text: Count only traits that are genuinely independent; two features from the same cause add little combined evidence.
A single common trait narrows the suspect pool little, but each independent, rarer trait multiplies the evidence, since the joint share of people matching all traits is tiny.
when: many suspects match any one feature

text: A vaguely recorded feature cannot be combined with others; clues must be noted precisely to be useful.
Each elimination step depends on the one before it, so a single false premise invalidates every conclusion that follows from it.
when: reasoning through a chain of date constraints
why: links in a deduction chain are cumulative

text: Assuming an intrusion happened during the event window can mislead reasoning when the enabling action, such as removing a key, occurred much earlier.
when: Reconstructing how a sealed space was entered.
why: The decisive action may predate the event by a long time.

text: 1) Identify the facts the witness is certain of. 2) Use dated outside records to find the earliest and latest possible dates. 3) Remove candidate days that fail each routine or absence constraint. 4) Settle the remaining candidate with a fixed later event.
when: testimony about dates is vague but independent records, schedules or calendars exist
why: each elimination narrows the window until one candidate remains

text: Confirm that a routine assumed to be fixed really holds before using it to exclude candidate dates.
when: a recurring schedule such as weekly visits is used as a constraint
why: an unverified routine can wrongly exclude the true date

text: On a uniform surface such as open water, rely on a fixed landmark, since visual judgment of position is unreliable.
why: Water looks alike across its surface, so position cannot be judged by eye.

text: An upright object's height equals a reference rod's height times the object's shadow length divided by the rod's shadow length, measured under the same sun angle.
when: when both shadows are cast under the same light conditions
why: Similar triangles make the two shadow ratios equal.

text: Miscounting scale markers, or counting from a different start each time, shifts the intersection and the located position.

1) List every route into the sealed space and who held its key or watched it. 2) Find the route with no accounted-for control. 3) Reason backward: the key was removed before the event, not during it. 4) Fix the timeline with dated testimony.
when: A sealed space seems impossible to enter and the record names keys, guards and times.
why: An unaccounted route usually reveals when the key was lost, which narrows the suspect list.

text: Offer a listening mode that lists inferred details with confidence levels.
Design ambient sounds such as wind gusts, creaks and drafts as false positives, including scripted ones that mask a real trigger, so players must verify cues before reacting.
when: Designing an audio environment with cues
why: Noise that mimics signals trains players to verify before reacting

text: Use sound cues such as jingling objects or coughing to convey an enemy's position or condition.
when: Designing enemies that should be locatable or readable by ear.
why: Audio gives the player information without line of sight.

text: Give audio clues a confidence level, such as a clear sound from nearby versus a muffled one through walls, and let players weigh them.
when: Designing audio clues.

text: Design sound cues so the player identifies the source from a distinctive quality, not from volume alone.
Use audio as a main feedback channel only if its cues are reliable, since misleading sounds undermine what the player tests.
when: audio carries key information
why: players act on what they hear

text: In a quiet level with sparse audio, small cues such as a tick or creak carry meaning for the player.
when: Designing a level for atmosphere
why: Few competing sounds make each cue stand out.

text: Use an audible cue, such as a chime followed by a crash, to tell the player that a protected space has been entered.
when: A vault or restricted area is breached off-screen or out of sight.
why: Sound reveals the event to the player when the guards have not seen it.

text: Tie sound cues to specific actions, such as a lock that clangs only when opened, so players infer state without seeing it.
when: Designing a hidden state players must deduce
why: Distinct sounds let players detect what happened out of sight

text: Plant a distinctive sound early and tie it to a returning enemy, so the player only understands its meaning at the climax.
when: Designing an audio cue that foreshadows an enemy's return.
why: A cue heard before its meaning is known rewards attention and turns a late appearance into a payoff.

text: Give a trick a distinct sound, such as a latch clanging down, so its timing is fixed to a moment the player can attach to a suspect.
A recording played at a set moment can make a listener believe a conversation is happening inside a room when no one there speaks.
when: A listener hears but cannot see the room
why: The listener relies on sound alone to judge who is present

text: A repeated ambient sound, such as a recurring musical figure, marks elapsed time and can set an ordinary tone against tense dialogue, sustaining suspense.
when: A long scene needs a sense of time passing.
why: A repeating cue gives the player a time reference and contrast with the emotional content.

text: Small sounds that steadily grow nearer during a silent wait keep players on edge before an entity appears, building suspense without extra scripting.
when: before a monster or NPC appears
why: Rising proximity cues sustain anticipation

text: Repeated sound cues lose their effect and stop signalling danger, so vary the signals used to show approach.
when: when a pursuit uses the same audio cue many times
why: Familiar cues stop signalling danger.

text: Sounds and traces reveal information only when they are placed where a listener can hear or notice them.
when: Placing audio clues in a level or scene.
why: Inaudible or unreachable cues go unused.

text: A sound cue that is missed or misread can send the player the wrong way.
Sounds heard from concealment, such as breathing, are easily misread, so audio cues need clear and unambiguous meanings.
when: the listener cannot see the source
why: the listener must infer the cause from sound alone

text: A timed playback device that fails to start on cue exposes the whole trick once the silence is noticed.
A sound cue that arrives too late reveals the entry only after the target has been taken, which removes the chance for the player to react.
when: Timing an audio cue for a breach.
why: The cue must play while the player can still respond.

text: Use misleading sounds from hidden spaces to point players to a false source, but make the true source discoverable, such as through a later corrective cue or investigation.
when: Designing sound cues from concealed areas
why: Misleading cues are fair only if the source can be found by investigation

text: Make an unseen object audible, such as a locked drawer being moved, to build tension during a confrontation.
Model room acoustics and door states so players can deduce who could have heard a sound or reached a room.
Use a sound such as a rattling key ring to hint at hidden storage without placing a marker on the map.
Use sound, cold wind and visual unease to convey guilt, but keep the clues themselves discoverable through play.
when: Designing mood for a site connected to a crime
why: Atmosphere sets tone while the mechanical evidence stays separate

text: Silence right after a startling sound, such as a scream cut off at once, extends tension and keeps the mystery open, feeling more threatening than the sound itself.
when: immediately after a startling sound

text: Faint small sounds, such as animals moving, become audible in a silent room and heighten the tension of a scene.
when: when a scene is quiet
why: Silence makes minor sounds prominent.

text: The investigator cannot know whether a diversion is genuine or staged, which adds uncertainty to the plan.
Create a distraction so that a searcher can work unobserved.
when: a search must happen while others are present

text: Place ambient distractions, such as a guard animal or a cheerful host, to draw the player's attention away from a restricted area.
when: When designing a restricted area that should stay hidden
why: Competing stimuli shift attention away from what is concealed.

text: Leave the cause of an ambient sound open, so the player hears it without the game settling on a single source.
Use pauses in narration or ambient audio to control suspense rhythm, letting tension build with repetition.
when: Timing reveals or threats in a scene.
why: Silence between cues sets pacing and anticipation.

text: Hide a second reading in an inscription's phrasing that emerges on closer inspection, so a player who re-reads it gains new meaning.
when: Writing a note, letter or inscription that the player will examine.
why: A reading that changes on re-examination rewards careful attention and deepens the message.

text: Keep a disruptive detail visible in the story so it can be recalled later to confirm a key fact.
when: when a detail will later support a conclusion

text: Leads that point away from the speaker, or away from the speaker's own history, deserve extra scrutiny.
when: When a speaker offers a culprit who is not themselves.
why: A lead that deflects blame may protect the speaker.

text: Ask questions whose purpose stays hidden, since a direct question about what matters would give the answer away.
when: The suspect is likely to guard a fact.

text: An audio-only hiding spot with one exit, such as a room behind a curtain, can deliver information like a route or password through overheard talk.
when: designing a guard conversation the player overhears

text: A missing sound that was expected can be as informative as a sound that is present.
Hearing an event without seeing its outcome, or hearing it from a locked area one cannot reach, withholds information and raises tension and a barrier to action.
when: An action's outcome is out of view or an event is audible but unreachable.
why: Tension depends on withheld information and barriers to action, not on the event being displayed.

text: A visible event elsewhere, such as a failed light, draws guards and visitors away from the true route.
A cry cut off mid-note locates danger without showing it.
A character kept busy with a task can cover a second action, hiding its real purpose when the audience sees events through one biased viewpoint.
when: events are shown through a single character's perspective
why: the audience's attention and bias are directed at the distraction

text: Keep a fetched fact's purpose hidden until a later scene, creating a why-mystery that pays off later.
Gloomy atmosphere and strange furnishings absorb attention and pull it away from the trail the player needs.
when: An area is dense with striking background detail near a key clue.
why: Striking surroundings compete with the important clue for the player's focus.

text: An NPC whose movements are heard but not seen leaves unobserved gaps that players can exploit through hidden routes.
when: An NPC's schedule is only audible
why: Unseen movement is not constrained by what the player can watch

text: An audible hint, such as a sob or footstep, lets players locate a hidden target without a full sweep, ending the search early.
when: A hidden NPC or target emits sound

text: Sensory signals of approaching pursuers, such as knocks, voices, footsteps and a lock being worked, tell the target that escape options are closing.
when: when a target is being pursued toward capture
why: Each cue signals proximity and removes an option.

text: Ambiguous sounds that are first dismissed and later reinterpreted leave the listener unsure whether another actor is nearby, building suspense.
when: ambient footsteps or noises occur where nobody is visibly present
why: reinterpretation reopens the question of who is nearby

text: Entertainment and playful speech can steer attention away from the serious matter at hand, so listeners end up engaged with the diversion.
when: A suspect uses amusement while business is in motion
why: Diversion lowers the audience's guard on the real topic.

text: A dramatic delivery can draw attention away from the claims inside a document, so judge those claims separately from the staging.
A distraction that draws attention to the searcher's own actions can alert the suspect.
Comic disruption dulls attention to the point that follows it, so a key clue should be placed after the interruption, not inside it.
when: when pacing a scene with a comic interruption
why: the listener's attention is pulled away by the disruption

text: 1) Post one visible watcher near the suspect. 2) Let the suspect be seen and followed so they choose to leave. 3) Time the move so the other target cannot be warned in time.
when: When a suspect must be drawn away from an ally.
why: A visible watcher pushes the suspect into movement that can be controlled and timed.

text: Do not use a diversion that could harm a bystander or expose the person who arranged it, such as one character's noise drawing scrutiny to that character.
Let players test audibility, such as closing a door and listening from another room; do not assume no sound carried, but test that claim rather than trust one informant.
when: Designing a timed puzzle built on witness sounds.
why: Active testing lets the player verify which sound matches the event.

text: Pace repeated matches between narration and ambient sound so listeners suspect a cause rather than chance; overly frequent or unpaced matches strain believability.
when: Pacing suspense through sound or read-aloud material, or using synchronized audio cues that mirror narrated events.
why: Apparent coincidence escalates tension when spaced and repeated.

text: Use ambient sound cues such as a creak or footstep to raise tension without guaranteeing that an enemy is present.
when: Building suspense in an area the player must explore.
why: Unconfirmed sounds keep players uncertain, sustaining tension without repetitive confrontations.

text: Check an apparent distraction against physical traces, such as footprints, before accepting it as genuine.
when: An event looks like a real emergency or distraction
why: Physical evidence can show whether the event was staged

text: Hide your purpose from witnesses who could be harmed or alarmed by knowing it.
when: Approaching a witness in a sensitive matter

text: Keep the real purpose of a feint hidden from its target, since the trick works only while the target does not see the trap.
Use an unplanned disruption to a prepared scheme to make the player suspect the wrong person.
Let an unreliable narrator admit one bias openly while concealing another, so careful players can find the gap.
when: designing unreliable narrators

text: Make fog or darkness a level mechanic that scrambles audio cues, so the player must triangulate the source rather than trust a single sound.
when: Designing a level where weather or darkness limits sensory information.
why: Requiring triangulation turns degraded perception into a challenge the player solves by combining cues.

text: Place a locked cabinet or posted rule as ambient detail, with NPC dialogue that names what it contains.
when: Populating a room with clue objects
why: Named contents make the object usable later

text: Trigger a major event in a busy area, such as a festival, so the player learns of it amid noise and distraction.
when: designing a story beat in a level
why: Distraction shapes how the event is received.

text: Use sounds such as bell pulls and rattled handles to pace an encounter, escalating in strength before the visitor is seen.
when: designing a visitor encounter behind a door
why: escalating sound builds tension without visuals

text: Withholding the purpose of a question keeps the subject unaware, but helpers who do not know why may cooperate less fully.
Use physical actions, such as a spilled drink or trembling hand, to mark emotional turns in a scene.
when: Signaling a shift in a character's emotional state
why: Concrete gestures make inner change visible and memorable

text: Walls, closed doors, bolts and bars attenuate sound, so witnesses in different rooms hear different things and a sealed-room listener may miss activity next door.
when: an event produces sound inside a building with doors and halls
why: walls and doors attenuate sound

text: Play dialogue through walls or doors so only tone and fragments are audible, forcing players to infer what is happening inside.
Speakers close to an open window carry their voices outward; a long conversation cannot be fully whispered, so a nearby listener is likely to hear it.
Distance, a wooden door, and an enclosed horn aimed at the door each blur a recorded voice's timbre, making it hard for a listener to identify it.
Singing carries farther than speech, so sung lines are often the only words a distant listener can make out clearly.
Sound carried by wind can travel a long way, so a distant source can seem close.
when: Judging the distance of a sound in an open environment
why: The transmitting medium distorts apparent proximity

text: A sound heard without a time anchor stays unreliable until a later sound, such as a gate clicking shut, pins its timing or marks a second party's arrival or departure.
when: Movements happen out of sight and the timeline needs an anchor.
why: Sounds are heard without being seen and can fix events precisely.

text: Before accepting an explanation or count for a reported sound, check it fits the sound's nature and timing; one heard shot may be a muffled one or two close shots.
when: A witness attributes a noise to a common cause such as a door closing, or reports gunfire or noise.
why: Plausible-sounding explanations are often assumed without testing.

text: A sound constrains timing but does not identify its maker or a hidden object's contents; confirm with more evidence before assuming.
when: a sound is linked to a suspect or an object is hidden from view
why: Sounds can mislead; timing evidence narrows events, not identities.

text: Verify a heard sound by measuring distance and sightline from the listening position on site, rather than assuming it was audible.
Make sound a clue, such as a groan behind a locked door that the player must interpret, and include a harmless noise as a decoy.
when: Designing audio-based evidence.
why: Ambiguous sounds reward interpretation and test the player's judgment.

text: Use ambient sounds such as ticking clocks, breathing or creaking floors as cues that signal danger before anything is seen.
when: darkness or stealth segments
why: Audio gives the player information in a dark space where visuals are limited.

text: Sound-alike fragments of a foreign phrase can resolve into a place name, after which other details can be read as parts of a route.
when: Partial speech is in an unfamiliar language.

text: Give a guard or NPC who overhears half a conversation a plausible but wrong reading, so players must assemble the full picture from other sources.
when: designing eavesdropping NPCs
why: partial information produces believable error

text: Do not assume walls block sound where rooms share open corridors or streets, since sound carries across them.
Windows, vents, doors, glass and curtains muffle ordinary dialogue, so outside listeners recover only fragments, with clarity depending on distance and obstruction.
Shared pipes, shafts and flues carry sound unexpectedly: neighbors outside the exchange can hear speech, and a muffled report missed on one floor may be clear below.
when: A hidden channel is shared with other spaces
why: Sound travels along the same route as the message; structures channel sound along unexpected routes

text: Hearing a cue before seeing its source builds dread and anticipation, as the audience imagines the unseen cause and prepares for the reveal.
when: an unseen threat or distressed character is present, or danger is hidden from view
why: Audiences need time to prepare for a discovery to land with force.

text: Opening a window or shutter slightly improves hearing, but the gain is limited because the action makes noise that can jar the listener.
when: when a window is raised as a lever
why: The gain is limited by the risk of a sudden jarring noise.

text: In a quiet, empty space small sounds carry and stand out, so an approaching footstep is heard before its source is seen and a faint noise builds suspense.
when: when ambient sound is sparse or a scene is kept still and quiet
why: Without competing noise, faint sounds remain distinct and draw attention.

text: Hearing depends on position: a corridor, a noisy room or distance from a door decides which words reach the listener.
A clue heard as a snippet through a door or wall can hold back its full meaning for a later scene.
A sound cue such as a voice or shout points to a region without naming a character, so players must weigh it against each candidate's route.
when: designing audio clues for investigation
why: an unnamed sound narrows location but leaves identity open

text: Flagged dialogue can trigger listener NPC reactions, such as turning away or denying, that the game records as clues.
A sound that draws a guard away from a chokepoint leaves the post empty, opening a timed gap that others can exploit.
Distance, several stairs, long halls and heavy doors together can keep a gunshot from reaching other floors or the street, especially with closed windows.
Closing a window or door cuts off all sound at once, so a closed barrier can end the flow of information at a dramatic moment.
Listening through a shared wall can reveal plans, so proximity or sound checks can change what nearby NPCs learn or say.
when: Designing stealth or information gathering through adjacent rooms.
why: Sound passes through partitions, so proximity determines what a listener hears.

text: Treating sound as proof is a common error: a closing door shows it closed, not who was on either side, so sound deductions need later confirmation or a contrary detail.
why: A sound confirms an action occurred but does not identify the actor or their location.

text: An unexplained sound left unresolved frustrates players. It needs a later explanation or a tie to another clue.
when: when a mysterious sound is used as a clue

text: A sound or sign that appears without prior setup has no emotional effect.
Footsteps carry far on still, quiet roads, so a follower can be given away by sound even when out of sight.
when: A follower moves on a quiet road or open ground.
why: Sound travels further when the surrounding environment is still.

text: Test a witness's claimed identification of a sound by comparing it with that sound's known source before accepting it.
when: When a witness says they recognised a particular noise.

text: 1) Drop a small object into the hidden shaft or cavity. 2) Listen to the impact and its timing. 3) Judge depth or emptiness from the sound, without opening the structure.
when: when a hidden space must be checked without opening it

text: 1) Form a guess about an unexplained sound. 2) Reproduce the sound with a candidate action. 3) Repeat the test before concluding.
when: a sound inside a room has no obvious source
why: reproducing the sound tests the guess directly, and repetition guards against a single coincidence

text: 1) Stand behind an obstacle that blocks the most watchful person's sight. 2) Map speakers by voices and silhouettes. 3) Improve hearing with small adjustments. 4) Withdraw at once if the window is opened by another.
when: when a closed room holds a plan and direct entry is impossible

text: Base elimination on sound observed facts, not on a hunch dressed up as logic, since the method depends entirely on the reliability of its facts.
Ask a witness directly whether they could swear to a sound, forcing them to separate firm impressions from doubt.
Let players test whether noise carries between rooms by making a sound and observing which guards react.
when: when a level's stealth depends on sound propagation
why: observable reactions make the propagation rule learnable

text: Abandon an eavesdropping position if targets sit far back inside a room, since little of their conversation will be audible.
when: when choosing a listening spot
why: Distance cuts sound too much to be useful.

text: Model sound propagation by room and by door, so listeners hear only what their position allows and audio clues can be checked on the map.
when: designing sound-based clues
why: Audibility should match the physical layout

text: Sounds through walls are hard to localise and can be attributed to a different location or person, so verify the source before tying audio cues to a location.
when: A sound comes from a hidden or adjacent space
why: Sound through walls is hard to localise

text: When sight is blocked, sounds such as footsteps, chair creaks, locks, lift sounds and doors reveal an occupant's identity, activity or route.
when: Stealth or detective scenes with limited sight
why: Sound conveys presence and action.

text: Do not assume two voices mean two people, since one performer can imitate a second voice; separate what is heard from how it was produced.
when: when speech is heard through a barrier

text: Trace a repeated phrase to its source before treating it as a name; it may be a routine like counting, a trap countdown, or a monster mimicking a voice.
when: when a fragment of overheard speech seems to name someone

text: A distinctive sound heard earlier can trigger memory and make a place feel concrete on a return visit.
A sound's distinctive feature, such as an echo that differs from the original, identifies its source more reliably than its loudest part.
A threat that depends on a small audible cue, such as a weapon being cocked, gives the listener a brief advantage if they react to the sound first.
when: Two parties face each other in darkness and one can hear the other's preparation.
why: Sound arrives before a visible action, giving reaction time.

text: A sound from an offscreen event can bridge a reveal, letting the audience connect distant events through audio cues.
when: the cause of an event happens out of view
why: Audio carries the link when the audience cannot see the source.

text: A half-remembered match between a sound and a known source is only a lead, not proof, and should be confirmed before acting on it.
when: A player recalls a sound they think they have heard before
why: Recall is unreliable and can be wrong.

text: A false voice that is too easy to spot feels cheap; give a subtle clue, such as a wrong position or a missing reply, instead.

1) Capture a sequence of sounds, not a single step, since gait and cadence identify the mover. 2) Rule out candidates whose movement type or rhythm does not fit. 3) Consider why the sequence would occur for the remaining candidate.
when: Deducing an unseen mover from audio, such as a suspect out of sight with a repeated sound signature
why: Gait and cadence carry identifying information; the full pattern reveals what no single step does.

text: 1) List known candidate sources of the sound; do not accept the first plausible one untested. 2) Reject each candidate whose expected features do not match. 3) Match the sound's unusual feature to the remaining candidate. 4) Confirm that source with a check.
when: when a sound's features do not match its expected source
why: Accepting the first plausible source untested leads to a wrong identification.

text: Let footsteps or voices identify nearby characters, so a player can confirm a target without line of sight.
Give hidden NPC state a distinct audio signature, such as footsteps, a lighter or smoke, so players can infer it without sight.
when: designing stealth encounters
why: audio lets players read state without seeing it

text: Use an imitated ally's voice as a lure only when players should learn to question what they hear.
when: designing a dangerous room with a deceptive sound

text: Let players verify a false voice by finding the real character elsewhere, so the reveal feels fair rather than arbitrary.
when: using an imitated NPC voice as a lure

text: Use setting mood to build tension, while ensuring the player can test each supernatural claim against evidence.
when: when a supernatural atmosphere is part of a mystery
why: Mood raises stakes without removing the player's ability to reason.

text: Gate an exit behind a payment so release has a clear mechanical cost and ends the branch.
For independent events such as dice throws, past outcomes do not change the chance of a future outcome.
when: predicting the next result of a random event
why: each independent trial has the same chance regardless of history

text: Set a deadline for a squeeze so the victim's remaining resources are drained before they can meet escalating demands.
when: Designing a pressure or extortion quest with a time limit
why: A fixed window forces the victim to commit everything before escape is possible

text: Do not assume an opposing contest is settled by one decisive move; in an evenly matched contest, control often stays uncertain for a long time.
when: when a plan assumes a quick, decisive victory
why: evenly matched sides can stay balanced, so control is not won in a single stroke

text: Attach a reward or permission to a timed condition, so the player's action before or after a threshold changes which NPC benefits or which door unlocks.
when: Designing timed outcomes in a game economy
why: Threshold rules let players reason about outcomes without the designer naming a culprit

text: When a single event order decides who benefits, small timing differences cause large outcome changes, making timing the contested stake and inviting interested parties to shade testimony.
when: Legacies are conditional on survivorship order, or a single event order decides who benefits
why: A threshold rule concentrates large stakes on a small timing gap, turning a small timing question into a contested, high-value point

text: When a recurring timed effect escalates, intervals shorten and required doses rise; designers can show this as a visible countdown so urgency stays legible.
when: when a timed effect or cover depends on repeated doses, or when designing escalating pressure on a player
why: Escalating frequency and dose demand increases pressure, and a visible, accelerating timer makes urgency legible

text: When parents transfer farms to children while keeping income, the parents' assessments fall as the children's rise.
Track the count of unique instances: total produced minus held equals sold, and sold minus logged sales equals untracked sales.
when: Designing limited-run or unique items in a game economy.
why: The running count shows how many instances are unaccounted for.

text: Estimated effect durations can differ from actual outcomes, so calculated timings should be treated as approximate and checked against observed recovery.
when: Predicting how long a dose or status effect lasts.
why: Calculations often miss real variation in recovery.

text: Dependence on a consumable supply makes recurring effects fragile: a low or impure batch can cause failure, and a timeline ignoring this hidden cause misleads.
when: when a character or cover relies on a recurring consumable, or when explaining the failure of a recurring effect
why: Supply quality and quantity become a single point of failure, and blaming the effect itself hides the real cause in the supply chain

text: Independence of events can fail when a system has memory, so test that assumption before applying independent-event reasoning.
when: applying chance reasoning to a game system
why: systems with memory make earlier results affect later ones

text: Give each party in a shared enterprise a stake value, so the game can show who gains most from a loss, not just who lost most.
Log NPC fees, seizures, withdrawals and transfers in an economy ledger so players can infer which character or party paid or gained, leaving intent to inference.
when: designing NPC economies with hidden transfers
why: Visible money flows let players deduce motives.

text: Creditors usually wait until a debt falls due, and blackmailers usually apply pressure where social shame is greatest; early or misplaced pressure is a lead.
Prisoners may be made to pay their own keep, adding a financial cost to being accused.
Credit a deduction more when the player kept several readings open until a second clue selected one.
when: rewarding player reasoning
why: holding alternatives open shows the reasoning was tested

text: Little cash on hand suggests the missing person did not prepare a trip.
when: when judging whether an absence was planned
why: a planned trip needs funds

text: A price or rent far below local norms, especially where many others were refused, is an anomaly that deserves explanation.
why: Unusual deals often have a hidden cause.

text: Log each transaction and the starting count of a game currency or inventory so suspicious changes are detectable and spending can be rebuilt and checked against the current balance.
when: A game tracks player purchases, payments or currency spending.
why: Recorded outflows can be verified rather than recalled from memory.

text: Track each NPC's income, debts and visible spending; luxury purchases or a residence without matching income prompt players to question the source and check claims against observed deposits.
when: When designing NPC wealth for a mystery system
why: A visible mismatch between income and spending creates a lead the player can pursue.

text: A spent casing found outside a window links the shooting to the area beyond it.
A fixed income drawn on by several claimants, each taking a set amount, can be nearly exhausted by a few claims.
when: Several beneficiaries each draw a fixed sum from one source.
why: Each claim subtracts from a limited total.

text: A loan with a fixed monthly percentage and interest deducted up front means the borrower receives less than the principal, giving a checkable calculation.
when: A lending system uses a set rate per period and prepaid interest.

text: Cleared, fenced land was taxed at a much higher rate than unimproved wild land, so tax rates reward improvement.
An assistant credited with others' ideas may repeat them without understanding them.
The person who bought an item and the person who carried it to the scene may be different people, so a buyer's name is not proof of use.
The place where a payment was cashed is not necessarily where it was drawn, so each location must be checked separately.
why: Transaction location and cashing location can differ

text: Public accounts can distort the sequence of deductions and assign credit to the wrong party, so expect this after a solution is announced.
Spreading a limited light supply across a search area, or spending it on the wrong spot, exhausts it quickly and leaves the search unfinished.
when: when light sources are finite
why: Each light covers only a small area and burns out.

text: A falling assessment can hide a transfer of wealth rather than a loss of wealth.
Trace cash found in a hidden stash back through the records to a payer or recipient.
when: Designing a discovery that links to financial records.
why: Tracing connects physical finds to the people involved.

text: Offer a small payment to buy a plain factual answer from someone with no stake in protecting the subject.
when: a reluctant source may know a checkable fact

text: Tie an NPC's debts or secret routine to a faction or economy system so the player can uncover motive through shops, lenders or servants.
when: designing a suspect's background
why: it links motive to observable game systems

text: Model an NPC's debt and need as a visible motive for their bargaining.
when: Designing NPC negotiation with financial stakes
why: Visible need makes bargaining behavior understandable and predictable.

text: A reputation or loyalty system that rewards NPCs with gold or favors can change their dialogue and later answers, revealing hidden influence to a player who notices the change.
when: Designing NPC loyalty or reputation systems that affect dialogue
why: Rewards shift an NPC's incentives, so their statements change in observable ways

text: Players who lose heavily at a chance-based game tend to attribute losses to bad luck and believe a betting system can win, unless the mechanism is shown to be controlled.
when: A chance-based game with a house edge is played for money.
why: Belief in luck and systems keeps players from suspecting the outcome is manipulated.

text: Each independent random trial has the same chance regardless of earlier results, so a number that came up repeatedly is no more or less likely next time.
Blackmail on a damaging secret keeps extracting resources, since each payment reveals new assets; a visible deadline such as a repossession visit forces the player to act.
when: A victim has a strong reason to stay silent and the cost of silence grows; when designing blackmail or debt quests with time pressure.
why: Fear of exposure makes payment seem cheaper than reporting; a visible timer converts gradual pressure into a decision the player must make.

text: Give each stolen-item report a precise inventory so the player can check it against items found in a suspect's room.
when: Designing theft investigations in a game.
why: Precise inventories let the player verify claims against physical evidence.

text: Accused people are charged fees for maintenance, transport, clerks, reprieves, discharge and execution; where cash is scarce these fall on livestock and crops, ruining families while owners are absent.
why: Little cash forces payment in goods

text: Raising search effort for a larger reward increases time and cost without improving insight, so search cost can be modelled as a resource separate from search method.
If a stolen item's value falls once its secret becomes public, holders face pressure to sell early, while holders expecting a rise may wait.
when: the item's worth depends on secrecy or timing
why: waiting either loses value or gains it, depending on how the value changes

text: Stolen money can be traced only if identifying details such as serial numbers were recorded at the transaction; without them recovery becomes nearly hopeless.
why: identifiers link a loss to a specific physical item

text: Seizing an arrested person's goods gives accusers a material motive to press charges, and can ruin families even after acquittal.
Stolen items that cannot be broken down or converted into currency need a willing buyer. Without a buyer market, theft yields no value and the goods stay idle.
when: When stolen goods are unique or hard to liquidate
why: Conversion routes determine whether theft pays

text: If stolen items sell only in certain markets, players must track where loot can go, turning fencing into a routing problem with a discoverable path.
when: In games with fencing or black-market systems
why: Restricted outlets give players reasons to follow sales

text: A public reward, offer or appraisal raises an object's perceived worth and the number of people who know of it, making it a more attractive target.
when: When a valuable item is publicly valued
why: Publicity increases temptation and awareness

text: Model investigation constraints as resource limits: search time, the duration of legal holds, and a finite number of guards.
when: a game requires the player to investigate under limited resources

text: 1) Track the victim's remaining resources as a state variable. 2) Scale each new demand to what remains. 3) Stop escalating when resources are exhausted.
when: Implementing an extortion mechanic in a game
why: Demands tied to remaining resources keep pressure meaningful without becoming impossible

text: Keep investigation savings in a bank and calculate spending closely, since funds limit how long a hidden party can last.
Treat a cash total that comes up short by a fixed amount as a clue the player can count and trace.
Route hidden economy transactions through brokers so players must follow intermediaries to reach a single NPC.
when: Designing a concealed market or trading chain
why: Forces the player to trace the chain step by step

text: For consumables, treat theft of part of a stock differently from theft of the whole stock, using quantity thresholds.
when: when designing a stockpile that can be partially stolen
why: partial and total losses have different consequences

text: A game's suspect logic can use untouched valuables to rule out robbery as a motive, which is a strong test separating robbery from personal motives.
when: when designing motive logic for a crime in a game
why: Untouched valuables contradict a theft motive

text: Destroying a container costs the container but can reveal its contents; it suits cases where the container's loss is acceptable.
when: Deciding whether a player may break a container to find an item
why: Destruction guarantees discovery at the cost of the container itself

text: Bribery can be a mechanic whose cost is weighed against how reliable the purchased information proves to be.
when: Designing a paid-information mechanic.
why: Players balance the price of information against its expected accuracy.

text: A keyhole view shows only what the viewer could see, so a blocked view means the room is unknown, not that it is clear.
when: Using a keyhole or narrow gap to check a room.
why: Partial sightlines can look like confirmation when they only cover a narrow area.

text: A closed door between two rooms can make an occupant unable to hear a disturbance, so access depends on layout as well as on ability.
when: When a sound or event in one room is meant to be missed by someone in an adjacent room.
why: Physical barriers limit perception and reach, so layout determines who could plausibly have acted.

text: A closed-cell escape puzzle is a locked-room problem in which the player reconstructs an exit from props, notes and a decoy placed in the room.
Make the suspected character appear to hold exclusive access to something, while the true route runs through a helpful-seeming character.
when: building a red herring
why: Visible exclusive access draws suspicion while the real access stays hidden.

text: A tracking mechanic such as dogs or guards can be set up so the culprit engineers it to point at an innocent party.
when: when a pursuit system is part of the investigation
why: The player must realise the pursuit was rigged rather than accept its result.

text: 1) When the trail stalls, return to the premise. 2) Re-test the starting assumption, such as the location. 3) Gather evidence on the corrected trail.
Build enclosure logic so breaches are possible and visible, otherwise a test seems to fail for no reason.
when: Designing a controlled-isolation puzzle or test

text: Investigators are cautious about arresting a prominent figure, because the arrest draws press attention and any error is costly.
when: the suspect is socially prominent
why: Public visibility raises the cost of mistakes.

text: People who loudly condemn the accused may later find themselves or their relatives accused in the same way.
Mass accusations resting on sight alone can yield many confessions and arrests, and most of those tried may later be cleared.
Include an honest-looking suspect with hidden financial pressure so that checking motive is meaningful.
Keep suspicions hidden while questioning so the witness does not adjust their story to fit what the investigator seems to expect.
An action that seems pointless often makes sense if a hidden party exists whose presence would change the outcome.
when: an act appears to have no purpose
why: an unknown party can give the act a reason

text: Let a confrontation scene change an NPC's trust or hostility according to which evidence the player shows, so the same scene yields different outcomes.
when: When designing an NPC dialogue encounter driven by player-chosen evidence.
why: Evidence-dependent reactions make the player's choice of proof meaningful.

text: Make the accuser share the outcome of an ordeal, so players see the risk and weigh the accusation more carefully.
Design an accusation puzzle where the player builds a checklist from clues and accepts only the suspect matching every point, rewarding thorough work.
When evidence is thin, keep several plausible suspects in view and wait for a focusing clue rather than acting on a weak guess.
when: evidence cannot yet single out one suspect
why: Acting early on a weak guess risks the wrong target.

text: Use a mock trial or accusation as a mid-story turn rather than as the final solution.
when: the reveal should redirect the investigation
why: a turn keeps the question open for later resolution

text: A jury that cannot agree produces adjournment rather than acquittal or conviction, and the accused stays in custody until a later session.
A suspect detained on a witness report of location can be cleared only by producing an alibi item or NPC testimony covering that window.
An accomplice's confession can change which character the player suspects, shifting the investigation.
Interrogation dialogue can branch on the accusation into denial, deflection or partial admission, and a stressed NPC may reveal a clue.
An accusation mechanic where the player presents gathered evidence can trigger a suspect's confession when the correct item is chosen.
when: the game has collectible clues and suspect characters
why: Matching the right clue to the right suspect turns evidence into a dramatic payoff

text: Quiet stretches read as lost time or stalling unless ongoing progress is signaled, such as a clue or hint; silence without forward signs loses audience attention.
when: a narrative slows after a burst of events, or a long investigation is paced without clues
why: Without any forward signal, waiting reads as stalling rather than building tension; silence without signs of progress loses momentum

text: A hung result can drift into a conviction without a fresh, clearly authorized decision, so the case must be formally reopened.
when: when a jury has not reached a verdict but the case continues
why: informal continuation can convert an undecided case into a conviction

text: A verdict reached quickly after a long list of accusations may reflect momentum rather than careful checking of each claim.
when: Many accusations are heard in a short proceeding
why: Accumulated pressure can outpace individual evaluation

text: Circumstantial suspicion, pressed by an emphatic summing-up, can settle a verdict before the facts support it.
when: A verdict rests on circumstantial evidence and strong framing.
why: Emphatic framing shortens deliberation and can override thin support.

text: A single loud remark can break a productive silence and end the exchange before the witness says more.
A quick recovery from an interviewer's slip can hide the error from both the interviewer and the record.
A coherent account can hide its weakest link, and the most important explanation is often the one left incomplete.
Treating the loudest account as the most credible is a mistake; separate the firm facts from the noise before judging.
The most vocal accuser is not necessarily the one who started a chain of accusations.
A gambit works only if the target can see the trap; hidden framing may be read as honest advice.
when: When designing manipulative advice for a character.
why: The target must perceive the framing for the trap to bite.

text: Each new accusation looks stronger because it follows others, even when the earlier ones were weak.
when: when a case is built on a sequence of related charges
why: Accumulated accusations create an appearance of corroboration

text: 1) Infer the offender's traits from the method of the crime. 2) List every trait as a required point. 3) Accept a suspect only if all points match; a partial fit excludes that suspect.
when: Deducing a culprit from the traces of a crime.
why: Requiring full agreement avoids accepting a plausible but wrong suspect.

text: 1) Record each arrest or verdict as a node. 2) Link each node to the accusers who named it. 3) Trace the graph back to the first accuser to show how the chain began.
when: when designing an accusation the player must reconstruct
why: A visible graph lets players see which first accusation started the chain

text: Gate accusations and confrontation behind enough proven clues; early wrong accusations fail with a visible cost, giving alternative explanations time to surface.
when: when designing accusation or arrest mechanics
why: Weakly supported accusations otherwise succeed by chance

text: Do not let an NPC's declaration of certainty trigger an ending; the final accusation should rest on several linked, recheckable clues the player found.
when: designing a culprit reveal
why: an accusation without proof would skip the player's investigation

text: Do not read a hung jury as proof of innocence; it shows only that the case failed to convince everyone.
Stage a loud event such as a performance, toast or quarrel during which a second action goes unnoticed, then let the player return to find the change.
Forbid hidden group members from going out alone or admitting visitors, to limit chances of exposure.
Write an NPC confession with exact, checkable details while a guilt or fear motive colors the rest, so the player must cross-check it.
Give the player an accusing note or rumor that names a checkable object such as a chest, ledger or grave, so they can confirm or dismiss it.
Require at least two independent checks before the game accepts an accusation.
Each object a confession explains must already exist in the generated level data, so the reveal recasts real content rather than adding new facts.
when: when a villain's statement explains planted level objects
why: Objects absent from the data cannot be fairly explained.

text: Store deferred payment and reversion terms as data, so a faction can gain or lose a holding over time as conditions are met or missed.
An accusation should fail if the player's evidence does not cover every required proof category.
when: the game evaluates an accusation
why: partial coverage leaves a weak link

text: Give confrontation visible costs, such as alerting other NPCs, so that patience and quiet observation have value.
Require motive, means and opportunity as separate evidence items before a case file allows an accusation.
Map each document requirement to a discoverable world state, so an accusation becomes justified once the player has verified the required facts.
Show collected clues on a labelled board in the final accusation scene so the player sees the full chain before naming a culprit.
Use an enforcement timer to force the final accusation, and have the accusation screen list the reasons in order.
when: when designing a final accusation mechanic
why: Timed pressure and ordered reasons support a decisive climax.

text: An ending can present a mock tribunal in which earlier choices and gathered evidence determine the verdict.
when: designing a moral resolution
why: the verdict reflects the player's own investigation

text: A threat is credible only when the actor can back it up, so bluffing without the means to act undermines control.
when: Making a threat in a standoff.
why: Opponents test bluffs, and an unsupported threat collapses.

text: Pick the target the opponent least expects, while still meeting the practical needs of the attack, by reasoning from the opponent's expected form of attack.
when: the opponent's model of the attack is known and can be exploited
why: Unexpected targets face fewer prepared defences

text: Conclude an event from several small anomalies that point to one cause, rather than from any single unusual sign.
when: Reading a scene from weak, individually ambiguous signals.
why: Converging signs are more reliable than any one of them alone.

text: Pace an investigation by alternating small confirmations with a setback that leaves doubt, keeping the player uncertain about the next step.
when: when structuring a long investigation

text: A hierarchy clue such as a uniform or footprint can be overturned by a later witness, forcing players to revise their working hypotheses about who is in charge.
A final accusation that requires evidence in a set order leaves the case unproven when items are wrong or missing.
when: a player must present clues to win an accusation scene

text: A detective can be right about one fact and wrong about its meaning, so each conclusion needs its own test.
when: An investigator's reasoning is partly sound.
why: Correct premises can still support a wrong inference.

text: A theory built on early assumptions can persist after evidence weakens it, because it already shapes how new facts are read.
A theory that explains one anomaly while ignoring another is incomplete, and a theory that explains every anomaly is not thereby proven.
why: Coverage of the evidence is necessary but does not confirm the explanation.

text: 1) Treat the case as open by default. 2) Build a profile of the culprit as a list of conditions. 3) Narrow the field only through evidence matching those conditions.
when: No motive is yet established.
why: Keeping the field open avoids concluding too early.

text: Make an accusation require proof across several categories, such as an object, a witness statement and a timing, rather than a single suspicion.
when: designing an accusation mechanic
why: a single suspicion is too easy to challenge

text: Build a mystery from a fixed set of explanations, each predicting a different clue, so the player can rule them out one by one.
Record evidence as smudged or partial, so players must combine several weak clues rather than rely on one clean result.
when: Designing an evidence system for players.

text: Have an NPC point at a rival with a motive, then let the player check the claim by finding another record.
Absence from a scene only exonerates a person if their timing is firmly fixed; never suspect or clear someone before knowing where they were.
when: Judging whether a witness could have committed an event
why: A person cannot be in two places at once, so unfixed timing proves nothing

text: A confrontation that lets the player stake partial evidence trades a possible gain in pressure against a penalty if the bluff is called.
when: designing a confrontation mechanic
why: Raising stakes rewards confidence but risks loss if the opponent is not fooled.

text: Accept a verbal promise of secrecy when a witness refuses to be bound by a sworn oath.
when: A witness will not take an oath.
why: A verbal commitment keeps cooperation without forcing a refusal.

text: A deduction journal can require enough clue coverage for each explanation before an accusation is allowed.
when: Designing a case-solving system with accusations.
why: Gating accusations on evidence coverage prevents premature or unsupported solutions.

text: A confessor's visible disfigurement or emotional cost makes a confession carry weight, so the revealed truth feels earned rather than merely stated.
when: A character confesses to a crime during a late reveal.
why: A visible cost to the confessor makes the admission feel consequential and believable.

text: Revealing your theory to win cooperation can tip off the suspect.
when: Persuading witnesses to help.
why: Witnesses may repeat the theory to the people being investigated.

text: Block accusations until corroboration (witness item or second testimony) exists, or allow premature accusations with a penalty; blocking suits proof-gated games, penalties suit games allowing early accusations.
when: a game requires proof before accusation or arrest, or accusations can precede complete evidence
why: Suspicion alone cannot justify punishment; unsupported accusations should fail, building tension toward proof; a cost for premature accusation makes gathering corroboration worthwhile.

text: An item that does not fit its owner, such as a costume bill or something too new or careless for them, signals a hidden motive or second life worth probing.
when: Reviewing items found in a scene.
why: Mismatches between an object and its context reveal something the owner would not normally have.

text: A record entry that sits in the wrong section of its original can expose a forgery even when its stated date looks correct.
A violent reaction to accusation shows a touched nerve, not proven guilt, and the same outburst may read as honesty or guilt depending on the watcher's mood.
when: a witness or suspect reacts strongly to questioning or an accusation
why: emotion reveals sensitivity, not factual truth; the watcher's mood colours the interpretation

text: Out-of-place traces or visual details, such as dress or bearing breaking social rules, mark a clue or person; compare each find with what its setting should contain.
why: Settings with exclusion rules make mismatched appearance readable at a glance.

text: An unnatural figure in a personal record, such as a suspiciously round sum, can signal a hidden transaction worth investigating.
when: When a record does not fit the owner's known habits or position.
why: Real balances and payments are rarely round, so the deviation invites a question.

text: When a normally tame creature or person acts out of character, look for a specific cause such as provocation, interference or outside control before accepting the change.
when: A familiar actor behaves in a way that contradicts its known habits.
why: Behavior that breaks a known pattern usually has a reason that can be found.

text: An item absent from a suspect's possessions, despite witness belief that they owned it, is itself a clue that should be investigated rather than ignored.
when: When witnesses expect a suspect to possess an item that is not found among their effects.
why: The absence contradicts witness expectations and may point to concealment or disposal.

text: Leave one anomaly unresolved on purpose. It holds tension and can be tied to a later reveal.
A sudden rise in spending that departs from a stable routine prompts questions, and the person who caused it must produce an explanation the household will accept.
when: A person's spending or resource use departs sharply from an established pattern.
why: Observers expect consistency, and a departure without a credible reason invites scrutiny.

text: Scattered debris on a road can reveal that an apparently accidental breakdown was engineered, which tests the official account of events.
when: When an incident is reported as accidental and the scene holds physical traces.
why: Deliberate placement of debris leaves physical evidence that contradicts an accident.

text: A vague warning can confuse rather than guide, so the clue must eventually become recoverable for the audience.

1) Identify the last known location of a missing person. 2) Collect institutional records such as payments, registers and staff contacts. 3) Use each record to name the next location or person. 4) Confirm each stage with a second source.
when: a person has gone missing after moving across several places
why: Chained records reconstruct a route when no one saw the whole journey

text: 1) Define search criteria precisely, such as region, date range, age, stated cause and the signer's qualifications. 2) Filter the records by those criteria. 3) Collect the candidates. 4) Check each candidate against the known story before travelling to it.
when: When one event must be found among many similar records.

text: An act or item that a hypothesis cannot explain shows the theory is incomplete and a key factor is missing; list every such unexplained item.
Hold stray anomalies aside as open questions, neither discarding nor forcing them to fit the theory, and treat any explanation as a hypothesis.
when: A theory's main chain holds but a few items do not yet fit it, or one element of a clue cannot be explained.
why: Unexplained items may later fit the revealed method or prove coincidence, so they remain testable; early conclusions can close off the true meaning.

text: Record every clue, even minor acts or anomalies like a figure entering a building, a key turning or a stumble, since omitted sightings can matter later.
when: during observation
why: A recorded small anomaly lets a later investigation reopen the incident and resolve its meaning.

text: Record every physical trace of a disguise before removing any layer, because washing or stripping destroys the evidence.
why: Removal alters the physical evidence the investigator may later need to check.

text: Give registries and ledgers an access log so NPCs who view restricted documents leave a trace the player can follow to a hidden party.
when: Designing a town record, guild ledger or similar archive in a game
why: Traceable access turns record checks into a usable investigation path

text: Give players an item whose origin is not shown, so they must decide whether to reveal it to NPCs.
In a case file, mark each timeline entry or link as seen, heard, inferred or proven, so players weigh unverified oral claims against sworn records and see where knowledge stops.
when: When designing an in-game investigation with uncertain reports.
why: Labeling evidence type lets the player judge reliability and see which parts are proven versus left to inference.

text: Store original clue text and exact NPC and companion statements, not just summaries, so players can verify links, re-read them after a reveal, and expose contradictions.
when: statements or clues will later be verified or challenged
why: Without originals, a digest cannot be tested for shaping or editing, and later contradictions cannot be pointed out.

text: Store unexplained items or coincidences as open leads for later review, not as proofs or forced explanations.
when: the game tracks clues or suspicions, or an object fits no current explanation
why: This separates tentative links from established facts, and the item may gain meaning once further facts arrive.

text: A journal or clue log that keeps the player's notes of key lines lets the clue survive after the physical object is burned, lost, or the world evidence vanishes.
when: world evidence can disappear during play

text: A journal or notebook can record small separate observations or partial clues that the player must link into a chain or combine over time to narrow suspects or locations.
when: designing deduction systems with fragmentary evidence

text: Let players pursue several parallel leads on a case board, tracking failed ones so remaining options stay visible and the lead that confirms a fact is revealed.
when: An investigation has many possible leads running in parallel
why: Most leads fail, and only one may reach the truth; listing failures narrows the open options.

text: Crimes share recurring patterns, so matching a new scene against past cases can suggest which clues to search for.
when: A scene resembles a known method and the investigator is expected to know history.
why: Shared patterns make past cases informative about new ones.

text: Record whether each fact was volunteered or asked for, since the difference can itself be a clue about a character's motives.
when: When tracking NPC dialogue in a game or case file.
why: Unprompted information can reveal what a character wants the player to believe.

text: A deduction board where players rearrange clue cards can trigger a solved state when the right combination appears, giving a sudden realisation.
when: Designing deduction interfaces for mystery content
why: Rearrangeable clues let players discover patterns by manipulation rather than only by reading.

text: Two quest threads can merge when the player identifies a common NPC with the required access to both, shown on a corkboard linking each NPC to open cases.
when: Designing multi-case investigations
why: A visible shared link rewards the player for connecting threads.

text: Running two deadlines at once, such as a return before an absence is noticed, compounds pressure and forces trade-offs in planning.
when: when a player faces more than one timer
why: each timer competes for the same time

text: Let NPC doctors keep ledgers players can audit, so a missing or inconsistent entry becomes a clue.
when: Designing medical or supply records in a game world.
why: Inconsistency in records gives players a checkable lead.

text: A game opening can make a minor delay, such as a missed meeting or late call, look consequential to hook the player into the case.
An NPC may withhold a detail or be unable to recall it, recoverable only by a specific follow-up question or earned trust, so the player must work to reach it.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that holds clues
why: Clues stay hidden until the correct question is asked.

text: Small mismatches or separate transactions reveal a pattern, such as common beneficiaries, only when grouped on one board or list, letting a cluster trigger a lead no single entry shows.
when: A case rests on many small transactions
why: Comparing records exposes common beneficiaries that individual entries hide.

text: Tagging dialogue lines by source, such as seen, heard, guessed, or loyal, lets players learn to weigh each line differently.
when: designing NPC dialogue that conveys testimony
why: visible source tags teach the player how reliable each statement is

text: Physical clues such as a note outlast witness memory and can later be traced to the person who wrote or caused them.
An interrogation dialogue can check player answers against world state such as logs and sightings; consistent answers are accepted, while contradictions raise NPC suspicion.
when: in a game with an interrogation scene

text: Building transit delays into letters makes a letter's send date differ from its arrival, which adds a timing clue for players to reason about.
A clue pointing at one suspect can be checked against recorded locations, so players see which other suspects it rules out.
Lore facts collected over time can later unlock a door or reveal a hidden route, rewarding players who kept earlier information.
Track the ratio of verifiable facts an NPC gives to trust requests it makes; a low fact ratio flags emotionally scripted dialogue.
when: when reviewing NPC dialogue
why: Heavy trust requests with few checkable facts signal evasion or scripting.

text: Organize each suspect's case under the same fixed headings (hypothesis, place, opportunity, time, means, motive, conduct, physical height), so filled and unfilled parts show and accusations can be checked.
when: When several suspects have overlapping evidence
why: Fixed headings show which parts are filled and which are only apparent, and a consistent structure makes accusations checkable.

text: A case can be assembled from three strands: motive, opportunity (who knew of and could reach the key item), and conduct before and after the crime.
why: separating the strands shows which parts of the case are still unsupported

text: An accusation can be tested against seven elements: admitted threat, motive, time, place, opportunity, conduct, and the criminal agent (instrument).
when: Before deciding whether an accusation is ready
why: A structured list shows which parts of the case are complete

text: Case levels are enquiry (a clue justifies a question), presumption (evidence justifies suspicion), and conviction (proof justifies a verdict); many clues stop short of conviction.
Collecting apparent slips and near-misses as evidence can inflate suspicion, since each one may have an innocent explanation.
why: Ambiguous behaviour is easy to over-read once a suspect is in view.

text: A clue shown without any marking of its relevance is more likely to be ignored than read as a clue.
why: Players do not recognize unmarked objects as significant.

text: 1) Have the witness restate the whole account from the start, even if part was already heard, including seemingly irrelevant details. 2) Let them pace it and include background. 3) Hold off on theories until all facts are given.
when: When a witness account is the only starting point
why: Complete detail is needed before patterns can be judged, and trimming can lose a small detail's link to a later clue.

text: 1) State what is established as fact. 2) Assess motive. 3) Link each physical trace to a possible route or person. 4) Test feasibility. 5) Weigh persons, labelling inferred points.
when: no witness saw the act and the case rests on traces
why: separating proven facts from inference prevents overclaiming

text: 1) Ask each witness to recount the same event. 2) Compare accounts for gaps and contradictions. 3) Check the accounts against facts that surfaced later.
when: several people shared one event
why: Independent accounts can fill each other's gaps and expose errors a single source would hide.

text: 1) Gather the available facts. 2) Keep the few judged essential and set aside the rest. 3) Arrange the essential facts in order to rebuild the sequence of events.
when: Witness statements, records and traces accumulate faster than they can be checked
why: Sorting and ordering turn a pile of facts into a chain that explains what happened

text: 1) Begin with the culprit's background and the hidden identity, confirmed by outside records. 2) Lay out motive and planning in order. 3) Explain each concealment as part of one design. 4) Explain the roles of others, including unwitting tools. 5) Admit unresolved gaps. 6) Return to ordinary matters to close.
when: when explaining a solved case to someone who missed the key events

text: 1) List each fact that implicates the suspect. 2) Ask what role the suspect could have played as a victim or intervener. 3) Reorder the timeline with that role reversed. 4) Check the physical record and planted items against the new sequence.
when: A suspect's apparent guilt rests on placed or circumstantial evidence
why: Reversing roles tests whether the same facts fit an innocent sequence

text: 1) Write each open question. 2) Attach the best candidate answer. 3) Mark any candidate with no supporting evidence as having no answer. 4) Review the list for gaps and new leads.
1) List known facts. 2) List open questions. 3) State each assumption. 4) Test each assumption against timing. 5) Ask which important questions have never been asked.
1) Shake the blotter or pad to see whether anything else falls out. 2) Hold the sheet only by its corners. 3) Seal it in an envelope. 4) Keep it in your own custody, not left in the room.
when: A loose sheet found among ordinary objects may be evidence.
why: Checking for other traces and limiting handling preserves the evidence.

text: 1) Examine a found object minutely, including linings, bands and hidden surfaces. 2) Look for makers' marks, initials or wear. 3) Check its fit against the suspect. 4) Compare it with a known original.
when: when a found object may link a person to a crime
why: Glancing at an object misses marks that tie it to an owner or source.

text: 1) List each candidate clue. 2) Ask whether it can be proven in court. 3) Record why each fails, such as being worthless, untraceable, missing or only showing motive.
when: when assessing which clues can support a case

text: Give each case-file report a provenance field recording its source and distance from the event, such as sworn deposition, later hearsay, local tradition or editor's note.
when: Designing a case file the player investigates
why: Provenance shows which source is weaker and which clues are firsthand versus rumour.

text: Have shops and merchants log purchases and sales, so the game can check whether a purchase fits a character's plan and players can trace where items went.
when: when designing shopping or crafting systems that support investigation
why: Without records the item trail dies and forces players onto another route.

text: Give players a notebook or case codex logging every NPC and object met, so later prompts recall them and the suspect list can be rebuilt and checked.
when: game with many NPCs
why: A logged record keeps the solution reachable by reasoning.

text: Provide a cast list at the start naming each character and role (victim, clerk, doctor, publicist, lawyer), so the audience can track presence and match people to functions.
when: Writing mysteries with several or many incidental characters
why: Clear presence tracking lets the audience test alibis and access, and prevents complaints of unfairness when minor characters matter late.

text: Keep a clue ledger marking each lead open, cleared or lost, recording negative results so players see progress and do not repeat exhausted checks.
when: a case has many simultaneous leads
why: A written record keeps cleared theories from retaining their place and lets players tell progress from confusion.

text: Keep a clue journal logging all observations, and every culprit-identifying clue before any accusation, so the final explanation or elimination can be traced back.
when: when designing a deduction game
why: A record of observations makes the solution and the elimination checkable.

text: Keep minor observations, such as a missing item or disturbed room, and flag mismatches in a visible list the player can review, so the pattern across them is readable.
when: a puzzle relies on many small clues
why: Flagging rather than filtering keeps mismatches available, and a reviewable collection lets the player compare items and see what they share.

text: Track whether each clue was noticed and whether it was acted on, so ignored clues can return later as legitimate leads.
when: Clues can be dismissed or acted on

text: Make omitted lines or qualifying clauses in in-game logs, letters or journals discoverable, so attentive players can recover what a partial record left out and reach its real meaning.
Log a minor NPC the first time they appear so a later link to the crime is still fair.
Build case files from several document types with dates and locations, such as receipts, logs and letters, so players can assemble a timeline.
when: designing an in-game investigation

text: Give a case file a dated event log so players can order events to test an alibi, and treat mismatched times as clues.
when: Designing investigation content.

text: When an NPC is removed, the case should persist in the world's records and pass to another character.
Give each suspect a discoverable stake, such as debts or an inheritance, so players can test motive for themselves.
when: designing suspects for a mystery

text: Record small sensory details such as a scent, sound or odd choice as they arrive, without interpreting them yet.
when: when a clue first appears
why: the meaning becomes clear only once later evidence supplies context

text: Keep a case journal of known facts and open questions, so players see gaps as hooks to pursue.
Collect all facts about a case impartially, without forcing them into an existing theory, and study each one however trivial it seems.
why: A theory chosen early decides which facts count as relevant and can hide the real evidence.

text: Track which facts the player has shared with each NPC, so a slip is recognised only when it matches a hidden fact the player has revealed.
when: Implementing reactive dialogue in a mystery game.
why: Matching slips to shared facts keeps reactions consistent.

text: Design a dialogue query such as asking whether a witness saw someone so that its correct answers depend on facts the player has learned earlier.
when: When designing witness dialogue trees.

text: Maintain a case file the player can search for matching methods, enabling links across encounters.
when: designing an investigation journal
why: searchable records make pattern matching possible

text: Offer a case-file mode where players solve a mystery from documents and interview logs without walking the whole map.
when: designing investigation gameplay

text: Make room objects collectible evidence that players can compare against testimony from characters.
Make facts that refute a hypothesis discoverable, so players learn to revise rather than cling to a first answer.
when: designing deduction puzzles
why: discoverable contradictions train revision

text: Make a preparation constraint, such as a task that cannot be done from bed, discoverable through an NPC's statement so it can narrow the suspect list.
when: when a constraint is needed to eliminate suspects
why: A constraint the player hears from a character can be used as a deduction tool.

text: Once several copies of an access item are found, collect them all so no other person can open the locked place.
when: A locked place can be opened by duplicate keys.
why: Leaving any copy available keeps someone's access open.

text: Store each character's roles, such as witness, accused or confessor, on a case board and update them as events unfold.
Include property records and lot boundaries as discoverable documents that let players confirm where a building or route actually was.
When an NPC reveals an apparently impossible secret, give the world an ordinary source, such as a relative, rumor, or old record, that the player can find.
why: Letting players confirm the channel makes the secret feel earned rather than arbitrary.

text: Give an accuser a private grievance the player can uncover through dialogue or a letter, so the motive can be deduced.
when: Writing an accuser NPC.
why: A discoverable motive rewards careful investigation and supports a fair reveal.

text: Give an NPC's anonymous note a phrase or piece of knowledge only that NPC has, so players can attribute the note to them.
when: Designing anonymous messages in games

text: Notice boards and handbills can serve as a reward system, but an NPC who cannot read will not see them.
Give players a clue log that records which NPCs could have overheard or learned a secret, so they can narrow the list of possible knowers.
Give each NPC suspect status and motive data, so players can build their own roster and mark who needs watching.
when: when designing a mystery with many characters

text: Record each evidence item with its origin, such as where it was found and who checked it.
why: Origin records let others verify how an item was obtained.

text: Track which facts the player has confirmed, and reveal the answer only after every rejected route has been ruled out.
when: designing a deduction puzzle
why: Gated reveals keep the deduction satisfying.

text: Store a player's collected knowledge in a container that survives character death, so progress is not lost.
when: When knowledge is central to progression

text: Check the institution's own records first; if nothing is missing, drop the explanation that depends on it.
when: a suspicion rests on an item having been taken
why: A complete record can close a line of inquiry quickly

text: Mark key assumptions explicitly in the case file so that a later clue can invalidate them.
Open several parallel objectives and attach a fallback path to each, so a failed line gives the player a named set of next steps.
when: when designing a quest system

text: Track NPC inventories so that when an item disappears or an extra copy appears, the mismatch can serve as a clue.
when: When designing systems where NPCs carry items.
why: Visible and consistent inventories let players deduce that something was swapped or removed.
