text: Provide a journal section where players record details that do not yet fit, and let them revisit it as the case develops.
when: when players collect clues that resist current theories
why: A dedicated log keeps unresolved facts available for later comparison.

text: A disputant facing a larger opposing crew may back off after counting forces, so the side with fewer men often yields without a full fight.
when: when a physical land confrontation is about to begin
why: the weaker side judges that continuing would be futile

text: A book cipher encodes a message as numbers giving page, line and word position in a reference book that sender and reader both hold.
A numerical cipher assigns a number to each letter, so a message is recovered by mapping the numbers back to letters once the assignment is known.
The frequency-and-common-word method works on simple substitution ciphers; it does not guarantee solutions for harder cipher systems.
Some people specialise in breaking ciphers, and a cipher that looks hopeless at first can yield to patience and structured analysis.
A victim's private papers may be written in code that needs specialists to decode, so their contents form a separate evidence source.
when: a victim left diaries or letters

text: In English E is the most common letter, but beyond E the frequency order is loose and can reverse in short samples.
when: using frequency analysis on short messages
why: small samples vary widely

text: Systematic symbol ciphers can be solved from samples, while a purely random code may be impossible to solve.
when: judging whether a cipher is solvable
why: structure gives patterns to exploit

text: A paper marker or the page a book falls open to shows what its recent reader was reading.
when: inferring a reader's recent reading from a left book
why: Pages stay pressed open after sustained handling

text: Spread a substitution alphabet across enough inscriptions to tally; make the commonest glyph and a repeated short sequence a learnable first-mapping hint, and let players record solved pairs.
when: designing a symbol puzzle

text: Repeated or clustered numbers in a book cipher can reveal its structure to a careful reader who suspects the system.
when: Analysing a suspicious sequence of numbers.
why: The encoding method leaves statistical traces in the number pattern.

text: A coded note can be written in two styles, and the planner can be identified from blanks and pressure marks left in the text.
Chain clues so a book found earlier supplies the key for a later encoded message.
Settle the source language first; wordplay like a pun on a name can hint at it, and a wrong language misleads the letter ranking.
Test cipher keys drawn from terms the story has made meaningful; arbitrary words from surrounding material rarely work.
when: when guessing the key of a cipher
why: a key tied to the story is more likely to be the one used

text: Make early cipher words easy and later ones harder, so a book-cipher puzzle teaches its scheme first and then tightens the search.
when: designing a book-cipher puzzle for players
why: an easy start teaches the method and rising difficulty sustains effort

text: Use readable label codes on objects as clues the player must match to the correct sample.
why: Codes give the player a concrete check that links objects to their source.

text: A repeated name or a predictable reply supplies several letters at once and works well as a crib.
when: a message has a likely known phrase
why: one correct guess reveals many letters

text: Copy every new message, since each fresh sample adds letters to the solution.
when: solving a cipher over several samples
why: later samples confirm and extend earlier guesses

text: A column marker before a number implies a double-column printing, which narrows the type of book the key must be.
when: when reading a book cipher's markers

text: Public notices such as classified ads can carry hidden messages; read their initials or codes as possible names and match them to pickup addresses.
when: a notice or register may link to a person
why: Coded messages hide in ordinary public channels.

text: Release a cipher's solution by method, such as letter frequency and crowding of characters, so each step feels earned.
In a book cipher, common early words get small line numbers near page tops, while rare words need long searches and produce high line numbers.
why: word frequency and position in the source text determine the numbers used

text: Each book-cipher number is a coordinate: page, then column or chapter marker, then word position. Without the matching book the numbers carry no meaning.
Anyone who identifies the shared book can read every message, so the choice of book is the weakest point of the cipher.
when: A cipher relies on a shared book as its key.
why: The book itself is the key, so exposing it exposes all traffic.

text: A static phrase passed along a chain of people is repeated and can be compromised by a single leak across the whole system.
when: A password is shared through a group
why: Repetition and transfer multiply the chance of leakage

text: A caption can claim more than its image shows, so check the picture itself before trusting the caption.
Searching a very large set of candidate words can consume hours without success, since the true key may not be among them.
A wrong key can produce partial sense, so any partial decoding needs a full check before it is accepted.
Assuming a message is a cipher when its numbers could be sums of money or a plain list wastes decoding effort.
A message of only a few symbols gives too little data, and several words may fit one pattern, so context must decide.
Editions of the same book can differ in pagination, so a correct key may fail until the sender's printing is identified.

1) Treat each distinct symbol as one letter. 2) Count symbol frequencies. 3) Assume the most frequent symbol stands for E, the language's most common letter. 4) Test repeated three-symbol groups ending in it as the most common short word. 5) Use likely words as cribs. 6) Rewrite messages with dots for unknown symbols.
when: solving one-for-one letter substitution with a long message
why: frequency and common words give the first mappings; cribs narrow the mapping step by step

text: 1) Collect a long run of repeated public text, such as back issues of a paper, since partial collections hide the pattern. 2) Extract only the relevant column. 3) Isolate repeated marks such as initials. 4) Compare what each entry requests. 5) Sort entries into sets and review for a pattern.
when: a clue is hidden in repeated public text
why: a full run reveals a pattern that partial collections hide

text: 1) Read the initials on a byline. 2) Match them against an independent source naming the author. 3) Replace a first guess that the source contradicts.
1) Complete a partial word by trying letters in each gap until one reading fits. 2) Replace solved symbols with letters, leaving blanks. 3) Use the new partial words to reveal more letters.
when: after several mappings are confirmed
why: each confirmed word narrows the remaining candidates

text: 1) Turn to the stated page. 2) Count to the first numbered word. 3) For each following number, count forward from the previous position.
when: A numeric message is suspected to use a known key book.

text: 1) Write a notice that reads innocently to the general public. 2) Embed a detail that only the intended reader will recognise. 3) Publish it where the target is likely to see it.
when: when a message must reach one hidden reader without alerting others
why: a double-reading lure reaches the target while appearing harmless

text: 1) Recount the disputed total to confirm the mismatch is real. 2) List the simple explanations, such as an earlier payout or theft. 3) Keep every explanation open until evidence decides.
when: a counted sum falls short of a claimed amount

text: 1) Find nulls and stop marks by repeated trial. 2) Choose a candidate key word linked to the story. 3) Map the key onto the number sequence. 4) Check that the full decoded text reads sensibly.
when: when a numerical cipher resists direct reading
why: nulls and stops must be known before the key can be tested

text: 1) Split the number sequence into groups and check whether each group reads as three values. 2) Estimate message length from the group count. 3) Test the scheme on the first few groups before decoding the rest.
when: numbers appear in grouped sets with no known text
why: confirms a reference scheme before investing in the full decode

text: 1) List books both sender and reader surely own. 2) Reject books with many editions or a small vocabulary. 3) Test each candidate's decoded words for sense, and reject any that yield nonsense.
Identify the shared key book before decoding, since a book cipher's numbers cannot be recovered alone; from outside, any book in the world could be the key.
why: the numbers only index a text the reader must possess

text: Make an in-world book or text the shared key for a numeric puzzle, placed where the player can find and carry it, and require the player to identify the edition.
when: designing a book-cipher puzzle in a game world
why: a findable key makes the puzzle solvable through play and interpretable; an unreachable key leaves it unsolvable.

text: Build puzzles around an expected event that fails, such as a guard who never reports a theft; reward players who notice the gap, as the absence itself becomes the clue.
when: designing clue-based puzzles or NPC-driven mysteries
why: players reason from expectations, which engages more than simple searching for hidden items

text: Give faction NPCs a passphrase or gesture that only members answer correctly, so the player must earn trust to pass.
when: Designing gated dialogue for a faction
why: A secret response tests whether the player has learned the faction's signs.

text: Disguise forbidden subjects with innocuous substitute words, so messages look ordinary to outsiders yet carry hidden meaning for insiders.
when: messages must pass unnoticed by outsiders
why: outsiders read only the surface wording

text: Use a short coded phrase when a contact must signal the investigator without alerting a target nearby.
when: when the target must not know they are being watched

text: Design a puzzle cipher around an in-world object so only characters who saw its location could produce the message, making the answer a deduction.
Use a wordplay signature as a hint players can decode.
why: decoding rewards attention

text: A generated list of absent NPCs with reasons can serve as an accounting puzzle, with each reason acting as a clue to narrow suspects.
when: when a nobody-leaves rule is in force

text: Flag a note whose tone breaks its author's usual style so players can notice it.
when: Designing notes or letters with author styles

text: Signal a hidden-message rule with a visible marker, because players who miss the marker cannot find the hidden content.
when: When a clue is hidden within ordinary text

text: Let the player write or decode a coded message from memory as a mechanic, instead of reading it from a stored document.
Provide a cipher's pattern through another clue, such as a cipher wheel or a repeated word, so the puzzle stays fair.
when: When designing a cipher puzzle for players.

text: Encode hidden coordinates in notes the player finds, and give them a chance to reread the note before acting on it.
when: Designing puzzles that deliver information through written messages.
why: Rereading lets players catch misreadings, making the message's challenge fair.

text: Send the cipher and the message separately, so that if one is lost the message is not exposed at once.
A small word list keeps the key obscure but forces a clumsy, compressed message, leaving part of the meaning for the reader to infer.
Plant a deliberately unreliable clue, such as a dream-sourced or garbled retelling, that players can correct by checking it against other evidence.
why: Fair misdirection rewards verification.

text: Build findable tells into staged or fabricated clues, such as a trimmed page, missing name or mismatched detail, and reward players who check them against NPC's known abilities.
when: Designing a fabricated document or staged clue
why: Tells let careful players detect the deception.

text: Treat absences as clues: a key NPC removed from a planned event, or a missing key, should be noticed and pursued by attentive players.
when: Designing an NPC-dependent event, or a missing key that could reveal an access route
why: Unexpected absence rewards attentive players; dismissing it removes the trail.

text: Gate progress either behind one timed, exclusive decisive clue, or behind a threshold of weak cumulative clues that must agree; contributory clues alone may not establish a conclusion.
when: Designing clue gates in a deduction mystery
why: A single decisive clue gives a clean conclusion; a cumulative threshold makes players assemble the answer through reasoning.

text: Fair play gives the audience the same characters and information as the investigator, showing every clue, suspect and fact needed before the reveal, so the answer can be reasoned out.
when: when designing a deduction-based reveal that must feel earned
why: Readers can check the explanation against the facts they were given, so the solution feels earned.

text: A fair-play clue sits in plain view from the start, presented as ordinary and unemphasised, so an attentive audience reconstructs its meaning only after the reveal.
why: Players can only reason from clues they actually saw.

text: Show a character's routine or behaviour before its anomaly, so a later reversal or changed signal is recognised as fair.
when: when a clue or twist depends on deviation from a routine or repeated action
why: Players can detect a change only if they first saw the normal state.

text: Deliver clues as offhand remarks, record them, and cross-check against objects and testimony, since a throwaway detail can become decisive.
why: A trivial-seeming detail can answer a question once a theory raises it.

text: Design a single odd object or trace, such as a patched sign or relabelled crate, with both an innocent and a criminal explanation so players must test which fits all the evidence.
when: when designing environmental clues or investigation puzzles

text: Named people, places and details from a delirious speaker are leads that can be checked, even when the speaker's mind is unreliable.
when: a delirious witness names specifics
why: concrete details can be verified independently

text: Holes in the ground combined with displaced material at height, such as loosened mortar on a wall top, can show where a ladder stood.
Let an independent source confirm a deduced conclusion, so the inference is tested rather than accepted as a confident claim.
when: A character or player reaches a conclusion from signs alone
why: An outside confirmation separates a sound inference from an unchecked boast

text: Plant earlier fair clues, such as a mismatched detail in clothing, so that a later reveal feels earned rather than like a trick.
why: an unprepared reveal reads as a cheat

text: An object's wear, engravings and marks can be read in layers to infer occupation, habits and companions, and each inference should be tested.
when: when reconstructing a person from a small set of possessions

text: Plant clues in offhand remarks, private fears or vague moods so the audience registers them long before their meaning is clear.
In a fair-play puzzle, state a physical fact early that a later event must either contradict or explain.
when: the solution depends on physical details the audience can check
why: an early fact gives the audience a way to verify the later event

text: Plant a contradiction early in the story, such as a voice or accent detail, so a later reveal of identity reframes earlier scenes fairly.
when: Writing a late reveal that recontextualises the story.
why: Clues seen before the reveal make the twist feel earned rather than arbitrary.

text: An obscure case signals that the matter is not yet understood, so keep working rather than treating it as settled.
Unfalsifiability matters most for claims with no independent measurable cause; claims that have one can be checked directly.
when: Assessing a hidden-cause accusation

text: Separate evidence players can verify, such as a found object or second witness, from evidence only one NPC can see, and give the latter a visible cost to rely on.
when: Designing witness or accusation systems.
why: Costly unverifiable claims discourage accusations based on them alone.

text: Repeat a puzzle with one parameter shifted, such as a marker's position, to test whether the player's deduction depends on the intended variable.
when: Designing or validating deduction puzzles in generated or authored levels.
why: A single-variable change shows which cue the solution actually relies on.

text: Silence can be data: an NPC who does not react to a noise may have known its source, which the player can read as a clue.
when: When designing NPC reactions to events in a level.
why: A non-reaction implies prior knowledge, which rewards attentive players.

text: Use readable but cryptic marks, such as letters that can be read in reverse, as a puzzle that rewards a second look.
when: Designing optional puzzles in generated environments.
why: Marks that resist a first reading reward closer attention.

text: A refusing NPC can set a flag the player must interpret, with later events confirming whether silence meant protection or guilt.
when: designing ambiguous NPC responses
why: delayed confirmation rewards reasoning

text: Include predictive clues, such as lit windows that should be dark if a place is empty, so players can test their theories inside the game.
when: When designing environmental clues for player deduction
why: Testable predictions let players confirm or reject their reasoning

text: A puzzle can require the player to check one precise fact, such as an angle, object position or hour, to confirm or reject a theory.
when: Designing a deduction puzzle.
why: A single precise check gives the player a clear, decisive test.

text: A trap can be driven by a slow process such as burning fuel, closing a gate or dropping a bar after the player has passed.
Give one object two meanings, a culprit's false clue and a victim's sign, so a player who reads it one way is led to the wrong suspect.
Let a well-hidden opponent be exposed when an unrelated event forces a choice.
Keeping word breaks makes frequency analysis easier, because one-letter words can validate a candidate solution.
Place an unexpected physical trace, such as a fresh chip in an odd spot, as a clue that links to a later mechanism.
Make paid or threatened informants give partial, cryptic clues that gain value only when cross-checked against other sources.
A clue item can carry a material property that is checked in two stages, first visually, then by test.
A coroner-style report can give a directional clue, such as a wound angle that places the shooter on a walkable staircase the player can reach.
Design a weak clue so that it pays off only when the player also finds a second, stronger clue.
when: Building a puzzle with clues of unequal strength.
why: Pairing clues rewards players who combine evidence.

text: Give evidence that a supernatural explanation covers everything, then offer a test that breaks it, so the player can rule the explanation out fairly.
when: A mystery is built on a supernatural or unfalsifiable cause.
why: A fair test lets the player reason to the answer rather than guess.

text: Place small, mundane objects, such as a stopped clock, a single glass or a dropped key, that players can read to reconstruct what happened.
when: designing a scene for investigation
why: ordinary objects feel discoverable and grounded

text: Place a crumpled discarded note in a room so players who search the grate can recover the lure and reconstruct its timing.
when: Designing a dungeon that rewards searching.
why: Players who search thoroughly can recover evidence of a trap.

text: A notepad can hold a reversed impression that a tool reveals as a fragment pointing to a location, confirmed by a full note found elsewhere.
Reason from the culprit's motives to find where a discarded object would physically end up, such as close to the scene and out of plain sight.
when: When a scene has been searched and a clue is still missing.
why: A person hiding an object avoids carrying it away and avoids leaving it visible, so the likely location follows from that behaviour.

text: Loose fibres, displaced material or an observer's nervous reaction can reveal that an item was concealed inside an ordinary container.
when: Reconstructing where an object was hidden among everyday things.
why: Disturbances to ordinary objects leave traces that a careful searcher can notice.

text: Design a clue's physical state, such as a crumpled note, so it supports more than one reading and can serve as a red herring.
when: Designing evidence that should not point clearly to one answer.
why: A single physical state can be read as hurried concealment or as an innocent return.

text: A puzzle can let the player plant a fake relic and observe which NPC reacts to it, giving a reliable tell.
when: Designing identification puzzles in a game.
why: The NPC's reaction to a planted object reveals hidden knowledge.

text: An item with no identifying marks still carries information, because the absence of marks can itself narrow or support a conclusion.
when: When a clue object lacks obvious identifiers.
why: The lack of markings is a meaningful observation, not a null result.

text: Design a series of traps or deaths that share one element, and let early ones look random, so the pattern rewards attention later.
when: designing recurring hazards

text: Build an impossible scene first, with a single locked entrance, no hiding place and distracted witnesses. The solution must break one of these assumptions.
Reward attention to small physical evidence, such as creases, reversed folds or wear, that proves a swap or tampering.
when: when a puzzle's solution must be verifiable
why: observable traces let players confirm a hypothesis

text: A decoy with mismatched details, such as seal, colour or address, can mislead players into believing the real target is a different item.
when: when placing a false lead
why: players read conflicting details as the true distinction

text: Open the mystery with a plausible natural explanation, then let one physical anomaly reopen the case at low cost to the player.
why: A calm first belief makes the later anomaly feel like a real discovery

text: A confessed detail that can be checked elsewhere opens a new line of inquiry, so the player is rewarded for verifying it.
when: designing an interrogation mechanic

text: A document with two layers of correction rewards careful inspection. A thorough reader who looks beneath the top change can recover the earlier version.
when: Designing a clue that can be altered and then concealed
why: Layers reward closer examination without making the clue unreadable

text: A glyph repeated at several trap or death sites lets players connect separate rooms to one hidden faction.
when: players must discover a hidden group through scattered sites
why: the repeated mark is the only visible thread linking the sites

text: Tie a physical clue's result to a specific examiner, so a player who requests a second opinion from a skilled NPC can change the outcome.
when: when designing evidence checks
why: different examiners can read the same sign differently

text: Once a material is identified, an ambiguous tactile cue can gain a new meaning, such as seams between plates, forcing players to revise their mental map.
A puzzle state that cannot be reached points the player back to an earlier assumption, such as a door believed to be locked.
A body dressed in a player character's clothes can carry one inconsistency, such as mismatched shoes or a hidden item, that a careful player can check.
when: Designing a body or identity swap for a mystery.
why: A single planted inconsistency lets an attentive player expose the swap.

text: A document found on a victim can supply a motive, so a physical trace carries meaning beyond its appearance.
when: When a found document may explain why a person was targeted.
why: Contents of a found document can reveal a financial or personal reason for the crime.

text: A scene can contain two crimes: a staged crime that is solved first and a hidden second crime that remains. A later killer may reuse the original planner's prepared devices.
when: Solving a staged death reveals unresolved anomalies.
why: The planner's devices can become a trap for a later offender.

text: Unverifiable evidence has three uses: opening an inquiry, adding presumption alongside other facts, or serving as sufficient ground for judgment. It should never be sufficient ground for judgment alone.
when: deciding what weight unverifiable testimony carries

text: A design that considers only the offender's route misses the investigator's route, so both routes must be written.
A single odd detail is a lead, not a conclusion, since many anomalies have ordinary causes and an incomplete pattern can still point at the right suspect.
when: when players build theories from one or two anomalies
why: Coincidence produces many false anomalies

text: Treating an obvious trace as proof while overlooking a quieter one can send an investigation toward the wrong suspect.
when: Several traces are present and one is conspicuous
why: Attention drawn to the loud trace misses the subtle one

text: A signal too obvious to the characters invites the audience to ask why others miss it, which can break believability.
when: A clue is visible to every character.
why: Characters who ignore an obvious signal look careless and undermine the mystery.

text: Searching obvious hiding spots first can miss a concealment that the routine suggests.
A single plan that shows only some sides of a property cannot fix its location with certainty.
Assuming a search was exhaustive, or that a weapon must look like a known type, can hide the solution in plain view.
when: when a method seems impossible given the items found

text: An imagined mechanism that outruns the evidence can waste effort, since a plausible-sounding idea can still be unsupported.
Too many clues that do not link together leave players with no clear path through the case.
Adding unneeded steps to a plan multiplies its points of failure, so extra complexity can make a mostly successful plan collapse.
when: A plan is extended beyond what its goal requires.
why: Every added step is another dependency that can go wrong.

text: A correct but limited clue can disappoint players if it leads nowhere, so even a narrow clue should point toward the next step.
when: A clue confirms only a small fact.
why: Players expect clues to advance the case, and a dead end feels like wasted effort.

text: 1) List every fact the solution needs. 2) Confirm each appears before the reveal. 3) Explain the answer step by step, linking each step to a shown clue. 4) Move or add any missing clue onto a route the player must pass. 5) Let the reveal read as recognition of earlier evidence.
when: when designing a mystery solution or reveal
why: Players can check each step against clues they already saw.

text: 1) State the case against one suspect alone. 2) Add a second suspect or fact, tying each addition to a specific fact. 3) Present the combined case with each layer visible.
when: evidence is circumstantial
why: each layer can be judged on its own

text: 1) Reread the whole work from start to finish. 2) Read it as a first-time audience would. 3) Note where the culprit becomes obvious. 4) Revise the structure from the start if needed.
when: checking whether a mystery gives away its answer

text: 1) Show the clue when it appears, with its sensory detail. 2) Withhold interpretation. 3) Supply context later that reveals its meaning. 4) Connect the clue to the answer in the final account.
when: when a clue must be paid off later in the story
why: the audience can catch up with the investigator

text: 1) Show the key detail early as an ordinary habit or object. 2) Withhold its significance. 3) Later, trigger recall with an unrelated cue that connects the detail to the solution.
when: Designing a mystery whose solution depends on a detail the audience has already seen.
why: A detail that seems ordinary when first shown can be recalled later as the answer, which makes the reveal fair.

text: 1) Give an inventory item wear, such as a chipped blade or worn sole, that implies a specific user. 2) Give one prop a condition that contradicts its expected owner. 3) Let the mismatch be the clue the player must notice.
when: Designing clue-bearing props for investigation play
why: Players infer ownership from physical traces, and a contradiction creates a discoverable deduction.

text: 1) Make the easy answer supported by visible evidence. 2) Leave one visible gap in that support. 3) Reward players who check the scene before accepting the group's view.
when: When designing a mystery with a tempting wrong solution
why: A gap in an apparently complete answer gives careful players a path to the truth without making the wrong answer unsupported.

text: 1) Check motive against financial or personal records. 2) Check means against a link to a workplace or training. 3) Check opportunity against a fixed schedule. Accept each layer only when records confirm it.
when: when testing whether a solution accounts for all the timing and means

text: 1) Define the trap as a chain of conditions, such as a note read, an item used and a timer. 2) Reveal the result to the player only through a later event.
when: Designing delayed traps or consequences in a generated level.
why: A chain of conditions with delayed reveal sustains suspense and pacing.

text: 1) Enumerate every access path to the victim, such as food, drink, water and room items. 2) Let the player close paths one at a time through investigation.
when: Generating a poisoning or sabotage puzzle.
why: Each closed path narrows the search and gives the player a sense of progress.

text: 1) Reconstruct the act that could have dropped the object. 2) Test whether the hiding place fits that act. 3) Accept the placement only if it is physically plausible.
when: When judging how a concealed object came to be where it was found.
why: A hiding place that matches a plausible action gives a credible explanation of the clue.

text: Every clue or fact a solution depends on must be shown before the reveal, in plain words without interpretation, so the solution is reachable; otherwise it reads as a cheat.
when: when designing or writing a mystery reveal, or promising a solvable mystery
why: Players accept only reveals they could have reasoned out from earlier evidence; holding back clues breaks the promise of a solvable mystery.

text: Plant small, seemingly irrelevant details early, such as a note, odd object or repeated phrase, and trace each later payoff back to them so the reveal feels fair.
why: Players can only accept a payoff they could have anticipated; fair-play reveals reward attentive players.

text: Use verifiable fixed anchors, such as timestamps, a bell or a door, and plant clock discrepancies the player can compare, so a reconstructed timeline is fair.
when: when players must check the sequence of events or alibis
why: Shared timestamps let players order events themselves; discrepancies give a fair route to the truth.

text: Require players to find in-world records, such as a bank ledger, rent receipt, laundry ticket or insurer's file, to verify a claim rather than guess.
when: when designing evidence the player must confirm
why: Verifiable records turn suspicion into a checkable fact, and locating them makes confirmation an active step.

text: Give a full, ordered record of what was discovered and when, with a recap showing each link, so the audience can check each step.
when: when the solution depends on earlier discoveries the reader must rebuild
why: Visible links let players confirm the solution follows from evidence.

text: Leave a clue's meaning open until later evidence settles it; ambiguity may stay unresolved in the background, since a guess presented as fact misleads later reasoning.
when: when a clue is meant to pay off later or its meaning is not yet supported
why: Unresolved meaning keeps the mystery alive; premature answers can mislead later reasoning.

text: Plant physical tells, such as a moved rug or fresh floor patch, so players can infer that a body was moved.
A fact used to contradict a commitment must be verifiable, or the resulting shift in view proves nothing.
Test equally placed suspects against the same motive question, so differences in the result come from their stakes rather than from how each was examined.
when: two or more suspects look equally placed

text: Restate the governing constraint of a key rule in plain, non-technical terms before the audience needs it, so they hold the same facts as the investigator.
when: A later deduction depends on a rule or limit the audience must understand
why: Shared facts let the audience judge later conduct as evidence rather than surprise

text: In a fair-play mystery, plant small observable reactions early so the audience can reinterpret them when the hidden fact comes out.
A mystery depends on keeping its answer hidden while still giving the audience fair access to the clues that solve it.
Give each suspect a schedule that the player can verify through NPC witnesses, and let the alibi break when the player finds a gap in it.
when: when designing a murder or theft puzzle

text: Confront a suspect with a verifiable document, such as a receipt found in a desk, rather than with an unsupported accusation.
when: When a suspect denies involvement and a physical record exists.
why: A document that can be checked is harder to deny than a claim.

text: Show or mention a concealed method earlier in the story; a method never shown will feel like a cheat to the audience.
Plant clues before a late identity reveal; withholding information that was never planted feels like cheating, not a fair reversal.
Plant a note with a tell, such as an unusual letter form or ink, tied to one NPC, and let players find it by comparing against a known sample.
when: Designing a clue that points to a specific character
why: A comparable sample keeps the solution fair and checkable

text: Plant a legend that players can verify through two independent sources, such as a shop record and a witness NPC.
Give each planted document an answer that the player can reach using evidence available in the level.
why: Otherwise the document reads as arbitrary rather than a fair clue.

text: Seed a chain of NPC deaths reported by different sources, and include one independently verifiable death so that players gain trust in the rest.
when: Designing a series of reported events
why: A verified event lets players judge which unverified reports are reliable.

text: Give letters a hidden layer, polite text that the player decodes using what they know of the sender's motive.
when: Writing a letter that carries a concealed meaning.
why: Players reward effort when surface wording must be read against known motives.

text: Balance temperament-based elimination with evidence the player can verify, so that elimination feels fair.
when: Designing suspect elimination in a game
why: Unverifiable profile reasoning feels arbitrary to players

text: State every contradiction in the evidence plainly so the audience can test explanations against it.
Plant the decisive clue early in the scene, visible but not emphasised, so a later reversal feels fair.
when: When designing a late twist that overturns the leading theory.
why: A clue that stands out gets noticed and spoils the reversal; a buried one feels unfair.

text: Write the true handler's habit into a readable detail the player can compare, so planted-item puzzles stay fair.
Let the audience test each competing theory against the available evidence before it collapses, so a false lead is discredited by facts rather than by decree.
Every clue needed for a final reveal or accusation must appear earlier, before it matters, so the player can rebuild the chain by their own reasoning.
when: Designing a mystery, deduction puzzle or late reveal
why: Fair play lets players reach the solution through their own reasoning.

text: Plant every clue needed for a late reveal or open question earlier in the world, so the final explanation recalls known facts and the ending rewards collection over guesswork.
when: Designing a late reveal, finale or open question
why: Clues placed early let the reveal recall known facts rather than introduce surprises.

text: Scatter distinct, linkable parts of an answer across sources such as a letter, record, portrait, memory aid, map fragment or worn mechanism, so only combining them reveals it.
when: Designing a mystery answer, sealed vault or multi-source investigation
why: Joining sources is the puzzle; no single source gives the answer.

text: Place important clues in ordinary or fringe props, visible enough to notice but not labelled as clues, rewarding players who study the whole room.
when: Placing ordinary objects that may matter later
why: Subtle placement rewards observant players.

text: Give hidden things a subtle visible cue, such as a loose bolt, open shutter or faint seam, early enough that observant players can notice it before the solution.
when: Hiding a secret, panel or solution the player should find
why: A cue lets observant players succeed; a solution they could not spot feels unfair.

text: Make damaged, wrecked or concealed items, such as a torn note's surviving word, point toward a specific room or object to examine.
when: Designing a damaged document or wreckage as a clue
why: A surviving detail gives a concrete place to investigate.

text: Place remains, ruins or cellar foundations that match or contradict witness descriptions and documents, so players confirm or refute a claim by finding them.
Record who knew a suspect and for how long, so a player can test a claim against verifiable history.
Give clues players can verify by inspection, and make sure a suspect's explanation can actually change the outcome.
when: Designing an interrogation or deduction
why: Testable clues and responsive explanations keep deduction fair.

text: Before accepting confirming evidence for a theory, state which observation would count against it.
why: A conclusion chosen in advance makes every outcome look like confirmation.

text: Design each rumour so a specific NPC can confirm or refute it, giving the player a clear route to verify it.
Use an inconsistency in an NPC story as a clue that points the player to a second source for checking.
Expose the reasoning path, from behaviour to pattern to motive, so players can test an inference rather than simply accept it.
Let a puzzle test a guessed rule, such as an NPC reacting to an item in a room, so the player can recreate the setup and time the response.
when: Designing a puzzle where the solution is a hypothesised rule
why: Repeatable setup lets players confirm or refute their guess

text: Give partial-match feedback: an NPC that deviates slightly should yield an ambiguous result rather than a clean yes or no.
when: A player's test of an NPC's reaction is close to but not exactly the trigger
why: Ambiguous feedback keeps the deduction open and reflects real variation

text: Fix the reference's page layout so decoding is repeatable, and give a fail state for a wrong edition.
Make environment features that enable climbing visible and inspectable, and signal an exceptional ability early, so an impossible-looking entry feels earned.
when: Designing a locked room reachable by an ability-based route
why: Visible features and earlier demonstrations make the solution fair

text: Set a reveal to the rules the player was given, so the solution reads as a clever use of allowed means.
when: Designing a puzzle solution in a generated level.

text: Build tracks puzzles so that two possible characters share a trace, forcing the player to find a second clue.
In an escape puzzle, show all obvious exits as checkable and closed, and keep the real route off the initial list so it is discovered only after elimination.
when: Designing a room or sequence where the player must find how an NPC or item escaped.
why: Players feel a satisfying reveal when the obvious options are exhausted first.

text: Make a riddle depend on an item found elsewhere and reward the player when the key connects the two.
when: Designing a cryptic clue
why: Ties exploration to puzzle solving

text: Keep at least one essential clue findable even when decoys and lost evidence are present.
when: generating or placing clues in a mystery level
why: Otherwise the player cannot reach the solution.

text: Ask a player who witnessed a destruction to vouch for it later, and let a puzzle hinge on whether they actually saw it happen.
Place a side passage or service stair in the layout as the answer to an access puzzle, so the solution is fair and checkable.
when: Designing a sealed-room puzzle
why: A visible, checkable route lets players verify their deduction

text: Place a small unexplained anomaly, such as an unlocked door, and explain it later through an NPC encounter.
when: designing a hidden arrangement the player will learn about
why: the anomaly rewards attention and sets up the reveal

text: Make the matching step a physical action the player performs, such as placing an object on a mark, so the test feels earned.
when: A clue must be verified by comparison.
why: Active testing makes the verification feel like the player's own discovery.

text: Describe a hidden object's location relative to a fixed landmark and a count, such as steps from an opening, so players can find the exact spot.
when: Placing a cache
why: Landmark plus count gives a checkable position

text: Make a scripted encounter look like a fair fight, while leaving a procedural oddity, such as a mismatched detail, that exposes the setup to careful players.
when: Designing a staged or deceptive combat encounter.
why: Players should be able to detect the trap through clues.

text: Give an unexpected location a fair-play clue on its approach path, so the solution can be discovered in hindsight.
Pair ambient foreboding with a concrete clue so the player knows what to watch for.
when: a level builds dread through warnings or ambient signs
why: Undirected dread gives the player nothing to act on

text: Design a puzzle sequence so the player can predict the next clue, and place the missing clue where the prediction points.
when: Building a multi-clue puzzle
why: Prediction rewards pattern recognition and confirms the solution path

text: Give a sealed room a stated boast, such as on a sign or in lore, and place the real weakness in an element the boast does not mention.
why: Players who look past the claim are rewarded.

text: Use a fixed physical trace, such as a device defect, to link an anonymous object to one person, and make the player locate that object to make the link.
Showing the audience every fact the investigator has, and the offender's actions, makes the challenge interpreting evidence rather than hunting for a hidden answer, but removes the whodunit surprise.
when: Choosing between a hidden-culprit mystery and full disclosure
why: Full disclosure shifts the challenge from identity to reasoning.

text: An identical object found in several places can link the people who carried it, but can also be a planted decoy pointing at the wrong person.
when: A single object type could have many owners and the question is who carried it and when.
why: Matching items prove a connection only if the placement can be attributed; ownership alone does not establish guilt.

text: Test a clue's value rather than assuming it from its label or convenience; discarding inconvenient evidence misleads as much as trusting it blindly.
when: Evaluating a lead marked as important.
why: Labels do not guarantee usefulness; confirmation bias favors whatever fits the current theory.

text: Dismissing routine records or items as unimportant can hide the real lead; keep dismissed items open and reassess them once new facts arrive.
when: Reassessing items after the obvious leads have been checked.
why: Initial judgements may be revised when new facts arrive.

text: Conspicuous investigative actions, such as visible protection, a loud canvass or an obvious grab, reveal interest, so suspects may change accounts, drop trails or lure the investigator.
why: Overt action reveals the investigator's interest.

text: When confessing brings visible suffering, others in the same position learn the cost of speaking, which shapes who will confess.
when: Punishment or torment follows confession publicly
why: Observers adjust their behavior to the observed cost

text: A victim's own item found beside them can show they were acting in response to a threat, which shifts how the scene is read.
when: When an object near a victim is interpreted as evidence of their intent.
why: The object reveals the victim's last action, which can point away from the intended suspect.

text: A hidden trace found by digging feels more convincing to people than one in plain view, because it appears as a secret that was uncovered.
when: When a clue is concealed and then discovered by the player or an investigator.
why: Discovery of a concealed item creates a sense of uncovering a secret, which increases its perceived weight.

text: An object is more likely to be picked up where it can be seen than where it cannot, so its location must be judged against lighting.
when: Interpreting where a physical clue was found

text: A small object concealed in an ordinary place can hold decisive evidence that goes unnoticed until a searcher knows where to look and what it opens.
A deeper inspection tool, such as a camera, can reveal traces hidden by cleaning or enemies that normal sight misses, rewarding thorough play.
when: Designing a tool that exposes hidden content.
why: A specialized tool gives players a way to see what normal sight cannot.

text: Players follow the most conspicuous element, so hide the real clue in a quiet element, such as a figure who waits unnoticed, forcing players to look past the decoy.
when: Designing a scene with a decoy and a real lead.
why: Salient elements draw attention before quiet ones, so chasing the loudest element rewards careful observation.

text: Hold back a clue that only one investigative frame reveals, so the player's choice changes what they can prove.
A disguised NPC can be unmasked through visible seams, such as a pale line or loose hairpiece, that players are invited to notice.
when: Designing an NPC whose true identity is hidden behind a disguise.
why: Fair visible clues let observant players deduce the identity before the reveal.

text: Use visual signals across a gap when direct contact is unsafe; avoid them when signals are too fast or irregular to be counted reliably.
Design item clues so their meaning depends on owner, location and time together; each one alone leaves the clue incomplete.
An incidental witness detail can become decisive when checked against a later physical find; its worth depends on how it relates to the other evidence.
A short unexplained gap in an otherwise complete alibi can be a clue the player is meant to notice.
when: An alibi is otherwise complete and well witnessed.
why: A small gap is easy to overlook but breaks the whole alibi.

text: Show witness statements pinned to clock times in a timeline view, with conflicts visibly highlighted, so the player can compare them.
when: Players must reconstruct a sequence from several testimonies.
why: Spatial placement of times makes agreements and contradictions easy to see.

text: Make trace markers visible enough that the player can find them; a clue nobody can locate does not help the player.
when: Designing passive evidence markers for a player to inspect.
why: Markers the player cannot find deliver no information.

text: A hint can unlock only after the player re-examines an item from a new angle, such as a different map view or a newly held inventory item.
when: Gating a clue behind a change of perspective
why: A changed viewpoint makes the hidden detail noticeable

text: When physical clues are thin, poor leads multiply, and investigators cannot invent evidence, so the case must be read from what exists.
A found item, such as a recording device, can reinterpret an earlier sound clue, and a shop or ledger can then confirm the explanation.
A stain's visibility depends on lighting, colour and the observer's suspicion, so dark or dirty surfaces hide marks from an unsuspecting observer.
Fog or night that limits sight and sound forces players to piece events together from partial information.
when: when a level restricts perception
why: Missing senses make the player infer what happened

text: If every witness vanishes at once, the audience sees the device and stops trusting the story; the remaining watcher needs a reason to stay.
when: Isolating characters for a plot beat.
why: Abrupt total removal looks contrived, and an unexplained absence of the remaining watcher invites doubt.

text: Watchers track the visible route, so an unexpected visitor to a third party's rooms can expose the meeting.
when: a discreet meeting depends on an alternate route
why: An unusual visit draws attention even when the main route is watched

text: A false confession can collapse tension, so the case must still be presented as open.
Dismissing each clue separately can hide the cumulative force of a pattern, and counting one fact under two descriptions falsely inflates confidence.
when: Evaluating a set of related clues.
why: Each clue looks weak alone, and double-counted facts create an illusion of independent support.

text: Ignoring unexplained anomalies until they undermine the whole chain causes a theory to collapse late and unexpectedly.
Writing on the back of an item is easy to miss unless the player turns the item over.
when: When a clue is printed on the reverse of a physical item.
why: Players inspect the visible face by default and skip the hidden side.

text: Investigators miss a swapped object when the replacement looks identical to the original and they have no record of its normal appearance.
when: Searching a room for a hidden item

text: A clue tied to the victim, such as the victim's own belongings, can mislead by suggesting an inward source when an outside actor was responsible.
when: When evidence links an object or substance to the victim.
why: The victim's own possessions can explain some traces without implicating anyone else.

text: A small visual detail can mislead an observer who has no reason to examine it closely, such as a partly visible object that appears complete.
when: Presenting evidence where a key detail is easy to overlook.
why: Without a reason to inspect, observers accept appearances at face value.

text: Tag vision or ghost clues pointing to a suspect as unverifiable; they may raise suspicion but need physical or documentary corroboration before unlocking an arrest.
when: designing clue gating in a mystery game
why: keeps unverifiable testimony from driving a final accusation

text: Show the case as one stated question with listed constraints, visible sub-goal status and searched containers, so players see untested leads and the obstacle blocking progress.
when: Designing a quest log or case board.
why: Visible status lets players track what must be proven and what is blocking them.

text: End a suspense sequence on a visible reveal, such as a figure leaving the scene, so the player sees the answer rather than hearing an explanation.
Give a suspect a visible, dangerous escape option, such as a hidden vial, so the accusation has an immediate consequence.
A rescue that fails should have a cause the audience can see, so the failure does not read as author convenience.
when: When designing a rescue that is stopped or interrupted.
why: Unexplained failure undermines trust in the story.

text: Release clues as raw facts and keep the logical link between them for the player to make.
when: when designing a deduction puzzle
why: Players gain satisfaction from making the link themselves.

text: During repeated questioning, have each answer add one new detail instead of revealing the full solution at once.
when: when a player interrogates an NPC several times
why: incremental detail rewards persistence and keeps each answer meaningful

text: Let a character withhold a clue until the player meets a condition, and make that condition visible to the player.
when: gating information behind progress
why: A visible condition tells the player what to do to unlock the clue.

text: Make public supernatural acts visible to several NPCs at once, so a player's claim about them has independent witnesses.
when: Designing a magic event that others must confirm.
why: Shared witnessing lets the player build a case that holds up to questioning.

text: Tie a hidden surface clue, such as an older sigil under a fresh coat, to a skill or knowledge check so that an observant, knowledgeable player gains it.
why: rewards observation and expertise rather than chance

text: Release clues in instalments through a journal or news feed, holding the decisive finding for the final entry.
when: When a game delivers story or clues through readable entries
why: Staged release builds suspense and keeps the key finding for the climax

text: Give each kind of trace its own visibility rule, such as a lighting level or NPC suspicion state, so players must examine items in the right conditions.
Give the player the same clues the investigator used, and do not withhold a clue needed to test the conclusion.
when: designing a deduction mystery where the solution must be reachable
why: a surprise the player could not predict feels unfair

text: Make some clues appear to confirm a player's assumption so that the player must test them before acting on them.
when: When designing clues that point toward a conclusion.
why: Clues that seem to confirm a belief can mislead, so verification keeps the player from acting on an unchecked reading.

text: Make tactile, olfactory and weight-based details reliable and distinguishable, so players who cannot rely on sight can still detect a fake or tampering.
when: Designing clues for players who cannot rely on sight or the visual channel is limited.
why: Non-visual clues give access to the same information through other senses.

text: Set out decisive physical clues at the start, such as size, sightline and residue, so the solution is fair even when the suspects seem unlikely.
A clue placed too prominently is noticed by everyone and loses surprise; one hidden too well is unfair, while one too conspicuous gives the answer away.
A visible presence deters crime but forgoes catching it in the act; concealment does the reverse.
when: Deterring crime matters more than catching it.

text: Hidden clues add mystery and search effort but change the puzzle; obvious clues keep the solution clear but give searchers nothing to find.
when: Deciding whether a clue should be concealed

text: A shuttered lantern lets the player briefly reveal details, trading visibility against attracting threats.
when: Designing a light-based mechanic for stealth exploration
why: Light reveals information but also signals the player's position

text: A soft-nosed projectile flattens on impact, causing a deadly wound and leaving a deformed round that can be recovered.
Several individually harmless failures occurring together can disable a defence that none of them would defeat alone.
Vary how precisely npcs describe threats, so players learn to weigh tone against content.
when: when writing npc warnings across a game

text: Prying or lockpicking mechanics can leave tool-specific damage patterns, so players can match found tools to damaged doors or locks.
when: designing lock and damage systems
why: Distinct marks give players a way to link evidence to a tool.

text: Hide one clue from a companion NPC so the player decides when to share it with them.
Pair companions with complementary strengths, such as a methodical fact-tracker and an intuitive noticer, because each is weak alone and effective together.
why: Each strength covers the other's blind spot.

text: Let a companion flag an unusual observation, such as a missing object, so the questioning character can pursue it.
when: Designing companion systems that support investigation.

text: Compact tools are efficient only at low and moderate detail but are still better than none; a simple fallback, such as a pocket lens, covers work beyond their range.
when: when a portable toolset must be small
why: carrying size limits what the tools can do

text: Layered concealments such as masks, hats and cloaks can make one person look like several people, and an alibi breaks once the disguise is identified.
when: when one character changes outward signs between scenes, or a disguise mechanic is designed
why: Observers track the visible figures rather than the single person behind them.

text: A missing or torn item within an otherwise complete or ordered set, such as an emptied frame, archive gap or torn leaf, suggests deliberate removal rather than loss.
when: a gap or tear breaks an otherwise complete setting, archive or document
why: A gap breaking a full pattern is unlikely to be chance, neighboring records survive in order, and binding or wear can reveal where a leaf was taken out.

text: A hidden item placed inside a common, routinely handled object in a familiar spot passes inspection, since searchers focus on pockets, containers and surfaces and overlook everyday fittings.
when: a hidden item must survive routine checks, or is swapped for an identical-looking object timed to a search
why: Ordinary appearance and handling draw no suspicion, and a substitution timed to a search goes unnoticed.

text: Culprits may plant, swap or reposition items, such as a suspect's garment or cleaned stain, to point at a false person, so a convincing marker alone does not settle identity.
when: clues were left by someone who may be hiding, or a matching item implicates a suspect who denies being present
why: Deliberately placed or altered items can imitate evidence of presence, and altering an object changes the story it tells about who handled it.

text: A person who finds incriminating writing may destroy it at once, before anyone else has time to consider it.
when: a written record could expose them
why: Destruction removes the record faster than analysis can.

text: A deliberately clumsy act makes noisy movement read as accident, so a noisy trip is less likely to draw suspicion.
when: An investigator must move in a way that would otherwise seem suspicious.
why: Observers attribute clumsiness to carelessness rather than intent.

text: People often keep a secret from the person most affected, judging that knowing would only burden them.
A witness who loves a suspect may flatly deny a sighting or statement, so a denial alone does not establish guilt or innocence.
when: A family member or close ally denies a claim in front of an investigator.
why: Loyalty and sympathy push people to shield those they care about.

text: A person may stay silent before authority when confessing a minor secret would cost them their livelihood, even if they are innocent of the main charge.
when: An innocent suspect hides a lesser wrongdoing under questioning.
why: Fear of losing their position outweighs the cost of concealment.

text: An NPC who is hiding something may lie further or fall silent when pressed directly.
when: when a concealing character is confronted
why: pressure threatens what they are protecting

text: Naming a witness's motive for silence, such as fear of a strict authority, can help break that silence.
when: witness refuses to speak
why: Acknowledging the fear removes part of its hold.

text: A personal object with sentimental value can lead its owner to act against their own interest, such as taking a risk to keep it.
why: Attachment can outweigh practical cost

text: When confessing offers survival and refusing means execution, most people confess for self-preservation, so the confession says little about whether the charge is true.
when: A confession is the price of escaping death or severe punishment.
why: The benefit of confessing outweighs any commitment to the truth of the statement.

text: Framing a forced choice as the other side's responsibility makes them feel in control of the outcome.
when: An accuser presents an ultimatum to a family.

text: After a violent act, an offender tries to remove blood and clothing, then acts composed in public and says nothing about what happened.
when: when a character must appear normal soon after committing violence
why: to avoid suspicion before traces are found

text: A guilty party removes items linked to a visitor from the scene and disposes of them at sea.
when: when an offender wants to erase a visitor's connection to a place
why: to remove evidence that someone else was there

text: Destroying a document does not erase its evidence: its burning can become a clue, and witnesses to its creation can still date it.
Destroying a document that would support an innocent suspect is suspicious conduct but does not establish a crime.
when: a suspect is seen destroying potentially helpful evidence
why: The act is suspicious, but its cause must be checked separately.

text: Hidden objects are often protected in layers: a decoy resembling the real item, a changed format, and a secondary hiding place.
A scene that is too tidy, too complete or too flawless for its event is likely staged, since genuine events show uneven, hasty disorder shaped by chance and error.
when: judging whether a disturbed or complete scene was staged or authentic
why: Deliberate staging follows a plan that real stress does not, and a perfect match to a template suggests arrangement.

text: Destroyed or broken objects leave readable fragments that reveal the original's purpose; when a clue is destroyed before examination, reason from surviving traces and log the loss.
when: evidence has been burned or broken, or a clue can no longer be examined
why: Destruction rarely removes every trace, and a fragment can still support or limit a conclusion.

text: Inspect a decorated or molded container's outer form and weight for anomalies; decoration hides contents, but molded layers still reflect the interior's outline.
when: an observer suspects a hidden item inside a sealed or decorated object
why: Decoration is designed to mislead but seldom erases the underlying form or weight.

text: Use plausible, mundane reasons for each removal, and do not rely on one removal alone; the effect comes from several removals in sequence.
when: Staging the isolation of a witness.
why: Individually reasonable reasons avoid showing the device, while a sequence of removals builds suspicion.

text: A pile of ash concentrated in one place may indicate a deliberate attempt to remove a document, so identify which remnants were destroyed and why.
when: Ash or burned material is found in an unusual concentration.
why: Intentional destruction leaves a pattern that accidental burning does not.

text: If a person who rarely leaves a place is removed from it, the removal was probably planned, and the plan points to what the removal enables.
Show partial words with blanks as a staged reveal, so each solved word unlocks the next clue.
A delayed reveal can withhold a theory until a final clue confirms it, while the supporting clues remain visible to the player throughout.
when: Designing a puzzle whose answer is confirmed late.
why: Visible clues let the player feel they earned the answer when it arrives.

text: A quest may stage an accident that seems natural, hiding a beneficiary whose records a player can uncover.
when: designing a mystery quest
why: Gives players a second layer beneath the obvious cause

text: Present a too-complete set of clues as a puzzle, where the player must notice that the evidence was staged.
when: when designing a deduction puzzle with a false solution
why: noticing staging rewards careful reasoning over accepting the obvious

text: A cover-up mechanic can let a villain pre-fill an official report, which the player later checks against physical evidence.
Sort each disturbed object in a scene into those that fit the stated motive and those that contradict it; the contradicting items are usually the strongest lead.
when: a scene shows many signs of disturbance and one explanation is accepted quickly
why: Most disorder can match a single story, while a few anomalies point to a second story.

text: Give a gang NPC a manufactured alibi that the player can break by checking a timeline, using a clock, a lit window or a witness's timing.
when: Designing an investigation with an NPC who lies about their whereabouts
why: A checkable timeline lets the player expose the lie through reasoning rather than luck.

text: Vary the sensory cue, such as a hollow sound, an unexpected weight or a turning handle, so the clue is solvable without pixel-hunting.
when: designing hidden items for players to discover
why: Distinct physical cues let players solve the clue through interaction rather than visual scanning.

text: Air moving through vents shows a hidden space is not fully sealed, so vents can point toward the space.
Burying an object deep in mud slows recovery, but does not remove the trail of where it went.
when: when an object is hidden in soft ground
why: depth slows recovery but leaves a findable trail

text: A legitimate commercial enterprise gives a central figure a reason to be present and draws little notice from curious observers.
Blend into a population by adopting a plausible costume, language, stock phrases and routine, so observers read the person as a local rather than an intruder.
when: when passing through a populated area unchallenged

text: A witness's mistaken conclusion is part of the confusion, so a reconstruction should explain it rather than discard it.
when: A witness reached a wrong conclusion about an event.
why: The misreading itself has a cause that the reconstruction can account for.

text: A suspect's attempt to end their own life after arrest may be read as a sign of a secret they are determined to protect, though it is not proof of guilt.
when: When a suspect's conduct after arrest is under consideration
why: People may guard a secret more fiercely than their own life, but this is a generalization without established frequency

text: Ask whether a suspect was often short of money and how often they sought support, since repeated requests reveal ongoing pressure rather than a single debt.
when: Assessing a suspect's financial motive
why: Recurring need signals stronger pressure than one-off debt

text: A witness protecting someone may say less in a group, so a private meeting is often more productive.
Secrecy in disposing of an item suggests the disposal is hard to undo.
when: Reasoning about why a culprit hid or destroyed an object.
why: Hard-to-reverse disposal is what a careful culprit would choose.

text: Destroying or hiding evidence changes what others can know, and the gap can be noticed, becoming a source of suspense and later clues, even when it protects a private matter.
Each cleanup action, such as moving objects, wearing gloves or discarding items, leaves its own physical or contextual trace that an investigator can check.
when: a culprit tries to remove or disorder evidence, or a staged or cleaned scene is designed or analysed
why: Cleanup is itself a physical act; using an incriminating item to wipe creates another clue, and a cloth used to wipe prints carries smudges of its own.

text: Burning or keeping a written note removes the paper trail, so the party holding it can deny or prove a claim depending on what survives.
when: a meeting turns on a written record
why: the surviving document decides who can prove what

text: Burning a message before it reaches its target stops it from arriving, so the recipient never learns its content and the sender's secret is kept.
An NPC dialogue can run in stages: scripted identity lines, a free-form statement, then pressure lines unlocked by stored contradictions the player has found.
when: Designing interrogation-style dialogue for a game NPC
why: Staging controls information flow and rewards players who gather contradictions

text: Fragile seals on doors, windows and objects show whether a space was entered unobserved; an intact seal indicates no entry, a broken one indicates entry.
when: A room is left unwatched and the player must learn whether anything passed through.
why: Each marker changes state only when disturbed, so its condition is a record of entry.

text: Refusal to speak may come from loyalty, shame or fear rather than guilt, so it proves neither wrongdoing nor innocence; treat silence as a motive to probe.
why: A witness may be shielded by a rule or fear.

text: A tidy or ordinary appearance is not proof of an untouched or genuine state, because restoration and staging are built to look natural and leave traces.
when: judging whether an object, document or arranged scene was handled or genuine
why: Restoration and staging target what is visible, so they rarely remove every chemical, sensory or positional trace.

text: Destroying an object removes the chance to recheck it, so destructive examination belongs last.
A concealed view is not necessarily unobserved; the watched party can notice the reflection and react to it.
Overrating your own deception is as dangerous as underrating an opponent; assume they know more than they show and treat easy acceptance with suspicion.
why: an opponent may be letting you win a point on purpose

text: A reconstruction that is too tidy can hide the parts of the record that do not fit.
when: Presenting a neat account of a confusing event.
why: Smoothing over contradictions removes evidence that could overturn the account.

text: Dust and polish depend on storage conditions, and a single fresh item can have other causes; use surface clues to narrow a search rather than conclude from them.
when: Interpreting wear or finish differences
why: Environmental factors and innocent explanations can produce the same surface signs

text: Assuming a clever purpose where none exists leads to over-reading; the purpose must be checked against the possibility that the position was random.
when: Interpreting a moved object's position
why: Not every displacement serves a plan

text: A refusal to give full identity can read as evasion, even when a stated reason is given.
when: a character withholds a name on a form
why: incomplete information invites suspicion

text: Withholding information for too long can frustrate the player and cause them to disengage.
when: Delaying answers in a mystery
why: Players tolerate uncertainty only while they expect resolution.

text: Declining an offer of shelter may reflect social manners rather than suspicion, so refusal alone should not be read as guilt.
when: when a witness refuses an investigator's offer of help
why: Social norms can drive refusal independently of guilt

text: A romantic or sentimental explanation can feel satisfying but fail against facts, so it should be checked before acceptance.
when: Forming a theory about a character's motive.
why: Emotional narratives are persuasive and can override the evidence.

text: A mark left in plain view can be noticed by other characters, so a hidden or less conspicuous placement helps keep the mark useful for the player.
when: A player-placed or world marker is meant to remain private to the player.
why: Visible marks can be spotted and removed or exploited by others.

text: 1) Sew a hanging loop inside the garment. 2) Suspend the object from the loop. 3) Hold its handle through a pocket so it does not swing or show. Concealed carry still ties up the hand and balance.
when: A weapon must be carried through public space unseen.
why: Supporting the object from inside the garment keeps it hidden and frees the hand from holding its weight, though the carrier's body must still support and hide the item at the same time.

text: 1) Remove the top layer first and record each item's position. 2) Sift and record each layer so small clues are not lost. 3) Infer that items higher in a stack were placed later than those beneath them.
when: When hidden evidence is stacked or sealed and placement order matters

text: 1) List each object's claimed role in the event. 2) Check whether it could have been affected by the physical forces claimed. 3) Check whether the object's state fits the order of events claimed. 4) Flag any object that could not have been affected as described.
when: testing whether a scene's details could have happened in the order claimed
why: A single object that cannot match the claimed mechanism can expose the staging.

text: 1) Note deviations from routine, such as an object placed somewhere unusual. 2) Compare the suspect object with a familiar one of the same kind. 3) Test the object physically by handling, twisting, weighing or bending it to reveal hidden contents.
when: A hidden item may be disguised as an ordinary belonging in a familiar place
why: Concealment in common objects works because they are overlooked, so physical testing exposes what looks normal

text: 1) Ask what the guilty party needs to do with an item and why. 2) Visit the location under the crime's conditions. 3) Count realistic hiding places. 4) Rule out places that offer none.
when: Explaining where a concealed object could have gone.
why: Conditions like time of day change what a location actually offers.

text: In poisoning or hidden-ingredient puzzles, let a strong ingredient or drink mask the substance, so players must match taste or residue to the right ingredient.
when: when designing food, drink or potion poisoning puzzles
why: A taste mismatch or residue gives players a checkable, concrete deduction.

text: Protect a witness with layered defences: an outside watch, a fireproof building, a watched and lit hall, a stout gate, and messengers who can summon help.
when: a witness must be guarded against attack
why: each layer covers a failure of another

text: Design the steps of a cleanup so that each one reveals something about the actor's knowledge.
when: Designing concealment in a scene

text: Make a note or item whose destruction changes what other NPCs learn, so that the player's handling of evidence becomes a real choice.
when: Designing evidence items that can be altered or destroyed
why: Consequential choices give players meaningful control over information flow.

text: Let rumours spread between locations in stages, adding detail at each retelling, so players can trace how a rumour grew.
when: when designing rumour propagation

text: Let a convincing trace point toward the wrong suspect, and provide a later check, such as drying time, that lets players correct the reading.
when: designing clue-based mysteries

text: Write hidden-item puzzles as explicit constraints, such as who was present, what could be moved and what went unobserved, so the player can derive the location.
when: Designing a puzzle where the player must find a hidden object.
why: Stated constraints make the answer derivable through reasoning rather than guessing.

text: Make control impressions from a known source using the same technique, so the method's own effects can be separated from the trace.
when: when preparing blood or print samples

text: Give an NPC a reason to conceal a fact that protects a third character, and make that reason discoverable through another clue.
when: Designing a suspect or witness who appears guilty.
why: Players must be able to find the hidden motive to resolve the apparent guilt.

text: Offer a consistency check, such as a careful NPC's usual habits, so attentive players can detect staged evidence.
when: designing planted clues
why: A checkable standard lets players spot fakes

text: Use a gift or item as a misleading lead so the most dramatic thread is not the one that solves the case.
when: designing false leads in a mystery
why: Dramatic threads otherwise tend to reveal the solution too easily.

text: Give players a way to explain or hide sudden wealth, such as a stated source or a hidden stash, so spending becomes a puzzle rather than a sure tell.
when: designing a wealth-based detection system
why: a counter-option keeps the check from being automatic

text: Burned evidence may support only conjecture when the key item is gone, but a destroyed container does not make its contents unknowable; other tests and records can narrow possibilities.
when: When the key item no longer exists.
why: Without the item, its contents cannot be confirmed or refuted, yet other tests can still narrow what it held.

text: Releasing NPC clues in stages gated by trust gives the player control over pacing, but the player must also decide what to keep private and what to share with allies.
when: When designing NPC-held information in a game.
why: Gating information rewards relationship building while forcing secrecy choices.

text: A target bound by good manners feels unable to leave a conversation without seeming rude, so a diversion can keep them in place.
when: when the target is polite and the other party controls the talk
why: Leaving early would break courtesy, so the target stays.

text: Offender profiling infers a likely mind from a crime's precision, pattern and apparent motive, then uses that profile to narrow the suspect group.
when: There is no physical evidence yet and the crime's design hints at a state of mind

text: A first-time offender has no file, no known habits, and no contacts, so records and informers return nothing useful.
when: the culprit has no criminal history
why: Without a past, there is no background to match against.

text: End a deduction puzzle with a journal or summary listing the clues found, how they connect, and the conditions the culprit meets, so the solution feels earned.
when: When a puzzle or mystery level ends with a solution.
why: Showing the chain confirms the player's reasoning.

text: Restrict a suspect pool by local population so a general profile becomes usable.
when: A broad profile is too general to act on
why: Small communities make a general description specific enough to search

text: A recognisable profile, checked against reference data on known dimensions and armament, identifies a known vessel type quickly.
when: when a known type is seen at a distance
why: the profile matches a catalogued type

text: Give NPCs personal histories and quirks that open or close motive paths, and let players uncover them through conversation.
A room whose contents contradict its owner's profile is a clue that may point to another occupant, a staged setting, or an unexpected interest.
when: comparing a room with its owner's known character
why: Possessions normally reflect the person who keeps them.

text: A combat signature can narrow the list of suspects, but a designer should also plant a misleading assumption that only one strong enemy could have acted, to test the player's reasoning.
when: designing an investigation where a combat method points to a suspect class
