why: A narrowing signature gives players a lead, while a decoy assumption checks whether they reason beyond it.

text: Store motive as a discoverable record in the level, leaving positive evidence as the deciding factor.
Make a rare trait of an item, such as an unusual feature of a worn object, the decisive proof linking it to one NPC.
A generator can draw a crime's motif and staging from a library of known templates, then fill in characters and rooms around that motif.
why: templates give a coherent crime structure that can be dressed with new content

text: Give a stranger NPC an unusual entry route and a specific, checkable cover story, such as a tradesman or neighbour with a plausible reason.
when: Designing an unexpected NPC who enters a restricted space.
why: A checkable story lets players test the NPC while the unusual route keeps them curious.

text: Where a delivered item mostly reaches certain groups, the offender probably had direct access to them. This inference is weak when the method is widely available.
why: Broad availability means many people could have used the method.

text: Ask a local specialist to fill gaps that general records cannot, since local variants such as slightly different schedules can change the answer.
when: when reference data leaves a key fact unresolved
why: local knowledge covers variations that general sources omit

text: In a social-deduction setting, NPCs whose choices under stakes reveal consistent tells can be used as evidence of character, provided their scripted outcomes are logged.
when: designing NPC suspects in a table-based deduction minigame
why: Logged reactions to scripted pressure let players compare behaviour against motive.

text: Give each non-player character a timed routine so the player can rebuild a timeline from overheard remarks and visible movements.
when: when designing NPC behavior for a mystery game
why: Routines give players a predictable baseline against which to detect discrepancies.

text: A uniform method across a body, repeated at every cut, points to one operator following one procedure rather than several people acting separately.
when: when the same cut style appears on several parts
why: consistency implies a single practice or plan

text: Rank suspects by who had both knowledge and opportunity, since a long undifferentiated list dilutes attention.
when: A list of suspects has grown large.
why: Filtering on both criteria focuses investigation on the most plausible candidates.

text: An offender's fear or haste shapes choices such as securing a tool, returning to the scene, or leaving items behind, and those choices create the traces left.
when: an offender acts under strong emotion or time pressure
why: state changes what the offender does, and what they do leaves evidence

text: An NPC with a second persona has different dialogue, access rights and routines, revealed when the player notices a mismatch in appearance or timing.
Narrating the crime from the offender's viewpoint reveals his routine, plans and handling of objects to the audience before the investigator arrives.
when: Designing a story where the audience observes the crime
why: Shared offender knowledge lets the audience watch the mechanism operate before consequences appear.

text: Track a character's resolve as a value that rises with shocks and falls without them, and let it decide whether a confession triggers.
when: a confession depends on the character's state

text: Inferring offender type from conduct after arrest assumes a clean split between habitual and first-time offenders, an assumption that is often untested.
when: When using post-arrest behavior to classify a suspect
why: Offender categories may overlap, so the classification may be wrong

text: A dramatic figure or effect can invite a magical explanation that hides a plain human plan, so players may dismiss the simpler solution.
when: when a puzzle centers on a striking figure or effect
why: Visual drama pushes players toward supernatural interpretations

text: Revealing the whole case too early lets a suspect adjust their account before it is tested.
Treating the heir with the most to gain as guilty without checking whether another person had the same access is an error.
when: Building a case around inheritance motive.
why: Motive alone does not establish means and opportunity.

text: Assuming a skilled or crude operator without checking the marks leads to wrong conclusions, since clean cuts and rough cuts each need evidence.
when: when judging the skill behind a physical signature
why: skill must be read from the marks, not assumed from the outcome

text: 1) Decide whether the acts look senseless or precise and planned. 2) Build a psychological model only from established facts and the traits they imply. 3) Hold the model fixed. 4) Test each suspect against it, not shaping the profile to fit a favoured suspect, and check for special pleading.
when: Narrowing suspects by temperament or building a profile from the method used.
why: Fitting a profile to a favoured suspect corrupts the test, as an investigator may bend the method's implications toward them.

text: 1) Describe the method: positions of victim and attacker, aim, choice of target, and how the scene was tidied. 2) Infer the culprit's temperament from it. 3) Eliminate suspects whose known character clashes with that temperament. 4) Check the remaining suspect against physical habits and facts.
when: Narrowing a suspect list from how a crime was carried out
why: Method reveals character, and character filters suspects before factual confirmation

text: 1) Lay out the offender's actions in order. 2) Tie each step to an observable trace. 3) Model the offender's state of mind at each step. 4) Predict the next trace that should exist and where to find it.
when: traces suggest a plausible sequence but the events are not yet confirmed
why: ordered steps tied to traces give investigators concrete places to look

text: 1) List what the object physically demands of its user, such as fit, pressure points, corrective strength and materials. 2) Convert fit into body measurements. 3) Look for signs that demand would leave on the body. 4) Mark each inference's confidence.
when: a single personal item is the only evidence about its owner

text: 1) Identify residue of the act, such as a blank wad. 2) Ask where a person would need to act to avoid being seen or heard. 3) Ask what the act needed in terms of safety and loss prevention. 4) Use the answers to infer the site and the actor.
when: A scene shows signs of a deliberate arrangement and the actor must be identified.
why: A staged act leaves traces of the stager's practical needs.

text: 1) List the opponent's goals and constraints. 2) Identify the option it would find least suspicious. 3) Check that option first, before searching hidden spots.
when: when a puzzle hinges on an intelligent opponent's choice
why: a target is often placed where the opponent expects searchers not to look

text: Give NPC equipment, wear, tan lines, posture, worn hands or old spectacles cues hinting at past occupation, such as soldier, sailor or miner, or at wealth, before any dialogue.
when: writing item, body and NPC descriptions
why: Cues let players infer character from small details.

text: Present each profile marker as a sign narrowing the search, not an identification; never name a suspect on a profile alone, since suspicion without evidence does not justify acting.
why: Each marker alone is only a sign; a list of indicators is not proof.

text: Filter suspects by fixed traits a disguise cannot change, such as height, build, scars or teeth, and give disguisable NPCs flexible traits such as hair or hats.
when: Designing an NPC that can appear in disguise.
why: Players can only identify a disguised character if some features persist across appearances.

text: Plant convincing false suspects, such as a hostile NPC with a personal motive or one with an innocent explanation, and reward players who verify rather than confront or accuse.
when: designing suspects who look guilty
why: Tests patience and judgement rather than reflex; verification rewards investigation over premature accusation.

text: Make a culprit's post-event actions and choices, such as cleaning a weapon, relocking a door or avoiding one object but using another, checkable against the scene and included in reconstructions.
when: When designing evidence of a culprit's actions.
why: Checkable traces let players reason about how a rational criminal would act.

text: Give antagonist traps, enemy behavior and NPC crimes a consistent style from a stable trait profile, so players can infer the faction, personality or author behind them.
when: When designing crimes committed by NPCs or enemy traps.
why: Consistent traits make a crime's style recognizable.

text: Use a culprit profile as a checklist for non-player suspects, testing each suspect's behaviour against it.
Build timed NPC events, such as guard rotations, so the player must compute whether a route or claimed location is physically possible.
when: When designing NPC schedules that players can verify
why: Timing constraints turn NPC claims into a checkable deduction

text: Give an NPC who heard nothing a stated sleep or distraction trait that players can verify.
Design a fixated guard or detective NPC so the player has a test to check that suspicion, such as a trace check or a distance check on a witness.
when: an NPC focuses on one suspect
why: Giving the player a test lets them verify or refute the NPC's conclusion.

text: When a scene search finds nothing, reason from a known offender's habits and methods, and question them or their associates rather than searching walls further.
when: A scene has been searched without result and the offender has a recognizable style
why: Habits point toward the person, while building searches follow old stories

text: Give NPCs personalities that colour their dialogue, such as a grumbler who volunteers useful timestamps, so players must read tone as well as content.
Give first-time culprits only scene evidence, so players must read the room rather than match a known pattern.
when: designing culprits with no history
why: Without habits to match, the scene is the only route to the answer.

text: Let an NPC's public speech and private letter disagree, and treat the gap as a clue to the NPC's real aim.
Let players deduce an NPC's motive from behaviour before the full plot is revealed, so the reveal confirms a suspicion.
why: Earlier deduction makes later confirmation rewarding

text: Store each character's known events as data, so a dialogue can be flagged as true yet incomplete when it skips an event that character knows.
when: when generating or validating dialogue
why: Tracked knowledge lets a system detect omissions automatically.

text: Before placing a proposed culprit at a scene, check that they could physically reach it under the level's own constraints.
when: A generator places characters who must reach a scene.

text: Give culprits a model of what the player is expected to find; a missed item should be an explainable exception the system can account for.
when: when generating hidden items or evidence for culprit NPCs

text: Give a quest ending a choice to keep or release evidence, with consequences for NPCs who depend on the secret.
Give culprits one distinctive feature, such as a ring or limp, so they can be separated from lookalike characters.
Structure a culprit-finding puzzle around independent conditions such as room access, device knowledge, tool skill and item possession, each checkable through in-game evidence.
Give a meticulous or short-sighted character a higher chance to notice fine details, so the search mechanic has a clear personality.
when: Designing character traits that affect searching.

text: Give each NPC a personality-based chance to react to provocation, such as raising an alarm, so players can plan around it.
Give each NPC a want, a fear and a loyalty, and use them to predict its actions and decide which clues it reveals or hides.
Let NPCs have reasons to accuse others to protect themselves, so accusation effects can chain across a settlement.
Profiles built from document conditions narrow suspects fast but may fit several people or be faked; treat them as provisional hypotheses, confirmed by physical, factual and disguise checks.
when: Choosing between profile reasoning and factual checks, or drawing a broad conclusion from a suspect's profile.
why: Profiles are fast but can match several people, while facts identify one; some traits can be faked more easily than expected, so a broad inference can mislead.

text: Listing every beneficiary with gain widens the puzzle with several motive-bearing suspects, while a short beneficiary list keeps the pool manageable though motive stays common.
when: generating a murder mystery or designing a murder scenario's suspect pool
why: Several motive-bearing suspects widen the puzzle; a short, manageable list keeps the investigation focused.

text: Explicit NPC trait tables let dialogue claims that contradict stated traits be flagged, so players can catch lies without a hard fact; tables should be written independently of designer assumptions.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that players must evaluate.
why: Behaviour then follows the data rather than designer expectations.

text: A partner who follows orders without understanding is easy to control but may misreport what was seen; a perceptive partner reports accurately but may challenge the player.
Narrowing candidates by assumed constraints or profile traits can exclude the true answer before evidence is checked; an all-or-nothing deduction is only as reliable as its profile.
when: eliminating candidate explanations from constraints or building a culprit profile
why: An incorrect assumption removes options that should have stayed open.

text: Establish clear routines, such as cleaner schedules or guard rounds, and a standard procedure, so deviations are recognisable and players can rule out explanations logically.
when: designing scenes where an alternative explanation is possible or a routine players can learn
why: Known routines turn exclusion into a checkable deduction; deviations read as meaningful only against a known sequence

text: A calculated, self-interested culprit may see the victim as a risk to remove rather than a person to hate, so the motive can be cool rather than emotional.
when: when reading or writing a planned act

text: Several independent matching clues that agree with one another raise confidence far more than each clue adds alone, while a common trait adds little.
when: Identifying a person or object from multiple details.
why: Each further matching detail multiplies the support of the others rather than adding a small increment.

text: Players who doubt a deduction often claim there is no positive evidence; restating the basis precisely usually makes the supporting facts visible.
when: A player rejects a conclusion as unsupported.
why: Evidence is easy to overlook until the reasoning's starting point is stated clearly.

text: An objection to a search can come from pride, insult or vanity rather than guilt, so the reason behind each objection matters.
when: when someone resists an inspection or search
why: people object for social reasons as well as to hide things

text: Vague doubt that does not commit to a testable claim does not advance an investigation; ideas must be tested, not merely accepted or rejected.
when: A player or character voices uncertainty about a theory.
why: Unfocused skepticism produces no new information.

text: Investigators tend to accept a substitution explanation over admitting an event is unexplained, so records shape their conclusions.
when: An escape or event lacks a clear cause
why: A neat explanation is preferred to uncertainty

text: Small illogical details are easily dismissed when many other contradictions are present, so players often miss them.
when: when a scene contains many conflicting clues
why: Attention is spread across many contradictions, so a single odd detail goes unnoticed.

text: Experts can overlook an obvious principle because it seems too simple to apply to a specific case.
when: when a case looks too complex for a basic explanation
why: simplicity seems beneath the problem

text: Players and characters judge a fact by what it can prove, not by how interesting it is; an unrelated line of questioning is usually set aside once its bearing on the central facts is questioned.
when: when a line of inquiry drifts from the central facts
why: relevance is judged by evidential bearing on the outcome

text: Players and observers who learn a regular routine notice a person who breaks it, and the deviation becomes a salient clue.
when: A place or NPC follows a routine that others can observe.
why: A known baseline makes departures from it stand out.

text: A straw man is a suspect built to be knocked down, so that later progress looks like real advance.
Backward (analytic) reasoning starts from a known result and reconstructs the events that produced it, while forward (synthetic) reasoning predicts results from known causes.
when: Investigating a known outcome such as a body or scene
why: Reversing the direction clarifies which causes fit the result

text: A departure is the starting point a solver needs before forming any hypothesis; without one, reasoning about an unexplained object cannot begin.
A closed crime is committed within a known circle of people; an open crime could have been committed by almost anyone.
when: Defining who could be the culprit in a mystery.
why: The size of the suspect pool changes how the case is reasoned.

text: Deduction supports suspicion, but proof requires physical evidence that can be presented to an authority; reasoning alone can be dismantled by a challenge.
A clue pointing to one person narrows the inquiry to that person and to others with access to the same source; it does not settle who is guilty.
In a closed setting every entry and exit route can be listed, so questions about who could come or go become checkable.
Not every noticed detail is a clue; judge it against the whole case before acting, and treat odd details as meaningful only when the theory gives reason to expect them.
why: Unexplained details can be noise rather than evidence.

text: Do not treat the suspect list as closed; ask who knew where an object was kept, since the first answer often omits outsiders who knew the secret.
when: several people might know a hiding place
why: Knowledge can leak to people who were never considered, so an unlisted outsider can go unnoticed.

text: Test the opposite explanation when one account fits neatly, since a fully closed chain of evidence can be staged to look probable.
when: one explanation fits the evidence neatly and no alternative has been examined
why: Staged accounts are designed to look probable, so plausibility alone rewards the deceiver; a perfectly closed set of alternatives may have been engineered.

text: Backward reasoning suits a known result needing its cause, while forward reasoning is more useful in ordinary situations.
when: Choosing a reasoning direction
why: Each direction fits different problems

text: After repeated checks find nothing, clear that character and redirect suspicion to another actor.
when: Repeated surprise checks produce no detectable wrongdoing
why: Keeps the player's suspicion from locking onto an innocent party

text: A search result that clears the obvious suspect can move the player's focus to another location or person.
when: Designing the progression of a mystery
why: Clearing the expected answer forces the player to reconsider

text: Treat everyone who has access as a suspect, however remote or trusted, so that no one is excluded by affection or habit.
Deduce an unknown fact from known facts step by step, as in solving for an unknown quantity.
when: when an investigation has partial information
why: Working from established facts keeps each conclusion checkable.

text: Clearing one suspect does not close the wider mystery, since the true actor may still be unknown.
when: a suspect is cleared but the puzzle continues
why: clearance removes one person, not the question

text: A case built from many facts pointing one way can collapse when one fact the suspect could not have done points elsewhere; treat that single mismatch as a break in the chain.
when: many facts lean one way and one fits only a different person
why: a single impossible act can invalidate an otherwise matching chain of evidence

text: When deciding which of two people was in a place at a given time, small traces often separate them more decisively than large, obvious clues.
when: Two possible people could have been in the same place.
why: Minor details tied to one person or place can break a tie that broader evidence cannot.

text: When a detail confirms a suspicion, ask one more question before moving on to the next line of inquiry.
Have a second party confirm a disclosed motive; once confirmed, the investigator can shift from pursuit to pardon in a single exchange.
when: a motive is revealed by an interested party
why: Independent confirmation makes the account trustworthy.

text: The outcome depends on the sum of evidence and mitigating facts, not on a confession alone.
when: resolving a case with several strands of proof
why: confessions are weighed alongside other proof

text: In a small, closed community with few people present, the list of possible culprits is short, so narrow suspects by checking each person's access and timing.
when: an accusation rests on a small group of possible people
why: isolation limits who could have acted

text: A suspect can be cleared when direct evidence is absent and an independent witness account does not fit them.
Do not dismiss a witness only because a detail seems odd; an unlikely detail is not automatically false and needs a physical test first.
when: When a witness's claim seems unusual.
why: Strange-seeming facts can be true, so they require checking rather than rejection.

text: Avoid too many suspects with equal weight, since an even spread dilutes the trail.
when: planning a mystery's cast
why: equal weighting makes it hard to follow any single lead

text: A clue's value depends on distinctiveness: a common item fits many owners, while a unique mark identifies one.
Give each culprit a defined set of facts, such as door codes or guard schedules, so players narrow suspects by which facts each could know.
Assume a careful suspect has rehearsed an alibi and test it against independent checks rather than accepting it.
Use the victim's profession to rule out missing items that someone in that role would be unlikely to carry.
when: Several items could have been taken
why: A victim's routine determines what they would normally carry

text: Ask who in a household shares an activity, since a shared activity narrows the pool of suspects.
Compare each small object against its expected context; an item that does not fit suggests a second object or a second person.
Handle accused people with previously unblemished reputations with extra care, because a sudden accusation damages them most.
Use elimination when the set of possible agents is small and known; when the set is large or unknown, exclusion proves little.
when: Choosing whether elimination can settle a cause.
why: Eliminating from a large unknown set leaves too many possibilities to rule out.

text: Let players filter a suspect list by scene-derived markers, and make profile items checkable through testimony so an accurate profile unlocks the correct suspect.
Present several candidate explanations with their supporting clues so the player can judge which fits the full set of evidence.
when: Designing a deduction or mystery interface
why: Players reason better when they can compare candidates against the same evidence

text: If an act targets a suspicion held by only one person, the actor must know that suspicion exists.
When no regular option fits a required time, the remaining option is likely a special one.
when: when known schedules constrain the options
why: regular options are ruled out by their timetables

text: Test whether a companion of the suspect could be the real actor, and require evidence before accepting that alternative.
when: A suspect has associates who had access to the scene
why: Accomplices or companions can be the true actors and are easy to overlook

text: A regularity can be recorded and used before its cause is understood, so players and designers can act on a pattern without knowing the mechanism behind it.
why: Noticing a pattern does not require explaining it.

text: Make the player's first interpretation of a scene plausible, then correct it with a visible clue such as a changed view or shifted object.
Before assuming a room is empty or private, check each person present, since an unnoticed occupant may have heard everything.
when: a conversation takes place in a room

text: A quest can restrict the player's knowledge to what an NPC reveals, then use a debrief scene to explain the full plan after completion.
When a barrier's resistance to forcing is offered as proof of strength, first consider whether its material is weak or cheap.
When a sealed space seems to forbid entry or exit, question the premise that something is wholly inside or wholly outside.
Let players gather terrain knowledge under safe conditions earlier, so they can recognise a decoy guide later.
why: earlier surveys give a baseline for spotting false signs

text: Compare a space with your memory of it and note anything out of its usual place or angle, since small displacements reveal recent activity.
when: a room looks untouched but may have been searched

text: Do not assume a locked room is impossible to enter; first look for a shared key or an open door.
when: when a locked space seems inaccessible
why: Locks often share keys or have unsecured entries

text: Give a prominent clue at least one plausible rival explanation that the player can build from other clues.
when: designing a crime or mystery scene

text: Physical arrangement, such as body position or the state of a latch, can rule out explanations that would leave different traces.
when: Testing whether an explanation fits the scene.
why: Each possible cause produces a characteristic physical state that can be checked.

text: Rule out ordinary explanations one at a time before accepting an unusual cause, using a specific test whose outcome is a clear yes or no.
when: player must choose between a natural and an unusual cause

text: Do not infer intent from every irregular act, since some deviations from a routine are harmless.
when: Interpreting an observed deviation from a routine.
why: Many breaks from routine have ordinary causes.

text: A sequence of confirmations, each narrowing the suspect pool, lets the audience follow the logic and makes the later reversal feel earned.
Each reappearance of a cryptic phrase that adds a detail, such as a count or a time, narrows the phrase from vague to a specific place or moment.
when: a riddle is spread across several documents
why: incremental detail constrains the set of possible meanings

text: When a sealed-room claim is disproved, the suspect pool widens to everyone with access through any adjoining room.
Each new name produced by an unverifiable witness widens the suspect group, spreading suspicion to people with no other link to the case.
A suspect board can close options as contradicting evidence is found, leaving one suspect who is provably the only remaining option.
A deduction board lets players assemble clues into a theory, and the system then reports which items remain unexplained.
A search by description returns several candidates, and each stable trait found removes others, so the field narrows only as stable traits are discovered.
when: Players search for a character from a partial description

text: The order in which evidence reaches an observer shapes their conclusions; someone who perceives the scene before learning identities and stories forms impressions from the senses alone.
when: When evaluating how a character or player interprets an unfolding scene
why: Early information frames later interpretation, so sequence controls which conclusions feel natural.

text: Physical evidence exceeding a cover's stated purpose, such as machinery far too powerful for the claimed work, exposes the false cover to a careful observer.
A single constraint may match dozens of entries in a large table; several constraints together are needed to narrow the candidates to a few.
when: when searching a large reference table
why: one shared property rarely identifies a unique entry

text: Hindsight makes deductions look trivial: audiences are surprised before reasoning is shown, then find it obvious. Test each link; show the sign and its meaning so reasoning keeps its credit.
when: a deduction is revealed to an audience or a solved explanation is reviewed
why: Each step looks obvious only after it is stated, and knowing the outcome biases perception of the path.

text: A clue that only the investigator understands can seem like a trick to the audience, so the reasoning behind it must be explained step by step.
when: A deduction depends on a reference the audience does not yet know.
why: Unexplained reasoning reads as arbitrary, so the audience does not accept the conclusion.

text: Layered deduction collapses if any figure is wrong or unsourced; it holds only when each number comes from an independent source the reader can check.
Each route deduction rests on assumptions, such as no side openings and shortest-route travel; test them before trusting the conclusion.
A list can make answers look settled when its candidate answers are only guesses.
Explaining the reasoning only after the event works for a reveal but leaves the audience uncertain during the scene.
A crowd tends to assume the strongest person is responsible when a crime seems to need extreme strength, and such extreme methods can mislead.
when: a crime's method appears to require unusual physical power
why: Assuming an extreme method points to an extreme person skips testing whether ordinary people could have done it.

text: Reading behaviour from a trace requires knowing how the act is normally performed; without that baseline, a staged trace can mislead in either direction.
when: the observer is unfamiliar with the activity

text: Clearing one suspect can open a second false lead, so the investigation may keep chasing decoys.
when: When suspects are eliminated one at a time
why: Each cleared lead can point toward another plausible but wrong suspect

text: Accepting an informant's theory because it fits the observed pattern makes the theory look more credible than its evidence supports.
when: An informant's account matches a pattern
why: Fit with the pattern is not independent evidence for the account.

text: A questioner's inference can be accepted by a witness who would not have reached it alone, so recovered details may be suggestion rather than memory.
when: When asking a witness to agree with a proposed inference.
why: Agreement is easier to give than independent recall.

text: Clearing an alibi can remove a witness who might have been useful later, especially if the investigator promised to keep them out of the case.
when: Clearing a witness's alibi.
why: A cleared person may still hold information of value.

text: Judging a person by one shelf is an error, since gifts, shared possessions, or unusual collecting can explain a mismatch.
when: a collection seems out of character
why: Ordinary explanations for odd possessions are common.

text: Starting from an object instead of asking why it was chosen can send an investigation the wrong way.
when: Investigating a crime built around a chosen item.
why: The choice of object often reveals the culprit's intent more than the object does.

text: Reading a new death through an old, similar one can push an investigation toward suspicion that the evidence does not support.
Assuming an offender thinks like an expert, or that high rank shields him from suspicion, can lead investigators to misjudge the culprit.
when: Building a profile of a skilled, careful criminal.

text: A valid syllogism can still be worthless when its premises already contain the conclusion, since its first step assumes the very point it claims to prove.
why: Analysing the same assumption again creates no new evidence.

text: The same calm can be read as a hardened criminal's habit or as concealed feeling, so one observation can support opposite conclusions.
An investigator who traces every strange event to one hidden source will over-read coincidence; accepting only what plain facts support counters this.
Stretching one innocent explanation to cover several incriminating items weakens the review, since each item needs its own support.
when: Building counter-explanations for a multi-item evidence list
why: A single explanation rarely fits unrelated facts

text: Using only physical evidence or only psychological inference undervalues one kind of reasoning; the two must be combined to reach reliable conclusions.
when: An investigation relies heavily on one type of reasoning
why: Each kind of reasoning covers gaps the other leaves

text: Assuming a room is the one expected from its position can send an investigator to the wrong place.
A problem stated too broadly can hide which goal should be pursued first.
when: Restating an investigation with several goals bundled together.
why: Bundled goals obscure priorities and which obstacle blocks progress.

text: Precedent matching fails when the method is new and no reference case covers it, so the theory cannot be checked this way.
when: when an investigation involves an unprecedented method
why: No documented case exists to compare against.

text: A person seen with others at one moment may still have had time to act alone, so an apparent alibi can be partial rather than complete.
when: Evaluating an alibi that covers only part of the timeline

text: Missing parts block any conclusion that depends on them, such as cause of death, and an absent feature cannot be read as proof it never existed.
when: when reasoning from incomplete remains
why: the missing part may hold the decisive evidence

text: 1) Examine each object for features and traces: maker, wear, dust, stains, smells, residue, missing parts, fittings, bulges. 2) Check each fact is specific and countable. 3) State each inference and its basis, marking certainty. 4) Infer height from where debris landed, then combine into a profile of build, age and habits.
when: the suspect is absent and objects or the scene are the only evidence about a person
why: Stating each basis lets inferences be checked, since objects carry traces of their users; showing facts before conclusions makes inference checkable.

text: 1) List every possible explanation or candidate cause. 2) Remove each one the known facts or scene rule out. 3) Treat the remaining one as the answer and check it against the evidence.
when: the possibilities can be listed and tested against known facts, such as when designing a puzzle with several plausible answers
why: Elimination narrows many options to the one the facts allow; players solve by elimination rather than guessing.

text: 1) Define the finite candidate roster, such as a manifest or participant list. 2) Eliminate candidates who cannot match each known attribute, such as physical profile. 3) Continue until one candidate remains. 4) Write each step so others can check it.
when: a finite roster of candidates is known and a suspect must be identified from a partial description or physical profile
why: A physical profile removes candidates systematically, and written sequential filtering narrows the pool to a checkable few.

text: 1) Collect partial facts from separate sources. 2) Combine them into a total or pattern. 3) Compare the result against the claim it may contradict.
when: Checking a partner's or suspect's claim about money, quantities or events
why: A sum of independent figures can expose a lie that no single figure reveals

text: 1) List the actions the crime required. 2) For each suspect, ask whether they could have done it without help. 3) Clear those who could not have acted alone and look for a third party who completes the set.
when: Several suspects each have partial access to the means of a crime.
why: A suspect who did not need an accomplice is unlikely to have sought one, so the logic points toward who must have assisted.

text: 1) List plausible candidates the witness might fear. 2) Name each one and watch the reaction. 3) Treat visible relief as a sign that person is not the feared one. 4) Ask about related traits to narrow further.
when: when a witness withholds a name but the questioner can list candidates
why: Reactions to each name rule possibilities in or out without the witness naming anyone.

text: 1) List candidates. 2) Exclude each one that observed physical facts rule out. 3) Explain the remaining facts with motive. 4) Check that explanation against all earlier evidence. 5) Obtain a test that confirms it.
when: a short list of candidates can each be checked against physical facts
why: exclusion narrows the answer, and motive and tests confirm it

text: 1) Collect every instance of the recurring token. 2) Match each token to physical objects tied to the incidents. 3) Link events only when the physical match holds, not memory alone.
when: a recurring mark appears across incidents

text: 1) Locate the traces using light that makes them visible. 2) Compare depth and direction of each set. 3) Combine with other facts such as load and timing. 4) State the conclusion with its supporting facts.
when: A vehicle or group has left a scene and tracks are the main trace
why: Combining independent facts supports a conclusion more reliably than track depth alone.

text: 1) List who knew of the task. 2) List who visited the location. 3) List who knew its layout. 4) Intersect the lists to narrow who could have acted.
when: An action must be traced to one of several people
why: Each condition removes suspects who could not have acted

text: 1) Start from one physical trace. 2) Ask what routine would leave it. 3) Link that routine to a habit, then to a person. 4) Connect the person to a recent statement or fact to reach a conclusion.
why: Each link is simple but depends on the one before

text: 1) Read a general trait from the trace. 2) Match the trait to a group, such as a trade. 3) Match the group to a known roster. 4) Find the one member who fits the remaining facts.
when: A culprit must be found from traces alone.
why: Each step narrows the field until a single person remains.

text: 1) Name the object or mechanism a theory implicates. 2) Inspect that object directly. 3) Compare its condition with the trace the theory predicts. 4) Accept the theory only if they match.
when: a theory names a specific object or mechanism
why: a physical match tests a claim faster than argument

text: 1) Establish what the person could physically reach 2) Check whether reaching the observed point would leave a mark 3) Eliminate the person if no mark or route exists.
when: Clearing a suspect who might have acted
why: Access and physical traces can rule out a person without a confession

text: 1) Test each suspect's alibi against a timeline. 2) Check whether one person could have caused the harm alone. 3) Check whether the suspect could obtain the instrument used.
when: filtering suspects in a mystery
why: timing, physical capability and access each exclude people

text: 1) State one undisputed fact narrowly. 2) List everyone who could have had access to the means that produced it. 3) Record each candidate's presence during the relevant window. 4) Mark each candidate against the facts. 5) Identify the candidate who had reason to be present but is unsuspected.
1) Note which object a suspect consulted. 2) Ask what purpose the consultation serves. 3) Propose a specific plan. 4) Verify the plan against the fixed schedule.
when: a suspect's attention reveals an intended movement on a fixed schedule
why: Checking the prediction against known facts makes it trustworthy.

text: 1) Compare accounts of one person from observers who saw different settings, such as work and home. 2) Treat sudden mood shifts or neglected routines as clues and ask their cause. 3) Note unusual requests and ask who handled them and what was said. 4) Check whether an action was hidden from normal confidants, and ask why.
1) Deduce from the facts that a clue must exist. 2) Predict where it would sit. 3) Direct a search there to confirm the deduction.
1) List each suspect's facts that incriminate. 2) List facts that clear them. 3) Weigh each item. 4) Test each suspect's account against independent facts.
when: when several suspects have mixed evidence
why: first impressions can mislead

text: 1) List everyone present when the crime was found. 2) Remove anyone who could not have acted unnoticed. 3) Remove anyone without knowledge of the key object. 4) Remove anyone lacking the needed skill. 5) Remove anyone who could not have reached the item in time. 6) Restate all conditions for the survivor.
when: several suspects share similar motives and physical clues must decide the matter
why: each condition removes candidates until a few remain

text: Build motive by chaining discovered facts, such as a secret marriage, a same-day announcement, a stormy confrontation, and a changed will, checking each link.
when: when assembling a case against a suspect
why: A chain of connected facts is stronger than any single fact.

text: 1) Match each physical trace to an item belonging to the suspect. 2) Check each link for an alternative cause. 3) Accept the suspect only if every link holds.
when: Physical traces in a confined space are compared with a suspect's belongings
why: Each link can be explained by another cause, so every step needs testing.

text: 1) Ask one question. 2) Confirm and mark the answer. 3) Ask the next only after the previous link is confirmed. 4) Summarise confirmed links. Close every gap before concluding, even if checks seem odd to others.
when: facts must be confirmed in order when building a multi-step explanation
why: one missing link breaks the entire chain of reasoning

text: 1) List the obvious alternative suspects or candidates. 2) Test each against access, character fit, physical capacity and any real link to the motive. 3) Discard each with a stated reason. 4) Confirm the last remaining candidate before accepting it.
when: initial evidence leaves several candidate explanations or the suspect list is short
why: Eliminating candidates on explicit grounds makes the final choice traceable; checking facts rather than instinct narrows the candidates

text: 1) List every possible route or place the object could have taken or be. 2) Test each against established facts or evidence. 3) Reject those that conflict. 4) Treat the single survivor as the answer once the list is confirmed complete.
when: a case seems unsolvable and the possibilities are finite and checkable
why: Elimination only yields the answer if no candidate is missing; fact-based elimination narrows the solution

text: 1) Write each assumption the current theory depends on, numbered. 2) Verify each with the simplest available source, including evidence never requested. 3) Drop or revise any failing premise and recheck every conclusion built on it.
when: A theory resists clues, an investigation stalls on one suspect, or before accepting a motive, alibi or timeline.
why: Stalls and tidy arguments often rest on an untested premise, and one false premise invalidates the whole chain.

text: 1) Give each suspect one test at a time. 2) Clear or hold each name. 3) Repeat until only the guilty remain. Partial coverage is not enough; any incomplete check leaves a suspect unexcluded and can derail the case.
when: A long crowd of suspects must be filtered using documentary and physical checks
why: A long list is hard to clear, and a gap in the search leaves a suspect unexcluded

text: 1) List every route into and out of the sealed location. 2) Give evidence ruling out each, checked against timing. 3) Leave at least one route standing, or admit an unknown method remains. Too many rejections frustrate players.
when: designing an impossible-access mystery
why: players test each candidate against evidence and accept the answer as fair only if every rejection holds

text: 1) List every condition the solution must satisfy, including minor details. 2) Propose a candidate answer. 3) Test it against all conditions. 4) Discard it if any condition fails.
when: when an official explanation leaves loose ends
why: One unexplained contradiction is enough to reject an answer.

text: 1) List who could physically have been at the scene at the event time. 2) Remove those with a verified alibi. 3) Check motive for the remaining people.
when: building a suspect list
why: Opportunity narrows the field before motive is weighed

text: 1) Pull a trade directory. 2) Filter it by trades that would plausibly use the vehicle or resource described. 3) Contact the candidates privately.
when: a new candidate pool is needed
why: filtering by plausible users keeps the pool manageable

text: 1) List the facts a crime depended on: who was present, who was absent, where the victim was, and the room layout. 2) Mark which facts an outsider could not know without leaving a trace. 3) Keep only suspects who could have known those facts.
when: when the crime's method shows precise local knowledge
why: the people who could know such facts are usually far fewer than those who could physically be there

text: 1) Check the collection for signs of use. 2) List its subjects, authors, and condition. 3) Compare the list with the owner's known interests. 4) Treat each unexplained gap as a question. 5) Record findings in writing, then ask the owner and others in the room.
when: a room's contents seem to belong to someone other than its attributed owner
why: A written comparison exposes gaps that a glance misses.

text: 1) List suspects who were dropped earlier. 2) List those never examined. 3) Test each against new facts.
when: a suspect list has stalled and new information has arrived
why: Earlier dismissals may no longer hold once new facts appear.

text: 1) Form a provisional inference from a sound or object. 2) Check it against the next piece of evidence. 3) Keep the conclusion provisional until a later detail confirms or contradicts it.
when: A puzzle should reward reasoning from indirect evidence rather than from direct statements.

text: 1) List each object and mark in the scene. 2) For each, ask who used it and for how long. 3) Ask what the arrangement was meant to show.

1) Examine construction: tool marks, timber density, ceiling height and the source of foundation stone. 2) Read the grounds for earthworks and old paths. 3) Compare with period surveys and plans. 4) Check deed and record wording for the named occupant.

1) Establish the observed effect and a reliable baseline of the prior state. 2) List the agents present. 3) Exclude each agent the evidence rules out. 4) Accept the remaining cause, noting that the list may be incomplete.
when: Tracing an effect with no visible cause and a short list of possible agents.
why: Elimination only works from an accurate baseline and a complete list of candidates.

text: 1) Pick a scene item. 2) Place matching items in a suspect's inventory. 3) Present each match in sequence, each plausible alone but damning together. 4) Add a common-item decoy.
when: when designing a deduction puzzle
why: Decoys force the player to judge distinctiveness.

text: 1) List the possible methods of the act. 2) Rule out each method that the traces contradict. 3) Treat the remaining options as the question still to answer.
when: several methods could explain an act

text: 1) Write the traits the culprit must have. 2) Apply each trait in order to the suspect list. 3) Keep only the suspects who satisfy every trait.
when: Many suspects and a clear chain linking the crime to specific traits
why: Each trait removes candidates, shrinking the list to survivors

text: 1) For each clue, ask what it rules in or out. 2) Apply the constraints one at a time to the candidate list. 3) Check the final candidate against every original clue.
when: when the search space is large and clues are cryptic
why: each clue removes a class of candidates

text: 1) Identify each person with motive, means and opportunity. 2) Check whether each person's conduct has another explanation. 3) Rank suspects by how many factors they meet and how unexplained their conduct is.
when: Direct evidence is missing and suspects must be ranked.
why: Circumstantial evidence can rank suspects when direct proof is absent.

text: 1) List every possible suspect. 2) Sort each into columns for means, motive and opportunity. 3) Mark uncertain entries with a query instead of deleting them. 4) Rank suspects with all three flags first, two flags second.
when: Many people had contact with a victim and the method limits who could act
why: A structured grid exposes gaps and forces each suspect to justify their place

text: 1) Name the ordinary principle that could cause the outcome. 2) Predict how quickly the effect follows and what visible signs it leaves. 3) Predict the traces that should remain. 4) Search for those traces.
when: when an outcome seems natural but circumstances suggest a deliberate method
why: a known principle can explain the case when experts overlook it

text: 1) Map the space of possible routes or answers. 2) Partition it into regions. 3) Test each region against a physical or logical constraint. 4) Dismiss a region only with a stated reason. 5) Repeat until one candidate remains.
when: The solution space is large and each region has a checkable constraint
why: Dismissals resting on stated constraints keep the elimination verifiable rather than based on preference

text: 1) Identify a measurable physical limit, such as height or reach, from the scene geometry. 2) Check which suspects can meet it. 3) Exclude those who cannot. 4) Inspect the remaining suspects' own objects to confirm.

1) List everyone who could have been in the space and time, including the culprit. 2) Compare the list with people actually seen together. 3) Clear any candidate seen alongside the culprit at the same moment. 4) Treat the remaining candidate as a hypothesis until physical proof confirms it.
when: The suspect set is small and the timeline is well recorded
why: Sightings at the same moment can rule out people and expose the hidden one

text: 1) Identify who had access to the target. 2) Check which of those suspects had the means to act. 3) Establish what evidence would settle the question, and weigh each suspect's initial likelihood before deciding.
when: Several suspects share a motive or a clue links to more than one person.
why: Separating access from means and proof keeps the case from closing on a single clue.

text: 1) List candidate objects. 2) For each, ask what trace it would leave. 3) Eliminate candidates whose trace does not match. 4) Keep the candidate whose trace fits best.
when: when several objects could have caused an injury
why: reasoning from expected traces narrows the cause

text: 1) Note details that contradict the stated purpose. 2) Build a timeline from physical limits. 3) Test the working theory against the clock. 4) Revise the theory as each new fact arrives.
when: Inferring where a suspect is really going

text: 1) List every access point to the restricted place or item. 2) For each, identify who held the means of access. 3) Check whether those holders kept that means on the relevant night.
when: an unauthorized entry or removal must be explained
why: Testing each access point rules people in or out by custody

text: 1) List each victim's condition at the time. 2) Find the state all victims share. 3) Infer methods that would work only on someone in that state. 4) Eliminate methods whose expected traces are absent.
when: when the method of harm is unknown but victims share a state
why: the shared state narrows which methods are possible

text: 1) Pick the least unlikely alternative from what is known about who is connected to the affair. 2) Give that person a motive that would explain the crime and justify framing the accused. 3) Build a step-by-step sequence of entry, means and planting of evidence that fits known facts. 4) List every condition the sequence requires, such as presence at places and dates. 5) Test the first condition, since the theory stands or falls on it.
when: when the accused's innocence depends on showing someone else could have committed the crime
why: A concrete set of checkable requirements turns vague suspicion into testable claims.

text: 1) Check each suspect's clothing against the outfit the item's carrier must have worn. 2) Test physical fit against the item's size. 3) Test access to plausible hiding places. 4) Search suspects' property for substitutes.
when: A suspect list is long and each suspect can be tested against one physical or logistical condition.
why: Each test removes candidates that fail a condition.

text: 1) Establish whether the witness stayed in one room throughout. 2) Collect each household member's movements and cross-check them. 3) Compare every other room with its earlier state. 4) Confirm each unchanged room, so the change is narrowed to the rooms left.
when: a set of connected rooms must be searched for who could have entered
why: Eliminating verified rooms bounds the set of possible entry points.

text: 1) Forbid anyone to leave. 2) Check each person's presence. 3) Require a list of absent people with their reasons. Together these account for everyone on site.
when: when a set of possible suspects must be accounted for

text: 1) List every impossible-looking element in a level. 2) Confirm each has a fair answer placed somewhere in the level. 3) Check that the constraints allow the intended solving order.
when: Designing a puzzle-driven level
why: Unresolved impossibilities frustrate players, and ordering tests solvability.

text: 1) Identify who entered the space. 2) Identify who was sent out. 3) Identify what was interrupted. Use the results to build the sequence of events.
when: reconstructing who touched what in a disturbed scene

text: 1) Describe the victim's condition. 2) Identify what method would produce that condition. 3) Work backward to when and how that method had to be applied. 4) Test each step as a separate numbered claim.
when: A crime's method seems to need an unlikely ability or circumstance.
why: The victim's state often reveals an earlier action.

text: 1) Fix a starting premise firmly. 2) Extend it one step at a time. 3) Test each new observation against the bounded set of what is already established before accepting it.
when: Working out a solution from incomplete evidence.
why: Building from a firm premise keeps conclusions consistent and blocks shallow guesses.

text: 1) Fix known hard facts such as date and time window. 2) Apply a physical constraint such as tide height. 3) Eliminate candidates that fail distance, direction or timetable checks. 4) Keep the result provisional.
when: when a time and place must be inferred from scattered clues
why: combining hard constraints shrinks the candidates until few remain

text: 1) Frame each possible explanation as a separate heading. 2) Record why it fails and why it might hold. 3) Use physical arrangement to rule options in or out. 4) Weigh the remaining options and state the result as provisional.
when: Organizing scattered observations into candidate explanations.
why: Separating hypotheses and recording evidence for and against prevents a favoured theory from hiding contrary facts.

text: 1) Note an object's abnormal proportions relative to its normal wearer. 2) Ask what would make it look that way. 3) Infer the unseen person's trait, such as height. 4) Filter suspects by that trait.
when: A suspect description is vague but an object or costume was seen clearly.
why: Object fit reveals hidden attributes that narrow the suspect pool.

text: 1) Make several items missing or altered in a way that shares one property. 2) Let the player list them. 3) Use the shared property to identify the thief.
when: designing an inventory-based deduction puzzle
why: A common property across missing items points the player toward a single cause.

text: Confirm a claim, especially a name recalled from memory, against records or the person best placed to know it before acting on it.
when: a witness names a suspect in a tense moment
why: an unchecked name can be wrong and then drive the investigation astray

text: Give players a fixed set of candidate causes or culprits, let observable clues eliminate them, and name the single answer only after enough independent clues exclude the rest.
when: when designing a deduction puzzle or game investigation
why: Premature single answers reward guessing rather than reasoning.

text: Give players candidates such as suspects, motives or locations, each paired with a checkable clue or stated constraint that rules it out, so elimination rests on evidence.
when: Designing a deduction puzzle with several candidates
why: Players can verify exclusions instead of guessing; elimination against constraints turns scattered clues into a solvable set.

text: Provide a visible deduction board where players list the crime's requirements, check each suspect against them, and drop theories that fail a check.
when: designing a deduction interface or elimination puzzle
why: Visible constraints let players follow the logic and see why theories fail; listing requirements makes elimination playable.

text: Keep a deduction journal of facts, open hypotheses and candidate sequences, marking which remain unverified so players can revisit them as new clues appear.
Design puzzles where players eliminate options using facts already revealed, and where each found object removes suspects so several clues must combine.
when: a puzzle asks which suspect or option is correct
why: elimination on revealed facts is solvable by reasoning rather than guessing; combining clues avoids reliance on one

text: Track eliminated leads and mark when a line of inquiry is exhausted, so cleared suspects no longer block progress and players switch trails.
Treat a guess about a person, a proposed access route, or an elimination conclusion as provisional until independent evidence or a verified candidate list confirms it.
why: a hunch can be wrong and acting on it early compounds the error

text: Confirm a reveal with an independent source, such as a prior photograph, so the identification does not rest on one observation.
Drop a candidate when their traits, such as character or age, contradict what the hypothesis requires.
In a deduction mechanic, present remaining suspects as a weighted list after ruling out causes, keeping the candidate set complete.
Let a narrow but true answer give the player a clue that becomes meaningful when compared with another character's account.
when: Designing dialogue that reveals information through comparison.
why: Clues that only pay off when cross-referenced reward attention and reasoning.

text: Only treat a trace as evidence if it can be matched to a specific object, using identical material or a known position, not mere resemblance.
why: resemblance alone can point to many objects

text: Give each suspect a list of evidence and let players weigh which items actually support guilt, rather than treating every item as equally strong.
when: several suspects carry circumstantial evidence
why: weighing evidence is the core of the deduction

text: Use shape-based clues only when the normal form of the object is known, since a deviation cannot be recognised without a baseline.
when: judging whether an object's shape is anomalous
why: Without a known standard, a deviation cannot be identified.

text: Let the game test a candidate explanation against facts the player has not yet seen, so the hypothesis can fail.
Give players a list of who knew each plan so they can deduce a leak by elimination.
when: designing mystery or stealth puzzles

text: Design each clue to rule out a different wrong answer, so only the correct answer survives every test; a game can check each condition the player proposes.
when: when building a deduction puzzle
why: Distinct eliminations make the correct answer the sole survivor.

text: Require two independent partial matches before a suspect is confirmed, so that one weak clue cannot settle the case.
when: designing suspect confirmation in a mystery
why: Independent evidence reduces the chance that a single weak match misleads the player

text: Check that every accused NPC has at least one clue against them and one defence, so no suspect is unfairly or trivially guilty.
when: when designing a set of suspects

text: Confirm that the receiving party's visitors are genuine and that they hold the right to the object before taking custody of it.
when: at a receiving point such as a shop or depot
why: a receiver who is not satisfied may refuse, and a wrong handover loses the object

text: Track which suspects have been cleared by confession, so the true culprit's lead remains available to reopen.
when: a quest or case closes on a confession
why: a closed lead can otherwise be lost for good

text: When a witness's claim does not match visible facts, leave the gap open as a question rather than confronting the witness at once.
when: A discovered mismatch is not yet strong enough to act on

text: In a tribunal mechanic, give the player's exculpatory evidence a clear route to the judge, and when a rule blocks it, show the block so the player can see the rigging.
when: Designing a trial or tribunal where the player presents a defence.
why: A visible block lets players detect rigging rather than assume the defence was weak.

text: A decree that invalidates a class of clues can remove an investigation branch mid-game without deleting the items involved.
when: designing a mid-game change to an investigation

text: Offer several candidate locations for one past event, with one explicitly ruled out by an NPC, so players learn that matches are only probable.
when: Designing a mystery where players link events to places.
why: Ruling out a candidate teaches players to treat matches as tentative.

text: Give a descriptive clue, such as height or build, that narrows the list of suspects the player may question.
Allow suspects to be eliminated only through in-game evidence, such as a verified location or documented trait, so the roster shrinks through play.
when: when designing suspect elimination

text: Keep the candidate set small and explicit so players can run the elimination, and introduce any hidden candidate before the final reveal.
when: a puzzle asks players to find the one actor who could have acted

text: Give each suspect a checkable movement window so players can test whether each alibi overlaps the time of the crime.
when: In investigation puzzles with several suspects
why: Players can only accept or reject an alibi if its times can be compared with the event.

text: After the player clears an NPC, recompute the suspect shortlist by filtering on who was in the room where the key item sat.
Track who has access to each key object, such as a potion or key, and remove suspects through state flags until a short list remains.
Give a second suspect equally convincing evidence so players must test which chain of evidence is complete.
Let players match a found object to a suspect's known routine, and reward them for reconstructing the sequence of events from it.
when: Building a deduction mode.
why: Linking objects to routines turns evidence into play.

text: A search mechanic that empties a character's pockets can clear an innocent character while revealing the item the culprit wanted hidden.
when: Designing a search or inventory check in a mystery.

text: Separate fact-gathering tools such as tracks, residue or scans from inference, letting the game supply facts while the player reasons about intent.
when: designing investigation mechanics
why: keeping data and reasoning apart makes deduction the skill tested

text: Show each eliminated candidate with the test that discounted them, such as access, strength or missing link, so the player sees why.
when: Candidate suspects are listed in a game.

text: Rule out a candidate when one measured dimension clearly falls outside the range of the trace, such as overall length or width.
when: comparing a partial trace to a known sample
why: A clear mismatch is reliable even when a faint trace cannot prove identity

text: Do not eliminate a suspect on one test alone, because a candidate may pass one check and fail another.
Let an absent weapon imply its wielder still carries it, so players deduce enemy loadouts from what is missing.
when: designing enemies whose equipment is hidden
why: Missing items give players readable information without a direct display.

text: Reason backward from a fixed conclusion: if the room was left by one route, that route must have closed itself after use.
when: the exit used is known but appears closed
why: the known outcome constrains which mechanism could have sealed it

text: Do not narrow options in a sequence where the player needs a clear path to a goal.
when: when the player must reach a specific destination

text: Plant one observable trace, such as a stain or worn step, and let the player derive each link from facts found elsewhere in the level.
Reward players who ask what a concealment protects, rather than what it claims to hide.
Reason backward from an object's placement to the motive that moved it, such as an object left at an awkward angle by someone rushing.
Let the player propose an alternative time window and have the game check it against recorded events, so the hypothesis is confirmed or rejected.
Clearing a convenient suspect early removes the misdirection; keeping it to the end requires a later reversal to sustain interest.
Elimination by presence works well with a small suspect set and complete records, but patchy observation across many people produces many false candidates.
when: Choosing whether to apply presence-based elimination
why: Short unseen gaps multiply possible candidates when observation is sparse

text: Deduction reasons from a fixed, supplied record with little fieldwork, but inherits every error in that record; induction gathers new evidence, costing more time but tolerating thin or incomplete records.
when: Choosing an investigation approach.
why: Each route trades effort against reliance on the available facts.

text: A fingerprint trace on a surface lasts until something touches or rubs it away, so it works as a durable physical trace.
when: A surface is left undisturbed after being touched.
why: Unless the surface is handled by others, the trace persists.

text: A proof the audience can watch being performed is more convincing than a verbal argument.
when: Delivering the key evidence of a mystery.
why: Seeing a test reproduced builds trust more than an explanation does.

text: Let players test a recovered item cheaply, so that a fake reads as a hypothesis to check rather than a settled fact.
A date given with a precise day may still be wrong if the record behind it was not written at the time.
when: Relying on a precise date from a later record or recollection.
why: Memory and later reconstruction introduce error even when the date looks exact.

text: 1) Record where and by whom an object was found. 2) Have a witness present at discovery. 3) Track who controls keys and containers. 4) Note the object's specific contents.
when: When an object's origin or who had access to it must be established
why: A witnessed, documented discovery with controlled access creates a traceable chain of custody

text: 1) Trace an object back to its maker or order. 2) Match the order to a specific description. 3) Confirm when it was worn through a witness account.
when: An object can be linked to a purchase or a date.
why: Provenance links an object to a person and a time.

text: Make a clue meaningless alone meaningful when an independent second source, such as a directory, map, ledger, NPC or object, matches it; mark single-source clues uncertain.
when: When designing clues that should gain meaning from a second source.
why: Corroboration converts an isolated detail into a verifiable connection.

text: Store an item's appearance, such as colour, shape and wear, as data so that a later clue can refer back to it.
Take a reference sample openly and beforehand when a suspect's presence must later be tied to a surface they touched.
when: A physical trace will later be compared with a suspect's reference sample.
why: A sample taken in a social setting can be questioned, and the reference should be clean.

text: Give players a way to verify a title through records, witnesses or a seal, so that acceptance has to be earned.
when: an NPC claims rank or lineage
why: Verification lets players test claims instead of accepting them on status.

text: A disguise trap alone does not prove guilt; the confirming evidence comes from a confession or from physical traces.
when: Designing a deduction case built on a disguise.
why: The reaction is suggestive, so a separate proof is needed to close the case.

text: Test a physical anomaly with a tool or second check before drawing conclusions, since most objects are what they appear to be.
when: A property does not match the expected identity.
why: Anomalies are not automatically significant, but untested ones are often missed.

text: Solving an unexplained clue needs both constructive imagination to form a guess and exact reasoning to test it.
Test a visible detail that seems to settle a question against independent facts, such as distance, since it may have another cause.
Test a clue that confirms the first theory too easily by asking who gains from it.
when: Evaluating evidence that fits a favoured explanation neatly.
why: Planted evidence is often designed to benefit the person who planted it.

text: Before committing to one reading of a clue, ask whether another explanation fits it equally well, and treat the current conclusion as a working hypothesis.
when: when one clue points strongly to a single place or person
why: A clue that fits a theory may have an innocent source, so the first reading can be wrong.

text: Character evidence shapes what seems likely but must be kept separate from proof when judging who acted.
when: When a suspect's personality or history is used to judge probable guilt.
why: Character makes an outcome seem likely without establishing that it happened.

text: Suspicious conduct, willful suppression of evidence and fabricated evidence can together create a strong presumption of guilt without direct proof.
when: Evaluating a suspect who hides or alters evidence.
why: Concealment and fabrication are read as signs of guilt when combined.

text: A clue that seems to prove one fact can mislead; if the find is only a limited fact, players who overstate its meaning will reach a wrong theory.
when: A discovered item appears to settle a point.
why: Stronger conclusions than the evidence supports lead the investigator and player astray.

text: Suspicion has three escalating levels: inquiry, a matter needing examination without implied guilt; presumption, strong enough to justify detaining a suspect; and conviction, which needs more again.
Coherent, tidy reasoning can look certain while being merely plausible; keep plausibility separate from confirmed evidence and still weigh evidence against the favoured theory.
when: Presenting a deduction result or evaluating an account that fits known facts well.
why: Tidy structure makes weak reasoning look certain, and fit with known facts does not verify parts only one party can confirm.

text: A choice that rests on a single report of no defences fails if that report is wrong, so the core assumption must be checked.
Losing a unique label reduces strong evidence to mere suspicion.
when: When the tag that identifies evidence can be removed or lost.
why: Without the tag, the physical object no longer links to a specific source.

text: Accepting a confession as fact because it is detailed and articulate overlooks the physical circumstances that could establish where the writer was.
when: Reviewing a volunteered confession

text: An object's position may be planted rather than where it was discovered, so a location inference needs a second test before it convicts anyone.
when: Interpreting where evidence was found.
why: The same location can be explained by concealment or by innocent placement.

text: Conclusions resting only on impressions the player cannot check leave the reveal unsupported and reduce trust in the investigator.
when: A clue or deduction is presented without visible reasoning.
why: The player has no way to verify or reproduce the conclusion.

text: A clue whose link to a person is disputed by witnesses is unreliable until its ownership and use are confirmed.
when: When witnesses disagree about whether a person carried or used an object.
why: Conflicting testimony leaves the object's connection to the person unestablished.

text: A fragment proves that a garment was torn, not that its owner wore it at the time of the event.
when: When a physical fragment is used to place a specific person at a scene.
why: Material evidence establishes the object's condition and match, but not the timing of the wearer.

text: A broken marker may have an ordinary cause, such as over-tension, so the reveal is spoiled unless the alternative explanations are considered.
when: A marker breaks and is meant to signal a hidden event.
why: Mundane causes can mimic the intended signal and undermine the reveal.

text: Practical reasoning about distance and noise stays a guess until supported by measurement or testing.
when: Inferring where a deliberate act would have been safe.
why: Unverified assumptions about distance and sound can be wrong.

text: Treating a few confirmed cases as proof of an entire compiled collection overreaches and hides errors in the unchecked majority.
when: Drawing conclusions about a whole collection from a small verified sample.
why: Verified cases are a non-random subset, so they cannot establish the reliability of the rest.

text: 1) State the baseline quantity. 2) Subtract known offsets to get the actual distance. 3) Divide by an assumed rate to get the time. 4) Flag which inputs are analogy rather than measurement.
when: Building a calculation that the player or reader must follow.
why: Visible premises let the reader see and challenge weak assumptions.

text: 1) Propose an alternative scenario that also explains the absence. 2) Name a concrete way to check that scenario. 3) Compare which scenario the check supports.
when: when a theory explains an absence of traces
why: An absence fits several scenarios, so only a specific check can separate them.

text: Track suspected and proven states separately; an accusation or arrest requires a specific recorded evidence item, while weak cues only raise suspicion.
when: When designing accusation mechanics for a game.
why: Separating the two prevents accusations on hunches alone and keeps plausible guesses apart from confirmed findings.

text: Tell the player which facts are settled so the remaining puzzle concentrates on the disputed points.
when: A deduction puzzle has both certain and uncertain elements.
why: Conceded ground narrows the search space and keeps focus on what is still open.

text: Distinguish a finding that is consistent with a hypothesis from one that is specific to it and confirms it; a consistent finding alone does not confirm the hypothesis.
when: when judging whether a new fact supports a theory
why: A fact can fit a theory without being specific to it, and a strong theory can make every new fact look like support.

text: Make a locked or jammed object state impossible to reset, so the player can trust it as evidence rather than treating it as a red herring.
when: Designing a clue that encodes a past event in an object's state.
why: A reversible or ambiguous state cannot be trusted as proof, and the clue loses its value.

text: A case can be strong enough to act on, such as charging or arresting, without complete proof; sufficiency for action is a lower bar than certainty.
when: when deciding whether enough evidence exists to act
why: Acting early risks error, while waiting for certainty can let the chance to act pass.

text: Place valuable loot in the same container as a small story-relevant item, so the player must decide what to keep.
when: Designing containers in a dungeon or level
why: The choice forces the player to evaluate the small item against the reward.

text: Plant an anomaly early, such as a missing physical feature, so the later reveal pays it off as a payoff rather than a surprise.
when: Designing a twist that depends on a physical clue.
why: A set-up anomaly makes the reveal feel earned and fair.

text: Place one clue in each suspect's room in an investigation hub so each clue shifts blame, forcing the player to re-evaluate the household.
1) Stage an early clue that clears the obvious suspect. 2) Later, stage a dense set of physical traces without explaining them. 3) Pay off each trace at the reveal.
why: suspicion then moves to the real culprits as evidence accumulates

text: A red herring must be fair: the clues that expose its falsity should already be available to the player.
when: Designing a misleading but reasonable conclusion before the truth is revealed.
why: A decoy that can only be disproved by unseen information feels like a cheat.

text: Build puzzles where one clue has two valid readings, and let a later clue select the correct one.
Let a puzzle clue point to two or three locations or characters, each confirmed by a different in-game check.
Give a concealed clue a unique tag such as a seal or label so the game can verify it, and do not let a generic version of the object solve the puzzle.
when: When a clue must link to a specific person, item or event.
why: A generic container or object cannot prove identity; only a unique mark can.

text: Spread several minor traits across a level, such as a scar, a gait and a voice, so that together they identify the culprit.
when: designing a mystery level
why: Players must combine clues, which rewards careful note-taking.

text: For each clue object, ask who placed it where it was found and why, before treating its location as evidence of its owner's involvement.
when: Evaluating physical evidence that appears in several locations.
why: Duplicates and planted items can mislead about who used them.

text: Antagonists can keep a target engaged and unsuspecting by staging spectacles, offering plausible alternative theories, and placing blame on other suspects.
when: A target must be kept interested or misled while the real plan proceeds.
why: Plausible decoys give the target a reasonable but wrong conclusion, so attention stays away from the true threat.

text: Let a misleading message be true in one sense, such as a note that really concerns the escape, so it misdirects without lying.
why: A literally true clue misdirects the player more convincingly than a false one.

text: Build one false answer that authorities accept and make it cheap to act on, so the player's test of it becomes the story.
