Establish whether the client seeks acquittal or a lighter outcome before starting work, since each goal requires different evidence and different effort.
when: at the start of a case

text: Gate each investigation step on its own evidence threshold: a rumor opens an inquiry, a physical clue allows detention, and two independent sources allow a verdict.
Choose a preservation method that can be carried out with materials actually at hand, not one that needs unavailable supplies.
when: Time is short and the preferred materials are missing.
why: A method that cannot be performed on site protects nothing.

text: Before acting on an unconfirmed theory, send word first, arrive with witnesses, and avoid forcing entry without cause.
when: When a theory suggests action but predictions are not yet checked
why: Acting on an unchecked theory risks error and harm

text: Carry the equipment needed to examine a scene on the spot rather than deferring analysis.
when: Planning an investigation
why: On-site examination captures traces that would be lost in transport or delay.

text: Hold back an arrest while gathering one more item of evidence, and keep the suspect under watch during the delay.
when: When the suspect may flee or destroy evidence, and watching will not tip them off.

text: Relay observations to the decision maker promptly, because a late report loses most of its value.
when: when a partner is reporting on a watched target

text: Acting on partial evidence saves time and prevents harm, but risks error and alerting targets; waiting for confirmation is safer but may let harm recur or leads fade.
when: Choosing between acting on partial evidence and holding an investigation open for full confirmation or a focusing clue.
why: Premature action risks alerting targets and error; delay risks recurring harm and lost leads.

text: A digression can waste time and let the witness steer the conversation, and allies kept unaware of the plan may lose faith in the investigator.
when: Using feigned indifference during an investigation.
why: Concealment that protects the suspect also costs time and team trust.

text: Following a departing target across open ground risks being seen, so spending the absence on searching the premises is often safer.
when: the suspect leaves on foot across exposed ground
why: a shadow on open ground is easily noticed

text: Deferring conclusions keeps the investigation open to new evidence, but it works only if the investigator can tolerate an unresolved state.
when: When facts are still incomplete and the investigator must choose whether to commit
why: Premature commitment closes off alternatives; indefinite deferral stalls progress

text: Taking a small risk for speed, such as a brief light flash, can expose the offender even when the rest of the cover-up succeeds.
when: An offender must act quickly during a cover-up
why: Speed reduces care and can leave a fresh trace

text: A key missing from where it should be can indicate who could have secured a room from inside.
when: Investigating a locked room.

text: One assumption can unlock a whole line of work, so state it explicitly and treat it as a hypothesis the next result may overturn.
when: A plan depends on a premise accepted without proof.

text: A high page number followed by a restart at page one suggests the key book is short, so the largest page number used gives a rough bound on its size.
when: the key book is unknown and the sender's numbers are available
why: a sender who restarts at page one reveals how far the book extends

text: Let players test a tool on a door or lock to confirm which object produced a scratch.
why: Hands-on testing turns a clue into a verified conclusion.

text: Make each kit item unlock one distinct action, such as magnify, measure, sample or seal, so choosing a tool becomes a puzzle.
Rotating a key item can change which lock it opens, so one key yields different outcomes and rewards experimentation.
when: The key's pattern changes arrangement with orientation
why: A changed arrangement matches a different target

text: A door handle with stripped mounting holes gives no grip, so the door cannot be pulled open even if the latch itself is free.
A container that opens only at a fixed future time protects its contents by schedule rather than lock, so anyone seeking them must wait or break it.
when: Designing a hiding place that reveals at a set moment.
why: Time-based access makes the location public while the contents stay hidden until opening.

text: A small offset in a measured bearing from a landmark can make a search miss entirely, so the failure can look like honest error, keeping a deliberate offset fair.
A theft-by-concealment puzzle hides the stolen item in the room it was taken from, so the reveal depends on a container already in plain sight.
A locked-room puzzle can be solved by a trained animal and an ordinary household object, so thefts that look like intrusion are an insider's method.
A missing key item lets its holder deflect questions by claiming it cannot be produced.
when: when an item central to the case is unavailable
why: the item cannot be checked

text: Failing to consider a second location can make an investigation look more hopeless than it is.
when: A person is missing and only one destination is checked.
why: The unchecked location may hold the answer.

text: A size-fit test can be defeated because an item can be carried rather than worn, so eliminate suspects on both wearing and carrying grounds.
A timed mechanism meant for one person to open is weakened when another person holds a key.
when: Designing a locked or timed container with access controls.
why: A second key holder can bypass the intended access restriction.

text: 1) Identify who ordered the lock. 2) List every key's holder and when held; confirm keys by tag or marking, locating the master key. 3) List who could hold a copy, such as tenants, staff, security or central office sets. 4) Narrow to holders with actual custody and reach to the container. 5) Test each holder's claim against other facts.
when: Access to a locked space or container is disputed, or few people could open it, and key holders can be identified.
why: Access records reveal who could have acted.

text: 1) Go to the suspected disposal spot. 2) Lift out each item separately. 3) Inspect and return it before moving on. 4) Do not rely on a quick glance over the pile.
when: when an object was seen dropped into a cluttered or burnable place
why: Small objects are missed by glancing or sweeping.

text: 1) Remove a key from a locked room's connecting route. 2) Have an NPC dismiss the key's absence as unimportant. 3) Prevent staff from searching for it. 4) Enter through the hidden connecting door at a time the owner is away.
when: When designing how a player can enter a sealed room without breaking the lock.
why: Controlling what others believe about the key keeps the loss from being investigated.

text: 1) State who holds keys to the space. 2) State what is sealed and which windows or doors exist. 3) State which force or methods are ruled out. 4) Plan entry only within those stated limits.
when: A locked space must be entered or explained and access rules can be stated
why: Explicit constraints define what counts as a valid solution

text: Let a minor character hide a detail, and let the player catch it by checking the story against a known fact.
when: designing minor NPC testimony

text: Design a missing key as a clue by leaving a trace, such as a call log or desk record, showing someone tried to get in.
Show the connection between a key and its lock, such as a matching pattern near the lock, so the solution does not feel arbitrary.
when: A hidden lock is opened by a physical key
why: An unshown link makes the solution feel like luck

text: Let an NPC carry a key that the player must find by searching them, and let a wrong key give a clue about its owner.
when: designing key puzzles

text: Require two items held by two different NPCs to open a vault door, so the player must recover both before entering.
when: When designing vault or door puzzles.
why: Split credentials turn the door into a multi-step objective.

text: Give an evidence room a timed unlock, or a door left ajar for a fixed number of turns, so the player can reconstruct who could have taken an item.
when: designing a clue location in a game
why: a bounded window makes the access question answerable

text: Make NPC and animal reactions or animations, such as a pause before answering, ambiguous, so players must compare them with other cues before judging.
Give evasive NPCs a dialogue state that refuses a topic, and let a narrower fact-based question unlock the answer.
when: Designing NPC dialogue for a topic the NPC will not discuss directly.
why: Players can still progress by asking answerable questions, which keeps the refusal meaningful rather than a dead end.

text: Track an NPC's reaction, such as a flinch or pause, as a tell, but require a fact-based confirmation before the player concludes anything from it.
when: An NPC reacts visibly to a player's question.
why: Reactions suggest a lead but are ambiguous, so confirmation prevents false conclusions.

text: Confirm a witness's history or routine claims by independent inquiry; independent corroboration, like staff recalling an event, is harder to dismiss than the questioner's opinion.
when: Relying on a witness for background facts.
why: Independent sources reduce the chance a single account is wrong, and people can contest an accuser's claim but struggle to dispute a neutral witness.

text: Test a beneficiary's account against their motive; in games, show each accusing NPC's visible relationship score so players can weigh their reasons to lie.
when: When a new account arrives from a party who benefits from its conclusion.
why: Self-interest can shape the account, so its contents need independent checking.

text: A hypothetical framed as being about a third party can be a probe, and a listener who reacts as if it applied to them reveals their stake.
when: someone poses a general case about a claim
why: a personal reaction shows where the listener stands

text: Third-person phrasing creates distance and formality, and a writer may struggle to keep it up through a letter.
when: A writer adopts an impersonal voice for a personal message.
why: Detachment is hard to sustain, so slips back into personal phrasing show the real stance.

text: A direct question about a third party can trigger sudden excitement and a rising voice, marking a sore point.
when: when asked about someone connected to the client
why: the question touches a sensitive subject

text: A subject can signal a third person from a distance to draw them away from a pursuer, a visible clue an observant player can notice.
when: a third person is in contact with a watched subject
why: signals pull attention away from the pursuer

text: A third party's offer of their rooms depends on trust, so a discreet plan can fail if that trust is misplaced.
when: a meeting relies on a host who is not part of the conflict
why: The whole arrangement rests on the host's willingness and discretion

text: When official requests for samples are refused, reference prints may still be found in unofficial sources such as personal collections.
Keep a close companion uninformed when that person could not play the grieving part convincingly.
when: Planning a staged death
why: A poor performance from someone who knows the plan would expose it.

text: Uniform, scripted denials from a group of NPCs can signal to the player that they share a secret.
Take witness accounts separately before reconciling them, so that shared details that survive independent questioning can be treated as firmer evidence.
when: Several people report the same event.
why: Separate accounts reduce contamination between witnesses.

text: Verify a frightened witness's account of danger by direct inspection, since fear can exaggerate the description.
when: A witness reports a threat or danger.
why: Emotion inflates descriptions, so key claims need independent checking.

text: Build an NPC report with a deliberate blind spot, so a player who asks about hard-to-fake details finds the report incomplete.
when: Designing an NPC whose testimony the player can test.
why: Blind spots reward players who ask probing questions over those who accept confident summaries.

text: A decoy witness can explain several early clues at once, so the player keeps the belief even when it is partly wrong.
why: One fiction accounts for many unexplained details, which makes it hard to abandon

text: A third person present in a conversation prevents two people who know each other from speaking freely.
when: Two acquainted people speak in front of a witness.
why: Their guarded speech changes when someone else can overhear.

text: Evidence held by a third party under conditions makes the object itself a source of suspense, since its release depends on who asks and how.
Negotiation conducted through formal written notes between intermediaries tends to stall, because each side refers the matter back to its principal before answering.
A witness told to omit something can reveal it later once the player builds trust or removes pressure, rewarding return visits.
when: When designing NPCs who withhold information.

text: A trusted NPC who can summon help adds a signal mechanic whose reliability the player must weigh.
An NPC's timed final statement can reach the player only through a second NPC, which adds a step at which the information can be doubted.
when: a quest where a dying character holds a key fact
why: each relay is a point where certainty is lost

text: An accusation made by a third party can taint a witness's answers, so each answer must be checked against physical facts.
when: when another party has already voiced a theory before the witness speaks
why: the witness may echo the accusation instead of reporting perception

text: Excluding someone because they were told nothing is an error, since being kept uninformed does not remove access.
Investigators tend to dismiss a trusted colleague without testing them, and this bias must be corrected by applying the same test to everyone.
when: An investigator's trust in someone shapes which candidates are examined
why: Unexamined trust skews elimination toward a favored suspect

text: A locked door is only as secure as the trust placed in whoever says a missing key does not matter.
when: When an NPC's word is the only assurance that a lock is secure.
why: A dismissed absence can hide a real route in, and a careful investigator would chase it down.

text: Vague answers such as 'I don't remember' should be recorded as gaps and revisited later, not treated as either confirmation or denial.
when: Collecting testimony from memory

text: An account that depends on one party's confirmation stays untested when that party denies it, and a denial leaves the account unverified.
when: When the only witness to a key moment is the person being accused.
why: With no independent source, no part of the account can be checked.

text: Do not assume a witness saw everything within their view; a witness's certainty about an exit is a claim that still needs confirming, including whether they left their post.
when: when relying on a witness's account of who passed an exit
why: witnesses can misjudge coverage or be absent from their posts

text: Agreement between witnesses who shared the same frightening situation and talked to each other is weaker evidence than it appears.
when: Counting agreement between witnesses as confirmation.
why: Shared fear and conversation make their accounts mutually influenced, not independent.

text: Verify a message against a third-party copy, such as a telegraph or cable office record, to confirm it independently.
when: A message's authenticity or content matters.
why: An independent record can confirm or contradict the copy the investigator holds.

text: Let hostile characters intercept messages, so players must choose a trusted route to pass information.
when: Designing message systems in games

text: Assign a trusted third party to handle formal steps, such as paperwork, that would otherwise expose the deception.
when: A deception requires official documents or formal processes
why: Formal records can reveal a trick that appearances hide.

text: Make an NPC who confirms player guesses unreliable, so players must seek a second source before trusting it.
when: designing NPC dialogue that offers information
why: Agreement alone should not settle a question

text: In a vouching mechanic, a failed contact raises suspicion of the vouched person; elsewhere, an unreachable reference proves nothing and counts as neither confirmation nor refutation.
when: A vouching mechanic requires verifying a reference in the world; other third-party reference claims are tested separately.

text: Approaching a third party carries a cost that must be weighed against the value of a confession from the principal.
Handing evidence to an authority secures it only if that authority is trusted; an obvious conflict of interest makes the handover unbelievable.
when: Choosing who receives a contested object.
why: The receiver's loyalty determines whether custody holds.

text: Let players search containers one item at a time, revealing items in turn with a record of what has been checked, so systematic search is rewarded over partial search.
when: When designing the interaction for searching a container.
why: Step-by-step search gives the player a process to follow and reveals items gradually.

text: Older marks such as scratched initials and symbols reveal earlier occupancy, separate from recent use.
Writing that is invisible under normal conditions can be revealed by heat, so a document can hide a clue until a physical process is applied.
An object too large to carry out unnoticed is probably still on the premises.
An object left behind by an absent figure promises their return and keeps the audience expecting them.
when: a character has gone missing or left the scene
why: a left-behind item implies the owner will come back

text: Searches for a discarded item long after an event are hard, so concentrate effort on the most probable hiding places.
why: Limited search time is best spent where the item is most likely to be

text: When testimony conflicts, look for one object that can settle who owned or touched something.
when: witness accounts disagree about possession or contact

text: A generic scan that returns nothing is a valid result; a second, location-specific action can be required before the clue appears.
when: designing search mechanics

text: Place a small residue in a hidden spot far from the central event, so players must reason about why the staging was done there.
when: Designing a hidden clue for a staged event.
why: Players who reason about the location of the act can find the trace through deduction.

text: Wearing an object for a long time can leave a lasting pale mark on the skin that matches the object's outline.
Exhaustive search through many mostly irrelevant objects without clear purpose tires players and invites hasty wrong guesses; give each search a clear purpose and readable result.
when: When a puzzle requires sifting through many mostly irrelevant objects.
why: Sustained fruitless search lowers attention and motivation, raising the chance of a rushed guess.

text: An inference from a missing trace is only as sound as the timing of the search and the accuracy of witness claims. A late or partial search weakens the conclusion.
why: A trace may have been removed or may have faded before anyone checked for it.

text: Collecting only the large pieces hides the shortfall or surplus that reveals where breakage happened.
A systematic search can still miss the opening, which may turn up by accident rather than by reasoning.
Assuming a tool was used because it was found near the damage can mislead, since proximity does not establish that the tool made the marks.
1) Examine the object's condition before disposal. 2) Weight it and open a way for water to enter. 3) Watch through a telescope until it vanishes. 4) Treat a longer float than expected as a warning.
when: when a guilty party disposes of a vessel or object at sea
why: verification confirms the disposal worked

text: 1) Search every surface in a fixed order. 2) If one trace type is erased, check other surfaces where it may survive. 3) Examine small fragments under magnification.
when: a scene has been cleaned, weathered or disturbed
why: Erased traces can leave residues elsewhere

text: Place clues so a systematic search finds them while a hasty first pass does not, rewarding careful play.
when: designing a timed search puzzle
why: thorough inspection should be rewarded over quick scanning

text: Give staged crime scenes a checklist of unchangeable traits, such as a ring, a scar or a bandage, so players can test the staged story against them.
when: Designing a scene arranged to mislead
why: A fixed checklist gives players a concrete way to find the contradiction.

text: Give hidden items in containers a physical property, such as weight or solubility, so the player can test a theory instead of guessing.
when: Designing a puzzle involving a sealed, cracked or bought container.
why: A testable property makes the puzzle checkable rather than arbitrary.

text: To establish who could open a secured object, determine who knew the access code, when it last changed, and whether anyone's memory of it is unreliable.
when: A locked object such as a safe or combination lock is involved
why: A key alone may not suffice, and the code's holder and timing decide who had access

text: Seed a puzzle object early with a plain, discoverable function, and keep the materials needed for its solution in the level before they are required.
when: when placing puzzle objects

text: Reassemble discarded items from fragments recovered from waste, turning waste into evidence.
when: A discarded object is found in a bin or dump.
why: Fragments can be pieced together to reveal the object's identity and link.

text: Players notice hidden connections when NPC actions fall inside the same visible time window, especially on a timeline view.
when: The game shows NPC actions on a timeline or in shared in-game time.
why: Shared timing invites players to infer a link between actions.

text: Keeping a search quiet, so suspects do not know a fragment matters, can add stealth and tension.
when: When designing stealth or tension around a hidden clue.

text: A log of recorded reactions lets the player build their own reading rather than accepting the first explanation offered.
Recording timestamps for game events lets players see gaps, revivals and cycles, including hidden triggers that reset after a quiet period.
when: when a recurring phenomenon is meant to be discovered
why: Comparing dates reveals a pattern that a single event hides

text: Limit the player's journal to the player's own observations, and deliver NPC statements through dialogue with the speaker named.
when: Designing a journal or case log for the player.
why: Keeping sources distinct preserves the player's reasoning about who said what.

text: Let the player choose an investigative frame, such as procedural or intuitive, so each frame highlights different clues in the same scene.
when: in an accusation system

text: Organise the player's notes around three questions (who, why, how) so their theories stay ordered.
when: Providing a journal or notes system for a mystery
why: A fixed structure keeps theories sorted by question

text: A quest log can split one investigation into tasks such as witness canvass, record checks, background reports and surveillance, each with a clear time window or location.
when: Designing a multi-step investigation quest.
why: Scoped tasks give the player concrete next actions.

text: In multiplayer deduction, give each player a private clue ledger and a clear rule for when clues become shared with others.
when: several players investigate one case
why: private clues keep reasoning independent while sharing stays controlled

text: Fingerprint comparison matches a scene print against a known sample from a suspect, detail by detail, and expresses the strength of the match as a probability.
A latent print is an invisible fingerprint left on a surface, which can be made visible with fine powder and compared to a known print by ridge features.
A print shows someone touched an object at an unknown time, so it may predate or postdate the event and cannot alone place them there.
when: Using prints to establish presence.
why: Prints record contact, not timing.

text: Writing pressed on a top sheet leaves an impression on sheets beneath, so a blotting pad can hold a reversed copy of the message.
when: a message was written over other sheets in the scene
why: pressure transfers the writing to lower layers

text: A print's depth and shape, such as a blurred toe or a deeply sunk heel, indicate the walker's pace and how weight was carried.
when: Reading individual prints in soft ground
why: Weight and pace change how the foot sinks

text: Experts may treat a fingerprint match as equivalent to an eyewitness account, though it carries different reliability.
A printed witness statement looks more complete than the questioning that produced it, because the back-and-forth is removed.
Examiners often followed a printed guide that listed signs of guilt and a rule for separating them from ordinary blemishes, so the guide shapes what counts as a finding.
Many footprints are identical, so tracking by footprints alone is a primitive method for identifying a person.
when: Relying on boots or shoes to identify a person
why: Common footwear produces indistinguishable prints across many people

text: An inked relief pressed onto paper can reproduce even small pores, so the copy can look indistinguishable from the original.
Print-lifting tools are two colors of fingerprint powder, brushes and a stamping pad for different surfaces.
A recovered print identifies no one unless it can be compared with a stored record, so clear prints are useful only when a reference set exists.
Prints of two different sizes in the same soft surface, such as footprints near a moved victim, show that two people passed the spot or moved them.
when: Several prints of different sizes appear at one scene.
why: Each person leaves prints of their own foot size.

text: Print shape can rule out familiar animals, but a new creature may fit a known family while being larger than any known member.
Printed capitals in place of handwriting hide the writer, but a torn word or an unnatural word form can still betray the disguise.
Fingerprints are most usable on smooth, undisturbed surfaces; frequently handled surfaces carry overlapping prints that obscure each other.
when: when choosing where to look for prints
why: Undisturbed surfaces keep individual impressions distinct.

text: Marks left by a previous reader, such as underlined words, can identify the correct copy of a key text.
If latent marks may be disturbed by brushing, photograph them before brushing.
when: Marks are fragile

text: Build a fingerprint puzzle as a chain of choices: powder, brush, photograph, then feature match, so the player practises each step.
Identifying marks such as indelible initials on recovered items can link them to a person, but must be checked against aliases before naming someone.
when: Recovered items carry names, initials or stamps.
why: Initials can point to the wrong person when an alias is in use.

text: Gating print recovery by surface type, prior handling, and item type makes the same dusting action yield different outcomes and directs the player's search.
when: in investigation mechanics; when designing a forensic interaction.
why: Restricting prints to specific objects directs the player's search.

text: Stored print records let a player compare a mark with suspects and rule characters in or out, narrowing the suspect list.
when: in investigation mechanics

text: Spelling in a printed document may reflect the printer rather than the writer, so it is weak evidence about the author alone.
when: Attributing a document's authorship from its spelling
why: Typesetting conventions can alter the writer's spelling

text: A near-complete match on a partial or smeared print is not automatically conclusive, because fewer comparable points remain.
A claim that two people share identical traces should be tested, not assumed, before it is used as evidence.
when: Someone asserts that two individuals' physical traces match.
why: An unverified similarity claim can mislead a comparison.

text: Claims that prints quickly identify culprits overstate the case, because comparison can require substantial time and skill.
when: Relying on fingerprint evidence for quick resolution
why: Careful comparison is slow and needs practice

text: 1) Lift prints from the scene. 2) Compare them against prints on file from known people. 3) Accept a match only when a known record identifies the print.
when: Physical evidence must be tied to a specific person.
why: A print is identifiable only through a comparison with a known record.

text: Compare lifted prints against all elimination sets; prints matching no known person are candidates for an unknown visitor.
when: Prints have been lifted from an object and elimination sets are on file.
why: Unmatched prints point to someone not yet accounted for.

text: 1) Trace a print onto paper. 2) Cut out the outline as a pattern. 3) Compare the pattern against other prints to test for a match.
when: Matching footwear prints to a candidate's shoes
why: A physical pattern lets prints be compared consistently

text: 1) Place a reversed negative of a genuine print over light-sensitive gelatine. 2) Expose to light, which hardens the gelatine under the ridges. 3) Wash in hot water to dissolve unhardened gelatine, leaving the ridges in relief.
when: A genuine print is available to copy.
why: Hardened and unhardened areas leave a raised copy of the original pattern.

text: 1) Dust a hard, smooth, non-porous surface with fine powder. 2) Brush gently with a soft brush to raise the marks. 3) Photograph them, placing dark paper behind glass for contrast. 4) Transfer the print to paper, dust both sides, and shake off loose powder.
when: Recovering prints from smooth surfaces

text: 1) Classify the pattern type, such as whorl or loop. 2) Count the ridges. 3) Note bifurcating ridges and scars. 4) Score how many features match the known print.
when: Comparing a latent print to a known print

text: 1) Dust surfaces with powder to bring out prints. 2) Photograph each print under controlled light and exposure. 3) Sort prints by likely owner.
when: prints may be faint or on a shared surface
why: Controlled photographs preserve detail for later comparison

text: 1) Dust a fine powder over faint marks and brush gently. 2) Use printer's ink on softer surfaces such as wax. 3) Photograph the marks before further handling. 4) Compare the recovered marks against inked impressions of each candidate.
when: Faint marks are left on objects and a suspect pool is known
why: Development and comparison includes or excludes each person in the pool

text: To judge a footprint's size, press your own foot into it and compare the fit; no tools are needed.
Set aside older and smaller impressions made by other hands before matching, so they do not produce false pairings.
when: when matching prints from a crowded scene
why: Overlapping or irrelevant prints can mislead the comparison.

text: Collect prints from a potential suspect only with a clear reason and the subject's knowledge, since unexplained collection can alert them or confuse the sets.
when: A person is a potential suspect.
why: Unexplained collection tips off the suspect and muddles the records.

text: A print shows that someone handled an object at some time, not that the person committed the crime.
Enforce test order so that a print check before the trace check forfeits the trace, teaching the player correct procedure.
A game can enforce a formal rule, such as two witnesses with a clear line of sight, so the player must arrange the setup correctly to succeed.
when: designing formal-procedure puzzles
why: Enforcing the rule makes the player engage with its logic

text: Offer a sealed case file solvable by deduction alone and a second mode requiring location visits and NPC questioning.
when: Designing investigation modes for players.
why: Both reasoning styles can be supported.

text: Expose the governing rule to the player; an unexplained premise that decides outcomes feels arbitrary and unfair.
Choose a response by weighing the resources at hand against how fast the threat is spreading.
when: A threat is growing and resources are limited

text: Place doorways, shop fronts and crates along routes a player follows, so they have places to hide from a target who looks back.
when: designing a route where the player tails an NPC
why: nearby cover lets the player break line of sight

text: A long chase exhausts the pursuer's transport and budget, because horses and drivers tire and each extra mile costs money.
why: Pursuit consumes finite resources at a rate set by its length.

text: A timed group decision can show a countdown and reactive NPC chatter that changes as progress is made.
when: Designing a group decision or timed puzzle with NPCs.
why: Changing chatter makes progress and time pressure visible.

text: 1) Move the player into a physical activity or new location 2) Deliver fresh material 3) Return the player to the puzzle with that material.
why: A stall needs a new stimulus to keep the player moving.

text: In stealth or urban detective levels, make pursuers react to sudden stops and doubling back, so players can learn to test for a tail.
when: Designing followers

text: Have the player keep pace with an NPC while staying out of sight, using crowds as a cover mechanic.
A stealth tail mission can model a building with two exits and a restricted room, requiring the player to cover both routes or use a disguise item.
when: Designing a stealth pursuit set in public spaces
why: Two exits make a single watch insufficient

text: Post a partner at a wall or doorway to cover an exit while the follower keeps the target in view.
when: A single pursuer risks losing the target.

text: A reply to a question that presumes an event reveals that the listener already knows of it, through the form of the answer.
when: a question carries a hidden premise
why: answers reveal knowledge the speaker did not intend to share

text: A mystery can be marvellous, meaning startling or supernatural, or complicated, meaning built from many interlocking parts; these two kinds must be kept separate.
when: when deciding how a puzzle or case should be structured
why: Mixing them makes a plain plan look like magic or a magic event look like a plot tangle

text: In a plain-view theft puzzle, the thief's intelligence rather than the object's hiding place is the puzzle, so the solver reasons about what the thief would choose.
Searching only for unusual objects misses the ordinary item that blends in; a stalled player may need a mundane solution in plain sight, like a common object used unexpectedly.
when: when the player is stuck on an overcomplicated theory

text: Build puzzle rooms from readable traces, such as forced-lock scratches, an outside bar, mismatched cigar ends, ash, scuffs or footprints, each pointing to a specific actor.
Hold back a puzzle answer behind a visible trigger or staged beat, releasing partial clues first; NPC hooks like 'wait and see' get resolved in a later scene.
when: Designing a puzzle or final reveal that resolves in a later scene.
why: Visible triggers let players know the answer exists and when it comes; staged release keeps trust and engagement.

text: Model a tampered or missing item as a chain of handoffs and open-access time window, then list everyone who could have acted within it.
when: When building a poisoning or sabotage puzzle, or investigating a vanished clue.
why: Players reconstruct who could have acted and when; the window narrows the set of possible takers.

text: Map a riddle's terms, such as stair counts, timed cycles, paces or landmarks, onto visible or journal-recorded level data so players filter candidate locations against each term.
when: when designing a riddle that points to a location
why: Each term can be tested against the level, and anchors must exist and be verifiable.

text: Treat a crime arising from human acts as a problem with a solution, reasoned from knowledge of human motive and action, rather than as an unsolvable mystery.
when: Framing a case that seems impenetrable
why: Human actions follow motives that can be reasoned about and checked

text: Design an official storyline that explains most of the scene but leaves one object, such as a key in an unexpected place, that the attentive player can use to challenge it.
A puzzle room can show a few items that jointly point to a guilty NPC, with one overlooked item that reverses the conclusion.
Do not make every gathering a clue dump, since crowds mostly obscure evidence.
Keep an investigation hidden, because an open appeal for information alerts suspects who may then flee.
when: when a suspect could escape if warned
why: publicity signals pursuit to the people being hunted

text: A mystery should be hard enough to resist guessing but never impossible, so players feel challenged yet not cheated at the reveal.
Trace a witness's hidden knowledge to its source, such as a written scrap in a drawer, rather than relying on the spoken answer alone.
when: when a witness seems to know more than they say

text: Hide a long setup in early scenes, such as a staged event or a gift, that looks random until the player links it to a later event.
when: when designing a fair-play sequence of events
why: the player can recall and connect setups once the payoff occurs

text: Prefer questions about hidden facts over visible ones, because a hidden fact is harder to obtain elsewhere and so tests the theory better.
when: when choosing which question to ask

text: Be wary when a mystery's evidence is hidden or invisible and an authority accepts it without checks.
Use transport schedules, walking times and opening hours as puzzle inputs, have each action consume game time, and hide the decisive act in the gaps between timed points.
when: When designing a timeline-based mystery in a game with a clock.
why: Players must order timed events from documents, and gaps conceal the key act.

text: Give a supply or key ingredient a plausible but thin in-world reason, and let a later location reveal its true use.
when: designing a dungeon's supplies or key ingredients

text: Design a choice where both options look identical to the player, and let the outcome depend on a fact the player can learn later.
when: Authoring a decision whose right answer should be discoverable
why: Hidden stakes reward investigation without making the choice arbitrary

text: A document split into fragments across several rooms can make a puzzle that tests whether the player matches each fragment to the correct source.
Introduce a puzzle object whose use is not yet explained, but make sure the facts needed to guess its purpose are already available to the player.
why: Lets the player earn the solution by reasoning.

text: Make a puzzle's key a name the player has heard in dialogue, and let players find the cipher's structure by trial before the key is needed.
when: when designing a cipher or code puzzle
why: a key tied to story is recognisable, and trial builds understanding first

text: Reward a partial solution with a readable fragment, so the player gains confidence and motivation before the full solution.
when: when a puzzle has several stages of solution
why: early partial success encourages further effort

text: Build a provisional model of a hidden plan from scattered partial clues, and test it later rather than treating isolated fragments as firm conclusions.
when: when only a few clues are clear and the meaning is unknown

text: Require exact event order only when a general window would not settle the outcome.
when: Deciding how precise an investigation must be
why: Unneeded precision wastes effort and invites contested testimony

text: Let a mundane system, such as a board game or a shop haggle, carry a state change that matters later.
Players enjoy solutions reached through logic more than solutions reached by instinct, so puzzles should reward reasoning from the presented facts.
when: Designing a mystery reveal
why: Reasoning from evidence gives more satisfying payoff than guessing

text: Set an explicit proof threshold in deduction puzzles, so a vague rumor plus any nearby object does not count as confirmation.
when: Designing deduction puzzles.
why: Without a threshold, any object can be read as confirmation.

text: A puzzle built on few simple rules and visible evidence tests analysis, while one with many interacting moves tests attention; choose the mix that matches the intended skill.
when: designing puzzles

text: Give players a partial view, such as a window, grate or wall gap, rather than full access, so the puzzle is solved by observation.
when: designing a locked-room puzzle

text: Plant origin mismatches on items as puzzle hooks, such as a label that contradicts where the item was made.
Repeated sequences in clue fragments, such as a list read in order with a note after each item, can reveal the structure of a lock or code.
An NPC who should have moved on but remains in place can serve as a clue, and a player who notices this has found the lead.
when: an NPC's behaviour is inconsistent with its scripted timing
why: A stalled NPC signals that something has interrupted the expected routine.

text: A puzzle can require three linked checks answered in order, with each answer unlocking the next.
when: Designing a puzzle built around a single clue.
why: Ordered unlocking keeps the player moving through the intended chain.

text: Avoid plausible but weak deceptions when facing a sharp adversary, since a flimsy lie fails under close scrutiny.
A timing puzzle can have the player decode times in a victim's notebook, with a fixed timer setting the window for the event.
when: Designing a deduction puzzle around written times and a timed effect.
why: Fixed timers give players a bounded question to solve.

text: An investigation puzzle can require the player to match three facts: who was present, who held the item, and who gained from its use.
when: designing a deduction puzzle

text: A contamination puzzle can require the player to trace the victim's unique habit rather than the obvious source.
when: designing a poisoning or exposure mystery

text: An impossible entry is fair when its mechanism is physical and can be inspected on the object itself.
A puzzle that requires the player to test each conjecture against known facts before the next step unlocks makes reasoning, not guessing, the path to progress.
when: Designing a puzzle that rewards deduction.
why: Gating progress on verified conclusions ties advancement to the player's reasoning rather than trial and error.

text: Adjacent cells and brief co-location of prisoners can set up a witness-collusion puzzle for the player to solve.
when: Designing prisoner placement in game levels.
why: Proximity creates opportunities for information exchange.

text: A hidden identity behind a mask can carry an investigation, and the audience's expectations are reversed when the identity is revealed.
A character can pass hidden knowledge forward to another with an instruction to recall it later, carrying the secret across time.
when: A reveal must be delivered after a delay

text: A faction's official theory sets which leads are pursued and which are dropped as dead ends, so modelling it as data shapes the investigation.
A hidden constraint on who may learn of the player's success restricts available actions and shapes the choices the player makes.
when: when designing objectives that involve secrecy
why: the constraint closes some options and pushes play toward others

text: When a clue contradicts a puzzle's starting assumption, players are forced to reopen the chain of reasoning and reconsider earlier conclusions.
when: Designing a deduction puzzle with an explicit starting assumption.
why: Contradiction breaks a settled path and prompts re-evaluation.

text: Removing nearby alternatives forces a target to search further, raising the chance they go to the spot where a substitute is kept.
when: a target can satisfy a need from several places
why: fewer local options shift their route

text: A key surrendered under pressure changes the NPC's relationship with the player, so it can work as a meaningful release mechanic.
Rate each knowledge area on a six-level scale: nil, feeble, variable, practical, profound, immense.
when: when building a character's skill or knowledge profile

text: Plasters, bandages and jewellery can be changed or added; confirm a trace before relying on it rather than assuming it is genuine.
Hiding a character's face or identity for too long makes the delay feel like a trick rather than fair withholding.
when: Withholding a reveal to build suspense
why: Excessive delay breaks trust and makes the withholding look arbitrary.

text: Puzzle reasoning can rest on a hidden premise, such as the identity of a body, and the answers may finally overturn it.
when: Solving a mystery where questions seem settled
why: Unexamined assumptions can block the correct explanation.

text: Some repeated actions are simply required procedure, so repetition alone does not prove hidden intent.
Assuming a surviving fragment tells the whole story leads to wrong conclusions; combine it with other records before reconstructing its meaning.
Correct guesses earn more praise than sound inferences with modest results, which encourages overconfidence.
A fixed goal can hide assumptions, so check that the endpoint is actually reachable before building the plan on it.
when: when an endpoint is set early
why: an optimistic target may rest on unexamined premises

text: Overlooking how a weapon or tool works can rule out a suspect entirely, so the mechanism itself should be treated as evidence.
when: Inferring the instrument behind a trace
why: The mechanism constrains who could have used it and how

text: A lure fails if others share the code, because the target may recognise the message as a forgery.
1) Run a continuous line through the hidden route. 2) Agree a tug pattern to confirm contact. 3) Agree a second pattern to signal that the exchange should continue.
when: Two parties must communicate through a concealed passage
why: A pre-agreed code avoids sound that could be overheard

text: 1) Choose a target and list what their world exposes: associates, residence, routine, transport, servants. 2) Plan access, delivery and safety. 3) Write the full case. 4) Write how it would be detected from the investigator's side.
when: building a puzzle or crime case
why: Covers both the offender's route and the discovery route

text: 1) Gather the day's personal notices from every relevant paper. 2) Read them in order for messages that fit the situation. 3) Check each candidate's details against known places and people. 4) Reply in a column the contact reads.
when: A hidden suspect is known to read a public column.
why: A reply placed where the contact reads it keeps the channel under the investigator's control.

text: 1) Create a town where one respected figure's accusation spreads through letters and sermons. 2) Make doubters risk punishment. 3) Require the player to identify which sources are independent.
when: Designing a community where belief spreads through authority.
why: The player must separate real corroboration from repeated authority.

text: 1) Present a will and a later deed that disagree. 2) Have the player check witnesses, dates and later transfers. 3) Let the player decide which document is valid.
when: Designing a document-based puzzle.
why: Players must weigh formal and temporal evidence, not simply trust one paper.

text: 1) Split the account into separate claims. 2) Check each claim against independent sources. 3) Accept or reject each part on its own, not the account as a whole.
when: when evaluating a multi-part statement
why: Separate judgement prevents a confirmed part from carrying an unverified part.

text: Design an incident as a set of candidate explanations, each requiring specific evidence, so the player can mark each off as evidence is found.
when: When designing a mystery or puzzle with several possible explanations.
why: Explicit candidates give the player a structured way to track progress.

text: 1) Locate residual marks such as impressions, dents, holes and dust outlines. 2) Infer each displaced object's original position from its marks. 3) Restore objects to those positions. 4) Trace lines of fire or movement through the restored layout.
when: Reconstructing an arrangement that was disturbed
why: Marks left behind are more reliable than the moved objects themselves

text: Design an ambiguous clue or action with two plausible readings, one false, and make the correct reading confirmable by a second checkable test.
when: A clue should mislead briefly without being unfair; writing an action with ambiguous meaning
why: A clue with only a false meaning cannot be solved fairly; single-cause motives leave players nothing to test

text: Tie each required condition, such as a debt, deposit or stolen item, to a playable trait or location, so players eliminate candidates who lacked it.
when: Designing a deduction or suspect-elimination puzzle around a required resource.
why: Players can solve the puzzle by eliminating candidates who lacked the needed resource.

text: Vary layout, method, reward and template details across generated or reused cases so earlier solutions don't carry over; repeat one signature deliberately only as a clue.
when: When generating many encounters or reusing a case template.
why: Variation prevents easy memorisation; unchanged details let players carry over the earlier answer.

text: Present a known result, such as a locked vault or dead guard, and let players reconstruct the event from body or object positions and missing items, not a cutscene.
when: Designing a mystery puzzle.
why: Backward reasoning gives players a clear goal.

text: A closing cutscene or journal entry can reconstruct the villain's plan in order, replaying events and linking each collected clue to its explanation so players can check them.
when: when closing a mystery in a game

text: Hide a key to an alias or a puzzle solution in in-game text, such as a referenced play, library book or codex item description, that players must find and read closely.
when: Designing puzzles around signatures, codes or items.

text: When a puzzle seems impossible, check ordinary movement and routes before accepting magical or supernatural explanations.
when: when designing or solving a seemingly impossible event
why: Most apparent impossibilities resolve into plain routes once checked

text: Design evidence so it supports both innocent and guilty readings, and let the player decide whether the explanation fits.
when: building mystery clues around a suspect's story

text: Do not rely on a staged threat against a target who can check the facts or call for help.
Avoid staging a confrontation while the evidence is still conjecture, since a reconstruction built on guesswork can be challenged.
Do not press a suspect toward a reversal of their account that the questioner cannot support with evidence.
Tie a puzzle to a visible timer, such as a bell or a patrol route, so the player must act within a window.
Hide the solution while showing NPCs' reasoning, so players can check deductions against the evidence themselves.
Let the player see a hidden event, such as a cutscene or remembered vision, that in-world characters do not know, to create dramatic irony.
when: Designing scenes where player knowledge should exceed character knowledge
why: Player knowledge that characters lack generates suspense around their actions.

text: Keep the resolution brief and confirm the outcome rather than revealing new information about the crime.
Let a quiet guide NPC seem uninterested while quietly tracking the real lead, revealing this only at the reveal.
when: designing a mystery
why: a concealed lead rewards later recall

text: Offer character-based tells as an alternate route when a timeline check fails, but require the physical mechanism for final proof.
Do not stage a false lead when it could harm an innocent person, or when the culprit is unlikely to react.
when: planning a bluff or misdirection
why: Misdirection costs more than it gains in those cases.

text: Gate an NPC's cooperation behind a wait or a shift in tone, so a suspected player must spend time before the NPC talks.
when: a puzzle NPC should pressure a suspected player

text: In a timed puzzle, use waiting periods, such as a transfer that completes after a set number of in-game days, so the player must infer its status.
Let an NPC offer a theory, such as poisoning, that the player must check with a test before acting on it.
Not all hidden or unsolved events in a game world should reach the player's investigation, so the visible cases should be presented as a sample.
when: Designing a world with many events and few player-facing cases.
why: Players then understand that unsolved mysteries are not the full set of what happened.

text: The designer should know the complete solution of a mystery from the start, even when the player-facing surface looks disordered.
when: Designing a puzzle with an exact, checkable answer.
why: A fully known solution lets every clue be placed consistently.

text: State the governing rule of a puzzle, such as what a lock accepts or what an item does, in plain text before the player faces the test.
when: A puzzle's solution depends on a stated constraint
why: A known constraint lets players reason to the answer rather than guess

text: Give puzzles a safe test, such as exposing a creature to a substance, so players can identify the dangerous item without losing the run.
when: when designing identification puzzles
why: A safe test lets players gather evidence through action

text: Make a motive discoverable through a recalculation puzzle that the player solves using figures given in the game.
when: A financial motive is meant to be found by the player.
why: Solving from supplied numbers rewards careful reading.

text: Put coded notices in an in-world newspaper or noticeboard, and let each message's content reveal its place in the sequence.
when: Designing an ordering or decoding puzzle
why: Players can rebuild the sequence from internal clues without dates

text: The true answer may be the least obvious one, provided it is the only explanation that fits all planted clues.
In a rotating-suspect puzzle, give each NPC a clue and a motive that makes them plausible until the player clears them.
when: designing a who-did-it puzzle with several NPCs
why: each candidate must seem viable until evidence removes them

text: Keep a puzzle's intended solution path out of UI, tutorial text and NPC dialogue, so players cannot adapt to it in advance.
State the intended sequence of events for a puzzle, then check that every clue supports it and that no clue points elsewhere too strongly.
when: When designing a mystery or deduction puzzle.
why: Misleading clues break the intended solution.

text: Use a family tree or inheritance record as a puzzle object, so players work out who gains before choosing a suspect.
when: when designing motive-based puzzles

text: Build puzzles whose answer uses a general rule players already know, such as a mechanical or chemical principle, to reward lateral thinking.
when: when designing deduction puzzles

text: Use objects with layered meaning, such as a sinister-looking item with a legitimate source, so players must check the source before drawing conclusions.
when: Designing a clue object for an investigation puzzle.

text: In a poisoning puzzle, make the food served to all guests safe, pushing the player toward the single item one NPC consumed.
when: Designing a poisoning mystery
why: Eliminating the shared source focuses the search

text: Make a puzzle's solution depend on information the player can reasonably gather, not on lucky timing, and include at least one fact that could contradict it.
when: designing a deduction puzzle
why: gatherable evidence keeps the answer fair and a falsifiable clue keeps it testable

text: Hold back one criterion until needed, so a final test can clear or condemn suspects late in the investigation.
when: Designing a multi-stage deduction
why: A withheld test keeps the final decision open

text: Let a dismissal or expulsion quest resolve through its procedural issue, while the real trigger surfaces through dialogue or documents.
when: designing a quest driven by a hidden grievance

text: In measured-search puzzles, let a first-marker mistake grow along a line, rewarding careful measurement and landmark checks.
Set a puzzle around a physical clock such as wet ink, drying blood or melting wax, so players can reconstruct when a door was opened or a trap set.
when: designing timing-based puzzles

text: Encode a puzzle solution in fixed objects, such as a seated figure or a chair facing a doorway, so the player can infer where a threat must be.
Make every item needed to unlock a puzzle visible before the unlocking step.
when: When designing a puzzle that depends on found items.

text: A room of scattered oddities can be a puzzle with several plausible readings, where only one covers every item and reveals a lore clue.
Let players restart a mystery from its first event after a failed theory, keeping earlier clues in place so the rerun is informative.
when: Designing a puzzle or investigation quest with several possible theories.
why: Retained clues let players rebuild the chain without losing progress.

text: Let players re-enact a scene with NPCs in set positions to test whether sound or line of sight reaches a given spot.
when: designing a physical reconstruction puzzle
why: the test uses the game's own geometry and audio

text: Use object counts or shelf orderings as puzzle inputs that match a place name or code.
Let players compare partial clues, such as a torn fragment or faint marking, and grade how strong each match is.
when: designing a clue-matching puzzle
why: Graded matches reward judgment about uncertainty

text: Switch the language of a puzzle so the player must reconsider earlier assumptions.
when: Designing a multi-stage text puzzle.
why: A language change forces re-evaluation of prior readings.

text: Make sure the true hiding location is among the candidates the player can check, or deduction by elimination collapses.
when: Designing a deduction puzzle around hidden items.
why: Elimination can only reach the answer if it is among the candidates.

text: Make paired puzzle objects differ in one visible detail, so the player notices it and infers that one was swapped or moved.
when: designing matched puzzle props
why: A single difference is discoverable without being obvious.

text: Make a constraint physical and testable, such as a binding that can only be freed with a specific tool, so the player can reason about what is possible.
when: Designing a restraint or obstacle with a clear limit.
why: A concrete constraint gives the player a definite rule to test against.

text: Design scenes where body position or items on a table encode what happened, so players must notice what seems off.
when: Authoring a crime scene that players inspect.
why: Visible posture and objects give players clues to reconstruct events.

text: Make the decisive test a repeatable demonstration, so the player can watch the mechanism work before the final confrontation.
Hiding middle links of a deduction heightens the reveal but can look like magic; show the clue so the audience can verify reasoning.
when: when a solution is revealed to the audience
why: Unverifiable reasoning makes the solver seem to have guessed.

text: Ordeal results can look random if hidden variables drive them, but hidden or arbitrary outcomes feel unfair unless rules are visible and testable.
when: designing trials, traps or tests of skill
why: Hidden variables, such as a weighted object or a known tide, can stay fair; players can only learn and trust a challenge whose outcome follows from visible rules.

text: A marvellous effect should still have a simple, discoverable mechanism, while a complicated puzzle should be built from many traceable steps.
when: when designing a puzzle with a striking surface effect
why: Surface wonder pleases players, but discoverable method keeps it fair

text: Puzzle-focused mysteries need full clue visibility, while mood- or character-focused stories can loosen fair-play rigour.
when: choosing a story's primary aim

text: Keeping a secret preserves leverage over the victim, while revealing or using it spends that leverage permanently.
when: A quest item or secret can be held or exposed.
why: A secret's value depends on staying hidden.

text: A cipher that is too hard stalls players, while one that is too easy gives the solution away, so difficulty should sit between these extremes.
A decoy that looks like the prize must be explained afterwards, or players may feel cheated.
when: A timed reveal delivers a substitute item.
why: Unexplained substitution breaks trust in the reveal.

text: Partial text becomes meaningful only when combined with a second clue found elsewhere, so split key information across locations.
A reconstruction puzzle can ask the player to order a set of tracks and check the answer against the ground layout.
when: When designing a tracking or deduction puzzle.
why: The ground layout gives an objective check.

text: An elaborate mystery rests on one simple core fact; its complexity is a set of distracting details arranged around that fact.
A path leading to a secluded spot is a shortcut for anyone using that spot, so the path alone does not identify one particular user.
Keep small past facts on record, since a fact from an earlier case may bear on a present one and can be drawn out when needed.
when: A past fact may relate to a current matter

text: A test-action mechanic lets players compare a character's attributes with evidence on site, turning a stat check into an investigation.
A requirement narrows the field only when requirements stack, since many people may share any single requirement.
Gate a puzzle's final solution behind separate checkable conditions, such as motive, means and access, so the player confirms each before solving.
when: Designing multi-step deduction puzzles.
why: Each confirmed condition gives feedback and narrows the answer.

text: A puzzle system can track a knowledge set for each secret, so an NPC knows a hidden location only if a named source told them.
when: designing secrets that spread through NPCs
why: tracked sources make knowledge spread consistently and checkable

text: A container can carry a state flag, such as handled or untouched, and the player must preserve that state for the evidence to stay valid.
Conditions can change between events, so an assumed snow cover or gap must be checked against the actual record before it anchors a window.
A predicted item may not exist, and an intended break in the pattern can make the prediction wrong.
when: Predicting a missing item from a sequence
why: Patterns are not always continuous by design

text: A sequence of only two or three points can fit many rules, so extrapolation from it is unreliable.
when: Inferring a pattern from few records
why: Too few points underdetermine the rule

text: A list of profile conditions written after a suspect is chosen can be tailored to fit that person.
when: Building a suspect profile.
why: Post hoc conditions confirm the chosen suspect instead of testing them.

text: 1) Tally every symbol's occurrences over the full message, noting the rarest ones too. 2) Equate the top symbol with the language's most frequent letter. 3) Verify the guess using another pattern, such as how often the symbol appears in doubled pairs.
when: simple substitution ciphers with enough text for counts to be meaningful; avoid short messages or ciphers designed to flatten frequencies

text: State a challenge's constraints exactly before the attempt begins, so players can judge whether any workaround is allowed.
when: designing a locked-room or restricted-resource puzzle
why: Written rules make the solution checkable and fair

text: Track 'death looks natural' separately from 'death was caused' in game state, so foul play must be established before the motive board opens.
Represent torn or split items with edge data so the player must rotate and match fragments to confirm they belong together.
when: Designing a fragment or clue item
why: Fitting gives the player a checkable, physical test

text: Let the player's own action, such as knocking on a surface, trigger the proof, so the reveal is interactive rather than read off.
when: designing the moment a hidden truth is exposed
why: The player feels responsible for the discovery.

text: Offer a replay mode that resets room conditions such as heat, locked doors and latch positions, letting players repeat or time an action under identical conditions to confirm a theory.
when: when designing a deduction mechanic involving room conditions
why: resetting state lets the player test a claim repeatedly

text: An absent key document can act as a quest pivot whose absence implicates a faction the player must work out.
when: designing a quest built on a missing item

text: Reward dialogue that pushes the player to stay or accept a gift can hide a binding mechanic the player should notice later.
when: Designing rewards that encourage a player to stay or accept an item

text: Recording an item's removal as a state flag implies a second actor and gives the player a concrete lead.
When a captured NPC refuses to answer, the quest flag stays locked, so the player must find another route, such as a document that the refusal protected.
when: An NPC refuses to give information in a quest.
why: The refusal blocks the flag, so the quest can only advance through an alternative path.

text: A prisoner held in an intermediate state, neither dead nor free, can regain a retrial when a stated condition is met.
when: a judicial outcome that is neither final nor clear
why: the condition keeps a path to retrial open

text: Keep a timeline of world events the designer can replay, so an apparent NPC delay can be traced back to a known cause.
when: Designing a simulated world where NPC actions must be explainable.
why: A replayable record lets designers verify that delays have causes.

text: Require two independent NPC witnesses before a quest flag advances, so one mistaken witness cannot trigger an accusation.
An opponent who has planned around a condition, such as a rival being incapacitated, will act on that assumption and may expose their plan while doing so.
when: an antagonist counts on a safeguard failing
why: they commit to the expected condition and act on it

text: Show contract terms and the consequence of failure on screen, so players can see what is at stake before committing.
When an NPC's stake changes, such as a rival's consent or a contract's worth after a world event, their motive weakens or intensifies, and players can recompute it.
when: Designing rivalries that evolve over a playthrough, or a world event alters an agreement's worth.
why: Incentives follow the current value of what is at stake, so changing stakes shift which rival has a motive.

text: An NPC who abruptly drops a demand signals that they learned something hidden, so the reversal can serve as a clue.
A reversed expectation at the end, such as a secured object found gone, produces a sense of impossible disappearance.
when: a locked or secured setup is followed by a surprise
why: the expected state is overturned after the object seemed secured

text: A recurring demand from an authority figure for a quick result can act as a timed pressure mechanic that changes available dialogue but not the underlying facts.
why: pressure alters options without altering evidence

text: Unresolved disputes compound over years or decades, with an early issue growing more violent until it erupts into a public crisis.
when: a community dispute is left unaddressed
why: Each unresolved wrong adds grievance.

text: Delay a completion reward until the quest-giver has been briefed, so payment follows completed duty.
when: designing mission rewards

text: Tie a mercy choice to a condition the player can check, such as whether the victim is still at risk.
Give each NPC in a conspiracy system a concrete reason to join. Players can then test a theory by checking each NPC's gain or loss before acting on it.
when: designing a game with hidden conspiracies
why: Motivated conspirators make the theory checkable and believable

text: Post bounty notices in towns describing a missing item or NPC, and let rumours spread so other NPCs carry the lead.
Allow an arrest on a case board only when motive, opportunity, and instrument are all filled.
when: When designing an accusation mechanic
why: Requiring key elements prevents premature accusation

text: Make opposing NPC factions co-own a shared task, such as a bridge repair, before a locked area opens.
Let an appeal to a higher authority revise a severe sentence into a lesser one, such as exile.
An arrest system where the accused must prove innocence can add restricted access and time limits, such as limited visits, that shape how the player can respond.
when: Designing detention or legal-process mechanics.
why: Limits on access create pressure and force the player to prioritize actions.

text: Execution permanently ends an accused character, while release on a condition removes them from the play space instead of killing them.
when: choosing an ending for an accused character
why: the two outcomes differ in finality and in whether the character survives

text: Place a decoy figure in the bed that the player is told to trust, then reveal it as a placed prop once the escape is found.
when: designing a locked room where the occupant appears to be present
why: A trusted decoy hides the escape until its falseness is shown.

text: Clear the most obvious suspect early with a timing alibi, so the suspect's hiding window is closed before the decoy item is found.
1) List everyone close to the object or with knowledge of the plan. 2) Note each person's presence, absence and access. 3) Extend the list to people who hold information but not physical presence.
when: A theft or secret depends on private knowledge or restricted access.
why: Mapping both presence and information reveals all plausible sources of a leak.

text: 1) List physical traces at the scene. 2) Infer one trait from each trace. 3) Intersect the traits into a single profile. 4) Check each candidate against that profile.

1) Show that the framed party is the easiest suspect. 2) Plant physical evidence with a timing detail that rules out later planting. 3) Reopen an early dismissed clue. 4) Prove the self-framing with a reconstruction.
when: Designing a mystery where the obvious suspect is innocent and the victim framed them.
why: The reveal inverts the case, and each step is visible before the final proof.

text: Record each NPC sighting with a confidence value, and require a suspect description to match at least one physical clue before an arrest is possible.
when: the player can arrest based on witness reports
why: Sightings alone are weak, so a physical match guards against wrong arrests.

text: A single obvious suspect carrying most suspicious clues makes the mystery easy to read, so a real route to the answer must run through a different character.
when: designing a mystery with a misleading suspect
why: Players who see every clue pointing one way suspect a trick and stop checking alternatives.

text: Observers side with a well-regarded or officially standing person when accused, since reputation makes the accusation seem implausible, leaving the accuser few supporters.
when: the accused is well-regarded or holds official standing in the community
why: Reputation biases judgment before evidence is weighed; public standing favours established authority.

text: Reticence, distant manners, unusual behaviour, sour looks or a difficult temper are not evidence of guilt; accusers may cite them as motive, so judge motive and opportunity separately.
when: a difficult manner, demeanour or unusual behaviour is cited as grounds for suspicion
why: Temperament is not evidence of action or motive; reputation gets confused with evidence.

text: Judging witnesses by reputation can mislead as easily as it helps: a poor reputation can decide the outcome even when the witness saw something real.

Reputation, manner, standing or reported accusation is not evidence, nor the main filter: a bad record is not proof of guilt, a good one not proof of truth, though it shapes how claims are read. Check each claim against underlying documents and a verifiable link to the act; substitution often goes unnoticed. Accusations can prove false.
A reputation for discretion can make a character both trusted with a secret task and unlikely to be suspected of wrongdoing.
when: a respected figure is asked to carry something
why: Reputation lowers suspicion and raises trust.

text: Witnesses of good standing can make a legend seem credible, so their reputation stands in for checkable detail.
when: A tradition rests on a respected witness's account
why: Audiences accept a trusted reporter's word in place of verifiable specifics.

text: A single unfavorable feature, observed in passing, can fix a lasting reputation for a person among observers.
when: When a neighbor or passerby forms a lasting judgment from one visible trait.
why: A striking feature overshadows the person's wider conduct.

text: Wary opponents suspect a decoy and may change the meeting, so a sting can fail in a way the player must notice.
when: the opponent is cautious and expects a trap
why: a suspected set-up raises the cost of walking into it

text: A neighbour's long-standing reputation for an unkind remark can turn into a charge once a misfortune follows, even without proven fault.
when: a bad event happens after a past dispute
why: People link misfortune to earlier words and old reputation.

text: Reputation may seed suspicion or serve as flavour only; require physical evidence before the player forms a firm conclusion.
when: designing suspicion mechanics in a game
why: Reputation suggests where to look; evidence decides.

text: Give a trusted NPC a reputation bonus that delays early arrest, and show the player when that protection is lost.
An apology or restitution can serve as a second layer of misdirection, making the guilty party look reasonable.
when: Designing a culprit who must appear trustworthy
why: Visible good conduct lowers suspicion

text: Show a public reputation in one place and a hidden lifestyle in another, so players must connect them through records.
when: when designing a character with a concealed second life

text: Record faction actions and reputation as visible facts so players can build a case from what a group did rather than from a confession.
why: Observable recorded actions support inference more than stated claims.

text: Give extra care to people with unblemished reputations, since an accusation can damage them before any finding is made.
Introductions and reputation can act as keys to escape, so a player with the right contacts has an easier way out.
when: when designing escape or release options
why: Social access rewards player relationships.

text: A respected figure can hide wrongdoing; check their claimed routines against records, especially activity kept out of public view, rather than trusting reputation.
when: A reputable person is named as a suspect.
why: Respectability does not establish honesty, and concealment can hide wrongdoing.

text: A village reputation system in which a refused trade raises suspicion among other NPCs, spreading through their dialogue, lets player actions shape community attitudes.
when: when designing NPC reputation that travels between characters
why: Small social slights can propagate into broad distrust

text: Model a town reputation value that raises suspicion on an NPC; only past a threshold does the NPC move to a magistrate for review.
when: Designing suspicion systems for town NPCs
why: A threshold keeps rumor from escalating without limit

text: A public act such as breaking a seal in front of NPCs can serve as the reveal event and change the world state.
A reputation system can reward open actions and penalise covert ones, so player standing depends on how investigation is conducted.
when: Designing a detective's reputation or morality meter.
why: Social standing responds to the visibility of a character's methods.

text: An NPC who helped condemn someone and then confesses publicly can unlock new quest paths or change faction standing.
when: a town event lets the NPC speak publicly
why: Public admission alters how other characters and factions treat the NPC and the wronged party.

text: Using force against an NPC in front of others can lower the player's reputation, since onlookers may frame the player as the aggressor.
when: Violence is used in view of witnesses.
why: Observers judge who started the conflict, not only who was right.

text: After cleaning up and changing appearance, a player who has been seen can move openly without drawing a second look from NPCs.
when: after being seen by NPCs
why: a changed appearance lowers suspicion

text: An NPC's suspicion can rise with the player's visible agitation and fall when the player shows resolve or sudden irritation.
Gossip flags can persist after a player disproves them, so one new fact should shift trust only partly and repeated proof should be required.
when: designing NPC reputation systems
why: slow updating matches how entrenched opinions resist evidence

text: A system where a false accusation costs the player money, reputation or an ally makes wrongful suspicion a consequential choice.
when: designing consequences for player accusations
why: Costs attached to accusation discourage careless blame and reward careful evidence gathering.

text: A reputation flag set by an accusation can be cleared by a later repair event, and the cleared state changes which factions accept the player.
when: a player is accused by a faction and later cleared
why: faction standing is tied to the flag state

text: Treating a strong suspicion built on an accuser's word and a suspect's bad reputation as if it were proof mistakes suspicion for evidence.
A profile built on reputation can harden into a fixed belief that filters out evidence contrary to it.
when: Profiling an offender from their reputation

text: Reputation can carry an accusation forward without new evidence, so the reputation itself becomes the charge.
when: An accusation continues after its original evidence weakens

text: A bad reputation can point to too many suspects at once, which dilutes the case; narrow the field by linking each motive to the crime.
when: a victim had many enemies
why: unconnected misdeeds do not identify the culprit
