text: A suspect's reputation can bias how a physical clue is read, making a weak clue seem to confirm what people expect.
Reputation protected some accused people but not others, so it cannot be relied on as a defence against accusation.
Trusting a respected figure's appearance or word can lead players to wrong conclusions, because a deceiver can imitate trusted people and engineer how they look.
when: when a character's reputation or look is used as evidence of innocence or guilt
why: Appearance can be manipulated, so visible identity may not match what is real.

text: Do not drop or clear a suspect because of a trustworthy reputation or fame; a respected person's motive must still be considered, since people routinely conceal real conduct.
why: Reluctance to suspect the familiar lets many crimes go undetected.

text: Model suspicion as a spreading state over a network of grudges and property ties, where each accusation raises the chance connected neighbours accuse too.
Make reputation a gameplay variable, so a trusted NPC can carry an item past guards who would search a stranger.
when: designing stealth or social checkpoints
why: Reputation changes what the player can get away with.

text: Make an NPC's stated request a cover for a final question about timing or access, so players must notice the real aim.
when: designing NPC dialogue with hidden purpose

text: A long record of escaping conviction can itself serve as evidence of a group's reputation, though it does not prove any specific act.
when: Judging a group's reputation from its legal history.
why: Repeated acquittals signal influence or intimidation, not guilt in a given case.

text: Have a quest giver exploit the player's reputation or identity in a scheme, so a later reversal changes the player's role.
Store each rumour with its source and a reliability tag, flagging secret or untraceable reports as unverified.
when: Designing a reputation or rumour system
why: Recording source and reliability lets the player weigh gossip rather than treat it as fact.

text: Tie restitution in a game to who petitioned, leaving unnamed victims without a remedy unless players find them.
Record public confrontations in game state so that later NPCs can reference the player's reputation.
Show the public record openly, such as completed quests, donations, and reputation, and keep the private deed in a hidden flag that a later scene reveals.
Give an avoidant NPC a hidden suspicion value, and let the player's questions raise how often the NPC deflects.
when: designing an NPC who avoids a topic
why: the avoidance then reflects the player's line of questioning

text: Store an accuser's suspicion as a weighted value that drops when contrary evidence appears, instead of locking it when an arrest is made.
when: Designing AI suspicion or accusation systems.

text: Withhold the decisive fact or document until the scene where it matters, delivering it at peak tension, when the audience is most surprised and has context to feel its weight.
when: staging a final revelation, or when a case or scene needs a turn
why: Timing maximizes surprise and makes the answer memorable; delivery at peak tension increases impact.

text: Gate an NPC's disclosure or an item's hidden content behind a condition, such as finding a document or recognizing a claim, so players must obtain it first.
when: designing items or NPCs that gate information behind progress

text: Give each withheld answer, such as a name, pending offer or key evidence, a firm point where it surfaces; overlong stalling frustrates and exhausts the audience and wears down trust.
when: when extending suspense, or when a reveal is held back many steps without new information
why: Players want resolution once they have enough clues and may reject vague build-up; long withholding without payoff makes readers lose patience, so balance the wait against the payoff.

text: A sentence that breaks off signals that a fact is being kept back, not that nothing is there, and a listener absorbed in their own feelings often fails to pursue the gap.
when: A character halts mid-sentence while speaking about something important
why: Distraction lets the listener miss the omission while the reader notices it

text: A character holding back knowledge often shows it through a shift in tone, a sudden hesitation, or a retort that sounds like a boast.
when: A character knows more than they have said so far.

text: Layered safeguards can make a planner nearly impossible to convict, even when the planner's influence is clear.
Institutional records, such as a patient or staff record, can confirm a person's presence at a place and time.
when: when verifying a claimed presence
why: Records made at the time are independent of the suspect.

text: Plant a chain of small cues, such as hints in early dialogue, that pay off later and teach players to notice details that matter.
when: designing a mystery, dialogue payoff, or reveal that will come later in the story
why: A planted hint lets the player connect the reveal to earlier evidence; noticing trains attention for the reveal.

text: Let each step of the solution arrive after a pause, tied to clues already in plain view, so the answer feels earned rather than imposed.
when: a reveal must feel fair or reward attentive players, especially a multi-step solution
why: Clues already seen let the audience match the answer themselves.

text: Spread a reveal across several scenes or explanations; answering every oddity or question at once overwhelms the audience, blurs the logic and deflates suspense.
when: when resolving a mystery or when a suspect's account explains an entire plot at the end
why: Dense exposition overwhelms the audience and blurs the logic.

text: Read responses before escalating; do not press every contradiction at once, moving on after a few, since escalation raises the witness's guard and may warn them.
when: several contradictions have been found in one interview
why: Escalating pressure on every point makes the witness more defensive and less revealing.

text: Withhold full answers near a key revelation or when a character is about to disclose something important, so the audience waits with the protagonist while tension lingers and stakes grow.
when: near a key answer, or a character is near a key disclosure
why: Delay keeps the audience waiting and attentive.

text: Show partial, precise details such as a partly seen hand or reflected light so the audience infers, then give a complete view as payoff when lighting aligns.
when: building a tense scene
why: Partial visuals direct attention and invite inference.

text: Hold a fact back and release it later as a favour to create a natural pacing beat in an investigation quest.
Introducing a figure through rumour or background before meeting them gives the later encounter weight and makes it feel earned.
Reveal facts in the order they were experienced rather than by importance, so the audience must reconstruct their significance later.
when: when the audience should reread for clues
why: Delayed understanding rewards attention to earlier details.

text: Uneven intensity within a mark, such as deeper marks at crossings, reveals the shape of the object that made it.
why: the object's structure is pressed into the mark

text: A secret message that is plainly simple, where a real one would be coded or technical, may be staged to be read at once.
when: Evaluating a note or message meant to be secret

text: Avoid heavy withholding in short scenes, because a delay without a quick payoff becomes frustrating.
when: short scenes
why: little time remains for the payoff to justify the wait

text: Reveal a central fact only after minor witnesses have built suspicion, because revealing it early leaves the suspense unbuilt.
when: the disclosure should change the audience's view of everyone present

text: End a section on a character's reaction to a new fact while withholding its content, shifting the question from what happened to what it means.
why: the reaction creates suspense before the detail is given

text: Sort known facts into groups that fit together and those that do not; a misfit element may be padding that hides the true purpose.
when: Public activities and private interests seem inconsistent

text: Establish a suspect's debts, dependencies and history early, giving motive without yet pointing at a specific crime.
Alternate heavy argument, sudden revelation and light relief to vary pacing, and place a jarring event where it undercuts the mood.
Open a mystery with an early paradox and several plausible explanations, so players test theories rather than follow a single scripted path.
when: designing the opening of an investigation
why: competing explanations invite active reasoning

text: Pace a long explanation through questions from another character, since a plain list of clues feels like an information dump.
Make a withheld entry the reward for a later investigation, revealing what the excerpted version hid.
why: Withheld content gives investigation a payoff.

text: How quickly an institution is set up and starts operating is a detail worth weighing when judging whether its proceedings were fair.
when: judging the fairness of a newly created body

text: Create quiet phases where players wait for a trigger, then cut to a scene showing the antagonist moving toward the player's goal.
when: Designing pacing for a hunt or pursuit.
why: The cut shows the threat advancing while the player is still unaware of it.

text: Let a discovery stay secret until the player chooses to reveal it, so the player decides when an NPC learns of it.
when: Designing hidden-evidence or stakeout mechanics.
why: Player control over disclosure makes the timing of exposure a meaningful choice.

text: Expect leaks and pre-label them as innocent defensive measures, so observers who learn of them interpret them wrongly.
when: when a hidden activity is likely to be seen
why: Observers accept an explanation given in advance more readily than one they discover later.

text: Set a reveal window a few months after the apparent death, when the opponent has already committed to its plan.
when: Planning when a survivor reappears
why: Commitment makes the opponent's plan hard to change after the reveal.

text: Hold a reveal with camera or cutscene pacing until the player has taken a step forward.
Ending a level section at a door that opens onto an unknown area invites the player forward.
when: closing a level section
why: An unseen space raises a question the player wants answered.

text: Withholding part of a character's reasoning while promising a later explanation keeps the audience uncertain about the next step.
when: a mystery needs tension before the answer is revealed
why: uncertainty about what comes next holds attention

text: Stage reveals as reproducible measurements or steps the player can follow and check, such as a measured line from a visible landmark, not a bare assertion.
Answer the first riddle early to correct a false belief, and leave the second open, so the player keeps a live objective.
Give an ambiguous event both a rational and a supernatural explanation, each backed by records or items the player can use to test it.
when: when designing a mystery the player must judge
why: The player can weigh evidence instead of accepting one authored answer

text: Place a trap or threat near the midpoint so the investigator's own safety raises the stakes before the answer is close.
when: structuring mystery pacing

text: Withholding a fact, such as stopping mid-sentence, refusing a topic, or promising a reveal, builds suspense; the open question makes the answer feel important and holds attention until it arrives.
when: A key reveal depends on information kept from the audience, the next fact will change the investigation, a long testimony requires a held question, or a character is near a key disclosure.
why: An open question creates a need to resolve it; the unanswered question keeps attention focused until the answer arrives.

text: Delaying the explanation after a reveal, or of how a conclusion was reached, opens a gap that builds tension; the audience anticipates a close but unstated answer as clues accumulate.
when: the audience already has most facts and only needs to see how they fit, or the clues are in place for the audience to check later
why: The open question holds attention until resolved; tension rises when the audience senses a hidden answer close but not yet stated.

text: A witness who refuses or evades a question, even under oath, reveals through avoidance; the gap may point to a protected third party, so ask what the account avoids.
when: a witness declines, evades or refuses a line of questioning, including a complete-sounding story with one part refused
why: Avoidance is a form of communication; concealment signals the hidden history bears on the case, and withholding is often protective.

text: Refusing to explain a surprising situation at the moment it appears lets the audience feel the question before any answer, which builds tension.
Withholding the end of a sentence creates suspense and prompts the listener to draw their own conclusion.
when: when a character is about to disclose a sensitive point
why: an unfinished statement invites the listener to complete it

text: Keeping key facts back from both reader and characters keeps their uncertainty shared, and the withholding itself signals danger.
when: The story needs tension before the answer
why: Shared uncertainty and implied scale raise suspicion without revealing the answer.

text: If the player chooses the order of revealed evidence, each reveal can change the NPC's available responses and options.
Withholding some names until early statements shape opinion lets the first accounts frame everything that follows.
when: an investigation controls the release of names
why: early accounts set the frame for later testimony

text: A bestiary or journal entry unlocked by matching a clue phrase can list symptoms as a checklist, letting players verify an identity before acting on it.
when: Designing lore that supports identification of an unfamiliar threat.
why: A checklist of symptoms converts recognition into verifiable evidence.

text: An outside interruption, such as an arrival or a warning of limited time, forces a decision and raises urgency at the moment of confrontation.
when: when the player is about to confront a suspect or reach a key revelation
why: A sudden external event compresses time and removes room for hesitation.

text: Over-explaining after a reveal, through overt warnings, repeated phrasing or spelling out the answer, drains surprise and gives the trick away; explain only what the audience cannot infer.
A reveal that lists too many details or narrates at length reads as a lecture and drains tension; keep each step short and tied to established clues.
when: writing a final explanation of a complex case, or narrating a reveal
why: Excess detail dulls the payoff and breaks the sense of a compact deduction.

text: Revealing evidence or your own theory early warns the culprit or allies, letting them reshape their account or act first, removing the chance of a slip.
when: the witness may pass information to the suspect
why: Frank disclosure gives the other side time to respond; the culprit has no chance to slip.

text: Stating a deduction or highly specific conditions in more exact detail than needed reveals its source and alerts a suspicious reader or suspect.
when: presenting a prediction to others
why: Precision beyond what is needed exposes the deduction's source.

text: Revealing a schemer's plan, a puzzle's purpose or a hidden motive too early removes what the audience would discover or reinterpret; hold it until the context is available.
when: staging a villain's preparations or a puzzle's purpose
why: Full disclosure leaves nothing to uncover; a hidden motive held back lets players reinterpret earlier statements.

text: A hint or hidden identity shown too plainly removes the surprise of the eventual reveal and can collapse its payoff.
when: planting clues for a later reveal

text: Overusing interruptions, or repeating the same cut, wears out the revelation's effect, makes the plot feel contrived and erodes trust.
when: when the same narrative cut is used across many scenes
why: Repetition makes the device predictable.

text: Overusing withholding makes a reveal feel like a cheat; a slow approach or long delay without new stakes or payoffs lets tension drop, so each stage must add something new.
Revealing the full significance of evidence before the suspect commits to an account weakens the test of that account.
when: during a witness interview

text: Too many officers approaching at once can provoke a suspect to fire first, which makes the sting dangerous.
when: When closing in on an armed target.
why: A cornered suspect reacts defensively when surrounded by visible threats.

text: Presenting a combined case as overwhelming can pressure the listener into agreement before they have checked each link.
when: a case is presented to a decision maker
why: the framing substitutes for independent checking

text: Entering too often can disturb a fragile person being cared for, so surveillance must be balanced against that person's welfare.
when: The watched party is a patient or other vulnerable person

text: Setting description that runs too long delays the plot.
A confession that tells everything removes suspense; withholding outcomes, such as a third party's fate, keeps tension alive until a later point.
when: when a confession is delivered in the story
why: Revealed answers leave nothing for the audience to anticipate.

text: A code explained in full detail by the people who use it can be decoded by an investigator who finds that description.
Treating weak leads as real clues to make an investigation look busy.
Hiding a clue too well makes the reveal feel arbitrary, while revealing the answer too early removes suspense and the chance to reason it through.
when: Pacing the disclosure of a mystery solution.
why: The reveal must be supported by earlier clues the audience could have assembled, yet withheld long enough to create suspense.

text: Explaining a trick at length can make the writer look as if they are hiding something; keep the debunking in character and in proportion.
Explaining every reinterpretation at once removes the audience's chance to deduce; hold it back until the earlier clue has been noticed.
when: designing a reveal that reframes earlier clues
why: deduction is what makes the reveal satisfying

text: Too much recap after resolution flattens the ending, so keep the summary short.
A participant who names the culprit early breaks the planned structure, so the reveal should anticipate a player who guesses ahead.
when: Designing a mystery reveal for players who may reach the answer early.
why: Early guesses short-circuit the sequence of clues the designer built to lead to the name.

text: An overexposed aim can be read as clumsiness rather than deceit, so the audience may underestimate it.
Too many promised reveals turn into a tease and frustrate the audience. Every promised payoff must arrive.
when: Planting multiple open questions or deferred answers.
why: Unfulfilled promises erode trust in the narrative.

text: Withholding a reveal too long lets the audience forget the earlier evidence needed to appreciate it.
why: Clues lose their force when distant from the reveal.

text: Showing a clue before explaining its history keeps a mystery open, but if the explanation never arrives the reader cannot learn how the object was moved.
when: When a clue is revealed early and its explanation is deferred.
why: Without a later explanation, the reader lacks the information needed to resolve the clue.

text: Using interruptions too often turns them into a predictable device that stops creating suspense.
when: when a scene repeatedly relies on an arrival or timer to force action
why: Predictable interruptions lose their surprise and urgency.

text: 1) Deliver the full answer with method, motive and timeline. 2) Hold back one final piece of information. 3) Reveal it, forcing the audience to reinterpret earlier evidence.
1) Introduce all characters present in the enclosed space before the incident. 2) Give a clear roster. 3) Let the player track who could have been where.
when: Setting up a whodunit or locked-space mystery
why: A fixed list of present characters lets the player reason about access and alibis.

text: 1) Show the marvellous surface first. 2) Withhold the plain method. 3) Reveal the mechanism behind the effect after players have explored its implications.
when: when pacing a reveal in a mystery sequence
why: Delayed explanation keeps the surface effect intriguing before it is explained

text: 1) Establish the motive question. 2) Present the physical clues. 3) Build the proof chain. 4) Name the suspect last.
when: Designing a finale where the audience must be able to follow the chain.
why: Building proof before the name makes the reveal the payoff rather than an unsupported claim.

text: 1) Offer the player a human or natural explanation first. 2) Let them test it against access and timing. 3) Reveal the supernatural cause only when the mundane options fail.
when: Designing a mystery whose reveal is supernatural.
why: The reveal feels earned when the player can confirm that no mundane explanation remains.

text: Every withheld fact or reveal must be paid off later and its clues placed in the record beforehand; overlong withholding without fair hints feels like cheating.
when: when information is deliberately kept from the audience or delayed for suspense
why: Unpaid reveals break trust; a reader can only judge a reveal fairly if the needed facts were available.

text: Hold the answer back until the evidence is complete, so an accusation cannot be disputed and the player's own deduction is rewarded.
when: timing a confrontation in a mystery
why: Incomplete proof lets the accused dispute the claim; a reveal given early leaves the player nothing to deduce.

text: Deliver the full motive as a retrospective account after the immediate question is answered, tying each revealed fact back to clues the player already holds.
when: Closing a mystery whose motive depends on earlier backstory.
why: Re-reading earlier evidence rewards the player and avoids a stalled recap.

text: Flag unusual details at intake, such as terms far beyond the normal rate, as signals that call for an explanation.
why: Anomalies often hide a strong underlying reason.

text: Let an early character warn the player about a named faction leader, creating a pending objective the player can act on later.
Place backstory items, such as a letter or a scandal record, early so they can later serve as motive or access clues.
when: designing background material for a mystery
why: items introduced early can be reused as clues without new exposition

text: Show a tool and its stated limits before the situation needs it, so its later use feels prepared rather than conveniently invented.
when: when a later scene depends on the tool
why: a stated limit makes later use believable and fair

text: Stage an unmasking before several witnesses so that its outcome can be verified.
when: Designing a reveal scene

text: Use a withheld fact to build tension only when the listener has a reason to suspect it.
Script a reveal in steps, breaking it at the most tense point and pausing briefly before the key item appears, so the audience wants the rest.
why: unresolved tension holds attention

text: Script some NPC reactions as instinctive and others as deliberate, so players can distinguish panic from premeditation.
Withhold a final document or revelation until the player meets a condition, and do not let it resolve automatically.
when: when designing a late reveal
why: A withheld final point keeps the reveal incomplete until the condition is met.

text: Keep the identity of an actor and the role of intermediaries unresolved until the player is ready for them, and mark each as an open question.
when: Narrative threads share a middle figure whose role is not yet clear.
why: Revealing those answers early removes the investigation's remaining tension.

text: Pace reveals so that a new development follows each moment the player gains sympathy for a suspect, keeping tension high.
Close a mystery quickly with a confrontation where the culprit's admission ends the quest, instead of staging a trial.
when: Designing the final act of a mystery quest
why: An admission gives a fast close without extra scenes

text: Use lighting, seat placement and a late entrance in the accusation scene to stage the reveal of the culprit.
Place a blocked route or a stranger needing help just before a key NPC, so the player anticipates the coming interaction.
when: Pacing toward an important character

text: Leave one reading unresolved after the tests, so the question can carry into a later quest step.
Gate cause-of-death or killer-identification steps so they unlock only after the victim is confirmed.
when: Designing investigation case files in games.
why: Prevents players from reasoning about motive or method before a basic fact is anchored.

text: Withholding a solution builds suspense until anticipation turns to boredom; long delays also lose the investigation's thread and let the culprit escape or destroy evidence.
when: Deciding how long to hold back a solution or reveal.
why: Each extra beat of delay raises the cost of waiting and the risk of loss.

text: Revealing evidence early lets the opponent investigate, search for the item, and build a counter-account before testimony is tested; a late reveal catches them unprepared but can look like concealment.
when: Deciding when to disclose decisive evidence or a witness account.
why: Timing trades the opponent's preparation time against the risk of seeming hidden; they can act while the account is still unmatched.

text: Giving an instruction before its reason builds suspense, but frustrates the recipient if the reasoning is never paid off.
why: The recipient must act before understanding

text: Withholding the full explanation until the end preserves suspense, but makes the solution feel unfair if the clues were not presented as the reasoning develops.
when: when planning how a mystery's solution is revealed
why: Audiences need premises stated before they can follow the conclusion.

text: Withholding the suspect's name gives the reveal payoff but risks losing the audience if the delay runs past the point where they can still follow the argument.
when: Choosing how long to hold back an identity in a mystery.
why: Suspense depends on the audience having enough clues to track the chain.

text: Offering choices at a reveal, such as accepting a bribe, pressing for confession or exposing the truth, branches the ending but must be recorded in world state.
when: Designing a scripted confrontation with a trusted quest-giver.
why: Branching outcomes require the game to remember the player's decision.

text: Offering a choice between revealing a truth and preserving an official story gives players a moral decision with consequences for NPCs who hold the public narrative.
when: Designing a moral decision about a public secret.

text: Make mystical effects real but bounded so players can test them, or resolve magical-seeming events with a testable physical cause, not an unexplained magic answer.
when: when designing supernatural or magical-seeming elements in a mystery

text: Check for a human cause, such as who touched or wound an object, before attributing unexplained behavior to supernatural forces.
when: An object behaves in an unexplained way.
why: Most anomalies have a mundane explanation that a witness can supply.

text: Breaking a rule of engagement that the player set corrupts the witness record, so the player's collected data becomes less reliable.
when: Players choose rules before an observation event
why: Rule violations change what was observed and how it can be compared

text: A procedure that looks complicated may still be lax in practice, so complexity should not be taken as proof that a system is secure.
when: Judging whether a routine or safeguard is reliable.
why: Staff or systems may skip steps even when the procedure appears elaborate.

text: A wait in which the player cannot act makes the tension feel scripted rather than interactive.
A search shows only what was found, so a negative result does not prove absence; ask what searchers sought and how they looked.
when: when evaluating a witness account of a search
why: a search in good faith can still miss the target

text: Search methods depend on lawful access, since legal powers such as warrants limit what investigators may examine.
Divide a large area into sections and test each separately, since an explanation may fit one section yet fail in the section that matters.
Secrets tend to sit in private spaces such as desk drawers and cupboards, so these are high-value places to search.
when: designing or conducting a search for evidence

text: An instruction to act alone makes the retrieval a private act and rules out witnesses.
when: when a clue should be done without observers

text: A visibly locked door that yields to a probing action, paired with an unnoticed second exit, rewards players who test barriers before accepting them.
Look for the one mistake a careful planner would overlook rather than for the most visible clue.
when: Examining a staged scene for the planner's error.
why: Careful staging removes obvious traces but rarely every subtle one.

text: Use a locked or restricted room as a clue, since a denied witness signals that someone wanted testimony kept out.
when: Designing investigation spaces where witnesses or evidence are restricted.
why: Denied access to testimony implies a motive to suppress it.

text: When a person is unfound after a search, the remaining possibilities are concealment or an exit that no witness could watch.
when: when an absence cannot be explained by a search alone
why: the two possibilities narrow the search to hidden spots and unobserved routes

text: Let the player choose when to probe, and let an early, premature probe cost them the witness's cooperation.
Discovery time depends on search thoroughness: a concealed object can stay unnoticed for days under casual search yet appear within minutes under systematic search.
Treating a large area as a single location skips its sub-locations, such as ceilings or fixtures, so a real hiding spot can be missed.
why: Candidate lists built from coarse assumptions omit hiding spots.

text: Fixating on one favored spot wastes search time when the opening lies elsewhere.
Searching a large table before ruling out whole classes of candidates wastes effort.
A sample container opened before use can contaminate the sample and make the result unusable.
when: a sample must be collected for later testing

text: Accepting a secret door as the answer to a disappearance without checking the geometry of the space skips the test that would confirm or refute it.
when: A player or designer explains a vanishing by a hidden route.
why: A hidden route must still fit the layout and the elapsed time.

text: A search made for a living person checks rooms and expects to see him, so it can miss a body hidden under furniture, in drawers or cupboards.
when: when a search is carried out for a missing person
why: searchers look where a person could be seen, not where a body could fit

text: 1) Conceal a reflective item while appearing occupied. 2) Angle it to view what lies behind you. 3) Look again, since a first glance may show nothing useful.
when: a direct view is blocked or watched

text: 1) Leave the hidden item where it is. 2) Control who is present and when. 3) Make the suspect believe the way is clear. 4) Watch where they retrieve it, instead of searching every surface.
when: the item's location is uncertain and a full search would be costly or destructive
why: letting the suspect reveal the spot avoids destroying the environment

text: 1) List all candidate containers. 2) Assign each a rough likelihood of holding the item. 3) Check the most likely candidates first. 4) Keep the remaining candidates under watch. 5) Destroy a container only when other checks fail and the cost is acceptable.
when: Several identical containers may hold a hidden item
why: Ordering by likelihood minimizes the expected effort to find the item

text: 1) Check whether the contradictory trace is genuine. 2) Identify the premise it contradicts. 3) Question that premise. 4) Search the locations no one considered, including the most unlikely ones.
when: A search is complete but yields nothing, or a physical trace contradicts the timeline

text: Place two spotters at known positions beside a scale marker so players can intersect their bearing lines, and mark that intersection on the player's map.
Collect candidate tools from everyone with access before comparing marks, since a trace that cannot be matched to a tool is lost evidence.
when: investigating a mark on a lock or surface

text: Before springing a trap or confronting a target, check the area for other people who might leave and change who is left alone with the target.
Give a search mechanic a fixed check order and escalating passes, so a tempting empty spot can be checked and rejected.
Store knowledge in a sealed item that opens only when a defined condition or date is met.
Check who may lawfully search a place before recovering a discarded item, because a refusal by the holder can make the evidence unusable.
when: Evidence sits in a space owned or controlled by someone else
why: Searching without required authority can lose the evidence or the case

text: Restore containers to their prior state when the player leaves, or show a visible mark that the search was made.
when: When a player has searched a container in a space the owner or an NPC might later inspect.
why: Consistent state keeps the search undetected or makes its traces discoverable.

text: A weapon that is never recovered leaves its owner unknown, and circumstantial links must then fill the gap, which can weaken the case.
when: When the key physical instrument of a crime is absent from the evidence.
why: Without the instrument, its ownership cannot be proven directly.

text: A torn fragment in a victim's hand that matches a suspect's garment creates a direct physical link between suspect and scene.
when: When a physical fragment found at a scene matches a suspect's possession.
why: A material match ties the possession to the scene, though it does not prove who wore it at the time.

text: Pair markers that fail in different ways, so a single marker is not a sole source of truth and the player must reason about which indicator to trust.
when: Designing evidence that should require deduction rather than direct reading.
why: Conflicting indicators force interpretation, and a single marker can be ambiguous.

text: Building a theory on one anomaly or a timeline on one estimate makes it look firmer than it is; forcing details to fit while ignoring timeline contradictions hides problems.
why: a single clue can be coincidental, forced fits hide contradictions, and a single source provides no cross-check

text: Relying on a single marker or chance encounter when other routes to the target exist makes the progression feel thin.
when: Designing a tracking objective
why: Players sense when success depends on luck rather than their choices

text: A false alarm loses its force when repeated, so use it once or space repeated uses far apart.
when: When a stop or reset event is used more than once in a scene or session.
why: Repetition makes the threat predictable, so players and agents stop reacting to it.

text: A method requiring specialised technique implies the actor's knowledge, such as chemical knowledge, while a crafted device implies mechanical skill.
Test whether a tool could have been used during an event by checking the physical actions it needs, such as the number of hands required to operate it.
when: a tool is claimed to have been used during a struggle
why: actions that were impossible during the event rule the tool out

text: Let a disguise or cover identity give the investigator access to a clue that would otherwise be unavailable, such as a sample of a suspect's handwriting.
when: When a key clue is held by someone who would refuse direct questioning
why: A cover role opens doors and conversations that formal questioning keeps closed.

text: Plant the solver's key tool in plain sight early, so that it can later serve as the answer to a puzzle.
why: Early planting makes the late use feel fair

text: Specialist inference from an object depends on the examiner's knowledge, and a non-expert or an expert outside the object's field may learn little or give no verdict.
when: Judging authenticity or origin of an object.
why: Recognising a fake depends on prior experience with that specific field.

text: Make detection of hidden items or residues depend on character skill, so the same object yields different results for different abilities.
when: Designing detection of hidden items, or residues meant to reward specialist characters.
why: Specialist readings reward investment in the skill.

text: Make small traces collectible only with the right tool, such as a lens or powder, so that tool choice matters.
when: designing item-based investigation
why: Gating makes tool knowledge part of the puzzle

text: 1) Hide concealed where you can see the room, watching the fixed hiding place from spaced positions so watchers don't collide and one can move while another observes. 2) Wait until the target commits to retrieving or exposing the item. 3) Move in once the target is committed and the guard drops.
when: a target must return to a fixed, known hiding place to retrieve or expose an item
why: Timing the strike to the exposure moment removes the target's chance to resist or flee

text: Perpetrators choose the moment to act when the target's activity is lowest, and they pick a time that leaves the most margin for escape.
when: Planning when an action should occur in a scenario
why: Quiet periods reduce the chance of interruption and extra time improves the escape margin

text: Cutting a room's lights at a chosen moment, especially its single controllable power source, removes sighted opponents' advantage, letting players who rely on sound or touch gain the upper hand.
when: a standoff or fight in a room with lights or one controllable power element
why: Darkness removes visual information and shifts advantage to whoever does not depend on sight

text: A sudden inner warning prompting immediate withdrawal can save the party just before violence strikes; tying it to past cases makes it read as learned, not random.
When a character loses a short interval of control and traces of the character's own actions appear afterward, players discover a hidden action through evidence.
A test that works only when the subject can see it makes the outcome depend on line of sight, which a player can exploit by repositioning.
Raising a signal for help after a disposal draws outside attention to the place the actor wanted kept quiet.
when: when an actor wants a scene to stay unnoticed

text: A suspect who checks the surroundings before exposing the item may escape, and crowds or passersby can force delays that blow the stakeout.
when: Running a stakeout in a public place

text: 1) Identify the defender's expected form of attack. 2) List candidate sites that suit your craft and resemble your starting region. 3) Narrow them by explicit criteria. 4) Prefer routes that are short and free of hazards.
Design puzzles where players anticipate a rival's move from known traits rather than from a visible clue.
when: when building a puzzle around an opponent

text: Use ambient warnings such as npc unease or glimpses of an unseen threat so players sense danger before they can act on it.
when: when building tension in a level or scene

text: Let a new arrival trigger a change in the active plan, so the player must adapt the search.
when: a visitor appears during an investigation
why: Changing plans keeps the scene responsive.

text: Offer a choice during a wait, such as holding a door shut or retreating to another room, so the suspense is interactive.
when: the player is waiting for an approaching threat
why: the player can respond while uncertain

text: A watcher gathers information unnoticed via a harmless, context-appropriate task keeping them moving; a concealed mirror aids observation. An out-of-place task makes the observer suspicious.
when: when a target must not know they are watched, or when designing or staging a covert action
why: A routine task that grows naturally from the situation is not questioned, so the observer is not suspected.

text: Offer disguise costume tiers, each opening a set of NPC conversations and blocked areas.
Make a stealth window depend on stated assumptions, such as guard attention, so the player can test them and discover when they fail.
A slow, silent action such as turning a knob gently suggests the actor wanted to avoid waking the occupant.
why: quiet movement signals intent not to be noticed

text: A diversion trap feels fair when the player can anticipate it by noticing the agent who staged it.
when: when scripting a distraction the player must overcome
why: visible setup lets players reason toward the trap

text: When a target notices a watcher and remarks on it, surveillance becomes a known threat, which raises the immediate stakes for the player.
when: when watcher NPCs are visible to the player
why: knowing one is observed changes how the target acts and how tense the scene feels

text: A staged noisy event draws a guard's attention away from a target, letting the player swap or retrieve the object unobserved.
when: when a scripted heist-style sequence needs cover
why: attention is pulled toward the noise, opening a window

text: Opponents watch whatever object is being manipulated, so an action on a controllable element must look innocent or it will be noticed.
when: manipulating a shared object in front of opponents
why: observers track changes to objects near them

text: 1) Watch the target's residence from a fixed spot. 2) Follow at a distance that keeps the target in view. 3) Note his stops. 4) If he uses a vehicle, hire another and follow it. 5) Record landmarks to memorise the destination.
when: The investigator needs a target's address or movements that the target will not volunteer.

text: 1) Build a timeline of when the target is busy and how long a usable window lasts. 2) Confirm the target's position before the diversion. 3) Fit the full action inside the window, with a margin for surprises.
when: a target's schedule is predictable and the action needs a short window
why: a reliable window is the only time the action can succeed

text: 1) Give the target a reason to leave the room or look away. 2) Post a lookout on the approach. 3) Keep a clear exit. 4) Retrieve the object before returning.
when: An object must be examined while the target is present nearby.
why: A distraction needs cover and an escape route, or the attempt is exposed.

text: 1) Give the suspect a credible warning whose substance is accurate. 2) Make the source seem authoritative. 3) Set a watch on the suspect and plan the follow in advance. 4) Follow the suspect to the hiding place they move the item to.
when: The suspect's move will reveal a hiding place or accomplice
why: A credible tip provokes movement, and the movement exposes the cache

text: 1) Survey a hostile room by listening and by fixing the positions of people, exits and windows. 2) Identify single controllable elements such as a light. 3) Plan the action around the elements.
when: entering a hostile room with limited sight
why: positional knowledge makes later action precise

text: A stealth mission can let the player adopt a disguise or assumed role to enter a restricted area or talk to a guarded NPC.
Let the player judge lighting, noise and timing when deciding whether an observation is safe.
when: designing stealth observation puzzles

text: Do not stay in one spot so long that passers-by or witnesses begin to notice the watcher.
when: During a stakeout.
why: A lingering, visible watcher becomes conspicuous and risks exposure.

text: Offer a stealth action that lets the player feign distress to be placed beside a target.
when: Designing stealth gameplay

text: Let a stealth disguise be tested by a physical action, such as wiping a face, that reveals the fake.
when: Designing disguise mechanics for stealth play.
why: A physical test gives the player a way to expose the disguise without relying on luck.

text: Build a timed stakeout mechanic that requires several in-game nights, a hidden vantage point, and a fatigue meter.
A stakeout works only when the cache location is known and the suspect's timing can be controlled; it fails if the cache may be elsewhere or the suspect is armed.
when: Choosing between a stakeout and other approaches

text: A controlled tip can move the item but may be doubted or checked by the suspect, and a false tip risks endangering innocent people.
when: Deciding whether to use a planted warning

text: Build a working conclusion from several minor signs that point the same way; no single fact is decisive, but independent weak facts reinforce one another toward one conclusion.
when: Hard proof is missing, each fact allows more than one reading, and a hypothesis is needed to test against further evidence.
why: Agreeing signs support a likely conclusion, while a single sign is too weak to settle the matter.

text: Offer a natural explanation alongside a human one, and let a test separate them, so the puzzle rewards careful checking.
when: designing a poison or disease puzzle
why: Players must test rather than assume.

text: End the escape with a counting detail, such as a headcount that exposes an extra person, so the exit can be proven.
why: A numeric check turns suspicion into verifiable proof.

text: Use a sensory clue, such as a scent, that the player can test against each suspect one at a time, eliminating suspects through repeated checks.
why: A repeatable test lets the player narrow suspects by direct comparison.

text: If an apparition stops once the suspect leaves a place, the cause may lie in that location or association rather than the person themselves.
when: Testing whether an anomaly follows a person or a place
why: Removing the person from a location separates location-linked causes from person-linked ones

text: Dismissing an explanation as absurd can miss a real event: an implausible theory does not falsify the coincidence, and a supernatural connection may grow harder to dismiss as evidence accumulates.
when: A coincidence or reported effect is explained by a theory the investigator finds absurd.
why: Absurdity of a rival theory does not establish that the observed event is false.

text: A test that yields no result can look as though it was never run; make the failure visible and meaningful to the player.

1) List each supernatural claim. 2) Find an ordinary mechanism for each; a known mechanism can expose a human act. 3) Keep only what ordinary mechanisms cannot explain. 4) Do not accept a claim merely because it fits the facts.
when: An event seems to have a supernatural cause.
why: A claim that fits every fact may still have a human cause, so each element must be checked separately.

text: 1) List every candidate cause, including the supernatural one. 2) Test each against the evidence using checks that can fail. 3) Eliminate causes; keep the dramatic one open only while testable rivals remain, stating which is unproven.
when: A reported effect fits several explanations, including a supernatural one.
why: Testable elimination separates real causes from dramatic ones; naming rivals openly prevents the only suggested reading from being accepted by default.

text: 1) List ordinary explanations: imagination, intoxication, excitement, sleepwalking, drowsiness, illness, observer error. 2) Check each against witnesses' actual conditions. 3) Keep unexplained details open rather than assuming a cause.
when: A case includes reported phenomena such as an illusion, a strange sighting, or an odd witness experience.
why: Checking witness state removes many apparent mysteries, since intoxication, drowsiness or illness can produce convincing but false perceptions.

text: 1) Ask a question only the culprit could answer. 2) Compare the answer against information the player has not shared with the NPC. 3) Treat a match as real insight only if no leak could explain it.
when: Designing tests that separate genuine insight from a cold read.
why: Questions that only the true source could answer expose trickery.

text: 1) List each reaction or clue that does not fit the working theory. 2) Check whether each is a real contradiction or a trivial anomaly. 3) Frame the remaining conflicts as a choice between two explanations. 4) Test the starting assumption before adding ingenuity.
when: Several clues conflict and the theory is not converging.
why: Revisiting a wrong assumption is cheaper than defending a broken theory.

text: 1) Group scattered anomalies that seem unrelated. 2) Propose a motive linking the people involved. 3) Reconstruct the sequence of events, from how parties met to what triggered the conflict and what was used. 4) Explain how any unseen party escaped detection. 5) Test the theory against physical clues elsewhere and list unresolved contradictions before acting.
when: several anomalies appear that no single explanation covers
why: a theory that explains all clues and exposes its weak points is more reliable than one built on a single anomaly

text: 1) Show an injury or clue that reads as guilt. 2) Let an unexplained phrase sit in the journal. 3) Hold a withheld interval of inspection. 4) Reveal a physical proof of the hazard, then recall the phrase.
when: Designing a mystery where the apparent culprit is innocent.
why: Recalling a planted detail at the end ties the hazard to earlier evidence and makes the reveal feel prepared.

text: 1) Give the player a test that checks an NPC's physical trait, such as a hand-touch check. 2) Use the result to learn a mechanic or expose an impostor.
1) Check the witness's record against the case file. 2) If no record exists, treat the testimony as fabricated. 3) Re-examine every planted object the testimony touched.

Rule out mundane causes one at a time, unlocking the supernatural option last. Offer a physical probe, such as throwing an item, that shows an apparition is not solid, letting the player try rational explanations first.
when: Designing a disturbance or an ambiguous, impossible object that could have a trap, monster, or other cause.
why: Sequential elimination gives the player a reason to test each option and makes the final cause satisfying.

text: Use motive as the test for an explanation: a mechanism that explains how something happened does not identify who had reason to do it.
when: Evaluating a supernatural or mechanical explanation in a mystery.
why: Method and motive are separate questions, so a complete answer must address both.

text: Give the player a simple test, such as a light flicker or a sound cue, that reveals a status effect or hidden state.
when: A game has hidden status effects or conditions.
why: A visible test lets players detect a state they cannot see directly.

text: Link each possible reading of a clue to an independent fact the player has already collected, so the player can rule options out.
Judge self-serving accounts, such as recasting an act as blackmail or a written confession, separately from the speaker's wish to be excused; candor is not proof.
when: A suspect offers a self-serving account or a written confession.
why: Self-interest can shape a confession even when it contains some truth, and accepting a reframing can mislead.

text: A suspect who hears a detailed recital of known facts may turn pale and sweat before speaking, showing pressure builds as evidence is laid out.
when: Known facts are recited in detail to a suspect.
why: Hearing the full case removes the option of maintaining a false account.

text: A suspect may reveal knowledge while answering about a related subject, so asking about neighbors of the target is more revealing than asking about the target directly.
when: A witness is likely to conceal a connection to a person or object.
why: The witness does not notice the real subject of the test, so answers carry unguarded information.

text: A witness's anxieties, such as fear of paying for damage, can color how they report times and events.
when: Interpreting a witness's account.
why: Emotional stakes bias recall and reporting.

text: A sudden, convenient error that forces an early exit is a warning sign and should not be accepted at face value; it may be a planned evasion.
when: A suspect's explanation for a sudden change of route conveniently removes them from tracing.
why: Planned decoys are designed to look like innocent mistakes.

text: A suspect dossier can list evidence for and against each suspect, leaving the player to weigh it.
Judge witnesses' trustworthiness by temperament, and do not depend on the discretion of one who is volatile or weak.
when: Choosing whom to confide in during an investigation.
why: Temperament predicts whether a witness will keep quiet.

text: An interrogation option that unlocks only when the player holds the right clue makes the confession match the evidence.
when: Designing dialogue challenges that reveal information.
why: Gating the option on evidence ties the outcome to the player's investigation.

text: Give each suspect a record of access such as keys, schedule and presence, and check it when a crime occurs.
when: Designing crimes where access determines who could act.
why: Recorded access lets the game and player test opportunity objectively.

text: Let players assemble a motive chain from evidence cards and present it to a suspect, with a confession or flight as the result.
when: A detective-style interrogation system is designed.
why: Presenting a coherent chain turns evidence into a social outcome.

text: When household members are absent, the premises become open to anyone who knows the arrangement, so absence can both explain and enable access.
when: Assessing who could have acted during a period when staff are out.
why: Known absences remove the people who would otherwise block access.

text: A bluff can turn into a dare, as the other side pushes harder once a party refuses to yield.
when: Both sides are bluffing during a negotiation.
why: Refusal to concede invites escalation rather than settlement.

text: The questioner's own prejudices can distort the reading of answers, especially judgments of manner or spending, so over-interpretation of indirect answers is a common error.
when: Interpreting indirect or ambiguous answers.
why: Personal judgment colors what counts as a meaningful signal.

text: Stating a conclusion too firmly gives the other side a reason to dismiss it, and trusting one's own sense of sincerity is risky when one sympathizes with the suspect.
when: Presenting a theory to a witness or interpreting their sincerity.
why: Firm claims invite rejection, and sympathy biases the read of sincerity.

text: A witness who reveals findings too early risks losing their advantage in the exchange.
when: Deciding how much to reveal during an interview.
why: Early disclosure gives the other side information to adapt to.

text: Assuming the closest household is the only possible source can miss leaks from outside people who hold information.
when: Tracing how a secret became known.
why: Information often travels through contacts beyond the immediate location.

text: Second-hand alibis need direct checking before they are trusted, and a stopped clock can mislead anyone who relies on it.
why: reports passed along by others can disagree or be mistaken

text: 1) Make the arrest formal, stating the charge and the caution that statements may be used. 2) Recite the known facts in detail to break pretence. 3) Offer a conditional incentive, such as no prosecution if an object is returned unopened. 4) Let the suspect explain in their own words. 5) Reduce the account to plain facts. 6) Verify each claim against objects and records.
when: There is enough independent evidence to test the suspect's account.
why: Laying out facts before the suspect speaks reduces room for a self-serving story.

text: 1) Choose a topic the person is likely to enjoy. 2) Observe physical traits during the talk without showing special interest in the person. 3) Confirm any noticed trait with a second observation before relying on it.
when: A suspect is recognizable but not yet confirmed and the trait can be observed without alarm
why: A casual remark is weak evidence, and a second observation strengthens it

text: 1) Hint at a discovery without revealing it. 2) Watch the other party's reactions for tells. 3) Ask hypothetical questions to learn their rules. 4) Trade information only after learning their position.
when: Both parties hold partial information and each wants the other's cards first.
why: Withholding keeps leverage while probing reveals what the other side already knows.

text: 1) Ask about a related subject instead of the target. 2) Compare answers across related subjects. 3) Hide your interest with a distraction. 4) Stop before naming the target. 5) Treat tone shifts and dismissive replies as data.
when: Probing a witness who may conceal knowledge.
why: Indirect probing yields hints about what the witness knows without alerting them.

text: 1) Withhold your own conclusion. 2) Make a bold, unexpected statement. 3) Read the reaction in tone, pauses and evasions. 4) Establish who was where using arrival questions. 5) Ask the other party to confirm or deny each point.
when: The other party controls information you need.
why: A withheld conclusion cannot be dismissed easily, and reactions reveal whether a claim touched something real.

text: 1) List heirs in succession order. 2) Note who is next if the chain changes. 3) Restrict suspects to those present in the household. 4) Check alibis last.
when: A death gives someone a gain through inheritance.
why: Ordering heirs and limiting to those present narrows the suspect pool before alibis are checked.

text: 1) Start from the physical object. 2) Identify its maker or source. 3) Trace the people connected to that source. 4) Assess the plausible motive for each link.
when: A single object must lead to a set of suspects.
why: Chaining from object to people builds a case step by step.

text: An absent sighting, expected trace or instrument reading is a clue: it narrows possibilities, can rule out false suspects, or points to a special cause; record it.
when: When a witness, artifact or instrument lacks an expected sighting, feature or detection
why: Absence read against the witness's position or the expected features narrows possibilities even though nothing was found.

text: Testimony collected by questionnaire is only as trustworthy as the questions asked and how answers were recorded; leading questions or editing can shape the results.
when: Evaluating a body of statements gathered by survey or inquiry.
why: Question wording and compiler edits can confirm what the collector already believes, and the originals are needed to detect this.

text: When earlier cases left no trace of a suspected agent, treat a new method as needing its own test rather than assuming it.
when: when earlier searches came up empty

text: Confirm a timing estimate from decaying objects against other traces, such as the count of glasses or cups present.
when: A timing estimate is drawn from a single decaying object
why: A single timing can be wrong, and other traces can corroborate or refute it

text: Compare a passive recording against a reliable baseline taken under normal conditions so that differences can be isolated.
when: Interpreting a faint or uncertain passive record.
why: Without a baseline, faint marks are easily misread.

text: Spot-checking a few independently verifiable statements confirms only those statements, not the rest of the collection.
when: Verifying a large body of testimony by checking a sample.
why: A confirmed sample does not establish the reliability of unchecked items.

text: Evidence objects with testable properties, such as scent, torn edge or a duplicate pair, let players compare two fragments to confirm they match.
A search that finds nothing shows only that nothing was found where it looked, not that nothing is hidden.
Competing motives can make a plan switch between methods, which wastes effort; choose one method and stay with it.
when: when conflicting aims pull on the plan
why: switching methods loses progress

text: Recovery after removing a suspected source is persuasive evidence, but other changes occurring at the same time may also explain the recovery.
when: Confirming a cause by observing improvement after removal
why: Removal and recovery are correlated with other changes that were not controlled

text: 1) Identify two candidate causes that produce similar effects. 2) Place a proxy subject in the suspected environment. 3) Observe the subject's reaction over a short exposure. 4) Remove the suspected source and observe whether the effect ends.
when: A source must be identified from its effects and the environment can be sampled
why: Similar effects cannot distinguish candidates alone, but timing and removal can confirm which cause operated

text: 1) Identify a physical property of the item that varies between sources. 2) Collect reference samples from each candidate. 3) Compare the item against each sample using a standard scale and chemical tests. 4) Exclude candidates whose samples do not match.
when: Ordinary identifiers such as handwriting are inconclusive and samples can be obtained
why: Physical properties can separate sources that look identical to the eye

text: 1) Give the player an authentic known sample. 2) Give a disputed document. 3) Let them compare magnified details. 4) Provide a confirming record that supports or refutes the match.
when: building an investigation puzzle around a disputed written item
why: Pairing a visual comparison with a verifying record makes the answer deducible instead of guessed.

text: Make some player checks return nothing, so players learn from negative results rather than only from successful ones.
when: When designing investigation loops in a game

text: Mark meaningful features such as islands, loops and bifurcations, not an arbitrary grid whose lines fall at random.
when: when comparing fingerprints

text: Plant an overt clue that could be a message or pure chance, and let the game confirm it against a second source before it counts.
when: when designing ambiguous clues

text: Have the player memorise key details rather than copying documents, and record notes only after leaving the scene.
when: a covert action must avoid carrying evidence

text: Test for concealed machinery with an instrument that would register its operation, so that a mechanism, if present, reveals itself.
A narrow test checks one substance and gives a clear answer, but the tester must already suspect it, and a negative result says nothing about others.
when: when choosing which lab test to run

text: A short test exposure may cause no lasting harm yet still show an effect, but extrapolating to longer exposure is uncertain and a single sample is weak.
when: Testing with a subject who bears real discomfort or risk
why: Extrapolation from short to repeated exposure depends on assumptions that one sample cannot verify

text: Hold a theory provisionally; test it against the timeline and remaining contradictions before acting, since plausibility and conviction do not establish correctness.
when: a working explanation is formed from clues before the evidence is complete
why: plausible theories often fail once fuller facts arrive

text: Reward players who track the in-game clock and map distances, since they can check claims that others cannot.
Reward a player for noticing that an object was sunk, burned or moved, and for finding the leftover trace of that action.
when: when designing disposal puzzles

text: Route bait replies and follow-up messages through intermediaries so the investigator stays hidden.
when: The investigator must avoid revealing their identity or the test.
why: Hidden senders keep the target and other parties from learning they are being tested.

text: A single matching reply is not conclusive when the predicted description is generic enough that many people could fit it.
when: The bait's criteria match a common profile.
why: Coincidental matches are likely when the description is broad.

text: Trust a witness's observation more when a second independent record, such as a photograph taken in calm conditions, supports it.
when: Evaluating a stressful witness account.
why: Independent records offset distortion in the witness's memory.

text: Many replies may arrive; each must be checked against the prediction, not accepted just because it suits the working theory.
when: A public test draws several responses.
why: Confirmation bias makes a loosely matching reply look like proof.

text: A plausible theory about where an item went stays a plan to search, not a finding, until physical evidence confirms it.
when: Reasoning about a drain, gutter or other hiding place.
why: Confident reasoning can run ahead of the evidence.

text: 1) Enumerate rival theories that fit the clues. 2) Test each against the same evidence, including the same timing and objects. 3) Test what each theory requires to be true, and reject one whose requirements are absurd. 4) Check that its reasoning is internally consistent.
when: several explanations fit the same clues
why: comparing theories on identical evidence exposes weak ones

text: 1) Derive what a theory would observably cause. 2) Design a public bait that only the predicted witness would answer. 3) Treat a matching reply as support and silence as inconclusive.
when: Two explanations predict different observable events that a public call could reveal.
why: A bait filters for the predicted response, separating rival explanations without direct proof.

text: Pair a public bait with a direct request to a better-placed informant to strengthen the test.
when: A second informant can confirm or refute the prediction.
why: A well-placed source gives stronger evidence than an anonymous public reply.

text: 1) Identify the lead. 2) Find an unnoticed clue that bears on it. 3) Test the clue directly, such as by sending a helper to check. 4) Keep or drop the lead by the result.
when: A lead is plausible but unconfirmed.
why: Direct tests separate real leads from decoys without relying on the most striking evidence.

text: 1) State the meaning an item seems to have. 2) Check it against domain knowledge or a second source. 3) If the inference fails, accept the narrower fact the item actually supports.
when: A clue seems to settle a point and must be verified before acceptance.
why: Expert knowledge or a second source can overturn a plausible reading of an object.

text: Let the game reveal the result of a player's prediction, so wrong guesses teach the underlying rule.
when: Players are invited to guess outcomes in a puzzle or system.
why: Visible results turn failed guesses into learning.

text: Let the player meet a rude expert who proves correct, and reward checking the expert's claims.
when: Designing an NPC expert who opposes a helpful NPC
why: Rewarding verification teaches players not to judge by manner.

text: Give players facts that contradict their first theory, and reward them for revising it, so revision becomes part of the play.
when: when designing investigation progression
why: Revision is a skill that needs rewarding feedback

text: Place a reward notice on a board or in a rumour system so that posting it prompts certain NPCs to come forward with information.
when: Quest design where information is held by unknown NPCs.
why: A posted reward gives NPCs a motive to act, so the player receives leads without direct contact.

text: Reward a confirmed theory by unlocking the next location or suspect.
Reward players who test a hypothesis against alternative explanations, and do not reward those who accept the first explanation offered.
when: Designing deduction challenges where players must judge a claim.
why: Testing alternatives is the step that separates a trick from a real cause.

text: A bait must describe the predicted witness closely enough to be recognized, but omitting details limits the risk of alerting authorities or the target.
when: Designing a public call that others will read.
why: Too much detail exposes the investigation; too little draws no reply from the right person.

text: Define a presence window, such as about ten minutes, in which events are impossible for a suspect; a longer claimed interval cannot fit and becomes a timeline problem.
when: A presence window is known or defined, or a longer interval is claimed
why: Narrows the search without a direct confession, since the claimed interval cannot fit inside the available time

text: When a timed object conflicts with testimony, the investigator must choose between trusting the theory and trusting the evidence, and must test which one to doubt.
when: a timekeeping object shows a time that conflicts with the believed time of an event
why: both the object and the testimony can be wrong, and the conflict forces explicit reasoning

text: A witness's time can be vivid yet wrong, and a nearby clock may be inaccurate, so any interval between events is only as reliable as the clock and memory behind it.
why: memory and timekeeping instruments both introduce error

text: A scene timer that contradicts the player's assumed sequence can be reset by an NPC and then re-verified by a second witness.
Give a found object a verified timeline by checking the finder's account of where and when it was found.
when: When an object's location must be tied to a time.
why: A dated, checkable account anchors the object's position in the sequence of events.

text: A locked container that opens only after a timed event can anchor a timeline the player must reconstruct.
when: designing a quest timeline

text: A timed event can be paused while the player gathers evidence and released when the player acts, so pacing follows player progress rather than the clock.
when: when a countdown or scripted threat would otherwise run unattended
why: Holding the timer keeps the player from losing options before they are ready.

text: A timeline puzzle can use world-state indicators such as shop prices, town notices or NPC gossip, letting the player date an incident without a witness.
A witness's account of when an object was moved can rule out a suspect by showing the planted object could not have been placed at the time claimed.
when: A suspect is charged on the basis of evidence whose placement time is in question.
why: Fixing the time of the object's movement removes the opportunity for the accused to have planted it.

text: Distance travelled can be estimated from fuel consumed. The result is a rough range to be checked against road distances on a map.
when: Fuel consumption is known or can be inferred

text: Bones clean of soft tissue and showing no fresh change set a lower bound on time since death, here at least eighteen months.
when: when estimating how long remains have been exposed
why: decay and cleaning take time, so their state gives a minimum interval

text: A timer based on fixed flow fails when the flow changes, so its calibration must be repeated whenever the rate may have shifted.
why: timing depends directly on rate

text: A quiet interval can look like the end of a recurring pattern when it is only a pause, leading players to a false conclusion.
A delayed cause can make a recent visit look harmless, and a single preparatory act is weak evidence unless it aligns with the timeline.
when: Evaluating suspects against a delayed mechanism
why: Delay hides the link between contact and effect, and isolated clues mislead

text: 1) List the chain of deductions that produced the impossible timeline or result. 2) Test each assumption about distance, sound or other physical facts. 3) Test candidate explanations against the physical facts. 4) If none fits, find the stated premise that is wrong.
when: A timeline or deduction looks impossible
why: An impossible timeline may rest only on an unchecked assumption, so assumptions must be tested before accepting the contradiction

text: 1) List every condition the apparently impossible action requires. 2) Identify which conditions the suspect lacks, testing each candidate explanation against all conditions. 3) Test simpler explanations first, accepting the ordinary route that satisfies every condition before supernatural causes. 4) Search for a place where the missing conditions do not matter.
when: A witness account or scene seems impossible given a person's known condition, yet evidence still constrains it
why: Necessary conditions narrow candidates until one ordinary route remains; impossible-seeming actions point to alternative explanations such as a hidden location

text: 1) Build a timeline for each incident in proper order, marking each time firm or estimate. 2) Record who was where, noting second-hand absences and observer gaps. 3) Place the central figure first, then move outward so each answer anchors the next. 4) Keep unplaced people as suspects; set aside anyone who could not have been present. 5) Use expected arrivals as deadlines.
when: Several incidents, several people, testimony given from memory, or assembling a timeline to test alibis and locate conflicts
why: Later facts can be fitted to earlier ones, missing information becomes a question rather than an accusation, and firm and weak times must be kept apart to judge alibis fairly

text: 1) Identify the object's maker or seller. 2) Obtain the sale or record date from that source. 3) Check the date against the timeline of events.
when: When an object's ownership must be established.
why: Dated seller records give an independent, checkable link between an object and a buyer.

text: 1) Find the known incubation or delay period of the cause. 2) Subtract it from the onset date to get the exposure window. 3) Clear suspects whose contact fell outside that window. 4) Cross-check remaining suspects against known whereabouts.
when: The mechanism works with a delay, such as an illness or slow poison
why: Working backward from onset narrows when the cause could have acted

text: 1) Give the player each staged event. 2) Let them attach a suspect, means and opportunity to each. 3) Reveal the consistent timeline only when all events are linked.
when: When designing a mystery or deduction puzzle.
why: Linking each event to a suspect, means and opportunity turns the mystery into a checkable timeline.

text: 1) Compare the time shown with the time of the event. 2) Ask whether the object was running or was stopped by the event; a stopped object records only when it stopped. 3) Check whether it could have been wound, started or moved afterward. 4) Weigh alternatives against other evidence. 5) Restore the object to its found state after examining it.
when: a timed object conflicts with testimony
why: a stopped or tampered timepiece can mislead anyone who reads it at face value

text: 1) Collect each witness's times from clocks, memory and estimates. 2) Set them side by side in one sequence. 3) Identify a single reliable fixed point to anchor the account. 4) Check whether the story of events fits the hours.
when: several witnesses give times that must be placed in one sequence
why: a fixed point lets conflicting estimates be tested rather than averaged

text: Do not resolve an impossible-access puzzle with an unexplained supernatural cause when the design promises a rational solution.
when: the design promises a rational answer
why: an unexplained cause breaks the fairness the player expects

text: Give players a timestamped event log with a discoverable constant offset, so they must detect and correct it before ordering events.
when: designing timeline-based puzzles
why: Correcting the offset is what makes the sequence solvable

text: Cross-check a timed record such as a log, message or clock reading against a suspect's claimed location to show who could have been present.
when: when a character offers an alibi

text: An observer who cannot see a scene can order the events by their sounds, using each sound as a marker for the sequence.
when: Visual access to an event is blocked or partial.
why: Audible cues such as shots and cries give a usable timeline.

text: Dates tied to known events such as weddings, sailings or recorded visits are more reliable than dates that depend on a witness's guess about another event.
when: Assessing how reliable a witness's date is.
why: A date fixed by an independent event can be checked, while a guessed date inherits the uncertainty of the guess.

text: Succession rules can change through legal challenges, so the line of heirs may not be stable.
when: Relying on a fixed inheritance order as a clue.
why: Disputes over birth or marriage proof can alter who inherits.

text: Leave one supernatural event unexplained while giving other events testable natural and hidden human causes, so the player must weigh the uncanny against the human.
when: designing a mystery with supernatural elements
why: A single open event keeps the player uncertain and invites weighing of explanations.

text: Look for periodic patterns, such as events recurring at fixed intervals or on the same weekday, to predict and check dates.
when: Events recur in a case and their dates are uncertain.
why: A regular interval lets the investigator predict the next occurrence and verify the timeline.

text: Use fixed timeline windows, such as a half-hour gap, so the player must reconstruct where a suspect was during that window.
when: when designing investigation timelines
why: Fixed windows give the player a concrete period to reconstruct.

text: Schedule an interruption, such as a rival entering, to force a decision at a critical moment.
when: when designing tense confrontations
why: A timed interruption compresses the player's decision window.

text: A title and estate pass along a fixed line of heirs, and the line can shift if the first heir fails to inherit.
when: A death gives someone a claim through inheritance or succession.
why: The order of heirs determines who benefits from each death.

text: 1) Anchor the timeline on an event with a certain date, ideally recorded in more than one place. 2) Date other events against the anchor. 3) Verify each key onset date against a second record before building reasoning on it.
when: A solution depends on precise timing of several events, who was where and when, or records conflict.
why: A fixed reference orders scattered dates, and a chain of dates is only as strong as its weakest link.

text: Explaining a plan before a stakeout turns the final scene into a test of that plan; hiding it turns the scene into a reveal.
Each reconstruction trial can change an investigator's assessment, so repeated trials turn a timing claim into measured evidence.
when: when testing a theory over several sessions
why: measured results replace speculation and shift conclusions
