text: A gate that closes a branch with no action when evidence falls below a threshold ends the matter without combat.
Holding a suspect on a weak charge risks release, and the offence may be reclassified by authorities.
1) Accept the witness's conditions only if she can be watched at all times. 2) Assess her mental state and involvement. 3) Judge whether her word can be trusted.
when: A witness imposes conditions on her testimony.
why: Monitoring confirms the bargain is honored and reveals whether the witness is reliable.

text: Do not accept a natural cause or an impossibility until physical traces have been examined.
Design a trial-style ordeal so that its outcome exposes the test's flaw instead of revealing the truth.
Build trials as staged mechanics, from charge to appeal, where each stage changes what the player can do.
Accepting a witness's conditions, such as a waiting period and a fixed meeting, gives time to confirm her account but also gives the suspect time to escape.
when: A witness will speak only on her own terms.
why: Delay trades the witness's cooperation against the risk of losing the suspect.

text: Breaking a suspected hidden part and seeing the illusion end confirms that the part caused it.
Tie a state flag to a player-visible object so the scene changes only after the player moves or interacts with it, such as a clock starting once wound.
why: Visible causes make later changes feel earned and readable.

text: A small physical arrangement, such as a cord hitched to a bell, can give a hidden actor both a reason and a window to leave a room.
A trap or event can chain small harmless states, such as a disabled alarm and an absent guard, so players can discover the sequence.
Casual handling of an object with a concealed mechanism can injure the person who inspects it.
when: An object looks harmless but contains a hidden trigger
why: The mechanism is designed to act when the object is disturbed

text: A door can look locked while its bolt is disabled, so an apparently locked door is not proof that the room was closed.
when: Judging whether a room was sealed
why: Visual lock state hides mechanical sabotage

text: Plans to disable a system depend on knowing how it is wired, and wrong assumptions about wiring can make the plan fail.
when: planning to disable a system
why: hidden wiring may not match expectations

text: Give players an examine or test action that confirms the mechanism, so they can move from hypothesis to proof.
when: when designing investigation interactions

text: No-slack plans fail at the first setback; one delay, such as a late arrival, can shift windows other actors depend on, so every timeline needs spare time.
when: Timed sequences where each leg is timed exactly or several actors depend on one another.
why: Any delay pushes the whole plan past its deadline or shifts the window the rest of the plan depends on.

text: Show a quest's remaining time, such as days left, and let players pick sub-goals before expiry; pressure grows as each interval passes.
when: Designing a quest with a fixed end date.
why: A visible countdown turns the timeline into urgency and makes choices meaningful.

text: Making a slow process's progress readable, such as a burned-down candle, lets players reconstruct when a trigger happened, so the mechanism itself becomes a clue.
Add a world rule change or deadline, such as a decree or curfew, that makes an NPC's death advantageous to a particular suspect.
when: when designing motives for a mystery

text: Pair an external threat that multiplies copies with urgency, so the player must act before the mechanism is fully proven.
Timed messages that delay a rescue or investigation's outcome make the player act while still uncertain.
Setting a time limit on recovering an item creates urgency, since each delay lets the item be copied or moved.
when: When an item can change state or location over time.
why: Elapsed time increases the chance the item is lost or duplicated.

text: Trail signs that fade as light changes impose a time limit, forcing trackers to act before the signs disappear.
when: when a tracking chase takes place in changing light
why: The fading evidence creates urgency

text: A fixed waiting deadline gives the culprit time to flee, and a witness's mental state can shift during the wait.
when: Setting a delay before a reveal.
why: Time lets the suspect act and changes the witness's reliability.

text: Repeating the same threat without change dulls tension; each beat should escalate or shift the threat.
why: the audience adapts to an unchanged threat and stops reacting to it

text: Show a clock during timed sequences, and let players extend it by completing tasks or by delaying the opposing character.
when: Designing escape or heist challenges

text: Do not hold back action when a victim may be in immediate danger, even if surveillance is still incomplete.
when: A victim may be in immediate danger

text: In poison or trap systems, make opportunity windows visible, showing when an object is unattended and who can reach it, so players can reason about timing.
when: when designing timed hazards or hidden acts
why: Visible windows let players work out the timing rather than guess.

text: A short deadline makes players act before evidence is certain, which speeds play but raises the chance they commit to a wrong trail.
when: timed investigation or rescue scenarios

text: Torn paper recovered from debris can be a multi-step task, where the assembled document unlocks the final dialogue.
Design each deduction branch to lead to an informative answer rather than an empty dead end, so each elimination advances the player.
when: Building a deduction puzzle with several explanations.
why: A dead end that gives no new information leaves the player with no progress, so elimination feels wasted.

text: Give the player early requests that seem harmless, such as money or shoes, and let them return later as escape tools or disguises.
why: Ordinary-seeming requests planted early pay off as concealed means when recalled.

text: A cluster of defensive measures around one location signals the real objective, since each measure can be read as harmless alone.
when: a boss or trap-setter places defenses
why: Players infer intent from repeated defensive placement around one spot.

text: A deceptive pretext can distort the judgment of helpers who cooperate because they trust the investigator, so the cost of deception falls on them too.
when: An investigator uses a false role to gain access.
why: Helpers who trust the investigator may act on that trust in ways that later cause harm.

text: A warning that always proves right removes tension; let some warnings be wrong or ignored, with the cost of ignoring them made clear.
Let a witness who saw the player act give a conditional warning, so the player may heed it or ignore it and face later consequences.
when: An NPC has seen the player's hidden action.
why: The choice makes the warning a decision, not just information.

text: Offer a bluff option whose claimed evidence can be checked later, so a bluff can be called and punished.
when: designing interrogation choices for the player
why: A checkable bluff makes the player's claim a risk rather than a free threat.

text: Make sensor loss a designed failure state so that players must act on partial information.
when: A player depends on a planted sensor

text: Make staged evidence verifiable through a second channel, so the player can confirm or refute it independently of the first source.
Let the player control different characters in turn, each with different knowledge, so the same event reads differently from each viewpoint.
when: Designing a multi-viewpoint mystery
why: Differing knowledge makes one event look like different events.

text: Expose an impostor through a skill check, such as a chess-like move or timed sequence, where a visual check cannot separate the fake from the real figure.
A witness at a fixed position reports only what that position shows, so events out of view must be inferred or left unknown.
when: A witness watches from a window, tower or other restricted viewpoint.
why: A vantage explains what was seen, not what happened outside the field of view.

text: A witness account needs independent confirmation, such as a matching physical trace, because vivid detail, pride, or a dramatic claim can make it persuasive yet inaccurate.
when: A witness reports a dramatic or checkable claim from a limited vantage, or describes a close call in vivid detail.
why: Physical traces can confirm or contradict a single observer, and memory can be misremembered while self-image colors the telling.

text: A surface handled by others loses its value as evidence, because a later trace may not be attributable to the intended person.
when: A surface has been touched by several people before it is examined.
why: Foreign contact makes the trace ambiguous.

text: A subject who notices a collection of records can change behaviour to avoid the check.
when: A subject knows their traces or identity are being recorded.
why: Awareness of the check prompts evasion.

text: 1) Set secrecy terms before sharing anything. 2) Share conclusions in measured amounts, promising to reveal the rest later. 3) Ask about delicate matters indirectly so the witness can reject a suggestion first.
when: Interviewing sympathetic witnesses who may talk too much.
why: Measured disclosure protects the investigation and gives the witness no ammunition to leak.

text: Let players notice when an NPC displays the wrong limb or side, as a clue that something is being hidden.
when: an NPC performs a display involving a body part
why: A mismatched display gives players a visible inconsistency to investigate.

text: Compare the weapon used against the other objects present; a mismatch with the violence of the wound or the available tools is a first anomaly to investigate.
when: the weapon looks wrong for the injury or the scene
why: An object out of place for its use can reveal who chose it and what they could do.

text: Use warnings instead of attacks when the antagonist aims to deter and the target needs a real choice.
when: The antagonist wants deterrence rather than a kill
why: A warning gives the target a decision before any harm occurs.

text: An attack usually produces more than one blow, and a second blow often lands on a raised arm defending the head, so a wound pattern suggests likely injuries.
when: Inferring a suspect's injuries from an attack
why: Defensive posture during a multi-strike attack leaves predictable injuries

text: Physical damage to an everyday object or weapon persists after the blow, such as a split; its state records how it was used and can be checked against an account of the attack.
when: An ordinary object is used in a fight, or items persist after combat
why: Damage persists after the act; physical state can serve as evidence

text: A damage system that records the pattern of a wound lets players deduce the weapon or creature from the detail of the injury.
why: the injury's shape carries information about its cause

text: The entry angle of a blade shows which side it was driven from; a slanted stroke cannot easily come from the opposite side.
when: the attacker's position is in doubt
why: entry geometry limits which positions could have produced the wound

text: 1) Identify the physical force the blow required. 2) List which suspects could generate that force. 3) List which suspects would choose the weapon used. 4) Keep only suspects who pass both tests.
when: a weapon choice and the force of the injury both point to a suspect
why: Strength and intent are separate constraints, and a theory must satisfy both.

text: Keep the cause of a wound separate from the cause of death, since a wound made during life can coexist with signs of drowning.
when: when a body shows both an injury and a fatal condition

text: If a weapon's state is shown early, such as an empty magazine or removed cartridges, later combat must respect that state.
when: a weapon's ammunition or condition has been shown to the player
why: a displayed state is a fact the player will check against later play

text: Bag a weapon in cloth to protect fingerprints, and record any hair or fibres stuck to it before further handling.
when: A weapon found at a scene may carry prints or fibres.
why: Handling without protection can destroy prints and loose trace material.

text: For stealth or puzzle AI, predict the player's next choice from observed habits, then respond one level deeper, so the AI adapts to the player's patterns.
when: Designing AI that adapts to player habits.
why: Responding one level deeper counters a player who anticipates the AI.

text: An NPC can anticipate a common player trick, such as a disguise, and answer with a counter-trap or a decoy.
When a player's theory fails repeatedly, offer a hint that points to the assumption most worth revisiting.
when: Players repeatedly reach dead ends in a deduction puzzle.
why: Redirecting attention to the faulty assumption restores progress without solving the case.

text: When a defense is escalated, an adaptive attacker switches approach and attempts again, so each new precaution is followed by a new attempt.
when: a defended target faces a persistent attacker
why: the attacker adapts to the defense

text: A prediction fails to prove a hypothesis if the other party has real alternatives the hypothesis ignores.
when: When testing a solution by predicting an actor's move.
why: A rational actor may choose a path the solver did not consider.

text: 1) State what the hypothesis forces the other party to do next. 2) Identify the constraints that action must satisfy. 3) Note what different evidence the alternatives would produce. 4) Wait for the event. 5) Confirm with a logical corollary.
when: When a hypothesis implies a specific future action by another actor.
why: A correct prediction discriminates between hypotheses when alternatives are ruled out.

text: Predictable personality traits let players plan counterplay, but predictable search patterns are exploitable; reasoning-capable opponents suit item guards, while stated traits suit antagonists.
when: designing opponents that players must outmanoeuvre or that guard an item
why: Predictability aids fair counterplay but invites exploitation of routine search behavior.

text: Wary creatures need more skill and care to catch than unwary ones, so catching them is a harder challenge.
Tune hider NPCs by intelligence: low-tier hiders use common spots, higher-tier hiders use unexpected ones, so the detective player must infer which.
when: Designing hide-and-seek or search encounters.
why: Varying hiding quality makes the search a reasoning task.

text: Let a suspect's strength attribute determine which weapons they can wield, so the player's weapon choice becomes evidence matched against each suspect's attributes.
when: rooms contain weapons of different weights
why: Gating deduction on stats makes the chosen weapon informative rather than arbitrary.

text: Give an antagonist a set of options so that the player's hypothesis predicts one required move, checked by a trigger.
when: Designing antagonist behavior for deduction puzzles.
why: Makes the player's reasoning testable against the game's response.

text: A symptom or test result that contradicts the apparent cause is read as a clue that the substance was altered.
when: when a diagnostic result disagrees with the obvious explanation
why: A mismatch invites the player to search for a masking or added agent.

text: Several traces can be left by people working in turns, so a single-actor inference is weaker when multiple people could have produced the traces.
when: Interpreting traces at a scene where more than one person could have acted.
why: Traces alone cannot distinguish sequential actors from a single one.

text: A found object such as a cause-of-death note or a stolen item can shift what the player can conclude, without naming the culprit.
when: When designing evidence items for an investigation.
why: Physical items narrow the set of plausible conclusions while leaving the final identification open.

text: A deduction journal can list premises, and evidence items can be flagged as verified only after the player cross-checks them against those premises.
when: Designing a player-facing deduction or clue system.
why: Verification gates keep unchecked clues out of the player's reasoning.

text: Give players a way to test an ambiguous scent or tracker result so its reasoning stays open rather than accepted at face value.
A document-comparison puzzle can ask the player to match a distinctive handwriting trait against a suspect's note.
when: Designing a puzzle built on written evidence.
why: A distinctive trait gives the player a concrete feature to compare.

text: The number and skill of distinct actions in a scene's traces can indicate how many people acted and what skill they needed.
when: A single-actor or locked-room crime must be analysed to decide how many suspects to consider.
why: Each action implies a particular capability, and a set of capabilities suggests one person or several.

text: A deduction system can let the player name acquaintances or factions to a reluctant NPC and read each reaction as a clue.
when: when designing reluctant witnesses
why: Reactions carry information without direct answers.

text: A case-file system can store event order as a chain, with absolute timestamps only where a record certifies them and relative ordering elsewhere; players can rebuild timelines from NPC accounts and a calendar anchored by a certified document.
when: Designing in-game records where some events have confirmed dates.
why: Relative ordering keeps a sequence usable when most times are unknown.

text: A timestamped event log of gate openings, patrol passes and door activations lets players rebuild who could reach a room and when, and game clocks that differ from an NPC's report create checkable contradictions.
when: Designing a dungeon or facility with tracked movement.
why: Logged times let players test claims against the recorded sequence.

text: A count of observed successes suggests a larger number of unseen attempts and failures, since a scheme that succeeds rarely was probably tried many times.
when: Estimating how often a repeated scheme was attempted.
why: Only some attempts are observed, so the observed count understates the total.

text: A collision during a chase may be accidental or deliberate, and the evader cannot always tell which.
1) List every observable feature of the target. 2) Mark each as stable over time or easily changed. 3) Match candidates using stable features first.
when: Identifying someone from a description

text: 1) Place a suspicious item with an innocent origin. 2) Let the player trace it to a mundane cause. 3) Allow the player to rule it out, while the item still changes what they do.
when: Designing a game where players investigate a suspicious item.
why: Ruling out an item without removing its effect keeps the investigation meaningful.

text: 1) Collect every candidate pair of footwear in the setting. 2) Compare each against the measured tracks. 3) Reject candidates with mismatched size. 4) Keep the remaining pair as the suspect.
when: A puzzle asks the player to match tracks to a wearer.
why: Size mismatch is a checkable filter that narrows suspects without relying on testimony.

text: Base identification or accusation on several converging weak clues rather than one decisive item, weighting each clue by how rare its trait is.
when: Designing a detective or identification check, or an investigation system with partial forensic results.
why: Combining independent clues makes identification robust and rewards player reasoning, because ambiguous single items cannot carry an accusation alone.

text: Keep prints ambiguous when several items fit, so that matching a print to an item does not give a single unavoidable answer.
when: designing puzzles where NPCs own footwear, keys or prints
why: Ambiguity forces the player to combine clues rather than match one item.

text: Give NPCs an accuracy value when passing information on, so relayed clues can arrive garbled.
when: NPCs share information with one another

text: Track which clues the player has shared with each NPC, since a shared clue can change that NPC's behaviour.
Keep a case journal that logs every clue, witness statement and object the player has encountered, so the final accusation can be replayed as a chain of evidence.
when: Designing investigation gameplay where the player must justify an accusation.
why: A replayable evidence chain lets the player verify and review their reasoning.

text: Record evidence disposal, such as removed cups, tools or stolen notes, as an event the player can detect by noticing missing objects.
when: A culprit has removed evidence from a scene.
why: Missing objects give players a detectable trace of the removal.

text: When material evidence stalls, introduce a psychological test such as a social game, so the player receives a new kind of clue.
when: The player has exhausted physical evidence.
why: A different clue type reopens the investigation without repeating earlier searches.

text: Design one definitive anchor plus several partial sources that narrow the range, so a missing source slows the player without blocking the case.
when: Designing a timeline puzzle.
why: Redundant partial clues keep progress possible when one source is lost.

text: A timeline that records where each character was at set times lets the player find contradictions between two accounts.
A time-stamped event log with measured travel times between map nodes lets players check whether NPCs could have reached a location in time.
when: Designing location-based alibi checks in a game world.
why: Physical travel constraints expose impossible claimed routes.

text: 1) Read the object's fixed state. 2) Confirm it could not have been altered after the event, since changeable states can be staged. 3) Compare the recorded time with the agreed event time. 4) Treat a match as supporting evidence only after step 2.
when: Using an object's condition to test a claimed time of an event.
why: A match alone does not prove the object was untouched; irreversibly fixed states are trustworthy, while changeable ones can be staged to match a story.

text: 1) Compare the design of the new case with earlier cases. 2) Compare its execution. 3) Check psychological features as well as physical ones. 4) Verify any match against the record.
when: a new crime looks similar to older ones
why: matching across several dimensions reduces false matches

text: 1) Check the claimed location against the physical layout of the area, such as how numbering runs along a street. 2) Confirm the result later when conditions allow. 3) Keep the written claim and test it against other evidence.
when: A character or player gives a location that can be checked against physical or public facts.
why: A stated location may be misheard, misremembered, or wrong, and a single check does not settle it.

text: 1) Fix the exact timeline of scheduled events, including departures, changes in service pattern, and arrivals. 2) Check each claim against those fixed points. 3) Separate ordinary runs from the disputed one.
when: A claim depends on a sequence of scheduled events.
why: Anchoring claims to a fixed timeline reveals which statements are consistent with the schedule.

text: In a locked-room puzzle, record every opening (doors with catches, windows, keys) and its state so players can test an NPC's sealed-room claim by elimination.
when: Designing a locked or sealed room that an NPC describes as sealed.
why: Listed states let players reason to a conclusion they can verify.

text: Show a fixed-time clock so players can check NPC time claims; it is a valid reference only if running and set by a known character.
when: Designing NPC time claims that the player must verify, or in-world clocks used as timeline sources.
why: Players can only trust a reading whose setter and running state are verifiable.

text: Let an NPC encounter use a message in an in-world code the NPC recognises; the player succeeds by timing the arrival.
when: A stealth or ambush encounter.

text: Require several independent clues before a solution is accepted, so one lucky find does not solve the case.
when: Designing a mystery or investigation system with a solution check.
why: Multiple required clues prevent accidental solves and reward thorough investigation.

text: Store investigation leads with a priority score and dependencies, so a check such as sampling a typewriter precedes its conclusion.
why: Dependencies prevent conclusions from being drawn before their prerequisites.

text: Leave one secured-looking route open, or give an NPC a key, so the elimination method misleads without being unfair.
when: Designing a sealed-room puzzle with a red herring.
why: A fair misdirection tests reasoning without cheating the player.

text: Make an item that slips from a guard's coat, or wear on a lever or handle, carry readable origin information, so players can trace who handled it and where.
when: Designing environmental clues in a level or dungeon.
why: Players can reconstruct events from traces that point to people and places.

text: Let players reconstruct a timeline from scattered entries such as letters, sightings and hiding spots, gating progress on the correct order.
when: Designing investigation progression across scattered clues
why: Ordering the clues reveals the hidden sequence and unlocks the next step

text: A suspect-deduction puzzle can offer several motives, with one fact contradicting the most obvious suspect.
when: Designing a deduction puzzle for players.
why: Competing motives and a contradicting fact reward careful reasoning over the obvious answer.

text: A denial is neither proof of innocence nor a sign of guilt; treating denial or defiance as guilt lets an investigator presume a culprit without proof.
why: a denial may reflect loyalty, fear or a promise

text: A suspect cornered by evidence may lash out in anger, sometimes making a threat or a move that shows guilt.
when: A suspect is confronted after being cornered.
why: Anger overrides composure.

text: People in despair take a high-risk pressure move as a gamble when no better option remains.
when: all safer options are exhausted
why: the cost of inaction seems higher

text: When an interviewer shows that the outline of events is already known, denying individual steps becomes costly for the witness.
when: the investigator holds evidence for the outline
why: Denial would contradict a visible, established sequence.

text: A suspect confronted with an accusation may answer to protect themselves rather than to answer the question actually put to them.
when: when a suspect receives a written or direct accusation
why: Self-protection can shape a reply more strongly than the literal question does.

text: A witness may deny knowledge directly while holding relevant information, showing through hesitation, manner shifts or a missed chance to speak.
when: A witness's denial conflicts with the observer's impression

text: A sudden sharpness in someone's voice when a topic is raised often signals a sore spot.
A suspect's amusement or defiance can conceal real fear, so their reactions must be read carefully rather than taken at face value.
when: Reading a suspect's response during a confrontation
why: Outward confidence can be a defensive display

text: A party that fears identification may deflect suspicion onto an unrelated person when offered a false lead, exposing its concern.
when: A fabricated target is presented to someone with something to hide.
why: Trying to stop identification drives the suspect to act in ways that betray their interest.

text: A suspect cornered out of witnesses' sight, with escape blocked, tends to answer with silence or a narrow excuse rather than a full account.
when: Confrontation happens on a quiet road or similar place away from onlookers, with the retreat blocked.
why: Pressure and isolation make a full, checkable answer less likely.

text: Suspects who answer only with flat denial give no testable content, leaving the investigator without evidence to check.
when: Questioning suspects at night or under pressure.
why: A bare denial offers no claim that can be confirmed or refuted.

text: A speaker caught making a remark can easily deny what was meant, and the hearer's own unease does not prove the accusation.
when: Confronting someone over an overheard remark
why: Meaning of words is contestable, so denial is cheap

text: Once a group accepts an accusation, it tends to read the accused's denials as distraction rather than answering them.
when: when an accusation has already been accepted by a group
why: Acceptance of the accusation shapes how later rebuttals are interpreted.

text: A suspect confronted with an accusing identity can deny it and adopt a new name, which blocks confirmation while the questioner lacks proof.
when: when the questioner cannot yet prove the identity
why: denial prevents the accusation from being confirmed

text: Predict a captor's behaviour by asking what it still wants from its captive and whether that goal remains reachable.
when: An abduction or hostage situation has a clear financial or informational motive

text: A cornered NPC with an escape option turns a conversation into a timed chase.
when: an NPC can flee during confrontation
why: escape adds urgency

text: A cornered or trapped suspect may fight or fire at close range, especially when armed, so the approach must expect a last-moment attack.
when: a confrontation has no exit, a hidden party is about to be exposed, or a lone pursuer closes on a trapped suspect
why: threatened people fight or flee; being cornered removes escape but not the ability to attack

text: Confronting a hidden weapon in a crowded place can endanger bystanders.

Corner a suspect in a bounded area: 1) assign one companion to each open side so the posts overlook the cover, 2) personally watch the one route they cannot see, 3) agree a signal for convergence, 4) enter slowly and quietly, 5) follow fresh tracks straight to the hiding place, 6) close in from behind.
when: a suspect is confined to a bounded area with a small number of exits
why: Covering every exit and approaching unseen leaves the suspect no unwatched route and no warning.

text: Separate what a cornered witness actually knows from what they only guess, since pressure can produce confused or partial answers.
when: a frightened witness gives a muddled account under questioning
why: Pressure blurs knowledge and speculation together.

text: Remove a threat's weapons as part of establishing control of the situation.
A target who fears public exposure may come forward to plead for help rather than confess.
when: The target reads the public record and fears being exposed.
why: Fear of exposure can push a target toward the investigator for protection.

text: Frightened NPCs can give fewer answers, so dialogue stays restricted until the fear passes.
when: an NPC is panicked or scared
why: Fear reduces an NPC's willingness or ability to respond, which limits what the player can learn from them.

text: Model panic as a state that spreads between nearby characters and can trigger avoidance of imagined threats.
when: when simulating crowd reactions

text: A single sudden alarm, such as a shout, halts all active conflict for a moment, then sends the crowd fleeing toward exits, clearing the space quickly.
when: When a scene needs an abrupt stop or a fast clearing of many agents.
why: A shared, unexpected threat overrides ongoing behavior and redirects everyone toward escape.

text: A dramatic spectacle draws crowd attention away from nearby objects, leaving a dropped object unwatched.
when: A chaotic event occurs near an object the player wants to reach.
why: Attention concentrates on the spectacle, so peripheral objects go unnoticed.

text: NPC crowds in a hall or courtroom can react to questioning, with mood shifting as the player's line of inquiry changes.
when: When designing public scenes where NPCs witness player actions
why: Visible crowd reaction makes the consequences of questioning legible to the player.

text: Questions asked in a public place can reach the person under investigation and reveal the investigator.
when: gathering information in public
why: the target can overhear or hear about the inquiry

text: To observe a target unnoticed in a public room, sit with your back to them and keep watching a second person's face.
when: watching a target in a crowded or noisy room

text: Use a hidden flag to change how a crowd or guard reacts, so the player understands tension the characters do not yet grasp.
when: Designing crowd or guard responses in a game.
why: Player knowledge of a hidden state creates suspense about the NPCs' coming misreads.

text: A fast crowd clear removes individuals from view too quickly for the player to track them, so avoid it when individual NPCs must stay followable.
when: When the scene requires following specific characters.
why: Mass movement at speed hides individuals in the flow.

text: Track topics the player raised with each NPC: list refused topics, mark closed if refused outright or deferred if an answer was promised, then check which deferred topics the player can reopen. Refusals or topic changes can raise suspicion or unlock a different reaction.
A character who blinks, looks away or turns the talk to another grievance when asked about a topic reveals that topic is a sore point.
when: A player raises a question the character would rather avoid
why: Avoidance marks sensitivity.

text: Let an NPC react to a trigger phrase only when the player holds a related hidden fact, and keep the reaction ambiguous so players must separate guilt from grudge.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that hints at hidden knowledge.
why: Ambiguous reactions require players to reason rather than read a clear signal.

text: A quest can post a description chosen by the player's theory, so only the NPC matching the predicted clue state replies, confirming or refuting that theory.
when: Designing a witness-reply mechanic for a detective game.
why: Tying responses to clue state makes the player's inference testable in play.

text: Make NPC reactions in interrogation scenes depend on the player's actions, so the player can test whether a reaction is genuine or staged.
when: Designing scripted NPC responses in interrogation or confrontation scenes.
why: A reaction that responds to player input can be probed, letting careful players tell real signals from arranged ones.

text: Make NPC recognition depend on which disguise features cover the traits each NPC remembers; changing visible traits such as equipment removes the cues NPCs use to identify the player.
when: Designing NPC recognition in a costume-based disguise system.
why: Recognition should follow what the NPC actually remembers, not a single global check.

text: A character's sudden silence, flush or fixed stare reveals recognition of a clue before anyone understands its meaning.
when: when a character sees a hidden clue
why: visible reactions signal recognition

text: Watchers accept a feigned illness or absence at face value, so a character who pretends to be sick lets others act freely.
when: A character must appear absent while others carry out a plan.
why: Watchers rely on the visible state of the character and do not check it directly.

text: A group can appear wholly indifferent to a stranger while closely watching him, and the watching shows in indirect movement rather than direct attention.
when: A group's behaviour is too uniform or convenient to be innocent
why: Feigning ignorance hides observation

text: At a distance people are recognised more by their back, shape and posture than by their face.
when: when observing someone from far away
why: Faces are hard to make out at range, while silhouettes stay visible.

text: Expose disguised characters through specific behavioural or context mismatches, such as a guard in the wrong room, running, or carrying wrong items, not general appearance.
when: when designing recognition of disguised enemies
why: Behaviour reveals a disguise that costume conceals, and a mismatch with setting is easier for players to test than appearance.

text: Do not identify a character by silhouette or voice alone; require a second cue such as a unique item, a mark, a visual cue, or a second guard.
when: When designing NPC identification for stealth or detection systems.
why: Shared visuals would let the wrong character be identified, and a mimicry trait can fool an NPC that trusts voice alone.

text: Let guards pass a disguised player when uniform and password match, and run recognition checks when any detail is mismatched.
Let a false identity's strength depend on which NPCs saw the player and whether those NPCs check records.
when: designing stealth or infiltration missions

text: Give infiltrators full, consistent daily routines matching their cover, so the only clue is a break in that routine.
when: when designing infiltrating enemies
why: a consistent routine removes all clues except a break in it

text: An enemy disguised as an expected guard passes patrol checks if its routine explains its presence; trigger recognition on a specific wrong detail, not general appearance.
when: when designing recognition checks for disguised enemies
why: a specific detail is a clearer cue than overall look

text: A disguise that copies a coat and hat should give the player a fair chance to doubt the identity.
when: When designing disguise mechanics.
why: Players need a way to detect the disguise so the reveal feels earned rather than arbitrary.

text: A stealth or disguise mechanic can grant access to a restricted NPC while the cover identity remains at risk of discovery.
when: Designing social stealth for a game

text: NPCs react according to the identity they believe the player holds, so hidden identities change reactions only after the player reveals them.
when: A player hides or claims an identity in the game world.
why: NPCs can only respond to what they know, so reactions shift when their knowledge changes.

text: Guards that judge a player by appearance let a plausible cover identity pass until a visible trait exposes it.
A stealth checkpoint can compare a disguised character's outfit against a target's signature items, with recognition chance falling as distance grows.
when: when designing guard perception for disguised characters
why: distance reduces the detail available to the observer

text: A target who stows a prepared disguise in a public locker can change appearance mid-pursuit and leave looking ordinary.
when: The target anticipates being followed
why: Removing the tracked trait breaks the pursuer's identification

text: An observer NPC can notice a mismatch between a character's displayed capability and its real capability, which exposes a feigned state.
when: a stealth or detective game lets the player hide strength

text: Resemblance alone is weak evidence, since many crimes look alike; a shared method must be confirmed.
why: similar surface features arise independently

text: A disguise that hides only the eyes or face can still be recognised at close range, ending the operation.
when: when approaching closely

text: A stand-in double who is never seen up close fails to fool watchers, because a direct check exposes the substitution.
when: Designing a character impersonation or double for deception.
why: Deception depends on watchers not inspecting the double closely.

text: 1) Enter the target household under a cover role. 2) Present a false identity that insiders know to be false. 3) Watch the suspect's reaction. 4) Add a second contact to test whether the suspect bargains or holds firm. 5) Confront with a trace the suspect cannot explain away.
when: The suspect is close to the victim and inside the household, so the disguise grants access.
why: A cover role provides observation from inside, and a guilty suspect's reaction under pressure exposes them.

text: 1) Create a companion disguised as the player character. 2) Use it to deceive patrols. 3) Let patrols act on the false identity until they inspect closely.
when: Designing a stealth mechanic that uses a disguised companion.
why: Patrols act on visible identity, and the disguise holds until close inspection.

text: Let a disguised character pass a first identity check but fail a second, such as a sound cue, missing item, smudged paint or wrong gesture, giving careful players a visible tell.
when: designing disguised characters or stealth past guards
why: Layered checks reward observation without making the disguise impossible to see through.

text: Make recognition of disguised characters depend on distance, posture, light and suspicion, so disguises succeed at range and fail up close; allow a second look to confirm identity.
when: Designing guard or NPC recognition of disguised players in stealth systems.
why: Varying conditions makes recognition feel fair and uncertain.

text: Give disguised characters a hidden fixed trait, such as a physical mark, tag or gait, that survives removable disguise elements so removing one exposes a mismatch.
when: Designing disguised characters or suspects who may wear removable disguise elements.
why: Removable elements can hide a mark the disguise does not cover, and a stable trait differs from the visible disguise so players can match it.

text: Model a disguised investigator NPC with a cover-integrity state that drops after a slip, raising suspicion in the NPCs being questioned.
when: when a character poses as a friend while gathering information
why: a broken cover changes what witnesses will say

text: In a restricted area, let guards and NPCs recognize each other, so a stranger triggers an immediate reaction the player can exploit.
why: Mutual recognition makes unfamiliar faces produce visible responses

text: Make disguise changes actions with a time cost so that the timeline can be checked for consistency.
when: Designing disguise mechanics in a timeline-based investigation
why: Timed disguises leave a verifiable trace in the schedule

text: In stealth games, let players use a costume and a faction's jargon to gain access to restricted areas or a suspect's trust.
when: Designing disguise mechanics in a stealth game
why: Matching appearance and speech lets players pass as members of a group

text: Create a role-based NPC such as a messenger or servant whom guards ignore and who can pass through restricted areas.
when: designing NPCs that cross guarded boundaries
why: Guards that filter by role will let ordinary-role NPCs through unchecked.

text: A suspect who senses pursuit becomes more careful, so a change of focus should be signalled late.
when: when a suspect may learn they are being investigated
why: a pursued suspect adjusts their behaviour to avoid detection

text: Fleeing away from a safe place rather than toward it signals severe fear and impaired judgment, so the direction of flight is evidence of a person's state of mind.
when: reconstructing a person's movement sequence after an event
why: Fear can override sensible escape choices, so the direction chosen reveals what the person dreaded.

text: A person facing ruin or exposure may have motive to disappear, and a murder can serve as the means of that escape.
when: debts or exposure threaten the person
why: A believed death ends pursuit.

text: A person planning to vanish prepares the means of escape in advance rather than at the moment of crisis.
when: a disappearance is deliberate
why: careful planning reduces the risk of being caught

text: A suspect under pressure may leave the room with an excuse; this can signal guilt or innocent distress.
A survey that ignores compass variation runs boundary lines inaccurately, so disputes over the line can persist until a corrected survey is made.
when: when lines are surveyed with a magnetic compass
why: uncorrected magnetic deviation shifts the measured bearing

text: List each exit of a sealed chamber explicitly and attach a check, such as footprints, dust or sound, so the player can eliminate exits one by one.
when: designing a sealed chamber puzzle

text: A route arranged to hide a destination is itself a clue to intent.
why: Deliberate concealment implies the destination matters

text: Ask why an actor would choose a longer or riskier route, to test whether a candidate exit is plausible.
why: A route that costs more risk or time is less likely to be chosen.

text: Perpetrators who choose vulnerable targets, use natural-looking methods, and avoid repeating their pattern are the ones most likely to escape detection.
when: Assessing why some crimes go unnoticed.
why: Each of these choices removes a trace that would otherwise reveal the act.

text: On entering a confined space, note the exact position of fast escape options, such as an emergency cord, so they are ready when needed.
Do not assume one object is the only route for a harmful substance; keep other routes open until each is ruled out.
when: More than one item or container could have carried the harm.
why: Ruling out routes one by one prevents a premature conclusion.

text: A fugitive in poor physical condition is unlikely to remain at large for long and tends to be found in public places, while people often return to places tied to a need or memory.
when: searching for a fleeing or missing person
why: physical limits and attachment to meaningful places constrain where they go

text: A pursued subject who travels faster than observers can leave their sight for a stretch of time, creating an unobserved window.
when: When a pursuit involves a significant speed difference.

text: An accomplice inside can open a route, let an entrant in, and reseal the route afterwards, so the gap disappears.
A pursued target who knows the district by heart can outpace followers who do not, so local familiarity gives a decisive edge.
A second event that does not change the central question adds noise rather than tension.
Improvised evasion can attract police attention and expose the evader, so its benefit must be weighed against that risk.
1) Survey the whole layout before entering. 2) List every possible route in and out. 3) Rule out routes blocked by terrain. 4) Treat the remaining passage as the only exit.

1) List every door, window and balcony of the room. 2) Test each for bolt or lock state. 3) Test each from both sides. 4) Check whether any opening leads outside. 5) Treat the remaining explanation as lying within the room or its access rules.
when: A theft or death occurs in a room whose exits can be checked directly
why: Eliminating every exit narrows the explanation to what remains

text: 1) List every route by which the poison could reach the victim. 2) Check each route against a timeline of who was where. 3) Close routes that fail the check. 4) Note which routes remain open.
when: A poisoning or similar act must fit a narrow time window.
why: Eliminating routes one by one narrows opportunity without assuming which route was used.

text: 1) List each possible escape route, such as a door or an unlocked window. 2) Judge which is more probable. 3) Prefer the route that implies less about the suspect.
1) Offer a reachable exit. 2) Build tension with an alarm, a crowd or an opened door. 3) Reverse the attempt at the threshold. 4) Leave the player in a more confined space.
when: when designing a stealth or escape sequence
why: Alternating build-up and reversal raises stakes each time

text: 1) List every escape option, such as door, window, neighbouring room and connected room. 2) Predict the likely flight route. 3) Place a guard on each option. 4) Secure all other exits so only the planned route remains.
when: the target's route is predictable and all exits can be covered
why: a target with an uncovered exit will escape through it

text: Show every exit's state (bolt position, frame condition, grate size, grille, bolts on both sides, sealed window, width, drop height, latch, sightline) so players can rule routes in or out.
when: Designing sealed-room or locked-room puzzles where players must reason about access.
why: Visible, testable exit states let players rule routes in or out by inspection or action.

text: Offer escape options such as doors with back exits, crowds, and fast transport, each with a clear check, to let the player shake a pursuer.
when: Designing urban pursuit or evasion options in stealth or chase scenes.
why: Clear checks make each escape route predictable and fair.

text: Give each exit a fixed open schedule, such as gate hours, lock timing or guard rotation, so players can reason from a clock about who could have left.
Map each room's exits and sightlines before placing puzzles, so that every way in and out is known and finite.
when: when building a locked-room or enclosed-space puzzle
why: A finite, visible list of exits makes the puzzle solvable

text: Look for a lever other than the obvious one; a trusted contact who vouches for you can secure release faster than a written plea.
when: when detained and a direct appeal seems the only option
why: A vouched introduction carries more weight than a stranger's own appeal.

text: Make the barrier to escape internal to the character, since an arbitrary external obstacle makes the reversal read as contrivance.
Plant a visible clue to an evasion route, such as a second exit, that the player can find by inspecting the building.
Place a locked exit behind the player's entry, so careless entry has a clear and fair consequence.
when: Designing a room the player enters through an unguarded door.
why: A visible consequence teaches the player to plan entries.

text: An escape route must fit the described geometry, because a route the layout cannot allow breaks fair play.
Place a missing item so the player can deduce who could have taken it from exit timing and guard positions.
when: Designing a theft clue in a level
why: Timing and guard coverage limit who had access

text: In a crowded area with few sight lines, tune passage timing so an escape is possible but tight, letting the player test whether it could have happened.
when: When designing a dense residential area for an investigation.
why: Crowds hide movement, and tight timing keeps the escape believable without making it trivial.

text: Model hiring an accomplice as a risk cost that the AI plotter avoids unless its design allows it.
when: an AI character plans a crime
why: each added accomplice raises exposure

text: Plan an escape against a capable pursuer in layers: an unplanned transport, a fast route, a changed vehicle, a trusted helper, and a disguise.
when: when the pursuer can deduce the escapee's moves
why: Each layer removes one way the pursuer could follow.

text: A suspect's escape may not end pursuit, since charges can be chosen while travelling; but a pursuer may estimate the time-gap lead and give up when it is large.
when: Deciding whether to keep pursuing a fleeing suspect.
why: Charges can be issued during flight; time lost at a barrier widens the gap, making capture unlikely.

text: An NPC's alibi should count as verified only if checkable via a watch, bell, schedule, or independent source like a servant's log or ticket.
when: designing NPC alibis
why: Unverifiable clocks cannot confirm the claim.

text: Loose ground and debris can hide footprints, but torn fabric caught on a fixed object stays as a visible trace.
when: A character tries to cover its movement
why: Cover actions erase only some kinds of marks

text: Wheel width in ground tracks identifies the vehicle type that made them.
when: Reading physical tracks left on terrain
why: Each vehicle type has characteristic wheel dimensions

text: Accept a claim that an area was already searched, or that no one passed through it, only after checking it against other evidence or a reliable searcher.
A tracking mechanic should reveal where a creature or scent went, not who it is, unless a separate clue confirms identity.
why: a trail shows movement, not identity

text: Simple markers such as thread across a door, a seal, or dusted floor change state when disturbed, so a flat, broken or moved marker shows that a player or monster passed.
when: Designing mechanics to detect unseen movement through a door or passage
why: The marker's physical change records the disturbance; cheap indicators give players readable evidence of unseen passage.

text: A tracking mechanic can leave markers on walls or floors that a second NPC or the player follows, with the key known to the player.
A game can remove suspects whose stated motive conflicts with world-state facts, letting the player eliminate candidates through action.
when: In investigation games with tracked world state.
why: Checking motive against recorded facts makes elimination a checkable player action.

text: A planted item can be made detectable by a later check, so the player's ability to uncover a frame-up depends on whether the planted clue is verified.
when: When designing a frame-up mechanic the player can investigate.
why: A verification step gives the player a path from a planted clue to its true origin.

text: A footprint or trail mechanic that contradicts a guard's denial forces the player to re-examine who could have entered the area.
when: designing a sealed-area investigation
why: Physical traces that disagree with testimony shift trust from witnesses to evidence.

text: A feigned death fails if the opponent can verify it independently, so uncertain evidence of death leaves the planner exposed.
why: Independent checks expose a death that was only staged.

text: 1) Note the target's regular routes and destinations. 2) Record where the target repeatedly loses a follower. 3) Keep tracking over time, not in one search. 4) Follow the pattern to the hidden destination.
when: a target's routine is regular enough to reveal a hidden location

text: 1) Compare the trace's form to known candidate forms. 2) Infer the instrument or mechanism that produced it. 3) Eliminate candidates whose features do not fit. 4) Check remaining candidates against a reference of where the traits occur.
when: A physical trace has a distinctive shape or mechanism
why: Each trait can rule out some origins, narrowing identity faster than any single feature

text: 1) Record each NPC's claim about an item in a state table. 2) Compare claims for contradictions. 3) Use contradictions as new leads.
when: when designing NPC testimony that the player must cross-check
why: Stored claims let contradictions be discovered and exploited later.

text: 1) Reach the contested object first during a distraction. 2) Hand it to a trusted authority rather than keep it. 3) State its importance to secure custody.
when: A rival is racing to claim an object during a chaotic event.
why: Official custody puts the object beyond the rival's reach.

text: A travel system can check whether an NPC could cover a distance in the claimed time; a message log recording each message's origin lets a forged message become a clue.
Track a suspect NPC's gold and purchases, so a sudden buy after a crime can trigger a reaction from guards or shopkeepers.
when: designing NPC suspicion reactions
why: spending becomes a observable signal

text: Build rumour networks where grudge-holding NPCs feed names to a volatile witness, so the player can trace who first named each suspect.
Track whether a letter has been opened, and let that status change how much the player trusts its contents.
when: Designing letters or documents that can be read or tampered with
why: Opened status is a checkable signal of possible tampering

text: Let journals or letters the player finds record physical traits, places and dates, and have later investigation check them against what an NPC says.
when: Designing player-found documents that support later questioning
why: Checkable details turn testimony into a verifiable test

text: Volunteered facts or accusations may steer an inquiry, so don't dismiss them as false merely for being offered; test content against evidence, since a mundane cause may explain them.
when: when a suspect or witness offers facts or accusations unprompted, e.g. about a missing object
why: Offering a lead lets the speaker control which path the investigator follows; volunteered claims may deflect rather than inform.

text: Each retelling adds embellishment and speculation, lowering reliability yet making the story seem more established and certain without new evidence, as listeners take embellishment for proof.
when: when a rumour or crime story passes through a community or chain of intermediaries
why: Tellers add details to make the story memorable, and repetition makes unverified talk seem like evidence.

text: Each retelling in a chain drops, alters or filters detail and context, so the final version differs from the original, lowers reliability and leaves sources impossible to check.
when: when information passes through several people or NPCs

text: Store rumours with their source chain and reliability value, which drops per hop, so players trace how far each travelled from origin and corroborate with a second independent source.
when: when designing rumours NPCs pass along that players must verify
why: Recorded provenance makes corroboration possible and lets players judge reliability.

text: Let a rumour's strength rise as more NPCs repeat it, paired with a verification step players or NPCs can perform to check the original source.
when: when designing rumour propagation among NPCs

text: Rumours passed among NPCs mutate, losing detail and gaining confidence with each retelling, so players trace each to its first speaker and see the chain's order.
when: when designing rumours or clues that move between NPCs
why: Tracing rewards checking sources, and each hop's variation reveals the chain's order.

text: Information volunteered freely by a questioner is often offered to draw a reply in return.
when: A questioner shares news before asking for something.
why: Offering information creates an expectation of reciprocity.

text: Observers in different positions can see the same facts differently, so one body of evidence can support different interpretations.
when: when several witnesses describe the same event
why: each position reflects different aspects of what happened

text: Once a suspect is blamed, observers tend to add later unrelated misfortunes to the same accusation chain.
when: after an accusation has been made
why: The accusation frames new losses as its effects.

text: Some people warn others not to spread malicious talk, which shows that such chains were already recognised as a concern in the community.
when: when a community is aware of harmful rumours
why: Public concern about gossip signals that talk is already spreading

text: Oral accounts mix real clues with invention, change with each retelling, and can outlive the events that produced them.
when: sudden events that spread by word of mouth
why: Each retelling reshapes details, so the story drifts from its facts

text: A rumour of a haunting lowers people's guard, so staged effects seem more believable.
when: a location has a known haunting reputation
why: expectation primes people to accept strange events

text: Community gossip assigns motives from stereotypes, so it supplies suspects rather than proof.
why: Stereotypes such as a widow's past or a servant's expected marriage fill gaps in what people actually know.

text: Identities passed by word of mouth grow more uncertain with each retelling, as each teller adds or alters details about who the figure is.
when: Information about a hidden character reaches the player through several NPCs
why: Each retelling introduces new interpretation

text: A claim reaching someone through an intermediary is often accepted at face value and then not tested, especially when the person challenged backs away from the complaint.
when: when a report reaches the judge through a third party
why: Untested second-hand reports carry the look of fact without verification

text: Known gossips or quarrelsome people can join an accusing circle, and their reputation for trouble widens it.
Gossip about private habits can turn ordinary conduct into an apparent motive, so a community may treat normal life as a sign of guilt.
when: A community has already talked about someone's private habits
why: Notoriety lowers the threshold for suspicion

text: A group that answers with strong, uniform conviction may be the most suggestible, which a player can use to trace where a rumor started.
when: Designing NPC witnesses whose testimony can point to a rumor's origin.
why: Suggestible sources adopt and amplify a shared claim, so their unusually strong agreement marks the likely spread point.

text: Use a market, tavern or temple as a rumour hub, since regular gatherings spread news faster than formal channels and seeded news reaches NPCs in a predictable order.
when: when designing rumour spread in a game world
why: Fixed gathering places and schedules make propagation predictable.

text: Let a tavern or cart NPC gossip about faction debts or succession, giving leads without formal questioning.
A town's gossip can carry a suspect's story, so embellished rumours change what NPCs believe and say.
when: designing town gossip in a game world

text: Warn colleagues before a conversation with a probing questioner so they do not reveal what they know.
when: A colleague is about to speak with someone who may extract information.
why: A brief warning prevents casual disclosure.

text: Track each suspect's rumor state as unknown, suspected, watched, complained-of or indicted, and change NPC dialogue at each step.
when: Designing a village with a suspicion system

text: Model rumour so each accusation raises suspicion on the accuser's rivals and social peers, with suspicion climbing with social rank.
when: simulating a town where accusations circulate

text: An NPC gossip system can spread false claims through a settlement, and player-revealed facts can change how those claims are believed.
when: Designing NPC information spread in a world with player-driven discovery.
why: Believed claims shift as new evidence reaches the people who hold them.

text: A false rumour can establish a false motive and send players to the wrong location, so make its planted origin traceable to a later discovery that exposes the source.
when: when designing rumour systems in a game world where NPCs share information
why: Rumours spread faster than verification and can be traced back.

text: Model gossip as a network of carriers such as servants, shopkeepers and guards, timestamping when each NPC learns news, so players can trace who learned a secret and its source.
when: designing NPC information spread
why: A network of carriers determines who learns what and in what order.

text: Officials travelling between settlements carry accusations outward and name new suspects along the way.
Rumour and frequent travel between communities carry case details, so later communities are likely aware of earlier cases.
when: When two communities are connected by trade or travel.
why: Information moves along existing contacts.

text: Cutting a suspect off from others leaves one remaining channel, which the observer can watch, so the suspect's choices are funneled toward the response the observer expects.
when: A suspect is able to act but cannot safely contact accomplices
why: Limited options make behavior predictable

text: A first-person account of a crime changes the information the audience receives, since the narrator controls what is shown and what is withheld.
when: choosing the narrative viewpoint for a mystery
why: Viewpoint determines which facts are visible, so it shapes both suspense and fairness.

text: Remarks pass between servants and then reach investigators, so information leaks through staff and can be distorted along the way.
when: Information passes through a household.
why: Each relay can change or expose what was said.

text: Information passed along a chain of speakers gains distortion and opinion at each relay, and each speaker conveys only what their own knowledge covers.
when: when a clue reaches the audience through gossip
why: Each relay adds bias or misunderstanding.

text: NPC gossip can carry a clue to the wrong faction, and a rumoured fact can let players or rivals defuse a trap.
Rumour can spread accusations through a community, so players must separate rumour from evidence.
when: A town or group repeats an unverified accusation
why: Repetition spreads accusation faster than evidence

text: Rumour passed through several people lets any speaker blame another link, making the original source hard to trace.
Fragments held by several ordinary acquaintances can be pooled into a detailed picture of a person's private affairs.
when: several people each know a small part of a matter
why: each acquaintance sees a different detail

text: A rumour-spreading NPC can pass on a false version of an event, so the player can trace which version came from an eyewitness.
when: Designing rumour propagation among NPCs.
why: Rumours mutate as they spread, separating them from the original observation.

text: A channel that spreads news widely carries wise and mischievous ideas alike, giving both the same reach.
A rumour can carry a reliability rating and unlock a quest only after a second independent source confirms it.
when: Designing rumour-driven quest hooks.
why: Confirmation gating prevents acting on unreliable leads.

text: A hidden drop or post-box mechanic lets the player send gathered information to an off-map contact.
when: Designing covert reporting in a game.
why: A separate private channel keeps reporting secret from the local population.

text: A game with rumour or news systems should model how information spreads, so the player's actions can leak to enemies through routes the player did not plan.
when: Designing information propagation between factions or characters.
why: Unplanned leaks create tension and make the player consider every channel.

text: Tag each NPC endorsement with the knowledge that NPC could actually have, so players can see where a claim goes beyond it.
A rumour or notice in the game world can contaminate later NPC testimony, so track when each statement was formed.
when: NPCs can hear or read world information before giving accounts.
why: Statements formed after exposure may differ from firsthand memory.

text: An NPC's willingness to reveal clues can be gated by a reputation value, so changes in reputation change what information the player can get.
Reputation and disguise can change how NPCs weigh the same testimony, so identical reports get different reactions from different appearances.
when: The player's appearance or reputation varies

text: Each NPC can hold a version of an event shaped by its own motive, so players must cross-check claims against physical evidence.
Information spreads through conversation: each character who hears a secret can later act on it, so tracking listeners shows who holds the knowledge.
when: Secrets are shared among non-player characters

text: Changing headlines in an in-game news feed can change NPC behaviour, such as prompting a target to leave a safe place.
Model a tavern or village as a rumour network where a local NPC supplies names and routines, with a risk that the target overhears.
when: designing information gathering in a social hub
why: local talk spreads and can alert the target

text: Model village gossip as a relay with its own reliability value, kept separate from direct testimony.
Gossip handed down through generations can feel like fact while having no traceable source.
Too many rumours make every one seem equally plausible and drain each of its value as a lead.
Letting gossip about a person's unease shape the suspect profile before facts support it biases the conclusion.
when: Reputation begins forming suspicion
why: Reputation is easily reshaped in memory after events are known.

text: 1) Trace each cited claim to its original source before relying on it. 2) Check whether that source reports first-hand or second-hand evidence. 3) Verify each link, since relays can distort or misreport.
when: when a claim reaches you through another person or a chain of sources
why: Intermediaries may add or misreport details.

text: 1) Identify a remark or secret. 2) List everyone who heard it, with their reaction. 3) Treat those listeners as the people who could have acted on it.
when: A remark was repeated in company and the culprit may have known it
why: Listeners are the only people who could have acted on the knowledge

text: 1) Identify the source of a remark about a person. 2) Ask how that source learned it. 3) Follow the link it names, such as a relative's trade or service, into the victim's family.
when: When a casual remark mentions a relative or occupation that might connect to the case.
why: Gossip chains often lead back to the people the investigator needs.

text: 1) Reconstruct the sequence of events leading to a reaction. 2) Ask what the affected people heard or read. 3) Identify the source of that information. 4) Trace each person who carried it.
when: A reaction or departure has no obvious cause.
why: Each link in the information chain may explain the reaction and point to the origin of a leak.

text: 1) Examine the physical medium for cost, stiffness and printed marks. 2) Read woven or printed marks as abbreviations. 3) Match fragments to reference sources. 4) Analyse phrasing for the writer's origin.
when: a found document has no date, signature or address
why: physical and linguistic traces can locate a writer when the text names no one

text: 1) Decide whether the person was forced or left willingly. 2) If willingly, find what prompted them. 3) List who wrote, who was known to write, and any new correspondent. 4) Trace each message's handling. 5) Check whether the message stayed with the person.
when: A motive depends on an outside message.

text: 1) List every channel by which a message could reach a hidden accomplice, including post, telegraph, telephone, couriers and printed media. 2) Guard the obvious ones. 3) Check which remain open.
when: A suspect may have an unknown accomplice and a time-sensitive reason to act.
why: Guarding one channel does not close the others, and an unguarded channel can leak the plan.

text: 1) List who was told of a discovery. 2) Check any vague statement against a second source. 3) When a suspect appears, see whether they already know the discovery.
when: When a discovery may have reached a suspect.
why: Tracking knowledge reveals where information leaked.

text: 1) Establish which facts were kept private. 2) List every legitimate route by which each fact could reach the suspect. 3) Check each route against the suspect's recorded contacts. 4) Mark routes with no recorded contact.
when: when a suspect reveals knowledge the investigation has not released
why: An unexplained route to a secret points to a leak or an informant.

text: 1) Follow each hidden transaction to its intermediary. 2) Repeat until a single name appears. 3) Check whether that name is the real origin or only another step.
when: A trail is covered by intermediaries
why: Concealment hides the origin behind several steps

text: 1) Identify the circumstance the message depends on. 2) List who could have observed that circumstance. 3) Narrow the suspects to those who could have known it.
when: a coded message or clue depends on a situation only some people could see
why: knowledge of the circumstance links a sender to the message

text: 1) List every fact that appears in a question but never came from the witness. 2) For each, identify who supplied it. 3) Treat a specific answer that echoes a question as no independent evidence.
when: reviewing any recorded interview or in-game dialogue log

text: 1) Record each rumour's source. 2) Record who relayed it. 3) Record any reason the relayer might distort it. 4) Provide an eyewitness the player can find to check the chain.
when: Designing rumours or gossip as clues in a game world.
why: Traceable sources let players weigh claims and verify them.

text: Let NPC gossip drop or alter details around one canonical fact, so players must weigh each source and cross-check retellings against first-hand accounts or other NPCs.
when: when designing NPC gossip or rumours passed between characters

text: Model how rumors spread through the game world so the player can see why a wrong NPC gets blamed.
Model a village rumor network in which feuds and land disputes shape who is suspected, and let players trace each rumor to its origin.
when: designing social suspicion in a settlement

text: Tag gossip facts with reputation and grudge weights so rumors grow as they travel; players must separate true facts from the chain built around them.
Design planted rumors and hired-guard notices so an attentive player can trace their source or check the guard's record to detect the bait.
when: Designing a quest-giver or rumor system that can be manipulated.
why: Traceable sources let attentive players uncover deception without it being arbitrary.

text: Let gossip NPCs mix true details with irrelevant chatter, so players must filter out what matters.
when: When designing gossip NPCs

text: Let a frightened NPC blurt a phrase that serves as a lead, withholding detail until players probe with specific questions.
Let gossip NPCs supply background profiles, and let a legitimate task unlock otherwise closed rooms as a pretext for entry.
when: designing information and access in dungeons

text: Let NPC gossip about a monster prove to be a misreading of a performer or trap, and reward players who test the rumour against physical clues.
when: When NPC rumours are part of the level's mystery
why: Testing rumours against evidence rewards careful players and makes the reversal satisfying

text: Model town gossip as an NPC rumour system that surfaces only to a player or NPC using the right cover identity.
when: When designing rumour or information spread in a game.
why: Identity-gated information rewards the right approach.

text: Let NPC chatter summarise a quest's result in a way that shows how the player's knowledge differs from rumour.
Model a gossip hub, such as a boarding house, where the player can gather rumour and identify a key NPC's attendant.
when: designing social information sources

text: Let an NPC pass on an unverified rumour, and have the player decide whether the target's later reaction shows guilt or just news.
Give an unwitting messenger character a summons whose origin the player can trace back to its true sender.
when: a trusted figure's message is carried by someone who does not know the plot
why: a traceable chain keeps the branch fair

text: Let NPC gossip spread through a community with a reputation cost, and make each NPC's access and motive to exaggerate traceable.
Let rumors gain detail with each retelling, and let guard or closed-gate responses make them seem more credible to other NPCs.
Track who told whom what, since rumours passed between factions can become a mechanic the player learns to use.
when: When modelling information flow between factions.
why: Information routing creates player-usable leverage.

text: Let town rumor systems generate red herrings, such as an NPC absent for unrelated reasons, so players learn to separate coincidence from proof.
when: designing town rumor or NPC systems

text: Keep rumor and documents separate so the player must compare what the community believes with what the records say.
when: Designing information sources in a mystery
why: Contrast between hearsay and records creates investigation

text: A parallel quest or rumor can absorb player attention and offer a false motive, provided the player has a way to check it.
when: Designing side content in a generated dungeon.

text: Place a rumoured villain whose trail leads nowhere so players chase an absent figure while the real threat waits elsewhere.
when: When designing misdirection in dungeon generation
why: Players spend effort on the rumour while the actual danger is unguarded

text: Track how NPC reactions escalate after a visible disturbance, and let attention reward the most dramatic performers.
when: when designing village rumour systems

text: Give two families overlapping claims to one plot, with one occupant defending it physically, so the grudge spreads to neighbours who were not party to it.
when: designing faction rivalries around land

text: Let NPC gossip point players toward a location, while the reward depends on finding physical evidence there.
Track which facts stay constant across NPC retellings and which change, to reveal a lying or biased NPC.
when: the player hears several NPC accounts
why: Changing facts expose unreliable sources.

text: Let a rival NPC pursue a wrong theory so the player must decide whether to follow it or correct it.
why: Creates a choice between accepting an authority's theory and testing it.

text: Tie authority-based actions, such as stopping a cart without a warrant, to player reputation so the system decides whether NPCs comply.
Make a stolen item sellable only at certain NPC shops, and have a bounty on it change those shops' behavior so they refuse it and lure the thief.
when: A game has a stolen-goods mechanic with NPC merchants.
why: Restricting the market and reacting to bounties forces the thief into a choice that can be exploited.

text: Guards can respond differently to a harmless disturbance, such as a moved item, letting the player infer who is hiding something.
Guards who trust a familiar figure will not examine a disguised stranger closely, so an unfamiliar face or voice exposes the disguise.
why: the disguise relies on watchers' trust

text: A guard animal that growls or flees at hidden enemies or disguised players can give a diegetic warning signal.
Observers alert on noticed cover-story mismatches; a staged distraction, such as a violent scene, diverts attention from the true path toward a hard-to-undo conclusion.
when: Designing guard or observer suspicion.
why: A noticed inconsistency triggers escalation, while distraction shifts attention away from the real route.

text: Repeated or unnatural noise raises a guard's suspicion, so players must vary their cover behavior rather than repeat the same action.
when: when a stealth agent perceives sounds from the player
why: Repetition makes ordinary activity look like a signal.

text: Harmless animals that look suspicious can trigger stealth or tracking systems as false positives, testing whether players read ambiguous cues correctly.
A bulge may be innocent, so acting on a single sign risks a mistaken confrontation.
A guard NPC can test a player's stated reason by walking to a visible object tied to the claim; the excuse fails if the prop does not match.
when: A player is challenged while doing something suspicious
why: Checking a physical prop is a quick way to verify a cover story.

text: Make guard checks escalate from a glance to a closer inspection, so a decoy that fools the first check cannot hold indefinitely.
when: when designing guard occupancy checks
why: Decoys succeed only against shallow checks.

text: Let a guard post log enemy movements over time and raise an alert only on a known sound or silhouette, not on any shape.
