Give guards fixed posts and shift times; coverage gaps are predictable, so players test a route by checking which posts cover it and when, and by counting guards present.
when: when designing guard schedules or testing stealth routes
why: Coverage gaps are predictable from the schedule and the number of observers.

text: Give watchers realistic gaps, such as bribery, distraction, or timed departure under bad weather, so players have a reason to probe the ring.
why: A perfectly sealed perimeter leaves no deduction to make, while a known gap rewards observation.

text: Confirming that no one crossed the perimeter narrows a hidden target's possible location to the enclosed grounds.
To locate a hidden observer, judge each candidate spot by its concealment and its view of the event; a spot with poor cover is unlikely to be the one chosen.
when: a scene has several candidate positions for a watcher
why: an observer wanting to stay unseen favours spots that hide them well

text: Give a guard or hermit a repeated door-checking routine whose timing and targets hint at an intruder, a stolen item or a hidden exit.
when: designing a locked-room puzzle or hidden passage
why: a compulsive focus on secure doors is a visible anomaly the player can investigate

text: When a patrolling NPC leaves a crowded hall, let the player choose between tailing them or cutting them off at a door.
when: designing stealth patrols
why: the choice creates a tactical decision

text: Give a guard at a single exit an attention or patrol schedule that the player must learn, and time movement against it.
when: When designing stealth or locked-room puzzles around a guard.

text: Keep armed backup available in case the target learns they are being watched.
when: a covert watch might be noticed
why: detection can turn a quiet watch into a violent confrontation

text: Keep patrol arrangements from staff who have access, since they may be the source of information leaks.
Let line-of-sight occlusion decide what each NPC sentry sees and what it assumes about unseen areas.
when: when designing sentry behaviour
why: occlusion limits what a sentry can perceive

text: Gatekeeper dated arrival and inquiry logs reveal where a rival has been and can set up a later encounter; some entries contain errors, so cross-check dates and descriptions against other sources.
Guards checking gates, lights and doors on fixed rounds record timestamped before-and-after states; comparing states between rounds shows when an intruder entered and left.
when: When a guard patrols or checks doors on a fixed schedule.
why: Each patrol or scheduled check gives a reference point for timing.

text: Relaxed or lapsed guard vigilance, such as in a calm lull or when attention wanders, creates a timing window a suspect or stealthy player can exploit to slip away unnoticed.
when: A watch is reduced during a lull or a guard's attention lapses.
why: Lax vigilance removes the checks that would otherwise stop an escape.

text: Patrol or scheduled guard visits open predictable windows usable only at set times; players who learn the schedule by observation can act unseen between passes.
A guard's shift schedule defines a window of opportunity; the player reconstructs it by combining logs, clocks and the guard's statements.
when: when designing NPC-guarded access

text: A fixed observer at a chokepoint, such as a guard at a gate, closes the routes it covers, so the remaining routes form the solution space.
when: Designing a level where a sentry or witness restricts movement
why: Observation removes candidate routes and narrows what the player must examine

text: Tying a patrol route to a fixed observation spot lets players plan around known routines, since the guard's timing becomes predictable.
Guard reports are the record of who entered a sealed scene, so gaps in those reports create openings for unauthorized access and for doubt.
when: a scene must stay undisturbed between searches
why: reports are the only evidence of entries

text: A tracking mechanic built on a list of checkpoints, each returning found or not-found, lets players see what has been ruled out, and a trail ending at a gate gives a clear reason to change approach.
when: Designing a tracking or investigation mechanic.
why: Recorded dead ends narrow the search and signal when a new method is needed.

text: An inspection routine that focuses NPC attention on forms or tasks can cause a visible clue to be overlooked.
when: when NPCs search the player or the environment
why: attention is diverted to the task

text: A conspicuous patrol can deter enemies and change their behaviour without a fight, since they avoid trouble once they are watched.
Observers placed at the wrong entry see nothing, however long they wait. A correct plan can still fail silently if the watch point is wrong.
when: Posting watchers for an expected approach
why: Watchers only detect movement through the spot they are guarding

text: A guard's report covers only their own shift, and an inattentive guard leaves the scene open; a report cannot prove that nothing happened.
1) Divide a long watch into timed shifts with fixed change hours, so someone is always awake. 2) Ask each outgoing guard what happened and whether anyone approached the door. 3) Log known visitors.
1) Let guards and witnesses file reports on a suspect. 2) Make each detail readable two ways. 3) Require the player to weigh the reports before trusting them.
when: when designing observer reports
why: Ambiguous details keep the player reasoning.

text: Place guards on chokepoints a player or patrol must cross, such as doors between wings, not just the objective; they catch movement the objective misses and report sightings over time.
when: when designing guarded passages in a level
why: Choke points catch movement that the objective alone would miss; a reporting guard gives players a source of movement data.

text: Stage a diversion, like a sound or dropped object, to pull a guard from a post or split two guardians, letting the player slip through or face them singly.
when: Designing stealth access through a guarded area or a stealth encounter with multiple guards.
why: A diversion separates guards so the player can face them one at a time; a guard drawn away creates a temporary opening.

text: Place guards at exits and leave a deliberate uncovered route, covered by the player's threat or a patrol; this keeps the space crossable and the trap solvable.
when: Designing a stealth area or a room where an enemy must be cornered.
why: Coverage gaps create meaningful routes without making the space impossible; the deliberate uncovered route keeps pressure on the player.

text: Gate some records behind an authority, so the player needs another route to reach them.
Set a fixed deadline, such as an NPC departure, to create pressure that drives NPC choices and player urgency.
Give a public NPC a persona and a hidden routine visible only in private rooms, rewarding players who explore beyond the social hub.
when: Designing NPC behavior across public and private spaces
why: Exploration exposes the hidden side and rewards curiosity.

text: Unlock an arrest or capture event only after the required evidence has been collected, so the trap triggers when the player is prepared.
when: Stealth or investigation levels that build toward a confrontation.
why: Gating ties the confrontation to the player's preparation rather than to chance.

text: Let players deduce an NPC's situation from when an action began rather than from a direct report, so the clue must be reasoned out.
why: Indirect clues reward inference over reading explicit text.

text: Give a drowsy or distracted NPC a roughly correct time, and let players verify it against a schedule or sound cue.
Run an in-game clock marked by audible chimes so NPC routines and player alibis can be checked against it.
when: when designing time-based schedules and alibis
why: A shared clock lets the player verify timelines.

text: Give NPC guards a watch schedule and a reporting route, so the player can detect or outwit a chain of observers.
when: When designing guard behaviour in a level.
why: A readable schedule and route give the player a pattern to exploit.

text: Add a passive log, such as an ink-use counter or a door-open record, that an informant NPC can read to the player.
when: When designing evidence the player can gather through NPCs.
why: A passive record lets the player infer habits and timing from it.

text: Prepare for several kinds of responder, including proxies and accomplices, so the trap still works when the expected target does not appear.
when: Designing a trap or lure encounter
why: Expected targets may not come, so the design must tolerate other arrivals

text: Place controls on the approach, such as a rendezvous point, a guarded checkpoint or an identity check, before the target is reached.
when: when designing a path to a protected location
why: checkpoints raise stakes and signal that the target is guarded

text: A reason for a guarded area should rest on real features the player can check, such as a gate, a valuable object, or a threat to defend against.
when: when designing a patrol or puzzle explanation

text: Require the player to verify a suspicion before a quest flag unlocks an accusation against an NPC.
when: A quest allows the player to accuse a character
why: Verification prevents accusations built on a single detail

text: Test a guard's report against physical evidence such as lock state, since the report is only as reliable as the checks behind it.
Keep a night watch with lowered lamps, silence and patience, waiting for a telltale sound such as a creaking step.
A concealed NPC who trails the player can be a guardian rather than an enemy; reveal this through a later clue.
Give guards firm rules: hold position until called, and do not enter or fire early.
when: coordinating a set of guards for a takedown
why: early movement alerts the target and breaks the plan

text: Post a guard at the chokepoint with a reserve guard nearby ready to respond, so the point is watched and can be reinforced.
Give each guard an explicit trigger, such as alerting the investigator whenever anyone touches the guarded door.
Chokepoint guards who each count passers-by let the player reconstruct an enemy's location, but a guard's attention and staying power create gaps the player can exploit.
when: designing guarded entrances that feed player deduction
why: Watchers only record what they see and may leave early, so their reports are incomplete by design.

text: Guard placement is a limited resource, so covering one person or route leaves another uncovered and the player must choose.
when: when designing escort or stealth missions
why: Limited watchers force prioritization between targets and routes.

text: A distinctive habit, such as opening a door, tapping fingers or lowering the eyelids, can link the same person across encounters.
when: A habit is established earlier and an unseen or separate-encounter person performs it again.
why: Recognizable routines are used as shortcuts to identity.

text: Inferences about how someone would normally act, including motives drawn from habit, are judgments rather than proof and should be flagged as such.
when: Reasoning that someone would not act a certain way or had a particular motive.
why: Habit is a guess about one individual, not a fact about the event.

text: A single habit or conspicuous item fails when copied, broken or removed; match several traits, check whether others share them, and confirm with more than one witness.
when: An identification or pursuit rests on one habit, gesture or item.
why: Imitation or coincidence can produce the same signature, and removing the item drops the trail.

text: A person who handles an object as though familiar, flinches at it, or takes a route without conscious thought may reveal knowledge or guidance from someone else.
why: Unconscious habit can reveal knowledge or outside guidance.

text: People often cannot prove where they were weeks earlier, because ordinary activity seldom leaves a witness who remembers it.
when: everyday, routine activity
why: no one notices or later recalls it

text: Witnesses often admit a routine once it is named directly, and their stated reason then becomes a checkable claim.
when: a witness denies an activity and is then asked about a known habit

text: Outsiders who do not know a person's habits tend to miss the spot that person would think of first.
when: Searching a stranger's space.
why: Hiding spots follow personal routines and preferences.

text: Routine behaviour that looks effortless can be indistinguishable from genuine habit, so observers may mistake a performance for innocence.
when: when judging whether a person's ease is genuine
why: ease that seems too natural is taken for real habit

text: A figure may look away just as it is recognised, leaving the observer only a fleeting impression to act on.
when: when a target is seen only momentarily
why: the observer has no time to confirm the match

text: Someone who keeps things orderly will read an out-of-place disorder as a deliberate message from a partner who knows that habit.
when: the partner knows the person's established habit
why: A deviation from a known habit stands out sharply

text: A person seen in an unexpected setting may feel familiar before the earlier context comes back, so recognition often comes in stages.
when: A previously seen character appears in a new role or place.

text: A person under stress often keeps small ordinary habits, which are easily overlooked as signs that routine continued.
when: when someone is in a disturbed state
why: habit persists under stress

text: A known personal habit, such as always leaving a gathering at a fixed hour, can serve as a timing anchor that fixes when a person was where.
when: A witness or character has a consistent, known routine
why: A routine gives a reliable time reference that other evidence can be measured against

text: Against a predictable alternating pattern, a skilled opponent who anticipates the prediction reverses it, so a player who only copies the pattern loses.
when: Two-player guessing games with repeated choices.
why: A rival who models the player's model defeats a shallow prediction.

text: A searcher who fixates on one attractive hiding place stops checking others, and an empty lead can drain attention.
when: a tempting opening looks like the likely hiding place
why: A promising lead diverts attention from systematic checking

text: An agent working to a fixed plan is reluctant to change its timing or route, so its schedule stays predictable.
when: when the agent follows a disciplined plan
why: a fixed plan is built around set timings and routes

text: Routine-based prediction works poorly against opportunists, whose behaviour follows no fixed schedule.
when: when the adversary acts opportunistically
why: opportunists have no fixed routine to predict

text: People often fail to recognise someone seen out of their usual uniform or role.
when: Judging whether a disguise needs to change clothing or role.
why: Context such as a uniform strongly cues recognition.

text: Calluses on the hands suggest sustained manual work, while badly blistered feet suggest recent long walking in tight shoes.
when: Reading physical signs on a person
why: Skin wear records repeated activity and footwear

text: Establish a person's established habit as a baseline before treating a deviation as meaningful, since anomalies show only against a known baseline.
when: A single act seems out of character or whether an act was out of character is being evaluated.
why: Anomalies are only visible against an established baseline.

text: Compare a suspect's unconscious habit or routine, even seen in a new setting, with a known pattern rather than the face; disguises alter appearance but rarely remove habits.
when: Face, age or build are changed by a disguise, or the suspect's routine is observed in a new setting.
why: Habits are unconscious and persist under a changed appearance.

text: Predict an adversary's likely moves from habits typical of its kind, phrased as a likelihood since habits describe typical rather than certain behavior; predictable timing and place allow interception.
when: Anticipating an enemy's route or timing when its methods are known to be disciplined.
why: Habits make timing and location predictable.

text: Identical measures across several items, such as cut length or dose, suggest a deliberate consistent habit rather than chance, and can be linked to a person.
why: Chance rarely produces the same measure in each item.

text: Test a first reading of a habit or found tool against all physical facts: an odd choice may have a practical cause, and a partial explanation can hide a remaining discrepancy.
when: Reading a character's choice in a scene, or a found tool seems to explain a trace.

text: A witness's usual habits can make testimony more or less credible; an unusual exception to a habit, such as waking, can strengthen it.
A trace tied to one person's personal habit, such as a particular tobacco brand, narrows the candidates far more than a generic sign.
when: Many people could have left the sign.
why: Only a few people share the specific habit.

text: An object at odds with the victim's known habits suggests that it came from someone else.
when: A found object is compared with what is known of the victim's life.

text: A small contradiction with a person's stated habit can count for more than a larger body of evidence and can reopen a line of inquiry.
when: when a stated habit or fact can be checked against the evidence

text: Relate a person's habits, such as handedness, to where an injury appears, which can narrow how the injury was produced.
when: Injury location seems unexpected
why: Habitual actions shape which parts of the body are exposed to a mechanism.

text: A habit the witness never mentioned to its owner was displayed without awareness, making it more trustworthy as an identifier.
People usually stay within familiar districts and routines, so their training, past work or regular errands can narrow a geographic search.
when: a person's movements are unknown but their habits are known
why: people tend to act within their own orbit

text: Weigh a witness's unusual observation less when the person is habitually of that disposition, since the observation is then less distinctive.
when: a witness reports an unusual observation about a usually cheerful or calm person
why: the habit makes the unusual detail less informative

text: An owner's habitual arrangement of objects is a baseline. When an item is out of place or handled differently, the change reveals the visitor's habits.
when: A visitor has disturbed a space with known owner habits
why: Deviations from the normal arrangement expose a different temperament

text: Two public identities held by one person can be linked by stable private habits, such as a preferred product, even when their stated beliefs differ.
when: Deciding whether two personas belong to the same person
why: Daily preferences change less than public positions

text: When several associates give the same stock reaction and no useful fact, record the uniform evasion itself as a finding.
when: Multiple witnesses respond identically with nothing concrete.

text: A uniformly clouded surface with no ridge pattern suggests the item was wiped or never handled by bare fingers.
when: a breath test shows no pattern
why: Oily ridges are absent when skin did not touch the surface.

text: Use a deadline such as daylight or an hour of departure to bound when an agent must return, narrowing its plausible locations.
when: when an agent must finish a trip before a fixed time
why: A return must fit within the remaining time, so distant places drop out

text: Identify what a target values most, since that attachment is the most predictable trigger for its action.
when: when a target is shut in or hidden

text: Plan inference from character works poorly when the plan depends on facts the reasoner cannot reach at all.
when: when a plan rests on hidden or inaccessible information
why: Character evidence cannot supply facts that are unavailable.

text: Criminals tend to repeat methods that worked, so a repeated method points to one offender.
when: comparing a new crime with earlier ones
why: human behaviour is largely unoriginal, inside and outside the law

text: A guard that checks a decoy at fixed intervals can be exploited, since the player can time movement to the interval.
Judge concealment by a pattern of posture, location, and gaze rather than by a single bulge.
An NPC whose communication with others is limited behaves more predictably, so a scripted warning can push it into a visible action the player is set up to witness.
when: An NPC's contacts are cut off or restricted by scripting
why: Fewer options narrow the NPC's likely responses

text: A target that slows or doubles back suggests it is nearing a goal, so changes in its pace reveal its intent to a tracker.
when: when a tracked agent's movement changes
why: Slowing often signals approach to a destination

text: Routine describes the usual, not the actual; do not let habit replace evidence of what happened, and treat a habit-narrowed list as a working hypothesis, keeping the full list.
when: Reconstructing a day from a routine or narrowing a search by assumed habits.
why: People do not always behave as their habits predict.

text: A plan fails if the target's habits differ from the assumption or it skips the predicted route; unwatched connections and unexpected occupants can block the path.
when: Designing schemes or traps that rely on an opponent's known character or route.
why: Predictions about behaviour are uncertain; unwatched connections break the assumed path.

text: A habit match helps only if the investigator knows the habit was present. A missing item shows removal only after its earlier presence is established.
when: Using a missing item as evidence
why: Absence means nothing without a known baseline

text: Assuming one period's knowledge was uniform hides dissent and minority views.
Ornaments and distractions can hide the very mark that would identify someone, so a feature that matters may go unnoticed.
Modelling an opponent by your own ideas of cunning leads to searching only where you would hide; the model fails against different reasoning.
why: Investigators assume the other mind thinks like their own.

text: Relying on one forecast of a character's reaction is risky; a plan should cover a second likely path, such as searching for proof.
A deduction built on an adversary's reputation may overrate their cleverness and miss a simpler explanation.
when: when inferring a plan from a reputation
why: Reputation can inflate expectations of the adversary's sophistication.

text: Reading one habit as a full profile of an adversary leads to wrong predictions, since habits guide conduct without fixing it.
Habit evidence, such as never wearing rings, is only as strong as the witness who vouches for the habit.
when: A habit is offered as proof that a suspect is or is not someone

text: 1) Identify the recipient's temperament. 2) Trace the likely sequence of actions after the news. 3) Identify what they would do to check the claim. 4) Choose between acting fast and waiting.
when: a chain of events depends on a character reacting to news

text: 1) State a specific predicted reaction for a suspect to a stated piece of news. 2) Deliver the news without preparation. 3) Compare the actual reaction with the prediction and revise the theory accordingly.
when: An investigator holds a theory that makes a definite claim about how someone will react.
why: A controlled test shows where the theory fails, but a single reaction does not prove guilt.

text: 1) Ask whether the disputed event recurred and how often. 2) Test the stated frequency against the routine. 3) If a pattern recurs, consider whether others could have known about it.
when: A witness describes a repeating event whose frequency matters.
why: A recurring event is predictable, so others may have observed or anticipated it.

text: Identify NPCs by a fixed trait, such as height, gait, a mark or voice, that a costume or disfigurement cannot change and the player has noticed earlier.
Do not rely on a reaction forecast when the character's temperament or condition, such as being drugged, drunk or ill, is unknown, because the prediction then has no basis.
Give recurring enemies a recognisable habit, such as a reused trap, weapon, tactic or meeting place across encounters, so players can link, predict and exploit it.
when: Designing enemy behaviour or routines across encounters.
why: Repeated signatures become readable and rewarding to learn; a recognisable pattern lets players recall and predict.

text: Give suspects characteristic habits as checkable constraints that let players clear or suspect them without extra dialogue, such as through a skill check.
when: Designing suspects for player deduction or elimination.
why: Observable habits let players reason about a character; constraints turn character knowledge into testable elimination.

text: Place traps on a creature's usual route, since animals reuse known paths, and make the trap fire only when the creature follows that path as a timing puzzle.
when: Creatures follow habitual routes between places.
why: Animals reuse known paths, which makes their movement predictable.

text: Catalogue a character's habits as data and treat each as a trait to explain, not something to assume.
Give items in the game world unique wear, scratches or stamps that players can match against a written description.
Tie a hiding place to an established character habit so the player can deduce it from the character's behavior.
when: Choosing where an NPC hides an item.
why: A habit the player has observed becomes a logical clue to the hiding place.

text: Let an NPC that used a tool once reach for it again under similar pressure, so the player can predict and expose the behavior.
when: Designing NPC repeat behavior
why: Predictable habits give players a way to set traps

text: Give NPCs fixed routines tied to in-game clocks, so the player can rebuild where each character should have been.
Use recurring environmental cues, such as unnatural stillness or an odd sound, to warn players that danger is near before they meet it.
when: Designing an area where a threat is coming but not yet visible.
why: Players learn to read recurring cues as signs of nearby danger.

text: Distinguish unsolved from solved-and-proven resolution states, so the game's outcomes match the evidence the player has gathered.
when: Designing mystery resolution and endings.
why: Outcome states that mirror the evidence keep the resolution fair and understandable.

text: Require a proof threshold before a player can name a character in an accusation, so suspicion alone is not enough.
when: Designing accusation mechanics in an investigation game.
why: Gating accusation on evidence prevents premature or unsupported claims.

text: Use a dream-like phase in which the player is apparently harmed but awakens in a changed version of the same location, letting the level alter its rules without breaking the world.
when: Designing a level that must change state or rules mid-story.
why: The framing lets the world change without contradicting its logic.

text: Define level rules as statistical tendencies rather than absolutes, so individual rooms stay unpredictable and a rule that fails in one case does not mislead the player.
when: Generating level content governed by common patterns.
why: Tendencies hold across many instances, and leaving exceptions preserves surprise without breaking expectations.

text: Unaided parties unfamiliar with formal procedure cause delays that irritate the judge; they may face a stricter judge or skilled opposing NPC, which a procedurally knowledgeable ally reduces.
when: Modelling a formal hearing in a game with an unaided party unfamiliar with procedure.
why: Procedural missteps slow proceedings and change how the decision-maker reacts; procedural knowledge offsets the advantage an opposing party gains from expertise.

text: A poison whose symptoms appear after a delay tied to dose and food lets the player test timing against a suspect's meal.
when: designing a poisoning mechanic
why: Delay that varies with dose and food gives the player a testable timeline.

text: Ask the player to keep a borrowed object intact and return it to its owner, so the object's condition remains a checkable part of the case.
when: Designing a quest that involves a physical item of evidence
why: Preserving the object keeps it available for later examination

text: Give a supernatural effect a physical source so it can be measured and traced to its cause.
when: when a ghost, spirit or magic event is part of a scenario
why: A traceable source lets players test the event and disprove the supernatural explanation.

text: Witnesses may describe two shots fired almost together as one loud report, so their accounts must be tested.
when: A witness reports fewer shots than the physical evidence suggests.
why: Sounds close together in time merge into a single impression.

text: When sight is removed, a character can locate others by sounds such as footsteps, breathing, heartbeat or the click of a weapon.
when: Visibility is removed and parties can still hear each other.
why: Audio cues remain available when visual information is not.

text: Ambient noise can mask footsteps, so a careful person can pass an observer unseen.
when: An observer relies on hearing or sight near a noisy area.

text: A solid surface and a hollow cavity give different tones when struck, so a tone change can reveal a hidden space.
Strong smell, such as tobacco smoke, can reveal a presence before any figure is seen, and it can arrive ahead of the occupant.
when: sight is blocked
why: scent travels and signals occupancy

text: In dim stealth areas, make sound the main clue, since reduced sight shifts attention to audio; limit voice recognition to a set range so players judge sources unseen.
when: Designing audio clues for stealth levels with low lighting.
why: Sound carries information when visuals are weak.

text: Sound cues such as footsteps or footstep patterns can reveal a presence, or who is passing, before sight confirms it.
when: Presenting a visual reveal in a dark area, or quiet corridors where no one is seen.
why: Quiet or dark spaces make sound carry information without visual contact.

text: Give sealed or hidden spaces distinctive sounds, such as grating hinges or hollow knocks, so players can connect a sound to a location.
when: Designing hidden rooms or vaults.
why: Audio carries traces the player can localize.

text: A witness with blocked sight can still infer route and location from sound, such as the surface underfoot, and from elapsed time.
when: a character has been moved or confined without vision
why: non-visual senses still carry usable cues

text: Staged noisy, memorable events make witnesses talk and fix a traceable route that pursuers can follow.
when: witnesses are needed to fix a route
why: Memorable incidents get repeated and remembered by bystanders

text: Stealth sections can use sound sources, such as creaking surfaces, as a detection mechanic that rewards careful movement.
Sounds or animal movement that come from or vanish into unseen areas hint at routes that are not yet visible.
When the camera or minimap is restricted, audio cues such as a bridge rumble or a turn carry the spatial information the player cannot see.
when: a vehicle, container or hidden section limits view

text: Stealth or siege missions can use sound cues from behind a door to reveal enemy activity, letting the player choose when to breach.
Add ambient sounds with no visible source, and tie each one to a hidden room or creature the player can eventually reach.
when: Designing unexplained ambient audio.
why: Unresolved sound creates curiosity that a later reveal can pay off.

text: Plant an unexplained sound with a plausible human cause, such as an unseen character, and let the player investigate who made it and why.
when: Designing horror or mystery scenes where a sound should raise questions without an immediate answer.
why: A human-caused sound feels grounded, and leaving its source open keeps the player curious.

text: A listener's or player's own noise, such as scraping, opening a chest, stepping on loose floor or loud movement, can mask sounds that others such as NPCs make.
when: A stealth or sound system is in use, or the listener is making noise while others speak or move.
why: Competing sound drowns out faint sounds for the listener.

text: Logged silent periods let a player infer that an NPC did not pass a checkpoint during a given time window.
when: when a checkpoint keeps a time-stamped log
why: Absence of a record is itself information.

text: A narrow gap restricts sight but carries sound, so a listener can learn plans and identify voices without seeing the room.
when: A partly opened door or gap connects to the room.
why: Sound passes through openings that block the view.

text: Deriving noise from actions such as forcing an object lets a stealth system decide whether a claimed silent entry was physically plausible.
when: a stealth system must judge whether an action is heard
why: Noise tied to the physical act makes silent entry a checkable claim, not an assumption.

text: Echoing footsteps in an empty space make the space feel watched, creating unease before any threat appears.
when: Quiet environments meant to build tension
why: Echo implies unseen listeners, which players interpret as presence

text: A sound cue that stops the moment the player enters a room signals that enemies are aware of the player but gives no identity.
when: Designing night or stealth scenes.
why: Silence reveals awareness without revealing who is present.

text: Ambient noise can mask a silenced attack, so nearby observers miss the shot only where the surrounding noise is loud enough.
when: A silenced attack takes place in a setting with loud background sound.
why: Background noise covers the reduced report, and in a quiet setting the masking fails.

text: Ambient noise, such as rough surfaces or rattling vehicles, can mask a struggle, so a witness's silence is weak evidence and a quiet room does not prove it was empty.
when: Judging whether a witness or room was occupied at a given time.
why: Ambient noise drowns out quieter events, and silence does not rule out a visitor who moved quietly.

text: Noise made while moving through a hidden passage can alert occupants of the area below, so sound cues can betray a stealthy player.
when: designing secret routes that pass near enemies
why: sound reaches the room below

text: Witnesses in noisy or poor conditions hear uncertain fragments that can mimic signals; treat their sound-based claims as hypotheses until a measurement or exposed object confirms them.
when: Key evidence is a sound or speech heard in noisy or poor conditions.
why: Wind, storms and old buildings mimic deliberate signals, and noise removes most of a conversation.

text: Use sound as testable evidence: make a sound checkable from another area, or plant a muffled shot or fall that supports one reading and can be tested against other clues.
Set NPC hearing and proximity ranges so silence is a usable clue, and record a shut door as an event so the player can deduce the route taken.
when: When designing stealth or investigation spaces.
why: Lets players learn that a quiet area can signal events elsewhere.

text: Make a night intruder sound-driven, so the player's listening decides how much they learn about him.
Avoid noise during a stakeout, such as tapping a floor or dropping an item, since it can reveal the watchers to the enemy early.
when: characters or players are waiting in hiding
why: noise is a clue that can give the ambush away

text: Do not force an opening beyond the point where it would make a sudden jarring noise.
End a wait with a sound cue, such as an approaching footstep, before the tension fades, forcing a quick, clean action.
when: A tense delay is building and needs a decisive end.
why: A sudden cue prompts immediate action before tension dissipates.

text: Give NPC tells ambiguous meanings with several causes, such as avoiding a task, prompting follow-up questions; never let one tell prove guilt; confirm with a second independent clue.
when: designing suspect behaviour, interrogation tells or NPC cues in a mystery; a reaction has more than one plausible reading
why: Single behaviours are ambiguous, so players should weigh alternative causes; ambiguity invites inquiry and avoids unfair verdicts.

text: Give NPCs readable tells, such as flush, shifted gaze, glance, pause, turned shoulder, tone or voice change, or delayed answer, when a secret is touched, to reveal what is concealed.
when: when a secret or sensitive topic is touched
why: Readable tells let players infer the secret being protected.

text: Treat NPC tells, such as a glance at a door, flinch, nervous laugh, hesitation, over-eagerness, interruption, denial, or blood on hands, as signals pointing to a suspect, never as proof.
A visitor who hesitates and fidgets usually brings a delicate personal matter, while a different kind of distress usually signals an injured party.
when: a visitor arrives before their problem is explained

text: A witness's silence can mean protecting someone or simply staying quiet. Ask what each reading predicts before choosing one.
when: a witness refuses to speak
why: silence fits both innocence and guilt

text: A panicked actor rarely leaves lights on in several rooms or pauses for minutes between actions, so such details suggest a calmer or staged sequence.
when: when a scene shows light states or gaps inconsistent with flight
why: panic usually produces hasty, uninterrupted action

text: The same visible distress from a suspect is read by different observers as either proof of guilt or proof of innocence.
when: a suspect shows emotion under accusation
why: observers interpret one signal through their prior assumptions

text: In a public panic, accusers tend to pick the most visible and respected people, and personal grudges steer which of them get named.
Watchers reveal themselves through coordinated behaviour, such as a silent signal between a loiterer and a figure at a window.
when: observing a suspected surveillance network
why: coordination requires communication that is visible

text: Small kind acts can support more than one reading, so a witness's charitable interpretation of them is not proof of the person's good character.
when: when praise rests on minor gestures
why: The same observed facts can fit a benign or a suspicious explanation.

text: Give NPCs observable tells such as posture, eye contact, sweat, hesitation, voice shifts and avoided topics, so players weigh behaviour as evidence alongside spoken answers.
when: designing NPCs who hold information they do not state
why: Players can read body language as clues without explicit dialogue.

text: Give NPCs small habits, such as a ring on one hand, distinctive cloak or favoured hand for cards, that players match to clues found through ordinary observation.
when: designing NPCs for an investigation or characters whose traits may serve as clues
why: Traits gathered during normal play feel earned rather than announced.

text: Tie an NPC's gaze target, idle animation or posture cue to a backstory fact or specific prop, so players can verify the inference and choose their next question.
when: designing NPC behaviour that reveals inner state
why: A tell linked to a verifiable backstory fact or prop can be checked by the player.

text: Let NPC reactions or a quiet non-verbal cue, such as a gesture or fixed camera, reveal the answer without a cutscene or direct statement.
Design NPC tells to be ambiguous, so avoiding a trapped chest could mean hidden theft or simply fear of the trap.
Give evasive NPCs a visible tell, such as a changed posture or repeated line, so players learn when to press.
when: When designing evasive NPC dialogue.

text: Use an NPC's emotional tell, such as turning away or breaking off speech, as a readable cue the player learns to interpret.
when: when designing NPC reactions to sensitive questions
why: learnable cues reward observation

text: Give NPCs dress, posture and tone that signal their state, so players can read their condition before any dialogue.
A row of stars or a blank in a timeline signals that information was omitted, which attentive readers can notice.
Tag each NPC on the items they touch; dusting an item reveals its tag set, which the player compares against a suspect list.
when: Designing evidence systems for NPCs and items.
why: Handling can then be traced like fingerprints.

text: Let a character's behaviour change after key events, with each change given a plausible innocent alternative the player can rule in or out.
when: designing suspect behaviour in a mystery
why: innocent alternatives keep suspicion fair and testable

text: A tan line or wear mark on an NPC can hint at an item they habitually wear, linking them to a crime scene item.
Visible anxiety among witnesses about offending a powerful person can suggest what they privately think about that person.
when: Witnesses are cautious when speaking about a powerful figure
why: Fear of giving offense can reveal a private view that the public statement conceals

text: Let an NPC blurt a line that conflicts with another NPC's account, and let the player press dialogue tells only when no companion is present.
when: When designing dialogue that should reveal hidden knowledge.
why: A contradiction gives the player a lead, and privacy mirrors a real private interview.

text: Tie NPC belongings' wear patterns, repair counts and contents to owner traits such as handedness, wealth and habits, so players can deduce traits before meeting the NPC.
when: When designing NPC possessions as information sources
why: Players can infer character from consistent physical signs

text: Give each generated NPC a financial or social pressure and a possible cover story, so the player can discover the hidden motive through investigation.
when: Populating a generated murder mystery with suspects.
why: Distinct pressures give each suspect a credible reason and a reason to lie.

text: Vary NPC response style by social position and history, so the same question draws different answers from different characters.
Give NPC witnesses a fear or fatigue value that lowers the accuracy or completeness of their answers when the player interrogates them harshly or keeps them waiting.
when: Designing NPC witnesses in a game.
why: Simulates how real witnesses become less reliable under stress and delay.

text: An NPC that pauses or hides information can signal a secret through a distinct animation or dialogue beat for each evasion type.
when: Designing NPCs that conceal knowledge from the player.
why: Varied, readable evasion cues let players distinguish hesitation, deflection and denial.

text: Turn a habit into a trigger: disturb the environment so the target's habitual need draws them to a chosen spot at a predictable time.
when: a target's habit is reliable
why: predictable needs yield predictable movement

text: Give a staged NPC symptoms that look real but betray a detail, such as timing that is too neat, so a careful observer can catch the performance.
when: Designing an NPC who feigns a condition.
why: Overly precise timing is a tell that rewards close observation.

text: Overdone distress and a defensive travel story can draw suspicion, but they are weak evidence on their own.
when: When assessing a witness whose emotional display or account seems staged.

text: An NPC's visible tell, such as a colour change or sudden topic shift, can mark a dialogue answer as possibly false for the player to test.
Give each lookalike NPC a fixed trait, such as a limp, scar or ring, that a disguise would not carry, so players can expose the impostor.
why: A visible unchangeable trait gives players a fair way to tell the double from the original.

text: Track an NPC's emotional state, such as pallor or trembling, and use it to signal which topic the player should press.
when: When an NPC reacts to a player's question.
why: Visible tells give the player a readable cue about which lead is sensitive.

text: Let the game flag contradictory readings of an NPC's behavior so the player must weigh the conflicting observations.
when: Designing evidence about a character that can support opposing conclusions.
why: Surfacing contradictions makes the player reason rather than accept one reading.

text: Give lying or evasive NPCs readable tells, such as pauses, manner change, visible hesitations or hedged answers, that players learn to read over time.
when: designing NPC dialogue or behaviour that conceals information
why: Consistent tells give players a fair chance to detect deception.

text: An NPC who reacts disproportionately, such as looking alarmed at a harmless question, gives a lead because the reaction does not match the question, so players can infer guilt.
when: designing NPCs that hold hidden knowledge
why: Disproportionate reaction is readable without explicit dialogue.

text: NPCs with visible bias, grudges or attitude shifts tied to the player's past actions reveal feeling-shaped accounts, so players should discount their claims or confirm them through other sources.
when: designing NPCs with personal stakes or attitudes that shift with player actions
why: Visible bias signals that the NPC's account needs independent confirmation.

text: An NPC's stance can soften from defensive to cooperative after matching evidence, convincing claims or an emotional scene, and the change is a clue to later answers.
when: when an NPC's stance changes mid-scene or the player presents matching evidence

text: When in-world authorities find a scene baffling, their reactions signal that the clue set is hard, so difficulty can follow NPC responses.
When players form impressions of an NPC from its observed habits rather than its claims, their shifting trust can be tracked as it changes.
An NPC who lingers near a crime and reacts to dialogue about it can give a behavioural cue, and reactions to specific clues can change available dialogue options.
when: When designing NPCs in a crime or investigation scene.
why: Visible reactions give the player evidence without stating a verdict.

text: A game can let the player name an NPC witness to a suspect and then show whether the suspect's reply shifts, revealing whether that witness was compromised.
An NPC who reacts differently to a known fact than to a bluff makes its reaction itself a readable clue.
Raising an NPC's stress can shorten its answers and add visible tells such as pallor, while the player's pauses and wording change how it responds.
A character's self-harm or escape attempt can act as a tell that shifts the player's view of the character and points toward a hidden secret.
when: Designing a dramatic reveal around an NPC's distress
why: A high-stakes act signals that the hidden material matters

text: Placing life cues around a still figure creates a contradiction the player resolves through checks, which can turn a search for a witness into a discovery.
when: When staging a discovery scene in a level.
why: A mismatch between surroundings and the figure prompts investigation.

text: An NPC's mood sets how long information stays available; the player must act while the NPC is still willing to talk.
An NPC's hidden fact can unlock when the player discovers the reason for its silence, often through a second clue.
An early player accusation can trigger NPC responses such as fleeing, hiding an item, or changing a guard's route, so the world reacts to incomplete information.
when: The player takes a visible action against an NPC before gathering complete evidence.
why: NPCs who learn of a threat act to protect themselves, which changes the situation the player must handle.

text: A character who sees through a staged trap can change how later NPCs respond to the player.
An NPC dialogue can reveal a hidden clue through a slip when the player stays silent or delivers a shocking statement.
when: When designing interrogation dialogue for a suspicious NPC.
why: Silence and shock pressure the NPC to respond, and the response can expose what they know.

text: Changing NPC states such as drunk, away or confined can break a plan built on their schedule, because the plan depends on those states holding.
when: a player plans an action around NPC schedules or conditions
why: A state change removes the assumption the plan was built on.

text: Track NPC reaction states such as suspicion, greed or grievance, and shift them when the player offers a claim or a bribe.
when: designing NPC dialogue responses

text: An NPC can display readable reactions such as a changed posture or pause after a specific player question, and each reaction should allow more than one reading.
when: Designing NPC interrogation or dialogue reactions.
why: Ambiguous tells require players to test them against other clues.

text: A routine, low-key interaction can test whether a hidden state is real without alerting the target.
A mood system can reveal partial information by state, keeping some internal states hidden until specific conditions are met.
when: Designing NPC or character state that players can read.

text: A character with a claimed background can be tested by a skill check; a mismatch flags a false identity for the player to discover.
when: Designing NPCs whose claimed identity may be false
why: A skill mismatch gives players a verifiable clue

text: Grief, anger and fear look alike and can have private causes, so a strong emotional reaction to bad news is one clue among several, not proof of guilt.
A nervous appearance has other causes, so visible signs at a door suggest eavesdropping but do not prove it.
A visible effect can be misread as to its cause; slow movement may come from a high gear rather than leisure, so check the cause before interpreting it.
An over-emphatic denial can reveal more than the denial itself, since excessive protest may signal the opposite of what is claimed.
when: A witness denies a claim with unusual force.
why: Excess emphasis often hides anxiety about the denied point.

text: A suspect who wanders is not necessarily making contact, so movement alone should not be read as a meeting.
when: A target stops at many locations during a trail.
why: Aimless movement and purposeful contact look similar from a distance.

text: A reaction showing only surprise is ambiguous; it can mean innocence or practised composure.
Reassurance given without authority overstates confidence in a plan and can backfire if the plan changes.
Showing interest in one answer tells the witness which answer matters, so questioners should hide their interest.
Repeating the same action too often makes a trap obvious before it springs.
when: when a trap relies on a repeated action

text: Assigning a motive from ties alone overreads loyalties; confirm the motive against what the account actually says.
Concluding that all apologies are sham from one insincere case is overgeneralisation; a single apology proves neither sincerity nor insincerity.
Assuming a character's state, such as drunkenness, excuses any action is a mistake; the test is what that state would realistically produce.
when: when judging whether a character's action is plausible
why: States constrain behavior, they do not explain every outcome

text: 1) Give NPCs visible tells such as pallor, sweating or looking away. 2) Change those tells when the player shows a relevant clue. 3) Let the player infer the truth from them.
when: when designing confrontation scenes

text: Tie small NPC tells, such as a blink, blush, blocking a passage or repeated anxious question, to a hidden secret or anxiety so players track them across encounters.
when: designing NPCs who conceal a motive or hidden state
why: Repeated tells let players build an understanding of hidden motives over time; subtle cues reward attentive players.

text: Trigger NPC tells such as hesitation, animation change, hand movement or tone shift when a sensitive topic or secret is touched, prompting the player to re-examine it.
when: designing NPC reactions to sensitive questions

text: Give NPCs readable facial or posture cues, such as a pause, flush or glance toward a hidden object, when a name or clue phrase is mentioned, so players test them.
when: designing NPC reactions to names or clue dialogue
why: Readable cues are signals for the player to test.

text: Mark NPCs with readable wear such as hands, boots, clothing or tattoos revealing past profession or homeland, so an appraisal skill can unlock dialogue.
when: designing NPC appearance to suggest backstory or generating NPC appearance details
why: Readable marks let players read backstory from appearance and give them a reason to appraise NPCs.

text: An NPC's readable reaction to a found or hidden item or symbol, such as freezing or dropping it, signals relevance and prompts the player to look further.
when: designing NPC responses to discovered or hidden clues
why: A readable reaction gives the player a next step.

text: Track each NPC's habits, such as withdrawing or confiding and normal gaze and answer patterns, flagging deviations when a key fact is mentioned as clues.
when: designing NPCs whose reactions should carry information or stay consistent with their personality
why: Consistent habits make reactions predictable; deviations from a known pattern are readable signals.

text: Keep NPC reactions ambiguous between guilt and fear, or heat and fatigue, so the player must weigh them against other clues.
when: writing NPC reactions to accusations or interrogation dialogue
why: Ambiguity makes the player weigh evidence instead of trusting tone.

text: Attach a visible tell to a hidden purpose, such as an object the NPC keeps handling or a topic they always steer away from.
when: a secret motive should be detectable
why: tells give attentive players a fair way to notice concealment

text: Give NPC dialogue small state cues, such as a pause, a change of color or a hand gesture, that the player can later connect to a hidden fact.
Give an NPC a scar or missing item that players must ask about to link a disguised character to their past.
An NPC's reaction to a contradiction should open a follow-up branch rather than end the conversation.
when: when the player presents a contradicting record
why: a reaction is a lead that can be pursued

text: A clean check should change an NPC's dialogue state without automatically closing the investigation thread.
when: A test on an NPC returns no evidence.
why: Keeping the thread open preserves suspicion and avoids a dead end.

text: Give NPCs checkable tells, such as a stated preference that contradicts an object the player finds, so a notice-and-check mechanic can expose the contradiction.
Let a villain's pre-built alibi leave trackable tells, so the player uncovers the plan through scattered traces.
Make an NPC's honesty and nervous cues depend on the character's situation, never on group identity such as gender or class.
Give NPCs small visible tells, such as a colour shift or a cut-off line resumed later, and use a pressure value to decide when a slip occurs.
Show an NPC reaction to an accusation so the emotional stakes of the reveal are visible to the player.
Interpret a tracker's reaction before treating it as evidence, because a non-verbal source cannot be questioned about what its behavior meant.
when: a conclusion depends on how an animal or other tracker behaved
why: its basis cannot be asked for

text: Give an unusual NPC emotional reaction a checkable backstory explanation that the player can uncover through investigation.
when: Designing a cold, suspicious or unexpected NPC reaction
why: A reaction with a discoverable cause lets players test interpretations instead of guessing

text: Give NPCs a small idle gesture that appears only when they lie or recognise the player, keeping it brief yet repeatable so players can confirm it.
when: designing NPC behavior

text: Give NPCs a genuine emotional state paired with possibly false claims, and make the player check claims against scene evidence, not performance.
when: designing npc dialogue

text: Define what each possible explanation implies for NPC behaviour afterwards, so the player can test a theory by watching what NPCs do next.
when: Designing a mystery with several possible explanations

text: Let an NPC's fear act as a readable clue to guilt, backed by physical evidence the player can check.
when: designing NPC emotional reactions

text: Give each NPC routines for how they store or use items, so a staged scene can contradict them and the player can notice.
Give NPCs visible reactions, such as a changed line or a flinch, that other NPCs can notice and misread.
why: observable tells create opportunities for misinterpretation and new branches

text: Let an NPC's look act as a tell, such as a cheerful guard whose gear shows signs of crime, and let players check the impression against other clues.
when: Designing NPC appearance clues.

text: Have an NPC who keeps reopening a settled issue signal a hidden goal, detectable by players through repeated dialogue loops.
Give NPCs reactions to fake leads and secrets, such as a fast answer, flash of relief, over-strong denial, or too-ready answer, that players can learn to read.
why: Readable tells reward players who observe closely.

text: Make an NPC's expected reaction explicit, so a missing reaction, such as a guard staying silent toward one character or staying asleep, reveals that character's identity or status.
when: Stealth levels where an NPC's reaction can flag a character.
why: An absent reaction tells the player something when the normal reaction is clear.

text: Give impostors and disguised NPCs behavioral tells, such as ignoring a required greeting or a fixed gesture or routine, that attentive players can learn to recognise.
when: When an NPC is meant to be an impostor or disguised.

text: Give a suspicious NPC tells that the player can probe with varied tests, such as a language check, a knowledge check, or a setting that changes their behavior.
when: Designing an NPC who may be lying about a hidden ability or knowledge.
why: Varied probes let players test the NPC rather than accept or reject it on a single clue.

text: Keep visual tells ambiguous at first so a player's initial judgment can be wrong and then corrected by later evidence.
when: designing NPC tells

text: Give characters distinctive footwear so the player can follow one NPC through a crowd.
Make an NPC's precautions, such as a hired witness, hidden exit or fallback meeting place, into clues pointing to the NPC's hidden plan and its target.
why: Precautions reveal intent and make hidden plans discoverable

text: When an NPC's attitude changes between two conversations, explain the change with an event the player can find.
Let NPC dialogue reveal a mannerism that identifies a suspect, and make it something the NPC noticed without intending to reveal it.
Give NPC dialogue deliberate slips that reveal knowledge the NPC should not have, and track NPC physical reactions to clues as data the player can read.
Let NPCs react to the player's noise, so the player must choose whether to cover a sound with speech or stay silent.
Make NPC reactions depend on the player's visible condition, such as wounds or intoxication, so guards and townsfolk judge them differently.
when: designing NPC responses

text: Model NPC posture and animation states, such as hands hovering over an instrument or leaving a room, as observable clues the player can log.
when: designing NPCs whose state should be inferred by the player
why: Visible states let players build evidence from behaviour rather than dialogue alone

text: Give a watcher NPC a view cone and a visible tell, such as a moving curtain, so an attentive player can detect the watch and turn it around.
Log changes in an NPC's reaction when specific facts are mentioned, and record them as tells of what that NPC knows.
when: when an NPC is questioned about known facts

text: Give suspect NPCs idle reactions to being watched, such as checking over their shoulder, so players can read guilt.
Make NPCs change their willingness to talk when the player presents evidence, so a confrontation produces information instead of a fixed refusal.
when: when designing an NPC who withholds information

text: Let NPC dialogue respond differently when the player holds a recorded trace, such as logged movement, that contradicts the NPC's stated account.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that depends on player-discovered evidence.
why: Confronting an NPC with a record can force a confession or open new dialogue.

text: Give NPCs explicit behavioral limits, such as a drunk NPC attacking targets rather than furniture, so that scene contradictions are checkable.
when: when NPC actions must be read as evidence
why: Predictable limits let players detect actions that break them

text: Give NPCs reactions such as hesitation or a follow-up question that reveal what they believe about a player's claim.
when: Designing dialogue where the player can bluff or probe.
why: Visible tells let players read the NPC's knowledge and adjust their approach.

text: Give NPCs traits such as risk aversion that constrain which actions they choose. A cautious NPC should rarely select violent acts.
when: When NPCs choose between actions with differing risk.

text: Vary an NPC's tell across repeated cues so the player cannot memorize a single reaction, and withhold some details until a later conversation.
when: Designing NPC reactions to player-supplied information
why: Fixed reactions become predictable and trivially exploitable; gated information sustains tension.

text: Attach each NPC tell to more than one possible cause, so players must combine tells with other evidence to reach a conclusion.
An impatient character who has resisted control tends to insist on acting alone and defends hard once their interests are threatened.
when: when predicting how an adversary will respond to a confrontation
why: Their known traits drive the response.

text: Bait-and-watch with an intermediary does not work against a lone opponent who acts entirely alone, since no contact will be made.
when: Choosing a counter-plan against a pursuer
why: No intermediary will be approached

text: Failed interrogation tactics raise NPC hostility, so the player's later options narrow over time.
when: when an NPC has a composure value
why: repeated failure hardens the NPC against the questioner

text: Tracking an NPC's health against a tipping point lets a discoverable event push a fragile character into death, rather than the decline being fixed in advance.
when: A chronic condition makes an NPC fragile.
why: A threshold turns a gradual weakness into a sudden outcome that an event can trigger.

text: Model NPC suspicion as a timer: NPCs stay calm through a short absence and grow suspicious after a set number of in-game minutes.
when: the player leaves an NPC gathering

text: A reputation or faction value can drive NPC hostility toward a suspect independently of what actually happened.
A strike launched on an ill-defined target can miss entirely, and the failure alerts the whole area.
when: An ambush is triggered on partial information.
why: Misjudged position both wastes the attack and raises alarm.

text: Gate an NPC's willingness to attack with separate stats for physical strength, moral permission and combat temperament.
when: designing NPC violence
why: a capable NPC should not act out of character

text: Do not make NPC killers return to the scene by default; script flight behavior explicitly instead.
when: Designing enemy or NPC behavior after a crime or attack.
why: Default return-to-scene behavior is unrealistic and predictable.

text: Let players present an item or keyword to an NPC and branch dialogue on the reaction, since involuntary reactions to a recognised item reveal guilt or knowledge.
when: Designing NPC responses to player-presented evidence
why: Involuntary reactions to recognised items are readable signals of knowledge

text: Record each interrogation answer as a committed fact, flag later conflicting answers, and track which claims repeat unchanged or are dropped when pressed.
when: Designing an interrogation scene in a game.
why: Conflicts between statements expose lies, and tracking repeated and abandoned claims reveals evasions.

text: Give a distraction NPC a timed task or scripted dialogue that covers a second action, so players must notice what it hides; a failed search carries a penalty.
when: an NPC is placed to misdirect the player or hold a target during a search
why: A timed task pulls attention from the concealed action, and the failure penalty keeps the choice meaningful.

text: Gather information through casual conversation, such as questions over drink, to learn a person's background without revealing the questioner's purpose or raising alarm.
when: when information must be learned without alerting the subject or arousing suspicion
why: a casual frame lowers the subject's guard

text: When an NPC has limited knowledge or deflects a question, let its evasive dialogue point to a second source, so the player can map the chain of information.
when: when an NPC has limited knowledge, refuses or deflects a question
why: redirecting keeps the information and clue chain moving without the NPC revealing it directly

text: Evasive answers or hesitations can flag a follow-up question or hidden branch; gating answers behind a timeline lets probing a hesitation reveal it.
when: designing NPC dialogue trees
why: Hesitation-triggered branches reward players who press the right questions.

text: Model pressing a defensive NPC as raising tension, with a threshold after which it refuses and closes the thread; show tells such as repeated gestures or changed wording.
when: Designing an interrogation mini-game or dialogue with a defensive NPC.
why: Visible tells let the player read a lie, and a threshold makes refusal a consequence of pressing too hard.

text: An NPC's claimed expertise can define a test's rules, so the player must work within conditions the NPC chose, and the request feels routine.
when: An NPC scoffs at a threat and then sets requirements for entry
why: Routine-seeming rules are accepted without challenge

text: Let an NPC who politely declines to ask about the player's business leave a hook suggesting prior knowledge, inviting the player to check what that NPC has seen.
Pick a persona that fits the source's expectations; a respectable figure in reduced circumstances invites trust that a plain stranger would not.
when: Planning how to approach a wary source
why: Expectations shape how much trust a stranger gets

text: Offer the player a choice to spare a guilty NPC once the main accuser withdraws, and show that choice's consequences later.
when: a case against an NPC collapses through a withdrawn accuser
why: a visible later consequence makes mercy a meaningful decision

text: Limit a disguised character's dialogue options to answers the persona could plausibly give.
when: when writing dialogue for a disguised character
why: out-of-persona answers would break the disguise

text: A player absorbed in an objective may stop tracking NPC routines; a missing guard or merchant can serve as a cue that rewards attention.
when: when players are focused on an objective
why: routine changes are noticed only when players still track them

text: Hold a suspect on a minor, provable offence while the main case is built, but only where the offence can be proven.
when: The main case is still open and the minor offence is solid.
why: The minor charge buys time and does not depend on the main case.

text: Let the player build rapport with a frightened NPC through patient dialogue choices, silence options and permission to continue an action, and record which alternative motives the NPC rejects.
when: Designing dialogue with a fragile NPC and a player theory to test.
why: Patient options build trust, and recording rejected motives lets the player eliminate theories.

text: An NPC interrogation can check a player's cover story against world state, such as a dropped item or a witness account.
when: when designing NPC questioning
why: the world holds evidence that contradicts false claims

text: An interrogation minigame can reward the player for choosing the trigger word that produces the strongest reaction.
when: Designing an interrogation minigame.
why: Rewarding the strongest reaction ties the player's choice to the revealed secret.

text: When an NPC volunteers a next step in a conversation tree, the interaction continues without the player having to force it.
Let a friendly NPC recall a remark, but reveal its full context only after the player asks the right follow-up question.
A public recantation can branch so that its wording decides whether players learn the real source or only a convenient excuse.
when: designing a recantation quest

text: A dialogue option in which an employer grants a guarantee can unlock testimony and set a quest flag.
Interview order can gate NPC dialogue, so staff testimony unlocks timing facts before the suspect is approached.
A character's knowledge store has limited capacity, so each new fact stored can push out older knowledge that is needed.
when: when designing knowledge, memory or inventory limits
why: Storage space is finite, so kept facts compete with one another

text: A game can offer a false or partial confession and let the player expose its gap through a second clue.
In dialogue trees, an early accusation can lock out later answers unless the player follows a specific order of topics.
A perception trait sets which behavioral tells a character can notice during questioning, changing what information that character gains.
An NPC's willingness to reveal information can depend on its state, so a sober NPC reveals more than an intoxicated one.
when: When designing NPC state variables for dialogue.
why: Changing state alters the information the NPC can or will give.

text: Payment and intimidation can change how an NPC speaks, with consequences for the player's trust in what the NPC says.
when: When an NPC's cooperation can be bought or forced.
why: Costs alter the NPC's incentive to be honest, which affects the reliability of what they report.

text: An NPC's answers to a player's hypothetical scenario can vary with what the NPC knows, so different answers signal different knowledge.
when: Designing an interrogation dialogue.

text: A threat bluff fails if the target does not believe it, so a confrontation relies on the target accepting the threat.
A brief, general questioning of staff does not replace a full interview; family members still have to be heard in complete detail.
Early answers from a frightened witness can be false, so they should be treated as unreliable until checked.
Accepting an expert's first explanation without checking the direction of force can lead to a wrong sequence of events.
when: an expert offers a quick explanation for damage
why: The first explanation may not match the physical evidence.

text: Confronting a suspect can turn violent, especially if they are armed, so interrogation should not assume a calm target.
1) Start with an open question. 2) Follow with narrower questions that unlock specific facts. 3) Tag each disclosed fact with whether the NPC saw it or only heard it.
when: When designing an informant NPC whose knowledge is partial.
why: Layered questioning gives the player facts in order, and source tags let the player weigh each claim.

text: 1) Hold each piece of collected evidence as a unlockable item. 2) Unlock the next line of questioning only when the player has the matching evidence. 3) Offer a timed bargain that forces a choice between handing over an item and facing a consequence.
when: Designing an NPC interrogation in a game.
why: Tying dialogue to evidence rewards investigation and makes the player's choices consequential.

text: 1) Caution the person before taking the statement, so they know it may be used against them. 2) Tell them of their right to representation. 3) Ask whether they have representation. 4) Record the answer.
when: A witness may become a suspect during questioning
why: Protects the statement's admissibility and the person's rights

text: 1) Pick each named place or person in the account. 2) Ask a plain follow-up question about it. 3) Note whether the answer shifts. 4) Compare the answer with facts already known.

1) Build the persona from the outside in, starting with visible details such as dress, grooming and wear. 2) Check each prop against what a close observer would examine. 3) Fix any detail that contradicts the persona.
when: when creating a disguise meant to survive close scrutiny

text: Give suspect NPCs a tell: a named place, person, object or loaded keyword that triggers a visible reaction, like a flicker of fear, which the player can notice and record.
when: a suspect NPC is exposed to a sensitive topic
why: a flicker of fear is a readable tell

text: Give interrogated NPCs a composure value that drops as the player presents evidence, and let the player switch between threat and empathy, with the NPC reacting to each.
when: when designing NPC interrogation or confrontation
why: the reaction depends on the NPC's composure

text: Branch a confrontation or interrogation on evidence the player shows: a refusal can be followed by presented evidence that opens a new option, making each discrepancy a meaningful choice.
when: designing NPC interrogation or confrontation scenes

text: Reveal facts in a set order through dialogue trees, so a hidden grudge or key clue unlocks only after follow-up questions in the right sequence; admissions can change later options.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that hides a motive or an investigation.
why: Sequenced questioning rewards systematic investigation

text: Let narrow follow-up questions pin down a witness's prior claims to reveal what they observed; each correct line gates the next piece of evidence.
when: Building a witness interaction or NPC interrogation with branching dialogue.
why: Players learn the true basis of a claim through questioning

text: Let players question an NPC about where its knowledge or position came from, and check the answer against a second source or what the player has seen directly.
Let guarded NPCs, such as servants, reveal information when the player shows sympathy or accepts a partial story, and flag the stated claim for later checking.
when: Designing an NPC that withholds information until rapport is built.
why: Interrogation is refused while sympathy invites volunteered information; flagging keeps the claim testable.

text: For an NPC witness, open with neutral earlier events and release partial information in stages to build trust.
why: Staged disclosure keeps the NPC cooperative

text: Let an NPC probe gently and show its surprise, so the player can tell which facts the NPC already knows.
when: during NPC questioning
why: visible reactions expose what the NPC knows

text: Offer dialogue prompts like 'what would they do', so players can draw out an NPC's opinion of another character's motive.
Let an idle NPC conversation hide a second objective, and leave a visible clue so players can spot the subterfuge.
Let a confrontation deliver unexpected news and record the NPC's response, branching dialogue on whether the player's choice was cruel or careful.
when: When designing a confrontation scene

text: Model a disgruntled ally who turns on his employer as a branch whose unlock depends on the player's earlier actions.
when: designing branching narrative paths
why: the defection should follow from what the player has done

text: Let an NPC on a fixed patrol find a planted item at a predictable point, so the player can steer that NPC's suspicion.
when: Designing NPC-driven detective or stealth scenarios
why: Fixed routes make the NPC's discovery of the item reliable and controllable.

text: Let players test two rival readings of the same detail, so the investigation branches on which reading they pursue.
when: when designing investigation logic

text: Separate the goal of catching the actor from the goal of breaking up the wider operation, and plan each as its own task.
when: A crime is tied to a larger criminal network.
why: Each goal needs different work, and doing both at once is hard.

text: Make an NPC's accusation rest on rhetoric, and reward players who notice the unsupported step.
when: Designing an NPC accusation in an investigation game.
why: Players who catch the gap engage with the evidence.

text: Let a suspect NPC ask the player questions in return, so the player's answers change what other characters believe.
Build interrogation scenes so NPC questions reflect facts the player has found; a question about an undiscovered fact implies another source, which can be a clue.
Interrupt a long NPC monologue at a meaningful point so the player must choose what to ask next.
Let an NPC's written or spoken ideology serve as a clue, with dialogue options asking the player to take a position on a hypothetical crime.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that reveals motive through belief.
why: A stated belief gives the player a lever to probe the NPC's motive.

text: Give NPC witnesses a reputation value that changes how much their testimony counts in dialogue or accusations.
Offer a leave-message option for absent witnesses, and let clues such as a remark or a note reveal where a witness has gone.
Do not treat stated denials or secrecy pledges as proof that a secret stayed contained.
Give npcs warnings that hint at a hazard without naming it, so players must deduce the danger from context.
when: when designing npc dialogue about dungeon hazards

text: Design a conversation option that seems sympathetic but carries a cost, so that a player's comment can close off an informant's cooperation.
when: designing NPC dialogue with informants
why: Makes social choices meaningful and risky

text: Attach a stake or bias tag to each NPC so the same event is described differently by allies and rivals.
when: designing NPC dialogue about shared events
why: Biased descriptions create contrast that players must resolve

text: Spread partial clues across several informant NPCs so the player must combine their fragments to reach the answer.
when: Designing a quest log with multiple sources.

text: Let dialogue options contradict later evidence so the player must remember what an NPC said earlier.
Use silence or a delayed NPC response as a dialogue mechanic to pressure a hidden reaction.
when: When designing confrontation dialogue.
why: A pause gives the player a choice to wait and lets the NPC's hesitation carry information.

text: Give a reluctant NPC an optional question they refuse to answer, record the refusal, and let the player return to it later.
Give an NPC with a personal link to the victim extra dialogue or hidden information.
when: Designing NPC information access.
why: Personal ties naturally open intimate detail.
