text: Let a player's chosen solution face a cross-examination phase in which challenger characters ask for corroboration and offer rival answers before the accusation is confirmed.
when: the game has a confirmation step for accusations
why: inconsistencies surface before the player commits

text: Let NPCs vary their tone by listener while core facts stay fixed, so a careful player can compare versions.
when: designing NPC dialogue
why: Fixed facts give the player something to check.

text: Track whether each fact an NPC states was volunteered or prompted by the player's options, and discount prompted facts as independent knowledge.
when: The player offers choices during dialogue
why: Player-supplied options can shape what the NPC says

text: In an interrogation, let a suspect's stress interrupt questioning, forcing the player to choose between pressing on and waiting for the suspect to recover.
when: Designing an interrogation system with a stress or emotion state
why: A forced choice between pressure and patience creates a meaningful decision

text: Broad questions fill gaps but invite broad answers that cannot be checked and drift from the key point; focused questions aimed at a specific gap stay on target and checkable.
when: Investigating gaps in several accounts.
why: More questions do not always clarify; direction matters.

text: Model gossip as propagation along relationship links, where NPCs repeat claims with a chance of distortion so the player can trace each claim to its origin.
why: Information spreads gradually along links instead of appearing everywhere at once, and tracing claims reveals their source.

text: An antagonist who keeps acting on outdated information, such as believing it still holds an item, commits to actions that can be turned against it.
when: The world changes without the antagonist learning of it.
why: Decisions based on stale knowledge lead to predictable mistakes.

text: Openly voiced plans, such as offers of bribes or talk of outside help, make watchers expect threats along that route rather than the real one.
Local supernatural rumours can hide a real sound and a real speaker; approaching the source reveals whether the cause is human or supernatural.
when: A setting has a supernatural reputation that may conceal a human presence.
why: Moving closer lets the observer identify the actual speakers, replacing the rumour with direct evidence.

text: Make biased, drunk, or emotionally driven NPC informants right on some points and wrong on others, and tag their gossip unreliable so players must corroborate claims through other sources.
when: When creating unreliable NPC informants, or dialogue and rumour systems that carry information.
why: Mixed or emotionally shaped reliability rewards players who verify claims and weigh sources rather than trust one voice.

text: Let a dying NPC give clues in fragments, with lucid moments timed so the player can gather the useful lines.
when: designing dying or ill characters as sources
why: fragmented information rewards attention

text: Witness NPCs can give accounts that conflict on time or appearance, and the player reconciles these conflicts to find the lying NPC.
when: When designing witness dialogue for a deduction puzzle.
why: Conflicting statements give the player a method to identify deception.

text: An NPC who later contradicts an earlier statement can trigger a mid-game shift in the plot.
when: an NPC's alibi changes over time
why: Contradiction creates new evidence and changes what the player believes.

text: Give an NPC contradictory reputation tags, such as generous and arrogant, that offset in a crowd's view so the net reputation stays neutral.
when: building reputation systems
why: opposing tags cancel in aggregate

text: Model an NPC's grudge, affection, or belief as a state that changes which clues it notices and how heavily it weighs them, so emotional investment can lead it to discount evidence.
when: An NPC has a personal stake in an outcome or a personal link to a case figure.
why: The state alters which leads the NPC pursues and how new information is weighed.

text: Assuming a remaining person is safe because the threat seems to have run its course leaves them exposed.
when: when a series of attacks seems to have stopped
why: Attacks may continue against the one person not yet touched.

text: Track each character's knowledge state explicitly, so the player's choice to tell or hold back has visible consequences.
when: Designing NPCs that react to information
why: Separate knowledge produces different reactions

text: Build NPC gossip so every accusation introduces new named suspects, and let players track the spread over time.
Tag NPCs with reputation values such as unreliable and let player actions change the tag, so NPCs ignore or misread clues according to it.
when: Designing NPC responses to player-supplied information.
why: Reputation shapes which clues an NPC accepts, and player action should be able to revise it.

text: Track each NPC's knowledge; have each revealed fact point to its giver and how they know it, setting a flag when mentioned early so the player can question the source.
A party who keeps an inquiry secret until holding a decisive clue hides the evidence from others, so their claims cannot yet be checked.
when: someone announces they are assembling a case in private
why: Evidence unseen by others cannot be tested or contradicted

text: Parties who meet somewhere secluded and away from their homes are avoiding witnesses, so the meeting itself becomes evidence of intent.
Knowledge kept secret and never shown tends to be read as sorcery, so its holders gain power because others cannot see how their results were produced.
when: when a community cannot observe how an outcome was produced
why: unseen means are attributed to supernatural causes

text: A character can expose that they hold a secret through questioning, not only by choice, so guarded information can still leak.
A motive rooted in a secret may surface only after the secret is shared with another person.
Subjects in induced trance often remember nothing of what they said afterward, so they cannot confirm or deny their own account.
A leaked or stolen secret can only come from someone who could know where it was; ask who could have known to narrow suspects to confidants or household insiders.
when: a threat reveals private knowledge or a secret is stolen
why: a secret has only a few possible sources

text: A mechanism with a secret input implies the culprit learned that input from someone who spoke it aloud.
when: a locked mechanism needs a code

text: A supposed secret cannot be hidden from the people around the suspect; if they already know it, it is not the hidden truth.
when: judging which secret an investigation should pursue
why: Information shared with bystanders is no longer concealed

text: Give NPC dialogue knowledge markers, such as asking whether an object was put back, that reveal who knew what and when.
when: Designing dialogue for a mystery.
why: Casual lines let the player infer knowledge without direct confession.

text: When a witness hides something, ask whether the secret concerns the crime or something unrelated to it.
when: a witness is concealing information

text: When a suspect knows a private fact they could not have witnessed, trace how it travelled rather than accepting it as proof of guilt.
when: Someone reveals information that was never shared with them.
why: An unknown transmission channel is a lead to investigate, not an answer.

text: Log NPC reactions to named people or places so the player can later read them as tells.
when: Designing NPC responses that carry clues
why: Recorded reactions let the player connect body language to hidden knowledge

text: Record what each NPC could know, and flag dialogue where the NPC's confidence exceeds that knowledge.
when: when building NPC dialogue that signals belief

text: Track what each non-player character knows and suspects, letting suspicion rise and fall with new evidence.
why: knowledge state drives believable reactions

text: Let an NPC's knowledge or disclosure depend on time of day, state or hidden mood, so the same question returns different answers; ask at the right time.
when: designing NPC dialogue

text: Each concession or added participant in a conspiracy widens the circle of people who share the secret.
Tracking which characters were told, read, or heard about a rule or secret, and when, lets the game model who knew what.
when: Designing secrets or rules that characters can learn about.
why: Knowledge state determines which motives and actions are plausible for each character.

text: Model an NPC's testimony as a changing state that a handshake, public hearing or accusation can flip, so the player can notice and exploit the shift.
when: designing witnesses who change their account during play
why: belief shifts make social events count as evidence

text: Record which characters know a secret as state flags, so an NPC reveals it only when its flag matches the player's actions.
when: designing a secret held by several NPCs
why: state flags keep disclosure consistent with what each character has learned

text: A game can track whether an item is hidden from a guard and change that guard's awareness only when the player acts in a set way.
when: Stealth or hidden-evidence mechanics where NPC knowledge should depend on player actions.
why: Tying awareness to specific actions keeps discoveries secret until the player chooses to reveal them.

text: Give each NPC a knowledge state, true statements and a disclosure threshold; pressure or clever questions reveal some facts while others stay hidden, one stage at a time.
when: designing an interrogable NPC or dialogue for a mystery
why: gradual disclosure keeps information controlled and lets the player test claims

text: Count every person in a small circle, including staff, overhearers and anyone passing a partly closed door, as a possible channel; track who was told, not only who promised silence.
why: Discussion and movement in a household reach more people than its family.

text: 1) List every communication channel and the hours each was open. 2) Note which channels were cut off at night, which stayed open, and whether each was used. 3) Use later actions to infer when the news arrived. 4) Identify who could be at the source during that window. 5) Combine with an access list, since someone unable to leave or call out was inside.
when: A group reacts to news and the source and timing of the news are unclear.

text: 1) Record which memories each NPC loses and when. 2) Attach a scripted recovery clue to each. 3) Trigger the clue only after the player finds the matching source.
when: NPC memories are part of quest state
why: tracked losses make recovery consistent and tie it to player actions

text: Track which facts each character knows, so concealment stays consistent and information leaking via staff can reach a suspect.
When an NPC learns a secret or a leak occurs, update what each other character knows and let their next behavior toward the player reflect it.
when: designing faction knowledge or branching dialogue with information leaks
why: Consequences of disclosure should show in later behavior.

text: Withhold each NPC's specific facts or key item until the player meets its condition, such as a dialogue choice, return visit, particular action or scene, not simple accusation.
Track NPC knowledge state so sharper or indirect questions, or built rapport, unlock detailed, firmer answers; vague questions get only vague replies.
when: designing NPC information or partial-memory dialogue

text: Log what each NPC could see and hear, with times and locations, so contradictions resolve by finding which NPC was positioned to perceive the event.
when: NPCs act as witnesses or give conflicting accounts
why: contradictions can be found by reasoning rather than chance; logged perception makes conflicts resolvable

text: Log each NPC's position and last-seen moment over time so players can reconstruct the timeline and spot gaps that conflict with another NPC's account.
why: Position history lets players find contradictions between accounts

text: Track which NPCs have seen which documents, sigils or objects, so a forged letter fails detectably for those who saw the original and each message's possibility can be checked.
Track which NPCs heard or were told of a discovery; some may relay it to the target, so a suspect's later appearance can reveal the leak.
when: When designing NPC knowledge in a mystery.
why: Some NPCs may relay conversations to the target and change how they respond later.

text: Model each NPC's knowledge and beliefs about others' identities or judgments, and show the gap to the world state so the player can test and exploit the error.
when: an NPC's judgment about another is wrong
why: The gap makes the NPC's error discoverable.

text: Treat an unknown companion kept secret from others, yet trusted for a long time, as a lead to pursue.
why: secrecy combined with trust suggests a meaningful relationship worth tracing

text: Track which characters know which secret, and direct the player to question the ones who can explain a hidden history.
Give NPCs secrets that explain behaviour the player misreads, and let the reveal change how earlier scenes look.
Give NPCs knowledge flags separating 'saw it' from 'heard about it', so dialogue reveals narrow truths that the player must test against other sources.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that conceals information
why: Narrow, source-tagged answers create verification gameplay

text: Chain the password through several NPCs so the player can trace who knows the answer.
when: Designing a password that spreads through a group
why: Tracing knowledge reveals the group's connections

text: Have an informant recap the facts the player knows; the player confirms or corrects each one, and the game records which facts were confirmed and which disputed.
when: designing dialogue that checks player knowledge
why: Recording confirmations and disputes tracks what the player actually believes.

text: Keep an antagonist NPC from learning the player's findings, so the player can act before the antagonist reacts.
when: when designing antagonist knowledge

text: In a poisoning or locked-room scenario, narrow candidate NPCs by the locations and times each could reach, given their schedules.
when: designing a mystery where the culprit must have had access
why: Schedules make access checkable, so the player can test each name.

text: Use a secret errand as a red herring that the player must investigate and then dismiss.
when: designing a misleading subplot
why: Investigating and dismissing it rewards testing.

text: Make NPC confidence depend on access: detailed knowledge without any written record implies the NPC was at the scene, which players can verify against other clues.
when: designing NPC knowledge in a mystery

text: Give each witness NPC a record of access (where they stood, who they know) and a loyalty that may bend their phrasing.
when: Designing NPC witnesses for an investigation
why: Access and loyalty give players the context needed to interpret each witness's words

text: Treat knowledge of secrets or future events as evidence of a hidden pact only if no human skill, reason or revelation can explain it.
Limit each NPC's reports to what its position let it perceive, so NPCs at different positions report the same event differently.
when: designing NPC dialogue about past events
why: Each report should match what that NPC could actually sense

text: Log unusual NPC actions as flags the player must interpret, rather than explaining them to the player immediately.
why: interpretation keeps the player engaged

text: Store each NPC's claims in a log that other NPCs can contradict, so cross-checking has consequences.
Scope non-player character knowledge so only the appropriate character can report a given detail.
when: Assigning facts to characters
why: Limiting who knows a detail keeps clues consistent with each role

text: Expose a suspicion state for NPCs that changes their routine after the player is noticed, so later behavior produces different clues.
when: When designing stealth or observation systems.
why: Changed routine keeps detection consequential.

text: Log each NPC's interactions with the player and other NPCs, so a rival or friend can confront the player with that record.
Keeping a plan secret stops the opposing side from adapting, but it leaves allies and loved ones unable to judge the strength of the case themselves.
Fog, smoke, low light and distance reduce what an observer can confirm and shorten tracking, so identification weakens and sightings end abruptly, leaving gaps.
when: sight lines are obscured or long, or when designing line-of-sight or witness systems
why: Degraded visibility removes identifying detail and shortens tracking.

text: Give each NPC sighting a confidence value that falls with distance and poor light, and adjust it for time of day, observer fatigue, illness, intoxication, and familiarity with the subject.
when: NPCs report what they have seen
why: View conditions and observer state determine how reliable a sighting is.

text: Cautious actors avoid a target while a more dangerous opponent guards it, and strike when the target is left unprotected.
when: A group chooses when to act against a defended objective.
why: Each actor minimizes the risk of encountering a stronger defender.

text: NPCs that notice mud, dust or other traces on a player reveal the player's past route as an observable clue.
when: when a player has traveled through dirty or dusty terrain

text: A high-skill NPC can react to the player's appearance and manner, so the player's cover must hold against a perceptive character.
NPCs may change their behavior when they know they are watched, so surveillance itself alters the situation.

text: An enemy who isolates a target from friends must eventually communicate with someone close to the target, so an intermediary can expose the approach.
when: The pursuer relies on allies or contacts to reach the target
why: Isolation cannot be complete without some outreach

text: An open doorway shows a watcher only a slice of the room behind it, so a witness's view covers less than the whole room.
Position an observer close enough to read faces and gestures, since distance hides the details needed for identification.
when: identity or fine detail matters
why: far vantage points lose key visual information

text: Act when a concealing person is alone, close to an exit, and their hands are still occupied, to limit their response.
when: when a hidden threat must be exposed

text: An NPC walking past a hidden item creates a risk of discovery that makes the concealment itself a timed challenge for the player.
when: Designing a hidden-item scene with patrolling or passing characters.
why: The passing character changes the chance that the item is found.

text: Guards with long sight detect moving characters before still ones, so a player who holds still at range can stay hidden.
when: Guards detect by sight at distance
why: Motion is a stronger detection cue than static presence

text: A light exposes whoever carries it to anyone facing it, while a light switched on behind a group dazzles the group and leaves its holder unseen.
why: glare blinds those looking toward a light, and the holder stays outside their view

text: Model NPC detection using lighting, distance and attention, so a disguised player passes in darkness or at range but fails in bright, close or attentive conditions.
when: designing stealth or disguise detection for NPCs

text: A watcher viewing through a narrow gap gets partial, unreliable evidence, and can be deceived about another's position.
when: An observer must watch a target without being seen.
why: Limited view leaves the target's exact position and shape ill-defined.

text: An NPC that watches through doors or windows reacts when the player gets too close to a hidden area.
A lit window nearby is the main hazard to a hidden listener; rustling clothing and loose objects can also betray a position.
The intermediary must be seen often, or the enemy may never make contact.
when: Setting up a bait position
why: Without a visible routine the approach does not happen

text: A second stranger asking questions draws local gossip and can alert the target.

1) Use questions to pin down what the watched person is doing, when and why. 2) Position yourself in darkness at an angle from which the watcher can be seen but cannot see you. 3) Once the watcher appears, leave by the planned route and ignore him.
when: a watcher threatens a character and must be drawn away unseen
why: the observer's attention stays on the decoy target

text: 1) Tell the observer in advance what to watch, so the test is fair. 2) Have them record specific features. 3) Compare their inventory with the facts to see what was really noticed.
when: Judging how much weight to give a witness's observations.
why: A fair standard in advance prevents the test from being biased by hindsight.

text: Simulate each witness's line of sight, hearing range and ambient noise, including partial views through doorways, mirrors and screens, so testimony reflects position and players can cross-check it.
when: designing witness NPCs whose observations matter
why: Perception limits set by position make witness claims checkable.

text: Model each guard's line of sight and alert state so players can learn what it can and cannot see and detect surveillance they set up.
when: designing guards or watchers in a game
why: Readable sight limits let careful players find unwatched routes.

text: Let an NPC being trailed by the player across several transports react when the player is spotted.
Track what each NPC can see, so an item pocketed from view stays hidden from observers in the inventory system.
Simulate hearing and visibility so a missing reaction follows from the setup rather than from arbitrary design.
When an uninjured person may be the next target, assign watchers to them rather than forcing them to stay.
when: when a remaining person may be the next victim
why: Forced detention creates new risks and legal problems, while surveillance protects without restraint.

text: Station an NPC near a target and have it watch the target repeatedly, giving the player a suspect with visible behavior and a reason to be there.
Let NPCs notice a hiding or feigning player, and let the player spot surveillance in return.
Let NPCs revisit a scene and notice changes the player made, giving the player a second chance to catch the mistake.
Give perceptive NPCs an error margin when reading the player, so they can still misjudge a deceptive character.
when: Designing NPCs that evaluate player behavior.

text: Give NPCs daily or weekly routines, such as deliveries, patrols or meals; a skipped or changed routine, such as extra patrols or avoided eye contact, is a visible clue.
when: Designing NPC schedules or guilt-hinting NPC behaviour.
why: Schedule breaks reveal hidden activity, especially at crime time; nearby NPCs reacting to a skipped routine signal players to investigate.

text: Players infer when a room is unguarded by noticing NPCs' scheduled shifts, which opens gaps they can use.
when: NPCs follow visible shift schedules
why: regular absences reveal predictable unguarded periods

text: Give each NPC a routine model, track it over time, and flag even small deviations, such as unusual purchases or a shifted patrol, as clues or quest triggers.
when: Designing NPC schedules that should reveal hidden actions through deviation.
why: A routine gives the player a baseline, so deviations become meaningful clues rather than random events; a deviation can open a new quest or lead.

text: Establish a learnable routine, then break it at a key moment; the scripted break becomes the clue prompting the next question, and trusting players may miss it.
when: Designing NPC schedules tied to story beats or daily routines.
why: A learned pattern makes a deviation noticeable and meaningful; players who rely on predictable schedules overlook changes.

text: Tie NPC witnesses' timed memories to shift or routine endings; precise times are more reliable because the routine gives a reason to remember them, so players can fix a timeline.
when: Assessing a witness's timed memory or designing NPC witnesses.
why: People watching a clock for a routine end, such as a shift, remember when it happened.

text: Repeated sightings reveal habitual movements and likely destinations, so a regular haunt makes a good stakeout; a single sighting is weak evidence of a routine.
when: Tracking a suspect's habits over several days, or a suspect seen at a regular haunt.
why: People keep to habitual places and times, so a pattern needs repeated observation before it is trusted.

text: Let town NPCs hold routine knowledge that players collect through repeated conversation, with several NPCs confirming the same schedule.
when: Designing information gathering in towns.

text: Give the world a schedule of expected events, such as faction messages or market reactions, so that a missing event signals a change in the plot.
A movement that a schedule cannot support is a strong lead against a suspect.
Build a time window from schedules, such as last sighting and transport departure, and let the player test each hypothesis against it.
when: Designing a deduction puzzle with a timeline.
why: A fixed window makes competing explanations checkable.

text: Check a suspect's account of small details against the schedule; a detail, such as a meal that could not fit before a train, can be decisive.
Log NPC routines with timestamps and allow an innocent reading of errands, so a player who reads them as a plan can be proven wrong.
when: When designing NPC schedules that players will follow.

text: Test whether an act fits a known gap in a fixed schedule, such as a short errand within a ten-minute interval.
Assign each NPC specific locations at set hours so the player can build timelines and a suspect list that grows as new associations are found.
when: Generating a mystery with NPC suspects
why: Scheduled locations make alibis checkable and let suspects be added or removed as the player learns more

text: A fixed NPC timeline can be checked by the player against other NPCs' schedules, with repeated questioning revealing shifts.
when: Designing NPC schedules and dialogue for a timeline puzzle.
why: Cross-checking schedules exposes inconsistencies the player can act on.

text: Schedule NPC movements so the window closes before a discovery, and the player must prove who was present within it.
when: Designing a discovery event with a limited suspect window.
why: A closing window makes presence within it the key question.

text: Give each NPC a schedule with checkpoints, so the player can reconstruct who could reach a restricted area during a gap.
when: Designing NPC movement for a stealth or investigation level.
why: Checkpoints turn unobserved time into a reconstructable window.

text: A puzzle can present a routine explanation that fails when a missing item is one the routine would never take, prompting the player to look further.
Make a puzzle require checking a schedule or record rather than appearance, so the player learns to test testimony.
Let the player tail an NPC through a town, with each stop unlocking a clue about that NPC's plans, such as an evening appointment.
when: designing NPC routines
why: route stops reward careful observation

text: A distraction timed to a target's routine only works if the planner knows that routine; a poor timing match reveals limited knowledge.
when: Judging whether a staged event was planned with insider knowledge
why: Routines reveal what the planner actually knew

text: Give escort or timed-delivery NPCs more than one schedule, and show the alternative through an earlier clue so the player's estimate can fail fairly.
when: when designing timed escort or intercept missions
why: A fair, foreshadowed failure lets the player adjust rather than feel cheated.

text: Use a moving character's timetable or onward route to infer where it is heading, rather than reading only its current position.
when: when a character follows a fixed schedule
why: routes reveal likely destinations

text: Let NPCs ignore familiar routine noise, so a player who moves during that noise can pass unseen.
when: when designing NPC awareness and stealth cover
why: Expected sounds are filtered out, creating cover from routine activity.

text: A fixed routine works as a reliable timer only if no one has ever broken it; verify that before relying on it.
when: A routine is used to fix a time.

text: Build NPC schedules so a target is present only during a defined window, forcing the player to arrive within that interval.
when: Designing a quest that depends on catching an NPC in place.
why: A bounded window turns travel and timing into the challenge.

text: Give NPCs routines such as meals, walks and shift changes so players can build a timeline asking who was free during a window.
when: Designing a time-based puzzle
why: Routines give players a schedule to reason against.

text: Give NPCs a schedule and witnesses who can confirm it; a player breaks an alibi by finding one contradicting sighting.
when: Designing NPC alibis that the player can test
why: A single contradicting sighting exposes a false schedule

text: NPC routines can change at dusk, so a player can infer a hidden schedule from when people appear and disappear.
when: Designing day and night NPC schedules

text: A fixed routine forms a baseline; a missing, moved or changed behaviour, such as an absent guard or item removed from its usual shelf, becomes a visible clue.
when: A predictable routine or spending pattern that players can learn and monitor.
why: Observers compare new behaviour against the established norm, and routines run on the in-game clock; players can only notice departures from patterns they have seen.

text: A scheduled patrol, inventory or fuel check works as a timer: players who learn it can plan around or exploit it, and a concealer must act before it arrives.
why: A fixed schedule sets a deadline the player must meet or exploit.

text: Scheduled NPC shifts, patrols, deliveries or doors open or close predictable windows of access that players can learn and exploit; events can fire only while the target is away.
when: Designing events that depend on guard, NPC or delivery timing.
why: Presence and access change with the shift, and schedules make the target's position predictable.

text: Household routines and sleep times, such as who is awake at a given hour or who locks up at night, set windows where movement goes unnoticed; deviations become clues.
when: Planning movement through a building or designing household NPCs.
why: Routines determine when people are watching; a deviation from a household baseline is a meaningful clue.

text: Scheduled NPC movements let a player who tracks the clock establish which character was where at a given moment.
when: NPCs follow fixed schedules in a game world
why: Fixed schedules make positions predictable from the clock

text: A game clock combined with NPC routines lets a player reconstruct where a character could have been and when they would have been visible.
when: when NPCs follow scheduled routines

text: Routine schedules create predictable gaps in which an event can occur unobserved, so tracked NPC routines reveal when and where to act.
when: when NPCs follow timed routes or schedules
why: Predictable behaviour leaves regular windows without witnesses

text: An NPC's illogical path can signal hidden knowledge or intent, so players who notice such deviations gain evidence about that character.
when: When an NPC moves in a way inconsistent with its stated purpose
why: Actions that serve a concealed goal look wrong when judged against the public one.

text: An NPC schedule that logs actions by time can flag gaps where a character's location is unknown, and travel times can reveal which alibis are impossible.
when: Designing NPC routines that the player can verify.
why: Logged times and travel durations expose physically impossible claims.

text: Random failures such as a misfire or a grazing hit change an encounter's outcome and can expose a weapon's condition as a clue.
when: A combat encounter uses probabilistic weapon outcomes

text: A missed NPC meeting can open a new location, moving the player from waiting to investigating.
when: Player's planned meeting fails

text: A timeline log of NPC movements lets players cross-check alibis, and distinct sensory cues such as a unique smell or visual sign help players identify who was present.
when: Designing NPC movement logs and clue-based identification.
why: Logged movements allow cross-checking, and distinct cues make a person recognizable.

text: If an NPC's sleep skips time out of step with the game clock, the player can spot the mismatch between the NPC's account and the world.
A hiding place tied to a routine, such as scheduled worker access, can be found by watching that routine. Let an NPC use the access point on a schedule.
when: Stealth or investigation levels with scheduled NPCs.
why: Concealment that depends on a repeated action reveals itself to anyone who watches that action.

text: A plan built on a target's routine can be defeated by a single false assumption, such as a fixed schedule, even when most gathered details are correct.
when: Planning an entry or meeting that depends on an NPC's habits.
why: The whole plan rests on one timing assumption, so its failure collapses the sequence.

text: An NPC's routine, such as chores or patrols, can be faked by another character, so the player's timeline checks mislead until a contradiction emerges.
when: When designing NPC schedules that players use to build timelines
why: Forged routines create false timelines that a later contradiction can expose.

text: NPC routines run on a clock, so a patrol gap or a closing time gives the player a window to check an alibi.
when: Guards or merchants follow scheduled routines.
why: Scheduled absences create predictable moments when claims can be tested.

text: An NPC's scheduled routine, such as a delivery at a set time, can be exploited as cover when the player wears a matching disguise.
when: The routine is usually punctual
why: Watchers expect the figure they see at that time

text: Routine NPC schedules can include a deliberate exception, such as an NPC present when the schedule says absent, creating surprise for the player.
Gating an NPC behind unavailability, such as being away or not yet reachable, paces the investigation by controlling when information arrives.
when: Pacing a game investigation with NPC access.
why: Temporary unavailability holds back information until the player is ready for it.

text: NPC schedules and a timestamped event log let players reconstruct who was where and when.
when: Designing a mystery where player reconstruction of movements matters.
why: Recorded times let the player cross-check accounts.

text: Model an NPC's daily schedule as timestamped entries, with uncertainty windows where the schedule is missing, so the player can reconstruct movements.
when: Designing NPC movement that players must reconstruct.
why: Timestamps plus explicit gaps let players infer where a character was.

text: A schedule-based window or habitual-delay deadline assumes the pattern held exactly; delayed or missed schedules invalidate the reasoning built on it.
when: Relying on a timetable or predicted response time to fix when an event happened.
why: Real schedules are often delayed or missed; a countdown is only as accurate as the pattern it is built on, and irregular schedules make it unreliable.

text: 1) Estimate travel time for each possible route. 2) Compare each route time with the timestamps in the sequence. 3) Reject any step whose route cannot fit the clock.
when: testing a reconstructed movement sequence

text: 1) Establish the routine's fixed timing and ask whether any single occurrence ever broke it. 2) Ask who knew the timing, to learn how widely it was known. 3) Establish where the witness stood to observe. 4) Check the conditions of observation, such as lighting, and whether visible fixtures actually work.
when: A routine is used to fix a time in an investigation, or a witness vouches for it.

text: 1) Learn another person's timetable. 2) Schedule your own movements around it. 3) Act within the window when that person is expected to be absent.

1) Leave a visible note at departure, addressed to someone who would notice the absence. 2) Time each leg of the journey. 3) Name a witness who can confirm each leg or stop. 4) Anchor arrival to a timed landmark.
when: reconstructing a traveller's movements
why: each leg then has someone who can confirm it

text: 1) Record the witness's stated route and each named stop. 2) Compare each stop and timing against the travel record. 3) Note any stop that cannot be reached in the stated time.
when: A witness gives an account of movements that can be checked against transport or location records.
why: A stated itinerary is only credible if its places and times are physically possible and match independent records.

text: 1) Identify the collection or event schedule. 2) Define the window between the two nearest scheduled times. 3) Check whether opening hours or other constraints rule out alternative methods.
when: Limiting when an act could have occurred using a timetable.
why: A schedule bounds the time and facts like closures eliminate options.

text: 1) List the planned timed items in order. 2) Assign each an expected duration. 3) Compute when each should have ended. 4) Compare with the actual clock to find the gap.
when: When measuring whether a character's day has drifted from plan.
why: A cumulative gap reveals that something has gone wrong, and the list makes it visible.

text: Give NPCs timestamped schedules with map travel times and waiting periods, so players can test whether a suspect, or two suspects, could reach a location in time.
when: Designing NPC schedules for a mystery in a world with travel.
why: Checkable timing lets players build and test timelines, measure alibis against real distances, and reject accounts that could not physically have happened.

text: Give NPCs timestamped events such as arrivals, exits or shift changes so claimed whereabouts can be checked against other NPCs' accounts or sightings; contradictions or confirmations reveal the truth.
when: Designing NPC alibis, stated locations or investigation routines.
why: Two independent accounts of the same time can contradict each other; shared timestamps make inconsistencies checkable.

text: Give NPCs scheduled routines, such as a set walk or fixed closing hour, so a claimed alibi or errand can be checked against the clock to prove or break it.
when: Designing NPC schedules that support alibi checks, especially where positions are tracked over time.
why: Schedules make claims testable; a logged schedule of NPC movements turns each alibi into a checkable claim.

text: Give NPCs daily schedules with unobserved gaps, so players rebuild the timeline from witnesses and clocks, testing who had opportunity; unknown gaps become investigation hooks.
when: Designing NPC routines or a generated mystery around a crime.
why: Unobserved windows are where opportunity lives; each witness saw part of the day, and the player fills gaps using clocks, receipts and witness times.

text: Let an NPC leave or arrive at a set time so the player can exploit or miss that window.
Give each NPC a location and schedule so the game can check whether they could have heard or seen an event.
Build NPC movement schedules that let the player reconstruct each character's location from clock chimes and patrol times.
when: Designing a game where NPC positions matter for deduction
why: Checkable schedules let players test alibis

text: Give every NPC a daily schedule with timed anchor points, such as bells or shift changes, so the player can test whether that NPC could have been at a scene.
Make non-player characters' timing claims checkable against an in-game schedule, so that contradictions reward players who catch them.
when: dialogue includes claims about time or movement
why: checkable slips give players a reason to compare records

text: Give NPCs timed routines, such as shop hours, patrol routes and meetings, so players can rebuild a timeline by questioning several characters.
when: designing a mystery that depends on whereabouts
why: Schedules give players a verifiable timeline to reconstruct

text: Treat an arrival or departure that departs from a stated schedule as a deviation that opens a gap in someone's alibi.
Let an NPC's routine or repeated habit be a motive clue that the player connects to a later event.
when: Designing recurring NPC behaviour
why: Repetition makes a habit memorable and later meaningful

text: Give NPCs ordinary lines that reveal a schedule or appointment only when combined with a location or time, so the player makes the connection.
when: designing NPC dialogue that hides information

text: Use NPC routine logs to define an administration window, showing who had access to the victim or item during that window.
Let an NPC repeat a second-hand alibi so the player must verify it through another witness.
when: When designing alibi chains between NPCs
why: A second-hand alibi forces the player to find an independent source before trusting it.

text: Let non-player character schedules define alibi windows, so a player can check whether a suspect could reach the crime scene within its time frame.
Give NPCs daily routines so several bystanders observe the same person, letting the player rebuild that person's movements from their remarks.
when: when designing suspect or witness characters
why: overlapping observations form a reconstructable timeline

text: Schedule a key NPC as unavailable until a specific in-game date or condition, so a reveal is delayed in a controlled way.
Give each suspect a schedule so players can check who could have been in a given room at a given time.
when: when designing crime or heist puzzles

text: Give each NPC a schedule that another system can confirm, such as a shift log or guard roster, so players can verify alibis.
Let an NPC interview walk the player through a day in order, unlocking a timeline entry for each answer.
when: When designing NPC dialogue for an investigation.

text: Track an NPC's repeated action at fixed intervals so players can learn the schedule before acting, and make the item state a routine-minded NPC checks, such as position or count.
when: When designing NPC routines that players can exploit.
why: Visible state and fixed timing let players predict whether a swap is noticed.

text: Schedule NPC arrivals to interrupt the player's investigation at tense points, and let the newcomer's appearance hint at his role.
when: placing NPCs in a dungeon investigation

text: Tie NPC routines to in-world clocks so the player can build an alibi grid from observed times, and use a summons with a deadline to create a timeline puzzle.
when: designing NPC schedules for investigation
why: observed times let the player infer who was where

text: Give an NPC a visible fixed route, then let the route break off in one district, so players who follow the pattern find the hidden location.
Have NPC dialogue give events without exact dates or as date ranges, and let some NPCs contradict others so the player must cross-check records.
Give NPC and player routines fixed schedules, such as empty rooms at certain hours, so habitual paths become patterns players learn and plan around or exploit.
Anchor each NPC's position to a timestamped event, like a sound; give set travel times or map distance and movement speed, letting players check who could reach the scene in time.
when: Designing NPC movement for alibi checks or timing puzzles.
why: Known travel times make claimed movements testable.

text: Make NPC movements carry narrative meaning: fleeing in an unexpected direction or waiting at an odd place should signal fear or a planned meeting.
when: designing NPC routes and idle locations
why: Players read movement as evidence of intent, so odd movement prompts the next question.

text: Give NPCs routines, such as lighting a fire at a set hour, so a missed routine signals a change the player can notice.
Leave deliberate gaps in NPC schedules so an alibi can be broken by a route the player discovers.
when: when designing suspect alibis

text: Track NPC movements on a timeline so players can test whether an alibi holds: a distant guard is cleared, while a patrol that never arrives raises questions.
why: Logged positions let players compare claimed and actual locations

text: Model NPC routines such as daily cleaning or deliveries, so that each routine defines the window in which a related clue can exist.
Time an NPC's return to a schedule, such as the end of a ceremony, so the designer controls when the player is interrupted.

text: Give every actor a shared clock with fixed appointment times, so each participant knows the window in which events must occur.
when: Scheduling NPC movements or meetings

text: Infer an agent's next move from its constraints, such as waiting to see whether pursuit has stopped, and treat that inference as a hypothesis to test.

why: Constraints make some next moves more likely than others

text: Let the player infer enemy positions from voices and silhouettes behind a curtain before entering the room.

why: Cross-checking rewards players who compare sources.

text: Compare an NPC's known resources with what a crime would gain them. Hidden debts or needs can be unlocked later to revise the motive.
when: When NPCs must weigh a crime
why: Resource gaps reveal plausible motives

text: NPCs with hidden plans reveal them only through observable actions, so players discover the scheme by watching behaviour.
1) Identify what the opponent can observe. 2) Infer the decision rules they likely use, not your own. 3) Predict their next choice. 4) Adjust for whether they anticipate your response.

why: Predictions must match the actual intellect of the opponent.

text: 1) Start from the adversary's known habits and traits. 2) Judge how capable the adversary is of planning. 3) Work out what the adversary must foresee for the plan to work. 4) Lay out options and test each outcome. 5) Admit unknown moves may remain.

text: Let an NPC hold secrets or hidden intent the player cannot see, flag its interactions, and let the player's inference diverge from the NPC's motive to create tension.

text: Give an NPC's question an innocent-looking reason while a hidden flag stores its real purpose, so players can later find the mismatch.
Give an accused NPC a dialogue option that offers proof or lets the player drop the question, so the player can test the NPC's reaction.

why: Testable reactions let the player discover whether the accusation holds

text: Set NPC testimony reliability from the speaker's location, awareness, grudges and relationship to the listener, so identical statements carry different weight.

text: An uncertain NPC accepts the first plausible item the player names, so quest logic should expect and handle that acceptance.

why: Uncertainty makes plausible suggestions easy to adopt

text: Pause between questions so the NPC's pressure builds before the player returns with a new question.

text: Have an NPC ask the player a test question before answering, so the player's own knowledge decides what the NPC reveals.

text: Test a witness with an itemized account of specific features, since a long inventory shows attention but does not establish accuracy of inference.

text: An unexpected question can change an NPC's behavior, such as making it flee or draw a weapon, as an immediate response.

text: Let players route a question through another NPC, with a chance that the answer returns changed.

when: An NPC's testimony is known to be incomplete due to a condition.

text: A disguised NPC voice can serve as a clue, and a claimed family tie can be disproved by a checkable fact.
when: Designing clues around impersonation.

text: A claimed fact that is hard to verify directly, such as a detail visible only to a close acquaintance, limits how strong a test of the witness can be.
when: Checking a witness's claim about a feature that few people can confirm.

text: In an interrogation system, let the player find a suspect's secret or second motive and use it as a lever to force a confession or a choice.

text: Give each NPC witness a stated interest and a hidden stake, so the player must weigh their testimony rather than accept it at face value.

text: Keep an NPC's retracted memory in its state so it can be resurfaced later in the conversation.

why: testimony then responds to player progress

text: Attach a partial clue, such as a place name or family detail, to each refusal so the player still makes progress.

text: Witnesses who withhold information out of social pressure can require persuasion or a different question to reveal it.
when: Designing interrogation or dialogue for reluctant witnesses.
why: Changing the approach matches the obstacle that silence represents.

text: An NPC witness system can store each witness's description with one differing feature and a confidence value, so the player must reconcile conflicting accounts.
when: Designing witness memory in an investigation game.
why: Stored confidence and distinguishing features create reconcilable conflicts for the player.

text: An NPC testimony system lets players verify claims through independent sources; NPC reputation can set how much weight a claim carries.
when: When designing dialogue-based investigation in a game.
why: Weighted, verifiable testimony rewards players for cross-checking rather than accepting claims.

text: A message carried by a companion the target trusts lowers the target's guard.
Give informant and witness NPCs a reliability rating from reputation and sources; show whether info is a transcript or live report; players verify checkable details by asking other NPCs.
when: Designing informant or witness NPCs whose information the player must weigh.
why: Explicit credibility lets players judge reliability, and cross-checking with other characters shows which claims to trust.

text: Model a gatekeeper NPC whose report decides admission as a flag set by the player's appearance, disguise or reputation.
when: Implementing an NPC that admits or refuses based on how the player looks.
why: A flag makes the admission rule explicit and lets appearance systems feed into access.

text: Use a lure the subject responds to strongly; a preferred food is a stronger lure than a common treat for a creature already accustomed to it.
when: A trained animal or creature must be induced to perform a behavior.
why: Stronger motivators produce more reliable responses.

text: Give each NPC a discretion value, so some relay the player's questions to others while others keep quiet.
when: Designing NPC information flow.
why: Varied discretion makes information leakage a meaningful system.

text: A sleeping or unconscious NPC can still trigger dialogue flags when a player speaks nearby, creating stealth and eavesdropping choices.
when: When designing NPCs who may be unaware of player speech
why: Hidden awareness rewards players who speak carefully.

text: Have a decoy keep the target occupied with a plausible small request, buying time for responders to arrive.
when: A target must be held in place while others close in

text: A staged lure works only if the victim accepts the bait, so a cautious victim who does not help breaks the trap.
when: when designing an ambush or trap that depends on player action
why: The trap's success depends on the target's cooperation, so caution defeats it.

text: Alibi networks modelled as NPC witnesses who confirm one another let the player probe for the weak link.
when: Designing witness interactions where alibis are mutually supporting.
why: Interlocking confirmations create a structure whose single weak point can be found by questioning.

text: In a lineup with decoys, a witness picks the true culprit consistently only when the culprit is actually present.
when: Designing a lineup mechanic in a game.
why: Consistent selection of one person signals genuine recognition, while random choice signals none.

text: A decoy prop, such as a lit silhouette or statue, can project a character's presence, so an enemy's targeting is drawn to the decoy rather than the player.
A hostage threat fails if the opponent does not value the captives, and a nervous opponent may act on fear, so commands can provoke the movement they aim to prevent.
when: Using hostages or threats to control an opponent.
why: Hostage logic assumes the opponent cares about the captives, and fear can trigger action.

text: 1) Plant a false report where the target will hear it. 2) Watch who reacts with fear beyond their usual calm. 3) When the frightened party asks for help, offer a route to the hidden person. 4) Require the recognition signal before any handover.
when: A suspect hides a second person reachable through a go-between.
why: Fear shows the report landed, and the signal confirms the contact.

text: A gatekeeper NPC who opens doors only on a signal acts as a controlled access system, and the signal should be a learnable clue.
when: Designing access controlled by NPC behaviour.
why: A learnable signal turns access into a puzzle rather than an arbitrary block.

text: A quest-giver NPC can request an action with a stated reason that differs from the real one, with the true reason revealed after a later discovery.
when: Designing a quest whose true purpose is hidden.
why: A discovered later fact can reframe the request and reward the player's attention.

text: Tie an enemy's compliance to captives or hostages, so that any movement by the enemy puts a captive at risk.
when: Designing a standoff where the player can compel an enemy's behaviour.
why: A credible threat against valued captives can restrain an opponent.

text: Create a rival NPC that mirrors the player's visible equipment or class and appears in different hub areas, revealing its identity only after repeated encounters.
when: when designing a mirror rival in an open game world
why: matching visible traits makes the rival read as a double

text: Give NPC testimony emotional, social, or stake-based bias tags that are perceptible, so the player can discount a witness's claims accordingly.
when: Designing NPC testimony in games with contested facts, or NPCs asked about others.
why: Stake and bias affect how far a witness can be relied on, and rewarding careful players who check biased claims

text: Witnesses open up more readily when the interviewer shares history or trade with them, such as recalling a shared past moment or favour, or speaking their own trade talk.
when: interviewing a reluctant witness or needing witnesses to open up
why: Shared history signals good faith; shared occupation makes the investigator seem an insider

text: A witness who begins to name someone and stops is holding something back, and a prompt that presses for the name often ends the disclosure.
when: A witness trails off mid-sentence on a sensitive point.
why: Fear or distress makes the witness retreat when pushed.

text: A listener accepts a witness's account according to their relationship with the witness, not only its content, and a trusted liar can plant a false story the listener defends.
when: a statement comes from a family member, patron or close ally
why: Affection and what the listener needs to believe shape what they accept.

text: Use a trusted agent to handle the investigator's daily needs and watch from a distance, so the investigator can stay unseen.
when: the investigator must remain hidden while working
why: Delegated support keeps the investigator's presence secret.

text: A quarrel settled by a figure trusted by all sides tends to leave no new enemies.
when: choosing who should judge a local dispute
why: Universal trust makes the ruling acceptable to every party.

text: Gate NPC information behind trades, and give a reaction cue such as a pause or changed line when a hidden fact is near.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that withholds knowledge.
why: Players can detect the cue and learn that a fact exists, making the trade meaningful.

text: Model NPC reluctance as a trust value that rises with patience, bribes, or proof of authority and falls with pressure, so raising trust unlocks more disclosure.
why: Witnesses reveal more to those they trust

text: Affection or trust values can bias how NPCs describe or perceive a suspect, producing biased testimony the player must weigh rather than accept.
why: A biased observer yields an interesting view of events that the player must weigh

text: An NPC can refuse to disclose information until a trust threshold or condition is met, and a contradiction between two NPCs can unlock a new line of questioning.
when: When designing NPC dialogue with restricted information.
why: Gated disclosure forces the player to earn trust or find a contradiction before progressing.

text: A companion NPC's attachment to a suspect can bias what it reports, so the player must cross-check that companion's testimony against other sources.
when: Companion characters know or favour a suspect
why: Attachment colours what the companion notices and says

text: A flustered NPC gives scrambled answers until calmed by an item or dialogue option, after which its account becomes coherent.
when: in an interview mechanic

text: When a player uses knowledge of an NPC's secret as leverage, the NPC's reaction reveals whether the accusation is true.
when: when an NPC hides information the player can threaten to expose
why: Reactions under pressure expose whether the accusation is true

text: A suggestion from someone who holds authority in the setting is accepted more readily, so the same approach varies with the setting.
when: when a character's influence depends on their role in the scene
why: Authority lowers the listener's resistance to the suggestion

text: A servant NPC reveals information only when it believes the information matters, so a specific question can change its answer.
A suspicious stranger who becomes charming can dissolve the observers' suspicion, and they settle on a flattering explanation.
when: An observer first suspects intoxication or wrongdoing.
why: Charm changes how the observer interprets the same behavior.

text: Companion reactions to a staged act show whether the performance works, giving players feedback on the deception.
when: A companion witnesses a staged act
why: Their response reveals whether observers believe it.

text: An NPC with a composure value can reveal hidden information when surprise or accusation lowers that value; once the player has used the surprise, the NPC should become guarded.
when: Designing NPC reactions to player pressure
why: Lowered composure weakens resistance, and repeated tactics are anticipated

text: A trusted observer or intermediary may withhold key testimony or leave out parts that do not suit their purpose, so their account carries its own filter.
when: A helper seems an outside observer or a trusted intermediary relays the story.

text: A companion may be deceived too, so the performer must explain the act or rely on the companion's cooperation.
when: Using a staged act with a companion present
why: An uninformed companion may react in ways that expose the performance.

text: Treat a clearance claimed by a character as an assertion until its evidence is shown, since the claim may rest on the speaker's own belief.
when: a character reports a suspect was cleared
why: an unshown basis cannot be checked

text: When a trusted person dismisses a witness's fears, the witness can seem unreliable, and the investigator may wrongly discount a genuine account.
why: Isolation from help makes a witness's account easy to dismiss.

text: A red herring can seem true when an official investigation has already endorsed it, leading investigators to accept it without testing.
when: An official conclusion rests on a suspicious clue
why: Authority lends credibility, which reduces the scrutiny the clue receives.

text: Acting on an unverified claim creates commitments that are hard to reverse.
Accepting a witness's description of appearance without considering deliberate disguise can miss the culprit.
Believing a close relative on demeanour alone can miss a motive to shield them.
A witness who trades facts for requests for trust, and calls demands for facts unfair, is likely evading the question.
when: when an interviewer presses for specifics
why: Shifting to trust avoids checkable claims.

text: 1) Record each fact an NPC volunteers. 2) Note what the NPC gains if the player acts on it. 3) Let the player later see whether the offer served the NPC's goals.
when: When an NPC gives unrequested information.

text: Make NPCs who fear informers withhold information from strangers, so the player must earn trust before receiving testimony.
Track trust earned in earlier scenes and use it to change how an official responds to later requests.
Gate a character's secret behind trust or sympathy checks, so a gentle approach reveals more than an aggressive one.
Give a trusted NPC a personal loss that can flip their stance, and write dialogue variants showing either genuine change or rationalisation of the old belief.
when: A reveal depends on an insider changing sides.

text: Let an NPC who refuses to talk reveal information through a second channel, such as a bribe trail or stated motive, rather than repeated dialogue.
when: designing NPCs who withhold information

text: Track an interrogated NPC's composure and surface tells, such as a pause, a change of tone or an unforced gesture, for the player to read.
when: building an interrogation mini-game

text: Record the topics an NPC avoids and the third party each avoided topic involves, so the game can reveal the connection when the player asks the right follow-up.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that hides information.
why: Avoided topics then carry a traceable link that rewards questioning.

text: A trusted local introducer opens doors to a reluctant witness, but the introduction also colours what the witness will say.
when: When access to a witness depends on a local contact

text: A person lying on a high limb above a path can watch those passing below.
why: Height gives a view down onto the path.

text: A hidden activity may be visible from only one position, so identify the single observation point that reveals it.
when: The activity happens at a known location.
why: Only one view may expose it.

text: An intruder's choice of a spot with a view of an exit reveals escape planning.
Use a vantage point with a clear view to tell the player how many witnesses could have seen an event.
when: When designing a scene where a crowd or audience matters to the story.
why: Visibility sets a plausible limit on witnesses, which makes the scene believable.

text: Build guard patrols and NPC schedules so some sightings overlap and others leave a short, learnable blind spot.
when: Designing NPC movement that the player must read and exploit
why: Predictable short gaps reward observation without making stealth arbitrary

text: Repeated observation of a room across in-game days can reveal a patrol or signal pattern a single visit would miss.
when: Designing covert observation mechanics for players.
why: Patterns emerge only from repetition over time.

text: A patrol system that logs a character's last sighting and marks the exit as unconfirmed leads the player to search for hidden routes or sound cues.
when: A character is seen entering an area but its departure is not observed.
why: The unconfirmed exit creates doubt about whether the character is still present.

text: Model patrol routes and NPC schedules so players can reconstruct where a guard was at a given time.
A patrol that handles routine infractions and also raises alarms for fire or attack lets one guard system drive both stealth and urgent events.
A rotating patrol assigns two trusted members to each day's duty, so a community observes its own people through scheduled, named watch shifts.
when: Setting needs a community that watches itself through formal, recurring duties.

text: Guard patrols leave gaps between rounds, and a culprit can use a gap to act unseen.
1) Assign two patrollers per day. 2) Patrol from a fixed start point. 3) Record absent or loitering members. 4) Report names to authority. 5) Notify the next patrol before ending the shift.
when: Designing a recurring patrol that must observe and report.
why: Fixed rounds and explicit handoffs keep coverage continuous and accountable.

text: Give enemies a habitual route, such as avoiding the direct corridor and using a service passage, so players can learn the pattern and exploit it.
when: designing patrols or thieves

text: Give a patrolling or stalking NPC a line of sight that the player can exploit by standing in darkness and watching from an angle.
Let patrol groups split into direct-trail and flanking roles so that a player's decoy produces a real response from the pursuit.
when: designing search or patrol behaviour
why: split roles make a decoy change the pursuit's movement

text: Track unaccounted gaps in a character's route, since those gaps are where a hidden action could occur.
when: Reconstructing a route or movement history.
why: Unobserved time is where an unseen act can take place.

text: Regular patrol schedules let players form testable timing predictions the game can confirm, while varying timing across visits makes repeated observation pay off on different days.
when: Designing guard or NPC routes that a player may watch and learn.
why: Regularity lets players reason and experiment; variation prevents a single pattern from solving the puzzle.

text: Fixed patrol start points make timing predictable so players can avoid the watch, but they also let players learn and exploit the pattern when paired with named pairs and handoff rules.
when: Designing guards meant to be read and outwitted.

text: Assuming the only threat lies ahead, or splitting the party or carrying a single light, leaves the rear uncovered to ambush.
why: an opponent can approach from behind while attention faces forward

text: A strong foreign odour can pull a tracking animal onto a false trail that looks like the real one.
when: A competing or contaminating source lies near the trail
why: Trackers follow the strongest nearby scent

text: Scent carried on banknotes can link cash to the person who concealed it in their clothing.
when: cash has been carried on a suspect's body

text: If a scented object would have scented anyone who handled it, a person without scent suggests a tool was used to hold it.
Let NPCs notice traces the player leaves, such as moved objects or trampled plants, so the world visibly reacts to the player.
why: responsive worlds make player actions feel consequential

text: Before reading a contaminant as deliberate misdirection, check whether it is common in the area, since ordinary substances can explain a misleading scent.
when: A strange scent appears near a trail
why: Common substances often have innocent sources

text: Use a scent marker and a trained tracker when the target is alert and its route cannot be followed openly.
when: the target is alert to followers and the route is hidden
why: sight-based tailing fails

text: Confirm each trail sign with repeated markers at intervals rather than relying on a single sign.
when: when tracking a target through an environment
why: Repetition distinguishes a real path from a chance mark

text: A scent or residue left by a target can serve as a tracking signal that an NPC follows or matches to a suspect.
A scent on a moving vehicle lets a tracker follow its real route, including detours, when visual tailing fails.

1) Count the candidates who could carry the trace. 2) Calibrate by smelling the found trace and your own hands; clean hands and use clean materials. 3) Sample each suspect in turn with a question at close range. 4) Compare scents, ruling out near-matches. 5) Confirm each hit with a second trace.
when: A found object carries a distinctive personal odor that can be sampled directly from each suspect.
why: Calibration, contamination removal and repeated sampling separate true matches from look-alikes.

text: 1) List every object carrying the odour. 2) Identify which object others touched or were wrapped in. 3) The object that transferred scent to the others is the likely source.
when: deciding which object carried an odour

text: 1) Establish a distinct marker the target carries or leaves. 2) Confirm the marker against a comparison sample. 3) Judge whether it will persist given the trail's age and conditions. 4) Follow the strongest signal and adjust when it weakens.
when: A tracker must follow a suspect along a path
why: A known marker gives the tracker a signal to follow reliably

text: Give the player a scent item to follow an NPC, and route the trail through decoy paths.
A stealth system can let the player mask their own scent or leave a scent trail for enemies, with the trail changing as items are touched.
NPC willingness to talk can build gradually with accumulated time and player behaviour, or be gated by a single defined trigger such as a second visit or specific event.
when: Gradual build fits accumulated time and player behaviour; defined trigger fits a specific event or second visit.

text: Repeated visible captures or a scripted capture moment can lower a watcher's alertness, so it stops searching for the real method while the player works another route.
when: a sequence of plausible attempts is caught one after another, or a scripted capture occurs
why: Each catch feels like closure, so the threat seems exhausted

text: A sudden accusation can produce the same physical signs of nervousness in an innocent person as in a guilty one, such as sweating, shaking, dilated pupils and pallor.
when: Judging a suspect's reaction to an accusation.
why: Shock from an accusation triggers physiological responses regardless of guilt.

text: Under confrontation, people show anxiety tells such as coughing, shrugging, nervous laughter, fidgeting, avoiding eye contact, and claiming to be unafraid before any accusation.
when: a person is questioned about a sensitive matter
why: Anxiety and guilt both produce visible signs.

text: A visible alarm or sudden relief at a specific question suggests the question has struck a real hidden fact.
when: When a witness reacts strongly to a particular topic.

text: A witness who shows alarm at an invented claim is likely hiding relevant knowledge, so a false statement can test what they actually know.
when: an investigator makes a fabricated claim to a reluctant witness
why: the claim touches something the witness wants to protect, so the reaction exposes it

text: A person who has just passed a tense exchange often reveals relief or worry through small follow-up questions, such as asking whether anyone has called.
when: after a stressful meeting ends
why: anxiety leaks through trivial questions

text: A person who suspects they are being watched is tormented by the suspicion, whatever they actually do.
when: someone believes they are under observation
why: the suspicion itself causes distress

text: Repeatedly bringing a character to the edge of disclosure and then interrupting builds anticipation, and sustained pressure keeps the audience waiting.
when: the audience should expect a disclosure
why: each near-answer keeps the unanswered question active

text: Under sudden alarm, a person rushes to secure what they value most, which can reveal where a hidden object is kept.
when: a sudden alarm occurs and the target's valued object is hidden
why: under alarm, attachment drives the first action

text: A person hiding in a concealed space may leave it when a convincing alarm sounds, because they lack the nerve to stay still.
when: An occupant of a hidden space is threatened by an apparent emergency
why: Fear of danger overrides the instinct to stay hidden

text: Waiting with repeated checks of a visible timer builds tension toward a known hour, and a single event at the end releases that tension.
when: A player must wait for a scheduled moment
why: Anticipation grows as the expected time approaches

text: Alarm before composure shows as a start, a fidgeting of hands, or a glance away, and a composed recovery can hide a real reaction.
when: A suspect hears a fact they may have reason to fear
why: Involuntary reactions precede deliberate control, so they appear first.

text: An anxious person doubts that their own inspection of evidence is reliable, so self-checks feel untrustworthy.
when: Checking items under fear
why: Fear degrades confidence in observations

text: A target who notices a follower may turn back, use side roads, or detour to shake the pursuit.
when: the target suspects being followed
why: alerted targets actively test for tails

text: A sudden exodus of staff carrying luggage, followed by a site being locked up, signals a planned closure and an imminent move.
when: watching a site for a coming departure
why: Hurried packing and locking up suggest the occupants are leaving for good.

text: Scripted events on fixed in-world clocks let the player verify when an NPC was where.
when: Designing timed events the player can check.
why: Fixed clocks give players a shared reference.

text: Use a concealed-reveal clue only when the required condition is one players can reasonably reproduce.
A reflective surface can give players a fair, visible route to observe a hidden room or target.
when: Designing a concealed space players must find.

text: Script a collapsing beam or falling trap to look accidental, while giving players clues that distinguish it from a deliberate act.
A scripted scene can use a dramatic non-player event to draw the player's attention while an item changes hands, and the event should match established traits.
why: a mismatched event reads as a designer's cheat

text: A searcher stops only for an unexpected find and otherwise keeps working through the checklist.
Reverse a question's form to test an NPC: a scripted responder gives the same answer regardless of wording, while a responsive character answers the new form.
Log timestamps when guards are alerted. A short gap between an escape and the guard reaction suggests the alert came from someone inside the fortress.
when: Designing a fortress with alert systems the player can observe
why: Timing reveals the alert's source and lets players infer insider knowledge

text: Frame scripted alarms as routine patrols, so a player who notices them draws the wrong conclusion about what is happening.
A timed accusation mission has an NPC promise to name a culprit at a set in-game hour, with the player required to protect and follow her.
when: Designing a suspenseful reveal mechanic.
why: A fixed deadline creates tension and gives the player a clear timeline.

text: A scripted signal, timer or routine such as a guard's leave or a shop's closing time can remove an NPC, opening a short window the player can notice and exploit.
when: When designing scheduled NPC absences.
why: Routine schedules change where NPCs are at a given time.

text: Torn cloth or dropped items can serve as clues that alert patrols and send them back to search an area.
when: A traced item is found by searchers

text: An object left disturbed in a stealth search can alert the occupant, so the state of each searched object must be tracked.
when: an occupant may return during a search
why: Visible changes give the occupant a reason to become suspicious.

text: Moving a body can be designed to change when a patrol discovers it.
when: When a scene can be reset by player action.
why: Discovery timing then becomes a consequence of the player's choice.

text: Running parallel events such as guard patrols, escapes and traps on one shared simulated timeline lets players perceive them as happening together, raising tension.
when: Several world events occur concurrently
why: Shared time makes simultaneity legible

text: A calm, orderly setting placed against a violent event heightens the sense of wrongness and draws attention beneath appearances.
when: When staging a dramatic reveal or investigation hook.
why: Contrast makes the violence feel more out of place and more striking.

text: Holding attention on a visible object lets an attack come unseen from behind.
when: When staging an ambush
why: Attention fixed on the display leaves the attacker's approach unwatched

text: A stationary device can fire while its setter is absent, triggered by a cord linked to a panel that the victim opens.
when: when an event must occur with no one present at the trigger
why: the trigger transfers the action to the victim, removing the setter from the scene

text: A scripted interruption, such as a guard's footstep, can force a rushed AI action that leaves state behind.
when: An NPC is interrupted during a task.
why: Interrupted actions do not complete their cleanup, so traces remain.

text: A scripted reveal can trigger a special NPC line when the player mentions a secret the NPC believed was hidden.
A scene lockdown that restricts movement and handling forces the player to act before careless NPCs disturb evidence.
Sealing a room has three parts: the door handle, the window shutters and the power supply. Disabling any of them can trap occupants inside.
when: When designing a sabotage or locked-room scenario

text: A mundane physical detail that stops or changes, such as an unwound watch, can later serve as a signal that a character has died.
when: A character appears alive but is actually dead.
why: The detail was present earlier, so the player can reread it as evidence in retrospect.

text: An agitated listener reads ordinary noise as significant, and expectation can shape what they think they hear.
A staged alarm reveals the hiding place but also tells the target she has been betrayed, giving her a chance to react.
1) List each assumed event in an NPC's scripted plan. 2) For each, define a fallback state for when the event is cancelled. 3) Check that no fallback creates an unplanned extra dependency.
when: Generating or scripting NPC plans in a dungeon.
why: Scripted plans that assume fixed events stall or break when the assumption fails.

text: 1) Create a disturbance that draws everyone's attention away from the search area. 2) Search the target area while attention is held. 3) Return to normal before attention shifts back.
when: A search must happen while suspects or guards are present
why: Attention drawn to the disturbance leaves the search area unobserved

text: 1) Record each evasive answer and its topic. 2) Let later questions revisit that topic. 3) Open new lines of questioning when a answer contradicts a logged fact.
why: Logged evasions give the player leads to return to.

text: 1) Withdraw to a distance where the site is still observable but the watcher is unnoticed. 2) Report the observed signs to a response team. 3) Let the response team act on the report.
when: a watcher sees signs of a planned escape or closure
why: Remote observation keeps the watcher hidden while the report brings help.
