text: Use a timed or scripted interruption, such as an alarm or messenger, to escalate tension at a key moment, then hold a quiet period before the next clue appears.
why: Interruption and waiting build tension before the reveal

text: Use a scripted loud event, like a battle, cutscene, NPC performance or repeated dialogue loop, to cover an NPC's movement or a crime elsewhere; let players notice the absence.
when: Designing NPC movement or hidden events that should go unnoticed.
why: Spectacle holds attention, so other events and NPC absences pass unnoticed unless the scene makes them noticeable.

text: Schedule a visible decoy event elsewhere, such as a light failure or alarm, to pull a guard or patrol away from the true route or chokepoint, opening a stealth route.
when: Designing a stealth dungeon.

text: A silent space where a smell or sound is expected can serve as a clue pointing toward a false front or illusion.
when: when designing environmental clues

text: Tag procedural events with shared attributes such as place, person or record, and surface a connection only after the player has seen enough shared elements.
when: Generating events that should form discoverable patterns
why: Players need several overlapping elements before a link feels earned

text: Script an alarm that makes an NPC leave her post and reveal a hidden stash the player can then retrieve.
when: a stealth or heist level needs a hidden item revealed
why: a scripted reaction makes the hiding place visible to the player

text: Make a signal interruption readable: the player should be able to date the break and reason about what triggered it.
when: when designing NPC signalling
why: A break the player cannot time or interpret gives no usable clue.

text: Script hazards to trigger when their intended victims are predictably absent, so players can deduce the plan from the timing.
when: Designing traps or environmental hazards

text: Leave physical traces such as worn spots or holes where a fixture was, implying a hidden mechanism or a swapped object.
when: Designing a scene that hides a mechanism
why: Traces let players infer what is concealed without it being shown directly.

text: Split the party so one controlled character faces danger alone, while others respond only through sound and a rope or tool.
Delay a reveal until the player reaches a second location, so the level's structure carries the suspense.
Let a secret open from a physical nudge rather than only a labelled button, so discovery feels accidental but earned.
Lock doors and station guards at the moment of a murder, so the player works with a closed set of suspects.
when: Designing a murder event in a game level.
why: A fixed suspect pool makes deduction tractable and prevents the culprit from simply leaving.

text: Model a second likely NPC reaction, such as searching a room, alongside the first, so the world responds to what the player leaves behind.
Place a friendly NPC on a predictable route so that a hostile NPC's messenger or spy must approach them, revealing the enemy's plans.
when: Designing hostile NPC spy or messenger behaviour
why: A predictable target draws the enemy into view

text: Let a hidden player plan a response to a visible sign, so they decide whether to act on incomplete information.
when: designing hidden-state tension
why: a readable sign turns uncertainty into a choice

text: Script enemies to hold position until a staged drop in pressure makes them move, so their movement becomes a readable signal for the player.
Tie NPC attention to scripted events such as festivals or boss roars, so attention windows are predictable and players can time hidden actions.
when: designing NPC awareness or stealth opportunities
why: scripted peaks of attention create openings the player can read

text: Implement an NPC threat as a claim reacting to a visible item rather than a real weapon, so players weigh the claim without a verified danger.
Give an alerted NPC a visible signal, so the player receives a readable tell that they have been noticed.
Record a player's reaction to an ambiguous signal so that NPCs can respond to it later.
Require a higher evidence threshold before a town turns on an NPC, so rumour alone cannot trigger a mob.
why: Rumour spreads fast and can otherwise drive collective action without a finding.

text: Each person's movement produces a distinct vibration signature tied to body weight and gait, so walkers can be narrowed by comparing recorded traces.
when: An unseen intruder's movement is recorded and suspects differ in weight or gait.
why: Heavier or lighter bodies transmit different vibrational patterns.

text: An intruder avoids routes passing many occupied rooms and accepts a riskier entry with fewer witnesses.
when: planning an unobserved entry
why: Witness risk outweighs the difficulty of an unusual route.

text: Enemies that answer a recognisable signal, such as a whistle, let the player learn a code and use it for stealth.
when: Designing stealth encounters with signalled enemies.
why: A learnable signal turns enemy communication into a mechanic the player can exploit.

text: Use companion animals as threat detectors that react to danger before humans understand it.
when: Signaling a hidden threat to the player without explicit exposition.
why: Animal reactions give early, readable warnings.

text: Let ambient noise such as machinery or crowd chatter determine whether nearby guards hear a silenced attack.
when: Designing stealth detection in a loud environment.
why: Environmental noise makes detection depend on context rather than a fixed radius.

text: An enemy can commit to a set action inside a timed window while hidden allies position to spring a trap at the decisive moment.
when: designing a stealth or puzzle encounter
why: a committed action in a known window gives the player a clear intervention point

text: Markers covering a whole area can be read by an opponent who knows they are there, so consider what the opposing side can perceive.
when: Designing traps or markers that enemies move through.
why: An informed enemy can detect and avoid or disturb the markers.

text: 1) Move a light slowly before the subject's eyes. 2) Watch for the expected response. 3) Set the light down once the response is confirmed.
when: Checking a suspected condition or status without a full examination.
why: A simple response test can confirm a hidden state quickly.

text: 1) Fix a main direction of travel from the first signs. 2) Check the trail at regular intervals. 3) Chain signs together, reading changes in pace. 4) Act before fading signs disappear.
when: when a moving target leaves intermittent signs but cannot be seen
why: Chaining intermittent signs reconstructs a path that no single sign shows

text: Give a creature's repeatable routine a trigger that is harmless if guessed wrongly, so players can test a deduction by observing the lure-triggered response.
when: Designing a creature or NPC that lets players test a deduction through play.
why: Low-cost testing encourages experimentation, and a repeatable behavior gives a reliable test.

text: Have a monster move between two spots so players must track its position rather than assume it.
when: Designing an enemy that repositions during an encounter.
why: Tests whether the player keeps tracking or relies on assumption.

text: Give NPC witnesses attention states, such as being busy with a task, and record what each perceived from its position.
when: When designing NPC perception for investigation.
why: Attention and position determine which details an NPC can later report.

text: Still observers hiding close to NPCs overhear private talk on patrol schedules or vault codes and see actions open observers cannot access; NPCs never address them.
when: an observer hides at close range
why: Stillness keeps the observer unnoticed while proximity gives access to the conversation.

text: Wait for the opponent to act first, since their response to interference reveals their aims.
Treat light sources as a gameplay resource, since the carrier of the only light is at a disadvantage.
Place a stealth observer in a hiding spot near an NPC event, with a timed sound cue setting the window for action.
when: When designing a stealth scene in a level.
why: The player watches and times their move from the cue.

text: A stealth system can record footstep vibrations by weight class so the player can match an intruder to a suspect, and include control recordings so normal activity is learnable.
when: Designing stealth detection and tracking puzzles.
why: Players learn what normal activity looks like only with a baseline.

text: Guards or townsfolk can feign ignorance of the player while tracking movement, and the player can detect them through indirect routes and sudden idleness.
when: Designing NPC stealth or surveillance behaviour

text: Games with many varied moves let lapses of attention decide outcomes, while games with few simple moves let analytical skill decide them.
A decoy that moves on a timer can draw an enemy into an ambush while the player watches from hiding and reads patrol patterns.
when: a stealth level with enemy patrols

text: An NPC who spots a tail and warns others escalates the encounter and draws further reactions from the group.
In stealth levels, guards who fail to react to a disturbance show they were out of earshot, which makes silence meaningful.
Misdirection depends on watchers accepting the feigned state; a check that inspects the person directly exposes the deception.
when: Designing AI guards that can observe a target's state.
why: Direct inspection reveals the mismatch between the claimed and actual state.

text: A usable window can be only minutes long, which leaves almost no margin for an extra actor or delay.
when: planning a multi-step action against a routine
why: short windows fail when any step runs late

text: Losing sight of the target at a crossroads or in gardens can force a return to slower foot-tracking.
why: Branching routes and obstacles break line of sight.

text: A hidden observer's safety depends on the target looking away, so a single turn of the head can expose them.
when: Designing a stealth observation.
why: Detection depends on the target's attention, not only on the observer's cover.

text: 1) Give one NPC scripted small talk that keeps the player in place. 2) Start a timer. 3) Let a second NPC reach the unguarded container. 4) Log whether doors and containers stayed open during the hold.
when: in a stealth or heist room
why: The player can later reconstruct the window and see what was exposed.

text: Let players create noise, such as a dropped object or a shouted argument, to draw guards away from an action.
when: designing a stealth or distraction mechanic
why: noise pulls guard attention to a chosen spot

text: Use lighting, distance and view duration as explicit mechanics that determine whether the player can recognise someone in a stealth scene.
when: Designing recognition checks in stealth or observation gameplay.
why: Making these conditions explicit lets players understand why a recognition succeeds or fails and reason about it.

text: Reward the player for observing sight lines and sound before committing, and present a clear order of rooms to check.
when: Designing a stealth or investigation level.
why: Clear structure makes observation useful and keeps the player informed before risk.

text: A stealth mission can let players take on a role or disguise to gain access to a restricted area.
when: Designing access restrictions in a stealth scenario
why: A believable role offers an alternative to forced entry

text: In stealth, let doors or curtains change state between checks, so players peeking through a gap see only a cone and their reports conflict.
when: Designing stealth areas with partial sightlines.

text: Let the player eavesdrop, intercept messages and tail an NPC, with the NPC able to notice and evade the player.
when: stealth system design

text: Let pursuing NPCs appear repeatedly so the player can notice a tail, and offer a cheap confirmation test so tailing feels deducible.
when: Designing stealth pursuit systems
why: Deducible pursuit feels fair, while repeated sightings reward attentive play.

text: On high ground, stay low until the target has crossed the crest, since a target above a follower can see down over cover.
when: The route rises and the follower is near a hedge or ridge.
why: Elevation gives the target a view over cover.

text: A large visible force deters the target from moving; a small hidden watch lets it act and be caught, trading containment for surprise.
when: when deciding how to confront a mobile target
why: A visible presence is noticed, so the target may never leave its hiding place

text: An alert target quickly notices a follower whose movement is unnatural, such as zigzagging, sideways moves near walls, answering while walking away, or staying in one place.
when: a target is alert to being followed, or observers pretend not to notice a player
why: unnatural movement draws attention

text: Restricting outside access to a witness, or keeping the secret holder busy and never alone, isolates testimony, so no confession or independent check can occur.
when: a single authority controls access to a witness or account
why: Without outside contact, no one can test or contradict the account.

text: Watchers kept on a week of nights grow worn out and their motivation fades; some nearly quit while others persist out of stubbornness.
when: a long stakeout with no result
why: fatigue accumulates over repeated nights

text: A target who suspects or discovers observation alters habits or acts for the watcher, so covert watchers are unsafe and lose value once noticed, and quiet records may mislead.
when: when a target suspects or discovers observation
why: Awareness of surveillance alters habits, and the suspect adjusts to the observer.

text: Uncertainty about being observed produces a constant sense of being followed, so a person sees danger everywhere and tension stays high, even without any identifiable watcher.
when: when someone senses surveillance without proof or suspect, or a suspect is kept waiting with no active questioning
why: Feeling threatened does not require an identified source; uncertainty about being observed produces the feeling of surveillance.

text: A motionless figure seen in dim light is ambiguous; the observer cannot tell calm from sleep or waiting, so stillness itself breeds dread.
when: A figure is visible but poorly lit.
why: Uncertainty about intent fills the gap with fear.

text: A character who controls the delivery point can read incoming letters first and conceal the tampering, so the recipient never learns the message was seen.
when: When a character positioned at the door or mail basket receives correspondence meant for another.
why: Physical control of the delivery point gives first access to messages and leaves no visible trace.

text: A target who has already seen a stranger may form a poor first impression and watch that stranger closely, so the approacher is also being investigated.
when: the target has had an earlier encounter with the approacher
why: a spoiled first impression persists and makes the target suspicious

text: A secret faction known only through its effects seems all-powerful, because its methods stay hidden and the mind fills the gap.
A watched party who notices surveillance often redirects attention, dismissing the observer or closing off the view rather than confronting the watcher openly.
when: a person realises they are being observed

text: Those who defend a contested site bear repeated intrusions, which can turn neighbors into enemies.
when: a site is claimed by more than one party
why: defending it puts the occupants in ongoing conflict

text: An observer infers an unseen occupant from physical traces such as a worn seat or a disturbed chair.
when: Examining a room after an event.
why: Traces imply the presence of someone who is not visible.

text: Approaching a person from hiding frightens them, while approaching along a route they can see lowers that risk.
when: when confronting a subject from a concealed position
why: A sudden appearance causes alarm; a visible approach gives warning.

text: People trying to go unseen keep close to walls and stay out of the sightlines of windows.
when: moving past watched windows or doorways
why: Windows reveal movement along open lines.

text: Watched people and bystanders may notice a watcher through small traces such as a face at a curtain, a repeated figure or a lingering stare.
when: a watcher is posted at a fixed point
why: fixed watchers leave repeated, visible traces

text: A searcher who is confident an object is absent tends not to recheck, so an object hidden in a previously searched place can go unnoticed.
when: A person has already searched a container or space
why: Confident denial stops further checking

text: A target who believes a rival is dying may visit to gloat, revealing intent in person.
when: The target has a motive to see the victim and a vindictive or vain character
why: Vanity and vindictiveness make the target want to witness and confirm the outcome

text: A person standing and gazing into shop windows looks occupied rather than loitering, so a stationary watcher draws less notice.
when: Waiting on a public street with a subject in view.
why: Browsing gives a plausible reason to stay in place.

text: When trapped occupants smell burning or see smoke, urgency rises and they force a breakout rather than wait for rescue.
when: Occupants are trapped in a room with smoke present
why: Danger raises urgency

text: People stop watching someone they find laughable, so a trivial or ridiculous persona can protect an investigator from scrutiny.
when: An investigator must move among people who would stop talking if they knew who he was.
why: A ridiculous appearance lowers others' attention and suspicion.

text: Observers who see a condition as beyond ordinary human capacity tend to accept supernatural explanations for it, even without independent evidence.
when: when a bodily or behavioural feat looks impossible to the observers
why: A perceived impossibility makes a natural explanation seem unlikely.

text: A watcher's attention keeps returning to particular visible cues, such as clothing, which reveals how the watcher picks targets.
when: Observing a watcher in a crowd

text: When people abandon ordinary business to watch a stranger, and resume it once he leaves, the routine itself is a sign of surveillance.
when: NPCs stop routine activity when the player is nearby
why: Idle gathering that dissolves on departure signals watching

text: Silence from a busy watcher is weak evidence: an arrival matters only if the witness was placed to notice it, and a missed route is not proof none exists.
when: when judging an unseen arrival or using guard or sentry reports to rule out entries
why: Silence only means something when the witness could have seen; observers have blind spots.

text: A suspect's eager consent to a test and a non-matching result only exclude the suspect from that physical evidence, not from the crime itself.
when: When interpreting a suspect's cooperation and a negative forensic comparison.
why: Cooperation and non-match address one piece of evidence, not overall guilt.

text: A back route that staff do not watch can explain how someone left a building unseen during a gap in the timeline.
An action performed where no one can see it leaves no witness, so only the actor knows its outcome until someone notices the result.
Watch the suspect rather than the object or crowd everyone else watches, since the audience is distracted and the hider's reaction shows what others miss.
when: when observing a reaction in a group, or a suspect reacts to an arrival or event
why: the crowd's attention is fixed elsewhere; audience attention drifts

text: Signal a hidden participant or overlooked detail before the reveal; otherwise a late reversal feels arbitrary, and unease about a missed detail builds suspense.
when: a reversal depends on a hidden participant, or a mystery approaches its reveal
why: An audience that saw a trace accepts the reversal, and a sense of a missed detail pulls attention toward the answer.

text: When an object is probably carried on a person, watch for the exchange instead of demanding it, since a demand invites denial or destruction.
when: when the holder could deny or hide the object

text: A character who watches a sleeping NPC or a sealed door can signal danger before any battle starts.
A witness who watches one fixed spot for hours can bracket long periods of a suspect's absence and presence.
Setting a small controlled test and watching the reaction reveals more than asking directly, because the response shows what the person knows.
when: a suspect will not answer directly
why: reactions expose knowledge that statements conceal

text: Leaving a suspect unpressured while watching their reactions can reveal a hidden party they expect to reach.
when: A suspect is a likely channel to someone behind the scheme

text: A clue that disappears and returns after the room empties suggests someone watching that room who knows its routine. The watcher's identity can remain unknown.
when: A clue is moved only during quiet periods
why: A watcher who waits for an empty room avoids being seen

text: Detect watchers through small sounds such as a rustle or creak, then keep acting unaware while adjusting the plan.
Check the vantage points a watcher would choose, such as a lobby view of the elevators, when looking for a follower.
A watcher's report lets their employer prepare for the expected location before the observer arrives there.
why: reports pass knowledge to whoever gave the order

text: A visible watcher turns an ordinary departure into a moment of danger and reminds the audience that the antagonist is still active.
In a game, delivery systems delayed by watched routes make players reason about who observed whom and when.
when: messages travel through surveilled routes
why: observation limits what senders can send unnoticed

text: Observers placed near a hiding place make retrieval dangerous, discouraging a culprit from returning to recover the evidence.
Hidden listeners can be made detectable through noise and changed NPC behaviour, creating suspense around what is overheard.
when: Designing a scene where a character may be eavesdropping.
why: Signs of a listener let the player sense danger without seeing the listener.

text: A guard NPC can be set to surveil a suspect without alerting him, and questioning can be unlocked only when the suspect's state allows it.
when: Designing stealth or investigation encounters around a suspect.

text: A single-entrance area can be contained by posting a watcher at each route and having each record passers-by, which narrows the suspect pool and makes the timeline checkable.
when: suspect pool is small and the area has few entrances
why: Each watcher's log constrains who could have been where, so the reports together fix the order of entries.

text: Npcs that track a player's movements turn each visible action into a possible risk, so stealthy inspection costs more than an unobserved one.
when: when a player inspects a site under watch
why: watchers notice who is looking at what and report it

text: A hidden recording device that captures NPC conversation can turn private talk into an actionable location clue for the player.
when: Designing an information-gathering trap in a mission.
why: Overheard NPC speech gives the player a concrete target to act on.

text: A watcher absorbed in duties such as running equipment or answering calls, or in a loud performance, loses track of who is absent and for how long, leaving gaps.
when: a witness was busy with a task during the alleged period, or a loud performance coincides with another's absence
why: Divided attention leaves gaps an alibi-holder could use; attention is captured by the visible performance.

text: Inferences from a figure's stillness rest on the observer's theory of that person and are often wrong.
Dropping a recurring figure without any resolution leaves the audience a loose thread that can feel unfinished.
Watching a family home can alienate the household and drive the sought person away.
A visible observer or badly timed test disturbs the encounter and spoils the identity check.
when: Setting up a staged identity test
why: The subject reacts to the watcher or misses the planned moment

text: A companion may never be fully identified, so the player must accept partial results from a tail.
A delay before a search gives time to remove or add items, so evidence found later in an unsecured space proves less.
Any change to a body or prop can be noticed later, so even careful handling can reveal that someone interfered with the scene.
when: When examining evidence before the official inquiry.
why: Investigators compare the scene against what they recorded earlier.

text: A person who watches a room is not necessarily the one who committed the crime. Keep surveillance and guilt as separate conclusions.
when: Inferring a suspect from observation alone

text: A watch lapses when the guard favors a particular person; keep watchers impartial and instructed not to relax.
Watching an object while ignoring the people who can reach it or summon help leaves gaps in the watch.
A claim that a power has vanished, never demonstrated, cannot be tested and should not count as evidence.
Long, quiet waiting dulls attention, so a watch must stay alert for the moment that matters.
when: Designing a stakeout or long waiting sequence.
why: Extended monotony reduces the player's readiness at the critical moment.

text: Unconfirmed sightings stack into a theory when separate reports are merged, so observed facts must be kept apart from inference.
when: Multiple weak reports point at the same suspect
why: Merging unconfirmed reports makes an assumption look like evidence

text: An observer with limited view may miss or misidentify a watcher, since seeing the watched area requires a particular angle.
Watchers can be disabled before a watch begins, so the plan must not depend on every observer being active.
why: an incapacitated observer leaves a gap in coverage

text: Watchers working the same ground can spot each other, so an independent route risks detection by an unseen patrol.
Leaving a door shut or other traces visible can alert a watcher, so control what is visibly left behind.
Warning a watched target ends the surveillance before it yields any information, so observation of NPCs must stay hidden.
when: Player tailing of NPCs

text: 1) Release a detained suspect under watch. 2) Wait for the suspect to contact associates or recover resources. 3) Move in with a prepared warrant at the decisive step.
when: A suspect has a hidden group, the investigation has stalled, and the expected payoff justifies the risk.
why: A suspect lacking money, housing or contacts will eventually act, creating observable signals.

text: 1) Search the hair, beard and mouth for hidden glass or notes. 2) Recognise these as the usual means of cutting bars or passing messages.
when: A prisoner is searched on booking.
why: These are common hiding places for escape tools and messages.

text: 1) Stop suddenly in a quiet place and look back. 2) Double back past suspected watchers. 3) Note which one moves away and which stays. 4) Memorise the face of anyone waiting nearby.
when: Suspecting being followed in a city
why: Sudden movement exposes pursuers who must react

text: 1) Start from the last confirmed sighting. 2) Check each standard source in a fixed order, such as ticket offices, staff, inns and official posts. 3) Record every negative result as carefully as positive ones. 4) Stop when the list is exhausted and state the matter is unresolved.
when: A trail has a clear starting point and a fixed set of sources.
why: A fixed checklist with recorded dead ends prevents premature conclusions and shows what has been ruled out.

text: 1) Let the suspect believe he is leading the investigators. 2) Watch his route from outside vantage points. 3) Give him a reason to enter, such as a low perceived risk. 4) Close in once he is committed.
when: A suspect is expected to act on a plan and can be observed doing so.
why: Letting the suspect lead keeps him unaware of being followed while his moves can be tracked.

text: 1) Send an operative to a place where gossip circulates. 2) Have them identify the person who attends the target. 3) Have them find that person's weakness. 4) Set a fallback goal if the key item is elsewhere.
when: the investigator is stalled and must choose whom to watch
why: the vulnerable associate is often easier to reach than the principal target

text: 1) Restrict access to the scene. 2) Forbid touching anything. 3) Keep the central evidence hidden from newcomers. 4) Observe everyone present as they react.
when: when a crowd of possible suspects is on site and none can yet be ruled out
why: unprompted reactions reveal more than answers to direct questions

text: 1) Infer where targets will sit from what they plan to inspect. 2) Count windows and note which are empty, occupied or lit. 3) Compare approaches and choose the least risky. 4) Remove noisy gear and extinguish lights.
when: when a listener must overhear a conversation unseen
why: Each step reduces the chance of detection.

text: 1) Choose a cover position with a view of the meeting place, such as behind a grave or hedge. 2) Wait until the participants leave. 3) Wait until their voices fade before moving, then follow by a route that stays out of sight.
when: A hidden observer must watch a meeting and then follow the participants.
why: Waiting for the parties to leave keeps the observer unseen, and sound cues show when it is safe to move.

text: Assume a concealed watcher can itself be observed, since targets may notice others in nearby cover, and feigned sleep or hiding gives the watcher away.
Route contact with a witness through a controlled intermediary or private channel when official attention may make them withdraw.
when: when a witness may change or retract an account under exposure
why: control keeps the lead protected

text: Look for signs that a subject has noticed observation, and reread later quiet reports in that light.
when: When a subject may have detected surveillance.
why: Detection changes the meaning of subsequent negative results.

text: Do not offer a release that removes the investigator's duty to the wronged party without that party's consent.
Restrict handling of key papers to one holder, so the delivery stays controlled and traceable.
Watch a suspect rather than question him directly when a direct question would alert him and end any chance of learning more.
when: A suspect may be helping a fugitive or hiding something.
why: Alerting the suspect removes the investigator's advantage.

text: Ask each watcher whether anyone else entered during the watch, phrasing the question to cover the whole period rather than a single moment.
when: when establishing who could have passed a guarded point
why: a narrow question leaves gaps the witness may not think to mention

text: Place a watcher out of sight of the entrances people use, so the watcher observes unnoticed.
when: observing a suspect or a meeting
why: Visibility to others would expose the watcher.

text: In crowd scenes, let NPCs look toward a suspect or hidden clue, and make these glances a detectable pattern the player can track.
when: Designing crowd scenes that hint at a hidden connection.
why: A consistent gaze pattern gives the player a readable signal to follow.

text: A watched home location can serve as a trigger for a return event.
Wait until the target is fully inactive before acting, and keep the observer hidden in an adjoining space.
when: A character must ambush a sleeping or stationary target.
why: Acting early exposes the observer and alerts the target.

text: Log each NPC's position over time so the player can check which witnesses could see a given doorway at a given moment.
when: a stealth or investigation system tracks witnesses
why: Logged positions let the player verify alibis and witness coverage.

text: Keep the investigator out of view when the target is alert to watchers and would recognise them.
Leaving a suspect free may gather evidence when they act, but it risks further harm during the wait, so the danger must be weighed.

1) Start from the act or traces and list each distinct action required. 2) Attribute each action to one person where possible. 3) Build a skill profile from the combined actions. 4) Rank suspects by fit, restricting to those matching the profile.
when: Building an inference system for a crime, or traces are available and the suspect pool must be narrowed.
why: Ranking from the act avoids matching a single trace to one suspect; a consistent profile excludes suspects who cannot have performed the actions.

text: A suspect who fears a skilled investigator may change behaviour, which creates a tension-based encounter.
Let the player list suspect evidence and mark each item as confirmed, weak or contradicted, so a wrong conclusion must be defended by the game's logic.
when: Designing an investigation journal or suspect board
why: Explicit status marks make the reasoning inspectable

text: When an alibi clears one suspect, shift the remaining suspects' priority automatically.
A suspect's arrest that is justified by one clue can be undercut by the next clue, which shifts suspicion without fully clearing the earlier suspect.
when: Designing a suspect-gate chain where each arrest unlocks new evidence.
why: Partial contradiction keeps earlier suspects relevant and the player's belief in any single answer unstable.

text: 1) Filter suspects by access to the victim. 2) Remove those with solid alibis. 3) Remove those whose relationship with the victim had ended. 4) Rank the remainder by character and motive.
when: narrowing a list of suspects with incomplete evidence
why: Each filter removes candidates by a different kind of evidence, keeping the list short and fair.

text: 1) Identify the place or item the fugitive is drawn to. 2) Check that location repeatedly. 3) Alert relevant public places with a physical description so sightings are reported.
when: tracking a person who has a known pull toward a place or item
why: return visits to meaningful places make the fugitive predictable and interceptable

text: Let players list identity candidates and strike each off with a recorded reason, so the list visibly shrinks and elimination stays reviewable.
when: When players deduce from elimination; when designing deduction or tracking screens
why: Visible progress makes deduction easier to follow; recorded reasons keep the elimination reviewable.

text: Make corroborated and uncorroborated claims visibly different in the notebook, including alibis backed by independent confirmation versus those depending on one interested NPC.
Track each suspect's alibi and motive in a data structure so the game can determine which suspects remain viable.
when: a game must check suspects against evidence
why: viability is computed from stored alibi and motive

text: Report a suspect's fit to a crime as a probability, not a verdict, so the system keeps the question open.
Let players question suspects about physical details, and reward a suspect who reveals knowledge they should not have.
Give the player a journal that tracks each suspect's motive, claims and observed conduct, so statements can be checked against behavior.
Give each roster entry a short tag, so later clues can refer to characters the player already knows.
Keep dropped suspects reopenable in the suspect list so players can revisit them when new clues appear.
when: designing a suspect or clue tracking interface
why: Players can reconsider earlier dismissals as the case develops.

text: Show the spread of an accusation on a map so the player can trace it moving outward from its origin household.
Score each observed trait, weight rarer traits more, and name a suspect only when the combined score passes a threshold.
when: the player identifies a culprit from gathered clues
why: Combined rare traits can identify a person where single traits cannot.

text: Show a full roster of relevant characters at start and let players reopen it when many characters matter; a small cast players will remember needs no roster.
when: Many characters matter to the solution, versus a small cast the player will remember.
why: Players must fix each name in memory before clues depend on it, and refer back to track relationships.

text: A wary target sends a scout ahead and stays put when something looks wrong, so an ambush must anticipate both scouting and delayed movement.
when: when the target suspects it is being watched
why: Targets protect themselves by checking the route and waiting out danger

text: A subject avoiding main roads by taking side streets produces a zigzagging trail that the tracker must follow turn by turn.
when: The target is trying to avoid observation
why: Evasive routing breaks the straight line a tracker would otherwise follow

text: A tracker that circles at a corner and then picks up a stronger scent and resumes indicates the subject changed course at that point.
when: Reading a tracker's pause at a junction
why: A pause marks a decision point where the signal changed

text: Enemies that tail the player can break off when the player turns to confront them, which rewards patient play over sudden pursuit.
when: when the player reacts to being followed

text: A lured target's first question reveals what they assumed about the sender, which shows what the trap relied on.
A pursuer relying on a single sighting at a fork can fail if the target has unobserved alternatives or a head start.
when: When the pursuer predicts a target's route from limited observation
why: Unobserved options and a head start can let the target reach the goal before the pursuer intercepts

text: Following a target across open ground is much harder than in crowded areas, since cover is scarce and a follower's movement is conspicuous.
when: A tail must follow a target through open countryside.
why: Few obstacles exist to hide the follower from view.

text: Follow by positioning rather than speed: keep a greater distance on quiet streets, while crowds, fog and dusk let a follower close in unnoticed.
when: tailing a suspect on foot
why: quiet areas expose the follower, crowds and cover conceal them

text: Tail a suspect when its movements or contacts are the main evidence; observed behaviour can confirm or refute circumstantial evidence, and a mismatched destination exposes a false story.
when: when an NPC's stated plans are doubtful or its movements are the main evidence; designing surveillance gameplay
why: Observed movement can contradict spoken claims; observed behaviour can confirm or refute what the evidence suggests

text: A pursuer that predicts your choices acts a step ahead; ask what you would do in its place and plan your move one step ahead of its prediction.
when: when a pursuer reasons about or models your movements, such as enemy AI modelling player decisions
why: A pursuer who thinks as you do will likely take the obvious route; each side's model of the other shapes the next move

text: A recurring hazard that works only when the target is exhausted can be designed as a readable clue chain the player can learn.
when: designing traps tied to a character's state

text: Encode readable tells, such as wound angles or stain patterns, that reveal where a hidden enemy stood.
Splitting a pursuit lets one watcher question a witness while the other keeps the subject in view.
Let a tailing NPC question a local and learn of a second exit, then lose the trail, so the player can break a tail through a building with a rear door.
when: Designing a tailing or stealth chase
why: Locals provide information that resolves a pursuit, rewarding player observation

text: An NPC who ignores the player in an unexpected way can start a tail sequence; the player's follow confirms a destination that adjusts the next encounter.
when: designing NPC follow sequences
why: a surprising action invites investigation

text: Tie an interrogation subject's health or stress to a limit on questions, so the player faces time pressure before the subject collapses.
Check the surface a trail lies on: a trace on a footpath suggests a walker, while one on a roadway may come from a passing vehicle.
when: Interpreting a trace of movement
why: The surface constrains what kind of source made the trace

text: Fresh footprints in soft ground lead directly to a hiding place, so follow them straight instead of searching the whole area.
when: tracks are visible in soft or wet ground
why: Fresh tracks mark the most recent path, so following them narrows the search quickly.

text: When a pursuer describes a target's clothing down to small items, the trail has been followed closely rather than guessed.
when: judging how closely pursuers track a target
why: fine-grained knowledge requires recent observation

text: A blocker in the path can be cleared with a quick improvised move, which can leave pursuers behind.
Obstacles blocking a pursuer, such as crowds or a moving vessel forcing a swerve, cost it time and lead; each lost moment widens the target's head start.
when: a pursuit passes through a crowd or along a route with moving hazards
why: Each lost moment widens the gap the target can use; blockages and forced detours cost pursuers time, narrowing or reversing their advantage

text: Pursuers converging on one crowded choke point block each other and fall behind, so do not assume a pursuer keeps pace through it.
Reusing a place where an event occurred before lets the audience anticipate its return and raises tension.
Letting players reach a partial objective easily signals through the route itself that a stronger challenge, such as a boss, waits ahead.
when: Designing a path that leads toward a major encounter.
why: Ease of progress conveys the intent of the level without explicit warning.

text: Each delay in recovering a lost item or suspect lowers the chance of finding it, so timers or pursuit states raise pressure during investigation.
when: when a search has a time limit or a moving target

text: Patrolling guards or follower NPCs can lose track of the player when the player moves through many corridors.
A fuel or stamina limit caps how far a mobile agent can travel, so its reachable area can be estimated from the resource remaining.
when: when an agent's movement depends on a consumable resource
why: Once the resource runs out, the agent cannot go farther without a refill

text: Rain, age, and heavy traffic can wash out or blur a scent trail, and the tracker should ignore competing smells and keep to the strongest remaining signal.
when: A scent trail is old or crosses busy areas
why: Environmental factors weaken the signal and add noise to it

text: Following by vehicle lets a watcher keep distance and pursue at once if the target changes transport.
when: when a target is likely to travel by vehicle

text: Pursuers divide: some follow the direct trail into a valley while others circle to cut off the target, so the fugitive's lead is measured in time.
when: a group pursues across broken ground with a glen or gully between them and the target
why: searchers cover both the direct route and possible escape routes

text: Pursuers that follow the most recent or loudest cue can be drawn away from a route by a planted decoy sound.
Pursuit AI that logs repeated sightings of the same character lets a player break contact by changing route or vehicle.
When a tailed target vanishes, offer a fallback NPC who gives a partial lead to keep the player progressing.
A stealth tail mechanic can have a patrolling NPC follow the player, with route loops or second exits as tests of whether it keeps pace.
when: Designing a stealth or tail mechanic

text: Pursuers rely on relays and pre-agreed markers; fleeing targets rely on decoy vehicles and crowd cover.
A suspect who senses a tail may change route, double back to test whether it keeps up, or confront the watcher, turning surveillance into pursuit.
when: the suspect has noticed or suspects a follower
why: Awareness lets the target act against the observer; a sudden change of course reveals whether the follower keeps up

text: A missed mark sends the follower the wrong way.
When a tail loses its target, the failure may mean the tail was noticed or anticipated, so the failed follow is itself information.
when: when a suspect escapes surveillance
why: A target who escapes cleanly may have been warned or prepared

text: Practical limits such as hailing transport, running, drawing police attention, or running out of money can end a tail abruptly.
Acting on impulse at a key moment, such as at a door, breaks the discipline a tail needs; hold to the plan.
A visibly clumsy chase can push a suspect into escalating hostile action rather than revealing their concerns.
when: The suspect notices they are being pursued.
why: A pursued suspect perceives threat and responds defensively.

text: Following at too great a distance can lose a moving target at a turn before the observer can react.
Losing one watcher does not rule out others, and your own movements can reveal contacts to the watcher.
when: Evading surveillance
why: Multiple pursuers and observed meetings can expose the investigator's network.

text: Loop-based tailing checks work poorly on quiet streets.
when: The area has few other people
why: A single watcher there is easy to spot and easy to avoid.

text: A tail can be drawn off by one visible movement, so the observer must watch the whole area rather than a single path.
A vehicle can hide a subject's real route, so a dismissed cab does not mean the subject has left the area.
when: the subject leaves by transport
why: the observer cannot see the subject's movement after it boards

text: A follower can be exposed by an odd coincidence, such as meeting the target again at a later point, which makes the target suspicious.
when: a tail is repeatedly seen by the target
why: repeated appearance looks deliberate to the target

text: Waiting too long before following lets the target get far ahead, so the pursuer may lose them.
when: Following a target after a meeting.
why: Delay increases the distance and reduces the chance of tracking the target.

text: A single look back or a standing movement at the wrong moment can expose a tail and end the follow.
when: A tail is close to a target during a long pursuit.
why: One visible movement is enough for the target to notice the follower.

text: Canvassing or asking questions can make the searcher visible to the person being sought, and a visible threat can drive a fugitive into risky behaviour.
why: the fugitive reacts to perceived pressure

text: 1) Keep to the side of the street with a clear view, switching sides roughly every fifty paces. 2) Stay about two or three yards behind, outside the subject's line of sight. 3) Stop and look, then resume at a distance that keeps the subject visible without contact.
when: A follower must track a moving subject on foot along a public street without being recognised.
why: Distance and cover keep the follower unnoticed while maintaining the trail; these values keep it near enough to track but not obvious.

text: 1) Keep the subject in view. 2) If the subject is lost, reason about where they must go. 3) Learn their schedule from people who know their routine. 4) Arrive at the destination first and wait.
when: Tracking a subject whose movements are predictable.
why: Anticipating destinations recovers from lost tracking and keeps the pursuer in position; a pursuer given a learned schedule can arrive before the target does

text: 1) Notice whether the same person recurs in several places; a single glimpsed face is often a false alarm. 2) Confirm by walking to a set destination, or by crossing and recrossing to loop back. 3) Someone who keeps pace through the detour is probably following you.
when: You suspect a follower, or a face is seen during an escape.
why: Repeated presence across unrelated locations is unlikely by chance and a repeat test confirms it; false alarms waste time and effort

text: 1) Turn away rather than chase openly, since chasing reveals your interest and can end the pursuit. 2) Hire a second vehicle at a distance, or go to the likely destination and wait.
when: when a watcher is spotted
why: Patience avoids revealing interest and lets the watcher come to a known point

text: 1) Keep a set distance behind the target. 2) Switch sides of the street periodically. 3) Re-acquire the target at turns. 4) Stay out of the target's direct line of sight.
when: following someone without being noticed
why: a moving target can be followed without alerting it

text: 1) Enter one vehicle. 2) Leave it by its far door. 3) Board a second vehicle that departs at speed, shedding the follower.
when: A target is tailed closely in a street where vehicles are available.

text: 1) Halt the vehicle in traffic. 2) Step out into the crowd. 3) Board a second vehicle that heads the opposite way.
when: a pursuer is following by vehicle

text: 1) Arrive before the target and observe from a spot you cannot be seen from. 2) Buy a ticket covering every likely destination. 3) Let the target pass before following. 4) Confirm the destination at a checkpoint. 5) Note late arrivals and where they board.
when: the target is unaware and exits are limited

text: 1) Identify the path between two points. 2) List spots along it where a waiting party could hide. 3) Compare those spots with physical obstacles such as fallen debris that may block or reveal them.
when: testing whether an ambush or interception was feasible
why: Physical layout limits where a hidden party can wait unseen

text: 1) Agree on visible marks before the chase begins. 2) If one watcher must break off, mark each junction on walls, shutters or shopfronts. 3) Mark the direction with a long streak.
when: Dense urban pursuit where a watcher may lose the subject.
why: Pre-agreed marks let a partner keep following through crowds, quick turns and busy streets.

text: 1) Return to the point where the tracker hesitated. 2) Find where two trails diverge. 3) If they run opposite ways from one point, the wrong branch was taken. 4) Follow the other branch.
when: A trail seems to break or split
why: Recovers the true line after a false lead

text: 1) Follow at a distance. 2) Remove noisy footwear. 3) Test each surface before putting weight on it. 4) Wait until the target is absorbed in a task.
when: Pursuing someone over noisy ground at night.
why: Noise can betray a pursuer, and a distracted target gives cover.

text: 1) Follow the moving target with a second vehicle, keeping out of sight at the end of the route. 2) Record each location, who enters and leaves, and what is carried in. 3) Report to the coordinator before acting. 4) Obtain legal authority before entering a private location. 5) Plan authority first, then approach.
when: A suspect is moving and the location is uncertain
why: Watchers stay hidden and the decision to act is made by someone else

text: 1) Release the suspect as bait. 2) Follow at a distance over a long route. 3) Position watchers to cover every exit. 4) Expect blind spots and plan for the target slipping out of sight.
when: A suspect is likely to act on hidden goods or contacts and the exits can be covered.
why: The target may lead to accomplices or a cache that the pursuers cannot otherwise find.

text: 1) When suspects separate, check tickets or destinations to decide which one matters most. 2) Follow that one yourself. 3) Call an ally to take the other.
when: two suspects separate

text: 1) One investigator enters the target's building. 2) The partner waits nearby. 3) They agree a signal, such as a dropped object, to start the follow.
when: one target can be covered by two people

text: 1) Assume the target may have left by another route. 2) Confirm departure through a plausible pretext, such as a delivery to someone inside. 3) End the watch only after confirmation.
when: A target has been out of sight for a while
why: Waiting without confirmation can waste time on an empty exit

text: 1) Keep a set distance behind the target. 2) Close the gap at junctions and in dim light. 3) Check the target against a written description. 4) If it is absent, search other likely carriers nearby.
when: an observer must follow a moving target unnoticed
why: Distance limits detection, but too much distance risks losing the target at turns.

text: 1) Use the map to list the routes the target can take at each fork. 2) Remove branches that are blocked. 3) Use scheduled timings to set a place and moment for the intercept. 4) Move to the point where the remaining routes meet.
when: When a fleeing target's destination is limited by fixed schedules and a small set of routes
why: Predicting a place and time, not only a direction, lets the pursuer arrive before the target

text: 1) Board transit and leave at a stop the follower may not expect. 2) Enter a building by its front and leave by its rear. 3) Cross to a parallel street to break line of sight.
when: You need to lose a follower before a meeting or return home
why: Route changes and sight-line breaks force a pursuer to lose track.

text: 1) Match the subject's pace and stop when it stops. 2) Stay close enough to see it but out of its sight. 3) Break off once it notices you and the pursuit becomes a confrontation.
when: the subject is moving and the observer must learn where it goes

text: 1) Let a messenger leave first. 2) Follow at a distance, staying out of sight behind a bend. 3) Track the delivered item to its destination. 4) Identify the target building from its marking.
when: A suspect's contacts are unknown and the hidden location must be found from a few clues.
why: Following covertly reveals the target's location without alerting it.

text: 1) Keep a fixed gap behind the target. 2) Wait behind one bend until the target passes the next. 3) Move along soft edges to muffle steps. 4) Cross hedges only where the road is straight and open.
when: A target's route is long and open and the follower must stay unseen.
why: Bends and cover block the target's line of sight while preserving the gap.

text: Cover every exit of a building before waiting at one; an unplanned route, such as a stairway, lets the target bypass all observers.
when: A target enters a building with more than one entrance.
why: A second route can defeat a single watch; uncovered routes let the target bypass all planned observers

text: Do not tail a target who knows your face or can see the whole area; use a two-person tail for a sole lead, not when it knows one investigator.
why: A familiar face or open view exposes the follower; recognition ends the tail

text: Vary a tail's distance and position rather than keeping them fixed, so a target who turns back does not see the same figure repeatedly.
when: following a target on foot
why: a fixed position makes a tail obvious when the target turns

text: Define enemy escape routes in level scripts so the flight path is predictable and the player can cut it off.
when: designing stealth or ambush encounters
why: a known route gives the player a chance to plan an interception

text: Plot each patrol's sightlines and timing so players can learn coverage gaps, and reward that learning by letting them exploit the gaps.
when: Designing stealth patrols
why: Learnable gaps turn observation into a skill

text: Let an NPC tail mission log each stop it makes, so the player rebuilds a timeline from scattered reports.
when: When designing tracking missions

text: A tail mission can require the player to follow a target unseen, with failure detected by distance or line of sight.
Let an NPC who follows the player after a conversation create suspicion without explaining the purpose.
If an enemy's appearance misrepresents its speed, give a readable visual cue so players can learn its real pace.
why: Players cannot anticipate speed they have no way to read

text: Use counter-surveillance when a tail is suspected or when moving a valuable person or item across a city.
A waiting partner should not speak to the one inside, in case the target is watching.
Assign a second unseen agent to follow the suspect so movement is still recorded after the first watcher is withdrawn.
when: A suspect is tracked covertly and the first watcher may be exposed or pulled away.
why: A concealed second observer keeps the trail alive without the suspect knowing.

text: Require a tailing mission to follow an NPC to a payment point, with timing set by the NPC's known motive.
when: Designing a stealth or tailing objective
why: Motive-driven timing makes the target's movement predictable and learnable

text: Marking a route keeps a fallen-behind follower on track but costs time; a follower who stops to mark it can lose the target entirely.
Letting a target go to raise an alarm trades the risk of losing one subject against the risk of losing the investigators or the wider operation.
when: a watcher can either keep following or report to a response team
why: A report can bring help that a lone watcher cannot provide.

text: A target who trusts a sender tends to accept a matching invitation without verifying it, because the message fits what the target expects from them.
when: The sender is someone the target would obey.
why: Trust lowers the chance of checking the source.

text: A trusted ally can extend a player's view by checking a location and reporting back, or by keeping watch for them.
A trusted companion who can unlock a reticent NPC works as a gating mechanic that rewards relationship building.
when: Designing NPCs who only talk to certain companions
why: Trust transferred through an intermediary opens dialogue that direct questioning cannot

text: Modelling an NPC's trust as a state that drops under hurried interaction creates a deception mechanic.
Track trust status per NPC, so a guard admits a familiar voice but not a stranger, and the admission rule can be checked by the player.
when: Designing NPCs that decide whether to let others pass.
why: Per-NPC trust gives access decisions a consistent, testable basis.

text: Use a trusted helper rather than hired staff for escape roles, since a hired person can leak the plan.
when: when the plan must stay secret
why: Paid strangers can disclose details to the pursuer.

text: An ally NPC can offer a hiding place with a double purpose, leaving the player to decide whether to trust the offer.
when: Designing an ally whose help may serve another goal.
why: Ambiguous motives create meaningful player choice.

text: Use audio cues like a striking clock, footsteps, and a ringing bell as countdown signals in pursuit or timed evasion, building tension and rewarding players who read them.
when: Designing suspense in a stealth, pursuit, or timed evasion scene.
why: Sound cues signal approaching danger and shorten perceived time; audio gives players readable information about time and danger.

text: A sudden loud noise after a quiet passage restarts momentum and redirects attention.
when: A scene has gone quiet and needs renewed pull.
why: Abrupt sound breaks the calm and forces the player to react.

text: A light swung briefly across a figure can illuminate a face for a moment, revealing who is there.
when: When a light source moves past a character in darkness
why: Brief illumination exposes features that stay hidden in darkness

text: A small concealed device producing a sharp sound on cue can create an effect that observers attribute to a supernatural cause.
when: Staging an effect that observers will misread.
why: A hidden, timed sound is convincing when it matches what observers expect.

text: Ambient sounds such as passing traffic can give rough timestamps when no clock is visible, while observers hold position.
when: when a timeline needs rough reference points
why: Recurring sounds mark elapsed time without requiring an exact measure.

text: Cut ambient sound and pause before exposing a hidden antagonist, so the silence heightens the reveal.
when: Scripting a dramatic identity reveal.
why: A sudden drop in sound draws attention to the moment.

text: Give injuries a direction and location in the game, so a wound read from one side can imply the attacker's stance or handedness.
when: when designing injury feedback or forensic clues
why: Directional wounds let players infer attacker positioning

text: Make enemies seen only as silhouettes against a bright exit require the player to move closer or test a detail before identifying them.
when: When enemies are initially backlit or distant
why: Forcing closer inspection turns identification into an active choice

text: Animate small reaction cues, such as a paling face or a hand to the chest, so players can read a suspect's reaction without a text prompt.
Fog that hides and reveals in patches, with lamps struggling against it, makes the surroundings feel threatening and leaves the watcher uncertain.
when: when fog or partial lighting covers a space
why: Partial visibility keeps the observer unsure what lies beyond the reach of light.

text: A character who dozes and loses time creates a gap in the timeline that the player must explain.
when: A mechanic lets a character lose time unnoticed.
why: The unexplained interval forces the player to reconcile the sequence.

text: Moving light that flashes objects into view and removes them again makes ordinary objects seem to appear, vanish and watch, so dread comes from lighting and motion rather than the objects.
when: Static objects should feel threatening without adding enemies.
why: Shifting light and shadow give still shapes apparent motion and intent.

text: Alternate long quiet passages with sudden interruptions, releasing tension when the threat is left behind and rebuilding it in a new space; contrast makes each break land harder.
when: Shaping a sequence of encounters or building dread before a reveal
why: Contrast with quiet sharpens the impact of a sudden event; constant intensity flattens the effect.

text: Use stealth or ambush sequences when they depend on patience and sensory cues rather than constant action.
Place each pause just before new information, since a pause with no payoff turns suspense into boredom.
when: pacing a suspense sequence
why: pauses gain value when they lead to a reveal

text: Wind, storm, darkness and drifting debris make a player flinch and raise tension, amplifying the emotional weight of an approaching reveal.
when: Staging a tense scene before a discovery
why: Environmental pressure heightens the sense of threat without new information.

text: Surfaces that creak give away a hidden player while silent surfaces do not, so surface material becomes a stealth mechanic.
when: Designing stealth movement across floors or stairs.
why: Surface sound determines whether movement is detected by nearby characters.

text: Let a shadow or cloth fold read as a threat in a dark room and then reveal it as harmless, but require a visual check so sound alone never settles whether a threat exists.
when: Designing horror or tension in a dark environment.
why: Fear is built by ambiguity, and a check prevents sound-only cues from being unfair.

text: Constant action keeps energy high but dulls the impact of each moment; quiet stretches sharpen interruptions but risk boredom if too long.
when: Pacing a chase or encounter sequence
why: Contrast gives impact, while sustained intensity loses its effect

text: Footprints stay sharp enough to read when there has been no new snowfall since the event and the surface is frozen, while heavy traffic, thaw or fresh snow erases them.
when: Judging whether outdoor traces can still be read
why: Snowfall, thaw and foot traffic overwrite impressions and remove the evidence

text: Touch-like cues such as a draught or contact can signal a nearby presence before it is seen.
when: visibility is poor

text: Environmental disruptions such as a fire or light change can break a trick, creating a timed mechanic.
when: Designing a trick that depends on lighting or fire.
why: Changing conditions reveal or defeat the trick and can be used as a timed challenge.

text: Attach a timestamp to each trace so stale evidence does not mislead the player, since a stain's inference about timing fails once it is no longer fresh.
when: Designing visible physical evidence such as stains or wear
why: Freshness determines what a trace can tell, so stale traces must not imply recent events

text: Convey speed through bodily sensation such as sway, hill climbs and a braking stop, so the player feels motion when the view is restricted.
when: the player cannot see the route

text: A controlling person may deny holding a key and later produce it, so the lock works as leverage.
A culprit may close the entry point after using it, hiding the means of entry from occupants who then cannot see how the room was reached.
when: Entering through a route left open
why: Concealing the route delays discovery

text: A gatekeeper may refuse visitors a known party vouches for, admitting only someone it personally recognises from an earlier event.
when: The gatekeeper lacks a current guarantee
why: Personal recognition outranks third-party assurance

text: Rooms that connect, such as a bedroom suite or another occupant's quarters, offer routes bypassing the main door, which overlooked connecting doors can hide.
when: Analysing how a building can be entered or exited, or reconstructing access to a room.
why: Interior connections create routes invisible from the main entrance.

text: A key bent or twisted at its ring suggests it was wrenched free, and a new-looking duplicate on the owner's ring suggests another person used the original in a lock.
Walls with no waste space or hidden entrances rule out a secret-passage explanation for a sealed room.
A credible report that a route was open at the time of the crime can collapse a conclusion that only one route existed.
A simple bolt on a door can be worked from outside with a thin tool, so a locked door is not always sealed.
when: A door's lock is a basic bolt or latch.
why: Basic fastenings can be manipulated from the other side.

text: Use a key's inside or outside position to separate accident from deliberate act and reveal who handled the lock, since a key found moved shows someone had access.
Read door, lock, bolt and light states as evidence of who had access, by what route and when; each limits who could pass, and combined they rebuild event order.
when: Reconstructing how someone entered, left or moved through a room or sealed space.
why: Each state records a moment of access, and together they reveal the order of events.

text: The force used to enter reveals intent: stealthy intruders pick locks, while intruders confident no one is inside may break the door; doors can encode this for players.
when: Several people could have entered and the method suggests their goal or skill, or when designing doors and locks that show intruder type.
why: Different intruders have different goals, so the way they enter reflects what they want; readable entry signs let players deduce intruder type.

text: A dust-free area on a knob or bolt shows recent handling; an untouched marker on a door or lock shows it was not used, separating door entry from hidden entry.
when: Checking whether a door was opened recently, or designing evidence of how a space was entered.
why: Hands leave dust-free areas, and a marker that stays untouched shows the door was not used.

text: Give a sealed room more than one plausible entrance, with at least one non-obvious, so players must search beyond the locked door and weigh explanations.
when: Designing sealed rooms in a level.
why: A hidden route rewards thorough checking and avoids a single fixed answer.

text: Treat a key's position, and a locked room's obstacles, as evidence the player can see and reason about.
when: Designing locked spaces or key items in a mystery
why: Position and obstacles constrain what could have happened

text: An intruder without a key to the main entrance must use another route, which can point toward people already inside the building.
A key left in a door can signal carelessness or a deliberate arrangement rather than a secured room.
when: Investigating a locked room.

text: A suspect who could not have arranged the event that made the crime possible is less likely to be responsible.
when: When a crime depends on a prior event that someone else controlled
why: Whoever controls the enabling event controls the opportunity.

text: Keying a message to an item one character always carries limits who can decode it, so only that character's possessions can unlock the message.
when: designing a message puzzle tied to a character
why: restricting the key to one carrier controls who can read the message

text: When a lock requires two independent conditions, such as a key and a code, narrow suspects by which condition each holds and by who can know the second.
when: Determining who could have opened a secured object.
why: Two conditions held by different people imply that the act needed collusion or a route through their shared circle.

text: An unlocked door may simply have been left open, so check the time and the habits of its users before inferring intrusion.
why: people leave doors unlatched for ordinary reasons

text: A player who avoids long exposure to risk is more likely to choose the access route with the shortest time at risk.
when: Several access routes carry different exposure risks
why: Longer presence inside a risky space raises the chance of detection

text: Hide a vault behind ordinary objects such as a wall of bones or stacked crates that the player must notice and clear.
when: Designing concealed storage or secret areas.
why: Mundane facades reward careful observation.

text: Check what lies between an entrance and its target, not only whether the door is unlocked, before assuming open access.
Build each exit, such as a door, window, water route or tunnel, as a checkable route with ownership or access records the player can consult.
when: designing exits from a sealed location

text: Access to a space can itself be a clue: an apparent vanishing often has a simple explanation based on who holds keys or knows an unlisted route.
when: a character seems to disappear from a location
why: control of access explains movement

text: When a direct route is sealed, look for a link through an adjacent room, such as a connecting door.
when: A locked room blocks the intended path.
why: Adjacent spaces often share a connection that bypasses the lock.

text: When a locked door resists, check easier alternatives such as a window before forcing the door.
why: A simpler route may exist that the obvious barrier hides.

text: The absence of forced entry suggests the intruder knew the house or was admitted by someone inside.
when: A locked room shows no signs of forced entry.
why: Someone with access or knowledge could enter without breaking anything.

text: Avoid entering the target's room directly, since a sound or sudden entry gives the target time to flee.
when: approaching a target who is still inside a room
why: the target reacts to noise and surprise before the trap closes

text: Model doors with physical barriers that need effort as well as social barriers, and track who can open each door.
when: Designing access control for rooms in a level.
why: Layered barriers make access depend on both effort and social expectation.

text: Track lock state, key location and sightline for each door so the player can work out which routes were possible.
when: Designing locked-room puzzles.
why: Recorded door states let the player reconstruct movement and reason about access.

text: A two-part token, a spoken phrase plus a gesture, verifies identity; both must be given before an NPC reveals information.
when: A contact cannot check a face or papers
why: Two checks are harder to fake than one

text: A door's swing direction hides or reveals an adjoining room depending on the side someone approaches from, so the same door can block sight from one side and open it from the other.
when: when a door separates two rooms with a sightline concern
why: the door panel itself blocks the view on one side of its swing

text: A site reachable only on foot or by a narrow track restricts vehicles and so narrows who could arrive or leave unseen.
when: A theory about movement depends on who could come and go.
why: Limited access removes routes that would otherwise let people pass unobserved.

text: A concealed passage known to only some characters gives them unseen access, so routes can be hidden from others.
When locks are rare as a world rule, access depends on social custom, so any entry becomes a question of intent rather than of physical barrier.
when: A world has few physical locks.
why: Without barriers, the meaning of entry shifts to who is allowed and why.

text: An open window or other opening that connects two rooms can serve as an access route, so its open or shut state matters to the event.
when: two rooms share an opening or adjacent exterior route

text: A gummed flap can be opened and resealed covertly, while a wax seal resists covert opening, so breaking one leaves visible damage.
when: Modelling sealed containers in a game
why: Seal type determines how tampering can be hidden

text: A sensor that signals each entry, like a bell over a door, can log the order and spacing of visits, so repeat traffic becomes readable.
High or hard-to-reach containers can require a specific tool, such as a ladder, before they can be searched.
Test barriers from both sides: a bolt checked from one side says nothing of the far side, and a room sealed on one side may open through an adjoining room.
when: Checking a room that appears sealed, or a connecting or communicating door.
why: The far side can be bolted or unbolted independently of the near side.

text: Do not assume a returned key was never used: a briefly lost key can be impressed and duplicated, and a locked room can have other entrances.
when: A key is out of its owner's control even briefly, or reasoning about access to a locked room.
why: A duplicate key gives access without forced entry, and keys can be copied.

text: A closed gate or eliminated exit does not prove no one passed: a modest gate can be climbed, and someone hidden inside may leave later than expected.
Entry method alone does not prove identity, since a skilled intruder can change the method deliberately and a signature needs corroboration.
when: An entry method is used to name a culprit.
why: Method can be chosen to mislead, and one signature does not establish identity.

text: An unmanned checkpoint records no witness, so passing through it leaves no evidence that can confirm a route.
when: a route depends on an unattended door or gate

text: Omitting the exterior from a plan can hide entry or exit routes, such as terraces, ladders or outer towers, that the interior alone does not show.
when: Mapping a building for movement puzzles
why: Exterior features create routes that an interior plan does not reveal

text: 1) Enumerate every opening of a space, such as window, door, lock or catch, with its state. 2) Test each claimed barrier yourself and cross off barred or fastened openings. 3) Test remaining routes against every anomaly any explanation must account for.
when: A closed space is found and the question is how a person could reach the victim, or openings can be listed.
why: Claimed barriers may not work; elimination narrows routes, and anomalies verify which remaining route is real.

text: 1) Decode the message with the candidate key; a length match alone does not confirm it. 2) If output lacks sense, discard that key. 3) Search the scene for another text the sender could have used.
when: Choosing between candidate key texts, or a decoding attempt yields nonsense.
why: A single loose fit is easily produced by coincidence; nonsense output signals a wrong key rather than an unreadable message.

text: 1) List every exit and barrier limiting access. 2) Note whether each was watched, locked or open, and when it could have changed. 3) Compare each lock time with the victim's arrival, discarding exits blocked before arrival. 4) Test remaining routes against the physical scene.
when: A closed building or space seems to block entry or exit, and a suspect's route must be narrowed.
why: The window of opportunity is where barriers and timing allow access; routes closed before arrival could not be used afterward.

text: 1) Locate the entry point. 2) Ask who could physically reach it. 3) Test each route against access, such as keys or ladders. 4) Keep only suspects who could use the remaining routes.
when: a crime has no clear or unexplained entrance

text: 1) List every entrance to the restricted area. 2) Note which entrances can be seen or reached from outside. 3) Ask each candidate about rules and hours. 4) Remove candidates who cannot reach the area.
when: when a shared resource must be traced to a person

text: 1) Test an insider acting alone. 2) Test an insider who holds a key. 3) Test an accomplice. 4) Test the victim leaving a window unfastened. Test each in turn against the traces.
1) Establish what was known about a risk. 2) Establish what advice was given and how it was answered. 3) Establish who was told.
when: when reconstructing a decision
why: ordered questions expose who knew what

text: 1) List every holder of a key, any master key, and who guards it. 2) Account for each key: confirm its holder had it at the time and record where it is. 3) Treat an unfound key as a sign its holder was absent or that it was taken on purpose.
when: Entry or re-entry to a locked room is central to the case.

text: 1) List who holds a key to each door. 2) Check whether the door was locked at the time. 3) Study lighting and routes through the layout. 4) Look for signs of forced entry. 5) Consider what the visitor knew of the occupant's habits.
when: a locked or semi-secured entrance decides who could enter
why: access depends on keys, locks, layout and knowledge

text: 1) Map which areas are sealed and who holds a key to each. 2) Note who lacks access. 3) Record each person's position and distance. 4) Build a timeline from sounds and events.
when: narrowing the people who could have acted in a sealed or partitioned space
why: Combining access, position and timing reduces the set of candidates.

text: Confirm who held keys to a locked space; key holders could enter without forcing access, and if one person held the only key, possible entrants narrow.
when: Assessing who could have entered a locked room.
why: Keys remove the need to break in, shrinking the candidate list and the suspect pool.

text: Model each key as an item with owner and custody history, recording every change of holder, so the game can show who could have opened a locked vault and when.
when: Designing locked-area puzzles or theft investigations.
why: Recorded handoffs let the player derive who had access at each moment.

text: Log each entrance's state (locked, relocked, briefly opened) as timestamped events, so the game can compute which rooms were reachable in a window and verify claims.
when: Designing locked-room puzzles, alibi logic, or multi-room spaces.
