Let a word on a note point to a location the player must find in the world's atlas or codex before they can proceed.

text: Plant an object with an odd feature, such as a mismatched mark, and log it in the journal to be explained once the player gains a key.

text: Highly detailed clue instructions turn solving into mere transcription, while sparser instructions keep solving but risk unfair failure.

text: Model line of sight from windows and balconies, so witness reports match what the player can verify from a given spot.

text: Searching the obvious room first and skipping closets or cellars leaves routes unchecked, so cover every area in a set order.

text: Place a small unexplained object or footprint that players can return to after learning the solution.

text: A cue the player can see may also be seen by enemies or other observers, who can read it and exploit it.

text: 1) Place physical signs of use in the hidden area, such as fresh straw, lantern light, or a worn ladder. 2) Let the player notice them. 3) Let the player conclude the myth is cover.

text: 1) Describe the scene before touching anything. 2) Examine the body or key object for clues to cause. 3) Check each exit and hiding place in a fixed order. 4) Read traces of age and use at each. 5) Rule out escape routes before searching desks and papers.

text: 1) Present a vague impression that fits several suspects. 2) Let the player narrow candidates only after finding one specific matching fact.

text: 1) Schedule a late cluster of clues. 2) Unlock them when a new character arrives. 3) Let the second half of the investigation open after a pause.

text: 1) Plant a rumor that points to a region. 2) Add a boundary marker that narrows it. 3) Add an ownership record that confirms it. 4) Hide the target so all three clues must be combined to find it.
Make observation conditions such as distance, light, and obstruction checkable so players can judge how reliable a clue is.

text: Check the edges of a room and interactive fixtures such as vents, registers or closed openings, since clues often lie there.

text: Let a character's fear or stress state change what they notice, so some clues appear only under high tension.

text: Keep an inventory of each container's contents so that a missing item becomes a clue the player can notice.

text: Place a clue in the environment, such as a dated record that stops abruptly, so the player infers a mechanism without the game stating it.

text: Show an item's origin through packaging or workmanship differences, giving the player a route to its source.

text: A recurring sound or symbol can be planted as a clue and later revealed as misdirection or as a true sign.

text: Plant small physical evidence such as wet prints, smell or disturbed dust, so the player can check a trick against what they observe.

text: Marks lined up across terrain can act as a breadcrumb trail leading the player to a hidden site.

text: 1) Place atmosphere and omens early. 2) Place NPC testimony in the middle. 3) Place the key document or test late.

why: Escalating clue types match the player's growing ability to interpret them.

text: Address a quest item to a similarly named NPC so players must inspect the item's reverse to find its true recipient.

text: Position overheard lines and reflections where the player can watch unseen, and tie each one to a later place or character.

text: Place a physical trace such as dust, cobweb or rust at each exit so the player can rule routes in or out.

text: Fatigue and slippery footing change step length, so a count taken under those conditions cannot be trusted as a measurement.

1) Walk through the rooms and grounds. 2) Understand how the building fits together. 3) Only then draw conclusions about movement.

text: 1) Place a matching fragment on the victim. 2) Hide the matching item in a diggable location. 3) Let the player discover both and decide whether the fragment and the item agree.

text: Plant a small verifiable number in an alibi record, so a player who notices it can unlock the contradiction.

text: Keep the candidate list visible to the player so each filtering step is fair and verifiable, and give partial clues such as an initial, a color or a limp that narrow it.

text: Design a second source that can confirm or break a character's alibi during play, so the alibi is tested rather than simply accepted.
Separate witness-only claims from claims backed by objects or positions, so players can tell which evidence they are able to verify.
when: when placing clues in a level
why: Players need to know which claims they can check against the world.

text: Store each self-report with a verification status so that later evidence can confirm or contradict it without overwriting the original.
when: designing a data model for NPC claims and player knowledge
why: Keeping the original claim lets later evidence change its status

text: Let players check identity through faction or guild records, so a fictitious character's absence from the records becomes a discoverable clue.
when: a game has organisational records

text: Matching ballistic or print evidence across scenes can confirm a link between crimes, which strengthens a case without proving identity alone.
when: comparing evidence from multiple crime scenes
why: Shared evidence connects scenes even when the culprit remains unknown.

text: Flag any log claiming a confession that the scripted process could not have produced as false.
Verify every advertised or stated claim about a location against physical reality before trusting it, since posted notices and NPC statements can be wrong.
when: A player must act on a sign, notice or NPC's description of a place.
why: Stated locations can be false or outdated, so verification is needed.

text: Offer the player two candidate explanations, human action or environmental change, and let a material test such as heat, time or moisture decide between them.
when: designing a clue with two possible causes
why: A test the player can run turns a guess into a checkable choice.

text: Let a player compare identifying marks on a corpse's head with its body, so a substituted head can be detected.
when: sealed scenes with a discovered body
why: A visible mismatch gives the player a checkable way to detect a substitution.

text: Keep one or two effects deliberately unexplained, so a mechanical solution does not close the entire mystery.
when: When resolving a haunted-level puzzle
why: Leaving residual mystery sustains player curiosity

text: 1) Show the player a scripted illusion or vision. 2) Reveal the true state of the room. 3) Let the player learn to check perception against the environment.
when: Designing a puzzle built on deceptive perception.
why: The contrast teaches the player to verify what they see.

text: 1) Present two competing explanations. 2) Require the player to choose one before a door opens. 3) Lead each choice to a different witness.
when: Designing a gate that forces a theory choice.
why: Each explanation yields distinct evidence, so the choice shapes what the player learns.

text: Give a strange event both a mystical label and a checkable natural cause, so the player decides between explanations by checking evidence.
when: when designing an encounter that appears supernatural
why: The checkable cause rewards attentive players without removing the mystery's atmosphere.

text: Make the competing theory testable at the same time as the supernatural one, so the player can disprove both.
when: when a scenario offers several explanations for one event
why: Players need a path to eliminate each explanation, not only the favored one.

text: Inspecting a hidden spot with a light or by moving a panel is risky, because the light and movement can expose the observer.
A concealed space's size, shape and construction suggest what it held: a small flat pocket points to a flat, light object such as paper, and a cramped gap to small or forbidden objects.
when: Interpreting a concealed space.

text: Objects players dismiss as set dressing, such as chairs or cabinets, can conceal a trigger; placing it early among decor lets a later targeted check reveal it fairly.
when: Designing a room with a potentially dangerous or functional item.
why: Early, unobtrusive placement makes later recognition fair and satisfying.

text: A physical sign shown at a critical moment, such as a change in skin colour, may be misread at the time and only understood later.
when: During a tense scene
why: Urgency leaves no time to interpret the sign

text: A person hiding evidence tends to choose a place that searchers cannot reach without being told where to look.
when: when concealing a physical trace from a search
why: Keeps the trace outside the house, where only an informed person can find it.

text: Observers believe only what they see, so an object moved out of their view before a reveal stays hidden from them.
when: a character hides an item in plain sight of others
why: Watchers judge by what is visible to them.

text: A hider who believes a threat to a hidden item is real and imminent will retrieve it early, exposing themselves before the deadline.
when: when the hider thinks discovery is about to happen
why: the deadline removes the option of waiting

text: Small signs, such as a handle that turns and returns without opening, suggest someone inside is listening.
A concealed method can use an ordinary object delivered through a normal social action, so the mechanism stays hidden until the object is found.
A personal desk can hold records of wealth its owner hid from others, so documents kept in furniture can reveal concealed income.
A concealed object may show as a bulge or stiffness in clothing; a single such sign is only a lead.
Open flat ground gives little concealment, so a visible tail tends to fail; hedges and fields provide cover.
In busy, open spaces an intruder can pass unnoticed, so routine inattention by staff excludes few people as suspects.
when: A location is crowded and open to many people.
why: Activity and openness hide individual movements among ordinary traffic.

text: Open moor with no trees or shelter offers almost no cover, so a hidden person there depends on hollows and crouching rather than structures.
when: a level is open and flat
why: cover needs height or obstacles to block sight

text: Clothing such as gloves or sleeves can disguise a body part, and a refusal to remove it can be concealment rather than an innocent excuse.
when: A character's apparel or refusal to remove it conflicts with the rest of the evidence.
why: Re-reading earlier details in light of a reconstruction can reveal that the item hid the true means of action.

text: Concealed items are often hidden in bulky, decorative or dismal everyday objects and places that others dismiss, so careful inspection of mundane objects finds what a broader search misses.
when: When a room or set of belongings with many ordinary objects is searched.
why: Everyone sees such objects and few examine them, and people overlook what looks unimportant.

text: Hide clues among ordinary contents of storage like costume chests or wardrobes; they draw little suspicion and are searched least, so the clue surfaces only when moved or collided with.
when: Placing a hidden item among household or everyday objects.
why: Routine objects draw little suspicion and get the least inspection.

text: Check whether a concealed surface has been disturbed by comparing it against the surrounding material, since matched repairs still differ from the original.
when: Investigating a suspected hidden space.
why: Disturbance leaves differences that a careful inspection can detect.

text: Disturbed soil or a glint within it can signal that someone buried an item to keep it out of sight.
A culprit who cannot destroy evidence may place it in an ordinary, visible spot and rely on others overlooking it, if the culprit controls who passes the spot.
when: Concealing an item that cannot be destroyed.
why: Visible objects tend to go unnoticed when nobody expects them to be connected to a crime.

text: A concealed object is usually kept close to its owner and under the owner's control, not entrusted to a third party.
when: The object is small and the owner is its only custodian; less applicable if a third party holds it.
why: Owners prefer to keep valuables within reach and personal control.

text: Objects thrown into water or otherwise removed may have been the former contents of a container, disposed of to hide evidence.
when: Recovered objects do not fit the scene's purpose
why: Removing evidence is a common way to conceal a crime.

text: Evidence concealed inside ordinary objects and places is found by searching the spots where it could plausibly have lodged.
A careful hider avoids eye level and places a concealed object above or below it, since a loosened item at eye level is noticed in a close search.
when: Judging where a hider would conceal an object.
why: Eye level is the zone most often inspected closely.

text: Look for changes that contradict what was known earlier, such as a room now open that was known closed, and ask what the change removes.
when: A scene differs from its earlier recorded state
why: A culprit often alters the scene to erase traces of the method.

text: An object turned to face the wall and covered in dust suggests someone wanted it out of view.
A puzzle can use a concealed item that the player must learn to operate, with a limit on what the item can move.
when: Designing a puzzle built on a hidden tool.
why: Learning the tool and its limits makes the puzzle satisfying to solve.

text: Place a hidden location under the player's own resting spot to create dramatic irony that rewards careful inspection.
when: Designing a secret near a safe area the player frequently uses.
why: The player's proximity to the secret makes discovery feel earned and tense.

text: A mundane facility such as a salvage or construction site can hide a different function, such as military defence, so judge its purpose by what it could conceal.
when: when a commercial site appears to have an innocent purpose
why: a cover activity can conceal a real purpose

text: Hide a device among objects that suggest disuse, and disguise its container with a familiar label, so close inspection tends to pass over it.
why: Signs of disuse and familiar labels discourage a closer look

text: An unused room with its door open is a natural hiding and ambush site when NPCs walk past.
when: Designing opportunistic hiding places in a level.
why: An open empty room gives a place to step aside and wait.

text: A pursuer can hide under a stopped vehicle to see where the target steps out, rather than following into the open.
Make a late reward container empty, and plant a small trace, such as a fresh scent or a missing key, that suggests it was emptied on purpose.
when: Placing a chest or stash the player expects to hold loot
why: The trace lets the emptiness read as deliberate concealment rather than a broken reward.

text: Hide a substitution behind a visible disguise that the player sees but is not told to examine, then make searching candidate locations the objective.
Concealed, locked objects whose key is carried by a suspect often hold the decisive evidence about the suspect's secret.
when: A suspect hides an object or mail that is central to the secret
why: Locks and custody control access, so the contents reveal what the suspect is hiding

text: An object hidden in an ordinary storage place can survive a search, so a search that misses it must be explained rather than assumed complete.
when: when an object has been concealed in household storage
why: searchers may skip places they do not expect to hide an object

text: A room search that requires opening containers and moving objects defines hiding spots by what the player can disturb.
A concealed release such as a hidden panel or keyhole, set into ordinary architecture like wainscot or angled walls, stays hidden until found by testing, not sight.
when: when a room's exit must be hidden but reachable by someone who knows the mechanism
why: Hiding the trigger in ordinary architecture makes discovery depend on interaction.

text: Hiding evidence makes the person who hides it look guilty and harms the inquiry, such as when a witness hides an object to protect one person.
Each concealment step, and concealing an object's route, creates traces such as scraped surfaces, fresh copies, dust, damage or handling habits that a careful observer can notice.
when: When concealing an object or hiding from pursuers.

text: Attempts to hide traces by rubbing, rolling or re-roughening paper can leave signs of their own.
when: Someone tries to conceal an alteration on a document.
why: Physical concealment damages the surface in detectable ways.

text: Hiding that evidence was damaged is itself a risk to the case; report the disturbance openly so others can judge what remains.
Hiding the empty container in the same spot as the loaded one is a natural move that can also reveal the swap.
when: When concealing a swapped container.
why: Keeping the substitute beside the original makes the swap easy to detect.

text: Assuming objects remain where you last left them can fail when someone else has entered the room.
A hidden eavesdropper can be noticed by a second, silent character present, so concealment must account for every observer.
when: a stealthy listener is in a shared space
why: other present characters can perceive the watcher

text: Searchers who follow their own impulses leave gaps in coverage; without a shared division of the area, some corners are never checked.
1) Obtain a search warrant. 2) Open the claimed trunk with a locksmith if needed. 3) Open it in the presence of an official.
when: a suspect says belongings were left in a container
why: An official present makes the search verifiable

text: 1) Remove or weaken a corroborating trace. 2) Make a duplicate of the item before any inventory check. 3) Keep the original locked away out of view for later use.

1) Test several candidate spots. 2) Choose one that is easy to reach but hard to see from the usual path. 3) Place the object out of view. 4) Grip it with a tool kept in the same spot. 5) Before use, check by feel that the cache is intact. 6) After use, return the tool to restore the cache.
when: when an object must be hidden and later retrieved without direct hand contact
why: retrieval without touching the object avoids leaving new traces on it

text: 1) Empty each pocket in turn, not just the first one felt. 2) Examine and record each item. 3) Return each item after checking it.
when: when searching a body or container

text: 1) Search large furniture first. 2) Open locked containers. 3) Inspect compartments inside each container, such as pigeonholes and small cases, before moving to the next object.
when: a scene holds furniture and containers that may conceal evidence
why: hidden items often sit inside other objects, so a surface check misses them

text: 1) Replace the real document with a blank or decoy before a search. 2) Hide the real pages inside an ordinary object. 3) Move them to a place searchers are unlikely to take apart, when watchers are least alert.
when: when a captive must keep a document safe under observation

text: 1) Check the item's last known location. 2) Check its usual container. 3) Check the people and bodies involved. 4) Record which places were empty.
when: searching for a missing item
why: ordered checks reveal each empty place in sequence

text: 1) Search the person carrying a sealed object for keys 2) Try each key found against the lock 3) Force the lock only if no key fits.
when: a sealed object is held by someone

text: 1) Stage a disturbance that draws the target's attention away. 2) Exchange the object during that moment. 3) Leave a convincing substitute in its place.
why: Each step covers the next so the exchange goes unseen

text: 1) Check the searched character's clothing and footwear. 2) Check waistband and pockets. 3) Check the enclosing space, including bedding. 4) Test fixed fixtures one by one by force, noting any that loosen.
when: a searcher must leave no part of a confined space uncovered
why: A fixed order makes the search systematic so no hiding place is skipped

text: 1) Stay still until the approach is clear. 2) Slip into a side room out of sight. 3) Secure the entry so it cannot be opened.
when: a visitor approaches a room the player occupies

text: Place a key item or clue inside a mundane or unexpected container, such as a drawer in an already cleared room, that the player must deliberately open and inspect.
when: Designing a clue or key item.
why: Thorough searching and deliberate inspection reward attention.

text: Do not declare a place empty until each floor and room has been checked.
when: When deciding whether a location is unoccupied
why: A quick look at the main area misses rooms where occupants or clues remain

text: Place a single breaker or gas meter in a room, since switching it off can hide player movement and NPC sightlines.
Build a pleasant or dreamlike area that hides a hazard, and give a clear warning cue before the danger appears.
Place a concealed item in a room that an NPC's patrol schedule avoids, so players must learn the routine to find it.
when: Designing a hidden collectible or clue
why: Makes the schedule itself the way to discover the item

text: Gate concealed spaces behind specific tools, such as probes for soft fillings, a light for dark gaps, or a lift for fixed fittings.
Design NPC scenes that draw attention, and give the player a cue that reveals when the real goal is being hidden.
when: an NPC stages a scene to cover another action
why: the player can then notice the misdirection

text: Set a covert meeting point out of sight of the main building, using back routes, small gates and tree cover that block line of sight.
when: Designing a secret contact location
why: Layout determines which watchers can see the meeting

text: Place small trace objects where a larger object would be overlooked, so careful players can find them.
when: Designing clue placement in a level
why: Small clues reward close inspection without being obvious

text: Hide the stolen item inside an object the player has already searched, so the search itself is what conceals it.
Plant a visible concealment, such as a wig or mask, as an early passing remark, so the player does not treat it as the solution but later connects it to the reveal.
when: Using appearance as a clue to an enemy's or NPC's identity
why: A casually stated clue is noticed but not overvalued, so its later payoff feels fair.

text: Key items in the most obvious nearby spot reward players who check close by; when hiding from pursuers, avoid routes and places searchers check first.
why: Players search nearby spots quickly, but hiding where pursuers expect to search gives them an easy find.

text: Place hiding spots by function: drains, laundries and unlit alleys each support a specific kind of concealment and item type.
when: Designing concealment locations in a level.
why: Matching location to function makes hiding plausible and discoverable.

text: Place hidden items where a plausible action would send them, and make the hiding place explainable afterwards.
when: Designing where a key item is concealed in a game world.
why: A player who searches beyond the obvious floor finds the item and can understand how it got there.

text: Key clues can be hidden in ordinary, conspicuous objects that searchers overlook because they look first at obvious hiding places.
when: Designing a clue that must be discoverable but not obvious.
why: Experienced searchers check secret or unusual spots first and skip mundane items.

text: In a bare room, few hiding spots exist, so every fixture becomes a suspect and any hidden spot is itself a clue.
when: Designing a sparsely decorated room.
why: Limited cover concentrates suspicion onto the few features that could conceal something.

text: Lighting controls what observers can perceive, so darkening a scene removes the evidence needed to see an act.
when: A hidden act must happen unseen in a scene
why: Observers can only perceive what light makes visible

text: 1) List every fixture, opening, shadow and bare surface in the room. 2) Identify which features could hide an object. 3) Choose a placement that uses a shadow or fixture for concealment. 4) Test visibility from the observer's position.
when: A site must be covertly monitored and its layout limits hiding options.
why: Mapping features before placing equipment reveals the few viable concealment spots.

text: Size hidden alcoves to match the objects they conceal, so a player can infer what was stored there.
Let neglected features such as dry wells or overgrown shrubs mark places where items can be hidden and later found.
Make the plan specific enough to measure; a vague plan cannot guide a physical search.
when: Designing a hidden feature that players must locate from clues.
why: The search method depends on measurable distances.

text: Use fog, lamp coverage and footstep audio to hide and reveal enemies, letting sound warn of approach before sight.
when: when designing enemy visibility in a dark or foggy space
why: Sound preceding sight gives the player warning while concealment preserves tension.

text: In a room whose lighting can change, place a light source the player can reach at a critical moment so the reveal is earned rather than purely random.
when: Designing a hidden enemy action or trap trigger in darkness
why: Player-accessible light makes discovery a matter of skill and attention

text: Let a victim's condition point the player back to an earlier action, such as a drink taken at dinner, so the clue reveals the method.
when: Designing a poisoning or drugging clue.
why: Symptoms can link the outcome to a prior event.

text: Hidden changing spots, such as an empty waiting room, can serve as clues that reveal the disguise method to a careful player.
when: Designing clues for disguise mechanics.
why: A discoverable location lets careful players work out the method.

text: Place an item or independent record, such as a receipt or gate log, that contradicts an NPC's testimony or stated story, so checking it exposes the lie.
when: Designing clues that test an NPC's testimony or a character's claims.
why: Physical items and records are harder to rehearse away than speech; discovering the contradiction rewards attention.

text: A trace mismatch proves an object was moved but not why; a rearrangement narrows the question without answering it.
The detail that contradicts a story is often a small, ordinary object rather than a dramatic clue.
When pieces refuse to fit one attractive theory, examine the misfits before accepting it; they usually signal a wrong assumption, not a missing piece.
When stolen goods do not fit the thief's apparent aim, or valuable items were left untouched, consider that the random haul is a disguise hiding a targeted motive.
when: When valuable items are ignored or the haul makes no sense together
why: Random additions can make a targeted crime look like an ordinary burglary

text: Objects that conflict with a household's stated routine reveal what its occupants do not admit. Ask what each unexpected object would be needed for.
when: an object's presence or position conflicts with stated routine
why: the conflict shows an activity the occupants hide or do not mention

text: Note a mismatch between two traces, such as a broad mark and a set of prints, before trying to explain it.
when: two traces differ in shape

text: A strong mismatch between a suspect's capacity and an act's demands should lower their rank, not prove innocence.
when: A capacity check reveals a clear mismatch
why: The suspect may have had help performing the physical part

text: An item on a body that does not match the victim's own kit suggests the kit was kept elsewhere and the victim was prepared there.
when: Cosmetics, tools or supplies on the body differ from the victim's usual set.
why: The victim's own items would have been used if the preparation had happened at the scene.

text: Behaviour that does not fit a stated motive is a clue; contradictory signals, such as generous offers from someone claiming poverty, suggest a hidden purpose or a played role.
when: a character's words and actions point in different directions
why: a true motive usually produces consistent action

text: Give the player a copy and an original; a layout mismatch, such as a blank line on the wrong page, becomes a checkable clue.
when: when a document must be verified
why: Comparison turns a discrepancy into a fair, testable clue.

text: Use small stains, such as a few drops of blood, to confirm that a trail is correct and to show which person was injured.
when: A trail needs confirmation from a second trace
why: A minor physical clue corroborates a trail without requiring a larger scene

text: Place a clue that contradicts a convenient theory later in the investigation, so the player's own hopes are tested.
when: a mystery encourages an appealing wrong theory
why: late contradiction forces the player to revise

text: Plant deliberate contradictions in clues and let a case board flag them, so players can resolve them.
when: Designing a mystery's evidence.
why: Visible conflicts give players a clear target for deduction.

text: Not every discrepancy is a lie; memory, fear and accomplices can all produce differences between accounts.
when: Judging a witness whose accounts differ.
why: Innocent causes produce mismatches as readily as deception.

text: A recreated test may give a false result if its conditions differ from those of the original occurrence.
1) Confirm that two traces that should align really do not. 2) Propose a rearrangement that would restore agreement. 3) Check whether a second trace fits that rearrangement.
when: A scene was kept in position and then altered.

text: Keep a clue that contradicts the obvious answer, such as clean cut debris far from its source, so checking players can reject the decoy.
when: Building a fair mystery where the decoy can be disproven.
why: Fair clues let observant players reach the truth.

text: When a new observation or custody account contradicts a prediction or working theory, revise the hypothesis rather than treating it as an investigation failure.
Use a mismatch between a room's disorder and its contents as a designed clue that the apparent motive is false.
why: valuables left behind contradict a theft reading for careful players

text: Give a wrong suspect a plausible motive, a missing object and a suspicious manner, and include enough contrary evidence that a player can detect the flaw.
when: when designing a red herring NPC case
why: a fair red herring rewards correction without giving away the true solution

text: When a physical state contradicts a reported event, such as a door found unfastened after being reported locked, explain the contradiction before accepting either account.
why: Either the report or the physical evidence is wrong, and the contradiction points to where the story fails.

text: Build a sighting that conflicts with expectations, such as a child where an adult was expected, as a clue pointing to the true occupant.
Confirm that a withdrawing party has actually left before continuing, so no one can reverse the decision and reclaim the scene.
Design clues so rival explanations predict different observable results, letting players test and separate them.
when: designing mysteries with several plausible causes
why: distinct predictions allow evidence to decide

text: Provide two or three sources that can be cross-checked, so players must reconcile conflicting records to proceed.
when: When designing investigation puzzles with record sources.
why: Requiring reconciliation tests player reasoning rather than rewarding a single lookup.

text: Include a scene object that contradicts a naive reading, such as a neatly placed container, to prompt players to revise their first explanation.
when: designing a crime or event scene
why: a contradicting detail rewards players who question the obvious story

text: In a staged room, place a small trace that contradicts the staging, such as a half-eaten dish or unexpected light, that careful players can match against a character's habit.
when: Designing a room whose arrangement should be questioned.
why: Small contradictions reward observant players without making the staging obvious.

text: Place traces such as drag marks or blood pools that are consistent with the action that supposedly occurred in the scene.
why: Consistent traces make the scene's story checkable by the player.

text: Place dated objects so the player can find one whose date contradicts an NPC's testimony, giving them a lead to pursue.
In dim light a victim close to an attacker may still have seen him, so if she never names him, her silence becomes evidence to weigh.
when: a victim or witness saw an attacker at close range in low light
why: Low light still gives some visibility, so darkness alone does not rule out recognition.

text: In darkness, a witness's eyes adjust slowly, so they may believe they see more than they do or mistake faint light for a clear view.
when: the witness has moved from light into dim or dark conditions
why: eye adaptation lags behind the change in light

text: A dim or shaded room limits what a witness can see, so their account depends on where they stood.
when: The scene is lit by a single lamp or otherwise darkened
why: Darkness hides identity and detail

text: In darkness, witnesses may report only what they could touch or hear, not what they could see.
A person groping toward a switch suggests the room was dark, and their route should match where the switch sits.
when: a witness describes moving through a dark space
why: Reaching for a switch reveals the lack of light

text: Darkness is not a clean alibi when many people saw who was near the controlling switch.
Contrast a lit, crowded public area with narrow dark lanes; the change of light and noise marks the approach to danger.
when: When designing a route into a dangerous place.
why: Light and sound shifts build suspense.

text: A dark observation post with a view into a lit space lets the observer watch while staying unseen, because light contrast hides the watcher.
when: Placing a watcher's position in a level.
why: Lit areas are visible from outside while dark areas conceal the watcher.

text: Use a low-light room with an unclear figure to hide a body or trap until the player commits to looking closer.
when: Designing a dark room with a hidden threat.
why: Players must commit to inspection before the threat is revealed.

text: In a dark room, an attack from behind leaves only a partial account, so the investigation depends on physical traces and the victim's limited perception.
when: A victim is attacked where vision is limited.
why: Limited sight produces a narrow witness account.

text: Removing or breaking a light source creates a darkness window in which a concealed actor can move unseen.
Brief, dim lighting makes it easy to swap two similar objects and return the wrong one.
A map made in good light can miss details that matter in darkness, such as which doors were closed.
1) Use the scene to infer the most likely hiding spot. 2) Spend light only on that spot. 3) If nothing is seen, feel the surface by touch. 4) Lift any loose piece and check beneath.
when: when light is scarce and the search area is large
why: Targeted light and touch conserve a limited supply.

text: 1) Switch off the room light 2) Show the object with its faint distinguishing mark 3) Ask a witness to name the object.
when: a witness must identify an object in poor light

text: Let dark or fogged areas be mapped through counted, paced movement, paired with map fragments or wall features so players cross-check and correct step-count estimates.
when: dark-area mapping or puzzle

text: Make lighting a gameplay variable: in dim areas, detection is less accurate and objects can look like something else until the player moves closer.
when: Designing detection in dim or dark areas

text: Darkness hides an act well but is fragile: one light source or lucky glance can break it, while it also hides the actors' own movements.
when: Choosing darkness as the mechanism for a hidden event
why: Concealment strong enough to hide acts is also prone to sudden exposure

text: Lure a guard off post with a fake errand or decoy NPC quest, with the player's cover identity as the key to the approach, for a set window to take a route or search or swap an item. Plant earlier the dependency that makes the guard's departure plausible.
when: Designing a stealth or distraction mechanic that pulls a guard away from a protected area.
why: A controllable absence gives a timed opportunity; players and guards need a believable reason to move, or the decoy feels arbitrary.

text: Place harmless-looking decoy faction, quest line, or staged evidence on the map's far side, away from the true objective in a less noticed area.
why: Staged props draw the search away from where the event happened.

text: Offer two plausible culprits or routes, with only one carrying the real clue and the other a convincing decoy.
when: When designing a mystery or branching investigation space.

text: A decoy that is partly true and explains only half the event can lead the player toward a second clue needed to complete the solution.
when: When designing misleading clues in a mystery.
why: A partial explanation satisfies the player temporarily and motivates continued search.

text: Place valuable-looking loot to suggest a theft motive, and leave decoys unlinked to the solution so the player must check each one against the scene.
when: When designing misleading objects in a level
why: Unlinked decoys force the player to verify rather than assume.

text: A decoy event or sound in the same timeframe absorbs traces or draws guards' attention, letting the real actor or intruder act unobserved.
why: A plausible alternative cause diverts attention from the real one.

text: Include a decoy item or route that looks like the answer, with a clear test, such as a record, a skill check or a reagent, that eliminates it.
when: Designing false leads in a level
why: Players learn by testing and eliminating decoys

text: Place a loud, harmless event such as a vendor, festival, or fight near a quieter clue the player must find.
when: Designing a scene where a clue must be noticed.
why: The distraction draws attention while the clue stays available nearby.

text: In locked rooms, place a decoy object that appears to solve the room, so the player is misled until the real mechanism is found.
why: A convincing wrong answer delays the solution and rewards close examination.

text: A conspicuously absent key item can be placed deliberately, leaving the player to infer it from wounds, terrain and remaining traces.
when: When designing a puzzle or mystery where the answer or key object should be inferred rather than found.
why: The absence itself becomes a puzzle the player solves by working out why the item is missing from indirect clues.

text: A destroyed item can leave a permanent gap that the player must reason around, rather than being restored by the game.
Withholding one body part, such as a skull, blocks one line of deduction until the player finds it.
when: when designing a remains puzzle with staged deductions
why: the missing part removes the evidence that depends on it

text: Place missing elements, such as a blood trail or a dropped key, as deliberate clues that point toward a hidden route.
An inventory puzzle can present a set with one deliberate gap, so the player notices the absence and traces the item to another room.
Let a common-looking item, such as scrap or chips, hide a rare material, and reveal it only when the player tests it with a tool or second opinion.
Plant two identical items as a trick that tests whether the player checks what is real.
when: Designing a clue or item that tests verification
why: Players who assume identical objects are equivalent miss the difference.

text: Give a lab set of clean tests with one container out of its usual place, so placement rather than test results reveals it.
when: designing a forensic room
why: placement is a clue the tests cannot cover

text: A lab puzzle can let the player test residue or blood against a control subject, using labelled items and a numbered key.
when: Designing a forensic or lab-based puzzle.
why: Controlled comparison gives the player a traceable route from evidence to source.

text: A communication line cut by a hidden object can appear dead before its cause is known, so the dead line itself becomes a clue to investigate.
Place a visibly disconnected pull or lever so a player who tests it discovers that it is a dummy.
when: Designing puzzle rooms with false clues.
why: Testing lets players learn the fixture is non-functional.

text: Fresh stitching or disturbed material at a hiding place shows that someone has tampered with it before the investigator arrived.
when: Evidence has been hidden and may have been reached by others.
why: Disturbed concealment leaves physical signs of recent handling.

text: A person who tries to clean a stain has likely known about it.
when: A stain has been partly removed or tidied.
why: Cleaning is a deliberate act driven by awareness of the mark.

text: An object disguised by dirt is usually noticed only by a searcher who is looking for that specific item.
when: When searching a scene for a specific object.
why: Dirt makes the object look like ordinary debris.

text: A departure from an expected layout shows that something was moved, but not who moved it.
when: an investigator finds a disturbed item
why: the layout reveals change, not the cause

text: In a concealed killing, disposing of the body is a harder problem than the means of death.
when: When planning or analysing how a death is hidden.
why: Remains that are found or traced create the link that a killer most needs to break.

text: An emptied container with a known opening time gives the player a clue about when a theft occurred.
Cleaning, repair, replacement or disturbance of a scene or object before examination erases or fakes the traces, so do not rely on them as reliable evidence.
when: when an object or scene may have been cleaned, restored or altered before inspection
why: Cleaning and handling remove or change the marks that would have been read; disturbance erases or fakes the traces the method depends on.

text: Ordinary traces such as a stale smell, thick dust, unlatched case, open empty drawer, paint smear near a lock or lockless cabinet show a space has been used or disturbed.
when: when deciding which spaces to search first or signalling disturbance
why: Such traces reveal past or recent activity in a space that appears closed.

text: Disturbed furniture, such as a rumpled couch, can show where something was hidden and later removed.
when: an item may have been concealed in a room

text: An object lying out of place on the floor can point to something hidden behind nearby furniture.
why: Moving the furniture may reveal a concealed compartment.

text: A room with dismantled shelves and open drawers shows that someone searched it hurriedly, and that search can be read as a clue.
An overturned object beneath an exit, such as a chute, can be the only sign of how an escape was made.
Cleared desks and neatly arranged papers suggest someone has already searched the room before you arrived.
Before treating a disturbed trap as proof of intrusion, check whether an innocent cause could have moved the marker.
when: A trap or marker shows signs of disturbance.
why: A disturbed trap shows that the place was touched, which can have an ordinary explanation.

text: Objects left in shared transport are often cleaned the same night, so tracing must begin before that cleaning routine.
Titles of disturbed books reveal the reader's interests, but such an inference must be tested before it is treated as evidence of a particular person.
when: reading the titles of books handled in a room
why: A title suggests interest, yet a single item alone does not establish who handled it.

text: A bent or disturbed fixing beside an empty slot suggests the item was pulled out quickly rather than removed carefully.
A scrubbed spot, moved rug or missing cloth can indicate that a killing happened elsewhere and the room was tidied afterward.
A door found locked and later found open shows that someone passed through in the interval, which suggests an unseen movement.
when: a room's entrance changes state between checks
why: a state change records movement the witnesses did not see

text: Set markers at points an intruder would not expect to check, such as an item's position or a faint residue, and check those points rather than only where things are stored.
when: Designing a space or object that players or NPCs may search or handle without authorization.
why: Intruders focus on hiding what they took and often restore visible order, leaving unexpected spots unchanged or altered.

text: Debris such as shells or moss on an injured character or item can point players to a specific area, like a flooded passage or submerged structure.
when: when designing environmental clues

text: Disturbed furniture, displaced cushions and crushed carpet show how a person sat and moved.
Faint traces rarely survive in a room that has been heavily handled or cleared, so survey it before disturbance erases the marks.
when: when deciding whether a room is worth a trace survey
why: disturbance destroys faint marks

text: Retain sweepings from cleaned areas for sifting, since small clues such as ticket stubs can turn up in debris.
Signs a concealment leaves behind, such as disturbed ground, scent and routine, can be read in reverse to expose a hidden act.
when: A scene depends on whether a location shows signs of disturbance.

text: Concealment depends on removing every sign of disturbance from the ground, not only the most obvious one, so the surface matches its surroundings.
when: Hiding a trap, pit, or dug area.

text: A visible change in the surface, such as freshly turned soil, can signal that a hidden cache has already been disturbed and moved.
when: Designing hidden caches that players search for
why: Disturbed ground betrays past activity and gives players a clue to the true location

text: A brief stall or slowdown in a guarded transit masks an exit, because observers' attention and any alarm are overwhelmed by the ambient disruption.
when: A transit route has predictable slow points such as junctions, tunnels or traffic.
why: Noise and the momentary halt drown out the signal that would otherwise expose the escape.

text: A visible disturbance draws attention away from the action the disturber actually wants, so the real act goes unseen.
why: Observers focus on the most visible event

text: Recording when each surface was cleaned lets a trace's age become a usable clue for the player.
when: designing time-based evidence

text: Residue left by a cleanup, such as powder grains lodged in glue, shows that handling happened after an object was used and can exclude some sources.
A disturbed-room system that tracks displaced furniture lets players deduce a hidden item's location from which objects have moved.
when: a room tracks object displacement

text: An object found in a different position after its owner was away shows that someone visited and handled it.
why: Physical state changes record access to a private space

text: Disturbed ground or a dropped object shows someone passed without entering a room, which narrows the list of suspects.
Handling the key book visibly can alert the suspect, so fetch it without any tampering he could notice.
Items found away from a body do not by themselves show who discarded them. Many chances to dispose of them exist, so location alone leaves the culprit open.
Assuming a sealed room must have been entered through its door hides the real access route.
Searching after bystanders or first arrivals have moved things loses evidence of original positions.
Items may be hidden by disposal in water or drains, and burned or torn papers leave fragments the player must reassemble to recover information.
when: when designing hidden evidence in a scene
why: Disposal and destruction create search targets and reconstruction puzzles.

text: Locking a room behind you can keep others out of the evidence they need to examine.
1) Give the corpse items that suggest an identity. 2) Include a feature that cannot be altered. 3) Require the player to find and check that feature before confirming identity.
when: Designing a body-identification puzzle.
why: The player must weigh misleading items against decisive evidence.

text: Leave damaged, moved or disturbed objects and room states, such as a moved chair or wet path, that players can read as signs of recent handling and search direction.
when: when designing a scene that implies a recent event or placing clues
why: Players reconstruct recent activity from disturbances, and disturbance implies someone touched or moved the objects.

text: Design a ransacked room so its disorder shows what the searcher wanted, letting players infer the search goal from the scene.
when: when designing disturbed scenes
why: Disorder that reveals intent gives players a readable clue.

text: Add detection risk when the player moves a curtain or screen that hides them.
when: designing stealth cover that can be disturbed

text: Mark a shifted board or disturbed debris as a visible clue that guides the search, and let touch or a close look confirm what lies beneath.
when: when hiding loot in a dark area
why: Physical disturbance signals a hidden space without requiring full light.

text: Give containers physical states such as resealed flaps, altered dates and stains that the player checks in a fixed order.
when: Designing containers that carry evidence of handling
why: Concrete physical traces give the player something specific to examine and reason about.

text: Make containers, props and cosmetics inspectable, with a turn or twist mechanic that reveals hidden items, so players learn to test objects rather than only read them.
when: Designing props or containers in a dungeon or level
why: Players then learn that objects reward manipulation

text: Give each disturbed area its own texture and scent, so a careful player can notice a mismatch with the ground around it.
when: Designing hidden or disturbed areas in a level.

text: Disturbing a target's space can trigger the desired search but may alarm them into fleeing or destroying evidence.
when: choosing whether to tamper with a target's environment
why: the same disturbance can prompt escape

text: Thick, undisturbed dust and cobwebs show a room has stood idle a long time, since footsteps disturb dust and the layer records absence of recent entry.
when: judging whether a room was recently entered or how long it has stood idle
why: footsteps disturb dust, so an undisturbed layer records absence

text: A permanent timed object such as a sundial keeps a steady record for decades, making it a durable reference for dating events.
Report durations at a coarse grain, such as under a minute or under two minutes, so readers can judge how fast a danger closed in.
Count elapsed time since an event in days or years, giving a second anchor that helps recall and check the event.
Estimate the time since the last sighting, then combine it with known conditions such as tides to narrow where the person could now be.
Test whether a claimed action could realistically take the stated time, which can expose a false alibi without any extra clue.
A witness's judgement that they would have noticed an arrival before a given time sets the earliest possible bound on that event.
when: Estimating how early something could have happened
why: If the witness would have seen it, earlier arrival is unlikely

text: As elapsed time since an event grows, its subject can be spread across a wider area, so a fixed local search succeeds less often.
when: a subject must be found after an event
why: the subject has more time to move away

text: Sand, dust or ash in a corridor can record when a hidden door was opened or which creature passed, and the prints can be read on return.
Measuring elapsed time for each leg of a journey shows where a timeline runs behind schedule.
Dust shows only the surfaces you can see, not every route in and out; a visitor may have stayed outside or left another way.

1) Identify a consumable trace at the place that burns, melts or builds up at a known rate. 2) Confirm nobody has handled or replaced it. 3) Count units used or judge its state. 4) Multiply by per-unit burn time, adjusted for conditions, to estimate elapsed time. 5) Compare that estimate with the claimed sequence of events.
when: the time spent in one place, or a claimed sequence of events, needs a rough duration
why: consumed items burn at roughly known rates, so counts give durations

text: 1) Estimate how long the journey or task takes physically. 2) Subtract that from the witness's stated times. 3) Treat any unexplained surplus as a place where hidden activity may lie.
when: when a stated timeline leaves a gap
why: A surplus longer than the activity suggests concealed action.

text: Count elapsed days between dated events to measure how long a delay lasted.
when: a sequence of events includes a delay
why: Duration can change how events relate.

text: Use stocked provisions and cooking equipment in a room to signal that someone has been living there for some time.
when: designing environmental storytelling for a hidden room
why: supplies and cooking gear are signs of extended occupancy

text: Use dust layers and freshly disturbed objects as flags that show a room was used recently, so players can infer activity.
when: When dressing a laboratory, studio or workspace.

text: Visible watchers make threats readable so players can react, but when a trap needs a subject to enter, visible guards may frighten the subject away.
when: placing watcher NPCs at a hub's entrances, or guarding a location where a trap relies on a subject entering
why: Noticing a watcher lets the player respond to the threat themselves; a visible threat causes the subject to flee rather than enter.

text: A watch post is an observer stationed at a single passage who records who moves through it during a set period while the investigator works elsewhere.
Show the player an antagonist's preparations, such as a changed meeting point or a waiting figure, that the protagonist cannot see, so the coming encounter carries known risk.
when: when setting up an encounter
why: visible but unseen-by-protagonist threats raise tension without revealing the plan

text: Move covert work to a spot where any approaching footstep gives warning.
when: designing hiding places for stealth play

text: When a guard is drawn away, the location is left unwatched, so any unexpected arrival creates risk for the person inside.
A hidden watcher behind a slightly open door can be noticed by the people being watched, so concealed observers may give themselves away.
when: placing hidden NPCs who observe visitors
why: the watched party can notice the door moving

text: Give sensory warnings, such as a smell, sound, hiss or touch, before a hidden threat appears, so the player has time to react.
when: a threat is about to appear in a level, or a dark room holds an enemy the player cannot yet see
why: Early warnings let the player prepare instead of being surprised.

text: End a dungeon section or encounter on an unresolved state, such as an ajar door, an unreadable message or a low-health fall, to pull the player into the next area.
when: designing the end of a section or encounter
why: Unfinished encounters prompt the player forward.

text: Let a close pass identify a watcher who can later reappear in the level.
when: Designing recurring pursuers

text: Tell the watcher the purpose of the watch so they know what to notice.
why: A watcher unaware of the purpose misses relevant events.

text: Absence is negative evidence: a passage missing from the blueprint eliminates its location; a 'nothing unusual' NPC report points to a constraint like a wall, distance or closed door.
when: when a hidden passage is absent from the plan or an NPC reports no observation of a sound or event
why: A null report still narrows where the event could have occurred.

text: An architectural anomaly is a part of a building that its layout or function does not account for, such as a fireplace with no flue.
when: inspecting a building for hidden spaces
why: unexplained elements can signal concealed structures

text: A smoking chimney shows that someone is present in a building, even when no one is seen, but not how many people are inside.
Objects and rooms that reflect a location's history carry implicit evidence, so an atmosphere matching a family's past supports the story.
when: when designing a location tied to a backstory

text: A climbing puzzle can leave handprints at a height so the player can deduce the size or reach of whoever climbed there.
when: When designing a climbing sequence in a level.
why: Marks at height reveal the climber's reach.

text: Make the environment's orientation a readable clue so the player can resolve the geometry before solving the mechanism.
when: When the layout of a sealed space is ambiguous.
why: Unresolved orientation blocks the search itself and frustrates the player before the puzzle begins.

text: Chained mirrors can relay an image so that a person appears far from where they actually stand.
A bright spot draws the eye and can hide what lies at the edges of the room.
when: Lighting a key area of a level

text: A tree screen hides a site only while its canopy stays intact.
Make a room's most anomalous feature the intended key, so the puzzle does not rely on spectacle alone.
Read level architecture as evidence: a moved chimney or a foundation with no building above can signal a later addition or a lost structure for the player to investigate.
Use boundary deeds with exact measured lines as physical clues that can settle a land argument.
Give corpses, containers and drawers wear patterns, missing items or small leftover objects that reveal their user's habits or prior visitors, so players can deduce what happened.
when: when designing level props

text: Give unusual observations or test results a visible in-world explanation, such as age or fear level, so surprise feels strange without being left unexplained.
why: Players can then interpret surprising results

text: Seed an ambiguous inscription or readable object early, without a prompt, so its meaning emerges when the player finds the matching object, location or NPC interaction.
when: when seeding a clue for later payoff
why: The player can notice it later without being told; a clue connecting to a later find rewards exploration and recall.

text: To outsiders, specialist knowledge seems trivial or like eccentric minutiae, even though it is the key that makes a trace meaningful.
when: when a character's expertise is dismissed by others
why: detailed lore appears unimportant until it solves a case

text: Vague testimony or uncertain recollection becomes useful when confirmed against a second source, such as a logbook, footprint or found journal, turning vagueness into a puzzle.
when: When designing lore that pays off after a second find
why: Partial information gains value when corroborated

text: Signs such as thieves' slang, a lookout, and gambling tables show who controls an area and who knows it.
when: When designing environmental clues about a criminal network.

text: Objects left at a scene, such as a dropped case or torn notebook pages, can carry a message and point to where further evidence is stored.
when: A scene contains objects that seem out of place
why: Deliberate or accidental markers often direct the investigator onward.

text: Mud tracks, fresh breaks in surfaces and cold drafts signal recent activity, and players learn to read them as signs of presence.
Spotless surfaces in a room can suggest an orderly, strict occupant, so environmental details can be used to hint at character.
Local tradition is a valuable lead but can be wrong about location, so test it against terrain and records before accepting it.
why: Traditions often preserve events while misplacing where they occurred.

text: A journal collecting several NPC accounts can be sorted by time, so the player can see gaps in the story.
when: designing quest logs with multiple accounts
why: chronological order exposes missing events

text: Schedule a key lore reveal behind a sealed item or timed delivery, so players anticipate the content before learning it.
when: When a major lore reveal should build anticipation
why: Waiting for a delivery builds expectation

text: Leave unanswered petitions and character witnesses as open plot threads that the player can revisit later.
when: when writing a legal storyline
why: unresolved requests create lasting narrative leverage

text: Keep room motifs consistent so they point the same way, and use single unrelated objects as red herrings.
Give a location a mood that contradicts the public face of its owner, and let details such as cold rooms or bare walls hint at private trouble.
when: designing a location whose owner has a public image
why: A contradiction between surface and setting invites players to look beneath the facade.

text: Encode a scene's story in props such as a dropped book, a clutched blanket or a lit lamp, so the player can read the sequence of events from them.
when: when designing environmental storytelling
why: Props reward observation and let the player infer what happened.

text: A stopped object, moved chair or half-dressed character can convey a timeline, so players reconstruct events rather than read a log.
when: Designing scene clues for a mystery or story-driven level.

text: Let an unrelated lore text, such as a plaque or a building's history, hold the clue for a hidden passage.
Place many odd events with mundane causes, such as drafts, loose boards or previous occupants, and reserve the truly unusual cause for a few rooms.
when: Designing a level with mysterious events
why: Keeps player trust in the investigation meaningful

text: Place a cult belief as an early room description or inscription, then let a later document recast it as a witnessed event so the same location reads differently afterward.
when: When building a dungeon or location whose meaning should change after a late reveal.
why: A location's description gains new weight once the player learns the belief was a real event.

text: A specific trace, such as a particular tobacco ash, narrows the search sharply when the lore maps it to few possible sources.
when: when a trace is distinctive and its lore is known
why: the fewer matching sources, the smaller the suspect pool

text: Props such as weapons, containers or animals can be placed so that they confirm or rule out each candidate explanation for a supernatural-looking event, rewarding careful checking.
when: Designing a level with a mysterious event that has several mundane explanations.
why: Physical evidence in the environment lets players eliminate candidates.

text: Furniture that makes a relaxed posture plausible supports innocent readings of a figure and can hide the dangerous one.
1) Seed a region's lore with several stacked pressures. 2) Record them as dated chronicle entries. 3) Let the player build a timeline of unrest before the main event.
when: Building background lore that explains local hostility.
why: A dated timeline makes the causes of suspicion discoverable and credible.

text: Make lore documents' figures, claims, dates and authors checkable against other clues or world state, so a bad number, false claim or forgery can be exposed.
Let players corroborate clues against in-world books, journals, archives or directories, so checking a hunch can itself reveal further clues.
when: Designing clue sources for a mystery

text: Repeat a symbol or consistent staging style, such as a trap pattern, across locations so players link each encounter to one faction or recurring villain.
Build a reconstructable sequence in a game scene from connected physical clues, such as a broken object, a dust mark and a stain, so players can deduce events without dialogue.
when: When designing environmental storytelling for a staged event.
why: Connected clues let players reconstruct the sequence through reasoning rather than exposition.

text: Use book titles and margin notes as environmental hints about a hidden mechanic, and mark each trace with enough detail that a player can link it to a later find.
Record a lore note's chain of custody, such as who wrote it and who copied it, so players can judge how far to trust it.
when: Placing written lore that players may need to weigh.
why: Provenance gives players the information to assess reliability themselves.

text: Gate a puzzle behind lore, such as a poison, plant or dialect, that the player learns from in-world codex entries before a trace becomes meaningful.
when: when designing a clue that requires specialist knowledge
why: in-world learning makes the lore a discoverable key rather than an arbitrary requirement

text: Have an in-world character explain the solution, so the player can check their own reasoning against it.
Place memorials, inscriptions, or reliefs that can trigger a visible NPC reaction, and use the reaction to hint at that NPC's past.
why: the environment can carry evidence that dialogue does not

text: Place props such as journals, half-made items or a turned-away portrait that encode motive without giving a single answer.
when: When building environmental storytelling.
why: Props that hint without settling let players interpret and compare clues.

text: Give found letters a typewriter defect or watermark, and found clothing embroidered initials, so the player can link each item to one sender or owner.
when: when designing found documents and clothing

text: Give a game's backstory named documents and dates so the object feels real, and let the player's journal or an expert NPC confirm or deflate some claims.
when: Designing lore for an object or faction
why: Verifiable references reward investigation while keeping the world believable.

text: Give rooms and objects checkable state, such as warmth, arrangement and disorder, and flag contradictions with NPC claims while leaving the player to decide what they mean.
when: Designing environments that support dialogue checks
why: Object states let players test claims and make environmental storytelling interactive.

text: Build a game's past from in-game documents such as letters, court records and diaries, and from locations matching their descriptions, leaving the link partial.
when: Designing backstory for an event the player must reconstruct.
why: Partial links make the player judge how well evidence fits, which rewards investigation.

text: Place reversed inscriptions on blotters or rubbings so players can read a message from a damaged note.
when: designing readable clues from damaged documents
why: reading reversed text is a satisfying discovery

text: Give NPCs props consistent with their stated activity, since a wrongly rigged tool or badly cut herb can contradict a cover story.
when: designing NPCs with a stated occupation or pretext
why: mismatched props expose the lie to observant players

text: Make some props distinctive and others generic, so only a few traces point to a specific NPC.
Build crime scenes whose staged method conflicts with the physics the game enforces so players can detect the mismatch.
Give a lore NPC one fragment of a dead figure's history, told with a reason to shade it, so players must weigh the source.
when: Designing lore delivery about a past figure.
why: Partial, biased sources make players reason about the history rather than receive it whole.

text: A missing stretch in a character's recollection can signal that a place was visited but not remembered, serving as a level-design hook.
when: Designing a character backstory that a level should reveal.
why: The gap invites the player to find the place that the memory lacks.

text: Plant ominous signs, such as a warning or a fork the player only understands later, to set dread without revealing the outcome.
when: Designing a dungeon that should build unease.
why: Signs that gain meaning later reward attention and sustain tension.

text: Place an element whose purpose is not yet clear in one area, and explain its cause in a later area's notes or environment.
Place a written warning at an entrance to set expectations and raise stakes without dialogue.
when: Designing the entry to a dangerous area.
why: Text at the threshold communicates stakes efficiently.

text: Put a secret's full history in optional lore such as letters or diaries, while main dialogue hints at it earlier, so progress is never blocked.
when: Designing how a late-revealed motive is delivered in a game.
why: Optional lore rewards curious players without gating the main case.

text: Environmental clues such as cellars and overgrown roads can reveal a former settlement, and a surviving family name can tie a living household to a documented event.
when: When designing environmental storytelling for an in-game world.
why: Physical details let the player infer history without reading a document.

text: Expose variables like water depth, temperature or flow as readable numbers, so players reason whether an event could have occurred and can test conditions to isolate its cause.
when: Designing an effect that varies with the environment.
why: Testing conditions lets players isolate the cause.

text: Leave readable traces such as wet footprints, dust, missing keys, wear marks, debris or spill patterns whose placement records what happened, so players reconstruct the event.
when: Designing puzzles or spaces that tell a past event based on physical evidence.
why: Readable traces let players reconstruct what happened, and consistent placement lets them infer the sequence.

text: A defensive position inside an isolated room protects its occupant but brings no outside help.
Dry, flaky snow can make it impossible to tell whether a line of prints was walked inward or outward, so the doubt should be recorded explicitly.
when: reading direction from prints in dry, flaky snow
why: The surface may not preserve the orientation of the walker's steps.

text: The pattern of studs or prints pointing inward or outward shows the direction someone moved, so footprints can indicate entry or exit.
when: Footprints are visible on a surface
why: Print orientation records the direction of travel

text: A container with mechanical features such as chains or a hasp can be used to sink an object and retrieve it later, so its features hint at how the item was hidden.
when: Assessing an object's function from its physical features.
why: Mechanical features reveal the intended method of hiding or recovery.

text: Keep creature reactions consistent so players can reinterpret them when new information arrives.
A hidden cache behind a wall can leave signs such as fresh mortar, texture mismatch or dust that a careful player can find.
when: Designing concealed objects in walls or floors.
why: Recent alteration usually differs from the surrounding surface.

text: Plant an object or unexplained sound early in a level so a later reveal feels fair to the player.
why: clues seen earlier make a reveal feel earned rather than arbitrary

text: Let players find disguise pieces in a shop or costume chest, so the impersonation becomes a discoverable trail they can follow.
when: Designing a mystery where players must reconstruct a disguise.
why: Traceable supply sources let players infer the impersonation.

text: In a locked-room puzzle, snow or mud tracks serve as a fixed record that narrows the possible escape routes.
when: designing locked-room or sealed-location puzzles

text: Give weapons or tools a handling trace, such as grip wear or unusual prints, that reveals how the act was done.
Environmental interruptions such as fog or a bell can delay a reveal and control its pacing.
Plan leads that deliberately fade and return later, since a paused thread keeps suspense alive between active discoveries.
when: When designing the sequence of leads in a mystery or quest chain.
why: Lulls between discoveries give tension a second wind when the thread returns.

text: Place a single piece of furniture in front of a locked connecting door so that a careful player can discover the listening spot.
when: Designing a level with adjoining empty rooms.

text: Earthworks, old paths and worn ground can show how long a site was used and by whom, without any written record.
when: Designing historic sites
why: Physical wear communicates use

text: Naming how many others know a secret and a witness who will attend makes the recipient believe the matter is contained and cannot be quietly buried.
when: when confronting a person who may try to evade or hide facts
why: A visible, limited circle of knowers removes the recipient's hope that the matter will fade.

text: Environmental objects can carry state, such as a crumpled note beneath a body or a burned scrap in a grate, encoding a hidden event the player can reconstruct.
why: Physical arrangement records what happened in a place.

text: An environmental cue such as an animal disturbing soil can reveal a buried item, rewarding careful searching.
Stride spacing and stumble marks can reveal a figure's state, such as fleeing or injured, through the physical record left in the level.
when: a tracked figure moves through the level
why: gait changes reflect the figure's condition

text: A vessel that grounds on a falling tide stays stuck until recovered, so grounding is a costly failure when water levels drop.
when: when water level is falling during a crossing
why: the water drops below the hull and the vessel cannot float free

text: Newer floor decals such as dust, blood or water overwrite older ones, so the visible layer shows the latest movement and players must infer the earlier sequence.
when: Floor decals record movement in a dungeon.

text: Marks left in the environment, such as footprints, dents and cut grass, record the direction and force of past actions.
Rain, trampling and routine use can blur or erase prints, or create false marks, so examine the scene quickly before evidence is lost.
when: When evidence depends on weather, elapsed time or foot traffic.
why: Environmental change removes the traces an investigation needs.

text: 1) Collect the times of every check on a door. 2) Order them with the last sighting of the occupant. 3) Bound the period in which the door's state changed using the nearest checks on either side.
when: When a door's state change must be dated
why: Bounding the window between checks narrows when the change could have occurred.

text: 1) Mark each faction victim's body with that faction's symbol. 2) Add the symbol and its meaning to the player's journal lookup. 3) Let players match the symbol to the victim and group.
1) Sort footprints by owner using size, sole pattern, patches and wear. 2) Eliminate candidate owners whose known prints do not match.

1) Give a disguise a visible oddity that makes it seem trivial. 2) Let the odd trait be inconsistent in private. 3) Let attentive NPCs have a way to see through it. 4) Reveal the true role at a scripted story beat.
when: Designing infiltration or stealth disguises.
why: Trivial appearance grants access, while the tell gives attentive observers a route to suspicion.

text: Give environmental inscriptions and damage marks at least two plausible readings, so player interpretation changes a route, key or door and can be tested against other clues.
when: Designing puzzles in a game level.
why: Interpretation then has consequences in play.

text: Add physical evidence such as casings, holes, scorch marks, disarray, damp clothing or fresh tracks that can support or contradict an NPC's stated account or location.
why: Physical evidence gives players a check on what they are told.

text: Place environmental triggers such as heat, light, or movement so that the player's elimination of them leads to the hidden cause.
when: Designing an unexplained effect, such as a sigil that appears in a level.
why: Players can rule out visible conditions and reach the hidden trigger by elimination.

text: Let a damaged journal or inscription show gaps, and accept any completion that fits both the visible letters and the surviving sense.
when: Designing a text puzzle built from fragments.
why: Multiple valid completions let players reach the same conclusion by different routes.

text: Support player deductions from odd behaviour, such as a locked door or a startled reaction, with clear environmental cues.
when: Players must infer something from an NPC's unexplained action
why: Clear cues let players reason to a checkable conclusion

text: Place mud, dust or sand where creatures move so footprint sizes and strides reveal how many moved a victim.
when: Designing environments that record movement.
why: Printed traces convey count and role.

text: Make the environment leave expected traces, such as wet footprints or dust, so their absence becomes a meaningful clue when the setting should have produced them.
when: A scene where the player is expected to read tracks.
why: A missing trace only tells the player something if the world normally produces it.

text: Place one unexplained action in a level, such as a door opened for no clear reason, as a designed clue that the player must interpret.
when: Puzzle or mystery levels.
why: An unexplained action invites the player to form and test hypotheses.

text: Make a trap mechanism discoverable from the object itself, so a careful player can notice it before triggering it.
when: Designing a puzzle item with a hidden danger
why: Fair discovery makes the harm a lesson rather than an arbitrary penalty

text: Place small environmental tells, such as a curtain out of place or a figure angled wrongly, that a careful player can notice.
when: Building a staged scene that should hint at deception.
why: Subtle tells reward observant players and make staging discoverable.

text: Offer a disguised survey of a location before the main puzzle, so the player learns the layout as a different character.
Offer a staged-accident explanation that careful players can disprove by checking floor layouts and NPC positions.
when: Designing a misleading accident in a fair mystery.

text: Place disguise tells such as ill-fitting clothing or a spotted false feature in the environment for observant players to notice.
when: When a level contains a disguised character
why: Rewards observation with a clear, discoverable clue

text: Show footprints in mud, snow or dust, and let an object in the wrong spot reveal recent movement.
Use countable features such as steps, doors or windows as puzzle keys, so a count that matches a clue identifies the right location.
Make a prop's residue purpose discoverable from the game world, such as a workshop tool or lubricant, so players reason from it rather than guess.
when: a prop carries residue that links to a puzzle

text: Make ambient sounds diagnostic: a lever click or a dropped object in an adjacent room should be reproducible by the player to test a hypothesis.
when: designing environmental audio clues
