why: reproducible sounds let players test their reasoning

text: Let environmental objects carry meaning the player can work out from the room layout.
Place environmental inconsistencies, such as light levels, patrol routes, or blood placement, so that only together do they point toward the real scene.
when: Designing a crime scene the player must reconstruct.
why: Each clue alone is ambiguous, so the player must combine them.

text: Disorder can signal haste or struggle, yet may be innocent once the room's purpose is known; the most dramatic reading is not always the real one.
when: When interpreting debris, disturbance or scattered objects after an event: treat disorder as evidence of urgency, but check the room's purpose before concluding a struggle.
why: Disorder signals urgency and can point to what happened, but ordinary disorder may have an innocent explanation.

text: Place a decoy item or sign initial at a suggestive location as a blind the player must test rather than trust; it misleads until a later clue exposes it.
when: Designing environmental clues or placing hidden objects in authored or generated levels

text: Hold an arrested companion until the player finds a witness who contradicts the physical evidence, so the false solution can be overturned.
when: A false solution has been reached but the real culprit is unknown.
why: A gate tied to contradicting evidence rewards continued investigation.

text: A false trail can lead out of a location while the decisive object that disproves it is hidden on an inside floor of the same location.
when: Designing an outdoor or multi-floor level with a misleading path.
why: The player follows the outward trail and only finds the inside evidence by searching thoroughly.

text: Place a decoy objective that looks like the real goal but resolves to nothing, to test whether players check their assumptions.
Arrange areas so each yields a plausible culprit and a fresh discovery in the next area breaks it, forming a chain of false solutions.
when: Structuring a multi-area investigation level
why: Each new area overturns the previous suspect, sustaining progression.

text: 1) Place a decoy clue such as a glowing object or a set of tracks that points to a dead end. 2) Let the player's failed search expose the decoy.
when: when building a mystery or dungeon that should mislead before revealing the true source
why: The decoy is believable enough to be pursued, and its failure teaches the player to test explanations.

text: Use an inconsistent loot choice as a counter-clue that signals a non-obvious actor.
when: Designing evidence that conflicts with a default culprit profile
why: Odd choices of items raise doubt about an obvious suspect

text: Make the easiest reading correct for early events and let it fail only when a later event arrives.
when: when designing a sequence of clues that should mislead before revealing the truth
why: The player commits to a plausible model that a later event must then correct.

text: Furniture clamped to the floor keeps a constant position relative to nearby fixtures, giving players a stable reference for planning paths or traps.
Physical features carry meaning, such as a line of floating barriers marking a tidal approach to a settlement.
Show a routine, such as a steady wind, water level or guard rotation, before changing it, so the change reads as a clue.
Equipment such as a hidden-lining helmet or a traceable loot item can reveal who was prepared for a fight.
when: designing items that carry clues about their owner
why: Preparation shown through gear tells players who anticipated conflict.

text: A feature seen earlier in neutral form changes meaning when it reappears under new conditions, becoming a route or a warning.
when: when the same environment element returns later
why: the changed context gives the old detail new function

text: Failed forced-entry attempts can leave persistent scratches as world state that guards can later discover.
when: a lock or object is tampered with and not repaired

text: A found object that raises a new question can serve as the trigger for the player's next goal.
A fixture that changes state, such as a phone marked out of order, redirects where people go and what they do in a space.
when: When a fixture's state affects movement or access.

text: A switch can be operated from beneath the floor by a line through a floor hole, cutting power without any visible wiring.
Give each room or character a known set of expected items, so a missing item such as a key, tool or cup becomes a clue about who moved it.
when: Designing a space or character with possessions, or rooms with clue objects
why: Known sets make absence readable.

text: Test whether a fitting performs its apparent job; a mismatch between construction or position and function may mean it is a dummy or a conduit to another space.
when: A fixture's appearance suggests a plain use.
why: Appearance alone does not reveal whether a fitting works.

text: Show the player a partial trace of a hidden change, such as a missing item or fresh mark, so it can be deduced.
Hide a key or document in a pocket or torn seam on NPC or player gear, and let a tear show that an item was pulled out in a fight.
Connect a fixture to a route, such as a vent into an adjacent room, so players must reason about what could pass through it.
Place injuries, fixtures and furniture so the player can measure their relation, such as a wound matching a lamp bracket's height.
Name locations so the label hints at their function, such as a name fragment that suggests a sluice, so players can reason from the name.
Make a recorded or automated sound suggest a room was occupied at a time when it was not, giving players a false timeline to test.
when: designing a timed clue for players
why: players must test the timeline against other evidence

text: Plant a device that fails under certain conditions, so the player's trial and error reveals how the mechanism works.
Hold a ranged device on a fixed line with a clamp or fixture so its shot travels in a predictable direction.
when: when a device must hit a specific point without a person aiming it
why: a steady mount keeps the trajectory consistent

text: Give hidden-object puzzles one partial change that fits no obvious purpose, to signal an unfinished plan or a second actor.
when: designing a hidden-object clue
why: A purposeless partial change invites the player to question the obvious explanation.

text: Evidence of forced entry, such as a broken window, can reveal a route that the visible layout alone did not show.
when: when a hidden route must be discoverable
why: Physical damage signals a passage the map did not mark

text: A lock opened without tool marks or damage suggests a genuine key or copy, since forcing or picking usually leaves visible marks.
why: Visual evidence tracks how the lock was opened.

text: A forced lock is evidence in itself: an intruder who accepted a visible risk of discovery probably valued the object inside.
when: when a sealed space or locked container shows signs of entry
why: the intruder accepted a visible risk

text: Someone already inside has no need to force a barrier, so signs of forced entry suggest the person came from outside.
when: A barrier that could be opened from inside shows signs of forcing.
why: Forcing is needed only by those without access.

text: A tool made for forcing locks points to illegal entry and narrows the set of people likely to have used it.
Forcing a joint during rigidity leaves it loose afterward, so a limp joint amid set joints signals tampering.
when: A body is rigid except for one loose joint
why: Forcing breaks the joint's stiffening

text: Forcing a barrier can destroy the traces of earlier tampering, so the act that seems to confirm the lock hides the trick.
when: the barrier is forced open by those trying to help

text: A fragile prop left in a covert entry path can add a penalty, rewarding players who clear it before entering.
when: designing covert entry routes

text: Forcing a locked door takes several attempts and leaves damage, and the broken bolt becomes a physical trace of the entry.
when: when a key is missing and the lock must be defeated

text: A locked obstacle can resist a weak first attempt and yield to a stronger second attempt, signalling the player to find better means.
when: designing locked doors
why: Graduated failure teaches the player that the obstacle is passable.

text: Forcing a door can injure people, destroy evidence inside, or make the scene look different from how the intruder left it.
when: Deciding whether to break into a locked room.
why: Force is destructive and irreversible, so it must be weighed against what the room may hold.

text: Forcing a lock or door is loud and dangerous, alerting those inside, so bystanders must be kept clear.
why: Force produces noise that alerts those inside.

text: 1) Record the lock and frame condition before forcing. 2) Force the door. 3) Lock the affected rooms and secure their keys to keep the scene closed.
when: when a door must be broken open to enter a sealed room
why: forcing destroys the original state of the lock and frame

text: 1) Identify the tool that could make the mark. 2) Confirm the mark matches that tool. 3) Confirm the suspect possessed the tool. 4) Confirm the suspect needed to force the entry.
when: A barrier shows signs of forcing and the question is who forced it.
why: Each link must hold, so a weak link breaks the whole inference.

text: 1) Listen at the door to judge the threat. 2) Plan the breach so one person forces the door while others wait ready nearby. 3) Enter, then search the scene in order.
when: when delay could cost a life
why: coordinated entry keeps the breach controlled

text: 1) Check every access point to the locked room, such as keyhole and second door. 2) Announce identity and the discovery, and give the occupant a chance to open. 3) If there is no reply, force the door.
when: A locked room may hold a witness and all other access has been tried.
why: Escalating in order gives the occupant a fair chance and confirms that force is needed.

text: 1) Concentrate force on the bolt and a nearby bar until they weaken. 2) Drive a heavy movable object into the door as a ram. 3) Repeat until the fastening gives.
when: When a door is fastened and no other exit exists

text: Forcing a sealed room gains access and information but destroys the original scene, so breaking in trades speed against evidence.
when: when designing a barrier that players can break

text: Build some forgeries into the game with a detectable mismatch, so a careful player can catch them.
when: Designing deceptive in-world evidence
why: A detectable flaw rewards attention and keeps deception fair

text: In a forged-letter puzzle, the player should compare the document's contents, not only its seal or handwriting, to find the forgery.
when: Designing a document-forgery puzzle.
why: Content can reveal inconsistencies that surface imitation hides.

text: A lock or code can reject a forged key by checking for impossible perfection, such as an exact copy of a seeded random flaw.
when: when designing anti-forgery checks

text: Build a fake death from checkable pieces such as a grave, register entry and body, and let the player check each piece.
when: When designing a staged death in a mystery
why: Each verifiable piece gives the player a way to expose the lie

text: Let a found letter's physical details, such as trimmed margins or mismatched paper, lead the player to a room in the level where it was made.
when: Designing a document puzzle in a level.
why: Physical traces give the player a concrete route back to the source.

text: Build item puzzles in which a forged letter's handwriting does not match a sample the player has found, so the mismatch is discoverable.
when: Designing document-based puzzles for a game.
why: A discoverable mismatch rewards the player for comparing evidence rather than trusting the document.

text: Give an npc's handwriting a distinctive letter form that players can spot across several documents, so forged notes can be matched against it.
when: Designing forged-note clues.
why: A recurring distinctive form lets players compare documents.

text: Let the player send an NPC a forged message with scripted reactions such as pausing, looking around, reading or hiding, so the reactions reveal the NPC's allegiance.
when: Designing a loyalty or deception check in a game.
why: Observable reactions give the player evidence about hidden allegiances.

text: End a dungeon with an in-world record giving a false official explanation, and let the player's findings contradict it so the player decides which account to trust.
Give the player a fake trail, such as a footprint or item, plus a second object that exposes the forger, such as a shoe or tool the suspect holds.
when: Designing a puzzle where a clue has been planted.
why: The second object gives the player a way to detect the forgery.

text: Give a forged in-game letter a correct hand but wrong directions; players who visited can catch the errors, and their pattern hints at the writer.
when: designing a forged document players must evaluate
why: checkable errors let players test the letter against what they already learned

text: A quest can deliver a forged letter from an NPC to lure an enemy to a set location and time.
when: Designing a lure or trap quest.
why: A trusted-looking letter gives the player a reason to set a trap and the enemy a reason to walk into it.

text: Build haunted-seeming effects from hidden mechanisms, such as a creaking panel, wire, secret stair, or an actor moving objects on a scripted path, that players can find; track who could reach each spot.
when: Designing a haunted, trick-based, or ghost encounter in a location
why: Discoverable mechanisms let apparent supernatural events resolve into traceable physical causes

text: Use weather, lighting and changes to landmarks to signal dread without dialogue.
when: Setting a tense mood in a location
why: Visual and environmental cues convey threat efficiently.

text: Use a ritual or performance as cover for a character's exit, and reward players who watch the performers rather than the spectacle.
when: Designing a scene where a character must leave unnoticed.
why: Spectacle draws attention, so a watchful player can catch the departure.

text: 1) Give the haunted effect a hidden human or mechanical cause. 2) Offer rival explanations, each leaving distinct checkable traces, such as a hidden door versus a sound effect. 3) Let an NPC offer a supernatural excuse the player can test against the traces.
when: Designing a supernatural encounter or haunting with an unclear or rational cause
why: Distinct traces let players test which explanation holds and reach the truth through testing

text: Seed a mundane hazard, such as a lamp, oil spill or flammable drape, early in an NPC joke, complaint or note so the player recalls it when it becomes relevant.
when: when a later event depends on an earlier hazard
why: A casual mention hides its significance until the player needs it.

text: A dropped flame can ignite nearby flammable material, so a light source used carelessly near fuel can start a fire during a search.
when: when light is used near fuel or fabric
why: Flammable material catches fire from an open flame.

text: Place dangerous tools in plain sight in a room and let them become relevant in a later scene, while attention stays on other things.
when: When designing rooms with potentially lethal objects
why: Visible but unremarked items become meaningful once the player needs them

text: Attach a hazard to retrieving or reading the final document, such as a collapsing stack or timed trap, so the reveal itself becomes a risk.
when: When the final reveal is placed in a physical location.
why: Making the reveal dangerous to reach ties the narrative payoff to the gameplay tension.

text: A periodic hazard that publishes its cycle lets the player plan a crossing inside a safe window, so timing itself becomes the puzzle.
Irregular timing of an effect, such as lights failing at random intervals, prevents anyone from catching the method while keeping the effect mechanically fair.
A timed hazard, such as fog rolling over the route during a climactic encounter, closes the map's path and forces the player to act before it disappears.
A drugged or altered state inside a sealed room can serve as a time-gated hazard.
when: dungeon or locked-room hazard design

text: Use a moving hazard as a clock. Estimate the minutes left before it covers the route, and act early to keep a safety margin.
when: when an environmental hazard closes an escape path

text: In a stealth room, place two sensor points with overlapping sightlines and tie a visible world cue, such as a lamp going dark, to a shared alert.
when: designing a room with multiple guards or detection points
why: the shared cue tells the player the alert is linked

text: Make a hazard's true source a separate actor, such as a hidden NPC or past event, that the player can find and identify, and let the player's first explanation be plausibly wrong.
when: Designing a level hazard that hides a deeper cause.
why: A wrong first explanation drives investigation toward the real source.

text: Build a sanctuary that is actually a trap, with locked doors and an NPC host whose manner shifts from welcoming to threatening when the player is cornered.
when: Designing a safe-seeming location that becomes dangerous.
why: A shift in host behavior signals the change of state to the player.

text: A hazard can be disguised as an environmental event, and the player must find the underlying mechanism to tell the two apart.
when: Designing traps that resemble environmental effects
why: Players who investigate the mechanism distinguish a designed trap from natural danger

text: Use a threatened frame as a mid-game escalation that forces the player to protect an ally before the main truth is available.
when: Escalating stakes in the middle of an investigation.
why: Protecting an ally raises urgency before the core answer is reachable.

text: A bait mechanic lets the player place a lure with the right properties to force a hidden enemy or clue to appear.
when: when designing a puzzle around a hidden enemy or clue
why: The player's correct setup produces a visible response they can act on.

text: When a crowd is about to lock its verdict, give the player a timer to reach a specific witness, so exposure becomes a race against the crowd.
1) Start with a watch on a door. 2) Force a breach. 3) Enter a cabinet or inner room. 4) Yield a new document at each stage that raises the stakes.
when: Structuring a level that builds toward a reveal
why: Each stage raises tension and gives a new piece of information, so the player's stakes grow steadily.

text: 1) Place a poisoned object the player must avoid or swap. 2) Let the player's deduction determine which object is dangerous. 3) Resolve the case when the culprit consumes it.
when: Designing a climactic mechanic for an investigation
why: Ties the final action to the player's reasoning rather than a cutscene.

text: Give players a prearranged visible cue, such as a light or sound, that tells them when a planned action is safe.
when: A plan depends on a timed moment the player must recognize.
why: A clear cue lets the player act at a set moment instead of guessing.

text: At a climactic door, make the expected boss absent and place a lesser enemy's corpse on the floor, reversing the player's threat model within one room.
when: Staging a boss reveal that changes what the player believes
why: A single room that overturns expectations changes the player's model of the threat immediately.

text: State the lure's required conditions, such as freshness or strength, in the environment so players can work out the correct setup.
when: when a puzzle depends on a lure with specific properties
why: Explicit cues make the solution deducible rather than guessed.

text: Escalate across encounters, using a false victory followed by a new threat, and plant the cause of the later threat in earlier rooms.
when: Designing a dungeon's encounter sequence
why: Returning players can reinterpret earlier rooms once the cause is revealed

text: Give players a brief warning cue before a danger, such as a sound or light change, and vary how reliable that cue is across the level.
when: before traps or ambushes

text: Give players a partial map and require them to pace out distances before probing walls for a hidden feature.
when: Designing a concealed door or secret puzzle.
why: Measuring turns the search into a skill rather than a guess.

text: Hidden routes such as trapdoors, screens or ceiling openings can be found only by reasoning from sounds or damage, which makes them discoverable through deduction.
when: Designing a sealed room with a concealed entry.
why: Indirect clues reward reasoning and keep the route from being trivially visible.

text: Assuming a secret entrance explains a crime is a mistake when the attack itself could not be carried out by an ordinary person present in view.
1) Wait for darkness. 2) Enter through a rear barrier. 3) Stay out of sight of windows. 4) Ambush whoever opens the door.
when: Forced entry carries noise risk and the approach must stay hidden until the occupant comes out.
why: Concealment keeps the element of surprise and avoids alerting the occupant before the door opens.

text: Avoid hiding a clue in a place the story marks as secret, because searchers check those spots first.
when: Choosing a hiding place for a key clue.
why: A hidden drawer or similar marked spot is the first place investigators search.

text: When no physical route fits the time available, signal the gap with a hidden passage or an explicitly unexplained effect rather than leaving the player to assume a route exists.
when: Designing a space where a figure can vanish.
why: A player who cannot find a route needs a clear cue that the impossibility is intended.

text: Make hiding spots finite and checkable: state traffic patterns, sightlines, exits, open-plan layout and features such as furniture height or drawn curtains, so players eliminate spots by logic.
when: Designing a space where something or someone is hidden and players must search or deduce its location.
why: Explicit information lets deduction replace luck, and controlled sightlines keep the set of possible hiding places small enough to verify.

text: Hiders exploit searchers' reluctance to recheck places already dismissed or finished, choosing a spot judged unlikely or a site where a search has ended.
when: a disappearance is planned, or a hidden item must survive a completed search
why: searchers rarely re-check places they dismissed and treat a finished search as exhaustive

text: An anonymous writer who omits names and signature, disguises the hand, and delivers in person expects to be recognised by the recipient.
when: An anonymous note is delivered in person

text: A person disposing of an object often picks a mundane spot that looks like it will destroy it, such as a fire or a pile of fuel.
when: when concealing an item from searchers
why: An apparent destruction discourages a closer look at the spot.

text: Owners tend to hide valuables in places they consider safer than the obvious container, so the obvious container may be a decoy.
when: when a theft involves an obvious safe or chest
why: owners treat the obvious hiding place as the one thieves check first

text: Elaborate precautions can also serve to draw attention to one expected route and make observers overlook another.
when: A suspect's protections focus on one obvious route.
why: Attention concentrates on the most visible safeguard, hiding an overlooked route.

text: A person who fears exposure may give only a partial name in a record, keeping others unsure of where they are or what they look like.
when: a written identity could expose the person to strangers
why: a fully traceable record creates risk

text: A figure who hides and keeps distance is read as a stalker, though the same behavior can be protective.
when: A character follows another unseen.
why: Concealment is interpreted as hostile intent.

text: A person who has hidden something tends to add a second obstacle at each access point, because the secret seems obvious to them and they assume others will find it too.
when: when concealing a secret the hider already knows well
why: Having found the secret easily, the hider overestimates how easily others will find it.

text: A person who believes they are hidden tends to stay still and wait for a passerby to leave, rather than act.
when: a hidden person sees someone approaching
why: they assume they have not been noticed

text: A person behind a closed door may also be listening, so they can react to sounds made outside.
when: a listener is outside a closed door

text: People and animals avoid isolated, dangerous places, so anyone seen going there stands out.
when: In a remote location with a known hazard
why: Avoidance makes visitors conspicuous

text: Valuables a person keeps hidden on their body reveal what they value and expect to need in an emergency.
Concealment often targets what an object would reveal about its owner's identity, rather than the hider's own needs.
Concealed spaces behind removed boards or panels can hide a person or object from search.
Hidden items are often kept in clothing linings, sleeves and pockets, where the holder expects no one will search.
A hiding place fails in full view of a main entrance or constant foot traffic, but evidence in a confusing, rarely visited area stays concealed because few pass through.
when: judging whether a concealment was feasible, or placing hidden evidence in a level
why: observers and passersby would notice movement in busy spots, and low traffic lowers the chance of discovery

text: Blend a clue among ordinary or similar items rather than letting it stand out; players then find it by comparison, and conspicuous clues trigger suspicion and reduce fair surprise.
when: Placing clues for later discovery in a collection of objects.
why: Similarity disguises the one item that differs, and conspicuous clues trigger suspicion.

text: A hiding place works best among features people do not examine, such as service access points or loose boards left for routine maintenance.
when: Choosing or searching for a hiding spot in a building.
why: Ordinary structure is rarely inspected, so a concealed item there looks unremarkable.

text: Rarely worn clothing and seldom-opened containers are good places for small items to be hidden or forgotten.
when: A small item is missing and some garments or containers have not been used recently.
why: The owner is less likely to check places they have not handled for a while.

text: A hunted party can stay unseen by settling in a crowded, poor district, where strangers draw little notice.
when: a party must disappear among ordinary people and cannot rely on authorities
why: Few idle watchers and busy residents mean strangers go unremarked.

text: Ask whether a hiding place fits the effort spent obtaining the item; a careless spot for a hard-won object can count against the theory.
when: An item was concealed and its concealment is part of the explanation.
why: Concealment that does not match the value of the item is less likely.

text: Strong light on a space can exclude it as a hiding place for a person.
why: a hidden person would be exposed in strong light

text: To make a clue harder to notice, remove it rather than alter it, so the player must search for the absence itself.
when: designing a concealed clue
why: A changed object invites comparison with its earlier state, while a removed one does not.

text: A small hole sealed with matching material shows where a substance was inserted, and it is easy to miss on the surface.
why: the repair hides the entry point from casual inspection

text: Plant movement patterns, such as use of a back door, as readable tells that signal concealment.
when: designing NPC routes and behaviour
why: players learn to read movement

text: Hidden items are often placed in an ordinary routine setting, such as a repair shop, where they look normal rather than in hard-to-reach spots.
when: when designing or searching for a concealed object
why: Legitimate-looking settings draw less suspicion than unusual hiding places

text: A hiding spot that projects from a wall can give a view of the room while keeping the observer concealed.
Hiding places are usually where searchers do not look first: high above the floor, inside tall or decorative furniture, or behind ornament.
when: When placing hidden compartments or secrets in a room.
why: Searchers check eye-level and obvious surfaces first, so unusual positions go unexamined.

text: Place hidden listening spots behind thin walls adjacent to unused rooms, such as an empty, locked-off or to-let room, and show the layout early.
when: Designing a concealed observer or eavesdropping position.
why: An unused adjoining room gives an unseen place to stand and listen.

text: Placing a hidden target in the last-checked, most enclosed space creates a natural climax for a search.
when: Designing a search sequence that builds to a finale

text: Add a route with recognisable points where the player can be spotted, so stealth and disguise choices matter.
when: designing tailing routes
why: known detection points give stealth meaning

text: Define a location by the things it could conceal, such as loose floorboards, cramped gaps between floors or screened shrubbery.
when: a location must hide something or record a past action

text: Hide key proof in a location only one character knows, so the hiding place is itself a secret clue the player must discover.
when: When designing a clue that must be reached through knowledge of a specific place.
why: Restricting knowledge of the hiding spot makes the location part of the puzzle.

text: A search tool that gives a sound cue on contact helps the player find hidden items out of sight.
when: When designing hidden items in a game world
why: Audio feedback locates objects the player cannot see

text: Hide a container's key on a routine item the owner carried, so a search of personal belongings reveals what a room search misses.
when: When placing the key to a locked container in a mystery space.
why: Players search habitual items and effects, rewarding attention to character routine.

text: Hide a disguised entity in plain sight, such as an ordinary-looking mount or an NPC's equipment, so a recognition check exposes it later.
when: Designing an enemy or threat disguised as something common.
why: A disguise visible in the scene rewards observant players and makes the reveal fair.

text: Each added precaution creates a new witness who can contradict the story, so more precautions add exposure rather than safety.
Removing a postmark or similar marker erases where a message came from and how it travelled.
when: A message's origin must be hidden
why: Postmarks are the physical record of origin and route

text: Moving through lit, open spaces can draw less suspicion than hiding in dim corners, since observers search hidden places first.
when: Designing a stealth or disguise path
why: Suspicion tends to focus on concealed spots.

text: Items left in an open shared container, such as a bag in an open hall, can be reached by anyone with access during a diversion window.
when: when a diversion leaves a space unattended
why: The target is absent, so the container is unguarded.

text: A player who moves alone is more vulnerable to ambush, so solo movement carries a visible risk.
when: A player separates from companions in an area with hidden threats
why: A lone target gives a watcher an opening

text: Restraining a concealing person's arms forces their hands forward, lifting the coat and revealing what they hide.
A building with a second exit lets a moving target lose a follower, who is left stranded at the first entrance.
A stealth or stash mechanic can score candidate spots by observer count and sight lines, and the scores can shift as NPC routines change.
when: Designing a system that lets an agent choose hiding spots.
why: Observer counts and sight lines change with NPC movement, so the best spot changes too.

text: A hiding place chosen from the owner's known habits is predictable, so anyone who knows those habits can find the object; assuming a careful person hides predictably can mislead investigators.
why: A hiding place is only concealed if it does not follow a pattern others can read.

text: Objects moved or handled before investigators arrive alter traces, can drop out of the record, and mislead about the original scene and who was present.
when: Investigating a scene others had access to first.
why: Prior handling alters traces, and an object's later presence then suggests the wrong people were on the scene.

text: Searching a hideout can alert the person hiding there, so plan the approach first.
Elimination of hiding places depends on assumptions about how the hider thinks; if the hider thinks differently, the deduction points to the wrong place.
when: Reasoning about a hider's choice of location.
why: The constraints used depend on the hider's reasoning, which may differ.

text: Containers and tools used to hide an item carry their own traces, such as scent, that can reveal what was hidden and where.
A precaution against one trace can leave another, such as changing footwear to avoid soft-ground prints while hard surfaces still show prints.
Once players learn that obvious objects can hide clues, every openly placed object looks suspicious and the concealment effect is lost.
when: Plain-view hiding is used repeatedly across a game.
why: Players generalize the trick and begin searching obvious places.

text: Ignoring masking factors such as engine noise, distance, or hidden injuries leads to misreading silence as meaning nothing happened.
Assuming concealment is safe is a mistake: a nearby person reaching toward the hiding place can nearly expose the observer.
when: the observer is close to the people being watched

text: A hiding place obvious to a searching NPC defeats its purpose, so search routines should check the most likely spots first.
when: Designing NPC search behaviour for hidden items.
why: A search that checks likely spots first finds the obvious concealments.

text: 1) List every concrete place something could be concealed. 2) Rule each place in or out with a specific reason, such as fire risk or areas already searched. 3) Keep the open places and check them against the hider's likely habits.
when: Locating a concealed object whose owner could reach it but a casual searcher could not, or deciding who could have been concealed and where.
why: Constraint elimination narrows the search to the most plausible place.

text: 1) List who visits the place on weekdays and weekends. 2) Estimate how often each group visits. 3) Compare the visit rate with the claimed hiding period.
when: a theory depends on how long an object sat in a place before discovery

text: 1) Rule out unusable hiding places by elimination. 2) Choose the most sensible remaining cover. 3) Copy the look of the crew so you pass as one of them. 4) Move quietly and stay still until needed.
when: movement is confined to a vehicle and a cover identity exists

text: 1) Identify the trace the suspect's action was meant to remove. 2) Check whether an existing protection already covered that trace. 3) Judge whether the stated reason fits the action.
when: A suspect's action can be explained by a precaution.

text: 1) Find a hidden vantage point with a view of the target's location. 2) Make a small opening for observation. 3) Keep the watch running over several nights until the target's pattern is caught.
when: a secret act must be witnessed

text: 1) Move into a setting where observers have not seen you. 2) Adopt that setting's routines fully, not just its costume. 3) Keep every routine consistent with the new role.
when: when a suspect must pass among people unfamiliar with them in the new setting

text: 1) Keep one party talking while facing away from the likely hiding place. 2) Coordinate a second party silently to watch from cover. 3) Watch for the listener to move or reveal themselves.
when: When a listener is suspected but a direct approach would alert them
why: Speech that rewards approach makes an eavesdropper move into view without confrontation.

text: Check who could have shared a holding cell with a suspect, since placement can allow contact with the culprit.
when: suspects are held in shared or nearby cells

text: Place occupancy traces in a hideout to signal that a character is nearby, and use a planted note to show the hidden NPC knows of the player.
Keep suspicion of a leak hidden where possible, because a visible reaction alerts the culprit, who will then change the plan.
when: a leak is suspected
why: the culprit adapts once they believe discovery is possible

text: Do not treat an over-careful setup as proof of guilt, since an innocent person may also take precautions.
when: Weighing a suspect's elaborate safeguards.
why: Caution has many innocent causes.

text: After observing, remove any sign of approach, such as a ladder, and hide in cover so the observer is not noticed.
when: leaving an observation point

text: Treat avoided locations as private meeting places, so their presence on the map becomes a clue.
when: When placing locations

text: Place cover positions that give a full view of the target, so the player can watch a route without being exposed.
when: The target is in an open area

text: Make a culprit's concealing action leave a trail, such as a vent opened after a death, so players who notice the unnecessary change can find the route.
when: Designing a puzzle in which the intruder hides the method
why: The act of covering tracks becomes the clue that reveals the method.

text: Define a route as an ordered sequence of doors and occluders so the game can answer whether a path was observable from a given vantage point.
Use an unexplained danger to deter exploration and protect hidden content, such as an NPC or smuggler, in a cursed zone.
when: Designing a level with a secret area that should stay hidden.
why: Players avoid the feared zone, so the hidden content goes unnoticed.

text: Hide a key item inside an unexpected container, such as an animal or bag, and let the player find it through examination or inventory.
why: Unexpected hiding places reward inspection and make the item's location a discovery.

text: Use a physical puzzle, such as a measured spot, to trigger a hidden cellar or pit as a late-level reveal.
Hide a key item in a trusted NPC's private room, so the player finds it by tailing that NPC at night.
Hide a timed sound source behind furniture so it can be found only by a specific check, not by casual inspection.
Hiding evidence in a visible spot can be safer than a concealed hiding place, but both depend on the culprit controlling who passes the location.
when: Choosing how to dispose of incriminating evidence.
why: A concealed item looks more suspicious, while a visible one risks being noticed by an observer.

text: A resource-limited agent is easier to predict and search, while an agent that can restock anywhere is harder to bound.
when: when designing an enemy or pursuer's movement
why: Limits create predictable search areas but can be broken by restocking

text: Tune the distance and sound volume of an approaching entity so its reveal lands on the chosen beat of an encounter.
when: when scripting an approach-and-reveal sequence
why: Distance and volume control when the threat becomes visible

text: A recap screen that lists each clue the player found makes a final reveal feel earned.
when: Designing a game's final-act reveal.
why: The player sees the evidence chain assembled before the conclusion.

text: Leave a visible loose end at the close of a resolved mystery, such as an NPC escaping with a clue, so the player can follow it later.
when: Ending a level or case that should lead to further content
why: An unresolved thread carries the player's interest forward.

text: 1) Define the required linked clues. 2) Allow a partial accusation that leaves one inference open. 3) Show the player which link is missing. 4) Offer an ending that accepts the partial solution with uncertainty.
when: Designing a mystery whose final verdict can be incomplete.
why: A partial ending respects what the evidence supports without forcing a false certainty.

text: 1) Place a trap room where a suspect's reaction to a false clue exposes guilt. 2) Make the player's deduction the trigger. 3) Provide a hazard the player can swap or neutralize as the climax.
when: Designing the final encounter of an investigation level
why: Letting the player act on their own deduction turns the reveal into an interactive decision.

text: Design an ending that releases the agent with partial consequences so the level state persists after the reveal.
when: Concluding a supernatural encounter in a level.
why: Lasting changes make the resolution feel consequential.

text: Tie each lock to its known keyholders so players narrow suspects by method and intruders stay few when entry to a sealed space must be restricted.
when: Designing a locked-room or break-in clue, or a room that must be kept from unauthorised entry.
why: Method-based filtering turns a lock into a deduction tool.

text: Attach each key to a specific NPC and log every handover; track door states like locked, unlocked or bolted, recorded at intervals so players see each carrier and read changes.
when: Designing key custody and locked doors for an investigation game.
why: Logged handovers and door states let players reconstruct access and reason about who could have entered.

text: Track each key as an owned item in game state, so removing or moving it changes who may enter and when a theft could have occurred.
when: Designing locked-room puzzles, lock-and-key puzzles or theft-based mysteries.
why: Custody state keeps access logic consistent and gives the player a basis for timeline deduction.

text: A key's lock type can identify which entry it opens, linking an item to a specific door or route.
when: an item looks like a key with no known lock
why: the lock type narrows which entry the key belongs to

text: Place each object where its owner could reach it, so a missing item can be traced to who had access.
when: designing object placement in a scene
why: Location links an object to a set of possible people.

text: Place a sealed door's key with another character or in another room, so entry becomes a locked-room puzzle with an intended bypass.
when: Designing access puzzles.
why: Separating the key from the door forces the player to find the key or a different route.

text: Place keys in unexpected locations so that access to a locked container changes depending on who holds the key.
when: When designing locked containers and their access rules
why: Misplaced keys shift suspicion to people who could not have been expected to reach the container

text: Label each locked container with the key that opens it, and place the keys where the player can find them, so no lock is a surprise.
when: Designing locked containers and their keys in a level.
why: Identified locks let the player plan their search instead of being blocked by hidden obstacles.

text: Place a copy of a key elsewhere so a key the player believes is unique can be duplicated.
when: Designing key-based access puzzles.
why: Hidden copies reward players who check whether apparent exclusivity holds.

text: When one person holds the only key to a locked room, treat that person as the natural suspect and build the mechanism within the room's fixed fixtures.
A key that opens a container passes custody between holders; if carried away after each use, it limits who can open the container at any moment, learnable from NPC dialogue.
when: when a restricted container is designed
why: the key's movement controls when access is possible

text: Model keys as an ownership graph with holders, copies and past uses, so players deduce who could enter and when from key state.
when: Designing keyed access or a locked room the player must investigate.
why: Graph and key history give the player concrete evidence to reason from.

text: A single lock can fail and be retried repeatedly, so a door and key alone buy only seconds of protection.
Verify who actually held each key, since key ownership may be shared or disputed.
when: an access claim depends on who held a key
why: A recorded owner may not be the person who actually had the key at the time.

text: A lock that opens too easily wastes tension, so the key should cost the searcher some effort to find.
when: When setting how hard it is to open a container.
why: Effortless access removes the sense of discovery.

text: Move a key through NPCs and containers in a fixed order across scenes, requiring two characters to agree before it opens, and log each transfer so players can trace its path.
when: Designing a key item's route or a quest item that passes between NPCs.
why: A visible, defined trail lets the player reconstruct the key's history and sequence.

text: Model lock states and missing keys as a set of routes the player can rule out one at a time.
Turn an item's route through staff routines, such as cleaning schedules, into a tracing puzzle the player can follow.
Require a paired item to open a two-part lock, such as a double key with two ends, and provide a diagram that matches the level layout.
when: when designing locks that need two parts to open
why: Pairing items creates a dependency the player can verify against the plan.

text: Make a key held by an NPC who recently left an area a traceable item, so players can reconstruct where a captive was taken.
when: Designing an item trail that leads to a hidden location
why: Item possession ties an NPC to places and times

text: A key ledger works well when entry is central, but it is weak when keys can be copied or the lock can be bypassed without a key.
Let shared pipes carry sound so NPCs in adjacent spaces can overhear the player.
when: Designing connected rooms or cells
why: Overheard speech creates tension and new information paths

text: Not every hole in a wall should be a passage; some openings can lead to dead-end shafts, so players learn that openings need testing.
when: generating wall breaches or openings in rooms
why: a mix of real and dead-end openings teaches players to verify rather than assume

text: Scatter personal items along approach paths so players can prove a character passed by, even when the room looks untouched.
A chance encounter can open a new area, but the game should also give the player a way to reach it through search.
A floor plan showing where each room sits and who sleeps where indicates which lit opening deserves attention.
when: choosing which opening to observe

text: Let a location change over in-game days through repairs, new structures and new occupants, so early visits preserve evidence that later visits lose.
when: designing an investigation location
why: Time pressure rewards prompt visits

text: Design an NPC's unusual arrival so a player watching the wrong angle misses it, while one watching the right angle catches it.
when: Placing a sightline-dependent event in a level.
why: Rewarding good observation makes the event feel earned.

text: Use a fixed landmark such as a beacon or lit tower as a navigation anchor while the rest of the map grows darker and more dangerous.
A route that looks impossible for one person may work with a helper, so consider whether an accomplice could make it possible.
when: Only one person seems able to reach the route
why: A second actor can complete what one cannot

text: An approach builds tension only when it leads to a clear end point; a long approach without landmarks or pressure drags.
when: when pacing a long journey
why: suspense needs a destination and interim pressure

text: Compare two maps made for different purposes; a feature drawn on one but absent or different on the other can expose something hidden.
when: when one map may omit features another shows
why: the gap between maps can reveal hidden works

text: Give a target location a second approach that avoids the main alerting point, such as a side entrance that bypasses a doorbell.
when: Entry at the usual point would give the party away or is guarded.
why: A silent alternate route keeps the approach unnoticed.

text: Expect unmapped branches in a pursued passage; a plan that assumes one route fails when a second route is used.
when: pursuit enters terrain that has not been mapped
why: an unknown branch can carry a second party into the encounter

text: Fog, dim light, weather and endless or unfinished streets build unease during an approach; a lit entrance and a briefly blocked key door add hesitation before the reveal.
when: designing the journey to a destination; staging an approach to a boss or reveal
why: Atmosphere, disorientation and pacing make the approach feel threatening and shape anticipation.

text: A region graph can tag each edge with a required capability, such as a vehicle, climbing or a key; the player removes edges by finding the matching gate or witness.
when: Generating a level whose routes are gated by abilities
why: Capability tags turn traversal options into a checkable elimination space

text: A lookout whose line of sight is blocked gives a built-in, in-world reason for a witness account to be incomplete.
An angular error at the start of a bearing grows with distance along the line, so a small starting miss can put the endpoint far off.
when: measuring a line of direction
why: the error scales with the length of the line

text: Colour-coded rooms and coloured light steer the player's eye through a layout and can discourage entry into particular areas.
when: A layout needs to guide or deter movement without signage.
why: Colour draws attention and signals which spaces are open or dangerous.

text: When every object has a fixed place, a moved or missing item stands out at once, so departures from the layout reveal tampering without a full search.
when: a space's expected arrangement is known
why: a planned baseline makes deviations obvious

text: If an area's boundaries are never made clear, players cannot test claims about who passed through them.
Assuming a clear sightline when foliage, a curtain or other cover blocks the view leads to wrong judgements about who was seen.
Proposing a route, such as a chimney or roof, before the window and other routes are checked leads to unsupported answers; check routes in order.
when: Reasoning through a sealed room
why: Guessing skips the evidence

text: Accepting a single witness's assurance that no exit exists, without checking the room plan, can hide the route that was actually used.
A checkpoint's records cover only its main route, so a visitor who enters another way passes unrecorded.
when: a guarded area has more than one entry
why: the log only captures traffic through the watched gate

text: Stacked floors and open shafts make it hard to track who was where, so investigators easily lose the sequence of events.
when: Scenes with vertical layouts such as lift wells or multi-storey buildings.
why: Vertical separation hides positions.

text: A layout that seems too familiar may be skipped by players, so the designer should make the key constraints explicit.
A layout is useful only when its features are recorded accurately; approximate plans can mislead the investigation.
when: a plan is drawn from memory or rough notes
why: Errors in the plan propagate into every test

text: An unguarded exit can look like the obvious escape route while its lock state is never checked, so verify it physically.

1) Start from one verifiable fixed point. 2) Place each boundary from that point using bearings and distances. 3) Cross-check against deeds naming neighbours. 4) Confirm with surviving features. 5) Combine independent plans so two fixed boundaries locate a third. 6) Mark each site's confidence.
when: the exact position of a site matters to the sequence of events
why: A single anchor and measured offsets fix positions, while cross-checks and confidence marks limit errors.

text: 1) Anchor the level to one landmark. 2) Place rooms by bearing and distance from it. 3) Check the layout against scattered reference notes. 4) Adjust any room that conflicts with a note.
when: building a level from scattered reference notes
why: A single anchor keeps the layout consistent, and reference notes catch placement errors.

text: 1) Make every visible approach fail the visibility test. 2) Leave one concealed route. 3) Let the player deduce that route by elimination.
when: When designing an ambush or apparition puzzle
why: Elimination of visible options guides the player to the hidden route without explicit hints.

text: 1) Note the building's road frontage. 2) Note its orientation. 3) Match these against old map records. 4) Confirm against present land plots.
when: Locating a building from historical records.

text: Map every route and mark which are visible to NPCs; guard routines should contain predictable gaps, with patrol schedules defining time windows the player can exploit.
when: designing level routes, guard patrols and locked areas guarded by NPCs
why: Visibility and timing define when a route is safe; predictable routines create openings that reward observation.

text: Make a visible sign, such as a forced or broken door or a cleared shelf or tidied area, indicate a second or concealed exit the player must find.
Generated dungeons can place waypoint markers at each junction to support tails and escorts.
Provide a directory or map of candidate locations and let a note's constraints, such as floor count, distance or landmark, eliminate all but one.
why: Explicit constraints make elimination a solvable puzzle

text: Build a dead-end chamber with the same mechanism to confirm a solution, rather than making the first hidden door the answer.
when: Designing hidden door puzzles
why: A repeat confirms the route

text: Apply a consistent supply-path rule to generated items so that trace clues remain coherent across the game.
when: Generating a set of items that players may trace.
why: Contradictory supply paths make trace clues unreliable.

text: Define region boundaries with landmarks such as bridges or roads, and make a dispute depend on which landmark the player finds.
Keep the full solution of a generated mystery as a fixed data record while the player-facing layout varies between runs.
when: Generating mysteries procedurally.
why: A stable solution keeps clues consistent while the presentation changes.

text: Place a marker item the game can check on return, so players can confirm their own route through a dark area.
Let an NPC's directions reference physical landmarks, such as an arch, steps or a name plate, that the player can verify in the layout.
when: A game NPC gives navigation help
why: Verifiable landmarks let players test claims

text: Mark access lines such as paths and their bordering features on the map, connecting the map layout with the physical traces found on site.
when: when preparing a site survey

text: Give players a way to map a level and record doors and sightlines so that navigation in darkness remains fair.
when: in levels where light is limited

text: Use a visible lure, such as a rumored vault, while keeping the true route in plain sight.
Make the necessary route through the level geometry visible, so a careful player can reconstruct how an event such as a disappearance happened.
when: when an event's solution depends on movement through space
why: Players can only solve what the layout lets them trace

text: Make back lanes and service routes look like background while connecting rooms the player is not expected to reach.
when: designing hidden connections
why: plain routes can be found by careful players

text: Give each possible exit of a sealed puzzle room a visible, testable state, such as latch, window or flue, so players can rule options out.
when: designing a sealed room puzzle
why: players can only eliminate options they can check

text: Build a finale room where suspects converge, and let each evidence piece the player assembles unlock the next step of the reveal.
In stealth levels, offer a visible route that guards watch while a hidden route serves as the real exit.
Make hidden routes visible only from certain angles, so players can test their reasoning about exits.
Build branching paths where one option is blocked, so the player's choices narrow naturally.
when: When designing routes where players choose a direction
why: Blocked branches reduce options and point the player toward the remaining route

text: Build entry routes as separate access points with different risk levels, so the player must weigh them.
when: Designing ways into a restricted area
why: Players then make a meaningful risk-versus-timing choice

text: Use exits and sightlines to block a visible culprit's route, so players who test the obvious theory against the layout find the real path.
when: when designing a decoy suspect
why: Testing the decoy reveals the true route.

text: Treat a witness's claimed route or landmark that does not exist on the map as evidence that the account is false.
Waiting at an earlier point or changing elsewhere may reach the same connection with less risk, at a different time cost.
when: when a planned connection is at risk
why: each alternative trades time against safety

text: Fixed landmarks such as carpets, pillars or tiles can serve as measuring references for a puzzle that requires counting movements.
when: Designing a puzzle that depends on counting movements
why: Visible fixed references let the player measure and compare movements.

text: Limit the player's first visit so that the real test becomes a return visit.
when: Designing a location the player must investigate covertly.
why: A first visit is constrained, and the return visit is where the test pays off.

text: A layout whose rooms lead back to places already passed leaves no one able to reconstruct who went where.
when: visitor movement must be hard to trace
why: revisited spaces erase the sequence of movement

text: Overloading a setting with detail, including decoration that serves no purpose, makes the one feature that matters later hard to notice.
Design disorienting layouts that conceal routes, and require the player to work out a path back.
Light sources and angles determine what players see: place an NPC so lighting favours the player's view of their face; a lantern behind the player lights a suspect's face.
Changing light, such as a moved torch, can expose details or figures that earlier lighting hid, so a scene can be re-read once conditions change.
when: When a reveal depends on what the player can see, or when designing visibility-dependent clues.
why: Lighting changes let players re-observe a scene and find what was hidden.

text: Dim light and distance can reduce a viewer's perception to a silhouette, so identification may rest on a single cue such as voice.
when: Viewing a person in low light or at a distance.
why: Features cannot be made out, leaving only partial cues.

text: A mechanism shown in full inside a playful or fairy-tale frame is easy to read past, even though it is fully disclosed.
when: a key detail is presented within a whimsical story or game fiction
why: the light frame lowers attention to the detail

text: A shadow cast across a lit path is an early visual trace of an intruder who is still out of view.
when: a lit area is watched at night
why: Light casts a visible shape before its source is seen

text: In a dark space, one small lit detail can reveal a hidden person's presence through its movement and a distinguishing feature.
when: an unlit area with a moving light source
why: motion draws attention and a lit detail stands out against darkness

text: Lights seen in rooms known to be empty are read as proof that someone is moving about and that something is wrong.
when: when a place expected to be unoccupied shows activity
why: the contradiction with what is known signals danger

text: Light exposure gradually changes fabric colour, so a shade difference between matched items can reflect where each one stood.
when: comparing fabric or padding of matched objects
why: Sunlight and lamplight fade materials unevenly over time.

text: Use light and weather to set mood; they shape what players notice and how a room feels, so soft light can make a scene dreamlike or ominous and support suspense.
why: Lighting controls what is visible and how the space reads.

text: Scan to both sides of a search path, since unexpected evidence may lie off the predicted route.
Items lit but barely used suggest abandonment, while items burned down suggest a longer stay.
Seed background facts lightly early, such as a financial position or a rumour, so that a motive can be picked up later.
when: establishing characters before the plot turns
why: early seeds become usable motives without needing exposition later

text: A performance can cover a simple fact, so look through the performance to reach the core.
when: when a character's behavior seems staged

text: A killing at an hour when the scene has no light implies darkness or a light source the actor carried; if neither is plausible, the scene is probably wrong.
when: Time of death and lighting conditions are known.
why: A violent act needs enough light to be done as described.

text: Keep a hidden inscription invisible until a light source touches it, and let the reveal lapse quickly so players must time their action.
Trigger a resemblance puzzle only when the player passes a specific light source or window, with an NPC crossing the view on a timer.
when: designing a recognition puzzle
why: position and timing control when the clue appears

text: A lit window usually signals that someone is inside, so a visible light can serve as a presence cue.
Build a junction so a short time window shows two NPCs without guaranteeing what the player will see.
why: brief windows create suspense while keeping outcomes uncertain

text: Do not assume a sightline is complete; partial views and angles change what can be seen.
Light levels that change as the player moves toward a key site can increase tension in a confrontation.
when: Staging a confrontation in a level.
why: Shifting light changes visibility and the mood of the encounter.

text: Use dim lighting at a doorway or archway so an NPC's identity is not clear until it is close.
when: When designing a reveal of an approaching NPC
why: Poor light delays recognition and heightens the moment of reveal

text: Gate detailed inspection behind a lighting or time-of-day condition to reward patience.
when: Designing environmental clues

text: A room can have a power or lighting system the player can short out, changing enemies' ability to see, and a puzzle can rely on a fault visible in a separate box.
when: designing a room with controllable lighting
why: tying visibility to a controllable system creates tactical options

text: Light one person's face while the observer sits in shadow: the lit person's reactions stay readable, and the observer watches every movement while staying partly hidden and unnoticed.
when: Arranging a room for questioning, confrontation, or a scene where some characters must watch unseen.
why: Light makes the lit person's reactions visible, while shadow conceals the observer; darkness hides observers while light draws attention to one area.

text: Light sources decide what the player and NPCs clearly see and what sits in shadow; a lit corridor exposes a figure while cluttered dim space lets it hide.
when: Designing lighting for stealth or investigation levels, or deciding where characters can be seen.
why: Light sets what can be perceived and shows who could observe whom in a room.

text: A caller on unlit steps cannot be seen through glass, so the occupant must recognize them by voice.
when: Judging whether an occupant could identify a visitor visually.
why: Poor lighting and sight lines limit what can be seen.

text: A figure that draws back into shadow as others approach stays unidentified, and it is revealed only when it steps into light.
Placing an act where a visible light source makes it possible lets players infer the actor's needs from the location.
when: designing where an event happens in a level

text: A single controllable light source for a room lets one person change what everyone in it can see.
Low raking light across a surface makes shallow depressions visible that flat lighting hides.
when: when inspecting a floor, rug or carpet for impressions
why: shallow relief casts shadows at a low angle

text: Dim light or moonlight can hide a key detail, so give the audience enough light to notice the clue needed later.
when: when lighting a scene that holds a later clue
why: A clue the audience cannot see cannot be used when the reveal comes

text: Colors that look identical under artificial light can differ in daylight, so test shades under the lighting the original witnesses had.
A changed lighting condition can reveal a difference without explaining its cause, so the cause must still be identified separately.
when: When varying conditions makes a detail visible or invisible
why: Revealing a difference is not the same as identifying what produced it

text: Shadowed areas and places a follower cannot enter let a tailed target slip away, so these gaps need covering or accounting for.
when: Pursuit crosses dark or restricted terrain.
why: Line of sight breaks down where light is low or access is blocked.

text: Searching only in lantern light misses small items; a magnifier and a slow careful sweep find what a quick pass overlooks.
1) Observe whether a glowing object lights the nearby floor and walls. 2) If it does not, treat it as a non-emitting appearance rather than a true light source.
when: Deciding whether a glowing object is a physical light source.
why: A real light source spreads light onto surrounding surfaces.

text: 1) Place the clue in a niche the light does not reach. 2) Provide a movable light source. 3) Let the moved light expose the clue to the player.
when: hiding a clue in plain view
why: a clue in shadow is missed on a first pass but found once the light changes

text: 1) Pace along a wall and count steps as a rough size. 2) Mark the start with a fragment of cloth. 3) Probe floor and walls by touch, arms extended, before moving. 4) Drop an object and listen for it landing.
when: reconstructing a layout in darkness

text: 1) Assign a watch at a likely meeting point. 2) Add an observer who can make the identification. 3) Record what is seen separately from what is inferred. 4) Resolve the figure before acting.
when: Following a suspect whose identity is uncertain
why: Structured observation separates confirmed identity from assumption

text: Light tense rooms with one shaded lamp so the player sees only what their position reveals; partial visibility delays understanding, raises tension and makes the audience fill gaps.
when: Designing tense or secretive rooms, or scenes that are dark or lit by a single source.
why: Limited light adds tension and controls information.

text: Tie a hidden item's or body's visibility to lighting so it stays unnoticed in dark or cramped spaces and is found only when lighting changes.
when: Designing dropped, hidden items or bodies in dim, dark or crowded areas.
why: Visibility depends on light and sightlines; scheduled lighting changes can reveal concealed content.

text: Shadows from moving objects, such as branches or swinging lanterns, can resemble a figure; tag such ghostly sightings as lighting effects so players learn to discount them.
Map limited perception onto limited vision or fog: give sound, touch, duration and landmark cues instead of full view, so players narrow location from partial information.
when: Designing fog-of-war, blinded, dim or dark sections.
why: Partial cues let players deduce location and keep the search active.

text: In a dark level, limit light sources such as torches or lamp fuel, so that light becomes a scarce resource the player must manage.
when: when designing a dark area
why: Scarce light forces deliberate choices about where to look.

text: Give players a level map showing sightlines, access lines and nearby buildings, so they can plan routes and identify who could have seen what.
when: when designing a level for stealth or investigation

text: Place mirrors, glass or water so players can see hidden NPCs or objects indirectly, and make clear which surface reflects what.
when: Designing a space where key information should be visible but not directly accessible.
why: Players can only use reflections if they understand the surface's geometry.

text: Offer a hidden vantage point with a limited view, so the player needs a second angle to read the full scene.
Signal hidden occupants with indirect traces such as gloved marks and rubber-soled prints, so players infer presence without seeing NPCs.
Let sunlight or lamp position act as a clue, so a changed shadow reveals that a door or hatch was opened.
Store line-of-sight data for a level so designers can verify which approaches a player could have been seen on.
when: When building stealth or ambush encounters
why: Verified sightlines prevent unfair or unintended exposure.

text: Make a clue that shows only under a certain light, such as a lantern or torch, depend on a light source placed in the scene.
when: a hidden trace is meant to be seen by an observer
why: without a plausible light source the clue cannot be seen

text: Use night or low-visibility scenes so the player must read traces and sounds without full sight; avoid them when evidence should be easy to inspect.
when: Designing investigation scenes.
why: Limited sight shifts the challenge to reading indirect clues.

text: Do not assume an open or lit room means an accomplice was present; several explanations are usually possible.
when: Interpreting a room left open or lit.
why: Ordinary reasons can explain the same state.

text: Rank a missing person's likely destinations by both plausibility and risk, using local geography; hazard zones such as docks can be probable endpoints.
Search for missing items against a written list of expected objects rather than doing a general search.
when: checking a space for absences
why: Without a list, missing items are easy to overlook.

text: Give a locked space several admission routes, like a window, service stair, loose panel or hidden entrance, so the first deduction is not final and the lock becomes a puzzle.
when: When designing locked spaces in a level.
why: A discoverable alternate route turns a barrier into a problem to solve.

text: A locked or bolted door or container proves little about access alone, since someone using another entrance, route or key may still have entered.
when: When designing or reading a locked room.
why: Players assume a locked door blocks all routes, so an unseen second entrance surprises them.

text: A locked-room puzzle seems impossible because its only entrance appears fastened from inside; that impossibility rests on the claim, which must be tested rather than assumed.
A locked-room puzzle is solved by accounting for every entrance and exit of a sealed space, including minor and service routes.
A locked drawer gives weak protection while the means of access to the room stays unguarded.
Scratches on a lock's ward can show that a tool was pressed in to turn a key from outside, revealing the means of entry.
If the victim had no key and the door was secured, access must have come from another person admitting him or from an unlisted route into the house.
when: Reasoning about a locked-room death.

text: A locked door and its keys show that a room was closed, but not who entered it or why.
A sealed chamber whose method is visible but misread gives the player a fair puzzle.
Before accepting a room is sealed, check its fastenings from the other side, other doors and windows, and trapdoors or fixture openings; ignoring adjacent rooms also misleads alibis.
when: A victim is found in, or an alibi depends on, a room that appears locked.
why: Apparent sealing often has a hidden or overlooked route; unchecked locks and adjacent spaces are common blind spots.

text: Use a locked room to hide an event only briefly, not as the sole source of mystery.
why: A single hidden event carries little weight if it is the only puzzle.

text: When a sealed room seems to rule out the culprit's escape, ask whether the culprit was already inside before it was sealed. Earlier presence removes the apparent impossibility.
when: a sealed or locked scene appears impossible

text: A locked room can hide an absent character, and a trace inside, such as a prepared bed, tells the player she left in a hurry.
when: rooms the player cannot enter directly

text: A locked container with its key left in the lock narrows the people who could have known what it held to a small group.
why: Knowledge of the contents is limited to those with access to the container.

text: If no key holder can be identified, the lock itself becomes the question, and the investigation shifts to how it was opened.
when: No one can be identified as a key holder.

text: Combine a physical key with a changeable code so the player must learn who knows the code and when it changed.
when: Designing a locked-room or safe puzzle
why: Two access layers force the player to gather information from NPCs and timelines

text: Hide items in containers with a mechanical quirk, and give an earlier hint about the quirk so the discovery feels earned.
when: When placing concealed items in furniture or chests
why: A prior hint makes the discovery fair and satisfying

text: When every entrance is sealed from inside, observing through a partial opening such as a window becomes the main way to gather information.
when: direct entry to a space is blocked

text: Make a sealed room's lock obvious while leaving a second access route that looks secure but is not fully fastened.
when: The room's apparent security is central to the story
why: A visible seal convinces people that nobody can enter, so the gap goes unseen

text: A person who stayed inside a locked building can leave only when its doors reopen, which narrows an unknown intruder to a limited set of possibilities.
when: a building has fixed hours and attended or timed exits

text: A fortified enclosed room suits puzzles where exits can be listed and closed one by one; it does not suit puzzles that depend on a hidden passage.
when: choosing a setting for an entry-and-exit puzzle

text: Do not accept a claim that a key never left its holder without counting how many keys exist for the lock.
when: Assessing whether a locked object could have been opened without force.
why: Unique locks still have a limited number of keys that can be accounted for.

text: When a room is locked from outside, look for an exit route beyond the room or through a passage that staff or allowed roles can use.
when: A sealed room seems to have no way out
why: A lock blocks the obvious exit, so the solution usually lies in an allowed or overlooked passage.

text: In a locked-room puzzle, give several access points with real and missing traces so the player learns to test each one.
when: when designing a locked-room or sealed-scene puzzle
why: Testing every access point rewards systematic investigation over a single guess.

text: Track each door's lock state and the keys issued to each character in a locked-room puzzle so the player can check inventory against the sealing.
when: Designing a locked-room puzzle with keys.
why: Checkable key and lock records let the player test theories fairly.

text: A locked-room puzzle can state its premises openly, so the player can identify which premise is false, such as an unchecked sightline or a hidden passage.
when: When designing sealed-room puzzles.
why: Stated premises give the player a fair path to the false assumption.

text: A space built for performance likely has trapdoors, trick exits, and screens that hide performers, so presence counted by roll call may be false.
when: A location is a stage or set with concealed fixtures.
why: Stage design includes features that hide movement and people.

text: A locked room with a sound from inside, such as a cry, hides an event for a short time and builds suspense while its cause stays open.
why: Withholding the explanation briefly keeps the scene tense.

text: If NPCs cannot tidy or move a scene's evidence, and the player has a clear preserve action, the evidence stays available for investigation.
when: Designing scenes where NPCs might disturb clues
why: Protecting evidence from NPC action keeps the clue accessible for the intended deduction.

text: A locked room controls who can enter, leave, or be heard, so a trapped person has no witness and no easy exit.
Hiding a key item across several containers lets a player who overlooks one still find it in another.
when: Designing a hidden item in a level
why: Redundant hiding spots reduce the chance of total failure while preserving discovery

text: A melting candle propping up a latch holds the lock open. When the wax softens and bends, the latch drops and seals the door.
A mechanism's effect can depend on location; a bypass near a blockage can reroute the effect, so exceptions must be considered.
when: when predicting the outcome of a known principle

text: A locked room's sealed features, such as reinforced walls, a single latched door and an unreachable window, define which escape routes the puzzle allows, since each closes one route.
when: designing an enclosed space meant to resist entry or exit
why: each listed feature removes one possible way out

text: Evidence can disappear during any interval when a room is left open, since everyone who enters during that window could have taken it.
when: when a scene or storage room is unlocked for a period
why: the open window lets unknown people reach the item unobserved

text: A door locked from both sides makes a room seem sealed, and forcing it reveals how much time an escape would take.
when: A room appears inaccessible from outside.
why: Physical forcing exposes the real escape time and the traces left behind.

text: A spring latch can be a small upward-pushing moulding, and a tug on nearby mouldings can release it, so the hidden panel opens without a visible control.
when: Designing a concealed door with a non-obvious opener
why: Hidden triggers reward careful manipulation of the surrounding detail

text: Locked and unlocked doors, switches hidden behind furniture, and lights that show recent use can form a locked-room puzzle with several solvable routes.
when: Designing a locked-room puzzle.
why: Multiple routes let different players reach a solution by different reasoning.

text: An apparent impossibility can dissolve once a physical remainder is found, revealing the real route an event took.
Locking a key clue behind a condition, such as a later quest, keeps the player under pressure from an unknown answer while exploring.
why: Unresolved uncertainty motivates continued exploration

text: A door locked with a key that is then removed seals the space behind it, and the missing key's whereabouts become a question pointing to who held it.
when: A space must be closed off to all but those with access.
