why: The lock and the key's location together restrict entry and implicate the key holder.

text: A scene plan keyed by letter marks each position, including the victim, empty seats, aisles, exits and staff stations, so claims about location can be checked.
A locked room with a stolen item has three clue types: the chain of custody, the list of key holders, and any preserved proof of the item.
when: Designing a locked-room theft.
why: These three clues let the player reconstruct how access was possible.

text: Unverified assumptions about a lock's type or state, including trusting one witness, can overturn an entire chain of deduction.
A lock's state shows who would need to lock it, not who was inside, so a locked door alone does not establish the occupant's whereabouts.
when: Inferring who was in a sealed room from its lock.
why: Locking can be ordinary caution by the occupant, so the lock alone proves little about presence.

text: Treating a locked door as proof that no one left is an error, since the room may have other exits or false impressions.
when: reasoning about an enclosed space
why: constraints can be bypassed

text: Treating a strong lock as proof of innocence is a mistake, since it only moves the question to who held the keys and secrets.
when: When a secure container is cited to clear suspects.
why: A strong lock limits the method, not the person who had access.

text: Assuming a locked store is secure overlooks copied keys and people who have seen the key being used.
when: when judging who could access a locked item
why: locks are defeated by copies and observation

text: Investigators who lock onto the first premise, such as a misfired plan, read every new fact through it and miss alternatives.
when: Early in a case where one assumption shapes the whole inquiry.
why: Confirmation bias makes consistent facts seem to support the first reading.

text: A deduction about occupancy assumes how people normally lock up, so a known alternative exit can break the inference.
when: Relying on routine behaviour to solve a locked-room puzzle.
why: Unusual exits invalidate assumptions about normal habits.

text: A locked room becomes a dead end unless it offers a way out, such as a key, a second door, or a sound that carries.
Measurement errors can create apparent hidden rooms, so a dimension discrepancy must be confirmed before it is treated as a concealed space.
when: Inferring a hidden room from a measured discrepancy
why: Small errors in measurement look like concealed space

text: Messages appearing inside a sealed structure pose an impossible-delivery puzzle the player must solve to find the source.
when: Designing a sealed space with unexplained messages
why: Sealed access makes the source a deduction challenge

text: Forcing a lock can damage what it guarded and destroy evidence of how the container was closed.
A locked room is only impossible if its constraints are complete; a missed key holder or hidden route breaks the puzzle.
when: Designing a locked-room puzzle
why: Any unlisted access route makes the puzzle solvable in unintended ways

text: 1) List every entrance and exit of a closed room, including doors, windows, vents, chimneys, ceilings, floors and hidden doors. 2) Test each route against the evidence and check its state, such as bolts or catches. 3) Record what each check rules out. 4) Keep only routes still possible until one is found or all are excluded.
when: A room appears sealed from inside or on all sides, and the question is how someone entered or left unseen.
why: A complete, recorded check finds the real route and avoids overlooking an exit, instead of relying on a claim that none exists.

text: 1) Record each barrier and visible exit as open or closed. 2) Search hiding places such as under furniture, behind objects, chimney and walls for traps or panels. 3) Only after all listed exits are excluded, consider unlisted routes; accept impossibility only if none is found.
when: A suspect appears to vanish from a watched or sealed space, or a puzzle requires accepting that a sealed space cannot be left.
why: Systematic elimination separates the real mechanism from apparent impossibility, and a documented search makes the impossibility fair.

text: 1) List every key, duplicate and handoff, and who holds each and where it is kept. 2) Establish how long each has been kept there and whether it ever left the owner's control. 3) Check the lock for forced-entry marks. 4) Look for timed records. 5) Ask narrow questions that close alternatives.
when: A locked space has a small, known set of keyholders, or its access is tied to a limited set of keys.
why: Tracing each key's holders and history narrows suspects to those who could really open it.

text: 1) Survey the outside, including grounds, road and approaches, for any entry from outside. 2) Check each door and window against its locked state. 3) Count barriers such as dogs and household routines. 4) Once outside entry is ruled out, narrow suspects to people already inside. 5) Verify every route yourself.
when: when goods are taken from a locked building and every entry point can be listed

text: 1) List every entry to the room, including doors, keys, skylights, windows and adjacent rooms. 2) Record each lock's state. 3) Identify who held keys and who could have locked it.
when: Reasoning about a room found sealed.
why: Listing every opening exposes overlooked routes, and key holders show who could have sealed the room.

text: 1) Examine the door and lock from both sides. 2) Check the key, including any found inside. 3) Check any bar or barrier. 4) Inspect furniture. 5) Inspect the body and its surroundings.
when: the crime seems impossible because the room was secured
why: A fixed order ensures each physical element is checked for traces of entry or action.

text: 1) List every possible exit, including ordinary doors, bolted entrances, service doors and staff or watchman routes. 2) Close each exit with a fact. 3) Time each closure. 4) State what remains as a hypothesis to test.
when: A suspect appears to vanish from a sealed space.
why: Turning how-did-they-escape into checkable eliminations makes the answer testable.

text: 1) Place a locked container in the level. 2) Assign its key to an NPC who carries it. 3) Make the key itself a route to a puzzle.
when: Designing a secret hidden in a locked container
why: Tying access to a carried key makes the NPC a source of progression

text: 1) Jam the bolt with a piece of metal so the door closes without locking. 2) Prepare an unseen second route for the exit. 3) Pause about ten minutes before leaving, long enough to wake and dismiss a witness.
when: Designing a locked-room or alibi puzzle
why: Each step keeps a closed-looking scene passable and removes a witness

text: 1) Establish the physical constraints of the place. 2) List every method that remains possible. 3) Measure the layout, such as distances and heights. 4) Verify the chosen method by observation under the needed conditions. 5) Check corroborating traces.
when: A crime or action seems to defy access to a location
why: Closing alternatives and testing the method turns an improbable claim into a confirmed one

text: 1) Map each room, its exits and window positions. 2) Mark which exits are visible from the main building. 3) List each possible route out. 4) Remove routes the layout cannot allow. 5) Keep routes that are unseen and plausible.
when: A culprit has left a locked room and the exit route must be deduced.
why: Checking geometry and sightlines narrows the routes to those that fit the setting.

text: 1) Identify how the barrier is secured. 2) List every route past it, such as a key, pass-key, accomplice or hidden passage. 3) Check each route against a physical survey.
when: when a crime occurred behind a secured barrier

text: 1) Pull the handle and listen for a clank. 2) If the door clanks against a hook, the fastening was set from inside. 3) Conclude someone is still inside. 4) Act on that conclusion, such as posting a watch and waking others.
when: Solving a locked-room problem through the door's fastening.
why: Testing the mechanism yields an inference about occupancy that drives action.

text: 1) List the keys and who holds them. 2) Identify open or unlocked doors. 3) Determine which guards or patrols were present and when. 4) Test each access route against independent witness accounts.
when: when examining how a sealed or restricted space could have been reached
why: Access routes are found from shared keys and open doors before assuming a room was impossible to enter

text: 1) Establish the normal entrance and confirm it is locked. 2) Rule out that entrance. 3) Reveal the unlisted second entrance an NPC described earlier. 4) Let the player enter through it within a time window.
when: A player must enter a sealed space by a route other than the door.
why: Ruling out the obvious entrance directs attention to the hidden route.

text: 1) Record the room's state: door and window locks, keys, lights, fires. 2) List every possible exit. 3) Rule out exits that are sealed, observed or too narrow. 4) Test the remaining exits against measured physical reach.
when: When a room appears sealed and an escape or entry must be explained.
why: Systematic elimination and measurement find feasible routes that an assumption would miss.

text: A door locked from inside rules out that exit, so a low window or detour path can be tested for physical possibility.
Build a locked-room puzzle from candidate doors, bolts, keys and lookouts, each with an observable, checkable state; players rule them out one at a time, leaving one route open.
when: When building an enclosed-space or sealed-room puzzle.
why: Discrete, observable states let players eliminate routes systematically, and a final open route rewards careful elimination.

text: Map and make explicit every access route of a locked room, including doors, windows, vents, lifts, service doors and hidden stairs, so players can test each one.
when: When designing a locked or sealed room.
why: Players can only solve an access puzzle if all routes are knowable.

text: Keep one plausible hidden route in a locked-room puzzle so that the player's elimination process ends in a satisfying discovery.
when: Designing a locked-room puzzle with a solution.
why: A reachable hidden route rewards systematic elimination.

text: Track each exit's state and the last time a guard or trigger observed it, so the player's exit deduction can be checked.
when: Designing a locked-room puzzle.
why: Checkable state makes deduction fair.

text: List every sealed feature of a locked room, including all doors, windows and shared passages, so the solver cannot find an unlisted route.
when: building a locked-room puzzle
why: an incomplete list invites the solver to hunt for the one missing route, which makes the puzzle feel unfair

text: Treat a locked door or gate as a control point that limits who can enter or leave an area.
Use keyed doors and hidden gates so that the key holder, not the layout alone, determines who may pass.
when: designing restricted access
why: access then depends on possession

text: Lock a key deduction behind a specific clue, so the player can only reach it after finding that clue.
when: designing a mystery level with a central reasoning step
why: gating preserves the reveal until the player has the needed evidence

text: Keep a threatened witness's clues locked until the player intervenes or removes the threat that silences her.
when: a witness's knowledge is blocked by an intimidating party
why: Releasing the clue only after the threat changes makes the cause and effect legible

text: Make a locked-room solution use a route whose use exposes a different suspect, so the solution carries its own red herring.
A locked room whose owner refuses access creates a known gap that can be investigated later.
when: designing a locked space the player cannot search at first
why: A recorded gap gives the player a clear target for later investigation.

text: A lock should have a clear in-world reason to exist; a locked room that is only a formality weakens the scene.
Lock a puzzle room from inside with an NPC holding the key, leave neighboring rooms empty and nearby NPCs absent, so the player must find another route out.
Allow exceptions in the rules at specific places, so a clever answer can fail there and add depth.
when: when designing system rules for puzzles

text: A double-locked door signals guarded privacy and marks who controls access to the room behind it.
when: a door shows extra locks
why: Extra locking indicates restricted control.

text: Give locked rooms layered access routes, such as keyhole, second door and force, with each step revealing something new to the player.
when: Designing access to a locked room.
why: Layered access rewards exploration and makes each failed attempt informative.

text: Build locked-room puzzles whose solution is a key copied during a small event the player can observe, such as a key dropped and returned.
when: Designing a locked-access puzzle
why: A visible custody gap gives players a fair path to the solution

text: Design locked rooms with a fixed sequence of barriers and times, so players can work out which window allows entry.
Encode the entry method in a locked-room puzzle so players can deduce how the room was reached and who had access.
when: Designing a locked-room puzzle.
why: Players can reason backward from the method to the access it required.

text: Make intrusion events depend on discoverable prerequisites, such as a weakened wall, unlocked door or guard routine, that players can trace back.
when: Designing an event where an intruder enters a space.
why: Traceable prerequisites turn the intrusion into a deduction task.

text: Map every route into a restricted room so designers can verify which characters can reach a lever.
Use a locked room as a constraint puzzle: the solver must find a hidden route or a reason the occupant never left.
when: designing an enclosed space puzzle
why: constraints force creative deduction

text: Place a key, exit or boss where the player's search habits do not look, but keep it reachable by a route the level has already taught.
Give forced and keyed openings different visual wear so players can read how a container was opened.
when: Designing damage states for locks and containers.
why: Distinct wear lets players infer the method and find the true key holder.

text: A bolt on the inside of a door means the door can be secured only from within, or by someone with access to the bolt from inside.
Build a puzzle whose solution hinges on a key missing from its usual hook, and include expected-location checks in the search mechanic so players can detect the gap.
when: Designing a locked-room puzzle

text: Hide a physical route in a locked-room puzzle, such as a remainder in an adjacent room, that players find by searching around the apparent impossibility.
when: designing impossible-looking events or locked-room puzzles

text: When a locked door hides a sound from an occupant, break it open rather than searching for a key.
when: when a locked room suggests a captive or hidden person

text: Use a private room as a locked-room questioning setting, with no other characters present to overhear the conversation.
when: Staging a sensitive interview

text: Offer a locked room one unusual route, such as a gap too small for a player character, so players must deduce the mechanism from the room's state.
when: Designing a locked-room challenge
why: A non-obvious route rewards deduction from fixed conditions

text: When early rules rule out destructive force, the designer must still leave at least one fair path to entry.
when: Limiting methods in a locked-space puzzle
why: Without a fair path the puzzle becomes unsolvable

text: A game lock puzzle can list its constraints in-world, such as key holders, noise rules, and sealed walls, so the player can reason toward a fitting entry method.
when: Designing a lock puzzle the player must solve
why: Visible constraints let the player reason rather than guess

text: Give a sealed room a few countable entries, such as one door, one key holder and a few hatches, so the player can check every route.
Close an area once its central evidence is recovered, so the player cannot re-check the story.
when: When designing the ending of a mystery area.
why: Locking the area preserves the conclusion without further verification.

text: A nearer target reached by a simple, hazard-free route can outweigh a farther one, but only while the defender stays unprepared at that target.
A locked door the player first assumes belongs to an enemy can later be revealed as the protagonist's own access point, with the key planted early and its owner changed late.
when: Designing a locked door whose owner is hidden
why: Reassigning ownership late recasts an earlier obstacle as a personal link, adding a twist without new geometry.

text: Locked doors and a limited set of usable rooms define an investigation area's scope, so the player knows what remains to check.
when: Defining the boundaries of an investigable area
why: A defined scope lets the player track what has and has not been searched.

text: Set a lock's difficulty by how much force its weakest point requires, and let players test tools to see which leave the matching marks.
when: Designing lock or safe puzzles.
why: Designers then control how plausible a break-in is and players learn from tool marks.

text: 1) Fix a precise moment using several witnesses' statements. 2) Check each account against independent sources. 3) Establish who was within reach of the victim. 4) List every entry route. 5) Search walls, floor, ceiling and roof systematically.
when: a crime seems to occur with no one nearby in a sealed room

text: Let a key location fade from the map over time so the player must search for it using clues from locals.
when: A quest depends on finding a place whose location is no longer known.
why: Searching for a lost site turns lore into gameplay.

text: Let an NPC interrogation offer a legal or social pretext, such as a warrant, so the player gains access to a locked room.
when: Designing a locked room that the player must enter legitimately.
why: A pretext gives a plausible in-world reason for the search.

text: Build locked thresholds with a physical mechanism such as a bar or bell, and make its operation a clue to who controls the exit.
when: Designing exits that a player cannot easily leave.
why: A visible mechanism gives the player a lead on the controlling party.

text: Seal doors and stairs with a fragile mark; an unbroken seal shows the space was not entered.
when: Tracking whether a room was entered while unobserved
why: A broken seal is a clear, checkable record of entry

text: Use a timed journey, such as a train or boat schedule, as a lock: the player must know the schedule to see that a claimed location was impossible.
when: when a claim depends on travel time
why: The schedule is the missing knowledge that turns a claim into an impossibility.

text: Small measurement errors compound over distance and can miss the exact target; verify a bearing-and-distance result with a physical check before committing.
when: When locating a spot by paces, bearings or projected shadows, or a search depends on a measured offset from a reference point
why: Each small offset compounds over a long measurement, so an unverified bearing can miss the target though it may confirm the general path.

text: Judge objects and traces by measurable properties, such as weight or how far a stub was smoked, rather than appearance or brand, since surfaces can hide differences.
when: When two objects look identical or a trace is judged by a surface feature
why: Appearance can hide a difference in material or construction.

text: Check a witness's measurements against the place itself, since a claim built on dimensions can be tested directly.
when: when an account depends on measured quantities such as distances or heights
why: Measurements can be verified on site where memories of events cannot

text: Where an object contacts the body, its width and placement suggest body measurements, such as nose-base width or eye spacing.
Measured distances, such as how far a car went before a look back or how far a body lay ahead, act as checkable constraints on the timeline.
why: Distances turn vague recollections into values that can be tested against travel times.

text: When a witness recalls a physical state, ask for a measurement, since even a rough estimate gives a checkable value.
Tie examination rights to a permission token such as a badge, and let partial permission unlock only limited tasks.
when: when designing access to evidence or locked areas
why: partial grants give a sense of progress without full access

text: Give the player a small set of observable tests, such as a handle pull or keyhole check, so a locked-room deduction has footing.
when: Designing locked-room puzzles.
why: A deduction needs tests the player can actually perform.

text: Whenever a witness claims to have seen something across a space, verify the geometry, including distance, lighting and reflection, against the plan.
when: a witness reports a sighting across a shaft or room
why: Lighting and reflection can extend what is visible beyond what a plan suggests.

text: Let containers hold a countable amount, so a player can deduce how much was used by measuring what remains.
when: designing consumable containers as clues
why: A measurable quantity lets the player check a theory numerically.

text: Make a substitute's description almost match the target but differ in one detail, so the mismatch becomes a clue.
when: When designing impersonation or substitution clues
why: Near-matches are plausible at first but reveal the fraud on closer inspection

text: Let the player replay a room's noise levels to check whether a reported event was possible.
when: Designing an investigation of a reported event.
why: Replaying conditions lets the player test witness claims against the setting.

text: A route whose required reach or height is a measurable value gates access, so players deduce it from their character's stats; confirm feasibility by measuring rather than assuming.
when: In level design with climbing or reach-based traversal, when designing or evaluating routes requiring a specific height or ability
why: Measured values turn a plausible claim into a testable one, and tying access to a measurable value lets players deduce the route from their character's capabilities.

text: Measured distances given in old or unfamiliar units can be misread, so the searcher must confirm the units before digging.
when: Distances are recorded in historical or unfamiliar units
why: A unit mismatch places the search at the wrong distance

text: Log exact measurements alongside notes; dimensions may either confirm or exclude a match.
Use measured physical evidence, such as a demonstrated height or reach, to test whether a suspect fits the act.
when: When the act depends on a physical attribute
why: Measured fit is more reliable than impression

text: Build impossible-seeming access, such as a moving vehicle or high window, that players can measure and test.
when: Designing a location with an apparently inaccessible entry or exit
why: Measurable access lets players reason their way to a confirmed solution

text: Tie a hidden stash to a routine the player can observe, such as when keys move, so players learn the access pattern before using it.
Make a thrown object's landing spot or a wound's position reveal who acted and how, so players can measure and compare them.
Show a discrepancy the player can measure, such as a feature differing slightly between two states, rather than a vague change, so it can lead to a hidden mechanism like a secret door.
when: Designing a clue that hints at a hidden door or moving wall
why: A measurable difference gives the player a concrete lead to follow

text: Let the player remove one component at a time from a machine to find the part that triggers a hazard.
when: Designing a puzzle around a malfunctioning machine.
why: Isolating components gives the player a logical path to the cause.

text: Break a hidden mechanism in front of the player, then explain it, placing every clue earlier so the explanation feels fair.
when: Designing a game mechanism that is revealed to the player.
why: Physical evidence before explanation makes the reveal believable.

text: A handheld detector that reacts to hidden magnetic or electrical triggers lets players test a suspicion before acting.
when: Designing investigation tools for hidden mechanisms.
why: Players can verify a suspicion through a tool rather than guessing.

text: Include a replica room the player can build or walk through to test a sound or path hypothesis.
when: A mystery depends on a sound or route heard from another location.
why: Letting players rebuild the setting turns a heard clue into a testable one.

text: A supernatural-seeming effect can be traced to a device with a signature and a hidden emitter, rewarding players who look for patterns.
when: Designing a puzzle with an unexplained effect.
why: Pattern-seeking turns the effect into a solvable mechanism.

text: A test action, such as adding water, can reveal a hidden state like residual heat that confirms or breaks an NPC's statement.
when: puzzle that checks a claim
why: residual heat is held in material

text: A mirror shows a reversed, indirect view, so identities seen in it must be confirmed directly rather than trusted from the reflection alone.
when: Observation through mirrors, glass or windows.
why: Reversal and indirection make a reflection easy to misread.

text: Concealed lines remain visible to anyone who traces them back along their route.
Let a trivial action, such as moving an object or interrupting dialogue, trigger a hidden record, and make the cause traceable so the player can link the result back to it.
when: When designing a hidden discovery triggered by a small action.
why: Players can only learn from a result they can trace to its cause.

text: Oil or worn stone on a passage floor suggests a mechanism was worked from the far side and needed lubrication.
when: Finding wear near a sealed wall
why: Use shows where a mechanism is

text: A missing refill or maintenance step can serve as a clue, letting the player infer an NPC's presence from what the NPC failed to maintain.
when: designing environmental clues about an NPC's activity
why: Omitted maintenance reveals that a specific NPC was present or absent, which players can deduce.

text: A sensor or indicator in the level can act as an independent check, letting players confirm or reject a reconstructed mechanism.
when: Designing puzzles that depend on a hidden mechanism
why: An independent readout gives players a way to test their hypothesis

text: Timed mechanisms such as clocks or pressure plates can be set by a character, so let the player learn who set one before trusting its reading.
Missing items can show that someone cleared evidence from the scene.
Design each absence so the player has a checkable question, such as whether its cause is accidental, natural or deliberate.
when: building a clue around something missing
why: A specific question gives the player a route to a verifiable answer.

text: Make a vanished key item the clue: end a section with it missing from its expected place, so the player's next task is finding where it went.
when: designing a search puzzle or closing a section on an open question
why: an absence gives the player a concrete question to pursue

text: Make an expected item missing from a victim's or NPC's inventory or equipment a clue, so players must find where it went, who had access, and reason toward the culprit.
when: designing inventory-based clues or missing equipment
why: absence prompts a search that leads to new suspects and reasoning from absence

text: Put a misplaced object, such as a ladder, in an unexpected outdoor spot so players must infer an entry route, linking an interior puzzle to the open map.
why: A misplaced object signals a route the player has not yet explored.

text: Place small anomalies, such as misplaced or dropped items, loose planks, patched walls, or mislabelled crates, that careful players notice and trace to a hidden actor, route, or routine change.
when: when hinting at a hidden actor, event, or route
why: Players connect distant but similar anomalies as a trail; noticing a mismatch rewards the player.

text: A found page's high number or a ledger's missing page implies missing entries; players must find another copy to recover them and finish the story, rewarding exploration and cross-referencing.
when: designing a document-based clue
why: Recovering a missing entry rewards exploration and cross-referencing.

text: Plant a weapon where it suggests a different room or owner, so players must test where it was actually used, which can uncover a second, unrelated crime.
Let fragments of an unseen object turn up in another location, creating a new clue that leads the player to a new area.
A garment or item left by mistake can lead the player to the real owner of an item that was taken.
Place a document in an unexpected spot to signal that someone visited after it was written.
when: Designing clues about a character's movements
why: Players infer later visits from displaced evidence

text: Reading a map can reveal what a site is for before anyone visits it.
Give corridors fixed names and number each person, seat, exit and access point on the map so routes, sightlines and positions can be checked unambiguously.
when: Designing a venue or building where movement sequence or position claims must be verified
why: Fixed names and numbers keep route descriptions unambiguous and let claims about position be tested against a map

text: Omit one feature from a puzzle sketch or map; players who rotate the item, change light or examine it closely will find the hidden detail.
Mail, telegrams and forwarding addresses can serve as location markers that lead the player from one place to the next.
Have an NPC give step-by-step directions to a crawl route, then set a time limit on the search.
when: Designing a timed passage through a tight space.
why: Directions reduce guesswork while the time limit adds pressure.

text: A map feature noted during first exploration, such as a small window, can later become a stealth route on a return visit.
when: Designing a level that is revisited
why: Features the player noticed early reward them when they return

text: Landmarks that persist while nearby features change let players reconcile old maps with the present.
A returning player's map memory can disagree with a rebuilt layout; landmarks that shift in size become a puzzle the player must test.
when: when a layout changes between visits

text: A difference between maps alone is not proof, since features may be absent from one map for legitimate reasons.
why: maps differ due to purpose, age and scale

text: A bearing taken from the wrong landmark sends the search to the wrong place, so the reference point must be fixed and correctly identified.
when: Using a landmark to locate a hidden object
why: Errors in the starting point carry through every subsequent measurement

text: 1) Start from named landmarks in old records that still exist. 2) Fix each lot by the described positions of its neighbours. 3) Match changed wording of the same bound across records. 4) Check the candidate against physical features in the description. 5) Grade the conclusion only after records and tradition agree.
when: when records give relative positions and named bounds but no coordinates
why: Several independent clues together narrow the location more reliably than one

text: 1) Walk each room and note entrances, passages and fixtures. 2) Note which doors are closed or sealed. 3) Record sightlines from key positions. 4) Write the map down for later study.
when: before acting in a dark or confusing location
why: light may be unreliable during the action

text: 1) Identify a fixed, known landmark as the reference point. 2) Set a compass bearing from it. 3) Measure the stated distance along that bearing. 4) Probe the marked spot to confirm the target.
when: A hidden location is defined relative to a known landmark and measured with simple tools
why: A fixed reference and measured offset locate a target that cannot be seen directly

text: A room whose orientation or gravity flips is fair when the flip rule is stated in an earlier room or a readable note.
Place distinctive landmarks along the route as navigation clues that reward players who notice them before reaching the goal.
Give NPCs physical tells, such as a dropped object, pause or pet's retreat, tied to sensitive topics, readable as clues rather than verdicts.
when: When designing NPC reactions for confrontation scenes or sensitive subjects.
why: Visible tells let players read stress without relying on dialogue, and add information while leaving room for ambiguity.

text: In any room where a private talk happens, check large cupboards and similar enclosures for space to conceal a listener.
why: Concealed observers can hear conversations that seem private

text: A rustle outside a locked room suggests someone is listening, so check the hall and consider what an eavesdropper would want to learn.
when: A noise is heard outside a room where a conversation takes place.
why: A listener in the hall may be watching the investigation.

text: A hidden access point lets a player overhear targets who believe they are alone, and their unguarded talk can reveal plans.
when: a hidden access point lets the player stay unseen near the targets

text: Give a fallback NPC instructions to reveal the solution if the player fails to return in time.
when: Designing a time-limited reveal that depends on the player's return.
why: A fallback keeps the reveal from being lost if the player misses the window.

text: In a gathering scene, each character's reaction to a shared event, including tone and omissions, can expose motives.
Hide an acquaintance between two NPCs, revealed only when the player asks the right question or cross-checks a record such as a guest list.
when: Designing social connections the player must uncover.
why: Hidden links reward investigation and make cross-checking records meaningful.

text: Let an NPC show several cues, such as untidy dress, a half-finished meal and nervous speech, that the player combines into a guess.
when: When designing NPC behavior that lets the player infer recent activity.
why: A set of cues supports inference, while no single cue gives the answer outright.

text: Show a character locking a door as a visible tell that they are concealing a state from others.
when: When designing a character who keeps others out of a room.
why: A visible lock signals concealment to the player.

text: Let an NPC's sudden movement toward a key object signal that the object matters, so the player notices it.
when: Designing NPC behavior around important items
why: Physical tells direct player attention without exposition

text: Give a non-player character one habitual behaviour that players learn to read, so they can predict how it will act in an unscripted encounter.
when: Designing NPCs whose behaviour should be learnable
why: A consistent habit lets players form and test predictions

text: Tie an NPC's decline to a visible change in a gameplay object, so the player can track progress without relying on dialogue.
why: A visible state conveys progress

text: Set window heights, ledges and reach distances so that the player can infer which character types could have entered a location.
when: When designing a location that restricts which characters could have acted.
why: Physical limits let the player eliminate suspects using only the scene.

text: Let gossip NPCs seed suspicion about a faction, and require the player to find a record such as a ledger or arrest entry to turn rumour into proof.
when: Designing a faction that the player must investigate.
why: Rumour motivates investigation, while records supply verifiable proof.

text: Place a helper NPC inside a sealed room whose timed action reveals the hidden access route.
Make hidden contact messages refer to real location details so players can verify them against the game world.
why: Verifiable details let players judge whether a message is genuine.

text: Hide a key character in a location the player has already cleared and labelled a dead end, then expose them through a small domestic clue.
when: designing a character who must be found later

text: Show an ally's disappearance first as a clue, then reveal its cause once the player reaches a specific location.
Have a captive NPC give the final clue after the player frees her, unlocking the last room of the reveal.
A brief sighting of a servant near a building confirms that staff are present, though not whom they serve.
Place clue objects where the character who hid them would logically keep them, such as under cushions, in a purse, or in a locked room, so searches follow character habits.
when: designing hidden items in a level
why: plausible hiding spots make discovery feel earned

text: Use a recurring in-world sound, such as a bell or gong at fixed intervals, to mark elapsed time and trigger NPC or enemy behavior on a schedule.
when: Designing a timed event in a level.
why: A steady audible cue lets players and characters know the time from sound alone.

text: An NPC sent to a hidden place can be scheduled to appear when the player needs them, so the player finds them at the right moment.
when: Controlling when a witness becomes available
why: Scheduled availability paces the investigation

text: Stage the first contact between an NPC and a target as a seemingly chance event, so the player sees only the opening step.
when: designing an NPC plot
why: an innocent-looking start hides the scheme that follows

text: Scheduled openings of a service door can serve as the intended way for a player to bypass a locked area.
When many people gather, absences, seating and gifts become readable clues, so a feast or wake can serve as a staging area.
why: small social signals become meaningful in a crowd

text: Give each crowd member a defined exit route so the space empties in a readable order, letting the player notice what was left behind.
when: When a space must be cleared of many NPCs in a visible way.
why: Ordered exits make the clearing legible and reveal remaining objects or clues.

text: A barrier that changes state on a schedule, such as a bridge raised at dusk, defines when access is possible.
A timetable giving daily routes, weekly calls and arrival times narrows when a party could have reached a given place.
when: travel routes must be checked against schedules
why: Fixed calls and arrival times bound the possible times of presence

text: Mistaking an old removal for a recent one happens when a witness's memory predates the window being investigated.
when: dating when an item went missing
why: Old memories can attach to the wrong time window.

text: Build timetables of scheduled departures, including conditional entries like weather-dependent stops, and tie NPC exits to them so players test alibis against a second time source.
when: designing alibi checks
why: A shared schedule makes claimed movements checkable.

text: Store container, door and object states so a later visit reveals changes; an object appearing since the last visit becomes a lead.
when: when designing rooms that change after events
why: Persistent state makes changes detectable on return.

text: Script patrols, NPC routines or moving platforms to slow at known points or after a diversion, opening a short window telegraphed by sound or animation.
when: designing timed stealth or action sections
why: Visible, readable windows let players plan and time moves, so timing becomes a skill rather than luck.

text: Anchor generated NPC routines to a fixed event time, so each suspect's movements can be checked against that moment.
when: when generating suspect schedules for a mystery
why: a shared fixed time gives the player a common reference point

text: Give a level a shared clock, bell or scheduled light change so the player can place events on one common timeline.
when: a level contains events the player must order in time
why: A visible shared time reference lets the player sequence events without guessing.

text: Use a broken routine as a clue, such as an NPC who always carries a key but has none, or a usual object missing from its room.
when: when designing puzzle clues

text: Script an offender's route through the level and place a trace at each step, so the player can rebuild the sequence.
when: designing a past event the player must reconstruct
why: one trace per step gives the player a complete chain to follow

text: Let players build timelines from overheard reports, and use windows when staff are away as a mechanic for unobserved action.
when: Designing investigation or stealth mechanics around NPC schedules.
why: Scheduled absences create safe moments for player action.

text: Give the player a social entry route, such as an introduction from a known NPC, that unlocks a building, and let the host resist until a persuasion check succeeds.
when: when a locked building is controlled by an NPC
why: A social route offers an alternative to force or stealth.

text: Shop opening and closing hours constrain when a player can make a purchase inquiry, so purchase time is a gameplay constraint.
when: When designing timed inquiries in a town.
why: Inquiries are only possible while the shop is open.

text: Script an NPC's route so it passes the player's trap while the player watches from a fixed vantage point.
when: Designing an ambush or trap the player must set.
why: A fixed vantage point lets the player observe the NPC's path without being seen.

text: Tie a hidden item's location to an NPC's daily schedule so the player finds it by working out when and where the routine opens a window.
Schedule timed events from a discovered pattern so the player learns when to act.
when: Designing timed events tied to clues
why: The pattern tells the player when the window opens

text: Use scheduled events, such as a guard arriving at a set time, to give the player a deadline that explains a hidden character's choices.
when: A hidden character acts under time pressure.
why: A fixed deadline makes the character's timing understandable.

text: Let a fleeing NPC carry a key item out of the level, so the player must decide whether to pursue.
Fixed routines leave findable unobserved windows and let impossible alibis be exposed via modeled distances and vehicle stats; varying schedules makes learned plans fail and need rebuilding.
when: timing-based stealth or investigation puzzles; fixed routines suit deduction, varied schedules suit learnable stealth levels
why: Predictable schedules let players deduce gaps; varying them forces players to re-check assumptions.

text: Record fixed routines, such as a chest emptied at dusk or room lights and shades, as world state; players learn the baseline and treat deviations as clues.
when: Designing containers, vaults, NPC schedules or timed level behavior
why: A broken routine signals that someone with access arranged the change.

text: Give NPCs fixed, readable timed routines so players can reconstruct who was where and deduce when opportunities arise.
when: When designing NPC schedules that create opportunities for events.
why: Readable routines let players deduce positions and timing from observable patterns.

text: Access to a room can be limited by fixed schedules, such as cleaners and watchmen who open it at set times and no one else.
Furnish rooms so worn stairs, scorched flooring near a hearth, unslept beds, half-packed bags or cold cups reveal routine and recent events without dialogue.
when: Designing rooms that tell the player what happened recently.
why: Ordinary objects in disturbed states give time-stamped clues.

text: Plan any search or observation around the target's routine, since routines set both who is present and which evidence remains.
when: planning an entry or observation of a place with fixed habits
why: routines determine occupancy and evidence survival

text: Gate NPC knowledge by role and timing: a new hire knows only recent events, and a veteran knows the full history but speaks only when given a reason.
when: when designing NPCs who hold story information
why: Gating makes each NPC a distinct, useful source.

text: Make an NPC's stated schedule a timeline the player can verify by observing the level at the given times.
when: An NPC describes when they or an event will occur.
why: Verifiable schedules let players test dialogue against the world.

text: Fixed occupant routines leave rooms predictably empty or occupants busy, creating windows of unobserved access that players can time entries and searches around.
when: a place with habitual occupant schedules
why: predictable absence lets the player time an entry

text: A vault or guard gap can open only when an NPC's routine changes, such as a late request or an absence, so the player can trigger the window by influencing that routine.
when: Designing stealth or heist encounters
why: Routine exceptions give players a timing puzzle to solve

text: Routines are not perfectly fixed; absences and unusual days break the pattern, so a plan built only on routine can fail.
why: plans assume a regularity that exceptions disrupt

text: 1) Place one unidentified NPC in several scenes. 2) Make each appearance plausibly innocent or purposeful. 3) Later either resolve the NPC's purpose or keep the NPC as a deliberate red herring.
Protect a secret by paying informants to stay silent or by soundproofing its room, forcing the player to find another route to the truth.
when: when a secret should be reachable only by indirect means
why: blocked direct access rewards alternative investigation

text: Do not stage an opportunity where no routine has been established, since the encounter will feel arbitrary to players.
Give a routine NPC role, such as a delivery worker or servant, a route out of a sealed area so players check roles rather than assuming guards are the only exit.
when: Designing an escape or locked-room puzzle
why: Players who notice ordinary roles can discover the hidden route.

text: Give NPCs schedules with travel times between locations so players can detect impossible alibis by checking whether travel is feasible.
when: Designing timeline puzzles with NPC movement.
why: Makes alibi checking a matter of reasoning from concrete constraints.

text: Give NPC directions that the player must verify on the level, so a wrong reading produces a visible, informative failure.
when: Designing puzzles where an NPC gives spatial or relational instructions.
why: Verification turns the hint into a deduction the player can test.

text: An NPC who relays a message can give a deliberately vague description, so players must check the account against other sources.
when: Designing message-relay or testimony content
why: Vagueness forces players to cross-check

text: Build a quest around a single witness with a route to them and a deadline, and provide alternative sources so the player is not blocked if the witness is missed.
when: When designing a quest that depends on one NPC.

text: Give the game world daily routines, such as cleaning schedules and nightly fires, that leave timestamps the player can use to order events.
when: designing traces for a mystery
why: scheduled activity makes traces datable

text: Have a secondary NPC report an absence that the player can verify through a phone call or message check.
Have NPCs react visibly to world events, so a missing reaction becomes a readable clue about where that NPC was.
Keep two plausible culprits viable until the player's clues separate them, and give each rival its own gaps.
when: designing a whodunit
why: rivals that can be dismissed on evidence feel fair

text: Include a wrong-person arrival as a misdirection that forces players to change their plan.
Give witness NPCs partial, confident memories that are useful but need confirmation, so they cannot simply hand over the answer.
when: When designing witness NPCs who identify characters.
why: Partial memories keep players working to confirm rather than being given answers.

text: Let a visitors' book or guild register produce a list of candidates for players to narrow with extra clues.
when: When designing investigation content around registers.
why: A candidate list paired with clues creates a narrowing puzzle.

text: Scatter unexplained vacant positions in crowded scenes so an observant player notices them.
when: Designing crowded scenes with clues.
why: Gaps in a dense crowd draw attention.

text: Place NPCs in adjacent rooms with thin walls so that overheard dialogue gives the player clues before any direct conversation.
when: designing NPC placement for investigation
why: overhearing offers clues without a formal conversation

text: Place information hubs such as kitchens, markets, or stables where scattered NPC chatter holds clues.
when: Designing where players gather rumors in a level.
why: Hubs concentrate chatter that players can piece together.

text: Give NPC sources such as reporters or informants a friendship, rivalry or agenda that biases what they share, so players must weigh or cross-check the information.
when: Designing NPC summaries of events, or NPCs who provide clues or story information
why: Omission by a biased reporter is a source of uncertainty; biased sources make players verify rather than accept at face value.

text: An NPC's alibi can be checked against a shop's opening hours or a patrol schedule, so a false claim is exposed when the player checks.
when: Designing NPC alibis in a game world.
why: Fixed schedules kept by other parties provide independent records the NPC cannot control.

text: Keep NPC statements ambiguous so players must judge which were meant for an audience and which carry the true meaning.
when: Writing dialogue for NPCs in monitored scenes.
why: Ambiguity makes the player weigh the speaker's motives.

text: Give captured NPCs a fear or temperament trait that changes how they answer threats, so players must choose their approach.
when: Designing captive NPCs who may be interrogated.
why: Different traits call for different approaches, making the choice meaningful.

text: Give attendant NPCs visible clues, such as grooming reactions or leftover objects, that the player can read as evidence.
when: When designing servant or companion NPCs who share private spaces with another character.
why: Physical traces from private moments give players evidence without dialogue.

text: A child NPC who repeats overheard lines can supply true but incomplete clues, and an adult who interrupts them signals hidden influence to pursue.
when: When designing a child NPC who overhears adult conversations.
why: Children repeat what they heard, and adult control over them points to a further lead.

text: Let a feverish or disturbed NPC produce fragments that hint at secrets and mark them as unreliable, so the player must verify them elsewhere.
when: Designing dialogue for a disturbed character who holds clues.
why: Fragments that are unreliable keep the player searching for proof rather than accepting the hint as fact.

text: Give the player a letter or journal item that resolves a location's mystery in an NPC's voice, leaving one moral choice unresolved.
Place an observer in a hidden spot so a confession is overheard rather than told.
A guardian NPC who offers to waive access to some rooms steers the player toward other areas.
Blocking onlookers' view of a scene hides who was watching and how they reacted, removing witness information.
Turn an NPC's claim, such as a hidden partner or having locked up, into a checkable world state like a scar, tool, record or locked room players can inspect.
when: Designing NPC testimony that the player must verify.
why: Verifiable details let players separate truthful claims from fabricated ones.

text: Write a hint-giving NPC to challenge the player's assumptions rather than confirm them.
when: Designing advisors in a mystery game.
why: Challenged assumptions push players to re-test their reasoning.

text: Give a sensitive area's NPC a reaction or hidden item that supports both an innocent and a guilty explanation, so the player must weigh both.
when: The player approaches a sensitive area or object.
why: Two-sided evidence keeps the player's conclusion open until confirmed elsewhere.

text: When a guard describes only a cloak, the player should match the description against other clues such as height, voice or gait before accusing anyone.
when: Designing evidence that offers only partial identification.
why: Partial evidence narrows suspects without naming one, so further clues are needed for a fair accusation.

text: Offer a bluff option whose success depends on facts the NPC has already learned, and let a second NPC verify the claim so a failed bluff becomes a failure state.
when: Designing dialogue challenges with consequences.
why: Tying success to prior knowledge makes the bluff a fair test of what the player has learned.

text: Give a sighting an ambiguous location, such as an adjacent room or the target room, so the player must resolve the doubt.
Give NPC storage a canonical orientation, so a moved item betrays a visitor who did not know the room.
Make NPC predictions checkable by recording whether each warning came before the harm, so players can verify the claim against the timeline.
when: when NPCs make predictions about future events in a game
why: Checkable predictions let players judge whether a prophecy is genuine or reconstructed.

text: Give two NPCs separate memories of one event that include a detail also present in the level, so players can verify the link.
when: Two NPCs share a past event.
why: A world detail lets players confirm or refute the memory.

text: Make an item an NPC remembers, such as a coat or towel, a checkable clue rather than background detail.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that mentions possessions
why: A remembered item lets players verify its absence

text: Build a sequence of NPC statements that each get retracted, so every retraction opens a new area or ability for the player.
An NPC's willingness to reveal a secret can depend on how much the player has paid, insulted or threatened them.
when: When designing NPC dialogue that gates secrets behind player actions.
why: Past treatment shapes how willing an NPC is to disclose.

text: Give an informant NPC dialogue options at different confidence levels, with a specific question unlocking a more exact answer.
when: When designing an NPC with partial knowledge.
why: Graded answers reward precise questioning and let the player build knowledge step by step.

text: A masked NPC can demand a player's oath before naming a target, so the player commits before learning the secret.
when: when designing festival or costumed NPCs who hold secrets
why: The commitment creates tension and later accountability.

text: Place a sealed note or journal in a container that opens only after a major fight, so it carries the level's explanation at the moment the player can absorb it.
when: Delivering lore or explanation tied to level progression
why: Gating the explanation behind a fight rewards progress and gives the player the answer when it has the most impact.

text: Vary an NPC witness's report confidence by distance, lighting and duration of observation so players learn to weigh testimony.
when: when designing NPC reports for the player to evaluate
why: Observation conditions teach the player to judge reliability.

text: Plant an NPC who claims credit for the player's work, then reveal in a late scene that this NPC is responsible.
when: Designing a dungeon or quest with a deceptive ally.
why: The player retroactively reads earlier interactions differently once the reversal lands.

text: A sealed note carried by a servant or errand boy can be watched or intercepted along its route, and misread if the carrier is untrusted.
when: a message must pass through a third party

text: A language barrier limits what players can learn from certain NPCs until a translator or tool is found, narrowing information flow.
when: Designing information gates in a world
why: Access tools control information

text: Fog, darkness or a cut sensor feed can hide information players need to act; critical information needs a backup channel.
when: when atmosphere is used heavily in a play space, or when sensor feeds may cut out
why: Concealment that blocks needed information prevents informed decisions.

text: 1) Have the NPC hold a key fact back. 2) Place matching physical evidence elsewhere. 3) Trigger the scripted reveal when the player finds that evidence.
when: A boss or NPC holds information that the player must earn.
why: The reveal feels earned because the player supplies the link.

text: Plant an NPC's odd gesture in an early scene and reward the player when the gesture later becomes meaningful.
when: Designing character-driven reveals.
why: Players who notice early details feel rewarded when they pay off.

text: A change of occupant shows up as a mismatch between what a household expects and what it observes.
A small object found at a scene can prove a person was there even when that person denies it.
when: a suspect's account conflicts with an item at the scene
why: an item tied to a person places them physically in the space

text: Fixtures and decoration reveal who used a room, and a layout plan shows where those traces should appear.
when: identifying a room's occupant
why: Personal objects link a space to a person

text: Look for occupancy traces such as bedding, ash, empty tins and bottles, food and water supplies, and warmth from a heat source that leaves no smoke.
when: Investigating a room or hideout suspected of being occupied
why: Physical traces reveal use without anyone being seen

text: Combine several small physical signs, such as stains, smells and marks on the body, to infer a person's occupation.
when: A person's job is not stated.
why: Several weak signs together point to a profession more reliably than one.

text: Record objects lying near a victim, such as a weapon or a glove, since they may belong to someone who was present.
Good muscle with clean, unworked hands suggests a person who did not do manual labor.
when: when inferring a stranger's work from the body
why: hands and build record how a person has used them

text: Half-used items such as cigars or cigarettes left behind indicate that people were recently present and left quickly.
Mostly closed blinds suggest that much of a building is unused, so window coverings are a readable sign of occupancy.
when: Judging whether a building you cannot enter is inhabited
why: Visible signs carry information about use

text: A door left unlocked by habit can provide a second path into a locked building, though it remains bound by the same timeline.
Track NPC occupancy and sightlines as data, so an NPC's presence can rule a route out.
when: When designing sealed-area puzzles with NPCs.
why: Recorded positions let the game check whether a route was observable.

text: A door fastened by a hook from inside clanks when pulled, showing someone is inside, while a key locked from outside shows the room is empty.
when: Reading a locked door to infer whether someone is inside.
why: The fastening's side and sound reveal who set it.

text: 1) Note disturbed dust and fresh footprints. 2) Check for swept corners. 3) Note consumables such as candle stubs and dated newspapers. 4) Infer recent occupancy and its rough timing.
when: estimating recent use of a hidden place
why: residual traces reveal use without naming the user

text: Leave countable traces such as cups, cigar ends or footprints so players can deduce how many characters visited a room.
when: Designing a room that implies past occupants
why: Matching counts let players reason about the number of visitors

text: Calm stretches before or between threats, like scenery, small talk, exploration lulls or quiet rooms, make the next danger or ambush land harder through contrast.
when: Leading players toward danger; designing encounter rhythm or a sequence of dangerous spaces.
why: Contrast with calm moments makes threats sharper; a lull builds expectation that the strike releases; recovery sharpens the next threat.

text: Pause or remove ambient sound, such as dripping water or a clock, just before a reveal or threshold opens, so the stakes register and the next sight or sound stands out.
when: Designing a threshold or major reveal moment.
why: Delay makes the opening feel consequential; silence makes the next sound or sight stand out.

text: Reveal events out of chronological order through found notes or journal fragments, and control when each actor appears, so information reaches the player in a shaped sequence.
when: Pacing a scene or investigation that reveals clues.

text: Use NPC interruptions in dialogue as a pacing lever that delays a reveal without removing it.
Let an NPC warning that the player ignored return as the means of escape, rewarding players who heeded or noted it.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that foreshadows a later event
why: Delayed payoff makes earlier choices feel meaningful and rewards attention

text: Environmental triggers such as sudden stillness or stirring leaves before an ambush can warn players of nearby danger.
when: Designing an ambush or hidden threat in a level.
why: Players learn to read such cues as signs of an imminent encounter.

text: Delay revealing a link between events until the player has enough evidence, so the connection feels earned.
when: When designing a multi-event mystery or quest chain.
why: A connection revealed too early feels arbitrary; one earned through evidence feels satisfying.

text: Rotating suspicion through NPCs, each shift triggering a set-piece event, can pace a level.
Letting a wait run too long makes its cues stop feeling meaningful, so the buildup loses its force.
when: a suspense sequence holds the player in waiting
why: Cues depend on the player still associating them with an approaching event.

text: Ending the mission cleanly right after a reveal can leave the player feeling the solution was hollow; withhold or undercut the reward to keep consequences meaningful.
when: a reveal is the climax of a mission or quest
why: A reward taken or a culprit released makes the outcome feel unresolved and memorable.

text: Too many false alarms dull the audience, so each should lead somewhere or be verifiable later.
when: Pacing ambiguous cues in a level
why: Unresolved false alarms lose their tension over time

text: End each level area on an open detail, such as an unexplained locked door, that becomes the next objective and gives the player a reason to keep moving.
when: Structuring a sequence of level areas or a level meant to sustain forward motion.
why: An open question the player carries keeps the level pulling them forward.

text: Pair every stall point with a new stimulus, like an alarm, a visitor, or a fresh clue, so players keep moving.
when: designing paced puzzle or investigation sections

text: Alternate open exploration with confined interview spaces so attention narrows gradually toward key rooms and witnesses.
when: When structuring the pacing of an investigation area.
why: Shifting space types steers focus.

text: Show a deadline on screen alongside reversals, such as a secret found already gone, to keep pacing tight.
Introduce a noisy or joke item, such as a bell or chime, early with recorded properties, so a later puzzle can refer back to them.
End a scene at the peak of danger with the outcome withheld until the player makes the next choice.
when: Designing a scene's ending.
why: Withheld outcomes keep tension and force a decision.

text: Use a scheduled gathering as a suspense gap, and let players pursue other investigation threads during the wait.
when: A main objective is temporarily blocked by a timed event.
why: Parallel threads keep players engaged while the blocked objective resolves.

text: Obstacles such as forced doors or embedded projectiles add urgency and keep players moving, but a run of delays without progress makes them impatient; alternate obstacles with progress.
when: Pacing a long route, investigation, or sequence of obstacles leading toward a hidden outcome.
why: Each obstacle costs time so pressure builds before the outcome, but consecutive delays turn eagerness into impatience.

text: Give remains or disguised NPCs permanent marks such as rings, scars or tattoos that the player can check against a missing NPC's known features or an unmasked identity.
when: When designing bodies, remains or disguised enemies as clues
why: Checkable permanent marks turn identification into a player inference, since costumes can be changed.

text: Scorch marks, ash rings, warm or damp objects, residue, smells and stains reveal recent activity, giving a timeline or contradicting a claim.
Physical traces such as dust and cobwebs are less reliable when others may have disturbed them.
when: others may have entered the scene

text: Tracks in loose ground show that someone has moved through a space even when no one is seen.
Disturbed wrappings and a missing object at a body show that it was touched and what was taken.
Let a player inspect an NPC's wound with a light or magnifier, and make its pattern contradict the NPC's stated cause to point to a suspect.
when: Designing clue-based wounds on NPCs
why: Inspection with a tool turns a mismatch into a discoverable clue.

text: Let players order events from body signs such as pooling, temperature or stiffness, and give an NPC medic a time range they must narrow with other clues.
when: When designing a corpse or collapse puzzle
why: Signs the player can read make the timeline a solvable inference rather than a guess.

text: Let physical states that change over time, such as stiffening or moved furniture, reveal the real cause of an event and reward players who inspect late.
A stealth or tracking mechanic can use intermittent signs such as ripples, ash, footprints and sounds that the player must chain together.
when: when designing a pursuit or stealth encounter
why: Chained clues reward attentive players

text: When a key witness cannot speak, leave physical clues they left behind, giving the player another route to the answer.
when: A witness is unable to give testimony.
why: Environmental evidence can substitute for lost testimony and keep the investigation going.

text: Place a clue on a surface the player inspects with a tool that reveals invisible traces, and let a skilled actor's technique leave a recognisable residue.
when: Designing hidden-trace clues.
why: Missing traces then point to method, which the player can learn to recognise.

text: A wound on a creature can be mirrored on a linked NPC, letting the player verify the connection by inspecting the mark or attacking and observing the result.
when: When a creature and a character are linked in a game
why: Checkable mirrored injuries let the player confirm the link through inspection or direct action.

text: Neglected features such as an idle well handle or rotten rope show that nobody visits, so objects hidden there can stay unseen for a long time.
when: a location shows signs of disuse
why: disuse means fewer visitors who might discover concealed items

text: A smooth surface can look like a protective covering; examining only one side of a residue fragment can lead to a wrong identification.
why: Both faces of a fragment must be checked before deciding its origin.

text: Trails that lead into corners and back again suggest a search or an unknown intruder rather than a single route.
when: Interpreting a messy footprint trail
why: Looping paths indicate searching, not one clear passage

text: 1) Find traces at each affected site. 2) Connect them in order of occurrence. 3) Check for sites with no traces. 4) Read the line of traces as the actor's path and target selection.
when: Reconstructing where an unseen creature or NPC moved through a space.
why: Sites with no traces show what the actor avoided or ignored.

text: Build a death scene with a deliberately absent struggle, and let players check the verdict against physical traces such as footprints and servant accounts.
when: When designing a death scene that appears self-inflicted.
why: Absences invite the player to test the apparent explanation.

text: Reward players for inspecting objects before moving on, since decay-based room-state puzzles depend on that inspection.
when: Designing puzzles that use object state as a clock
why: Clues are only usable if the player examined them

text: Let a broken object's rust or wear show how old the damage is, rewarding careful inspection.
Keep at least one reliable physical feature in a deceptive space, since a place that misleads on every detail becomes arbitrary.
when: Designing a setting whose appearance is partly misleading.
why: A fixed reference lets players judge which other details to trust.

text: Use footprint trails as tracking evidence that leads toward hidden rooms or a locked door that has been opened.
when: Designing clues that point to secret areas
why: Trails turn a visual trace into a navigation lead

text: Compare any time-stamped physical trace against each account, since physical records are harder to bias than recollection, which cannot be checked when no object survives.
when: Physical evidence is available alongside witness statements
why: Physical records are harder to bias than human recollection.

text: Give horror scares discoverable mundane traces, such as a sound, moving object, injury, damp clothing or fresh tool mark, specific enough that players can choose them over the supernatural reading.
when: designing anomalies in horror-leaning levels or haunted locations
why: Specific clues give players a checkable alternative to the supernatural reading.

text: Hurried acts leave marks on surfaces that a careful examiner can read, so the rush itself becomes evidence alongside the tool.
when: an act is performed in haste
why: abrupt movement during haste causes the marks

text: Chloroform signs found at post-mortem are mostly negative, so the body alone often under-reports the cause and the scene carries much of the proof.
when: When a death may have been caused by an agent that leaves little trace.
why: Volatile agents evaporate and leave few physical marks on the body.

text: Soot or burn marks on skin around a wound show that the muzzle was close, so their absence suggests the shot came from a distance.
when: Judging whether a gunshot wound was self-inflicted
why: Close-range discharge leaves residue on nearby skin

text: Hairs lifted with tweezers can show a person was present in a place; coarse fibres can suggest a material such as a sheet used for an improvised rope.
Judge whether a mark is fresh before linking it to a timeline, since fresh residue, such as wet finger marks, shows something was touched recently relative to earlier events.
when: a mark is found on a surface after an event

text: Test a witness's identification or account against physical details such as a ring, missing item, footwear or gear, which are hard to fake consistently.
when: When a witness identifies a suspect or describes clothing or gear, and physical details may not match.
why: Physical details are harder to fake than general impressions.

text: Check dust, cobwebs and rust, which signal long disuse, before judging a door, route or broken part as recently used or damaged, since a fresh-looking break can mislead.
when: judging whether a route or object was used recently
why: Slow-forming traces accumulate only when nothing has disturbed them.

text: Test a stated journey or timing against a physical condition it implies; a contradiction can overturn a claim the group accepted.
when: a witness's account of distance, time or effort conflicts with a physical state
why: a physical condition constrains what could have happened

text: An absence of fog or condensation in a room can suggest it was kept closed through the night.
A clean test result may mean the tested item was swapped before testing, so consider substitution as an explanation.
Claiming an incriminating object as your own before others attach it to a crime can explain it away.
when: when an object links you to a crime

text: Test a witness's stated need or motive against visible possessions, clothing or behaviour. A mismatch is a lead about hidden purpose, not proof of wrongdoing.
when: A witness gives a reason that can be checked against visible wealth or behaviour

text: A locked container with no outward damage that was later relocked was probably opened with a key rather than forced.
when: Inspecting a container that shows no sign of tampering.
why: Forced entry leaves visible marks, so their absence points to legitimate access.

text: A genuine trace carries random individual imperfections, so a copy that matches the original, flaws included, is suspicious.
when: when a trace is presented as strong proof
why: random flaws do not repeat exactly across independent traces

text: Identify fibres by type and dye colour under magnification; a mix of furnishing-type fabrics points toward an indoor, furnished place.
why: furnishings are normally found in habitations

text: Let an item carry a trace such as a fingerprint that links two personas, so an inventory check can connect them.
Food quality can reveal a person's means or tastes, and a mismatch with the rest of their appearance is itself a clue.
Deliberately scuffed trails can plant a clue that a subject tried to hide movement, leaving players to judge how far to trust them.
when: Designing a clue that involves concealment.
why: Players must weigh a disturbed trail, which keeps the clue ambiguous.

text: Use a plain, low-contrast surface under a fine layer, so later disturbance is easy to read.
Leave physical traces such as cut glass, trampled objects or dropped items that players can read to show the entry route and the thief's knowledge.
when: Designing scene evidence for a break-in.
why: Readable traces let players reconstruct the method.

text: Wear on objects, such as edges rubbed from handling, shows how often something was used and supports claims that it was kept and read.
when: a document or item must show past use
why: Physical wear records handling that testimony cannot.

text: Give rooms door seals that the game checks on return, and flag a breach as a clue.
when: When designing a room that the player may leave and revisit
why: Persistent state changes let the player detect unseen entry

text: Use a small clothing or equipment detail, such as mismatched footwear, as a physical clue, and hold back its explanation until later.
when: Creating a clue that gives an identity or timing contradiction
why: A detail noticed early but explained late rewards careful observation without giving the answer away.

text: A late physical lead can overturn an earlier elimination, changing the whole inquiry and forcing earlier notes to be revisited.
why: Eliminations rest on facts that a new discovery may contradict

text: Items on a corpse or in a container can hold clues, such as food residue or unusual materials, that a player reads only with the right tool.
when: When designing evidence in a game world.
why: Tool-gated reading turns minor objects into meaningful discoveries.

text: A found object can lead the player through a sequence of stops back to its owner, turning one item into a multi-step quest.
when: In investigation games with physical clues.

text: Pre-placed markers, such as chalk or a dropped item, let a player recover a lost trail without breaking the chase.
Wear marks on a lock, chest or door persist as world state, letting players infer which tool was used and who has been there.
when: a world object is used repeatedly

text: Forged or removed items can carry physical marks, such as ruling, trim size or a count one short, that the player can match against a stack or set elsewhere in the level.
why: Matching physical details across locations turns scattered objects into a discoverable link.

text: Residue such as clay or sawdust can link a suspect to a specific place, such as a pit or workshop.
A grip that uses one hand where two would normally be needed leaves the other hand free for a second action, which is a usable physical clue.
when: A restrained or held target shows a grip that is physically weaker than expected.
why: The free hand is available for another task, such as taking an item.

text: Absence of powder marks does not prove no shot was fired; poorly fitted cartridges can spurt back and many shots leave no sign, so a clean weapon proves nothing either.
Reading meaning into an object before checking how it came to be there leads to false conclusions. Verify its origin first.
Restricting the search to an area already inspected can miss the evidence that matters most.
A closed door does not mean an empty or safe room, since fumes can linger and become deadly in a small enclosed space.
A clean inspection of a letter does not prove that no one read it.
Assuming a near-fatal wound was deliberately aimed, without checking whether the victim's movement changed where it landed, can mislead an investigation.
why: a small turn can shift a shot's path

text: Reading a clean fogged surface as proof of no handling is an error, since wiping and no handling look identical.
when: interpreting a breath-test result
why: Both leave no ridge pattern, so the result cannot separate them.

text: Generic traces such as common dust may be too general to identify a particular owner.
when: when residue is common across many places

text: Squeezing through a narrow opening risks breakage and injury, and can nearly fail the entry altogether.
when: entering through a small or upper window
why: tight gaps and fragile glass make the route dangerous

text: 1) Compare the timing of each discovery against prior communications. 2) Ask whether objects could have been placed after those communications. 3) Test the evidence before accepting the clue.
1) Look at the body for pallor, glassy eyes, and stillness. 2) Touch a hand and note coldness or stiffness. 3) Listen at the mouth for breath. 4) Feel for a pulse at the heart.
when: When a person appears unconscious or dead.
why: Each check is more decisive than appearance alone.

text: 1) Note each fold, seal and crease on the object. 2) Establish the order in which these marks were made. 3) Check whether that order fits the owner holding and dropping the object, or someone inserting it later.
when: An object was found beneath a body or in a disturbed place.
why: A consistent sequence supports the owner's use, while a conflicting one suggests later placement.

text: 1) Present the physical item. 2) Ask whether it could fit the witness's account. 3) Record any agreement as a checkable fit, not as confirmation of the claim.
when: when a witness's memory concerns an object
why: a physical match turns vague memory into testable evidence

text: Lie flat on a waterproof sheet and use a magnifier to inspect the ground closely.
when: Traces are small or faint.
why: Low, steady viewing reveals faint detail.
