text: 1) Compare a witness's account with physical signs such as marks or injuries. 2) Where they contradict, identify the exact points of conflict. 3) Press on those points directly and factually.
when: A witness's account is smooth but a physical sign suggests otherwise.
why: Targeting the conflict draws out what the witness has left unsaid.

text: 1) Read any name or mark on the item to establish ownership. 2) Count the remaining rounds or uses to check whether it was fired.

1) Examine the door frame where a bolt is claimed to be shot to confirm it. 2) Unbolt and reopen the connecting door repeatedly, examining the bolt each time. 3) Collect any tiny residue from the bolt and seal it. 4) Test adjoining doors, relocking each after inspection.
when: when a closed-room claim is made

text: 1) Compare the object with its original record, such as purchase or inventory details. 2) Look for mismatches in shade or material. 3) Check whether adhesive or residue dates the replacement. 4) Ask why the object was changed.
when: An object has been moved, replaced or cleaned and the reason is unclear

text: 1) Take a finding from one source. 2) Look for the same trace at a second, independent location. 3) If they agree, the finding gains support. 4) If they disagree, reconsider the finding.
when: when a finding needs verification
why: a mismatch shows the finding may be misread

text: Leave wax, footprints, smudges or scattered objects along a route so players can trace the culprit's path and confirm they are on track before the final location.
when: Designing a path the player must reconstruct or a tracking route in a level
why: Traces let players reconstruct movement without a witness and verify they are on the right path.

text: Let a witness's described route leave footprints, disturbed dust or other traces the player can revisit, so an inconsistent route exposes the lie.
when: an NPC describes events along a route
why: Visible movement traces let players verify stated routes and test claims directly.

text: A puzzle room can leave bullets, broken glass or scraped floors as traces that reveal events without the weapon present.
Store physical traces such as drag marks, scorch patterns, and broken railings in a level so players can rebuild what happened.
Before accepting an identification, ask whether the witness saw the person up close rather than only glimpsing them.
when: when a witness claims to recognise someone
why: a recognition based on a glance is weak evidence

text: In a feast or potion mechanic, log who consumed each item, so the player can rule items out by checking who was unaffected.
when: A game has shared food or drink that can cause harm.
why: Consumer records turn a shared item into a checkable clue.

text: Log item movement through the level so a player can check whether an item left a room.
when: Building a stolen-item puzzle.
why: A checkable movement history makes the route deduction fair.

text: Place residue, scorch marks or stored raw material that contradicts an NPC's stated purpose so players can infer the real activity.
when: Designing environments that reveal NPC lies.
why: Physical contradiction rewards inference.

text: Give the room a physical signature, such as marks or stains, that matches the intended method.
when: Designing a scene that implies a specific action
why: Matching traces let players confirm the method from the environment

text: Place residue such as soot, blood, or putty as negative evidence that rules out a route.
Record the player's own traces, such as disturbed dust or items left out, to create tension about whether they left evidence behind.
Make burnt or half-destroyed items sift-able and partly recoverable, so players reconstruct content from remnants.
when: Designing destructible or burnt clue items
why: Partial recovery turns damage into a usable mechanic

text: Build rooms whose residue is readable, such as empty frames, missing toiletries and dated calendars, so players can reason about what happened and when.
why: authored traces give players evidence to build a timeline from

text: Leave physical remnants such as cellars as clues that can confirm or contradict a written record.
In a locked room, plant one trace that breaks the impossibility, such as footprints ending at a threshold or a mark near an object, so players can deduce the route.
when: Designing a locked-room puzzle with a solvable route.
why: A single clear trace gives the player a concrete lead without solving the puzzle for them.

text: Leave visible residue such as scorch marks or footprints in a dark room so a player who searches afterward can reconstruct what happened.
when: Designing a space where events occur in darkness
why: Physical residue lets players infer hidden actions after the fact

text: Make a wrongly accused person's innocence provable only by one specific physical trace, so the player must search for that exact trace.
when: Designing an accusation the player must overturn
why: A single decisive object gives the search a clear target.

text: Use an object's physical detail, such as a symbol, inscription or broken pattern, as a key matching a door, chest or empty slot elsewhere in the level.
when: Designing a puzzle where the player must link an item to a lock, container or empty slot.
why: A matching physical detail gives the player a concrete link to follow.

text: A ledger or shop book can be a puzzle object in which the player notices a missing charge and infers who stayed there.
when: designing a record-based puzzle
why: Players deduce from absence and pattern without dialogue.

text: A puzzle item can carry a pattern impression that the player must cast or copy and match to a character's trait, such as a bite or glove mark.
when: When designing evidence-matching puzzles.
why: Pattern matching turns physical evidence into a checkable clue.

text: An ordinary object such as a coat or lantern can serve as a trigger that the player must notice moving, rewarding attention to small changes in the scene.
Place a carved inscription behind debris or a removable panel, and store the fuller account elsewhere, so players must visit both to assemble the story.
Hold back a found object's full story until the player has physically recovered it, and let its use become clear through application in a set order.
when: Designing a puzzle room or item whose purpose is revealed through use.
why: Tying the explanation to possession and action makes the discovery feel earned.

text: Place an inspectable artifact in a public space, such as an item implying a missing person, to open a quest whose cause is discovered later.
An unopened pouch keeps its contents unknown until opened, so whether someone checked it becomes a puzzle for the player.
Keep a fragment unusable until it is paired with a second location, so the player must connect two areas.
Props such as a loose sheet, a wrecked toy or a rigged fitting can be placed so an attentive player can connect them to a method.
Withholding clues for too long leaves the player unable to track the evidence already gathered.
when: Pacing a gradual reveal
why: Too much unresolved information overwhelms memory

text: 1) Place a readable codex in a single room that explains the cause of the scene. 2) Link the final interaction to the completion of a gameplay object.
End each level or reveal scene on an unresolved item or beat, such as a stray item in a cleared room, half-burned note, collapse or shut door, pulling the player onward.
Show the premises of a deduction puzzle clearly, so the player can locate a weak assumption and reason about its effect on the answer.
when: Designing a puzzle that requires computing a route or time from in-world figures.
why: An unstated chain reads as arbitrary and cannot be challenged.

text: Place an item with no obvious use in a room and resolve it later, rewarding attentive players.
Open a level with unexplained hooks, such as lights switching off or a silhouette at a window, before the main objective is revealed.
when: designing the opening of a level
why: hooks pull attention and create questions before the goal is stated

text: Place a clue object in one room and its matching document elsewhere, so that matching them becomes the unlock for a later step.
when: designing a multi-part identity puzzle

text: Hide a key in an unexpected spot in a locked room so players can solve the puzzle by checking the room's props.
when: Locked room puzzles with a vanishing or trap element.

text: Let the key proof item look like a collectible or quirk, so players pick it up early without treating it as clue-bearing, then reuse it as the final proof.
when: designing a puzzle or secret whose solution depends on items found earlier
why: Players do not expect a decorative item to become the answer, so the later payoff feels earned rather than arbitrary.

text: Make the solution a physical object already on the table and used in the open, so its role is in view but easy to overlook.
Place a solution's key object in an early, unremarkable location so the final confrontation pays it off.
when: Designing the layout of a puzzle or mystery level.
why: An object seen early becomes a meaningful payoff when revealed later.

text: Use a missing item or body part as a puzzle lock, so the player recalls a prior fact such as an unremovable ring to see the link.
when: designing a puzzle around an absence
why: Requiring recall of an earlier fact makes the solution feel earned rather than arbitrary.

text: Give each candidate cause its own test in the room with a distinct result, such as sounding a wall or measuring a gap, so players eliminate options by evidence.
when: Mystery levels or puzzles with several possible answers or hazards
why: Separate tests let players narrow candidates rather than guess, so the solution feels earned.

text: Let the player compare a written theory with an observed mechanic, such as a vortex or rising water, so the theory's failure is found through play.
Place a mirror clue in a nearby room so the player can test the reflection explanation before the reveal.
Make an apparent solution feel too easy so players examine the objects that do not fit it.
Give small feedback, such as a shift or sound, for each tested point, so the player can tell whether a point is correct.
when: When a hidden mechanism responds to specific contact points.
why: Without a signal, a systematic search gives the player no way to make progress.

text: A test-and-result step, such as growing an old seed to check viability, can unlock a later area while the environment reacts visibly.
when: Designing a puzzle that gates progress behind an experiment.

text: 1) Collect earlier items that each hold part of the answer. 2) Place them in a final challenge room. 3) Require the player to match them against each other to reach the conclusion.
when: designing a climactic reveal built from items the player already holds
why: Assembling known evidence rewards attention and turns the finale into a deduction rather than a surprise.

text: Make exits that look blocked testable, such as a barred window to force or a window too small to pass, so each claim can be confirmed or refuted.
when: When designing blocked exits in a puzzle room
why: Testing and failing a route teaches the player why it is closed; a test turns a looks-blocked claim into a checked result.

text: Require a hidden mechanism to respond only to specific contact points, not any force, so brute force fails and testing each point in turn finds the correct one.
when: When designing a sealed entrance or hidden door with an unknown trigger
why: A puzzle is only a puzzle if the correct input is distinguishable from wrong ones; a specific-response mechanism only reacts to a particular pressure point, so only methodical testing finds it.

text: Make props that look operational testable, so a player can check whether they work; otherwise they serve only as misdirection.
Encode a hidden route through testable features such as slope, dryness and species, so players can verify their deduction.
Plant false leads that players can test by checking the named suspect's location and the speaker's history.
when: When designing red herring content.
why: Testable false leads reward verification without being unfair.

text: Keep each tested object within the player's reach, so substitution becomes an option the player can investigate.
Let the player test a reconstructed sequence by checking staff answers or measuring a bed.
when: designing deduction puzzles

text: Give planted clues a test the player can run, such as a handwriting comparison or a check of who held a key, rather than accepting them at face value.
Place a submit-your-answer moment before the reveal so players can test their deduction against the designer's answer.
when: Designing a mystery ending
why: Players can compare their reasoning with the actual solution

text: Build room puzzles from dust, disturbed items and handedness so the player can test which side an object would fall from.
when: designing an environmental deduction puzzle
why: physical habits and layout give checkable answers

text: A timed quest with a conditional penalty, such as an item sent to an authority if a vault is damaged, uses the same structure as narrative deadlines.
when: Designing timed objectives with consequences in a game.
why: The same deadline-and-consequence structure creates pressure in both stories and quests.

text: Covert collection, such as taking a coat or cup unseen, can be a stealth objective whose results are sorted by owner.
when: Designing a stealth objective involving evidence gathering.
why: Unseen collection creates tension while producing ownership-linked evidence.

text: Present an apparent dead end or closed quest, then reopen it when a previously seen item or NPC reveals the truth, with every prior clue available to the player.
when: Designing a quest that the player believes is finished.
why: Reopening through known clues rewards attention without cheating.

text: Let a hidden human faction emerge from a location the player has already cleared, so the earlier search is rewarded.
1) Hide the nature of a past offense behind a locked record or a reluctant NPC. 2) Show the offense's consequences first. 3) Reveal the offense only after the player has seen those consequences.
when: Designing a quest built around a past wrong.
why: Consequences shown before the cause create suspense that the reveal then resolves.

text: Treat a missing body as a possibly living victim, and let the player's search reveal the victim's own movements, such as missing clothing or cleaned traces.
why: A living victim who left alone is a plausible answer to a vanished body.

text: A missing object from a body or altar can be a deliberate puzzle state that the player must restore.
Give players runnable tests, such as checking line of sight from outside or walking a claimed route, to confirm or reject a theory.
Test reach from each tile or position a person could occupy, since a control may be unreachable from a resting spot yet reachable along an unintended route.
when: when verifying who could operate a control, or when a puzzle must be solved only along a designed path
why: a control may be out of reach from a resting spot; unintended reachable positions let players skip the intended sequence

text: Let players test an object's path by throwing or dropping it down a designed slope to see whether it reaches a target ledge.
when: designing a physics-based puzzle
why: trial and observation make the solution discoverable

text: Give the player an in-game measuring tool, such as a ruler or stick, to test whether an upper route is physically reachable.
when: Designing entry-route puzzles with height-based access
why: Measurement lets players verify routes through evidence rather than guesswork.

text: 1) Identify the suspected feature from the map comparison. 2) Physically inspect it, measuring depth or width. 3) Accept the feature only if the measurements match what the map difference implies.
when: when a map difference suggests a hidden feature
why: measurement separates genuine features from map artefacts

text: 1) Map every door, switch, window and balcony. 2) Mark where the victim or subject was found. 3) Check which door links to which room. 4) Test each account of movement against this geometry.
when: an account of movement in a room must be checked
why: Physical space reveals which routes were possible

text: 1) State who could reach the object and from where. 2) Physically recreate the route, including clothing or obstacles that alter reach. 3) Check whether the impossible result is possible from the other side.
when: An event appears to defy physical limits, such as an impossible reach through a gap.
why: Rerunning the act with real positions often shows that the apparent impossibility rests on a wrong assumption about who could reach where.

text: Compute, or let players time, travel between locations so a claimed location or time window is tested as physically possible.
when: designing alibi or movement puzzles, especially when the claimed location depends on route length
why: reachability turns a claim into a testable fact; a timed route makes the claim testable

text: Check any assumed reach, such as a ledge height or stretch needed to climb, against the actual geometry of the scene before accepting it.
when: When a conclusion depends on whether someone could reach a point.
why: Reach estimates that ignore real dimensions can rule out the true route or accept an impossible one.

text: Hide the solving object or detail, such as furniture, an NPC, or an early minor clue, behind a dramatic threat like a boss or curse that draws attention away.
when: When hiding a solution in plain view or under a major encounter
why: Players spend attention on the dramatic threat and skip familiar or early minor details.

text: Place a misleading prop, such as a weapon found far from the scene, that fixed room details or the crime's path contradict, so checking exposes the frame.
when: Designing a red herring for a deduction puzzle, or a scene whose evidence should point to an NPC
why: Contradictions reward players who check the prop against the rest of the room; a prop that cannot physically belong exposes the frame.

text: A private secret can explain a suspicious absence so neatly that the audience stops asking about the crime itself.
when: A character's disappearance has a plausible personal explanation
why: A tidy motive for the anomaly closes the open question

text: A red herring is a plausible false lead that draws attention from the true line of inquiry, often a suspect, clue or theory that appears to point at the answer.
why: It works when it is specific enough to act on.

text: A red herring is typically built on a real fact attached to the wrong person, fits some evidence but not all, and resolves as innocent or unrelated once tested.
why: It exploits what the audience expects.

text: A red herring can make an innocent person with plausible motive and access look like the obvious suspect while the real culprit stays hidden.
Red herrings can arise from wishful thinking, public assumption, a deliberate joke, or an offhand remark or sighting with an innocent explanation; test them against facts.
Design a misleading suspect or theory to fit what the investigator already suspects, such as a convenient suspect with an obvious motive, since confirmation is accepted with little testing.
when: A character already has a suspicion that a misleading clue matches.
why: Confirmation feels like insight and reduces scrutiny; investigators examine expected fits less critically.

text: Give each clue two or more readings or suspects, such as a sound meaning arrival or departure, and reveal the correct one through a further clue.
when: Designing investigative clues in a game or mystery.
why: Multiple readings keep players reasoning and keep suspicion open rather than accepting the first conclusion.

text: A red herring works best when its innocent explanation arrives after suspicion has already settled.
when: Reader should share the investigator's wrong assumption for part of the story.

text: Incidental details can act as red herrings: they look significant, draw attention, and leave the true solution intact.
when: a mystery needs plausible details that appear significant but are irrelevant

text: Give the correct reading of a clue the same visual prominence as the wrong one, and reveal the true purpose of red herrings later.
when: Placing red herrings or ambiguous clues
why: Equal prominence lets players recover the correct interpretation

text: A red-herring event similar to the main case can seem to explain it, letting players test whether the link actually holds.
Plant a plausible wrong match, such as a second NPC with the same item, to act as a red herring.
A brief, uncertain sighting can serve as a red herring that the player must confirm or discard.
Leave one trait of the culprit ambiguous so that a rushed player accuses too early.
Scatter an ominous but misleading detail, and place a contradicting object nearby so a careful player can expose the cover.
Plant an arrival with no witness, so the player must work out how the character got back into the area.
when: Designing a clue that points to an unseen movement.
why: Unexplained arrivals prompt players to reconstruct the route.

text: Plant a red herring with a prepared fallback, so a lesser clue can draw a probing NPC away from the true objective.
Build a common shortcut that seems to rule out a threat, then let later clues show it fails, rewarding players who test their conclusions.
when: when designing misdirection in a level
why: players trust a plausible safe conclusion until evidence contradicts it

text: Use shifting shadows as deliberate red herrings, giving them a mechanical tell that players can find by looking from a second viewpoint.
when: when designing misleading visual cues

text: Include a scapegoat NPC, such as a guard or gatekeeper, whose apparent guilt fails when timing or evidence is checked.
when: Designing false leads in an investigation.
why: A false lead that fails under checking rewards careful play.

text: Give eerie sounds and drafts a mundane, testable source, such as a hidden switch, and reveal a contradicting fact later to drive the next step.
when: When designing haunted locations or eerie sounds in a level
why: Testable explanations keep the supernatural option open until they fail, and teach players that the cause is mechanical.

text: Give an unexplained event or several suspects plausible explanations, such as supernatural and human, each leaving a distinct checkable mark, so a visible detail rules out the wrong one.
when: When designing a spooky or ambiguous event, or a mystery with several suspects or causes
why: Competing checkable explanations turn atmosphere into an investigation; distinct marks give the player a fair way to eliminate options.

text: Make a haunted-looking room a red herring by placing ordinary physical clues inside it that explain its eeriness.
when: When designing spooky locations in a mystery
why: Players can resolve the eerie feeling through verifiable human evidence

text: Keep spooky cues such as legends or odd sounds separate from verifiable evidence, so the eventual reveal is human and checkable.
when: When designing investigation content with eerie elements
why: Distinct cues and evidence let players test explanations independently

text: Let an NPC offer a ghost story, then reveal a real person behind the legend.
when: When designing NPC rumors in a mystery
why: The reveal rewards investigation and reframes the legend as human action

text: Plant a red herring, such as a blackmail-like payment, that explains part of the evidence and invites a wrong conclusion.
when: Designing a misleading clue for a mystery
why: A clue that explains part of the evidence feels convincing enough to pull the player toward a wrong answer.

text: A red-herring explanation can be a fake mechanism that the player disproves with an in-world experiment.
when: Designing a mystery with a misleading explanation.
why: A testable false mechanism rewards the player for experimentation.

text: Include a shared detail in each record that the natural explanations do not cover, and make that detail the key to the puzzle.
when: Designing a set of records or inscriptions as clues
why: A detail that no explanation covers keeps the pattern from reading as a mere list

text: Give a level a rival faction with a clear reason to sabotage the player, and make its traces verifiable so the real threat stays hidden.
when: When designing faction-based suspicion in a level
why: Verifiable traces make the false lead believable while the true threat remains open

text: Build an environmental misdirect, such as a bright landmark that is really a sign of altitude, and let the player correct it through observation.
Clear a false suspect first, then reveal the real culprit through a clue that appears only after the first accusation.
when: when structuring a multi-stage mystery
why: A clue gated behind the first accusation keeps the investigation advancing after the initial answer fails.

text: Place environmental anomalies, such as a stopped clock or an out-of-place delivery, that the player can ignore, with an optional reward for noticing them.
when: Adding detail to a level that rewards attentive play.
why: Optional anomalies reward observation without forcing the player to investigate.

text: A hidden secret, debt, affair or mundane cause can explain a suspicious absence, lie or grotesque detail, clearing the suspect of the central crime without resolving it.
when: Writing suspects with private lives, or a suspect's odd behaviour has a plausible, checkable everyday cause.
why: Ordinary or decoy motives give innocent explanations, so the player must separate them from real evidence.

text: A vivid but unsupported suspect draws attention away from the real clue, so the audience searches there before finding the true trail elsewhere.
when: A character is made to look suspicious but is tied to no actual evidence.
why: Attention follows the most striking impression rather than the most reliable clue.

text: A red herring works because every piece of evidence against the decoy is true; only the inference drawn from that evidence is wrong.
Give a suspect a documented, real grievance, but make the true culprit's reason differ, so players must check each motive against the suspect's gain.
when: Designing motive-based decoys in a mystery.
why: Documented grievances look convincing and need checking against gain.

text: A dismissive NPC's mundane or bodily explanation can serve as a red herring, which a second source such as a door or footstep log can confirm or refute.
Ambiguous behaviors such as packing, idling or unusual errands can serve as red herrings when a later reveal explains them differently.
when: When planning clue reveals in an investigation.

text: A fabricated monster in a locked outbuilding can be heard and glimpsed, through noises and a door, before its artificial nature is revealed.
A body resembling the target may be a disguised fugitive; a dropped item lets the player correct the false belief at that checkpoint.
Accepting a convenient explanation that conflicts with the scene, or a reassuring one placed so the investigator stops looking, leads to a wrong conclusion and an early halt.
why: A quick reassuring resolution removes the worry that would keep suspicion on the main case.

text: Chasing a red herring can erode an investigator's confidence in their own judgment.
A red herring can be built from a true fact that is attached to the wrong person, so the evidence is real but the conclusion misleads.
when: Designing misleading clues for a mystery.
why: Players check facts for accuracy, so a true fact misdirects more effectively than a false one.

text: Overusing red herrings exhausts audience trust in the story's clues.
when: Scattering misleading clues across a narrative
why: Too many false leads make players distrust all evidence

text: A pattern found in a small set can be coincidence, so test whether it predicts something else before trusting it.
Taking a deterrent rumor as a supernatural explanation can hide a human explanation that fits the evidence better.
when: An unexplained phenomenon or rumor is being investigated.
why: A false myth can mask ordinary human activity.

text: When closing a mystery, explain each misleading element in turn, resolving every red herring and decoy through a reachable, testable explanation; untested or unexplained misdirection makes readers feel cheated.
when: when closing a mystery
why: Unresolved secrets and figures given attention without payoff frustrate players.

text: 1) Plant items, such as a note or photograph, that implicate a wrong faction or person. 2) Place later evidence that exposes the false cue or shows it proves a different point. 3) Confirm the player can reach that evidence.
when: Building a mystery or investigation sequence that misleads before resolving.
why: A red herring stays fair only if the correcting evidence is available; the reversal rewards attention.

text: 1) Build a chain of zones. 2) Give each zone a plausible false solution. 3) Let the next zone refute that solution with new evidence.
when: Designing a multi-zone investigation level.
why: Each refuted false solution moves the player forward and keeps the chain of suspicion moving.

text: Mark some anomalies, such as a displaced object, as accidental on purpose, so players learn one anomaly need not overturn a theory.
why: Players learn to set aside coincidences rather than treat every clue as meaningful.

text: Design false leads that fail a checkable test, such as a missing track or timing mismatch, so verifying players are rewarded without ending the search.
when: Designing misleading clues or false leads in a mystery level.
why: False leads that fail under testing reward careful checking; a testable alternate explanation makes players reason rather than guess.

text: Pair each plausible wrong explanation with a checkable fact, such as a motive, alibi or physical detail, that undercuts it, so careful players can correct their theory.
when: Designing misleading clues, a red herring pointing to the wrong suspect, or a wrong but coherent solution.
why: An uncorrected red herring is unfair to careful players; a fair undercutting fact lets players correct a wrong theory through play.

text: Attach a rival explanation, such as bribery or coercion, to each clue so players must rule out alternatives and weigh evidence rather than accept the first answer.
when: Designing a clue with more than one plausible cause.
why: Competing causes force players to weigh evidence.

text: Plant plausible leads, such as an old relationship name or a faction-feud rumour, that players can chase, then reveal what the lead really was.
Use vivid spectacle, such as a monstrous silhouette, open window or bloodied item, to point at a harmless NPC; a later record resolves it while mundane evidence stays overlooked.
when: Designing misdirection in a level or quest.
why: Spectacle absorbs attention, so the mundane clue is easier to overlook.

text: Give a red-herring character an apparent motive, false links or plausible resemblance, and suspicious item with no real tie to the crime, so players must test each claim before accusing.
when: Designing a mystery where the obvious suspect should be misleading.
why: Testing forces examination of the evidence rather than accepting the first chain; verification beats quick arrests.

text: Seed false-lead suspects with real but incomplete evidence, like panic, a secret or no alibi, and hide the true clue in an overlooked routine known to few.
when: Designing a mystery with several suspects.
why: Partial evidence feels convincing until tested, and a fair clue remains available.

text: Stage fabricated tracks or a planted item toward a false suspect, but leave a discoverable contradiction that rewards players who test the opposite explanation.
when: Designing misleading clues or a deceptive staged scene in a puzzle.
why: Evidence looks authentic at first glance, yet testing the opposite explanation exposes the staging.

text: Plant items or a recent note making an innocent NPC look like the target, then leave a checkable fact or contradiction that clears them.
when: Designing a mystery with a misleading suspect or misdirection.
why: Planted evidence makes the obvious answer wrong without being obviously false; a plausible wrong lead rewards checking.

text: Use an official theory as a visible cover story, partly self-serving and chosen for convenience, and give players a route to find evidence contradicting it.
Place a decoy accomplice or front NPC with a cover story, plus a clue that exposes it on inspection, so players have a fair way to discover the false lead.
when: Building a misleading lead or deceptive setup into a mystery.
why: Players must have a fair way to discover that the lead is false.

text: Place visible bait, such as a left object, moved NPC or lit lamp, to draw a suspect or hidden trap into a predicted action players can watch.
when: Designing a trap for an NPC or a bait interaction.
why: A visible object invites the target to return or act.

text: Make an NPC's record match a different crime's method, so the player must compare modus operandi before concluding guilt.
when: designing a red herring suspect
why: method comparison reveals the mismatch

text: Place an item that looks like the key tool of the crime but is not, so a careful player can rule it out by checking.
Make a red herring plausible enough to hold attention, but not so obvious that it invites disbelief.
Mark which leads are red herrings so the player can drop them without losing progress.
when: Designing a mystery with several plausible leads.
why: Players can abandon false leads without feeling their progress was wasted.

text: Stage a ransacked room with missing loot that points to a plausible wrong culprit, while the true cause lies elsewhere.
when: When generating a crime scene for players to investigate
why: A credible surface explanation delays discovery of the true cause

text: Show a short, alarming note with no stated cause, and let players name a suspect they can later check.
when: Designing mysteries

text: Make some partial traces deliberately ambiguous so the player must combine several traces to identify a person.
when: Designing multi-clue identification puzzles.
why: Combining incomplete traces rewards synthesis over a single lucky find.

text: Give lure items a checkable mismatch so players who verify details before trusting an offer are rewarded.
when: A lure item is offered to the player as a shortcut.
why: Verification then pays off and careless trust is punished.

text: Check an object's ordinary explanation against records before reading it as incriminating; smears or missing prints do not prove guilt.
when: An object in a private space looks suspicious.
why: Legitimate items, such as valid prescriptions, can look sinister until their source is confirmed.

text: Make a benign-looking item become evidence once the player links it to the scene, creating an item-interaction puzzle.
when: Designing investigation puzzles
why: Recontextualizing ordinary objects rewards connecting clues

text: Give a rival detective NPC a false theory that the player can disprove.
when: When designing rival characters who pursue wrong leads.
why: A wrong theory gives the player a case to test and overturn.

text: Give a plausible NPC a recent visit to a room, so the player's first conclusion is wrong and a later clue corrects it.
Make chasing a red herring cost time without blocking the true path.
Give each planted disturbance a plausible motive that the player can infer.
Give a pattern an innocent explanation as a red herring; testing it teaches something without revealing the answer.
Plant false evidence implicating a suspect, such as a rival's objects or a staged intruder trail, that a careful check exposes via material, handwriting, or inside-made footprints.
when: when designing misdirection in a crime scene
why: A false trail that can be exposed rewards careful checking without being unfair.

text: Change the cost of each failed escape attempt, since repeating the same reversal in the same way flattens pacing.
Let a non-hostile group be caught doing something suspicious but harmless, so the player's suspicion is tested rather than rewarded.
when: When placing neutral NPCs in a level
why: Players should learn to test suspicion, not only confirm it

text: Red herrings build misdirection and suspense, but a misleading clue that cannot be verified or dismissed later, or is dropped without explanation, feels like a cheat and frustrates.
when: The story must steer players toward a wrong suspect or cause; choosing whether to plant a diversion

text: Cleaning, dust, fresh sand, new stock, footprints or disturbed objects reveal a recent visit or new occupant, letting players test claims, though the reading may be wrong.
Show recent occupation via warm embers, half-eaten food or a freshly made bed; with a defined routine, deviations like a half-filled lantern or cold brazier reveal events.
when: when designing rooms that should suggest a recent occupant or environmental storytelling
why: Traces of recent presence prompt players to investigate; defined routines make deviations readable as evidence of recent activity.

text: Let props change state or record past events, such as a container's level, rumpled rug or wedged block, so players reconstruct and test event sequences.
when: when designing environmental storytelling
why: Changed props let players infer off-screen actions and give them something concrete to verify.

text: Tie item retrieval or evidence availability to a natural cycle such as a tide, day, patrol timing or dawn, so players must plan a timed follow-up.
when: when a hidden item or evidence is reachable only at certain times

text: Plant an early schedule, record or classified notice whose meaning appears after a later event or whose check overturns the apparent answer; players must reread or verify it.
Reopen previously cleared NPCs or locations as the story advances, so players who revisit them are rewarded.
Let message origins encode the mode of travel, so the player must infer the mode to set a deadline.
when: designing deadline puzzles
why: inference from origin rewards attention

text: Give each room a material palette, such as rug fibres, ash or grit, so players can match a carried trace to the room it came from.
Place a conspicuous note or an open door as a deliberate clue, where the player cannot miss it.
A reconstruction scene can let the player replay positions and spot contradictions between NPC accounts and the physical layout.
Objects that reset unless touched let a displaced item show the player that someone was there.
An environment can change when the decisive clue lands, marking the turning point for players and separating it from the minor clues before it.
Tracking a room's item state lets a gap prompt the player to ask where the removed item went, turning an inventory gap into a clue.
Withholding information from players or NPCs can be modeled as a visibility flag, which changes what the player can learn and when.
when: A game hides a fact until a condition is met.
why: Flags control which information becomes available to each actor.

text: A bill shows one room's occupancy, not where the occupant was at night.
when: using a bill to place a person at a time
why: Billing records track rooms, not the locations of people.

text: A clue placed in shadow is overlooked until the player searches deliberately.
A search during an empty window is still risky if someone notices the visit, so empty time does not guarantee safety.
why: observation can occur from outside the room

text: Timestamp room state changes, such as alarm raised, door opened or torch burned out, and record time since last disturbance, so players reconstruct timelines from residual lights or doors ajar.
when: A world records the aftermath of actions.
why: Stored timestamps let players date events; leftover state persists after the actor leaves and reveals the sequence.

text: Store room state such as fire level, window state, furniture position, lights, open or locked doors, noise gaps or cluttered ashtrays so players reconstruct earlier events and test accounts.
when: when building a room or scene that players investigate or must reconstruct
why: Persistent state lets past actions leave readable evidence and gives facts against which accounts are checked.

text: Track dust, snow, mud, blood trails and object states over time, such as wiped handles or moved books, so visits leave readable changes players can date.
when: when designing environments that record visits or movement
why: Persistent, readable traces let players reconstruct sequences and infer who was present and when.

text: Save a baseline or per-event snapshot of clue state so the game can diff against it and tell whether a clue existed beforehand or was added afterward.
when: when clue timing matters to the mystery or rooms may be altered during play
why: Without a stored baseline the game cannot check when a clue appeared or report what changed.

text: Place a distinctive, harmless-seeming object or habit early, like a cloak, key or boots, so a later cue prompts recall and links it to the answer or an NPC.
when: when a solution or clue chain depends on an earlier detail
why: A later cue rewards attention without signposting; early mundane links point to a character later.

text: Use dated in-world items such as newspapers, receipts, journals, inscriptions or photographs to bound when events occurred, what an NPC knew, or a household's history.
when: when a game needs a player-reconstructed timeline or time-sensitive knowledge clues
why: Dated items give objective time bounds; dated documents tie knowledge to specific moments.

text: Record each room's openings, shared walls, doors or service routes with states such as barred, fastened or passable, so claims can be checked against the layout.
when: when rooms must be reasoned about or sealed-room claims checked
why: Explicit states let players rule out routes without trial and error.

text: Place torn cloth, stains or missing items so players can rebuild what happened in a room.
when: Designing a crime scene for the player to solve
why: Physical remnants let players infer past actions

text: Use a level reset or replay to recreate a room's exact state, so the player can test a theory of how an event happened.
Store the real heights of furniture, doors and props so an NPC's height can be deduced from where it leaned or reached.
when: designing scenes for height deduction

text: Give sealed rooms environmental clues such as scent, sound or residue at the door, so players can judge danger before entering.
when: Designing hazardous rooms in a generated dungeon.

text: Place objects whose wear, debris direction and quantity imply an occupant's size or number, so players can infer creature details from the scene.
when: generating environmental clues about occupants
why: props can imply presence

text: Give a narrow hidden shaft a size clue, such as a matching object that fits only that passage, so the player can discover it.
when: when a secret passage should be findable through logic
why: a size clue links the hidden route to something the player can test

text: Let hotel or inn staff record room use, so the designer can hide relationship clues that the player collects.
Generate murder scenes as closed with a fixed NPC cast or open with any wandering NPC possible, since this changes how many suspects the player must check.
when: Generating a murder-mystery room.
why: Suspect count sets the deduction workload.

text: Let disposable items such as wrappers, torn notes and bin contents persist in the world so that a player who searches bins can find them.
when: Populating a dungeon or environment with clues.
why: Discarded items reward thorough searching and feel believable.

text: Place props such as fuel, tar or tools so they imply a process, letting players infer events that no NPC describes.
Encode a building's period in its construction details, such as hand-hewn beams, low ceilings and rough foundation stones, so players can date it from its walls.
when: Generating historical buildings
why: Visible construction lets players read history without text

text: Give a returning player a visible trace, such as a stain or dirt, so an NPC can recognize them on the next visit.
Track which conditions the player has restored, and show when a missing object blocks the test.
Let the player prove an enemy was inside before doors locked, using uncleaned blood or left-behind objects, so the sealed-room puzzle has a findable solution.
Where rooms look alike, use their contents, such as an occupant's belongings, to correct a mistaken assumption about position.
Place a crime inside a window between two known events, so the player can test the gap between them.
when: When designing a timed mystery puzzle
why: A bounded window gives the player a concrete interval to check against alibis.

text: Record the state of each door and switch in a level, so the player can rebuild who had access and in what order.
when: Designing a level where access must be reconstructed.
why: A recorded state history gives the player a timeline to reason from.

text: Plant clues such as an open door, a left-behind key or an unlatched bolt early so the player can see them before the reveal.
why: Players need prior exposure to find a clue fairly

text: Build rooms as readable scenes, so leftover objects reveal who was present and what happened.
A reset that restores props every cycle erases player disturbances; keep the state of objects that clues depend on.
when: a level resets objects between sessions or cycles
why: clues that rely on moved props break when reset

text: Store dust, ash and cleanliness as room state so the game can show the player when a document or fire was recent.
Store a clearing of an accused character as an explicit world-state flag, so later dialogue and reactions reflect the reversal.
when: A character's status changes after an accusation is withdrawn
why: Without a flag, NPC dialogue can contradict the new record

text: Make two views of the same space share viewpoint and scale so that differences between them can be checked.
when: Designing a discrepancy the player must compare, such as a before and after state
why: Comparison fails when viewpoint or scale differs between the two views

text: Author a puzzle room or hub with defined zones so the player can enumerate every reachable location and every character inside it.
when: Designing a bounded hub or puzzle space.
why: A finite, visible set of zones lets players reason systematically about who could have acted where.

text: A reset of a hiding spot can leave a trace such as a slightly raised stone or disturbed soil, which gives a checkable clue to a detective NPC or player.
when: A hiding spot has been restored to look untouched.
why: Even careful restoration rarely leaves no evidence.

text: A ring of trees on a rise can hide the interior from outside observers even when the ring is not solid.
Physical features such as walls and dense vegetation constrain where events could plausibly occur, and so limit which stories a scene can support.
Check whether an access route would be seen by patrols or a watchful street before accepting it as viable.
Model a player's view through a doorway or window as a limited sightline, so clue text shows only what that viewpoint could reveal.
A physical route counts only if it actually connects to the destination; check each route's geometry, such as whether a ledge reaches the target room.
Plant a physical route and a social cue early as ordinary detail, so they read as harmless until later used for access.
when: when a route or cue will matter in a later beat
why: ordinary detail is not questioned until its use is revealed

text: A mirror angled at a target's window lets a watcher learn when the target is asleep, with no direct view into the room.
when: Watching a target without line of sight.
why: Reflection carries the view around an obstacle.

text: Reflective or repeated spaces make one figure seem to appear many times, so witnesses lose track of who is actually present.
What a person can see or reach from a spot depends on room geometry: door placement, furniture position and distance set what is visible and within arm's length.
Random events such as a patrol changing route can break a player's plan and add variance to level play.
when: Designing level events that are not fully scripted
why: Unplanned changes force the player to adapt

text: Different ways into a blocked room, such as force, persuasion or another route, change what the player learns from it.
1) Let the player visit a location once. 2) Record its layout, stair counts, sounds and occupants. 3) Reward the player's recall of those details on a later visit.
Give a physical guide, such as a stick laid along the bearing, so the player can follow the line exactly.
when: for hidden locations reached along a fixed line

text: Design corridors and gardens with few, readable entry points so players can reason about who could reach a point.
Place routes and landmarks so the player can infer the likely approach path, and seed search zones where items are likely to be dropped.
Plant climbable escape routes, such as ivy beside a window, as options when the player must leave unseen.
when: Designing a location the player may need to exit covertly
why: Visible exits let the player choose a route without being caught.

text: Give players a room map with sightlines, so a locked-room puzzle can be solved by checking windows and walls.
Create a hazard area, such as a bog or fog zone, where visibility is reduced and players must rely on audio cues and a direction tool.
when: designing a dangerous traversal area

text: Use exterior cues such as blinds, smoke and staff movement as readable hints about which interior rooms are in use before the player enters.
when: Designing a building the player views from outside first
why: Exterior signs prepare the player for what is inside

text: Place identifying signs such as house numbers and painted names on doors, so a follower can confirm a destination by reading the environment.
when: designing a location the player must find by tailing
why: lets the player confirm a room without entering it

text: Use the map to limit which routes a prisoner or cart could take, and let players deduce the route from it.
A roof route carries its own risks, while a ground-floor approach exposes the listener to far more danger; the lower-risk option is usually preferred.
when: when two approaches to a listening spot are available
why: Each route has a different cost of detection.

text: Packed luggage and an open box signal that a departure is underway.
Staff who saw someone leave can often recall the direction taken and the person's state of mind, such as a remark made in passing.
when: A departure is being reconstructed.

text: Families leaving a settlement and abandoned sites mark where residents chose to leave, a trace that a record of arrivals alone would miss.
Cliffs, ravines and waterfalls can close an area as effectively as walls do.
A detour path around a building can let a person leave without being seen from the building.
Builders more often create a hidden space with a false inner partition than by thickening an outer wall, so inner walls are the likelier location.
when: Searching a building for concealed space
why: An inner partition is cheaper and easier to hide

text: Ask why an object departs from ordinary practice; the departure is often a clue, but a deviation is not proof of wrongdoing, so test innocent explanations first.
Level wear, damp, echoing ambient sound, rodents, drafts and wet floors can hint at a hidden room or passage without placing a map marker.
when: generating areas with secrets
why: environmental cues let players infer hidden space

text: Compare recent behaviour and scene states, such as shades, windows and lights, against established routine; deviations often reveal more than the routine and are worth recording.
when: a timeline contains an unexpected visit or change; scene departs from habit
why: unusual states suggest someone acted differently

text: Treat a secret passage as both shortcut and risk, and give the player a test, such as a sound check, before committing.
A single directional mark, such as a drag, handprint or scraped gravel, suggests a route, while a trail that ends abruptly suggests escape.
A trampled strip running beside a path suggests someone deliberately walked next to the path rather than on it.
when: When a trodden margin is found near a path.
why: People avoid a path to avoid being seen or to avoid leaving clear tracks.

text: A stated route that forces a large detour from the expected path is evidence against the account.
Recorded departures and returns, such as leaving at six and returning at nine, bound a timeline into known intervals.
Where a character flees to, not only what they say, reveals where they feel safe and who they trust.
when: A character runs to someone after an incident and their account is being tested.
why: Choice of refuge is a behavioral trace that can contradict a simple story.

text: Make hiding logic differ from search logic, since a search over a fixed list of containers and surfaces will always miss items hidden by rules off that list.
when: designing hidden items and the searches that find them

text: Let a pipe or shaft serve as a hidden communication route, with a tug code that players can learn to signal contact.
when: Designing secret routes in dungeons
why: Hidden routes reward players who discover and decode them

text: Place a hidden room where a systematic player will reach it, with an ordered set of likely candidates such as walls, fireplaces and roofs.
when: Generating a concealed room the player must find.

text: Make a simple-looking scene hide a second layer that rewards players who consult a reference or notes system.
when: designing an investigation scene
why: Players who check their notes gain access to the hidden layer

text: Hide a transfer in a moment of distraction, such as a dropped item during a conversation, so the gap is fair and can be noticed later.
when: designing a handoff the player should be able to detect afterwards
why: a visible but easily missed moment makes the later clue fair rather than arbitrary

text: Seed a scripted escape earlier in the level, so a player who noticed the watcher can understand the reversal when it happens.
After narrowing the possible routes, look for side passages, service stairs and side doors to identify which route was actually used.
when: More than one route remains possible
why: Secondary routes are often overlooked when attention stays on the main entrance

text: A feature that refuses to move was likely never designed as a door, so it should not be treated as an entrance.
when: testing a sealed feature for an opening
why: a design intended to open would respond to attempts to open it

text: Leave one entrance as the only possible route in and lock it, so every intrusion funnels to a known point.
when: one entry is cheaper to defend than several

text: Position folk tales about a haunted corridor or wall noises close to actual hidden passages, so the story masks how the passage works.
A confirmed sealed exit does not rule out a hidden passage elsewhere; check other walls before concluding a space is closed.
when: a room's only known exit has been sealed
why: a sealed exit may be the known route while another remains hidden

text: A straight, labelled channel where a natural stream meanders suggests human engineering.
when: when comparing map representations of a waterway
why: straight forms rarely occur naturally

text: Offer a second route into a locked room, such as a connecting door in an adjacent room, with a stiff bolt that rewards patience.
when: Designing a locked-room puzzle.
why: A second route lets players solve the puzzle without the main key.

text: A room with no tracks on a route can tell the player that nothing has entered by that route.
when: Movement traces are used as level feedback.

text: Add a fallback route, such as a slower alternative, so a failed path lets players revise their plan instead of being stopped.
when: Designing timed routes with failure risk

text: A feature that disappears on a second look should hint at a hidden mechanic or concealed passage rather than being treated as an empty room.
when: A room or object changes between visits.
why: A change in the environment usually signals something the player has not yet discovered.

text: Hidden or rarely open passages can be signposted by an NPC remark, so the player has a reason to check the route.
A level can record a last-seen entry point without a matching exit record, pointing players to where they should search.
when: Designing a location clue that directs player investigation.
why: An unbalanced entry and exit record turns the location into a meaningful search target.

text: When a window escape seems to lead only downward, check for upward routes such as sills, gutters and gable faces within reach.
when: When evaluating escape routes in multi-story or elevated spaces.
why: The downward assumption is natural and hides upward options that may be reachable.

text: A disproved alibi can unlock a new area or route, turning an investigation step into exploration.
Replace an imagined hidden route with a physical route the player has already seen, so the solution is grounded in the environment.
when: when an escape or access route is revealed late
why: a route already seen feels earned, not invented

text: A known departure time limits who could have caused an event: an actor who left before it, or cannot cover the travel time, could not have been there.
when: when a precise departure time, such as a fixed train, is known
why: travel takes time

text: Footprints or dropped items act as directional clues that point the player along a route.
when: Guiding the player between scene locations
why: Traces oriented in a direction reveal the path an actor took

text: A concealed passage between rooms gives a second route the watcher does not know about, letting someone cross unseen.
when: The route is the only way to cross unseen and the far exit is known

text: A hidden passage offers a plausible route by which an item could be swapped without anyone being seen.
when: explaining how a switched item reached a location
why: concealed routes allow unobserved movement

text: A hidden-room mechanic, such as a swinging bookcase, can be revealed when the player points to it at the right point in dialogue.
Attackers who leave before witnesses gather go unseen, because the crowd arrives only to find the aftermath.
when: An attack is followed by a gathering crowd
why: Witnesses arriving late cannot place the attackers at the scene.

text: Deep soft ground slows mounted pursuers, and a flooded obstacle forces the escaper to change plan, so terrain can shape a chase's outcome.
when: when designing a chase across open ground
why: terrain changes pursuit speed and route choice

text: A barrier can look secured while a hidden support has been weakened beforehand, so the first inspection misreads its real state.
Environment tiles such as dry creeks or dust can rule out escape routes like water or footprints, letting players deduce by elimination.
A hub can require the player to propose a locality first and then unlock a limited search, and a failed search can cost time and reduce NPC trust.
when: When designing investigation structure in a game.
why: Limiting search scope makes deduction meaningful and gives failure real consequences.

text: A hidden reflective panel in a corridor can make an enemy's silhouette resemble the player, so the designer controls when the misidentification is revealed.
Terrain concealment defeats distant ground-level observers without optics, but fails against observers with height or optical aids.
when: when choosing a hiding place for a site
why: elevation or optics reveal what ground level hides

text: An outer wall that blocks sightlines from the main building hides anyone leaving through an exit on that side.
when: Testing whether an escape route would be observed.
why: A blocked view removes the risk of being seen while leaving.

text: A single-access room with a side passage to an outer court limits who can enter while still offering an escape path the player must rule out.
why: A restricted entrance narrows suspects, while the secondary exit keeps the puzzle from being closed too early.

text: A seemingly impossible crime can be solved by a hidden route, such as a freight door or train, that the player uncovers by checking schedules.
when: designing an apparently impossible scenario

text: A known departure does not prove absence or action: the record must also include the return trip, since a confirmed train departure shows only opportunity.
why: opportunity is not action

text: A place that is both eerie and vital leaves players unsure which signals matter.
A thorough search of ordinary hiding places can still miss the real hidden route, so the search must also consider routes absent from the initial exit list.
when: Searching a space for an escape route after ordinary checks fail.
why: The real route may lie outside the set of places the searcher expected.

text: A seemingly secure opening may not be secure: a second door or freight entrance can contradict a claim that only one entrance exists.
why: witnesses often describe only the main route

text: 1) List every route into the scene. 2) Note the barriers and exits on each. 3) Decide who could have used each route.
when: the scene is enclosed and the routes can be listed

text: 1) List every possible route out of a sealed location, including water. 2) Test each route in turn against ownership and availability records. 3) Rule out each route that fails.
when: a location appears unreachable
why: each route is a separate exit to check

text: 1) Place open rooms first in the search order. 2) Place locked rooms after them. 3) Add a sensory clue such as dust, odor or a displaced object to guide the player.
when: generating a hidden-room puzzle
why: Gives the player a method of search rather than random guessing.

text: 1) Test whether the candidate surface is fixed; if it is secured, rule it out. 2) Find the object that is clear of clutter, as the likeliest entrance. 3) Spread a fine layer, such as ash or dust, in front of it. 4) Leave, return and read the disturbed marks.
when: the surface is likely to show handling and can be left and returned to without disturbing the layer

text: 1) List surfaces and fittings no one has searched yet. 2) Inspect them for fresh holes, tool marks or disturbed parts. 3) Test the proposed route against the marks found.
when: A room seems to have no other exit
why: Overlooked fittings often hold the route

text: 1) Find features whose function the design does not explain. 2) Measure them against the design. 3) Separate a true void from a chamber by size and disturbance. 4) Test whether a sealed feature was meant to open. 5) Treat unexplained damage as evidence of someone else's search.
when: searching a building for a concealed space
why: measurement and inspection separate real hidden rooms from structural features

text: 1) Use the building's history to guess where a hidden space would be built. 2) Tap walls and note dull versus hollow sounds. 3) Pace the distance between rooms. 4) Convert paces to length to narrow the search. 5) Rule out unlikely surfaces.
when: Locating a concealed passage in an existing building

text: Disguise a hidden route, sealed passage or trap as ordinary scenery, such as a drainage sluice, storeroom or solid wall, sized to match decor so it reads as ordinary.
when: when designing a secret passage between rooms
why: matching the decor hides the route from casual inspection

text: Make hidden door traces findable, such as a drilled hole, clean patch, fresh scratch or altered bolt, so close inspection can reopen a dead end.
when: Designing secret entrances or a mystery where players reach a dead end
why: traces let players infer a hidden route; a small physical clue rewards careful inspection

text: Give locked vaults, screens and windows signs of forced entry, such as a scratched lock or moved item, as physical evidence that narrows the suspect list.
why: physical damage gives a clear clue

text: For a locked room, list all exits including overhead openings and let the player mark each as checked; place a fair, non-obvious route that elimination reveals.
when: Designing a sealed room or hidden-exit puzzle.
why: A hidden route that follows from elimination rewards careful observation without being arbitrary.

text: Show every exit to the player and make each checkable in the world, such as through bars, bolt type or lock state; an exit hidden from the player breaks deduction.
when: when building a deduction-based or sealed room puzzle
why: Players cannot rule out routes they cannot see

text: Make hidden exits and mechanisms discoverable through visible clues; an exit or mechanism appearing only at the reveal, or leaving no trace, breaks fair play and the solution.
when: when designing a secret mechanism or exit players must discover
why: players cannot deduce a mechanism or exit they have no evidence of

text: Plant a clue to a hidden exit, such as a scuffed floor or draft in the first room or inspectable materials named early, before the trap activates.
when: Designing a sealed room with a hidden exit.
why: An exit that appears only at the last moment reads as an arbitrary cheat; players need a checkable trace that leads to it.

text: Give a sealed room a hidden second route, such as an old wing, cellar or passage, revealed by clues or by opening a container such as a worn safe.
when: Puzzle levels with locked areas or any locked space that needs a way forward.
why: Players stop at a locked door unless clues show another way in.

text: Generate each exit as sealed by a logged event or deliberately open, logging its time; a checker can compute usable exits and players can test claimed routes.
when: Generating a locked-room puzzle or a level with doors that record or reveal passage.
why: A complete, logged exit list lets the game verify the solution; a logged route lets the player verify or refute a suspect's account.

text: Hide a main or secret space behind terrain, mist, a turning corridor or a ring of terrain, revealing it in pieces as the player moves and climbs.
when: when designing a secret area or hidden main space
why: terrain forces exploration to reach it

text: Do not enter a hidden route whose return is uncertain, because a route you cannot exit safely can trap you.
Build a sealed wing guarded by a keyholding NPC to create a natural hidden-captive or hidden-item puzzle.
when: Designing a locked-area encounter

text: Keep a hidden captive behind a locked room, with the guard giving a false reason for the locked door.
Let returning an item be a deliberate move that closes a line of questioning, and let the player recognize and test it as a possible bluff later.
Hide a compartment in an NPC's pouch that requires a second search action to find.
Give locked rooms an inspectable entry mechanism, such as a bolt that shows wear, leaves residue or works from both sides.
Offer an apparent entry route that the player can disprove by testing the ground beneath it, such as a smooth bed beneath a tree.
when: Designing entry points and route puzzles.
why: Testing an apparent route teaches players to verify routes rather than trust appearances.

text: Give doors audio cues, such as a shifting foot or a touch on the handle, so the player can infer an NPC waits behind.
Place a hidden closet or cellar that contradicts a respectable facade, so the gap between image and act becomes the discovery.
Check who knows about a back or disused entrance and who holds its key, since such doors can serve as secret routes.
when: assessing who could enter or leave unseen
why: Hidden entrances bypass normal observation.

text: Provide a hidden vantage point from which the player can watch NPC responses, rewarding attentive play.
when: Designing stealth observation spaces.
why: Players gain information by observing rather than acting.

text: Place a hidden NPC who watches a private action and can later alter a weapon, lock or trap.
Give a room one exit or a single choke point, so the player can watch every NPC who passes, which suits stealth or tailing puzzles.
when: when designing stealth or tailing puzzles
why: one exit forces all traffic past a single watch point

text: Shift the active investigation to a new location when a lead moves, so the location change drives level progression.
Design the grounds so retreat routes are visible and their exits are known, since layout defines an intruder's escape path.
when: designing outdoor areas where intruders flee

text: Make the most striking anomaly the lead clue, such as a missing item or an odd tool, so the player has a thread to follow.
when: Designing the opening clues of a mystery level.
why: Players need a specific thread to start investigating.

text: Fix all watcher positions before any light is extinguished, and keep light sources covered so the watchers stay unseen.
Give levels service ducts, pipe access panels or loose floor tiles as concealment spots, each with a visible but unremarkable sign.
when: Designing hiding spots for items or clues.
why: A concealment spot that looks ordinary is easy to overlook, yet discoverable by a careful player.

text: Give stealth exits a disguised escort NPC or a reserved path that enemies cannot easily follow.
when: when designing an escape sequence
why: Hidden allies and routes keep the player ahead of pursuit.

text: Search all rooms connected to a scene, because residue such as clay or sawdust can fall in several places.
Describe a hub's atmosphere through threat cues so its mood hints at what the player will find there.
when: designing a hub area

text: Give hidden voids a measurable size and a telltale anomaly so players can detect them by reasoning rather than luck.
when: designing a concealed space in a level
why: detectable clues make discovery a matter of reasoning

text: Let a sealed vault be glimpsed through a window or from another door, creating a contradiction the player files away for later resolution.
when: when a locked area should stay a mystery until later
why: A partial view creates tension without giving away the solution

text: A partial crossing must be fair: it needs visible physical traces the player can inspect, not a casual trick.
Design routes with hidden access points, such as service gates and paths behind hedges, so players can discover and map them.
Give players a visible sign that points to a concealed route, and make the rule linking sign and route readable.
Place a visible second route, such as a rope or ladder, that the player finds only after forcing or inspecting a locked door.
when: Designing a sealed room with a hidden escape.
why: The route rewards investigation and explains how an escape was staged.

text: Place stairs or hidden routes so players must reconstruct unseen movement and test it on the level.
Avoid a second route where the investigator would disturb the scene or warn the suspects.
Do not bury a lead so deeply that the player has no route to reach it; keep at least one reachable path to every key clue.
Use fixed landmarks and sightlines in stealth spaces so that guard routes and cover points are checkable by the player.
Record recent movement through tile-based state such as broken foliage, footprints and ground firmness that changes when a character passes.
Gate access to a water area on a character trait, such as swimming ability, and let the player learn that trait through NPC talk or a record.
When a witness disproves a key clue, move the player to a new lead, so the investigation keeps moving rather than stalling.
when: a clue is disproved during play
why: a fresh lead prevents a dead end

text: Hide a puzzle's mechanism in the room's structure, such as under the floor, so players inspect switches rather than hunt for a key.
Place an exit that looks open but is locked by a mechanism the player learns about only by talking to an NPC.
when: Designing exits in a locked-room puzzle.
why: Dialogue reveals the hidden constraint.

text: Place a discoverable alternate route to a locked room in plain sight, such as a connecting door, spare key or forgotten lever, so a careful player finds it.
when: When designing the entry path to a locked room or restricted area.
why: A visible but overlooked route rewards careful observation without hidden knowledge, and players accept a lock more readily when a discoverable alternative exists.

text: Let the player see the approach to a sealed area while its contents stay hidden, adding a small clue at each step toward it.
why: the approach builds suspense before the contents are shown

text: Introduce a hidden bypass route through dialogue before the player needs it, giving directions and a time limit.
when: Designing a sealed room that has a concealed second entrance.
why: A route set up in advance reads as fair, while an unexplained one feels like cheating.

text: 1) Scout the site when its structure is most plainly visible. 2) Take bearings and note what matters. 3) Keep the notes so the route can be followed later in worse conditions.
when: before acting in unfamiliar or dangerous terrain

text: Use ruins and foundation outlines to confirm that a location existed before the player arrives, as a check on a rumor or map.
Let a location carry a legend, but tie it to real NPCs, rent, ownership or hidden passages so the player can find a mundane explanation.
when: when designing a haunted or mysterious location
why: Concrete links give the player a path from myth to ordinary cause.

text: A supernatural message can be tied to a living person with knowledge of the location, which then becomes the next lead for the player.
when: Designing a mystery where an apparent spirit message has a human source
why: Linking the effect to a person turns it into a traceable clue

text: A public notice can draw out the holder of a traced item, turning a dead end into a direct interview.
when: Tracing an item whose current holder is unknown

text: A place with a supernatural reputation deters visits, so it can serve as an unwatched hiding spot even though the rumor is false.
when: A location is avoided because of a rumored danger.
why: People stay away from a feared place, leaving it unobserved.

text: Give players a second, physical source, such as an object's state or a door's state, to confirm an NPC's report of a voice or movement.
when: when an NPC reports sounds or movement
why: A physical source lets players verify a partly true report

text: Give rumour clues a source label so players can judge reliability, as a careful investigator would weigh each account by its origin.
when: when players receive clues from several informants
why: Source information lets players decide which rumours to trust.

text: Place rumored hidden passages in lore or room descriptions so the player's search can reveal them later.
when: Designing a locked room with a possible secret route.
why: Foreshadowing makes the eventual discovery feel earned.

text: Rusty bolts and worn fittings can stick or make noise, so they need patient handling.
when: Opening an old or worn door.
why: Age and corrosion increase friction and sound.

text: A staged stimulus meant to flush a hidden occupant must be safe; one that risks fire or harm must not be used.
when: Designing an alarm or trap to draw out a hidden person
why: Harm to the occupant or surroundings makes the method unacceptable

text: Let the player's hypothesis be tested by a cheap, safe check before the expensive or dangerous one.
when: Designing investigation sequences where the player tests a hypothesis
why: Ordering checks by cost lets players rule out causes before risking more

text: Show alternative routes with different time costs, so the player must trade safety against speed.
when: when designing route choices
why: a visible time cost makes the choice meaningful

text: A sailing chart shows only features useful to mariners, so inland features are often missing or simplified.
when: when comparing charts with land maps
why: each map is drawn for a different purpose

text: Hide layered history in searchable objects, such as luggage labels and letters, that the player unlocks by searching.
when: designing an investigation space
why: Searching rewards careful inspection with backstory and clues.

text: Split clue parts across separate locations, pages or fragments, such as ledger, bank record and order book entries, so players must combine them.
when: Designing a deduction puzzle, written clues in a dungeon, or fragments that form one usable clue
why: Players who gather and combine sources feel the reveal was earned; combining parts makes the clue require attention

text: Partial traces such as visible stairs, footprints toward a back door or a moved mat can point to an entrance or hidden passage the player has not seen.
when: Designing a hidden passage, or a player must find an entrance from incomplete evidence
why: Traces left by occupants point toward access routes

text: Scenes can record a sequence through footprints, dropped items and disturbed objects, so players can reconstruct events.
Loose particles lying in a pile, such as spilled sawdust, can reveal what was spilled and where the container stood.
when: when debris lies near a mark or impression
why: spilled material falls from its source

text: A waste pile or abandoned site can hold a discoverable clue in its debris; scatter items the player must sort to infer what each implies.
Scattered finds across separate sites can look connected; keep them unlinked until the player compares the exact items.
when: when designing several finds that should form a pattern
why: the apparent connection is only confirmed when the specific items match

text: A crime scene can hold several traces, each pointing to a different location, letting the player reconstruct a path from them.
when: when designing a investigation space
why: Multiple pointing traces turn a single room into a route the player must solve.

text: Scatter small traces such as scents, wood shavings or dropped items, each tied to a room and time, so the player can link an NPC to a location.
why: Each trace provides a partial connection that the player assembles into a chain.

text: An object bouncing down stairs leaves repeated scrapes on consecutive treads, then a stretch with no contact, then a dent.
when: reading marks on a staircase

text: Searchable refuse piles can hide items, with later layers making some clues harder to reach than others.
when: When designing searchable sites in a level.
why: Depth of covering layers sets the effort needed to reach each clue.

text: A cache of mixed partial clues forces the player to compare items and see how they connect, which turns the cache into a pointer to further sources.
when: When a container holds several kinds of material.
