why: Comparing fragments produces understanding that no single item provides.

text: A single unverified clue can mislead; confirm a hidden route by finding the same mechanism repeated in a second place.
when: Accepting a solution
why: A first lead may end in a dead end

text: Concealment fails if one sign is left, such as a smell or a broken track, because that one trace can expose the whole setup.
Stacking too many traces makes them compete so that none stands out as a clue.
Place a key clue visible from only one window or balcony, so the player's choice of position becomes the puzzle.
Scatter disturbed objects around a room to signal that an enemy searched it, and let the player compare against the undisturbed state.
When several events occur at once, let the player reconstruct them one at a time from scattered traces such as dropped items and sounds.
when: A level contains overlapping simultaneous events.
why: Scattered traces let the player separate sequences that overlap in time.

text: Examine a scene before others alter it, since traces degrade when characters walk through or handle objects, such as footprints being walked over.
when: when a scene is at risk of contamination by other characters; designing investigation scenes with fragile evidence
why: Handling by others can destroy traces the player needs; time pressure adds stakes to first inspection

text: Reward players who cannot see a room but can hear it by letting them learn plans from sound before entering.
when: Designing rooms where sound carries information.
why: Sound gives players advance knowledge that changes how they approach the room.

text: An NPC's partial, subjective description of a stranger can be matched by the player to a physical marker placed in the level.
when: Designing NPC clues that point to a level object.
why: Incomplete descriptions reward the player for linking clues to the world.

text: A framed character who never resists weakens the story, so show their attempts to defend themselves.
A suspect is not cleared when only one condition has been tested; every condition must be checked before dropping them.
Dusting, cleaning or relighting a scene before inspection destroys evidence and makes later observation unreliable.
1) Measure distances between marks with a tool. 2) Inspect written or marked text closely, character by character. 3) Collect loose material samples into a container for later analysis.
when: when examining a disturbed or contested scene
why: Measured and preserved evidence can be analysed after the scene changes

text: 1) Clear the empty room first. 2) Search the room where the disturbance was heard. 3) Search the place where the injured person lay.
1) Read posture, object positions and lighting as traces of events. 2) Propose a sequence of events for each victim. 3) Mark each reading as a hypothesis and test it against other traces.
when: when reconstructing a scene from physical evidence
why: A single reading can fit posture yet miss the actual route taken, so cross-checking is needed.

text: 1) Control all exits so people leave only through checked routes. 2) Search each person and parcel at the checkpoint. 3) Sweep every zone for small items. 4) Collect and log all fragments before releasing anyone.
1) Partition the space and assign each searcher a side or set of containers. 2) Work toward the middle. 3) Compare notes where the sweeps meet.
Protect a scene with a covering, barrier or marker so repeated foot traffic does not destroy or confuse its evidence.
why: Repeated foot traffic can destroy or confuse evidence.

text: Let witnesses give partial descriptions, such as height or build, so the player can narrow suspects without a full identity.
Let a distinctive but partial NPC description drive a search across a bounded area, such as one town block.
Record each object's position and state when a scene is first examined, so later disturbances can be detected against the original.
Track the time since each scene was last inspected, so the player can judge whether a trace would still be present.
when: Levels where traces decay, such as footprints fading or water drying.
why: Players can reason about trace survival only if they know how long ago the scene was examined.

text: Let players examine how a scene was arranged, such as tie patterns or disturbed objects, to detect a false trail.
when: When a level includes a staged scene the player can inspect
why: Inspectable arrangement turns the scene into a detectable false trail

text: Offer a secure-the-scene action that seals rooms and designates a key custodian; each choice carries a time or reputation penalty.
Flag a scene as altered when someone disturbs it without authority, and record that it was disturbed.
Search the floor with a lens and a close crawl for small or faint traces before the scene is disturbed further.
Design scene evidence whose meaning depends on a second observation the player can make, such as checking the weather.
Plant early staging clues, such as a blood-free or wet trace or an odd light or lock detail, so a staged obvious site misleads until close inspection exposes it.
when: Designing a culprit-arranged scene where the most visible location is not where the event actually happened
why: Careful players notice the inconsistency that a casual look misses, and the staged site draws investigation away from the real site until the clue exposes it.

text: Encode a scene's story in body position, disorder radius and lock state, making each clue reachable by the player.
when: When designing a crime-scene room
why: Reachable clues let the player reconstruct the event.

text: A room or NPC carrying two readings, such as a sleeping figure that may be a corpse or an ally, can be settled by a later event like a noise or light change.
when: Designing a space with an ambiguous figure.
why: A dual reading holds tension until a later cue resolves it.

text: Finding no hiding place does not prove a crime was impossible; re-check witness reliability and who held the key before concluding.
1) Stage an impression or dent in the scene. 2) Let the player place a matching item on it. 3) Confirm the event sequence when the impression reproduces on a second surface.

1) List each actor's position and weapon at the moment of the first fall. 2) Note which weapon is dropped, hidden or still in hand. 3) Check the timing of the fall against the shot. 4) Compare the result with the apparent cause.
when: A scene's apparent cause of harm conflicts with the physical evidence.
why: Positions, weapons and timing expose a reversal that the first impression hides.

text: 1) Let the player reproduce the original conditions of the event, such as dose, deprivation or timing. 2) Use the reproduction to unlock a hidden object.
when: The final puzzle must reveal a hidden object tied to a past event.
why: Letting the player recreate the conditions turns a past event into an interactive solution.

text: Encode events in body positions, scorch decals and footprints for reconstruction; hide traces only when a trap or secret must leave no visible evidence, e.g. via spring-hinged resetting panel.
when: Deciding whether a scene should show evidence of past events.
why: Visible traces let players reconstruct events; a reset removes visible evidence of the action.

text: A physics puzzle can require players to rig a weight and line to reproduce a scene clue, and a matching result confirms their theory and unlocks the next step.
when: Designing a puzzle where players must verify a theory about a scene.
why: Players gain confidence when their own setup reproduces the evidence.

text: A room whose state changes over time, such as a missing object already gone, forces the player to reason backward about who acted first.
Require players to preserve a scene and summon an examiner before the body can be examined, then fix the time-of-death estimate at that point.
when: Designing a discovery mechanic
why: Correct handling ties evidence to the timeline

text: A room with no visible disturbance is a useful clue only if obvious exits are visibly closed and shown; unrevealed gaps feel like cheating.
when: Designing a locked-room puzzle or clue.
why: Obvious exits must be closed before a hidden route is plausible, and gaps the player never saw make the solution unfair.

text: Define each barrier separately, such as a locked door, inside bolt, barred window, fastened shutters, light source and witness, so the player can verify no visible route exists.
when: Defining a sealed room, vault or locked-room puzzle.
why: Explicit, checkable barriers make the impossibility verifiable rather than asserted.

text: Build sealed-room puzzles with a stated time window, a clear last-seen timeline and NPC positions logged at fixed moments, so players can test who could have acted.
when: Designing a sealed-room puzzle.
why: Players can then check claims about who was where and when against the room layout.

text: Build sealed-room puzzles with several openings, such as door, hatch, ladder and empty neighbouring building, plus keys and scheduled events, so players can enumerate, test and deduce the route out.
when: Designing a sealed-room puzzle.
why: Enumerated components give the player a complete set to reason over.

text: A spring lock relocks when its door swings shut, so entry requires a key even when the door is closed behind you.
Hold a reveal behind a sealed door or item that opens on a deadline or checkpoint; record the solution in advance and let an NPC note promise the explanation.
when: Designing a delayed reveal in a quest.
why: A fixed record guarantees the reveal happens at the intended moment.

text: Physical security does not stop an attack via a utility shared with other rooms, such as a lever or pipe network, so a trap there can be operated from another room.
when: Analyzing or designing a locked-room situation.
why: The attack path runs through shared infrastructure, so a locked room can be solved without breaking its door.

text: Place a trap or poison on a shared object such as a chest, potion, or gift, so whichever character picks it up can be struck, and model the handover chain so players trace it.
when: Designing a trap that can hit an unintended NPC.
why: Handover chains give players a route to deduce the intended target.

text: Build a sealed chamber so the player checks each exit in a fixed order, and each failed check narrows the options.
when: Designing a locked-room puzzle.
why: A fixed order makes elimination systematic and fair.

text: Make a sealed room less certain by leaving a second-person trace inside, such as a half-eaten object whose state changes over time.
A sealed room can look empty on first inspection, with its hidden route revealed only after the in-game timeline is checked.
when: when designing a locked-room puzzle
why: Timeline checks reveal what visual inspection misses

text: Place a sensor on each door in a multi-door level so a player who hears a noise can work out which room it came from.
when: a level has several doors near a hidden event

text: Seal a setting with visible barriers, such as collapsed passages or locked gates, cutting off outside help so only intended suspects or threats remain and the setting bounds the puzzle.
when: Designing a self-contained area for an encounter or mystery, or when the people involved should be confined.
why: Visible barriers and cut-off conditions remove outside options and focus events on those present.

text: 1) List every exit, such as doors, hatches, chimneys, windows, roofs, hidden spaces and adjacent buildings. 2) Test each against a checkable physical property. 3) Rule out routes with stated evidence. 4) Accept a surviving route, even if improbable, only once any proposed mechanism is confirmed by experiment. 5) Re-examine nearby features for overlooked routes.
when: A room seems sealed or a crime seems confined to it.
why: Stated reasons show which exits were ruled out; a locked door hides other openings.

text: 1) List every possible entry and exit. 2) Check each for a physical trace. 3) Rule out exits with no trace. 4) Weigh the remaining explanations.
when: a death or event seems to have no explanation

text: 1) Rule out ordinary exits by checking doors and windows for disturbance. 2) If none show it, infer a hidden route. 3) Search for wear, oil or scuffs that a mechanism leaves.
when: A room is sealed and no forced entry is visible
why: Elimination narrows the search to concealed routes

text: 1) List every exit and access point. 2) Check each against the guard posted there and its physical state. 3) Bound the escape window using observation times. 4) Cross-check with an independent question. 5) If all exits are closed, the culprit is still inside.
when: A crime occurs in a space with a limited set of controlled exits and a known observation window.
why: Each exit is ruled in or out by evidence, so closed exits leave the culprit inside.

text: 1) Establish each seal condition, such as locks, checks, light and witnesses, before breaking it. 2) Let the player verify each condition. 3) Break the seal in a scripted event showing the room empty and undisturbed.
when: Designing a fair locked-room impossibility.
why: Verified constraints make the impossibility fair and invite deduction.

text: Use a self-relocking lock to force the player to carry or find a key to re-enter a room.
Link two separated scenes through a shared object the player can recognise, so they connect the scenes without explicit explanation.
when: A scene jumps in time or place
why: A recognised object bridges the gap

text: Make a sealed room an optional mechanic that the player can choose to enter, rather than a fixed barrier.
Let a sealed room open through a mechanism tied to its occupants or contents, so players test people and objects instead of walls.
when: Designing a sealed vault puzzle
why: Checkable routes that are ruled out move attention inside the room

text: In a room with no forced-entry marks, offer hints toward an NPC holding a key, a servant's route or a hidden passage.
Pair a secret with a simple lock so that keys the player has found are rewarded.
why: A concealment that relies on secrecy can be opened by any found key.

text: A sealed room should still have at least one route the player can discover through clues.
when: designing a sealed or locked space
why: A sealed space with no discoverable route frustrates players rather than challenging them.

text: Use a sealed grave or container as a forced escalation point: opening it at the player's decision triggers a new scene.
when: a hidden object is needed to advance the story
why: Player-initiated opening turns pressure into a concrete action with consequences.

text: Let players reveal item properties or a sealed container's contents through non-destructive checks such as weight, feel, colour or a scanner, so the object survives.
when: Designing item inspection that should yield hints, or when the answer is inside a container the player must not break
why: Non-destructive checks reward attentive players while preserving the item; the player proves the theory without the level being destroyed

text: When evidence disappears, resume the search where the hypothesis says it should reappear.
Repeated advice from characters to seek a particular person sets up a thread the audience expects to follow.
when: opening a story or case
why: An expected thread gives players a goal to pursue

text: Look an odd object up in a reference source to find a known practice that explains it, making the object make sense.
Knowledge of a hiding place narrows suspects only if it can be shown to be restricted. If many people saw it, the suspect pool stays wide.
When a theory fails, drop its conclusions and return to the established facts before building a new one.
when: An investigation's working theory is contradicted.
why: Clinging to a failed conclusion distorts how new evidence is read.

text: Restrict observers' access to the accused, so the player must find another route to the truth.
when: designing an investigation with a controlled interrogation
why: Blocked access forces alternative investigation.

text: Trace responsibility by asking who could have stopped a process with a word, and whether anyone with standing demanded delay.
when: assessing who is accountable for a process

text: Wet floors, dust, or mud can record NPC movement, letting players reconstruct a route through the space.
when: A level has surfaces that hold impressions.
why: Visible marks turn environmental detail into a traceable record of movement.

text: Ledgers kept in a level can be cross-checked against each other, such as a supplier list against a detailed book, to reveal a chain of transactions.
Include plausible but empty leads on a quest map, such as an address, shop or contact, that resolve quickly and point the player back to the real clue.
when: When designing an open quest map with multiple leads
why: Quick resolution keeps the player moving and reinforces the true path.

text: Let the environment confirm a claim during a short wait, so suspense builds before the payoff.
Reward cross-checking, for example where a missing key proves a witness's claim about a lock wrong.
Tag each district with a particle profile, such as mill dust or coal soot, and let players match residue on an item to a district.
when: when designing location-finding puzzles

text: Do not sweep an entire area at random when geography already suggests a direction; search the likely path first.
A dormant site such as an abandoned workshop can be inferred from ownership change combined with remaining physical traces.
when: a site's use ended without a recorded reason

text: A distant fire, smoke or light seen from one spot can have several sources, so the player should check the map before settling on one.
when: Designing an ambiguous distant visual cue
why: Multiple plausible sources keep the cue open until the player investigates

text: State the limits of help the NPC will give during a search, such as no assistance or hints, so the rule of the search is explicit.
when: Designing an NPC who stands aside while the player searches.
why: An explicit rule prevents players from expecting help that will not come.

text: Design a reconnaissance phase in which players gather identities, codes or records before the final entry, rewarding patient observation over direct force.
when: Designing a protected location with a final entry challenge
why: Information gathering makes the entry feel earned and lets players succeed through observation

text: A string of empty results builds tension before a turn, so it works as a deliberate pacing device.
when: When pacing a mystery or investigation sequence.
why: Repeated dead ends raise expectation for the next reveal.

text: Assuming a room is empty after a first search found nothing can lead past the real hiding place; check its contents, since an absent occupant still leaves traces.
why: absence of a person does not erase what they left behind

text: 1) Visit every residence with a view of the scene. 2) Record who saw nothing as well as who saw something.
when: start of an investigation with few leads and many possible witnesses
why: negative results narrow the field

text: Re-test each eliminated route before treating it as closed, since an elimination can rest on a mistaken time or witness.
Station a watcher inside the location during the danger period under a plausible pretext, so the watch stays where the threat lies.
when: a further crime is expected and suspects are confined to a known location

text: Describe a place from a stated vantage point, and say why it was chosen, since the viewpoint determines what the reader can see.
Leave a trail leading to a lucky find so the discovery feels earned rather than arbitrary.
Build indirect leads, such as asking an associate first, as a branching route that reaches the same record.
when: When a direct route to a record is locked or unclear.
why: Alternative routes let players reach the same information in different ways.

text: Let a quest require the player to revisit an earlier area and search for details missed the first time.
when: Designing a reopened-case or revisit quest
why: Returning with new knowledge rewards attention and reinforces the reopened question

text: Give each zone or wall a visible cleared or completion flag, and mark each container as checked, empty or holding an item, so players track remaining coverage.
when: a hidden target is searched for across a grid of zones
why: each cleared zone narrows where a small hidden target can be

text: Hide a clue or key item in a searched room so the search feels full, or report nothing so the player learns it is elsewhere; choose by intent.
when: designing a clue in a room the player has already searched
why: a place that seems searched is rarely searched again; the earlier search pattern explains why it was missed

text: Full zone sweeps find small traces but are slow; skipping a few spots with a visible tell, hiding an item there, invites return. Choose by whether completeness matters.
when: designing or searching a bounded room for a small hidden target
why: full sweeps catch traces in corners; an incomplete search signals something remains and gives a fair discovery route

text: Players and characters pass over plain packing materials and boxes on high furniture, because such things blend into the surroundings and go unnoticed.
when: moving through a room without searching it
why: they offend no eye

text: Spatial deduction rebuilds a hidden layout from limited senses, using step counts, marked starting points, touch and sound when sight fails.
when: a character or player must map a space without light

text: A full search of a large building can take months, making exhaustive search impractical for an investigation.
when: a crime scene is a large building with many rooms

text: When obvious places fail, check overlooked containers such as bins, baskets and drawers, and sift mundane material and every fragment.
when: an expected item is missing from obvious places, especially where the owner's habits explain its presence
why: careless habits make items survive in neglected spots

text: Give a covert search a narrow checklist of specific items to find, rather than letting the player browse the whole space.
when: a stealth mission requires locating information
why: targeted search is faster and reduces exposure time

text: Make a blanket search of all staff low-value in the game, and reward players who narrow the search to those who knew the goods were there.
when: Designing investigation rewards in a mystery level.
why: Rewarding targeted reasoning over brute-force searching teaches the intended deduction.

text: Compare the effort needed to leave a scene with the effort needed to enter it, because the easier direction often shows how the person actually left.
when: When an intruder's route in and out is uncertain.
why: Exits from a raised position can be a single step, while entry may require climbing.

text: When a target could be in many rooms, wait at the exit instead of searching, if the target's route is predictable.
Structure search phases so each area yields less than the last, pushing the player toward the next lead.
Give the player a reason to examine a low-stakes side quest closely, since a main-plot item can be hidden inside it.
when: Designing side quests that connect to the main plot
why: Expectation of triviality makes players skip details that matter

text: Study soft ground at close range, lying flat, rather than surveying it from above.
when: When traces are likely on soft outdoor surfaces; hard, dry ground holds tracks poorly.

text: When an NPC is missing, prompt the player to search the expected locations first, since the search itself can reveal clues.
Nested containers, such as a desk holding a pigeonhole that holds a small case, reward thorough searching and give players a reason to check every compartment.
when: designing hidden items for a search-based puzzle
why: players who learn that compartments hide items will check each one

text: A scripted search order can guide the player through rooms so the most urgent space is checked first.
Place two observers with overlapping but different sightlines, so each covers the other's blind spot.
when: one vantage point cannot cover every route
why: the overlap closes the gaps each observer leaves

text: Treat a negative search result as conclusive only after every zone has been checked and nothing has been found.
State a puzzle's search boundary in advance, saying the clue is in this room and visible and touchable, without naming the exact item, so the player searches within a fair limit.
when: Designing a search puzzle where the player must find a clue.
why: A defined search area keeps the puzzle fair and the answer still open.

text: A search mechanic that appears to clear an area gives the player a false sense of safety, and a later disruption then creates suspense before the reveal.
when: Designing a search or clear-the-area moment before a twist.
why: A sense of safety makes the later disruption more startling.

text: A container that has not been emptied keeps items from earlier dates, so its contents bound when an item could have been placed there.
when: When a housekeeper or other source reports when a container was last cleared.
why: Unemptied containers retain items for the period since the last clearing.

text: Measurable cues such as step counts and sound differences can narrow a secret door's location to a short span, letting players search only that area.
when: Designing a secret door that players must locate
why: Quantified clues convert vague searching into a bounded search

text: An aerial observer flying low over a valley makes previously safe places less safe, so a fugitive must reassess which routes are hidden.
when: an overhead observer is active
why: height gives a view that ground routes do not

text: Mapping every surface on a fixed grid of about six inches, and sounding each square, ensures no panel or cavity is skipped.
A careful or single-method search can miss items hidden outside its assumptions, and a finished search then falsely suggests absence; cover all likely places and check personally.
when: a lost item is being searched for
why: limited coverage produces false negatives

text: Failed checks, empty observation sessions or silent witnesses do not prove absence; the target may lie at the next location or appear on another day.
when: a search produces repeated negatives, a stakeout is empty, or no witness reports seeing the person
why: routines vary by day, so one null result is weak evidence; repeated failures do not show the item is absent

text: Attention on the most suspicious object, like a lock or obvious spot, misses surrounding frame and fittings, and thorough searching there wastes effort while decisive traces lie nearby.
why: attention settles on the most suspicious object

text: Checking only hidden nooks, or expecting containers to be empty, misses items in ordinary visible containers; check every container fully.
when: the search space contains both hidden and visible spots
why: expectation lowers attention; the search pattern assumes concealment

text: A failed register search may mean the name is false rather than that the person never stayed, so pair it with an alias check.
when: A name is absent from every register checked.
why: A false name would leave no record under the real name.

text: Checking a long candidate list in person is tedious and draining, so ordering and recording the work keeps it manageable.
when: the candidate set is large
why: repetitive legwork wears down the investigator

text: Choosing a search direction arbitrarily wastes time and invites regret, so an ordered plan should be set before the search begins.
Judging a crowd only by close-up details misses the pattern that distance reveals.
1) Handle every ordinary object, not just look at it or read it. 2) Squeeze, shake and turn each one. 3) Notice any wrong give, sound, weight or crackle that marks a hollow.
when: searching for items or messages hidden inside everyday objects
why: looking alone misses hollows; concealment inside ordinary containers is invisible to visual checks

text: 1) Open and search each container or drawer in turn, separately, since a later one may hold what an earlier search missed. 2) Record its contents. 3) Return every item to its original place so nothing looks disturbed.
when: the room must stay undisturbed for later examination
why: orderly searching keeps traces of the search hidden

text: 1) Search every wall and corner for a second opening. 2) Divide the suspect area into wall and floor sections. 3) Test each section and record which are ruled out before concluding no hidden door exists.
when: a room appears to have no exit
why: hidden exits are often placed where the first search did not look

text: 1) List every route into and out of the room: doors, windows, transoms, air-shafts, dumb-waiters, side doors, spare keys. 2) Check each at every height, including low door gaps, upper transoms and cracks. 3) Test each against physical evidence. 4) Conclude a route was used only when evidence supports it; treat sealing as proven only when every route is closed.
when: a room looks sealed on first reading
why: sealing one height does not rule out another; a locked door alone does not prove a sealed room

text: 1) List every candidate who passed through the relevant area. 2) Question each one. 3) Follow up on every lead that comes out of the answers.
when: Tracing a vehicle or person through a region.
why: Systematic coverage avoids missing the one candidate who matters.

text: 1) Narrow candidate locations using the target's likely habits and motives. 2) List every remaining candidate. 3) Check each in order and record its result. 4) Mark each candidate as checked.
when: the target's trail is missing but the candidate set is finite
why: an ordered, recorded check covers every option without repeats or gaps

text: 1) Empty the container onto a clear surface. 2) Examine each item one by one. 3) Do not look only for the item already in mind.
1) Visit a fixed list of sites in set order. 2) Justify each visit with a cover story. 3) Pay small sums for access. 4) Keep spare money so the canvass can continue.
when: Searching many locations for one item or person.
why: A fixed route and cover make the search systematic and sustainable.

text: 1) Have the responsible official conduct the search. 2) Lay each item out in view. 3) Record every item as property as it is handled.
when: when personal effects are searched as evidence
why: a record of handled items supports later proof

text: 1) Scan the edges of cover for odd shapes. 2) Check protruding parts such as limbs. 3) Mark the spot before anyone moves closer.
when: Searching open ground for a body or hidden object.
why: Bodies often show as small irregularities at the edges of vegetation.

text: 1) Start at a stated end of the guide. 2) Feel along the guide step by step. 3) Follow a cord to the point where it enters a hazard.
when: for clues that require a precise search method

text: 1) Check each sense or channel in turn for anomalies. 2) Return in better light or conditions. 3) Find the spot that stays still against moving background. 4) Search that spot directly and repeatedly.
when: a small clue is lost among moving or busy surroundings
why: stepwise checks catch what one glance misses

text: 1) Strike the surface with a tool. 2) Listen for a change in tone. 3) Repeat strikes in steps across the area to narrow where the hollow lies. 4) Measure from a known reference. 5) Compare the result with what is expected there.
when: a cavity may lie under a floor or behind a wall

text: 1) Strip or sound walls, floor and ceiling to detect hidden openings. 2) Inspect the door for removable panels or weak points. 3) Consider whether a person could pass under furniture near the door. 4) Check the window and adjoining space as a route of flight.
when: A room seems sealed and the apparent seal is the central problem.
why: Each structure is a distinct possible exit that needs its own test.

text: 1) Lie low so the surface is seen at a grazing angle. 2) Sweep a light across the floor. 3) Look for seams between blocks. 4) Clear rugs away and check again.
when: a floor may hide a concealed cache

text: 1) Turn the handle slowly in small steps. 2) Stop when pressure goes beyond a point, which signals a bolt. 3) Restore the handle to its original position before releasing it.
when: Testing whether a door is locked from the other side.
why: Gentle probing avoids noise and leaves no sign of tampering.

text: 1) Inspect every access point (door, window, roof) for marks of passage. 2) Check supporting marks such as ladder marks or footprints. 3) Search every place a hidden object could sit, including storage. 4) Complete the search before forming a concealment theory.
when: when a scene appears closed but someone must have entered or left
why: Missing a storage space or access point leaves concealment untested.

text: 1) Divide the area into enclosed spots by type. 2) Check each type in a fixed order. 3) Follow any sound from the target at once, ending the sweep early.
when: The target could hide in several enclosed spots in a small, bounded area

text: 1) Split the area into zones so no corner is left out. 2) Assign each searcher one zone. 3) Check every zone fully. 4) Recall the team once all zones are checked.
when: A hidden target could be in any small space and helpers need a shared plan.

text: 1) Circle overhead and lower height to spot the target through optics. 2) Advance ground searchers in a line across the area, like beaters sweeping cover. 3) Keep the line moving until the area is covered.
when: a target is hidden across open terrain
why: height reveals figures and a line sweeps ground systematically

text: 1) Fix a sightline using visible landmarks. 2) Hide where the view is clear. 3) Count time to measure the target's actions. 4) Wait a set interval before moving.
when: a hidden action must be seen unnoticed or repeated at the same spot
why: landmarks and counts let a later repeat be matched precisely

text: 1) Observe the building from a public route. 2) Make repeated passes rather than approaching the entrance. 3) Note window coverings, smoke and movement.
when: You need to learn occupancy without entering
why: Repeated passes from outside avoid drawing attention

text: After a failed search, test where the object went by searching surroundings methodically, not assuming it is elsewhere; someone else may hold it, so suspicion should move on.
when: a search comes up empty
why: absence in one place does not clear the item's whereabouts

text: Search every kind of hiding place beyond the main scene: gardens, sheds, conservatories, pavilions, kennels, top branches of each tree, cloakrooms, sweepings, waste containers, lounges and restrooms.
why: clues outside the building are easily overlooked when searchers check only the inside

text: Record a negative result, since a fully searched area with nothing found narrows where a hidden object can be.
Give counts and measures such as dimensions, door offsets and window numbers, so the reader can build an accurate mental map.
when: when the layout matters later
why: exact figures make the map checkable

text: Give each chamber with a corpse or wreck a fixed inspection list of posture, bedding and objects so players can search systematically.
Make in-game ledgers searchable by date so players can narrow entries to the probable date of an event.
Search a small group in one room with outer doors locked, and search people of the same gender together, so the search is seen as fair.
when: A small closed group shares access and a search is socially acceptable.
why: Locked exits and same-gender searches reduce objection and keep the process credible.

text: Let players search a group of NPCs in a room, set a remembered flag when someone refuses, and track reactions as behavior clues.
when: Designing an interrogation or search mechanic.
why: Persistent flags let refusal and reactions affect later inference.

text: Give NPCs searchable items, such as a key with a coloured tag, that point to a specific door or room.
when: an NPC carries an item tied to a location
why: searchable pointers turn NPC inventory into navigation clues

text: Let players stash an item in a high, partly hidden spot and retrieve it with a tool, so the item never needs to be held in hand.
when: in stealth or puzzle levels

text: Route item searches through logical locations so players learn the layout while looking.
Assume players and NPCs will recheck a stash, so give a hidden item a second hiding place.
when: placing a hidden item
why: a single hiding place is likely to be found

text: State the limit of search coverage, such as dim light, and do not treat one failed check in a partly seen area as ruling out a hiding spot.
Escalate to a second, more thorough search when a first pass finds nothing and suspicion of hidden activity remains.
When the number of actors is unknown, add coverage rather than assume a single actor, since a group may be present.
when: the number of people involved is not known
why: A lone-actor assumption misses accomplices who may act unseen.

text: Give each character a fixed vantage point so its claims about what it saw can be tested against the level geometry.
Repeated failed searches raise pressure while the answer stays unknown, or flatten interest and tire a watcher into exploitable lapses when they add nothing new; choose by the effect wanted.
A methodical search keeps the room tidy but takes longer; a rushed search finds the likeliest spots sooner and leaves disorder behind.
when: under a time limit
why: speed and tidiness cannot both be maximised within one window

text: Give each trace one consistent source condition so that a rival explanation fails under a check the player can perform.
when: Designing physical clues that players must test.
why: A rival explanation then becomes testable and can be ruled out.

text: Make an object examination change meaning once the player reads an in-world text, so the same object reads as a clue after reading.
when: Environments with inspectable artifacts
why: Reading supplies the cause the object lacks

text: Giving an evidence object a secondary use, such as a scrap that resembles a tool, makes the player explain why it was placed where it was found.
why: An object with a plausible alternative function creates a question about its actual purpose.

text: Make the final confrontation depend on evidence the player collected several zones earlier, not on a new key item.
Place secrets above normal reach so the player must find a ladder, climb, or use a tool to reach them.
when: When designing hidden areas in a 3D level.
why: Height adds a deliberate search cost without hiding the secret from a determined player.

text: Let a locked object's secret be known to a small set of NPCs and plant clues so players can build the holder list and work out who could have opened it.
when: Designing a locked object opened by a secret
why: A bounded holder list turns the solution into a deduction rather than a guess

text: 1) Record a baseline measurement of an identity early as a routine habit. 2) Record the same measure later. 3) Compare the two records; a mismatch exposes the hidden identity.
when: a character's true identity must be proven from records kept at different times
why: Comparing a fixed early record with a later one gives a checkable proof that a player can reproduce.

text: Soundproofing, restricted locks and fixed seating can signal a room set up for private, planned gatherings.
A visible parked cart, carriage or known route can expose a hidden meeting, since observers infer it and a bystander can later confirm or contradict accounts.
when: Players or NPCs approach a hidden meeting, or a meeting site with parked transport is designed
why: Observers infer the meeting from peripheral signs

text: A spring-hinged cover that snaps shut after use leaves no visible sign that it was opened, erasing evidence of the route.
when: when a hidden mechanism should leave no trace after use
why: the automatic closing resets the visible state

text: Keep construction tasks, such as building a device, separate from analysis tasks, such as reading a scene, and judge each on its own terms.
when: designing multi-step investigation challenges

text: Place the murder room and the dump site apart, and leave clues on the route between them so players can trace how a body was moved.
Give each witness a bounded vantage point (window, doorway, mirror, screen, corridor) and record its duration, place and closeness so players can check claims against the layout.
when: testimony depends on sight lines, such as designing NPC witnesses for a mystery level
why: a confident account can hide a partial view; players can then judge which testimony to trust

text: Observers at the same vantage can see the same scene yet draw opposite conclusions, because each brings different assumptions to what they see.
when: two watchers share one observation post
why: interpretation depends on prior assumptions

text: Witnesses who glimpsed a scene at a distance or under stress often garble incidental details, such as a sign's wording or an animal's colour.
when: reporting brief or stressful sightings
why: attention is limited, so peripheral details are recorded weakly

text: A vantage point gives sight without sound: a watcher on a hill can see a meeting clearly yet cannot hear what is said.
when: The meaning of an event depends on words.
why: Distance blocks sound, so sight alone is insufficient.

text: Rooms with undrawn curtains can be seen into from the grounds, so anyone outside may have observed the interior.
when: Hot weather, when curtains are often left open

text: An image can be arranged so that it reads correctly only from one viewpoint, limiting where observers can verify it.
Elevation lets a viewer see over obstacles that hide the same ground from ground level.
Walls and buildings block sightlines from a house, so a character can move between them without being seen by an observer inside.
A locked store's position relative to an external opening determines who could reach it from outside and by what route.
when: when assessing access from outside a building
why: proximity to openings sets the possible approach paths

text: A pulled-out chair can hide a table and whatever sits on it from anyone entering through the door.
when: Furniture stands between a doorway and an object
why: Displaced furniture blocks sight lines to what lies behind it

text: A room corner, especially a sharp acute one, is hard to see into without strong light.
when: Deciding whether an observer in a corner can be seen.
why: Lighting limits sight lines into corners.

text: Thin partitions carry speech between adjoining rooms, so private conversation in one room can be overheard from the next.
when: walls between rooms are flimsy

text: Judge a claimed sighting by the witness's position, obstacles, distance, light and whether the observed looked toward them; a claim outside these sight limits is implausible.
when: a witness claims to have seen someone through a door, crowd, across distance or an act
why: A half-open door can hide a person from one observer but not from another.

text: Let one room be seen from several vantage points and record the differences between views, since they reveal what a single view cannot.
Check each alibi witness's sightline to confirm they saw the suspect continuously; a continuous, complete view strengthens a sequence more than a partial view.
why: A badly placed witness leaves room for an unseen departure.

text: Events falling within the same short window are candidates for a causal link, but overlap only prompts investigation and is not proof.
why: Coincidence in time is common, so overlap alone does not establish a connection.

text: A witness's account of where an item was dropped narrows the search more than the item itself does.
when: when a searcher has a reliable sighting of a disposal
why: The sighting points to the exact container or spot to examine.

text: A sound many people heard, such as a clock chime, can anchor an hour that several witnesses can confirm independently.
when: when witnesses need a common reference time
why: several people can confirm the same sound

text: A witness's casual sighting fixes a point on the timeline and tests a stated alibi, but only if the time and place of the sighting are known.
when: A witness recognises someone while passing by.
why: An unlocated sighting cannot anchor a timeline or contradict a claim.

text: A witness who admits taking no notice of the people involved adds little evidence.
Before accepting a witness's description of a figure's shape, check the angle, lighting, reflective surfaces and objects between observer and figure.
when: when a witness reports an odd or monstrous shape

text: Check a witness's timing against where they stood. A view from a different floor or angle limits what they could have seen.
Record why a witness was positioned to observe, since that reason is part of judging how reliable the account is.
when: Assessing a witness account from a hidden position.
why: Motive for watching explains the vantage and affects how much attention was paid.

text: Where witnesses disagree about who passed a point, check which witness could actually see that route, since honest witnesses may lack a view.
Map homes, meeting places and travel distances to judge which witnesses could have seen or heard an event.
when: testing a witness's account
why: physical access limits what a person could observe

text: A connecting door that is never used can be made discoverable as a shortcut into a hidden area.
when: Designing secret routes

text: A stealth encounter can use silence and a narrow sightline so the player learns the enemy's movement without alerting it.
when: Designing a timed stealth encounter.
why: Limited vision rewards patient observation and builds tension through restraint.

text: In dark stealth areas, place a trackable sound cue, such as a clock or creaking floor, that the player must follow to avoid detection.
when: generating dark stealth rooms
why: Sound cues give the player usable information when light is limited.

text: Place a room or lodging with a view of a target's door in the level as a stakeout spot for the player.
when: Designing surveillance or stakeout missions.

text: Place a high vantage point so the whole trail is visible at once, letting players read the clue before they reach it.
Place landmarks along routes so players can correct distance estimates that darkness or sealed windows have distorted.
Make a question such as why a room was chosen answerable by examining the building's layout and routines.
A stairway or archway with a fixed sightline makes witness positions in a level meaningful.
Map a setting's isolation to the availability of witnesses and rescue, and let the player judge access from the layout.
when: Designing a location where witness presence affects the story.
why: Layout-based cues let players infer access without explicit explanation.

text: Verify a stealth rule, such as a guard not seeing a doorway, by checking line of sight from the guard's actual position in the layout.
when: when a layout must hide an area from an agent
why: geometry, not intent, decides what the agent sees

text: Let a player on a tower or roof see into zones hidden from ground level, rewarding height and exploration.
when: when designing vertical level layouts
why: height reveals areas that ground movement cannot

text: Choose exit routes that avoid windows and open ground under observation, and use roofs or pipes as hidden traversal paths.
when: when designing or planning a route past watchers
why: Exposed open ground and watched windows make detection likely, while vertical routes stay out of sight.

text: Store positions a witness describes as data and check them against level geometry, so testimony the layout makes impossible can be rejected.
when: in games with NPC witnesses
why: geometry determines what a sight line allows

text: A plain building layout can decide what is possible, since limited entrances and passages define the routes a culprit could take.
when: Route of access is central to the puzzle.
why: Physical constraints of the layout determine which paths are feasible.

text: Place a witness at a deliberate sightline and time so the player's own timing check becomes a test of whether a claimed account holds.
when: An NPC claims to have been somewhere or seen something.

text: Use a concealed watch point with partial cover, and remember that the watched may look up and see the watcher.
when: Designing a hidden observation position in a street or building.
why: Concealment is reciprocal; the observed can spot the observer.

text: Show only part of a room, such as through a door or cutaway, and follow it with a character's reaction to build tension before the clue appears.
when: Designing a reveal in a room the player is about to enter.
why: A reaction without a visible cause raises curiosity.

text: Use a reflector or window across a shaft to let a player see a hidden space, so the sightline itself becomes the clue.
when: designing a hidden room visible from elsewhere
why: The player discovers the room through the geometry rather than through text.

text: A person hidden from one watcher may be visible to another watcher at a different angle, so each sightline needs checking.
when: Placing NPCs who can observe a meeting area
why: Coverage differs by position, so one blind spot does not guarantee privacy

text: Give familiar props or NPCs an alternate state visible from a particular angle, rewarding players who inspect from new positions.
when: Designing hidden detail in a known environment.
why: Changing position reveals information that default viewing hides.

text: A sightline from a fixed position defines what a watcher there could see, so a sighting depends on the doorway or viewpoint.
when: when judging whether a witness could have seen an event

text: A window overlooking a busy area makes an outside intruder unlikely, since the entry would be seen.
when: An intrusion theory is weighed against the layout.
why: Visibility to others raises the risk of entry and so lowers its likelihood.

text: A structure such as a parapet can hide an actor from street-level observers, letting an act happen unseen from below.
when: an act happens above a public space
why: blocking sightlines removes observers

text: Corridors or rooms that look alike can supply a believable wrong-turn explanation for how a character reached a restricted area.
when: Explaining how a character entered a restricted room
why: Visual similarity makes a mistaken route plausible

text: Layout features such as a tunnel under a road and two gates shape an escape route and determine where pursuers search.
A secret site stays hidden when nearer terrain blocks every outside sight line, and observers assume the object went elsewhere.
when: when the site sits on a rise with blocking features between it and the usual approaches

text: Floor layout limits who can reach which room; a wing with no direct link to another removes that wing as an access route.
when: when judging who could have entered a room

text: Peepholes or sightlines through a room let guards watch the player, and darkness can let the player avoid being seen.
when: Designing rooms that are monitored.
why: Darkness cuts off the watcher's view.

text: Track or wall curvature can hide most of a long moving object from witnesses in other parts of it, so visibility depends on layout.
when: deciding which observers could see an event
why: geometry blocks sightlines

text: Room layout, not only furniture, determines who can reach a listener and who can overhear them.
Who can see or reach a spot depends on walls, balconies, bay windows, gates, alleys and locked doors, which together set sightlines and entry points.
A conclusion drawn from one short window of observation can miss a route used at another time.
A short unexplained absence can look sinister or be innocent, so gaps need checking rather than assumption.
Relying on sight alone misses differences that a magnifier would reveal.
when: inspecting matched objects
why: Small details fall below ordinary visual detection.

text: Agreement among people in one room is not independent corroboration when all of them accept the same unverifiable report.
A single check shows only the state at the moment it was made, not that the state never changes.
A location clue is only as precise as its landmark; a vague feature such as a round tower leaves the exact point unclear.
A single disturbance read in isolation can mislead, so test it against the rest of the scene before drawing a conclusion.
A watcher who hears nothing may assume nothing happened. Ask about sounds as well as sightings.
why: Events can be heard without being seen.

text: The observer's own noise, such as a knocked table, can be mistaken for an event. Note self-caused sounds.
when: when the observer is moving or working nearby
why: Their own actions can produce events that look external.

text: A single watch post fails to cover a building that has several unguarded entrances.
A route that avoids windows can still pass a sleeper who wakes, so sightline safety does not guarantee an undetected route.
when: when relying on sightline-safe routing
why: Unplanned events such as waking occupants can expose a route.

text: Trusting a witness's route through a dark room without checking it against the layout can hide impossible movements.
when: a route is described from memory in poor light
why: Dark rooms make descriptions unreliable

text: A sweep that checks only eye-level surfaces misses what sits above or behind normal reach.
A claim that a watcher would have seen an intruder is unreliable when the guarded area is dimly lit.
when: when judging whether a watcher could have observed an entry
why: low light limits what a watcher can actually perceive

text: 1) Stand where the witness claims to have been, or locate their window or room. 2) Check what they could see or hear from there, including whether any door is visible.
when: A witness claims to have seen, not seen, or heard something, or claims a sight line or shot position.
why: Position limits what could be seen, so standing there tests the claim.

text: 1) Establish the distance. 2) Establish the lighting. 3) Establish the angle and any obstructions. 4) Establish the time of observation. 5) Compare the account to the resulting sightline.
when: when testimony concerns an event seen through a barrier, at night or from a distance
why: a claim that cannot physically be seen should be doubted until these conditions are checked

text: 1) Take the witness's stated sequence of events. 2) For each step, ask where the person was heading, not only what they did. 3) Compare the direction of travel with the scene of the event. 4) Probe the unobserved gap after parting from companions and before the next known point. 5) Ask about things the witness did not volunteer.
when: A witness's account includes movement or times that can be measured against a map or clock

text: A level can be restored to a saved state, and replayed player routes can check whether a trap, pickup, or enemy still gives the same result.
when: Testing whether a placement behaves consistently across runs.
why: Replaying the same conditions isolates the effect of a single placement.

text: 1) Pick two distant landmarks. 2) Stand at a fixed spot from which they appear in one line. 3) Use that line as a precise bearing to the hidden position.
when: for placing a hidden object that is visible from a fixed point
why: A line of sight through two landmarks gives a bearing that a reader can follow exactly.

text: 1) Name each landmark passed on the route. 2) Keep a mental map of direction from the sequence of names. 3) Note where orientation is lost, such as in fog.
when: when a traveller must track an unknown route
why: named landmarks let a traveller keep bearings that fog or darkness would erase

text: 1) Identify the vulnerable points of the building. 2) Assign one watcher to the exit the suspects would use. 3) Place others behind cover to close in together. 4) Cover each remaining exit with a separate group.
when: setting an ambush before suspects arrive
why: every escape route is blocked before the suspects act

text: 1) From the observer's position, check whether one fixed light or point hides another behind it. 2) If they line up, read the alignment as a danger signal.
when: Testing whether a signal or hazard is aligned to a spot

text: 1) Sketch the room and any adjoining room as a plan, marking doors, windows and furniture. 2) Stand at the position a witness describes. 3) Look through each opening and record what is visible. 4) Confirm fittings work before concluding.
when: when a witness's account depends on what could be seen from a location
why: claims about visibility are only checkable against the actual layout

text: 1) Map walls, gates and entry points. 2) Mark which windows and balconies have a clear view. 3) Note obstructions such as foliage. 4) Keep the diagram as a permanent record when it bears on the solution.
when: question is who could see or reach a location
why: obstructions change the answer

text: 1) Position the observer behind a narrow gap, such as a half-open window or a gap in a blind. 2) Observe the subject without alerting it. 3) Record only what the gap reveals.
when: The subject must be learned about without being warned.
why: A narrow sightline limits what the observer sees and keeps the observer hidden.

text: 1) List every exit of the building. 2) For each exit, record which witness or sight line could observe it. 3) Mark exits with no observer as candidate routes for an unseen departure.
when: when someone's absence must be explained by an unobserved route, or when designing a hidden exit
why: gaps in observation reveal where an unseen exit may lie; observer positions give a fair, observable basis for deduction, rewarding careful observation over guesswork

text: 1) Place windows, glass partitions and lamps so each hidden spot gives a specific view. 2) Let the player test each sightline on a map.
when: Designing hiding spots and observation points in a level.
why: Defined sightlines make hidden positions readable and testable by the player.

text: 1) Fix the vantage point from which an immobilised player views the room. 2) Place layout, patrol routes and key items within that view. 3) Set critical enemy dialogue or planning where the sightline is clear.
when: A player is immobilised by a trap, cutscene, or sleep effect but must still learn the situation.
why: A deliberate vantage point lets the player learn the threat before they can respond.

text: Provide a second exit or hidden passage, such as a back exit no guard watches, so the player can discover a route and watch a room unseen.
when: Designing a stealth space where observation is part of play.
why: A second route lets the player watch and escape unseen.

text: Give stealth scenes watcher NPCs with limited sightlines and use windows, doors and corridors as sightline puzzles, so players find unobserved routes that reward route planning.
when: designing a stealth or surveillance encounter
why: Blind spots turn observation into a puzzle the player can solve

text: Provide a readable level plan showing entrances, doors, stair destinations, passages, switches, sightlines and cut-off areas before the investigation starts, so players can test routes and NPC accounts.
when: opening a setting that will be investigated
why: known routes give players a baseline for judging later movement and accounts

text: Place balconies, bay windows, windows, doorways and screening trees so players can check who can observe each key spot and confirm or exclude witnesses.
Check the room's geometry before reasoning from a sound, since mistaking a window for a door changes the possible sources and can derail the reconstruction.
when: a sound is traced to a room
why: openings determine what could have made the noise

text: Make some traces visible only from particular vantage points and signpost those points, since a clue seen from one spot is easily missed if players never go there.
Make each locked room's entrances and each eliminated option visible through sight lines or map features, so the player can check exclusions and see why they are closed.
when: When designing a sealed room puzzle
why: Visible, listed routes give the player a clear elimination process.

text: Place a grille or window that gives a partial sight-line as a concealed vantage point from which the player can watch a target.
when: when designing hidden observation spots

text: Use shared rooms and thin walls as overhearing opportunities, but treat overheard speech cautiously if the listener was distracted or had a stake in the outcome.
when: When a room is shared or walls are thin.

text: Let doors, vents and corridors carry sound or sight to NPCs, so players learn things they were not meant to hear.
when: designing spaces where NPCs may overhear

text: When a fugitive NPC escapes, make the next lead a contact the player can tail rather than the fugitive's known location.
when: Designing the lead after an NPC escapes.
why: Tailing a contact keeps the trail alive and rewards patient observation.

text: Build stakeout and tail mechanics with fixed watch positions, line-of-sight checks and a risk that the target notices the player.
why: Positional checks turn surveillance into a skill test with a clear failure state.

text: A reversal of who watched whom can serve as a late twist that retroactively explains a locked room.
when: when designing a late-game twist

text: Record how long a guard stays away from a post, and let the player test whether a planned sequence fits that window using an in-game timer.
when: Designing timed stealth sequences in a level.
why: Measurable windows let players check their plans against real timing data.

text: Place light switches and connecting doors deliberately, since they set which routes, lighting and sounds are possible in a space.
when: generating or hand-placing rooms
why: These elements determine reachable routes and perception

text: Make the required viewing position itself a clue, such as a ledge that fits only one seated position, to confirm the intended vantage point.
Use line-of-sight and sound rules to limit what the player sees and hears, and flag NPC reports that cover only part of an event as partial.
when: Designing observation and eavesdropping in a level.
why: Partial information should be marked so players weigh it correctly.

text: Give the player two sightlines and a visible approach path so that both stealth and direct confrontation remain viable.
Let the player spot a following guard through a window or reflection, so the watcher works as a clue.
when: A guard or spy follows the player out of a room.

text: Open a level on a disorienting view of a landmark that the player understands only after reaching it.
when: Designing a level opening around a landmark
why: Seeing the landmark out of context creates curiosity

text: Route the player past named landmarks, use fog and lighting for tension, and end the approach on a reveal of the target location.
when: when designing a level path toward a reveal
why: named landmarks orient the player and the reveal rewards the journey

text: Place a mirror so a hidden observer sitting in the dark can see a door or window opposite without being seen.
when: a watcher must observe unseen
why: a reflected sightline keeps the observer in shadow

text: Make witness corroboration a puzzle: the player confirms a claim by finding a matching physical trace in the environment.
Use line-of-sight checks to show where an enemy could watch the player without being seen, and make those unseen views discoverable.
when: designing enemy placement in a search or stealth area
why: players can then deduce hidden watchers from the layout

text: A capture tool that records a scene from a fixed list of viewpoints gives players a reusable, checkable record of the space.
when: Designing an in-game photo or scan mechanic
why: Fixed views let players compare and recall the layout later

text: Make reach constraints explicit, such as a key on a high ledge, so players can infer a character's height or ability; add furniture like a step that changes the estimate.
when: designing objects placed at set heights

text: Render distant crowd members as grouped silhouettes and reveal individual tells only up close, since visual resolution falls with distance.
when: Designing crowds or enemy groups seen from afar, or where an observer views a group from different distances.
why: Distance limits what the eye can resolve, so individual detail disappears at long range.

text: Use eye-height line-of-sight tests to decide which characters or positions a puzzle can include or exclude.
Place residences with sightlines to a scene on the city map, so a canvass yields a mix of witness and null results.
Let an unobstructed window supply testimony that players can reach only by moving through the map, so location gates the clue.
Assign each observer a fixed post covering part of an area and mark the posts on a plan so overlaps and blind spots are visible.
when: Several observers cover overlapping but imperfect views
why: Fixed posts make coverage gaps predictable

text: A hidden listening post works best when the room beside the target is empty and locked from the target's side.
Let a gap or crack in a wall give the player an unseen view into an adjacent room.
Let a building's position and the roads around it limit what a witness could have seen, so the map itself works as an alibi check.
when: designing witness testimony in a game
why: players can test claims against the geography

text: Design a house layout as a crime scene map, with rooms and access routes that determine who could have been where.
when: Building a mystery location.

text: Keep a hidden character out of view so that the player's knowledge of their state stays partial, as the observer's is.
Give guards or NPCs in a crowded hall sight cones, so a player-seen event may go unnoticed by others for a logical reason.
when: When designing a crowded scene where NPCs react to player actions.
why: Limited sight lines make missed observation believable and fair.

text: Place partial views such as a gap in a fence or a window that signal a presence without identifying it, rewarding players who wait and watch.
when: Designing hidden presence clues in a level.
why: Partial information invites patient observation and inference.

text: Build sightlines and blind corners into the layout so a player can find a hidden spot from which to watch or act unseen.
when: when designing an area meant for stealth or surveillance
why: Blocked views from nearby windows let a visitor proceed unobserved.

text: A vantage point that reveals more should carry detection risk: a larger concealed peephole shows more but attracts attention.
when: when placing a hidden observation spot
why: unpunished vantage points make information gathering trivially safe

text: A distant location lowers exposure to observers but lengthens travel time, increasing the absence that may be noticed.
when: Choosing where a player or NPC must go under a deadline.
why: Safety from observation and time spent away pull in opposite directions.

text: A chokepoint is a location with a single practical approach, which limits who can arrive and gives a clear point to watch.
when: Designing a map or location with a limited entrance.
why: A single approach concentrates arrivals and visibility at one point.

text: Use one controlled crossing, such as a single bridge, to fix the player's route into an enclosed area.
When a crime seems to have only one route, confirm every other route is closed before accepting that conclusion.
A map with one main approach gives the player a clear point to watch and gives the game a clear point to spawn arrivals.
when: Designing a location that the player defends or monitors.
why: A single entrance concentrates both player attention and enemy or NPC arrivals.

text: A late-arriving document can gate the final reveal room.
A reveal that depends on a single light source fails if that source changes unexpectedly.
when: Designing a reveal lit by one source.
why: Without a backup light, the intended moment can be lost.

text: 1) Design each mystery with at least two entry points. 2) Let a blocked player approach from a known event elsewhere. 3) Set the cost of a fact request to match the question's importance.
when: Building investigation content that a player may get stuck in.
why: Multiple entries prevent a single blocked location from ending progress.

text: Balance access so progress is not fully blocked, but is not so smooth that it looks staged; vary route smoothness to keep progress feeling earned.
when: Designing progression through a space with opponents or obstacles.
why: Overly smooth paths reveal the designer's hand and undermine the sense of earned progress.

text: Use soft surfaces such as sand, mud or dust, which keep the shape of each step, so routes can be reconstructed and players can deduce who entered and when.
when: Designing traceable movement or an entry or exit puzzle on a surface that holds impressions.
why: Recorded traces let players reason from evidence rather than guess.

text: Record footprints on soft ground such as mud or grass, but let them vanish on paved surfaces; a path leaving no prints becomes a cue to deduce rather than track.
when: When designing ground surfaces that affect tracking.
why: Tracking has natural limits, and surfaces that hide tracks shift the challenge from tracking to deduction.

text: Scent, residue or disinfectant can mark a hidden room or NPC as a discoverable clue for the player.
Record footprints in soft ground so overlapping marks reveal the order in which the player or NPCs passed.
when: When designing environmental storytelling in a level.
why: Layered tracks create readable history.

text: Inspect objects for recent repair signs: a glue line still tacky, a patch with mismatched colour, and dust or powder caught in fresh bonding.
when: an object may have been handled after an event
why: Fresh repairs leave traces that aged, intact material does not.

text: Dust, mud or snow on a level can record player movement, and a designed trail can end at a hidden exit the player must notice.
when: When designing tracking puzzles on surfaces that can hold impressions.
why: Visible traces let the player infer routes and hidden exits.

text: Footprints leading to each closed door and under it show a route, and the last print can reveal where movement ended.
when: Tracing an intruder's path through a space
why: Physical trails record movement across the floor

text: Soft ground, dust or snow can record footprints whose shape and depth vary with footwear and weight, letting the level identify which character passed.
when: A level includes receptive surfaces
why: Impression differs by foot and load

text: A sign of unknown authorship invites guesses, and a later discovery can either settle those guesses or reverse them.
when: A world element has no known author or origin
why: New evidence changes the meaning of old marks

text: Record tracks as persistent terrain marks, with tread or wheel width identifying which route was used, so players can trace movement.
when: Designing a level where movement should be traceable
why: Readable marks let players reconstruct routes and vehicle types

text: When a measured space seems larger than expected, or a feature looks like a secret entrance, first check structural projections and partitions, since they often explain the apparent hidden space.
when: a measured gap exceeds the visible room, or an element seems to conceal an entrance
why: structural elements often account for the extra dimension, and many features serve only a structural role, so a suspicious element is not proof of a passage

text: Key layout constraints should be stated before they matter, since a reader or player needs the map in advance to check each route.
when: Access routes are central to a puzzle.
why: Constraints revealed only at the reveal break fair play.

text: Test walls and moldings by tapping for hollow sounds, and lift loose fittings, since hidden items can sit in cavities behind surfaces.
A sealed room with no physical trace gives the player nothing to reason from.
A trap that depends on exact fit fails if the passage and trigger component differ even slightly in size.
when: when a mechanism relies on a component passing through a narrow route
why: small size mismatches block the component or change its path

text: Sounds carry unevenly through a building, so check any claim that someone could hear an event from another area.
when: a witness claims they could hear a distant event
why: Walls, floors and distance change what is audible, so earshot claims can be wrong.

text: Treat gates and doors as deliberate thresholds that change who enters and what they face, since choke points concentrate tension and clues.
when: Laying out a level's passages.

text: A staged reveal shows a scene in parts over time rather than at once, using fog, a winding route or a gate to control what is visible.
when: the reveal should build gradually

text: Make a staged room detectable through inconsistent details, such as a made bed lacking sleeper's habits or uncut pages and unused objects, rewarding observant players.
when: when designing environmental clues in a mystery level, or making a room feel staged or lived in
why: Inconsistent details reward observant players; detail states communicate how the space is used.

text: End a level section at the moment of recognition, so the reveal becomes a cliffhanger.
Visible marks of an unseen past add atmosphere and suggest that a clue may mean more than it appears.
when: Designing a setting with history
why: Hints of history invite players to look closer

text: Let players infer planned traps from setup clues, such as a guard swapped at a set time or a tool kept in an unusual place.
when: designing a trap or puzzle
why: visible preparation rewards players who notice it

text: Pair a serene location with a hidden danger so the setting itself gives the player a hint that the calm is misleading.
when: When designing a peaceful area that hides a threat
why: A mismatch between appearance and history prompts the player to look closer.

text: Use staged scenes, such as a notice or a board, to give players a sense of place and show which details matter to a character.
when: Designing scenes that carry memory cues
why: Environmental detail signals relevance without explicit exposition

text: A level can carry a secondary map, such as a surveyor's record, showing a changed feature; hide the difference so careful comparison reveals it.
when: when designing a discoverable change to a location
why: careful players are rewarded for comparing sources

text: Separate level sections so that a player's theory about one area is disproved when they reach the next.
A schematic map shows routes with conventional symbols that omit exact positions and minor detail, so players must learn precise paths through observation.
when: when designing a simplified map
why: symbols give a guide, not a complete record

text: Stagger reveals across rooms and use ambient sounds or clock objects as timers to pace the player's progress.
when: Designing the pacing of a multi-room area

text: Arrange objects so that a forced grip or misplaced item signals a staged scene, prompting the player to question the setup.
A recorded admission triggered by a hidden event can serve as a reversal in a multi-stage investigation.
when: Structuring a multi-stage mystery
why: A late reversal rewards players who followed the earlier clues

text: A final set-piece room can gather NPCs under a timer with an evidence display, and lighting or a decisive player action can trigger the reveal.
when: Designing a finale encounter
why: Environmental timing and staging concentrate tension

text: Show the final clue last and summarize the rest, giving the player a satisfying payoff.
when: Structuring the reveal of a mystery
why: Withholding the decisive clue preserves tension until the end

text: Show a first answer early, then reveal the true location after a later region or document unlocks, so the first answer becomes a stage.
Landscape, weather, season and architecture set a mood that shapes how players read events, building dread or suspicion before facts are known.
when: at the start of a case when facts are few, or when designing the atmosphere of a crime scenario
why: Mood influences expectations, which affect how players read ambiguous events.

text: A scripted NPC action can expose a hidden chamber, so the player learns its location before deciding whether to enter.
A forced lock is suspicious when a simpler entry route, such as a key, would be available, because forcing it then serves to display a break-in rather than achieve one.
when: Evaluating visible damage to a lock or container.
why: A rational actor with easy access gains nothing from a noisy method.

text: A staged collapse can reverse the apparent roles of attacker and victim, so a 'dead' actor may still be armed and the one who approaches to help may be the target.
when: A scene presents a fallen character as a victim and a nearby character as the culprit.
why: A feigned collapse exploits the watcher's expectation that a motionless body is harmless and that a helper is safe.

text: A single tone can mislead, so repeated strikes in a pattern are needed before trusting a reading.
A garden's appearance reflects the season as well as care, so judging neglect from an empty-looking lawn is unreliable.
why: Season and weather change how grounds look

text: 1) Start with a bright public area. 2) Move into dark, narrow lanes. 3) Cross a hazardous passage. 4) Reach the hideout. Pace the reveal through these spaces.
when: When designing a visit to a dangerous location.
why: Each step increases tension and reveals more.

text: 1) Agree a signal in advance that the target will trigger. 2) Place a hazardous object where the target will be seen handling it. 3) Position waiting responders to move on the signal. 4) Warn responders to handle the object carefully, since it may later be evidence.
when: The target will act at a known place and time
why: The signal tells responders when to move and the object becomes evidence

text: 1) Order the locations from small to large and central. 2) Assign each location one new kind of evidence. 3) Let the picture grow in layers as the player moves through them.
when: Evidence is revealed gradually across several spaces
why: Layered reveals build understanding while keeping information withheld

text: 1) Summon the culprit for a set time. 2) Lock the room. 3) Lay out the evidence together. 4) Allow the culprit to flee, turning the escape into a tactical moment.
Stage the final reveal inside a location the player has already visited, such as the crime scene, a trap or stakeout, so they can return to the evidence.
why: Familiar space makes the climax readable and ties back earlier exploration.
