text: Include one prop in a staged scene that contradicts its stated purpose, so attentive players can spot the staging without it being spelled out.
when: designing a fake robbery, planted camp or similar staged set-piece
why: players who check purpose against details can detect the deception

text: Stage a search or excavation with empty results, a disturbance, and partial finds before the main reward, and defer the puzzle explanation until after the reward is seen.
when: Designing an excavation or hidden-vault sequence.
why: Staged finds raise expectation and make the eventual solution feel earned.

text: Show the public performance and the private reality side by side so attentive players can compare them.
when: Designing contrasting behavior for the player to notice
why: Direct comparison makes the discrepancy visible to attentive players.

text: Release information in stages, so each partial answer narrows the search without solving it.
Give shocking set pieces an in-world explanation that clears them while still rewarding curiosity.
Let players inspect items in stages, with hidden details appearing only under magnification or at close range.
when: Designing examinable clue objects in a game world
why: Progressive disclosure rewards careful inspection and keeps casual players from solving the clue instantly.

text: Stage disturbances such as a broken window or spilled goods to lead guards and players along a chosen path.
why: Visible disruptions give players and guards a readable direction to follow

text: Make empty areas risky: a lone character should be more visible to patrols, so solitude carries a cost rather than offering safety.
when: designing quiet or empty zones in a level
why: patrols notice isolated characters more readily than crowds

text: Plant a staged battle scene in which a bound prisoner's knots or a tool mark reveal the truth to a careful player.
when: When designing a staged combat scene as a misdirection
why: A physical detail rewards players who examine the scene closely

text: Give the antagonist a hidden escape route, such as a locked gate with a concealed mechanism, so a trap has a second phase after it springs.
when: designing a confrontation that ends in a trap
why: a second phase keeps the climax from ending too early

text: Give a scripted scare a checkable tell, such as residue on a costumed character's hand, so a careful player can expose the staging.
when: designing a fake supernatural event

text: Before a final reveal, give the player a short confirmation step, such as checking a route or record, so the answer rests on facts they have verified.
when: Designing the approach to a puzzle's final solution.
why: Verified facts make the eventual conclusion feel credible rather than arbitrary.

text: Let the player deduce the culprit from how a scene was staged, using several clues, rather than from a single item.
when: Designing a deduction puzzle around a crime scene
why: Multiple converging clues make deduction feel fair and reduce guesswork

text: Release exiting groups in sequence so each area empties before the next is searched.
Let a journal entry or cutscene give the player the answer while the detective NPC still searches, then return control to the player at the NPC's point of confusion.
when: Creating dramatic irony in a game.
why: The player acts on knowledge the NPC lacks, which creates suspense.

text: Tag each NPC statement as lead, background or proof, so players learn what each one actually supports.
when: Designing an interview or deposition system
why: Labelled statements teach players how to weigh them

text: Give players a discoverable inheritance record so they can infer who benefits from a missing item.
when: Designing a missing-item or theft quest
why: Players reason from benefit to suspect

text: Letters or ledgers can carry dated instructions that supersede one another, letting the player choose which instruction is valid.
Mark reconstructed or partial text in the game so players can tell which parts are inferred.
when: When a clue is assembled from incomplete fragments.
why: Clear marking keeps the player's understanding accurate.

text: After leaving an observation point, listen for footsteps to check whether anyone is following before continuing.
why: A watcher may be watched in turn.

text: A guarded locked room can be entered through an approach the guards do not watch, while a distraction draws them to a different area.
when: A protected room has guards watching one approach.
why: Guards respond to the most salient threat, leaving other approaches open.

text: A sequence of barriers, namely baize doors, curtains and a small circular hall, separates the approach from the inner room and controls who can reach whom.
when: when designing access to a protected room

text: Routes along a narrow ledge above water carry the risk that one misstep ends the whole plan.
1) Map guard and servant schedules. 2) Identify sleeping or distant observers. 3) Pick the weakest barrier as the route. 4) Time movement to the quiet window.
when: Designing a stealth or heist route for the player.
why: Schedules and weak points define where the player can pass unseen.

text: 1) Display guard sight cones and patrol timings. 2) Let the player compare coverage across exits. 3) Reward finding the one route no guard watches.
when: when designing a stealth level with an unwatched route
why: visible coverage data turns the route search into deduction, not guesswork

text: 1) Have the player wait in a vault for a threat. 2) Capture one enemy. 3) Let a second enemy escape through a hole the player can later revisit.
Place a small object such as a torn cloth or rope end on a high ledge or hook that links a room to a route the player thinks is sealed.
Require the player to choose a disguise and backstory that stay consistent with any reference the game can check.
when: Designing an infiltration mission with identity checks.
why: Consistency with checkable details makes the player's choices meaningful and testable.

text: Lead players along a winding, poorly lit route to a guarded area, and place reusable landmarks along it so the route still supports later deduction.
when: Designing an approach to a protected area.
why: Disorientation adds tension while landmarks keep the route usable for later reasoning.

text: A noisy lock or dense plant cover at an exit adds risk, since audible tells can alert others, so sneaking out costs both time and sound.
when: when designing a stealth exit route
why: Noise and cover impose costs that make the exit a choice rather than a free escape.

text: On a quiet street, a watcher hears an approaching footstep well before the figure is visible, so sound gives early warning of a match.
when: when ambient noise is low and sightlines are blocked
why: Small sounds carry in quiet surroundings, so they arrive before sight.

text: Use shifting light and line of sight to hide a threat until the player moves into position, so a harmless-looking shape becomes an enemy.
when: Designing lighting for a stealth or reveal moment, or placing enemies in low-visibility areas.
why: Changing light alters what the player perceives, and delayed visibility creates surprise and rewards careful movement.

text: A stealth or infiltration mission with a costume or alias disguise, where NPC reactions depend on identity and a reputation check fails if the disguise is too well known, adds replay and tension.
when: Designing stealth or infiltration missions where the player takes on a false identity.
why: Identity-dependent NPC reactions and a recognition check make the disguise consequential and tie it to the player's notoriety.

text: Place cover objects such as graves or hedges near meeting points so the player can watch unseen and follow after participants leave.
when: Designing a meeting space for stealth play.
why: Cover supports watching, and the player can then track the group's movement.

text: Create patrol windows and chokepoints where the player can wait, with sound cues that reveal approach, and vary guard route timing so the player must watch at different hours to find the pattern.
when: when designing guard routes and waiting spots
why: Sound reveals approach before sight, and varied timing forces the player to observe over time.

text: Use light, sound or fire as timed checkpoints in a level so the player can build a timeline, and give NPC alibis that the player can check against them.
when: when designing time-based clue systems
why: Environmental timers let the player verify alibis independently.

text: A hidden device placed in furniture or a floor seam and discovered late can produce a dramatic payoff in a stealth or setup puzzle.
when: Designing a stealth or planting puzzle where the player places a hidden listening device.
why: The delayed discovery turns concealment into a payoff rather than a dead end.

text: A disguise or pretext item can unlock a guarded area, with a guard who may check it.
when: Designing a guarded area that the player must enter.
why: A verification step creates tension and a risk of failure.

text: Let players map sightlines and choose where to place a tool, rewarding them for noticing the one hidden spot.
when: Designing a stealth or surveillance puzzle in a fixed room.
why: Reading the room becomes the skill being tested.

text: Hidden surveillance suits events whose location is known in advance and where responders can wait close by; it fails when the sensor can be found or destroyed.
when: Choosing whether a covert sensor fits an event

text: Place a key event in a blind spot, such as off-screen or behind an obstruction, and reward the player for returning to examine it.
when: Designing a critical event the player must later discover
why: Events outside the player's view are easy to miss on first pass

text: Let a hidden character watch a room the player thinks is empty, revealed only after the player has acted on a wrong theory.
when: Designing a reveal in an enclosed location.
why: A late reveal of a watcher reframes the player's earlier actions.

text: A stealth level where one NPC can change outfit or role makes the player's sightings conflict until they find where the swap happened.
when: Designing disguise mechanics in a game.
why: Conflicting sightings drive the player to discover the swap location.

text: Track whether a character is present in the scene versus visible, so a scripted alibi can be broken by a hidden route.
when: A character's alibi relies on a headcount or witness observation.
why: A person can be counted as present while being out of sight.

text: A watcher who is seen loses the advantage, so a watch post must stay concealed.
when: when the player or guard holds a surveillance position
why: Discovery turns the watcher from observer into target.

text: 1) Pick a hidden post with a clear view of a fixed destination. 2) Watch at varied times of day so no period goes uncovered. 3) Stay out of the line of sight. 4) Wait until the target arrives.
when: when the target has a fixed destination and the watcher cannot approach directly
why: Covering all times and staying hidden keeps the watch effective.

text: 1) Count the doors between the listener and the unseen source. 2) Mark each door so any movement shows. 3) Note which marked door moved to locate the event.
when: a sound is heard but its source cannot be watched

text: Give a non-human agent observable limits, such as one item at a time or no speech, so players can deduce its role from its behavior.
when: When designing a creature or automated agent that players must reason about.
why: Clear, observable limits let players infer what the agent can and cannot have done.

text: Avoid a stakeout when the target has an independent way in, such as a key, because the watcher cannot stop the entry.
when: when the target can enter without passing the watched point
why: Watching a fixed point cannot intercept an alternate route.

text: Include deliberate distractions such as a character who changes the subject, and mark them so players can tell them apart from real clues.
when: when placing red herrings in a mystery
why: Clear marking keeps the distraction fair while still misleading careless reasoning.

text: A hidden observer with a dark background, unlit face and silhouette, or light behind, is detected less and can watch and listen unrecognized; lit or pale features draw attention.
when: choosing a stealth position near light sources, or in lit or dark areas
why: Lighting and cover keep the observer's face obscured, while light-coloured or lit features contrast with the background and draw attention

text: A bystander's reaction, such as a guard's tense posture, can be a designed tell that the player learns to read.
when: reacting to a revealed name or secret
why: consistent body cues become learnable

text: Rivals who fear publicity more than suspicion tend to avoid overreacting and stop probing once a plausible explanation is offered.
when: when the rival has more to lose from exposure than from uncertainty
why: exposure risk makes quiet responses more attractive

text: A secret operation can be hidden behind a visible, ordinary activity so that observers take the hidden work for routine business.
Concealed actions, such as a figure bending low over a vehicle, are visible only to someone close.
Treat silhouette bulges larger than the hands could explain, and rigid hands with a fixed gaze toward the chest, as tells of a concealed object or threat; show them visibly.
when: when judging a person's silhouette or posture
why: so players can spot concealed threats before combat begins

text: Wait in a busy place, where loitering is less noticeable, though a cautious target can still spot the watcher.
A courier who must deliver information in person can be intercepted at a known time and place, which makes a natural set-piece.
when: when the enemy's information must travel by hand
why: in-person delivery cannot be done remotely

text: Covert observation works best on a target in an open area with a known routine; unpredictable movement weakens it.
when: Planning a stealth watch

text: Offer party-splitting as a designed choice: one character scouts while another holds an exit and waits for a signal to rescue.
A covert signal should be a single, simple cue disguised as ordinary activity, since a signal that is long or repeated draws attention.
when: when two actors must communicate under observation
why: Simplicity lets the receiver decode it, while deniability keeps the watcher from registering it as a message.

text: Give an actor a plausible reason for being in a room, such as a casual errand, so their presence and movement look natural to watchers.
when: when an actor must act unnoticed in a location
why: An explained presence lowers suspicion about activity there.

text: A covert search suits a suspect who may be lying only when the premises can be reached unseen and the search fits within the available time.
why: a visible approach or short window makes the search fail

text: Stealth levels can use sightlines, lit windows and noisy gear as mechanics, giving players a lower-risk route with its own constraints.
when: when designing stealth spaces
why: Readable hazards let players plan approaches.

text: A stationary object amid moving elements such as water, foliage or crowds stands out when attention is focused on it, so it can be made findable.
when: placing a clue in a busy, moving environment
why: motion contrast draws the eye to still items

text: A stealth level can place a dark alcove with a view of a lit hall, letting the player observe while remaining unseen.
when: Designing a stealth space.
why: Light contrast gives the player concealment and a clear view.

text: Use hollows and low movement to stay out of view when open ground offers no structures, keeping the profile low against the skyline.
when: fleeing across open ground
why: low profiles and dips break sight lines

text: Signs that a target is evading a watcher include dismissing a vehicle, passing through a transit hall without buying a ticket, leaving by a second exit, and checking around before re-entering.
when: a target is followed through transit or buildings
why: Each action tries to shake off a follower or conceal a destination.

text: A cover identity can require a skill check whose difficulty depends on how well the costume matches the local role.
A search that yields nothing deflates expectation and resets the investigation, so the next lead starts from a clean slate.
when: a planned excursion produces no evidence
why: the failed effort lowers hopes, shifting focus back to open questions

text: If a post-holder leaves the post at any point, coverage has a gap, which opens a window in which access to the guarded point is possible.
when: when a guard, watchman or attendant may step away

text: Sudden total darkness covers movement, because everyone loses sight at the same moment with no gradual fade.
Street crowds, stalls, accidents and blocked vehicle lines give a fleeing target cover that breaks the pursuer's line of sight.
Detection chances can scale with distance, cover and noise, so the player's position and actions shape the risk of discovery.
A guard that checks for gaze exposure can detect a reflection-based peek and respond by redirecting the player's attention.
Ambient noise that drowns out an observer's alert lets the player act unseen, but the observer's sighting can still be recorded for later investigation.
when: Designing stealth with environmental noise.
why: Masking the alarm does not erase the NPC's perception of the event.

text: A guard that re-checks line of sight after each turn of the target makes the player's timing of hiding and movement matter.
when: a guard patrols with a stealth state
why: the recheck forces the player to break line of sight quickly

text: Give stealth or eavesdrop mechanics a visibility range, so a hidden position lets the player hear dialogue unseen.
when: designing eavesdropping
why: A hidden position makes overhearing possible without detection.

text: A route close to a building but hidden from its view suits secret meetings or concealment, because it is near enough to use yet unseen.
when: choosing a path for covert movement
why: proximity with no sightline offers cover

text: A cue such as a moving object or an animal's reaction draws attention to one spot, letting the real action happen unnoticed elsewhere.
A stealth sequence can let the player appear to rest while preparing an ambush, with an ally who believes the cover story.
Assuming a crowd will hide you fails when the target is cautious or has already left.
Relying on fog or the sea to hide a disposal fails when tide and visibility change.
when: when an actor uses weather or water to conceal evidence
why: conditions that hide evidence now may shift later

text: Marks that the subject or bystanders can read, or that stand out, expose the pursuit.
Moving to act while a still posture would hide the watcher exposes the watcher to detection.
when: A watcher is near a target and needs to stay concealed
why: Movement breaks the camouflage that stillness provides

text: Unseen observers can be present; an unexpected listener can change the picture, so any timeline must allow for hidden watchers.
Relying on an excuse whose prop the checker can inspect is risky, because a mismatched or empty prop collapses the cover.
1) Pick a concealed spot with a full view of the target. 2) Watch it over time and record its routine. 3) Act only once the routine is clear.

1) Pick a believable pretext for asking about an absent person. 2) Judge the witness's evasiveness at the door. 3) Watch from cover until the witness leaves. 4) Enter by the least conspicuous route. 5) Search quickly and exit before the witness returns.
when: a witness may be lying and must stay unaware of the investigation
why: the search depends on the witness not knowing about the inquiry

text: 1) Watch from concealment before approaching. 2) Check for pursuers and onlookers. 3) Speak quickly. 4) Leave at once.
when: when a person avoids being seen
why: Checking for witnesses reduces the risk of exposure.

text: Give stillness a concealment bonus, since a motionless figure blends into a background similar in colour or texture, while movement draws the eye; this rewards patient play.
why: Movement draws the eye while stillness merges with the surroundings, making stillness a meaningful choice

text: Give stealth spaces hidden vantages, like a pipe, balcony or window, with a clear view of the target and no sightline back, so players gain information without entering the room.
Provide cover props or excuses, such as a forgotten item or a distraction, that the player can invoke to continue an action.
when: designing interruption events for stealth

text: Have a guard issue a challenge whose answer the player can learn by eavesdropping on earlier dialogue, turning the gate into a deduction puzzle.
when: Designing a gate guarded by a password
why: Eavesdropping gives players a fair path to the answer

text: Make a scripted reaction detectable by letting it always stop on one specific action, so a careful player can spot the trick.
For stealth, place vantage points close enough that a player can read faces or objects once in position.
when: designing observation spots
why: detail must be readable for the player to act

text: Place a watch point with a narrow but controlled view of the passage, and keep its openings clean enough to see through.
when: when a player or NPC must observe a bounded point
why: a controlled sightline lets the observer watch without being seen

text: In stealth areas, include shadows that turn out to be harmless, so players learn that movement is not always a threat.
when: Designing stealth detection and enemy visibility.
why: Players calibrate their caution from what proves harmless as well as what proves dangerous.

text: During a crowd event, make guards watching the spectacle less likely to notice a thief at a side door, so a scripted theft can succeed.
when: Designing a stealth or theft scenario during a festival.
why: Guards' attention is pulled toward the event.

text: Make observed detail depend on light, distance and observer state, so a witness in darkness or fog reports less detail or less consistent detail.
Use a hedge or screen to limit a witness's view so the figure is glimpsed rather than fully observed.
when: Designing line of sight for witness scenes

text: Add a harmless-looking nuisance, such as a recurring noise or scattered debris, that quietly hides a movement.
when: when designing ambient hazards or distractions

text: Step counts estimate size well in simple spaces but diverge from true distance in spaces with many angles or turns, misplacing markers at a circuit's end.
when: choosing between counting and other mapping methods
why: the true extent exceeds the assumed size

text: Worn or repaired surfaces keep traces of disturbance after a room has been tidied.
Marks such as scratches and dents, plus displaced objects, can rebuild what happened in a scene nobody observed.
Let footprints or blood drops lead players into concealed areas; a trace ending at a spot points to a hidden area, so do not treat dead ends as final.
when: Tracking or exploration levels; closed spaces holding traces that lead into hidden areas.
why: Traces point to places the player has not yet searched; a trace ending at a spot directs the player to search there.

text: Place boot wear, soot or staining on a corpse or ruin so players can work out who was there and how recently.
Removing items from their settings leaves empty fittings that betray the theft.
when: A stolen item was set in a mount
why: Missing pieces show what was taken

text: Rule out floors and ceilings with practical risk or visible seams. A floor covered wall to wall in carpet shows no seam where a hidden access panel could be.
when: Narrowing where a concealed access point could lie
why: Hidden access leaves physical traces that can be ruled out

text: Ask how a culprit would obtain a material and whether they could avoid leaving a trail; the answer shows where to look for its source.
when: Tracing where a rare substance came from.

text: Encode clues as traces, such as scorch patterns, residue or missing marks, that players check with the right tool.
when: Designing rooms that hold evidence

text: Surface material decides which traces survive: footprints show on bare gravel or soft carpet but not grass or bare hard floors, so sweep and examine loose debris instead.
when: When choosing where to look for impressions.
why: Traces are readable only on suitable surfaces.

text: Environmental change such as a rising tide, lifting fog or shifting weather can erase footprints or clues on a timer, forcing action before evidence fades.
when: Outdoor levels with weather or tide states that change over time; designing timed evidence destruction.
why: Environmental change limits how long clues stay available.

text: Mud, dust or snow tiles can record footprints, so a tracking puzzle can let the player match tracks to a boot or shoe found elsewhere.
when: designing a tracking puzzle
why: soft surfaces store impressions the player can compare

text: When traces degrade over game time, investigating early yields more evidence than investigating late.
why: Degraded traces are harder to read, which rewards prompt investigation.

text: A hidden mechanism can be made discoverable through a chain of traces, such as a smell, a pipe, a control tap and a concealed outlet, each leading to the next.
when: Designing a hidden hazard or device that players must uncover.
why: Each linked clue gives players a reason and a path to the next one.

text: A good-looking surface can hide poor condition, so only close inspection reveals the truth and distant views mislead.
Place readable wear, dust, disturbed furniture, half-finished drinks or fresh scents against stale air so players learn how recently a room was used, even with no one present.
when: A place must reveal recent activity without characters on stage.
why: Physical traces imply recent use; players who check surfaces learn it.

text: Let players compare mark spacing with each candidate tool's dimensions to identify which tool made the crossing.
Let scene traces encode the number of actors, such as one drag trail versus several footprint sets, and add a later clue when a lone actor is mistaken for a group.
when: Designing a crime scene for players to reason about.
why: Players can infer who was present, and a second clue can correct a wrong assumption.

text: Leave a crime scene unchanged, treating its lighting and furniture as affordances that let the player read the room's history.
why: Placement and light carry the room's story without text.

text: Encode an NPC's height and mood in stride and weight, and design investigations that reward players for cross-checking two traces.
when: Designing a footprint-based investigation
why: Cross-checking tests whether players verify evidence

text: Place timing traces such as dropped embers, melted wax or muddy steps so players can estimate how long an NPC waited.
Place destroyed or hidden papers in a room whose traces point toward a motive, and make the player confirm that motive in another location.
when: Designing clues that suggest a hidden motive.
why: A single trace should not settle the question on its own.

text: Give marks a clear sequence so players can tell which event happened first.
Let a small, specific trace such as a material or residue identify a creature or room type, and let the player confirm it elsewhere.
Let a plain object carry a trace matching an NPC's record, so the player can link the object to that suspect.
when: designing clues for an identification puzzle
why: the match turns an ordinary item into evidence

text: Pair each physical trace in a level, such as footprints or dust trails, with a question about purpose, so a match alone does not resolve the puzzle.
when: Designing evidence that records movement
why: Purpose questions keep trace-matching from solving the puzzle without reasoning.

text: After an ambush, leave physical traces such as a broken lock, broken window or a scratch that identifies an item, so players can reconstruct the attack.
when: Designing evidence in an attack or theft scene.
why: Traces give players concrete evidence to reason from.

text: Place surviving traces such as foundations or walls in the scene as evidence that a building once existed.
Raise a suspicion meter only on physical evidence, not on atmosphere alone.
when: When designing a suspicion or threat indicator.
why: Atmosphere can mislead, so the indicator should track verifiable evidence.

text: Make identity checks in a mystery level require two or three independent clues found in different rooms.
when: Designing a mystery that depends on confirming who someone is.
why: Several separated clues prevent a single missed item from blocking progress.

text: Each misidentification can unlock a new zone, so players must revisit earlier clues instead of moving strictly forward.
A false suspect can carry a visible, damning item or mark that leads the player to a dead end.
when: designing misleading clues

text: A suspect who is watched rather than confronted can produce a long sequence of clues and behaviour changes that the player follows.
when: Designing a suspect who should be observed over time.
why: Ongoing observation yields a stream of reactive clues instead of a single confrontation.

text: In a hub, let each character's suspicion rise as the player finds items, with the victim's effects updating the accusation.
when: Designing a hub-based investigation with multiple suspects.
why: Item discovery gives the player a reason to revise accusations over time.

text: Hide the true culprit behind an authority NPC's wrong theory, and give the player a physical check, such as a route or item, that exposes the error.
Giving each candidate door its own marker turns an unlocated sound into a located event, though every added candidate adds another check.
Model each suspect as an area chain: entering each new area unlocks a clue contradicting the previous suspect, and the culprit's signature items sit in the last-visited area.
when: Generating or authoring investigation levels
why: Late-visited areas hold the decisive evidence while early areas build a misleading case.

text: Make two enemies that share a key or access route potentially the same entity in two states, and let the player discover the link on a second encounter.
when: Designing encounters where the player sees a locked access point used by a second enemy
why: The shared key creates a plausible reason to think two foes are different, so the later reveal rewards attention to the access clue.

text: Let an NPC witness a transformation in a locked room and deliver the reveal, with the room's contents as physical proof, rather than having the protagonist discover it alone.
when: Revealing a hidden transformation to the player in a level
why: An outside observer provides a credible account, and the physical proof in the room backs up what the player is told.

text: A familiar-looking enemy or NPC can plant doubt about identity, to be resolved later by an in-game check.
End a level with a confession encounter whose proof is an object the player carried through the whole level.
Examine items closely and cover walls, floor and ceiling systematically rather than relying on a quick glance that finds everything at once.
A person whose tool or pipe is blocked will search for a replacement, drawing them toward where that replacement is likely kept.
when: a habitual need is blocked or missing
why: an unmet need drives search behaviour

text: A room can be searched while its owner is away for a set time, forming a timed window whose outcome stays open; an empty result still counts as a step.
when: Looking for traces of a suspect who is out for a set period, or designing a room search with a suspect away

text: Gate each search step with timed events, such as a train departure or deadline, and sort collected leads by priority so players weigh them by urgency.
when: Designing a time-limited investigation or a search in a mystery level
why: A deadline forces the player to prioritise checks, and time pressure with priority ranking reflects how investigators triage leads.

text: Let walls or floors give hollow or responsive sounds when struck, so a player's test of a surface can reveal a concealed space.
when: Designing hidden areas that players might search by probing.
why: Audible feedback rewards testing and hints at hollow spaces.

text: A fixed-order room search suits answers hidden among many small containers in one enclosed space.
when: The target may sit in one of many small containers in an enclosed room.
why: Systematic order ensures no container is skipped.

text: A visual sweep does not test a surface's structure, so items hidden inside walls survive it and need a targeted, structural check.
One observable condition can rule out most candidate locations on a map, shrinking a radius-based search dramatically.
when: a search is bounded by travel distance from a point
why: a condition implying limited travel excludes far locations at once

text: A search that tests only surfaces or easy-to-reach spots can miss small or hidden evidence, so an empty result may reflect the method rather than the evidence's absence.
why: Surface searches miss small or hidden evidence.

text: Searching by genre tropes can waste time when the real release is a simple mechanism.
Searchers tire, so late searches are the least careful unless the work is kept under time pressure.
A single visible trace is enough to redirect an entire search toward one spot.
A quiet search is not unobserved, because a sound made during it can draw a checker to investigate.
1) Walk from object to object. 2) Inspect containers such as basins and dishes. 3) Check gaps, folds, and cracks. 4) Bring small items close and examine them up close.
when: Searching a room for traces that may be small.
why: Small traces collect in ordinary containers and gaps that a casual look skips.

text: 1) Empty drawers and closets. 2) Move furniture to check beneath and behind it. 3) Log each object in order with where it was found.

1) List the places the owner says they already searched. 2) Search systematically in places outside that list, including rarely used containers and clothing. 3) Pair results with when and why the item was last used.
when: An item is reported missing.
why: Repeating the owner's search repeats the owner's blind spots.

text: 1) Keep the room exactly as found. 2) Post a lookout on the occupant. 3) Go through luggage and papers. 4) Arrange questioning so the occupant is unaware of the search.
when: the occupant may return during a discreet search
why: A fixed order protects the search from discovery.

text: 1) Separate the suspect from others present. 2) Keep the room in view while searching. 3) Examine each garment piece by piece with hands as well as eyes. 4) If nothing is found, redirect suspicion to the next likely holder.
when: when a small concealed item must be found quickly
why: Systematic search finds hidden items and avoids missed areas.

text: 1) List the named target objects. 2) Search the likely surfaces first, such as writing tables. 3) Move to other rooms in sequence. 4) Check pockets of hanging clothing. 5) Record what is found and what is absent.
when: When searching a room for specific physical evidence.
why: Expectation guides the search and an ordered sequence avoids gaps.

text: 1) Predict how the item was concealed. 2) List plausible locations. 3) Check each in order and record results. 4) Observe the found target before moving in.
when: when a missing object is among many similar possible locations
why: An ordered, recorded search avoids repeats and covers every candidate

text: 1) Check the obvious spots, such as drawers. 2) Check the room's ordinary structure, such as floor boards and pipe access points.
when: Searching a room thoroughly.
why: Searches limited to obvious spots miss hiding places built into routine structure.

text: 1) Count the barriers between the character and the goal, in order. 2) Note routine visit or patrol times. 3) Read sounds and sights for unseen geography. 4) Infer hidden routes from unexplained movement.
when: planning an approach before acting
why: A survey turns a closed space into a plannable route

text: 1) Fix a reference object and note its position. 2) Sweep surrounding surfaces at low height, then raised overhead. 3) Repeat the sweep around the reference. 4) Split heights between searchers if reach is limited. 5) Test each element for looseness.
when: a hidden object is believed to be in a confined space with a known reference point
why: Height-separated sweeps cover surfaces one searcher cannot reach

text: 1) Identify the likely approach path from the layout. 2) Sweep rough ground in parallel lanes. 3) Search dense cover such as vegetation along the inferred path.
when: searching for a lost object
why: a structured sweep finds items a casual look misses

text: 1) Divide the scene into zones and search them in a fixed sequence. 2) Mark each find at its exact position. 3) Move to the next zone only when the current one is complete.
when: a scene is large or has several areas that may hold evidence
why: a fixed order and recorded positions prevent missed areas and preserve find locations

text: 1) Survey each object in turn and form a clear picture of it before moving on. 2) Examine the floor with a lens, eyes close to the surface. 3) Record every faint mark found.
when: when a room may have held an object that has since been moved
why: objects are easier to test against traces when each one is understood first

text: 1) Search every closet and waste space in order, starting at the lowest level. 2) Move upward through the building. 3) Do not skip spaces that look empty. 4) Check rooms unused for years and test whether they are locked.
when: searching a building for concealed evidence
why: Hidden compartments often sit in spaces that look unremarkable.

text: 1) Finish one area before starting the next, without going back. 2) Open every container, locked or unlocked. 3) Test soft objects by feel and sound for hidden items. 4) Check room structure: under rugs and furniture, inside blinds, window ledges. 5) Check unusual spots such as jars, atomizers, drains and cisterns. 6) Record negative results.
when: A small object may be hidden in a confined space and the searcher has time and a plausible reason to be there.

text: 1) Start in the place the person was last known. 2) Search adjacent spaces in a fixed order, moving outward. 3) Check each candidate hiding spot. 4) Check exits last.
when: when a person has gone missing from a known place
why: A systematic order covers the likeliest spots first

text: 1) Divide the room into its walls. 2) Search one wall, then its opposite, covering all furniture on each. 3) Open every container, including drawers, bowls and spaces under cushions. 4) Examine objects closely, checking each card and shaking books. 5) Reach high places with a ladder. 6) Mark empty containers as checked before moving on.
when: Searching an enclosed room for a hidden item.
why: A fixed order ensures no container, surface or object is skipped.

text: 1) Decide whether the player searches for an NPC or an object. 2) If searching for a corpse or hidden item, open containers and under-furniture spots. 3) If searching for a person, check rooms and visible spots.
when: when designing a search action in a game
why: the search method must match the target to be fair

text: Search a room's corners and directly behind and beneath furniture, since a quick glance misses small traces and hidden compartments there.
Search padded or lined objects and their seams by touch as well as sight, since a surface-only look misses linings and a trained hand can find what the eye misses.
when: An object could hold a concealed item

text: Search interiors room by room, moving furniture, opening cupboards and drawing back hangings, working from upper floors down to the cellars.
Hide traces such as a scrubbed patch under a rug, and reward players who check beneath movable objects.
Give a player search action per-room completion flags, with an optional companion NPC who rechecks finished rooms.
Plan a level as a sequence of rooms, each unlocking one evidence type, with a timed event at the end of each act.
when: Structuring an investigation level
why: Each room adds a layer and the timed event sustains pressure

text: Let a target's possible locations widen after a set number of in-game days, expanding the area the player must search.
when: designing a missing-person or fleeing-target search
why: elapsed time makes the target harder to find in a fixed area

text: Systematic sweeps find items hidden in containers, while a thorough search can still miss items in plain sight, so a failed search does not prove the item is gone.
why: Full coverage removes the advantage of plain sight.

text: A thorough search costs time, which rewards careful players while penalizing hurried ones.
when: Giving search actions a time cost

text: Store witness statements as dialogue lines so players can compare two NPC accounts side by side and discover contradictions themselves.
when: when building NPC testimony
why: side-by-side versions expose differences

text: Flag testimony as unreliable, such as a dying NPC's last words or claims about a missing item, until a second witness, physical clue or player confirmation verifies it.
when: A quest or puzzle relies on what an NPC says.

text: Include bluff dialogue options, such as false claims or pretending to already know, where NPC responses reveal whether it knew the fact and whether it talks or shuts down.
when: designing dialogue systems with deception or bluffing
why: Lets players test NPC knowledge and unlock or close disclosure.

text: Overheard speech in a language the player cannot follow yields only partial data that the player must infer.
Track which NPC observed which detail, so a player who hears a secondhand description has a reason to doubt it.
when: Generating multi-witness investigations
why: Knowledge provenance lets players judge reliability

text: Host the first step of a scheme in a public space or town event, leaving the player to trace how the contact develops.
when: designing a scheme that spans locations
why: public settings make early steps look incidental

text: Let a partly open door or vent carry an NPC exchange to the player, so overheard talk changes what the player knows before entering.
when: Designing a room where the player can hear NPCs talk.
why: Overheard fragments create anticipation and shift the player's expectations.

text: Give a suspect NPC a dialogue option that changes tone when the player presses a contradiction, offering an apology and promise in return for dropping the topic.
when: Scripting a suspect's reaction to a challenged statement.
why: A tonal pivot gives the NPC a believable escape route and keeps the scene dynamic.

text: Let an NPC who answers a question with a counter-request or refuses until a condition is met gate a clue, requiring a favor before the truth is given.
when: Designing a dialogue tree that withholds information.
why: A conditional refusal turns the clue into a reward for a favor, adding a choice to the scene.

text: Script a deflecting NPC so the player must ask the same question again to get the real answer, and let repeated attempts unlock different dialogue.
when: Designing an NPC that avoids a topic.
why: Repeated attempts reward persistence and reveal the boundary the NPC will hold.

text: Let an NPC's refusal state a conditional or hinted boundary, telling the player what remains possible even when the answer is withheld.
when: Writing an NPC who refuses a question.
why: A stated boundary keeps the player informed about the path forward.

text: If a player alarms a contact on the trail, the contact can vanish or change route, so the trail goes cold.
when: A player is too visible while following a contact.
why: Noticing the watch causes the contact to act to avoid it.

text: A talkative NPC can yield extra dialogue that the player may need to verify later, with a noted word triggering a follow-up question.
when: Designing dialogue-heavy NPCs
why: Flagged words create optional follow-up threads that reward attention

text: An NPC can store a remembered sound or sighting that unlocks only when the player asks the right question at the right in-game time.
A character's vague answer can unlock a dialogue branch when the player finds a location that matches part of it.
A voice heard through a door may not belong to the expected character; reveal the true speaker only through sight or a second clue.
when: Designing audio-only clues
why: Audio alone can mislead players

text: 1) Ask how a secured route came to be secured again. 2) Ask who changed its state and when. 3) Treat the answers as reopening the entry problem.
when: when a single-route conclusion depends on a lock's state

text: Tag each testimony with its source (access, witnessed, heard directly, or secondhand), distance from the event, and witness condition such as drunk, fearful or self-interested, so players weigh reports by tags.
when: designing NPC testimony systems
why: tags make source reliability visible

text: Store each NPC's testimony with timestamps and positions so the game can flag contradictions with scene state and players find the account that does not fit the timeline.
when: designing a mystery level

text: A tavern NPC who gossips after being bought a drink can reveal a quest clue, and the player's pretext or timing before a rumour spreads can change what they learn.
when: Designing gossip-based information gathering.
why: Gossip content and willingness depend on approach and timing.

text: A thief NPC can offer to return stolen goods for safe passage, giving the player a choice between confrontation and a negotiated outcome.
when: designing a theft quest

text: Write an NPC who insists on a false explanation as an unreliable witness, so the player must test the claim.
Let a hired informant deliver a report after a set in-game time, and log the evidence it delivers as a timeline entry.
Offer dialogue options that let the player probe an NPC with what-if questions, so the NPC's reaction sets a flag without a full confession.
when: Designing dialogue systems for suspect interrogation.
why: Partial reactions let the player learn without forcing a full admission.

text: Let witness NPCs supply testimony that changes an outcome, such as a lighter sentence or faction trust, rather than a simple yes-or-no verdict.
Give the player two accounts of one boundary dispute, one from each neighbor, so the gap between record and memory becomes a clue.
when: when designing a dispute as a discoverable mystery
why: contrasting accounts make the difference itself informative

text: Let players question a survivor about route and timing, so the answers change which room is safe to enter.
when: designing NPC information that guides exploration

text: Use a journal entry or NPC remark as a recall trigger that lets the player sense a missed detail before the game names it.
when: Building suspense toward a puzzle solution in a game.
why: A remark can bring a forgotten detail back to mind without stating the answer.

text: Give a refusing witness a pressure point, such as a relationship or secret, that players can use to reopen the dialogue.
when: When designing witness NPCs who refuse to talk.
why: A pressure point gives players a path forward without forcing the answer.

text: In a puzzle, give each testimony a checkable prediction, such as a broken object, a hole or a footprint, that players can verify.
when: when building clue-based puzzles
why: verifiable predictions let players test claims themselves

text: Resolve conflicting NPC accounts with a verifiable environmental mechanic, such as a door, stair, weather, a lever's pivot or a reflection, so players need not decide who lies.
when: Two NPC accounts of the same event disagree
why: A verifiable physical cause lets players resolve the contradiction without deciding who lies, and rewards careful observation.

text: A social hub can host several NPCs whose versions of an event differ, so the player must cross-check their accounts.
Keep tells ambiguous so a faint or tears could be innocent, which keeps the player assembling a case rather than reading a flag.
when: When designing NPC tells that signal guilt.
why: Ambiguous reactions require the player to combine evidence rather than accept a single signal.

text: Require a final accusation to rest on several linked clues, and make each link visible so the player can see which inference is still missing.
when: Designing a final deduction or accusation mechanic.
why: Visible links let the player judge their own reasoning and find the gap.

text: Track whether the player accepts an NPC's pivot, and if they do, mark the contradiction as unresolved so it can return later.
when: A player lets a suspect's emotional pivot end the questioning.
why: Keeping the contradiction open lets it resurface as a later hook.

text: Reveal motive through a sequence of NPC conversations, letters and locations visited in order, each adding a piece.
when: When designing a backstory the player must assemble
why: Ordered pieces let the player build the motive progressively.

text: Opportunity alone does not prove guilt, but it reduces the set of candidates who could have acted.
when: physical access limits who could have committed an act
why: Excluding people who could not reach the scene shrinks the suspect pool without proving anyone's guilt.

text: An NPC interrogation can offer a timed question with a short window, and a companion's glance toward the speaker can serve as a visible tell the player must notice.
when: Designing an NPC dialogue with multiple speakers
why: Timed prompts and visible tells reward attentive players

text: For a mystic NPC who claims magical sight, give the player a test, such as whether the NPC could actually have seen the object, to separate showmanship from real knowledge.
when: A mystic NPC claims knowledge of an event.
why: A checkable test exposes whether the claimed power matches the actual access.

text: A physical trace that contradicts an NPC's testimony can prompt the player to revisit a locked door or check a second route the NPC denied.
why: The conflict between evidence and account gives the player a reason to re-examine the scene.

text: Accepting that a door or window is found fastened without checking its mechanism, or dismissing a route as impossible because it looks awkward.
why: appearance and difficulty are not evidence that an exit is closed

text: A misfit noticed from one angle may vanish from another, so note a tell at the moment it is first seen.
Interpreting facial expressions as a specific emotion is subjective, since the same expression can reflect several different emotions.
when: when reading a victim's expression as evidence
why: Expressions are ambiguous and open to several interpretations.

text: Tie a confession opportunity to a place or schedule the controlling figure rarely leaves, so the player must time the approach.
Give each suspect a fixed trait, such as temper or hobby, so players can rule out suspects whose traits do not fit the crime.
when: Building a murder-mystery scenario with several non-player suspects.
why: Fixed traits let players eliminate suspects by reasoning rather than guesswork.

text: Use a trusted authority figure with a visible motive and a physical link to the crime, so a late reveal recasts earlier clues.
Build puzzles that combine a character trait with a scene feature, such as a non-swimmer and a pond, so the player can rule out a route.
Time a withheld name, shown only in a later scene or record, to match the player's readiness to act on it.
when: A key identity is revealed in a game
why: Revealing too early or too late reduces the impact of the reveal

text: Let the player control the order in which suspect NPCs are presented during the reveal.
Plant a found item in an NPC's inventory, and place a witness NPC who saw the act where the player can find and question them to clear the accused.
A tide or water-level variable determines which routes are passable at a given moment, so a puzzle or claimed event can depend on timing.
when: when an event or puzzle depends on timing of the environment
why: water level controls whether banks are covered and whether a vessel can float free

text: Some routes stay covered at every tide while others dry wholly or partly at low water, so timing decides which routes can be used.
when: when a route depends on water level
why: a route passable at one tide can be impassable at another

text: Gate a route with a tide or patrol schedule so players can deduce an NPC's destination from its time windows.
Use a timed object such as a clock strike, sundial or bell as a fixed point to place uncertain times on a timeline.
when: building a timeline from unsure observations
why: an exact time gives a reliable reference

text: Build deadlines and timed events, such as a scheduled knock, into puzzles with checkable intervals that narrow possible solutions and make the deadline fair.
when: Designing puzzles with deadlines or timing clues.
why: Checkable intervals give a verifiable constraint and make the deadline solvable.

text: A timepiece that stopped and was never reset keeps its last set time, which can serve as a fixed point to build a timeline from.
when: The object was wound or set at a known moment and not adjusted afterward.
why: A stopped mechanism freezes the time it last showed, so it stays readable long after the event.

text: Stage timed NPC arrivals, such as stakeouts or reveals, with readable approach cues like footsteps so players build suspense while they wait.
Use timed interruptions, such as patrols passing, an accident or an alarm, to shape confrontations, forcing the player to decide whether to act now or later.
when: designing confrontation scenes
why: Interruptions create time pressure and let the suspect escape.

text: Use the tide or fading light as a deadline, since they can erase traces before the investigation is finished.
when: Traces are on a surface that the environment will erase.
why: Natural erasure sets a limit on how long evidence remains available.

text: Give a climax a clock, such as a head start or a closing window, so that each lost moment raises the stakes.
when: when designing a chase or final action
why: A visible deadline makes every delay feel costly

text: Schedule an arrival so the target is still in place and the timing looks ordinary to them, not earlier or later than a normal visit would be.
when: A target's movements depend on a short window of opportunity.
why: Unusual timing can make the target suspicious and prompt them to leave or react.

text: Use unseen messages and timed appointments as quest triggers that open new areas or scenes.
An NPC with a timed daily schedule gives the player a baseline, and missed appointments can trigger alerts or reveal someone's removal from the scene.
when: When designing NPC schedules that feed game events.
why: A deviation from a known baseline is detectable and can drive consequences.

text: A short, repeated, timed sequence of events can explain a situation more fully than its final outcome alone.
when: when the order and timing of visits matter
why: the sequence carries the story

text: A timed world event, such as a flooded chamber draining at a set hour, can prompt an NPC to move a hidden item only at that moment.
when: when designing NPCs that hide items

text: A sudden event such as a scream or flicker of light can draw the player's attention while a real change happens elsewhere in the scene.
when: designing a scene where a hidden change must go unnoticed
why: Sudden stimuli capture attention, leaving other changes in the scene less likely to be perceived.

text: Give timed events short, stated intervals so the player can reconstruct the order of a trap sequence or collapse.
Use a timed countdown with a short open window as an event, and check NPC timelines and alibis against it.
when: when designing a time-limited event
why: timelines reveal who could have acted in the window

text: Give a timed window, such as a tide, patrol or guard rotation, some slack so the arrival window is achievable but still demanding.
when: when designing a time-limited opportunity
why: a window with no slack is effectively impossible

text: A level can run a timed schedule of events that the player orders from witness accounts, with gaps the player closes by finding traces.
Pair a traveling key character with an announced deadline, so the player must reach them or defend the route in time.
when: A key character is away from the player's location and an outcome depends on their arrival.
why: A visible deadline converts waiting into an active objective.

text: Schedule timed events, such as guard rotations or departures, and let players work backward from fixed times to find a safe window.
when: Designing timed events the player must plan around

text: Let the time of day change an NPC's alertness, so an early or late encounter yields different answers from the same character.
when: designing NPC responses across a day
why: fatigue and timing change how guarded they are

text: Choose the moment for a risky entry when the target's attention is engaged elsewhere, and avoid times when an alarm makes entry impractical.
when: Entry into a guarded room is planned.

text: Divide a watch into timed shifts with agreed handover times, so the post is never left unattended.
Weather changes can serve as timers, and a stopped or skipping clock can serve as level dressing that signals an unreliable world.
when: Designing time pressure or atmosphere in a level.
why: Environmental timers create urgency without interrupting play.

text: Signal a timed event such as a patrol or messenger with a sound cue before its source is visible to the player.
when: When designing approaching NPCs or timed events
why: A sound cue builds anticipation and lets the player prepare

text: Use an external deadline, such as an escape window, as a level timer that rewards the player for tracking the right suspect early.
A guard's or partner's timed departure, such as a patrol leaving a room, opens a short window to search or act, which closes when they return.
when: stealth sections with leaving or patrolling NPCs

text: In a timed investigation, delay is costly: evidence fades, suspects flee and leads close, so the quest should change or fail if the player waits too long.
when: designing time-sensitive investigations
why: Time pressure makes the player prioritize questions and prevents indefinite stalling.

text: NPC timetables showing who is absent or where, and quiet periods of low traffic, reveal windows in which a concealed act can run uninterrupted, findable by checking routes.
when: a crime or action depends on an absence, routine or deadline, or on NPC routes in an investigation
why: Timing both enables the action and exposes it to someone who reconstructs the schedule; reduced observation in quiet periods opens the only undetected opportunity.

text: A timed staged event can hold one occupant's attention for a set period, opening a window for an accomplice to act in another room.
when: A crime depends on removing a guard or occupant for a limited time
why: The occupant's attention is committed to the event for its duration

text: Accomplices can cover a decoy's movements and trigger small visible acts, such as a gate bolt pushed shut, as signals in a timed sequence.
A sedative timed to the victim's expected sleep lets a plot proceed during the victim's unconsciousness, so the timeline must be rebuilt around that window.
when: A crime depends on the victim being unable to wake.
why: Timing ties the method to the intended moment of the crime.

text: A timed trigger works like an alarm clock: it starts a playback at a set moment with no one present.
when: a device might have run unattended
why: the trigger separates the sound from the person who made it

text: In a timed negotiation the NPC's tone shifts as the clock runs down, adding pressure on the player to accept terms.
Timed world events, such as a debt falling due or a festival, can draw a hidden NPC to a place where the player can watch.
Overlapping scheduled movements of several NPCs let a player who tracks them order events and uncover meetings the player did not see directly.
when: a level schedules NPC movements that intersect in time
why: Players who track multiple schedules can reconstruct events that occurred off-screen.

text: Place a shared timed event, such as a clock striking, that two characters must meet at, and reward players who track it.
A location that closes on a timer can cut off a conversation mid-answer and send the player back for the rest of the information.
when: Designing time-limited locations with information

text: Timed doors and guard routines placed in a level let players learn which exits were open at which times by checking logs.
when: designing locked-room or closed-building puzzles

text: A scheduled mechanism that releases evidence at a fixed moment makes the release time itself a clue, since it can show when the evidence was placed.

A timestamped quest log lets players reconstruct which NPC learned what first, and a chain of messages where each reply triggers the next lets a delayed or skipped message change the state the player finds.
when: Designing NPC information flow and quest state.
why: Timestamps preserve order, and each message in the chain conditions the next state.

text: A timed requirement, such as needing a key or warrant before entry, forces a choice between waiting and acting.
Replaying a timed sequence, such as an exit followed by a wait and a knock, lets a player confirm a clue's timing before acting on it.
when: a clue depends on the order and interval of actions
why: Timing claims are easier to trust when the player can rerun the sequence and observe it.

text: Periodic events such as recurring attacks can serve as a level clock the player reconstructs by eliminating dates against external records.
when: a sequence of events repeats on a schedule
why: regular intervals let the player order and test events

text: A degrading object such as browning fruit, a burning candle or a torch works as a timer, since its state at discovery gives the elapsed time since a second person was present.
Player arrival close to a scheduled event, such as the day before, creates near-miss tension.
when: Designing scheduled events the player must reach in time.
why: Arriving with almost no margin raises stakes without ending the chance to act.

text: A role-based disguise cannot be kept up for long, so the scheme must be timed tightly around the event it serves.
when: Planning a disguise that must hold through a limited window
why: Prolonged exposure increases the chance of being recognised.

text: Time pressure forces a search to end early, and the unsearched space can hide the target item.
when: When a search is interrupted by a deadline or an arriving person.

text: 1) Arrange an ordinary-looking reason to draw the occupant away. 2) Wait until the agreed time. 3) Enter the marked room and act quickly while the occupant is absent.
when: a person must be absent for a search or confrontation
why: an ordinary reason draws the occupant away without alerting them

text: 1) List who will be present, away or incapacitated at the planned time. 2) Identify anyone who could raise an alarm. 3) Neutralise those people. 4) Set an arrival window. 5) Recheck their states before entering.
when: the next action must wait for a known window and witnesses could raise the alarm
why: Planning around the actual state of people reduces the risk of discovery.

text: 1) Walk or run the route between two points. 2) Time it against a watch at each checkpoint. 3) Compare the measured time with the stated timing before accepting the route.
when: A route between two points matters to the case.
why: Measured timing tests whether the stated route is physically possible.

text: 1) Leave a suspect alone with the object for a fixed, timed interval. 2) Time the wait from outside. 3) Examine the result of the interval as the key evidence.
when: testing a suspect's actions during a short unobserved period
why: A fixed, checkable interval makes the result interpretable.

text: 1) Test the passage both ways before committing, going down and back. 2) Place a marker for the return route and note where the steps begin. 3) Advance and, when the watcher approaches, leave by the far end. 4) Return by the same path, timed to stay out of the watcher's sightline.
when: Using a hidden route to avoid a watcher

text: 1) Observe in timed blocks at different hours. 2) Log every block, including empty ones. 3) Treat repeated visits, not a single empty session, as the basis for a pattern.
when: Building a routine model of a moving subject.
why: Empty sessions are informative, and one session can mislead.

text: 1) Let an enemy or hazard act on a timer across several visits. 2) Make each act slightly stronger or closer. 3) Show a visible sign that the threat is still active during quiet periods.
when: Designing pressure that builds between encounters
why: Visible persistence lets silence read as danger rather than safety

text: A timed distraction, such as a helper's false errand, fetch quest or dropped object, can clear the room and open a window to inspect a hidden item unobserved.
Give world events such as guard patrols and chimes fixed timestamps the player can reconstruct from clocks, bells or NPC routines, letting conflicting times become a puzzle.
when: Designing a world where the player must order events.
why: Reconstructable times reward attention and make conflicts meaningful.

text: Give NPCs timestamped scheduled movements so players can check who was present at a moment and which witnesses could have seen a crime window.
when: Players must reconstruct what happened at a given time.
why: Known timed schedules let players test who was present or positioned to observe an event.

text: Use in-game time to gate events, such as a guard shift, merchant's closing hour or secret meeting window, so players must find the exact window an NPC could act.
when: Designing scheduled content or time-gated scenes.

text: Deliver clues via letters, field-agent reports or scheduled check-ins timed to player progress, pacing discovery across locations and bridging gaps the player cannot reach.
when: The player must receive information away from the main scene or across several locations.
why: Timed delivery paces discovery; timing controls pacing and forces prioritisation.

text: Use timetables and fixed-time anchors, such as a set departure hour or a vehicle's arrival, to eliminate escape routes and narrow where a suspect could have gone.
when: Designing a suspect's possible escape in a timed world.
why: Schedules constrain where a suspect could have gone.

text: Build time-window puzzles from overlapping NPC schedules and events, letting players narrow an interval with several constraints until only one window fits.
when: Designing timed events in a mystery.
why: Overlapping schedules let players deduce the time of an event.

text: Gate an NPC's departure or a plot event on a timer, such as a wedding or a train, so the player must decide when to act.
A timed trap or poison with variable delay should be reasoned from the player's route and the likely delay, so the trigger time is inferred.
when: Designing a delayed hazard that a player must reconstruct.
why: Players can then work backward from their route to find the trigger.

text: Fix a time and place for a confrontation so the characters must plan around it, creating a ticking clock.
Give a doubting NPC a chance to speak; if no one voices doubt, let the panic escalate on a timer.
when: when modelling mass accusation in a game town

text: In a timed quest, let a key NPC arrive at the last moment if the player was told where to look, so the arrival reads as a payoff.
why: A signposted arrival turns a late event into a planted payoff rather than a surprise.

text: Make in-world event timers vague at first, and narrow the player's estimate as more clues arrive.
Schedule a locked clue to become readable at a chosen in-game turn or event, using timed reveals to pace content.
Give a timed window a fixed duration and mark the target room clearly on a map, so the player knows where to go and how long they have.
when: a timed infiltration window is designed
why: a clear target and known time keep the window fair and readable

text: In a timed level, set a clock that closes off options and make the missing evidence the goal.
Stage two events in a level, one real and one staged or misread, and require the player to assign each trace to the correct event.
Create timed movement puzzles where the gap between a log entry and the physical route reveals a hidden step, such as a secret passage used in that interval.
when: when designing route-based clues
why: Mismatched time and distance signals a concealed route.

text: Give a timed NPC rendezvous a visible countdown or a shadowing agent who reports the NPC's location, so the player feels the pressure of the meeting.
when: Designing a meeting the player must reach
why: Visible time and location cues build tension

text: Use regular intervals as a timer the player can predict and exploit.
when: Designing recurring events or schedules in a level
why: Predictable timing lets players plan actions around it

text: Set a promised confrontation behind a time gate, so the reveal waits until the player returns to the location.
when: A reveal depends on the player's schedule or revisit

text: In a timed-clue puzzle, place clues across locations so players must check whether a suspect could cover the distance in the time available.
when: Designing an alibi that the player can test.
why: Travel times expose a claimed alibi that looks plausible on paper.

text: Make timed puzzle routes depend on fixed-time events, and let a mistimed action break the plan visibly; timestamp each event in a log so players can find the conflict.
when: Designing timed puzzles with guard shifts, scheduled doors or similar events.
why: Visible failure and a readable event log let players reconstruct the sequence and locate the error.

text: A journal or diary found early can set the schedule for a later timed event, such as a trigger or a timed door.
Trigger timed events from a specific observable cue, such as a phrase or light change, so players know exactly when to act.
when: Designing timed events in stealth scenes

text: Timestamped NPC movement logs with room entries, exits, sightings, carried items and patrol times let players disprove alibis by finding a suspect elsewhere or a claim conflicting with the log.
when: designing a world where players check NPC alibis or timed NPC movement
why: A shared timestamped record gives players a neutral reference for testing timing claims.

text: Timestamp and source every game event, including NPC movements, door openings, purchases, trap triggers, alarms and state changes, so players can rebuild who was where, when and in what order.
when: designing a quest log, journal or mystery's event history where order and timing matter
why: Ordered, sourced timestamps let players compare accounts, test consistency, find contradictions and recover where a sequence breaks.

text: Timestamp and place events such as calls, messages, sleep requests, departures, arrivals, deliveries and sightings, with carried items, so each NPC's claim can be checked against independent sources.
when: for timed events and sightings recorded in a game
why: Timestamped sightings let players test whether a watcher could have seen what they claim.

text: Store each NPC statement as a timestamped, fixed record so players can review it, catch contradictions when new clues appear, and test it by confronting the witness.
when: designing dialogue systems that track NPC testimony
why: Timestamps let contradictions be discovered later, and a stored claim becomes checkable through live questioning.

text: Idle occupants who stay in a building still restrict movement, so a time when people seem inactive is not automatically an empty window.
when: occupants are idle but indoors
why: their continued presence limits what an intruder can do

text: Common journey delays include a mechanical breakdown, a chance encounter, removed navigation signs, an interrupted conversation and a closing time.
Test whether a timeline is genuine by asking who could have made a key call or action at the moment the event is fixed.
when: when an anchor is a recorded call or a similar action

text: Use travel time across the setting to limit where a missing person can be, since a place crossable in a fixed time bounds the search.
when: Reasoning about whether a missing person is still nearby.
why: Distance and travel time constrain possible locations.

text: Record the questions asked in witness logs, so players can see how a statement was extracted.
Track each location's traffic, including patrols, NPC routines and weekday schedules, letting players judge whether a stashed clue could survive.
Include visitors who arrived too late, so the player learns that the site was used on a schedule.
Set the intervals between a scream, a silence and an arrival as tuned triggers for patrols and guard movements.
when: Designing timed reactions to in-world events

text: Use a dated backward trace on a case board, where each record found unlocks the next location in a fixed order.
when: Designing investigation progression in a game
why: Ordered records gate progress and keep the player on a clear path.

text: A locked-room puzzle can log a door-state change caused by an NPC, giving a timestamp the player must reconstruct from other events.
when: when designing a locked-room puzzle with NPC movement
why: Logged state changes make the timeline a task the player can solve.

text: Plant a timed object, such as a stopped watch, whose recorded time can be compared with other locations to test who was where.
when: Designing a clue that tests alibis or movements.
why: A recorded time can be cross-checked against other locations and witnesses.

text: Make an alibi a physical object or timed fact the player can check, such as a telegram or a timed event, so its falsity can be proven by a later clue.
when: Designing a suspect's cover story
why: An alibi that can be tested gives the player a real route to disproving it.

text: Build a timeline puzzle around a single hinge event, such as a checkpoint, so the player must work out a character's state before and after it.
when: Designing a timeline puzzle in a level or case.
why: A single hinge gives the player one clear point to test all other facts against.

text: A game timeline built from timestamped events and NPC schedules lets players reconstruct a crime window themselves.
Matching torn edges of paired stubs shows whether the holders were issued or presented them together; mismatched edges indicate separate entry, even if arrivals were close in time.
when: Paired physical tokens such as ticket stubs are recovered and the question is whether two people entered together.
why: Tickets torn in one act share matching edges, while tickets torn at different times do not.

text: A half-finished action, such as a drink or meal left unfinished, shows the action was interrupted and gives a cue for dating events.
A sudden stop in a visible signal, such as a lantern flash or whistle, can tell the player that an NPC has spotted them or is about to act.
when: in a level where NPCs signal each other
why: A break in a readable pattern carries information the player can reason about.

text: Timing a bribe so that an interruption cuts off the reveal creates a ticking-clock encounter that rewards quick action.
when: Designing a reveal that a player must race to hear.
why: The interruption forces the player to decide quickly.

text: A recurring trap that fires at a fixed interval can be made discoverable from a log of firing times, so players infer the interval rather than reading it as a stated rule.
when: When designing periodic hazards or events in a level.
why: Players learn the pattern by comparing timestamps side by side, which makes the discovery feel earned.

text: Store each NPC's movements as timestamped events against a game clock, so players can assemble timelines from several accounts, find contradictions and check who could have heard an event.
Leaving a post to chase a sound opens the gap that an intruder needs to pass unseen.
Leaving the most enclosed spots for last means the hardest checks fall when the search has already run long.
1) Count tickets sold from the sales record. 2) Count stubs recovered at the scene. 3) Subtract to find the unaccounted tickets.
when: Sales logs and collected stubs are both available.
why: The difference reveals tickets that never returned to the scene, which can point to hidden or absent parties.

text: 1) Log each trap or event with its cause and trigger. 2) Store the order of occurrence. 3) Replay the log to show the solution step by step.
when: a level needs a reconstructable solution
why: Logged causes allow the sequence to be shown

text: Log door and gate timestamps, sounds, consumed resources, delivery crates and guard patrols, so players can rebuild who entered and spot gaps revealing a hidden visit or open path.
when: designing a game where players reconstruct past events
why: Logged traces give players checkable evidence for testing timing answers.

text: Keep one shared, timestamped event log the player can query, so every character's account or testimony is cross-checked against one sequence.
Timestamp room visits and events, such as lock states, item drops and guard patrols, so players can check when a victim was last alive or when a last-person rule breaks.
Label clocks that run fast or slow; with several regional clocks or time skips, store each event's reference time so doubt about one source does not spread.
when: a clock is used as evidence or several regional clocks or time skips exist
why: Unlabelled inaccuracy makes all timings uncertain.

text: Give placed or disturbed objects time markers, such as fresh soil, wet paint or fresh dust, so players can tell current traces from older ones.
when: designing evidence that changes over time
why: Timing lets players separate current traces from older ones.

text: Timestamp found documents and in-world objects, such as logged notes, so players can place clues on one shared timeline and anchor reconstructed sequences.
when: when clues must be ordered in time or in a timeline-based mystery
why: Concrete timestamps let players place clues on one timeline and anchor sequences.

text: Anchor timed events to in-world references players can observe or verify, such as bells, landmarks, shift changes, patrol times or posted schedules, so they can order events.
when: designing timed events or story sequences the player must reconstruct
why: A verifiable shared reference gives players fixed points for ordering events without a written log.
