text: A crime-scene clock or watch can be set to a false hour, and checking whether its mechanism still runs can reveal the tampering.
when: Designing a timing clue in a scene.
why: Players can detect tampering through physical inspection.

text: Use a witness arrival or outside pressure to pause a search and force the player to decide what to reveal.
when: Ending a scene or raising tension during a search
why: Interruptions create decisions and suspense

text: Give in-game events timestamps and distance estimates so players can assemble the sequence of a timing puzzle themselves.
Give world events timestamps so players can check whether an NPC could be in two places, and let them compare clocks, dated letters and schedules for contradictions.
when: designing a mystery or alibi puzzle
why: Timestamps let the player find contradictions themselves.

text: Log who proposed each plan in NPC conversations so that later clues can depend on attribution.
Generate motives from a relationship history of timestamped events, so the player uncovers the layers in order.
Learn a target's routine before placing a clue; if the routine is unknown, delivery depends on luck.
Let items a character leaves behind show which exit was used and when, giving the player a timeline to reconstruct.
when: Levels that reconstruct a past event.
why: Left-behind objects give the player concrete evidence that orders events.

text: Stage an identity switch during a journey between two locations so neither persona is seen leaving its home.
Check a door's security at the time of the crime, since the time it was secured may differ from the time it was last checked.
Tie a missing item count to a character's earlier visit, so the player connects the loss to the right suspect.
when: Designing a clue based on a missing item.
why: A visit gives the player a reason to suspect a particular character.

text: Design a location that holds the record of an earlier event, such as a house where a past crime occurred, so the player reads its traces.
Log purchases and item acquisitions as timestamped planning evidence that the player can cross-reference with other events.
when: Building a game where earlier acquisitions can implicate a character.
why: Acquisitions that match later events let the player reconstruct intent.

text: Log time-stamped actions so a game can show when a character was absent from a post during an event, and derive alibi checks from those logs.
when: A game tracks character presence during events.
why: Timestamps let the game verify claims about who was where.

text: Log ticket or key issuance as queryable data, so unclaimed slots near a crime become clues a player can check.
Make an offered explanation checkable against the level's timeline, so an attentive player can catch the gap.
Place ambient sound events from other areas as location and timing clues, so the player can order events.
when: designing a sealed space where events occur out of view
why: Sounds from elsewhere let the player reconstruct a sequence without seeing it.

text: A single watcher over a long period becomes unreliable without a relief watcher or a written log.
when: when a watch lasts a long time
why: Attention fails over long periods.

text: Let players build a timeline from NPC routines, delivery times and key-holder notes to find when an item was swapped.
when: Designing a schedule-based investigation puzzle.
why: Combining routines and access records lets players deduce the window of opportunity.

text: Events that draw occupants away reduce the number of people who could observe an intruder, opening unusual access windows.
when: a community event pulls people out of a building
why: fewer observers lower the risk of being seen

text: A timed check is only as reliable as its starting time; if the starting point is an estimate, the computed window may be wrong.
when: The start of a timed chain is not precisely known.
why: Errors in the first timestamp propagate through every later calculation.

text: 1) Anchor each planned action to a fixed day or event. 2) Order actions so that the target is acted upon before a suspect can respond. 3) Verify facts before the schedule forces action.
when: Designing a timed investigation sequence
why: A deadline creates pressure, and acting before the suspect can react preserves the advantage.

text: 1) Record the timing of each event in the case. 2) Lay the accounts against one another. 3) Mark where accounts conflict. 4) Let the player compare accounts against that timeline.
when: Building a timeline for player-facing investigation
why: A shared timeline makes conflicts between testimonies visible and gives the player a structure for deduction.

text: Model patrols and transit as fixed timetables that players can check against suspects' claimed routes and use to predict locations and plan an intercept.
when: When designing NPC movement that players should be able to anticipate
why: Predictable schedules make interception a skill rather than a matter of chance

text: Give NPC couriers a fixed role, such as a servant who cannot read, so a message can be carried without its contents being revealed.
when: when designing NPC message delivery
why: A set role makes the courier's knowledge predictable.

text: Require a timed investigation to be checked in fixed order, with each check unlocking the next lead while a clock runs toward a deadline.
Give an escape puzzle a fixed deadline and a fixed meeting point, so the challenge has a clear finish and a clear test of success.
Give NPC routines such as rent collection that run on a schedule, so a missed payment prompts the player to ask where it should have come from.
when: designing a town economy that can carry a clue
why: A break in a scheduled routine is noticed only when the player knows the routine exists.

text: Accumulated residue such as fallen cigar ash gives a rough duration for how long someone stood still.
Time covert actions for a quiet window, and use ordinary routines such as staff departures or cleaning as cover.
when: a player must act unobserved

text: End a level phase on a breach of an area the player was told is secured, creating a turn in pacing.
when: the player has just been assured that an area is safe

text: A timed challenge can keep its rule limit hidden, so players must track the limit through the events of the level.
when: Designing timed challenges

text: A timed gate such as an arrival date or opening day forces the culprit to act before a fixed deadline.
when: When designing time-limited actions in a mystery
why: The deadline constrains the culprit's options and the player's window to intervene

text: Plant a false lead, such as a letter pointing to a rival faction, and let its timing reveal the trick to players who check it.
when: designing a false lead in a level

text: Give a guard or servant who tends a shrine, cache or prisoner irregular patrol times, so the player can catch tampering and feel the suspense of a surprise check.
Add an event in which the target NPC relocates before the player arrives, so the player's reconnaissance becomes outdated and the trap hits an empty room.
when: Designing a stealth or assassination quest.
why: Stale information forces the player to re-scout, adding tension.

text: Time a planted cache to appear when the player expects it, and let a later clue reveal who placed it.
Give a poison or trap an onset time, so players can deduce that dosing occurred near the victim within a fixed window.
when: When designing a poison or trap as a clue
why: A known onset lets players infer proximity and timing from the effect.

text: Make a timed object such as a clock or candle readable in two ways, and reward players who test whether it was moved.
when: Designing a time clue in a locked-room puzzle
why: Checking the object's state reveals a falsified timeline

text: Make a locked gate open on a set day and let players learn its schedule from in-world information.
when: Designing an access restriction that should be predictable
why: A learnable schedule turns the gate into a timing puzzle rather than an arbitrary block

text: Destroy a dangerous document before the player reaches it, leaving visible residue such as ash or a half-burnt scrap, and hide a copy elsewhere so players can recover what was lost.
when: Designing a room where an NPC or event destroys evidence.
why: Visible residue gives the player a clue, and a hidden copy rewards searching.

text: Cleaning or restoration erases handling marks, so players must notice what is missing as well as present; a spotless space may hide tampering.
when: The environment can be altered by characters or events, or repeatedly reset to a known state.
why: Missing evidence carries information as much as present evidence, and restoration removes traces that show interference.

text: Give each ambiguous clue, such as a smell, sound or trace, two possible sources, so players must test it with a second clue before committing.
when: Designing a clue that could mislead if taken at face value.
why: Requiring confirmation makes careful reasoning pay off.

text: Cleaning leaves traces: a patch cleaner than the surrounding dust, or an unusually wiped object, shows someone wiped it, so tidy scenes can hide disturbance.
when: Inspecting a dusty surface or a cleaned room.
why: Wiping removes marks but leaves contrast.

text: Place a chain of NPCs along an item's path, each holding a readable record, so every handler leaves a clue that narrows the next search.
when: Designing an item-tracing investigation in a level
why: Each record gives the player a concrete lead toward the next link

text: A change in stride or trace pattern at one point along a route can mark where a person's behaviour changed.
Give physical traces such as footprints, dropped objects or scuffs properties comparable to a suspect's gear so the player can match them.
when: designing traces in a level
why: matching requires the player to have a comparable attribute

text: Marks left on a body or object can be stored as checkable facts that confirm or contradict a testimony.
Cleaning routines that skip some surfaces let dust-based traces persist, so which clues survive depends on which tasks are done on which days.
why: a cleaner who skips dusting leaves dust evidence intact

text: Let a hidden item leave a detectable trace, such as a scraped surface or missing match, so a careful player can uncover the concealment.
Make a removed body or object leave no drag marks, blood trail or dropped item when it was not moved by force, giving players a deduction hook.
when: Designing a room where a body or object is apparently taken
why: Missing traces reveal that the removal was voluntary, rewarding inference

text: Give a hidden or lethal hazard a subtle visible tell, such as a misplaced item, an exterior flaw, or residue on a lamp shield, so careful inspection can reveal it.
when: Designing hazards that should be fair to careful players, including in closed rooms
why: A visible tell rewards careful inspection and keeps the hazard from feeling arbitrary.

text: Create a sealed room with a timed hazard so the player must make decisions under pressure, and count down the shrinking space to make the threat visible.
when: Designing a trap or escape encounter that needs urgency
why: A visible countdown turns an abstract timer into concrete tension

text: Time a trap to the moment an earlier event is believed to have occurred, so the expected event becomes the trigger.
If a lure is suspected, letting the target leave on it can remove them from the scene while you prepare a counter.
when: When you expect the lure to be followed by an attack.

text: An ambush prepared by an opponent can be turned against it when the defender anticipates it and surrounds the waiting attackers.
when: When the defender knows the opponent is setting an ambush
why: The opponent's waiting becomes a trap for the opponent.

text: A trap built on a belief about how a watcher behaves works only if that belief holds. Test the belief before committing resources, because a false one leaves the trap empty.
when: Designing a trap or ambush for an observing agent
why: The trap's outcome depends entirely on the single assumption it rests on

text: Show a trap's components as ordinary decoration, such as inscriptions or altar fixtures, so careful inspection lets players deduce the mechanism early.
Send the player to a location as a decoy, and trigger a trap, such as gas or a shock, through a signal the player can hear or see.
when: Designing an ambush or trap encounter.
why: The player feels the trap was set by a clue they could have noticed.

text: A prepared object catches only a suspect who touches it; one who avoids contact leaves no trace, so a trap's proof comes from the target's own act.
when: The trap relies on the target acting freely
why: The target, not the investigator, controls the decisive action.

text: A marker placed on a hiding place, such as a hair on a drawer lip, moves or falls when the place is opened, signalling that it was searched.
when: A hidden object must be guarded and the owner needs to know whether it was touched.
why: The disturbed marker acts as a silent alarm that needs no witness.

text: A trap that fires when triggered can signal the trapper, who waits nearby and times a return to the sound of the trigger.
A light-sensitive trigger hidden behind ordinary objects completes a circuit when light reaches it, sending a signal to a remote point the target cannot see.
when: a confrontation is staged in a room the target controls
why: concealment keeps the target from knowing the signal exists

text: A hazard disguised as an accident depends on the victim's expected mistake, so a small out-of-place container or item near it can reveal the true intent.
when: when designing a trap that looks accidental
why: Disguises rarely remove every trace; the leftover anomaly lets careful players detect the hazard.

text: A timed sting has five parts: a hidden listener, a concealed response team, a visible trigger cue, a decoy who stalls the target, and a standby exit with open comms.
when: Designing a covert ambush or sting event
why: Each part supplies one need: information, surprise, timing, delay or escape.

text: A lure that a careful reader can see through fails, so the message must hold up under scrutiny.
when: when writing a coded notice or false lead
why: suspects who examine the message will recognise the trick

text: A disturbed trap proves that someone touched the hiding place, but it does not reveal who did it.
when: A trap has been triggered and a suspect is being named.
why: The trap records the event, not the identity of the person who caused it.

text: A trap whose timing depends on uncertain transit can fail when delays, such as weather, upset the schedule.
when: the target's arrival time is set by travel

text: A decoy that never moves gives itself away as fake; movement is needed to keep the bait believable.
A signaller may be left stranded and hesitate about entering danger if the expected follow-up never appears.
why: no instructions cover the case where the expected event does not happen

text: Entering a venue whose activity holds you in place can trap a follower, who then becomes the one pursued.
when: Following a subject into a shop or room that requires participation.
why: Required participation keeps the follower stationary while the subject moves on.

text: Moving or handling a concealing object can set off a hidden trigger by accident, so its placement must be checked before the trap is relied on.
A hidden trigger depends on its power source and signal timing, so a failure in either silently disables the whole response.
1) Hold an independently verified timeline. 2) Ask about a detail the target could only know by being present. 3) Compare the target's answer, including any substitute detail, against the timeline.
when: A target claims to have been somewhere or seen something, and dates or times can be checked.

text: 1) Approach slowly. 2) Operate a suspected switch with an improvised tool. 3) Scan the room for signs of danger. 4) Examine common everyday objects first.
when: When an enemy has had access to a room
why: An improvised tool keeps the hand off possible hazards, and everyday objects are the ones people are most likely to touch.

text: 1) Stretch fragile traces, such as threads, across the room at the height and route a visitor would cross. 2) Place a marker on a door or lock. 3) Check the traces and markers afterward. 4) Compare disturbances with the expected routine to confirm an entry and its route.
when: When you need proof that a room was entered and the route of entry matters
why: Traces disturbed in an unexpected pattern reveal movement that bypassed the door

text: 1) List every candidate container. 2) Order them from oldest to most recent. 3) Inspect each in turn, checking for recent handling. 4) Do not guess which one matters.
when: An investigator must search many similar containers for hidden evidence.
why: Methodical ordering prevents missed containers and avoids guesswork.

text: 1) Build a trap with a visible flaw in its mechanism. 2) Let a careful player notice the flaw. 3) Make the confession or later dialogue reveal the trap's concealed purpose.
when: Designing a trap that serves as a murder disguise and a clue.
why: A visible flaw rewards observation and lets the reveal be checked against the environment.

text: Give a trap a clear trigger condition so the player knows what they have set in motion.
when: Designing player-triggered traps or ambushes
why: Players can plan only when the outcome of their setup is legible

text: Place a watcher or trigger at the expected exit so the player's observation of the reaction advances the plot.
Let a trap or elevator be set in one room while its effect appears in another, so the timing of that effect becomes the evidence.
why: Separating cause and effect in space and time creates a deducible puzzle

text: Place trip-wire alarms on routes into a base, and let the player detect and avoid them through careful movement.
when: A base has known approach routes
why: Alarms that ring on contact reward a defender who knows the approaches

text: Link a trap's trigger to an everyday object that players are tempted to reposition.
when: When designing traps in rooms players will search and handle

text: A trap room that leaves a body behind can be designed so the player's exit looks suspicious to NPCs who did not see the entry.
Place a trigger inside an ordinary object and route its wiring along walls, so the target neither notices the components nor trips over the wire.
when: a hidden trap or alarm must stay undiscovered
why: discovery or accidental disturbance makes the trap fail

text: Stage a supposedly cleared suspect's final confrontation in a room the player has already explored, as a trap.
when: when planning a late-game confrontation
why: Familiar space makes the trap feel fair and lets the player recall earlier clues.

text: Structure the final confrontation as a trap sequence, such as a locked door and smoke, that forces the culprit to confess.
when: when staging a climactic confrontation
why: Physical pressure leaves the culprit few options except a confession.

text: Plant small visible traces, such as mud on boots, a missing button, fresh wear, dents, scuffs, dust disturbance or missing footprints, so careful players can deduce hidden mechanisms.
when: Designing environmental clues
why: Careful observation rewards players without needing text explanation; visible traces let players deduce hidden mechanisms.

text: A visible surface effect, such as trembling ground at the turn of the tide, signals a hidden danger beneath.
A setting visible from many windows makes a witness feel she could be seen and heard, yet it gives no protection against a quiet threat.
when: a public location with many sightlines hosts a private conversation
why: Visibility is felt as safety even when no one can intervene in time

text: Give a cover-up a visible but easy-to-miss mismatch, such as a replaced rug or fresh paint, spotted with a tool or good light, so careful inspection rewards.
An unusual event in a level can serve as a strong opening clue that narrows the player's search.
when: designing the first clue of a mystery
why: an unusual event points to a smaller set of explanations

text: A fixture that looks decorative but is placed in an odd way may be the hidden mechanism, so treat no visible detail as trivial.
when: placing secrets in a room
why: players who inspect odd details are the ones who find the secret

text: Place a warning at a feature, such as a well, fountain or locked gate, with a casual reason, and make the real reason discoverable later.
when: Designing environmental hazards tied to a feature.
why: A casual warning stays a live clue until its reason is found.

text: Show a re-fitted or freshly scratched lock as a visible trace, placed alongside an innocent explanation the player can weigh.
when: When designing evidence of tampering that should not be conclusive.
why: Ambiguous traces keep the player reasoning rather than receiving a flag.

text: Place visible but unremarked clues in rooms, which only an attentive player or a perception check will pick up.
when: Clues should reward attention without being flagged.
why: Attention and skill checks separate observation from mere seeing.

text: Trigger a hidden passage with a visible cue, such as a flash from a fixture, so attentive players can connect cause and effect.
when: Designing hidden doors
why: The cue links the action to the reveal

text: Make a hidden timed trigger fire on a visible NPC action, so the player must watch the same cue the witness watched.
Avoid overloading an opening with description that no later scene uses.
Hide a distinguishing detail that is visible only at close inspection, such as in an enlarged portrait, to reward players who examine carefully.
when: Designing a clue for identifying a culprit
why: Careful inspection then yields a clear and satisfying discovery.

text: Show the final mechanism in plain view early, such as a fake or dummy element, so the eventual explanation feels fair and retrospective.
when: Designing a trap, route or device that the player will later understand fully.
why: Players accept a late reveal more readily when the components were visible earlier and simply misread.

text: Use cheap, durable environmental anomalies, such as a closed window or an object built after death, as tells the player can notice and revisit later.
when: Adding clues to a scene for an investigation
why: Persistent details let the player return to them once the context that explains them is discovered.

text: A witness who says a person 'looks like' someone is weaker than one who is sure, so do not treat the two as equal.
A witness who says a detail 'may have' been present has not confirmed it, so the detail must not be recorded as fact.
Hedged, vague predictions cannot be disproved, so trust rests on the performer's claimed past accuracy rather than on the forecast itself.
when: A reader offers forecasts with limited stated expertise.
why: Unfalsifiable statements make audiences trust reputation instead of testing claims.

text: A sudden, unexplained departure from a gathering can signal a quarrel with someone in the victim's circle.
when: A character leaves a social setting abruptly
why: Abrupt exits often follow a confrontation.

text: Work left mid-process, such as paint on a palette or brushes standing in solvent, suggests sudden abandonment that needs explaining.
A route that travelers abandon loses its legal use and can be plowed back into fields, so it disappears from the landscape and survives only in records, stones and fences.
Abandoning the past entirely can miss clues that only past testimony or records can supply.
when: past records or witnesses can still be checked

text: A major event reported in a brief passage with little reaction can feel abrupt, so it needs a short emotional beat.
An abrupt interruption ends an exchange before more is learned, so keep the questioning at a steady rhythm.
Abandon a conspicuous object rather than keep it when pursuers could identify it quickly once found.
why: a found object alerts pursuers rapidly

text: A missing expected entry, such as an unpaid fuel charge, is evidence only once the expected pattern is known.
when: reading a ledger or account book
why: Absence means something only against a known norm.

text: A forensic finding that no poison was swallowed contradicts a suicide-by-ingestion reading and suggests the drug was administered by another person.
when: A death first read as self-administered poisoning.
why: A missing trace in the body is a physical fact that can overturn a method-based assumption.

text: A presumption of death after a short absence requires evidence that makes death highly probable, and the shorter the absence, the stronger the evidence must be.
when: Deciding whether to presume a person dead after they disappear.
why: A short absence leaves many innocent explanations open, so stronger evidence is needed to rule them out.

text: Absence of a visible sign or of anyone hearing an event does not prove nothing happened; check whether the setting could mask it.
when: An examination finds no marks but the witness reports an injury, or nobody heard the event.
why: Some effects leave no visible residue, and the setting may mask the event.

text: Having no other candidate is an argument from absence, not proof that the chosen suspect is guilty.
Silence in a report or record does not prove an event or claim never happened; it may fall in a blind spot, so treat the gap as a question.
why: A report may omit a fact because it was never recorded, and some families had disappeared or received no notice.

text: A missing expected reaction, such as grief, pain, tears or a fit, is weak evidence of guilt, since age, illness, fear, pride or habitual silence can suppress it.
when: A test relies on an expected bodily or emotional reaction
why: Many innocent conditions suppress the reaction, and the same outward appearance can arise from different causes.

text: A missing expected person or object is a clue only when an established routine or habitual baseline makes it expected; without a known baseline, do not over-read the gap.
when: Someone or something is expected in a location and does not appear, or a gap is judged for meaning
why: Breaking an established pattern makes a missing element significant; without a known baseline, a gap may be ordinary.

text: A missing expected trace, like hoof marks, should be checked at the site before accepting a supernatural reading, since it counts against the claim that would have produced it.
when: Testimony conflicts or a reported trace is missing or moved
why: Absence is easy to over-interpret when the expected trace is not found.

text: Absence alone is not proof of guilt; keep innocent causes like illness or servants' routes open, and do not accept a routine explanation until confirmed.
when: A person is missing, unaccounted for, or absence is used as evidence of avoidance or guilt
why: Absence has many innocent causes, and both guilt and innocence need evidence beyond the absence itself.

text: Lack of sightings can be informative when nearby people are busy, but silence means little when witnesses were not positioned or expected to observe or report.
when: When asking witnesses whether they saw someone leave or return, or inferring from absence of reports
why: Busy observers miss unnoticed departures, so silence reflects attention and position rather than absence.

text: Once expected people are missing, others treat their absence as meaningful, so an absent person quickly becomes a default suspect.
People who stay away from public gatherings get marked as suspect once the crowd has committed to a cause.
when: when a community is mobilised against suspects
why: absence reads as disagreement with the group

text: A key figure who is absent, glimpsed or only reported second-hand builds anticipation, so the audience expects the encounter before it arrives.
when: setting up a major character or confrontation
why: withheld presence keeps the audience waiting for the figure

text: A host tends to read an absent invitee as a deliberate insult, though absences often have innocent causes.
An offender who shows no remorse may be isolated by others, who distrust him and give reasons that differ from the real ones.
when: a character's lack of regret becomes known
why: peers judge the person by visible guilt rather than the act alone

text: A stated, ordinary plan, such as a visit to a relative with a planned pickup, explains a long absence and keeps it from looking suspicious.
when: when someone is unseen for a long stretch
why: an ordinary explanation accounts for the gap

text: Observers treat absent signs, such as missing breath or no movement, as evidence, so silence itself comes to carry meaning.
A person who is missing and whose body is not found does not automatically count as dead, because no positive proof of death exists.
when: A character's status is uncertain and no body or direct evidence is available.
why: Lack of a body leaves death unproven, so a formal finding of death requires more than absence.

text: Absence of fingerprints does not show the offender feared prints, since gloves explain it equally well.
when: when interpreting a clean scene
why: a gloved offender leaves no prints without any deliberate wiping

text: A missing expected item or presence, in a scene, body or routine, is as revealing as an unexpected one that turns up, and should prompt an explanation.
when: When examining a scene, body, routine or belongings for clues
why: An expected thing that is absent signals a change in events; checking absences against what is normally there reveals removal or hidden events.

text: A missing valued or concealed item narrows suspects: its taker must have known it existed and had access, and the reason for taking it points to who wanted it.
when: A private, concealed or valued item is absent from where it should be
why: Taking an item requires knowing about it, and the reason for an absence points to who had access and what they wanted.

text: A character absent from a key scene is evidence of a gap to investigate, not a neutral fact.
Notice when a person who should have been present is missing, since that absence can be the result of a deliberate act.
when: A scene lacks someone who normally or expectedly would be there.
why: Engineered absence removes a witness and can hide a second actor.

text: A missing action that an innocent person would normally take can be evidence, because its absence points toward knowledge or guilt.
when: a key person fails to do what they would be expected to do
why: innocent people usually act to clear themselves, so their silence is informative

text: Ask whether an absence fits the other known facts; if it needs its own separate explanation, the inference drawn from it is weaker.
When someone fails to know a widely reported event, treat that gap as a clue about where they were.
Note what reports leave out. Gaps mark where to seek details from the people directly involved.
when: public records give few details
why: the missing parts need primary sources

text: A missing part of a matched pair suggests the item was disposed of nearby, so start an investigation from what is absent.
Treat missing traces, such as absent blood or a missing ticket, as evidence that points to where an event happened.
A scene can be read by what it lacks, such as missing stuffed gaps or an unblocked transom, to narrow the possible routes.
A theory that depends on an absence, such as no wound, can be exposed by a single later test of that absence.
when: Checking a theory that assumes something did not happen.
why: One test can falsify a claim that rests on something missing.

text: Build a payoff where the expected target is absent and a different one takes its place, with earlier hints the player could have caught.
A deleted line, blank stretch or sudden silence in a written account can indicate what the writer avoided, and should be weighed as a possible signal.
when: Reading a written account or witness testimony for clues.
why: Writers often leave out what they did not want revealed.

text: Treat an expected event or object that is missing as evidence in itself. Ask what should have happened and did not, and require any theory to explain that gap.
when: A theory feels complete but has not been checked against what did not happen.
why: Missing expected details reveal intent, pace or care that present details alone do not show.

text: An expected item that is missing from a person's usual state, such as jewellery a visitor would normally wear, can serve as a clue to an earlier event.
when: A person's appearance does not match their usual habits.
why: Absences from normal patterns are informative when the pattern is well established.

text: An abandoned location can carry a timeline the player reconstructs from an NPC's account and traces such as moved furniture or a dropped key.
An empty space can be evidence: a vacant spot marks where an object used to be and can be read like a present object.
An absence of footprints on a surface below an entry point can indicate that no one landed there, which the player must reason about.
when: when examining the ground beneath a window or drop
why: Missing traces constrain how an intruder could have entered or left.

text: An absent item is not proof of wrongdoing, since it may have been moved legitimately.
Do not treat a missing sign as proof alone; it gains weight only when a later test confirms a second cause.
when: when using an absent or contrary result as an investigative clue
why: An anomaly without confirmation can mislead the investigator.

text: A deliberate absence of a tell can itself signal that a character is hiding something.
An unexplained absence following an unexplained scene can become the clue itself, holding the audience's question open until the cause is revealed.
when: a figure vanishes without explanation
why: the missing figure invites inference

text: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence; a missing witness does not prove no one was present, so inference from what is missing stays provisional.
Absence-based deductions, like no footprints or dry clothing, are weak unless the search covered where a rival would leave traces and the evidence should have appeared.
when: A search finds nothing or a deduction relies on something missing
why: Silence supports a theory only when the search could have detected the rival's traces.

text: An absence can support almost any theory, so a missing-item investigation can end in dead ends.
Nobody having suspected anything is not evidence that nothing happened; an error can stay hidden until a sealed space is opened years later.
A conviction obtained in default rests on the accused's absence and says nothing about guilt in itself.
when: Interpreting a verdict reached without the accused present.
why: The verdict reflects procedure and absence, not an evaluation of the evidence against the person.

text: An expected person's absence is easy to overlook as routine, though it can contradict a stated plan.
when: Reviewing a timeline for missing people.
why: Absences look normal unless compared against the plan.

text: Absence and a shared common object are not proof of guilt, yet they can build a convincing false lead.
when: a suspect is absent and matches a common clue
why: many people share the same trait or circumstance

text: Lack of rebuttal may reflect limited access rather than truth, so establish whether rivals could actually read and answer the account before inferring its accuracy.
A departed visitor is not evidence of who the visitor was; treating an absence as proof of identity is an unsupported inference.
A clean-looking cloth does not prove a stain was absent, because what the cloth shows depends on how it was handled.
why: handling can remove or hide a stain

text: Assuming an item was burned or destroyed ends the search too early; partial survival such as a half-burnt item may still be enough.
Sending away the only witness can itself draw notice, because an unusual absence of staff becomes a pattern that others can observe.
when: A suspect removes servants or observers to cover a movement.
why: Unusual absences are noticeable in their own right.

text: Silence in response to an appeal can be read as refusal or death, but it may simply reflect an unrecognised name.
why: Non-response has several causes that the notice itself cannot distinguish.

text: Indirect answers can carry no information when the witness lacks the relevant knowledge, so a null answer should not be read as evidence of absence.
when: an investigator interprets an answer that avoids the target subject
why: A witness who knows nothing relevant gives an answer that looks informative but tells nothing.

text: 1) Model the person's habits and the items they imply. 2) List what they usually owned, bought or carried. 3) Compare recovered items against that list; treat each unaccounted item as an open question. 4) Search the most likely storage places thoroughly. 5) If none are found, conclude it was probably never present, provisionally; revise if it turns up.
when: An expected item cannot be found or a scene is checked for gaps
why: A gap is visible only against a known baseline, and a thorough search makes the absence conclusion trustworthy.

text: 1) List what was removed. 2) List what was left. 3) Find the element common to the removed items. 4) Use that element as the motive clue.
when: when damage or loss looks organized

text: Present an NPC's convenient absence or travel as a time window the player can plan around; it also constrains when the culprit can time a crime.
when: Designing NPC travel or timing in a mystery
why: Windows let the player plan and let the culprit time actions.

text: Give an absent NPC a motive trail built from documents such as a map, letter or diary so the player can reconstruct the crime.
when: when designing a crime in the player's past
why: documents let the player reason backward to the motive

text: Record where blood is absent as well as where it is present, since missing blood on a hand or floor constrains how an act could have occurred.
when: when documenting a scene with a wound
why: Absences limit the possible sequence of actions

text: Check for expected traces that are missing, since their absence shows what probably did not happen.
Check a reported absence, departure or illness by contacting the place the person should be, and do not accept the claim unconfirmed.
when: A second party reports that someone left or is unavailable
why: Reported absences are claims that need independent confirmation

text: Let gaps in the records be real, so the player infers events from surviving documents and places rather than finding a complete record.
when: Designing the information available in a mystery
why: Incomplete records make inference a real part of play

text: In an inventory system, the lack of expected accessories or duplicates can signal that a character never carried them, letting players deduce it.
when: When designing character inventories that players can inspect.
why: Absence of expected items is readable as information.

text: Before dismissing a missing item as unimportant, check whether it was actually expected at that location.
when: an item's absence seems to have no obvious cause
why: Assuming no one expected it skips the check that could reveal a meaningful gap.

text: Use absence as storytelling: tracks with no livestock, or a patrol route with no guard, can signal that a disguise is in use.
Place an absent object, such as a missing lamp, as a clue the player must notice and reason about.
Design a timeline puzzle by giving each character an absence window so that exactly one window fits the event, and players must find it.
Absent marks suggest no passage only where the surface would record it, like soft ground after rain showing only investigators' prints; on surfaces that hold no traces, absence proves nothing.
when: When reading a scene for entry, exit or route evidence
why: Passage leaves marks only on surfaces that record it, so a clean surface shows nobody else passed only in that case.

text: Absent residue on expected surfaces can rule out a mechanism, but a missing weapon, cloth or trace cannot prove no method was used; absence settles only what tests could detect.
when: When using missing residue or traces to rule a method in or out; choose which tests are worth running

text: Absences matter: missing expected traces or damage, such as scorch marks, and conflicting traces, such as soot without fire marks, can rule out an assumed cause like fire.
when: a hypothesis predicts a visible trace, or when testing a proposed explanation for a scene

text: Absence and residue, meaning what a room has lost, left behind or left untidy, can show how and when someone departed.
An absent sound can be evidence, since a slow, quiet action differs from a slammed one and produces no matching noise.
Negative claims are hard to prove, and the same objections can apply to arguments on both sides.
when: when a case turns on proving absence

text: The absence of a smell of anaesthetic at a scene narrows the possible methods, but does not settle who the culprit is.
when: Investigating a suspected drugging during a crime.
why: Method evidence narrows options but rarely identifies the person alone.

text: Missing or non-identifying remains are still informative: their absence narrows what can be inferred, but other parts may still support conclusions.
when: Evidence includes parts useless for identification.
why: Investigators can still learn from remaining traces even when some parts cannot identify a person.

text: A failure to find expected traces, such as footprints, mud, tracks or a body, is itself a finding that can rule out hypotheses and should be reported and reasoned from.
when: the ground or surface would normally record traces, or the scene is checked for what should be present
why: the absence narrows what could have happened

text: Compare what should be present with what is found: an expected object that is missing is evidence, and an absent personal item suggests the actor carried it away.
when: an object expected at a scene is missing or no longer where it should be
why: The actor may have chosen to remove it, which reveals their equipment.

text: A negative check, such as an empty search or no calls charged to a room, narrows suspects, leads or explanations and is worth recording.
why: Ruling out a lead removes it from consideration

text: Repeated empty checks or a negative expert report eliminate one line and may mean the target is wrong; re-examine the theory, not just close the case.
when: lab results are negative, or repeated checks produce nothing that fits the theory

text: The absence of forced entry does not prove no one entered; the history of keys and access is the relevant trace.
when: Investigating how a locked space was accessed
why: Duplicates leave no visible damage

text: Missing tracks on wet or soft ground can mean deliberate care, so check for their absence before assuming nothing happened there.
when: Ground should record prints but shows none
why: A careful mover leaves no mark

text: When a wound looks suspicious, check for what it lacks, such as bleeding or clothing stains, and what was overlooked, such as foam on the lips.
when: Assessing a cause of death.
why: Missing or overlooked signs often point to the real cause more reliably than the obvious injury.

text: Missing marks are evidence: someone who never left a room leaves no marks outside it, so test their claimed movements against where tracks are absent.
when: A suspect claims to have moved through an area that shows no traces.

text: Ask witnesses what they did not see; negative observations can narrow the field of suspects.
An empty pen or missing writing tool can serve as negative evidence that someone was not writing, but it suggests rather than proves the absence of action.
when: Assessing whether a person wrote something around the time of an event.
why: Absence is open to other explanations, so it is only a tentative inference.

text: An absence in a record means little unless the routine that would have logged the item was actually checked.
When every copy or item at a candidate source is accounted for, that source is eliminated, so a negative check is as useful as a positive one.
when: Checking a candidate source of an object.
why: Confirming that all items are present rules out the source as the origin.

text: Absence of trace is itself informative. When no footprints or witnesses exist, an investigator has neither direct nor circumstantial proof.
when: A culprit's entry or exit leaves no physical sign

text: The absence of an item that a person's habits predict can be evidence that the item was never carried.
when: When a person's habits imply a predictable set of items.
why: Expected items should be present if the habits held.

text: After a failed search, question the search location rather than concluding the object is absent from the building.
A result that contradicts a long chain of reasoning often has another explanation, so check the test itself before abandoning the chain.
when: when a new fact conflicts with an established theory
why: Tests can fail for reasons unrelated to the theory

text: Record a negative test result as evidence too: if no one reacts to a tested sound, that absence supports the conclusion that it was not heard.
when: when a test produces no observable reaction
why: an absent reaction is informative when the test was properly set up

text: A difference between a reproduction and the evidence is a finding in itself, since it can show who could or could not have caused the result.
Repeated reports of nothing suspicious narrow suspicion but do not prove innocence.
when: When surveillance or search returns no evidence.
why: Absence of evidence lowers some probabilities without ruling everything out.

text: A check that yields nothing, such as a witness with no new information, still narrows the field of possible explanations.
Absence of traces is not proof of innocence or skill on its own; combine it with other findings, since reading it as skill is an assumption without independent support.
when: a scene shows no trace of the actor, or a conclusion rests on something that is not there
why: lack of traces has many possible causes

text: A failed test does not prove a substance or cause was absent; a negative analysis only removes one test, so other possibilities remain open.
when: Testing consumed items for a drug, or a negative analysis of a death.
why: Some substances have no taste or odor.

text: Not seeing a pursuer does not prove you are unobserved, so keep checking.
when: Assessing whether you are still followed

text: Absence of theft does not prove a motive: a thief may be scared off, or may choose to take nothing.
A negative conclusion must be checked, not assumed; if it rests on one witness's account, that account must be verified.
when: Concluding that an item was never acquired
why: Negatives are easy to assume and hard to prove

text: A trace can be a dead end, so test each trace before building on it, and avoid searching many items when the target is likely elsewhere.
when: Many marked items are candidates for a clue.
why: Broad searches of unrelated items waste time.

text: Observers may explain away a failed result as success, so decide pass criteria before running the test.

1) Record unexplained marks and defer their interpretation, since premature explanation can fix a wrong reading. 2) Keep a running list of unexplained items. 3) Revisit each item as new facts arrive. 4) Raise open items at the next interview or check. 5) Mark each as fitted, coincidental, or still open.
when: A mark is noticed but its cause is unknown
why: Premature explanation can fix a wrong reading

text: 1) Exhaust every lead, including contacts of contacts. 2) If new names stop appearing, reassess the working theory. 3) Consider that the theory may be misdirected before investing more effort.
when: Repeated inquiry produces no new name.
why: Continuing a wrong line wastes effort.

text: Absent sightings narrow where observers could have been if their positions are known; a negative canvass across a time window alone proves only that no one was found.
when: a search for witnesses or sightings within a time window returns none
why: Absence of reports is not proof of absence of the event.

text: A missing person leaves no physical trace in a busy room, so a failed search there tells little about whether the person was present.
when: When a search fails in a crowded or busy location.
why: Many people and movements erase traces, and a search can miss a person who left.

text: Give a clear reason for why witnesses are absent, so the audience does not question why no one checks the scene.
when: Staging a scene where bystanders are removed.
why: Unexplained absence breaks plausibility.

text: If nearby helpers would have come had they been allowed, their absence is informative and suggests they were prevented.
when: A request for help or a visit went unfulfilled.
why: Expected presence gives a testable baseline.

text: A witness who passed the location and did not notice an item suggests the item may not have been there when they passed.
when: Checking whether a found item was present at a given time
why: A person who walked the spot would ordinarily have seen a conspicuous object.

text: A fixed-position witness who saw no one enter or leave during an interval bounds when access was possible.
when: checking who could have reached the scene
why: Absence of sightings closes windows of possible access.

text: A vanished witness with no record on file can be the pressure point that forces the player to reconsider earlier testimony.
A witness who was not watching a spot, or failed to describe someone, cannot prove nothing happened or nobody was there; the gap stays open.
when: A witness claims nothing could have passed unseen or nobody was seen.
why: Witnesses cannot observe places they were not positioned to watch, and crowded places can hide people.

text: When the official holding the warrant is absent, accusations can spread largely unchecked.
when: When the authority who signs detentions is away from proceedings.
why: No one with power over warrants reviews the accusations.

text: A witness who is awake but paralysed can report only what happens around them, so gaps in their knowledge remain.
when: A narrator is incapacitated and relies on their account.
why: Limited perception leaves events outside view unknown.

text: A key witness who vanishes, especially after handling a key object, is a central lead; do not accept a theory relying on them without asking why they are absent.
when: A key witness cannot be found, does not testify, or vanishes after contact with a key object.
why: Disappearance removes the chance to verify the account, and a central witness's absence may itself be evidence.

text: The absence of people who could have been witnesses, by chance, does not clear a suspect.
In a case file or quest log, leave a key witness statement absent so a player who notices the gap can go find the missing testimony.
when: Designing investigation content with missing evidence.
why: Noticing a gap prompts the player to seek the missing information.

text: Preferring a subtle, vivid, or clever explanation over a plain, tested one lets an impressive theory become fixed belief, since elegance can feel like evidence.
when: several explanations fit the facts, or a frame is accepted
why: Elegance or vividness can feel like evidence even when a plainer account fits better or the frame has not been tested

text: Audiences accept a character's plausible innocent explanation for an oddity or illness as settled and stop examining the detail until a crisis contradicts it.
when: a character offers a reason or natural explanation for a suspicious detail or strange events
why: a stated reason closes the question; ordinary-seeming accounts are taken at face value until evidence breaks them

text: Explanations that are flattering or spare painful outcomes are readily accepted, and a person with a personal stake builds argument after argument for them.
when: the explanation is flattering or removes a painful or threatening outcome
why: Wishes and social comfort shape what witnesses accept; the wished-for result drives the reasoning

text: A witness shielding someone may disclose her situation when asked a general moral or legal question about it, because impersonal framing feels safer.
when: the subject discusses her own problem in abstract terms
why: reasoning about a general problem lowers her guard and exposes her position

text: People often accept an accusation against another party because it is easier to believe than a harder truth closer to home.
when: A close party is implicated by evidence
why: Blaming an outsider spares those nearest the crime from a painful conclusion

text: A witness's dislike of the accused or loyalty to a friend shapes what they notice and report.
when: when a witness has a personal attitude toward a party
why: Attitude filters attention and memory toward favoured or disfavoured facts

text: Once a group holds a belief, ordinary misfortunes such as dead animals, sick children or quarrels are read as signs of the same guilt.
when: A community already suspects someone
why: The belief filters new events so they confirm it

text: Prejudice spreads through a household as casual remarks that others repeat, making it feel ordinary.
when: A group shares a bias against one member.
why: Repetition normalises the bias.

text: A trusted insider who is personally harmed by a belief-based system may reverse their stance, recognising the injustice they had helped enforce.
when: The insider's own family or close circle is hit by the accusation.
why: Direct personal experience of harm can outweigh an abstract framework they had accepted.

text: Believers who meet contrary evidence often keep the framework by adding an explanation that absorbs it, such as a hidden deceiver who mimics innocence.
when: A held belief is challenged by a case that does not fit it.
why: Adding an exception protects the whole framework instead of revising it.

text: Emotional conviction can override evidence, and intense certainty can rise as evidence worsens, so conviction is not a measure of truth; a player may hold a conclusion physical facts contradict.
when: a witness insists they just know
why: feelings can persuade without proof

text: Let the audience accept an ordinary cause for now, but leave a clue that disagrees with it so the question can return later.
when: a mystery needs a temporary explanation
why: A surviving contradiction keeps the mystery alive.

text: Treat a quick, convenient explanation for an object as suspect when that object would be absurd for the use it is given.
when: an object is explained as harmless but could serve another purpose

text: When a person accepts an official order without protest, the usual grounds for later challenge to that order are removed.
Accepting the most confident account or accuser without corroboration, or ignoring their stake in the outcome, is a mistake: confidence and motive are not evidence.
when: when an account or accusation is delivered with confidence or force
why: confidence does not establish accuracy; confidence and motive are not evidence

text: Accepting how a scene looks or an official explanation without rechecking the objects it relies on lets investigators miss what actually happened; appearance can hide the real sequence.
when: examining a crime scene or when an official account explains a scene
why: The objects may contradict the explanation; appearance can hide the real sequence of events

text: A neat, confident explanation from an authority, especially one arriving early, can end inquiry; test it against the one fact that could break it, physical evidence and unexplained details.
when: A plausible complete account arrives early and seems to close the case.
why: Coherent stories can feel conclusive while leaving key objects or traces unexplained; a neat answer left unchecked stays unverified

text: Accepting neat evidence or the most visible explanation as proof without asking who arranged it falls into the staged-trace trap; repeating the suspect's preferred reading reinforces the staging.
when: when an investigator adopts the most visible explanation or neat evidence
why: Staged evidence is designed to look conclusive and exploits the tendency to accept the reading the culprit wants

text: Accepting a claim because it sounds authoritative or is repeated by many sources is a common error; check its premises first.
Accepting the official reading of a noise or event without asking what it would have required leads to missed possibilities.
Accepting a witness's claim that nothing was touched at a scene, without checking the physical evidence, lets the claimant control the investigation.
when: The witness reports the scene as undisturbed
why: Whoever describes the scene first shapes what others see.

text: Relying on accepted maxims rather than the facts of the case misleads an investigator, even when the maxim feels reliable.
when: reasoning from a rule of thumb about crime
why: maxims ignore specific case facts

text: A tidy explanation can be accepted before anyone checks where suspects actually were.
when: investigators are under pressure to close a case
why: unchecked whereabouts leave theories untested

text: Taking a victim's stated cause at face value can miss the real cause, which may sit in the victim's past.
why: A general cover story, such as a burglary or vague threat, can hide a personal motive.

text: Accepting an agitated witness's out-of-order account leaves the timeline wrong; ask them to put events in sequence.
Accepting cash or documents on trust, without comparison or recording of identifying details, leaves the receiver exposed to fraud.
Accepting a helpful offer without asking what it removes from your control can give the helper power over timing, departure, or who stays with you.
when: when an ally offers help that separates the group
why: help can serve the helper's own plan

text: Accepting an in-world curse as the explanation without checking whether any person profits from it can hide a human killer.
Accepting a confession because it is sincere or emotional ignores whether it fits the evidence.
Accepting a stated emergency at face value is a mistake when the stated reasons contradict the body's own earlier recorded views.
when: A procedure is bypassed citing urgency.
why: Stated urgency can hide a reversal of prior judgment.

text: A firm belief is not automatically a motive; it matters only if it actually drives the person's behavior.
Accepting an explanation by default, because no other has been found, rests on a weak basis.
when: An event has an explanation that has not been tested against alternatives.
why: Absence of an alternative is not evidence for the default.

text: Accepting a witness's explanation for their silence without testing it against what they do later leads to misjudgment.
when: A witness withholds information and gives a reason
why: The stated reason may be self-serving or incomplete

text: Accepting the first plausible reason leads to false conclusions, and dismissing a witness too quickly can waste a lead.
why: Early explanations are often incomplete and witnesses may hold useful knowledge.

text: An official can accept a convenient explanation when the victim's known mood supports it, so the ruling should be tested rather than accepted.
when: When a death is ruled quickly on the basis of the victim's mood.
why: Confirmation of an expected story discourages further checking.

text: A supernatural explanation can excuse reckless action, such as firing into a dark scene without checking the target.
when: when a supernatural belief shapes how people act under threat
why: Belief in an unseen threat can justify actions that ordinary checking would prevent.

text: Accepting a reported theft at face value, without checking delayed inspections or an insurer's silence, lets a staged loss go unexamined.
why: Those gaps are signs that the claim may be fabricated

text: Once impossible options are excluded, accept the remaining explanation even if it seems unlikely, provided it fits every clue.
Accept a case with a hidden client only when the apparent motive is honorable and the facts can be checked independently.
Having the ability or opportunity to reach an object or location does not show that a person acted; keep access separate from motive and evidence of action.
when: a suspect had the means to be present but no proven act
why: Many people can reach the same object, so access alone narrows little; opportunity alone does not establish involvement.

text: Close access to events does not guarantee an accurate account, since a well-placed witness can still be wrong or biased.
why: Position gives opportunity to know, not proof that the knowledge is correct

text: Who holds a key, which door a person uses, and how a household runs all reveal who has access to a place.
when: when establishing who could have been present at a scene
why: Access control and routine define the set of possible actors.

text: Test a claimed entry route by checking whether it was visible from the road or locked at the time.
Tracing where a concealed means came from, such as a social circle, points toward people who had access to it.
Make the access check a required sub-goal that gates the final accusation.
when: designing the endgame of a mystery

text: Rule out a hiding place by checking whether physical access to it is possible, given the observed state of doors and paths.
when: when testing whether something could be hidden in a room
why: Physical access can make a hiding place implausible.

text: Narrow an access inquiry by asking where the item was kept, what lay beside it, and which person carried each item, moving from location to handling.
List everyone who entered a room after an event and narrow the suspect field to that list.
when: an event occurred in a room with controlled access
why: only people who entered could have changed the scene

text: Evidence against one suspect is weakened when another party had access to the same spot shortly before.
when: Assessing a clue tied to a single location.
why: Another person's presence offers an alternative explanation for the trace.

text: Access narrows possible actors but identifies no one; moving from who could handle an object to who took it, without a witness or trail, yields only suspicion.
Elimination by access rests on the premise that only insiders could act; if that premise is wrong, the whole shortlist is wrong.

1) Order the events in sequence and mark each window in which an item could have changed hands, such as between the last sighting and a fixed event. 2) List who had access within each window. 3) Test each person against it.
when: A crime must have occurred within a narrow time span, or the sequence must be reconstructed before naming a suspect.
why: A bounded window narrows the set of people who could have acted; restricting attention to access windows narrows the field of suspects.

text: 1) Identify what opening the object without force requires. 2) List every holder of that secret and every route by which it could leak. 3) Cross the list with routine facts.
when: A protected object opens with no sign of forced entry and few people could know the secret
why: Access lists narrow suspects to those who could actually have acted

text: 1) Describe the route room by room: connecting rooms, which door opens onto which path, and the target's position. 2) For each candidate, ask whether they could pass unseen. 3) Include furniture as sight blockers. 4) Test every candidate against the same route.
when: a crime requires a person to move through a space unseen

text: 1) List every lock or barrier guarding the target. 2) Name who holds each key or access item. 3) Check for unrecorded duplicates. 4) Track whether each item left its holder's possession.
when: a mystery involves keys or restricted entry
why: Access chains reduce the suspect pool to those who could physically reach the target

text: 1) List each person's absence times, such as days off and return times. 2) Record who holds each key and when it is used. 3) Check each store's position relative to windows and routes. 4) Shortlist those who could reach the item in that window.
when: when identifying who could reach a restricted item before naming a suspect
why: schedules and layout define who had access and when

text: 1) Confirm no published or circulated report existed that the speaker could have read. 2) Check whether the speaker's detail exceeds those reports. 3) If so, infer presence or access.
when: deciding whether a speaker was present at an event
why: The inference fails if written reports were available to him.

text: 1) Fix the time window when an object could be tampered with, between its delivery and its first use. 2) Use routines and watch records to narrow when the target was vulnerable. 3) List everyone with access during that window.
when: An object passes through several hands before it is used and suspects must be narrowed.
why: A bounded window with a list of access holders reduces the field of suspects.

text: 1) List who holds keys or access to the location. 2) Compare access rules with the real routines of those people. 3) Check whether any person with access could act unseen.
when: When a closed-access claim seems to rule out human involvement
why: Stated restrictions often hide a second route or a person who can act

text: 1) Take an impression of the key without drawing attention. 2) Have a duplicate made. 3) Enter without changing the keeper's routine.
when: Access to a locked space must avoid alerting its keeper
why: Covert duplication keeps the keeper's routine unchanged.

text: Use a guardian's absence to open a window for an NPC's act, and let players learn its timing from clues, so the act can be anticipated and observation is rewarded.
when: designing a scripted act an NPC performs while a guardian or boss is away
why: Learnable timing lets players and detectives infer the act from the absence and anticipate it in hindsight.

text: Let a later clue challenge the access premise so the suspect shortlist can change.
when: the player builds a suspect shortlist from access
why: A premise that can be overturned keeps the shortlist open to revision.

text: Test whether a person could approach a victim unnoticed by checking the physical evidence against medical testimony.
when: When access to a victim is in question.
why: Physical and medical facts constrain what was possible.

text: Eliminating a suspect by access does not prove innocence; it only removes that person from those who could have acted.
Use key or access tokens to narrow the suspect list, so only NPCs holding a given key remain in the frame.
Encode a site's access limits, such as no vehicle route, in NPC dialogue so players can deduce them and use them in a later puzzle.
Keep every access route open until it has been tested, and reject only the routes that are truly impossible.
when: When investigating how an event could have happened.
why: Dismissing routes early can exclude the one that actually occurred.

text: Access narrows suspects when entry is restricted or recorded, since the culprit must have lived in the building or stayed overnight; where a place is open to all visitors with no records, access adds little.
when: deciding whether to analyse entry and exit, or building a suspect list
why: A culprit without access cannot commit the crime; without records or restrictions, access does not narrow the suspects.

text: Investigators tend to read a found object as an accidental drop, so well-placed plants are accepted rather than questioned.
when: a planted item is found during an ordinary search
why: people assume items were dropped by accident

text: If a community believes an enemy can act at a distance, a missing visible cause is read as proof of guilt rather than as a gap in knowledge.
when: when the believed powers are wide and unlimited
why: the frame explains any unexplained harm as concealed agency

text: An apparent accident can be a deliberate act, such as an attack, a distraction, or an attempt to disrupt an investigator.
Accident explanations are supported by crossings, roads or paths to the scene, fences with or without gates, and a reason for the person to be there; their absence weighs against accident.
when: When assessing whether a death at a location could be accidental.
why: These physical features make an accidental presence plausible.

text: The strongest threat to a plan is an accident the planner could not foresee, such as an object carrying an identifying mark the planner cannot remove.
when: A culprit has hidden or removed evidence
why: Some traces sit in things the planner cannot replace

text: When a hired attacker gains nothing from an act, the real motive usually lies with a hidden employer who does gain from it.
A coincidence may be a mere accident, so leave it marked as unresolved rather than forcing a link.
An object out of place at a scene that belongs to the victim links the victim to that scene, even if it was left by accident.
when: A personal item is found where it should not be.
why: Accidental leftovers are less likely to be staged.

text: When a trace should be explained by a source that is missing, the trace may be a deliberate imitation rather than an ordinary result.
when: A set of traces looks ordinary but the expected cause is absent.
why: The missing source leaves the trace unexplained.

text: A death that looks self-caused or accidental can still be murder if the act and its result are separated by time or by a mechanism.
when: a victim's death looks self-caused and the timeline needs testing
why: A delayed or mechanical link hides the act behind the apparent cause

text: Reconsider the premise: the apparent victim may have authored the staging rather than only being its target.
when: A staged death contains details that do not fit an ordinary crime.
why: Staged scenes are often planned by the person who appears to be harmed.

text: A pair of changes that both serve the same purpose, such as two windows open where one would be natural, is a stronger anomaly than a single change.
when: Reviewing environmental changes at a scene
why: Redundant changes suggest deliberate clearing of fumes or traces rather than chance.

text: Check an apparent accident, such as a dead power source or a missing bulb, at its source before accepting chance as the explanation.
why: Deliberate tampering can look like bad luck

text: Let the killer's own chance accidents expose them, so the final reveal follows from the story's logic rather than luck alone.
when: writing how a culprit is caught
why: Accidents rooted in the killer's own actions feel earned, while random exposure feels contrived.

text: An unplanned event can break a long-prepared concealment scheme and make the evidence suggest a different explanation, such as one person killing another.
An independent record can reveal an unplanned duty that places a suspect elsewhere, removing that suspect from the timeline.
when: when a claimed alibi is checked against records

text: Accidental leads arise from unforeseen witnesses, third parties' unplanned acts, and objects carried by chance into new places.
Accepting an early benign explanation, such as a natural-cause verdict or a familiar legitimate use, without testing alternatives against the physical pattern can let tampering go unnoticed.
when: A death is quickly classed as natural, or an initial explanation fits a known legitimate use.
why: Early verdicts stop further investigation, and a familiar explanation can close inquiry too early.

text: A crumpled object can result from accident as easily as concealment, so confirm the sequence of events before concluding that someone tampered with it.
why: Disturbed objects look similar whatever caused the disturbance.

text: Accepting each incident as an accident without comparing them lets the attacker continue.
when: a series of incidents is explained one at a time

text: A meeting that seems accidental may later be recognised as the first step of a plan, so its timing matters.
when: an early encounter is reinterpreted after events unfold
why: the significance of a first contact only shows in hindsight

text: Treating an estimated time of death as exact is a mistake, because a medical estimate usually gives only an approximate interval.
when: When building a timeline around a time of death.
why: Estimates have a range that must be respected.

text: Showing an unprepared visitor a corpse may cause them to faint and alter the scene in the process.
A challenge spoken half-seriously can bind a party to an unplanned path that neither side intended.
when: When a casual dare is taken literally.

text: An accidental-looking mark counts as a clue only if the player is shown how it was produced; otherwise reading it is interpretation.
When confidential information is accidentally shared with someone outside the circle, acknowledge the breach at once and ask them to keep it secret.
When damage looks accidental, examine where the break started and how the edges look before deciding how it happened.
when: a platform, floor or object fails
why: break origin and edges reveal forced or staged damage

text: Consider an accidental cause, such as a carried light, before assuming deliberate arson when a fire is reported.
when: when a fire or damage is attributed to a deliberate act
why: an accident may be the real cause and must be excluded first

text: Accomplices expect quarrels over shared gains and fear counter-plots, so they read each other's disguises and moves as possible traps.
when: A criminal partnership with a pending division of spoils
why: Each partner knows the other could betray them for a larger share

text: A new or slow helper may fail to raise an alarm, letting a brief absence of the guard go unnoticed.
when: A guard is absent for a short time and a less experienced helper is present
why: Unfamiliar or slow responders may not recognise a problem

text: An accomplice alibi is a cover in which a partner builds a timeline so the crime appears to happen while the suspect is elsewhere.
Mutually distrustful accomplices often keep letters or other records against each other, and those records can later be recovered and used.
when: When accomplices have quarrelled or do not trust each other.
why: Distrust leads partners to hoard evidence that can be turned against them.

text: Judging a disguised person's physical capability can reveal that a different, more active person is involved, suggesting an accomplice.
when: when a disguise's physical demands do not match its wearer
why: Physical actions expose the true actor behind a disguise

text: A staged death usually needs an accomplice, and the accomplice is often bound to the plan through a personal interest.
when: a false death requires help from outside the subject
why: the plan cannot run without someone to handle the arrangements

text: Model accomplice NPC loyalty as tied to leverage, so the player can turn, threaten, or expose their partner.
when: designing accomplice NPCs

text: Accomplices tend to hide their valuables before fleeing, so valuables left behind suggest a person who left in haste without preparing.
when: When a vanished person's behavior must be inferred from what they left.
why: Preparing to flee is a deliberate act that an unprepared departure would skip.

text: When a theory needs two or more people to coordinate, check what each would gain or lose by joining. Discard the theory if a partner would lose money or standing by taking part.
when: a plot requires coordination between characters
why: People rarely cooperate against their own interest, so such a theory is unlikely

text: An accomplice's written confession that shifts blame can make the accused drop a defence and admit earlier lies.
Separate who committed an act from who assisted it, since a person may have had a hand in an event without being its author.
when: Investigating a crime with possible helpers
why: Assistance and authorship imply different suspects and different questions.

text: Accomplices who are paid, threatened, or sustainedly pressured may crack and expose the plot or turn on the one applying pressure; expect them to give the game away eventually.
when: A conspiracy or false death depends on reluctant, paid, threatened, or several silent partners
why: Cruelty, sustained pressure, or loyalty bought by money or fear is unstable

text: Accepting an accomplice explanation too easily is a mistake when the physical evidence does not fit that explanation.
1) Have a frightened suspect write a note to an accomplice setting a time and place. 2) Use the threat of police as the lever. 3) Let the accomplice walk into the trap at that time and place.
when: When a suspect has a reason to cooperate and an accomplice is still outside.
why: The suspect's own note draws the accomplice into a controlled meeting.

text: Split investigation tasks among non-player helpers by region or suspect, so partner characters cover different ground.
As matches accumulate, a suspect's answers may shift from agreement to weak explanations before they stop arguing.
when: when a suspect faces a growing set of matching traces
why: Each match weakens the suspect's denial.

text: Circumstances can change quickly; a cheerful letter can be followed by a short one reporting a broken engagement, so compare sequential letters.
when: reading a series of dated letters
why: Sequential letters reveal a shift that a single letter hides

text: When a condition worsens suddenly, first check what was administered, since an overdose is a common early suspect.
Every claim should trace to an accountable person who can be questioned, rather than to an unnamed or anonymous report.
when: A story relies on many claims about contested events.
why: Accountable speakers can be questioned, so claims can be tested.

text: Separate the story people tell about an event from the mechanism that actually produced it.
when: A supernatural or hard-to-verify explanation is offered for an event with natural causes.

text: A long quiet period followed by abrupt new urgency suggests that something entered the situation recently, and that recent arrival is the likely cause.
when: An opponent or character's behavior changes sharply and the change has a visible starting point.
why: The timing of the change narrows which new factor could have caused it.

text: Shared belief can hold for a long time, then fail quickly once a trusted figure is accused and the accusers' claims are doubted.
A witness whose detail changes only after challenge, or after a reward or deal, should not be trusted without checks; the change may reflect pressure rather than memory.
A door's state may look different depending on which account is accepted, so compare several accounts before relying on it.
