Treating a witness's sudden change of account as the truth, without independent checks, is a common and serious mistake.
Trusting a witness's sudden reversal just because it is emotional or made in public mistakes intensity for reliability.
why: emotion and public display make a changed account feel more certain

text: 1) Split the account into separate checkable claims, setting aside colourful detail and untestable motives. 2) Match each claim to a record that could confirm or refute it. 3) Check every date against a calendar. 4) Trust only what sources confirm.
when: when a story mixes checkable facts with motives, or one teller is the only source of a dramatic event, especially if interested or theatrical
why: each claim can be confirmed or refuted on its own; confident or partisan tellers can embellish claims others can check

text: 1) Invite a full account, and offer a stated benefit for it. 2) Test each claim against physical facts such as timing. 3) Hold judgment open until the story is checked.
when: when interrogating a captured or cooperative suspect
why: A full account gives more claims to test, and withheld judgment prevents early acceptance of a self-serving story

text: 1) List the expected occupants of each room. 2) Check each room in turn. 3) Note which occupants are absent or unused. 4) Reframe the question from who is hurt to who is unaccounted for.
when: first stage of an investigation

text: 1) Bring in a second person to confirm or add details. 2) Note any difference between the two accounts. 3) Ask about a related past event to test whether the account holds together.
when: when a single account needs testing
why: contradictions between accounts and related events expose weak claims

text: A suspect's self-serving account of motive or actions, including a narrator who is also a suspect, should be compared with other sources and treated as a defence to test.
when: A suspect explains their actions or motive with a self-serving story.
why: Self-interested accounts can distort facts and shift blame.

text: Test a suspect's explanation against observed facts and secondary claims; plausibility alone does not settle a disputed statement.
when: interrogating a suspect or witness who offers a justification or explains a statement
why: A plausible account can hide a false one.

text: Test each account against independent records, a timeline of who was where, and other witness accounts, so every claim is confirmed by more than one source.
when: The suspect's story or a witness account rests on claims others can confirm or contradict.

text: State how an account reached the reader, and mark which details were relayed second-hand rather than taken from firsthand records.
When a visible story conflicts with small physical details, trust the details and test the story against them.
A suspect's statements about other people can be unreliable, so they should be checked rather than accepted, even when offered sincerely.
when: When a suspect vouches for or describes a third party.
why: A person may misjudge others or have reasons to shade testimony.

text: Flight, shrieking or collapse by a confronted person can look like guilt, but fear, shame or an innocent explanation can produce the same behaviour.
when: when an accused person reacts to the supposed victim or a suspect's behaviour appears to indicate guilt
why: Fear and shame produce dramatic reactions regardless of responsibility; surface behaviour is ambiguous and the true reason can be benign.

text: A distressed witness shows tells such as fidgeting with nearby objects, glancing around the room, flushing, or pulling a hand away.
when: A witness is avoiding or struggling with a topic.
why: Discomfort leaks through small bodily movements.

text: Strong involuntary signs such as clenched hands, trembling lips, or a hateful stare can signal that a person is feeling strong emotion about a trigger.
when: A person reacts sharply to a stimulus connected to a concealed matter.
why: Strong feeling about a secret shows in the body before the person speaks.

text: A witness who feels guilt or fear may confess with a motive that shapes what they stress and what they leave out.
when: A witness with a personal stake in the events
why: Guilt or superstition gives them reasons to speak beyond what they saw

text: A guilty suspect may react to an accusation against a loved one with an outburst that reveals guilt, even while insisting the charge is false.
when: A suspect hears an accusation against someone they care about.
why: Strong feeling can expose a concealed involvement through an involuntary response.

text: Accusing a suspect in a populated scene exposes each listener's stake, because everyone reacts at once and their reactions are visible to the others.
when: a disclosure is made in front of a group
why: Listeners have their own interests, so their reactions reveal loyalty and knowledge.

text: When the culprit is a trusted friend, the audience feels the unmasking emotionally as well as logically, because trust raises what the revelation costs.
when: when the culprit is a character the audience has trusted

text: A guilty party may reveal themselves after hearing an unverified report that someone else has confessed.
when: a suspect is pressed and then hears of another's confession
why: fear of exposure can push a guilty person to act

text: A suspected affair that a household never discusses openly can still create lasting strain that acts as a motive.
when: A relationship is suspected but not confronted.
why: Unspoken suspicion builds emotional pressure without resolution.

text: Apparent willingness to take guilt on oneself can earn leniency from judges, even when the motive offered is weak.
when: a culprit appears to exaggerate his own guilt
why: contrition is read as a mitigating sign

text: Officials record a suspect's pallor, stammering and near-collapse as observations, so physical distress becomes part of what they believe about him.
when: a suspect is visibly distressed during questioning
why: questioners interpret physical signs as evidence about the person

text: A target who trusts and loves the requester, and who feels guilt, may yield to a request framed as saving the requester's life.
when: when the target cannot easily verify the threat
why: guilt and tenderness override refusal

text: An openly violent character draws suspicion as the obvious danger, pulling attention from a hidden threat.
The most visible person with obvious motive and contact tends to become the focus of attention, even without stronger evidence.
when: An investigation has one person with a conspicuous link to the victim.
why: Visible motive substitutes for checked evidence and is easy to act on.

text: A warning that silence may cause suspicion can be heard as a threat, even when the speaker denies any threatening intent.
when: a witness with a stake in the outcome hears a caution
why: The listener interprets the consequence as coercion regardless of intent.

text: A guilty person who feels exposed often takes unnecessary steps to cover traces, and these steps can draw attention and reveal them.
when: a suspect feels threatened by an inquiry
why: Fear of exposure pushes them to over-act

text: A suspect may confess and give a full account when loved ones are present to press them.
when: confronting a suspect with family present
why: pressure from people close to the suspect weakens resistance

text: An unwelcome visitor is read as a threat, which raises suspicion among the people already present.
when: a newcomer is unwanted by the people in the room

text: A guilty person checks every hiding place and detail with dread, fearing a single overlooked trace could become decisive.
when: a person has hidden something incriminating
why: fear makes ordinary traces seem dangerous

text: A guilty person may treat a stranger as a witness even when the stranger knows nothing, so fear itself becomes part of the evidence.
A visible, emotional motive such as jealousy can draw investigators toward a false cause while the real concern stays hidden.
when: when an obvious emotional motive fits the situation
why: A plausible surface motive is accepted before its fit with all facts is tested

text: A charge withdrawn with no evidence offered clears the accused differently from an acquittal on the merits.
A grand jury presentment rests on general reputation and formally delivered testimony, refers suspects to a higher court for custody and further proceedings, and states suspicion without proving it.
Innocent people sometimes enter a guilty plea as a tactic, so a guilty plea does not reliably show actual guilt.
Objects show how they were used, not the intention behind it, so motive must come from other evidence.
when: reconstructing a scene from traces alone

text: A weak motive does not exclude a suspect, since motives for serious acts are sometimes weak, and careful planning can indicate a motive strong enough for deliberate action.
when: Judging whether a proposed motive is sufficient
why: Motive strength is not the same as proof of action

text: Hold quietly gathered findings and the decisive accusation until the end of an exchange, so they carry more weight and tension builds across it.
why: Delayed presentation can make evidence more persuasive.

text: A promised reward must have a source, so the person who made the promise is the one to find.
when: evidence suggests someone was paid to act or stay silent

text: The order in which evidence is presented can differ from the order of events, so the audience meets clues in a constructed sequence.
Move from a physical trace to the writer's intention: a later line may have been added to produce a particular effect on the reader.
why: the sequence of writing reveals a deliberate choice

text: Treat a name for a figure known only through reports as a working label, not a conclusion, until other evidence confirms the identity.
when: A suspect is discussed but never seen clearly
why: Reports can be wrong, and an early label shapes all later reasoning

text: A mismatch between refined presentation and neglected habits can be the clue itself, because the contrast points to an inconsistent person.
when: When a person's appearance and habits seem to belong to different backgrounds.
why: Real people rarely have uniform traces across every area of life.

text: Credit rivals for correct observations even when their conclusions were wrong, so every contributor stays inside the shared work.
why: the reveal then completes common work rather than defeating opponents

text: Weigh a claim of a hidden bargain more lightly when it offers nothing that could be checked, and prefer a rebuttal backed by inspectable evidence.
when: when comparing an accusation with a rebuttal
why: unverifiable claims cannot be tested against physical facts

text: A public, costly confession by someone who helped cause a wrong can reverse how the whole story is read, while a free or unwitnessed confession has little effect.
when: a character must admit an earlier role in harming another
why: Witnessed cost gives the admission weight, and the reversal depends on that weight.

text: Guilty people often reveal themselves through other behavior and traces, so look for independent signs beyond the accusation itself.
when: when an accusation lacks other support

text: Hedging phrases such as reluctant qualifiers often come just before an admission, and signal that a follow-up question is worth asking.
when: A witness hesitates or qualifies a statement
why: Hedges mark the boundary between a denial and a partial admission

text: A witness who watched the street through a crime window clears the street but not the household, so it narrows only the external route.
when: using a watcher's report to exclude outsiders
why: Street observation rules out passage outside but not inside the house.

text: Do not sum motive or evidence weights naively; the combined effect of two motives can differ from the sum of their separate strengths.
when: A suspect-scoring or decision system combines several factors.
why: Motives and evidence can interact in ways a simple total misses.

text: An accuser who presses hard for one conclusion may be signalling confidence or a stake, so examine why they press before accepting it.
when: A prosecutor or accuser is insistent
why: Eagerness can reveal grounds or interest that bear on the case.

text: Untested suspicion of a person spreads as gossip among neighbours and within a community, hardening into accepted fact or a formal accusation before anyone checks it.
when: when a person is publicly suspected before any charge is made
why: Talk among neighbours reinforces suspicion until it is formalised.

text: Public accusation or examination can cost the accused their reputation, support and livelihood before any finding, even if the accusation later fails.
Acting on incomplete evidence can alert suspects, letting them move assets, destroy proof or prepare alibis before the case is ready.
when: Evidence is incomplete and suspects can flee or destroy proof.
why: A warning reaches the target before the investigator can secure the full case.

text: A culprit who tightens a frame against a target can expose their own trick, so a visible overreach is a satisfying way to undo them.
when: Designing how a villain is caught.
why: Excess effort to incriminate leaves a trace that contradicts the original deception.

text: A confrontation overheard in a public place spreads through a town, so a stranger becomes known there before his claims are verified.
when: A stranger clashes with officials in public
why: Public exchanges are repeated, which builds a reputation regardless of accuracy.

text: Arrests made on thin grounds tend to collapse once movements are documented, so detainees with no case against them get released.
Publicly asking a witness whether they noticed a sign forces them to agree or appear foolish, which pushes the group toward the investigator's finding.
when: An investigator confronts an expert or official in front of others.
why: Refusing to agree in public risks looking incompetent.

text: A vague but heavy warning about a powerful antagonist raises dread without spelling out the consequence.
Acting on an insufficient accusation can bring consequences from authority figures, such as a reprimand, so procedural error carries its own cost.
Accusations move from vague descriptions to named people, and first names are drawn from those the public already distrusts.
Competing claims to the same ground can build lasting hostility between families and neighbours, supplying a motive that later shapes who gets suspected.
when: two parties hold overlapping rights to one plot
why: Contested ground keeps rivalry active across years

text: A scripted accusation can prompt a guilty NPC to act, and the reaction itself can expose a clue the player can notice.
when: the NPC is designed to be guilty and the trigger is a stated claim
why: a direct claim provokes a response the script can use

text: A suspect's capacity for a violent act has three separate parts: physical ability, moral acceptance, and nervous capacity for violence.
when: testing whether a theory fits a suspect
why: each part can fail independently

text: A witness's guilt, shock or fear can distort what they perceive and hear, so their certainty or claim may reflect their fears rather than the events.
Fixing on an early suspect before evidence is fully examined makes investigators gather only incriminating evidence, ignore contrary traces and clearing checks, and stop seeking other culprits.
when: An early favourite emerges in an investigation.
why: Commitment to one explanation filters what counts as relevant evidence.

text: Confronting or accusing someone in public warns the culprit and associates, giving them time to act and ending any chance of watching them quietly.
Accusing or acting before evidence supports it outruns proof, risking a wrong arrest or exposing the wrong person.
Judging people by visible company or affiliations, such as kinship, service or friendship with a convicted person, widens suspicion beyond evidence.
when: when a community meets a newcomer whose visitors or affiliations are visible
why: Associations are easy to see and offer a ready explanation where direct knowledge is missing.

text: Vague warnings, notices or planted motives feel like padding, draw irrelevant replies or get discounted; tie each to specific names, dates, places or details.
when: when writing public notices, warnings or motive clues
why: generic gossip carries little weight as evidence

text: An untested suspicion kept private or left as a loose thread is never confirmed or dismissed, hiding the truth; track such suspicions for pursuit or dismissal.
when: when someone has a suspicion but doubts it, or a suspicion is raised in dialogue
why: Untested suspicions cannot be confirmed or dismissed, so the truth stays hidden.

text: An accusation made in distress can be undermined when the accuser later calms down and denies it.
why: Emotional state can distort what a witness reports.

text: Confronting a witness too early reveals what you already know and lets them adjust their story.
Announcing an accusation too early ends the interview and removes the chance to observe the suspect's reactions.
when: when running an interrogation scene
why: Early accusation makes the suspect guarded and transparent.

text: Confronting a suspect before the physical test is complete weakens the case, because the match is not yet confirmed.
Challenging a suspect too early can provoke a physical response that overpowers the investigator.
when: confronting a suspect before gathering enough evidence
why: Premature confrontation gives the suspect a chance to act while the investigator is unprepared.

text: Vivid impressions of guilt, such as a shifty look, are weak evidence and can mislead as much as they point toward the truth.
why: A striking appearance attaches suspicion to a person without supporting evidence.

text: A vague label for an impulse can stand in for a verified cause and hide the real motive from the audience.
Reading a suspect's distress at arrest as a confession ignores that a clever suspect could explain the same reaction another way.
Sales records may state only a vague purpose, such as general medicinal use, which tells the investigator little about the buyer's intent.
Assigning a trait to one parent without evidence, when the behaviour could come from either, misleads the reader.
when: Inferring a trait from a child's conduct
why: The child's conduct alone cannot identify which adult caused it

text: A public confrontation gives a suspect an audience and sympathy, and onlookers can turn against the person doing the confronting.
when: when an arrest or accusation is made in front of a crowd
why: onlookers side with the person being pressed

text: Treating every normal routine as suspicious is an error, because ordinary households are usually ordinary and an innocent surface is not evidence of guilt.
why: suspicion must be targeted to inconsistencies, not to all normality

text: Vague official causes of death, such as heart failure after shock, are hard to test and can close an inquiry without settling it.
Treating every silence as proof of guilt leads to false conclusions; a withheld topic is an inference to be tested, not a confirmed fact.
when: Silence has an obvious innocent cause or no link to the crime.
why: Silence can come from many motives unrelated to the crime.

text: A joke about guilt left unaddressed can later be taken seriously, so the writer must track such remarks to avoid an unresolved loose thread.
when: A suspicion remark is dismissed as a joke and not followed up
why: Dropped remarks read as careless when the story later depends on them

text: An overheard threat can be misjudged by the listener, and the speaker's explanation may be impossible to test.
when: when a threat is heard from another room

text: Inferring a culprit's great skill from one neat arrangement overrates them, since a neat setup may be the product of a simple plan.
when: Assessing a suspect's capability from staged evidence.
why: Tidy evidence can look sophisticated without reflecting real ability.

text: A suspect who looks guilty may still be guilty; clearing them by constraint works only if the facts behind the constraint hold.
when: when clearing a suspect on physical grounds
why: An unreliable premise can clear the wrong person.

text: A suspect who is ill, poor or upset can look guilty through erratic behaviour alone, and interrupting him blocks the explanation that could clear him.
Accusers who keep naming ever more respected people overreach, and a trusted target's innocence can expose the whole accusation.
why: Doubt spreads once a trusted name is hit.

text: A vague charge such as works beyond nature can cover almost any misfortune and needs no clear link between act and harm.
when: A charge names no specific act or victim
why: Nothing in the charge can be tested

text: A speaker who reports talk rather than facts often stays vague on purpose, which makes rumor hard to check.
Hope that a favoured suspect is guilty makes an investigator want a match, so the measurable test must still be run.
when: A suspect fits the investigator's theory emotionally.
why: Desire for a conclusion biases how the evidence is weighed.

text: Pallor and silence on recognition can signal fear of the investigator, grief or guilt, so the reaction alone does not decide which.
when: when a witness reacts strongly to being recognized
why: Several emotions produce the same visible reaction

text: Relying on folk beliefs that guilty people always give themselves away or return to the scene can lead to wrong conclusions, since most killers escape detection.
when: Reasoning about who committed a crime from assumptions about guilty behaviour.
why: Such beliefs are not supported by evidence and mislead the investigator.

text: Accusing someone without showing evidence invites a firmer denial and fills the silence with unprompted details and protests.
when: Confronting a suspect with a claim alone
why: Without proof the suspect has nothing to retract and every incentive to push back.

text: Blaming the tracker before checking the environment for other sources of the same smell misreads a fault that lies in the scene.
when: A tracker goes wrong
why: Other sources can explain the error

text: 1) Collect physical proofs for each required category. 2) Explain or remove every unexplained gap. 3) Condense the evidence so the accusation arrives backed by proofs.
when: preparing an accusation for a sceptical reviewer
why: unsupported links invite rejection

text: 1) List evidence that could vanish, such as witnesses who may die or lose their faculties. 2) List the readings still open. 3) Accuse only after testing the perishable claims.
when: before a formal accusation

text: 1) Give the subject assurances of safety first. 2) Unveil the object slowly, under good light. 3) Link its history to the crime. 4) Watch for changes in expression and speech.
when: confronting a suspect with an object
why: lowering the subject's guard first makes reactions easier to read

text: 1) Identify who benefits from the death, such as through a will. 2) Identify who controlled access to the victim. 3) Ask who arranged each change in personnel or affairs.
when: When a death follows unusual statements, staff changes or legal arrangements.

text: 1) Lay out the sequence of actions as a numbered, precise account. 2) Name the witnesses. 3) Recall small details to show nothing was overlooked. 4) Offer closure if the suspect confesses before others. 5) Warn of harsher measures if refused. 6) If denied, turn the factual question into a moral one, such as ingratitude.
when: a suspect must be pressed publicly
why: detail and witnesses make the accusation credible, and the offer makes confession the price of closure

text: 1) Collect the history of disputes, marriages, refused dowries and business ties among the parties. 2) Date each episode from testimony. 3) Treat the present accusation as the latest step in that history.
when: building a motive for an accusation
why: Motive is usually traced through a long history of relations rather than the single event under dispute.

text: 1) Record each loss or harm in a community. 2) Link it to any earlier recorded dispute with the blamed person. 3) Show the player how the accusation formed from that link.
when: when designing an in-world accusation the player must trace
why: Visible causal links let players reconstruct how suspicion grew

text: 1) Accept the test's rule as the accuser states it. 2) Apply the same test to the accuser under the same conditions. 3) Check whether the accuser passes or fails by that rule.
when: a case rests on a test whose validity has been accepted without checking
why: A rule the accuser cannot pass exposes inconsistency in the accuser's own standards.

text: 1) State the conclusion first. 2) Name the sources of the facts. 3) Accuse plainly. 4) Offer a bargain for a confession. 5) State the consequence if the confession is refused.
when: when silence is driven by shame or social standing and partial evidence needs a confession to complete it
why: Naming sources shows the case rests on testimony, and an explicit consequence makes the choice concrete.

text: Shock, grief, fear, worry or illness produce signs like guilt, so never read distress as proof of guilt or knowledge; check it against other evidence first.
when: when judging a suspect or witness by emotional or body signs
why: distress has many causes besides guilt

text: Unverifiable testimony or accusation can justify opening an inquiry but must never alone settle a person's identity or guilt, since it can implicate innocent people.
why: Prompting investigation and proving guilt are different functions of evidence.

text: Make threats and accusations in scripted scenes checkable against other NPCs' claims and scene objects, so players can expose lies through facts rather than the designer's word.
when: when writing NPC accusations, threats or timelines
why: Checkable claims reward investigation and let players test the accuser instead of simply trusting or distrusting them.

text: Let a suspect's reaction reveal something but keep it ambiguous, so it is never proof on its own.
When a suspicion cannot be confirmed, keep distance from the suspect anyway.
when: strong suspicion remains without a verdict
why: avoiding the suspect limits risk while the question stays open

text: Record vague plans and unverified suspicions as vague or unverified, not as settled fact.
when: a witness mentions a plan without details, or a suspicion is presented
why: Loose talk of a project is not evidence of a decided course of action

text: Present an identification with independent pieces of evidence, such as a photograph and several witness descriptions, and check whether doubt remains.
when: Concluding an identification in front of others
why: Independent sources make an identification more persuasive than a single claim

text: Offer a present-evidence dialogue option that changes NPC behaviour, such as hesitation, shifted posture or a slipped name, so the player can read those tells.
when: designing NPC confrontation dialogue
why: Visible reactions give the player a checkable reading of the NPC.

text: When designing a guilty NPC's path, list every action it requires and check each against its motive and risk.
Score each non-player character by motive, access to the scene and ability to act, and flag any who hide or alter evidence.
when: Building a guilt-tracking system for NPCs in a mystery.
why: Structured scoring makes suspicion trackable and consistent.

text: Design interrogation dialogue so a player can see when a question presupposes guilt.
when: designing interrogation dialogue

text: Track which NPCs believe which accuser and why, so the player must examine the motive as well as the claim.
Make the scene of the crime a place the culprit is drawn back to, so the player can catch the culprit returning.
An open unresolved suspicion keeps the true cause hidden, but feels like cheating if never settled, so firm information must arrive in time.
when: a suspected crime is used to hide the real cause
why: unfinished theories erode trust in the story

text: A public confession ends the matter, while denial keeps the accusation open and invites harsher measures; the audience raises the social cost of denying.
when: the player should choose between confessing and denying

text: An accusation resting on unverifiable testimony builds tension, but gives the player no fair test to disprove it.
when: Designing a story accusation the player cannot check.

text: Weigh claims from a party with a personal stake or plausible motive to mislead, such as a grudge or rejected deal, and limit that party's authority until checked.
when: A complaint or claim comes from someone who gains from the outcome or has a clear reason to lie.
why: Personal feeling or motive can distort judgement and what a source reports.

text: Do not accept an alibi or accusation from an interested party without independent physical or documentary corroboration, rather than judging by standing or temper.
when: A witness has a stake or motive to accuse or protect.
why: An interested witness can shape a story to protect themselves.

text: Observers weigh a culprit's stated motive by its frankness and justification; a blunt, unjustified motive can count against him.
when: a court or community judges a confessed act
why: an unjustified reason reads as crude and less forgivable

text: A withheld alibi may protect someone else's reputation, and outsiders often read that silence as guilt, so find the reason for refusal before judging.
when: A suspect has a verifiable alibi but declines to disclose it.

text: Weigh a suspect's rebuttal on its argument as well as on the emotion it shows, since a reasoned defence can still be evaluated.
Close a final accusation on motive reasoning rather than physical proof, and deliberately leave one loose thread unresolved.
when: Writing the resolution of a deduction-based mystery.
why: Motive reasoning fits a deduction ending, and an open thread keeps the mystery memorable.

text: Accusation case template: 1) the afflicted accuse a person 2) neighbours' misfortunes and quarrels accumulate as suspicion 3) a confession or claimed sight serves as proof 4) a verdict closes the case.
when: designing a trial or accusation sequence
why: A repeated template makes the outcome predictable and builds suspicion step by step.

text: Do not test an alibi where no one can confirm times, because the timeline then has nothing to anchor it.
why: Unanchored times cannot be compared against a claimed schedule.

text: Weigh a source's family ties, reputation and institutional links before accepting its account, but do not discard the source solely because it has a motive.
Check the accused party's own records, such as treatment dates and counts, against the timing of the complaint.
when: Assessing a complaint against a professional

text: When a central clue collapses, the authority may shift the charge to a different offence rather than drop the verdict.
when: A case built on one piece of evidence loses that evidence.
why: The institution needs a conviction, so it substitutes another charge.

text: Let a captured antagonist falsely accuse an ally, forcing the player to produce proof before the scene resolves.
when: Designing a late-scene twist with a captured enemy.
why: A desperate false accusation creates a misdirect that only evidence can clear.

text: Build an accusation where players must disprove each false claim against physical evidence before a final confrontation with a culprit-only detail.
when: Designing a deduction climax
why: Stepwise disproof makes the final reveal a result of the player's own reasoning

text: Make the most aggressive accuser a suspect, since visible exposure behavior draws attention away from their own act.
Make an absent rival the default suspect, so suspicion flows outward toward them and the insider in plain view is overlooked.
when: building a red herring for a closed-setting mystery
why: A visible threat from an absent figure absorbs suspicion that would otherwise fall on those present.

text: A mystery can clear each suspect in turn through a test or witness, shifting blame back toward whoever controlled the key objects, so the handler of the evidence becomes the final suspect.
when: Designing a whodunit where several characters are plausibly suspected in sequence.
why: Each cleared suspect removes an alternative, and the person with exclusive access to the instruments of the crime is left standing.

text: Each accepted accusation hardens the official story, so the next suspect is judged against a settled account.
when: a sequence of wrong suspects
why: each arrest makes the official account harder to challenge

text: Equating the ability to act with the likelihood of having acted leads to accusations on weak grounds.

1) Place several cheap minor clues, such as an object, a dropped word and a timing. 2) Require the player to link them before an accusation is possible. 3) Let an NPC voice the chain as a dialogue trigger that reveals a reaction.
when: Designing an accusation mechanic built on several minor clues.
why: Minor clues that combine make the accusation a reasoned act rather than a guess.

text: 1) Keep a written tally of each clue and whom it implicates. 2) Note when several clues from different sources point unanimously to one person. 3) Confirm the pattern before acting on it.
when: When no single clue is conclusive but several point the same way.
why: Converging weak points can form a pattern that a single clue cannot.

text: 1) Give the player a suspect with a motive and a visible alibi. 2) Add a physical or timed clue that disproves that suspect. 3) Repeat with the next suspect until the remaining one seems guilty. 4) Overturn that final answer with a late clue.
when: Designing a whodunit whose suspects are removed one at a time
why: Each elimination feels like progress, and the last overturn delivers the surprise.

text: 1) Accuse the culprit procedurally by listing faults in the earlier investigation. 2) Press the culprit until a confession behind a closed door.
when: when staging the reveal of a hidden culprit
why: Procedural faults build the case before the culprit cracks.

text: Give each false culprit a checkable detail, such as a timeline, letter or object, that a clue already on the table can break, so the reversal feels earned.
Do not treat a witness's anger or grief as proof of error; keep open both that they are right and that their judgment is disturbed.
Unlock an accusation only after the player has collected convergent clues from a minimum number of different categories.
when: When designing an accusation mechanic in a mystery game.
why: Requiring varied convergent clues prevents accusations from resting on a single source of evidence.

text: Write accusations as templates with slots for accused, act, harm and consequence, each mapped to a clue the player can check; let the accused's story shift under follow-up.
when: Designing accusation-based quests or NPC-to-NPC accusation dialogue.
why: Verifiable accusations let players test claims, since each slot becomes something they can verify or disprove.

text: A final accusation scene that walks through the crime step by step lets the player see the full logic before choosing a confession or a fight.
when: Designing the climax of a mystery.
why: Showing the full reasoning makes the player's final choice informed.

text: Pushing a witness past her composure with an accusation rather than reassurance can shut down cooperation.
when: When a witness is close to an admission
why: Accusation raises defensiveness and ends the exchange

text: 1) Place the culprit in a constrained position. 2) Name the method step by step. 3) Name the motive. 4) Force the culprit to surrender the stolen items.
when: when the solution must be explained directly to the culprit
why: the culprit's presence adds tension to the explanation

text: 1) Reconstruct the crime step by step: motive, background pressures, method and cover story. 2) Deliver the reconstruction calmly. 3) Offer a way out, such as a confession in exchange for a settlement.
when: A case is circumstantial and a confession would settle it.
why: A calm, complete account convinces the suspect the case is solved and makes confession the easiest option.

text: An accusation test should show a reaction the player can read and state its limit, rather than automatically clearing the suspect.
when: Designing an accusation or ordeal scene.
why: Stated limits keep the test from being mistaken for proof.

text: When accusers are questioned together, each may blame the other for who first named a suspect, deflecting responsibility.
when: when multiple accusers give joint accounts
why: shifting blame protects each accuser's own position

text: Accusations travel by word of mouth, and a public outcry can lead others to avoid the accused household.
when: when a claim is voiced in a public gathering
why: Social avoidance spreads quickly once a claim is shared

text: Raise the chance of formal accusation as disputes accumulate between factions in a closed community.
when: designing a closed community with rival factions
why: Each unresolved dispute adds grievance that can turn into a formal charge.

text: Each newly named suspect prompts further warrants and examinations, so a household accusation widens across the community with every round of names.
when: people in a close community know one another

text: Warrants can spread across neighbouring settlements within weeks, naming people far from the original case.
Accusers meeting privately can hand new targets to one another, so accusations grow through peer suggestion.
when: when a group of accusers meets without outsiders
why: each suggestion is accepted within the group

text: An accusation can grow from a household episode into a crowd and then a formal hearing, as each new group accepts it as more credible.
when: When a private claim is repeated and publicized.
why: Each audience's acceptance raises the claim's apparent weight for the next.

text: A physical clue used to accuse can be turned back on the accuser, and once the same mark is shared it becomes a general claim, not a single finding.
when: an accusation supported by a physical sign
why: the accused can show the sign exists elsewhere

text: Model an accusation as a chain: a first suspect, a failed hearing, and a second suspect pulled in by the same rumor, so suspicion visibly moves.
when: designing investigation plots
why: A moving target keeps suspicion visible rather than letting it vanish.

text: Accepting a volunteered culprit at face value, or ignoring the speaker's past connections to the crime's pattern, can lead to a wrong conclusion.
when: When evaluating a suspect's offered explanation.
why: Diversions can be false, and connections to the crime's pattern reveal the speaker's involvement.

text: Make a mocking or false accusation cost the player rather than being free of consequence.
Accuse only after two or more independent verified clues converge, stating openly what remains unproven; one suggestive clue cannot close a case.
when: designing a mystery quest; no single clue settles the matter

text: Accusing a respected figure without firm proof provokes outright rejection and may get the accuser dismissed as unbalanced; withhold until evidence can be shown.
when: culprit is socially protected and early accusation would fail
why: Without proof the accuser has no standing and the accusation is discredited.

text: Do not act on or name a suspect before proof is secure; with a wary suspect and costly false move, early action warns them, and early naming risks false accusation.
when: investigator has a theory but insufficient proof, or a match is still being tested
why: premature action warns the suspect and loses the case

text: A wrongful arrest of a bystander raises pressure without ending the investigation, because the real question stays open.
when: mid-case, when an innocent suspect is detained
why: the arrest raises the stakes while the actual culprit is still unknown

text: Pressured suspects discredit the accuser: framing the accusation as mental illness, turning the accuser's intellect against them, or calling the investigator mad and threatening confinement.
when: when a plain accusation lacks a prepared answer to a rival explanation, or when the suspect is confronted with strong evidence
why: Discrediting the accuser contests the case without answering it; a prepared alternative frame can move the conversation even if not fully accepted; the threat can visibly unsettle the investigator.

text: A suspect's visible reaction, such as a drained colour, is read before any dialogue, so it works as a clue in its own right.
when: the accused is named in front of others

text: An accused person under pressure may name others, sometimes out of concern for the other's soul, and such accusations can seal a co-accused's conviction.
when: when a confession includes accusations against family or associates
why: the confession's accusatory content carries weight in the proceedings even when its origin is pressure

text: Accused people may answer with lawsuits, and a counter-suit can be read as proof of innocence or as a way to hide guilt.
when: when an accused person sues an accuser or a witness
why: the same act can signal either innocence or an attempt to shift suspicion

text: Under confrontation, a suspect typically denies the facts, appeals to the investigator's right to question, or breaks down emotionally, rather than confessing.
when: when shown evidence that contradicts their account
why: Pressure first produces defensiveness and distress; admission is not the usual immediate response.

text: An accused person's own defensive or self-damaging remarks, such as a wish to be tested, are recorded and read as evidence against them.
when: an accused character speaks during an investigation
why: the listener interprets speech through the existing accusation

text: An accused person who refuses a verdict can be read by the deciding authority as more guilty, so defiance adds pressure while damaging her own case.
when: a character is pressed to accept a judgment
why: refusal is taken as a sign of guilt by those deciding the case

text: Every response from an accused person, including denial, calm, eye movement or head shaking, can be read as guilt, so no response can exonerate.
An accused person who names others may be trading accusations for a reprieve, so every name carries its own motive.
Do not judge denials by manner: calm, reassuring answers can make a question seem settled, and stout or sharp denials are easily misread as guilt.
when: when assessing a suspect's denial during questioning
why: composure can substitute for evidence; tone and demeanor are weak indicators, and treating them as evidence of guilt tends to convict the innocent

text: Reassurance after pressure draws out admissions more reliably than pressure alone.
when: When a witness has become guarded or distressed
why: Pressure alone can shut down cooperation

text: Repeated reassurance and claims of acting without counsel often signal what the writer is anxious about.
Withdrawing a confession can bring renewed or harsher custody, since a court may respond to a retraction by tightening custody, risking liberty and life.
when: a confessor is already in custody or retracts after pressure
why: the retraction exposes the person to harsher punishment, so withdrawing a confession takes great resolve

text: Reassuring text placed beside an unexplained threat makes the threat more unsettling, not less.
Taking a reassuring first sentence as the author's position while the operative clauses say otherwise.
why: Readers stop at the opening and miss the clauses that decide the outcome.

text: Accepting a general claim of good health or a clarifying story without particulars or confirmation can mislead an investigation.
when: When a witness offers reassurance rather than specifics.
why: General claims cannot be tested.

text: 1) Record the speaker's exact words. 2) Note what question or pressure prompted them. 3) Note who heard them. 4) Check whether the speaker later repeated or denied them.
when: Interpreting a recorded statement that may count as an admission
why: The same words can mean guilt, bravado or distress depending on context and listener

text: Offer a reason to cooperate, such as a warning of consequences or a favourable word, but never promise protection the questioner cannot provide.
when: a witness must be persuaded to speak
why: The method works only if the witness believes the offer.

text: When a suspicion is shown to a witness, reassure them that the disclosure stays private, or they may stop talking.
when: A witness has been confronted with a suspicion they fear.
why: Fear of exposure can make the witness withdraw the moment their secret is named.

text: In dialogue puzzles with two-reading lines, let players re-ask the NPC with the exact line to hear the speaker's explanation.
when: when a line can be read two ways

text: Let a later recantation reopen a closed case by exposing the pressure behind the original confession.
Let a witness recant when confronted with a prior statement, and reward players who keep records of what each NPC said.
when: designing witness confrontations in a mystery

text: Use a recording or hidden device to turn suspicion into an admission the accused cannot deny.
when: when a suspect must be confronted with evidence of a plot
why: A recorded admission removes the accused's ability to dispute the accusation.

text: A witness who records what they cannot explain, such as the source of a feeling, is more credible than one who hides the gap.
when: when assessing a narrator's reliability
why: Acknowledged uncertainty signals honest reporting rather than a tidy but unsupported story.

text: End a reveal by admitting what remains uncertain rather than claiming total certainty.
when: Closing a mystery's explanation
why: Acknowledged loose ends seem more credible

text: A reveal in which the solver openly names their own earlier mistake feels earned rather than lucky.
when: Writing the moment of solution
why: Acknowledging error places the lesson on reasoning rather than chance.

text: An investigator's admitted errors must match the clues actually shown, or the reveal loses its fairness.
when: the investigator confesses missed signs
why: Mismatched admissions break the fair-play contract

text: Treat a witness's admitted missed details as weak evidence, and fill those gaps from other sources.
why: A witness who lost track of events cannot vouch for them

text: Disclose known defects before a deal is made; a flaw named in advance cannot later be claimed as concealed.
when: parties commit to a space or agreement with hidden drawbacks
why: prior disclosure removes grounds for later complaint

text: State plainly when data is missing, and do not reach a conclusion without it.
why: Conclusions without supporting data are guesses.

text: Threats or promises of penalties or rewards that cannot be enforced or delivered weaken pressure and expose the bluff; penalties deter only when actually enforced.

Agreement between separate witnesses or confessions raises reliability, but shared bias, interest, or pressure can produce matching accounts; check whether sources are truly independent and test core claims apart from details.
when: When witnesses or confessions confirm the same claim.
why: Independent sources support shared facts, while shared misconceptions, motives, or pressure can mimic independent confirmation.

text: A recipient with no warning identifies an unexpected visitor from partial cues and prior assumptions, and forms plans about the visit before checking them.
when: an unannounced visitor appears
why: no time or information to verify identity and purpose

text: Paying a blackmailer cannot end the threat, because the blackmailer keeps the secret and can sell it again.
A conditional deal can be a dialogue choice whose consequences depend on whether the item is returned.
when: Designing negotiation dialogue in a game.

text: Give partner NPCs unequal stashes of compromising letters so an alliance breaks when one side holds more proof than the other.
when: Designing a faction or accomplice alliance
why: Imbalanced leverage makes betrayal a credible and discoverable outcome

text: A blackmailer who waits years before acting is unusual, so the delay can be used to test whether the blackmail claim is plausible.
when: Assessing a claim of blackmail that has a long delay before any demand.
why: Blackmail typically follows soon after leverage exists, so long delays suggest the claim may be false.

text: A witness who agrees with every party in turn carries no information about the facts.
why: Agreement with all sides is independent of the truth

text: A deal that unlocks a witness's full statement should let the player check it against logs or receipts.
when: designing witness deals

text: Heirs who unanimously ask for an estate to be divided by an informal document signal trust and family harmony, though this does not prove fair dealing.
A reward offered to a rival in exchange for a hearing secures that rival's cooperation only for as long as the argument lasts.
An agreeable question that the subject accepts and restates fixes their terms on record, so their commitments can be referred back to later.
A weak person who finds a secret, is tempted by easy money, and grows greedy will overreach, be exposed, and may commit a desperate act before turning calm.
when: designing a blackmail plot or an NPC under pressure
why: Each demand raises pressure until the person reaches a breaking point.

text: Once information leaves one desk, it can spread through connected organisations even without coordination, faster than anyone can recall it.
when: A story passes between related outlets or departments.
why: Duplicate channels republish independently, so no single holder controls the spread.

text: Release, reward, or a new role after a defection exposes a hidden scheme, because it shows what the switch gained.
when: Designing a double agent or turncoat ally
why: The payoff for the switch is a clue the player can reconstruct.

text: A dealer or witness may not recall a sale, so records should back up memory.
A reported fact may never reach the official who should act on it, so confirm that a report was followed up.
A signal with no agreed meaning gives the watcher nothing to act on, and a repeated or missed signal delays the response.
A deal struck before the witness is secured can be overtaken by events if the witness is interrupted or dies.
when: Negotiating with a witness in a dangerous situation.
why: Events can end the witness's ability to deliver before the terms are fulfilled.

text: An instruction given without confirmation can let an object slip away, because an ambiguous handoff creates a window for loss.
when: when an object changes hands in a hurry

text: Offering a suspect terms in exchange for a confession carries risk to the investigator.
Assuming an intermediary is the natural choice, such as a lawyer to draw up a will, can mislead; an unusual choice needs an explanation.
If the player is expected to trace how news or rumour travelled, the transmission channel must be shown clearly, since vague or figurative explanations leave the route impossible to pin down.
when: Designing how information moves between NPCs and locations.
why: Players cannot reconstruct a chain of knowledge that the game never shows.

text: A confession obtained through a deal may be disputed later, so the terms should be recorded.
when: Accepting a confession in exchange for an agreement.
why: Unrecorded terms are easy to contest afterward.

text: 1) Collect each person's account of the same place and overlapping times. 2) Align all accounts on one timeline. 3) Note disagreements and omissions. 4) Treat each gap as a lead to investigate.
when: several people were in the same place at overlapping times
why: A shared timeline exposes which accounts cannot be true together.

text: 1) Give a free item on the first visit. 2) On a repeat visit, let the visitor ask for more. 3) Then demand payment, so the player sees the concession and its cost.
Make checks unannounced and at irregular times so the watched person cannot rehearse a false appearance.
why: Predictable visits let a subject prepare

text: Trust a physical profile only when several traits agree; overcommitting to one trait produces wrong conclusions.
Use unequal payouts as a faction clue, pointing to the family or patron that the payment favored.
Use an unannounced visit as a surprise only when the audience does not need to know the recipient's prior state.
Leave an unverified cover story with a visible gap so the audience can notice it and return to it later.
when: A character's alibi or account is accepted without check.
why: A noticed gap can be used by later sections.

text: Someone who handles a mechanical object can leave it in a changed state, such as running, that occupants have not noticed.
An account resting only on one person's word, such as an alibi or a claim of being alone, cannot be checked and should be treated as unverified, leaving a gap filled by guesswork.
when: A suspect's alibi or a witness says they spent time somewhere without anyone else present.
why: Without independent confirmation, the claim cannot be cross-checked.

text: Absence of sightings neither proves nor disproves a visit; an unseen visit that was never searched stays unconfirmed, supporting suspicion but not proving it happened.
when: A timeline is built from witness sightings.
why: Absence of observation is not evidence of absence.

text: Travel plans announced in advance can change without any record of the change, making the announced plan unreliable.
when: A stated schedule is used as the baseline for checking a suspect's movements.
why: Unlogged changes make the announced plan look valid when it no longer applies.

text: Trusting a witness's stated time without checking it against an independent event leads to false timelines.
when: A witness gives a precise time for an event.
why: Independent events are needed to verify a witness's clock.

text: 1) Note the visitor's route and who knows it. 2) Overlay the claimed visit on each occupant's movements. 3) Check arrivals that overlap the visit. 4) Phrase the claim conditionally and keep belief separate from reported appearance.
when: a death or disappearance is linked to a claimed visit with no witnesses
why: Access routes and occupants' movements bound what could have happened

text: A fabricated alibi is a witness account that places a suspect elsewhere, where the witness is the suspect in disguise, so the account is planted to mislead.
A household member's habitual heavy sleep, especially after illness, creates a predictable window when an unseen exit is most likely.
when: A suspect plans a movement through a house at night.
why: People who sleep heavily early in the night are less likely to notice movement.

text: Fix each step of a sequence to a clock, a dated record, or a published schedule rather than to memory alone.
when: A timeline must be checked against independent evidence.
why: Anchored steps can be tested, while memory-only steps can drift.

text: A group alibi is strong only if the timeline covers the exact moment in question, since a continuous routine gives general but weaker corroboration than a specific witness.
when: Evaluating a group account of where people were.
why: A routine running without interruption does not prove each member was in view at the critical moment.

text: Store events on a global clock with local time offsets so the player can line up records from several locations.
when: When a game spans several locations with separate records.
why: A shared clock lets the player match events across places and find meaningful overlaps.

text: Dust accumulates on undisturbed surfaces, so clean and dusty patches show when an object last covered or left a surface.
when: a surface is under or around an object
why: covered areas stay clean while uncovered areas collect dust

text: A cover story that a witness can verify and find false damages trust, so keep any pretext simple enough to hold up under checking.
when: When an investigator adopts a cover identity or story
why: A discovered pretext makes the investigator's other statements suspect.

text: 1) Pick fixed landmarks such as floor pattern or wall marks. 2) Measure each movement against them. 3) Count steps or turns against the reference.
when: Recording a moving target's path in poor visibility
why: Fixed reference points make movement records measurable and comparable.

text: 1) Identify the latest moment a missing person is certainly known to be alive. 2) List every place they may have gone and the possible order of visits. 3) If an unobserved visit may have come later, add the shortest travel time between the two places to the last sighting.
when: A person has vanished and a timeline has unknown visit order.
why: The last certain moment of life governs legal questions such as inheritance and succession.

text: 1) List everyone who could have acted, including performers, staff, guards and investigators. 2) Eliminate each person by a specific placement, such as a sound or presence they can be heard or seen from. 3) Identify the independent witnesses. 4) Ask whether each witness could have left their position.
when: Several people give a shared alibi covering the same moment.
why: A group account can hide individual gaps, so each member's position must be checked separately.

text: Explain why a scripted delay happens so players feel uncertainty rather than confusion.
when: A planned moment is postponed to build suspense.
why: An unexplained wait reads as a bug or confusion, not as tension.

text: Let a false solution's own evidence cut against it later, such as an alibi that fails under a second check.
Make a false alibi depend on one unverified fact, such as a timing, so that a single independent record can break it.
when: Designing a suspect's alibi that the player must test.
why: A single hinge fact is easy to check once the player knows to look.

text: Do not build a timeline on one witness's clock or memory, especially when the witness was asleep or emotionally shaken; one faulty time marker can shift every dependent event.
when: The timeline depends on a single time source, such as a witness who reports a time while impaired or distressed.
why: Sleep and strong emotion distort time perception and recall.

text: An alibi resting on one document can collapse if its timing was faked or the message was sent in advance or by someone else.
when: When an alibi depends on a single message or record.
why: A document proves only what its timestamp and sender actually establish.

text: Give a single object a second reading that becomes available only after the first suspect has been cleared.
why: The new reading then has no earlier answer to conflict with.

text: Anchor a case on one exact physical match, precise enough to carry weight beyond testimony.
when: Building a case against a suspect alongside witness accounts.
why: A precise physical match gives the case a fixed point that testimony alone lacks.

text: An alibi places a suspect elsewhere at the critical time; it excludes only if timed overlapping accounts cover that moment and a third party or record confirms them.
when: A suspect's movements at the critical hour are disputed.

text: A witness's silence does not prove nothing happened, since sleep depth and window position limit what they could hear, so a lodger's claim depends on their alertness.
when: when assessing whether a witness's silence is meaningful, such as a lodger vouching for a sleeping suspect
why: Hearing a movement depends on the listener being awake and attentive.

text: Respectable conduct or good humour does not prove innocence: it can conceal forgery, and letting reputation settle the question lets social impression override evidence.

1) Place each person's statement on one timeline and compare accounts of the same event to locate conflicts. 2) Ask which claims someone other than the speaker can confirm; treat a claim as supported only if independent witnesses agree. 3) Check records such as registers or manifests.
when: Several people claim to have last seen the victim or left a place at different times, or to have been somewhere at the same time.

text: Check an NPC's alibi against a second NPC's independent statement, and show both to the player so discrepancies point toward the true source before judgement.
when: Designing witness-checking gameplay or NPC testimony.
why: Two sources let the player judge.

text: A suspect who refuses a private interview and insists on witnesses limits the questioner's pressure, because others present make direct pressing costly.
when: when a suspect controls the setting
why: observers constrain what the questioner can press

text: A witness who depends on a party for position or income tends to shape testimony in that party's favour.
when: Weighing a witness's evidence
why: Dependence gives a reason to be careful with the truth

text: A timing that does not match expectation may be dismissed without comment, which signals that it did not fit the theory.
when: A reenactment's measured time conflicts with the working theory.
why: Investigators often set aside results that do not support their view.

text: Colleagues may accept a confident but unproven claim provisionally because they trust its source.
when: An investigator asserts a conclusion before proof is found.
why: Trust in the speaker lowers the demand for evidence.

text: A player with no prepared lines for a cover stalls at the first question, which exposes the pretext.
when: improvising a pretext
why: no rehearsed lines exist to answer the first challenge

text: A reply showing the witness already checked for a possibility is a tell that they had considered it before the question was asked.
when: A witness answers a question about a possibility they should not yet have considered.

text: A suspect who explains a visitor before being asked is perceived as anticipating suspicion and trying to pre-empt it.
when: A suspect volunteers an explanation no one requested
why: An unprompted account signals the suspect saw a risk of being suspected

text: After disturbed sleep, people cannot always separate what their imagination produced from what they actually observed.
when: a witness recalls events after disturbed sleep or strong fear
why: Dream images can blend into waking memory.

text: Prisoners' statements can shift to match what questioners already expect to hear, so the examiners' hypothesis shapes the testimony they produce.
when: questioning follows a hypothesis set by the investigators

text: When a jury cannot agree, the accused may be held in custody and the jurors kept ready, pending further direction from a higher authority.
when: when a jury deadlocks on a capital case
why: a hung verdict cannot be entered, so the case is held open for a higher decision

text: A suspect with excuses prepared in advance meets each accusation with a ready defence, so direct challenges lose force.
Players catch an unreliable claimant when the claimant's behavior contradicts the story, such as never acting on a supposed reward.
when: A source claims value or action that its conduct does not reflect.
why: Inconsistency between words and deeds signals doubtful testimony.

text: People misjudge elapsed time and distance, often underestimating or overestimating how long an action took, so recalled timelines are unreliable.
when: witnesses recall time after a social event or walk
why: memory of duration is distorted

text: A culprit can stage sightings of the victim at a late hour to place death after the suspect was already elsewhere, and can have witnesses confirm a fabricated timeline.
when: When a suspect's alibi depends on witnesses placing the victim alive later
why: Witness testimony can be shaped to build a false timeline that clears the suspect.

text: An absence on a key night looks suspicious to observers even when it has no link to the event.
when: a character is missing at a moment the audience expects them
why: absence on a critical moment is read as meaningful

text: Witnesses often forget brief separations from a group, so a short gap can vanish from memory unless checked against other sources.
when: Reconstructing group movements from recollection
why: Short absences do not seem significant when remembered

text: An alibi is a claim about where a person was at a given time, and it needs independent proof to carry weight.
An alibi places a suspect elsewhere at the critical time, and can be broken by showing that someone else could have occupied that place.
An alibi is a claim that a person was elsewhere during a window of time, and it must be judged against how long the act takes.
A companionship alibi is a claim that a witness stayed with the suspect throughout a period. It rules the suspect out only for events that fall within that exact period.
when: a single companion vouches for a suspect

text: An opportunity window is the span of seconds during which one person is alone with an item and could tamper with it, measured between handoffs.
An alibi is an account placing a suspect elsewhere during a critical time window; it is only as strong as its corroboration and must be checked before counting as evidence.
Concrete details of a journey and a third party's confirmation at the destination both corroborate a traveller's account.
Provisional bookings on several vessels can explain why a traveller's name appears on a list while the traveller's actual movements remain uncertain.
when: when a passenger list is used as evidence
why: a name on a list does not prove the person boarded it

text: A second identity is far easier to sustain when built over years in advance than invented at the last moment.
Four methods used on suspected witches to extract confessions were pricking, waking, watching and testing.
An alibi can be genuine yet carry little weight if it cannot be supported against the prosecution's case.
If death followed an act within minutes, the act likely happened in the presence of the victim. Short onset narrows who could have performed it.
when: When a medical estimate gives a short time between an act and death
why: A fast-acting effect requires the perpetrator to be close to the victim when the act occurs.

text: An empty seat at a stated time shows that its holder had not yet arrived, which can date arrival.
when: Attendance at a fixed event is observed at a known time.
why: Occupancy at a specific moment bounds when a person could have come in.

text: A ticket holder may sit somewhere other than the assigned seat, so the seat alone does not prove where a person was.
when: Location is inferred from a ticket's assigned seat.
why: People can move or swap seats, so assigned seats are weak proof of actual position.

text: A claim of sleeping through an event may be a lie or unreliable perception, so test it against the scene and ask how many distinct sounds were heard.
when: a witness says they slept through or heard nothing of an event
why: People vary widely in what wakes them, and waking perception separates distinct sounds that sleep would blur.

text: An alibi is weak when witnesses share the suspect's loyalties or interests, or were not truly at the claimed place; checking records against timed events tests it.
when: Testing a suspect's alibi
why: Witnesses bound to the suspect may lie, so their independence sets the alibi's strength.

text: Alibis need confirmation by another person at each stage, not only being seen elsewhere; unwitnessed intervals, such as time alone in a room, stay open.
when: when evaluating an alibi
why: Only independent confirmation closes an unverified interval.

text: An alibi holds when several independent witnesses place the suspect at a known location at the critical moment, with each time source checked; lone proximity without vouching is weak.
when: Comparing alibis for a time-bound event, where testimony about time is the only way to exclude a suspect.
why: One witness can be mistaken, so independent corroboration is much stronger; independent witnesses confirm position at the moment that matters.

text: A detail confirmed by a second, independently positioned witness is stronger than a single account; for arrival or departure times, several independent staff agreeing on the hour is most reliable.
when: weighing a witness's claim, or fixing when a person arrived or left
why: Independent agreement reduces the chance of a single error.

text: Signs of preparation before a break-in, such as an unlatched window or bound guard, suggest knowledge of the routine or inside help, but not proof; check access records.
when: A break-in looks too precise for an outsider, or an insider is inferred from signs of planning.
why: Preparation usually requires access to the place, yet outsiders can also prepare and records show who truly had access.

text: Model each suspect's alternative or arranged story as a hypothesis with explicit, checkable requirements, tested against new facts rather than treated as settled.
when: Handling multiple suspect accounts or a suspected arranged alibi.
why: Explicit requirements make accounts testable.

text: Second-hand accounts of when someone was last seen need checking, since absent witnesses may repeat what they were told, sincerely; another witness must verify them.
when: A timeline depends on second-hand accounts, or an alibi rests on what someone else told the witness.
why: Those absent can only repeat what they were told, and sincerity does not make it accurate.

text: Accept a provisional point and return to it later rather than resolving all at once; a claim lacking a motive stays provisional, not proven.
when: a serious claim lacks a complete motive
why: A missing motive is not a reason to halt investigation, yet acceptance must stay provisional.

text: Define the crime window from the gap between last sighting and discovery, then check which alibis within it have an independent witness; a bounded gap gives a clear question.
when: Designing a deduction question about a victim's death window, or a suspect claims to be at home or asleep over a long period.
why: A bounded gap gives players a clear question to resolve.

text: Describe a clue's distinctive features before the object appears, so the audience can recognize it when it returns.
A suspect who stages a visible quarrel or refusal may be building a later claim of innocence, so ask whether the account was prepared in advance.
when: when a suspect's defence depends on a witnessed dispute
why: A staged scene can make a later claim look credible.

text: An actor's movements over several days form their own timeline, which can be checked against deadlines and other events.
why: Movements recorded in sequence reveal preparation and timing.

text: Confirm a reaction across more than one moment, since a single observation can overturn a settled belief.
A plausible excuse given right after a slip suggests it was prepared in advance; check it against what information was available at the time.
when: When a suspect explains knowledge they should not have.

text: Infer an adult's character from the behaviour of children or dependants in their care, treating it as grounds for suspicion rather than proof.
when: An adult's behaviour is hard to read directly
why: A dependant's behaviour can reveal household tensions

text: Split a large search area so each searcher covers one side of it.
A respectable role can hide a personal interest; let that interest stay concealed behind the role until a clue exposes it.
An actor who wants to secure an object tends to act early, before the loss is noticed.
when: when estimating when a theft most likely occurred within a window
why: Early action reduces the chance of discovery.

text: Evidence that a party tried to prevent the harm can complicate a simple motive reading.
Wait until an impaired suspect recovers before questioning, but words spoken while impaired can still be used as leverage.
A timed decision, such as a choice made after an interruption, can be confirmed by asking the person who relayed the message.
when: A witness's timing depends on an event that others observed.
why: A relay witness can corroborate when the decision was made.

text: Route marks and purchases show opportunity and preparation, but rarely prove an alibi false on their own.
when: Evaluating physical or behavioural evidence against a stated alibi.
why: Each item fits many innocent explanations until combined with timing and testimony.

text: When witness times are unreliable or absent, use objective measures such as fuel use and mileage to reconstruct when events happened.
when: no reliable witness time exists
why: objective measures do not depend on memory

text: A suspect far from the scene can be cleared by distance, but the times of their arrivals and departures must still be checked.
when: a suspect's location at the scene matters
why: Distance clears a suspect only if their movement timing also fits

text: Whoever knows what a suspect is doing can get in front of them; one who only guesses at it must keep behind.
Compare an estimated dose with the quantity of medicine dispensed and remaining; if the amount cannot account for it, accidental overdose is excluded.
An observed onset far later than a substance's known onset is a mismatch to investigate, not proof of any particular cause.
The posting or delivery time of a document can be evidence when reconstructing an event.
when: a document arrives close to a key moment
why: timing links the document to what could have been known

text: Prepare verifiable proof before a confrontation, since an alert opponent can infer hidden preparation.
Have an NPC who believes a false cause state it with real certainty, so players must test the claim before accepting it.
Ask about details the subject could not have prepared for, since accurate answers to those reveal real knowledge.
when: testing whether a subject's account is genuine
why: A rehearsed story rarely covers unexpected specifics

text: An unusual choice, such as a later train over an earlier one, is a point to probe.
A companion's testimony that leans toward a suspect should be checkable against other sources, so the player can detect the lean.
when: designing a companion who testifies
why: checkable testimony keeps bias from going unnoticed

text: Occupancy and rough timing can be established from traces even when no clue to the occupant's identity exists.
Test the weakest alibi first, since breaking it earns the cooperation needed to test the stronger one.
A witness's claimed timing can be tested against a public schedule that no one present controls. If the claimed hour conflicts with it, the alibi fails without a second witness.
when: A witness's timing is tied to a public event with a known schedule
why: A fixed public schedule is an independent anchor the witness cannot alter

text: Whoever prepared a masking agent probably also added the harmful agent. Check who had access to both the preparation and the dose.
when: when a harmful agent was hidden in a prepared item
why: The same person often handles both steps, linking the preparer to the harm.

text: Dialogue systems that let players ask NPCs about routines and times make contradictions checkable.
Weigh a claimed absence against how long the trip would take; a short errand covers a gap only if its timing fits within that gap.
when: A suspect says they briefly left and returned
why: A trip that cannot fit the gap cannot cover it

text: A single motive label can hide two emotions aimed at two different people, so split it when new facts reveal this.
when: when a crime involves several interested parties

text: Unfinished obligations due soon after a disappearance suggest a sudden break rather than a planned departure.
when: when judging whether an absence was planned
why: someone preparing to leave usually settles pending deals first

text: A plausible physical excuse such as fever is often accepted too easily, so the designer must decide whether the NPC believes it.
Agreement between companions proves less when they shared the same expectations.
Partial reports from several witnesses of one event corroborate the story where they overlap.
when: When multiple people saw different parts of one incident.
why: Independent partial views that agree support one another.

text: Treat a physical absence as a clue that needs interpretation, not as proof on its own.
when: A search finds only a missing part or an empty space.
why: One absence can be read in several ways.

text: Judge a person's character from surface behavior only provisionally, since hidden inner states are not a reliable basis for accusation.
when: Assessing a suspect whose motives are not visible.

text: Leave some links in a generated history unverified, so the chain has honest gaps that players can choose to investigate.
when: Designing a discoverable backstory.
why: Unresolved gaps give players something to pursue and avoid presenting a suspiciously complete history.

text: Filter suspects by hard-to-fake attributes, removing easily disguised features from the comparison so that the remaining traits decide who matches.
when: Generating or resolving a set of possible culprits.
why: Easily faked features cannot reliably separate suspects.

text: Make some alibi witnesses members of the suspect's faction so the player must weigh their testimony against other evidence.
Keep an unidentified victim a mystery until players gather identity clues that unlock the case.
Have a guard or innkeeper claim a room is full while an unlocked empty room is nearby, so the player exposes the lie by looking.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that the player can verify in the level
why: Letting players test claims turns dialogue into discoverable clues

text: A warning that arrives late is worth less than one that arrives early, and delaying a response gives the enemy the advantage.
Timing that breaks the expected order of events, such as an item collected before it could have been needed, can itself become a clue.
Deduction from a timeline works best when a plan is bounded by a physical clock such as tide, schedule or fuel.
when: A suspect's route depends on a limiting physical factor
why: Fixed limits turn a vague plan into testable time windows

text: A gap in a sequence is meaningful when the missing value has a reason, such as a non-working day, rather than being accidental.
Test a witness's account by asking whether their route and timing make sense given what they knew at each moment; an odd path choice is a clue to conduct or intent.
when: When a witness includes an action that seems unnecessary or contrary to their stated purpose
why: Actions that contradict the stated goal often reveal knowledge, intent, or concealment.

text: Reward specific, checkable information more than pleading, so players learn to test claims instead of accepting emotional appeals.
when: when designing NPC dialogue rewards
