why: Rewards shape what players learn to trust.

text: Give a clue object such as a pocket watch a fixed game-time value, so players can rebuild event order from known schedules like guard rotations.
Model an alibi as a timetable the player checks against timed events, and place one contradiction in an unrelated object found while searching for something else.
when: designing a mystery with a claimed alibi
why: a checkable schedule gives a fair test and an incidental clue rewards thorough searching

text: Record when the last known baseline was taken, since every change must fall after that moment.
when: dating a discovered change
why: Anything earlier is already reflected in the baseline.

text: NPCs who believe culprits must be clever will read an alibi gap differently from those who do not; let the player judge which NPC reasons sensibly.
when: NPCs comment on a suspect's lack of alibi
why: Beliefs about cleverness shape interpretation of the same fact.

text: An NPC can bluff by behaving as though the player's case is complete, prompting a culprit to act and reveal themselves.
when: designing a culprit's reaction to pressure
why: Feigned certainty triggers a response the culprit would otherwise hold back.

text: A timetable can make an alibi seem objective; a staged or misleading timeline can make a suspect appear cleared, so check the timeline the alibi depends on.
when: A suspect's innocence rests on a sequence of times or events.
why: A designed timeline can look innocent while hiding the actual sequence.

text: Check a witness's time claim against a neutral, independent source, such as another witness whose own timing is fixed, since witnesses share clocks and memories that may be wrong.
when: A witness states when they saw someone or when an event happened, from testimony alone.

text: When several parties move to the same place within a short window, they probably had a planned meeting rather than a chance encounter.
when: movement times and destinations line up closely
why: Matching schedules are unlikely to occur by coincidence.

text: Split a covert meeting into separate roles so that no single observer can prove the whole arrangement.
when: a group must meet discreetly under possible surveillance
why: Each observer sees only a fragment and cannot connect the parts

text: Give each alibi a player-performable check, such as a cell record or time-stamped movement log, stored in the game so the claim can be tested.
when: designing alibis for suspects in a mystery
why: Movement records give the player an independent source to test a claim against.

text: A candle that has not guttered shows an opening was open only briefly, which narrows the window of access.
Vouching passes trust from a trusted local to a newcomer without proof, forming a chain the player can trace to its source to judge reliability.
when: A stranger's cover is backed by someone locals trust, or characters who have not met need trust built.
why: Trust passes from the vouching person to the newcomer; traceable vouching lets the player judge reliability.

text: Official obstacles such as hearings, bail and a magistrate extend the wait and keep the character from acting.
when: A reveal must be delayed

text: An NPC's refusal can be a state that other actions change, and an unprompted remark can open a new lead.
A continuous alibi removes its suspect and any theory requiring their presence, closing the line of inquiry that pointed to them.
when: An alibi is verified by independent sources.
why: A proven position in the crime window rules out the act within that window.

text: One person can pose as two witnesses who are never seen together, each seeming to vouch for the other's absence, so non-overlapping sightings hide a single actor.
when: A suspect's alibi depends on sightings that never overlap.
why: Non-overlapping sightings hide a single actor.

text: Model witness NPCs to give partial, hedged statements with gaps the player fills from world state, so inconsistencies become discoverable and the player must weigh what they hear.
If an observer is alert, a suspect's movement out of a single-exit room is limited; if the observer is inattentive, the alibi collapses.
when: When an alibi depends on a guard stationed at a room's only door.
why: The observer's attention is the only barrier to leaving.

text: When several independent informants describe the same routine, confidence in that routine rises.
An arranged alibi works as insurance: if the act goes wrong, the culprit can answer any accusation with a powerful witness.
why: the witness's standing serves as the defence

text: Fog and slow signals make positions hard to confirm, so a person can move between hidden sections of a journey unseen and a claimed route can conceal a different one.
why: poor visibility weakens the link between a stated position and actual movement

text: An NPC's claim such as hearing nothing can be tied to a bell or door the player can test, making dialogue checkable against the world.
when: When designing NPC dialogue that players should verify.

text: Incapacitating a guard removes the one observer of a route, opening a path that was previously watched.
when: A guarded passage whose watcher is drugged, distracted or absent.
why: Without a watcher, the route's only check is gone.

text: An accuser who claims the accused acted through an invisible agent makes the alibi irrelevant, since no record of absence can refute the claim.
when: A suspect has a strong alibi
why: An unobservable method cannot be disproved by location evidence.

text: Praise for a witness's honesty from an opposing party adds weight beyond the witness's own words.
when: A dispute involves a record of the witness's honesty.
why: Such praise is costly to give against one's own interest, so it signals credibility.

text: NPC schedules and night logs let players assemble a timeline from witness entries and find where the entries break.
An NPC claiming an official role can be checked by a second NPC or an in-game record; a mismatch can trigger a hostile reveal.
when: Designing NPCs whose claims the player may test.
why: Cross-checking exposes the lie and changes the NPC's behaviour.

text: Let an NPC's written report be contradicted by the player's own memory log, so the player must decide whom to believe.
when: Designing conflicting testimony between an NPC report and player knowledge.
why: Conflicts force the player to weigh sources rather than accept one passively.

text: An alibi resting on people who did not notice the suspect is hard to disprove, but becomes fragile once someone starts searching for the suspect.
Let companion characters unintentionally reveal clues about other NPCs' motives and temperament through idle chatter, opening paths the player can exploit.
An alibi can be a recorded sound played by a timed device, such as a voice or scream, that a witness takes for a living person's presence.
why: Witnesses trust what they hear, so an audio trick can fake a person.

text: A reconstructed absence, such as a disguise followed by an exit and a false alibi, can be set out as a chain of linked facts.
when: when a disguised or staged absence can be listed as ordered actions
why: Ordering the actions makes each dependency between steps visible.

text: Prepared answers can be modelled as dialogue branches where questions outside the script receive deflecting responses, letting a clever player test the performer.
when: When designing dialogue for a deceptive NPC.
why: Off-script questions expose the limits of prepared content.

text: Grade each alibi into one of four tiers: witnessed with a specific time, witnessed but vague, self-reported only, or purely negative with no one seeing the suspect.
when: deciding whether a suspect stays in the case
why: corroboration varies in strength

text: An alibi can be a constructed story designed to place the accused elsewhere, so it is not automatically a true record of movements.
An alibi or reconstruction fails if its assumed time is wrong, such as a presumed time of death resting only on identification, or a time of tearing or writing.
why: The alibi depends entirely on the fixed time it is measured against.

text: Splitting attention or a watch between two people leaves each exposed: a target may move unexpectedly, or coverage is lost if one is reassigned without notice.
An alibi with gaps can look solid while every link depends on the person who gave it or on their own account rather than independent records.
An alibi supported by a companion or witness who cannot be questioned loses its support and stays unverified.
Consistent or coordinated accounts do not clear anyone: mutual vouching can be circular, especially with a shared interest, since agreement shows fit, not absence of opportunity.
when: Several suspects share the same window and their accounts interlock.

text: A check made at one time, such as a morning lock inspection, says nothing about events in the earlier hours.
when: a status is confirmed only at a later time
why: the check did not observe the intervening period

text: An alibi based on a door being locked fails if the door was never secured, so check the lock before trusting the alibi.
Forgetting that a dependant can raise an alarm leaves a plan exposed, so every person able to alert others must be accounted for.
when: a plan focuses on the main target and ignores others present
why: Any person who can call for help can ruin a timed action.

text: Letting a suspect's household open the door before investigators are inside gives the suspect time to flee.
A respectable or saintly reputation does not remove a beneficiary from suspicion, and motive may exist that the records do not show.
when: clearing a beneficiary on character or on the records alone
why: Motive is defined by legal stake and personal knowledge, not reputation.

text: A planted item is only as strong as its stated reason; a weak cover story leads the audience to question the item.
when: the explanation for an item is thin
why: audiences test explanations and find gaps

text: A witness who answers 'I am not sure' marks a gap rather than a guilty answer, and a witness who was away gives an absent alibi, not a confirmed one.
when: Interpreting uncertain or absent alibi testimony
why: Uncertainty and absence are unconfirmed positions, not proof of innocence or guilt.

text: Assuming a suspect will remain in place while a game or scene continues is risky, since a deadline can end the wait early.
when: the suspect is free to leave
why: suspects act when the scene's pace changes

text: Companions who withhold their own findings create a false sense of progress.
when: when several characters share investigative work
why: Hidden findings look like advancement while no shared picture forms.

text: An alibi that cannot be verified can make an innocent person look guilty, because the gap invites the worst reading.
when: when a witness's whereabouts cannot be confirmed
why: Unexplained time is readily read as concealment.

text: A departure time given by a servant may be imprecise. Note the imprecision before relying on it to build a timeline.
A witness who was off duty cannot confirm a routine on the critical day.
when: Relying on staff testimony about a specific day
why: Absence means no observation of that day

text: A suspect with a prepared medical explanation can use it to account for physical traces, so the explanation must be tested before it is accepted.
when: A suspect offers a health-based explanation for physical evidence.
why: A ready story can cover real traces and delay scrutiny.

text: A corroborated cover story can still be false, because a plan can hide behind a believable research explanation.
A scheme that depends on a stranger's unseen cooperation has many points of failure.
Reading packing as a getaway can be wrong: the same preparation may come from a suspect who plans to surrender.
when: When a suspect's preparations suggest flight.

text: An alibi strong for one event can be weak for another, so test each suspect against the same moment.
when: Several events with different suspects' alibis.
why: Coverage of one time does not extend to others.

text: Treating a claim of sleep as proof of innocence ignores the chance that the claim is false.
why: sleep cannot be verified by the investigator

text: An alibi relies on witnesses failing to connect the victim's summons to the danger, so witnesses who are calm while the victim is sent to harm give the alibi its force.
why: The alibi works only while the witnesses do not connect the events.

text: Using the time help was summoned as the time of an event's onset can misplace the events, since discovery may lag the event by a substantial interval.
when: Building a timeline of a sudden event such as a collapse.
why: Summoning help is a later event than the thing it responds to, so treating the two as one shifts the whole sequence.

text: A witness who was in company may pass over a gap in the timeline as if it were spent at home.
when: Evaluating an account given by someone who was with others.
why: Shared company can make unaccounted time seem accounted for.

text: Unplanned participants can change a timed plan without warning, so model their likely arrival as a risk.
when: a plan relies on a fixed sequence of events
why: extra actors alter timing and outcomes

text: A late arrival in a usually punctual routine can force a rushed plan with almost no margin, so timed plans need slack.
when: The plan depends on a single scheduled event

text: Assuming people who met at a station went to the same destination afterward is an error; a missing shared destination proves little.
An absence used as an alibi needs checking for when it started and ended, and whether the absent person could still act through others.
Trusting an alibi because it is stated firmly leads to missed contradictions; a confident claim is not verification.
when: When a suspect delivers a confident alibi
why: Confidence of delivery is not evidence that the events occurred.

text: 1) Use a message's dated write and receipt times to fix the sequence of events. 2) Note who knew what and when. 3) Check the sequence before questioning other witnesses.
when: A written message is near an event in time, or a dated written statement frames the sequence.
why: Timing of communication can establish that an event followed or preceded it; the fixed sequence frames later questioning.

text: 1) Identify the source of an alibi document or counter-alibi. 2) Verify the source independently. 3) Accept it only if the source is confirmed; never take a documented alibi at face value.
when: A witness or suspect offers a document as proof of location, or a counter-alibi is offered.
why: Unverified documents can be false or misattributed.

text: 1) Split the alibi into time and place claims and the witnesses who confirm them. 2) Separate claims resting only on the subject's word. 3) Test verifiable claims first against independent sources. 4) Ask each witness how they know the hour. Breaking the alibi into parts exposes points of failure.
when: A suspect presents a neat or airtight alibi, a complete timeline, or a time-and-place defence.
why: Each part can be tested separately.

text: 1) Record each person's claimed location, span and activity per time slot, noting who confirms it. 2) Find an independent source for each point. 3) Mark unsupported points as weak or open. 4) Re-examine weak entries first.
when: An alibi or event timing is in question, or several people give overlapping accounts of the same hours.

text: 1) Fix the crime window and order independent timed sightings or records around it. 2) Ask where the suspect was during each part and mark gaps between consecutive fixed points. 3) Check whether travel, walks and calls fit each gap. 4) Treat the alibi as broken if any leg cannot be covered in time.
when: A suspect's whereabouts during a crime window are disputed, or they could be in two places within the window.
why: Physical travel time decides whether a claimed alibi is possible.

text: 1) Estimate earliest possible departure from realistic travel speed. 2) Add time for each small delay, such as dressing or starting a vehicle, and weigh reasons for any delay. 3) Compare the result with the stated arrival. 4) Check fixed times and side evidence against independent records or witnesses.
when: A suspect's whereabouts are claimed for a specific window, or a reconstruction depends on journey times, opening hours or call logs.
why: Timing shows whether the alibi is physically possible, and small delays can decide whether a timing holds.

text: 1) List each claimed action and its time. 2) Estimate the minimum time each takes and compare the total with the available window. 3) Name who confirms each claim and whether they are independent of the suspect. 4) Note steps no witness could confirm.
when: Checking a suspect's account of a period, especially one that depends on one person or a tight schedule.
why: Shows whether the schedule is physically possible and where it depends on unverified or non-independent claims.

text: 1) Anchor each timeline to fixed independent events, such as recorded times, medical estimates, a phone call or other observers' schedules. 2) Ask each person where they were in the window. 3) Check claims against records and room layout, and whether timing permits later events. 4) Mark gaps and contradictions.
when: The crime time is narrow and several people claim alibis, or several independent clocks or observers are available.

text: 1) Have each person state their claimed time and position in their own words, pinning vague answers with specific questions. 2) Record clock times for movements, checkpoints, absences and returns. 3) Compare each claim against a physical record such as tickets or logs, and test other witnesses against it. 4) Compare movements across people to see who could have acted.
when: Several people's movements or overlapping claims must be compared.
why: Matching recorded times shows who was in position to act; building the timeline from the suspect's own words makes any later contradiction clear and fair.

text: 1) Fix the window in which the act could have happened. 2) List everyone who could have been near the victim, not only obvious suspects. 3) Check each claimed location against that window and verify it independently. 4) Test whether a substitute could have occupied the suspect's place.
when: Assessing a suspect's alibi when the crime time is narrow and several people had access to the victim.
why: A claimed location counts only if it fits the minutes the act could have occurred; a wide list prevents tunnel vision and independent verification prevents accepting a firmly stated alibi.

text: 1) Fix the exact time of the act and the clock times each alibi witness gives, aligning the clocks they came from. 2) Line up each alibi window with the crime window. 3) Measure the gap between them. 4) Reject the alibi if the margin is too small to be credible.
when: An alibi depends on a short time window, or a suspect's exact location at a precise time is contested.
why: Times must be checked against a clock, since a loose estimate leaves little room for error.

text: 1) Agree rules in advance. 2) Stagger each person's movements. 3) Stage a brief quarrel loud enough to be heard. 4) Give each accomplice one task so no one performs the whole act and no single person is seen doing it.

1) Describe the act in physical terms, such as lifting a weight or crossing a difficult route. 2) Compare those demands with the suspect's age, health and mobility. 3) Note any mismatch; a claimed action may be impossible for that person.
when: Deciding whether a suspect could physically perform an act, or a claimed action involves a physical skill.
why: Tests capability directly against the requirements of the act.

text: 1) Ask for exact times and places rather than general accounts. 2) Pin each stage to a location. 3) Check each fixed point against other evidence. 4) Note every interval the witness cannot account for.
when: when a suspect's account places them near a crime
why: specific claims can be tested against the clock and other evidence

text: 1) Record each party's departure time and destination from witnesses. 2) Note any arrival times. 3) Align all times on one clock. 4) Look for overlaps that reveal a shared destination.
when: witnesses can give times and destinations, even roughly
why: Aligned times show which parties were heading to the same place.

text: 1) Ask indirect questions about the suspect's movements during the crime window, not whether they have an alibi. 2) Keep your reactions neutral. 3) Build a timeline of the suspect's arrival, departure and destinations.
when: a close companion of the suspect is available to question
why: Indirect questions let the witness volunteer details freely.

text: 1) List everyone who could have learned the secret. 2) Record where each person was at the relevant time. 3) Keep those with access and opportunity as possible actors.
when: An event's cause depends on who knew of a hidden object or secret.
why: Presence at a place and time determines which actors are possible.

text: 1) Note the reason given for a sudden departure. 2) Check it against an independent record such as a telegram, ticket or travel log. 3) Weigh it against known facts about the people involved.
when: a suspect or witness leaves at an awkward moment with a stated reason

text: 1) Fix the known times: calls, appointments, arrivals, departures and the discovery time. 2) Ask who can confirm each step. 3) Check the route taken. 4) Measure the unwitnessed gap between the last contact and the death.
when: Testing a suspect's claimed movements before a crime.
why: Fixed times and witnessed steps show where an account is unverified.

text: 1) Establish when the dose was delivered and when it was consumed. 2) Look up the known onset time of the substance. 3) Compare the observed onset with the expected onset. 4) Weigh each alternative explanation by the size of the gap.

1) Make a room look used, such as a rumpled bed. 2) Use a known harmless habit as cover, such as a long bath. 3) Keep the noise long enough for listeners to settle, then reduce it. 4) Arrange lights and doors to suggest someone is home. 5) Set up a prior excuse for absence.
when: when someone must appear present to a witness checking at a given hour
why: Staged signs of routine make an absent person seem present, and the cover depends on the household's habits.

text: 1) Establish a person's fixed hours and day off. 2) Identify the free periods in which they could have been elsewhere. 3) Check those periods against the event window.
when: testing whether a person could have been at a location
why: routine fixes the times they were unaccounted for

text: 1) Take the last time the victim was seen alive. 2) Take the time the body was found. 3) Check whether the suspect had access to the agent during that span.

1) Anchor the timeline to a witness-recorded time. 2) Establish the suspect's known movements. 3) Work out whether the suspect could travel and act within the gap. 4) Add corroborating times. 5) Check the suspect's belongings and state against the timeline.
when: When a suspect claims to be elsewhere or a witness gives a time
why: A claimed alibi can only be judged against checkable times and travel possibilities

text: 1) Identify the object and when it was unguarded. 2) Identify who could reach it during that interval. 3) Check whether the interval fits the act's duration.
when: when a poisoning, trap or theft must be timed
why: Comparing the window to the act shows whether a suspect could have done it.

text: When a witness's timing seems off, press for the exact hour; a firm answer shows whether the discrepancy is real.
1) Take one witness aside for a private talk. 2) Have a partner search the rest of the scene while the talk continues.
when: when two parties must be occupied at once
why: Separation creates time and space for a search.

text: 1) Get each companion's own account of the same event. 2) Compare what each perceived. 3) Note what each expected beforehand. 4) Treat differences as clues.
when: two or more people shared an experience

text: 1) Separate the time a message was sent from the time it was delivered. 2) Compare each time with where the suspect was seen. 3) Estimate the travel time for the key journey. 4) Count the free minutes left to the suspect. 5) Check who handled the message and whether a copy exists. 6) Test the suspect's likely next move against the schedule.
when: When a claimed alibi depends on stated times that others can verify.
why: Converting suspicion into a checkable schedule reveals whether the suspect had the opportunity to act.

text: 1) List every possible route into or out of a place. 2) Check each route for the marks it would leave. 3) Exclude routes whose expected marks are absent. 4) Test remaining marks against known sources.
when: Deciding how someone reached or left a place.
why: Systematic exclusion narrows the route to the one that matches the evidence.

text: 1) Find physical traces of passage, such as torn cloth or a fresh gap in a barrier. 2) Measure the height needed to reach the gap. 3) Test the route physically to confirm the traced trait.
when: Reconstructing how a person moved through a barrier.
why: Testing the route checks measurements that can be wrong on paper.

text: Do not accept an alibi resting only on the suspect's word, or on relatives' or a spouse's or close associate's testimony; seek a second, independent source.
Treat the whole chain as sound only when every link holds; one unverified step leaves the whole reconstruction open.
when: when judging a reconstructed alibi
why: A chain holds only as strongly as its weakest link.

text: Weight a vouching witness's alibi by their own reliability and independence from the suspect; a spouse's vouching counts for less than an independent witness, so confirmation needs a second source.
when: when one witness vouches for another's whereabouts, or when designing alibi characters
why: A vouching witness can share the same interest or bias, so their support adds limited weight.

text: Check times recalled from memory against dated or logged records before relying on them, since a witness's sense of elapsed time can be badly wrong.
when: a timeline relies on remembered times
why: Memory of clock times is error-prone and drifts.

text: An alibi resting on one person's word stays unproven, especially if that witness has a motive or could be removed. Seek an independent record before accepting it.
when: an alibi depends on a single account
why: Accepting an unverified alibi leaves the case open to a false claim; a compromised witness cannot anchor an alibi.

text: Accept an alibi provisionally and mark a weak one unverified rather than discarding it, testing it against an independent source before relying on it.
when: an alibi lacks independent confirmation

text: Corroborate an alibi with two or more independent sources, such as a guard log, door state, footprint or staff member, not the alibi holder's own account.
when: when verifying a whereabouts claim
why: One source can be wrong or controlled, and independent confirmation can refute a story that fits what listeners want to hear.

text: Write NPC dialogue claims about times, places and objects that players can check against inventory items, records or room state, so contradictions become discoveries.
when: when writing NPC or witness dialogue in a mystery
why: Checkable claims reward attentive players and let them catch contradictions between witnesses.

text: Give NPC alibis concrete, checkable details such as which hand was used, work in progress, a meal, weather or passing train that players can cross-check against other records.
when: when writing an NPC's account of their whereabouts
why: Checkable details let players test claims instead of simply accepting them.

text: A usable NPC alibi names a specific time and place and has at least one independent source, from someone present, that can confirm or contradict it.
when: when judging or authoring an NPC's whereabouts claim
why: Vague claims give no timeline and are easily broken; checkable times let players test claims.

text: Build NPC alibis from in-world records or world conditions the player must find and check, such as tickets, guard logs, storm logs, closed gates or patrol schedules, not dialogue alone.
when: when designing alibi puzzles

text: Schedule NPC routines with hourly locations and travel times so players can test alibis against the in-game clock and find the gap in a suspect's route.
when: when designing NPC routines or timed alibis for a mystery
why: Schedules give the player a clock to check claims against; a gap in one path can point to the true culprit.

text: Use travel times between map areas to set how much time a suspect actually has, so whether they could reach the scene in time can be checked.
when: when designing movement and alibi windows
why: Travel durations convert stated times into a measurable window of opportunity.

text: Do not build a case on a single timing inference or small detail; confirm it with other corroborating evidence first.
when: an interval is central to a case, or a small detail is used as a clue

text: A suspect's concealment or refusal to account for their time does not prove guilt, but the gap stays open until explained or verified.
when: a suspect hides where they were or declines to say how time was spent
why: Concealment damages credibility without establishing the crime.

text: Give each NPC informant or witness a reliability value tied to motive, since one with reason to hide their own part or exaggerate is less reliable.
when: NPCs supply information or testimony to the player
why: Motive affects whether an account is complete and honest.

text: Make each NPC explanation, including false ones, checkable against a second or physical source so players can tell a true recollection from a convenient one.
when: when NPCs explain events

text: Place alibi witnesses in the world and let players check a claim by visiting them in turn, showing any gap no one can explain.
when: designing alibi checks or verification in a game
why: Verification becomes an active player task.

text: Give an NPC's alibi or claim to have heard, or heard nothing, a positional basis the player can verify, such as distance, walls, doors or sound propagation.
when: when an NPC offers an alibi or says they heard, or heard nothing
why: The player needs a checkable sightline or earshot to judge the claim.

text: Model alibis as traversable routes with real geometry, including exits like balconies, so players can test whether a sleeping or stationary suspect could have left unseen.
when: when a character's whereabouts are disputed or claimed asleep or stationary
why: Players can only check an alibi if the layout and paths exist; unobserved exits make stationary claims unverifiable.

text: When a companion or NPC offers an alibi, make the player verify it against the named witness or a transport or door-log record before it counts as established.
when: designing an NPC-provided alibi
why: A checkable alibi gives the player a verifiable way to test it.

text: Give an NPC who matches a rumored description and sits near the crime a checkable alibi.
Plant two NPC accounts of one event that conflict on a name, direction or time the player can verify elsewhere.
when: Designing contradictory testimony for players to resolve.
why: Checkable mismatches let players detect the liar through evidence.

text: A companion can change a line of dialogue to hint at knowledge before the full information is available to the player.
A companion can withhold a location or event until a trigger, using dialogue lines that carry two meanings depending on what the player later learns.
Before a risky meeting, check a third party who may share the key fact, since a secret known only to two people is hard to confirm.
when: before confronting a person who holds a key fact

text: Treat pursuers' and witnesses' descriptions as provisional, since they may be wrong and are often corrected in conversation.
when: Relying on a description to identify someone
why: Observers can be mistaken

text: Let a player's alibi check rest on dated records they can rebuild, leaving one gap that a single witness can fill.
Give each NPC time-stamped statements covering different windows, so the player must find the moment where no statement overlaps the critical event.
when: designing a timeline puzzle
why: An uncovered gap becomes the clue the player has to locate.

text: When a private clock is disputed, establish when it was last set, since a recent reset limits how far it could have drifted.
when: a witness's timing depends on a private clock

text: Let a suspect narrate the crime in dialogue while the player verifies each claim against objects collected earlier in the game.
Let a companion character give incomplete reports, so the player discovers what was missed by examining the scene and comparing it with the companion's account.
when: when designing companion dialogue in a game investigation
why: the gap gives the player a reason to examine the environment

text: An alibi that survives a timing check is stronger than one that was never tested.
Leave part of the evidence for official investigators to find and keep part for one's own analysis.
when: Collecting evidence that others will also examine
why: Shared discovery supports the official record while retained material allows independent checking

text: A person proven elsewhere during the crime window could not have carried out the act then, but knowledge or access may still link them.
when: when testing an alibi

text: Make an NPC's cover story checkable against records the player can search, such as shop logs, journals or book collections.
when: designing NPC alibis or explanations

text: When a pretext is weak, invent a plausible reason for unusual behaviour, such as slow progress or frequent stops, before it is questioned.
Let a companion keep a secret that is revealed only when the player's trust reaches a set threshold.
Do not rely on a silhouette alibi where a clear view of the face is possible, and state the similar profile to the player before any reveal.
when: Designing a witness-based alibi or disguise reveal.
why: A visible face defeats the substitution, and an unstated profile makes the reveal feel unfair.

text: Make a physical mark, such as a scar or tattoo, a checkable identity feature that players must confirm before trusting an NPC.
Keep a character-based conclusion provisional until the question of who acted has been answered by evidence.
Treat the moment a poison is given, the moment it takes effect and the moment of death as three separate events, each opening a different window of suspects.
when: when establishing when a poisoning could have happened
why: Assuming they coincide leads to wrong suspect windows

text: Let a companion character reach the solution from the same material, giving the player a fair chance to match it.
when: A companion accompanies the player through an investigation.
why: Shared material lets the player verify the companion's conclusion.

text: Do not treat an alibi as broken when independent physical evidence already fixes the time of the event.
when: When physical evidence and an alibi conflict
why: Fixed physical evidence can outweigh an uncertain witness account

text: Check whether a document places the suspect himself, or only a vehicle, a driver or paperwork; a document may prove one without the others.
when: Evaluating a documented alibi

text: Build a timeline table for a level with each NPC's movements and sounds, and mark the alibi windows the player can check.
when: designing a multi-NPC mystery
why: visible time windows let players reason about who could have acted

text: Check for a mechanical cause before reading a habit into a placement; a catch that snags fabric can force one orientation.
An alibi exculpates only if the facts it relies on come before the disputed act; a cover that falls after the event does not help.
when: Evaluating a suspect's cover story for a specific act
why: Presence after the act says nothing about presence during it

text: Do not accept an alibi because the person is respectable or high-ranking; social status does not verify a claim.
when: Assessing an alibi from a trusted or prominent person.
why: Reputation is not evidence of where someone was.

text: Let players build an alibi timeline from scheduled NPC routines, and flag any claimed emergency that does not match the in-game clock.
when: Designing alibi and timeline puzzles.

text: Include a suspect's physical capacity in the timeline, since an injury or lack of transport can make reaching a distant scene impossible regardless of intent.
when: when a suspect is accused of travelling to a scene
why: presence requires the ability to get there

text: Make alibis depend on physical access, such as locked doors and window size, rather than on claims alone.
when: designing alibi checks in a game
why: physical constraints can be tested while claims cannot

text: Log timed events and NPC movements so the player can reconstruct who was where, and record a player's detour as a stall that can change what guards know.
when: a world tracks player movements over time
why: logged history supports reconstruction and consequences

text: Give NPC statements a reliability value that drops when the NPC is impaired or coached, so the player must cross-check those claims against scene evidence.
when: when designing NPCs who may give partial or misleading answers
why: it lets the player treat impaired testimony as leads

text: Attach a clear gain or loss to each suspect so players can test motive rather than react to mood.
Generate murderers with explicit financial motives, such as an inheritance, an insurance payout or a debt that changes on death, so players can verify them.
Use burning candles, half-melted torches, drying puddles and settled dust as ambient clocks so players can judge how long an NPC has been present.
when: Designing rooms where NPC timelines matter

text: Split a backstory clue across two documents, such as a letter and an obscure journal, so the player must combine them and check dates to solve it.
when: designing a hidden backstory revealed through documents
why: Combining sources and checking dates is what turns a puzzling phrase into a resolved fact.

text: Place a deed in one location and its counter-deed in another, so players must visit both to learn the real terms.
when: designing a land or ownership dispute in a game world
why: The true terms appear only when both documents are found.

text: Have a companion question an NPC's vagueness and respond to it in dialogue, so the evasion is visible to the player.
Let the player unlock pre-written excuses as they gather evidence, so cover stories grow with the investigation.
Use a victim's hidden favours and past dealings to seed extra motives and widen the suspect pool.
when: generating a murder scenario
why: the victim's history creates new interested parties

text: Track two evidence tiers per suspect, suspicion from circumstance and proof from direct observation, and gate arrest or accusation on the proof tier.
Build a suspect web listing each NPC's room access and how long each has known the target, so the player can see which questions to ask.
when: Designing a mystery with several NPCs who had access
why: Access and familiarity guide which accounts the player can test

text: Let an NPC's alibi be an absence from a location, which the player can verify by checking that location's logs.
Score each alibi by its number of independent witnesses and timestamps, and reveal partial results rather than a clean yes or no.
why: graded results match partial evidence

text: In a torn-document puzzle, use the gap size as a constraint on the missing text so the answer stays bounded.
when: when designing a fragment-based clue
why: Constraints make the puzzle solvable and checkable.

text: Give NPC witnesses schedules and departure dates, so the player must reach them before they leave the map.
Build a verification path where the decoy's alibi can be tested, so it clears them only when the player goes looking.
Define several opportunity windows across the in-game day so that players must identify which window fits the event.
when: when designing a case with multiple possible times
why: Multiple windows turn timing into a deduction task rather than a single obvious answer.

text: An NPC-set time limit can serve as a timed mechanic the player must respect or exploit, and each timed event should have a witness NPC who can confirm or contradict it.
when: designing timed events in investigation
why: the player must build timelines from several sources

text: Give shops, guards and offices fixed opening and closing times, so the player must plan routes around them and deadlines create real pressure on choices.
when: designing a town with time-restricted locations
why: fixed hours turn movement into scheduling

text: Rule out a route when earlier walkers would have passed the spot, since they would have noticed anyone there.
when: When a location was recently traversed by known observers
why: Prior traffic through a spot makes concealment there unlikely.

text: Explain an apparent timing discrepancy with a specific, checkable cause, and verify that cause with an independent witness.
when: A person's movements seem to conflict with the timeline.
why: Vague excuses cannot be tested, while specific causes can be confirmed or refuted.

text: Show a timed escape or guard schedule through ambient cues such as bells or footsteps, so the player feels the clock.
when: when designing timed sequences in a level

text: Scatter traces such as blood, tracks or dropped items so their order implies events, letting players assemble a timeline in a journal.
Give a level a clock puzzle: the player aligns a timed event such as a bell, rainfall, or locking door with an NPC's claimed schedule to expose a lie.
Let a companion NPC carry a task list the player assigns and return results on a timer.
when: Designing companion-driven investigation tasks.
why: A timed, prioritized task keeps the player's investigation moving.

text: Build rescue or alarm systems whose timing can be checked, so that a late response becomes evidence a player can use.
why: Measurable response times turn delays into readable clues

text: Give staff or guard testimony small timing facts, such as who left last, that the player can check against the level layout.
Empty an area of potential witnesses on a schedule to define the window in which a character has an alibi.
Give an alibi puzzle a timestamped token, such as a gate log, that places a suspect while leaving identity open for a second clue.
Give an NPC an alibi of illness for a span of in-game days, and provide a witness or record that contradicts it for the player to find.
when: designing NPC alibis

text: Give NPC investigators a stock explanation that the player can test and find lacking.
when: designing NPC investigators who offer a theory

text: Encode whether an NPC's omission is an oversight or deliberate in its behaviour, letting players infer intent from what it leaves out.
Store each NPC's statements so the game can flag contradictions between them, such as conflicting durations or sources.
when: when NPCs make checkable claims
why: contradictions expose lies

text: Build an alibi from many small, checkable claims that each pass on first check, so the player trusts the whole account.
when: when writing a false alibi
why: Each passed check adds to trust in the full account.

text: A flawless alibi often rests on arranged details, like a convenient clock or witnesses who never lost sight, though true ones can look staged; weigh objective evidence.
when: Judging an alibi that looks flawless or unusually complete.
why: Arranged details are the usual weak points, yet appearance alone can mislead in both directions.

text: An alibi from witnesses related to the suspect, or from witnesses who saw the suspect only briefly, is less conclusive than one from independent, sustained observation.
when: when weighing alibi evidence

text: Verifying a method that needs specific conditions, such as a stopped vehicle, makes the plan depend on chance.
when: The method works only under transient conditions
why: If the condition never occurs, the method cannot be tested or used

text: Passing evidence to a trusted companion moves it out of your hands, but its safety then depends on that person's loyalty.
when: Concealing proof from searchers
why: Control transfers to another person

text: An opportunity window is the interval in which an object is unguarded and a person can reach it, measured by duration and by who has access. Only people present during it could have acted.
when: when assessing who could have moved, taken or acted on an object
why: Opportunity links a person to the act through timing and access.

text: Opportunity and mechanism show how an act could happen, while motive shows why someone would do it; the two must not be confused.
A locked, scheduled collection system, such as a sealed box emptied at a fixed time, produces a known sequence of records.
Opportunity and presence can be manufactured or shielded, so they cannot by themselves settle guilt.
when: When a suspect's presence or access is established
why: Presence can be arranged or concealed

text: A vague alibi lacking names, times or places, such as not remembering clearly, is not an alibi; it leaves a gap to test, not proof of guilt.
when: an alibi lacks names, times or places

text: Give NPCs fixed daily schedules with clear time windows so players can infer who had opportunity at a given time, and let a break in routine become a detectable change.
when: When designing NPC schedules for a mystery or investigation.
why: Players can only reason about opportunity and anomalies if the baseline is explicit.

text: A route shown to be feasible is not thereby proven; feasibility only means the act could have happened that way.
when: testing an inferred route
why: possibility differs from evidence that it happened

text: Test a route's feasibility against observer timing, such as patrol passes and quiet hours, to see whether an approach could go unseen.
when: an act could have been done unobserved
why: observer schedules determine exposure

text: When a remark implies knowledge of an act, infer the act happened at the first opportunity rather than later.
when: A remark suggests someone knew an event had occurred.
why: The earliest window of opportunity is where the act most likely took place.

text: A single fragile link can be gnawed or snapped, so a hidden channel needs a backup or a sturdier material.
when: Relying on a thin link to carry messages
why: Losing contact removes the only route of communication

text: A perpetrator avoids notice by acting at low-traffic hours and wearing clothing that does not draw attention.
when: Assessing how a culprit moved unseen.
why: Empty corridors and plain dress reduce witnesses.

text: Check first any alibi that depends on a single witness or a single record, since one failure removes the whole claim.
when: when a suspect's alibi rests on one source
why: a single source has no backup if it is wrong

text: A false alibi is fragile, and a detective who suspects it will attack its weakest link, such as the timing of transport.
when: An alibi is suspected to be false.
why: Weak links in a fabricated timeline are easier to break than the whole story.

text: Assume that any information shared with several people may leak, and plan for it.
Ask whether a claimed action is practical under the conditions the suspect describes; an account that is hard to carry out may have been built to be believed.
when: A suspect's account involves an unusual or difficult action.
why: Constructed stories often favor plausibility on the surface over practical feasibility.

text: A staged scene can present a false cause of death; the player finds a missing object and works out how it left the scene.
when: designing a misleading death scene
why: Recovering the object's route exposes the staging

text: Treat vague quantities such as 'about' a given acreage as ranges, since they can support both sides and must be checked against the physical record.
when: a grant or deed gives approximate measures
why: Approximate wording invites competing readings.

text: A stealth level can use a guard or merchant's schedule as a timing puzzle, with a window of a few hours for the player to act and a clear closing signal when it ends.
when: Designing a stealth or infiltration puzzle
why: A readable schedule lets the player plan around it, and a closing signal makes the deadline fair

text: Design NPC alibis around scheduled public events, and record which witnesses saw the NPC there.
Include a later timestamped sighting that breaks a presumed death time, so players must revise their timeline.
Place a timetable or schedule in an NPC's room with marked entries that indicate a route, letting players predict the next move.
when: designing clues for NPC movement
why: Players can act on a readable schedule to intercept the NPC.

text: Show each NPC's schedule on a timeline panel, so the player can align sightings and locate the gap where a suspect could be elsewhere.
when: Designing an investigation interface with NPC movement.
why: Aligned schedules expose the windows in which an account can be false.

text: Use quest timers, NPC daily schedules and routine events such as meal service to test which NPC could have been at a given place and time.
A scene-investigation system can use decay timers: weather erases traces, and NPC memories fade after a set number of in-game hours.
when: when designing investigation mechanics with time pressure
why: Decay makes the timing of player action matter

text: Treat a shared room as only a partial alibi, and check who was awake and whether an open door limited what each could see.
when: Two people sleep in the same or adjoining room
why: Proximity gives partial cover, but an open door limits what each could observe.

text: Clear the leading suspect with a documented alibi at the midpoint so the investigation must find a new suspect.
when: Structuring a whodunit around a strong early suspect.
why: A verified alibi removes the leading suspect and forces a fresh line of inquiry.

text: Compare a principal's known absence dates with any act credited to them, since an act performed during their absence points to a deputy.
when: A title or act is ascribed to a senior figure who was away.
why: Only someone present could have performed the act, so timing exposes the real actor.

text: Culprits faking time often assume all timers stop alike and miss the one still running; a timepiece set by hand to a false hour keeps working, exposing the tampering.
when: when staging a false timeline, or a timing claim rests on a damaged or staged timepiece
why: Hands moved by hand leave the mechanism working while the setting is false.

text: An NPC's routine, such as locking up or watching a window, can serve as an alibi the player must test against what they observe.
when: When an NPC's routine is used as evidence in a level.
why: Routines create expectations that the player can check for gaps.

text: Schedule-based alibis let a player verify NPC locations through independent NPC or log records.
when: When designing NPC movement and alibi checks.
why: Scheduled positions create records that can confirm or refute claims.

text: A suspect who believes he is cleared may act on his own, producing new movements and disclosures the questioner can observe.
when: when the questioner withholds a contradiction
why: confidence leads the suspect to take steps he would avoid if alarmed

text: Presence can serve as a shield: a guilty person may be absent while an innocent person is present, and a crime can be carried out at a distance through an agent on the scene.
when: Investigating who was present at a crime or where the culprit went.
why: Physical presence and absence can both disguise the actual perpetrator.

text: Flagging which NPC claims conflict and letting the player choose which to verify turns contradictions into investigation targets.
when: When NPC schedules overlap in a shared space.

text: Showing the stolen item at the right moment can break an insider's composure or alibi, so the confrontation should be timed around revealing the object.
when: Confronting a suspect who denies knowledge

text: A large dose of a fast-acting poison should act within roughly an hour, so a long delay between dose and collapse counts against the simple theory.
when: when testing a poisoning theory against the clock

text: A chain of times or sources breaks if any one link is wrong; check each link, since one wrong time breaks every later inference.
when: a chain of events relies on several sources
why: One weak link undermines the whole sequence.

text: Character is an assumption about behaviour, and strong emotion can make people act out of character, so do not rule out a suspect on temperament alone.
when: A suspect has been cleared only by temperament.
why: Emotion and pressure can override usual behaviour.

text: Reading imprecise witness times as evasion ignores that stress weakens time sense and short-interval memory is unreliable; check remembered durations against physical signs.
when: a witness gives imprecise times about a tense event, or a timeline depends on remembered durations
why: Stress weakens time estimation, and memory of short intervals is unreliable.

text: Assumed waiting, travel or lead times can be wrong; a procedure may run faster or the adversary may be further ahead, so check assumptions and recompute when new evidence arrives.
why: Unverified assumptions carry into the conclusion and can understate how much time is lost.

text: Accepting a single vague time as an exact fact distorts the timeline.
why: approximate times carry a margin of error

text: Timelines built from vague periods such as a month or five weeks are hard to reconcile; make dates firm wherever a later test depends on them.
A schedule with vague durations cannot reveal a gap, so the timeline cannot be reconstructed from it.
when: When writing or auditing a timed schedule meant to expose deviations.
why: Without numbers there is no baseline to compare against.

text: A vague claim such as 'I was out that night' gives no timeline and can be broken by any single counter-witness.
Inferring the number of culprits assumes the group behaves rationally, so careless groups can produce traces that mislead the reasoning.
when: Inferring a group size from traces.
why: Groups can act carelessly, which the inference does not account for.

text: Dismissing a suspect because a plot seems unwise assumes a rational culprit, yet hired killers can themselves be dangerous.
when: a suspect is cleared on the basis of plot sense
why: the culprit may act irrationally or hire a risky accomplice

text: A deadline that is vague or never felt by the audience does not create tension.
A witness who seems insensible may still be listening, so the questioner should not assume they have stopped attending.
Assuming a sleeper would wake from any disturbance is a mistake; check how loud the disturbance would actually be first.
when: a claim says someone nearby heard nothing
why: Many actions are too quiet to wake a sleeper, but others are not.

text: An account of whereabouts with no names, places, or titles cannot be checked, yet it may be accepted because it sounds like work.
when: when a suspect explains an absence in general terms
why: vague specifics sound credible

text: Assuming everyone present in a scene was active can hide a silent or already incapacitated participant.
when: A witness describes several people in the same place.
why: Presence and activity are different and are easy to conflate.

text: Assuming an offender always acts in character can be exploited by one who deliberately changes methods.
when: Predicting a known offender's next move

text: A time window built on an assumption can make a valid alibi look false, or a false alibi look valid.
A witness who assumes a benign cause for a missed routine event may delay raising an alarm.
when: A regular event such as a meal is missed.
why: The witness explains the absence with an expected reason and waits too long.

text: Naming a character type from clothing and manner builds a label on assumption rather than evidence.
Assuming a seated person was present throughout an event. Absences during long thinking go unnoticed unless the timing record is checked.
Assuming an actor always acts sensibly makes the inference unreliable; it holds only when the actor's goal is understood.
when: Reasoning backward from an odd action.
why: Without the goal, the act's purpose cannot be reconstructed.

text: An alibi that depends on a third party's silence or ignorance is fragile; travel records and direct inquiry can expose it.
A shared boundary or old feud shows that someone could make an accusation, not that the accused actually caused harm.
why: Opportunity and motive do not establish that an act took place

text: Losing track of a person who leaves the group breaks the alibi chain and hides their movements.

1) State the physical access the act required. 2) List who was present and could reach that place at that moment, given access controls, such as staff and guests. 3) Note when the victim would have been unguarded. 4) Review each candidate on that shortlist.
when: a crime requires access that only some people had, or when assessing whether a suspect could have acted
why: Access and timing limit who could physically commit the act, so the shortlist rests on opportunity.

text: 1) Fix a clock time for each event. 2) Compute travel time from distance and vehicle performance for each pair of places. 3) Compare gaps and overlaps with the account. 4) Check each link against independent facts. 5) Identify the weakest link and seek an explanation before accepting the account.
when: When an alibi depends on movement across distance and a fixed schedule, or a suspect lacks an alibi and event times are known.
why: A sound-looking chain can hide one assumed step; gaps and overlaps show whether a person could have reached a scene in time.

text: 1) Ask a broad question about where the suspect was. 2) Narrow to destination, departure time, transport, companions and arrival time. 3) Ask for names of people, venues and transport.
when: an alibi is a sketch with blanks where names and times should be
why: Specific details can later be confirmed or contradicted.

text: 1) Record fixed times and when the house or place is empty. 2) Note known absences that open a window for entry. 3) Use routines and ordinary pretexts that allow access. 4) Count elapsed time since the last confirmed sighting. 5) Verify whether the clock itself is reliable.
when: Opportunity or an alibi depends on timing.
why: Knowing when a person could act requires both who was absent and whether the timekeeping can be trusted.

text: Vague times leave room for doubt; reject an estimate or alibi that fixes only a general period, press for an exact time, and treat its absence as a weak point.
Release clues through an in-world bulletin or news system on a schedule the designer controls, so information arrives in stages.
when: when designing a case that unfolds over time
why: Controlled timing paces discovery and prevents early disclosure.

text: Do not assume who was present; check the assumption against the witness's own description before acting on it.
when: Investigator holds a working hypothesis about a visitor
why: A hypothesis can make the investigator hear the expected answer.

text: Tie an NPC routine to a fixed day or hour, so the window in which the player must act is set by the routine.
when: a visit or action is allowed only at certain times
why: a time-limited routine creates a deadline

text: Use schedules such as patrols, shop hours and collections to set time windows that the player must reconcile with other evidence.
when: Designing time-based clues in a world.
why: Schedules give players a concrete timeline to check against other clues.

text: Time an accuser's relief to the suspect's restraint as a red flag the player is meant to notice.
when: when designing a false-accusation scene

text: Generate physical limits such as injury or a locked stable as constraints that rule a suspect out of a scene.
when: when designing suspects for a mystery
why: constraints let the player eliminate suspects through world state

text: Give an absence an ordinary cause, such as a meeting or a delivery, so players accept the wait before they learn it was suspicious.
when: when building delay into a timeline
why: An ordinary explanation makes the delay look harmless.

text: Keep one alibi link that depends on a fact outside the alibi's own frame, such as a boat's sailing time or a switchboard record.
why: An outside fact can break a claim the suspect controls.

text: Vague time intervals suit natural storytelling but frustrate players who need exact times to check an alibi; exact times allow checking.
when: when choosing how a timeline is presented to players

text: Chronological ordering helps most when evidence arrives piecemeal, and adds little when every event is witnessed and precisely timed.
when: deciding whether to build a full timeline
why: Precise timing already gives the order, so the extra work yields little.

text: 1) Fix the event's time window from independent clocks and observers. 2) Record each suspect's time claim and each sighting time. 3) Compute the gap between last sighting and discovery. 4) Check each account fits that gap, cross-checking witnesses covering different parts. 5) Test physical ability to reach the scene. 6) Keep competing causes on record.
when: when a suspect must be placed away from a scene at a given hour, or a timeline is contested, such as testing whether a person could have acted within a bounded window
why: Anchoring the window first keeps suspects' claims from defining it; bounded gaps show which accounts must be explained.

text: One broken link collapses a circumstantial chain however strong the others are, so to break a chain, seek one fact undermining its premise rather than attacking each link.
An alibi that checks out can overturn the investigator's working theory, so be ready to revise it.
Where a trail breaks off, reason about how the walker could have avoided leaving marks, such as by wading through water.
when: A track ends abruptly at water or hard ground.
why: Knowing how the walker avoided marks helps the investigator predict where to look next.

text: Link earlier insults to later misfortunes only with a visible causal trace, or players will read the link as unfair coincidence.
when: designing narrative consequences in a game
why: Unexplained links feel arbitrary to players.

text: When an accusation rests on what was seen, catch the suspect in the act, because otherwise the blame falls back on the accusers.
Disprove each false solution with a physical clue the player has already seen, such as footprints, a count of objects, or a record.
when: a suspect is ruled out during an investigation
why: Physical clues already in view make each correction verifiable and fair.

text: A broken alibi shows only a gap in location, not intent, so it should not be treated as proof of guilt.
why: location and motive are separate questions

text: A tightly bounded set of accepted facts excludes useful evidence that lies outside it, so the boundary should be widened when new credible evidence appears.
when: Maintaining a set of established facts during investigation.
why: An overly small set rejects clues that could complete the picture.

text: Trusting an alibi because it is detailed is a mistake, since specific detail is cheap to fabricate.
when: Evaluating a witness's account of their whereabouts
why: Invented specifics can be as convincing as true ones, so detail is not evidence

text: 1) List everyone with access to the scene, or the means and chance to act. 2) Establish the crime's time window. 3) Confirm each person's alibi against that window. 4) Clear those proven elsewhere; keep the rest for further testing.
when: when several people had access to the scene or the means and chance to act

text: 1) Establish motive. 2) Establish means, such as how the weapon was acquired. 3) Establish opportunity. 4) Argue each link in turn.
when: when no direct witness exists

text: 1) Identify the premise the alibi depends on, such as a sealed place or a fixed schedule. 2) Look for a gap in that premise, including unguarded routes. 3) Build a timeline from independent clocks and routines. 4) Place each witness's observation on it.
when: Testing an alibi that claims a place was sealed or a schedule was fixed.
why: An alibi is only as strong as its premises, and a timeline shows where a premise fails.

text: 1) List who had a motive to accuse. 2) Separate harm that followed a quarrel from harm the accused actually caused.
when: investigating an accusation built on a sequence of misfortunes
why: Sequence alone does not establish causation.

text: 1) List all possible explanations for a result. 2) Drop each explanation that conflicts with the facts. 3) Accept the remaining explanation, after checking the candidate list is complete.
when: Several causes could explain a result
why: Elimination narrows candidates to what the evidence supports

text: 1) Attend the scheduled event yourself rather than relying on memory. 2) Record when each suspect is absent from the scene. 3) Compare absences across suspects to find who had an unobserved window.
when: A crime occurred during a scheduled event with clear entrances and exits.
why: Direct observation produces reliable absence records that memory cannot.

text: When motive reasoning reaches a deadlock, introduce a new clue that breaks the tie.
when: two suspects remain equally plausible after motive tests

text: Make the real culprit's alibi a witnessed event whose sightline misleads, and make the witness's account something the player can check.
why: A checkable sightline lets a careful player catch the deception.

text: A missing alibi may be neutral (no witness, unwilling silence, or no deliberate cover) or raise suspicion as an unfilled timeline gap; it never proves guilt alone.
when: when a suspect's movements cannot be corroborated
why: The same gap has several causes; many innocent people lack alibis; a missing alibi is a problem of evidence, not innocence, and an unverified claim is not a false one.

text: A stated alibi can be tested by checking it at a second location, such as an office or inn, which shows whether the claim holds.
when: A suspect's whereabouts matter to the case
why: A second location provides independent confirmation.

text: Every detail a witness repeats becomes a claim that can be checked, so alibis hold only while stories stay consistent and timing holds.
when: when assessing or building an alibi
why: Repeated details create a trail that others can test.

text: Make every acquittal or alibi reveal a new secret instead of ending the case.
when: when a witness clears a suspect
why: Clearing a suspect should move the investigation forward, not end it.

text: Make the alibi that clears the primary suspect and the disguised witness the same event, so clearing one exposes the other.
when: Writing an alibi that must also reveal the true culprit.
why: A shared event means the alibi cannot be accepted without re-examining the witness.

text: Tracking alibis as sworn records makes a disproved alibi visibly collapse a suspect's standing.
when: A suspect's alibi is contradicted by new evidence.
why: Visible state change lets the player see how evidence reshapes suspicion.

text: A single credible alibi can overturn a chain of suspicion built on physical clues, shifting the player's belief to another suspect.
when: a suspect has been built up by circumstantial evidence
why: Testimony that breaks a theory forces the player to abandon a chain of reasoning, reopening the case.

text: A trusted narrator's alibi for a suspect leads the audience to assume the narrator is protecting that suspect.
when: a narrator vouches for someone
why: Trust in the narrator transfers suspicion onto the vouched-for person

text: An alibi supported by family and servants may be sincere yet shaped by loyalty, so it is not fully independent.
when: An alibi rests on witnesses bound to the suspect.
why: Social ties can bias testimony even without intent to deceive.

text: 1) Send the one witness who could see you away on a plausible errand. 2) Wait for a quiet interval after their movements fade. 3) Choose the exit least likely to be watched. 4) Leave the way back in unbarred.
when: A suspect must leave a house unseen and knows the household's routines.
why: Removing observers and timing the exit lowers the chance of being noticed.

text: 1) State each witness's vantage point. 2) Record the time each witness reports. 3) Compare the accounts side by side. 4) Mark where they agree and where they conflict.
when: Testing a suspect's alibi against several witnesses
why: Conflicts between witnesses and vantage points become timeline clues

text: 1) Ask the suspect where they were. 2) Ask whether anyone can confirm it. 3) Mark any period without an outside witness as unverified.
when: when testing a suspect's account of their movements
why: A suspect's word alone cannot establish an alibi.

text: 1) Identify the suspect's known location at the time of the crime. 2) Check whether that location could be reached and returned from in the available time. 3) Clear the suspect if the trip is impossible.
when: a suspect is accused and has a claimed whereabouts
why: a verified alibi removes a suspect from consideration

text: 1) List each character's expected location for each hour from their routine. 2) Confirm each routine with observation. 3) Identify which characters could have acted at each hour.
when: A crime is assumed to have happened at night
why: Schedules turn alibis into positions in time that can be tested.

text: 1) Write down the suspect's claimed whereabouts and time. 2) Find a record kept by someone the suspect did not control. 3) Compare the record with the claim. 4) Compare the timeline with arrival and departure moments of others.
when: A suspect's account of where they were can be tested against records kept by others.
why: A planned alibi can be built to match the suspect's own story, but independent sources are harder to shape.

text: An alibi holds only if its timing and location can be checked against independent evidence, such as travel records or a message timed to the event.
when: A suspect's account depends on travel times or a single witness, or when checking whether the suspect could have committed an event at a given time.
why: Unverifiable timing and place leave the alibi open to challenge; a timed message or independent travel record makes the claim checkable.

text: An alibi is only as strong as the time window it covers; check for unaccounted intervals before accepting it.
when: Evaluating an alibi
why: A gap in coverage leaves room for the act.

text: A confirmed alibi shows only absence from the scene, not non-involvement, yet it can end a suspect theory; a missing motive should first prompt checking for an unfound form.
when: When a confirmed alibi or a missing motive challenges a suspect theory.
why: Premature dismissal and stubborn defence both distort the investigation, and involvement can occur without physical presence at the scene.

text: Dated documents such as letters, receipts or absence records can support an alibi, verified against an independent travel or movement log or by others' confirmation.
why: Cross-checking independent dated sources tests a claimed whereabouts.

text: An alibi or quarrel account is only as strong as the independent witnesses who saw events; named witnesses who cannot be found or whose roles do not fit are fragile.
An alibi is a dead end if its witness cannot be named or questioned, and weak when no one can confirm the suspect's location or the alibi witness is unreliable.

1) List each sighting of the suspect's two identities. 2) Check whether any moment shows both together; a missing joint sighting is an easily overlooked gap. 3) Look for arrivals or departures no one saw. 4) Test whether the absence matters before concluding impersonation.
when: A suspect's whereabouts rest on sightings of separate identities, or people described as separate may be one person.
why: Gaps in witnessed overlap reveal possible impersonation.

text: 1) Take the last sighting alive as earliest bound and discovery time as latest. 2) Narrow the range with maximum survival time after a known poisoning. 3) List each witness's position and view. 4) Check whether each suspect was covered in the window.
when: Testing whether a suspect could have been present when the time of death is uncertain but independent times exist.
why: Two bounds plus a known duration limit the window; an alibi is only as strong as the timeline and witness coverage.

text: 1) Record where each witness was and measure the distance to the place described. 2) Stand there and look along the claimed line of sight. 3) Reject observations from places the witness could not have reached or seen from.
when: Testing a witness's claim to have seen an event.
why: A claim requires physical presence and a clear line of sight.

text: Keep timestamped logs and telemetry, such as power or water use, of NPC movements and events, linking each whereabouts claim to them so players can rebuild order and find contradictions.
when: When designing a mystery or witness system where timing or whereabouts matter.
why: Ordered, recorded entries let players check consistency; contradictions become discoverable by comparison.

text: Test an alibi against the household routine, which must itself be verified; a claimed location conflicting with usual pattern, like a room found empty when occupied, exposes it.
when: A witness claims to have been somewhere during a routine period, or when evaluating a character's whereabouts against a routine.
why: Deviations from habit are hard to explain away; a routine never observed is only a claim.

text: Clearing a suspect with several independent checks makes exoneration credible and gives separate steps; one concrete physical detail is quicker and more convincing.
when: When exonerating a suspect seen near the scene or in a mystery.
why: Several checks add verifiable steps, while a single specific detail is faster to state.

text: Testimony from brief, dim, crowded or shocked sightings, including of disguised people, yields only general impressions and must be tested before trust.
when: poor lighting, distance, crowding, disguise, brief glimpses or shock
why: Recall depends on what observers could see and what they were attending to.

text: Sleep is a weak alibi: a sleeper cannot vouch for their own timing, so the claim is unverifiable and the timeline must rely on other evidence.
when: When an alibi rests on being asleep, or a timeline is built from testimony during a night event.
why: Unconscious time is unobserved and unverifiable; sleep disrupts awareness of time.

text: Callers' visits and calls can serve as a second record of who was present in a place and at what time.
when: When corroborating a household or location timeline with outside observations.
why: Independent witnesses to presence cross-check the routine.

text: Several independent alibis from separate sources count for more than one unverified claim, since each source can be checked on its own.
when: Ranking suspects by alibi strength
why: Independent sources do not share the same error or motive

text: Household records of times out and in confirm departure and return but say nothing about what happened in between.
when: when using door or entry records to check a suspect's timeline
why: Entry times bracket a period without showing activity within it.

text: A fixed timeline can look trustworthy at first, then be exposed by checking it against a second clock source that reveals the timings were staged.
when: Designing a mystery where a character's alibi relies on a timetable or clock.
why: A second independent time source can contradict an apparently solid timeline and expose the deception.

text: Playing the reproduced sound can serve as its own proof of an audio alibi, so no witness is needed to establish the trick.
why: The sound itself matches the claimed alibi.

text: Ask where unstated time went and check the edges and exceptions of long or fixed alibis, since short absences and unobserved gaps may hide there.
when: A timeline has silent periods, an alibi covers a long span, or a schedule seems fixed.
why: Silent windows and window edges can hide movements the account omits.

text: An alibi resting on one uncertain sighting, or on a sighting covering only part of the required interval, is partial and should not clear a suspect.
when: when the witness admits the sighting may be mistaken, or covers only part of the span
why: Sightings can cover only part of an interval, so partial or uncertain coverage cannot clear the whole window.

text: An untested alibi or unrecorded gap should stay open and be reopened when new evidence fills or changes it, since a claim is not verified until checked.
Check an alibi through independent accounts covering each hour in question; detailed, corroborated records can clear a suspect despite an early failure to account for time.
when: verifying a suspect's movements
why: independent coverage of each window tests the claim

text: Check a detained person's identity before treating them as the target, since a plausible arrival can be the wrong person.
Let NPCs accept a cover identity only when they lack a verifying contact, so a player who learns the network can expose the impostor.
when: Designing NPC trust in an impostor plot
why: Gating acceptance on verification gives players a route to expose the lie

text: Combine a process-based time window with each person's last-seen time to narrow who could have acted.
why: Intersecting two independent time constraints eliminates candidates.

text: Use a third party's sighting to test a claimed alibi when that party was positioned to see the departure.
when: Checking whether someone was where they claimed
why: A positioned observer can confirm or break a claimed location

text: Before trusting a report of hearing nothing, ask what the observer's own noise and attention were at the time.
when: a witness says they heard nothing
why: The observer's conditions may have masked what others could hear

text: Tie an alibi to other characters' sightings and a travel time, so the claim can be checked against the distance involved.
when: when building a character's alibi
why: checkable claims make deception testable

text: An alibi based on being elsewhere can be arranged to avoid a suspected item, so verify the absence itself.
when: a suspect's alibi is an absence

text: Corroboration from a suspect's own companion carries little weight, since that witness shares the suspect's interest.
when: when assessing an alibi supported only by a companion
why: A companion may be unable or unwilling to contradict the suspect.
