text: Check a suspect's claimed history of odd episodes against the timing of the suspicious act and against other witness statements before accepting it as the innocent explanation.
when: A suspect's past episodes are offered to explain suspicious conduct.
why: A convenient explanation may be invented or misdated, so it needs independent checking.

text: A leg that the first object cannot explain can reveal a second object or a hidden handover between parties.
Record when a clue was removed and when it returned. The gaps between these times show when the room was empty and when someone could have handled the clue.
when: A physical clue moves within a room whose occupancy you can track
why: Movement timing reveals the handler's routine

text: Give several NPCs overlapping schedules, each with a plausible alibi, so players must test opportunity rather than consistency.
when: designing suspect sets
why: alibis that look consistent force players to check access instead

text: When a group of related items is missing, check that group's records instead of dropping the gap, since clustered absences can share a cause.
when: Several linked items have no recovered record
why: Clustered absences can point to a shared event

text: A verified location at the time of an alleged act contradicts the claim and suggests the account was fabricated.
when: when the time and place of the act are reasonably reliable

text: Several broken routines together are stronger evidence than one missed routine, which alone proves little.
Letting a sceptic check a detail personally turns doubt into belief more effectively than assertion.
when: Persuading a doubter of a physical claim.
why: Being able to verify a detail removes the need to trust the presenter.

text: Build a cover story from real, checkable particulars, because mixing true details makes the lie easier to hold.
when: when a cover story must survive checks
why: true details are consistent with what the questioner can observe

text: An arrival that no one witnessed, when a normal means of transport would have brought the person to the door, is a gap to investigate.
when: A suspect's return home is unobserved.
why: Unobserved movement can hide a swap of identities.

text: Build a timeline by lining up dated events, witness ages and intervals from several testimonies; a timeline that fits all of them is more credible than one that fits only some.
when: When reconstructing events from partial records.
why: Independent dates and ages can be cross-checked against each other to expose errors.

text: An absent principal with an alibi can be used to avoid suspicion, so the player must find the party who actually acted.
when: Designing a mystery where the planner is away
why: Distance from the crime protects the planner and shifts investigation

text: When an alibi cannot be checked, it is not decisive, so weigh it against the other available evidence.
when: When an alibi has no independent check.

text: A sighting placed around midnight is only as reliable as its time, so find a source that can fix the hour.
why: approximate times weaken a sighting

text: Design NPC alibi statements that can be checked against other clocks, since a claimed location cuts down the possible window.
when: when designing suspect statements in a mystery level
why: Checkable claims let players narrow the timeline and test the suspect.

text: A stated schedule can be false, so check an alibi against independent sightings and physical evidence.
when: Evaluating a suspect's claimed whereabouts
why: A written or reported schedule can be fabricated

text: A fact that seems to clear a suspect should be checked for who could have produced it, since a planner can stage an alibi.
An alibi given by an associate of a suspect is weak support, and it can keep that suspect in the frame.
Timed records (a driver's trip, a performance, a train departure, a published timetable) fix a person to a place and hour, confirming or breaking alibis against witness times.
when: Designing alibi or transit-based investigation, including NPC alibis players can check.
why: Matching times across independent sources exposes contradictions.

text: A timed absence can give a suspect an opportunity to act, and the resulting changes become evidence for the player to find.
when: When designing timed or absence-based investigation mechanics
why: Removing observation creates a window in which hidden actions occur and leave traces.

text: A letter from a trusted intermediary vouching for a bearer lets an unknown stranger be accepted when combined with the token.
when: A stranger is introduced to a contact they do not know
why: Endorsement from a trusted party carries weight with the person approached

text: An alibi covering a gap can be exposed by asking whether the claimed hours could physically hold the claimed actions, given the true timeline.
when: A suspect's account relies on undocumented events filling a time gap.
why: Invented events must fit the physical constraints of the time window to hold up.

text: An alibi is contradicted when a measurable interval between known points is much longer than the travel time between them, leaving an unexplained gap that may cover the crime.
when: When a suspect's account of a short interval can be measured against travel times
why: The unexplained surplus of time is the window in which the suspect could have acted.

text: Guard patrol schedules define alibi windows, so a player who checks the rounds can find the gap in which a theft was possible.
when: Designing alibis or timing puzzles around guard routes.
why: Patrol gaps create opportunity windows that players can reconstruct.

text: A solid alibi keeps suspicion from settling on a suspect until new evidence breaks the alibi.
An alibi made of many small claims can pass each check alone yet collapse when the claims are linked, so the lie appears only when checks are combined.
when: when a suspect's alibi is tested
why: Each claim looks independent, so its failure is hidden until the claims are compared.

text: Model NPC verification in three tiers: some never check, some check one record, and some check everything.
when: designing NPC checks on player identity

text: An alibi or timeline resting on a single source, such as one person's word, one watch reading or one police check, is unverified and needs independent corroboration.
when: A schedule or alibi depends on one source or one outside check.
why: A single source can be wrong, incomplete or influenced, and unchecked claims cannot be confirmed against independent facts.

text: Accepting an alibi or a witness's explanation of presence without checking its exact hours, or timings never checked against each other, lets a suspect pass with a gap.
Relative phrases such as 'about thirteen years ago', and dates taken from secondary accounts, must be checked against other dates or primary records, since errors shift the timeline.
why: Relative phrases drift and can point to the wrong year; a secondary account's error spreads through everything built on it and can move a case to the wrong decade.

text: Trusting a device's reading without asking whether it runs true lets an uncorrected offset silently distort the whole timeline.
Counting repeated events such as laps or rounds without a record produces vague estimates of how many occurred.
A first check on an alibi can be too thin to catch a lie, so follow up with deeper verification.
when: When an alibi has been checked only once
why: Shallow verification misses fabrications that deeper testing would expose.

text: Vague dates with no in-character reason for the vagueness feel like authorial convenience rather than character.
why: Readers accept vagueness only when it has a cause

text: Accepting an alibi without checking its timeline for gaps, or keeping a theory after the suspect is cleared, leads to wrong arrests and wasted investigation.
Confirming one link of an alibi does not confirm the whole chain, and a partly true story can hide the time that matters.
when: when evaluating an alibi with several steps
why: Each link must hold on its own for the chain to hold.

text: Fixing the suspect window on the moment of collapse ignores earlier dosing and can clear the real culprit.
Assuming an object's place of origin equals the place of the crime ignores its transit history, since items can be moved, re-addressed or reused to mislead.
when: when an object's origin is used to locate an event
why: Objects travel through several places, and their labels or wrappers may not reflect where they were last used.

text: A witness who offers a useful accusation may still be lying about their own movements, so check both.
A distance or alibi test works only when each witness's location is recorded in the sources.
A theory that fits the timing of deposits may still be wrong, so hold it as provisional until a second source confirms it.
when: Adopting a leading theory from financial records.
why: Timing agreement is one signal and does not establish cause.

text: A sleeping witness cannot confirm his own activity, so an alibi resting only on his presence proves little.
when: when an alibi depends on the alibi holder's own presence or activity
why: The witness cannot observe the claimed activity while asleep

text: Self-reported durations can hide errors, since people often estimate how long an activity lasted from their own sense of it.
when: A witness gives the length of a noise or activity without a clock
why: Subjective time perception is unreliable

text: An unexplained delay in an account, such as a short errand taking long, is itself worth examining.
when: A witness's stated duration for a simple task seems too long.
why: The gap may hide the actual activity.

text: An absent alibi is not proof of guilt; an unconfirmed alibi is an open checklist question, not evidence against the person.
why: Two innocent and guilty readings of the same gap are both possible.

text: A suspect's irregular habits make an alibi from a household member weak.
when: when a household member vouches for a suspect's movements
why: Erratic routines are hard for others to track reliably.

text: Dropping alibi checks once a case feels settled lets an apparent solution hide the real lead.
when: A case appears resolved early
why: Settled-feeling cases stop being tested

text: A self-reported alibi should not be treated as settled; check it against other events and records.
when: Assessing a suspect's claimed whereabouts
why: Self-reports can be wrong or deliberately false and need independent corroboration

text: 1) State the claimed location, time and companion. 2) Find an independent record, such as a doorman's log or establishment time-clock, that the claimant does not control. 3) Confirm whether the claimed event occurred there; accept the alibi only if the record supports it.
when: when an alibi rests on an arrival, appointment or presence claim
why: Only evidence the witness did not control confirms a claimed hour, place or companion; the suspect's own account alone is weak support.

text: 1) Bound a person's movements with timestamps from their last sighting and report. 2) Test the alibi against several independent witnesses at different times and points. 3) Weigh whether coincidental sightings are linked or unrelated.
when: when verifying a suspect's account against a timeline or when an alibi rests on sightings
why: Several independent sources make an alibi more reliable; one vague witness can be mistaken or lying, and independent observers at different points make movement hard to fake.

text: 1) Record every event time against one shared reference clock. 2) Log later checks at fixed times. 3) Test each reported time against those recorded points.
when: Alibis or movements depend on times within a building, or several alibis fall within one window.
why: Shared clocks prevent inconsistent memories from distorting comparison; reconciling reported times with clocks actually read prevents memory errors.

text: 1) State the claimed identity, title or document. 2) Find an independent record, such as an authoritative reference, handwriting sample, laundry mark, directory or insurer's registration, that can confirm or exclude it. 3) Check the record against the claim. 4) Note what the record cannot show.
when: when an identity, title or document must be confirmed before it is accepted
why: Independent records test a claim, while a claim with no independent check rests on assumption.

text: 1) Record each event with its time. 2) Compare event times with witness-stated times and activity durations. 3) Test whether each claimed movement fits the gaps between events.
when: a suspect's movements are in doubt, witnesses give different times, or events are reconstructed from observations
why: Repeated time-ordered records let investigators rebuild where a vessel or person moved and rule possibilities in or out, showing whether a claimed position was physically possible.

text: 1) Note the time and place of the claimed engagement. 2) Send a note to the named other party through a third person. 3) Use the reply to confirm or contradict the claim. A dead party cannot confirm it, so the appointment stays unverified.
when: a suspect names a specific appointment, or a witness claims an arrangement with someone who has died
why: Only the other party can confirm the arrangement, and an independent party can verify the claim.

text: 1) Split the suspect's account into separate, checkable movements, with times, places and sums. 2) Find an independent source for each, such as staff accounts, purchase logs, shipping manifests, telegrams or people with no stake. 3) Mark unconfirmed or contradicted steps and weigh them rather than dismissing them.
when: a suspect or witness claims a place and time, or gives a timed account with several checkable steps
why: Each movement must stand on its own evidence; a precise, checkable account is harder to fake than a vague one.

text: 1) Identify the witness's position. 2) Determine what could physically be seen from it. 3) Separate what was observed from what was assumed, and check the observation is possible.
when: when judging any eyewitness account or claim to have seen something from a position
why: Physical visibility can rule out an observation regardless of the witness's sincerity.

text: 1) Fix each claimed time from a witness. 2) Estimate travel time between claimed positions, to the scene and back. 3) Check whether the gap allows the claimed location to be reached and returned from in time.
when: testing whether a suspect could reach the scene or a claimed location

text: 1) Write the claimed route with its times. 2) Check whether visibility and timing allow unseen positions along it. 3) Test secondary records such as tickets, timepieces and dated vouchers against the route, since checking only the headline misses cover-ups.
when: checking whether a claimed alibi holds
why: Secondary records can contradict a claim that looks correct at first.

text: 1) Identify who vouches for the suspect and when each saw them, or the exact time and place of a specific sighting. 2) Check that the witness's coverage spans that time and place. 3) Rule the suspect out only if the window covers the crime moment.
when: a suspect claims to have been elsewhere during a narrow window, or a specific sighting contradicts or supports presence
why: An alibi clears a suspect only if its window overlaps the crime; a broad alibi can fail to cover a narrow sighting.

text: 1) Identify the alibi's claim and its vague points. 2) Note where timing or location is uncertain. 3) Test the weakest point first against the suspect's behaviour, seeking direct confirmation from the source rather than a written summary.
when: checking a suspect's alibi, especially one reported second-hand
why: Vague alibis hide weak points, summaries drop details that expose them, and a suspect's later response can reveal them.

text: 1) Ask a second NPC about the same person, or ask the speaker to repeat a detail. 2) Check every newly named person against other witnesses. 3) Accept identity only when the checks agree.
when: when a player must verify who is speaking or who has been named
why: Independent checks turn a cue into confirmation.

text: 1) Ask who could have been elsewhere at the time. 2) Identify independent witnesses who could confirm the claimed whereabouts. 3) Check the distance and travel time between places against the claim.
when: when testing whether a suspect was elsewhere
why: independent confirmation and travel feasibility decide whether the alibi holds

text: 1) Verify the alibi documents. 2) If they hold, drop the suspect. 3) If they are false, keep the suspect in play.
when: before clearing any suspect

text: 1) Fix the timeline with exact times for each event. 2) List the physical traces the account implies. 3) Search for marks that differ by direction of movement. 4) Recover any objects said to have changed hands. 5) Use a plausible pretext for inspection.
when: when a suspect's alibi rests on a private meeting no one else can confirm
why: Physical traces and fixed times test whether the account is consistent with the scene.

text: 1) Note the unknown sighting. 2) List every household member. 3) Place each one at the relevant time by direct observation or report. 4) Rule out those placed elsewhere. 5) Keep narrowing until the gap is small.
when: when a sighting or noise must be placed among known people

text: 1) Choose the time of an event. 2) Look up where each suspect was at that time. 3) Flag any conflict between a suspect's location and the event as a clue.
when: when the player checks suspects against an event
why: Conflicts in location and time become discoverable evidence

text: 1) Record the exact detail of the alibi document, such as seat, row and date. 2) Compare it with an independent record. 3) Treat a mismatch as a contradiction of the alibi.
when: a suspect's alibi rests on a ticket or similar document
why: independent records are harder to alter than a suspect's account

text: 1) Identify people with no stake in the outcome who were near the place. 2) Ask each specific questions about the suspect's presence during the window. 3) Record which claims each one confirms.
when: when a suspect's presence at a place and time is central

text: 1) Map the claimed location and the route to it. 2) Look for physical traces of a route out and back. 3) Time the trip against the critical window. 4) Check the suspect's recent purchases for preparation.
when: A suspect claims to have been elsewhere and the layout of the location may decide whether that is possible.
why: Geometry, timing and possession together show opportunity and planning that a bare claim does not.

text: 1) Record the suspect's claimed location and time. 2) Gather accounts from people with no stake in the claim. 3) Find accounts that place the suspect elsewhere during the same window. 4) Attack the single conflict rather than the whole story.
when: a suspect's account depends on being somewhere else
why: One independent contradiction can break an otherwise coherent alibi.

text: 1) Build a timeline of the suspect's stated movements. 2) Confirm each step through sources the suspect does not control. 3) Request replies quickly so they can shape the next step. 4) Compare travel distance with the time window.
when: When testing whether a suspect could have been present at a crime.
why: Independent records are harder to fake than a suspect's own account.

text: 1) Pin down the exact date by asking the witness directly. 2) Ask whether a specific person was involved before accepting any description. 3) Test the record against other facts before building a timeline on it.
when: a minor official recorded who passed and when

text: 1) Identify the alibi-giver. 2) Ask whether the alibi-giver would swear to the account under legal scrutiny. 3) Check the account against transport or witness records.
when: An alibi depends on one person's word.
why: A sworn account exposes weak or false claims to challenge.

text: 1) List the claimed times: departure, arrival, and activity between. 2) Identify who can confirm each step. 3) Note weak links. 4) Corroborate each step with independent records or witnesses. 5) Keep a separate timeline per person and compare them.
when: when a suspect offers a timed account of their movements
why: An alibi is strong only if each of its times can be checked independently.

text: 1) Fix the suspect's location with witnesses at the trigger time. 2) Have the victim move to the danger zone at a chosen moment. 3) Keep witnesses' attention away from the danger.
when: a suspect must appear innocent while the crime is timed by them
why: Combining a witnessed location with a victim's timed movement breaks the link between suspect and crime.

text: 1) Establish the departure time and the announced route. 2) Estimate expected arrival from usual travel time and the shortest route. 3) Contact the expected destination to learn whether the party has arrived. 4) Choose how fast to act from the lead.
when: a witness's account of movements can be checked at a fixed point
why: a check at a point someone else controls turns an estimate into a verified fact

text: 1) Have the suspect confirm the exact time of the claimed event. 2) Establish whereabouts across the whole crime window. 3) Compare the claimed behavior with the person's known routine. 4) Note hesitations or self-corrections.
when: an alibi depends on a claimed time or place
why: a claim is only as strong as its time and location

text: 1) Pin the suspect to a location at the exact hour of the crime. 2) Question everyone present where the suspect claims to have been. 3) Canvass the route between that location and the crime scene. 4) Seek one reliable witness who places the suspect near the scene in the window.
when: a suspect has a claimed alibi that can be checked
why: one reliable sighting turns an alibi into circumstantial evidence

text: 1) Identify the suspect's claimed time and place. 2) Ask the people who were with them then. 3) Cross-check each account against other reports for shared contacts or conflicts.
1) Start from an unaccounted group of seats or tickets. 2) Get the specific seat numbers. 3) Check them against unsold-ticket stock and issuing records.
when: a group of tickets or seats is unaccounted for, or attendance contradicts the normal pattern

text: 1) Mark fixed event cues on a shared timeline. 2) Mark when each person had to be present. 3) Find the gap that would let an absent person leave and return unnoticed.
when: An alibi depends on minutes within a scheduled event.
why: A timeline anchored to fixed cues exposes the windows where a person could act unseen.

text: 1) Record each suspect claim about movements, possessions or state. 2) Link each claim to a named witness or dated record. 3) Mark which claims others confirm or contradict.
when: a suspect's whereabouts are the central question
why: each claim can then be tested against independent sources

text: 1) Identify the independent witnesses who can confirm an alibi. 2) Check the alibi against each witness's account. 3) Treat an unverified alibi as unproven, not cleared; an alibi resting only on the suspect's word is weak.
when: A suspect offers an alibi.
why: Independent confirmation is needed; a given alibi may be weak or stronger than believed.

text: 1) Pin the alibi to an exact time. 2) Check the physical route between the claimed place and the scene. 3) Look for a third party's timestamp that fixes the suspect's movements. 4) Measure travel time against the gap.
when: Testing whether a claimed whereabouts can be true.
why: A time-bound claim checked against routes and independent records can be confirmed or broken.

text: 1) Fix each person's arrival, location and last sighting of the victim. 2) Treat each claimed meeting as a hypothesis. 3) Test it against independent witnesses, records and physical traces. 4) Record who gave each statement and when.
when: A suspect's presence depends on memory or a single uncorroborated account.
why: Independent checks separate verified facts from unsupported claims.

text: 1) Record the time and place the suspect names. 2) Compare them with the timeline of the act. 3) Look for a witness who can confirm the location.
when: A suspect offers an alibi against a specific charge
why: A time alone, without a witness, is hard to prove

text: 1) Identify the traces that must exist if the account is true. 2) Check the site for each one. 3) Note which traces are absent or contradicted before accepting the claim.
when: A witness describes entry or exit through a closed space.
why: Physical traces test whether an impossible route really happened.

text: Place each suspect's location at relevant hours, and confirm what each person could have known, such as whether the owner knew the contents of a secured place.
when: Establishing who could have acted during a time window
why: Locations and knowledge at specific hours separate possible actors from impossible ones

text: 1) Pin down the time span when the offence was possible. 2) Test other plausible time spans. 3) Compare the suspect's known activities against sightings in each span. 4) Ask who could have taken the suspect's place.
when: a suspect's whereabouts at a precise hour decide the case
why: an alibi holds only if it fits the window the evidence supports

text: 1) Identify the time gap the alibi must cover. 2) Establish what was physically possible in that window. 3) Anchor the timeline to independent dated events. 4) Verify claimed communications with the source system, not the recipient.
when: Testing a suspect's alibi against other evidence.
why: Recipients can confirm a message arrived while the system record shows it never happened.

text: 1) Fix the timeline of the evening with known times. 2) Measure the intervals between known points, starting with the most measurable one. 3) Use the measured travel time to test each explanation the suspect offers. 4) Press on duration when the suspect says time simply passed.
when: When testing a suspect's alibi against a crime time
why: Measurable intervals give a fixed reference that vague explanations cannot easily cover.

text: 1) Identify the chain of people the lead passed through. 2) Discount the teller's emotion and prejudice. 3) Test the named person against an independent record. 4) If no match, try other records or regions before deciding. 5) Make further discreet inquiries rather than accepting or dismissing the claim.
when: Information arrives through several relays, especially from a biased teller.
why: Each relay adds distance from the original event, and a failed match in one register does not prove a claim false.

text: 1) State a prediction with an exact time and place. 2) Synchronize all clocks beforehand. 3) Place the observer where they cannot be seen, with a plan for afterward. 4) Watch and record the outcome, including if nothing happens.
when: when a theory depends on a person's routine or on something being perceived
why: shared time and hidden position make the observed result trustworthy

text: 1) Revisit the scene to test its layout, sightlines and exit routes. 2) Question each witness about timing. 3) Test the times against each other. 4) Note every vehicle or visitor present.
when: Timing and positions at a scene are unclear.
why: Witnesses often know parts of a sequence but not all of it.

text: 1) Record every stated time. 2) Compute the intervals between them. 3) Check whether each movement fits its gap. 4) Mark unaccounted windows. 5) Treat estimates such as about or nearly as ranges.
when: Reconstructing a sequence of events from a confession or witness account
why: Laying out intervals shows what was physically possible and where the account fails

text: 1) Follow a subject with a tail. 2) Have the tail report each sighting with its time and place. 3) Link sightings into a route.
when: A subject's movements must be tracked across a location.
why: Timed, located reports build a route that can be checked.

text: 1) Collect dated church votes, diary entries and wills. 2) Order them by date. 3) Cross-check each date against a second source where possible. 4) Use the ordered list as the timeline.
when: When building a town or institution's history from documents.
why: Dated documents give fixed points, and cross-checking catches conflicting dates.

text: 1) Identify the time window a suspect's account fixes. 2) Find a physical trace that could test that window, such as weather marks or dust disturbance. 3) Confirm the environmental fact from an independent source before drawing a conclusion.
when: When a suspect's account fixes a time window that a physical trace can test.
why: Independent confirmation prevents an innocent cause from being mistaken for guilt.

text: 1) Ask the NPC who arrived when and by which route. 2) Compare the account with recorded arrivals. 3) Confirming or contradicting the account unlocks the next line of questioning.
when: Building alibi checks in an investigation game.
why: Arrival records give a checkable structure for testing NPC accounts.

text: 1) Ask how long the witness believes an event lasted. 2) Compare that against dated, independent records such as registers or logs. 3) Check any physical trace that fixes when the event ended.
when: when a witness's timing is central to an alibi or to a claim that events lasted longer than records show
why: Independent records are not shaped by the witness's memory

text: 1) Time the alibi and identify the window in which an absence could occur. 2) Identify each confirming source. 3) Ask whether each source had a stake in the outcome. 4) Seek independent support for interested sources.
when: Assessing an alibi confirmed by family or associates
why: Interested witnesses may shade their account, so independent support is needed

text: 1) Place each event on a shared timeline. 2) Test each alibi against the recorded times. 3) Check each claimed location against the travel routes of the people involved.
when: Several people claim to be elsewhere

text: 1) Write down every day and place named in each statement. 2) Compare each claimed location against an independent source such as a schedule or log. 3) Note the day where a record contradicts a claim. 4) Compare each person's claimed visits against the record.
when: Two accounts of the same time conflict, or a record can confirm or refute a claim
why: Independent records expose contradictions that the accounts themselves conceal

text: Verify an alibi through a source the suspect does not control, such as a third party's call or an employer's shift log, rather than the suspect's own word.
when: When checking a suspect's stated whereabouts.
why: A source the suspect controls can confirm a false story; a bare statement clears no one until verified.

text: Accept an alibi only when independent, disinterested witnesses confirm the exact time window that matters; discount confirmation from someone with a stake, such as a spouse.
when: Assessing an alibi that rests on witnesses.
why: A confirmer with a personal interest has reason to shade the account; disinterested witnesses are less likely to.

text: Check a mutual alibi against a separate independent source, and whether the two vouchers were ever observed in the same place at the same moment.
when: Two witnesses vouch for each other.

text: Let the player confirm an NPC's alibi with a second NPC; a mismatch exposes the lie, so record each NPC's reliability in its character data.
when: Designing alibis in a game, when an NPC gives a claimed whereabouts.
why: Independent accounts can conflict.

text: Give each NPC a schedule players can verify through clocks, bells, guard rotations or travel times, plus an alibi checker comparing NPC statements against them, letting characters contradict one another.
when: Designing a game with NPC alibis.
why: Travel-time checks make alibis testable through play.

text: Every leg of a claimed schedule needs an independent witness, such as a clerk, conductor or companion, who saw the person at that place and time; unwitnessed legs stay unverified.
when: A suspect offers a detailed schedule.
why: Unwitnessed legs cannot be verified.

text: Do not accept a schedule-based alibi or timestamped purchase until the crime time is confirmed by an independent source or fixed in the game state.
why: The alibi holds only if the time it rests on is genuine; it can only be checked against a known event time.

text: Treat an alibi as something to actively disprove, tested by investigators against physical and timing evidence; the suspect need not prove it.
why: Checking is the investigator's job.

text: Test a stated alibi against a source the suspect does not control, and check whether the claimed place and time were physically possible.
when: A suspect gives a specific time and place.
why: Proof supplied by the suspect can be fabricated; only an outside source can confirm it.

text: Treat an alibi as unconfirmed when its owner refuses to say where they were, since silence cannot verify absence.
Undated or estimated times cannot support a timeline check, so mark them as unverifiable rather than as established.
when: a witness gives vague times
why: Vague timing cannot confirm or refute presence

text: Check an alibi against how the person would plausibly have behaved, since a claimed alibi can fail on behavioral grounds alone.
Design alibi documents with a detectable mismatch so the player must spot the inconsistency before an NPC is cleared.
Verify a claimant's description of the item against the item itself before handing it over.
when: When a person comes forward to claim a found object
why: A claim that matches the item is far more likely to be genuine than one that does not.

text: Test a claim of continuous presence against a machine record, and discount any log kept by the person whose claim is being tested.
when: when a witness claims to have been present throughout
why: a self-kept log is not independent

text: Contact a person named on a found item directly, such as through a listed number, and ask them to attend before trusting the link.
when: A found item names a person
why: A direct check reveals whether the name belongs to the case

text: Clearing one party of a link to a crime does not clear another suspect; assess each suspect's evidence separately.
when: a finding absolves one person linked to the case
why: a partial clearance does not transfer to other suspects

text: Test each alibi with an independent witness, ideally at a separate location, who recalls the suspect at a stated time.
Build alibis that hold in some NPC accounts but not others, so players must check public activity to find the truth.
When several alibis rest on the same witness, test each against the corrected timeline, since one timing error affects all of them.
when: Multiple alibis come from one witness.
why: A shared source spreads its timing error across each claim.

text: Judge each suspect by whether they could independently have acted, not by how well their accounts fit together.
why: a shared alibi can look convincing while proving nothing

text: Use alibi witnesses who can state where the suspect stayed up to a stated hour, and check that their account covers the whole window rather than one moment.
Attack an alibi by naming the exact time in question and pressing it with independent written evidence rather than another person's word.
when: a suspect claims to have been elsewhere

text: Check each alibi against independent records, such as staff-confirmed room occupancy, and flag it when the claimant's own description contradicts those records.
why: Records made by others are harder to bend than the claimant's account.

text: Give each NPC alibi a checkable record, such as a ticket, call log or timestamped message, that a neutral NPC can confirm or refute.
when: Designing alibi puzzles.
why: Players verify claims rather than accept them.

text: Accept an alibi only when the timeline and the people vouching for it line up with each other.
why: An alibi that conflicts with the timeline or its witnesses is not reliable.

text: Design alibi puzzles where the player compares each character's claimed actions with task durations and with what could be heard.
when: Building a deduction puzzle around schedules
why: Gives the player concrete values to test claims against

text: Do not split a line of inquiry that depends on one witness who must be seen first; keep that line sequential.
Before accepting an accusation, check whether the accused could physically perform the act given strength, reach and timing.
when: evaluating a suspect's confession or accusation
why: a claim the body cannot support is unreliable

text: Use patrol routes, shift logs and door logs as alibi evidence, since they reveal who was absent at a critical time.
why: Logged movement from other areas can confirm or break a claimed location

text: Use published notices or posted schedules as independent sources that can contradict an NPC's stated alibi.
when: Designing a mystery where an NPC's account can be checked.
why: Independent sources let the player test claims without relying on the NPC.

text: Test a suspect's stated location independently, since an alibi can misplace where the suspect was even when the account is confident.
Make an impostor's identity checkable against a witness list so the player can verify the alibi independently.
when: Writing a disguise or false-identity twist.
why: Checkable alibis let players test the solution against the evidence rather than accept it on authority.

text: Plant an alibi's witness in the first act, but delay testing the alibi until suspicion has been spent on other suspects.
why: A late test then reads as a reversal rather than a repeat of earlier doubts.

text: A narrow crime window makes alibi checks useful, while a wide window or a suspect-only source of movement data makes them less informative.
when: When deciding how much an alibi check can reveal
why: A narrow window constrains which claims matter; a wide one lets many claims fit.

text: Mark an alibi supplied only by a spouse or servant as unverified, and give household witnesses extra scrutiny because shared interests bias what they report.
when: when no outside witness confirms whereabouts or when weighing alibi witnesses
why: that person's reliability is limited, and shared household interests create bias toward the accused

text: Close associates such as a spouse or valet can make an absence invisible by repeatedly confirming the story to the household.
when: a claimed absence is supported by people close to the person
why: The household believes the person is at home, so each repeated claim strengthens the story.

text: Survival by less than a minute has decided succession to property, so timing precision in a last-known-life timeline can carry legal weight.
when: A timeline determines inheritance or succession.
why: Legal outcomes can turn on very short intervals.

text: Household talk about a lodger's trade, habits, visitors, odd possessions and payments gives cues for identifying and locating them.
Scattered events that look unrelated can form one sequence once placed together on a single timeline.
when: when several separate events seem disconnected

text: A reconstructed sequence exposes hidden steps, such as a message passed to a second party who consults a decision-maker before a plan forms.
A figure seen performing an ordinary task near a victim can be read as proof the victim was alive, though the figure may be the killer in disguise.
when: A witness account is used to fix a victim's last known time alive.
why: Witnesses take an ordinary activity as evidence of the victim, so a disguise is hard to spot.

text: Unstated travel times, vague markers such as 'immediately afterwards', and unaccounted intervals hide gaps; fill them deliberately, since they can make an alibi impossible or conceal the key action.
when: when a timeline has unstated travel or unaccounted intervals
why: the missing time may contain the key action

text: An alibi can be prepared in advance and still be false, so the same fact can support innocence or a planned cover.

1) Question each household member separately so no account shapes another's. 2) Collect small observations: meals, orders, visits, departures, and changes in mood or health. 3) Combine them into a timeline spanning several days. 4) Record disagreements and resolve each against other evidence. 5) Check the timeline against physical findings and official reports.
when: when a suspect's whereabouts must be reconstructed from many observers
why: independent accounts combined and checked expose gaps

text: 1) Start from small traces not yet understood. 2) Order the actions by what each required, such as hiding, entering, unbolting, escaping and covering tracks. 3) Explain which traces were left and which were not. 4) Account for unrelated facts within the same sequence. 5) Ground each step in the actor's motive. 6) Present the theory as a chain where each step causes the next.
when: Many small clues point to an unseen act and no single clue explains them.
why: A single ordered chain explains all traces together and exposes gaps.

text: 1) List each witness's timed sighting. 2) Map each described route. 3) Identify gaps between sightings. 4) Test each account against physical evidence.
when: Several witnesses give times and routes that must be reconciled
why: Ordering the accounts exposes contradictions and the gaps that matter.

text: Store each character's claimed times for players to line up, and let a time stamp or travel record contradict an alibi so players find the gap.
when: Designing alibi clues or mysteries where alibis can be contradicted

text: Hide an NPC's trait behind rumour, but leave a service routine that reveals it to careful players.
Give an investigation board a household roster with arrest and location dates, so players can deduce which figure in a sighting was present.
Log every event a quest NPC or tracker produces with a timestamp so the game can rebuild the sequence in the player's journal.
when: when designing quest tracking or journals

text: Let players arrange found letters on a timeline, so that contradictory dates can serve as the route to the solution.
when: when designing document-based puzzles

text: Model alibis as sets of observers with explicit positions, so the game can check which claims are consistent with each other.
when: Designing alibis or witness systems for a game.
why: Explicit positions let the system test whether testimonies can all be true together.

text: When a crime is a secret faction or inner allegiance with hidden members, infer it from indirect marks such as missing persons and rifled stores.
when: An investigation relies on indirect evidence, such as when the crime is defined by belief or a secret pact.
why: proof must be sought in indirect marks

text: Association alone, such as faction membership, alliance, or loyal service, does not prove conspiracy or innocence, since a faction may be one side of a dispute and sincere devotion can be mistaken.
when: Judging someone by their faction, allies, or the loyalty of those who serve them.

text: Accusers may avoid a respected figure directly and strike at his daughters, grandchildren, in-laws and servants, reaching him through his household.
when: when a prominent person is protected by standing
why: attacking close relations pressures the person without a direct confrontation

text: People bound by friendship or shared membership often act from a common stance, so their parallel choices reflect the bond.
when: Two allied figures make parallel decisions about the same matter.
why: Shared ties create shared expectations.

text: A witness publicly tied to a party may disapprove of its course yet record the outcome indirectly, so the disapproval shows in the wording.
when: A witness associated with someone whose conduct they disagree with.
why: Public ties discourage open dissent.

text: Group initiations can test nerve and pain tolerance as part of admitting a new member.
Make a mentor-style character sharp but incomplete, so the player must check claims independently.
Paying bail or legal defence for captured agents keeps the chain loyal.
when: When captured agents can be supported by the organization.

text: NPCs speak differently depending on their perceived allegiance to the player, so the same question can yield a different answer.
Tying the consequences of how much truth a player tells an ally to that ally's loyalty and discretion makes disclosure a meaningful choice.
Let an ally share the quest goal while keeping back the personal reason, and hint at it through a locked or partial dialogue topic.
Reveal alliances in council scenes through seating and past favours rather than explicit statements.
when: Designing a council or vote scene.

text: An ally who promises to keep a visitor's presence quiet protects them, but may repeat the story and spread the cover beyond control.
A suspect who sees a formal search coming and has no time to destroy the object is likely to hand it over.
why: Resistance no longer helps and the evidence is at risk

text: Acting on a coerced confession can alert the other side, who may respond with a quick ambush.
when: A suspect yields information that is then acted on.
why: The opposing party learns of the investigation through the action taken.

text: An ally who holds a wrong belief creates a gap between their conclusion and the evidence, which a player can exploit to reach the truth first.
when: investigations with an official NPC ally
why: the ally's conclusion is visible but not supported

text: Give a trusted ally a visible heroic act, since that act becomes the strongest cover for revealing them later as the real antagonist.
when: planning a hidden-boss twist
why: Heroism raises trust, which hides the true identity

text: 1) Give the captive paper and a pencil for a written reply. 2) Read the answer. 3) Judge whether the written answer is likely to be true.
when: a captive cannot speak

text: Ask an ally of the adversary for a written account, stating that it will be demanded if refused, so a record exists.
Secure pledges of silence from witnesses and from anyone with an interest in the case, since a witness not properly bound may speak to others.
why: Information flows only where the designer or investigator intends.

text: A label or form written in an unfamiliar hand suggests someone else has altered the object, which is a lead worth following.
why: A second writer means the object was touched after its creation.

text: Check the seam of a cut-and-patched label or document, since altered papers often show an uneven edge where the edit was joined.
when: a document or label may have been changed
why: joins are hard to make invisibly

text: When a document seems altered, ask which change would be easiest for a forger. Changes between similar-looking characters, such as one day name for another, are the most likely.
when: A date or figure looks changed
why: Easy substitutions require minimal effort and avoid detection

text: Claims by a party, such as petitions or records by those who acted, are advocacy that softens or omits their own role; check them against the other side's account.
A cover-up that alters dates on records can reveal the true day, because the altered date conflicts with the real schedule.
Dates can be wrong or added in later copies, so check the original record where possible.
when: when working from copies of documents

text: The same parcel's size can be recorded differently across successive documents, so area figures alone cannot identify a lot.
when: when matching a parcel across several records
why: Measurements were often re-estimated at each transfer

text: Trusting the top layer because it is most visible can hide the true record beneath an overlay.
when: An object carries multiple labels or markings
why: Newer surfaces are designed or accidentally placed to overwrite older information

text: Plant a faint, later-looking note in a document as a clue that the record was altered after the fact.
when: when designing in-game clues

text: Place an edited archive copy whose key word points to one suspect, with the original as the evidence that unlocks the truth.
Treat a discrepancy between an official document and a rumored version as a clue about who may have altered the text.
when: When a document exists in more than one version.
why: Differences between versions point to the party who changed them.

text: The same fact can support opposing conclusions depending on framing, so a clue tied to two places cannot single out either one.
when: A clue points at a suspect and also at other possibilities.
why: Shared relevance to several candidates dilutes the inference toward any one of them.

text: Doubt about how a legal rule applies can itself create a motive when one party gains if the doubt favours them.
Detective fiction often gives a clue only one correct reading, whereas real clues often admit several readings.
Leave some props unexplained as later payoffs or a closing hook, and keep a quest log of open anomalies revisited as facts arrive.
when: Designing a mystery with layered clues
why: Open items keep the investigation alive and give the player reason to revisit earlier evidence.

text: Choose even vague hints deliberately, since an ambiguous sign should still rest on a definite underlying form.
when: writing suggestive clues
why: vagueness without structure reads as noise

text: Offering two paths, telling the truth or facing a stated penalty, makes silence costly and pushes the suspect toward a choice.
NPC claims can be designed to conflict on purpose, so the player must cross-check them against earlier dialogue to find the truth.
when: Building a mystery plot with dialogue-based clues

text: Place a term with two meanings deliberately and reward the player who learns the specialist sense.
Design case files so two conclusions both fit the clues, and place a clue that eliminates one only after the player has committed to considering both.
when: Designing deduction puzzles with competing answers
why: Players must weigh consistent evidence instead of spotting a single obvious answer

text: Build crime scenes so each trace supports or undermines a set of hypotheses, leaving some traces ambiguous to reward deduction.
when: when designing a scene meant to be solved
why: ambiguity forces the player to weigh evidence rather than read one clue

text: Pair two clues from one system with a third from a separate system to reward cross-referencing.
Design clue sets so no single item solves the case, but combinations rule out some suspects, rewarding players who read the set as a whole.
when: When designing investigative puzzles with many minor clues.
why: Combination reasoning requires the player to synthesise, not just find, clues.

text: Place a locked-door detail mid-case; it can read as fear or as staging, and its meaning changes once the key holder is known.
when: a locked room is part of the scene
why: An ambiguous detail stays open until the key holder is revealed.

text: An ambiguous clue can still establish a general fact, such as that a person is probably dead or that one of a small group handled the body.
when: A clue does not identify a single culprit.
why: A clue can narrow the field without pointing to one individual.

text: A single physical object, such as a footprint, can support two opposing readings, and the reading shifts as later objects are found.
when: Writing evidence that must be re-interpreted during an investigation.
why: Holding the mismatch detail visible from the start lets the eventual reversal feel earned.

text: An incident can be split into a real first phase and a later phase that was staged or misread. Witnesses may hear the second phase without seeing it.
An ambiguous remark gets fixed to the reading that suits a favored theory, especially when the speaker is absent to explain it, sending the investigator down the wrong path.
Ambiguous wording can confuse innocent listeners as well as guilty ones, so a double meaning alone cannot show guilt.
A deliberately incomplete record should not be assumed complete, since removed pages are an absence an investigator must account for.
Storms, wind and old buildings produce sounds that resemble deliberate signals, so a heard noise should not be read as a signal without checking.
A flawless offender makes the investigation feel arbitrary; the criminal needs a gap for the solution to feel earned.
when: When designing an antagonist's plan.
why: Readers accept a solution only if the offender could have slipped.

text: A witness's ambiguous answer can be recorded as a stronger statement than intended, so the transcript may not match what was said.
Ambiguous phrasing may come from habit or self-deception rather than deliberate deceit, and the speaker may sincerely believe the claim.
when: reading a suspicious statement
why: Deliberate concealment is not the only cause of ambiguity.

text: 1) Give one clue, such as a residue that is poison or medicine, two plausible readings. 2) Place a second test or witness trace later that favours one reading. 3) Let the player resolve the ambiguity by finding it.
when: When designing investigative clues in a level.
why: Two readings make the player weigh evidence instead of accepting the first answer; a single reading gives no decision to make.

text: 1) List every candidate who fits the shared name. 2) Weigh each candidate's place in the list, formal rank and seniority. 3) Weigh which names were left out. 4) Choose the best-supported candidate.
when: A document names one person only by a surname shared with others of similar title
why: A shared name leaves identity open, so context must decide

text: Leave a deliberate gap, such as a question an official never asks, that a second, more specific conversation or later quest can close.
when: Designing an unresolved thread for later payoff

text: Leave one clue element unexplained, such as ink with no visible pen, until a later location, document or character resolves it, so the gap drives the player forward.
when: Designing multi-location clue chains or pacing a mystery's reveals
why: An open question sustains curiosity until a later location answers it.

text: Treat a blotted, missing record or envelope as a designed gap the player must fill from another source, such as another NPC, object or records office.
when: A key detail is missing from a written record.
why: Gaps force players to seek corroboration elsewhere.

text: Plant an accident that can be either a trap or bad luck, and give both readings some visible support so the player must weigh them.
Place a visible but misleading clue, and give the player a test that corrects the path, so the red herring teaches rather than wastes time.
when: when designing a mystery

text: Let an NPC detail that seems to clear a suspect also fit a disguised culprit, so the player can work out the second reading.
when: designing witness clues
why: Ambiguity rewards careful reasoning.

text: When two explanations fit the facts equally well, test which is true rather than adopting the first plausible one.
when: A clue has two plausible readings.
why: A single wrong choice can send the whole investigation the wrong way.

text: Ambiguity should come from the text itself, not from a character refusing to explain, and should be used only where the clue is meant to be unclear.
when: Deciding how to make a clue uncertain.
why: Ambiguity from evasion feels like withholding, while textual ambiguity invites reasoning.

text: Show unknown intervals in a game's record, such as a missing witness or unreachable log, so the player has a concrete gap to pursue.
when: When designing mystery or investigation content.
why: A visible gap gives the player a next step, while a hidden gap gives none.

text: Leave one ownership link deliberately unexplained, and let the player infer it from a related document.
when: Designing a document-based puzzle
why: Inference from a related record rewards players who connect documents

text: Have an NPC describe an item or room almost correctly, then let the player confirm it by finding the real item, rewarding cross-checking.
A word an NPC emphasises on purpose can be a designed signal that the player is meant to notice.
Use an accidental-looking mark, such as a scrape on a crate, as a hint, and define in advance what it means.
when: designing environmental clues
why: a mark the player can read consistently becomes a usable lead

text: Place ambiguous ornamental clues in rooms and let the player decide whether they matter.
Pair each clue in an investigation journal with a counter-explanation, and keep it unresolved until a second clue supports the explanation.
when: Designing a generated mystery or investigation journal
why: Players need visible open questions that resolve through corroboration

text: Include one or two clues that resist every available explanation to serve as the deductive anchor of a generated case.
when: Generating a mystery with several explainable clues
why: A clue no explanation covers gives the case a fixed point for deduction

text: Chain clues through shops and staff lists, and use a trigger phrase so an NPC can signal the player without alerting a target.
when: when designing multi-step investigations

text: Keep at least one piece of physical evidence ambiguous so the player cannot close every thread.
when: Closing a mystery with a late reveal
why: Leaving one clue unresolved preserves doubt and makes the solution feel less mechanical.

text: A flawless public surface can be innocent or concealing; it only reveals the truth when the observer is away from the performer.
when: Judging a suspect whose presence seems perfect
why: Presence itself makes the performance persuasive, so independent observation is needed.

text: Players hold two interpretations at once when a physical clue carrying the suspect's mark has a second plausible reading.
when: An accusation rests on evidence with an alternative explanation
why: Neither reading is ruled out, so the question stays open and the player keeps reconsidering.

text: An antagonist whose candour fits both innocent and guilty readings cannot be dismissed by the player, so suspicion stays alive.
when: Writing an antagonist who gives open, plausible answers.
why: Openness that serves two readings keeps the player weighing the character rather than discarding them.

text: Hold several readings of an ambiguous clue open and revise them as facts arrive; early commitment can yield a plausible but false reconstruction.
when: A scene raises a question before its answer is available, or few fragments remain and a partial word or name has several plausible completions.
why: Partial sight supports several plausible readings until further evidence settles one; early commitment can produce a plausible but false reconstruction.

text: An NPC that swings between theatrical and lucid gives players two readings, eccentric or conspiratorial, and later evidence should settle which one holds.
when: designing a suspect whose behavior is unclear

text: A clue can be written so its meaning changes once a second clue is found, rewarding players who keep it.
when: when placing a written clue on a body or in an item
why: Two-stage meaning makes early findings pay off later.

text: A cryptic hint delivered before a crowd leaves listeners puzzled rather than persuaded, and the hint gains meaning only when a later event confirms it.
when: The speaker has a reason to conceal what they know.
why: The audience cannot yet connect the hint to any fact, so it stays open until the event.

text: A single observed sign often has several innocent explanations, so a conclusion built on trivial signs can seem unconvincing.
when: When building a case from minor details such as appearance or a changed habit.
why: Each sign can result from many causes, so only the combination carries weight.

text: Vague, ominous lines from a witness can be read as either threat or admission until follow-up questions settle the meaning.
1) List every explanation the clue allows. 2) Test each against independent facts already known. 3) Eliminate explanations the facts contradict. 4) Accept that the question may remain open.
when: a clue supports several readings

text: Ambiguous clues should be resolved by later facts; ambiguity that is never resolved leaves the player with no way to choose a reading.
when: Planting an unclear clue or figure.
why: Unresolved ambiguity frustrates players who cannot test their interpretation.

text: Choose a bait that fits the culprit's psychology, such as an offer the culprit expects to accept.
when: designing a trap that lures a culprit into the open
why: A bait the target expects to take draws them in without suspicion

text: Let a set ambush produce an unexpected arrival, so watchers witness a false suspect's innocent action and clear that suspect.
when: during a watch on a disturbed object

text: Let an ambush fail with a fleeting glimpse rather than a clean capture, so the culprit stays at large and tension carries forward.
when: when a trap is set for the culprit
why: a glimpse keeps the threat alive and gives a clue for later

text: A thief who has taken a valuable must find a buyer; a public reward notice makes the usual market hostile, so the thief must either stay hidden with unsellable goods or come forward.
when: A thief must eventually move stolen goods and the item is identifiable.
why: Notices alert sellers, closing the usual channels for disposing of the item.

text: 1) Let the culprit act while the detective watches from concealment. 2) Recover the stolen item at the moment of the act. 3) Confront the culprit with the item and the route taken.
Ancient sorcery was not originally classed as morally evil; the devil-based interpretation developed later.
Authority drawn from ancient texts can stop officials from asking whether the alleged crime was possible at all.
Apparition cannot prove guilt, since a deceiving agent may take an innocent person's shape; treat its accusation as a reason to investigate, e.g. questioning or examining the accused.
Make an oracle's apparently impossible insight trace back to a visible human source, such as a note, a witness, or an observed tell, that the player can reconstruct.
when: Designing a supernatural-versus-human puzzle or fortune-teller NPC.
why: A traceable source lets the player separate apparent magic from ordinary information.

text: Accusations voiced in anger reveal suspicion between speakers, often in both directions, but they are charges made in heat, not findings.
Animosity or jealousy can push an investigator to conclude before facts are in, so they stop verifying, read later facts through that conclusion, and may make unfounded accusations.
when: The investigator is emotionally invested in the outcome.
why: Emotion replaces verification as the basis for acting.

text: Statements made under anger, including confessions, mix truth with overstatement and spite, so a calm admission carries more weight; record exact wording and check each slip against other evidence.
when: A suspect speaks under emotional pressure.
why: Emotional speech mixes truth with overstatement and spite.

text: Antagonism with an official team reduces its cooperation, so an outside investigator's requests lose effect when the tone turns hostile.
when: an outsider works alongside an official inquiry
why: Officials act less on requests from people they resent

text: Anger can reveal the questioner's own weak position as well as the other party's.
Animals near a panicking person often react to that panic, so the animal's behaviour can reveal the person's emotional state.
when: A companion animal is present during a frightening scene
why: Animals respond to their owner's emotional state

text: Animals and small movements can register as signs of recent presence, prompting unease without establishing a conclusion.
when: When a sudden animal flight suggests someone was recently nearby.
why: Disturbed animals signal recent human or other activity.

text: Measured tracks can reveal the size, body plan and behavior of a creature no one has seen.
when: When tracks are the only record of a creature and can be measured reliably.

text: Footprints on paved or newly surfaced ground often vanish, so a trail may end where the surface changes.
A tracking source can find a known individual but cannot identify an unknown one, so its result does not name who it has found.
Animals may detect cues such as smell that humans miss, so an abrupt change in a companion animal's behaviour can reveal a hidden change, while people may supply wrong explanations.
when: A companion animal's behaviour changes abruptly, or a character has changed in a way others cannot see
why: Animals react to what people miss, so their behaviour reveals the truth early.

text: Bite marks can support a species-level guess about an unseen animal by judging the width of the jaw.
when: when an animal is implicated by marks but not observed

text: Animals found inside a sealed space without passing its door suggest another opening exists, which can be searched for.
If a tracker ignores an object it should have reacted to, doubt any inference drawn from its reaction to a different object.
why: the expected reaction did not occur

text: A dim or partly hidden feature, such as a faded numeral, can turn a passing glimpse into a trackable identifier.
A biological sample such as blood or hair can match a specific animal location, narrowing the search to one building.
when: when a trace points to a place with animals
why: Animal-specific traces link a suspect to a particular site.

text: Deeper wheel or cart tracks mean more weight on that wheel, so comparing depths reveals which vehicle carried more load or how a rider's weight was distributed.
when: Comparing two sets of tracks from vehicles that left the same place
why: Ground compresses more under greater weight.

text: Fresh snow or mud records every track entering and leaving a place, so finding only inbound tracks suggests no one left on foot.
when: conditions such as fresh snow have preserved the record
why: the surface keeps a record of movement

text: Tracks alone do not prove who made them; reading them well requires knowing what a staged version would look like.
An animal's fearful reaction is not testimony and should be treated as atmosphere unless other evidence supports it.
when: When an animal reacts to a person and the reaction is being used to infer guilt.
why: Animal behavior has many causes and cannot establish a person's intent or actions.

text: 1) Measure stance spacing, the distance from fore-foot to hind-foot, using prints where the animal stood still. 2) Add neck and head length to estimate body length. 3) Compare stride length to body length to infer leg length. 4) Note toe count and claw marks, and compare print shape against known animal families.
Do not treat an animal's behaviour as proof alone; combine it with other evidence before drawing a conclusion.
Test a tracker's conclusion by repeating its behavior under controlled conditions where possible, and accept it as proof only after that test.
when: the source's behavior can be repeated

text: Give non-player animals guarding behavior, such as pacing or staring at a patch of ground, as readable tells instead of map markers.
when: designing puzzles around hidden items

text: Use an animal threat as a visible symptom of a hidden human state, so tracks and sounds make the threat real before its nature is known.
when: When an unseen supernatural cause must feel present early
why: A physical sign gives players concrete evidence to investigate while the underlying cause stays hidden.

text: Track evidence is strong on wet or soft ground but weak on dry ground or with indistinct prints, where no reliable reference sample can be made.
when: Choosing whether to rely on footprint evidence
why: Surface condition determines whether prints can be compared at all.

text: Tie a mystery flag to a specific premise so the system can check whether a claimed anomaly depends on an unstated assumption.
when: Implementing a mystery or anomaly flag in a game.
why: Explicit premises make a flagged anomaly verifiable rather than vague.

text: Introduce small unexplained anomalies sparingly and plan their payoff before planting them, so the player carries them forward as live questions.
when: when seeding details the audience will track across the story
why: planted questions give the audience a reason to keep reading

text: Treat a character's apparent madness as a possible deliberate test, so the reader's suspicion becomes the setup for a later reveal that recasts earlier dialogue.
A set of strange clues may all be one motive seen from different angles, so the player should look for a shared cause rather than separate explanations.
when: many odd clues point in different directions
why: A single motive can unify anomalies that look like unrelated sacrilege, madness or intrusion.

text: Interpreting an animal's internal state is uncertain; an observer cannot fully gauge what an animal feels.
when: Drawing conclusions from animal reactions
why: Animal reactions are observable, but their inner states are not directly accessible.

text: 1) Treat the frightening appearance as a surface. 2) Check what behaviour or motive it could hide. 3) Look for a human cause behind it.
when: Investigating an apparent supernatural event

text: An apparent impossibility, like an unnoticed event or a result in a sealed or controlled situation, is often planned by someone who knows a system's gap, not luck.
when: a sealed or controlled situation yields a result that seems impossible
why: people who know the system's weak point can produce effects that look uncanny to outsiders

text: Seek a mundane mechanism fitting every detail before accepting the supernatural; yet if all anomalies are ordinary, the supernatural never feels real, so keep a few truly unusual.
when: a strange sighting has specific reported features
why: a mechanism that fits all details is stronger than a vague supernatural explanation; uniform natural explanations remove the stakes of the unusual

text: People sense a deviation as wrong only against an established routine or expected behaviour, often feeling unease before naming the cause; without a baseline, a clue goes unrecognized.
when: a sign departs from an established pattern; an ordinary-looking action may be a clue
why: a deviation needs a baseline to register as meaningful; anomalies are defined relative to expectations, so the observer needs a reference point

text: Players who meet a striking physical anomaly with no known purpose often read it as supernatural or careless rather than deliberate.
when: a conspicuous trace whose purpose is unclear
why: unexplained anomalies invite convenient stories that fill the gap

text: An anomaly is a mismatch between an object and its apparent origin or source.

Acts that contradict expected behaviour or the efficient choice, such as taking originals when copies would suffice, are distinctive clues to flag and treat as questions; unexpected choices reveal intent.
when: a single act seems to serve no purpose; a choice departs from the expected efficient option
why: actions that break expected behaviour can reveal motives or circumstances hidden by routine behaviour; unexpected choices often reveal intent that routine actions conceal

text: Record every anomaly, even one contradicting the working theory without explanation, and test it or compare it with later details; unexplained oddities pay off when revisited.
when: a detail breaks the expected pattern and may matter later
why: an unexplained oddity pays off when it is revisited; filing an anomaly away untested lets it lapse

text: Keep a running list of small anomalies; each may be explicable alone, yet together they can point to a pattern no single item reveals.
when: no single clue is decisive
why: links across items form evidence that individual items do not

text: An odd trace may look like coincidence at first; do not treat every mark as meaningful, but return to an anomaly once its position and cause can be matched.
why: a trace placed wrongly can point the inquiry the wrong way

text: A single small oddity on an object is a lead to test, not proof of wrongdoing, and it may point to a careless handler rather than the sender.
when: Interpreting one anomalous detail found during inspection
why: Small anomalies have many innocent causes, so they must be checked before drawing conclusions.

text: Each unusual feature of a scene may be possible alone, but several together weigh against a simple account.
when: when judging whether a story fits the scene
why: Improbabilities accumulate, even when each has an innocent explanation.

text: Substitutions are easier to spot when routines are documented and cross-checked, since a deviation then stands out clearly.
when: routines are recorded
why: a baseline makes deviations visible

text: The detail that does not fit the simple account marks where further investigation should focus.
when: A case appears settled but one element remains unexplained.
why: Unexplained details are the points where a flawed theory is most likely to break.

text: An unusual change in a fixed detail, such as a missing lamp, suggests someone has handled the scene.
when: a routine detail differs from usual

text: Dress-based reasoning is weak when the stated circumstance is unusual enough that almost any clothing could be justified.
why: Without a clear norm for the activity, mismatch carries little evidential weight.

text: A physical sign that breaks the expected progression carries a trace that needs an explanation, and one asks who or what produced it.
when: A body or object state does not match the expected pattern
why: Deviations from a known pattern indicate interference or a cause to find

text: Read a case through its apparent contradictions: clues that fit too neatly can signal deliberate design rather than chance.
Coincidental resemblances, like a theme recurring across unrelated leads or an object's theme matching the crime, can be chance and create false links; test them independently before accepting them.
when: the same pattern recurs across separate leads; an object's theme overlaps the crime
why: chance repetitions look meaningful but establish nothing on their own; thematic overlap needs independent testing

text: If a deviation gives no explicit signal, players may sense something is off without understanding it, and the anomaly passes unnoticed.
Anomalies generate puzzles, not answers; a culprit should not be named from theories that still fail to fit the details.
A theory that explains one anomaly through an assumed sequence of events may misplace another anomaly, so the sequence needs independent confirmation.
when: When a theory accounts for an odd detail with an unverified sequence
why: Assumed sequences can fit one fact while contradicting others

text: 1) List each puzzling fact as a separate anomaly. 2) Ask which single cause could produce each one. 3) Link the causes into one sequence that explains all the facts.
when: when several unrelated facts may share one hidden cause

text: 1) Notice an action that breaks the usual pattern. 2) Compare it against what the situation would normally produce. 3) Test the mismatch with a plain challenge and observe the reaction, which then becomes evidence.
when: a minor detail looks ordinary but may reveal a hidden intent
why: A mismatch against the baseline gives a concrete starting point, and the subject's response can confirm or refute it.

text: 1) Before the interview, list every loose fact tied to the witness. 2) Ask about each fact separately and have the witness explain it in their own words. 3) Cross-check each answer against other witnesses' accounts.
when: A guarded witness must explain specific anomalies rather than make a general admission
why: A separate question per anomaly gives the witness fewer places to hide and makes contradictions visible

text: 1) State what a normal sequence would have produced. 2) Note the actual absence. 3) Consider design, necessity or carelessness as causes. 4) Reject theories that call the anomaly an oversight without support.
when: An expected detail is missing from a scene.
why: Dismissing an anomaly as carelessness closes the question before the evidence has been used.

text: 1) Treat the apparent supernatural effect as impossible until tested. 2) Apply graded stimulus to the body while watching its vital signs. 3) Trace the physical chain of causes back to its source.
when: A seemingly supernatural death or revival needs explanation

text: 1) Obtain the record for the event period. 2) Obtain a control-period record from a comparable time. 3) Check whether the anomaly recurs at the same hour. 4) Test the record with a known load to confirm it responds.
when: a record shows an unexplained anomaly
why: repetition separates a systematic event from a one-off with an innocent cause

text: 1) Find a detail the reconstructed story cannot explain. 2) Ask why the object is in its current state. 3) List possible explanations. 4) Test the cheapest, most mundane explanations first. 5) Accept a dramatic explanation only after the simple ones fail.
when: A physical object looks too neat or contradicts a known habit.
why: Mundane causes like spare items are often the true answer and must be eliminated before accepting dramatic ones.

text: Tie any count anomaly to a known starting figure; an anomaly with no verifiable baseline cannot be used as evidence.
when: When a count is the basis for a claim
why: Without a baseline the discrepancy cannot be confirmed

text: Resolve every behavioural anomaly in a theory before trusting it; an unexplained refusal or offer is evidence the explanation may be wrong.
Test a suspicious record against an independent source, such as another office's totals, before accepting it as a motive.
when: Before drawing any conclusion from a financial anomaly.
why: A single record can mislead; a second source confirms or rejects it.

text: Treat an anomaly as a hypothesis with several possible explanations, such as gambling or other spending, until a source confirms one.
when: When an anomaly points to a hidden stake.
why: The anomaly shows a stake exists but not which explanation is true.

text: Treat a physical anomaly as a clue and keep it separate from any conclusion about the perpetrator it might support.
when: An unexplained physical feature appears in evidence.
why: Separating observation from inference keeps the investigation open to other explanations.

text: A habitually truthful figure's unprompted exact falsehood is read as changed intent, yet observed changes in a person may support either an honest or deceptive reading without inside knowledge.
when: a character known for honesty lies
why: the contrast with a known habit makes the lie stand out

text: Investigating every odd detail wastes time under pressure; keep pursuing the main objective while logging minor oddities for later.
when: a deadline or time limit applies
why: time spent on minor anomalies can cost the main goal

text: An unsigned warning lowers the credibility of its information, since the recipient cannot verify or trace the source, so the claims may be dismissed without a fair check.
