when: Passing on accusations or evidence without attribution.
why: Anonymity removes accountability, so recipients have reason to doubt the claims.

text: An unsigned accusation plants doubt rather than proof, and the doubt persists after the message is destroyed.
when: a recipient receives an anonymous accusation about a trusted person
why: Suspicion outlasts the paper it was written on

text: People who want to be unknown tend to choose large cities, where neighbours rarely know them and newcomers are seldom noticed.
when: a person is hiding or disappearing by choice
why: anonymity is easier where people do not know their neighbours

text: An anonymous message that names a recipient's location and time shows that its author has detailed knowledge of the recipient's routine.
when: When an unsigned message contains specific information about a target.
why: Specific details about a routine require observation or access.

text: A message that mixes warning and threat, or signs itself as someone the recipient dreads, blurs its motive and can serve either purpose.
when: When an anonymous message's tone is ambiguous.
why: Mixed tone makes intent hard to read and may be a deliberate tactic.

text: An unsigned letter reveals things about its writer through handwriting, wording and knowledge of the subject, but these clues describe the writer and do not prove the letter's claims.
An unnamed tip, such as an anonymous letter, can complete an identity that physical evidence left incomplete.
when: a body is unidentified and has no papers

text: Identify an anonymous note through phrasing, habits and references only one person would know, since disguising handwriting leaves these traces.
when: A note is unsigned and the hand is disguised

text: Attribute an anonymous writing by its initials, style and reasoning, and present the result as the weight of evidence, not certainty.
when: no signature identifies the writer
why: style-based attribution is probabilistic

text: A list of rivals kept in someone's private notes can mark who that person intends to target once power shifts.
A gift or favour from an unnamed giver can be a clue that the giver wanted influence over the recipient.
when: a benefit arrives without a traceable source

text: A message claiming open watching and no wish to hide suggests the sender may be deliberately unconcealed, which warrants checking whether the claim is true.
when: When a follow-up message announces ongoing observation.
why: Stated openness can be a bluff or a real intent to intimidate.

text: Discovering a private letter can expose a secret that triggers family conflict and drives the plot forward.
An investigator who keeps a theory private risks the household drawing its own conclusions.
A private record can overstate a feeling, so the written wording may diverge from the writer's own later recollection of it.
Assuming the apparent sender wrote or posted a message, without checking the chain of handling, misleads the investigation.
A reveal that depends on the investigator's private knowledge seems unfair unless that knowledge is shown in the dialogue beforehand.
when: when a solution rests on unseen knowledge
why: Unshown premises feel like cheating.

text: A private journal entry does not establish that a person wrote a formal report or signed an order.
why: Personal writing and official acts are different kinds of record.

text: Judging a message a hoax or a warning merely from its tone is unreliable; the content, delivery and physical evidence must be weighed together.
when: When classifying an anonymous message.
why: Tone alone can mislead, since genuine warnings and hoaxes can sound alike.

text: 1) Find booking records for private rooms. 2) Ask staff who served the pair whether the pattern recurs. 3) Have staff identify the people from photographs.
when: A booking hints at a hidden relationship
why: Staff can confirm a pattern and identify people

text: Let an anonymous note in a dungeon name a room and a time while leaving the author open, so players must deduce identity from other finds.
when: When designing a written clue in a generated dungeon.
why: An unresolved authorship invites inference and connects the note to other clues.

text: A private record of suspicions helps track evidence as a case develops, but it cannot prove anything and is hard for others to share or check.
when: an investigator tracks suspicion without a formal case file
why: privacy aids tracking and limits verification

text: Make a charming ally the disguised threat, withholding the reveal until the final confrontation backed by an earlier planted clue, so trust lands on the wrong person.
when: designing a companion or helper character, or when the antagonist hides behind a trusted name
why: A trusted figure's secret identity gives a reversal, and a planted clue makes the reveal fair and earned.

text: Show an ally's habits early so a later clue can be checked against earlier scenes; a new fact then reframes those already-shown traits as evidence without changing their scenes.
when: Revealing or planning a twist where a trusted character is the hidden culprit.
why: Habits and traits seen earlier make the late reveal fair and checkable rather than arbitrary.

text: Keep bystanders present during a reveal, since their reactions and whispers add pressure and show who is afraid.
when: Running a group reveal
why: Observers amplify tension and expose hidden anxiety

text: A plan stated in advance gives a fixed expected schedule that later actions can be tested against.
when: A character announces a plan before an event
why: A recorded expectation makes departures from it visible.

text: Let the antagonist's death end the threat, which keeps the reveal in an emotional register and avoids a trial.
when: Closing a mystery where the culprit is exposed
why: A death resolves the threat quickly and shifts focus to the emotional fallout.

text: When the antagonist's own failed plan or rash letter triggers the crisis, the conflict arises from the character's choices rather than external chance.
when: Building the climax of a plot where the villain's plan must unravel.
why: Self-caused crises feel earned and keep the outcome tied to character action.

text: When an announced antagonist never appears, the reader's assumption that the author of the threat is in the room is overturned, and the threat becomes a phantom.
when: a threat figure is announced early but withheld from the scene
why: The expected confrontation is replaced by an unresolved relationship, which raises tension and surprise.

text: The person who gains from a missing item is not thereby guilty; the benefit is a motive to test, not proof.
1) Hold a working hypothesis that someone is shielding another. 2) Ask which person and how much help was given. 3) Keep the theory open until a planned test is run.
when: Evidence suggests a suspect had outside help
why: A confident theory can narrow the search before it is tested.

text: Plant the true culprit early as a bystander with a motive and a noted presence, expressed in passing, so the reader trusts them as harmless.
when: Hiding the real antagonist in plain sight
why: A character seen as a witness is rarely suspected, so a later admission surprises the player.

text: Have the suffering character reveal the origin of their affliction; this makes the reveal personal and removes the need for a detective figure.
Use witnesses with a known history together to establish a baseline of normal behaviour against which unusual reactions can be compared.
when: Assessing whether a witness's reaction is abnormal
why: A known baseline gives a reference for judging deviations.

text: Appearance unreliably signals guilt: a calm culprit may seem innocent, and a suspect who looks guilty from appearance or record may be innocent.
when: When judging suspects by demeanor, appearance, or past record
why: Composure can mask guilt, and appearance or record can mislead.

text: A trait presented with affection can read as romance rather than information, so the audience may fail to register it as a marker.
A visible behavioral change is a clue only against a known baseline, and it is not proof of guilt because many causes can produce it.
when: When interpreting a suspect's changed manner as evidence.
why: Without a baseline and alternative explanations, a change can mislead.

text: Excluding a suspect because their character seems unfit for the crime ignores that character is often misjudged and that self-interest can be hidden.
when: When ruling out suspects by judging their personality.
why: Personality impressions are unreliable, and concealed incentives can override them.

text: Once an item traces to a household, family and friends become suspects by association alone. Spread accusations via relationships and rumour; separate true suspects from those caught only by association.
Relatives can be on opposite sides of the same long dispute, such as a contested land claim.
Accusations follow kinship, neighbourhood and rivalry lines rather than spreading at random; tracing who accuses whom reveals grudges that testimony hides.
when: when accusations centre on one household, faction or a group facing suspicion
why: People act through their closest ties, which shape who is noticed and blamed

text: Let dialogue puzzles present trigger words to NPCs and time replies; quick ordinary replies show nothing hidden, while delayed or unexpected replies, flagged as clues, point to a hidden association.
Scan a register or guest list for names linked to a known person, revealing who else is present and possibly why.
When motive is possible, ask personal questions about the witness's relationships to the victim, since a relationship can become the central line of inquiry.
Before first contact, identify the target's known associates and avoid them, since they could expose the cover.
when: a persona must be introduced to a new target

text: A judge's citation of a writer's work as authority can link that writer to the proceedings, but establishes association rather than responsibility.
why: Citation shows reliance on a source, not endorsement of every action taken.

text: Accusations spread along kin and neighbour networks: accusers and accused, often rivals, are neighbours bound by marriage, debt or local disputes, and harm to one household reaches connected ones.
When one partner's self-image clashes with the other's wish to leave, the conflict can escalate toward violence and supply a motive.
An NPC may remember a fact only after the relationship with the player changes, which can trigger new dialogue.
Accusing a stranger without knowledge invites conflict that can overshadow the real problem and leave the accusation unresolved.
when: a confrontation starts from a misidentification
why: the dispute draws attention away from the actual issue

text: 1) Ask for the relationship in fixed categories, such as friendly, strained or hostile. 2) Make the witness choose one. 3) Note vague words used for events. 4) Ask follow-ups on those words.
when: A family or business dispute must be assessed for motive.
why: Fixed categories force a concrete answer that can be compared.

text: Do not treat a grudge, an unrelated absence, a misplaced source or a person seen with money as proof that a document is a hoax.
why: these connections are loose and establish nothing

text: Use association results to choose a line of questioning and check them against facts, since reading the answers depends on interpretation.
Store relationship events such as quarrels, letters and insults so the game can show the player the chain of hostility behind a frame.
when: building NPC relationship state
why: recorded history lets the game surface motives for players

text: Use relationship data between NPCs to narrow suspects, but require physical or testimonial evidence before an accusation counts.
when: when designing suspect logic based on NPC relationships
why: Relationships suggest motives but do not prove them

text: Revising a single assumption about a witness's knowledge can overturn the whole reading of an event.
A wrong assumed dimension, tool, or any unchecked assumption propagates its error into every dependent deduction and plan, so confident conclusions and plans fail.
Explanations of a plotter's hesitation rest on assumptions about their reasoning, which cannot be tested directly.
why: Motives and judgments are not observable, so the explanation remains provisional.

text: Assuming a reconstruction is complete can mislead, because a single overlooked small object can change how an event actually happened.
Mixing a witness's assumptions with their observations leads to false identifications.
Accepting the first explanation that matches an assumption, such as a belief that a given person would never commit a crime, closes off the real line of inquiry.
Challenge the shared assumptions of witnesses and officials about who acted and how they escaped, and test each assumption rather than accepting it.
Record which assumption the player accepts during a leading interrogation, so later evidence can reveal the assumption as wrong.
An attractive theory feels settled when stated in orderly steps or when other links are plausible; each link still needs its own evidence.
when: when assembling a case from several partly supported facts
why: Plausibility elsewhere does not verify a specific link.

text: Do not trust a routine or social norm about what someone does without checking when circumstances, such as weather, could have broken it.
when: When inferring behavior from routine or social expectation
why: Circumstances can override habits that people usually follow.

text: Record each fact's origin (rumour, document or place) with a reliability tag, marking rumours unverified and separate from firsthand observations so players can weigh each.
when: when recording witness information or presenting clues in a journal
why: Players cannot judge trust without knowing the source type.

text: One confirmed fact can suddenly re-sort many small earlier oddities into a single pattern, making them feel connected.
Audiences assume the poorer party in a secret relationship is the one under threat, and they accept that reading until something contradicts it.
when: A hidden relationship with an expected victim-and-aggressor dynamic
why: Stereotyped expectations about wealth and power shape the first theory readers form

text: Raw facts gain meaning only through inference; gathering facts without organising and interpreting them leaves a case unexplained.
when: An investigator relies only on collected facts.
why: Facts do not explain themselves.

text: A witness who listened without looking has only sound-based evidence, which supports weaker claims about what happened than sight does.
when: when a witness reports events only through sound
why: sound conveys less specific information than sight

text: Local talk is often affectionate or hostile, so separate what people remember from what they merely assume.
when: when collecting community accounts

text: A guess thrown out to unsettle a witness may draw admissions, but a lucky hit does not prove the guess.
when: An investigator uses a speculative accusation to provoke a reaction.
why: Reactions to a guess can be coincidental or caused by pressure.

text: Facts that affected parties never disputed at the time and that were never later refuted can be treated as settled.
when: Reconstructing a past event where contemporary parties were in a position to challenge claims.
why: Lack of contemporary or later challenge is weak but real evidence of accuracy.

text: Set a counter-argument against an observation and treat the observation as suggestive rather than proof when the counter-argument has strong grounds.
when: Reasoning from observation that conflicts with a theory.
why: Observations can be misleading, so they should not be treated as settled.

text: Adopt a working premise, such as the subject's innocence, before weighing evidence. The premise determines which evidence is sought and which lines of inquiry are pursued.
when: when deciding what evidence to pursue

text: Check a fresh theory against the clue it accounts for least well, since a theory that fits that clue poorly is weak.
when: a new theory competes with an existing one

text: When several predicted facts all hold, the chance of that happening by coincidence is low, supporting the theory.
when: Several independent predictions are confirmed.
why: Joint coincidence is unlikely if the theory is wrong.

text: Separate confirmed facts from inferences in the case file, and let players run experiments such as a climb or a cut to verify a route.
when: building an investigation journal
why: players need to know which claims are verified

text: Once sedation takes hold, the actor becomes inert and sleeps, and on waking has no memory of what was done during the night.
when: A person passes from a stimulated state into deep sedation.
why: The sedative phase blocks the formation of memory.

text: Seating placement determines who sits near whom, and this proximity shapes which conversations happen at a table.
Investigation divides into gathering facts from physical traces and interpreting them through method, sequence and psychology, which are separate tasks.
why: traces supply facts, but meaning requires reasoning about intent

text: Explanations accepted unchallenged, such as an object's first plausible reading or a settled claim from an official-sounding source, can yield a confident but mistaken reading; test them.
Dismissing a detail as trivial, or because its theory is weak, can hide a real clue resolving a contradiction; check it against physical evidence.
when: when judging whether a detail matters
why: A weak theory does not make every related detail false.

text: A conclusion built on an unexamined premise can make an investigator overlook the evidence that would refute it.
A theory that rests on an unproven assumption is weaker than one that explains each fact; check whether key evidence is assumed rather than shown.
why: An assumed premise can carry a whole explanation without support

text: A place that looks secluded is often busy in practice, so its seclusion should be verified rather than assumed.
Treating an attractive hypothesis as settled before testing it lets unrelated events appear to confirm it.
when: a case dominates the investigator's thinking
why: fixation makes coincidences look confirming

text: Assuming others are ignorant of a matter without checking is risky, since a wrong guess changes what should be done.
when: Deciding who knows what

text: Taking the list of stolen items at face value sends the investigation after a generic thief instead of the actual motive behind the crime.
when: When a theft's loot list looks like ordinary opportunism
why: The cover story hides the real aim until the motive is found

text: A least-observation conclusion depends on assumptions such as no accomplice and no silence by witnesses; each assumption must be stated and tested.
why: Hidden assumptions can make a plausible timeline wrong.

text: Confusing a fact with its interpretation, or treating the obvious solution as proven, produces a conclusion the evidence does not support.
Plausible but unsupported claims, such as an unnamed party's warnings, should be marked unresolved until evidence arrives.
when: a theory depends on an unseen actor
why: plausibility alone does not establish a fact

text: A bluff that the target sees through weakens the interrogator's position.
Assuming a source's motive is obvious without testing it can lead the investigator to misjudge both the source and the claim.
Treating a rule drawn from finite cases as absolute leads to dismissing exceptions that should be considered.
why: Absolute assumptions block consideration of counterexamples.

text: Matching one shared trait to one category commits the undistributed middle error, treating a common trait as identifying a single category.
Treating an accurate forensic match as final proof ends the inquiry too early. Popular belief overrates the evidential value of prints.
when: when a single match seems to settle a case

text: Reading a deviation as meaningful without knowing the normal routine leads to false conclusions.
when: Interpreting a change in a setting's behaviour.
why: A change is only evidence relative to a known baseline.

text: An explanation that accounts for every observation can still be impossible to prove, so it needs a test that could fail.
Clearing one suspect can cause tunnel vision toward the remaining suspect, so re-check the rest of the field.
Assuming a crime was unplanned because it looks violent can mislead, since that reasoning rests on habit and character rather than evidence.
A demonstration that answers one objection can leave another open, so each separate objection needs its own test.
when: a reconstruction addresses one doubt but others remain
why: One successful test does not settle questions about other actors or sequence.

text: Frustration can make a line of questioning look pointless to teammates, causing it to be dropped before its value shows.
when: A line of questioning yields little at first.
why: Impatience hides slow-building evidence from the people judging the work.

text: Concluding that there is no reason for a suspicious act, such as an alias, because no motive has been found is an assumption, not a finding.
when: When an investigator explains away an anomaly for lack of a discovered motive.
why: Failing to find a motive does not establish that none exists.

text: Assuming the window was the only exit from a room can mislead, since other routes may remain open.
when: when deducing how an intruder entered or left
why: Overlooking an alternative route leads to a wrong conclusion.

text: Inferring the perpetrator's skill from one feature can mislead, since different backgrounds can produce the same result.
when: A profile of a culprit rests on a single technical feature.
why: Several kinds of training can produce identical physical outcomes.

text: An unexamined assumption about what a witness knows can invalidate an elimination.
when: When excluding a suspect based on a witness's recognition.
why: The witness's knowledge is often assumed rather than established.

text: 1) Build a base layer of facts that no one could reasonably deny. 2) Keep interpretations and rumours apart from it. 3) Test each interpretation against the base layer.
when: Many accounts conflict and the investigator must decide what is established
why: A clean fact base keeps theories from being mistaken for evidence

text: 1) Write down what is established. 2) Name each assumption and the facts it rests on. 3) Find an alternative that fits the same facts. 4) Decide what evidence would separate the two. 5) Test the most fragile assumption first.
when: When a theory depends on an assumed route, timing or method

text: Log observations and inferences as separate journal entries, marked suspected or proven, so players see which conclusions need verification and revisions don't alter what was seen.
when: when a journal or case log records clues or witness statements
why: Inferences are often revised as new evidence arrives, so separation lets players revisit conclusions.

text: Before using an account, separate firm observations from guesses and assumptions, for witnesses and investigators alike, such as a shocked witness's belief an object was gone or window open.
Keep independent confirmations of each minute, and who could confirm it, separate from the suspect's own account, and check any published report against them.
When explaining a solution, open with facts found yourself and label each revealed fact as confessed or deduced; presenting confession facts as deductions breaks fair play.
when: when reconstructing or explaining how a solution was reached

text: Separate observed facts from interpretations such as motive or character, and record each with its own confidence level.
when: when a witness mixes what they saw with what they believe about it
why: interpretations can be wrong even when observations are right

text: Keep a clue's raw fact apart from the interpretation attached to it, such as where an object was found versus who is guilty.
when: Evaluating any physical clue
why: The same fact supports different conclusions depending on the account placed around it.

text: Separate established facts from hypotheses and hold both to the same standard of proof.
Let players mark a theory as a guess until they have checked it against the physical evidence.
when: players form hypotheses from physical clues
why: marking guesses separates untested theories from confirmed conclusions

text: Separate 'seen' and 'inferred' entries in a clue journal so players can test an NPC's account against other evidence.
Tag each witness statement as seen, heard or inferred, so players can weigh how much each line is worth.
Separate a witness saying they saw something from being able to identify it; a sincere witness with conflicting details is still weak evidence.
when: Judging how much a sighting can support a conclusion
why: Sincerity does not make a detail reliable

text: Set explicit evidence thresholds and show the gap between accusation and proof in the game's journal.
why: players can see how far they are from a conclusion

text: Keep uncertain identifications separate from confirmed ones, so weaker evidence does not inflate the strength of the case.
when: Compiling a list of evidence
why: Mixing confidence levels overstates what is actually known

text: Keep evidence separate from the conclusions others draw from it, and keep testing alternative explanations until the evidence settles them.
Separate a biased witness's factual claims from their judgments and opinions, keeping the facts and discounting the judgments.
when: When a witness is biased but may still be a source of reliable facts.
why: Biased people can still report accurate events.

text: Discard speculation about a suspect's race or nationality, since it is unsupported by evidence and misleads the investigation.
Separate what records document from what is inferred, such as motives, when identifying a figure from household records.
why: identifications built on inference are weaker than documented ones

text: Let players hold two conflicting readings of one note and resolve them only after finding physical evidence.
Make the victim's rank a variable in investigation depth, so a high-status death triggers a fuller inquiry and the player can see the difference.
when: Designing how thoroughly a death is investigated.

text: Let players collect accurate clues that point to the wrong suspect, then reward the clue that breaks the chain.
Show confirmed links with check marks in a deduction interface, so the player sees each fact established.
Keep emotional scenes that raise NPC trust separate from evidence flags, so players do not confuse emotional rapport with proof.
when: Tracking NPC relationships and case evidence.
why: Trust and evidence are different states and should not be merged.

text: Log which lines the player has heard, and surface them when matching evidence appears, so delayed recall feels earned.
Let a clue journal retag earlier entries with new meaning when a key revelation fires, so players see links they had missed.
Keep retracted NPC accusations in the dialogue log as valid clues the player can revisit.
when: an NPC withdraws a claim during dialogue
why: Withdrawn claims can still carry usable information

text: Let players tag which collected NPC statements they trust, then check those tags against later evidence.
when: players gather testimony in a journal or dialogue log
why: tagging makes the player's judgements visible and testable

text: Tag dialogue lines that matter so the game can guide the player's attention without a direct hint.
Store second-hand facts, such as an NPC's claimed hour, as uncertain so a later discovery can correct them.
Let players choose between watching a suspect and acting on them, with a visible cost for waiting.
Atmosphere frames a mystery but is not proof: test each eerie cue against physical evidence, like a hidden chest or drawer, since mood can color ordinary facts.
when: When evaluating eerie details in an investigation or a scene relying heavily on tone.
why: Physical evidence distinguishes human work from supernatural causes; mood alone cannot establish facts or let players make progress.

text: Ornament untied to plot dilutes attention when evidence is needed, and overused cues without payoffs lose force, so tie each cue to a following event.
when: Repeating mood imagery across a story, or when the reader needs evidence.
why: Cues without payoffs become empty and reduce trust in future warnings.

text: When a decisive fact is disclosed to a hushed room, the audience's attention turns to the implicated person, who is watched closely for a reaction.
when: a decisive fact is disclosed in front of a group
why: people look for signs of guilt in the accused

text: Audience sympathy can override evidence, so a case may turn more on who seems wronged than on the facts.
when: A trial or judgement is made before an audience with emotional stakes.
why: People favour the party they sympathise with over what the evidence shows.

text: Public appeals address an audience, while private praise addresses an ally whose support is needed.
when: A writer sends a flattering private letter to someone whose backing they need.
why: The recipient's support is the real target.

text: Words spoken for an audience, including denials, may mislead anyone who takes them at face value, so separate what is said for watchers from what is meant.
when: Interpreting dialogue in a monitored or hostile setting.
why: Speakers shape words to deceive listeners who may be watching.

text: Atmosphere such as darkness, silence, oppression, and matching weather sets the pacing and mood, reinforcing the protagonists' gloom.
A narrator kept in the dark can make the audience feel excluded from the solution.
Too much staging, such as dramatic arrivals or shouting, can pull attention away from the real clues.
when: A confrontation is heavily dramatized.
why: Spectacle captures attention that should go to factual evidence.

text: Describe the setting's mood as part of the mystery, showing danger and violence as ordinary, so the place itself signals threat.
Explaining away every eerie detail drains dread and dismissing all atmosphere leaves the world flat, while explaining nothing loses the audience's trust.
when: When resolving a horror mystery or designing an investigation with an eerie setting.
why: Full explanation removes the unknown and removing all atmosphere drains mood, while no explanation makes the story seem arbitrary.

text: Make an authority figure's wrong theory plausible at each stage so the player's correction must be earned by evidence and the real culprit stays hidden until a final logic check.
when: Writing an official investigator whose conclusions the player must challenge, or the real culprit must stay hidden late in the story.
why: A weak wrong theory makes the correction trivial and removes tension; the audience accepts an official theory and stops testing alternatives.

text: A disturbance reported by a judge or authority figure can damage that figure's composure, and others may read the shaken state as evidence.
when: When an authority figure reports a disturbing event and shows distress.
why: Visible distress by a figure of authority changes how others interpret the event.

text: When an authority figure misjudges publicly, players can see the error and doubt the conclusion, which invites them to question the official theory.
when: A respected character publicly names the wrong suspect.
why: Visible error on the authority's part lets players discount the stated verdict.

text: Let a recurring authority figure dismiss the protagonist's theory, so the protagonist's later correction feels earned.
when: a protagonist must prove a theory against official opinion
why: The dismissal sets up a visible contrast that the correction then resolves.

text: A trusted authority figure who seems to have closed a case may have concealed the truth, so a late confession can reveal complicity and reverse trust in official accounts.
when: An official account has been accepted without question.
why: Audiences trust officials, so their concealment is a strong late reversal.

text: When the false explanation is offered by a credible authority figure, the player must defeat a trusted voice rather than a rumour, which raises the difficulty of the reveal.
when: Designing the misleading explanation in a mystery.
why: Authority makes the false answer more persuasive, so disproving it requires stronger proof.

text: When an authority figure closes a line of inquiry too early, players trust the decision and only later notice the gap it left behind.
when: a trusted investigator dismisses a suspect's alibi
why: Players defer to the authority's judgment.

text: Assuming a judge will always give an untrained party full consideration is a mistake, since judges may carry biases from their background or dislike certain witnesses.
when: Planning a formal hearing where one party is untrained.
why: Personal bias and prior experience can shape how fairly a judge weighs a party.

text: Test a respected authority's theory against an alternative explanation when new evidence arrives, rather than treating the theory as settled.
when: A respected expert holds a theory that new evidence may not support.
why: Settled conclusions receive less scrutiny, which lets errors persist.

text: Place the true antagonist in an authority role the player has no easy reason to suspect, and let that role supply the information they need.
when: Designing a hidden culprit who holds an official position.
why: Trust in an official's role masks the influence they exert on the case.

text: Judge disputed authorship by a controlled side-by-side comparison with a known sample from the supposed writer; never link a document to an author on one telling feature alone.
when: A document or object can be compared with known samples
why: One feature can mislead, and confirmation needs a fair comparison

text: Physical evidence is only as strong as its attribution, so a genuine trace can still point to the wrong person.
When a cry or exclamation could come from several suspects, establish what each could have been doing at that moment before attributing it.
when: a sound is linked to multiple candidates
why: a sound alone rarely names one person

text: When no record names an author or place, combine deeds, handwriting comparison and registers to narrow the candidates.
Hostile writers may exaggerate and sympathetic writers may excuse, so weigh each account against its author's motive before trusting its details.
when: When sources are partisan.
why: Both kinds of bias can distort the same events in opposite directions.

text: Let a document's flaws point to whoever handled its drafting, so players can trace responsibility.
when: Designing documents that hide a collusion trail.
why: Errors left by a drafter can be followed back to them.

text: Testimony that names who gave an order ties an act to a specific person, making responsibility easier to test.
when: when an act's responsibility is disputed
why: a named authority can be confirmed or denied

text: Accounts naming several people, such as he says or she says, make it easy to lose track of who gave which claim, so record attribution for each claim.
Long chains of second-hand attribution can hide where a claim first came from, so trace the claim to its origin.
A message written for an audience can guard its true meaning, so its apparent content may mislead.
why: Coded or public wording is meant to be read by many people, not just the intended recipient.

text: A depicted person or artwork is not evidence of a relationship on its own, since it may have an ordinary explanation.
A genuine-looking report can still be a mistake or a deception, so authenticity is not the same as reliability.
A letter that only praises its writer invites suspicion; the audience should be able to question it.
1) Compare the handwriting with a known sample. 2) Check the signature. 3) Accept a letter that reverses a presumed fact only after both checks pass.
when: When a letter contradicts an established fact.

text: 1) List what the writer must have known. 2) List what access the writer needed. 3) List what materials the writer could obtain. 4) Keep only candidates who meet every condition.
when: when an anonymous message reveals what its author must have known
why: each condition filters the pool of possible writers

text: Do not assume who wrote a typed letter just because someone had access to the machine; test authorship independently.
Do not link an anonymous act or document to a named real person without concrete evidence; a guess about authorship is not attribution.
why: tying a real person to an event without evidence can misrepresent that person

text: Authenticate every document used in a reveal, or the audience may dismiss it as forged.
when: when a reveal relies on papers
why: unverified papers can be waved away

text: Ask about physical attributes a method requires, since one answer can close an entire line of theory.
Author dialogue tells, such as an over-emphatic denial or a question that exposes fear, as signals the player is meant to notice.
when: Writing NPC dialogue that hides a truth.
why: Visible tells reward attentive players.

text: Ask who proposed an action and who agreed to it, since attribution of a suggestion can matter more than the action itself.
Show each in-game record's author and place of writing, so players can judge the motives behind it.
Vivid, uncheckable backstory details reveal a speaker's character and state more than they establish facts; do not read detail as evidence.
People perform routine acts, such as securing a loose item, almost automatically, so a missing habitual act signals a changed plan or state.
when: when a habitual act is absent from an account
why: routines run without conscious thought

text: Background facts show that an act was possible for a person, not that they committed it. They must be combined with physical evidence.
when: when history is used to support a suspect
why: Possibility is weaker than proof and can be shared by many people.

text: Background about a person's marriage, finances and reputation can supply a motive and shape how relatives are seen.
Check a body against unalterable traits, such as a long-worn ring or scar; an item that cannot be removed from the real person betrays a substituted body.
when: A body may have been replaced
why: A ring worn for years cannot be removed from a substituted body, so its presence or absence reveals the swap.

text: Verify a newcomer with a second source; one accepted on a third party's word, without references, may be a plant, since a convincing story can hide a false identity.
Gather a suspect's background through acquaintances, since relationships, family objections and money controls can supply a possible motive.
when: Building a motive profile for a suspect.
why: Personal and financial dependencies often explain why someone acts.

text: Treat an unusually polite request from an unlikely source as a warning sign; the length and location of a talk matter more than its content.
when: when an unexpected party asks for a private conversation
why: Such talks can hold a target in place while something else happens nearby.

text: Backstory such as lost fortune, family history or wounded pride explains why a threat was so intense.
when: A grudge needs to feel strong enough to justify violence

text: Uneven wear on a body, such as one hand larger and more developed than the other, suggests habitual manual work.
when: a person's body shows lopsided development
why: repeated use develops the body unevenly

text: Give look-alike characters one unchanging visible trait, such as eye colour or a crest, so the player can match identities later despite the disguise.
when: when several characters share a silhouette or face

text: Trace a suspect's history for past dependence, mistreatment or ties to a criminal family, since these shape their state of mind.
when: when a suspect's behavior seems unexplained
why: Past experience explains why an act felt possible to the person.

text: Tie NPC grudges to a concrete asset such as a house, salary or vote, so players uncover allegiances by reading records.
when: designing NPC factions for a game
why: A visible stake makes allegiances traceable through documents.

text: Tie a threat to the protagonist's past so the persecution has moral logic.
Give a character's claimed backstory one checkable contradiction against other NPCs, letters or records, so verifying players discover a slip that unlocks a branch.
when: designing character claims the player can verify

text: A character's personal history, such as a grievance or lost prospects, colours how he speaks about others and reads evidence, and others may notice his unguarded remarks.
when: When a character's history might affect how he treats witnesses or interprets the scene.
why: Private resentment and sacrifice bias perception and speech, so the character's view is not neutral.

text: An object described briefly as background early in a story can later return as evidence, so readers and players who noticed it hold information the offender may have missed.
when: Designing mundane props that later matter
why: Items noticed once and then ignored are recalled as significant when they reappear.

text: A background check reveals motive hints only when a real link exists, so routine checks are informative but do not always pay off.
A disguise never shown or hinted at makes the reveal feel unfair; show the costume early with clear ownership.
A backstory revealed only at the end feels unearned unless earlier scenes plant the threat.
when: Revealing a hidden motive late in a story

text: Accepting a close relative's identification without testing it means the identity rests on emotion as much as on proof.
when: an identification comes from someone who wants it to be true
why: emotional certainty can replace evidence

text: A striking skill, such as recognising faces from eyes alone, must be tested before it is trusted, because prior knowledge or rigging can explain the result.
when: when a character's skill is used as evidence
why: Hidden knowledge can mimic genuine ability.

text: A routine known to one character but not another can make the second character misjudge who is present at a given hour, ruining an alibi.
An unusual request for lodging can be noticed and remembered by staff, which undermines the cover identity.
when: A newcomer asks for an odd or inconvenient place to stay.
why: Staff remember out-of-the-ordinary requests.

text: A profile built on one unverified trait can mislead, so every attribute needs its own traceable source.
when: Building a description of an unknown person
why: An unsourced trait can send searches to the wrong people

text: Access gained through an assumed name fails once the household checks the claimed background, so the cover depends on no one checking.
A replacement explanation can rest on an unexamined assumption, such as that a missing person existed, even when its attacks on the first theory are sound.
when: building a new theory after refuting an old one
why: refuting one story does not validate another

text: If no one questions a persona, the audience has no reason to revisit it when contrary evidence arrives.
when: When a persona is presented without any doubt raised
why: Unquestioned surfaces are not reconsidered

text: Accepting other characters' descriptions without testing them lets reputation serve as misdirection.
1) Learn the victim's identity, origin, habits and known enemies. 2) Only then judge the scene's details against that background.
when: beginning an investigation of a death
why: Background gives the details a frame for judging witnesses.

text: Mark a character's self-reported backstory, single-NPC lore, or claim no one else can confirm as unverified until a second source or physical object confirms it.
when: A new character, witness or NPC gives a single-source account or self-explanation.
why: Self-reported details can be false, and recording unconfirmed claims as fact corrupts the case record.

text: Deliver backstory as ordered dialogue beats, each a checkable claim the player can test against the world.
when: An NPC explains past events
why: Checkable claims let players weigh information instead of accepting it passively

text: Do not rank suspects by background traits such as origin or language skill alone.
why: such traits are weak grounds for suspicion and easily mislead

text: Treat a trace as meaningful only when it exceeds the natural background level for that substance.
why: Common substances occur naturally in trace amounts

text: Establish hostility between two characters early, as known background history rather than as a clue.
Establish the background fact, such as a known opposition, before inferring belief from a group's choice of advisor.
why: A choice only signals allegiance when the advisor's known stance is established.

text: Tie a natural or elemental threat to a buried, ancient cause rather than a present villain, so the source lies in the past.
when: When a supernatural hazard needs a deeper origin
why: An ancient cause gives players a discoverable backstory that explains the threat.

text: Deliver the motive in a separate backstory block after the present crime is solved, so the past recasts the crime rather than being explained by the investigation.
when: a mystery whose present crime is already solved
why: the investigation stays on who did it, while the past gives the crime its meaning

text: Presenting a long provenance story before naming a value makes the listener accept the high value before bargaining begins, but the story must hold up if tested.
when: A seller or persuader sets a price or claim after a narrative
why: Accepted framing anchors later negotiation; unverified detail risks exposure.

text: Ask concrete questions about food and drink; the answers show how long a captive was held and whether the account fits the known facts.
Judge whether a behaviour was unusual only against a baseline of the person's normal habits, such as usual drinking or seating.
Compare an object's current state with its known earlier state. The difference between two observations can be the clue.
when: when a scene's objects have a known or recalled earlier state
why: A change is only visible against a baseline.

text: Compare a found object with the victim's own belongings; a mismatch lets that object be excluded as theirs.
A control sample gives a baseline, so a reaction in a test sample means something and false exoneration or false accusation becomes less likely.
1) Speak close to the patient's ear. 2) Press the patient's hand. 3) Lift an eyelid. If there is no reaction, the patient cannot yet give testimony.
when: before relying on a bedside statement
why: Testimony needs a responsive witness.

text: 1) Find the sign that looks like evidence. 2) Survey how often the same sign occurs naturally in the area. 3) Treat the sign as meaningful only if it is unusual compared with that baseline.
when: a sign such as a broken twig or disturbed foliage appears
why: the environment can produce the same sign without any crime

text: Check a suspect's basic facts, such as finances, shared profits, spending and character, before accepting their guilt.
when: A suspect is under pursuit.
why: Neglected basic facts let a wrong explanation survive.

text: Record a starting count of a small countable item before it changes hands, so later disputes about it can be tested.
when: A countable item is central to a suspicion
why: A fixed agreed number turns a claim of loss into a checkable fact.

text: Ordinary routine, such as sport, polite drinks and a tidy house, reads as innocent and makes investigators drop lines of inquiry they should keep open.
when: investigating a setting that outwardly looks domestic
why: familiar signs of harmless life lower expectations of threat

text: People with an orderly view of the world find it hard to accept that rank does not guarantee virtue, so they resist accusations against office holders.
why: they expect judges and clergy to be upright

text: Ordinary crimes with many plausible motives and methods are harder to solve than unusual ones, since they lack distinguishing features and each explanation seems equally possible.
when: a case looks routine and several explanations seem to fit
why: no single explanation is favoured by the evidence, and nothing focuses the investigation

text: Before accepting apparently supernatural knowledge or a spectacle as supernatural, check ordinary channels first: gossip, a relative, an earlier record, or whether a skilled performer could produce it by ordinary means.
when: a witness reveals something they could not have observed directly, or a spectacle seems supernatural
why: ordinary sources can account for knowledge or feats that appear impossible

text: Ordinary states such as a mount's freshness or dry boots can test an NPC's account of travel, so use them as checkable clues.
when: an NPC describes a journey
why: everyday conditions reflect the effort of travel

text: Describing a culprit as unremarkable is typical of hidden masterminds, so blandness can itself be a clue.
when: a witness describes the suspect as ordinary
why: hidden masterminds are deliberately forgettable

text: When a key object disappears from its last recorded location, check ordinary explanations such as cleaning or routine disposal before assuming tampering.
when: A recorded object is missing from where it was last seen.
why: Mundane causes are more common than deliberate removal.

text: The most ordinary reading may be right in one respect yet miss the case, so each reading must be tested against the other facts.
when: an event has a mundane explanation
why: partial truths can hide the real cause

text: Assuming that because an ordinary person cannot do something, nobody could, overlooks routes that exceptional abilities open.
when: Judging whether a suspect could reach a sealed place
why: Ability differences are ignored when the route is judged by normal capability

text: The norm departure method depends on the investigator's knowledge of normal practice, which can itself be wrong.
why: A mistaken idea of normal practice makes ordinary behavior look suspicious.

text: Assuming a nominal ruler acts independently is a mistake when advisers and early contacts shape his views and decisions.
when: a figurehead holds formal power

text: 1) List the usual practice for each actor in the story. 2) Compare each reported action against that practice. 3) Treat each mismatch, a departure from common practice that suggests a hidden purpose, as a lead to test against the explanation.
when: a witness account must be checked for plausibility
why: practice is predictable, so a departure from it signals a motive

text: 1) Observe and record the scene before the event. 2) Compare the scene afterwards against that baseline. 3) Treat any change as evidence that someone handled it.
Do not treat ordinary conduct, such as a lively household or a lost temper, as proof of a crime.
A witness whose conviction-supporting account rests on seeing or hearing must rely on ordinary human faculties, not on claimed perceptions only they have.
when: when judging whether a witness account can support a verdict

text: Investigators should use the same lawful methods for every crime, instead of special tests or procedures for one kind of offence.
when: when investigating a crime that seems to need special handling
why: Ordinary methods can be checked, while special tests are easier to bend toward a predetermined result.

text: Suspicion is reasoned doubt justifying keeping someone on a suspect list; proof is specific evidence holding under scrutiny that justifies accusation. These are distinct stages; each claim must be provable.
A case record can differ from what investigators believe happened, since unproven crimes stay unrecorded.
Treat a plausible story as a conjecture, not proof; keep rival explanations open until evidence separates them.
when: evidence is partial and one story fits neatly
why: a neat fit can still be wrong

text: Do not assume a blackmailer and a murderer are the same person without evidence; keep the possibility open.
Suspicion built from rumour, coincidence and character reading can add up to a strong feeling but does not prove guilt.
why: Each weak cue can have an innocent explanation, and agreement among them does not remove that possibility.

text: A character's false belief can reveal their state of mind and motive, especially when the error is explained and connected to the case.
A false belief survives after part of it is disproven, because it still explains real clues that the player has already accepted.
why: Each lie accounts for some existing evidence, so the player keeps the belief

text: Eerie atmosphere or emotion, such as imagined apparitions, is not a clue and must not replace checked facts; only verified facts advance the inquiry.
when: Interpreting eerie or emotional imagery, or feeling an eerie presence around a case.
why: Mood can feel like proof while carrying no factual weight; feeling is not evidence.

text: Threatening consequences alone may not produce a confession; an obstinate suspect can withstand pressure without proof.
when: When pressure is the only lever used in questioning
why: Pressure works best when backed by evidence the suspect knows is real

text: Confirming that an event happened does not confirm what was said during it; only one party may report the content.
when: when a call or meeting is confirmed
why: Confirmation covers the occurrence, not the content.

text: Treating a theory about an unwritten document as proof is a pitfall; it needs support from other evidence before it is accepted.
A surmised motive is not evidence of identity; a theory must be confirmed before it can establish who did the act.
when: An investigator builds a case on motive alone.
why: Benefit does not automatically identify the actor.

text: A found object can look like it confirms a theory when it only fits the theory loosely, so it should not count as proof on its own.
when: Interpreting a single physical find
why: One object usually establishes only a limited fact

text: Keep belief separate from proof and base decisions on evidence alone: mark proven conclusions versus suspicions; a conviction may be stated openly while admitting it cannot yet be demonstrated.
when: A case rests on inference or the decisive evidence is not yet in hand.
why: A strong belief can feel like knowledge; stating the gap keeps the accusation honest.

text: Pressure alone neither proves guilt nor shows the accused knows what the scene reveals; accept a pressured confession only once its statements match what was observed.
why: Pressure can produce false admissions as easily as true ones.

text: Keep an investigator's proof separate from their reputation, so accusations are judged by evidence rather than by standing.
when: Rumour attacks the credibility of an accusation.
why: Mixing proof with reputation lets rumour decide what is true.

text: Mark which parts of a speaker's account are confirmed by other sources and which are only that speaker's belief.
Separate confirmed case journal entries from rumour entries, so players build the base layer of facts before forming theories.
when: Designing a case journal or investigation log
why: Players who see rumour mixed with confirmed facts may build theories on the wrong base

text: Keep a witness's belief separate from physical evidence. A physical trace is data, while the claimed nature of a creature is only asserted.
when: when a witness describes an unusual cause

text: Store financial motive and personal motive as separate values, so the player can weigh greed against grudge.
when: when modeling NPC motives for a mystery or inheritance plot
why: separate values let players judge which motive best explains an action

text: Treat a confirmed difference between matched objects as a lead, then check whether the object was moved or the difference was always present.
when: a feature of a matched object does not match its pair
why: A difference may be innocent and predate the event.

text: Keep the source of each pressure separate from the evidence; record only what the facts support, not the frustration that outside remarks produce.
Separate the stated charge from the underlying cause, and check whether the official reason explains the outcome fully.
when: Analysing a persecution, expulsion or punishment whose official reason seems incomplete.
why: The stated charge can hide a different motive, such as control of property or office.

text: Present a reconstructed decision as a probable explanation, not proof, when records are missing.
why: Hedged words such as probable mark conjecture, and readers often mistake them for settled fact.

text: Keep the question of whether a harm occurred separate from the question of who caused it, and require independent evidence for the second before resolving an accusation.
when: An accuser reports harm and names a specific person
why: Accepting that harm occurred can quietly stand in for proof of who caused it

text: Treat a suspect's conviction about an explanation as an argument to weigh, not as proof; the arrangement of objects decides.
Give self-interested NPCs biased accounts with visible motives so players can test which claims hold up; never discard a biased account, since it may still contain a true fact.
when: designing NPC testimony
why: Visible motive lets players discount bias without losing the true details.

text: Give some NPCs biased opinions about others, so players must weigh the source of a claim as well as the claim itself.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that expresses judgements about other characters.
why: Players then evaluate testimony by its source, which deepens investigation.

text: Treat an NPC's claims of certainty as biased, and let the player verify each factual claim against the world.
Give a powerful NPC advice that seems neutral but binds the player to one faction, and let reporting it to rivals change faction standing.
when: When designing faction-based choices.
why: Reporting gives the player a lever over allegiance.

text: Let a biased NPC withhold an exculpatory document, so the player must find it elsewhere to reach the truth.
Give an NPC a briefing about another character before they meet, and make the briefing's bias discoverable, so the player can check the NPC's view against the world state.
when: designing NPC dialogue where one character's opinion of another is shaped in advance
why: Players can then detect where an NPC's view is wrong and reason about why.

text: Stakeholder records (diaries, published case records, accounts clearing or shielding others) shape what is included and omitted; confirm them independently.
when: Relying on a diary, published case record, or witness record as evidence.
why: Self-regard, bias, or a held conclusion can shape even a detailed record toward its writer's aims.

text: An official with a standing grudge, or who arrested the witness and wrote the record, can steer players toward the wrong suspect; test their conclusions against evidence.
1) Write the journal entry from the author's stake and mood. 2) Tag it with the writer's stake. 3) Provide a second source the player can cross-check against it.
when: An NPC with a grudge or personal interest writes a journal or quest log.
why: Tagging the stake teaches the player to discount the entry, and a second source lets them test it.

text: Include a biased character's document with a note of its writer's involvement, so players can weigh its claims themselves.
when: designing in-game documents

text: Bizarre crimes often prove less mysterious than they look, and the bigger the crime, the more obvious its motive tends to be.
when: A plot seems inexplicable.
why: Large schemes need large motives, which are easier to identify.

text: Provide a bestiary of reference descriptions so players can match a physical trace to a creature entry.
when: designing traces that point to a creature
why: a reference lets players compare traces with documented features

text: A suspect who explains a contradiction by claiming the questioner misunderstood is likely patching the story rather than telling the truth.
when: A suspect is confronted with their own earlier words.
why: Reframing as misunderstanding is a common way to defend an inconsistent account.

text: A partner who senses betrayal may respond with mockery and open threats rather than negotiation.
when: a partner believes they will be sacrificed

text: Under pressure, a witness may accuse another person to protect themselves, and the accusation often contains a true, checkable fact.
when: a frightened witness is pressed by questioning
why: self-protection pushes suspicion toward someone with a plausible link

text: When a belief places an enemy among one's closest circle, the nearest and most prominent people become the most dangerous suspects, because their betrayal feels deepest.
when: a fixed belief casts the enemy as hidden inside the community
why: Betrayal by a close person carries more emotional weight than by a stranger.

text: When pressed, accusers who blame one another reveal that their account is unstable.
Officials who blame agitators for a dispute may leave the original accusations unexamined.
when: When authorities attribute unrest to people who stoke it.
why: Blame moves attention away from whether the claims are valid.

text: A small, legally pending dispute can serve as the procedural vehicle for a larger grievance, so an action taken over the minor issue may really answer the larger one.
when: a formal action cites a minor pending dispute

text: People often shift blame for a loved one's faults onto outside companions, moving guilt away from the loved one.
when: a parent or guardian judges a child's misconduct
why: protecting the loved one from blame

text: Someone who acted on false information may be less culpable than the person who deceived them, so blame can shift away from the helper.
Model blame moving through a town after a disaster as rumour that grows by repetition, and treat individual guilt as a separate matter to show.
Place a suspect who is blamed for an environmental hazard, such as a trap or creature, while the real cause is visible only in a later test.
when: Designing a mystery where a hazard is wrongly attributed to a person.
why: Blaming the wrong agent keeps the real cause hidden until a test exposes it.

text: Misfortunes generated by the world can create new suspicion, so the player sees a belief feed itself as events accumulate.
when: Designing a village with a suspicion system
why: Each misfortune is read as evidence, strengthening the belief

text: When a loss follows a recent quarrel, the losing party tends to blame the quarrel partner, turning misfortune into an accusation.
when: when an animal, crop or household suffers a loss after a dispute
why: People look for a cause, and a recent quarrel offers one

text: A plausible explanation that names a convenient culprit with a motive can steer an inquiry away from the real cause.
when: a suspect offers an explanation for a crime
why: a motive that fits the first suspect discourages further search

text: A late reversal can shift blame to a procedural argument, reopening guilt after the culprit is exposed, so long as the argument rests on facts the audience already had.
when: Final resolution depends on a detail that reframes responsibility.
why: A reversal consistent with earlier evidence keeps the fair-play promise; one contradicting shown facts breaks it.

text: Accusing a suspect over misfortunes such as livestock deaths, especially after a quarrel or curse, rests on slender grounds: presumption, not proof, without a separate causal link.
A confession may shift blame onto others, so every claim in it should be verified before it is accepted.
Assigning all blame to a hidden party hides the human motives and consents that actually made the harm possible.

1) List exactly who knows the secret. 2) Confirm that nobody else knows it. 3) Require a secrecy pledge and a conduct pledge together. 4) Attach checkable conditions. 5) Have each party confirm the account aloud.
when: a small group shares a sensitive fact
why: a defined circle makes later suspicion easier to assess

text: A bluff about information the target lacks reveals its reaction, but works only while the target believes it, and its force comes from the target's own fear.
when: The bluff depends on information the target lacks, or the questioner claims evidence it cannot produce.
why: A bluff relies on the other side not knowing the truth; belief, not proof, gives the threat its effect.

text: A bluff about evidence collapses once the other side can check it, so avoid bluffs where checking is simple; rely only on claims unverifiable on the spot.
when: The other party has access to a means of verification.
why: Unsupported claims cannot survive an independent check; verification exposes the false claim and removes its leverage, and a checkable false claim destroys credibility and control.

text: A bluffed claim about nonexistent evidence or knowledge is likely to be tested and exposed, ending trust and cooperation for the rest of the exchange.
when: Claiming evidence or knowledge the questioner does not have.
why: A suspect or witness who can check a specific claim will often do so, and a disproved claim weakens the whole approach.

text: A bluff can backfire if the witness sees through it, feels threatened into silence, or concludes its knowledge is worthless and stops talking.
when: Using an implied threat or bluffed claim of knowledge to pressure or test a witness.
why: A witness who detects the bluff may withdraw or resist when threatened; one who feels dismissed may withdraw.

text: Mocking a subject keeps listeners from asking what a procedure is really for, so they focus on the claim rather than the method.
when: A character dismisses a practice with ridicule while controlling it
why: Derision discourages scrutiny of intent

text: A witness may reveal a hidden connection when offered a choice between two candidates, because a pause, flinch or unusually quick denial signals a link.
when: Questioning a witness who withholds a secret that direct questions will not reach.
why: Reactions to a concrete pair of options expose what words conceal.

text: Bluff a calm, guarded suspect by claiming you hold more than you reveal, without naming a source, and watch his reaction.
when: The suspect has already made a statement that can be checked.

text: Use a bluff when the suspect is anxious, time is short and a credible threat exists; avoid it when the claim is easy to check.
Prepare a list of key people and memorised notes before a bluff, so the pressure is consistent and well informed.
when: planning a confrontation built on partial evidence
why: Inconsistent claims under pressure are easy to expose.

text: Openly name a suspect's stance as a bluff, then see whether the suspect's answers hold up against the facts.
A bluff that the case is complete works only while suspects believe it; revealing the trap early ends its effect.
when: Using a feigned exit or feigned weakness to make suspects speak freely
why: Suspects speak candidly only when they think the pressure is gone

text: Naming a detail the suspect hides, like a second name or a visitor they met, makes them believe you know more, so they may confirm or supply it.
when: When a suspect is frightened and may reveal more if they think you know.
why: A suspect who believes you know a hidden detail may confirm it, and a third party may supply it.

text: A suspect who stages a test visit to read the investigator's reaction treats a lack of reaction as proof of safety, even though the investigator may be concealing knowledge.
when: a suspect has one investigator they fear and can arrange an inspection
why: Silence is ambiguous, so a suspect who reads it as safety can be misled by an investigator who does not show what they know.

text: A bluff offered to a suspect, such as a claimed poison on a harmless item, exposes the suspect when their reaction contradicts what they should know.
when: when a confession is absent
why: A guilty suspect's reaction reveals knowledge they should not have.

text: A rigged examination can set seating, restraint, required gaze, a recited prayer, a touch test, staged cures, and limits on contact, each step able to turn compliance into guilt.
when: analyzing or designing an ordeal
why: Each procedural rule can be bent toward a predetermined result.

text: A bluff or accusation can provoke a revealing reaction, but fright or innocence can mimic guilt and leading questions can elicit expected answers; treat reactions as leads, not proof.
when: Using a bluffed claim or accusation to test a witness.
why: Shock and guilt can produce similar reactions, and a reaction shows concern that may have innocent or guilty causes.

text: A bluff or accusation without real evidence held fails or backfires if wrong: it yields no useful reaction, lets the witness discredit the investigator, and ends any chance of confession.
when: Deciding whether to challenge a witness's account or accuse a suspect.
why: A suspect who sees the claim is unfounded keeps denying; an unsupported accusation lets the witness discredit the investigator.

text: Stating an unverified fact as if it were known risks exposure, since the witness may check it and reveal the bluff.
when: When pressing a witness with an unconfirmed claim.

text: A bluff can produce an object that proves less than hoped, so an extracted item should be checked before it is treated as decisive.
A rigid script can make the interviewer miss answers that fall outside the prepared topics.
An improbable method still needs a physical test. Assuming it works without checking timing and distance is an error.
when: A surprising method is proposed for a crime
why: Plausibility on paper does not confirm that the method works in practice

text: Trusting a trap's result before its sample is analysed risks a false conclusion; the reading should rest on the sample and the reaction together.
A feint that no one tests feels too convenient to believe, so a visible test or plausible cause is needed to make it credible.
A bluff built on a weak explanation exposes the investigator when the suspect's reaction shows the explanation has gaps.
when: the explanation behind the pressure is unsound
why: Pressure only holds up when the reasoning behind it is sound.

text: A reveal based only on inference can feel unfair if the earlier action was never shown to the audience.
when: when a twist depends on unseen actions
why: the audience cannot check the inference

text: A test whose result always confirms the examiner's belief is not evidence; it is a rigged clue that can never disprove the accused.
when: Assessing a test used to establish guilt
why: Outcomes fixed in advance carry no information

text: An earlier lie gives the other side leverage, so a bluff in one direction makes the liar vulnerable.
when: when a character has told a lie
why: A false statement can be exposed or used as a threat later.

text: Bluffing without a plan for the suspect's likely reaction, such as running for the door, can leave the investigator with no control.
1) Offer the suspect something that seems to invite checking, such as a key. 2) Watch answer timing and reactions. 3) Physically verify the offer before trusting it.
when: The suspect is confident and a direct question would be deflected.
why: A generous-seeming offer draws out a reaction, and verification exposes an empty offer.

text: 1) Claim knowledge you cannot yet prove. 2) Watch the listener's reaction for hesitation or a pointed reply. 3) Press the advantage where they seem unsure. 4) Break off as if you revealed too much, so the slip reads as confirmation.
when: The other side's knowledge is uncertain and there is time to probe.
why: Reactions expose what the listener does and does not know.

text: 1) Let the suspect believe you hold proof they cannot dispute. 2) Keep the real evidence hidden from them. 3) Keep allies unaware of your true knowledge. 4) Observe the suspect's action on the false belief.
when: When a suspect will deny an act unless convinced you hold proof.
why: A false belief removes the suspect's chance to deny, so their own move can reveal the truth.

text: 1) Plant a false report whose details matter only to the person you want to draw out. 2) Watch whether that person reacts. 3) Verify the reaction before trusting it.
when: Someone is hiding and has a strong personal stake in a particular detail.
why: A false detail that only the target cares about flushes them into view.

text: 1) Present a worthless object as valuable. 2) Watch whether the suspect shows strong interest or agitation. 3) Treat that reaction as evidence of knowledge. 4) Reveal the object's real value in front of the suspect.
when: A suspect has a visible interest in a specific object and the evidence is circumstantial.
why: A desperate interest in a worthless object exposes knowledge the suspect should not need to show.

text: 1) Lay out the crime sequence in order: arrival, method, the victim's state, result. 2) Make a bold claim about a hidden object to test the reaction. 3) When the suspect breaks, offer secrecy or protection for the full account.
when: You hold partial proof and the suspect is emotionally strained
why: Each detail acts as a hook, and an assurance lowers the guard

text: Offer a bluff dialogue option that changes the NPC's response, and record that reaction as a clue so the player can read hidden knowledge from it.
when: Designing dialogue that can expose a character's secret, where the game tracks reactions.
why: Players can use reactions as evidence when the game tracks them.

text: Give NPC bluff checks where confronting with an item reveals a clue if correct and a harmless denial if wrong; add a reassurance option unlocking further dialogue.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that hides information.
why: Both outcomes keep the player engaged without punishing a guess.

text: Back any bluff with real evidence the other party can check, and state it openly with supporting facts attached, since unbacked claims are exposed when tested.
when: When confronting a suspect with a reconstruction or partial proof.
why: A bluff built on guesses fails under challenge and destroys credibility.

text: Do not use a staged bluff that could endanger an innocent person or the investigator, or push an innocent person into a false confession.
when: Considering a bluff against a suspect.
why: The bluff may provoke a second crime.

text: Do not bluff with challenges that depend on details the suspect could check, unless independent evidence exists.
when: when no independent evidence supports the accusation
why: a bluff collapses once the suspect can verify the detail

text: If a player falsely accuses, track the consequence of the accusation, not only the reveal.
when: a player makes an accusation that proves wrong
why: consequences give the accusation meaning in the game world

text: Let the player choose between a bluff and a promise of protection, with each choice changing what the witness will reveal.
Do not use a bluff as a substitute for evidence where a legal or formal standard must be met.
when: the outcome requires proof for a court or formal inquiry
why: A bluff creates pressure, not admissible proof.

text: Let the player watch a suspect stage a test visit to check the detective's reaction, so the player sees the suspect's reasoning and the risk it carries.
when: designing a scene where a suspect probes an investigator
why: Showing the test lets the player judge whether the suspect's conclusion is justified.

text: Pressing a convincing but unproven theory early can force a guilty party to act, but may reveal how little evidence is held and warn them investigators are guessing.
when: Choosing when to press a suspect on a convincing but unproven theory.
why: Pressure can force a guilty party to act and reveal themselves; early pressure exposes how thin the evidence is.

text: A bluff of partial knowledge can shake a guilty party, but exposure ends cooperation and destroys trust; a promise of protection keeps cooperation possible.
when: Choosing whether to bluff or how to press a witness.

text: A bluff tests a suspect but tips them off if the claim is wrong; a direct question alerts no one yet is easily deflected.
A bluff can force a guilty party to act, but the action may endanger others, so the risk must be weighed against the gain.
when: deciding whether to use pressure on a suspect
why: provocation can produce a new crime

text: A bluff mechanic lets the player claim evidence they lack, where later matching clues reward the gamble and failed bluffs cost trust.
when: Designing a player-facing bluff or pressure option in a dialogue system.
why: Rewarding successful bluffs and penalising failed ones makes the gamble a meaningful risk.

text: A bluff can extract reactions, but it proves nothing alone and can make the investigator seem unreliable to people he needs.
when: An investigator considers feigning knowledge or withholding facts
why: Reactions are suggestive evidence, and a deceptive investigator loses trust.

text: A bluff can backfire if the suspect can check the object's value before the reveal, so the bait must survive independent checking.
when: Using a worthless object as bait.
why: A verifiable bluff exposes the investigator instead of the suspect.

text: Observers tend to read a blunt, businesslike manner as a sign of honesty.
when: Judging a witness's trustworthiness
why: Plain style signals sincerity to many readers

text: A culprit who believes pressure falls on someone else, and that proof is thin, may make a bold move that exposes themselves.
when: an investigator openly admits weak proof
why: The culprit's perceived risk drops, so caution gives way to action.

text: Do not discount a bold reconstruction merely for being bold; check it against the facts, since such stories can be right or wrong.
when: an amateur builds a dramatic account from a single clue
why: boldness does not indicate accuracy

text: A bold, direct act at a dangerous spot suggests nerve and planning rather than impulse.
when: Inferring temperament from a crime's method
why: Acting with composure in a risky position requires control that impulsive acts lack

text: A blunt weapon implies that great force was needed to use it.
A blunt guess can read as an insult, so the investigator must let the subject supply the answer rather than state it.
when: Confronting a suspect with an inference.
why: Direct accusation damages rapport and can end the exchange.

text: A bold bluff is risky and costs credibility if exposed; it works only when the reconstruction matches what the suspect knows.
when: Using an unverified reconstruction to pressure a suspect
