text: An investigator who acts impulsively under pressure, such as physically grabbing the suspect, can undermine the scene and the credibility of the case.
when: During a confrontation with a cornered suspect
why: Adrenaline and urgency override deliberate judgment

text: 1) Ask a sudden, blunt question about a specific fact. 2) Watch physical reactions such as breathing, standing up or tears. 3) Follow up on what the reaction reveals.
when: when a witness's spoken answer seems incomplete

text: Blunt pressure or interruptions can yield a quick admission, but they wound the speaker, reduce cooperation, and may push them to withhold more.
A motive stated openly risks being dismissed as melodrama, while one stated as a whim or joke stays visible but can be missed.
when: Deciding how directly to reveal a character's motive early on
why: Directness aids comprehension but can reduce believability

text: A missing blood trail and a missing outer garment suggest the person left under their own power rather than being carried away by another.
when: a body is missing and the case is open

text: Adipocere, a waxy residue formed by wet decay, is absent in dry environments or when most flesh is removed before bones enter water.
when: Reading decay residue on remains to infer environment or prior handling.
why: Adipocere forms only under wet, anaerobic decay conditions.

text: Stage an accident via an early quarrel and push, letting one noticed but unpursued flaw slip by, so a later murder reveal turns earlier details into proof.
when: Writing an accident that will later be revealed as a planned killing.
why: A noticed but dismissed flaw signals the cover story to attentive players and makes the confession feel earned; the reversal gives incidental earlier details new meaning.

text: A killer can leave no visible injury, so a lack of marks does not settle whether a death was natural or staged.
Make the proof a trait of a person's body that the player could have checked, such as an arm or hand, so an impostor is exposed by something visible.
A victim-may-be-alive state lets a missing body later be found moving under its own power, so disappearance does not always mean death.
when: When designing encounters where a body disappears.
why: Keeping the victim's status open creates a reversal the player can discover.

text: Make some deaths clearly accidental so that suspicious deaths stand out and players can separate conspiracy from chance.
when: When designing a set of witness deaths.
why: Contrast with clearly natural deaths makes the suspicious ones meaningful.

text: Physical marks such as thickened ears, hand calluses or partly erased tattoos hint at a person's past trade, habits or attachments.
A body found at a set time gives the latest possible time of death, while the last confirmed sighting alive gives the earliest.
Body position and orientation relative to doors and objects can show how an event happened and the direction the victim was moving.
when: When reading a body at a scene
why: Position records movement and force that the scene itself may not show.

text: Body position after an injury can show the sequence of a struggle, such as a blow from behind that catches a crouching person.
when: A body is found at a scene with signs of violence.
why: Posture at impact reflects the victim's stance and the attacker's direction.

text: Follow a trail in both directions; prints that lead in but none that lead out point to where the subject stopped or stayed.
Compare the body's location with the wound and the scene; a lack of blood at the site suggests the killing happened somewhere else.
when: The body's location seems inconsistent with the wound
why: Blood at a death site reflects where the fatal event occurred

text: Moving a body or item toward a door versus a hiding spot can encode whether the actor sought help or concealment, giving a readable choice to interpret.
when: Designing a scene where a body or item is moved.
why: Direction of movement carries an interpretable intent.

text: Moving a body away from the scene can delay its discovery rather than hide where the crime happened, so the timing of discovery is itself a clue.
A victim's physical state at discovery, such as warm body temperature, bounds how recently the act happened and narrows the window of the crime.
when: a body is found and examined
why: physical cooling rates give a measurable elapsed-time estimate

text: A body may be in a state that contradicts the scene's story, such as being alive under a drug, so check its condition against the timeline.
when: when a body is assumed to be dead
why: appearances can mislead about condition

text: 1) Watch institutional intake for a body of similar build. 2) Swap it for the victim's body at the point of storage. 3) Move the victim's body to where the substitute would be found. 4) Alter the features others will check.
when: When a concealment plan relies on a body already held by an institution.
why: Each step removes a link between the killer and the body while placing the substitute where expected.

text: Check the body's position against the wound; a posture that prevents the hand reaching the wound argues against self-infliction.
when: when deciding between suicide and homicide from an injury
why: Posture can make a self-inflicted wound physically impossible

text: A route that stays on open ground leaves traces, while a route over roofs in rain is screened. Route choice trades physical exposure against difficulty.
when: When moving a body without being seen.
why: Concealment cover reduces observation but may make the route harder or riskier.

text: Measuring the spacing between footprints gives stride length and direction of travel.
when: a sequence of prints is visible
why: regular spacing reflects gait and heading

text: Mechanical noises such as a click or grinding reveal how a device works, but a device designed to be silent removes that clue.
An object sized to one original can fit two people differently: too loose on one, too tight on the other, which reveals a difference in hand size between the two.
when: A worn object's fit is used to infer a physical trait.
why: Object fit is set by the original's dimensions, so a mismatch between wearers exposes bodily asymmetry.

text: The entry angle of a gunshot wound can estimate the shooter's height range, which can exclude suspects who are too short or too tall.
when: a forensic clue is used to narrow suspects
why: Trajectory geometry links the angle to the shooter's position.

text: Stride length on soft ground gives an estimate of a walker's height, which can be checked against another trace such as writing height on a wall.
when: Estimating a walker from footprints
why: Writing height is a second independent trace

text: A long, unhurried step over an obstacle suggests a walker's age and fitness.
when: Reading a footprint pattern
why: Stride style reflects physical condition

text: A strong corrective measurement suggests a long-standing condition, which should leave matching physical signs on the body.
An enemy patrol can be identified by its footstep cadence, and changing that cadence when alarmed, such as from walking to running, gives the player a readable signal.
when: Designing patrol detection and alert states
why: Audio cues let players detect threats without line of sight.

text: Footstep cadence conveys distance: steps that grow louder and more distinct signal a closer threat.
when: a threat approaches on foot
why: the player reads closeness from the sound

text: Shared audible timers, such as hourly chimes, give every character a common timeline and can give a level a rhythm players learn to read.
Footstep rhythm and range reveal agitation: stride changes across a room or back-and-forth pacing within a few yards signal a rising-mood occupant.
when: footprints or footsteps are readable across a space or audible from a hidden position
why: Agitation alters gait; rhythm and range reveal emotional state

text: The delay between dropping an object and hearing it land or splash grows with pit depth, so a listener can estimate a hidden drop without seeing it.
1) Listen first to locate the occupant. 2) Interpret sound cues such as footsteps and locks. 3) Look only after the cues establish position.
when: a hidden observer must gather information
why: sound gives position before risky sight

text: 1) Map each distinct sound, such as a pause, a door, a switch or a crash, to a stage 2) Listen from concealment 3) Track the sequence stage by stage.
when: observing an event without line of sight
why: sounds give reliable stage markers

text: 1) Pick an observable act the witness will notice. 2) Calibrate the recording's replies to its pauses. 3) Start playback at the act so the cue lands at the right moment.
when: A timed audio trick must match a visible action

text: Use an outside sound such as distant music as a timer, since its rhythm marks time passing and makes silence around the action more oppressive.
when: When a scene needs a sense of passing time.
why: A regular rhythm makes waiting felt.

text: Use footstep sounds of differing weight and count to signal how many people are present and whether they are advancing or retreating.
when: designing audio cues for groups moving nearby
why: Mixed step sounds reveal multiple presences

text: Human hair grows about six inches a year, a rate that lets traces along a strand be dated.
To infer a hidden person's height, start from an object of known size and the height at which they touched it.
when: the person is unseen but has leaned on or handled an object

text: Height from marks is not conclusive on its own, so combine it with other evidence such as a physical trait before identifying a person.
when: When identifying a person from marks.
why: Many people share similar reach.

text: Hand condition, such as broken nails or hard skin, can contradict a person's apparent class or occupation.
Record a victim's normal daily routine and health, so a sudden decline is judged against a known baseline.
when: Harm appears suddenly after a day of ordinary activity.
why: Without a baseline, normal and abnormal condition cannot be told apart.

text: Incomplete remains can still indicate age, build and health, so a partial body can narrow identity even without identifying parts.
when: Only some remains are available for analysis.
why: Size, bone structure and wear reflect a person's physical characteristics.

text: An injury pattern may suggest a left-handed attacker, but treating that suggestion as proof of who acted confuses a narrowed possibility with identity.
Heritable physical traits, such as build, ear shape, face shape, and pigment, can support a hypothesis of kinship but are not confirmation alone.
when: When suspecting a family link from appearance
why: Resemblance suggests a relation but does not prove it

text: A booking made at a travel office creates a dated, witnessed record that fixes a planned movement.
why: The clerk who takes the details becomes a witness.

text: Left-luggage staff may log a deposit time yet be unable to describe the depositor, so a stored object can preserve traces that human memory loses.
A game can model booking as a logged inventory where any missing or changed item becomes a clue.
when: Designing item tracking in a custody or inventory system.
why: Logged items make discrepancies detectable.

text: A booking alone does not place anyone at a scene, so corroborate it with other evidence.
Include a clerk's name error that players can catch by cross-checking names, and reward the catch with a corrected timeline.
Give shopkeepers, clerks or ledgers records that players can cross-check, and let a contradiction trigger new questions.
when: When designing record-keeping NPCs or objects in a game world.
why: Checkable records let players test testimony and generate follow-up investigation.

text: A witness's account that sounds too much like a familiar story may be borrowed from something heard or read rather than remembered.
A matching permit or real person's documents does not confirm identity: permits can be used by others, and false identities can be built on real people's papers.
when: When verifying a visitor against an access record
why: Permits can be obtained under a pretext and used by an impostor

text: Endorsement by a higher authority or respected figure can lend legitimacy to weak evidence or accusations without testing them.
A helper who presents a planted conclusion as their own discovery may come to believe it is theirs, which weakens their credibility under questioning.
Dismissing an object on another person's authority, without testing it, can lose a real clue.
Copied descriptions suggest fabrication and warrant tracing; repeated phrasing across speakers may just reflect a shared source, so note it without concluding.
when: Copied descriptions in one source suggest fabrication; a phrase reappearing in another speaker's account is only noted
why: Reuse can indicate a shared source or an adopted framing

text: A witness who wants a deal shows it through physical cues, such as touching an object and a change in facial expression, that signal the offer has landed.
when: An offer is made during an interrogation.
why: A tempting offer produces involuntary reactions before words are spoken.

text: A suspect who moves from defiance to requesting specific terms reveals exactly what he is trying to protect.
when: during confrontation
why: concrete demands expose priorities

text: Bribery fails with witnesses whose loyalty to a leader outweighs money, so offers work better on those with weaker loyalty.
A bribe offered to a suspect signals how much the offerer values the matter and hints at what they know; the size of the offer is evidence.
when: A character offers money to keep a matter quiet.
why: No one pays heavily over a trivial matter, so a large offer implies high stakes.

text: An offered bribe during questioning signals the witness's fear and motive.
when: A witness offers money to avoid questioning.
why: Attempts to buy silence reveal that the witness has something to hide.

text: Payment can buy only partial information from an informant, so the player may need several sources to complete the picture.
when: A game NPC sells information
why: Paid information is limited in scope

text: A confirmed bribe shows that an alibi was false, but it does not establish that the alibi-holder committed the crime.
when: When an alibi is revealed to have been bought or coerced
why: A false alibi proves a lie, not the identity of the culprit.

text: A witness who was paid to keep quiet may feel insulted by the payment, and that resentment can turn the bargain into a threat that loosens the silence.
when: When a witness has been bribed to stay silent and feels underpaid or demeaned.
why: Wounded pride and grievance over the payment can drive the witness to confess.

text: A secret held by one person can leak to another under pressure, but the leak alone does not prove the source is guilty.
when: A character is confronted and reveals information
why: The disclosure may be coerced rather than voluntary.

text: A suspect who pays or befriends a witness before questioning can shape what that witness later says, so the account reflects the people who will be asked about it.
when: A witness's testimony will decide the outcome and the witness has an incentive to be unhelpful
why: Goodwill and payment give the witness a reason to confirm the suspect's version

text: Testimony obtained through money or favour needs caution; a suspect's assurance that a witness will stay quiet proves nothing, and purchased silence can be bought again.
1) Offer a reward for a specific identifying detail. 2) Gather testimony from many sources. 3) Cross-check the accounts against each other before acting.
when: Searching for an unidentified person
why: A targeted reward drives collection of usable testimony

text: Use a friendly or bribed non-player character as a plot lever that the player must find and test.
when: Designing hidden allies or informants.
why: A compromised witness creates a discoverable but risky source.

text: Give NPC bribes or deals an unusually broad clause so that a player who notices it gains a motive clue without a confession.
when: Designing NPC offers in investigation games.
why: Lets motive be inferred from wording rather than stated outright.

text: Restate a key clue plainly, without revealing its meaning, near the reveal and more than once; a single mention among jokes or details is easily missed.
when: A key clue appears early in a long text, among jokes, or among other descriptive detail.
why: Players forget or skim clues, and a single, one-time description reads as an afterthought.

text: A final word naming a category, such as a type of enemy, may point to a group rather than a single attacker.
when: A dying speaker names an enemy type
why: A category describes many possible perpetrators, not one person.

text: Use a word from one scene to unlock a clue in a later scene, so the player feels the click of recall.
Leave disposal traces that a player can find when designing a hidden-body or cover-up puzzle, since concealment is hard under physical constraints.
when: Designing a hidden-body or cover-up puzzle.
why: Physical constraints make concealment leave findable traces.

text: Leave one physical seal or marker unexplained, so the player carries an open detail into the climax and can revisit it later.
when: Structuring clues in a mystery
why: An unresolved detail keeps the player engaged and rewards revisiting after the main reveal.

text: Burying a clue in NPC asides lets players catch it, but within fact lists or long digressions it looks like background and gets skipped; bury only where still catchable.
when: Designing NPC dialogue or long texts that hide clues.
why: Clues buried in asides or lists can be found, but clues inside lists or digressions look like background and are skipped.

text: Searching for hidden remains exposes the crime and its participants, while leaving them buried keeps the truth concealed; each choice carries social or legal cost.
when: Physical evidence is hidden at a place with a known history
why: Recovery produces proof but also public consequences

text: Body language during a call, such as a flushed face, rigid posture, or turning away, can reveal an emotional bond the speaker hides.
when: Observing a person during a phone call or interview
why: Involuntary cues leak feelings the speaker does not state

text: A telephone call or booking can fix the caller's location when only one reachable point could have sent it.
Calm demeanour, including calm acceptance of an accusation, fits both innocence and guilt, so it does not separate them.
when: when a suspect appears composed under detention
why: Composure can come from many causes, including self-restraint.

text: People who expect no audience record or state plans, motives, debts, deadlines and who benefits candidly, so private notes or exchanges can reveal intent.
when: private records discovered after events, or private exchanges between characters
why: Writers and speakers do not expect anyone else to read or hear them, so they speak candidly.

text: A composed denial is unremarkable when the accused has no hidden stake, so on its own it reveals little.
Someone who accepts a refusal without protest, despite claimed urgency, is probably not the genuine need they describe.
when: a claimed need is refused
why: Genuine urgency usually produces resistance or pressure

text: A calm reminder from a third party to be gentle can quiet an aggressive questioner, and it also halts the outburst.
when: A bystander intervenes during an escalating interrogation.
why: The intervention looks like kindness while redirecting the questioner's momentum.

text: A suspect who refuses to lie even to protect themselves can see suspicion against them grow.
when: the suspect is confronted with incriminating facts
why: Others may read a candid refusal as a sign of guilt.

text: A witness who admits being at the scene can become a suspect while their testimony clears others, so frankness can shift suspicion onto them.
Calm refusal and feigned boredom give an interrogator no visible reaction to read.
when: when a suspect is pressed without evidence in hand

text: Alternate calm stretches with sudden shifts or new events, placing calm before an event so it hits harder and keeps the audience pressing forward.
when: pacing a tense or long narrative section
why: Contrast makes the shift more noticeable and keeps attention from settling.

text: Question a witness about a reaction only once they are calm enough to answer.
A promise made by someone who openly admits their limits is more credible than one from someone who denies them.
when: evaluating a pledge
why: honesty about difficulty signals the promise is considered

text: Making candor the condition of help can get a reluctant witness to speak more plainly.
when: the witness is guarded about their own role

text: Keep questioning even in tone; a cooperative witness answers more fully without alarm.
when: questioning a cooperative but unobservant witness who overheard a conversation
why: pressure raises alarm and shuts down answers

text: When help is traded for candor, later NPC answers can depend on whether the player kept that promise.
A calm surface over hidden pressure heightens expectation, because the audience senses that something is being held back beneath it.
Advice that looks like protective care can be a method of controlling a witness's movements and access.
when: An investigator directs a witness to hide or wait
why: Concealed control can pass as concern

text: Trusting a calm or confident witness over a confused one can mislead.
A candid admission of motive can be a way of appearing above suspicion, so openness is not proof of innocence.
why: A clever suspect may choose which motive investigators find.

text: Brevity alone is not evidence of omission, since a short speaker may hide nothing at all.
1) Demand a complete, true account, stating that gaps or invented details will be exposed. 2) Confirm each part against known facts. 3) Use the confirmed account to unlock further evidence.
when: questioning a suspect whose evidence is already partly known
why: a checked account anchors the story in fact

text: Calm, cooperative manner or a direct denial of lying is not proof of honesty; observe it as behaviour and treat tone changes as signals to question.
when: A witness appears composed during questioning.
why: Composure can be practiced or feigned.

text: Admitting one's own fault without excuse can raise credibility; yet frank admissions of minor faults can hide a central fact, so check what the account leaves out.
when: when assessing a witness's or narrator's admission of their own wrongdoing
why: Unflattering admissions are less likely invented for advantage, but a candid admission can still conceal the central omission.

text: Telling a truthful account protects you when the other side can verify your facts, since hiding checkable facts looks suspicious. It fails when one checkable fact would expose the whole cover story.
when: when a questioner can check facts independently
why: concealment of verifiable facts signals guilt, but one exposed fact can unravel a fabricated story

text: A candid approach is trusted only when the interviewee will take it seriously, while a pretext can be exposed by a single detail and fail on contact.
when: When choosing how to approach an interviewee
why: Candor depends on the listener's trust, and a pretext depends on being believed in its role

text: Wide canvassing or paid rewards draw in suggestible witnesses who describe whatever resembles the picture they were shown.
when: circulating a picture to find witnesses
why: Witnesses want to match what the investigator seeks.

text: Checking addresses by pretext is slow; wrong names and moved households waste many checks.
1) Obtain names and addresses of every operator in the stated area. 2) Visit each establishment in turn. 3) Note closed yards and refusals to show records.
when: Records of several operators must be checked for one event.

text: An investigation can close without legal proof: circumstantial evidence and an outside event, or a procedural step such as a charge dropped without trial, ends the case without a positive finding of innocence.
Under close questioning, apparent knowledge of a secret tends to collapse, and the speaker becomes confused and vacant.
when: a witness is pressed for specifics

text: Once one piece of a constructed case is shown to be false, the rest of the planted evidence tends to fail with it.
when: when a single fact is disproved
why: Planted evidence depends on each piece supporting the others.

text: A coerced confession can open leads that look strong but collapse when the player finds no physical support.
when: A player follows a lead from a forced confession
why: Physical evidence decides whether the lead holds

text: A character's refusal to learn the truth can fix the outcome, leaving a crime unresolved and the authority figure permanently uninformed.
when: when an authority figure chooses not to receive information
why: Withholding knowledge closes off paths that would have led to resolution.

text: A case collapses when a confession separates the real threat from the accused and the victim disowns the accused as the attacker.
A late ruling that invalidates a whole category of evidence can overturn a case without any new discovery or witness.
when: a case resting on one kind of proof
why: the change is in the rule, not in the facts

text: 1) Open with a stated claim or puzzle. 2) Log concrete physical details without explaining them. 3) Settle on a plausible wrong explanation. 4) Add a crisis that rejects it. 5) Reconstruct the case from the logged details with physical proof.
when: structuring a single investigation scenario
why: Logged details that later return as proof make the final reconstruction feel earned rather than arbitrary.

text: A lenient or private outcome keeps focus on the puzzle, while a full legal aftermath pulls focus away from the mystery itself.
when: closing a case

text: A clue given as a partial phrase, with the missing part recoverable only through a later action, makes the player reconstruct its meaning and invest in the discovery.
when: Designing a clue delivered in fragments.
why: The player must act to complete the sentence, so the answer feels earned.

text: A reconstruction that is only partly right can be overturned by one further clue, so the solution is revised rather than discarded.

1) Group questions by source document. 2) For each question, offer a motive and test it against the actor's known behavior. 3) Set a greater motive against a lesser one to explain a single act. 4) Label answers as probabilities, not certainties.
when: A case has many separate actions that must each be explained.
why: A chain of reasons makes an otherwise arbitrary actor's conduct discoverable.

text: 1) Reconstruct the disputed event step by step in front of witnesses. 2) Present the identifying object as proof. 3) Let witnesses accept the account, turning a private admission into a public verdict.
when: ending a mystery with a confrontation
why: A public account with witnesses fixes the outcome in a way a private confession does not.

text: 1) Name the hidden actor behind the disguise; 2) link them to a witness's testimony that explains the sighting; 3) confirm with an independent record that breaks the alibi.
when: Delivering a reveal that exposes a disguised actor and a false alibi.
why: Naming, linking and confirming makes the reveal clear and checkable.

text: A collection of case studies can be built on one repeated formula: an accusation, a build-up of testimony, a turn that reframes the evidence, and an outcome set by a formal authority.
when: Designing a series of similar encounters rather than one continuous plot.
why: A stable cycle lets each case feel distinct while the player learns one pattern to test against.

text: Release quest information through a chain of messages, with each step revealing more than the last, and gate the next revelation behind a timed event.
when: Designing message-based quest progression
why: A chain with timed gates gives the player a real reason to wait and a growing picture

text: A chain-of-investigations mystery widens the case: each new client, body or suspect opens a fresh question, growing from a small missing-person case into a larger conspiracy.
Letting the client set investigation priority can push the investigation away from authorities who may be needed later.
when: A reluctant client avoids official channels and sets the agenda
why: Client priorities may exclude help that becomes necessary later

text: 1) Stage a crime that looks impossible, motiveless, or misread, within a plausible premise. 2) Make a plausible or convenient suspect or official explanation the first accusation. 3) Reverse it with a planted physical trace, changing culprit or events late. 4) Expose the culprit with a trap or confession.
when: Designing a series or a set of self-contained mysteries.
why: A repeated structure makes each case recognisable and testable.

text: 1) Deliver a found item as the first link. 2) Send the player to a destination that the item points to. 3) Reveal a dead witness's record as the final link. Each link unlocks the next.
when: When a reveal should build dread through delay and partial evidence.
why: A chain of partial items controls what the player learns and when, and holds back the most disturbing detail until late.

text: Structure a quest as a chain in which each clue leads to the next, so each new clue becomes a further thread to pull.
when: Designing a multi-step investigation.
why: A chain of linked clues sustains progression.

text: Give a closed set of NPCs shared routines and let community gossip supply partial, biased clues that players can verify or discard.
when: Designing a village-based cast of characters.
why: Shared routines make each character's movements checkable, and biased gossip rewards verification.

text: A person can insist little time has passed despite evidence otherwise, and that stubbornness can make lost time visible to an audience.
when: When a character's perception of time conflicts with a verifiable clock.
why: Confidence in a wrong estimate contrasts with the actual elapsed time.

text: Non-human explanations for a death include self-inflicted harm, an accident, a fall of heavy objects during a struggle, and fate or divine will.
Some insurance policies forfeit premiums if the insured takes his own life within a set period, such as one year after the policy begins.
A suicide can supply a motive for one death without explaining the other killings in the same case.
Alkaloid poison can cause asphyxia and failure of the heart and lungs, producing a death that looks supernatural.
When a body shows no visible wound, infer the cause of death from the surrounding situation rather than the body alone.
when: Cause of death is unclear from the body
why: Scene context can reveal causes the body does not show.

text: A cause that acted long before a death is a weak explanation for it, because it should have worn off by then.
when: When comparing a candidate cause with the time of death.

text: If a symptom appears before the suspected cause could have acted, the suspected cause is doubtful.
when: checking a claimed cause against a timeline
why: A cause cannot produce effects that come before it

text: A fast-acting dose suggests a liquid taken by mouth, which narrows the container to look for.
when: the speed of an effect is known
why: Effect speed reveals how a substance was delivered

text: Stupor and a flushed face can indicate that a person was given drink or drugs, which hints that they were deceived.
A person with no known means who suddenly spends freely is a prime suspect.
when: the person's finances are known and the change is observable
why: a sudden source of money needs an explanation

text: A death ruled self-inflicted rests on absence of struggle, absence of noise and the victim's known low mood, so each premise should be checked.
when: When assessing a death that appears self-inflicted.
why: The ruling depends on what is missing as much as what is present, so each absence needs verification.

text: Check an apparent cause of death, such as an accident or collapse, against the body; the physical signs can overturn the obvious explanation.
when: When a surface cause of death must be verified
why: Injuries may have been inflicted after death, making the obvious cause misleading.

text: Cooling after death depends on surroundings: shade and damp grass slow it, so the same body cools at different rates in different places.
when: when estimating time of death from body temperature
why: environment changes heat loss

text: A settled cause of death does not name a culprit, so keep cause and culpability as separate questions; players may mistake the answered how for the whole case.
when: A key forensic fact has been established
why: Answering how something happened leaves open who did it

text: A death caused by a sudden movement can look random, which hides the real cause unless its timing is checked against the dose.

1) List every candidate cause. 2) Rule out each cause one at a time with a specific physical check. 3) Check each cause's timing against the death. 4) Read the body for signs. 5) Eliminate causes until a remaining one is supported or unexplained.
when: When a death is sudden and the stated cause does not fit the body or timeline.

text: 1) Start from an observed effect. 2) Establish a normal baseline. 3) Ask about exceptions to the baseline. 4) Pursue a candidate cause with specific questions. 5) Check details that link the cause to the event.
1) List the candidate causes. 2) Rule out each cause the observed signs contradict. 3) Match the remaining cause against known case records. 4) Confirm with an expert who recognises the pattern.
when: A cause of death is unclear and the body still holds traces
why: Elimination narrows causes, and expert records confirm the match

text: 1) Take the time-of-death estimate made at the examination as a range. 2) Subtract the known interval between observations to bound the state at the earlier one. 3) Check the bound against testimony.
when: A precise time of death matters and two observations have a known gap

text: 1) Find when the victim was last seen well. 2) Find when the victim was first seen unwell. 3) Treat the span between them as the window in which dosing could have occurred.
Store each death's posture and wound type so the player can read how an NPC died.
Ruling out one cause of death does not establish when the death occurred; treat cause and time as separate questions.
When a death could be suicide or murder, keep both readings open until physical evidence or a contradicting note settles which one fits the scene.
when: A death scene supports both a self-inflicted and a staged reading

text: A contact may first deny knowledge, then offer a cautious hint while noting that it has passed through many hands.
when: When a contact is asked about a sensitive matter.
why: Denial protects the contact, and a hint lets them help without full exposure.

text: Do not treat a later, more cautious retraction as the truth just because it came later.
Use a cooperative approach with reachable witnesses, and be cautious with frightened ones, for whom any warning can feel like coercion.
when: choosing an interview approach

text: Read a witness's claim in light of its qualifications and circumstances rather than discarding it outright.
when: Assessing a witness who has real knowledge but a conflict of interest
why: Charity means interpreting the claim fairly, not rejecting it by default

text: An interrogation system that tracks whether a caution was given can mark later statements inadmissible when the caution was skipped.
A cautionary phrase can mislead a careless reader into thinking the source opposed a practice it endorsed in other clauses.
why: Endorsing clauses can outweigh qualifying words.

text: Treating caution as guilt in itself is a mistake, since a sensible person also takes precautions.
when: interpreting a character's defensive behavior
why: Precaution alone is not evidence of wrongdoing.

text: Blood cell shape distinguishes sources: mammal corpuscles are round, while camel-family corpuscles are oval, separating some stains from bird or human blood.
when: When identifying the animal origin of a blood stain.
why: Cell morphology differs between animal groups.

text: Use a precise physical detail, such as a wound's location or a scar on a specific limb, as a checkable trait; a suspect cannot easily hide it, and it can be verified against evidence.
when: A description or witness claim needs verification against physical evidence.
why: A physical mark can be tested directly, unlike a general description; precise details can be confirmed or refuted.

text: 1) Confirm the comparison list is complete. 2) Include the victim and the scene as possible sources. 3) Check whether the trace could have been placed after the fact. 4) Only then trust the match or non-match.
when: A trace matches nobody on a suspect list, or matches someone strongly
why: An incomplete list or a planted trace can make a match or non-match misleading

text: Separate prisoners into different cells to prevent exchange of information between them.
when: Multiple prisoners are held in custody.
why: Co-location allows communication and collusion.

text: Prefer checkable physical facts such as eye colour, facial marks and clothing over impressions of character when describing a person.
why: Physical facts can be matched against later sightings, while impressions cannot.

text: End a chapter on a reversal when the reframing will carry the player into the next chapter.
when: end of a chapter or act
why: Reversals create suspense and invite continuation

text: A public ceremony that acknowledges past errors gives a divided community a shared end point.
when: a conflict has ended and trust must be rebuilt
why: Shared ritual marks a common transition.

text: End a mystery with a light, closing gesture after the reveal to release tension, especially when the cause is unusual or the resolution informal.
when: Writing the final scene after a dramatic reveal.
why: A lighter ending releases the tension built by the reveal and softens an informal outcome.

text: A public ceremony of confession can be read as proof that the wrong was real, when it may only show that the authority could enforce silence.
when: A public confession or rebuke is offered as evidence.
why: Compelled public acts reflect the power of the enforcing authority, not the truth of the charge.

text: Close a quest beat on a message or NPC reaction that starts the next objective.
A witness who claims to report only facts often mixes in opinion, praise and moral judgement.
when: a witness states a principle of giving pure facts
why: Judgement slips in through selection and interpretation

text: A trial held in default, without the accused present, can still yield a sentence, so absence itself can produce a legal outcome.
when: The accused cannot appear for trial.
why: Legal systems may proceed without the defendant, so the result rests on the defendant's absence rather than on a direct test of guilt.

text: A witness may report a sound without knowing its cause; state how sure the witness is before reasoning from the report.
when: Taking a witness's account as evidence

text: Tagging witness claims with confidence levels lets hostile or flustered NPCs lose confidence under repeated questioning.
when: Designing NPC testimony that the player can probe.
why: Repeated pressure reduces stated certainty, which the player can exploit.

text: Certainty, whether a witness's, accuser's or defender's, does not establish what happened; sincere witnesses can be wrong, so confident claims must be tested against other facts.
when: a witness or party states a claim with strong conviction
why: Conviction and accuracy are independent; confidence reflects how sure someone feels, not whether perception was accurate.

text: A claim presented as certain, or an explanation that smooths over odd facts, can close inquiry early; test it rather than accepting it.
when: an expert presents an identification as certain, or several explanations are offered for an anomaly
why: Smoothness and confidence are not evidence; authorities tend to accept confident claims without testing them.

text: A conclusive-seeming trace or physically plausible act can mislead; check its timing, context and third-party records before treating it as final.
why: Records can contradict a plausible performance; physical plausibility does not settle a timeline.

text: Treating a witness's confidence about small details as evidence can hide an unverified assumption.
When police efficiency is judged by convictions, effort can narrow onto one suspect and neglect alternatives.
A conviction formed from feeling can outlast the evidence, and an investigator may avoid the subject while half expecting to be wrong.
A claim that matches information the witness already had, such as where they were hurt, is weak evidence because it may simply repeat what was known.

1) Ask the question. 2) Note any hesitation or hedge, separating firm details from half-recalled ones and recording each hedge. 3) Ask again, pressing on qualifiers such as 'appears' until their meaning is clear.
when: a witness hedges or gives a single-word answer
why: Qualifiers often hide the answer the witness is least sure of; hedges mark which details are firm and which are shaky.

text: When a speaker or narrator claims to know an absent person's mind or feelings, ask what that claim rests on; confidence alone is a claim to test, not evidence.
when: someone speaks for another person who is not present
why: Confidence about another's thoughts can exist without any basis.

text: Ask whether a witness could have known a claim directly, not from rumor or feeling; confidence doesn't prove vantage, and trusting it over observation conditions makes poor placement look reliable.
when: a witness reports something they did not see
why: Confidence does not show the witness could actually see the event.

text: Do not convict on stacked presumptions; a verdict requires sufficient proof, and certainty is easy when unverifiable evidence counts as proof, so presumptions only justify further examination.
when: deciding whether a case warrants a formal finding

text: Give a witness NPC's description confidence levels tied to lighting and distance, so the player learns which parts to trust.
when: designing a witness description for a mystery
why: the player can weigh clues by how well the witness could see

text: A staged death must convince the opponent, since the opponent is the audience whose behaviour the deception needs to change.
when: Staging a death to mislead enemies

text: A copied record certified by its owner's signature can be used as formal evidence.
A written account that names people, times and objects can be checked against physical clues, which makes it more useful than general impressions.
Keep a message or call log that players can check against the timeline they build, so records can confirm or expose claims.
why: independent records make claims testable

text: An official's private judgment about acceptable methods can be checked against other records from the same period before being taken as fact.
A signed register entry that records buyer, purchase and date turns a packet into a documented transaction that can be checked.
when: Linking a physical item to a sale
why: A written record gives an independent point of verification

text: Changing signatures between sends breaks a simple link between letters, so linking requires other shared traits.
when: linking anonymous messages
why: Surface identifiers can be varied on purpose.

text: Photographs of a scene that has since changed can mislead about what the scene looked like at the time.
when: Comparing old records with the present state of a place
why: Later records reflect later conditions

text: 1) List each step of the verdict or claim. 2) Locate each cited source and confirm it exists with the stated details. 3) Check that the source applies to these facts, not only the general field, and judge the claim by what it says.
when: a decision or record is justified by citing earlier sources

text: When a document is reported to have changed, ask who gains or loses from that change.
when: a will or contract was reportedly altered
why: Gain and loss expose motive.

text: Record every handler, container and timestamp in an item's custody log, so swaps can be reconstructed; an item leaving custody unrecorded cannot be checked again.
when: designing item provenance systems
why: A full log makes swaps discoverable.

text: Check a document's provenance, such as its envelope, postmark, prints, filing or handwriting, before relying on its contents or accepting its account of delivery.
Chain of custody is the recorded sequence of holders and locations of an object or document, which determines whether it can later serve as evidence.
when: when a document or object changes hands
why: Gaps in the record make the evidence doubtful.

text: Provenance is tracing a found object back to its source by matching details such as type and edge wear.
Under the procedure governing accused persons, the investigating magistrate may impose measures such as solitary confinement for the prosecution's interest, within a legal framework of state custody.
when: Deciding how to hold a suspect during an investigation.

text: A chemical reagent that reacts only to a blood protein separates blood from look-alike stains such as mud, rust or fruit juice.
A suspect's death in custody can close a case without trial, leaving beliefs about earlier crimes unproven.
Tracing a chain of strangers depends partly on luck and partly on sustained effort, since the right person must be found at the right moment.
A sender's signature, handwriting and wording can identify them across documents, even when the letter comes through an intermediary.
Trace the chain of hands an item passed through, since each handler may hold the next clue and their traces reveal how many hands it passed through.
Model bodies as quest items with a recorded chain of custody, so the player must trace each transfer to reconstruct what happened.
when: When a body or artefact moves between locations or people in a game.
why: A recorded custody history makes transfers traceable and gives the player a path to follow.

text: Use initial-only signatures and recognisable handwriting so players can match a sender across multiple documents.
when: Designing anonymous documents for players to link.
why: Recognisable traits let players connect separate clues.

text: Assign a provisional name to a set of traces as a hypothesis, and drop the name once the evidence contradicts it.
when: Traces point to a person but their identity is not confirmed.
why: A working label organises the evidence while staying open to revision.

text: Ask why a source sent a warning at all. Silence might have invited scrutiny that endangered the sender.
An object's provenance, such as a previous owner's mark, is weak but real evidence linking it to a person, to be weighed with other facts.
A written order transfers custody of a prisoner to a bearer and relieves the original keeper of responsibility until the prisoner returns.
when: A prisoner is moved between sites.
why: Formal transfer shifts legal responsibility.

text: If an object never left its owner, any theft involving it must have occurred before or after certain events, which constrains the order of the timeline.
when: Reconstructing when an object could have been taken.
why: Custody limits which actors could have touched the object at each moment.

text: A provenance record of past holders lets a player judge how reliable an item's identity and history are.
An object's provenance can be traced through its chain of custody, from sale to one holder, to resale, to reclaiming, identifying each holder in turn.
Confessed people kept in custody can be controlled and prevented from withdrawing their statements.
when: a confessor is held after making a statement
why: custody limits access to the confessor and their retraction

text: When a confessed person names associates, each new name can pull more people into the case, so suspects multiply quickly from one informer.
A fictional witness can sustain a chain of false beliefs: first a lead, then a conspiracy, then a lure, and each stage collapses in turn.
why: Each stage holds the player's attention while exposing the next layer of deception

text: A trace's meaning depends on its chain of hands, the sequence of people who held it, and any link in that chain can be planted.
when: a trace must be tied to a person
why: Each handoff is an unverified step that may be arranged by someone else.

text: A seller may recall a purchase but not its purpose; buyer identification is only as good as fading memory, so treat it as probable and ask about appearance and companions.
why: Recall degrades and can be filled in by expectation.

text: A custodial condition without a believable reason reads as a convenient delay and undermines the reveal.
Assuming an object stayed with its owner can build a wrong timeline, and uncertain custody must be verified before it constrains the order of events.
when: Reconstructing a timeline from object custody.
why: Unverified custody leads to a wrong order of events.

text: Official pressure may tempt a custodian to open sealed evidence early, which defeats the purpose of the delay.
A chain of custody is unreliable if earlier handlers searched or altered an item before handing it over.
Taking an object without recording its origin leaves a gap in its chain of custody, so later claims about it cannot be verified.
when: When an object is moved or collected during an investigation
why: Without origin records, the object's history cannot be proven

text: A room kept locked after an event leaves open who entered it while it was shut, weakening the chain of custody.
when: A scene is sealed after an incident
why: Unrecorded access breaks the record of who could have altered the scene

text: 1) List each handoff in order with its holder. 2) At each handoff, ask who had access to it. 3) Mark every span when the object was out of anyone's view. 4) Check each holder's memory of its state. 5) Test each handler's denial against the other handlers' accounts. 6) Identify a plausible reason for each transfer.
when: when an object's location, presence or identity changed between points and must be explained
why: Each handoff is a point where the object could have been swapped, diverted or moved unnoticed.

text: 1) Identify the printed fragment on the document. 2) Match it to stock taken in a known theft. 3) Link that theft to a place. 4) Trace the route the document took from there.
when: Tracing where a document or object came from

text: 1) Supply the pen yourself. 2) Have each person who handled the object sign or mark the page bearing the trace, in small writing. 3) Take custody only after signing. 4) Keep the signed page with the object.
when: an object with a trace may become evidence
why: Fixes its state at handover, so later tampering claims can be answered and signing stays under your control

text: 1) Ask where the object was kept. 2) Ask who could have taken it. 3) Ask when it was last used. 4) Link the answers into a chain of handovers and mark each gap as a possible access point.
when: Establishing who could have used a key, bag or weapon

text: 1) Place a small, ordinary-looking mark on an object before it leaves your control. 2) After its return, check the mark to confirm the object was away. 3) Verify that nothing was swapped or missing.
when: When evidence can be taken or swapped out of sight and custody must later be proven.
why: A prior mark is the only reliable record that an item was moved, and an obvious mark invites reproduction.

text: Do not treat an inferred chain as established until independent evidence, beyond a single testimony, supports each of its links.
when: When judging whether an evidence chain is reliable
why: Independent verification guards against a single faulty source.

text: Check an object's provenance against the account given, comparing dates and receipts, since the item may turn up somewhere the account says it could not be.
when: when an object's history is part of a claim

text: Test a custody alibi by asking whether the confined person can still communicate with outsiders; confinement alone does not stop messages, accomplices or inside help.
when: a jailed or distant suspect seems to rule out involvement
why: A confined person may still act through others, so the alibi must be tested rather than accepted.

text: Discount evidence whose provenance is unclear, such as an item with no traceable date or a finder who could have placed it.
A found object is not automatically the lost one; its chain of custody must be shown before it is treated as the same object.
when: A replacement or recovered object is presented as evidence.
why: Objects can be swapped or confused, so provenance must be established.

text: Check who moved or touched a body before attributing stains or marks to the attacker, since helpers can leave marks that look identical.
when: Blood or marks are found on a body or its clothing.
why: People who carry a body can transfer blood and leave marks resembling those of an attacker.

text: Run a provenance check when a source's only support is its own assertion, asking where its material came from.
when: a source's sole support is its own claim

text: Collect each sample in its own labelled container tied to its exact location, so later tests remain traceable to where it was found.
when: Collecting residue or other trace material

text: Before accepting an object as evidence, confirm it stayed in a secure place and check who had access to it before the event.
A stated reason often shifts over time; the first explanation is often incomplete, and a move from not knowing to a simpler reason suggests improvisation.
when: A listener asks for the basis of a claim about motive.
why: The teller may have no real basis and improvises.

text: Record each revision a speaker gives under pressure, including shifting motive, such as account, then denial, then partial admission; check each against others and physical facts before accepting the last.
when: questioning presses a suspect or witness repeatedly
why: Pressure produces successive versions; shifts between them are worth comparing.

text: Shifting testimony is weak evidence of guilt, not proof; nervousness, confusion or better recall can cause it. Check when each version was made and what the speaker then believed.
when: a witness's statement changes or answers contradict under questioning
why: Innocent people also produce changes and contradictions, possibly from an honest shift in belief about timing.

text: An unchallenged account is not verified: silence may be strategic, and an unchallenged witness can still be wrong, so test it against the facts.
when: a party leaves a witness account unchallenged
why: Silence reflects no judgment on accuracy; lack of objection is not verification.

text: An uncorroborated account, whether a suspect's bare denial or an honest witness's true testimony, can be dismissed just as easily, so a plea alone rarely settles where someone was.
when: when a suspect offers only a bare denial or a witness's account lacks corroboration

text: Do not build a reconstruction on unchecked second-hand claims; hearsay gains authority through repetition, especially when it points an investigation one way.
when: when rumours from servants or bystanders circulate
why: unverified claims gain authority through repetition

text: An answer that changes under repeated or small follow-up questions signals uncertainty, a bent fact, or an account fitted to a story.
when: a witness is pressed on the same point more than once, or a small follow-up changes details
why: A speaker who is unsure or hiding something revises the answer under pressure.

text: A coached witness repeats a fixed answer smoothly under gentle questions but breaks under sharp repetition, a change of language, or separate questioning, where co-witnesses contradict.
when: a witness has been told what to say, or several witnesses were given the same script
why: A memorized line is comfortable only while the question stays familiar; it breaks under follow-up questions.

text: Bystanders tend to accept an official's confident pronouncements without challenge, so the confidence goes unexamined within the scene.
when: an official speaks with confidence in a group
why: social deference discourages questioning

text: Defenders often rely on character testimony describing a long, known way of life when no accuser or evidence is named, since reputation becomes the remaining counterweight.
when: when an accused has no physical defense and accusers are unnamed
why: a respected record of conduct is the only evidence left to offer

text: Character testimony establishes habits, character and motive, not how an act was done or whether it occurred; once the act is established, it shapes how intent and punishment are weighed.
An uncorroborated statement from a dying person is open to challenge, and its weight depends on a second witness.
An accused person connected to respected families often gains neighbors and clergy who speak for their character.
when: When a family with social standing is accused.
why: Social ties mobilize defenders.

text: Ask whether an independent fact confirms an account; unconfirmed testimony stays a loose lead, not a finding, especially from witnesses with partial knowledge or a stake in the outcome.
when: a claim cannot be checked against other evidence
why: partial knowledge and personal stakes can bias the account

text: Give testimony concrete, locatable details or figures, such as an amount of money, which can be checked against physical evidence; vague claims cannot be tested.
when: a witness gives concrete, locatable details, or when designing testimony players should test
why: Specific details make false accounts easier to expose; a stated number can be confirmed or refuted.

text: When a witness revises a time or gives a second account of the same evening, compare versions and record the change; a correction can hide an earlier statement.
when: A witness gives a second statement that differs from the first.
why: Memory and motive can shift timing details between tellings.

text: Secure a witness's signed statement while they are still committed, since a witness who has signed finds withdrawal harder.
when: when a witness may change their mind
why: Commitment makes retraction costly.

text: A lead can be built from a chain of brief, partial sightings by different witnesses, each adding one fact, weighted by how well each could observe.
when: The case depends on strangers who saw something briefly

text: A plan changed at the last moment often reveals the planner's reasoning, so note which flaw forced the revision.
when: the culprit's plan was altered shortly before the act
why: the revision exposes what the planner feared would fail

text: Treat a witness whose judgments of others reverse within hours as unreliable about character.
When a witness claims a larger role in the events than before, treat that change as a point to examine rather than accept it.
when: A witness's described role in events shifts

text: One admitted fact can expose a related fact the witness did not intend to reveal, so each admission opens the next line of questioning.
why: facts in a case are connected, so confirming one narrows the others

text: Accepting a suspect's explanation or a witness's word as proof, without an independent check, closes the inquiry before the claim is tested; a common error.
Accepting a suspect's or household member's statement before checking it against the scene can build a case on claims that do not hold.
when: a suspect's or household member's statement is accepted without checking
why: unchallenged testimony can shape the official record

text: Accepting an event sequence or a conceded fact without checking its timing and surrounding steps against other evidence leaves the story only partly verified.
when: when a suspect concedes one fact, or a witness gives a sequence of events
why: surrounding steps and timing can still be false

text: Reading a person's state or temperament from appearance, expression or posture is a hypothesis needing corroboration; a confident detail given in haste from a dim encounter may need revision.
when: a clue about inner state rests only on outward signs, or a first description comes from a brief or dim encounter
why: Expression and posture are ambiguous and can mislead; hasty recall of minor details is unreliable.

text: A claimed vision cannot be cross-examined, so its contradictions are easy to dismiss and its weight tracks audience trust and staging rather than facts.
when: testimony that only one witness can perceive
why: no one else can contradict it

text: A confession matching the accusers' claims is not independent corroboration, since questioners supply the content; where one group interrogates and applies force, no one can test it.
when: A confession agrees with the accusation, or one group both interrogates and applies force
why: the match may come from coaching; nobody is positioned to test the confession

text: A witness may reverse a story once they realise its danger, so record their first account before they learn why it matters.
when: a witness's account could implicate the suspect
why: Realising the stakes can change what they say.

text: Obvious narrator unreliability with no later check reads as lazy writing; the contradiction must be something the player can actually test.
when: Designing a narrator whose account is meant to be doubted.
why: Untestable contradictions give the player no way to confirm the gap, and unchallenged self-exculpation loses the fair-play signal.

text: Accepting an answer without asking how it is known, or letting emotion or digression replace the answer, weakens the interview.
A partial account later revised can leave the audience with a wrong picture of what happened.
Trusting an account of a past case without checking its record can import false facts into the present investigation.
Failing to ask a witness about every person they noticed leaves a gap that one simple follow-up question could have closed.
1) Hold an independent timeline. 2) Note slips such as shifting pronouns or compressed stretches. 3) Ask one clear question at a time about each omitted leg.
when: a witness summarises events and the listener has a separate timeline to compare against
why: Summaries hide gaps, and a direct question about a skipped stretch is what brings them out

text: 1) Repeat the question in a firmer, more detached voice. 2) Rephrase it or switch to the witness's own language. 3) Ask who told the witness the answer and when. 4) Calm the witness before asking more. 5) Show knowledge of the core truth.
when: A witness repeats a fixed phrase that seems rehearsed.
why: Each step removes comfort from the scripted answer and invites the real memory.

text: 1) Compare the recantation's wording with the accounts of the people it harmed. 2) Note whether it blames an outside cause. 3) Note whether it admits faults in the witness's own statements.
when: a witness recants earlier testimony

text: Present an NPC's unverified feeling or report as a weak lead the player must corroborate with a second clue before it becomes fact; it may be wrong until checked.
when: When an NPC reports a feeling or impression no other evidence supports, or supplies information about a suspect
why: Uncorroborated impressions are not hard evidence and can mislead the player; checking makes the report a lead rather than a fact.

text: Do not rely on a companion's account when they are likely coached or protecting the suspect, since it may be a constructed alibi.
when: a witness has motive to shield the suspect
why: Protective accounts can be fabricated.

text: Design informant interrogations so each answer unlocks the next question and points to a new lead.
when: When designing an informant scene

text: Flag a witness who recites details already circulated as coached, so players can detect planted testimony.
Flag a witness NPC's account that depends on a vision as uncorroborated, and withhold any verdict until a physical trace supports it.
when: Designing a witness whose claim only they could perceive
why: Players accept a verdict only when evidence they can check supports it.

text: A source that cannot be questioned or held to account must not be accepted as a witness, even if it offers an oath.
when: when deciding whether to accept testimony from a supernatural or hidden source
why: An oath has weight only when the one swearing can be examined and judged.

text: Do not accept a candid partisan's conclusions because his details feel vivid and honest; judge the conclusions separately from the details they report.
when: the only surviving source comes from one side of a dispute
why: Vivid detail can carry a conclusion the evidence does not support.

text: Let a culprit NPC's dialogue shift as cover becomes belief, giving the player an account that changes over time to compare.
when: Writing a culprit NPC whose attitude evolves.
why: A changing account lets the player detect the gap between performance and belief.

text: Use established character to narrow suspects, treating the judgement as support, not proof; confirm with physical facts, since character cannot show how the act was done.
when: when ruling a suspect in or out by traits, or when a motive reading points at one suspect
why: a plausible character can still be wrong without physical evidence

text: Knowing a person's self-destructive tendencies makes a self-inflicted explanation a live hypothesis, so disposition can make one explanation more plausible than another.
when: weighing theories about how a death occurred
why: Known dispositions raise the likelihood of some explanations

text: A witness who speaks freely about a side topic may reveal their attitudes, such as contempt for a group, without any direct accusation.
Character evidence describes a person's habits and disposition. It argues that a charge clashes with known conduct but does not disprove a specific event.
A character certificate is a signed statement from people who knew the accused for years, attesting to good conduct.
Character evidence cannot disprove a claim that the court refuses to examine.
Habit testimony can weigh against violence, but clearing a suspect on temperament alone is unreliable, since a quiet nature can hide dangerous potential.
when: when assessing a suspect's likelihood of violence
why: character evidence lowers suspicion but does not prove innocence

text: Use a suspect's character and motive to rank suspects for checking, not to convict them, since character arguments are weak proof.
when: Deciding who to investigate first.
why: Character inferences can mislead.

text: A witness account that conflicts with what is known of the subject's character should be doubted until confirmed independently.
When several people's complaints about one person contradict each other, each complaint weakens the others and the reputation becomes unreliable evidence.
when: assessing a person's reputation from others' accounts
why: conflicting claims cancel out

text: Character readings from letter shapes are interpretive and weaker than matching recurring forms, and observers may disagree about them.
when: Judging a writer's temperament from a sample
why: Shape readings depend on the reader

text: Distinguish controlled from open emotion; a speaker's restrained agitation can be stronger than another's loud distress.
Check whether a suspect's reputation fits their account, and treat a convenient detail, such as a spouse's refusal, as a point to test.
when: a suspect supplies a convenient explanation
why: details that suit the suspect may be invented

text: A character's temperament can rule out a deliberate, elaborate plan, though it cannot rule out a sudden act of passion.
when: An elaborate method suggests a calculating planner.
why: Impulsive anger produces spontaneous acts, not long-prepared schemes.

text: Center the inquiry on one figure whose access and interest connect to the event, then check that figure's conduct closely.
why: A single connecting figure keeps the search focused.

text: Judge whether a prime suspect's known character fits the crime separately from whether the evidence points at them. A fraud may still be unlikely to commit violence.
when: When the suspect fits the motive but not the temperament.

text: Consistent statements by the accused over time are harder to fake than a single outburst, so they count as character evidence.
Use witness descriptions of a person's character to judge whether a document's unusual terms fit the person who wrote them.
when: When a document contains odd or unexpected terms.
why: A known trait such as stubbornness can explain otherwise puzzling content.

text: Attacking a witness's character targets the reliability of the accuser rather than the event being described.
when: when a witness's account is challenged

text: Cross-examining a witness about a person's conduct and manners can build a counter-impression that makes a motive seem implausible.
when: A prosecution rests on a motive of temper or jealousy
why: A witness's picture of the person shapes how the jury judges whether that person would act

text: Strong character evidence combines five kinds of source: the accused's written plea, a spouse's statement, a clergyman's oath, magistrates' affirmations, and a neighbors' petition.
A character argument or remark that someone is incapable of a deed is opinion, not evidence; with no link to physical evidence it can be dismissed as speculation.
A reading of character can silently replace a reading of the facts and colour judgment of a person without establishing anything about the event.

Judging a story true from the teller's foolishness, or an account true from its extraordinary people, substitutes character for evidence; suspicion from character or shock is insufficient for accusing.
when: accepting a story on the teller's personality, or naming a culprit after a shocking event
why: a clever liar could produce the same details; character and feeling cannot establish what happened

text: Appeals to the unknowability of a person's character can end an investigation too early, before motive or physical evidence is tested.
A source's characterization of other people is not independent evidence about them.
Building a theory on an assumed character type is speculation unless evidence shows the emotional tie existed.
Character testimony can excuse as well as condemn, so keep the uses for mitigation and for establishing guilt separate.
A summary calling a document full of a theme can be false when the quoted entries show no such content.
when: Judging a secondary summary of a primary document.
why: Summaries can assert tone the actual text does not support.

text: A plea of good character set against testimony, without fresh evidence, leaves the verdict in the accusers' favour.
when: when the defence offers only reputation

text: Character testimony describes a person's general nature but does not prove a specific act, so it cannot settle a case alone.
when: Testimony is offered to vouch for an accused person.
why: Judgment built on long acquaintance rests on observation, not on proof of the act.

text: Judging a witness only by reputation discards useful content, while judging only by the transcript misses how the testimony was delivered.
when: Assessing a witness's trustworthiness
why: Both reputation and transcript give incomplete evidence

text: 1) Hear an outside warning about your involvement. 2) Examine your own feelings honestly. 3) Set explicit rules that keep dealings strictly professional. 4) Let duty to the case outrank the attachment. 5) Check any exceptions made for favoured people.
when: An investigator notices personal interest or affection for a witness, which can make a reading lenient or harsh
why: Self-judgement is coloured by the same emotion, so outside views and fixed rules add checks; the evidence alone does not justify such leniency or harshness

text: 1) Ask a companion to describe the person without polite restraint. 2) Ask for recent episodes such as quarrels and plans. 3) Note habits, grudges and how the person took offence. 4) Note the person's mood just before the event.
when: Profiling a suspect through a companion's talk

text: 1) Compare the costume and other fixed visible traits against the earlier image. 2) Check persistent features such as the face. 3) Offer an object that triggers memory. 4) Ask indirectly and read the response.
when: A character cannot reliably state who they are and must be identified through objects and senses.
why: Recognition is a chain of matching steps, so confidence builds from several checks rather than one leap.

text: Treat a mismatch between a suspect's known character and the act as a flag to investigate; excluding or accusing on that basis without a physical check risks wrongly clearing or implicating them.
when: when the suspect's known behavior does not match the crime
why: a mismatch may point to error or concealment rather than innocence

text: Make traits testable by showing the NPC acting against them, and tie each inferred trait to an independent clue, such as a physical or timeline fact.
when: when designing NPC traits as puzzle clues, or before clearing or condemning a suspect
why: character alone is a soft clue and cannot settle guilt; a second clue lets the player confirm a guess

text: A character who withholds a fact must have a believable in-world reason for doing so.
why: Unexplained silence reads as authorial convenience rather than character

text: Give an NPC an odd prejudice or rule that drives the quest's central choice.
when: Designing a character whose attitude shapes the plot
why: An irrational-seeming attitude can force decisions and create conflict

text: Record a suspect's past outbursts as character evidence that the player weighs as a reliability factor, not as proof.
Give important NPCs an unusual, visible trait, such as a deformed hand or missing finger, so that a damaged or hidden body can still be matched to them.
when: when a character's identity may need confirming later in the game

text: Record each character's weaknesses, hobbies and follies beside their official facts, so a motive can be matched to the right suspect.
when: tracking many suspects or NPCs

text: Reject a theory that requires a character to act far outside their established temperament and habits.
when: testing a suspect against a theory

text: Check each suspect motive against the NPC's established traits, and narrow the clue chain until only one solution fits that character.
when: designing or solving motive and clue sets
why: a solution consistent with character is the most probable one

text: Separate a person's character or status from the evidence; lack of success does not establish guilt.
when: judging a suspect
why: Status is not a finding.

text: Accept character evidence only from someone who knew the accused well over a long period.
when: when weighing a character witness

text: A charming person can earn trust while contradicting evidence accumulates, or carry out a flawed plan; charm proves neither innocence nor competence, so check claims against behaviour.

A pleasing appearance can hide a serious character; an observer's interest in a witness, face-value reading of a suspect's self-presentation, or admirers' framing clouds judgement and misleads the investigation.
when: when interviewing witnesses who are loyal to the suspect
why: admiration and shared sympathy repeat the suspect's framing

text: A character discredited by a listener's existing low opinion of them is accepted more easily, because the listener already has a prior assumption that fits the explanation.
when: The listener already trusts the speaker more than the accuser
why: Prior assumptions make a dismissive explanation feel like an answer

text: A charming character who occupies a host with questions about a building can divert attention from the real interest in that building.
A warm word from an employer is not proof of influence; influence is indicated by a promise tied to a specific act.
when: Inferring bribery or loyalty from an authority figure's manner
why: Kindness is common and does not establish a bargain

text: Let a charming suspect leave a visible gap that the player finds only by asking targeted questions.
when: designing suspect characters

text: Treat a child's account as a lead to check against other evidence, not as direct proof; it may serve as an unreliable witness whose statement conflicts with others.
when: A child witness provides information about a case, or a story needs unreliable witnesses.
why: Unverified child testimony can be mistaken or exaggerated.

text: Use a child NPC as unreliable testimony through fear or repeated prompting, leaving prompting clues in dialogue; or as a reliable observer the player must verify against environmental evidence.
when: Designing child NPC testimony or an NPC who reports a sighting.

text: Vulnerable witnesses such as children may be pressed to testify against relatives, so their testimony reflects that pressure.
when: authority figures question a child about family members
why: pressure from authority shapes what a child says

text: A child's testimony can be valuable for vivid, unfiltered detail, but the same account mixes real events with gossip, games and invented material.
when: An investigator takes testimony from a child witness.
why: Children mishear, exaggerate and repeat adult talk, so their accounts need filtering.

text: When an adult interrupts or repeatedly tries to hush or remove a child witness, treat it as evidence that the adult is controlling the account and protecting a secret.
when: When a child witness is questioned in the presence of adults or an adult tries to remove a child from an interview.
why: Adults who silence a child may be shaping what the child reveals, since controlling a child's speech is a way to protect a secret.

text: Claims of illness, delirium or unusual lucidity made under suspicion deserve scrutiny, since they are a common way to deflect questions.
when: A suspect volunteers a claim about their own mental state while under suspicion

text: A child or paid witness may hide part of the truth, so a figure they give can be understated.
when: a witness has been paid or wants to please
why: Payment or a wish to please shades what is said.

text: A child's memory of an outing can fix the scene accurately while blurring the details.
when: when testimony comes from a witness who was young at the event
why: Children retain vivid scenes but not precise particulars

text: Adults may overrule a child's account to avoid a disturbing conclusion, which can cause an important observation to be lost.
