when: When an adult dismisses a child's report because the conclusion is unsettling.
why: Avoidance of a disturbing conclusion can override the evidence.

text: Do not press or question a child to the point of pressure, since it can cause distress and harm the child.
when: An investigator interviews a child about a sensitive matter.
why: Pressure can distress the child and upset the adults caring for them.

text: Do not rely on a child's recall of events the child slept through, though details the child remembers may still be useful.
when: When a child is offered as a witness to an event.
why: A child who did not witness an event cannot testify to it, but repeated details can still point somewhere.

text: Restating a document's import in one's own words is paraphrase, not quotation, and its fairness must be judged separately from the text's accuracy.
A party's paraphrase of a document may not match what was written, and without the original text, disputes over wording stay unresolved.
when: A written claim is being used as evidence
why: Memory of a document's exact wording is often unreliable.

text: Later writers who paraphrase a source without citing it hide their dependence, so check the texts themselves, not only the citation lists.
Check the reverse of a scrap, since printed or blank forms on it can reveal the paper's source.
when: when a clue is a loose paper

text: Check a claim from an interested or boastful claimant through a second source, and confirm that source is independent, since the claimant may have chosen it.
when: When a lead comes from a claimant who benefits from its acceptance.
why: Confidence and personal interest can make an unreliable claim seem credible.

text: Persuasive stories, sympathetic or dramatic witnesses, emotional appeals and confident explanations are not proof; weigh them only after checking against corroboration and known facts.
Let players test an NPC's claim against a second source or a checkable action, such as opening a locked item or visiting a place; raise trust only after the check passes.
when: when designing verifiable in-world claims
why: A claim that survives an attempted contradiction earns trust.

text: Mix checkable claims with deliberate lies or contradictions in NPC testimony about sightings, injuries, routes or times; each fails a specific test against world records or objects.
when: Designing NPC dialogue, testimony or backstory delivery.
why: Rewards players who check claims against evidence.

text: Tie each clue and claim to a checkable source, such as a device, dated document, travel record, clinic ledger, ship manifest or sworn statement; unsupported assertions cannot be confirmed.
when: Designing clues or forensic evidence.
why: A clue can only be tested against a known source; concrete records let players test claims.

text: Classify witness statements and mark each claim unverified until a physical trace or independent source confirms it, especially a claim only one NPC perceived.
when: Handling witness statements, including dungeon generation with NPC witnesses.

text: Verify dates and implied days against a calendar before building a timeline from undated, conflicting or altered documents; a plausible mapping can be false.
when: Using undated, conflicting or altered documents as evidence.
why: A wrong date can reverse the apparent order of events.

text: A test that worked once may fail when repeated, so past success is no guarantee that the same result will follow.
Unsupported written assertions can be used as evidence against the person who made them, since their unproven claims can be read against them.
when: A written statement is read in court or to an audience
why: Assertions without support can be turned by the other side

text: Give two NPCs slightly different versions of one event or explanation; players compare dialogue to find the discrepancy, and the difference points to the liar.
when: when designing a mystery with unreliable witnesses or two characters describing the same event
why: Conflicting versions create a choice that rewards careful comparison.

text: Log each NPC's claimed whereabouts with a time window and an independent verifier; check claimed travel against map distances and surface mismatches as follow-up clues.
when: Designing alibis for characters in an investigation game.
why: Independent verifiers and time windows make claims testable by the player.

text: Give an NPC a believable cover story or lie with a checkable contradiction in a reachable object, room or physical evidence, so the player can expose it.
when: When designing an NPC who hides a secret or makes self-serving claims.
why: The player can expose the cover story by investigating what is reachable.

text: Make clues specific and testable, with names, places or predicted object locations an independent source can check; vague hints fit any outcome and prove nothing.
when: Writing clues or NPC claims meant to pay off later.
why: Specific, checkable details can be confirmed or refuted.

text: Test physical assumptions directly on site, such as a restraint's position relative to a hazard or whether a path exists, before committing to a plan built on them.
Judge a suspect's account mainly by how much of its checkable parts outside witnesses, records and observations confirm, and weigh demeanour only as a minor factor.
when: when a story contains many checkable claims alongside a key claim that cannot yet be checked
why: Instinct about manner can err, while independent confirmation is more reliable.

text: Tag information gathered from NPCs as unverified so the player can choose whether to trust it.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that offers schedules or habits.
why: Marking uncertainty lets players weigh the risk of acting on it.

text: Two NPCs describing the same event with different detail corroborate it, and their disagreements can be designed as leads for players.
An NPC's claimed relationship can be checked by a second character who should know the real person, with that character's reaction serving as a cue.
when: Designing a dialogue where an NPC's identity is in doubt.

text: A false claim is easiest to catch when the listener already knows the true fact, such as having seen the speaker's real ability.
Check a claimed injury against who visits, who speaks for the person, and whether they act like someone in pain.
when: a medical excuse covers a long absence

text: Check a sensational report against behaviour the player has already seen before the report is accepted.
when: An NPC delivers a dramatic accusation or diagnosis.

text: After probing a witness's view of a person's mood or behaviour, ask for objective evidence such as copies, drafts or old papers to test it.
why: subjective impressions are weaker than documents

text: Test a new reading of a scene against other witnesses' times before accepting it.
when: A reinterpretation changes the timeline of a scene.
why: A reading that fits one account may conflict with others.

text: Make each contradiction a checkable item, such as a missing garment or an untouched item, that falsifies a theory when inspected.
when: Designing evidence that disproves a theory
why: Concrete items can be verified

text: Make a false identity or mix-up follow from a visible, checkable step, not from luck alone.
when: When designing a plausible deception or belonging swap.
why: Audiences and players can later trace the error back to something they saw.

text: Let NPCs give different accounts of the same location depending on who asks, rewarding the player for cross-checking.
An apparent large conspiracy may be a fabricated setup, so verify its scale before reacting to it.
when: When a threat seems much bigger than its visible evidence
why: Constructed hoaxes can make minor sources look like organized plots.

text: Test a claimed timeline by asking about a related, hard-to-invent detail such as a meal or weather. Rehearsed accounts often omit such specifics.
when: When a timeline rests on a single witness.

text: A recorded statement is only as reliable as the checks made on it afterwards.
Partial checks give partial confidence, so record the remaining doubt explicitly and decide whether it is acceptable to proceed.
when: verification is incomplete
why: unrecorded doubt is easily forgotten and distorts later decisions

text: Verifying existing alibis tends to eliminate suspects rather than produce new leads, so it should be paired with questions that open new lines.
when: Investigating with little new evidence.
why: Checking confirms or refutes existing claims but does not generate new ones.

text: Narrow factual questions that can be checked against dates and records break evasion better than general accusations.
when: A witness gives vague answers about a past event.
why: Specific answers can be verified, which makes evasion costly and gives the witness less room to deflect.

text: A fixed-point check is unhelpful when the expected destination cannot be reached or the schedule itself is unknown.
Check the timing of a side detail before trusting it, since a real detail can still be a dead end.
Let confirmation rest on a document the other party can read, not on the investigator's word alone.
when: Presenting a deduction to others

text: Test a claim of unusual strength against the claimant's known training or physical history before treating it as a supernatural effect.
Claims about when a specific route was abandoned should follow the surviving record, since no fixed rule dates such changes.
A false claim can be exposed by asking for a detail that only a real witness could know, and whose answer can be confirmed apart from the witness's word.
when: A witness claims to have observed something that others can check.
why: A checkable answer exists independently of the witness, so it can confirm or refute the claim.

text: A statement written to defend a person or group often shifts emphasis toward that party's favored framing compared with earlier accounts of the same events.
when: a later account is written or circulated to protect a reputation
why: a defensive purpose changes what gets stressed or omitted

text: An account with concrete, checkable specifics gains trust when no one challenged them, because a false specific would likely have been refuted.
when: an account names times, places or words
why: false details are easy targets for rebuttal

text: Test an explanation by restoring the lost item: if that ends the trouble, the ordinary explanation is at least as strong.
when: Choosing between an ordinary and a supernatural cause of loss
why: Ending the trouble by ordinary means points to an ordinary cause

text: When a witness's stated belief shifts, examine how the question was framed before accepting the statement.
Give players a test kit with a clear detection threshold, so a clue's type is verified before it is trusted.
Let a fragile rope be upgraded to a sturdier cable as a progression step, so the player's channel becomes more dependable over time.
when: Designing gradual progression through a traversal or communication system
why: Visible upgrades communicate growth and reduce the risk of losing a route

text: Give each source trace an unrepeatable feature so that only a careful check exposes a copy.
when: Designing traces that can be forged.
why: Unrepeatable features keep copies imperfect and reward thorough inspection.

text: When no independent source exists for a claim, judge it on other grounds rather than treating it as verified.
A puzzle to tell whether an NPC is dead or unconscious can use checks with clear, distinct results, such as a pulse, a mirror or a responding limb.
Use a checkable marker such as a plate or inscription so players can confirm an identity they must verify.
when: crypt or graveyard levels

text: Rank clues by how tightly they bind to one place: common clutter should count for less than rare, localised traces.
when: when weighting clues

text: Place low-value props that carry checkable data, so thorough players are rewarded while the main path does not depend on them.
when: When designing optional detail in a level.
why: Optional depth rewards exploration without blocking progress.

text: Make variables such as tide, time of day or weather checkable, so players can test whether a claimed sequence was physically possible.
when: when designing a past-event puzzle
why: checkable constraints let players verify the reconstruction

text: Make records such as a roster or ledger checkable, so players can confirm or disprove a claim by visiting a second location.
Separate a claim that a place holds a supernatural trace from evidence that a human act occurred there, and test the claim before accepting it.
when: When an atmosphere or local legend is offered as explanation for an event
why: Ordinary houses can conceal crimes without leaving visible traces, so setting alone proves nothing

text: Casual remarks give hints rather than proof, so confirm an offhand connection with a second independent source before relying on it.
when: Using gossip or chance remarks to advance an investigation
why: A listener can misread a remark, and hints alone do not establish facts

text: Treat claims of a perfect record, such as many cases without failure, as unverified when no checkable detail about those cases is given.
Let an NPC state a negative confidently, then offer a follow-up question that exposes what they did not check, so the player must verify it.
when: Designing an NPC testimony that can be challenged.
why: A follow-up question turns an assumed claim into a checkable one.

text: Introduce a late counter-objection that breaks a neat solution, forcing players to recompute the timeline rather than accept the first answer.
when: The mystery is approaching its apparent solution around the late middle or final stretch.
why: A last-minute challenge keeps players reasoning instead of settling early.

text: An NPC's report of a sound, missing item or routine, or what a servant or object shows, can contradict a suspect's stated movements, creating a clue the player must reconcile.
when: Designing NPC testimony in a game.

text: An NPC formally questioned may later give a changed version, which the player can detect by comparing its statements against earlier ones.
why: A formal statement creates a record that later accounts can be checked against.

text: A dialogue system can store an NPC's earlier answers and flag contradictions when the player returns to the topic.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that must stay consistent.
why: Stored answers let the system detect and surface contradictions.

text: Accepting a verified detail as proof of the whole account is a mistake, even if framing is doubtful; each claim in a timeline or chain needs its own check.
Each elimination filter, plan or route deduction rests on assumptions, such as a sound's source; verify them, since a contradicting result collapses every branch built on them.
Treat an inferred entry route or location from residue as a hypothesis until logs, witnesses or on-site checks confirm it, since inference chains can hide fallacies.
when: when reasoning about how someone got into a location or from residue to location
why: Inferred routes can be wrong without corroboration.

text: A theory may fit most clues or one clue yet contradict or miss another, such as a shot time or body position; test every condition before trusting a confident solution.
when: Evaluating a theory against the full set of evidence.
why: An unexplained detail can overturn an otherwise convincing answer.

text: Accepting a sealed-room or constant-presence statement without asking when it was true or cross-checking it creates false impossibilities or false eliminations.
Confirming harmless details in a document can make its accusations seem proven, even though accuracy on minor points says nothing about the central claim.
why: Correct description proves familiarity, not guilt.

text: A clear, persuasive argument can blind a listener to its own weakness, especially when the weak point wounds their pride.
A reproduction test is only as strong as its match to the original conditions. Loosely matched conditions can make a result look like confirmation when it is not.
when: Interpreting the result of a reconstruction test.
why: Differences in weight or position can produce a trace that the original did not.

text: A verified detail is true but not necessarily meaningful; confirming a fact does not show what it means or who is responsible.
Saying that a check was already made can stop others from repeating it, even when its result is unknown to them.
when: Reporting that a forensic or other check has been done.
why: Listeners assume the matter is covered and do not pursue it.

text: Claiming superior hidden means of verification without carrying out the checks signals skipped verification and leaves the case unsupported.
A persuasive connection that goes nowhere can consume time that belongs to new evidence.
when: a connection seems meaningful but cannot be followed
why: Attention spent on a dead end delays productive lines of inquiry.

text: Repeating a staged test for an audience rewards the performer and adds no evidence, since the same reaction is simply shown again.
when: A test is staged and repeated for observers rather than varied.
why: Repetition for onlookers gives the performer more stage time, not new information about the claim.

text: Relying on a single lie to hold fails when the claimed absence can be verified.
when: when an alibi or excuse can be checked

text: Accepting a physical trace as proof that a person was somewhere, without asking who else could have moved it, leads to wrong conclusions.
A player theory that rests on a mistaken assumption can be exposed by a cheap verification step such as a ledger or record check.
when: Designing a deduction puzzle where players reason from assumed facts.
why: Cheap checks let bad deductions be caught rather than rewarded.

text: Confirm a check's coverage before ruling out a room, feature or item, or calling a search thorough or a container empty; limited checks miss items among ordinary contents.
when: Deciding whether an object, feature or room has been found, is absent or can be eliminated.
why: Limited surveys can miss features or items that exist; unchecked eliminations can hide the real route.

text: A claim nobody can check leaves the story stalled; the player needs a path to corroboration.

1) List each factual claim in the statement. 2) Compare each claim with facts you already hold, such as a price. 3) Record wrong claims and the correct version; a mismatch shows the story cannot be complete.
when: a statement describes events you can check
why: Claims are tested against known evidence, not tone.

text: 1) Note the suspect's claimed skill or background. 2) Ask for a demonstration of that skill. 3) Repeat the demonstration in any other languages or forms claimed. 4) Treat a mismatch as a flag for a false identity.
when: A suspect claims a skill or background that can be shown on request
why: A live demonstration tests claims that a story alone cannot confirm

text: 1) Check whether the claim would be valid under the stated rules if its facts hold. 2) For each factual element, ask what source could show it. 3) Check whether each source still survives. 4) Note what support remains.
when: a claim rests on a formal or legal conclusion

text: 1) Identify a claim checkable against records held by others. 2) Run a cheap test. 3) Let the result confirm or rule out the lead.
when: A claim or location can be checked independently.
why: Independent records give cheap, decisive checks.

text: 1) Compare the stated times with other timed events. 2) Compare stated positions with where objects or people were found. 3) Record each mismatch.
when: a witness's story can be checked against objects, positions or times

text: 1) Identify the exact arrangement shown in the scene. 2) Take test prints of the same digits in that arrangement. 3) Compare the test prints with the scene under matching conditions.
when: when a claimed pose seems physically impossible
why: a fair comparison needs the same conditions as the scene

text: 1) Store each NPC claim as a record with a time and place. 2) Let the player choose which record to present against a suspect. 3) Compare the chosen record with the NPC's answer.
when: when building an interrogation system in a game
why: structured claim records make contradictions checkable by the player

text: 1) Ask the witness to look again without naming the feature. 2) Record whether they still report it unprompted. 3) Discount any detail that appears only after a suggestion.
when: a claimed detail came after a suggestion
why: Suggested details often disappear when retested.

text: 1) Compare the statement with what other people report seeing. 2) Compare it with the physical record. 3) Note any period or contact the statement leaves out.
why: Independent sources reveal omissions that a consistent account hides.

text: 1) Record each verified event with its time. 2) Order the events chronologically. 3) Link consecutive events by the travel or interval between them.
when: Building a timeline from verified times.
why: A chain of confirmed times reveals where each person could have been.

text: 1) Form a conclusion from the pattern. 2) List each supporting fact. 3) Confirm each fact separately using a record or a targeted question. 4) Reveal the conclusion only after every link is confirmed.
when: a conclusion is clear but unconfirmed
why: each link is weaker than the conclusion until checked

text: 1) Take a stakeholder's events one at a time. 2) For each, ask where, when, why and how it happened. 3) Settle that event before opening the next. 4) Check it against physical traces and other accounts.
when: Checking an account from a witness or suspect

text: 1) Find a complete copy of the source if one survives. 2) Compare its omitted passages with the quoted ones. 3) Note which omissions change the conclusion.
1) Find a small object near the crime. 2) Test it against its most likely match, such as fitting a key to a damaged lock. 3) Treat a successful fit as confirmation of the link.
1) Let the subject approach far enough for a clear view of the face. 2) Keep the observer in a dark spot. 3) Confirm identity at close range before the subject escapes.
when: A suspect must be identified at close range before escape.
why: Close, unhurried viewing gives a reliable identification while the observer stays concealed.

text: 1) Obtain a baseline from someone who knows the space, including recent movements. 2) List every item that should be present. 3) Check each listed item for absence. 4) Treat any unexpected object as a change made after the baseline.
when: a space should match a known state and changes must be found
why: Comparing against an explicit list and a known baseline reveals what was added, moved, or removed.

text: 1) Treat a damaging, unverified claim as a lead rather than a verified fact. 2) Seek independent confirmation before acting on it.
when: An informant brings a claim that would harm the target if believed.
why: Unverified accusations can mislead and cause harm if acted upon.

text: 1) Note a witness's claim. 2) Compare it against what other people or records show. 3) Use any mismatch to decide where to press further.
when: A witness makes a claim that cannot yet be verified.
why: Mismatches identify weak points to investigate, without being proof on their own.

text: 1) Identify the NPC's motive for the account. 2) Find a second source that can confirm or contradict a key claim. 3) Act on the claim only after the second source is checked.
when: When designing a dialogue system in which an NPC offers a self-serving account.
why: A second source lets the player test an interested party's claim before acting on it.

text: Tag each NPC claim as seen, heard from another character, or guessed, and note any interest that may bias what that NPC reveals, so players can judge reliability.
when: when writing NPC dialogue that reports events in a mystery
why: Tags make the epistemic status of each claim visible.

text: Verify a witness's central or checkable location claim immediately, before building on it; keep trust partial until the check passes and state the cost of a false claim.
State the limits of a reasoning method, such as secondhand reports or the point where the signs stop, rather than implying certainty beyond the evidence.
when: when a deduction reaches the edge of what the signs or access allow
why: Explicit limits keep the reasoning credible.

text: State key constraints and premises plainly, such as no key on the body or an object's starting state, before the conclusion so the audience reasons from the same facts.
when: when writing a locked-room puzzle or presenting a deduction
why: Shared premises let the audience check the reasoning.

text: Store each NPC or suspect claim with time, place and verification status so players can check it against other NPCs, ledgers or world records; testimony becomes checkable evidence.
when: when designing NPC dialogue or an investigation system
why: Checkable claims turn dialogue into gameplay evidence.

text: Compare each NPC claim with stored records and observed behaviour, flagging conflicts and any claim that exceeds what that NPC could have known.
Let players cross-check NPC statements and reconstruct sequences from fragments, deducing who saw what and from where; fragments form a sequence only when compared.
Make an unverifiable note or document a claim that players must corroborate before relying on it.
Tag clues as misleading, suggestive or conclusive, so players learn which kinds of evidence to trust before naming a culprit.
when: when designing a deduction puzzle with several clue types
why: Explicit reliability tags teach players how to weigh evidence.

text: Let an NPC state a small fact, such as which item was used, that one found clue contradicts; make that clue decisive so the NPC cannot explain it away.
when: Designing a puzzle where the player catches an NPC lying.
why: A single decisive contradiction gives the player a clear, fair way to expose the lie.

text: Do not accept a pattern-based motive or dismiss a suspicious clue as a blind until the victim's background or a confession or record confirms it.
when: Interpreting a suspicious clue or inferred motive at a crime scene.
why: Background facts can override a misleading pattern and fix the real motive.

text: Treat a neat deduction as a conjecture and require a verification step, such as a search, so correct answers are confirmed by observation and wrong ones are exposed.
when: Designing a deduction puzzle, including one whose solution is inferred from constraints.
why: Observed confirmation makes the answer feel earned and prevents lucky guesses; tidy reasoning can still be wrong.

text: Offer a plausible but wrong explanation players can verify, and treat a leading explanation as a starting point to verify before committing resources.
when: Designing a puzzle, or before committing resources to one line of inquiry.
why: A careful player who verifies still reaches the real answer, since the obvious reading is not automatically correct.

text: Let the player check an NPC's account, especially one that cannot recall events, against objects the player can examine.
Give NPCs sincere but wrong causal explanations, so players must test them against items and locations before accepting them.
why: a confident wrong explanation rewards checking rather than trust

text: Check your own figures as carefully as the suspect's, since a corrected number can change the case.
Verify explanations such as a loan or sale against records rather than dismissing them.
Let a suspect make a public statement the player can check against evidence, so the claim can be tested.
when: When designing suspect dialogue

text: Keep each discrepancy checkable by the player so that noticing it is rewarded.
when: when designing clues

text: Give an NPC who claims to know the dungeon a boast that the player can check against the map or a rival's account.
When a witness claims to see inside a closed space, check the claim against the sightline through its openings, such as windows, gaps or doors.
when: when a witness describes the interior of a room they could not enter
why: openings define what can physically be seen

text: Do not treat a firm statement as settled until its basis, including distance, light, sobriety and the source of any time given, is known.
when: A case rests on a witness's firm claim
why: A confident account may rest on weak conditions

text: Make a dialogue confrontation require a verified detail, so the suspect's account unlocks evidence and changes later options.
when: designing suspect dialogue
why: the player's earlier work gates the new information

text: Each criminal act needs its own evidence; a person's record should not be treated as one bundle that proves every offence.
when: assigning guilt for multiple offences
why: offences differ in method and proof

text: Do not drop a suspect on the strength of one document; seek partial or independent answers from multiple sources.
when: when a single record seems to clear a suspect
why: one source may be incomplete or misleading

text: Let an NPC accept a player's cover story, then create later conflicts that expose its flaws so the player must manage the lie.
when: designing deception-driven quests

text: Script two NPC experts to disagree about one piece of evidence, and provide a verifiable third source the player can consult to settle it.
Challenge a claim with a pointed question to test whether the other party concedes what they do not know.
Identify and state the limit of an alibi, naming which parts no one could observe.
when: Summarising how well an alibi is supported
why: Makes clear what remains unverified

text: Give an NPC story many details the player can check against records, other NPCs and the world map, while leaving one core claim open for later.
when: when writing an NPC's account
why: Verifiable details build trust, and the open core keeps the mystery going.

text: Flag contradictions between an NPC's established personality and the evidence against them, so the player can weigh the mismatch.
when: When generated evidence conflicts with an NPC's traits
why: Showing the mismatch invites the player to reason about it

text: Check for innocent explanations before treating a gap as proof of a crime, since a gap alone does not establish one.
Create a timed clue from contradictions between two NPCs who both protect a third, so the player must resolve the conflict to fix a time.
Check the alibi of every named person, not only the main suspects, since a minor name can prove decisive.
Check every possible exit, not only the obvious one, before accepting that a place was sealed.
when: Assessing a locked or guarded location.
why: An unguarded route can make a seemingly sealed location passable.

text: Give an NPC a gap between its stated attitude and its actual schedule, so an observant player can detect the contradiction.
Give an NPC an innocent explanation for an incriminating item, and let players check it against records or ownership marks.
Judge a character's claims by their checkable content, separately from the manner of delivery such as tears, kneeling or pleading.
why: Manner does not establish whether a statement is true.

text: Require a verifying find, such as a document in a hidden place, before a case can be marked closed.
Gate a final accusation behind a checklist of verified links, so the player must confirm each one before the reveal.
Treat an anomaly as a clue only after it is verified, and test it rather than assume an innocent or sinister cause.
when: An unexpected object or mark conflicts with the apparent story
why: Unverified anomalies can have innocent explanations that mislead

text: Do not rely on evidence whose original form was never examined, such as a postal envelope that was never seen.
when: when evidence depends on a document or package that was not inspected directly
why: Without examining the original, its postal or transit details cannot be trusted.

text: Place checkable clues earlier in the level rather than revealing the answer only in a final cutscene.
Make clue wording matter, so near-synonymous descriptions lead to different solutions and players must read carefully.
when: Writing text-based clues for puzzles
why: Precise wording rewards close reading

text: Make an accident verdict checkable by requiring players to find the object the verdict assumed was used, or to notice that it is missing.
when: designing a crime scene with an official accident verdict
why: a checkable verdict rewards careful inspection

text: Give the player a case journal that automatically lists found clues, so overlooked items become visible.
when: Designing investigation-based gameplay.
why: An automatic list reduces the chance a clue is forgotten.

text: Separate checkable details from hearsay, and verify the checkable parts directly rather than accept the relayed claim.
when: Weighing a secondhand account
why: Only verified details can support a conclusion

text: Let a culprit's borrowed justification be checkable at its source, since the culprit may have avoided checking it.
when: A culprit cites a precedent or authority.
why: Exposing the source can undermine the rationalization on which the wrong rests.

text: Check a claimed family relationship or identity against an independent verifiable fact, such as the claimed person's physical condition at the time.
when: A caller or visitor claims a relationship to someone.
why: A checkable fact can prove a claimed identity false.

text: A challenge-countersign check tests knowledge, not identity, so anyone who overhears the exchange can pass as a legitimate visitor.
when: Relying on a password to admit visitors
why: Knowledge of the phrase can be obtained by eavesdropping

text: Use one shared clock, such as the in-game clock, to order witness statements and logs; lining them up exposes contradictions among them.
when: Several records or accounts describe the same events.
why: A common reference lets players line up accounts.

text: Estimates of when an event happened from physical evidence are approximate, and should be stated as ranges rather than exact times.
when: when deriving a time from decay, temperature, or similar physical state
why: physical clocks vary with conditions and are imprecise

text: Some people track time through recurring markers, such as a weekly day, and can report events in order without knowing the calendar date.
when: a witness cannot read or write
why: Recurring markers preserve sequence even without dates

text: An interval between a lightning flash and the following thunder, about a minute and a half, can serve as a readable clock that shows a calm, controlled sequence.
when: A storm scene where a flash and thunder are used to mark time.
why: The delay between light and sound lets the observer measure elapsed time and infer deliberate timing.

text: Do not rely on a witness's sense of time; take the date from a record instead.
Repeated sounds and clock readings make elapsed time visible, so the audience senses the hours passing.
Explicit times of day give a timeline fixed points against which other events can be measured.
An unreliable clock or a wrong forecast is itself a clue: it undermines trust in the world's timing, and the reader should not assume it is accurate.
when: Using time markers or predicted events as narrative tools.
why: A faulty timekeeper can mislead the reader as much as the characters.

text: A changed object or unfinished work records when events happened and how long a process took, so it fixes timing for investigators.
A fixed offset between two clocks, such as a one-hour time-zone difference, shifts every reported time by the same amount and can turn an apparent contradiction into a consistent timeline.
A pre-recorded voice played after a death makes witnesses hear the victim alive later, shifting the apparent time of death.
when: a voice is heard but the speaker is not seen
why: Listeners cannot tell a recording from a live speaker.

text: A cigarette burns for about twelve minutes in calm weather and about eight minutes in gusty weather.
when: estimating how long a cigarette was lit outdoors
why: wind speeds up burning

text: Treating one witness's time as exact is a mistake when other witnesses differ, since times from different people can vary by several minutes.
when: When witnesses give different times for the same events.
why: Each witness's clock or memory carries its own error, so a narrow timeline built on them can mislead.

text: 1) Compare the witness's clock with a reliable reference at the same moment. 2) Compute the offset. 3) Apply the offset to every time the witness reported, keeping relative order and durations intact.
when: Building a timeline from a witness's timestamps, especially when the timing device is known to drift.
why: An uncorrected clock shifts every event it recorded, and a uniform shift keeps order and durations intact.

text: 1) Note clock times from watches or timestamps. 2) Record how long ago earlier key events occurred. 3) Compare sequences to place events relative to one another. 4) Accept that the timeline shows when events happened, not why.
when: ordering several people's movements

text: 1) Use regularly repeated sounds, such as bell quarters, as units of time. 2) Count the units between events. 3) Cross-check the total against memory of other landmarks.
when: no clock can be trusted

text: 1) Check whether the object's winding or power has run out. 2) If stored run remains, treat the stop as possible interference. 3) Test the object directly, which settles whether the stop was natural faster than debate.
when: an object has stopped unexpectedly

text: 1) Subtract the elapsed time recorded at each checkpoint to get the duration of each session. 2) Compare each player's totals. 3) Estimate the length of a long calculation and place it within a time window.
when: An alibi rests on continuous presence and a time-stamped record exists.
why: Timing gaps reveal periods when a player may have been away from the table.

text: Do not assume a clock is accurate without knowing whose it is; confirm it still runs and check its drift against a known event before trusting it.
when: A timeline depends on a clock, watch or other timer.
why: Damaged or drifting devices can show a time far from the true one, placing events at the wrong times.

text: Collect or record a time-sensitive trace in an exposed scene early, before weather or tide erases it.
when: investigation scene exposed to weather or tide where delay is part of the case
why: Erased traces cannot be re-examined later.

text: Record NPC grudges as explicit, time-stamped threats so that a later death or theft can be traced back to a stated motive.
when: Designing NPC rivalries that feed a later crime
why: A recorded threat gives the player a traceable motive

text: Correct a clock's reading only when its error is known; a guessed offset adds false precision.
when: the source's error is unknown
why: An invented correction looks exact while being unsupported

text: List everyone with access to a closed space to narrow suspects, and check whether each control was real.
when: Investigating who could have entered a restricted room.
why: Access controls differ in strength, so the real list may differ from the apparent one.

text: Access rules limit which NPCs could have taken an item, so the player can eliminate suspects by location and skill.
when: In games where NPCs have locations and abilities.
why: Restricted access makes elimination a fair deduction method.

text: A chain of mundane causes can explain how and why a discovery happened, but it does not substitute for evidence that identifies what was found.
when: Presenting a discovery whose circumstances are plausible but unidentified.
why: Explaining access is distinct from establishing identity.

text: Hint at the final hiding place through an architectural feature early in the setting, then open it only late, so the solution is anchored in the location.
when: planning a concealed room or route that resolves the case
why: A feature seen early but used late makes the reveal feel grounded rather than invented.

text: A forced waiting period with no available action builds frustration and tension, since the investigator cannot advance the case.
when: Access to a key witness is postponed by a scheduled event.
why: Lack of agency during a wait increases the pressure to act.

text: Keeping the player close to each suspect makes later reversals feel earned rather than arbitrary, because the player has seen each suspect's behavior first-hand.
A closed-room death accepted as accident can be a murder by a visitor, proven by a second person's trace left inside the sealed room.
A typical mystery sets an apparently impossible or sinister act inside a closed setting, puts forward a plausible suspect, clears that suspect, and explains the act through an overlooked detail.
when: structuring a closed-setting or locked-room mystery
why: Clearing the first suspect and exposing a small detail drives the solution.

text: Treat an apparent impossibility as evidence that a stated premise is false; a claim that no one could enter often hides a second route, so conclude someone moved the object.
when: When evaluating whether a space was sealed or an act was impossible
why: Unverified access claims can conceal entry paths

text: A witness who identifies a person by clothing or outline, especially at a distance or in poor light, can be wrong, because common outfits are shared by many people.
when: When a witness describes a suspect only by outfit, hat or silhouette.
why: Shared clothing gives many people the same outline, so the match can be coincidence.

text: Several simple changes together, such as shaving, a false hair frame and tinted lenses, can alter a person's appearance completely.
Clothing and footwear record recent movements, such as mud on shoes or wet trim that points to rain.
A detached fragment of clothing can link a wearer to a scene and may leave no fingerprints.
when: prints are absent but a fragment is found
why: Fragments can identify a wearer where other traces fail.

text: Finer fabrics still leave marks, and each layer of a garment can leave its own impression on the bullet.
Clothing worn in an unusual combination can signal haste or deliberate intent, especially when it departs from the person's established habits.
when: when a person's dress differs from their normal routine
why: people rarely break habitual dress without a reason

text: Disguising a person with another's clothing can make observers misidentify them, especially in poor light when observers expect to see a familiar figure.
when: poor light and familiar expectation
why: clothing cues dominate quick recognition

text: Relying on common clothing descriptions to pick out a person in a crowd often fails, since many travellers wear the same outfit.
when: Searching for a person in a crowded place.
why: Common clothing matches many people and identifies none.

text: A cut-out label on a garment can suggest deliberate removal of identity, but it may also mislead investigators.
when: Interpreting a removed tag or mark on discarded clothing.
why: The removal can be read as a clue when it has another cause.

text: Do not convict on a clothing description alone, and give little identifying weight to common garments, since many people wear them and they narrow the field very little.
when: The only evidence against a person is a description of their clothing, or identification rests on clothing alone.
why: Common clothing matches many people, so it cannot single out one individual.

text: Show an unresolved clue, such as a missing companion, early with its meaning withheld, so attentive players can notice it and accept the later reveal as fair.
when: Planting a clue that contradicts the main theory, or showing a clue early with its meaning withheld
why: Early visibility rewards attentive players, and the player already had all the evidence needed to reach the answer.

text: A minor anomaly kept open across many scenes can gain weight and recast the story, but if left too long unresolved it reads as an authoring error.
when: A minor clue, such as a missing object or early planted detail, stays unresolved across many scenes
why: Sustained open questions keep readers tracking the detail until it resolves, while long gaps make the detail look forgotten.

text: Raise a question about a visible fact that does not match the stated account, and leave it unanswered for now.
when: A character's appearance, wealth or circumstances conflict with the official story.
why: An open anomaly invites the reader to investigate and keeps a lead alive.

text: A visible detail, such as an object in a photograph, can overturn an explanation that seemed settled.
A single reaction or calm response is one signal among others, not proof, so keep the reading open until more evidence comes in.
when: Interpreting a suspect's expression or demeanor.
why: Innocent reactions and calm can look like tells or cover when read alone.

text: Give the player a visible, wrong answer that the evidence supports, so that a later reversal feels earned rather than arbitrary.
when: planning a mystery's false solution
why: A wrong answer grounded in visible evidence makes the eventual correction read as deduction, not invention.

text: Leave a loose thread, such as an unexplained name, as an optional lead even if the story does not pursue it.
when: when a narrative has spare detail
why: An open lead adds texture and invites player curiosity without needing resolution.

text: Having the investigator stumble on a key fact that was never mentioned earlier breaks fair play, because the audience had no chance to connect it.
when: Resolving a mystery through a sudden discovery.
why: The audience cannot make the link without a prior mention of the fact.

text: An anomaly that is never explained undermines trust in the whole story, because the audience feels the clue was a cheat.
why: audiences stop investing in clues they expect to be ignored

text: Players feel cheated when a clue seems to point at a culprit and is never confirmed, so state whether the ambiguity is intended.
when: a clue points toward a culprit without resolution
why: unmet expectations from a pointing clue

text: If the audience sees a removed clue vanish, a shifted charge can look contrived.
when: A case changes its charge after a clue is discredited.
why: The visible disappearance makes the substitution feel arbitrary.

text: When a clue is revised, show the cause of the revision, such as cleaning or new evidence, or the change will seem like a cheat.
when: Correcting an earlier clue's reading.
why: A visible cause makes the change credible.

text: Having a suspect repeat a statement aloud and confirm it under oath fixes the wording, so it can be checked against later statements.
when: A suspect's account must be locked in for later comparison.
why: A fixed wording gives a stable reference point for detecting contradictions.

text: When a key source is unreachable, wait for confirmation rather than assuming the answer.
Do not repeat an event at the same level; each repetition should change something the player can detect.
when: Repeating a threat or event across scenes
why: Identical repetition becomes predictable and stops producing tension

text: Give an unexplained clue in a verbatim form the player can record and check later.
when: Writing a cryptic clue meant to be solved later.
why: A recorded exact wording lets the player test it when new information arrives.

text: Leave some clues unexplained and mark them for later, so the audience senses that the system is wrong.
when: Writing an investigation whose resolution is institutional rather than a revealed culprit.
why: Unresolved details make a later reversal feel more credible.

text: A gap in observer coverage at the critical moment is a place to investigate, not proof of guilt.
why: Gaps can arise from fog, cover or weak sightlines as well as wrongdoing

text: A later disturbance of a covering can expose an earlier one, so the sequence of disturbances shows how an object was hidden and then found.
A covering can hide the moment an object was dropped, so track when the object was last seen.
Leave deliberate gaps in a route record for players to fill through observation and deduction, rather than supplying a complete log.
when: Designing a character's movement or whereabouts as a clue.
why: Gaps invite players to reason about the missing parts.

text: Evidence that is too complete or points neatly at one person may be staged or planted to frame a scapegoat; check it before trusting it.
when: evidence or a clue seems to point too clearly or unusually well to one suspect
why: real events rarely produce a perfectly consistent trail; planting can aim evidence at a scapegoat; over-convenient evidence reads as contrivance

text: A suspect's account or a theory that fits every fact with no leftover detail may be constructed; persuasiveness is not proof of truth.
when: choosing between candidate explanations, or a suspect's account matches all the evidence
why: a perfect fit can indicate a constructed account; tidy stories can fit visible facts without being true

text: A pair that differs in every visible trait suggests a staged arrangement, since real rivals usually share some point of contact that makes them clash.
when: A set of people or objects looks suspiciously symmetrical
why: A complete reversal leaves nothing pushing against anything, which natural contrasts rarely do

text: When events seem too well timed to be spontaneous, check who benefits from each development and look for a pattern across several events.
why: A single coincidence is weak evidence, but a repeated pattern of benefit is stronger.

text: Placing a dense cluster of clues at the start of each case, followed by one or two misdirects and a sharp late cluster before the reveal, gives players early useful information.
when: Structuring the clue pacing of a mystery case.
why: Early density orients the player, and the late cluster sets up the reveal.

text: Too many red herrings or false leads dilute the real danger and make the mystery feel arbitrary; each false lead should be knocked down by a visible fact.
Planting many minor details without distinguishing the useful ones dilutes the important clue, so players cannot tell which detail matters.
when: planting several small clues
why: too many trifles compete for the player's attention

text: Repeated false alarms without progress make the audience lose patience, so the suspense collapses rather than grows.
when: Staging delays before a reveal.
why: Setbacks without advancement stop feeling meaningful and the audience stops caring.

text: Trying too few patterns can lead the solver to give up or settle on a false reading.
Assuming a clear-looking set of facts is complete is a mistake; distrust tidy facts and ask for the detail that would test the theory.
Too many unresolved questions at once frustrate the audience, so close some threads as new ones open.
Asking a dying speaker too many questions is unrealistic and can break the scene's credibility.
when: When a dying witness is being questioned
why: Excessive questioning strains plausibility

text: Make a clue appear only when the player chooses a specific dialogue topic, so exploring the conversation tree reveals it.
Drip clues steadily through the story, then cluster the decisive ones late so the final reveal draws on many earlier threads the reader can connect.
when: Pacing clue release across a mystery
why: Early clues need time to be noticed; a steady drip keeps suspicion moving; late clusters make the reveal click and reward accumulated attention.

text: Clues often surface by chance, such as a fragment found while searching for something else, and the finder's reaction signals the clue's significance to the audience.
when: Introducing a clue through an incidental search
why: Incidental finds feel natural and the reaction tells the audience what matters

text: Key discoveries often depend on small accidents, such as an interruption or a forgotten gesture, that look minor when they happen.
when: When explaining how a critical finding came about.
why: Trivial actions can set off the chain of events that leads to the finding.

text: Front-load the earliest clues to set the central question, drip later clues steadily through the middle, and cluster the strongest plants and identity reveals late-middle before the climax.
when: Pacing clues across a mystery or concealment plot
why: Early anchors establish the case, steady dripping sustains interest, and late clustering builds to the reveal.

text: Mark clues as corroborated by a second independent source or as memory only, so their reliability is visible.
when: Organizing clues or testimony for a case or game.
why: Distinguishing supported clues from unsupported ones guides how much weight each receives.

text: Test each apparently meaningful clue as a hypothesis, drop what the evidence does not support, and treat suggestive clues such as initials as possible blinds.
when: Several explanations fit the surface facts
why: A suggestive clue can send the investigation toward the wrong party

text: In a scene arranged with deliberate balance, a single feature that breaks the pattern is likely to be meaningful and points to something hidden, moved or missing.
when: The surrounding scene is so ordered that any deviation reads as a deliberate choice by its arranger.
why: A meticulous arranger would not leave one feature lopsided without reason, so the anomaly signals a hidden action.

text: Drip clues steadily through the first half, then cluster them at a midpoint trial and before the finale.
why: Clustering raises tension at key turns.

text: Place clues in front-loaded, mid and late clusters so suspicion shifts at each stage of the story.
Cluster the decisive clues into a late public scene, so a reversal of suspicion lands at once rather than drifting.
when: when suspicion must move onto a new suspect
why: a dense cluster of proof makes the reversal feel conclusive

text: Scatter clues across the middle of the story and let them converge just before the reveal, so suspicion builds toward a single payoff.
why: Clues converging at one point make the reveal feel inevitable.

text: Clues cluster in the first 10-20% of a story, then arrive as a steady drip; late sections bunch them into a single cluster of argument.
Clues arrive in three patterns: front-loaded at the premise, a steady drip through each stage, or a late cluster just before the proof.
when: pacing clues across a mystery
why: Each pattern controls when the audience gathers the evidence they need.

text: An event that looks like chance, such as an extinguished candle, may be part of the scene's design.
when: when a minor event seems accidental
why: Coincidence in a staged scene can carry the mechanism of the crime.

text: Several apparently independent clues may trace back to one earlier inference, so their agreement can be an illusion.
when: When counting clues that seem to support a conclusion.
why: Shared origins make clues look more independent than they are.

text: Front-load clues in the opening scene, deliver the middle as a steady trickle of testimony that shifts suspicion, and hold the decisive proof for a late cluster.
why: Early clues seed every suspect; late proof resolves the case.

text: Anchor a late reversal to a physical clue the audience already saw earlier, so the confession feels earned rather than arbitrary.
Build a cluster of physical clues so that no single clue carries the case; the rest survive when one fails.
when: Designing evidence for a case that may later be challenged.
why: Redundant evidence keeps the case standing when one item is discredited.

text: Recurring a clue keeps it familiar for later reinterpretation, but an unchanged return feels redundant and loses force.
when: Repeating a motif or clue across the investigation.
why: Familiarity aids recontextualization, while unchanged repetition gives no new information.

text: A physical sign can be shown before its meaning is explained, with its significance depending on later testimony.
when: Introducing an unexplained physical clue.
why: Withholding meaning keeps the clue open until corroborating testimony arrives.

text: A change in a person's routine, such as moving their work to a different room, is a signal that can reveal a shift in their state or activity.
when: Interpreting a character's behavior in a mystery.
why: Deviation from habit is noticeable and carries meaning.

text: Retrospective narration that marks a detail as significant before its meaning is known signals to the audience that it will matter.
when: Foreshadowing a reveal in first-person or retrospective narration.
why: The framing invites attention without disclosing the answer.

text: A single conclusive item can close off a whole group of explanations at once, so one find can rule out many candidates.
when: Designing a mystery where clues eliminate branches.
why: Grouping explanations behind one decisive clue lets a single discovery restructure the player's options.

text: Words that show knowledge beyond what the suspect should have, such as the names or labels used by the investigation, can reveal inside knowledge of the case.
when: A suspect uses terms or refers to people only the investigation would name
why: Slips of vocabulary expose prior access to information

text: Plant a written clue the player can reread after the reveal, so the earlier text gains meaning once the cause is known.
Plant a shared identifying detail, such as a birth date or matching item, in a notebook or dialogue that players can check later.
when: when a hidden link must be discoverable
why: checkable clues let attentive players confirm the link

text: Hide the key fact behind a social assumption the audience accepts, such as a character being a bachelor, so the reveal reverses the assumption.
Let a silent object carry the threat until it is explained, since an unexplained reaction to it builds suspense.
when: introducing an ominous prop early in a scenario
why: Unanswered reactions prompt players to speculate, and a later explanation pays off that tension.

text: Leave one or two secondary clues unexplained after the main reveal, so the audience keeps reasoning past the solution.
when: Concluding a mystery with a satisfying main answer
why: Open loops sustain curiosity and reward later investigation.

text: Attach small contradictions to ordinary routines so players can catch them without specialised knowledge.
when: Designing clues that reward attentive play.
why: Everyday facts are accessible, so the contradiction is noticeable.

text: A foreign or oddly capitalised word can carry a second meaning, such as a place name rather than an object, so solving it requires a lookup.
when: When designing word-based puzzles.
why: A surface reading can mislead, and the second meaning rewards map or lookup use.

text: One tell, such as a tear or a trembling hand, has many possible causes, including grief, shame, fear, or guilt, so it cannot identify the cause alone.
Shared geography, such as a find on a suspect's land or near their home, does not establish a connection to them and needs independent support.
when: A discovery is located near a suspect.
why: Location alone is coincidence; it does not identify the victim or the culprit.

text: A label or sign used by many groups cannot identify one culprit alone; check whether it points to a single group or to many.
when: a generic name or sign appears in the case

text: A single marker proves little; rely on several matches that reinforce one another.
when: Establishing identity from clues.
why: One match can be coincidence or error.

text: Link recalled sensations and past events into a sequence, rather than treating them as separate anecdotes, to build a usable hypothesis.
when: When collecting witness details about a pattern
why: A sequence of linked details is easier to test than isolated memories.

text: Seed warnings and hesitations from a character whose true role is hidden, so they read as ordinary behaviour until the reveal.
Reuse the same kind of clue across cases, such as a sighting, a key item, or a handwriting mismatch, so players learn to read the pattern.
when: building a series of mysteries
why: Repeated clue types let players anticipate where the reversal lies.

text: Plant each part of a trick separately in ordinary-seeming moments, so no single clue reveals the mechanism until the parts are assembled.
Seed doubt early with a dismissive remark about a suspicious detail, so the player senses a timing problem without learning its mechanism; hold the proof until the end.
Place key clues early so the audience can test theories and later material handles aftermath; or use one tight late cluster just before reveal so pieces combine at once.
when: Planning the timing of clues for a mystery's reveal.
why: Early clues let the audience test their own theories before the explanation arrives; a compact late cluster lets the mechanism's pieces combine into the explanation at once.

text: Before a reveal, show the chain of earlier clues and draw only on that evidence in a short reversal, so players can rebuild the solution.
why: The reversal reads as fair deduction rather than invention, and players must be able to rebuild the solution from clues they already saw.

text: State the decisive clue in plain text within the account before the final explanation, so the player can connect it at reveal.
when: Withholding the method of a reveal, or designing a twist that relies on a fact the player already holds.
why: A clue never shown makes the explanation feel like a trick; a twist is fair only if the player had the information needed to work it out.

text: A writer can shape a case by omitting evidence, hedging a claim, or moving a document's context, and comparing the published account with the original reveals these moves.
Side plots can pace a mystery and hide the real line of inquiry, provided the true clues remain fair.
Signpost withheld entries or cut passages so players know a gap exists rather than assuming the record is complete.
when: A narrator's account or journal is deliberately incomplete
why: Visible gaps prevent players from trusting an incomplete record

text: Re-read the same evidence from another suspect's viewpoint, since identical facts can carry a different meaning.
when: Investigation has fixed on a single suspect.
why: A single viewpoint can lock the investigator onto one reading.

text: When a witness signals a gap, treat the account as incomplete and gather indirect evidence instead of waiting for the witness to disclose.
when: a witness starts to speak then stops or avoids a subject

text: Older favourites left on shelves mark earlier stages of interest, while recent titles and a concentration on one subject show current interests.
Put the final missing link in a place the player has already visited but not searched.
when: Placing the last clue of a mystery
why: Revisiting a known location rewards attention without adding new travel

text: A clue that makes sense only in hindsight must be planted earlier so it can be recognized when later facts arrive.
when: When designing clues meant to pay off later.
why: Hindsight recognition requires the earlier clue to have been seen.

text: Place the decisive clue in ordinary, early contexts so that a later reveal pays it off without feeling like an afterthought.
when: Designing a mystery in which the solution must be fair to the audience.
why: Clues seen early feel earned, whereas late clues feel like cheating.

text: A cleaned item can hold a hidden trace, such as a stain in a seam, which the player must find after the obvious cleaning was done.
when: when designing a physical-evidence puzzle
why: A residue the cleaning missed rewards close examination.

text: Give each clue an innocent reading when first seen, and only reveal its significance when the pieces are linked.
when: writing a mystery whose solution must stay fair
why: Innocent readings let the audience accept clues without suspecting them, so the reveal feels fair when linked.

text: A clue can sit in plain view as an ordinary detail and become meaningful only once its underlying mechanism is understood.
when: A means of harm is carried openly by a person as a tool, item of dress or familiar gesture.
why: The ordinary context makes the object read as décor, so recognition arrives only after the mechanism is revealed.

text: A dramatic side lead, such as a past romance or a missing man, can absorb time without advancing the case.
1) Test each side clue. 2) Resolve it or set it aside. 3) Keep focus on clues that bear directly on the central question.
when: A case gathers many unrelated secrets or alternatives.
why: Unresolved side clues dilute focus.

text: 1) Present a witness statement and a ledger side by side. 2) Let the player find the single line that conflicts with the record. 3) Use the conflict as a clue.
when: Designing a document puzzle.
why: Players learn to compare testimony to records and spot the decisive discrepancy.

text: 1) Plant low-weight clues in ordinary talk. 2) Deliver one strong document as a hook. 3) Test that document with a cluster of clues. 4) Close with a late cluster of proof.
when: when structuring a mystery's reveal
why: Ordinary clues build trust and the cluster removes doubt in stages.

text: Make a prior investigator's known conviction and its blind spot visible, so the player knows which question is still open.
Show a character's reaction to a sensitive topic without revealing its cause, so the clue stays open for the player to interpret.
why: An unexplained reaction keeps the mystery active and invites the player to test theories.

text: Signal that an answer is near, such as through a changed environment or rising sound, to build suspense before the reveal.
Show the consequences of solving a case in the game world, such as factions changing behaviour or rewards being given.
Show players which argument moved which NPC, rewarding those who learn each character's reasoning.
Show a rationalizing NPC's reasoning alongside the raw observation, so players can see where the explanation goes beyond the evidence.
Let a shrine or statue point away from a hidden chamber, with the real entrance placed elsewhere.
when: Designing a hidden location tied to a visible landmark
why: Misdirection rewards players who check the landmark against other clues

text: A fair-play clue must supply both the reference needed to decode it and the link between them, so the player can solve it with information the story provides.
when: when the solution depends on a fact the player can verify within the game
why: a clue without a decoding path frustrates players rather than rewarding them

text: Build a confirming check, such as a mirror or second witness, into a discovery so the player tests the clue before acting on it.
A clue shown to the audience supports an earned reveal; a clue held only in the detective's knowledge leaves the audience unable to check the solution.
Throwing with the non-dominant hand reaches much less far, so a thrown object's landing distance can expose the thrower's handedness.
A clue that fits both an explanation and a rival cannot discriminate between them and settles nothing alone; check whether a match actually discriminates.
when: Two readings fit one piece of evidence
why: Matching patterns can arise whether an item is genuine or forged; a clue that supports more than one account cannot settle the question alone.

text: An expected action that never happens can count as evidence of what is not occurring.
Treating a physical test as conclusive is a mistake when the tester's strength or skill differs from the suspect's.
when: a test is run by someone with different physical capability
why: The result shows what that tester could do, not what the suspect could do.

text: A reveal that depends on a clue the audience has never seen leaves the audience unconvinced.
when: Planning the final reveal of a mystery.
why: Audiences cannot verify a solution built on evidence they never encountered.

text: Do not treat every clue as planted; decide whether the offender could have placed it before accepting or rejecting it.
when: Evaluating a clue that may be staged
why: Some clues are genuine, so blanket suspicion discards real evidence

text: Give each major clue at least two plausible readings so a later discovery can flip the player's conclusion.
when: designing key evidence in a mystery
why: ambiguity lets new facts reverse the player's interpretation

text: Give every false solution a real, checkable clue, so each wrong suspect is supported by evidence the player can test.
why: Each suspect survives until its own clue is disproved

text: A clue can be planted in an ordinary object that the investigator rejects at first, then retrieves later so the reader sees it existed before its importance was clear.
when: A later revelation depends on a document or fact the reader has already seen.
why: Early dismissal hides the trace in plain sight, and retrieval later makes the reader feel the clue was fair.

text: Track which clues the player has witnessed and which were dismissed, so later reveals can point back to earlier moments.
when: Designing a mystery with delayed reveals

text: A clue hidden inside a widely distributed document survives the loss of its author or memory, because many copies keep the information available.
when: when a secret must outlast its keeper or a long time gap
why: Redundancy across many copies preserves the key even if the original holder is gone.

text: 1) Show the object early as ordinary, with a reading that seems to confirm a simple story. 2) Reveal a new source or cleaning that corrects the reading. 3) Let the corrected reading change the object's meaning.
when: A detail must look innocent at first and gain meaning later.
why: A visible correction makes the revised meaning feel earned rather than arbitrary.

text: A fair-play clue must stay readable: include enough detail for the audience to recover it, and never withhold it entirely, since total concealment removes the payoff.
when: Designing a hidden clue meant to be solved by the player, or concealing information in a scene.
why: Withholding all details makes the solution impossible to reach fairly; a clue must remain legible to be recognised when the key appears.

text: Make a planted detail memorable enough that the audience can recall it when it matters; a detail too minor to recall breaks fair play.
when: Planting a clue meant to be recalled later.
why: A clue the player cannot recall cannot be connected to the later question.

text: Show each misleading clue openly and note its oddity in the text, so the eventual reveal is fair.
when: Planting a clue that points to a false suspect.
why: Readers can only reinterpret evidence they actually saw and had reason to notice.

text: 1) Front-load setup clues in the opening; 2) release physical evidence and small details steadily mid-case, building suspicion gradually; 3) save the motive-explaining cluster for late.
Let an informant NPC's dialogue give everything in one visit, or signal that the informant's willingness will fade if the player delays.
when: designing a cooperative NPC who holds key information
why: Players who delay may lose the chance to exhaust the contact's knowledge.

text: Design each layer so it can be checked independently, so players can reject a weak link without losing the whole case.
when: designing a multi-layer case
why: independent layers localize failure

text: Lore in a game is spread across journals, NPC dialogue and inscriptions, and the player assembles the truth by cross-checking them.
when: Designing a lore-driven story
why: Distributed sources reward player deduction and make the story feel discovered.

text: An NPC informant can reveal information only after the player invests time or money in rapport, with dialogue unlocking as trust rises.
when: Designing informant NPCs
why: Gated trust makes information feel earned.

text: Give a deceptive character a brief, honest moment that a player can notice and act on.
Let NPCs notice details according to their role and interests, so a guard who misses a disturbed tile tells the player something about the guard.
when: designing NPC awareness of the environment
why: what an NPC misses reveals their priorities

text: Puzzles that require connecting an earlier overheard line to a later character reward player attention more than brute-force search.
when: When designing clue chains based on conversation.
why: Connecting remembered details feels like insight, while searching exhaustively feels like grinding.

text: Show a clue and then remove it, leaving a gap the player can revisit and try to fill.
Paid NPC informants can answer with short lines that reveal more when probed, and their dialogue can change when the player shows knowledge.
Harmful acts are often reached by first moving a target to the edge of what is permitted, then applying a small final push that carries them over.
An NPC's replies can change as the player presents contradicting evidence, so a confession becomes available only once denial is hopeless.
when: designing NPC confrontation dialogue

text: A scene can stay locked to the player until a higher-ranked NPC signs off on the investigation or leaves the area.
Accepting a mechanism because it is ingenious rather than checking it against the evidence is a common error.
Explanations for why a building took its shape are inferences and should be labeled as such, not stated as established fact.
A key clue placed in a scene the audience never revisits, or never clearly shown, makes the final explanation feel unfair.
when: Planting clues for a later reveal.
why: The audience cannot connect a clue it has not properly registered.

text: 1) Present each trace to the suspect one at a time. 2) Ask what it means and let the suspect commit to an explanation. 3) Only then reveal the next item. 4) Compare each trace to its known source.
when: Physical evidence and witness accounts are available to test a suspect's statements
why: Committing to an explanation before revealing more exposes contradictions

text: 1) Hold a concrete piece of evidence. 2) Confront the suspect directly with it. 3) Treat the reaction, whether confession or refusal, as data.
when: when the suspect is not yet cooperating
why: A suspect's reaction to evidence is informative even when it does not answer the question.

text: 1) Block access to a restricted source in the scene. 2) Log the refusal. 3) Let the log point the player toward alternate sources for the same information.
when: when an NPC must refuse a question about a restricted source
why: the player keeps a path forward without the blocked answer

text: Confrontation dialogue should require presenting a specific evidence item, offer options stating known facts, and vary NPC tells and bargaining with revealed evidence.
when: designing accusation or confrontation scenes
why: Evidence-dependent responses turn confrontation into a reasoning task and reward careful investigation.

text: Store the exact wording of disputed statements and written messages in the quest log so players can detect contradictions and check paraphrases against the original text.
when: two parties give conflicting versions, or written statements are part of the story
why: Exact lines allow reuse and contradiction detection, and let players compare paraphrases with what was actually written.

text: Give a dying NPC brief lucid moments as a timed dialogue window that the player must use before it closes.
when: designing dialogue with a dying character

text: Let puzzle objects such as coins or phrases in letters carry clues that players read only after gathering a related lore entry.
when: when designing lore-linked puzzles
why: Gated clues reward exploration and link objects to the story.

text: Design puzzles where the player infers the thief's choice from what is absent, narrowed by the victim's known habits.
when: Designing a deduction puzzle
why: Known habits give a baseline that makes absence informative

text: Let an NPC scholar verify a lore claim, and keep verified facts visibly separate from unverified ones in the player's notes.
when: When designing lore-driven investigation in a game.
why: Players need to know which facts are established and which remain open.

text: Give NPCs evasive replies that open new leads, and let players press them with a timer or pressure meter.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that resists direct questions.
why: Evasion that yields new leads keeps the player pursuing the case.

text: Let players wear a disguise or take a false role to enter a restricted area, and have NPCs react differently to the persona.
when: Designing restricted areas guarded by staff or NPCs
why: Persona-based access rewards players for role-play choices

text: Let a former guard or officer who recognises a suspect give that fact more weight than a common villager's claim.
when: Designing NPCs who identify a suspect.
why: Authority and past experience make recognition more credible.

text: Use a recognition cue, such as a whistle or silhouette, so an NPC can identify the player without alerting guards.
when: Designing stealth encounters with allied NPCs.
why: A cue that only the ally understands lets contact occur without raising the alarm.

text: Let players deliberately decline to investigate a clue, keeping it available as an unresolved thread for later.
Let a reveal unlock a true answer only after the player observes evidence in a fixed order with witnesses present; do not harm a companion through delay without the player seeing why.
when: Designing a staged reveal with companion characters.
why: A fair order makes the answer earned and avoids unexplained harm to allies.

text: Key evidence gated behind conditions, such as needing a witness present, delays and shapes how the audience learns the truth, at the cost of making the reveal depend on player circumstances.
when: A key document should count only under specific conditions, or the expert community is divided.
why: Conditions and disputes control when and how the truth is learned.

text: Ordinary finders who read an item belonging to someone else become interpreters of its meaning, and each may read it differently.
when: an item passes from one finder to another
why: printed names and handwriting invite judgment about importance

text: Ask witnesses about trivial details, including names and places, since any detail can prove relevant and may surface facts the witness did not volunteer.
When a character finds an item missing, treat the absence as a question to answer, and fix the time and position with instruments to build a timeline.
when: a disruption leaves a character checking belongings and surroundings
why: fixed times and places make it possible to reconstruct what happened

text: Start an investigation from a detail that seems trivial, such as shoe wear or a mark on the skin, since small traces can reveal recent history.
A trivial incident early in the story can prove central later, so plant it in plain view.
