An assurance of secrecy may not hold, and other people may still face consequences after a confession.
when: Offering protection to a suspect in exchange for a confession

text: 1) Tell each person only what their role requires. 2) Withhold the cause when it would harm them or the case. 3) Give each listener a clear, limited role. 4) Ask them for discretion about what they learn.
when: An investigator must inform or enlist people during a sensitive case.
why: Narrow disclosure protects the case and gives each person a defined part to play.

text: Information given in confidence limits how it can be used and blocks the checks needed to test it, so verify a damaging claim before relying on it; a relative may be shielding someone.
when: An informant or relative gives information in confidence, or asks that a damaging claim be kept secret
why: Confidentiality blocks the very check the investigator needs to test the claim.

text: Ask a person for discretion rather than silence: name what they may keep to and what they should avoid saying.
when: Enlisting a bystander who must not spread sensitive information.
why: A specific request is easier to follow than a general demand for secrecy.

text: Block a question about a protected source or an unhelpful opinion only after checking whether the answer would change the outcome, not merely because it is uncomfortable.
when: when a question touches a sensitive source or is uncomfortable to answer
why: uncomfortable questions can still bear on the outcome

text: Confining a suspect does not limit an accusation that claims unnatural powers, since such powers are assumed to exceed ordinary restraints.
when: A jailed suspect is blamed for harm elsewhere
why: Belief in unnatural agency is assumed to defeat physical containment.

text: Confinement suspense holds a character in a murky, airless place, building tension through worsening physical danger, unseen threats, and false hopes of rescue.
A secret confided to only a few people stays contained and limits who can reveal the truth.
Use confinement to slow the pace and build dread before a reveal, and sustain engagement with a sequence of rising hopes and failures.
when: Before a reveal that needs build-up.

text: Confining suspects can breed resentment that colors their testimony.
1) Let the barrier begin to yield, showing light through a crack. 2) Let the threat escape through another opening, so the rescue turns into a new danger.
when: Building the climax of a confinement sequence.

text: Open a confinement scene with an unexpected closure, such as a door that locks itself with no visible means of opening it.
when: Starting a scene where a character becomes trapped.

text: Hold action until one decisive confirming fact is found when evidence points one way but lacks confirmation, since acting early risks exposing the plan or failing.
when: a case rests on circumstantial points and a conclusive fact may still emerge, or a suspicion exists but acting early would warn an opponent
why: A decisive fact resolves uncertainty that the tally cannot.

text: Confirm a surprising observation by looking again under the same conditions before relying on it as evidence.
Before drawing conclusions from two similar sets of tracks, confirm the direction of each set.
when: Track sets look alike
why: Similar marks can belong to different movements.

text: A message arriving mid-scene that confirms a player's hunch rewards inference, because the player reached the conclusion first and the message only verifies it.
when: when a scene is designed to reward deduction
why: confirmation feels earned when the player has already guessed

text: A witness may confirm a fact just to end an interview, so the answer may reflect a reaction to pressure rather than a real recollection.
when: a witness is pressed or wants to leave
why: agreement is a quick way out of an uncomfortable exchange

text: Confirm a heard or recalled remark before relying on it by asking the speaker to verify the exact wording, since remarks are often misremembered.
when: a key word was heard in a stressful or chaotic moment, or a remark is recalled

text: Confirm a fact only with two or more independent observers or sources, especially one deciding whether an item was consumed; revise the working theory only after such confirmation.
when: a new fact rests on a single secondhand claim
why: A single memory is fragile and easy to distort.

text: Treat stated plans and claimed errands as claims to be confirmed, not as established movements.
why: A stated plan shows intent, not what was actually done.

text: Confirm a physical match before confronting a suspect, because a confirmed match turns a theory into a checked fact.
Agree a signal in advance, such as a lit match, so that a watcher can confirm the target has acted.
when: Covert observers must report a hidden party's action without contact.
why: A prearranged signal conveys a specific result without requiring communication.

text: Confirm a reading of habit-based traces with witnesses who know the routines, since interpretation depends on that knowledge.
Do not assume a path without evidence; confirm the traces before they settle the question of where the crime occurred.
when: A route seems plausible but is unverified
why: Plausible routes can be wrong when the traces are not checked

text: Confirm the final solution with a witnessed document and a private confrontation, not a public accusation.
why: A witnessed statement is hard to dispute, and a private setting lets the culprit admit the truth

text: Acting now on partial evidence risks a wrong move; waiting risks losing the window in which evidence stays available.
when: Deciding whether to act on partial evidence or gather more
why: Some evidence decays over time while some errors can be corrected later

text: Make an NPC's flat denial a branch that a later sighting or discovery contradicts, so the player must choose between exposing a lie and embarrassment.
Witnesses may give opposite accounts, and confident claims may rest on partial knowledge, so compare conflicting versions, each from a different source, rather than accept the most confident one.
when: When two witnesses describe one event differently.

text: Give witnesses timing claims that conflict with each other or with another clue, so the player must work out which account is reliable and build a coherent timeline.
when: Designing testimony or investigative narrative with multiple witnesses.
why: Conflicting testimony makes the player weigh evidence instead of accepting a single source.

text: Conflicting accounts do not prove a lie: memory failure and differing vantage points, roles or attention can cause them, so weigh each source on its own record.
when: When several people describe one incident or accounts of one event disagree.
why: Disagreement can come from different vantage points, not deceit; vantage point, role and attention differ across observers.

text: Drop an explanation that physical evidence contradicts, rather than adjusting evidence or excusing contradictions by an outside cause, which hides flaws in testimony.
when: When accusers and confessors disagree or physical evidence contradicts a theory.
why: Reshaping evidence to save a theory corrupts the reasoning.

text: Weigh conflicting witnesses by observing conditions such as position and noise, giving more weight to the account made under better conditions rather than a trust ranking.
when: When two witnesses' accounts conflict.
why: Conditions explain disagreement better than a trust ranking; better conditions give more reliable perception.

text: When two statements, such as two NPCs' accounts, cannot both be true, their contradiction is itself a clue marking where the facts must be tested.
when: When two witnesses describe the same event differently.
why: The conflict marks where the facts must be tested.

text: When witnesses disagree about an agreement's terms, lay each account beside the dates of the offers and votes it describes.
why: Matching accounts to dates shows which version fits the record.

text: Let witness details conflict in small ways so the player resolves each conflict using other evidence.
why: conflicts teach the player to test sources rather than trust them whole

text: Read contradictory replies with care, since distress affects speech as much as it affects the facts being reported.
when: A witness gives inconsistent answers while in distress.
why: Confusion can produce contradictions without any change in the underlying facts.

text: When an object's location contradicts an owner's account, treat the contradiction as a lead to press, not as proof of guilt.
when: When a found object places its owner somewhere they denied being.

text: Compare reactions across people: both surprise and its absence are signals, so note who shows none when others do.
Withhold news from a suspect, then compare how each person responds; differences in concern are harder to fake than direct answers.
when: the suspect does not already know the event
why: reactions to identical news are harder to fabricate than direct answers

text: Contradictions inside one witness account, such as denying a problem while describing it as severe, mark exactly the claims that need checking.
why: inconsistent statements show where the account is unreliable

text: Reports that contradict the expected route may point to a second person or a false trail and should be recorded, not discarded.
when: When sightings do not fit the route being tested.
why: Contradictions can reveal an accomplice or a misdirection.

text: A detail that conflicts with what people have said about themselves or each other is worth recording as a clue.
when: when a remark does not fit the expected pattern
why: Mismatches between statements can point toward concealment or error.

text: Any statement made under any circumstances can be contested, so the goal is to judge which way the probabilities lean rather than to reach certainty.
Compare accounts of the same event point by point, looking for differences in emphasis or detail.
when: Accounts of one event conflict.

text: A muted reaction to a fact can give way to strong shock when the real news arrives; compare the two responses to judge what was expected.
Compare testimonies from multiple witnesses; a contradiction between two accounts can force a fuller account from the one who lied.
when: Two witnesses give accounts that cannot both be true
why: Confronting one account with another exposes the weaker claim

text: When two testimonies conflict, offering a plausible innocent alternative keeps the choice genuinely open for the player.
when: when two accounts contradict each other
why: a credible alternative prevents the obvious answer from being automatic

text: Give companions conflicting reasons to blame each other, so the player must weigh each accusation against the timing data.
when: Designing suspect dialogue in a mystery
why: Conflicting accusations make the player check evidence instead of accepting claims

text: A witness detail that seems to weaken a theory may strengthen it; ask what the theory predicts before dismissing the detail.
when: the theory predicts unusual behaviour the detail could show
why: Predicted unusual behaviour can look like a contradiction.

text: Agreement among several witnesses on raw observed facts carries weight even when their interpretations differ.
when: Judging whether multiple testimonies establish a fact.
why: Independent agreement on what was seen is harder to produce by chance than shared interpretation.

text: Discount witness descriptions of a person's mood or sanity when those descriptions are themselves disputed, since they cannot settle a timeline.
when: witnesses disagree about a suspect's mental state
why: subjective impressions are weak evidence for factual timing

text: Judge testimony by consistency and tone; plain, steady accounts that do not reveal partisanship deserve more weight.
Compare a reported remark with the speaker's own account, since the reporter's bias may shape how it was passed on.
when: When evaluating a secondhand quotation.
why: Relaying introduces the reporter's slant.

text: Let NPC reports conflict with what the player observed, and let the player choose which witness to trust.
when: when designing testimony in a mystery
why: Choosing a source makes the player responsible for the conclusion

text: Let at least one identity proof conflict with the true answer, so the leading theory is tested rather than simply confirmed.
why: A clue that resists the answer keeps the player's belief in the solution under genuine test.

text: Tracking what each witness saw and assumed lets inconsistent accounts generate new questions the player must resolve.
Witnesses who disagree on a person's description or a key object weaken any identification built on it, since inconsistent details cannot merge into one reliable image.
when: When several witnesses describe the same person or object differently.
why: Inconsistent details do not combine into a single trustworthy likeness; disagreement undermines the shared basis for identification.

text: A mismatch between traces, such as a lens fitted to an older person than the body, is a reason to look closer, not a conclusion.
A precise threshold invites narrow, contested testimony, so every witness account may be treated as suspect when stakes are clear.
when: Witnesses must fix an exact time that decides an outcome
why: Interested parties have reason to shade precise timing claims

text: Speaking freely in a contested forum can hand the opposing side a formal charge, so statements should use exact, defensible wording.
when: a statement is made where it can be formally tested
why: loose words can become legal grounds against the speaker

text: Recording a claim beside facts that contradict it, with neither tested, gives the claim standing it has not earned.
When a tenant and an owner both claim the land, the question of who may speak for it is itself contested.
when: Tenant and owner both assert a claim to the same property
why: Competing claims make authority over the land part of the dispute

text: 1) Record each claim from every statement separately. 2) Line up spoken and written versions claim by claim. 3) Note which details change and who gains from each version.
when: A witness gives a spoken account and a written one, or two accounts at different times.
why: Discrepancies between accounts are the first lead in identifying inconsistencies.

text: 1) Record each statement in the order it was given. 2) Mark firsthand details separately from told or read details. 3) Compare prepared answers with recalled answers. 4) Flag any version that changed after a prompt or document.
1) Record each version and who received it. 2) Ask what each witness could physically perceive. 3) Test whether each version fits the timeline and public records.
when: when two parties describe one event differently
why: the discrepancy is evaluated against each witness's access

text: 1) Present disagreeing accounts side by side. 2) Let the player see which claims conflict. 3) Ensure at least one verifiable detail can settle each conflict.
when: designing a mystery where witnesses disagree
why: The player must decide which facts can be verified, so each contradiction needs a checkable resolution.

text: 1) List every statement with its date and speaker. 2) Mark who first introduced the claim. 3) Weigh earlier recorded accounts above later revised ones.
when: When a witness's story has changed or a claim may have been suggested.
why: Earlier accounts are less shaped by later pressure or retraction.

text: 1) Find the original file behind a published account. 2) Check each cited document's date and whether it was presented at the proceeding. 3) Note exculpatory material the account omits. 4) Judge whether the writer knew of it.
when: A published account and an original file both exist.
why: Exclusions and misdated evidence are visible only in the original.

text: 1) Date each statement by one source. 2) Note its intended audience. 3) Note its purpose. 4) Decide which version to trust using those three facts.
when: two statements by one source disagree
why: date, audience and purpose reveal the pressures that shaped each version

text: 1) Let the player interview several NPCs who claim to have been present. 2) Collect their versions, which may contradict each other. 3) Treat the chain of who told whom as the puzzle to solve.
when: when designing an event witnessed in fragments by several NPCs
why: Contradictions require the player to reconstruct the sequence

text: 1) Compare reports from two observers standing at the same spot. 2) Check light, angle and position at that moment. 3) Accept the alarming report only if the physical conditions support it.
when: when two observers of the same spot report different things
why: A second viewpoint can expose an ordinary cause

text: 1) Compare competing accounts of the same events. 2) Weigh each by detail, caution and inclusion of key documents. 3) Note what is missing. 4) Trace the status of any lost source through correspondence about it.
when: Testimony about one case exists in more than one version, or a source is lost.
why: Comparing accounts and tracing provenance reveals which record is most reliable even when the best source is gone.

text: 1) Place each witness's interpretation beside rival interpretations. 2) Identify what each witness gains from a particular reading. 3) Weigh the accounts against independent evidence before settling on one.
when: Two or more witnesses offer conflicting explanations of the same event
why: Motive and partial knowledge can bias each account, so none should be accepted alone.

text: Conflicting descriptions may mean a disguise, a different person, or an innocent cause, so treat the mismatch as a possibility to test, not proof of identity.
when: Several witnesses describe the same person differently.
why: Descriptions can be wrong, and mismatches have innocent causes.

text: Let an NPC's stated plan or claimed departure be contradicted by a later clue, such as their movements or an item they would not have left behind.
when: When designing NPC dialogue or a missing-character quest.
why: A checkable contradiction rewards attention to behavior.

text: Let NPC factions or sources pass rumours of differing accuracy, so the player weighs each against the scene and what they know and reconciles conflicting figures.
when: When designing gossip or rumours about a shared event in a game world.
why: Reconciling competing sources turns hearsay into a reasoning task.

text: Record conflicting witness answers or perception logs on the same point and leave the disagreement open for the player to weigh, rather than resolving it automatically.

Let several NPCs who share knowledge of an event give partial, conflicting accounts, reconcilable through physical evidence such as footprints, broken locks, wounds, dropped items, ammunition or keys.
when: When designing contradictory testimony or branching investigation dialogue.
why: Resolving conflicts through evidence makes the player's deduction the source of truth.

text: Have NPCs describe the same sighting or exchange differently, including those kept in the dark, so the player must reconcile the accounts rather than trust one.
when: When designing witness testimony in a mystery.
why: Conflicting accounts require the player to weigh evidence.

text: Make NPC tells and claims conflict with each other or with scene evidence, so the player must weigh them rather than accept one clear signal or speaker.
when: When designing clue sets or an NPC's account of events.
why: Forces players to judge reliability rather than trust the speaker.

text: Mark the time each witness gives for the same event side by side; conflicting times and routes show which accounts need checking.
Build a contradiction into two NPC accounts so the player must find a third source to decide which account is accurate.
when: when designing witness dialogue

text: Let a puzzle NPC mix truth and falsehood in directions, and track contradictions across conversations so the player can detect them.
when: Designing a helpful but unreliable NPC
why: Tracking contradictions rewards careful listening

text: Compare a witness's retellings for constant facts and for changes in details, not for changes in manner.
when: a witness has told the story more than once
why: Tone changes easily, while factual inconsistencies reveal problems.

text: Break a claimed alibi with one reliable sighting that contradicts it; that single contradiction can overturn the claimed location.
When a story is split among several narrators, compare their overlapping events to check each account against the others.
Have several NPCs agree on a character's key features but vary on minor ones, so players can assemble a composite description.
Do not treat one observer's reading as the truth. Compare it with another observer's account, since interpretation bias can change what is reported.
Give NPCs statements that can contradict one another, so the player must compare sources and find the account that was prompted by someone else.
when: in designed witness or dialogue scenes
why: Contradictions give the player a reason to cross-check.

text: Give a claim one confirming witness and one contradicting witness, so the player must decide which witness to question first.
when: when designing npc dialogue around a disputed claim

text: Build a landmark whose layout contradicts an NPC's story about it, so the player can test the tale against what they see.
when: Designing NPC stories about landmarks.

text: Have two NPC authors publish conflicting views, so the player must reconcile them.
Testimony rejected as unreliable in one kind of case, such as from a distracted or possessed person, must be rejected in every similar case.
when: when judging witnesses across different charges
why: Applying different reliability rules to the same kind of witness is inconsistent.

text: Place conflicting NPC testimony in different rooms so players must decide which witness to trust.
when: When designing witness NPCs whose accounts conflict.
why: Spatial separation makes players weigh sources instead of receiving a single answer.

text: Present conflicting in-world sources, like a witness annotation correcting an earlier one or two side-by-side documents, so players judge which account to believe and why, weighing author motives.
When an owner's belongings point to a different origin than their stated identity, keep both readings open rather than trusting either.
why: Objects and people can point in different directions, so one clue alone does not settle origin.

text: Conflicting facts are a starting point for ordering a case, not a sign that the investigation has failed.
In-world maps that describe the same landmark differently across versions force the player to compare sources and decide which is right.
when: when designing map artefacts for a mystery or exploration puzzle
why: Differing descriptions create a comparison task that rewards careful reading

text: Two conflicting times often describe two separate events rather than a contradiction, so check what each time measures before ruling one account false.
when: a clock time and an event time disagree
why: different clocks and different events are easily confused

text: Ignoring conflicting dates across a source chain hides errors; the reader must decide which source to trust and note why.
when: Sources give different dates for one event

text: When two dated instructions conflict, the later one, especially if marked urgent, supersedes the earlier; the date sequence decides which instruction stands.
Include in-world documents that conflict with a later NPC's legend, and let players verify the claim by visiting the site.
Two characters in the same household can give opposite readings of one person's behavior, and each reading reflects the observer's assumptions.
when: Characters with different relationships to the same person describe that person's mood or conduct.
why: Observers interpret behavior through their own expectations, such as gratitude or dullness, so their readings diverge.

text: Pressuring or bluffing a suspect can provoke a drawn weapon, so plan bystander safety and account for violent reactions before confronting.
when: An interrogation is scripted in a crowded or armed setting, or the suspect may carry a weapon.
why: Pressure can provoke a weapon the investigator has not accounted for.

text: A confrontation option may need to close off the escape route an NPC would otherwise use.
when: Designing a confrontation the NPC could dodge.
why: Without closing the exit, an NPC can answer with a technically correct refusal and end the scene.

text: Confront a suspect with a direct question about a hidden fact only the culprit would know; this breaks a prepared story.
when: The suspect has a rehearsed account
why: Unexpected knowledge disrupts composure

text: Answer a weak explanation with a specific contradicting observation rather than a vague doubt, because concrete sightings are harder for the speaker to explain away.
Base each challenge on evidence the suspect cannot be sure the investigator holds, so denials carry risk.
when: when confronting a suspect
why: uncertainty about what the investigator knows makes the suspect hesitate

text: A confrontation scene can draw attention to one character while the real clue remains elsewhere.
when: staging a dramatic encounter in a mystery
why: the emotional focus pulls the player away from the key evidence

text: You can accept an opponent's premises and still mount a sound challenge by showing that their conclusions do not follow from those premises.
A dialogue system can unlock a confrontation option only after the player presents the matching piece of evidence.
when: In dialogue systems tied to an evidence inventory.
why: Gating confrontation on evidence rewards the player for gathering it first.

text: A challenge-and-countersign or knock signal sorts arrivals by demanded replies: a wrong reply marks an outsider, and watching exchanges reveals each member's type.
when: A gate or group admits people through a ritual exchange without knowing each visitor personally.
why: Members can perform the ritual correctly, so the exchange tests password knowledge rather than identity.

text: In a dialogue system, an NPC statement can be challenged with evidence the player has gathered, and each contradiction unlocks a follow-up question.
when: NPC statements conflict with evidence the player has found

text: A half-serious challenge, once accepted, becomes a binding commitment that sets the next investigation steps and the challenger's obligations.
when: When a character's pride or dare opens a new investigation path.
why: Acceptance turns a casual claim into an agreement with terms.

text: When a conviction transfers property or fees to officials and tradespeople, each conviction gives them a reason to pursue further accusations, so accusing can spread through a system.
when: Where confiscation and fees follow a conviction.
why: Each conviction pays the people who profit from the next one.

text: A timed confrontation forces the final admission without a conventional proof puzzle, because the guilty party reacts to pressure before evidence is complete.
when: Evidence is short but the culprit is known to the player
why: Pressure at a fixed moment can make the culprit reveal themselves.

text: Confronting a character with a claim that has a plausible innocent explanation makes them close up and withdraw.
Attacking a procedure while leaving its premise intact can let an unverifiable source stay in use for long periods.
when: when critics challenge a court's methods
why: the premise keeps the source credible

text: 1) Claim more knowledge than you hold. 2) Offer terms such as immunity. 3) Set a deadline. 4) Withhold source names. 5) Watch the suspect's reactions.
when: A guilty party must be pressed into revealing a position
why: Pressure and uncertainty make denial harder to sustain

text: 1) Establish the suspect's past and who could identify them. 2) Lay out evidence one item at a time, naming each before adding the next. 3) Remind the suspect of any earlier warning. 4) Read their reaction after each item. 5) Press on while stakes rise.
when: Confronting a suspect with strong evidence
why: Sequencing lets each item land and exposes the suspect's responses

text: 1) Assess the witness's fitness beforehand. 2) Plan the confrontation with the risk of a breakdown in mind. 3) Bring a companion to take notes so statements can later be verified.
when: Preparing to question a witness who may be fragile or under stress
why: A breakdown can come without warning, and unrecorded statements are hard to prove

text: 1) Approach from behind and force a bolted door together. 2) Cover the suspect with a weapon and order them still. 3) Have helpers restrain the arms and move the suspect away from the equipment. 4) Explain the mechanism aloud. 5) Confront the suspect with the physical evidence. 6) Keep the captive away from the apparatus while securing evidence.
when: A suspect is caught in the act and may resist, escape or destroy evidence

text: Make the premise of a case, not only its individual links, something the player can challenge.
Include stated assumptions in npc relative dialogue that the player can challenge with other evidence.
when: designing witness dialogue
why: Players engage when a witness's claim can be tested

text: Press with a pointed question only when independent facts are available to check the answer; without them it signals suspicion but proves nothing.
Declare any personal link to a suspect, victim or witness openly, then decide whether to recuse or hand the case to someone else.
when: a personal connection to someone in the case exists
why: disclosure lets others check the investigator's fairness

text: Confront a witness only with a claim the investigator can show to be false, and have documents ready to prove it.
when: the witness is committed to a checkable falsehood
why: Without documents the witness can simply deny the claim.

text: Design a confrontation where an NPC's flinch or hidden item, prompted by a culprit-only question, produces the next clue.
when: Designing a suspect confrontation scene

text: Stage a reveal in dialogue where an NPC must confirm a physical discovery the player made, turning the solution into a confrontation.
When two testimonies directly conflict, hold the conflict open and check other facts before choosing which account to accept.
Reward players for reconciling conflicting accounts, and make an unexplained gap the trigger for the next lead.
when: Designing progression in a testimony-based investigation
why: Reconciliation is a skill-based reward and gaps drive exploration

text: When a complete-looking case feels wrong, name the specific flaw; a gut conviction alone does not settle the question.
when: A detective doubts a theory that seems logically complete.
why: A tidy theory can still be wrong, as juries also resist neat cases.

text: Let players choose which accuser to bring forward and which question to ask, with each response revealing a different clue.
when: when designing a confrontation scene

text: Use a trap that tests a suspect's reaction so the culprit exposes themselves through a choice rather than a confession.
when: Climax of a mystery where a confession is unlikely or impossible
why: A reaction under pressure gives proof without requiring the culprit to speak.

text: Confronting a suspect now can close off further information, while waiting keeps information open but lets delay cost something important.
when: when a witness is cooperating and the matter is not urgent
why: a direct challenge may end the cooperation

text: When incidents seem unrelated, check which location, person or record recurs across them.
when: Reviewing a set of seemingly separate incidents
why: Recurring elements are the associations that connect events

text: A secretive person usually confides in someone close, so a close associate of the subject is the most likely source of hidden facts.
when: someone holds key facts but keeps them guarded
why: people tend to share concealed matters with a trusted intimate

text: An object found at a scene is weaker evidence when its finder had other chances to move or plant it.
when: The finder had access to the scene before the discovery
why: Access gives the finder a plausible route to placing the item.

text: A sudden rush of connections feels like proof but must be checked link by link, since it can still be wrong.
1) Identify the next link, such as an agent or trade house. 2) Contact that link in the next location. 3) Give instructions and repeat until the suspect is reached.
when: a suspect has moved across several locations and must be followed through contacts
why: each intermediary holds the lead to the next

text: Follow at a distance and on the same side of the street, planning position so the target does not easily recognise the follower.
when: tailing on foot
why: a suspect may still recognise a follower

text: The amount each person consumed from a shared object reveals who handled it and in what order, which can point back to the intended target.
when: Several people shared a poisoned or trapped object.
why: Consumption differences trace the object's path and show who was meant to be harmed.

text: Show the consequence of a disclosure in the next scene rather than in the reveal itself.
A holder's account of keeping an object continuously in sight shrinks the window of possible access to the time it was out of their sight.
A bait the player sets, such as an advertisement, can cause a later death, and the resulting guilt steers the player's next choices.
A partly consumed object, such as a half-full glass or burned-down candle, can be read as a clock to estimate when an event occurred.
when: An object burns, melts or accumulates at a known rate
why: Its state works as a clock only while nobody has handled it

text: A small early action with a dangerous side effect, such as a dropped light source, can set up a later disaster that it explains.
when: Planting a cause that pays off later in the plot
why: A seeded consequence makes the later event feel earned rather than arbitrary

text: Stating the legal or personal consequences of an act, and showing how much is already known, adds pressure on a suspect.
Contingency plans for a crime can include four parts: an escape route, a cover story, a reserve of money, and a disguise.
Give ultimatum choices explicit consequences, so that a confession branch has a visible and meaningful effect on the outcome.
when: when designing a confession or refusal option
why: Vague consequences make the choice feel empty and weaken the branch.

text: A continuous timeline keeps simultaneous threads and builds tension but may feel long; discrete sections isolate units but repeat shared background and fragment the thread.
when: Several threads run at once
why: Structure choice trades felt simultaneity against standalone readability

text: A tragic outcome deepens the aftermath but removes any trial, while an arrest allows a trial but gives a plainer close.
when: when choosing how the culprit's fate closes the case

text: An investigator who notices a tell and moves on without pursuing it lets the subject recover, which keeps them talking.
when: when questioning a reluctant suspect
why: Pressing an embarrassing reaction tends to end the conversation, while sparing it keeps information flowing.

text: The evidence required for a conclusion should rise with its seriousness: a grave conclusion needs stronger proof than a provisional one, and an early accusation must not be treated as settled.
when: Deciding whether evidence supports an accusation or a formal finding.
why: Serious consequences require stronger certainty, while preliminary steps need less.

text: Keep evidence intact and warn suspects against destroying it, since suspects may try to destroy proof.
when: Confronting a suspect with evidence

text: One illicit act often forces the next, as each step taken to conceal or cover an earlier wrong creates a new one.
when: when a character commits an initial wrong under pressure
why: Covering an initial act requires more acts, each harder to undo.

text: A case built on one kind of evidence collapses once it reaches a respected person, since the accusers' credibility is then exposed.
when: An accusation based on a single evidence type extends to a figure the community trusts.
why: Accusing a respected person makes the weakness of the evidence visible.

text: Returning evidence to a suspect can alert them, so the timing of returning or showing an object matters.
when: Deciding when to show an item to a suspect.
why: Showing evidence gives the suspect information to react to and adapt.

text: A lead that fits one clue but fails a later test leaves the investigation stuck; the false account is exposed once the search turns up nothing.
when: when the suspected cause is searched for and never found
why: The explanation covers the original evidence but not the absence of the predicted result.

text: Accepting visible damage at face value is a common error, because crash damage can conceal the real cause.
End the falsely accused thread with a visible cost or profit to the accused, so the consequences of the frame are shown.
Close an investigation by making the evidence inaccessible, so that the player's final knowledge is what they carry rather than what they can check.
when: When ending a mystery on an unresolved, uncertain note.
why: Removing the ability to verify leaves the player with belief instead of proof, sustaining the sense of unease.

text: A witness who cannot speak freely gives an account shaped by fear or emotion, so the statement needs checking before it is trusted.
when: a witness is afraid or cannot speak openly
why: fear or emotion shapes what is said

text: A costly or distance-constrained action taken before a claimed time is strong evidence that the actor knew something earlier than they admitted.
when: an independent action conflicts with a stated knowledge time
why: the action required prior knowledge to be taken

text: 1) Clear bystanders from the room, or restrict who may speak, before a sensitive exchange so a fragile witness is not confused or steered. 2) Restate the demand plainly. 3) Repeat it without following tangents, mockery or changes of subject until answered.
when: Interviewing a witness who may speak more freely alone, a fragile witness with several people present, or a suspect dodging a plain question.
why: Removing bystanders and limiting speech reduces evasion and steering, and repetition blocks topic changes that would otherwise deflect the question.

text: 1) Set the money visible on the table. 2) Seat the witness facing the light. 3) Sit the interviewer apart. 4) Keep the manner gentle, so the witness stays at ease while the interviewer keeps control.
when: Interviewing a nervous witness who must be kept calm.
why: A comfortable witness speaks more freely, and the interviewer's position keeps the exchange under control.

text: 1) Open with a low-stakes question to build rapport. 2) Ask about the relationship with the subject. 3) Ask about their habits and character. 4) Ask direct questions on dependence and grievance. 5) Check their account against other sources.
when: The subject is the only source for a relationship and cannot be questioned freely
why: Answers can supply or rule out motive and need corroboration

text: 1) Wait for a natural opening in the conversation. 2) Ask the sensitive question as it arises rather than opening with it. 3) Add an explicit exit so refusal is easy. 4) Let the subject narrate.
when: A direct question would make the subject defensive or end the conversation.
why: Easy refusal and a narrated answer lower defensiveness and invite fuller disclosure.

text: Limiting replies keeps questions pointed, but long written exchanges slow the pace and become tiresome, so keep the constrained exchange short.
when: choosing how long the captive's replies should run

text: The same evidence can support opposing verdicts, so an examination can be adjourned for closer testing before a finding is fixed.
when: a physical finding is disputed
why: Incomplete or contested evidence can be read both ways.

text: Log each stray remark or NPC line with its trigger, listener and whether the speaker confirmed it, then link it to later facts it may explain.
when: Recording stray remarks or NPC dialogue that may serve as evidence.
why: A remark's meaning depends on the situation or question it answers.

text: Judge a found object by the conditions under which it likely reached its position, not only by what the object is.
when: Evaluating an object as evidence

text: Supplying missing background can change the meaning of earlier clues, so the audience must reassess events it already witnessed.
when: a reveal supplies context not previously available
why: meaning depends on context the audience lacked

text: Context explains why people believed or acted but does not prove a factual claim or what a specific person did; using it to excuse unsupported conduct replaces evidence.
when: Context is used to soften judgment of a person's actions or to support a factual claim.
why: Broad conditions do not establish what a particular person did or knew.

text: A single overheard exchange taken without context can suggest a motive that is not really there, since ambiguous phrases mislead.
Set out the conditions a community lived under before judging its conduct, so the reader can weigh its actions against the pressures it faced.
when: Evaluating a community's cruelty, suspicion or decisions.
why: Pressures such as hardship, fear and loss explain conduct that looks inexplicable in isolation.

text: Weight NPC recognition by context match, so a face seen at a matching location is more reliable than one seen elsewhere.
when: Designing NPC recognition rules in a game
why: Recognition should depend on the viewing conditions, as in real witnessing.

text: Flag a claim that a person's situation contradicts, such as claiming independence while others clearly control them.
Give NPC testimonies overlapping details that contradict one another, so the player must find physical evidence to decide which account is true.
when: Designing a mystery where player judgment depends on evidence.
why: Contradictions that only physical evidence can resolve reward investigation over trust in dialogue.

text: A dialogue option to withhold news can set a flag that later changes an NPC's trust or what that NPC will reveal.
When witness accounts cannot fit one sequence, store each version and flag the mismatch for questioning, not silent resolution; the player exposes it by presenting conflicting statements.
why: Lets the player discover contradictions through play.

text: A quest system could flag when a convenient event lines up with the player's stated goal, prompting a check before action.
Flag unverifiable events as unverifiable rather than folding them into the record as fact.
Design NPC lies to contradict known routine or world-state traces, so attentive players can detect them and advance the case.
when: When designing NPC lines that may be false and can be checked against the environment.
why: Exposing a lie rewards the player and moves the case forward, and a lie that conflicts with known habit gives attentive players a fair way to detect it.

text: Keep a supernatural agent's behavior consistent, such as blocking prayer, speaking and urging harm, so the reader can track its escalation.
When a statement from an impaired state also appears in the character's lucid speech, treat it as a stronger indication of the character's true motive, though not of fact.
when: Judging a character's motive from statements made in different mental states.
why: Agreement across states shows a stable belief, but the belief can still be wrong about what happened.

text: Stage a conversation the player overhears to control what the player believes while hiding the true facts.
when: A scripted scene must mislead the player on purpose.
why: Overheard talk is trusted as context and shapes belief.

text: A character who provokes conflict while appearing calm and detached draws less suspicion than the people who react to them.
when: when designing a manipulator who must stay hidden
why: Visible emotion draws scrutiny, so the calm instigator is overlooked.

text: Track a match in the player's journal as a separate state from confirmed and ruled out, so consistent but unverified matches remain visible.
when: Designing a journal or record for mystery clues.
why: A third state preserves partial progress without implying certainty.

text: One sighting that conflicts with a stated schedule can break an alibi and force the whole movement record to be reexamined.
when: A witness places a suspect somewhere the schedule says they were not.
why: Once the stated timeline is shown false, every other claim in the record becomes suspect.

text: Repeated questioning from several angles, with each answer checked against earlier ones, can expose a false account, since one noticed slip may unravel the whole story.
when: A suspect's account has already changed once and can be compared against known facts.
why: Each answer becomes a commitment that later questions can test for conflict.

text: A visibly loaded threat can be secretly harmless; revealing this afterwards keeps tension high while the outcome stays under designer control.
when: A confrontation where a weapon or danger is shown.
why: Players feel real tension, and the later revelation resolves the threat safely.

text: 1) Limit the scene to a known set of usable rooms and access points, locking the rest. 2) Research the place's history before the test. 3) Run a fixed routine of checking every room and lock. 4) Observe covertly and keep notes.
when: Testing a suspected place for an unseen factor
why: A known set of access points and a fixed routine make later changes stand out.

text: 1) Give the hidden agent a material form by a lure with known properties. 2) Ensure the lure meets its stated conditions, such as freshness and strength. 3) Observe the response so the agent becomes visible.
when: when a hidden agent cannot be observed directly
why: A controlled lure forces the agent to act within a condition the investigator set.

text: Allow a player to pin one NPC statement against an item or another NPC's testimony to expose contradictions.
when: designing investigation interfaces for testimony
why: direct comparison lets players test claims against evidence

text: Control who can hear a sensitive exchange by lowering the voice or speaking aside, so the subject misses remarks not meant for them.
when: A conversation contains information meant for only one listener.
why: Deliberate audience control lets the questioner speak freely without alerting the subject.

text: Control what each character learns. Let them hear only what serves the scene, so the player can later discover the gap between what is known and what is hidden.
when: Writing dialogue where some characters should remain uninformed.
why: Selective knowledge creates tension and a fair later twist.

text: Let a witness see something that contradicts their own belief, such as a supernatural explanation, so the belief fails fairly.
Check each account against other accounts and observed details; a single contradiction, such as a conflicting remark or denied knock, opens a line of inquiry, especially who-where-when disagreements.
when: when witness accounts disagree with each other or with observed details, or when choosing which answers to challenge
why: Conflicts point to the account that is false or incomplete, and timing and location conflicts are where accounts can be tested

text: Store contradictions between statements or facts; each unlocks follow-up questions on a single detail, including flagged evasive answers, so the player can press for resolution.
when: when designing interrogation dialogue or NPC testimony
why: Contradictions create a new goal, pushing the player to investigate further

text: Record every NPC statement and build contradictions into witness accounts that players can expose by comparing statements, rewarding those who spot them rather than excusing them.
when: when writing multiple NPC statements
why: exposed contradictions reward careful comparison

text: Design contradictions visible only when two answers or records are compared, so players must cross-check; reward those who note days and times.
when: when writing interrogation dialogue or clues that depend on cross-referencing
why: Hidden contradictions reward careful note-taking and make the solution feel earned

text: Let a cover story vary between repetitions, since inconsistent versions can reveal the truth to a careful listener who compares them.
Place objects or later clues that contradict an NPC's stated habits or public image, such as a feeding dish with no listed pet, so players must ask or compare sources.
when: when designing NPC rooms with stated habits or public images hiding a different truth
why: the mismatch prompts inference; comparing sources rewards careful players

text: Test NPC and witness claims against checkable world state, such as timestamps, positions, locked doors, logs or a second witness, treating each account as true until contradicted.
when: when designing witness statements, NPC testimony or alibis
why: Checkable contradictions give players a fair way to find inconsistencies

text: Present contradicting or ambiguous clues that a later clue, such as a map or receipt, resolves, so players reason through competing evidence instead of receiving one answer.
when: when a clue has two valid readings or investigation design needs competing evidence
why: A corroborating clue narrows the readings without removing the puzzle

text: Use several converging traits, each eliminating candidate origins, and confirm the surviving match with a later physical find; a lone mark proves little.
when: when authoring physical evidence or a clue database for a mystery
why: Only converging marks make the inference reliable; layered elimination lets players reason to an answer

text: Make ambiguous NPC phrases resolvable only by checking the room, not by dialogue alone.
A flawed line of inquiry can still lead to the truth, so keep checking other leads instead of abandoning the investigation.
When a client's stated view contradicts their request, treat the mixed signal as something to clarify before proceeding.
when: when a client both disbelieves and fears an explanation

text: When a witness's account contradicts a known fact, the contradiction shifts doubt onto whoever produced the conflicting event.
when: a claim about a detail conflicts with verified evidence
why: The conflict shows which account fails to fit the record, pointing scrutiny at the party it implicates.

text: When a fact contradicts a theory, look for one plan that explains both, then test each hypothesis that results.
Test a witness's account against a physical item or verifiable record the witness did not expect the investigator to have.
when: A witness's account is rehearsed or plausible
why: Prepared stories hold against expected questions but not against unanticipated evidence

text: When two accounts of one event conflict and both parties are present, comparing them against the original document exposes contradictions.
when: Two parties give conflicting accounts of the same event
why: The original text is the only fixed reference both sides must accept.

text: When two records disagree, weigh the keeper's motive, check what each omits, and use the richer source where the other is silent.
When sources disagree on identity, prefer the account closer to the event, but check how each document was made before trusting either.
when: A first-hand letter conflicts with a formal record.
why: A formal record may rest on second-hand answers.

text: A writer's contradictions and hedges may hide unfairness, so check whether they blur facts or shift blame.
when: A writer's logic does not follow consistently.
why: Confusing logic can conceal partiality.

text: Make the weak reason behind an NPC's claim discoverable so a careful player can catch the gap.
when: when designing NPC testimony that may be wrong or self-serving
why: discovery rewards careful checking and makes the reasoning feel fair

text: Phrase a prediction as a checkable statement, such as a departure in N minutes, so the player can confirm it against an in-game schedule.
when: writing clue text
why: A verifiable claim rewards careful checking and builds trust in the clue.

text: Give a test result that contradicts an NPC's claim, forcing the player to revise the plan.
Give a speaker a plausible reason to deny an overheard remark, so the player must cross-check with another witness.
when: Designing overheard NPC lines that serve as clues
why: A deniable line forces the player to gather corroboration

text: When some traits of a substance match a known compound and others do not, expect the identification to need extra analysis to resolve the conflict.
Attack a consensus point by point, pairing each claim with a counter-clue, rather than rejecting it wholesale.
Let a culprit's own statements contradict each other so the player can catch them out.
when: when writing a suspect's testimony
why: Contradictions give the player a way to expose a lie without a confession.

text: Design clues with a known comparison source, such as mud matched to a room floor, or a ledger or NPC record, so players can test statements.
when: Designing physical or environmental clues
why: A known source gives players a concrete test to apply

text: A conversation system can compare an NPC's spoken claims against stored verbatim records or recorded facts, flagging conflicts the player exposes through questioning.
when: when the game stores a witness's words or facts that NPCs may contradict
why: Verbatim records make earlier statements retrievable and comparable, so the contradiction becomes detectable through the player's questions

text: A clue that conflicts with the known timeline or working theory, such as an obedient servant, forces the player to revise who could be present or the whole account.
when: when designing a mystery puzzle or a mystery where the player holds a working theory
why: The conflict forces reassessment of an assumption

text: Minor out-of-place details each mean little alone, but together they reveal one actor's deliberate pattern once the player collects enough of them.
when: when a hidden actor leaves small anomalies across several locations
why: A pattern only becomes visible when several anomalies are compared

text: A measured discrepancy between a room's dimensions and its plan can be placed as a clue that reveals a hidden room, and the reveal should stay visible to the player.
when: Designing a level with concealed rooms
why: The player who noticed the mismatch earns the payoff when the room is revealed

text: A contradiction can arise from honest error, confusion, fatigue or forgetfulness as easily as deceit, so treat it as an error to check, not automatically a lie.
when: when a witness's account conflicts with known facts
why: Honest memory errors also produce contradictions

text: Investigators tend to inflate a minor oddity, such as one open window, into a conspiracy, giving it disproportionate weight; look for other evidence before building a plot around it.
when: when a minor object or fact conflicts with the expected picture
why: Anomalies stand out against the expected pattern and accumulate in attention

text: An investigator who warns about hearing errors must apply the same caution to their own inferences.
when: when an investigator critiques others' testimony
why: Self-made inferences are also prone to error.

text: Describing the same trace differently in different scenes confuses the reader unless the change is clearly marked.
A time reported by a witness may not match the moment of the act, so timelines should allow for delay between event and report.
Dismissing a contradiction between two witnesses instead of asking what each could hear hides the explanation.
when: two accounts of sound disagree
why: Positional differences often explain the conflict

text: A statement can reject one thing and accept it in the next clause, so a contradiction may sit inside a single passage.
why: Close reading is needed to catch a reversal hidden within one sentence

text: 1) List each unresolved thread. 2) Assign each a concrete outcome, such as money, income or management of assets. 3) Resolve the last emotional thread.
1) Identify the conflicting detail between accounts. 2) Return to the witness with a specific question about that detail. 3) Accept the account that holds under that question.
when: When two descriptions of the same person or event disagree.
why: A specific question tests which account is accurate.

text: 1) List the innocent explanation, such as a memory error. 2) List the deliberate explanation, such as withheld information. 3) Test each with a separate check.
when: A witness's account contradicts what was found.

text: 1) Identify which referent the witness had in mind. 2) Check whether the witness can recall the date. 3) Test whether that reading explains the conflict without requiring forgery.

1) State the statement that existing facts seem to contradict. 2) Search outside sources for a connecting fact. 3) Read the wording by the customs of its period. 4) Test the proposed answer against dates. 5) Check whether it explains other odd facts.

1) Record each conflicting statement with its timestamp. 2) Lay the statements on one timeline. 3) Find the point where two accounts cannot both be true. 4) Test the claims on each side of that point separately.
when: Several accounts of one period conflict.
why: A shared timeline exposes the exact contradiction that needs resolving.

text: When a fact contradicts a theory or deduction, doubt the premise behind it rather than bending or discarding the fact.
Have two or more NPCs give conflicting accounts of the same event or third person, so players must weigh sources and check which matches physical evidence.
Give two NPC experts conflicting readings of one object, such as a diagnosis or poison, and let the player settle it with the right follow-up question or verification.
when: Designing identification puzzles

text: Log or file contradicting answers for later review rather than smoothing or discarding them, since a later player may need the conflict to resolve the case.
Reveal or resolve a withheld purpose later; otherwise the ominous action feels arbitrary.
Let players keep a contradiction list on a mystery board, where each missing or conflicting detail is resolved by later evidence.
when: designing a mystery that players solve through evidence

text: Accept an explanation for a document contradiction only when it fits the physical evidence; then the document can be returned safely.
When an object contradicts a witness's claim, verify both the claim and the object's context before accepting either.
when: When testimony and physical evidence conflict.
why: Either may be mistaken or false.

text: Give observers biased theories so their notes need cross-checking before the player trusts them.
when: when designing observer NPCs

text: An NPC whose behaviour contradicts their stated reason can form a deduction puzzle in which the player assembles who was present, what was said, and what the NPC does next.
when: Designing an NPC whose stated reason conflicts with observed conduct.
why: Contradiction invites the player to reconstruct the scene.

text: Reward players for checking a written clue against independent sources, so that accurate details build trust in the note and accusations need separate proof.
Attach small, unreliable witness details to the case file as corroboration rather than proof.
when: Populating a generated case file with witness information
why: Partial details accumulate into a stronger case without a single decisive clue

text: Tag each story claim as core, affecting the solution, or flavour, never checked, so the player is not required to verify decorative details.
Give a legend or in-world history several contradictory versions, then let the player check each against a physical record to find the reliable one.
when: when generating lore or documents

text: In pursuit encounters, let NPCs give conflicting descriptions that are corrected mid-exchange, so players must reconcile them.
when: Designing NPC dialogue during a chase

text: Plant a blank or altered document in an NPC's possession, and offer the dismissal as a dialogue option that a later reveal can reopen.
when: Designing NPC-held clues

text: Design a clue to point one way while surrounding context points another, so the player must weigh both before deciding.
when: designing clue sets
why: conflicting signals make deduction meaningful

text: Give players an item whose state contradicts the expected story, such as a costume on a body that its owner would not wear, and let the answer come from a second item elsewhere.
when: Designing physical clues for a mystery.
why: Contradictions invite inquiry, and a second location forces the player to connect separate clues.

text: Resolving a recurring figure later pays off the setup. Leaving him a red herring tests the player's judgement but risks the thread feeling unfinished.
when: Designing a figure who appears across several scenes

text: A witness can contradict themselves on a simple matter, such as whether a door was open or closed.
Asking a subject to engage with something they hold dear reveals how much it matters through hesitation and rising tension.
A game can seed an improbable lead that pays off as side information, rewarding players who try unusual routes.
when: Designing optional clues or routes in a game
why: Unusual routes that yield information reward exploration

text: A single mismatch, such as a misremembered day, is an open question needing further testing, not conviction; treating it as conclusive is an error, and impression-based doubt is not evidence.
why: A single mismatch can have an innocent explanation.

text: A series of clean checks shows only that nothing was detected; it weakens suspicion without clearing the suspect and should be combined with other signals.
when: A physical check shows no marks.
why: Absence of a visible mark does not rule out other involvement.

text: Check each explanation for the new objections it creates; a story that explains one oddity while introducing several new anomalies is weak, so count them.
when: A proposed explanation answers a specific objection.
why: Each explanation can introduce its own physical or logical problems.

text: Before dismissing a contradiction as careless, check whether a swap, disguise, or shrewd actor explains it, e.g., a cheap item taken while a valuable one is left.
when: Evaluating a contradiction between witness accounts or an actor's choices.
why: Deliberate substitution can produce honest-looking error; conflicting signs may reflect a shrewd or unusual mind.

text: A single anomaly, such as a failed seal or unusual detail, neither proves interference nor can be dismissed; record it as one data point, since weak evidence supports several explanations.
A single spatial or timing mismatch is one check among several, not proof on its own.
Choose where to post a notice by reasoning about where the true owner would look.
when: When placing a lost-property notice
why: An owner who lost something valuable is likely to watch the places where such notices appear.

text: Choose which theory to put to a person by asking which one would provoke a useful reaction from them.
When a reliable NPC contradicts the player's model, design a hidden motive that explains both the NPC's account and the observed facts.
One physical mismatch with the real person's record, such as the wrong missing limb, can expose an entire disguise.
Check even weak leads when checking costs less than a missed identity.
A single odd detail does not prove staging. Confirm the anomaly against the medical report before drawing a conclusion about how the scene was altered.
when: An investigator notices one posture or item that does not fit.
why: Many innocent factors can displace a body or an item.

text: Pair a character's generosity with harm so the player must reconcile both before judging them.
why: Forced reconciliation avoids flat good or evil judgments.

text: Place paired clues, such as a boot and its matching print, so each gains weight only when both halves are found.
Plan a reveal as already-placed clues, such as a note or object, whose meaning changes once a forgery is known.
when: Designing a twist in a generated mystery.
why: Reinterpretation lets the same placed objects support a new conclusion.

text: Let NPC dialogue reveal a secret location through an offhand remark, so the player must infer who has knowledge.
when: writing NPC dialogue with hidden information
why: Indirect clues reward attentive players.

text: Place environmental clues as a set that partly contradicts itself, so the player must sort them against an NPC's established routine.
when: when designing clues for a deduction puzzle
why: contradictions require the player to model the character rather than read one clue

text: Place a puzzling or purposeless disturbance at a generated scene, so the player must reason about the culprit's motive to explain it.
when: Designing a crime scene for investigation.
why: Unexplained details invite reasoning about intent rather than simple lookup.

text: Make a suspect NPC over-cover one minor detail, so repeated denials become the target of a precise follow-up question.
Keep contradictions unresolved until players have the information to explain them, rather than letting an early explanation close them.
Treat a contradictory sighting as a gap needing further checks, not as proof of wrongdoing.
when: A single witness conflicts with an official account.
why: The contradiction shows the official record is unreliable without establishing what really happened.

text: Loud public clamour from affected families, combined with adviser pressure, can push an authority toward a special commission.
when: When public pressure grows around an accusation case.
why: Official action responds to visible public demand.

text: A level can seed a distinctive visual cue, such as a gloved hand or a particular item, early and pay it off later.
when: Designing long-range clue payoff in a level.
why: Early seeding creates recall when the payoff arrives.

text: A search pass can miss a tool hidden in a pocket, and a later recheck of the same spot reveals it, rewarding repeat searching.
why: Recheck mechanics let players recover clues they first overlooked.

text: Repeating a crime's signature lets players who notice the repeat predict where the next event will occur.
A rare method narrows the suspect pool more than a common one, so a generator can tune clue strength by rarity of the required lore.
when: Generating a trap, lock, or potion whose method requires specific lore.
why: Fewer people can know a rare method, so it excludes more candidates.

text: A single slip or contradiction is a lead to test, not proof: it can point at the wrong person, and reading too much into one word sends investigations astray.
when: When a witness's phrasing seems to betray knowledge.
why: One word rarely carries enough weight to establish guilt or knowledge.

text: Assuming a culprit must be clever enough to prepare cover can lead investigators to read an honest person's gap as innocence or dismiss it entirely.
when: judging a suspect with no alibi
why: The assumption about cleverness drives the reading of the gap.

text: A frame can be undone by one detail the planner did not foresee. Small overlooked items often expose the staging.
why: a planner cannot control every detail the accused might carry

text: The same checklist can fit more than one person, so a fully matched list alone does not single out a suspect.
when: When several people share similar circumstances
why: Shared opportunity and motive can fill the same entries

text: Two sincere witnesses can disagree about the same conversation, and choosing the version that fits a theory can distort the record.
when: when witness accounts of one event conflict
why: sincerity does not guarantee accurate recall, and selection bias can enter the evidence

text: 1) Record each version of the central event. 2) Mark where the versions differ. 3) Keep only the elements that all versions share.
when: when a case rests on retold accounts that cannot all be true

text: 1) Write a few plain sentences of what is known. 2) Ask what was actually seen and heard. 3) Turn that into one concrete question to pursue next.
when: when theories multiply without evidence
why: plain statements restore a practical view

text: 1) List each timed event with its source. 2) Check each clock's reliability. 3) Anchor on the most precise time. 4) Test other events against it. 5) Confirm the full sequence fits one consistent order.
when: when several witnesses and devices give times

text: 1) List who was present at each time. 2) Match each claim to that timeline. 3) Weigh a secondhand repetition below a first-hand account unless it is independently confirmed.
when: when one claim is repeated secondhand and conflicts with a first-hand account

text: 1) Pair former rivals in shared tasks. 2) Formally revoke verdicts that still stand in the official books. 3) Prepare the group before the vote. 4) Lead the question rather than waiting for public pressure.
when: a group must keep working together after a bitter internal conflict
why: Shared work builds cooperation, and formal revocation corrects the record that outlasts the conflict.

text: Accept a theory only after every known fact and each detail is checked; a neat theory can still be wrong, so rebuild it if one fact breaks it.
when: A tidy explanation fits the known facts.
why: A coherent theory can still be wrong.

text: Reconcile conflicting traces, such as a stab wound and a blunt blow, into one account before concluding, not discarding one; a clue can show presence despite another trace suggesting absence.
Test each inferred sequence against independent evidence, such as a later expert report, before treating it as fact.
when: A timeline is built from many small traces.
why: A neat, confident reconstruction can outrun the evidence behind it.

text: Before a long backstory begins, signal the reader or player to set aside prior assumptions, because confusion follows otherwise.
when: Introducing a long backstory section.
why: Prepared attention makes the later reveal land more clearly.

text: Let witness NPCs report partial or conflicting sounds that players must reconcile against the conditions each witness was in.
why: Reconciling conflicts makes testimony an active puzzle

text: Test a client's own theory rather than adopting it, treating even a plausible theory as provisional until confirmed.
Close every decoy with a checkable fact, since a lead left open makes the audience feel cheated.
Check every stage of a handoff chain, since a swap or alteration could have happened at any point along the route.
Design a too-convenient found item as a planted clue with contradictions the player can expose.
when: when placing clues in a dungeon

text: A portrait or family likeness can link a present NPC to a past culprit, but the link should be confirmed by another source.
when: Designing clues that connect characters across generations.

text: Make an NPC explanation fail only when two of that NPC's own claims are placed side by side.
when: scripting NPC alibis or explanations as puzzle content
why: the contradiction is then discoverable through the player's own comparison, not arbitrary

text: Checking every factor thoroughly costs time that could go to the central question, so weigh each check against its likely value.
when: Deciding how far to verify minor facts.
why: Investigative time is limited.

text: The suspects that an accusing theory names are often the most convenient to blame, so they should be tested as possible decoys.
A witness who switches sides at a convenient moment may be running a cover story, so check the timing and what they gain.
when: A witness changes position and is then released or rewarded
why: Benefits from a switch can reveal coordinated intent.

text: Fixating on the most convenient culprit can absorb the whole investigation, hiding the real mechanism or skipping the real method behind the event.
Accepting a convenient answer too early closes the question and loses the lead.
when: a witness offers a neat explanation
why: Neat answers often end inquiry before it is tested

text: Evidence or messages arriving exactly when they help may be staged; scrutinize undated or unstamped documents as possible plants and ask who benefits from each arrival.
why: documents that conveniently surface are unusual; timing that is too convenient may be staged

text: Ask whether the scene conveniently supplied tools used or tracks sit in a convenient spot, such as a lone damp patch; convenient setup can point to planning or staging.
A convenient delay in calling outside authorities can serve investigators as much as a suspect, so weigh who gains from it.
A convenient coincidence in timing invites scrutiny, so an alibi built on it must hold up against independent records.
when: An alibi depends on an alarm or event arriving at a convenient moment.
why: Timing that suits the suspect too well draws suspicion.

text: 1) Compare a second-hand technical term with its likely meaning in context. 2) Check the term against the original wording where possible. 3) Correct the term if the context shows it was garbled.
when: A relayed report uses a technical term that seems wrong
why: Relayed terms are often misquoted, and context reveals the intended meaning

text: Let the protagonist's early impression be wrong, then correct it with an objective artifact such as a photograph, teaching players to trust evidence over impressions.
Have a second expert examine the evidence before removal, so a surprising conclusion rests on more than one opinion.
when: When an expert conclusion overturns the obvious explanation
why: Corroboration guards against a single opinion sounding settled too early.

text: Several independent observers or sources who describe the same events consistently strengthen a claim more than a single account, and a repeated telling by the same person adds nothing.
when: when weighing character evidence, witness accounts or rumours
why: Independent confirmation makes claims checkable and reduces shared error; a single record can be forged or misremembered.

text: Two independent sources that agree beat either alone, and a mismatch points to a lead; e.g., a suspect's admission and an independent source, or local knowledge and a physical survey.
when: A single account is contested or hard to verify, or a deduction needs confirming.
why: Independent agreement makes it unlikely either account was shaped to match the other; two unrelated sources make the conclusion more convincing, so the match feels earned.

text: Witnesses who share a grudge, rely on each other, or repeat one source add no independent weight; matching accounts can share the same error and need independent testing.
when: Multiple witnesses agree on the same accusation, or several people report one account from one source.
why: Shared motive or shared source makes agreement a single voice; shared origin is not independent confirmation.

text: 1) Separate what a witness saw directly from what they were told, including reports by others on a record. 2) Mark each claim as first-hand or hearsay. 3) Weigh each source on its own.
when: Evaluating testimony or a record that mixes observation and report.
why: Witnesses often present hearsay as if it were observed.

text: Corroborate a witness's account with a second independent source before it supports a charge or key claim, and show any dissenting view.
when: A testimony claim is checkable against records or other people, such as a child's age or a contact's letter.
why: A single account can be mistaken or biased, and single-witness claims can be wrong; independent checks reveal errors. Two agreeing observers carry more weight than one.

text: Testing a claim's origin means classifying it as original, suggested by someone else, or revised later under pressure.
when: When an accusation may come from another person's suggestion or a witness changes their story.
why: It shows whether the claim came from direct knowledge or from outside influence.

text: Examination rules that bind only the accused make the accused's compliance look like proof, while the accusers' conduct goes unchecked.
Matching witness accounts strengthen a claim only if witnesses did not hear it from each other or coordinate on the point, since shared sources or coordination can produce agreement.
when: multiple witnesses give matching accounts, or a second witness matches on a point the first had no reason to coordinate
why: Uncoordinated agreement is less likely to be shared invention; shared belief can also produce agreement without observation.

text: Back a single witness's identification with an independent observation, such as a separate description or a second witness recognising the same detail, which strengthens it more than either alone.
when: identifying a person from a witness's description, when an identification rests on one witness
why: Independent agreement reduces the chance of error.

text: Check testimony against physical traces or objects and locations whenever both exist; treat it as established only after corroboration.
when: a story covers actions that left traces, testimony is central, a witness describes how an object was handled, or a witness and an object point in different directions
why: Physical facts confirm or contradict claims independent of the speaker; each source can mislead, so agreement between them is stronger than either alone.

text: Traces confirm or contradict only parts of an account, so check each part of a doubtful account against physical traces rather than treating a trace as proof of the whole.
when: a witness account is unreliable or lacks direct verification
why: Traces support parts of a story without confirming the whole; a trace can confirm the part that happened even when the rest is doubtful.

text: Let players test an NPC's travel, purchase or history claim against an independent transport log, ledger, archive, letter, register, timetable or ticket record.
when: an NPC makes a claim about travel or purchases, and the player holds data the NPC cannot control
why: Records from separate game systems are independent of the NPC's story, so a false account can be exposed; independent logs let players test claims directly.

text: Check a disputed recollection against dated records and schedules rather than trusting how someone looked; a matching entry turns the memory into corroborated evidence.
when: the outcome depends on exact wording or dates
