text: When a primary witness cannot confirm a date or event, a second independent record, such as a transport order-book, can add facts no one else recorded and extend the timeline.
when: the primary witness cannot confirm a date or event
why: A backup record keeps the timeline provable.

text: When one clue or symptom fits several causes, test each explanation against an independent trace or fact, such as a second sense, since a matching feature fits all equally.
when: one observation supports two readings, a single physical clue has several possible causes, or a visual clue seems significant
why: An independent trace can separate the possible causes.

text: Witnesses who share a suspect's group, interests or ties, were chosen by one party, or can be bribed form one echo, not independent confirmation; check before accepting corroboration.
when: a witness supports an alibi or corroborates a story, or judging how strongly a corroborating source supports it
why: Shared loyalties or sympathy can bend an account, so an outside party's record weighs more than friends' support.

text: Settle a person's status or identity on several features that agree, not on a single feature such as a shoe or a gesture.
Do not treat a single trace as proof; build the inference from several traces that agree with one another.
when: when concluding a suspect's size, gait, equipment or injury
why: one trace can be coincidental or misread

text: Confirm a measured value against an external record, such as a seller's stock, rather than relying on the subject's own word.
when: A subject claims a size, identity or origin
why: An outside source cannot be shaped by the subject's claim

text: Settle a disputed fact against official records, which can resolve it even when an admitted fault is also on file.
when: a disputed fact can be checked against records

text: A witness report can justify action, but a claim of awareness or movement stays unverified until physical evidence corroborates it.
To test a claim quickly, find an independent witness who could have observed the same visitor, such as household staff.
when: when a claim about a visit cannot be checked directly
why: observers without a stake provide a separate check

text: When a lead moves to a new place, shift the inquiry there rather than continuing at the old location.
Have an NPC confirm the details of a recovered note, such as age, clothing or direction, before a new quest branch opens.
when: gating a quest branch on evidence
why: checking details verifies the player's findings

text: Test a lead's importance before spending more time on it, but do not drop it merely because it is inconvenient to follow.
Have two observers count the same signal independently and compare results, which catches counting mistakes that one observer would miss.
A physical trace already on record, such as a footprint outline, can support an eyewitness sighting and strengthen a weak description.
A detail offered late, such as a half-seen movement, is hard to verify and should be treated as a lead rather than an established fact.
Check an unfamiliar term or name against an independent reference, such as a manual or blotter, before relying on it.
when: A term or name found in evidence is unfamiliar
why: An independent source confirms or corrects the reading

text: Witnesses who disagree about whether others were present open gaps that an opposing side can exploit.
An alibi is strongest when several unconnected people confirm the same minute.
A pickup-point NPC who records each claimant creates a chain of witnesses the player can question one by one.
Test one witness's account against another's by setting the statements against each other until one side must concede.
when: two parties give conflicting accounts
why: Direct contradiction forces a check against independent facts.

text: Inspect physical objects before recollection and rumour, since objects stay put while accounts drift.
when: early in an investigation
why: memory and testimony change over time

text: A separate contact that points to a broader interest can strengthen a motive hypothesis, though it does not prove it.
Favour a witness whose account links to independent records, such as who admitted a visitor, over one whose account stands alone.
Corroborate a lead with a separate record, such as a news item placing an event at the same location during the subject's stay.
Treat a witness's certainty about an object's identity with caution when they saw it briefly or in poor conditions.
when: brief or poor-condition viewing
why: Certainty does not guarantee that the object was the genuine one.

text: An account of someone's movements that depends on a watcher reveals a source; ask who supplied the information.
Corroborate a compromised witness with an independent account of the same state or scene before relying on their memory.
Accounts that agree on small details, such as menu items and preparation, strengthen each other.
when: Comparing several witness accounts
why: Matching specifics are harder to coincide by chance

text: Do not conclude from one shared feature; several independent features should agree before a document is linked to a common source.
why: a few defects can overstate a match

text: Rank competing leads by how likely each is to yield a motive or suspect, and pursue the one with concrete next steps first.
when: Several investigation leads compete for attention.
why: Concrete next steps show quickly whether a lead is productive.

text: Physical evidence such as forged documents or traces carries stronger reasoning than motive alone, so build deduction on the physical trail.
when: When structuring an investigation's reasoning.
why: Physical traces can be tested; motives are only backgrounds.

text: Corroborate private remarks from an insider by checking them against external facts before relying on them.
when: Information comes from a servant or other insider with access to private matters.
why: Insider access makes information revealing, but it still needs independent confirmation.

text: Anchor a timeline with physical traces such as impact position and freshness, since they can rule out explanations that relayed statements cannot.
when: When a case includes objects, marks or damage that can be dated or placed.
why: A trace records an event directly, so it constrains the story more reliably than hearsay.

text: Let a crowd repeat the first claim it hears, so the player must find a second, independent source to correct it.
when: Designing crowd dialogue that carries misinformation

text: Separate what is observed from what is told when using objects and places as evidence.
when: Reading a scene that combines physical traces with stories.
why: Legends can attach to objects and look like proof.

text: Use a written report as corroboration when a suspect's memory is unreliable or self-serving.
when: A suspect denies or fails to recall the event.
why: Corroboration from a second source compensates for the suspect's unreliable account.

text: When witnesses conflict, corroboration from those with extended, direct observation can outweigh a weaker, shorter account.
Repeat a physical examination with a different examiner. Disagreement between reports suggests the first examiner may have been biased.
when: When a single examiner's finding is decisive.
why: Independent observers reduce the effect of one person's expectations.

text: Trust a second-hand account less than one backed by physical traces; corroboration by records or objects matters more than who told the story.
when: when an account arrives second-hand

text: Use logs, rosters or visitor books as search filters, so the player narrows locations by elimination.
when: Designing a location search in a game
why: Elimination through records turns investigation into a readable process

text: A single fact rarely proves a conclusion on its own, so it should be corroborated by independent evidence before being relied on.
when: A clue appears to decide a case alone.
why: One premise cannot establish a conclusion without support from other facts.

text: Two absences that point the same way, such as a missing item and a missing record, strengthen the conclusion that the item was taken.
When several independent witnesses report the same pattern or thing across separate inquiries, a conclusion gains credibility and a simple imagined explanation becomes less likely.
when: A mystery must be made to feel established; judging whether a reported sighting is real.
why: Independent agreement reduces the chance that one observer's error stands alone and reduces the chance of shared illusion.

text: Count sources by independence of origin, not number: sources drawing on one authority are not independent, and two accounts count only if from different first-hand sources.
when: Weighing agreement among multiple sources, or two witnesses reporting the same claim.
why: Repetition of a single origin inflates apparent support; two people repeating one source add no independent confirmation.

text: Let earlier environment or NPC details gain meaning when a later reveal or new document changes the motive or beneficiary; re-run the case file so clues are reinterpreted.
when: A new discovery changes the likely motive or beneficiary in a generated mystery.
why: Reinterpreting existing clues keeps the mystery coherent and rewarding.

text: Build a case in layers: each independent confirmation adds weight before the conclusion is stated.
Claims about one event that appear in several accounts, such as an agreed meal, may be reliable while disputed details such as money or objects need separate testing.
when: Witnesses agree on some points and disagree on others.
why: Agreement on incidental facts does not confirm the contested ones.

text: Identity is stronger when several traces, such as a fragment and a location, are gathered together and point the same way.
when: Weighing evidence that links a person to a place or event.
why: Converging independent traces are harder to explain away as coincidence or planting.

text: Use two independent witnesses to reinforce a false time, so the error appears verified and the player stops questioning it.
Lighting, distance and fear shape how many details a witness can report, so poor conditions yield vague or uncertain accounts.
when: Evaluating eyewitnesses at a scene
why: Weak perception reduces what can be sworn to, even when witnesses are sure of the event.

text: When the same phrase appears in a second independent source, it connects two separate events that the first source alone did not link.
Physical traces such as wasted muscle or wear on an object can test an NPC's claim about its past condition, giving the player a way to check a story.
when: Designing an NPC whose backstory can be verified.
why: Physical evidence lets the player test a story rather than simply accept it.

text: An accuser's account gains strength when a named bystander who was present is asked to confirm what they saw.
when: when a case rests on one person's word
why: a third party who saw events can confirm or contradict

text: A busy public location where an NPC handles steady trade acts as an observation post; its traffic and transaction records yield a timeline of who was present and when.
when: Designing a shop, tavern or market as a source of witnesses and movement records.
why: Regular, continuous traffic creates a sequence of observable events the player can reconstruct.

text: A case is built as a chain of links, and tracking which link is still missing shows what must be proven next.
when: when organising evidence toward a conclusion
why: Each link must hold for the chain to stand, so the gap is visible at the weakest link.

text: Accounts of a dispute often come from one side only, and a record written by one side is not impartial; the full facts may never be recoverable.
when: when reconstructing a dispute from testimony or a published account
why: The party who tells the story has a stake in its version; a published account can shape opinion before anyone tests it.

text: Agreement is not independent confirmation when witnesses share expectations or agree with a detail offered to them, since they may all be wrong in the same direction.
when: many people agree an object is familiar, or a witness confirms a detail that was offered
why: Shared expectations or offers produce agreement without evidence; agreement and recollection look the same in the record.

text: A wrong time in a public notice can mislead the whole timeline, so official documents must be checked against what witnesses actually observed.
when: a published document sets a time or fact

text: A witness's statement that they were never alone with an item is unreliable unless timing and sightline are documented, because the real access window is often wider.
Anyone who heard the original conversation could have written a letter, including the apparent recipient, so keep authorship open.
If the audience cannot tell which speakers are drunk, biased or passing on gossip, every statement feels equally reliable and the mystery loses its texture.
A record that quotes one side's report can be contradicted by the full examination, so compare the two before accepting either.
when: when working from a summary or secondhand account

text: Physical traces such as marks or objects can look objective, yet they may be matched to the accusers' own claims and so prove little.
A group that agrees together can look like independent corroboration when its agreement is only deference to a leader.
A second anchor that depends on the same unverified source is not independent, so it does not confirm the first line of inquiry.
when: An investigator treats two leads as corroborating each other.
why: Shared origin means both leads inherit the same error.

text: 1) Assign one watcher per target. 2) Give each watcher a separate reporting channel. 3) Obtain records at their source and cross-check the reports against each other.
when: When suspects move apart and one observer cannot cover them all.
why: Separate channels and cross-checking keep multiple observers reliable and independent.

text: 1) Record the disputed account in writing. 2) Gather independent sources such as diaries, letters, official records and other witnesses. 3) Check each source against the others. 4) Form a judgement only afterwards.
when: A single account conflicts with the record

text: 1) Collect details that condemn and details that favour the accused. 2) Take the accused's account as a working hypothesis. 3) Follow where it leads and test it against each witness's stated limits.
when: Testimony contains both incriminating and exculpatory details
why: Selective reading of witness details distorts the case

text: 1) List the physical traces the described event should leave, such as powder marks, footprints or impact range. 2) Compare each trace with the account. 3) Doubt the account where traces contradict it, even if witnesses agree.
when: a witness gives a detailed account of a fast event

text: 1) Find people who knew the person involved. 2) Look for letters or records. 3) Compare them with the witness account before accepting it.
when: when a single account is the only source for a fact

text: 1) Compare the official account with personal first-hand observation. 2) Ask the witness for the private facts behind it. 3) Check the record against physical evidence. 4) Note which observations were made before the scene was disturbed.
when: when an official finding seems to close a case too quickly

text: 1) Name the source of the lead. 2) Check whether that source actually holds the item or fact. 3) If every source is negative, close the branch and return to other evidence.
when: A lead is taking time without yielding results.
why: Closing an empty branch frees effort for leads that can move the case forward.

text: 1) Compare each witness statement with physical facts such as the body, the doors and the keys. 2) Mark each conflict. 3) Keep the testimony provisional until the conflicts are resolved.
1) List each claim in the testimony. 2) Match each claim to a physical item or record. 3) Re-ask the questions and note which answers change.
when: Assessing a witness or suspect's account.
why: Physical checks reveal contradictions, and shifting answers reveal weak claims.

text: 1) Take the witness's account of an event. 2) Check it against other facts and reports. 3) Look for a physical trace confirming it. 4) Compare timing with separate accounts. 5) Check that the witness had access and time to plant the object.
when: a witness's account links a person to an object or place

text: 1) Ask each witness for times and locations. 2) Link each account to the next. 3) Test the linked accounts against physical evidence.
when: when several witnesses give partial accounts

text: 1) List each incident with its source. 2) Mark which incidents are independently verified and which rest on one informant. 3) Count only independent links toward a pattern. 4) Keep the pattern provisional while sources are second-hand.
when: Building a case from reports and accounts
why: Only independent evidence can make a chain of events trustworthy.

text: 1) Identify the person who actually saw the event. 2) List every person who repeated the account. 3) Mark which parts are first-hand, reported, or the teller's guess. 4) Check each link against an eyewitness.
when: Presenting or auditing a clue delivered through hearsay.
why: Explicit chains let the audience judge reliability link by link.

text: 1) Identify which accounts copy or borrow from others. 2) Trace each copy back to its original witness. 3) Count independent witnesses only. 4) Check claims against any direct chain of evidence.
when: Sources quote or borrow from each other
why: Copies add no independent confirmation

text: 1) Record the exact kind of object found at a scene. 2) Trace its source by inquiry. 3) Search other scenes for the same kind. 4) Confirm by physical comparison where possible.
1) Count the events the scene implies. 2) Match each event to a physical mark it left. 3) Investigate any event with no matching mark, or any mark with no matching event.
when: when a scene's physical record seems inconsistent

text: Corroborate a confident report or family retelling against independent records before relying on it; confidence does not guarantee accuracy, and retellings can hide errors and bias.
when: a witness's confident account of the past shapes the next lead

text: Separate what a witness observed from how they report it: a stake or pride can bend the report even when the observation was accurate.
when: judging a relayed account
why: Heavy stress on certain words often reflects pride rather than fact; the report can bend toward a purpose while perception stays correct.

text: Let a second, independent clue test an item's owner rather than simply telling the player; a single clue is easy to dismiss, while two can cross-check each other.
when: revealing the owner of a found item or designing an object-based clue
why: A player who tests the identity earns the conclusion.

text: Do not rely on one witness when physical traces can check the account; test a stated time against a clock, a log or a door's state.
when: A key account rests on one person
why: Physical traces do not depend on memory or mood

text: Check claims against independent sources before building a theory or case, especially claims only one or two people can confirm; do not build a theory on a single odd remark.
Do not treat a single trace as proof; each detail needs a second independent trace before it anchors a theory, especially when several explanations fit.
when: Evaluating a single physical clue.
why: One trace can be misleading on its own.

text: Cross-check each testimony against other accounts of the same moment and independent observers; a claim conflicting with a reliable observation must be questioned.
Offer cross-checks for each claim from a biased source: bias can make a true claim look false and a biased witness can report wrongly; judge each on its own evidence.
when: When a witness shows clear bias.

text: Compare a character's earlier spoken account with a later written or physical record; a mismatch is a lead even when the speaker seems honest.
when: the claim can be checked against an object or place the speaker could not easily alter
why: Contradictions can expose hidden facts that sincerity does not rule out

text: Require a second independent clue before the player's character can make an arrest or accusation.
when: when designing accusation rules in a mystery game
why: A single weak lead should not be enough to act on.

text: Let an NPC's statement look consistent with the chart on the surface, so the player must check details to find the lie.
Offer the sources behind a claim for direct inspection, so others can verify them instead of trusting the reporter.
Let players bring a second NPC who holds a separate view, creating a meaningful verification step in the scene.
why: An independent view makes verification a real choice

text: Do not rely on a single barrier; an impossibility is credible only when several independent checks agree.
Test a witness's account by checking whether each described physical action is possible given the scene's geometry and objects.
when: When a witness describes reaching, climbing, tying or moving something.
why: An impossible action shows the account is wrong or staged.

text: Require formal follow-up on a witness who offers a sworn statement, or the alibi stays unconfirmed on the record.
Do not rely on a handwriting match alone; treat it as one clue that needs corroboration.
when: Using writing comparison as proof
why: Matching handwriting can be coincidental or imitated

text: Do not treat a single overheard phrase as proof of motive; require independent corroboration before drawing that conclusion.
when: a motive is inferred from one overheard line
why: a fragment can be misread, so it needs support

text: Keep corroborating evidence in the world for true testimony, so a player who believes an honest NPC can still prove it.
Independent checks complement direct questioning of everyone present; they do not replace it.
Separate a statement's source from its claim. A statement may reach you through an intermediary, so it counts as that intermediary's testimony, not the original speaker's.
when: When a key claim is relayed rather than heard directly.
why: Relayed claims can be altered or invented without the original speaker's knowledge.

text: Do not rely on a one-sided record, or one assembled by someone with an agenda, without independent corroboration.
Treat testimony as a lead, not proof; a witness's trust in someone reveals the witness's state of mind, not the facts of the event.
Verify a privately disclosed account through separate sources. A confidence given in return for discretion does not establish that the account is true.
when: When a witness's private disclosure is relied upon for the case.
why: The witness's motive to shape the account is unchanged by the promise of privacy.

text: Watch one suspect through several channels at once: follow them in person, listen in on their calls, and intercept their written notes.
when: When a suspect's contacts and intent cannot be learned from a single source.

text: Track which witnesses share a grievance so the game can flag testimonies that are not independent of each other.
Make a witness NPC's expected mention of an event a testable gap, so that skipping it gives players a clue.
Check an anchor's installation time against a second source before building a timeline on it, since second-hand timing is weak alone.
Make stated amounts such as rewards match or conflict with actual loot, so a mismatch becomes a clue.
when: Designing bounty or reward text
why: Conflicts give investigators a lead

text: Give players a case log of stored statements that they can reread at any time, so claims remain available as a record.
when: when a mystery spans many NPC conversations
why: a persistent record lets players compare claims over time

text: Tag each witness NPC with a reliability value and a motive, and let players cross-check reports against neutral NPCs who were present.
when: when designing witness networks
why: explicit bias makes reports checkable

text: Do not accept a rational explanation when an independent observer reports the same event in a place the proposed mechanism could not reach.
when: Evaluating an explanation against witness reports
why: An explanation that cannot reach the reported location does not account for the event

text: A case that moves from an unverifiable accusation to conviction on loose supporting evidence has no real corroboration standard.
why: Any trifle is accepted as confirmation once the accusation is heard.

text: 1) Find a second source for the claim. 2) Compare the two. 3) Treat agreement between an official and an informal source as strong support.
Check that accounts are independent before treating their agreement as corroboration; copied accounts or sources who have spoken to each other may agree from a shared origin or bias.
when: Two accounts agree on a point, or two witness statements are being compared
why: Copied accounts repeat a single source and so do not confirm each other; shared conversation can produce agreement that reflects shared bias rather than truth.

text: Require two credible, independent witnesses who each attest firsthand to the act before accepting an accusation, or require a confession that is matched to the physical fact it describes.
when: Formal accusation or conviction is being decided
why: A single or uncorroborated account can be mistaken, shaped by pressure or motivated

text: Require two separate witness NPCs before a quest accuses a character of magic, and distinguish those who saw an event from those who only heard of it.
when: Scripting an accusation that changes the quest state.
why: Direct sight and a second witness reduce false triggers caused by rumour.

text: Testimony that costs the speaker standing or safety signals sincerity and is more credible than disinterested testimony. Make speaking for a suspect carry visible risk.
when: a witness speaks for another at personal cost
why: A defence that implicates the speaker is harder to dismiss as self-serving.

text: Delaying a conclusion, such as slow evidence-gathering, lets evidence surface and guards against error but costs time; when a stakeholder needs a fast result, delay can damage the outcome.
when: a stakeholder is waiting for a result

text: People sometimes make small trades to prove to themselves they could do more, so a small trade signals intent without proving motive.
when: A small transaction seems out of proportion to its gain
why: Small trades can serve as tests of capacity

text: Cost ledgers for a formal process can reveal how routine and indifferent its handling was, an attitude that witness statements may not show.
Lavish payment for a trivial task implies the stakes for the planners are far larger than the task itself.
when: A plan's expense is out of proportion to its visible work.
why: Rational planners spend only in proportion to what they stand to gain.

text: Compare the effort a suspected plan would need with the value of the goal. If the effort is out of proportion, the motive is probably different from the one assumed.
when: Judging whether a suspected plan or motive is plausible.
why: An expensive method for a small prize signals a different underlying reason.

text: When someone gives up a benefit they would normally keep, the sacrifice suggests an urgent, time-bound need.
when: a choice contradicts the person's stated interests
why: Giving up a lasting gain only makes sense if a more pressing need outweighs it.

text: Weigh what an act costs the actor against its gain; a theft that harms the actor's own prospects is a weak motive for that actor.
when: judging whether a suspect would plausibly commit an act
why: Rational actors avoid acts that undermine their own goals

text: An action that looks costly or unnecessary often reveals an adversary's plan; ask what the action achieves.
Move from dialogue to the scene in a single transition, so stakes rise without a pause.
when: When a conversation should lead directly into the next location or action.

text: Pursuing a dispute through formal challenge can cost more than available resources, and an unfunded claim can ruin the pursuer before the truth is established.
why: Formal processes have high costs and long delays.

text: A false lead that costs the player nothing feels pointless. Make its cost visible, such as an unwatched area or lost time.
Slow, cautious movement and stops consume the margin in a timed plan, so a plan with little slack can be overrun by ordinary delays.
when: When an actor must complete actions within a fixed window.
why: Each delay reduces the time left before the deadline.

text: A statement taken without a proper caution or notice of representation may be challenged and excluded, even if it is carefully recorded.
Long gaps between reports make a story feel slow and build irritation during the wait.
when: The protagonist is kept inactive for long periods
why: Waiting without progress frustrates the audience

text: Too much slow detail stalls a story, so every descriptive passage should serve tension or information.
Costs can be recorded in detail while the reasons for an arrest go unrecorded, so harm alone does not reveal intent.
Do not press a witness who is cooperating and has no conflicting facts.
when: A witness answers openly and their account matches the evidence.
why: Extra pressure adds risk without new information.

text: Gate a witness behind a social rule, such as a faction that punishes anyone who asks questions, so the player can detect the lock by noticing which NPCs refuse to talk.
when: Designing a quest hub or investigation with restricted witnesses.
why: Social refusals and past discipline reveal hidden access controls.

text: Make recovering key evidence a real decision with costs such as an inquest or exposure of an ally, rather than a free pickup.
when: Designing a discovery of pivotal evidence
why: Costly choices give the discovery moral and strategic weight

text: Sinking or destroying a vehicle removes it from the record, but also removes the means of travel.
A count of missing items can rule out a simple explanation; a partial count can fit neither an accidental nor a deliberate single-dose cause.
when: Physical evidence includes a countable quantity

text: Count independent sources or matching details, not repeats: shared-loyalty witnesses add nothing new; several independent matches point to one author, a single match may be chance.
why: Shared loyalty makes their views a single source

text: A small mismatch between an expected count and an observed count is often the first sign that someone acted outside the stated story.
when: When a known starting figure exists to compare against
why: Mismatches reveal actions the account omits

text: Report a tally built on a range estimate as a range, not a single exact figure, since the width of the range shows how far the total may be off.
when: Some recalled payments are uncertain and given as alternative amounts.
why: A single number hides the uncertainty carried by the estimate.

text: Counting accusers or incriminating items is a pitfall; each item must be weighed, since volume of accusation is not proof and merely counting misranks suspects.
when: Weighing suspicion against a person
why: Volume of accusation is not the same as proof

text: A single counting slip shifts every later word, so the decoder must recount.
Changing the count of items is a detectable error, so a swap must keep the number the same.
1) Count accusations within a small area. 2) Note how many accused had blameless lives. 3) Track growth in accusers over time. 4) Count outcomes for accused who denied guilt.
when: a body of testimony looks suspicious as a whole

text: Give a game's council or jury seat rules that exclude parties with a stake, so the player can check the body for bias.
A cover that depends on distraction or on not being examined becomes a clue under careful, repeated inspection, and the staging fails.
when: a disguise or deception depends on preventing close examination
why: Careful attention exposes the mismatch; a cover that relies on not being inspected fails once inspection is repeated with comparison.

text: Cover-up efforts leave their own evidence; an altered or replaced object and its materials can reveal what it was meant to hide. Doing nothing afterward is hardest to catch.
when: after a crime has been committed
why: Cover-up actions leave traces of their own.

text: Demands for silence and checks for eavesdroppers signal that a cover protects something real.
When a visitor's behaviour is out of proportion to the stated goal, suspect the request is cover for another aim.
when: a visitor's request and reactions do not match

text: Concealing one fact often leaves a second, small contradiction in an unrelated object, such as a note written on the back of a paper.
why: people who hide one item seldom clean up every item they handled

text: Cover is weakest where routine observers see both identities, and staff familiar with the second identity can react to it at an unusual hour and expose the arrangement.
when: when a hidden identity is exposed to people who know both roles
why: Familiarity with one identity lets observers connect it to the other under unusual conditions.

text: End a case with an aftermath that shows the consequence of the concealed act, closing the loop the reversal opened.
A cover story fabricated for one crime can later be exposed by facts, and its details can reveal a repeated pattern.
A cover identity or story collapses if one relative, mutual contact, or independent check can confirm or deny it, so the victim must be isolated from people who could check it.
when: Maintaining a false identity
why: One independent check can expose the entire lie.

text: If a slip exposes the questioner's real role, witnesses change what they say, so the cover must be maintained throughout.
A cover can break through a single slip, or through a suspect who notices a stranger's unusual interest.
Half-truths tend to be found out, and the discovery of concealment can do more damage than the truth would have.
when: When a character's partial account is likely to be checked later.
why: Hidden information that surfaces later erodes trust in the whole account.

text: A cover persona that slips in its slang or details can expose the investigator.
when: Maintaining an undercover identity over time
why: Inconsistent details invite suspicion from those who know the group

text: Sharing a cover identity with an ally adds risk, because the ally's questioning can expose the cover.
when: Two or more people operate under a shared cover.
why: An ally who is questioned may reveal the shared story.

text: A cover role may hold up against ordinary staff but fail if checked by someone with authority over the site.
when: Choosing a pretext for entry.
why: Authority figures are more likely to verify credentials.

text: Distrust fluent answers that fit every trap, since rehearsed replies fit any follow-up; a clever liar may overplay wit or seem too composed, so waiting often exposes the slip.
when: A suspect is skilled at controlled speech, or a witness's answers are prompt and seamless.
why: Over-control and rehearsed polish are unnatural, so fluency alone does not show truth.

text: Partly verified details from an informant or witness create unwarranted confidence, and blended fabrications survive; check each detail separately.
when: An informant's or witness's claims are partly confirmed.
why: One verified detail does not validate the unverified rest.

text: Treat a suspect's specific excuse as a checkable statement, and test a narrow excuse offered under pressure against the wider record.
when: A suspect offers a specific prior engagement or narrow excuse under pressure.
why: Excuses can be tested against other sources and the wider record.

text: A cover story must match every earlier statement and everyone who might hear it, and be backed by documents establishing the claimed identity; one inconsistency exposes it.
when: A character maintains a false account across several witnesses.
why: Cross-checking exposes contradictions in a scripted lie.

text: Avoid vague bluffs; back a cover with a plausible, checkable backstory, since suspicious people can test its details and a single slip exposes it.
when: Maintaining an alias during questioning; using a pretext to gain access.
why: Checkable details give a suspicious observer a way to expose the cover.

text: A pleasing, courteous, or attractive suspect can lower an observer's or official's guard, so charm may be mistaken for innocence and hide motive.
when: A suspect is polished, respectable, courteous, attractive or charming.
why: Impression and attraction shape judgment, and pleasant conduct draws attention away from purpose.

text: A conspicuous cover draws attention to the secret it claims to hide, so observers fixate on that claim while the real secret goes unexamined.
when: a visibly displayed concealment
why: visible concealment invites the question of what it protects, and the answer offered is accepted

text: People explain a short absence with ready-made reasons such as nerves or a clothing problem, and these reasons lose credibility as the absence lengthens.
when: a person leaves a social scene briefly

text: A witness facing a contradictory sworn statement may claim confusion or a disturbed state of mind to explain it away.
when: a witness is confronted with an earlier statement
why: A claimed mental state offers a ready explanation for the contradiction.

text: A detail framed as a joke is rarely treated as a clue, so players notice its significance only in hindsight.
A sudden show of pleasantness from a suspect after a threat appears can be read by an observant audience as a warning rather than reassurance.
when: A suspect becomes unusually polite or attentive after a visit or threat
why: Players who know something is hidden interpret friendliness as a cover.

text: An investigator who looks at objects rather than the person addressed hides what he has noticed, and observers struggle to read his thoughts.
when: An interrogator wants to keep suspicions from a suspect.
why: Eye contact is a channel for revealing attention, and averting it withholds that signal.

text: A weapon that a stranger shows briefly and then hides invites suspicion from observers.
when: A stranger reveals and conceals a weapon

text: A caught suspect often claims he was lured, showing he is already building a counter-story.
when: A suspect is caught in a trap
why: Self-defence leads the suspect to blame the trap's setter

text: A plausible cover story can make a source speak freely, even when the cover story is false.
when: when a source is given a believable reason for being questioned
why: plausibility lowers suspicion

text: When someone erases marks, the erasure itself shows care and expectations about what investigators would find.
when: Some marks are missing or clearly removed while others remain.
why: Erasing selectively implies the actor anticipated scrutiny of certain traces.

text: A bluff is reinterpreted afterwards once the listener knows the pressure was staged.
when: a listener learns that a deadline or message was fake
why: knowing the staging changes how the pressure is understood

text: A witness's certainty can shift after speaking with a third party, so a changed account should be treated as a new statement to test.
when: when a witness changes account after talking to someone else

text: A suspect may avoid a particular change if they fear the investigator has already seen it, choosing caution over a clear commitment.
when: When a suspect has partial knowledge of what the investigator has observed
why: Avoiding a detectable commitment protects them if the trap is already known.

text: Eager or careless speech often reveals information the speaker did not mean to share, such as a plan not yet announced.
when: in casual conversation

text: A person hiding their inquiries about a sensitive matter may seek advice from strangers under another name, leaving few direct traces.
when: Investigating whether a suspect sought advice about a sensitive matter.
why: Using an alias avoids involving trusted advisers who might grow suspicious.

text: A witness who claims not to remember a particular topic may be concealing something, and the questioner must decide whether to press.
when: A witness avoids or disclaims a specific topic
why: Selective forgetting can be a way to withhold information

text: A person who hides an embarrassing but true fact, such as paying a blackmailer, can look guilty even when innocent.
when: When a witness denies a meeting or payment.
why: Concealing shame is read as concealing a crime.

text: Demanding one specific falsehood from a written claim shifts the burden of proof, and disputants often reject the whole document instead.
when: A long written accusation is contested
why: Locating one error is harder than rejecting everything at once.

text: A concealer keeps re-checking the hiding place for signs of disturbance, so a concealment is never fully trusted.
when: A character has hidden something and remains nearby.
why: Doubt about whether the hiding will hold drives repeated checks.

text: Others read a conspicuous silence on a topic everyone else avoids as a sign that the silent person suspects something.
when: a person never asks about a subject others steer around
why: the absence of a question is noticed and interpreted as evidence

text: Visible props, such as spare clothing packed for show, make a hasty departure look ordinary and support a cover story.
when: Someone must leave quickly without drawing notice
why: Plausible surface evidence hides the real motive

text: Authorities may adopt a convenient public theory that excuses their failure, presenting selected evidence while leaving contrary evidence unmentioned.
when: when an official explanation protects the force from blame
why: Protecting reputation makes a convenient explanation more attractive than an accurate one.

text: A suspect asked about an odd appearance or absence often gives a plausible reason, and several such reasons may conflict with each other or with what others saw.
when: when questioned about a conspicuous detail or unexplained absence
why: People improvise explanations under questioning, and the improvised reasons often do not fit together.

text: A culprit who rehearses a deception until it becomes automatic is more convincing under questioning, and a rehearsed cover can be tested against the investigator before acting.
when: a planned deception must survive an inspection
why: Practice removes hesitation, and a test lets the culprit decide whether the investigator is a threat.

text: A cover story is a plausible explanation for odd behavior or an activity that hides the real purpose and discourages checking, steering observers wrong.
A cover name is an alias two correspondents adopt, so their letters are addressed to a false identity and remain private.
when: when a hidden correspondence channel is needed
why: The false identity hides who is actually writing.

text: Confusion during an event can shield a prominent participant from later scrutiny.
Surviving records often cannot separate a witness's honest hallucination from deliberate fabrication.
Hiding a body is easier to conceal when the site is unexamined, and removal is too risky when neighbors may notice.
when: Choosing between disposal options.
why: Visibility and exposure shape which concealment method is viable.

text: A witness opens up more when the questioner's cover story flatters her importance, so acknowledging a witness's standing can increase cooperation.
when: When a witness is reluctant and the questioner uses a cover identity
why: Feeling important lowers a witness's guard and increases willingness to share.

text: A cover identity can build trust yet not fully remove suspicion, so the investigator may still be questioned about who they are.
when: Relying on a persona to resolve a suspect's doubts
why: Trust built by a persona is partial and can be re-examined

text: Base a cover story on real events or profession with a few details changed; true details are harder to expose and easier to maintain under questioning.
when: when building a false pretext or a character must mislead a listener
why: True details lend credibility and survive casual questioning.

text: Make NPC testimony partly true, such as a reported movement later confirmed by a find, so players learn selective trust and explore without the answer being given away.
A cover must hold under direct testing: a thin one fails after a few questions, so learn the target's domain facts first, or the interview ends.
Judge an account by consistency of voice, gesture and detail; a confident delivery can still betray a lie through changed voice or avoided eye contact, and such judgment can err.
A cover story built on one true, checkable detail is hard to break, though it can still hide a lie about the purpose of contact.
Build a false identity on a core of truth, so the cover can explain any slip in speech or manner.
when: An investigator must pass as someone else in conversation.
why: Facts from one's real life are easier to recall consistently under questioning.

text: Choose a cover that gives a natural reason to ask questions, such as a purchase or a trade.
when: Planning an investigator's false role
why: A plausible reason makes questions feel ordinary to the subject

text: Use a plausible cover story, such as a reserved seat or a stated decision, to justify presence, and ask for discretion so it stays quiet.
when: when an investigator needs a reason to be somewhere
why: A believable cover is accepted and keeps the real purpose hidden.

text: Give each cover identity a reason to exist in the world, such as merchant, pilgrim or tax collector, so each disguise opens specific dialogue.
when: Designing player or NPC disguises
why: A grounded role gives the disguise dialogue options that fit it

text: Use the target's own interests as an entry point, since showing knowledge of their subject builds trust quickly.
when: the target shares a belief or interest you can match

text: Arguments aimed at one conclusion show their weakness in what they omit.
A cover story about a third party can carry a real truth, because listeners see their own situation in it and react to that recognition.
when: An investigator uses a fabricated tale to prompt a confession
why: Listeners project their own circumstances onto a parallel story

text: A suspect's generous offer may aim to close a matter rather than confess; ask whether it exposes the culprit, protects the victim, or buys silence.
when: A suspect's cooperation seems too convenient

text: Conspicuous courtesy can coincide with a covert purpose, but not every courtesy is sinister; suspicion shapes how it is read.
when: A suspect's courtesy overlaps with unexplained absences
why: Observers primed by suspicion over-read ordinary behavior.

text: Test a stranger's cover story and stated address by checking whether the place it names matches the claim.
Townsfolk who repeat the same cover story can be marked as sharing one origin, so their agreement counts as one source.
Give a planted item a plausible cover story that explains its presence as ordinary character detail.
when: an item is introduced for a later reveal
why: a believable reason keeps the item from looking like setup

text: When a contact cannot check a stranger's face or papers, a shared phrase or gesture can verify the bearer's identity.
when: A contact and a stranger share a secret in advance

text: Give each audience a different version of the cover story or decoy, designed around what that recipient needs to believe.
Use a cover story when the real purpose would alarm others; use a decoy when you want a target to focus somewhere else.
Anticipate the obvious objection a listener will raise and answer it within the replay.
An account that fits the schedule is not proven by fitting it; a consistent timeline only shows the claim is possible.
why: Many false accounts can also match the timeline

text: A minor witness's simple, checkable answer about where someone was on given days can corroborate another person's account.
Confirm a half-remembered line with a document found elsewhere, so the hint is checked rather than taken at face value.
Let the official reason be partly true, so a careful player can separate it from the hidden cause.
when: Designing a faction-driven town where a public crime covers a private struggle.
why: A partly true reason gives players a fair route to see through the cover story.

text: If an item needed only to be destroyed, elaborate precautions would be unnecessary, so elaborate care in handling an item usually points to concealment or retrieval.
when: Judging why someone took special care with an object.
why: Destruction needs no means of recovery, while hiding does.

text: A cover story's absurdity can make it harder to disprove, since few would invent something so ridiculous to hide a crime.
when: Judging a suspiciously silly explanation
why: People assume no one would fabricate something so unlikely.

text: A half-truth linking an innocent person to the crime can mislead more effectively than an outright lie.
Do not accept a plausible explanation merely because it is offered first or with confidence.
when: Weighing competing explanations for an event.
why: Order and confidence of delivery do not establish truth.

text: Keep an assumed identity consistent once adopted, since switching names invites contradictions in the story.
when: A stranger is using a false name

text: Act out the cover persona's habits, speech and manners fully, not only its surface look.
when: when maintaining a cover under questioning
why: behaviour that fits the persona is harder to doubt

text: A suspect's behaviour can change when a new servant appears, so the player must keep the cover story consistent.
when: when a disguise or cover requires NPC substitution
why: Inconsistent cover details alert observers and break the plan.

text: Ground a cover-up in a routine the audience already knows, such as a bath or a hospital delivery, so the cover story feels ordinary.
when: designing a mechanism of concealment
why: Familiar routines seem innocent, so the audience does not question the cover story.

text: Suspects mix a convenient lie with accurate details or silence on the key point, then may admit a lie and concede some truth, shaping the listener's conclusion.
when: A suspect must look cooperative while concealing a key fact; when questioned about a detailed story.
why: A single false claim, surrounded by truth, shapes the listener's conclusion.

text: A cover story holds when observers are incurious and records are hard to check, and fails once claims can be verified.
why: Distance and lack of curiosity protect the story

text: An invented disappearance or crime can explain both a missing person and missing assets, so one fabricated event covers two losses.
when: When a missing person and missing money appear together
why: A single story that accounts for both losses is more convincing than two separate explanations

text: A motive can be hidden by staging a cover story, such as making a killing look like an unrelated crime so suspicion does not fall on the real beneficiary.
when: A culprit wants to deflect suspicion from a clear motive.
why: An unrelated explanation draws the investigation away from the person who gains.

text: A cover story collapses once the questioner already knows the real identity, however convincing the details are.
when: when the questioner holds the real name and face
why: a known identity makes the cover's claims false

text: Mood, family history and dark backstory can pull player attention away from concrete clues toward emotional leads that cannot be checked physically.
when: when a mystery surrounds the crime with atmosphere
why: Emotional content is vivid and easy to follow, so it competes with less memorable physical traces.

text: A group story holds only while every party repeats the same line; one party breaking ranks, or physical evidence contradicting it, causes it to collapse.
when: Multiple parties coordinate a shared account
why: Coordinated stories depend on unanimous repetition and consistency with physical facts.

text: A hidden second identity is supported by a separate residence, separate money, a forged signature and staff briefed in advance, so the public party keeps a clean alibi.
when: when a character must act covertly while keeping a public alibi
why: Layered separation keeps the second identity from being linked to the first.

text: A simple, tidy explanation from a suspect or official can close inquiry and hide the single lead that counts.
when: when a suspect offers an account of a death or an authority offers a sensible reason for a witness's account
why: A reasonable theory satisfies listeners and ends inquiry.

text: A cover story used to gain entry can leave an impression on those inside, and one too convenient makes a doorman or porter question the visitor.
when: using a cover story for entry
why: suspicion rises when a story seems too neat

text: A cover explanation for one detail can deflect attention from a more significant item it mentions, so check what the explanation draws attention away from.
A cover story that is only partly true can cost trust, and the questioner may have to correct it before the witness will continue.
when: An investigator explains their stake to a guarded witness
why: Partial truths get exposed and make the witness withdraw cooperation

text: A partly true story can unravel from one inconsistency, especially when an ally can check its details against facts they know.
A suspect who knows the consequences may give a half-truth or a false denial rather than a full confession.
Speaking too freely in a bluff reveals the limits of what you know.
when: Maintaining a bluff under questioning.
why: Every extra detail gives the listener something to check and test.

text: Overplaying a bluff makes the suspect cautious rather than frightened, which defeats its purpose.
when: a bluff is performed with too much force
why: a cautious suspect hides more carefully

text: A plausible reason can be a cover story. An audience that accepts it unchecked lets the suspect control the narrative.
Discarding a whole account because one part is false is an error, since even a fully false account still leaves gaps to examine.
An account partly true in spirit but false in detail is hard to separate, and one early lie can colour later trust in every source.
when: a source has mixed accuracy
why: errors spread into judgment of the whole account

text: A casually stated reason can read either as a cover story or as ordinary character, so players may misjudge which it is.
An alibi given by a close associate is open to challenge, especially if the associate has little contact with the person they vouch for.
when: Evaluating an alibi from a companion.
why: Limited acquaintance makes the claim hard to verify and easy to dispute.

text: Relying on an account that suits everyone who hears it, since such accounts are easily shaped to fit.
An offer shows what the sender believes, not what is true; a suspect's guess about the sender's knowledge may be wrong and must be checked.
when: A suspect interprets a bribe as proof of guilt or knowledge.
why: Reasoning from an offer is inference, and inference can fail.

text: A visible alibi can be an artifice, so confirm the movement between the two points, not just the appearance.
Overplaying a character's harmless cover can turn them into a joke that never recovers, weakening the later reveal.
when: When a persona is played for comedy over a long stretch
why: Audiences stop taking the character seriously

text: Plans stated as future events in testimony can be overtaken by later changes, so the sequence needs revising whenever new facts appear.
A target who sees through a bluff can call it, so a bluff needs displayed evidence that looks convincing.
Pretending to know a witness's secret can make them reveal more, but the pressure coerces rather than establishes the truth.
why: Fear produces disclosure whether or not the claim is accurate

text: Viewers who share a protagonist's bias may read a cover action as a personal slight and miss its covering function.
when: a distraction is seen through a biased viewpoint
why: the emotional reading takes precedence over the plot function

text: Signs of wealth or novelty, such as new clothing, can betray a cover and expose the investigator.
when: Maintaining a disguise among people who know each other's routines.
why: Unfamiliar or new items stand out against the community's established appearance.

text: Maintaining a deceptive persona can cause inner conflict and guilt, which may degrade the performance of the person wearing it.
when: a long-running deceptive cover
why: moral cost weighs on the player

text: Tidiness proves neither truth nor falsehood: a complete story can be persuasive yet wrong, and rejecting a plausible ending only for being tidy can hide the real answer.
why: Coherence is easy to build from partial evidence.

text: A plausible excuse can conceal the real reason for an arrangement, so excuses should be weighed against what they hide.
A cover story that depends on a partner who does not know their role adds risk of exposure.
when: Staging a cover involving more than one person
why: Uninformed partners can contradict the cover at the wrong moment

text: A decoy lure is only as good as its cover story, and a fabricated report can be traced back to its source.
when: Planting a false report to draw someone out.
why: If the fabrication is traceable, the lure can backfire on its author.

text: A person who acts to create a belief in their own death bears the consequences of that belief.
when: When a presumption arises from someone's own conduct.
why: The law holds people responsible for beliefs they deliberately produce.

text: A cover story never revisited can leave the misled person confused about what was actually done.

1) List every plausible explanation for the odd act, including one not yet named. 2) Keep the list open rather than settling on an authority's preferred one. 3) Test each separately until one survives.
when: An unexplained act has several candidate causes, or early evidence fits several explanations.
why: A closed or early explanation can omit the true cause.

text: 1) Identify evidence the witness cannot account for. 2) Offer a neutral, innocent explanation that fits the facts, not an accusation. 3) Watch whether the witness adopts it, and how.
when: a witness cannot account for evidence and a neutral explanation exists
why: A calm, fitting explanation is less likely to provoke defence than an accusation.

text: 1) Identify the suspicious features of the explanation, such as false names or repeated acts. 2) Find sources the suspect does not control. 3) Check whether those sources support or contradict the explanation.
when: a suspect offers an innocent explanation for suspicious acts
why: independent records are harder to bias than the suspect's own account

text: 1) State the coherent theory against a suspect. 2) List every objection the theory cannot answer. 3) Check each objection against evidence to keep or drop the theory.
when: A convincing suspect appears early
why: Explicit objections turn elimination into a testable task rather than an instinct.

text: 1) Ask the staff who clear the location or hold lost property whether the claimed item was found. 2) Treat a missing record as evidence against the claim.
when: When a witness claims they lost an item at a location
why: Records kept by staff provide an independent check on the claim.

text: 1) Offer a plausible cover explanation for a sensitive topic. 2) Refuse to discuss it on a stated grounds. 3) Let a later clue expose the cover as false.
when: Designing dialogue where an NPC hides the truth
why: A plausible cover misleads on first pass, and the later clue rewards careful players.

text: Keep a cover story simple, repeatable and matching visible facts, such as a name on clothing that others can read and repeat.
why: Visible facts are checked first and must agree, and visible details reinforce the cover through repetition.

text: Give a disguise an ordinary routine, such as an activity that explains repeated presence, so observation of suspects does not raise alarm.
when: A disguised character must observe others over time.
why: A plausible routine supplies a reason to be present.

text: Claim only beliefs you can defend. A target who tests a claim will catch any mismatch.
Check a cover story against direct observation, and drop it once observation contradicts it.
when: When a suspect offers an easy explanation for odd behaviour
why: Direct observation is more reliable than a convenient account.

text: A cover story or reveal must account for physical traces such as clothing or body positioning, since any contradicting trace exposes the lie or gets the reveal rejected.
when: someone offers an explanation for an act; solving a staged crime
why: Physical details are the evidence a staged plan must account for.

text: Make each alibi checkable through a witness, receipt, logged route or environmental clue, such as a sound trigger or arrival time, that the player can reach and test.
when: designing NPC alibis
why: A checkable alibi turns testimony into a puzzle the player can solve.

text: Avoid a cover story whose claims touch records, witnesses or accents that will be consulted, such as a stranger checked against records or a native speaker catching an accent.
Script half-confessions with missing words recoverable from other clues; a gap is a clue only when the investigator notices it and asks.
when: designing NPC confessions in a mystery

text: Agree a common account with a companion before being seen together, since a shared story is harder to break than a single one.
Control people close to a secret by restricting their movements and binding them to silence.
Use a false cover when a subject would refuse to speak to an official, and avoid it when the subject has seen the investigator before or may recognize the cover.
when: Choosing between official and undercover approaches
why: Recognition ends the cover and the access it provided

text: A cover story must explain the secrecy, the odd hours and the hidden workplace together, surviving a glance while failing a closer look.
when: a world needs a reason for hidden activity

text: Correct wrong conclusions openly, since a mistaken reading can still show where the truth lies.
when: when an investigator's earlier deduction proves partly wrong

text: Make rumours of supernatural events partly true but misattributed, so players must check which witness actually saw what.
when: designing rumour-based clues
why: Partial truth rewards verification of the source rather than the claim.

text: Use specific details in an alibi reply, such as arrival time, meals and departures, as checkable points, and check whether a booking reported as made actually led to travel.
when: When evaluating a reply from a distant source.
why: Concrete details can be verified and expose false stories.

text: Use a cover only with a background that can be checked, since an employer may test the applicant with background questions and a named reference.
when: Entering a household or job under a false identity.
why: Reference checks expose any claim that cannot be verified.

text: Offer interview dialogue a partial truth with a stated consequence, letting the player choose between pressing for detail and offering discretion.
when: Writing confrontation dialogue for a guarded character
why: Offering a choice with a clear cost makes the interview an informed decision

text: Send a cover witness ahead of the main investigator so that arrivals look unrelated and the coordination goes unnoticed.
Offer a cover-story dialogue option that unlocks access or new branches, with consequences for the NPC's trust.
when: designing player deception options

text: Record an NPC's agreement to a cover arrangement as a game flag, so a restricted area opens only when that flag is set.
when: when designing access to a restricted area

text: In a deduction puzzle, hide an item where the placing character's limits (keys, ownership, time) allow it, so players can narrow the candidate locations.
when: Designing a hidden item or body for players to find
why: Known limits reduce the search space and make the puzzle solvable by reasoning

text: Trace the source of any written argument a suspect presents, and check it against known works in the world before accepting it as the suspect's own reasoning.
when: A character submits a written defence or document.
why: A borrowed argument shows dishonesty about its origin even when its content is sound.

text: Build a cover story so a contradicting independent witness can expose it, and let the player compare repeated wording against another source.
when: designing an antagonist's false explanation in a game
why: exposure requires an independent check

text: Verifiable cover details build credibility, but one easily checked claim exposes the persona; when a questioner can verify facts, stay vague on testable points.
when: a follower must explain their presence and a questioner can verify facts
why: Verifiable claims are tested by the target; a verifiable invented claim exposes the persona.

text: Describing a source through a cover account protects a person's relationship or position, but risks distrust if the true route to the evidence comes out.
when: Evidence was obtained in a way that could embarrass a person or strain a relationship.

text: Cutting and burning, burying, dumping in a well, or shipping out each have physical or practical costs; the choice depends on which risk is least acceptable.
when: Selecting a method to dispose of a hidden object.
why: Each method exposes the culprit to different detection risks.

text: Use an ordinary cover story only as far as needed; a more elaborate cover risks exposing the inquiry, so keep the purpose hidden without adding unnecessary detail.
when: When a questioner needs a pretext to ask about something without revealing the inquiry
why: A simple cover keeps the inquiry discreet, while excessive detail draws attention.

text: A bluff that lands can be misread as real knowledge, so the questioner may not understand why the witness reacted.
when: A questioner states a guess meant to force a denial.
why: A strong reaction to a guess looks the same as a reaction to proof.

text: A bait is a message written to provoke a specific reaction from a suspect and placed where the target will see it. The investigator watches for the predicted reaction.
Covert inquiry gathers information without alerting the suspect, using a hidden investigator identity, a stated pretext and a paid lure so the witness answers freely.
A physical act can demand knowledge of a site, a suitable build, care with gloves, strength to lower a weight, and composure when handling a body.
Use an advertised item, quest hook or harmless planted note as bait, and track which NPC or faction responds so the player can trace the responder.
when: Designing a lure or faction/NPC tracking within a game world.
why: Tracking responders turns the bait into an investigation thread.

text: An NPC may act differently when believing they are alone, so a hidden observer or a scene where they think no one watches can reveal the truth.
when: Designing an interrogation or a suspect's private moment
why: Unobserved behavior shows what the character hides in public

text: Following a suspect unnoticed gathers more information than confronting them, because the target keeps behaving naturally.
when: gathering evidence before acting
why: a confrontation changes the behaviour being observed

text: Ask about an acquaintance under cover of an ordinary question to get informal confirmation without revealing your purpose.
A message may be planted by an opponent as bait, so solvers should consider who wrote it and why before acting on it.
A prized missing item can be a bluff: the culprit may want it searched for, so its apparent importance should be treated with suspicion.
when: A missing object appears to be the key to a case
why: A search for the object can serve the culprit's diversion.

text: A public offer of something the suspect values, such as return of lost property, can draw the suspect out into the open.
when: When the suspect has a clear want that a notice can address without revealing the investigation.
why: People respond to offers that touch a want, which exposes them to observation.

text: A locked-room impossibility can rest on observers' assumptions about a barrier's condition rather than on a true physical impossibility.
when: a sealed space seems impossible to enter or leave

text: Hide an unusual activity inside an existing routine that nobody questions, so it looks like normal activity.
why: The cover only holds if the routine already exists and is accepted as ordinary.

text: A pretext check can be a mini-game with a fail state, where a poor cover is exposed by one odd remark.
Offer players a controlled test, such as a lure they set, and require a blind rerun before a suspect is confirmed.
when: Designing investigation puzzles

text: Design stealth or dialogue sequences where an NPC observer records what is said on an in-game cue, and let the player review the transcript later as evidence.
when: Designing stealth or dialogue sequences
why: A reviewable record turns overheard talk into usable evidence

text: Bait works best when the target believes they are gaining something they want, so a tempting offer can draw out a cautious person.
when: Designing a lure to draw a specific target
why: Desire can outweigh suspicion, and a target who suspects a trap may still check it

text: Covert dialogue options that require special knowledge can pass unnoticed by NPCs, letting players probe without alerting them.
A sting lures a guilty party with a paired reward: one for the object and one for the person, so anyone bringing the object in is caught holding both.
when: Target is motivated by money and must pass through a predictable channel such as pawnbrokers.
why: The bait exploits greed and the assumption that a thief will sell the stolen item through known channels.

text: A lure can alert the target, closing other leads and causing behaviour change before the test completes, so use it only when that cost is acceptable.
when: When the bait is public and the suspect can see or hear about it.
why: The same notice that invites a response also signals that someone is investigating.

text: A false threat or bait fails if the target doubts it, consults another person, checks identity independently, or an authority calls the plan impossible.
when: A scheme depends on a target not verifying information.
why: Independent contact exposes the decoy.

text: A cautious target who recognises bait as a trap may send a proxy in their place, so the lure reveals an intermediary rather than the target.
when: Designing a lure against a suspicious target
why: Suspicion lets the target avoid exposure by delegating the risk

text: A bait notice can attract the wrong party as well as the right one, so every visitor must still be checked.
when: When a lure is used to draw out the true claimant
why: Anyone interested in the item can respond to the notice.

text: Baiting a suspect whose intent is unknown can turn dangerous, so the bait should be controlled and the suspect's possible violence planned for.
when: the suspect's motives or mercy cannot be trusted
why: a bait that succeeds can still provoke a violent response

text: A bait can reach and endanger people who are not the suspect, and can provoke an outcome worse than the one investigated. Weigh these costs before using it.
Steam, blades and re-gumming can leave traces that a careful owner might notice, so covert opening carries detection risk.
when: Opening a sealed item without the owner's knowledge
why: Tampering methods leave physical evidence

text: A courier who stops or wanders can alter the evidence, so the handoff to the lab must be direct and unaltered.
A reluctant observer who skips parts of the conversation leaves gaps in the record.
when: Relying on a hidden recorder
why: An unwilling recorder does not follow the agreed plan

text: A sting is only as good as its premise; if the lured object was never stolen or never existed, the trap catches nothing.
when: The lure depends on an unverified object.
why: No culprit will come forward for an item that is not in play.

text: A sting that runs too long, or an alert outsider studying its structure, can expose it to the target or to gossip.
when: A trap stays open over an extended period.
why: Time and outside reasoning let the target recognize the scheme's shape.

text: 1) Predict the suspect's likely reaction. 2) Place the bait on a channel the suspect monitors. 3) Watch for the predicted reaction. 4) Use the reaction as evidence.
when: the suspect is likely to act on information
why: A bait turns a prediction into an observable test

text: 1) Send a bland message with no meaningful content to the suspect's channel. 2) Observe the reply or any follow-up. 3) Use the response to identify who is watching or passing messages.
when: When a suspect is hiding behind an intermediary.
why: Only the watcher reacts to content that means nothing to others.

text: 1) Hide your real identity behind an alias, including bookings and advertisements. 2) Adopt a plausible pretext that gives the witness a reason to talk. 3) Offer modest payment and ask for secrecy. 4) Question the witness on details only the true source would know.
when: when a direct approach would warn a suspect who could destroy evidence or coach witnesses
why: the suspect cannot link the inquiry to the investigator if the alias stays hidden

text: 1) Name a specific item the suspect wants back. 2) Offer its recovery through a reward in a notice. 3) Require claimants to describe the item, which filters out people who do not know it.
when: luring a suspect who avoids attention
why: the tempting recovery draws the suspect out while the identifying test screens false claimants

text: 1) Publish a notice naming the missing people and offering a reward for information. 2) Give a code number to route replies privately. 3) Treat each reply as a lead to verify.
when: People with knowledge are unknown but likely to read a public notice.
why: A reward gives a reason to respond, and a code keeps the investigation hidden.

text: 1) Open with innocent questions. 2) Watch whether listeners react; silence suggests they do not understand. 3) If there is no reaction, escalate to riskier questions within the same exchange.
when: When others may overhear but cannot understand the language, and the questioner has that advantage.

text: 1) Test the suspicion quietly first. 2) Restore the original situation. 3) Announce a false plan that threatens the hidden item. 4) Watch who acts before the stated deadline.
when: when a hidden item must be flushed out

text: 1) Wait for darkness and watch the building. 2) Approach quietly, stopping to listen at each movement. 3) Look through gaps before entering. 4) Secure the exits. 5) Check rooms from the ground floor up, noting objects in each.
when: A team raids a suspected hideout where the number and position of suspects is uncertain.
why: Watching first and moving in a fixed order limits the suspects' warning and gives a clear picture of the interior.

text: 1) Create bait, such as a withheld or sealed document, expected to draw out the hidden leader. 2) Treat the bait as working only once the adversary's response confirms it.
when: Trying to expose a concealed leader who controls an organisation.
why: Responses confirm whether the adversary took the bait, avoiding reliance on untested assumptions.

text: 1) Position out of sight near the people talking. 2) Listen without being seen. 3) Note any motive or pressure the talk reveals. 4) Approach the person using that knowledge.
when: A meeting between a suspect and another person can be watched unnoticed

text: 1) Invent a plausible reason for being at the place. 2) Adjust the helper's appearance and props to match that role. 3) Plan views from fixed viewpoints in advance. 4) Set the camera so fine detail is captured. 5) Keep the investigator apart from the helper.
when: When a scene must be documented without alerting people who may be involved
why: A believable cover and planned views avoid suspicion and produce usable records

text: 1) Soften the gummed flap over steam. 2) Slip a thin blade under it. 3) Lift the flap cleanly without tearing. 4) Read the contents, holding the flap folded back. 5) Dry the flap, re-gum it and press it down.
when: A gummed envelope is the only barrier and the contents must stay undetected
why: The method restores the seal to its prior state

text: 1) Create a plausible vacancy in the target office. 2) Place a trusted agent into it. 3) Give clear instructions on what to listen for and how to act unobtrusively. 4) Have the agent report back regularly.
when: Direct questioning of the target would be refused.
why: A placed insider hears staff talk that outsiders cannot access.

text: 1) Write a message in a trusted person's name and voice. 2) Post it from a distant point. 3) Give the target an exact place, time and recognition signs. 4) Keep the real associate under watch. 5) Hide officers near the meeting spot and close in from both ends at once.
when: Luring a suspect into a controlled arrest when a meeting can be set.
why: A trusted-seeming message gets the target to the spot, and simultaneous approach limits escape.

text: 1) Approach a nervous informant away from others and speak quietly. 2) Pass written instructions discreetly so only the two of you see them. 3) Assign the follow-up to a trusted subordinate. 4) Plan a fallback, since the errand may fail.
when: official search would draw attention or a suspect might be tipped off
why: Discretion prevents tipping off suspects; informants may be fearful or unreliable.

text: 1) Watch a suspect's routine until a repeated action recurs at a fixed interval. 2) Obtain a duplicate that matches visible markings and placement. 3) Swap the duplicate in while keeping the item count unchanged. 4) Study the original at a safe place.
when: When an object is in a suspect's routine and cannot be kept in place.
why: A matched duplicate lets the investigator study the object without the owner noticing.

text: 1) Keep the subject on the topic where he is most likely to betray himself. 2) Let him speak freely and use tact to decide when to encourage a line of talk. 3) Seat the hidden observer out of the subject's sight but within the questioner's view. 4) Agree start and stop signals beforehand. 5) Have the observer record passively without hinting or commenting.
when: Interviewing a suspect who would alarm easily at open note-taking
why: A covert observer captures statements without disturbing the subject's behavior
