text: Let players write a reply in the open channel that sets a meeting place, time and payment, and see whether the hidden NPC arrives.
when: The player must reach a hidden contact through an open medium.
why: The contact expects replies through the watched channel, and player-set terms give agency and test understanding of NPC motives.

text: In a game, a posted notice can act as bait that triggers a hidden NPC's reaction. Script the expected reaction and a visible follow-up to reward the player's prediction.
when: designing antagonist reactions
why: Rewards player deduction with a visible consequence

text: Keep the real deadline hidden from the suspect, because the trap depends on the hider acting before it.
Collect suspect evidence in secret, since discovery would alert the suspect.
when: when gathering reference samples from a suspect

text: Keep identifying details out of bait messages, so the recipient cannot trace the bait back to its sender.
why: Traceable bait gives away the test.

text: Avoid covert placement when it could expose the investigator or harm the people involved.
when: Considering placing an agent in a target's workplace or home.
why: Exposure and harm outweigh the information gained.

text: Avoid covert inquiry when the witness is likely to repeat the conversation to the suspect, unless the questions are carefully controlled.
Enter a room on a harmless pretext to observe the objects people use there without arousing suspicion.
Do not treat a confirmed presence at a scene as proof of the act; being there and committing the crime are different claims.
Design the agreed recording cue so it looks like ordinary behaviour, because a signal the subject notices alerts him.
when: Setting up a covert recording cue
why: A conspicuous signal reveals the observation to the suspect

text: Hide wires along floor seams and room edges, and cover them, then check the concealment more than once.
when: Running wires for a concealed device.
why: A visible wire alerts the people being watched and ends the advantage.

text: Covert methods gain information but carry ethical cost; one proposed limit is to use improperly gained information only when it reveals criminal activity.
when: When deciding whether to use information from questionable surveillance.

text: Leaving the room to let suspects speak freely gives access to private talk, but the device must stay undiscovered until the chosen moment.
when: Planning a covert listening operation.
why: Early discovery of the device ends the advantage.

text: A creature that needs food and shelter is unlikely to persist for years in an unoccupied place, so its presence there is doubtful.
when: when a sound or sign suggests an animal in an abandoned place
why: food and shelter are needed for long-term survival

text: Weigh a creator's own denial or claim about their sources alongside the physical evidence rather than dismissing it.
when: Judging whether a work was modeled on a specific real place or event.
why: A creator's statement is itself a source about how the work was made.

text: Witnesses usually recall events, sights and sounds, but rarely recall the dates or the intervals between events.
when: Eliciting testimony about a sequence of events

text: Witnesses of the same event often recall small details differently, so minor disagreements do not by themselves show that one is lying.
Ask whether a witness's clock runs true; a known offset from true time lets the investigator correct the time the witness reports.
when: A witness's timing depends on a household or public clock, or the witness mentions keeping their clock off true time.
why: Knowing the clock's bias lets the investigator adjust the reported time.

text: A survivor who saw companions fall bounds their deaths to a short time window.
The same timing can support opposing claims, so apply the feasibility check separately to each claim rather than to one favoured story.
Timing data gathered over a short period may not reflect the subject's full range of behavior.
when: when estimating a subject's schedule from limited observation
why: Short samples miss variants the subject uses at other times.

text: Fix the crime to a precise minute so that alibis and the crime can be measured against the same clock.
why: A shared clock makes each alibi's window directly comparable to the event

text: Anchor witness times to events others can confirm, such as a clock striking, a bell, a door closing or a vehicle leaving.
An alibi is judged against the time a crime was believed to occur. When that believed time shifts, an earlier statement can change meaning.
An object seen before one time and gone at a later check bounds when it was present; the window lies between the two observations.
when: A witness reports an object at two observation points.
why: Absence at a later check limits how long the object could have been there.

text: A sequence of symptoms that worsens in fixed stages acts as a clock, showing the victim nearing a fatal end and creating a deadline.
when: A threat progresses through ordered stages.
why: Each stage signals proximity to the final outcome.

text: Witnesses may misjudge how long a process takes; check the duration against a second source where possible.
why: A wrong duration shifts the entire computed window.

text: 1) Pick a vivid event both witnesses remember and fix its date. 2) Place other events before or after it. 3) Verify the anchor first, because a misremembered anchor shifts the whole sequence.
when: Witnesses give conflicting times and need a common reference point to order events.
why: Without a shared reference, the sequence of events cannot be built reliably.

text: 1) Lay all accounts side by side on one timeline. 2) Mark which times are fixed by outside events and which are only estimates. 3) Test each alibi and claimed time against the fixed points.
why: Alibis are only as strong as their anchors.

text: 1) List the scheduled events, such as NPC routines and phone calls. 2) Record each as a checkable time window. 3) Let the player compare windows to find who had the opportunity.
when: a game needs a shared timeline of character movements

text: Anchor each event to one time source shared by all observers and the reader, such as a public clock, a watch set by someone else, or a standing meal time.
when: when several observers record events
why: A shared clock lets every time-stamped event be compared directly; a public clock lets several witnesses check it independently.

text: Map each witness's claim to the exact moment they could have observed it, and discard claims whose timing their position could not allow.
when: reconstructing who was where and when
why: a claim is usable only if the witness was positioned to see it

text: Ask handlers whether they noticed the individual feature and when; a recollection made before the event is stronger evidence.
Ask a witness to tie each event to a clock time rather than a loose period, so the account can be checked against other facts.
when: When re-questioning a witness whose account is vague
why: Exact times can be cross-checked, loose periods cannot

text: Let a faction's influence shift over time, such as after a vote, to model a weakening hold that opens a window for a new approach.
when: designing faction power that changes across the game

text: A controlled press notice is a deliberately vague public statement that hints at a breakthrough, planted to provoke a reaction from a target.
Persuasive weight and formal proof are separate standards; corroboration may convince yet fail formal acceptance, and stricter standards reject evidence lower ones accept.
when: Judging whether supporting evidence will convince an authority or be weighed by different people.
why: Lower standards accept a neat conclusion that stricter ones reject.

text: Proof is either direct, such as an eyewitness to the act, or circumstantial, a chain of linked facts pointing to the act. Direct proof is often unavailable.
when: Deciding how a case can be established.
why: Many crimes leave no witness, so inference from linked facts is the usual route.

text: Stories in this formula close on the protagonist's death rather than an arrest or trap, using a note, letter or editor's statement to end the frame.
To link a fragment to its source, recognising its design or pattern matters more than knowing its value, age or maker.
Use a sudden personal crisis that forces intervention, so the truth comes out before the suspect can escape.
when: a suspect is about to flee or conceal the truth
why: Intervention compels disclosure within the scene.

text: Make the act of discovering a hidden space hazardous, so the reveal becomes a survival scene and not only an explanation.
why: Physical danger turns exposition into action and raises stakes at the reveal.

text: A custody record such as a pawnbroker's duplicate names an owner and a value, and can conflict with a story told about the object, exposing a second account.
when: An object's history is recorded by a third party
why: Independent records often contradict the account given by the person holding the object

text: Describing a family's desperation makes an unusual source acceptable, because the audience understands why people turn to it.
when: An unconventional source or remedy is accepted by characters.
why: Desperation provides the motivation that makes the source credible within the story.

text: A brief cross-examination of a witness can be read as weakness by observers, even when the examiner has little to gain from a longer one.
when: When a party chooses to question a witness briefly.
why: Observers judge the length of questioning as a signal of strength.

text: A hidden mark on a key item, tracked across scenes, lets a game detect whether an NPC or player moved the item and confirm its later return.
when: In games where key items may be moved or stolen.
why: Persistent state on the item records its movement history without relying on player memory.

text: A deadline reversal, where relief such as a pardon arrives already overtaken by events, resets the stakes and changes the whole situation.
The detective story formula: the reader sees the crime or its setup early, then watches the investigator read physical traces that overturn an official belief about who did it or how.
why: Each story turns on a wrong suspect or wrong explanation, with the solution coming from forensic detail that authorities dismissed or missed.

text: 1) Identify what should have remained at the scene if the object or body was moved. 2) Inspect the route between the scene and exit for those traces. 3) Ask household witnesses whether any item is missing. 4) Infer whether the subject left under its own power.
when: A body or object appears to have vanished
why: Systematic checks separate forced removal from voluntary departure

text: 1) List each strange effect separately. 2) For each, ask which ordinary act could produce it. 3) Identify the device or mechanism behind it. 4) Trace where any concealed route leads.
when: When a reported phenomenon has several distinct effects
why: Breaking effects into ordinary causes exposes the mechanism behind each

text: Be wary of a guide who advises avoiding other acquaintances and trusting no one unknown, since this keeps you dependent on that guide.
when: when a source advises restricting your contacts
why: Limiting access to other sources makes the guide the only channel of information.

text: Stage the final reveal as a demonstration with physical evidence rather than a verbal accusation alone.
when: resolving a mystery with a hidden culprit
why: Physical proof makes the reconstruction verifiable within the fiction and harder to dispute.

text: A person may remove labels or empty bottles to keep others from blame, which alters the physical record of a death before anyone examines it.
Excess precaution is often cited as a cause of detection, but the claim is drawn only from detected cases and cannot estimate how often precautions succeed.
Use a plausible, harmless role or pretext when direct questions would alert a suspect or make staff guarded.
when: When an investigator needs information from people who would refuse formal questioning
why: A non-threatening cover gets people talking and opens doors that stay shut under direct questioning.

text: Preparatory acts made before a delayed event, such as protective measures taken shortly before, can reveal that the act was planned.
when: Investigating a delayed or planned harmful act
why: Advance preparation shows the agent anticipated the outcome

text: Keep physical proof separate from early assertions, so players must search the world for it rather than accept the claims.
when: when a claim needs verification
why: found evidence feels more authoritative than stated claims

text: Stage a reveal as a sequence of partial proofs, each confirming one suspicion without giving the full truth.
when: Building a multi-step mystery
why: Each partial proof keeps tension while the complete picture is held back.

text: Keep the detective's private preparation visible but unexplained so that its later use feels earned.
when: Introducing a protagonist's hidden work early in a story.
why: Visible but unexplained preparation rewards the player when it pays off.

text: Build the opposing case complete on paper, so the protagonist's doubt, not a hole in the evidence, drives the story.
why: A convincing case forces the solver to find a deeper flaw

text: A grave may hold a planted corpse standing in for the intended victim, so exhuming it can expose the substitution and the plot behind it.
when: A burial or funeral appears to mark a known death.
why: A body in a grave is usually taken as proof of death.

text: Each added precaution taken to hide an act adds a trace someone can later examine, so extra care can itself cause detection.
1) Move the obstacle without disturbing the trace. 2) Lift the trace with careful fingers and avoid crushing it. 3) Unfold it gently so that surface residue such as dust stays in place.
when: Recovering a small fragile piece of evidence
why: Handling that preserves residue keeps the trace a record of where it lay

text: Leave objects in place so the scene can be read as it was, and do not disturb evidence before it is examined.
Stage the final proof so it is performed in front of the culprit, not only described afterward.
when: writing the climax of a mystery
why: A proof the audience watches happen is more convincing than a proof reported after the fact.

text: Give the first theory a physical prop that later reads as staged, so the obvious suspect seems guilty until the prop is reinterpreted.
when: building an early false suspicion
why: A prop that seems to prove guilt is later shown to have been placed.

text: Judge a crime by its conception and execution, which reveal its psychological signature (personality and method), not only its physical traces.
A case built on an old crime and a family inheritance combines three elements: a motive, a hidden object, and people with a stake in finding it.
A crime's style can be analyzed along seven dimensions: approach, conception, technique, imagination, attack, method, and organization.
when: When comparing a crime's style with candidate suspects
why: Separate dimensions allow a structured comparison of personality

text: Let players match a crime's style against NPC personalities, not only against physical clues, so character reading becomes a route to the answer.
A recurring signature can signal one responsible person, so compare incidents for it; yet it may also mislead, inviting a single-author assumption while the real link lies elsewhere.
when: When several incidents may share a responsible person; when linking several crimes in one investigation
why: Shared patterns suggest common responsibility; but a shared pattern invites assuming one author when the real connection lies elsewhere.

text: Build a scene timeline the player reconstructs by questioning NPCs, giving each a different time window so accounts combine to fix when an event happened.
when: Designing a generated mystery scene.
why: each partial window is incomplete alone but adds up when combined

text: The crime window runs from the last certain sighting or last moment the victim is known alive to the first known death or latest possible time; the event lies between.
Compare device readings with other clocks and testimony, and treat an unexplained discrepancy as an open question, not a minor detail.
why: a small mismatch can hide a hole in the timeline

text: Give NPCs a behavioural timeline so players can build a motive profile by comparing what different observers saw.
Bound a missing person's possible departure by the period when the place was unobserved; this turns an open question into a limited search window.
Use a loud, timestamped event as a timer: players compare when they heard it with when they last saw the victim.
A scripted errand that splits the party creates a timed window for another actor; log the window so the player can reconstruct what happened.
when: Scripting events during separation
why: Recorded timing lets players test alibis against the evidence

text: Make each NPC reaction, such as hiring guards or sending for help, a visible timeline step the player can track.
when: designing deadline-driven quests
why: Visible steps let the player sense progress toward the event.

text: Keep an event log of NPC locations, so a watchman NPC's logged visits can contradict a suspect's claim.
A candle's burn state gives a rough elapsed-time interval rather than an exact clock; a candle that has not guttered shows the open period was short.
when: Using a burning candle as evidence of elapsed time.
why: Burn length indicates a rough duration, not a precise time.

text: A near-miss event such as a door tried and left closed lets a player feel the threat without being caught.
when: When designing tension in a timed sequence.
why: A close call heightens threat while preserving player agency.

text: A brisk walk can cover a route in about three-quarters of the time a normal-paced walk takes.
when: Estimating walking times for a route.

text: Duration estimates depend on how the captive experienced time, so verify them against an independent clock when one exists.
when: a witness estimates how long a journey took
why: perceived time under confinement can differ from actual time

text: Confusing not later than with exactly at leads to false precision about when an event happened.
when: Stating a time of death from bounds
why: A bound is a limit, not a measurement

text: Stating a time window too loosely lets every suspect fit, so it stops filtering anyone.
when: Witness times are vague.
why: A wide window includes everyone's movements.

text: 1) Extract any stated date or time from an NPC's offhand remark. 2) Compare it against the in-game calendar or known schedule. 3) Note whether it coincides with the event.
why: turns casual dialogue into a lead

text: 1) Estimate a rough time window for the crime. 2) Place each claimed movement inside or outside that window. 3) Check each account against the others. 4) Treat approximate times as ranges rather than exact moments.
when: event times are estimates and alibis rest on one person's word
why: timelines reveal gaps and contradictions

text: 1) Record the exact time of each event as witnesses report it. 2) Mark the gaps between events. 3) Use physical states as clocks. 4) List who could have been present during each gap and who was seen leaving.
when: reconstructing when a crime occurred and who could have done it
why: physical evidence and witness reports together bound the window

text: 1) Create darkness or stillness so the audience has no other way to pass time. 2) Add recurring time markers. 3) Escalate faint warnings: a glimmer, then a smell, then a hiss. 4) Deliver the climax, then return to quiet.
why: Layered, escalating cues keep the wait meaningful and make the climax feel earned.

text: 1) List each theft's location and timing. 2) Find the time when the affected places were empty. 3) Use the window and the places to narrow the suspect pool.
when: a series of crimes needs a bounded time and place
why: A shared window of opportunity shows who could have acted.

text: 1) hook 0-4%: show method, no case yet; 2) inciting case 4-13%: missing person, recurring payment; 3) summons and confession 13-27%: push party, reveal first motive; 4) crisis 27%: a death makes a suspect obvious; 5) false solution 34-42%: arrest, reconstruction names second culprit; 6) pursuit 42-74%: river chase, false lead collapses; 7) reveal 74-98%: empty container, confession, final culprit.
Give each NPC a logged route or timestamped departure and arrival, so players can compare tickets, keys or door logs to find unaccounted gaps.
when: Designing a deduction puzzle around NPC movement.
why: Checkable logs turn gaps into discoverable contradictions.

text: Give NPCs daily schedules logged per time slot so players can spot absences and build alibi tables by questioning companions at the right times, checked against statements.
when: designing suspect schedules
why: schedules make absences checkable

text: Trust a stopped timer as an event time only after cross-checking it against another independent timer.
when: multiple timers on the same scene disagree
why: a single timer may be wrong or altered

text: Check a suspect's account of intervals against other witnesses, since recalled durations may conflict between sources.
Flag NPC alibis that no other character confirms, so players know which accounts need a second source.
Design an NPC to behave differently when the player leaves an area, and make the change visible when the player returns.
when: When designing state changes that depend on player absence
why: Visible change after absence rewards players for revisiting and reinforces the sense of a living world.

text: Have NPC dialogue state times and places that the player can check against other NPCs' accounts.
when: When designing NPC testimony in a game.
why: Cross-checkable details let players test consistency.

text: Proving an alibi for the wider period does not help if the critical window itself is uncovered.
Let NPC alibi witnesses change their dialogue state after the player applies pressure or offers a bribe.
when: When designing NPC dialogue that responds to player actions
why: Dynamic state makes the witness's testimony a result of the player's choices.

text: An NPC scripted to be in a guarded place at the moment a trap fires gives an apparent alibi that the player can break by checking the trap's trigger time.
when: designing NPC schedules around a trap or event
why: Trigger-time checks let players test an apparent alibi against the event.

text: Use NPC dialogue to reveal schedules, such as a guard leaving duty at a set time, that the player can then act on.
Give an afflicted state a bounded schedule of days or rests, so testimony follows a checkable calendar the player can compare with other events.
Store an NPC's alibi as a time window, and let the player break it by finding a clue that places the NPC elsewhere.
when: Designing an NPC with a claimed whereabouts
why: A time window gives the player a specific claim to test

text: Build a night timeline puzzle from fixed points, such as a visit, a departure and a dropped item, leaving one unverified interval for the player to resolve.
when: when designing a deduction puzzle around a suspect's movements
why: fixed points give the player anchors and one gap gives a goal

text: Make each individual incident look like a mishap, so the shared mark is the only way players can see that the incidents are linked.
Money obtained through a crime may be paid out if no crime has been formally charged.
Treat a crime as a network: the person caught is often one link, and the one who ordered the act lies further along the chain.
Compare testimony from witnesses of different status, so each account can be weighed against the others.
Disputes across several arenas at once, such as records, shared grounds, land and boundaries, feed each other, so each challenge or reversal draws in more of the community.
1) Collect each witness's independent account of one event. 2) List the concrete physical details in each. 3) Compare the details for exact matches. 4) Treat matches as links and mismatches as leads.
when: Two witnesses must be tied together by a shared event.
why: Checkable details separate real connections from coincidence.

text: Offering a detail another witness reported can revive a memory, but the recall may then reflect the prompt rather than perception.
why: suggestion can blend with genuine perception

text: Cross-check independent records, such as chemists' receipts and nurse-kept books, against one another.
when: Several records cover the same supply.
why: Agreement between separate records is stronger than one record alone.

text: 1) Identify a lead from an object. 2) Send inquiries to each possible source. 3) Compare replies against each other. 4) Re-check any conflict before drawing a conclusion.
when: When tracing an unknown person through objects and records.
why: Independent sources reduce the risk of acting on a single incorrect record.

text: 1) Keep a private notebook of names, initials and facts. 2) Record every name or alias seen in each source. 3) Look for matches across unrelated sources and link threads through them.
Give diaries, accounts and case files dated, cross-referenced entries that players check against other clues, such as receipts or patrol schedules, to place events on a timeline and spot conflicts.
when: When designing a document-based investigation.
why: Cross-references turn separate records into a checkable sequence.

text: Give each in-world document a known author and known bias, and let the player cross-check documents against each other and against related dates to rebuild an event.
when: When designing in-game ledgers, letters or court notes as clues.
why: Known bias lets the player weigh each document rather than accept it as neutral truth.

text: Do not rely on one document alone, since a register or log can be incomplete, and cross-check it with other records where possible.
Let a specific word, item or place presented to a character trigger a reaction that unlocks a dialogue branch.
when: Designing character interviews
why: Cues make dialogue respond to what the player actually shows

text: Design each reading of a cryptic clue to lead to a distinct, checkable location, so each reading can be tested.
when: Writing an ambiguous inscription or message that points to several targets.
why: Distinct, checkable targets let players test readings instead of guessing.

text: A cryptic remark spoken in front of others can warn the target and let them prepare.
why: the target learns that the speaker knows more than they should

text: An interpretation built on a few visible cues can be overturned by fuller observation that the witness did not weigh.
1) Deliver a short, cryptic message to one suspect with no explanation. 2) Observe the reaction on the spot. 3) Note any follow-up question or request to repeat.
when: when testing whether a suspect knows a specific fact

text: Offenders do slightly more than the crime requires; concealment steps, especially those needing fine control, can leave traces the actor would otherwise avoid.
when: When a crime was staged or concealed by the offender.
why: Concealment adds steps, and each extra step can leave evidence of intent.

text: Suspect a deliberate act only when some detail resists the accidental explanation; evidence of intent rules out explanations that require chance.
when: When weighing a natural versus a deliberate cause.
why: Otherwise every mishap looks suspicious.

text: A deliberate act is unlikely when it would defeat the culprit's own aim, such as burning a scene when concealment was the goal.
why: A culprit normally avoids actions that expose the plan.

text: A character designed to be flawless removes the weak point an investigator needs; leaving a plausible overlooked detail gives the story a way to be discovered.
when: Writing an antagonist or planner whose plan must be discoverable.
why: Without any overlooked point, there is no hook for detection.

text: Hide the key document with the culprit, and let its later appearance prove the fraud the culprit committed.
when: a document is central to the motive
why: A document the culprit controls exposes the fraud when it surfaces, rather than being found by chance.

text: Each incident can be waved off as accident, so a campaign built from single deniable events stays hard to prove even when its cause is certain.
when: when a rival uses small, plausible-looking hostile acts
why: Deniability protects the planner, since each event has a harmless explanation on its own.

text: A suspect who believes they were seen may act to correct the timeline, which can create new evidence.
when: A suspect fears a sighting has exposed them
why: Corrective actions leave traces that can be followed

text: A narrator who presents as detached may still reveal a personal stake through partly denied motives and minimised admissions, which readers can reread after the reveal.
when: when an unreliable narrator hides a motive
why: Concealment in narration leaves traces that become clear only after the twist.

text: A contradiction planted early, such as luxury against a claimed poverty, is read as character detail rather than clue, so it works as a later clue.
when: when an early detail conflicts with a character's stated situation
why: Audiences file contradictions as personality until they become relevant.

text: Culprits in mystery resolutions may be punished publicly, escape through social standing, or be handled privately to avoid scandal.
when: deciding how a mystery ends
why: Social position and discretion can change what justice looks like.

text: Hide the culprit in a familiar, constantly seen role or routine, such as a waiter, postman, servant, or habitual task in the victim's space, so their presence goes unremarked.
when: Hiding the culprit among ordinary scenes or choosing a hidden culprit
why: Routine and familiar presence is seen constantly and rarely examined, so suspicion does not fall on the culprit early.

text: A culprit who volunteers unprompted explanations, such as motive asides, leaves a checkable slip in their own dialogue.
when: writing an antagonist's dialogue
why: unrequested explanation can contradict later facts

text: Make an antagonist dangerous through clear internal logic and motive rather than arbitrary irrationality.
when: Designing a villain
why: Consistent motive makes a character both frightening and understandable.

text: Trigger a reaction when the player presents a detail that only the culprit could have known.
when: Designing a confession or exposure moment
why: Exact private knowledge is a strong signal that breaks a suspect's composure

text: Reject a culprit theory when physical traces, such as hair or marks, fail to match the proposed agent.
Turn a character's obsession into a concrete act, so the reveal shows a violation rather than an abstract fixation.
Let the lure used to trap the culprit be the culprit's own advertisement or message, so the trap feels like a discovery rather than a coincidence.
when: designing a trap or lure for a hidden antagonist
why: A lure drawn from the antagonist's own behavior is more believable to both the antagonist and the player.

text: Place the true director among the searchers or helpers, and give him a useful investigative role, so he stays close to the case without drawing suspicion.
why: Proximity to the investigation hides the culprit and gives him access to evidence.

text: A trusted helper whose knowledge is precise from the start can be revealed as the true antagonist later, and the reveal feels fair because the early clues were visible.
when: Designing a twist where an ally turns out to be the controlling party.
why: Precise early knowledge is a clue the player can later reinterpret, so the unmasking reads as a payoff rather than a cheat.

text: A culprit who knows enough to act but not enough to conceal leaves traces that a specialist can read.
when: When an offender's method is clumsy, unusual, or uses non-specialist tools.
why: The gap between acting and concealing exposes what the offender did not intend to show.

text: A mystery can open with a visible but dismissed detail, such as a figure seen in the garden, and later pay it off as the true mechanism behind the crime.
when: planting clues in a scenario's opening scene
why: Early dismissed details are remembered and recontextualized once the real mechanism is revealed.

text: Treating a private conviction as if it were evidence can lead an investigation toward the wrong conclusion.
when: An investigator is certain of a suspect's guilt or innocence.
why: Certainty substitutes for proof and skews what is pursued.

text: 1) Ask who profits from a death or crime. 2) Check whether that person's stake actually points toward the crime. 3) Map each victim against any payout threshold and the effect of each death on the beneficiary's claim.
when: Ranking suspects by gain, especially when rewards depend on conditions.
why: The beneficiary's real stake determines whether the gain supports or undercuts suspicion.

text: 1) Define the culprit's grievance, fear or passion. 2) Imagine planning the act from that state. 3) Check whether the act is consistent with that state. 4) Read the physical evidence from that viewpoint.
when: The puzzle turns on why a person acted or who would act that way
why: Motive-led reasoning narrows suspects before physical evidence is tested.

text: Let the culprit make a mistake that a witness can later recall, so the mistake becomes the trigger for the reveal.
when: when a disguised culprit must be exposed
why: a remembered remark connects the disguise to the person hidden beneath it

text: Plant the true culprit's motive early in a minor scene so the reveal recontextualizes known material instead of appearing from nowhere.
Keeping an investigator's role hidden stops the other side from adjusting its behaviour, but the advantage ends once the role becomes known early.
when: An investigator can act more effectively if the opposing side does not know their involvement.
why: Secrecy removes the chance for the other side to counter; early disclosure removes that advantage.

text: Culprits often return to the scene of their crime at least once, driven by unease, unfinished business or an unexplained pull.
when: Investigating a crime with an unknown perpetrator, or when a scene is revisited after time has passed.

text: Offenders often break down at the disposal step, even intelligent or careful ones; impulsive offenders rarely plan elaborate disposal, and intelligence does not guarantee clever concealment.
when: Modelling or predicting how a culprit conceals a crime or behaves after it.
why: Disposal demands sustained planning and composure, and physical constraints can defeat intelligent offenders.

text: A guilty party's written account explains, excuses and inflates its author, so it reads as a narrative with a purpose rather than a neutral record.
when: a suspect writes their own account of a crime
why: Self-justification and vanity shape what is told and omitted

text: A culprit can predict how investigators will behave and prepare goods to be found at the right place and moment.
Culprits prepare cover answers in advance, such as a partly false letter or a borrowed name, so they have something ready if questioned.
when: a culprit expects that an object or act may be questioned
why: a borrowed name avoids an obvious link to the culprit's own

text: A reader who sees a name they associate with a known person reads the message with matching expectations and may not question the sender.
when: a letter is signed with a name the reader links to someone
why: expectation shapes how the message is interpreted

text: A culprit may frame a deception as a kindness and recast the accuser's suspicion as spite, turning attention onto the accuser.
when: a suspect is challenged about a concealed act
why: Redirecting motive shifts scrutiny away from the concealed act.

text: A host may assume a motive, such as debt, that explains a party's secrecy without requiring an explicit lie.
Questioners who assume guilt before a hearing ask leading and trapping questions and read refusal to confess as stubbornness.
when: interrogations where the questioner has a stake in the outcome
why: Assumed guilt makes every answer look like evidence for the charge.

text: A clever culprit who believes they are safe may make a false move that reveals them, so waiting can expose a guilty party.
when: The suspect is active and may act to cover their tracks.
why: Confidence can lead a suspect to act in a way that betrays them.

text: A person with a motive too weak to convict them may still fear being blamed, and that fear can drive a second, lesser act.
when: A suspect is threatened with suspicion but has no decisive motive.
why: Fear of exposure can motivate action that looks more guilty than the underlying motive.

text: A culprit's motive can combine a belief in his own exceptional ability, contempt for other criminals, and a wish for absolute power outside the law.
A culprit's own retrospective or private written record can reveal motive, self-image and plans directly, without investigators discovering them through others' testimony.
when: Telling a story where the reader learns the motive from the culprit.

text: Assuming a suspect is lying can be a useful check, but it misleads when the suspect is telling the truth.
Reason from how a culprit would normally behave; an outsider rarely bothers to tidy a weapon, reload it, and relock a door.
when: When no direct witness exists and the case relies on post-event actions.
why: Unusual actions after an event reveal the actor's likely familiarity.

text: Let the solution rest on an element the audience has already seen as harmless, so the reveal recasts that element as the cause.
why: A familiar, dismissed detail becomes surprising once its true role is shown.

text: Hold a trusted ally back as the final suspect, so the elimination ends on the hardest case.
Record what a culprit believed about the player character, so the belief can serve as a hook for later confrontations.
Make the culprit someone the reader and characters rely on, so earlier signs of suspicion become proof once the answer is known.
Assume everyone involved may have something to hide, and press each witness on what they have not disclosed.
when: A witness's account may conflict with another's or contain an omission.

text: Use a perpetrator's known care elsewhere as a baseline; a trace that contradicts that pattern is suspect.
when: judging a clue against the culprit's established habits
why: A clue that breaks the pattern of care stands out

text: Show the contradictions in a culprit's inner logic, such as devotion beside anger, because they reveal motive without over-explaining it.
when: A culprit's psychology should explain the crime.
why: A rationalization that is too neat reads as a device rather than a person.

text: Rotate the culprit archetype across cases, such as insider, outsider or trusted helper, so a familiar structure stays unpredictable.
when: Varying a series of mystery cases built on one formula.
why: Repeating the same culprit type makes the answer predictable even when the structure is familiar.

text: Give a hidden culprit a sympathetic motive, such as grief, so the reveal reads as a human cover-up rather than a villain's plot.
A reversal mechanic can change which NPC is marked as culprit once a hidden item is traced to them.
Accepting a culprit's stated cause as the whole truth closes the case without further checks and ignores other readings, since a confession can be partial.
when: Weighing a confessed motive or writing a reveal that depends on it.

text: Assuming the obvious heir is the beneficiary, without tracing each transfer or reading the document's terms, can send an investigation to the wrong person or hide the real motive.
when: Following an estate's transfer chain or weighing an heir's apparent benefit.
why: Transfers can pass through several people before reaching the real gainer, and the terms of a document can change who benefits.

text: Assuming a second person exists because a threat feels external is a mistake; the source may be one actor wearing two masks.
Assuming a suspect is responsible because of one damaging act overlooks helpful acts they also performed.
A culprit who assumes an incriminating document was destroyed may not search for it, so the document survives and exposes the culprit later.
when: when a culprit's assumed destruction of evidence is never checked
why: Assumptions about what was destroyed can be wrong.

text: Treating an assumed link between a clue and a trait as proven is a common error that can misdirect the whole case.
Ruling out a suspect by assumption, without checking, can hide a real motive, so each weak candidate needs an actual check.
when: Dismissing candidates during motive enumeration.
why: Unchecked exclusions leave real motives unexamined.

text: Asking who benefits from a death is too broad a test, since many people would benefit from almost any death.
when: When weighing benefit as evidence
why: Broad benefit describes many people equally

text: Assuming the culprit took a missing item, without checking the timeline and who had access, is a mistake.
Assuming a crime follows a known pattern can lead investigators to search for a familiar signature that is absent.
when: a crime does not match known habits
why: The search wastes effort and can mislead.

text: Assuming a suspect's gender or social role without evidence can make investigators overlook the real culprit.
A theory can quietly assume the criminal's knowledge or preferences exactly where the theory needs them.
Place incriminating items where the culprit did not search, and make the omission traceable to the culprit's assumptions rather than convenient.
when: when planting an overlooked clue
why: A convenient oversight without a reason invites doubt.

text: Establish that a crime occurred before building a motive, since a motive only means something once a death is shown to be a murder.
Do not conclude that a witness is lying just because statements conflict; test which version the physical facts support first.
why: Conflicts can arise from honest error as well as deceit.

text: Unfamiliar customs such as tipping, seating, greetings and dress are read by outsiders as insults, threats or signs of character.
A custom only carries weight if it is widely shared; where habits vary across people, a broken habit proves little.
when: Habits vary widely across the people involved.

text: Treat an NPC's ward or talisman as a clue to their belief and fear, not as proof that magic exists.
when: Designing an NPC who carries a protective object.
why: The object reveals psychology while leaving the cause of events open.

text: Some strangeness is real but lies in human choices, such as the obstinate retention of a damaging wording, rather than in hidden forces.
when: when an odd document or motive resists easy explanation
why: human choices often produce oddities that look uncanny

text: A long-repeated folk belief passed through many speakers gains a false air of truth and shapes what people perceive without their noticing.
Folk beliefs about guilt, such as a murderer unable to bear the victim's blood, and links between hair or build and temperament are superstition, not proof of guilt or character.
Choosing the most dramatic, mystical reading of a foreseen event over a mundane explanation such as coincidence leads investigators astray.
A family prophecy can be reused to explain every later sudden death, turning separate events into a supposed pattern.
A folk rule about reading faces, such as distrusting direct eye contact, can confirm the observer's existing suspicion rather than reveal anything about the person.
why: The rule supplies a reason to believe what the observer already expects

text: A folk saying can recast a frightened person's flight as superstition, so the real cause of their fear is never examined.
1) Collect the incidents from the relevant period. 2) Filter for ones of the same kind. 3) Check each pair for a shared location, person or record.
when: Starting a search for links between incidents
why: Builds a candidate set of events that might connect

text: Cursed-relic lore or a seer's hint serves as misdirection: players blame a curse or monster; a human NPC culprit is revealed by a rational check such as the operator's influence.
Give staff NPCs a reference or record with flaws the player must weigh, rather than ignore or accept outright.
Plant a folk saying early that later proves literal, so a casual phrase becomes a key to a later puzzle.
Make a cursed-object clue that names a suspect contradict the timeline or physical evidence, so careful players can detect the mismatch.
Give a cursed location a sound clue with a mundane source, and let its lore shape interpretation while allowing a rational check.
A body with an unrecognisable face is often accepted, because examiners cannot swear to who the face belongs to.
Make one timestamp deliberately damaged so the player must infer the missing digit from other clues.
why: Inference from other clues turns the gap into a puzzle rather than a dead end.

text: Let a damaged or burned object support an inference about its material, and have players record that inference as uncertain.
Destroying an item does not destroy what is attached to it, and burning materials such as felt can produce smell that draws attention.
when: Attempting to destroy evidence by fire
why: Fire leaves fragments, fittings and odours that persist and can be noticed.

text: A report cut short leaves the key fact unknown, so the investigator must return to the source to confirm it.
Broken edges and other damage on the object do not reflect tooth marks, so exclude them from the comparison.
Partly destroyed or broken evidence can mislead when the surviving fragment is read on its own.
1) Test the altered residue with a flame. 2) Dissolve the residue in alcohol. 3) Examine it under a microscope for fibres and binder, then compare with a known sample.
when: the original material is burned or altered

text: Flag erased or worn words as unreadable, not filled with assumed content; never read a gap as containing the answer it lacks; record a missing final answer as a gap.
when: transcribing damaged records
why: assumed content can pass as evidence

text: Make a wound or damage pattern readable: its angle and location should reveal the attacker's position and the victim's posture to the player.
when: when designing environmental or body damage as clues
why: readable damage lets players deduce the event

text: Treat weather or wear as lowering a clue's legibility rather than erasing it; partly readable evidence still carries information.
Dated records fix event order, show who was present and who had motive, and can reveal a writer's unstated intentions.
when: Investigating presence, opportunity, motive, or a diary or log.
why: Dates create a cross-checkable sequence; entries reveal intentions.

text: Date each in-world journal or diary entry and show its heading, so players can order events and place entries against the events they describe.
when: Presenting a story or writing in-world documents through dated records.
why: Dates and headings give context that shapes how the text is read.

text: Store dated in-world documents, portraits, letters and deeds as quest-log entries so players order them, spot turning points, gaps and contradictions between official and travel records.
when: Designing mysteries or investigative quests built from dated records.
why: Visible ordering lets players find contradictions, turning points and gaps themselves.

text: Store NPC letters and statements as dated versions so players can spot contradictions between letters or with later statements, and detect revisions and retractions as clues.
when: Designing NPC dialogue memory or narrative clues where an NPC can change or retract a statement.
why: Dated records make change over time detectable.

text: Confirm recalled and single-source dates against a second independent record before building a timeline; one error can break every dependent link.
when: Building a timeline from recalled or single-source dates.
why: Memory of dates is unreliable, and one record can be mistaken or incomplete.

text: Dated sequences can reveal a rival's escalation campaign that single incidents hide, yet ordering events can make a trend look inevitable when it was not.
when: Attributing rival hostility favours the sequence view; presenting a chronology as progression calls for caution.
why: Sequence turns scattered events into a pattern, but also suggests direction and causation that may not exist.

text: A day-by-day ledger of an NPC's movements makes unexplained gaps visible, letting players notice what the NPC did not account for.
when: players review an NPC's recorded movements
why: Gaps stand out when events are laid out in sequence with their times.

text: People struggle to fix a past date without a written note, and alarming events further blur the timing.
when: a witness is asked when something happened
why: Without records, memory of dates degrades

text: People dismiss a time reading they believe is inaccurate, such as a bell that seems wrong, even when other sources agree with it.
when: time sources conflict
why: a prior belief about one clock overrides the other evidence

text: A dated message fixes a person's travel and timeline, giving a checkable point in a sequence of events.
A dated, step-by-step record shows who was summoned, what they were asked, when they replied, and how they answered.
when: reconstructing a community dispute from documents
why: Sequence and dates make each step checkable.

text: Without a clock, a steady bodily rhythm such as pulse can be counted to estimate elapsed minutes.
when: when no clock is at hand

text: Compare dates across documents to expose impossible sequences, such as a person shown alive or travelling when a record says otherwise; one inconsistent date marks a cover story's weak point.
when: A claim about death, whereabouts, travel or a cover story depends on dates.

text: Fix an undated or uncertain recollection by linking it to a memorable event, such as a public holiday or a fault costing a day's trade; confirm with a second witness.
when: A witness gives an undated or unsure recollection of a day.
why: Tying a date to a notable event makes recall more reliable.

text: Estimate how long an object has been in place from its condition, such as mildew, matting or overgrowth, by comparing it with known growth or decay rates.
when: An object is found away from the main scene, or a physical condition is used to date an event.
why: Weathering accumulates over time; a known rate converts condition into elapsed time.

text: Estimate unused time from dust depth or decay such as mould: dust builds at a steady rate, so heavy layers mean long neglect, light layers or none mean recent use.
when: Estimating how long an object has been unused or unattended.
why: Decay and dust accumulate at roughly known rates, so their state tracks elapsed time.

text: Dated repeated incidents can reveal a recurring interval no single event shows; trust the cycle only once exceptions are explained, since an unexplained one may mean the model is wrong.
when: A series of incidents may share a hidden schedule.
why: Single events look random; their dates together expose the cycle.

text: A date of death earlier than an event can remove a person from consideration as a claimant or heir.
when: when ruling out candidates by timeline

text: A dated item written on a day its supposed author was away on public business deserves a second look before that author is credited.
when: Candidate author's travel or duties are recorded
why: The author could not have been present to write or seal it

text: Prefer day-by-day dated records when reconstructing a sequence of events, since undated accounts cannot establish order.
Later actions reveal earlier knowledge: a group that changes plans before dawn must have learned of the problem during the night.
When a person claims knowledge of an event, check when that knowledge was first voiced, since it may show whether they could have known it beforehand.
when: when a witness's knowledge of a night's event is in question
why: Knowledge that appears only after the event may have been learned from others.

text: Date an object from the condition of what it touched; a snapped but still living stem suggests the object landed recently.
when: estimating when an item was placed
why: living surroundings show little time has passed

text: Date a change in a person's behaviour or mood to when it began, since that onset fixes a point in the timeline; household members often notice it first.
when: building a timeline of a suspect's conduct
why: A change with a known start is an anchor for other events.

text: Use a dated sequence of movements to test whether a witness could have been present at a given time.
when: checking an alibi or presence claim
why: Dates make presence testable

text: Verify a stated timeline against independent official records before trusting it, since the claimant's dates may be false.
when: A character presents a schedule as fully controlled.
why: Official records register events on their actual dates and can contradict a self-serving account.

text: Date a found object from its context, such as the coins it contains or the rulers named in the text.
when: when identifying an object from clues alone
why: Known historical sequences narrow down when an object belongs.

text: Judge how recent a scratch or cut is by contrast: fresh damage shows bright, unoxidised material, while old damage has dulled to match the surrounding surface.
when: When deciding whether damage happened before or during the current scene.
why: Exposed material darkens and dulls with time and exposure.

text: Dated in-game documents can establish a deadline, so a player who notes the cut-off can see why one NPC benefits from an event before it.
A dated object bounds events: it cannot have reached a place before its date, and its travel time limits when it could have been brought there.
when: placing events on a timeline using dated items
why: physical objects move at limited speeds and cannot predate their date

text: Attach a confidence level to each dated entry, so approximate dates count for less than firm ones.
when: building a timeline from uncertain records

text: Contemporaneous letters fix a person's intentions and mood at specific dates, and later statements can be checked against them.
when: a victim's own writing is the main record of their state of mind
why: Writing made at the time records circumstances before any later change

text: A dated item left in a room, such as a tear-off calendar showing a given day, can fix the day a person left.
Date and identify a building from its construction traces and surveyed plans, ranking specific evidence above local tradition.
when: Confirming a surviving structure's age or original occupant
why: Physical and documentary evidence can be checked; oral stories often cannot

text: Date an undated document by reasoning from where its examination took place and who in the surrounding area is named.
Ordering dated depositions, votes and orders shows what was owed and known at each moment, and can expose an action as breaking an earlier agreement.
when: Checking claims about who owed what, and when.

text: Compare a person's stated role against behaviour recorded on the same day, since a claimed role can contradict a dated record.
when: a person's public image conflicts with a diary entry

text: Disputed dates can be argued from the season a given month falls in and from the dating conventions of the period.
when: Two sources give conflicting dates for an event.
why: Seasonal and period conventions limit which dates are plausible.

text: A dated record that matches an undated entry by name, place or event can fix the identity and date of the undated one.
when: When a dated primary record exists alongside an undated fragment.
why: Matching shared details links the two entries to the same event.

text: Log a faction dispute as dated in-world entries, so contradictions between entries and later claims become clues the player can check.
when: designing a readable document trail for a quest
why: Dates let players sequence events and test claims.

text: Dates tied to personal events such as a birthday, a journey, or a death are sturdier in memory than bare numbers.
when: When reconstructing dates from recollection.
why: Personal events are more memorable and more likely to be recalled accurately than abstract dates.

text: Undisturbed dust on a surface can date marks: marks with no dust over them are recent, because dust had not yet settled on them.
when: When the object's history of being undisturbed is known.
why: Dust accumulates over time, so its absence on a mark indicates recency.

text: Use a contemporaneous diary or log as the primary source for exact dates wherever one exists.
why: Written records made at the time are more precise than recollection

text: Establish a baseline before dating marks or dust: misreading old dust as recent, or recent handling as old, misleads conclusions about who entered.
when: Interpreting footprints, marks, dust or disturbed ground.
why: Mark age decides which event produced them; dust baselines must be known before disturbances can be dated.

text: A narrator's dates may be accurate while the account of intent is not, so dated facts and claimed motives should be assessed separately.
when: Evaluating a first-person account.
why: Accurate timing does not guarantee accurate reasons.

text: An estimate off by more than a decade signals either a flawed method or a different document than assumed.
when: Comparing a dating estimate with a stated date
why: Large gaps indicate a problem in the method or in the document's identity

text: A date error may be innocent, so verify it with another source before reading guilt into it.
A dating conclusion depends on the assumed growth rate and on the trace moving at a steady pace; check both before trusting it.
A date alone does not confirm content, so check the wording against how the event must have worked.
Keeping a position number in memory while counting is fragile; record positions with physical markers instead.
1) Collect every dated entry on the subject. 2) Order them chronologically. 3) Check each against the others for conflicts. 4) Mark gaps and overlaps. 5) Decide which matter for the question.
when: Sources are partial or unevenly dated, or claims and alibis are checked against dated entries.
why: Sequence exposes contradictions, gaps and overlaps, showing what was possible and what was disputed.

text: 1) List each event with its date. 2) Add purchases, absences and arrivals. 3) Check the order of events. 4) Test each claimed cause against the sequence before accepting it.
when: a witness reports a cause that must be checked
why: a sequence shows whether a supposed cause came before or after the effect it explains

text: 1) Examine period-specific letterforms and conventions before reading the content. 2) Estimate an age range, ideally within about a decade. 3) Compare the estimate with any date written on the page. 4) Record any gap as a finding.
when: A document's age or authenticity matters and a period reference is available
why: Physical conventions change over time, and reading content first can bias the dating

text: 1) Recall the scene's state at the last check. 2) Compare it with the current state. 3) Treat any object that has appeared since then as recent.
when: the timing of an object is the key question

text: 1) Compare the date a letter was written with its arrival date. 2) Estimate transit delay from its routing. 3) Check the writer's stated expectations against that timeline.
when: Using dated documents to fix a sequence of events
why: Indirect routing can make arrival far later than sending

text: 1) Name the witnesses to the document's creation. 2) Ask each for the time. 3) Offer a candidate time and see whether witnesses confirm or correct it. 4) Narrow the date to the window all accounts support.
when: when a document's date is uncertain

text: 1) Collect dated records such as orders, dispatches and appointments. 2) Order them by date. 3) Check whether preparation predates the event an alibi covers. 4) Treat earlier preparation as evidence the alibi was arranged.
when: an alibi covers a journey or event
why: Dated paper trails can show that a plan began before the apparent alibi

text: 1) Date the record. 2) Match its date to the moment of a key event. 3) Use it to establish what a person was reading or knew at that time. 4) Check the content against an intact copy.
when: A dated document links to a key moment.
why: Dates tie documents to events and reveal what people knew.

text: 1) Collect the witness's account as a sequence of dated facts. 2) Restate the whole account in order. 3) Let listeners check the restated order against the facts.
1) List each dated act or statement. 2) Note its speaker. 3) Mark which voices or parties are absent at each point.
when: When several dated documents must show how opinion changed.
why: Ordering the record reveals trends and silences.

text: 1) Record the date each document can support. 2) Order events so no document precedes an event it refers to. 3) Check each date against an independent record. 4) Use a third party's diary to fix contested days.
when: Dates on letters, diaries, warrants and reprieves are the main clues
why: Ordered dates expose impossible sequences

text: 1) Collect indirect signs of time, such as temperature, unlit fires and completed or unfinished tasks. 2) Compare them against the routine of the person. 3) Estimate the death window from the mismatch.
when: When rebuilding when a death occurred without a firm medical time
why: Indirect environmental and routine signs can bound the hour when direct evidence is weak.

text: Log dated household events such as repairs or faults so players can order them, use them as fixed timeline points, and test alibis; such events may later prove decisive.
when: Building a timeline the player can inspect.
why: Dated events give players fixed points to reason from; a minor event can anchor the order of other events.

text: Stamp world items with dated, location-based records such as receipts or ledgers, so players can check NPC dialogue against them.
Keep dated records in the game world so players can check when a claimed piece of knowledge could have reached a character.
Let players assemble dated official returns into a timeline of who was where, supporting alibi checks.
Record each statement with its date and attach it to the case file so later readers can see who said what and when.
when: When collecting formal testimony.
why: A dated, attached record makes the sequence of statements checkable.

text: Shift NPC dialogue or routine after a key event so players can date when the NPC's attitude turned.
Give an elder's account of an old event a date, an age at the time and a stated uncertainty, so the player can weigh it.
when: designing NPC testimony about past events
why: Memories of old events drift, and the player needs cues to judge reliability.

text: Give players a dated case file with entries from several offices, and leave one outcome for a later document they must find.
Use dated reversals, such as a town revising its verdict years later, as late-game revelation beats.
when: When planning story twists in a long-running timeline.
why: Delayed reversals pay off earlier events.

text: Log threats with dates so players can check whether the misfortune actually followed them.
why: Dated records let players test the sequence instead of accepting it.

text: Recognising a dead person is weaker than recognising a living face, because appearance changes after death.
A rumour of past deaths can be set up early as village memory and dismissed by the protagonist, then overturned by later physical evidence.
when: Designing a mystery where the reader should initially accept a false explanation
why: A dismissed rumour lowers suspicion of the real cause, so later evidence can shift belief sharply.

text: Place plausible dead ends that a player has a real reason to test, since an unworthy lead will not mislead anyone.
when: When designing false leads in an investigation
why: A lead that nobody pursues cannot misdirect.

text: Most leads in an investigation end in dead ends, and only a few prove useful.
when: Planning how many clues to follow.
why: Investigation is mostly elimination.

text: When a physical trail ends at a dead end, shift weight to other evidence so the case still moves forward.
when: a clue matches no known source

text: A dead-end clue still informs: a trace that leads nowhere can reveal that another route into the space exists.
when: a physical trace that yields no passage or answer
why: the failed lead itself narrows the possibilities

text: A negative result, such as a shop lacking an item or a negative lab test, can close one branch while pointing the player to where to look next, keeping the mystery moving.
A dead NPC's belongings in an attic or chest can carry a half-finished plan, which the player reconstructs from the objects and where they were stored.
A timed group decision ending without a verdict feels like a dead end unless it opens a second attempt with a new objective, mirroring a retrial.
when: A timed group decision fails to reach a result.
why: Without a new objective the audience has nothing to pursue; a new objective keeps the player engaged after failure.

text: A reveal delayed without interim evidence, or with no new clue in the next scene, reads as a stunt and frustrates the audience, who may start to mock the character.
when: A reveal is delayed without interim evidence.
why: Without partial evidence the delay reads as vanity rather than method.

text: A conclusion formed early can bias how later facts are read, so each confirmation should be checked on its own terms.
when: An investigator forms a conclusion before gathering all evidence.
why: Early commitment makes later evidence seem to fit more than it does.

text: A wrong early assumption, such as the size of a mark, corrupts every later inference built on it, so each premise should be verified before building on it.
when: Reconstructing a process from partial evidence
why: Downstream deductions inherit the error

text: A trail that ends at a stranger, bookmaker or shop is often a dead end, so plan the next verification step before the interview.
Dismissing a message because its obvious explanation seems adequate.
why: The obvious explanation can hide the real meaning of the clue.

text: Refusing every inference can mislead as much as jumping to one, because caution taken too far blocks inference entirely.
An owner may dismiss an early count as unimportant, so a loss can be noticed without being acted on until a direct question.
when: A count comes up short but seems minor.
why: Small discrepancies are easy to ignore until later evidence gives them weight.

text: Reading a document's presence in a place as proof of a person's presence there is an error; the copy may have gone elsewhere.
when: Inferring who was somewhere from a found document
why: Documents travel independently of their handlers

text: A normal test result can end an inquiry prematurely, so a scenario should let a failed test still lead onward.
when: when a diagnostic test is the player's main route to the answer
why: A passing or inconclusive test can close the investigation if it is the only path.

text: Treat a dead NPC as a possible alternative state, and reveal the true identity only through a grave check or body examination.
when: designing a character whose death may be staged
why: a hidden identity keeps the death ambiguous until tested

text: When a clue leads to a dead end, offer the player a different route to the same goal so they are not left searching at random.
when: Designing a clue chain for a player-driven investigation.
why: A dead end with no alternative pushes players into aimless searching.

text: Do not abandon a lead after one failure; check whether the failure has a cause, and treat it as direction for a new search.
when: A lead produces no result
why: A failure may have an identifiable cause that points to another line of inquiry

text: Delaying questioning allows a witness to be traced less easily, so each postponed interview can cost time in which evidence is lost.
when: When a witness's silence delays the investigation.
why: Trails cool and witnesses become harder to trace over time.

text: A deadline the audience cannot track, or that never visibly changes the target's behaviour or gets acted on, loses tension and feels arbitrary or like a cheat.
when: Setting deadlines in a story.
why: Tension depends on the audience seeing the deadline affect outcomes and follow-through.

text: Treat a reconstructed timeline as unconfirmed until each link has its own cited source, such as verified witness accounts or records; loose estimates do not settle it.
when: When a reconstructed or inferred timeline is presented as fact in an investigation.
why: Inferred times can be wrong, and weak sources produce timelines that fall apart.

text: Trust a witness's timing detail only after independent verification; a single observer's confident wording carries little weight, and one unchecked time can shift the whole sequence.
when: A detail comes from a single source, or a witness's stated times anchor a timeline.
why: Confident wording is not physical evidence; one unchecked statement can make a suspect appear cleared or guilty.

text: Use an external deadline, such as a hearing, trial date or approaching authority, to keep the investigation moving, force evidence out and cut off stalling or bargaining.
when: Pacing a long investigation, or when authorities or escape threaten to arrive.
why: A fixed external deadline creates pressure, and time pressure limits the suspect's options.

text: Reject any proposed explanation for a note whose timing does not fit the time available.
why: a plausible story fails if it cannot happen in the window

text: An externally logged event, such as a recorded phone call, gives a checkable anchor for a timeline.
why: It can be verified independently of anyone's memory

text: An unusual arrival time is significant only once its cause is known; ask the person directly and check their reason against the record.
A fixed deadline builds expectation toward a set moment, and a story can defeat that expectation when it arrives.
when: when a threat is tied to a date
why: The deadline focuses attention, and its subversion or fulfilment drives the climax.

text: Attach a specific consequence to each deadline, so failing a condition triggers a defined outcome.
when: Designing timed pressure in a story or quest.
why: Concrete consequences make the deadline meaningful and let players plan around it.

text: Withhold the culprit's name until a stated deadline to build anticipation before the naming.
when: at the climax of a public reveal
why: a fixed deadline gives the audience a clear point of anticipation

text: A fixed, publicly known deadline gives a countdown that charges each intervening day with worry and shapes every character's plans.
when: A fixed, publicly known future moment is announced in advance.
why: A visible countdown turns each day into a reminder, and shared knowledge makes choices urgent and comparable.

text: Presenting a report as the first and only source creates urgency.
An external event that shortens a deadline can force hidden actors to act sooner, driving the plot forward.
An unaltered second timer can expose tampering with the first, because its reading reveals when its hands were moved.
when: two timers on a scene disagree
why: the untouched timer keeps honest time

text: An external event that draws a crowd can interrupt a confrontation and delay the decision it was building toward.
Verify clocks, timestamps and delivery assumptions before concluding who acted; unverified or unreset clocks, and one person's hour assumed exact for another, can overturn a timeline.
why: Wrong timing assumptions produce a confident but baseless reconstruction.

text: One unverified fact, such as an unconfirmed appointment, can undermine an entire timing chain.
Too much waiting drains tension, so each delay should change the situation or raise the stakes.
why: Repeated waiting without change loses the audience.

text: Skipping too much time can leave the audience feeling that something important was missed.
A trap question built on a wrong timeline can clear a guilty target or expose the questioner, so verify your own dates before relying on the test.
why: A test is only as good as the timeline it is checked against.

text: Repeating the deadline too often dulls suspense, because reminders lose their force once they become routine.
when: A countdown is restated frequently.
why: Constant repetition makes the date familiar and less alarming.

text: A deadline can be defeated by a trick that changes who must attend the scheduled event.
when: A character needs to avoid a fixed-time obligation.
why: Changing the participants can invalidate the deadline without changing the time.

text: Too many simultaneous deadlines make the sequence of events hard to follow.
when: Several time limits run at once.
why: Competing clocks overload the player's tracking of what matters first.

text: When decay or ageing acts as a timestamp, expose its rate so players can check the reasoning rather than guess.
Do not commit to an action while its timing cannot be checked.
when: the window for acting depends on information that cannot be confirmed
why: Acting on unverified timing risks walking into people who are no longer incapacitated or away.

text: Do not accept a departure time when the only witness admits they did not see the movement; leave the timeline unverified.
when: When a timeline depends on an unseen movement.

text: Use the timeline to name the time windows that lack witnesses, and direct questioning at those windows.
Track the in-game day explicitly so the player can catch a witness who misstates it.
when: Designing a game with witness testimony tied to time.
why: An explicit calendar gives the player a reference to test claims against.

text: Set a deadline for the final act only if it is credible, since an arbitrary deadline weakens suspense.
when: Adding urgency to a climactic investigation stage.
why: Audiences discount deadlines that feel contrived.

text: A poisoning scene can hold a label or packet that a player matches to a shop, and a tidying NPC can erase it unless the player acts first.
Ligaments outlast muscle, so bones still joined by ligament suggest most soft tissue was gone before separation.
when: Judging how a skeleton was handled or how far decay had progressed before it was separated.
why: Ligament persists longer than muscle through decay, so joined bones indicate soft tissue loss before separation.

text: A body altered after death to imitate another victim leaves a physical detail, such as a removed item, that reveals the true sequence of events.
when: when a false scene is staged to hide the real crime
why: the alteration requires an action that leaves physical evidence

text: A death can be caused by a psychological event, such as a sudden shock from seeing a person, so the apparent murder is not a physical attack.
when: Designing a death scene where the cause is not a physical attack.
why: Reinterpreting the cause removes the crime and dissolves the investigation without a culprit.

text: Remains evidence requires knowledge of decay and handling; without it, the same marks carry no meaning.
when: Interpreting physical traces on skeletal remains.
why: Trace meaning depends on understanding how decay and handling produce them.

text: Loose debris lying beside a damaged spot shows that the damage is recent, because nobody has yet cleaned it away.
when: When a damaged surface may have been made just before the scene was examined.
why: Debris is removed by dusting or handling, so its presence indicates little time has passed.

text: Look for debris, such as mould knocked from soles, on hard surfaces where prints stop to find evidence of the route.
when: prints end at a hard surface
why: loose material is shed where the walker crossed

text: Debris landing on a high surface suggests the hand that caused it belonged to a taller person than the expected suspect.
when: broken items scatter across a scene
why: landing height depends on where the breaker stood

text: Debris type suggests a location: sawdust points to a carpenter's workshop, a dead leaf to a garden or common, a cobweb to a wine cellar or potting shed.
An official verdict can be reasonable given the information it received, even when a better-informed party holds facts that were never disclosed.
When two experts disagree, find the single question whose answer separates their readings, and put it to the witnesses.
when: A cause or diagnosis is disputed
why: One decisive answer can settle a disagreement

text: Treat the reliability of the decision-maker as a separate question from the reliability of the testimony.
when: when a verdict is contested
why: a flawed judge can reject sound evidence, and a sound judge can accept weak evidence

text: 1) Reduce the case to one decisive question. 2) List each explanation. 3) Record the facts each explains and the facts each leaves unexplained. 4) Prefer the explanation that accounts for most facts.
when: A case rests on one contested item
why: Separating explanations by the facts they cover shows which one is best supported

text: 1) Give the full timeline of events. 2) State the conclusion. 3) Ask the listener to judge whether the evidence holds. 4) Offer a conditional exit, such as dropping the matter if told to. 5) Record the reply.
when: when a listener's decision determines whether the investigation continues
why: Making the listener's choice explicit turns the briefing into a decision point with a recorded outcome.

text: Decline a hidden-client case when the unknown interest could compromise the investigation or when uncertainty builds on several sides at once.
Decline an offered test when accepting it would expose the cover, and keep reading the suspect's reaction to the offer.
when: a cover identity is at risk
why: Declining protects the cover while the reaction still gives information

text: A decisive clue that is re-tested can dissolve after it has done its work, removing the basis for the verdict while other evidence remains.
when: A case rests heavily on one physical token and the token can be examined again.
why: A second examination can undo the first without any new evidence entering the case.

text: A single checkable discrepancy, such as a date conflict between two records, can be the decisive proof where broader argument fails.
when: building a case
why: verifiable contradictions are hard to dismiss
