Credit between rivals with different strengths alternates, since each side's method wins some rounds and the other's wins others.
when: Two investigators with contrasting methods share a case

text: Evidence that helps one suspect often also gives that suspect a motive, so each fact must be weighed against everyone involved.
when: Several suspects share a set of facts.
why: A fact favouring one person may incriminate them.

text: An unverifiable account shows only that it cannot yet be checked; it establishes neither innocence nor guilt.
Publicly known crimes are skewed toward detected failures, because successful crimes are never reported, so the visible record does not represent all crimes committed.
when: Learning from famous or documented cases.
why: Only discovered cases enter the public record, and discovery usually follows a mistake.

text: Most people reason forwards from events to results, and few can reconstruct the path back from a given end.
Each resolved answer or constraint narrows the next, since constraints interact, keeping a single-trace inquiry focused and reducing directions to check.
when: when reasoning through a mystery's facts or an investigation has a single trace with several linked questions
why: One resolved fact points to further conclusions.

text: Puzzles and journal entries should match clues found earlier, so the player's prior knowledge confirms the answer rather than introducing it.
when: designing investigation puzzles
why: Matching rewards the player's prior knowledge.

text: Set explicit evidence tiers, such as lead, supporting and proof, and make the game enforce the difference between them.
when: Designing investigation or accusation systems.
why: Explicit tiers stop a lead from being treated as a verdict.

text: Track confidence in each deduction separately, distinguishing suspected from proven, so players can act on a suspicion before it is proven.
when: when designing a deduction or journal system
why: Players reach suspicion well before proof, and labelling the difference keeps their reasoning honest.

text: Players read a crooked chain of cause and effect as a sign of a human plan, so a convoluted puzzle reads as deliberate rather than supernatural.
when: when a puzzle's mechanics involve several indirect steps
why: Winding, traceable paths communicate intent to the player

text: The more exact a parallel between two cases, the more likely it is a coincidence rather than a rule; use it to suggest questions, not to settle answers.
when: using a previous case to reason about a new one
why: a striking match is often accidental

text: A partial, unfinished change shows both what was done and that someone may return to complete it.
When a decision arrives through a chain of replies, each document can be checked against the others to make the order of decisions visible.
when: Several letters or messages each prompt the next.
why: Each link is a separate document, so the sequence of decisions can be verified link by link.

text: If a task is too heavy for one person, assume a helper was present, and that the helper had to be close enough to avoid detection.
when: A physical task exceeds one person's strength
why: Physical limits constrain how many people were involved.

text: Ask who a person was waiting for, and why they waited at that particular place rather than at home, to infer their intent.
when: a person is seen lingering somewhere unusual
why: The choice of location reveals an expected meeting or departure.

text: A document can confirm one fact while leaving the key question open; note what each clue establishes and what it does not.
Argue from checkable detail rather than claimed witness, so the detail carries the argument and not the speaker's authority.
Leave the purpose of an antagonist's arrangements unstated, so the eventual reveal remains open.
when: when showing a schemer's actions before the reveal
why: an unexplained purpose keeps the reveal available for later

text: When a physical estimate contradicts a timeline built from other clues, treat the conflict as a lead to resolve rather than something to ignore.
when: a timeline and a physical estimate disagree
why: one source must be wrong, or the event happened earlier than assumed

text: A substance used to make a mechanism run silently suggests its user wanted silence, which narrows the list of people who needed quiet.
when: the residue has a known purpose

text: Before relying on an unusual physical action in a reconstruction, test whether it is feasible and whether anyone would have noticed it.
when: when a reconstruction depends on an action few people would perform

text: Build a chain of small checkable facts toward a conclusion, verifying each before using the next.
when: Assembling a case from many minor findings
why: Each verified link supports the next and limits error

text: A match between a trace and a suspect shows presence, not purpose, so ask what the person intended as well as who made the mark.
when: A physical match links a suspect to a scene
why: Motive and method can differ from what the traces alone suggest.

text: Rank candidate explanations by how probable each is given how a person of that character would realistically behave, not by whether it is merely possible.
when: several explanations are offered and one must be chosen
why: many explanations are possible, but few are probable

text: Physical constraints such as layout, sightlines and access points can rule out most candidate methods quickly.
A link to the crime that cannot be traced to any one suspect usually signals a missing fact, not proof of guilt.
when: a connection exists but points to no specific person
why: The unresolved link often reflects an unknown fact.

text: A crowd that agrees quickly has often been shaped by a few voices, so quick agreement is not proof.
when: when judging whether public consensus is genuine

text: Rank dated records above self-reported figures and oral tradition, and check any one person's claim, such as a count of descendants, against independent records.
when: sources disagree about a family's history or numbers
why: A self-report is one person's claim, and tradition is weaker than a dated entry.

text: Require stronger evidence at each escalating stage, so detention and especially conviction need more than a claim of a supernatural sighting.
A puzzle can ask the player to reassemble a torn map or ledger, using edges and margins as matching hints.
when: Designing document-based puzzles in generated levels.
why: Matching fragments rewards observation and gives a clear solution path.

text: Gate hidden information behind dialogue that requires the player to reconstruct the suspect's actions exactly, unlocking secrets only after an accurate account.
when: When designing interrogation or confrontation dialogue
why: Requiring an accurate reconstruction rewards careful reasoning over guessing

text: Let geometric clues such as wound angle, trajectory or footprint direction eliminate some suspects but not all, so the player checks the remaining options against room positions.
when: building a deduction puzzle around a physical clue
why: keeping several options open leaves the final choice to the player

text: Let a body's injuries contradict a staged scene so a careful player notices the mismatch.
Link dying-word fragments to locations or characters players have already met, so they know where to follow each fragment.
when: When placing hint fragments across the level
why: Familiar anchors tell players where to go

text: Rules valid for physical quantities hold only within their domain and may not transfer to motives, social behavior or psychological evidence.
when: Applying a quantitative rule to human choices or motives.
why: Parts do not always add up to the whole outside their domain.

text: Clients often mix what they know with what they assume; separate the two and check each against independent sources before accepting them.
when: Taking a client's account at the first interview
why: Assumptions presented as facts can mislead the investigation.

text: When each dead end gives a clear, checkable result, the pattern of falsehood itself becomes information that points toward the truth.
when: When a chain of false leads is followed in order
why: Repeated failures of a similar kind reveal a deliberate design behind them.

text: One sound inference tends to suggest others, so a single absence can open a chain of further reasoning.
why: Each conclusion creates new expectations that can be tested.

text: Equally strong evidence against two suspects leaves an audience with no clear answer about which one is guilty.
Each new fact, such as a destroyed document or a jammed key, shrinks the pool of people who could have entered.
Unforeseen events chained together can push a concealed plan into the open, even when each event alone is minor.
An ambiguous clue carrying two meanings stays open until one discovered object resolves which meaning holds, so the player reasons toward a single answer.
why: A single decisive object closes the question that ambiguity left open.

text: Forensic reports can give a time range rather than a single time, and different examiner NPCs can give different ranges with stated reasoning for the player to compare.
when: When designing forensic evidence in a game.
why: Ranges and disagreements make the player weigh reliability rather than accept one answer.

text: A detective combines three faculties with logic: close observation of details, knowledge of how people think, and insight into motive and feeling.
when: Designing an investigator character or deduction system.
why: Each faculty supplies a different kind of input, and reasoning joins them into conclusions.

text: A solution is a chain of inferences where each link depends on the one before; one wrong link, such as a single wrong date, invalidates the whole conclusion.
Accepting a confession without testing its details against physical traces lets false or incomplete admissions pass.
Deductions must rest on facts shown to the audience; a clue held privately or a reveal built on unseen facts cannot be weighed and reads as a cheat.
when: Writing a reveal that depends on information the player has not seen.
why: Players cannot reproduce a conclusion built on hidden facts.

text: A single indicator, such as a pulse or a shift in language under pressure, has several possible causes and is weak evidence that must not be overread.
when: when one sign or reaction is used to judge a condition
why: Different causes can produce the same sign, and the reaction may have innocent causes.

text: Accepting an explanation for a trace without identifying the person who gave it leaves the link unverified, and any third party it names still needs identifying.
why: The explanation may be invented to cover the link.

text: One wrong or newly discovered fact can undermine a whole reconstruction, letting the suspect dismiss it and forcing the theory to be rebuilt from scratch; overstating costs credibility.
why: Overstating a deduction costs the investigator credibility.

text: Verify assumed facts first: an unverified anchor, personal detail or link passes its error to every later inference, even where later details seem confirmed.
when: when a conclusion depends on one assumed fact about a suspect
why: A knowledge-based deduction inherits the uncertainty of its premises.

text: Confidence does not track accuracy in poor light, weather, crowds or strong emotion; observers give conflicting directions or confident identifications, and excitement can inflate impressions.
when: when evaluating a witness report, locating a sound or event, or spreading a sighting
why: Each observer fills the gap with a different guess, and confidence and emotion inflate impressions beyond the observation.

text: Confidence in one explanation or one reading of a tell, even an expert's, can close off other leads and make the real suspect easy to miss.
why: Certainty closes off other leads.

text: Reading 'consistent with' as 'proves' leads players and reviewers to accept a conclusion that only one reading supports.
when: Evaluating evidence that fits a claim without excluding alternatives.
why: Consistency with a claim does not rule out other explanations.

text: Dismissing an objection without testing it can hide a real gap in the reconstruction.
Accepting a convenient reinterpretation without testing it is a mistake, even when it dissolves the contradiction.
Keeping the anchor fact broad, such as naming a culprit, lets one dispute collapse the whole chain; a narrow time-bound fact is safer.
when: Stating the basis of a deduction.
why: A broad claim invites challenge, while a narrow one survives scrutiny.

text: An inference built from a visit, a letter and a manner of speech can feel like proof while each link is unverified, and one new fact can collapse it.
Inference chains can seem far-fetched to listeners until their basis is stated, even when each conclusion is correct.
when: a conclusion is shared without its evidence
why: listeners cannot judge a leap they cannot follow

text: A witness who claims honesty too often invites suspicion; such claims should appear only where the character would plausibly make them.
why: Repeated protestations read as performance

text: Treating a witness's clenched hand or nervousness as proof of a lie leads an investigator to conclude guilt from a subjective impression alone.
when: An investigator is certain of a witness's dishonesty based only on body language.
why: Body language is ambiguous and the investigator's impression is not verifiable evidence.

text: A summary that lays out a chain of beliefs and events but leaves the conclusion unstated shifts the burden of testing onto the listener.
why: The listener must then test the chain personally rather than hear a finished argument.

text: A staged meeting only works if the target is confident enough to attend; a wary target will not walk in, so the trap fails before it can close.
why: The plan depends on the target's own expectations, not on the investigator's control.

text: A stated reason for a choice that others cannot reproduce cannot be checked, which weakens any account built on it.
A claim repeated by several people is not the same as a checked record, so each link in a custody chain must be confirmed independently.
when: Tracing an item through several hands
why: Repetition can make a weak link look strong and hide the link that matters most

text: A test that depends on an unverified handoff proves little either way, whether it passes or fails.
If a captive can answer freely, the reply constraint loses its meaning; keep the limit in place and its reason clear to the player.
Accepting an official's quick categorisation of an event, such as calling it mischief, without checking the facts can miss a deliberate act.
An overly literal reading of a clue can exclude the correct answer.
Over-eager helpers can reveal an investigator's presence and turn a quiet signal into an alarm.
when: Relying on third parties to pass on or respond to a signal.
why: Excess activity draws the attention of watchers.

text: Treating every possibility as equally likely leaves an investigation stuck in an endless might-have-been stage with no progress.
Claims about evidence that has been destroyed cannot be checked, so they should not be relied on without independent support.
when: When a witness says a document or item existed but no longer exists.

text: A verification answer from an unknown party does not prove who is speaking, and a plausible reply can still be false.
An overlong or pedantic expert account can seem more authoritative than it is; judge it by the evidence it actually gives.
when: An expert gives a long, detailed explanation.
why: Length and detail can be mistaken for certainty.

text: Estimates offered as guesswork are easy to over-trust, and a witness's own timing also depends on fallible memory.
A random-killer or copycat explanation fits any crime without naming anyone, so it narrows nothing and can serve as a red herring.
Answers obtained under a false identity or an overstated threat are not clean evidence and should be checked against independent sources.
why: the method itself may have shaped what the witness said

text: Building a theory on the everyday meaning of a technical term can mislead, because specialist vocabulary often means something different.
when: a clue is a title, term, or jargon

text: Admitting a statement is not the same as weighing it; decision-makers may accept accusers while setting character evidence aside.
An honorific can attach to a deputy acting in an absent officeholder's place, so check who was acting before naming the holder.
when: The office holder was away when the document was produced
why: Titles can outlast the actual holder's presence

text: Once an unverifiable kind of evidence is admitted in any form, it can control every case and make corroboration add little.
why: Admission gives the evidence power that other evidence cannot match.

text: Judges without legal training may lean heavily on counsel from a single source, which narrows the range of views the verdict reflects.
when: when a court has no legal expertise among its members
why: without independent expertise, the judges depend on the advice they receive

text: A chain of misfortunes can look like a pattern when each link rests on a single neighbour's report.
when: when a series of harms is attributed to one person on one witness's word
why: a linked sequence feels convincing even when each link is unverified

text: Finders tend to assume more meaning than partly legible writing supports; read damaged evidence carefully before drawing conclusions.
when: when a clue is partly illegible
why: gaps invite overinterpretation

text: Some supposed proofs, such as ordeal-style tests, are themselves unsound and can introduce error rather than provide evidence.
Once a hidden deduction is explained, it can seem absurdly simple, which undercuts the player's sense of achievement.
Confidence in a first theory makes contrary facts look like errors, so people discard evidence that should prompt revision.
when: when players or characters hold a settled theory
why: Commitment to an explanation filters out opposing data

text: Settling a method on the claim that a victim could not have been woken is fragile; if that claim is wrong, the whole chain fails, and alternatives need direct checks.
when: A reconstruction depends on a victim's sleep or incapacity.
why: A single unverified assumption can break an otherwise consistent theory.

text: Reasoning that only adds the most obvious next step, such as another exit, is shallow and can overlook the real explanation.
when: Proposing explanations for a puzzle.
why: The obvious continuation is often the first thing considered and may miss the actual cause.

text: Treating a routine household sound as proof of a particular person's presence is an error, since many people can produce the same sound.
when: A witness links a common sound to a specific individual
why: Routine sounds are shared by everyone in the household

text: Vague labels make later comparison impossible; each label must describe exactly what was tested.
when: Recording physical samples
why: Unclear provenance cannot be compared later

text: A claim that nothing could pass through an opening is only as reliable as the inspection behind it, and unchecked openings invalidate it.
when: Ruling out entry through windows or doors.
why: Each untested opening, such as rear windows or interior doors, can still provide a route.

text: 1) List every plausible explanation, such as accident, illness, flight, arrest, suicide and murder, or state the contradiction precisely. 2) Test each against known facts. 3) Discard contradicted explanations, keeping untested ones open. 4) Gather new facts when none survive.
when: Early in a case with scattered facts, or when facts seem to contradict one another.
why: Testing rival explanations narrows the field without fixing on a first guess and exposes the assumption to drop.

text: 1) List each known fact as a numbered point. 2) State what each point implies. 3) Test each conclusion against the others. 4) Revise the list when a new fact changes the picture.
when: several facts must be weighed together

text: 1) State what each small fact implies. 2) Link the implications into a single hypothesis. 3) Test the hypothesis against a witness or record before accepting it.
when: several small observations may share a common cause
why: loosely related facts can point to one answer

text: 1) Lay out a reconstructed sequence of events in order. 2) Ask the suspect to confirm, deny or correct each step. 3) Revise the sequence using every correction.
when: the investigator has partial knowledge and needs confirmation

text: 1) Start from one simple visible sign. 2) Reason one step at a time to a next inference. 3) State each step separately so it can be checked.
when: Evidence is sparse and only small signs are available
why: Stated links can each be tested, so errors are found.

text: 1) Derive physical or temporal constraints from the clue. 2) Obtain a complete candidate list from an authoritative source. 3) Filter candidates by constraints. 4) Check the remainder through reconnaissance and records.
when: a clue constrains the search space and candidates can be listed
why: Constraints cut a large field to a checkable short list

text: 1) Ask why the lead was offered, not only whether it is true. 2) Check it against facts the speaker should not know. 3) Verify it independently, such as by searching the named person's location.
when: When a suspect volunteers a rival culprit.
why: A volunteered lead may be honest help or a diversion that shifts blame.

text: 1) Check where each relevant object was at the time. 2) Check who could physically reach it. 3) Check whether the timing allows the act. 4) Check what the method required and whether that was available.
when: when testing an accusation

text: 1) Link the item to the act. 2) Link the act to a physical trait, such as the hand that held the weapon. 3) Link the trait to a suspect. Test each link.
when: a physical clue is used to point at a suspect
why: Each step is an assumption until it is verified.

text: 1) Arrange physical proofs in order, such as photographs, samples and clues. 2) Confront the suspect with them. 3) Reveal that an earlier decoy was invented. 4) Check the suspect's detailed admissions against the assembled traces.
when: When the suspect has been misled and the evidence is concrete
why: Ordered, physical proof lets the suspect's account be tested step by step

text: 1) Separate what is known from what is inferred. 2) Walk through the chain of inference step by step, linking each step to an earlier clue. 3) Keep the recap short and specific, adding no new facts. 4) Reveal the motive as the final link.
when: Closing a mystery to show how the solution follows from clues
why: Traceable steps make the solution feel earned rather than conjured

text: Check each premise or link in a chain separately before accepting its conclusion; a chain is only as sound as its weakest link, and gaps can hide unshown steps.
when: Validating a reconstructed sequence of events or any chain of premises.
why: One false premise can make correct reasoning give a wrong answer, and a chain may look continuous while resting on unsupported connections.

text: Store case facts as a graph and show a conclusion only when every fact fits; check chain completeness before allowing an arrest.
when: Designing a deduction system or generating mystery content with linked clues.
why: A graph lets the game verify that each link is present and lets players check their reasoning.

text: Give every apparently supernatural or ambiguous event a rational explanation players can find, since an unexplained impression reads as a cheat.
when: Designing mysterious events in a game.

text: Present a deduction as a short chain of facts, each resting on the one before, and list the queries or inquiries that would test each step.
when: Presenting a deduction.

text: Present competing readings or conflicting sources side by side and let the reader weigh them, rather than forcing one story.
when: A document, remark or record supports opposite conclusions.
why: Openly stated readings keep the evidence weighable and the reader engaged.

text: Deliberately discount your own expectations when weighing evidence, because they shape what you notice and how you read silence.
Do not confuse an unusual case with an unsolvable one; the oddities of a case often point toward its answer.
when: when official explanations have stalled

text: When a theft or fraud affects several parties, check whether each loses the same amount rather than assuming the largest loser is the only interested party.
Do not claim certainty about a sample that was never tested; state the gap openly rather than filling it with guesswork.
When a companion character withholds a hint, reveal a checkable basis for it later in the game.
when: an NPC guide keeps a deduction back
why: a hidden basis that never appears feels like teasing

text: When evaluating an argument, ask what facts were left out, and check the connection between each piece of evidence and the conclusion.
when: A case is presented persuasively.
why: Persuasive presentation can hide missing links.

text: Let players combine a deed, a handwriting sample and a map location to deduce who wrote an anonymous note.
when: designing a detective mode
why: matching several evidence types gives a stronger deduction

text: Resolve a contradictory testimony with a test, such as moving the suspect into full light, rather than explaining it away in dialogue.
Begin an inquiry with independent evidence rather than the accusers' claims, so accusations do not set the agenda of the proceedings.
when: When running a hearing based partly on accusations.
why: Starting with accusations lets them frame what counts as evidence.

text: Do not conclude a witness is lying from a timing discrepancy alone, since memory and wording can produce it.
when: A witness's account conflicts with another clue.
why: Discrepancies have innocent causes as well as deceptive ones.

text: Keep personal interpretations out of the factual record so the notes can be checked later.
Track which hypothesis the player holds so later clues can be written to fit both readings of an ambiguous sound or sight.
when: When a level contains an ambiguous event two characters could have caused.
why: Clues matched to both readings keep the mystery open for longer.

text: Let a forensic minigame require sorting samples under magnification, and let a residue tied to a trade narrow the list of NPC suspects.
when: Designing a forensic investigation minigame
why: Trade-linked residue gives the player a concrete way to filter suspects

text: Let each damaged object record whether its damage happened during the event or afterward, so staged scenes can be exposed by inconsistent timing.
when: building a damage system for a scene
why: Timing of damage is a checkable clue that separates genuine events from staged ones.

text: Design a code whose rule, such as interval, weekday or letter match, a careful player can infer from several observations, rather than a random lookup.
when: Creating puzzle codes or hidden schedules in generated content
why: A rule-based code rewards deduction while a random lookup only rewards memorization

text: Let players test a hypothesis at a search point, such as searching a location where a trace would be if the hypothesis holds.
why: Testing a route hypothesis gives a clear yes or no result.

text: Let players confirm a document fragment against an in-world record, such as a harbor log, to unlock the next location.
when: when designing a fragment-based clue
why: Confirmation against a second source rewards careful matching.

text: Build the case from several confirmatory items that converge, rather than relying on a single decisive proof.
when: No single item is conclusive but each supports the same conclusion
why: Individually weak clues become strong when they point to the same suspect together.

text: Do not conclude from style alone; each feature inferred from writing needs corroboration from other evidence.
when: when drawing conclusions from a document's style
why: Style reflects habits and hostility as much as intent

text: Present physical evidence rather than describing it, because a bare claim invites the question of where the evidence is.
when: Arguing a conclusion before a sceptic or authority.
why: Shown evidence can be checked, while a described clue depends on trust.

text: Check whether a simple, obtainable test, such as comparing a known handwriting sample, was ever requested before concluding a question is unanswerable.
when: A question about a document or item seems unresolved.
why: A cheap test can settle a question that reasoning alone cannot.

text: Admit sensory reports as evidence only after checking them against a firmly held reasoned premise, never letting raw perception override logic.
when: Sensory reports conflict or are heavily emotional.
why: Senses are unreliable alone and must serve reasoning to be trusted.

text: Do not treat an immediate reaction to a touch or a glance as proof of a person's guilt or power.
when: when a reaction is the only evidence offered
why: reactions have other causes, including fear and expectation

text: Build a tally-based clue with one deliberately uncertain figure, so players must reason from the range to locate a character's whereabouts.
when: Designing a clue puzzle from payments or purchases.
why: A range keeps the answer deducible without making every figure exact.

text: Show how the player reached a conclusion as a flourish, rewarding attention without forcing an accusation.
when: Presenting a deduction to the player.
why: Visible reasoning rewards observation while letting the player keep control of the confrontation.

text: Make the reveal a conclusion drawn from records the audience already saw, rather than a confession, so the scene rewards reasoning.
when: designing the moment a hidden identity or swap is exposed
why: Deduction from known evidence feels earned, while a confession only delivers information.

text: A suspect's silence alone is only a suggestion that must be backed by evidence; combined with known contact with the victim, it can justify holding them until they explain.
when: Silence is used as evidence; holding is justified only when known victim contact is also present.
why: Silence has many possible causes and does not prove guilt, but it gains weight when linked to a known connection.

text: A piece of evidence can support both a suspect and an alternative; an item that suggests a marked assailant may also count against the apparent suspect.
when: Evidence seems to implicate one person
why: Physical details must match the suspect as well as the theory.

text: Make NPC claims checkable, such as warnings or a guide's walk duration tested against a timer or map, so their words gain meaning and the guide's fairness can be tested.
when: An NPC gives a warning the player might dismiss, or a trusted guide gives a timing claim
why: A later confirmation rewards attention, and a checkable claim lets apparent fairness be tested.

text: A checklist of case elements orders what must be tested; it is not proof of guilt.
Ask for one precise fact from a source rather than a general account, so the query is fast and the answer narrows the search.
when: An investigator needs a specific detail to move forward.
why: A narrow question gets a usable answer without long delay.

text: A crime-scene mode with a numbered checklist turns each step into a recorded observation that feeds a final deduction, and negative results still move the player forward.
when: Designing investigation gameplay
why: Recorded observations accumulate into a conclusion, and eliminations keep progress visible

text: An argument-driven mystery uses timeline and identity challenges to move suspicion between suspects, ending on a physical lead rather than a full on-page reveal.

A mystery format where a stationary solver reasons from reported facts, an official solution forms and an innocent suspect is arrested, then a hidden detail reverses the case and the solver reconstructs the truth by argument.
when: designing reasoning-driven mystery cases told through reports
why: The reversal reframes existing evidence, so the player experiences the solution as an inference rather than a discovery.

text: A single check does not establish truth: cheap surface answers mislead, and a cover story passing one known test can still fail another, since planners rarely anticipate every method.
when: Investigating a case with planted misdirection, or assessing whether a cover story will hold
why: Surface answers are easy to produce and planners rarely anticipate every verification method.

text: Advice that sounds protective, such as destroying a dangerous item in a way that keeps it in use, can shift the risk onto the target.
when: an NPC gives the player safety advice
why: The safe-sounding action actually increases danger, so it can serve as a trap.

text: Building a larger conspiracy around a foreign or official-looking detail without checking its purpose leads to false theories.
when: When a single striking clue suggests espionage or a big plot
why: Dramatic details invite elaborate explanations that the actual facts may not support.

text: 1) Set out every plausible explanation, including accidental ones. 2) Test each against the evidence. 3) Only then conclude the most likely cause.
when: Forming a conclusion about a cause or culprit.
why: A rival explanation left untested can overturn a theory built on a single suspect.

text: A witness who insists a person is honest and did nothing wrong can make that defense itself look suspicious.
when: a witness defends someone unprompted

text: Defending an accused person in public can cost a witness socially, so pressure to apologize or retract tends to silence the defense.
when: a witness speaks for an accused during a public panic
why: The social cost of testimony can outweigh its benefit to the witness.

text: A surviving defence document does not prove that decision-makers read or considered it.
when: Evaluating whether a defence was heard in a tribunal.
why: A document can exist without reaching the people who decide the case.

text: A plausible defence can reframe an account, so a statement must be tied to what the physical record shows.
A heated defence signals the defender's feelings more than the facts, so weigh its force separately from its evidence.
Even defensive answers can reveal more than intended, so each reply should be checked for what it implies.
Pressure can make a witness defend the person being asked about, which hides the information the questioner needs.
A defender may have their own reasons to protect a suspect, so their endorsement must be read with that stake in mind.
A defence that reasons toward another source of harm can be recorded as an accusation against a third party.

1) State the theory outright early so that questions can be aimed at it. 2) Identify the links the theory needs, such as possession, knowledge and intent. 3) Prove each link. 4) Test the theory against the link that is weakest.
when: Building a defense or accusation that must hold up under questioning
why: A stated theory directs questions and lets listeners judge the purpose of seemingly odd questions

text: Let a player's defence be answerable by specific clues, so the verdict depends on the case the player has built.
when: when designing a trial where players argue their case

text: A defense can name people who knew the accused longest and were of good report, and ask that they testify under oath.
when: an accused person cannot plead their own case

text: When the physical facts are settled, the defense can shift the contest from what happened to who and why by reshaping the motive and character of the parties.
when: Forensic or physical evidence is overwhelming and hard to challenge
why: Challenging settled facts is futile, so the contest moves to motive and character

text: A visible change in manner tends to fade over time as the person's habitual pattern returns.
when: When a suspect's unusual behavior is observed across an extended period.
why: Sustaining a concealing manner is effortful, so habits gradually reassert themselves.

text: Let players trust a document for a long stretch before undercutting it, so the reversal changes meaning rather than just adding information.
when: when planning a late reversal of a settled belief
why: a belief held long enough makes its overturning a shift in understanding

text: Show a premise clue early as trivial; it can later become a key piece of evidence once its context is revealed.
Let the investigator defer accusation and let the staging show itself, so the proof is visible rather than asserted.
when: writing the final confrontation
why: Visible proof persuades more than a direct charge.

text: Withholding what is seen, and letting light or argument change over time, builds suspense before the reveal arrives.
when: Designing a scene that builds toward a reveal.
why: Uncertainty about what is present keeps the audience engaged until the reveal pays off.

text: A lost interval that the protagonist explains away as a dream can hide a deed, so the reader treats the gap as harmless until physical traces contradict the explanation.
A device left under a door latch after the culprit exits can make a room look sealed from inside, creating a false alibi for the moment of death.
A delayed frame reveals an arrival's identity and motive first, and only later reveals the true direction or mechanics of the events that brought it.
A confident, detailed witness is not necessarily accurate; detail can coexist with inference, bias, or repeated hearsay.
when: When judging a witness's reliability.
why: Confidence and detail do not establish that the observation was firsthand.

text: Labelling a strange event as a trick can dismiss a real unexplained detail that the trick does not account for.
when: Explaining away an event as a prank.
why: A single explanation may cover only part of the evidence, leaving some details unresolved.

text: Delaying an explanation too long confuses the audience when the scene depends on its logic to follow.
when: The climax needs the logic to be understood.

text: When a narrator labels a character's remark as superstition, readers may discount the remark entirely, even if it later proves meaningful.
when: An omen is voiced by a character marked as superstitious.
why: The label signals the remark is unreliable, so the audience ignores it.

text: Accepting a deferred meeting wastes time and may let the witness be warned or prepared, while social settings add people who shape the answers.
when: A witness can only be reached at a later scheduled event.
why: Delay gives the witness time to prepare and brings in other voices.

text: A deferred offer buys time, but if the target takes it seriously it creates an obligation that is hard to withdraw; use it only when the offer can be cancelled.
when: when using a fake or conditional offer to delay someone
why: Accepted offers create commitments that the offering side cannot easily undo.

text: Faint, seemingly arbitrary details gain meaning only after a reveal; withholding their purpose rewards careful notice without signalling importance when they appear.
when: The solution depends on details that look arbitrary when first encountered.
why: The later explanation reframes the earlier details.

text: A sealed item or packet with a stated release condition defers its content while staying visible, and can give a second, personal account; the wait builds interest rather than confusion.
when: Designing a clue that pays off after a set condition, or when the answer should arrive in stages.
why: Withholding content defers the payoff while keeping the item visible; the reader waits for a condition they can follow.

text: A painful disclosure that is put off repeatedly is rarely made; concealment grows by inertia rather than by a decision.
when: a character holds a secret that causes guilt
why: Each deferral lowers the odds of ever speaking

text: Each retelling of a rumour adds vivid physical details, while the cause of the event shrinks to a few words.
when: Event relayed through several people.
why: The most dramatic version tends to travel fastest.

text: When the audience knows a scheme that the target does not, the target's calm moments become tense, because each ordinary action is read against the threat.
when: when building suspense before a confrontation
why: knowledge of the hidden plan changes how the audience reads ordinary moments

text: Dramatic irony is the gap between what an audience knows and what characters understand, so the audience sees more than the speakers do.
A delayed reveal withholds the full explanation of an event until after it happens, then reconstructs the plan in a debrief.
Delayed disclosure is a message held by a third party and released only after the sender's death or on a set date.
Delayed reveal withholds a central fact across repeated pauses, so the audience waits for it while the pauses build suspense.
News can reach a character days late, so knowledge lags events; a delay, such as a misdelivered letter, changes what each party could know and when.
when: Modelling what characters know at a given time.
why: Information travels with delay, creating gaps between events and awareness.

text: A substance's effects can change with dose and stage, so assuming one simple effect can mislead a timeline.
when: Reasoning about when a substance acted.
why: Effects vary over time and quantity.

text: Reveal a hidden fact or threat late, after suspicion has built, since showing it early would resolve the tension that depends on uncertainty.
when: a fact would resolve tension too early if shown sooner
why: The reveal lands harder once expectations are built, and suspense depends on uncertainty.

text: Leave a damning clue unexplained and name the witness, step, or journal entry that will explain it later, so players can check their own deduction.
Frame a request for delay as a condition of the inquiry, or as a branching choice that changes what the player learns next, to secure time from a reluctant witness.
Do not press a hinting witness at once; reopen the topic at a later pretextual meeting, or wait until your position lets you press without losing access.
when: A witness has hinted but not disclosed, or the investigator is a guest or otherwise restricted.
why: Early pressure makes the witness guarded and closes off information.

text: Mark a costly choice with a retrospective narrator line or journal hint, so the player later links the choice to its lasting consequences.
when: Designing a decision whose consequences appear after the choice.
why: Hindsight hints darken what came before; a later reflection links the choice to its outcome.

text: Explain a dangerous action or withheld reasoning only after its danger has been felt; the explanation then follows the tension and lets the earlier scene reread as a clue.
Defer the core reveal to the final moment so that the audience's curiosity stays unsatisfied until the end.
Delay explaining how an impressive feat is achieved, and reveal the method later in the playthrough, so the mystery sustains engagement.
when: A character performs a feat whose mechanism would spoil tension if shown immediately
why: Withholding the method keeps the mystery alive while the player still has motive to pursue it

text: Hold back the full explanation until records and evidence align, so the reveal rests on corroboration rather than assertion.
when: revealing a solved mystery
why: corroborated reveals are more convincing

text: Deliver the most damaging point deliberately, since a shocking fact forces the witness to respond and reveals how they react to the truth.
when: the interviewer has a decisive fact
why: A shock produces a visible reaction that can be read.

text: Withholding the explanation until after the events lets the audience's expectations be challenged alongside those of the characters.
when: designing a mystery where the audience follows the investigator's wrong view
why: Delay keeps the audience inside the misdirection until the reveal.

text: A retrospective account can list the disguised person's movements that earlier scenes only hinted at, completing the reveal.
Design an NPC who refuses to account for themselves so that a later clue, rather than the refusal, reveals where they were.
A brief pause before a key line marks emotion and builds suspense, but frequent pauses drain tension rather than build it.
Announce a delayed decisive element publicly so the audience knows an outcome is pending, turning the wait into suspense rather than confusion.
when: The outcome depends on a witness or item that can plausibly be delayed.
why: Advance notice sets expectations and makes the eventual arrival feel earned.

text: A narrator can frame a chance delay as decisive in hindsight, building suspense and signalling stakes before the disruption is explained.
when: Building anticipation before a disruption.
why: Hindsight claims make the audience expect consequences.

text: Time a delivery to a target's known daily routine so it arrives when the target is present.
A single pointing gesture naming the accused can serve as the climax of an accusation scene.
when: the reveal is staged before a group
why: a clear gesture focuses attention on one person

text: A delay before an admission builds tension when it shows the gap between the speaker's inner resolve and outward hesitation.
when: The climax of a scene is a confession
why: The audience feels the cost of saying the words through the visible struggle.

text: Promising a full reveal later builds suspense, and the wait for it, rather than the disclosure itself, drives most of the tension.
when: A secret must be held back for dramatic effect
why: Anticipation sustains attention longer than the fact does

text: Delaying the opening of news and withholding its details builds suspense, because the audience anticipates the answer before it arrives.
when: Pacing a moment where a key fact is about to be revealed

text: The time between an event and a later reference to it can measure how little progress followed.
when: When a later document recalls an earlier proclamation or act.
why: Long gaps show the issue stayed unresolved.

text: Delay revealing a plan to build tension, provided the player has enough information to avoid unfair losses.
Keep the real purpose concealed until the last possible moment, so the cover stays intact for as long as it matters.
Reveal an ally's debts and principles in a later scene, so the player reinterprets his earlier dialogue in light of the new motive.
why: A late motive gives earlier lines a second meaning.

text: Place the motive in a document the player reads early but cannot interpret until a legal rule changes its meaning.
Giving the audience a fact characters do not weigh creates dramatic irony: the audience sees the plan or danger a character walks toward, making each decision feel fraught.
when: when the audience has information a character lacks

text: Holding back a key fact or source and delaying its reveal raises expectation, so each delay makes the eventual reveal carry more weight, especially when it reinterprets earlier events.
when: the reveal reinterprets earlier events, or a long investigation promises a next source
why: A late reinterpretation lands harder than information given up front.

text: A notice sent by post or carried by a courier can sit undelivered, so the recipient learns of an arrival only when the visitor appears; reveal the missed delivery later.
when: plot depends on information reaching a character late
why: An undelivered message removes the recipient's warning.

text: An earlier clue gains meaning only when a later revelation links it to a name or fact, so unexplained clues should be kept on record until then.
when: Clue is planted long before its explanation
why: The link is recalled only when the late fact arrives.

text: Postponing a key witness while a deadline stays fixed extends the unresolved wait and raises tension.
why: Each postponement adds time in which the stakes remain undecided.

text: A requested delay combined with a pending action, such as an arrest, raises tension because the audience cannot know whether the action will happen in the meantime.
when: a reveal is postponed while a threatened step is pending
why: uncertainty about the outcome raises the stakes

text: Holding back a confession just before it is spoken builds suspense, and each postponement raises the stakes.
when: a reveal depends on a delayed decision
why: anticipation grows with each delay

text: Delivery routes and day schedules constrain when a sent item can arrive, so arrival timing can serve as a clue pointing to a later event.
Delaying the alarm lets the body cool and stiffen, which blurs any later estimate of when death occurred.
when: when the discovery of a body is delayed
why: post-mortem changes alter the evidence over time

text: A hidden witness who cannot leave without revealing their presence is forced to wait, and that waiting builds suspense.
when: When a character is concealed near an event and must stay put.
why: Inability to act while close to danger raises tension.

text: Showing the reader the crime and the culprit's identity before the investigators learn them creates dramatic irony and suspense, while clues remain fair because the reader has witnessed them directly.
when: Designing stories where audience knowledge should drive tension
why: The audience holds information the characters lack, so each character action carries suspense.

text: Delaying disclosure builds tension, which is released when a full reconstruction makes the solution verifiable.
A blocked route can delay a hearing and let whichever party is present act first, creating an organic deadline that shifts control to another faction.
when: a legal or political process depends on travel or timing
why: Delay changes who is able to act before others.

text: Delay can be used to hold an outcome back, such as a confirmation left pending for long periods or a meeting postponed.
Dramatic irony arises when the audience sees the gap between an outsider's reading of a group and what the group actually means.
Withholding the culprit's identity until the supporting proof is laid out builds suspense, and a pause before the accusation lets the accused react and extends tension.
when: A climactic reveal where the audience should be able to follow the reasoning.
why: Delay raises anticipation, and an ordered presentation of the case lets listeners verify each step before the payoff.

text: Withholding what is happening and giving a single partial clue sustains tension and drives characters to act before the full picture is known.
A delayed-onset effect keeps open only those earlier stages that could still have acted before symptoms began, so onset time narrows the window.
when: a harmful effect takes time to appear
why: A stage cannot cause symptoms that appear before it could have acted

text: Holding the full backstory until it is complete makes the later reveal more meaningful, but long withholding costs audience engagement as attention wanders.
when: Choosing when to release backstory.
why: Delay increases impact but risks losing the audience.

text: Revealing an inheritance chain link by link forces the player to establish each relation before the motive becomes clear.
when: a motive is spread across several documents
why: Sequential revelation makes the player check each step rather than jump to a conclusion.

text: Testimony given at a dramatic moment may be shaped by surrounding events, and dramatic reports mix real events with imagination; check for that influence and separate the two before concluding.
Later confessions and reflections can shift blame and simplify a messy process, so they must be dated and checked against events recorded at the time.
Withholding the explanation too long after the reveal can make the solution feel like a trick rather than earned.
when: Deferring a solution until after a reward is shown.
why: A delayed explanation loses its link to the reward and reads as artificial.

text: Withholding a hidden identity or map area too long feels like withholding; reveal it once the escape has begun, so the reveal feels earned.
when: a restricted section ends and the player exits
why: a reveal tied to the escape feels earned rather than arbitrary

text: A dramatic reversal, such as returned stolen goods or a motive explanation, can pull attention away from how the culprit got in.
when: Investigating a crime with a striking twist
why: Stakes and motive compete with the method question

text: Attention fixes on dramatic changes and misses ordinary habits that continued, weakening the reading of the scene.
Delay can make a timeline harder to rebuild, because witnesses' memories fade while the investigator travels.
Long environmental surveys before a reveal slow pacing and can drain tension from the discovery that follows.
when: a discovery is close
why: description delays the payoff

text: A delayed reveal is believable only when the character has already shown careful reasoning in the open.
when: A character announces a hidden answer.
why: Audiences trust a withheld answer only after seeing the character reason well.

text: Delaying disclosure of a clue the investigator already holds can look like concealment and undermines fair play.
A delayed response can be innocent, so check the times before assuming the delay was designed.
why: Delays often have ordinary causes such as distance or confusion

text: A plan with a narrow timing window and long transit leaves no slack, so any delay can cause the whole operation to fail.
when: when travel or preparation is long
why: no margin remains once the window is set

text: A recipient may read a delayed instruction as sentiment; the message should state plainly that it is part of a plan.
Waiting for public demand before correcting a verdict can leave the record uncorrected for years.
A delayed trigger's timing is hard to predict, so an early or late activation can expose the plan.
when: the trigger depends on an estimated rate of change
why: the actual rate depends on conditions the actor can only guess

text: Delaying the reveal too long drains the tension it was meant to build.

1) Replay the chain of inference in the order evidence was weighed. 2) Tie each conclusion to an observation shown earlier. 3) Mark which steps the player found and which were only confessed. 4) Keep the replay short, as a checklist rather than a second plot.
when: Ending a mystery where clues were encountered earlier, so the player can verify the solution's fairness.
why: Showing the logic and re-presenting clues makes the solution feel earned and reachable rather than arbitrary.

text: 1) Withhold the hidden identity until the climax. 2) Pause the action with a stretch of silence. 3) Speak the identity aloud. 4) Recap hidden earlier acts so they read as managed events rather than misfortune.
when: Structuring a mystery whose antagonist is concealed until the end.
why: A timed reveal and retrospective recap make earlier events reinterpreted as clues.

text: 1) Show the reaction first. 2) Withhold its cause. 3) Deliver the reason through a secondary source, such as a lore book, after the reaction is registered.
when: a clue's meaning should follow a surprise
why: the audience forms an expectation before learning the explanation

text: 1) Note the delay as a gap in the timeline. 2) List known constraints such as surveillance or routine. 3) Propose an explanation that fits them. 4) Test it with an independent check.
when: a message or report arrives much later than expected
why: constraints narrow the explanation and an independent check tests it

text: 1) Keep the narrator or guide ignorant of the plan. 2) Show each needed clue early in a neutral form. 3) Stage the event. 4) Reconstruct the sequence in a debrief that links each clue to its meaning.
1) Pause the present-day case. 2) Deliver the motive through a self-contained embedded story. 3) Return to the present case with the motive now known to the audience.
when: The motive for a crime depends on events that happened long before the present investigation.
why: Giving history separately keeps the audience informed without losing the thread of the active case.

text: Each step of a repeated or delayed reveal must add a new fact; repeats without new information dull tension and cause frustration.
when: a disclosure is built up for suspense

text: Declare each delayed effect as a testable rule, not a generic excuse; if observed timing diverges from the expected delay, suspect another source or an interfering factor.
Do not treat a dramatic lead or result as proof, since it can hide weak reasoning; check it against physical evidence before acting on it.
when: a striking message or claim draws attention
why: Attention is not proof.

text: Place a physical sign, such as a mismatched ticket half, that stays inert until a later explanation reframes it, and show the concealed action in the scene itself.
when: When designing a clue.

text: A later reveal, such as dialogue, can recast an earlier event or completed quest, so design outcomes to read differently once new information arrives.
when: Designing a late plot revelation.
why: New information changes the meaning of details already seen.

text: Note an unexplained word or claim and hold it for later follow-up rather than pressing on it now.
when: A suspect uses a term or claim that is not yet explained
why: Deferred questions preserve a lead without tipping the suspect off

text: Delay revealing the cause of a character's reaction, letting it stand unexplained for a while before the reason is shown.
when: a character's knowledge is suspected but not stated

text: After a confession, re-tag earlier objects and events with their true purpose, so replaying the game reveals new meaning from the same content.
when: when a reveal recasts earlier content
why: Objects gain significance once their purpose is known.

text: Use delayed reveals at a climax, where partial information raises stakes, and end the scene before the full picture is shown.
when: at a climax

text: If a substance could not have acted by the stated hour, that hour is ruled out as a time of effect.
when: Testing a claimed dosing time
why: Physical timing rules out impossible claims

text: Give each listener a distinct reaction, such as shock, cold distance, declared loyalty or collapse, so each reaction reveals where that person stands.
when: writing a group reveal

text: Leave the physical or mental cause of a sealed room's mystery open until enough clues have accumulated to support one.
why: Premature answers close the puzzle before the evidence is gathered.

text: Delay revealing a character's identity until a set point, such as a doorway or ladder, to build suspense without cheating the audience.
when: Introducing a character whose identity should be revealed gradually
why: Withholding the face or identity briefly builds tension, while withholding it too long feels like a trick.

text: Delay a key reveal by interrupting the speaker or withholding the explanation until others have acted on the evidence.
when: A character holds knowledge the audience needs later
why: Postponing the explanation keeps the question open and the tension high.

text: Hold back an NPC's secret until repeated questioning or a later event, so the reveal works as a payoff.
Decide the feeling the player should have first, then make every element serve that effect, with no detail left idle.
when: Designing a mystery or puzzle experience.
why: Working from the effect keeps all parts pointed toward one centre.

text: Delayed clues reward recall but can frustrate players if the payoff comes too late; an obvious clue avoids that frustration.
Delaying a reveal builds suspense and lets the audience watch reactions to each step, but it gives the suspect time to escape.
Witnesses questioned right after an event may offer nothing, while a later, calmer round can recover recollections the first round did not trigger.
when: witnesses are excited or busy immediately after an event
why: Immediate stress and duties crowd out recall that returns with time and different questioning.

text: Long-delayed testimony can contain vivid, precise detail that is still inaccurate, especially if the witness only began to suspect something during the event.
when: testimony given long after the event
why: memory is reconstructed and shaped by later suspicion

text: Once a name is spoken, forgotten remarks and small incidents return with new meaning, as memory reorganises around the revealed identity.
when: A key identity or fact is revealed late
why: The revealed fact reframes previously ignored details

text: A delayed check lets a suspect's situation change before you verify it, so verify claims as early as possible.
When several people have motives and opportunities, delay settling on the most convenient suspect until each suspect's evidence has been weighed.
when: multiple suspects look plausible
why: early settling on the convenient suspect can hide the real answer

text: A delayed-reveal mystery moves through six phases: frame, arrival, accumulating clues, escalation, testimony, and exposure with aftermath.
when: Designing a story where a hidden identity is revealed late.

text: 1) Suspend the detective's thread. 2) Supply the hidden answer in a digression using facts shown earlier. 3) Return to the detective at the point of confusion.
when: Structuring a mystery so the audience outpaces the investigator.
why: Reveal through digression keeps the reader ahead while the investigator's uncertainty creates suspense.

text: Statements from a feverish or delirious person are unreliable but informative: they point to leads and concerns, so verify before belief; repeated names show what troubles them, as impressions not testimony.
when: When interpreting a feverish or delirious person's speech
why: Delirium gives hints about concerns without giving reliable statements.

text: Witnesses may present a sleep- or fear-born event as a waking observation; ask whether they mix dreams, belief or superstition with real events before accepting their account.

Do not dismiss dream-framed testimony automatically; it may honestly reflect the witness's state or hide behind uncertainty, so treat details as probable but unproven and test them against other evidence.
In a disordered mental state, dreams can feel more real than ordinary memory and contain details that seem too fitting to have been invented while awake.
when: A person is ill, feverish, distressed or intoxicated.
why: A disturbed state heightens the feeling of reality without improving accuracy.

text: Witnesses often recall distant events only in outline, remembering a general fact such as a resemblance while missing the specifics.
when: asked about a childhood or long-past detail
why: Memory keeps the gist more reliably than particulars over time

text: A small public disturbance fixes a person's presence in other people's memory, because disputes and unusual appearances get recalled.
when: a minor dispute occurs at a public event
why: unexpected friction makes witnesses notice and remember details

text: Witnesses often recall a distinctive object before a face, so the object can be the more dependable anchor.
when: a fleeting sighting
why: attention fixes on distinctive items first

text: Vivid, disturbing experiences stay long in memory and strongly affect an overwrought nervous system, so their lasting force is not evidence of their truth.
when: A recollection feels powerful and persistent.
why: Emotional intensity strengthens memory regardless of whether the event was accurate.

text: A distressed witness's visions are uncertain, because senses can deceive and deception is hard to separate from the witness's own condition.
Delirium can make a true statement sound false and a false one sound true, so delirious speech cannot prove a claim alone.
Weigh a delirious witness's statements by when they were made, checking them against the speaker's lucid moments.
when: a sick or dying witness speaks
why: reliability varies with mental state

text: Dream or vision fragments can foreshadow a location or event the player will reach later.
A sale unlike a shop's usual stock is easier for a seller to remember, so it makes a stronger link to the buyer.
why: unusual transactions stand out against routine ones in memory

text: Before dismissing an odd statement from a dying or delirious person, test whether it reflects real knowledge, using questions that separate hallucination from delirium.
when: the statement could point to a real fact
why: delirium and hallucination can both produce similar words

text: Planted information stays dormant until a later sighting matches it, at which point the earlier remark is recalled and gains meaning.
when: when a later piece of evidence matches the earlier remark

text: Delirium lowers a character's guard, so they drop words that show they knew far more than others assumed.
when: a character is in a fever or delirium state
why: the character no longer filters what they say

text: A widely shared delusion gains strength when a community's gathering network repeats it to many listeners.
Assuming all of a delirious speaker's words are nonsense, or that all are true, both lead to error.
Assuming a word spoken in delirium names a specific person is an error, since such words may point at several people.
A patient's fear of being harmed may be a symptom of illness, so it cannot prove or disprove a plot; treating it as proof or dismissing it outright are both errors.
A real delusion can mask a real act, so dismissing a confession entirely is also an error.
Resolve a quest where two NPCs disagree about a past detail only by finding the artifact that matches one of the accounts.
A suspect who leaves no proof and has a clean past can resist questioning by denying everything, since investigators must prove what is refused.
when: the suspect has covered their tracks
why: The investigator must establish the facts without the suspect's admission.

text: Witnesses who deny unfavourable facts, or who refuse to lie even when the truth hurts them, both shape what investigators can prove.
when: when a witness is questioned about damaging facts
why: each choice either removes or preserves evidence

text: A denial aimed at one specific claim may show that the rest of a reconstruction is close to the truth.
when: a suspect is confronted with a detailed account

text: A suspect challenged on an alibi may deny the claim while asserting that no one saw them, keeping the statement literally correct.
when: when a suspect's whereabouts are questioned
why: Literal accuracy lets the suspect avoid stating a falsehood while concealing contact.

text: A suspect who claims not to recall an act can be contradicted by an official written report from an independent party.
when: A suspect's memory is self-serving or convenient.
why: Independent records can establish facts that the suspect's denial does not account for.

text: Public pressure to name a culprit pushes accusers to name people, and names come out one at a time in an order that favours those wanting them named.
when: when a community demands a culprit
why: accusers respond to pressure by supplying names

text: A recantation that denies any source for the accusations removes the claim that they rested on hidden or outside information.
A denial of incriminating items is a fact to weigh, not proof; test it against what others heard or observed, and keep pressure low if the witness may be honest.
A demonstration does not end a dispute: a suspect may dismiss the evidence, and persuasive demos don't dislodge physical evidence, so keep open questions visible until resolved.
Focus questioning on what evidence can actually be shown, since a firm denial holds only while investigators lack proof.
when: a suspect's story stays fixed

text: A serious question answered with a flippant reply is a probable sign of hidden knowledge, though only a rule of thumb.
when: Interpreting a witness's manner under questioning

text: Question a witness further when a firm answer on one point is paired with evasion on a related point.
when: When a witness is confident on one matter but reticent on a connected one.
why: Mixed signals suggest the reticence may hide relevant information.

text: Use a firm, businesslike tone to bring a flustered witness back to the facts.
Under emotional appeals, acknowledge the cost to the suspect while holding the factual argument unchanged.
when: when a suspect uses affection, tears or appeals during an accusation
why: Empathy with firmness keeps the case intact.

text: A rival or authority figure who demands proof before acting makes the player trade information for cooperation.
A character who denies or hides a reaction adds a second layer of ambiguity to the clue.
Denials count for little when the accused has no counsel and no practice at cross-examination, so the accusation stands unrefuted.
An unchecked accusation during a panic can escalate from arrests to mass punishment as more people are drawn in.
when: during a panic

text: Silence, denial or refusal to confess can be read as guilt and recorded as evidence, bringing harsher treatment; the accused cannot clear themselves by refusing.
why: denial is treated as defiance rather than an answer

text: Firm or calm delivery is not evidence of truth; practised lies can sound convincing and end questioning early, so test claims against physical evidence.
when: when assessing a reply or a claim delivered with strong emphasis
why: Confidence or calmness of delivery is not reliable evidence of accuracy.

text: A witness's denial of seeing a scene or knowing a matter may be honest, defensive, incomplete or concealing, so it cannot clear them; sightline or ignorance alone cannot decide.
when: a witness denies seeing a scene or knowing the matter

text: A claim lacking corroboration is not proven false, and an uncontradicted whereabouts is not confirmed; some claims have no possible independent source.
A suggestion put to an expert and rejected should not be recorded as a finding, even if it was raised in questioning.
when: Questioning proposes an explanation that the expert denies.
why: Questions can introduce a theory that the evidence never supported, and treating it as established misleads later reasoning.

text: Clearing suspects without new evidence makes the solution feel arbitrary, so each exoneration should rest on a fact.
when: a suspect is ruled out
why: an unsupported clearing looks like authorial convenience

text: A bluff must be sustained across later exchanges, since each new question risks exposing it.
Demanding certainty that medical evidence cannot give leads to frustration and false confidence in rough estimates.
when: An investigator presses an expert for a precise answer.
why: Medical evidence usually gives probabilities, not certainties.

text: Accepting that nothing unusual happened, without checking the normal routine, misses the deviations that matter.
When the questioner already assumes guilt, a denial can be treated as proof of falsehood, especially when witness reactions seem to contradict it.
1) Set aside the competing theory. 2) List only facts no witness disputes. 3) Build every inference from that list.
when: Several accounts compete and a fixed starting point is needed.
why: Disputed starting facts make every later conclusion unreliable.

text: 1) Check the pulse. 2) Apply smelling salts and brandy. 3) Treat a steady pulse as a sign that the feint is holding.
when: judging whether a collapsed person is genuinely unconscious
why: Each test gives a sign that either supports or exposes the feint.

text: Treat an unconfirmed claim, such as a visit or dinner with no witness, as a weak timeline link or weak evidence until a second source corroborates it.
Do not make threats or hint at evidence you cannot back up; an unsupported pressure bluff exposes the investigator and weakens the case.
when: when using pressure in an interrogation or hinting at evidence not yet secured
why: Unsupported threats are exposed and damage credibility.

text: Require a verifiable physical token or specific proof before accepting a claim about identity, status or reputation, since repeated talk can be accurate yet unprovable.
when: weighing a claim about a person's identity, status or wellbeing, or secondhand reports about a person or group
why: Checkable proof can be verified; unsupported claims cannot.

text: Ask a pressured suspect for a demonstration of cooperation rather than trusting their word.
when: When a suspect offers to cooperate under threat or leverage
why: Observable action is harder to fake than a verbal promise

text: Insist that a witness state where each person was and when, since precise times and places are what expose contradictions.
Use a feigned state when a character's location or knowledge must stay hidden from those around them.
when: a character needs to listen or move unseen
why: Feigning explains the character's presence without drawing suspicion.

text: Plant a claimed connection, such as a shared acquaintance, that a character uses to gain favor but that is never verified, so the claim's credibility is left open.
when: A character's claimed background is used to win trust.
why: Unverified claims can carry tension and invite the player to doubt them.

text: Test any suspect flinch or reaction mechanic against a decoy NPC who triggers the same reaction; otherwise players learn the reaction tells them nothing and ignore it.
Give any claimed power a demonstration the player can try to reproduce or disprove.
when: when a character claims a supernatural or special ability

text: Make denial and demands for proof dialogue options, each unlocking or closing off later confessions.
when: Designing confrontation dialogue
why: Branching reactions make the player's pressure choices matter

text: Firm pressure on a key holder can make them surrender the key, but it works best on a reluctant holder who already fears exposure.
when: A key holder refuses to hand over a key.
why: Fear of consequences can overcome reluctance, but pressure applied to the wrong person can backfire.

text: Acting on belief alone is fast but risks wrongly punishing the innocent; demanding proof is slower but keeps the outcome grounded in evidence.
when: a confrontation after a reveal where the accused denies the secret

text: A deposition is sworn testimony taken to fix a witness's memory on record, so it can be used later.
when: A witness is old or a dispute may return to court
why: Recording testimony early preserves it against the loss of memory or the death of the witness

text: A sealed deposit ties the suspect's safety to the investigator's, because any harm to the investigator would expose the suspect.
why: Release is triggered by the investigator's absence

text: A sealed deposit is useless if the recipient is untrustworthy, late or absent when the release time arrives.
why: The method depends on the recipient acting as instructed

text: A suspect who learns of a sealed deposit may demand its destruction, so the plan must allow for that demand.
Enmity recorded in a deposition is a motive to examine, not proof of guilt.
Specific details such as colour, texture and shape are more useful for identification than general terms, since general terms cannot be checked against a suspect.
when: writing or reading a physical description used for identification

text: Overusing a symbol such as weather, or heavily emphasising a plant, reads as a signal to the audience and removes the surprise of the later payoff.
why: Obvious emphasis tells the audience what matters too early.

text: Heavy vocabulary can bury the point a message must make, so the formal tone may obscure the accusation.
when: when writing an accusatory document
why: Stiff phrasing competes with the content for the reader's attention.

text: A failed appointment, where the expected person had already left, changes what the suspect does next, so record it as an event that branches the timeline.
Let an NPC's protective excuse appear in dialogue so players learn to test excuses against physical evidence.
Tagging each account with its speaker's stake lets a designer plant motive early without a direct exposition dump.
when: Delivering backstory through dialogue.
why: Speaker motive carries information that a flat recital would lack.

text: Quote sources at length so readers can see gradual shifts in wording that a stripped excerpt would hide.
Deliver the missing steps of a reconstructed sequence through a short dialogue that closes the gap.
when: When the player needs a brief explanation to complete a timeline.
why: A concise spoken account closes gaps without a lengthy info dump.

text: A long backstory monologue delivered after the climax can drag and undo the tension built by the discovery.
when: Delivering exposition following a major reveal.
why: Extended explanation after the peak of tension lowers momentum and pacing.

text: 1) Keep the exchange going by asking one follow-up question after another. 2) When the witness mentions something unexpected, ask an open follow-up rather than a closed one. 3) Invite their opinion, then test it against what else is known.
when: a witness is willing to talk
why: Open follow-ups surface leads that closed questions would end

text: Set explicit terms before work begins: agree expenses plus a fee and lawful scope; for challenges needing the challenger's help, require full cooperation and dropped objections.
when: When accepting a job or a challenge.

text: Explain your purpose to a witness in plain, conversational terms; an overly formal explanation can lose their attention entirely.
Ask witnesses for facts rather than verdicts, so they do not steer the account toward a conclusion.
Stage the full explanation as a scene where the detective already knows the answer, so tension comes from how the room reacts rather than the solution.
Design an NPC offer whose meaning shifts with the player's knowledge, so a player who recalls a fact hears the same line as a threat.
when: writing dialogue with hidden meaning
why: the same words carry different weight given what the listener knows

text: Let an NPC withhold a fact until the player has combined the contradictions or gaps they noticed, and present the dialogue as a sequence of inconsistencies the player can point out.
when: Designing dialogue that reveals a secret through player reasoning.
why: Each point the player raises unlocks the next admission, which rewards collecting evidence.

text: Delivering the full explanation at once reads as a lecture and drains the reveal's impact; spread it out so the audience can confirm it from earlier clues.
when: the full solution is delivered at once
why: Too much exposition at once overwhelms the audience

text: Leaving an overheard scene early can miss the rest of the statement, which may change its meaning.
