1) Withhold the conclusion while planting the clues. 2) Reveal the conclusion at a chosen moment. 3) Walk through the reasoning in order, linking each early clue to the answer.
when: Closing a mystery where the solution depends on earlier clues.
why: Ordered recaps let the audience see how seemingly minor details form the solution.

text: Script a confrontation so a line of dialogue reveals a language or ability the player can notice and act on.
when: when an NPC has been described as lacking a skill
why: contradictions between description and speech reward attention

text: Layered presentation makes each link checkable but can make the combined case look stronger than its foundations, since stacked inferences add apparent weight.
when: a case rests on inference rather than physical proof
why: each added layer can seem to confirm the last

text: Layered testimony makes an account partly unreliable without making it false, but stacking too many filters leaves the audience unable to tell what happened.
when: Designing how much intermediation a story uses
why: Each filter adds doubt, and too many erase the core facts

text: Flag sore-point cues such as hesitations or stressed keywords; a question touching one unlocks a new line, and a changed line or animation marks the reaction.
when: Designing dialogue that rewards careful questioning
why: Signalling cues in speech lets players discover new lines of inquiry from how an NPC answers.

text: Requests for small commitments made during an emotional appeal are attempts to extract agreement the speaker can later use.
when: when a speaker pleads for a quick favour or meeting

text: A speaker's cut-off or pointed remark can carry a warning that a listener, bound by his own assumptions, reads as rudeness or small talk.
when: A character's dialogue hides information the listener lacks
why: The listener interprets words through his own assumptions, so the hidden sense appears only on a second reading.

text: Secondary characters often reveal knowledge or shared feeling through unguarded interjections that the main account omits.
when: Several people give accounts of the same event
why: People are less guarded when they are not the primary speaker, so their remarks can contradict the main story

text: Offering a drink is a social move that both sides use to signal they are not hostile.
when: at the start of a tense meeting

text: A sudden shift in a witness's mood or topic usually marks a sore point worth pursuing.
when: During an indirect interview

text: In social scenes with several NPCs, let body language and glances between characters hint at who is hiding what.
Scatter casual dialogue from several sources, such as a guard's mention of a flooded drain, so that it pays off later when matching evidence appears.
why: small talk from several sources can combine into a pattern in hindsight

text: A furious NPC line can hint at a different target; players uncover the true object of anger through a second dialogue or a written document.
when: Designing NPC dialogue with hidden motives
why: Second sources confirm or correct the first

text: Question a reticent witness one fact at a time, using narrow questions, so each answer narrows what can be inferred.
Run NPC interrogations on small talk with branching remarks, letting the player infer what the NPC knows from shifts in tone and pauses.
Allow players to skip optional rambling dialogue, but never skip dialogue that carries a critical clue, and keep a direct route to the lead.
when: Designing a rambling quest-giver who delays a clue.
why: Characterful digression should not block progress or hide essential information.

text: Use a plausible social pretext, such as a small delivery, to give a reason to visit and to carry messages.
A respected member's action can make others follow: handing over keys speeds compliance during group searches, and objecting to an unjust case makes others defer.
when: during group searches, or when a dispute involves an unjust action
why: Others follow or defer to the respected figure's standing and judgment.

text: A false persona or assumed role, such as a nurse or relative's agent, unlocks access or disclosures, including indirect accusations, that the true identity would be refused.
when: an investigator must enter a home or restricted place, or access depends on a role
why: Access is granted to the believed identity, not the true one; roles carry consequences that change what NPCs reveal.

text: Let answers vary with question phrasing, and make checkable details reachable only through precise, verifiable questions, rewarding precision as a skill.
when: designing dialogue for hypnotized, delirious or altered characters, or for checkable details
why: Rewarding precision gives players a reason to refine questions and makes answers testable.

text: A character who is not the main offender may answer a notice, because avoiding it gives them little reason.
when: character is a partial participant, not the principal culprit
why: fewer reasons to hide reduce the urge to avoid exposure

text: A witness who refuses to accept a correction to a recalled remark may reveal what the original words meant to them.
when: When an interviewer corrects a witness's recalled phrase.
why: Holding to wording often signals private knowledge.

text: A suspect who asks that an overheard exchange be kept from authorities reveals that they fear its content more than the investigation.
A witness's wording that names a source, such as having been told something, reveals how the knowledge was acquired.
Extreme personal reserve can unsettle others and be read as suspicious, yet it suggests a motive without proving one.
A partly true threat of legal consequence can turn a hostile gatekeeper cooperative.
when: the threat has some basis in fact
why: a credible threat raises the cost of continued refusal

text: A subject who knows the examiner's dislikes tends to shape answers toward what the examiner wants, so the answers mirror the examiner's beliefs.
when: The subject can learn the examiner's known prejudices during the test.
why: A performer reads the audience and gives expected answers rather than true ones.

text: Saying one will forgive and wait can make a pressing aim look patient rather than urgent.
Accused people in such records respond in three ways: they confess, they refuse to plead, or they confess and later withdraw the confession.
Order NPC conversation from background to events to opinions, and let an NPC tell its full story before handing out clues, so players gather facts before theories.
when: designing dialogue that carries clues
why: Complete context lets the player interpret each clue correctly.

text: Ask witnesses about peripheral details they may have seen unnoticed; answers reveal whether the account was observed. A prompt asking if an NPC noticed a detail unlocks otherwise hidden observations.
Give NPCs unprompted plausible explanations for traces, and let each cover story hold until the player finds a conflicting fact, turning the explanation into a test.
when: designing NPC dialogue that hides a truth
why: Delayed contradiction turns a stated explanation into a puzzle the player can test against evidence.

text: In dialogue, give a key word two valid meanings tied to different items or places, so the player must test each reading.
when: designing clue dialogue
why: the player must weigh alternatives rather than accept one

text: Structure quest-giver dialogue as a checklist of topics the player must cover before the NPC reveals a key fact.
when: Designing gated dialogue.

text: Test an NPC's claimed identity with a dialogue branch that offers a choice and a warning, showing a visible behavior change if the claim is false.
when: Designing a dialogue where an NPC's identity can be challenged.

text: Offer a dialogue option that lets the player threaten to reveal a secret, with the NPC responding differently depending on trust and evidence collected.
when: when designing NPC interrogation
why: leverage gives the player agency and makes NPC responses depend on prior play

text: Asking what someone said as they departed can expose their intent, since farewell remarks often carry it.
Patience and small personal rapport keep a suspect talking better than force does, while the core secret stays protected.
when: when a suspect guards a central secret
why: rapport keeps the subject talking

text: A suspect who asks to postpone questions while promising a full account later is making a telling move worth noting.
when: a suspect reacts with a request to defer questioning
why: deferral often signals something being held back

text: When a suspect's performed image conflicts with a genuine emotional reaction, the mismatch is a clue that can expose the performance.
when: a single event reveals the suspect's true reaction
why: People performing a role tend to show the emotions that fit the role, so a genuine reaction breaks the pattern.

text: Script an informant NPC with a grudge to reveal a location or object when the player gives a partial answer, and include self-justifying lines that the player must weigh.
when: Designing an NPC informant in a dialogue-driven game
why: Partial answers and biased framing make the reveal feel earned and keep reliability uncertain

text: Use a pause once, and use a physical prop to focus attention on the key evidence; repeated pauses dull the effect.
when: Staging a reveal's climax.
why: A single well-placed pause and a visible prop direct attention without fatigue.

text: Broad questions return generic or vague answers that unlock narrower questions once a related clue is held; hedged answers can be flagged low-confidence.
when: designing an NPC conversation with a sequence of questions
why: Gating keeps the conversation following the order in which evidence is found.

text: In dialogue, an NPC's guard can drop when a sensitive topic is raised, unlocking lines that are otherwise hidden from the player.
when: A dialogue system ties hidden lines to an emotional topic.
why: Raising a sensitive subject reduces the NPC's defences and reveals more.

text: A dialogue system can let an NPC decline a topic in a way that reveals a concern, and the player can learn more by trying related topics.
when: when designing NPC dialogue
why: Declined topics become an inference puzzle rather than a dead end.

text: An NPC suspect's cover explanation can be tracked against whether the player accepts it, challenges it, or reveals knowledge, changing what that NPC believes the player knows.
when: when designing a suspect NPC at a crime scene

text: Let an NPC revise its answer after another NPC reminds it of an event, and tag which details are firsthand and which are reconstructed.
why: Lets the player trace how the memory changed.

text: An NPC interrogation can be staged in phases: a hostile opening, a run of narrow factual prompts, then a reassurance node that unlocks the confession.
when: Designing a dialogue sequence that extracts a secret from an NPC.
why: Each phase changes the NPC's state, so the confession follows from the earlier phases.

text: An NPC's first answer can be deliberately wrong, with the corrected answer unlocked only after the player shows a matching object or logged event.
A suspect who suspects a trap may perform innocence, so the observer's reading of the reaction can be misleading.
when: A decoy test is used on a suspect who may be alert.
why: A deliberate act can imitate the reaction of an innocent recipient.

text: Staying passive while detained lets the opponent act freely; relying only on your own standing can fail when you are a stranger.
A restated answer can be taken as a commitment the subject never made, so restatements should be checked with the subject.
When the exchange turns personal, the interview can end early and the questioner loses control of it.
Gathering all parties into one room reveals motives, but witnesses may then perform for the room rather than report honestly.
when: A group confrontation is staged
why: People adjust their statements when others are watching.

text: Sincere penitence does not prove the earlier testimony was true.
1) Tell the other party you already know part of the matter. 2) Ask them to supply what is missing. 3) Note which parts they correct or react to.
when: Interviewing someone who would refuse a direct question

text: 1) Gather concrete points of evidence. 2) Secure endorsement from independent authorities. 3) Make the accusation only after that support is in place.
when: When an extraordinary claim meets resistant listeners
why: Independent endorsement counters the suspicion that the accuser is unbalanced.

text: Let weakened NPCs (injured, sick, exhausted, or rescued) give partial answers first; repeated prompts, rest or later progress unlock fuller testimony.
when: designing dialogue for an injured, sick, exhausted or rescued character
why: Staged disclosure rewards persistence without giving everything at once.

text: Let an NPC summarise a route or events while omitting a key stop or scene, which follow-up questions, a later conversation or a found letter reveal.
In dialogue trees, let neutral or sympathetic player prompts unlock more NPC disclosure, and track which claims the player has already heard.
when: when authoring branching NPC conversations
why: Sympathetic prompts make NPCs talk more freely.

text: Do not repeat a bluff that has already failed to move the suspect.
Let an NPC argue against the player's theory using stakes the player has not considered, so the theory must be retested rather than accepted.
when: Writing dialogue that challenges a player's deduction.
why: New stakes reveal gaps in the player's reasoning.

text: In a dialogue system, force the player to ask questions in an order that narrows the NPC's options, and track each answer for consistency.
Let NPCs keep talking by offering follow-up topics tied to what the player has just learned, instead of ending on one fixed line.
why: Linked topics reward the player's recent discoveries

text: Give an NPC a dilemma the player can discuss; the NPC's response reveals a choice that can unlock a hidden location or item.
when: designing NPC dialogue that hides optional content

text: In a dialogue tree, let an NPC volunteer a motive when asked about their last contact, and unlock a hidden line through a follow-up question.
when: When designing NPC conversation branches for investigation
why: Layered questioning rewards players who probe rather than accept the first answer.

text: Build dialogue options that are true but unhelpful, so the player can deflect without giving new information.
when: Designing evasive dialogue choices.
why: Deflection options let players protect information without lying.

text: Offer dialogue options with different wording, such as stranger, visitor, or anyone carrying cargo, so the choice of framing becomes a fair-play puzzle.
when: when a question's wording changes the answer
why: Precise framing exposes answers that broad framing hides

text: Make NPC dialogue literally true yet misleading when the player's knowledge is incomplete, and let later evidence revise earlier statements in the player's notes.
when: When designing NPC testimony in a game.
why: Lets players discover that accurate words can still hide the truth.

text: Open a new NPC question only after the player has overheard and recorded an exact phrase from another character, rewarding careful listening.
when: designing dialogue progression
why: quotations link conversations and reward attention

text: Build reticent dialogue options that signal hesitation without stating the secret, so the player senses something is held back.
when: Designing dialogue for a character who knows more than they say

text: After an NPC reacts strongly, offer a later return point, since forcing dialogue then can shut it down.
when: An upset NPC ends or refuses conversation.
why: Pressing an agitated character closes off further dialogue.

text: Model NPC interviews as dialogue options for sympathy, pressure and bribery, each changing what the NPC reveals and how reliable it is.
when: designing NPC interrogation

text: Write witness dialogue with perspective bias so players can compare two accounts and spot the distortions.
A dialogue system can offer an honest option that an NPC reads as a joke or lie, with the reading depending on the NPC's traits.
when: When designing dialogue choices that depend on NPC personality
why: NPC traits change how the same truthful statement is interpreted

text: Write NPC dialogue with filler and a few key facts, so the player must sort useful lines from noise.
when: When writing long NPC monologues
why: Filler makes the key facts a test of attention, giving the player an active role.

text: Design NPC dialogue to open with fixed low-stakes questions that record a baseline, then branch on the reply to a pointed question.
Let an NPC answer aggressive dialogue options with silence, while a respectful or culturally specific option unlocks a structured account.
Let players receive partial payment first and the rest after proof, so the mechanic tests NPC sincerity.
Let NPCs sign public statements of good character that the player can collect as a counter-case.
Let a boastful NPC mention a location or name in passing, so the player's deduction, not the NPC's intent, delivers the clue.
when: designing NPC dialogue

text: When a suspect offers to waive or dismiss a source as unimportant, check that source, since it may be something they want hidden.
when: A suspect offers to let the investigator skip a document or area.
why: Volunteering to drop a source can keep the investigator from examining it.

text: Unguarded behaviour is often more reliable than deliberate statements, so witnesses to such moments deserve extra weight.
when: Weighing a character's words against their actions
why: People control what they say more than what they do unseen

text: A dialogue line that slips out unintentionally can be stored and revisited later, so a hint of hidden knowledge pays off when the player returns.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that may hide knowledge.
why: A remembered slip rewards attentive players and links later scenes.

text: Overheard or relayed dialogue delivered with uncertain accuracy prompts the player to verify it with a second source.
when: Designing dialogue delivered through an intermediary
why: Uncertain accuracy makes cross-checking a meaningful action

text: A volunteered denial draws attention to the denied topic and can make an innocent witness look guilty, since audiences read unprompted denials as signs the denied thing is real.
when: a witness offers a denial unprompted
why: the denial signals that the topic matters to them

text: Vague answers such as 'some business' should be followed up before committing to a theory.
when: A suspect gives an unspecific reason
why: Unexamined vagueness can hide the truth.

text: A callback must point to an accessible scene, since a vague reference cannot be checked and the reveal then feels arbitrary.
when: Referring back to earlier material in a reveal.
why: A reference the audience cannot locate gives no means of verification.

text: An obscure remark reads as a random outburst unless it is tied to a visible motive.
when: Writing a cryptic line for a character.
why: Without a visible motive, the audience cannot see why the speaker would hint at all.

text: Tag dialogue lines that have two readings so that a suspicious listener selects the damaging literal reading.
when: Writing dialogue that can be misread by a skeptical NPC.
why: Ambiguity becomes a mechanism when listener bias chooses between readings.

text: Count every response, including a single word, nod or head shake, as an answer to be interpreted.
when: When a witness gives minimal or non-verbal replies.
why: Small reactions carry information that an investigator can miss if they listen only for full statements.

text: A dialogue system can time player or NPC answers and flag unusual latency on keyword prompts.
when: Designing a dialogue or interrogation system that uses response timing.
why: Latency on trigger words can signal that the character is hiding something.

text: Let a witness give a hesitant partial answer that the player can later confirm elsewhere, turning the answer into a verifiable dialogue puzzle.
Redirect a question with a small, unremarkable topic so the change of subject feels natural rather than evasive.
An NPC's hesitation before naming something signals that the answer lies nearby and can point the player to a hidden inspection action.
when: Writing dialogue for an NPC who knows part of the answer.
why: Hesitation draws attention to a topic the player should examine.

text: A dialogue tree can unlock follow-up questions only after a prior answer is confirmed, so questioning proceeds in steps.
when: Designing NPC dialogue for an investigation.
why: Gating follow-ups on confirmed answers enforces a logical order.

text: Dialogue can track an NPC's composure so that revealing answers unlock only after its theatrical display drops.
Reassurance options in branching dialogue can unlock additional detail from a reluctant NPC, so the player must choose the right tone to proceed.
when: In dialogue systems where NPCs guard information.
why: Reluctant NPCs release information when they feel safe, so tone choices gate later content.

text: An NPC's teasing remark about another character can set a flag that unlocks a later lead once the player records it.
when: In games with branching dialogue and flagged world state.
why: Recorded dialogue flags let early conversation gate later content.

text: A dialogue tree can present two suspects, with the character's reaction revealing a hidden link to one of them.
when: Designing an interrogation dialogue that surfaces hidden information.
why: A reaction to a specific option discloses knowledge the character would not state directly.

text: A dialogue option that deflects an NPC's question can carry real consequences for what the NPC does next.
when: player chooses a deflecting dialogue option

text: Emotional reactions, such as a defensive remark, indifference or boldness after identification evidence, are clues to weigh with other evidence, not proof of guilt or innocence.
when: Interpreting a suspect's or witness's early or emotional reaction to a remark or identification evidence.
why: A defensive reaction alone does not establish guilt, and composure has many causes unrelated to the facts being tested.

text: A partial admission or accusation against another party can be a deflection that redirects attention; treat it as a lead to investigate, not a finding.
when: When a witness makes a partial admission or points at someone else as the culprit.
why: Apparent admissions and blame can redirect attention or avoid scrutiny of the witness's own conduct.

text: Professional courtesy is easy to mistake for personal warmth, so a change in tone needs context before it is read as sincere.
when: Reading NPC dialogue tone

text: 1) Grant the opposing side's central claim where it is strong. 2) Test whether it implies a different motive. 3) Propose a rival explanation and check it against the evidence.
when: When the opposing claim is strong and a rival theory is available.
why: Granting a strong claim removes it from dispute and lets the rival theory be tested directly.

text: Keep a running log of every NPC statement, keeping both versions when an NPC changes a statement after new evidence, so players can replay it and detect contradictions.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that the player may re-check or that responds to player evidence.
why: A complete record makes inconsistencies detectable, and preserved contradictory versions let the player test the NPC's reliability.

text: Give each suspect NPC a dialogue state that changes after the player says a name or shows an item, with reactions readable in more than one way.
when: Designing suspect NPCs in an investigation game.
why: Changing states and ambiguous reactions make the player weigh evidence instead of reading a single signal.

text: Record which of the player's claims an NPC has accepted or challenged, and unlock new answers only when related evidence is shown.
when: When building a dialogue system with evidence-gated answers.
why: Tracking claims lets the NPC respond consistently across the conversation.

text: A dated diary can give a checkable timeline and show its writer's state of mind, but it does not prove the events it reports; leave the author's bias for others to weigh.
when: Designing found-document clues or assessing a diary as evidence
why: Timestamps can be checked against other events, and motive remains open to judgment.

text: A written account left by someone who has departed can answer a mystery, supply a motive and fix a timeline.
A personal record with side remarks is vivid but may reflect the keeper's feelings and grievances.
Misspellings corrected by another hand suggest a text was written from dictation rather than composed freely.
when: A draft shows corrections by a different hand.
why: A dictated text carries errors that a free composer would not make.

text: Journal entries about other characters show where a culprit's plan was exposed and where he misjudged people, so they can serve as evidence.
Use a culprit's written record to prove the reveal after identification; it does not help identify him beforehand.
Diary entries reveal motive as well as mood, so read recorded prayers, requests and remarks for the interests they serve.
why: Personal records expose priorities that formal statements conceal.

text: Separate what a source knows from what it hopes or fears, since wishes shape what a letter or warning emphasises.
when: Evaluating a letter, warning or advice from a third party.
why: Motive and emotion can make a source's claims unreliable even when sincere.

text: A diary written by an NPC who misreads events gives the player information the NPC lacks, letting the player act on the gap.
when: a found journal is placed in a game world
why: the player's knowledge exceeds the writer's

text: Let written diaries or notes act as items that anchor NPC testimony to specific dates.
Check a diary's dates and wording against other accounts before using it as a timeline or as a record of events.
Do not promise a reduced penalty that cannot be delivered; state any lighter outcome only as a possibility.
when: offering incentives for a confession
why: unkept promises damage trust in the exchange

text: Observed behavior near food, such as climbing toward caged prey, can reveal an unseen animal's diet.
when: When an animal's actions near food can be observed or inferred.
why: Actions near food indicate what the animal eats.

text: Digestion timing is an estimate, so test results must be read with care about expected timing.
when: Interpreting stomach contents for time of ingestion
why: Digestion varies, so timing carries uncertainty

text: A key fact that reaches the player only through a second character is held with less certainty, and players tend to test it rather than accept it.
when: a reveal delivered by an intermediary
why: the source is one step removed from the event

text: A direct indication shows presence outright, while a circumstantial indication only suggests it; clues differ in strength and should be sorted by this.
A plausible route by which a witness could have absorbed relevant history unknowingly can explain knowledge they claim to have gained elsewhere.
Traces the investigator did not see personally rest on other people's descriptions and should be treated as less certain.
1) Tag each report by source. 2) Mark whether the speaker saw the event or repeated what others said. 3) Weigh firsthand reports above relayed ones.
when: When a case rests on many small reports, some of them relaying speech.
why: Relayed speech adds a link where error or bias can enter.

text: Separate what a source directly observed from what it was told, and note where each source's knowledge stops.
why: Secondhand accounts can sound as firm as eyewitness accounts while hiding how little the source actually knows.

text: Separate what a witness saw and heard firsthand from what another person told them afterwards, and flag any parts they cannot repeat accurately.
when: A witness reports a private exchange or a later account
why: Relayed or remembered speech is easier to distort than direct perception

text: Examine the physical evidence directly rather than accepting a lead offered by someone else.
when: when a colleague or witness offers a ready explanation
why: direct reading keeps the investigation honest

text: Require character testimony to come from people with direct, long-term contact with the subject.
When data reaches you through a trusted intermediary who reads figures aloud, record that person as the source of the timeline.
why: The source's reliability shapes how far the timeline can be trusted.

text: Demanding direct proof for obscure matters may leave no verdict possible, while accepting circumstantial proof lowers the bar in practice.
when: when the crime is hidden and direct evidence is scarce
why: Circumstantial proof can fill the gap but makes wrongful conviction more likely.

text: A culprit may discard an item they would be exposed by carrying farther, showing awareness of what the item reveals.
Physical evidence discarded before inspection cannot be rechecked later, so its state must be recorded when it is found.
Discarded objects often end up in nearby concealed spots such as gardens or bushes, where they can remain for a long time.
Keep a record of facts set aside during early sorting, and do not discard facts that disagree with the working theory, since the discarded fact may be the decisive one.
when: Facts are being filtered before they are tested, or when they disagree with the working theory
why: Early selection or theory-driven discarding can throw away the fact that matters and hide evidence that could overturn the theory.

text: Discarded clothing can show that a suspect changed appearance after leaving the place where they were seen.
when: Searching for someone who may have changed their look
why: Changed clothing reveals a deliberate change of appearance

text: Discarding the only escape vehicle a fugitive needs looks like a diversion rather than a real act of flight, and should be treated as suspicious.
A passage a writer deliberately removed may reveal a revision made after reflection, so note what was left out.
why: Deletions can show how a position changed.

text: Everyday refuse such as wrappers and discarded letters often survives destruction by chance, and can carry more useful information than deliberate evidence.
when: Physical trail is thin and suspects have tried to destroy items.
why: People tend to destroy deliberate evidence but overlook packaging and scraps.

text: Discarded documents survive when layered under later refuse and ash, since each layer adds protection from decay and disturbance.
when: When designing hidden or buried clues in a level.
why: Successive covering layers shield fragile material from being destroyed.

text: Declaring evidence worthless without testing it can lose the key clue, since an item that seems meaningless may solve the case.
when: Assessing a seemingly trivial or suspicious item
why: Apparent worthlessness is not verified until the item is examined.

text: Discarded items can be recovered, and items hidden in water still give investigators reason to search.
A discarded forged message can be recovered later, so the forger leaves a paper trail that investigators can use to reconstruct the lure.
why: Discarded paper is rarely destroyed completely.

text: Discarding packaging removes the only independent test of an account of how an item arrived.
Disposing of items in several places multiplies the locations an investigator must search, and each location can yield a trace.
when: A culprit spreads discarded items across different places.
why: More disposal sites mean more chances for evidence to be found.

text: A narrator's rational dismissal of a witnessed anomaly can keep the clue from being examined, and it may be lost.
when: An observer notices an anomaly and another character explains it away
why: Explaining away prevents further examination

text: Dismissing a witness as insane, unwell, or hysterical ends inquiry or lowers their weight without disproving the account; test strange details, since illness alone does not make it false.
when: A character or investigator discounts a witness's emotional, ill, or strange testimony.
why: Emotional delivery or illness is not the same as falsehood.

text: Discount embellished accounts, including a witness's self-praise and partisan or dramatic framing, and keep only the bare facts reported.
when: A witness's account is wrapped in enthusiasm, self-praise, or strongest-colour framing.
why: Exaggeration and vivid framing can inflate the facts beyond what the evidence supports.

text: Do not dismiss a biased, vague, or unreliable witness outright; their usable facts, leads or event details survive, and dismissing all testimony discards real information.
when: A witness has a motive, weak memory, or vague dates but offers concrete information.
why: Bias distorts content, but underlying facts or directions can be correct, and reliable parts are lost when all testimony is dismissed.

text: Discrediting a witness for questionable conduct or poor moral character can discard accurate testimony, since conduct and character are separate from factual accuracy.
when: A witness's own behaviour is questionable or their character is poor.
why: Conduct and character are separate questions from accuracy.

text: Discount testimony from people close to a suspect or quarrelling with the accused unless checked independently; dismissing it outright may discard claims that are true or confirmed elsewhere.
A dismissed or careless-seeming witness may still be right; re-check sightings conflicting with the official view and minor conflicts with a confident theory before rejecting them.
when: A witness's account conflicts with the official view or a confident theory.
why: The witness may be right about a detail the theory missed.

text: Weigh a stakeholder narrator's account against his own admissions and against other witnesses before accepting his version of events.
when: A narrator has a stake in how events are judged.
why: His self-serving framing and admitted errors make his account partial, so independent checks reveal the facts.

text: An NPC who notices a pattern can warn the player while a powerful figure dismisses the warning, creating tension the player can exploit.
when: Designing faction conflict around a discovered pattern
why: The gap between warning and dismissal gives the player a reason to act.

text: Set a suspect aside with stated reasons rather than dismissing them outright, so the discount can be checked later.
when: A suspect looks guilty because of a convenient role.
why: Explicit reasons make the discount testable and fair.

text: Reframing a disputed claim as open questions for decision makers keeps it in play while formally disowning it.
Once a listener accepts a general theory that the accuser's mind is disordered, every protest from the accuser can be read as further proof of illness, so the claim cannot be tested in conversation.
when: A specific but unverified accusation is answered by questioning the accuser's sanity
why: An unfalsifiable framing absorbs all counter-argument

text: Dismissing an early warning or anonymous note as a prank can miss a pattern across later incidents or discard the only insider clue.
why: Notes can carry access information.

text: Dismissing a frightened witness as mistaken, or a fear as baseless, before testing the setting can discard a true account or a real hiding place.

Absurd-sounding explanations may hold the true mechanism, and unlikely second-hand reports may be right; discard an explanation only on direct testimonial contradiction, after checking first-hand sources.
when: Choosing between candidate explanations or a theory is dismissed as fanciful.
why: Likelihood is a weaker basis than contradiction; dismissal based on strangeness can discard the explanation that fits the physical facts.

text: Dismissing a child's warning too quickly can hide a true clue; weigh it against known facts instead.
Dismissing a reasonable lead with contempt can shut down a line of inquiry before its value is tested.
A witness who says they know nothing relevant may still hold the decisive fact. Check what a source contains before treating it as irrelevant.
when: when a source seems unhelpful
why: People often disclaim relevance while holding information they did not think mattered.

text: A quick dismissive explanation for a gap may be a deflection; check it rather than accepting it.
Dismissing the explanations people give as cover for a real motive turns the inference into the observer's assumption rather than evidence.
when: a character's stated reason conflicts with the investigator's theory
why: the investigator stops testing and starts projecting

text: Dismissing a recantation as a lie because the original confession is already on record ignores the conditions the recantation exposes.
When a watcher is dismissed or caught, trigger a dialogue or event so the failed tail has consequences.
Discount accusations offered as personal opinion that no evidence supports, and do not treat them as findings.
when: A witness accuses someone without backing.
why: Opinion without evidence is unverified.

text: Do not dismiss a credible expert merely because the investigator dislikes the conclusion.
When disputing a published claim, produce the relevant documents in full rather than summaries, so readers can judge the disputed passages themselves.
Discarding testimony that conflicts with established facts keeps the record clean but may lose real information that the witness did provide.
when: witnesses conflict or a suspect's account seems tailored
why: every rejected account carries a cost as well as a benefit

text: Discrediting a rival's clue by attacking the rival wins the moment but can cost standing with factions who see the attack as partisan.
when: when a dialogue option attacks a source instead of the evidence

text: Discovery order reflects the search, not true sequence; ordering events or traces by it can falsely link independent things or separate connected ones, and misreads a depositor's route.
A discovery that follows closely after public accusations deserves scrutiny, since it may have been arranged to fit them.
Objects left a long time in a busy public spot would likely have been noticed, so their remaining undiscovered suggests a shorter placement.
when: judging how long objects were left unseen
why: busy places make discovery likely

text: Direct attention to the part of a person or object that takes repeated contact, such as trouser knees or sleeves, where traces accumulate.
when: examining a suspect's clothing or belongings
why: repeated contact concentrates wear

text: Finding a body does not itself implicate the person who finds it, because someone must discover every crime.
A system that controls which characters learn a discovery, and in what order, changes how each character reacts.
Being discovered while hiding or tailing can end the investigation.
A discovered covert placement can end all cooperation with the household.
why: Discovery makes the target distrust every future approach.

text: Present a timeline in true order even when the investigator discovered the events in another sequence.
when: Giving the player a case-file or recap of a solved mystery.
why: Reversed order confuses the audience; the true order makes causes clear.

text: Do not treat where a body or object is found as where the crime happened; separate the discovery site, the killing site and any site where remains were moved.
why: remains and objects can be placed or moved after the act

text: Make a hidden errand discoverable by letting players ask the right question of the right NPC.
Test a claimed discovery for physical plausibility, since an item in a pocket is unlikely to fall out without rough handling.
when: an item is said to be found on a body
why: ordinary positions do not dislodge items

text: A witness who learns the investigator must share information with colleagues may immediately ask how discreet those colleagues are.
when: When an investigator states that information will be passed on to others.
why: The witness's concern shifts from the facts to who else will learn them.

text: Offer the player a discreet way to end a blackmail threat, such as a trusted authority figure, so it resolves without public exposure.
when: Designing a blackmail quest
why: Victims often avoid authorities who might expose their secret, so a trusted channel must exist

text: Recruit agents from people whose circumstances make them easily employed and discreet, drawing on a prepared register of such people.
when: A network of covert agents is needed quickly.
why: Ready candidates shorten placement and reduce the risk of indiscretion.

text: Request comparison material without revealing the aim of the examination.
when: comparison material is held by others

text: Promising discretion in return for a disclosure can stop the investigator from checking the disclosed account with others.
when: When a witness offers a private account in exchange for confidentiality.
why: A promise of secrecy creates a social obligation that discourages verification.

text: 1) Split the investigation into discrete tasks. 2) Give each task a named place, a time and a target object. 3) Ask for a report on every result, including negative ones.
when: an outsider without official powers wants to steer an existing inquiry
why: Narrow, checkable tasks are easier for the official team to act on

text: Keep surveillance discreet and avoid alarming people close to the trail, because visible pursuit ends the chance of learning more.
when: Shadowing a contact who may lead to an accomplice.
why: Visible approaches cause the contact to notice the watch and change their behaviour.

text: When a questioner who stands to gain presses for information, give answers that are true but reveal nothing new.
when: A friendly-seeming questioner asks about sensitive matters.
why: True but unhelpful answers protect what is known without deception.

text: Offering discretion is cheap and can draw out fuller detail from a witness, but it trades away pressure and may protect a guilty party.
when: Choosing how to press a reluctant witness who fears exposure
why: The assurance costs the questioner little and removes the main risk to the witness, but it costs leverage and risks protecting the culprit.

text: Treat witness discrepancies as contradictions to resolve and clues to observer state, not noise; call them evidence, not proof, until you know what each witness could perceive.
when: when accounts of one event conflict
why: Differences reveal each observer's state and vantage, and a witness may have inferred rather than observed.

text: Decide between rival readings of a trace by naming and applying a test whose outcome differs between them, such as whether enough material remains to analyze.
when: When a trace fits more than one explanation.
why: A named test turns an open question into a checkable one.

text: Test a theory by asking for something it predicts a guilty party would refuse, so the answer discriminates between the theory and innocence.
when: a theory predicts a specific reaction
why: A yes or no then carries information

text: A detail that fails to match the expected fact, such as a house number differing from the given address, signals a deliberate misdirect.
why: Checking small inconsistencies exposes a planted lure

text: 1) List each point where the witness's account conflicts with the evidence. 2) Order the points from least to most dangerous. 3) Put each point to the witness in turn. 4) Record each answer exactly as it is spoken.
when: a witness has already given a checkable statement
why: Ordered questioning builds pressure gradually and keeps answers reliable.

text: 1) Establish a known inventory of the container or space. 2) Compare its present state against that inventory. 3) Treat a missing item as evidence only if it was known to be present before.
when: When a space or container may have been entered or disturbed.
why: Comparison against a known baseline is what makes an absence meaningful.

text: Question a witness about discrepancies only when you hold independent evidence to test any admission against.
Design a puzzle event so some hypotheses are clearly ruled out, and avoid events that every theory explains since they give the player no information.
when: When scripting a deduction event for the player
why: Only outcomes that discriminate between hypotheses advance the player's reasoning.

text: Matching voice and manner reinforce a costume-based disguise, making a substitute harder to detect in brief contact.
when: when an impersonator speaks to a witness
why: voice and manner add cues to the outfit

text: The relationship between a subject and a visitor, such as client, friend or lover, implies different likely places for a hidden object, so identify it early.
A regular, unremarkable scene that hides a death suggests the killers disguised the cause, because a visible murder would have required a hidden grave.
when: A death appears natural or routine
why: Concealing a violent cause is more likely than hiding a normal one.

text: A cover story repeated without any variation can seem rehearsed to a careful observer.
Let observers misidentify a disguised character in low light or brief sight, then let the player exploit that mistake later as a clue.
when: designing a mistaken-identity encounter
why: low visibility makes misidentification plausible and creates a clue

text: True facts, such as debt, can seem to confirm a theory they do not support; a lead built on them can close a question too early and needs separate testing.
when: A widely accepted story seems complete.
why: Correct facts can support a false conclusion when combined with a plausible but wrong interpretation.

text: Change appearance and adopt a false identity when known faces would be recognised, since recognition makes sources refuse to talk or ends an infiltration at its first step.
when: sources or watched people would recognise the investigator's known face
why: recognition makes sources refuse to talk and would end the infiltration

text: Tie every disguise to the plot as a mechanic that stages late reveal scenes, since a costume that links to nothing leaves readers feeling cheated.
when: when a mystery relies on a character concealing identity
why: mechanical use of disguise creates the reveal scenes that drive the resolution

text: A planner who expects scrutiny may build an alibi beforehand by being seen in public places where others will remember them.
when: when the planner expects an investigation
why: later witnesses can confirm their presence

text: A striking, memorable feature draws observers' attention so strongly that they fail to notice the face beneath a disguise.
when: a disguise includes a conspicuous scar, lip, or hair colour
why: observers fixate on the most distinctive feature rather than the underlying person

text: A disguise lets an investigator move among servants and tradespeople unnoticed, so they can approach households and their contacts without drawing attention.
when: Investigating a closed household or group.
why: Low-visibility cover opens access that open questioning would not.

text: A party with something to hide may confess selected faults to key listeners in its own framing, presenting itself as a victim and warning that accusers are malicious.
why: Prior framing makes later accusations sound like attacks from known enemies

text: A message sent in another person's name can pass unnoticed by a recipient who barely knows that person's voice, so the recipient may not question it.
when: the recipient has little contact with the supposed sender
why: unfamiliar voices are hard to recognise

text: A striking act reported publicly can be imitated by others, so the behavior spreads through a group like a rumor.
when: the act is dramatic and widely reported
why: people copy visible, reported behavior

text: A small item hidden among many similar-looking objects is hard to notice as missing, because it blends into the crowd.
when: Items of similar appearance are scattered or stored together.
why: Visual similarity removes the cue to check for a specific item.

text: A few visible traits, such as height, a beard or a steep forehead, can name a figure only tentatively when the view is brief.
when: when observation is partial, brief or distant
why: incomplete features leave the match uncertain

text: A passing sight can supply a later false identity: a remembered detail, such as a book title, can be reattached to a remark and mistaken for a clue.
when: A player or witness links an incidental detail to a claim
why: Incidental details are easily recalled and reinterpreted

text: Rehearsed forms of deference can gradually become sincere, so a pretended role can turn into real attitude.
when: A character repeatedly performs a role they do not hold.
why: Habitual performance shapes the performer's actual feelings over time.

text: A double identity: one person keeps two identities in one community, each covering the other; the second life, with one confidant, explains absences and lets an apparent victim vanish.
when: a character must be unrecognisable to people who see them daily

text: A disguise works mainly through role and manner, a performance a culprit can put on and off; a cover persona may hide a trained performer.
A disguise often betrays itself through a thin visible seam, such as a pale line at the hairline, where an artificial layer meets real skin or hair.
when: A character's appearance relies on layered parts such as a wig, beard, or stained complexion.
why: Attachments and cosmetics leave edges that a careful observer can notice.

text: A beard or dark clothing can hide a protector's identity from the person they guard.
A substitute body may come from an institutional source, such as a dissection supply, that is unlikely to be questioned.
when: a false death requires a body to pass as the subject
why: an unquestioned source avoids scrutiny of the body's origin

text: A disguise can hide a threat behind a mask of concern, such as a guardian enforcing a rule under an outside identity.
Small changes such as an altered brow line, a hairpiece, hidden shoe lifts, and a cap and apron can disguise a person from people who know them.
when: A person must avoid recognition by acquaintances.
why: Recognition depends heavily on familiar features and silhouette, which these changes alter.

text: A disguise prepared in advance, with a false identity and supporting paperwork, can look ordinary to routine checks.
Grease paint around the eyes is enough to change how observers read a face.
A disguise changes hair, clothes, face and manner, but usually leaves habits, expressions and physical traces such as fingerprints unchanged.
Footwear and posture can add a little height, and a small feature can be built up, but a large feature cannot be reduced quickly by disguise.
when: Judging which traits a disguise can change
why: Disguise methods add material or alter posture but cannot easily remove bulk.

text: A substitute who matches the suspect in height, voice, gait, dress or disguise can make a false alibi appear to hold.
when: when a suspect's alibi rests on being seen elsewhere

text: A strong smell or sudden scent change may hide another odor; ask what the masking covers and why it is so strong.
when: A room has an odd smell or new finish, or a suspect's scent is unusually strong or changes after an event.
why: Concealment often leaves a suspicious surplus of one cover scent; a strong masking odor can hide the original trace.

text: When a bitter or unexpected taste appears, ask what strong-tasting or effervescent agent could mask it, and test the drink for taste before accepting that.
when: when a substance may be concealed in food or drink
why: Masking covers taste, so a clear taste test separates masked from unmasked cases.

text: Give disguised NPCs a consistent tell, such as a scar, accent, ring, gait, habit, repeated gesture, dropped item or careless remark, so an attentive player can unmask them.
when: when an NPC changes appearance with a hood, mask, hair or disguise
why: Description checks fail once appearance changes, and a tell gives attentive players a checkable clue.

text: Plant a disguised character's trait or belonging, such as an accent, repeated gesture, story mismatch or knowledge a stranger should not have, early so the later reveal feels earned.
when: Designing a character who will later reveal a disguise.
why: Prior clues let the audience accept the reveal instead of feeling cheated.

text: Let a disguised NPC hide identity during a scene while leaving a recognizable detail, such as clothing or voice, for later recovery.
when: Generating masked or hooded characters
why: Players can later connect the hidden figure to a known person

text: Do not assume the deeper the inquiry, the closer the truth; in important matters the answer often lies close to the surface.
when: an investigator digs ever deeper without progress
why: searching harder in one place can miss what is obvious nearby

text: A clue that the victim did not react suggests the attacker was trusted, which can steer the player's suspicion toward known characters.
when: when designing a murder with a known killer
why: lack of reaction implies familiarity

text: Give NPCs visible signs such as tan lines, worn uniforms or tattoos so players can infer their past, and let a later character confirm it.
when: Authoring NPC backstory that should be discoverable through play
why: Readable signs reward observation, and confirmation makes the inference feel earned

text: A double identity is weak when one observer knows the face and habits well, or when the disguise leaves traces a search can reveal.
A disguise can explain why a witness was frightened without revealing who was present; identify the person separately from the reason for the scare.
when: a witness reports a phantom or unidentifiable figure
why: the scare and the identity have different causes

text: Coats and similar identity items are easily swapped; confirm which garment is genuinely linked to which person before relying on it.
A companion with a transparent manner reveals private suspicions through behavior, so withholding a theory from them keeps the test honest.
when: when a theory is kept from someone who could betray it
why: a transparent manner leaks suspicion

text: An NPC's quest can match identities by description and known aliases, so a player who asks the wrong question is not dead-ended.
Use a cover story that is plausible for the searcher, so the people questioned have no reason to suspect a real inquiry.
when: When gathering information from people who might be alarmed by a real inquiry.

text: A person who tries to obtain a substitute key, such as by impersonating its owner on a call, needs access they lack.
When a document shows one traveller but a second person was expected, consider that someone else was used in the person's place.
when: A register or bill covers fewer people than the case implies
why: A stand-in can carry the documented identity

text: The person chosen for impersonation reveals what the manipulator knew about the target, so the choice of impostor is itself a clue.
when: a message was faked in someone's name
why: the choice reflects the manipulator's knowledge

text: Compare a speaker's exact wording against earlier statements, since a changed qualifier or stressed detail can reveal concealment.
when: The speaker's earlier statements are available for comparison

text: Track whom an NPC hires, invites or sends for; these readable signals let players infer allegiance without confession.
why: Visible associations convey alliances without explicit dialogue.

text: Separate the two impostor roles so each guards the other from exposure, and let the player connect them through one unchanged detail.
when: designing a quest where two characters share a false identity
why: Keeping roles apart limits what one discovery reveals, and a shared detail rewards careful observation.

text: Encode a character's identity across many small props, such as trade-specific items and habit traces, so a careful player can assemble a profile.
when: A hidden culprit must be discoverable from the scene.
why: Players reward attention when clues from several props converge on one identity.

text: Give NPCs a hidden true-identity field, revealed through an earlier detectable inconsistency that players can notice.
when: Generating NPCs with secret identities.
why: Players need a fair chance to spot the inconsistency.

text: Give two characters a similar build or coat so a witness misidentifies one, creating a false identification the player must correct.
Give a disguised NPC partial cues, such as a gait or voice line, that the player must match later, and let each cue carry some uncertainty.
when: Designing a disguised character for identification.
why: Uncertain partial cues make the later match a reasoned judgement, not a lookup.

text: Do not make a disguise the only route to a solution, since that route depends on the audience accepting the reveal.
when: Designing a solution path that depends on a disguise
why: A single route fails if the reveal does not land

text: A lookalike decoy wearing the same outfit lets the player eliminate suspects by checking a distinctive trait.
Let a disguise mechanic open access to guarded NPC groups, with each cover story unlocking different dialogue and information.
when: Designing stealth or social infiltration.

text: Check each disguise prop against what an observer would expect, and raise suspicion per mismatch rather than for the disguise as a whole.
when: when designing a stealth disguise system
why: per-detail checks show the player which element failed

text: Tie recognition to outfit: a player in other garb may pass unnoticed, while the same player in a known outfit is spotted.
when: when designing a disguise recognition system
why: observers match the outfit as well as the face

text: Decoys can nest, with a container meant to fool a thief holding a second decoy inside it, multiplying the layers of deception.
when: when designing hidden loot in a dungeon

text: A disguise need not be perfect; a plausible setting does most of the work in passing an impostor.
when: when planning a substitution
why: observers judge the setting before the person

text: When a target uses an alias, match descriptions, appearance, or possessions rather than names, and offer an alternative route such as a witness who knows the face.
when: Designing a search for a wanted NPC under a false name
why: Names fail for an alias, while physical traits remain identifiable.

text: Let one character appear as two separate people, betrayed by a distinctive physical trait that a careful observer notices.
when: designing an impostor reveal
why: Players can connect the trait only if they examine people closely.

text: Altered features, changed clothes and a new haircut let one person pass as a different person, so appearance serves as cover for identity.
An impostor can swap costume items such as cloaks, cards and wigs; checks against a register, a witness or unchangeable traits expose it better than appearance.
when: Designing an NPC that impersonates another character.
why: Verification methods determine success, and changeable items are defeated by unchangeable traits.

text: A visible impersonation at a remote place makes the act seem to occur elsewhere, so the impersonation itself becomes the cover for the crime.
why: observers take the visible presence as proof of location

text: A disguised person who changes appearance gradually, copying another's build, hair colour and dress, may pass unnoticed by people who see them daily.
when: A character must pass as another person without being detected by close acquaintances.
why: Slow change avoids the sudden contrast that would alert observers.

text: A culprit who surveys a location under a disguise, such as a delivery role, learns its layout without being recognized and can plan the crime accordingly.
A clue given an ordinary, reasonable-sounding explanation draws attention away from its real meaning, so the explanation ends further questioning.
when: a clue has an innocent-looking explanation offered
why: the explanation sounds natural and satisfies the need for an answer

text: An NPC's written description of a missing person can be compared against items the player has found, turning dialogue output into a checkable clue.
Presenting a story as a true account with disguised names gives its invented documents the weight of real evidence rather than a fictional device.
when: when a fictional document must feel credible
why: the framing lends authenticity to the device

text: Pre-answering each likely question leaves an official little to probe, so the inquiry closes early and controls what authorities hear.
when: a party wants an inquiry to end quickly
why: ready answers remove openings for follow-up

text: Discovering a substitution changes who could have acted, and can show that a plausible plan was pre-empted by someone else.
why: The swap alters the facts that earlier testimony depended on.

text: A ticket for one destination can disguise the real route, making an event appear to follow a later journey from a different place.
when: a document points to a false travel path
why: the document supports a misleading timeline

text: A disguised character is exposed when their claimed location, behavior or known details contradict facts the player can observe and check.
when: designing an impersonator or disguised NPC
why: Contradictions between the disguise and checkable facts give players a way to detect the deception.

text: Information from a deceiver is worthless even when partly true, since mixing truths with lies makes the lies believed.
A guard who logs visitors can build a trail: a permit issued under one name but used by someone with different features lets players deduce the impostor.
when: Designing an access-log puzzle
why: A mismatch between recorded and observed features reveals the impostor

text: A guard animal that reacts differently to a disguised player exposes an impostor without dialogue, when its reaction is readable at a predictable moment.
when: Designing a disguise or impostor encounter
why: Animal recognition gives a non-verbal test the player can set up and read

text: An identity-swap mechanic lets the player replace one corpse with another, and inconsistencies in the swapped features create detectable clues for NPC investigators.
when: When designing corpse-based puzzles in a game.
why: Checks against recorded features expose mismatches the player must avoid.

text: A disguise mechanic with a removal moment lets the player use a disguise, and the removal changes the situation.
when: a stealth or infiltration mechanic

text: NPCs recognise a disguised player only after a trigger, such as a repeated gesture or a particular conversation topic.
A disguise system can let player clue-hunting reveal the real identity behind an altered look, turning recognition into a deduction task.
when: when a disguise mechanic is part of play

text: A person can appear to be somewhere they are not by sending a stand-in of similar build in their clothes, supported by a written token that explains the absence.
when: A character needs to fake presence elsewhere
why: Observers who see clothing and a note assume the person is present

text: When a player stages a disguise to test a guard's story, dialogue can branch on whether the claim survives the test.
when: A player tests an NPC's claim through a disguise
why: Claim outcomes depend on whether the story holds up under the test

text: Impersonation can break an alibi: each sighting is genuine but attaches to the wrong identity.
when: Witnesses place one person in two places at once.
why: Genuine sightings misattributed to different identities create an apparent contradiction without any false statement.

text: One person can cover several identities with few accomplices, so three characters can be played by two people.
when: A household or group is suspected of using disguises.
why: Shared roles let a small group produce many apparent witnesses.

text: A cover role such as a posed professional can grant access to a suspect who would refuse an open investigator, letting them speak in a relaxed way.
when: The suspect would refuse an open inquiry
why: The cover lowers the suspect's guard

text: A supernatural frame, such as a hooded or masked figure, keeps observers from looking closely at the person beneath.
when: when a disguised or hidden person must avoid scrutiny
why: the frame discourages close inspection and invites belief instead

text: Disguise preparation can be cheap and quick: a card printed on demand, a second-hand uniform, and a beard and wig from a costumier are enough for a convincing impersonation.
when: Estimating how hard a disguise is to obtain in a game world.
why: Cheap materials make impersonation a realistic option for characters.

text: A disguise can combine a grown beard, eyeglasses, speech mannerisms borrowed from the impersonated person, clothing bought elsewhere and a documented persona.
Changing only surface details, such as clothing, is quickly seen through; matching appearance without matching behaviour, name or details, also fails under scrutiny.
why: Gait and manner are strong recognition cues that clothing does not hide.

text: A witness's later identification can rest on inference; separate cues actually seen, like voice or gait, from assumed ones and from conclusions reached by later reasoning.
when: A suspect was disguised during the observed event, or a witness names someone after reflecting on it.
why: Witnesses fill gaps with inference, and later reasoning can reconstruct an identity never seen.

text: A disguise is only as good as the target's experience; someone who has practised deception may recognise the costume.
Overconfidence in one's disguise, driven by pride, misjudges a skilled observer and invites exposure.
A disguise can defeat assumptions about age or gait, so one observation should not settle a suspect's identity.
when: when judging a disguised person's identity from appearance
why: Disguises alter the visible cues people rely on

text: Accepting an identity based only on voice or sound as certain, when it is an impression rather than proof.
when: A witness identifies someone without seeing them
why: Sound cues are ambiguous and can be mistaken

text: Assuming a disguise must be elaborate, or trusting a uniform, title or card without checking it, leaves investigators open to con artists.
when: Evaluating whether a claimed identity is genuine.
why: Small, well-timed changes can be enough to deceive.

text: A substitute body depends on passing as genuine, so a witness who knows the person can expose the substitution.
when: a body is presented as a known individual
why: someone familiar with the person can spot the mismatch

text: A plausible reason for knowledge, such as a newspaper report, can cover a real slip, so check the claimed source against what was actually published.
when: a suspect explains away what they know
why: a convincing cover can hide genuine insider knowledge

text: Forgetting a drink's own strong taste, such as coffee's bitterness, can wrongly exclude a candidate, because that taste may hide the poison.
A disguise that build and bearing give away conceals little; judge whether the disguise hides identity before relying on it.
A substitute identity is convincing only if the features others check are the ones altered. Changing unchecked features does not protect the disguise.
when: When faking the identity of a body.
why: Investigators verify specific identifiers, so alterations elsewhere are irrelevant.

text: Do not accept a double identity on one trait; check complementary features against independent records.
why: a single shared feature can be coincidence

text: A hint can arrive disguised as a question about a hobby or entertainment, so it is easily missed.
A visual disguise can cover the face while a small trace, such as an ink mark, remains on the hands, so a check limited to appearance can miss it.
when: When verifying a suspect's identity or activity.
why: Searchers who focus on the face overlook evidence elsewhere on the body.

text: If a roster is the only place a character is described, later clues about that character are easy for the player to miss.
A name that fails to match one register does not prove it false, because other registers or regions may hold the record.
when: Checking a name against a single reference source.
why: Records are incomplete and spelled or filed differently across sources.

text: A disguise that works only at distance or in poor light will be dismissed as implausible by the audience.
A visitor's apparent frailty can be a disguise or a tactic to gain time, so physical signs alone should not be trusted as evidence of honesty.
when: Assessing a stranger's account.
why: Sympathetic appearance can lower an interrogator's guard.

text: 1) Prepare a duplicate in advance. 2) Create a pretext that brings the valuable within reach. 3) Take the real item while the owner is expected not to notice quickly.
when: reconstructing how a theft was planned

text: 1) List every appearance of the suspect. 2) Sort the features by how easily each can be altered. 3) Build a profile from the hardest-to-change traits. 4) Generate candidates matching the profile and eliminate them using checks until few remain.
when: One person appears under several disguises
why: Hard-to-change traits survive disguise and make the candidate pool small.

text: 1) Identify where the scene's object is sold locally. 2) Visit each shop and show a photograph of the suspect. 3) Record the time and any clothing descriptions the shopkeeper gives. 4) Report findings so their weight can be assessed.
when: When the object is sold commercially and sales are not logged.
why: Shopkeepers may recognise a face and link it to a known time and place.

text: 1) Note what the outline alone shows. 2) Identify a physical attribute the outline cannot settle. 3) Test that attribute directly at closer range.
when: When an outline is ambiguous and the identity matters
why: A direct physical test resolves what appearance from afar cannot

text: 1) Show the image to several people, not one. 2) Ask the witness to fix the time of the sighting. 3) Collect concrete descriptors such as height, clothing and speech. 4) Separate direct observation from inference.
when: Testing a witness's recognition of a person from a photograph.
why: Several viewers reveal whether recognition is reliable, and concrete details can be checked.

text: 1) Study the target group's current slang and manner. 2) Adopt a cover identity that uses them consistently. 3) Build trust through in-character behaviour. 4) Confirm any partner knows and plays their assigned role.
when: An investigator must gain trust from a suspicious group
why: A convincing, consistent cover draws out information while avoiding exposure

text: Tie guards', merchants' or staff's identity to a name, badge, invitation or item check, so players judging by role-typical looks are not misled.
when: NPCs can be disguised by swapping outfits; designing identity checks in a game.
why: A checkable credential lets the player catch impostors.

text: Keep a disguise consistent in manner, objects, voice, appearance, gait and invented ailments; otherwise acquaintances who know the real habits will expose any mismatch under scrutiny.
when: Acting a disguise before people who know the real person.
why: Mannerisms are harder to fake than looks; habits betray a disguise that looks sound.

text: Choose a substitute body of similar height, build and hair colour, dressed in the target's clothes, rings and personal items, so a casual viewer accepts it.
when: when a fugitive needs a death accepted as their own, or a body is too damaged for face identification
why: Items and shared features are easier to fake than unalterable traits.

text: Do not rely on costume alone where people who know the person, such as guards familiar with regular staff, would see their face at close range.
when: when judging whether a disguise will hold
why: close familiarity uses facial cues that costume cannot fake

text: Give each NPC fixed outfits and body sizes, and let outfits decide who can pass guards, so clothing and fit checks rule suspects in or out.
when: designing a suspect-elimination or stolen-item puzzle with guards
why: fixed attributes make eliminations checkable; outfits constrain who can plausibly carry the item

text: Gate a player disguise behind acquired skills or profession facts, so NPCs accept the persona only after the player has learned the required knowledge.
when: designing player disguises or cover-identity mechanics
why: the persona is credible only to someone who earned it

text: Documents and clothing can be copied, so confirm identity through a physical trace or behavior discrepancy the impostor cannot match.
when: designing identity mysteries or a disguised NPC could be mistaken for a wanted figure
why: paper passes but behavior and physical traces are much harder to fake

text: Let a disguise or forged permit grant restricted-area entry, with checks that expose false pretexts and NPC reactions to a test item revealing what they hide.
when: a game has guarded or restricted areas or when designing stealth
why: a pretext system gives a non-combat way in; disguise and tests turn stealth into information gathering

text: Make every visible detail match the persona, since one prop signalling a different origin or class can expose a disguise that observers inspect up close.
when: when observers will inspect the disguised person up close
why: a single inconsistent detail can expose the whole disguise; observers examine details rather than glancing at the face

text: An investigator's disguise must suit the setting, match a common local role, and hold up through extended conversation.
why: a costume that fits the local type is accepted without scrutiny

text: Use a disguise only when the disguised person has a plausible reason to be in place.
when: when a character adopts a false identity

text: Make a helper NPC the disguised antagonist, planting an odd habit or item early so the later reveal reframes it.
Design a minor NPC as a hidden antagonist, using its ordinariness as deliberate disguise.
Give concealment a plausible motive such as protection, so the audience is unsure whether it is kind or sinister.
when: A plot depends on one character's knowledge being kept back.

text: Model a voice impersonation as a timed action that leaves a sound event on the world timeline, so later checks can use it.
Track every claim made under a cover story, since any witness who remembers it could later expose the cover.
Make a disguised character's tell noticeable but not conclusive, and give it a fixed pattern that a careful player can catch.
why: the player must corroborate it

text: Track NPC identity across scenes so that a former servant or guard who reappears in a new location is recognisable.
Give an impersonator a plausible routine, and place one environmental slip that corrects it.
when: designing a disguise puzzle
why: A single slip lets a careful player detect the substitution

text: Trace every planted link, such as an order, a delivery address or a collected parcel, since each can lead back to whoever arranged it.
Give each watcher a plausible cover role, such as a vendor, a worker or an acquaintance, so their presence in the area needs no explanation.
when: watchers must stay near a location without drawing attention
why: an ordinary role explains presence and is seldom questioned

text: A substitution theory needs independent confirmation of the trip before it is treated as proven.
Link NPCs by marriage and property so rivalries can be found by reading records rather than stumbled upon.
when: designing NPC relationships for a game

text: Vary an NPC's name spelling across in-world documents so that a player who links the variants must solve an identity puzzle.
when: designing document-based clues

text: Cross-check NPC ages against a parish register, so a claimed age that does not fit the record becomes a clue.
Give NPC judges, guards and witnesses an allegiance attribute; when one faction staffs a tribunal, players should read its verdicts differently.
when: designing a tribunal or court in a game

text: Place discarded clothing or items in rooms as physical traces that show a character changed identity.
when: Populating rooms with evidence

text: Let the player check credentials or membership in an in-game database to detect impostors.
Let players pass guards by changing costume, and base recognition checks on outfit and behavior, not only identity.
when: Designing guard or NPC recognition systems
why: Outfit and conduct are the cues a real observer would use

text: Give NPCs several visible tags, such as clothing, gait and voice, so a witness's description can be matched to one NPC.
why: a description can then single out one character

text: Let players copy an NPC's action, such as raising a lantern, to trigger a hidden response elsewhere in the level.
Make a trap or weapon look like a harmless accessory, so the player finds it by examining NPC belongings or testing the gesture that delivers it.
A disguise mechanic can let a character pass as someone else for a limited time, with a visible tell such as a changed feature.
when: when designing identity mechanics

text: Give a disguised character a fixed bodily tell, such as a burn, missing finger, hand or gait, visible only on close inspection so players can unmask them by looking closely.
when: Designing disguised characters

text: A disguise made from a wig, false beard and costume can conceal a younger person's identity, especially when family portraits show a strong resemblance.
when: A character is seen in a costume that imitates an older person.
why: Costume pieces hide surface features, while shared family features remain visible to those who compare portraits.

text: A disguise can survive a search when it is hidden under a covering such as a glove, so a refusal to uncover a body part is worth noting.
Disguises usually change clothing, hair and manner, so look past targeted features; fixed marks like scars or moles in unexpected places are hard to disguise and can confirm identity.
when: A disguise is suspected and the person controls the features others normally check
why: Clothing, hair and manner can change, while permanent marks usually cannot

text: Tie one fixed, verifiable mark to a schedule others know, such as tides, bells or shift changes, to anchor a timeline when witnesses are unreliable.
when: Witness memory is clouded or witnesses disagree about when events happened.
