text: Prove a disguise with several independent physical traces, such as smell, sweat and stray hair, rather than one observation.
when: a suspect's identity is hidden by disguise
why: multiple corroborating traces make the deduction hard to dismiss

text: Loose garments, veils and large hats hide height, shape, dress and face, so witnesses describe only partial features that do not narrow identity.
when: A culprit disguises appearance with loose clothing or a veil, or witnesses saw the person briefly.
why: Covering the body or face removes cues witnesses use to recognize people, and partial concealment is enough to block recognition.

text: A flamboyant cover can make the real secret look ordinary, pulling the investigator toward the wrong question.
A disguise such as a veil or mourning dress hides exactly the features investigators need to match a suspect.
Build scenes where authorities accept a cover story while the player notices anomalies, and reward players who test the staged plot against its flaws.
when: When designing an investigation with an official explanation
why: Players who spot flaws the authorities missed gain a sense of insight

text: Plant a suspect's evasion or visible lie early to keep a spouse or associate under suspicion while the real suspect is developed.
when: Writing a mystery where an obvious suspect must stay under suspicion for a time.
why: A visible lie gives the wrong suspect a reason to be watched, which buys time for the real suspect.

text: A change of clothes in an empty place leaves no witnesses, so the change itself is hard to detect.
when: A disguise is put on or removed where no one is present.
why: Without observers, nothing records the change.

text: A disguise can be very small, such as a veil, a hat or a coat, and still be enough to fool witnesses.
when: Assessing whether a suspect could have disguised themselves.
why: Minor changes often suffice because observers focus on whole appearance.

text: 1) Adopt a disguise that fits a community whose members talk freely among themselves. 2) Ask about a relevant subject that leads to the person who witnessed the target. 3) Gather the witness's description of the target's movements and appearance.
when: Local knowledge is needed and the community speaks to outsiders on its own terms
why: Insiders share information with those who appear to belong, while strangers are noticed

text: Identify a disguised person by traits a disguise cannot change, such as gait, build, silhouette, voice, dental work, nose, eyes, mouth or a fixed item, not face, clothing or name.
when: two people claim different identities, or a disguised character must be recognised
why: Disguises alter surface features like hair, facial hair and clothing, while body-level traits and underlying proportions persist.

text: Tinted glasses, an altered voice and false whiskers are typical signs that someone is concealing their identity.
when: A witness reports unusual appearance features.
why: Such changes are deliberate and hide who the person is.

text: A disguised threat that proves empty can serve as a scripted reveal, provided the disguise appears earlier in the story.
when: Staging a reveal that changes how a threat is understood.
why: Earlier setup makes the reveal feel earned rather than arbitrary.

text: A physical match can disambiguate between candidates who share a clue such as an initial.
A disguise test needs the real person's physical details on record, because without them the investigator cannot spot a mismatch.
when: the impersonated person's physical details are unknown to the investigator

text: A found object can be matched to a missing one by comparing its dimensions with an empty frame or container.
Test an unnatural appearance with a physical action, such as rubbing the face, to reveal whether a disguise is applied rather than grown.
when: When a suspect's appearance seems wrong, such as a mismatched mustache or stiff hat.
why: Applied disguises can shift or lift under contact in ways natural features do not.

text: Disguise items dropped at a scene, such as a wig lost in a struggle, and leftover application or removal materials are evidence that identity was concealed.
when: Designing or investigating a disguise
why: Concealment steps leave physical traces

text: A disguised suspect can produce honest but contradictory reports from different witnesses, since each saw a different partial view.
when: a suspect has altered their appearance
why: each witness completes a different partial glimpse

text: A disguise that changes only conspicuous features can be detected through careful questioning of witnesses about close-up details.
when: when designing NPC disguise or impersonation
why: questioning exposes mismatches the disguise did not cover

text: An NPC who knows a specialty can test a disguise with questions that only real knowledge answers.
when: a disguised player speaks to a specialist NPC

text: A disguise hides a character's identity until it is removed in a reveal, so concealment and reveal are arranged together as one structure.
when: identity is central to the plot

text: A disguise fails in private: housemates' intimate routines expose it, and a faked tell that vanishes in private conversation reveals the cover.
when: the disguised person lives among others, or the disguise includes a faked trait
why: Intimate routines are hard to keep up in disguise, and inconsistency between public and private behavior reveals the cover.

text: A disguise worn in a place where one is known can be discovered and raise suspicion.
A changed appearance breaks physical description matching, so a disguised person can pass a check that would otherwise expose them.
Pointing too hard at a disguise makes it obvious; let the detail be half-noticed and then dismissed, so readers can catch it later.
A disguise tell noticed too late leaves little room to conceal it, so early detection matters.
A disguise is not reliable under close or repeated scrutiny.
when: The cover must survive sustained inspection.
why: Close observation can reveal details that the disguise does not hide.

text: 1) Write a full description of the suspect. 2) List features a disguise can change, such as hair, beard, age, clothing, glasses, false whiskers or voice. 3) Keep stable features, such as skull shape, height and build, and compare them across sources.
when: a suspect's appearance or voice may have been altered
why: Remaining stable traits are more reliable for identification.

text: Reveal a disguised identity through a physical change, such as a cloak falling away, rather than through speech alone.
Stage a disguise reveal for effect by removing a key disguise element in front of the people who failed to recognise you, exposing the whole disguise at once.
when: Payoff moment after a disguise has passed scrutiny
why: A sudden full reveal lands harder than a gradual one

text: Disguise by changing the cues people use to recognize someone, such as the eyes, rather than costume alone. This applies to dungeon NPCs too.
when: a character must pass as someone else
why: recognition depends more on cues like the eyes than on costume

text: Let a player hide costume details in a portrait or wanted poster and compare the face underneath, since disguises can conceal identity.
when: Designing a disguise puzzle
why: Covering distinctive costume features can reveal the underlying face

text: Let a final-act reveal show that a friendly NPC was an investigator in disguise, with earlier clues explaining the change.
A disguise helps avoid recognition but risks being seen both disguised and undisguised by the same people, which invites distrust.
when: when deciding whether to change appearance

text: Hint at a concealed identity with small cues, such as changed appearance or banter, and introduce the disguise's physical features early, so the reveal is surprising yet fair.
when: Early chapters of a disguise plot, or when planting a costume that will be revealed later
why: Naming the disguise before it is shown makes the reveal fair and memorable.

text: A disguise usually covers the face and clothing but not body proportions such as height, or the hands, which can betray a hidden identity.
Conspicuous features like hair, beard and nose are easiest to counterfeit, so witness memory of them is unreliable; eye markings, fingernail shape and ear set are hard to fake.
when: when checking whether a person is who they appear to be, or identifying a person from witness descriptions
why: Eye-catching features are chosen for disguise because they draw attention, while hard-to-change features are rarely altered.

text: Let an NPC wear another character's cloak to fake a presence, and let a written note serve as a false alibi that the player can test against other evidence.
when: Designing disguise or alibi mechanics
why: Visible tokens create apparent presence, and the player can expose them through timing or witnesses

text: A test can be hidden behind a harmless request, such as fetching an item, so the subject's behavior is judged without their awareness.
when: Checking whether a person resembles someone or matches a clue.
why: A concealed purpose yields more natural reactions than a stated test.

text: A disguise is easiest to expose through non-visual traces, such as smell, skin warmth or the way hair is set, which the wearer cannot easily hide.
when: when a witness's visual description may be unreliable because of disguise
why: Disguise materials and construction leave traces outside what the eye checks.

text: Let a disguise pass on sight by matching a shared dress code, but fail on sound or behaviour, so an observant player can still catch it.
when: hiding a living intruder among staff or a uniformed group
why: Visual checks are easy to satisfy, while sound and movement are harder to fake.

text: Assuming a witness who saw someone in unusual clothing is mistaken, rather than checking whether that clothing was worn by someone else, is a mistake.
when: A witness reports a person in atypical attire.
why: The clothing may be a disguise worn by a different person.

text: 1) Note conspicuous visual features. 2) Check hard-to-fake features. 3) Check sensory traces such as smell and skin. 4) Treat each trace as weak alone and suspicious only when several agree.
when: when judging whether a person is in disguise
why: Single traces have ordinary explanations, but agreement among small details builds real suspicion.

text: Give a disguised NPC a sensory clue such as a scent, sound or visible seam so players who check non-visual cues can expose the impostor.
when: when designing disguised characters

text: Use a disguised confrontation to force a confession when the culprit has no witness.
when: No witness exists and the culprit can be reached in person.

text: Disguised handwriting suggests concealment; study strokes, capitals and spacing, but a single known-sample comparison is weak evidence since disguise can match by chance.
when: When analyzing an anonymous or unusual handwriting.
why: Disguise can match or mismatch a sample by chance.

text: A disguised handwriting does not hide the writer from a physical trace such as a thumbprint, which can identify them.
why: physical traces are independent of how the writing looks

text: When disguise hides common letters, a single recurring habit carries much more weight as evidence of a shared author.
when: Samples are deliberately disguised
why: Disguise removes most ordinary letter cues

text: Speech that sounds unnaturally exaggerated may indicate a deliberately disguised voice, suggesting concealment of identity.
when: when a speaker's manner seems artificial
why: Disguise is a common way to hide who is speaking.

text: Include lines of questioning that seem irrelevant to hide the real purpose and avoid alerting other witnesses.
when: a group shares one story and one member could warn the others

text: A disguised NPC can be identified by a voice line, distinctive gesture or uncovered feature rather than appearance, and a player's disguise can fail on a fixed detail a guard remembers.
when: designing disguise mechanics for characters
why: fixed details give players and NPCs a way to detect disguises

text: Model disguised speech or hidden faces as partial information with a reveal condition, so identity is only confirmed once the condition is met.
when: when designing concealed identities
why: Gating reveals keeps uncertainty meaningful.

text: Word-based conclusions mislead when the writer chose words deliberately for disguise, and others may reasonably contest them.
Press witnesses and suspects on small incidents or details they wave off as unimportant, since dismissed details often prove central to the case.
when: when a witness or suspect waves away a specific detail
why: Dismissing a detail under pressure is often a sign that it touches the truth.

text: A clue that seems trivial, fits a held theory, or lies outside the current objective is often dismissed and understood only later.
when: an offhand remark does not match the current theory, or concerns a topic outside the current objective
why: commitment to a theory, a sense of triviality, or attention filtering out off-task information hides its meaning

text: Peers and listeners may wave off a subtle inference or visible hesitation as imagined or high-sounding talk when they want the conclusion to hold; test it rather than argue.
when: the group is invested in accepting the solution
why: doubts that threaten a wanted conclusion are easy to discount

text: Investigators often ignore an unexplained clue until someone forces it into view, after a theory has been accepted.
when: A favored theory has already been adopted.
why: Commitment to a theory reduces attention to the facts that contradict it.

text: A recipient may wave away an anomaly that someone else reports, and may deny having noticed it, avoiding investigation.
when: An outside party reports a suspicious detail to someone involved
why: Reporting through another party lets the recipient deny awareness

text: Household members may dismiss an outside investigator's foul-play theory as a specialist's private obsession, so resistance should be expected.
when: when an outside investigator proposes that a death was a crime

text: An assumption that a case is trivial lowers the investigator's guard, so the clue that matters is dismissed before its significance appears.
when: A case looks harmless with a small apparent loss
why: Expectations of low stakes reduce attention to details that could signal serious offence

text: Reasoning that others dismiss as not really evidence can still shape a group's vote.
Audiences who saw a warning dismissed as fancy recall it when danger escalates, so cashing in a dismissed clue feels satisfying.
when: a warning was described and then explained away
why: They registered the clue as description, so it reads as earned when it returns.

text: A group can keep members ignorant of a crime so they have nothing to testify to and cannot be forced to speak.
Place the clue in plain sight within a dismissed conversation or physical scene so the player sees it without registering it until the late reveal.
when: hiding the solution in plain sight
why: a dismissed detail is recalled differently once revealed

text: Dismiss an early clue, such as burnt paper, in a neutral voice so players treat it as irrelevant, then reopen it when a later test or reveal makes it key.
when: planting a clue whose function is revealed later in the scenario or at the climax
why: A dismissed clue is easily forgotten, and its return rewards attentive players and makes the solution feel inevitable.

text: Plant early clues, including the true explanation, that an authority figure dismisses, so attentive players can later reinterpret them to overturn the accusation.
when: opening a mystery with an official dismissal
why: Players who recall the dismissed clue gain a sense of insight when it is later vindicated.

text: Dismissing an obvious question quickly can make the audience stop asking it, which can be used deliberately to steer attention.
Plant a vivid but ambiguous observation early, dismissed at the time, so its meaning becomes clear when later facts arrive.
when: a clue must be understood only later
why: delayed recognition makes the clue feel earned

text: A link dismissed as coincidence delays the real connection, and the dismissal is later shown to be wrong.
when: when a character explains away an early clue
why: the rejected link is the one the story needs to reach the answer

text: Dismissing a small or mundane detail as accidental or trivial, without evidence, can hide the real clue; routine marks may be decisive when read with timing and sources.
when: Reviewing ordinary-looking evidence.
why: Minor details may prove relevant, and routine marks may carry the decisive information.

text: Dismissing a small mark or detail as unimportant can lose the case-resolving clue; apparent importance is unreliable, and trivial details gain meaning when linked to other facts.
when: A small mark or detail seems too trivial to test.
why: Apparent importance is not a reliable guide to relevance.

text: Dismissing a trace because it does not fit the favoured theory discards evidence that may later prove relevant; a fixed theory leads investigators to treat conflicting clues as unimportant.
Ignoring contrary evidence, including residue that does not fit the theory, lets a wrong explanation stand unchallenged; contrary traces must be explained before a conclusion is accepted.
Dismissing evidence as planted or deceptive without testing it is as unsound as trusting it blindly; each item still needs its own test.
Ignoring a retraction made after the pressure ended discards the accused's correction and evidence of how the confession was obtained; a false confession may stand.
when: A confession is later withdrawn.
why: The retraction is evidence about how the original statement was obtained.

text: A half-remembered resemblance dismissed as a side effect of repetition is effectively lost, so the clue must be made recognizable on its own.
when: when a clue sits in a confusing or repetitive scene
why: repetition overloads memory

text: Dismissing a tell because it was brief causes an observer to lose evidence that could be recalled and checked again.
Dismissing a clue because its meaning is unclear when first noticed can lose the detail that the solution later needs.
Dismissing a clue because its reference is unrecognised can discard the key evidence; the investigator's ignorance is itself a risk.
Missing a small moved object that others dismissed as unimportant can hide the key trace.
when: A minor detail is set aside by others
why: Small disturbances often carry the decisive evidence

text: Players and investigators often drop small oddities as trivial, though the smallest detail may reveal how an act was done.
why: Minor-looking details are easily filtered out as noise.

text: Dismissing a small loss or detail as harmless can leave a trace that others later connect to the act.
A small delay or odd address on a sent item can be the key clue; dismissing it as unimportant can lose the lead.
A clue dismissed as trivial can misdirect an inquiry for a long time, because the dismissal shapes everyone's later reasoning.
Dismissing a small mark as trivial, without checking when its material was wet, can assign it a wrong and ordinary cause.
A clue dismissed early and never revisited becomes noise, so the contradicting detail must be kept alive for later return.
when: writing or designing a mystery
why: An unresolved detail loses its meaning when forgotten.

text: Dismissing an inconvenient object as coincidence can hide the truth, and investigators who do so leave the strongest clue unexamined.
when: A physical clue conflicts with the favoured theory.
why: Waving away the clue removes the test that could expose the error.

text: Dismissing a sound or clue because it seems unlikely for the culprit to produce it can cause the investigator to overlook the culprit's real choices.
when: An investigator judges a clue against an assumption about how the culprit would act.
why: The assumption about method may be wrong, so the discarded clue may be the true evidence.

text: Dismissing an odd detail without conviction can leave a real threat unexamined.
Ignoring the direction a trace runs makes any inference drawn from it unreliable.
Dismissing a small trace as trivial can delay an inquiry, because seemingly irrelevant details such as diet can later prove meaningful.
when: When a small residue seems unimportant to the case.
why: Minor traces can connect to places or people not yet known.

text: Overlooking a trivial remark or minor detail can miss the clue that reopens a timeline, since idle talk often points back to an absence.
why: Casual comments can carry facts that matter once a sequence is checked

text: A tiny trace is easily dismissed as debris; the investigator must ask why it is there.
Clumsy-looking incidents are easily dismissed as unimportant, so a plan can go unnoticed until the full chain is read.
when: when investigating a crime with many small events
why: each event seems harmless when viewed alone

text: Assuming a sound is harmless because nothing visible is present is a mistake, since the sound may still signal a real threat.
when: Deciding how seriously to treat an unexplained noise.
why: Absence of visible evidence does not rule out a hidden presence.

text: Dismissing an answer that contradicts a favoured theory, before asking what that theory predicts, discards possible evidence.
Ignoring traces of a second person because a confession names only one actor leaves the case incomplete.
Dismissing a witness's description of a suspect's temper or speech can hide an early clue that only makes sense later.
when: when a witness offers a passing remark about a character
why: Trivial-seeming remarks can gain meaning once background is known.

text: Dismissing an offhand remark as unimportant can delay the lead it points to, until it is recorded in full and tested.
when: Reviewing a passing comment in testimony.
why: Remarks that seem trivial may later prove to be the key lead.

text: A single lit detail can be dismissed as imagination, so an observer's doubt may be the only thing stopping it from being acted on.
when: a brief sighting of one detail
why: one brief detail is easy to doubt

text: Ignoring a contradiction because it seems minor can delay the answer for days.
Dropping a lead because it seems absurd or comic can cause the investigator to miss the real clue it contains.
Ignoring the accuser's grievance, property or income when weighing testimony is a common mistake.
Answering a counterargument by calling it emotion dismisses it without addressing the question it raises.
Dismissing a theory only for being improbable can be as careless as accepting it only for being neat.
when: Evaluating competing explanations.
why: Both shortcuts skip checking the premises against evidence.

text: Dismissing a small measured difference is a mistake, since a very small discrepancy can be decisive.
when: Evaluating a forgery with minor measured variation
why: Forgeries are often exposed by differences too small to notice without measurement.

text: Dismissing a clue through a character's stupidity makes the reveal feel cheap.
why: The reveal depends on the character's error rather than on the player's reasoning.

text: A detail offered casually at the end of an interview can be dismissed as trivial when it may be significant.
when: When a late remark does not fit the main line of inquiry.
why: Incidental remarks can carry clues that the questioner has not yet connected.

text: An interviewer who dismisses trivial details discards the very details that carry the timeline.
when: Questioning a witness whose account is built from everyday routines
why: Mundane details serve as cues for the sequence of events

text: Ordinary details are dismissed as coincidence until the investigator has a reason to notice them.
when: A small detail seems too mundane to matter
why: Without a link to the timeline or people, the detail looks harmless

text: Before dismissing a frightened witness's sighting as nerves, inspect the physical scene for traces that would confirm or refute it.
why: A dramatic sighting can rest on something real

text: Discount an individual mark when it could have been made after the event or when no one saw it before the event.
Dismissing a motive or lead without checking its evidence, especially because it conflicts with a favoured theory, can hide the real explanation; recheck the stated reason for rejection.
when: An investigator rules out a suspect's apparent motive; a theory conflicts with a character's own explanation.
why: Unchecked elimination removes the correct answer; the theory is preferred over direct testimony.

text: Judge the argument, not its framing or speaker: dismissing a respectable suspect, a modest or disliked witness, or a self-promoting observer mistakes standing or presentation for innocence or accuracy.
when: A witness is modest, timid or disliked by peers, or a second observer contradicts an established authority.
why: Social standing and framing do not determine whether an account is accurate; readers and characters discount opinions by how they are framed.

text: Use a plausible gain-based or financial motive as a deliberate red herring, not the real cause, so the player must test and discard the obvious reason.
when: Designing red herrings in narrative or dungeon generation.

text: Personal dislike and property disputes give suspicion its direction, so an accusation often targets someone already disliked or in conflict over land.
when: when analysing why a particular person was accused
why: Accusers' stakes in property and position shape whom they name

text: A red herring is a motive that seems believable but is inconsistent with the nature of the act, pointing investigators away from a larger plan.
Make suspicious-looking traits such as accent, job, jealousy or nervousness red herrings, and keep guilt signs ambiguous while placing real clues in the suspect's actions.
when: when designing suspects and clues for a mystery
why: Ambiguous cues keep players from accepting the first answer.

text: A sighting that vanishes on approach can work as a deliberate red herring that rewards players who verify before acting on it.
when: when designing misleading clues

text: Make a suspect's guilt rest on companions and one published accusation alone, so players must test the claim before accepting it.
when: Designing a red herring character.
why: Untested association can look like evidence, which rewards investigation.

text: Clear each suspect with a specific test, so suspicion rebounds across suspects without stalling the case.
when: a suspect is accused
why: a concrete clearing keeps the case moving

text: A flamboyant conclusion can be a red herring; a contradicting sighting widens the field of suspects and undermines the dramatic theory.
when: a witness reports a sighting that does not fit the favoured suspect
why: an alternative observation reopens the case

text: A plausible rival suspect with a physical match can divert suspicion, and the player can later disprove that match with evidence.
when: designing a misdirection in a mystery
why: a convincing alternative delays the correct conclusion until it is refuted

text: Setting aside a suspect's denial leaves the accuser's account unchallenged, letting a weak link stand and tilting the case toward the accuser.
when: A motive chain is already built, or a suspect denies a vision reported by an accuser.

text: A red herring with a real motive stays convincing until its supporting facts are checked.
why: motive alone can make a false lead look solid

text: Dismissing a belief entirely can miss its influence on the people who hold it.
Dropping a whole case on one fact can be as hasty as accepting it on many facts; weigh the anomaly against the rest of the evidence.
Dismissing people as uninvolved causes missed clues; keep everyone present open as a suspect until evidence excludes them.
A suicide motive can be built on the same facts a murderer would use to disguise a killing, so motive alone should not settle a death.
Each new plausible claimant pulls attention away from the real question, such as who benefits from the current arrangement.
Dismissing a hobby as harmless without checking it is a mistake, since it may hold evidence of activity.
Spreading suspicion over several weakly connected suspects can dilute the case against the one with the strongest motive.
Dismissing a decades-old grievance as ancient history can brush aside a real motive too quickly.
A discharged suspect is not thereby innocent in the community's eyes; people may still treat them as under suspicion.
Dispute or dismissal events are possible motives that do not automatically point to the culprit; a dislike alone is not a motive, since many disputes are unrelated to crime.
when: A witness reports hostility between people.
why: Ordinary quarrels are common.

text: Do not dismiss a suspicion merely because the case looks arranged or its conclusion seems too wicked; wary witnesses may reject correct suspicions for that reason.
Show that an accusation is too weak by listing its essential gaps; proving innocence is not required to block an arrest.
when: a character proposes arresting someone on a thin case
why: a case with missing links fails without an alternative culprit

text: Give an NPC a note naming a powerful figure that the player must check through a direct meeting, while the real connection lies elsewhere.
when: Designing a misleading clue
why: The check resolves the lead and redirects the player

text: Do not dismiss strange impressions as nonsense merely because no explanation is yet available.
Disorder shows what searchers wanted, but it can also point away from where the object really is, so test it against the physical scene.
when: a room shows signs of a violent or unexplained search

text: A search that restores objects to their original order is hard to do perfectly, and a neatly rearranged space can itself be a sign of tampering.
when: A character searches a room or belongings and tries to leave no trace.
why: Perfect restoration is difficult, so small irregularities or unusual neatness reveal the search.

text: Sudden disorder pulls everyone's attention away, leaving an object unwatched for a moment.
Treating disorder as proof of theft is a guess: it can be staged or have other causes, and it shows a search only if the undisturbed baseline is known.
why: a messy scene has several possible causes; without a baseline, disorder proves little

text: Do not assume one person caused the disorder; check who else had access before attributing it to a single intruder.
Disordered or unfastened clothing supports a sudden change of purpose rather than a planned sequence.
Check whether a person's clothing and equipment fit the stated purpose; a mismatch contradicts the account and becomes evidence.
when: A stated motive or activity implies particular clothing or equipment.
why: People dressed for an activity usually match their attire to it.

text: Clothing that is torn or badly fastened can show that someone else dressed or disturbed the wearer, possibly with clumsy hands.
Disordered rooms (clothes on floor, pockets out, open drawers) may show a hurried occupant search or panic, or a search by someone else; do not assume the occupant caused it.
An object lying far from a body on a still day suggests it was thrown or placed afterward, which contradicts a simple accident account.
when: reconstructing an accident scene
why: no wind or ordinary motion explains the distance

text: Fear directed at a red-herring legend draws attention away from the real threat, which can then be held back until it is revealed.
when: a larger threat is hidden behind a more visible one
why: the audience's attention follows the legend

text: An item moved from inside to an unexpected outside location raises a second question about who moved it and why.
when: When a missing object is found somewhere it should not be
why: Displacement implies a further action

text: A harmful object aimed at one person can strike another when it passes between hands, so the actual victim may differ from the intended target.
when: A poison or trap sits on an object that is handed on.
why: Each handover moves the object to a new holder, changing who is exposed.

text: A recorded item can be disputed later, so sealing evidence in the suspect's presence protects its integrity.
A displaced target can make a crime look random, hiding the real intent for too long, so the intended victim should be stated clearly at some point.
when: Writing a crime whose surface victim differs from its intent.
why: Without a clear statement of intent, readers lose track of who was meant to be harmed.

text: An object found far from its owner may have been planted or moved, so its route must be explained before it is used as proof.
Note objects out of usual place and ask occupants what normally sits where; displacement means little without that baseline, or once the scene is cleared or no routine exists.
when: when the household's routine can be learned
why: A displacement only means something relative to the usual arrangement; without a baseline no comparison remains.

text: Removing a disputed fence at once concedes the ground immediately, while letting it stand until the bounds are fixed keeps the claim open.
when: when a neighbor disputes the line of a structure
why: each option trades an immediate concession against an unresolved claim

text: An ostentatious, ugly cover can signal that the wearer wants it noticed, so display suggests pride rather than shame.
Give characters a displayed face or bearing that can differ from their hidden stance, so a player can notice a mismatch.
when: designing NPC tells

text: Open disapproval of an accusation can make the dissenter a target, so doubt becomes risky to voice.
A single insulting label applied to critics can make them seem odious and end their objections.
when: A faction names those who doubt its proceedings.
why: The label shifts attention from the objection to the critic.

text: Allies may resist an unfamiliar method, so the investigator must explain the procedure clearly.
when: when proposing an untested investigative method to a group
why: Unclear procedure breeds doubt even when the method is sound.

text: Give objecting characters the ability to restrict rooms or postpone the investigator, so their dissent changes the player's options.
Give each NPC a distinctive script so the player can match a forged note to its writer.
Spread facts across NPC witnesses or objects, each holding a different timeline part with recognition cues, so players must reconcile accounts; empty containers count as independent evidence.
when: designing witness testimony and clues in a mystery
why: partial knowledge requires cross-checking, which rewards deduction and makes objects carry testimony

text: Parties to one incident often describe it differently, so an event one side calls rough play may be read by the other as an attack.
when: when two people describe the same event
why: each party frames the event by its own stake in it

text: Characters given different versions of a secret can each reveal only their own partial account, so an investigator must track who was told what.
when: A secret is held by several characters and each is told a different version.
why: Each character's knowledge limits what they can reveal, and selective accounts can be mistaken for the whole truth.

text: A document addressed to someone else can misidentify its bearer, so an introduction may point to the wrong person.
Confessions reported after a story ends can confirm a deduction, giving closure without a full on-page reveal.
A question of whether a claim was ever true can require checking several sources, such as records, witnesses and physical traces, before accepting the conclusion.
when: Designing a puzzle where the player must verify a historical claim.
why: No single source is sufficient, so cross-checking builds confidence in the conclusion.

text: A reliable-seeming third-party manuscript can override earlier rational explanations and convert a prior belief into an eyewitness event, closing the investigation.
when: Late in an investigation, when the reveal is delivered as a document from a witness the player trusts more than the investigator.
why: A first-hand account from a separate source carries more weight than the investigator's theories, so it reframes all earlier clues.

text: When each later document overturns the one before it, the believed answer keeps flipping until the final sealed proof settles it.
when: when building a lore-document mystery
why: the chain sustains uncertainty while preserving a single final truth

text: A clean result from a physical check is not conclusive, because its reliability depends on when and how the check was made.
when: When a physical check finds no trace.
why: Traces may have been removed or may not have been present at the time of checking.

text: When an NPC presents a conclusion, offer at least one other reading of the same clue and let the player choose which to pursue.
A document kept by one party can threaten another if a single accident puts it in the wrong hands.
when: when a secret record is kept by someone with a conflicting interest
why: Exposure risk depends on who can reach the record.

text: A document can be presented to a court long after it was written, so its writing date and its filing date must be tracked separately.
Confront a suspect with documents or objects from their possession so they must account for each, and watch for manner shifts revealing knowledge of contents they claimed not to know.
when: When a suspect holds case-linked items or may recognise a document they claim not to know.

text: An NPC who offers a written statement can carry false information, which the player must verify against objects in the scene.
when: Designing NPC-provided documents
why: Written testimony should be checkable against the world.

text: Use official notices, letters or bounty bills that look like they concern the main case but resolve into a side quest.
When the audience cannot judge written documents, handle letters and records carefully and rely on clearer forms of evidence.
when: Presenting written evidence to readers or listeners with limited literacy or expertise.
why: Audiences that cannot evaluate documents may misjudge their weight.

text: A search of documents may fail to answer the question at all, so plan a second line of inquiry rather than relying on one archive.
Record and honour a party's request about who receives a copy of a document, rather than routing it by default.
when: Handling copies of agreements for interested parties.

text: Record the bait announcement in writing and have it signed, so the bait itself becomes a documented step.
Ask how a document reached its holder; the delivery route can be as informative as the document's content.
Give an in-game note checkable requirements, such as knowledge of a password, access to a machine or a specific material, so the player can deduce the author by elimination.
when: when designing a letter or note that identifies its author

text: When a lock must be forced, do it in front of witnesses so the opening is observed and documented.
Give each in-game document its own gaps and bias, so cross-checking produces a different picture than any single file.
Require the player to gain permission or a ruling before a sensitive document can be used as evidence.
when: Designing a document that is contested or private.
why: A gate adds a step that delays the reveal and raises stakes.

text: Use a reconstructed document, like a letter or sealed declaration from within the affected family or group, as final proof where testimony cannot settle the case, not a new witness.
when: resolving a mystery's central secret
why: Documents from within the story carry authority and keep the resolution tied to material the player already knows about.

text: A written statement is evidence, but its reliability depends on the writer's state of mind, its internal consistency, and how it compares with the writer's earlier statements.
Check a document's addressee before acting on its contents, since a shared name can make a letter belong to someone else.
when: Items that identify or introduce a character by name.
why: Similar names let an item reach the wrong person unnoticed.

text: Check how a document arrived, including postmark, envelope and delivery record, since a note from a private route changes its meaning.
when: when a document's route to the investigator is unclear
why: Delivery route is evidence about who sent it and how.

text: A harmless message can still prove a link, because the sender's knowledge of the hidden party is the valuable part.
A frame-narrative investigation moves through linked documents, each pointing to the next source, so understanding widens in time and place while the explanation keeps shifting.
when: When structuring a mystery told through found documents.
why: Each document narrows or expands the protagonist's belief, sustaining the investigation.

text: A grieving or angry writer may exaggerate or contradict themselves, so vivid accusations need corroboration before they are believed.

1) Write the letter, journal or contract with deliberate gaps, such as a missing name. 2) Let each gap reveal an author's blind spot. 3) Place the document where the player can find and examine the gap. 4) Place a second source so that finding it opens the gap as a quest hook.
when: Designing written clues in a level
why: Gaps the player can interpret give a specific place to look and an inference to make; a missing detail motivates the player to search for the corroborating source.

text: Let a threat exist only in documents, so the player must verify its existence before accepting the accused as guilty.
Use a physical proof that is hard to fake and easy to test, such as prints on an object, as the decisive reveal.
when: when the solution must convince an official audience
why: A testable proof resists counterclaims and makes the conclusion checkable.

text: Make a document, not a character's speech, deliver the final reveal, so the reader can check it against earlier scenes.
when: Choosing how to deliver a major plot revelation.
why: A document can be examined and compared with earlier evidence, which makes the reveal verifiable.

text: A summary built from selected entries or a condensed record can mislead, and the selection is open to the same scrutiny. Check it against the original text.
when: A document, deposition or transcript is summarized through selected entries or condensed form.
why: A single sample or compression may drop or distort key details and not match the whole.

text: A report that credits work to a group rather than one author can make the work seem more objective and later claims more credible.
when: writing reports that will face later scrutiny
why: Collective credit reads as less self-interested.

text: Witness reports often comment on the investigator's manner, so interviews reveal witnesses' attitudes as well as case facts.
when: During sequenced interviews

text: A reporter's prejudice against a group can colour how they weigh a report. Check the source's bias before trusting the account.
when: When the reporter dismisses a whole category of evidence.

text: A first, mechanical reading of a document often misses distinctive traits, which become visible only on a later, deliberate reading.
when: reviewing a document for physical clues
why: Attention goes to content during a first reading

text: Readers of an endorsed, reprinted account often treat it as proof, which strengthens the case in later minds.
when: When a printed account is reissued in another place.
why: Repetition and endorsement signal authority.

text: Facts a speaker reports without conclusions are often more reliable than conclusions built on them. Keep reporter asides and opinions separate from the evidence.
why: Interpretation adds a layer of error, and mixed asides blur evidence and interpretation.

text: Read a written statement or note first for its aim (what it demands, forbids or threatens), then for tone, omissions and rewrites, since wording reveals the writer's intent and stance.
when: A letter, note or written statement is a clue, or makes claims about other people.
why: Writers reveal purpose through choices of phrasing and what they leave out.

text: Treat a shadowing report only as a lead until other facts confirm it.
When checking a record for a transaction, start with its most recent entries, since recent payments are most likely to be relevant.
How an incident is reported indicates its nature; a call that brings in a specialist suggests violence rather than a mere accident.
when: Judging the kind of incident from the report that triggered an investigation
why: Response level reflects what the reporters believed occurred

text: Have a role holder report suspicious outsiders to a nearby liaison who can act immediately.
when: when an outsider threatens a covert plan
why: quick reporting limits exposure

text: Re-examine a clue that everyone reads one way, and ask whether its wording fits live speech or a recorded or read text.
Ending a report with a prediction or a sign that the next step is near builds anticipation for the next delivery.
when: Writing a report that leads to a later event
why: A forward-looking close creates suspense

text: A report that an object was lost is a claim to test, not a fact to accept.
when: A witness says a key, tool, weapon or document is missing.
why: The claim may reflect the witness's belief about where the item was.

text: Consider a reporter's physical and mental state, such as fasting, sleep loss or strain, when weighing their account of unusual experiences.
when: A report of unusual experience comes from someone under physical or mental stress.
why: Physical strain can distort perception and produce imagined experiences.

text: Show the player dated entries such as letters, logs and refused visits so they can build the sequence themselves.
when: when presenting clues for player reconstruction
why: Players who order dated evidence derive the timeline rather than receive it.

text: Read a monument or document for what it claims and what it deliberately leaves unclaimed; wording that avoids asserting a fact may be innocent or deliberate.
when: Interpreting a grave, plaque, or official document for its assertions.
why: Omissions in a record can be deliberate or innocent, so the reader must weigh which.

text: Check a document's date before interpreting its content, since a date lag can reverse a belief that an earlier, undated source encouraged the reader to hold.
Public reports of a grave condition can reinforce an opponent's sense of success, which can change their timetable.
Repeated reading can make an investigator see patterns that are not there, so record what has been checked and how.
why: Expectation shapes what a rereader notices

text: A reviewer who repeats an official stated ground may be reading the document at face value rather than concealing anything.
why: repeating a record is not evidence of deception

text: 1) Collect the reported facts as a timeline, such as travel, a timed conversation, a visit or a departure. 2) Ask for specific missing details that would confirm or refute each theory. 3) Reason to a solution from those facts.
when: case fully described by a source

text: 1) Look for recurring visitors or routines. 2) Note entries linking several people. 3) Check for missing days. 4) Flag ambiguous references. 5) Mark names for follow-up rather than treating entries as proof.
when: When a victim's private diary or notes may show contacts or changes in routine.
why: Structured reading separates patterns from speculation and keeps follow-up open.

text: 1) Treat fragments at a torn edge as partial words, not complete ones. 2) Test candidate completions for each gap by checking whether they form coherent words. 3) Compare hypotheses about writing order. 4) Keep the one that predicts the available evidence.
when: a damaged document may hold a clue in its missing part

text: 1) Identify the grantor and the grantee. 2) Note what was given in exchange. 3) Note any attached condition. 4) Record the date to order the events.

1) Read the whole passage, including every qualification. 2) Follow each qualifying clause to its end. 3) Compare the passage with the same author's other works. 4) Decide what the source asserts from the full context.
when: A testimony or confession seems to say two things at once.
why: Qualifiers can reverse the apparent meaning.

text: When new facts undermine the motive behind a suspicious behaviour, reread the behaviour rather than defending the earlier reading.
Place a matching fault that is visible only on a second or third reading, so a puzzle rewards careful rereading of documents.
when: designing document puzzles
why: Clues that need deliberate attention reward careful players

text: Use periodic report checkpoints that summarise discovered clues for the player, giving a regular review of progress.
when: when designing turn-based or daily investigation structure

text: Deliver the largest reveal as a document within a document, and let each artifact point to the next location or source.
when: When placing the climactic clue in a document chain.
why: Embedded documents carry the reveal while directing the player onward.

text: Record damage, wear and destroyed evidence as facts; a burned remnant with no legible fragment is itself information.
when: A fragile document is being examined or preserved, or evidence has been destroyed.
why: Fragile originals keep deteriorating, so the record may become the only full view.

text: A tear where an item would be pulled out suggests it was snatched in a rush rather than removed carefully.
Search the remains of a fire or grate, since partly burned material may survive and carry evidence.
why: Destruction is often incomplete

text: Record the exact fragment, list every possible reading, and test each reading by how well it fits the torn edge rather than by expectation.
when: A document is incomplete and its wording is disputed.
why: Strong expectations bias readings, while edge fit is a more objective test.

text: A torn edge in a record may be deliberate or accidental, so do not assume significance until the record is compared with an intact copy.
when: A record shows damage near relevant content.
why: Damage can be innocent, so comparison is needed before drawing conclusions.

text: Make a discarded or burnt document reconstructable from fragments, and match printed fragments to a known source such as a dated publication.
when: A document has been destroyed but the player should still be able to recover part of it.
why: Partial recovery gives the player a reason to search and assemble clues.

text: Reconstructing lost words can change a document's meaning, so mark supplied words, since inferred words look identical to original ones.
when: Using or completing a partly damaged or fragmentary document.
why: Supplied words can alter the sense of the original text.

text: Sentences cut from a real source and reassembled can appear to say something new, as satirical dialogues built from fragments show.

1) Gather every related account of the events, including printed reports, confessions and depositions. 2) Note what each includes, omits, agrees on or conflicts with. 3) Date each record and flag undated, incomplete or lost ones. 4) Align dated entries on one timeline. 5) Label conclusions as documented or inferred. 6) Cross-check with surviving physical evidence.
when: Reconstructing events from several partial or fragmentary sources.

text: 1) Collect all fragments, including those found on a second search. 2) Match edges using margins, partial words and machine-cut versus torn edges. 3) Space pieces as a standard sheet to count missing strips. 4) Use partial words and dates to estimate contents.
when: Physical evidence is partly destroyed and its layout matters.
why: Edge matching and layout reveal page order, missing pieces and sometimes the writer.

text: 1) Lay a torn fragment over a complete copy to see what is missing. 2) Turn the fragment over and read its reverse side. 3) Check whether adjoining or reverse text changes the fragment's meaning.
when: a torn or partial document is found
why: Alignment shows the gap, and the reverse can hold text that changes the reading.

text: 1) Record the document's full state, including worn margins, before any trimming. 2) Note any mounting or treatment that changes its appearance. 3) Record the scale whenever the image is reduced.
1) Find the written item in the place the person was known to use. 2) Record where it was found. 3) Bring it to the investigator with that account of its location.

1) List surviving word fragments and note which letters remain and where they break off. 2) Complete each fragment only with words the visible letters allow. 3) Add connecting words the sense requires. 4) Judge the restored whole by its general tenor.
when: A torn or partly burned document must be restored to understand its general content.
why: Restoring tone and content avoids overclaiming exact wording that cannot be recovered.

text: 1) Check the top sheet for impressions. 2) If it is blank, check blotting pads and lower sheets. 3) Tear off a strip and read the reversed impression by turning it over.
when: a message may be hidden in lower layers
why: lower layers often keep a clearer copy

text: 1) Collect the surviving words of a lost document or statement. 2) Gather related behaviour and threats. 3) Narrow what the missing content must have said.
when: a document or statement has been destroyed or withheld
why: surrounding words and behaviour constrain the missing content

text: 1) Locate the source the fragments came from. 2) Match fragment edges to that source. 3) Mount the fragments on stiff backing so the text can be read and kept. 4) Compare the text with a known sample by the same writer.
when: a damaged document is physically present and a reliable comparison sample exists

text: 1) Check whether the recovered object is authentic. 2) Test it by weight, appraisal or a second source. 3) Reopen the timeline to see whether the real event came earlier. 4) Only then close the case.
when: A recovered item seems to prove a suspect's guilt
why: Authenticity and timing can overturn an apparently conclusive find

text: 1) Search the waste and recover the fragment. 2) Unroll and smooth it. 3) Match its edges precisely to the tear. 4) Measure the blank gap. 5) Check the reverse side. 6) Acquire the same day's original edition from its office. 7) Compare entries by time, origin and destination. 8) Mark the matching entry; keep the fragment as exhibit.
when: when a discarded document may hold information about a place or person
why: Systematic matching identifies the removed text reliably.

text: Reassemble torn fragments like a puzzle to recover a message that no single piece shows.
when: when a clue is a torn document

text: Let in-world journals or case files carry redacted entries, and let players recover the struck text through a lore or light puzzle.
when: Designing in-world written material that hides information.
why: Recovering hidden text rewards the player's attention and reading.

text: Make burned or altered items still identifiable through a test such as flame or solvent, so the player can recover their identity.
Let players recover discarded drafts, each with different wording or tone, so they can see the writer's hesitation.
when: Designing written clues in a game or puzzle.
why: A draft reveals hesitation only if the player can actually find it.

text: Let a torn note's missing letters be recovered by overlaying a second fragment, and require the player to check the restored words against the scene.
when: designing document puzzles

text: Compare the torn or cut edges of two halves directly; edges that do not coincide rule out a link between them.
when: when two halves of an object may come from the same source

text: 1) List each document's date. 2) List the events it describes and the relevant trial dates. 3) Flag any document dated after the moment it could have been used. 4) Pursue every mismatch as a lead.
when: when verifying a written record

text: A terse official record can hide how contradictory the facts are, while full notes let an audience later check what was visible from the start.
Physical traits like machine faults or paper watermarks narrow a source but rarely identify it alone; confirm a dating estimate with a second feature, since forgeries copy one period style.
when: Judging whether a document is genuine
why: A single matching feature can be imitated more easily than several

text: Treat a document's physical form, including its handwriting, signature and wear, as evidence in its own right.
when: Authorship or authenticity of a document is in question
why: Physical features can reveal who wrote it and how it was handled

text: A journal that records the player's own assumptions gives later evidence something to test, which rewards careful reading.
when: when designing in-world records
why: Written assumptions can be confirmed or contradicted as the story unfolds.

text: Let a later in-game chronicle state an interpretation that players can test against original letters and site clues.
when: Designing in-game histories

text: An intact wax seal and undisturbed dust in a document's folds suggest it has not been altered since it was sealed.
Check authorisations against the signatures they carry, because a repeated forged signature can hide withdrawals from a fund.
when: when a fund's withdrawals look approved

text: A genuine document can contain errors, so one failed check does not prove forgery; several failed checks together strongly suggest it.
when: when evaluating a suspicious document
why: Genuine documents can have minor inconsistencies.

text: A written document can look damning out of context and harmless with background; establish its context before deciding what it proves.
when: Interpreting a letter or record as evidence.
why: Meaning depends on the reader's background and the referenced papers.

text: A found letter can carry a watermark or paper type that matches a map region, letting the player link the document to a location through an in-world reference.
A forgery can copy a known handwriting yet still fail on facts, so check a suspiciously detailed document's facts against the established record.
when: a document claims to come from a known person
why: matching handwriting does not confirm the content is accurate

text: Test a standard of evidence by parallel: if accepting an unverified kind of testimony would also require accepting equally unsupported claims, the standard is shown to be too weak.
when: defending a standard of proof for unverified claims

text: Players should compare a found letter or diary with environmental clues before acting on its claims, since documents can be biased.
when: Designing found documents as story information.
why: Checking against physical evidence prevents the player from acting on a biased source.

text: When a document fits later events too neatly, check whether the events were arranged to fit the document rather than the reverse.
when: A document appears to anticipate later events.
why: Reversing the inference can reveal a scheme that exploited the document.

text: Let a forged document fail an independent check, such as a date or material compared against a record found elsewhere.
why: A checkable record gives the solver a fair route to expose the forgery

text: Documents capture only their wording, not intentions or later events, so treating one as proof of motive is a mistake.
when: Interpreting a letter, contract or memo as evidence
why: Documents do not record motives or what followed

text: Inferring forgery from format alone, such as a typed letter with a signature, is a mistake; it makes the document suspicious but not proven forged.
when: A document lacks handwriting but carries a signature.
why: Typed documents are unusual but can be genuine, so format is only a reason to examine further.

text: A suspect who notices a mismatch in a forged message's handwriting or wording may refuse to attend the meeting.
when: When a bait message is imitated from a real person's writing.
why: A careful target compares the message to known samples and rejects it on any discrepancy.

text: When the original document is never found, a claim resting on a copy or on one person's handwriting cannot be verified and the explanation stays untested.
1) Pick a specific detail, such as a letter shape or signature mark. 2) Compare it against known genuine examples. 3) Judge authenticity by any mismatch found.
when: a transaction depends on whether money or a document is genuine
why: comparison with genuine references reveals forged details

text: 1) Gather known specimens from the same person. 2) Compare them with the questioned document on distinctive features. 3) Rule out forgery first. 4) Only then have a specialist vouch for authorship.
when: When a document's origin matters to the case
why: Authorship cannot be confirmed while forgery remains possible

text: 1) Compare the handwriting with a known sample of the author's hand. 2) Confirm the date. 3) Check named people and places against other facts. 4) Establish where the document was kept.
when: Before relying on a written document as evidence.
why: A document's contents count only once its authorship and date are checked.

text: 1) Keep the document's text unaltered. 2) Obtain endorsement from witnesses who can attest to the facts it records.
when: A document must be presented as genuine.
why: Unaltered text and endorsement by knowledgeable witnesses let others judge its authenticity.

text: 1) Identify the writer from handwriting or other markers. 2) Record postmark, date and signature gaps as facts, not proof. 3) Keep the meaning open until a second source confirms what is referred to.
when: Evaluating an unsigned or undated document.
why: Markers establish provenance, but meaning needs independent confirmation.

text: 1) Request the original from its official source rather than trusting the copy in hand. 2) Compare the copy with the original. 3) Check independent witnesses against both versions.
when: when a crucial document is in doubt
why: The original is the reference point that copies can be tested against.

text: 1) Compare the paper with the supposed sender's normal stock. 2) Check the form of production, such as typed versus handwritten. 3) Compare signatures and initials with genuine examples. 4) Judge what the writer knew. 5) Trace where the materials came from.
when: when a document is central to the case and its authorship is in question

text: 1) Collect specimens from each candidate machine and each paper supply. 2) Compare typeface, ink and paper separately against the questioned document. 3) Exclude sources whose specimens differ.
when: An anonymous document has no handwriting or signature

text: 1) Match specific details between two cases. 2) Check whether independent sources note the same parallels. 3) Infer copying only if they do.
when: When a later event closely resembles an earlier published account.
why: Resemblance alone may come from shared conditions.

text: 1) Compare the document's date with each candidate's recorded whereabouts. 2) Count the actual signatures. 3) Scrutinize undated or untitled items. 4) Check titles against who was acting. 5) Note the addressee.
when: Authorship or authority is disputed and candidates' movements are recorded
why: Dates, signatures, titles and addressees each reveal who really wrote or sanctioned a document

text: Test a document's or testimony's claims against independent, checkable facts or records, such as logs, receipts or reports, not its appearance.
when: when a document supports a claim

text: Let a forged-papers mechanic require a past record that a gatekeeper checks against stored files, so a mismatch is caught.
Compare a document's paper type, watermark and typing with the stationery of the suspected source before accepting it as genuine.
when: when a document seems to come from a specific place
why: Differences in paper or typing show the document came from elsewhere.

text: Check a tradition about an event's location against records and practical constraints; a plausible tradition still needs reasoning to confirm it.
Show documents in a case file with provenance, including who wrote them, who copied them and what was lost, so players can weigh them.
when: Designing in-world documents or case files.
why: Provenance lets players judge reliability rather than trust every document equally.

text: A witness's stated reason, such as money, is a claim that can be checked against records like bills.
when: A witness gives a motive for an action
why: Records provide independent confirmation or contradiction.

text: Reviewing back issues of a public notice column for repeated signatures can reveal a hidden channel linking a victim to a secret party.
when: A private arrangement may run through published messages.

text: Place the cause of a visible effect in an inset text, so the reader learns the mechanism at the same moment the protagonist sees the effect.
A death-investigation plot can be built as a chain of corrections: each reveal overturns the current belief and reassigns suspicion until a final confession closes the case.
when: designing a mystery with several suspects
why: Each reversal makes the player re-evaluate who is responsible

text: A found document that explains everything removes the need for deduction; let it raise questions as well as answer them.
A suspect who claims powers or behaves sinisterly is not thereby guilty of the act in question; the claim and the deed must be assessed separately.
why: Showmanship and claimed power are not evidence of a specific crime.

text: 1) For each object, ask who had access to it. 2) Check whether it fits the rest of the scene. 3) Treat it as possibly planted if it does not.
when: An investigator must weigh clues against the chance they were placed.
why: Planted evidence can look convincing in isolation.

text: 1) List each detail in the retold story. 2) Check each against known facts. 3) Treat matches as real knowledge and unmatched details as possible cover. 4) Wait for a pattern before concluding.
when: A suspect recounts a fictional case while avoiding direct questions.
why: Matches reveal what the teller actually knows, while a single invented detail is weak evidence.

text: 1) Quote each condition in the will exactly. 2) Check each part literally against the facts. 3) Name the beneficiary or executor only after every condition is confirmed.
when: A motive or control of property depends on the wording of a will.
why: A paraphrase or assumption can yield a different beneficiary than the literal clause.

text: Check claimed explanations, such as no fire or no recent use, against the object's physical state; separate the room as it is from the room as felt.
when: Evaluating an account in a mystery
why: Perception and physical record can diverge, especially under altered mental states.

text: Check specific facts in personal documents, such as appearance, dates and places, rather than judging only by the tone or praise.
when: Reading a personal letter as evidence
why: Warm tone can hide concrete details that matter to the case

text: Compare a reading of a writer's state with what the writer later says before treating the reading as reliable.
when: Interpreting a document before meeting its author.
why: Only a later statement can confirm or correct the reader's impression.

text: Separate the truth of a claim from its source: a claim can prove accurate while its origin stays unresolved.
when: Designing a mystery where the supernatural origin of information is left open.
why: Confirmed accuracy can settle the claim without settling how it was obtained.

text: When a reader holds facts a diarist lacks, the reader feels suspense while watching the diarist's entries misread events.
when: a character's diary is shown to the player alongside knowledge the character does not have
why: the reader can see the gap between what the writer knows and what is true

text: A letter can instruct its recipient to keep an identity hidden for a set period, writing the concealment into the document itself.
Readers can project meaning onto ordinary diary entries when the dramatic tone is strong, and missing days may hide what matters.
when: interpreting an incomplete or emotionally charged diary
why: tone and gaps both invite over-reading

text: 1) Gather dates from separate sources that do not know about each other. 2) Compare them on a shared date. 3) Measure the gap between them. 4) Treat a tight gap as a link, not proof. 5) Record each source and speaker so dates can be weighed later.
when: Two people or records claim to describe the same event or identity.
why: Independent sources give a measurable constraint without a single verdict.

text: Treat a personal diary as a partial record, since the writer's feelings and incomplete knowledge shape what is recorded.
when: using a diary as a source of information
why: its author's affection and fear filter every entry

text: Give players a document that contradicts an earlier one, so they must compare the two to find the lie or the change.
Use the route-elimination method when a crime seems to have no entrance or when door and window evidence contradicts.
Dialogue can mark which statements are confirmed and which remain open, so the player decides what to trust.
when: Designing witness dialogue in a deduction game.
why: Explicit status markers make verification visible and keep judgment with the player.

text: Check dates retold in secondhand accounts against original records, because dates drift as they are passed along.
when: when a timeline relies on recounted information

text: Use a second, independent source, such as an old letter or deed paper, to show that a suspect misled the investigator about a genuine record.
why: An independent source can overturn a suspect's claim the suspect controls.

text: Make a supernatural claim concrete and checkable before asking the audience to doubt it, so they have specific details to test.
when: Introducing a spectral or otherwise unverifiable source of information.
why: Specific details such as a wound, a description or a name change give the audience something to test.

text: Delay verification of a supernatural claim until the end of the case, so the claim stays in play throughout.
when: Structuring a mystery whose central claim comes from an unverifiable source.
why: Early confirmation would close the question before the audience has been held by it.

text: Use a searchable in-world case file accepted as precedent as a source of false belief whose cover story contradicts later facts; let the player correct it with new evidence.
when: when designing world history that shapes current beliefs
why: Precedent carries errors forward until someone tests them.

text: Worn or missing words force players to infer gaps from what remains; a wrong reading can send them chasing a red herring.
Old records may be incomplete, memory fades and accounts reflect writers' purposes, so check each source's reliability; narrators should acknowledge gaps.
when: Using a recording narrator to report investigative detail.
why: Admitted gaps mark where the record is firm and where it may drift.

text: Log every money transfer and place receipts, inventories and payment logs in-world so players reconstruct who paid for what and why; unrecorded deals become clues.
when: when designing NPC transactions

text: Do not treat a record as independent when its controller is the person being checked; a single party-held record can be incomplete or altered and needs verification.
when: choosing records for corroboration, or when the only record of a visit or event is controlled by one person
why: Controlled records can be arranged to match the claim, and gaps or changes can hide a contradiction or make a false claim look true.

text: A recognition by a former authority figure carries more weight than local rumour, and changes how others treat the person once confirmed.
when: An official with past experience identifies a person from a record.
why: Specific, documented confirmation is more credible and status-changing than general talk.

text: An official statement made right after a harsh act often aims to stop public sympathy from forming.
Judges and jurors bound by statutes in force apply them even when doing so risks serious personal consequences.
when: when the law in force is harsh
why: They are expected to apply the law as written, and refusal is not reasonably expected.

text: Internal evidence is information a text supplies about what its writer expected to happen, revealed by the terms it contains.
when: Analysing a written document such as a will or contract
why: The writer's assumptions show through the wording

text: An inquest gathers witness accounts early, before police work is advanced, and can surface facts that no one has yet connected.
why: Memories are fresh and the facts have not been linked yet.

text: A claim that a document was destroyed cannot be verified directly and can only be reconstructed indirectly from surrounding evidence.
why: The destruction itself leaves no content to examine.

text: Phone calls record who spoke to whom and when, so the phone itself becomes a timeline record.
Phone calls can establish a person's whereabouts and state of mind, but the listener's account of a call is often partial.
Hotel registration records typically show arrival date, city of origin, baggage and calls charged to the room.
In many past periods a stepparent was commonly called by a parent's title, so an odd family label may reflect custom rather than error.
when: interpreting old records that name family relations
why: Customs of the period shape how relationships are worded.

text: A deed takes effect during the giver's lifetime, whereas a will takes effect only at death.
when: choosing how to transfer property or honour a promise
why: The timing of effect differs between the two instruments.

text: What looks like ignorance may have been the accepted learned philosophy of the period, taught in universities and applied in law and medicine.
Official parish records typically list votes and proceedings of legally called meetings and omit outside events.
Grammar norms of earlier periods differed from modern rules, for example singular verbs often followed plural subjects, so modern grammar is a poor test of a writer.
One official's hand recurring across many records reveals who drove the procedure and who wrote most of its examinations.
When oral tradition is thin, deed and will registers are often the main source for locating past events and people.
Petitions record who survived and who pressed a claim, so they show who could seek relief.
Spelling in original records is often inconsistent, even within a single document.
An official arriving later may inherit many reported victims and prior arrests, so early reports can set the agenda before facts are examined.
when: When a new authority takes over an ongoing accusation case.
why: Inherited records frame the official's first decisions.

text: Official records can be lost or withheld for decades, so early accounts built on incomplete material may later need revision.
why: Access to primary records can arrive long after events.

text: Periodical collections can mix original papers, letters, diaries, biographical notices, proceedings, notes and queries, reprints of rare tracts and miscellany, each attributed to named contributors.
Early legal codes protected testimony and courts through harsh penalties for witness intimidation, false testimony and judicial tampering, and they relied on written records.
A shop, tailor or economy that logs every sale, pickup and transfer of a unique item lets the player trace its path and learn who bought it.
when: Designing a trace that leads from an item to a buyer, or unique items the player can track.
why: Complete transaction logs make item provenance recoverable; records connect objects to people through a verifiable source.

text: Hide a key item or document in an unexpected location or among routine papers, so thorough search or patient reading reveals the motive.
when: Designing motive discovery in a level or a social-stealth puzzle.
why: Unexpected placement rewards thorough search without being unfair; patient readers find what quick ones miss.

text: Read a strange message as possibly hiding a second text, such as one readable by every third word or every second letter.
when: When a document seems innocent but its context suggests a hidden meaning.

text: Test official or first-responder reports against physical facts before acting; a hasty first reading or standard-phrased announcement can hide a false lead others will act on.
when: reports from officials or first responders; reading police or authority reports
why: Others may act on the early reading and delay the correct response; public statements may conceal a false lead.

text: Compare units produced with units recovered; a gap signals a hidden possession, but only when the owner can state how many units should be present.
why: Every produced copy must be somewhere; without an expected number there is no baseline to compare against.

text: A case that looks insoluble to officials may be solvable, since their confusion often reflects their method rather than the case itself.
When case files lack a motive, published records such as biographical dictionaries and family histories can supply one.
when: A conflict between people with unknown histories, or behavior that suggests a private grudge.

text: Rank an official record above an informal statement, since a spoken proof can be fabricated or improvised.
when: Sources disagree on a checkable fact
why: Records are harder to improvise than a witness's word

text: A detective game can gate a clue behind archive work, such as photographs, passenger lists and a timeline the player assembles.
A partly recovered message can still steer the next objective if the surviving words name a danger or an ally.
when: only fragments of text survive
why: fragments carry enough meaning to direct action

text: Officials usually refuse direct requests for another person's records, so access often needs a formal authority or a plausible pretext.
when: When a record is held by an official who has no reason to share it.
why: Officials protect records from unauthorised disclosure.

text: A retailer's pay records give the last date a person was paid, which can be compared with a sale date to place that person in time.
when: when dated payment or sales records are available for a suspect's workplace
why: Dated payments link a person to a place and period.

text: In-world bulletins or news tickers can carry a faked status, adding suspense about what the rival believes.
A dispute resting on an old or unusual record is worth investigating, since its outcome is uncertain.
