Keep the most personal record on your person, where it never leaves you.
when: when a search may take items
why: it cannot be seized from a hiding place

text: Record loyalty, resentment, fear and past history early, since they shape what each witness will admit.
Notes, journals and letters can carry clues through style, smudges and crossings-out that hint at the writer's condition; keep inferences open so players must confirm them elsewhere.
when: when designing readable documents as clues
why: Open-ended inference makes players verify rather than accept the clue

text: A document lacking a clerk's signature or proper legal notice carries less authority, so lower its weight in case reasoning.
when: Judging the reliability of a recorded decision.
why: Missing formalities weaken the record's legal standing.

text: When testimony claims knowledge no one can verify, check whether the procedure can separate truth from delusion before accepting it.
when: when a claim rests on supernatural or unobservable sources
why: a test that cannot tell truth from delusion gives no support

text: An in-world note can sound protective while its instructions still grant access. Build such notes so attentive players who read the full text catch the mismatch.
when: Designing written in-world notes, such as a warden's memo with conditional warnings.
why: Players who read past the opening reassurance can detect the contradiction.

text: A forged note misleads a player only if its details are plausible given what the player already knows.
Give each suspect a timeline of signed records such as ticket stubs or guard logs, and let the player find the entry that breaks the chain.
when: when designing an alibi-breaking puzzle
why: Locating the one inconsistent record rewards careful reading of timelines.

text: Tickets, badges and tags generated with serial numbers or torn-stub patterns let the player cross-match them to expose a timeline problem.
when: Designing collectible items that players cross-check.
why: Matching serials or tear patterns give players a verifiable clue.

text: Show the player only discovered incidents and keep some unnoticed ones hidden, so the player's model of the world stays biased toward what was noticed.
when: designing a detective or crime-tracking system
why: Players reason from what the system reveals

text: Document each entry into a controlled stock with its source and authorization, so that unauthorized entries stand out.
when: items arrive through a controlled supply
why: Known sources make anything outside them conspicuous

text: Keep a partial observation open by listing who belongs in the scene and who the observed figure could not be, instead of filling in the missing identity.
when: An investigator has one incomplete sighting.
why: A guessed identity from partial evidence is often wrong and closes off other explanations.

text: Use historical records to fix time, place and fate of a figure, such as crimes, dates and former locations.
when: Building a backstory for an identified figure
why: Dated, located records make a reveal concrete and checkable.

text: An accusation system can show a suspect with motive and no alibi, while a planted document later invalidates the motive.
when: when designing a suspect that the player may wrongly accuse
why: A later document lets the player correct an early error.

text: An ironic final image that echoes an earlier clue ties the ending back to the mystery.
Hand over the solution through an in-world document instead of an investigation scene, so the explanation comes in the character's own voice.
A copied or translated in-world record can diverge from its original, so comparing versions can expose an altered clue.
An in-world quoted decree that silently drops a clause becomes a discovery when players compare it with a full copy found elsewhere in the game world.
when: In-world documents exist in partial and complete versions
why: Comparison reveals hidden omissions

text: Placing the explanation in an embedded document a character reads aloud delays the reveal and sets the document's origin before its contents.
when: when the solution depends on events the investigator did not see
why: The source and framing shape how the contents are received.

text: Official doubt about an object can delay the connection between that object and the solution, acting as misdirection.
when: when authority figures dismiss a clue
why: the dismissal removes the obvious link until the player assembles the evidence

text: Official responses such as gathering people in a shelter or sending reinforcements make a rumor seem more serious, which raises fear further.
when: a rumor prompts visible authority action
why: official action is read as confirmation of the threat

text: A council convened with a majority chosen by one party can turn public opinion toward the party it targets.
when: a dispute is settled by a council
why: visible unfairness shifts sympathy

text: A faction that enters its own account into an official record can recast a rival's intervention as an accusation against that rival.
when: two factions contest authority over the same case
why: Official records carry legitimacy, so the account written into them gains weight with observers.

text: An official act such as a seal or closed gate can reveal who held authority at a given hour, so players can infer control from visible acts.
when: Authority changes over the course of the game world
why: Official acts are observable evidence of who is in charge

text: An NPC's official status can differ from the player's knowledge, such as a wanted figure marked presumed dead, so the game world tracks a record that the player may see differently.
when: A character's status is uncertain and the official record is updated separately from the truth.
why: Records are changed by procedures and authorities, which may lag behind or contradict what actually happened.

text: A player can take a suspect's physical records, such as prints, and compare them with scene clues, so the match or mismatch changes which suspects remain in play.
when: When a game offers forensic comparison as a mechanic.
why: Comparison turns physical evidence into a decision that narrows the suspect pool.

text: A puzzle can hide a deliberate discrepancy that the player detects by comparing a record, such as a receipt, with the current state.
when: Designing an inventory or evidence puzzle

text: When the audience knows a hidden relation the characters do not, ordinary acts such as punishment or appeals for help acquire tension, since the characters misread them.
when: The story depends on what characters will misjudge.
why: Audience knowledge turns the characters' misreadings into visible stakes.

text: Official reports and verdicts can skip the small detail that matters or miss a trace only a close observer saw; check the raw evidence yourself.
when: when relying on an official finding

text: Officials trust what they saw directly and may accept a plausible cover story, while flaws stay visible to a closer observer; subtler inferences lose out.
when: When authorities investigate a staged disappearance.
why: Official investigators may not test the internal consistency of a plausible account.

text: Plausible but unverified figures can grow into strong suspicion; verify them before acting on them.
when: financial or gossip information seems to fit a theory
why: plausibility feels like confirmation

text: Partial reports from witnesses can mislead an arriving character, so the audience should be told how little that character knows.
when: A character arrives after events and relies on fragments

text: A partial reproduction gives a weaker conclusion, since missing conditions such as mood or state of mind can change the result.
when: Recreating an original act with some conditions unmatched
why: Unreproduced factors can alter the outcome, so a match is less conclusive

text: Omitted passages can hide information needed to check a timeline, and a narrator's stated limit does not guarantee completeness.
when: Verifying a sequence of events from an edited account
why: Edits can remove facts needed for verification

text: A large archive of familiar cases can make ordinary incidents feel dull to the investigator.
Partial overheard words invite confirmation bias, so a name heard in fragments may point to the wrong person.
when: When a single name or word is the only clue from overheard speech
why: Incomplete information is easily fitted to a preferred suspect

text: A hurried reading can invert a note's instruction, so reread a message before acting on it.
when: Acting on a short or urgent note.
why: Brief wording is easy to misread, especially under pressure.

text: Official-looking paperwork is not proof, since a neat, authoritative document can be forged.
Assuming a single shipment when paperwork may hide a second, similar one can mislead the reconstruction.
Following a recorded address without checking it wastes effort, and the trail goes cold when the address was invented.
Visitors with official standing may go unlogged and unquestioned, letting unrecorded access pass as legitimate.
Named sources and titles alone do not establish a claim's truth; citations without checking give false confidence.
when: Evaluating a story that relies on references
why: Listeners may act on the appearance of documentation rather than its substance.

text: Early surveys made by walking or rough measurement were often poor, so grants overlapped and maps seem more precise than the original surveys justify.
why: Rough measurement cannot support the precision a drawn map suggests.

text: Paper records are partial, and a lost or missing deed can start a real dispute, so a gap in the record can itself matter.
A reversal or remedy limited to those who petitioned leaves unnamed victims unrestored.
An editor's correction can itself be an error, so corrections should be checked against the source where possible.
when: when relying on an edited or annotated transcription
why: Editors work from the same imperfect records and can introduce mistakes

text: Totals counted from a partial list can mislead, because the final count depends on which cases are included.
Dramatic irony is flat if the audience has no reason to care about the hidden truth.
when: Creating a secret the audience knows.
why: Irony needs stakes to produce tension.

text: Approximate or inconsistent dates produce illusory patterns, so a timeline must be reliable before matches are trusted.
when: When event dates come from sources of uneven accuracy.
why: Noise in dates gives the appearance of correlation where none exists.

text: 1) Look up each principal's name in reference works. 2) Read the family's record, not only the individual's. 3) Follow each record to its consequences. 4) Read later generations' entries for inherited grudges.
when: A case has an unexplained conflict between people with unknown histories.

text: 1) Search old records for events similar to the current case. 2) Check whether an earlier unresolved case shares motive and method. 3) Verify the pattern against the present details before applying it.
when: A current case may echo an earlier one
why: Past patterns can explain present events but may be misapplied

text: 1) Collect every notice from the open channel. 2) Order the messages by content, since dates may be missing. 3) Record the medium's details, such as column and position. 4) Match the channel to other evidence to identify the sender.
when: Secret messages are passed through a public medium
why: A rebuilt sequence and a traced channel can reveal who is communicating

text: 1) Compare the disputed sheet's watermark with known stationery to find its source. 2) Compare the handwriting with a sample the suspect is known to have written. 3) Re-examine the first impression closely. 4) Send both documents for specialist comparison and record remaining uncertainty.
when: Authorship of a letter or order is in question and a reliable known sample exists.
why: Watermarks and first impressions can each mislead, so a layered check is needed.

text: 1) Note the document's date and production time to set its earliest appearance. 2) Count copies and assign each to a recipient or file. 3) Record the last time the document was seen on its usual surface. 4) Treat a copy found somewhere illogical as evidence of someone else's handling.
when: A written record serves as a link in a timeline
why: Accounting for every copy shows whether a document was moved and when

text: 1) Extend the sequence beyond its last known item using the same interval and rule. 2) State the predicted position as a testable hypothesis. 3) Link the predicted position to a known event. 4) Treat the prediction as a lead, not as proof.
when: A strong pattern across several records suggests a missing member
why: A prediction gives a date and a reason to search, without assuming the item exists

text: 1) Write the letter to name specific checkable leads, such as witnesses and locations. 2) Ensure those leads can be reached from other sources. 3) Let a suspect destroy the letter while the leads stay available to the player.
when: Designing a document that points toward the truth but can be destroyed.
why: Destruction removes one copy, and leads elsewhere keep the mystery solvable.

text: Present in-world archive documents, such as letters, earlier verdicts and jury notes, in full with their provenance so players can cross-check them against present testimony.
when: designing an in-game archive

text: Give in-game documents distinct authors, handwriting and attestation details so players can judge each source's reliability and compare them.
when: when designing in-game documents
why: Players weigh sources by their provenance.

text: Treat an official's confident conclusion or closed verdict as a claim to test, separating forecasts drawn from reputation from demonstrated proof.
when: when an authority figure declares a suspect guilty or a case is closed
why: Confidence and proof are different things; official verdicts can be confident and still wrong.

text: Locate and record where a document is hidden, such as a locked or secret drawer, before relying on its contents.
Write in-world journals, letters and diaries as partial testimony with deliberate omissions that players can notice.
when: when designing documents for players to find in the world

text: Provide an in-world ledger of entries and appointments that players can consult on demand as a reference record.
Place a removed page in a ledger or shop book so the player can find a hidden payment by reading its last entries first.
when: designing a record-based clue

text: Give in-world documents period-appropriate spelling, paper and script, and plant a near-correct forgery so an observant player can catch it.
when: Authoring letters, maps or ledgers for a game world
why: Players who know period conventions can judge authenticity and gain clues about the forger

text: Give in-world letters and notices regional wording or spelling that signals their true author, and let players compare terms against an NPC's stated background.
when: Designing in-world documents that serve as clues
why: Players can detect a false origin by comparing the language with what they know

text: Use a suspect's past offences to narrow the search only when the method of the past crime closely matches the new one.
when: deciding whether a criminal record is relevant
why: matching method gives real evidence

text: Send a sensitive written message by a courier instructed to hand it to the addressee personally, so it cannot be lost or opened by others.
when: when the message must reach one specific person intact
why: Personal delivery prevents interception and keeps control of the document's contents.

text: Design in-world newspapers or bulletins with errors the player can correct using other evidence, so the document is a source to test rather than a fact.
when: When an in-world document conveys story information.
why: Players then learn to cross-check sources instead of accepting printed claims.

text: Give an in-game letter or journal a later-added line in a different ink tone or smudge, so a careful player can infer an edit.
when: designing document clues
why: physical cues reward close inspection without hiding any text

text: In-game newspapers and letters can serve as dated lore, and a collection can hide one entry the player must find.
In a forensic game, withhold the method behind an expert's report and let the player reconstruct it from other clues, or leave gaps they can infer.
Place wills and inventories in the world as documents that reveal ownership and which rooms were restricted.
Record the scene at discovery with a photograph or snapshot before others arrive, fixing evidence that later clues can be checked against.
Write journal entries that players can re-read after a reveal, so earlier notes take on the new meaning.
Build a missing-person quest as a chain of records, such as a receipt, ledger entry or station register, each naming the next location.
why: Chained records give players a traceable path

text: Design broken floors or scorch marks with readable edges that reveal whether a collapse was forced or staged.
when: generating environmental damage as evidence
why: damage should carry checkable information

text: Link a physical clue to a document clue, such as a receipt or delivery log, so finding an object leads the player to a record.
when: when designing clue chains

text: Make destroyed documents recoverable, by keeping a copy elsewhere or scattering pieces to reassemble, so players can compare a witnessed account with the record or race to rebuild it.
when: a plot document is destroyed, torn up or lost
why: Copies let players check testimony against the record, and recovery turns destruction into a playable challenge.

text: Give in-world documents a provenance tag, date and drafting history; mark undated or omitted material, and let later editions correct earlier ones with their own timestamp.
when: presenting letters, depositions, reports or case files as evidence; designing contracts, wills or maps as clues
why: Readers need to judge a source's reliability and completeness, and provenance, dating and metadata let players weigh sources and test whether later events fit by design.

text: Give in-world letters a readable aim, such as a threat or a demand, so the player learns to read the sender's motive.
Give shops ledgers of pledged items, so player-owned objects become traces that an investigator can check.
Model legal documents as game state: a filed document with the right authority changes inheritance, so players must learn that rule before using it.
when: a game includes deeds, wills or similar papers

text: Tie each document to its finding location, since where a document was found changes what it means.
Have an examine action log counted, verifiable details, such as the number of steps or the marks on an object, so the player can reach the same inference.
when: Clues are physical objects in the game.
why: Verifiable details let the player reason rather than guess.

text: Build document checks into the inventory, such as a ledger or receipt that confirms or refutes a claim, so players can test NPC statements.
when: when designing verifiable clues
why: Physical documents give players a way to check claims.

text: Design multi-step delivery puzzles so each handoff is recorded, letting the player see where the item went.
Include every person who matters to the solution in the roster; any omitted person forces the player to guess.
why: An omitted person breaks the fair-play contract.

text: Give each rare item to only a few characters so that matching an item to its carrier is meaningful.
when: designing item ownership for dungeon or level content
why: Widely held items cannot identify a single owner.

text: Record cryptic NPC lines in the player's journal so they can be recalled and linked when the related event occurs.
when: Designing hints that pay off later in a game.
why: Players forget ambiguous lines unless a record preserves them.

text: Keep alternative motives open when interpreting a clue, and do not treat a hint as proof.
when: Reasoning about a clue that suggests one suspect.
why: Overreading a hint can mislead investigators toward a wrong conclusion.

text: An in-game archive with missing records or incidental receipts forces the player to combine documents to reconstruct events, and a historian NPC can offer partial records the player must judge.
when: When designing an in-game archive or case file.
why: Incomplete evidence makes the player reason across sources rather than read a single answer.

text: A letter is testimony that cannot answer questions, so its claims should be checked against observed facts and cannot replace questioning.
when: Documents or letters are used as evidence.
why: A document cannot be cross-examined, and its author may have written it with an agenda.

text: A written notice can act as a barrier, setting the terms of contact and shaping expectations before any dialogue occurs.
when: A suspect communicates access terms through a written warning.
why: A written warning frames the encounter and raises stakes without direct confrontation.

text: A written statement of cause, shown to the examining doctor, records the cause in writing and can prevent others being suspected of poisoning.
Naming independent witnesses to a document's signing gives a revealed document standing as valid once its hidden text is exposed.
when: Resolving a dispute over a document's validity.
why: Witnesses to the signing support the document's claim to be genuine.

text: Writing a sensitive reveal instead of saying it aloud makes the claim seem discreet and gives the reader a reason to hide the method.
when: Delivering a private reveal in a performance.
why: Written delivery frames the claim as confidential, which lends it credibility.

text: A single document that explains several earlier anomalies at once makes the proof feel satisfying and complete.
when: confirming a hidden cause near the climax
why: One source accounting for many clues ties the investigation together.

text: Introduce an unexplained document early, so a later reveal can reclassify it, such as proving it a forgery.
If an observer's accurate work is never shown, the audience will also discount them, so the device has no payoff.
when: Using a discredited character as a clue source.
why: The audience judges the character by the same label the group uses.

text: Wide distribution helps a hidden clue survive but also lets other readers find it, so the designer must accept that others may discover it.
when: when choosing how many copies of a clue-bearing document exist
why: Every copy that aids survival is also a copy that the wrong person can read.

text: Deliver the climax as a found document that reframes prior scenes, but a single hidden document feels contrived unless foreshadowed early; alternatively corroborate with several documents and confessions.
when: Designing the climax reveal of a mystery.
why: A found document reinterprets prior events and lets the audience deduce the answer; late, unforeshadowed documents read as contrivance.

text: When a source makes a claim the narrator distrusts, frame it with explicit doubt while still following its instructions, so the audience sees both caution and compliance.
when: An unlikely document or source must still be acted on.
why: Explicit doubt keeps credibility in question without rejecting the source outright.

text: A signed record listing every attending witness makes a summary feel authoritative.
when: Presenting an account the audience may find hard to believe.
why: Official sign-off signals verification.

text: Letting a vivid report shape the hypothesis before its specifics are confirmed makes a general report seem to identify a specific person.
why: the jump from a general finding to a specific identity is unsupported until details match

text: Update a game journal after a reveal so earlier conversations gain new, clearer meaning.
when: A reveal changes the meaning of past dialogue.
why: Re-reading earlier entries lets the player see the new meaning.

text: Mark journals and letters with a reliability level so the player must judge how far to trust them.
when: Designing in-world documents.
why: Varying trust makes documents a reasoning challenge rather than a fixed answer.

text: Plant early, checkable clues about a doubling or disguised character, such as matching name, birthday or appearance, or an odd stare, and leave them unexplained until the reveal.
when: when planning a rival, mirror or disguised character
why: early, checkable traits or oddities give players a fair thread to verify and pull later

text: Reveal each disguise as an impostor so the antagonist resets to a new face while the same enemy persists, letting the player meet it again in a new form.
when: Designing a recurring antagonist who keeps hiding.
why: A new face gives a fresh reveal without changing the threat.

text: Give the enemy a repeated signature, such as a number or a trace, that appears across different suspects so the player can link the crimes.
when: Tying together crimes by a disguised or hidden enemy.
why: A recurring mark lets the player trace the enemy even when the face changes.

text: Stage the protagonist's apparent death at the midpoint, then let the player's assumption of safety become the trap for the next scene.
when: Planning a midpoint pivot in a suspense story.
why: The false death resets the stakes and makes the player doubt their sense of safety.

text: A character who shares the protagonist's name, appearance or birthday produces unease that grows as each shared trait accumulates.
when: when introducing a doppelgänger rival
why: each matching trait is noticeable and adds to the suspicion

text: A character's repeated habits, such as nightly checks or fixed watching, create standing unease and suspicion before any proof exists.
when: A character is suspicious but has no hard evidence yet.
why: Recurring behavior signals menace that players read as a threat without proof.

text: A blackmailer who seems to be an outside stranger can be a second agent of the victim's own family, hidden by costume.
when: Blackmail or extortion plots with an apparently external threat
why: Costume hides the family link, so the outsider assumption survives until the disguise is exposed.

text: One antagonist can appear under two personas, each carrying a different clue; the player must notice that the clues belong to the same person.
When the audience knows more than an authority figure, dramatic irony builds, but its emotional payoff depends on showing the cost of the gap.
when: when the player knows a truth that an ally does not
why: Tension from the gap lands only when its consequences are shown.

text: When the audience knows what a character does not, suspense comes from the gap between knowledge and power: the character acts in ignorance or cannot respond.
when: The audience must learn information the protagonist cannot share or act on; the reveal should drive tension rather than surprise.
why: Knowledge without power drives suspense; knowledge gaps convert the character's ordinary actions into tense ones.

text: A clue that characters dismiss, such as a report called a joke, stays available to the audience and creates dramatic irony that rewards attentive players.
Drop a hypothesis once a test or confirmed fact refutes it, since clinging hides the true answer; yet treat rejected explanations as branch points, not dead ends.
when: A tentative theory or candidate explanation is refuted by a test or confirmed fact.
why: Holding onto refuted theories wastes effort and misleads the inquiry.

text: Dropping a dissenting conclusion from the record hides an unresolved possibility that later evidence may need.
when: when a participant holds a different verdict

text: Dropping explanations too early can hide the true cause, so keep alternatives under consideration until testing rules them out.
when: When reasoning toward a single explanation.
why: A premature conclusion can close off the correct account.

text: Dropping a planted contradiction without a later answer leaves the player with an unresolved and frustrating loose end.
when: a statement conflicts with another
why: each contradiction needs a later resolution

text: A reconstruction can drift away from its purpose; once the reason for the tally is lost, the arithmetic answers no question.
when: A person starts a sum and forgets why they began it.
why: A tally is only useful for the question it was meant to answer.

text: An investigator may drop a case when the key witness will not testify and the offender has shown real remorse, rather than prosecute a case that would collapse.
when: the case depends on an unwilling witness and the offender is remorseful
why: a prosecution that would collapse gains nothing, and punishment may prevent reform

text: Drop a candidate explanation when no motive can be found for it, even if it was briefly considered earlier.
when: evaluating a candidate explanation

text: Drop a theory when a verified timeline places the suspect elsewhere at the critical time. Reopen the question if the alibi witnesses are themselves involved.
When two identical items exist, a matching trace implicates whoever held either one, so the evidence stays ambiguous until ownership is checked.
One matching item may be ordinary, but a second matching item turns an apparent accident into a suspicious duplicate.
A stolen valuable replaced by a convincing copy hides the theft, so a witness who examined the object may have confirmed only the copy.
when: an item's identity or value matters to the mystery
why: A good duplicate is hard to distinguish from the original without expert inspection.

text: Removing one copy of evidence does not erase it if duplicates exist elsewhere. Investigators should look for copies before assuming the evidence is gone.
when: Someone attempts to destroy an identifying item
why: Copies made earlier can survive the removal

text: Identical names can belong to different people, so check each index entry against its source before merging them.
Assuming a river or road keeps the same name across periods leads to misreading older documents, since one physical feature may carry several names over time.
when: reading records from different periods
why: names change while the feature stays in place

text: A dying speaker's fragmentary words, possibly partly delirium, can carry motive or knowledge but are inference, not a full statement or literal clue.
when: A key witness cannot give a complete statement.
why: Delirium distorts speech, and a fragment can be read to fit many theories.

text: A deathbed statement may be sincere, but fever, drugs, drink, pain, spite or fear can distort it; weigh motive and the speaker's state, and seek corroboration before relying on it.
when: when the only witness is dying, feverish or drugged
why: Impaired state reduces the reliability of memory and perception.

text: Have a dying NPC give garbled words that form a partial clue the player must combine and cross-check with other evidence to reach the meaning.
when: Designing NPC dying words as clues.
why: Partial clues keep mystery open while requiring player verification.

text: A dying person may leave a deliberate sign for the living, or may only repeat a fixed idea without understanding it.
when: A victim leaves a final mark or word
why: A deliberate message and a delirious repetition look alike at first.

text: A dying statement can be dismissed as delirium, so its weight depends on whether others are willing to credit it.
Treat a dying person's accusation as hearsay: a lead showing where to look, not proof of identity or intent, to be checked against the physical record.
when: investigating a dying person's accusation
why: Delirious statements lack independent weight and cannot be cross-examined; they may mislead.

text: Give a dying word two readings, such as an external cause and the real killer, so the player weighs both; reveal the intended one only at the end.
when: Writing a cryptic last utterance that serves as a clue.
why: Ambiguity keeps the decoy plausible while the true meaning stays available to attentive players.

text: A dying statement or witness account is only as reliable as the conditions under which it was heard and spoken.
A dying speaker's words are more reliable when they had no reason to deceive; a faked message would be spoken clearly, so broken speech suggests a genuine one.
when: A witness gives a partial utterance near death.
why: A deliberate fake is usually delivered intelligibly.

text: Hide a dying clue as a partial string that the player completes against a map or list of locations.
Use an NPC's dying words as a fair clue to the culprit, such as their gender, even while others dismiss them as delirium.
Use a dying victim's message as late corroboration of a mechanism the audience has already been shown.
when: confirming a hidden method near the climax
why: A message from the victim confirms the method without adding new explanation.

text: A remark made by a cornered or dying speaker can carry meaning only for an audience that shares the reference it relies on, so the clue is unlocked by knowing that reference.
when: A dying or cornered character speaks a line that seems out of place for their class or setting.
why: The meaning of a fragmentary remark depends on a shared frame of reference, which the audience must possess to decode it.

text: Timing a new revelation just after a sympathetic figure dies can turn that death into a fresh source of fear.
A last-moment confession can seem too convenient, so the audience must trust the source and the timing for it to land.
when: when a culprit confesses at the end, especially near death
why: Convenient timing can look like a device rather than earned revelation.

text: Dying speech is short and fragmentary, so plan in advance what information the audience must learn before the speaker dies.
when: Writing a dying character who must deliver a clue.
why: A cut-off speech may end before the key information is delivered.

text: 1) Record a dying person's exact words, treating them as a partial message. 2) Keep that wording separate from interpretation. 3) List each plausible reading and weigh it against other evidence.
when: when a victim speaks final words before dying or losing consciousness and the statement is ambiguous
why: Interpretations are often accepted as fact before wording is secured; a dying speaker may leave only a few words, easily misremembered if not recorded exactly.

text: 1) Determine where death happened from room evidence, not where the body lies, since the body may have been moved. 2) Compare the wound's shape and depth with the surface it struck. 3) Use both to test the stated account.
when: a scene looks orderly or theatrical
why: The body's position can differ from the place of death.

text: 1) Fix a starting time from a reliable record. 2) Fix an end time from a witness who heard the next event. 3) Treat the interval between them as the frame for testing every alibi and sound.
when: when a death must be placed within a bounded window
why: A bounded interval gives a common frame for all accounts.

text: 1) List each candidate explanation for a death. 2) Gather facts about the deceased's circumstances, the body, and the spot where it was found. 3) Check each explanation against each fact set. 4) Eliminate explanations that conflict with the facts, and test the remaining one.
when: At the start of a death inquiry, before findings are settled.
why: Structured elimination shows which facts still need gathering.

text: Let a dying character's words name a suspect, but make the player able to test those words against objects and traces in the scene.
when: designing an NPC's final testimony in a mystery
why: checkable testimony keeps the accusation from deciding the case alone

text: Use dying words or fragmentary notes as clue text that points to a location or time, to be combined with other evidence.
when: Designing clue text

text: Make an NPC's dying line ambiguous so the player must interpret it against the scene, and let a later NPC correct or contradict an earlier lie.
when: Designing dialogue-based clues.

text: Cap the number of exchanges with a dying or injured NPC, offering only a few short hints under a timer.
Hold a survivor's testimony back until a dying confession, which resolves a lost-person question and revives the missing character.
A witness who asks eagerly about a particular time usually has a stake in that time.
when: a witness presses on the timing of events
why: they want the time to fall in a way that favours them

text: An eager, unsupervised bystander may volunteer details that supply clues without knowing their significance.
Speech overheard through a wall arrives in pieces: muffled sound gives way to sharp, clear words, so a listener catches only parts of the exchange.
A hidden device can capture what people say when they believe they are unobserved, using a black box, wiring and a receiver to magnify and transmit sound.
when: Suspects are likely to talk privately and the setting allows concealment.
why: Speakers lower their guard, and whispers near the device are still captured.

text: An NPC hidden in a room can overhear player dialogue and react later, so a scene should not be treated as private.
when: designing dialogue in rooms that may hold unseen characters

text: When a conversation cannot be heard directly, a hidden vantage point, such as a nearby tree, can still reveal the scene to a watcher.
when: a private room or talk is out of earshot

text: Sounds through a closed door, such as scuffling, dragging, a heavy crash or a cut-off cry, indicate violence in progress.
when: when a person inside may be in danger

text: Echoing architecture garbles speech, so a distant listener receives only isolated words and broken phrases.
when: a listener is at an echoing corner or distance
why: reflections overlap and blur the words

text: A player hears full lines from one speaker and fragments from another, and a noise that interrupts the talk drops lines from what is heard.
when: Eavesdropping through a scene with ambient noise or distance
why: Distance and interruption limit how much speech reaches the listener

text: A hidden watcher who sees a private act and later changes the situation creates dramatic irony, since the target does not know the state has changed.
why: The target acts on outdated assumptions

text: When speakers sense a listener, they lower their voices, so the listener's own noise changes what is said and what can be learned.
Listeners who catch only fragments fill the gaps with guesses shaped by their assumptions, so conclusions drawn from overheard talk can be wrong.
when: a listener hears speech only partly or uses overheard talk as evidence
why: Fragments lack full context, so partial hearing invites guessing.

text: Revealing surveillance too early lets the suspect change tactics before the trap closes.
when: When planning a watch on a suspect.
why: Once a suspect notices watchers, they adjust their behaviour and the advantage is lost.

text: Each adjustment raises the chance of discovery by sound or by someone moving nearby, and a partial gain may still miss key words.
Speakers wrongly assume privacy when they think a listener cannot understand them, so overheard talk can reveal what they hide.
when: someone is said not to understand the language
why: people assume unintelligible listeners are harmless

text: 1) Make the target believe you are incapacitated. 2) Hide a trusted witness where they can hear but not be seen, near the antagonist. 3) Offer a believable pretext that invites gloating. 4) Ask specific leading questions about the means. 5) Reveal the witness and call for help once the admission is made.
when: A suspect or antagonist is likely to boast or reveal details if they think no one can use them; staging a confession for a player-triggered scene.
why: An antagonist speaks freely when they believe no one can hear, and a concealed witness makes the confession usable as proof.

text: 1) Find a concealed opening above or beside the target room. 2) Conceal it from the target's view. 3) Observe and listen from a fixed position over many days.
when: A suspect's routine is the best evidence and direct questioning has failed.
why: Repeated observation reveals habits a single visit would miss.

text: 1) Note when the key talk took place. 2) Note when the suspected listener arrived or came within range. 3) If they arrived after the core of the talk, they could not have heard it.
when: testing whether a listener could have heard what they claim

text: 1) List every door, bolt and wall between the listener and the sound. 2) Judge whether each one blocks hearing. 3) Accept or reject the claim accordingly.
when: when testing a claim that someone could or could not hear something
why: Unmapped barriers make hearing claims unreliable

text: 1) Listen unseen to unguarded talk. 2) Note the grievances, boasts and claims heard. 3) Approach the speaker in person and question them, using the overheard content as the opening.
when: the listener can stay out of sight and the speaker is unguarded

text: Give voiced NPC lines readable tells, such as a pause, a changed line, a repeated word or a shift in vocal pitch, that signal concealment or lying.
when: Recording dialogue meant to hint at hidden knowledge.
why: Audible tells let players read deception without explicit text.

text: Trigger an NPC's spoken line when the player is hidden nearby, gating it behind a stealth check.
Build a hidden informant into the design so the player has a second route to the secret beyond the obvious circle.
Make eavesdropping yield a partial line that raises a question without giving the answer.
when: Designing an overhearing interaction for players
why: Partial information keeps the player inquiring rather than solved

text: Let an NPC who appears dead overhear the player's conversation and reveal what was said later.
when: designing a fake death that conceals an NPC
why: A hidden listener can expose information the player assumed was private.

text: Let an unseen character's voice carry their state, since sound can reveal distress without the player ever seeing the person.
Place a hidden listener so gaps in what they hear feel natural. Avoid positions easy to discover, and speakers with no reason to talk freely.
when: Staging an eavesdropped scene
why: Plausible positioning keeps the scene believable

text: Confirm a secret through overheard dialogue rather than a confession, so the first direct evidence is heard and the accused can still deny it.
why: This keeps the reveal a matter of judgment rather than settled fact.

text: Targets find a request framed as a moral duty hard to refuse, even when the request arrives on forged letterhead.
when: When a lure can use real letterhead and an appeal to duty.

text: In the first half hour after a drug taken by mouth, its symptoms closely resemble feigned illness, so an early diagnosis cannot easily expose faking.
why: symptoms have not yet diverged

text: Move a guarded witness onto familiar local topics to get fluent talk and lower their guard, then return to the question that matters.
when: a witness resists the key question
why: Comfortable topics relax people, making them easier to draw out.

text: A talkative witness reveals more when the listener seems sympathetic and responds with short encouraging remarks rather than direct questions.
when: when interviewing a motivated witness
why: Feeling heard keeps the witness talking about what they believe.

text: Check deeds, wills and estate records before accepting a person's social status from earlier accounts, which may understate it.
why: property records can overturn accounts based on reputation

text: Releasing a witness before the whole truth is known risks losing cooperation; release only once the remaining stakes are minor.
An earlier statement is only as reliable as the note-taking that recorded it.
when: Relying on a prior written record to test a witness.
why: Transcription errors can make a record disagree with what was actually said.

text: 1) Ask questions that let each party state their own account. 2) Note exactly where the accounts disagree. 3) Weigh each account against checkable facts.
when: gathering testimony about one event

text: 1) Promise confidentiality to the suspect. 2) Ask for a complete written account. 3) Check the account for gaps against known facts.
when: A talkative suspect may withhold details that matter to the timeline
why: A confidentiality promise encourages fuller disclosure, but does not guarantee completeness.

text: 1) Let suspects talk freely about the topic. 2) Introduce a remark that invites a reaction. 3) Listen for repeated phrases or details only the culprit could know.
when: Interrogating a suspect without a full accusation.

text: 1) Let the witness narrate freely first. 2) Return to specific senses: darkness, sounds, touch, smell. 3) Offer concrete cue prompts for impressions not yet verbalized. 4) Ask whether the presence felt familiar or unknown. 5) Test each detail from another angle.
when: when questioning a witness who was frightened or asleep during an event
why: fear and shock blur memory, but accurate sensory detail often survives if prompted gently

text: Frame a suspect's obligation to speak as a duty to free someone wrongly accused, separate from any blame for the crime.
when: suspect is not culpable but holds knowledge
why: people cooperate more readily when their silence would harm an innocent party

text: Plant an odd question from an NPC early, such as one about rare poisons, so the player can recall it when a related clue appears.
when: designing NPC dialogue for a mystery
why: a planted question becomes meaningful when a later clue connects to it

text: When every alternative fails the evidence and no other path remains, the survivor becomes the working answer, but it must still pass the chain check.
when: Several explanations are dismissed one by one, or every rival has been eliminated.
why: Elimination can justify a conclusion when proof is impossible to obtain directly.

text: Make innocent handlers an explicit elimination step so players learn to exclude them before accusing anyone.
when: Designing investigation puzzles with shared objects.
why: Excluding innocent handlers prevents false accusation.

text: Test an early lead against later clues before trusting it, since first impressions can aim at the wrong suspect.
Use a partial clue as a filter: rule out candidates that fail each known detail until the remaining set is small.
when: Investigating an incomplete description
why: Known traits reduce the possibilities

text: Exclusion is stronger than matching, since a few samples can miss the actual source, so treat a match as a lead rather than proof.
Eliminate options by logical exclusion; for example, an exit locked before a certain hour rules out using it after that hour.
Narrow suspects by asking who could reach the contaminated means at the right moment; positively excluding people from access sharply shrinks the remaining field.
when: A poison or substance could have been introduced by a limited set of people.
why: Access removes people who could not have acted.

text: Eliminating rival explanations or routes shows only what is impossible; it does not explain the act itself, which still needs explanation from further clues.
when: Rivals or routes have been ruled out.
why: Removing wrong answers does not supply the right one; impossibility narrows the question rather than answering it.

text: The last candidate surviving elimination only fits the description, not proven guilt; treat it as a suspect needing a confirming test, since disguise or later contradicting evidence can defeat it.
when: Concluding a suspect from attribute filtering or a shrinking candidate list.
why: Elimination only shows who matches the description, and descriptions based on appearance can be defeated by disguise.

text: A false trail or premise that is too easy to disprove wastes time; choose one plausible enough to provoke a reaction and make the player doubt the real clues.
when: When designing false leads.
why: A lead that collapses at once gives the player no reason to doubt the real clues.

text: An elaborate alibi invites the question of why it was needed, which can make the whole story suspect.
An alibi covering only the early evening leaves the critical hour open, so it does not exclude the suspect.
An elimination that ignores unknown motive makes the answer look simpler than the case really is.
why: Missing motive leaves a gap that elimination cannot fill

text: Eliminating a theory point by point risks overlooking an alternative explanation that fits the remaining facts.
when: Testing a theory by ruling out its parts one at a time
why: Each elimination is judged against the current theory, which can hide other explanations

text: An unexplained interval does not prove guilt; treating it as proof assigns opportunity to anyone present.
when: A suspect cannot account for a period
why: A gap shows only that the time is unknown, not what happened in it.

text: 1) List every candidate explanation, such as suicide, accident, justified homicide and murder. 2) Test each against the evidence in turn. 3) Reject contradicted explanations. 4) Accept the remaining one as the working answer.
when: Several explanations for one event must be narrowed, or a small known set of explanations exists.

text: 1) List every possible agent who could have acted. 2) Eliminate each candidate in turn using the evidence, or a denial or changed reaction that behavior contradicts. 3) Repeat until one remains. 4) Accept it only if the list was complete.
when: The pool of suspects is small and the scene limits who could act.

text: 1) Trace the physical means and list every explanation and person who could have acted. 2) Reject those the evidence contradicts. 3) Test the survivor's motive and the facts it rests on against independent evidence.
when: A case has a short list of suspects or rival theories.
why: Elimination is only as sound as its starting facts.

text: 1) Start from the apparent impossibility. 2) List every physically open route or explanation. 3) Remove each option that observation rules out. 4) Hold the remaining option as provisional until it is checked. 5) State each step aloud so others can challenge it.
when: the set of routes or explanations is finite and checkable

text: 1) List possible ways a fact could have been produced. 2) Judge each by how much risk its perpetrators would have accepted. 3) Discard options that are too risky to be plausible.
when: Several explanations fit a fixed fact
why: Assessing the cost of each option to its perpetrators removes implausible explanations.

text: 1) List each candidate source of a poison. 2) Test each container. 3) Apply known properties such as taste threshold, onset time and dose to exclude candidates. 4) Reason from the remaining facts.
1) Clean each person's fingers. 2) Press them onto an inking pad. 3) Roll them onto smooth white paper. 4) Label each impression and file it as an elimination set.
when: Traces on an object must be attributed to people with legitimate access.
why: Known prints let remaining prints be assigned to an unknown party.

text: 1) Check each person's alibi against the window. 2) Set aside those whose alibis hold. 3) Treat the remaining people inside the window as suspects.
when: Access to the scene was controlled
why: Elimination focuses suspicion on those with access

text: 1) List every candidate hiding place for the object. 2) Check and exclude each external place. 3) Search the most likely internal place last.
when: Searching for a hidden object when the candidate places form a finite, checkable set.
why: Systematic exclusion narrows the search until the remaining place must hold the object.

text: 1) Ask closed questions about specific possibilities. 2) Record whether each is denied. 3) Use the pattern of denials to narrow the explanation under test.
when: Testing whether a suspicious act or idea was ever raised
why: Consistent denials of specific possibilities narrow the candidate explanations

text: 1) Reduce the account to a short list of fixed premises. 2) Identify the premise that must be false. 3) List everyone who could physically reach the object. 4) Test each suspect against that list.
when: When an object seems to vanish from a sealed place.
why: An apparent impossibility means a premise is wrong, and narrowing access finds who acted.

text: 1) Test ordinary explanations first: records, local history, prior exposure, and the witness's state of mind. 2) Assess only what remains unexplained as supernatural or psychological.
when: when a mystery has a supernatural reading not yet ruled in or out
why: Ordinary causes are checkable and often account for odd details before any unexplained remainder is considered

text: 1) List every agent the reports allow. 2) Exclude anyone a witness who knew them would have recognized. 3) Discard candidates who could not have acted in time. 4) Discard candidates who gain nothing from the act. 5) Treat any survivor as provisional until confirmed.
when: When one fact requires a single actor and several candidates remain.
why: Systematic elimination narrows candidates using checkable constraints.

text: 1) List each claimed action of the suspect separately. 2) Test each against the evidence and rule out those it contradicts. 3) Revise the theory around what remains. 4) Confront the suspect with a detail only the guilty party could know.
when: A theory is built from many small inferences that can be tested separately
why: Removing false parts of a theory leaves a narrower case that a guilty detail can break

text: 1) List each safeguard such as locks, passwords, signatures, keys and staff checks. 2) State the assumption each safeguard makes. 3) Rule out the crude route first, such as force against a hardened building. 4) Test each remaining route one safeguard at a time.
when: Finding how a heavily guarded place could be breached
why: Listing assumptions narrows the field to the single weak link

text: Exclusion yields only a probable answer while unobserved options remain; conclude from it only when the candidate list is complete.
Eliminating a suspect on an assumption rather than observed fact invalidates the deduction; record each elimination's premise so it can be reopened if that premise fails.
why: An elimination is only as sound as its underlying assumption.

text: Include one trace that eliminates the most obvious suspect, so players deduce who is present rather than guess.
Treat the ease of an explanation as a sign of missing evidence rather than a solution, and test a simple answer before accepting it.
when: an obvious explanation comes to mind early in a case
why: simple answers often fit because important evidence has not yet been found

text: Elimination works with a small, known candidate group but weakens when many could reach the means or candidates are open-ended; the answer is only as good as the alternatives considered.
Excluding a party from findings protects the investigation, but it can breed resentment and leave the excluded person feeling wronged.
Fear and expectation inflate confidence in brief or partial sightings, so frightened observers may report imagined threats, such as faces in windows, as clear proof.
when: a witness is under fear, or an area is already alarming
why: Fear fills gaps in partial views, making accounts more vivid than accurate.

text: Separate a witness's feelings and judgments from their factual claims; emotion distorts interpretation more than recalled facts, so concrete timings and signals can stay reliable.
when: A witness speaks with strong feeling, such as bitterness, intoxication or emotional investment, about events.
why: Strong feeling colours interpretation and reporting.

text: Frightened or emotional witnesses give vivid but imprecise timelines, and fright distorts the sequence of events; check their times and order against independent records.
when: a witness recounts events from memory
why: Vivid recall is not accurate timing.

text: Emotional force, vivid detail, or the fear a story provokes is not evidence of accuracy; intensity makes an account more persuasive, not more accurate.
Fear turns ambiguous movement or shapes, such as a startled jump or an unanswered knock, into perceived threats; separate what was seen from what was interpreted and felt.
when: a witness fears for someone's safety, or an observer is anxious and the cue is ambiguous
why: Fear and anxiety make observers read ordinary events as threats or messages.

text: Frightened witnesses may exaggerate or minimise events, and their strongest sentence is not necessarily the strongest fact; judge reliability on its own terms.
when: when a witness reports events under fear
why: Emotional intensity raises the apparent weight of a statement.

text: Strong emotion, such as fear, grief or pity, makes some details vivid and drops others, so a missing answer does not prove the detail was absent.
when: a witness is frightened or emotionally connected to the people involved
why: Emotional salience selects which details are remembered.

text: Fear of a feared or criminal group, or of informers, may silence witnesses until the threat is exposed or removed, so silence can reflect fear rather than ignorance.
when: witnesses decline to speak about a feared group or secret organisation
why: Fear of retaliation or informers suppresses testimony independently of what the witness knows.

text: Fear, illness or strong expectation shapes what is heard, so sounds are recalled as more than was perceived and ordinary noise is read as threat.
when: a witness is agitated, already expects something, or hears sounds after a frightening event
why: Emotional and bodily states and prior expectation colour what is heard and remembered.

text: Flush, pallor, trembling or sudden tone change is a sign to note, not proof of deception; innocent fear or embarrassment can cause it.
when: a witness or suspect reacts strongly to questioning or shown evidence
why: Emotion has many causes, including fear, embarrassment or protecting someone.

text: Awkward manner, avoidance, tears or reticence often come from embarrassment, fatigue or a wish to bury a matter, as well as guilt.
when: a witness avoids a painful subject or seems awkward
why: Embarrassment and fatigue look like guilt from outside.

text: A frightened or guilty listener may mishear speech and fill in missing words, so their account of what was said can be wrong.
when: a witness recounts a conversation or sound under fear or guilt
why: fear and guilt shape what a person perceives and recalls

text: A frightened or grieving witness may fit an ambiguous word to a familiar idea, so their interpretation of it needs checking.
Anxiety and fear of appearing weak can push an investigator to settle on a theory before the facts are gathered.
A witness speaking in anger or grief describes a suspect's character in detail, often revealing traits and motives without meaning to.
when: Interviewing an emotionally involved witness
why: Strong feelings loosen restraint and invite characterization

text: A witness who fears for their life may shade or withhold what they say, so the account can be less complete or less accurate than their knowledge allows.
when: when a witness is threatened or frightened
why: fear changes what the witness is willing to reveal

text: Posture and facial tension before a person speaks can signal fear, and an investigator can use that reading to choose how to approach them.
when: a person arrives visibly distressed
why: body language shows emotion before any words

text: A guarded witness may suddenly become warm or genial when offered a tempting claim, revealing an interest they had been hiding.
when: the witness is offered something they want
why: the reaction shows what the words conceal

text: People may delay approaching a feared person or scene, so discovery can come hours after an event and stretch the timeline.
when: a discovery is delayed
why: fear of the person or scene

text: A suspect subjected to a pointed test may hold back anger and comply, and the restraint itself becomes evidence of how they respond to pressure.
when: A suspect is challenged in private.
why: Controlled reaction under suspicion reveals character as much as the test result.

text: Words heard during an emotional moment stay vivid in memory, making the witness feel their meaning is reliable even when the interpretation is wrong.
when: a witness recalls words spoken in a charged moment
why: emotional tone strengthens memory of the words but not of their meaning

text: Fear, tears and confusion make witnesses poor judges of what their words might damage, so their statements can harm or help a party unintentionally.
when: when a witness is distressed
why: Strong emotion impairs judgment about consequences.

text: A person who fears assassination may suspect even trusted employees, so a victim's fears can point suspicion toward insiders.
when: a victim expressed fear of being killed
why: fear extends to people close by

text: A strong fear or feeling is not evidence, but it is a useful cue to search the place it points at.
when: when a character feels a strong unexplained fear
why: Fear can point to a real hiding place even when it proves nothing.

text: A suspect who asks how much you know reveals their own fear; vague answers grow that uncertainty.
A suspect may pause before answering a question about a fact already stated, and the pause can signal concealment.
when: when asked to repeat or confirm an account already given
why: a false version must be recalled and defended, which causes delay

text: A person who fears detection may remove one piece of evidence and forget that an existing precaution already protected it.
when: A suspect removes an object from a scene after a crime.
why: Fear of one trace can override knowledge of other protections.

text: Servants or staff who fear blame may deny involvement, so their denial is weak evidence of innocence.
when: staff are questioned after an incident
why: Fear of consequences motivates denial regardless of guilt.

text: A witness who fears being blamed adds self-justifying asides and makes sudden topic changes, which colour what they say.
when: when a witness is under suspicion
why: Fear of blame shapes what the witness chooses to emphasise.

text: A witness who fears losing their job may be guarded and glance at a supervisor, which can shape what they admit.
when: when a witness is watched by an employer
why: Fear of losing a job affects admissions.

text: A sudden revelation of a secret provokes a reaction that shows whether the witness already knew it and whether others shared that knowledge.
when: A witness knows a sensitive fact and will not state it directly.
why: A strong reaction or a question about how it was learned betrays prior knowledge.

text: A person may use grief, tears, affection or a sudden accusation to steer an interview or to test the listener's reaction.
when: when an interview turns emotional
why: a display can serve a goal even when it looks sincere

text: A grieving person's accusation can shape suspicion even when it rests on emotional state rather than evidence.
when: when a bereaved relative accuses an investigator
why: Emotional certainty is persuasive to observers.

text: Fear and a wish to appear respectable make a witness's account hurried and incoherent, lowering how far it can be trusted.
when: when a witness is frightened or concerned for reputation
why: emotion and self-presentation colour what is reported

text: A known threat or grudge can shape the images a witness later recalls, so a dread can reappear as a detail of a supposed event.
when: the witness had an earlier fear of or dispute with someone
why: Prior fear primes the imagination.

text: A sudden change from warmth to a cold, fixed look can reveal the real mood beneath a performance.
When respected members of a community are jailed, every household feels exposed, and fear spreads well beyond the accused.
when: prominent members are arrested during a campaign
why: Anyone in the same community can plausibly be next.

text: Strong dread combined with light falling on a face can leave a viewer unable to decide whether the face matches what they expect.
when: Close examination under emotional stress.
why: Emotion and light both alter what is perceived at close range.

text: Fear slows a person's understanding of a sudden threat, so their reactions and comprehension lag behind events.
when: A sudden danger unfolds around the person.
why: Fright delays processing of what is happening.

text: An uncanny image seen from a distance draws attention and frames a place as threatening until later evidence explains it innocently.
when: a frightening detail appears before its cause is known
why: Players attend to threat cues and let them set the explanation.

text: Hurried or barely legible handwriting can indicate that the writer was frightened when writing.
when: messages written under threat
why: Stress disrupts careful writing

text: A frightened witness may invent supernatural or unlikely details to cover a real absence.
when: A witness under pressure offers fanciful explanations.
why: Fear pushes people toward inventions that deflect suspicion.

text: Fear and the sense that help is close shape choices, so a frightened character may avoid calling a guard who is only feet away.
when: tense scenes with an ally nearby

text: A witness who shuts their eyes in fright observes poorly, so a description given in fear is weaker evidence.
when: the witness was frightened during the event
why: fear impairs what is seen

text: Emotionally involved discoverers can hold a wrong idea about a victim's identity, and that idea can persist and resist correction.
A lie about one's whereabouts can come from fear rather than guilt, so a false statement does not prove culpability.
when: A suspect is caught in an inaccurate account
why: People lie to avoid suspicion for reasons unrelated to the crime

text: Fear can recast an unexplained extra figure as a supernatural presence, so belief shapes how an observed count is interpreted.
when: an unexplained figure appears in a tense situation
why: Emotional state pushes observers toward supernatural explanations for anomalies.

text: Jealousy, resentment or fear can bend how an investigator reads a clue, shaping their interpretation of another person's motive.
when: An investigator has a personal stake in the people involved.
why: Strong feelings shift attention and reasoning toward conclusions that match the feeling.

text: A character's own question about whether they would be silenced if discovered reveals inner fear and makes the threat feel personal.
when: A character is in danger of being discovered
why: Internal doubt shows the stakes from the inside.

text: People spread fear faster than facts, often assuming the worst, such as a dangerous weapon, before anything has been confirmed.
when: when a frightening event is reported second-hand
why: Alarm moves through rumour faster than verification.

text: A person who fears being seen avoids actions that expose them, so a choice that risks exposure suggests the person did not fear discovery.
when: Deciding whether an action was accidental or deliberate.
why: People weigh exposure risk when they act, so risky choices reveal intent.

text: Emotional drama draws attention away from a quiet object lying on the floor.
when: a tense or tearful scene is unfolding
why: Strong emotion captures attention and hides small details.

text: A fear of public shame can drive a character's money and relationship decisions as well as their social choices.
why: the same underlying fear shapes several parts of life

text: Fear can attach significance to ordinary things, making a guilty person treat even trivial objects as possible witnesses.
when: a person is afraid of being discovered
why: fear inflates the meaning of small details

text: Peripheral witnesses who believe they are under suspicion grow frightened and deny knowledge before real questions are asked, making their later answers less reliable.
when: A witness is peripheral and their status is unclear, or they expect to be blamed.
why: Fear and fatigue make people defensive, and prolonged waiting or heavy questioning increases anxiety.

text: A decision-maker afraid of error may stop weighing doubtful evidence and defer to an expert instead, letting the expert's view replace their own judgment.
when: when a judge doubts the case but fears being wrong
why: fear of error discourages a full, independent summing-up

text: In a fearful community, the same figure can appear in many people's dreams, so contagion reinforces testimony.
Frightened, overwhelmed people treat trifles as strong confirmation, which makes a weak corroboration standard effectively empty.
when: Under fear or pressure.
why: Heightened alarm lowers the bar for what counts as evidence.

text: After one member recoils, a group tends to draw near together, so the discovery becomes a shared first account.
An alarm that rings on every entry unsettles whoever is inside, so the sound itself adds tension to each arrival.
when: when an entry alert sounds in an occupied space
why: each ring announces an unexpected visitor

text: A witness under emotional strain may project meaning onto moving light and water, then report that meaning as something actually seen.
when: when a character is frightened or distressed
why: Mood shapes perception, and imagination fills in shapes

text: Some people faint or react strongly at harmless objects, so a fit triggered by a look or object does not by itself show that any harmful cause is present.
when: when a strong reaction follows a sight that seems to prove a cause
why: a phobic response can mimic a real effect

text: A persuasive, emotionally charged plea can hide evasion, so a moving account does not guarantee an honest one.
when: when a witness's account is persuasive but thin on checkable detail
why: Emotion engages sympathy and can stand in for verifiable content.

text: Weeping, visible fear or self-harm is not reliable evidence of innocence or guilt; check statements against physical facts and independent support.
when: a suspect shows distress during questioning
why: Shock or feigned emotion can cause it, so it establishes neither truth nor guilt.

text: A sudden shift from hostility to generosity, or from guarded to talkative or cooperative, calls for more caution; check the new account against facts.
why: Fear or a tactic can drive sudden candour rather than truth.

text: Read a suspect's nervousness as a possible sign of guilt, not as a settled fact, and test it against other evidence.
when: a suspect's emotional reaction is offered as evidence

text: Let an NPC's fear or injury change what they report, so players must check statements against the environment.
Mix true and false details in a frightened witness's account so the player must cross-check each claim.
when: designing a witness who is afraid
why: Fear degrades reliability, so the account needs external checking.

text: A witness's strong feelings such as horror or a sense of guilt are impressions, not observations; treat them as clues to the witness's state.
The person who gains materially is not always the culprit; someone protecting a loved one can have the strongest motive despite gaining nothing.
why: Emotional ties can outweigh material gain as a driver of action.

text: Add a slight mismatch in an NPC's reaction to a discovery, hinting that it was staged and rewarding attentive players.
Record subtle reactions to pointed questions, such as a faint smile, as signs worth noting rather than ignoring them.
when: a person is asked a pointed question about an event
why: Small involuntary expressions can reveal how a question landed.

text: Give an NPC a stated fear of an object in dialogue, then place that object in a later puzzle so players connect the two only at the payoff.
Strong judgements about a person's danger or capacity for violence are opinion and must be checked against facts.
Show a character's fear through physical cues, such as a racing heart as they approach danger, to build tension.
A dramatic, emotional speaker can still give specific, checkable facts such as dates, sums and events; separate those from self-justifying claims.
when: when a witness is both drunk and dramatic
why: verifiable details can coexist with motive-driven rhetoric

text: Track an NPC's emotional state as a flag between dialogues, so a sudden change in manner prompts the player to question them again.
when: Designing repeatable NPC conversations

text: Emotion that exceeds the stated purpose of a visit, such as terror beyond ordinary anxiety, can signal a concern the person is not voicing.
when: A visitor's stated reason does not match their emotional display.

text: A suspect may be moved more by fear of public exposure than by a formal penalty.
when: the suspect has a reputation to protect
why: reputation can matter more than legal consequences

text: Separate facts from repeated emotional narration, since lamentation can bury key facts and an account must be read against physical evidence.
when: a witness or report is heavy with emotion
why: Strong feeling repeats itself and can crowd out the concrete details that matter.

text: Fear and an instruction to stay still can fix attention on one spot, so ambiguous shapes such as a fold of cloth are perceived as a threatening figure.
when: A person is frightened and told to remain still while in an unfamiliar or dark space.
why: Focused attention plus fear makes ambiguous stimuli read as threats.

text: Fear of convicting an innocent person raises the proof threshold, so doubtful reviewers tend toward acquittal.
when: reviewers face an uncertain case
why: the cost of error makes them demand more

text: A scene of fear can freeze pursuers, giving the attacker time to escape.
when: an attack is staged amid fear
why: Fear paralyses pursuit.

text: After a hidden event, a witness's fear shifts to the practical problem of escape, with time pressure set by others' movements.
when: After a concealed witness has observed an event.
why: Practical urgency replaces fear and keeps tension.

text: A character who can only wait under a deadline feels intensified pressure, because the lack of control adds to the time threat.
when: when the character cannot act on the deadline
why: loss of control compounds the time threat

text: A witness's fear of consequences is the lever that draws out a concealed connection; visible panic signals that the witness is ready to talk.
when: A witness is caught hiding a connection that matters.
why: Fear makes the cost of silence feel greater than the cost of speaking.

text: Strong emotional shock changes what people reveal and how clearly they recall events, so reports taken during distress are less reliable.
when: when a witness is interviewed right after a frightening or distressing event
why: Intense feeling disrupts memory encoding and willingness to disclose.

text: Personal feelings such as grief, resentment or wounded feelings can give certainty the evidence does not support, reading a scene as betrayal and mistaking emotion for evidence.
when: a character has wounded feelings about the people involved
why: Emotional conviction substitutes for evidence.

text: Treating a witness's fear, hostility or strong reaction, including jealousy or love, as guilt is an error; innocent people react strongly to ordinary things.
why: Stress and emotion can mimic guilt regardless of wrongdoing.

text: Testimony under fear can be partial, tailored to please, or mix seen, heard and feared content; check it against independent evidence before trusting it.
why: Fear pushes incomplete disclosure, answers the listener wants, and distorted recall.

text: Emotional appeals, confessions or confrontations can replace checkable facts and crowd out fact-based questioning; return to verifiable details, not feeling.
when: a suspect pleads, confesses emotionally, or a questioning session turns into a quarrel
why: Emotion persuades without establishing what happened or when; the record is the stronger lever.

text: Ranking suspicions by emotional closeness or affection rather than strength of evidence distorts judgment; suspects shift with doubts, not only proof.
when: reviewing evidence about someone one has feelings about, or weighing several suspects
why: Personal feelings decide which items feel damning and which doubts feel urgent.

text: Personal feelings cloud judgement, and an emotionally involved investigator may doubt their own reasoning and lose speed.
why: Emotion distorts assessment of which explanations are trustworthy

text: An investigator who lets emotional appeals decide the matter can be exploited into accepting an unverified account.
why: Appeals move the listener without establishing facts.

text: Linked events that feel unsettling to see together can make the connection seem stronger than the evidence supports.
why: Emotional reaction raises perceived certainty independently of the evidence.

text: People tend to accept a theory that explains the emotional story while overlooking the physical facts it leaves out.
why: Emotionally satisfying explanations are easier to believe than dry physical evidence.

text: Emotional involvement can colour what a person relays, so reports from those close to a case need checking.
A witness's fear can be genuine while the cause or danger it is attached to is wrong, so verify that cause separately from the feeling.
when: a witness links an emotion to a specific person, event or danger
why: Strong feeling makes a guessed cause seem certain.

text: Eloquence, sincerity, steady gaze or facial features are not evidence; they can sway observers for a moment, so conclusions about character must not rest on them.
A witness's emotional state or protest, such as about a route, is not evidence of guilt or innocence, and a guilt reading can persist after the evidence has changed.
A confrontation that frightens a suspect may make them lie more carefully, so check the source of any information obtained.
when: Pressuring a suspect into a confession.
why: Fear can increase the care with which a suspect deceives.

text: Fear can make a witness's refusal look more or less cooperative than it really was, so read refusals in context.
Relief that comes too easily weakens the danger, so the threat loses its weight.
Eccentric habits can mask genuine concealment, and an observer may mistake one for the other.
Emotional outbursts and family remarks can mislead the listener about who is really concealing something.
An emotional tone can lead a listener to take a speaker's attitudes for facts, especially when the attitudes concern third parties.
Losing the central suspect can collapse the whole theory. Keep alternative explanations open to avoid being left with nothing.
A victim's short phrase expressing fear, given without detail, should not be read as an accusation.
