A fragment that flatters a listener's fears is believed more readily than one that does not, so the listener's prejudice shapes what he thinks he heard.
Suffering after a confession does not show the confession was accurate; it can reflect punishment for speaking rather than truth.
when: A confessor is punished or tormented after testifying
why: Harm to the confessor is a cost of speaking, not evidence of content

text: A person in fear may act in ways that look irrational to an observer, so reading their actions only through rational choice can mislead.
when: interpreting a frightened person's actions
why: Fear distorts judgment, so a purely rational reading misses the real motive.

text: Anxiety explains a character's behaviour but does not establish that they committed an act; motive alone is not proof of guilt.
Fear can make a tester dismiss results or distrust their own senses, so the test may be run badly and its findings misread.
when: Testing a sound while frightened.
why: Emotional arousal impairs careful observation and interpretation.

text: Do not mistake a witness's genuine distress for unreliability; emotion calls for patience, not dismissal of the account.
when: when a witness is emotional or agitated
why: Strong feeling is common in people who have witnessed or suffered something real.

text: 1) Approach slowly and pause often. 2) Before asking about events, reassure the witness you are a friend, offer water and a familiar presence, and tell her to take her time. 3) Let her continue her ordinary task. 4) Advance in small steps, from circumstances to helpers to family and friends.
when: Interviewing a frightened, injured, held or exhausted witness whose next answer matters.
why: Calm and silence build trust, and a comfortable witness talks more readily; shock makes early questions unreliable, and small steps avoid overwhelming her.

text: 1) Give a character a hidden fear. 2) Reveal it through overheard questions the character asks. 3) Use the fear as a quest hook.
Cross-check a frightened NPC's sighting of a monster or ghost against other witnesses, since it may be a disguised ally.
when: designing fear-driven testimony

text: Give suspects behavioural tells, such as an odd refusal or offer, that the solver must explain; a solution that ignores them should be flagged as weak.
when: when designing a mystery's suspects

text: Treat enthusiasm for a topic as weak evidence of cover, since people often simply care about what they are talking about.
Nervousness may hide knowledge of who was present, yet a frightened innocent witness can look guilty; evasion alone does not establish concealed knowledge.
when: a witness is anxious or evasive when questioned about a location
why: Fear of consequences can hide knowledge, and fear and guilt look alike in manner.

text: A frightened witness may lose a sequence, so ordered questioning yields less; yet reassurance, then ordered recall and specifics, yields checkable detail.
when: a witness is frightened or distracted; ordered questioning helps mainly after reassurance
why: Fear weakens sequencing, but lowered fear enables ordered recall.

text: Physical reactions and manner shifts like hesitation have many causes; treat them as leads to test against documents or further questioning, not as proof of guilt, lying or supernatural claims.
when: reading a witness's body language or manner
why: Emotion and agitation can arise from many causes besides guilt.

text: Physical tells in a character's manner, such as sweating or a shaking hand while recounting a story, hint at a hidden history the audience can later connect.
An attentive observer may sense that a polished, friendly surface is deliberately maintained rather than natural.
A change in manner when the questioner speaks can matter as much as the answer itself.
when: a witness is questioned directly
why: tone shifts can reveal discomfort or evasion

text: A listener can read withheld information from a speaker's face and manner, treating demeanor as evidence of concealment.
when: A speaker gives a shortened account
why: Nonverbal signs leak what the words omit

text: Listeners who hang on a witness's answer reveal what they fear, which can be as informative as the answer itself.
when: Observing family or associates during questioning
why: Anxious reactions expose the stakes people attach to the outcome

text: Physiognomy is the practice of judging a person's inner nature from appearance, including face, hands, hair, and movement.
A person under strain can show both careless and careful details in the same scene, so mixed traces do not automatically indicate one state.
when: when a scene contains traces pointing in opposite directions
why: agitation affects some habits while leaving others intact

text: An ordeal reads a physical outcome as moral judgment, yet the result says nothing about the act being judged.
A mismatch between friendly manner and watchful attention signals a hidden interest, but does not prove guilt on its own.
Low spirits together with mounting money pressure can point to a motive, though a single observed manner is weak evidence.
when: Motive must be inferred rather than proven.
why: Money trouble often shows up as a change in mood.

text: Enemies who check written messages and watch for pursuit often miss physical signs left in a room.
A sudden shift in mood shortly before an event is worth recording as a clue.
An involuntary physical reaction can reveal a staged performance more clearly than the words that accompany it.
when: when a witness's account sounds practised

text: Concrete environmental details such as light, fire and objects set a mood that makes a later shock land harder.
when: building the setting for a scare
why: a grounded setting heightens contrast

text: Frame hints as mood rather than fact, so the audience feels unease while the speaker stays uncommitted to any specific claim.
when: the audience needs unease before facts are available

text: Rapid shifts in an informant's mood suggest the report is shaped by their feelings rather than by the facts.
when: An informant swings between sympathy, anger and friendliness during a report.
why: Emotional volatility indicates that feelings are steering the account.

text: Choose each remark in an interview to produce a specific feeling in the listener, so the emotional beats steer the exchange.
when: Scripting an interview or dialogue scene with a strong emotional goal.
why: Deliberate emotional targets make the scene's direction clear.

text: When a reaction is far stronger than its stated cause, the stated cause is probably not the real one. Search for a stronger, hidden cause.
when: When an outburst seems out of proportion
why: Intensity points to a deeper motive

text: Mood or atmosphere, such as a funeral's, establishes no fact and cannot replace corroboration; it should support the evidence instead.
when: when writing tense scenes meant to drive a mystery
why: Players need concrete clues, not just tone.

text: Inferring motive from mood, such as a cold house, alone misleads, since one manner may have other causes; link the mood to a concrete act first.
when: building a motive from the mood of a place or household
why: Atmosphere is suggestive but not proof, so it needs a concrete link to an act before it supports a conclusion.

text: Eliminating a suspect by social standing, manners, size or strength risks error, as such traits prove no innocence; a timed record of presence at the right time is stronger.
when: when considering removing or narrowing a suspect
why: Physical guesses ignore whether the suspect could have been present at the right time.

text: A physical trait such as an injury can point at a suspect too early; it may be the answer or a red herring, so wait for other evidence.
Building suspicion on a single physical resemblance, such as a matching injury, invites a false accusation against whoever seems to fit.
Prolonged silence or stillness becomes tedious unless the tension source is varied.
when: extended tense sequences
why: Without variation, the audience's attention drifts.

text: Reading mood changes as lies can mislead, and an investigator's own view of the suspect can shape that reading, so the reading must be checked.
A receiver's current mood, rather than the visitor's actual purpose, can drive the first judgment of an unexpected arrival.
A narrator's emotional distress can distract from factual clues being planted in the same scene.
when: Writing a scene that is emotionally intense and contains plot information.
why: Strong emotion draws attention away from details the audience needs.

text: Check prints for missing digits, since a suspect with a missing finger can be excluded when the prints show that finger intact.
when: When marks show fingers and a suspect's injury is known.
why: A visible trait can rule a person in or out.

text: Do not treat a relaxed, candid mood as proof of truth, because a witness can be honest on one point and silent on another.
when: when assessing a cooperative witness
why: candor on one topic does not guarantee accuracy on others

text: After stating an accusation, watch the suspect's physical tells and treat them as further evidence, not as proof.
Show distress cues such as hesitation or crying, and open a new dialogue branch when the player presses the right point.
Stage an early, seemingly trivial encounter whose meaning becomes clear later, rewarding attentive audiences.
why: hindsight rewards attention

text: Conflict between allies adds pressure without adding plot facts, so it can sustain tension between discoveries.
Place a revealing, emotional line that the player only hears if they keep talking to an NPC, since unguarded moments tell more than refusals.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that hides information
why: Emotional slips leak information that a guarded refusal does not

text: Convey an NPC's reliability through emotional tone in dialogue, such as panic or bravado, rather than through a stated reliability value.
when: Scripting NPC reports whose weight should vary.
why: Tone signals credibility implicitly and keeps the report diegetic.

text: Let the accused's shame carry the scene, so pressure on the victim drives the drama until the reveal.
An emotional scene can move the witness toward belief in the suspect's innocence, which can defeat the planned pressure.
A pointed remark made before enough is known can alert the subject before the investigator can use the reaction.
Emotional confrontations can stall pacing; keep exchanges short and return to the facts.
when: when an accusation scene grows emotional
why: Long emotional beats delay resolution.

text: Track NPC emotional state to gate dialogue: open with ambient topics, unlock sensitive ones only after tells show readiness, so player care or refusal changes what is revealed.
when: Designing NPC or companion dialogue, especially with sensitive subjects.
why: Premature sensitive topics cause the NPC to shut down.

text: Change NPC dialogue with the player's discoveries, so asking the same question again yields a new answer.
Let NPCs respond to player actions with emotional displays, and make the player judge whether each display is genuine or aimed at a goal.
when: when designing NPC dialogue that reacts emotionally
why: it makes the player weigh NPC motives

text: An empty room shows only that the person is not there, not where they went; their location needs other evidence.
An empty container that was opened with a key suggests papers were removed, which can be checked against the dates of those papers.
when: A container is found empty after being opened without force.
why: Removed papers may contradict a claimed purchase or timeline if their dates fall later.

text: Empty pockets are evidence in themselves: they leave the victim unidentified and should be recorded as a finding.
Check which items are missing from a container; an emptied box opened on the night of a crime is a physical trace linking the object to the timeline.
Treat unexpected empty positions in a crowd as deliberate features to explain, not as details to ignore.
When a container is found empty, its maker, markings and history can carry the clue in place of its contents.
when: the container is found empty

text: Before searching a place a clue points to, confirm it is occupied; a location that has stood empty for weeks is likely a dead end.
when: when a clue points to a vacant building
why: searching a deserted site wastes effort

text: An empty container built up as a reward can carry more narrative weight than its treasure, because its absence becomes a question the plot must answer.
when: A sealed reward is promised and built up, so the audience over-values it.
why: Removing the expected prize removes the obstacle driving conduct; disappointment makes the player seek the reason for its absence.

text: A missing key item from a known place tells the player that someone has been there, so it works as a trigger.
An empty room or container can mislead searchers into thinking the search is finished while other rooms or leads remain.
when: Clearing a building room by room.
why: Searchers can mistake one clear room for a clear building.

text: Endorsement by respected authorities can lend a spreading belief credibility and remove remaining doubt, since people defer to authority when judging unfamiliar claims.
when: when respected figures publicly support a claim or a crowd still has reservations
why: people defer to the judgement of respected figures when judging unfamiliar charges

text: Endorsement, approval or praise reflects an authority's standing, not verified accuracy; judge the claim itself rather than treating endorsement as evidence.
when: when a reference text or source is trusted because of endorsements or praise
why: approval reflects status and authority rather than checked facts

text: Accepting a single reference without seeing the referee or the institution makes the whole judgment depend on one unverified source.
why: A single source can be wrong, biased, or unavailable.

text: Trace each endorsement to its source and ask what the endorser actually saw; a secondhand vouch may say nothing about the conduct in question.
when: A suspect's character is argued from third-party endorsements

text: In an episodic mystery collection, each case closes quickly, so the collection's pacing relies on the repetition of one story arc.
Set a fixed deadline for replies to inquiries and decide beforehand what a missing answer would mean.
when: Waiting for responses that will test a theory
why: A deadline turns open waiting into a test that can be passed or failed, and prevents rationalizing silence.

text: Separate a mystery's force from its director so the source can be a distinct, findable actor with its own history.
Delays such as travel, illness or waiting periods stretch the interval between news items and raise tension.
when: Pacing the release of information through in-world events
why: Each wait holds the next revelation back and gives the audience more time to anticipate it

text: When exits close step by step, each small refusal or delay tightens the situation, so the character's way out narrows as the hour grows late.
when: A night-long or timed scene that should grow more threatening

text: A cold or similar environment can keep a body undiscovered until the victim dies, so a staged activity that delays discovery can shift the apparent time of death.
when: A death depends on environmental conditions and the timing of discovery.
why: The environment finishes the killing while the staged activity keeps the body hidden.

text: Episodic mysteries can share one investigator while each case is self-contained, opening with a crime that looks impossible or motiveless and solved from physical clues.

A linked episode story opens with a theft that is announced, staged or impossible-looking, shown from the victim's side, with misdirection from a visible suspect or sealed scene and a solution that reverses who controls the situation.
when: designing a run of linked mystery episodes with a recurring thief protagonist
why: The repeated shape gives readers a predictable frame in which the surprise lies in who is really in control.

text: Over-explaining the outcome of a mystery's ending can flatten it; tying up every thread leaves the reader with nothing to think about.
when: Writing the closing section after a case is solved
why: Full explanation removes the reader's reason to keep reflecting on the case

text: Escalation without a planned payoff exhausts the audience, so the climax should be planned before the first repetition.
why: Rising tension needs a resolution or it wears out the player

text: Ruling out a route because it seems hard can hide the one that is merely tedious.
when: Eliminating options in a theft or breach analysis
why: Difficulty and effort are different, and a tedious route may still be viable

text: Use the final beat only when no unanswered questions remain, since an ending cannot resolve them.
Stopping a plan early frees the suspect to try again, while letting it proceed risks the victim's safety and timing errors.
when: deciding when to intervene against a known plan
why: early intervention preserves safety but leaves the threat active

text: A searcher who fails to find the target tends to destroy more of the room as the search goes on, so the wreckage records the growing panic.
when: a search repeatedly fails to find its target
why: frustration grows with each failed attempt

text: An interrogator whose answer disappoints tends to escalate pressure, such as tearing up a reply and threatening the captive, which signals desperation.
when: a captive's answer disappoints the interrogator

text: A threat the audience already expects still shocks when it arrives, so foreshadowing does not remove the impact of the event.
when: a horror event has been announced or foreshadowed in advance
why: dread about how the event will land persists after it is anticipated

text: State a specific prediction, such as when a key event will happen, to set a clear expectation that the next scene can pay off.
when: Building anticipation toward a scene that will confirm or defeat the prediction.
why: A concrete expectation gives the audience something to watch for.

text: A threat made publicly in anger is strong motive evidence, especially when the threatened act later occurs.
when: Building a case around a suspect's stated grudge

text: Announce an expected visit in front of several characters, so their knowledge of the meeting is fixed before the crime occurs.
when: A crime depends on who knew of a visitor and when

text: If someone announces in advance that they will reveal a particular culprit, treat the accusation as produced by the announcer rather than discovered.
when: When an accuser promises to name a specific person before any evidence is shown.
why: A stated plan to name a target signals the accusation was intended, not observed.

text: End an area on a half-seen threat so the player keeps moving toward it.
when: an area should lead onward
why: an unresolved threat pulls the player forward

text: Time a rising storm or other hazard to build as an investigation or boss approach nears, so the hazard acts as a visual tension meter.
Hazards such as rotten boards and unstable stairs test a visitor's nerve, and each step should add tension.
when: When designing a hazardous passage.

text: Infer intent from a chain of escalating demands rather than a single outburst.
when: When judging whether a grievance amounts to a motive
why: A documented series of pressures shows purpose more convincingly than one emotional moment.

text: Escalate hints from vague to specific across a story, so each step raises stakes before the explanation arrives.
when: Building anticipation before a mystery's answer.
why: Gradual escalation keeps the audience engaged without giving the answer early.

text: Announcing a final threat in advance builds suspense toward a later confrontation.
when: A boss or major threat is scheduled
why: Anticipation raises tension before the threat arrives.

text: Moving an inquiry to a higher body changes its authority, audience and stakes, so the transfer can shape the outcome more than the local events do.
when: a case moves from local officials to a higher body

text: When a local jury refuses to convict, accusers may move the case to a higher tribunal with broader reach.
when: a first venue fails to deliver the desired verdict
why: Venue choice can decide an outcome that the evidence alone would not.

text: Layering dangers of increasing severity, each followed by short relief, keeps tension climbing across an extended sequence without needing one big climax.
when: danger must build gradually across an extended sequence

text: When an investigator lacks decisive proof, announcing the suspicions to an interested party can force a guilty person to confess, because the disclosure pressures them.
when: Physical proof is absent, a deadline looms, and the suspects' loyalties, fears and self-interest can be judged.
why: Confession from an involved party is the only remaining source of the missing proof.

text: An unexpected incident that repeats an earlier threat's symptoms with a new victim raises stakes and drives the audience toward the answer.
why: Repetition signals that the threat is ongoing and growing.

text: Escalating warnings, each more direct than the last, raise stakes while leaving the target free to choose a response.
when: An antagonist warns a target before acting
why: Growing directness increases pressure without forcing the target's decision.

text: A planned action that never happened, such as a planned change to a will, can still supply motive if its outcome would have helped or hurt someone.
Remarks egged on by others escalate tension in a crowded scene, and the rising tension can be used to pace a reveal.
When an accuser's account conflicts with the accused's denial, pressing the accuser for a more specific charge escalates the conflict instead of resolving it.
Once accusers gain attention and public confidence, they have no safe way to retreat, so their motives shift and the affair escalates.
A claimed threat from a jailed person increases restraint: if spirits could roam from jail, heavier chains were ordered whenever one was claimed.
why: each claimed threat justified stronger measures

text: Worsening conditions such as bad air or heat act as a timer: the longer a trapped character stays, the weaker they become and the greater the danger.
when: A character is confined in a space with a rising hazard.

text: If gaps between escalating events are too long, tension sags or a wait with no incident frustrates; if events are too similar, they stop feeling new.
when: Pacing an escalating sequence of threats
why: Tension depends on both interval length and variation between steps

text: Promises the investigator cannot keep, including protection, undermine the case and end informant cooperation; a false promise leaves a grievance that can bring the witness back.
when: Negotiating with a suspect or informant, or offering assurance to an informant
why: A broken promise ends cooperation

text: Threats or warnings that are never followed up make the threat feel empty and waste audience trust, so every announced threat must be paid off.
when: a warning or threat is introduced
why: Empty threats reduce belief in later warnings

text: A promised reveal or announced solution that never arrives makes earlier delays read as padding and frustrates the audience.
why: The promised answer goes unsupported.

text: When escalation outruns the available clues, players lose the thread; each new event should connect to the previous one.
when: Designing a multi-step mystery with escalating events
why: Players need a link between steps to keep tracking the threat

text: A flood of retroactive meaning can make earlier scenes seem more sinister than they actually were.
An expected threat may never arrive, so a rumoured deadline can mislead a player as much as it creates tension.
When examiners announce an outcome, observers' own perceptions can be overridden by the announcement.
why: Authority pronouncement outweighs direct observation.

text: 1) Claim evidence and watch the reaction. 2) If the suspect keeps refusing, threaten a formal search. 3) Keep courteous pressure until the suspect hands over the object.
when: a suspect resists a bluff

text: 1) Begin with a small, ambiguous threat. 2) Place each new threat closer to the target. 3) Increase its severity with each step. 4) Space the steps with gaps for reflection and evidence gathering. 5) End with a clear deadline.
when: A threat must grow steadily and the audience needs time between escalations
why: Rising intimacy and severity build dread while the gaps let the player gather clues

text: 1) Shift the surface from chop to a directed current. 2) Make the water go still. 3) Raise a copper-colored cloud fast on the horizon. 4) Overcast the sky within two minutes.
when: building a learnable warning sequence
why: a fixed order lets players learn to read the warning

text: 1) Name the leverage. 2) Refuse a small payment. 3) Demand a humiliating concession. 4) Set a short deadline. Each step weakens the suspect's resistance.
when: a suspect is holding back a secret
why: Escalation wears down resistance until a confession comes.

text: Explicitly promise a later payoff to sustain expectation without revealing the answer, and deliver it at a known, reachable point.
when: Holding an answer back for later in a story.
why: A stated promise keeps the question open, but only delivery justifies it.

text: Have the NPC carry out a conditional threat when the player breaks the condition, because untested threats lose force on later encounters.
Stage a puzzle as escalating contingency behaviours, such as escape routes and disguise attempts, that the player can follow to the culprit.
Show a hazard openly before the player commits to the area, so it cannot be dismissed as an unfair trap.
when: a room or path has a dangerous feature
why: prior visibility makes the hazard a fair choice

text: Attach sound triggers or expected alarms to routine events, so the player can notice when a reaction that should happen does not.
when: Stealth or investigation levels.
why: A missing reaction is only noticed when the player has a clear expectation of it.

text: A glowing light in a dark area can act as a moving enemy's tell, rewarding players who stay still and read the signal.
Make the antagonist's counterattack credible, such as threats or a claim that the investigator is unreliable, so it becomes a second conflict.
Announcing suspicions can harm an innocent person and warn the guilty, who may hide evidence or flee; the method rests on a fallible prediction of character.
when: Using a disclosure as a last-resort pressure tactic.
why: The disclosure is public and cannot be withdrawn, and character predictions can be wrong.

text: A staged ambush can invert a suspect's identity rather than only add danger, but it reveals the hidden figure's role and may collapse the suspect list at once.
when: Choosing how a hidden-character encounter should advance the mystery.
why: Using an ambush for identity reversal adds information, while using it only for danger adds tension without narrowing suspects.

text: A subject who suspects being watched may leave by another exit or vehicle, so followers lose them.
when: the subject is being tailed
why: Secrecy avoids observation

text: Over ten years, thirty escape attempts from prison vans were recorded: twenty-five failed absurdly, four were stopped early, and one man got out and was recaptured within fifty steps.
when: Assessing the rarity of escape during transport.
why: Successful escape from transport is very rare.

text: Name each blocked direction in turn, such as foes ahead and behind, with a hazard to one side, to make the narrowing options plain.
when: when showing a fugitive's closing options
why: a clear count makes the shrinking options felt

text: A concealed object in a mundane place, such as a heap of paper or rubbish, is a clue in itself because its location suggests cleverness or intent.
when: An object is hidden in an ordinary setting.
why: The choice of hiding place reveals something about who hid it and why.

text: An irregular route, such as one used for exit and a different one for return, can indicate that someone else used the route earlier.
when: A person's movements do not match the normal pattern
why: Route irregularities often trace to another actor using the same path.

text: Repeated near-escapes that reverse at the threshold raise tension, and each failed attempt can make the confined space feel more oppressive.
Do not accept a claim that nobody came in or out until the watcher's blind spots have been closed.
when: When a witness says no one passed the checkpoint
why: The statement is only meaningful if the watcher could see every route

text: Treating 'no other way in' as settled ignores that an admitted visitor leaves every barrier intact, so elimination does not prove the entry route.
when: Concluding an intruder used the only open door in a sealed scene.
why: Admission by the occupant bypasses locks entirely.

text: An endpoint watch fails when no predictable event exists or when the target can act well before the date.
Assuming a culprit fled in the most natural direction can leave the real escape route unexamined.
A hidden observer on a route someone may use is at risk, since a sharp-eyed member's glance can nearly expose them.
when: Choosing a hiding place near traffic or sight lines.
why: Hiding places on frequent routes are often checked by people passing them.

text: 1) Trace the object's chain of custody. 2) Find a predictable date, deadline or expiry. 3) Watch the point where the object must be collected in person. 4) Identify who collects it, since that person is the real target.
1) Keep the target in sight from a distance. 2) When the target turns back, use cover such as a shop window or doorway. 3) Feign a small task. 4) Step aside until the target passes.
when: the target may look back or double back
why: cover and a feigned task avoid face-to-face contact

text: Make reaction tells point to more than one possible hider, so players weigh the evidence rather than reading a single guilty face.
End a peril segment on an open state, such as a character fainting, so the suspense carries into the next scene.
when: transitioning from a dangerous sequence to another scene
why: An unresolved end keeps the audience's attention on the open question.

text: Sudden flight can signal intent and justify acting immediately; without evidence of plans to leave, do not assume an escape motive.
when: a suspect flees
why: Flight reveals intent.

text: Letting a trapped culprit slip away keeps tension and avoids a contrived ending, but weakens the sense of closure.
when: Resolving a confrontation in a thriller after the main threat is caught.
why: A surviving threat keeps tension to the last beat, but a lingering escape weakens closure.

text: Leaving the killer's fate unconfirmed after escape keeps the ending open, at the cost of leaving the official resolution unsatisfying.
when: when ending a mystery where the culprit vanishes
why: An open fate reflects the limits of the investigation but withholds closure.

text: Essential circumstances are causally tied to how a mystery resolves; incidental circumstances merely accompany the event by chance and do not determine the outcome.
At case end, replay the clues the player collected and link each to the conclusion, so the reasoning can be checked.
Mark one essential clue as must-remember so it is not lost among many weaker leads.
Do not withhold facts the audience needs in order to follow the present action.
why: Hidden information needed now leaves the audience unable to follow events

text: End a level with a debrief that recaps each misleading clue and its real cause, leaving one optional thread players can follow.
Do not leave open any point the player needs to finish the case; only minor or background details should remain unsettled.
when: Deciding which details stay unresolved
why: Unresolved essentials block progress and frustrate players

text: Front-load the core questions in the opening so that mid-game clues can make them concrete.
when: a multi-stage investigation
why: later clues then have questions to resolve

text: Heirs from an earlier marriage may suspect a later spouse of gaining undue influence over the dying person and judge the resulting will unfair.
when: a will favors a later spouse over earlier children

text: Family traditions can keep the sentiment of an old grievance accurately while confusing the details of what happened.
when: A descendant repeats a story about an ancestor's enemy.
why: Sentiment is passed down more reliably than facts.

text: When a person leaves no will, inheritance usually follows fixed default rules, so the outcome can be worked out from the family position.
when: when a victim left no will

text: An estate with no eligible heir may pass to the state rather than to any private party.
Entailed title and land pass along a fixed line of succession, and the successor may also take the money unless the owner's will redirects it.
when: an estate is entailed
why: Entail limits the owner's control over who inherits.

text: An heir who has not yet made a will leaves the estate's future open, which is itself a question for motive.
when: an heir's estate plan is unknown
why: Without a will the eventual distribution is uncertain.

text: Examining estate and inheritance terms can reveal a motive, but the terms matter only once they are fitted into the wider picture.
when: Looking for a financial motive in a case.
why: A single fact gains meaning only when it is placed against the other evidence.

text: Inheritance disputes draw in relatives, creditors and parish bodies, not only the heirs.
Inheritance terms create economic motives: state each rule explicitly and check who gains a share from a death, with or without heirs.
when: a will or estate division determines who gains from an outcome
why: Outcomes become checkable when each rule is stated.

text: Infer a plot's motive from what it makes possible, not from its stated cover reason, especially when that reason seems odd.
when: A plot element seems to serve no purpose beyond its stated reason.

text: Map the heirs of an old estate and how much each received, to list people with a stake in a missing object and their possible motives.
when: A crime involves an inheritance or a hidden object of family value.
why: Each heir with a share has a reason to find or hide the object.

text: A target's indifference to a fact can indicate that they have nothing to hide about it.
when: a fact touches the target's own interests

text: Crimes are usually individual acts rather than coordinated group efforts, so look first for a personal motive.
when: choosing which suspect to investigate
why: a single actor's motive is more specific than a vague group assumption

text: A will that passes property to a person on the owner's death or long disappearance gives that person a motive to hurry the outcome, once they know of the will.
when: a beneficiary learns of an inheritance tied to death or absence
why: waiting costs them the gain, so they may act sooner

text: A warning that more harm is coming and cannot be stopped makes the threat feel inevitable and raises dread.
when: a story needs tension before a climax
why: Perceived inevitability increases unease

text: A contest over a dead person's estate can absorb a family member's attention and pull them away from their duties.
A descendant who keeps a family grudge alive can offer a quest hook, and the player can check the story against records.
Guilt over an unjust inheritance can carry forward to later heirs who keep the property, shaping how they act.
Track changing wills as items in an NPC's file, so players can compare versions and see who benefits.
when: Designing an inheritance or quest system where wills change.
why: Versioned records let players reconstruct the beneficiary history.

text: A motive stated by one witness may be incomplete. Ruling out a plausible motive early can be a mistake, since it may return as relevant.
A motive based on inheritance is valid only when the beneficiaries are confirmed and the facts match.
Family ties and connections show who had influence, but not that the influence was actually used.
1) Note the suspect's unusual behaviour. 2) Match it to a pattern from earlier cases. 3) Propose a motive that explains several odd facts. 4) Choose the next check that would test it.
when: no hard evidence yet

text: 1) Identify what silence costs the person. 2) Infer the likely hidden reason and any third party it involves. 3) Test that inference against other evidence before acting on it.

1) Reconstruct the person's movement from available traces. 2) Judge whether the sequence fits a calm or a panicked state. 3) Infer the fear or expectation behind it. 4) Test each inferred step against other evidence.
when: a motive or fear must be inferred to direct an investigation
why: Each inferred step is a hypothesis, not fact, until other evidence supports it.

text: 1) Collect facts about the hidden reason from separate locations and conversations. 2) Check the ally's behaviour against them. 3) Accept a motive only if the evidence supports it.
when: a withheld personal reason matters to the case

text: 1) List every bequest by category: fixed sums, life income, specific gifts, residue. 2) Note who receives each. 3) Set aside charitable gifts as low-interest for motive.
when: Reviewing a will or estate during an investigation
why: Categories show who gains and how much, so motives can be ranked

text: 1) List every life that stands between a sum of money and a suspect. 2) Trace each legal link, such as will, life interest or policy, to the suspect. 3) Confirm each link before concluding the motive.
when: a suspect's financial gain from a death must be established
why: Only lives still in the way give the suspect a direct interest, and a missing link leaves coincidences instead of a motive.

text: Present inferred motives as hypotheses marked as such, not as established fact, and leave unproven links visibly open.
Run an estate lawsuit alongside the main investigation, so its papers serve as a source of motive clues.
Design a character who inherits a feud without sharing its origin, so players can separate the person from the side they were born into.
when: when designing a character tied to a feud

text: Travel time and distance estimates from a witness's judgment are ranges, and a travel maximum is an assumption unless it has been measured.
when: when timelines depend on witnesses' impressions of journeys
why: Witnesses judge distance and duration from expectation, not from measurement.

text: Compute alibi checks from inspectable positions and timers, not hidden flags, and leave checkable traces such as footprints or timestamps, since chance incidents make unreliable systems.
when: Generating suspect-tracking and alibi logic
why: Traces let players test an accuser's claim of unseen means.

text: Treat rough time estimates and witness clocks as provisional; do not treat a time gap as settled until travel times and clocks are confirmed by independent accounts.
when: When an alibi depends on a witness's recorded time
why: Unverified clocks and travel estimates can make an impossible movement look possible or the reverse

text: Dividing a poison into equal portions lets whoever prepares it control the total dose taken.
Treat a time-of-death estimate as a range, not a moment; treating it as exact can wrongly exclude innocent people, and a wrong estimate changes the conclusion.
Narrow the candidates by matching a witness's time window and description against each operator's records.
An alibi anchored on an arrival time does not cover the earlier window, since the gap may lie before departure or after arrival.
when: when a suspect's alibi rests on a known arrival

text: An alibi whose witnesses appear only after the relevant window does not cover that window.
when: checking whether an alibi covers the crime period

text: Test witness times against official records, since a time written at the moment of an act can fix when it happened.
when: Checking a witness's stated timing against documentary evidence
why: Contemporaneous records are harder to fabricate than later recollection.

text: An alibi holds only within its time window, so a slightly off estimated hour can collapse it; include the estimate's margin when testing routes.
An alibi covers a time window, and the decisive gap is between the last point where the suspect is accounted for and the critical moment.
when: checking whether an alibi excludes a suspect
why: An alibi can be detailed for one period and still leave the critical moment unaccounted for.

text: If a crime's apparent time is moved, an alibi built on a fixed departure can make a suspect look far away at the stated hour.
when: a suspect's whereabouts depend on a schedule
why: a fixed transport time is checkable, so a false crime time makes the alibi look solid

text: Model each character's alibi as a time window testable against shared anchors, such as a shared game clock NPC accounts reference; create windows the player must reconcile.
Estimated intervals are imprecise, and interested parties may shorten or stretch them, so timelines built from recollection can mislead.
when: Times come from witness estimates rather than fixed clocks
why: Stress degrades time memory and self-interest biases it

text: An alibi placing a suspect at known public venues proves little about the minutes that matter.
when: when a suspect's alibi relies on visible public locations
why: being seen in public does not cover the critical interval

text: A matching time does not prove presence, since a single sighting can be mistaken.
Phrases such as in a week are estimates, so treating them as exact dates creates false precision in a timeline.

1) List each suspect's timestamped movements in time order. 2) Match every interval to a landmark or event. 3) Mark windows no one can vouch for, flagging those before the key event. 4) Keep any window long enough for the act, even a short one.
when: Testing alibis against a crime, or when a suspect's whereabouts are described only loosely
why: A quick act needs only a short unobserved interval

text: 1) Mark fixed times such as departures and arrivals. 2) Add reliable travel times. 3) Find the gap a suspect could have used. 4) Check whether any decoy's movement fits that gap.
when: when a suspect's alibi covers a single known window and travel times are reliable

text: 1) List the moments when the suspect's location is already known. 2) Use a schedule to find the earliest departure and latest return that allow presence at both places. 3) Focus checks on that window.
when: the main question is whether the suspect could physically have been somewhere and schedules exist
why: Only the window decides whether the alibi holds.

text: 1) Measure the spacing and height of handprints on a surface. 2) Compare the reach with a known person's reach. 3) Allow for the posture the person used.
when: When marks show where a person's hands rested and a suspect's reach is known.
why: Reach from marks gives an approximate size estimate.

text: 1) Note the height of the object the person reached. 2) Note the posture used, such as standing on tiptoe and which surfaces were gripped. 3) Apply standard body proportions to estimate height from that reach.
when: a visitor left no direct record but the scene shows reach-dependent placement

text: 1) Note the origin of the postmark. 2) Record the dates of the message and the event. 3) Subtract the mail transit time from the total gap to estimate the sender's extra travel time. 4) Infer the vessel type from that time.
when: the sender's location and speed are unknown and only the postmark is available
why: the gap measures travel beyond the mail

text: 1) Perform the same action yourself. 2) Judge how much strength and practice it demands. 3) Compare that requirement with each suspect's physical capacity.
when: A physical attack must be matched against possible suspects.
why: A suspect who looks frail may still have the strength the attack required.

text: 1) Ask for departure and arrival times. 2) Compare each gap with the expected travel time. 3) For each gap, ask what was done and who could confirm it. 4) Log each unverifiable claim as a task to check independently.
why: Each interval is a separate claim that needs its own support.

text: 1) Fix the time from a verified timer 2) Look up the external schedule 3) Identify which scheduled event occurred at that minute and location.
when: an in-world timestamp must be linked to real-world events
why: schedules can explain what happened at that moment

text: Any alibi must cover the whole relevant window from when the suspect left onward, with a witness for every stretch; any unwitnessed gap lets the suspect slip away.
when: when verifying a suspect's alibi
why: A gap anywhere in the window lets the suspect slip away unseen; an unwitnessed interval is a gap an alibi cannot close.

text: Require the player to confirm a suspect's whereabouts through a separate source, such as a guard log, servant or timed door, not dialogue alone.
Build alibi clues such as a location log, a guard's shift record or a door timestamp that makes a claimed sighting impossible.
when: when designing an investigation

text: Before accepting an alibi, check whether its window is long enough for the act and whether witnesses can confirm it.
Verify alibis quietly so suspects do not learn what is being checked.
why: knowing the check lets suspects adjust their stories

text: Set the standard of proof so that letting several guilty parties escape is preferable to condemning one innocent person on indirect evidence.
Let each NPC's alibi be checked by a separate source that is individually true, while one hidden link, such as a mismatched identity, breaks the whole story.
why: Players must test links, not just individual facts

text: Give suspect NPCs a travel record, such as a ferry log or fare receipt, that lets the player verify their alibi.
Show scheduled meetings across a day in an in-game case log so the player can check alibis against the clock.
Store each suspect's claimed time intervals with the locations and NPCs who could verify them; if a verifier is removed, another route to that fact must remain.
when: designing a solvable alibi system
why: Removing a verifier must not make the puzzle unsolvable.

text: Give each suspect an anchor-event timeline, and make one alibi depend on an NPC reachable only through a clue such as a hotel or train record.
why: The player must follow the clue to verify the alibi.

text: Institutions may hide identities by recording people only by location or role rather than by name, which limits what staff can later reveal.
when: when an institution is a source of records about visitors
why: Routine practices deliberately or habitually obscure identity.

text: Legal proof, which must persuade a court and the public, is distinct from a privately held conviction, which can be firm without evidence to support it.
when: Deciding whether a conclusion can be acted on publicly.
why: A conviction felt strongly is not admissible support for an accusation.

text: Revealing a sympathetic character as the true instigator can invert the audience's earlier sympathy.
Granting mercy after a confession tends to buy gratitude and silence rather than the truth.
when: When a confession is followed by a lenient outcome.
why: The confessor's incentive shifts from accuracy to keeping the benefit.

text: Raise dread by making the danger seem intelligent and aware of the characters watching it.
when: Designing an antagonist or hidden threat.
why: A watching, thinking enemy feels more menacing than a mindless one.

text: Individual deaths or events may each have ordinary explanations, yet the record as a whole can make those explanations less convincing.
when: Several incidents share a condition and each has a separate natural cause
why: A common pattern across many cases is harder to attribute to chance

text: Close a solved mystery with mercy or restitution where it fits, so the solution changes the situation rather than only ending a fight.
when: choosing an ending for a solved mystery
why: Restitution gives the solution consequences beyond punishment.

text: An investigation can close through an institutional reversal, such as an authority withdrawing its charges, without any single culprit being unmasked.
when: A mass accusation is wrong and no clear culprit is found.
why: The authority's withdrawal ends the case even though the underlying mysteries stay unexplained.

text: A cluster of accusations can collapse together when an authority reverses, so the acquittal of many at once makes earlier false confidence visible.
when: A case has accused many people on the same testimony.
why: A group reversal exposes the shared weakness behind the earlier accusations.

text: Treating a formal legal finding as established fact misleads investigators, since a court may declare someone dead who is alive; rulings reflect admitted evidence, not necessarily reality.
when: When interpreting an official ruling about a person or event.
why: Legal records decide on admitted evidence, not necessarily on what is physically true.

text: A character whose indifference is too complete makes later sharp deduction feel unearned.
why: Readers cannot believe a sudden turn to acuity without earlier signs of capacity.

text: Ending by leaving the official inquiry to others gives moral closure but leaves the legal outcome unresolved.
when: choosing how a mystery ends
why: The investigator's judgement is settled while the formal verdict stays open.

text: Test a frightening or confidently told account against independent checks before accepting it; vivid, emotional detail can make a sinister reading seem proven.
why: A sinister reading may rest on a wrong premise, and emotionally loaded accounts lead to false threat assessment.

text: Prove the culprit with the stolen item and the trace of its movement; without physical proof an evidence chain is only testimony that can be rationalised away.
why: Physical proof is harder to dispute than the word of others.

text: Accusers find inspectable objects harder to dismiss than verbal assurances, so an accused person who shows the means of an outcome can rebut a hidden-cause charge.
when: when an accusation rests on a cause no one can see
why: objects can be examined by accusers, unlike claims about hidden causes

text: A suspect's excuse relayed by a third party, with no reason given for it, can be mistaken for evidence.
when: A third party repeats a suspect's explanation.
why: Stated explanations sound credible without support.

text: Evidence only one person can observe, such as a vision, is hard to check and tends to be weighed by whether it can secure a conviction.
why: No one else can test the claim against the world.

text: The prosecution, not the accused, must prove guilt, so an accused can insist that the burden stays with the prosecution.
The arrangement test is weaker when experts dispute the physical evidence itself.
Weigh a witness's inferences, including beliefs from out of earshot or sight, below direct observations, especially where hedges such as I think or I can't tell mark them.
when: when testimony mixes seen events with reasoning, or the witness was out of earshot or sight
why: Inferences are less reliable than directly perceived events; secondhand knowledge is inference.

text: Visible evidence endorsed by experienced staff tends to outweigh a theory built on subtle inference from one remark.
Witnesses rarely give major revelations, but one faint clue can matter, so collect even weak leads.
An inference drawn from a purchase needs an independent check before it is treated as proof.
Build a conclusion about a hidden action from several small facts together, such as an adversary's sudden change, rather than from one observation.
when: an adversary's behaviour changes suddenly and the reason is hidden

text: Give a sympathetic NPC a visible injury that contradicts their cover story, so a player who looks closely can catch the discrepancy.
when: Designing character clues.

text: A single small mismatch is weak evidence; it gains weight only when combined with an independent fact that could explain it.
Keep an inferred reading of a witness's evasion separate from what the witness has actually stated.
why: evasion suggests but does not prove

text: Physical evidence that fits a gap, such as cut pages matching pasted words, can outweigh moral argument or testimony.
when: testimony conflicts with a physical object

text: A tentative match from partial traces is worth using to direct the next inquiry, provided it is not treated as confirmed identity.
when: only partial or low-quality traces exist
why: A tentative lead focuses effort without overstating the evidence

text: Narrow means by asking who could obtain the specific substance or tool without difficulty, such as a prescriber or a person with ready access.
when: The method requires a specific substance or tool
why: Limiting access to the method narrows the suspect pool

text: The weapon or method of a killing can indicate how much forethought the killer had; a brutal improvised method suggests an unplanned act, while a prepared weapon suggests planning.
when: The weapon or lack of one is known.
why: Prepared weapons imply planning, while improvised violence suggests a sudden impulse.

text: Resolve a reversal by letting documents carry the proof rather than staging a confession scene, so the player assembles the chain of evidence.
why: Assembled evidence feels earned and avoids a single convenient admission.

text: Witnesses often present an inference from an indirect cue, such as loudness, marks or earlier statements, as if they observed the act.
when: when a witness names or describes someone or an event they did not clearly see or hear
why: Witnesses often do not distinguish their conclusions from their perceptions; indirect cues mislead when treated as observation.

text: An observer who forms a theory early, or delivers it confidently, may report the conclusion as something actually seen.
when: when an observer forms a theory before examining the evidence, or delivers an inference confidently
why: Expectation and confident delivery override raw input when reporting.

text: Accusations are not proof of guilt: they follow proximity and rivalry, and many accusers without added verification establish nothing.
when: when judging whether accused people are guilty
why: Accusations follow proximity and rivalry as much as conduct; volume adds no proof.

text: A well-argued supposition, or treating an accusation as a game, can pass for proven fact; label hypotheses clearly so argument polish is not mistaken for evidence.
when: a hypothesis is presented with a strong, detailed case
why: Coherence of reasoning is easily confused with proof; persuasive performance is not demonstrated fact.

text: An untestable claim is not evidence merely because it cannot be disproved, nor proof of a lie; demanding doubters disprove it shifts the burden; physical checks need a verifiable trace.
when: only someone's word is available about events that left no trace
why: Absence of a check leaves the claim unresolved, not false.

text: A vivid story that fills evidence gaps, or a lead made significant only by vivid or repeated telling, can be mistaken for proof.
when: when reconstructing an unseen person or event from a few traces, or when a lead is vivid or repeated
why: Narrative detail and repetition feel convincing even when the supporting traces are few or the lead is untrue.

text: A partly visible or poorly reproduced detail, such as a cut-off inscription, supports an inference rather than a fact and should be weighed, not treated as proof.
why: A poor reproduction can hide the features needed for identification.

text: A perfect match does not prove identity: a forged trace may be copied from the suspect, or one trace copied from the other.
when: when a trace seems to match exactly
why: A perfect match can equally mean one trace was copied from the other.

text: Treating an observer's inference from a signal, such as a light or moving shadow, as a direct sighting of the event itself.
why: A signal suggests an event but does not record it.

text: Meaning inferred from partly understood speech, such as one repeated word, is provisional and can mislead.
when: Speech heard in a language only partly followed

text: Several conclusions may rest only on inference, such as a death by fright or a creature heard but not seen, and they remain unproven without direct evidence.
when: when a case depends on unseen causes or unobserved actors

text: A poorly linked cue reveals nothing, so cues must be chosen for a clear connection to the matter being tested.
when: Selecting cues for recall tests
why: Without a meaningful link, the subject has no reason to react

text: Treating an inference as a fact inside a list carries the error forward into every later step that depends on it.
Linking a sudden new document to a quarrel is an inference, not proof, even when motive and timing line up.
An anomaly can have an innocent cause not yet discovered, so it must not be read as proof of guilt.
when: A physical sign is out of pattern
why: Unexplained is not the same as culpable

text: A shared meal is weak evidence of intimacy on its own; stronger proof comes from records of private use.
An accusation made in anger does not count as evidence, and should not stand in for proof of what happened.
when: A claim about a weapon or a poisoning is made emotionally without support

text: When authorities assume witnesses are honest, the burden shifts to the accused to explain the witnesses' behavior.
A procedure can be bent to exclude someone without any explicit vote against them.
when: reviewing how a body made a decision

text: Observations that are not truly independent of one another add little confirmation, so the chain should be checked for overlap.
when: Several clues are presented as confirmation of one conclusion.
why: Overlapping evidence looks like more support than it actually provides.

text: Narrowing suspects by a shared trait, such as formal dress, does not identify the culprit and may still leave many candidates.

1) Establish what was bought and from where. 2) Infer the item's purpose from its type and quantity. 3) Check whether the time available could produce it. 4) Link the purchase to a missing or altered item. 5) Note what remains unexplained.
when: when a purchase or supply record may match a missing or altered item

text: 1) List each separate fact. 2) For each fact, remove the candidates it rules out. 3) Check that the remaining candidate agrees with every fact.
when: when no single clue is conclusive
why: each independent fact narrows the candidates, so the conclusion rests on several

text: 1) Build the accusation from motive, opportunity and means. 2) Question the suspect about a specific physical detail of the scene. 3) Note whether the suspect reveals knowledge that was not public.
when: After evidence has narrowed the field of suspects

text: 1) Identify the constraints on the people involved, such as secrecy, poverty, tenancy and timing. 2) Consider what a secret or hurried act would require. 3) Check opportunity and legal title. 4) Combine the constraints to narrow the options. 5) State confidence, and raise it only when independent evidence agrees.
when: No witness or document records an act, but motive and means can be constrained
why: Constraints can point to the most probable outcome when direct records are absent

text: 1) Identify the expected sound or event. 2) Check the listener's distance, hearing and sleep habits. 3) Only then weigh its absence as evidence. 4) Confirm the inferred route with physical traces.
when: When drawing a conclusion from an absent sound, sight or movement.
why: Unverified silence can support a false route.

text: Separate inference from proof: a converging-clue conclusion is plain inference, not settled, until a witness, document or decisive source confirms the link.
Label a conclusion drawn from circumstance or timeline as inference built on the evidence, not proof, until confirmed.
Check an inference from a physical sign against a second independent sign or direct question; do not rest it on one observation or tone alone.
when: A sign could be explained by more than one cause, or an inference rests on a single observation or tone.
why: A single sign often has several plausible causes, and one can mislead.

text: Do not dismiss inconvenient evidence, even a small fact; test each explanation against the facts it cannot explain, since a small fact may matter later.
when: several explanations fit the first observation
why: Choosing between explanations depends on what each fails to explain.

text: Treat a motive inferred from an unexpected choice, or an intention known only from an uncorroborated remark, as speculation until a separate record confirms it.
why: An inference is only as strong as the facts known about the actor; no one else can confirm the remark.

text: Explain a conclusion step by step with the evidence shown, so the audience can verify it; an unexplained accusation or twist feels arbitrary.
when: when an expert presents a conclusion from a physical object, or when delivering a solution to a suspect or audience
why: Visible reasoning builds trust and makes the twist feel earned without requiring acceptance of the expert's word alone.

text: Let a rumor-based clue be real but weak, with a physical check such as a test or trace that can confirm or refute it.
when: Designing a clue that rests on rumor
why: A checkable physical test lets players resolve a weak clue rather than guess

text: Let an object's meaning depend on a second clue, so players must check their reading against other evidence.
Present a circumstantial inference as an inference, not as proof, and be ready to show the link when it is challenged.
when: When communicating a conclusion drawn from indirect evidence.
why: Overstated certainty invites rejection when an alternative appears.

text: Do not accept a conclusion that outruns the visible signs; a chain of inference that goes beyond its evidence should be questioned.
Draw conclusions only as far as the evidence supports, and do not theorize beyond the data.
when: deducing from physical traces
why: unsupported leaps make reasoning wrong

text: Keep gaps in a log visibly empty so players must infer rather than receive false certainty.
when: When designing timeline clues

text: Show players a visible list of open questions and the clues each competing theory fails to explain.
when: Designing a mystery that players must solve by reasoning.
why: A visible gap list directs players toward what remains unresolved.

text: Design confrontation options so that an accusation's reaction exposes hidden knowledge, and reward the player for it.
when: When designing confrontation or dialogue mechanics in a game.
why: Reactions that reveal knowledge let players advance by reasoning rather than guessing.

text: Do not accuse anyone on a name alone; treat the inference as a hypothesis until other evidence supports it.
Ask a witness how they know a claim, since an impression can be thin support for a conclusion.
when: A witness states an inference about another person's state of mind.
why: A conclusion resting on impression rather than observation is weakly supported.

text: Hold paper to the light to check for a watermark; a matching watermark links two notes to the same paper stock.
when: when linking an unsigned document to a sender or to other documents

text: Treat an inference drawn from a trace as a hypothesis and check it against other evidence before relying on it.
why: Cluttered scenes produce false traces.

text: Present a conclusion about intent as an inference, and keep it open to revision if the missing item later turns up.
when: Concluding from an absence
why: Inference from absence is weaker than direct proof

text: A warrant listing several sentences cannot be dated earlier than the last of those sentences; the latest referenced event sets the earliest possible date.
Keep observed facts separate from inferences, so a wrong inference can be found and dropped without losing the evidence.
why: mixing them hides which conclusions are weak

text: Keep a deduction's conclusion to what the facts warrant, stating only the general category they support rather than a specific name.
when: A clue points to a set of possible causes.
why: Narrowing to a category is justified; naming one member needs more independent evidence.

text: An outside examiner should work only within the permissions officials grant, and stay inside a partial grant rather than exceeding it.
when: when an outsider must work alongside officials who control access
why: officials' authority limits what can be examined or done

text: A method of crime narrows the likely motives but is not proof of emotion or intent.
Accept a hidden code only if it holds across every item, not from one coincidental match.
A longer chain of inferences reveals more about a person but adds doubt at each step, so keep each link checkable.
when: an object supports several inference steps
why: each added step can be wrong, weakening the whole conclusion

text: Responding visibly to a suspected leak alerts the culprit and may forfeit the advantage, while changing a carefully made plan is costly and some changes may be impossible.
when: choosing between responses to a leak

text: A reasoned reversal is a mystery where deduction from a physical detail overturns the lead suspect, rather than a new witness or confession alone.
Set up a plausible early impression, then overturn it with a hidden clue players can verify independently; reward those who find it over those picking the expected answer.
when: designing clue sequences or pacing a mystery's early scenes
why: Unsettled expectations keep attention engaged.

text: A witness who saw only the end of a chain can confirm the outcome but cannot explain how the object reached that point.
when: A witness joins the story late or from a distance.
why: Without the earlier events, the witness has no basis for the earlier links.

text: A baseline built from partial records, such as one person's memory, can produce false gaps that do not reflect real absence.
when: Records are incomplete or come from a single source
why: Missing records look like missing objects

text: If a verification method is later ruled unlawful or unusable, every result it produced loses standing, even results that were presented as proof at the time.
when: a trial or check whose method is later judged invalid
why: its outcomes depended on the method's legitimacy

text: Frame a visible suspect with overwhelming evidence and one contradicting clue; reinterpreting a dismissed clue can clear the suspect and redirect the case.
when: designing mystery plots

text: A general rule is overturned only by a competing general rule, not by a few counterexamples.
Reject an explanation whose key act would simply be overridden by a later event that could happen, since that act cannot explain the puzzle.
when: an explanation relies on an action that a later action would reverse
why: a reversed action does not account for the observed result

text: Moving or searching a body or objects before investigators secure the scene, even by the first entrant, destroys or contaminates evidence and makes later accounts describe an altered scene.
when: a scene is accessed before investigators secure it
why: disturbance changes the original configuration

text: Physical evidence found on ground a suspect crossed shortly before is weak proof against that suspect, since their presence may have moved or deposited it.
A spilled substance on a floor leaves a footprint outline that can be followed, so the contaminant works as a tracking marker across a space.
when: when a character or route must be traced through an area
why: the spill transfers to footsteps and marks the path

text: A crime-scene system can log who entered each room and what each person touched, so evidence contamination can be modeled.
Blood added to a weapon after handling cannot show whether it was present before the struggle, so the question may become permanently unanswerable.
when: a weapon was handled or injured someone after the event
why: the timeline of traces is lost

text: A second event that removes or moves key evidence overnight signals that someone active in the setting is managing the scene.
when: Plotting a mystery where the culprit must hide evidence.
why: The removal itself is a clue about who is acting and shifts suspicion toward the actor.

text: Once a theory has been revealed to a witness, that witness can no longer serve as an independent check on the theory.
why: Their later account may echo what they were told.

text: If the central witness is heard first, peripheral witnesses may be shaped by what has already been said.
Testing an object can change its state, so record what is found before any further handling.

1) When transcriptions conflict or are hard to read, re-examine the originals. 2) Check dates, gaps and page placement against the original, not a certified copy. 3) Treat earlier compilations as secondary until checked against them.
when: when a copy, summary or earlier transcription of court or archive papers is offered as proof
why: Mismatches in placement can reveal forgery that a copy hides; transcription errors propagate through later accounts.

text: Tag each claim by source and confidence (direct observation, opinion, first-hand, repeated, gossip, third-party hearsay, suspect's report) so players can trace it and weigh each class differently.
when: when designing witness dialogue or evaluating a chain of testimony
why: Visible sources let the player judge how reliable each claim is; secondhand claims depend on their informant.

text: Give each in-world document visible provenance (author or holder, date, bias, whether its container is present) so players can judge reliability and cross-check accounts of the same event.
when: When authoring in-game documents as clues or recording one event from different sides.
why: Visible provenance lets players assess a document's reliability instead of guessing.

text: Reading a source only as far as suits the speaker, or cutting the clause that carries its warning, changes the conclusion drawn from it.
Memory of an ordinary day fades quickly when nothing distinguished it from others, so witnesses are often unsure of the specific day.
when: when a witness is asked about a routine day
why: Without a distinguishing event, days blend together in memory.

text: A document cannot predate the machine used to produce it, so its equipment can contradict a date the document claims.
when: checking a document's claimed date
why: A machine's manufacture date sets the earliest possible date for its output

text: Yellowed edges and an old erasure suggest a sheet was kept for years, and an erasure can preserve faint earlier writing that is still readable.
Parish membership and rate lists follow residence on land, recording legal membership rather than friendship or private loyalty.
Church and baptismal records establish a person's standing and family links.
A sworn statement that is dated, taken before a court and closed by a named clerk can have its origin and authority checked.
when: when judging how much weight a written account deserves
why: a named recorder and date make the record traceable

text: Names in old court records may contain clerical errors that complicate later reconstruction of who was accused.
when: reconstructing cases from historical records
why: Scribes can misrecord names.

text: A prosecution case built on one trace is prima facie, meaning it is an apparent case that still needs testing. It is not a conviction.
Mirror placement affects both what can be seen and where light reflects, so mirror positions must be recorded room by room.
Treat a clue confirming a direction, or a reproduced match, as a lead or plausibility, not proof; probable clues may be accidental, so be wary if the holder is evasive.
when: when a reconstruction matches the original mark

text: Give each evidence item a log in the player's record of who examined or handed it over, when, and what was found, with a signature or stamp at each handover.
when: Designing evidence tracking in a game
why: A structured, timestamped log lets players compare findings and supports later checks.

text: Before treating a piece of evidence as proof, check who produced it and which part of it actually carries the claim.
when: a note, signature or object seems to prove guilt directly
why: strong-looking evidence can carry little information when it rests on an unexamined assumption

text: Test each suspect against several independent observations. One matching detail may be chance, but a set of matching details is strong evidence.
when: a hidden agent has left traces across different sources
why: Coincidence can explain a single match, but not many independent matches

text: Tag each clue with its real origin, so a knife or note can belong to another character and let players reject a false link.
when: authoring clues in a mystery
why: clear origin enables correct rejection of false links

text: Expensive, stiff paper suggests a writer of means, so the medium itself can narrow the field of possible writers.
Record who gave each personal item, since a gift traces back to a relationship that can reveal a connection and a possible motive.
Ask whether an item was worn openly or hidden under clothing, because visibility limits who could have seen it and recognized the wearer.
when: testing who could have known the wearer from an item

text: A damaged or partial document, or one carried by someone, can be read as significant or innocent; keep both readings open until other evidence settles it.
Plant a strong-looking clue that points at the wrong character, and make it resolvable by a second check the player can perform.
when: Designing misdirection in a mystery
why: A resolvable red herring is fair and rewards careful play

text: Checking which hand an item is made for can narrow suspects by a physical trait such as handedness.
when: a worn or held item fits only one hand

text: Judge whether a found item was delivered deliberately, and who presents it, before accepting it at face value.
when: An object is handed over or turns up at a convenient moment.
why: A planted object can steer an inquiry toward a chosen suspect.

text: Record who knew an object existed; wide knowledge of an item widens the set of people who could have moved it.
when: an item has disappeared
why: Knowledge of an object is not limited to its owner.

text: When a document's key term carries an argument, compare its rendering with the original wording before accepting it.
when: the term may have been chosen to suit a patron or theory
why: renderings can be shaped to fit a theory

text: A writer who revisits a document at different moments may cite different sections, so date each citation before reading it as the writer's settled view.
when: The same author quotes a document at more than one time
why: Stakes and opinion shift, changing what is cited

text: Do not treat a suspect's manner alone as evidence of guilt; check the account against documented records.
Items passed between NPCs can carry a custody history, so a puzzle can reveal whether a clue was altered along the way.
Place discarded disguise items as findable clues in a drain, river or bin, so disposal leaves a trail rather than a clean escape.
A matching item in one location can link two places, letting a found item connect the player to a shop or room.
Check a trivial detail against physical inventories: a missing or matching item can link a gossip thread to a physical clue.
when: when a peripheral fact may connect to an object

text: Rank clues by reliability and spend effort on the strongest first; keep weak clues as long shots that matter mainly alongside a stronger one.
when: Multiple clues differ in strength and effort is limited.
why: Weak clues rarely succeed alone but can confirm stronger leads.

text: Let players sample a clue with a tool, seal it, and receive lab results after a delay, making evidence handling a playable step.
Give each scene object a plausible role, such as a ladder, a removed plank or a cut, so the player forms and tests a hypothesis.
when: designing a crime scene
why: plausible roles let players reason about how the act was done

text: An object's position shows where a person had to stand to use it, so players can infer where someone was.
when: A functional object such as a bell rope or lever is placed in a room
why: Use requires physical presence at a specific spot

text: A permanent change to a character or item, like a scar or breakage, can serve as a fixed check that it could not have been somewhere else.
when: when designing identity or location checks

text: Check any object out of its usual alignment, since it may hide something beneath it.
Movable props such as lamps or fires make a room feel alive and can set up later reveals.
when: designing a room for atmosphere and later payoff
why: interactable objects invite attention

text: When tracing many items, divide them into categories, assign each category to a different searcher, and let item quality suggest where to search.
when: when tracing a large set of items

text: Form a provisional interpretation of a clue quickly, then revise it as later evidence arrives.
when: Early evidence is ambiguous
why: Fast provisional readings let the player act and later correct wrong guesses.

text: Item size or wear can encode ownership, letting players match items to NPC profiles.
Use a physical substitute to break a chain of custody, so the apparent captive is not the real threat.
when: a trial or capture scene
why: Substitution invalidates the assumption that custody guarantees containment.

text: Confronting a suspect with an item can branch their replies and open new lines; an item contradicting a denial can trigger the next interrogation step.
when: designing an interview system with evidence items

text: A trail that weather or chance can erase rewards quick pursuit, and any delay in following it can lose the case.
when: tracking a fragile trail
why: traces are lost to events that accumulate over time

text: If a test works regardless of trace age, better tools gain value. Freshness-dependent methods lose value as in-game time passes.
when: Evidence decays over in-game time.

text: Make some evidence destructible, so that cleanup by a culprit leaves fragments players must reconstruct.
when: Designing evidence that can be destroyed.
why: Partial remains keep the investigation alive.

text: Evidence a suspect discards in an ordinary place can be recovered when a witness with a hidden sightline sees the disposal and keeps the item, though luck, not method, decides whether this happens.
when: A suspect disposes of evidence in an outdoor or public container
