why: Witness sightlines and retained items create recovery chances, but unplanned keeping is unreliable

text: Requiring a second clue before an accusation counts as solved, with different proof levels producing different outcomes, rewards thorough investigation over guessing.
when: A player makes an accusation in a mystery game.
why: Multiple proof tiers make weak accusations fail and strong ones succeed.

text: Moving an item changes which clues remain in the scene, so player actions on evidence should have consequences.
when: designing interactable evidence
why: Irreversible handling makes player choices meaningful.

text: Each handover of a valuable object between locations creates a window in which it can be seen or taken.
Accumulating small independent findings progressively narrows the set of plausible explanations, until the remaining candidates share a common origin.
when: When several minor clues are collected over time
why: Each finding eliminates alternatives that are inconsistent with it

text: A missing item, such as a disposed key, becomes a clue in its own right, since its absence is a gap in the record.
when: An expected object cannot be found at a scene
why: Absence of an expected item breaks the chain of evidence

text: A case can be built as a chain of linked facts in which each fact confirms the one before, and the final link connects to the suspect.
when: When assembling an accusation from several facts
why: Linked facts show how each element supports the next

text: A land record chain logs each grant with its date, each sale with its buyer, and owners at a later date, linking people across holdings.
when: tracing who was connected to whom through property

text: Identifying someone by a ring, clothing, record, interested party's claim or family recognition is weak until independently compared; items swap and records match substitutes.
when: when establishing who a body or person is
why: Items can be swapped or planted and records can be matched by a substitute.

text: A matching item in a suspect's room or a paper trace shows access or location, not who wore, wrote or caused the event on a given night.
when: when a suspect's item is found at a scene
why: Objects can pass through many hands before and after an event.

text: Handling evidence destroys or contaminates traces like stains, alignment or prints; touching adds new prints. Examine before repeated handling, since early contact removes traces tests need.
when: when handling evidence before examination, such as for a fingerprint check
why: Early contact removes or alters traces, and added prints confuse the original trace.

text: Handling evidence before its meaning is understood can delay or lose its value.
Clerks may refuse information out of professional discretion or annoyance, which can cut off a trail.
Public suspicion can rest on partial knowledge, since the detailed terms of a private agreement are often unknown to the community.
A clerk's added comments can tilt a deposition toward guilt, so additions must be read separately from the witness's words.
when: When a record contains marginal or appended notes.
why: Annotators may bring their own views into the account.

text: A medical or natural verdict offered before access is resolved closes the question too early.
A plausible sequence built from guesswork can fit the facts without being true, and unexplained facts such as an unrecorded visit must be addressed or the theory looks weak.
when: when assembling an alternative explanation
why: Fit alone does not establish truth, and unexplained facts expose the gaps.

text: A fixture that looks newer than the rest of the room may mark a deliberate change rather than a repair.
why: Recent-looking additions can be intentional.

text: Withholding findings from those who must act on them can be read as insubordination and breeds mistrust.
A trace that was not anticipated, such as a small personal object, can still connect the scene to the offender.
when: An offender cleans up but misses an item
why: Removal efforts focus on expected traces and miss others

text: Handling a trace object early, especially in front of others, can contaminate or confuse it, and a quick deduction from it can be wrong until a second source confirms it.
when: Examining a small object at the start of an inquiry
why: Careless handling can destroy the trace and tempt an unconfirmed conclusion

text: Inspecting a physical object late in the investigation can lose context and cause important evidence to be overlooked.
why: Details noticed early are tied to the scene and people present at the time.

text: Treating a coincidence in time, such as a storm at the same hour as an execution, as a cause or sign of guilt is an error.
when: When two events occur together and one is read as explaining the other.
why: Simultaneity does not establish causation.

text: A state that ends on its own may be mistaken for the effect of an intervention performed just before it.
A mark placed on an item other than the one that was moved proves nothing about the item that mattered.
when: When applying custody marks to evidence.
why: Only the mark on the actually moved object records its absence.

text: 1) Identify the item and the shared space it passed through. 2) List each person who held or was near it. 3) Mark who had access, who was positively excluded, and follow the chain back to its owner.
when: when an item may have been handled by several people or may link a person to a place or event

text: 1) Establish how many identical copies were produced. 2) Account for each copy's known holder. 3) Attribute any unaccounted copy to a hidden holder, likely the commissioner; a single recovered copy does not prove the case, since a second identical item may exist elsewhere.
when: when a weapon or token exists in several identical copies
why: Counting reveals possessions no witness mentioned.

text: 1) Label each item separately as collected, with description, date and source. 2) Record who handled it. 3) Obtain signed statements for identity, sampling and analysis. 4) Lock and log storage. 5) Hand to analyst with a written request.
when: Any sample may be needed later in court or comparison
why: A signed chain keeps results usable even when inconclusive.

text: 1) Find the full original source. 2) Compare the excerpt against it, noting unmarked omissions, especially cuts that remove material undercutting the claim. 3) Check disputed words against standard definitions. 4) Check claims of non-reading against cited sources. 5) Note what was removed and why.
when: when a claim depends on one quoted passage
why: Cuts can silently remove the evidence that weakens the claim.

text: 1) Gather corroborating letters and documents. 2) Interview the people who can confirm or contradict the account. 3) Arrest only once the evidence is sufficient.
when: when a suspect's guilt rests on presumption
why: Corroboration prevents an early strike from failing and damaging trust in justice.

text: 1) Pull out each specific, checkable claim in the document. 2) Compare each one with known facts. 3) Record which claims hold, and keep those results separate from the accusations.
when: A single unsigned document is the only lead and it contains checkable facts.
why: Verified details show familiarity with the subject, not that the accusations are true.

text: 1) Let the player collect each clue. 2) Have the player present the chain of evidence to a group of NPCs. 3) Make the NPCs respond to the chain.
when: for a final reveal in a game
why: presenting evidence to NPCs turns collected clues into a scene with consequences

text: 1) Compare each printed entry with independent accounts from family or witnesses. 2) Note any conflict in names or dates. 3) Record verified names and dates in your notes.
1) Empty each container of evidence. 2) Sort contents into groups by type, such as papers, coins and keys. 3) Record every item before bagging, so nothing is lost or confused.
when: When collecting items from pockets, bags or other containers.
why: Logging keeps each item traceable.

text: 1) Name who recognised the item. 2) Name who confirmed ownership. 3) Note how that confirmation was obtained. 4) Judge the clue's weight from these answers.
when: Assessing an object offered as evidence
why: Provenance shows whether a clue's link to a person is independent or shaky.

text: 1) Compare the entry's date with the events it describes. 2) Note hedged wording that avoids admitting fault. 3) Check the setting where the act took place. 4) Test whether the claimed event could have happened as described. 5) Read who was present or absent as a sign of intent.
when: an official record conflicts with other sources about who acted and why
why: Each check exposes a different way that a record can soften, omit or invent events.

text: 1) Count how often each writer cites each source. 2) Trace the common root of the citations. 3) Treat agreement between writers as corroboration only after steps 1 and 2.
when: a long chain of writers seems to confirm one view
why: a shared origin makes apparent agreement weaker than it looks

text: 1) Record the witness who sees the disposal. 2) Record who keeps the item. 3) Obtain the lawful access permission or key. 4) Recover the item. 5) Pass it to the analyst with custody documented.
when: Designing or tracing a recovered physical clue
why: An explicit chain keeps the evidence admissible and the discovery fair

text: 1) Identify the maker's mark on each object. 2) Check the maker's customer records for duplicate or matching items. 3) Use the maker's profile of customers to judge how likely a matching purchase is.
when: Objects carry manufacturer marks and records of sales are available.
why: Records link an item to a buyer and show whether a match is expected.

text: 1) Write every gathered clue in one list. 2) Mark which clues have been followed. 3) Check the list for omissions. 4) Prune leads as dead ends appear.
when: Many clues are gathered and the central clue is not yet clear.
why: A complete list exposes overlooked items and limits wasted effort on dead ends.

text: 1) Test every arrangement and discard impossible ones, or 2) hold all elements in view until a combination appears. 3) Test the sudden combination against the facts before trusting it.
when: Scattered clues need to be linked into one explanation
why: Systematic elimination and holistic recognition are both routes to a solution, but insight needs checking.

text: 1) Label each exhibit at collection. 2) Record where and from whom it was taken. 3) Keep items separate to prevent mix-ups.
when: Collecting physical evidence during an investigation.
why: Clear provenance prevents confusion between items and supports later proof.

text: Give items a provenance log of owners, sales, locations and confirmers so players can verify claimed owners, argue from it, trace stolen items and flag wrong-person or mismatched-inscription finds.
when: Designing evidence items, clues tied to objects, or a stolen-item mechanic.
why: Recorded owners and locations make the item's history checkable and give players a traceable path.

text: Check a claim resting on one author's reading against the sources that author cites; a citation alone confirms nothing until its source actually supports the claim.
when: when a claim about the past depends on one author's reading

text: Make key items leave a record, such as a log entry or an NPC who saw it, so they cannot be removed or denied without a trace.
when: before a key item is formally secured
why: A routine observer's account is hard to dismiss.

text: Take discovered evidence to one authority and examine it in their presence, keeping a documented chain of custody from discovery onward to prevent disputes over where it was found.
when: when physical evidence is found during an investigation
why: A documented chain protects the evidence from dispute.

text: Let items show history through physical state, such as a scuffed grip, a strap worn to one size or an unexplained detail no NPC understands, so players infer earlier holders.
when: when designing items with a history or environmental storytelling through objects
why: Physical state can communicate history without dialogue.

text: Test a written statement against the physical form: an unusual cut, an incomplete page or a handwriting mismatch undermines its claimed origin.
when: Examining a document presented as testimony
why: Physical inconsistencies reveal forgery or staging.

text: A lock, ID, or trace that appears to prove identity should require a second independent check, such as a matching key or alibi record, before being accepted as proof.
when: Designing a clue that the game treats as conclusive.
why: Independent checks prevent a single clue from closing the mystery too early.

text: Let looted items carry wear and marks that players learn to read as backstory; repairing or cleaning an item erases that evidence, which is a deliberate design choice.
when: when designing item histories
why: wear makes objects narrative and cleaning becomes a meaningful choice

text: Give items recorded origin tags, such as a shop mark, guard post, chest or workshop, so players can trace each item to its source and the NPCs with access.
when: designing item provenance or generated items that serve as trace clues
why: Origin tags link items to characters.

text: Track each evidence item's custody and owner history so players can ask and trace who handled or held it and when.
when: designing items that move between characters or clue items for investigation
why: A recorded chain of handlers makes item provenance a usable clue, and ownership makes an item's meaning depend on who handled it.

text: Give objects persistent states such as indentations, stains, fresh residue, broken, wet or scorched, encoding time and cause so players can compare them with a claimed timeline.
when: designing environmental storytelling
why: States act as readable evidence of past events and of recent use or movement.

text: Keep physical-possibility clues (time, means) separate from psychological-fit clues (character); a suspect may pass one and fail the other, and opportunity alone does not establish guilt.
when: designing suspect clues or narrowing suspects in a mystery
why: Opportunity alone does not establish that a suspect is the culprit.

text: Give found items provenance: who gave them, where they came from and who sold them, so each object can open a new line of questioning.
Collect every scrap of evidence, but read it without a fixed preconception, since gathering alone does not prevent distorted interpretation.
Give each evidence item several possible owners but design the correct one to match properties the player can inspect, such as colour or length.
when: Designing evidence that can be attributed to more than one character.
why: Inspectable properties let careful players rule out rival owners.

text: Track each key item's ownership and location history, so routine NPC tasks such as laundry or delivery create checkable evidence.
when: Designing items that move between characters in a generated world
why: Movement history turns routine activity into testable clues

text: Check a document's claims against other clues so it works as evidence to weigh rather than as a plain answer.
When a formal document decides who has a claim, check its exact wording before deciding who must be told.
when: Disclosure would harm a third party, or a document governs inheritance

text: Record what was left behind as well as what was taken, since remaining items show what was not needed and can reveal which exit was used.
when: Investigating a departure or disappearance.
why: What remains in place narrows the possible exit and time of departure.

text: Track which character holds a key item, so progress requires delivering it to the correct authority.
Establish an object's earlier location or ownership before treating it as evidence; a found item proves little on its own.
when: an item is found at a scene
why: its significance depends on when it arrived and who owned it

text: Examine each fact before dismissing it, because its evidential value is unknown until it has been examined.
when: Early in an investigation, when evidence is thin and many facts look equally unimportant.
why: A trivial-looking object can become key evidence once its properties are checked.

text: Show the initial meeting or event openly, so later clues can be traced back to what the audience has already seen.
when: Planting clues that should pay off later
why: Clues linked to earlier shown events feel fair and rewarding when they return.

text: Check each claim against the means the witness says they had of knowing it, such as seeing, hearing or inferring.
Scale a clue's reliability rating by how close the listener stood and whether the listener was interrupted.
when: Assigning a confidence level to overheard clues
why: Proximity and clean hearing make the captured words more trustworthy

text: Make booking clerks NPCs who remember names and dates, so a player who asks the right questions can recover an alias.
when: designing service NPCs
why: Remembered details reward careful questioning.

text: Give a clue an identifying name or mark that reveals its owner simply by being seen.
Mark each clue as material (timeline, records) or inferential (behaviour, tells), so players know which kind of evidence they hold.
when: when designing investigation clues

text: Attach a grudge to a specific item in game lore so a non-player character's behaviour toward that item becomes a motive hook the player can uncover.
when: writing character history for a game
why: A visible symbol makes hidden motives discoverable.

text: Use a clerk's sworn statement that an entry was written in his presence as a provenance check.
Scatter partial archives across a generated world, with a missing page the player must infer from surviving series.
Let an in-game pamphlet or sermon label a faction, and reveal the motive behind the label so players can judge it.
Order testimony so the final witness carries extra weight, and make that ordering visible so the player understands it matters.
Log an item's contents and any return condition at each transfer, so the player can later verify claims about its ownership.
when: In item-transfer systems that carry conditions.
why: A stored record lets the player check what an NPC or item history says.

text: Keep an access log showing which NPCs handled food, so players can eliminate suspects by opportunity.
when: when generating poisoning mysteries
why: Opportunity records give players a checkable basis for elimination.

text: Give crates, keys or letters a movement log, so that a leg that does not match the record can expose a second item.
Encode inheritance rules as data so each heir's share recalculates when an NPC dies, letting the player see shifting stakes.
when: when building a game with inherited wealth or property
why: recalculated shares make the consequences of each death visible

text: When a player destroys a document, keep its authors and witnesses reachable and let them be re-interviewed, so the loss does not feel complete.
when: Designing evidence that players can collect or destroy
why: Removing only the paper leaves sources who can still testify

text: Log which character handled each object during a set-piece, so a later puzzle can reconstruct who moved what.
Give each key or relic a logged history of holders and locations, so players can reconstruct who could have opened a given door.
Use object states such as a hung cloak or an open door as timestamps when no NPC was watching.
when: Designing environmental clues for a time-based puzzle
why: Environmental state can record events without any witness

text: Let volatile clues such as smells or residues decay on a timer, rewarding players who examine a scene early.
when: Designing evidence that changes over time
why: Time pressure gives examination a reason to happen promptly

text: Design partial-state clues, such as a half-cleaned statue or moved object, that imply an NPC will return so players can wait and watch.
Make each seal's state observable, such as a raised bridge, lit lamp or drawn curtain, so players can reason about entry periods.
Compare claimed possessions with physical proof; a stated large sum with no trace of the goods is a warning sign.
when: A party claims to hold valuables or funds.
why: Unverified claims can be fabricated to support a scheme.

text: Do not count evidence awaiting confirmation, such as a pending expert report, as proven.
when: when reviewing a case before an arrest or theory is committed

text: Before shipping, confirm that every clue needed to reach the solution is placed and reachable.
when: when validating a mystery level

text: Record each clue's source and timing, so designers can see which explanations depend on unverified assumptions.
when: When building a mystery or evidence system that must be checked for consistency
why: Provenance and timing make contradictions and unverified assumptions visible before the content ships

text: Rank clues by how usefully they trace to a person: location clues like postmarks are useful, while mass-produced items cannot identify a buyer and should be deprioritised.
when: Choosing which clues to pursue in an investigation.
why: Pursuing untraceable clues wastes time.

text: Once an envelope is opened or a paper is handled, it no longer proves who sealed it, so its trustworthiness should be lowered accordingly.
when: Judging the reliability of a sealed document
why: Breaking a seal or handling a paper removes the guarantee of origin

text: Preserve and record a bite impression before confronting the suspect, or the impression can be lost.
Confirm a container was not reopened after packing before trusting what it shows.
Hiding a clue in plain view conceals it from players who expect hiding, but makes it easy to miss entirely; a must-find clue needs a more reliable placement.
when: The clue must be reliably found for progression.
why: Obvious objects can be overlooked even when visible.

text: Cutting an object reveals its internal mechanism but destroys evidence that must stay intact. Cut only when preservation is not required.
when: when the object may be needed in court

text: Weather, drying, sun, trampling, repairs and other visitors erode traces such as blood and footprints, so delayed examination yields less or ambiguous evidence; examine early and carefully.
when: A scene is examined after a delay or left exposed
why: Exposure erodes marks that were clear when fresh

text: After a physical trace is erased, only a witness's recollection or a preserved copy remains as evidence of it.
Microscopic cell examination becomes useless once stains are a few hours old, while a protein-based test still works on older stains.
Disturbed ground and torn vegetation near an edge mark the final stretch of a struggle or flight, and show where movement became most violent.
when: Traces cluster near a drop or edge
why: Concentrated disturbance marks the point of greatest activity.

text: Erasures made after writing carry a different meaning from those made during writing, so the timing of an edit should be established before interpreting it.
when: Analyzing deleted text in a document.
why: The meaning of a deletion depends on when it was made.

text: Degrade some document clues with faded ink, missing lines or folds, so players must cross-reference them with other sources.
A physical trace can reveal recent human activity even when no one is seen.
Assign each trace to the phase that plausibly left it. Blood, objects left behind and uncleaned marks usually belong to the first phase.
when: a scene may contain traces from two separate events

text: Concern about disturbing traces matters less when many people have already handled the scene; prioritize tests that can still reveal new information.
when: when many people have already entered the scene

text: Date a trace by its time signatures, such as wetness, freshness, colour or smell, which show how long it has been there.
when: Estimating when a trace was made
why: Some properties change predictably with time

text: Date a physical trace by comparing it with daily routines, such as scheduled cleaning or nightly fires, which bound when the trace could have been left.
when: the routines of the place are known
why: a trace can only be made between routine events

text: A dropped habit-specific item can fix the moment a person passed, so the sequence of events can be reconstructed from where it lies.
why: The item is left at a specific point in time.

text: A trail of blood on plants, stains on the path and a side-slip together record a wound, a stop and a remount, in that order.
Weather, delay and fading memory destroy evidence that cannot be recovered later, and later questioning of witnesses yields less detail.
when: when time passes between a crime and its investigation
why: Witnesses forget details and deem earlier details unimportant over time

text: Clues tied to perishable landmarks, such as blazed trees or stone heaps, can decay with in-game time, forcing players to triangulate from surviving features.
when: landmarks are used as quest clues

text: Physical evidence can decay if not collected quickly, such as items disposed of or moved by an NPC.
when: Designing evidence in dungeon or narrative generation.
why: Delayed collection lets NPCs remove traces.

text: Reading a fresh trace as old, or the reverse, happens when weather or other events have altered it since it was made.
Opening windows or doors can dissipate smells and other traces before a later examiner arrives, so the evidence is lost.
when: A scene is opened or aired out before it is fully examined.
why: Airflow removes the physical traces that the investigation depends on.

text: Brushing, shaking or wiping clothes destroys or moves traces, so untouched items are needed to read where a person has been.
Erasing a public message destroys evidence of how a rumor spread and who might have passed it on.
1) Read the item's current state. 2) Infer how much time that state implies. 3) Check the implied time against a fixed schedule such as deliveries or service times.
when: fixing when an event happened

text: 1) Note any visual trace, such as a shadow or light patch, that changed during the event. 2) Reconstruct the sequence as it was seen, not as it was expected. 3) Repeat the action under the same conditions. 4) Compare the trace step by step; a mismatch rules out that explanation.
when: A witness's visual recall seems to conflict with what they heard.
why: A replay under matched conditions tests whether the recalled trace could have occurred.

text: 1) Convert the trace's position to an approximate date. 2) Compare that date with dated events such as purchases or illnesses. 3) Reject the story if they conflict.
when: a claim depends on when an exposure happened
why: Dated traces can confirm or break a timeline

text: 1) Check whether old traces cross a line of the current text. 2) If they do, the old text was not erased from that sheet. 3) Compare trace length with the expected length of a standard phrase.
when: Judging whether a document's text was altered or erased.
why: Erasure removes the upper text but cannot remove marks that were struck through the later line.

text: Set aside found evidence and keep it sealed, marked and unaltered so it can be preserved intact and examined again later.
when: A death may be natural but leaves material that could be retested
why: A preserved sample keeps its value for a later investigation

text: Note where a trail stops, such as paved or trampled ground, and treat that point as a place where evidence was lost rather than as the end of the route.
when: When tracking a route across mixed ground.
why: Hard or heavily used ground erases tracks without showing where the person went.

text: Keep evidence under watch by combining observers with sight of entrances and windows, an agent with the object, monitoring of communications, and a log of every visitor.
Keep objects found on a body away from the suspect until they are used to confront that person.
when: when a suspect has not yet been confronted
why: Early exposure lets the suspect adjust their account.

text: Describe an object by its make and features without handling it, so the object stays intact as evidence.
Keeping evidence on one's person risks a search, and destroying it removes the proof; leaving it among ordinary items can be the least bad option.
when: when a culprit holds incriminating evidence

text: Suppressing records can protect against present accusations but removes the evidence later needed to vindicate the suppressor.
Players who see evidence apparently destroyed often stop searching, so a convincing destruction can misdirect them away from the real item.
when: An investigation where a key document appears burned or lost.
why: Apparent closure signals that the trail is exhausted, which ends further inspection.

text: Water washes off visible traces, but only thorough cleaning defeats a sensitive biological test.
Brush or cleaning marks on a surface are a trace to check against the account of who cleaned there and when.
when: a surface shows signs of recent sweeping
why: cleaning marks can contradict or support a witness account

text: Check hearths and grates for partly burned papers, since ashes and fragments show that records were destroyed.
when: a suspect may have destroyed documents

text: Clean-up by a bystander can destroy the one clue that separates an accident or suicide from murder.
when: a death could be read as homicide
why: loose papers and labels can be lost among ordinary clutter

text: Make a destroyed or withheld item a meaningful clue, and let the NPC's account of it be checkable.
when: an item is removed or destroyed in a mystery
why: a checkable account lets the player test the explanation

text: Build the solution from several kinds of evidence, such as confrontation, documents, testimony and physical proof, rather than one decisive trap.
when: presenting a late-stage solution

text: When damning evidence is presented in full before the standard that invalidates it is named, the audience accepts the apparent guilt until the flaw is revealed.
when: a reveal built on a standard of proof that is stated late
why: the audience can see the flaw without being told what to look for

text: Open a mystery on a striking image whose cause is withheld, so the audience holds a question while the explanation is delayed.
when: Starting a mystery or investigation
why: A held question pulls attention forward

text: Open an interrogation with a confident claim the suspect cannot easily disprove, and offer a clear reason to be candid.
A container opened with a key rather than forced suggests the opener had access, and a thief with a professional aim would not usually take papers.
when: Judging who opened a container and why.
why: Method of entry reveals access, and professional thieves target valuables rather than documents.

text: Displays that recur at moments useful to the accusers, such as new arrests, suggest the display is directed rather than spontaneous.
Early inquest-style evidence such as a weapon by the body, a quarrel and doubtful timings can make the audience believe the accused is guilty.
when: opening a mystery with circumstantial evidence against a suspect
why: Strong-looking circumstantial evidence sets a convincing false conclusion early.

text: A recorded or timed playback can make a victim seem alive at a later time than the real moment of death, shifting the apparent timeline.
when: a voice or sound at a given time appears in an alibi
why: playback reproduces a voice without the speaker being present

text: A confession that merely restates what the investigator already proved feels like a shortcut and weakens the payoff of the reveal.
1) Give a formal warning that the words will be recorded and may be used. 2) Confirm the medical urgency. 3) Record the words exactly. 4) Question briefly after the continuous account.
when: A suspect may die or be unable to speak later.
why: Without urgency, a formal statement would normally wait for a later hearing.

text: 1) Record every exchange with a hidden stenographer. 2) Establish who was present and their roles. 3) Take the account in sequence, from the start to the final hour. 4) Restate key times and names as questions. 5) Repeat names and hours at the end. 6) Type and copy the record at once.

1) State the full theory to witnesses in order: method, physical proof, source of the document, access. 2) Hold back one link until the suspect's position weakens. 3) Recite each linked fact when the suspect denies. 4) Make the arrest rest on physical proof.
when: The accusation must be made before witnesses
why: Each link supports the next, and physical proof resists argument

text: 1) Show a physical discovery. 2) Add a checkable fact that contradicts the official story. 3) Add a late confession. 4) Add witness accounts. 5) Explain the full mechanism last.
when: When a hidden truth must be proven to the reader before the final explanation.
why: Independent layers make the explanation credible and let it arrive after the danger has passed.

text: Record a suspect's statements and the questions asked word for word, since meaning depends on the question and wording can carry unintended meaning.
when: A suspect's words are recorded and the question can be reconstructed.
why: So the questioning itself can be checked later.

text: Record off-topic answers and unguarded slips immediately, since they may later connect to alibis, access or other facts.
when: A witness gives an answer or remark that seems minor or off-topic.
why: Their meaning often emerges later, so noting them at once preserves evidence.

text: Record what a witness was offered, what they refused and their stated reason, since refusals can reveal the other party's preparation and be tested.
when: a refusal is used as evidence
why: Unrecorded reasons leave the inference untestable; these events can reveal the other party's preparation.

text: Record a suspect's statements as claims and a witness's impressions of appearance or mood as impressions, never as established observations or facts.
when: a suspect's account is evidence or a witness gives impressions
why: A claim is not an observation and should not be treated as one.

text: Make each reveal rest on one physical exhibit the player can reach and inspect, rather than an unexplained expert claim or only deducible evidence.
when: Designing the proof of a staged scene or a reveal.
why: A single inspectable proof is more convincing than an unexplained expert claim, and players trust what they can verify by hand.

text: Record every response to a test, including a later loss of response, because the subject's condition can change during observation.
Record a witness's earlier admissions word for word, so later denials can be checked against them.
Record which witnesses each expert interviewed, so players can see who was overlooked.
when: Designing investigation records
why: Overlooked witnesses expose gaps in an expert's inquiry

text: Record each agreement made between factions, so a later betrayal can be traced by checking the records.
when: when designing faction agreements in a game

text: Present trivial objects in an opening scene as ordinary, so their significance is recognised only in hindsight and rewards a player who noticed them.
when: Designing an opening scene that contains later clues
why: Ordinary presentation avoids signalling importance, yet preserves the clue for later recognition.

text: End a puzzle chain with a diegetic recap that links each strange event to the object or mechanic that caused it.
when: closing a puzzle sequence in-game
why: the player sees how the clues combine into the answer

text: Record an expert's unease about a surprising analysis made at a bad moment as a fact in its own right.
when: An expert hesitates over a result.
why: Hesitation may reveal a concern not yet stated.

text: Record even a false statement and compare it with other accounts, since a lie can itself be significant.
Record each stated duration, source and timeline, because an unchecked claim can later prove false and expose a contradiction.
when: when interviewing a witness or suspect
why: contradictions surface only when claims are kept

text: Let the player check a claimed injury or substance by touch or with an in-world tool, so the check itself confirms what the thing is.
Record ambiguous statements in full, noting every plausible reading, and do not settle on one reading after the fact.
when: A suspect's statement could be read as either a confession or a denial.
why: Choosing the reading afterwards lets the interrogator decide the outcome.

text: Present depositions and records without a comparison table, leaving the reader to compare them, so the presentation does not push a view.
when: Presenting conflicting testimony or documents to the player.
why: Unguided comparison lets the player form their own conclusion from the evidence.

text: Do not present an ambiguous clue as decisive; show the alternative reading alongside it.
when: A clue points to a suspect but also to other explanations.
why: Showing both readings lets the player test the inference.

text: End a mystery by explaining the solution in front of the suspects or authorities, using physical proof rather than confession.
when: Staging the resolution of a mystery.
why: Public physical proof makes the answer convincing and leaves the guilty party exposed.

text: Showing the full evidence chain lets the reader test the conclusion, but too much detail makes the chain hard to follow.
when: designing a mystery that the player must solve from clues
why: fairness requires visible reasoning, while clarity requires selection

text: Gather complete evidence before forming a theory, since an early unverified claim or theory makes later findings be read through it rather than assessed on their own.
when: when analysing a case or playtest result, especially at the start while evidence is new and assumptions untested
why: Premature conclusions bias judgment; early theories formed on thin evidence bias which facts get noticed and kept.

text: Record attested observations and actual words separately from the witness's interpretation or claimed cause, and check each on its own terms, since a sincere explanation can mislead.
when: when recording testimony or collecting witness statements, or writing NPC dialogue, about an event that comes with an explanation
why: An attested event does not verify its explanation; mixing what was seen with what was concluded hides the error in the inference and makes evidence look more certain than it is.

text: Treat a suspicious feeling as a prompt to seek physical evidence, not as proof, and separate it from proven fact before acting.
when: When an investigator's suspicion arises from unease or dread.
why: Unverified suspicion can harden into an unjustified accusation; feelings can reflect warning or fixation, and only physical evidence separates them.

text: Observation gathers raw facts from the scene, while deduction chains those facts together into an inference about what happened.
Finding a hidden item answers where it was kept but does not always establish what it proves or who acted.
when: After recovering evidence from a hiding place.
why: Physical location and evidentiary meaning are separate questions.

text: Ask a witness for an opinion before asking for facts, so they commit to a position that can be tested later.
why: a stated position can be checked against later evidence

text: Describe a character through precise, observable detail so the audience infers traits from what they see rather than being told them.
why: precise detail makes the audience feel the observer absorbs the scene

text: A witness's opinion about another person's private life is weak evidence, especially when the witness admits it may be imagination.
when: a witness judges someone's private conduct
why: opinion about private matters is seldom observed

text: Keep a witness's opinion separate from observed behavior, since an argument about rights is not a fact about what happened.
when: When a witness offers a moral or legal view alongside testimony.
why: Stated opinion can be mistaken for established fact if not separated.

text: Hold a conclusion open until later events confirm or refute it, while more evidence can still arrive.
when: when a team or investigator is split over an inference

text: Separate what a witness saw, heard, and understood, because a witness may report a vivid visual detail while missing the words or subject of a dispute.
when: Evaluating a witness's account of an argument.
why: Visual and emotional detail can make a weak account seem strong.

text: A dialogue system that separates an NPC's stated opinion from observed fact lets the player test one claim against the other.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that carries opinions and facts.
why: Separated claims give the player a basis for checking and contrasting what an NPC says.

text: An official finding can stand while an unproven insinuation about it keeps circulating as gossip.
A strong fit to facts does not prove a motive or story; showing no other explanation fits is stronger than showing that one does.
why: A motive that fits many facts can still be wrong.

text: A witness can accurately see an act while the explanation the actor gives for it is wrong, so an observation alone is not enough.
when: A witness reports what someone did and the actor offers a reason.
why: Actors can reinterpret the same act to suit their own account.

text: Strong observation and deduction still fail when specialist knowledge is missing, so both observation and lore are needed.
when: when an investigator is skilled at reasoning but lacks domain lore
why: deduction needs precise facts to act on

text: A witness's opinion of someone's character is not evidence that the person was present at an event.
A gap in observation is not evidence of an act. The contents of a sealed item remain unknown until it is opened.
Readers may take a character's reading of another's feelings as proof of that reading, though it is only an observation.
A confident but unverified opinion, even from a knowledgeable character who admits lacking proof, is a lead to test rather than a fact.
Attentive observation without empathy can miss what matters most to the people involved.
Two people can see the same object and read it differently, so record what was observed separately from what it is taken to mean.
when: When multiple observers examine the same physical evidence
why: Noticing a detail does not guarantee understanding its meaning

text: Failure of one theory does not confirm another; a rejected explanation leaves the question open.
why: a rival theory still needs its own evidence

text: Opinions presented as facts mislead an investigation and must be kept apart from verified statements.

1) Separate what the witness observed from the inference drawn from it. 2) Judge each part against known facts, listing facts the inference leaves out. 3) Test the inference against them, keeping the observed core even if rejected.
when: when a witness mixes fact with belief

text: 1) Ask whether the witness actually looked at the condition. 2) Separate direct observation from assumption. 3) Accept a claim about a physical state only if it was observed.
when: Checking a witness claim about a door, lock or similar condition
why: Assumed conditions are easily reported as observed facts

text: Record opinions of people, especially character judgements, separately from observed facts and check each claim about a person against observation, since opinions are weaker evidence and can replace it.
why: Opinions are not observations, and a narrator's opinion colours reports and can stand in for evidence.

text: Sort each witness claim into what was seen, heard, or guessed, weigh each category differently, and mark gaps in overheard speech rather than filling them in.
when: when evaluating any witness's testimony, including overheard speech
why: A witness's opinion can be mistaken for an observation; overheard speech is incomplete.

text: Let some NPCs report only what they saw and others report assumptions, so players learn to separate observation from inference.
when: Writing witness dialogue
why: Players must learn to evaluate claims by their basis

text: When reviewing a witness account, separate observed facts, such as what was said or where someone went, from interpreted states such as grief, madness or calm.
Mark which parts of a witness account are firm observations and which are inferences, since an inference is not an observation.
When weighing testimony, separate what a witness observed from what they interpreted, since fear can blur direction and source.
Keep observed conduct separate from inferred motive. Do not treat a suspected motive as an established fact.
when: Reading a suspect's actions as evidence of intent
why: Conflating what was seen with what was assumed produces false certainty

text: State which parts of a joined inference are firm and which are guesses about missing pieces.
when: A conclusion rests on partial sources

text: Keep identification by sight separate from identification by reasoning about motive, since they are different kinds of evidence.
when: Weighing a witness's naming of a suspect
why: Motive narrows suspects but does not show who acted.

text: Separate what is directly observed from what is inferred when stating a cause or time of death.
why: inferences are weaker than observations and must be labelled as such

text: Do not treat a physical fit between fragments as proof of intent; it shows only what was read or kept.
when: when a discarded document is recovered
why: A match establishes contact with the document, not motive.

text: When questioning a witness who is unsteady, restrict them to answering specific questions rather than volunteering opinions.
when: A witness's account is useful but unreliable due to intoxication or emotion.
why: Unprompted opinions from an unsteady witness add noise rather than verifiable facts.

text: A claim that an opinion was widely held at a time, passing through recognized writers, must rest on documents showing that transmission, not on reputation alone.
Track evidence as proven or inference-only, and let the player decide when to present a theory, since presenting it changes which NPCs trust them.
when: designing player-held deductions

text: Count matching reports as corroboration only from independent sources; one shared cause, such as one disturbance heard by two people, yields matching reports.
when: When checking a witness account against another person's memory.
why: Separate memories reduce the chance of a shared error.

text: Objects, marks, hiding places and small scene changes reveal who was present, how they moved and what they intended, and can confirm or contradict testimony.
Later evidence of the same pressure, such as a broken engagement over money, corroborates a confession's account of that pressure.
when: a confession describes financial strain
why: Independent events matching the motive support the claim

text: Passers-by can corroborate only what they directly saw, such as a figure in a window, not the identity behind it.
Weigh testimony by independent corroboration, not by how vivid, confident or socially respected the witness is; independent confirmation adds weight.
when: Evaluating a report, a named suspect or a claim resting on a witness.
why: Vividness, confidence and status do not establish truth.

text: When testimony conflicts with physical facts, give physical facts extra weight; facts witnesses cannot explain away should anchor the case.
when: When a witness's account contradicts the scene.
why: Physical traces are harder to shape than spoken accounts.

text: Require corroboration before naming a suspect when a witness's account is incomplete.
Ask a suspect for corroboration such as a named person, receipt or document; when none is offered, the account rests on the suspect's word alone.
when: Assessing the strength of a suspect's account.
why: Uncorroborated claims cannot be independently confirmed.

text: Corroboration through outside accounts matters less when the evidence can be physically examined or independently observed.
Independent corroboration strengthens a witness account but does not prove it completely; the claim remains partly open.
Weigh an alternative explanation by its source: an expert offering an implausible theory deserves closer scrutiny than a layman's guess.
when: Evaluating a theory offered by a witness or suspect
why: An expert should know better, so the choice is telling

text: Where no independent check exists, weigh an account for plausibility rather than treat it as proved.
when: When no witness or record can confirm a timeline
why: Unverified accounts support only tentative conclusions

text: A container much heavier than its size suggests may hide contents, a trace that can be noticed before anyone opens it.
Discount single facts that connect to nothing else, and weigh patterns that recur across many observations.
when: when evaluating scattered observations
why: isolated facts are easily coincidental, while patterns are more reliable

text: Weigh a witness's own certainty lightly when observation conditions were poor.
Ask who gains from each version of a secondhand account, and treat the most direct witness as more reliable than retellings.
when: several characters report the same hidden event
why: reporters may have reasons to shade what they say

text: Authored NPCs can hold back facts until the player finds corroborating evidence, rewarding investigation over guessing.
Physical findings such as wounds, bruises and clotting, recorded and examined by a qualified examiner, can contradict rumor or spectral accusation and establish how a death occurred.
when: A death must be classified as natural, accidental or murder and a body or wound survives
why: Concrete bodily traces are checkable facts that outweigh unverified claims

text: Confirming a witness was present does not confirm the rest of their account; corroborating one detail is not proof of all of it.
when: a witness's location is verified
why: presence and identity are separate claims

text: Physical evidence has also condemned innocent people, so it must be checked against motive before it is trusted.
why: traces alone do not establish intent

text: Rejecting a whole account over one doubtful detail, or accepting it because of one vivid detail, are both errors.
A single financial gain does not prove guilt, since several motives can point at the same person.
1) Identify the source's vantage point, timing and purpose. 2) Check which quoted figures it could actually have measured. 3) Test its claims against direct observation.
when: A mystery presents conflicting reference works, maps or witness statements.

text: Block a formal accusation based only on witness-only clues until a physical trace or a second independent source confirms them.
when: when designing an investigation system with perception-only evidence

text: Require independent corroboration from a second source before recording a witness claim as a confirmed fact.
why: A single claim should not settle a case.

text: Require physical corroboration before a verdict counts a claim, and track how many accusations rest on a single source.
Require independent corroboration before testimony the accused cannot rebut carries weight in a verdict.
when: Accusers' testimony is the main evidence
why: Unrebuttable testimony can decide a case without any outside check.

text: Weigh each account by how closely its source saw the matter, and do not treat gossip as established fact.
when: several people describe the same event
why: distance from events reduces the reliability of testimony

text: Seek other corroboration for a key fact rather than letting the case stall on one unreachable source.
when: When a single source holds a critical fact.
why: Backup sources prevent a blocked investigation.

text: Build a reconstruction on physical traces such as recovered ammunition; treat testimony about a missing weapon as weaker.
when: A weapon is missing but its ammunition or mechanism remains.
why: Physical traces are harder to misreport than recollection.

text: Mark which statements need independent corroboration before they are relied on, and do not treat hesitation, evasion or grief as proof of guilt.
when: When sorting testimony in a case.
why: Emotional or evasive answers have many causes.

text: Weigh official accounts such as sermons, epitaphs and histories against private talk and domestic testimony, since formal sources often conceal truth that private witnesses reveal.
when: Building a character's reputation from multiple in-world sources.
why: Authors of public records know they are on record and tend to flatter.

text: Weigh each claim by its source and checkability, since the fullest account is not necessarily the most reliable.
when: When comparing several accounts of one event.
why: Length and detail do not establish accuracy.

text: A practitioner's assertion is not an independent test, and experts or advocates with a stake, such as a reputation, may minimise mistakes, so claims need independent verification.
when: When an expert's own practice is under review or a claim rests only on the person promoting it.
why: Self-interest colours professional accounts; advocates have a stake in their claims.

text: Require a second, independent source before adopting one expert's conclusion or approval; expert opinion alone may fail to secure a verdict and enthusiasm can override judgment.
when: When expert opinion is offered as the main support for a case.
why: Expert testimony may not outweigh the rest of the proceeding; enthusiasm can override careful judgment.

text: Listeners who accept a confident expert's theory become less likely to question it, so a wrong theory can hold a whole group's attention.
when: an authority presents a plausible but untested account
why: trust in expertise lowers scrutiny

text: A player who knows how a craft is normally done can spot a prop that contradicts a character's stated activity, rewarding expertise.
when: a player has domain knowledge of the activity
why: recognising the normal way exposes the wrong detail

text: Formal procedure, such as assigned roles and a majority vote, can lend a weak accusation credibility it has not earned.
when: a red herring is presented in a structured forum
why: the form of a trial signals rigour regardless of the case's quality

text: Judges and audiences often defer to a prestigious expert's word on a disputed matter, so the expert's reputation can settle a verdict without adding evidence about the case.
when: when an expert testifies to facts in dispute
why: status is mistaken for proof of the particular claim

text: A belief endorsed by judges and learned figures as well as ordinary people is hard for any single observer to question.
when: when a doctrine has institutional and popular support
why: broad sanction makes dissent appear unreasonable

text: A confident interpretation from a respected authority can end an investigation early, so people stop testing a sighting once it is declared a message.
when: A public figure endorses a supernatural reading of an event
why: Trust in the authority replaces further checking

text: Experts' confident identifications can be wrong, and their doubtful picks may lean the same wrong way, so confidence does not guarantee accuracy.
when: experts identify genuine versus counterfeit items
why: Observed in a controlled sorting trial

text: A qualified denial answers only the literal question asked, so it can be true while still leaving a false impression.
when: A suspect's statement is narrow or carefully worded.
why: Literal truth and misleading implication can coexist when the question is narrow.

text: Experts can read the same physical signs differently, and testimony such as handwriting comparison can be contested by both sides, so interpretations need checking and questions may stay unresolved.
when: When specialists disagree or read signs differently.
why: Expert methods have limits and interpretations differ.

text: Expert status can extend belief into areas where the expert has no testing method; check whether their knowledge bears on the specific facts in dispute.
when: When a verdict rests on an expert's word.
why: Expertise in one area does not confirm claims about a particular case.

text: Treat an expert's explanation or framework as a hypothesis, weighed separately from the evidence it cites, since expert knowledge can be wrong and a confident conclusion is not evidence.
when: When an expert offers a theory or framework about a case, especially one pointing away from those involved.
why: Experts can be wrong or misdirect, and a framework needs evidence.

text: Have an expert check a working conclusion when a wrong one would have serious consequences, since a reasonable trace can still mislead.
when: A wrong conclusion would have serious consequences
why: An expert can reveal that the true condition differs from the working theory

text: Stage a reveal as an explanation given to people who know the field, so the solution is tested against expert judgment.
when: when the solution must feel credible
why: experts can check the reasoning and expose weak logic

text: When a skilled culprit makes a major blunder, the surprise itself invites scrutiny of the culprit's assumptions.
when: when a culprit's expertise makes an error look unlikely

text: Before accepting an expert's time estimate, check its stated basis and the confidence the expert expresses about it.
when: When comparing conflicting expert opinions on a timeline.
why: Estimates grounded in specific findings are more reliable than unsupported ones, and hedging signals uncertainty.

text: A witness's qualifying phrase, such as saying anyone might have used a route, is a new fact about access and should be recorded.
Separate what an expert knows directly from what they infer, and verify an expert's correction against the sources it cites rather than treating it as settled.
when: an expert offers a correction or gloss on a clue

text: Advice from a body with its own interests should be read in full, since cautious general wording can still endorse prosecution in particular cases.
when: when a court relies on written opinions from clergy or another interested body
why: a general call for caution may coexist with a specific recommendation to prosecute

text: Consult someone who knows how a mechanism is built, since they can often rule out a theory faster than testing each one.
when: many escape theories are proposed

text: Check advice from anyone with a reason to mislead independently before acting on it.
when: the advisor has a stake in the outcome
why: someone with a stake may steer you wrong

text: An expert's time-of-death estimate is a range, not a clock time, and should not be turned into a minute-level alibi.
when: Using a medical or forensic estimate in a timeline
why: Such estimates carry wide uncertainty and are often admitted to be guesswork

text: An adviser who repeatedly tells a witness they need not answer takes over the pace of the exchange and blocks further questioning.
Advice given to a subject can directly change her next action, so an answer to a hypothetical question can trigger the behavior the questioner then observes.
A game can represent symptoms and time of death as ranges, so the player learns to reason from uncertainty.
when: Designing a forensic or medical clue.
why: Ranges reflect real uncertainty and reward careful reasoning over guessing.

text: A mystery's misdirect can be placed in an expert's own explanation, so the audience's trust in the expert becomes the obstacle to the truth.
when: Designing a misleading explanation in a mystery.
why: Expert credibility makes the mathematical or technical explanation feel conclusive.

text: Treating a hedged expert finding (partial resemblance, 'probably') as full confirmation or denial hides real uncertainty; investigate further instead.
when: When an expert gives a hedged judgment on a match, identity or estimate.
why: Hedged findings carry limited certainty, and treating them as absolute drives wrong decisions.

text: Deference to a confident senior voice or expert standing can settle a group's view and end inquiry before the evidence has been tested; the explanation still needs testing.
Agreement between experts who examined the same set is not independent confirmation; shared examination shares the same biases, and even two people reaching judgment independently can both be wrong.
why: Shared examination shares the same biases.

text: Physicians can carry their own assumptions, so their conclusions about a body need checking against the other evidence.
Deferring to the expert's own perception over a witness's report can discard a real clue, such as a sound the expert did not hear.
An expert's confident-sounding opinion can change or dissolve under a direct question, so ask for specifics before accepting it.
when: An expert's testimony is the main basis for a theory of how a person died.
why: Opinions hedged under pressure reveal weak support.

text: A list of sources shows that a field's general standards were followed, not that each source was correctly applied to the case at hand.
Publishing a public action without consulting a partner can damage trust, even when the action serves the shared goal.
when: A team member plans an action that affects others.
why: Partners who are excluded from decisions feel bypassed and lose confidence.

text: An expert's admission of uncertainty is easy to miss beside a confident conclusion, so readers may skip the caveat that limits the claim.
when: a confident conclusion sits beside a caveat

text: 1) Describe the observed effects. 2) Ask an expert which causes would produce those effects. 3) Test whether any proposed cause is supported, and treat the lack of a supporting basis as a reason to doubt it.
when: A suspicion about cause, such as poisoning, needs checking against observed symptoms.
why: Experts can rule out causes that do not fit the evidence, narrowing the explanation to what is possible.

text: 1) Ask the expert to explain the relevant effects in plain terms. 2) Test that explanation against the known times of events.
when: An expert's account of a substance bears on the timeline.
why: Checking against known times exposes a wrong explanation.

text: 1) Mix known genuine and fake samples in equal numbers, numbered. 2) Record the true answer key. 3) Keep the expert away from how samples were made. 4) Have the expert sort them. 5) Compare picks with the key.
when: testing a claimed expert skill that controlled samples can check
why: Shows whether the expert's claimed skill holds up without revealing the answer

text: 1) List the specific claims: names, dates, works and authorities. 2) Ask an expert whether each one exists and is accurate. 3) Ask the expert to keep the material confidential while checking it.
when: When a claim depends on specialist sources the investigator cannot assess alone.
why: Specific, checkable claims give the expert something concrete to confirm or refute.

text: 1) Send a trusted contact a request for a specialist with the needed experience who will keep confidence. 2) Accept a short reply giving name, location and confirmation. 3) Use the specialist's judgment to settle the disputed claim.
when: A case turns on a question beyond the investigator's competence, such as a suspect's mental state.
why: A specialist can give a verdict the investigator cannot, and that verdict decides the next step.

text: Do not treat an expert's confident conclusion on timing or cause as proof; test it against the timeline and the evidence it rests on, since confidence is separate from accuracy.
when: When an expert gives a firm opinion on timing or cause, or when an expert's timeline supports a conclusion.
why: Confidence does not establish the facts, and experts can be confidently wrong.

text: Use a specialist's findings to test your theory rather than replace it; test a preliminary expert account of cause, shot count, weapon or time window against your own observations first.
why: Preliminary accounts can be incomplete or wrong.

text: Let an expert's questions follow physical evidence, asking about approach, speed and origin rather than repeating the witness's account; questioning the wrong witnesses misses key facts.
when: When judging an expert's investigation or framing its questions.

text: State the margin of error when reporting an expert's estimate, since such estimates are often given with more confidence than they deserve.
when: reporting expert reconstructions
why: Overconfident estimates can mislead later reasoning.

text: Do not let an expert's verdict settle a dispute unless the reasoning behind it is shown.
when: Accepting a specialist's conclusion
why: An unexplained verdict can hide errors

text: Have a person who knows an object identify it, and record the confidence of each identification.
when: An object must be tied to a person or place
why: Familiarity makes identification more reliable, and confidence shows how much weight it deserves

text: Tag qualifying phrases in dialogue as clue flags that link to another character's statement, and trigger a follow-up when the player notices a mismatch.
when: Designing dialogue systems that carry implicit information
why: Linking hedges to other statements lets the player discover implications through comparison.

text: Design evidence of death, such as remains or reports, so that the player can later question it.
when: Designing a character's apparent death
why: Questionable evidence leaves room for the reveal and for player investigation.

text: Show clearly who actually holds authority when a seal or decree is issued by an acting officer, so players are not misled by official-looking marks.
when: An acting official's seal is used in the game world
why: Official marks alone can mislead about who approved a decree

text: Advisers' opinions inform a decision but do not bind the judges, who remain responsible for the verdict.
when: when judges receive opinions from outside advisers
why: the decision rests with those who hold judicial authority

text: Bring a colleague who can read the message independently, and agree on the risk with them before acting on the tip.
when: a tip carries possible risk
why: an independent reading catches errors and shares the decision

text: Do not reject an expert merely for being an expert; judge the claim against the facts and evidence.
when: Weighing expert testimony

text: A trained specialist supporting official responders can recover evidence that untrained handling would lose, though it requires involving expertise early.
when: Responding to a scene with time-sensitive physical evidence
why: Trained handling preserves traces that general responders may not recognise or protect.

text: Keeping the expert's method partly unexplained preserves authority, but the proof itself must stay inspectable.
why: Authority depends on mystery, while trust in the conclusion depends on verifiable evidence.

text: Treat a witness's proposed explanation as partly true, accepting it for the symptoms it covers and rejecting it for the rest.
when: when a witness blames a mundane cause for a whole set of symptoms
why: Most explanations cover some effects but not all.

text: Offering a rational explanation, then letting the protagonist's past or the final scene unsettle it, keeps the reader from ever fully settling on one account.
Explaining most anomalies or one mechanical event does not solve the whole case. Leftover unexplained items must be stated plainly, not hidden.
A hoax can explain some effects while others remain unexplained, so one solution does not close the whole mystery.
when: When one trick is found in a multi-effect haunting
why: Some effects can have independent causes

text: 1) List each reported detail of the event. 2) Propose one physical mechanism for each detail. 3) Accept only the mechanism explaining every detail; a plausible ordinary cause alone does not close a strange event.
when: when a witness describes an event that seems to break physical rules

text: Investigators keep a favoured theory despite counter-evidence, or after its supporting physical evidence weakens, especially when a key fact stays unexplained or a vivid fact anchors belief.
when: a favoured theory faces contrary evidence, or its supporting evidence is lost or cleared
why: Attachment, trust in a companion, and a vivid fact anchoring belief more firmly than its later support can outweigh contrary evidence.

text: Advocates may keep a favoured theory after admitting the central question is unsolved, so the theory persists without new evidence.
when: repeated searches have failed to confirm the theory
why: Commitment to an idea can outlast the evidence for it

text: Investigators who accept correction without argument when shown an error avoid compounding that error.
when: A colleague shows a flaw in an investigator's reasoning.
why: Defending a mistake keeps the wrong theory in place.

text: Players and investigators readily adopt a plausible alternative theory as their working explanation, especially when an authority figure endorses it.
when: When a credible substitute explanation is presented.
why: A plausible decoy gives a ready answer, so it is accepted without testing.

text: A suspect offered money tends to infer the offerer's hidden knowledge from the offer itself, reasoning that a sensible person does not pay without cause.
when: A suspect receives an unexplained payment proposal.
why: People read motive backward from unusual behaviour, which can be right or wrong.

text: A widely held assumption about a kind of person can steer inquiry toward the expected suspect and away from others.
A witness who hears an alarming sound may explain it away with a benign assumption and not investigate, and may later regret that choice.
when: A witness hears a disturbing sound and leaves the scene
why: An assumption formed at the time can replace checking what happened

text: A theory linking many facts to a larger hidden network attracts belief because it explains everything at once, even when it is only conjecture.
why: explanatory breadth feels like confirmation

text: Witnesses treat a coincidental effect as confirmation when it matches the accusers' story, such as fits stopping at a touch.
Several weak clues, each modest alone, joined into one sequence can look unbroken and persuasive, even though no single link is strong.
when: several small incriminating facts point the same way
why: Joined links appear complete, so the sequence feels proven.

text: An inference reveal overturns a belief by combining evidence from several source kinds, such as tradition, testimony, records and comparison, rather than a confession or found artifact.
when: a truth must be deduced because no single item shows it

text: An investigator explains the reveal in dialogue, while a narrator often confesses under pressure to an unseen or unwilling listener.
An explanation accounting for every known fact, including rarity and secrecy, outranks one accounting for most, and is stronger than one fitting only the fact supporting it.
when: Comparing rival explanations of a clue
why: A theory that leaves facts unexplained is easier to undermine.

text: Test each premise of a tidy chain separately; each step feeling convincing lets a single weak link pass unnoticed and carry a wrong conclusion.
when: An explanation or suspect assessment is built from several steps or smaller clues.
why: Logical neatness and apparent support between steps do not show that each premise matches the facts.

text: Trace one established fact back to its causes and forward to its likely results, building the chain from that single link.
when: a reasoner has one reliable fact
why: a known link constrains what came before and what follows

text: Lay the facts out in order so their relative importance and their links to each other become visible.
when: A set of established facts must be reasoned about
why: Order reveals which facts bear on the conclusion

text: Explaining too little is better than explaining too much, so leave some details unexplained rather than forcing every object into the solution.
An explanation that accounts for symptoms can itself raise a new question about access to its source; check that before accepting it.
Judge an explanation by how well it fits the surrounding circumstances, not by a single fact taken alone.
when: When several explanations fit one event.

text: A planted-object explanation holds only until a forensic or ownership check disproves it.
Check a volunteered explanation against the speaker's own earlier statements and memory, since a conflicting recollection exposes the cover story.
Separate misleading evidence caused by bad luck from errors caused by poor method, and judge each on its own cause.
when: An investigation yields a misleading trace.
why: Misattributing the cause of error leads to wrong fixes.

text: An explanation that works only if a character was feigning turns their behavior into an unverified performance, so test it closely.
A test with a visible result, such as a colour change, bubbling or smoke, can support a rational explanation of an impossible effect.
Distinguish a state, such as sleepwalking, from the cause of an event, since a state explains behaviour without proving a supernatural source.
when: when a character's unusual action is explained by a condition
why: Conflating a condition with its cause hides the actual mechanism.

text: Let the detective reach the answer through a single theory that links separate pieces of evidence, rather than through isolated facts.
when: writing the climax of a deduction-based mystery
why: A unifying theory explains why the clues fit together and makes the breakthrough feel earned.

text: Once a community accepts an expert's verdict of an outside cause, other lines of inquiry are closed off.
when: when an authority offers a ready explanation
why: the accepted explanation leaves no reason to look elsewhere

text: Conclusions often form by linking small visible signs into a chain of inference, frequently so fast the reasoner does not notice each intermediate step.
when: A player must reach a conclusion from several observable details
why: Each sign narrows the possibilities, and the chain can feel instantaneous even when it is long

text: Explaining anomalies one by one protects the first theory while hiding what it cannot explain; each added rescue seems ingenious yet adds no evidence and more risk of error.
when: an investigator faces contrary facts
why: Rescue explanations make a theory look more persuasive without supplying evidence.

text: Explaining away the first tell generously can make later reactions look innocent too, so each tell needs its own check.
Trivial details are easily explained away as accidents; require a second explanation before dismissing a clue.
Inventing a fact to explain away a conflicting description replaces assessing how reliable the witness was.
A tidy explanation of a sound can leave the essential question open, since it does not settle who was present afterwards.
An explanation that fits one detail can contradict another, so every proposed explanation must be checked against all the details.
A plausible chain of inferences can lead away from the truth, and a single purchase is not proof of intent.
when: Building a theory from a suspect's purchases and possessions.
why: Each link may seem reasonable while the overall conclusion is wrong.

text: A clear, plausible motive can make a theory feel certain before the physical facts are checked.
when: Forming a theory from motive alone
why: Narrative coherence is mistaken for evidence.

text: A bound person may be free, so restraints should be tested rather than trusted to hold.
when: When evaluating whether a restrained character is still constrained
why: Restraints the bound person tied can be loosened by that person

text: A watcher often assumes the target is unaware because nothing overt happens, which can lead to a poor plan.
when: A target shows no visible reaction
why: Absence of overt action is mistaken for absence of awareness

text: Assuming the records are complete is an error; a count that does not reconcile signals missing entries.
when: Totals from records do not match the known number of items.
why: Unrecorded transactions leave a gap that only the count reveals.

text: A plausible explanation that is convenient for the speaker and accounts for an earlier lie should not end the inquiry.
why: Convenience and a prior lie are reasons to doubt the explanation.

text: 1) Take each apparent impossibility in turn. 2) Identify the mundane means that could produce it and how it was physically made. 3) Check that chain against the physical facts of the setting and link it to an earlier planted clue.
when: a striking trace or mystery effect looks supernatural
why: Ordinary causes are testable before any supernatural reading is accepted.

text: 1) List each step of the inference. 2) State the assumption behind each step, such as an object's height or the tool used. 3) Treat early findings as provisional until confirmed.
when: deducing a person's traits from physical traces
why: Explicit assumptions show where an error would enter the chain

text: 1) Collect the witness's full account before judging any fact. 2) Arrange the facts in order and check that each links to the next. 3) Mark every missing link as a significant gap.
1) List every plausible explanation, such as accident, error or deliberate act. 2) For each, state the consequences it would produce. 3) Seek evidence that separates the explanations.
when: Direct evidence is missing or several explanations fit.

text: Explain surprising observations and each deduction step from known principles, not bare assertion, so listeners can verify the conclusion.
when: Presenting a conclusion drawn from physical traces or a surprising observation
why: Listeners cannot accept or verify a leap they cannot follow.

text: Test each explanation of a suspicious fact against verifiable records, such as bank deposits or ledgers, before accepting it.
Refuse to witness or sign a document until its terms have been explained, and say so openly.
when: Pressed to commit under time pressure
why: Understanding is needed before commitment

text: Store whether an NPC accepted the player's explanation of a clue as checkable state, so later questions can depend on whether the player pressed the point.
Fear, excitement, strain or strong feeling about a person can project a dominant image onto a glimpsed figure, so an identification made under emotion is unreliable.
when: A brief glimpse under fear, excitement or strain, or evaluating an identification of someone the witness dislikes or fears.
why: Expectation and emotion shape perception and bias recognition.

text: Identifying someone from height, clothing, build or colour alone, at a distance, in poor light or from fragments, matches many people and invites false matches.
when: Matching a partial description or brief sighting to a suspect.
