text: A final chamber can hold physical evidence that recontextualises earlier clues, such as a lure quest or misleading document.
when: Designing the last reveal of a mystery.
why: Physical evidence confirms the solution and gives earlier clues a new meaning.

text: A case-notes or solution screen can reveal the method first and keep the suspect's identity locked until a condition is met.
Gate a reconstruction screen behind key evidence recorded in the player's journal.
Leave one or two details unresolved before the final confession, so the confession adds information rather than repeating what the player already knows.
when: when designing a game investigation's clue structure

text: A detective's claim to predict an outcome is fair only if the clues supporting it were visible to the audience.
A reversal of an earlier claim feels fair only when the earlier fact is shown to have been ambiguous, not when it simply changes.
Match time of day, light and door states when replaying an event, so the comparison is fair.
why: Unmatched conditions make the comparison unreliable.

text: Let players present accumulated clues in a final confrontation, with NPC admissions unlocked only by correct evidence.
when: Designing the climax of an investigation
why: Tying admissions to evidence rewards the player's reasoning

text: Let a late-arriving clue invalidate an earlier elimination, so players must revisit their notes.
when: designing deduction puzzles
why: Revisiting notes keeps the investigation open

text: Use a late-game reveal in which two NPCs with separate records share one underlying identity, deducible from complementary traits.
A fair-play reveal lands when clues planted earlier pointed to the revealed person, even if the player did not expect that identity.
Have the investigator admit their own missed signs, so the audience can see what should have been noticed earlier.
when: writing a solution reveal
why: Admitted blind spots keep the reveal honest and fair

text: Use NPC names or UI labels to frame how the player expects a character to behave, and treat that framing as a possible planted misdirection.
when: When naming characters or labelling interface elements
why: Players form expectations from labels before they observe behavior

text: Make a document's full text readable only after interaction, so the first glance creates suspicion that the full reading then resolves.
Leave the last decision to the player after the proof is delivered, rather than resolving the outcome by script.
Make exposing the truth carry a cost beyond the reveal itself, such as a loss of reward or a failure of justice, so solving the mystery does not end the story cleanly.
when: designing the aftermath of a twist or the resolution of a mission
why: A reveal that restores everything leaves no lasting weight, while withheld victory keeps the consequences felt.

text: A culprit's death before trial closes the case without formal judgement, but leaves the investigator to weigh the ethics of the outcome alone.
when: Culprit dies before trial

text: Money is rarely the only driver: jealousy, revenge, relationships, secrets, or quarrels over manners and records often operate alongside it, so do not let financial motive stand alone.
when: when a financial motive is found early or appears to explain a suspect's act
why: Investigators stop searching once a plausible explanation is found; money explains who benefits but rarely all reasons, and several motives often operate together.

text: Infer motive by asking who gains from a death or crime, who bears its cost, and who is under pressure the gain would relieve.
when: investigating a suspect's motive, especially when several people had access or the gains are concrete
why: Gain and pressure together explain why a person might act, narrowing the suspects; gain is a common reason to act.

text: Financial pressure (debt, large unexplained payments, speculative losses) can explain why a suspect might act, but alone does not link them to a specific act or prove intent.
when: when financial motive is the only link to a crime
why: Debt is common without criminal action; money alone does not prove intent.

text: Financial trouble, such as a closed bank or missing securities, can motivate flight or disappearance, but motive alone does not prove the act or any foul play.
when: when assessing a disappearance or flight with a financial angle
why: A person may leave voluntarily for money reasons, so motive is not proof of harm.

text: Financial motive can be real yet not the actual reason; debts can mask an unrelated cause, so check it against other evidence before concluding money was the reason.
when: when money pressure seems to explain a suspect's actions
why: Financial pressure is visible and can mask a different cause.

text: Tie a suspect's motive to a traceable resource (key, debt, safe, inheritance) with an explicit link to a specific actor so players can reason to the culprit.
when: designing a motive that players must trace through the game or uncover
why: Players can only reason to a culprit if the motive is traceable to a specific person.

text: A past dispute over money can make a person's honour seem doubtful to an accuser, so earlier quarrels shape how later claims are judged.
when: an accuser weighs someone's reputation
why: Earlier conflict colours present suspicion

text: A suspect whose clear motive is stated openly is easy to blame, because the motive needs no digging to be stated.
when: a motive is strong and visible
why: Investigators can name a visible motive at once.

text: In a new fight, an unresolved old debt or grievance is often voiced as justification, showing that the confrontation has a longer history.
when: a fight appears to have sprung from a single incident
why: Unsettled grievances carry over into later confrontations

text: A person under financial threat may read pressure from dependents as a threat to expose their secret, and anger toward them can reveal underlying fear.
when: when a suspect is being pressed for money by someone who knows a secret
why: Fear of exposure drives hostile reactions that can expose the suspect's concerns.

text: A death can end a suspect's income, such as a paid case or engagement, so that person may appear to have no motive.
Past divorce and custody arrangements can shape present relationships, so trace them as background before judging current ties.
when: A family's history includes separation.

text: Financial motives can be documented through three records: a will favouring a beneficiary, a life insurance policy, and a mortgage that ends on death.
When householders are made responsible for funding a shared office, the right to decide its pay and property becomes the basis of local power and dispute.
when: a community must fund a shared office such as a minister
why: Payment duties determine who holds a vote on money and property.

text: Property disputes between factions can remain unresolved in court for years.
Investments made by guardians or trustees with another's money leave deed and transfer records that can reveal actions the trustee never announced.
A will refused probate has no legal effect, so a legacy clause in it cannot be carried out.
Gambling losses raise the general risk of embezzlement. They are a general risk to weigh, not proof that a particular theft or killing occurred.
why: Risk patterns describe populations; individual guilt needs direct evidence

text: Sabotage can be motivated by money: betting that a stock will fall lets a saboteur profit if a disaster drops its price.
why: A financial stake can hide behind a political or accidental appearance

text: Show a death's financial gain through wills, debts, policies and transfers, tracing the estate's legal path to the true beneficiary rather than assuming motive from wealth or the obvious heir.
when: when a death or disappearance has a financial benefit or a suspect's benefit is in question
why: Motive often lies in who gains from the estate, not in the obvious heir; wealth alone does not show who benefits or how.

text: When motive is hidden, financial records such as lender and trader figures on debts and spending often reveal more than testimony, exposing pressure that suggests motive.
when: when a suspect's account is in doubt or a suspect's motive is unclear
why: Financial records can expose pressure that testimony leaves out.

text: Objects and signs of strain, such as pawn tickets, repaired worn clothing or footwear, reveal financial pressure a person has not mentioned and bear on motive.
A witness with a debt, pledge or payment at stake may shape the story; a promised payment shows willingness to deal but does not guarantee the information is true.
when: when a witness has a debt, pledge or payment at stake, or information is offered for money
why: Interest can bend what is told; motive to be paid can encourage a witness to say what is wanted.

text: Check actual holdings before accepting a money motive: a verifiable financial position weakens a theft motive, since someone who can raise funds quickly has less reason to steal.
when: when a suspect's motive rests on money or theft
why: Assumed wealth can be wrong, and the motive disappears once real holdings are known.

text: Treat a debt as motive only after checking who else had reason to act.
Judge whether an accused person had reason to act by checking their finances, character and the value of what was taken; a theft with no apparent gain looks unlikely.
when: when weighing a suspect
why: Without a gain, the act has no evident purpose.

text: Combine a gap in a record with the timing of a visit and the demand made before inferring a payment motive.
A personal object such as a photograph can reveal a link between two people and so carry a motive.
when: When a found item suggests a relationship between suspects.

text: When a scheme looks absurd, infer its purpose from the costs and fixed routines it demands, then ask which single purpose would justify them.
when: An investigator must find the function of a bizarre plot.
why: Costs and schedules reveal what the scheme must achieve.

text: Examine who controls the money and who would benefit from an inheritance or trust, since financial control often reveals motive.
when: a case involves an inheritance, trust or income
why: Those who control or draw on funds may have reasons to act.

text: Rank suspects by motive, starting with who urgently needed a large sum of money.
when: suspects may have a financial motive

text: A suspicious figure such as a large recent cash withdrawal is a lead to carry forward, not proof of guilt.
Large payments to a person suggest a financial tie, but do not prove that person holds the key secret; test that assumption separately.
A fact left unmentioned may still matter, and silence about it can have a deliberate motive behind it.
A large policy taken shortly before a death, combined with financial ruin, is a motive signal worth checking.
Heavy reworking of a piece that departs from copied styles elsewhere can signal personal purpose behind it.
Link motive to financial records: a debt or cash need that the victim could resolve gives a concrete reason for the act.
A person in financial trouble who courts someone with an expected inheritance has a money-based motive worth checking.
when: Someone's finances are strained and an inheritance is expected.
why: The inheritance would relieve the financial problem.

text: Infer a suspect's motive from who had access and who gains, then confirm or refute it with a later clue.
Follow prices, partial payments and mortgages as evidence of a party's finances; a debt cleared years later marks the point where its plan succeeded.
when: a party's economic situation or plan is unclear from narrative alone
why: Money trails track how finances changed over time.

text: Ask who gains from each accusation to uncover the real motive behind suspicion.
when: designing faction rivalries that drive accusations
why: Beneficiaries are the likeliest source of the accusation.

text: When testimony is disputed, use financial records to infer the attitudes of those who ran a process, not to establish a person's guilt.
when: testimony is disputed and a financial or physical record exists

text: Use tax and rent records to estimate who had the most to lose from a dispute, and whether a landholder was newly exposed by a transfer.
Trace a building or burial ground through marriages, sales and descendants to see which families held it and whether they still do.
when: linking a physical site to named people
why: ownership records connect a place to a lineage

text: Compare payments across cases; unequal allocations, especially to witnesses with influence, can reveal favoritism or a patron's sway.
Compare each payment against its case's outcome; a payment to a pardoned party far above one to an executed party's family signals unjust distribution.
Trace who held property and office before and after removals, since changes in ownership reveal what was at stake.
when: Investigating whether an expulsion or punishment served economic or political interests.
why: Ownership and office changes show who gained from the outcome.

text: A small first exchange can be framed as the first real result of a plan, marking a turning point in the situation.
A large unexplained payment to a victim's family can suggest blackmail, giving a second motive to check.
when: a payment is linked to a secret or a signed document

text: Institutional records, such as bank accounts, can reveal assets a suspect holds that the physical scene does not show.
Ask who gains from the uncertainty itself, not only from the death, when a disappearance affects inheritance or payments.
when: When investigating a disappearance tied to a legal or financial outcome.
why: A party that profits from an unresolved state may prefer the state persist.

text: Trace a suspect's motive to a specific pressure, such as debt, and check whether the act would bring the gain they need.
when: when a stated reason for a crime seems vague or grand
why: Concrete financial pressure usually explains actions more reliably than broad claims.

text: Mounting debt narrows a character's options, raising willingness to accept a deal they would refuse; track what they own, owe and have sold, since each debt adds pressure.
when: when a character is under financial pressure or is designed with a financial motive
why: Fewer alternatives make the bargain more attractive; each debt adds pressure and narrows choices.

text: Once an accusation exists, minor earlier quarrels are reread as evidence of harm, so a rival's frightening encounter is presented as proof of guilt.
when: a new accusation is made against someone with a past quarrel, or an earlier dispute resurfaces during an accusation
why: Accusers and audiences reinterpret prior events to fit the new charge; earlier conflict already gives a motive to read into events.

text: A debt with a fixed due date creates urgency that can push a person toward risky choices.
when: when a character owes money on a set date

text: Dated property transfers can explain later meetings held on that land, since groups often gather where a sympathetic member controls the space.
Concrete property such as land, a house or a salary turns personal feuds into formal legal action.
A deed or old grant can give one family a motive against a rival, and the player can find it in an archive.
when: Designing faction motives tied to land or property.

text: An accusation that reaches a patron's own family can cost the patron the support they had given the prosecution.
Motive can be read from who gains or loses money or status, and the same facts can be argued to support opposite conclusions.
when: Assessing whether a suspect gained from a death.
why: A loss to one party can be presented as a gain to another, so the reading depends on who is counted.

text: A staged theft of a replica, insured at full value, can disguise a loan, turning the insured value into cash for the owner.
why: The insurance payout converts a hidden asset into money without an apparent sale

text: Financial gain establishes motive, not action, and is only as strong as each link in the chain; the beneficiary may have a clean explanation for the missing link.
when: when a suspect profits from a death or disappearance and the motive is used as evidence
why: Motive is circumstantial and does not prove that a person acted.

text: Paying a dependent for silence invites repeated demands; each payment shows silence can be bought and each new demand raises its price, so look for the next pressure point.
when: when a secret is bought, as in a blackmail or hush-money situation
why: Demands continue as long as the secret remains valuable to the holder.

text: A large sum shows that money moved, not who received it or why; the recipient and purpose still need separate evidence.
A financial match shows that a link exists, not why it exists.
A map of property motive is weak when accusers have no material stake, and seeing property motive everywhere can hide sincere belief.
Accepting a livestock or crop loss as proof of a supernatural cause skips the ordinary explanations that must be ruled out first.

1) Read the seller's name from the item's label. 2) Visit the seller and find its sales register. 3) Narrow to entries near the probable date of the event. 4) Read the buyer and witness names from the matching entry.
1) List each beneficiary of a death or event. 2) Record the amount each receives. 3) Note the legal terms governing it. 4) Ask whether each beneficiary knew of the gain beforehand.
when: a death or threat might be financially motivated
why: Sorting beneficiaries by stake and knowledge shows who had a motive.

text: 1) Trace the suspect's business connections. 2) List recent large sums they received, and check the source of each.
when: a financial motive has been identified
why: hidden income can supply both motive and funds

text: 1) Identify the most recent document. 2) Check whether a marriage or later act revoked earlier ones. 3) Find the beneficiaries under the valid document. 4) Treat their gains as candidate motives.
when: when a death may bring inheritance gain

text: 1) Map the inheritance chain across generations. 2) Identify who was passed over. 3) Identify who gains from a death. 4) Check each claimed motive against records before accepting it.
when: when a death or disappearance may relate to property

text: 1) Establish whether a will exists and compare all versions. 2) Trace money flows such as royalties and copyright to named beneficiaries. 3) Check for insurance and who held an insurable interest. 4) Examine debts that may shrink the estate. 5) Separate those who profit from the death from those who profit from its publicity.
when: Testing whether a death served someone's financial interest.
why: Financial gain is traced through documents and flows, and publicity gains can mimic motive.

text: 1) Trace each transfer forward through successive deeds. 2) Identify the earliest owner and how they acquired the property. 3) Test an uncertain link against a related document. 4) Use lawsuits to show possession where title is unclear. 5) Keep proven and conjectured links separate.
when: A claim of ownership or inheritance must be checked, or one missing transfer is central
why: A structured chain shows where ownership is documented and where it is only inferred

text: Do not use financial beneficiary analysis as the only motive test, since a beneficiary who gains nothing may still have a non-financial motive.
when: Confirming or dismissing a motive for a death.
why: Financial gain is one motive among several.

text: Express a suspect's motive through observable signs, such as debts in a ledger or nervous habits, for the player to interpret.
why: Visible signs let players infer motive rather than be told it.

text: Give characters a believable reason for omitting a fact, so hidden presence can be explained once it is discovered.
In an in-game property ledger, give each building a sequence of owners, and make a missing transfer a clue the player can reconstruct.
when: Designing property history for a game world
why: A gap in the sequence prompts players to infer the missing transfer

text: Let property change hands after an accusation, so the motive becomes visible in the world state.
Paying a witness loosens their tongue but sets expectations of judgment; paying in front of others can make them greedy or distrustful and alter what they say next.
when: when offering incentives to an informant or paying a witness
why: Payment alters the witness's incentives during the exchange.

text: A financial motive is practical and clear when its figures are stated, but it adds nothing unless the figures connect to the plot's choices.
when: choosing a motive for a character

text: Financial motive has three forms, robbery, insurance and inheritance, and each requires a different method and a different holder of interest.
when: Sorting money-based motives in a case.
why: Each form implies different actors and different evidence to check.

text: Observers who did not see why someone fled read the flight as guilt, while the person may have acted from shock.
when: a witness reports that a household left during a crisis
why: the same act reads as guilt or shock depending on what the observer knows

text: A person who flees on seeing a stranger often warns others, which indicates the household expects visitors who mean harm.
when: When a witness runs or alerts someone upon meeting an unknown visitor.
why: Prior threats or expectations make strangers feel dangerous.

text: To test whether a person could have fled, add each leg of the journey, including wait, transit and walk, and check whether the total fits the gap.
when: a sequence of alibis or an escape must fit a time window

text: Reading a hurried exit or flight as guilt without other evidence is a mistake, since innocent people sometimes flee in panic.
Treating a servant's flight as proof of guilt, without the victim's plan in view, can mislead the investigation.
why: Flight may follow orders or fear, not complicity

text: Let a suspect's flight or dismissal open new paths, such as a changed location or a new hiding place.
Do not treat flight as proof of guilt when a verifiable, independent cause for it exists.
Place decisive clues early in testimony, scenes, or passing mentions (e.g., a culprit's errands) so the solution is fair yet easy to overlook and reveals read as recognition.
when: a mystery's answer depends on a clue the player has seen
why: The solution stays fair yet easy to overlook, and players accept late reveals more readily when they can recall information already on screen.

text: Mention a hidden room in an early document, before it is physically visible, so an attentive reader can anticipate it when the room is later reached.
why: Early hints let the reveal confirm a suspicion instead of arriving from nowhere.

text: Plant the mechanism of a later reveal in an innocent-looking early scene, then pay it off with a repeat appearance when the stakes rise.
A small ritual error or superstitious remark can plant unease that pays off later, since readers recall half-noticed details when the reveal arrives.
when: The eventual reveal depends on the audience remembering an early detail.
why: A trivial detail becomes a sign only in hindsight, once a later event gives it meaning.

text: Foreshadow that an ordinary document will form part of later evidence without naming what it proves.
why: Naming the evidence too directly spoils the reveal and removes suspense.

text: Plant an unexplained timer, count, or question early, and let only the climax reveal its purpose.
when: Opening a mystery whose answer comes late.
why: An unresolved detail keeps the audience reading later events for its meaning.

text: Plant a sound anomaly early, before its meaning is known, so the player hears it and can connect it to the answer later.
when: designing a mystery whose solution is hidden in the scene
why: A heard cue that is explained later rewards attention without giving the answer away.

text: Unpaid planted events, foreshadowed dangers, hooks, teases, flagged motives, cliffhangers and withheld facts feel like a cheat or broken promise, eroding trust; open threads must be answered.
why: A setup without payoff signals a loose thread; a withheld fact also needs an earlier clue to feel fair.

text: Mark one unresolved thread as unknown, such as an open-question quest log entry, so players can pursue it in a later session.
when: Designing a missing-person mystery.
why: A marked gap gives players a reason to return.

text: End a scene on an unanswered question, withheld fact, unresolved offer or danger so the audience carries the tension forward.
when: Closing a scene, chapter or section before a reveal, decision or next step.
why: Open questions make the following scene feel necessary; uncertainty sustains attention.

text: A closing warning aimed at an unnamed party keeps the observer's suspicion alive for the audience without resolving it.
when: a scene ends with an unresolved threat
why: An open warning leaves the audience expecting a further revelation

text: Close a seemingly resolved scene with a single-line threat that reopens tension, shown only after the characters have been reassured.
when: Ending a chapter or scene where the party believes the danger has passed.

text: Close a confirmed chain while leaving the final outcome open, so a loose thread carries into later play.
when: A mystery's middle links are resolved but its ending is not yet reached.
why: An unresolved thread keeps the player engaged and gives a basis for a later part.

text: A closing section resolves threads by deciding what evidence is kept or destroyed and what the public learns, once the central question is answered.
Ask a witness directly whether they saw anything relevant. A clear negative closes that lead quickly and frees effort for others.
when: a lead depends on one witness's report

text: End a tense segment on an unexpected encounter that changes the stakes, so the next scene begins from a shifted situation.
when: closing a stealth or tension segment
why: A changed situation at the end pulls the audience forward.

text: When doubt is high, show proof openly, since visible documents can establish good faith.
when: when the other party is suspicious

text: End a scene with a decisive fact to drive pacing into the next investigation step.
when: structuring a sequence of scenes
why: a strong ending creates a hook for the next scene

text: Use a closing recap to fix the outcome and settle relationships, but skip it when major facts are still uncertain, since it would add confusion.
Use a timed group decision as a scene's climax only when the audience must feel time running out.
when: Choosing a climactic structure for a scene.
why: A decision without time pressure loses its urgency.

text: A true-account mechanic can ask the player to fill the missing act of a reconstruction, rewarding correct sequencing.
when: designing reconstruction puzzles
why: the player must order events correctly

text: An inventory screen can mark one out-of-character item to trigger a side quest.
Store a dialogue line that foreshadows a later event as a quest hook that resolves when the player reaches the matching location.
when: Writing NPC dialogue that predicts a future event.
why: Hooks link early dialogue to later payoff and reward attentive listening.

text: Let an NPC's dying words give two or three fragments that players must combine with other clues to reach the next lead.
when: When designing a quest hint delivered by a dying NPC
why: Combining fragments makes the hint active rather than passive

text: A mysterious NPC who follows the player and leads toward a location can drive a quest, with the player checking what that NPC could have seen from there.
Plant a prophetic parting line early that players can recall when stakes rise.
when: Setting up a future callback or escalation.
why: A remembered line makes later escalation feel foreshadowed.

text: A suspect escaping through a crowd or train can be a branching point where the player chooses between a new watch and a fresh line of inquiry.
when: Designing a pursuit or lost-suspect event
why: A lost lead forces a choice of next investigative path

text: A status effect that repeats an earlier event works as foreshadowing, which players recognize on second encounter.
A motive or reveal that appears from nowhere or contradicts established evidence without earlier hints feels unfair or cheap to the player.
A hidden presence introduced only for a jolt, with no later payoff, feels cheap to the audience.
why: a threat that goes nowhere wastes the tension it built

text: A quiet period without new information feels like wasted time and can cause the audience to lose interest.
when: a lull is not followed by new facts
why: Waiting only builds tension if it resolves in new information

text: Withholding evidence without a clear reason or a plan to disclose it later leaves the investigation stalled and unaccountable.
In an open setting, spotting a stranger proves little, so the method only works where the population is closed.
why: Where many people come and go, an unfamiliar face is normal

text: A reversal or doubted decision made earlier that the final reasoning never justifies erodes the audience's trust in the solution.
An open threat made during pressure can be used by the suspect against the questioner.
Letting vague hints accumulate with no later payoff leaves the audience with open threads that never resolve.
1) State plainly the facts that are known. 2) State what remains unknown. 3) Point to the single clue toward the solution, confirming clues already given rather than introducing new ones.
when: Closing a mystery with an open or partly open answer.
why: Lets the audience check the outcome against earlier evidence.

text: 1) Restate the evidence in chronological order. 2) List each possible conclusion. 3) State what each conclusion must explain to be accepted.
when: several explanations remain open
why: Weighing each option explicitly prevents a premature verdict.

text: 1) Script each escalation step, such as a knock, a second knock and a forced entry, as a sequential trigger. 2) Let each trigger alert nearby NPCs. 3) Leave a memory of each trigger the player can check later.
when: when a reveal should build tension

text: Leave one thread unresolved, such as an object tied to an unknown figure, to seed follow-up and keep the ending believable; many open threads make closure feel missing.
when: Designing the end of a case or chapter.
why: One open hook invites continuation; a reveal explaining everything feels mechanical.

text: Close every lead and red herring with a specific checkable fact, not a general impression, showing which parts were false; unresolved red herrings become plot holes.
When a search line yields nothing useful, record that it was checked and closed rather than leaving it unstated.
Gate reveals with unresolved lines, letting players overhear an alarming statement and learn its context later.
when: Pacing a reveal in a quest or scene.
why: Unresolved lines create curiosity that a later reveal satisfies.

text: Keep the release brief after a long build: resolve the climax in a few quick actions.
why: a short release follows the long build

text: Resolve personal tensions and loose ends in the same closing scene as the case, such as rewards, reconciliations and future plans.
when: after the central reveal
why: unresolved threads leave the outcome unclear

text: Keep a scene open after an arrest so new evidence can still appear, rather than locking it once a suspect is held.
when: an investigation system holds a suspect
why: late evidence can overturn or confirm the arrest

text: When a quest branch can fail, keep a path to the truth through other clues so the player can still solve it.
Record a failed attempt to reach a character, such as a call with no answer, as a timed event that can change later options.
Use strength or stamina feats as puzzle gates, so only a character with the recorded capability can move a heavy object.
when: when designing physical obstacles

text: Stating or repeating that harm will come, without disclosing its outcome, builds dread and expectation, so a later return or reveal feels earned rather than arbitrary.
when: A story must promise later difficulty or reveal without disclosing it.
why: Anticipation of a known future event heightens tension.

text: Tie each forward hint to evidence the audience already has, and never let foreshadowing replace the evidence that would confirm or refute it.
when: Using prophetic or ominous hints in a story.
why: a hint with no visible basis reads as an arbitrary promise.

text: Normally people turn toward a sudden crash; someone who does not may have expected it, so the missing reaction is evidence.
when: someone witnesses a sudden event they would ordinarily react to
why: An expected event draws less surprise, so a muted reaction can signal prior knowledge

text: Foreshadowing hints at a coming disaster while denying specific knowledge of it, building suspense and misdirecting the listener without committing to facts.
End a section with a foreshadowed misfortune to create dread and prompt players to reread earlier dialogue for hidden meaning.
A spontaneous remark counts as foreshadowing only when later suggestion did not shape it.
when: a remark seems to predict a later event
why: suggested remarks may be reconstructed to fit what happened

text: Show an NPC's leverage through dialogue so that a later betrayal feels foreshadowed rather than arbitrary.
A narrator who points forward to later events signals that the present scene is the start of a longer story.
A forward hint that later events will be stranger than the present raises pressure on the audience.
when: a mystery is approaching a climax
why: anticipation of something worse keeps the audience engaged

text: A remark about a future event plants a question that the story can answer later, which keeps the reader's attention on that thread.
when: A character predicts an event or outcome.
why: An open question prompts the reader to track its answer.

text: Warnings from minor characters that point at a dangerous figure without describing him build suspense about a threat the player cannot yet see.
when: opening a story or case
why: Hinted danger raises tension before the threat is revealed

text: A departure record or forwarding address points to the next destination, letting a trail be followed step by step.
Foreboding needs concrete events and a later payoff; without them it reads as filler and drains credibility.
Overusing death imagery makes warnings feel clichéd, and unfulfilled dread becomes noise that weakens later tension.
when: Using repeated death images or warnings for foreshadowing.
why: Repetition without payoff dulls the audience's response to real danger.

text: 1) When a past event or disputed item cannot be checked directly, follow it forward through later records such as catalogues or sales rather than retracing the past. 2) Note where the chain breaks.
when: Verifying the history of a disputed item or transaction, or a past event that cannot be verified but a future event can be observed.
why: Tracing forward reveals gaps that suggest concealment or loss; retracing the past wastes time and effort.

text: Use throwaway lines as foreshadowing and record them in the quest log so the player can connect them later; unpaid foreshadowing reads as a loose thread.
when: Writing offhand dialogue meant to pay off later
why: Logged lines let players link early remarks to later events

text: Foreshadow danger through a remark or an innocent-looking setting, and make sure the foreshadowing pays off later.
why: unpaid foreshadowing leaves the audience with a false warning

text: Keep forward-looking leads, such as scheduled events, in the case log, and lock past events until new evidence unlocks them.
Use retrospective phrasing to flag that a minor event matters, without yet revealing how it will matter.
Foreshadow an ending by having a character predict it, then confirm the prediction in the closing section to reward attentive players.
Do not use foreshadowing when the audience already knows the threat, since warnings then only repeat what is known.
when: deciding whether to foreshadow a danger
why: foreshadowing adds tension only while the threat is still unknown

text: Do not let a foreshadowing hint reveal the solution; use it to build anticipation for what follows.
Tag foreshadowing lines with the characters who heard them, so players can deduce which character had the knowledge an event required.
when: Designing foreshadowing for a mystery

text: Plant a guiding character's parting line early so players recall it when danger peaks.
when: When a mentor or guide leaves before the climax
why: A remembered line turns a farewell into foreshadowing and raises tension at the climax.

text: Plant anomalies early and resolve them late, so a detail waits for its explanation and rewards the reader who noticed it.
when: Seeding physical or circumstantial details in a mystery
why: Delayed explanations make the reader revisit the detail and trust the eventual solution.

text: A matching signature does not prove common authorship: marks can be copied or names used as cover, so shared patterns may indicate a shared source; physical evidence must confirm authorship.
when: Attributing a document by its signature
why: Signatures can be copied or falsified

text: Crimes are sometimes imitated from earlier high-profile cases, so a precedent using the same method can support a copycat theory.
Do not drop a shop-based lead just because a careful culprit might have avoided it; such a lead is cheap to check.
when: a source inquiry is available at low cost

text: When a detail's importance is unclear, a sidelong check costs less than a confrontation.
A substitute who copies a target's most distinctive garments can pass for the target to witnesses who see them only at range.
when: when an impersonation must deceive a witness
why: distinctive clothing is the cue witnesses rely on

text: Once a target's measurements are known, forged physical traces become cheap to make, so a culprit of similar build can copy a rival's footprints and matching footwear.
why: copying measurable features is inexpensive

text: Counting a copy's agreement with its original, or later writers repeating one error, as independent confirmation inflates apparent evidence, since they often copy one original mistake.
when: Several secondary accounts agree on an identity or date.
why: Agreement among copies adds no new evidence.

text: Identifying a person by easily copied features such as a beard, glasses or distinctive clothing can be mistaken, since anyone willing to copy them can match the description.
when: when a witness names a suspect by appearance
why: conspicuous features are easy to imitate

text: Disguised people may copy a known habit on purpose, so a matching habit does not by itself prove identity.
A matching description does not prove ownership if the description itself was copied.
Resemblance to a maker's standard design proves little, because others can copy the design to create a false trail.
Early disturbances that gain attention are often copied, so the first symptom may not be the real story.
when: when investigating the origin of a crisis

text: A surviving copy of a record may not keep its original dates, so dates taken from a copy must be treated with care.
why: The original may be lost, leaving no way to verify the copy.

text: 1) Photograph the original printed record. 2) Turn the photograph into a raised relief plate. 3) Ink the relief. 4) Press it onto a new surface to produce a copy.
when: When a forger has access to a printed record but not the original object.
why: A faithful copy can be made from the record alone.

text: Make forged NPC messages checkable by giving the real NPC a phrase or habit that an impostor is unlikely to copy.
Settle an accusation that one writer copied another by comparing their citation lists rather than by assertion alone.
when: a rival accuses one writer of taking cues from another

text: Make a forged clue imitate a known pattern from elsewhere in the setting, so the decoy is believable within the world.
when: designing a false clue

text: Separate deliberate forgery from honest error by including at least one genuine clerical mistake, so players do not treat every odd detail as evidence of a plot.
when: Designing environmental clues in a mystery or puzzle scenario.
why: Otherwise players over-read every inconsistency as deliberate and lose trust in their reasoning.

text: Plant a forgery's contradiction in a checkable property, such as paper, ink, handwriting or a machine's purchase date, and name that property before the player needs it.
when: Designing a document that may later prove to be false.
why: A checkable contradiction lets the player expose the frame by their own deduction, and a fair reversal needs a way to test the document.

text: Records and staff accounts that use false names confuse the official trail as well as the people searching it.
Confirm a hidden-name link only on an exact letter match; loose resemblance or shared sounds are weaker evidence and easily overread.
when: Testing whether an alias hides a known name.

text: Give the true culprit a motive that appears early, such as a quarrel or absence, but leave it unremarked until the reversal.
when: Writing a mystery where a secondary character hides the real crime.
why: An early but unemphasized motive is fair play that the player can recall once the twist lands.

text: Split trusted allies with a forged message, and plant a small detail, such as a misspelled signature, that exposes the forgery.
when: creating a false belief between protagonists
why: A detectable flaw lets the audience and characters recover the truth

text: Forged or conspicuously intact evidence may be a planted misdirection, so check whether its presence looks deliberate before accepting it.
when: a forged letter or wrapper survives the investigation unchanged
why: Evidence that is too convenient may have been placed to mislead

text: A deception holds when a forged document and a conversation the victim overhears agree with each other, since the paper gains believability from the context and the context gains weight from the paper.
when: A deceiver wants a victim to accept a false situation without outside checks.
why: Both channels must agree, or the victim may notice a contradiction.

text: A document that looked authentic, once shown to be forged from trimmed or mismatched stock, flips belief from the apparent author to the forger.
when: A key document is revealed to be fake.
why: Physical traces of forgery overturn trust in the document's apparent source.

text: A forged document can be found later, and a staged story can be exposed by a single contradiction.
when: A deception relies on one convincing scene and a document.
why: Overconfidence in one scene can make the deceiver careless about the rest.

text: A seal that delays the answer too long can make the reader forget its release instruction.
when: when the gap between seal and release is long
why: The instruction fades from memory before the release arrives.

text: A document can be false, and a list of names proves contact rather than guilt.
when: Relying on written records as evidence

text: Present a forged or altered document that the player must check against a second source, such as a ledger or witness.
when: Designing a puzzle built on a document that may be false.
why: Requiring a second source makes the deception discoverable by fair play.

text: A forged invitation can pull suspects into one room, but it also means the expected threat may never show, so the lure must be paid off by another event.
when: gathering suspects for a confrontation
why: The lure creates pressure and a single setting, at the cost of a possibly empty payoff.

text: Tag in-world documents with source and editing, and store them as dated objects with occasional conflicts, so players judge reliability and build a timeline by cross-checking claims.
when: Designing in-world documents or a mystery-driven quest.
why: Source tags let players weigh claims; cross-checking makes the player an active reader of evidence.

text: A forger may produce a clumsy, easily detected forgery so that it is discarded and an earlier valid document stands.
when: A forged document appears alongside an earlier genuine one.
why: Exposure of the forgery removes it, which can leave the earlier document as the controlling version.

text: A witnessed transfer is an exchange of an object before a third party, whose presence creates a record independent of either principal's account.
why: A third-party record can settle later disputes about who held the object and on what terms.

text: A calling card taken from a real person can be used to implicate that person further, since it links the impersonator's actions to a real identity.
when: An impersonation plot needs to shift suspicion onto a real individual.
why: Authentic-looking props make a false trail more convincing.

text: A well-made forgery can be so exact that its maker cannot tell it from the original, even when they are placed side by side.
why: Appearance alone cannot prove a trace is genuine.

text: A document written on a standard printed form is easier to forge quickly, since the template is widely available.
when: Assessing how hard a document is to forge.
why: Common templates reduce the effort required.

text: Documents dated after the event they order or report expose later insertions or forgery; papers were sometimes procured later to support a verdict, and readers consulting them miss this.
when: Accepting a complete-looking archive as a whole, or checking a suspect document.

text: Give authoritative-looking forged letters checkable errors, such as a postmark or seal conflicting with the date, route, named place, handwriting, signature, paper or form, so observant players can catch them.
when: Designing a forged document clue.
why: Verifiable details reward careful players and keep the puzzle fair.

text: Plant a gap or discrepancy in a document timeline, such as a blank day or one guest where two were expected, so players must find the missing record elsewhere.
when: Designing a readable document as a clue source.

text: Give forged notes a recurring habitual quirk, such as a letter form or machine trace, that players match against known samples, since disguises hide obvious traits but rarely habits.
when: Designing a forgery reveal or a puzzle around a forged document.
why: Repeated habits give players a checkable pattern.

text: A clause written in smaller hand and fainter ink than the surrounding text may be a later addition, so check ink and hand.
Traces seen by many observers at once are more credible than traces seen by a single party.
when: weighing physical evidence in a case
why: Shared observation is harder to fabricate or misremember than individual observation.

text: Stationery such as a letterhead ties an object to a past source, and that old relationship can explain how a person came to hold it.
when: the paper bears a firm's or source's marks
why: past dealings can explain possession long after the link ended

text: Give forged documents plausible sources, dates, names and an intermediary, so players must judge the chain of trust against other evidence.
A body that is wrapped or tied suggests it was carried from elsewhere rather than harmed at the spot where it lies.
when: a body is found bundled or bound
why: bundling is a sign of transport

text: Letterhead details such as a crest, place of writing and date can indicate a writer's rank, location and time.
when: A letter carries printed or written header details.
why: Stationery reflects the writer's status and circumstances.

text: Two drinking vessels set out for a guest, with none of the host's drink present, point to a visitor rather than a resident.
when: reading drinking vessels in a room
why: set-out vessels show who was expected

text: Tracks showing no wear on heels or soles, or new-looking heels, are unlikely to come from independent walkers and may signal staging.
An item that routine staff checks would have caught or handled differently can indicate it was planted to mislead.
when: an item's presence does not fit normal practice
why: fabricated evidence often ignores routine procedure

text: A forger NPC behind a copy can serve as a later reveal that changes the quest's objective.
when: when designing a quest around a valuable object
why: a discovered forger reframes the goal

text: Give each NPC a writing sample so players can match an anonymous note to its writer through in-game comparison.
when: Generating written clues
why: Comparison turns a note into a deduction task

text: Track which characters walk where so their footwear carries plausible traces that point players toward the route they took.
A journal item can carry a culprit's plans and misjudgments about other NPCs, letting players verify a reveal from a primary source.
A forgery or crafting mechanic can require a reference record and a specific tool, with a chain of steps such as photograph, copy, and press.
when: When designing a crafted-forgery system.
why: A multi-step chain gives the player a meaningful process to solve.

text: Let a player frame an NPC, and make the frame hold only if the NPC's authority incentives and a physical match the player can test both support it.
when: when designing a framing mechanic
why: the frame then depends on checkable conditions

text: Compare the layers of a forged item; a detail missing from one layer but present in another can expose the forger.
Residues such as mud or puddles that dry over time let the game estimate when an action happened; decay states show how long an object stayed in place, revealing staging.
when: When a game records residue or props whose state changes over time.
why: The rate of change gives a time reference for the event; condition reveals how long an object was there.

text: A copy of a person's trace can be made from an impression taken earlier, such as a seal pressed into soft material, and later transferred to a scene.
when: When a trace matches a suspect too neatly.
why: A stored impression lets someone reproduce the trace at a time they choose.

text: A forgery mechanic can let a player copy a seal, key impression, or handprint from a source item, with the copy passing inspection unless a hidden deviation exists.
when: Designing forgery or counterfeiting mechanics.
why: Hidden deviations give careful inspection a payoff without making copies obvious.

text: A forged document delivered through a trusted person can establish a false identity, because the target accepts it through a channel they already trust and cannot check it independently.
when: A false identity must enter a household or group
why: Trusted delivery and lack of an independent check let the claim pass

text: Destroying a document in front of witnesses makes the act public and removes the paper as a later source of evidence, while witnesses can later vouch for its loss.
when: a party wants a document gone and controls how its story is told

text: A weakened heart makes a dose of an anaesthetic more likely to be fatal, which explains an outcome without proving who administered it.
when: When a medical cause of death is consistent with an agent but the agent's administrator is unknown.
why: Pre-existing weakness changes the lethal threshold, so the cause of death can be explained without identifying the person responsible.

text: A pencil with broken shavings and a worn tip shows hurried work and the need to repair the tool mid-task.
A forged record can be made by changing a few words that pass a quick reading, and the forgery often leaves a trace in another witness's account.
when: when a document passes through a suspect or third party
why: Small edits escape casual checking, but other accounts may not match.

text: A forged message signed with a trusted name can lure a target to a chosen place, and its success depends more on the forger knowing who is trusted than on the message's wording.
when: The target must be moved quickly to a specific location.
why: People act on urgent messages from names they trust without checking them.

text: Volatile substances evaporate, so a long delay before examination can erase the trace, and a small dose may leave no detectable sign.
Attempts to buy a valuable object make its worth known, which can prompt a forger to make a copy.
when: when a buyer or rival shows interest in a treasure
why: public valuation signals a market for copies

text: Discovering a forgery can overturn the group's assumptions and expose a party they trusted as the source of the copy.
when: when a treasure is revealed to be fake

text: A threat against a witness should flag the case and make the threatening character a suspect in the investigation.
when: when a game has witnesses and intimidation events

text: A poorly concealed trace such as a scorch mark or blood trail can carry information about who tried to remove it and with what tools.
when: Designing hidden-cover-up clues in a game world.
why: Imperfect concealment leaves readable traces of the actor's method.

text: Attaching a timing window to tampering evidence lets the player narrow down when the tampering happened.
when: Designing investigation puzzles with time-based evidence.
why: A time bound lets players eliminate suspects by alibi.

text: Detecting a forgery does not identify its author or beneficiary, so combine it with evidence of motive or a second clue.
when: Investigating who produced a forged document.
why: Knowing a document is false does not identify its author or beneficiary; detection and attribution are separate steps.

text: A forged message or document is exposed by a simple check at its claimed source, since forgers rely on no one consulting the original; plans must allow verification.
when: A decoy message is used to move a character, or a forged document is circulated.
why: Easy verification undoes the deception.

text: A message that appears to confirm a threat can be fabricated even when its details are accurate, so a convincing message is not proof of genuineness.
when: a single message drives a serious decision
why: a forger may have researched accurate details

text: Assuming a forgery requires the original object is wrong, since a copy can be produced from a printed record.
why: Access to a record can be enough to fake a trace.

text: A stamp or mark identifies a location, not a person, so it must be linked to someone before it is treated as a lead.
Handwriting and enclosed objects can be forged or taken from someone else, so a physical document alone cannot prove its source.
when: Relying on a document or enclosed item as proof
why: Imitation and theft break the link between the physical item and its true author

text: Washing or disturbing a surface can erase or mislead traces, so a clean area may hide where someone walked.
when: When a scene has been cleaned or handled after an event.
why: Cleaning removes the impressions that would otherwise record movement.

text: Packaging shows where the wrapping material came from, not who wrapped the goods or when, and a discarded item may have been passed on.
A matching print can produce a false match that appears to implicate someone the investigator wants to trust, so matches need independent confirmation.
when: A print match points toward a favored suspect
why: Investigator bias can make a weak match seem decisive

text: A fingerprint impossible to produce by pressing all digits at once suggests forgery, since a forger may press each finger separately to match a record.
when: when examining a print matched to a suspect
why: Simultaneous impression mechanics expose a print assembled from separate pressings.

text: 1) Establish who had seen the true handwriting sample. 2) Examine the forgery for details only a non-viewer would get wrong, such as a misspelled signature; forgers copy visible script but often miss spelling. 3) Match the error to that list.
when: when a written clue could have been produced by more than one person.

text: 1) Check each visible feature, such as a stamp or postmark. 2) Cross-check the dates and routes they imply. 3) Compare handwriting against an available specimen. Forgers who anticipate single checks are caught only by linked checks.
when: Verifying a document that claims a distant origin or specific author, or rests on one visible proof.
why: Each faked feature answers one check, so only cross-checking the chain behind them exposes the forgery.

text: 1) Compare entry dates and density across the document. 2) Check for missing leaves and frayed or pruned edges. 3) Check whether a stretch shares one uniform style, suggesting a single writing session.
when: when a written record may have been altered
why: edits leave gaps in dates, physical damage, and uniform writing

text: 1) Identify the expected source of the trace. 2) Check whether that source is absent. 3) See whether the pattern varies as one source's movement would. 4) Check for a means of imitation, such as freshly altered objects.
when: A trace looks ordinary but may be fabricated.
why: A missing source plus a source-like pattern points to imitation.

text: 1) State what a display or arrangement should contain. 2) Compare the actual contents with that expectation. 3) For any gap, inspect its fixing for signs of hasty removal. 4) Ask why that specific item would be taken.
when: when a display, inventory or regular arrangement should be complete
why: a gap in an expected arrangement can be evidence

text: Reconstruct a tampering sequence in order: select the items, open an entry point, remove the original contents, insert the substance, refill, reseal, and restore the packaging.
when: physical evidence suggests an item was altered after it was sealed
why: ordering the steps shows how the act could have been carried out

text: Give forged or swapped items a precise original state with detectable differences, so players who compare them with the original can spot the substitution.
when: Designing a substitution or trap quest.
why: Detectable forgeries reward attention.

text: Give forged documents physical details, such as mismatched stock, typeface, print, letterhead or trimmed edges, that point to a visitable source device or place, so checks narrow suspects.
when: A document is the main lead in an investigation or quest.
why: Physical traces link the document to its production source, so checking them shrinks the candidate pool.

text: Make a broken or damaged unique item a lock-and-key clue: players search the level for its missing piece or match its damage to a door or suspect's knowledge.
when: Designing physical clues that connect to locations or characters.
why: Matching a distinctive feature to its source is a satisfying deduction.

text: Mark which in-world documents each report draws on, and count reports that share one origin as a single witness when players weigh evidence.
when: building a case file of in-game reports

text: Let a forged quest note be contradicted by an offhand remark from a background NPC, opening a new branch.
when: when designing forged or altered quest material
why: Background detail gives players a way to detect the forgery.

text: Place in-world reference books, chronicles or family registers that the player can read to uncover a historical grudge behind an NPC.
when: Designing clue content that explains NPC motives.

text: Let an inn register record every traveller's name so players who check it for a false alias can find a suspect who used a different identity in each town.
when: Designing traveller records in a game world.
why: Registers give players a searchable trail across locations.

text: Let characters leave fibres of a set colour on objects they snag, so the player can match an item to a suspect.
Record change dates in an inheritance or contract system so the player can check whether a change came before or after a crime.
when: Designing a documentary inheritance or ownership mechanic
why: Timing lets players test whether a change could be a motive

text: Give the game an official summary of an event that omits one detail, so players who visit the scene can find the missing trace and correct the record.
when: when designing in-world records or reports

text: Let environmental clues decay over time, rewarding players who investigate quickly.
why: Time pressure makes early investigation valuable

text: Let abandoned routes leave the playable map but persist as plowed boundaries, fence lines or old labels that players can rediscover.
Offer a quest with a possible feigned death, leaving the player to decide whether the witness is genuine.
A feigned harmless, flustered or weaker persona makes targets underestimate visitors, reveal more and speak freely, but an overplayed act can be noticed.
when: An investigator or character hides capability or adopts a gentle, scattered manner around a suspect.
why: People relax around someone who seems unthreatening or unobservant.

text: Adopt a false role when officialdom is blocked or targets would refuse an identified officer, but avoid it where it exposes the investigator to legal or ethical risk.
when: When the official approach is blocked or a false identity could expose the investigator to legal or ethical risk.

text: Judge an explanation for a found object against the likely intent of the act; an explanation that contradicts that intent is weaker.
A freshly placed object in a disturbed scene may be a deliberate signal left by the searcher for investigators.
when: when a new object appears in a disturbed scene
why: Searchers sometimes leave messages.

text: Planted evidence takes five forms: a placed trace, a motive document, staged props, removed belongings and a substitute item.
Treating a found object as proof that an event occurred at its location, or that someone intended the act, is a pitfall when you do not know where it lay and for how long.
Let a single found object seed deduction about a larger faction when its features point to that faction's history.
when: a found object carries faction-specific features
why: a clue with faction-specific features opens a larger line of inquiry

text: A journal found in a hidden place can carry a location's backstory; describe its discovery place and seal first.
when: when designing story documents for players to find
why: The discovery context shapes how players weigh the contents.

text: Give found in-game documents deliberate gaps, guessed labels, or misspellings that players must detect, and flag which entries are verified originals versus uncertain copies.
when: Designing player-found documents
why: Source reliability becomes a playable skill.

text: Physical evidence such as torn paper degrades over time, so some traces may not survive long enough to be recovered.
when: Evidence is old when investigated.
why: Time erodes materials and removes traces.

text: Use pressure on an emotionally fragile witness with care, since it can produce a statement shaped by the questioner.
when: interviewing a vulnerable witness
why: Pressure can distort what the witness says.

text: A single observer or witness can be mistaken, lying, or forgetful, so an alibi or clue resting on one memory is fragile; long night watches also make observers drowsy.
why: A single unverified recollection can be wrong or forgotten.

text: A voice-imitation cover rests on luck about distance and light; a single close observer can break it.
A password taken on trust from a doorkeeper can pass a first checkpoint, but it is fragile because the group may change it.
when: Relying on a borrowed password to enter a group's space.
why: Passwords are shared and can be rotated, so they expire as cover.

text: Small traces are easy to overlook, and handling them can destroy them, such as brushing residue off a sleeve.
Physical evidence is easily lost, and heavy handling by many people makes it hard to establish who touched an item.
when: Investigating an object that passed through many hands.
why: Each handler is a possible source of contamination or misattribution.

text: A planted witness relies on events the planner cannot control, so the whole chain breaks if an ordinary arrangement changes.
why: the witness's presence depends on routines that can shift

text: A concealment that depends on one unlucky lighting moment feels arbitrary if the reveal is only bad luck; give the player a way to find the truth beforehand.
when: Designing a reveal that depends on timing
why: Chance-only reveals feel unfair without earlier discoverable evidence

text: Do not use a staged reveal as a trap on someone already fragile; let them recover before the conversation continues.
Make physical clue items fragile or losable, so players must protect and memorise them.
Handle evidence through a clean cloth and hold it by its edges to preserve surface marks for later examination.
when: When collecting objects that may carry fingerprints or surfaces to examine.
why: Bare-handed handling can disturb marks needed later.

text: A fragment supports several readings, so without its surrounding words or fit with the rest of the record it leads to conjecture; keep context and check consistency before trusting it.
when: using an incomplete, garbled or partial fragment as evidence
why: Partial text supports many readings, so only context or consistency with other evidence makes its meaning reliable.

text: A fragment that matches a known item or gap, such as a garment, ties its owner or origin to the place where it was found.
when: A torn or broken fragment is found in a room or at a scene
why: A matching source connects its owner or origin to the location.

text: A listener who hears only fragments fills the gaps with their own fears, expectations or distrust, so the fragment is evidence about the listener too.
when: when overhearing a partial conversation or when the audience receives partial information
why: Missing words invite the listener's assumptions; people fill missing parts with what they expect or want.

text: Hosts extend hospitality, such as clothing and a bath, to a guest vouched for by a trusted sponsor, without knowing the guest's name or checking identity.
when: a sponsor's word is offered for a guest
why: trust transfers through the sponsor rather than through direct verification

text: Partial damage can destroy a name while a surviving fragment, such as a printed corner or a postscript recovered from ash, still identifies the document's source or writer.
when: A burnt or torn document is examined
why: Partial survival can still identify its writer.

text: Surviving archives are often scattered, damaged and partly abstracted, with only a few items reaching repositories by chance.
An entry with no name, sex or date cannot establish who was involved on its own and must be matched against other sources before it supports any conclusion.
when: When a record mentions a person without identifying details.

text: Dismissing a fragment as meaningless or over-reading it both mislead; test it against all known facts, and treat any pieced-together meaning as a lead until checked.
when: a dying phrase, odd note or pieced-together fragments are interpreted
why: Fragments can seem trivial yet matter, or create a false pattern when over-read.

text: A fragment may seem meaningless or unimportant until a later fragment links to it or to earlier clues, so compare separated parts before judging its meaning.
when: A late fragment refers to earlier clues, or a character hears a place name or phrase without grasping its importance
why: Meaning depends on links found later; connections to earlier material make the story cohere.

text: At each link in a chain of testimony, ask whether the speaker saw the event or was only told about it.
when: Testimony reaches you through other people.
why: Second-hand reports can look like first-hand ones.

text: Write a dying character's lines as fragments whose neighbours constrain the missing words, so players assemble the meaning themselves.
when: for dialogue meant to be pieced together by the player
why: Constraints from surrounding words let players infer meaning without it being stated.

text: A clue that names a person and implies a stake, without explaining the matter, tells the audience someone holds a key without revealing its purpose.
when: when introducing a clue ahead of its meaning
why: Partial information creates a question the audience wants answered.

text: Place dialogue fragments mentioning an NPC's name or a quest item so the player must connect them, leaving room for a misreading.
when: designing partial dialogue for discovery
why: connection effort makes discovery feel earned

text: A cut cord with an intact knot shows how a parcel was opened and suggests the knot itself carries meaning worth examining.
when: When reconstructing how a sealed package was handled
why: The manner of cutting or untying reveals both handling and significance

text: Consider who made a claim, who was present, and what they gain from the suggestion.
when: when a single explanation rests on one source's word
why: A source with a stake in the outcome may mislead.

text: The shape of a cut can match a particular tool, so repeated curved cuts suggest a tool with a bent blade.
why: Blade geometry leaves a characteristic mark

text: Check whether a witness's stated source fits her confidence; a claim to know only a dead man's past yet speak surely about his death is suspect.
when: A witness's certainty seems greater than her stated access to information.
why: Confidence beyond the source suggests inference or invention.

text: Keep any fragments found stuck together by accident, since they can be the most valuable clues.
when: When searching a fragmented clue site.
why: Pre-joined pieces preserve context that scattered pieces lose.

text: A small fragment can prompt a hypothesis about a larger missing part, and a search guided by that hypothesis may locate the rest.
when: A small piece of evidence suggests a larger missing object or body part.
why: A fragment identifies the structure it belongs to, pointing the search.

text: Clue-matching puzzles can present a sequence with deliberate gaps that the player must align against the evidence.
when: Designing matching puzzles

text: A line cut through a surface that deepens toward a door shows the direction the object was pulled.
A physical marking too subtle to see can reveal itself through differing effects in use, so testing an item can expose what inspection misses.
Taking an overheard fragment as the whole statement, or a relayed phrase as verbatim, misstates what was said.
when: when using eavesdropped or relayed speech
why: Fragments and relays lose content.

text: Treating words from a speaker in shock as a complete statement, when they may be only the end of a longer thought.
when: The speaker was in shock or delirious
why: Shock fragments omit context that the full thought would supply.

text: An accurate fragment can distort a motive when read alone; another witness's added context can change its meaning entirely.
when: Interpreting a partial overheard statement.
why: Missing context shifts how a fragment reads.

text: Forcing a fragment to fit when its edges do not match, or missing that a document runs across several pages, produces a wrong reconstruction.
when: Assembling torn or burned documents.
why: Edge evidence must agree before pieces are joined, and multi-page documents can hide pieces.

text: Constant cutaways fragment attention when no thread is resolved, leaving the audience without a clear sense of progress.
when: Many threads run in parallel without resolution
why: Too many open threads dilute focus

text: A dedication, reprint, or later notice shows someone was alive at one moment, not where they went afterwards.
Identical colour and printing do not show that two pieces came from the same source; only the fit of the torn edge settles it.
when: Pieces match visually but have not been fitted
why: Many items share colour and print

text: Joining fragments by assumption can yield a fluent but false phrase; fit must be verified against the physical edges.
when: Piecing together torn text without clear edge matches
why: Plausible wording can hide an incorrect join

text: 1) Read only the words that survive. 2) Set aside weak fragments at first. 3) Keep partial observations on record and reread after new facts arrive. 4) Use the result as a lead to test, not a final answer.
when: interpreting a partly legible document
why: New context can change what surviving words mean; a fragment can later become evidence.

text: 1) Learn the shorthand conventions, such as underlines, dashes and short phrases. 2) Link key words into a coherent story. 3) Test the story against dates. 4) Note the gaps the story leaves unexplained.
when: a community or habit gives the shorthand shared meaning
why: Shared conventions give fragments a common meaning.

text: 1) Collect every fragment, including small ones. 2) Fit them together. 3) Count missing or surplus pieces. 4) A complete set means breakage at the find site; many missing pieces mean the rest lie elsewhere, while surplus or shortfall suggests another place or cause.
when: investigating a broken object

text: 1) Identify an unusual, specific feature of the object. 2) Compare it, with its type, edge wear and discolouring, against the suspect's or source's possessions. 3) Confirm with a second, independent feature that only one source could match. 4) Check that source's remaining stock for matching items.
when: a found item may come from a suspect's possessions or a household or workplace inventory

text: 1) Give a dying character a partial message. 2) Scatter the remaining parts across locations. 3) Make each fragment point to a place the player can reach.
when: designing a quest hook built from a dying character's words
why: The player must be able to complete the message by visiting the places the fragments name.

text: 1) Bring the two torn pieces together. 2) Try each orientation: front to front, back to back, and back to front. 3) Accept a match only if the torn edges coincide in one orientation.
when: Two physical fragments look alike or must be matched

text: 1) Check the page number; a high number implies many missing pages around it. 2) Count the gap to the surrounding pages. 3) Look for shifts in narrative voice or point of view. 4) Note handwriting and provenance that tie it to a household.
when: a document fragment is the only surviving evidence

text: 1) List the objects that could have made the mark. 2) Recreate the mark with each candidate. 3) Compare each result with the original. 4) Keep the candidates that match and narrow the suspects.
when: a specific mark is found and the set of possible tools is known

text: 1) Name each mark and the question it answers. 2) Measure overall size, span and proportions, recording them apart from the visual impression. 3) Eliminate candidates with clear mismatch. 4) Report any match as tentative.
when: only fragments of a trace survive
why: Measured records and explicit tentativeness keep conclusions from outrunning faint evidence

text: 1) Record the damage and infer the tool's shape from its marks. 2) Locate candidate tools. 3) Compare each candidate's marks with the damaged surface. 4) Measure and sketch each tool so the comparison can be repeated. 5) Test the fit with the actual tool.
when: damage suggests a specific tool was used
why: A repeatable, measured comparison is more reliable than judging fit by eye.

text: 1) Sort each fragment into a flat container in the order found. 2) Find a pre-joined clump and use it as the central anchor. 3) Build outward from the anchor. 4) Mark any filled-in gaps as inferred.
when: When reassembling a torn or fragmented document.
why: A stable central piece gives a reliable starting point and keeps each addition traceable.

text: Split a fragment that carries writing on both sides to create a blank backing before reassembling it.
when: When reconstructing double-sided paper fragments.
why: A blank backing lets the piece join without covering one side's text.

text: 1) Sort fragments by edge: straight edges with text starting at them mark an opening. 2) Join pieces by overlapping torn words. 3) Check each join against edges and neighbouring words. 4) Keep alternative readings open until another clue decides.
when: A document has been torn and its fragments are available to align
why: Edge shape and overlapping text constrain which pieces fit together

text: 1) Take the broken fragment found on the body. 2) Pass it with the second fragment found elsewhere to the decision group. 3) Let each member check whether the ends fit. 4) Confirm the match is clean before accepting it.
when: Proving that two broken pieces of an object belong together before a group.
why: Letting several people check the fit independently makes the match more credible.

text: Partial fragments often cannot be reconstructed reliably; state any inferred reading as an inference and do not complete it with more meaning than the trace supports.
when: clues are damaged or incomplete
why: missing parts cannot be recovered with confidence.

text: Never let a single fragment or mark carry a conclusion alone; building a large theory on it inflates weak evidence until other evidence corroborates it.
when: a clue or lone physical trace is the only support for a conclusion
why: A fragment alone offers no way to verify it.

text: Confirm a partial text or impression's source against a known sample, such as handwriting, and recover its full text rather than inferring contents from the fragment.
why: A partial impression can be misread, and a fragment cannot establish contents.

text: When a story has passed through several hands, go back to the original place or witness, or question the first informant directly, to check the details.
when: A reconstruction depends on accounts that passed through several reporters.

text: Assemble partial documents from several locations so the player must collect each fragment to reconstruct the whole.
when: Designing a letter or record split across the world

text: Confirm a dying message fragment with other evidence before committing to a course of action based on it.
when: a partial message would drive a major decision such as an accusation or pursuit
why: Fragments are partial and can be misread, so unconfirmed meaning may mislead.

text: Do not name a culprit on the strength of a dying fragment alone.
when: a dying message is the only evidence against a suspect
why: A few incomplete words cannot establish guilt.

text: Match a torn fragment to a known item by close examination of its fibres, such as a fringe, against a known sample.
when: a fragment is found at a scene and the owner's garment is known

text: Track which message fragments the player has heard, so earlier words gain meaning when a later fragment arrives.
when: a game lets players collect message fragments over time
why: Fragments only gain meaning when linked, so the game must remember what was heard.

text: Verify a claimed source by asking details that only the true source would know.
