Reveal a non-verbal character's past only in fragments that the player must assemble.
when: designing non-verbal companion NPCs

text: Mark which conclusions a player can prove and which remain suspicions, so the game clearly separates belief from evidence.
when: Designing an investigation where the player forms theories.
why: Players can misread suspicion as fact unless the game distinguishes them.

text: Sort overlapping prints and smudges by source before concluding that they came from one person.
why: Superimposed marks can look like a single source

text: Hide clues in burned or torn remnants that the player must combine, as in an inspection or crafting puzzle.
Match the full sequence of marks, including the gaps, rather than relying on a single distinctive mark.
when: Comparing a partial trace with a candidate

text: Who is present in a house decides who would be framed, so the obvious suspect shifts with the people who were there.
A scapegoat with a verifiable alibi or clean record is unlikely to be framed successfully, since others will check those facts.
when: Assessing whether a frame will hold
why: Verifiable records let investigators disprove the accusation

text: A frame feels arbitrary unless the framed character has a real tie to the scene, so give the accused a believable link to it.
when: Choosing who to frame
why: Unconnected frames look contrived

text: Compare planted evidence with the habits of the person it implicates; physical traces can be planted, but personal habits are harder to fake.
when: When evidence looks too neat or too consistent with one suspect.
why: Staged items often contradict the routine of the framed person.

text: A mistaken shared frame tends to survive argument and gives way mainly when events contradict it.
when: when a community clings to a doubtful belief despite critique
why: people revise frames under observed failure more than under reasoning

text: NPC responses that change with how the player frames a question let a tone choice unlock different information.
Extra steps taken to shift blame create additional traces that a player or investigator can find, so they can serve as deliberate detection points.
when: Designing a scripted cover-up or frame-up.
why: Each added action leaves a further record or inconsistency.

text: A frame is a set of planted items that all support one false story, such as a booking, cash, a disguise and a stated motive.
when: when a culprit wants blame to fall on a specific person
why: each item reinforces the others and makes the story believable

text: Framing a question or presentation can change how a statement reads or how an expert's estimate is answered, with no new facts. Tie each reading to the facts.
when: when an estimate is questioned under pressure or a statement is interpreted
why: framing changes the answer or reading given, not the evidence

text: A frame with gaps invites questions, and an unexplained key or exit route gives the defence its strongest arguments.
when: A planted frame is built
why: Unexplained details become points of attack

text: 1) List everyone who could have entered the place. 2) For each document, ask who could have written it or swapped a page. 3) Note when each access could have happened.
when: items may have been planted

text: Let an NPC copy another character's outfit or tracks to frame them, and give the player a visible mismatch to detect.
Frame a witness interview as voluntary and private, asking for help rather than making a charge, so the witness feels free to cooperate.
when: questioning a witness without formal authority

text: Place a planted item pointing at an NPC with a test, such as an alibi or time record, that players can run to discover the frame.
when: Designing a false lead in a quest.

text: Keep the framing questions alongside recorded answers, since answers alone hide the premise that shaped them.
when: recording interrogations

text: Treat a relative's complaint or serious accusation as a claim with possible private motive, not as proof of intent or truth.
when: A relative complains about an estate division or makes a serious accusation.
why: Grievances are often voiced as bluster, and family ties give the accuser access and believability while grudges can drive the claim.

text: A frame is a false reconstruction of a past event, built from planted facts and withheld accounts, that shifts blame onto an innocent party.
A framed person can appear guilty through motive, testimony and circumstance until a late fact overturns the reading.
when: An innocent person is set up to take the blame
why: Each piece of evidence fits the false story when read alone

text: A person facing financial crime may fake their death to escape pursuit and later enjoy the proceeds in safety.
when: someone is under threat of prosecution for money crimes
why: a presumed death ends the pursuit

text: A respectable surface can conceal wrongdoing from observers and from the wrongdoer, so a polished image does not reveal what lies beneath.
Planted evidence may be fabricated if it seems too convenient, sits oddly, or shows fresh scarring or a timing mismatch that a careful examiner finds; check how it got there.
when: Evidence seems to point neatly at one person.
why: A framer places items where the blame will land.

text: A real object or signal can be turned against an innocent character, so suspicion falls on someone who did not commit the act.
when: when designing suspicion among NPCs
why: Players must weigh competing evidence, which makes the framing a meaningful test.

text: A reported sighting that cannot be true may be invented, and the invention itself points toward the fabricator's motive.
when: a sighting conflicts with physical or timing facts
why: a false report is made to serve a purpose

text: Charge an official with deliberately letting offenders escape only on the strongest evidence; hidden shielding by subordinates is usually the more plausible explanation.
why: Deliberate complicity is a heavier charge than suppression by intermediaries.

text: Plant evidence giving an innocent character both means and motive, such as revenge against someone with a grievance, so the true actor stays out of view.
when: A scene needs a second suspect to draw attention from the real actor.
why: Planted items that fit a plausible motive can redirect suspicion.

text: A framer picks a target with suspicious circumstances, such as debts or hidden attachments, and supplies a story that explains the evidence, so the false case is built from partly true pieces.
when: Someone wants suspicion to fall on an innocent party
why: Partly true evidence makes the false conclusion harder to detect

text: A false suspicion that is acted on costs something, such as a lost ally or wasted time, so wrong inferences have consequences.
Actions an accused person takes after a frame can read as guilt, so the frame strengthens as the person responds.
when: A framed character acts to defend themselves
why: Staged context reinterprets innocent acts

text: Give a character a visible false motive, and place the true motive on a separate trail the player must find to see the real plan.
when: A character's known grudge could explain the events
why: A visible motive absorbs suspicion

text: An expected gain can be tied to a feared future change, such as a new will after a rival relationship forms, which raises the motive.
A culprit can steer an investigator toward a false suspect by feeding an existing grudge, so the suggestion feels confirmed and attention leaves the real secret.
when: The investigator already holds a suspicion about someone.
why: Confirmation of a prior belief makes the false lead feel reliable.

text: Fabricated accounts gain trust through five devices: a named credible source, an intermediary, exclusivity, admitted editing, and concrete specifics.
Claimed visions and unverifiable testimony can be invented, e.g. by a skilled deceiver showing innocent people to halt pursuit; check the gap between claim and source.
when: when a source of testimony cannot be checked
why: Nothing in the report can expose a staged or invented vision.

text: Reports can build a false impression of activity or contact even when the sources behind them have no real knowledge of it.
when: when press reports are used as evidence
why: Parties with a stake in an outcome can shape what is published.

text: A confident public account that offers a false motive can spread quickly and be taken as true, even when its facts only repeat unverified memory.
Too much staged noise makes a trail look accidental rather than planned, weakening the misdirection.
why: Excessive disturbance reads as chaos instead of deliberate design

text: 1) Leave an incriminating item where the suspect's household will find it. 2) Remove items that point back at the framer or reveal intent. 3) Erase traces that would clear the suspect. 4) Lock the door so the household seems to have sealed it.
when: A culprit wants an investigation to target a chosen suspect
why: Selective traces steer the investigation

text: 1) Show the framing threat on the page. 2) Let the player see the plan forming. 3) Spring the trap only after the threat is visible.
when: Escalating mid-game tension around a possible frame-up.
why: A visible plan makes the trap feel earned and lets the player act before it closes.

text: 1) Show the killer buying or preparing the tools early. 2) Place planted evidence where a plausible suspect will find it. 3) Reveal the purpose of the preparations only after the frame takes hold.
when: when designing a frame-up plot
why: Preparations shown early make the later frame legible on reflection, and the planted evidence arises from the game's own logic.

text: Lure an NPC away with a fabricated message or invented story whose real purpose is the absence; give the player a limited window before the NPC returns.
when: designing a timed search puzzle
why: A false pretext removes the NPC from the scene without a hard block.

text: Let an unsigned note in a dungeon push players toward a particular NPC, even when the note is a lie.
Before using a false or partly invented accusation, weigh the harm it could do to an innocent person and to bystanders who may take the words as fact.
why: listeners may treat the speaker's words as established fact

text: Use gossip or rumour items to supply false motives that the player must weigh against physical evidence such as signs of violence or messages at the scene.
when: designing red herring story items
why: players must test motives against proof

text: A frame needs a stated motive and a believable chain of evidence. Without a motive, planted items look arbitrary.
when: when constructing a false implication against someone
why: motive gives the planted items a reason to exist

text: Treat a frame-up as a hypothesis to test, not as a default explanation for every case.
why: Most cases with strong evidence are not staged.

text: A witness who fears punishment may stop contesting a false statement, believing a retraction will not be credited over a confession.
when: a witness wants to take back testimony under threat
why: examiners credit confessions over denials

text: A grand jury can return a no true bill, ending the case before trial; the accused may then be released on paying costs.
Read each article of a multi-part verdict separately, since one ruling can condemn one act, clear another, and make a sanction conditional.
Insist on guarantees that do not depend on the suspect's word before accepting a restitution offer.
why: A verbal promise cannot protect the victim

text: A guarantee answers only the fear it addresses; other fears the witness holds remain, and should not be assumed gone.
Define a game crime by intent or allegiance, so players prove guilt through plot evidence such as letters, meetings or pledges rather than a physical act.
when: when designing crimes in a game world

text: In a setting where a law criminalizes an act, require players to prove the act happened, not the magical effect the law assumes.
when: Designing in-world law for a game

text: Gate a sensitive detail or evidence behind a rapport or trust meter, an earned trust cue, or a set game point, so players build a relationship before it is revealed.
when: designing NPC dialogue that hides key information

text: Start dialogue with low-stakes topics; unlock pointed or sensitive questions only after rapport, supporting evidence or a trigger, since pressing too early closes later options.
when: designing a dialogue system with sensitive subjects
why: Early trust makes sensitive topics less likely to shut the conversation down.

text: Plant a passing remark that pays off later, even one a speaker laughs off; have the reveal explicitly recall it, since casual lines are easily overlooked.
when: when planting information for a late reveal or constructing clues for a mystery
why: casual mention is easily forgotten and feels fair when recalled

text: Hide a key document or locked compartment in a hidden drawer or passage, signal its existence elsewhere, and make it a reward giving a reason to return.
Show a threat or trace only in part, holding back its full meaning so the audience supplies the rest and connects it to later evidence.
when: building suspense before a reveal or when a trace will matter later in the story
why: partial views activate the imagination

text: A passing remark by a tavern or casino NPC can gain weight once a later room or item is discovered.
when: placing dialogue early in a game
why: a remark that seems idle becomes meaningful with later discovery

text: Tell the audience what to compare before the reveal, so the recognition has context to land.
why: a clue needs a reference point to be recognised

text: A detail a speaker mentions in passing, such as an unusual pay arrangement, is worth a short confirming question before moving on.
why: Incidental details often expose inconsistencies or motives

text: Design some NPCs to reveal information only when no other NPC is present, so the player must separate characters to learn it.
Weigh what each possible actor gains from a hidden outcome; a motive is more plausible when disclosure would publish damaging facts.
when: choosing suspects from a set of possible actors

text: Divide clues into those that point toward a suspect and those that prove guilt, so suggestive evidence cannot unlock the final accusation.
when: designing an investigation with several clues

text: Use delayed news such as a notice or rumour to pace a mystery, so the player waits between revelations.
when: Pacing a mystery across a generated level or quest.
why: Spacing revelations creates anticipation between discoveries.

text: A constraint, such as needing a second person, can point the player toward where a helper is hidden.
when: Designing NPC locations for a puzzle
why: The constraint narrows the search space for the player.

text: Present conflicting clues first and let the planted order emerge only as the player assembles them, rewarding players who keep unexplained facts.
A confidant who holds a secret can serve as a gated information source that the player must earn.
A quest can end a scene on uncertainty, such as a sound behind a door, so the player must continue to learn the cause.
when: when designing a quest scene ending
why: unresolved cues motivate the next step

text: Let a secret held by one NPC be leaked when a second NPC applies pressure, and make the leak a trigger for the next quest stage.
when: Designing progression through NPC secrets
why: The leak connects two characters and advances the plot.

text: An NPC offering several opening lines can unlock a hidden topic, with the player's tone or choices determining whether the NPC reveals it.
when: when a clue is hidden behind a reluctant character
why: Multiple entry points let different approaches reach the same secret

text: A later event that matches an earlier joking remark turns it into a confirmed prediction, shifting listeners from doubt to belief.
Small items such as a button, a torn wrapper or a stain can persist in the world and be found later, letting the player rebuild a sequence of events.
when: designing a clue system
why: the items keep their state until discovered

text: A delayed discovery sets the time window for a crime in a level timeline, since the event could have occurred any time before discovery.
Treating each clue as a filter condition and counting NPCs that satisfy all of them lets a generator tune how hard a deduction is.
when: Generating clue sets for a deduction puzzle.
why: Each added condition narrows the candidate set.

text: Evidence can be revealed in tiers: each accepted clue unlocks the next line of testimony, so progress is gated by the proof the player presents.
when: when designing an interrogation scene that the player drives with evidence
why: Gating testimony behind clues rewards careful evidence use over guessing.

text: A non-player investigator holding a private theory reveals it only when the player supplies matching evidence, which paces disclosure.
when: when designing an NPC who knows more than they say
why: gated disclosure ties information release to player progress

text: Social events such as dinners or festivals can open conversations that remain locked outside them, rewarding patient play.
when: Designing gated NPC dialogue.
why: Shared hospitality lowers guard and creates natural openings.

text: Model clues as a graph where a physical item links two or more characters, and lock dependent clues until the identity node is confirmed.
when: Generating interlinked investigation content
why: Gating prevents players from building conclusions on an unverified identity

text: A list makes weak points look as strong as firm ones unless each item is graded by how well it is supported.
A partly visible clue may read as a smudge and be missed by the searcher.
1) Write each deduction as a separate claim. 2) Grade it as established, probable or speculative. 3) List the events that support it.
when: building a conclusion from many events

text: 1) Begin with a slow approach. 2) Add a detour that delays arrival. 3) Give a last chance to leave. 4) Present the player's choice to confess or flee.
when: Staging a climactic confrontation before a key choice
why: Each gate adds pressure before the decision, making the choice weightier.

text: 1) List every clue placed in the content. 2) Check that each clue appears in at least one step of the replayed sequence. 3) Flag any clue that no step uses.
when: generating a case that must be solvable
why: A clue no step uses is either noise or a broken chain

text: Promise a payoff for every open question or promised reveal and never leave threads permanently unresolved, since an unpaid question frustrates the audience and erodes trust.
why: An unpaid question frustrates the audience.

text: Unlock dialogue bluff or sharper follow-up options only when the player holds a matching clue; store an omitted detail as a hidden flag that only that follow-up reveals.
when: designing interrogation or NPC dialogue that withholds information
why: Bluffs should rest on something the player actually has.

text: Gate a motive reveal or character-related reward behind a second independent NPC who confirms the claim, so corroborated claims unlock more than single-source ones.
when: designing reveals
why: Corroboration makes the reveal credible.

text: Gate a level's key reveal behind a sequence of scenes or locations, each ending on an unanswered question that the next partly resolves, so anticipation accumulates.
when: designing multi-location investigations or sequencing reveals across levels
why: Sequenced gating paces the reveal and keeps the player moving.

text: Open on a mystery only when the question will be paid off later; an opening puzzle should not be left hanging.
when: Planning an opening image with a hidden cause
why: Players expect opening puzzles to pay off

text: An NPC gatekeeper can withhold a clue until the player meets a condition or gives a reason for asking.
when: Designing an NPC who guards information
why: Conditioned release makes the clue feel earned and ties it to the player's reasons

text: Let a confidential NPC reveal background only when the player asks the right question, which can open a new investigation branch.
A payoff should follow from a detail introduced earlier, never appear for the first time at the reveal.
Unlock each next quest question only after the previous fact is confirmed, so the quest log follows the chain.
when: designing quest logic

text: Gate a key reveal on the player's own committed conclusion, so its arrival tests and rewards revising that theory.
Let an NPC share a secret only after the player brings a proof-of-goodwill item.
when: designing dialogue that withholds information
why: the item signals trust and unlocks cooperation

text: When a second entry route is raised, pay it off later, since a route never mentioned again leaves the audience feeling cheated.
Gate the reveal of a distinguishing trait behind a skill check or a dialogue with the right character, so the player must earn the identification.
when: when the trait is a key clue for a puzzle or quest

text: Gate finer readings of physical traces behind a specialist NPC who can interpret them precisely.
when: designing layered clue reading
why: Specialist access gives players a reason to seek out NPCs

text: Let an NPC accept a pretext only after the player has asked the right other characters first.
Gate a key NPC clue behind earlier dialogue answers, and let the NPC's reaction vary with which clue is shown first, so question order matters.
when: When designing dialogue that reveals evidence
why: Rewards careful sequencing

text: Let the player propose a theory, list its implications, and mark which implications the game's known facts contradict.
when: Designing a deduction interface for players.
why: Making implications explicit lets players test theories against evidence.

text: Reward players who ask what a large object was for, not only those who search for small items.
when: Designing clue discovery paths.
why: Rewarding functional reasoning supports varied investigation styles.

text: Give each generated clue a strength rating and a list of innocent explanations, and require a corroborating clue before an accusation unlocks; tag clues sharing a source as correlated.
when: when building a case-file system
why: keeps players from over-trusting clues that come from one NPC

text: Use a cancelled appointment in a character's schedule as a hook that leads the player to a second character.
Tag each clue item as traceable, untraceable or contextual so the generator and the player know which clues can identify a person.
when: Building a clue system for a generated case.
why: Explicit tags keep clues from failing silently.

text: Use a closed counter or locked door as a constraint that eliminates an option, and present it to the player as a clue.
when: Designing access constraints in a level or investigation.
why: Eliminating options through visible facts makes deduction satisfying.

text: Require proof before a character concedes a point, so the concession becomes a gated objective the player must earn.
when: When designing quest progression involving a stubborn NPC.
why: Conditional concessions turn persuasion into a clear task with a defined reward.

text: Make destructive actions such as cutting or breaking available only after gentler checks have been tried, then reveal hidden contents.
Make a ledger or inventory record accessible only after an NPC grants permission, with the NPC's willingness as the unlock condition.
when: Designing gated information in a game
why: Conditional access ties information reveal to relationship and trust

text: Let an NPC give partial information with tells such as hesitation or evasive phrasing, so players can detect omissions and press to unlock the rest.
when: Designing dialogue that reveals information gradually
why: Visible tells reward attentive questioning

text: Let a non-player character reveal a secret only after the player mentions an item, name or event they have already found.
when: Designing dialogue that gates information

text: Reveal a checkable NPC detail only after the player has separated the claim from the evidence.
when: Sequencing NPC information reveals.
why: Gating detail behind sorting rewards careful reasoning over passive listening.

text: Gate NPC information behind trust and tag sensitive topics, so a keyword that triggers a visible reaction shows the player where to press.
when: Designing dialogue that reveals secrets.
why: Visible reactions guide players toward the lines of questioning that matter.

text: Offer questions that do not name the target, but surface a clue only when the NPC holds the relevant fact, so information is gained by inquiry rather than by name.
when: designing dialogue options that reveal a hidden subject
why: Indirect questioning keeps the suspect unaware, and it rewards players who ask the right general questions.

text: A gatekeeper may hint at a next source or character without naming it, or at a condition pointing to a second location or later quest trigger, admitting nothing outright.
when: gatekeeper will not confess directly; designing gatekeeper NPC dialogue
why: hints move the story forward while protecting the gatekeeper; the refusal's stated reason and conditions give the player a path to hidden material

text: When a gatekeeper bound by client constraints blocks access to a witness or location, plan a second route to the same facts.
when: a formal channel refuses access to a witness or location
why: Formal gatekeepers follow their client's constraints, which limits what they will share.

text: A gatekeeper may yield a partial answer, useful only with another fact, after appeals to honesty or a credible claim of skill, even while doubting it will help.
when: requester argues an amateur can succeed where professionals cannot; or when building an interrogation scene

text: A gatekeeper's report about a visitor's appearance can decide whether she is admitted, and the gatekeeper's own opinion filters that report.
when: A visitor must pass a reporter before meeting the person in charge.
why: The reporter's words reveal their own taste and bias as much as the visitor's qualities.

text: Getting information from a gatekeeper depends on how the request is framed, on showing the requester can handle risk, and on accepting a partial answer.
when: player must extract information from an official through dialogue

text: Dialogue extraction suits an official who holds needed information; a gatekeeper with no reason to share will not be moved.
when: choosing whether an official can be used as a source

text: A gatekeeper NPC can refuse access to a witness until the player builds trust or gives a reason, and the refusal can be framed as protection.
when: When designing access restrictions to an information source.
why: Access gated by trust creates a meaningful progression.

text: Trust built in an earlier encounter lets a gatekeeper listen before any request is made, which changes how they respond.
when: character has met the gatekeeper in a previous scene
why: past favorable contact lowers guardedness

text: Let a gatekeeper NPC ask a fixed set of questions drawn from lore the player may have found. Answers matching the world state open the way.
Let gatekeeper NPCs be persuaded by a cover story or small bribe that opens a locked location or reveals a contact.
when: designing NPC access checks
why: cheap persuasion gives players a route that avoids combat

text: A gatekeeper NPC answers with true but general statements until the player shows a specific clue, then gives a partial fact.
when: When designing an NPC that guards information.
why: Specific evidence unlocks specific answers, which rewards investigation.

text: A general principle or belief, even when an authority endorses it, does not prove a specific accusation or claim drawn from it.
Stereotypes or motives assigned to a whole group, such as clergy or a nationality, lack case evidence and do not prove any individual's intent or conduct.
why: Group-level attribution unfairly implicates individuals who acted otherwise.

text: State what you know only in general terms, and let the suspect make the next move, rather than naming the culprit outright.
when: Questioning a suspect during an investigation.
why: A general statement invites a response without warning the culprit.

text: Each observer group sees only the role it expects, so assumptions about role let a person pass unnoticed among them.
when: A character crosses between social groups
why: Expectations filter what observers perceive.

text: A genuine victim can look staged, and a staged scene can still include real harm, so neither appearance settles the question.
when: Judging whether a scene was arranged.
why: Appearances mix real and arranged elements in the same event.

text: Assuming a culprit's identity from a general theory about who commits subtle crimes biases the search. Treat such theories as questions to test.
when: a general theory about offenders is offered

text: A grand motive can justify action against any suspect, so it does not prove that a particular person is guilty.
Generalizing about a whole group from a few incidents makes the observer blind to individuals who differ from the group.
Over-reading a common scent or paper type leads to false matches, so weigh how widely the material is available.
A symbolic gesture passed around a social table is read at once by those present, so its meaning must be clear in context.
A gesture or body position is not proof of guilt or a particular cause; first ask what innocent or injury-driven explanation exists.
why: Pacing is common when people are memorising material or under stress, and the same posture can result from different causes.

text: Victims found with open hands and extended limbs, showing no struggle, were probably taken by surprise.
Impressions implying a posture no one would choose freely suggest the subject was placed there, or could not move, which points toward restraint.
when: Measured distances between marks and the body suggest an unnatural pose
why: Free movement leaves a different pattern

text: A person still in the position they held at a known earlier moment probably has not moved since then.
when: Checking whether someone has left a place since a known moment

text: A body position that contradicts a stated account, such as a victim who supposedly ducked and fell forward, is a strong test of that account.
A character's habitual gesture, such as a handshake or toast, can carry a hidden function that the player recognises later.
when: Designing an NPC interaction with a concealed mechanism.
why: Routine acts are unlikely to be questioned, so the means of harm blends into normal behavior.

text: Posture and nervous gestures let the player read a character's state without dialogue.
Comparing one's own reach with a handprint is only approximate, since the result depends on the posture the person used.
why: Different postures change the reach without changing height.

text: A crouch or stoop widens the shooter height range, so the posture assumption must be stated and checked.
Hospitality, gifts and favours from a powerful host can be an attempt to buy goodwill, revealing what standing the host wants to secure.
when: a host offers gifts or advice to a visitor
why: goodwill can serve as a bid for influence

text: A courier chosen for discretion, and unable to read, keeps message contents hidden even under questioning, though she still knows where she went.
when: when a message must be carried without revealing its content
why: Inability to read removes the content from her knowledge.

text: A gift that the recipient is unlikely to use can be a plant, so an unusual gift is worth reading as a clue.
when: when a crime seems prepared in advance
why: an odd choice of gift can serve a hidden purpose

text: Routing a gift through an intermediary while keeping the giver unnamed lets the giver gain hidden influence over the recipients.
when: Modelling patronage or faction influence through gifts
why: The recipient does not know the source, so gratitude and control are not directed to the giver

text: Generous or friendly behaviour, especially when given publicly, does not establish innocence; it can frame self-interest as disinterest and lower others' guard.
when: a character offers gifts or favours, especially publicly while holding a private aim
why: kindness can be a tool for pursuing a hidden aim, and visible kindness lowers others' guard

text: A favoured reading may fail to explain parts of the evidence, so check the preferred reading against the facts it cannot explain.
A will favoring one person can be read as motive while another real beneficiary of other arrangements goes unnoticed.
Allowing a generous margin for travel time can hide how early a suspect could have left, so estimates should use realistic speeds.
why: padding travel time shifts the apparent earliest departure

text: A favour granted to a contact can be remembered as a debt that may cost the investigator later.
Treating a gift as proof of guilt is an error, because a gift can explain a trace without implicating the giver.
when: a trace came from a gift
why: The giver may have had no part in the act.

text: A promise of reciprocity makes an informant's account look more useful than it is.
when: An informant offers information in exchange for a favour.
why: The expectation of return inflates the perceived value of the information.

text: Let an NPC's offer of gifts, safe passage or shelter carry a hidden condition the player can discover later.
Use a generous-seeming offer as a red herring, and let the player test it against another NPC's warnings.
Record a favour given to an informant as a cost that affects later dialogue with that informant.
when: Designing information trades with NPCs.
why: Recorded costs make reciprocity have lasting consequences on relationships.

text: Use moved furniture, open doors and changed room use as clues that a presence is active in a space.
when: Designing environmental storytelling for a haunted or occupied location.
why: Physical rearrangement implies recent activity without dialogue.

text: Furnishings and marks in a room reveal what its usual occupants do there, letting an observer infer routines and hidden purposes without dialogue.
when: A setting must signal a social routine, habit, or hidden purpose without explicit exposition.
why: Objects are physical residue of repeated activity, so they carry evidence of who uses a space and how.

text: A witness's fear can make an ordinary event seem supernatural, but the fear may be real even when its supposed cause is not.
when: A witness reports an uncanny event while frightened
why: Fear shapes perception and turns a crime into a legend, yet the emotion itself is genuine

text: Fog and smoke reduce visibility, leaving distant objects indistinct and sometimes losing moving animals from view.
when: An observer looks across a foggy or smoky space
why: Reduced visibility blurs distant detail and hides moving targets.

text: Gothic atmosphere can make an ordinary human explanation seem supernatural, so do not accept a supernatural reading while a human one remains available.
when: A scene is staged with dark or eerie atmosphere.
why: Atmosphere raises the sense of mystery and lowers scrutiny.

text: A bounded setting can create false comfort, since the obvious suspects nearest the scene may be the only ones examined while others go unchecked.
when: Investigating within a small, enclosed location.
why: Proximity to the scene draws attention, and an apparently complete list can still miss people further away.

text: Let a repeated test change a sound's rhythm so players can tell an echo from a second source.
when: Designing responsive audio in a level.
why: Changed timing gives players evidence that separates an echo from an independent source.

text: Public consensus shifts with attention and can be wrong, so it is weak proof of what happened.
when: When an event is accepted because many people believe it
why: Shared belief spreads without independent evidence

text: A confident account from one character can set the group's expectation, so the audience adopts the wrong motive and stops checking it against the physical evidence.
when: a suspect or witness offers an early theory
why: People accept a shared explanation before testing it.

text: A confident group consensus about cause of death can be wrong. Check the wound directly rather than trusting the earlier assumption.
Consult several experts on an ambiguous rule, since conflicting readings show how uncertain the motive really is.
Visitors who seek out accusers for help carry the accusations home, so the accusations reach communities far from their origin.
when: when accusers offer consultations to outsiders
why: each visitor becomes a new channel for the claim

text: Group consensus among officials can outweigh a correct minority view, so a lone investigator may be overruled.
when: officials disagree about a suspect's identity

text: Agreement among authorities can hide a shared error, because later sources often repeat the same premise rather than test it.
1) Identify each source that supports a belief. 2) Trace where each source's authority came from. 3) Merge sources that share an origin. 4) Count the remaining independent sources.
when: Judging whether apparent agreement is independent evidence.
why: Consolidating shared origins reveals how much real support exists.

text: Do not dismiss a consensus merely because it is consensus, since experience counts and officials are not always wrong.
Offer a compare-notes action that lets players collect contradicting accounts, and use the group's silence as a clue.
when: When designing a player action to gather witness accounts.
why: Comparing accounts tests reliability and surfaces what no one saw.

text: A grudge shows who had a reason to act, not who did, so check opportunity and whether the money would have passed to them anyway.
Grudges outlive their holder: resentment over a lost inheritance passes to heirs, and faction resentment spreads house to house, keeping hostility toward later leaders.
when: a family member lost money through a passed-over inheritance
why: a grudge can outlive the person who first felt it

text: Accounts from someone holding a grudge are shaped by spite, so discount their harsh claims; a speaker's grudge or an observer's disapproval colours what gets reported.
when: a witness has a visible grudge against the subject of their testimony
why: Hostility shapes what a speaker emphasizes and how they describe others.

text: Misfortunes, such as illness after a rival's visit or a run of mishaps after a dispute, get blamed on the feud, since an existing quarrel supplies a ready cause.
when: harm follows soon after a visit or confrontation with a rival, or a run of misfortunes follows a dispute
why: the existing grudge or quarrel supplies a ready cause

text: A judgment of a new person can rest on earlier grief or resentment toward someone similar, so the verdict reflects the past more than the present.
when: a character judges a person resembling a lost or disliked one
why: prior loss shapes present perception

text: A witness report can be honest and still unreliable, because grief and anger fill in what was not observed.
when: A witness who suffered loss reports events
why: Strong emotion supplies the missing details

text: A grieving or horrified witness describes the victim's body in emotional terms, and the first impression is dominated by the body rather than by the surroundings.
when: when a witness first encounters a death scene
why: strong emotion takes over attention, so the room is recorded later

text: A witness with a grudge may volunteer complaints about a third party that a neutral witness would keep back.
when: a witness has a personal grievance

text: A witness's grief at seeing evidence can show that the working theory is wrong, so the investigator should revise it rather than defend it.
Suspicion often follows existing quarrels, property disputes and family tensions more than fresh evidence.
when: when a new accusation targets someone already in conflict
why: people reach for a known grievance to explain events

text: When a legal dispute stalls, disputants often move the contest onto the ground, such as by felling a disputed tree or mustering crews.
when: when a land dispute fails in court
why: physical contest continues where legal channels have failed

text: Grief over a death can push a person to blame a nearby figure for it, so emotional strain can act as a hidden motive for an accusation.
when: an accuser has recently lost someone close
why: Blaming someone gives the loss a target. This is a hypothesis to test, not a fact.

text: A pending land lawsuit can make a rival a source of sworn accusations, and the accused may still never be tried.
Communities tend to treat whoever clears and fences land as its rightful owner, since labor is seen as adding most of its value.
when: land is cleared and improved by a settler
why: labor is seen as the main source of land value

text: An accusation from a witness with a long-held grudge is easy to dismiss, because the listener sees the accuser's bias and stops there.
when: the accuser has a long-standing grievance
why: bias is visible and tempting to treat as the answer

text: Boundary controversies between neighbors can later aggravate larger feuds that surface under pressure, even when each quarrel was handled courteously at the time.
when: when a land quarrel between households precedes a larger conflict
why: earlier disputes leave a ledger of grievance that later conflicts draw on

text: A grievance plot is driven by a rising run of small humiliations and quarrels, and its central question is who is deceiving whom, not a single whodunit.
A motive can originate in events long before the crime, such as a secret past that threatens a person's reputation or legitimacy.
when: A crime is tied to a hidden history rather than a recent event

text: A witness who only fixes when they parted from a suspect sets a timeline boundary but does not prove where the suspect was during the crime.
Disputes that move through petitions, town votes and higher approval leave a dated paper trail that shows how tension escalated.
Creditors may pursue a deceased person's estate, or even the body, over debts, so grievances can continue after death through legal channels.
Land disputes produce sworn depositions, lawsuits and lasting rivalries that record who had a stake in a boundary.
when: Assessing who had an interest in a piece of land
why: Disputes make the stakeholders and their claims visible in formal records

text: Legal fees and imprisonment costs can be paid by seizing a household's goods, so a lawsuit can fall on property itself.
when: A family faces legal action and penalties
why: Fees and costs may be recovered directly from movable possessions

text: Local sayings about a feud show that a community has already framed the grievance as a motive.
Treat an accusation from someone with a grievance against the accused as a lead to test, not a finding, because a grudge can steer testimony.
when: a suspect is named by a person with a personal grudge, or a witness points at a household member
why: a grudge can steer testimony

text: Before accepting an accusation that matches a grudge, ask who supplied it, who quarrelled with whom, and who gains from the outcome, since the grudge may have produced it.
A dispute record can supply a suspect's motive without revealing who acted, so players can use it as a lead rather than a verdict.
when: Designing a motive for a suspect in an investigation
why: Shared motive narrows suspicion but does not identify the actor

text: Informants with grievances, such as dismissed servants, can reveal internal household secrets but may exaggerate, so their claims need corroboration.
why: Grievance motivates disclosure and also distorts it

text: Judge a bereaved person's emotional demeanour against their relationship history and known character, not against a stock script of how grief should look.
when: A witness's reaction after a death seems odd or muted
why: People express loss differently, and relationship history often explains a reaction that a generic script would misread

text: A past partnership that ended in threats is worth testing as a motive, because the reason for violence is already on record.
when: When a past dispute has been documented.
why: A recorded conflict gives a concrete reason rather than speculation.

text: Resolve a feud gradually, removing root causes in well-timed steps, rather than relying on one decisive act.
when: mediating a long-running conflict
why: Root causes return if only the surface is addressed.

text: When accused families hold land that rivals claim, old land grievances often overlap with the accusations.
Map property stakes and grudges when several accusations come from one circle, since accusers may gain from the accused's seizure.
when: several accusations come from the same circle

text: Let a rival NPC voice a suspicion so the player must test it rather than being told the answer.
Allow small or personal motives, such as revenge or minor gain, to drive NPC plot events.
Limit how many parallel secrets exist in one area so the mystery stays readable.
when: Populating an area with side mysteries.
why: Too many simultaneous threads overwhelm the player.

text: A grudge or a wish to protect one's position can colour every detail of an account, so each detail needs independent checking.
A quarrel over a boundary, shared property or livestock plants a grudge that resurfaces as a formal accusation and can draw in a wider circle of people.
when: after a dispute between neighbours over a boundary or livestock
why: unresolved grievances persist and get reused when a new accusation is needed

text: A private dispute can draw in neighbors through testimony and gossip, so people with no stake in it still take sides.
when: a dispute is discussed publicly or given as evidence
why: testimony and talk spread involvement beyond the parties

text: Accomplice NPCs with grudges can leak information when offered protection, so distrust can be modelled as a stat that changes what each NPC reveals.
when: When designing NPCs whose willingness to share depends on relationships.
why: Grudges lower loyalty, making protection a lever that opens disclosure.

text: A change made in many small steps can pass every single check, so only the trend across checks reveals it.
when: Appearance or identity changes over time
why: No single check sees a break

text: A grudge can pass through family ties: a refused match between two households can later reach a third person through a marriage link.
why: Kinship links carry old disputes into new accusations.

text: A prolonged estate dispute can strain a whole household and may contribute to later distress in one of its members.
why: The strain is a plausible contributing cause, not a proven one.

text: Encode NPC relationships as a graph of marriages, inheritances and alliances, and let grudges propagate along those edges to new NPCs.
when: when designing NPC relationships in a game

text: Repeated land lawsuits keep contested claims in public view and sustain feuds between neighbours over many years.
why: Each new filing reopens the dispute in front of the community

text: A boundary defined by a particular house can turn a small dispute into a dispute over the whole community.
A map layer of land claims and parish lines defines which NPCs side with which faction, so a boundary change creates new suspects.
A relationship or grudge flag that changes how later clues are read lets a past dispute distort the player's interpretation of evidence, and each rumour's source should be visible.
An NPC's acceptance of a player's accusation can depend on the strength of the evidence and the NPC's standing with other characters.
when: In quest and faction design
why: Credibility is shaped by both proof and social standing.

text: Track rumours along NPC relationships, so a grudge between two NPCs raises the chance that one accuses the other, and the player can trace who started the story.
Model property and inheritance records as a searchable motive system, letting players trace deeds and probate documents to find who gained, lost or was trusted.
Trusting a witness who holds a grudge, or an accusation it drives, can fix an investigation on the wrong person and waste the search for the real culprit.
A document that records a family grievance creates a possible motive without proving the grievance led to an act.
when: Evaluating a bitter document as motive.
why: Resentment recorded in writing is not the same as action taken on it.

text: Witnesses may downplay a relationship or claim slight acquaintance, so casually described ties need corroboration from others.
Mistaking a suspect's real grief or sincerity for proof of innocence, or accepting a folk ordeal as a valid test.
when: Judging a suspect after an emotional scene.
why: Emotional sincerity and superstition do not establish facts.

text: Taking a stated grievance at face value, without comparing it to what was already agreed, misreads the dispute.
Buying unrelated goods to justify your presence costs time and money and can still fail if the subject leaves while you wait.
why: The cover consumes resources without guaranteeing the trail.

text: Treating neighbours' quarrels and livestock losses as proof of guilt is fragile: an accuser acting from spite can break the whole chain.
when: evidence is built from social grievances
why: Small grievances can motivate the accuser, so the chain is only as reliable as its motives.

text: 1) Record which families sit on each committee or seat. 2) Trace recurring family names across years to follow a grudge over time.
when: a community has long-kept records
why: Recurring names expose enduring rivalries that single events hide.

text: Record disputes such as boundaries, debts or broken promises as discoverable motives, and let a rival's accusation point to an older grudge revealed through household or property records.
when: when building a motive for an NPC-driven crime or designing accusation quests
why: Discoverable motives let players judge plausibility.

text: Let an NPC's old grudge or minor insult become a rumour that grows as characters repeat it, each repetition tied to a named accuser.
when: designing village rumour systems

text: Plant an NPC with a grudge against another as a red herring, and reward the player for recognizing the grudge as the motive behind the accusation.
Use a grudge as motive only when a source ties it to the act itself, not merely to the suspect's character or past quarrels.
when: when a grudge is offered as the motive for an accusation
why: an older quarrel does not establish that the suspect committed a new act

text: A witness's quarrel with the accused explains why they may speak, but does not by itself show that their account is false.
when: When judging a witness with a known dispute.
why: A motive makes an account suspect, not wrong; its content must be checked separately.

text: Give each suspect a motive the player can rate, and let a weak motive still matter when combined with other clues.
when: Designing suspect motives in a generated mystery
why: Players weigh motives, and weak ones gain value through combination

text: Design NPC motives so one motive explains two roles, and let the player find the link through evidence.
when: When designing linked NPCs in a mystery.
why: One motive connecting two roles rewards deduction.

text: Model property boundaries and shared fences as triggers for disputes, and track each NPC's grudges over time so they can later become accusations.
when: when generating neighbouring households or villages
why: boundary disputes give durable, traceable motives

text: Store grudges with timestamps and let them fade, so an NPC acts on an old feud only while the grudge is still held.
when: NPCs carry memories of past incidents
why: Stale grudges create false motives

text: An extra or missing guard in a count signals a disguised or dead character, making headcount discrepancies usable as clues.
when: a count of guards or NPCs is shown to the player
why: Discrepancies between expected and observed numbers point to hidden status changes.

text: A guard animal's silence is evidence of no intrusion only if its reliability is known.
Give a guard NPC an entry log so players reconstruct a sequence by asking about count, order and appearance, not by receiving a single name.
when: Designing an NPC witness in a dungeon or level
why: Partial sequences make players reason rather than look up an answer

text: Let a guard stationed at one door act as a witness, and use line-of-sight and audio cues so players can check what the guard could see or hear.
when: designing guard NPCs near key chokepoints
why: limits on sight and sound make the guard's report testable

text: Give a guard a motive, such as a personal attachment to a prisoner, so players have a reason to question the guard's report.
when: designing guard NPCs who report events
why: a bias gives players grounds to doubt the report

text: A repeated guess hardens into assumed fact without new evidence; label inferred steps as guesswork and promote a reading only when evidence supports it.
when: A character, player or source reuses an uncertain interpretation or conjectured link.
why: Repetition feels like confirmation; labels separate confirmed timeline entries from assumptions.

text: People facing a visible mark with several plausible readings tend to choose the reading they want, so their guesses reveal their hopes.
when: A mark, sign or inscription has no settled meaning
why: Interpretation is shaped by what the reader wants to believe

text: Use a guess as a probe: the subject's confirming, correcting, or despairing reaction reveals their view or confirms the guess, without a direct accusation.
Treat a guessed routine or a hider's habits as a question or ranking only; confirm it against physical evidence before trusting it.
when: Deducing a hiding place or routine from another's habits.
why: Reasoning about another person's mind is uncertain and can mislead.

text: Offer a guessed name and invite correction; people often fix spelling or form, confirming identity without a direct accusation.
when: verifying a name tied to an alias
why: correction is a neutral reaction, not an admission

text: Asking the listener to guess draws them into deduction, so the reveal is earned rather than simply told.
when: A secret is about to be disclosed
why: Active deduction makes the listener a participant in the reveal.

text: Speculative reconstruction built on unknown circumstances tends to be wrong; reasoning should rest on known facts rather than imagined scenes.
when: Judging how an event probably happened when key circumstances are unknown.
why: Filling gaps with invented detail produces reconstructions that often fail.

text: Each unverified link becomes the premise for the next, so a chain drifts beyond evidence; check each link independently before trusting it.
when: An investigator builds a conclusion from a partial clue or guess.
why: Unchecked inventive links can drift far from the evidence.

text: Keep each hypothesis provisional, whether tidy, plausible or intuitive; a neat story or motive can harden and steer the investigation down a false path.
when: Reasoning through competing accounts, a plausible motive, or an intuitive guess.
why: Attachment to a neat story hides contrary facts; an intuitive guess without evidence is only a suspicion.

text: Guessing who made an improvised repair from its look, such as assuming a sailor tied it, or acting on a guessed ability rather than a demonstrated one, turns a theory into an unproven accusation.
An explanation that fits only the headline facts can leave one clear detail unexplained, so accepting it early misleads the investigation.
Attacking a witness by attributing views they never held is a distraction; the witness can ask which claim is meant and expose the misattribution.
Invented detail can be disproved later, and one disproved claim discredits everything else the speaker said.
why: a single checkable falsehood undermines the whole account

text: A claimed loss can be invented to explain why someone possesses an item.
A target under questioning may invent a plausible substitute detail, so a correct-sounding answer does not prove innocence.
why: Stress pushes people to fill gaps in memory with convincing details.

text: Headings supplied by guesswork in an earlier transcription can assign a document to the wrong case or date.
Guessing contents from a partial or abbreviated label can settle on a wrong but common substance.
why: fragments invite the most familiar reading

text: Treat a strong intuition as a pointer toward a relevant parallel, and test it against case facts; resemblance alone is never proof.
why: a parallel can feel right yet fail the evidence

text: Hail a fast vehicle from a point away from the usual stand, so foot pursuers cannot keep up.
when: Needing to break a pursuit in a city
why: Foot pursuers cannot match a fast vehicle

text: 1) Obtain known samples of the writer's hand and signature. 2) Judge the disputed writing on its own, then place it beside them, reproduced at the same scale. 3) Compare letter forms line by line, noting shared forms that differ in slope or detail. 4) Judge authenticity or single authorship only from that comparison.
when: A document's authenticity or author is central to a claim or in doubt.
why: Authenticity can only be assessed against known samples; step-by-step comparison exposes resemblance and difference rather than a quick verdict.

text: Compare anonymous writing with known signed samples and interlineations of similar length and type; a match ties the writer, but may point to more than one writer.
when: Attributing anonymous writing to a person, especially when a name or seal cannot be trusted alone.
why: Samples of similar form make the comparison meaningful.

text: Handwriting resemblance is not identity: carelessness, disguise or gloves can change a hand; report attribution hedged, open to more than one reading, never as proof or from handwriting alone.
why: Handwriting alone has limited reliability.

text: Handwriting is weak evidence and experts may disagree, even on disguise; relying on an expert without noting limits invites being overturned under challenge.
when: Handwriting is offered as proof of authorship, or expert readings of a damaged document are used as evidence.
why: Expert opinions have bounded confidence that opposing sides can attack; disguised script gives too little to conclude reliably.

text: Handwriting conclusions need known comparison samples from the suspect or a second source; testimony about the writing is not proof, so do not authenticate an unfamiliar hand without them.
why: Without comparison material, conclusions are easily overclaimed and rest only on whoever holds the papers.

text: Model handwriting or prints as puzzle mechanics: give players a suspect's known sample to compare against a forged or altered note; comparison is a concrete, checkable method.
when: Designing document-based deduction puzzles or forgery clues.
why: Comparison lets players test authorship themselves.

text: An unfamiliar handwriting on a known person's document often looks like a forgery, until a physical condition such as an injury explains a slow, cramped or awkward script.
when: A known person's writing looks unfamiliar
why: Players and characters assume forgery before considering physical causes

text: Handwriting can improve with practice; hurried or shaky script can reflect the writer's agitation and focus, and imitation leaves its own traces.
why: Writing quality reflects state of mind.

text: Handwriting in an unsigned document usually reveals little beyond a rough education level, since a faint or blotted hand gives few clues to identity.
Pen and pencil leave different impressions on lower layers, so the writing tool affects what can be recovered.
A short handwritten note can compress a whole plan into routes, times, places and open questions, so it carries much in few words.
Witness signatures show that others were prepared to swear to a record, but they do not by themselves prove that its contents are accurate.
Edges worn beyond normal and creases matching old folds show a sheet was refolded and resealed, which a careful player can read as tamper evidence.
Writing signed in gloves under a false name can produce unusual handwriting that resembles a disguised hand.
when: A suspect signs a register while trying to hide identity.
why: Gloves and deliberate writing change letterforms, creating an atypical signature.

text: Phrasing and structure of an unsigned letter can hint at the writer's sex or background, weighed against other evidence; incoherent writing can raise doubts about state of mind.
Unusual word choice, word order or sentence structure can point to a writer's native language or origin, letting the player narrow the writer down to one region.
Ink stains on a writer's fingers, especially on the outer edge with the pen type, can link a suspect to a writing act; check hands as well as face.
when: Investigating a suspect connected to written messages, or a writer's hand bears ink marks.
why: Small traces remain on the body after the act; writing habits leave consistent marks.

text: Handwriting matches are strong only with distinctive features; generic script proves little, and several agreeing distinctive letterforms together are stronger than one, since one may match by chance.
when: Comparing a handwriting sample with a suspect's writing.
why: Shared generic features occur across many writers, while rare features point to one person.

text: Two distinct handwriting styles on one document indicate that different people wrote it.
why: Hands differ in pressure and letter form

text: Compare stroke strength, such as the crossing of t's, across words to attribute each word to one writer.
A difference in ink shade between two parts of a writing can imply a pause, suggesting the writer stopped to look something up and was unfamiliar with the content.
when: Judging a written note's composition from its appearance
why: Ink dries and fades over time, so a shade change marks a break in writing

text: Compare the tone of different lines; a dark and a pale ink in one document suggest separate moments of writing.
when: a document's wording or hand seems to change partway through
why: separate writing moments leave marks of different freshness

text: Handwriting that differs from a person's usual hand suggests disguise or that the writer is not who is assumed.
Combine material clues with a messenger's description to infer the social circle of the document's writer.
when: A document's writer is unknown but a messenger was seen

text: Straggling letters, a broad pen with poor ink, and a corrected spelling together suggest a writer of limited education who is unfamiliar with the place named.
when: When assessing a writer's background from handwriting and spelling
why: Multiple small writing signs reinforce one another

text: When one writer leaves blanks that a second writer must fill, the writer who left the gaps wrote first and planned the text.
Read the steadiness of a rushed record as evidence of conditions: neat writing suggests stillness, shaky writing suggests movement, and the worst writing suggests a bumpy or jolting ride.
when: When a written record was made under physical conditions that are unknown.
why: Writing quality changes with the motion or stress of the writer.

text: Compare handwriting by letter forms, stroke length and line steadiness; disguised writing often shows an uneven upstroke or letters that straggle as if the hand shook.
A pseudonym or wordplay signature may be a deliberate choice meant to be noticed, but should not be read as a confession.
why: signatures can signal intent without admitting guilt

text: Minor wording variation is normal, so ask whether a variation changes substance before treating it as a contradiction.
when: Comparing two accounts of the same event.
why: Most differences are phrasing, and only substantive ones undermine a claim.

text: A dead NPC's letter hidden in a mailbox or journal can carry times, names and objects that the player must cross-check against other clues.
A print with an identifiable scar can be matched to a known person, while smudges repeated over several surfaces can suggest gloves.
Use handwriting features such as letter size, irregularity and underlining to infer something about the writer, with emphasis marking deliberate stress.
when: A written document has distinctive handwriting or marked words
why: Writing habits reveal education level, intent and sometimes identity

text: Offer two plausible writing orders for a document and let the game check which one matches the item's recorded history.
when: designing document puzzles

text: Handwriting can estimate age within about a decade: steady bold hand suggests youth, broken declining hand suggests age, but illness or weakness can make it look older.
A handwriting match alone is weak since any hand can be imitated; weigh it alongside other evidence and confirm with a second independent source.
why: Forgers can copy a writing style; handwriting rarely settles who wrote a document on its own.

text: Paper stock and colour are common across households, so a bare match proves little; a match needs distinctive features such as defects or matching ruling, combined with other traits.
why: Widely shared materials produce matches by chance.

text: A later narrator or listener can change exact wording, turning a loose account into apparent proof, so compare original phrasing with retellings.
when: A story is retold across records or time, or a private remark is reported by a second person.
why: Memory and interpretation alter exact words, so the original claim may never be fully settled.

text: Relying on handwriting alone works only once the list of who had seen the true sample has been established.
A case sheet that fills every heading can still be wrong, and circumstantial evidence can be stacked against an innocent person.
when: When a case looks complete on paper
why: Filled headings reflect assembly, not proof

text: Assuming record writers shared a reader's values misreads routine entries, which may reflect norms different from the reader's own.

1) Obtain two independent records of the same event. 2) List the details each keeps and drops. 3) Treat differences as evidence of the recorder's choices, not of what happened; they show which points each emphasized.
1) Compare a handwritten item's signature with a signed sample from a known source. 2) Flag a likely match for formal laboratory confirmation.
when: when the authenticity of handwriting matters

text: 1) List recurring letter forms across the disguised samples. 2) Check whether the same forms recur in each sample. 3) Compare them with a known hand to confirm or rule out a match.
when: Two writings may share an author
why: Habitual letter forms are hard to disguise consistently

text: 1) Identify distinctive letter forms in the disputed sample. 2) Compare those same forms in a known sample. 3) Record the result as full, partial, or no match.
when: Checking whether a disputed writing belongs to a known person.
why: Focusing on distinctive forms gives a more reliable comparison than general impressions.

text: 1) Note the audible fragment of a word. 2) Match the fragment against a map or list of names, allowing for the hidden letters. 3) Check each candidate against independent background facts.
when: a dying utterance or partial word is heard
why: a fragment can be completed by matching it against a known list

text: 1) List the visible fragments. 2) Propose several candidate readings. 3) Match each candidate to the surviving marks and discard those that fit poorly. 4) Test survivors against the likely author and context.
when: A partial or damaged document is the only source of a fact.
why: Testing candidates against marks and authorship filters out plausible but wrong readings.

text: 1) Collect a known sample of the suspect's writing and the paper it is on. 2) Compare both with the note. 3) Compare with a second person's writing to rule out a match.
when: A note must be tied to a writer
why: Matching paper and hand together is stronger than either alone, and a control shows discrimination

text: 1) Obtain known exemplars from the suspected machine. 2) Examine the questioned item and exemplar closely before consulting others. 3) Compare them side by side at the same scale. 4) Identify several shared flaws. 5) Have others check the comparison.
when: matching a questioned document to a machine
why: independent examination first limits outside influence, and several shared flaws are needed for a sound match

text: 1) Notice the visible marker. 2) Apply the fixed selection rule, such as taking every nth word. 3) Read the resulting words. 4) Interpret them as coordinates, times or instructions.
when: When a short text carries a hidden message
why: A fixed rule plus a marker turns innocent-looking text into a decodable message.

text: Separate the words actually spoken from the meaning later attributed to them; knowing vocabulary does not mean knowing the sense, so each can be disputed alone.
when: A remark is later interpreted as a serious claim, or a fragment is heard.
why: An ambiguous remark can be read as stronger than what was said.

text: Keep an independent duplicate of an in-game record out of the forger's reach, and make forged entries complete but in another hand, so players detect them by comparison.
when: Designing alterable documents such as ledgers or shrine records, or placing in-world records.
why: A second source exposes the forgery.

text: Record a witness's account in their own words, so nuances an interpreter might flatten are preserved.
when: taking statements that will later be interpreted

text: Do not present a witness's words as proof of a fact the witness did not assert.
when: Using testimony to support a claim

text: Compare a written instruction against another copy, since a single dropped word can change where the search should go.
when: when a riddle or document exists in more than one version
why: Copying errors can alter the meaning of a direction.

text: Make a written description complete, since it may later be circulated for identification and every omission weakens it.
when: A witness's description will be used to identify a missing person or item
why: Gaps reduce the description's usefulness

text: Give NPC ledgers or receipts a deliberate anomaly so a player who questions it uncovers a hidden transaction.
when: When designing NPC-owned records for a mystery.
why: Questioning an anomaly rewards observation and drives discovery.

text: Write found letters so their meaning shifts with what the player has already learned, rather than fixing a single reading.
Give documents fixed entry slots so that a deleted entry shows as a gap, letting players detect tampering from layout alone.
when: Designing in-game records meant to be checked

text: Use an introduction letter from a trusted NPC as an item that gates access to a faction or location.
Hide information on a document's reverse side, and let an object's scene location carry part of the story.
when: designing clues that reward close inspection
why: Hidden layers and placement add meaning beyond the visible text or item.

text: Let a note's handwriting or wording carry clues about the writer's physical condition, such as a cramped script or a left-handed slant.
when: Designing written clues in a game
why: Physical details in writing give players a testable link to a character's state

text: Give an NPC a distinctive written trait, such as a letterform or phrasing, so players can match it against a note found elsewhere.
when: Designing written clues that link to a character
why: A matchable trait lets players connect documents to characters

text: Record which features were compared when an expert judges handwriting, rather than letting a quick verdict settle the matter.
when: when relying on an expert's opinion on authorship
why: Unrecorded reasoning cannot be checked or challenged.

text: Environmental hazards such as cold can cause death without visible struggle, so a staged accident may leave no sign of violence.
A hazard that strikes just when its apparent targets are elsewhere suggests the planner knew their movements.
when: A hazard hits a place its likely victims have left

text: Unseen harm is assumed to have a human agent, so the investigative question becomes who is responsible.
when: illness or injury has no visible cause
why: an agent is sought for every harm

text: Assuming a cause without testing it closes off alternative questions, such as whether the victim's identity is confirmed, and can be overturned by a replica or reenactment.
when: A cause appears obvious early in an investigation
why: Assumed links stop the investigator from checking alternatives.

text: A reversal caused by a rule the audience never saw feels arbitrary and cheats them, so state the rule early.
Recorded losses are not proof of cause; a grudge can be mistaken for motive when the link between threat and loss is never shown.
Separate proof that harm occurred from proof that a specific person caused it; with no one observing the act, harm is not evidence of cause; guilt must be shown, not inferred.
why: a victim's suffering does not identify the agent

text: Let environmental hazards act as the mechanism of an apparent accident, and reveal tampering through small inconsistencies such as neatly folded clothing.
Avoid tests that harm people, even when the method is effective.
when: when designing an investigation or trial that might injure someone
why: A harmful method is unacceptable even when it would produce a clear result.

text: Do not use force near live equipment until its safety has been explained.
Do not use planted bait when it could reach innocent people or cause them harm.
Forcing a locked door saves time to open but damages property and can delay or spoil what the investigator needs, so forced entry carries real costs.
when: when choosing between forcing a lock and waiting for a proper key or tradesman
why: Force is fast but destructive and may compromise evidence.

text: Separate what a person saw directly from what they heard, and record who told each claim, since each retelling loses detail, adds guesses, and lets assumptions pass unnoticed.
when: a clue reaches you through other people

text: Second-hand or relayed reports have limited reliability; verify them with the original observer or an independent source before relying on them, since each relay adds a distortion layer.
why: Distance from the original source removes direct confirmation.

text: 1) Ask each witness who said what to whom and mark each statement as direct or relayed. 2) Trace each relayed step back to its first-hand source, counting retellings. 3) Weigh each account by its distance from observation.
when: A case or story depends on hearsay passed through several people.
why: each retelling is a step away from the original event and can alter it

text: Trace relayed claims to a first-hand witness; treat the chain as a lead, not proof, and rely on neither version when gossip conflicts with an official account.
when: A clue or claim reaches the investigator only through intermediaries.
why: Secondhand versions drift from the original event; relayed claims can be distorted at any link.

text: Mark hearsay as hearsay; do not treat a relayed or final rumour, or a precise time no witness observed, as firsthand, even when the relay claims exact knowledge.
when: When a witness repeats or describes events they did not observe.
why: Hearsay can be presented as firsthand knowledge.

text: Label rumour and hearsay with its source and confidence, distinguishing it from firsthand reports so players know what is unverified; keep it for later even if unhelpful now.
when: When gathering history from hearsay or presenting rumour in a journal or dialogue.
why: Hearsay may be wrong; heat or indignation in gossip does not indicate knowledge of events.

text: Hearsay drifts and grows with each retelling as listeners add or alter detail, so the most elaborate version is often least reliable and far from its origin.
when: a secret or story passes by word of mouth through several people before reaching an investigator
why: each retelling adds material and loses the original source

text: A witness's report reaches a listener already shaped by the witness's wording, emphasis and wish to look competent.
when: a character passes on information they did not see firsthand
why: Speakers select and stress details to protect their own standing.

text: Hearsay about hidden secrets and family history suggests intrigue, and witnesses weigh such surmise differently, so each source's reliability varies.
when: Witnesses repeat rumours about a person's past
why: Surmise is offered without evidence

text: A go-between relaying a story may betray their own doubts through hedged tone.
when: when a third party carries another person's account
why: The go-between may privately doubt what they carry.

text: Hearsay is a claim relayed from someone else, such as a dying person's words, and it is harder to verify than a witness's own observation.
when: when a key account comes secondhand
why: The reporter may not know the points relayed, and the original speaker is unavailable to confirm them

text: Second-order knowledge is what one party knows about another party's knowledge, such as a holder knowing that the victim knows the holder has a secret.
Hearsay is a witness repeating what others said, while direct observation is what the witness perceived personally.
Second-hand statements by a person who cannot be questioned are often inadmissible as proof, even when they contradict a suspect.
when: in legal settings
why: such statements cannot be tested by cross-examination

text: A key event can be relayed through an absent witness, so the audience must reconstruct it from a report they cannot question directly.
when: a central witness never sees the event

text: Reports relayed by others are secondhand and shaped by the teller, while physical traces must be examined before they are read.
A conclusion relayed from another person, such as a diagnosis, is a judgment built on a few observations, not a raw fact.
when: when someone repeats an expert's opinion

text: A witness who knows an event only through rumour or sounds heard from afar gives second-hand testimony with limited evidential weight.
when: A witness did not observe the event directly.
why: Rumour and distant sounds convey incomplete and possibly distorted information.

text: A published report may be a corrected, amplified or annotated version of a shorthand record, so its claims pass through several editing layers.
when: Evaluating a document that reports events witnessed by others.
why: Each editing layer can change what the reader sees.
