text: Information relayed through intermediaries, such as over a phone call, tends to be partial and garbled, so it carries less weight than firsthand accounts.
why: each relay step can drop or distort details

text: Judge a relayed report by each link's access to events, how it was known, honesty and motive; note who first observed each step.
when: evaluating testimony passed along by others
why: access to events determines how reliable a report is

text: Attach a confidence value that drops at each relay step, so an NPC's claim passed through another NPC is weaker than a direct one, modelling unreliable hearsay.
when: generating NPC testimony about events
why: each translation step can lose or distort the core fact

text: Second-hand reports of a dying person's words are open to several readings and cannot settle a matter alone.
Second-hand testimony needs its own reliability check, since the original source may be wrong or self-interested.
when: A person is known only through what another person reported
why: Each retelling adds a layer of possible distortion

text: Secondhand accounts relay what others saw; weigh them by who told them and how they came to know it.
A witness who relays the questions they were asked reveals what the questioner was probing for.
A first-person account gives the absent party's own testimony rather than observers' guesses, but it still needs checking.
NPC dialogue that relays events secondhand can contain deliberate gaps that players must close with follow-up questions.
Information overheard or relayed by another person is secondhand, and should be weighed as weaker than direct observation, although a matching physical detail can still strengthen it.
when: When a witness reports what they heard through a door or from someone else.
why: Secondhand accounts can be incomplete or mistaken, but independent matches add credibility.

text: Rumoured sightings relayed secondhand have weak reliability and should be weighted lower than direct observation.
when: a supernatural claim rests on rumour
why: Each relay adds distortion and no direct check.

text: Ask how a second-hand reporter knows a fact, and whether its details match what is already known. A detail that changes between tellings is a warning sign.
when: When a rumour or reported fact contains a decisive detail.

text: Weigh a report from a hired observer, telegram or distant letter against physical facts and the observer's own reliability, even when it looks authoritative.
when: when an absent party's movements rest on secondhand messages

text: A fact passed on secondhand is still usable, but its reliability must be judged separately from its usefulness.
A motive can be inferred from a third party's report of a document the investigator has not read firsthand; treat the report as a lead to test.
when: a document's content is only reported
why: Secondhand reports can carry motive but may be inaccurate.

text: Ask how the same phrasing would be judged coming from a friend, to separate what is said from who said it.
If a speaker confidently describes evidence never reported in writing, he probably heard it in person, since hearsay usually produces hedged language.
when: a speaker claims detailed knowledge of unpublished proceedings

text: Second-hand accounts carry the relayer's own opinions, so check them against what can be observed about the person described.
Mark entries that rely on secondhand reports as unconfirmed, and weaken any timeline that depends on them.
when: A movement is reported by someone who did not witness it.
why: Second-hand accounts can be wrong and should not carry the same weight as direct observation.

text: Separate a witness's quoted words from their commentary on those words, since admiration or disgust can colour the commentary while the quoted words remain usable.
Corroborate a rumor from a second, independent source before acting on it, especially for exact amounts or dates.
when: A secondhand report is about to drive a decision.
why: A single relay may carry noise.

text: Treat secondhand accounts as incomplete, but still extract the facts they reliably state, such as dates, places and listed items.
when: When only press reports or hearsay are available.
why: Reports often omit essential facts yet keep dependable details.

text: Each person who relays a claim adds distance from the original observation, may embellish or misremember it, and loses precision, so reliability drops with every link.
when: a claim reaches a listener through intermediaries
why: each relay adds distance from the original fact

text: Each extra teller in a chain of sources adds framing and distance, so the audience must judge how far the account can be trusted.
when: A story or clue reaches the audience through intermediaries.
why: Every relay can reshape the account, and its origin becomes harder to verify.

text: Evidence relayed through several retellings loses reliability at each link, so the chain of who saw what and who repeated it should stay visible to the audience.
when: A case depends on what one person says another person saw.
why: Each retelling adds distortion, and the audience must judge every link to weigh the account.

text: Information passed through several speakers shifts in wording and meaning, so it must be checked against the original speaker.
when: When testimony reaches the investigator secondhand
why: Each relay adds a paraphrase and the relayer's colouring

text: Testimony relayed through another person is filtered twice: by the original witness's memory and again by the teller's retelling.
why: Each retelling adds room for gaps and error

text: A simple prearranged signal, such as a light in a window meaning the coast is clear, can be read by a relay who does not know the full plan.
when: an accomplice must pass status without knowing the purpose
why: the reader needs only the part of the meaning that concerns them

text: A person who relays a suspicion while disliking the suspect can carry that hostility into the rumour, making it sound more certain than the evidence supports.
Each relay in a gossip chain can add, drop or distort details, so information passed through servants or several people loses precision and gains exaggeration.
when: Information reaches a character through several people.
why: Each retelling reshapes details; each intermediary can misremember, mishear or reinterpret them.

text: Each relay adds the teller's interpretation, emotion, gossip or slant, so an account may be overstated, lose detail, or gain unintended meaning, though useful detail often survives.
when: accounts or clues pass through several people before reaching the investigator
why: every retelling is an interpretation

text: Second-hand news and vivid hearsay can be mistaken for firsthand observation, so note whether each report is firsthand or secondhand and check it against its source.
why: vivid detail sounds like something the listener saw

text: Building motive on a friend's gossip about rivalry or romance treats hearsay as fact; hearsay about character can suggest motive but cannot establish facts.
when: when a third party supplies motive information

text: A reaction reported second-hand, whether by another person or through a letter, is already filtered by the reporter's memory and attention, so its details may be incomplete.
when: when a reaction is relayed by another person or a letter

text: A messenger's bias, competitive spirit, dislike or stake can shade or misreport relayed words and tone, corrupting a message or a probe's result.
when: when a character relays an authority's words or a probe is relayed through a messenger
why: the messenger's own opinions or stake colour the retelling

text: Relayed testimony can lose its exact wording, so accepting the first natural reading without checking the original words can lock in a wrong interpretation.
Witnesses often rely on others for key events; a central event no reporter saw directly is the weakest link, since each retelling adds error or shading.
when: the central event was witnessed by someone other than the reporter
why: direct access to key events is often limited

text: A relayed account can distort both what was asked and why, since the relayer shapes it with their own ideas.
A message passed through intermediaries, such as a secretary, becomes a chain of hearsay that can distort its meaning, so trace it back to its originator.
why: Each relay can alter, shorten or obscure the content.

text: A secondhand report depends on the reporter's notes and memory, and may drift from the original account.
when: A timeline is based on a report passed along by another person.
why: Each retelling can change details without the teller noticing.

text: Each handoff can drop or shade details, so an early relayed report should not be treated as final.
Claims about staged events that rest on people who did not see everything are weak evidence and should be checked.
A track account that comes from a family story is secondhand. Confirm the snow record itself before treating it as proof.
when: a track claim comes from a witness account

text: Confident testimony can rest on second-hand sources, so the chain of transmission must be checked before relying on it.
A sincere but second-hand account accepted to keep rapport can be wrong, so it must be verified later.
when: A witness reports something they did not witness directly.
why: Sincerity does not make secondhand information accurate.

text: Secondhand retellings distort facts, and a garbled or exaggerated version can spread and fuel disbelief in the original event.
A relayed written account filters both words and tone, so the reader cannot judge the original speaker's manner or sincerity.
when: evidence reaches the player second-hand in writing
why: Only the relayer's wording survives

text: Predictions reported secondhand are only as reliable as the person who relays them.
when: a prediction about future events comes through another party
why: Each relay adds a chance of error or distortion

text: Others' reports of a suspect's absence can shape the investigator's view before the suspect is questioned directly.
A chain of hearsay can carry an identification that no one has checked, so its reliability is uncertain.
when: When an identification reaches the investigator through intermediaries
why: Each relay can distort or omit the original verification

text: A story relayed by a third party carries that party's stake in it, and the relayer may have arranged the account with the suspect.
when: when a suspect's story reaches you through another person
why: The relayer may share an interest in the same account.

text: Treating a secondhand published accusation as a verdict on a person's character, without hearing the original act, lets reputation replace evidence.
Trusting a respected name or a striking anecdote without having seen the event itself makes a claim unverifiable.
when: when relying on reports rather than direct observation
why: Reputation and vivid stories can stand in for checked facts.

text: Hearsay from drunk or frightened sources can compress or stretch time, so each stated interval should keep its source label.
Names relayed by accusers through intermediaries and written into a complaint without checking can point to the wrong person, especially when names are common.
when: When a complaint names someone from another person's report.
why: Unverified intermediaries can mistake which person was meant.

text: Curiosity, affection, gossip, and old resentment can all color a secondhand account before it reaches the listener.
Accounts relayed through several tellers, or told long after events, can carry the teller's assumptions, so the original facts may be lost.
Secondhand press accounts are often incomplete or wrong. Do not treat them as full records of an event.
A secondhand report can itself be wrong, so a small checkable detail in it should be verified before relying on the testimony it supports.
when: relying on a report passed through another person
why: A wrong detail in a relayed account weakens everything built on it.

text: Repeating hearsay as fact, or letting a relayer's disgust or prejudice shape what you take from the report.
when: Using secondhand information as a basis for conclusions.
why: Hearsay carries the teller's bias and unverified claims.

text: A relayed opinion can look like a relayed fact, so separate what was said from what the speaker thought it meant.
when: A reported statement mixes report with judgment.
why: Interpretation blended into quoted words can be mistaken for objective content.

text: Treating an unverified second-hand report as proof of a shared past or hidden link, without checking it, builds a conclusion on hearsay.
Debts and conflicts reported by servants are hearsay until verified against records or other witnesses.
when: When household gossip is the source of a motive
why: Secondhand reports can be wrong

text: Relying on second-hand reports of an offer's terms without checking the exact wording can miss the clause that carries the clue.
when: When evaluating a deal or bargain.
why: Paraphrases drop the conditions that reveal intent.

text: Hearsay can omit the one fact that changes the answer, so do not rule out a possibility based on an omitted detail until it is verified.
when: When relying on incomplete accounts.
why: Absence from a report is not evidence the event did not happen.

text: Information passed on verbally, such as an address, can be misheard or misunderstood, so it should be tested against the world before being trusted.
when: A player or character receives a location or instruction through dialogue.
why: Spoken details are easily garbled and may not match physical reality.

text: 1) Separate what the witness personally saw, heard and inferred. 2) Ask explicitly for the personal part. 3) Weigh each as distinct evidence and record heard or inferred parts as hearsay or opinion, since inference mixed with perception overstates what was known and can distort the timeline.
when: when weighing any witness account, especially one that seems to settle a scene's reconstruction
why: firsthand knowledge carries more weight than relayed or inferred claims

text: 1) Trace the chain of people back to the first holder of a suspicion. 2) Record who knew what and when. 3) Note who failed to report it in time.
when: An investigation begins from relayed suspicion rather than a formal accusation.
why: Relays change detail and can delay evidence.

text: 1) Identify the key facts in a witness account. 2) Separate them from irrelevant digressions. 3) Check only the key facts against other evidence.
when: A witness mixes relevant facts with digressions
why: Digressions can bury the facts the audience needs

text: 1) Separate what each person saw firsthand from what was reported secondhand. 2) Record who saw what. 3) Reconcile conflicts only after the sources are clear.
when: Witness accounts conflict
why: Mixing direct observation with hearsay makes conflicts impossible to assess

text: 1) Identify the damaging claim and its source. 2) Test whether the claim is true. 3) Test where it came from. 4) Weigh which is more probable: the accused acted as reported, or the informant is wrong. 5) Judge against the accused's known character.
when: A damaging claim about a person arrives second-hand and cannot be checked directly
why: Separating the claim from its source and weighing both by probability avoids accepting a rumour on trust.

text: Treat secondhand testimony relayed through intermediaries as weaker than direct observation, since each relay can shift meaning and lose tone and context.
when: when knowledge passes through several people
why: every intermediary can distort the picture

text: Separate firsthand observations from relayed accounts and tag each testimony or detail as firsthand, hearsay, or read in a document, so readers can weigh each claim by source.
when: when assessing any witness account
why: second-hand details can be repeated with the same confidence as firsthand memory

text: Treat an account relayed through another person as unverified and record who passed it on, since a repeater adds no observation and must be checked against the original source.
why: relayed details can distort or lose context

text: Treat hearsay, rumour, gossip and relayed observations as unconfirmed leads that direct inquiry, not timeline facts or findings, until direct evidence checks them.
why: relays lose precision, and the original observer's viewpoint may have limited what was seen

text: Second-hand alibis and claims about what another person did need separate confirmation rather than acceptance from the witness who reports them, since they are weaker than direct observation.
Make relayed clues, including a quest-giver's rumour, verifiable: they keep the core claim but lose specifics, so give players a way to check or contradict them before acting.
when: designing secondhand information
why: relayed claims need a route to checking

text: Limit each narrator to what they personally saw and heard, naming the source when relaying others, so readers can assemble the truth from overlapping firsthand accounts.
when: when a story depends on several people's testimony or viewpoints
why: readers can weigh each claim only when they know who observed it

text: Separate relayed observations from the conclusions drawn from them, and check each conclusion before relying on it.
when: several people relay the same event

text: Separate dramatic detail and personal commentary from the observed facts before weighing a witness's account.
when: when a witness's account is vivid or emotionally charged
why: embellishment can make weak observations seem stronger

text: Record hearsay with its source, and treat it as evidence of motive only after the original report is confirmed accurate.
when: when a witness repeats what someone else said
why: Hearsay is only as reliable as its original source

text: Separate reported times and facts from a publication's editorial speculation before using them.
Do not rule out a suspect on a third-party description alone; confirm the relevant trait directly, since gossip about age or health can be wrong.
when: Relying on gossip or hearsay about a suspect
why: Secondhand claims are often inaccurate

text: Do not treat relayed information as confirmed until a second, independent source checks it.
when: a fact arrives through an intermediary
why: relayed accounts can carry distortion

text: Trace a go-between's message to its original sender, since the messenger may distort it, add content, pursue their own motive, or not share the sender's purpose.
when: A key message reaches the investigator through a go-between.
why: The messenger may not know or share the sender's true purpose.

text: Do not rely on eavesdropped or relayed testimony for precise facts without a firsthand source or corroboration.
when: when a fact rests on overheard or relayed speech

text: Trust a message passed through an intermediary only when it carries a credential the recipient can recognise, such as a name or code phrase.
when: When a message arrives via a third party.
why: A credential lets the recipient verify the sender.

text: Add a dialogue option where the player relays a cryptic line, and let the NPC's next line depend on whether they understand it.
Use remembered secondhand accounts for description, and mark any inference drawn from them, such as materials guessed from how objects were disposed of.
Give the player two linked rumours, one blatantly false, that together lure them toward a trap location.
when: when designing quest hooks or lures

text: Relayed lore adds distance and uncertainty that can enrich a story, but each extra layer adds reading load that is wasted if the source's reliability does not matter.
when: Deciding whether a clue should pass through an intermediary.
why: Layers add atmosphere but also cost the player attention.

text: A reconstructed account keeps the event offstage, but an audience that needs direct evidence to believe the central mystery will reject it.
when: the central mystery is at stake

text: Induction is reasoning from many particular observations to a general likelihood, producing a provisional conclusion that ranks possibilities rather than proving them.
when: When an investigator must reach a conclusion from incomplete evidence.
why: Induction yields probable readings, which remain open to challenge.

text: Present sensory readings as inference with visible confidence, not as verified fact.
why: Sound-based inferences can be wrong.

text: Treat an inference from partial information, like a completed witness story, as a hedged hypothesis, not settled fact, especially when evidence is a single or trance-derived account.
when: Stating a theory from limited evidence
why: Hedged claims signal uncertainty and prevent a weak theory from being taken as fact.

text: Present a rival hypothesis as a guess to be tested, and acknowledge that guesses may miss, since a wrong guess costs little.
when: When proposing a theory that lacks full evidence.
why: Openness that a guess is a guess keeps the reasoning honest and the cost of error low.

text: A vague standard for accepting inferences lets decision-makers split the difference, while a strict standard risks rejecting a true conclusion built from linked facts.
when: Setting how much evidence a final judgment requires.
why: Without a clear threshold, the verdict depends on how each judge reads what counts as a just inference.

text: Witnesses leak views via hedges, qualifiers, tone and indirect phrasing even when content sounds innocent, such as implying someone else disagrees; treat it as a clue.
when: Listening to a witness who gives a qualified, unusually framed or indirect statement
why: Speakers often leak implications through hedges and manner; restraint leaves a trace in phrasing that reveals a view they would not state outright.

text: A listener who hears a speaker hedge after a promise may read the hedge as concealment and suspect that something is being held back.
Record a witness's hedged identification, such as 'might have been', or sighting as uncertainty: weak alone, neither discarded nor firm, but usable as a lead to pursue.
when: when a witness is unsure of an identity or sighting
why: uncertainty limits evidential value

text: Weigh hedged witness claims such as 'almost sure' or 'not certain' lower than firm ones, judging them by specificity and agreement with other evidence.
when: recording witness claims
why: hedges reflect the witness's own confidence

text: Hedged or vague answers, such as a 'figure of speech', are weak and mark where to press with specific follow-up; make NPC hedging a visible cue to the next answer.
why: Visible hesitation tells players where to continue questioning

text: State conclusions from physical traces or traits, such as a profile, as hypotheses or likelihoods, since one trace rarely settles a question; say plainly what cannot be known.
when: Physical evidence supports an inference.
why: Traces support probability more than proof.

text: Give NPC witnesses a mix of hedged and flatly contradicted statements, so the player must check each against logs and other sources.
when: Designing testimony in a game investigation.

text: Give NPC witnesses confidence levels tied to how much they observed, so a partial glimpse yields a hedged statement.
when: designing witness dialogue
why: Confidence should track the quality of the observation.

text: Treat a physician's guarded readings as limited evidence, since experts may hedge to avoid committing to a conclusion.
when: when a medical opinion is non-committal
why: hedging avoids overclaiming

text: Track hedging words such as 'maybe' or 'appears' as dialogue flags or branches; hesitant or hedged replies unlock follow-up lines or leads the player can later expose.
when: designing dialogue systems

text: Turning a hedged statement such as 'probably right' into a fixed fact about a faulty source corrupts any timeline built on it.
Mark interpretations as guesses with hedges such as 'probably' or 'seems'; read hedged claims as impressions, not verified facts, until other evidence confirms them.
when: reasoning from partial evidence
why: an inference can look like fact once stated

text: Let a forensic NPC give a hedged diagnosis that the player can firm up only by asking the right follow-up questions.
when: Designing a forensic-style NPC.
why: Follow-up questions reveal how much the expert actually knows.

text: Let players notice hedged or indirect dialogue as a clue, and reward them for weighing it against the speaker's position.
when: Designing dialogue that hides information
why: Rewarding inference makes indirect speech a playable clue rather than noise

text: A helpful character who volunteers information and then arranges privacy can look supportive while isolating the accused.
when: writing a character who seems allied with the player
why: Helpfulness can disguise control, so players should not trust helpfulness alone.

text: A guide's familiarity with a route makes an outsider dependent on them and signals local knowledge.
when: When a player or character enters an unfamiliar, dangerous area with a local guide.
why: Outsiders cannot navigate safely without local knowledge.

text: An NPC led through a sequence of stops to a chosen place can be reconstructed by the player if each stop is shown.
when: Designing an NPC movement sequence
why: Visible stops let players trace the route

text: Reading each action against the person who performed it turns helpful acts, such as urging a meeting, into evidence for the opposing side.
when: analysing the conduct of a suspect or a go-between
why: Interpretation is tilted toward the frame of the accusation

text: A helper's own doubts about the errand can disrupt the collection, so a plausible cover story is needed.
when: a helper must carry out a task without knowing its full purpose

text: Give a mastermind or witness NPC a helpful-sounding suggestion that quietly steers the inquiry toward an innocent target or convenient theory.
Let a helper NPC's letter or codex supply a motive chain that players must verify against in-world facts.
when: when delivering lore that bears on a mystery

text: Family history or hereditary risk is not proof of any act; an inherited tendency may or may not appear and cannot establish what a person has done or is doing.
when: Using inheritance to explain or prove behavior
why: Inherited traits do not establish present or past conduct; a tendency is a possibility, not a demonstration.

text: An inherited grievance deepens when one side blocks a shared resource while the other side grows poorer and keeps asking.
when: A feud spans generations over a shared asset.
why: Repeated refusal and worsening hardship keep the dispute alive.

text: When an investigator's reasoning rests on a mistaken identity, every later inference inherits the error and must be rechecked.
when: An early identification shapes later deductions.
why: Errors in a foundational premise propagate through the whole chain of reasoning.

text: A hidden-accomplice explanation can seem rational but fails once every exit is still secured.
A hired party may stay hidden, even from the investigator, so the case must be judged on its own facts.
A game handler can know a masked NPC's true identity while the player does not, with the reveal triggered by a specific player action.
Formal office can hide who actually decides; trace who selected each officer and who had their ear.
when: judging who controls a government or council

text: Hide a rescuer NPC in plain sight by marking their gaze early, so players recall the figure when the rescue happens.
when: Designing a later-revealed ally.
why: An early marked detail makes the late identity feel earned.

text: A faction's hidden boss can issue orders through agents, so catching and replacing agents reveals the boss's presence without exposing them.
A hidden antagonist's harm can follow a chain of roles: an accuser presents charges, an authority grants permission, and an executor carries out the harm.
when: explaining harm that has no visible perpetrator
why: A staged chain of roles makes unseen causation legible and reconstructable.

text: Build a hidden antagonist whose agents act openly, with each action benefiting the antagonist and traceable to a shared location.
when: designing a conspiracy in a game

text: Give a hidden antagonist a concrete motive, such as envy or a grudge, so its choice of targets makes sense to players.
when: designing a hidden or unseen antagonist

text: Build a helper who doubles as the trap by offering visibly too-precise knowledge, then unmasking them as the source of danger.
Early naming of a hidden antagonist and goal gives audiences a question to pursue, but a fixed early identity removes reason to investigate; keep identity as rumour until direct evidence.
when: an unseen boss drives the plot
why: A named target gives the audience a question to pursue; a fixed early identity removes the reason to investigate

text: Hide a decisive item inside ordinary-looking set dressing or a mundane container so it becomes a key only when combined with a later clue or its revealed purpose.
when: When placing a valuable clue in a scene or designing item-based progression in a level.
why: A mundane container avoids suspicion; ordinary-looking items reward attention and tie earlier and later discoveries together.

text: A key left on a wall can seem to clear a suspect, but a spare or second key may exist, so the key's presence does not rule out another route.
when: when a key appears to rule out a suspect
why: Visible keys do not exclude duplicates.

text: 1) Take a directional reading while the suspect source is active. 2) Repeat it after conditions change to check the bearing stays fixed. 3) Confirm with a second, independent observation before naming the source.
when: a signal or cause cannot be seen directly
why: one bearing gives direction only, not distance or identity

text: Let a boastful NPC's exaggerated claims contain a real clue hidden among the exaggerations.
when: Designing a boastful NPC who carries information.
why: Players who sift the boasts can find the genuine lead.

text: Hide the explanatory key in a memory or record the protagonist cannot reach, then give the player a way to reconstruct it.
when: Designing a reveal that reverses an accusation
why: The character's ignorance keeps the explanation hidden from the reader until the reconstruction.

text: Plant the real killer's tells in plain view, such as a distinctive ring, a missing coat, or a night visitor, so the reveal feels inevitable in hindsight.
Recover a hidden original record late in the story to confirm that a suspect's written account was false.
why: A late physical proof settles what earlier documents only suggested.

text: An unseen investigator can gather fragments of speech and visual reflections that point toward hidden matters.
Overheard but unseen voices narrow possibilities: their number, kind, and voice quality can suggest who was involved without identifying them.
when: when the people present were heard but not seen
why: Partial sensory evidence narrows possibilities even without identification.

text: Treating an unlocked space as closed to everyone, or a locked space as safe from insiders, leads to wrong access conclusions.
when: Judging whether a space was accessible.
why: Locks indicate physical control, not who holds keys or has permission.

text: Searching unrelated events, such as birthdays or weddings, for a link produces false patterns and wastes effort.
Do not rely on an unexplained secret passage as the answer to a locked-room puzzle; use it only as a passing guess.
when: Resolving a sealed-room mystery.
why: An unexplained passage feels like a cheat and leaves the puzzle unresolved.

text: A person may reveal knowledge of a secret through an offhand remark rather than a direct confession.
when: questioning a witness about a hidden item
why: Casual speech often exposes what a person heard or saw.

text: A character's fear of interception may be well founded or mistaken, so make clear which one it is.
A visitor who taps a window instead of using the bell suggests the visitor knew the household well enough to skip the formal signal.
when: A visitor's method of announcing arrival differs from the normal one.
why: Skipping the usual signal implies familiarity with the occupants.

text: Hide the decisive trait behind a missing or damaged component so that identification requires a second discovery.
when: Designing a body identification puzzle.
why: Withholding the confirming detail turns a partial match into a reason to keep searching.

text: Hide a clue in a detail visible only under magnification or an overlay, so the player must inspect closely to find the inconsistency.
when: designing a clue meant to reward careful inspection
why: Requiring a deliberate inspection action turns discovery into an active choice rather than a passive reveal.

text: A message released on a condition lets knowledge and instructions outlive the person who wrote them.
A suspect who knows a detail no one disclosed to them can be flagged, so the knowledge itself becomes a clue the player tracks.
Clues or anomalies the player cannot see or hear feel unfair, so reveal incidental clues to both sides and make character dismissals follow visible clues.
when: Hiding a clue in casual conversation or an object, or having a character dismiss an anomaly
why: Players cannot reason from information they never perceived.

text: A covert change the player cannot notice or learn about removes their agency over the outcome.
when: the player is meant to act on the outcome

text: A joking answer to a noticed reaction can bury the clue, leading the observer to dismiss the reaction along with the joke.
when: A character deflects a question about a revealing reaction with humour.
why: Humour ends the question without answering it, so the reaction is easily forgotten.

text: Recording failure at an unrelated test, such as reciting a prayer, as evidence of guilt substitutes an irrelevant test for proof.
Invisible threats seen by only one NPC need corroboration from another NPC, an environmental trace, or a logged event.
Hide the true mechanism in an ordinary object that the player has no reason to test until a sample is taken.
when: when designing a concealed method of harm or deception
why: Players test objects they find suspicious, so an everyday object stays unexamined.

text: Hide a person in the room and reveal them through a mechanism, such as a swinging panel, rather than through testimony.
A dialogue clue can be kept fair yet unobvious by letting the protagonist's bias hide it until a later reveal recovers the sense.
when: A clue must be fair but must not look like one
why: A bias-driven misreading hides the clue, and the reveal rewards a second reading.

text: Plant a culprit's or second culprit's presence in ordinary acts, like an everyday request, noted time, limp, case or repeated check, so it reads as background until reveal.
when: When hiding a culprit present throughout the story, or a second culprit.
why: Unremarkable details are passed over on first reading and gain meaning when the reveal recontextualizes them, so the reveal reads as fair.

text: Do not fix on the most visible grudge; a suspect with no obvious grudge can still hold the motive that explains the crime.
when: When a single obvious suspect is emerging early in an investigation.
why: Visible motives can distract from concealed ones.

text: Unexplained personal spending can be the root of a debt that drives later crime, so note private obligations even when they are not fully explored.
when: when a financial problem has no clear origin
why: Private expenses often start the chain of pressure that leads to misconduct.

text: Give an alibi witness a motive hidden in plain sight, so a neutral-seeming account becomes damning once the witness's identity is exposed.
A witness found in a place they should not be can be more credible, since their presence exposes them to risk.
when: When assessing a witness discovered in an unexpected location.
why: Accepting risk to be present is costly, which makes the account more believable.

text: A culprit's signature clues can stay in plain view while being attached to harmless explanations, so readers attribute them to an innocent suspect until a late search exposes the true author.
when: Designing a mystery whose solution is hidden behind a frame on another character
why: Readers accept an explanation that fits the planted clue, so suspicion runs opposite to the truth until new evidence appears.

text: A protective device that seems strange may conceal a private motive; tracing its origin and what it currently guards can reveal the real purpose behind it.
when: A protective device or ritual seems inexplicable and needs a personal or material explanation
why: Origin and current use together often explain behavior that looks mad on the surface

text: A jailed mastermind who still directs the scheme is a twist whose misdirection is the belief that imprisonment ends the threat.
when: designing a captive antagonist reveal
why: Confidence in containment makes the reader accept the threat as ended.

text: Keep a hidden leader masked and offstage until the reveal, appearing only in group meetings and unmasking late.
when: A secret organisation whose leader is also a suspect or friend.
why: Limited exposure protects the identity and keeps the reveal dramatic.

text: Twins share a resemblance that makes a swap of identity easier to believe.
when: A plot involves a substitution between related people.
why: Close family likeness lowers observers' suspicion.

text: If two apparent people are never seen together and one appears only when the other is away, suspect they are the same person in disguise.
when: Witness sightings show a pattern of alternation.
why: Mutually exclusive appearances suggest one person changing appearance.

text: Hide a late motive in a document the player can read, so the final reveal feels earned rather than invented.
when: planning a mystery's final motive
why: A motive the player could have read earlier makes the reveal a recognition.

text: A harmless-seeming character can be a hidden protagonist; show the disguise on the page, then disclose the identity in dialogue afterward.
why: A disguise visible on the page makes the later disclosure fair.

text: Keep the accuser's grudge off-page until late; a credible witness whose motive is hidden can become the real suspect.
when: designing a witness twist
why: The revealed motive reframes the witness.

text: A disguised ally's true identity can be revealed fairly if the physical proof, such as a planted card or plate, has been set up early and recurs.
when: a late reveal depends on an object the reader has already seen
why: Planted and repeated clues make the reveal feel earned rather than arbitrary.

text: A mystery built on two swapped identities, where the victim and the person present are both misidentified, so the solution reverses who died and who was there.
when: designing a murder whose key error is identity
why: Reversing both identities at once doubles the reframing of the evidence.

text: A mystery can separate the letter-writer, the intruder, the disguised ally and the killer as distinct identities, so the expected controlling figure can be absent from the scene.
when: designing a mystery with a planner or threat figure
why: Keeping roles separate lets the reader's assumption about who is in control fail when the planner never appears.

text: Two names do not prove two people, since a fictitious identity can be made to look real.

1) Identify the formal record that the hidden party touched. 2) Find the clerk or official who handled it. 3) Trace the people connected to that official. 4) Follow an intermediary link to the party who made the request.
when: A hidden actor's identity must be recovered from a logged action
why: Indirect ties often reveal a name the direct record hides

text: 1) Search records for the person's past under any false name. 2) Identify associates who recognise the person. 3) Link past events, such as old thefts or sentences, to the attackers.
when: A person is attacked and the real identity or motive is unknown.
why: Records and associates reveal a real identity that a false name conceals, and link it to the motive.

text: 1) Link incidents that share a thread. 2) Follow each link upward through its agents. 3) Stop when the chain reaches one controlling figure.
when: When tracing a conspiracy to its planner.

text: 1) Examine every possession of an unidentified person, including inside and both sides of objects. 2) Review papers for any name. 3) If no name appears, ask whether anyone came looking for the person.
when: An unidentified person is connected to a scene.
why: Belongings and visitor questions can narrow the search even without a name.

text: In an infiltration plot, hide the protagonist's real allegiance in dialogue until the trap room, then drop the disguise and disarm enemies.
Personal items such as rings, pins or clothing can be carried by someone other than the owner, so make them the clue players trust, letting their failure become the main twist.
when: A body or person is identified by belongings and the identity is central to the plot.
why: Players rarely question items accepted as proof of identity, and matching possessions does not prove who the person is.

text: An identifying trait is a physical detail, such as a limp, cane or face shape, described early as characterization and later used to recognise the person.
A body or character presented as one identity can be re-matched to another when a later item, such as a name, clothing mark or sample, is found.
Use a single recurring phrase or inscription to link a dead NPC to a past wrong and a hidden enemy.
when: Designing a thread that connects a victim to an unseen antagonist.
why: A repeated phrase gives the player a concrete lead that points to the past.

text: Establish an impostor through physical evidence such as footwear, fingerprints or mismatched belongings before naming any human suspect.
when: when a character's identity is in doubt
why: Physical traces are harder to explain away than testimony

text: A document that reveals a hidden identity can open a new route, letting the player use the disclosed identity to progress.
when: Quest items that disclose a secret.

text: A single character's identity can be revised several times by successive clues, moving between honest, impostor, accomplice, target and noble, so the player must keep re-evaluating.
when: a mystery centres on who a character really is
why: Each new clue changes which category the character fits, keeping belief unstable longer than the case's main answer.

text: A victim is killed before a checkpoint, and a disguised impersonator boards there, so a witness's sighting creates a false alibi for another suspect.
when: Building a false timeline where a disguise covers a death.
why: The impersonator's appearance replaces the victim's, so the timeline appears intact.

text: Reassurance grounded in a person's standing rather than facts can stop a listener from checking the actual claim.
when: A listener is told a report is false because of who is involved.
why: A reputation argument is not verification and can end the search for facts.

text: 1) Collect several independent physical markers from the subject. 2) Compare each marker against a separate record. 3) Confirm the identity only when the matches reinforce each other.
when: Identity is in question and the body or subject is too decayed to recognise.
why: Several independent matches are much stronger than a single marker.

text: 1) Use the posting location and any first name as partial identifiers. 2) Link the writer to a person through later references in other documents.
when: A letter is unsigned or signed only with a first name.
why: Partial clues combine into an identification that a later clue can complete.

text: 1) Have the witness produce a sketch of a face or figure. 2) Find a historical record that matches it. 3) Ask the witness to confirm the match.
when: Identifying an unseen figure from a witness's description
why: A witness's recognition of a match identifies the figure more reliably than a description alone.

text: Keep the investigator's method partly hidden until the reveal, and withhold conclusions until the proof is in place.
when: When designing the reveal of a mystery.
why: Concealed method preserves surprise and makes the proof land.

text: Hide the investigator's own surveillance from the player until a late turn, so the sense of who is watching shifts at the reveal.
A murder weapon that is a common object already present in the scene is accepted more readily once revealed, because it was in plain view and was misread as ordinary.
when: Planning a concealed-cause twist such as an accident that turns out to be murder.
why: Players recognize the object in hindsight and feel the clue was fair rather than arbitrary.

text: After a reveal, earlier insignificant details are recognized as clues, and spontaneous events are re-read as deliberate arrangements, with details recast as planted lures without contradicting earlier scenes.
when: when a reveal recontextualizes earlier scenes
why: Hindsight reframes earlier details as evidence; retrospective meaning changes how innocent details are understood.

text: Praise for a dead person that carries implied fault can reveal a speaker's blame, so such remarks can be treated as possible evidence of motive.
when: a witness speaks warmly of someone who has died
why: blame often surfaces disguised as praise

text: Hindsight makes a clue reading seem obvious though it was unclear when first observed; presenting the solution as obvious hides that earlier uncertainty, making the reasoning look unearned.
Hindsight makes a plant look obvious; a real decoy should be checkable from the evidence available at the time.
Hindsight can make a whole period look careless; a fair account first reconstructs what the period knew before judging its conduct.
Motives that look clear in hindsight may not have existed when the act was committed.
when: Reconstructing why someone acted in the past.
why: Later knowledge projects a motive backward onto earlier choices.

text: Release hints in a fixed order, starting with a general rule and then the specific target, so the player builds the theory step by step.
when: Designing how a mystery's clues are revealed to the player
why: A general-to-specific sequence lets the player construct the explanation incrementally.

text: Open rewards for information draw many unreliable claimants, who waste investigative effort.
why: Anyone seeking the reward will offer an answer, true or not.

text: Hints that never connect to a later event read as padding. Each hint should link to a later test or escalation.
when: Scattering clues through a mystery.
why: Unconnected hints waste the audience's attention and erode trust.

text: Offer optional backstory only when the player's conversation reaches a matching point, not from a menu, and include an explicit option to decline.
when: Designing NPC backstory delivery.
why: Contextual timing and a safe exit make players more willing to reveal and engage.

text: An optional explanation of how an item was taken rewards curious players, but it removes the mystery that a fully unexplained default preserves.
when: choosing how much of a mystery to resolve by default
why: Explaining everything satisfies some players and deflates the mood for others.

text: With no clue, move through oddities the pursued target would also have noticed, since what caught the pursuer's eye may have caught theirs.
when: no solid lead exists

text: Finding a modern cause for one sighting does not prove every other claim about the event false.
A moving farewell can bind the reader's emotions to one reading of events, so the reader accepts the explanation it suggests.
Modern tombs can look old, so check the date of construction before treating a monument as historically original.
when: Judging a monument's age from its appearance
why: Weathering and style can make recent structures seem to date from earlier periods

text: Test a monument's name against documents and tradition before accepting it as evidence of a location, since the name carries unearned authority.
when: A memorial is presented as marking where something happened
why: A name on a marker can make a claim seem established without support

text: A guilty speaker may test a confidant by describing a crime as a general or hypothetical method, then watch the listener's reaction before committing.
when: A suspect is likely to test a confidant before revealing guilt.
why: A hypothetical frame lowers the risk of exposure while still gauging the listener.

text: Avoid hypothetical probing with hostile or guarded subjects, who will simply refuse to commit.
when: when the subject is hostile or guarded

text: Frame a sensitive topic as a hypothetical so the witness can consider it without committing to an answer.
when: A witness must be drawn toward a painful subject.
why: A hypothetical lowers the stakes of answering.

text: Ask one precise question that a reliable source can answer and that would confirm or refute a specific theory.
when: when a theory depends on one hidden fact

text: A hypothetical question put to a witness, such as asking whether someone was named, is a probe; its answer is not a finding.
A theory built on a hypothetical event, such as a document that was never made, fails once a reliable source denies that the event happened.
when: a theory assumes an unverified action
why: the theory's foundation depends on an event that may not have occurred

text: A joke or hypothetical can harden into a suspect in others' minds.
when: A speculative idea is repeated in a group
why: Repetition turns speculation into perceived fact

text: A hypothetical that is too specific can reveal your own suspicions, and a sharp listener may read it as a test.

1) Ask the person to suppose a condition that bears on their view. 2) Get them to commit to their position under that supposition. 3) Reveal a verifiable fact that contradicts the commitment. 4) Observe whether they shift.
when: when a person holds a fixed belief you need to test and is willing to talk

text: 1) Describe a general case rather than accuse. 2) Ask the subject to judge it. 3) Watch colour changes and pauses. 4) Note verbal slips. 5) Ask a neutral question about a third party and see if the slip repeats.
when: a direct question would be refused
why: A judgement on a general case touches the subject's own stake.

text: 1) Choose a hypothetical case that mirrors the suspect's secret. 2) Tell it while watching the suspect's face. 3) Record each change in reaction and what was said at that moment.
when: a suspect's guilt is likely and direct questions yield nothing
why: A mirrored story can prompt a reaction the suspect cannot easily hide

text: 1) Frame a fictional scheme that mirrors the case, so the listener can discuss it without feeling accused. 2) Ask them to suggest methods, alibis or ways to shift blame. 3) Watch hesitation, quick dismissals and topic avoidance. 4) Note any legal obstacle they raise and whether they propose a workaround. 5) Probe the scheme's weak points.
when: A suspect will talk but would refuse or rehearse a direct question.

text: 1) Ask an insider a general hypothetical about how an object could be hidden. 2) Record the negative facts in the answer, such as absent structures. 3) Verify each negative claim with a second specialist. 4) Keep the question general so the subject does not feel accused.
when: after a search fails and location depends on building construction
why: Insider answers rule out whole categories of hiding places without alerting the subject.

text: 1) Pose a hypothetical about a third party in a similar situation. 2) Ask what that person would do. 3) Ask why, to draw out motive without a direct accusation.
when: A witness knows a sensitive relationship or fact they will not state.
why: Opinions about someone else's behavior can reveal motive without a formal accusation.

text: Offer players hypothetical or suppose-style dialogue options so the NPC's committed answers reveal its beliefs without committing the player.
when: when designing dialogue trees for information gathering or for NPCs holding views
why: hypotheticals invite estimates without commitment

text: Offer a hypothetical dialogue prompt whose reply sets NPC flags that change later lines.
when: designing branching dialogue

text: Ask a witness a hypothetical about what they would do in the same situation, and press for an answer, to draw out their stance.
Overconfidence in a safeguard becomes a serious risk mainly when it causes lax habits.
A mystery can open on an unidentified corpse and be driven by the question of who the dead person is, with identity itself as the central puzzle.
when: designing a detective plot built around a body
why: Identity uncertainty gives the investigation a question that drives every scene.

text: A person may mistake an intruder for someone else and freeze in surprise until a voice reveals the truth.
when: explaining a delayed or absent reaction to an intruder
why: misperceived identity delays response

text: Let an NPC misidentify a character under certain question orders, and let the player re-ask with different phrasing to get a more reliable answer.
when: Designing NPC witness dialogue that can err
why: Misidentification becomes a puzzle when the player can test it.

text: Read a character's odd conduct against their occupation and habits before treating it as guilty; the same act may be routine for them.
when: A suspect's behaviour looks suspicious
why: Habits give innocent explanations that an outsider's standards overlook.

text: Keep the cast minimal: a companion should supply context for the scene, not take part in the investigation.
when: Single-scene mystery with few characters
why: Extra investigators dilute the reveal

text: Pair each identity clue with a second independent clue so the eventual explanation has more than one support.
when: Building toward a disguise reveal.
why: Two independent supports make the final explanation more convincing and fair.

text: A guest or servant who seems harmless can be revealed late as a disguised criminal or supernatural being, overturning the audience's expectation of an outsider.
when: Late reveal of a trusted or ordinary-looking character.
why: Audiences assume the threat comes from outside the household.

text: 1) List the conditions: length of absence, expected inquiries, and whether a sealed place would hide a body. 2) Ask whether those conditions favour concealment. 3) Separate possible from probable. 4) Find the plan's weak point.
when: a suspect's motive or access is known but the act is unproven
why: Judging opportunity by conditions gives a structured test rather than a guess

text: 1) Offer a plausible identity for the victim. 2) Back it with a witness. 3) Test it against physical marks. 4) Discard it with a contradiction. 5) Move suspicion to the next candidate.
when: structuring a whodunit where the victim's identity is disputed
why: Repeated test-and-discard cycles keep the reader's belief moving and build toward the real answer.

text: Leaving the final identity open when the enemy's body is unrecognisable keeps the threat alive for a sequel but withholds closure; confirming identity gives satisfaction and ends the thread.
why: Each option trades lingering tension against a clean resolution; an open identity keeps the disguise chain available for later encounters.

text: Players accept an identity introduced by a character they trust, and do not question it when witnesses agree with that identity.
when: A character is introduced with an identity that others confirm.
why: Shared acceptance by multiple witnesses removes the impulse to test the identity.

text: An anagram alias rearranges every letter of a true name, hiding identity in plain sight until the letters are compared.
A notice that names a person fails silently when the person travels under a false name, even if they are alive and nearby.
when: The sought person is known to use an alias
why: Recipients cannot link the notice to the person without recognising the name.

text: 1) Show the character under one name. 2) Show a related name earlier in a separate context, sharing letters or sound. 3) Deliver the link at the moment of exposure. 4) Confirm the identity through a second independent witness.
when: A hidden identity must be revealed at a climax without a separate explanation.
why: The reader already holds every fact and needs only the recognition, and two sources make the reveal feel earned.

text: Give an NPC an almost-recognition moment that stops short of naming someone, and use it to unlock a later identification.
when: planting a future identity reveal
why: A hesitation the player notices makes the later identification feel earned.

text: A convenient coincidence may be a deliberate arrangement, and a case that fits too neatly is suspicious since a shrewd culprit can plant misleading loopholes.
when: A coincidence fits the timing and people involved, or a circumstantial case fits together too cleanly.
why: A shrewd culprit can leave misleading loopholes that look like a tidy theory.

text: Objects with a hidden second layer, such as a label revealed by scraping or a seal, can reveal a second identity.
when: Designing an item that hides a second identity.
why: Revealing an underlying layer rewards players for careful inspection.

text: Attach the identity clue to a shared physical object that only a few named characters touched, so the suspect list stays small and the clue is fair.
when: a reveal depends on one physical trace
why: A short named suspect list lets the audience test the clue

text: A physical identifier such as a scar or a fingerprint is useless until it is matched against a second independent record, such as a witness description.
An antagonist can remove an investigator from the scene using a formal, legitimate-looking process timed to a window of opportunity.
when: when an opponent has a plausible legal or social means to stop the protagonist
why: The process looks lawful, so it is hard to resist directly.

text: A plotter can make a location predictably empty at a known hour by arranging a servant's leave, travel times and a planned outing.
when: When a plan requires a location to be unobserved at a specific time.
why: Scheduled absences remove witnesses at a chosen moment.

text: A stopping point that depends on a person's inability to sense a condition suggests the conditions were engineered rather than arising by chance.
when: an incomplete action coincides with a sensory limitation of the actor
why: A limitation the actor cannot sense explains why the stop occurred only if someone arranged the situation.

text: A suspect can secure an alibi by being in a witnessed place when the crime happens, while the crime itself runs without them.
when: a non-present suspect needs confirmed innocence
why: Independent witnesses confirm the suspect's location at the critical moment.

text: A staged death can invert identity: the body may be someone else, or the man presumed dead or living may be the impostor.
Identifying marks can be altered after death to create a false identity, so a match holds only if the body has not been modified.
A person who knows someone well can recognise them by gait or posture even when a disguise hides the face, since habitual movement is harder to disguise than appearance.
when: Identifying a person through a recurring trait, or a disguised figure near someone familiar with them.
why: Movement is harder to disguise than appearance and can link identities.

text: A recognition signal is a spoken phrase that must receive a set reply before any message or item is handed over.
Fingerprints are permanent and unique, unlike face, hair, height or build, which can change or be duplicated, so they serve as a more reliable identifier.
when: When identifying a person from physical evidence.
why: Permanence and uniqueness make the mark a stable identifier.

text: Displaced sheets, fresh work or rotted boards on surfaces and fittings can mark recent work and where something was hidden.
Specific details of a victim's flight, such as clothing or a weapon seen with a pursuer, can point to an unlisted suspect.
when: A pursuer is glimpsed but unidentified
why: Distinctive details narrow the search to someone not yet considered.

text: A distinctive mark recorded in a list can be spotted by the player in a crowd or portrait, so the player can confirm a dead or missing character's identity.
when: Designing missing or dead character clues
why: A specific, recordable feature gives a checkable link between a character and a clue

text: Assuming a recognition phrase stays secret once the carrier knows it is a mistake.
A changed appearance, such as a new shave or disguise, cannot confirm identity, and a sighting proves nothing when an unseen agent could copy that appearance.
A suspect's self-description or bold self-declaration is not evidence: a profile built from their own opinions restates them, self-assessment echoes praise, and admiration does not confirm the claim.
A witness's claim of sanity or wellness does not prove accurate perception, and may make them least reliable about own actions; impairment can affect one task while another seems fine.
A character who jokes about being suspected can make suspicion seem harmless, and the joke draws attention away from the real trail until evidence arrives.
when: A character volunteers a damning-seeming motive or suspicion early in a mystery
why: A light tone lowers the audience's guard against a remark that may later be taken seriously

text: Changing visible appearance, such as clothing or footwear, hides a traveler from pursuers who identify people by face or dress.
Physical strength and appearance can diverge, so delicate build or movement does not reliably show weakness.
Different records may give one building different names, including a common term for dwellings of the period, so a differing name does not necessarily mean a different place.
when: Matching records about a building
why: Naming conventions vary across records

text: When a witness disclaims their own accuracy, weigh each detail separately: they may be right on key points, while blamed conditions can hide gaps or be self-serving evasions.
when: A witness's account matters for later reasoning and the witness has disclaimed their own accuracy.
why: Explicit disclaimers signal observations made in a compromised state; self-disclaimers can be partial truths or evasions.

text: Appearance-based first impressions are only hints to test against later facts; they distort judgment, especially when signs contradict each other.
When appearance conflicts with behavior or a stated claim, weigh both signals and record the conflict; neither alone decides, and the conflict is itself informative.
when: A suspect's look conflicts with their behavior or what they say about themselves.
why: Either signal alone can mislead, and their conflict is itself informative.

text: Appearance, clothing, footwear and manner poorly indicate guilt or social rank; respectable, pious people have committed murders, and observers may misread who holds authority.
when: When judging suspects or ranks by how they look or act.
why: Culprits who seem ordinary force players to rely on clues rather than instinct.

text: Appearance reveals recent activity: loosened clothing or ongoing activity suggests how long someone has been in a place, while clean, mud-free clothing suggests they stayed indoors.
when: Inferring a person's recent movements or time in a place.
why: Dirt and wear accumulate from outdoor activity.

text: Treat a character's claim of skill, past events or relationships as untested until it is checked against something observable.
when: the claim matters to the plot
why: self-reported accounts may be biased or mistaken

text: If a supposed force would act the same way elsewhere, a limit tied to one location is a weak point in the claim.
when: when evaluating a supernatural claim

text: A physical trace, such as a ticket stub, that does not fit the described appearance of the occupant points to a different person.
Each check confirms that someone did what a story claims, not that the central subject is who they seem to be.
A harmonious portrait can hide one jarring detail, which may be the thread worth examining.
when: A victim or subject is described as uniformly admirable.

text: A colour mismatch can look like a dead end; inspect the disguised area up close, because older marks may show faintly through the new layer.
when: a disguise seems to fail at first glance
why: thin or uneven coats let earlier layers show through

text: A neat, self-supplied alibi can be deliberate: a careful culprit planning for safety would arrange exactly that kind of paperwork.
Show a witness's own disclaimer in dialogue to warn the player that the testimony is incomplete.
when: An NPC witness has a known condition affecting their testimony.
why: Transparent warnings give the player fair notice of unreliability.

text: An item chosen to match a target's known preference suggests the actor knew that target's habits.
Visible sentiment toward one person can mask a concealed purpose aimed at another person.
An identification puzzle can use several NPCs who partly match a description, with a distinctive mark as the decisive clue.
when: designing a character-identification puzzle
why: partial matches create ambiguity that a single clue resolves

text: A manufactured-identity mystery chains identity proofs, each partly wrong; the answer emerges only when the proofs are reconciled and their conflicts explained.
when: designing a mystery whose hidden character must be identified from clues
why: Single proofs mislead, so the solution depends on how the whole chain fits together.

text: A witness's or narrator's claim of candour or fairness is an assertion to test against conduct; volunteering damaging facts can be impression management, not proof of sincerity.
why: Stated fairness is easy to assert and can earn undeserved trust; confession alone does not establish sincerity.

text: Judging a witness's credibility by clothing, status, accent or nervousness biases the account's reception; appearance should not decide truth, and sympathetic readings stay unverified until checked.
when: Assessing a witness's credibility, especially a low-status witness giving an account to an official or court.
why: Appearance is judged before the account is heard.

text: Records under another person's name mislead investigators who check only the suspect's name; a name missing from one record but present in a related one may reveal an alias.
when: A suspect may travel or register under an alias.
why: The person may have used another name in that record.

text: A search can find nothing and still be incomplete. A scene can look clean to the person who made it, so a concealer's confidence is not evidence.
Do not treat a name or origin given at registration as verified; it may be false and may give no address.
Judging a stain by appearance alone can mislead; confirm what a fluid is with microscopic or chemical testing.
A witness who admits their own anger may still be shielding someone, so the bystanders' accounts must be checked against theirs.
when: when a witness is a participant in a quarrel
why: self-criticism can make an account more credible while still concealing facts

text: Judging age by appearance alone can be wrong by years, so check the estimate against other dated facts.
A false name can be exposed when it is linked to the investigator's real business or address, so the alias must be kept apart from those links.
A confessed bad motive, such as being blackmailed, can redirect suspicion onto others, so it should be weighed carefully.
when: Suspect admits a motive while denying the act
why: An admitted motive shifts blame elsewhere

text: A self-declared expert whose accusations keep multiplying can damage a whole region until exposed as a fraud.
Naming the attacker from the side of a wound alone is a mistake, because the same wound angle can fit more than one person.
why: position narrows suspects but does not single one out

text: Identifying a substance does not prove who used it or when. A separate step is needed to establish administration.
when: a test confirms what something is
why: a positive test shows possession, not the act or its timing

text: 1) Plant an object suggesting a habit. 2) Add a second object that confirms or refutes it. 3) Require that verification before the player names a suspect; checkable habits, such as never wearing a ring, can rule an NPC out.
why: Keeps player inference checkable.

text: 1) Check the history of any named reference person. 2) Query contacts abroad where the claim places the subject. 3) Circulate the subject's photograph to many authorities.
when: a suspect's claimed identity cannot be confirmed directly

text: 1) Collect the cryptic signature or alias. 2) List sources the suspect may have read, such as plays, histories or cultural texts. 3) Search them for the term. 4) Keep a match only if it ties to the people and facts.
when: a signature or alias has several possible meanings
why: a source the culprit drew on can narrow the meaning

text: 1) List identifiers to collect: name, address, occupation, marital status, family, and links to third parties. 2) Collect physical description and habits from witnesses. 3) Check each candidate against records. 4) Reconstruct meetings using event records like guest lists.
when: The only known link to a suspect is a face, voice or name
why: Memory alone is vague, and records fill the gaps

text: 1) Compare shared generic traits such as hair, skin and build first. 2) Compare distinctive marks such as scars against the body. 3) Compare objects that touch the body, such as rings and locket hair. 4) Compare the same fingers and marks in both cases.
when: When matching a body to a missing person
why: Shared traits carry little weight alone, while distinctive marks and objects carry more.

text: Do not accept an alibi resting only on the suspect's own word, servants or fellow group members, since they may be complicit; track which parts independent others corroborate.
when: Evaluating a suspect's whereabouts or alibi.
why: Self-report and interested parties are not independent verification.

text: Hide an identifying mark under clothing so the player must expose it, for example by rolling up a sleeve, to verify identity.
Mark one visual feature on a hostile figure so that a later encounter can be matched to an earlier sighting.
Do not decide whether a person is alive or dead from appearance alone, since deep sleep and death can look alike.
when: When a person is motionless and still.
why: Visual signs overlap between unconsciousness and death.

text: Build identification puzzles so the player must consider the alternative hypothesis, that two appearances are the same person, before the trick becomes visible.
when: designing a puzzle that hinges on recognizing someone
why: the player must weigh both possibilities before the answer is clear

text: Answer whether two traces share a source separately from whether two cases are linked.
why: A matching pair of traces can settle one question while leaving the other open

text: Let item details such as monograms, shades and key types encode an owner's name and habits, so players can deduce identity and eliminate non-matching suspects.
when: Designing mystery-item puzzles.

text: Claiming authority you do not hold can win cooperation, but if the witness checks the claim, it can backfire and damage the case.
when: when a volatile witness may refuse or retract

text: A council chosen by one party rules only on the evidence that party supplies, whereas a jointly accepted body can issue a verdict both sides must respect.
Plant a distinctive, persistent cue the player sees early, such as a tool, cord or remembered item, so a disguised or masked figure is recognised fairly at the reveal.
when: A recognition beat depends on noticing a clue; a confrontation at a deadline in a crowded location; a character's identity was hinted at earlier.
why: A visible constant cue makes recognition fair and solvable, letting players resolve confrontations quickly and feel the reveal is earned.

text: Witnesses who omit or withhold a detail may recall or confirm it once a specific named item or guess is offered; general questions miss it.
when: Asking about a detail the witness left out or seems to withhold.
why: Specific cues retrieve memories general questions miss, and a concrete proposal is easier to confirm than an open question.

text: A suspect asked to list people present gives names reluctantly, and recalls a forgotten person only when the interviewer offers a name already known.
when: when a suspect is asked to list people present
why: recall is cued by a specific name rather than generated freely

text: A close relative's recognition of a personal item tends to be emotional and is often accepted as the strongest confirmation.
when: a relative of a missing person sees a possession
why: personal attachment makes the relative's identification feel certain

text: A witness who cannot recall a person's face may still recall their name when it matches something already known to them.
when: when a witness cannot describe a face clearly
why: A shared detail anchors recall.

text: A character recognises a distinctive object only if they saw it before, so recognition depends on earlier exposure.
when: A worn or distinctive object reappears later in a story
why: Recognition requires having seen the object earlier

text: A recognized personal item can show that someone knew the wearer even though the wearer did not know them in return.
when: an onlooker recognizes a marked item on a person
why: the mark reveals the wearer's identity to the viewer

text: A witness may be sure of a face yet unable to recall a name, so an identification of a face does not establish a correct identity.
when: When a witness claims to recognize someone but cannot give a full identity.
why: Face memory and name memory are separate, and confidence attaches to the face.

text: A witness may reverse an identification made in a charged moment once she recognises someone close to the accused, and then decline to prosecute.
when: when the identified person is known to the witness
why: Personal relationships change the stakes of testimony.

text: Observers recognise a distant figure by build and gait before seeing the face; this can beat a close view of a disguised face.
when: identifying someone at a distance or behind a disguise
why: silhouette and movement are harder to alter than facial features

text: A witness who saw only part of a figure, such as its back or a voice, forms an identity from cues and expectations, so a missing face goes unnoticed.
when: the witness saw only part of a person and expects someone familiar to be present
why: expectation fills the unseen parts of the perception

text: A witness who sees only part of a person, such as gait, build and a distinctive coat, can recognize them with confidence, though less surely than from a clear face.
when: the view is partial, such as from behind or at a distance
why: Recognition combines partly seen and partly remembered features.

text: Offering a list of names can reveal a witness's knowledge: a witness who denies knowing one name may still name someone else from the same situation.
when: When a witness conceals knowledge of people connected to a case.
why: Witnesses concentrate on the names they fear and can slip on the rest.

text: Witnesses can recognise a person from small habits the witness never consciously noticed, such as a repetitive fidget at the table.
when: a witness has observed the person at close range
why: habits are registered without conscious attention

text: A single witness identification placing a suspect at a site and time can justify arrest, though it is a fragile basis for the case.
A witness identification informs a case, but the decision to charge depends on whether the whole case holds together.
Establishing identity between close lookalikes, especially from personal recognition alone, is among the hardest questions to settle.
when: a claim depends on who someone is
why: resemblance undermines recognition

text: A person can be linked to an identity through marked objects, physical descriptions, or third-party references, and each method needs its own check before it is trusted.
why: Each link method can mislead in a different way.

text: Recognition is often partial: a witness may know a voice without recognising the face, and may confirm only height and general look.
when: identifying a person from voice or appearance

text: An identification method works only if someone is known to keep the records it needs, such as dental records kept over years.
Feeling certain does not guarantee an accurate identification; a confident memory of a face is a claim to test against the person actually in view.
when: A sighting or memory of a face is the basis for identifying or linking a person.
why: Identification depends on memory, condition and confidence.

text: An engraved or monogrammed item can link an unidentified body or injured person to its named owner when papers are missing, but its presence alone does not prove identity.
when: A body or injured person has no papers but keeps personal items.
why: An object can be worn or passed on by others.

text: A failed identification still narrows possibilities without eliminating the suspect; it does not prove innocence until the witness's view, limited by lighting and distance, is known.
when: A witness is shown a lineup or a person and cannot confirm them.
why: Lighting and distance limit what a witness can see, so a near miss may be a poor view.

text: A partial identifier, such as a vehicle plate from a particular region or its first digits, narrows a search without solving it, since it shrinks candidates rather than isolating one.
when: A full identifier is not available.
why: Partial information shrinks the candidate set but rarely isolates one answer.

text: A remark revealing knowledge the speaker could not have had should be challenged, since it can betray involvement; asking whether an item was returned implies they could not check.
when: A speaker says something showing what they knew, or a suspect speaks of details only the culprit could know.
why: Offhand remarks often expose information the speaker did not intend to share.

text: Vague descriptions widen the suspect pool while precise ones narrow it; test how many people a description fits, since one matching a large share identifies no one.
when: Identifying a suspect from testimony.
why: A description identifies someone only when few people fit it.

text: Record people through what they repeatedly do, such as watching or drinking, rather than only through labels, since habits reveal more than descriptions.
