Name the specific people who use a place and why, which turns a general claim about traffic into one that can be checked.
A distinctive personal item can stand in for a person's face when the owner was never seen clearly, linking an unexplained event to that person.
when: a figure was seen at a distance or cannot be named
why: an item unique to a person can carry identity where a face cannot

text: Naming specific verified facts, such as a known meeting or offer, can push a guarded suspect toward confession.
Before trusting a conversation, consider whether a listener behind a door is an ally or a rival.
when: a private exchange may be overheard
why: Listeners carry different loyalties and can change what is said

text: Choose a time and lighting in which the target has the least reason to recognise you, such as after seeing you only in darkness.
when: planning a covert approach
why: recognition depends on conditions as well as appearance

text: A culprit who wants a body unidentified tends to strip its most recognisable items. Identifiable items found apart from the body suggest the discard was deliberate.
when: Interpreting where identifying belongings were left after a death.

text: Check objects against the identity they claim; a detail such as clothing sized wrong for its owner can expose deliberate misdirection.
when: an object seems to belong to someone it does not fit
why: Misdirection often leaves a small inconsistency on close inspection.

text: Naming the consequences of continued silence before leaving can prompt a fuller account.
A distinctive mark such as a brand on the forearm identifies a body once clothing slips and exposes it.
When a face is hidden by a mask, veil or covered hair, identification depends on whatever partial features were actually seen.
when: A victim or suspect was disguised
why: Concealment limits identification to visible traits

text: Test a claimed identity by introducing the claimant to someone who knows the real person; a failure of recognition exposes the false claim.
when: A claimed identity is doubtful and a related person may be hiding behind it.
why: Someone who knows the real person can recognize an impostor.

text: A substitute chosen for partial resemblance makes each outside check confirm something true, strengthening the deception.
when: Choosing a double
why: Matching facts pass verification

text: Close scrutiny of a stranger's face and clothing can defeat a disguise, since a careful observer registers details that a costume leaves unchanged.
when: a disguised suspect is in view
why: Detailed observation exposes features a disguise cannot fully hide.

text: A witness who names the giver of an object, retracts, then restates the claim is showing unreliable memory or concealment.
An identification based on a known habit depends on that habit, not on the object's own features, and should be weighed as such.
Do not treat a face or outline as identification without checking for disguise.
when: a witness saw a person only briefly

text: A half-formed recognition of a voice is weak evidence and should not count as identification until it is tested.
when: when a witness recognizes a voice only partly
why: Partial recall is easily mistaken.

text: When a body's face is destroyed by burns, identity becomes a legitimate doubt that a test can confirm or rule out.
when: A victim cannot be recognised visually
why: Visual identification is unavailable, so other evidence must decide.

text: A single meeting is weak evidence of identity; repeated meetings need checking before they support a link between people.
when: Connecting a person seen in passing to a suspect or name.
why: One sighting can be mistaken, while repeated sightings can be tested.

text: Verify identities in records before trusting counts, since two people with the same name can make totals unreliable.
Match characters on traits that survive wear and change, such as expression, because they still show through decay and ageing.
when: A person's appearance has changed since the earlier image.
why: Surface details fade over time while core features endure.

text: A physical description that matches a suspect is only a starting point, because broad descriptions fit many people and need corroboration.
when: Matching a suspect to a witness or record description.
why: Common physical traits are shared by many individuals.

text: Verify a stranger with a shared sign or challenge, like a known alias; a bluffer fails, but a real contact may lapse, so one miss is weak evidence.
when: Checking whether a stranger belongs to a group; a contact must verify identity without revealing much.
why: Only someone who knows the sign can answer it correctly; memory lapses happen even for real contacts.

text: A buyer who gives no address can still be identified by a detail such as appearance or payment habit that picks them out from a crowd.
when: Tracing a customer who left few personal records
why: Distinctive traits can single out a person even without contact details

text: Remarks made within hearing of accusers can suggest names, and those suggested names are then acted on.
A player-mentioned name can set a hidden flag when an NPC hesitates, letting later dialogue react to the NPC's unease.
when: Designing NPC reactions to named characters.
why: Hesitation is a detectable signal that can change the NPC's future responses.

text: A recognition trigger, such as a particular word or symbol, can unlock a memory of an earlier encounter.
when: a character must reconnect to a past event
why: the trigger reactivates the associated memory

text: Recognition cues such as a garment, hat or posture can stand in for a face, so an impersonator needs to copy only those cues.
A recognisable outline, such as a silhouette, or a deliberate cue, such as a loud song, lets a watching contact identify a person without names.
when: A contact must recognise an investigator who cannot be openly identified.
why: Distinct visual or audible signals convey identity to someone who knows what to look for.

text: Giving each persona a small habit fingerprint, such as a brand of product, lets players link two characters when the fingerprints match.
when: Designing NPC identities that can be linked
why: A shared private habit is harder to fake than public identity

text: Each named person, place or transport gives a detail that can later be confirmed or contradicted by other evidence.
when: a witness gives an account with specific names

text: Documents with deliberate name variants or errors force the player to reconcile them with a second document, turning each conflict into a cross-check puzzle.
when: when in-game letters, ledgers or depositions are generated with inconsistencies
why: Conflicting records require comparison to resolve, which makes the discrepancy the challenge

text: Identical-looking items defeat tracing and can mislead reconstruction when assumed to be one object or several without checking distinguishing features recorded when placed.
A reaction to a named person shows familiarity or unease, not its content or guilt; it justifies further investigation, not a conclusion.
when: A name probe produces a visible reaction.
why: Unease has many causes, and a reaction confirms familiarity but not what the knowledge is.

text: Naming people during questioning can plant those names in the witness's mind and make later answers unreliable.
when: When testing a witness with names of possible suspects.
why: A witness may adopt a name suggested by the questioner rather than recall it independently.

text: Linking two people as one because their descriptions overlap is unsound; a description match alone does not establish that they are the same person.
A partial match on a shared model can be coincidence, since many copies of a product share the same features.
Fixating on a minor name in a file can absorb attention while the central question stays unanswered.
Recognition after a long gap can be mistaken, so a remembered identification should be checked against earlier sightings.
when: A witness identifies someone seen only once, long before.
why: Memory of appearance fades and can drift over time.

text: Naming one's own bias does not remove it; a witness may admit prejudice and still have answers coloured by it.
A fragment that names a person without implying a stake carries little weight.
Identifying a person or object under public pressure, in poor light and with a crowd watching, is fragile and often unreliable.
when: A character is asked to identify something quickly in a tense setting
why: Pressure and poor visibility reduce accuracy

text: A description alone is weak where the target can blend into a large city.
A correct match showing whose trace it is does not show when the trace was made. A planted mark can match the right person perfectly.
when: When evaluating a trace that identifies a suspect.
why: Identity and timing are separate facts that a single comparison does not establish.

text: Assuming the person who arrived is the same as the person who left is a common error that hides an occupant substitution.
Assuming a body's identity is certain can hide a staged death.
Relabelling a character after the fact can mislead audiences about who is present and what role they play.
when: When editing a story's labels or framing late in production
why: Audiences build their model of the cast from the labels they are given

text: A sign of identity can be recognised by the wrong people as well as the right ones.
A direct question about a name fails if the target uses an alias, producing a false negative that looks like a dead end.
A caller who quotes another person's name does not thereby become that person; a name in a message is not proof of who is speaking.
when: when a message names a speaker
why: A name can be borrowed or false.

text: Handling a sheet by its face can destroy fingerprints or other marks the investigator wants to keep.
when: Collecting loose paper as evidence.
why: Contact with the surface disturbs traces.

text: Treating a face as a mirror of the soul traps a reader or investigator once later events overturn the first impression.
A description that fits a real person's appearance looks like corroboration but does not prove the perceived event occurred.
Assuming a repeat visitor is a stranger ignores visible traces that link the two visits.

1) Drop or ask about a name or visitor the witness should or should not know. 2) Observe stammering, denial, blushing, embarrassment, sudden anger, colour change or asking who talked. 3) Treat reactions as leads to test, not proof of guilt.
when: Testing whether a witness knows a particular person, or a suspect holds information you need.
why: Recognition or unease is revealed more reliably by reaction than by spoken answers; an unexpected name triggers fear of exposure.

text: 1) Identify the features the disguise hides or alters. 2) Obtain one hard-to-change feature, such as a scar, from a witness who saw the person closely, and examine permanent marks up close. 3) Compare marks with records of past injury or background. 4) Match each mark against candidate identities.
when: A suspect's name or papers may be false, or a disguised person is suspected.
why: Disguises rarely alter physical marks.

text: 1) List each claim the stated identity makes, such as name and address. 2) Check each claim against independent records, such as criminal records, property histories and physical descriptions. 3) Flag mismatches; record each match as a link between person, place and victim.
when: A stated identity may be false and independent records about people, places or crimes exist.
why: Independent records expose inconsistent claims, and independent matches build a chain harder to fake than a single claim.

text: 1) Start from a past fact the suspect once revealed. 2) Trace the records of that past role. 3) Match descriptions, names and corroborating details from several sources. 4) Accept the identification only when independent sources agree.
when: A suspect has changed name or appearance but left a traceable past; the record may use a different name.
why: A name can change while descriptions and records persist, so a match may rest on descriptions rather than the name.

text: 1) Collect every name variant and title. 2) Link variants to one identity using family ties, residence and repeated sworn testimony. 3) Accept a link only when it rests on more than the name.
when: Before comparing dates, places or alibis across documents.
why: A name alone cannot confirm identity, so context must support each link.

text: 1) Ask a witness for the unseen person's build, complexion and whiskers. 2) Verify any rough description before acting on it.
when: a witness can describe a third party

text: 1) Collect a physical description, such as height and build. 2) Fix the time of the event. 3) Note what each observer did. 4) Match the description and timing to the most probable person.

1) Gather people who knew the person's appearance. 2) Check a physical marker, such as an engraved item. 3) Combine their evidence with the discovered facts. 4) Test the doubted claim against that combined result.
1) Ask an open identity question. 2) Ask a follow-up about shared context. 3) Offer a familiar everyday cue. 4) Accept the identity only after two shared facts match.
when: a character must confirm who another is from memory

text: 1) Estimate when an absence would first cause concern. 2) Estimate when that concern leads to a published notice. 3) Search the press around that date. 4) Match identifying marks, such as initials, against the notice.
when: identifying an unknown victim through the press

text: 1) Collect the partial identifier, such as initials. 2) Test it against local knowledge and records. 3) Accept a match only when several corroborating local facts support it.
when: A witness or document gives only a partial identifier
why: A single initial match is weak and can mislead

text: 1) Note the first identification and its emotional weight. 2) Check features not yet examined, such as a beard, scar or tattoo. 3) Link borrowed or traced items to their source. 4) Revise the whole reading of the event.
when: when a first identification may be wrong

text: 1) Pick a predictable moment when the suspect must slow down. 2) Station a hidden observer. 3) Release a familiar animal at that moment. 4) Read its reaction as evidence of identity.
when: A person's identity or a substitution is in doubt and a familiar animal is available
why: The animal's recognition is hard for an impostor to fake

text: 1) Ask whether the witness would pick the person out of a group later. 2) Test the answer with a lineup that includes similar people. 3) Accept the identification only if it holds.
when: A key identification rests on a witness's memory of a common-looking person.
why: Recognition among similar people is weak, so a lineup tests whether the memory can actually single out the person.

text: 1) Record the lighting, distance, duration of view and any face-obscuring items. 2) Weigh the identification against those conditions. 3) Treat a poorly lit, brief or obscured view as weak evidence.
when: Assessing how far an eyewitness identification can be trusted.
why: Each limiting condition reduces what the witness could actually perceive, so the identification carries less weight.

text: 1) Ask the identifying witness whether the suspect is the person. 2) Record a denial and any alternative description given. 3) Compare the alternative description against the suspect's actual features.
when: A witness is asked to identify a suspect and may deny the identification.
why: A denial and a differing description can cast doubt on the original identification.

text: 1) Adopt a plausible official role. 2) Ask a neutral question, such as about household members. 3) Confirm or discard the identity from the answer, without revealing interest.
when: checking whether a named person is at an address
why: a neutral question avoids alerting the subject

text: 1) Have the witness examine the body or image long and carefully. 2) Ask whether they are sure. 3) Ask which specific marks the identification rests on.
when: a witness gives an identification from partial evidence
why: Confirms the basis is specific marks rather than a general impression.

text: 1) Note features that survive disguise, such as build, height, beard, bodily marks, voice, accent, and speech habits. 2) Track each unidentified person under a stable label. 3) Check each feature for reliability.
when: a witness sees only parts of several people
why: Disguises hide the face but not every trait, so some features remain usable.

text: 1) Note the familiar face and the feeling that it is known. 2) Place it in the earlier context where it was seen. 3) Confirm the identity with a direct question.

1) State the investigation goals before questioning anyone. 2) Review physical and medical facts, such as cause and approximate time of death. 3) Filter a records list by sex, age, area and description. 4) Confirm each candidate with a non-physical detail, such as clothing or possessions.
when: a victim is unidentified and a records list exists
why: Filtering narrows candidates, and a non-physical detail can confirm or eliminate them.

text: 1) List the habits and possessions each persona is known to use. 2) Compare the lists for overlap. 3) Check where the shared items were, and whether they disappeared when one persona vanished.
when: Linking two identities by evidence

text: 1) Raise the name the witness currently uses. 2) If they deny a connection, press on the name. 3) Once they show distress, reassure them to draw out an admission.
when: When a witness is hiding a family tie
why: Name challenges unsettle concealment and reassurance encourages honesty

text: 1) Name a witness to the suspect without revealing more. 2) Observe whether the suspect mentions, avoids or contacts that witness. 3) Record the reply as an inference, since the witness may now be prepared.
when: A suspect has omitted a witness who logically should have been mentioned

text: To test identification, have the witness view the body or item and confirm the person who did the action.
1) List the features in the description. 2) Approach the candidate under similar viewing conditions. 3) Check each listed feature against the person before accepting the match.

1) Match names, dates and places across sources. 2) Label each identity as stated, inferred or assumed. 3) Use only the stated and inferred identities as a basis for conclusions, and flag the assumed ones.
when: When cases rest on fragmentary, undated or annotated records.
why: Explicit labels stop an assumption from being mistaken for a documented fact.

text: 1) Approach the subject while they are visible. 2) Ask them to show their face. 3) Tell them recognition is intended. 4) Fix the image in memory for later identification.
when: when a face must be recognised later and the subject can be approached
why: A deliberate look at a face produces a more reliable memory than a passing glimpse.

text: Require two or more independent identifiers or sources before accepting an identity, so one compromised or unreliable witness cannot close the case alone.
when: Designing quest or case completion in a game; a body's or person's identity rests on a single compromised source.
why: One unreliable witness can mislead the conclusion; a single source may be wrong, shaken or biased.

text: Verify an identity link before relying on dependent clues; an identity inferred from a single report can be wrong and silently invalidates every clue that follows.
when: A clue chain depends on who a person is.
why: A plausible chain can look complete yet rest on one false premise.

text: Record a witness's identification confidence separately from its accuracy; confidence can rest on a partial view, like a lit face through a window, and still be wrong.
when: Photo or lineup identification.
why: A sure witness can still be wrong.

text: Test claimed identity with hard-to-disguise marks or routine behaviour an impostor fails; use marks only alongside other evidence, since they can be altered or engineered.
Recognition depends on attention and motive, such as vanity or gain; don't accept a recognition claim alone, check it against the witness's motives and opportunities.
when: A witness identifies someone at a distance, after a long gap, or in changed circumstances.

text: When a witness omits a step, name that step explicitly and state they have not told everything; the gap exposes a flaw and invites further questions.
when: When listening to a witness's narration or when a witness's account seems incomplete.
why: Naming the gap signals that the story is not accepted and invites more detail.

text: Establish a person's identity from official letters, licences and lodging addresses, and record letters as evidence once read.
when: A person's background is unclear.

text: Use wanted posters, prison records and newspaper notices as in-world sources that can either hide or reveal a character's identity.
when: Worlds where characters have pasts that players can uncover.
why: Ordinary public records give players diegetic ways to discover identities.

text: Matching a physical feature requires expertise in that feature; without it, the comparison is only a guess.
Make an NPC's recognition question change how the NPC treats the player, so a wrong answer alters the NPC's willingness to help.
when: designing NPC contacts who verify identity
why: a visible consequence makes the challenge meaningful

text: Make identity cues in NPC dialogue something players must verify; a voice heard through a wall should not confirm identity automatically.
when: when designing identity clues
why: Unverified cues can mislead players.

text: Let vendors or passersby describe the expected pattern so players can detect a missing element without being told directly.
Ask what a witness could actually know before weighing their testimony, since recognition depends on prior acquaintance.
when: When a witness's account would rule out a suspect.
why: A witness cannot recognize someone they never knew.

text: A close associate may miss a disguised person when key cues like look or manner changed, since appearance overrides memory; yet a spouse often recognises the face through long familiarity.
when: A disguised person meets someone who knew them well or is in close contact; recognition by a spouse or long-time associate holds when familiarity is long.
why: Appearance and manner can override memory, while long familiarity gives recognition cues others lack.

text: Naming a witness to a suspect can yield information, but it may let the witness be coached, destroying the independent check that witness could have provided.
when: Only one independent source of verification exists

text: When documents fail to prove identity, a rival's recognition of a personal tell can serve as proof; documents are stronger evidence but slower to establish.
when: a reveal depends on identifying a disguised character
why: Recognition resolves the question in a single scene, at the cost of being less legally rigorous.

text: Plant the key identity clue, such as a portrait, record, object, or gesture, in the first act in plain sight, so the answer is visible before the reveal.
when: Writing a hidden-identity twist

text: Deliver an identity reversal through a document or incidental aside rather than a dramatic accusation, so it reads as a discovery.
Plant identity clues early and feed later evidence in a steady trickle, so the question stays open until the late reveal.
Reveal a stranger NPC's identity through an in-world log or record after the player leaves a zone, enabling a late callback.
when: Designing a delayed identity reveal.
why: Records let identity be disclosed without interrupting play.

text: Hold back the culprit's full identity until a late reveal that proves it, rather than disclosing it piece by piece in private.
when: when the culprit has been hidden behind a trusted role

text: A twist that a character is a second self can be built by planting two separate facts early, such as a key and a will, which the audience reads as unrelated until a later reveal links them.
when: Designing a reveal where two apparently different characters are the same person
why: Separate early facts let the audience hold both pieces before knowing they connect, so the reveal reframes rather than contradicts them.

text: An identity-swap reveal hides that one person has taken another's place, and is built from partial exposures, each confirming a suspicion but not the full truth.

1) Let an authority figure gather physical proof, such as a grave, tomb, or working object. 2) Stage the reveal as a public or semi-public act. 3) Close with a brief aftermath where the narrator leaves, carrying lasting unease.
when: Designing the climax where a hidden identity is exposed.
why: Physical proof lets the audience verify the solution rather than accept a claim.

text: 1) Exchange roles so the suspect and staff see the wrong person in the wrong role. 2) Arrange the scene the suspect will enter. 3) Keep the people who know the truth apart.
when: The suspect has never seen the real person.
why: A swap works only while those who know the truth stay separated.

text: Break one identity into stages, such as stranger, performer, former lover, and parent, each revealed in a separate scene so understanding changes in steps.
If a claimed result needs many separate unlikely accidents, treat the claim as suspicious and examine it more closely.
An explanation is weakened when the action it implies is unlikely for the actors involved, such as a family hiding a dangerous person at home instead of sending them away.
A theory can be improbable and still a serious candidate if every rival explanation is also improbable.
When a method seems implausible for ordinary people, check whether it really excludes them rather than accepting the obvious suspect.
when: a method appears to require an unusually strong or skilled person
why: Implausibility can clear some suspects while leaving the true culprit's capacity unexamined.

text: A claimed duration far longer than the expected travel time for a short journey is a point to probe.
When a stated reason looks too minor to explain the outcome it produced, look for a larger pressure that the complaining party chose not to mention.
when: an official ground seems out of proportion to an action

text: Quest hooks that promise improbable rescues can tempt players into investing in the wrong lead; give players a way to recognize that mistake later.
when: Designing tempting but false leads.
why: Players need a discoverable signal to correct a misreading.

text: Confusing an improbable truth with a planned lie is an error; a self-serving or unlikely account may still be true.
when: when judging a witness whose account seems too convenient

text: Improvised detail added under pressure creates new checkable claims that can be exposed later.
Accept an improbable explanation only after the likelier explanations have been tested and failed, or closed off by physical constraints.
when: Several explanations remain, one of them improbable
why: Eliminating the easier options leaves the improbable one as the only consistent answer

text: When a sighting or normal explanation seems impossible, examine the means of access and test it; uncanny explanations are premature because the gap usually lies in a checkable route.
when: A sighting seems impossible on its face, or a normal explanation appears closed off.
why: Apparent impossibility often reflects an unexamined assumption about the system.

text: Treat a sealed-room claim as a method question, not proof of impossibility: keep asking how anyone could enter or leave and whether the space was truly empty at the event.
when: A room or crime appears sealed or impossible given its enclosure.
why: Sealed-room claims often hide an overlooked route or timing gap.

text: A citation pointing to a location that does not exist signals an error, and the surrounding context often reveals the intended reference.
An item in a place it should not be is itself evidence, because its presence shows that someone had access to it.
When a room seems unreachable, look for a route that a person with an unusual ability could use, once that ability is known.
when: A locked or sealed room appears impossible to enter
why: Known abilities can make an apparently impossible route plausible

text: If a perishable still shows a state that heat or elapsed time would have destroyed, it must have arrived after that period.
when: checking a delivery's timing

text: Open with a stated physical impossibility, then supply a mechanism that explains it, so the audience gets a fair puzzle to attempt before the solution is revealed.
when: A mystery should feel impossible yet remain fair.
why: Stating the impossibility first gives the audience a puzzle to attempt before the reveal.

text: A planted clue fails when its staged action is physically impossible, so a wound angle or grip can serve as a checkable puzzle condition.
when: Designing a staged clue the player must test
why: A physical check exposes staging that a story alone would hide

text: A report of something impossible can distract from the practical facts that can be tested.
when: a witness reports a supernatural or impossible event
why: Focusing on the impossible claim leaves the checkable details unexamined.

text: 1) List every access point, including doors, windows, side entries and overhead openings. 2) Verify each lock's state independently and rule out exits that fail established facts. 3) Set the physical facts against the anomaly and keep the route that fits all of them as the method. 4) Ask what that route hides. 5) Identify the author only after the method is determined.
when: A scene seems sealed and every obvious exit has been checked, or someone's entry or exit from a secured space must be worked out.
why: Elimination against fixed facts exposes overlooked routes that a first look misses.

text: 1) List the physical traces each proposed explanation must leave. 2) Check each trace against the scene. 3) Discard any explanation with a missing trace.
when: a scene seems sealed and several explanations compete
why: Traces make explanations testable.

text: 1) Open with an impossibility, such as a death with no heard shot, smoke or weapon. 2) Let the player investigate it with specific tools. 3) Resolve it through a chain of physical clues.
when: when designing an opening mystery built on an impossible scene
why: A concrete impossibility gives the player a question that physical evidence can answer.

text: 1) Count everyone who had access to the place. 2) List the access methods such as keys, passwords and signatures. 3) Test each human explanation against those methods to find who could act.
when: An apparently impossible event occurs in a controlled place
why: A finite set of access holders converts a supernatural-seeming event into a checkable human mechanism

text: When testimony or an answer seems impossible, ask which further facts would make it possible instead of discarding or rejecting it outright.
Do not accept a claim that no one could have done something until it is checked against every other handler's account.
Medical examination can fail to establish a cause of death when injuries obscure the mechanism of harm.
when: when injuries are severe to the relevant body region
why: Heavy damage can hide the evidence the examination needs.

text: 1) Build a theory from second-hand information gathered in casual conversation. 2) Ask the informant small, relevant questions that each check one point. 3) Avoid stating the accusation. 4) Let the subject volunteer the answer.
when: The subject is guarded and a direct accusation would end the conversation.
why: Single-point questions confirm a theory without revealing it, keeping the subject cooperative.

text: Age, build and dress can be inferred from small cues heard without sight, such as a walking stick.
1) Note the objects and marks in a space. 2) Infer the routines that would produce them. 3) Hold the inference provisionally. 4) Test it against observed behaviour of people in the space.
when: Judging who uses a room and for what, from physical evidence alone.
why: Objects suggest routines but cannot prove a particular person's presence or conduct.

text: Judge a paid or interested source by testing checkable claims against independent records, since verified claims lend credibility to unverified ones; payment gives reason to shape the story.
when: The only available witness is paid or has a stake in the outcome.
why: Checkable claims give an independent measure of the source's accuracy.

text: Give informants a visible price, bias or stated stake, such as payment or grudge, plus a real chance of false names, so players must weigh their reliability before acting.
when: Designing informant characters, especially NPCs who trade information for leniency.
why: Reliability becomes a meaningful choice.

text: Unwitting bystanders, such as fellow travellers, can repeat what they heard without grasping its significance, so their reports carry information they do not understand.
when: A target's movements are being traced after the fact.
why: Casual conversation reveals details the speaker does not recognise as significant.

text: An informant's cooperation can depend on payment, and once paid, the informant may give help and leave without further commitment.
when: A street informant is offered money
why: Reward, not loyalty, drives the exchange

text: An informant with a stake may try to steer the investigator's suspicions toward another person before those suspicions form.
when: The informant fears suspicion falling on someone they protect
why: Shaping the imagination first can steer conclusions

text: When paid seats go unused after sales errors are ruled out, the non-use is likely deliberate; check records rather than accepting a witness's claim of non-use.
when: A witness claims a paid seat or channel went unused.

text: Treat information bought for money with caution, especially cryptic warnings that are hard to test.
Gather information from nearby bystanders by questioning them rather than approaching the subject, and keep one's own purpose hidden.
when: Learning about a target without alerting them.
why: Questioning others keeps the target unaware.

text: Unusual limits on contact, such as allowing only untraceable correspondence, are a signal worth noticing and investigating.
when: someone arranges communication in an unusual, hard-to-trace way
why: Restricting traceable contact can hide a person's identity or whereabouts.

text: Use an unexplained cryptic message to test whether a suspect knows a specific fact without asking directly.
Explain how a suspect learned of an opportunity through overheard or indirect knowledge.
Check whether an accuser is paid per accusation, since that income gives reason to keep finding targets.
Let NPC gossip carry concrete physical details marked as unverified, so players can check the world state and see whether the rumour holds.
Give a late arriving character a risk, such as forcing the player to expose a secret they hold, so the choice changes later encounters.
why: A costly choice makes the arrival meaningful rather than a passive event.

text: Release a dying or fearful NPC's information in steps: a hint, a related question, then a physical object that proves the point.
when: An NPC holds key information in a game
why: Staged disclosure keeps the player engaged and lets the proof carry the final weight.

text: A servant or informant who knows secrets can gate late-game information, with their trust earned through earlier tasks.
when: When designing an NPC who holds hidden knowledge
why: Earned trust makes the reveal feel earned rather than handed over.

text: Offering a witness control over whether a secret is published or suppressed, or dropping a charge, for a full account prompts fuller, candid answers than formal questioning.
when: A witness has a reason to hide a relationship or the whole truth, and a credible reason to speak.
why: The witness weighs the consequences of disclosure.

text: Leverage from a held secret lasts only while the item stays hidden and unused; using or revealing it ends the power over the victim.
when: A character holds damaging information over another.
why: The power depends on the threat being unspent and the victim knowing of it.

text: An informant's answer can disclose a fact the questioner could not check otherwise, which makes the exchange valuable.
A credibility value on each informant, lowered when that informant is exposed, cascades to every clue they supplied, reducing the weight those clues carry.
when: Designing NPC informants in dungeon or narrative generation.

text: In an information-trade mechanic, the NPC's reaction to an offered item signals how much it has to hide.
A player-controlled network of informants, each placed in a different location, can supply gossip and clues across the map.
when: A game world spans several locations.
why: Distributed sources report on places the player cannot watch directly.

text: A social-network view that records relationships learned from gossip lets the player map a community as they learn more about it.
A found item that contradicts an NPC's story can trigger a confrontation, turning a clue into a dialogue encounter.
when: In investigation games with NPC testimony.

text: Informant NPCs who can be bribed or threatened into a covert task should carry real risk and a chance of failure, and a failed errand can branch the mystery rather than close it.
When suspicion is high, NPCs refuse to trade or help, which hides clues and narrows the player's options.
when: when a game uses community suspicion as a mechanic
why: Refusals block access to information and resources

text: An informant's account often has three layers: what they saw, what they heard from others, and what they conclude from both.
when: Evaluating a claim from an informant who followed or observed a target.
why: Separating layers shows which parts are direct observation and which are inference.

text: A feud can be modeled as a rising tension meter: each dispute raises tension, and clear triggers push it toward a public accusation.
when: designing community conflict systems
why: Visible escalation lets players anticipate crises.

text: An unrecorded handoff can be overlooked by both the investigator and the audience if it is never written down or shown.
when: a key transfer happens off the page or off screen
why: nothing in the record points to it

text: A message repeated from memory can differ from the original, so check its wording against the account's other claims before trusting it.
An informant's stiff, flat delivery can make a scene feel colder than the news itself.
A false summons only becomes evidence once the claimed sender is shown not to have sent it.
when: A message claims to come from a particular person who was absent.
why: Until the claimed source is checked, the message can be taken as genuine.

text: An overly eager informant or an implausible cover story can alarm the community and end the inquiry.
An ally who blurts out the investigator's true knowledge can ruin a bluff, so control what each party knows.
when: When other people are present during a bluff.
why: Revealed knowledge tells the suspect the claim is false.

text: 1) Ask how the informant learned the fact. 2) Check claims for self-consistency and directions against landmarks. 3) Note what reward the informant wants and what they gain. 4) Verify key claims against independent accounts before acting on them.
when: Assessing any informant, especially when the informant is the only route to a fact or place.
why: Informants can contradict themselves, mislead and act for pay.

text: 1) Identify the source's grudge. 2) Offer small courtesies that signal respect. 3) Let the source talk first. 4) Reveal only what is needed to steer the conversation.
when: When questioning a witness or informant who is reluctant to share.

text: 1) State what you already know, so lying clearly costs more than the truth. 2) Reveal hidden dealings to show concealment has failed. 3) Name the motive. 4) Show a real pending consequence. 5) Demand one specific act in return.
when: Real leverage over a suspect exists and can be shown.

text: 1) Use short neutral prompts that invite elaboration. 2) Show insight into the source to unsettle them. 3) Offer a small payment. 4) Press for precise details.
when: a source is motivated by money or vanity

text: 1) Identify the fact you need. 2) Have a trusted contact fetch it without revealing why it matters. 3) Deliver the result to the subject and watch their reaction.
when: A direct question would alert the subject.

text: 1) Approach the source through a mutual acquaintance in an informal setting. 2) Start from the source's own interests. 3) Introduce the real subject only after rapport is established. 4) Record the exchange as dialogue, noting evasions and omissions.
when: The source talks freely informally and would close up under direct questioning
why: Informal rapport loosens speech, and recorded dialogue reveals pressure points.

text: 1) Confirm there are no signs of forced entry, such as a picked lock, forced bolt or marked panel. 2) Conclude that an accomplice admitted the culprit. 3) Rank occupants by how much access each had.

1) Establish the stranger's identity and set the conditions for sharing news. 2) Probe who is involved and how the informant learned it. 3) Test the claim against a fact already known. 4) Ask for a verifiable anchor, such as a location and return meeting, to hold the claim to account. 5) Note the subject's physical bearing.
when: A witness offers a serious, checkable claim.
why: Sequencing identity, sources, verification and anchors exposes unsupported claims before action is taken.

text: Attach a reliability value to informant answers that depends on the informant's current condition, such as fatigue or confusion, which can also end a session early.
when: When designing informant answers.

text: Keep rumours as unverified leads: weigh them against evidence rather than dismissing them as improbable, and do not treat them as clues until checked.
when: A rumour contains improbable details.
why: A rumour may still hold a true detail; treating gossip as a clue chases noise.

text: Give some NPCs stock answers and others richer, linked knowledge, so players learn which informants to trust.
why: Depth contrast teaches players to judge sources

text: Give an informant NPC hurried or illegible notes written under pressure, as a reliability cue the player can read.
when: designing informant characters

text: In a leverage mechanic, give the NPC a deadline and a required action, with options to threaten or to bargain.
Test an informant's claims against dated, independent facts such as letters, reports and the timing of earlier events.
when: an informant gives an account
why: dated records can confirm or contradict the claims

text: Give a trusted local a specific watch brief, such as reporting motors or aircraft, to turn them into a reliable informant.
when: monitoring a region for pursuers
why: a narrow task gets clearer reports than a general request

text: Give an informant NPC a sample collection quest with ordered steps the player must follow exactly, such as sealed kit, timing and delivery.
when: designing NPC-driven investigation tasks

text: Plant a paid-but-never-used lead that players can verify against venue records.
Make an informant reachable only through a specific intermediary or channel, so players must plan how and when to make contact.
when: when designing hidden informants

text: Trigger an NPC reaction, such as an attack or flight, when the player shows the correct item at the right moment.
Paying or flattering a witness secures cooperation and can yield more detail, but the incentive can lead them to invent, exaggerate or shape the account; cooperation never establishes accuracy.
when: A witness is offered money or favours.
why: Payment changes the witness's incentive to please the questioner.

text: A paid informant can reach places and routines the investigator cannot, but each claim they sell is shaped by payment and must be verified.
when: the investigator lacks access and can later check the claims
why: the informant's money motive can bias what they volunteer

text: Pressuring an informant with a dependence you hold can yield the name, but the information gained this way is tainted by the abuse of position that produced it.
when: A trail depends on a reluctant intermediary who relies on the investigator
why: Coerced information is less trustworthy and costs the investigator moral standing

text: A reluctant witness can be moved by a threat, a favour or money, and the interrogator should choose the lever that fits the witness's motive.
when: A witness has a clear motive to trade information.
why: Each lever suits a different motive, and a mismatch makes the offer fail.

text: Keep assistants and allies uninformed of covert plans or extra insight, since they may reveal it by look or act.
when: Running a covert operation with a helper, or writing an investigator with more insight than the cast.
why: A helper may give the plan away unintentionally; keeping the player ahead sustains suspense.

text: A written approach to a suspect can confirm that findings exist and who holds them, while keeping the conclusions and reasoning private.
when: when a suspect may be warned or may shape a story
why: Revealing possession of evidence prompts a response without giving the suspect the investigator's reasoning.

text: In a feud with several parties and shared assets, who controls a committee or fund often matters more than the stated complaint.
Control over who knows a death, when they learn it, and what is opened shapes how others read the death and the people connected to it.
Staging who learns what and when keeps each person calm and cooperative, and withholds what would make them act rashly.
when: An investigator controls what each character knows
why: Partial or premature knowledge can trigger reactions that damage the investigation.

text: A staged departure only works if the suspect hears the news through a channel the investigator controls; if that route fails, the deception collapses.
when: planning a feint
why: The false belief depends on the suspect receiving it.

text: When the witness starts asking questions, the questioner may be forced to disclose information before intending to, such as confirming a detail under direct questioning.
when: A witness turns the questioning around
why: A direct question can compel an answer the questioner had not planned to give

text: 1) Run the in-world test on a character known to be innocent. 2) If it returns the same guilty result, treat the test as unreliable. 3) Use that failure as a mystery beat or reversal scene.
when: designing lie detectors or trap tests in a game
why: A control exposes tests that cannot distinguish guilt from innocence.

text: Agree a visible cue and tell allies to stay quiet, so you control what the public, press and suspects learn and when.
when: A trap or investigative plan depends on secrecy.
why: Each leak can warn the culprit or ruin a planned trap.

text: Set a fixed reporting schedule and forbidden zones, and route urgent messages through one channel, so contact stays controlled.
Use one instructed spokesperson to relay the false status, since controlled bulletins shape what rivals believe.
Let players compare an item against a control set of similar items, so the clue carries meaning only through contrast.
Check the answer to a neutral dialogue question against logs or other testimony to measure consistency.
when: designing a dialogue-based truthfulness check
why: a checkable answer lets players judge consistency

text: Track what has been disclosed in dialogue so later questions and answers stay consistent with earlier ones.
when: Designing a dialogue system with ongoing questioning
why: Inconsistent disclosure breaks the player's trust in the record

text: Do not dismiss an unexplained phenomenon; admit the gap and keep it open for later weighing.
when: an event resists explanation
why: Honest uncertainty keeps the player weighing both explanations.

text: A short message that omits size, comfort and crew, and asks for odd items, invites the reader to guess a hidden purpose and keep reading.
when: when a message should promise more than it tells
why: missing details invite the reader to supply suspicion

text: A missing address or name can stop a message from reaching its recipient, delaying the truth as effectively as deliberate concealment.
when: A clue or message depends on a recipient's location or identity
why: Without the correct information the delivery fails, regardless of intent

text: Too much information can bury the one vital fact among many irrelevant ones, so the decisive clue goes unnoticed.
Partially briefed allies can act independently and change the situation, so withholding information from people who must act together can backfire.
when: Coordinating a group that must act quickly
why: Partial knowledge leaves allies unprepared and prone to uncoordinated action.

text: Explain odd sensations, sounds, knocks or ambiguous signs with ordinary causes, such as a respiratory complaint, before concluding a scene is staged, sinister or supernatural.
when: a witness reports unusual sensory details or an odd sound has a plausible ordinary source
why: Ordinary objects frequently account for strange impressions.

text: Test physical traces for mundane causes, such as evaporation for an empty lamp, and check evidence rules them out before concluding an event occurred; weigh against other traces.
when: A trace fits a dramatic explanation and also a common one.
why: Common actions can leave the same marks as unusual ones.

text: Test each link in an accusation chain for an innocent explanation, such as an ordinary cause for a vehicle fault; one plausible alternative can dissolve the whole pattern.
when: building or checking an accusation; a link has a plausible ordinary explanation
why: a chain is only as strong as its weakest link; ignoring innocent explanations inflates apparent strength.

text: 1) List everyone who gains, linking each to a visible benefit such as a vacancy, promotion or rival's removal. 2) Note who does not gain; absence can be a clue. 3) Verify each gainer's movements, removing those whose alibi holds and keeping unverified alibis open. 4) Use the remaining list to narrow suspects, without naming a culprit from benefit alone.
when: Investigating an event with unclear cause or purpose, early in the investigation.
why: Beneficiary checks remove suspects cheaply; visible gains give a concrete basis for motive.

text: Victims are drawn into a trap by innocent-seeming lures, such as a letter in an unfamiliar hand or a polite encounter.
Details of habits and travel times can pass through innocent conversation, so a suspect may know them without intent.
when: a suspect appears to have insider knowledge
why: Casual talk spreads private routines

text: A suspect seen by a witness may already have an innocent reason for being there, so a firm sighting is not automatically damning.
Innocent people may refuse a search out of embarrassment or privacy, so a refusal is ambiguous evidence.
when: the request touches private belongings
why: Refusal has motives other than guilt

text: A natural cause, such as a physical predisposition triggered by emotional crisis, can make a suspicious death look ordinary to observers.
Ordinary objects can carry clues, such as a dropped key, a clock stopped at a set time, a partly drunk glass, or a footmark on a chair.
A witness can be innocent of the crime under investigation and still guilty of a lesser secret.
when: when a witness's past is uncovered
why: Hidden lesser faults can be exposed without solving the crime.

text: Holding a belief, even one that accepted decisive evidence of its day, does not by itself show malice; a person can be judged free of vindictiveness.
When a detail contradicts an account or stated habit, look for an innocent explanation, such as a round trip, and check rather than accuse.
when: a physical detail seems to contradict an account
why: an innocent cause can explain the detail without refuting the account

text: A damning-looking fact often has a mundane innocent explanation, but a plausible one is not shown innocent; check it against evidence rather than stopping there.
when: A suspicious fact has a plausible harmless explanation.
why: A plausible explanation lowers suspicion, so investigators often look no deeper until new evidence forces a second reading.

text: Concealment or evasion may be innocent, such as protecting someone else; check for an innocent cause before treating a revealed omission or evasion as evidence of guilt.
when: a suspect conceals or refuses to explain their actions
why: Many motives for evasion are unrelated to the crime.

text: A death that looks natural is not closed: ask what routine checks would miss and what evidence the culprit would lose, rather than dismissing a motive.
when: analysing an apparently natural death, or medical opinion says the death was natural
why: Points to the concealed cause and the evidence to look for.

text: Check whether a mark has a mundane mechanical cause, such as friction from a pulled chain, before treating it as a separate attack.
when: A mark lies in the area of a struggle.
why: Ordinary mechanics can produce marks that look like wounds.

text: Check plausible natural causes before a deliberate one for a physical trace, since warm places can attract insects or similar traces.
when: A trace could be innocent or planted.
why: Natural causes are often overlooked when a culprit is suspected.

text: When a death is attributed to natural causes and occurs close in time to another violent event, check whether the two are linked before accepting the verdict.
when: A natural-causes verdict and a nearby violent death appear together.
why: A deliberate trigger can act on a body that an illness has already weakened.

text: An innocent explanation for an object does not prove it irrelevant; test that explanation before accepting it.
when: An object has a harmless purpose that also fits the scene
why: The explanation may account for the object without ruling out its role in the crime.

text: Do not assume every innocent-seeming story is a red herring; some stories are true, so test each one rather than dismissing it.
Place the party who benefits from the confusion among the helpful onlookers, so their interest stays hidden while they watch the suspect closely.
Someone may benefit from an object being destroyed by accident, not only from selling or using it, so include them among suspects.
A rival who gains from a failed arrest may quietly encourage it, so ask who benefits before acting.
when: when a confrontation could collapse
why: a failed arrest can free a competitor to act

text: Before accepting an apparent second attack, test mundane causes such as a nightmare, a fall, or an accidental discharge.
Choose clue objects with a plausible everyday purpose so each reads as harmless when first mentioned.
when: planting an object meant to matter later
why: an innocent purpose keeps the object from drawing suspicion early

text: An innocent history for how an object was acquired does not explain why it is arranged the way it is.
Before reading a timeline gap as sinister, list innocent explanations for it, since many gaps come from ordinary errands.
when: a suspect's timeline has a gap
why: Ordinary activity often fills gaps that look suspicious

text: When an item goes missing, first test a harmless cause, such as it was moved for safety, by questioning those who handled it.
when: when an item is missing from its expected place

text: A plausible record can look like evidence of a plan until an ordinary error, such as a clerk's mistake, explains it.
A repeated remark is often an innocent disclosure, not a leak; check the reason for repeating it before treating it as a breach.
Innocent suspects can usually show where they were, so a suspect with no way to confirm their whereabouts deserves closer scrutiny.
Plant clues that each have an innocent explanation and reveal the true cause later, so players must test the pattern rather than accept it.
when: designing mystery clue sets
why: players learn to question coincidence

text: Give an innocent character an odd routine that a search would expose, and make the item that clears them findable in their own space.
when: Designing a suspect who looks guilty but is innocent.
why: A visible oddity invites suspicion, and a findable clearing item lets players resolve it.

text: Give an early suspect an innocent-seeming remark that a later solution reframes as a meaningful clue.
when: planting clues in a suspect's dialogue
why: Readers reread the remark once the reframing exposes its relevance.

text: Keep one or two clues with an innocent explanation until the late convergence, so they can be reread as evidence when the case closes.
An innocent character can look guilty through her own visible actions, such as making a call or tending a suspicious process, because those actions are read as evidence.
why: Visible actions are read as evidence even when their purpose is innocent

text: Giving an innocent NPC a plausible motive forces the player to test their theory against physical evidence instead of accepting it on motive alone.
why: Motive creates a convincing but false suspicion that only evidence can resolve.

text: A new fact that shifts who gains most from a death reframes the earlier evidence, so the most likely culprit changes.
when: A new fact changes the likely beneficiary of a crime.
why: The benefit-based theory of who committed the crime depends on who gains, so reassigning gain reassigns suspicion.

text: Once the means behind an effect is identified, the supernatural cover is removed and the staged elements of the scene become legible.
why: identified causes turn mysterious effects into understood ones

text: An absence can have a mundane cause, such as an item moved, lost or stored elsewhere; check that assumption, and keep the gap open until the item is located.
when: Reasoning rests on an item having been taken

text: A shared or disputed trait is weak evidence until innocent sources, such as an old machine in common office use or many small causes, are ruled out.
why: Suspects can offer benign explanations; many small causes can explain one object's stability.

text: A found object can have an innocent explanation; check for one before treating it as incriminating, since a plausible explanation leaves no firm proof linking it to the crime.
when: When a found object seems to link a person to a crime.

text: Drinking, nerves and restlessness have innocent causes and can mislead an audience about guilt.
Silence or absence can have innocent causes such as travel, so it should not be read as guilt on its own.
Treating a bloodstain as proof of violence ignores innocent transfer, such as blood from carrying a body by the shoulders.
when: Interpreting stains or residues on a suspect
why: Helping move a victim transfers blood without any involvement in the act

text: An innocent motive for one suspicious act does not prove innocence of the central crime, so the suspect must still be tested separately.
when: A suspect is cleared of a side issue.
why: Clearing one suspicious act leaves other links to the crime unexamined.

text: An innocent person can be detained on weak evidence, so a false lead must be tested quickly before the cost grows.
A small difference between two versions of an item may be innocent, such as a second version taken in the same session.
Unwitting participants in an arranged plan can be wrongly treated as conspirators, so each person's knowledge should be established before accusing them.
why: innocent go-betweens may only have carried a message

text: A discarded document may have been thrown away for innocent reasons, and interpretation such as assuming interest in a target can outrun the evidence.
when: when reading meaning into discarded papers
why: Innocent explanations are often overlooked.

text: A clean surface or missing item can have an innocent cause, such as routine cleaning, so each trace must be weighed against ordinary explanations.
when: When interpreting cleanliness or absence as evidence of intrusion.
why: Routine activity produces the same traces as an intrusion.

text: A frightened witness may offer a false but plausible explanation for their fear, which should be checked against other evidence.
when: When a witness explains a reaction in a way that deflects attention.
why: People often invent innocent-sounding reasons to hide their real concern.

text: 1) Name the innocent explanation for a trace. 2) Compare it with the known routine habits of the person who could have caused it. 3) Keep or drop the explanation on that basis.
when: an innocent explanation must be excluded before accepting a conclusion
why: Routine habits show whether an explanation is plausible

text: Give each suspicious clue an innocent explanation via an NPC or document, such as a weak seal, offered before the darker one; players must weigh both.
when: designing a red herring suspect or ambiguous clues
why: keeps the player from assuming guilt; ruling out innocent causes makes the eventual payoff stronger

text: Benefit from an event establishes a reason, not a deed; when several parties gain, it narrows suspects without naming a culprit.
when: several heirs or interested parties gain from a death
why: Several people may have reasons, so motive alone does not settle who acted.

text: A mundane crime should carry more distinguishing clues per suspect, because many motives seem plausible on their face.
when: designing a routine crime with several suspects
why: without distinguishing clues, every suspect looks equally likely

text: Exhaust ordinary explanations before accepting an unusual one. Give supernatural claims a fair hearing, but test them last.
when: when an unusual explanation is offered
why: Accepting an uncanny explanation early can end the investigation before ordinary evidence is gathered.

text: Ask where an object would naturally fail or wear, then check whether the actual break or damage is at that point.
when: When an object's condition may have been arranged to look accidental.
why: A break at an unnatural point is a sign that someone interfered.

text: Use an innocent-looking setting as a deliberate red herring, and reward players who keep their suspicion alive by finding the one wrong detail.
when: designing a hideout or suspect location
why: rewarding persistence keeps the deception meaningful

text: Accept a natural explanation only where it can be demonstrated, not merely described, since an incomplete visible explanation can still leave the real cause unexplained.
when: when judging a claimed natural cause
why: demonstration tests the explanation; description does not

text: Give a key item an inscription with a name, date and place tying it to a character and occasion, so finding the item links it to that character.
when: designing a clue item tied to an NPC

text: Give a scene an inspectable fake forced-entry mark so players can judge whether it is staged or real.
when: Designing a mystery scene with a staged clue
why: Players who examine closely can catch the fake.

text: Give crafters or merchants production records the player can inspect to uncover a missing copy.
when: designing a clue chain around crafted items
why: records turn a count discrepancy into a discoverable lead

text: Make dated photographs or portraits in an inn interactable, so they identify characters and confirm when those characters lived.
when: when placing environmental lore clues

text: Leave an inspectable flag behind any in-world excuse for a failed testimony.
Use environmental text such as tombstones, plaques or ledgers to imply a fact without confirming it, so players must weigh what is stated against what is left out.
when: Designing in-world text that players must interpret.
why: Implied facts invite players to reason rather than simply read a confirmed answer.

text: Write an antiquarian document, such as a ritual or inscription, as a set of instructions that point to a physical place.
when: designing a clue hidden in an old object or text
why: An ordinary-looking relic then works as a map the player can follow.

text: Inspect seams and joints where grime gathers, rather than only the visible outer surface.
when: Looking for traces on an object.

text: Ask indirectly and lightly, in passing or by waiting for openings, when a direct question would alert the subject or was refused, so they cannot adjust their story.
when: A direct question would alert the subject or a witness refuses direct questions
why: Indirect approaches avoid triggering the same deflection

text: Ask open questions, offering named options only after they fail. Suggested details get absorbed as memory and confirmations may echo prompts; record each detail's source and prompted points.
when: Interviewing any witness, especially when unsure, vague, or asked who or what they saw
why: Suggested details cannot later be told apart from observed ones, and offered options are easily adopted

text: Record every interrogation answer and let later questions reference earlier ones, so contradictions are detected automatically instead of relying on memory.
when: Systems tracking dialogue or testimony across multiple interrogation turns
why: Stored, cross-referenced answers make contradictions checkable and link facts

text: Log overheard and trivial remarks, and partial or evasive answers, so they can later unlock dialogue, change NPC behaviour or become clues.
when: The player overhears or receives partial information, or dialogue may later gain meaning once the player learns the background
why: Delayed relevance rewards keeping notes; partial answers carry value for later questioning

text: Suspects' startled reaction, indignation, flat denial, appeals for help, embarrassment, anger or evasion signal discomfort or a lead to investigate, not proof of guilt.
when: When a suspect is shown evidence or observed under confinement.
why: Guilty and innocent people both react defensively to surprise and accusation; discomfort can produce the same outward signs as guilt.

text: A sharp, unexpected answer or visible reaction to a pointed question about a relationship or grievance is itself a clue worth following up.
when: Pointed questions touch a relationship or grievance, including when suspects are questioned in front of one another.
why: Unexpected reactions can reveal hidden feeling; the questioner reads the reaction as an answer.

text: A suspect's assurance weakens as each specific detail of his movements is recited back to him, so pressure builds with every fixed point.
when: When a suspect hears his own night narrated precisely.
why: Accumulated specifics make denial harder to sustain.

text: When a suspect hears a precise, correct account of his unseen actions, his reaction and choice of defence can reveal facts the investigator could not prove.
when: during a confrontation built on an ordered reconstruction
why: Facing a sequence he did not expect to be known, the suspect tends to react and pick a defence that exposes what happened.

text: Witnesses who want to do right or be seen as fair often volunteer details they never meant to give, such as a private letter or a payment made.
when: When the witness is trying to be helpful
why: The wish to appear fair lowers caution about what is revealed

text: Under pointed follow-up questions, a witness often retreats from a certain identification to a weaker claim, separating what they observed from what they inferred.
when: A witness is pressed on the basis of a claim
why: Questioning forces the basis of belief into view

text: A suspect under threat denies key actions and shifts blame onto companions, so each denial and accusation needs independent checking.
when: when a suspect faces consequences
why: Self-protection pushes suspects to minimize their own role

text: When a suspect learns that a clue matters, they may destroy the rest of it.
when: When investigators reveal a clue's importance to suspects.
why: Suspects who understand a clue's value have reason to destroy the rest.

text: A suspect at a scene often asks what witnesses heard or saw, to learn what they know and what he fears they know.
when: when a suspect arrives after a death and speaks with witnesses
why: the questions reveal the suspect's anxieties

text: A suspect's visible relief when witnesses accept his explanation signals what he feared they might discover.
when: when a suspect's explanation is accepted
why: relief reveals the concealed concern

text: A suspect who feels watched lies low, but a false sign that the pressure has lifted can prompt him to move or act carelessly.
when: the suspect is monitoring the investigators
why: he acts only when he feels safe

text: A suspect may not know the grounds of suspicion, because public reports can mention a clue without describing it.
Public threats, quarrels and rushed actions by a suspect are remembered and weighed as evidence of motive, so conduct alone can make a person look guilty.
when: A suspect threatens, quarrels or acts hurriedly in front of others
why: Observers recall motive statements and scene behaviour more readily than the underlying facts

text: A witness pressed on a painful point often answers in clipped, deliberate, precise terms rather than volunteering more.
when: A direct question on an emotionally charged matter

text: A suspect may request a pause on a pretext, such as giving household orders, and use the time to stall, so the delay must be checked.
when: the suspect asks for time or a break
why: Stalling delays questioning without answering it.

text: A suspect who does not mention a witness who could confirm a claimed past service may be concealing something. Note such silences.
A suspect pressed with a sudden, direct question may flush or show a sharpened look, and these physical tells can be observed.
when: when asked a sudden, direct question
why: Sudden questioning leaves less time to control reactions.

text: A reconstruction that removes a favored suspect can meet strong resistance from the people involved.
why: People invested in a conclusion resist evidence that overturns it.

text: A suspect may refuse to name a third party until they have spoken to that party.
when: when asked who is behind their actions

text: Under questioning, both the suspect and the questioner notice small hedges and qualifiers, and each reads them as possible signs of unease or concealment.
when: A suspect speaks at length during an interrogation or accusation
why: Each side monitors the other's wording for hidden meaning

text: A suspect who decides the questioner is bluffing may treat every true statement as a trap, especially when the questioner's own claims are inconsistent.
when: The questioner's claims contradict each other
why: Inconsistency gives the suspect grounds to dismiss every reading as a bluff

text: A person wanting a private conversation may bring in a third party to stand by, partly to guard against a later accusation and partly to shape what that witness recalls.
when: when a talk may later be disputed
why: a neutral listener can later confirm or contest what was said

text: Vain or talkative suspects are more likely to try to display mastery of the case, which makes them easier to press with contradiction-based questioning.
when: A suspect who wants to appear clever or well-informed is questioned.
why: Wanting to show command of the facts leads them to over-explain and expose gaps.

text: A suspect's remarks about the case can be read as alliance with the accusers' enemies, which deepens suspicion against them.
when: when a suspect comments on an ongoing investigation
why: ambiguous statements fit suspicion already held

text: A hostile reply to a challenge about one's presence tends to escalate a dispute and can lead to dismissal or departure.
when: Being challenged about a presence at a sensitive place

text: Sharp, pointed questions reveal what the questioner is trying to learn, and bystanders can pick up the tension they create.
People waiting for an answer grow impatient when reasoning is withheld for a long time, even when the wait is justified.
when: a conclusion is held back for a decisive reason
why: the wait is felt as delay regardless of its purpose

text: A guilty suspect shown a victim's body may change colour and lose composure.
when: a suspect is confronted with a victim's remains
why: Guilt produces visible stress reactions that an investigator can read

text: A loyal witness may shield someone in their answers, so their replies reflect loyalty as much as memory.
when: When a witness is close to the accused or a protected person.
why: Loyalty biases which facts a witness offers and how they phrase them.

text: Witnesses with a stake in an outcome give urgent advice that is not neutral, because fear for someone's safety or soul drives it.
when: When weighing warnings from interested parties
why: Personal fear biases the advice given

text: Interrogation confronts a suspect with specific facts in a planned sequence under pressure, noting concessions; the questioner controls which facts surface and when.
when: during a suspect questioning scene

text: Witnesses who hold a post or keep a watch define who could have entered a place and when, which gives a fixed frame of times and places.
Psychological pressure applies delay, feigned friendliness and tone shifts to a suspect's nerves instead of hard evidence, aiming to make him talk or reveal himself under strain.
The same timing question can support a suspect's defence or test the suspect, depending on whether the death occurred before or after the moment asked about.
when: when interpreting a timed answer
why: The meaning of a time depends on its position relative to the death.

text: In English practice, a prisoner who stood mute was called to plead three times, warned of the consequences, and then subjected to weights on the chest until he pleaded or died.
when: Describing the historical procedure for a defendant refusing to plead.
why: The procedure had a defined sequence for refusal, which is what made standing mute possible.

text: State commissions authorized named torture instruments to extract confessions from the accused.
A private contact line lets an intermediary keep communication open without exposing the principal's identity.
Treat a suspect's self-description or stated intent as a claim to test, not a fact; talk of family or status may be performance, and self-reported motives can be self-serving.
when: When a suspect describes himself or explains an action as harmless or protective.
why: Threats can serve to protect his own position.

text: Treat witnesses a suspect offers, or says have no connection to him, as leads to check, since close associates may be biased toward the suspect.
Bluff with evidence you do not yet hold when a confident suspect would deflect a direct question; a changed story suggests the claim touched something real.
when: Questioning a suspect who may be hiding something or is confident.
why: A bluff forces a reaction that a direct question does not.

text: Keep questions short and narrow so a witness cannot retreat into generalities; after a refusal, keep the next question short and direct.
Let the witness give the account from the beginning, then move from open recall to specific checks, such as where furniture stood relative to a door.
why: Open recall surfaces facts narrow questions miss; early specific questions can shape what the witness reports.

text: With a guarded witness, open with easy conversation, then approach the central subject sideways through earlier, safer events before showing sensitive evidence.
when: A witness is reticent or guarded and early memories are warm or neutral.
why: Comfort and safe recollections make a witness more willing to engage and open the way to harder memories.

text: Choose when to ask a pointed question, since timing shapes the reaction; leave the most important question to the end and deliver it as if unimportant.
Reveal a discovery and watch for shock, fear or a forced laugh; a flicker of fear or broken composure is more telling than composure, since it shows the reveal landed.
when: Evidence is weak and the suspect may know more, or a confrontation exposes a hidden fact.
why: The reveal has landed when the suspect's composure breaks.

text: A deadline set by a suspect can be used to rush the investigator, so the investigator should not accept the time limit without checking it.
when: a suspect imposes a time limit on questioning
why: artificial urgency reduces careful verification

text: A single word in a question can carry the clue, so exact phrasing should be preserved when it is later reported.
Design interrogation so that refusing to account for one's time raises suspicion without triggering conviction.
when: writing suspect interrogation
why: suspicion should not equal proof

text: Store witness accounts as structured facts that unlock later dialogue and link events into a timeline.
Judge a witness's answer against what the expected record would normally contain, since a mismatch exposes a gap in their account.
Place a hidden listener in cold, cramped or dangerous positions only where the scene justifies the risk, since that danger gives discovery its weight.
Name a suspected person only after rapport is built, so the involuntary reaction arrives before the witness can compose themselves.
when: a witness has avoided naming someone
why: a witness who has not yet composed themselves reveals more

text: Ask precise questions about visible details; each answer narrows the set of possible interpretations.
A witness already attentive to the relevant route is a more dependable observer than one with no reason to watch it.
why: Existing attention makes observation more reliable.

text: In an NPC interrogation, present known evidence as a settled premise and let the player choose how to frame each question.
when: designing interview dialogue for a game

text: When a trapped suspect acts, his own words and possessions can become evidence against him.
Sow distrust in a network only after it depends on trust and has suffered a series of losses; a loyal group with no shared losses resists it.
when: a network depends on trust

text: A suspect's own scheduled appointments can fix his timeline at the critical hour.
when: Checking whether a suspect could have been elsewhere.

text: Press a witness who is cooperative on surface facts but evasive about history or motive.
when: Choosing how hard to question a witness.

text: Avoid pressing a grieving or deferential witness, since early attempts at questioning yield little.
when: Choosing how hard to question a witness.

text: When a trace is suspiciously perfect, check for duplication and for the means of production rather than judging by appearance.
when: When a trace might have been copied, or the original record was accessible to someone.
