why: Forged traces can look identical to the real one.

text: A psychological explanation that fits a character's manner must still be checked against the documentary record before it is accepted.
Ask what the other person already knows before revealing your own conclusions, so you keep control of the exchange.
when: when questioning a suspect

text: Do not press an informant who has already given a full account; ask a direct question only when the story seems to be missing something.
Stating that clues are openly left invites the audience to follow them and test their own solutions against the story.
Keep a suspect under watch instead of arresting at once while evidence is incomplete, since that leaves time to gather more clues.
when: evidence incomplete
why: Early arrest closes off investigation paths.

text: Judge a questioner's aim by which questions a witness answers and how the witness reacts when pressed.
Present a new timing claim to a guarded suspect so they feel pressed to defend their account, then state the stakes plainly.
when: A suspect's account conflicts with a checkable fact
why: A new claim forces a defence the suspect must support with detail

text: Ask narrow factual questions that a truthful answer would fix, such as whether an action happened once or twice; inconsistency across them exposes a false account.
Expose a suspect in separate steps: first raise doubt, then show the alibi holds, then suggest a third party acted first, each step resting on facts already shown.
Schedule a pretext approach for hours when targets are likely home, since the wrong hours can yield almost nothing.
A story that grows more emotional with each retelling usually signals a speaker with a stake in the outcome.
when: An account changes as it is passed along.
why: Emotional embellishment often serves the teller's interests.

text: Stage the environment so that an attempt to flee runs into a prepared party, rewarding the player's confrontation choice.
when: Designing a scene where a suspect may try to escape.
why: A staged trap turns a predictable escape into a test of the player's reasoning.

text: Requests that are broad or vague tend to be dismissed as unhelpful, so keep each request narrow and specific.
when: asking another party to act on an investigation
why: Vague requests cannot be carried out without wasting effort

text: Narrow questions close off escape routes and can expose a suspect's hesitation, which often marks a weak point in the account.
Weigh the suspect's own risk: a trap that exposes him to arrest or discovery is less likely than a plan to flee.
when: judging whether a tip is a trap
why: a trap that endangers the sender is less attractive than an escape plan

text: A timing detail, such as a change in appearance after a key date, can single out one candidate from a list of replies.
when: several replies are plausible
why: timing ties a candidate to the event more strongly than general fit

text: Track suspicion and confirmed guilt as separate states. Keep more than one explanation for an NPC's behavior until new evidence decides between them.
when: Modelling a character who behaves suspiciously
why: Separate states prevent a suspicion from becoming a conviction

text: Read a suspect's body and manner when verbal answers are evasive and the suspect is likely managing composure.
when: verbal answers are evasive

text: Check a suspect's offhand advice or steering toward an innocent party for a deliberate setup, especially when it seems too neat.
Following a suspect after an interview tests whether their stated account is true, since a tail can expose contacts they denied.
when: After a suspect has given a statement about their movements or associates.

text: After a detail returns, play it down so that further recall comes voluntarily rather than under pressure.
Control the emotional setting of an interrogation, such as who may be present, since it shapes how the suspect responds.
Psychological pressure works best when suspicion exists, physical evidence is thin and the suspect is high-strung; it weakens against a calm suspect.
when: suspicion exists but physical evidence is thin
why: pressure exploits nerves rather than proof, so it needs a nervous target

text: Base a misdirection on a timing estimate, so the diversion ends when the scene is ready.
when: Using a false lead to draw someone away.

text: Show the player's suspect tree as a quest log, linking each branch to an inquiry method and an elimination check, and design cases where one branch is cleanly eliminated while the favoured branch still leaves a detail unexplained.
when: Designing investigation content with multiple suspects or explanations
why: Visible branches and checks let the player reason through options and keep the case engaging.

text: A witness who narrowly denies attending one stage while staying silent about another invites the question of whether he attended the silent one.
when: a witness's denial is precisely worded and omits a similar event

text: Show a portrait to an NPC who claims not to know the figure, and give a brief animation, pause or colour change as the tell.
Show each testimony's scope on screen and mark entries learned second-hand, so players can judge where a source ends and how reliable it is.
when: presenting witness logs
why: visible scope helps players weigh reliability

text: An idle listen option can reveal more dialogue than a direct question, because it lets NPCs talk without being pressed.
Relative timestamps in dialogue, like a count of days since an event, let players order events without a clock interface.
Offer precise dialogue options that check the state of one object, and record each answer as a timeline entry.
when: the player needs to verify a specific physical detail through an NPC

text: Interview a witness away from companions and the crime scene, since a private setting makes a candid account more likely.
when: interviewing a witness who may be guarding information
why: others present and the scene raise the stakes of admitting anything

text: An interrogator who reveals what they already know too early lets the suspect repair the story.
when: Running an interrogation scene where the suspect can adjust answers.
why: Early disclosure gives the suspect information needed to make the account consistent.

text: Pauses between witnesses build pressure only when each pause is followed by new information or a sharper question.
when: Pacing an investigation with waits or adjournments.
why: Delay without new content drains attention.

text: Pressing a source for disclosure while offering protection in return can draw out information when the source has something to lose by staying silent.
when: the source has an alternative to offer and risks something by silence
why: a protection offer gives the source a reason to trade secrets for safety

text: Pose the question the clues answer in public, then defer the full explanation to a later scene.
when: when a solver must act before explaining
why: deferral without a stated reason can feel like withholding, so the question should be posed openly

text: Interrogation dialogue can branch on evidence the player presents, unlocking options or a confession only when claims are backed by a full set of supporting clues.
when: Designing NPC interrogation or dialogue that rewards deduction.
why: Gating ties the option to demonstrated reasoning rather than chance.

text: An NPC interrogation logs every stated fact and flags conflicts with earlier statements or world records, unlocking new questions and reveals.
when: Designing NPC interrogation in a game.
why: Logged statements make conflicts detectable.

text: An interrogation can branch on questions about routines, associates and recorded events, revealing what the character knows and changing the available dialogue.
when: When designing NPC dialogue in a mystery or dungeon-style game.
why: Different questions open different information paths, so the player's choices shape what is learned.

text: A dialogue option whose reply varies with an NPC's knowledge lets players extract hidden information through the form of the answer.
In a stimulating drug phase, the most vivid recent worry can harden into a fixed idea that overrides judgment and drives purposeful action.
when: A person is in the stimulating phase of a drug.
why: The stimulated state narrows attention onto one dominant concern.

text: A questioner can extract information indirectly by letting a second person supply the answers, and a witness who notices this can limit what she gives away.
when: Someone questions a witness while an ally or third party steers the exchange.
why: Helpful-seeming suggestions and interruptions redirect the witness, and a pressing follow-up can make her disclose more than intended.

text: Timing answers that narrow as the player supplies more events reward systematic questioning over guessing.
when: an NPC answers questions about when events occurred
why: each new anchor shrinks the possible window

text: Naming a consequence for silence makes a partially cooperative NPC more likely to yield further detail.
A suspect character can carry timed watch states that log messages and calls, which the player can intercept or overhear.
when: In games where an NPC's communications should be trackable.

text: A dialogue system can gate information behind keywords, so a player who uses the right term, such as a place name or repeated phrase, unlocks the next line.
An interrogation system can lock NPCs in separate rooms and sequence them, letting the player revisit lines in a fixed order.
Each approaching signal removes an option, so the target must weigh escape against hiding or stalling, which creates a real decision.
when: at the climax of a pursuit
why: Tension depends on choices that have real consequences.

text: A second NPC who watches an exchange can check the first, letting the player test the claim against an independent reaction.
A rival NPC who asks friendly questions can extract information, and the player's choice between evasive and candid answers can carry different consequences.
when: Designing dialogue with rival or adversarial characters.
why: Information leaks create stakes for how the player answers.

text: Present the interrogation as an ordered timeline or question tree where each answer unlocks or locks the next step, so the player cannot skip steps.
when: Designing a witness questioning interface
why: Ordered unlocking guides the player through the sequence

text: An interrogation system can let the player ask indirect questions and watch for tells, without revealing what the player already knows.
when: When designing an interrogation mechanic.
why: Indirect probing gives information while protecting the player's knowledge state.

text: An unfinished claim or half-sentence invites the listener to complete it, so the listener supplies the content and the speaker reveals a motive without stating it.
when: when a speaker is reluctant to state a sensitive fact directly
why: The listener's own completion makes the hinted meaning feel discovered rather than told.

text: An NPC interviewed in a scene can only answer about what they could observe from their own position, so the player must cross-check answers.
when: when designing NPC answers in an interrogation
why: Limiting answers to observed positions makes contradictions discoverable.

text: Interrogators unsettle a suspect with three tools: an accusing timeline, a bluff, and a fixed steady stare.
A query that omits the one decisive detail returns an answer that is technically correct but useless. Frame questions around the detail that matters.
when: when questioning NPCs or records
why: The wording of a query limits what the answer can contain

text: Letting the witness or suspect steer questioning, such as by asking what will be done with the information or accepting their explanation of a concealment, shapes the outcome.
Sharp, hostile or escalating questions can make a nervous or defensive witness shut down, refuse to talk and produce anger and few new facts.
when: Pressure beyond the witness's tolerance, sharp questions to a nervous witness, or a hostile tone toward a defensive witness.
why: Under strain, a witness may withdraw to protect themselves; felt pressure triggers resistance.

text: Aggressive or coercive pressing can produce a bluff or confident but unreliable answers shaped by the questioner's framing rather than what happened.
when: Cross-examining or pressing a witness who resists answering.
why: Pressure produces confident statements that reflect the questioner's framing.

text: Witnesses who confirm a prepared account, or staff matching an employer's story too neatly, may shield others; agreement is not proof, and weak confirmations may not fix the critical hour.
when: When witnesses confirm a prepared account, or staff may shield employers.
why: Agreement with a prepared story does not show the story is true.

text: Favouring one suspect early, or suspecting a discoverer merely because of their role or appearance, leads to a wrong conclusion; favour the most consistent explanation and check conduct against evidence.
when: One suspect is favored early, or a discoverer is suspected because of their role.
why: Suspicion attaches to appearance or role, not to fit with the facts.

text: Startling, probing or chasing a suspect before ready can cost the chance to observe them, risk injury, or provoke a dangerous reaction; time tests and pursuit carefully.
A fixed questioning sequence can be learned and anticipated by a suspect who has been questioned before.
when: When the same interrogation order is reused with repeat suspects
why: Repeat suspects can rehearse answers to a known sequence

text: Repeated near-confessions read as stalling unless each one adds new pressure or cost.
Holding too many alternatives open can stall a case, so each rival explanation needs a test that can rule it in or out.
A polite questioner may hide a motive, and a warning to leave can be an attempt to clear the scene rather than an expression of concern.
when: an interested outsider questions a household
why: courtesy can conceal a self-interested aim

text: Records the suspect could have produced, such as an application or referral, are weak proof that an independent person exists.
A delay that runs too long reads as stalling rather than struggle, and the tension it was meant to build is lost.
when: Stretching a pause before a reveal
why: Audiences stop reading hesitation as meaningful once it feels like filler.

text: A correction delivered in a sharp tone can itself shift the room's attention away from the claim being corrected.
Visible agitation from the questioner, such as pallor or a trembling voice, tells the suspect the accusation is personal and lets them guard against it.
when: An interrogator is emotionally invested while questioning.
why: The suspect reads the interrogator's state and adjusts their answers defensively.

text: An admission made near death can be narrower than the accusation later built on it.
when: A condemned person makes a statement before execution
why: The statement may admit only rumor or uncertainty

text: A witness who designs a test and then reports its result is interpreting their own experiment, so the report is not a neutral observation.
A witness who returns mid-search can catch the intruder, who may not know whether suspicion has already been raised.
when: the search runs past the witness's absence

text: Insinuating questions about inheritance can reveal the questioner's bias more than the witness's guilt.
when: Questioning a witness about a motive they may dispute
why: Pointed accusations shift focus to the questioner

text: Making a witness look foolish in front of others can damage the interviewer's relationship with them and hurt later cooperation, even if the method works.
when: Interviewing in front of colleagues or other people
why: Public embarrassment creates friction that outlasts the interview

text: Asking what a witness saw after naming a cause invites the answer the questioner has already set up.
Repeating a point can persuade as much as it clarifies, so repetition may tilt the audience.
why: Repeated emphasis is perceived as importance.

text: Too many simultaneous speakers blur which remarks matter, so important lines can be lost in a crowded scene.
Promises made under strong emotion may not be kept, so a pledge given during a plea is weak assurance.
when: Accepting a suspect's promise to end a matter.
why: Emotional states drive promises that the speaker's later conduct may not honour.

text: Pressing a close friend or sensitive source too hard can end the conversation and leave the questioner without the answer.
1) Begin with broad questions, such as about general life, whether anything unusual caught attention or someone appeared uneasy. 2) Then narrow to specific points or the key event.
when: Starting an interview with a witness whose account matters.
why: Broad questions surface details before the witness is led, and the wider picture makes later answers easier to judge.

text: 1) Put the witness at ease. 2) Ask short, specific factual questions. 3) Fix each answer to a clock time covering arrival, departure, meals and lodging. 4) Build one timeline; treat each answer as a fixed point later answers must fit. 5) Locate the unaccounted gap and press on it.
when: Questioning about who was where and when, where accounts can be checked against places or events.
why: Exact times expose the unexplained interval, which is usually the core of the case; fixed points expose inconsistencies in later statements.

text: 1) Fix the crime's narrow time window and location, and the window in which a suspect had to reach it. 2) Record each suspect's whereabouts across that window. 3) Rule suspects in or out by comparing logged locations against it.
when: Building a case around a timed offence.
why: A window narrows which suspects could have acted.

text: 1) Fix anchor times such as closing hours, last sightings and transport schedules. 2) Split the route into legs, each with a time and place. 3) Check each leg with an independent witness or record. 4) Mark unconfirmed legs and gaps openly.
when: Several people claim positions at fixed times, or a suspect gives a detailed account of movements.

text: 1) Fix the order of events by asking step by step what happened at each stage. 2) Question each witness separately. 3) Compare accounts against one another and against each witness's position and timing. 4) Re-question overlapping witnesses until the timeline has no gaps.
when: Several witnesses can each confirm or contradict who passed a point and when.
why: Cross-checking overlapping accounts exposes omissions and contradictions.

text: 1) Observe the suspect discreetly and list his movements in time order. 2) Open with facts you already hold, such as a call, an appointment or a time of death. 3) Lay out the sequence so he sees how much is known. 4) Have him confirm the timeline, then ask about the disputed matter.
when: Physical proof is incomplete, or a suspect's partial facts match the record but a purpose is withheld.
why: An ordered reconstruction shows the investigator knows more than the suspect expected, which pressures him to explain.

text: 1) Fix the time first. 2) Ask what was said. 3) Ask for the exact wording, in original order rather than a summary. Move from general questions to narrow ones.
why: Summaries lose sequence and wording that carry evidence.

text: 1) Fix a checkable fact, or state a deliberately wrong detail. 2) Let the witness correct it, treating the correction as a concession. 3) If needed, offer a second, slightly different wrong detail. 4) Ask where they were, narrowing each answer to close vague options. 5) Confirm via a second source; summarise what was learned, not denials.
when: A reluctant witness gives vague answers or withholds details.
why: People correct errors more readily than they volunteer facts, and small concessions build toward narrower questioning.

text: 1) Let the witness narrate without interruption, noting every skipped step or point where they were cut off. 2) Ask concrete questions about those moments, appearance and items. 3) Return point by point, seeking admissions without new facts. 4) Steer back when they drift.
when: Interviewing a cooperative, semi-cooperative or self-protective witness whose statement seems incomplete.
why: The unprompted version is captured before the interviewer reveals knowledge, and revisiting in order surfaces inconsistencies without tipping the witness off.

text: When a suspect or NPC witness invokes counsel and goes silent, do not argue; hold them separately and pursue contradictions with other evidence. Whether the request is honoured can change the outcome.
when: A suspect invokes rights and stops talking.
why: Holding a suspect without pursuing contradictions only delays the problem.

text: 1) List each suspect's whereabouts over time. 2) Mark the minutes that no account covers. 3) Check those gaps against physical events such as body warmth and departures.
when: several accounts overlap and no single account covers the whole sequence
why: Combining accounts exposes unobserved minutes that single testimony hides

text: 1) List physical traits inferred from marks and wear. 2) Add habits and distinctive features found at the scene. 3) Infer the vehicle from tracks or its draft animal's marks. 4) Present each item as an indication to test.
when: An investigator has a scene but no suspect.

text: 1) Estimate each attribute from a specific trace, such as stride for height or wound side for handedness. 2) Record the source of each attribute. 3) Combine independent attributes into one profile. 4) Check the profile against candidates.
when: Several traces point to the same unseen person
why: Each attribute with its own source makes the profile checkable

text: 1) Open with identity questions to size up the suspect. 2) Read out the suspect's prior record to undercut their claimed respectability. 3) Ask for a free narrative of events. 4) Attack gaps in that narrative. 5) Keep your own knowledge hidden. 6) Raise consequences last.
when: Scripted questioning where the goal is a full account from someone with reason to hold back
why: Each stage limits what the suspect can prepare for, and the order builds control over their account

text: 1) Confront suspects with the victims' remains. 2) Question the cab driver, concierge, landlady, neighbours, suspect's companions, and the owner of the tavern where the victims were last seen.
when: planning interviews after a crime
why: Start with the step most likely to provoke a reaction, then gather witness accounts in order

text: 1) Drop a pointed remark that only someone with guilty knowledge would fully understand. 2) Watch for a sudden change in attention. 3) Treat that change as a sign the suspect knows more.
when: when direct questions would only get polite denials

text: 1) Establish the actor's usual method. 2) Ask the victim about daylight, nearby people, whether the appointment was kept and whether they travelled alone. 3) Score each answer as on-plan or a departure. 4) Treat departures from plan, such as an early arrival or an unplanned companion, as factors that reduce the risk.
when: reconstructing an attack or incident from a witness

text: 1) Read the document aloud to the witness. 2) Ask narrow questions on checkable details such as apparent age and clothing. 3) Count each confirmed detail as a match across two sources.
when: testing a witness's account against a document
why: checkable details resist shaped answers

text: 1) List each claim in the theory. 2) Check each against the records and witnesses. 3) Note which contradictions remain unexplained.
when: testing a theory before presenting it
why: systematic checks expose weak points

text: 1) Ask routine questions about role and location to build a baseline. 2) Narrow to specific times, rooms and objects, comparing answers. 3) Show a physical object and watch the reaction. 4) Ask the witness to explain it.
when: a witness's account has gaps testable against physical facts
why: baseline answers make later contradictions easy to spot

text: 1) Split the mystery into who the victim is, why the killing happened, and who did it. 2) Answer the earlier questions first, since each makes the next easier.
when: Structuring a murder mystery or whodunit investigation
why: An early answer narrows the possibilities for the later questions

text: 1) Gather background facts first. 2) Move to the events of the day. 3) Ask about incidents the speaker called trivial. 4) Ask about vantage points. 5) Ask for opinions last.
when: interviewing a stakeholder whose facts are scattered
why: Recording facts before opinions keeps the speaker's interpretation from shaping the record

text: 1) Ask background questions about visitors, habits and who goes out to establish the normal pattern. 2) Ask what the authorities concluded and where they searched. 3) Ask about unusual behaviour. 4) List each step the simplest explanation requires and test whether it is workable.
when: questioning a client or witness early, while the account is emotional and facts are tangled
why: baseline routine makes deviations visible

text: 1) Bring the witness in as a planned part of the session. 2) State the stakes plainly. 3) Reconstruct events in outline. 4) Let the suspect correct it and add details. 5) Check added details against physical evidence.
when: the suspect's account is the only source for events inside a closed space
why: A witness can later confirm what was said, and corrections often supply checkable physical details.

text: 1) Warn the witness that the account may be used as evidence. 2) Secure the scene and move to a private room. 3) Listen to the full sequence. 4) Split it into timeline beats. 5) Test each claim against the scene and records.
when: A witness offers a long personal account of past events
why: Warning, isolation and testing keep the account legally usable and reduce contamination and error

text: 1) Ask a simple question. 2) Narrow it to specific facts. 3) Compare each answer with earlier answers. 4) Ask the same question another way. 5) Ask the witness to begin from the start.
when: a witness's account needs to be tested

text: 1) Ask where the key evidence was found. 2) Ask whether anyone else passed the spot. 3) Ask about past associates and whether any former contact could explain the motive. 4) Ask about past escapes or incidents in the suspect's history.
when: When the suspect's account can be checked against third parties and records and a prior connection could explain the motive.
why: Answers can be tested against other witnesses and physical records, and past links may reveal motive.

text: Ask each witness what their own description implies, so the contradiction surfaces from their words rather than from the investigator's accusation.
when: when witnesses describe something that seems impossible

text: 1) Open with sympathetic questions about identity and the last sighting. 2) Warn the witness that a painful question is coming. 3) Ask the direct question once you have a reason for it.
when: Questioning a witness on a sensitive point
why: Gentle framing lowers guard, and the warning prepares the witness for escalation

text: 1) Lay the groundwork with earlier questions. 2) Make the leverage explicit. 3) Ask the decisive question once, pointing at the specific relationship.
when: when a witness is likely to conceal a sensitive relationship
why: a single well-timed question is more revealing after trust is built

text: 1) Ask a pointed question that tests a claimed sighting. 2) Watch whether the witness improvises or recalls. 3) Note where the answer strains.
when: When testing a witness's story.
why: Improvised answers under pressure tend to reveal the weak point.

text: 1) Compare notes with your partner right after questioning. 2) Agree on what to say next. 3) Only then answer further questions.
when: when a team is questioned together

text: 1) Ask a general question about the relationship. 2) Quote the exact words of an earlier exchange. 3) Press for a direct answer, leaving no room for a vague denial.
when: a witness has given a partial account and an exact phrase is available
why: a quoted phrase is hard to dismiss with a general denial

text: 1) Read trigger words one at a time at a steady pace. 2) Record each answer and how long it took. 3) Flag replies that break the expected association. 4) Reconstruct which memory links each flagged reply to its trigger.
when: a suspect claims to know nothing but may hold a specific memory
why: Hesitations and unexpected links expose hidden associations.

text: 1) List what each suspect stands to gain or lose from the outcome. 2) Note each stated motive. 3) Record every contradiction between statements. 4) Keep each contradiction open for later resolution.
when: building a set of suspects before a crime is solved
why: a mapped web of stakes shows who could act and where accounts conflict

text: 1) List each source's facts separately. 2) Combine them on one shared record. 3) Look for contradictions between sources. 4) Form theories and test each against all the combined facts.
when: when several sources each hold partial information
why: combined facts can expose contradictions that no single source reveals

text: 1) Open with a broad question about someone else. 2) Read the witness's reactions. 3) Narrow to a named person and a specific relationship. 4) Restate the question in plainer words.
when: when a witness has partial knowledge and is evasive
why: broad questions reveal reactions that justify narrowing the focus

text: 1) Let the witness talk, answering with encouraging remarks. 2) Ask neutral open questions on each topic. 3) Ask for dates so claims can be checked later. 4) Record opinions separately from reported facts.

1) Take each account in a fixed order: background, prior events, then the timeline. 2) Record every answer. 3) Pin each event's time and each person's position. 4) Ask the witness's own theory, then ask whether any other explanation fits. 5) Ask what was omitted and confirm negatives, such as no one leaving by a given exit.
when: Accounts must be tested rather than accepted.
why: A fixed order and recorded answers make contradictions visible.

text: 1) Question each witness alone. 2) Let them speak fully without revealing your suspicions. 3) Pin down exact words and how they knew the speaker. 4) Compare each statement against the others.
when: after an event where several people saw or heard parts of it
why: Crowds make witnesses alarmed and less forthcoming, and group talk blends accounts.

text: 1) Open with formal courtesy and routine questions. 2) Narrow step by step from what happened to specific details. 3) Compare each answer with other statements. 4) Ask the most pointed question last, plainly.
when: After other accounts have been checked, so answers can be compared with solid facts.
why: A witness settles and talks more freely when questions start easily, and a plain final question shows the witness's reaction.

text: 1) Fix dates from the suspect's own records. 2) Let the suspect describe events freely. 3) Probe a specific claim with a targeted detail. 4) Ask for the names of everyone present. 5) Question each witness separately.
when: when a suspect's statement can be checked against named witnesses and records

text: When a witness says they cannot tell, follow up with narrower questions about what they actually saw or heard.

1) Establish how household routines normally run, such as handling doors, lights and shades. 2) Take each witness through the exact order of their actions. 3) Fix a clock time for each step. 4) Ask who saw the subject's movements.
when: early, before confronting anyone
why: a routine baseline lets deviations stand out

text: 1) Ask one narrow question at a time. 2) Record each denial as a fixed statement. 3) Check each fixed statement against later evidence for contradiction.
when: A witness gives vague or evasive answers about specific events.
why: Narrow denials can be checked later, while broad answers cannot be contradicted.

text: 1) Open with a soft question. 2) Follow with a sharp demand that breaks the suspect's rhythm. 3) Return to calm, specific questions about names, times and places.
when: suspect is stalling or evasive
why: Alternating tone disrupts rehearsed answers while calm specifics expose contradictions.

text: 1) Reassure the witness they are not accused. 2) Let them tell the account in their own words. 3) Ask a question about each step they describe. 4) Have them confirm key words by repeating them exactly. 5) Press directly on suspected omissions.
when: interviewing a witness whose account may be incomplete or hide a motive
why: Reassurance lowers defensiveness, and direct questions expose gaps that a fluent narrative can conceal.

text: 1) Give the NPC shared facts first 2) Shift to a friendlier tone 3) Lock the NPC into a refusal that opens only after the player shows a matching new item.
when: designing NPC questioning

text: 1) Open with neutral factual questions. 2) Move to pointed pressure questions. 3) Watch voice, body and colour for reactions. 4) Probe the answerer's core belief. 5) Press a painful point until it breaks, then step back.

1) Mark confessions gained through promised release as unreliable. 2) Reward players who spot the inducement. 3) Let a later record contradict an accepted verdict, showing that confirmed verdicts can still be wrong.
when: Designing an interrogation mechanic or case system.
why: Players learn to test statements against their incentives and to doubt verdicts that merely feel settled.

text: 1) Map the ties linking accusers, accused and their rivals. 2) Weigh each claim only after those ties are known.
when: a suspect list is built from social ties rather than physical evidence
why: Ties reveal which accusations serve an existing rivalry.

text: 1) Present last-seen questions first. 2) Ask about the person's state. 3) Ask about actions taken. 4) Ask about security. 5) Unlock follow-up questions as each answer is given.
when: designing a player interrogation interface

text: 1) Question each witness alone. 2) Re-question a key witness so their answers can be compared with others.

1) Choose a controlled intermediary, such as a servant, who is close to the suspect. 2) Prompt them with questions on a sensitive theme. 3) Observe their emotional reactions for attachments or hidden secrets the suspect might use.
when: A suspect is hard to question directly; designing a servant or intermediary character
why: A trusted subordinate's emotional responses expose hidden relationships and loyalties

text: 1) Ask direct questions in sequence. 2) Note the literal wording of each answer. 3) Record reactions that do not match the words. 4) Compare words with reactions to find gaps.
when: Questioning a subject who may be hiding information.
why: A narrow or evasive answer paired with a contradicting tell can reveal concealed information.

text: 1) Frame questions as a harmless topic, such as a wager, that gives a reason for asking. 2) Ask questions that reveal concern with a hidden subject. 3) Observe the replies for a state of mind the questions did not state.
when: A person hides a motive and will not answer a direct question.
why: A harmless frame lets the hidden concern surface through related questions.

text: 1) Open with a pointed question that assumes the hidden fact. 2) Watch the suspect's reaction. 3) After a denial, lay out the evidence in order. 4) Shift to a calmer tone and offer a candid account in return for fair reporting. 5) Have the suspect describe the method and check it against the scene.
when: When there is one strong line of evidence and one principal suspect with access to the scene.
why: A presumed fact gives the suspect no neutral reply, and the method can then be verified.

text: 1) Withhold the decisive detail. 2) Offer a partial or half-true premise. 3) Watch the reactions of the suspect and bystanders, not only the speaker's answers. 4) Release further information in measured steps.
when: A suspect is likely to lie about what they know
why: Reactions to withheld or partial facts reveal knowledge that direct questions would not.

text: 1) Ask the witness to repeat the exact words. 2) Ask which part was missed or unheard. 3) Mark the surviving fragment as partial. 4) Interpret only after the gap is identified.
when: A witness reports a clue heard only in part.
why: Separating what was heard from what was assumed prevents a full meaning being built on a fragment.

text: Ask narrow, time-specific questions rather than general ones; each committed yes, no or time becomes a fixed point to check against other evidence later.
when: Questioning a witness about a sequence of events.
why: Narrow prompts jog memory better than broad ones, and committed answers expose later contradictions.

text: Separate witnesses and suspects before questioning, question each singly, and control movement between them, so no one can compare, coordinate or align their accounts.
when: More than one witness to the same event, or a limited group such as a household.
why: Shared discussion lets accounts converge and hides contradictions.

text: Do not accuse or name anyone aloud before evidence is secure; a list of possible suspects is not a list of guilty people.
when: Planning a confrontation.
why: Premature accusation can warn the suspect and prompt flight, and naming without evidence can be unjustified and harmful.

text: Justify a delayed reveal as deliberate, explaining why an earlier answer would spoil the plan or lacked proof; an unexplained silence makes the audience feel cheated.
when: A character withholds a conclusion for a while.
why: A stated reason keeps the delay believable, and the eventual reveal must explain the earlier silence.

text: Let players choose lines that narrow an NPC's statement and expose contradictions, or set two NPCs' statements against each other; the game checks consistency.
Ask who saw a suspect during the relevant window, because without witness questions only physical evidence remains to test their movements.
when: investigating a suspect's movements
why: Witnesses are the most direct channel for corroboration.

text: Let interrogation answers branch on which documents the player has shown, varying with whether the NPC read the whole record or only a summary.
Use a negotiated outcome only when a public case would harm innocent people more than the guilty party's punishment would help.
Do not reveal the answer early when the scene is built to lead toward it; keep the solution back until the staged moment.
when: a scene's structure depends on building toward a final answer
why: An early reveal removes the anticipation the scene relies on.

text: Judge a witness's reliability through a direct interview as well as their written report.
Answer optional witness questions from the level's actual state, such as dust, doors and smells, so players can check answers in the world.
Openly invite a rival to respond to a theory, so suspense becomes a contest of reasoning between two minds.
when: Two characters hold competing explanations.
why: Open challenge makes the eventual outcome feel earned.

text: Offer an interrogation phrase option tied to a hidden fact, and let an NPC tell such as a colour change, pause or walking away unlock a new lead.
when: designing NPC dialogue for investigation
why: the tell gives the player a visible clue to follow

text: Write interrogation dialogue with closed, checkable questions, and give a warning NPC a motive the player can later expose.
when: designing an NPC who questions or warns the player
why: checkable answers and hidden motives reward follow-up investigation

text: When a sealed space shows signs of entry, shift the question from whether it was locked to by what route and for what reason.
Explain in a covering note why the delay matters, so the holder trusts the plan instead of demanding immediate verification.
Treat a remark made under pressure as a lead needing independent checks, not proof; flag coerced answers as unusable evidence, and show what forced statements can and cannot prove.
when: A suspect speaks under questioning; writing interrogation content
why: Pressure can produce statements that do not match what happened, and players should learn the limits of forced statements

text: Show behavioural tells such as stalled speech, stiffening posture, a sudden request to stay, a twitching lip or shifting gaze as clues beyond dialogue, so players can judge answers.
when: Writing scenes or designing suspect NPCs who may be hiding something

text: Require precise follow-up questions before confirming a contradiction, and offer a repeat-plainly option that rewards pressing again after a non-answer.
when: Designing interrogation mechanics or dialogue responses to evasion

text: Give interrogation dialogue several pressure points, such as reputation or exposure, so a suspect's stated fears and motive let different levers or tones yield different confessions.
when: Designing an interrogation scene

text: Weight which suspects the game surfaces first by their motive ranking, so the player meets the strongest-motive characters early.
when: Ordering investigation leads for the player
why: Ranking by motive gives the player a sensible path through the suspects

text: Build a dialogue tree where players ask for timelines, ask for alternative explanations, and receive yes-or-no checks on claims such as whether anyone left by a door.
Ask whether a witness heard an event and at what time, since timing questions can expose an earlier false answer.
Design an interrogation as a chronological statement with checkable claims, where the subject volunteers some facts and withholds others.
when: when designing an interrogation mechanic

text: Tag each NPC with traits so the player's deductions can filter the suspect list.
when: Building a suspect system
why: Trait data makes deduction computable and checkable

text: Let NPC informants answer narrow questions without revealing the player's overall goal.
when: Designing NPC information exchanges.
why: Limited questions keep the player's purpose hidden.

text: Control the physical setting of an interrogation, such as lighting that falls on the suspect's face while the questioner stays in shadow.
why: Leaves the suspect exposed while the questioner stays unseen.

text: Give interrogation dialogue options such as pressure, bluff, and silence distinct NPC reactions, so each choice produces a different response.
when: when designing a dialogue system

text: Information an interrogated NPC gives after a long ordeal should be checkable against the world, not only what the interrogator wants to hear.
Let an interrogation clue be a visible mismatch between what a witness said and what the interrogator reports, so players can catch the distortion.
Do not discard a claim just because its source is suspect; test it against independent evidence before deciding.
Let other NPCs change behaviour after a suspect is removed, and treat that change as a clue about who was involved.
Design a request whose refusal or acceptance reveals an NPC's hidden state, such as consent to search belongings.
when: building an investigation puzzle
why: The response becomes the clue

text: Do not treat a request for silence as neutral; it changes what the investigator can rely on, and its cost to justice must be weighed before honouring it.
Give a recurring NPC a distinctive tic that the player learns to recognise even when the NPC is disguised.
When the player cannot move or hold items in a scene, let dialogue choices carry the motive and relationship clues.
when: An interrogation scene limits player actions
why: Without props or movement, dialogue must deliver the information

text: In an interrogation system, present evidence in order and vary the suspect's reaction with each item shown.
when: Designing an interrogation mechanic
why: Sequenced reactions make each piece of evidence feel consequential

text: Confront the person a damaging claim concerns directly, rather than accepting a third party's discovery as final.
Lock some evidence from a suspect NPC so the suspect cannot react to clues the player has already found.
when: When a suspect could otherwise react to the player's discoveries.
why: Preventing reactions keeps the suspect's responses consistent with what the player can know.

text: Check the room for listeners before a subject speaks freely, since the setting itself can shape how much a subject is willing to reveal.
when: Conducting an interview on a sensitive subject.
why: Fear of being overheard suppresses honest testimony.

text: Offer a press option that yields a more specific answer at the cost of the NPC becoming hostile or closing the topic.
when: When designing dialogue that lets the player push an NPC for detail.
why: Pressing trades information for relationship cost, which makes the choice meaningful.

text: Staged overhearing or a false role may be seen through, prompting the suspect to mislead in return, and overacting raises suspicion; yet deceiving the accused or setting snares risks entrapment.
when: Deciding whether to use staged overhearing or a false role in questioning.
why: Plausible restraint limits detection; deception can produce false confessions and undermine the case.

text: Pressing a reluctant subject yields information sooner but can close off later answers and end the conversation; waiting keeps them talking at the cost of time.
when: Deciding when to press a hesitant subject or designing interrogation pacing
why: Premature pressure can end the conversation and forecloses options that patience would keep open

text: Pressing a witness hard can end cooperation; asking one clear question at a time keeps the conversation open while still exposing gaps.
when: questioning a cooperative witness
why: Pressure makes the witness withdraw, while focused questions keep the exchange going

text: Separating a hostile suspect from companions removes their support and leaves fear as the main lever, but coerced answers are less reliable than confirmed ones.
when: A hostile, frightened witness holds key information and time is short.
why: Isolation shifts the suspect's options toward compliance rather than truth.

text: Asking the key question early risks losing a fading witness before the answer comes; asking it late risks losing the answer altogether. Timing must balance both risks.
when: witness may lose consciousness or strength
why: the witness's remaining time is limited

text: Closing a door before a witness speaks limits eavesdropping but removes the investigator's own view of what was said.
when: A witness asks for privacy before speaking
why: Privacy protects the witness from overhearing but leaves no observer of the exchange.

text: A repeated interruption can serve propriety while also monitoring the people present.
when: a third party repeatedly enters a private conversation
why: the visit is socially justified, so it covers the observation

text: A suspect who recovers from a break and turns warm signals that control of the conversation has changed hands.
when: after an interruption breaks a tense exchange

text: A sudden interruption, such as an urgent summons at a tense moment, sharply turns the scene and heightens its tension.
when: a scene is building toward a climax
why: An unexpected interruption resets the audience's expectations

text: A steady signal that stops suddenly, mid-message, suggests something went wrong, likely a new event interrupting it, rather than a normal ending; the break is evidence.
when: when a steady exchange stops at a moment that can be dated
why: A sudden cut points to a trigger rather than a planned end.

text: Remnants of an unfinished activity, such as brushes left clogged in solvent or a tense mid-play board layout, show it was interrupted or recently stopped, not completed.
Interrupt a long narrative with a specific question, such as asking for the one vital reason, that the speaker must answer, so the key point is not buried in detail.
Use an interruption within a conversation to pull out key information at the right moment.
when: when timing of a revelation matters
why: interruptions create pressure that releases the fact

text: Cut off a revelation just as it is about to be made; the interruption holds attention and sets up the next scene.
when: At a scene break where the answer should come from elsewhere
why: A withheld payoff pulls the audience forward

text: Interruptions that cut a witness off at a sensitive point signal that the story holds more than is being given, to both witness and examiner.
when: A witness is repeatedly stopped just as the account reaches their own whereabouts.
why: The interruption reveals that the examiner suspects a gap in the account.

text: Cutting off a sound, event, or conversation before its explanation or outcome defers the answer, so tension grows while the payoff is postponed, not lost.
when: Pacing a scene with a planned confrontation or revelation
why: Unfinished tension keeps attention and anticipation high, and the audience stays waiting while the story continues.

text: A message cut off before its key detail gives partial clues and an open question, which sustains suspense until the gap is resolved.
when: Early story hook
why: The audience needs the missing part

text: A character who enters just before a countdown ends can interrupt it and halt the scripted outcome.
An outside interruption can cut a probe short before anything is admitted, forcing the questioner to find another opening.
A small sound, such as a footstep, interrupting a silent scene tests the characters' nerves and raises the stakes of the wait.
when: A quiet scene is building toward a decisive moment.
why: An unexpected small sound forces a reaction and reveals how the characters cope under pressure.

text: A sound from outside can end a questioning scene and force the characters to drop their plan and hide, reshaping the timeline.
Interrupting a revelation with a new arrival slows the scene, raises tension, and gives the audience a new character to judge.
when: a reveal is in progress
why: a fresh presence pauses the reveal while adding information

text: An outside interruption such as a guard entering or a bell ringing can pause a revelation, and offering a choice to resume gives the player control over timing.
when: Designing dialogue or cutscenes with a key reveal.
why: The pause builds tension and lets the player decide when the scene continues.

text: Interrupting a witness too soon breaks a fragile chain of memory and loses the details they would otherwise give.
when: a witness is recalling events in sequence

text: An interruption that replaces a needed explanation or revelation without a later payoff frustrates the audience; every cut must lead to an answer they can reach.
when: When a revelation is cut off
why: Unanswered cuts read as evasion

text: Trying to interrupt a talkative witness usually fails, since they swamp the questioner with talk.
when: a witness buries answers in digressions

text: Interrupt an NPC's confession with a scripted event, then resume it later; the secret stays intact while stakes rise, so disclosure is deferred, not lost.
Do not treat an interrupted record as a complete account of what followed; the gap is a question to investigate, not a fact to fill in.
when: A diary or log stops mid-entry.
why: Filling gaps with assumed detail can mislead the investigation.

text: Interrupt prepared speeches and keep the suspect close, so that pleading or flirtation does not break off the questioning.
when: when a suspect tries to steer the conversation with emotion
why: interruption keeps questions on the sequence of facts

text: An interruption should not fully replace the lead being followed; the original line of inquiry must stay open.
when: a new arrival breaks a scene
why: dropping the lead wastes the investigation

text: Players can interrupt rumour escalation by gathering contrary evidence early, before official steps lock in.
when: When a rumour has not yet triggered official action.
why: Early counter-evidence stops later steps from gaining credibility.

text: Have an adult NPC interrupt a child NPC who is about to reveal something dangerous, so the interruption itself signals a secret.
when: When staging a child informant near a dangerous or hidden fact.
why: The interruption signals the stakes and invites the player to pursue the child later.

text: Interruptions build tension, but overuse, or ones that change no order or facts and are just delays, feels arbitrary and contrived; reserve them for key scenes.
when: Adding interruptions to scenes
why: Interruptions without plot effect frustrate audiences

text: Interrupting a witness early loses their sequence of events, while letting them run on unchecked leaves claims untested.
when: Questioning a witness whose account has checkable claims

text: 1) Open with a vague remark that invites others to speak. 2) Let them volunteer what they know before questioning directly. 3) Pin down who made each specific claim.
when: interviewing witnesses, especially when the community talks freely

text: Do not press a witness who is distressed, likely to shut down, or hesitating; change subject instead. Avoid pressing when the investigator is angry and may lose control.
when: a witness hesitates, grows evasive, or is distressed, or the investigator is angry
why: pressure at that moment raises guardedness

text: A suspect who first denies everything may break down and confess when confronted with a checkable fact, or abandon denial once investigators visibly know more than expected.
when: the evidence is real and cannot be dismissed easily, or the suspect sees investigators' knowledge exceeds expectations
why: A precise, verifiable fact removes room to deny; visible knowledge removes hope of concealment.

text: A casual or idle-seeming question does not trigger defensiveness, so a witness who cannot see the questioner's aim may reveal facts they would hide under direct questioning.
when: a direct question would alert the subject, or a guarded witness is questioned about a sensitive subject in a casual setting
why: Casual framing hides the purpose and lowers the listener's guard.

text: Reminding a suspect that his own conduct will shape the outcome tends to lower his confidence.
Asking how an offence happened, rather than whether it happened, moves a witness from flat denial toward explanation.
when: the investigator already believes an act occurred
why: presupposing the act removes the easy option of denial

text: Cross-examination can unsettle a witness until they withdraw even a claim of recognition.
when: A witness is questioned repeatedly or aggressively.
why: Pressure erodes confidence in uncertain memories.

text: People questioned about a private matter often show hesitation and embarrassment, which can mark a topic the family would rather not discuss.
when: investigators press on a victim's personal life
why: the subject exposes private matters

text: A suspect may surrender to shift suspicion onto a lesser charge.
when: A suspect faces a serious accusation.

text: Re-examining an object after a new idea arises often reveals changes the first look missed.
when: when a new question prompts a review of earlier observations
why: The first look was not framed by the new question.

text: Readers file an object introduced for a joke as comic detail, not clue, so its later reinterpretation as evidence can surprise them.
when: A prop appears in a light, comedic scene.
why: A humorous tone lowers attention to the object's details.

text: A short written refusal carries weight when the writer's character is known, since brevity itself signals resolve.
when: A person known to the investigator refuses in writing with few words.
why: Brevity from a known character reads as deliberate and firm.

text: An ambush question placed before a hostile audience can turn sympathy toward the witness and against the questioner.
when: Confronting a witness in front of an unfriendly group
why: Audiences react to perceived unfairness, weakening the questioner's position

text: A witness who challenges a claim by demanding proof invites the investigator to produce documents, so the challenge can be answered with evidence.
when: the investigator holds documents supporting the claim
why: A demand for proof gives the investigator a reason to present evidence.

text: Asking who gains from an event, or floating an impersonation, provokes a reaction the questioner can read.
A listener who sees that advice would isolate them from rivals may read it as a trap rather than sincere counsel.
when: When advice would alter a listener's alliances.
why: Awareness of the consequence reveals the hidden intent.

text: A witness asked about surrounding events rather than the target often gives answers that reveal more to the investigator than to themselves, because they do not know what matters.
when: a witness does not know the significance of what they know, or direct questions would alert a suspect
why: Indirect questions avoid triggering guarded answers, so the investigator learns facts the witness does not realise are relevant.

text: A suspect who asks to hear the investigator's method before giving an account reverses the usual questioning order and shifts control of the interview to the suspect.
when: A prepared suspect opens negotiations before any statement is given.
why: The suspect has anticipated the inquiry and wants to set the frame first.

text: Cross-examination tests a witness by putting pointed propositions one after another, forcing a choice between admission and denial, and looking for conflicts with the known record.
A line of inquiry closes when the people who could confirm it are gone, so the investigator must turn to other sources.
A third party may arrive mid-interview and cut it short, so interviews can end before the questioner gets the full account.
Partial disclosure of suspicions or withheld evidence gives the witness leverage to judge how much to trust the questioner and how much to reveal.
when: When an investigator discloses some suspicions but withholds other evidence
why: The witness uses what she knows about the investigator's position to decide what to say.

text: Draw out guarded, reserved or hostile sources through casual conversation, shared meals, neutral subjects and tactful indirect questions, since blunt questions make them defensive.
when: A source is guarded, emotional, hostile or reserved
why: Direct questions trigger guardedness and close the channel.

text: Question a suspect unexpectedly and early, before a cover story is settled, since warning or delay gives time to build a false account that cannot be checked.
when: A suspect is likely to prepare answers if warned, or their account is not yet fixed
why: Time to reflect lets the suspect prepare a false, uncheckable account.

text: Question the person whose duties cover a given detail, since they are most likely to have noticed it.
when: Seeking information about a specific detail
why: Routine responsibility gives the most reliable knowledge of that detail

text: A suspect questioned early, when woken, hungry and half awake, is less guarded than one questioned at midday.
when: choosing when to confront a suspect
why: fatigue and hunger lower defences

text: Hold a strange remark open, since it may show knowledge or merely seek attention, until more evidence arrives.
when: a witness says something ambiguous
why: one remark cannot tell knowledge from attention-seeking

text: Arranging facts in order of occurrence can reveal links between events that seemed unrelated when reported out of sequence.
A hidden state can be inferred from what a correspondent avoids saying, such as repeated direct questions that receive no direct answer.
when: The reader must infer a state from a correspondent who will not state it.
why: Persistent evasion on a specific point signals something being withheld.

text: When a witness knows a detail not in the record, ask directly where it came from before assuming a secret, since simple misremembering also explains it.
when: a witness appears to know something unpublished
why: witnesses may simply misremember a source

text: When a skeptic objects that the target seems unrelated, ask what the sender gained and what they wanted the recipient to know.
when: Judging a motive is unclear
why: Purpose often explains a message even when the target looks unconnected.

text: An interview may need only to see the witness and their setting to build a clear picture, not to extract a full statement.
A visitor who asks more about consequences than about the facts needed reveals priorities worth testing.
Frame recall questions open-endedly so the witness answers from memory, not from the interviewer's own theory.
Re-examine physical details that witnesses remember poorly, since such details are easy to misstate.
Ask about habits and locations, such as where an item was kept, before testing a suspect's claim.
Unusual precautions taken by a witness, such as bolting a door or borrowing a weapon, should be questioned for their reason.
when: A witness reports a precaution out of the ordinary.
why: Unusual precautions can signal prior knowledge or fear that bears on the case.

text: Let an evasive person describe events in their own words rather than leading with direct questions, which can draw out more voluntary disclosure.
Ask specific closed questions about when, where and purpose; their answers can be checked against other evidence.
when: interviewing a witness about events
why: specific answers can be verified, unlike vague ones

text: A question that seems to ask about distance may really test what a suspect possesses. Ask what each question is meant to reveal.
when: Interviewing a suspect whose answers may conceal planning.
why: Innocent-sounding questions can expose preparation the suspect did not intend to reveal.

text: In a fixed, fully known population, a single unexpected person stands out at once, because routine makes any deviation visible.
when: the suspect pool is small and fixed
why: Known routines make a stranger's presence conspicuous

text: Probe what a sincere but confused witness cannot describe; the gaps reveal how little their claim actually rests on.
Confront a witness with a document or record when they have a motive to distort it and the record must be explained.
when: a witness has a motive and a record needs explaining

text: When a target may conceal identity, ask about descriptions and dates, not only names.
when: when a target may use an assumed name

text: If an adversary acted on information only later, someone must have passed it on. Ask when the adversary learned a fact to infer who their source was.
when: Tracing how sensitive information spread.
why: The timing of knowledge reveals the chain of communication.

text: Turn a question back on the questioner to avoid revealing your own view.
Ask what happened after each step, and look for the one unexplained move in an otherwise tidy chain.
An engaging NPC who asks questions about a location can be designed so that the questions reveal what the player is really seeking.
Open questioning with irrelevant small talk, then strike with a pointed question, so the suspect lowers his guard before the key point arrives.
when: the pointed question is the real goal
why: a relaxed suspect is less prepared to deflect

text: When a volunteered account seems loosely connected to the case, press for exact times, outcomes and departures to test whether it fits the rest of the evidence.
when: When a witness offers a detail that seems convenient or peripheral.
why: Specific, checkable details are harder to fabricate consistently than vague accounts.

text: When a witness says something happened 'at the time', ask for the exact time to force a precise sequence and expose hidden contradictions.
when: a witness gives a vague time reference
why: vague timing hides gaps in the sequence of events

text: Open a conversation by praising a witness's work or interest, then listen; private worries and relationships tend to surface while they talk about it.
when: witness is talkative or trusting
why: people share more when they do not realise their words are being weighed

text: Ask indirect questions, such as who the witness remembers visiting, to draw out details that a direct question about a named suspect may not reach.
when: Witness will not share directly

text: Ask the person who made a stain before relying on a laboratory, since their account may be faster and sufficient.
Let co-interviewers signal each other privately, so questioning keeps its rhythm and the witness does not notice the interruption.
when: when two people question one witness

text: Pressing a suspect to speak works best when the suspect's account can clear an innocent person and the key facts are already largely established.
when: Deciding whether to press a suspect for a full account
why: Known facts let the suspect's account be checked and make the cost of silence concrete

text: Ask direct questions about the suspect's known secrets, such as an unexplained payment or an item found in their property.
Hint at the truth through facts and suggestions rather than an outright accusation, so the other party reaches the conclusion alone.
Ask witnesses directly about prior acquaintances, since a hidden link may only emerge when someone asks the right question.
when: Interviewing witnesses in an investigation.
why: Unprompted accounts omit links that the witness considers unimportant.

text: Probing for hidden motive matters less when the visitor openly explains the request.
Open with a sound, object or short reply that signals a death or major event before any name is given.
Brief, closed questions get terse answers, which questioners tend to accept as clear, so the pace of the exchange controls what gets heard.
A claim of a hidden ability can be tested by varying conditions and asking for tasks that a true possessor could pass but a performer could not.
when: A claim depends on a hidden ability or reaction, and conditions can be varied.
why: Varied conditions separate a real ability from a performance that only fits the examiner's expectations.

text: An NPC who bans public talk to prevent unrest can serve as a suppression obstacle that players must overcome.
when: When designing authority figures who restrict information.
why: Restriction creates a barrier for the player to break.

text: Ask what a request for documents aims to achieve; records requested to answer critics may serve as a defense rather than neutral record.
when: Documents are requested or circulated during a dispute.
why: Stated purpose can differ from recorded purpose.

text: A direct, plain question often provokes a flustered denial that exposes an evasion more readily than an indirect approach.
when: When a witness appears to be concealing an intent or fact.
why: Direct questions leave less room for a prepared, smooth answer.

text: Avoid open identification demands when a witness has already refused to name a candidate, since they tend to backfire.
when: A witness has resisted naming a suspect
why: Direct pressure can harden refusal and undermine the witness's later cooperation.

text: Ask background questions about a witness's reading or past to check whether their knowledge came from an outside source.
when: when a witness shows unusual knowledge of a subject
why: Outside exposure can explain knowledge a witness attributes to experience

text: Closed questions that fix one fact at a time narrow what can have happened, since each negative answer eliminates a possibility from the timeline.
when: confirming a timeline before confronting a suspect

text: Each unanswered question can point to another person to check, so an open-question list tends to grow in several directions at once.
Give NPCs secrets that players can pry loose by confronting them with a verified fact.
An NPC who feels unthreatened by the player gives more information, so the player's choice of tone changes how much is revealed.
when: Designing dialogue where the player questions a suspect.
why: Lower perceived threat reduces guardedness, so disclosure rises with a relaxed approach.

text: When dialogue options differ in phrasing, neutral questions can return a fuller NPC description than leading ones, so phrasing changes the information received.
when: Designing dialogue options

text: A reveal can be triggered by asking the right question at the right moment rather than by a fixed dialogue option.
when: Designing interrogation-driven discovery.
why: Context-sensitive triggers reward good questioning.

text: A comic beat after a tense peak releases built-up pressure and resets tension before the next section.
when: a scene has reached a peak
why: humour breaks the pressure

text: An authority that refuses joint meetings and sees people one at a time forces each witness into a separate account, which lets players gather corroboration.
A question that reveals what the investigator knows, through its content or its order, tips off the witness and invites a prepared answer.
Asking a witness about details outside their knowledge yields unreliable answers.
when: Choosing whom to question
why: Guessing replaces knowledge when a witness has no real basis

text: Losing temper hands the other party an advantage and makes the interviewer appear the aggressor.
when: An interviewer faces repeated evasion.
why: Visible anger shifts sympathy to the evader and weakens the interviewer's position.

text: A comforter's follow-up questions can shape the account a witness gives, so the exact wording of questions should be recorded with the answers.
when: a witness is questioned after an emotional moment
why: Questions frame what the witness recalls and how they describe it

text: An interviewer's own visible embarrassment at a name can alert the source and reverse the balance of the exchange.
when: when questioning someone who reads emotional cues
why: Reactions signal which facts matter.

text: Thorough questioning is not the same as checking; pressing a witness hard without testing answers against the clock leaves contradictions unexposed.
A threatened suspect may shift blame onto others to save themselves.
Questions that depend on one another can loop back to the start, so the list makes no progress without new evidence.
Overusing sudden threats dulls tension.
Reassuring a witness with promises that cannot be guaranteed turns comfort into deception.
A witness with privileged access to the scene may frame the story to suit themselves.
Warmth in an interview can disarm the interviewer as much as the witness, causing the interviewer to miss gaps.
when: when an interview becomes friendly
why: rapport lowers the interviewer's guard against inconsistencies

text: A probe can backfire: an accepted cover story invites further testing, so each new claim adds to the risk.
Rephrasing the same question often only reconfirms the same answer; switch to a new angle such as finances or contacts.
Asking an acquaintance to pass on what they heard can apply pressure rather than gather neutral facts.
when: Seeking information through an intermediary who knows the subject.
why: The intermediary is shaped by their relationship to the subject.

text: Marking every helpful character as a suspect destroys the signal, so suspicion stops distinguishing the guilty from everyone else.
Reading meaning into a silent person's signals invites projection from the reader's own feelings, and the impaired person may also read the reader as a symbol.
why: Interpretation runs in both directions and distorts both readings.

text: Baiting a suspect can make later answers more guarded, and a reaction indicates concern rather than guilt.
when: Using a bait fact to test a suspect
why: Suspects who sense a test grow careful, and worry has many causes besides guilt.

text: Relentless pressure can make a witness faint or break down, ending the examination before the account is complete; get key facts on record first.
1) Re-ask the detail in neutral wording or a different form, avoiding hints of the answer. 2) Compare it with the verbatim earlier record. 3) Note any change and ask why it happened.
when: a witness or suspect's account of a key fact may be inconsistent
why: Leading questions shape answers; rephrasing shows whether an answer is stable or invented.

text: 1) Ask one short, narrow factual question at a time. 2) Have the witness answer only what was asked, steering rambling replies back. 3) Ask for the witness's own impression separately from what they claim to know.
why: Keeps the account clean and checkable.

text: 1) Record the witness's firm claim and ask for exact times, names and actions. 2) Ask about conditions of observation and what was seen directly versus inferred. 3) Ask about incidental details and how sure they are. 4) Offer a plausible alternative. 5) Keep the claim only at the level answers support.
when: A witness is certain but the view was brief, partial or poor, or an identification is being tested
why: Certainty about minor details often exceeds what was observed; confidence does not guarantee accurate details.

text: 1) State a fact or inference aloud, real or pretended. 2) Watch for denial, evasion, sudden admission or visible fear. 3) Offer a second hypothesis and note which answer is guarded. 4) Use the visible fear to draw out the missing detail.
when: when testing a specific point in a suspect's account or a suspect is withholding a detail
why: Reactions show which point the suspect protects; naming the inference makes fear visible.

text: 1) Ask about a specific detail, such as colour, count, or who handed over an object. 2) Record the answer. 3) Ask a follow-up that the answer must match. 4) Compare the answers for consistency.
when: Questioning a witness whose account cannot be checked directly.
why: Each specific detail creates a point that a later answer can contradict.

text: 1) Repeat key questions in different wording and watch for hesitation or pallor. 2) Narrow to specific dates, places and reasons. 3) Check answers against records the witness cannot easily change.
when: a witness gives a partial story and may be concealing part of it

text: 1) Ask the witness to begin well before the event of interest. 2) Move forward point by point in sequence until reaching the event.
when: the witness is not a practised narrator and sequence matters
why: Starting early and advancing in order produces a plain account without gaps

text: 1) Ask a plain question about enemies or who benefits. 2) Hold the witness's gaze. 3) Record any hesitation or vague answer. 4) Repeat back a recalled remark exactly, including its pronouns.
when: When a polished witness might reveal knowledge through one phrase.
why: Exact repetition and attention to hesitation expose what the words meant.

text: 1) Learn the household through casual sources such as neighbours, tradespeople and servants before any formal interview. 2) Use a pretext and small courtesies to open conversation. 3) Clarify your purpose so gatekeepers admit you.
when: Gathering information before a formal interview.
why: Informal sources often know more than formal witnesses and are easier to approach.

text: 1) Adopt a persona or disguise that allows indirect speech. 2) Tell a story that hints at the secret. 3) Watch the target's reactions in order. 4) Weigh the reactions as evidence against innocent explanations.
when: when a target has motive but is unlikely to admit it

text: 1) Confirm the inquiry's official progress. 2) Set a trap that tests the suspect. 3) Question each key party in turn. 4) Examine documents such as receipts. 5) Raise public stakes last.
when: when a witness is hiding knowledge
why: each question narrows the field of possible answers

text: 1) Open with neutral or general topics far from the subject. 2) Build rapport through flattery and shared sympathy. 3) Ask many small indirect questions. 4) Note which answer lands.
when: When a direct question would be refused or met with silence
why: Lowering the witness's guard brings out facts a direct question would not reach

text: 1) Have the suggestible subject focus on a fixed stimulus. 2) Ask questions in a fixed order, moving from route to possession to timing. 3) Note any pause before each answer.
when: When questioning a compliant or suggestible informant
why: A fixed order can draw out knowledge of plans

text: 1) Ask for exact words, order and setting. 2) Ask directly what was left out. 3) Check the answers for gaps.
when: interviewing a witness through a relay
why: Specific detail and direct omission questions expose gaps

text: 1) Ask numbered questions one at a time. 2) Hold each answer before moving on. 3) Note each refusal or evasion for later. 4) Use the answers to decide the next terms.
when: A bargaining scene where one side controls the setting
why: Each answer reveals what the other side knows and how much leverage remains

text: 1) Address the source with deference and praise their judgement. 2) Ask guessing questions that let them confirm or correct your guess. 3) Ask open questions about their interests. 4) Ask one targeted case question. 5) Keep your own statements short and vague so the source does most of the talking.
when: Source is talkative and vain; guarded sources will not respond the same way.

text: 1) Open on a neighbouring subject. 2) Watch for involuntary signs. 3) Ask a follow-up question to test any sign. 4) Ask the subject to justify why you asked. 5) Ask agreeable questions to fix their stated terms.
when: A direct question would make the subject guarded and you need their own framing of their stake.

text: 1) Prepare a checklist of topics. 2) Open with small, checkable questions. 3) Raise sensitive topics later. 4) Strike off each topic when covered. 5) Restate answers for confirmation.
when: Running a formal interview where terms must be confirmed.
why: A checklist keeps coverage complete and the record clear.

text: 1) State the suspect's position as an impartial observer would. 2) Ask narrow questions about the unexplained item. 3) Separate admissions from refusals and treat each answer as narrowing the field.
when: The suspect refuses to explain a possession and has limited information to offer.
why: Framing the case calmly and asking narrow questions can draw partial admissions.

text: 1) Open with a broad request. 2) Build background about who the person is and where they came from. 3) Ask the critical question directly. 4) Pull drifting answers back by matching reported words to facts already known.
when: When a witness holds partial, second-hand knowledge that comes out in pieces.
why: Background builds rapport, and direct questions prevent a frightened witness from shutting down.

text: 1) Break the account into small steps: timing, door state, objects present and order of events. 2) Ask about small physical details the witness may not have rehearsed or noticed. 3) Compare each answer with known facts about the place or object.
when: a witness's account is smooth, may be assembled from a story, or may have missed details
why: Fabricated accounts and missed details tend to fail on small points the witness did not prepare or notice.
