text: 1) Ask a broad question about who else was present. 2) Only then name the person sought. 3) Show a photograph and ask for confirmation.
when: a witness saw a stranger earlier
why: naming the target early can seed the witness's memory; a plain who-else-was-present question can move a witness from denial toward confession

text: 1) State the events in order. 2) Establish a fixed routine as the baseline. 3) Fix the times of each event. 4) Cross-check times against each other. 5) Theorise about causes last.
when: a case needs a clear account of what happened and when, before explaining why
why: A fixed sequence of events prevents explanations from distorting the facts.

text: 1) Make a specific false claim about a shared past, such as meeting at an event. 2) Observe whether the witness denies it. 3) Treat a firm denial of a detail as informative, without accusing them directly.
when: a witness may know more than they say
why: a witness who knows the truth will tend to deny a false detail

text: 1) Ask whether a crime occurred. 2) If so, ask what it was and how it was done. Use both questions to set the scope before analysis.
when: at the start of any case

text: 1) Give an ordered, precise account of the suspect's actions. 2) Present physical evidence they cannot easily refute. 3) Offer protective terms if they cooperate.
when: suspect is present, evidence is specific, and a private resolution is possible
why: Specificity makes denial hard, and protection gives the suspect a reason to confess

text: 1) Ask leading questions about the stranger's purpose and past. 2) Note any trouble or violence he admits to. 3) Observe his temper when warned. 4) Compare his answers with what others report.
when: A stranger's background is unknown
why: Answers, conduct and reputation together give evidence about who he is.

text: Ask who else knew of the meeting, whether valuables are kept, whether theft is feared, and how long the witness has lived there, then compare answers with other evidence.
when: questioning a witness about a planned meeting or property
why: these questions narrow the list of people with knowledge and motive

text: 1) Ask short closed questions to fix the witness's exact claim. 2) Return the witness's own words to expose an assumption. 3) Ask them to explain a mechanism to test plausibility. 4) Bank admissions for later argument.
when: Questioning a witness who is precise.

text: 1) Ask whether the event was recorded at the time. 2) Ask how the date was fixed. 3) Ask what written record exists. 4) Press each answer with narrow follow-up questions.
when: a witness is certain of an identification
why: certainty can outrun documentation

text: 1) Start from the first fact the audience knows. 2) State the motive, then the link to the suspect, then the means. 3) Eliminate alternatives in turn. 4) Answer the questions left open.
when: at the reveal of a mystery solution
why: each inference rests on facts already shown, so the answer feels earned

text: Accept a witness's account as partial, then ask why each action was taken, since the reason is often withheld until pressed.
Test an apparently sealed barrier with a probe or push before accepting it; a probe through a keyhole can show whether a key sits in the lock from the other side.
when: Investigating a room that appears locked.
why: A locked state can be weaker than it appears.

text: 1) Ask an open question so the witness recalls freely. 2) Record that free account before adding your own frame. 3) Narrow with specific questions, noting which details came from you.
when: questioning a witness whose memory could be shaped
why: the witness's own memory is captured before the investigator's framing is introduced

text: 1) Make a small, harmless change in the suspect's surroundings. 2) Observe whether the reaction is immediate, absent or unusually quiet. 3) Weigh the reaction against the wider pattern.

1) Begin with a broad request for everything observed. 2) Interrupt if the witness jumps to a conclusion, and return to the order of events. 3) After the full account, ask directly about any odd point. 4) Shape each next question around the last telling answer.
1) Ask neutral questions about a place or event. 2) Record each answer. 3) Compare answers across suspects and note contradictions with earlier statements.
when: when a suspect cannot be pressed directly

text: 1) Open with a claim the witness would find hard to defend. 2) Use an earlier fact the witness remembers to test memory. 3) State each accusation as a proposition. 4) Record every denial. 5) Cover alternative explanations in turn.
1) Watch for pauses, blushes or sudden topic changes when a witness answers. 2) Ask a narrow question about one specific object or fact. 3) Let the narrowness make a simple denial hard.
when: a witness is partly truthful and one precise fact is being withheld
why: a narrow question leaves little room for evasion and exposes the withheld fact

text: 1) Ask for an exact moment of an event. 2) Ask who left first. 3) Repeat for each step of the meeting, so every step is pinned down.
when: when a suspect's timing forms a gap
why: Exact sequence questions expose inconsistencies that vague answers hide.

text: 1) Use a cover story that grants access. 2) Drop a small test remark. 3) Watch who reacts and how. 4) Discard answers that do not bear on the case.
when: a target is guarded and a direct question would alert them
why: Indirect tests reveal reactions without tipping off the target

text: 1) Open with a neutral shared interest, such as a local activity. 2) Let the talk drift to related people and places. 3) Turn to the people or events under investigation.
when: when an informant is reluctant or guarded
why: a neutral start lowers resistance

text: 1) Ask yes-or-no questions that narrow the field. 2) Use each answer to eliminate options and choose the next question. 3) For spelled-out answers, confirm each uncertain letter before moving on. 4) Repeat and confirm slow or ambiguous signals.
when: The subject can answer only briefly, or one fact is needed at a time.
why: Accuracy depends on confirming each step.

text: 1) Get a formal denial on record before the subject narrates. 2) Let the subject give a complete account in chronological order. 3) Review the notes and ask pointed follow-up questions. 4) Ask for exact counts, durations and times. 5) Ask for a witness to each movement; log unnamed gaps as open tasks.
when: when interviewing a suspect for a full account

text: 1) List every known event with its date or time. 2) Order events by when they happened, not when they were learned. 3) Put undated facts in a separate list. 4) Scan the sequence for patterns and gaps.
when: evidence arrives piecemeal from several sources
why: Discovery order can scramble the real sequence and hide patterns.

text: 1) Open by stating the known case against the suspect and advising that candor serves their interest. 2) Cover topics in order: acquaintance, disputed possessions, timeline, finances. 3) Return to any point the suspect avoided.
when: A suspect holds information and a non-coercive approach may still work.

text: 1) Open with an apology and a framing remark to lower the suspect's guard. 2) Ask about the past relationship in an incurious tone. 3) Put the sensitive question directly and note the reply.
when: Suspect has an obvious reason to deny
why: A lowered guard makes later denials easier to read

text: Question peripheral witnesses first and compare their timing and sound accounts before questioning the central witness.
why: earlier interviews fix the baseline that later ones are checked against

text: Open with establishing questions about location, hearing and sight, then narrow to doors, locks, light and movement.
1) Note any detail a witness volunteers before being told it. 2) Ask where they heard it. 3) Name a key person or fact to test their reaction. 4) Watch for changes in posture and speech.
1) Let the suspect give their own account first. 2) Quote the disputed words exactly. 3) Ask what the words meant, not for a yes or no.
when: when a statement has two plausible readings

text: 1) Restore order with a firm rebuke when a suspect loses control. 2) Return to a calm, ordinary question.
1) Ask general questions about the household or group. 2) Move to the people most closely involved. 3) Keep the most sensitive questions for later, once witnesses are at ease.
when: A case involves many relationships and motive is unclear.
why: Starting broad lets witnesses speak with less embarrassment.

text: 1) Declare the category of crime at once so everyone understands the stakes. 2) Assign searches to named helpers in advance. 3) Question witnesses one at a time, pinning each to a specific fact. 4) Record exact words. 5) Use scene watchers to fix the timeline and cross-check.
when: At first arrival at a scene while witnesses are still present.
why: Accounts are fresher and not yet shaped by one another.

text: 1) Lay out the physical evidence first. 2) Ask the suspect to explain it. 3) Test each explanation against an independent source. 4) Press on the motive until the suspect explains.
when: a suspect offers an explanation that may be true but is unverified
why: evidence fixes the facts before the suspect's account is judged

text: 1) Frame a personal question as an impersonal or literary point. 2) Invite the suspect to recognise himself in a category. 3) Treat refusal or defiance as evidence.
when: Probing a suspect whose writings or beliefs may reveal motive, and who would refuse a direct question.
why: An indirect frame makes the suspect react, and the reaction becomes the clue.

text: 1) Keep the target talking through small talk and silences. 2) Drop a specific known detail. 3) Watch the reaction. 4) Shift topic suddenly. 5) Compare answers with known facts.
when: there is no decisive proof and the aim is to see how a suspect handles pressure
why: reactions and fit with known facts reveal knowledge without an accusation

text: 1) Ask rapid, direct questions about who, what and when. 2) If answers stay thin, drop that line rather than force it.
1) Begin with an opening ritual. 2) Question the accused in sequence. 3) Read witness statements aloud. 4) Let witnesses contradict the accused. 5) Record each answer.
1) Make a suspect believe a key matter is important to them. 2) Leave them unobserved for a set period. 3) Check for a physical change that reveals their action.
when: When a suspect is likely to act to protect their position and the action leaves a trace
why: Perceived freedom to act makes the suspect more likely to reveal themselves through a checkable change.

text: 1) Check the pretext's basis by asking others whether the item belongs to them. 2) If the target offers no opening, create one with a plausible excuse. 3) Ask a question that invites advice. 4) Use the target's own suggestion to extend the contact.
when: The target will not invite contact or sits alone.

text: 1) Raise one implausible point lightly. 2) Accept the defensive reply and note each new detail it adds. 3) Ask about motive or access without accusing. 4) Mark checkable details as leads for later.
when: A witness's story is plausible but has one weak point.
why: Each defence adds verifiable facts without provoking the witness into closing up.

text: 1) Agree a time limit openly with the suspect before the interview begins. 2) Have an officer record the statement. 3) Let the suspect speak at length, noting the sequence of events and the gaps. 4) End the interview when the agreed time expires.
when: A suspect is willing to talk but controls the pace.
why: Open terms and a recorded statement keep the interview constrained and usable as evidence.

text: Question witnesses privately, dismissing other staff or keeping only a reliable witness present, so no one overhears. Others present make witnesses close up and raise the cost of honest answers.
when: a witness is reluctant to answer in front of others, or sensitive relationship questions are asked
why: Witnesses close up when observed by colleagues or subordinates.

text: Ask how a witness knows a claim and what evidence supports it; accept the claim only with a stated source.
Let the player choose an interview venue, private or public, since each choice changes what NPCs say and who overhears.
Do not use a cruel or harmful disclosure as a test of reaction, even when it might reveal the truth.
Use a public disruption, such as a performance breaking down, to open a private dialogue option with a second NPC.
when: a scripted scene can be interrupted by one character's distress
why: The disruption creates a moment where a bystander can speak privately

text: Take a statement only once the witness can give it clearly; interviewing too early can lose the evidence.
Use interviews for motive and context, and keep physical traces as the evidence the player must find.
Question a match before accepting it as a conclusion, and ask what further evidence it needs.
Ask what was said and who said it, rather than whether the statement is true, when assessing a witness's testimony.
when: Evaluating a statement from a witness
why: Attribution and wording reveal the speaker's position and hidden views, which a bare truth check misses.

text: Ask whether anything else weighed on a person's mind, and accept a flat denial as the answer rather than pressing it further.
Make a sudden request, such as borrowing money, a quest trigger that players can trace back to its cause.
Use a shared signal, such as a familiar whistled tune, to open a contact so both parties recognise each other and build rapport.
why: a shared cue creates a sense of belonging between strangers

text: Question witnesses about all visitors, not just those they consider expected or important.
Keep questioning on points relevant to the case, since off-topic questions weaken the examination.
when: when examining a witness
why: Irrelevant lines waste time and give the witness cover.

text: Ask for physical proof of claims, and when none can be produced, record that the claim cannot be checked.
Offer interview options such as a legal warning, a personal appeal and a precise follow-up question, each producing a different witness response.
when: designing witness dialogue

text: Stop pressing when continued questions would make a bystander's position worse, even if more information is still available.
In a death inquiry, ask a witness directly whether any suicidal remarks were made, and record the answer even when it is negative.
when: the cause of a death is uncertain
why: A recorded negative answer is still evidence that the question was asked

text: Let a yes-or-no oracle NPC or device narrow a name, location or code, so players reach the answer through structured questions.
Explain at the start that withholding information is risky and that what is said will be kept confidential.
when: when opening an interview
why: sets expectations for a full account

text: Use a direct question when the witness is likely to answer honestly, and reserve indirect probes for partly cooperative witnesses.
why: Indirect probes are less efficient than direct questions

text: Track each suspect's concessions as state, since pressure can lower trust or open a false-confession branch.
when: designing NPC questioning

text: Do not use indirect probing on a target who already recognises it; they will read the method as an accusation.
Ask a witness a closed question about one physical object's state at one fixed moment, and require a positive answer rather than a general account.
when: a witness's general account is clear but a specific physical state is needed

text: Separate an interview phase from a formal hearing; an NPC who denies attending the hearing leaves the interview open as a question for the player to probe.
when: designing an investigation with several stages

text: When records are silent, infer an event from surviving documents and physical traces rather than stating it as recorded.
when: A historical event has no direct documentation
why: A silent record supports inference, not a stated fact

text: Let an NPC ask probing questions and react to the player's answers, so the player's reactions become information.
when: when designing NPC dialogue that tests the player

text: Prompt a character with an object rather than a direct question, so they reveal what they recall without being forced to testify.
when: Eliciting information from a reluctant or confused character.
why: Indirect cues lower pressure, so the response shows genuine recall.

text: Chronological retelling from before the key moment suits non-practised narrators and lets order emerge; some ask every witness, yet it adds little for crisp accounts or single facts.
why: Sequence matters only when the account must be built step by step.

text: Probing questions gather evidence but can expose the investigator's interest, and a neutral inquiry can quickly turn personal. Holding back preserves secrecy at the cost of detail.
when: the investigator is hidden and the suspect is unaware
why: each option trades information against exposure

text: Closed questions reliably pin down specific facts or a precise witness but limit what is volunteered. Open questions yield fuller accounts at the cost of precision and risk losing control of a confused witness.
when: choosing a questioning style

text: Asking openly for an item reveals your role, while taking it covertly avoids that but risks discovery and delays awareness of any reaction.
when: when an item would be refused if requested openly

text: Open inquiry preserves social trust but cannot reach what covert methods uncover; splitting the work between two investigators covers both at the cost of coordination.
when: Dividing investigation methods between characters.
why: Each approach has reach and cost that the other lacks.

text: Naming a key subject early can expose a guarded witness, but it also alerts them, so later questions lose their element of surprise.
when: a probe is used on a subject who is already guarded
why: the witness adjusts their guard after the first reaction

text: Indirect questioning through a witness's interests works with talkative or trusting witnesses but yields little from guarded ones who recognise the questions.
when: choosing an interview approach
why: guarded witnesses notice what is being asked

text: Direct questions gather facts quickly but may close a witness; indirect casual conversation reveals behavior more slowly but yields more candid answers.
when: when deciding how to question a witness or household
why: direct pressure can make people withhold information they would otherwise share

text: Voicing an unusual theory risks being thought absurd, while holding it back risks losing a lead.
when: a witness holds a theory the inquiry did not ask about
why: fear of ridicule versus loss of evidence

text: A direct accusation reveals a reaction quickly but can end the exchange; a softer probe keeps talk going but reveals less.
Harsh labels a witness applies to others reveal the speaker's own values and prejudices as much as they describe the people labelled.
Showing insight into a source's identity makes them more forthcoming, though they may also become unsettled.
Accusers who blame a loss on a particular person may attack that person's house and body, for example with stones.
when: A loss is blamed on a named suspect

text: A defeated adversary who keeps leverage, such as an insurance copy of the evidence, can still threaten the protagonist after losing the object.
Keep a visible formal consequence in reserve while speaking calmly, so pressure toward candour stays credible without overt threats.
when: interrogating a suspect
why: a visible option makes refusal costly

text: In a dialogue state where a visible weapon is shown and then reassurance follows, an NPC's trust and offered options can shift, opening more answers.
why: threat followed by a promise of safety changes how the NPC weighs cooperation

text: A reprieve followed by a fresh threat keeps stakes rising, because relief that is immediately undercut sustains tension.
when: When a tense scene resolves with temporary relief
why: New threats prevent the tension from ending

text: Sympathy that is not sincere is a manipulation the subject may later recognise, which undermines the cooperation it was meant to win.
Pressing a denial harder without new evidence gets the same unchanged answers.
when: questioning a suspect who holds a fixed story

text: A repeated line can carry the weight of first-hand knowledge in the listener's mind, alarming a target who assumes the speaker knows details.
Severe penalties for witnesses can deter honest testimony as well as false testimony, so witnesses may stay silent.
why: Fear of punishment affects every witness, not only liars.

text: Statements obtained through coercion may be incomplete or shaped by fear, so they need checking.
1) Note the slip and its exact words. 2) Ask the suspect to justify it, such as by asking why they mentioned the name. 3) Compare the forced explanation against other facts.
when: Suspect has let slip a name or detail
why: A forced explanation often deepens the slip rather than covering it

text: 1) Note the specific avoidance. 2) Name it openly and calmly. 3) Ask the witness to explain their reluctance before revealing your inference. 4) Separate firsthand knowledge from assumption. 5) Check the answer against physical facts.
Harsh pressure or forced confession can close a witness off for good; note what a refusal implies, not a false answer, and press with restraint, keeping the topic open.
when: when a witness declines to discuss a subject or is fragile or protective
why: Forcing a confession can close the topic for good.

text: Do not discard a theory because of one gap, but do not accept it while unexplained gaps remain.
when: A theory has one or more clues it does not explain.
why: One gap may be a detail, but unresolved gaps indicate the theory may be wrong.

text: Holding a suspect against their will carries legal risk, and the suspect may sue for unlawful restraint.
when: An investigator locks a suspect in a room.
why: Restraint without lawful authority is a civil or criminal wrong.

text: A confident motive can be invented to fit the facts, and destroying evidence can look like concern or privacy.
when: evaluating a suspect's explanation or removal of an item
why: both can hide the real cause while appearing innocent

text: An apparent delay or hesitation by a plotter often has a risk-based cause, so ask what the actor would find safest.
when: A gap in a plotter's behavior looks odd.
why: Careful actors avoid unnecessary risk, so waiting usually has a reason.

text: Repeated passes of a figure across the same frame build rhythm; place the clue on the final pass.
when: staging a recognition
why: the rhythm primes attention for the reveal

text: A road's course may have changed, so deeds written for the old course can mislead a reader using the current route.
when: Interpreting a deed that refers to a road
why: Old descriptions no longer fit a road that has been rerouted

text: Ritual acts that look like investigation, such as burning animal parts, produce no evidence.
when: A ritual is used to identify a culprit
why: The act looks rigorous but tests nothing

text: Partners in a crime may cooperate while each suspects the other would abandon them in danger.
when: two accomplices must work together
why: Each partner's cooperation is also a reason they might betray the other.

text: Two investigators can exchange meaning through a glance, conveying understanding that a third party only partly grasps.
when: Multiple investigators question a witness together.
why: Shared context lets a brief look carry meaning without words.

text: Investigators pool information, so an officer may already know a person's background from records rather than needing to deduce it.
when: A mystery where investigators have access to records
why: Shared records can supply facts a detective would otherwise have to infer.

text: Have two staff members give partial accounts of one event, so players must compare them to find the contradiction.
Let a rival or mentor supply the final synthesis from documents, so the last step is deduction rather than combat.
when: resolving a mystery's final step
why: Deduction from documents resolves the case without requiring a confrontation.

text: Give a trusted ally a useful role in the investigation, so his presence in the case keeps him plausible as a helper and his later exposure reads as a betrayal.
why: An active role inside the case makes the ally appear trustworthy and gives him reasons to be present.

text: When the player's chosen companion changes who is present, the observations the player receives also change, because an absent character can reveal different clue text.
when: The game lets the player choose which NPC accompanies them.
why: Each present character filters what is noticed and reported.

text: A witness who is also a party to the dispute can appear neutral when they are not.
Keep an observing companion uninformed of your theory so their impressions form independently and can be compared with your own conclusions.
why: An observer's impressions lose their independent value once they have heard the investigator's theory.

text: Split investigation between the player and an NPC partner, with the partner handling covert actions.
when: Designing cooperative investigation gameplay.
why: Division of methods lets each role fit its character.

text: Agree on signals with a companion before questioning, and have them keep a record ready even while appearing inattentive.
when: Two people question one subject together.
why: Signals coordinate action, and a ready record preserves evidence without alerting the subject.

text: Give a companion NPC the role of recording a suspect's statements so the player's journal can log them for later reference.
when: Designing dialogue scenes where statements may later be disputed
why: A recorded statement can be shown as fact

text: Leaving a suspect unattended to fetch another opinion or ally gives the suspect the chance to leave, so the investigator trades control for outside help.
when: An investigator considers bringing in a second party while a suspect is present
why: An unattended suspect can depart, creating a sudden loss of the subject

text: Anomalies are often in the fringes of a scene rather than the central event, so peripheral oddities deserve close scrutiny.
Distance travelled can be estimated as fuel used divided by consumption rate, giving a check on a claimed round trip.
when: a journey claim is checked against fuel consumed
why: the estimate depends on the assumed consumption rate

text: A forecast can be far off; when the predicted time passes with no change, the state may persist for much longer than expected.
If the investigator learns the content of a destroyed message by accident, the cost of destroying it disappears.
Information given freely may be harmless, while a gatekeeper's hint may steer the player into danger; weigh each before acting.
1) State a proposed explanation. 2) List every later event it must account for. 3) Reject the explanation if any later event contradicts it.
when: an explanation fits only one moment
why: A cause must hold across the whole sequence

text: Store in-world lore fragments and documents in full so a lone fragment cannot mislead; let players find partial excerpts in rival reports, so comparing them exposes omissions.
when: Designing in-world records and rival accounts.
why: Players can detect what a partial copy hides.

text: Do not accept a mechanism that explains the main sight but leaves a smaller detail unexplained.
Record even a fruitless search, noting what was absent and where you looked, because an empty result still carries information.
After an inquiry escalates, the scope tends to widen quickly, with more warrants issued and more people accused.
when: an inquiry has just moved to a higher body

text: Keep only details tied to the central purpose of the story and leave out domestic events that do not advance it.
why: Off-purpose detail dilutes the main line

text: Common known methods of exposing a stage trick include cabinets, dark clothing, soft-soled shoes and dimmed lights.
Use searches and accusations that clear suspects as steps in the investigation rather than dead ends.
when: When a search yields nothing and the investigation must keep moving
why: A negative result still narrows the field and advances understanding.

text: Recovery of a victim can take priority over capture of culprits, so the client's stated goal can set the investigation's order of action.
when: A client's goal conflicts with pursuing the culprits
why: Immediate harm to a victim usually outweighs later capture

text: Merging the evidence-gathering stage with the later trial in memory hides where the evidence was actually built.
when: reconstructing how a case was assembled

text: 1) Split the event into ordered stages. 2) For each stage, ask when a harmful agent could realistically have been added. 3) Discard stages the victim was never alone for. 4) Discard items others consumed unharmed, unless dosed separately. 5) Test each stage against how fast symptoms appear.
when: several people could have acted and the method is known or suspected
why: Stage-by-stage checks narrow the list using access and timing

text: 1) State the first question the case must answer. 2) Settle it with evidence. 3) Pose the next question only after that answer is known.
when: Working through a large, multi-part mystery.
why: Later questions often depend on earlier answers.

text: Define a separate evidence threshold for each escalation stage, such as suspicion, detention and accusation, so the player must earn each step; skipping stages lets suspicion jump straight to conviction.
An investigator's manner, such as feigned complacency or a leading question, can mislead others about what is already believed, letting the investigator test a different theory.
when: An investigator questions a person whose belief is being tested.
why: Leading questions make a person state a belief that can then be checked against evidence.

text: An investigator may recognise a disguised person early and keep silent until the moment is right, holding knowledge back from others.
When an investigator hides their real purpose behind a feigned ailment or dismissive talk, the people being watched tend to relax their guard.
when: an investigator conceals their purpose
why: the cover story makes the investigator seem harmless

text: An investigator who withholds a solution for a personal aim adds a moral twist, because the player must judge the withholding.
when: Writing a detective whose goals diverge from justice.
why: A morally questionable choice by the investigator complicates the player's trust in the solution.

text: An investigator should check their own motives as well as the witness's, since a prior relationship can bias how a witness is trusted.
when: when the investigator has a history with someone involved

text: Investigators' own footprints can contaminate a scene, so check what they touched before attributing a trace to someone else.
when: Investigators walk over the same ground as the suspect.
why: Mixed prints make it impossible to tell whose movements left which marks.

text: Harsh or hostile confrontation gives a suspect material for counter-accusations and can shift suspicion onto the investigator, so keep manner measured.
when: Confronting a suspect who denies everything.
why: Denial plus perceived hostility turns the accuser into a target, and visible harshness supports claims that the accuser is unstable.

text: Chronology errors in the investigator's own file can send a case in the wrong direction.
An investigator's own first theory can become the suggestion that corrupts a witness's later account.
Revealing your identity and evidence can make you the target. Sending every investigator into one confrontation risks losing all evidence holders at once.
when: When the suspect may retaliate or destroy evidence after a confrontation.
why: Concentrating both knowledge and people in one exposed encounter leaves no one in reserve.

text: Investigator overreach or poor procedure can sink a case and bring a reprimand, even when the underlying evidence has some weight.
An investigator who acts on an unconfirmed report can be misled as much as a suspect, so confirm before acting.
Expected results depend on the investigator's own knowledge of how an act works, so that knowledge should be checked.
An investigator linked to the victim, who leaves a scene quickly and withholds a source, can become the prime suspect.
when: when the investigator was following the victim
why: Circumstantial links look like guilt to authorities.

text: Withholding information can make the investigator look evasive to the one person whose trust they need.
when: An investigator keeps names or facts from a companion
why: Concealment is read as distrust even when it has a purpose

text: A forbidding entrance can make an investigator more eager to press on, since pride and resistance raise commitment.
when: Access to a suspect is made difficult.
why: Obstacles can strengthen the investigator's resolve rather than deter them.

text: A test that reveals the investigator's interest can warn the wrong people, so it must appear ordinary to the subject.
when: Verifying a suspect's identity or links
why: Suspicion alerted early lets the subject or their associates adjust

text: Keep the investigator's own name out of a witness's account when it would turn the witness hostile.
An investigator may decline covert tactics such as eavesdropping and deception, leaving covert inquiry to a partner.
when: Designing investigation roles or a character's code of conduct.
why: Self-imposed limits shape which methods a case can use.

text: Mark explicitly which facts the investigator cannot disclose, so the reveal stays honest about the limits of what is known.
when: A story reveal leaves some facts unexplained or privately held.
why: A stated boundary keeps the reveal credible instead of arbitrary.

text: A disguise may draw more candid answers from wary staff, but a slip reveals the investigator and ends cooperation.
when: questioning people who distrust officials

text: Calling in an investigator fast protects the scene, while publicity around the call can make the household reluctant to consent and changes how much trust the investigator receives.
An investigator's personal bias, such as jealousy or dislike, can make a red herring against a suspect look convincing; a biased guide adds doubt beyond the evidence.
when: The investigator has a personal bias toward a suspect, or a detective guide leads the player's reasoning.
why: Emotion distorts how plausible a misleading lead appears, and a biased guide makes the player question conclusions rather than accept them unexamined.

text: Keep evidence of intent or a plan separate from evidence the act occurred; a reasoned motive account does not prove the act was done.
when: A mystery turns on whether a scheme happened, or a character's plan or reasoning sounds like a confession.
why: Documents of intent alone do not prove the act; players should notice the gap before proof of action arrives.

text: Let the investigator's first reading of people be partly wrong, so a private suspicion becomes a usable lead.
why: A mistaken but plausible suspicion drives investigation and later correction.

text: Establish an investigator's idle habits early so that a later change in behavior reads as meaningful rather than convenient.
when: The story depends on the protagonist's later close attention to ordinary things.
why: A established baseline makes a shift in attentiveness feel earned.

text: Widen the investigation timeline by requesting records from well before the crime, since the relevant date may be earlier than the event itself.
when: When a crime's origin is unclear
why: Motive and setup can predate the act by years

text: The player's expectation of a monster can be inverted by making the threat a person in a disguised state.
when: Designing a reveal that subverts a monster expectation

text: Insert a pressure event, such as an attack or threat, during the investigation to test the protagonist's resolve.
when: the investigation is gathering clues
why: Pressure forces the protagonist to act, which exposes character and advances the plot.

text: A common mystery structure makes the apparent investigator the hidden criminal, so the solver's own tools and actions steer belief away from the truth.
A case file that is also the culprit's confession reframes each entry as evidence, so the investigator is the culprit recording his own crime.
when: when the narrator of an investigation is the killer
why: Each recorded detail becomes evidence once the frame is revealed.

text: Dismissing a tight evidence chain merely for being improbable returns the investigator to where they started.
when: Evaluating a convergent body of evidence.
why: Improbability alone does not refute a chain that fits the facts.

text: Assuming the intended victim from a poisoned item's delivery route can mislead, because the route may be set up to point at the wrong target.
when: a poisoned item was delivered to one person
why: A staged delivery route can make the wrong person look like the target

text: An immobile witness who perceives everything needs a clear in-world reason for stillness, or the scene looks contrived.
when: Placing a helpless character who overhears or sees the whole scene.
why: Without a reason, the convenient vantage point breaks believability.

text: An investigator who reveals too much to a witness cannot later tell what the witness saw from what the witness was told.
when: Deciding how much theory to share during questioning
why: Shared theory becomes indistinguishable from independent observation.

text: Keep one secret in the investigator's hand, such as a hidden family link, and reveal it late through the investigator's own knowledge.
when: a mystery depends on a concealed link between characters
why: Investigator knowledge makes the late reveal feel earned

text: Casting the investigator as culprit gives a stronger twist; it works fairly only when each trusted tool appears as ordinary detail before its meaning is revealed.
when: Deciding whether the solver is the culprit, or the investigator is also a suspect.
why: A hidden tool that appears only at the reveal feels like a cheat; the reversal reuses the trust already placed in those tools.

text: Official investigators often withhold information from outside parties, treating them as interlopers, so outsiders have limited access to the case.
when: A non-official character seeks details of an ongoing investigation
why: Authorities control who learns what to protect their process

text: Let each interview name the next source, so one witness leads to another who holds further evidence.
when: Tracing a trail of witnesses

text: A local body unsure of its authority over a serious case should refer it to a higher court rather than decide it alone.
Stepping away from a conflicted case protects fairness but may look like avoidance; staying on is defensible only after honest self-examination and external checks.
when: a conflicted investigator is deciding whether to continue
why: each option trades perceived integrity against risk of bias

text: A single trace read in isolation can mislead; check normal behaviour and test each alternative explanation against other evidence before concluding.
when: When interpreting a trace or physical evidence with several possible explanations
why: Ordinary sequences can produce changes that look suspicious, and alternatives can fit one reading but fail under other checks.

text: People in lonely houses who know little of the law may never complain about mistreatment, so abuse can continue unreported.
when: When residents are isolated and have little legal knowledge
why: They lack nearby neighbours to notice and little knowledge of how to seek help.

text: Distance from neighbours and authority makes a crime less likely to be noticed or reported, so a remote location gives a perpetrator more room to act unseen.
when: When judging how easily a crime could go unnoticed in a location
why: Few people are nearby to witness events and few authorities are close enough to respond.

text: Individual records or facts look harmless or confused alone; their connections and meaning emerge only when compared against each other.
when: Reviewing individual transactions or facts in isolation
why: Single entries lack the context that a comparison supplies.

text: Suspicion gathered around an isolated group can make it look guilty of later events without direct evidence.
Judge a witness's written report by its meaning, separating the message from poor spelling.
A conclusion drawn from joined partial sources rests on the join itself, so no single fragment needs to be strong for the inference to hold.
when: Several weak sources must be combined

text: Enemy or boss cycles can be made discoverable by giving players dated journal entries or logged timestamps, so they can infer the schedule themselves.
when: Designing hidden recurring behavior in a game
why: Players find patterns only when the dates are available to compare

text: A journal entry can flag a case as the start of a longer campaign without revealing its solution.
A note stating a room and time can direct the player to a meeting spot, with wording understood only by its intended reader.
when: a clue must point to a place and moment
why: specific cues guide the player while staying opaque to others

text: An anonymous note can contain correct details of a real NPC or location that the player can confirm, while its accusations stay unproven until a separate clue supports them.
when: Designing written clues that mix verifiable facts with unverified claims.

text: A notice or message that gives a specific time and a list of items lets the player plan a response and reveals what the sender knows.
when: placing quest messages
why: Concrete details give the player an actionable plan and a clue to the sender.

text: In-game mail can carry disguised handwriting or postmarks as clues that point toward a hidden NPC.
when: designing message-based clues
why: Physical traces in messages give players a route to the sender.

text: Locations taken from later road or property records may not match the original layout.

1) List the terms as numbered items. 2) Cover duration, duties, pay, residence and required references. 3) Compare the list with what was said orally. 4) Confirm ambiguous words. 5) Judge the offer on the written terms, separately from any unease about it.
when: Evaluating an offer or agreement presented in writing
why: Written terms give a fixed basis for judgment

text: 1) Confirm who was physically present. 2) Confirm each witness could see the signer write. 3) Confirm witnesses signed in the signer's presence. 4) Judge whether the room and sight lines allow genuineness.
when: checking a signing for validity or staging
why: A formality can look complete on paper yet have been staged

text: 1) Identify the exact source text, including its edition. 2) Find each coded word from its page number, line number and word position. 3) Read the located words in order to recover the message.
when: a code is built on a known shared book

text: 1) Identify who published the record. 2) Check whether its author could be questioned. 3) Measure how widely it circulated. 4) Check whether anyone disputed its specifics at the time.
when: weighing a published account from an earlier period
why: exposure to challenge at the time signals reliability

text: Keep an objective record, such as a message log, shift bell or sensor reading, that can contradict or overturn a witness NPC's claimed account or sequence of events.
when: designing witness testimony or verifiable clues
why: Objective records let players test claims and detect false accounts.

text: Use a journal's dated entries to reveal motive and schedule, and leave its final page unfinished to create a question the player resolves elsewhere.
when: Designing a journal item as a story clue.
why: Dated entries give timelines to cross-check, and an unfinished end drives discovery.

text: A quest journal can list unresolved questions alongside candidate answers the player wrote, flagging any candidate a clue has disproven.
Store the reasoning behind a puzzle solution in a journal and unlock it at a chosen story moment.
when: the player has a puzzle solution that needs explaining
why: timed unlocks keep the reveal under designer control

text: Place a key-text code in a library book, and identify the correct edition through a previous owner's marks.
Make the correct reading of jargon in codex entries, books, or inscriptions reachable through an NPC expert, a glossary, or a consultable source.
when: in-game text uses specialist vocabulary
why: a literal reading should not be the only one available

text: Give players a journal they can compare against timestamps, so an unexplained blank period becomes visible and invites investigation.
why: Comparing records exposes gaps the player must explain.

text: Give documents a layered history with erased lines, earlier impressions and traces that a player can inspect with a tool such as a magnifier or lamp.
when: Designing readable documents as clues.
why: Layered histories reward careful inspection.

text: Notes, journals, or inscriptions can hide a second layer; compare emphasis and omissions across documents to infer what the author feared.
Use a journal or memory fragment to carry a character's rationalization as a clue the player can challenge.
when: Revealing a culprit's justification through a document.
why: A written justification gives the player something concrete to test and contradict.

text: Present an observer's log as an in-game journal with unreliable entries, and let the player check it against scene evidence.
when: designing diegetic records
why: checking a flawed record against evidence rewards player deduction

text: Present facts in a journal and let the player assemble the answer, without the game stating the conclusion outright.
when: designing a mystery that rewards deduction
why: Leaving the inference to the player makes solving it an active achievement.

text: When a culprit's own mistake, such as taking the wrong coat, leaves a material trail, the investigation can proceed without a confession or lucky break.
when: when a thief or killer escapes a crime scene
why: The physical error gives the investigator something recoverable to trace.

text: A contact who knows a market reacts to a shown object with detached knowledge rather than surprise. Their reaction reveals what they know.
when: When an expert examines an object linked to a case.
why: Genuine expertise shows as recognition, not astonishment.

text: A community leader's public statements can change how townsfolk treat a suspect.
when: When a respected leader speaks publicly about the accused or related beliefs.
why: People follow the stance of trusted leaders.

text: Showing that a writer knew the true facts does not settle guilt or innocence; competing readings of the same document can remain.
Legitimate sources of a fact include the victim, interviewed staff, the police and the press; each must be checked against the suspect's contacts.
Leading thinkers of an era can reject ideas that later became accepted, so great minds share the blind spots of their period.
Give the player a knowledgeable NPC who can confirm or reject a hypothesis, turning a guess into a quest step.
when: designing investigation quests
why: verification gives the guess a consequence

text: Reveal a fact the suspect believes you lack; a denial that conflicts with it shows their knowledge exceeds what they admit.
Knowledge of a test is itself a clue, because it narrows who could have planned a substitution.
when: when a scenario hinges on who knew about a test
why: Only people aware of the test could have prepared to defeat it.

text: Inferring knowledge from a method does not show where that knowledge came from.
when: Using a method to infer a suspect's expertise.
why: Knowing that someone had specialised knowledge does not reveal how they acquired it.

text: 1) Ask what the other side already knows before stating your own facts. 2) Withhold your own information while they speak. 3) Compare their claims with what you know.
when: when you need facts from a party without revealing your hand
why: the exchange becomes a comparison of two fact sets

text: Separate what a witness actually knows from what they hope or have persuaded themselves to believe, since protective bias and feelings are not evidence.
why: Protective bias can distort testimony, and feelings are not evidence.

text: Tag each NPC's knowledge by how it was obtained, such as seen directly, overheard or heard secondhand, and show that tag to the player.
when: Writing NPC dialogue that carries information
why: Players can then weigh claims by their source

text: Present confirmed facts separately from working theories, and keep unresolved questions open rather than auto-solving them.
when: Designing summary screens or case journals.
why: Keeps the player's model of the case accurate about what is established.

text: Once a suspect is given a label, the powers associated with that label, such as affliction or apparition, become the evidence expected and accepted.
when: A suspect is labelled and then examined in an investigation.
why: The label sets the frame in which testimony is interpreted and accepted.

text: Treating a label, such as 'maniac' or a charged term like 'spy', as an explanation of behavior adds no evidence and leads to unfounded conclusions.
when: when a testimony or observation offers a charged term
why: the label feels like an answer but adds no evidence

text: Label conclusions that go beyond the evidence as guesses, and do not present an untested hypothesis as established fact.
when: presenting a theory drawn from a physical trace
why: unverified reasoning can look certain if not labelled

text: Use labels that match the names used in the explanation, so the audience can follow each item the argument mentions.
Treat a label or brand name as a claim and check it against the contents before relying on it.
why: Labels can be wrong or shared across different products.

text: Use an accusation's chosen label as a clue, since a different label would have pointed to different evidence and a mislabelled suspect can reveal investigative bias.
when: Designing wanted posters, accusations or clue ledgers that name suspects.
why: The label shapes which evidence is sought, so the choice of label exposes the investigator's assumptions.

text: Observers tend to treat the last testimony heard as decisive, so the order of evidence can shape a verdict without any new fact.
Give the victim a partial dying message that a tool or map can complete into a place name outside the scene, rewarding attention to what was left behind.
Last-minute changes to a plan, such as a missed transport, can break an alibi or create one, so schedules must account for disruptions.
when: when an alibi depends on a planned route or meeting
why: Unplanned events alter who was where and when

text: Cluster the decisive clues late as several small facts, so suspicion cycles through earlier suspects and the final deduction gains weight.
when: structuring the final act or climax of a deduction-based mystery
why: Late clues keep earlier suspects plausible, and a dense late cluster lets the player assemble the answer.

text: Place a late cluster of clues that fit several theories at once, so the reader must choose between them.
when: Entering the final act of a mystery with competing theories.
why: Ambiguous evidence forces the reader to weigh each candidate explanation.

text: A late witness account that contradicts the accepted suspect cracks a wrong solution and reopens the case.
when: when a false solution holds the story
why: A contradiction from a witness exposes the gap in the accepted explanation.

text: Stage a confession letter as a late cluster that rewards the player for solving the room before an NPC confirms it.
A later stop or cancellation order can reverse an earlier assumed sponsorship, revealing that the party the reader trusted quietly halted the plot.
Investigations fail from missing the moment evidence is available, not from lacking it; traces degrade or become unreadable, so late discovery may arrive too late.
when: An investigation stalls despite evidence existing
why: Traces can be lost or cease to be readable after a limited time; hidden evidence may lose value before it is found.

text: Search where the sought item is least expected and in less-searched, out-of-the-way places, since evidence often turns up where it was not anticipated; treat such finds as serious leads.
when: a case hinges on one item whose origin is still open
why: out-of-the-way locations are less searched and may hold overlooked evidence

text: A visitor arriving at an unexpected hour can shift the scene without warning.
Recover physical proof late from the suspect's own belongings, so the confirmation comes from evidence that is hard to explain away.
why: Evidence found among the suspect's possessions is difficult to dismiss and rewards late investigation.

text: Introducing a critical fact, decisive clue or new person only at the reveal or climax feels arbitrary and cheats, since the audience cannot check it against earlier clues.
why: The audience cannot check it against anything shown earlier and could not have reached the answer from what it saw.

text: A count taken after an item has left its owner's control cannot establish a baseline for a dispute.
Narrative pressure from a locked room feels unfair when the key's whereabouts are unclear.
Evidence gathered late and in poor light is partial, and once disposed of by others it cannot be recovered.
Plan a late independent confirmation, such as a confession or confirmed record, that tests the player's deduction from public sources, rewarding fair reasoning.
Converge decisive documents and physical proof into one tight late cluster, supported by everything already seen, so each remaining alternative falls at once.
when: at a mystery's climax, once the player has accepted a different culprit
why: Clustered failed claims change belief at once, giving the strongest reversal and leaving no open threads.

text: A sudden noise or fearful NPC reaction can trigger a search task whose outcome stays uncertain until it is checked.
when: when designing reactive events for players
why: Uncertain outcomes keep players investigating rather than assuming.

text: Reveal a detail the suspect did not expect to open a new line of questioning, rewarding players for collecting clues.
Introduce a final, decisive clue without comment so it is noticed only when the explanation arrives.
why: an uncommented clue invites the audience to reread it after the reveal

text: Scrutinize testimony given long after events, especially under custody or mainly to sway an audience, by checking independent corroboration before using it as proof.
when: A witness's account changes, first appears after a long delay, or is admitted mainly to persuade.
why: Late recall can be sincere yet unreliable; time and persuasive intent distort memory, and corroboration separates reliable accounts from distorted ones.

text: A targeted lab analysis for an unconsidered substance can overturn a settled explanation and change the meaning of the whole case.
when: A natural cause is accepted but circumstances remain unexplained.
why: A specific test can reveal a hidden cause that earlier evidence missed.

text: Key test questions are often asked too late; ask questions that could eliminate hypotheses early.
Let a non-player character remember new details after a trigger, but only if the detail is consistent with recorded events the player can check.
when: Designing NPC memory reveals.
why: Checkable consistency keeps new recollections fair and meaningful.

text: Check whether a later clause cancels an earlier disclaimer, such as admitting that evidence could still be received and acted on.
when: A passage opens with a disclaimer.
why: Later admissions can override the disclaimer.

text: 1) Give each listener a cover story shaped to their role. 2) Keep the stories consistent with each other. 3) Set timing so no one can check the absence before the window closes.
when: when a character must be unaccounted for during a window of time
why: Each witness confirms only part of the picture, so the whole story holds.

text: Separate eye-catching disguise features from hard-to-fake features so that players checking only obvious traits are fooled while careful players can catch the lie.
when: when designing disguise detection challenges

text: A layered misdirection presents one clue under successive readings, each backed by a different authority, before its true origin is revealed.
Place the central fact late, and let it turn a distant threat into a present one, so the stronger fact changes the reader's sense of danger.
when: A mystery needs a climax that raises stakes.
why: Late, close-to-home facts carry more weight than early, abstract ones.

text: Layer two plots: a small, quickly solved crime, and a larger planned one that the solution exposes, with the minor culprit as a frightened accomplice whose weak motive leaves the mastermind open.
when: Designing a mystery with more than one crime.
why: The second layer gives players a reason to keep investigating after the first is solved.

text: Two linked misdirections can be undone together when one second witness and one physical object reframe both at the same time.
When a captured thief's identity reveals a worse crime than the initial theft, the stakes of the chase rise and the quest moves from theft to murder.
when: a pursuit follows a robbery and the captive's past is revealed
why: The reframed crime raises the threat level and the reader's investment after the apparent resolution.

text: Stacking a reconstructed impostor, a false alibi and a later confession keeps a reveal fair when each explanation is physically grounded and overturns the last.
Reversing the roles of investigator and criminal, so trusted detectives are exposed as culprits, recasts every earlier scene once the masked leader is unmasked.
when: Designing a late twist that overturns the reader's trust in the investigators.
why: Earlier scenes are re-read with the new identities, so their evidence seems to have pointed to the truth all along.

text: A layered reveal moves through setup clues, disguise hints, a false trail, a false conclusion, a documentary link, a confession and a late reveal.
when: designing a multi-stage twist in a story or investigation
why: each stage builds on clues the audience already holds

text: A layered reveal stacks false solutions so each reveal reframes the one before, moving blame between suspects and finally to whether a crime happened at all.
A layered identity reveal peels back a hidden antagonist in steps, each exposing a more trusted figure, so the final reveal lands on the character the audience trusted most.
when: designing a mystery with a hidden antagonist who may be a trusted ally
why: Each layer reuses audience trust as cover for the next

text: A layered mystery runs in phases: fixed evidence, several false solutions each undone by a counter-source, a late reversal cluster, then reconciliation of partly true solutions.
1) Clear the innocent suspects first. 2) Confirm the evidence matches. 3) Explain the mechanism of the crime. 4) Name the culprit last.
when: Building a climactic accusation after the evidence is laid out.
why: Ordered layering lets the audience accept each step before the final naming.

text: 1) Let one character confess a lesser crime. 2) Use the confession to reopen a solved case. 3) Reveal a second culprit whose role reframes the earlier map.
when: Designing a climax that should change the player's understanding of the whole level
why: Layered revelations keep the player re-evaluating after apparent closure.

text: 1) Introduce a plausible but wrong culprit with physical links. 2) Let investigators build a case, then have them admit it is weak. 3) Replace it with a second suspect whose evidence seems stronger. 4) Break that reading with a physical test.
when: Mystery plots that need suspicion to move several times before the real answer.
why: Each false solution that is disproved raises confidence in the eventual solution.

text: 1) Confront the culprit with witness testimony. 2) Put physical evidence on the table. 3) Let the culprit confess. 4) Have the investigators explain how they reached the answer.
why: Several independent confirmations make the reveal feel complete.

text: Place the decisive reversal near the end so a sudden late event breaks the closing belief; guilt reassignment surprises once each earlier correction is accepted as truth.
when: planning the climax of a mystery
why: A late shock overturns the audience's settled conclusion, and the reversal works only when earlier corrections were accepted as truth.

text: Open layouts with little room to conceal a person narrow the hiding places available in a small setting.
when: A bounded setting has open sightlines and few enclosed spaces.
why: Visibility limits where a person can stay unseen, making remaining hiding spots finite and checkable.

text: Layout shows only what was possible, not what happened, so it cannot replace witness testimony.
The layout of doors, gardens, alleys and rooms holds evidence about how a person could be reached, watched or taken.
Question a suspect about the layout a crime required, so the answers test whether they could have acted.
when: checking a suspect's plausibility
why: Describing the scene reveals whether the suspect knows its details.

text: Map a scene's layout for access routes, such as balconies, windows and drops, to see how someone could reach a room.
when: A crime method depends on reaching a particular room.

text: Boundaries described by landmarks such as trees, stumps, pens, bridges, roads or lines drift or become disputed when a landmark moves or the description is vague, becoming hard to relocate.
when: when a boundary is defined by physical markers
why: landmarks are not permanent and their positions drift

text: A room arranged to attract paying guests may reflect the landlord's intent rather than the occupant's own taste.
A rearrangement that explains the layout can still hide the true cause, so keep testing after it fits.
Assuming a building's later appearance matches its use at the time of the events can mislead a location check.
1) Locate the scene on a large-scale map. 2) Mark neighbouring sites and points of interest within a set radius. 3) Note distances to the nearest dwellings and how isolated the site is.
when: when a site is remote and a map is available before any visit
why: Study can happen before a visit and shows which people could have witnessed events.

text: 1) Collect every reference to the person. 2) Order them by date. 3) State what each shows and what it does not show. 4) Mark where the trail ends.
when: A person vanishes and leaves no final record
why: Scattered fragments reveal a last likely sighting only when ordered and bounded explicitly.

text: Before an overhearing scene, establish the layout constraint that keeps the listener in place, such as a single exit through the room.
when: a character must overhear a secret
why: otherwise the audience asks why the listener did not leave

text: A question that presumes an answer, such as guilt, steers replies to follow the premise and the investigator's view before evidence is checked.
when: questioning that assumes an answer
why: The framing of a question supplies the shape of the answer; assumed answers bias what the investigator sees.

text: Agreement with a suggested name, event or version is not independent confirmation; the witness may simply follow the question's wording.
when: the questioner offers a candidate name or event, or a suggestible witness with uncertain memory is asked a question carrying the expected answer
why: Suggestible witnesses may adopt the questioner's version rather than recall their own; agreement is easy when the question supplies the answer.

text: Witnesses who hear a theory or are shown where to look may report matching features, so findings can reflect suggestion rather than the actual body or event.
when: a witness hears a theory or others' guesses first, or observers are directed to a body area or object
why: Expectation and suggestion shape what people think they saw and how they describe it.

text: Pressing a witness with suggestion can harden a vague recollection into a firm fact and inflate confidence; a later near-certain claim may reflect the suggestion, not new recall.
when: when the witness is uncertain or the interviewer's suggestions are not recorded
why: Suggestion shapes answers and inflates apparent confidence.

text: Do not embed an assumed answer, desired content or conclusion in a question; ask what the witness saw, since the wording removes innocent or true answers.
when: Framing a question to a witness.
why: A leading question tells the witness what to confirm, weakening testimony so the answer reflects the question rather than the events.

text: A witness with a partial view and an unclear memory can be led to a new reading of events by a plausible alternative explanation.
when: the witness is unsure of what they saw
why: A suggestion can replace a vague memory rather than refine it.

text: Questions put in front of others can shape a witness's answer, and objections from an adult can signal that the account has been influenced.
when: A young or suggestible witness is questioned in a group
why: The witness takes cues from the questioner and the audience

text: Questions that presuppose details the witness never observed invite invented answers or collapse under pressure, especially from elderly or eager witnesses.
when: Questions assume an unobserved fact such as appearance or clothing
why: Witnesses feel pressure to answer rather than admit ignorance

text: A person with no prior suspicion can settle on a specific neighbor after hearing vague, fated claims from an outside visitor.
when: When an anxious person hears general, ominous statements from a stranger.
why: Vague claims invite the listener to fill in a named target.

text: A witness who is asked a leading question and then agrees with the offered wording tends to adopt that wording as their own recollection.
when: An investigator supplies a term before the witness describes what they saw
why: The sense of being understood makes the witness accept suggested language.

text: A leading question is one whose wording carries content, such as a name or trait, that the witness may then repeat back instead of recalling.
A witness who insists on a direction, vouches for an associate or volunteers an outside suspect may be steering attention; test the claim before acting on it.
when: a witness pushes the investigator toward a place or person
why: a decoy can send investigators away from the real answer

text: Question a witness step by step, through small concrete questions, to recover precise details that a broad question misses.
After a refusal, shift to a shared task to keep access to the witness open.
A dramatic word or familiar outside group that explains a case too neatly should be tested against physical facts before it is accepted.
when: an explanation fits the case suspiciously well
why: suggestive words and known groups can absorb attention and hide the real mechanism

text: When a lead proves false, ask who shaped the search toward it.
Point a searcher toward an ordinary explanation and withhold the anomaly, so the search appears to confirm the ordinary account.
when: A suspect or NPC is conducting a search that could expose the investigator's knowledge.
why: A search that seems to confirm a mundane answer ends further scrutiny.

text: Digressions cost time, so steer a witness back to the point when the story wanders.
Offering a specific detail to investigators can steer them toward a test that leads to a dead end.
A non-player character who accuses under suggestion can serve as a plot device, letting the player discover who planted the idea.
when: When designing an NPC whose accusation should trace back to another character.
why: Revealing the source of a suggestion creates a discovery beat.

text: Pressing an NPC with leading questions lowers the confidence of its testimony, so its later claims should be weighed less.
why: Suggestion weakens the reliability of what is then reported.

text: A character can be sent to a location someone else selected by a plausible reason for not going there themselves, so they go alone.
when: Directing a character to a place without appearing to control them.
why: A stated constraint on the director makes the redirected character the only one who can go.

text: Leading questions, such as 'was it right?', can plant answers or conclusions the witness never observed, knew or reached, so replies echo framing even without harmful intent.
why: Suggested content is absorbed into the witness's account and mistaken for knowledge.

text: Repeating a suggestion or filling memory gaps about unclear details can produce confident false memories that are reported as observed facts.
when: questioning a witness about details they did not clearly see
why: Suggested details are absorbed into memory and then reported as observed facts.

text: Leading questions can make a witness confirm the investigator's theory or identification, so answers must be tested against independent facts before they are accepted.
when: when questioning a witness with a fixed theory, or when confirming a witness's identification
why: Suggested answers can be mistaken for true ones; the questioner's framing can make a weak claim look settled.

text: A leading question can plant a detail, so a witness's later report of that detail may reflect the question rather than memory.
when: the questioner names a detail before the witness has mentioned it
why: witnesses may adopt details suggested to them

text: Suggesting a gender, identity, or size to a witness can plant a belief that the witness then adopts as their own memory.
when: when asking about a figure the witness only partly saw
why: witnesses under stress tend to accept supplied details

text: A leading question can plant the answer it seeks, so the phrasing of key questions needs care.
A numbered list of suggestive items can look stronger than it is, so hedged wording should mark how far each item actually supports the conclusion.
when: presenting several weak indications
why: list formatting implies equal weight

text: Leading questions can plant answers in the witness; keep answers her own rather than shaped by hints, and ask questions whose implication she may not notice.
Rapid, leading or harsh questioning can produce the answer the questioner wants, or make an honest witness look evasive.
A sick or sedated witness may agree to whatever is suggested, so confirm key facts with independent records.
Ignoring that a claimant may be steering the witness toward a desired answer.
when: When assessing testimony obtained through a motivated intermediary.
why: A party with a stake can shape what a witness reports.

text: Asking a leading question, such as about a specific habit, can shape the answer the subject gives.
when: Questioning someone about a possible cause of a physical sign.
why: A suggested answer can steer a subject toward confirming it.

text: 1) Ask open, neutral questions first, since leading questions confirm a client's assumption instead of testing it. 2) Only then put the suggested answer and test whether the witness confirms or rejects it.
why: a leading question can make a witness simply agree

text: 1) Open with a formal, neutral request. 2) Press with pointed questions when answers are evasive or minimal. 3) Watch the witness's colour, speech and posture. 4) Use deliberate provocation sparingly to test whether a reaction is genuine, and note any refusal to answer.
when: a guarded witness has specific facts to test
why: escalating in stages reveals genuine reactions before the investigator risks losing control

text: 1) Open with a calm, general question and let the witness talk. 2) Narrow to specific points such as visitors or sounds. 3) Test claims against a physical fact. 4) Note changes in posture, tone or repeated lines. 5) Follow any unexpected remark with the next question.
when: When questioning a cooperative witness who may hold back or minimise.

text: 1) Open with easy factual questions that fix a baseline. 2) Re-ask a key point in a different form to test the account. 3) Ask the sensitive question casually. 4) Watch for small changes in expression. 5) Follow brief remarks with narrower questions.
when: interviewing a witness about a sensitive matter
why: routine answers fix a baseline, so deviations stand out

text: 1) Ask when the witness last saw a key object. 2) Ask where they went. 3) Ask when they last saw a key person. 4) Ask about background concerns that may explain their actions.
when: when a witness's movements and contacts must be reconstructed
why: staged questions build a fixed sequence of events

text: 1) Have the witness recall the day's events in order. 2) Anchor the recall with facts already known. 3) Ask the essential question only once the familiar account is secure. 4) If refused, state the consequence of silence.
when: witness is weak, fading or emotionally tied to the suspect
why: familiar material builds recall before the critical question is reached

text: Calm a shaken witness by asking a concrete question about a physical object they carry, giving the conversation a fixed point.
why: a physical object anchors attention and restores composure

text: Stop the interview when a weakened witness becomes agitated; pressing on yields unreliable answers.
Give a low-status NPC a plausible motive to steer the player toward them, then supply a clue that clears them.
when: designing a suspect for a mystery
why: A plausible motive makes the detour convincing; the clue makes it fair.

text: A torn-out cheque leaves its stub blank, because the amount was written on the removed leaf rather than the stub.
A bank account acts as a compressed record of movements, since a payment shows where money went and can identify a connected person.
why: Financial transactions expose relationships and destinations

text: A pale line added after a finished letter suggests the writer returned to the page later rather than writing in one burst.
why: a second writing session leaves a distinct mark

text: A bearer instrument is payable to whoever presents it, so possession alone allows money to be collected.
Charge-waiver thresholds on absent days turn a per-day billing ledger into a timeline of a guest's absence.
when: a hotel or service waives charges after a set number of days away
why: Billed and waived days record when the guest was not present.

text: Use this check when a claim rests on a recomputable number, scientific principle or observer viewpoint; it is weak if the checker lacks reference knowledge.
In a ledger most entries are routine, so an entry whose amount breaks the pattern stands out as a clue.
Dated merchant or guild ledgers can tie an NPC's employment or payroll to the moment of a theft.
when: when designing guild or merchant records for a mystery
why: Dated records connect people to events in time.

text: Treat a mismatch between a shipping receipt and actual arrival as evidence, not clerical error.
A later document can override an earlier one, so the outcome may depend on which paper a court accepts.
when: Two documents with different terms compete.
why: Later transfers or deeds may reflect a more recent or more valid decision.

text: A late document that contradicts an earlier court ruling can signal a settled grievance, but that reading is an interpretation, not proof of motive.
when: A character's final will or letter defies a legal outcome.

text: Ledgers, bills and sudden withdrawals can show who has been paid and when, so check them against other evidence.
when: when investigating hush money or a motive tied to finances
why: Financial trails record transfers that a witness may not reveal.

text: A late annotation added to a document can change how the earlier text reads, producing a twist at the end.
A player-facing ledger of payments shows which NPCs have been paid, giving clues about who is under pressure and who might talk.
when: when the player can track bribes or payments made to NPCs
why: Visible payment history reveals both pressure points and loyalty risks.

text: The size of a court bond gives a rough measure of how large a person's personal estate was.
when: estimating personal wealth from probate records
why: A bond is set relative to the estate's value.

text: Later-written sources can place events at dates the records do not allow, or compress and misplace them, so treat their dates as claims to check even when aligned across sources.
why: Later accounts may compress or misplace events.

text: Reading an inheritance only for totals and missing the survivorship clause leads to wrong conclusions about who gains from each death.
when: when analyzing a will or contract that shifts shares
why: the clause that changes shares as people die is easy to overlook

text: A ledger records costs, not causes, so reading it as a complete account of an event overstates what it shows.
Later additions and repairs change a building's appearance, so separate original fabric from later alterations before dating it.
A name written later in a different hand reflects a later reader's belief, not the original author.
A later public repudiation of an earlier role does not erase that role; the earlier participation stays open to judgment.
when: a participant later disavows past actions
why: a late change of stance is not a full cleanup of the record

text: 1) Ask for a relevant independent record, such as a ledger, catalogue or sale record. 2) Read its entries closely. 3) Note which entries support and which contradict the witness's account.
when: when a witness's means or behavior can be documented, or a verbal account can be compared to ledgers, catalogues or sale records
why: Long-running records are costly to alter consistently; records can confirm or refute claims.

text: 1) Take the claimed distance or size. 2) Divide it by the stated magnifying power or scale factor. 3) Compare the result with what an observer could actually resolve.
when: a claim rests on a number that can be recomputed

text: 1) Find the document that sets a financial motive. 2) Recalculate its value under current conditions. 3) Use the recalculated figure, not the original, to judge motive.
when: A suspect's motive rests on income or property.
why: Market or price changes can shift a payout far from its nominal figure.

text: Read each receipt item for what it shows about time, place, money and the kind of establishment, not only whether it matches what you searched for.
