Design unexplained transfers and matching amounts between NPC payment logs to reveal hidden payments and relationships, rewarding players who compare ledgers.
when: Designing financial clues in a game.
why: Unexplained entries invite the player to trace hidden flows.

text: A late reveal that clears an earlier suspect should force the player to update their notes and assumptions.
when: designing mid to late reversals
why: revised assumptions keep the reveal meaningful

text: Use a late document or epilogue to explain the full plot logic and show why earlier red herrings misled, once the audience has the whole picture.
why: hindsight makes earlier misdirection visible

text: Log each item's handover in a shop or guild ledger so players can reconstruct where an object went.
Let a later recorded entry contradict an NPC's earlier statement or action, so players can expose it by laying out the calendar.
when: Designing a mystery with contradicted testimony.

text: Officials may protect powerful parties' arrangements, and examiners can be pressured or bribed, so inconvenient findings get stalled, which shapes whose account is accepted; secure the original report.
when: An investigation touches a wealthy or powerful party, or findings are inconvenient to them.
why: Institutional incentives favour the influential; examiner methods and records determine how far a finding can be trusted.

text: Endorsement by a respected expert or leader gives an unverified claim or accuser's story weight, so audiences accept it without checking the evidence.
when: When a respected leader or persuasive expert endorses a claim in front of an audience.
why: Public standing or demonstrated skill substitutes for independent verification.

text: Do not accept an official's verdict because of rank or claimed competence; check who judged, how, and the evidence; overturn it with harder evidence, not rank.
when: When an earlier official judgment about a person is used as settled fact.
why: A self-described authority may be biased or mistaken.

text: Accepting a satisfying reconstruction or an arrest as the end of inquiry leaves unexplained gaps and alternative explanations unexamined.
when: A plausible story is offered in a formal setting, or a suspect has been arrested.
why: A satisfying story or arrest reduces the appetite to question further, creating a false sense the matter is closed.

text: Pressure from a superior for a quick answer can make an investigator vouch for a suspect and say reassuring things he does not believe.
when: a senior figure demands closure
why: external demands shape statements independent of evidence

text: In an interview, a senior person's dismissive remark can end a junior's protest, showing who controls the room.
when: a protest is raised during questioning

text: A nuncupative will is a spoken will, declared orally rather than written, offered in place of a written one to show a person's wishes.
Two situations are recognised exceptions to the need for material proof: a suspect caught in the act, and a suspect who confesses.
when: deciding whether an accusation can stand on inference alone
why: these are the named cases where proof is not required

text: Without formal authority, investigators may only watch, and the required approval can arrive too late to act.
Props signaling authority, such as a card, uniform, sash, or fur coat, can command trust and make a target hand over valuables.
when: A con relies on the victim accepting a claimed identity.
why: Visible markers of rank short-circuit careful verification.

text: Authorities may withhold information without giving a reason, so their silence on a lead does not prove the lead is worthless.
Objects bearing the searcher's own address show that the other party already knows where to find the searcher.
when: when a found item carries the searcher's details
why: Such items reveal the opponent's knowledge of them.

text: A person can decline a role on a record because signing under their own name would make them legally responsible for it.
why: Legal duties attach to the name written on a document.

text: Remind a witness they are under oath before key questions, which changes the stakes of every answer they give.
when: when questioning a witness whose answers matter for the case
why: Awareness of a formal obligation raises the weight of each answer

text: A weaker side in a formal dispute can survive by following each procedural step exactly, leaving the stronger side no valid ground to override it.
when: formal rules govern the dispute
why: strict compliance removes grounds for dismissal

text: Letting the player examine a corpse for expression, smell and blood, with each observation ruling causes in or out, makes examination a reasoning step.
when: Designing a body-examination interaction
why: Each observable narrows the candidate causes of death

text: An official diagnosis that implies hidden agents nearby sets the frame, so accusers are primed to find suspects matching that premise.
why: The accepted explanation determines which targets seem plausible.

text: Confessions take on a common shape when examiners supply it: a yes to a leading question is expanded by the questioner into a full narrative the accused did not originate.
when: Questioners ask leading yes-or-no questions and then elaborate the answer.
why: The accused adopts the framing offered, so independent detail is missing.

text: Signs from examination may reflect the examiner's assumptions or methods, which subjects echo back; judge each sign by whether the examiner could have caused it.
when: When a suspect's behaviour or answers are observed during questioning.
why: Subjects may simply give the examiner what it expects; interrogation methods can produce the reactions they appear to reveal.

text: Searches justified as diligence can still reach private property and damage trust, so respect propriety and record every search step carefully.
Authority does not validate a method; arguments from appeals to authority or principle are only as strong as their sources, and results may depend on facts unrelated to the question.
when: When evaluating a written argument or the validity of a test.
why: Status is mistaken for verification.

text: A general attack on institutions can replace argument about the evidence, so keep criticism of sources separate from examination of the claim.
Forcing an unusual exception to a rule draws attention to it, so the request must be prepared in advance to avoid being noticed.
when: An exception is needed to bypass a protective rule
why: Unusual requests stand out to those who watch the routine

text: A stated refusal to use covert methods can weaken under urgency, and self-imposed limits can slow progress.
when: A character's principles meet high stakes.
why: Pressure erodes early commitments and restrictions cost time.

text: Authority figures who treat a prisoner's silence or repeated denials as proof of guilt will ignore the true explanation unless the player corrects the record.
when: An NPC authority interprets a silent or denying suspect.
why: Prisoners' claims of innocence are assumed routine, so their silence gets read as confirmation.

text: A sincere-sounding oath of innocence proves nothing about the act it denies, and it can be delivered as a performance.
when: A suspect ends a confrontation with a solemn declaration.
why: Staged emotion can persuade listeners without providing evidence.

text: Keeping outside authorities out of a scene removes an independent check on the evidence.
when: A scene's evidence is interpreted by only the investigating party.
why: Without an outside check, errors and bias go uncorrected.

text: A search depends on control of the subject and fails once the subject can act or others may interrupt.
when: when planning a search
why: Control is the precondition for the procedure.

text: A respected figure's later account can contradict his own earlier record, so authority does not replace checking statements against the record.
when: When a prominent witness gives a revised version years later.
why: Status makes a changed story seem credible without comparison.

text: Missing official roles, such as who drew up a warrant or order, cannot be filled in by assumption.
why: Unsupported role attribution produces false conclusions about responsibility.

text: A permission granted for one purpose, such as opening an inquiry, is easily stretched to decide the case once a suspect is named.
why: Once a suspect is named, the limit on use is easily forgotten.

text: A legal rule explained only once may be forgotten before it matters, so it should be reinforced or planted early and reused.
when: A rule the player needs later is taught in passing.
why: Players forget one-time exposition before its payoff.

text: 1) Brief authorities in advance with names, locations and weapons. 2) On arrival, present suspects and exhibits. 3) Name each exhibit and state each suspect's role.
when: when handing a solved case to outside authorities
why: Prepared handover lets authorities act at once.

text: 1) Disarm the subject first. 2) Check coat and body for other concealed items. 3) Empty every pocket onto one surface. 4) Examine each item patiently. 5) Open containers to check for hidden compartments. 6) Check the subject's pulse before continuing.
when: when a person is subdued and a search is allowed
why: A fixed order avoids missing items and protects the subject's safety.

text: 1) Mark sections omitted from the excerpt. 2) Compare the wording with a complete copy to find unmarked edits. 3) Locate a full text. 4) Separate quotation from paraphrase. 5) Date the citing text against the author's changing purpose.
when: A retelling is the main surviving version of a document or its author had a stake in it
why: Excerpts can silently drop, alter or reframe content

text: Treat confident claims from authorities or the press as hypotheses to test; confidence resting on someone else's word is not direct evidence.
when: A conclusion is supported only by someone else's word.
why: Trust in the source is mistaken for proof.

text: Confirm a rumour with an authority that has standing; a legal check can turn an opinion into a finding or show it has no basis.
Confirm the right to search before forcing a locked space, because entry without authority can damage the case.
when: evidence may be concealed in a locked room
why: Improperly obtained evidence can be rejected or weakened.

text: Let authority NPCs turn on the player based on observed actions, requiring new evidence to clear the name.
when: when designing a suspicion system
why: Observed actions drive suspicion.

text: The evidence required for a capital charge must be as strong as for any other capital crime, with no lower threshold because the crime is unusual.
when: when a charge is exceptional, hidden or hard to observe
why: Lowering the standard lets unusual crimes convict on weaker proof.

text: State the governing legal standard early, then make each later clue a test of that standard.
when: Structuring a sequence of accusation-driven scenes.
why: A standard set up front gives the player something concrete to check each piece of evidence against.

text: Removing a suspect to search can expose the investigator to later legal questions about how the search was conducted.
when: An investigator searches while a suspect is removed.
why: Improper searches can have consequences beyond the immediate scene.

text: A fast, thorough physical search finds concealed items quickly but can cause real distress; privacy and consent may matter more than speed.
when: when deciding whether to search a person
why: Speed gains are paid for with the subject's distress.

text: An unrepresented party in a formal process may be out-manoeuvred by opposing counsel, who knows procedure and can respond to surprises.
when: A party acts alone in a formal or procedural setting.
why: Unfamiliarity with procedure leaves the party exposed to a more practised opponent.

text: A suspect's explanation that cannot be checked is read by the system as evasion and as proof of guilt, keeping the case closed.
when: A suspect offers an explanation the investigation does not pursue.
why: Without checking the source, the system has no reason to accept the explanation.

text: Compare the terms offered to two people, such as pay, since a difference between them can hint at differing motives worth investigating.
when: when two people with a shared link receive different terms
why: Unequal terms can reflect different interests or stakes.

text: A reveal lands when the wrong suspect was shown every incriminating fact but no exonerating one, so the player never had grounds to clear them.
A vigil case has the investigator stay in a haunted place, watch an apparently supernatural presence act, then find a physical or human mechanism behind it.
Using unlawful methods carries a cost to the investigator that must be weighed before acting.
Vague answers such as 'usually' or 'I did not look' leave gaps that independent evidence must fill.
when: A key holder gives non-specific answers about custody.
why: Vague statements cannot establish access on their own.

text: An insufficient-proof or reasonable-doubt acquittal frees the accused without clearing their name; a defamation verdict likewise leaves suspicion, and both verdict and doubt can be recorded.
why: Doubt about guilt is weaker than a finding of innocence

text: A prosecutor who values a clean record will drop a doubtful case rather than risk losing it, and will accept one conviction over a tangled multi-defendant trial.
when: when deciding whether to pursue a messy case
why: clean outcomes protect the record

text: Official proceedings can omit the investigator's evidence, so the player's knowledge may outpace the court's.
when: when designing an official resolution
why: Institutional limits can leave the truth known to the player but unresolved in the world.

text: An intent-based offence is defined by a malicious intention or an allegiance, so guilt can rest on proving that link without showing any harmful act.
A pledged object usually carries a set term after which its owner may redeem it, creating a predictable date.
A person can be legally accountable for a loss, such as missing property, while not being morally responsible for it.
An inquest can return an accident verdict, a self-infliction verdict, a deliberate homicide verdict, or an open verdict when the evidence is insufficient.
when: When a death inquiry must record a finding.
why: Verdict categories let the inquest distinguish cause from proof of means.

text: Related legal acts, such as a power of attorney and a will, differ in meaning, so confusing them changes what a visit implies.
A correct clue can appear wrong when it omits a procedural detail, such as the direction to turn a dial first.
when: An attempt based on a partial instruction fails.
why: The missing step makes a valid sequence look invalid.

text: A formal inquest asks narrow questions and rarely invites a witness's own theories about the cause.
Disputes that run through formal rules over testimony and convening can be decided by procedure, not only by which side holds the stronger position.
when: a conflict is governed by formal rules on who may testify or convene
why: rule compliance can outweigh a weaker side's position

text: A rule that a harmful agent may appear in an innocent person's shape removes innocence as a defense.
why: Appearance becomes evidence the accused cannot disprove.

text: A defendant who pleads not guilty puts themselves on trial, so the case moves toward a verdict.
A rule can make a case legally valid without establishing the underlying fact that the act could cause the harm alleged.
Ask who actually sent an inquiry, not just who it was attributed to, since a rival usually sends their own agents.
when: an inquiry has been traced to a feared person
why: the sender may be someone else

text: Infer how an item was processed by reasoning about normal handling, such as whether a laundry would starch it, to judge its origin.
when: An ordinary item is found in an unusual state
why: Normal treatment practices show whether the item came from a usual source

text: An arrest dialogue can record the player's exact words so they have consequences later.
Opposition to a faction that has long dominated a community adds a political motive to accusations against its opponents.
Check whether a tribunal was formed through normal legal channels, since a special body set up without usual representation may lack lawful authority.
when: a special court handles a case

text: Separate condemning unjust statutes from blaming officials who were bound to apply them.
when: assessing officials who enforced harsh laws

text: Test an explanation by asking whether it would change if the accused were innocent; if not, it cannot be checked.
when: Evaluating an accusation or deduction
why: An explanation that stays the same either way gives no evidence.

text: Build a kangaroo-court encounter where one NPC is judge, prosecutor and jailer, so players must find an outside authority to get a hearing.
when: Designing corrupt legal encounters.
why: Concentrated roles force players to seek an external check.

text: Pair an intent-only law with a clue showing the intent was never real, so players can challenge the verdict.
when: Designing in-world law for a game

text: Weigh irreversible penalties more cautiously: a guilty person left alive can be judged later, while an executed innocent person cannot be restored.
when: when a verdict cannot be reversed
why: errors that cannot be corrected justify more caution

text: Each arrest or unresolved hearing produces new accusers, so a single entry point can escalate within days into dozens of arrests.
Procedures with built-in waiting times, such as clearing a cheque between banks, delay outcomes, so a pending status can be inferred from when the process began.
why: The waiting period means the result is not yet settled at the time of the action.

text: A framer who aims for arrest rather than conviction expects a weak trial to leave the suspect exposed and easier to pressure.
when: A frame is designed to be used after a failed case
why: A flawed case still weakens the suspect's position

text: A procedural delay before a reveal builds tension only when it is tied to the stakes; otherwise it deflates tension.
A legal rule about inheritance or residence can turn a grievance into a practical plan by deciding who gains and who must stay.
when: when a motive depends on property or living arrangements
why: Rules set the conditions under which a resentment becomes an actionable option.

text: A procedural motion can defer a question for a set period, so the matter is neither closed nor pursued.
why: the deferral suspends the issue without resolving it

text: A decree that favors one group over an earlier settlement can seed a grudge that outlasts the lawsuits and resurfaces in later disputes.
when: when an authority reassigns land already settled by others
why: the displaced party keeps the unresolved loss in memory

text: When power shifts between factions, members of the losing side may be endangered, exiled or ruined.
A new decree that redefines a crime can reverse which characters count as guilty, so players must notice and track the change.
Rebuking juries that depart from public mood pushes verdicts toward crowd opinion rather than the evidence.
When accused people must pay board, jailer's fees and court costs before release, the process gives officials and creditors financial stakes in seizing property.
A procedural condition, such as a witness being unable to testify in the accused's presence, can control how fast a proceeding moves.
An indictment has four parts: the accused, a place and trade, the act, and the statutory consequence.
Estimating a natural process's duration from general experience can mislead when local conditions differ from the usual case.
Repeated withholding with no payoff frustrates the audience, so deferred questions must eventually be resolved.
when: Pacing a long mystery with multiple deferrals.
why: Endless postponement reads as a broken promise.

text: A legal framing can hide the human stakes of an outcome, and the author's own bias toward a drafted settlement can color the account.
when: A rule-based explanation covers personal consequences
why: Technical language shifts attention from who is harmed.

text: A single preparation, such as a repeated outfit or a common object, can have an innocent explanation and should not be treated as proof of planning.
Arresting a convenient suspect can close a case too early, creating an appearance of progress while the real culprit remains free.
when: A case has a suspect who is easy to arrest but weakly linked.
why: Arrests give an impression of progress that can mislead the inquiry.

text: Promising authorities a result before the evidence is in hand creates pressure the investigator may not be able to meet.
A defendant's use of procedural rights, such as challenging jurors, does not by itself protect against a biased verdict.
when: when a fair trial is assumed from its forms

text: A council hears only the evidence put before it, so its ruling is shaped by what the parties supply.
A confession taken after arrest, in a hostile setting, can be the least reliable part of a case.
when: A confession is taken from a detained suspect
why: Hostile settings add pressure that distorts statements

text: Procedural stages can turn on decision-makers' private doubts rather than a clear legal standard, making the outcome hard to predict.
Arresting someone on suspicious silence alone can hide the truth and make real witnesses less willing to speak.
A defense may attack procedure, such as the handling of evidence, instead of the facts, even when the underlying fact is established.
when: Evidence handling is challenged in court or inquiry
why: Technical objections can cloud a fact that stands on its own

text: A procedural argument that reverses guilt feels like a cheat if the governing rule was never established earlier in the story.
when: A verdict changes on a procedural point the audience never saw.
why: Players cannot anticipate a rule they were never shown, so the twist reads as arbitrary.

text: 1) Start with routine facts such as identification and timeline. 2) Present technical findings. 3) Follow with emotional personal testimony. 4) Add minor witnesses. 5) Deliver the central disclosure late. 6) Close with a verdict.
why: each step prepares the next

text: 1) List the next lines of inquiry as a short set. 2) Give each line a clear test that can confirm or rule it out.
1) Comfort the witness first. 2) Then collect facts: when things began, who knew, and what was said. 3) Assemble them into a timeline of relationships, quarrels and motives.
when: A witness has made an emotional confession.
why: Comfort restores trust, and the timeline later supports reasoning about motive.

text: A capital prisoner's jury must be the jury that decides; a verdict reached after the panel is replaced or re-polled can be challenged as unlawful.
when: a juror is absent or replaced, or a deadlocked group is replaced or re-polled, before a verdict is returned
why: changing the panel breaks due form of law and undermines the verdict; legitimacy depends on who made the decision

text: Let trial systems route uncertain cases to a higher court, since its outcome can differ from the local one, including full acquittal.
when: when the local authority is uncertain

text: Before any irreversible decision, establish the matter as true and certain through diligent search, and never rest it on bare presumptions alone.
when: a capital or otherwise irreversible decision rests on contested evidence

text: Let quests shift a power balance by returning or replacing a secret item rather than by combat, so the change comes from knowledge rather than force.
when: Designing blackmail, faction intrigue or secret-based quests.

text: Do not let a personally aggrieved official hold exceptional power over a detained person; resentment can turn that power into harm.
when: someone with a grudge controls a prisoner's custody or treatment
why: private resentment can drive actions outside procedure

text: When reassuring someone bound by a pledge, do not shrink the difficulty; measure the commitment against the longer, harder struggle.
when: a person is asked to keep a promise under emotional strain
why: understated stakes make the promise fragile

text: When a suspect is cleared, keep looking for positive evidence of the real culprit.
Charge only offences the evidence can support, even when a theory about other crimes is firmly believed.
when: when framing a case for legal proceedings
why: Belief alone cannot secure a conviction.

text: Make an arrest only after the object's location is linked to the suspect, not before.
why: an early arrest can lose the link that the rest of the case needs

text: Let a private intervention by the player skip the public stage of a hearing.
when: a private act can settle the matter

text: Use unverifiable testimony to open an inquiry, never as sufficient grounds for condemnation.
when: A case rests on claims no one can confirm.
why: An inquiry is a lead, not a verdict.

text: Ask whether a claimed objection appears in any document; a witness who never objects in writing cannot be read as having objected.
when: A witness claims to have protested or opposed something
why: An undocumented protest is weak evidence of opposition

text: Penalize an official who alters a sealed verdict heavily, remove them from the bench, and bar them from hearing that case again.
when: when a game's court system needs checks on rulings
why: This blocks officials from quietly changing outcomes.

text: When a scenario builds a conflict of interest into an investigator character, offer the player a recusal or reassignment option.
when: a conflict of interest is part of a case
why: it gives the player a way to respond to bias

text: Give restraint of a character, such as locking a door on a suspect, a consequence like escape or a legal penalty.
when: Game state lets the player hold an NPC.
why: Consequences keep restraint from being a free action.

text: Make an arrest a scripted sequence with a clear signal, so the player understands the moment of commitment.
Require the player to restrain an enemy's hands before opening a pocket, so searching carries a hidden-weapon risk.
when: Designing search interactions with armed enemies.
why: The risk makes the search a meaningful decision rather than a free action.

text: A new procedural route needs its own proof and cannot simply reuse the reasoning of the earlier verdict.
when: Reopening a closed verdict through a different channel
why: Each procedure requires evidence that satisfies its own standards

text: In a formal hearing, raise only what can be shown on record; an unproven inference will be dismissed as conjecture.
when: a hearing that accepts only evidence

text: Intent-only liability can punish acts that could never cause harm, but proof rests on testimony about the accused's mind or associations, which invites bias.
when: A law punishes intent to harm

text: Strict legal order can slow action when speed matters most, yet after a confrontation the formal process should be kept intact rather than shortcut.
A warrant or formal action cannot be undone once issued, so it should be weighed before a bluff is made.
when: threatening formal action
why: a bluff that must be carried out binds the investigator

text: Offering a choice between arrest and restitution gives the player a trade-off, with each option leading to a different ending.
when: A dialogue choice resolves a crime.
why: Competing outcomes make the decision meaningful.

text: Following disclosure procedure promptly protects a suspect, while postponing it for personal feeling weakens the appearance of good faith even when intentions are sincere.
Present a will as a readable in-world document so players can compare each beneficiary's stake themselves.
when: Designing estate or inheritance story content
why: Players then reason about motive from the terms rather than from a summary

text: Let players present evidence to an in-game council whose verdict depends on the quality of the rebuttal they offer.
why: the outcome then rewards argument and evidence

text: Let an NPC justify a decision by citing in-world laws, and let the player check whether each cited law actually applies to the case.
Let a faction publish its own ledger or proclamation that shifts reputation, and let players find a rival's contradicting entry.
Treat rumour as testimony with a source: ask who repeats it and weigh each strand by its source, keeping physical traces separate from sighting claims.
Treat a local legend as framing rather than fact; a legend tied to an object adds weight without proving it, so check claims against records.
when: when a folk story is tied to a case

text: Let players check a retold rumour against a physical or primary record that confirms or contradicts it.
when: when designing NPC gossip and clues
why: Retellings can mutate as they pass between people.

text: Tag each rumour retelling, and claims from unreliable NPCs, with a confidence level so players weigh them before other evidence confirms them.
when: when designing rumour propagation

text: Present rumours as partial observations from several tellers who each add opinion, so players compare accounts and sort fact from framing.
when: Designing rumours in narrative or dungeon generation, or news passing between residents of a small community.
why: Each teller frames the story with personal views.

text: Ambiguous remains found in a secluded place can prompt townsfolk to form a foul-play theory that is repeated as hearsay without proof.
when: remains are partial and mixed with unrelated debris
why: partial evidence invites a dramatic story that gossip spreads without checking

text: Rumour about an investigator's competence shapes how everyone reads the evidence, so the investigator's reputation can become the weakest point of the case.
when: Rumours question an investigator's judgment.
why: Colleagues interpret evidence through their view of the investigator.

text: People may reject a legend's literal claims yet privately accept its moral, such as crime bringing its own punishment.
when: when a folk story offers a moral explanation
why: a moral frame can feel satisfying without evidence

text: Local legends can present unverifiable witness reports as proof of supernatural events, and such stories persist through repetition.
A family belief in a curse may have grown out of a documented prophecy, and a later fictional curse may echo that belief, so cause and effect can run either way.
when: Tracing how a legend and a recorded event relate.
why: Legends and records feed each other, so the order of influence is often unclear.

text: Let the player correct a rumour by reaching the first-hand witness, who holds the original version of events.
Tie a rumour's reliability to the speaker's relationship with its subject, so biased speakers yield less reliable information.
when: Designing or evaluating rumours in a game.
why: A speaker with a stake distorts what they pass on.

text: Check a witness NPC's account against a time-stamped log so players can catch a rumour that contradicts an eyewitness.
Test a legend's internal logic against the setting, such as whether a claimed haunting fits the place where the claimed crime happened.
Test an inherited explanation against the physical form of the site it describes; layers, sizes, and positions that contradict it weaken the explanation.
when: A received account conflicts with what can be seen of a site or object.
why: Physical arrangement is evidence about how a site was made.

text: Require a rumour to be confirmed by two sources before it is trusted, so players cross-check claims rather than accepting one.
when: Designing rumour systems.

text: When separate accounts do not fit together in sequence, assume the joints were distorted, with each person telling either less or more than they know.
when: Several people give separate chronological accounts.
why: Mismatched sequences more often signal selective telling than simple confusion.

text: Separate rumour and suspicion from positive evidence when judging a case, since many facts can be read in two ways.
Trace whether a legend has a documented origin or only repeated tellings before accepting its supernatural claim.
when: A local tradition claims a supernatural witness

text: Later embellishments of a story are weaker evidence than the core elements that every retelling keeps.
A local legend can encode a rule about what a sign means before the event occurs, so it should be checked rather than dismissed.
when: When a folk tale describes a signal or trap behavior
why: Legends often carry usable information about how a phenomenon works

text: Legends spread through talk among neighbors and grow with each telling, so the most repeated version often drifts from the original.
A folk legend or natural cause can hide a human agent by placing a death outside human hands, such as blaming fright or a weak heart.
when: a death is attributed to a supernatural or natural cause
why: A cause beyond human reach discourages further investigation.

text: A culprit who learns a local legend can stage a death to match it, so the crime looks supernatural and investigators are steered away from a human agent.
when: a local legend is known to the culprit
why: A supernatural frame directs suspicion away from people.

text: A local ghost legend can absorb unexplained events, so a household ready to blame the uncanny stops looking for physical causes.
when: unexplained events occur in a place with a ghost legend
why: the legend supplies a ready explanation that ends investigation

text: Model a rumour as a message that gains or loses detail as NPCs repeat it, letting the player trace its origin.
Rumour repeated in talk or print passes as fact; accept it as evidence only after weighing it, since dismissing it outright loses partial truths.
Hearsay built on unverifiable perception, or early rumour, is no independent check on later testimony; stacked reports look like more evidence, and stages may be driven by fear or grudge.
Eager witnesses and well-meaning gossips, wanting to help or love talk, may add detail never observed, so each report needs checking.
why: Desire to help can produce invented detail.

text: Local legends may be exaggerated or distorted in retelling, so their details can mislead.
A bystander's remark is not itself a timeline and needs checking against fixed times before it can support a conclusion.
when: A witness offers an informal observation as evidence of timing.
why: Remarks lack fixed reference points and can be wrong.

text: Treating a rumour as proof, or assuming a secret is unknown because the people involved never spoke of it, leads to false conclusions.
A vivid, detailed description can make a rumor feel verified when later tellers added the detail.
A legend offers a ready explanation that can stand in for evidence, and a frame that explains everything blocks testing of ordinary causes.
Public accounts can credit the wrong people and misstate motives, so how a case is perceived can matter as much as what was done.
Rumour can misdirect an audience and make it reject correct evidence, so it should create tension rather than settle the story's logic.
when: Designing public opinion or gossip within a mystery.
why: Rumour is persuasive but unsupported, so it can outweigh facts that point the other way.

text: Searching for hidden passages because of old stories wastes effort when the building has none.
when: Investigating a sealed room
why: Folklore replaces evidence about the building

text: A sign that matches a legend exactly is suspicious when the legend may have been constructed from the sign, so check which came first.
when: a symbol seems to confirm a legend
why: Stories are often shaped to fit existing signs, reversing the apparent evidence.

text: Mixing legend and documented fact in the final account corrupts the conclusion.
Calling a legend proven while presenting it as a theory that explains a pattern overstates what the evidence shows.
1) Record the original witness of an event. 2) Log each person who relays it and count the hops. 3) Note the details each hop added or removed.
when: Designing or tracking a gossip or rumour system.

text: 1) List each claim with its source. 2) Separate physical traces from sightings. 3) Check each trace against the record and the actual scene. 4) Tag each claim by how well it is supported.
when: when rumours must be tested before they are used
why: Vivid rumours can pass as fact without checking

text: Label secondhand NPC reports as rumour, opinion or verified fact, keeping direct witness testimony distinct, since rumour lacks direct basis and can mislead the timeline.
when: designing dialogue about a suspect, or gathering witness accounts
why: Labels let players judge reliability without a separate check.

text: Use a rumour to open a lead on where to search or whom to question, but resolve it only with a verifiable clue, never as grounds for an accusation.
why: Rumors start inquiries, while verifiable clues close them.

text: Let a legend be partly true and partly embellished, with relayed details shifted, so players must check each retelling against physical evidence in the world.
when: Designing a rumour or legend within a game world; designing npc gossip
why: A mixed legend rewards checking claims against evidence rather than accepting or rejecting it outright.

text: Label journal entries as rumour or fact so players know which leads still need verifying.
when: designing player journals or logs
why: Clear labels keep unverified information from being treated as settled

text: Let an unreliable NPC reveal a real fact in distorted form, so players must cross-check the claim against the environment.
Let a legend predict signs that vanish under close inspection, rewarding players who check facts over folklore.
Test a supposed supernatural threat with a physical test, such as wounding it, that shows whether it is mortal and therefore an ordinary creature.
when: a supernatural explanation is proposed
why: A mortal result removes the supernatural premise.

text: Take an unusual witness report seriously, but look for the mechanism that could produce it before accepting the supernatural explanation.
when: When a witness reports an apparently impossible event.
why: Most unusual reports have a physical cause that can be identified.

text: Give a haunted sound a findable physical cause and a documented source, so the legend stays testable hearsay rather than unexplained lore.
when: Designing a local supernatural legend
why: Players can then check the claim against the location.

text: A rumour of a supernatural or monstrous secret can keep people from looking closely at a mundane concealment.

1) Hide a key or code between pages stuck together in a lore book. 2) Let the player reveal it by cutting or parting the pages. 3) Place an inscription chain across several NPC hands for the player to read in order.
when: Designing hidden clues in in-game lore items.
why: Physical concealment rewards thorough player inspection and sequence reading.

text: Seek admission of a lesser offence before a greater one, since a suspect who denies the serious crime may still admit the smaller one.
when: a suspect is accused of several crimes
why: smaller admissions are easier to obtain

text: Pressure a lesser informant with arrest threats and reminders of past offences, then offer a choice of cooperation.
when: a witness has partial knowledge and something to lose

text: Pursue a minor culprit for a small provable offence to unlock the main investigation, or leave them unpursued to reach the figure behind them; choose by whether they lead upward.
when: a small-time accomplice is involved in a larger scheme
why: Detaining or exposing the lesser culprit opens the main case, while leaving them free may lead to the figure at the top.

text: Mix opinion with fact, or one true and one false fact, in dialogue so players must cross-check claims against other evidence.
when: designing dialogue for a deceptive or unreliable character
why: Sorting mixed statements becomes a rewarding task.

text: When an offer is questioned, a suspect who shifts to a new offer shows that the plan is being improvised.
when: A suspect is pressed on a gesture

text: A suspect who knows he is exposed will watch the people who threaten him, check their outgoing messages, and destroy evidence.
when: The suspect has learned that someone is closing in.
why: Exposure gives the suspect a reason to protect himself.

text: A guilty party may reframe the act with softer, mitigating language, insisting on terms that cast it as justified.
when: a suspect confesses but resists the word for the act

text: Witnesses answer the sense they infer from a question rather than its literal wording, so a truthful denial can still hide a fact.
when: when an NPC denies something that physical evidence contradicts
why: People filter questions through what they think the asker wants

text: Loose talk in a casual setting often reveals rivals, disputes and habits beyond the topic that was asked about.
when: a suspect or acquaintance talks freely over a meal or drink

text: A confession made in mockery is often retracted at once, so it needs support from other clues to hold weight.
when: A speaker admits something and then laughs it off.
why: Retreating into jest lets the speaker deny the admission.

text: People whose knowledge others cannot follow are often suspected of sorcery, because their skill looks unexplained.
when: a learned person's methods are hidden from the community
why: Opacity invites supernatural explanation.

text: When questioned about a visitor's absence, a guilty party offers a false explanation, such as a departure aboard a passing vessel.
when: when questioned about someone who has gone missing
why: to account for the absence without admitting involvement

text: Captors who cannot verify a concealed threat tend to comply when a visible cue makes the threat appear real.
when: When a captive makes a threat that cannot be checked
why: An unverifiable threat backed by a visible cue is treated as genuine.

text: Marks in exposed places, such as sand, damp ground and fallen leaves, are erased by wind, rain and tidal action.
A failed physical check does not prove a witness lied; it shows only that the sign is weak evidence.
Ask why a witness misleads: a false account where refusal was possible signals concealment; a lie about one fact often protects someone present, so ask who it shields.
when: a witness gives a false account instead of declining, or misstates one fact about a visit or event
why: People lie most readily about facts that would expose someone they want to protect.

text: Gate information behind a bluff or implied threat, and let a failed bluff trigger a clear consequence such as a cooperation penalty, locked door or guard response.
when: Designing a dialogue system with pressure options.
why: A penalty for failed bluffs makes the choice a risk, not a free reveal; the outcome feels earned.

text: Concede a smaller, defensible fact so an opponent believes they have seen the whole picture, while the real line of inquiry stays hidden.
when: when the opponent has something to lose from exposure and will accept a plausible explanation
why: a satisfied opponent may stop probing

text: A competitor who lets the opponent win early and then wins quickly lowers the opponent's guard and gains the advantage.
when: Designing an opponent in a game of skill
why: A feigned concession relaxes the opponent before the decisive move.

text: When a suspect denies knowing a fact that the displayed evidence implies, treat the denial as a sign they do know it.
Model a suspect's lie as an attempt to avoid a larger danger, so a player who finds the lie can also find its reason.
why: A motivated lie gives the player a path from contradiction to motive.

text: A plan that requires many exposed steps with no clear gain is suspicious and deserves closer scrutiny.
when: an account requires a long, risky sequence of actions
why: Each exposed step is another chance to be noticed, so the sequence is hard to justify.

text: Challenge a witness's lie by reasoning about who else could have acted; the logic can expose the lie even without direct proof.
when: the witness's account depends on who else was present

text: Expose a concealed truth when a false account would wrongly blame an innocent person by name in lasting form; stay silent when the falsehood only praises the dead.
when: Deciding whether to reveal a memorialised falsehood.
why: Harm to the innocent outweighs harm to a reputation.

text: A habitual liar's additional falsehood reveals little, so the lie-as-tell signal works only against a clear honesty baseline.
when: when a character often lies
why: without a baseline, one more lie breaks no pattern

text: When a suspect is caught in one false detail, re-examine every other statement they gave, since a lie about one detail weakens the rest.
when: A suspect's account contains a proven falsehood.
why: A fabricated detail suggests the other claims may also be constructed.

text: Let an NPC's theory be wrong in a checkable way so the player can disprove it with a found item.
Test whether a claim survives its strongest alternative explanation before treating it as established.
when: Weighing an inference drawn from physical or testimonial evidence.
why: An inference that an alternative undermines is weakened, as with wound placement that a second cause can produce.

text: Offer a clear-the-room dialogue option that removes bystanders before a sensitive exchange, and let persistent questions resist topic changes so NPCs cannot dodge them.
when: Designing dialogue for sensitive conversations.
why: Removing observers and persisting questions preserve the focus of the exchange.

text: Dialogue can branch on reaction tags such as pale or halting speech, not only on yes or no answers, and a tag can be tied to a secondary fear the player must verify.
when: Designing dialogue that reads NPC emotional state.
why: Richer tags let the player interpret NPC behaviour and avoid acting on a single misleading signal.

text: Offering a fair hearing, protection or immunity to a candid suspect or witness facing consequences draws out motives and accounts they would otherwise withhold.
why: Fear of consequences makes full disclosure risky until terms are offered; those who expect fair treatment volunteer reasons they would hide.

text: Literally accurate statements, such as a bare phrase about nothing left undone, can conceal a key action and leave a false overall impression when read in context.
In an interrogation mini-game, the NPC's response can depend on which evidence the player presents, and its denials can reveal what it knows.
A partner's own exposure can serve as leverage, since someone who would be exposed by speaking has reason to stay silent.
Let players expose a propaganda document by comparing it with an original record or the scene it describes.
When a found material does not match what a person claims to have used, the item likely came from another source, possibly another person.
when: a claimed use is compared with residue found on the item

text: A confess-for-leniency branch changes a suspect's later behaviour and the case outcome, so the choice should carry lasting consequences.
Witness dialogue can be made fallible, so an NPC misremembers a detail such as a room unless the player passes a perception check.
NPC dialogue can carry an explanation that a later observation contradicts, letting the player catch a lie without a direct accusation.
when: when a stated explanation can be checked against a later event
why: Letting the player spot the contradiction rewards attention without requiring an explicit accusation.

text: Model interrogation as gated questions, where some answers unlock only after a fact is established elsewhere.
A bluff holds only until tested: an unexecuted threat or a single check by the opponent exposes it and reveals the questioner's limits.
An exposed bluff or easily checked pretext makes the suspect more guarded for the rest of questioning, so avoid cover stories the subject can verify.
when: the subject has ready access to verify the claim
why: exposure gives the suspect a reason to resist and conceal

text: Accusations and pressed testimony often mix true and invented details; label and check each claim piece by piece, since speakers and listeners can lose track of what is real.
why: The lure can confuse its own user as well as its target; stress blends accurate details with self-serving claims.

text: Emotionally loaded framing or hypotheticals can make a witness defensive and end answers, or push them toward the investigator's theory so it confirms a guess rather than reveals truth.
A bluff about knowledge can be exposed, and a suspect who sees through it may then answer falsely to avoid trouble.
A bluff about authority can be exposed later, and the cooperation it earned is then lost along with the investigator's credibility.
why: the witness learns the claim was false

text: A withheld plan can leave a subordinate exposed to suspicion if he is followed.
A partial claim that is false and easy to expose will be called a bluff, so the interviewer must be ready for correction.
when: Making a partial claim that the other party can check

text: Reading stated affection literally misses a letter's real purpose, which may be financial or manipulative.
when: A warm letter seems to express friendship.
why: Affection is often used as a means to a practical end.

text: A failed trap can expose its planner, so a prepared fallback explanation is often needed for a plan that might not work.
when: when a hidden plan depends on a device working correctly
why: failure leaves evidence that points back to the planner

text: Stating the pressure method openly lets a sharp suspect recognise it and refuse to react.
People who seem clear and open can be deceptive in depth, so an observer's confidence in reading them is itself a warning sign.
A lie can be a cover for an innocent reason, so a detected falsehood does not by itself reveal the motive behind it.
why: a lie signals concealment, not its purpose

text: 1) Identify each odd event. 2) Ask what it requires and who gains from it. 3) Run a test that exposes whether the event is staged.
when: A case contains several staged or misleading events.

text: 1) Show the suspect proof that you know their past. 2) Lay out the evidence you hold. 3) Ask for the one missing fact. 4) State the deal and its alternative plainly.
when: the suspect knows a needed fact and the evidence against them is strong

text: 1) Identify checkable figures, dates and claims in a witness's account. 2) Compare each with sources the witness does not control. 3) Flag disagreements for follow-up.
when: a witness's account includes verifiable details
why: Independent sources expose claims the witness may have invented.

text: Do not treat a detected lie as proof of guilt; treat it as a lead needing corroboration, and weigh innocent explanations such as fear first.
when: a statement is contradicted by evidence
why: Contradictions can have innocent explanations; fear and embarrassment produce lies without guilt.

text: Make NPC claims checkable against neutral scene evidence, such as scorch marks, mud prints, weapon range, inventory items or records, so players can separate fact from bias and catch lies.
when: designing NPC testimony or dialogue with factual statements
why: Verifiable claims let players weigh accounts against evidence; neutral evidence separates fact from bias.

text: Do not accept a confession alone; verify it against objects, records, map and other witnesses, and author confessions with checkable details so players earn the truth.
when: Designing an NPC confession in a game.
why: Checkable claims make the player's verification the path to the truth.

text: Flag testimony from a witness or accuser with a personal stake, since anger or reputation distorts it, and require an independent source before acting on it.
when: a witness or accuser has a personal stake in the outcome, or an NPC's claim benefits them
why: Emotion and reputation distort what is reported.

text: Keep sensitive material and trap staging out of observable channels and openings, since outsiders who see contents or setup expose the plan before it is sprung.
when: A prepared ambush room has openings to the outside.
why: Observation along the way exposes contents; visible preparation exposes the plan before it is sprung.

text: Let the player bluff a suspect with a note showing knowledge, unlocking a confession branch in dialogue.
when: Designing dialogue puzzles where the player holds hidden knowledge.
why: Showing knowledge rewards investigation and opens new dialogue paths.

text: Use overheard monologue as a dialogue trigger, letting the player collect fragments that combine into a theory.
Design dialogue so a lie-detecting pretext triggers a different response, rather than a plain refusal.
why: A changed response keeps the conversation useful.

text: Let NPCs answer literally so that players must ask precise questions to get information.
Let an NPC admit one lie while insisting on a core truth, and let players check each detail against world records.
when: when designing a suspect's story

text: Give a faction NPC a fixed premise, and let the player expose it by finding a fact the premise cannot explain.
when: designing a cult or faction with a belief that drives its actions
why: Players can defeat a closed belief system only with evidence it cannot absorb.

text: Let a false informer be exposed later, with consequences for the NPCs they falsely named.
Keep a cover story consistent with earlier statements, so it fits what the opponent has already heard.
Let in-world judges sometimes ignore contradicting evidence, so players learn the system is biased and must seek independent proof.
when: when designing a judgment system in a mystery
why: ignored evidence teaches players to verify independently

text: Feign distress or an ailment only when the performance can be made convincing to those watching.
when: Using a staged illness to gain access
why: A weak performance draws suspicion rather than cover.

text: An NPC can withhold information until the player meets a trust or favor condition, and the refusal can be logged.
Store partial confessions as flags so that a later denial can be checked against them automatically.
when: when an NPC makes a partial admission
why: stored flags expose inconsistent later denials

text: An open accusation warns a suspect and may force early action, while feigned ignorance lets them act on a false belief but risks surprise and exposure.
when: A direct accusation would warn the suspect before evidence is secured.

text: A long closing speech adds moral and emotional weight but slows pacing and can dull the final beat.
Militia titles were kept for life, so a former junior officer might still be styled by a higher title.
Household servants, shop assistants and others in a victim's circle are the likeliest readers of an appeal to identify them.

Test even the most probable explanation against evidence: 1) State the proposed mundane cause. 2) Check it against every observation, including timing and the person's reaction. 3) Accept it only if it fits the whole pattern.
when: When an eerie event is given a natural explanation
why: A cause that fits only some observations is a red herring, not an answer

text: Do not stack many revelations at once, or the audience loses track of which claim is being tested.
when: during a multi-claim reveal

text: Astronomy, chemistry, optics, pneumatics and geography were largely undeveloped in the period, so ordinary events lacked natural explanations for those who saw them.
Restricting what a character can see keeps destination and outcome hidden, so the character must infer the situation from sound, motion and fragments of sight.
when: a sequence where the reveal of place or identity matters
why: inference from partial cues builds suspense

text: A witness reports only what they could see from their position; looking up a stairwell gives a limited view, so coverage must be checked.
Use a limited viewpoint when the reveal depends on facts the observer could not know, but never hide clues the observer would reasonably have seen.
when: Writing a narrator with restricted knowledge
why: Hidden obvious clues make the reveal feel cheated

text: Make a note writer's knowledge visibly limited, so the document itself reveals how much the writer knew.
when: when designing npc-written documents

text: Consistency checks on motive and conduct do not always settle a suspicion, because a guilty mind can be hard to read.
A specific test can separate human blood from animal blood, so a claimed animal-accident explanation can be checked.
A demonstration shows that a mechanism works as described, not that it caused the harm in question.
when: A defence rests on a device test

text: A negative test on the wrong sample proves nothing about the item that matters; check whether the suspect item was included in the tests.
when: a lab test clears a case
why: a negative result only rules out what was tested

text: A test that fails to detect a substance may reflect the limits of the tools rather than the absence of the substance.
when: A search or chemical test returns nothing and is taken as proof of absence.
why: Detection methods have thresholds and blind spots, so a negative result is weaker than it appears.

text: Do not use physical tests to judge intent or motive; they show only what an action could physically achieve.
when: a claim concerns why someone acted
why: Physical evidence cannot reveal what a person intended.

text: When a test cannot separate two relevant sources, such as the blood of two similar animals, use a different test for that question.
A complete-looking taxonomy does not prove every case is covered, and the most interesting crime may sit outside every category.
when: Relying on a classification scheme to solve a case
why: Schemes are built from known motives and can miss unfamiliar ones

text: A reductio against an accuser shows inconsistency in the accuser's standards but does not establish the innocence of the accused.
A weaker print from one foot suggests less weight was placed on it, which points to a limp.
when: Prints from the same shoe differ in depth.
why: Reduced weight shows as a shallower impression.

text: 1) Present several candidates who partly fit the description. 2) Have the witness signal rejection of each under an agreed sign. 3) Log each candidate as seen.
when: a witness must identify a suspect from several people
why: an agreed procedure keeps the identification controlled and recorded

text: 1) Assemble a parade of similar decoys with the suspect. 2) Have the witness pick a person. 3) Check whether the witness repeatedly picks one person or simply agrees with the suggested suspect.
when: Testing whether an identification is genuine.
why: Decoys reveal whether the witness discriminates or is merely confirming a suggestion.

text: Lingering anxiety after a detail resurfaces suggests the detail matters to the witness.
A person who lingers at a door before knocking, looking pale and shaking, may have been listening.
A suspect whose thoughts still dwell on an earlier story may link a trigger word to that story rather than its usual meaning.
when: a suspect recently heard a story tied to a key object
why: Recent attention primes an unrelated association.

text: A formal disclaimer does not stop a vivid theory from shaping how people interpret later facts.
An unexplained sense of dread with no traceable cause stays with the audience as a mood to recall when later events give it meaning.
Leave some final signal unexplained so the audience remains uncertain after the reveal.
when: Closing a multi-stage mystery
why: Residual doubt preserves suspense beyond the apparent resolution

text: Connect separate records or sources sharing people or places; overlaps reveal links no single one states, building a sequence of events, such as a trip abroad before a death.
when: when multiple documents or sources mention related people or places
why: Overlaps between separate accounts expose links no single source states.

text: Separate incidents that share an unusual detail, such as a method, object or location, can be seen as unrelated for a long time until a chance remark links them.
when: When several incidents occur with a recurring unusual detail.
why: People judge each incident in isolation, so a shared trait stays hidden until someone compares them directly.

text: A chain of linked documents, such as a petition followed by an order to an officer, shows how a decision moved through a chain of command.
An object in one location that matches the material or style of an object elsewhere can tie their owners together.
A found object gains evidential weight when it matches a known item from the event; an object with no established link should stay unresolved.
when: a button or wrapper is found at a scene
why: matching evidence to a known source separates relevant items from coincidental debris

text: Recurring signatures across unrelated incidents can reveal a single organizer behind them.
Repeated incidents that look accidental can be linked through the victim's fixed habits. Compare each incident against the routine rather than accepting it as chance.
when: a series of similar incidents keeps being explained as accidents
why: a fixed routine can be exploited each time

text: Link each trace to a specific owner or item so the player can verify the match directly.
when: when designing clues that point to a suspect
why: a clue tied to a checkable owner can be confirmed or refuted

text: Test a working theory that links several incidents into one plan, but judge each incident on its own evidence.
when: when several incidents seem related

text: Link an unfulfilled intention to a suspect by asking who would lose or gain if the planned change had happened.
A connection between a person and an object shows where to ask next, not who is responsible.
when: Before drawing conclusions from a link
why: Links are leads that need corroboration

text: Two events, such as a dismissal and a missing sum, can look connected when they are not; an unknown detail leaves the link unproven.
1) Ask who else could have known the information, to trace how it spread. 2) Collect odd details from each source. 3) Place the details side by side and look for a shared pattern.
when: a hidden agent is suspected from scattered traces

text: Do not conclude from one trace alone; connect it with other traces, such as a bracket mark and a rope break, before deciding what happened.
when: When a single physical clue seems to explain the whole event.
why: Linked traces support each other, while an isolated trace can mislead.

text: 1) Find a physical detail shared by separate incidents, such as a maker's mark or description. 2) Trace the mark to a source that can identify the person. 3) Treat the link as provisional until proven.
when: Two unrelated reports may concern the same unidentified person.
why: A shared physical detail gives a lead, but proof is still needed.

text: One account can join unrelated facts into a single sequence and point to where to look next.
List every reading a single clue supports before accepting any one, since one physical fact can support several contradictory deductions.
when: when a single clue is treated as proof of one identity

text: In lists of officials, the first-named of several same-surname people is usually the one with the presiding office or longest service.
when: Ordering follows local convention and the reader accepts that convention
why: Writers tend to list by office and seniority of settlement

text: Ordering conventions vary between writers and places, so an inference from list order holds only if the reader accepts the convention in use.
A listener checks a relayed account against what they already know and reacts openly where it strains belief, showing the audience where to doubt.
when: An in-world listener hears a claim that seems implausible.
why: Prior knowledge gives a basis for judging how credible a claim is.

text: Witness accounts are shaped by who is listening and when they are recorded, so alibis offered late are often recorded and then set aside.
when: When an alibi or account is first offered after an accusation.
why: Late statements look self-serving and are harder to check.

text: Each teller tends to supply the detail that suits the listener, so repeated retellings shift emphasis away from what was originally known.
when: A story is passed on to different listeners.
why: Tellers adapt content to the audience.

text: Digressions can contain useful names or objects, so listen for them within irrelevant talk.
Pay close attention to details a witness offers unprompted, since small asides can point to important leads worth pursuing.
when: A witness volunteers a passing remark during questioning.
why: Unsolicited comments often reveal knowledge the witness did not intend to share.

text: 1) Listen before acting. 2) Stay silent so the intruder does not learn you are present. 3) Avoid sudden movement that could reveal your position.
when: an unseen visitor is moving nearby in the dark
why: Sounds reveal what the intruder is doing, and silence keeps the observer hidden

text: 1) List every apparent impossibility as a separate question. 2) Target a different assumption in each: weapon, silence, access, exit, sequence. 3) Answer each in order. 4) Require each answer to fit all constraints.
when: A scene has several inconsistencies that no single theory explains
why: Each question narrows the explanation, and an answer must satisfy every constraint, not just one.

text: 1) List everyone who could have learned the secret or hidden object's location, such as visitors and staff, before concluding no outsider knew it. 2) Test each person for access, presence at the key time, and a provable alibi. 3) Count each person once.
when: a secret or object's location is believed known only to few people or insiders
why: access to the secret is the central question

text: Assuming every trace belongs to a living suspect overlooks the victim and the scene as possible sources.
when: Interpreting an unmatched physical trace
why: Traces can come from the body or the environment itself

text: Keep NPCs who have access to a crime as live suspects with testable evidence, not fixed red herrings that the story dismisses in advance.
when: Designing mysteries where several characters could have acted
why: Players can only reason fairly if each suspect stays open until evidence rules it out

text: Record a local informant's rejection of a common explanation and weigh it seriously rather than dismissing it.
Assuming a motive must lie locally can send the search the wrong way when the cause lies far from the scene.
A local postmark removes the travel delay, so the time available before the event is short.
when: the sender's origin is near the event
why: no transit time is needed

text: Let a local character who knows the terrain supply a fact about hidden features, which can rule out routes or explain how an event happened.
Local sources such as a tavern or village often yield more useful detail than distant inquiries made elsewhere.
when: gathering information about a community
why: local talk gathers what the whole neighbourhood knows

text: Local sources often misremember names and histories, and a claim repeated many times is not thereby confirmed.
when: when relying on community gossip for identities or backgrounds
why: Repetition spreads errors just as easily as it spreads truth.

text: When a case depends on local memory, ask who worked longest alongside the people involved, since long-serving locals often hold the best history.
when: when reconstructing a community's past

text: 1) Compare the outward relationship with later changes in behaviour. 2) Find the point where the attitude turned. 3) Look for a trigger, such as a disclosure. 4) Check whether the hostility was concealed.
when: A private grievance is not visible in the public record

text: When one witness is the only link, shift the work from questioning to tracking them down, and plan concrete steps such as visiting a set location.
when: When the key witness is absent or unreachable.

text: In a small community with few civilians, a distinctive appearance is easy to notice, so a description narrows the search.
when: the target is local and must be found within a bounded area
why: few people means a distinctive look stands out

text: Use a precedent's motive to identify who would have been harmed by the event, then search among those people for the hidden party.
when: the precedent involves a motive that blocks someone's goal
why: the motive narrows the field of possible culprits

text: When a contact has moved, follow the record of the move rather than ending the line of inquiry.
when: Investigating through a chain of contacts
why: The move record can lead to new sources and reveal hidden links.

text: 1) Ask acquaintances, such as club members or servants, for the witness's address. 2) Get their travel route and a rough return date. 3) If the witness is still absent, leave a written message to keep contact open.
1) Write to an intermediary who may have been in contact with the witness. 2) Ask that replies be forwarded or sent to a distant post office to protect the search.
when: a witness's location is unknown and the search must stay discreet
why: Intermediaries relay addresses, and distance hides the searcher

text: 1) Check registries for the target vessel. 2) Cross-check its name against origin records. 3) Confirm the crew's whereabouts with a contact at the dock.
when: tracking a target that is travelling

text: 1) List the places a hidden person could have been placed. 2) Check the most likely places one by one until the person is found.
when: when a person's location is concealed
why: Ordered checks of likely places are efficient.

text: 1) List every household member. 2) Record each member's location and any marriage, move or arrest with its date. 3) For the sighting date, remove those who were absent. 4) Weigh the remaining candidates.
when: an unexplained figure appears at a known household
why: physical presence follows documented movements

text: An NPC's most important secret is often the subject it works hardest to close off, so players can spot it by watching deflections.
A room with one exit watched by a trusted observer works as a human substitute for a locked room.
A small craft with few hiding spaces makes concealment hard, so a thorough search is harder to resist.
when: when hiding items in a confined space
why: few hiding places leave little room for concealment

text: Use independent indicators of location, such as lights lit elsewhere, to test a theory that places someone in a particular spot.
when: A theory depends on where a person was
why: Outside evidence can undercut a theory built on the scene alone.

text: Use a location that shows the crime's path: objects there connect the body to the scene and to the person who was present.
A slow entry method can hide an extended presence, so the time it requires must be considered when reconstructing events.
when: Reconstructing how long an intruder was active.
why: Slow methods imply the intruder stayed unnoticed for a long period.

text: A witness's account of a door is weak until a second source confirms it.
when: A door's state is reported by one person.
why: One account can be mistaken or incomplete.

text: A surviving cellar or foundation proves a site existed but not who lived there at a given time; pair physical remains with dated documents.
Matching a real location to a story creates false certainty; several sites may each seem to fit, and none may be the actual model.
when: Linking a historical event to a physical place.
why: Partial resemblance is easy to find, so a fit can be coincidental.

text: Players who accept a staged location at face value stop reconsidering the premise and miss that the event happened somewhere else.
1) List the physical traces the visitor left. 2) Estimate height from marks at a reach height. 3) Estimate age and agility from the feats the traces imply. 4) Infer habits from residue left behind.
when: An unseen visitor left several small traces.
why: Each trace narrows one trait, so a sketch can be built from many small clues.

text: 1) Examine the outer boundary first. 2) Record the traces there before entering. 3) Enter afterward, so the traces are recorded before anyone is alerted.

1) Describe the setting as named places with clear edges. 2) For each place, record who was inside, who passed through, and who would have noticed a stranger. 3) Treat the boundaries as hard limits. 4) Check each witness against the boundaries.
when: A person vanishes inside a small, bounded place.
why: Fixed boundaries turn an open-ended disappearance into a finite list of places and people to check.

text: Do not search a location where physical evidence already excludes the object being sought.
why: Effort is better spent on places still open.

text: Let the decisive evidence come from a location the characters have not yet searched, so the player feels the discovery is earned through exploration.
when: Revealing the culprit in a mystery
why: Discovery in an unsearched place rewards exploration and keeps the reveal plausible.

text: 1) Name the place where the body was found. 2) List every fact that conflicts with a crime happening there. 3) Test each conflict on its own. 4) Reject the place if several conflicts hold.
when: A body is found somewhere that does not fit how the death occurred.
why: Each conflict may be weak, but together they can rule out the obvious location.

text: A note written from a post the author could not leave places the author there on that date.
when: A dated note mentions the writer's duty or location.

text: The place where an act occurs can reveal what the actor needed, such as light, so consider why that location was chosen.
when: an act happened somewhere odd

text: If the seals on other doors stay whole while only one room's seal breaks, the disturbance stayed within that room.
when: Comparing physical markers across a building
why: Intact markers elsewhere localize the cause.

text: A trace that places a caller at a public location narrows the search but does not identify the person if no one saw them.
when: Relying on a telephone or location trace
why: A place gives direction of travel, not identity

text: A locked-room impossibility is partly real and partly staged; its solution depends on who controlled the door, window and timing, not on a hidden passage.
when: designing a sealed-room mystery

text: A locked-room mystery presents a crime whose scene seems impossible to enter or leave, and is solved by explaining how that impossibility was produced.
A locked-room shooting staged with no weapon and no motive gives an investigator an impossible premise to solve.
A locked connecting door whose key is missing limits which rooms could be reached, so note access points when reconstructing movement.
A locked door whose key sits with one suspect explains why rescue was blocked. Breaking the door in the dark then adds confusion to the scene.
A locked-room plot runs: method shown, impossible crime, conflicting testimony, false solution on an innocent, mechanism analyzed, then a trap forces a confession.
A locked-room reveal runs in five beats: sealed-room setup, a staging hint, a competing mechanism, a confession, and corroboration with aftermath.
A locked-room mystery runs in seven phases: hook, first suspect, open verdict, pivot to new suspects, crisis, trial, reveal.
Assuming a container is secure because it has a lock; check whether it was actually locked and how often it is routinely opened.
Characters and players often treat a route as impassable because it was checked from one side, missing a concealed mechanism.

1) Establish the door, its lock and where the key was. 2) Record who had access to the key and corridor at the time. 3) Note whether the occupant reacted to the lock's sound. 4) Check for any other exit the occupant could have used.
when: Solving a locked-room mystery where the key holder is in question.
why: Access records and exit checks narrow the set of people who could have locked the door.

text: 1) List every exit, key and timed event in the room. 2) Check each exit against the events. 3) Use timed observations to narrow when the person could have left.
when: when an impossible exit is the core of a locked-room puzzle
why: Enumerating exits and timings narrows the possible routes.

text: 1) Establish whether duplicate keys exist and where they were kept. 2) Establish who held the key on the critical day and when it changed hands. 3) Ask whether the holder had reason for access and whether they asked why the key was wanted. 4) Ask whether the key was returned and whether the holder can identify it. 5) Test the holder's account against the physical record.
when: A locked entrance is central and the number of possible key holders is small.
why: A sequenced custody trace links access to people and times, and tests accounts against records.

text: 1) Show physical traces without explaining them. 2) Build a first route through testimony. 3) Break each route with a new fact. 4) Fail an ambush with a fleeting glimpse. 5) Name the culprit with proof.
when: when structuring a locked-room mystery

text: Use a key-duplication shop as a location where the player discovers who made a copy and when.
when: Designing a location tied to a copied key.
why: A craftsperson's record can reveal who ordered a copy.

text: Verify each lock on every door and identify who held the keys, since access controls determine who could reach the sealed object.
Model keys as items with a custody history that logs holders, transfer times and last-seen locations, and let NPC answers be checked against that log.
when: Designing locks and keys in a game.
why: A custody log lets the player test NPC claims against recorded facts.

text: An intact lock suggests key use and narrows suspects to key holders; but locks don't prove exclusive access, since copies let outsiders enter, so don't assume an insider too quickly.
when: A sealed room shows no forced entry or an undamaged lock.
why: Absence of damage points to a legitimate key rather than a break-in; other routes or copies can produce the same undamaged result.

text: Hotels and furnished lodgings must record every guest's name, even for a single night, so their registers cover a wide range of people.
when: Tracing a person through lodging records.
why: Legal record-keeping obligations apply to all tenants.

text: Log each NPC or interrogation question and suggestion with its presumptions, so players can reconstruct a hidden goal or spot when a question assumes guilt.
