Let dialogue or interrogation systems express hidden thoughts through glances, pauses and dropped objects, and log these cues so players can reconstruct the link.
when: designing NPC systems that conceal intent
why: logged cues give players anchors to reason from

text: A timestamped log of each character's location lets a player reconstruct a timeline, and any gap becomes a lead.
when: when designing an in-game event log for mystery play
why: Missing entries show the player where to look next.

text: 1) Record each witness clue separately. 2) Note what was volunteered versus asked; log volunteered statements as unverified and reserve judgement until checks confirm or contradict them. 3) Mark each open thread as a task to investigate.
when: Interviewing a witness who gives partial or evasive answers, or offers history, motive or character unprompted.
why: Separating clues keeps unverified impressions distinct from checkable leads; unprompted material often shows what the speaker wants believed.

text: 1) Log each fragment the player hears. 2) Record where it was heard. 3) Revisit the log when the wider picture arrives so the player can weigh each fragment.
when: when a game delivers clues as partial overheard speech
why: Source and context let the player reassess earlier fragments.

text: Log suspicious NPC dialogue and behaviour early as clearly recallable world events, so a later reveal about a trusted NPC can recontextualize them via moments already seen.
why: Hindsight reinterpretation only works if the detail can be recalled; a late reveal is backed by moments the player already saw.

text: A dialogue system should log each suspect's exact words so the player can later confront him with his own recorded statements.
Offer a humorous deflection and record it in the dialogue log, so the player can return to the question later.
when: An NPC avoids a sensitive question with humour.
why: A logged deflection keeps the question open rather than letting it disappear.

text: Record incidental bystanders even when their role is unexplained, since they may matter later as witnesses or alibis.
when: when observing a scene
why: Unexplained figures can become important once the picture changes.

text: In a questioning system, log contradictions between an NPC's answers and show them when the player presents a conflicting fact.
Log NPC threats and public quarrels so they can be reused as motive evidence when the player later confronts that suspect.
when: Designing NPC interactions that may matter to a later accusation

text: Log the timing of events the player witnesses, so a character's spoken timeline can be checked against the game's own record.
Log only facts the player has actually seen, so the final explanation reinterprets earlier events rather than introducing new facts.
when: designing a quest log

text: Check a death or trap-triggered event in a game against logged evidence such as inventory counts, timers and wounds, and record each failed check.
when: When designing game events that must be explainable.
why: Recorded checks let the player and designer trace the cause.

text: When accounts conflict, let a fixed sequence of logged events, such as calls and sightings, decide which account to trust rather than memory.
why: memory of time is unreliable

text: Script NPC reactions to specific words or items and log them as clues the player can review later.
A relief scene that runs long drains the tension that the misdirection depends on.
An item belonging to someone missing for years, with no word since, is especially significant, since it may be the first sign of their fate.
when: a found object connects to a long-missing person
why: the absence of news makes any trace of the person unusually valuable

text: Use a delayed-disclosure secret when it must stay hidden across many scenes while the character's inner conflict builds.
Anonymous summons and recurring symbols keep a hidden history alive until a confession explains it.
Plant an old feud or past crime that the present suspect inherits, adding a second story layer behind the immediate case.
Observers can mistake a closely resembling person for the target without any lie, and trusting a witness's sense that someone looked right lets an impostor pass unnoticed.
when: two people closely resemble each other

text: Witnesses often misidentify a person in a group when individuals arrive together, linger, or enter in quick succession.
when: Several people arrive or move through a space close together
why: Brief, grouped movement makes individuals hard to separate in memory.

text: Two people who look alike in daylight can be mistaken for each other in dim light, so a brief sighting in low light is unreliable for identification.
when: Witness accounts of a figure seen briefly in low light
why: Poor light blurs distinguishing features.

text: Identifying someone by one common trait can mislead, because many people share it, so a single match should not be treated as proof.
why: common traits occur by coincidence across many people

text: Use a look-alike relative in a character dossier as a red herring, so players must check a physical detail before accepting an identity.
when: Designing a misidentification in a mystery.

text: A caution given loosely may fail to protect the statement that follows it.
when: Cautioning a witness informally or hastily
why: The caution must clearly convey the statement's risk

text: A partial or vague clue supporting many readings widens the search, because a reading flexible enough to fit every hiding place rules none out.
when: A clue is partial and admits many interpretations.
why: Generous readings match many locations, so the search spreads without narrowing.

text: A loose match between a description and a record needs a second independent check before it is relied on.
Do not reject a theory merely because one detail is unexplained; check whether that detail really falls outside the theory.
when: a theory explains most evidence but leaves one detail open

text: A loose joint can have more than one cause, such as deliberate handling in care settings, so it must be interpreted carefully.
when: Interpreting a loosened limb
why: Innocent handling can mimic tampering

text: Inconsistently applied or loosely used labels can mislead, so a term's meaning should not be treated as fixed; records show motive only when clearly linked to the outcome.
when: Reading case records or historical/in-world labels for suspects where terms or records are used inconsistently.
why: Vague or overlapping terms shift meaning between accusers and courts, and weakly linked records can imply a motive the evidence does not support.

text: Do not reject a theory only for one loose point; that point may be a detail the theorist has not yet explained.
Unguarded speakers who vent, complain or boast while believing no one is listening let slip grievances, money complaints and facts such as times.
when: A witness is complaining or boasting, or believes they are alone.
why: Their guard is down, so they say more than they would in company.

text: A suspect may reveal guilt through an unprompted remark that shows knowledge only the culprit could have.
when: A suspect has partial knowledge and is questioned on a related topic.
why: Knowledge slips out when the suspect is not guarding that detail.

text: A slip can betray a hidden purpose when the listener is reading the speaker closely and the speaker accepts a question as shared experience.
when: a listener probes a character's assumptions
why: the slip reveals knowledge or feeling the speaker tried to keep back

text: A trusted confidant may receive a disclosure and accept it as a plain fact without comment.
when: a secret is shared with a trusted person
why: trust makes disclosure feel ordinary

text: Players often accept an odd detail that comes with a brief, offhand explanation and move on without probing its real purpose.
when: an unusual item or action is given a dismissive, plausible reason
why: a casual explanation seems to close the question

text: Investigators tend to suspect people whose earlier remarks seem sinister, which makes them easy targets for planted evidence.
when: a suspect has made an earlier controversial statement
why: Prior impressions bias which person is considered suspicious

text: A confidante who has long shared a household's private matters can serve as a witness to them.
when: when a character has heard household secrets over time

text: A belief voiced casually early can later shape how the audience reads a related object or event, when it is recalled at the right moment.
A chance companion, such as a stranger who knows a family's lawyer, can supply facts about debts, inheritance and heirs.
Share a sensitive fact only with people who cannot be kept from learning it otherwise, since shared confidences spread beyond the intended circle.
when: when deciding whom to tell a secret
why: Information reaches people who cannot be excluded.

text: A plan can advance through a seemingly casual meeting that a natural occasion explains, with trust built across several steps.
when: an outsider needs access to a household or group
why: each contact looks ordinary alone, so the plan goes unnoticed

text: A hint dropped in a careless tone may be deliberate, so the listener must decide whether it was meant.
A captive who cannot speak openly can leave a sign that means nothing to captors but is meaningful to a partner who knows their habits.
Place a casual NPC comment or ambient detail naming a location from a document the player has read, so it links two threads of the story.
why: A small, offhand connection can make the player see a link between separate leads.

text: Let NPCs repeat dialogue exactly so players can compare versions and catch contradictions.
when: Designing NPCs whose statements may later be tested for consistency.
why: Identical wording gives the player a fixed reference for detecting changes or lies.

text: A public briefing that discloses only accurate facts and withholds witness testimony can lull a guilty party into false security.
when: when investigators want to buy room to work
why: the guilty party relaxes and acts less carefully

text: A bulletin board or rumor system can expose a player's private actions, and the details in each note can reveal which NPCs were present.
when: Designing public rumor or notice systems.
why: Public notes carry details that reveal the observers' positions.

text: Letting one's own knowledge spread through casual conversation alerts the culprit to what is known.
A sympathetic confidant can leak a private plan without meaning to, especially when trying to offer reassurance.
Treating a casual remark as settled testimony is a common error; asides need checking before they count as facts.
1) Ask a witness to repeat a written or spoken statement several times. 2) Compare the versions word for word. 3) Fix the exact wording for analysis once it stays unchanged.
when: A written or spoken statement is central evidence and its author is defensive or unknown.
why: Identical repetition shows whether the witness recalls a fixed text or rebuilds a story each time.

text: 1) Have the witness repeat the exact key questions and answers. 2) Record the wording verbatim. 3) Compare it with the relayed summary before accepting it.
when: When fixing testimony that passed through intermediaries
why: A paraphrase can shift meaning

text: 1) Have an intermediary raise the topic casually. 2) Watch the listener's face and answer. 3) Follow up gently later on any omission.
when: The witness is open to talk, or the questioner wants to avoid signalling interest.

text: Record suspect and witness statements word for word, so exact phrasing can be read back or compared later.
when: Conducting interviews whose accounts may be checked later.
why: Paraphrase loses the details that reveal contradictions.

text: Introduce a minor character or detail casually early; later show why it mattered when the player revisits that thread.
when: Designing clues that seem trivial when first introduced.
why: Delayed significance rewards players who remember and revisit earlier details; significance often depends on corroboration arriving afterward.

text: Let a confidante NPC reveal secrets only after the player earns trust, and mark those secrets as testimony.
when: when designing a confidante NPC
why: Trust gates information and gives it evidential weight.

text: Raise a confidant's rivalry or loyalty once, then let it return when the related character's name draws a suspicious look.
when: Writing secondary characters with ties to suspects
why: Reintroduced loyalties add suspicion without new exposition

text: Use an NPC's silence in a bulletin or feed to hint at coming events without confirming them.
when: Designing news or notice feeds in a game world
why: Absence hints at change while keeping uncertainty

text: Give a confidant NPC who supplies an alibi a reason to protect someone, so players must weigh the testimony.
when: designing alibi-giving NPCs
why: motive turns the alibi into a judgment call rather than a plain fact

text: When a detail appears in public that its owners denied supplying, treat the leak as a question to trace to its source rather than a closed matter.
when: Private case details appear in press or public reports
why: Denials do not rule out leaks from anyone with access elsewhere

text: A motive inferred from a loose timeline can be wrong even when it fits the people involved.
Leave an unverifiable claim as a loose thread that players can test later, paying off only if a living witness confirms it.
A loot pattern that takes only one kind of material from a shrine suggests a particular taker and reason, so the player can infer an NPC's motive.
Let a defeated NPC's inventory carry letters, tickets and other items that point to other places or people, so loot doubles as investigation.
when: when designing NPC inventories
why: Clue-bearing loot links the investigation forward.

text: Ask what a record leaves out: one unlisted fact can reconcile contradictions and reveal a pattern's structure; a missing consequence shows what a complete account must contain.
when: when known facts do not form a coherent reading, or an account is detailed but skips a logical consequence
why: The missing item often explains contradictions that look unrelated.

text: Mark which records survived and which are lost, and build an in-world archive with lost, partial and undated records, so players must piece together the timeline themselves.
Grounds for strict examination of a suspect, such as notoriety, a co-accused's naming, or unexplained harm, are not sufficient for conviction on their own.
when: when deciding whether a clue justifies questioning
why: suspicion can open an inquiry but cannot by itself establish guilt

text: Gaps in a split account show events no narrator witnessed, which a reader must treat as unknown rather than as nothing happening.
A gap in a diary may mean nothing happened or that the entry was never written, so a blank day cannot be read without further evidence.
when: When an expected entry is absent from a personal record.
why: Absence is ambiguous between no event and no record.

text: Many original records are removed, transferred to other archives, lost, or held privately, so copies can lack pages or sources.
A missing part or original may have an innocent explanation; test that explanation rather than accepting or dismissing it at once, and ask for the original rather than a summary.
when: a part or source document is absent from its expected place
why: The original's wording can be compared against a summary.

text: A single gap in an otherwise maintained set is a trace; compare it with untouched matching items nearby to see whether it was singled out.
when: a set of objects is normally kept in order by someone
why: Deviation from a consistent standard suggests a different handler or a disruption; the maintainer would not normally allow it.

text: Treat gaps in a witness's account, such as a blank stretch or unnamed employer, address or identifier, as signs to examine, though some omissions are trivial.
when: when an account is internally consistent but skips a period or contact, or a witness cannot name an employer, address or other identifier
why: Some omissions hide significant events while others are trivial; missing identifiers can point to concealment or an unverifiable story.

text: When an action leaves one part behind, like a spilled match or torn document, search pockets and nearby belongings for the missing counterpart.
when: when a partial record or item is found on a body or at a scene
why: The missing half is likely kept close at hand by whoever took it.

text: A missing document is evidence: reason about what the lost set would have proved, and treat the gap as something the story must explain.
when: A key document is absent from a case.

text: Check unexplained gaps in time against known cycles or schedules, since a gap matching a schedule suggests an interruption rather than a break.
when: a long unexplained interval appears
why: schedules can account for gaps that otherwise look like abandonment

text: When a lead dismisses a case as routine, the gap this leaves lets a junior actor investigate without formal approval of the theory.
The intervals between dated events, such as a reversal within a day or a slow worsening over days, show how a situation shifted.
why: Change in a situation appears in the spacing and direction of dated events.

text: A missing public report that should exist, such as news of a death, is evidence that the matter is being concealed.
Reward players who find gaps or conflicts between witness statements that questioning has not yet closed.
why: discovering contradictions is the act that moves the investigation forward

text: Local memory can lose a site's history; land records can recover who owned or used a place earlier.
Note missing closing records, such as formal releases or farewell letters, as explicit gaps in the trail.
when: Reconstructing a departure with no final document

text: A missing document needed to make a plan work is itself a clue pointing to who must explain the gap.
Internal gaps make a story look disconnected, and a target may come to suspect a fabrication designed to frighten.
Details lost from memory stay unrecovered without new evidence, so the trail goes cold.
why: Memory cannot regenerate specifics that were never retained

text: When supporting records are lost, a claim falls back on the claimant's sworn word, which a contradicting sworn witness can overturn.
Evidence written off as lost can later arrive through an unexpected outside channel, which can reopen an investigation.
When key physical evidence such as a grave is lost over time, the investigator is left with testimony and no object to examine, and the missing evidence drives the search.
when: A key site has been removed or no living person can locate it.
why: Without the physical object, the investigator cannot confirm the story.

text: The blank space left by a removed section, divided by line spacing, estimates how many entries were removed.
when: when a torn document has a missing section above surviving text
why: Gap size bounds the amount of missing text.

text: A gap in an archival record is not proof that nothing happened; missing entries say nothing about omitted events, and an argument from absence needs independent support.
when: When inferring intent from a gap in documents.
why: Gaps can result from archival loss.

text: A timeline gap or inconsistency is not proof of guilt or falsity; treat it as a question to test, since a claim with gaps can still be true.
why: A gap has many innocent explanations until it is checked; inconsistency gives grounds for doubt, not a verdict.

text: Without an established normal pattern, a later spike or deviation gives the observer nothing to compare against, so it goes unnoticed.
when: Designing a pattern meant to reveal an anomaly.
why: An anomaly is detectable only relative to a known baseline.

text: Losing or failing to date a document can remove the evidence that would have settled the question.
when: Handling written evidence

text: A missing letter removes the means of knowing the lure, so gaps in evidence need other routes to recover them.
Skipped diary entries and late-arriving letters change what each character knows at a given point, and missing records invite readers to fill holes wrongly.
when: Reconstructing a timeline from incomplete records.
why: Gaps alter what characters could know, and readers tend to guess at what is missing.

text: A missing spare key is suggestive of a hidden copy but does not prove one exists; it should be treated as a lead rather than conclusive evidence.
why: Absence of a duplicate may reflect incomplete searching rather than its non-existence

text: The most important link often sits inside an unexplained gap, so a chain with gaps must not be treated as complete.
Missing a will made casually or stored outside official papers can hide the real motive from the start of an investigation.
when: Searching for a beneficiary
why: Informal documents are often filed away from official records

text: Keeping notes only of conclusions loses the facts that support them, making later checking impossible.
why: without the underlying facts, conclusions cannot be tested

text: Ideas stated in writing may be misread or exaggerated by others, so an author's position should be checked before it is used as a motive.
when: Using a character's written ideology as evidence.
why: Readers and critics can distort a text's meaning.

text: Not every gap in a text is meaningful; some come from damage, padding or later editing, so treat readings of gaps as interpretations.
when: Interpreting erasures or missing stretches as clues.
why: Gaps have many causes, and reading one as meaningful can mislead.

text: A gap in the record may come from exclusion of the defence rather than from the absence of a defence, so do not conclude that no answer existed.
when: Reading a trial record with little or no defence testimony.
why: Exculpatory evidence can be blocked from reaching decision-makers, leaving no trace in the outcome.

text: A missing entry can make an event look as if it never happened, and an extra entry can do the reverse, so first check whether the record should contain it.
Losing track of who held an object and where it was kept breaks the logic of a locked-room event, since the custody record is what makes the impossibility checkable.
when: An object moves between locked or guarded places.
why: Custody gaps let the player doubt the event instead of testing it.

text: Citation markers placed inconsistently, before or after the claim, can attach a reference to the wrong statement.
Failing to record an appearance, through no photograph or few meetings, leaves a search dependent on fragile memory.
when: when a suspect's appearance is not documented
why: Without a stored record, recognition depends on individual recall.

text: Read each gap in an event sequence as a question about who had opportunity during that interval, and ask what the unseen party did there, since unexplained time is where unseen actions hide.
when: when an interval between two events is unaccounted for
why: A gap only matters if someone was present to act within it; unexplained time is where unseen actions can hide.

text: A missing lot in a record is evidence of absence, not proof of innocence.
when: A record shows no trace of an item or transaction.
why: Absence may reflect concealment or lost records equally.

text: Count a lost record as evidence neither for nor against a claim.
Record a broken item's missing piece together with the owner's account of it, since the gap itself can be a clue.
Hours without coverage must be filled with evidence from outside the window, such as companions' accounts of where a person was.
when: a suspect was unobserved for a stretch of time
why: Unobserved time cannot be cleared by coverage alone.

text: Turn missing pages into a deliberate investigation hook, with a surviving copy held by an NPC who may or may not share it.
when: Designing a clue trail built around a partly lost document.

text: Let a missing register entry or an inscription that avoids a claim matter to a later puzzle.
when: Designing a puzzle that depends on an absent or non-committal record.
why: Gaps in records give players a clue to pursue.

text: Items are rarely truly lost; people more often believe they have lost something, so a loss report often reflects their habits of storing things.
when: A person reports losing an item.
why: People tend to misremember where they last used or put an item.

text: A stored item's absence is often discovered only when someone needs it, so the loss is revealed at the moment of use.
when: A small or personal object is kept out of sight.
why: Nobody checks for an item until it is required.

text: The person who carried an object may notice its loss quickly, which can expose a theft sooner than the thief expects.
when: when an object is regularly carried by one person
why: the carrier is most likely to notice missing items

text: Place dropped or lost-and-found items in a level as trace evidence that players can link to an NPC.
When a hidden item is sold within an undifferentiated lot, its trail ends with the buyer unless the seller recorded where each unit went.
A lost item that is later stolen creates a loss-then-theft sequence, so the order of events itself becomes a timeline clue.
A list of losses alone does not identify a culprit; it needs surrounding context before it can point to anyone.
1) Ask the owner to list what is missing. 2) Compare the list with the scene. 3) Infer the likely culprit's kind or purpose from which items were taken.
when: a reported loss can be checked against the scene
why: the set of missing items is itself evidence

text: 1) Determine the quantity taken. 2) Compare it to a known harmful or significant threshold. 3) Judge the theft's seriousness from that comparison.
when: when a missing object could be a weapon, clue, or means of harm
why: the same loss matters differently depending on how it relates to a threshold

text: Use a lost-item hook to start dialogue with an NPC who would otherwise refuse to talk.
Treat overheard rumours as low-reliability clues or log entries, upgrading them only when an independent second source confirms them.
when: When designing rumour clues or building a witness log for an investigation.

text: Rooms holding items of little resale value are unlikely to be disturbed by thieves, so their hidden contents tend to stay undisturbed.
why: Thieves seek goods they can sell.

text: A small payment paired with a claim that the evidence is worth little can prompt a source to offer more to prove its value.
why: Sources may want to defend their worth.

text: Low-status workers such as stable-hands or servants often know routines, visitors and habits, see more than the powerful suppose, and share for small rewards, but are unreliable by default.
when: Seeking routine information about a target.
why: Routine contact gives them observations others lack.

text: Several facts pointing the same way do not prove guilt when none shows timing or exclusivity; they remain circumstantial.
when: Building a case from circumstantial evidence.
why: Coincidence can explain several weak facts together.

text: When available valuables are small, a theft motive looks implausible, which pushes players toward other explanations.
Use magnification and raking, low-angle light to reveal small traces that plain lighting hides.
when: When a scene is weathered or handled and remaining evidence is faint or small.
why: Low-angle light casts shadows that bring out surface relief.

text: Use small, low-stakes probes when proof is lacking or a direct accusation would cause scandal.
Typewriters develop individual wear over time, so characters degrade in distinctive ways and two machines rarely produce identical output.
A hidden item can be found through a physical snag that the searcher recognizes from earlier experience, making the snag the moment of discovery.
when: When evidence is concealed inside furniture or containers
why: Earlier experience links the jam to its cause

text: Independent machine records, such as utility load curves, fix event times without depending on witness memory, so they are preferred when witness times are unreliable.
when: witness times conflict or are doubtful and a machine record exists
why: instrument timestamps do not depend on recall

text: 1) Collect a sample from the suspect's device. 2) Compare its defective characters with a known sample under magnification. 3) Count how many defects match across the sample.
when: A suspect's device could have produced a written or printed document.
why: Shared, distinctive wear indicates a common source.

text: 1) Match the suspected object's weight and position to the original. 2) Set up a substitute that holds it at a fixed distance. 3) Release it and check whether it leaves the same trace.
when: A trace has a plausible cause but the mechanism has not been shown to work.
why: A reproduction that matches the original turns a theory into repeatable evidence.

text: A machine-based match identifies the device, not the user, so a machine trace should only narrow suspects and a second independent source is needed to name the person.
when: Designing clues that narrow but do not name a suspect
why: Two independent sources are needed to pin down an identity; the link is to the device, not to the person

text: Use a mechanism-driven reveal only when the timing of the reveal is itself a clue; crimes without a performance need only discovery.
A maker can identify its own product from construction features such as material, reinforcement, fittings, and standard sizes.
when: an object carries a maker's mark or has distinctive build features

text: A manufacturer's stamp on an object can point to a retailer, opening a separate line of inquiry.
when: an object carries a maker's name
why: a traceable source links the item to a shop and its customers

text: An honest maker's account can contradict a suspect's version, so the discrepancy needs explaining rather than dismissing.
when: a maker's records conflict with a suspect's statement
why: either account may be wrong, and the conflict often hides the key fact

text: 1) List distinctive faults or traits, such as machine, paper or handwriting, in each document. 2) Compare the lists across documents. 3) Link documents only when several matching traits agree, not on a single shared fault, to expose a shared author or source.
when: two documents might share a source, or a document's origin is disputed
why: Several matches give a stronger link than one

text: 1) Read the item's labels and marks. 2) Contact the retailer or maker. 3) Check its staff or customer records to narrow the candidates.
when: when a clue is a manufactured object such as clothing or paper

text: Compare a trace item against the local stock or household supply to identify its type and narrow where it came from.
when: When an item is common enough that its origin is in question.
why: Matching to local stock reveals which source it likely belongs to.

text: Keep a current table of symbol-to-letter pairs once several are known, so mappings do not get confused.
Old luggage labels can reveal a person's earlier ships and hotels, giving a traceable past.
Make mail and notes into items, since the address on a letter reveals who knows where the player stays and interception creates risk.
when: Designing in-game correspondence.

text: Marked correspondence can separate secret items from ordinary mail and fix a timeline when dated records note the marking.
when: Letters carry a distinctive mark or handling instruction
why: The marking signals restricted content and can be matched against dated notes

text: Design a marked item so each handoff leaves a record, letting players trace its path through the world.
when: when building clue trails for a mystery

text: A marked object given to one of two look-alikes ties suspicion to that person, so its theft or disposal can shift who looks guilty.
why: the object links identity to a physical trace

text: A stamped mark or initials can identify an object's owner and link it to a named person, but shows ownership, not action; someone else may have placed or altered it.
Examine every item of correspondence, not only the expected ones, since a witness's written account can arrive after that witness has died.
Show dream or flashback scenes in rich detail while marking them as unreliable, so players must test them against other clues.
when: Presenting a character's memory or dream in a game journal or cutscene.
why: Rich detail with an unreliability marker invites verification rather than blind trust.

text: Hide matching objects in two locations and require several matched objects before a quest state changes, so single common items act as hints rather than proof.
when: Designing evidence checks in a game.
why: Multiple independent matches give more reliable confirmation than one common item.

text: Pair the method of the act with its motive when disclosing the solution, so the audience understands both.
when: at the final reveal

text: Matching amounts between two people's payments can reveal a hidden link, such as dependence or a secret deal.
when: when two people's finances show regular, matching flows

text: Ask how the suspect came to hold the agent at that moment; a proposed mechanism without a means of access remains unsupported.
Reason about means from the victim's surroundings, since an alternative tool is likely to exist nearby and the suspect may know of it.
when: When the primary means is unrecovered or unclear
why: Familiar environments supply tools that people can use

text: Link a poison to a workplace or to the suspect's training, such as a firm that uses the substance or a chemistry background, to establish means.
Give each suspect a motive and an opportunity, and let a new witness reframe a relationship so the player reconsiders motive.
when: Designing suspects for a mystery
why: Opportunity plus motive gives the player grounds to test each suspect

text: In a suspicion analysis, weigh motive, knowledge of the setting, and opportunity separately; a suspect who has all three is the strongest candidate even without proof.
when: A case has a sincere-seeming ally who knows much about the victim and setting
why: Combining the three factors narrows suspicion.

text: Several suspects can each satisfy every apparent requirement of guilt while being innocent, because weak individual links can look persuasive when accumulated.
when: A case has many suspects with circumstantial evidence
why: Each thin link appears stronger in combination than it is alone

text: A strong motive combined with no provable alibi can build a convincing case against a person who is innocent.
when: when a suspect has a clear motive but cannot confirm their whereabouts
why: Motive and unverifiable alibi together create an apparently complete case.

text: Naming a hidden mastermind without evidence can send an investigation after the wrong person.
when: Suspecting a concealed controlling figure.
why: A suspicion without support diverts attention from the people actually involved.

text: The most visible motive can still be false, so a motive alone should not settle the question.
when: A suspect has an obvious motive.
why: Visibility of a motive does not establish that it caused the event.

text: Opportunity alone does not show motive, and motive alone does not show access. Each category must be established as a separate deduction.

1) State what the act was meant to achieve. 2) Identify the outcome that serves that purpose. 3) Look for the person who needed that outcome. 4) Match the motive to the actor who carried the act out, which may differ from the beneficiary.
when: An act's purpose is clear but its doer is not.
why: Narrowing suspects by purpose targets the person who needed the result.

text: A medical cause of death explains how the body failed, not who or what set that failure in motion.
Medical time-of-death estimates rest on signs like stiffening and wound angle; they are judgments with wide margins, such as a seven-to-ten-hour window, not a fixed hour.
when: Using a medical estimate in a timeline.
why: Medical evidence narrows time only within its margin.

text: Treat a condition confirmed by medical evidence as an observed fact rather than a claim.
Read medical findings as consistent with several scenarios rather than as proof of one specific cause.
why: Many different events can produce the same physical result.

text: Let a medical NPC give a range rather than a single time, and let players combine that range with other NPCs' sightings.
when: When writing medical or forensic dialogue for a mystery
why: Ranges invite cross-referencing, which makes the player's deduction active.

text: A disguised person who fears being watched chooses a private spot off the road to talk, since anyone nearby might be observing.
when: A disguised character arranges a meeting in public
why: Suspicion of watchers moves the meeting to a hidden place

text: A character who frames a private matter as a business transaction reveals where their priorities lie.
Observers often miss earlier warning signs and notice only a sudden change in another person's manner.
when: tracking changes in someone's behaviour
why: Gradual signals fade into the background until a sharp shift

text: When a person fails to return at the expected time, list other places they could have gone before treating the absence as serious.
when: An expected return does not happen.
why: Alternative locations often explain the absence.

text: A missed routine is evidence: an unserved breakfast alongside a slept-in bed can point to an early departure.
A missed meeting can itself be a clue: check whether the witness has left, or whether a shadowing agent has reported on their movements.
A recurring private act of penance gives a character a visible sign of lasting guilt that players can learn to read over time.
Sort testimony into what one person reports alone and what several people can check. Sincere witnesses can still be wrong, so this sorting tests evidence, not honesty.
when: Evaluating testimony about unseen events

text: Missed appointments can each name someone waiting, which reveals who will notice the absence.
when: When a character fails to meet scheduled commitments.
why: Each missed commitment has a dependent who registers the failure.

text: A scheduled meeting that fails to happen shrinks the time left and forces a decision, so suspense rises as waiting or acting becomes urgent.
when: A long-awaited revelation is scheduled
why: Failure removes the expected path and raises the stakes

text: A private reaction noticed by another person can be turned into a public confrontation, making unease a visible event.
A missed promise or appointment can have an innocent explanation, so treat the gap as a point to test; in game design, give the player a discoverable innocent explanation.
when: an NPC or person misses a promise, appointment or deadline
why: The same missed obligation supports both guilt and innocence, and the gap alone is not proof of wrongdoing.

text: A witness who turns away during an unmasking can miss the moment of reveal, so the investigator must keep watching the subject closely.
when: A distressed or sensitive witness is present during the reveal.
why: Emotional withdrawal can take the witness's attention away from the decisive moment.

text: A witness who moves the talk to a private setting narrows who can verify their account, even when the stated reason sounds plausible.
A staff member who was out of the room may simply have missed an arrival.
when: Relying on the absence of a sighting
why: People cannot see everything in their area

text: Use a signal code only while it stays private to its users, since a code others can read stops protecting them.
when: when choosing how to communicate a secret

text: Agree a regular contact schedule and treat a missed message as a signal to return at once, which can trigger a new event.
Verify one witness claim privately, since asking about it in company can alert others involved.
Let an NPC privately confirm whether another character was present, and record that answer as a checkable alibi.
when: When designing alibi systems for a game.
why: A private confirmation gives the player a source they can verify against other evidence.

text: A message left in a hidden cache may describe an observer and warn of future meetings.
When an adversary passes intelligence in person, a mail channel is unlikely to be their route for the secret.
Use in-world dialect or code words as signals that identify a faction or origin.
The height of a wall message shows the writer's posture; a message low to the floor suggests the writer was lying or sitting there.
A message that points to a specific object, with no prior agreement, implies its sender saw that object up close, making the message evidence of that knowledge.
A message or call arriving at the peak of expectation can give a new lead and send the protagonist away.
A notice left in plain view can force a culprit to change the staging of a crime.
A hired hand may not know who hired them, so an investigation can stop at the middleman.
1) List every person a message passes through. 2) Note whether each actually saw the next. 3) Confirm the final recipient received it.
when: when a claim depends on a message passing through several hands
why: Anyone who handled a message had a chance to read or change it.

text: 1) Examine typeface and paper to exclude source categories. 2) Detach fragments and check their reverse side for printed text. 3) Match the printed source to a physical object.
when: a composed message made of printed fragments

text: 1) Note the initials and pickup address in the notice. 2) Ask the holding clerk who claimed the item and when. 3) Question each claimant. 4) Link the claimants to the notice.
when: a message is held for pickup at a post office or register
why: Claim records turn an anonymous address into a chain of people.

text: Use a message's content as a clue only when its tone or wording differs from the sender's usual style.
when: Reading a short or unusual note

text: Printed appeals reach only people who can read, so an illiterate person must be reached by word of mouth instead.
Track each message's writer, poster and reader, so the player can rebuild the prompt behind an NPC's action.
Deliver a faction's story through in-world documents such as notes or newspapers, released as the player progresses.
Date a received message and check what it prompted afterward, since that link can explain later actions that otherwise look odd.
when: when a later action has no obvious cause

text: Do not treat an intermediary's account or advice as neutral; relayed information is weaker than direct observation, and each go-between's stake shapes it.
when: a third party or go-between relays information, gives advice, or later describes a dispute they calmed
why: Calming a scene shapes its outcome and how it is later reported; intermediaries often have stakes in the outcome they recommend.

text: An object can pass during distraction or a routine gesture such as a handshake, so the holder may not notice and bystanders register nothing unusual.
when: an exchange happens while attention is elsewhere, or the gesture is familiar and the effect minor and fast
why: attention is focused elsewhere, or a routine action is not perceived as an event, so the transfer leaves no memory

text: A person who restates news shapes it through their manner and wish to calm others, so the official version reflects the speaker's purpose.
The person who introduces an outsider may gain the most from the scheme, so control over it is not always obvious.
when: a scheme involves an introduction
why: the introducer can benefit while appearing peripheral

text: Wording in documents from unfamiliar periods or conventions can mislead modern readers, so the phrasing itself is evidence to be read carefully.
why: Terms can carry meanings that differ from the reader's current usage.

text: An anonymous or private record could never have been publicly checked, so the absence of challenge says nothing about its accuracy.
when: assessing an anonymous or private account

text: Treat an unfinished message as a hypothesis, not proof: the writer may have been interrupted or lost consciousness.
when: a found document ends mid-sentence
why: Readers tend to fill gaps with their own assumptions.

text: Track which object passed through which person's hands, since a handover is often the decisive step in a chain of evidence.
why: Transfers between people are the points where an object's link to a person can be established.

text: Passing the story from one NPC's testimony to another can reveal different parts of the same event.
when: Structuring a story across several narrators
why: Each narrator sees a different part of the event

text: Examine the medium of a message, such as handwriting, to check whether it matches the named sender, since the writing can reveal who actually produced it.
when: A message appears to hide its true author.
why: The physical form of a message can carry evidence that its stated sender did not write it.

text: An introducer's endorsement should start a verification check, not replace it. The examiner still tests the claimant before trusting them.
Uncut pages suggest an owner never read an item, but unread items may be display pieces rather than signs of concealment.
when: judging whether a possession was used
why: Display items are kept without being used.

text: Add a mediator NPC trusted by every faction, so the player can end a feud without taking sides.
when: designing faction conflict resolution
why: Universal trust removes the need to choose a side.

text: Each handoff of an object, such as a repair, sale, resale or handover to outside staff, creates a record or witness held outside the owner's control that can trace it.
when: an object passes through third parties such as repairers, sellers or staff
why: Third parties keep their own records, which can reveal movements the owner hoped to hide.

text: A go-between who is not the named recipient may refuse to deliver an item, which forces the recipient to come in person.
when: An item must reach a specific person who is not reachable through an intermediary.
why: The intermediary is bound by the instruction that the item goes only to its named recipient.

text: A warning passed through an intermediary lets a hidden actor act without exposing themselves, adding a second line of action.
An intermediary can carry an offer while the sender stays hidden, so the terms are delivered plainly and the sender remains out of reach.
when: A character wants to negotiate without being seen.
why: Separating sender from message protects the sender and keeps the terms impersonal.

text: A report that an official never reads forces the player to follow up through another route.
when: designing reporting systems between NPCs

text: Intercepted correspondence can name a meeting or reveal overheard talk, opening new lines of inquiry.
Intercepted correspondence reveals an address a target is known to use, so that location becomes the first place a pursuer would watch.
when: A pursuer reads a target's letters.
why: People tend to return to trusted contacts and known places.

text: A clue that is never reinforced may be forgotten entirely, and a clue heard before the wider picture forms may have no context to attach to.
Media coverage of a lead, such as touched-up photos and features, raises public belief in it and sustains the decoy.
Subordinates may hush or intercept complaints aimed at powerful people to win favor, so the powerful appear to escape scrutiny without any direct order from them.
when: complaints or reports point toward a faction's leaders
why: Subordinates gain standing by pleasing those above them.

text: If the named recipient of a withheld item is unreachable, the clue it carries becomes a dead end.
A message passed through several paid intermediaries can hide its true sender, and a poor description can send investigators after the wrong person.
when: Tracing the origin of a message or action
why: Each link adds distance and can conceal the origin

text: An introducer's presence can invite confidences that the introducer would rather not hear.
when: When an introducer sits in on an interview

text: The trusted go-between may end up exposed to the same risk, so weigh that before setting the bait.
when: Planning to use a trusted person as bait
why: Contact that exposes an enemy can also expose the intermediary

text: A concealment that relies on an unread document can collapse if that document says something different.
A partial clue that is never completed frustrates the audience unless the gap is explained later.
when: Using a cut-off clue
why: Unresolved gaps feel like errors

text: Every key handoff widens the set of possible suspects, so an owner's habit of sharing keys can multiply the people who could have acted.
why: Each person given access becomes a candidate

text: When one person passes a message or object to another, that link is often the weakest point in the chain.
when: Tracing a message or item through several people
why: Handovers are rarely witnessed or recorded

text: Repeating an account without noting how many people have passed it along hides how far it has drifted from the original event.

1) Identify the subject's routine from repeated sightings at the same place and hour. 2) Estimate the arrival time with a margin. 3) Check the estimate against every known alternative schedule before committing.
when: when planning an intercept, rescue or observation of a routine subject
why: Repeated sightings separate routine from chance, but a single assumed schedule can fail.

text: 1) Ask why the messenger came. 2) Identify who sent them. 3) Establish what that sender directs them to do. 4) Note who the messenger reports to.
when: Tracing a message passed through several characters
why: Each link shows who controls whom and whose interests the message serves.

text: Make a messenger's motives visible through distress, insistence or evasion, since these signal stakes and whether a delivered lead is real or false.
when: a go-between delivers a message with emotional intensity or specific handling demands, or NPC messengers deliver leads
why: Emotional cues and handling instructions reveal the stakes behind the message; visible motives let players judge a lead's trustworthiness.

text: Do not let a secret channel carry a plot point without showing who could intercept it, since mail routed through others may be opened before arrival.
Do not treat press reports as evidence, since parties with a stake in the outcome may have shaped them.
when: when weighing published accounts
why: Stakes give sources reason to distort what is published.

text: Let an intermediary NPC pass along a witness's location and reward players for tracing that relay.
why: Relays turn the search into a chain of discovery

text: Let a friendly intermediary with standing unlock a locked location or body for the player.
Unlock the true version of a document only after the player finds the contradicting physical detail in the decoy.
when: designing a document-based reveal
why: Gating the true version on discovery ties progress to observation

text: After a briefed handover, let the in-world authority's response confirm the state of the case.
when: when designing a case-closing step
why: The response gives the player clear feedback on the outcome.

text: Have a messenger linked to the target summon the player at a key moment, and let the player decide whether to trust the call.
Confidence in one's own method and pride can lead an investigator to dismiss a rival approach, which shows a personal stake in the answer.
Method of exclusion: after ruling out other causes, the remaining candidate gains suspicion even on thin evidence.
when: the list of possible causes is complete

text: Reviewing past cases can show which forensic methods would have changed their outcomes, supporting evaluation of new techniques.
Ask whether a suspect would act this way, not only could; a method clashing with their habits or a tool ill-suited to the task suggests another actor or staging.
when: A suspect has a motive but the method, staging or tool seems out of character or ill-suited to the task.
why: Possibility alone does not establish the act; out-of-character details point to a different doer or a staged scene.

text: Treat the choice of method as evidence: ask why it was chosen and who would think of it, since the answer reveals needs and narrows the suspect pool.
when: A crime or visitor uses an unusual or particular method.
why: Uncommon methods reflect specific knowledge or interest, which narrows the suspect pool.

text: Offenders tend to reuse effective methods, so incidents sharing a distinctive method, or a present crime matching a documented earlier one, may link to one actor or an accomplice.
when: Several incidents or a present crime share a distinctive method with records of earlier cases.
why: Criminals reuse what has worked before; method fit, not only the target, supports the link.

text: Body disposal is hard: bulky, heavy, chemically unstable, emit strong odours, and retain identifying structure; realistic options reduce to burial or dismemberment with dispersal, both tending to lead to discovery.
when: Judging whether a concealment or body disposal is plausible.
why: Physical properties of remains make concealment hard, and each option leaves traces investigators can follow.

text: A cold, methodical killing can be read as the act of a mind that is mad in a method-driven way, shifting the inquiry toward the killer's mental state.
Judge a physical detail by what a skilled practitioner would normally use or do; deviations from expected practice suggest a different source.
when: Assessing whether an explanation fits the evidence
why: Professional methods leave characteristic traces.

text: An investigator should reconstruct the method of a crime, not only identify the weapon, because the method explains how the act was done unseen.
Ask how a clue was made. If no tool that could make the marks is found, the method stays open even when the source matches.
when: a clue's source is confirmed but its means is not
why: a clean source match does not explain the method

text: Sound detection rests on a method rather than inspiration, and that method is what checks a gut feeling.
Reconstruct a hidden method from what is absent, such as smell, supply lines or residue, and from changes that would clear evidence of it.
when: Ordinary examination finds no cause
why: A method that leaves no positive trace is revealed by what is missing.

text: Trace each method in the solution to a known precedent so the way the plot was built feels plausible.
when: explaining how a plan or trick was executed
why: Documented precedents make the method credible

text: A cleaned scene still records the cleaning, so reason backward from what a concealer destroyed and what they missed to learn what they feared.
when: A scene shows wiping or tidying more elaborate than the crime needed

text: Use cleanup evidence to establish how a concealment was done, not who did it.
To explain why a community acted on a now-doubtful assumption, reconstruct the shared frame that defined its evidence rather than judging each person's choice alone.
when: when analyzing a past group decision
why: the frame determines what each member could treat as proof

text: An unusual scheme signals unusual means of execution, not that the case is impossible.
when: A crime seems impossible under ordinary assumptions
why: Atypical methods can satisfy conditions that ordinary ones cannot

text: Read the method of dismemberment or damage as a profile of the perpetrator's skill, such as clean joint separation suggesting anatomical or butchery training.
when: Physical damage shows a consistent and deliberate method.
why: Technique reveals the skill and training of the person who carried it out.

text: A method copied from a published account may fake an effect or serve as cover, so it can point to the wrong suspect, since a human actor can produce the reported result.
when: A documented technique is used to fake an apparent supernatural event or to cover a death.
why: Published accounts are easy to imitate, so the reported result may come from a person rather than the method's author or the claimed cause.

text: Treating a similarity of method as proof of an accomplice is a leap; it stays a suspicion until evidence supports it.
A conclusion about who did it, without an explanation of how it was done, invites ridicule and resistance.
Explaining how an effect happened does not by itself reveal who caused it; the mechanism still needs a link to a person.

1) Fix the physical setting and its constraints. 2) List candidate methods, simplest first. 3) Imagine the act step by step inside it. 4) Test each candidate against evidence and physical possibility; discard failures and keep the fit. 5) Predict where a key object should be and search there.
when: Reconstructing how a crime was committed, especially a locked-room attack.
why: Reasoning from mechanism reveals the path that apparent security hides.

text: 1) Scout the target alone, ideally at night. 2) Brief the team on the layout. 3) Set timing and charges. 4) Withdraw to cover before the effect.
when: Planning a direct assault on an isolated building.
why: Solo scouting gives accurate layout detail before committing the team.

text: 1) Identify the object or means used. 2) Describe how it was delivered through a normal action. 3) Check what bystanders could actually have seen. 4) Trace who had access to the means.
1) State the observed facts in the order they were gathered. 2) Explain what each fact indicates. 3) Infer the method linking them. 4) Withhold identifying or confidential details.
when: explaining a solved case to a listener

text: 1) Compare the room's state at two times. 2) Ask why each object is in its current state and whether that state has a plausible reason. 3) Work out which action would produce it.
when: After a scene is secured and before it is handled
why: Backward reasoning from disturbances reconstructs earlier events

text: 1) Lay out the offender's actions in order: approach, entry, the act, exit. 2) Add any changes made along the way. 3) Place each physical clue at the step it explains.
when: closing a case with a fair-play reveal
why: A step-by-step replay shows the crime was possible and every clue fits

text: 1) Get the medical account of wound path, depth and nearby organs. 2) Reconstruct the victim's posture at firing. 3) Infer attacker position and intent from the angle. 4) Check the scene for facts that contradict an accident. 5) Weigh the physician's alternative readings against those facts.
when: wound position can be compared with the room layout
why: physical evidence reveals how an attack unfolded

text: 1) Describe the proposed method. 2) Check how it actually behaves: targeting a moving target, wear on the tool, where objects would land. 3) Check the victim's timing and ability to react. 4) Flag each mismatch as evidence.
when: the scene looks too neat or the proposed method looks implausible

text: 1) Identify the method and how rare its knowledge, supply, or skill is. 2) Sort possible users by how deliberately they would have acquired that knowledge. 3) Narrow the suspect pool to those in the deliberate tier. 4) Confirm the profile with a separate line of evidence.
when: The method is uncommon and its requirements can be checked.
why: Rare methods exclude most people, but the profile is only reliable when independently confirmed.

text: 1) Start from the culprit's motive. 2) Reason forward through the steps needed to act. 3) Give each link a form a witness or record can confirm. 4) Label unsupported links as guesses. 5) Prefer the reconstruction whose links are each supported.
when: a crime seems to need several coordinated steps
why: each link can then be checked separately

text: A slow-acting method is a poor tool for robbery, because the victim cannot be quickly overpowered; filter motives by the method they would require.
when: Filtering candidate motives against the chosen method.
why: The method's speed and effect limit which motives it can serve.

text: Revealing only the method protects a suspect's identity but leaves the audience unable to judge the full solution; revealing the ending allows judgment but exposes the person.
when: closing a case

text: Use an attack on the investigator at the midpoint to raise stakes without resolving the central mystery.
when: Planning the middle act of a mystery.
why: A threat to the protagonist raises tension and keeps the mystery moving.

text: A midpoint false solution, in which the apparent threat dies or flees, convinces the audience the case is closed and raises the impact of the later reversal.
when: pacing a mystery's middle act
why: Relief from a false ending makes the later reversal hit harder

text: Let the investigator's own theory be confidently wrong at the midpoint, sending the story in a new direction.
A culprit-planted object chosen to be noticed and point at the obvious suspect can mislead investigators; it feels solid until revealed as staged in final reconciliation.
when: A scene contains an object that seems to explain the crime
why: Objects placed deliberately to be noticed steer interpretation; obvious planted evidence feels solid until the reasoning shows it was staged.

text: A red herring is a plausible, dramatic explanation that lacks supporting evidence and draws attention away from the true lead.
A planted-evidence twist has a character frame an innocent person in public with a planted object, then a witness who saw the sleight exposes the frame.
Let the protagonist's concealed plan turn out to be a decoy, so the player's trust in the ally's secrecy becomes the trap.
when: Writing a twist that uses the player's trust in an ally.
why: The player feels pleased to be surprised by someone they already trusted.

text: Casting doubt on whether a central object or claim ever existed shifts investigators from asking where it went to asking whether they were deceived.
when: When a theory depends on one unverified object or claim.
why: Questioning existence undermines the premise, so attention moves from the object's location to the reliability of the observers.

text: A red herring can look like the main event, so always test what the act actually changes.
when: when evaluating a distracting event

text: Plant a false lead, such as a rumoured affair or motive, that players can check and dismiss to test their reasoning.
when: Designing clue sets for a mystery

text: A rational false explanation placed early, then corrected through the protagonist's own reported observations, makes the correction feel earned and punishes the player's skepticism.
when: When designing a mystery's first misdirect.
why: The player commits to the plausible explanation, so the later evidence carries weight.

text: Use the strongest official theory to hide the true cause, such as blaming an arrested suspect or a convenient group.
when: Building a misdirect in a mystery.
why: A well-supported wrong theory keeps the player from looking at the real cause until late.

text: Offer mundane explanations, such as mental or financial motives, to hold back a supernatural or hidden cause until late.
when: the true cause would be surprising if stated early
why: Plausible everyday explanations keep the audience's expectations grounded until the reveal.

text: A plausible outside suspect or public explanation, such as a feud, draws attention away from insiders while the true evidence builds inside the location.
when: an identity or staged-death mystery
why: Searching for an outsider keeps the player from testing the insider's account.

text: A motif repeated across many sources steers interpretation toward one frame, acting as misdirection that pushes the audience toward a supernatural reading.
A frame-up stays hidden from the characters but not the audience when the sleight is shown openly, because the audience sees the setup while the group believes the accusation.
A mystery can be built as a chain of misdirections, each stage shifting suspicion to a new suspect before a final reveal exposes a schemer hiding in plain sight.
when: designing a multi-stage whodunit
why: Each shift delays the true answer and keeps the audience guessing.

text: Misdirection by allegiance keeps the reader focused on foreign figures and outsiders while the real answer sits among the investigators and their trusted friends.
when: Designing a mystery with a hidden culprit who is part of the investigating group.
why: Readers assign suspicion by social distance, so the closest allies stay unsuspected while outsiders absorb blame.

text: A reveal can plant a wrong attribution in a source the reader trusts, then replace that identity with a second holder that independent dates settle.
Planted doubt can point an investigator in the wrong direction without changing their core belief, so the investigator may still hold the wrong conclusion.
when: When a misdirection is used against a skeptical investigator.
why: Doubt redirects attention but does not necessarily overturn an existing conviction.

text: A decoy that is too obvious leads the player to dismiss the real clue along with it.
when: when placing a distraction near a real clue

text: 1) Ask what the disturbing act actually changes. 2) List who benefits from those changes. 3) Test motives such as theft against the valuables present. 4) Discard theories that do not fit the facts.
when: when a strange act seems pointless
why: The effects of an act reveal its purpose more reliably than its appearance.

text: 1) plant an early misleading reading of a clue; 2) correct one reading in the same scene; 3) repeat the clue at a later point to make the false pattern look stronger; 4) confirm the author in a late confession.
Let the most obvious helper carry the central action without drawing attention, since errands look like ordinary service.
Keep an outside-intruder theory alive through an official voice, so the player is misled by apparent authority.
Audiences weigh conspicuous facts, such as a payment, showy accessory or boastful talk, over quieter clues like an object's construction; look beneath them.
when: a conspicuous fact is presented early or a character volunteers attention-grabbing details about an item
why: Striking facts draw attention away from the underlying cause and decisive link, so attention fixes on apparent meaning rather than function.

text: Check physical origins and possibilities before accepting a supernatural cause for a striking object, sealed scene, or loss; people otherwise skip ordinary inquiry.
when: a scene appears sealed or a loss or damage has no obvious cause
why: A mundane path is easily overlooked when a dramatic cause is assumed first.

text: Ground each misdirect in a real fact, such as a visit or borrowed item, so the false alternative is credible; weak alternatives deceive no one.
when: when designing a misleading explanation or red herring
why: Players weigh only credible alternatives, and misdirects grounded in true facts reward careful reading when overturned.

text: Reversing who threatens and who is threatened hides the motive: a character who seems to threaten the protagonist is revealed as the victim.
when: when the audience holds a strong expectation about a relationship or a late reveal reverses perceived danger
why: A coherent wrong theory is accepted in place of checking hidden dynamics, and earlier choices are recast once the threat is reversed.

text: Plausible false targets, such as a familiar cause or an early living suspect, absorb attention and worry, so the real danger goes unexamined and arrives unexpectedly.
when: A real threat is present but a more familiar cause or an early living suspect is available.
why: Plausible false targets absorb worry and attention that the true source of danger needed.

text: Readers accept a claimed security guarantee and dismiss a watching character when a confident expert declares the system impregnable, so clues placed there are easily overlooked.
when: clues are planted early and a character dismisses them
why: confident dismissal by an authority lowers the reader's suspicion of what is dismissed

text: Before accepting a plausible explanation or single-clue reading, ask what it accounts for and leaves unexplained, and check it against other evidence.
when: a conclusion rests mainly on appearances or a single clue suggests a tidy explanation
why: Plausible stories can point investigators at the wrong explanation; surface resemblance does not confirm it, and the gaps reveal red herrings.

text: Seed a plausible wrong theory early, before the solution, and label it as misdirection so players cannot tell whether it is true.
when: planning the reveal of a mystery
why: This gives the design a fair-play structure; an unresolved alternative keeps the player uncertain until the reversal.

text: Front-load a misdirect, amplifying evidence against the false suspect openly, while planting the culprit's clues early in passing and holding the decisive physical trace until mid-case.
when: Structuring clue distribution across the acts of a mystery.
why: Casually presented clues are discounted, while prominently displayed clues dominate the reader's suspicion.

text: A surface explanation for a death can be presented as a verdict the player is invited to test.
Hold a striking coincidence as an open lead rather than dismissing it or treating it as proof.
when: an unexplained coincidence links to a theory
why: it may be meaningful or merely chance

text: A scene's surface can support a neat, socially expected conclusion that is wrong, so look for a detail that fails to fit.
when: a scene suggests a simple explanation matching the people's class or occupation

text: Include some strange details in a mystery, since ordinary crimes offer few distinctive features to deduce from, while unusual details narrow the possible explanations.
when: when designing a mystery's clue set
why: Each unusual detail carries information that filters suspects

text: A surface's drying or wear pattern can expose a recent repaint and older marks beneath it, so read the pattern, not just the colour.
when: a surface looks freshly altered or mismatched
why: the pattern records how the layers were applied

text: Check a summons from someone linked to the target, since it may be a diversion that pulls watchers out of position.
A blind, such as a visible line that appears to end elsewhere, misleads only observers who look at the wrong end.
when: Concealing the true path of an operation.
why: Misdirection works only when observers attend to the decoy.

text: Let a mundane explanation carry the misdirect, so the audience accepts it before the physical proof is shown.
A character's stated fear can point the reader toward the wrong suspect, so the stated cause should be checked against other evidence.
when: A character confides a fear about another person

text: Give an innocent suspect a prior criminal record, which makes their guilt look plausible and pulls the player's first suspicion onto them.
Name plausible outside beneficiaries, such as rivals or foreign powers, to draw suspicion away from trusted insiders.
A sudden movement or noise in the dark reveals the observer's position, so the intruder may flee before being seen.
A sound such as a cart heard at speed makes a household look outward, away from the house where the real act occurs.
when: An ambiguous noise occurs near the scene
why: People interpret sounds through the context already in their minds

text: A culprit may spread suspicion across several people, so investigators holding conflicting evidence split their attention away from the real actor.
when: Several suspects have plausible but conflicting evidence against them.
why: Equal weight on many suspects dilutes focus on the one who actually acted.

text: A secondary mystery can absorb the audience's attention, and reframing it midway shifts the focus onto the real answer.
when: layering two linked mysteries in one story
why: The audience invests in the first question, so reversing it redirects belief toward the hidden truth.

text: A supernatural explanation can lead players to dismiss a clue with a plain physical cause; keep the physical reading checkable.
when: an unexplained sound is blamed on the supernatural
why: Players may accept the ghostly reading without checking the sound's ordinary cause.

text: A striking supernatural explanation distracts from and ends the search for a mundane one, so it should not be a last resort or be taken as proof.
when: designing a mystery's resolution for a sealed-room puzzle
why: A supernatural answer removes the need to reason about evidence, leaving the real answer undiscovered.

text: Dismissing an object because its surface meaning seems obvious, such as treating a stained item as plain evidence against its owner, hides its real value.
why: The surface meaning is assumed rather than tested.

text: Attributing harm to an unseen cause removes from view the human agents who relied on the claim.
why: The unseen cause draws attention away from the people who acted on it.

text: Declaring an event supernatural to avoid explaining it costs the reader's trust, especially if the claim has no checks the reader can apply.
when: Resolving a mystery with an impossible element.
why: Readers trust a puzzle more when its impossibility can be tested against evidence.

text: A narrator's emphasis on one detail can be misdirection rather than a signpost, so the player must judge which it is.
when: a detail is stressed
why: emphasis looks the same in both cases

text: Strong insistence on one person's innocence steers attention away from other suspects and can serve as misdirection.
when: a character is defended repeatedly
why: repeated defence draws attention away from others

text: A simultaneous disturbance, such as a light going out during a sound, can cover someone's movement.

1) Plant a misleading fact early. 2) Have a trusted witness fix it. 3) Let an authority dismiss a contrary clue. 4) Reopen that clue later through a lower-status witness. 5) Confirm with testimony and physical evidence.
Withhold the solution or a fact only if every clue needed to deduce it is shown on the page or in the game.
when: when delaying a mystery's answer or designing a twist or hidden solution
why: Hidden clues make the answer unfair and unreachable; a missing fact must be given first.

text: Show a deduction's reasoning clearly enough to be checked; withhold reasoning only if the detective's full explanation is given later.
when: revealing a solution to a mystery or a deduction is kept back
why: Unexplained leaps make the solver appear to have supernatural insight, and an unexplained deduction feels like a cheat if never revealed.

text: Use a supernatural explanation as a red herring, but keep visible physical traces pointing to a human actor so the eventual reveal feels earned, not a trick.
when: when a level or mystery offers a supernatural explanation for events
why: Traces that contradict the supernatural reading reward close looking, and a visible physical clue makes the natural solution feel earned rather than arbitrary.

text: Let a supernatural or unverifiable clue, such as a dream or ghost's word, open inquiry, but require a second observer or physical trace before accusation.
when: Designing investigation or accusation systems.
why: Physical traces or independent witnesses keep unverifiable clues from ending an investigation alone.

text: Pair an ambiguous gaze or object-focused hint with a second, checkable clue so players are not misled.
when: Designing NPC hints that players must interpret.
why: A lone ambiguous tell can send players down false paths.

text: Every superstitious explanation an NPC offers should come with a fair check the player can run.
when: Designing NPCs who suggest supernatural causes
why: Misdirection stays fair only if it can be tested

text: Strangeness becomes a problem only when nothing independent supports the claim; judge the support, not the oddness alone.
when: when assessing an unusual witness account

text: Do not use darkness to hide clues the reader needs to test fairly; keep needed evidence visible enough to check.
when: mystery scenes
why: hidden evidence cannot be tested

text: A sympathetic NPC who misleads is designed misdirection; reward players for testing claims rather than trusting character warmth.
Frame physical clues inside a supernatural premise so they read as part of the mystery rather than as its solution.
when: when designing a mystery where the player might otherwise solve the case early
why: The supernatural frame makes physical evidence look like atmosphere, so players underweight it.

text: Hide the decisive clue inside a conversation or joke so the audience hears it without weighing it.
when: when a clue must be present but not yet recognized as important
why: attention is spent on the banter, so the clue passes unexamined

text: Answers built from shown details are recognizable on reflection, while reveals that introduce unseen information surprise but cheat the audience.
A clue traced back to the victim can mislead the player into thinking the victim controlled events, when another person did.
when: a purchase or record leads to the victim
why: Tracing a clue to its owner feels like progress even when it points the wrong way.

text: Physical traces such as footprints can belong to a visitor who frightened the victim, not to a killer, so their meaning should be reinterpreted late.
when: Writing evidence that initially suggests an attack.
why: Reinterpreting an early clue changes the case without new physical evidence.

text: Mislead with a gendered or appearance-based description and let the reveal correct it, so players form a wrong picture of the hidden character.
when: describing an unseen or hidden character early in a scenario
why: Players accept the first description and only revise it when a later reveal contradicts it.

text: An object that looks like a plain fact can actually be a message; its meaning stays hidden until later evidence reframes it as a route or identity clue.
when: Designing a mystery where an item is found early but interpreted late
why: Players reread a mundane item differently once it gains a new meaning, which rewards careful attention.

text: Negative test results can mislead players into trusting the source they were told to ignore; the one unverified source is often the true culprit's domain.
when: Lab tests or analyses clear the obvious suspects early in a mystery.
why: Clean results appear to close the question, so the unexamined source stays hidden.

text: A planted clue that is too neat, pointing obviously at the wrong person, can betray the staging.
when: Designing or judging planted evidence.
why: Conspicuous pointing reads as artificial.
