text: Let a confession mislead the audience by seeming to resolve the case, then show it is false through later evidence.
when: a false confession is used as a reversal
why: A believed confession makes its overturning feel stronger

text: Give each false solution one fact that is true and one interpretation that is wrong, so the suspect stays damning until a later fact reframes it.
why: A true fact makes the wrong inference feel reliable.

text: Treating disorder, burning or an incidental item carried from a scene as proof of guilt closes off other explanations; presence alone does not establish the crime.
when: Interpreting signs of destruction or incidental items at a crime scene.
why: Disorder has many causes, and presence at a scene does not establish that the person committed the crime.

text: Two independent unlikely matches together can exceed what chance allows, though a single common match proves little.
A common name slows a search; a distinctive detail, such as a religion or a family placement, narrows the candidates quickly.
when: a suspect's name matches many people in the records
why: the detail excludes most candidates at once

text: Let the dialogue system record the cause of a misread, such as a visor or poor lighting, so players can correct the impression.
when: When an NPC reads a player's stance or gear as hostile for a visual reason.
why: A recorded cause lets the player understand and fix the misjudgment.

text: Use protagonist misreading when key information is held by a group the protagonist does not yet understand; avoid it if the audience must share the blindness throughout.
A trace is often explained by its most familiar source, but the familiar source can hide a rarer one, so check the material before accepting it.
when: a trace resembles a common residue or object
why: familiar explanations are reached quickly

text: NPC rumours of being watched, with no identified source, create paranoia and ambiguity without resolving anything.
An official account can absorb an early physical oddity, so a deliberate insider murder passes as a natural death or intruder's work until the oddity is re-examined.
when: a death that looks natural or external

text: A false lead or decisive fact withheld, never corrected or signalled later, reads as unfair cheating rather than a fair trap; players cannot check what they never had.
when: When withholding a decisive fact or leaving a false lead.
why: Players cannot reason toward a fact they never had a chance to check.

text: Reading a sound as the event it resembles, such as a blind flapping for a groan, creates false certainty.
when: A witness hears an ambiguous noise.
why: Familiar explanations are accepted before alternatives are considered.

text: Chasing a detail whose significance is unclear can lead to a false trail.
A misread letter or signal can send an investigation after the wrong person.
Hope can read a brief stir from an unconscious patient as meaningful speech or hearing, when it may not be.
when: a dying or unconscious witness shows a faint sign

text: An animal's aggression may be aimed at something other than the person it seems to target; revise the reading once the true cause is found.
Accepting the most common motive, such as silencing a blackmailer, without checking whether it is proportionate to the suspect's position.
when: A familiar motive is offered for a crime.
why: Familiar motives are adopted without testing their fit to the suspect.

text: Digressions that do not connect back to the main case stall the pace.
why: they delay without adding to the payoff

text: A rumour that is wrong in an unmarked way can mislead the audience permanently if no later passage corrects it.
when: when a clue is delivered through gossip
why: Without correction, the false version stands as accepted fact.

text: A hint shared with only one person can leave the audience unsure what was passed, so the later payoff must make it clear.
when: A hint is delivered in private

text: If a protagonist's misreading is never corrected, the audience cannot tell the character's mistake apart from the author's intent.
Errors compound when one unconfirmed guess becomes the basis for the next inference.
when: building a chain of deductions

text: A cold or confident manner is not proof of guilt, since it may be affectation or simply temperament.
when: Judging a suspect by demeanour alone.
why: Personality traits can look like evidence while meaning nothing about the act.

text: A record naming the wrong person may be the only surviving trace of an event, so it can mislead investigators.
A momentary quiver can be dismissed too quickly, leaving the observer confident in a wrong reading of consciousness.
when: When observing a sleeper for signs of awareness
why: Brief signs are easy to miss or explain away.

text: A flushed face may come from embarrassment about an unrelated matter, so a reaction must be interpreted against the topic that caused it.
when: Interpreting a witness's visible emotional reaction.
why: The same physical sign can arise from different causes.

text: Record ambiguous sightings and unexplained odd behaviour as unconfirmed leads, not as proof, and leave them uninterpreted until evidence arrives.
when: when a witness reports something that fits no explanation yet
why: early interpretation of an ambiguous detail can harden into a false conclusion

text: Plant a misleading reading of a clue that the player can see through only with a later key.
when: mystery clue design
why: the player holds the error until the key arrives

text: A concealed motive can make a sincere act look suspicious, because observers see only the act and not its hidden cause.
when: a hidden reason explains behaviour that observers misread
why: the real explanation stays hidden from observers

text: An observer who misreads another's fear or attachment may admit the error later in the same scene, correcting the misjudgment.
A single odd remark can show that the subject assumed a different visit, so a pretext can be read wrongly.
An observer can misread a face or expression as hostile when a mundane cause, such as poor eyesight or effort to focus, produces the look.
when: When judging mood or intent from a person's facial expression.
why: Physical strain or impairment can mimic anger or ill will.

text: A concealed motive misread as guilt can send an investigation after the wrong person.
A reaction read as guilt may be interest, embarrassment or irritation, so the observer's hopes can bias the reading.
Letting an offender go rests on the investigator's judgement of remorse, which can be wrong.
Do not treat a missing motive as proof of innocence; keep alternative explanations open until each one is checked.
when: when no motive has been found for a suspect
why: an unfound motive may simply be unrecorded

text: Anomalous clues or mismatched records get dismissed as untidiness or process error and recognised only later; plant mismatches so a second-event reading stays available.
when: An anomalous detail is seen on arrival, or two records or entries fail to agree.
why: Observers do not interpret a clue until it connects to a broader pattern, and a plausible administrative explanation hides it until wider evidence supports another reading.

text: Give each misreading a factual alternative that fits both the honest and the deliberate interpretation until a decisive clue arrives.
when: A player is led to a wrong conclusion about an incident.
why: Players accept a misreading only when the evidence genuinely supports both readings, so they do not feel cheated when corrected.

text: A satisfying solution can still be wrong, so the investigator must keep looking for the fact it fails to explain.
when: A theory feels complete and resolves most of the case.
why: Satisfaction is not proof, and an unexplained fact may reveal the real cause.

text: A flattering or romantic reading of an object can lead an investigation away from the plausible explanation.
when: when interpreting an object with emotional appeal

text: A social scandal is not automatically a motive for murder; check whether it actually connects to the death.
when: A witness reveals an embarrassing private matter.
why: Scandal is common and often unrelated to crime.

text: Pressing ordinary acts for hidden meaning produces false significance, and a character's agitation can grow beyond what the facts support.
when: A character or investigator is anxious or suspicious.
why: Anxiety reads ordinary actions as signs of a concealed purpose.

text: Investigators can be misled more by implication than by direct statement, so a sincere-seeming hint can shape judgment without being proven.
when: weighing an observer's impression of a suspect's hesitation or remark
why: implied suggestions carry emotional weight beyond their evidence

text: An emotionally charged reading of document fragments can impose a false sense, such as threats where none are intended.
when: Interpreting partial text with strong expectations about its content
why: Preconceptions about the writer or situation shape how fragments are read

text: Avoiding the front of a house can mean concealment or simple convenience, so routine behaviour needs a second explanation before it is read as hiding.
when: when interpreting an unusual movement pattern
why: The same behaviour has more than one plausible cause.

text: A moral or spiritual explanation can stand in for a concrete human cause and feel more satisfying than the evidence supports.
when: when an investigator interprets an unusual appearance or event
why: Moral framing offers a clean answer that avoids checking the mundane facts.

text: Vivid supernatural imagery can make an investigator see the supernatural where only a human pattern exists.
when: when a mystery is described in intense or unusual terms
why: Striking imagery shapes perception before the evidence is weighed.

text: Assuming an angry remark targets the person it names can mislead; the anger may be aimed at a third party.
when: When interpreting heated statements
why: Named targets can be stand-ins

text: A missing-body mystery can resolve as self-removal: the supposed victim was alive, moved away alone, and planted a forged note to frame another person.
A missing document can supply motive, but its existence must be proved from another source such as a copy elsewhere.
when: when a document is missing but its contents matter to motive
why: An absent document cannot be assumed to have existed without corroboration.

text: Examine what a document leaves out, such as a missing fallback for failure, because gaps can show the writer's assumptions as clearly as the terms do.
when: Reading a document whose wording looks absurd or one-sided
why: An omitted contingency often shows the writer never considered it

text: A missing record can freeze a legal or administrative process, such as an estate, even when it does not prove the underlying fact.
when: a process requires proof that a record provides
why: Institutions act on documents, so a gap halts action regardless of what it implies.

text: Missing one document, such as an unsigned will, can change who benefits from a death and invalidate the apparent motive.
when: When an inheritance seems fixed
why: Unfinalized documents leave benefits open

text: 1) Compare the account against the expected facts. 2) Note any omitted item. 3) Ask about the omitted item directly. 4) Ask for small details, since they often give the best clues.
when: A witness's account skips a key fact.
why: Gaps in testimony often point to the most important evidence.

text: 1) Work out the legal consequence of the document's absence for each party. 2) Identify who would lose or gain. 3) Establish when it was last seen and who could reach it. 4) Check for duplicates or records elsewhere.
when: a missing item has financial or legal consequences

text: Note what a fragment is missing, such as the sender or date, and do not treat it as proof of authorship or fill the gaps with assumptions.
when: Using an incomplete record as evidence
why: Missing parts limit what the record can prove

text: Before reading deliberate intent into a gap in a document, check whether the gap is actually significant; many omissions are blind spots rather than planned outcomes.
when: Interpreting an apparently strategic omission
why: Treating every gap as malice leads to false conclusions

text: Missing knowledge is evidence: a forger often knows a name but not internal details, so gaps in a writer's knowledge can expose a fake.
A missing acknowledgment of receipt leaves a gap in the paper trail that a careful checker will notice and question.
why: Gaps in a chain of custody invite doubt about the whole transfer.

text: Let a note left by a missing NPC, delivered to the right faction, explain a disappearance and give players a motive thread.
when: designing NPC disappearances

text: Scatter fragments such as a letter, a debt entry, or a later reference so players can reconstruct a missing character's last known location.
when: Designing a missing-person mystery
why: Players can only deduce a location from clues they can assemble themselves.

text: When an expected item is missing from an inventory, point the player toward the owner's most likely confidant.
when: designing an item-tracing clue

text: Build a missing-person quest where each trace, such as a messenger, ticket or carriage, is a node that the player follows to find the failed link.
when: Designing a search quest.
why: Sequential traces give the player steps that can each be checked.

text: A conspicuously missing trace where others should appear may show that the area was deliberately cleaned.
when: a trace is absent from a place where it is expected
why: A deliberate act can remove evidence.

text: When expected traces are missing, propose alternative causes, such as another means of transport or wind dispersal, and test each with a targeted check.
when: when the traces a method should leave are absent

text: A writing tool may be missing from the body, so its absence must be checked rather than assumed.
A claimed trace that cannot be found later neither confirms nor refutes the claim, since its absence has many causes.
when: when a witness reports a feature that has since vanished
why: evidence that is gone cannot be checked

text: 1) Establish the original count of a set of similar objects. 2) Count the members present. 3) Count the separated pieces. 4) If a piece is unaccounted for, estimate what it held from its size.
when: a set of standard objects such as cut sheets or tickets has a discrepancy
why: A count mismatch shows that a member is missing, and its size limits what it could have contained.

text: 1) Confirm the display's contents with someone who knew it well. 2) Confirm which item is missing. 3) List everyone who had access to it.
when: A weapon is missing from a known display
why: Confirmed absence and access narrow who could have taken it

text: A missing-item puzzle can show the player the gap first, letting them infer the owner, the weapon type and the time it vanished.
when: designing a missing-item puzzle
why: Inference from a visible gap rewards attention.

text: Treat a missing page or item in a record as a clue, since the gap may show someone wanted a particular entry hidden.
when: A record is incomplete.
why: Deliberate removal often signals a concealed entry.

text: Absence of an expected trace rules out its cause only if removal is unlikely; if cleaning or purging could erase it, absence is inconclusive; search for the trace.
when: A suspected cause should leave a physical trace, such as a residue, stain, marker or footprint.
why: Cleaning, purging or vomiting can remove residue, making absence inconclusive.

text: Sincerity does not establish accuracy: keep good faith separate from reliability, since a sincere witness can misread reflections, misperceive and discount a sound, or report objects only they perceived.
when: when evaluating a witness whose account seems trustworthy
why: Sincerity and reliability do not guarantee accurate perception.

text: A witness can sincerely recall a vivid sound or face at a wrong time; when the recalled time conflicts with fixed evidence, reconcile the two rather than discard either.
when: Testimony conflicts with a fixed timing such as time of death
why: Memory of a vivid event can be confident yet mistimed

text: Witnesses often cannot recall the exact words of a brief exchange, so their account of it has gaps that must be filled from other evidence.
when: a witness reports a short exchange
why: brief speech is rarely fixed in memory

text: Use a sincere but mistaken witness when the audience should see how an error arose, not when testimony must be fully reliable.
when: when designing a witness whose account misleads
why: Visible error mechanisms teach the audience to test claims

text: Even sincere witnesses misremember or overreach, so questions should aim at specifics rather than general impressions.
when: taking any witness account
why: specifics expose memory errors that general impressions hide

text: Following too far or in the wrong place, or too closely on open ground, loses the target; in crowds, keep pace with a fast walker to stay in sight.
Protective advice can be lost when the person it protects judges it unnecessary, leaving that person exposed to the threat.
why: the protected person dismisses the warning

text: Repeated hearsay loses its original source at each retelling, so the chain must be traced back before its claims are trusted.
when: when a claim has passed through several people
why: Each retelling removes the link to the first observer

text: A missed chance to act, taken because of caution or chance, can be judged a failure by others even when caution was reasonable.
when: reviewing a confrontation that did not end in capture
why: Hindsight and outside observers often weigh the missed moment heavily.

text: Minor threads, such as an injury noted early, can drop from attention; track each open thread until it is resolved.
Treating a sincere denial as proof that nobody was present is a mistake when the question was framed around suspicion.
when: when a witness denies a presence and the question was narrow
why: Narrow framing excludes ordinary-looking people

text: Losing confidence just before a tell is confirmed can lead the investigator to apologise and withdraw, letting the suspect escape the trap.
when: the reveal is near completion
why: doubt surfaces at the moment of commitment

text: A sincere witness can still be wrong about times, so vagueness in an account should be treated as a lead to pursue, not a verdict.
when: When a witness is honest but imprecise
why: Honesty does not guarantee accurate memory of time

text: If the culprit dies before further questioning, unresolved threads must be settled in the account already given, since no later questions are possible.
when: Culprit is lost before follow-up
why: Gaps left open cannot be closed later

text: Recording only the answers and not the witness's state of mind loses information about how reliable each answer was.
A witness can misidentify the day, and without an outside reference the sequence of events cannot be fixed.
when: Reconstructing a timeline after an impairment or long sleep.
why: Without an external date, an incorrect day skews the whole sequence.

text: A secondhand description of a lost item can miss details that matter, so the clue must be verified through notes or recollection.
when: the physical item is no longer available

text: Sincere belief in a flawed standard can produce testimony that is honest but still wrong.
A lost or delayed notice makes the person receiving a visitor misread the visitor's intent, because they judge without the information the notice would have given.
Do not build an exact sequence from a witness who admits lost memory. Mark that stretch of time as unknown.
when: A witness admits memory loss for part of the events

text: Build a lost-event mystery from dated letters, a sealed file with a suspicious insertion, and a grave or house whose layout tells part of the story.
when: designing a game investigation about past events
why: each clue type lets the player reconstruct events from different evidence

text: Trace unexplained withdrawals and large payments to infer a motive and who was being paid, then rank suspects by their ability to pay or need for money.
when: investigating who had a motive for a crime
why: Money movements often reveal who received payments and why.

text: 1) List every inflow and outflow over the period. 2) Total the holdings at the end. 3) Compare that total with the figures in the account.
when: A money movement must be checked over a period

text: 1) Find withdrawals from a known account shortly before the death. 2) Follow the cash to where notes are spent or cashed. 3) Check wills and contracts for a motive. 4) Check whether money is missing from the scene.
when: a financial record gives a timeline, a sum or a beneficiary

text: Moral disapproval, such as of a suspect's luxury or unsavoury past, can replace evidence; it is opinion, not proof, and skips motive, opportunity and reliable clues.
when: When a judgement about lifestyle or past is used to infer guilt.
why: Disapproval feels like proof but is an opinion, not a fact.

text: A confession can resolve a moral question rather than a legal one, leaving the culprit unpunished by law.
when: ending a mystery where justice and law diverge
why: Motive and remorse can close the story without a formal arrest.

text: Moral or circumstantial evidence, such as motive, presence or manner, supports likely guilt; legal proof needs direct evidence, like witnessing an act or a physical link.
why: the two standards differ in what they require

text: Moral certainty is a strong belief in guilt, whereas legal certainty requires evidence that can be shown and sustained.
A moral impossibility is an act a person would refuse because it clashes with their instinctive manner, even though they could physically commit it.
Judge a document by what it can actually establish; a short later letter may give only moral support, not decisive proof.
when: Weighing how much a document settles a question.

text: A mission frame can justify a group's general policy as well as its individual prosecutions, so suspicion gains a purpose beyond each case.
Praise for those who refuse to confess is moral judgment and does not prove innocence.
Offering moral judgement on a witness's personal relationships can end their cooperation and lose the detail the investigator still needs.
Letting an offender go spares them punishment but removes accountability and may let them wrong others later.
when: dropping a case against a remorseful offender

text: A motive is a gain or fear giving someone reason to commit the act; slight, odd or disproportionate motives, such as revenge or small gain, still count.
Treat an inferred motive as a provisional hypothesis, not a verdict, that points to what to check next until facts or behavior confirm it; a correct motive can still mislead.
when: forming a theory about why an event happened
why: Untested motives mislead; a correct motive can still mislead about the action it produced.

text: Frame the case around motive: ask who gains from an event, such as a death or disputed document, and apply it to every suspect.
when: identifying suspects after an event with a financial or inheritance outcome, such as a will
why: The beneficiary of an event is a common source of motive; motive links otherwise separate facts.

text: Inferring a witness's motive without independent facts is guesswork; a stake does not prove a statement false, only that it needs independent support.
when: when a witness has a stake
why: stake raises doubt but does not establish error

text: Do not infer guilt from motive alone; motive shows who could gain or desire an outcome, not who acted.
when: judging an accusation with little direct evidence
why: Motive shows who could gain, not who acted.

text: Leaving a late-revealed culprit's motive unstated can weaken the reveal, but a one-word motive such as 'spite' lets players fill the gap so the reveal lands on their own assumptions.
when: revealing a culprit's motive late; an unstated motive weakens the reveal, while a minimal motive works when players can supply the reason
why: Players may notice an unexplained gap after exposure, whereas a minimal motive is completed by the player.

text: A confessing character may name an impulse as the motive and disclaim any cause and effect, yet describe events in an order that links them.
when: A suspect's statement supplies its own motive.
why: Stating a motive as impulse can hide the planned or caused sequence behind it.

text: Colleagues envious of a person's pay or lifestyle are quick to attribute vice or loss to them, so their opinions reflect resentment as much as observation.
when: Witnesses share a workplace with the accused
why: Envy colours perception and interpretation

text: Among a few possible culprits, the one with both motive and opportunity draws suspicion even when evidence against them is slight.
when: the suspect pool is small
why: Exclusion narrows the field, so remaining candidates attract attention.

text: Envy can explain a rival's ordinary, skilled success as supernatural, turning competence into an accusation.
when: a neighbor outproduces others on modest resources
why: Envy seeks an explanation that is not the rival's effort.

text: Everyday disputes over boundaries, lent tools and refused help give accusers both a motive and a ready list of incidents to cite.
when: small communities with frequent daily dealings
why: Familiar grievances are easy to recall and easy to connect to later misfortune.

text: A harmful plan can grow from an idea picked up by chance that fits a pressing need, rather than from long premeditation.
when: when explaining how a character came to a scheme
why: Chance information that matches an existing need is readily adopted.

text: Motive explains why someone acts; means and plan explain how. Knowing where a valuable is kept shows access, while wanting it is a separate question to test.
Many people could name someone they wish dead, so starting an investigation from motive narrows little and can point at several people, including associates.
when: judging a suspect by motive, starting an investigation from motive rather than evidence, or using motive to choose a suspect
why: Wanting harm is common, so motive does not discriminate between people.

text: Mistaking the motive is the greatest obstacle to solving a crime, so motive and search pattern should be kept distinct when reasoning.
when: When investigating any crime with an unclear purpose.
why: Conflating the two hides the true aim.

text: Murder motives fall into three broad kinds: material gain, a passionate crime, and a killing for an idea that suggests mental derangement.
Confessed motives often arise from social pressure such as poverty, fear of poverty, or the wish for better social standing, and are presented by the teller as self-justification.
when: A character explains a past act
why: Social pressure supplies motive, while the teller frames it to justify the act

text: Past marriages, rivalries, business disputes and romantic competition can each give several people a motive at the same time.
A motive can arise from a long-standing legal restriction and an inherited grievance rather than from a single event.
when: Investigating property, inheritance or shared-resource disputes.
why: A standing agreement can be the real source of conflict between parties.

text: Motive alone does not establish guilt; a suspect must also be shown to have means, opportunity and knowledge.
A motive that explains why two events happened does not reveal who acted; treat motive and identity of the actor as separate questions.
when: A found motive suggests a plausible cause but no suspect.
why: Motive narrows the reasons, while identity needs direct evidence about the person.

text: Debt and low income can be read as a real reason behind a bargaining clause, which makes a financial motive visible.
when: A party's debts or income are described beside a clause that benefits them
why: Financial need explains otherwise odd terms.

text: The size of an estate indicates how desperate a suspect might be; a large fortune raises the stakes enough to justify desperate action.
when: weighing suspect motive
why: Greater gain makes greater risk plausible.

text: Motive options that imply a specific person narrow the suspect list fastest; when several motives fit the facts, the motive is the hardest point to settle.
when: Several candidates remain and motives compete.
why: Each motive points to a particular relationship, and several fitting motives leave the choice open.

text: Link an unseen movement to a motive, which explains why the route was hidden.
Treat a stated value as evidence of motive, not proof of the deed itself.
Everyone has a sore spot; look for it in a suspect's known reactions to see what provokes strong feeling.
When one act is given several different motives, the number of motives can signal a weak case, since each must be judged on its own support.
when: A case offers several explanations for one event.
why: Multiple motives may indicate that none is well supported.

text: Be skeptical of an impulsive-violence explanation when the scene shows deliberate staging, since it may not fit the arrangement.
Infer a crime's motive from the victim's livelihood: identify what the income practice needs to keep working, then expect the supporting records to exist and to explain the killing.
when: Designing or solving a murder whose victim had a business or income.
why: A practice that depends on documents or secrets leaves traces of what was held, and someone may have acted to stop it.

text: Motive multiplies when many people resent a victim, so check each motive separately.
when: several people had reasons to harm the victim
why: Each motive must be linked to presence and action on its own.

text: A statement given to win mercy can still be true, so judge its motive and its truth separately.
when: when a statement benefits the person who made it

text: Remarks showing that a person was weighing options indicate inclination, not a settled decision, and should not be read as an agreed outcome.
when: evaluating what someone said about future plans
why: Speculation about possible plans differs from a committed choice.

text: Use a rival's envy as the motive behind a false clue, which the player must debunk to reach the truth.
when: designing misleading accusations
why: The motive exposes the clue as unreliable.

text: Use motive mapping of shared assets for feuds with several parties, not for puzzles with a lone actor and no shared stakes.
Motive shows who could gain from an accusation but is not proof of guilt or malice, and a reputation can hide what someone gained.
For a deliberate crime, centre the search on motive rather than on incidental details, since a planned act is driven by purpose.
when: a group decides which line of inquiry to follow
why: a deliberate crime reflects intent

text: Model a character's motive as a concrete object, such as valuable jewellery that creates a dispute, and let the player uncover it by asking the right questions.
when: when designing hidden motives in a story
why: A tangible object makes the motive concrete and gives the player a clear thing to discover.

text: A suspect's choice to remain at the scene can be inconsistent with a self-preservation motive, which points toward other motives such as robbery.
when: When a suspect's action at the scene conflicts with a presumed motive.
why: Behavior that a motive would not predict is evidence against that motive.

text: Assign each character a motive and make the most obvious motive a decoy so that the less visible motive must be found.
when: When designing suspects for a mystery.
why: Players tend to accept the first plausible motive, so a hidden one rewards deeper inquiry.

text: Give NPC witnesses motives and knowledge gaps, and let the player cross-check their statements against objects and other testimony.
when: Designing NPC witness dialogue in a game
why: Players engage more when testimony must be verified rather than accepted at face value.

text: A person who holds secrets of their own has a motive for silence and for controlling others who might learn them.
Check whether a fact cuts against a motive, such as a lawful remedy that removes the need for revenge, before accepting the motive.
when: when a motive is central to an accusation
why: A lawful alternative can weaken the claim that someone acted out of revenge.

text: Test a suspect's motive by asking what they actually gain and whether it can be turned into value. A theft with no payoff points to another motive or a cover story.
when: When a suspect's motive is examined
why: Gain and resale ability show whether an act was worth doing

text: Plant the culprit's motive early as a visible but unfinished fixation or past tie, such as a former romance, so the player connects its object to the act when revealed.
when: planning the culprit's backstory
why: A partly visible motive becomes plausible once the culprit is exposed; an earlier fixation pays off later.

text: A motive grounded in relationships between characters, such as a threat against an impending marriage, gives a clear reason to act.
when: Constructing a motive for a suspect.
why: Relationship-based motives are concrete and easy for players to verify.

text: Read motive from the wording of a legal instrument rather than from the reputations of the people involved.
when: A motive is tied to inheritance or control of property.
why: The conditions determine who gains, regardless of who is suspected.

text: Ask why an act seems pointless, which invites the suspect to explain motive.
when: Interrogating a suspect whose motive is unclear

text: Give a reveal a human motive, such as debt, a threat or a wish to stop a reckless plan, so the solution carries emotional weight.
when: when writing the motive behind a culprit's act
why: Relatable motives make the revelation meaningful, not merely mechanical.

text: Prefer motives of ambition or respectability over romance when they better fit the crime's method.
when: when ranking possible motives for a crime
why: calculated motives match planned crimes more closely than passion does

text: A respectable person may commit a crime to protect standing, since losing reputation is the most serious loss to them.
when: when a suspect has a reputation to protect
why: threats to standing motivate people who have little else to lose

text: Leave a character's motive unexplained when the story does not need it, so an unresolved flight or escape adds tension.
when: A secondary character's motive is not central to the reveal
why: An open question keeps the audience engaged after the main twist.

text: A late reversal or sudden public generosity reframes earlier suspicion, so audiences move from suspicion to gratitude: apparent culprits become sympathetic and coldness reads as mercy.
when: a suspected person changes their public image, or a late reversal occurs
why: The audience re-reads earlier behaviour in light of the new fact.

text: A motive makes a suspect plausible without proving the act, so players will suspect a motivated character before any access is established.
when: motive is visible early but access is unverified
why: Motive is a cheap signal that raises suspicion faster than evidence can confirm it

text: A motive such as blackmail can organise scattered clues into a coherent path that the player can test.
when: When designing a mystery's underlying story.
why: A motive links clues so they form a testable explanation.

text: The same distress and avoidance can signal guilt under one motive and innocence under another, so a clue's meaning shifts when its assumed motive changes.
when: A suspect's behaviour is read against an unverified motive
why: Behaviour has no fixed meaning apart from the motive assumed for it

text: A story can expose motive when the teller invents one to defend a rival suspect.
when: A suspect's fiction assigns motives to other characters.
why: Inventing a defense for someone else reveals what the teller thinks is plausible and what he cares about.

text: Several private documents from different writers that point the same way build a motive more strongly than any single one.
when: Building motive from letters or diaries.
why: Independent sources that agree are harder to dismiss than one source.

text: Motives split into irrational (homicidal mania, irrational antipathy) and rational; rational motives include revenge and practical aims, and prudential ones divide into gain and prevention.
when: Listing every possible reason a suspect could have
why: A complete list prevents fixing on the first motive that comes to mind

text: Motive shows who benefits or has reason to act, not that they acted; pair it with opportunity before implicating anyone.
when: concluding guilt from benefit, or evidence establishes a motive only
why: Gain shows incentive, not action; wanting something is not proof of doing it.

text: Motive alone does not prove guilt: innocent people can look guilty when a motive is visible, and sincere anger may never be acted upon.
when: a suspect has a visible reason to act, or had a reason to kill but no proven act
why: Motive is compatible with innocence.

text: Motive can be supplied by imagination; gaps filled this way should be treated as provisional until the facts are checked.
when: A motive is accepted without supporting evidence.
why: Imagined links feel convincing but may not match what happened.

text: Assigning intent from a single remark or a single gap risks error; rule out an innocent explanation before settling on a motive.
why: one cue rarely supports a motive without alternatives being excluded

text: Reading motive into an emotion that has another cause, or mistaking coincidence for sabotage, leads to wrong conclusions.
A relationship detail creates only a possible reason and is not an accusation, so it needs evidence before it is treated as guilt.
when: Presenting a relationship detail during an investigation.
why: A possible motive can be mistaken for proof if not checked.

text: A rival's motive is not evidence that the rival was present at the scene.
Building a motive on past resentment alone, without evidence that the benefit was actually at stake, is a common error.
A stated motive or a chain of links built by one interested party can look like proof when it is only a story.
when: an accusation rests on one party's account of another's reasons
why: The party presenting the chain has a stake in its conclusion

text: Attacking a witness's motive shifts the debate from the content of the evidence to the witness's character.
A written motive can support two readings depending on who wrote it and whom they feared.
when: Interpreting a motive stated in a personal record.
why: Authorship and fear shape what a text really means.

text: Framing the motive question too narrowly can point the investigation at the wrong target.
Seeming inadequate is not evidence of innocence.
A motive can remain real even after the person who held it has died, so do not dismiss it for that reason alone.
Assuming every missing record is a cover-up overlooks loss through neglect, such as records never kept or not preserved.
Envy often presents itself as public concern, which hides a personal motive behind a moral framing.
Judging a possible accomplice only by financial self-interest can miss non-financial motives such as fear or loyalty that would make joining rational.
Motives built on hidden secrets are hard to check and can be invented to fit a theory.
Letting a motive stand alone without checking the alibi or the physical evidence leads to an unsupported accusation.
when: when building an accusation from motive
why: A motive does not establish that a person acted.

text: Dismissing a motive because a suspect looks well off misses hidden debts and private money needs, which often surface only later.
when: When a suspect appears prosperous
why: Visible wealth hides financial strain

text: A strong motive can fill gaps in weak evidence and make the case feel conclusive when it is not.
when: A suspect has a compelling motive but thin physical or testimonial evidence.
why: Motive is persuasive, so it can mask missing proof.

text: 1) List each party's debts and financial stake. 2) List legal stakes: inheritance position, any marriage settlement, pending divorce. 3) Ask who gains from the death and whether that gain is documented.
when: building suspect motives after a death
why: Written financial positions and legal stakes can be checked against records, while rumoured motives cannot.

text: 1) List every party with an interest in the death. 2) Eliminate each by a distinct argument, such as their physical state, their character, or whether the plot suits them. 3) Widen the search to the victim's past dealings.
when: ranking suspects by motive
why: listing every interested party avoids stopping at the first

text: 1) Ask who wanted the victim dead. 2) List motive lines: business enemies, including anyone whose fortune the victim may have ruined; romance rivals; jilted suitors; former partners of rivals. 3) Answer every question each line raises before reporting.
when: starting a case with several possible motives
why: it organizes the search into separate lines

text: 1) List the outcomes a character gains from an act. 2) Propose a motive that produces them. 3) Test the motive against further evidence, including the character's own account. 4) Keep the conclusion provisional until it survives testing.
when: inferring why a character acted
why: explicit steps expose assumptions before they harden into conclusions

text: 1) List who dies and in what order. 2) Note what each death yields and to whom. 3) Use the chain as a lead to be tied to means and opportunity.
when: Building a motive chain for several linked events.
why: A written chain shows how sequence shifts rewards, and a motive is only a lead until tied to means and opportunity.

text: 1) List what the crime did not take or gain. 2) Rule out motives the evidence contradicts. 3) Take the remaining motive and find people with a grudge or gain from it. 4) Test each candidate by character and self-interest.
when: When the purpose of a crime is unclear and suspects must be narrowed.
why: Eliminating contradicted motives leaves a smaller field of plausible explanations.

text: 1) List the apparent motives for the event. 2) Test each against the facts. 3) Remove suspects whose motive makes no sense given those facts.
when: When many people are connected to an event and several motives seem possible.
why: Testing motives against facts removes suspects without a plausible reason to act.

text: When ordinary motives all fail, consider less obvious motives, such as protecting a reputation or hiding a loss or fault.
when: When the usual motives do not fit the facts.
why: Hidden motives often explain actions that obvious motives cannot.

text: 1) Where the surface shows no grievance, trace the suspect's past relationships. 2) Interview people who saw the relationship from different angles. 3) Follow the history through the places it unfolded. 4) Link the grievance to a specific need or object.
when: When a case has no obvious motive on its surface
why: A motive built from documented history is easier to connect to the crime than one assumed from appearances.

text: Motive is a starting point that makes a suspect plausible, not guilty; before naming a culprit, show opportunity, means and a physical link to the scene and time.
when: A theory rests mainly on why someone might have committed a crime, or when judging a suspect in a mystery.
why: Motive explains willingness, not whether the act happened; resentment is common, so it cannot separate the guilty from the merely hostile.

text: A known quarrel establishes only that a motive could exist, not means or opportunity; the most suspicious person can still be the wrong one.
when: documented conflict, or a suspect's motive is obvious but access unproven
why: Possibility is not evidence of action; motive alone does not establish the act.

text: A financial motive or matching money is only a lead to test; pair it with physical or witness evidence before naming a culprit, since innocent explanations exist.
when: a suspect has a motive or matching funds
why: Treating it as a conclusion ends the inquiry too early; motive and money can have innocent explanations.

text: A motive without means or opportunity proves nothing on its own; pair financial gain with timing and access before suspecting anyone.
Do not dismiss a suspect on motive alone when an accomplice could have acted; separate the motive question from the accomplice question.
when: a suspect lacks a motive but could have had help
why: A person without a motive may have acted with someone who had one.

text: Organize the search around human motives such as hatred, revenge, silencing the victim and greed, rather than around objects alone.
when: Structuring an investigation.
why: Motives link otherwise scattered clues to people.

text: Pair a withheld motive with a later discovered note, so the player can work out why the door stayed shut.
when: An NPC refuses access or information and the reason is not stated.
why: A later clue lets the player reconstruct the motive from the evidence.

text: Use an in-world artefact, such as a newspaper caricature, to plant a motive the player can revisit after the reveal.
Do not imply a consequence the writer has no intention of pursuing; such a bluff is dishonourable.
when: when trying to draw a reply from a suspect
why: The writer judges a bluff below the standard the approach should meet.

text: Give suspicious NPC behaviour, such as nervousness or tears, at least two possible motives so a misread clue can be reread later.
Use motive to direct investigation toward a suspect's history, not as the sole proof of guilt.
Give witnesses a motive flag, such as blackmail or fear, that the player can discover by searching the NPC's belongings.
Explain motive through the suspect's character and wider aims, not only through the act itself.
when: revealing why a culprit acted
why: Character and aims make the motive feel earned

text: Have a journal entry or NPC gossip mention a changed document, giving the player a motive lead to pursue.
when: designing narrative clues in a mystery
why: Indirect mention creates a motive without solving the case.

text: Make each NPC's motive visible through several actions so players can test their inferences against later observations.
when: designing NPC motive systems
why: multiple observations let players confirm or reject a reading

text: Model each NPC's grudges, debts and property stakes as weighted links, and let those weights decide which NPC suspicion falls on.
Design hidden-item puzzles so they reward reasoning about the holder's motive over checking the expected container first.
when: designing puzzles around hidden items

text: Give an NPC a wager or riddle whose replies reveal a hidden motive to a player who asks the right follow-up.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that conceals intent.
why: A harmless frame lets the hidden motive appear through follow-up questions.

text: A past grievance supplies motive, but it should prompt testing rather than serve as proof of guilt.
when: when building suspicion from a character's history
why: Motive makes a suspect plausible without establishing that they acted.

text: Hold back one motive until a later clue, and show the gap as an open item in the player's notes.
Hold the motive reveal until after the culprit is identified, so the victim's reputation is reframed late in the case.
Check a reconstructed motive against documents and relationships before adopting it.
when: After proposing a new explanation for a reaction
why: Unverified theories can mislead

text: Make an outside motive concrete with a written or printed trail that the player can follow.
why: A tangible trail lets players verify a motive rather than guess it.

text: An NPC's journal or confession can state its own motives, and the player can compare those claims against the scene's setup to test them.
when: When designing NPC testimony that the player must verify.
why: Stated motives become checkable against physical evidence, so the player weighs claims instead of accepting them.

text: A prevention motive is killing to stop someone from acting, such as a blackmailer, a political rival, or an inconvenient spouse.
when: Classifying a suspect's prudential motive

text: Treat an apparently simple death as a claim to test, and check facts that would contradict the obvious explanation before accepting it.
when: a death or loss looks ordinary
why: A simple-looking case can hide a different cause

text: When a dispute is framed as principle but a specific office is at stake, control of the appointment may be the strongest motive.
when: a dispute involves a contested post or succession

text: Building a conspiracy from anecdotes that share a single source produces a pattern that depends on one unreliable account.
when: Several reports seem to confirm one another
why: Reports from a common source are not independent confirmation.

text: Explaining a conflict only by one party's personal ambition overlooks long-standing feuds that divide the community.
Treating a neighbor's anecdote about a different case as proof about this one; an analogy from another situation is not evidence here.
when: When a prediction or verdict rests on a story from a different context.
why: Different circumstances can make the comparison invalid.

text: Give an NPC a will or contract that creates motive, and let the player decide whether it is genuine or a lure toward the wrong suspect.
A suspect gains from an outcome only if they knew its terms. Establish that knowledge before counting the outcome as a motive.
why: Benefit without awareness of the arrangement gives no reason to act

text: Secondhand or relayed accounts can be unreliable: each retelling may add or drop details, and gossip bends stories to fit expectations, so informants must be corroborated.
when: When a motive or claim rests on secondhand or relayed sources.
why: Informants may be biased, and every retelling can alter specifics the original source held accurately.

text: Rumours from people with a grudge can spread without any firsthand basis.
when: When rumours circulate about a person's origins or conduct.
why: Grudges motivate spreading claims that no one has witnessed.

text: If the full motive is revealed too early, a character's misreading loses its tension.
when: Structuring a secret the character misjudges.
why: The gap between the character's guess and the truth creates the suspense.

text: 1) Give an NPC's claim about another NPC a stake the player can discover, such as marriage or inheritance. 2) Let the player judge the claim against that motive. 3) Offer a rival NPC reading the player can choose to trust.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that the player must evaluate.
why: Discoverable motive makes accusations something the player weighs, not just receives.

text: A line of testimony drawn from gossip can seem to implicate a suspect, but its unreliable origin reduces its weight until stronger evidence removes it.
when: A witness repeats hearsay that points at a suspect.
why: Unverified origin lowers credibility, so the hearsay can be discarded once proof arrives.

text: A person may frankly state a self-interested motive, and this candor can be a performance that must be checked against what the person actually does.
when: When a witness volunteers reasons for their actions.
why: Frankness about motive does not guarantee honesty, so behavior is the test.

text: A motive a suspect openly admits, such as a planned legal action, should be recorded even when the suspect denies intent to harm.
when: when a suspect admits a grievance but denies violence
why: An admitted motive is evidence regardless of the denial.

text: A secret that depends on a holder's false belief collapses once that belief is corrected, and delay from missing information can look like deliberate withholding.
when: Designing secrets supported by a character's mistaken belief or an information gap
why: Correction removes the secret's basis, and unclear causes make players misread intent

text: 1) Date each diary entry and letter. 2) Reveal them in date order. 3) Let the player see motive build from a long gap, a sudden change, then a shift in feeling.
when: Presenting a sequence of documents to the player.
why: Chronological order shows cause and effect in the subject's own voice.

text: What a thief takes and what they miss reveals what they expected to find, which is evidence for analysing a theft.
when: when analysing the pattern of a theft
why: a thief's choices follow their information about the target

text: The party who gains from a missing item is most likely to press a theory that it was stolen.
when: Several parties have competing claims on the item.
why: They have a direct stake in the outcome.

text: A gain motive is killing to obtain what another person holds, by theft or inheritance.
when: Classifying a suspect's prudential motive

text: If goods were taken, a paid job becomes likelier; if nothing was taken, a financial motive weakens and a non-financial one such as punishment gains ground.
when: Deciding between a paid crime and a revenge crime
why: Robbery marks profit as the aim, so its presence or absence separates the two motives.

text: When a stated motive seems too slight for the action taken, search for a hidden trigger in a passing detail or overheard remark.
when: a narrator's reason does not match the consequences
why: A small trigger can sit behind a casual explanation.

text: Revealing that apparent victims staged the affair turns the thief from actor into pawn, reversing his role in the story.
In a theft mystery, offer a cheap supernatural rumor alongside a plain thief, and let the return of the item separate them.
when: Designing a theft quest with competing explanations
why: Returning the item gives the player a test that favours one explanation

text: Suspicion resting only on a weak or unflattering motive should not be acted on alone; but real murders often have thin motives among cohabitants, so thinness alone need not refute.
when: Judging whether a weak motive justifies acting on, or dismissing, a suspect.
why: Close relationships produce frequent conflict, and violence often follows trivial triggers.

text: An unsigned promised gift generally does not pass property after the giver dies, and an estate with no will passes to legal heirs.
Goods bought for cash without a maker's mark or sales record leave no trace, so tradesmen checks on them may fail.
when: When an item must be traced through its seller or maker
why: Cash transactions often generate no record for the investigator to follow

text: Untouched valuables or unspent proceeds make robbery less likely as the whole aim; theft stays possible, so keep rival motives open and ask what else the act was for.
when: When valuables are left untouched or stolen goods are unspent.
why: A thief who keeps the money untouched suggests a different underlying purpose.

text: A person who accepts far less than normal pay for a post may have a hidden reason for wanting that position.
when: A character's terms are unusually favourable to the other side.
why: Unusual willingness usually points to an unstated gain.

text: A literal-minded thief values an object at its market price, while an abstract-minded person does not steal a physical object they see as trivial.
when: when matching a theft to a suspect's temperament
why: a literal mind reads value in market terms, an abstract one does not

text: Assuming deliberate intent without evidence is as misleading as dismissing it.
Assuming a will or inheritance without evidence builds a false motive; verify the document before using it to accuse a suspect.
Treat a rumoured motive as unverified until a record, such as a will, confirms it; do not upgrade gossip to fact.
when: A motive comes only from gossip or staff suspicion
why: Gossip can point to a motive without proving it

text: Motive is often inferred from changes in conduct, unexplained requests or concealed errands, and these clues also point to the time the suspect is buying.
A person may perform an ordinary act for a motive they cannot name, and may then search that act for hidden meaning it does not have.
when: Someone acts without being able to state why.
why: Unacknowledged motive leaves the actor uneasy about their own reasons.

text: Infer motive by asking what purpose a chain of acts serves; if no purpose is visible, suspect a hidden design behind them.
when: a crime's pattern is clear but its reason is not

text: Look beneath the surface of a person's acts for the impulses and motives behind them, rather than accepting visible behavior at face value.
A sympathetic motive, such as protecting someone from violence, should shape how the investigator chooses to act.
when: deciding the outcome for a suspect
why: motive changes the moral weight of the crime

text: Test a motive against the suspect's known character; a crime that clashes with their habits and temperament weakens the theory.
when: A motive points at a suspect whose known behaviour does not match the act.
why: Character fit is evidence, and a mismatch suggests another actor or a cover story.

text: Pair an inferred motive with known deadlines; a scheduled visit shows when discovery will come, which explains why the actor acted when they did.
when: A fixed arrival or event is known.
why: The deadline shows what the actor had to beat.

text: When a character's route does not match their stated purpose, suggest an unspoken motive worth probing, without concluding guilt from that single act.
when: A stated errand and the path taken diverge.
why: A mismatch points to a hidden goal but does not prove one.

text: A carefully staged, fitting revenge indicates a personal motive rather than a financial one, which points the investigation toward the hidden injury.
when: A larger plan is designed to match an earlier wrong.
why: Deliberate fit between act and grievance reveals the emotional source of the plan.

text: Envy shows through comparison with another's rise, such as a former subordinate's new status, and can make a witness hostile to that person.
when: A character's envy should shape their statements or actions.
why: Comparison makes the resentment concrete and affects the witness's reliability.

text: A motive reconstructed from a confessor's own reasoning may describe a belief they held, not what actually happened.
The motive for a denial cannot be read from the denial alone; it may be deliberate concealment or simply lack of nerve.
A motive does not identify its holder; the same history can support a different actor.
when: When a motive is used to name a suspect
why: Shared history can implicate several people who had the same grievance.

text: 1) Record each relevant action with its witness or source. 2) Order the actions chronologically. 3) Confront the suspect with the sequence and test their explanation against it.
when: motive is not confessed and must be inferred

text: 1) Imagine the suspect's inner state with ordinary common sense set aside. 2) Ask which motive that state would act on. 3) Keep only the suspects whose temperament fits the crime.
when: when narrowing suspects by motive
why: a temperament that fits the act is more likely to have committed it

text: Let motive emerge from fragments the player finds, such as NPC dialogue or a marriage record and will draft, with each deduction unlocking a new branch of the investigation.
when: when designing a mystery's motive
why: Step-by-step discovery builds a case the player owns.

text: Do not infer motive from one act alone; a violent or clumsy act may still serve a goal, so check what the actors were pursuing first.
when: judging why someone acted
why: clumsiness and motive are independent

text: Use financial motive to explain an action only once opportunity and a link to the crime are already in view.
when: building a case against a suspect
why: motive is supporting context, not a starting point

text: Vary each NPC's dialogue response to a search by motive, such as pride, fear or greed, so the reaction gives clues without explicit text.
when: when scripting NPC reactions to investigation
why: motive shapes reaction more than guilt alone

text: Separate personal motives, such as family ties, from impersonal ones, such as loyalty to a system, because each calls for different pressure.
Prefer surfacing motive through personality clashes over announcing it, but state it openly when a suspect will be cleared later or a character announces a framer's motive.
why: Conflict reveals motive more vividly than statement; a candid remark reads as trivial, so its weight is discounted until it matters; announcing lets the reveal land without group deduction.

text: Working out what a crime gained shows how far culprits will go to protect it, since a large gain raises the incentive to protect impunity.
when: Estimating a culprit's willingness to act against exposure
why: Gain indicates what the culprit has to lose.

text: Test a candidate motive by asking what the death gained a particular suspect; suspicious conduct alone does not supply motive, and a missing one weakens the case.
when: when a suspect looks suspicious, was chosen by elimination, or a candidate motive's credibility is judged
why: motive separates culpability from suspicious conduct; motive is a standard test of plausibility; a jury would expect one

text: Scale motive to the act: a grave crime needs a reason of comparable weight, and an obvious motive with small gain against violence may be a decoy.
when: deciding whether a suspicion is enough to act on, or the apparent motive is simple and obvious
why: Disproportion suggests the obvious motive is a decoy.

text: Test each candidate motive against a physical fact and discard any motive that fact contradicts, keeping the rest open until evidence settles them.
when: Several motives are possible and each can be checked against physical evidence
why: Testing against facts separates plausible motives from impossible ones

text: A motive that cannot account for a violent act cannot carry the case, however plausible it looks on its own.
Motive is a weak test of guilt because nearly everyone has some motive to harm someone, while a hidden or sudden motive can be more telling.
when: When many candidates share an apparent motive
why: Common motives do not distinguish people

text: Prefer a shared ideological motive when group actions exceed what individual grudges or documented gain can explain; otherwise prefer those simpler motives.
A motive can be modeled as a chain: a threat to the character, the options for removing it, why each option fails, and the resulting decision to act.
when: when reconstructing or writing a suspect's motive
why: a stated logical motive can be more convincing than an emotional one

text: A strong motive can bias reasoning toward a convenient suspect, and competing theories expose that danger.
Using a motive to dismiss an accusation replaces checking the claim, so true testimony can be discarded, and the bias can run either way.

1) Read the motive from the document. 2) Check what it would have required the person to do. 3) Compare against the person's known character and independent accounts. 4) Keep the motive open only if it fits; a mismatch makes the link doubtful.
when: A motive is proposed from a document such as a will.
why: A document can show a grievance without showing the person acted on it.

text: 1) List every candidate motive. 2) Take each separately and check its evidence support. 3) Check what the suspect would gain from the act. 4) Drop a motive only when evidence is absent; move to motives needing hidden preparation.
when: Several explanations for a plot are possible, or a suspect's stated motive is being evaluated.
why: Systematic elimination keeps a plausible motive from being dismissed unchecked; a motive must be supported and offer a plausible gain.

text: 1) Name the claimed motive. 2) List what was taken and what was left behind. 3) Check whether the left goods fit that motive. 4) Check whether the room's original state is known before reading disorder as proof.
when: a single apparent motive rests on timing or on a reading of disorder
why: a motive is only credible if the outcome matches what the motive would produce

text: 1) Build a motive as a chain of links. 2) State each link as a claim. 3) Check each claim against evidence before accepting the whole.
when: reasoning about a suspect's motive
why: a chain is only as strong as its weakest link

text: 1) State the suspect's gain from the act. 2) State the risk the act carries for them. 3) Judge the gain against the suspect's means and position. 4) Check whether the accuser holds evidence that could convict.
when: An official theory rests on one motive that seems out of proportion.
why: A motive is only credible if the gain is worth the risk for this particular person.

text: 1) Settle the suspect's identity first. 2) List plausible motives. 3) Test each against the evidence. 4) Set aside unsupported motives while keeping their underlying possibility open.
when: when a figure close to the crime may be complicit but evidence is unclear
why: motives can be tested one at a time without forcing a verdict

text: 1) Sort possible motives into a few categories. 2) For each suspect, check whether they gain from the death in each category. 3) Rule out suspects who gain from none.
when: when a suspect's motive is proposed or several suspects are possible
why: Categories let an investigator eliminate suspects systematically rather than by assumption.

text: 1) List the standard motives: habitual overuse, self-harm, money trouble, romantic involvement. 2) Ask about each. 3) Note which denials are complete.
when: Testing whether a denial hides a motive
why: A fixed list stops the questioner from skipping likely causes.

text: 1) List broad motive categories such as passion, money, blackmail, suicide and homicidal impulse. 2) Split each into concrete candidates. 3) Filter each candidate by feasibility and timing.
when: Early in an investigation when no suspect is favoured.
why: Mapping the full field prevents a plausible motive from being overlooked.

text: 1) List the relationships among people in the group. 2) Propose each candidate motive. 3) Keep a motive only if it explains every other fact, including the staging, not just the killing.
when: Choosing among motives in a small-group crime
why: A motive that explains the act but not the scene is incomplete

text: 1) State the motive as a claim backed by concrete evidence, such as a sum on a document plus testimony. 2) Check whether the pressured party and the killer are one person. 3) Adopt the branch needing fewer unknown people, keeping the other open. 4) Test the motive against behavior.
when: When a private transaction involves several people with a possible stake.
why: Branching avoids committing early while favouring the simpler explanation.

text: 1) List the missing person's finances, debts, routines, vices and other partners. 2) Check each one and rule out motives that do not fit. 3) Read the absence from what remains.
when: when someone vanishes and no crime is yet evident
why: each ruled-out motive narrows whether the absence was voluntary

text: 1) List each motive factor separately. 2) Check how the factors interact. 3) Rank the factors that bear directly on the act, and keep the ranked few rather than the full list.
when: Explaining why a character acted as they did.
why: Long unranked factor lists dilute the case.

text: 1) List every suspect. 2) Assign each a motive in the taxonomy. 3) Check that each suspect's motive fits a category, and note any that fit none.
when: Building a suspect list for a mystery
why: Confirms coverage of the cast and exposes motives outside the scheme

text: Discount a witness who has reason to shift blame, protect themselves, or fit the story, such as facing a charge or expecting a reward.
why: Their own outcome depends on what the story shows.

text: Design motive clues so players can rule out suspects whose motive does not match an observed behaviour change, and include tests of motive hypotheses that yield nothing.
when: Designing suspect sets and motive clues.
why: Elimination by motive gives players a method for narrowing suspects.

text: Use a motive as a basis for a theory only when its supporting evidence cannot be read equally well as innocent.
Ask whether a motive exists, not whether it seems adequate.
Motive pointing away from a fitting explanation: pursue the motive when facts fit, but test the timeline before discarding a theory, since motive can mislead.
when: when an explanation fits visible facts but the motive points elsewhere, or a suspect's motive seems to rule out a candidate explanation
why: Motive can mislead, while timeline facts are more checkable.

text: Combine a culprit's psychological profile with physical facts, since motive alone rarely settles who committed an act.
when: Solving a mystery
why: Physical evidence confirms or rules out what the motive suggests.

text: Rank suspects by motive, such as desire for credit or reputation, as well as by access; motive can point to a different suspect than access alone.
when: Several suspects could have performed an act.
why: A suspect's desire may point to a different kind of act than the one committed.

text: Mystery proof takes one of four kinds: a reconstructive test, a document, a trap, or a confession.
when: choosing how to confirm a hidden mechanism
why: Each kind gives the audience a different form of certainty.

text: Motive and suspicion are far weaker than proof of an act; a stated motive can explain a relationship without any crime, so motive alone does not establish that an act occurred.
when: Building a case on motive; evaluating a suspect's stated reason
why: A plausible reason for an act does not confirm it occurred; a motive describes intent or interest, not the action itself.

text: Romance and money motives are easy to over-weight, so check them against evidence before building a story around them.
when: Assigning motive to suspects

text: Keep the final proof narrow and personal; a confession can carry the reveal when the physical chain is thin.
when: when the reveal lacks a full physical evidence chain
why: A personal admission gives the reveal weight without a complete case file.

text: When suspects have comparable, established access, rank them by motive: who gains from the act and whether the gain is worth the risk.
when: Several suspects have comparable or established means and opportunity.
why: Motive can separate suspects that opportunity cannot.

text: Actions arise from several interacting drives, such as vanity, ambition, credulity, sincere belief, resentment, desire, jealousy or gain; identify the strongest.
when: A suspect's or character's motive or record is mixed, such as admirable and harmful acts together.
why: A single motive explains too little of a mixed record; money is often only one drive.

text: Accusations that carry a clear motive, such as inheritance or wealth, seem convincing even when unsupported.
when: several characters have plausible reasons to act
why: a stated motive gives an accusation weight before evidence is checked

text: A theory built on psychology and motive, such as hatred toward a rival, can point to a suspect without any physical evidence connecting that suspect to the act.
when: an explanation rests on motive rather than physical evidence
why: Motive is easy to imagine, so it can make a suspect seem guilty even when the act was physically impossible for them.

text: A belief in a cosmic enemy can be held across learned circles far from the community, making it a shared motive rather than local vanity.
Rank suspects by what each gains from a death, such as an inheritance or debt relief, to see who has a reason to act.
when: Early in an investigation with several suspects, especially where a death has financial consequences.
why: Known motive narrows who needs closer examination and shows which facts to check first.

text: A victim's known condition can link an object-based clue to a motive, because the condition explains why the clue matters.
when: an object clue depends on a person's limitation
why: Knowing the limitation connects the clue to the person who could exploit it.

text: Evidence of heavy physical work at a scene, such as digging, weighs against suspects who could not have done that work alone.
why: Labour requirements limit who could have acted.

text: Weigh a motive against medical and legal facts; a motive that could never be acted on, such as through an unmade will, weakens.
when: when a motive depends on a document

text: A broad motive that every character shares can hide the one person who had both motive and access. Look for the overlap of motive and opportunity.
when: when many characters have the same grievance
why: Shared motive makes everyone look equally suspicious, which hides the one person who could act.

text: Blame in a feud is often shared; when both sides escalate with uncharitable words, assign fault to both rather than one.
Do not reduce a character's conduct to one explanation: deliberate fraud, self-deception and partial madness can coexist, and cunning does not rule out madness.
when: judging a suspect's mixed or changing motives

text: Shared ownership of a plot gives several characters a motive to hide or reveal a crime.
When the stakes of a rivalry change, such as a consent being granted, the rival who stands to lose changes, and so does who has reason to act.
when: A rivalry's prize or conditions shift during the story

text: When a shared cost, such as paying a minister, falls on sub-groups whose interests differ, the community splits into factions that dispute the terms.
when: a community pays for a common institution
why: Groups with different stakes in the cost push for different outcomes

text: Model character motives as a shared pool where each character holds a stake, and one character can exploit another's stake to frame them.
when: when designing suspects with interlocking grievances
why: Interlocking stakes let false accusations feel plausible.

text: Motive alone does not identify a culprit; it ranks suspects by possible gain and can wrongly implicate an innocent person.
why: Motive shows possibility, not action, so accusation needs access and evidence.

text: Assuming the largest beneficiary or the first motive match is the culprit misleads, since several people may share the same financial stake or strain.
when: Multiple suspects have money troubles, claims on the estate, or one motive is found.
why: Financial strain can motivate many people, not only the direct heir.

text: Agreeing witnesses with a shared interest, such as protecting the same person, may give coordinated matching accounts; those who saw only part of an episode are also weaker.
when: Witnesses or tellers have a common stake in the outcome, or two accounts agree.
why: Agreement from interested parties does not independently confirm the facts.

text: Motive reasoning alone can deadlock: each suspect is cleared morally while the physical question of where the object is stays unresolved.
when: motive is the only sorting method used
why: Motive answers who, not where

text: 1) List each suspect's opportunity to overhear plans. 2) List direct gain. 3) List family links. 4) List possession of key objects. 5) Compare the lists to rank suspects.
when: Several suspects have overlapping opportunity and motive.
why: Structured comparison exposes which suspects have the most incriminating links.

text: 1) List everyone with a motive. 2) Ask which of them would take the risk. 3) Link facts such as sightings, quarrels and purchases. 4) Narrow the pool to those whose links reinforce one another.
when: Investigating a crime against a widely disliked victim
why: Many motives exist, so the pool must narrow through linked evidence

text: Treat a motive-based conclusion as a suspicion rather than a finding until independent evidence supports it, and ask whether it would survive later developments.
when: A theory is driven by motive or judgment about a suspect's character.
why: Motive reasoning can be persuasive without being proven.

text: Give an NPC several motive tags and let the player learn the dominant one through dialogue and history records.
when: when designing suspect motives for a mystery
why: Layered motives make the suspect more believable and reward attention to records.

text: Give each NPC a public reason for an action, such as a debt, fee or permit, plus a separate hidden grievance, and store both so players can connect them.
when: designing NPCs whose actions need a plausible surface cause

text: Create a moment where a character must publicly admit or deny a relationship, and let the response change the player's standing with that character.
when: Designing social consequences in a narrative game.
why: A public choice with lasting effect makes relationships feel consequential.

text: Keep some motives private, stated as the character's own matter, to create a hook the audience wants resolved.
when: Revealing a character's reasons.
why: Withheld motives create curiosity.

text: Stage an identity reveal in a public setting where witnesses can confirm it, using a physical item as proof.
when: when a hidden identity must be made undeniable
why: witnesses and proof remove the chance of explaining the anomaly away

text: Show a suspect's temper in public before the crime, so later evidence against them feels earned rather than invented.
when: Planting a suspect who will later be framed or accused.
why: Prior visible behavior makes later accusation credible to the player.

text: A quarrel overheard by others seems decisive because its emotional heat is taken as evidence of intent, even when it serves a different plan.
when: when a public or overheard argument precedes an event
why: Observers weight emotional intensity more heavily than context.

text: Heavy publicity of a lure, notice or reward warns the target as well as intended audiences; weigh wide reach against tipping off the wrong people.
when: Publicising a lure, notice or reward.
why: Wide exposure reaches unintended audiences along with the target; the same announcement that attracts informants also tells the thief what is being done.

text: An official's loaded characterization of a crime can prejudice listeners against the one suspect; a neutral, clear question is safer.
when: When an authority figure addresses a public audience during an investigation
why: Charged wording shapes judgment before the facts are established.

text: Jumping to a motive before the mechanism is clear invites unsupported answers; settle the motive by a test rather than assumption.
Taking a publicly stated motive at face value can hide the real stake; check it against the legal facts.
why: Stated motives may be incomplete or convenient for the person giving them.
