text: Gate some clues by language or background so only certain characters can understand them, turning the difference into a deduction.
when: Designing NPC dialogue or glyph clues
why: Knowledge gaps give players an inference to make.

text: Pair a limited light source with a short fuel timer, so brief flashes reveal the room layout in intervals.
when: designing dark exploration areas
why: Timed light forces the player to build a mental map from partial views.

text: Lighting, weather and sound can amplify a reveal, such as opening a hidden chamber during a storm at night.
when: Placing a hidden area or secret reveal in generated content
why: Environmental conditions heighten the emotional impact of the discovery.

text: A non-player character who starts a sentence and stops can mark a hidden room, item or fact that a later event reveals.
when: Placing secrets for players to discover
why: Interrupted dialogue signals hidden content without giving it away

text: Record which non-player characters know about a hidden treasure, so the player's suspect list is limited to those who know.
when: Designing a mystery where the treasure's location is secret.
why: Knowledge tracking narrows the suspect pool.

text: Let dialogue overheard during ordinary movement carry a hint whose meaning resolves only after a later event tests it.
Give an NPC approximate, somewhat generic details, and let a second source narrow them down to a specific identity.
Give NPCs small tells, such as a glance toward a companion, and time reactions to a known figure's arrival, so players can detect suspicion without dialogue.
when: designing non-verbal cues for suspicion
why: visual tells reward players who watch characters rather than objects

text: A minor NPC who observes a destroyed note can later report it, letting the player reconstruct a missing clue.
when: When designing evidence that is destroyed in-game.
why: Witnesses to destruction preserve the content indirectly.

text: An NPC with memory loss answers only about events after a set trigger, so the player learns the boundary of what can be asked.
when: Designing an NPC with amnesia.
why: A defined boundary makes the limit legible rather than arbitrary.

text: NPCs can be built so that two identities are never on screen together, and the player must catch the moment they overlap to reveal the deception.
when: Designing a double-identity mystery.
why: Overlap detection rewards careful observation of timing.

text: Suspecting insiders with access to a captive or record on presentiment alone, without proof, misdirects inquiry, diverting effort and weakening colleagues' trust in the investigation.
when: A leak or sabotage is suspected inside an investigating organisation, or an investigation turns toward internal suspects without proof.
why: Rivalry and access create plausible motive that pulls attention from evidence; unverified accusations divert effort and weaken confidence.

text: Trusting an insider's account as neutral observation is a mistake when the account is itself part of the campaign it describes.
An insider premise can exclude outsiders too early and shape every later question, so keep an outside accomplice open as a possibility.
A naive map overcounts witnesses; foliage or other obstructions can leave only one window with a usable view.

1) Estimate the risk the insider takes. 2) Offer compensation matched to that risk. 3) Give a written guarantee of safety and protection. 4) Schedule contact around the target's routine, away from observation.
when: when you need an insider to control access or a record
why: Money, guarantees and safety address the insider's personal risk.

text: 1) Ask a question only an insider would know. 2) Withhold the expected answer. 3) Reveal it and watch for a reaction that betrays prior knowledge.
when: Checking whether an evasive suspect actually has insider knowledge.

text: Model each NPC's line of sight through windows, gaps and light levels, so players check sightlines against geometry; a reflection or candle can make a claim plausible or impossible.
when: When an NPC's claimed sightline or witness account must be checkable against the environment.
why: Physical constraints and geometry let players test claims against the world.

text: Make overheard NPC conversations at doors or vents partial, so players infer context, may guess wrong, and combine fragments with other sources to uncover hidden factions.
when: When designing overheard dialogue as a clue.
why: Incomplete context creates inference the player must test; overheard fragments hint at hidden factions without a direct scene.

text: Keep a turned insider inside their normal role so they keep the appearance of innocence and can keep helping.
when: when the insider's cover is needed for later actions
why: Visible involvement exposes the insider.

text: Store observer notes as a log the player can review later, with each detail tagged for its later relevance.
when: when designing observer records

text: Stage a lineup where an NPC notices one candidate among several placed unannounced, so the player sees a spontaneous reaction rather than a prompted answer.
when: when designing an NPC identification moment
why: unprompted reactions carry more information than answers given after prompting

text: Track what each NPC saw separately from what they heard, so the player can weigh the two kinds of evidence differently.
when: when logging NPC knowledge of events
why: sight and sound differ in reliability and detail

text: Give each NPC witness a knowledge limit, such as illiteracy or fear, that changes how they respond to a note or question.
when: when designing NPCs who can testify or be influenced
why: limits make responses believable and varied

text: Let players probe an NPC on a side topic to reach the desired information, and give the NPC motives that colour how they interpret the player's questions.
when: When designing dialogue for a guarded or hostile NPC.
why: Indirect approaches and motive-coloured answers make the same question yield different responses from different NPCs.

text: Let a quest-giving character react differently when questioned alone versus in front of others, so the player can infer which of their claims is false.
when: When designing NPC dialogue that depends on social context.
why: Changing reactions by context gives the player a way to test claims.

text: Give an informant NPC in a heightened mood partial reports with gaps, and let the player fill them by checking a document or another NPC.
why: Rewards careful cross-checking

text: Give NPC witnesses traits such as heavy sleep or a faulty clock that players must factor into how much they trust each testimony.
Model NPC recognition so a witness can identify the wrong person, and let the player pick a suspect from descriptions in a line-up.
when: Designing identification mechanics for suspects in a game.
why: Wrong identifications create tension and force the player to test descriptions against evidence.

text: Build each motive around a specific non-player character so players can test it.
when: Designing motives for a murder-mystery scenario.
why: A motive tied to a concrete character can be checked by the player.

text: Let a witness NPC recognize a player character while misremembering a name or place, and require the player to cross-check the claim against an in-world record.
when: When designing recognition scenarios.
why: Misremembered details force verification through records.

text: Let an NPC witness an argument and report its tone but not its content, leaving the player to find the subject elsewhere.
when: Designing a witnessed event that carries a hidden subject.
why: Partial testimony prompts the player to investigate further.

text: Place an NPC conversation the player can overhear from cover, and let its content change how the player approaches a later encounter.
Move NPC dialogue through stages (guarded, pressured, conceding), unlocking information through raised stakes or by the player presenting a document.
when: Designing NPC interrogation dialogue

text: Give NPC sightings time windows rather than exact times; overlapping windows create real alibi questions the player must resolve.
when: when designing npc movement and alibis
why: Overlap produces genuine ambiguity.

text: Track what each NPC believes against the true world state, so that reassurances and claims can be checked by the player.
when: an NPC's dialogue may be wrong or incomplete
why: Comparing belief to truth turns NPC statements into testable information.

text: Let an NPC voice certainty about what investigators can find, so the player can later contradict that statement.
when: Writing NPC dialogue about detection.
why: A confident claim becomes a checkable statement that the player's findings can refute.

text: Split an NPC's knowledge across several conversations, releasing the decisive fact only after the earlier clues have been collected.
Let the player's questions about how an NPC knew something change what the player can deduce about that NPC's knowledge.
when: When an NPC holds information that the player must trace.
why: The source of knowledge is itself evidence about the NPC's role.

text: Attach knowledge flags to witnesses, such as knows the victim or has seen the face, that determine whether their testimony can rule out a suspect.
when: Implementing witness systems in games.
why: Keeps testimony logic tied to what each character could plausibly know.

text: Readers trust a quiet, harmless-seeming companion, so ordinary actions by that companion are read as innocent even when they are preparation for a crime.
when: a companion's ordinary action is visible early in the story
why: The surface reading of harmlessness hides the planning, so the reader misses the clue until a deduction.

text: A nominal intermediary can be named on paper to protect a real investigator's role, even if the intermediary does little of the work.
when: A hidden party must be formally represented without revealing their involvement.
why: A formal name can shield the true actor from being identified.

text: Model each character's knowledge and their contacts, so the player can trace where a secret leaked through the network.
when: Designing secrets that spread among NPCs.
why: Explicit knowledge and contact links make leaks traceable and fair.

text: A rival or official NPC holding private information can release it through conversation, a permit or a favour, giving the player a reason to pursue relationships.
when: Designing information access for an NPC faction
why: Gated information turns social actions into progress

text: An NPC's willingness to disclose responds to the player's tone, so reassuring dialogue can draw a fuller answer than pressure does.
when: player chooses reassuring or pressuring dialogue

text: Withholding too long leaves the audience feeling cheated and without footing; each reveal needs enough earlier facts understood to land.
when: Planning how long to delay key information.
why: Without context, a reveal feels arbitrary rather than meaningful.

text: Promising more than you can deliver, such as absolute discretion, creates risk when your obligations to others limit what you can keep private.
Leaving a client waiting while attending to another matter can cost goodwill, so manage the client's perception of attention.
when: When an investigator must juggle several threads at once
why: Visible neglect of the client's concerns damages the relationship.

text: Track a hidden trust or fear value per NPC; let it change how much they reveal and how reliable their information is.
when: Designing NPC interrogation scenes or information-giving NPCs.
why: Trust and fear determine willingness to disclose and reliability, so the player must judge trust in context.

text: Give each NPC a stated stake in what they say, so players can judge when a witness is protecting someone.
when: When designing NPC testimony.
why: Knowing the stake lets players discount biased claims.

text: Build NPC dialogue so each NPC reveals only part of the truth, with each holding a different slice and a different stake.
when: When designing a mystery with several informants.
why: Partial, self-interested accounts require players to combine sources.

text: Post a notice or bounty naming a ship, guild or location tied to an NPC's past, so the player can deduce the connection.
when: Designing world notices that link to NPC backstory.
why: Known connections let players infer ties without being told.

text: Give NPC witnesses a loyalty or price value, and change their statements when the player bribes, threatens or befriends them.
when: Designing NPCs who witness a crime
why: Witness statements then depend on the player's actions

text: Model servants and gossips as relays that pass information with noise, so a rumor may name the wrong amount or culprit.
when: Designing an NPC gossip or rumor network.
why: Noise in relays makes the player verify before trusting.

text: Give each NPC a hidden secret that offers a second motive, so the player must test which motive explains an act.
Let an NPC withhold information from another NPC so the player must choose whom to tell.
when: when designing NPC knowledge systems

text: Observers classify an object by the nearest group it appears with, so grouping steers interpretation before any deduction begins.
when: an object is displayed among other items
why: people assign a category from their neighbours

text: Let a local answer questions with the subject's name and occupation, then add a second question that tests the player's interest.
when: Designing NPC information exchanges.

text: Judge a tip by its source's motive and track record as well as its content.
when: a tip comes from a source with a known motive or fallibility
why: A source's history shapes how far its content can be trusted

text: Do not press a contact on topics they steer away from. Their redirection signals a line they will not cross.
Mark which characters stay silent at a key moment, since silence in a timeline can point to a later confrontation.
when: When designing a timeline of NPC statements.
why: Absence can foreshadow conflict.

text: Use a town-scale investigation when rumour spreads and many suspects appear at once; a closed circle of suspects suits a single-scene mystery better.
End a scene on an NPC's departure to create a new objective to find him.
when: Closing a confrontation scene
why: A sudden exit converts the scene's tension into a search goal

text: A shop ledger in the game world can confirm or contradict an NPC's account of a sale; a matching entry builds trust, a missing line opens a new branch.
when: Designing NPC sale claims verifiable through in-world records.
why: Records give players a way to test NPC statements.

text: A shop NPC who recognises a mark can offer a lead, so a dialogue check becomes a clue source.
when: designing dialogue-based clues

text: In town, neighbours' indignation and nearby justice let a single complaint set an investigation in motion quickly.
why: Close neighbours and authorities are able to act on a report almost immediately.

text: A matching print shows someone touched an object, not that they used it to commit a crime; pair it with other evidence before concluding intent.
1) State a limited aim honestly. 2) Show the object. 3) Invoke shared history. 4) Let the contact choose what to share. 5) Follow up discreetly.
when: When approaching a contact who knows a specialised market.

text: Let related NPCs be referred together, but require the player to separate each person's individual evidence from the shared reputation, since grouping lends each case unearned weight.
when: Designing or referring linked suspects in one document
why: Shared grouping makes each case look stronger than its individual evidence supports; shared reputation can hide weak evidence.

text: Treat ordinary conversation with side characters as an information-gathering action.
Make contact NPCs return nothing useful for a culprit with no history, so the player cannot solve the case by asking the wrong source.
when: designing informant characters
why: Otherwise a wrong source would give a shortcut.

text: A ghost NPC that names a culprit should give the player a lead to check, not a verdict, and the game should tag such claims as unverified.
when: designing ghost or spirit witnesses

text: Make debt ledgers and inheritance documents discoverable through conversation or records, so players can cite debts, deadlines and inheritances as motives pointing to specific NPCs.
when: Designing NPC motives in a narrative game
why: Visible financial stakes let players build cases from in-world facts.

text: Leave an NPC's motive real but partly open, so players must test it against evidence and decide how far to trust what the NPC says.
when: designing a suspect NPC or writing NPC dialogue with uncertain reliability
why: A testable motive keeps the investigation open, and partial ambiguity makes trust a player decision rather than a given.

text: Profit is not the sole possible reason for murder, so each motive category must be tested against evidence rather than assumed.
Let different NPCs accept or refuse the same bribe, so players learn what each NPC values.
Seed each motive line with a different NPC so the player's questions lead to separate characters.
when: designing a multi-motive mystery

text: Let a final reveal reframe an NPC's motives and attach a choice that rewards mercy or the withholding of punishment.
Give NPCs backstories that supply motive, and let players uncover them through informants who disagree with each other or have a stake.
Give an NPC a motive to conceal, so the player must find the reason before the testimony becomes usable.
Let an NPC's stated fear become a quest hook whose outcome depends on the player's choices.
when: Designing a quest triggered by an NPC's worry.
why: A fear the player can act on gives the quest personal stakes.

text: Give each non-player character a motive from the categories so the cast includes at least one gain-based and one prevention-based suspect.
when: Populating a mystery with suspects
why: A mixed cast keeps the player's suspicion divided between different kinds of motive

text: A helper whose motives are hidden so thoroughly that their choices seem arbitrary loses credibility.
when: Writing an ally who offers help during a pursuit.
why: Players need enough information to interpret an ally's actions.

text: Give two or three suspect NPCs stated motives such as debt, rivalry or inheritance, so the player can rank suspects and check each before accusing.
when: designing a mystery with several possible culprits
why: A ranked suspect list gives the player a starting point, and several plausible motives keep the solution open.

text: Give NPCs motives such as rivalry or family ties that shape their reports and interrogation choices, so hostile accounts visibly differ from neutral ones.
when: designing NPC investigators or NPC testimony
why: Visible bias lets the player learn to discount it.

text: Give an NPC a stated reason and a hidden agenda; let hesitation, evasion, slips, or a cost or quantity mismatch with the stated reason reveal the agenda.
when: designing a character with secret motives
why: Players discover the agenda through play rather than being told, and reward reading small tells.

text: Give NPCs explicit incentives such as debt, pledge or forfeiture, so players can judge whether a witness is self-serving.
when: designing NPC witnesses
why: Visible stakes let players weigh bias

text: When an NPC reports another character's motives, write the claim so it can be wrong, and let physical evidence confirm or refute it.
when: when an NPC explains someone else's reasons
why: motives are inferences, so the player needs an external check

text: Give an NPC a changed decision as a motive, paired with an emotional and a material explanation, so the player must weigh both.
Tie NPC motives to status and reputation, revealed through dialogue, gifts and gossip rather than through a stated goal.
when: designing NPC goals
why: players piece motives together from behavior

text: Build a motive board for each NPC listing what each gains from a crime, and seed at least one conflicting statement per suspect.
when: designing NPCs for a murder or theft mystery
why: each suspect then has a reason to act and a testable inconsistency

text: Tag NPCs with motives such as pride, debt or ambition, so their offers and threats read as motivated rather than arbitrary.
when: designing NPC dialogue and behaviour
why: visible motives make actions legible

text: List what each NPC gains from a frame or setup; when one gain matches an earlier quarrel, flag it as a lead for the player.
when: designing accusations or frames in a story
why: matching gains and history give players a traceable lead

text: Tie an NPC's odd behavior or missed appointments to a pending inheritance case, so the player can trace the cause through records.
when: designing NPC behavior in a mystery

text: Track an NPC's motives as a list that can change and grow as the story escalates, such as notoriety followed by fear of consequences.

Build NPC relationship graphs covering friendships, feuds, inherited grudges, marriages, property claims and financial stakes, so players map motives and predict who testifies, stays silent or slants stories.
when: Designing characters for a mystery, social dispute or populated world with witnesses and factions.
why: Mapped stakes make motives discoverable; ties drive testimony and silence.

text: Each party in a probing exchange may read the other's lack of knowledge as confirmation of its own theory.
when: when two parties each hold a partial view of the same matter
why: silence and ignorance are easily misinterpreted

text: Observers without a shared baseline for normal bodies disagree about what counts as an unusual mark, so their findings conflict even when they look at the same body.
when: When examiners must judge whether a mark is abnormal.
why: Each observer compares the body against a different private sense of what is normal.

text: Unspoken distrust in a relationship can persist despite a person's will to dismiss it, and explains why earlier warning signs went unacted upon.
when: A character ignores warning signs about someone close
why: Intuition and long-held unease resist deliberate reasoning

text: End a resolved story with ordinary everyday talk to show that normal life has resumed.
How each person sees the other can drive an intrigue, so track both sides' self-regard when reconstructing motive.
When NPC relationships determine who accuses whom, suspicion follows the social graph rather than chance, so relationships drive the outcome.
when: A game where NPCs react to each other's behavior.
why: Suspicion travels along existing ties, so changing a relationship changes who is accused.

text: When each party withholds information, each suspects the others, creating a deadlock where cooperation becomes awkward.
An informant NPC can change its dialogue when the player names a suspect, confirming the link and unlocking the next lead.
Bribery and cover stories offered in dialogue can change how an NPC behaves afterwards.
when: the player persuades or pays an NPC

text: A note or dialogue line can carry two meanings, each pointing toward a different suspect, room or solution.
when: Writing a clue with two intended interpretations.
why: Each meaning gives the player a different lead to test.

text: Two statements that agree do not prove either is true, since they may simply share one version of events.
Recognition can run both ways, so an investigator who is spotted may not be able to rely on staying hidden.
when: staging a confrontation with a disguised suspect
why: The suspect may recognise the investigator in return.

text: 1) Rank each NPC by age, then office, then property. 2) Choose dialogue honorifics that match that rank. 3) Let rank decide whose accusations others credit.
when: NPC standing affects whether others listen to them

text: 1) State the damage a public case would do. 2) Require the return of stolen goods and receipts. 3) Verify the recovery. 4) Offer the exit only after verification succeeds.
when: an investigator considers letting a guilty party go

text: Let small talk on unrelated topics raise a guarded NPC's trust, unlocking deeper dialogue and behavioral clues in later talks instead of direct questions.
when: Designing dialogue or open-world social interaction with guarded characters.
why: Rising trust gates access to sensitive information; rapport from casual talk can open disclosure.

text: Let an NPC reputation system weight a character's word by their standing and history.
when: designing NPC reputation systems

text: Do not drop a case while the wronged party is still in danger.
when: the victim faces ongoing risk from the offender

text: Give NPCs emotional bonds in a relationship graph, and design a protective NPC's cover story with a tell the player can expose.
Let an NPC who hides a relation be exposed by a name challenge in dialogue, with a reassurance branch that unlocks the confession.
when: When designing dialogue for a hidden relationship
why: Branching dialogue lets the player choose pressure or reassurance

text: Track NPC relationship values so an NPC's answer about a rival changes with which relationship the NPC chooses to admit.
when: A player questions an NPC about another character.
why: Admitted relationships shape what the NPC says.

text: Route a rumour through several NPCs so the player must trace each link back to its source.
Track what the player has shared with a companion, and let that companion's stance change when they could act on the secret.
when: Designing companion NPCs who receive player secrets.
why: Shared secrets create consequences that make companion relationships meaningful.

text: Keeping allies uninformed protects the plan and makes their behaviour read naturally to watching suspects, but leaves them unable to judge their own risk.
when: When allies must stay separate from the real plan, especially if observed by suspects.
why: Uninformed allies cannot give the plan away through their behaviour.

text: A mutual information trade shows what each side will risk, but offering your information reveals your own hand, since the other party learns what you already hold.
Model NPC rivalries with grudges, and let rivals leak information to one another so the player can overhear and act on it.
when: When designing NPC relationships that carry story information.

text: If a player provokes an NPC into violence, let the consequences fall on the player and the NPC's situation, after a clear prior warning.
Have an NPC press a rival explanation, so players must test it against evidence rather than accept it.
when: when designing misleading NPC pressure

text: Let a family's social connections, not only guilt, decide whether an NPC is protected or exposed.
when: when designing NPC consequences in a game

text: Let an NPC hint at a coming threat without specifics, record the hint as a flag, and let a later event confirm or contradict it.
A protagonist's confident conclusion is overturned when the authorities already hold the key evidence, obtained through a minor character she had overlooked.
when: a reveal must overturn the protagonist's theory
why: the decisive clue sat with a character the protagonist never considered

text: Social invisibility is a culprit hidden by an everyday role that people stop noticing, so the culprit is present in the scene yet never seen as a suspect.
A quest where one NPC is sent by another lets the player trace the original instruction and discover who controls whom.
when: Designing NPC quest chains
why: Tracing the chain of command reveals hidden power relations.

text: Delay a scripted arrival with dialogue beats that build toward the reveal of a masked contact.
when: Scripting the appearance of a key contact.
why: Dialogue during the wait keeps the anticipation active until the arrival.

text: Give the player an NPC who can confirm a clue, with a second source available if that NPC is removed or lies.
when: A clue depends on one character's testimony.
why: A backup source keeps progress possible.

text: A restrained or injured NPC can be the conspirator rather than the victim, so do not assume a bound character's role until evidence confirms it.
An NPC who claims neutrality can be scored by their gain from each outcome, so the player must infer their real loyalty from incentives.
when: Designing NPC allegiance that is not stated outright
why: Incentives reveal loyalty more reliably than declared positions

text: A misdelivered item that shares a surname can look like a deliberate link between two characters and mislead the reader.
why: Overlapping names make coincidence seem like intent.

text: A returned character's explanation for missing time should match physical marks such as injuries or damp clothing.
Tag each piece of NPC information with its source, such as seen directly, heard from someone, or told by a dead person, so players can judge trust.
when: Designing an interrogation or information system.
why: Source tags let players weigh reliability instead of accepting all claims equally.

text: After an event, NPC behaviour drifts back toward its baseline over time, which creates a window for detection.
when: An NPC has changed behaviour after a major event.
why: Old patterns return gradually, revealing the change.

text: Let an NPC remove clues on a schedule, so the player must reach the scene before cleanup or question the NPC about what was removed.
when: Designing an NPC who tidies a room in a game
why: Time pressure and questioning turn cleanup into a playable challenge

text: Give NPCs routines so that a change in schedule or a hidden item becomes a readable tell for the player.
when: designing NPC behavior for player observation
why: a stable routine lets deviations signal meaning

text: A person who tidies clothes or hair before an authority figure is often trying to appear composed, not showing vanity.
when: when a suspect prepares to face an authority
why: Presenting oneself well is a common response to a formal meeting.

text: An impossible or grotesque form of a myth can discourage close questioning, since witnesses are reluctant to examine something so strange.
when: a hoax needs to avoid scrutiny
why: Strangeness makes witnesses reluctant to test the details.

text: Make a gentle-seeming NPC the antagonist, with earlier hints that players can recognize in hindsight.
Gentle prodding, such as offering help or asking whether more time would help, raises stakes without pushing a stalled group too hard.
when: A group is stalled in a timed decision.
why: Mild pressure keeps the group moving without forcing an outcome.

text: Appearing weak or unthreatening can lower a suspect's guard, leading them to speak more freely and reveal hidden intent.
when: Interrogating a suspect who may be on guard
why: A suspect who believes the investigator is harmless may disclose information or intent

text: Keep praise plausible and in character, since heavy-handed flattery telegraphs the trap.
when: Writing a character who lures through praise

text: Script an NPC's courtesy to escalate as the player is pulled deeper, so warmth reveals intent over time.
when: Designing an NPC who may be setting a trap

text: Gathering all suspects in one enclosed place creates social pressure and lets their reactions be observed.
Gate some answers behind an NPC's trust rather than evidence, so the player unlocks them through relationship instead of investigation.
when: Designing case files with confidant NPCs
why: Trust is a separate unlock path

text: Excessive praise can lower a guest's guard and keep him in place, and its real purpose may be hidden behind its warmth.
when: A character's praise is out of proportion to the act praised
why: Flattery softens targets and binds them to a group

text: Grisly detail can overshadow the investigative point, so the physical clue should stay the focus.
1) Estimate the likely emotional cause of the witness's distress. 2) Name it gently. 3) Let the witness confirm or correct it instead of accusing them.
when: A witness shows distress or defensiveness about a sensitive subject.
why: A witness who confirms a point discloses more reliably than one who is accused.

text: Gather documents that show contact with a relative or other leverage before confronting an adversary.
When an NPC reports fear without detail, prompt the player to gather specifics before the report counts as evidence.
when: an NPC voices vague dread about another character
why: Unspecific fear cannot support a conclusion until its basis is found

text: Give NPCs observable tells such as glancing away, hesitating, or shifting posture and expression, so players can read their state when sensitive subjects come up.
when: designing NPC dialogue
why: Visible state changes give players a readable channel for information not stated in dialogue.

text: An unguarded flash of surprise can reveal that an opponent's assumption about your motive was wrong, and they lower their estimate of you.
when: Watching an opponent during a bargaining exchange
why: Unguarded reactions expose assumptions the opponent did not mean to show

text: Make an NPC's reaction a readable signal so players learn whether a hidden line landed.
Give a rival a backstory, such as a lost inheritance or a fallen family, so the player can read the grudge as motivated.
when: Presenting an NPC's grudge to the player
why: Backstory makes the reason for the grudge clear

text: An NPC who believes the player holds proof can be made to reveal a hiding place or act on it, so bluffing about knowledge can change NPC behavior.
when: In dialogue systems where NPCs track what the player appears to know.
why: Actions taken on false beliefs expose hidden information.

text: In an interrogation system, emotional reactions can change an NPC's state without unlocking a confession, so the player must still gather proof.
why: Separating reaction state from proof prevents emotional responses from acting as a shortcut to admission.

text: A readable mark is also a clue for whoever holds the object, and may expose the owner as well.
when: A marked item is in a thief's possession
why: The mark can be read by anyone holding it

text: Record treatments in a chart the player can read, so the question of what was given and when becomes a deduction.
when: medical or poisoning mysteries

text: Record an NPC's debts or prior dealings in a log the player can read, giving motive before the event.
Give NPCs readable wear, such as boot type, sunburn, or mourning colors, so players can infer backstory from them.
when: when designing NPC appearance
why: Visible details let players reason about a character's past.

text: Build a retreat state where a guarded NPC withdraws and returns later with different dialogue options.
when: Designing NPCs who react to pressure.
why: A retreat state makes pressure have lasting consequences on dialogue.

text: Script confrontations between an NPC and two possible culprits, showing a reaction cue that can be misread by the player.
when: designing a confrontation with ambiguous culprits
why: a readable but misleading cue creates productive uncertainty

text: Build physical tells such as a tremor or limp into NPCs as observable clues that change with stress.
when: Designing NPC appearance and behaviour that conveys condition or history.
why: Changing physical signs give players observable evidence to interpret.

text: Small signs like face, hesitation and manner can leak inner state, but the same reaction is often read in opposite ways, so treat it as interpretation, not evidence.
when: Observing suspects or people hiding emotion in conversation
why: Involuntary signs can leak state even when words do not, yet expressions carry no fixed meaning.

text: Log every NPC statement verbatim with a timestamp so later contradictions, including denials of words used, can be flagged and shown to the player as clues.
when: Building an NPC dialogue system or player journal for a mystery.
why: Timestamped, verbatim records let the game and player detect contradictions across time.

text: Attach a source to each NPC accusation, such as the room the speaker was in, so the player can judge how far the claim reaches.
when: Designing NPC accusations in a game.
why: A stated source lets the player weigh a claim's reliability.

text: A dialogue system can have an NPC demand a decision after a player's report and log which names the player withheld, so later reactions reflect that choice.
when: when the player reports a suspicion to an NPC with authority
why: Recording withheld information lets later dialogue respond to what the player chose to conceal.

text: 1) Record every claim a witness NPC makes. 2) Log the relevant game-state facts, such as door locks or light sources. 3) Flag any claim that conflicts with the logged state.
when: Designing an NPC whose story the player can test.
why: Later contradictions can then be surfaced in dialogue.

text: Have an NPC write a word or sign a line through a plausible request, unlocking a later comparison puzzle.
when: Designing handwriting or signature matching puzzles
why: The player gets comparison material without the NPC knowing it matters

text: Give NPCs a verification step, such as asking a clerk, so a player's cover story can be confirmed or exposed in play.
when: a player invents a story to approach an NPC
why: verification makes the player's choices consequential

text: Log NPC state changes with their triggering events, so the player can see each sudden change and its known cause.
when: Designing NPC behaviour that shifts over time.
why: Linked logs let players reason from behaviour changes to motives.

text: Record each NPC's witness state as saw, heard or assumed, and let contradictions between states unlock an accusation.
when: Designing investigation mechanics with multiple witnesses
why: Distinguishing knowledge types makes contradictions detectable

text: Store an NPC's scripted line separately from its true memory, so repeated or rephrased questions can expose the difference.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that can be coached or concealed.
why: Separating the two lets the game reveal the real answer under pressure.

text: Flag an NPC who readily accepts a suggested story for further checks when the player offers an explanation for a found item.
Give each NPC statement a checkable part and an uncheckable part, so the player can choose which claims to press.
when: Designing NPC testimony.

text: Let the player check an NPC's record: who they vouched for, who they accused, and what they did afterward.
A remark that provokes a visible flush or resentment indicates it has struck a nerve, which other listeners can read.
when: A casual or teasing remark draws an unusually strong reaction.
why: Visible embarrassment or resentment signals that the remark touched a sensitive point.

text: Let NPCs react differently to a bluff, and let a guard who seems told the truth betray knowledge through a pause, glance, or quick denial.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that responds to player probing
why: Reactions carry information the player must read and interpret.

text: Pressing a suspect hard or probing overtly makes them conceal everything, including unrelated truths, since they sense interrogation and stop speaking freely.
when: Interrogating a suspect who is already defensive or may hold back knowledge.
why: Heavy pressure shifts the suspect from correcting a story to withholding all information.

text: Give NPCs strong reactions to specific news, objects, or ordinary-looking figures to direct investigation; give the NPC a weak excuse a companion can question.
when: Designing NPC reactions that prompt player investigation.
why: Strong topic-specific reactions make a subject stand out, and the mismatch creates a reason to revisit the NPC later.

text: Script subtle tells, such as brief animations, dialogue pauses, or feigned ignorance or disdain, that attentive players catch on a second conversation but careless ones miss.
when: Designing NPCs who hint at or conceal hidden knowledge.
why: Subtle tells reward observation and repeated play without giving away the answer.

text: Use suspect tells sparingly, since too many make every character look guilty.
when: when writing character reactions in a mystery
why: Constant tells dilute their meaning and remove the signal that marks a real secret.

text: Key NPC tell animations to specific player questions, and offer a face-saving dialogue option that lets the NPC continue.
when: when designing interrogation or dialogue in a game
why: Matched tells make the NPC's reaction legible, and an exit keeps the dialogue from stalling.

text: Show a character's dramatic outburst as a reaction rather than the solution, so the player does not mistake the reaction for the answer.
when: A character reacts strongly during a mystery scene.
why: A vivid reaction can look like the key clue when it is only a response.

text: Give NPC tells, like nervousness or sudden topic changes, a test players can run, such as a follow-up question or second look, so manner is never the verdict.
when: Designing NPCs with a hidden stake in an outcome.
why: Observable tells invite investigation without giving away the answer.

text: Build non-player character theories as specific, checkable claims, so the player can disprove them and learn from the failure.
why: vague claims cannot be tested or refuted

text: A confused NPC may retain one clear memory; let that fragment serve as the clue rather than the whole speech.
when: Designing an NPC whose memory is declining or fragmented
why: A single clear fragment can carry a clue without making the NPC seem fully lucid

text: Author physical details on NPCs, such as a bandage or a missing shave, as small tells that connect to the mystery's solution.
when: Writing characters who hide a connection to the crime
why: Visible details reward attention and can be explained only by the solution

text: A rare trait that appears in only one character's description can let the player identify a body, while a second character confirms a fact but declines to explain it.
when: Designing a mystery where a found body must be matched to an NPC.
why: Rare traits act as unique keys, and partial knowledge from different NPCs keeps the player reasoning rather than receiving a direct answer.

text: Give NPC testimony a way for players to test it; testimony players cannot check should count only as presumption.
when: designing NPC testimony in an investigation

text: NPC dialogue can contain a plausible lie that the player tests against a known constraint, such as when an item could have been changed.
Track which NPCs are drawn in by testimony and keep their personal attitudes separate from their family's.
Denials by people who would have received or seen something can work as negative evidence that undermines a stated purpose.
when: A claimed reason for an action is contradicted by those who should know
why: The absence of the claimed item or event among those expected to have it weakens the claim

text: Let NPC dialogue contradict scene data so the player can catch a lie or confusion, and let vantage rules limit what each NPC can report.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that interacts with world state
why: Contradictions and vantage limits make testimony a puzzle the player must solve.

text: Each consultation with a non-specialist creates a record of what the culprit attempted, which can later be used to reconstruct the method.
when: When a culprit sought outside help or information.
why: Outside contacts can remember or document the offender's intentions.

text: Make an NPC's account detailed about the wrong moment, so the player notices what the account skips.
when: Writing an NPC who gives a testimony about a scene
why: Detail in the wrong place draws attention to the gap

text: Gaps across several NPC accounts signal either a lie or a missing witness, giving the player a lead to follow.
An authority NPC holding a biased theory can be challenged by letting the player's alternative theory be tested against evidence, rewarding players who question the official line.
when: Designing an investigation where an NPC authority is wrong.
why: Testing an alternative gives the player a meaningful way to overturn the wrong conclusion.

text: Give NPC witnesses a reliability value and a motive or bias tag; low-character or intoxicated witnesses give partial information that players must cross-check.
when: When designing NPC testimony for a game.
why: Explicit tags make contradictory accounts a reasoning task, and partial, biased information rewards player verification.

text: Give witnesses a reliability score; tag claims as facts or impressions, testing facts and discounting impressions; fearful witnesses may change details under pressure.
when: When designing NPC testimony or interview dialogue.
why: Impressions carry less certainty than observed facts, and opinions cannot be verified the way facts can.

text: Give an expert NPC a plausible but misleading lecture that sends the player toward the wrong district or faction; the player must decide whether to act on it or verify it.
when: When designing misdirection through an expert character or any NPC who gives information.
why: Plausible misdirection tests whether players verify claims, which makes information gathering a decision.

text: Let NPC explanations be testable against the scene, such as a mundane source like wind or a draft, or whether a burial site holds the remains claimed.
when: When designing NPC accounts of strange events or on-the-spot explanations.
why: A testable explanation makes the player's investigation determine the outcome.

text: Give NPC testimony a stated vantage point and confidence level so players can judge its reliability.
when: When designing NPC dialogue that reveals information.
why: Players can weigh statements only when they know how the speaker knows them.

text: Let a second NPC partly confirm or contradict the first and leave the gap for the player to resolve.
when: When designing linked NPC testimony.
why: Partial overlap creates a puzzle the player must reason through.

text: Give two NPCs opposed opinions about the same figure, so the player must decide whom to believe and why.
when: Designing a conflict of testimony for the player to resolve.
why: Opposed accounts force the player to weigh reliability.

text: Let NPC witnesses report partial observations with gaps, leaving the player to fill in the rest and check each claim.
when: designing witness dialogue for a mystery
why: Partial and interpreted reports keep the player an active evaluator rather than a recipient of settled facts.

text: Do not treat a suspect's outburst as proof on its own; link it to physical evidence or a previously established clue.
why: Outbursts are ambiguous and gain weight only when tied to other facts

text: Some accused people choose death over coercive interrogation, so refusal can be extreme when every outcome seems unsurvivable.
when: torture is threatened
why: they see no survivable path through the process

text: Let the player check NPC claims against evidence: stated sacrifices against observed actions, item handovers against the receiver's log or inventory, stated conditions against symptoms and schedule.
Build NPC testimony about another NPC's feelings as a claim the player must check against logged actions or other characters' statements.
when: an NPC describes what another NPC thinks or feels
why: Testimony about inner states is only useful when cross-checked

text: Numbered official messages that reply to earlier ones let an investigator trace a chain of communications between parties.
why: each reference links a message to its predecessor

text: Items that carry serial numbers, makers' marks or issue records can be traced to a single source, such as a shop, bank or issuer.
when: When a subject carries an object with identifying numbers or marks.
why: Issue records link an object back to its origin and possibly to a person.

text: A written list rearranges existing knowledge and cannot replace new information.
Numbered or anonymous labels can make people seem like abstract roles, causing investigators to overlook their real identities.

1) Write each open issue as a separate numbered question. 2) Mark which questions depend on others. 3) Reason through each item separately. 4) Test a dependent question only after the questions it rests on hold. 5) Join items once new evidence links them. 6) Restate what remains as practical questions.
why: Separate threads stay clear until evidence connects them.

text: 1) List each detail as a numbered point. 2) Read the list as a whole rather than item by item. 3) Test whether the details form one consistent picture. 4) Note any mismatch between parts.
when: When several minor clues must be assessed together.
why: Numbering forces the investigator to consider the set instead of isolated items.

text: Present an accusation as separate numbered grounds, so the suspect cannot dismiss one point without facing the rest.
when: when cornering a suspect with a multi-part case
why: Separate points resist piecemeal rebuttal.

text: Compare a claim's ratios with established values; a basic ratio error exposes a fabrication even when the surrounding detail is vivid.
Do not let a rare exception stand in to explain every outcome; if it can cover any result, it explains nothing.
A small tally mark can understate or overstate evidence, so a single entry may feel more decisive than it is.
when: evidence is recorded as simple counts
why: a simple count can hide how strong each item is

text: Rarity does not prove ownership unless the true sales area of the item is known.
when: judging whether an item points to one person
why: Items may be common in areas the investigator has not considered.

text: A complete copy of a document may be rare, so an apparently verified excerpt may rest on a single surviving text that is hard to check.
A miscounted start or end point changes the measured interval, so confirm both points before comparing with a limit.
Check an explanation against the actual amounts involved, and reject it if the quantity is too small to produce the claimed effect.
when: an explanation depends on a substance or dose
why: Amounts can make a proposed cause impossible

text: Characters can express tension through an object handled during a scene, letting mood show without direct speech.
when: a tense exchange where direct speech is avoided
why: the object carries emotion the characters will not state

text: An object that fails on first use reads as dead to the player, so its later working surprises them.
when: a device appears broken before it is used
why: The early failure sets the expectation that the object is inert.

text: An object's meaning depends on who finds it and how they read it; the same object can be a red herring for one investigator and a clue for another.
An object tying a suspect to public news of a crime can serve as a link between them and the crime.
when: when a found item relates to reports of a crime

text: One physical trace can carry a message and a memorial together, so an object may serve emotional and evidential roles at once.
An object bearing a victim's name, such as a carved door or ship, prompts the audience to ask why that name is there.
Give book and letter items inscriptions and loose notes that the player finds by inspecting each one, grouping the most relevant ones together.
when: Designing collectible items that carry story information
why: Inspection rewards thoroughness, and grouping directs attention to the important items.

text: A short, quickly extinguished burn on an item usually indicates a secondary use rather than its intended one.
when: When an item shows a burn far shorter than its normal use would produce.
why: Its brief burn does not match its primary function.

text: An object kept apart from memory cannot be reshaped by recollection, which makes it a more reliable check than another person's memory.
An object found later, such as a veil under a seat, can connect separate witnesses and the places where they saw people.
when: A physical item is discovered after witness accounts are taken
why: Shared physical traces tie separate observations to the same people or vehicle.

text: A found object proves its owner was present at one point, not that they committed the act or what happened afterward.
when: when interpreting an object found at a scene
why: presence at one moment does not establish later events

text: An object found in a corridor cannot by itself show who put it there.
An object that implicates an innocent person can mislead the investigator about who was present at the scene.
Judge a witness's account by checking its specific claims against independent objects, not by how confidently or vividly it is told.
When a physical object found away from the scene contradicts a witness's account, reopen the timeline and explain both the object and the testimony rather than dismissing either.
when: A physical clue conflicts with a witness's account of a locked or sealed place.
why: A contradiction forces reconsideration of what was possible.

text: Do not treat an object as significant until its location and history in the scene are established.
when: an object is found in an unexpected place
why: Where an object lay can matter as much as what it is.

text: Reveal motive through a found object such as an inscription rather than a confession.
when: Explaining the cause of a haunting or threat
why: An object carries history and identity without requiring a character to admit guilt.

text: A sample or fabric impression match shows only what material a projectile or object touched; it does not show who held, fired, or is responsible.
when: using physical comparison as evidence
why: A match describes material, not the person who handled it.

text: Compare two similar objects, such as identical steps at two houses, to find which one saw more use from a difference in wear.
Comparing parts of one object helps: a worn, discoloured part beside a new one suggests a replacement, and the wear estimates its age.
Compare a physical trace with how the normal version of the act would leave it; a mismatch can expose a staged reason for someone's presence.
when: a person gives a routine reason for being somewhere
why: staged routines often leave traces that differ from genuine ones

text: Beyond obvious defects, check fourteen further machine characteristics; a match across many independent traits is stronger than one shared defect.
1) Judge the suspect object against the similar objects beside it. 2) If something differs, inspect every comparable object. 3) Treat the trace as meaningful only if it is unusual across the set.
Keep both the first reading and the revised reading of a clue in view, so you can see how its meaning changed.
Do not judge divergence between a figure's public and private stance from a single surviving document; comparison needs at least two.
when: Only one document survives.
why: Divergence cannot be seen from one statement.

text: An everyday item's properties can reveal its user's habits and conditions; matches that light easily and are hard to put out suit lighting a pipe in bad weather.
Examine ordinary objects such as books, music, handwork, clothing and marks on glass for signs of their owner's habits and for signs that a hidden person is present.
when: A suspect is absent or another person's presence must be inferred from a scene.
why: Objects carry traces of character and history that reveal concealed presence.

text: Note an object's shape as well as its location, since a trace that looks wrong for its owner's usual habits can point to a deliberate act.
when: an object shows a cut, wear, or form that seems atypical
why: Mismatch between a trace and its owner's habits suggests another person or intent.

text: Read inscriptions, dates, and object placement in a room to infer relationships and history.
when: searching a room for background information

text: Make an object's state, such as a window left open a set distance, a fact the player can verify by asking an NPC who observed it.
Ask what purpose a small object served and how it was handled; its wear, placement and marks can reveal how it was used and sometimes by whom.
when: When an object turns up where it has no obvious reason to be, or its state does not fit normal use.
why: Use leaves characteristic marks that differ from ordinary handling.

text: Wear and condition show how a possession was used; compare wear across items, since a lightly used item may show more wear than expected elsewhere.
when: When reading an object's history from its condition
why: Differential wear reveals how each item was handled.

text: Note how an item was found, such as turned inside out, since the condition at discovery can show how it was removed.
when: When recording an item's state at the scene
why: Physical state records the manner of handling.

text: An object that was never modified keeps its original dimensions, so its fit is a reliable physical record of the body it was made for.
when: Using an object's fit as evidence of identity or physique.
why: Alterations change fit, so only unmodified objects preserve the original measurement.

text: Physical state such as dampness, wear or age records how long an object was kept and where, so the object itself carries a timeline.

1) Read physical wear first. 2) Treat engravings or dates as a working hypothesis. 3) Check the hypothesis, including any personal trait, against an outside record before treating it as proof. 4) Chain related inferences, such as an item tied to a career change suggesting a junior rather than senior role.
when: when deducing facts about a person from objects

text: 1) Examine the object by eye for overall wear. 2) Use magnification to inspect fine marks. 3) Compare marks across the object for repetition. 4) State inferences as balances of probability.
when: when reading an item for backstory
why: layered examination recovers evidence that a glance misses

text: 1) Compare the object with its stated source or origin. 2) Read accompanying documents such as labels or leaflets. 3) Inspect the object's form and surfaces for signs of concealment. 4) Examine it closely with a lens. 5) Only then consider destructive examination.
1) Note an object that suggests a relationship, such as a figurine of a person. 2) Form a hypothesis about the relationship it implies. 3) Confirm it by asking, and watch how the person reacts.
when: When a personal space holds objects hinting at relationships.
why: An object may have an ordinary explanation, so inference needs confirmation by questioning.

text: Inventory every object and its position against the expected count; a shortfall is evidence, identified by its markings, and an item found elsewhere can complete the count.
when: Checking the contents of a scene or examining a scene
why: A missing item signals removal or displacement, and objects and gaps both reveal who was present.

text: Sketch a suspected object with accurate dimensions so the design can be compared with later finds.
Ownership marks such as stamps, monograms or shared identifiers can be duplicated or made by many owners, so they prove nothing until the owner and context are confirmed.
when: Using a manufactured, copied or personal object as proof of identity.
why: Stamps are easy to duplicate; multiple people may own identical items, weakening a claimed link.

text: Possessions can be read as proof of theft, so a witness who owns visible luxuries may be suspected because of what they own.
when: A theft investigation involves valuable possessions
why: Inventories of wealth invite inference of guilt

text: An ordinary object can carry both the method of a crime and the proof of it, with its danger hidden in its mechanism.
when: A crime uses a concealed device
why: The device that harms also records how the harm was done

text: Read every physical trace through its owner's routine; an unusual movement or object is more informative than a usual one.
why: Routine sets a baseline against which the unusual stands out.

text: Read an object's wear against its owner's known habits; a deviation from those habits gives the wear its meaning as a clue.
when: The owner's habits are established, so a deviation stands out.
why: Wear alone is ambiguous; only contrast with normal treatment shows it is out of place.

text: Test a colour difference that nobody has noticed by asking the owner when they last saw the object.
when: a replaced part looks new or different
why: The owner's memory of the earlier appearance can confirm the change.

text: Recognising an object as belonging to a particular person is often the decisive step that ties a trace to an identity.
A matching object proves nothing unless its owner can be tied to the scene, so an object should be linked to a person before it counts as evidence.
If an owner knows an object's location without public reports explaining it, that knowledge needs its own explanation; the owner is not automatically the offender.
Possessions, clothing and purchases can reveal spending beyond known means and suggest motive, even without direct proof of wrongdoing.
when: When assessing a suspect's motive from their lifestyle.
why: Visible spending can contrast with stated income and point to a need for money.

text: An absent owner's habits can be inferred from wear, repairs, cost and damage on an object they handled daily, with each inference resting on a specific, checkable sign.
when: When the owner is absent but left a habitually used object behind
why: Daily handling leaves consistent traces of habit and means

text: Checking found garments and items against a record of who used them narrows the question of ownership and can contradict a claimed owner.
when: Several items are found and their owners are disputed.
why: A record of use is independent of the witness's account.

text: Use readable deeds, wills and registry entries as props with dated terms, so the player must order ownership changes to understand the situation.
when: designing document-based puzzles
why: Dated transfers force sequencing.

text: A marked item in an NPC's inventory can link the player to a hidden character, so the hidden identity can be deduced from the object.
when: Designing an alias reveal.

text: An object's size and weight suggest the kind of work it was used for, and so narrow its likely owner, such as a tool kit item rather than a personal item.
when: Linking a found weapon or tool to a person
why: Physical properties reflect the tasks an object was made for

text: Use the investigation's own tools as clues: equipment only an insider could access points to the culprit without a separate accusation.
when: A forensic or investigative tool leaves traces at the scene
why: Access to specialized tools narrows the suspect pool more reliably than a motive alone.

text: Pledge records and queryable registries of an item, showing owner and location history, link its owner to a place and time, letting investigators trace the person.
when: Investigation games with trackable objects, or items pledged to third parties.

text: An object left by an absent owner can reveal an unfinished plan the owner meant to carry out.
why: The owner's death or absence interrupted the plan.

text: Object state such as plant growth or residue type can encode elapsed time and identity, letting players date events and identify habits.
when: Designing world objects that record history.
why: Physical change accumulates over time.

text: An object that is normal in its usual place becomes evidence when found in a crime setting, because its owner's habits link it to that person.
when: A familiar item turns up somewhere unexpected
why: Its owner's known routine ties the item to the owner's presence

text: Accepting an owner's claim that a key never left their hands misleads when others also held it; treat the claim as testimony to check against other facts.
Assuming an owner would notice a change they never examined closely is an error.
when: relying on the owner to report a change
why: Unnoticed changes stay unreported.

text: Assuming an object's owner from its position alone can mislead until witness accounts are heard.
An inference chain can break at the ownership step, since an object may have been picked up from someone else by mistake.
Similar-looking damaged items may not be the same object, so confirm that a mark is unique before linking two scenes.
A change of owner does not by itself prove why a use stopped; an inferred abandonment is probable, not confirmed.
when: ownership changes are the only evidence of a stopped use

text: Many signatures can make a claim look firmer without making it more verifiable.
Treating an identification as settled when the reference record may be unreliable or outdated leads to false conclusions.
when: when matching against stored records

text: Assume an object's owner is not necessarily the person who hid something in it.
when: Attributing a concealed item to a character
why: Items change hands, and ownership alone does not establish who placed a hidden object

text: A dated inscription can belong to an earlier owner, so it can mislead about current possession.
why: Items change hands, and the writing records only the past.

text: 1) Measure the object tied to a person. 2) Compare the measurement with each candidate owner's known habits. 3) Note which owner the measurement fits.
when: an object is found with a person and its owner is assumed rather than established

text: 1) List every item a person carries. 2) Mark items that are out of character for them. 3) Test each marked item against an independent source before drawing conclusions.
when: a person's belongings include an item that seems out of character
why: Ordinary possessions reveal a hidden life only when one item does not fit.

text: 1) Check whether the object's design is exclusive to one owner. 2) Check how the identification was made. 3) Weigh a suspect's denial against the link.
when: One object is claimed to tie a suspect to a scene.
why: Ownership claims are only as strong as their exclusivity and method.

text: 1) Open a hidden cache carefully. 2) Inventory its contents item by item against the owner's list. 3) Note every listed item that is absent.
when: a cache is found and the owner's list exists
why: the missing items reveal what the owner or thief took

text: 1) Present an object bearing a marker, such as an initial, as if found in a shared space. 2) Ask whether it belongs to a named person. 3) Record the immediate reaction. 4) Compare the answer with other facts.
when: A suspect may deny a link to a place or person.
why: An object with a marker can test a connection without revealing the true purpose of the question.

text: 1) Have the witness describe the marks before showing the object. 2) Compare fresh samples under magnification with the original evidence. 3) Confirm that the shapes and alignment agree.
when: When identity rests on a mass-produced product
why: An independent description checks the match

text: 1) Identify physical objects linked to the method or scene, such as rope. 2) Trace each object to its owner and time of use. 3) Check whether the owner's account fits the trace.
when: When a physical object is connected to a death or attack.
why: Ownership and timing link physical evidence to people.

text: Ownership shows who owns an object, not who used it; track owner and user as separate facts, and establish access separately.
when: Linking an object found at a scene to a person, or when its registered owner may not be its user.
why: Ownership and use are different facts, and access connects the two.

text: Track who held each evidential object and when, since each handler can alter, remove or reinterpret it and a label alone can be altered.
when: Designing or investigating scenes where several characters touch evidence, or using a labeled object as identity evidence.
why: Each handler can alter, remove or reinterpret what is left; without a custody record, a label can be altered or misattributed.

text: Examine a body for the marks it should have, including injuries under a bandage, not only for what is visibly present.
why: Coverings can conceal the injury a story depends on, so the check must look beneath them.

text: Have someone who knows an object confirm its identity, tying it to a specific place.
why: Confirmed identity links physical evidence to a location.

text: Make props offered as proof, such as tickets or receipts, checkable against a world-state record so they can be confirmed or exposed.
when: When designing evidence items.

text: Do not conclude a trace was planted until the owner's possessions have been checked.
when: A clue seems to implicate a specific person
why: Checking inventory tests whether the trace fits what the person actually had

text: Make written inventories that can be checked against physical items, so the player can detect a missing or misreported object.
Do not treat an object found in a place shared by many people as proof of its owner's intent unless its custody is traced.
why: Anyone with access could have placed it there

text: Let an object's history, such as being stolen or moved, serve as the player's time anchor, but allow that anchor to be wrong.
why: a plausible anchor that can mislead rewards checking other evidence

text: Ask the owner whether the item was ever missing and when the loss was first noticed.
when: Investigating a suspected stock loss.
why: The owner's answers date the loss and may reveal an earlier shortage that went unexamined.

text: Track each item's owner and history so the player can trace a weapon or key back to the person who gave it.
Let the obvious suspect hold the murder weapon, and reveal that another character had access to it.
when: authoring a mystery where the weapon points to a wrong suspect
why: Shifting from ownership to access reframes the weapon as evidence against someone else.

text: An object found in a place where its ordinary use would not occur, with no sign of that use, suggests it was carried in rather than used there.
when: When a used item lies in a room where it was not likely used.
why: The absence of the expected context, such as a missing holder or unheard action, points to transport.

text: Work out an object's original position before it was found; an item placed to block a route was positioned there, not dropped by chance.
when: an object found in a route may have been moved

text: The placement of objects around a room, such as bottles, glasses or clocks, can reveal who handled the room.
Treat a prominently placed object as likely important, since its position signals its significance to the occupants.
when: interpreting items in a room

text: Forcing damage placed where it defeats a mechanism with least force suggests professional knowledge, while crude, misplaced damage suggests amateur use.
when: Judging the skill behind a forced entry

text: Brackets and placement can signal that a passage was never presented as evidence; check these marks in every edition, since later editions may drop them.
when: Reading a printed transcript or deposition.
why: Readers lose the signal when cues are dropped.

text: An object found out of its usual place points to the person who moved it, and its label or appearance can mislead until it is examined.
when: an object is found away from its normal location
why: Displacement is a trace, and misleading labels hide its meaning until examination.

text: Tracking where a small physical item moves between places can reveal who was present at each point and what they did.
when: the item passes through a household or routine
why: each location and handover leaves a trace in the item's path

text: An object's location near a possible route does not prove the route was used; the testimony that contradicts that route must still be explained.
why: Location shows where an object lay, not how it got there.

text: An object left behind after a scheme can be found by accident and become key evidence.
1) Read the date on the found document. 2) Match it against the event date. 3) Place the document on the timeline only if the match holds up under checking.
when: When a found document must be dated to fit a timeline
why: A matching date can be coincidental or misleading

text: 1) List every step needed to prepare the object. 2) Identify the physical ability each step requires. 3) Check which suspects can meet every requirement.
when: when an object must be prepared before use
why: Required steps narrow the set of people who could have prepared it.

text: 1) Count what each person left with. 2) Identify what the taker must have left behind in exchange. 3) Check which exits were unguarded, and when.
when: A missing item must be traced to a taker and a route
why: Counting constrains who could have carried the item out

text: 1) Check whether the object could have reached its position by its own motion given the layout. 2) Compare dust cover on the surface beneath it. 3) Test clean and dirty contrast with similar material. 4) Check the suspected placer against who had access to the room.
when: judging whether an object was placed or moved
why: layout, dust and access together test a placement claim

text: Deliver a sealed account directly to the people best placed to open it, where it cannot be missed.
Model stains and wounds as a placement puzzle where the player positions victim and attacker so that the marks are consistent with their positions.
when: building a deduction puzzle from physical marks
why: A consistency check gives the player a verifiable solution.

text: Hide the item in containers tied to the NPC's habits, so searching them reveals something about that NPC.
when: An item is hidden by or for a character.
why: Habit-linked places make the search itself informative.

text: Inscriptions from successive owners, each adding a link such as a gift or transfer, trace an object's chain of ownership, linking present owner to past one.
when: An object carries inscriptions from several owners over time.
why: Successive hands document the object's chain of custody.

text: Stains found on a weapon can reveal its earlier history rather than the identity of the current attacker.
when: Forensic analysis of an object used in a crime.
why: Analysis answers the question it is asked, and the object may carry traces of unrelated events.

text: An item sent through a trackable channel, such as mail, leaves a timed trace that may lead to a holding location without naming the recipient.
Speech accent, cap insignia, dress, grooming, inscriptions, vessel names or a small object's brand, type or habit can reveal a region, affiliation or owner; identify origin before concluding.
Initials, monograms, brands, shades, tools, rust specks or storage location can point to an owner and narrow suspects; each inference stays a guess until confirmed.
when: An object is found without a clear owner.
why: Distinctive features narrow which owner and storage place the object came from.

text: A message that refers to the recipient's past, such as an old identifier, narrows the list of possible senders.
when: a sender is unknown but the message reveals shared history
why: few people share that history with the recipient

text: An unaddressed item carrying an identifying line can link a found object to its sender.
A worse tool is chosen only when the best option is unavailable, so an improvised object at a scene dates the moment the better option was lost.
when: a fallback object appears where a better one would be expected
why: the choice reveals the actor's constraints at that point

text: A careful actor discards a weapon out of sight, so a weapon left in a convenient place suggests haste or framing rather than a coolly planned act.
Improvised repairs such as knots carry the habits of whoever made them, so they can help identify a person.
An item's origin can be traced to a known place, which links the item to a specific location and person.
when: an object is found at a scene and its source may be known
why: A traceable origin connects the object to a location and can narrow the suspect pool.

text: An item prepared in view of witnesses and never sent out of their sight has a fully traceable path, so its contact with the victim can be checked.
when: An item is made at the table and shared.
why: Its handling is observed from start to finish.

text: Town NPCs such as clerks or porters can hold trace data that the player must earn or buy to rebuild a suspect's route.
when: Designing a town with investigation content

text: Let a clue object show its own history, such as repairs or handling marks, as part of the evidence.
A concealed object that pairs with an earlier object can link a present event to a past tragedy.
when: When designing clues that connect the present to backstory.
why: A household item with a known partner ties two events together.

text: Trace an object's history of owners and givers, since a recognised object can link a crime to a known circle of people.
when: an object is found at a scene

text: A lock that needs two separate secrets held by different people narrows suspects to those who hold both, and a strong lock shifts the question to who held its credentials.
when: When a container is protected by a key and a secret, held by different people.
why: Opening requires legitimate access to both credentials, so the question becomes who had them.

text: An item left at one scene and carried to another location acts as a traceable record of who was where.
when: a personal object moves between places during an event
why: The object carries a person's presence from one location to another

text: A single person linked to several unrelated objects creates a web that an investigator can trace back to that person.

1) List every stage the object passed through. 2) Mark stages where no one observed it. 3) For each unobserved gap, compare its length with the time the suspected change would need. 4) Confirm identity at each stage using weight, fittings, contents or other physical features.
when: An object must have stayed intact along a chain of handoffs between NPCs or rooms.
why: Testing gaps against required time shows whether a change was possible, and physical traits persist through handoffs.

text: 1) Note where the object sits at each scene. 2) Record each handover or hiding and who did it, including when it entered and left each location. 3) Arrange these into a custody timeline showing who controlled it when.
when: When an object's location or ownership matters to the question.
why: Ordered records make transfers of control visible.

text: 1) Start from the object's current location or from the first record naming a handler, such as a supplier, employee or address. 2) Check each recorded destination against reality. 3) Trace each prior handler, confirming every link by record or questioning, until reaching the origin or crime.
when: An object has changed hands and each handler left written records or can be questioned.
why: Each confirmed link supports the next, and each record names the next handler, so the chain depends on every link.
