text: 1) Start from the item's origin. 2) At each stage obtain the seller's sales records listing every buyer of the item. 3) Treat each buyer as a possible holder and narrow to a short named list.
when: Tracing a physical object that carries a label, licence or signed record through a chain of trade records.
why: Each record stage shrinks the set of possible holders.

text: 1) Record the object's history from owner to finding place, including its route. 2) Take the object to its maker and compare the maker's order and dispatch records with the account given by the person who moved it. 3) Explain every discrepancy before accepting either account.
when: An object links a person to a scene and its ownership or history must be documented back to its source.
why: The maker's records may contradict the suspect's version.

text: 1) Identify who could recognize the object. 2) Reconstruct its custody chain through each place it was moved. 3) Check for missing parts and their causes. 4) Note expected publicity that did not occur.
when: an object at a scene links a suspect to a place or time
why: each step tests whether the object's movement and the owner's knowledge fit together

text: 1) Check the owner's sale catalogue. 2) If a notable item is absent, assume it was given or sold earlier. 3) Identify the most likely recipient, such as a close friend. 4) Work outward from that circle of people.
when: an object has passed through several hands and its owner's records are incomplete
why: An absent item points to a transfer that happened before the sale

text: 1) Trace the item's movement through the suspect's belongings. 2) Check what was bought, destroyed or moved. 3) Rebuild the sequence from hiding to later movement.
when: a suspect is linked to a stolen or hidden item

text: 1) Gather every plausible candidate object. 2) Test each against the trace. 3) Keep the candidates that fit and rule out the rest by their measurable features.
when: a trace is left in soft ground and candidate objects are finite
why: physical testing narrows possibilities to the true source

text: 1) Assess the object's condition, such as whether it looks new. 2) Ask staff who know the container's normal contents when it was acquired. 3) Match residual traces, like cut hairs, to a suspect.
Ask where an object was bought, and for whom, to connect it to a relationship rather than to the scene where it was found.
when: An object's link to a person is unclear.
why: A history can place the object within a personal connection that explains its presence.

text: 1) Identify where the object was last seen. 2) Find the staff who handled that place. 3) Question them under a simple pretext about the object's whereabouts.
when: a lost object was last seen in a staffed place

text: 1) Examine the packaging as well as the object. 2) Identify each mark, such as punctures, folds or print marks. 3) Match the mark to a candidate source location. 4) Check each candidate source directly. 5) Keep or eliminate each lead based on what is found.
when: An object's location of origin is uncertain but its packaging carries marks.
why: Physical marks on wrapping can link an object to a specific place, and checking sources confirms or closes each lead.

text: 1) Record each weapon's owner and its history. 2) List who had access to it and when. 3) Compare each party's account against the weapon's physical state.
when: A dispute arises over who owned or used a weapon

text: 1) Describe the stolen item to museums, collectors and dealers, including those abroad. 2) Treat any offer or sale as a traceable lead.
when: When a stolen item is distinctive enough to recognize
why: Circulating the item turns loot into a trackable object

text: 1) Ask one narrow, specific question at each source, such as whether a particular item was made there for a customer. 2) Repeat across sources until one answers yes.
when: Tracing an object back to its maker or buyer
why: A precise question gets a clear answer from makers who recognise the item

text: Trace an object's handling route and timeline, with witness accounts, before treating it as proof; owning an object does not establish that its owner used it.
when: An object is linked to a person through a place, visit or unusual position.
why: Objects are often carried or handed over by ordinary actions, so an object alone can be explained innocently.

text: Give weapons provenance records, such as owner's name or loaded count, so a found blade reveals its holders and the player can verify claims about it.
when: Designing weapons that serve as clues.

text: Test an unusual physical object, such as a small scrap of paper, by asking each involved person whether they recognise its origin.
when: when an unidentified object turns up in an investigation

text: Stamp found items with a maker's mark and a shop, so a player can trace each item to a merchant NPC who keeps a sales record.
when: designing clue items for a mystery or investigation
why: the mark gives the player a route from object to person

text: Attach a traceable item, such as a cap with a maker's mark, to an NPC, and let its trace fade on dry ground.
when: Designing a clue that links an NPC to a scene.

text: Track where keys were lost, claimed or returned, since those intervals are when keys can be copied.
when: Determining how a locked space was reached
why: Custody gaps are the moments of possible duplication

text: Check a character's stated origin for an object against the object's marks before accepting it.
why: marks can reveal a different source than the one claimed

text: Give objects or secrets an explicit in-world value so players understand why factions compete for them.
Place an accidentally dropped object in a crowded setting as a traceable trail the player can follow.
when: Designing a clue that moves through the world
why: The object's journey gives the player a path to follow

text: Give each in-world typewriter or printing press a distinctive fault so the player can match a forged note to its source.
when: designing forged documents in a game
why: Matching faults let the player trace an item to its origin

text: Flag which NPCs handled an object, so their recollections become usable clues.
when: An item passes through several characters before reaching the target.
why: Handlers can recall details that the player can check.

text: Give items traits tied to one handler, so a document or item traces back to a single source and sets a concrete exploration goal.
when: When designing clue objects in a game

text: Decide which items carry traceable marks, since this sets which leads the player can follow.
when: When designing items that players may trace
why: Marked and unmarked items determine whether a trail exists at all

text: Mark original objects with a distinguishing label and wrap them for transport so they remain identifiable.
Tracing an item to its maker or shop narrows possible owners, but depends on records that may be incomplete.
when: When an item's origin is used to identify its owner
why: Origin links are useful but limited by what the records capture.

text: Objects left in a habitual place, such as a coat on its usual peg or smoked cigarettes, can be linked to a timeline bounding when a person was present.
when: No witness saw the person arrive or leave
why: Objects left behind record that someone was present

text: A worn seat can show that someone repeatedly stood on it to reach something high. Wear records habits.
Heavy folds and faded ink suggest a document was read many times and may have lost legible words.
when: Examining a physical document.
why: Repeated handling wears paper and ink.

text: Ask whether light objects could have stayed in place through the disturbance described; if not, they were likely placed after it.
when: a scene claims heavy traffic or struggle around fragile items
why: objects cannot persist unmoved through heavy disturbance

text: Worn cuffs and a smooth patch on the elbow suggest long hours of writing at a desk.
when: clothing shows wear at the sleeve and elbow
why: resting the arm on a desk wears those spots

text: Damage concentrated on one side of an object can reveal which hand the owner uses.
when: When an object shows one-sided wear or charring
why: Habitual handling places stress on the dominant side

text: Wear on a personal object, such as tooth marks on a pipe mouthpiece, can reveal its user; compare the wear with the traits the presumed owner should have.
when: when the owner of an object is in question
why: physical wear records how the object was used

text: Compare a print against footwear by its wear, not only its design, since identical shoes can be told apart by wear on their studs.
when: A print is matched to a pair of shoes
why: Wear is individual while design is shared across many owners

text: A physical object's count or arrangement that looks wrong can carry evidence; check it before dismissing it as coincidence.
A container with no name or route gives no travel trail, so its contents and origin must be established by the owner rather than inferred from where it was found.
Wear and staining accumulate with repeated use and handling, so wear depth shows how much traffic a surface had, and personal objects record their owner's habits, finances and character.
when: when reading an item's history
why: repeated use and handling leave physical traces

text: Fading ink and worn margins help date a book and show where pages were handled most, since physical wear is evidence of use.
Objects in a game can record who touched them and when. A clean object can signal a careful culprit, and matching records link suspects to the scene.
Tag each object with a trace state such as fired, cleaned or handled, so an expert character can report conclusions the player can verify by inspecting the object.
when: Designing evidence that depends on an object's history.
why: Explicit states let expert conclusions be checked against the object itself.

text: Treating a stopped timepiece as exact assumes the owner's winding habits. Without knowing how it was carried and used, the anchor is weaker than it looks.
when: Using a timepiece's last set time as proof of when something happened.
why: Unknown carrying and winding habits leave the stop time open to error.

text: Inferring an object's type from a tear or a pocket's shape is a hypothesis, not proof, until confirmed by other evidence.
Old damage can be mistaken for new, and weather or other people may have altered the ground, so the age of a sign must be judged.

1) Examine the wear marks, which can reveal a previous owner whose build differs from the current holder 2) Compare them with the current holder's body 3) Identify who else in the case has that build.
when: an object may have changed hands

text: 1) Build a duplicate of the object. 2) Run it under the same conditions as the original. 3) Measure a quantity such as burn time. 4) Compare the result with the observed remains.
when: An ordinary object was used and left in a recognisable state
why: A matched duplicate turns a remaining trace into a measured estimate of past use

text: 1) Establish when the area was last cleaned or reset. 2) Check whether the object could predate that point. 3) Test the witness's claim against the object's timing and location.
when: When an object's presence conflicts with a claim.
why: Timing determines whether the object contradicts the claim.

text: 1) Identify the object's source. 2) Find the source's customers. 3) Check which customer could have produced the object's use. 4) Link the customer to a person.
when: An object with a known source turns up at a scene.
why: The trace moves from object to supplier to customer to person in order.

text: 1) Take a sample of the old item. 2) Use it for its intended function under normal conditions. 3) Judge whether it still works from the observed result.
when: An found object's age or condition is in doubt.

text: Show an object's contents and condition to both parties before handing it over, so its state is fixed at the moment of transfer.
when: When the object's state may later be disputed.
why: A fixed starting state gives both parties a reference point for later claims.

text: Show object age through wear and dust, so players can tell a fresh disturbance from an older one without reading text.
when: When a scene must communicate when something happened.
why: Players read visual wear as a time cue.

text: Do not treat an object as standalone proof; connect it to the timeline and to the people present before drawing a conclusion.
when: A single physical item seems to point to a suspect
why: An object alone can have innocent explanations

text: Witness perception in darkness or poor light is uncertain and may be admitted; a witness may still report a detail with false certainty, since poor conditions limit what is seen.
when: Evaluating a witness's visual claim, especially in poor lighting or at distance.
why: Poor viewing conditions limit what can actually be seen, and the witness may admit the uncertainty.

text: Staging a chance encounter to watch someone can reveal the observer's intent to the person being watched.
Artificial light can hide or distort fine marks, so examine them under suitable light before judging them.
when: Examining a scene at night or indoors

text: Check every sense when searching a scene, including smell, because a scent can identify a visitor who leaves no visible mark.
when: A search focuses on visible traces.
why: Scent and residue persist where visual evidence does not, and they are missed unless someone checks for them.

text: Check the witness's state at the moment of observation, since drugging or drunkenness can cloud what they remember.
Before accepting a witness's claimed observation, check the light, distance and alertness under which it was made.
A witness's physical reaction can exceed the question asked, such as a shudder or grip tightening once a suspect is described, and this signals recognition.
when: A description of a suspect provokes a reaction in the witness
why: The reaction reveals recognition the witness may not state

text: A person who keeps busy with a task without looking up may be listening closely while concealing their attention.
when: Someone appears absorbed in an unrelated activity during conversation.
why: Apparent distraction can mask focused listening.

text: Show a character's reaction in front of the whole group, giving the audience observed behaviour rather than the narrator's interpretation.
Small behavioral anomalies, such as an unexpectedly muted emotional response, can direct attention without proving guilt.
when: Setting up suspicion around a character.
why: They prompt the audience to look closer while remaining inconclusive evidence.

text: Recording every physical movement of a suspect aloud turns demeanour into evidence, so ordinary movements can be read as guilt.

1) Position yourself to see the subject's face and hands during evidence. 2) Track changes over time: colour, sweat, repeated gestures, eye focus. 3) Note silence and absent gestures. 4) Record minor details for later use.
when: when watching a suspect receive damning evidence
why: Physical reactions can reveal shock where speech stays controlled.

text: Record observable behaviour as plain facts, kept separate from both the meaning assigned to it and the observer's likes or fears about the person.
when: when a character's behaviour or demeanour is used as evidence about their state or character
why: Feelings and interpretations distort reports, while recorded observations remain checkable and can be reinterpreted later.

text: Omission may stem from restraint, fear, protecting the reader, or private reasons, so treat it as a clue to check, not proof of deception.
A teller who gives a partial account signals the gap, and a listener who asks directly for the missing part often gets it.
when: A speaker's account is incomplete
why: Partial accounts leave visible seams that careful questioning exposes

text: A suspect's account can leave out a visit that a neutral record, such as a station log or staff memory, would reveal.
Omission deceives more quietly than false statement: the listener hears a trimmed version without any claim being false.
An omitted detail can be the key clue, especially on timing or cause, so probe what a teller did not mention, even if they judged it unimportant.
when: a second-hand account lacks a detail the first witness noticed
why: Tellers often drop facts they judge not worth passing on.

text: A name conspicuously absent from a group appeal or petition may show the writer judged that person beyond persuasion, a possible sign of distrust or grudge to confirm elsewhere.
when: a person expected in a group appeal or petition is left out, especially in a dispute
why: Deliberate omission can carry meaning and reflect the relationship.

text: If a source never mentions something it would have to know about, the omission suggests it did not know.
when: the source would naturally mention the item if aware of it
why: Silence about an expected detail signals ignorance

text: Omitted exculpatory testimony from a writer who must have known of it signals selective reporting; do not assume omission was innocent without checking what the writer knew.
when: A writer covers a case but leaves out defense witnesses.
why: Selective inclusion can shape the case.

text: A written account that describes a person in detail but omits the name the writer would know is unnatural and suggests another hand composed it.
when: when checking the content of a supposed confession
why: Writers normally name people they know well.

text: A name missing from one witness's list of people present is worth checking against the other accounts.
A suspect who omits a witness that would support an alibi, even when that witness is named, suggests the witness was not compromised.
why: A compromised witness would normally have been offered as an alibi earlier

text: Failing to sign a corrective statement, when one could help, can indicate the person did not help correct the record.
Make the omitted passage the clue: the summary says one thing, and the complete text contradicts it.
when: designing discovery of hidden lore
why: Omissions can be checked by a motivated player.

text: A document that says little about the writer's life can still be informative through what it omits and through its date and place.
when: Reading a sparse personal letter
why: Absence of detail and the metadata of date and place can carry meaning

text: An omitted statement matters most when it would settle a question, so check whether a key observation was actually recorded.
when: Assessing a case file, report or witness account for gaps.
why: A missing observation that would decide a question is a meaningful gap.

text: A frame can survive without outright lies: each planted clue stays consistent with the false story until one withheld account contradicts it.
why: Silence leaves the evidence looking coherent while hiding the decisive fact.

text: Cutting the part of an answer that addresses the central question, or qualifiers from a quotation, changes its meaning even when the excerpt looks complete.
when: Reviewing summaries or excerpts of testimony, advice, confessions or documents.
why: Removed responses or qualifiers change meaning while the excerpt looks complete.

text: A witness's summary often skips steps they did not observe, so those steps must be reconstructed from evidence.
when: when relying on a secondhand account
why: unobserved steps are missing from the summary

text: If a withheld fact is too prominent, players dismiss the witness as a liar rather than as a fallible observer.
A clue left out of the first review may never be tested, so its significance stays hidden.
when: Reviewing a set of clues.
why: Unlisted items do not get checked against other evidence.

text: A missing clause shows that something was left out, not what it was, so identifying the omission needs a second source.
Reading an omission in a record as proof of a fact is an error, since careful wording may be innocent.
when: Drawing conclusions from what a monument or document does not say.
why: An absent claim does not establish the opposite claim.

text: Treat excised or omitted passages as evidence: writers' beliefs and compilers' purposes decide what appears, so gaps in an abridged text can say as much as its printed content.
Ask which fact a witness has left out, since a conspicuous omission can expose a contradiction with physical facts.
Weigh what a writer leaves out as well as what they say, and follow up any gap the writer admits to.
Treat an omission from a formal complaint as evidence of a hidden motive only when independent corroboration supports it.
when: a complaint leaves out a matter that seems central
why: silence alone is ambiguous

text: Keep a thread open after clearance or the main solution, such as an item's chain of custody or why only one character saw a figure, so the world feels larger.
when: when designing post-clearance investigation or ending a mystery arc
why: open threads keep the mystery active and suggest a wider world beyond the story

text: Explicitly leave specific questions unanswered, such as why someone cannot return, what caused a new bond, or an unknown identity, so the audience keeps tracking them until they pay off.
when: when a mystery is in progress, an early scene ends, or a news item or report is left incomplete
why: unanswered questions stay active in the audience's mind until resolved

text: Log a half-recognized character or possible identity match as an unresolved lead the player can revisit, inviting them to keep searching.
when: when a record or NPC is half-recognized or its identity may match another
why: an open question gives the player a reason to keep searching

text: Keep rival explanations, such as illness, natural death, accident, robbery, deliberate act or fled companion, open side by side until evidence settles them.
when: when a single neat or official explanation appears early or is pressed
why: premature acceptance hides contrary evidence; a grudge-to-harm link should stay a hypothesis

text: Keep an explicit journal of open questions (who, where, what next), stalled leads and dismissed clues, updated as facts arrive, so players can revisit them.
when: when designing investigation interfaces or quests, or when multiple leads and clues accumulate over a long investigation
why: unrecorded clues are easily forgotten, so players cannot connect new evidence to them

text: Open questions in a case list typically concern access (who could enter), motive (why someone acted), and identity (who an unseen person was).
A practised gatherer of plants usually leaves long stalks, while hurried snatching tends to leave them short.
when: judging whether a gathering trace is genuine
why: different habits and haste leave different marks

text: Keep seemingly minor details on file, since they may answer an open question or gain meaning when later facts arrive.
when: when gathering evidence over a long investigation
why: background knowledge can change what an earlier detail means

text: Keep every witness fact, including odd or jumbled ones, until its relevance is tested, since an odd detail may match an earlier planted fact.
when: when a witness gives full but jumbled testimony

text: Keep small personal details, such as work hours or pay, because they may connect to the wider matter.
when: When recording a witness account
why: Details that seem trivial can later prove central to the case.

text: When a future plan cannot be known, answer with a range of possible options instead of one certain answer.
when: when a reveal leaves a question about what comes next
why: it marks the limits of what could be known

text: Use unexplained items in the world as hooks, since each signals that the player's current theory is missing a piece.
Let the investigator narrate their reasoning openly, so each conclusion can be traced back to the observations behind it.
when: when writing a mystery's deduction scenes
why: Traceable reasoning lets the audience follow and check the logic.

text: Use contact attempts with recorded times that went unanswered as anchors showing when a person was probably not at a location.
when: When calls or visits were logged at known times.
why: A logged failed attempt is a dated fact that narrows where someone could have been.

text: When a witness says a cry went unanswered, test the claim against who was close enough to hear it, since an explanation for why no one came can be constructed.
when: A witness explains why no one responded to a sound

text: A missed-clue marker can show where a suspicious detail was available, making the design visibly fair.
when: the player has solved or failed a puzzle
why: Shows the player the sign they could have caught

text: Mark unresolved points as open rather than forcing a conclusion from incomplete evidence.
when: an account leaves gaps
why: premature conclusions hide what is unknown

text: Introduce the central name or key clue at the opening, so every later clue points back to it.
when: starting an investigation plot
why: A fixed anchor makes later clues cohere

text: Leave one clue deliberately unresolved to add texture without blocking progress.
why: Optional lore enriches a level without gating it.

text: Failing to ask who could still confirm a key claim leaves that claim untested and the case weaker.
A reveal that answers a question the audience never asked feels arbitrary, so each explanation should answer a question the story raised.
when: Writing explanations at the end of a mystery.
why: Unraised questions make the solution seem contrived.

text: Open group discussion can become confused and let the examiner lose control, and accused people present may coordinate their stories.
If the hidden party never reacts to outside sounds, the listener's inference has nowhere to go.
1) Let the witness narrate freely at first. 2) Listen closely without interrupting. 3) Steer back to the subject only when the witness drifts too far off track.
when: early in an interview when it is unclear which facts matter
why: A witness may reveal the key fact while wandering.

text: Track each accepted premise and flag unchecked ones in a to-verify list, plus unrequested tests, unchecked items and secondhand leads, so players see which conclusions rest on assumption.
when: when building a player-facing evidence log, or when the player has unconfirmed information
why: exposes untested reasoning; separating confirmed from unconfirmed facts reduces confusion; visible open leads guide players toward unexplored reasoning

text: Record each unanswerable question, such as a footmark's direction, with its best candidate answer and what each answer would mean for the case; this separates suspicion from known fact.
when: when evidence cannot settle a question but the answer would change other conclusions
why: keeping open questions visible prevents later reasoning from assuming an answer that was never established

text: Keep several suspects open rather than committing early, including respectable-seeming people, since dropping them risks clearing a guilty person or losing the chance to prove guilt.
when: at the start of an investigation
why: avoid risks in either direction

text: Keep an unexplained fragment or phrase, such as an overheard remark or a term a witness never clarifies, as an open lead, not attached to a person until confirmed.
when: when collecting partial remarks without context, or when a witness repeats a phrase they do not explain
why: a fragment attached to the wrong subject produces a false conclusion; unexplained details point toward further evidence

text: Keep unresolved leads open after an accusation, so the player can still find evidence that points elsewhere.
List open conditions in the quest log and mark each one resolved as the player eliminates alternatives.
when: when tracking a deduction-based investigation
why: a visible checklist shows progress toward the answer

text: Let a summary state what the player has not yet established, so the next step is clear.
when: A game summarises the player's investigation progress.
why: Explicit gaps direct the player toward the next action.

text: Do not close an inquiry while contrary traces remain unexplained.
Do not discard a witness merely for bias, since a biased witness can still report accurate detail.
Keep a person on the suspect list when they have a motive, even a small one, until that motive is ruled out.
when: when a suspect has any motive

text: Before naming a culprit, check whether any question remains open, including how the means of access was achieved.
when: when a motive and one link look convincing

text: Do not demand the source of a suspect's information, since that keeps the suspect cooperative.
when: questioning a suspect who has revealed knowledge

text: Keep the question of guilt open while a suspect is too unwell to be questioned properly, and resume questioning once they recover.
Do not drop a weak alibi; mark it unconfirmed and keep it open.
why: weak evidence is still uncertain

text: When an official verdict closes a quest stage, record the unanswered questions as open journal flags.
when: Closing a quest stage with unresolved elements.
why: Players need a trace of what remains open.

text: Keep the open question on the player's journal during light interludes, and reward the player when later evidence supports or undercuts their suspicion.
when: When tension is reset between investigation beats.
why: A persistent open question keeps the mystery active after relief.

text: Let an NPC's reaction open a new branch, such as a request to recover the item, rather than settling the question.
when: designing dialogue responses to an item reveal
why: a branch keeps the question open and rewards further investigation

text: Use locked doors and disposable notices to show a quest-giver's situation has changed, prompting the player to investigate further.
Open narration surfaces unknown facts but takes time; direct questions save time but miss key facts or leave evasive witnesses unchallenged, since witnesses volunteer only what they are asked.
when: choosing an interview style or interviewing a witness
why: key facts stay hidden without a pointed question

text: A single act can support opposing readings, such as vengeance or reconciliation, so an interpreter should not present only one.
why: The same act can carry two meanings depending on the intent assumed for it.

text: In a public calamity, some people exploit the disorder for private gain, including by making false accusations.
when: a disaster or crisis disrupts normal order
why: Disorder gives cover for private gain.

text: An opponent's reply to a lead can reveal how much the opponent knows.
when: A lead ends in a direct contest with a suspect
why: A counter-move depends on what the opponent has learned

text: Test an opposing timeline for its weakest point; one decisive witness can reverse a window that looked settled.
Repeated private meetings and passed messages between dissenters are a sign of organized opposition, and authorities tend to treat them as a threat.
when: a divided group with rival camps
why: Coordinated contact points to a shared aim rather than scattered complaints.

text: Frame a conflict as a contest between opposed systems to absorb local disputes into one larger story.
An opponent's own account of a quarrel's origin can contradict the motive claim, so check the accuser's records before accepting the accusation.
When a hidden leader is removed, the organization collapses: its members flee and leave incriminating papers that authorities can act on.
Give opponents a fixed decision window, about two hours, before moving on; this creates suspense and forces them to reveal their position.
Setting one witness's opinion against another can make a disagreement look settled when it is only two opinions.
when: Presenting conflicting witness views
why: Opinions carry no more weight than their reasons

text: Accounts that agree in outline can still disagree on times or on who was present, so agreement in general shape is not corroboration.
1) List the clues. 2) Group them by the motive and action they imply, not by object. 3) Look for the grouping that explains the most clues. 4) Test that grouping against remaining evidence.
when: Many clues appear to conflict and the investigator is stuck
why: Grouping by motive reveals the overall pattern that individual objects hide

text: Let an NPC give a long, ordered account, with optional branches for each detail so players can ask for everything.
when: Designing NPC dialogue for clue delivery.

text: Add neglected checks, such as a will, a partner's share or a lock's key holder, as optional tasks that let the player reopen a closed case.
when: Designing a case that can be closed too early.
why: Overlooked basic facts give the player a route back to the truth.

text: A small practical explanation for an observed state, such as opening a window to clear smoke, can change what that state means.
Read the operative sentences of an argument, which show what is actually recommended, rather than only the cautious qualifiers around them.
Optional small-talk dialogue branches that look unrelated can record an NPC's attitudes or knowledge for later use.
Red herrings trade off: optional innocent-resolving clues reward exploration without false solutions, while hidden NPC side-secrets consume player effort without advancing the answer.
when: Designing false leads or red herrings.
why: Clues that resolve innocently reward exploration; side secrets generate real leads that cost effort.

text: A claim that an event already produced a result is false if the event had not yet occurred at the claimed time.
when: when an account reports the outcome of a dated event
why: an outcome cannot exist before its event

text: When no direct record of an outcome survives, infer it from later documents, such as evidence that a person was alive years after a sentence.
When an impossible event occurs, begin with an ordinary explanation such as illness, and proceed cautiously while testing it.
when: an impossible event is witnessed
why: ordinary causes are more likely than the impossible

text: Revealing an outcome early, paired with an open question about how it came about, sustains suspense.
when: Structuring a mystery's reveals.
why: The open question holds attention after the answer is known.

text: Discovering a culprit can do more harm than the crime itself, so weigh the outcome of action, not only the fact of guilt.
when: deciding whether to pursue formal action
why: exposure has its own consequences

text: A conviction can persist after the evidence behind it has been repudiated, so a verdict's continued existence does not confirm its truth.
why: Courts may keep enforcing a judgment long after the evidence supporting it is discredited.

text: A procedure that declares an accused person innocent can still kill them, so its verdict does not prove the test was sound.
Claims about how something was done need evidence of the mechanism, not just the outcome; the number found in a result cannot settle the method used.
why: Several methods can produce the same observed result.

text: Ordeals such as heated iron, water, or swimming tests should not be accepted as evidence of guilt, as they are superstitious.
when: when considering physical tests as a basis for proof
why: they do not reliably establish the facts of an accusation

text: If a person acts against their own interest, look for an outside influence that prompted the act.
Use a third sample from a new location to redirect the investigation from the scene to the outside world.
Outside evidence such as a departure notice can reveal an opponent's escape plan and shift the investigation's deadline.
Information from outside, such as a newspaper's description of valuables, can prompt an outsider to form a plan.
when: a scheme targets a valued possession
why: public descriptions reveal targets and their worth

text: Leaving a locked room whose key is outside requires reopening the door, which exposes the leaver to anyone nearby.
why: Reopening the door takes time and makes the leaver visible.

text: A reveal resting on a single outside insight feels unearned if the supporting clues were never shown.
why: The audience has no way to check the insight against evidence.

text: Do not accept a stated account, such as an itinerary, until an outside witness confirms it: identify someone in a position to know, send a written question, and compare the reply with the account.
when: when the account rests on the teller's word, especially when the teller benefits from it
why: An outside reply is an independent check.

text: 1) Negotiate which bodies may sit, excluding any whose members pushed for the council. 2) Add neutral members at trusted advice to reduce the initiating party's control.
Engage an outside examiner who receives only the case detail the task requires, and cross-check their findings with interviews.
when: Financial or transactional records must be read
why: Limited information keeps the examiner's reading unbiased, and interviews check what records alone show

text: Have an independent specialist classify a physical material so the conclusion does not rest only on the investigator's judgment.
when: identifying material from a trace
why: Outside classification adds an independent check.

text: A narrator who openly admits lapses or skipped parts signals gaps in the record, so the reader should weigh that account less.
when: A narrator reports events while admitting inattention
why: Admitted gaps mean the record is incomplete

text: Sounds from outside raise a trapped character's hope, but when their signals go unheard, the failed rescue deepens despair.
when: Outside activity is audible but cannot reach the trapped character.
why: Hope raised by sound turns to despair when it is not answered.

text: A crime can seem incomprehensible from outside yet make sense from the perpetrator's inside perspective, so an outside observer must study it differently from an insider.
when: a story presents a crime from the criminal's viewpoint
why: The perpetrator's logic is hidden from outsiders, so the same act reads differently depending on the viewpoint.

text: A narrator who frames their own conduct as unavoidable and steers how the listener judges others controls what the listener sees.
when: when a witness or suspect tells their own account

text: Private talks between a dissenting group and outsiders are often logged as suspicious contact, which casts the group as coordinating against the authority.
when: a faction meets outsiders during a dispute
why: Hidden contact is read as conspiracy.

text: A newly arrived authority forms first impressions from those who meet him first, and they can steer his movements and decisions.
when: an outsider takes up a post
why: Early contacts control the information the newcomer receives first.

text: An outsider entering a tight group reads its jokes, ritual phrasing and silence through his own habits, so they can look like insult or evasion.
when: a newcomer observes a closed community with its own idioms
why: the newcomer applies only his own social norms

text: An outsider's explanation of a private misfortune can turn it into a public accusation by naming a neighbour as the cause.
when: A family illness is attributed to a person outside their household.
why: Naming a culprit gives a private trouble a social target.

text: Reject outsider theories only when access to the means is restricted to a known group; if entrances were open, alibis cannot exclude an outsider.
when: Access to the means of a crime is restricted to a known group.
why: Explanations needing an unseen intruder add unverifiable assumptions the evidence does not require.

text: Assign narrators by presence at events rather than cleverness or rank, so each account covers what its narrator actually witnessed.
when: choosing who tells part of a story
why: presence determines what a narrator can know

text: A barrier set from outside a sealed door after the intruders left implies an accomplice was on the far side of the door.
A plot that depends on an outsider acting at a moment they could not have known about is less likely than one that depends on information they had.
Use an outsider's misreading of a community when the group's rules are not stated openly to the reader.
when: the player must read a faction, guild or village with its own idioms

text: When the narrator does not know the plan, the audience shares the surprise and experiences the event as it unfolds.
when: surprise matters to the work
why: the audience has no more knowledge than the narrator

text: Specific detail in questions that outsiders could not have known shows the questioner prepared from prior information, not from the witness.
Emotional stance or hindsight can colour a narrator's account of people and events, including a victim's private feelings; partisan narrators need extra checking.
when: The narrator praises or condemns people involved in the events
why: Emotional stance colours what is remembered and how it is told

text: Personal narration drifts easily toward the narrator's own life, pulling the account away from the central events.
when: a narrator writes a first-person account
why: self-focus competes with the case

text: Multi-narrator framing breaks down when a narrator relays others' accounts beyond their own knowledge.
when: Narrators pass on information they did not witness
why: Relayed accounts blur the reliability each source is meant to carry.

text: Another person may use the same confusion to follow the target, so a pursuer should not assume they are the only one watching.
why: crowds can hide several followers at once

text: A request for a signed or handwritten statement from a newcomer can gather a handwriting sample for forgery, so such requests deserve scrutiny.
when: a newcomer claims an identity or role and is asked to write
why: Forgery needs time to learn a person's handwriting, which a routine-looking request provides.

text: With no strong suspect, investigators may fix on whoever is new or unfamiliar, which is a bias rather than evidence.
An outsider's first impression of a person's role or relationship can be wrong in either direction.
Ask who else could speak; silence cannot be assumed when others have interests that may align with the accused.
Frame a question around how outsiders would judge the matter, so that a private concern feels like a public necessity.
when: when a witness resists answering a personal question
why: a public stake can override reluctance to speak privately

text: Attach titles or subjects to books and documents so that the content of disturbed items can hint at an NPC's interests.
when: populating a room with readable items
why: Item content gives players a clue to an NPC's identity or habits.

text: A setup built to block every suspicion can look rehearsed, so observers may read the safeguards as evidence of foreknowledge.
when: A suspect's safeguards are elaborate and cover every route.
why: An innocent person rarely guards against an accusation not yet made.

text: Treat unusual over-precaution as a lead toward a concealed act, not proof of it; attributing motive to over-caution without other supporting evidence is unwarranted.
A writer who runs characters together to hide a message often leaves unusual crowding at the points where a natural pause would fall, and these gaps reveal the message's structure.
when: A message is deliberately run together to conceal it.
why: Writers tend to over-correct for concealment, leaving irregular spacing at phrase boundaries.

text: Guarding hard against a small risk can create a visible sign, and that sign can expose an otherwise careful plan.
Seeing a frame-up in every odd object makes an investigator dismiss real evidence; some are innocent oversights. Keep the other possibility open until evidence settles it.
when: a real clue looks suspicious
why: Premature doubt blocks the true explanation

text: Making the framed party's innocence too obvious removes the doubt that misdirection needs.
when: Writing a mystery with a red herring
why: Doubt must persist for misdirection to work

text: A watcher so careful not to be seen can lose the subject, which defeats the watch.
Treating every setback as staged wastes time chasing a genuine loss.
A witness who seems unusual may still be right; dismissing an unlikely account without testing it against records can discard the truth.
why: Over-correction treats oddness as falsehood.

text: A routine assumed too strictly can be broken by an unscheduled visit, so schedules must allow for exceptions.
when: Relying on a fixed schedule to rule out visitors
why: Unplanned visits fall outside the expected pattern

text: Hold a question open when the most forceful speaker is certain, rather than letting confidence settle the matter.
Logging every day produces a record so long that the important signal is buried.
Interrupting a narrative too often can drop the context that later explains the key point.
A withheld disclosure that stretches too long reads as evasion, especially when the audience needs the information to follow the scene.
when: When a disclosure is delayed across several scenes
why: Extended withholding feels manipulative

text: Excessive subdivision fragments tension and hides links between parallel events, and can overwhelm readers the way endless numbered headings do.
Pressing a witness too hard can make them close off, stop cooperating, and turn a neutral party into a defender of the person questioned.
Pushing a suspect too far can cause them to object and withdraw, and a question refused early may be impossible to ask again in the same form.
when: Interrogating a suspect who may deny everything under pressure.
why: Excessive pressure damages trust and closes the line of questioning.

text: Pressing a witness too hard can look like badgering, and the other side may argue the loose phrasing was innocent.
when: Repeatedly questioning a witness about a loose answer.
why: Persistence without restraint can damage the questioner's credibility.

text: Pressing too hard can end the conversation before the visitor reveals the motive.
Pressing a reluctant witness too hard makes them close up, so stop once they have given a checkable fact.
when: Questioning a reluctant witness.
why: Excessive pressure triggers withdrawal and ends the flow of information.

text: A dramatic or attractive theory, such as romance, must be tested like any other and must not replace evidence or force an interpretation onto an unexplained clue.
when: An attractive theory appears early, or an investigator wants closure on an unresolved clue.
why: Its appeal explains every anomaly and discourages testing alternatives; a premature answer replaces the open question with a wrong one.

text: Expecting a decisive clue, or fixing a thesis, makes investigators over-read ambiguous events; the same facts often support the opposite reading.
why: Ambiguous events are easily reread to fit a fixed thesis, and disappointment follows when a clue proves only suggestive.

text: Show the player a sign related to a held-back fact without revealing the fact itself, to create tension.
when: a fact must stay hidden for dramatic reasons
why: the related sign signals that something is unresolved

text: When a search yields nothing, reinterpreting a small physical detail can open a new route of investigation.
when: When a line of investigation has stalled
why: A fresh reading of an overlooked detail can redirect the search toward a productive lead

text: Fragments and gaps invite over-reading; hold each fragment as a hypothesis until other evidence checks it, rather than building an elaborate story from it.
when: a document has gaps or a fragment is open to several readings
why: Incomplete words attract guesses and assumptions; readers project more meaning than the sentence holds, and imagination generates ideas but is a poor judge of conclusions.

text: One overheard phrase, a turn of phrase, or tone alone, without context or corroboration, must not build a theory; distress is not guilt unless other clues support it.
when: a single line, tone or distressed reaction is read as evidence
why: Such readings mislead when no other clue supports them.

text: Ordinary surprise, a glance, posture or injuries should not be read as guilt, rage or hidden knowledge; such signs support a hypothesis but do not prove it.
when: A character reacts strongly, or body language and injuries are used as clues.
why: Gestures and wounds have many ordinary causes, and readers tend to seek dramatic explanations for them.

text: Do not conclude a scene is staged, or that a torn item shows struggle, from one oddity or stressed detail; test each detail against physical facts and corroborate first.
when: a trace looks suggestive but unusual, or a detail seems staged
why: Unusual details invite stronger readings than the evidence allows, producing false readings in both directions.

text: Ambiguous marks or alterations, such as a highlighted phrase or changed text, may be innocent, like a clerk correcting an error; do not read them as fraud.
when: Interpreting an ambiguous mark or document alteration.
why: Ambiguity does not establish intent, so reading it as fraud can produce a false accusation, and a highlighted phrase may mean nothing.

text: Trying to connect every detail to the chain of evidence is a sign of inexperience and causes a mystery to explain too much.
Readers may over-read a passing detail; keep an unexplained bystander as a loose thread, not a confirmed clue.
Dramatic staging can overshadow the logic if it is not followed by a clear reconstruction.
when: Revealing a solution with a flourish
why: Spectacle without a chain of reasoning leaves the solution unconvincing.

text: Resolving every ambiguous glimpse as harmless drains the suspense that earlier sightings built.
when: Using ambiguous sightings to build tension.
why: Repeated harmless resolutions teach the audience that tension is not meaningful.

text: Over-arguing a case for someone's madness signals steering, and makes the listener more suspicious of the speaker rather than of the accuser.
when: Discrediting a witness through a long argument
why: Excessive persuasion is itself visible as an agenda

text: Dismissing every strange detail as human can blind an investigator to a real anomaly, while a place's reputation can misdirect attention from a human suspect.
when: When investigating eerie events
why: Both blanket dismissal and reliance on reputation distort the investigation

text: Treating a recurring word or mark as significant before its context is known can mislead the investigator, who cannot yet link it to the danger.
when: Early in an investigation with partial evidence
why: A repeated detail feels meaningful, but without context it may not connect to the threat.

text: A fair-play reveal reorders facts the audience already has and never introduces a new fact; players feel cheated when a reinterpretation relies on information never shown.
when: when writing a mystery's final explanation
why: Fairness requires that every key fact was available to the audience.

text: Plant an ordinary or literal-sounding line in a journal or letter whose meaning changes after a related object or writer's health or history fact is found; resurface it then.
when: designing a clue that pays off later
why: A harmless line can become sinister once new facts are known, so written clues should be reread after each discovery.

text: Accepting an accusation or lead because the claimant sounds certain leads investigators to the wrong person; confidence is not evidence.
when: when an accuser or claimant is emotional, insistent, or pushes a lead despite doubts about the witness
why: Strong conviction is easy to mistake for accurate knowledge; it can override the listener's own reservations.

text: A confident delivery can make an unproven claim sound settled and mislead readers or investigators; the most forceful claim is often least supported, since persuasion is not proof.
when: when presenting a conclusion in fiction or argument
why: Strong delivery suppresses alternative explanations.

text: A witness's confidence about what they would have seen should be weighed against their vantage point, light and distance.
when: A witness's certainty is the main evidence for a claim.
why: Confidence is not reliability; poor light and distance reduce recognition more than witnesses realise.

text: People recall a promise of secrecy differently, so a confidence shared privately may be remembered and repeated in conflicting ways.
when: when a private remark is shared with several people under a promise of secrecy
why: Memory of a confidence varies with each listener's interest and recall

text: Investigators who have had repeated success may treat their conclusions as settled and scrutinize new contrary evidence less.
when: An authority figure has a string of earlier successes.
why: Past success builds confidence that can reduce willingness to re-examine a conclusion.

text: Confidences limit what a witness will offer, so investigators often must work from partial information.

Conclusive signs are inconsistent answers under deliberate questioning, a complete set of required causes, a free confession joined to full evidence of the act, and matching gestures among co-accused.
when: when classifying evidence in a suspect case
why: These signs are strong enough to found a conviction when they are documented.

text: A witness's certainty and accuracy vary independently, so check emphatic claims against the physical record; treating them as proof is a mistake, especially if the supporting item is gone.
when: when a witness speaks firmly about a detail the scene can test
why: certainty and accuracy vary independently

text: Confident expert opinions and reassurance can fail; probe them with the alternative reading, and verify any claim that everything is accounted for.
when: when an expert or authority states a firm conclusion or reassurance
why: Confidence does not guarantee a conclusion survives scrutiny, and confidence can be wrong.

text: Treat strong personal certainty in an investigator as a warning that the inquiry may have closed too early.
when: reviewing an arrest or accusation

text: Confident tone, manner, or certainty is not evidence of accuracy; a confident speaker can be wrong even about facts they are sure of, so all claims need checking.
why: Confidence is a delivery trait or belief, not a check on the facts.

text: A witness's firm assertion about a disputed detail or identification is not evidence of accuracy and is often immune to proof.
when: when a witness holds a contested point or identification firmly under challenge
why: Certainty and correctness are separate properties of testimony; confidence reflects belief, not the fact.

text: A confident witness may be reconstructing the past; a certain-feeling recollection can be shaped by fear, shock, or retelling, so confidence does not prove accuracy.
Fondness or claimed intimacy can make a witness describe someone favourably; neither confidence nor closeness makes such claims accurate, so check them against behaviour.
Certainty born of wounded feeling is not knowledge; an emotionally charged detail or character judgment needs evidence, since hurt can yield confident conclusions.
when: Weighing a witness's emotional judgments
why: Hurt can produce confident conclusions without evidence.

text: A confident manner or high rank is not evidence a reading is correct; an authoritative speaker can make a guess sound certain and steer the inquiry wrong.
when: when an official presents a settled explanation

text: A confidently stated time may be vague, so an approximate time needs a fixed reference, and the more certain the speaker sounds, the more the timeline needs checking.
when: when a witness gives an approximate time
why: Confidence does not make an estimate accurate.

text: Confident views from colleagues can pressure an investigator into accepting a rival account before the evidence supports it.
why: Social pressure can substitute for testing.

text: A confidently stated theory can be wrong; check it against physical evidence such as the cause of death before accepting it.
A witness's certainty is not evidence of accuracy; the first explanation that fits their fear is often wrong.
Confident, detailed claims are not evidence; informants often sound most certain when they know least, and their stories grow as real knowledge shrinks.
A verdict reached under strong feeling is not more reliable for being certain.
Confidence in a conclusion tends to grow faster than the evidence supporting it, so each step needs a second check before it is treated as settled.
when: Building a conclusion from several inferences.
why: Each inference feels reasonable on its own, and the accumulated certainty is not matched by the grounds underneath.

text: An investigator may be sure of a hidden cause yet have no proof, because individually plausible accidents resist proof.
A confident local theory can close off other lines of inquiry.
Confidence in spotting lies from demeanour can blind an investigator to a concealed witness, because a steady, plausible speaker may be unreadable.
A confident inference from character can mislead even when it turns out right, so confidence is not evidence.
A confident guess about what an anomaly means is an assumption, not a finding, until a source supports it.
when: When an investigator or character states a cause with certainty.
why: Confidence can substitute for evidence.

text: An accusation can feel certain to its author yet fail to satisfy an audience, because confidence is not the same as evidence.
why: the author's conviction rests on indirect material the audience does not share

text: A confident denial by a servant or participant is not independent confirmation; it is an explanation that can close the question without evidence.
A confident tone can reflect belief rather than knowledge; the access test shows presence or access, not accuracy.
when: using a speaker's confidence as evidence

text: Assuming the person who sounds more confident or expert is correct lets manner decide a disputed detail that evidence should settle.
when: two memories of the same event conflict

text: An investigator's confidence that the end justifies the means is itself a bias that can distort judgement.
Label each conclusion as proven, likely or speculative, keeping levels separate and not presenting a probable answer as settled.
when: when recording conclusions before a decisive test
why: stating a probable answer as fact misleads others and the player

text: Do not claim certainty for a deduction before independent evidence confirms it; a sense of certainty is no substitute for a test.
Suspicious conduct justifies investigation, but confirm identity before acting against a person, since an investigator's sense of certainty can outrun the evidence.
when: a suspect looks guilty but identity is not yet confirmed
why: Suspicion alone can point at the wrong person.

text: Give a sleuth NPC an early, confident accusation that the player can test against later clues.
Do not treat a confident statement about another person's reasons as established fact without evidence.
why: Confident claimants often read their own assumptions into another person's act.

text: Store background facts with confidence labels such as first-hand or hearsay, and consider an opt-in personal grudge that changes available dialogue.
when: Building a case knowledge system
why: Labels let players weigh reliability, and grudges make dialogue reflect personal stakes.

text: Let NPC dialogue carry confidence levels, so a guard may recall a night but not the hour, and the player must cross-check the claim.
why: Partial confidence invites verification rather than blind acceptance

text: Speakers who treat someone as absent, such as a silent bedside watcher, reveal what they did not mean to share; listeners pick up clues from tone, fragments and context.
when: People speak in front of a silent or watchful bystander.
why: Speakers do not account for someone they treat as absent.

text: Treat an overheard argument or partial plan as a lead, not a fact, until independent evidence confirms it, since fragments give only an outline without context.
why: Overheard information is often partial, so a listener may assign the wrong meaning.

text: Test each detail of an overheard motive or confession against other evidence before accepting it, since it may open a new line of investigation.
when: After overhearing a suspect's admission or motive.
why: Overheard speech is partial and can be misread.

text: Partly overheard speech is incomplete, so the listener fills gaps with existing suspicion and expectations, producing a plausible but wrong story.
when: inferring motive or acting on a conversation that was low-voiced or only partly heard
why: Missing words and context are completed by assumptions or prejudice.

text: A single overheard word or fragment is not proof of intent or confession: it can read several ways, may describe a harmless secret, and depends on context and the hearer.
when: Relying on a single overheard word or line to imply guilt or a confession.
why: Partial, ambiguous words admit innocent readings that corroboration must rule out.

text: Overheard speech with unclear pronouns or vague references invites overreading: the listener must guess the referent and may read an accusation into it, so conclusions outrun the evidence.
when: A listener catches part of a vague remark through a door or window.
why: Missing context forces the listener to guess the reference.

text: Witnesses who eavesdrop or hear through a barrier recall only fragments, so their account is partial even when sincere, and may be qualified or withheld out of loyalty.
when: A witness reports an argument, private exchange or talk heard while busy or through a door.
why: Limited hearing, partial memory and social loyalty all shape what gets told.

text: A person alone may speak aloud what they fear others know, so overheard monologue can reveal hidden knowledge.
when: when a character speaks alone

text: Players learn a third party's schedule more readily from overheard passing conversation than from direct questions, and the information feels like chance.
when: A key routine fact should reach the player indirectly
why: Passive listening feels unforced and leaves no trace back to the listener

text: A person who overhears another's sleep talk may gain a clue that they later reconsider.
when: someone speaks in sleep near others
why: overheard speech can be connected to other facts later

text: Once an overheard rumor is accepted as proof of supernatural insight, the same reasoning tends to be reused against other targets.
when: a community accepts a rumor of overheard talk as supernatural knowledge
why: The accepted logic becomes a template for new accusations.

text: A listener can weigh overheard talk far more heavily than the speakers intended, even when the speakers do not care about the listener.
when: When a character takes casual remarks about themselves as a verdict.
why: Personal relevance amplifies the impact of words not directed at the listener.

text: Players who hear only part of a conversation at a door tend to keep listening to hear the rest.
when: partial dialogue is heard at a door
why: the incomplete exchange creates curiosity

text: A remark heard from a group has no clear owner, so the hearer can identify the words but not the speaker.
when: A clue is overheard among many voices
why: Group setting hides the individual who said it

text: Overheard remarks can reveal attitudes and motives that people would not state publicly, but overhearing is selective and may be taken out of context.
when: Using overheard speech as evidence
why: Listeners capture fragments and miss the surrounding context

text: An overheard trap is a conversation staged so that a hidden listener's reactions reveal feeling or knowledge without a direct accusation.
Listening in on a phone line can capture a suspect's words to others, giving a source independent of the suspect's own account.
Speech can be overheard through a partition wall and repeated later by the listener.
An overheard name or reaction can redirect the investigation to a new suspect or start a surveillance lead.
When a witness reports overheard words, confirm who the speakers were and who could have heard them, and from where; one exchange makes a fragile motive.
when: A witness reports an overheard quarrel, threat or conversation.
why: Overheard accounts carry limits that seen events do not.

text: Speech overheard under shock or during sleep is weak testimony: weigh it, don't treat it as proof, since its meaning is ambiguous and it cannot be confirmed.
when: A listener hears speech made under shock or in sleep.

text: Give a servant-type NPC who overhears and repeats facts a habit of blurting clues at a scripted moment, shifting a tense conversation.
when: Designing clue delivery through conversation, with a minor character within earshot of a tense exchange.
why: A chatty bystander gives a natural delivery route for information.

text: An NPC's slip in small talk can unlock a clue or option only when the player listens to the right conversation, if room layout makes the listening position clear.
A witness can reliably establish a motive or a conversation even when the identity of a speaker stays uncertain. Keep what was established separate from who said it.
when: A listener caught only part of a conversation
why: Partial hearing can still give a firm fact with a loose attribution

text: An overheard exchange can reveal a hidden connection between characters without a direct scene.
when: introducing an unseen link between characters

text: Give each overheard fragment two or three plausible readings, and let a later clue confirm one of them.
when: overheard NPC dialogue the player must infer

text: Let players discover that a suspect's knowledge came from overheard conversation, resolving the lead without contradiction.
An overheard NPC line can seed a later lead that surfaces when the player reaches the matching location.
Overheard fragments should be kept as separate items to test, not accepted at face value.
Split a key overheard clue across fragments so the player's first half needs a second encounter or source to complete it, rewarding attention.
when: Designing dialogue clues delivered through eavesdropping.
why: Incomplete information invites the player to search for the rest, connecting separate scenes.

text: A character who overhears a secret can make a decision based on it that the speakers never intended to share.
when: a listener learns information the speakers wanted hidden
why: the listener acts on knowledge no one gave them openly

text: Overheard admissions of debt or despair can give a listener a motive that later drives a bargain, such as trading a secret for a share of money.
An NPC who overhears a conversation can be logged as a witness whose later dialogue reflects their relationship with the speaker, so players can test that account against other evidence.
when: when designing NPCs that overhear conversations

text: Letting players overhear NPC plans from hiding can change the next objective, rewarding stealth with information.
An NPC can overhear a conversation within a set radius and store only some lines, so the player must ask about the rest to learn it.
when: When designing NPC eavesdropping mechanics.

text: Accusations heard through a wall or door lack a clear sender and context; assuming who the unheard speaker is from few words invites error.
when: Identifying speakers or weighing a key accusation heard through a wall, door or from a third party.
why: Partial hearing leaves identity underdetermined; without face, context or confirmation, meaning depends on who is believed to have spoken.

text: A witness can misread accurately reported words; one misheard term or sibilant changes the reading, and allusive technical speech hides meaning from anyone lacking shared context.
Signals between servants can be heard by the wrong person, so a warning meant for one listener may reach another.
when: a signal is given in a shared space
why: Audible cues are not private.

text: Once a household knows it is being overheard, everyone starts listening, and secrets spread faster.
Overhearing can depend on luck, so do not build a plan that relies on it.
1) Ask the source directly what they actually heard and gather specific details. 2) Ask whether the words could bear another meaning. 3) Accept only if the hearing supports it.
when: An accusation or lead rests on an overheard exchange or unsolicited remark.
why: Overheard words are often ambiguous and partial, and unquestioned remarks give shallow support.

text: 1) Place a line of NPC self-talk where the player can overhear it. 2) Word it to hint at a consequence without naming it. 3) Pair it with a visible reaction for confirmation.
when: When designing revealing overheard dialogue.
why: Hinting preserves mystery while the reaction confirms the line matters.

text: Write overheard lines as partial fragments heard through walls, specific enough for players to reconstruct a sequence by combining them with other clues.
when: Designing NPC dialogue heard by eavesdropping.

text: Overheard evidence is second-hand: it counts only once the listener reports it, and its reliability depends on how well they heard and understood it.
when: When a witness says they overheard a conversation.
why: Partial recall limits what it can prove.

text: Let players overhear NPC talk through a gap while staying in shadow and unseen, so motive clues like debts surface without confrontation.
when: Designing NPC conversations in a game investigation.

text: Record an overheard exchange in detail, including alternatives offered, and mark as partial what the witness admits they did not hear.
why: A later choice between alternatives may matter.

text: Let overheard lines reveal motive while leaving the object or location unclear, so later clues can supply it.
Use overheard lines to raise a question or suggest a motive, not to settle it.
when: Writing partial dialogue as evidence
why: Fragments are too ambiguous to prove anything

text: Let an NPC in the next room overhear the player and change its later behaviour based on the overheard line.
Let a tavern scene overlap several NPC voices so most lines are garbled, leaving the player one or two clear facts to act on.
Plant a secondhand report of a confession as a clue, with the original record available for the player to check.
when: when building document-based mysteries

text: Treat overheard fragments as proof that two parties communicate, not as proof of what they meant.
why: Tone and partial words reveal relationship but not motive.

text: Overheard testimony reveals intent without confrontation, but it is weak for exact facts and times and cannot be verified by the listener.
when: speakers do not know they are observed

text: A staged overhearing can pressure a guarded suspect, but the cost may fall on a fragile witness instead.
when: Use when a guarded suspect answers direct questions only with refusals.

text: Record even small, seemingly futile or unclear observations, such as timing details or a victim's details, before judging relevance; minor details often prove significant.
when: Reviewing evidence during an investigation.
why: Minor-seeming details are dropped from working lists unless deliberately tracked.

text: Report small or odd details early, such as a missing weapon, quantity or left-behind object, and return to them later; they can reverse a settled conclusion.
when: when a later reveal depends on an earlier detail
why: Details dismissed as minor can gain meaning once the solution is known.

text: Even carefully planned crimes leave incidental difficulties and small traces that chance or overlooked details can expose; these are often the most instructive details.
when: when designing how a culprit's plan fails, or building a final reconstruction
why: Unplanned details and luck create believable exposure without contrivance.

text: Minor details gain weight when they match a pattern in other facts, but they may be red herrings; treat them as proof only after corroboration.
Keep clues at the edge between plausible and supernatural, so each can be explained either way and stays ambiguous.
why: ambiguity keeps the reader uncertain

text: Add a second, overlooked opening such as a skylight to a sealed room to keep the puzzle fair and solvable.
when: Designing a locked-room puzzle.
why: A visible alternative route makes the sealing solvable without arbitrary cheating.

text: An in-world notice or item description can carry a partial clue that prompts the player to find a second witness.
The most obvious inference is often the one people overlook. Check it explicitly before reaching for more complex explanations.
when: when an investigation stalls on complex theories

text: Let clues reach the player by accident during ordinary activity, such as a small item among a scatter of objects, rather than only at a marked objective.
when: when placing evidence or hints

text: Small incidental marks, such as an urgent label, a smudged note or a half-remembered rumour, can carry weight later, so plant them deliberately.
when: when planting clues in documents or dialogue
why: readers treat minor details as significant once suspicion is raised

text: Set aside incidental details such as manner or bearing unless they connect to another fact.
Seemingly idle personal facts, such as a dentist's name or a physical ability, can serve as connective points that link people or test a claim.
when: Routine or physical details might connect to the scene or to records

text: Ask about small unprompted details, such as unanswered calls, to surface witnesses the subject did not plan to mention.
Minor characters often turn out to matter greatly, so their introduction should be recorded in a way the audience can recall later.
why: Late-revealed relevance of incidental figures can make a solution feel unfair if the earlier appearance was not retained.

text: A culprit who cleans carefully often misses one conspicuous object, so check for ordinary items that are out of place in the crime setting.
when: The scene looks orderly after the culprit had time to clean
why: Cleaning targets obvious traces and not familiar belongings

text: Information delivered in idle talk or ordinary records drops listeners' guard and leaks details; listeners' reactions to a mentioned name become evidence in their own right.
when: A character hears a relevant fact unprepared, or should reveal information without knowing it matters.
why: A casual tone signals no test, so listeners do not brace and speakers leak details carelessly.

text: A dropped personal item links its owner to a place or another person more strongly than a general impression, once its source and contents are known.
when: A dropped item is found by a character who did not own it.
why: The item carries the identity of its sender, connecting otherwise separate parties.

text: A witness can give up a clue incidentally, such as mentioning a fought-over object, without realizing its importance.
when: When a witness describes a conflict or argument.
why: Witnesses report details of an event without knowing which ones matter to the case.

text: An outside observer who reads an incidental clue, such as leftover wine, can reshape suspicion against a whole group, though the culprit never planned that reading.
A clue remembered only from memory, with no label or markings, can support many different identities, so its identity stays uncertain.
when: A physical trace is described from recall without a surviving label.
why: Without recorded features, several objects match the remembered description equally well.

text: An object dropped at a measured point lets its owner return to the same spot later, even when conditions have changed.
when: a route or site must be revisited
why: the recorded position persists

text: Observers miss small physical traces, which look like debris from standing height, and fixate on color and fashion; small details, not the general impression, carry key information.
when: viewing a scene from a normal standing position
why: A small link looks like debris from a distance, and attention goes to appearance rather than wear.

text: Investigators overlook clues already in view, such as an address on an envelope, which may become meaningful only when a related reference is read.
A withheld fact that is never hinted at again reads as a dropped thread rather than a deliberate secret.
when: A secret is planted without follow-up
why: Readers lose trust in clues that go nowhere

text: A partial clue invites players to complete it by assumption, which can produce a confident but wrong theory.
Everyday structures such as pipes or creepers can offer a route that is missed when only obvious entrances are examined.
when: Checking how a window or high opening could be reached
why: Ordinary features can give footholds that are not immediately noticed

text: Investigators often overlook the suspect's own room, where items are moved or destroyed. Search there as well.
when: tracing a hidden or stolen item
why: items are often moved or destroyed at home

text: A closed circle can still hide an outsider who is simply overlooked, so a known population does not prove that no intruder is present.
why: Familiarity can cause people to stop noticing someone who does not belong

text: A trace can be missed even by the person best placed to see it, so being present at a scene does not guarantee a detail was noticed.
when: An investigator examines a body or scene they were present at
why: Attention at the time may be directed elsewhere

text: Identifying someone from voice and symbol without a clear view of the face shows how partial cues can mislead.
A reporter who judges a detail unimportant may omit it, so a key anomaly can survive only in secondhand talk.
when: When information passes through several reporters
why: Each relay filters details by perceived importance

text: An earlier version of a will can be overlooked, leading the investigator to the wrong beneficiary.
when: Identifying who benefits from a will.
why: Only the latest version is often checked, though a change of beneficiary may have occurred.

text: Treating a minor inconsistency as proof of lying, when it may reflect confusion or the wording of the question.
Fixating on a small wound or a fallen object can make the investigator overlook an alternative cause of the same event.
Investigators who accept a first clue at face value can waste long periods pursuing a false trail.
when: When a plausible clue appears early in an investigation.
why: A convincing false clue can mislead even an expert until its true origin is explained.

text: 1) Turn a small remark into a checkable fact, such as a date, name or cargo. 2) Check it against a reference source. 3) Branch parallel inquiries to each place the subject may be found. Check even minor timing details; a neutral fact confirmed by a third party can fix whereabouts.
