when: Verifying a suspect's account or a witness's trivial-seeming remark.
why: A checkable fact can confirm or rule out a line of inquiry; trivial details become decisive when tied to a timeline.

text: Do not dismiss a slight or minor-looking detail, such as an event's day or a witness's remark; it may resolve contradictions or carry the whole case.
why: Neglecting small details can lead to error, and they often decide between conflicting accounts.

text: A dropped item such as a hat or badge can point players to a missing NPC; have several NPCs independently recognise it to build confidence.
when: designing a clue that links an item to a missing character
why: independent recognitions make the link believable

text: Let a conversation system ask NPCs about incidental details such as seats, light sources or wall objects, marking answers that match or contradict what the player saw.
when: designing NPC conversations

text: Mark an overlooked NPC as a witness on a second visit, so players who return can resolve the clue.
Let a minor oddity, such as an offhand remark or a worn object, look trivial until a later reveal gives it meaning.
when: Planting clues that must pay off late.
why: Players pass over oddities they do not yet have a reason to question.

text: Repeated ordinary details are often filed as habitual color and missed as evidence, while recurring background noise is overvalued because repetition is mistaken for significance.
when: A clue is repeated in an ordinary context (missed) versus recurring incidental chatter (overvalued).
why: Repetition makes details seem habitual to some readers and meaningful to others.

text: A hint can take the form of a parallel case whose structure mirrors the answer without stating it.
when: the answer must stay hidden but should be recognisable
why: the audience can map the parallel onto the answer

text: A parallel case can guide reasoning about an undocumented act, but it is not proof that the same act occurred here.
when: A similar recorded case exists for comparison
why: Similarity suggests a pattern without establishing the specific event

text: A detailed parallel between two cases tempts reasoners to treat them as identical, though small differences can send the cases in very different directions.
when: a previous case seems to explain a new one
why: the match feels convincing even when key details differ

text: 1) Pursue a promising lead briefly. 2) If it leads nowhere, park it. 3) Revisit it when new facts arrive.
when: A lead looks promising but produces no results.
why: Parking keeps effort focused while preserving the lead for later.

text: Cut between parallel locations with rising stakes to keep several threads running at once.
Juggling several cases or leads spreads effort thin and invents false links; focusing deepens analysis but delays others. Test each lead, including self-offered experts, as a possible distraction.
when: when multiple open cases or leads compete for attention

text: Record partial testimony with its gaps and limits visible, and seek another source rather than reading more into the words, so readers can judge how much weight each part bears.
Make NPC dialogue accurate but partial, leaving players to infer what is omitted and cross-check it with other NPCs and environmental evidence.
when: When designing clue dialogue or NPC dialogue that withholds information
why: Accurate partial statements force players to compare sources; selective truth rewards inference and keeps dialogue honest.

text: Eavesdropping or glimpsing yields fragments; an observer often cannot see and hear at once, so the pieces must be combined.
when: a character learns part of a situation through a keyhole or partial view
why: A single sensory channel gives only part of the event.

text: A dying or badly injured witness gives partial, broken words, so the questioner must draw out the rest through short, targeted questions.
when: When a dying or incapacitated witness must reveal information
why: Severe distress limits speech

text: An NPC may give partial dialogue, so the player must follow up with specific questions to obtain the key line.
Witnesses are interested and partial, so they can stop short of the most disturbing part of an event.
when: a witness is asked to record a distressing detail
why: self-interest and distress make full disclosure unlikely

text: Overheard speech through a closed door is usually partial, and different listeners may catch different fragments of the same exchange.
when: When witnesses hear a conversation without hearing every word
why: Distance and barriers filter what reaches each listener

text: Make an NPC's first disclosure partial, such as 'I took it, but it is gone', as a branching clue that points elsewhere, so its fuller account must be verified.
when: When designing dialogue branches or NPC lines that reveal incomplete truths
why: A partial admission signals hidden information without confirming the whole account, which keeps the hidden fact worth pursuing.

text: Give witness NPCs in chaotic scenes fragmentary, lower-reliability dialogue so the player must cross-check several accounts.
when: Designing NPC dialogue for a fire, collapse or similar scene
why: Several partial accounts force the player to reason from evidence

text: Give an NPC a partial memory, such as a clear face with a vague name or hair colour, so the player must judge which details to trust.
when: when writing NPC recollections
why: mixed reliability forces the player to weigh evidence

text: Information from a reluctant or captive source usually arrives in fragments the questioner must assemble.
A dying or broken accusation names a suspect or motive but must be confirmed against evidence before it is accepted as the answer.
when: a witness's last words or fragmentary statement point at someone
why: partial words may have been caught or interpreted wrongly

text: Fragmentary recall from a dazed witness can still identify a key object, though details may be confused.
A suspect's reaction can change dialogue state, so a pressed NPC may reveal a second route or item.
when: designing reactive NPC dialogue
why: pressure unlocks new information

text: An informant NPC can give part of an answer for a price, unlocking the second half only after the first is delivered.
when: Designing staged information from NPCs.
why: Staged payment controls how much information the player gains at each step.

text: When an NPC corrects an earlier lie, record which statements are retracted and which remain standing, and open new questions from the admitted detail.
when: Writing dialogue that allows an NPC to change its account.
why: Tracking retractions keeps the player's picture of the case accurate and gives new leads.

text: Let a test confirm the mechanism while leaving one question unanswered, so the reveal feels proven yet a thread stays open for later.
when: Ending a reveal test
why: A full answer closes the case, while a partial one keeps the player engaged.

text: Test a witness's account by checking each detail separately, since a witness may be right on one point and wrong on another, which shows which parts to trust.
why: Mixed accuracy lets the reader judge which parts of a testimony can be relied on.

text: A reveal built from successive partial readings, each factually fair and each overturned by the next, makes the final answer feel earned rather than sudden.
when: Designing a multi-stage mystery reveal.
why: Every stage is supported by evidence, so overturning it teaches the player that the search was too narrow.

text: A witness who withholds the key point frustrates the audience unless the withholding is justified by the witness's own distress.

1) Record each fragment exactly as spoken, leaving blank gaps between them. 2) Fill each gap with a phrase that fits the words on both sides. 3) Revise until the whole sequence reads naturally in both directions.
when: when a speaker's account survives only in broken pieces that context can bridge
why: Fitting gaps to their neighbours recovers the sense of missing words without inventing unrelated content.

text: 1) Make NPC dialogue through a door partly audible. 2) Leave the missing words to be pieced together from other sources. 3) Let the player assemble the full statement.
when: when designing overheard dialogue

text: Give witness NPCs partial knowledge, such as height and beard but not eye colour, so players must combine fragments from several sources.
Have NPCs give partial or biased accounts, and let the player check them against a register, ledger or town record.
Trigger a player's public confrontation only when their evidence is ready; if it is premature, nearby NPCs should side with the suspect.
when: when generating crowd reactions to an accusation

text: Mark an NPC's testimony as partial and give a later journal entry or item that reveals the shielded fact.
when: When an NPC has reason to hide information.
why: A later reveal rewards careful players.

text: Ask what a witness did not say, since an honest speaker can omit the detail that matters.
when: Evaluating a witness account.
why: Sincere testimony is often partial, so omissions can carry the key information.

text: Make a suspect's conduct suspicious through a pattern of individually defensible actions rather than one damning act.
when: writing a suspect whose guilt should be inferred
why: Each step keeps an innocent reading, so the pattern carries the suspicion.

text: Track how a pattern, such as call frequency, changes over time, since a shift can mark an event worth checking.
when: Reviewing a record of repeated contacts

text: Reveal a pattern in observable responses to changing conditions to overturn a false explanation without naming the true cause.
A rival who keeps reappearing across different locations turns single surprises into a recognisable pattern the player can follow.
when: when a rival must be tracked over a long campaign
why: repetition across places makes the rival's presence a pattern, not a one-off

text: 1) Note events that recur on a schedule or share a trigger. 2) Check the pattern against an independent record. 3) Treat the match as a lead, then run a test before accepting a cause.
when: When scattered events seem random but may share a hidden trigger
why: An independent record can confirm a schedule, but only a test can establish the cause.

text: Confirmation bias or a theory built to fit a pattern can make ordinary events look connected, so weigh the chance that parallels are unrelated.
Treat repeated unusual details as leads, not proof; do not group incidents into one pattern until each is independently linked, since shared sources or causes can mimic a pattern.
when: Incidents share a signature, shared person, or warning but may have different causes.
why: Shared sources or coincidence can make unrelated events look connected; different methods may mean different actors.

text: Accusers often offer a pattern across many events as proof of a link, even when no single case is shown.
when: A group's guilt is argued from a list of incidents without direct evidence for each.
why: Repetition feels persuasive, though it does not establish the link in any one case.

text: A single odd action, such as an unusual payment or a stray item, can serve as the hook for an investigation if it is observable and can be reinterpreted later.
when: designing the opening clue of an investigation
why: A small, observable anomaly gives players an entry point and a reason to revisit it.

text: Repeated back-and-forth movements can be invisible when each event is examined alone but become clear when events are arranged in time order.
when: several similar events occurred at different times
why: Ordering reveals the rhythm of repetition that single events hide.

text: A single disturbed detail is weak evidence. A consistent pattern across several disturbed details, such as arrangement and handling, strengthens the inference about a visitor.
when: Interpreting disturbed objects as evidence
why: Multiple consistent traces are less likely to be coincidence

text: When several cases with different views share the same outcome, the common cause is more likely a policy than separate private quarrels.
when: Multiple similar cases are being compared to find the real motive.
why: A shared outcome across unrelated cases points to a systematic cause.

text: Pattern matching only singles out one source when the pattern is distinctive; a common pattern shared by many candidates cannot identify one.
when: Choosing whether a trace can identify its source

text: Regular anonymous sends of money or letters reveal a deliberate schedule, and changes in the amounts over time can signal intent.
when: an unknown sender acts repeatedly through indirect channels
why: Consistent timing and amounts are harder to disguise than names or handwriting.

text: Wills, intestate division, inherited judgments and inherited houses constrain the living, so past arrangements shape present action.
A pattern of quarrels preceding a harm is not proof of guilt without a separate link between the accused and the harm.
when: when evaluating a case built mainly on prior disputes
why: Disputes are common and do not establish causation

text: A patient plan can still fail when the target behaves unexpectedly, so it needs contingencies for other behavior.
A reconciliation vote that passes does not mean reconciliation is complete, since a minority may still dissent.
Reasoning from patterns across earlier cases to a new case is unreliable, because a pattern is not an infallible rule for an individual case.

1) Gather incidents that look separate. 2) List what they share. 3) Examine how the shared element is meant to work and why it might fail. 4) Note the conditions under which failures occur. 5) Compare against cases lacking the factor.
when: several events share a rare feature

text: 1) Gather records covering many cases. 2) Filter the cases matching a specific condition. 3) Count and compare the matching cases to reveal a shared pattern.
when: A pattern across many records must be assembled from several entries
why: No single incident shows the pattern, but counting across records does

text: A pattern of omissions is not proof on its own; independent evidence is needed before treating the inference as established.
why: The pattern may have an innocent cause.

text: Make a clue's power lie in a pattern across many entries, possibly in the owner's own handwriting, so the player must read the collection in sequence to see it.
when: Designing a document-based clue.

text: Repeat a sensory motif, such as recurring imagery, until it forms a pattern players can notice before they understand it.
when: When hinting at a hidden nature without stating it
why: Repetition turns scattered impressions into a recognizable pattern the player can later interpret.

text: Under fear, surprise, or fatigue, observers misperceive details, such as doubled figures, changed room size, or a living person taken for a spirit in poor light, and recall of event order breaks down.
when: An observer is frightened, surprised, or fatigued during an event
why: Stress and poor light distort perception; stress affects both perception and memory, not only later recall.

text: Let a stressed NPC misremember a detail that the player can later confirm with a record, which gives the player a reason to revisit evidence.
when: Writing NPC testimony that the player must verify.
why: Confirmable errors motivate investigation and reward checking.

text: Early boundary points were often removable or perishable objects, such as marked trees and heaps of stones, so original surveys of such boundaries frequently do not survive.
A disturbed scene that persists, such as a pulled drawer or a displaced book, signals a prior intruder and can tie an object's state to a character's habits.
when: Designing rooms that record past visits
why: Lasting disturbance gives players evidence of who was present

text: 1) Find the interval when the key person was away from the victim. 2) Find when the victim was next seen or re-entered. 3) Test which phase fits inside those bounds.
Model perishable evidence, such as a briefly speaking witness or an item whose condition records time since placement or delivery, to create time pressure and serve as a clock.
Initials, a monogram, or a name entry is not proof of identity, since many people share the same initials or names.
when: Using a marked object or record entry to identify a suspect or identity.
why: Shared names and initials can point to several people.

text: Personal objects link a person to places, times and actions. Tracing an object's path and condition can connect an unidentified body or missing person to a known life.
Some physical features vary enough between people to serve as individual markers.
Initialed items on fallen adventurers or NPCs can serve as identifiers that unlock dialogue or quests.
when: designing dead or injured characters in a game

text: Let a small personal object carry the identity question, and test it against each candidate owner using a physical feature such as wear, residue or damage.
when: designing an identification puzzle or whodunit
why: A concrete object can be matched to several suspects, so the answer becomes checkable rather than asserted.

text: Initials on an object may not match its owner. Check that they belong to the owner before reading them as the culprit's mark.
why: A coincidental match can send the investigation after the wrong person.

text: 1) Check where ownership is usually written, such as the flyleaf or cover. 2) Check the rest of the item. 3) Compare names, initials, and handwriting against the known owner. 4) Check the leaves for loose scraps of paper. 5) Note what each item reveals and set aside those that might help.
when: Examining a set of personal items for names, dates, or hidden notes
why: A systematic order ensures ownership and concealed notes are not overlooked.

text: Identify a specific object by an accidental, individual flaw such as a crack, damage or repair, rather than by its general type.
when: when several identical objects could be the one in question

text: Plant identifying marks such as a brand, a ring or a card in the opening scene so the player can later check them against the twist.
when: a body or character is presented as a known person
why: Early checkable marks let the player verify the reveal instead of accepting it on trust.

text: A photograph shows one instant and fixes a face and date but not relationships, so confirm what it shows and interpret it with surrounding evidence.
why: One instant can mislead without context.

text: Staff who saw published photographs can recognise a person, so a face on record can expose a false identity.
A photograph records fine physical features, such as the shape of a person's ears, that witnesses cannot reliably describe in words or memory.
when: Identification depends on subtle physical features
why: A photograph keeps exact visual detail that memory loses.

text: Labelled old photographs can identify who appears in an image and when it was taken, where written records are absent.
Circulate a photograph widely when a face is the only link to a claimed past identity.
Read a photograph closely for distinctive features, such as hair, beard, moustache and eyebrows, to build a description to test against later reports.
A photo-based identification may reflect politeness, suggestion or the shown image rather than memory of the original encounter, so it is weaker than it seems.
when: Using a photo identification as evidence, or showing witnesses a photo before or during identification.
why: The shown image shapes what the witness reports; recognition can be driven by the image rather than memory.

text: 1) Present a set of photographs to each witness. 2) Record which faces each witness recognises. 3) Confirm any identification later with independent evidence.
when: Identifying a person from memory of their appearance.
why: Structured recognition gives checkable identifications.

text: 1) Show a photograph of the suspected stand-in to people who knew the real person. 2) Record whether they recognise the face. 3) Treat recognition as identity evidence only if the witnesses are independent.
when: Testing whether a documented person was actually present
why: Recognition by people who knew the real person links the face to the identity

text: 1) Anchor the witness to a narrow time window and a specific location. 2) Check both directions of a route. 3) Show the photo to several witnesses separately. 4) Record each negative answer as information.
when: Testing whether a suspect was at a place and time.
why: Narrow anchors make recall specific, and several separate witnesses cross-check each other.

text: Show a photograph to witnesses to test identification rather than assuming a suspect is recognised.
A physical trace can jog memory, but a speaker may recall where something came from only after being given the specific figures.
when: an object or purchase connects to a disputed sum
why: recall is cued by concrete facts more than by general questions

text: The state of a container, such as locked, forced, or empty, can differ from the rest of a scene and suggest a different actor or motive.
when: A container's state does not match the rest of the scene.
why: A mismatch between the container and the scene points to a separate person or purpose.

text: A contributory clue points toward a suspect without proving guilt; a decisive clue is timed and exclusive, tying the act to one suspect at a known moment.
when: Grading the strength of evidence.
why: Decisive clues are needed before an arrest.

text: Rough contact can transfer fibres from clothing to a surface, revealing the garment's colour and fabric.
when: a coat or cloth brushes a wet or rough object

text: A missing contact mark from a firearm pressed against the head makes close-range self-harm less likely but does not rule it out.
when: when judging wound features against a self-inflicted explanation
why: contact marks are common but not guaranteed

text: Plant physical details, such as sensory specifics or an object's weight or material, in an opening or dialogue so their later meaning or use feels fair and recognisable.
when: Writing an opening, dialogue or clue that will return later, such as a late reveal or a lock's key
why: Early specifics give later scenes something to match; objects read as scenery, so later significance surprises without feeling unfair

text: An act at a scene that does not serve the suspect's apparent purpose suggests a different actor or motive.
when: A detail of a crime seems out of character for the suspect.
why: Purpose and character are both evidence, and a mismatch points away from the expected person.

text: The quality of consumables an owner buys can hint at their means, especially when a premium item is bought by someone who could economise.
when: When assessing an owner's wealth from purchased goods
why: Choice of quality reflects available money

text: Compare the physical dimensions of a container with what it is meant to hold; an unusual size can reveal a hidden extra item.
A conspicuous object can betray its holder over a wide area, so it is often the most dangerous trace to keep.
why: it is easily identified across a region

text: Make the physical condition of an in-world document, such as a missing leaf or frayed edge, an observable clue players can examine, not only text to read.
when: when designing in-world records
why: physical state can carry evidence that the text omits

text: Physical details of an object, such as a bend or a fitting, can indicate how it was displaced, supporting a reconstruction of the event.
A specialized object unsuited to its carrier's apparent purpose can imply planned intent, and item descriptions can hint at that purpose.
A very small physical trace, such as a torn label or residue, can link an object to a source more strongly than many larger finds.
when: Assembling evidence that connects a substance to a purchase
why: A specific identifying detail can establish a link that bulk cannot

text: A physical act done in public, such as removing a false marker, makes the truth visible and hard to undo.
Measure how far an actor's hand or body falls short of a target and use the gap to estimate how much bigger the actor must be.
when: When a physical mark shows how someone reached a high point.
why: The gap between a reachable point and the target gives a measurable size difference.

text: A physical detail, such as a damaged item found in an unexpected place, can overturn an accepted story by showing the damage happened earlier than claimed.
when: A physical clue conflicts with the accepted timeline
why: Physical state records a sequence the story did not account for.

text: A hidden item can be concealed by swapping its container for a similar empty one, and the empty substitute must then be hidden too.
when: When someone wants to hide the contents of a container.
why: The swap keeps the outward appearance intact while moving the contents elsewhere.

text: Let an NPC confirm an item with a stated confidence level, so the player must decide how much to trust the identification.
when: Designing item identification interactions
why: Confidence levels create uncertainty that players must weigh

text: An item bearing identifying information, left where it is easy to find, is suspicious and may have been deliberately positioned.
why: easy discovery suggests intent

text: A link that rests on physical description alone, with no name, is weak and needs further corroboration.
when: When the identity of a suspect or rival is unknown.

text: Give found items physical features, such as ink colour, paper type, material, wear and craft skill, as leads to the type of person who left them.
when: generating items placed in a level

text: Make the flipping statement reachable through earlier dialogue so the reversal feels earned rather than arbitrary.
Publish a physical detail when it could prompt a witness to come forward.
when: an investigation needs witnesses
why: a public detail can reach people who saw the matter

text: Keep one inspectable physical clue that connects the planner to the method, so the reveal rests on something the audience can examine.
why: the reveal survives if the object is later destroyed

text: Inspect ordinary containers by opening them and examining contents closely, even when they are messy or dirty.
when: a scene contains bins, crates or similar containers
why: key evidence can sit inside clutter

text: Do not drop a noticed physical clue because testimony sounds certain. Set the clue aside as unresolved and reopen it when a new question arises.
when: When a physical clue conflicts with a firm-sounding testimony.
why: Testimony may be wrong, and physical traces stay available for later questions.

text: Use physical habits such as clothing, seating position or how a weapon is carried as checks that can rule out an otherwise plausible suspect.
when: Eliminating suspects after temperament analysis
why: Physical details are checkable facts that temperament reasoning cannot supply

text: Ask whether each door was locked or unlocked, since this determines which areas an intruder could reach.
when: when reconstructing who could access a room
why: door state defines the reachable space

text: Give players a physical clue, such as a reflection, draught or echo, that explains a local legend once they know the period's rules.
Let a journal list the possible meanings of an item so the player can test each one.
Test whether a trace's position or a claimed action is physically possible; an impossible arrangement, such as an awkward grip for the claimed blow, exposes staging.
when: A trace's position or claimed action conflicts with the account
why: Physical limits cannot be faked; an impossible arrangement points to staging after the event

text: A matching mark can still prove the wrong thing. Check whether it could physically have been made in the recorded pose, not only whether it matches.
when: when a single match carries the case
why: a match shows similarity, not who made the mark

text: Logical checks on physical states, such as a window closed at one time and open later, bound what must have happened in between.
when: when a physical state changes across the timeline
why: A state change implies an event occurred in the interval.

text: Rule out a suspect by a physical capability only after establishing the limit that applies, such as whether the person could make a given jump.
when: Ruling out a person by physical ability.
why: An unestablished limit can wrongly exclude the real culprit or wrongly accept a disguise.

text: Physical constraints, such as wound logic, the need to conceal traces, or measurable facts like water depth, can exclude whole classes of explanation or a suspect's actions.
A locked-room theft that seems impossible for an adult can be solved by a small intruder through a route that only fits a child, reversing the assumed size of the thief.
when: designing an impossible-theft solution
why: The size assumption is the unstated premise, so overturning it resolves the paradox.

text: 1) Identify what the event requires physically. 2) Compare the pattern of the event with the limits of a candidate agent. 3) Narrow candidates to those that fit. 4) Test each step against the evidence before accepting it.
when: When an event seems supernatural or impossible.
why: Physical constraints can rule out candidates and turn an uncanny event into a solvable cause.

text: 1) List the fixed physical conditions of the scene. 2) Determine what a normal actor would have had to disturb to create them. 3) Identify which unusual agents could satisfy every detail. 4) Test each candidate against the whole arrangement.
when: The usual suspect is excluded by the scene's fixed details
why: Working backward from the arrangement isolates explanations consistent with all evidence

text: Check the rules of the scene before using a physical test on a suspect, since some tests may be unlawful or unfair.
when: planning a physical test on a suspect
why: Tests that break rules can invalidate the result or harm the investigator's standing.

text: Do not treat a physical match as identification until a detail such as clothing or jewellery agrees.
Make the reveal turn on a physical constraint the audience can check, such as a jump distance or a locked gate, so the solution is fair.
when: when a reveal rules out a suspect
why: a physical fact the audience can verify makes the deduction feel earned rather than arbitrary

text: Build distinct damage signatures into objects so players can match one wreck to another and find shared causes.
Showing that a wound was inflicted after death reframes the case: the assumed murder becomes a staging, and the apparent victim's identity becomes uncertain.
when: A murder is solved by a physical finding that contradicts the first account.
why: A changed cause of injury alters what the reader believes happened and who is dead.

text: An obstacle found exactly where it was left in a gap shows the gap was not used, because a person could not easily restore it.
when: When an entry point is blocked by an object that could be moved.
why: Restoring an obstacle precisely is hard, so its unchanged position is evidence.

text: A place left unchanged for years can be misread if the investigator does not know what has already been removed.
Do not assume a stain is the suspected substance before testing it.
Testing only the full containers can clear the real route, since the wrong sample can rule out the true source.

1) Examine every part, not only the most obvious damage. 2) Look for signatures a crash alone would not produce, such as burned insulation and fused wires. 3) Use intact parts to exclude causes. 4) Compare separate wrecks for shared damage. 5) Lock wreckage away unchanged after inspection.
when: a failure is blamed on ordinary causes but the damage looks unusual

text: Plant an odd, unexplained object early and pay it off in the final scene without explaining it.
when: when building an eerie or ambiguous story
why: The object keeps the reader attentive while leaving the cause open.

text: Confirm an environmental fact such as weather from an independent source rather than from the suspect's own account.
when: When a conclusion depends on a weather or condition claim.
why: A suspect has a motive to misstate conditions that affect their alibi.

text: Burning a document removes its content but leaves residue such as cinders, and an observer can read that residue as proof the document was burned.
when: A character destroys evidence in a visible place.
why: Destruction by fire leaves physical traces that can be inspected after the act.

text: A match between identical common items is consistent with a theory but not conclusive, because such items are widespread.
when: Weighing a match between two common objects.
why: Widespread items appear in many places, so a match alone does not identify an owner.

text: Who finds an item, and when, is itself part of the evidentiary record and can carry meaning.
when: Interpreting the discovery of a clue.
why: The finder's identity and timing can reveal access, intent or opportunity.

text: Pair an object that seems to confirm a theory with one that contradicts it, so neither evidence settles the question alone.
Among a set of similar items, compare appearances to find the one that differs, and test that one first.
when: Several near-identical items may hide something.
why: A difference in appearance flags the item most likely to hold a hidden property.

text: Make the container itself the evidence: a labelled item shown early can hold the key document, teaching players to inspect objects rather than only their contents.
when: Designing a document-based clue.
why: Players focus on what they see, and inspecting the container reveals the hidden evidence.

text: A place where used containers accumulate in order works as a log that can be checked later, preserving a history of use.
when: used containers are kept in sequence
why: stock order records what was used and when

text: Do not assume a debris pile holds evidence; examine it before claiming any clue from it.
Accepting a recurring correlation as a cause before running a test risks a wrong conclusion.
when: When a pattern matches a trigger but the mechanism is unknown
why: Matching timing does not prove that the trigger produces the effect.

text: Sweeping every surface evenly can dilute the one spot that matters, so a general sample reads clean even when the trace is present.
1) Read a vehement or self-contradictory document twice. 2) Compare it with the writer's earlier statements. 3) Note any change in tone or claim. 4) Ask what happened between the two statements.
Check every container and packet at a scene for names, since an overlooked one can implicate a third party.
Destroyed documents can still be recovered through the leads they name, but when a destroyed physical artifact cannot be examined, only the destroyer's account remains.
when: Key evidence is destroyed: recovery works if other sources name leads; if no other record survives, verification depends on the destroyer.
why: Leads named in a document exist independently of it, but without the physical record, claims cannot be verified.

text: Paint generally resists water, so a spot that washes off with water is unlikely to be paint.
A hazard delivered through a physical object in the room, such as a poisoned lamp, is a stronger mystery element than a hidden attacker.
when: designing lethal environments in a closed space
why: The threat is already present and discoverable, so players investigate the setting rather than search for an intruder.

text: A route across space that has been occupied for a long time is unlikely to pass unseen, and nearby rooms may show whether a ladder or path was in use.
when: When judging whether a route could have gone unnoticed.
why: Sustained occupancy and sightlines make a route visible to observers.

text: A missing item can point to a recent action, such as removal shortly before an event, so note what is absent as well as what is present.
when: When a person's usual belongings are absent from a scene
why: Absence can record a deliberate or hurried action.

text: Look for an object present at one visit and absent at another; its presence or absence can settle which visit came first.
when: Two candidate visit orders exist and one physical item links to only one of them.
why: A dated physical state orders events that testimony alone cannot.

text: Let a hidden object be examined for an innocent reason, so the audience files it in the wrong category until the reveal corrects it.
when: when an object is central to the eventual reveal
why: a harmless first impression keeps the true nature hidden

text: Offer a small object tied to a stated habit; if the person's behavior with it contradicts their claim, the claim is weakened without any accusation.
when: when a witness asserts a personal habit that can be checked
why: Actions reveal what claims cannot, and the test stays informal.

text: An out-of-place or abandoned object with an unusual feature, such as unusually strong cord, can point to a planned method.
Let a found item's stains and wear imply its owner's habits and situation, giving the player a profile to search by.
Pair two pieces of physical evidence so that one explanation, such as a disguise, accounts for both at once.
when: Resolving contradictory physical evidence.
why: One explanation that covers both pieces feels more convincing than two separate ones.

text: A missing object such as clothing or a collar can stand in for the missing person until a later reveal gives it meaning.
when: A body or person is absent or unidentified in a scene.
why: The object carries the question until its meaning is supplied.

text: An object that carries too many hints at once loses its force, so spread clues across separate objects.
when: Designing a clue object.
why: Too many simultaneous hints dilute each one and make the object hard to read.

text: A person who destroys evidence in panic often ignores the visible traces left behind, and a surviving duplicate defeats the purpose of destruction.
when: A character destroys a document under emotional stress.
why: Strong emotion narrows attention to the act itself rather than the aftermath or copies.

text: A missing item is evidence only once someone knows it was present, so witness memory of an item gives its absence weight.
when: Judging whether an absence matters
why: Without knowing the item existed, its absence is not noticed

text: Even skilled readers of remains can reach a wrong answer if they misjudge the decay environment.
when: Interpreting remains when the burial or submersion environment is uncertain.
why: Decay signatures depend on environment, so a wrong environment yields wrong conclusions.

text: Treating an object's found location as proof of custody without tracing its earlier positions.

1) Bring the scene object close to a matching item in the suspect's space. 2) Compare the two for an identical mark. 3) Record the match. 4) Combine it with other independent matches before drawing a conclusion.
when: Checking whether a scene object links to a suspect or location.
why: Careful comparison yields a record that gains weight only when combined with independent evidence.

text: 1) Start with the least destructive method, such as feeling, weighing or comparing. 2) Escalate to opening or breaking only if the first methods fail. 3) Keep the evidence intact throughout.
when: Evidence might be destroyed or changed by opening or breaking it.
why: Destructive tests can ruin evidence, so they should be a last resort.

text: 1) Give the stolen item a chain of owners, such as a sale, a club, or a market. 2) Make each owner a separate interview that narrows the search. 3) End the chain at the insider who handled the item last.
when: Designing a theft investigation
why: Each interview eliminates candidates and the chain converges on the true thief.

text: Keep the central object in motion, changing hands at intervals, so the goal stays open and each new holder redirects the pursuit.
Plant a small voice or phrase clue, and log every detail the player sees, so an idle-seeming detail returns as proof in the reveal.
when: Authoring clues in a mystery scene.
why: Rereading or a returning detail turns an overlooked item into proof once the truth is known, rewarding attention.

text: Reconstructing the physical scene can reveal a hidden mechanism without witnesses, yet physical traces can suggest a false cause that testimony must correct.
when: When a case rests on physical clues: reconstruct to show the mechanism, and check each inference against testimony when no eyewitness confirms it.
why: Scenes can show mechanisms directly, while witnesses can correct traces that suggest false causes.

text: Involuntary reactions escape control: a brief change in expression can expose known hidden information, and a flinch when a covered area is touched can reveal a concealed mark.
when: A suspect sees unexpected evidence, or a concealed bodily mark is suspected; provoke the reaction rather than asking directly.
why: Reactions escape control for a moment and are harder to control than spoken answers.

text: Household members notice distress signs, such as red eyes after lawyer visits or long closed-door talks, which signal conflict before any proof exists.
when: When a conflict is developing privately
why: Visible changes in habit reveal tension early

text: A careful hoaxer can restore disturbed objects, but traces such as wet prints and displaced items can remain.
when: When checking a staged event for evidence of tampering
why: Restoration hides some traces but rarely removes all of them

text: Circumstantial evidence links modest facts through time, place and records, without an eyewitness; none proves the act alone, but together they can implicate even the least likely person.
when: No direct proof or witness exists and the case must be built from documents and dates.
why: Convergence of connected circumstances can establish a conclusion that no single fact shows.

text: A witness who cannot read cannot check a written record put to them, so their answers rest on memory alone.
when: questioning a witness about documents
why: reading is needed to verify written content

text: The arrangement of teeth in a bite can be distinctive enough to help identify its maker, much as a thumbprint or signature does.
A stopped clock or other striking detail can draw remark while proving nothing about the event.
when: When a conspicuous object seems to offer a clue
why: Vivid details attract attention regardless of their evidential value.

text: Ordinary arrangements such as furniture set for an absent person or doors held open can serve as traces pointing to a second party.
A sealed container can be imaged with X-ray to reveal its contents without opening it.
when: Contents must be known without destroying the container.
why: Imaging shows internal contents while leaving the container intact.

text: A rough surface produces an irregular spot border regardless of drop height, so surface texture must be considered before reading height.
Routine chores such as dusting leave traces of who opened a container, even when the container was never locked.
why: Dust on ledges shows that drawers had to be opened to be cleaned.

text: Check every link in a circumstantial chain: one missing or unprovable link weakens the whole inference and can free a suspect.
when: Building a case from several modest linked clues, where no single fact is decisive.
why: Each inference depends on the one before, so chains are only as strong as their weakest link.

text: Answer a prosecution chain of inferences one link at a time rather than only rebutting the overall story.
when: When a case is built from a sequence of linked claims.
why: A weak link can break the chain even when the overall story sounds plausible.

text: Listeners often read an ironic remark literally and reason from that reading as if it were a serious argument, which can seal a damaging label.
when: A character's remark has two possible readings.
why: Literal interpretation is the default when the irony is not signaled.

text: Match a bite by its gaps and irregularities, such as a missing tooth in each jaw, rather than overall shape; a person with a full, regular set cannot have made it.
Separation by pulling and separation by a blade leave different marks; the absence of blade marks suggests the bones were pulled apart.
when: Determining how bones were separated from one another.
why: Cutting and pulling produce distinct traces on bone surfaces.

text: A closing explanation can resolve the main question and leave minor details open, which makes the world feel larger than the player's knowledge.
when: The main mystery is solved but the setting should feel deeper
why: Some open detail signals a world beyond what the player has learned

text: When a standing restriction lapses or an owner dies, ask who gains control and who is affected, to find the parties with a stake.
when: A restriction, charter or shared right changes hands.
why: A lapse shifts who can act, so it reveals who benefits.

text: Test a claimed account against where an object was found; if the claimed actor could not have reached that spot, the account conflicts with the evidence.
when: A reported self-inflicted or staged account is given.

text: Hesitation, such as hanging back before one person goes to a target, is a behavioural clue worth recording.
Physical trace reading is less useful when the scene has been cleared or the setup happened elsewhere.
A planted item made from a traceable source can betray its maker, since its fit with another fragment shows a shared origin.
Demonstrate the investigator's method in an unrelated scene before the crime is described, so the reader trusts the later reading.
Use a lure built from the villain's own medium, such as a note in the code they use, to force contact.
Let an ambiguous household trace, such as extra food or ash, carry the proof, provided it is backed by physical evidence.
Use an injury, such as a sprained ankle or a stocking-clad foot, as physical evidence that points at the wrong person, making the reader's suspicion feel earned.
when: a suspect's body shows a clue that resembles the culprit's
why: A bodily sign is persuasive, so the false lead convinces the reader before it is overturned.

text: Explain the mechanism of a trap or clue by demonstrating it to a character who witnesses it, so the explanation is shown rather than only told.
when: Resolving a clue whose logic the player must understand.
why: A demonstration makes the solution vivid and verifiable.

text: When a character removes or lures a nearby observer, the set of characters able to witness other actions changes, altering what the world notices.
when: A player or NPC sends away, distracts or lures a guard or witness.
why: Observation depends on who is present, so removing one observer opens unwatched space.

text: The route to a protected suspect can itself reveal evidence, and a disorienting route prevents the investigator from later reconstructing how they arrived.
when: A suspect is reached through a long, dim or shifting route.
why: Disorientation erases the investigator's memory of the path while the setting still tells something about the person.

text: Linking two locations through one shared object gives the investigator a route between them and a second place to search.
A group's verdict on a speaker, once settled, persists and gets reinforced by later discussion, outliving the remark that caused it.
when: A reputation has formed in a group.
why: People interpret new evidence to fit the existing verdict.

text: Limited light radius leaves the upper part of a room in darkness, which can make the space seem taller than it is.
when: An observer relies on lamplight in a dim room
why: Unlit regions are lost from view, so the perceived dimensions drift from the actual ones.

text: A mundane cause can explain early anomalies, then a later clue the cause cannot explain reveals a deeper source.
when: when structuring a mystery over time
why: The unexplained residue appears only after the mundane answer has been accepted.

text: Being the last person seen with a victim places that person at the centre of the timeline, making their account decisive.
when: when reconstructing the final movements of a victim
why: The last contact is the reference point for everything that follows.

text: Open safes, ransacked boxes and stripped fittings can contradict a suicide story and point to a slow, deliberate robbery.
Physical traces such as trampled ground, drag marks, and a repurposed cloth can show that one actor did the work, undermining a group theory.
Pair a mechanical clue with a human motive, so one device explains both the original death and a later death.
why: A device linked to a motive explains more than one event.

text: Labelling an act as 'mad' replaces the question of what can be proven and closes investigation early; keep the diagnosis and the evidence separate.
when: Explaining an odd event or behaviour with a diagnosis or label.
why: Labels stop investigation before the evidence is examined and hide the purpose of the act.

text: A single physical mark does not prove guilt, since it may have another cause and an observer can misread its color or age.
when: Drawing conclusions from one physical trace
why: Alternative causes and reading error are both possible.

text: Hindsight makes a chain of events look inevitable, though the path to a discovery was often fragile and accidental.
when: When explaining or evaluating how a discovery was reached.
why: After the fact, minor accidents are reinterpreted as deliberate steps.

text: Clues written as ordinary words or phrases can hide their meaning; a reader who takes the wording at face value misses the reference.
when: clue text that uses a local term or place name
why: readers assume ordinary meaning unless prompted otherwise

text: A lure frightens innocent people as well as guilty ones, so a reaction does not by itself prove guilt.
Overlooking the object that explains how a victim was incapacitated can stall an investigation.
Finding an object at a place shows that a visit happened there, but not when it happened.
when: An item is discovered at a location during a timeline reconstruction.
why: Presence at a place does not fix the time of the visit.

text: 1) Publish a notice in a public channel that names the target's known connection, such as a ship, place or guild. 2) Promise secrecy and a private meeting time. 3) Wait for the target to respond.
when: The target is known to be connected to a specific name or place.
why: A notice tied to a known connection draws out the intended person through their recognition of it.

text: 1) Revisit the scene and compare it with the written account. 2) Note what is missing, out of place or discarded. 3) Walk any claimed route to test whether it is possible.
when: a scene can still be examined

text: 1) Record the scene, including labels, bottles and loose papers, before anyone tidies it. 2) Only then allow clearing and handling.
when: a death scene is being investigated

text: 1) Hide the identity of each sample from the examiner. 2) Mix the suspect's sample among known control samples. 3) Record the examiner's identifications and compare them against the true sources.
when: When an identification must be defensible and chance could explain a correct match.
why: Hiding identities prevents the examiner's expectations from influencing the match.

text: 1) Oil the object to protect it. 2) Cast the clearest impression in quick-setting plaster. 3) Fit the object back onto the mold to see whether the projections fill a suspect's teeth gaps. 4) Make a second mold from the same object and compare the two.
when: When a bite or patterned mark is left on an object that can be preserved and cast.
why: Casting captures the impression, and fitting tests whether a suspect's teeth match.

text: 1) Obtain a map of the scene 2) check spatial relations between places 3) test whether a witness's route or distance is physically possible.
when: when a case depends on where things happened

text: 1) Watch the suspect's residence to learn their routine. 2) Create a moment when they believe they are alone. 3) Give them a reason to retrieve the hidden item. 4) Observe or swap the item before they can check it.
when: when a suspect is known to hide an item and return to check it
why: A suspect who believes they are unobserved is likely to reveal their interest.

text: 1) Compare the bones with possible sources. 2) Note that graveyard bones are usually weathered and incomplete. 3) Note that dealer and dissecting-room bones often carry drilled holes or red-lead marks. 4) Choose the source that fits the traces.
when: Identifying where a set of bones probably came from.
why: Each source leaves characteristic marks that distinguish it from others.

text: 1) Record the claimed event with an instrument the believers do not control. 2) Place the recorder while the believer is absent, and remove any sign of setup. 3) Review the trace for the pattern of events. 4) Locate the source by testing surfaces for matching sounds.
when: An effect is claimed to be non-physical and can be measured
why: An independent record separates the event from the witness's account

text: 1) Check whether the dispute assumes only two states and look for a third condition. 2) Focus on the disputed object and how it behaves under real conditions. 3) Test the candidate mechanism against the recorded facts, including environment and equipment state. 4) Use any independent technical check to confirm whether the mechanism was altered.
when: Two sworn accounts clash and the disputed physical object is central
why: A mechanism that makes both accounts true can resolve a contradiction without a liar

text: 1) List every way the suspect could have carried out the harm. 2) Record where the suspect was at that time. 3) Keep only methods the suspect could physically have used.
when: when assessing whether a suspect could have caused an incident
why: A plausible method is worthless without access and opportunity at the moment it mattered.

text: 1) Post a lure that draws the real culprit to a set place. 2) Lock the exit behind them. 3) Reveal a weapon to force a confession.
1) Gather traces the player can collect, such as possessions and skill marks. 2) Infer the culprit's profile from them. 3) Bait a trap that draws a matching person to a chosen room.
why: the lure becomes an earned step rather than a guess

text: Design a chain of independent physical traces, such as ash, wax, an unlit grate or a ledger entry, linking across rooms and NPCs to a culprit or mechanism.
when: Designing a mystery with physical evidence.
why: Linked traces reward observation, and several unrelated matches are harder to dismiss than a single clue.

text: Give each found or staged object a precise, checkable physical detail, such as a time, engraving, length or placement, so players can test a theory or confession.
when: Writing or introducing a physical clue meant to support a theory or a staged tool.
why: A checkable detail can be compared against other facts, turning acceptance into testing.

text: Use a depiction as an impression that raises suspicion, not as proof, when a portrait or document image is evidence about a person.
when: A portrait or document image is part of the evidence

text: Use a physical comparison between a trace and a known reference, so the player's deduction can be checked rather than guessed.
Do not release a lure where a false alarm would cost the investigation its credibility.
Ask what was not searched as well as what was; log every container and piece of furniture checked and leave gaps to be revisited.
when: A search for a person or object in a room is being assessed.
why: A search carried out to find a person, rather than to check every hiding place, can miss the person hidden there.

text: Design a household that maintains a pretence to reveal its real beliefs under pressure or through small slips.
when: Building characters who hide beliefs behind a shared fiction.
why: Pressure and slips expose beliefs that the fiction conceals.

text: An unauthorised search risks an investigator's career even when it succeeds, so searching requires proper authority.
when: Considering a search without formal permission.
why: Acting outside authority exposes the investigator to dismissal regardless of outcome.

text: A physical claim, such as bloodstains on clothing, can be checked directly on the object, turning a vague statement into something testable.
when: When a witness describes a physical trace on an object.
why: Objects retain evidence that can confirm or contradict a verbal claim.

text: A physical clue can point toward foul play while forensic findings show no violence or poison, so the clue must be checked against the body.
A thorough search can still miss the decisive trace when it skips the most unlikely location, such as a body or the victim's gear.
when: After a search is judged complete
why: Searchers stop at obvious surfaces and never examine objects they assumed were irrelevant

text: Test a theory or unexplained event physically before accepting it, such as firing a shot or checking whether a signal is visible from outside, since physical interaction leaves checkable traces.
when: A witnessed event may or may not be physical
why: Physical interaction produces traces that can be checked

text: Treat a physical mark a witness offers as support as a claim to test, since it may have a cause other than the one claimed.
Evidence that lacks a matching injury, such as blood with no wound on the person present, shows the injury belonged to someone else.
when: testing a theory against physical evidence
why: traces must correspond to the claimed event

text: Test a presumed culprit against physical traces, such as the method of attack and the physical effort the scene shows, since a contradiction can overturn the theory.
A guard's account that conflicts with a door's state or a footprint gives the player a lead they discover themselves.
when: designing an NPC statement that a world state can contradict
why: Players who find the contradiction feel they solved it.

text: Compare marks on a witness's body with their account; marks showing someone else applied restraint rule out a claim of self-restraint.
when: witness claims unassisted restraint

text: Physical findings that conflict with the activity an official account assumes, such as a meal too heavy for a light outing, weaken that account.
when: evaluating an accident or activity verdict
why: the evidence no longer matches the assumed activity

text: Physical details of a captive's state, such as dress, food or restraints, can serve as test clues the player checks against the NPC's story.
An object still in its original state, such as an item left in a coat pocket, shows it was never handled.
Do not accept a locked door at face value; ask whether it was really locked or only appeared so, since an incomplete account can make a door seem secure.
when: a closed room is reported as sealed

text: Specific physical facts such as injuries, damp clothing and requests for secrecy can overturn an eerie interpretation and reveal a living person.
when: When a supernatural reading is challenged by evidence
why: Concrete details are harder to explain away than atmosphere

text: A setting that looks non-flammable can still hold recent heat, so the appearance of a place is not proof that it is harmless.
1) State a hypothesis about how an event happened. 2) Check it against conditions at that time, such as tide, water depth or access by sea. 3) Discard it if conditions make it impossible.

1) State a physical hypothesis about the evidence. 2) Obtain an item from the suspect's own belongings that can test it. 3) Compare the item against the traces. 4) Accept the hypothesis only if the item fits exactly.
when: A trace such as a track or mark needs a test.
why: Testing with the suspect's own items gives a direct, checkable match.

text: 1) Open the container. 2) Confirm identity with a marker such as a plate. 3) Post a lookout against interruption. 4) Keep a witness so the act is on record.
when: identity depends on physical evidence

text: Check a suspect's claim, such as a loss, physically against the item instead of debating who is lying or accusing; the check yields evidence without alerting them.
when: when a claim can be checked against a physical fact
why: the check gives evidence without alerting or accusing

text: Confront a suspect with a physical item linked to the scene and note their reaction; purely theoretical evidence is easily dismissed as invented.
why: it can connect them to the place

text: Check an individual mark against a physical measure, such as fitting a damage shape to a known hand or dimension.
Keep claims of physical acts seen by present witnesses separate from visions, dreams or apparitions reported by one person.
when: Evaluating an accusation that rests on supernatural events.
why: A vision cannot be checked against the physical world, while an act observed by several people can.

text: A permanent feature that should appear in a trace but is absent is a clear mismatch.
when: when a trace is compared with a reference record
why: permanent features do not disappear

text: Confirm a permanent injury through independent records, such as medical files and the treating surgeon's account, before relying on it.
when: when a trace depends on a known physical feature
why: independent records check the reference

text: Use a height or reach requirement, such as a ceiling-level lever, as a physical constraint that filters suspects.
when: When an action requires a particular physical capability
why: Physical constraints remove candidates in a clear way

text: Make observation the gate to clues, since a clue the player never notices cannot be used in deduction.
when: Designing clue discovery in an investigation game.
why: Deduction depends on the player first perceiving the evidence.

text: Give objects with physical constraints such as catches, hooks or weights a required orientation, so a wrong return reveals an unfamiliar visitor.
Mark clues perceived by only one character, such as something seen under a status effect, so players must find a second source before acting.
when: Designing clues in a game

text: Re-search or re-test a physical token before a verdict; a token that vanishes on a second search undermines the case.
when: a verdict rests on a found object
why: The first finding may be an error or a plant.

text: A distinguishing mark, such as a secret sign on an envelope, lets a recipient identify which correspondent wrote a given letter.
when: when several secret senders use the same channel
why: The mark identifies the author without opening the letter.

text: A trail of blood or drag marks along a path shows that a body was moved from one place to another.
why: Dragging leaves continuous marks that reveal the route and direction.

text: A worn or odd object stands out and can become a trace that others remember, so it can later link a person to a place or time.
Distinctive marks such as a crest, initials or brand tie an item to one person; record small finds, and count a physical match only if its feature is rare.
Distinctive prints, such as very high narrow heel impressions, tiptoe marks or squared-toed boot prints, separate one walker's track from others at a scene.
A specific distinctive mark, such as a scar, is a stronger identifier than general appearance and can be checked directly.
when: appearance is ambiguous and a mark can be checked
why: a distinctive mark is rarer than shared features

text: A repeated individual defect, such as a bent character or a chipped type face, is unlikely on other machines and can distinguish one device from many similar ones.
when: a document's origin is disputed and a machine is suspected
why: individual wear is rarer than shared model features

text: A distinctive damage mark, such as a burnt corner, lets an investigator recognize the same object across different scenes when no paperwork exists.
An unusually distinctive landmark marking a hiding place can also be remembered and found by an adversary.
when: Choosing a marker for a concealed cache.
why: Memorable features are easy for anyone to recall.

text: 1) Inspect the victim's injuries directly and deliberately. 2) Note each mark's location and appearance. 3) Record them in a form that can be used as evidence later.
when: when injuries may be needed in a formal complaint or testimony
why: Records made at the time carry more weight than later recollection.

text: Give suspects and clue objects distinctive visible marks; unlabelled items, such as clothing without maker's marks, block identification and stall the investigation.
when: when writing suspect descriptions for a mystery or designing objects meant to identify their owner
why: Distinctive details narrow identity and let players link witness accounts or items to one individual; unmarked items cannot be traced.

text: Objects, marks and the state of a room record past actions and can testify as clearly as people.
why: Traces persist after the event and reveal what was done

text: Compare a message's physical details, such as an earlier firm envelope and a later shaky letter, to infer the writer's state of mind.
Compare physical records side by side without the suspect present, rather than accepting their word or letting them adjust their account.
when: Checking a claimed presence against a token or log.
why: Hiding the comparison keeps the suspect from adapting their story to it.

text: An unusually rigid or deep sleep state is a strange observation to record, not proof of innocence.
when: when a suspect is found in an unusual sleep state
why: An anomalous state invites suspicion but does not establish alibi.

text: Physical states such as wet ink or fresh adhesive reveal how recently a message was made or placed.
Physical details, such as an object's location or a person's dress and appearance, can fix when an action or disturbance began and test the accounts given of it.
when: when timing an event is uncertain

text: A visible physical change in a character can appear before its explanation, serving as foreshadowing of what is to come.
Real illness is hard to fake, so when a suspect's symptoms appear at a time that conflicts with a faked story, treat the timing as a test of that story.
when: A suspect is too ill or silent to speak and the cover story depends on the timing.
why: Genuine physical symptoms follow biology, not the timing a guilty person would choose.

text: Ask why an item appeared in its exact place and at that time; the placement often reveals whom the item was meant to implicate.
Physical changes that accumulate over time, such as growth of stubble or wilting, indicate how long ago an event happened.
when: when estimating elapsed time without a timestamp
why: Such changes progress at roughly steady rates, so their extent measures duration.

text: A confession gains weight when a physical consequence confirms it, such as a body returning or an object appearing.
when: a character confesses to a hidden act

text: Keep the decisive proof physical and inspectable, such as a ballistic trace, so the accusation rests on an object the player can examine.
A chemical interaction that the player can test, such as precipitation, can serve as the final proof, turning an earlier trivial container into the key clue.
when: Building a poisoning or mechanism-based reveal.
why: A testable reaction makes the proof checkable, and the container was seen earlier as trivia.

text: 1) Run a private physical test on the suspect, such as a touch, measurement, or staged trip that exposes a lie. 2) Observe the reaction. 3) Reveal the answer to the group only after the test confirms it.
when: Confirming a suspect before a public reveal, without tipping off the suspect.
why: A physical test gives proof that does not depend on confession, and a covert test confirms the theory while keeping the suspect unaware.

text: 1) Ask precise questions about physical evidence first. 2) Ask for general impressions only after the facts are laid out.
when: Interviewing a witness about a death or incident.
why: Facts anchor the witness's later feelings and keep interpretation from running ahead of evidence.

text: Place a physical contradiction shortly before the trap springs, giving players a last chance to notice what the story hides.
Pay off a hidden test with a physical effect that repeats an earlier event, so the reveal is proven by something the player has already seen.
when: Resolving a trap that was set up by an earlier test.
why: A repeated physical cue makes the reveal concrete and memorable.

text: Use a physical test to settle a hidden state, such as a working device on an apparently dead body, so the audience can verify the truth.
when: A character's condition is uncertain and cannot be seen directly.
why: A working object gives the audience concrete evidence rather than a claim.

text: Demanding a high proof standard prevents wrongful accusation but can leave an investigator stuck when the needed evidence is hard to find.
when: Setting how much evidence is needed before naming a culprit.
why: A strict threshold protects against error at the cost of progress.

text: People fill missing information with guesses, so an imagined version can be worse than fact; witnesses then repeat those assumptions as observed fact.
why: People reconstruct missing information instead of leaving it blank; memory and expectation complete what was not clearly seen.

text: Give each trace at least two reasonable readings, mundane and suspicious, so players must check against other testimony or a second item before accepting either.
An offender who cleans a scene tends to remove traces that identify him personally, such as his hair colour, leaving others that point toward a chosen conclusion.
when: A scene has been deliberately cleaned, or an offender knows which traces could link him to it.
why: Selective cleanup controls which evidence the investigator sees, and attention focuses on identifiers the offender knows he leaves.

text: With no witness, reconstruct events from soil impressions, disturbed vegetation, wax drips, oil, displaced duplicate objects and markers or messages; these reveal route and habits.
when: A scene is the only testimony left, or no witness saw the culprit.
why: Traces persist after the people who made them are gone, so they become the main evidence.

text: A distinctive garment seen on a corpse can briefly make a living person seem like the dead one.
when: a glimpse of a person wearing a familiar garment
why: A memorable item triggers an association.

text: Signs of forced entry, such as fresh scratches and an abandoned second attempt, indicate the intruder's skill level and what they will try next.
when: Reading physical traces left at a locked location.
why: Traces record the actions taken and hint at the likely next step.

text: A listener tends to read a fragment containing their own name as being about themselves, which can bias their reading.
when: fragments of speech include the listener's name
why: personal relevance draws attention and interpretation

text: Once social explanations are exhausted, an unexplained physical object in a suspect's possession remains as the main anchor of suspicion.
when: Several incriminating items have innocent explanations but one physical item does not
why: Physical objects resist plausible social explanations, so they keep suspicion alive

text: Players and investigators overlook the edges of a building, such as a sill, where a small trace can still show an entry point.
when: Searching a scene for entry evidence
why: Attention focuses on the main path, so edge traces are easy to miss without deliberate inspection

text: Observers who notice ordinary details, such as mismatched clothing or uneven grooming, can infer recent hurry, action or lighting conditions that others overlook.
when: A character's appearance could indicate recent events
why: Attention to ordinary details, rather than special tools, reveals what others take for granted

text: Audiences use a repeated signature to link separate incidents to one author, but the motif stays ambiguous until the link is actually established.
when: a distinctive mark appears in several separate incidents
why: the shared mark invites a connection without proving it

text: A physical trace can be read in several ways, and a trace seen through a favoured theory is easily taken as proof of it.
why: expectation shapes how evidence is read

text: A prop hidden in plain sight is more likely to be noticed by an experienced observer than by a less experienced one.
when: When a staged effect uses ordinary objects as tools.
why: Experience helps observers recognise how ordinary objects are used to deceive.

text: People who believe they emptied their pockets trust their belongings without checking, so a swapped item often goes unnoticed at once.
when: When collecting belongings after a token-based check-in.
why: A belief that was never tested feels like knowledge.

text: A walker who keeps behind a line of trees rather than in the open is likely trying to avoid being seen.
when: When tracks run out of sight behind cover.
why: Staying hidden is a deliberate attempt to avoid observation.

text: A person who trusts a familiar form and is hurried through a stack of papers tends to sign without reading the rest.
when: when a routine-looking stack is presented in haste
why: Familiarity and speed lower the urge to check each page.

text: People notice an altered object by comparing it with its earlier state, but rarely notice an object that is simply gone.
when: an object has been removed rather than changed
why: An absence offers no earlier state to compare against, so it prompts less suspicion and less memory.

text: Readers who first find a plain list of facts dry come to rely on it, because dated facts give a clear, checkable picture over time.
when: A long series of dated updates is read over months
why: A timeline of facts can be followed and verified step by step.

text: An investigator can infer a writer's state, effort, and relationship to the recipient from handwriting, length, word choice and omissions in a note.
when: when a document is one of few traces of its writer
why: Writing style reflects mood, skill and effort

text: Witnesses test a suspicious substance by rubbing it between their fingers, a direct physical check they use to decide whether it is real.
when: an unfamiliar substance must be judged as real
why: touch offers a check that testimony cannot

text: A guilty party can forget small incriminating details, yet each one remains a usable link for the investigator who gathers them.
when: A suspect has acted and time has passed.
why: Minor details are easily overlooked by the person who produced them.

text: A person who controls a scene may gather and remove traces such as dropped items, torn papers and disturbed objects before others examine them, so the scene no longer shows the original evidence.
when: A character with control over a room learns that an intrusion has happened
why: Clearing traces lets the controller shape what others can later find

text: Physical marks such as blood flows and injury signs can record a body's position and the order of events, letting an observer turn them into a timeline.
Reconstructing an event from physical traces means reading the marks left in an environment, then testing a theory by repeating the action.
A physical trace is an object a person drops that later links that person to an event or to their plans.
Soft ground such as sand or mud records footprints showing who passed, which direction, and weight, stride and foot size.
when: Evidence includes footprints in soft material.
why: Soft surfaces hold the shape of pressure.

text: Walking leaves even footprints, while running leaves deep toe marks with barely visible heels; print spacing and pattern reveal how someone moved.
when: Soft ground holds prints.
why: Gait changes the pressure pattern of each step.

text: Blotting paper absorbs wet ink and keeps a reversed impression of recent writing, readable by holding the sheet to light; a repeatedly tried word reveals the writer's focus.
why: Pressure from writing transfers to the blotting paper placed beneath.

text: Struck-out or overwritten text often stays partly legible, and a top layer may look blank while lower layers still hold a legible message.
A rare feature such as a scar crossing the ridge pattern sharply reduces coincidence odds and can make identification conclusive.
when: A print contains a rare feature such as a scar that breaks the ridge pattern.
why: Each independent rare feature reduces the chance another person shares the whole pattern.

text: Physical traces such as scuffs, displaced objects, dirt and small fragments can show how someone entered and left, and in what order, when read carefully.
when: when witnesses are unreliable or absent

text: Different heat-revealed inks show writing in different colors, so the color can help identify which ink was used.
Impressions of garments, such as the mark of a cloak in soft ground, add identifying evidence beyond footprints.
Objects and traces record where a person went, what they did, and what they intended. A single well-chosen object can establish a sequence of actions and a motive.
Physical traces such as tyre marks can identify a vehicle, its direction of travel, its speed and an injury to its rider.
The same hiding place can read as concealment or as carelessness, and the surrounding context determines which.
Footprints showing movement in but not out of a location suggest the relevant act happened inside that location.
when: Reconstructing where an act took place from tracks.
why: Tracks leaving no exit trail narrow the scene to the enclosed area.

text: A method run through a shared system can leave traces on its fittings, such as tarnish or wear where contact occurred.
A weapon held in a way that gives up its reach suggests close-range use, since length is an advantage in a lunge.
when: when reading a handling trace on a weapon

text: Small traces such as a half-written word, soil on a floor, footprints, and a key with a mismatched ring can be chained into conclusions about who acted and when.
Ground marks can be read in two directions; a handprint may mean someone pushed up from the ground or was pulled along it.
why: The same mark can result from opposite movements.

text: A set of footprints that never overlap cannot show whether the maker entered or left; a single trace can point either way.
when: when reading tracks along a single path
why: without overlap or a second reference, direction is undetermined

text: Blotting after a later addition shows the writer checked the page again before sealing it.
why: blotting follows a finished pass and is done before sealing

text: Ordinary fingerprints identify little without a comparison sample.
when: a print is found on a dramatic object
