why: a print means nothing until it is matched to a known source

text: Ambiguous physical evidence often admits several explanations, and each must be weighed against what the witnesses say.
Prints found on different objects can be compared, and a match ties both objects to one person.
when: Linking physical objects to a suspect
why: Matching traces create a physical connection between separate items

text: Prints can overlap and be superimposed, but a sufficiently distinct set may still be identified.
when: Several people handled the same object.
why: Superimposition blurs impressions without erasing them entirely.

text: Thinning oil paint with turpentine or another flatting agent makes it dry within about an hour, but the finish is dull rather than glossy.
With a stiff arm and raised shoulder, the height of an aimed weapon tracks the shooter's height closely, so weapon height gives a usable estimate.
A typed note's typeface, faded ribbon and fold pattern can link it to a particular machine and a route of delivery.
why: typewriter and paper traces are physical signatures

text: Some executions are recorded as probably resting on confession, though the basis was assumed rather than documented.
Small objects can be identified at a distance through glass by their shape and color.
An empty hiding place proves only that the object has moved, not that it has left the area.
when: A concealment has been searched and found empty
why: The object may have been relocated within the same space

text: A draught that carries a smell upstairs shows an opening existed while the event occurred.
Dust or grime on glass can block what a view shows, forcing the scene to be read from another light source.
A physical trace such as a fingerprint can be copied so closely that inspection of the copy reveals no difference from the original.
A forger needs access to a genuine sample to copy it, so access to the source is a precondition for forgery.
Fine airborne dust that settles into cloth can record where an object has hung over a long period.
Rough or rusty surfaces do not take fingerprints, so a blank surface of that kind carries no information about handling.
Control of a key, including one worn on the person, limits access to its holder and anyone they gave it to. Tracing key movements is needed to establish who could enter.
when: When a locked room's key is central to who could enter
why: Access to a key defines the set of people who could have opened the door.

text: The time a message is sent and the time it is delivered can differ by a large margin, and that gap can decide who could have acted.
when: When a message's timing matters to an alibi.
why: Delivery delay creates an unobserved window.

text: Ordinary household habits, such as a window left open or a door left unbolted, can provide routes into a room that appear locked.
Former homesteads often survive as cellar hollows, stone heaps or scattered bricks, which can corroborate written records.
People with plain voices and ordinary builds offer few distinguishing features, so many suspects remain unidentified.
A physical trace such as a fingerprint or bloodstain is one fact among others. Its evidential value depends on how it came to be where it was found.

Trifles that can form a circumstantial chain include a scrap of paper, a torn garment shred, a coat button, an incautious word, a letter fragment, a door's sound, a shadow on a blind, and a precisely timed moment.
when: Assembling a case from small clues.
why: Each item is minor alone but can link into a chain.

text: Physical traces require a surface that records marks; hard or dry surfaces that keep no impressions offer little evidence.
Fused wiring and burned insulation point to a high-energy event rather than impact damage alone.
Faint trickles of water in sand can show a body was carried in or moved by a current.
when: Examining wet ground near a body
why: Water flow leaves marks that record movement

text: Sympathetic ink stays invisible until heated, so applying heat to a surface can expose hidden writing in a single action.
when: A document with hidden text.
why: Heat changes the ink's visibility, so a simple action exposes text that looked blank.

text: A visible mark such as blood on a suspect's hands has many innocent sources; check its origin, timing and who else was present before treating it as proof.
when: A mark or injury is offered as evidence of an event.
why: The same mark can result from several causes, and the account of its origin may be incomplete.

text: Do not let a single trace settle a question or count as conclusive; confirm it with a second, independent source such as other marks and times.
Infer a watcher's purpose from deliberate placement or preparation, such as a weapon within reach, and use it to predict what happens next.
when: A person's location seems deliberate, or a trace suggests someone was waiting for an occupant.
why: Placement usually reflects purpose, and preparations reveal planned action.

text: Read disorder, including sheets on the floor, on a table and in their original spot, as a record of what an intruder did, in what order, and where they stood.
when: A scene shows several displaced objects.

text: Check for recent presence, such as warm fire, living animals, burning candles, fresh food, scent, residue or supply movements, even where nothing visible shows it.
when: When a location's occupancy is in question.
why: Recent use leaves warmth, sound, living things and objects that a quick look may miss.

text: Place traces such as floor marks, tracks, overheard sounds and dropped items in sequence to reveal who moved when, who walked where and who could not have.
when: Reconstructing movements at a scene.
why: The order of traces reveals the movement sequence.

text: Writing marks such as scratches, ink rush, ink shade differences, blotting and pauses reveal a writer's pace and hesitation and how a document was produced and handled.
when: Analysing a handwritten fragment, or a document's authenticity or origin is in doubt.
why: Pen behaviour and handling leave physical traces that a careful reader can interpret.

text: Footprints that differ in size or sole shape from the occupants' shoes identify a separate visitor, and their order shows who came in when.
Objects arranged in a room signal an occupant's taste and routine, and readers can later interpret them as evidence.
when: when the occupant matters to the plot

text: Furnishing quality reveals an occupant's standing, so a single well-furnished room among plain ones can point to a particular occupant.
when: When rooms in one place differ sharply in furnishing
why: Occupants of means concentrate their comfort in particular spaces

text: Mud on clothing, marks on a body, stains, and a tool at the scene can link a suspect to an act when read together.
why: combined traces are harder to explain away than single ones

text: Infer causes from physical traces: a stopped mechanism shows someone touched it, dust shows where a visitor's feet rested, and used glasses show how many guests were present.
when: reading a scene

text: A hurried exit by a back route signals a wish to keep one's movements hidden.
when: a character leaves unobserved
why: avoiding witnesses implies concealment

text: A displaced piece of furniture bearing a footprint shows that someone stood at that spot.
when: Objects in a scene show displacement or marks.

text: Damp, mould-stained, muddy or torn belongings suggest recent outdoor activity, so an object's condition is read as a trace of what happened recently.
Matching wear across paired items, such as stains, worn fingertips and scratches, points to a shared rough activity.
when: when items come in pairs or sets
why: agreement between items adds weight that a single item lacks

text: Tiny spots of blood around the neck suggest the victim was gripped by the throat.
A heavy, dragging step visible in prints can suggest the walker's age range, such as middle age.
when: prints are readable

text: A small physical disturbance, such as a moved object, can carry evidence even when its meaning is unclear.
Make a fight scene or bloodstain look incriminating to the player, and reveal the innocent cause through a later NPC.
Metal and other durable materials survive heat and ash, so a hidden object may remain recoverable even when a suspect believes it is destroyed.
when: when an object was burned or buried in a hurry
why: Non-combustible materials withstand the disposal method.

text: A blank stub beside a removed leaf suggests the payer wanted the sum kept off the record.
when: a record shows a gap such as a torn leaf, missing entry or missing receipt

text: Examine clothing item by item, since an ordinary garment can hide a feature, such as a homemade pocket, that shows what it carried.
when: a missing item is plausible

text: Describe key people with concrete physical marks, such as a scar or pierced ears, so a player can match a witness's description to a suspect.
when: designing suspects and informants

text: Destroying one item of evidence does not erase the rest; remaining clothing and lodging traces still point toward the truth.
Grass growing under an object shows how long it has lain there, so the amount of growth dates when it was placed.
when: An object has been left in one place outdoors.
why: Growth needs time, so it records elapsed days.

text: When an exterior feature and an interior feature are both shuttered or barricaded, check whether they line up to the same hidden space.
when: a sealed area is visible from outside
why: matching traces locate the hidden space

text: Wear on a shared item, such as cut versus bitten ends or differing brands, can show which person used it and how.
Ash deposits and the chair a person used can reconstruct where each person sat or stood in a room.
Blurred or indistinct physical marks are useless as proof and should not be treated as confirmation of a claim.
Treat small bodily or object wear, such as sole roughness, calluses or fingertip shape, as evidence of recurring activity and of a person's trade or routine.
when: When a character's job, habits or home are not stated directly.
why: Repeated actions leave consistent physical marks on people and their belongings.

text: A solid pipe with no side openings means animals that entered it partway probably traveled all the way to its exit.
A small object caught on fabric can prove that a hand reached into a place, linking the person to that spot.
when: a suspect may have touched a container or hiding place

text: An attempt to destroy a document signals that its holder knew its content was dangerous, which is itself evidence worth recording.
Judge a deceased person's belongings through their ties to the home's occupants rather than by contents alone.
Two traces running at right angles show order: the earlier one records the head's position when it formed, and the later one records a change in posture.
Read each object at a scene for what it implies, then check what that implication requires, such as who had access to the material or item.
Give lore carvings or signs two or more plausible meanings, and let an independent source decide between them.
when: a symbol is meant to support a legend
why: A single reading makes the sign either trivially true or unsupported.

text: Read a scene for what was disturbed in haste; a carefully planned stealth act leaves few traces to read.
Unmarked clothing, a weapon without fingerprints, and a wound without blood together suggest the killer wore gloves and the victim was already dead.
Sealed or concealed container condition shows whether it was opened: loosened fastenings mark recent handling, an untouched seal shows the item was not yet accessed, missing contents reveal removal.
when: A player inspects a sealed or concealed object for tampering or whether its hidden contents were accessed.
why: Physical wear and absences are readable clues of recent handling.

text: Positioning a figure so passers-by see its back rather than its face limits the chance of recognition.
when: when someone must avoid recognition in a corridor or crowd
why: faces are the strongest recognition cue

text: Prints laid over or under one another so that several people seem present at once are a sign of a staged trail.
Fresh paint odour and still-soft paint on a palette suggest work done within days.
when: When dating activity in a room.

text: Dust marks areas no one has touched, so the undisturbed zones of a room often show what a person avoided or was told to leave alone.
An object released too easily from a dead grip suggests the hand was never clenched at the moment of death.
when: Examining a corpse's grip on an object
why: A clenched hand resists removal

text: A disturbance left in a space, such as displaced papers or disturbed dust, can reveal an activity that no one saw.
Blurred or smudged marks carry little evidential weight and should not be used as a basis for a reconstruction.
Individual wear, such as misaligned parts or scratches, can identify one object among many identical copies of a model.
Two apparently separate people who never appear together may be one person if their traits complement each other, such as contrasting habits, beliefs or skills.
when: people seem different but never appear together
why: complementary features fit one person keeping two lives apart

text: Small physical details such as wear, scent, brand and layout reveal habits and interrupted activity; read them as a set, not one at a time.
Where a person keeps belongings shows where they actually lived or prepared, and can contradict a claim of being elsewhere.
when: when a suspect claims to have been elsewhere

text: Ordinary possessions such as passports, letterhead and clippings reveal a person's contacts and intentions; read them as evidence.
when: when inventorying a person's effects
why: Everyday items record connections and purposes.

text: Read torn clothing, bruises, and wounds as a record of a struggle, and reconstruct the sequence of grabbing, pulling, and striking from them.
when: The body and clothing are intact enough to test an account.
why: Physical damage records how a person was held and how the struggle moved.

text: A traveller's physical condition, such as wet or dry clothing, can be used to test whether a claimed journey actually happened.
when: when a claimed journey is in dispute and weather conditions are known
why: Weather leaves measurable traces on people who travel through it.

text: Check candidate tools for transferred material, such as paint flakes, as an independent test of whether they touched the surface.
when: a surface has a coating that can transfer

text: Read a physical trace as evidence of a specific process by linking it to what that process produces, such as a smell suggesting a chemical copying method.
when: Interpreting an unexpected stain, odor or residue found on an object.
why: A sensory or chemical clue becomes meaningful only when matched to the process that would plausibly generate it.

text: Tie some clues to transient states, such as footprints in wet ground or an item that can be moved, to reward prompt investigation.
when: designing clues at a crime scene
why: Transient clues disappear unless found early

text: Let tools such as a magnifier or an ammunition count confirm each trace, so reconstruction rewards careful observation.
Preparation can be stronger evidence of intent than the act itself, so make it visible, such as a bag packed for flight, for players to read against an alibi.
Make an object's source ambiguous but traceable through its construction, so careful inspection is rewarded.
Shell or encrustation fragments in a wound can identify the object that caused it, since certain growths show the object was periodically submerged.
when: when fragments are found in a wound
why: growths on an object reveal its conditions

text: Separate physical traces are weak alone; each checked for origin and meaning, together they can close a case.
when: A case depends on several separate traces.
why: Each trace gains weight when it links to the others.

text: Wear on a fixture or a displaced part signals that the mechanism was used recently.
when: when a player must infer a mechanism's recent activity from the environment
why: use leaves physical wear or displacement

text: If a trace is further advanced in drying or decay than the stated timeline allows, it was probably made or left earlier than the event.
why: the trace needed longer than the stated interval to reach that state

text: Search for the residue a claimed action should leave; finding none after a real comparison supports the inference, but only if the comparison was actually made.
Look for a cluster of small mismatches, such as conflicting statements and behaviour, rather than relying on one oddity.
when: several plausible accounts describe the same person
why: Clusters of contradictions are harder to explain innocently.

text: Count the distinct sources of prints, footmarks and hair colours found together; more than one source indicates more than one person.
Trace a dropped object by its maker's mark, scent or label to link it to a particular person.
A tyre track that differs from a car's ordinary tyres, or an oil drip, shows which vehicle was present and that it stood still for a time.
Give surfaces physical properties; a surface that cannot hold a print makes a missing clue a readable signal rather than a bug.
when: designing clue-bearing surfaces
why: Material reasons make absences believable and interpretable.

text: An unfinished action can imply that the tool needed to finish it has been removed or lost.
when: a task is visibly incomplete at a scene

text: Treat a medical estimate of time as a range rather than an exact time, and combine it with other witnesses' sightings to set the window.
when: When using a medical opinion to fix when an act occurred
why: Estimates carry uncertainty, and cross-referencing with independent sightings tightens the window.

text: Objects left at a scene with social, occupational or personal markers let observers infer the owner's class or status, but the inference should stay provisional.
when: Scene contains objects carrying social or occupational markers
why: Such markers suggest identity, yet they are weak evidence and can be revised

text: Keep seemingly trivial details about objects and routines, such as key locations or depleted supplies, and defer judging their importance until more evidence arrives.
when: When investigating a scene where routine knowledge may reveal who had access.
why: A detail that looks unimportant can later prove decisive once combined with other facts.

text: When evaluating a cleaned scene, ask which traces remain and why, rather than only whether any traces remain.
when: When assessing staged or cleaned evidence.
why: The pattern of surviving traces reveals intent that total absence would hide.

text: Verify a measured discrepancy with more than one measurement, since relying on one enlargement or reading is weak.
when: Presenting a measured difference as evidence
why: Independent verification guards against error and makes the finding credible to others.

text: Pin the date of a sale by linking the item to a second item that has a dated record.
when: A sale's date is vague but a related item was sold with it.
why: The second item's record can fix the date of the first.

text: Treat a physical trace as a narrowing clue, not as proof; use it to prepare a specific question for a witness.
when: A trace has been found but not yet confirmed by another source
why: A trace can be misread, so it should be checked before it is relied on

text: The residue of many burned candles points to repeated visits; estimate how long it took to build that residue to judge how often the room was used.
when: interpreting candle or wax residue
why: Residue accumulates with each burn, so its volume reflects repeated presence over time.

text: Matching calibre across victims links shootings to one weapon, though it does not alone prove a single shooter.
when: comparing bullets from several victims
why: Shared calibre narrows the weapon but many guns share a calibre.

text: Repeated visits leaving similar prints at the same hour under the same weather suggest a habit or a deliberate pattern.
when: comparing prints made on several occasions
why: Consistent timing and conditions point to a routine rather than chance.

text: Compare each player's stated theory with the clues they have collected, since a stated preference can reveal which clues they already hold.
when: a multiplayer game records player votes or theories
why: stated stances can betray held information

text: Leaving one known unlocked gap in a secured space gives intruders a predictable entry point.
when: designing an enclosure with deliberate weakness

text: Vary the kind of remains along a path, such as large animal bones versus small human ones, so players can infer who passed and what they carried.
Give scene elements such as a broken rail an age or condition the player can inspect, so a false claim about them can be tested.
Place a blotter or drawer contents on a writing desk that record a prior letter, so the player recovers the message by reading the impression.
why: Environmental traces reward close inspection of ordinary furniture.

text: A trace with two possible causes or contrary readings proves little; keep both open and let a second trace or separating evidence settle which applies before committing.
when: a clue has two plausible explanations

text: Read the marks and objects left behind, then test one explanation against them before moving to another.
when: When solving a puzzle from physical traces
why: Traces constrain which explanations are possible.

text: An incidental physical mark such as a scar on the hands survives changes of name, clothing and disguise, so it can link a disguised person to an earlier sighting.
when: A disguise hides the face or name but not the body.
why: Clothing, hair and names are easy to change, while bodily features are hard to alter.

text: Build scenes with stacked traces, like scuffs, shifted crates and an item fallen near a ramp top, so players can piece together events.
A person's dominant hand determines which side they act from, so an item dropped during an action falls on that side.
when: reconstructing how something was dropped or handed over
why: the actor's position follows their dominant hand

text: Know a person's habits, such as avoiding a particular floor covering, before reading the traces they leave, since the habit changes what a trace means.
when: a witness's habits differ from the norm

text: Before dropping a theory whose test failed, check whether the failure came from the theory or from the investigation.
when: when a theory fails its first test
why: Investigative error can wrongly eliminate a correct explanation.

text: A careful search of a suspect's room should include clothing, residue, and the suspect's movements, since removing visible marks does not remove all traces.
when: When investigating a suspect whose room appears clean.
why: A clean room does not rule out traces removed from the person or movements through the scene.

text: Smoothing disturbed ground removes evidence, so a suspiciously tidied scene can itself be a clue.
When a body or object seems removed, first list the traces its removal should leave, such as blood, drag marks or a dropped item, and check whether they exist.
when: An apparent removal must be explained
why: Absent expected traces can show that no forced removal occurred

text: A physical item moved between places, such as a bag or key, can confirm a person's movements at a given time.
The state of a lock or latch records who last handled a door, such as whether it was left unlocked by a departing person.
when: When reconstructing who passed through a door
why: Lock state is a trace of the last action on it.

text: Separate traceable causes from untraceable impressions; only traceable causes count as established, while impressions remain open.
A bone lying in a position impossible for an attached limb shows it had come off the body before deposition.
when: Reading where bones lay in water or soil to infer how they were separated.
why: Attached limbs cannot take positions that detached bones can.

text: An unusual feature such as an open door has meaning that depends on who used it and why.
when: Interpreting an ambiguous scene feature
why: The same feature means different things for different users.

text: Make the final suspect's clue differ from the first in a small, checkable way, so the test rewards close attention.
why: A subtle difference rewards players who compare clues carefully rather than accepting the first match.

text: A forensic reading of the scene can overturn an official cover story, so build early clues the player can test before the official theory is discredited.
when: Designing a mystery where the official conclusion is wrong.
why: Testable early clues let the player challenge the accepted account.

text: Show a tool or test before its purpose is explained, so the later payoff confirms what the player was already prepared to expect.
When a source repeats an earlier account, trace it back to its origin, since a derivative report inherits the flaws of the source it copies.
Each independent trace narrows possible sources; several traces pointing to one suspect are harder to dispute than any single match, and no single match decides a case.
when: when several physical traces link a suspect to a scene or physical items are the main hard evidence
why: each trace removes candidates, so agreement across traces compounds

text: A trace's state changes at a predictable rate, so its condition indicates elapsed time; humidity and temperature change that rate, so the environment must be known first.
when: the trace's drying, aging or decay rate is known
why: condition changes steadily, so it encodes elapsed time; the same stain dries at different speeds in different conditions

text: Vehicles in a game can accumulate dust, mud or wear that reflects their recent routes, so a player can deduce where they have been.
Objects, marks and bodies record who was present, how they moved and what they used; a reader interprets each trace by comparing it with a known standard and noting its implication.
Skin missing from the palm shows a rope was gripped and pulled quickly, so the trace records how the person moved.
when: when a hand injury appears near a rope or climb
why: friction removes skin when a line slides through the hand

text: A clean gap in settled dust on a shelf shows that an object was recently removed from that spot.
Soot rubbed away in patches and faint discolouration on wood or stone can reveal where a body rested and where blood was present.
why: Surfaces record contact through disturbance and staining

text: Gravity sets the direction liquid runs, so flow running down the face shows the face was upright, while flow toward the back of the head means it lay horizontal.
when: interpreting a fluid trace on a body
why: gravity is a fixed constraint on how liquid moves

text: A slower-acting form of an agent, such as a tablet rather than a solution, can explain part of a timing gap, and the victim may move about before collapsing.
when: when a delay between dose and collapse looks too long
why: Delivery form changes the time to effect

text: Moisture condenses unevenly over oily fingerprint ridges, so breath briefly shows a ridge pattern on smooth non-porous surfaces.
when: breathing on a smooth surface
why: Oil and sweat in the ridges change how moisture condenses compared with bare surface.

text: An object found with one victim can connect separate events, such as a killing and a disappearance, into a single case with a common cause.
when: Two investigation strands seem separate and one item appears in both.
why: The item carries traces of each event, so it can show they share a source.

text: Random events such as weather or timing can expose a planned action, turning an unpredictable factor into a clue.
when: when a procedural world has random conditions
why: Uncontrolled variables can reveal what a planned action was meant to hide.

text: Small physical changes such as a stain, odor, or shifted position reveal that an object was handled, even when it has been restored to its prior arrangement.
when: An object or document has been handled and its condition can be compared with a known earlier state.
why: Restoring order does not erase every trace of a process, and chemical or sensory residue can betray what was done.

text: Let a game track stains and allow washing, but leave residual traces for later inspection, and store where each disposed item ended up.
when: when designing removable evidence states
why: cleanup feels effective while a findable trail remains

text: People carry traces from a scene on clothing and shoes, so matching a body's traces to known sources can link the body to a location.
when: a body or object was moved and the surface it touched is unknown
why: contact transfers material to what it touches

text: Physical traces such as burned debris or a strange odour suggest what happened and point the investigation toward a cause.
A footprint's age can be estimated from when its floor was last washed, since later cleaning would have erased it.
when: a surface is cleaned on a known schedule
why: A trace cannot survive cleaning that happened after it was left

text: A second reagent that dissolves a positive stain can separate a target substance from a similar one that gives the same first result.
when: two substances give similar results in one test

text: A tool used on a surface leaves marks that match its shape. Forced-entry damage, such as a torn opening, reveals the tool type and where it was inserted.
when: a lock, door, or wall shows damage
why: The contact shape of the tool is imprinted on the damaged surface.

text: Traces such as mud, dust, boot wear and grooming can reveal a person's habits and social station even when the person is disguised.
Small leftover traces such as used items, furniture positions and object placement let a reasoner reconstruct who was present and when, producing a working assumption that still needs testing.
when: A scene contains leftover objects and the question is who was present and when
why: Physical leftovers record past activity and narrow possibilities, while psychological reasoning alone can only suggest them

text: A game world with linked records, such as NPC databases, property deeds and tenancy logs, lets players connect a hidden identity to a place and a victim.
when: Designing investigation content with several record types.
why: A shared location or description connects otherwise separate records.

text: The height and angle of impact marks on a surface can be stored as world decals that hint at where a hidden target was struck.
Undisturbed lock states, such as unmarked paint and no forced entry, can be readable evidence that a room is unoccupied and was entered by key.
when: When designing environmental clues about whether a space is occupied.
why: Absence of disturbance signals normal entry and an absent occupant.

text: Rain blurs and erases footprints over time, and animals disturb ground, so traces may vanish before recording or false signs of activity appear.
when: A scene is exposed to weather or wildlife before examination.

text: Trampled plants and footprints of a given size and shape show that a person was present outside.
An item dropped by an intruder is first found and interpreted by the person who controls the room, so that person shapes what the item is taken to mean.
when: A scene reveals an intrusion through a dropped object
why: The controlling person decides how the clue is presented before others examine it

text: Spiked prints show on coarse cinders but vanish on hard ground, so their disappearance there can mean the wearer changed footwear before reaching it.
A worn, burnt or marked item can encode how it was used, letting players reconstruct an event from its state.
when: When designing environmental props that imply past events.
why: Consistent cause-and-mark pairs let players infer what happened.

text: A trained animal can carry small items between rooms, so its routine can produce thefts that look like intruder activity.
A higher drop spreads into a thinner spot with spatter or an irregular edge, while a lower drop stays thick with a smooth border.
when: a drop lands on a smooth, non-absorbent surface

text: A physical object that links a suspect can have an innocent explanation and a damning one; the next link in the chain often rules out the earlier suspect.
The reagent still gives a visible reaction when one drop of blood is diluted in a litre of water, about one part in a million.
Elapsed time equals the trace's distance from its root divided by the material's known growth rate.
when: the growth rate is known and steady

text: Relative positions of several features matching within about 0.01 inch suggest that one trace was copied from the other.
when: when comparing measured features of two traces

text: Physical evidence can be read by examining string, knot, wrapper, handwriting, container and contents, then interpreting them together rather than in isolation.
when: When physical evidence is at hand and the sender or owner is unknown
why: Each object carries partial clues about trade, region and schooling that combine into a fuller picture

text: Physical evidence takes four forms: prints left on surfaces, the absence of prints, objects hidden in ordinary places, and medical findings.
why: Each form needs its own interpretation, since a missing or unclear trace can mean several things.

text: A hub-and-spoke case structure places one central character who connects every lead, keeping the player's search focused.
when: Designing a multi-lead mystery.

text: An initial or partial marker can fit several owners, so check for rival matches and corroborate before assigning it to one person.
when: An object has a partial marker, or a record refers to someone only by an initial.
why: Many people share initials, and a rival owner can make the first reading unreliable.

text: A feature named in a record may match more than one spot, so the chosen location needs a second, independent check.
when: when a common landmark such as a rock or well is the only anchor
why: Common features repeat across a region

text: Common material, such as dust or a single common fibre, proves little unless distinctive; treat comparisons as corroboration that adds weight to other findings, not as proof.
when: When comparing ubiquitous physical traces.
why: Common materials match many places, so a match carries little weight.

text: Reading crumpled paper, a flush or a turned face as proof of one emotion overstates the evidence; it shows unease, not what is hidden.
Inferring too much from a single detail overstates the evidence, and keeping a first impression after evidence favours another reading produces false leads.
when: When a single forensic detail drives a conclusion, or one observation of appearance, wear or habit is read.
why: one clue rarely determines the whole picture; early readings are formed quickly and can fit the evidence poorly.

text: Widely shared traits, such as a common scent, object class, habit or tobacco blend, identify few people and weaken single-owner inferences; use them only with other facts.
when: When a shared trace, object or habit seems to identify one person.
why: Common traits match many people, so a match carries little weight.

text: Ambiguous signs, such as faint breath with a cold limb or bruising, fit several conditions or causes; several traces often support both readings, so they cannot settle a question alone.
why: most traces have more than one possible cause

text: Assuming a mark is old because it looks ordinary, or trusting a trace with unknown direction or size, leads to wrong conclusions; test assumed ages rather than accept first impressions.
when: When evaluating common-looking damage or partial prints.
why: Ordinary appearance does not establish when a mark was made; first impressions of age are often mistaken.

text: Assuming visible traces are the only ones, or the obvious suspect the only maker, ends inquiry early; overlooked small traces like particles or footmarks fix timing and route.
when: A scene seems fully explained by visible evidence.
why: Hidden traces or other makers may explain the same marks; minor traces often carry the most precise timing and route information.

text: A print or trace on a common surface or in an ordinary place may come from an innocent, unconnected person, so it proves little until linked to the event.
when: When a print or trace is found on a common surface or ordinary place.
why: An innocent touch is likely, so a print proves little without a link.

text: Do not assume a trace is ordinary because it is common; verify the expected source and record absences, since unrecorded absences are easy to miss.
Testing a trace only on a flat surface, when the real surface is curved, can give a misleading match or mismatch.
when: checking an impression against a surface
why: the wrong geometry changes how the trace fits

text: Heavy mildew or decay does not by itself prove long exposure, because growth and fading can run through short cycles.
why: decay cycles can be short

text: Staging judgments rest on an assumed picture of how a struggle looks; test that picture before relying on it.
why: a wrong model of the event produces wrong conclusions

text: Reading stories into tracks goes beyond the marks; certainty ends where the prints do.
when: Interpreting footprints into a narrative.
why: Prints show only physical marks, not intent or identity.

text: A monogram is ambiguous, since its initials may belong to the killer rather than the victim.
Calling a missing object thrown away is an inference, not a finding; label it as a conclusion that needs support.
when: When a key item cannot be located after a search.

text: A worn seat or a tied knot may be ordinary. Its meaning depends on the other traces around it.
A single disturbed branch or mark admits several explanations and should be treated as provisional until other evidence supports it.
why: One trace can have several causes

text: Owning a boat does not show who used it. Check whether the boat was available at the time instead of assuming use.
when: a vessel is a possible escape route

text: A common sound cannot tie a witness to a specific moment, so using it as an identifier in a timeline proves little.
when: the sound could come from many sources
why: If many sources produce the sound, hearing it does not locate the event.

text: Accusing a witness of complicity from a physical inference alone is unjustified; the inference needs other support first.
A conclusion drawn from one wound path depends on assumptions about the victim's position and should be checked against the layout.
Handling an object with bare hands adds new prints and can destroy existing ones, so the object should be held by a non-contact method.
Several objects can share an odour, so the direction of transfer must be checked rather than assumed.
Burned residue can change in appearance, so compare it with a known sample rather than judging by look.
Many doors can share one lock type, so a key match identifies only the specific door it fits and must be checked against that door.
when: When a key or lock is used to identify a location.
why: Lock type alone is not unique to one location.

text: A single trace, such as one hair, can mislead because several people may share it.
An ambiguous mark needs a resolved reading; if the reading stays open, the audience is left guessing rather than reasoning.
An object or trace may suggest an event (a death) or have an unrelated cause (cleaning), but stays a hypothesis until other evidence confirms it; near certainty overstates it.
when: interpreting ambiguous room objects or traces

text: A matching watermark or authentic paper shows only type or source; forgers can use genuine supplies, so authorship needs separate evidence.
when: Evaluating physical evidence in a mystery or document-based clue.
why: Authentic supplies are accessible to forgers, so material authenticity and authorship are separate questions.

text: A stain left for a long time and cleaned badly becomes hard to test.
Assuming a target will read a particular medium can be wrong. Confirm which channel the target actually uses before placing a bait.
Cleaning removes some evidence but leaves traces elsewhere, so a clean workspace does not mean a clean room.
A shared object may be known to many people, so check who had access to it at the moment the message depends on.
The same disturbance can support more than one reading. A book opened to a famous passage may signal a serious reader or a casual one.
when: Interpreting a visitor's taste from an object
why: Traces rarely carry one meaning on their own

text: A chair or step changes how high a person can reach, so note any furniture present before estimating height from reach.
Powder used to reveal fingerprints can leave grains that look like evidence, so record what was used and when.
when: collecting traces from a surface
why: Introduced grains can be mistaken for original traces.

text: A physical trait many people share does not single out one person; wear shows that a previous owner existed, not who that owner was.
A compulsive ritual may simply be illness; reading it as a clue without more evidence turns a symptom into a plot device.
why: behaviour alone does not establish a plot fact

text: A condition written into an agreement, such as requiring an old party's consent, can plant the seeds of later disputes.
An object can appear in a hand during a glance away. Record what each observer could actually see at each moment, or an unseen transfer will look like a sudden appearance.
when: When an object is found in a person's hand after a brief lapse in observation.

text: Physical damage proves little until it is dated; fresh and old wear must be told apart before the trace counts as evidence of an event.
why: Undated wear could predate the event under investigation.

text: Searchers who assume a hiding place is untouched may miss clues, since someone may have emptied it before they arrived.
Ground litter can erase tracks within metres, so trace evidence may be lost before a search begins.
when: A search follows a trail across litter-covered ground.

text: A cover story can fail on a second look if incriminating tools stay visible in the space.
when: a player carries tools into a shared area

text: Packing tools without matching them to tasks makes the right one hard to find under pressure.
Trusting a witness's account of a door's state without knowing when it was checked, or overlooking who else had a duplicate key or access.
when: When relying on testimony about a locked door
why: A reported state is only as reliable as the time it was observed and the access it allowed.

text: A physical change after a trap should be explained rather than merely observed, since the suspect may have acted for a different reason.
when: When interpreting a change left after leaving a suspect alone
why: The same trace can have multiple causes, so the explanation must be checked.

text: A substitute item offered in place of a sought item does not confirm the original claim; treat it as a different item.
when: When staff offer a different item after the requested one is not found
why: A substitute resembles the claim but does not verify it.

text: Assuming a route from one visible line of prints, such as entry without exit, ignores that the other half may have been swept or never made.
why: Partial trails hide the full movement.

text: A person in hiding needs food, movement and routine, and these needs leave traces that reveal their presence.
when: any concealed occupant
why: concealment cannot remove all contact with the outside

text: Accepting a trace's most visible explanation without checking how it was made can mislead, since similar marks have different causes; a trace must be explained before it is relied on.
when: When interpreting a physical clue.
why: Similar-looking traces can have different causes, and only the process of making them reveals which.

text: Restricting access to a body protects evidence but leaves doubt about tampering, and a confident first impression can later be revised.
when: handling a body or scene as evidence
why: Limited access makes later challenges to the findings harder to answer.

text: A dose count depends on the person who recorded it, so measurement results should be checked against that recorder's reliability.
when: a measured quantity relies on a recorded count
why: Recording errors can shift the apparent quantity taken.

text: Attributing a trace to one person without ruling out others who share the same habit, such as a second smoker or reader, can pin the trace on the wrong person.
Small, easily missed injuries can be the real cause of harm, while obvious bruising can mislead an investigator into looking no further.
Traces seen in haste or in poor light are easily misread, so inspect them carefully before concluding.
A museum-style inventory label presents a neat picture of contents; players and designers should test such framing against the object itself rather than accept it.
when: When an object's label or inventory card summarizes what the object contains.
why: Labels shape what viewers conclude, so an authoritative-looking summary can hide the real contents.

text: 1) Record a distinctive physical feature at first sighting. 2) Compare it deliberately with later sightings. 3) Treat a match as a lead, not proof, to confirm since others may share the mark.
when: Linking a stranger or a profile-matching witness report to an earlier sighting through a physical feature.
why: A passing glance proves little, and a shared feature needs confirmation before it identifies anyone.

text: 1) Measure print sizes. 2) Compare them and the distinctive sole features with a known pattern. 3) Check whether tracks run in one direction only. 4) Examine prints under magnification for wear marks. 5) Attribute marks only to sources matching all of them.
when: when footprints or marks must be linked to a person or shoe
why: Measurement and comparison reduce the chance of a false match.

text: 1) Photograph clear prints on the object or scene and lift marks from it. 2) Collect reference prints from people with access, without alarm, and photograph them. 3) Compare enlarged photographs side by side by ridge pattern, using innocent people's prints to sort overlapping marks. 4) Assign each matched print to a hand.
when: when a scene holds prints and reference prints from people with access are available

text: 1) Note each physical trace separately. 2) Combine the traces into one hypothesis that explains the whole set. 3) Test the hypothesis with an action or an independent second trace.
when: Reaching a conclusion from scattered physical clues.
why: Separate notes stop one striking detail from hiding the rest, and testing catches a wrong reading.

text: 1) List every odd fact that does not match the expected sequence. 2) Check its position against the obvious paths of the victim and passers-by. 3) Propose a physical cause. 4) Keep it only if the cause fits the scene.
when: a scene offers an anomaly

text: 1) Record each set of prints at the scene. 2) Compare them with reference patterns taken earlier. 3) Separate sets by any differing measurement, such as toe size. 4) Follow the matched set across surfaces.
when: two or more sets of prints at a scene

text: 1) Fit the trace to the correct geometry of the real surface or body part. 2) Compare it with a documented reference description. 3) Read the force or effort the trace implies. 4) Accept the trace only if the fit holds.
when: a physical impression seems to match no ordinary agent
why: a trace is evidence only when it fits the real surface and reference data

text: 1) Note the object's form, condition and use. 2) Infer the skill its use requires. 3) Note where it lay. 4) Rule out obvious owners. 5) Hold the inference as a hedged hypothesis.
when: a single object is the only trace

text: 1) Note the items a suspect carried. 2) Check whether those items turn up in a known location. 3) Have the owner or a witness identify each item. 4) Record where and when it was found.
when: A suspect has been in a public place where lost items are logged.
why: An object becomes evidence only once it is tied to the suspect and dated.

text: 1) State the trace that should appear under known conditions, such as weather or footwear. 2) Check for it promptly. 3) If it is absent, infer the alternative means used.
when: A scene should show a trace under known conditions and the trace is missing.
why: An expected trace that is absent constrains how the actor could have arrived or moved.

text: 1) Examine the material type and format of paper or objects. 2) Examine folds, seals and cut edges. 3) Compare handwriting for different hands. 4) Match each trace to a tool or person that could have made it.
when: a scene holds small objects or residue that may identify people or tools
why: Material traits narrow the set of possible makers

text: 1) Use magnification on small damage such as twisted or snapped twigs. 2) Compare the damage direction with plausible movement to infer what happened.
when: fine damage to plants or surfaces is found at a scene
why: Magnification reveals detail that unaided sight misses

text: 1) Identify the trace a method left at the scene. 2) Match the trace to a specific object. 3) Link that object to a person who had access to it.
when: when a crime or event involved a tool or method that had to touch the scene
why: each link is checked against physical facts, so the conclusion rests on verifiable evidence

text: 1) Find places where one track covers another. 2) Record which mark is on top in each pair. 3) Chain the pairs into a single sequence of events.
when: When reconstructing movement from tracks on soft ground.
why: Pairwise order links create a full timeline.

text: 1) Notice a small residue left after a touch or action. 2) Identify the substance by its typical use. 3) Ask what process would leave that residue and what the person needed it for.
when: a crime depends on a quiet action no one witnessed
why: a residue points back to the process that made it

text: 1) Measure stride length. 2) Measure how deep prints sink in soft ground. 3) Estimate weight and build from both. 4) Compare that estimate with the size implied by shoe prints.
when: when prints suggest a number or size of people
why: stride and sinking depth reflect weight, which shoe size alone does not

text: 1) Set aside testimony and traces. 2) Identify the exact act that was committed. 3) Infer the actor's options and habits from that act.
when: Interpreting ambiguous physical evidence.
why: A trace supports only the conclusions its act and context allow.

text: 1) Place the pair side by side under the same light. 2) Compare surfaces, underside, and fittings. 3) Look for shade differences in fabric or padding. 4) Ask the owner whether the pair was moved, repaired, or touched. 5) Check that the recorded provenance matches the present condition.
when: two matched objects should be identical but one differs
why: A structured comparison separates real differences from ordinary variation.

text: 1) List every ordinary explanation for the physical trace. 2) Check each against an independent fact, such as weather or a garment's cut. 3) Only after all are ruled out, let the trace shift suspicion.

1) Look for signs of ongoing systematic effort, such as cleared growth, propped plants or tidy soil. 2) Date the activity from fresh marks like cut limbs. 3) Eliminate suspects whose habits do not fit. 4) Keep the identity open until the actor appears.
1) Present scene-linked items one at a time. 2) Ask the suspect to compare each directly with their own belongings. 3) Record each answer. 4) Judge the full cluster of matches, not any one match.
when: when confronting a suspect with physical traces
why: Each direct comparison is hard to argue away.

text: 1) Examine each trace sample under magnification. 2) Apply a chemical test to each sample. 3) Compare the results to decide whether the samples share a source.
when: when a small trace can be compared with a known sample

text: 1) Drop a small object down a pipe or shaft. 2) Time how long it takes to strike bottom. 3) Use the delay as a rough estimate of depth.
when: A searcher needs a rough sense of how deep a hidden space lies.

text: 1) Clean and drain the object, then lay it on blotting paper. 2) Describe its shape, holes and any loose internal part in order. 3) Cut it lengthwise carefully to expose the mechanism. 4) Reassemble it and replay the action to test the reading.
when: when an object's function is unknown

text: 1) Clean the thumb with a soaked brush, rinse, dry and polish it. 2) Roll a thin film of ink on a plate. 3) Press the thumb onto the plate and then onto cards, taking several plain and rolled impressions.
when: when comparable samples are needed
why: Standardised impressions make comparison reliable.

text: 1) Draw dust from several marked spots with a suction extractor. 2) Put each area's sample on its own wetted slide. 3) Label each slide to its spot on a sketch. 4) List each slide's contents separately.
when: when sampling a garment for location evidence
why: separate samples show which particles are spread across the whole item and which are local

text: 1) Use a low-power magnifier to see cut edges and overlapping paper. 2) Use a stronger magnifier to check surfaces for detail.
when: A close examination needs more detail than the eye alone gives
why: Increasing magnification in steps reveals layers of evidence without overwhelming the observer.

text: 1) Establish the total number of units made. 2) Count the units still held. 3) Subtract to get the number sold. 4) Subtract the sales with a named record to find the untracked sales. 5) Reconcile candidate names against the count before concluding.
when: Records are kept per transaction and the total item count is known.
why: The count reveals how many sales are missing from the records.

text: 1) Treat the print trail as a starting hypothesis about movement. 2) Test the hypothesis against other testimony. 3) Revise it if testimony contradicts it.
when: reconstructing movement from a print trail
why: Prints suggest a route but must be confirmed by independent accounts.

text: 1) Ask a person to return an item to its storage. 2) Note its orientation and position. 3) Repeat with others. 4) Compare placements to see who knows the setting.
when: checking whether someone knows a storage arrangement

text: 1) State a candidate sequence. 2) Carry it out on the mechanism. 3) Accept it only when the expected sound or change confirms it.
when: Solving a combination or lock
why: Physical feedback checks the hypothesis

text: 1) Lift or capture a fresh trace from the subject and enlarge or copy it. 2) Compare it against each labelled reference record in turn. 3) Remove each candidate that does not match, noting any mismatch.
when: When matching a found trace against a collection of labelled reference records.
why: Enlargement exposes detail, and sequential comparison narrows the candidate set one record at a time.

text: 1) Take an impression or other trace left at the scene. 2) Obtain a reference from the suspect or victim, such as an impression or the suspect's own object. 3) Compare them; an exact fit confirms the match.
1) Identify the object's last known owner. 2) Note the route it has taken since separation. 3) Follow each record of custody to the next holder.
when: An object has been separated from its owner and must be traced
why: Each custody record narrows the search for the object and its holders

text: 1) Record a visible object such as a painted crest, noting its colour and form. 2) Keep it as a thread for later inquiry. 3) Match it against known records later.
when: A suspect is unseen but carries an identifiable object.
why: A durable mark outlasts the encounter and can link an unseen figure to a known source.

text: 1) Trace found items, such as cards, marked objects or a watch, to their owner. 2) List who had access to them. 3) Identify the person who could have taken them.
when: Physical items are found that point to a theft or fraud.
why: Tracing an object links it to a person with access.

text: 1) Follow each physical trace to the person who handled it. 2) Use the answer to open the next question. 3) Continue through intermediaries until reaching the person who arranged the act.
when: A physical object connects to a culprit through several people.
why: Each link narrows the chain toward the source.

text: 1) Compare a series of records for one person. 2) If one record does not match the others, check whether the sample was swapped before blaming a faulty label. 3) Verify the chain of custody.
when: When a mismatch appears within a series of records for one person.
why: A mismatch may signal substitution rather than a labelling error, so the cause must be checked.

text: 1) Compare the note's paper and ink with materials at the scene. 2) Compare its handwriting with a genuine sample of the suspect's writing. 3) Check unusual words for second meanings, such as place names.
when: When a written clue appears to identify a culprit.
why: Material and linguistic mismatches reveal where a note was written and whether it was planted.

text: 1) Ask whether the object could fit where the witness says it was hidden. 2) Ask whether it could be smaller than the claimed item. 3) Compare the answers against the physical facts.
when: A witness claims someone carried an object
why: Size checks can rule claims in or out without identifying anyone.

text: 1) Sample the room broadly, sealing each sample and keeping them apart. 2) If broad samples come up clean, keep the theory rather than dropping it. 3) Sample the surfaces where the hypothesised contact occurred last and most carefully, each separately.
when: a substance could be hidden in fine material across many surfaces

text: 1) Establish a precise dimension for the clue object. 2) Find a common tool that can measure it. 3) Measure the second object carefully and repeat the reading to confirm it before relying on the match.
when: A physical trace must be matched to a specific object
why: A precise repeated measurement can identify an object, while a single approximate reading is unreliable

text: 1) Note where the moved body was found. 2) Trace the water path back upstream. 3) Check the sites along that path for where the body entered the water.
when: a body or object has been carried by water
why: Current carries an object away from its origin, so the origin lies upstream.

text: Spending shows dependence, not intent, and the same figures can come from gifts, inheritance, private income or loans, so motive should not be inferred from spending alone.
when: when interpreting unexplained wealth or heavy spending on another person
why: The same financial evidence can arise from legitimate sources.

text: A trace counts as evidence only once linked to the scene; an identification shows whose mark it is, not when or how it arrived.
when: when a found item is used to contradict a witness, or after an identification is made
why: An unlinked trace may have arrived at the scene by other means.

text: Physical condition alone does not prove ownership; trace a small object's origin to a product, supplier or person, with staff or witness knowledge, before counting it as evidence.
when: a small object near a scene could link to a product or person
why: Many people may own or handle the same item, so its origin must be established first.

text: Physical geometry decides what access or sight was possible; discount a witness's claimed ability or observation, such as seeing through a thick wall without special equipment.
Check each explanation with a concrete physical question, such as whether the object fits, leaves residue, or can exert the needed force.
Do not rely on one trace alone; each trace must fit the others before it supports a reconstruction.
Examine the outside of a location as well as the inside, since broken foliage and marks in the earth can show that someone was present.
why: Entry and exit often leave traces outdoors

text: Give an eerie sound an in-world mechanical cause while leaving a detail, such as a sound with no visible source, as a persisting clue.
when: designing haunted or eerie environments
why: A lingering anomaly rewards players who revisit the mystery.

text: Record each clue's original in a hidden ledger, so an altered clue can be detected by players who find the source.
when: when generating or altering clues
why: A stored original makes forgery testable.

text: Search clothing for maker's marks and initials, since a small embroidered mark can provide the only identifying lead.
Show inherited features, such as in a family portrait or on a character's appearance, as a deduction clue linking two NPCs.
when: When designing clues about family relations
why: Shared features give the player a visible link to reason from

text: Test footprints for signs of oversized footwear or an unnatural walking pattern that suggests a false path.
when: footprints are used as evidence
why: Prints can be manipulated to mislead

text: Let a mismatch between map and ground, such as a wall or gate out of place after a collapse, serve as a clue to changed room footprints.
when: Designing an in-game space whose layout changed after an event
why: Players can detect change by comparing the recorded layout with the physical remains

text: Keep first examinations of suspects low-visibility, with few spectators and little publicity, so they are not exposed before evidence supports it.
Let ink stains or wear on a scroll or letter reveal who wrote it and when, giving players a physical identity clue.
when: A written document is an item in the game.
why: Physical wear links an object to its author.

text: Use a burnt-out lamp or spent candle to encode an in-game time that the player must work out.
when: Designing an environmental clue that conveys elapsed time
why: Burn state is a readable, reasoned clue that rewards inference

text: Recalculate match odds when the subject has an unusual feature, since odds computed for normal fingers no longer apply.
when: The compared print comes from an unusual finger.
why: Standard odds assume typical ridge structure.

text: Let players reproduce a pose with a test action, so an impossibility is verified by the player rather than simply asserted by the game.
when: when a clue depends on physical impossibility

text: Model physical traces as inspectable state, such as scuffs, displaced objects or unfinished actions, so a scene carries its own evidence.
when: when building crime or event scenes
why: Players can deduce only from evidence the game exposes

text: Give found items a tag or label recording their origin, so players can preserve them as proof and trace where they came from.
Check faint or smudged prints against photographs in detail before comparing them.
Let an enemy leave a recognisable symbol, such as objects arranged on a table, as a signature linking its encounters.
Give an NPC a verifiable proof item that the player must obtain earlier, so a bluffed deal succeeds only when the groundwork is done.
Count the contents of containers against the expected number; a full count suggests nothing was taken, and a shortfall or extra item signals tampering.
when: A container's contents may have been altered
why: Contents are a checkable state that changes when items are removed or added

text: Give tampered items physical traces, such as uniform dosing and a sealed hole, that a player must notice and reconstruct rather than being told the sequence.
why: noticing and reasoning from traces makes discovery active

text: Let players compare a suspect item against a clean control, so that the difference reveals the tampering.
when: a lab-style puzzle is designed
why: a control isolates what has changed

text: Model shop ledgers, ship manifests and guest registers as readable world records, and let a missing entry point to a suspect.
when: designing investigation content in a game world
why: Readable records give players evidence through routine documents.

text: Let a posted rule quote its key condition with the clause cut, so the full text found elsewhere changes the outcome.
Build a lie-detector artifact to fail when the player substitutes their own item, so that the refusal or failure exposes the trick.
when: when designing a truth-testing device controlled by an NPC
why: A rigged test is revealed when a neutral input produces a different result.

text: Reject a story whose key link requires actions that no one could carry out without leaving traces.
when: Evaluating a theory's chain of events.
why: An action leaving no possible trace is implausible and fails the test of evidence.

text: Design evidence in layers: a blatant signal for careful players and a faint signal visible only from an oblique angle or after a pause.
when: designing clues for players with different search habits
why: layers let both casual and patient players find the evidence

text: Let an NPC who controls a delivery point intercept a message, so the player discovers the clue through a missing letter rather than receiving it directly.
when: When designing how a clue reaches the player.
why: Discovering a clue through its absence adds tension and a reason to investigate.

text: Let a note passed between NPCs be a clue the player cannot read until a later piece reveals its meaning.
when: When designing clues that unfold over time.
why: A deferred meaning keeps the clue active across the story.

text: Information carried by an NPC's item, or returned by a remote reply, can unlock a new location or area.
Let an item's label name a shop and the shop's ledger name a buyer, so players must follow the chain step by step.
Where a trace in the game is unreadable, provide a second clue that answers the same question.
when: When a clue depends on lighting, weather or terrain that the player may miss.
why: Redundant clues keep the case solvable when the primary clue is missed.

text: Reuse an identical item, such as a rope or wire, in several rooms so players link scenes by collecting matching items.
Give a clue an unintended artifact such as a stain or tear that a forged copy inherits, so a magnifier or measuring tool can match the two.
when: Designing forgeable clues in a game world
why: Inherited artifacts give the player a concrete test for whether a copy derives from an original.

text: Give bodies and fallen enemies wound states that record damage order, so a player who inspects them can tell whether a fatal fall came before or after a blow.
why: Inspectable physical state lets players reconstruct a sequence of events

text: Build a vertical level where a body can fall through a shaft, so players must test whether the fall fits the victim's routine and the space.
when: Designing a death scene in a multi-level space.

text: Let a trace on an item match only one location on the map, so the clue points to a specific place.
Give items inscriptions, crests or regional idioms that point to a faction, so a player who reads several together can identify the group.
Include inspectable props that reward careful checking, rather than making them mere hiding places.
when: when placing interactive objects in levels
why: props that reward inspection make the search meaningful

text: Use worn paths in a location to encode a route or meeting place that players can read as evidence of who gathered there.
Layer scene traces such as dust, soot and moisture, let each degrade as NPCs walk through, and let players examine them with a magnifying tool.
when: Designing environmental evidence in a game
why: Degradation makes early inspection valuable

text: Let walls record scrape and soil marks when a character or item crosses them, so players can reconstruct the route.
Place traces in unexpected spots such as frayed edges, pocket linings and sock tips, so players must inspect the whole object.
Give scene objects inspectable physical state such as scorch, wetness, displacement and matching marks on both sides of a wall, so the player can solve the cause from them.
Place a key trace far enough away that the player must travel to confirm it.
when: Designing where evidence sits in the world.
why: Travel adds effort and makes confirmation feel earned.

text: When a non-human agent is identified, always ask who trained, owned or sent it, since stopping at the animal leaves the responsible person unidentified.
when: When an animal or creature appears to have caused an event.
why: Trained creatures act on human direction, so the human is the real cause.

text: Generate traces from a stored cause, such as a creature, tool or person, so players can match each mark to its source.
when: When procedurally placing marks or clues in a level.
why: A stored cause makes each trace matchable and fair to solve.

text: Traces must be consistent with the rest of the scene, or they undermine the logic of the clue structure.
Use a physical trace to link two events when it is the only available proof of the connection.
Handle suspicious substances with care: keep them away from the face and test them at a distance.
when: An object may contain a dangerous substance.
why: Hidden contents may be harmful, so direct contact or inhalation is risky.

text: When a witness reports an impossible entry or exit, check surfaces that record passage, such as soil, dust, wet paving or fittings; a missing expected trace undermines the claim.
when: The setting can record movement
why: Environmental records show whether a human passed through

text: Collect corroborating physical traces, such as a cloth used to wipe prints, a wrapper and a fiber of string, before explaining the mechanism.
why: Traces gathered beforehand form a proof chain for the device.

text: Establish the core forensic facts early, within roughly the first tenth of the session, so every later solution can be checked against them.
when: building a mystery with several suspects
why: Fixed early facts give the group a shared standard for judging later claims

text: Shoe size and sole shape can distinguish individuals, but similar boots leave the same mark, so a matching print often points only to a boot type.
A stain test can give an ambiguous result, so the player must choose between trusting an NPC's claim and trusting a lab report.
when: a stain requires a magnifier or solvent test

text: Authorship comparison works with a reliable known sample; without one, or when the paper is common stock available to anyone, it gives little.
A fleeing person throws an item to be rid of it, so its landing spot reveals who was actually targeted.
when: An object is thrown during an escape.
why: Escape aims to shed the item, not to deliver it.

text: A thumb meets a flat surface through its side, not its palm, so a print showing all five palm-side surfaces together cannot come from a hand pressed flat.
when: when judging whether a print's pose is possible
why: the contact geometry of the digits limits possible arrangements

text: Dragged bleeding differs from arterial tracks left by a victim who could still move, so compare a mark with wound evidence before interpreting it.
Read floor coverings and stains as a map: where a covering is missing or a stain pools shows where an event happened and how far it spread.
when: investigating a scene's layout

text: Use footprints that lead beneath a closed door as physical evidence that rules out a simple supernatural explanation.
Stalled threads compete with active ones for an investigator's attention, so unresolved leads can crowd out new work when many run at once.
when: When an investigation has many open leads at the same time.
why: Limited attention must be divided between pending and active threads.

text: 1) Compare paired parts on opposite sides for length and shape. 2) Match worn joint surfaces across separate finds. 3) Confirm with several independent features before concluding the parts belong together.
when: Deciding whether scattered remains come from one individual.
why: Several independent matches are much harder to produce by chance than a single feature.

text: 1) Record where each trace lies on the object. 2) Map the trace pattern onto the anatomy or structure to find which surfaces faced where. 3) Test each explanation for the arrangement against the physical state of joints or connections.
when: A minor physical trace follows a regular pattern and suggests how an object lay.
why: Placement of small traces can reveal orientation and whether parts were separated before deposit.

text: Measure distances from a suspected heat source and inspect nearby surfaces for effects, since both can rule that source in or out.
when: A heat source is suspected

text: Use a checkable physical detail, such as handedness, the side an object lies on, or blow force against a frail build, that the suspected character cannot match, reversing the suspicion.
when: A player has been led to suspect a character, or early evidence has set up a false suspect.
why: A physical, verifiable fact overturns suspicion without relying on the narrator's word; a capability mismatch lets players reverse suspicion through deduction.

text: A physical impossibility, such as a body with no bleeding at the scene, prompts players to infer a hidden act such as the body having been moved.
when: a crime-scene puzzle where the evidence contradicts the apparent cause of death
why: The mismatch between the scene and the stated explanation signals that something was hidden from view.

text: A physical trace is a small disturbance in a scene, such as a moved object, a dent, a torn fastening or a faint odour, that shows who was present and what they did.
Buildings and objects such as doors, bars, bells, rooms and lamps can reveal and hide information, so a setting can serve as both a clue and a trap for its occupant.
Treat physical traces such as containers, labels, residue and lab results as evidence that narrows possibilities, and note what each one cannot establish.
when: investigating an object-based clue
why: each trace supports only part of a conclusion

text: Physical signs on a person, such as a change in colour, can point to a likely source before the suspected object is examined.
when: A bodily sign hints at a hidden cause.
why: A visible symptom narrows the search to a plausible origin.

text: Reuse one physical sign across several scenes, so its meaning becomes clear only when the secret is revealed.
Use physical evidence that changes which suspect fits, so each new artifact shifts suspicion to a different character.
when: Mid-to-late mystery where suspicion must move between candidates.
why: Each artifact reframes the evidence, keeping the suspect field active.

text: A physical trace that points to the victim rather than the suspect can clear the suspect and link the death to the dead person.
Tying a twist to where a document was physically kept lets the player see the forgery only after learning the item's last location from witness statements.
when: Designing a mystery whose reversal depends on a document or object's location.
why: The location detail is needed to expose the substitution, so it must be learned before the reveal.

text: A physical trace, such as a flat mat or a trail under a door, outranks a witness's confident report; accounts backed by physical traces are more credible than bare sightings.
when: A witness's account conflicts with physical evidence or is weighed against evidence.
why: Physical traces are harder to mistake than memory.

text: 1) Map every trail: which marks lead in, which lead out, and where they stop. 2) Compare footwear with the surface. 3) Test whether the implied route is physically possible. 4) Check companions' prints and disturbed ground. 5) Date prints by their condition.
when: When a person seems to vanish and the ground or floor can hold impressions.
why: Traces record movement, and each check removes a possible explanation.

text: 1) State the established physical facts, such as blood loss and body temperature. 2) Infer when the injury occurred from those facts. 3) Check whether the conclusion follows before moving on.
when: When physical signs are used to reorder events
why: Each step rests on a checkable fact, so the conclusion can be tested rather than trusted on authority.

text: 1) State in advance that an injury to one entity will appear on a linked body 2) inspect that body 3) compare the marks with the injury.
Stage a reveal through physical evidence players can connect, such as a line of burnt marks or a missing item, so the solution feels earned.
when: When a twist depends on a hidden action by a character
why: Concrete clues let players reason to the answer rather than receive it as an arbitrary disclosure.

text: Watch a suspect in custody for sudden changes in colour, posture or responsiveness, and treat them as a signal of a crisis to be read rather than ignored.
when: A suspect's condition changes abruptly during questioning.
why: A sudden physical change can end the session and may indicate a means of escape or harm.

text: Damage in a room is often read as a sign of struggle, even when one actor caused it, such as a shot that struck a reflecting surface.
Blackened, burnt wound edges indicate a close-range shot, while wounds from a greater distance are less severe.
Busy entrances are poor sources of footprint evidence because many people have passed through them.
when: Searching a heavily used doorway.
why: Heavy traffic overwrites or hides individual traces.

text: The length left on a partly burnt item shows how long it was used, and a stub's condition can show who could have used it.
when: Inspecting partly used items such as matches or cigarette stubs
why: Burning and wear leave a measurable record of use and of the user

text: An object broken where it fell suggests accident, while one crushed deliberately suggests someone acted on it.
when: Judging how a broken object came to its state
why: The pattern of damage reflects the force applied

text: Make a physical detail falsify an assumed fact, so the reveal comes from the environment rather than new information.
when: building a late reversal
why: a visible detail is checkable by the player

text: An object taken in haste often leaves secondary damage, such as a pulled fastening or a torn tie, that reveals the urgency and purpose of the taking.
Physical traces such as footprints, damage and marks on a body can connect events and confirm a theory.
A broken personal item at a site points to a struggle or sudden loss rather than casual dropping, but the damage shows that something happened, not what.
Compare a damage pattern with what the assumed cause would normally produce; a mismatch suggests a different cause.
when: The cause of damage is unclear

text: Physical traces are harder to fake than sounds, so surfaces where a hidden mechanism would leave marks should be inspected directly.
when: Investigating a scene where a hidden device could explain sounds
