why: Physical marks persist and are less open to misperception than sounds

text: A bullet hole with splintering on the room side shows the shot was fired from inside toward the outside, implying a person beyond the room.
A polished joint surface indicates friction after cartilage loss, which can imply a joint disease, and from it a likely limp or pain.
when: Reading wear on a joint surface.
why: Loss of protective cartilage exposes bone to friction, and the resulting disease affects how a person moves.

text: A scene's physical record has three trace kinds: damage pattern, residue and marks, which are read together to reconstruct what happened.
when: Investigating a room or location

text: Calling damage vandalism without examining what was taken and what was left misses the organizing pattern.
Burnt paper does not prove when an action happened, since a fire may have burned out at another time.
A sample taken loosely, or one whose label is lost, can be useless or misidentified.
Leaving the cause of an injury unstated keeps the wound's origin open, but it can frustrate a player who expects an answer by the end.
when: A death shows a wound without an explained cause.
why: An unanswered cause can read as an oversight rather than deliberate ambiguity.

text: 1) Hold the item by its edge or tip. 2) Breathe gently on a smooth, non-porous surface. 3) Look for a brief ridge pattern as the fog clears. 4) Confirm with powder and photography where it matters.
when: checking polished metal for recent handling without equipment
why: A quick screen reveals likely handling without touching the working surface.

text: Use a physical oddity, such as a mismatched stain or a turned rug, that implies concealment without naming the thief.
Hand prints with fingers pointing up a slope, plus rounded knee marks, suggest repeated falls while climbing.
Treat a witness's statement that a door was bolted as testimony from the person who tried it, not as established fact.
why: the witness may be mistaken or lying

text: An object found partway down a slope suggests a fall was not unbroken, so something may have caught the falling person.
A body shot through the chest tends to crumple forward or down, while a body falling straight back stays extended, with items displaced behind it.
when: Judging whether a body's posture fits a claimed fall.
why: Gravity and the direction of impact determine how the limbs and loose items settle.

text: A single trace can be faked, since a cunning person can swap tyres to leave unfamiliar tracks. Check each trace against the others.
In a cluttered scene, many objects look irrelevant, so a meaningful trace can be dismissed at first.
Test each fastening on its own rather than assuming a seal is complete.
Each point or explanation can seem sound alone, hiding a contradiction or pattern visible only when judged together with specific testimony or other clues.
when: When a theory rests on several separate points or a series of plausible explanations is offered for clues.
why: The conflict lies between points, not inside any one; each explanation looks sufficient alone, hiding the pattern across them.

text: A plausible account, including a psychologically plausible confession, is not thereby true; plausibility is not verification and must be followed by confirmation.
when: When an account is judged credible on its face.
why: Plausibility only makes a claim worth checking.

text: Confirming each detail of a story separately can create false confidence when the records confirm parts but not the whole claim.
why: Individually accurate records can jointly support a false conclusion

text: A large, plain, obvious clue is revealed at once by direct examination, so peripheral search is needed mainly for faint clues.
when: choosing how to search a scene
why: obvious evidence does not depend on how it is viewed

text: State legal, technical or rule-based limits in ordinary words so a non-specialist can follow the constraint without expert knowledge.
when: A limit matters to later events and the audience is not expected to be a specialist
why: Jargon hides the constraint and weakens the later deduction

text: A plain cover identity, such as a common trade and modest occupations, that explains the party's behaviour invites fewer questions.
Concealment often happens in plain sight among other discarded items, so a second searcher may find evidence the first one missed.
when: evidence is hidden among other objects
why: clutter hides items from a quick search

text: Clues can sit in plain sight as ordinary objects or gestures whose meaning becomes clear only later, so the reader can notice them before understanding them.
when: Planting clues for a mystery.
why: Early visibility rewards attentive readers without giving away the answer.

text: Present an estate's inheritance rules to the player in plain terms so that outcomes and their motives can be checked.
when: Designing inheritance or settlement systems for players
why: Visible rules let players test claims about motive.

text: Keep background plain and checkable when the investigation needs facts, rather than dressing the setting in atmosphere.
when: Presenting setting information that will be used as evidence.
why: Checkable facts can be tested, while atmosphere cannot.

text: State a charge plainly in front of those present, and restate it when the suspect asks what it means.
Keep the reveal itself short and plain, stating the act and its consequences in flat words without elaboration.
when: Delivering a confession or admission
why: Plain statement carries more weight after a long build-up.

text: State an inference plainly so the listener can test it.
when: Presenting a circumstantial conclusion to others.
why: A stated inference can be checked, challenged or confirmed.

text: In a disguise scheme, the difficult part is the planning and nerve required, not the physical execution of the disguise.
when: Designing how difficult an impersonation should feel to the player.
why: Execution is easy; the challenge lies in timing and daring.

text: A crime's overall plan may be made in advance while its details are improvised on the spot.
An apparent timing contradiction may come from a planned delay, such as a letter mailed in advance. Check for one before assuming an error.
when: when a date or timing conflicts with other facts

text: Plans can slip, so compare the planned date with the date actually used; a one-day delay can explain why an act came late.
when: when an act appears later than the schedule predicts

text: A character's wrong assumption that is later corrected can serve as a planned reversal.
Check whether a planned arrangement matches the timeline, and ask why a plan changed at short notice.
when: A promised arrangement does not happen as expected.
why: A sudden change can mean someone wanted a person out of the way.

text: Ask whether a culprit could foresee every condition a plan relied on; a plan needing both precise foresight and favourable chance is improbable.
when: testing an explanation that depends on uncontrollable conditions
why: each dependence on luck or unforeseeable events lowers its likelihood

text: A deliberately planned alibi keeps to public places and normal behaviour among others, so test an alibi by checking the suspect's public activity.
when: verifying a suspect's alibi
why: careless alibis are a common failure to watch for

text: Tie the culprit's hidden planning to an unforeseen weak point, so the reveal shows the plan had a flaw all along.
when: when writing a mystery's final reveal

text: Check whether a change in venue or procedure was arranged before the hearing began; prior arrangement is evidence of planning.
when: a proceeding changes mid-stream

text: Comparing a written plan with what actually happened shows where a person's intentions failed, letting the reader judge the gap.
Ask what an explanation requires of the actor; a method that does not fit the claimed intent counts against that explanation.
A carefully planned act most often fails at points the planner cannot control, such as a witness assumed absent who turns out present or another person's unplanned action.
when: Designing or evaluating a plan that must stay hidden
why: Other people's memories and choices are outside the planner's control.

text: Carefully built plans often fail through one unforeseen witness and through panic afterwards, which can undo the preparation.
1) Count the time left before the deadline. 2) Treat the interval before it as the window to act. 3) Schedule the key step inside that window.
when: A plan must be completed before a fixed date.
why: A counted interval turns an open deadline into a concrete plan.

text: Check each claimed plan against schedules and travel durations to confirm it was physically possible in the time available.
when: a suspect's route or trip is part of the claim
why: Plans that fail the clock are leads to test

text: A persistent fixed idea can reverse a settled plan, so a character's stated intention is a weak predictor of what they will actually do.
when: A character has decided on an act but is preoccupied with a thought.
why: An obsessive thought can take over the decision that was already made.

text: Skill at planning a crime does not guarantee care with money, so careless spending can betray even a clever offender.
A mismatch between stated plans and actual whereabouts, such as a missed engagement, is a warning sign worth investigating.
why: People who skip planned events may have been doing something else.

text: A planned schedule, such as a pre-booked transport or a set meeting, shows what each person expected to happen, which is evidence of intent.
Separate the planner of a crime from the actor who carries it out; each role has its own route, motive and distaste for violence.
when: when a crime involves more than one person
why: roles differ in knowledge, exposure and willingness to harm

text: An appointment made for a time when a house is empty suggests planning and a known visitor.
when: When a visit occurs at a time chosen to avoid witnesses.
why: Choosing an empty time indicates prior knowledge and intent.

text: A scheme that sets two enemies against each other works by predicting each one's habits, so each motive and habit becomes a link in the plan.
when: when a planner manipulates several targets

text: Careless details, such as a payment left with a victim, can link the planner to the scene; one forgotten item can undo an elaborate deception.
A planner's own account can itself be part of the plant, and exposure of that account would expose the planner.
why: self-reports are shaped by the planner's aims

text: Investigate toward a defined goal with a plan rather than reacting to whatever detail or action comes next.
Test a circumstantial case against physical facts before acting on it, such as planning a confrontation with a suspect.
when: A plan depends on a theory built from indirect evidence.
why: Acting on an untested theory risks losing the chance to confirm it.

text: Place a survey plan or diagram where a player can find it, so it can confirm a place's identity when a label conflicts.
when: A location has conflicting labels
why: Documentary layout resolves naming conflicts

text: Separate a suspect's plan from its outcome, so that a correct suspicion of intent can still be wrong about what actually happened.
when: a suspect is correctly suspected of a plan
why: the plan and its result may differ, creating a late surprise

text: A premeditated plan is argued to stay hidden unless the planner is pressed for time or hit by an unforeseeable coincidence.
when: Assessing whether a deliberate plan can be detected
why: Pressure and chance are the two main sources of error

text: Shadowing without method produces noisy, unreliable reports.
Arrange an unobtrusive exit so the watch can end at any hour without drawing attention.
Flag an early hint as important and promise its full answer later, priming the audience to notice it while anticipation builds and the payoff is held back.

1) Plant an anomaly, such as a warning, unexplained sound or deflected question. 2) Withhold its explanation for now. 3) Answer every planted anomaly later, since an unexplained early remark about the past makes the audience feel misled.
when: Building suspense through unexplained details.
why: Unanswered hooks read as broken promises and erode trust; unpaid hints read as cheating.

text: Plant a visible emblem or mark, such as a scar, costume detail or symbol, early and let it return at the reveal, rewarding attentive players as proof.
A remark that means nothing to listeners can produce a visible reaction, such as a colour change, stare or abrupt departure, that reveals a hidden connection.
when: the target knows the reference but the listeners do not
why: the private meaning shows through the target's body language

text: Plant key clues early as innocent-looking habits or inside ordinary talk, so readers file them as background and accept them at face value, making later significance a surprise.
when: A mystery's late proof or harmful hazard must matter later yet stay fair.
why: Mundane framing keeps the detail from drawing early suspicion; quirks accepted at face value make the later significance a surprise, not a cheat.

text: Plant a glimpsed clue early, such as an emblem seen in poor light, and pay it off when the player is ready to learn the name.
Plant an early warning about a danger, such as a health risk, and echo it later so the dramatic event feels both fair and dangerous.
why: A foreshadowed danger gives the later event a cause the audience already knows.

text: A hint given before the full explanation must be specific enough to be recognised, or the delay reads as evasion.
A secret can be conveyed through a glance or line that only one companion understands, and the player then acts on it.
when: A hint must pass between characters without being stated to the audience

text: Record a clue while it seems trivial, then leave it untouched for a long stretch, so it pays off late without seeming planned.
when: a mystery's proof must be set up well before it is needed
why: A clue that was ignored for most of the story is remembered as fair when it returns.

text: Let an NPC's earlier statement gain meaning once the player finds new evidence, so earlier dialogue can pay off later.
An unrecognized disguised figure met early can be revealed later as an ally or the investigator, creating an emotional or intellectual payoff.
when: Planning a mystery with a disguised investigator.
why: A figure seen but not identified early becomes a satisfying reveal when its identity is finally shown.

text: Repeat a distinctive symbol across the early scenes so that it later pays off as a physical key or plate in the climax.
when: structuring clues for a late solution
why: Repetition builds recognition, so the final use feels like a payoff.

text: Plant small oddities early, such as contradictions in grooming or minor timing details, and pay them off at the breakthrough.
when: setting up clues for a late reveal
why: Early small anomalies look like noise, but they become decisive evidence when the answer is revealed.

text: Hold back the meaning of early foreshadowing until after the crisis breaks, so each hint pays off once the player has the context to read it.
why: Premature meaning removes the surprise, while delayed meaning rewards recall.

text: A prediction stated early and specifically, then confirmed later, turns the later event into evidence for the earlier clue, so the audience sees the payoff as earned.
when: A lead names a checkable person, place or event that a later event can confirm
why: Confirmed predictions make the audience trust the storyteller and reread earlier clues

text: A missing non-player character can be explained by a private secret that resolves the quest hook, while a separate hidden event is the real threat.
when: Designing a missing-NPC quest with a second, concealed danger
why: The secret answers the disappearance and diverts attention from the true threat

text: A planted item can be neutralised by the suspect's plausible account of how they found it, so a plant is only as strong as the lack of an alternative explanation.
when: A suspect is confronted with a planted item
why: A believable account offers an innocent route to possession.

text: A short hint with a few names, places and circumstances, supplied by someone holding resentment, is enough to steer a whole round of accusations.
Showing a method only after the fact, with its links hidden, can make the observer look as if they simply knew the answer.
Hinting at an object's significance can put a subject on guard or plant ideas, so reactions may reflect suggestion rather than knowledge.
when: observers want to provoke a reaction
why: people adopt ideas they are offered

text: 1) Plant an unfinished statement early. 2) Keep the hidden fact out of view. 3) Reveal it later through the character's thoughts or an outside observer. 4) Add hints in between so the reticence does not read as a dropped thread.
when: Planting a fact for later reveal
why: Reticence pays off only when the reader can connect the clue to the reveal

text: 1) Plant the setting, the attached presence, and the stated immunity early. 2) Keep the final reveal consistent with them. 3) Let the reversal of expectation land last.
when: Designing a twist that should feel surprising but fair.
why: Groundwork lets the audience reinterpret the reveal as foreshadowed.

text: Place clues early while they look trivial, optionally letting a character dismiss them, so a late proof recontextualises clues the audience already saw.
when: a late-stage test will explain earlier details
why: Clues that seem minor are retained, and late reveals feel fair when the audience has already encountered the evidence.

text: Offer dialogue options that hint at a hidden motive and unlock new information when the player returns with evidence.
when: designing conversation systems
why: Evidence-gated hints reward investigation.

text: Plant a false lead, such as a tempting key or suspicious NPC, that players can disprove with a fact found later.
Recover a failed plan through a cause planted earlier in the story, not through chance, or the solution feels arbitrary.
Give an NPC a vague reason for a hostile act, and reveal the small hidden trigger later through an overheard line or diary entry.
Seed the identity clue early, when it looks unimportant, so that it pays off when the pieces are assembled later.
Front-load the damning but unexplained objects, such as a key, a will or a payment, in the first scene, so a later explanation recontextualises them.
when: Opening a mystery that will reveal a hidden relationship later
why: Early objects that are later explained feel fair and tie the opening to the resolution.

text: Make planted items visible and specific from the start, so a late payoff feels like deduction rather than a trick.
when: Setting up a reveal that depends on earlier objects or details.
why: Arbitrary-seeming items with no clear role make the reveal feel unfair.

text: Make a harmless-seeming request, such as signing a document, the hidden first step toward a later forgery or impersonation.
why: The request supplies the culprit with material such as a sample of handwriting.

text: Plant the decisive word early and leave it unexplained until a late cluster of clues gives it meaning.
when: Setting up a late reveal around a single term.
why: A word met early and understood late connects the early and late parts of the story.

text: A planted instruction builds setup and payoff, but it announces itself to attentive players, so it cannot serve as a surprise hook.
when: choosing between a planted setup and a surprise
why: attentive players recognise planted rules

text: Plant decisive facts such as an injury, a route, or a missing guard, and unexplained clues like predictions, favouritism, or hints, early so the late reveal can recall them.
when: Designing a mystery with a late solution.
why: Facts introduced late feel unfair; early seeds and their payoffs make the reveal feel earned rather than arbitrary.

text: Plant visible physical details or anomalies early that look like mechanics, and resolve them later; left unexplained, they read as authoring error.
when: Opening the investigation of a puzzle scenario.
why: Early anomalies read as set dressing and pay off when the solution reframes them, so the later explanation feels earned.

text: Place a physical tell in plain view early as an unremarkable curiosity, not a clue, so players can notice it and reinterpret it later.
when: Designing a hidden clue in a mystery scene.
why: A visible but dismissed clue stays fair and rewards retrospective reasoning without revealing the solution.

text: A plant is an arranged element, such as a false witness, faked death, or planted document, meant to steer investigators toward a wrong conclusion.
When a planted clue points strongly at one suspect, test whether it was placed deliberately before accepting it as evidence against that suspect.
when: a single object implicates one suspect

text: Set up a fact early, then reveal it at the moment it explains the present situation, so the reveal feels earned rather than arbitrary.
Introduce a central object and its delivery rule early, without revealing its importance; the reasons can arrive later.
when: a central object must be established before its value is known
why: setup without explanation builds anticipation for the payoff

text: Give the culprit a planting route that the player can reconstruct afterward from the scene.
Give a destroyed or lost clue a second trace, such as a slit or worn patch, so a player's mistake does not leave them stranded.
when: a clue can be destroyed by player action

text: Plant the absence of an expected detail as a clue, so that its missing trace signals a staged scene.
Make a moral or occult explanation available early, then reveal the mundane cause, such as a secret, address or key, when the player checks the evidence.
when: when designing horror-tinged clues with a human explanation
why: Early availability sustains the mood, and evidence checking grounds the answer.

text: Plant a concrete physical mismatch early, such as a fitting that is too tight or a missing part, and have characters explain it away until it pays off.
when: when a clue must survive a long investigation
why: a concrete detail stays memorable and gains weight when it returns

text: Use several lures from different sources, each presented as genuine, so the target trusts each one and does not suspect a trap.
when: designing a trap that depends on the target believing a lure
why: Independent sources make the lure seem confirmed rather than contrived

text: Introduce a single unexplained detail early and keep it unresolved until the reveal pays it off.
why: An open detail keeps the player checking it.

text: Seed suspicion through trivial logistics such as odd equipment requests, so the player's first pass reads them as eccentricity rather than as clues.
when: Opening a mystery where the hidden purpose must stay unseen early.
why: Mundane oddities hide their meaning and only gain weight when later facts recontextualise them.

text: Plant small concrete tokens such as counts, objects or keys early, so they read as proof of premeditation when they recur later.
when: when designing a clue trail for a concealed crime
why: Early tokens gain weight when the audience recognises them again.

text: Plant a mechanism's clue as an ordinary-looking detail, such as a gesture or a reaction to a cue, so players see it before its meaning is clear.
when: designing a hidden mechanism
why: The detail is later recognised as the key clue.

text: Plant the means of a later reveal early, as setting detail such as a sealed chamber or structural flaw, so the eventual use feels earned.
when: the reveal depends on a physical location or object
why: Details seen first as scenery pay off as the solution.

text: An object found along a route may have been planted to mislead, not dropped by the escaper.
A presupposing question can plant a fact the witness did not know, so any confirmation must be checked against independent sources.
1) Show the object in everyday use without emphasis. 2) Have a second character comment on it. 3) Link it to a habit. 4) Plant a name or phrase that gains meaning later.
when: a later solution depends on an earlier detail
why: ordinary context lets the detail pass as character, then read as evidence

text: 1) Place a minor detail early in a plain scene. 2) Frame it lightly so it does not stand out. 3) Reference it again later, when it connects to other details.
when: when a clue must be revealed only in retrospect
why: A clue dismissed in its own scene must still be retrievable, or the planting fails.

text: 1) Rebuild the sequence of events step by step. 2) Check that the sequence explains every trace. 3) Test it against what household members know about routines.
when: a disguise or a replaced person must be inferred from traces
why: A sequence that explains every trace is more trustworthy than one that explains some

text: 1) Place a cryptic line early in the game. 2) Record it in the player's journal without an answer. 3) Pay it off once the player has the context to interpret it.
when: Designing mystery clues that reward later discovery.
why: Delayed resolution lets the clue become meaningful when context arrives.

text: 1) Place a small, ambiguous tell in a calm scene. 2) Have a second character offer a plausible but wrong reason. 3) Reveal the truth later, pointing back to the earlier moment.
when: Foreshadowing a hidden cause

text: Plant a memorable detail or NPC early and return to it later with a sharper cue, since readers may overlook it on first pass.
when: Writing a fair-play mystery.
why: A later event makes the player recall the detail and link it to a clue, because distinctive details are recalled and linked when the scene is reconstructed.

text: Plant apparently irrelevant early details, such as a dismissal, an offhand question, a skipped routine, or a secretive habit, so they later pay off as hidden motive or timing.
why: Players forget the detail, then recognise it as the answer when the reveal arrives; ordinary-seeming details gain meaning later, rewarding readers who notice them.

text: Plant the clues a late document will need in the earlier scenes that it later reframes.
Plant a seemingly idle line of dialogue about a minor detail that becomes relevant when a timeline is checked.
why: An early casual detail becomes evidence later, rewarding attentive players

text: Show a culprit's motive, opportunity and access early in the story, so a late reversal reads as deduction rather than accident.
Plant hints of concealed knowledge in earlier dialogue or records, and make idle-seeming remarks carry hidden meaning; otherwise the twist feels like a cheat.
Plant spatial observations early that seem idle, since they can gain meaning later and reward the audience for noticing them.
Plant facts in a villain's journal that the writer does not interpret, so the player can deduce the truth before the character does.
when: designing in-game documents
why: Uninterpreted facts let players reason ahead of the character.

text: Script related events within the same in-game hour when you want players to suspect a hidden connection between them.
when: Designing scripted NPC events meant to hint at a hidden plot link.
why: Players read temporal proximity as a sign of connection.

text: Place a clue on the reverse of an item, such as a map fragment or receipt, that players must flip over to discover.
Keep a planted item in a secure place until the reveal, since it can be lost or taken before then.
Plant one anomaly, such as cargo too small for its stated purpose, that contradicts the obvious story and rewards players who check it.
Scatter small anomalies that are each innocently explainable, and reward players who link them into a pattern.
when: designing deduction puzzles
why: linking rewards players while single items stay plausible

text: Let a planted item point at an NPC who never touched it, and reward players who check the chain of hands.
when: designing misleading but fair clues
why: Checking the chain separates a planted pointer from real involvement.

text: Mark prop-triggered reactions as scripted so careful players can detect that they are staged, and let players introduce their own props to see which NPC responds.
when: Designing puzzles or reveal scenes where a prop triggers an NPC reaction.
why: A player's own prop exposes an NPC who responds on cue, revealing the performance.

text: Plant testimony such as a log or note early, so a later revisit makes the missing key deducible.
when: Designing mystery clues that pay off later.
why: Early placement lets the player connect the clue when the context returns.

text: Plant the explanation for a character's fear early so that a later use of that fear as a counter feels fair.
when: When a later scene depends on a character's weakness
why: A clue set up before its use lets players recognize the solution as earned.

text: Place a false clue through a non-player character and give it a detectable inconsistency the player can find and link to a second action.
when: When designing a mystery with a misleading clue.
why: A detectable inconsistency lets the player expose the staging through the second action.

text: Set up the decisive detail in plain sight early, before its meaning is known, then return to it as proof, so the evidence was visible from the start.
when: Setting up a clue that will prove a key link later.
why: Early visibility lets the player connect the object once its meaning is revealed.

text: Plant the unexplained object early and hold back its cause until mid-story, so the later explanation answers the question the audience holds.
Present oddities or identity-revealing details as ordinary background early, so they are accepted without scrutiny and recalled or reread when a later line changes their meaning.
when: Seeding clues in a bargain or introduction scene, or setting up a disguised-character reveal.
why: Early oddities feel mundane, so they are remembered when they become significant; ordinary details are accepted without scrutiny and later read differently.

text: A clue planted in plain view should be explained by a later event, since an unpaid hint reads as a loose thread and erodes trust.
when: Planting a hint the story will later resolve.
why: Unresolved hints make the story feel careless and reduce reader trust.

text: Leave an unexplained detail, such as mismatched handwriting or a minor figure, as a hook that a later reveal turns into a clue.
when: Building clues for a twist that reframes earlier evidence.
why: A hook already in the report becomes meaningful when the reveal explains it, rather than seeming like an error.

text: Plant an object that looks like an odd detail, then use it to carry the reconstruction of the reveal, so the reader can recheck it against what they already saw.
when: Setting up a physical clue meant to be reinterpreted later.
why: Objects seen early can be re-read once their meaning changes, making the reveal checkable.

text: Use one physical object that passes between suspects, since it carries the player from one false lead to the next.
A planted inscription in a game room can name the wrong culprit; players should be able to test it against a second source to discover the plant.
when: When designing misleading written clues in a level.
why: A checkable second source rewards careful players without making the clue unfair.

text: A deliberately placed object can carry a hint, and the person most likely to find it is often the one who placed it.
when: Evaluating whether an object was planted.
why: A planter tends to know where the object will be discovered and by whom.

text: A clue that fits the theory or neatly names the culprit may be planted; check it against physical setting, materials and the writer's known habits before trusting it.
when: A physical clue appears to confirm a theory; a clue arrives neatly and matches a suspect's visible grudge.
why: Planted evidence can imitate genuine evidence and is designed to end inquiry early; fit alone does not establish authenticity.

text: A matching item found in a room proves only that the item was there, not who placed it or when.
when: Interpreting an object found at a location.
why: Presence of an object does not establish its owner or time of placement.

text: 1) Show a small, odd detail early without explanation. 2) Mention it again briefly with no comment. 3) Give it enough narrative weight that it returns in memory. 4) Reveal its meaning later.
when: Setting up a mystery clue the audience should notice but not yet understand.
why: A detail the audience dismisses early will not register when it later matters.

text: Overheard references to unexplained things can be planted as clues that stay uninterpreted until a later payoff.
why: Unexplained fragments keep a thread open and reward recall.

text: Plant every fact used in a reveal earlier in the story, tying each to an earlier mention.
when: Writing a reveal built on hidden information.
why: A reveal resting on unseen facts feels like cheating and loses credibility.

text: Place a key somewhere unexpected as a discrepancy that sends the player back to question its holder.
when: Designing investigation clues around keys.
why: A mismatch between an account and the item's location prompts renewed questioning.

text: A name or object dropped into ordinary talk can carry a hidden link between people, and its weight comes from how a listener reacts to it.
A planted claim is a false or unverified statement offered to test another person's reaction rather than to be believed.
End each partial reveal on a hook that pulls the player into the next room or chapter before the outcome is settled.
Plant a remark in an early NPC's dialogue that matters only after another clue is found, and log it in the player's journal.
Plant an unguarded slip early in dialogue and make a trigger keyword unlock a confession only when used precisely, so the player can recognise its meaning later.
when: Designing dialogue that rewards careful questioning.
why: Early plants let the player connect a remark to a later revelation, and precision rewards careful inquiry.

text: Designers can plant small repeated habits that reward attention and let players spot inconsistencies.
Deliver a reversal through outside witnesses or pursuers rather than the protagonist's own account, so the revelation does not depend on the narrator.
why: Independent sources make a reveal more credible

text: Plant a seemingly irrelevant digression, such as a historical tract, that later reveals the key clue to the solution.
Place the decisive fact in an item or scene the player examines early, so the later reversal is earned rather than merely announced.
Only unmask someone the audience had reason to suspect of hiding something; otherwise the reveal carries no weight.
Plant a suspicion early in an incidental line, then repeat it when the audience is most agitated so it returns with added weight.
when: structuring foreshadowing or a later reversal
why: a line primed early is heard differently when it recurs under tension

text: Routine acts such as buying supplies can be planted as clues that look innocent until compared with the stated purpose, when their scale becomes suspicious.
when: A character's routine purchase or action is later compared with a stated purpose

text: Flag a physical detail as one to remember, so the reader stores it and recognises it when a later payoff matches it.
when: planting a clue early in the story
why: a flagged detail is kept for later matching

text: An antagonist could plant visions through a seer, so the player must track each seer's reliability over time rather than trust them as fixed.
when: designing seer or prophet characters in a mystery
why: reliability can change through hidden manipulation

text: A detail that contradicts an assumption, placed inside emotional material, is registered by the reader as background and stays open for later return.
when: Writing a scene where a clue must be noticed but not pursued yet
why: Emotional focus draws attention away from the detail, so it is noticed without being examined

text: A casually left note may be planted to mislead as easily as it reveals the truth.
when: A note seems to have been carelessly left.
why: Apparent carelessness can be staged.

text: Rumours can be planted deliberately, so a rumour mistaken for independent evidence may actually be a manipulation.
why: A rumour's spread does not show that it is true, and its source may have had a reason to spread it.

text: A witness may repeat a false identity the subject supplied, and a repeated name can sound authoritative enough to mislead.
why: Repetition lends an unverified claim false credibility.

text: A witness may be a plant sent by the suspect to gather information, so the investigator must watch for this before trusting the answers.
A reveal feels fair only when every clue it relies on was shown earlier; facts introduced only at the end, unseen by the player, cannot support the solution.
when: Structuring a mystery's solution, or when the solution depends on facts outside the shown clues
why: Unseen information cannot be reasoned about by the player

text: Build the final reveal only from clues the player already holds, so it reorders known facts and confirms their findings rather than adding new facts.
when: Writing a mystery's reveal or ending

text: Place the reveal at the close of a mystery, after every clue has been planted and shown, and show its reasoning so the audience can recognise the logic and recap the chain.
when: structuring the reveal of a puzzle or mystery
why: the audience can then recap the full chain of clues

text: A reveal works only when earlier planted details or misdirection build the expectation it overturns, without giving it away; without that setup it feels arbitrary.
why: A reveal without setup feels arbitrary

text: Let the explanation come from the people involved, drawing only on facts already shown.
when: When writing the reveal of a mystery.

text: Plant a witness whose sincere but wrong sighting is later explained by a physical trace, rewarding players who test the claim.
Make each step of a reveal yield a new inference that follows from clues already shown, rather than summarizing events.
when: when writing a mystery's final explanation
why: new inferences keep the reveal tense and fair

text: Stage a confrontation reveal only if the proof is secured and the culprit can be forced into an observable reaction.
Plant an unexplained sense of recognition early as a clue, and pay it off later so the audience can carry it forward.
Plant an open doubt about a harmless persona early, where the audience can see it, then supply later evidence that contradicts the surface.
when: When a reveal depends on a character seeming harmless
why: Without a visible crack the reveal reads as a cheat

text: Plant a witness who saw one suspect at a timed location, letting players break that suspect's stated alibi.
why: a witness gives players a checkable contradiction

text: Plant an NPC's reaction to an object early, so a later deliberate use of that object exposes a hidden trait and changes the encounter.
when: When a later encounter should hinge on an earlier clue
why: Players who connect an early reaction to a later test find the outcome earned rather than random.

text: Planted evidence is an item placed to point at a convenient suspect, positioned where that suspect will be blamed.
A note pointing to a concealed space shows its writer knew of that space before anyone searched for it.
Ask whether a location was chosen to be found: places already under suspicion or being searched are likely sites for planted evidence, which proves little when found easily.
when: when assessing whether evidence was placed, or a clue arrives neatly where the investigator is already looking
why: Placement is most useful where evidence will be found, so someone wanting a clue found can place it there.

text: Ask whether an object at the scene belongs to someone with no link to the crime, since borrowed items may have been planted to connect an innocent person.
Ask why a convenient discovery, confession or death arrived at that moment, especially when a case has just stalled.
when: a convenient discovery arrives as a case stalls
why: timing reveals whether the event was arranged

text: Ask whether the person a trace points to could have arranged it, since a gift can make the trace a pointer placed by another.
when: a trace seems to implicate one person
why: Items passed between people can be used to misdirect.

text: A counterpart may stage a discrepancy as a test of how the other party handles it.
Plant a distinctive habit early so the audience can judge later inferences, and let a rival imitate it to mislead.
when: When designing misdirection around character identity.
why: A planted signature gives the player a basis to test the inference.

text: Plant a false trail, such as an incriminating item in a rival's pocket with a route pointing back to the planter, that the player must clear before finding the true culprit.
why: A convincing false answer delays discovery and raises the payoff of the reveal.

text: A note placed in plain view can be a plant, so its apparent authenticity should be tested against physical details of the scene and the purported author's habits.
when: A written statement appears to explain an event
why: Planted evidence can mislead the investigator into accepting a false explanation.

text: A returned notice reading 'not known' can be a planted contradiction that makes a documented story look wrong and prompts the player to re-check.
when: a documented story has an unexplained conflicting record
why: contradictions push the player to question records they had accepted

text: A planted object may implicate an innocent person; treating a discovered item as conclusive proof without questioning whether it was planted is the mistake a frame-up exploits.
when: when an object points neatly at a suspect or a recovered item seems to close a case
why: Planted items can look like genuine evidence and make the wrong person appear guilty.

text: Evidence can be planted to point at one person, so the most obvious clue may be the one someone wanted found.
why: A plant aims at the suspect whose access looks most obvious

text: A tidy room may have been arranged to create an impression, so test whether its dust and clutter are real.
A track that leads nowhere may have been placed deliberately. Compare it with other evidence before accepting it.
when: when a trail ends without a clear destination
why: A false trail can be made to look like a genuine route.

text: 1) Ask the target to state the evidence that would justify an arrest. 2) Plant the object where they will carry it. 3) Keep them talking. 4) Ask them to reach into the pocket holding the object.
when: a target has stated a principle that a planted item can test

text: Plant deliberate trace mismatches, e.g. spectacles too old for the body, a wrong fall position, a broken component, or a uniform contradicted by hair or boots, for players to notice.
when: when designing clues that reward attention, a scene the player must reconstruct, or a scene with a misleading surface
why: A mismatch gives the player a concrete lead to test and lets a careful player overturn the obvious reading.

text: Plant a detail that does not fit the decoy's story, such as a document useless to the thieves, so an attentive player can see through the staging.
when: When designing a false trail

text: Plant evidence for every suspect so a favored theory can be tested rather than confirmed by searching only where it predicts clues.
when: Designing a mystery with several suspects
why: Balanced clues stop players from confirming a favored theory

text: Plant a mismatch, such as a generous gift from an apparently poor character, as a contradiction the player can later uncover.
when: building a mystery with NPC wealth or status
why: contradictions reward attention and drive further investigation

text: Plant a plausible false culprit with a motive while keeping the real cause available for the player to find.
when: designing misdirection in a mystery
why: the player should be misled by a fair alternative, not by missing clues

text: A witness adopts a wrong theory of an investigator's motives when it fits visible facts such as age, relationships and an odd request.
when: An outsider hears an unusual request about a person in their circle.
why: Visible facts make the wrong theory feel plausible, so the witness treats the request as improper.

text: Make the official theory coherent and wrong only in its motive or cause, then let the true solution emerge from rereading the same evidence.
when: Writing a false solution for a mystery.
why: An internally logical wrong answer is more convincing than an absurd one, so the eventual correction carries weight.

text: Chain false solutions that each use real evidence read in a different frame, assigning the same shared facts to a different suspect each time, until a final inversion.
when: Structuring a mystery with several suspect theories.
why: Each theory is consistent with real evidence, so the wrong frame is hard to spot; a reading that fits real evidence is hard to dismiss without a new source.

text: Include decoy suspects who are real enemies with their own goals, so they feel plausible without being the answer.
when: When building false leads for a mystery
why: Decoys with real motives remain credible and therefore hold the player's attention.

text: Give the audience a plausible political or conspiratorial explanation that is wrong, so attention goes to the wrong motive.
when: Building misdirection into a mystery
why: A believable alternative explanation absorbs suspicion that would otherwise fall on the real answer.

text: A plausible everyday explanation that fits some of the facts can close inquiry and divert attention from the true cause; weigh it against the full scene.
when: A misleading explanation is offered for an event and covers part of the evidence.
why: A simple, familiar story is easy to accept before evidence is checked; partial fit makes it feel complete, so searchers stop testing it against remaining clues.

text: A plausible, true-seeming reason does not clear a suspect, since an account can be true and still misleading.
when: Evaluating a suspect's stated reason
why: Plausibility is not the same as full disclosure.

text: A tidy rational explanation offered early can mislead as much as a supernatural one, especially when it was built to make the event look like a delusion.
why: A rational cover story can be engineered to hide the real act.

text: Make an NPC's explanation partly true without being a plain lie, and require players to test it against physical evidence.
when: Designing misleading NPC gossip or rumor.
why: Confirmed detail lends credibility to the unconfirmed remainder, so a partly true story is more believable and forces players to verify rather than dismiss it.

text: Make each suspect's guilt, including a wrong one, plausible on the evidence the player holds at that moment, so an arrest or blame is accepted.
when: A suspect is arrested, named or led to be blamed.
why: A weak false suspect is dismissed quickly, which removes the trap; the player must be able to accept the arrest on what they know.

text: A suspicious act or calm, coherent explanation that accounts for odd details is accepted quickly, and inquiry stops, even when it fails to fit all facts.
when: when a suspicious act comes with a reasonable explanation, or two readings of an event are both plausible
why: A plausible reason answers the question, and coherence and comfort make a neat theory easy to accept.

text: Make the first explanation or suspect plausible, internally logical and partly true or wrong, with real evidence present; then overturn it with one decisive clue the player already saw.
when: Designing a mystery with a later reveal.
why: A plausible wrong answer makes the reversal land and feels fair rather than arbitrary.

text: Plausible chains of links are not proof: check each link separately, mark inferred links as conjecture, and confirm the theory with a witness or record.
why: Inferred links otherwise look as certain as recorded facts.

text: A story that explains every detail, fits timing, or rests on uncheckable premises can still be false or aim at the wrong object; test each detail independently.
A suspect may offer an explanation before being asked, which signals the question was anticipated.
when: When a suspect volunteers an answer to an unasked question
why: Anticipating a question suggests the suspect knows the weak point

text: A plausible reconstruction is a coherent account of motive, sequence and character, distinct from evidence that would survive challenge.
Compare a suspect's reaction to accusation with what a guilty or innocent person would plausibly do in that situation.
when: a suspect responds to an accusation
why: plausibility gives the reaction a reference

text: Judge an account by whether the teller's own behaviour is plausible, such as whether they would destroy the evidence that could check it.
A plan that would swap one accomplice for a more dangerous one is one a sensible plotter avoids, which can help eliminate a suspect.
when: judging whether a suspect would plan a crime through an accomplice
why: rational plotters avoid added risk

text: Keep 'possible' separate from 'probable': a strained explanation that could be true is not supporting evidence for it.
Strong positive evidence can outweigh doubts about how strong a motive is.
Plausible pressure aimed at a witness's specific fear can make a reluctant witness talk.
when: When a witness is cooperative in principle but unwilling to confess.

text: Odd features of older buildings, such as low ceilings, often had practical reasons like warmth, so judge them by period needs rather than modern expectations.
Explanations or coincidences fitted after a trace or event is known can match any result, so claims recorded only after confirmation prove nothing.
A plausible event or assumption about what someone ought to know is not evidence that they acted; linking a named suspect to it needs direct evidence.
A tidy, plausible premise or theory built on unchecked gaps feels like established fact, spreads unchallenged, and can steer toward a chosen suspect while hiding the real cause.
when: when the theory rests on gaps its proponent admits are unchecked
why: Plausibility is mistaken for verification, so the theory spreads before anyone tests it.

text: Plausible routes or methods can fail timing, channel-arithmetic or physical checks, such as groping through a space that would cause a fall; feasibility objections can outweigh theory, so test them.
when: when judging a proposed route, method or claim verified only by appearance
why: Plausible narratives often ignore physical constraints, which may not hold.

text: Accepting a story because the teller seems plausible skips verification, and the only vouching party may be the suspect's own partner.
when: Weighing testimony from a sympathetic or interested source.
why: Plausible delivery is not evidence, and a partner's vouching has limited independence.

text: A plausible explanation that reconciles conflicting accounts is only a hypothesis until a possible actor and a witness check support it.
why: Plausibility is not proof

text: A discrepancy can be explained away by a prepared story chosen to fit it; the story must be tested against evidence before it is accepted.
A witness's remembered date may be wrong, and a plausible date can hide that mistake.
when: a witness's timeline seems consistent with other facts
why: Consistency with other details can make an error look correct

text: A plausible theory can fail once a single discriminating fact is weighed against it.
when: Only one fact contradicts an otherwise coherent story
why: Fit with most facts does not guarantee the theory is true.

text: Treating a plausible timeline as proof of the events inside it is a mistake, since a timeline shows where a person was but not who was present or why.
when: a timeline is built from traces
why: location and time do not establish presence or motive

text: Isolation and personal stake make a chain of links look stronger than it is.
when: When an investigator works alone under strain on a case that matters to them.
why: Without outside checks, personal investment inflates confidence in inferences.

text: Make each suspicion rest on a plausible basis in evidence or motive, since misdirection works only when the reason to suspect is credible.
when: designing red herrings or rotating suspects
why: unfounded suspicion reads as arbitrary

text: Give NPC witnesses estimates that are plausible but wrong, so the player must cross-check them against other evidence.
when: When designing NPC witness testimony.

text: Before an official inquiry, those on site decide who holds the evidence, whether to summon an outside investigator, and how public the matter becomes.
Show the player the exact question an NPC was asked, so they can judge what was actually confirmed rather than assuming the answer proves more.
when: An NPC vouches for another character in a generated scene
why: Players can only weigh a confirmation if they see its scope

text: Let players test a theory by performing an action and watching an NPC's reaction, as a way to reveal what the NPC knows.
Let players check a character's stated route against a map overlay or a journal of timestamps.
when: Designing NPC alibis

text: When a player's advice changes an NPC's next action, the dialogue forks into a branching path that the player's words caused.
A noise or struggle just before an accusation raises tension and lets the audience anticipate the reveal before anything is said.
In a confrontation, the player's reconstruction can trigger a visible reaction from the suspect.
why: The reaction confirms the player's deduction on screen.

text: Let players choose when to share a clue with an ally or withhold it, and show later dialogue consequences of that choice.
Let an NPC ask the player to keep a request secret, and track whether the player honours it.
Let the player's dialogue choices reveal what the player already knows, so an NPC can react to prior discoveries.
when: when designing reactive dialogue
why: Reactions to known facts make the conversation feel responsive.

text: Let the player become the prime suspect of a scene they did not create, so they must clear themselves by finding contradictions in the evidence.
why: Tests whether the player can reason their way out of a false accusation

text: Record what the player did not check or was not asked, since an omission can serve as a clue.
Let the player state a deduction in a journal or companion dialogue and have an NPC challenge each step, showing whether the chain holds.
when: when designing a deduction system for players
why: Challenge exposes weak links in the player's reasoning.

text: Track which facts the player has established and which are merely assumed, so a wrong premise produces a plausible dead end.
when: When designing a puzzle with branching deductions.

text: When a game depicts an old event, let players reconstruct it from archives and physical remains while in-world characters hold only their own beliefs.
Have players reach the conclusion themselves by combining evidence they already possess, rather than receiving it directly.
A witness's disclosure can depend on their state: a sober or pressed witness may reveal more, while an intoxicated witness's account may shift from one telling to the next.
when: When interviewing a witness who is drunk or under strain.
why: Impaired memory and changing mood alter what the witness reports.

text: Some poisons mimic heart failure and leave no characteristic signs, so a routine examination can miss them; test a natural-cause verdict before accepting it.
when: A death appears natural.
why: Natural-looking death can hide deliberate harm.

text: Early symptoms of some poisonings are hard to tell apart from common illnesses, so a suspicion needs expert confirmation before it drives action.
A water container that a victim asked to have refilled but is found dry suggests someone emptied it, and a staff member's memory of filling it can establish that it was full earlier.
when: A missing or emptied container is linked to a poisoning.
why: A discrepancy between a request and the container's state is a lead that points to tampering.

text: A bullet hole in a sash, fired from inside, is physical proof that someone stood outside the window.
A drug can cause a person to act in a trance and leave them with no recall of the act afterwards.
An intoxicated or inattentive witness's account is unreliable: impaired memory yields gaps and errors, so check any timeline built on it before accepting it.
when: A witness was drunk, distracted, or admits heavy drinking.
why: Impaired observation and memory produce unreliable detail.

text: Drink and flattery loosen a witness's tongue, so an intoxicated speaker says more than intended; treat their relayed gossip and claims as unreliable.
when: When a witness is drunk.
why: Drink loosens control over what is revealed.

text: A shared dish is cleared only if all co-eaters stayed well; when they did, shift attention to what only one person consumed, but harm to any co-eater implicates the dish.
when: Investigating an illness with a possible shared source.
why: Healthy co-diners rule out the common dish; harm to any co-eater implicates it.

text: In a poisoning mystery, design symptoms so an expert can rule out some causes, leaving the player to identify the remaining one.
when: Writing a death or illness that the player must explain.
why: Ruling out possibilities through expertise narrows the search and guides the player toward the true cause.

text: A drink chosen at a scene can reveal the drinker's trade or background, since people tend to pick drinks familiar to their own life.
A wound alone does not explain a faint; check whether the person fainted or fell and struck their head.
Before testing an earlier-dosing hypothesis, ask whether an earlier death would change anything relevant, such as an inheritance, to judge whether it matters.
Make sure every shared dish was eaten by at least two people, ideally about four, so a poison in one dish would affect several witnesses.
when: Designing or investigating a shared meal.
why: More eaters means more witnesses to any harm.

text: Prepare for poisoning by having medical help and antidotes ready, since prompt treatment can save a victim and reveal how the poison was given.
when: a poisoning is expected

text: A poison given in a shared drink suggests someone both victims knew and trusted, which sharply cuts the suspect list.
when: The method of death implies inside knowledge or trust

text: Fast-acting drugs may cause sickness and giddiness; exertion can speed poisoning and trigger fatal collapse at a time unrelated to worst symptoms, making death look like strain.
when: When matching a death to the agent's expected effect.
why: Symptoms and collapse can follow different timelines.

text: A poison puzzle built on fixed rules, such as detection thresholds and onset delays, lets players deduce which item was tainted.
Swallowed liquid poison symptoms usually appear 1–2 hours after ingestion but range 15 minutes to several hours, depending on whether stomach is empty; hours-late onset suggests later dose.
when: Estimating when a poison was taken from when symptoms began.
why: Wide onset variation weakens any single-timeline inference.

text: Strychnine is detectable in solution at about one part in seventy thousand, so only a strongly flavoured drink is likely to hide it.
A witness who seems drunk or confused may have been drugged, so their recollection is partial and needs medical checking.
Clearing an item because others ate it unharmed fails when the harmful dose was aimed at one portion.
why: Targeted dosing leaves the others unaffected

text: Audiences assume drugs only stupefy, so explaining purposeful action under a drug must first counter that expectation.
when: Presenting a drug-driven act that seems out of character.
why: The common belief makes purposeful drugged behavior seem implausible.

text: Accepting intoxication as a stock explanation for conduct skips testing the claim; treat a drunk-state claim as something to verify.
when: a character explains an outburst by having been drinking
why: The excuse is easy to offer and hard to disprove without checking

text: A half-asleep witness can give confident, specific details that are wrong, so the sharpest details deserve the most suspicion.
when: the witness was dozing or only half awake during the event
why: drowsy memory fills gaps with plausible detail

text: Taking an illness at face value before checking the timing of its symptoms can hide a fabrication.
A body left in a tidal area for days can pick up debris after death, so debris alone may not show when an injury happened.
when: when a body was exposed to an environment before examination
why: debris can be acquired after death

text: A common everyday source can make a rare substance hard to trace, so tracing by source may fail.

1) Ask everyone present what they ate. 2) Record the exact onset of illness. 3) Check the preparation details of each dish. 4) Fix an absent person's whereabouts with a timetable. 5) Compare accounts for consistency on menu and details.
when: Investigating a poisoning or illness with a possible source
why: Onset times and alibis anchor the timeline

text: 1) Inspect the injured body and its wounds closely before any formal examination. 2) Use magnification and fine tools. 3) Look for foreign fragments inside and around each wound.
when: when a wound may carry evidence of its cause
why: fragments can reveal the object or environment that caused the injury

text: 1) Identify what the victim consumed that others did not. 2) Test common shared sources first. 3) Test the victim's own supply and empty containers. 4) Inspect containers with magnification, handling them minimally. 5) Swab interior surfaces and culture the sample on a nutrient medium at body temperature overnight.
when: a cause spreads through a household and the victim's habits set them apart

text: If everyone who shared a dish was unaffected, the substance was likely added to a separate portion set aside afterward.
when: when investigating tainted food
why: A shared dish that was safe for others points to a later addition.

text: Record the exact time of a shared meal, everything eaten and drunk, and who ate and saw each item served, so harm can be traced to one item.
when: A poisoning or harm must be traced to one item consumed by one person.
why: Recorded details give each shared item witnesses and let investigators narrow the cause.

text: Give a drugged or possessed NPC a short purposeful routine, then let players reconstruct it from partial evidence.
when: Designing an NPC whose actions are later investigated.
why: Purposeful routines leave traces that players can piece together.

text: Place the source of a rare poison in an everyday item in the game world so the player must work out how the culprit obtained it.
when: Designing a poison-identification puzzle.
why: A familiar source makes the trace a real deduction step.

text: Lawsuits over rent or lease reveal who occupied land, even where the question of ownership remains unclear.
when: Ownership is uncertain but occupation matters
why: Court actions record who was in possession of a place

text: An item that cannot slip off once fitted, if missing from remains, was most likely removed on purpose, so its absence implies intent.
when: an item that could not come off by accident
why: Physical fit limits accidental loss

text: A mismatch between a room's surroundings and its occupant's apparent means invites questions about who the occupant is and why they live that way.
when: A room's contents seem inconsistent with the apparent wealth or status of its occupant.
why: Contradictions between setting and status prompt the observer to seek an explanation.

text: A sale record shows who bought an object, not who holds it now, so records alone cannot locate it.
when: when using trade records to find a current holder
why: Ownership can change after sale.

text: A forger who copies a known sample can pass a single comparison, so check the writing against several independent samples.
why: One sample can be duplicated

text: A key holder's exclusive control may be an illusion because keys can be copied, so every copy must be counted before ruling anyone out.
when: Ruling suspects in or out based on key possession.
why: Duplicate keys give access to people who appear to have none.

text: Treat precedent as a hint directing the search, not proof; a single similar case cannot establish a general rule and only supports a specific mechanism. Complex cases still need on-site examination.
Compare a new crime with recorded earlier cases to test for a shared method, not just a shared story, since repeated methods leave recognizable patterns.
when: a new crime resembles an earlier one, or its scene's method is unusual but has possible precedents
why: Known methods leave known traces

text: A past case using a similar trick makes a human cause more plausible, though it does not prove the same method was used now.
when: Weighing a human explanation for a strange event.
why: Similar prior events show a method exists, but each case still needs its own evidence.

text: A crime that shares distinctive features with an earlier unsolved case suggests the culprit studied that case, though the parallel may also be coincidence.
when: Comparing a new crime to an earlier unsolved one.
why: Shared method signatures imply knowledge of the precedent or deliberate imitation.

text: 1) Choose a known precedent whose method, victim, physical trace and motive resemble the current case. 2) List each matching feature. 3) Use the stacked matches to form a working hypothesis.
when: a recognised pattern exists but hard evidence is not yet available
why: stacked resemblances make a shared pattern more likely than chance

text: A precise, confident detail is not proof of truth: the witness may be wrong, exaggerating or repeating hearsay, so check it against independent sources.
when: When a witness gives an exact date, name, number or time.
why: Detail and confidence can coexist with error or bias; precision can feel authoritative without being verified.

text: A speaker who answers pressure with feigned puzzlement, or over-explains to defend a point, discloses more than planned.
when: when questioned under pressure
why: explaining to defend a point reveals detail

text: A witness can recall names, places and dates exactly yet remain unreliable about motive and meaning.
when: Evaluating a detailed but sincere testimony
why: Precise recall of facts does not guarantee an accurate reading of why events happened

text: A precise detail, such as an exact timestamp, is easier to check and contradict than a vague claim, so precise alibi claims are more useful to test.
when: Evaluating a witness statement or stated alibi for verifiability.
why: A specific claim can be checked and contradicted, while a vague one cannot.

text: A specific reference to a place or person provokes visible reaction where broad accusations fail.
when: Testing a guarded witness for a hidden connection.
why: Precise references signal knowledge, so the witness's reaction is more revealing than a general question.

text: Exact dates, named places and precise times can make an account look reliable while vagueness hides what the author cannot defend.
why: Precision signals reliability to readers

text: NPC witnesses can give timestamped, precise notes, while others give vague accounts that the player must verify against the environment.
Give NPCs both precise and loose phrasings of the same fact so players can press for the exact detail.
when: Writing NPC dialogue that hides a specific fact.
why: Players can pursue the exact fact through follow-up questions.

text: An exact description of a missing item narrows the search for it.
when: an item has gone missing
why: Size, calibre or type eliminates candidates.

text: Pin down exact wording in a witness's statement, since a single word such as 'only' can change its meaning.
when: testing a witness's statement
why: Small wording differences can hide a changed fact.

text: Property settled by deed with precise boundaries reduces later quarrels between heirs.
A precise clock reading from a busy, distracted or tired witness may come from memory rather than a reliable clock, so precision alone does not make a time trustworthy.
why: Precision does not guarantee accuracy.

text: A cover story with extra steps or excess detail, or told too eagerly, invites more scrutiny than a brief, measured one, since each extra detail is another checkable claim.
when: when an alibi includes extra steps or errands beyond what was asked
why: each extra detail creates another checkable claim

text: A well-remembered account is not proof of staging, because honest memory can also be precise.
when: when judging whether a witness's detailed account is false
why: Precision alone does not show deception.

text: Precise times can give false confidence if the stretch between two timed anchors is left unexamined.
A motive that explains everything may explain nothing, and stacked hypotheses leave the case open to attack.
A witness who describes a suspect too well may reveal that the pursuers have already been briefed.
when: a description is unusually precise
why: precision suggests a prepared source

text: Offer a dialogue option that asks an NPC to be precise, and open a new line of inquiry only when the NPC has a real memory of the event.
Do not use relative-position reconstruction when a record gives a precise description that survives unchanged and needs no interpretation.
when: when a deed gives exact, stable coordinates or measurements
why: Interpretation adds error where the record is already unambiguous

text: If an offender used a vehicle or tool and abandoned it, the object should be findable, and any removed part should be traceable.
when: reasoning about what an offender must have left behind
why: the act of using and discarding an object leaves a physical record

text: Predict a suspect's next step from the delay, such as complaining to the bank and then approaching the executors, and state it as an expectation to be confirmed.
why: A stated expectation keeps the inference open to correction.

text: A tip's prediction that comes true soon after raises trust in the source's other claims.
An explanation that accounts for any outcome has no predictive value; test a theory by whether it rules out some possible observations.
when: evaluating a proposed explanation
why: an explanation that fits every result cannot be checked by evidence

text: Predict where traces should appear from what the act produces, such as bleeding from a stab wound, then search that spot.
Use a stakeout only when the target's route is predictable and a direct approach would warn them.
If a witness claims a patient is near death and that claim is later disproved, a later real death will seem expected and draw less suspicion.
when: When a death follows earlier statements about the victim's condition.
why: The earlier claim sets expectations that the death appears to fulfil.

text: A predicted notice date is only an estimate, so the search should also cover nearby days.
Letting a suspect go free depends on predicting his next move accurately, so a wrong prediction can ruin the trap.

1) Infer the actor's need from the costly act or the logic of the crime. 2) Predict what else must be done to meet it, such as ordering a second container after returning an empty one. 3) Check whether those actions leave traces.
when: A motive is suggested but not yet confirmed, or a movement record has a gap.
why: Predicted actions give testable consequences; the culprit's motive dictates the action taken.

text: 1) Read the partial change as evidence of recent activity. 2) Combine it with testimony. 3) Predict where the actor will return and choose where to wait.
Listeners who hear a neat, plausible explanation accept it fully without independent check and stop asking questions.
when: A second-hand account offers a clear cause, or a trace is explained right after discovery.
why: Plausibility makes listeners stop asking.

text: Treat a self-inflicted or accidental reading of a death as a trap: check tools, marks and residue against physical facts, since earlier threats or nearby self-harm can end search early.
when: a death first looks self-inflicted or accidental.
why: Players accept the easy explanation unless the evidence contradicts it.

text: A case or confirmation that feels complete ends inquiry early, so investigators stop checking, untested gaps stay hidden and missed evidence slips through.
when: A single explanation is accepted, or a circumstantial case appears convincing.

text: A satisfactory account or convincing demonstration can close an inquiry before an available direct check or other causes are tested.
when: An account is declared satisfactory, or a defence is being evaluated.

text: Conclusions stated before their evidence is shown get rejected as guesses or mistaken for proof; untested hunches should stay labelled until verification confirms them.
when: when an investigator presents a fast answer in a formal inquiry, or when briefing someone who has a prior belief.
why: formal inquiries need proof, not guesses; a bare conclusion gives the listener nothing to weigh, so they defend their existing view.

text: Seeking direct confirmation or confronting a suspect too early alerts the culprit, letting them adjust, destroying evidence and exposing the witness who revealed a discrepancy.
when: Investigating an ongoing scheme, or confronting a suspect with a discrepancy.

text: An official or familiar-category explanation, such as mistaken identity or a fitting motive, closes inquiry before the motive is examined and hides facts that do not fit.
when: An official gives a quick explanation, or a suspect matches a familiar motive category.
why: A familiar story is accepted before its details are tested; fitting one category feels like a complete answer.

text: An investigator with an early neat theory reinterprets or dismisses contrary facts, treating nervous behaviour as evidence, and steers toward a favoured suspect.
when: when an official or rival investigator holds a convenient suspect.
why: a plausible chain of common sense makes disconfirming facts seem explainable away

text: A preferred theory, whether one's own or an authority's, directs attention toward confirming evidence and leads investigators to dismiss contradicting evidence.
when: when an authority or respected figure favours one theory.
why: pride and preference for one's own view; the preferred theory directs attention toward confirming evidence

text: A person who has been fully won over may accept any further conjecture, even conjecture resting on thin evidence.
when: A listener has just become convinced of a theory.
why: Belief once gained stops being checked, so weak extensions pass unexamined.

text: Investigators, like other people, prefer a clean explanation, and that wish for a neat answer can colour how they weigh evidence.
when: Competing explanations exist and one offers a simpler resolution.
why: A desire for closure biases judgement toward the tidier case.

text: People who already hold opinions tend to settle on the easiest solution and stop searching once it appears to have no visible flaw.
when: When a group has reached a quick conclusion about a case or problem
why: A solution without visible gaps removes the incentive to look further, so confirmation replaces testing.

text: A witness who has settled on an explanation may stop noticing details that contradict it.
why: A confident explanation replaces continued observation.

text: Players often miss correct signs in early evidence when more prominent details overlay them, so early theories can be wrong even when the answer was present.
After an alarming event, people instinctively close and fasten windows and doors, so a seal often dates from after the event.
when: A sealed room is reported right after a shocking incident.
why: People instinctively secure a space once they feel threatened.

text: People reach for the most familiar or dramatic explanation of an event, such as a romance or a rival faction, even when that explanation fits the shape people expect rather than the facts.
when: Witnesses or NPCs explain an unexplained event.
why: Familiar narratives feel satisfying and close the question, hiding the actual cause.

text: Bring in an outside investigator early, before anyone disturbs evidence or handles the body, while the setting remains intact.
when: when foul play is possible
why: Untouched evidence remains usable for the investigation.

text: The earliest vivid account can shape public belief for years, and later corrections may take a long time to displace it.
why: first impressions anchor belief

text: A known medical history can supply an easy natural explanation, so a death may be certified without inquest and the case closes early.
why: The ready explanation discourages further examination

text: A neat, harmless explanation or plausible generalisation ends the question early and stops the search for a deeper cause; treat it as probable until an independent check supports it.
when: An ordinary cause or generalisation is offered for an eerie, suspicious or contradictory event.
why: A ready explanation satisfies curiosity before the evidence is checked.

text: Accepting a plausible explanation early, such as a faint or a warning, closes the question and stops the search for alternatives, possibly burying a clue whose meaning is unchecked.
when: An explanation appears plausible early, especially an innocent one.
why: Early acceptance stops the search for alternatives.

text: A plausible explanation covering only part of the evidence can hide a real threat or remaining facts, so weigh all evidence before accepting it.
when: An investigator has a theory or first natural explanation that fits part of the evidence.
why: Partial fit feels like proof, so contradicting facts are ignored until the theory breaks down.

text: Committing to a theory built from partial facts before witnesses are cross-checked hardens it, so later evidence is fitted to the theory rather than tested and misread.
Deciding guilt, or hardening a theory into a formal charge, before evidence is checked locks in an unverified conclusion and risks a mistaken arrest.
when: Early theories are acted on before verification.
why: Commitment to a first theory discourages later checking.

text: Clearing a suspect on partial proof, or on a judgment about their cover, is as hasty as accusing early; test that hypothesis before clearing them.
