Treating a probable reading, a striking clue, or a dramatic headline as settled closes rival explanations; keep them open until alibis and other evidence are checked.
when: An investigation is under public or internal pressure, or a striking find appears.
why: Vivid clues feel decisive and create a sense of resolution that discourages further checking.

text: Reading a key document dramatically, or through someone's summary, settles a case early; check the source text and its stated times against other evidence first.
when: Reading a key document in a case.
why: Dramatic framing and secondhand summaries replace checking the source text.

text: Labelling an anomalous act accidental, or an anomaly forgetfulness or a mistake, closes the question and hides the clue that would disprove a weak theory.
when: A missing detail or anomalous act is explained away without evidence.
why: An accident label closes the question before any alternative has been tested.

text: Explaining away a witness's report, or a quick label for a suspect's odd conduct, such as overtired, overexcited or mad, closes inquiry before the claim is checked.
when: A group explains away a witness's report, or a neighbour or biased informant offers a quick label for unusual conduct.
why: Attributing the report to the witness's state replaces checking the claim; a dismissive label ends investigation before the behaviour is understood.

text: Dismissing a lead or an improbable account before verifying the fact that closes it, or testing its details, can discard a real line of inquiry or a true report.
Assuming the subjects outmanoeuvred the searchers, or abandoning after repeated empty results, ends the search before untested leads are tried.
when: A trail goes cold after exhausting known sources, or many checks return nothing.
why: Assuming defeat stops the search before untested leads are checked; repetition creates fatigue and false closure.

text: Declaring a crime or method impossible before listing when each barrier was in place, and checking each step it requires, hides the window or explanation that allowed it.
Abandoning an explanation or timing mismatch for a new theory before checking the old one against expert evidence leaves unverified conclusions and the anomaly unexplained.
Naming a suspect without evidence for a withheld cause, or assigning ownership of a found object too quickly, can point at the wrong culprit.
when: A cause is withheld, or a found object is first attributed.

text: Accepting a neat clue sequence or one strong physical clue, and stopping once it seems complete, lets a wrong suspect or answer settle the case.
why: A single clue can mislead, and the first theory is often the least tested.

text: Early impressions from physical signs, or formed in darkness or confusion, are often wrong; treat them as provisional until checked against a reliable cue.
when: Bystanders interpret a body or scene before experts examine it, or impressions form in darkness or while confused.
why: Initial readings are made without full evidence, so they can mislead later investigation.

text: A theory defended by patches for each contradiction, or built from one plausible mechanism, must have each patch or mechanism tested independently against alternatives.
when: A theory is defended by successive explanations, or developed from a plausible mechanism.
why: Individually plausible patches can hide that the overall structure rests on unverified assumptions; confidence can hide untested alternatives.

text: Accepting a witness's account without independent confirmation early in a case can delay the investigation for a long time.
An investigator convinced of the culprit can stop testing other readings while the evidence still allows them.
when: before the suspect is questioned
why: certainty ends further testing

text: Clearing the wrong person too early, or with an unsound method, can make the public distrust the whole investigation.
Dismissing a character's claims too early can make a later reversal feel unearned.
why: players who ignored the claim cannot see why it was later vindicated

text: Acting on an unchecked label can produce a decision that later looks wrong, and doubts that arrive afterwards do not undo it.
A sorted list of clues is still a hypothesis; conclusions drawn too quickly should be re-tested against the facts.
why: Quick sorting can produce confident but wrong chains of reasoning

text: Forgiving a revealed motive can end the inquiry early and leave other threads untested, so do not accept a late confession as complete.
when: a confession resolves part of a mystery
why: Unexplained facts may remain.

text: Closing off every safe option too early leaves the protagonist's remaining risk looking arbitrary rather than chosen.
A rare explanation can be accepted too early; common explanations should be rejected first, with evidence.
A first-thought theory can survive only as narrowed by new evidence. Keep other candidate explanations open after a timing clue eliminates some of them.
why: Early favorites tend to persist even when the evidence only partly supports them.

text: Dismissing an unusual explanation early, based on a quick check of precedent, can close off the real answer; treat such checks as tests, not verdicts.
when: an event seems to fit no ordinary explanation
why: precedent can be incomplete, so early verdicts hide valid options

text: A clue can be dismissed on first reading and regain meaning only after a later event, so keep early clues on file for reexamination.
A firm witness claim may be a deliberate lie; accepting it early keeps the investigator treating a room as sealed when it is not.
Publishing a clue before it is understood can send a whole community down the same wrong path.
Early judgments drawn from appearance can close an investigation before the decisive question is asked.
when: An official reaches a conclusion before establishing the key facts

text: Resolving a threat too early leaves a later reversal with no weight, because the audience no longer fears the outcome the reversal would overturn.
Accepting a plausible decoy early ends the search for the fact that contradicts it, so the case stays closed on a false answer.
Public demand can push for disclosure before the solution is ready, so the reveal may be rushed.
when: Under public pressure before a solution is complete.
why: Audiences want answers and may press for them before the evidence is in place.

text: Abandoning a sound theory after one disappointing scene is overreaction, while explaining every anomaly as cover is underreaction; both stop the theory from being revised correctly.
when: when evidence contradicts a theory once or repeatedly
why: a theory should change in proportion to the weight of evidence

text: A failed public appeal can reflect a flaw in the method rather than an absence of witnesses, so check why it produced nothing.
Closing the supernatural question early on a mundane cause that fits only one observation leads to a wrong conclusion.
when: When an eerie event has a plausible natural explanation
why: Partial fit is mistaken for full explanation

text: Overusing official sign-offs can make a case feel closed too early and reduce suspense.
when: Writing investigation resolutions.
why: Verified-seeming outcomes leave nothing to uncover.

text: Dismissing a fated or supernatural explanation too quickly can hide a real human cause, so still check the arrangement of facts.
A neat match between a weapon and a fragment can close a case too quickly, before other evidence has been weighed.
when: A physical match appears to resolve the question.
why: A single convincing link can hide competing explanations.

text: Treating a lost stretch of time as supernatural before the dates have been checked jumps to a conclusion the records may explain.
Jumping to cause before establishing identity leaves every later inference without an anchor, and speculation treated as a finding weakens the case when contradicted.
when: Building or solving mystery narratives.
why: Unsupported inferences collapse when new evidence arrives.

text: Closing the case once the visible culprit is found can miss the planner behind the scene.
when: A minor culprit has been caught.
why: The visible act is not always the main one.

text: Mark the suspects who need the closest study as a separate priority group within the working roster.
when: when the roster is too large to study equally

text: 1) Collect the audience's guessed answers. 2) Eliminate each guess through plot changes. 3) Repeat until common guesses fail before the reveal.
why: Revision prevents the puzzle from being solved early by accident.

text: Do not name a culprit or share a conclusion until proof is complete, the group is ready, or the inquiry is finished; early answers mislead.
when: The true explanation depends on evidence not yet gathered.
why: An early conclusion can send the audience or group toward a wrong answer.

text: Confronting a suspect early can force a confession, but dismissal or departure may remove the only source of information.
when: when deciding whether to press a source now or later
why: Pressure can end access to a witness who could have supplied more.

text: Confronting a suspect with thin evidence risks a flat denial and a more guarded suspect.
when: when deciding when to confront a suspect
why: confrontation timing shapes the suspect's response

text: Arresting a suspect early may steady him or end the chance to gather more evidence; delaying keeps evidence coming but leaves the suspect free to act.
when: the case still needs more proof

text: Judge whether a crime was planned by gathering several arrangements, such as a watched target, a waiting substitute or a carried tool; they strengthen the case when they point the same way.
when: a crime shows signs of setup
why: several independent preparations are harder to explain innocently than one

text: Premeditation shows as purchases that each serve one purpose; ordinary items look harmless alone but become suspicious when combined, so check each item's probable use.
when: when a suspect bought items before an act

text: 1) Confirm the item was present and is now absent with no substitute left. 2) If the culprit planned the removal, expect a replacement or altered contents. 3) If neither is found, infer improvisation.
when: An unexplained gap is found at a scene
why: Planning usually leaves preparations behind

text: Make a prepared replacement or tool a visible sign of premeditation, so the player can read a planned act from the scene.
when: Designing a planned crime or action
why: Players reason from visible preparation

text: Check a theory's premises against relevant records and physical facts before building on it; one contradicting record or medical or positional detail can collapse the whole theory.
why: Records can contradict the premise outright

text: Overturning a story's central premise, such as a belief about a death, changes the whole motive, so earlier accounts built on that premise must be re-examined in full.
when: a twist reverses the premise behind a character's account
why: the earlier account rested on the false premise

text: A neat argument built on a mistaken premise weakens once the premise is corrected, however sound its logic seems.
why: the conclusion depends on the premise, not on the reasoning alone

text: 1) Name each assumption the conclusion depends on; mark observed premises and label the rest provisional, granted only for the argument. 2) Test every unmarked premise before accepting it by asking what evidence or what follows if it is false. 3) Use conclusions as premises for the next step, keeping the chain visible to expose the weakest step.
when: When several facts point in different directions or a case has closed on untested assumptions
why: Unverified premises can carry a wrong conclusion

text: A person who admits being at the scene while denying the act can remain a suspect if the timeline leaves them alone with the victim's belongings.
when: when a suspect admits presence but denies the crime
why: opportunity with the victim's possessions is still incriminating

text: A suspect seen in company when an event happens gets an alibi that witnesses tend to accept without question.
why: A companion's presence is taken as proof of where the suspect was.

text: A person's presence in a place can be established by others who were there the same day, which places that person within reach of the scene.
why: Shared presence with other occupants gives an independent link to the location.

text: A per-event presence list narrows suspects by showing who could have been present, excluding anyone absent from each event.
Overlap with events or confirmed presence shows only proximity, not connection; the case must also link the suspect to the crime itself.
why: Linking a figure only because movements overlap can send the investigation the wrong way.

text: A verified document can be a weak alibi if it proves presence in a place without proving who was there.
1) Test a claimed presence against a dated schedule of events. 2) Check the wording of any denial. 3) Check the witness's role. 4) Conclude only if all three agree.
when: judging whether a witness attended a stage of a proceeding
why: A narrow denial alone is not proof of presence elsewhere.

text: Do not treat a suspect's silence about his movements as proof of guilt; the real question is whether he was at the scene.
when: a suspect will not account for his time
why: silence alone does not place him at the crime

text: Confirmed presence in a place does not verify what the person did there or during an unexplained gap. Treat those parts as unverified.
when: when a confirmed alibi covers only part of a period

text: 1) Get the suspect to commit to a specific claim with a time and place. 2) Check it against an independent sighting or record they do not control. 3) Put any contradiction to them and note the answer or change.
when: A statement conflicts with another witness or can be checked against an independent record.
why: A commitment makes the contradiction harder to escape; a verified contradiction tests the account directly.

text: 1) Pick a specific fact you already hold that the suspect believes you know. 2) Confront them with it without revealing its source. 3) Note the details they give next.
when: A witness refuses to answer or has given an incomplete account.
why: Naming a fact they think you hold prompts them to fill in details without exposing the source.

text: Confront a suspect only when the proof is complete and each link can be stated clearly, since any gap lets the suspect deny or counter and destroy evidence.
when: Choosing when to confront a suspect.
why: An incomplete confrontation warns the suspect and lets evidence be destroyed; premature confrontation gives openings to deny.

text: Confront only with solid dated evidence, and ease pressure on sick, distressed, dying or fragile witnesses, since forced answers may be unreliable and excess pressure can cause collapse or self-harm.
when: Questioning a frail, distressed or frightened witness.
why: Fear makes witnesses withdraw or reshape answers; excess pressure can cause harm and produce no useful admission.

text: A detail that witnesses disagree on, such as a closed window, often surfaces only under repeated questioning, and each disagreement becomes a lead.
when: Multiple witnesses describe the same physical detail differently.
why: Pressing for detail exposes conflicts that a single account hides.

text: A witness confronted with the exact words of a quarrel may admit the quarrel but refuse to state its subject.
when: when a quoted phrase exposes a partial account
why: admitting the event is easier than naming its cause

text: Pressing an evasive speaker can make the questioner look rude, so a deflection works socially even when it answers nothing.
Test each link of an accusation chain separately, including awkward ones, since a suspect may steer attention toward a rival and an avoided question stays unresolved.
when: a suspect points suspicion at another party
why: A single persuasive chain can hide a weak or missing link.

text: Press hardest on the points a witness hesitates over, such as who suggested an action or who forbade an appointment.
when: during an interview where a witness pauses
why: Hesitation marks where the withheld information lies.

text: Test a proposed purpose for a victim against their clothing or state; attire that contradicts the purpose makes it unlikely.
when: a victim's reason for leaving or acting is proposed

text: Avoid heavy pressure on a witness whose cooperation you still need, since pressure can produce a prepared answer.
When a community turns against a successful member with no verifiable facts, test the claim against physical or documentary evidence wherever it exists.
when: an accusation rests only on rumor
why: Unverifiable claims cannot be settled by reputation.

text: Build suspense in a confrontation with silences, repeated actions and objects knocked over during the conversation.
A confession can be obtained by confronting one NPC's testimony with another's contradicting account.
when: Designing interrogation mechanics with multiple witnesses
why: Presenting a contradiction forces the witness to revise or admit the truth

text: A false claim by a witness or staff member can point the player toward the wrong suspect until a physical object contradicts it.
when: claim conflicts with an object found on the premises

text: Confronting a suspect with a full accusation before controlling the exits or securing the case can warn them, letting them flee or coordinate their story before investigators test it.
when: The suspect is confronted before the investigator controls the exits or the rest of the case is secured.
why: Pressure drives a guilty suspect to escape, and a warned suspect can align accounts with others.

text: Pressing a reluctant, protective or gatekeeping witness too hard, abruptly, after refusal, or by demanding memory proof, can make them withdraw and close off later cooperation.
when: Interviewing a reluctant or protective witness.
why: Pressure raises fear, and being asked to prove recall reads as an accusation, so the witness protects themselves.

text: Pressuring a loved one to extract a confession can damage the relationship and undermine the case.
Pressuring a witness over the phone can cost their cooperation, so the cost should be weighed before pushing a reluctant witness.
when: Witness is reluctant to talk

text: 1) Obtain a third party's account of the suspect's whereabouts. 2) Confront the suspect with its specific claim rather than accepting or rejecting it outright. 3) Compare the two accounts detail by detail.
when: a suspect's account conflicts with or supplements another witness
why: Specific comparison reveals agreement and gaps.

text: 1) Hold the confrontation back until the audience has context. 2) Lengthen the approach with dim light, weather and a glimpsed figure. 3) Pause before entry, using a plea to add hesitation. 4) Close with a quiet remark looking back.
when: building tension toward a key confrontation
why: withholding and delaying the final step raises the weight of the moment

text: 1) List every way in and out of the location. 2) Test the suspect theory against each route. 3) If the theory fails every route, discard it and check the remaining mechanisms.
when: a convenient culprit is proposed for a locked or sealed scene

text: 1) Check the scene geometry: exits, sightlines and who watches them. 2) Check the victim's known habits. 3) Check the logistics the theory needs. 4) If the theory fails, clear the suspect and shift to whoever has access, motive and means.
when: when a dramatic suspect's route to the crime seems too easy
why: Physical constraints can rule out an obvious culprit.

text: 1) Ask the accuser how they know the claim. 2) Check whether the timing fits the known events. 3) Check whether the accuser's motive fits. 4) Compare the claim with facts already established.
when: A character points suspicion at another person.
why: A claim that fails these checks may be a red herring or deliberate misdirection.

text: 1) Establish the broad motive pool for all suspects. 2) Ask the accuser for specifics. 3) Test those specifics against scene facts, such as how each victim was struck. 4) Reject claims needing impossible sequences or two culprits.
when: when one witness directly accuses another with little independent support
why: Motivated accusations must be checked against facts before they are accepted.

text: 1) Identify what the act was meant to achieve. 2) Check whether that aim fits the suspect's temperament and goals. 3) If it does not fit, consider a different actor or motive.
when: A crime detail is hard to explain.
why: Working from purpose narrows the explanations for an unusual act.

text: 1) Find when the alleged grudge began. 2) Compare that date with the date of the event. 3) If the relationship started after the event, reject the grudge as an explanation for the testimony.
when: A witness is accused of acting from a prior quarrel
why: A grudge cannot cause testimony that predates it

text: 1) State the accusation plainly. 2) Watch for fear and loss of composure. 3) Threaten exposure to what the suspect values most. 4) Note any shift from defiance to bargaining.
when: evidence is secure enough to accuse
why: reactions and demands reveal what is at stake

text: 1) State the claim's checkable prediction. 2) Search the most obvious place. 3) If it is empty, search a second place. 4) Rule out each rival explanation one at a time.
1) State the suspicion. 2) Check it against the known routine and access rules. 3) Discard it if the routine makes it impossible.
when: A witness offers an unfounded opinion
why: Routine checks expose suspicions that rest on no basis

text: 1) State the benefit given up. 2) List every rival explanation for giving it up. 3) Rule out those that fail. 4) Keep the remaining explanation provisional until an independent check confirms it.
1) Ask whether one event could have caused the other. 2) Check what each person knew at that time. 3) Reject the link if either check fails.
when: A suspected causal link between two events in a timeline.

text: 1) Name a plausible motive that the evidence suggests. 2) Offer an alternative explanation for it. 3) Watch the witness's response for shame or confusion. 4) If she shows neither, drop the motive and seek a different cause.
when: A motive looks plausible but is unconfirmed.
why: A calm, unembarrassed reaction to the alternative rules out the suspected motive, forcing the investigator to find another explanation.

text: 1) Accept the witness's denial at first. 2) Arrange a second view where the suspect's full face is visible to the witness. 3) Point the suspect out again and watch for colour change or stillness. 4) Redirect the witness's gaze and watch whether the suspect relaxes.
when: a witness's denial and a suspect's behaviour may disagree
why: a visible reaction can contradict a verbal denial

text: 1) Ask whether the suspicion comes mainly from personal dislike. 2) Test the suspect's motive. 3) Compare stated aims with conduct. 4) Weigh claimed sacrifices against known character. 5) Decide.
when: a suspicion rests mainly on feeling and must be checked before acting or accusing
why: feeling alone can mislead, so motive, statements and conduct give a firmer basis

text: 1) Refuse to excuse a reluctant witness when you have the authority to insist. 2) Press persistently until the withheld answer is given. 3) Weigh the disclosure, since the witness may be shielding someone or hiding their own part.
when: A witness's reluctance is itself a clue and the questioner can insist on an answer.
why: Persistent pressure can force disclosure of a third party's name.

text: 1) Rebuild the motive as a causal chain of steps. 2) Present the chain aloud to the suspect. 3) Invite correction. 4) Watch the suspect's response for signs of admission.
when: Evidence supports a motive but not yet a confession.
why: A coherent chain that cannot be disputed can force an admission.

text: 1) Show the suspect that the evidence is complete and escape is impossible. 2) Reconstruct the crime step by step from known facts. 3) Watch the reaction. 4) Ask for the true account of the missing act.
when: the facts are assembled and the suspect's own account is the missing piece
why: reconstruction removes the suspect's grounds for denial

text: 1) Fix the terms of the reward or agreement first. 2) State the accusation plainly, naming the responsible party. 3) Verify an outside fact before confronting. 4) Press for full detail until the account is complete.
when: Revealing that a powerful or trusted figure is responsible.
why: Settled terms and verified facts prevent denial and make the confrontation effective.

text: 1) Check the outsider claim against physical traces, such as footmarks along the border. 2) Check it against conditions such as weather and lighting.
when: when a single explanation depends on an unseen visitor
why: Physical and environmental facts often contradict an unseen intruder.

text: 1) Gain access with a brief, pointed message. 2) Confront the suspect with knowledge that makes denial costly. 3) Let the suspect speak, then test each claim against facts. 4) Set terms using the threat of consequences.
when: A suspect is guarded and holds information the investigator needs.
why: Known evidence makes denial costly and draws out a fuller account.

text: 1) Hear the witness's simple account. 2) Test it against independent physical traces such as a route or timing. 3) When the account conflicts with the traces, recite the full checked route. 4) Press with a direct accusation to force the witness to respond.
when: A witness's account includes a route or timing that physical evidence can check.
why: Presenting a verified sequence leaves the witness no room to dispute details.

text: 1) Weigh how unlikely the match is, and check whether the matching item is common. 2) Test each profile trait separately: means, knowledge, skill, access. 3) Widen the pool to everyone with the same access. 4) Weigh motive and relationship. 5) Check whether the suspect could have learned the knowledge innocently.
when: a clue appears to name a particular person
why: Keeps a match a hypothesis until independent evidence supports it

text: 1) Narrate the full sequence with times and each person's moves, including disposal of evidence. 2) Ask the listener to check each step. 3) Note what they correct, since corrections reveal what they most want to protect.
when: the suspect has already been placed at the location by evidence

text: 1) Identify the claim the sworn alibi cannot explain. 2) Name the specific lie, not the broader crime. 3) Apply pressure through what the suspect stands to lose. 4) Obtain a detailed admission. 5) Check one detail against independent facts before accepting it.
when: a sworn account conflicts with other testimony
why: a specific lie is easier to address than a general accusation

text: 1) Gather facts about the witness's past before the interview. 2) Put them one at a time in rapid succession, so each question names a real event. 3) Watch for the witness's physical reaction.
when: when a witness may hide a past
why: Specific, prepared facts make evasion harder.

text: 1) State the wrongdoing plainly and say the truth is wanted. 2) Ask one narrow question that is hard to dodge. 3) Give the witness a reason to talk. 4) Follow up on a related point.
when: questioning a frightened witness with a clear self-interest
why: A narrow question and a clear reason to cooperate lead a reluctant witness to fill in details.

text: 1) Present the evidence to the suspect face to face. 2) Ask a pointed question about who would gain from the suspect's death or disgrace. 3) Observe the answer and any secondary reactions. 4) Decide whether to withdraw or press further.
when: When the suspect's reaction is itself informative and a formal charge is premature.
why: The reaction to direct evidence reveals more than a formal accusation would.

text: 1) Open with familiar small talk to keep the relationship. 2) Cut the preliminaries with rapid, short questions. 3) Ask directly for the result until it is given.
when: A contact is reluctant to give information
why: Pressing briefly keeps the relationship intact

text: 1) Ask a narrow question that pins down a claimed item or detail. 2) Repeat the question when the answer conflicts with earlier statements. 3) Request a demonstration that tests the claim directly.
1) Name the motive and the suspect's inner conflict first. 2) Recap the chain of events in order. 3) State the terms plainly. Use a one-way channel so the suspect cannot interrupt.
when: the evidence is complete enough that denial would be pointless
why: an ordered recap and a controlled channel let the investigator control the telling

text: 1) Make a neutral request for information and wait. 2) If the suspect deflects, press in steps. 3) Raise the stakes with a formal consequence, then offer a choice between two formal options.
when: Suspect has a known relationship to the victim but says little
why: Escalating stakes gives continued silence a cost

text: 1) Separate the verifiable fact in an accusation from its emotional charge. 2) Test that fact on its own. 3) Ask follow-up questions and watch whether the accused's answers grow vaguer.
when: a witness accuses another person
why: isolating the fact keeps the emotional charge from deciding the question

text: 1) Stage a confrontation in front of the group. 2) Use a prompt that makes the guilty person act. 3) Let a sudden movement or reaction expose them. 4) Confirm the summary with a co-conspirator's confession.
when: When the reveal should be dramatized rather than explained.
why: A reaction under pressure makes the trait visible in the moment.

text: 1) Ask a direct question. 2) Allow a pause. 3) Note whether the answer deflects, contradicts, or fits the facts. 4) Judge each reply against the situation.
when: Questioning a suspect or NPC under pressure.
why: The pattern of response shows where the answer is hidden without relying on one reply.

text: 1) Tell the accused that accusations are being made against them. 2) Let them hear who the accusers are. 3) Have each accuser name the accused in turn. 4) Ask the accused to explain why they were named.

1) Move the conversation to a private room and close the door before speaking. 2) Ask about a named person and their history, not general matters. 3) Describe the suspicion without naming a source, saying others share it. 4) State the fallback route you will take if the witness refuses.
when: A witness is reluctant to answer

text: Gate a confrontation on the player holding a proven fact or enough collected contradictions, so it has a checkable basis and is not run without evidence.
when: Gating NPC confrontations or scheduling a confrontation scene.
why: A confrontation without proof can fail with nothing learned or test nothing.

text: Confront a bluffing suspect by opening with undeniable concrete items, naming corroborating witnesses, showing physical evidence, and laying out each detail rather than one accusation.
when: The suspect tries to deny or bluster during a confrontation with real evidence.
why: Undeniable, complete specifics are harder to deflect and establish credibility before harder claims are made.

text: Test a strong motive by asking whether it explains the act itself, not only why the suspect is blamed.
when: a suspect has a clear motive

text: Before accepting a grudge as the explanation for an accusation, test the actual claim, since a motive explanation can be plausible yet untested.
when: deciding whether a grudge explains an accusation away

text: Fire the confrontation event at the moment the player presents the final piece of proof, not earlier in the sequence.
Confront a suspect publicly only when the evidence is strong enough that onlookers' reactions cannot stop the confrontation from succeeding.
when: when planning an accusation in a crowded setting
why: a weak case collapses under crowd pressure

text: Do not confront a suspect when the account could be overheard or key facts remain unverified, since an interruption can derail the decisive moment.
Build a suspect's case from several weak clues, but include a contradiction the player can find, so a neat case is not automatically correct.
when: Designing a suspect the player can build a case against.
why: A findable contradiction rewards checking instead of accepting the first tidy theory.

text: Model a confrontation as a question sequence in which each answer unlocks the next fact the player can use.
Do not accept a witness's first refusal as final; press for the account, since reluctance often reflects loyalty rather than falsehood.
when: A witness declines to share what they heard.
why: Initial refusal is common and can be overcome by persistence.

text: Threats and provocation may draw a confession from a volatile suspect, but lose force against a composed, stable one, so pressure alone rarely works.
when: Pressing a suspect with no eyewitness and weak physical proof

text: Pressing a defensive, fragile or sensitive-topic witness too hard can make them order you out, withdraw, panic or give guarded replies, ending useful testimony.
when: Pressing a defensive witness repeatedly; a witness already holding back; probing a topic they avoid
why: Excessive pressure turns the exchange hostile and triggers defensiveness, closing the channel and reducing information gained

text: Threats and anger are tactics, not evidence; tag each confession with its pressure source, such as threat or despair, and require corroboration before acting on it.
when: Logging confessions in a case system
why: The tag reveals how far the statement can be trusted

text: Pressure exposes liars and forces clear answers, but also makes honest or reluctant witnesses lie, falter or withdraw; use it when exposure matters more than truth.
when: Choosing how hard to question a witness
why: Pressure cannot tell a nervous truth-teller from a liar, and raises stakes for the subject, who may protect themselves instead of answering

text: Equal depth in both tracks suggests a rider was forcing the pace, with weight thrown forward onto the handlebars.
when: Both tyre tracks show the same depth.
why: Pushing hard shifts weight forward, so the front and rear marks press equally.

text: Under pressure, a suspect's denial may contradict their own earlier words, a sign that the pressure is working.
Heavy pressure can make a loyal witness shut down completely, and repeated attempts may fail to break her loyalty.
when: under repeated questioning
why: loyalty can outweigh fear of pressure

text: Under sharp questioning a witness may show physical tells such as a drained face, a hand pressed to the chest or a sudden flush of anger.
when: a witness is pressed on a sensitive fact
why: pressure produces involuntary physical signs

text: A person who has escaped a pressing situation, such as an unwanted engagement, may have a motive to conceal events.
Suspects rarely disclose their whole story without sustained pressure, so psychological tactics alone seldom produce a full confession.
Use a clue that comes from pressure rather than calm planning when the plot needs a lapse by otherwise composed offenders.
when: Writing a mystery where the culprit is usually careful.
why: Pressure-induced mistakes are plausible and differ from the planned behaviour.

text: Use pressure rather than proof to draw out a visible reaction; a suspect who feels watched is more likely to make a move the observer can see.
when: A suspect can act and the observer needs a visible move
why: Feeling watched prompts action over silence

text: Silence, sudden accusations and unexpected known facts force reactions that reveal whether a suspect is lying or merely surprised.
Asking a witness what they mean by not recalling forces a commitment to a claim that can be tested.
when: a witness repeatedly answers that they cannot remember

text: Forced inaction raises pressure: when characters cannot act until a signal arrives, restlessness builds and the eventual action feels more urgent.
when: when the plot holds characters waiting for a message or event
why: Frustrated waiting makes the next development land with more force

text: A binary choice with no third option forces a concealed fact into the open, since the suspect must either admit it or accept the test.
when: when a rival or witness is holding back an item
why: Removing an escape option compels a visible answer.

text: Pressing a cornered or resistant suspect hard provokes hostility and objection that multiply dangers; calm, persistent questioning often works better.
Pressure can provoke an outburst that hands control of the room to the suspect.
Heavy pressure can backfire: a suspect may recast the questioning as persecution, forcing the questioner to soften manner to keep the interview going.
when: Interrogation becomes aggressive.
why: Perceived mistreatment gives the suspect sympathy and a reason to disengage.

text: Forcing a disguise off can expose the person who forces it to legal liability, such as charges for assault.
when: An unmasking is done without consent

text: Using force before establishing the facts shifts moral weight onto the accuser, who can be seen as the aggressor even if they were right.
A statement made under pressure can be passed on as settled fact by a listener who never witnessed the pressure.

1) Control the room so the suspect cannot leave. 2) Show a threat calmly without using it. 3) When fear appears, respond kindly and promise no harm. 4) Signal you already know more than they admitted.
when: suspect is frightened and holds only partial knowledge
why: fear, then reassurance, and visible knowledge lower resistance and remove the option of clever lying

text: 1) Recall the two alternatives offered earlier. 2) Set a public challenge against a quiet alternative. 3) Judge the likely response by how much the target fears exposure. 4) Send each contact with a specific purpose.
when: the target is sensitive to reputational damage and a legal option exists
why: the choice is defined by options already raised

text: Offer the player a choice between pressing an NPC now and waiting for a better moment, so restraint is a meaningful option.
when: when an NPC withholds information
why: the timing of pressure changes what the player learns

text: Use pressure tactics only when there is evidence to test the account against.
A pretext can open access and draw information that direct questions would not, but it fails once the claim is checked, can taint testimony, and exposes the investigator if discovered.
when: A witness is hiding a fact, or direct questioning would alert the suspect or fail.
why: Cover stories depend on claims not being verified, and deception carries ethical and practical risks.

text: Characters can hide real feelings behind a game or pretend role, and the true feelings tend to surface when the pretence breaks down.
when: two characters agree on a pretence about their relationship
why: the pretence gives safe cover for emotions neither will state

text: Use a small pretext, such as returning a found or dropped item, to conceal the real aim of observing a reaction or checking what is happening inside a room.
when: Planning a question that must not reveal its purpose, or checking what is happening inside a room.
why: A plausible reason lowers the suspect's guard and makes their reaction more revealing.

text: Check whether a stated reason for entering or acting matches the real situation, especially when the excuse is convenient.
when: someone gives an errand to explain their presence
why: a pretext can conceal the real purpose

text: Ask what pretext would let someone administer the method unnoticed; without a plausible pretext, a candidate is weakened.
when: Evaluating whether a suspect could have acted unseen.
why: Access without a believable reason is hard to achieve in practice.

text: Choose a pretext whose role fits the interviewee's standing, since a role that does not suit the person's status is likely to be rejected.
when: When selecting a cover story for an interview
why: A mismatch between role and status can lead to refusal or exposure

text: A legitimate task, such as helping finish a job, gives a character reasons to be inside an otherwise closed household or room.
Use a respectable pretext, a plausible reason for being there, to enter a place or join a group when access is needed.
when: Access to a place or group is blocked without a reason.

text: A plausible role that matches what the site expects to see can grant limited access, provided it is repeated consistently.
when: Entry is needed for a limited time.
why: A role that fits expectations draws little suspicion.

text: Framing a dialogue option as a pretext can unlock different NPC responses to the same question, depending on how it is framed.
when: dialogue choices that ask about an absent person

text: A pretext can fail: the witness may distrust the stated reason, and an unlikely lead can waste time at the first address tried.
when: When using a pretext or pursuing a long-shot lead
why: Unverified reasons and unlikely leads carry a real chance of producing nothing

text: A pretext that is out of character for the person offering it is easily recognised, which exposes the plan to the target.
when: when a cover offer comes from a character who would not normally make it
why: Targets notice inconsistencies between an offer and the giver's usual behavior.

text: 1) Find a talkative local witness. 2) Invent a plausible reason to speak with them, such as returning an item. 3) Sustain the pretext without exposing yourself. 4) Accept the witness's correction, which often carries more information than the original lead.
when: A local witness is talkative and a plausible pretext exists
why: A plausible reason opens conversation that a direct question would not

text: 1) Get an introduction from someone the host trusts. 2) Give a reason for the visit that is partly true. 3) Give a believable reason to stay. 4) Expect the host to scrutinize you.
when: when entering a private home or space without arousing suspicion
why: A trusted introducer and a plausible reason lower the host's guard, though scrutiny continues.

text: 1) Pick a cover role that supplies a credible pretext for questions. 2) Let a talkative witness run out of words before asking. 3) Ask general questions first. 4) Follow each answer with a narrower question until it is specific.
when: interviewing a talkative or digressive witness
why: a cover role gives a reason to keep asking, while waiting avoids being swamped by talk

text: 1) Name a plausible reason why you need the record, such as an omitted detail. 2) Ask to see the copy that would confirm it. 3) Use the record to pursue the next lead.
when: When a clerk or official holds a record that would advance an investigation.
why: A believable error or omission makes staff willing to show a record they would otherwise withhold.

text: 1) Invent a plausible reason for a visit that the target cannot easily refuse. 2) Prepare the cover by learning enough of the target's field to survive questions. 3) Pick a time the target is likely free. 4) Offer bait the target values. 5) Use the occupied target's time to reach the real objective.
when: the target is alert but has one weakness a plausible approach can exploit

text: 1) Choose a plausible pretext for contact. 2) Deliver it so the suspect must respond. 3) Watch the reaction, since a blocking or fierce response is evidence of temper.
when: direct questioning would be refused
why: a suspect's reaction to a plausible claim reveals character

text: 1) Choose a plausible reason to be near the suspect. 2) Observe others present and note what they overhear. 3) Record the suspect's questions and reactions. 4) Adopt a naive manner to draw the suspect out.
when: a guarded suspect must be questioned without alerting them
why: A believable reason and a naive manner lower the suspect's guard

text: 1) Adopt a plausible cover role. 2) Offer a small payment or favour. 3) Take a lead, such as an address, from an ordinary object. 4) Follow that lead to the witness.
when: a witness must be located without revealing the real purpose
why: a believable cover and small incentive open doors that direct questions cannot

text: 1) Open with a neutral pretext rather than an accusation. 2) Talk on a comfortable subject while observing manner. 3) Move gradually to the sensitive topic. 4) Use hypothetical questions to reveal how firmly the interviewee holds a position.
when: when questioning an expert whose claims must be tested without alerting them
why: A pretext lowers guard and buys time, and the reaction to each probe is evidence.

text: 1) Obtain a legal or formal reason to search, such as a general warrant. 2) Use that reason to search every room and container, even against refusal. 3) Insist on opening sealed spaces when the suspect objects.
when: A suspect refuses direct entry to a closed space.
why: A formal pretext justifies access that would otherwise be refused.

text: 1) Give the questioning a harmless cover such as a routine check. 2) Pair the cover with a plausible physical action while observing the reaction. 3) Build trust first, then press for facts, leaving the central question for later.
when: The witness is fragile and would shut down under a direct accusation.
why: A benign cover lowers the witness's guard so reactions are more open.

text: 1) Choose a plausible pretext that explains the visit. 2) Ask background questions such as arrival time and reasons for coming. 3) Let each answer shape the next question. 4) Test the suspect with a known name. 5) Change manner if the reaction is unclear.
when: The suspect has a reason to hide information and the investigator can reach them through a plausible role.
why: A pretext opens access, and adaptive questioning reveals background step by step.

text: 1) Lure the suspect to you with a plausible false pretext. 2) Display a physical clue in plain view. 3) Offer an invented but credible account of how the evidence was found. 4) Let the suspect's reaction reveal what cannot yet be proven.
when: Physical evidence points to a suspect but cannot yet prove the connection
why: A guilty suspect's reaction to a visible clue or bluff can disclose knowledge that direct questioning would not

text: Use a believable pretext, such as a charity collection or survey, to gain access to a restricted building or to ask questions that direct questioning would alert the target to.
when: Entry to a restricted building is needed, or direct questioning would alert the target.
why: A plausible purpose opens doors that a plain visitor would not and gives a believable reason for the questions.

text: Keep a pretext consistent and leave on friendly terms, since targets may see through an innocent-seeming cover and exposure ends cooperation.
when: When using a pretext to contact a witness.
why: An exposed pretext ends the witness's cooperation and can compromise the investigation.

text: Unlock information through a cover identity the player chooses, so the chosen pretext shapes what is revealed.
when: designing dialogue with disguises

text: Unlock pretext options from a character's background or reputation, with different outcomes for each.
when: When designing dialogue or social choices
why: Background-based options make player choices reflect the character's standing

text: Let a pretext character grant the player entry, such as posing as a tenant or delivery worker, whose claimed identity the player can check.
when: when an NPC gatekeeps a location or a person
why: a plausible cover opens access without direct confrontation

text: Without official authority, adopt a plausible outsider identity with a believable reason to ask, so that staff at private firms or front desks will answer.
when: the investigator lacks authority and the source is a private or front-desk employee
why: a plausible customer or client is answered where a direct request is refused

text: Question people under a false pretext when they would change their answers if they knew the real purpose of the visit.
A witness primed by earlier talk of a threat may perceive a figure that a calm companion does not.
when: a witness heard rumors before a shared event
why: Prior expectation shapes perception, especially under fear.

text: Have a character warn that the antagonist is cunning, so the audience expects a trap.
when: a scene is building toward a surprise or ambush
why: a stated warning sets an expectation that later events can play on

text: A manipulator can prime an intermediary with a false suspicion so that the intermediary carries out the plan willingly.
when: a plan requires a go-between
why: a believed grievance turns the intermediary into a willing tool

text: A prepared public address, delivered to an assembled and already moved audience, can turn vague fears into fixed doctrine and retroactively justify earlier actions.
when: a gathering follows a day of accusations and examinations
why: Listeners already primed by events accept the speech's framing of them.

text: 1) Brief a witness about a newcomer before the meeting. 2) Expect the witness to form a favorable view. 3) Treat that prepared view as a bias to discount, and check it against later evidence before trusting it.
when: an investigator or character needs a witness to hold a prepared view, or a character or player holds an impression set up by someone else
why: A briefed impression shapes judgment, so it is not independent evidence about the person. A prepared impression can be false, and trusting it leads to conclusions the evidence does not support.

text: Present rival theories before the solution so the audience is primed to question conclusions and test them against the clues.
Use an NPC's sightings that match a claimed cause as a clue to that NPC's bias.
A character who distrusts ordinary communication may send messages by a private route, and that choice reveals what the sender fears.
when: A character suspects the household post is monitored
why: Fear of interception drives use of a private route

text: Individuals may use a public crisis to settle a private score, so a public accusation can hide a personal motive.
when: A community is in a time of accusation or fear.
why: Crisis lowers the cost of accusing and gives private hostility a public outlet.

text: A private diary listing grievances reveals its writer's temperament as much as the claims it makes.
Question a subject alone, or send witnesses away before a confrontation, to get an unguarded, candid account, since others' presence can shape or distort the response.
when: When a subject's account or reaction may be shaped or distorted by the presence of others.
why: Without an audience, the subject speaks and reacts more freely.

text: When a culprit's motive is personal and emotional rather than criminal, let that motive explain the act and keep the resolution private and lenient.
when: When the culprit's motive is personal rather than criminal.

text: A witness's account of how she learned a non-public fact can reveal a private channel between people and show that she treated the information as secret.
A suspect who names a private detail that no one told them is stronger evidence than a vision alone; grade such a clue above unverifiable sightings.
When the culprit has social standing, end with a private confrontation rather than a public arrest, to keep the resolution contained.
when: When the guilty party is a respected or socially prominent figure.
why: A private resolution avoids a public trial while still closing the case.

text: A motive that depends on a suspect's private history may be hard to prove.
Giving accusers private communication with the examiner before and during hearings lets their views shape the outcome out of sight.
1) Put a precise accusation to the suspect in private. 2) Describe the suspect's actions step by step until the suspect believes he was observed. 3) Set terms and a deadline.
when: When a suspect has a hidden motive and strong interest in keeping it secret
why: A precise account of observed actions makes denial less credible and pressures the suspect to bargain

text: 1) Call the suspect in alone. 2) Promise that nothing said will be repeated. 3) Walk through the reasoning. 4) Give a clear chance to confess.
when: a confession is needed without public scandal

text: Tie a private appeal to a concrete request, so its flattery has a visible motive the player can exploit or expose.
When public behavior or agreement looks too neat, check private settings or records, since public unity can hide private disagreement.
when: Public behavior or agreement appears flawless
why: The contrast between public and private faces reveals the hidden side; people display unity publicly while differing in private records.

text: Evidence convincing to an investigator may still fall short of the proof a formal proceeding requires.
Omissions made for privacy may be innocent, but they still change what the reader can infer from the evidence.
Private letters can reveal plans, but some passages are not meant for public ears, so ask who holds a document and why.
Using a private document raises questions of consent and of what may be used afterward, so its contents deserve care.
A decision to withhold evidence based on belief in someone's innocence rests on an unproven judgement and can be wrong.
when: When an investigator decides what to disclose based on a belief about a suspect
why: Belief in innocence is not evidence, so withholding on that basis can protect the wrong person

text: Keep a character's private knowledge hidden from others so that what they know and what they say differ, creating a gap for the audience to notice.
when: Writing characters who withhold information from each other.
why: A knowledge gap creates tension and invites the audience to question motives.

text: Do not accept a supernatural or unusual explanation for private knowledge until you check how the knowledge could have been obtained.
when: when a witness knows what was said privately

text: Use private marginalia or personal notes as collectible clues that reveal inner state, while letting the investigator respect their privacy.
when: when placing personal documents in a mystery
why: Private material exposes hidden feelings and can be used as evidence without public exposure.

text: Investigating privately before informing authorities can save time when they are busy, but leaves the investigator to carry the risk alone.
when: official help is occupied elsewhere

text: Matching two facts, such as a witness's answer and a name, creates a strong probability of a link, not proof of identity.

Probable signs include strong suspicion, bad reputation, habitual hostile remarks, unusual physical marks, testimony of victims, and suspected family ties, each suggesting guilt without establishing it.
when: when classifying evidence in a suspect case
why: Each of these fits a suspect but could also arise innocently.

text: Probability depends on context, so a dramatic theory is not automatically the probable one.
A probable circumstance can be accidental, so treating it as proof of guilt or innocence confuses likelihood with certainty.
when: Reasoning from a single circumstance that seems to point toward a conclusion.
why: Accidents and coincidences can produce a probable-looking circumstance without any link to the outcome.

text: A motive can be invented to fit the facts, so answers should be labelled as probabilities rather than settled conclusions.
when: Reconstructing an actor's motive from incomplete facts.
why: Fitting a story to the facts after the fact can mislead.

text: 1) State the chain-of-evidence idea aloud to the suspect. 2) Watch the listener's reaction while speaking. 3) Treat the reaction as a signal, not as proof.
when: An investigator wants to test a suspect without presenting firm evidence.
why: Speaking a theory can expose a reaction that a plain argument would not.

text: State inferences drawn from appearance as probabilities rather than certainties, and keep the basis for each stated.
when: when reasoning from observed appearance

text: A promise can bind a witness to silence, explaining why they refuse to talk without revealing what they are hiding.
when: A witness stays silent despite having relevant knowledge
why: Loyalty or a vow can outweigh the urge to speak.

text: Check whether a confession was offered in exchange for a promised outcome such as a reprieve, since that promise is itself a source of pressure.
when: reviewing a confession made during custody or accusation
why: the promised benefit can push a person to confess regardless of guilt

text: Propose payment in advance to test how far the other side will go in revealing information.
Let a council in the game be pressured to act on unverifiable claims, and let players trace the consequences afterward.
An offer whose conditions reach beyond its stated purpose, such as holding even when the expected event does not occur, can hint at motive or private knowledge.
when: When an offer's terms are unusually broad.
why: Such reach serves the proposer's interest in the outcome, though greed can also explain it.

text: A witness promised protection may tell the questioner what protects them rather than what happened.
when: a witness gains from a promise of immunity
why: self-interest shapes what the witness chooses to say

text: A promise made under pressure may not hold, so an appointment set through a channel needs a fallback plan.
why: Someone pressed into a commitment may not keep it.

text: A demonstration offered only after pressure was prompted by the questioning and is not freely given, so weigh it accordingly.
Deliver every promised reveal or payment; track NPC promises, such as allowances or inheritances, as state variables and test each is fulfilled.
when: a character promises to explain something later, or an NPC promises an allowance or inheritance
why: unfulfilled promises turn anticipation into frustration

text: Do not offer leniency without authority to deliver it. Promise only that the matter will be considered.
when: a suspect asks for mercy
why: unauthorized promises create false expectations

text: A witness may limit an oath to the parts they can vouch for, and the unsworn remainder must not be treated as established.
when: when a witness can swear to only part of an account
why: an oath covers only what the witness swears to, so the rest stays unproven

text: Agreeing to a promise of no molestation until statements are finished buys cooperation and a calm interview, at the cost of limiting the investigators' freedom of action.
when: A suspect will talk only if the investigators promise not to act during the interview.
why: Promises bind the police and restrict what they may do later.

text: Separate an apparently natural or supernatural cause from a human act by asking who would benefit and what mechanism was available.
when: An event looks accidental or uncanny and the cause is unclear
why: Motive and means reveal whether a natural-seeming event was in fact engineered

text: Confirm a mystery's answer with both documentary proof and physical proof, so players can verify it in two independent ways.
when: when designing the final confirmation of a mystery
why: two independent kinds of proof reduce remaining doubt

text: Use a checkable, concrete inconsistency, such as a wrong face in a grave, as the mid-level clue that proves a death was faked or a person substituted.
why: A concrete fact the reader can check undercuts the official story more convincingly than an assertion.

text: Treating an unexplained behavior as proof of guilt or innocence before testing it can mislead an investigation.
when: When a suspect's action lacks an obvious explanation.
why: The behavior may have an innocent or unrelated cause that testing would reveal.

text: Trusting stated constraints or a thorough search without testing them can let a false premise stand, and a search that reassures everyone may still miss the object.
A weakly supported theory is easy to dismantle, and once the witness exposes it the questioner loses ground.
when: When pressing a witness with an unverified theory.
why: A theory that fails under one question leaves the questioner with no further lines of pressure.

text: Players who expect a supernatural reveal may dismiss ordinary clues, so ordinary clues must be specific enough to test.
why: Vague mundane clues cannot be checked and invite dismissal

text: Assuming a mechanism is silent or loud without testing it leads to false conclusions about who acted and when.
when: Reasoning about a witness's sounds
why: Mechanisms vary in noise and are easily misjudged from memory

text: An invented forensic method can serve as a story's internal logic, but it is not established science. Do not present it to players as real-world fact.
when: writing in-world forensic or pseudoscientific methods
why: Presenting fiction as fact misleads players and weakens the story's credibility when they check it.

text: Do not treat a theory as settled while its key proof is missing, even if it explains most of the facts.
when: A theory rests on a decisive item that has not been found.
why: Without the decisive item the theory stays unconfirmed and can be wrong.

text: A not-proven verdict means the case was unsupported, not that the accused is innocent; proven innocence is a separate, stronger verdict requiring positive proof.
when: Defining the goal or outcome of an investigation.
why: Keeping the two apart stops an inquiry from claiming more than the evidence supports.

text: Assemble proof from independent sources, such as a forensic match, lab analyses, a records audit, a physical object and a witness statement, since converging sources are hard to dispute.
when: building a final case against a suspect

text: Evidence tiers: a rumor opens a lead, corroborated testimony adds weight, physical proof closes a case; block accusation or conviction until physical proof is reached.
when: designing investigation gating, or when a suspect is known but evidence is thin
why: Tiering keeps the player from accusing on inference alone, since a skilled defence can dismantle inferences lacking physical support.

text: A correct motive-based inference is not proof; without a document to show, conclusions from motive and deduction stay unconfirmed until access and knowledge are verified.
Secure proof before confronting a suspect; a premature claim exposes the investigator's source and lets the accused recast the dispute as the accuser's fault.
when: Preparing an interrogation or accusation.
why: An unprepared accusation gives the accused room to counter-attack.

text: Stillness, absent pulse, pallor, lack of warmth and stiffening are each weak alone, because a living person in deep trance can show the same signs.
Investigating judges may accept presumptions, whereas jurors weighing both sides usually require physical, tangible proof.
when: a case is presented to different reviewers
why: reviewers differ in how much they accept inference

text: Proving a solution is usually harder than explaining it, so the evidence must be arranged to support the explanation.
Record an NPC's explanation as a claim with a verification state, so the player can later test whether the story holds.
Separate what evidence proves, such as a person's presence, from what it only suggests, such as intent.
when: Evidence is used to support a theory about someone's motive.
why: Presence does not establish purpose, so the obvious reading may be wrong.

text: Ask for proof of ownership; indirect support offered in its place signals that the claim lacks evidence.
Give each mystery case one test that separates the true mechanism from the false one, so the answer can be proven rather than asserted.
when: Designing the solution of a mystery case.
why: A physical or observable test makes the answer verifiable for the player.

text: Once a fact is confirmed, NPC reputation can change their behaviour toward the subject, so the player sees the effect of proof.
when: A confirmed fact about a character becomes known to other characters.
why: Confirmed status alters how others treat that character.

text: A timeline built by an enthusiast may carry that person's agenda, and stating specifics that cannot be proven gives the suspect a point to contest.
when: When an interrogator recites an unverified timeline.
why: Unsupported details undermine the whole account once one is disproved.

text: A supernatural or unprovable explanation cannot support a legal case, however convincing it seems to the people present.
when: when the proposed explanation lacks physical or testimonial proof

text: Smell evidence is unreliable when the tester's sense is weak or many odours are present; confirm it with another method.
An investigator may be unable to prove a denial false, even when suspicious, so denials must be probed rather than accepted.
A doctor who never treated the deceased may give a cause-of-death verdict that the evidence does not support.
A proven lie does not automatically discredit a witness when judges already favor the accuser.
when: when a court hears contradicting evidence
why: prior bias can outweigh a new disproof

text: A trace found by one person in a moment others cannot recheck is weak evidence, however clearly that person describes it.
A verdict without a written record can be changed quietly, leaving no clue that the ruling was altered.
An impossible claim is only rumour unless the physical object involved has been preserved and can be examined.
when: A claim rests on an object that vanished or changed.
why: Without the object, no one can test the claim against physical reality.

text: Treating an artistic impression as proof of guilt turns a suspicion into an unsupported accusation.
1) Establish how a statement was obtained, such as whether it was freely given after a caution. 2) Only then weigh what the statement says.
when: Evaluating a statement given during an investigation.
why: A statement's content is judged differently depending on how it was obtained.

text: 1) Record each point that can be proven. 2) Mark each deduction as inference only. 3) Hold the inference until the suspect is linked. 4) Pass the full reasoning to the authorities once the link is established.
Gate accusations and arrests behind an evidence checklist, such as a medical or forensic report, so the player can delay action to gather one more item.
when: designing a late-stage accusation or arrest

text: Accept testimony as proof only when detailed and checkable, such as specific meetings, physical marks or objects received, ideally including a detail the witness could not have known.
when: when building a clue the player must verify, or when evaluating a witness account
why: Detailed, checkable claims can be tested against the world; only knowledge outside the accuser's reach proves the account.

text: Judge a suspect's innocence by what the facts show, not by faith in the person.
Keep physical conclusions separate from judgments about a suspect's character; doubts about character must not alter what the physical evidence shows.
when: a suspect seems unlikely for personal reasons
why: physical facts and opinions about people are different kinds of evidence

text: An unmatched trace should not auto-resolve to an unknown intruder. The corpse or the room's own objects should be possible sources.
when: A clue system finds a trace that matches no non-player character
why: Other sources in the scene are plausible and must remain open

text: Do not spend effort on authorship checks when the authorship of a document is not in doubt.
when: Deciding whether a document needs expert comparison
why: Effort is better spent on questions that affect the case

text: Include an authority NPC who ignores contradictions, so players learn that proof must be presented in a form that cannot be dismissed.
when: designing an antagonistic authority in a mystery

text: Do not place the burden of disproving a confession on the accused; a confession that cannot be shown false should not by itself settle guilt.
when: A confession cannot be checked against independent evidence
why: Shifting the burden to the accused makes unverifiable claims decisive

text: Start reasoning from observed facts and test each candidate idea against them, rather than fitting facts to a conclusion reached first.
when: Building or evaluating a theory of a case.
why: Preconceived theories lead to searching for evidence that confirms them and to missed contradictions.

text: A defence needs only reasonable doubt about the accused, not proof that the alternative person is guilty.
when: when arguing an accused person's innocence
why: Showing another person could have committed the crime is enough to weaken the case.

text: Prove a hidden cause with a document, a physical object or a sound; use a confession to close the reveal only when no object is available.
Aiming to prove a case differs from aiming to find what happened; the two aims can conflict and shape which evidence is pursued.
when: Several parties want different results from the same evidence

text: Setting aside a tight chain of evidence only because it seems improbable, versus accepting an extraordinary conclusion, each carries a cost that must be weighed.
when: Evidence forces a choice between a closely fitting chain and a very unlikely conclusion.
why: Rejecting the chain returns the investigator to the start, while accepting the extraordinary conclusion commits to serious consequences.

text: Props in mid-use (half-finished meal, paused game) or moved/torn signal recent or past activity and who used the room, so players read them as evidence.
when: Environmental storytelling
why: Players read changed props as evidence of past events.

text: A staged scene is unlikely to leave its props in full view, so ask why each object was arranged as it is.
A small flaw on a common object, such as a hole, can change meaning once the player knows an event occurred, turning damage into a trace of that event.
when: the object is a familiar domestic item
why: the event explains the flaw

text: In a scene full of props, the important item is easily overlooked, so keep it visible but unremarkable.
when: a key item sits among many objects
why: crowding dilutes attention to any single item

text: A prop that copies a visible trait can itself expose the impostor, because the substituted detail may contradict the real person's record.
A physical object offered as corroboration shows only that someone held it, not when or where the holder was.
when: When a suspect offers an object to prove a claim.

text: Record a few concrete facts about a prop, such as its number, appearance, or price, so a later scene can check it.
why: Vague props cannot be tested or compared later.

text: Give props a usage pattern such as wear, length or scent that players can compare across rooms to link items to NPCs.
Place a mundane source such as an echo, draft or loose board in a room, so players can test it by acting with a clear result each time.
when: Designing environmental sounds in a level.
why: Testable sources let players reason about the environment rather than accept a supernatural answer.

text: Use props in a room to hint at a character's history, such as a poor room holding one rare object, giving the player a question to pursue.
when: Designing environmental storytelling that implies a character's past.
why: A contradiction between setting and possessions prompts the player to investigate.

text: Professional registers let an investigator find everyone who held a given job, so a past occupation can be used to locate a person.
when: A suspect's past profession is known
why: Occupational records list people by role rather than by current name

text: Give the protagonist an inner resolve with a set deadline, such as a day to test a suspicion, to pace the story and raise stakes.
why: a deadline gives the investigation a clock

text: Give the protagonist a motive for concealment, so withholding information becomes a source of tension in its own right.
A feature shared by a whole product line narrows the field but does not single out one person.
A professional may stay silent about an irregularity to avoid consequences, so a physical trace can be hidden by discretion.
when: A witness with expertise notices an anomaly
why: Self-protection can suppress reporting

text: Keep a diagnosis or working hypothesis provisional when proof is missing, even if one explanation seems most likely.
when: when the investigator has a strong guess but no confirmation
why: Holding the explanation open allows later evidence to revise it.

text: A suspect may have been able to act yet still be unlikely to have done so, given the risk, lack of positive evidence and open conduct afterward.
A provisional theory that is partly right keeps the audience engaged while the full mechanism stays hidden.
when: the true cause is still unknown
why: A partly correct explanation sustains interest without revealing the answer.

text: Treat every solution as provisional until physical evidence and a witnessed statement independently confirm it.
why: A belief resting only on inference breaks easily and undermines trust in the case

text: A theory tied to a location requires a search that may find nothing, and a place shows only where to look, not proof of a crime.
when: Reasoning about a crime from a location.
why: A location can suggest a theory without confirming it.

text: A clue that looks meaningless alone can mislead if its significance is assumed too early, before it is connected to other evidence.
A note that reveals method can answer a question too early unless it is framed as a boast or taunt.
when: when writing confession or taunting notes

text: A reading of a partly heard clue should remain provisional until a later action or source confirms it.
when: A clue is given as a fragment with missing words.
why: Filling gaps with expectation can produce a confident but wrong meaning.

text: Make each reveal change the threat's identity, so the player must rebuild their model of the enemy rather than confirm it.
Anger that breaks a guilty person's or witness's composure, such as lashing out at the accuser, can confirm a hidden link or fear more than denial would.
when: a hinted accusation hits a real secret, a witness's false claim is exposed, or a witness speaks harshly about the victim
why: Strong emotion weakens controlled self-presentation and reveals what is feared or hidden.

text: A guilty person who hears a direct accusation often feels compelled to answer or defend, and may reveal knowledge they meant to hide.
when: the accused knows the hidden facts
why: an unanswered claim seems to damage them, so they respond

text: A calm, unexpected question about identity or a charge can provoke a sharp physical reaction, such as a flush, a stagger or a changed voice.
when: when a suspect is asked a sudden accusatory question
why: surprise disrupts composure and can reveal hidden knowledge

text: A provocative accusation shows who answers, who avoids the question and who laughs, revealing differences in how people respond to pressure.
when: when suspects are not yet alert

text: Someone who finds a stranger exploring a sensitive area may act to stop him, which can give a motive for suspicion even when the observer's own motive is unclear.
when: a stranger is seen exploring a sensitive area
why: A protective response to intrusion gives an observer a reason to act

text: A provocative remark about a victim tests a suspect's reaction; a composed suspect answers with a single flat line and shows no fear.
when: when physical evidence is incomplete

text: Provoking a witness with a half-truth lets them correct their own story, revealing knowledge they meant to conceal.
when: A witness is concealing information and may correct a partial claim.
why: Correcting a claim can expose what the witness actually knows.

text: An NPC who becomes angry after provocation may leave or act, changing the scene, so provocation options should carry a real risk.
when: Provocative dialogue options are offered to the player.
why: Reactive NPCs change the state of the scene, which makes the choice consequential.

text: Rumours passed through a friend can prompt a target to discuss the matter, provoking a reaction that reveals knowledge or feeling.
when: Evidence is circumstantial and the designer controls what the target hears.
why: A reaction to a controlled prompt shows more than an unprompted account.

text: A hidden trace can reveal itself when a probing physical action, such as striking a surface, produces a response from the concealed space.
when: A hidden fact sits behind a surface that can be tested.
why: The test converts a concealed object into a detectable sound or reaction.

text: A casual remark can provoke hidden agitation that sets a flag, unlocking a later accusation.
when: a throwaway line touches a sensitive subject
why: the reaction exposes a concealed motive

text: Provocation can trigger flight or fight, ending the conversation before the questioner asks the remaining questions or learns anything.
Provoking a suspect can endanger a witness or bystander and make the questioner more visible, so plan timing and protection before applying pressure.
when: The suspect could harm or flee from a witness or bystander
why: A provoked suspect may act against the witness or bystander first

text: Strong reaction is not proof of guilt: innocent people react strongly too, and one expression can have several readings, possibly just confirming expectations.
Flattery, teasing or dramatic, aggressive questioning unsettles a witness, producing protest and defensiveness instead of the facts the interviewer needs.
when: Trying to draw out a reluctant or defensive witness.
why: Pressure triggers defensiveness, which hides the facts the interviewer needs.

text: Provocation shown in front of others can damage the investigator's standing as much as the witness's, and a hostile reply can reverse the exchange.
Suspects read probing questions as accusation, so keep the stated purpose clear or the questioner may be seen as acting for an opposing party.
when: Questioning a suspect or hostile witness
why: Unclear intent triggers suspicion and defensiveness

text: Tests that provoke a reaction can also expose the tester's own motives to the other party.
when: Probing a suspect with a physical or verbal test.
why: The act of testing can signal what the tester suspects.

text: 1) Keep your own manner mild and even. 2) Raise a sensitive relationship with a small pointed remark. 3) Judge the reaction: anger, evasion or silence. 4) Use the suspect's own words as the next question. 5) Watch for impulsive movement and stop if danger appears.
when: Use when a suspect has a concealed relationship and strong feeling, and a slip is more useful than a direct accusation.
why: Strong emotion can cause a suspect to reveal information that self-control would otherwise keep back.
