text: 1) Keep early questions measured. 2) Wait until the subject believes the exchange is finished. 3) Deliver a prepared pointed remark. 4) Watch for sudden changes in color, speech and posture.
when: subject is guarded and a direct accusation would only draw denial
why: a subject off guard may reveal knowledge that direct questions cannot

text: 1) State the suspicion directly. 2) Point out the suspect's slips. 3) Threaten a consequence, such as calling authorities. 4) Watch whether the suspect grows worried.
when: a suspect is under pressure and may slip
why: a confident bluff can draw out a reaction

text: 1) Summon the witness with a vague message that hints at evidence without naming its source. 2) Have an official present to take formal notes. 3) Present a partial fact and watch for involuntary reactions. 4) Offer the witness a chance to explain motive, and treat retreat into generalities as information.
when: A witness withholds information that a direct question would not get
why: Involuntary reactions and evasions reveal knowledge that a direct answer would conceal

text: Trigger an NPC confrontation after the player provokes them, so the response itself reveals the link.
when: when a player's provocation hits a secret

text: Do not provoke suspects who are already alert, since the probe may end the investigation.
Avoid provoking a suspect when they may turn violent or when the pressure could lead them to destroy evidence.
when: A suspect has a volatile temper or access to evidence.
why: Provocation can escalate into harm or loss of evidence.

text: Do not provoke a suspect who has nothing to lose, or push when the questioner has nothing firm to press on.
A cruel provocation tests whether a reaction is genuine, but it also lets the witness take the moral high ground.
Being near a passage does not guarantee perceiving someone who passes; assuming a witness saw an event because they were nearby accepts claims they were not positioned to observe.
when: when a witness's claim rests on being near a route
why: perception also depends on attention, noise and barriers

text: A threat carried out by a proxy with a disarmed weapon looks dangerous at the scene while the planner stays away from it.
when: a plot must threaten a victim while concealing the person who arranged it
why: the proxy performs the act and the planner keeps distance

text: Treating proximity to a scene, or a convenient departure, as evidence of guilt.
why: Innocent people near a scene can look guilty.

text: Being close to a witness, or being told a story by them, does not make the account reliable.
A figure who is merely near both events may be coincidence rather than a true connection.
When a suspected source is ruled out, consider that the visible effect may be a reflection or proxy of another source.
when: when an observed effect has no matching source

text: 1) Collect a figure's public and private statements on the same matter. 2) Check whether private tone matches a claimed moderation or distance. 3) Treat any gap as a test of sincerity, since gaps often reveal the real picture.
when: A figure's public stance and private conduct may diverge.
why: Gaps can reveal a stance that public statements disguise.

text: A celebrated public figure may act awkward or sulky in private, so public reputation can differ from private conduct.
when: A suspect is widely admired in public.

text: Once an actor's stance is entered on the record, retreating from it costs standing, so the actor may give up the contest rather than defend the stance.
when: an actor has publicly committed to a position that a record now exposes
why: Reversing a recorded position looks like admitting fault, which damages reputation.

text: People who believe they are unobserved can drop a composed public face, showing strain such as tears or anger that contrasts with their calm in company.
when: A suspect is alone after appearing calm before others
why: Public composure is kept for observers and relaxes when no one watches

text: Targets tend to volunteer their own beliefs and practices when the person they face appears receptive and sensitive.
when: an investigator adopts a listening, sympathetic persona
why: people speak more when they feel understood

text: A visible public record of offices, charity, and manners can stand in for character, discouraging observers from scrutinizing the person.
when: when judging someone of high standing
why: visible virtue substitutes for inspection

text: A soft, sincere manner combined with ready explanations can make a false account persuasive to someone seeing the speaker for the first time.
when: a suspect's story fits a convenient narrative
why: tone is read as honesty

text: A rough manner and quick temper can make ordinary disputes look like motive, so a person's quarrels are read as a reason to suspect them of harm.
when: when a character has a known temper and a dispute precedes a loss

text: Observers read pallor, trembling and agitation as signs of guilt or illness, and their suspicion rises or falls with the suspect's visible manner.
when: A person is questioned in a conversation or interrogation.

text: Substantive questioning often shifts to a private setting after a public exchange, once an adviser asks others to withdraw.
when: after a public confrontation

text: Over-reading meekness, blushing or embarrassment as proof of wrongdoing is a mistake, since these have innocent causes.
Escalating a matter a private talk could settle into a public hearing adds little to the case while spreading fear through the group.
when: a private conversation would settle the matter

text: Public actions such as visible travel or landmark visits create a timeline that others can reconstruct, exposing an alibi.
when: when a character tries to hide movements
why: Witnessed actions give investigators points to check.

text: A dramatic public account serves the investigator's interests without commitment, but misleading others risks the truth coming out later.
when: An investigator shares a story they do not fully believe.

text: A quiet early interview avoids exposing a suspect too soon but gathers less public pressure, while a public accusation carries real risk.
when: choosing how openly to confront a suspect

text: Frightened onlookers calm when a device's harmless mechanism is explained aloud, but only accurately; a wrong reassurance endangers the people it was meant to calm.
when: A frightening display is active in the room

text: Stagger contacts across a day, such as an early visit, a midday meeting and an afternoon report, so the sequence shows what was known and when.
when: when alibis depend on exact hours

text: Compare a publication's described purpose with its real aim; a work presented as a report may aim to stop opposition.
when: A document presents itself as neutral reporting.
why: A stated genre can disguise advocacy.

text: Release a story in stages: hold unverified detail back until the report is ready, and limit what staff say before then.
when: when facts must reach the public or a suspect at a chosen moment
why: Early release can tip off parties or spread incomplete facts.

text: Attach a reward and a reply route to a public appeal, so any witness who can act has a way to respond.
when: Publishing an appeal for information

text: Public mood counts as independent evidence only if formed spontaneously; mood shaped by the reports under review is not confirmation, though a spontaneous judgment may still be sound.
when: When judging whether a case is credible from general opinion.
why: Mood reflects the same reports under evaluation.

text: A person can keep a steady public manner while private manner changes over the months before an event, so public calm is weak evidence.
During a stall, press attention and official pressure grow, and speculation fills the gap left by missing new facts.
when: a case stops progressing in public view
why: Public interest persists without new evidence

text: In a public hearing where each side makes one-sided accusations, the outcome can follow the speeches rather than checked facts.
when: A public meeting settles a dispute after speeches.
why: Speeches are persuasive even when unverified.

text: Press or public accounts can mislead on method and outcome, possibly deliberately, and may repeat a false story without revealing full details; weigh them as testimony, not reliable records.
when: When using newspaper reports, public bodies, news or rumour as evidence.
why: Sources have purposes and access that shape what they say; public accounts spread the staged narrative rather than the facts.

text: A rumour gains partial support when an observer independently records the same sign that the rumour describes.
A crime in a busy public place can seem safer to the culprit, since a quiet exchange there draws no attention.
Sound out circulating views before committing to a conclusion.
when: Forming a conclusion about a public event

text: Public opinion can push an authority to act on a case even when the evidence is incomplete, producing an official outcome that may not match the truth.
when: Public attention or outcry is strong while evidence remains thin.
why: Authorities respond to social pressure, so a formal decision can precede or diverge from proof.

text: A rallying cry naming a valued item can keep a crowd moving from place to place in search of it.
Public scandal spreads through rumour and press beyond characters' control, forcing them to respond to a story they cannot shape.
when: When a secret is known to several people

text: Public speculation can spread a red herring as effectively as a planted note, because rumour and theory amplify a misleading reading.
when: when NPCs or media discuss a case
why: Repeated interpretations are believed without checking the evidence

text: Public attention can create a false impression: if the public believes the hunt is on the wrong trail, the fugitives relax and stay put.
when: when suspects are likely to read news about the search
why: a public trail changes what fugitives believe and do

text: Information about a community's members moves informally and quickly through the local area, so people often know movements they did not witness.
when: A small community where people share news face to face.
why: Gossip circulates faster than any formal record.

text: A public channel, such as a newspaper column, can carry messages between parties without direct contact when they have agreed a code in advance.
Public rewards and subscriptions can turn a search into a shared, visible project.
Information loses reliability as it passes through intermediaries, since each link adds distance from the original source.
Authorities who sound the alarm publicly can trigger arrests before any formal proceeding begins.
News of a ruling reaches allied parties informally before any formal decision, so some allies learn of it before the public does.
when: a decision is pending in a faction-based system

text: In a public hearing with spectators, accusers speaking aloud can draw in new accusers after each event, so the proceeding grows on its own.
when: a trial or examination is held before a crowd

text: Case reports pass through a chain of relays: housekeeper, local station, headquarters, duty officer, prosecutor's liaison, then on-scene detectives, each adding detail.
Public notices reach everyone: naming a target informs anyone who knows the name, and an appeal alerts opponents who may flee or turn against the publisher; plan reactions first.
when: When writing a notice or appeal that identifies a person.
why: Public text is readable by people who should not learn of the claim; reactions must be planned before publishing.

text: Public opinion shapes what witnesses say, so their conjectures can be mistaken for facts.
when: a case is much discussed locally

text: Pressing a suspect in public tends to provoke anger rather than candid answers.
when: in front of an audience

text: Public certainty about one suspect directs attention to that suspect and can blind investigators to alternatives.
Public consensus about a famous event does not mean the matter is settled, because it may rest on a concealment.
Outbursts from onlookers interrupt proceedings and must be stopped before questioning can continue.
Financial gains from a death's publicity can be mistaken for gains caused by the death itself.
when: Assessing financial motive after a death.
why: Sales or fees may rise after a death without anyone having a motive to cause it.

text: Treating a published account as neutral is a mistake when its printer or endorser promoted the case.
when: When a printed case includes an endorsing preface or a promoter.
why: Promotion gives the publisher a stake in the account.

text: A reputation inherited from a dead relative can make a living person look guilty without any evidence against them.

1) Send an informant to each candidate location. 2) Have them find a talkative local with a memory of the event. 3) Let the account come out through gossip rather than direct questions. 4) Have the informant repeat it back to test retention.
when: When local talk is likely to preserve a memory of an event.
why: Repeating the account tests whether the informant kept the facts.

text: Present an alibi publicly by naming each independent witness and the distances involved.
When reversing a wrong accusation, state the reason for clearing publicly, so the cleared person is not left with lasting doubt.
when: An accused person is cleared late in the story
why: A withdrawn charge without a stated reason leaves public suspicion

text: A public challenge exposes the target, while a quiet arrangement removes the victim from the situation without public cost to the target.
A public appeal can identify a victim quickly but may alert the guilty, so it suits cases where speed matters more than secrecy.
when: deciding whether to publish an appeal

text: Public reports can differ from what happened in the room, so audiences may hold incomplete or distorted facts.
A written account can serve to silence dissent, not only to record events, so later readers must untangle its agenda.
A published account of a past event can serve as a dossier, read by the examiner and used to question the claimant about it directly.
Test whether a reported event is plausible by asking whether it would be widely known. A famous victim's death would reach national news, so its absence is evidence.
when: judging whether a reported serious event actually happened
why: large events leave a public record

text: Use an official, public setting such as an inquest to force a revelation into a dramatic moment.
when: A reveal should happen in front of many people
why: Public settings raise the stakes of an answer

text: A building's public opening time marks the first moment its exits could be freely used, but it does not show who used them.
when: Exit timing is being checked against the crime.
why: Public access makes escape possible for anyone, not only the actor.

text: Place each document's publication date against the events, since timing shows what its author could know and say at the time.
Let the game's official record or town verdict sometimes differ from what the player has deduced, so the player's knowledge drives the next action.
Let a false story gain institutional force, such as a newspaper report, so the wrong target bears real cost even though the blame is never proven.
why: Consequences attach to the accused regardless of proof.

text: Actions logged in open registries leave readable traces, so an unexpected access can expose a party trying to stay hidden.
when: A suspect's action is formally recorded and the record is accessible to others
why: Anyone able to read the log can connect the access to its source

text: A published physical description of a missing person works as a search tool and turns attention toward that person as a potential witness.
when: When a missing person's features are circulated publicly.
why: Public recognition makes the described person a source of information about events.

text: Public records created by a culprit, such as anonymous letters or notices, can steer investigators toward a false suspect.
when: the culprit has a motive to mislead

text: A false public account carved into monuments, tombs, and tours can outlast the people who knew the facts, keeping the concealed truth buried.
when: A group has covered up a crime that is memorialised.
why: Lasting public markers repeat the story without witnesses.

text: A published account of a dramatic case can become a template that later communities copy in their own accusations.
when: When a vivid case is printed and widely read.
why: Readers learn the pattern of events and reproduce it.

text: A public notice or published discovery can alert its target, since anyone watching the channel or buying the paper sees it.
when: Communicating through a channel the target watches; a discovery is reported in a public paper.
why: Anyone who checks the channel or buys the paper will see it, including the target.

text: Records that anyone can read may be consulted by the person being traced, so the trail can be disturbed.
when: when a trace relies on an open record
why: Open records give the subject a chance to alter or conceal their trail.

text: A published agreement between two authors does not prove they agreed; they may hold different private views.
when: Relatives or partners publish together.
why: Joint publication can mask disagreement.

text: 1) Enter each timed entry from a public record on its own line. 2) Mark gaps and overlaps between entries. 3) Check absences, such as a missed visit or an unanswered call, against the other entries.
when: A case depends on where people were at given times.

text: Keep a witness's name and travel out of the public record unless needed, since unnecessary exposure can alert the suspect.
when: Information must be presented in an open inquiry
why: Public disclosure can reach the person being investigated

text: Keep public information limited. Do not reveal that a solution may lie close to one household or announce key missing evidence.
when: An investigation is still open and a suspect pool is narrowing.
why: Public disclosure can alert the culprit and compromise the inquiry.

text: A timed-effect system such as poison, a fuse or a delayed trap should publish exact delay values so players can verify a clue chain.
Give in-game courts or councils readable records, so that a rival's protection of a suspect can later be turned into a charge.
Publicly exposing evidence can establish justice but can also harm innocent people, so disclosure must weigh the cost to bystanders.
when: Deciding whether to publish sensitive evidence
why: Public exposure reaches people who had no part in the crime

text: A mystery can open with an arrest for murder and then run a long investigation in which confessions, suspects and documents keep shifting.
when: structuring a mystery that begins with an accused suspect
why: Opening on an arrest sets a clear stake that the investigation must resolve.

text: A public hearing can settle its verdict through who speaks to whom and who pressures whom, not only through the evidence presented.
when: designing a public meeting or trial scene

text: A repeated public hearing can turn a private lapse into a judgment the whole group must witness and vote on, so the procedure itself becomes pressure.
A public trial may expose innocent people and their names, while a negotiated release trades punishment for recovered goods and certainty that the matter ends.
when: a public case would harm innocent people

text: Physical objects bought or moved during a timeline suggest a purpose, even when no one states it, and should be weighed as evidence.
why: purchases reveal intent that a witness may not admit

text: Plain, undecorated goods suggest a practical buyer, such as a servant, rather than a wealthy one.
when: when a purchase is used to narrow down suspects

text: Small purchases and instructions to a driver can reveal a planned future appointment or destination.
when: observing a target's errands
why: preparations hint at what is coming

text: A purchase made shortly before an event is more likely relevant than an older one, since a substance is carried only for a limited time.
Verify who actually made a purchase or visit, because a lookalike's action can be attributed to a rival and turned into evidence against them.
1) Interview the sellers of an item. 2) Record the buyer's measurements and the item's description. 3) Ask each seller the same questions.
when: tracing a purchased item to its buyer
why: Identical questions let answers be compared across sellers

text: Log NPC purchases of tools that imply a plan, so players can deduce intent from what was bought and where it was taken.
when: Designing an NPC inventory or shop record that carries story clues.
why: Players can reconstruct hidden plans from visible purchasing behaviour.

text: Do not expect the tipping point of a collapsing belief to be predictable; opinion often shifts unseen for a long time before it becomes visible.
why: The exact trigger is often unknown even to observers.

text: Letting one reversal reset every earlier conclusion without leftover clues leaves the player nothing to reinterpret.
when: a reversal is introduced
why: earlier clues should remain visible and meaningful

text: A test is only as good as its preparation, so a lure that misses its required conditions will fail to reveal anything.
when: when a controlled test depends on specific conditions
why: Missing conditions break the causal link the test relies on.

text: A witness who resents others, or has a prior quarrel with a party such as a rival or neighbour, describes them non-neutrally; moral judgements are not factual testimony.
when: when a witness describes people they feel strongly about, or when a neighbor or rival testifies
why: Feeling colours perception and judgement; past hostility shapes how events are interpreted.

text: A heated argument absorbs a group's attention and can collapse the mood of the whole gathering until a host intervenes.
Suspicion tends to follow existing quarrels, land disputes and group allegiances rather than evidence of specific acts.
People closest to a secret decision-maker attract the most resentment, whatever role they actually played.
why: Proximity to power is taken as a sign of complicity.

text: A law may punish malicious intent to kill even when the means used could never cause death.
when: judging offences defined by intent
why: The wrong lies in the intention, so an ineffective method still counts.

text: Private anger can push an investigator toward plans outside procedure, even plans to harm a suspect.
when: an investigator's hurt turns into a wish for revenge
why: strong negative emotion can override procedural restraint

text: Do not treat a quarrel held in the heat of the moment as proof of intent. Weigh the witness's own anger alongside the words.
when: when a public quarrel precedes a death
why: anger distorts both speech and its interpretation

text: Do not treat a family quarrel as proof of wrongdoing; a dispute can be real without any criminal act behind it.
Let a quarrel in one village create suspects in neighbouring households, so the player can trace who had motive.
when: modelling faction and grudge networks

text: An NPC's half-finished remark can serve as a quest marker that resolves only when the player finds its subject.
when: Designing unresolved hints in dialogue
why: The open question sustains interest until the subject is found.

text: Give a quest-giver partial information and hold the rest back until the player earns it by visiting other NPCs; flag hedged dialogue as a possible hidden agenda.
when: Designing quest dialogue
why: Withheld information rewards exploration and tests the player's judgement.

text: Date each hostile event in a quest log, and let case files hold dated documents with editorial notes, so players compare them to rebuild the rival's timeline.
Attach a named source to each piece of evidence and each accusation, since players weigh first-hand reports and an unnamed accusation cannot be tested and stays unverified.
when: Designing a case file or evidence system
why: Named sources let players compare reports and judge reliability; a withheld name stops the listener from checking the claim.

text: A missing-person quest can require following records across several locations, each with its own registry.
Quest log entries that record NPC statements may exaggerate, so the player should be given a way to test them.
Teach players to ask what a fake quest makes possible, since that question tends to lead them to the real target.
Build a mystery quest log as explicit motive lines, such as revenge, rivalry and access, each with its own checklist.
when: designing a mystery with several possible motives
why: the player's question list drives discovery

text: Design a quest from its final state: define the endpoint first, then place each earlier objective to serve it.
when: when authoring a multi-step quest
why: a fixed end state gives each objective a purpose

text: Include near-identical documents so players must read exact wording before drawing a conclusion.
Quests can log item transfers through NPC records and handwritten routes, with dead-end addresses that the player must visit to verify.
when: designing a traceable item chase
why: verification in person makes records meaningful rather than just readable

text: An NPC-posted job can draw the true target into a set room, where a trigger fires once they arrive.
When a quest or faction requires corroboration, check that the witnesses are truly independent, since players can challenge a list that shares one loyalty.
why: Players spot shared allegiance and dismiss the verification

text: Ask narrow questions about a specific object or document, because vague claims of never having read something may hide selective memory.
Give each guard, servant or NPC a logged sighting so players bound a victim's time of death using the earliest and latest entries.
when: Designing a murder puzzle with logged witnesses
why: Combining log entries gives players a checkable window

text: Give each quest thread concrete next steps and avoid leads that only produce atmosphere.
when: Designing investigation quests.
why: Concrete steps keep players moving toward a resolution.

text: Document each NPC action as a question paired with a motive answer, so a player can rebuild the chain of reasons from a dossier.
when: Designing NPC behavior for a mystery.
why: A written chain lets the player reconstruct intent from the evidence.

text: A quest-giver can have the player held by a plausible official process, with a time limit and consequences for the investigation if the player does not act.
when: when designing a timed quest
why: A believable obstacle creates pressure without arbitrary rules.

text: A quest-giver's body language can signal the quest type, letting a player calibrate expectations before the dialogue begins.
Let a quest-giver's identity be revealed later, offering partial information at first and deferring the name until the player is ready.
A quest giver who claims poverty while displaying wealth gives players a lead, discoverable through inventory, clothing or dialogue.
when: Designing a quest giver whose stated situation can be checked

text: A secret request from an NPC can start a quest where the real stakes are found in a new location, even when the stated danger is minor.
when: Starting a quest from an NPC summons
why: The gap between stated and real stakes gives the player a reason to investigate.

text: Ending each segment at a point of interest postpones the outcome, because curiosity about the next part outweighs the urge to see the threat resolved.
Require a second independent source before a strong quest-giver claim is accepted as fact, especially when the giver has an emotional stake.
when: a biased NPC reacts strongly to a clue
why: a single emotionally charged source may be wrong

text: A quest-giver who insists the player meet a victim elsewhere can serve as a timed lure that creates a witnessed alibi for them.
when: designing quest-giver meeting places
why: A fixed meeting place ties both locations and timing together.

text: Let an errand NPC carry a note the player can follow or intercept, turning the delivery into a small investigation.
Tie a rival's payout to a missing NPC's status staying unconfirmed so that the player learns the rival wants the body never found.
when: When designing a quest where a rival's reward depends on an NPC's fate.
why: The conditional payout reveals the rival's preferred outcome to the player.

text: Ask what has happened that has never happened before, since an unusual event gives a sharper question than a routine one.
when: framing the central question of an investigation
why: a novel event narrows the field of possible explanations

text: A note can answer one question while leaving others open, so check which questions remain unresolved after reading it.
The wording and order of a question shape what a witness reports, so re-ask with different phrasing to check an answer.
when: Eliciting identification from a witness
why: Question framing can lead a witness to an unreliable answer.

text: A question whose answer would fit every competing theory cannot test any of them.
1) Ask about structure first, such as the first letter's range in the alphabet. 2) Narrow to a single letter. 3) Then ask for the full name. Use only yes or no answers.
when: Identifying a concealed name through questioning
why: Each yes or no answer eliminates candidates, so the name is reached without revealing more than needed

text: Let an NPC's answer name a different person than the player expects, so the player must check their assumption against the answer.
when: Designing NPC answers about who was present

text: Let player questions be closed prompts that can rule out a suspect's explanation, so a witness's answers narrow the possibilities.
when: Designing player dialogue for deduction
why: Closed prompts make denials informative

text: Questions naming the accused and act before a witness speaks make answers echo the wording; a questioner's bias can steer questions so commitments reflect framing, not real views.
An interviewee infers what an investigator suspects from the framing of the questions and uses that inference to judge how much danger they face.
when: during an interrogation or interview
why: Questions expose what the questioner already believes.

text: A questioner who controls a subject's responses can shape what the subject appears to reveal, so the answers mirror the questioner's wishes.
when: The subject is under suggestion or command.
why: A passive, compliant subject adopts the framing it is given.

text: A questioner's assumptions shape how an ambiguous phrase is read and every follow-up; a single phrase can be misread as proof of a hidden relationship.
when: a witness's wording is open to more than one reading
why: the listener's expectation selects one reading

text: An interrogator's curiosity can override caution, leading them to push a reluctant witness too hard.
A questioner's dislike of a witness can colour the questions, so the interviewer should set aside personal distaste.
A motive drawn from an earlier question can be an artifact of how the question was asked, not evidence of intent.
A questioner's own uncertainty can leak through in remarks and tone, signalling the gap in their knowledge to the target.
A witness can assume an investigator's questions come from a personal motive, such as romantic interest, and answer according to that assumption rather than the stated purpose.
when: An investigator's visible feelings or relationships are plausible grounds for a wrong theory.
why: A plausible alternative motive closes off the true line of questioning.

text: An interrogator who has already settled on an answer hears only what confirms it, missing contrary details.
when: Questioning a witness with a fixed view.
why: Prior conclusions filter what the questioner notices.

text: A delayed answer to a sensitive question, especially with belated emphasis or a long silence on money or shared events, usually signals concealment or an unwelcome truth, not ignorance.
when: A direct sensitive question is asked, or a character hesitates on a sensitive topic such as money or a shared event
why: Delay and emphasis signal effort to conceal; the speaker may be weighing how to avoid or soften the truth

text: A statement is only as reliable as the questions it answers; gaps in what a witness was asked are themselves a source of uncertainty.
when: When evaluating whether an account rules out a suspect or event.
why: Unasked areas remain unverified regardless of how confident the witness sounds.

text: A witness may admit a possibility only when asked directly about a specific detail, so precise follow-up questions reveal what broad questions miss.
when: a witness's account is partial
why: broad questions let witnesses avoid committing

text: Confirm only what is asked with a bare yes or no, which makes the other party supply details and reveals less to them.
when: Answering questions about a secret
why: Withholding unrequested detail keeps the questioner's work visible to the other party

text: A vague answer from the questioner can prompt a witness to volunteer the object the questioner was seeking, sometimes without the questioner having to reveal the purpose.
when: A witness is eager to share and the questioner withholds intent
why: The witness fills the gap with information they hold

text: Delaying a confrontation gives a suspect time to entrench behind an account that cannot be traced.
Ask about marginal figures and peripheral details in a testimony, since questions there reveal what the witness did not attend to.
when: Interviewing a witness about a central event
why: Peripheral questions reach details the witness never focused on

text: Delaying a revelation builds suspense but blocks audience action; give it a payoff, since long delays frustrate, and avoid delay when the audience must act on the answer.
A witness who gives a guarded first answer may add a fuller detail when a mild, repeated prompt asks again.
when: questioning a reluctant witness
why: First answers are often minimal.

text: Ask focused, specific follow-up questions; they can draw out details the witness saw only in passing or does not realize they hold, so dialogue should allow them.
Ask follow-up questions while a shaken witness is being comforted, since the calmer setting tends to draw out more of their account.
when: a witness is distressed but willing to talk
why: Comfort lowers guard and makes further detail easier to share

text: A witness's first unguarded statement is often more reliable than statements given later under pressure.
Ask what caused a claimed condition and what the person was doing at the time; the answer often leads to the activity behind it.
when: when a witness explains an inability with a cause
why: A cause often connects to an activity relevant to the case

text: Keep questioning of peripheral witnesses short and targeted; identify who was positioned to see or hear something rather than asking everyone broad questions.
when: Witnesses are peripheral and their status is unclear.
why: Long, vague interviews generate anxiety rather than useful testimony and waste time.

text: Once a witness begins guessing out of curiosity, they can supply the letter and then the full name, finishing the questioner's chain.
when: A witness is drawn into speculating about a hidden name
why: Curiosity pulls the witness past the questioner's stated aim

text: A recipient who confronts the suspect at once can alert the guilty party and lose the chance to verify the accusation.
A confident, firm questioner is not necessarily a fair one; aggressive questioning can bend the rules of evidence.
1) Ask a fixed opening question. 2) Let each answer unlock the next question. 3) Record physical details that link the informant's account to a suspect.
when: designing an informant NPC whose answers reveal clues

text: 1) Ask when the person was last seen and in what state. 2) Ask what the witness did afterward. 3) Ask whether entrances were secured. 4) Ask how each claim is known.
when: a formal interview must fix a sequence of events
why: A fixed order makes each answer a checkpoint for the next question.

text: Ask background questions in a fixed order covering family, foreign languages, clear memory and handwriting, and record each answer as a fact to check.
when: when interviewing an unknown person
why: a consistent order makes answers comparable and easier to test

text: 1) Get the witness to commit to a general principle. 2) Name each evasion as evasion. 3) List the unexplained facts in order, each with its motive question. 4) Press on each point until the next admission follows.
when: A witness withholds information but gives partial, inconsistent testimony.
why: Stated principles and ordered gaps make the withheld event visible without accusing directly.

text: Agree on the follow-up before the interview, such as which witness to question if the suspect denies a claim, so the denial cannot warn them first.
Reward players who ask follow-up questions about details that seem unimportant.
Ask every witness the same fixed questions: who knew the hiding place, who overheard talk of it, and whether anything was heard in the night.
After an innocent explanation, keep asking who owns or caused the source, since the answer may lead to new people.
Let the player question in a fixed order and flag any answer that conflicts with an earlier one.
Gate a follow-up question behind a how-do-you-know option, rewarding players who test what they are told.
when: Designing dialogue options.
why: Asking for a source is a deliberate act that should unlock deeper information.

text: Walk along the quietest available streets, looking back often, so a follower is easier to spot.
when: Suspecting a tail on an urban walk
why: Few other people make pursuers stand out

text: A death that seems to occur in a quiet place may have happened during a busy event; check whether a crowd timing explains the traces better.
when: reading a scene that appears to suit a lone culprit
why: a loud event can mask an act that looks isolated

text: Keep investigating quietly during a lull, and signal that work continues so the calm reads as preparation rather than lost time.
when: public progress has paused
why: Visible ongoing work prevents the lull feeling wasted

text: Ask about the quiet interval before an event and about the witness's views of others, noting hostility as possible bias.
Keeping a suspect under watch at home only works if the watch can follow them when they leave.
when: Surveilling a suspect to catch a meeting
why: Losing the subject at departure defeats the surveillance

text: 1) Begin the first questioning with few observers and little publicity. 2) Avoid exposing suspects before the evidence is in.
Keep sensitive leads and record requests quiet, made through a neutral intermediary, and monitor quietly to catch the culprit in the act.
when: Public or official alarm, an accusation, or a sensitive lead would warn the watched party.
why: A warned suspect destroys or alters evidence, removes it, and confesses nothing.

text: Watch a suspect's pauses, tone changes and body changes alongside the words after each claim, since reactions and aborted answers can reveal what landed or knowledge they should not have.
when: interrogating a suspect who may be composed, or a witness who may conceal knowledge
why: involuntary reactions can reveal information that spoken answers hide

text: A single reaction, such as pallor or surprise, is not proof of knowledge or guilt: fear, distress or a startled innocent person can show the same signs.
when: drawing a conclusion from a single tell, or reading surprise or pallor during questioning
why: fear of being suspected produces the same signs as knowing the answer; distress and suspicion look alike

text: An angry reaction to an innocent question often betrays a real concern; a strong anger when caught in a restricted area reveals more than spoken words.
when: an innocent question is asked, or a person is caught in a restricted area
why: the reaction exposes what the person wants to conceal

text: Alarm at an object found somewhere it should not be signals a link to known evidence; a surprised subject may freeze, drop what they hold and leave hurriedly.
when: an object turns up somewhere it should not be, or a subject unexpectedly sees a damning object
why: surprise and alarm betray knowledge of the object's significance and disrupt normal behaviour

text: A sudden, specific question or meeting a witness's eyes can cause colour change, rigidity or dilated pupils even when spoken answers stay smooth, signalling a hidden connection.
when: a subject gives smooth answers that leave something out, or a suspect meets a witness's eyes
why: fear and concealed recognition show involuntarily when a hidden fact is touched or exposed

text: A person's manner when an object is raised can reveal more than their words, so investigators watch the reaction closely.
A sudden change of tone after learning a secret can betray a person's real concern, such as a cool manner that turns into relief.
when: a character learns a fact that touches their interests
why: the shift reveals what they value

text: A person who pretends an identity can betray it through an involuntary reaction when addressed in the language they actually know.
when: checking whether a claimed identity or disguise holds
why: An unexpected trigger produces a reaction the pretence cannot control

text: A request for proof can be read as suspicion, so the person asked may react visibly even while denying distrust.
when: A character is asked to prove a claim
why: Being asked to verify implies doubt, which causes discomfort

text: A suspect who collapses or begs after a step-by-step reconstruction shows that the reconstruction has struck home.
when: a reconstruction of the crime is presented
why: the suspect recognises the facts against them

text: Mentioning a name the suspect cannot explain can unsettle them, and their reaction can show whom they fear most.
when: Probing a suspect with information they did not expect you to have.
why: A guilty or threatened person reacts strongly to a name tied to danger.

text: A person with nothing to hide tends to object at once to a small unexpected change, while one hiding something may stay silent.
when: testing a suspect with a harmless provocation
why: concealment makes a person prefer going unnoticed

text: When an interrogator stresses a single word, the witness often reacts visibly and reframes how they present the account.
when: an interrogator emphasises a word the witness used
why: the stress signals doubt about the claim

text: A sudden accusation made before others can provoke the guilty party into an outburst or rash move before they have time to prepare a denial.
when: when the culprit is confronted with evidence in front of a group
why: Lacking time to prepare a denial, the guilty party's reaction exposes them.

text: A witness confronted with a true fact may show visible physical distress, though such a reaction alone does not establish guilt.
when: when a true accusation is put to a witness
why: Pressure produces involuntary signs.

text: A suspect's physical reaction to an offered test, such as a tightened grip or a fixed gaze, is a readable signal.
when: a test is offered during questioning

text: A witness's manner can shift from defiant to frightened when told of a death, after which answers begin to come more readily.
when: A witness learns of a serious event tied to them.
why: Fear can overcome resistance and open cooperation.

text: Showing a person where a found object was located can provoke a strong reaction, which may reveal a connection or be caused by shock alone.
when: when an object found on a body is returned to its owner
why: Both guilt and shock produce strong, similar reactions.

text: Characters tied to an exposed past often feel shame and resentment and try to limit the damage to their family's name.
when: a hidden history touches a character's family

text: Witnesses' reactions can track testimony: they grow quiet when an account is accepted and distressed when it is denied.
when: group testimony is given in front of an audience
why: reactions respond to the account rather than to an independent event

text: Without sound, observers read meaning from body language such as trembling, turning away, and repeated leaving and returning.
when: observing a scene through glass or at a distance
why: sound is lost, so gestures become the only channel of meaning

text: A suspect who refuses a question with a crude, fierce reaction reveals more than a calm answer would, so design confrontations where refusal is itself informative.
when: a character is asked a question they do not want to answer
why: strong refusals expose temperament and stakes

text: A suspect whose face changes or who fails to deny a claim has shown a reaction the investigator can take as information.
when: A direct claim is made that the suspect cannot easily check.
why: Involuntary reactions and silence can betray what a suspect knows.

text: A shared glance between people in a tense group can signal strain between them, not proof of guilt.
A character's fearful reaction to a sign can show they know of a group but not its role in the crime, helping judge whom to believe.
when: A character reacts to a symbol or sign
why: Reactions reveal how much a person knows, which may differ from what they say.

text: A suspect confronted with an unanswerable claim often shows a visible reaction and then changes account.
A person intolerant of opposition on a side issue may be sensitive there while open-minded in their main work.
when: when a person's reactions seem inconsistent across topics
why: vanity can concentrate on one particular subject

text: A violent reaction to a question about a partner can itself reveal jealousy or control, which becomes evidence about the person.
A quick return to playful indifference after a reaction shows control, and that control is itself information about the subject.
People's reactions to a missing item, whether joking it off or showing fear, reveal how each person relates to that item.
when: a gap is noticed among a group
why: Each person's stake in the object shapes the reaction.

text: Observers read a listener's sudden reaction, such as drawing back or glancing toward an exit, as a sign of fear or concealment.
when: A named person or place provokes an unexpected response
why: Involuntary body language signals hidden knowledge to those watching

text: A character's unusually strong reaction to news can signal a belief they have not voiced, though the same reaction may also come from simple distress.
when: A character reacts strongly to a news item or found object without stating a belief.
why: Strong reactions are observable signals, but their cause is ambiguous and must be interpreted.

text: A long, silent look followed by calm speech after a hesitation can signal a shift in control of the exchange that alarms the questioner.
when: A questioner falters and the witness responds with a prolonged silent look.
why: Sudden stillness and composure change the balance of the encounter.

text: A character's sudden shift in posture, voice or gaze, triggered by one detail, can serve as a clue in itself, signalling knowledge the character has not stated.
A concrete reaction from a person can refute a favoured idea when that reaction contradicts it.
why: observed behaviour is evidence that can overturn a preference

text: Watch a listener's reaction, such as hostility, fear, a flash of anger, a pause or a follow-up question, to a name as evidence of hidden history and stakes.
when: a name or topic is raised in company, or touches a source's concerns
why: involuntary reaction can reveal past connections and expose hidden stakes

text: A character's visible reaction conveys a threat's stakes, a loss, or the importance of a trivial signal or item before details are explained, guiding attention.
when: a threat or death is revealed before explanation, a mysterious first signal is introduced, or an item matters to the plot
why: reactions tell the audience danger is coming and emotion conveys blows faster than facts; observed alarm lends a signal meaning it lacks alone

text: Treat a reaction as one signal, not proof; corroborate it with other evidence before acting, since fear, grief or guilt can each cause it.
when: interpreting a suspect's emotional response, or a reaction to a named clue or remark
why: the same reaction has several emotional causes beyond guilt

text: Treat a visible reaction to a remark or fact as a signal to investigate further, not a confession; a witness may be affected yet stay silent.
when: a suspect reacts strongly to a cryptic phrase, or a witness responds to a confronting fact
why: reactions can come from other causes such as fear of exposure; emotion shows engagement but not guilt or full knowledge

text: Record a witness's or listener's reaction before interpreting it and alongside what they say; check it against the character's other known traits, since a reaction has several readings.
Read a listener's face and demeanour, which can betray knowledge before words: missing surprise at startling news signals prior knowledge; going pale or starting can outweigh answers.
when: observing a group react to new information, or a confrontation where one party may already know a secret
why: expressions betray what a listener already understands

text: Reactions to a search, such as objection, refusal or fainting, are behavior clues about who may have something to hide, not proof of guilt.
when: Observing a group during a search.
why: Stress reactions vary, and the reaction itself is weaker evidence than the search result.

text: A suspect's unguarded reaction, such as a flare of pride, can confirm identity more strongly than an alibi.
when: deciding how to judge a suspect at the reveal
why: involuntary reactions are harder to fake than stated accounts

text: Show a physical item to a suspect when evidence is strong but the link to them is open, then watch their reaction as well as their answer.
when: evidence strong, link to person unproven
why: Reactions can reveal knowledge that spoken answers conceal.

text: A reaction to a staged test is a lead, not proof; confirm it through searches and outside records before relying on it.
A reaction system showing which fact or option an NPC reacts to most strongly, or a mismatch with an unpleasant option's class, points the player to what the NPC hides.
When accusers' reactions track a suspect's movements and are accepted as proof, the reactions themselves become the evidence, untested for whether they are staged.
when: accusers react to the suspect during an examination
why: Reactions that match the accusation seem to confirm it

text: A startled reaction or a concealed object can be read as guilt, but that reading stays a suspicion until a second source tests it.
when: A character's reaction or hidden item suggests guilt while an innocent cause is also possible.
why: Reactions and concealment are ambiguous signals, so they support several explanations.

text: A blocked question, together with a witness's visible agitation, can signal that the answer matters and that the witness should be revisited.
when: A question is stopped or a witness reacts strongly to it
why: Obstruction and agitation hint at a sensitive answer

text: Reading a pale face, nervous laughter or hesitation as proof of guilt is a mistake: the guilty may seem calm and the innocent nervous, since reactions have many causes.
when: treating a listener's reaction as proof, or evaluating a suspect's or NPC's demeanour or hesitation during questioning
why: reactions have several causes besides guilt, and each is only one data point needing corroboration

text: Treating an emotional or sudden reaction as conclusive proof of guilt or a hidden motive overreaches; it only justifies asking what the person knows or testing a hypothesis.
when: judging a witness's response without checking records, or interpreting a sudden or emotional reaction
why: the same reaction, such as jealousy, can explain behaviour without any wrongdoing

text: Answering a counter-accusation in kind can make the accuser look as culpable as the accused to outside observers.

1) Ask a sharp follow-up question naming the specific source of a key fact. 2) Watch for pallor, hesitation, halting speech or evasion. 3) Check each tell against secondary fears before concluding knowledge.
when: a suspect appears to hold information and a general question gives no clear reaction
why: naming the source sharpens the reaction, but physical signs can come from fear rather than knowledge

text: 1) Question the parties separately and alternate attention between them. 2) State the implication plainly and watch each person's reaction. 3) Confirm the suspicion without accusing directly, then require proof.
when: When a suspect is protected by status and cannot be pressed directly.
why: Reactions to a stated fact can expose hidden intent that direct accusation would not reach.

text: 1) Seat the subject comfortably. 2) Present a list of words from an unrelated topic. 3) Insert the crime-related word among them so it sits naturally. 4) Record physical response and manner at each word.
when: using a physiological test as a prompt for questioning
why: a response tied to one word may reveal recognition

text: 1) Ask a neutral, open question about a sensitive event. 2) Watch for a sharp reaction or sudden change of tone. 3) Mark that subject for follow-up questions.
when: when a guarded witness gives polished answers
why: Unplanned reactions reveal where the witness is sensitive.

text: Log NPC tells, such as silence, pacing, a flush, a pale face, an angry whistle, pauses or sudden interest, as readable concealment signals the player learns to interpret.
when: NPCs react to a tense interaction, or an NPC is questioned about a sensitive claim
why: recorded tells let players infer hidden states and how much an interviewee has to conceal, without explicit exposition

text: In accusation or confession scenes, let the guilty NPC's dialogue visibly change, or send a message implying the player knows more, and treat the reaction as a new clue.
when: scripting an NPC confession or accusation scene, or designing an accusation scene
why: a visible change in dialogue lets the player notice the guilty reaction; the reaction reveals guilt or innocence through behaviour

text: Reaction branches can be keyed to vulnerabilities the player learned about earlier in the game.
Follow a reveal with a brief reaction from a minor character to show how the solution is received.
when: Closing a revealed mystery
why: Shows the consequences of the revelation without more exposition

text: Validate any reaction-based identification with a control: a decoy who should not trigger the reaction, and an observer who does not know which person is the suspect.
when: a suspect is identified by a physical or visible reaction

text: A listener's pallor, stepping back, lowered voice or changed subject may show recognition, but reactions to a hypothetical also show only attitude, not guilt; weigh them with other evidence.
when: a listener responds to a hypothetical confession or scenario
why: physical shifts can signal recognition, but reactions are open to interpretation and not proof alone

text: A sudden flash of interest after a pointed hint can be a stronger tell than a flat denial, yet puzzlement at a cryptic message also occurs in innocent people.
when: after a suspect hears a hint only an insider would grasp, or receives a cryptic probe
why: a person who recognises the hidden meaning attends more closely, but real confusion and curiosity show the same signs

text: Let player-found items or witnesses expose contradictions in suspect statements; contradictions unlock dialogue options, a consistent cover story opens other options, and polished rhetoric is a red herring, not proof.
when: Designing interrogation dialogue with testable claims.

text: Let the player show an item to an NPC or stage a planted item in a location; a dialogue or animation reaction reveals whether the NPC recognises it.
when: Designing item clues or item-reveal interactions with an NPC.
why: A reaction confirms the item's significance and gives the player a result; prior description makes the reaction a readable signal.

text: A sharp reaction to a particular name, item or keyword can reveal a hidden trait before the character speaks.
when: When a character is confronted with a specific keyword in play.
why: Involuntary reactions expose what the character would rather conceal.

text: Revealing a fact that contradicts an NPC's earlier commitment can unlock a new dialogue branch.
when: in dialogue trees with commitment-based answers

text: A reaction system can unlock new dialogue options when a named location or object enters the conversation.
when: A named location or object is mentioned during dialogue.
why: The mention triggers a linked response, extending the conversation along the relevant topic.

text: Confronting one NPC with another's statement can open a branch in which the contradiction unlocks new evidence.

1) Log facts the NPC knows. 2) Compare each suspect answer with logged facts. 3) Unlock the confession only after enough mismatches; small inconsistencies can yield confession without decisive physical proof.
when: Designing an NPC interrogation dialogue that branches on contradictions, with thin physical evidence and measurable gaps in the account.
why: Tying the confession to accumulated mismatches makes questioning matter; each contradiction narrows the account until the suspect cannot hold every claim.

text: Track suspects' visible reactions, such as paling, flinching, withdrawal or topic change, as dialogue state; contradicting clues or accusations trigger them and flags accumulate toward a later reveal.
when: Designing suspect reactions in interrogation dialogue that build toward a confession.
why: A contradiction that cannot be explained produces visible stress; accumulated reaction flags make a later reveal feel earned.

text: Make NPC reactions to presented facts open new investigation paths and reveal hidden states rather than trigger automatic confessions or direct answers.
when: Designing NPC responses to accusations, cryptic clues or held-back information.
why: Players then act on evidence instead of receiving answers for free; a reaction reveals a hidden state without requiring confession.

text: Use separate summons and hidden positions for NPC suspects so the player can overhear reactions to an accusation as a clue.
when: Scripting a confrontation scene between NPC suspects.
why: Overheard reactions give the player evidence without a direct confession.

text: Show the player a contradiction in an interrogation, then offer a demonstration, such as opening a container, as the next step.
Let the player propose theories that NPCs accept or dispute, and resolve disputes by requiring the player to find corroboration.
when: designing conjecture dialogue

text: Separate 'considering' from 'committed' flags in quest state, so an NPC's musing about a plan does not count as an agreed outcome.
when: designing NPC plans and quest outcomes
why: Speculation should not trigger outcomes that only a firm decision should.

text: Give NPC dialogue branches that change depending on whether the player probes a sensitive topic, so probing opens or closes answers.
when: when designing conversation with a guarded character
why: Responsive branches reward careful questioning and make the NPC feel reactive.

text: Treat a stranger's background read from dress and bearing as a hunch, and weigh it against later behavior or an independent record before accepting it.
when: Outward signs are the main evidence available
why: Appearance is a first impression that later behavior can confirm or overturn

text: Readers stay engaged when the puzzle lies in the reasoning path and the chain of consequences, not in the offender's identity, so revealing the culprit early can still hold interest.
when: Choosing whether to hide the culprit's identity
why: Interest shifts from who did it to how the discovery is made when all facts are shown.

text: Audiences keep a wrong theory alive by assuming the rich never want more and that blackmail is always about money.
when: A cast includes wealthy characters and a payment-based threat
why: These two illusions remove the alternative motives from consideration

text: Clothing cut, footwear, worn hands, poor teeth or recent manual work can reveal background, occupation, modest means or a recent change in fortune, and can contradict a claimed journey.
when: Judging a person's background or claimed origin from physical appearance or bodily condition
why: Appearance and bodily condition reflect habits and history

text: Plant an anomaly where the audience can see it before the character does, so the character's dismissal creates dramatic irony.
when: The audience should notice a discrepancy first

text: A reader first takes an obsessive protagonist's behavior as madness, then as rational deduction, and finally learns that a key moment was a deliberate staged trick.
If a clue depends on the audience's unstated assumptions, the author has offloaded work that the clue itself should do.
A reading of a reaction depends on assumptions about how guilty or fraudulent people behave, and respected readers can agree on it and still be wrong.
One reported detail often fits several readings, and choosing the reading that suits the accusation rather than independent evidence is a common error.
A reader's inherited reverence or an old grudge can color how they read a stranger's face and bearing.
why: Prior feelings supply the interpretation the observer expects to find.

text: Polished or redundant prose can hide thin evidence, so writing quality should not be taken as a sign of reliability.
when: Judging a written account.
why: Fluent or elaborate wording can make weak evidence look stronger.

text: 1) Note visible cues such as tan pattern, posture, wear and carried items. 2) Tie each cue to one conclusion about background. 3) Check the conclusions against an independent record.
when: Judging a stranger's past before they speak
why: Explicit cue-to-conclusion links make inference checkable and less like luck

text: Let a character's silence leave a gap that a careful player can notice and later fill, rather than leaving the gap invisible.
when: When a character's silence matters to the plot.
why: Players reward noticing gaps and feel satisfied when they fill them.

text: Give the audience the same clues the investigator had, with key details recorded, so the solution can be followed and checked.
when: When revealing a mystery's solution
why: Unverifiable solutions feel arbitrary

text: A remark implying that someone lacks full knowledge hints at a hidden fact without stating it.
When every route to a conclusion is closed, re-examine the witness accounts behind the eliminations rather than accept an impossible result.
when: Every possible explanation has been eliminated

text: If an argument would prove too much in either direction, the inference has been stretched beyond what the fact supports.
when: Evaluating whether a clue supports a conclusion.
why: A reasoning pattern that supports any outcome carries no discriminating weight.

text: Benefit to one party does not prove that party arranged the scheme; the beneficiary and the arranger can be different people.
when: Assigning responsibility for an arranged outcome.
why: Gain and control over events are separate facts that must each be shown.

text: 1) List every claim each proposed solution makes. 2) Check each claim against fixed facts and later sources. 3) Credit the true claims. 4) Build one account that keeps all true claims and drops the false ones.
when: ending a mystery where players have proposed competing solutions
why: Partly correct theories reward attention across the whole session, not just one decisive clue

text: Have an in-world listener voice disbelief at implausible claims, so the player is alerted to doubt without the designer stating it outright.
when: A claim in the story is meant to be questioned.
why: A character's reaction signals doubt more naturally than narration does.

text: When an in-world authority judges a player's case, weight dated, signed records above the player's inferred reasoning.
when: designing judgement scenes
why: authorities trust records over inference

text: Weigh an explanation honestly to decide which way the probabilities fall, rather than building a case against the speaker.
Separate what is implied from what is proven, and do not rely on implied warnings where a mystery's fairness requires the fact to be stated plainly.
when: when writing clues for a mystery
why: implication alone cannot support a fair solution

text: Let one suspect's confession implicate another only when a second, independent clue confirms it.
when: Designing multi-suspect accusation systems.
why: A second clue stops a single claim from carrying two people to judgment.

text: Repetition makes a claim feel confirmed, even when it rests on one unverified root; repetition is not verification, and a planned deception gains strength from being repeated.
when: a claim must seem believable to several observers
why: Independent-seeming confirmation raises trust in a claim.

text: Vivid, memorable or unfalsifiable details feel reliable but are weak support, not proof, leading to untestable conclusions; prefer plain, checkable details with independent corroboration.
why: A detail that stands out is not thereby verified.

text: Once a suspect is labelled guilty, audiences and interrogators read denials as evasion, silence as confirmation, and new facts as support, so contrary evidence is ignored.
when: an accuser or interrogator holds a fixed suspicion
why: the accusation becomes the frame for interpreting new facts

text: A listener's jealousy or an observer's irritation can shape how a stated-versus-real mismatch or partial view is read as motive; such readings need more evidence.
Suspicion, fear or unease can make innocent details and objects look guilty or sinister, so record such feelings as feelings, not proof.
when: an observer holds a belief or is under suspicion
why: Fear can mimic evidence; suspicion colours how ordinary things are read.

text: Once suspicion settles on one person, later evidence and mishaps are read as fitting that accusation and alternatives go untested; the reading darkens with each added fact.
when: an investigator holds an early theory of who is responsible, a case builds against one person, or a suspect has been named
why: Fixation makes weak or unrelated facts look like support; each fact is read through the first theory.

text: A vivid, specific account can make a biased, gossipy or aggrieved witness seem more reliable, since the most vivid record may be the most biased.
why: Detail makes a witness feel credible regardless of bias.

text: Relief or a wished-for outcome, such as finding a guilty person, can decide which facts seem related or justify weaker proof; the desire must not override the standard of proof.
when: pressure to reach a verdict is high, or relief or a preferred outcome shapes reading

text: Emotional closeness, attraction or sympathy toward a suspect or witness colours how cues and later facts are read, even when the investigator tries to dismiss the thought.
when: suspicion falls on a person the investigator knows well, or an interviewer is emotionally involved with a witness
why: emotional closeness biases interpretation of new evidence

text: Players accept an object's look as its label, or a barrier's look as security, ignoring contradicting physical evidence like unexpected weight until testing overturns it.
when: an object's visible identity conflicts with how it feels, or a locked barrier is presented as impassable
why: Visual appearance substitutes for testing; a familiar identity removes the question the anomaly raises.

text: Several independent confirmations make an investigator feel the account is solid, even when the key question remains unanswered.
when: when multiple checks agree on secondary points

text: A witness's prior opinion of a person shapes how they interpret and report that person's behaviour.
when: when a witness has an existing view of the person

text: A person who walks straight to the correct door and office shows prior familiarity with a place, which can expose a claim of being a stranger.
when: A suspect claims never to have been in a location.
why: Unprompted navigation reveals learned routes.

text: Believing a person to be a seer gives followers a new purpose and binds them together.
when: Followers hold a belief about a mystical figure among them.

text: A suspect who names a fact before anyone has announced it reveals that they already knew it.
when: When news is shared in a group scene.
why: Early mention of unannounced information shows prior knowledge.

text: Frequent daily contact with someone does not protect others from being fooled by an imitation of that person's voice.
Listeners who owe the accuser a favor are more willing to hear an extraordinary claim out.
when: When a claim challenges what the listener believes
why: Past goodwill lowers the resistance that disbelief would otherwise create.

text: Investigators may feel sick about a close that leaves questions open, even when the legal outcome is settled.
when: when a case ends with unresolved questions
why: Moral questions can remain after the legal decision.

text: A witness who hoped to share in the prestige of an event may shape their account to fit that wish, colouring how they speak.
when: when a witness had a stake in being connected to an event
why: A desire for reflected status biases recall and tone

text: A crime staged to echo a familiar story gives observers a ready script they recognize at once, before its details are checked.
when: a scene repeats a known story, rhyme or name
why: recognition of a known script happens instantly

text: Courts and crowds can credit vivid unverifiable testimony even when the accused know it to be false.
when: Dramatic testimony is delivered before an audience
why: Vivid accounts carry authority independent of their truth.

text: A witness whose belief changes during a case may reshape the account to fit the outcome they now expect.
when: a witness changes their view mid-case
why: recollection is adjusted to match new belief

text: A listener who openly dismisses a legend can still react to an ordinary sound the legend predicts, showing belief that persists below conscious rejection.
when: a legend links an ordinary sign to a curse
why: long-held belief lingers beneath stated disbelief

text: Once an unexplained object's purpose is revealed, the solution seems obvious in hindsight, though it was not obvious before.
when: after a puzzle is solved
why: Revealed facts make the answer appear self-evident.

text: People who do not know a language judge it by intonation alone and still sound confident, so their certainty does not reflect competence.
when: when hearing speech in an unfamiliar language
why: they lack the words and grammar to judge accurately

text: A suspect's suspicious reaction, such as fainting, may have an innocent cause that must be weighed against guilt.
when: a suspect shows distress or odd behaviour during an investigation
why: emotional shock can mimic guilt

text: When sound cannot be heard at a distance, suspicion grows from what is seen and what is missing, not from confirmed facts.
when: when observing from far away
why: the observer lacks confirmed information

text: Investigators tend to dismiss a repeated token as a prank or coincidence when each incident, taken alone, looks like an accident.
when: each incident has already been ruled accidental
why: no single event looks suspicious, so the shared mark is not connected to the others

text: Players and investigators tend to accept the first complete explanation offered by a trusted source, even when it leaves a key detail unexplained.
when: A tidy solution from an authority or press account arrives early.
why: A complete-seeming story relieves the need to keep searching.

text: Suspicion of a stranger is raised more by others' reactions to him than by his own behaviour.
when: introducing an unknown character
why: Observers read threat from how a group responds

text: Opposing parties press the same timing data toward their own theories, so one set of facts can support both.
when: when a case has rival narratives
why: a range allows either side to pick the end that suits it

text: A target who believes he is being followed is unlikely to lead his pursuers to contacts or hidden goods.
when: A released suspect may notice surveillance.
why: Awareness of pursuit changes the target's behavior and ends the expected trail.

text: An investigator's assumption about a suspect's position can make the correct conclusion seem impossible and hide the answer already in view.
when: The likely answer conflicts with a player's assumptions about a character
why: Preconceived views about who could act filter out contradicting evidence

text: People look for a difference when they expect one and for a match when they expect a match.
when: comparing two faces, records or accounts
why: the expectation directs what the comparison searches for

text: A confident denial of danger from an authority can make the audience question the denial itself, since its certainty draws scrutiny.
when: a character insists a dangerous route is perfectly safe
why: overconfidence reads as a cue to test the claim

text: A witness absorbed in other business may not register a substitution at all, since attention is limited.
when: when a witness is occupied during the event
why: attention is limited and goes to what seems important

text: A person who offers an alternative theory may gain from steering attention elsewhere.
when: Someone proposes an explanation that benefits them
why: Their stake shapes what they suggest

text: Witnesses judge strangers by appearance and status, so a recognized face may be misfiled at first.
Audiences fixate on facts that are emphasised and miss facts presented as background, so a key clue can sit in plain view unnoticed.
when: a key fact is stated as ordinary scene detail
why: background details seem unimportant and are skipped

text: An offhand remark, once repeated by a character, can grow into a full theory the character then acts on.
when: a casual remark is repeated and elaborated
why: repetition makes a loose hint feel like evidence

text: Observers hold stereotyped expectations of how sincere and calculating people look, and they treat a match with that stereotype as confirmation.
when: An observer judges a person's intentions from manner.
why: Confirmation of a stereotype feels like evidence, even when it is not.

text: A second, more damaging version of the same secret shifts suspicion onto the person already suspected, even when a third party only asserts it.
when: A rumour reframes a known secret more harshly
why: Each new teller adds an interpretation

text: Opponents often underestimate a character they dismiss as foolish, but that advantage ends once they learn the character's true purpose.
When each linked identity is examined alone, the investigator may never compare them directly, so a shared link can stay hidden for a long time.
when: Investigating several related records one at a time
why: Separate examination frames the subjects as unrelated

text: When every character is listed as a possible suspect, players spread attention thinly and miss the few people with both motive and access.
when: when a large suspect pool is presented without filtering
why: Broad suspicion dilutes focus across too many leads.

text: Players judge who could act from how other characters describe one another, so those descriptions shape suspicion as much as the facts do.
when: Characters describe the people around a victim

text: A character who judges another by an assumed type will shape what they tell that person and what they withhold.
when: one character forms a quick opinion of another
why: The judgment, not the facts, guides the interaction.

text: People accept offers from a host who controls every step of a familiar routine, such as pouring and toasting, which makes a trap possible.
when: when an offer follows a social ritual
why: guests trust routine hospitality

text: Conspicuous behaviour such as stopping to dispose of something in a busy place looks suspicious to passers-by.
when: A concealer acts in view of others.
why: Unusual actions draw attention even when the object is hidden.

text: A target who cannot explain a discovered item sounds less credible when denying it, even if innocent, because the item looks more convincing than the denial.
when: A planted item is found and the target has no memory of it.
why: Having no account of the item weakens the denial.

text: Suspicion settles more readily on people already disliked, poor, or isolated than on fresh evidence.
when: a community is looking for someone to blame
why: few are positioned to speak for them

text: A private channel of influence is assumed to serve personal interests, even when its holder intends to help.
when: Decisions are made privately and their basis is hidden.
why: Secrecy makes benevolent and self-serving motives indistinguishable from outside.

text: One event, such as a sudden change of fortune, can be read as luck or as providence, so it supports opposing interpretations.
when: Observers react to a sudden change in a family's fortune.
why: Interpretation depends on the observer's framework, not on the event itself.

text: Distrust and attachment can coexist; an observer may suspect someone while remaining reluctant to lose sight of them.
Suspicion of a character shifts as new reactions and grudges appear, so earlier judgments of that character should be revisited.
why: New behaviour and disputes change how earlier actions read.

text: An investigator's cheerful or evasive manner can conceal progress and lead others to misjudge what is known.
when: A character hides their findings behind a light manner
why: Demeanour is read as a sign of state of knowledge

text: A belief frame is a shared doctrine that fixes in advance who is suspect, what counts as the offence, and what proof of it looks like.
A guess is a specific, definite conclusion drawn from facts that justify only a general, indefinite one.
A broad belief framework shaping speech, drama, tales and public ritual sets what a population finds plausible, and circulates before any accusation, making charges easier to accept.
when: assessing when a belief entered a community or what a population finds plausible
why: A prepared framework makes accusations easier to accept.

text: Evidence of an interest formed before an event supports both innocent research and early planning, so it does not settle intent.
