when: a subject interest is used to justify an act

text: Sincere decision-makers can be misled by admitted evidence and only later recognise their error.
Check whether the same behaviour was seen or recorded before: a repeated pattern suggests routine, makes an account more credible, and quickly tests whether a story fits.
when: judging whether an odd behaviour is significant or an NPC's account needs quick verification

text: Do not assume a biased witness is lying or treat deception as mere bias; they look alike but need different responses, and a disclosed bias can be corrected for.
when: assessing a witness with a personal stake, such as affection for a suspect
why: Disclosed bias can be corrected for rather than discarded; bias and deception produce similar surface behavior.

text: An investigator should set aside personal distress to examine and record marks accurately.
when: when documenting a painful case
why: Distress can make the record less accurate.

text: Early, when evidence is thin, list several plausible explanations and treat each as a testable theory.
when: Evidence is thin and the investigation has just begun.
why: Several testable explanations give the investigation direction without committing to one.

text: Trust a long, close acquaintance with someone's normal condition over descriptions of that person in an unusual or disturbed state.
when: judging a claim about a person's behavior at a particular time
why: long familiarity gives a stable baseline

text: A feature shared by two suspects can read as a pairing rather than as evidence, so check it on its own terms.
Two matching shared past events make a stronger identification than appearance alone.
why: Shared history is harder to fake than a face.

text: A beneficiary told of a gift in advance has a different relationship to the death than one who was surprised, so note foreknowledge when weighing motive.
when: assessing beneficiaries
why: Foreknowledge changes how a beneficiary relates to the outcome.

text: Rivals are sensitive to shared credit; a clear account of who did what avoids later friction.
Let an NPC confirm a plausible but wrong theory, then supply the contradicting clue at a later stage so players must revise it.
Test a supernatural explanation by asking who gains from the belief, instead of ruling it in or out in advance.
when: when a set of events invites a supernatural explanation
why: a belief that serves a person may be planted rather than real

text: Treat a witness's favourite explanation as information about the witness as well as about the crime.
Cryptic notes written in a shorthand players learn over time reward familiarity, since decoding gets easier with each exposure.
A victim's report of feeling unwell before leaving can rule out a dose taken after leaving, if the symptom came from the poison.
when: A victim describes early symptoms before a departure.
why: Early symptoms place the dose before the departure.

text: Doubt any theory that requires a person to act against deeply held principles, even if the theory is logically possible.
when: a suspect's behaviour depends on a change of character or belief
why: character constrains what a person would realistically do

text: Treat a convenient outside-intruder explanation as a hypothesis. Drop it when the evidence fits it poorly, even if it fits the first clues.
when: when the crime seems to point to an outsider
why: Early evidence can make a stranger look plausible while later traces contradict the theory.

text: Treat an investigator's personal tie to the victim as a possible motive, and test it rather than dismissing it quickly.
when: the investigator knew the victim closely
why: a quick dismissal of one's own motive can hide a real suspect

text: Agreement among authorities is not a reason to discount a well-informed view that is backed by data.
when: A dissenting view is supported by evidence.
why: Popularity does not determine correctness; evidence does.

text: Do not assume bias without evidence; establish it from documented actions and writings.
when: suspecting an official of partiality

text: Use ordeal verdicts when a setting's justice rests on divine or natural judgment, and make clear the result is a matter of belief rather than fact-finding.
Reward early hunches with progress, but keep the final accusation gated behind conclusive clues.
when: designing an investigation with several clues

text: When evidence is incomplete, weigh competing presumptions against each other, and when the balance lies with the accused, favor the accused.
when: evidence is incomplete
why: charity to the accused guards against wrongful verdicts

text: An early sense that two handwritings match is often overconfident and should be retested on closer study.
Life cues around a body, such as clothing, food set out, and a used dish, make observers assume the person is merely asleep.
when: When a still person sits in a room showing ordinary activity.
why: Signs of routine life suggest the occupant is only resting.

text: Track the player's personal bias toward particular NPCs, since bias can steer which suspects the player pursues.
A group that matches a public stereotype is easily accepted as a false lead, because stereotypes fill gaps in evidence and make innocent people look guilty.
when: When a suspect fits an expected profile too neatly
why: Shared stereotypes substitute for individual evidence

text: When a questioner shows doubt, push back against the doubt itself rather than defending the name.
when: when a questioner begins to disbelieve the cover
why: defending the name invites a closer check

text: Judgment of people improves when a natural instinct is made systematic through study of psychology.
A theory explaining every clue at once feels more certain than it is; treat it with extra suspicion and test it as rigorously as any rival.
when: a combined theory appears to resolve every clue
why: Persuasive completeness hides flaws; explaining every clue is not proof.

text: Trusting a source because it is emotional or vivid, rather than because it is first-hand, leads to error.
when: Choosing which account to believe
why: Vividness can substitute for direct knowledge

text: Principled belief or disbelief, like 'people do not do such things', should be a prior lowering likelihood, not a verdict; keep the test open since rare acts happen.
Model an early biased report that later evidence gradually corrects, giving players a slow reversal of belief.
when: designing a story where a reputation must be overturned
why: gradual correction feels earned

text: An observer who accepts an early explanation reads later anomalies as confirmation, so a confident unproven theory can end inquiry before it is proven.
when: observer has accepted a neat explanation, or an investigator holds an unproven theory and collects new clues
why: A fitting frame makes new facts look like support; early hypotheses shape how later details are read.

text: When reader and character share the same wrong assumption, the error stays hidden until a face-to-face meeting forces a check.
when: a story uses a misleading sender or identity
why: the meeting tests the assumption directly

text: A player's assumptions from earlier encounters bias how they read later evidence, which designers can use for fair misdirection.
Two characters who share one trait the player has not compared give a link that is discoverable only when the player looks for it.
when: Designing connections between NPCs
why: Unlinked traits stay hidden until the player compares them

text: When many judges, clergy and scholars endorse one belief, its apparent breadth can look like independent proof, even when all draw on the same underlying authority.
when: A belief appears to be supported by many respected figures.
why: Repeated endorsement from connected sources creates the appearance of separate confirmation.

text: A person caught near a crime scene is not necessarily the culprit; they may be a decoy or simply in the wrong place, so proximity alone should not settle guilt.
when: A suspect is found near the scene but has no clear link to the stolen goods.
why: Physical presence at a scene is weak evidence of responsibility.

text: Once a theory forms early, contrary facts are reinterpreted as support or dismissed as noise, while new clues are fitted to it, keeping the real culprit out of view.
when: an investigator commits early to a single theory or suspect
why: confirmation bias protects a settled conclusion

text: A private suspicion makes neutral replies, remarks or wording read as confirmation, so ordinary phrases start to feel like warnings or proof of guilt.
when: an investigator or reader already holds a prior suspicion or senses a concealed motive
why: Confirmation bias turns neutral remarks into apparent support.

text: Once a theory of guilt is held, tailing a suspect or existing expectations make each new act, even ambiguous laughter, be fitted to the theory.
when: a single theory of the suspect's guilt is already held
why: Investigators tend to see confirmation in what they already expect.

text: Feelings about a case, or attachment to a theory because it is coherent and exciting, make a plausible story seem certain before its links are tested.
when: forming a preferred theory during an investigation
why: Feelings about a case can tilt weighing of the same facts.

text: Clinging to one favoured theory as settled blinds the investigator to better hypotheses and filters contrary evidence; keep several explanations open until facts close them.
when: one explanation feels most likely early on
why: attachment to a theory filters out contrary evidence

text: Vivid, eye-catching clues are often overweighted, though the least damaging item may be the most striking one.
Vivid reconstruction can outrun the evidence, so flag uncertain details such as the presence of objects or people.
An investigator with a personal stake may read a sequence of actions as proof of intent, so the observer's own bias must be checked too.
An investigator who already suspects a person may read that person's probing question as proof of guilt rather than as a check on the claim.
when: The investigator formed the belief before the test.
why: Prior belief shapes how the same question is interpreted.

text: Personal stake or sympathy, such as rivalry, grief, anger or liking a suspect, can skew evidence and motive readings, persist against contrary clues, and hide clues otherwise noticed.
when: investigator has a personal link to a suspect, victim or witness, holds rivalry, grief or anger, or favours a character
why: Feelings shape what a person attends to and how evidence is weighed.

text: Affection, attachment, charm or social standing toward a witness, or personal unease, can bend an investigator's judgement of their account; feeling is not evidence of reliability.
when: weighing a trusted acquaintance's, charming or prominent witness's account, or contact goes beyond the professional
why: Emotion colours self-assessment, so the bias may go unnoticed.

text: Reading each new fact in a favoured theory's favour means it is never really tested; test a favoured theory as hard as its rivals, since one's own hypothesis can mislead.
A settled early view resists later evidence, and a motive-driven theory can be shaped by the investigator's prejudice as well as the suspect's apparent motive.
why: A settled conclusion filters how later evidence is weighed.

text: Reading a room or alarming fragment to confirm a theory yields findings fitting the theory, not the evidence; a fixed view of a suspect makes observers record matching details.
when: observers hold a fixed view of a suspect, interpret incomplete evidence under suspicion, or read a room to confirm a theory
why: Expectation shapes perception so unrelated facts look like support.

text: An early unverified assumption about who, when or what the case concerns steers every later inference and search; test it against data and revise when contradicted.
when: framing an investigation around an unconfirmed suspicion or assumption

text: Witness or group agreement can reflect shared expectations, a staff roster, a common story or cultural belief rather than independent observation; list shared assumptions before trusting it.
when: several witnesses or a group agree on a detail, account or explanation
why: Shared sources make agreement look stronger than it is.

text: A tidy, convenient or settled explanation discourages testing: convenience replaces evidence, other causes go unsearched, contrary clues are missed, and unchecked accounts get built upon.
when: a scene looks too tidy, a clue conveniently implicates one suspect, or an explanation is accepted as settled
why: A satisfying story reduces the felt need to check contradictions.

text: Vivid memory of a person, especially under stress, is not proof of identity or whereabouts; detail makes someone memorable without making them traceable or certain.
when: a witness describes someone in rich detail or relies on a vivid, shocked recollection
why: Memorable description supplies no verifiable identifiers; stress can make a chance resemblance seem certain.

text: Vivid, specific testimony can be sincere yet wrong, reconstructed later or uncorroborated, especially when it fits expectations; richness is not verification, so check physical facts or other witnesses.
when: a witness gives vivid, specific detail such as dates, escapes or personal objects, especially when it fits expectations
why: Concrete texture feels like proof even when no one has verified it.

text: Vivid, emotional accusations can pass as fact or silence a skeptic, and old phrases from angry speakers can sound like evidence; check physical support and origin before accepting the reading.
why: Drama and emotion make claims feel true; emotion gives hearsay the sound of proof.

text: Vivid phrasing or lively narration can replace the precise observation and blur what was seen with what was guessed; check the observation itself.
when: a witness uses colourful, emotive or lively narration
why: Memorable phrasing replaces precise detail and carries assumptions.

text: A vivid detail or explanation can pull attention from physical contradictions, seem central when it is not, and make a weak lead look stronger than the evidence supports.
why: Vividness captures attention before physical facts are checked.

text: A neat reversal, or a single confession that explains everything or adds unseen facts, can feel contrived to an audience, especially when introduced for convenience rather than planted earlier.
when: writing a final explanation of a mystery
why: Audiences resist explanations that look introduced for convenience.

text: Observers read a look or flush through their own bias; attractiveness or sympathy can pass for innocence and nervousness for guilt.
when: interpreting a character one finds appealing or unsettling, or a bodily reaction
why: Appearance and emotion distort how signs are read.

text: Attraction, greed or personal interest in an item or person can distort judgement; not every examined object is evidence, so irrelevant objects get overvalued.
Rumours about someone one likes or distrusts are weighed through pride, sympathy or prior suspicion; accepting one that fits a held suspicion leads to false conclusions.
when: assessing a rumour about a person one already likes or distrusts
why: Personal feelings distort the weighing of probability against character.

text: Once a reading, match or suspect is adopted, people seek confirming evidence, overrate a second match, and ignore counterexamples; test a pattern against cases that do not fit.
when: a new reading of a clue is adopted, a match is found, or suspicion attaches to one person
why: People favour evidence that confirms a hunch.

text: Clinging to a convenient accident explanation, such as a body knocked about by natural forces, can hide a wound made during life until physical evidence forces revision.
when: an injury could be explained by accidental movement

text: A clue matching an expected suspect profile or confirming an assumption, or one that looks deliberately placed, may be exactly what the offender intended.
when: an investigator's prior belief makes a clue seem to fit, or a placement looks deliberate
why: Preconceptions make planted evidence convincing; deliberate placement attracts suspicion.

text: The first plausible reading, often a habit of thought, may fit one detail yet fail the remaining facts; test it against all facts before accepting it.
when: decoding a fragment with several candidate readings
why: Early plausibility does not survive checks against the full evidence.

text: Treating an intuitive guess or chain of plausible guesses as established fact lets deduction outrun evidence; mark which steps remain unproven.
An investigator's own impressions of a witness can be as unreliable as the witness's impressions of the suspect.
when: When forming judgments about people from limited acquaintance.
why: Limited acquaintance lets feelings shape the judgment.

text: Reasoning from similar past cases helps, but it can push a deduction toward a familiar pattern and away from the evidence at hand.
why: past experience creates expectations that can override new facts

text: Settling on an unseen suspect's name early can end further inquiry, because the player stops looking for evidence that could contradict it.
why: A settled label feels like an answer

text: A witness's bias can colour a conclusion even when their facts are accurate. Separate what they observed from what they concluded.
when: when a witness has a personal stake in the outcome
why: Accurate observations can be paired with biased inferences.

text: Visible frustration in an investigator gives the suspect an opening and can reveal the investigator's theory.
Players may treat a confirmed prediction as proof of guilt when it only confirms a fact, so the payoff should be scoped to what it actually shows.
when: A verified clue points toward a suspect or conclusion
why: Confirmation of one fact is often mistaken for confirmation of a broader conclusion

text: A child's account can be vivid yet incomplete, with the observer's own idle time filling much of the report.
A witness who denies everything by reflex gives a record that changes with each question.
A reading shaped by suspicion can mislead, because traces that show some people were present cannot prove that others were absent.
when: Interpreting tracks while already suspecting a particular account
why: Absence of a trace is not evidence of absence of a person.

text: Accepting a witness's vivid impression over the limits they admit about what they could perceive.
An accused who claims to have been tricked may be believed by listeners unless the trap's logic is clear and recorded.
Treating the early favourite as the answer, or assuming proof against one suspect eliminates the others.
when: An investigation has settled on one person.
why: Other suspects are never tested once the favourite seems confirmed.

text: A thorough earlier search can wrongly convince investigators that a hidden object is gone, when it lies in a spot searchers never tested.
when: Reviewing what previous searchers covered.
why: A search covers only the places its method reaches.

text: Identity judged from height, build or clothing fails when a body part has been replaced or altered after death.
when: Identifying a badly damaged or altered body.
why: Whole-body impressions can be deliberately arranged.

text: A vivid story about the means can hide a missing reason, so the motive should be checked separately.
Making a withheld fact too blatant makes the reveal feel obvious, so omissions should be subtle yet fair.
Reading a biased witness's omissions as silence misjudges them, because a witness with a stake may leave things out on purpose.
An investigator's own secrecy and control over a group can make the investigator a target of suspicion.
A suspect's character or ideology can make a theory seem likelier than the evidence supports.
when: Judging a suspect by unpopular beliefs.
why: Disliked views bias judgment toward guilt.

text: Several sources confirming a suspect's story can be mistaken for proof of innocence, while the central question may still be open.
Building a motive first and then searching for evidence biases the search toward confirming that motive and overlooks evidence that contradicts it.
when: When a suspect or motive is chosen before the evidence is examined.
why: Searchers look for what fits the chosen explanation and discount what does not.

text: An investigator's impatience can close off useful testimony.
A time limit on early questioning can force a superficial first interview, so initial statements should be treated as provisional until later cross-checked.
when: Questioning must happen under a strict deadline
why: Rushed first statements omit details that later examination would surface

text: A bystander who moves evidence as a precaution can destroy clues, because moving an item removes the traces it carried.
when: evidence is handled before investigators arrive
why: Good intentions can erase the physical record.

text: A new detail that fits the theory is the most dangerous kind of testimony; test it against physical facts first.
why: A detail that confirms expectations is easy to accept without checking.

text: A uniform habit may belong to several people, so do not assign it to one person without checking who shares it.
An investigator's own temperament can decide which facts seem important; a reading based on atmosphere rather than evidence is unreliable.
Early theories that match a bias can close off other leads.
A visitor who has already searched or intruded may be lying about the reason for the visit.
Bias can pass for ordinary procedure when irregularities of every kind are allowed and no one checks the process.
Shared vocabulary shows that influence existed but does not identify who carried it; the carrier must be established separately.
A conclusion held in advance can blind a reasoner to the meaning of their own statements.
why: Prior commitment filters out evidence that cuts against the conclusion

text: Citing a past minor offence can lend weight to a new charge without showing that the new act was committed.
when: A defendant's record is used to support a new accusation
why: Past conduct is not proof of the present act

text: When belief fixes an ordeal's result, no evidence can exonerate anyone, since any outcome confirms the accusation.
Choosing the version that fits your own theory of the case is a common error when accounts conflict.
Confusing a vivid likeness with a fact about conduct; an image shows appearance, not what someone did.
when: When a striking image is taken as proof of guilt or behavior.
why: Visual impressions feel conclusive but do not establish actions.

text: When observers choose which movements count and the subject can see the test, the pattern may reflect what the observers expected rather than a real link.
when: A test is run by people who already suspect the subject
why: Observer selection and visible testing bias results

text: Vivid, repeated examples can replace a checkable tally of cases, so count outcomes against records rather than relying on memorable instances.
Prior-act evidence can build a character rather than prove the charge; keep it separate so players can tell proof from colour.
Looking only at the first available option can hide a better connection that costs less time or risk.
when: when choosing a transfer or route
why: the first option is not always the best

text: A visible correlation, such as damaged versus undamaged, may hide the real variable, such as entry time, so players can settle on the wrong cause.
why: Surface differences are easier to notice than underlying causes.

text: Rivalry within an investigation team spreads doubt about a theory, and hierarchy or jealousy can decide which theory is pursued.
when: A sceptical colleague or superior dismisses the investigator's theory.
why: Personal and status pressures bias what gets followed up.

text: Untested impressions, including intuition about people, can harden into certainty; check them against facts, since trained judgment is not infallible.
when: A conclusion rests on impressions rather than verified facts
why: Untested impressions are easily mistaken for established truth.

text: An interviewer's suspicions or private doubts about a subject leak through tone and questions, biasing recorded answers; the suspect may sense them.
when: When an investigator has already favoured one suspect or privately doubts a subject
why: Bias leaks through demeanour unnoticed by the one holding it.

text: Surface respectability, courtesy, or silence does not prove innocence, since a disguised or guilty person can display them too.
why: Those cues fit guilty knowledge as well as innocence, so they let disguised people pass unchallenged.

text: Searching only for confirming facts once an identity is assumed, and never testing the reverse hypothesis that the body is someone else.
when: When investigators settle on an identity for a body or remains
why: Looking only for confirmation leaves alternative identities untested.

text: Strong reactions can come from unrelated grudges, so a reaction to a trigger is not proof of guilt until checked against the reactor's other motives.
when: Interpreting an angry or hostile reaction from a suspect.
why: Personal hostility produces the same visible signs as guilty knowledge.

text: Mistaking suspicion for proof, or treating any one confirmatory item as conclusive, leads to wrong or premature conclusions.
when: Evaluating a case built on partial evidence
why: Strength of feeling and single items can look decisive without converging support.

text: Bystanders may judge an investigator's questions as pointless until their purpose is revealed, so a sound method can look inadequate.
Underrating a person because they seem simple is a mistake; a plain person can be more subtle than others assume.
Letting a witness's moral verdicts shape how you read other people's actions carries the witness's bias into your interpretation.
when: A witness judges the character of people involved.
why: Verdicts frame facts before the investigator has assessed them.

text: Relying on a witness's view of another person's mental state without checking it turns impressions into apparent facts.
when: A witness describes someone's inner state, such as fear or confusion.
why: Mental states are seldom observed directly, so the witness's reading may be wrong.

text: Revealing your suspicions tells the witness which answers matter, letting them shape answers around what you want to hear.
when: When interviewing a witness who may be hiding something
why: A witness who knows which details matter can tailor the account to them.

text: A proven lie about activity does not prove guilt of a crime; the contradiction shows the account is wrong, not why it is wrong.
when: Concluding guilt from a contradicted account
why: A false statement can have innocent motives, so moving to guilt is a risky leap.

text: A satisfying story can hide the real culprit, so a case that feels complete should still be checked against evidence.
when: when a suspect's guilt seems narratively satisfying
why: Narrative appeal substitutes for proof

text: Do not treat a performance as sincere merely because many observers watched it, since crowds are often equally deceived.
when: Assessing whether a witness's symptoms are genuine.
why: Shared observation does not reveal a skilled performance, so consensus can be wrong.

text: An investigator's own bias colours their reading of rivals, making their account of others' motives partisan.
A single vivid detail, such as a cry, can pull a timeline toward a conclusion before the time windows are checked.
when: when reconstructing a sequence from testimony
why: Vivid details attract attention and anchor judgment.

text: Assuming every changed mood conceals a plan is a mistake; a listener may imagine inattention that has no hidden cause.
Judging guilt only as premeditated overlooks wrongs that grow from small, thoughtless acts into a steady course of misconduct.
when: When assessing a pattern of wrongdoing rather than a single act.
why: Gradual wrongs arise from accumulated choices, not one decision, so they fail a test that looks only for a plan.

text: Before accepting a single witness at face value, check for a prior dispute, such as a recent quarrel, between accuser and accused.
A reflex shows that a mark exists but is not proof of guilt; combine it with other facts before drawing a conclusion.
when: a physical test produces a reaction
why: A reaction confirms a physical fact, not the motive or the act.

text: Use an NPC's stated beliefs or habits as a suspect filter, and let players test the filter with a search or check.
when: Designing suspect logic in a mystery.

text: Do not rely on shorthand alone when a wrong reading would send someone to the wrong place.
Let a suggested reading settle for a pause before pressing for an answer.
when: a witness is considering a proposed explanation
why: A hurried witness gives a less considered response.

text: Ask an expert for the basis of each estimate, and treat hedged estimates as ranges rather than fixed facts.
when: Medical or forensic evidence is central to a claim.
why: Estimates depend on assumptions, and the basis shows how much confidence they deserve.

text: Before judging a missing item, establish whether its earlier state is known, because an absence cannot be measured against an unrecorded state.
when: assessing a clue that has disappeared
why: Without a recorded prior state, no comparison is possible.

text: If a target was already being watched or threatened, treat an unexpected summons with extra suspicion.
Ask witnesses when they arrived and what they knew of the victim, which tests prior acquaintance and timing and can reopen earlier conversations.
Gather a subject's medical history before reading a physical sign, since a long-standing condition can explain a mark that examiners would otherwise read as significant.
when: when examining a person for signs of a condition
why: context from family or records can account for the sign

text: Vivid, personal events anchor timelines because witnesses date them consistently, yet vivid, confident accounts can still be wrong about order and dates; verify them.
when: Ordering events from memory
why: Vivid events are encoded more strongly, so dates are more stable across witnesses, but confidence does not ensure accuracy.

text: Acting on a false claim costs one thing and ignoring a true claim costs another, so uncertain claims can remain unresolved.
when: Deciding whether to act on an unverified claim

text: A wrong but believable public theory builds pressure on a suspect, but it muddies the record of what is actually known.
when: when pressure on a suspect is the goal

text: A reductio applies an accepted rule to its own proponent; if the proponent fails the rule, the rule's authority is undermined without being proven false.
A reconstruction of unseen movement must fit what was seen and explain what was missing.
Test any reconstructed sequence of events against the recorded positions of physical objects; a reconstruction that conflicts with an object's location is wrong.
Reconstruction works only while the location and marks remain intact; disturbed ground or objects make it unreliable.
A reconstruction that fits the evidence remains a hypothesis, not proof; test it against independent evidence, such as a confession, before relying on it.
A reconstruction can contain errors, so the method must allow revision when a claim is only partly right.
A timeline reconstruction is only as reliable as its map distances and the accuracy of each witness's stated time.

1) State the theory as a specific action the suspect should repeat. 2) Match the original conditions: place, objects, dose and companions. 3) Time each stage with a watch. 4) Record results and have witnesses sign them on the spot.
when: Testing a theory about what a suspect did under specific conditions
why: Matching conditions and timing makes the repeat test a checkable comparison

text: 1) Build a full account that explains motive, accomplice and sequence. 2) Identify the one fact the account must explain, such as a door's state. 3) Check whether the account truly addresses that fact. 4) Mark each step as resting on evidence or on assumption.
when: A reconstruction is complete and needs testing.
why: A consistent account can still be wrong if it does not explain the hardest fact.

text: 1) List small facts that do not fit the working theory. 2) Propose a sequence of events that explains them. 3) Test the sequence against each anomaly. 4) Rewrite the whole line of reasoning if the premise fails.
when: A theory explains some facts but leaves a cluster of contradictions.
why: Anomalies that cannot be explained by the premise expose its failure, and a corrected sequence accounts for them.

text: 1) Hold back the full explanation. 2) In the closing reconstruction, cite only physical objects the player already holds. 3) Link the objects into one account of the act.
when: Ending a mystery with a proof rather than a confession.
why: The reveal becomes a recap of earned evidence, not a new lecture.

text: Present a reconstructed motive as a possibility rather than fact when evidence is incomplete.
when: evidence is incomplete
why: gaps in evidence make the reconstruction uncertain

text: Treat a reconstructed sequence as testable claims, each pointing to a line of inquiry, and do not present imagined steps as established fact.
when: presenting an investigator's reconstruction of events
why: untested steps can mislead if taken as fact

text: Keep a reconstructed document separate from the surviving fragments and do not present the restoration as the original text.
when: Using a reconstructed document as evidence.
why: A reconstruction is a provisional inference, and treating it as original overstates what is known.

text: Treat a reconstruction as a working hypothesis, and mark unresolved routes as open while doors, keys or exits remain unaccounted for.
why: Claiming certainty over unexplained exits invites error.

text: Reconstructed speech recovers the thought underneath a speaker's words, not their exact wording.
A detective's full model of a crime can be held back and released in a closing reconstruction that cites objects the player has already seen.
when: Ending a puzzle or mystery with a complete explanation.
why: Connecting known objects makes the answer feel composed rather than announced.

text: Reconstruction from context is unreliable where the source can be re-interviewed or checked against independent evidence; check directly in those cases.
when: when deciding whether to reconstruct a gap or verify it

text: Reconstruct a damaged document for its general character and meaning rather than its exact words when the question is what kind of document it is.
when: Deciding how precisely to reconstruct a damaged document.
why: General meaning often suffices for present needs even when some words stay uncertain.

text: Reconstruct a sequence of events when a sealed or confusing scene needs explaining; it is less useful when no physical evidence survives.
Sources for reconstructing a past community include court files, church books, wills, inventories, parish reports, colonial records and letters.
When a primary record is lost, reconstruct the event from side records such as lawsuits, letters or ledgers, and label the result as indirect evidence.
when: When the primary record of an event does not survive.
why: Side records preserve fragments of testimony but are not the original account.

text: A motive reconstructed from another person's intentions is persuasive but not established by documents, and should not be presented as proof.
when: presenting a theory of hidden intent
why: intentions are inferred, not observed

text: 1) Collect dated in-game ledgers, gravestones and burial sites. 2) Order the dated items. 3) Cross-check them against one another. 4) Derive the town's timeline from the agreed order.
when: When designing a town's history for the player to rebuild.
why: Physical and written items together give the player a checkable timeline.

text: 1) Recognize when a line of inquiry is blocked. 2) Pick a different known fixed point, such as a death or a departure. 3) Reconstruct the unknown interval forward or backward from that anchor. 4) Ask targeted questions to the right source.
when: A suspect's background cannot be traced past a certain point, or a chain of evidence has a missing middle.
why: A second anchor bypasses a dead end without needing the blocked path.

text: Compare each claim with an independent record of a different type before accepting it; a claim on one source stays weak, while one matching outside records carries more weight.
Witness chains resting on one person's word, or repeated reports sharing one source or fear, are not independent; shared origin makes agreement look like confirmation.
when: When weighing community testimony, or alibi witnesses that trace back to one source.

text: Records may be incomplete or destroyed, leaving gaps such as an unrecorded hired vehicle or missing porter; surviving documents do not show the whole proceeding, so conclusions stay uncertain.
when: When a record query returns no answer or a negative answer.
why: Absence of a record reflects the state of the archive, not the subject's conduct, so a missing answer is not proof of innocence.

text: 1) Identify the writer's stake in the outcome, since a biased source can distort the account. 2) Note which biases they admit. 3) Check what they leave out. 4) Adjust how much weight their account deserves.
when: reading any witness account or in-world document
why: Stake, admitted bias and omissions shape what a source reports.

text: 1) Note how close the source is to the event. 2) Check whether it was written at the time or later; notes made in the moment outweigh later recollection. 3) Check whether its author had an interest in the outcome.
when: Weighing historical or in-game documents against each other
why: Sources close to an event and free of interest are more reliable, and recollection drifts after the fact while a record made in the moment fixes what was known then.

text: Mark claims or key facts resting on a single witness or source as unverified, so players can see which accusations remain open to doubt.
when: When only one witness or source can establish a key fact.
why: Single-source support cannot be cross-checked; an untestable source leaves the fact unconfirmed.

text: Audiences weigh two conflicting accounts of one person by the speaker's stake, admiring or dubious, rather than accepting either at face value.
when: Two characters give opposing views of the same figure.
why: Knowing a speaker's motive lets the audience discount or trust the account.

text: A written object found on a victim can prove a relationship or intent that the culprit believed had been destroyed.
Records taken amid disorder often omit material, so a transcript is partial and should not be read as a full account of the proceeding.
A verdict can follow established practice and still be wrong, because correct procedure does not guarantee a sound premise about the facts.
Bills and receipts give dates and costs that do not depend on testimony, so they can check the timeline independently.
Estimates drawn from an incomplete timing record are only estimates, and more data is needed before an estimate can be treated as certain.
Relayed reports can mislead: trace each claim to its observer, weigh intermediary or third-hand claims below firsthand sight, separate repeated gossip, and verify before acting.

Let several characters with a personal stake, such as rivals, voice a feud with slanted accounts that players can detect by comparing reports, so the audience must weigh who is pleading and who is accusing.
why: Comparing accounts exposes the slant.

text: Judge a document by who kept it, why, and what it leaves out, before relying on its content.
A claim resting on one interested source's record is weak until it is tied to outside accounts that others can check.
Weigh each source's reliability when building a suspect profile; public rumor counts as weak evidence.
when: A suspect profile draws on records, reports and gossip.
why: Sources differ in how far they can be trusted.

text: Tie a secret to a single informed NPC, giving the player one person to question or bribe.
Test a suspect record against an independently kept duplicate, treating the copy as a control so that differences between the two point to later tampering.
when: A record is suspect and an earlier independent copy exists
why: A copy made before tampering shows what was originally there

text: Use independent records that do not depend on one person's word, since a single document or witness can be disputed.
when: Establishing a timeline that must hold up to challenge
why: Independence makes the proof harder to dispute

text: Judge where a story came from, not only how plausible it sounds.
when: Weighing a witness's account against an offered explanation
why: Plausibility can conceal how a story was shaped

text: Independent records such as hotel registrations place a named person in a place on a given day and can anchor a timeline.
Treat a diarist's account of movement and posture as direct observation, but read a memoir's refusal to explain as a signal in itself.
when: Evaluating sources with different kinds of content
why: Sources differ in what they observe directly and what they deliberately withhold.

text: Discount the embellishments of a source with known biases, but keep the parts that can be verified independently.
when: A source has a known tendency to exaggerate or romanticise

text: A contradiction between two in-world sources can be designed as the clue that points to a hidden faction or identity.
A source accurate about one person may be badly wrong about another, so judge reliability claim by claim, not by speaker.
Independent records, such as a telephone exchange trace, can settle disputed sequences more decisively than any witness's recollection.
when: when witnesses disagree on sequence
why: Records do not depend on memory or bias.

text: Seek a second, independent expert judgement on an object's authenticity before relying on a single finding.
when: the object's identity affects the case
why: Independent agreement is stronger than one source.

text: Assess a source's reliability before using its claims, and separate general claims about a group from specific claims about a person, asking for particulars.
when: a claim about a person is passed along by others
why: General talk can mask a lack of specifics

text: Exact times and an admitted uncertainty about wording are signs of a reliable witness, though they do not guarantee accuracy.
when: assessing a witness's manner
why: careful witnesses separate what they know from what they guess

text: Weigh witness reliability when statements conflict or evasions cluster on one point; not for a calm, consistent, corroborated witness.
Ask several staff whether a given stationery is used there; consistent denials suggest the document came from outside.
when: when a document's origin is disputed
why: Staff who know the supplies can rule out the local source.

text: An irrelevant-seeming question can test a witness's reliability; check its answer against other evidence later.
Asking staff to keep an inquiry discreet affects how freely they share information, so the approach shapes what can be learned.
A sudden purchase with a plausible source, such as a loan or an earlier sale, is weak evidence against its spender.
when: the spender has a stated or verifiable source of money
why: the source explains the spending

text: A spouse's statement is partial by nature, so its value depends on other witnesses who corroborate it.
An event found only in one deposition and not in the official record should be judged separately from events several sources confirm.
when: Weighing one witness's testimony against an official record.

text: A work printed after its author's death without revision can contain errors such as wrong dates, so check its details against other records.
when: A source appeared posthumously without the author's final corrections
why: The author could not correct the printed text

text: Treat an account resting only on a private remark as unverified when the accused denies it, since it then depends entirely on the witness.
Depositions and sworn confessions are the strongest evidence because they carry names, dates and the exact wording of statements.
when: When choosing which record anchors a reconstruction.
why: Sworn, dated statements fix what was said and when.

text: Compare a will's date with its probate date and with later newspaper notices to test claims about a person's identity and inheritance.
when: When a claim about who inherited or who a person was depends on legal records.
why: Probate and notices create independent dated checkpoints that can confirm or contradict a claim.

text: A hedged or formal document can seem to warn against a practice while its operative clauses permit it. Check what the text permits against its reassuring opening and its stated outcomes.
when: A source is hedged, formal, or written in unfamiliar conventions and its conclusion matters to a decision.
why: Reassuring framing can mask operative clauses that grant ground for action.

text: Rank sources by proximity and access: a writer who saw records that are now lost can be more reliable than a later writer working from tradition, even if the later writer is more recent.
when: When choosing which account to trust in a conflict.
why: Access to original records outweighs a closer date of writing.

text: NPC gossip can be modelled as a relay chain with a reliability value per link, so the player must confirm a rumour in an in-game record before acting on it.
when: Designing rumours that travel between NPCs.
why: Weakening confidence with each relay makes unverified information less actionable.

text: Letters to a stranger or a consultation under an alias can be placed as findable records that show a character's awareness of a matter.
when: Designing evidence of a character's knowledge for players to discover.
why: Players can infer knowledge from records even when the character never states it.

text: Testimony inherits its source's reliability: a secondhand witness can only say they were told, so doubt about the informant transfers to the claim.
when: when a claim rests on someone else's report
why: the claim has no independent basis

text: Tagging an NPC source with a reliability level lets players learn over time which parts of its story to trust.
Trusting a single report or record without checking it against an independent second source can mislead the investigation.
when: When acting on an unverified report or record.
why: One source can be mistaken or compromised.

text: A single clock, spoken hour or witness's sense of time can be wrong or deliberately set and place events wrongly, so corroborate it with a second source.
A secret or trap that depends on one confidant's silence or one person's cooperation is only as reliable as that person's conduct.
Taking a popular theory as confirmation, without tracing where it started and who repeated it, leads to false conclusions.
Trusting one suspect's account of the timeline without independent checks lets an interested party shape the whole sequence.
Crowding-based segmentation fails when a skilled writer leaves no irregular spacing, because the method depends on the author's mistake.
when: Relying on spacing to decode a concealed message.
why: A careful author removes the spacing clue entirely.

text: Relying on one stopped device without knowing when it stopped or whether it was reset makes its reading unreliable.
Relying on slow channels of inquiry, when faster means are available, delays a case and lets it stall.
A keeper's account of cell events may be wrong or self-serving, so procedures do not guarantee that no communication occurred.
Relying on only the last witness can miss earlier sightings that establish a different timeline.
A neat theory built quickly from second-hand reports can seem convincing while resting on weak evidence, pointing an inquiry at an innocent person.
why: Second-hand reports can be incomplete or mistaken, so how well a theory fits them is not proof.

text: An official record can be correct yet incomplete, so a certificate should not be treated as proof of everything it touches.
when: Relying on an official document to settle a timeline.
why: Records often omit durations or circumstances that remain unknown.

text: A pleasant or generous manner can stand in for an explanation of unusual terms, hiding the anomaly.
Relying on a single source for who is away or sober is risky, because a person's state can change before the planned action.
when: a plan depends on one report of someone's condition
why: Conditions such as confinement or intoxication can change without the plan knowing.

text: A timing margin built on one assumed schedule can be entirely wrong if the subject takes an alternative route or time.
when: when estimating a subject's arrival from a known routine
why: Omitting alternatives leads to interventions that arrive too late.

text: A single record can test a claim only if the examiner knows the record is accurate.
Relying on one record set or one person's memory can mislead, so cross-check each identification against a second independent source.
when: Identifying a person or place from records or testimony.
why: Single sources carry their own errors and omissions.

text: Judging a reference by surface flaws such as spelling can discount a source that matters or trust one that should be doubted.
One cashed note proves little on its own, because money changes hands in many ways.
Assuming the official record of a person's locations is complete; a second residence may be known only to people outside that record.
why: a missed location leaves the search incomplete and the case falsely closed

text: Official lists may record people mostly by title and surname rather than first name, so a sought first name may not appear at all.
when: Searching a record for a person by first name.
why: Record format can hide the detail being searched for.

text: One dramatic document, such as a jealous letter, can fix the whole investigation on one suspect and hide other leads.
A narrator who is personally embarrassed can give a skewed account of what the investigator knew.
A polished secondhand account can read as more authoritative than a raw record of the same testimony.
when: Choosing between a published account and a primary record.
why: Polish signals credibility regardless of accuracy.

text: Household observations, such as a cleaner's notes, can be incomplete, so do not rely on them as a full record of an evening.
when: using a household member's observations as evidence
why: observers notice only part of what happens

text: Trusting one informant too readily can hide a gap that remains unanswered.
when: relying on a single source
why: one account may be incomplete

text: Records may omit what the holder chose to withhold, so a ledger can look complete while leaving out a transaction.
when: Relying on a holder's books alone
why: A holder who controls the records can keep some dealings out of them

text: Dismissing a fact solely because of its source is an error, and verified fragments do not validate every unverified claim.
when: Weighing testimony from a motivated or compromised source.
why: A source's motive is a reason for caution, not proof that its content is false.

text: Treating an unverifiable source as a witness makes the testimony impossible to test, since its claims cannot be checked.
Relying on one advocate's account when other sources exist in the same archive produces a skewed reconstruction.
why: Advocates select and frame evidence in favour of their position.

text: Accepting one hostile or sympathetic account as the full record misses the events that the other sources preserve.
Assuming one coordinated author behind several unsigned messages is unverified; they may have come from several people.

1) Label each source as eyewitness record, second-hand report or oral tradition, and state the chain of transmission. 2) Mark whether each claim was seen firsthand or heard second-hand. 3) Check second-hand claims against independent sources. 4) Flag unconfirmed hearsay as unverified.
when: When assembling evidence from sources or reports of uneven reliability.
why: Second-hand and traditional accounts carry more error than direct records, so source labels let readers judge how much weight each claim deserves.

text: 1) Split the account into separate claims. 2) Check each claim against independent evidence. 3) Mark each as confirmed, contradicted or unverified, and keep the document for later sentence-level checks.

1) List independent records, such as staff memory, the nearest official station and the surrounding roads. 2) Compare the witness's claim against each one. 3) Keep only claims that survive comparison.
when: A witness's account is a key source of location or time.

text: 1) Give each source a numerical reliability score. 2) Tally the scores for each stage of the story. 3) Find the weakest link to see how far each stage can be trusted.
when: several sources conflict and must be ranked before acting
why: scores make the trust level of each link visible

text: 1) Identify each passage's source. 2) Note any corrections, amplifications or omissions. 3) Weigh each passage by its source's reliability before relying on its claims.
when: Using a document that combines several reporting layers.
why: Reliability differs between first-hand records and edited accounts.

text: 1) Record each account as it is given. 2) Separate reported facts from interpretations. 3) Judge each claim by its support, not by how confidently it was delivered. 4) Use every account as evidence against the others.
when: several accounts disagree and no single account is wholly reliable
why: comparison separates accurate claims from errors

text: 1) Ask the source directly whether they are telling the truth. 2) Note evasion or shifts between cooperation and evasiveness. 3) Separate checkable claims from uncheckable ones before weighing the account.
when: An account rests on one source with no physical evidence.

text: 1) Date the document from its own internal dates. 2) Identify the scribe by handwriting. 3) Separate the original text from later additions. 4) Keep the original spelling and punctuation as evidence of the writer's literacy.
when: When a document is one of several records of the same events and its reliability must be judged.
why: Later annotations and different hands can alter a record, and a document's origin shapes how far it can be trusted.

text: Check a suspect's alibi against independent records the suspect did not control, such as transport schedules, not the suspect's own description of them.
when: Before relying on a suspect's statement or a document or witness offered as proof of location.
why: Suspects can shape descriptions to fit their story; records do not depend on the suspect.

text: A single timestamp or surveillance report decides an alibi and rests on one observer, so it is weak unless other sources corroborate it.
when: When a suspect's whereabouts are central to the case.

text: Tag each NPC or game claim with its source and reliability level, such as eyewitness, relayed or hearsay, so players must cross-check it.
when: When designing rumour-spreading NPCs, or clues and dialogue such as gossip or motive information that players must evaluate.
why: Players must learn to judge how far each source deserves trust.

text: Do not build a conclusion on one overheard phrase or sentence without confirming who spoke and what they meant; seek a second source, since partial clues mislead.
when: When the speaker or target of an overheard line is unclear.
why: A partial clue heard without context can mislead as easily as it informs.

text: Confirm an explanation or claim with an inspectable independent record, such as the original message or a seller's ledger, rather than recollection or testimony alone.
when: When such a record is available for direct inspection.
why: Physical evidence does not depend on memory.

text: Judge each background claim by its source, since reports from authorities or colleagues vary in reliability.
when: When assembling a victim's history from secondhand accounts.
why: Sources carry different credibility and can be biased.

text: Mark some NPC statements as reliable and others as lead-only, so the player must judge which claims to trust.
Do not rely on a single record such as a sign-in sheet, since time records can be incomplete or falsified.
when: verifying an alibi from a logbook

text: Give NPC witnesses conflicting accounts, with one reliable witness whose details a physical clue can confirm.
when: designing NPC testimony

text: Treat a loyal ally's praise of a witness's honesty as opinion about character, not as checkable evidence of what the witness did.
why: praise reveals the speaker's feelings

text: Give a keeper's log a visit history that the player must cross-check against other sources to reveal a pattern.
when: designing a clue that rewards comparison
why: the pattern emerges only when several records are compared

text: Every claim a witness makes must have a plausible source, because a questioner can check an invented detail against independent facts.
when: When a witness supplies a detail.

text: Make the most reliable source the one with direct access, and give rumour carriers a reason to omit inconvenient facts.
when: designing sources of information in a story
why: Direct access gives accurate detail, and motivated omission makes gossip unreliable.

text: Do not conclude from a single timeline conflict; a coincidence explanation remains plausible until further evidence appears.
Store the only record of a key timestamp in one location, so the player must reach it to verify the timeline.
Do not treat one stated time as exact unless a reliable source recorded it.
when: several witnesses give different times for the same event
why: Unrecorded times are easily wrong.

text: State what each source can and cannot show, and do not claim a verdict beyond what the sources support.
when: writing up a reconstruction
why: unsupported judgments overreach the evidence

text: Make some events exist only in one NPC's account, so the player must decide how far to trust that account.
Tag NPC sources that cannot be examined with a reliability value, and answer demands for proof with something checkable rather than assertion.
Rely on a direct chain of evidence when one exists; use general inference only when no such chain can be traced.
when: Deciding how to support a historical claim
why: Direct evidence outranks inference

text: Cross-check transcribed documents against each other and against editorial notes and indexes to catch copying errors and inconsistent names.
when: when reconstructing events from old or transcribed documents
why: Copying errors, shifting spellings and inconsistent names are common in historical records

text: Check each claim in a later account against the original documents it cites, so the claim can be verified rather than trusted.
when: A secondary account states a conclusion
why: Later accounts can carry interpretation or error

text: Sort in-world lore by source type, such as official papers, letters, notices, rumors and reprints, so players can weigh each item by its origin.
when: organizing lore for players

text: Prefer sources that cite their origin, such as register book and folio, so each claim can be checked at its record.
when: when evaluating how far a historical claim can be verified
why: A precise citation allows the claim to be traced to its source

text: Give an elderly NPC who hints at knowledge an explicit reliability cue, such as failing memory or self-regard, so players know how much to trust them.
Let clues be corroborated later through slow channels such as messengers or rumour, after the claim has already been recorded.
when: designing delivery of confirming information
why: Slow channels can deliver confirmation days later.

text: A single accuser's word should not decide a capital charge; one witness is not enough to take a life.
Record what each source actually said separately from your own impressions, so gossip and verified facts do not mix.
Use independent world records such as receipts, logs or schedules as anchors that a player can trust more than an NPC's recollection.
when: Designing evidence for a timeline or investigation.
why: Records not dependent on anyone's memory give firmer fixed points.

text: The gap-timing test is reliable when travel and handling durations are known, and weak when those durations are uncertain.
when: deciding whether a timing argument can support a conclusion
why: The conclusion depends on the accuracy of the time estimates.

text: A briefing that is the only source can reframe clues convincingly, but its reading may be wrong, so audiences should be allowed to doubt it.
why: the source admits its reading is uncertain

text: Record event times and durations as they occur, and record each witness's answer to time questions; precise logged times, like a call time, beat general recollection.
when: Collecting times or durations during an investigation
why: Recorded times can be compared and checked, while recalled times drift.

text: Recorded descriptions of people seen at a location, such as an inn, let players identify a forger later.
Record a visitor's habitual pattern, such as using only one hand or keeping a limb in a pocket, as evidence to compare later.
A fact nobody recorded or observed cannot carry evidential weight, so verify whether a key fact was actually witnessed.
when: Judging whether a key fact can support a conclusion.
why: Unobserved facts give no basis for inference.

text: A dialogue challenge that cites an observation the player has recorded can change the NPC's reaction, so earlier discovery alters the conversation.
Trying to record every detail overloads the investigator; keep only details that answer an open question.
A concealed witness who adds no new information makes the surprise read as a cheat.
1) Stay hidden where the speakers cannot see you. 2) Hold their exact words in mind. 3) Write them down as soon as possible while memory is fresh.
when: when a concealed listener needs overheard talk to count as evidence
why: Exact, prompt recall keeps overheard talk usable later.

text: Record witnessed exits in world state so later NPCs can confirm or deny that the player left through the door.
when: When tracking movement through a guarded exit.

text: Record which NPCs name an event before it is announced, and let the player notice the slip.
when: When designing scenes where news breaks.

text: A dialogue system should record an NPC's stated basis for a claim so that later questions can contradict it.
Record gaps about a companion the witness saw poorly instead of filling them in.
when: a witness saw a companion only partly
why: filling gaps creates false detail

text: Store each household's ties and known quarrels in game data so the player can deduce motive from the network of relationships.
when: Building a community with accusations or conflicts.
why: A visible network lets the player reason about motive without a stated confession.

text: A statement or letter gains weight when independent records, such as venue lists, visit logs or contemporaneous diaries, confirm its names, dates and places, or independent sources agree.
when: Verifying a witness statement or letter.
why: Independent records test a claim without relying on the source's word; contemporaneous records reduce reliance on later memory.

text: A dated record that contradicts a claimed timeline, or is dated after the event it describes, shows later writing or alteration and undermines every claim it supports.
when: when testimony depends on dates
why: Dating exposes fabrication that the record's content alone hides.

text: A burnt or torn document can still yield a lead: surviving words may point to intent or destination without proving authorship, so combine them with other records to reconstruct meaning.
when: A document is burnt, torn or otherwise incomplete.
why: Surviving content can point to intent or destination without proving authorship.

text: Show a comparable earlier event as precedent so an unusual mechanism or action seems plausible, then verify the same conditions existed in the present case.
when: a current contradiction or unusual action resembles a documented earlier event
why: A known precedent shows a mechanism is possible, but it must still be checked against present facts; shared practice lowers implausibility.

text: Sequentially numbered items were likely issued together, to one recipient, at about the same time.
when: When a set of numbered items shares consecutive serial numbers.
why: Sequential issue batches are typically handed out as a unit.

text: Discarded drafts show hesitation, so a polished letter reflects deliberate effort rather than spontaneous feeling.
when: A letter appears to be carefully composed.
why: Each rewrite reflects a choice about tone or content.

text: In a dispute with signed petitions, people who sign neither side's paper are read as sympathetic to the opposing side.
when: both sides circulate signed papers

text: Destroying a document does not remove the people who wrote, signed or witnessed it; their testimony and memories remain available to questioning.
A solitary record fails to convince others for three reasons: its circumstances lie outside ordinary experience, it embodies the recorder's own theory, and only the recorder vouches for it.
A witness who heard a dying person's words may be the only record of them, so that account carries special weight.
Outgoing letters placed in a shared collection bag leave no trace for the household, limiting what anyone can learn about one person's correspondence.
why: Once collected, the letter's contents are no longer accessible to those in the home.

text: Serial-numbered physical currency can be traced through the issuing institution, linking each holder to a place and time along its path.
A separate account under a second name keeps that identity's money away from the bank where the person is known.
A written document can carry evidence through its phrasing and omissions as well as through its stated facts.
Authority to dispose of land can pass from a central body to local towns, so a later grant must be checked against the body that actually issued it.
when: records that span a change in who controlled land disposal

text: Collecting case reports from many correspondents and printing their replies creates a shared reference set that other communities can read and copy.
when: When case accounts are gathered and published.
why: Printed collections make one case's details available elsewhere.

text: Authors rearrange real details to suit their purposes, so documents supply raw material rather than a finished account.
when: Interpreting a work that draws on historical records.
why: Creators select and reshape evidence to serve the story they want to tell.

text: A printed date on a document can fix when the material it contains was obtained.
when: when dating physical records

text: A dated document signed by several participants gains weight; record each signatory in the game so players can trace and question every person named to check it.
when: Verifying what was said at a past event.
why: Multiple signers allow the account to be cross-checked against living witnesses.

text: Record small or odd details, such as where a screen stands or which light is off, since they can later serve as reference points or prove significant.
when: a scene will be revisited later, or a detail seems trivial.
why: Fixed details give later events a comparison point; trivial anomalies can later prove significant.

text: Treat press reports as data to compare with each other and with physical records; repetition in a published account can make an unverified claim look settled.
why: Repetition in a report can hide that no one actually observed the claimed fact.

text: Let NPCs hold letters as key items, and let the player obtain them through a cover story the NPC offers.
Documents help answer questions about ownership, inheritance or the intent behind an act.
A late letter from a distant NPC can confirm where a stolen item went, leaving a loose thread for a sequel.
when: A stolen item must be traced to a remote location late in play.
why: A distant witness can supply confirmation without resolving the whole case.

text: Do not assume a notice came from the person it names; check the details it contains against known facts.
why: A notice's named sender can be a cover for another writer.

text: Separate conversations in which each NPC reacts differently to the same item let the player identify which one is lying.
when: when the player can question several NPCs about one object
why: inconsistent reactions expose the liar

text: Keep a factual written record of case events that stays separate from the recorder's own role in them.
Give unidentified NPCs a dossier of blank fields that the player fills through conversation, documents and records, and track which fields remain empty.
when: Designing investigation-driven NPCs
why: Gradual field filling gives players a clear sense of progress

text: Use separate notices for the body and for individual garments, so that each lead can be followed on its own.
Repeat a witness's testimony at different times and favor the sober version when the player holds a verifying record.
when: designing repeated testimony

text: Accommodating a neighbor's boundary claim, even with a small concession, tends to prevent later lawsuits that would otherwise harden into long feuds.
when: when a minor boundary quarrel arises between neighbors
why: early concessions keep a quarrel from becoming an entrenched legal record

text: Deeds and wills record transactions, not feelings, so a stated affection in a document does not prove the real closeness of the parties.
A lore codex can hold an abridged letter whose full original, kept in another archive, contains an omitted line that changes the reading.
when: designing lore documents with hidden context
why: Players who find the full text reinterpret the summary.

text: Note how an entry was squeezed or slanted into place when comparing hands, since layout can reveal how the writing was made.
when: comparing handwriting across entries

text: Administrative bills for lodging and transport show which venues were used for an event and how heavily each was employed.
when: reconstructing where official proceedings took place

text: A person named in a later account but absent from contemporary petitions or certificates weakens the claim of their role.
Let in-world ledgers or deed books hold several small transfers so the player must compile them to see that one party gains control of a district.
when: Designing investigation content in a generated world
why: Compiling scattered records rewards the player with a discovered pattern.

text: A clue journal can use one tab per suspect plus a general tab, and flag when two accounts disagree.
when: designing an in-game clue log
why: Makes conflicts visible side by side

text: A character who records details carefully signals that the record will matter later, so the note works as a clue flag.
when: a character writes down dates or details
why: careful record keeping implies future use

text: A letter written for private reasons can later serve as evidence, because affectionate or detailed description may record facts the author never intended to preserve.
when: A personal letter is later used by an investigator
why: The author wrote for emotional purposes, so specific details are incidental and can be checked

text: Record a stated explanation alongside the physical evidence so the player can compare them, rather than being told the answer.
when: Designing a clue that tests a claim
why: Side-by-side comparison lets the player reach the conclusion.

text: A found document gains credibility when it states who wrote it, how it was recovered, and what was left out.
when: when a story relies on a recovered record
why: Provenance lets the reader weigh the evidence before trusting the content.

text: Dialogue choices that record promises let later NPCs check whether the player kept them, creating consequences.
when: when designing branching dialogue with promises
why: Tracked commitments turn choices into later consequences.

text: Fresh mud prints found after a dry week were made that day, and their presence in one place can show which entrance was used.
Read a record for repeated annotations and gaps, since a recurring mark may look significant without context and a sudden stop often signals a change in routine.
when: Interpreting a diary, log or dated record found in the world
why: Patterns and gaps point to events, but the meaning of a repeated mark stays uncertain until connected to other evidence.

text: Record unexplained anomalies as open rather than forcing a verdict when the evidence for and against a human cause is balanced.
Make the proof a records trail, such as an order or registry entry, that can be checked within the story world.
when: providing evidence for a late-stage reveal
why: Checkable records make the solution verifiable rather than a bare accusation.

text: Third-party logs, such as exchange records of long-distance calls from a house or postal delivery, link a clue or claimed call to a specific person and can expose a pretence.
when: when a suspect claims to have made a call at a set time
why: Third-party logs exist independently of the suspect.

text: Incriminating letters bind the partner who holds them and also expose the writer, so written evidence used as leverage cuts both ways.
when: Accomplices have written proof of each other's part in a crime
why: Written evidence creates shared exposure, not one-sided control

text: A signed or filed document changes recorded ownership, and that record, not physical reality, determines inheritance and tax outcomes.
when: ownership or inheritance is disputed

text: A slowly growing material records past exposure: a substance absorbed at the root moves outward with growth, so its position along the strand shows when exposure occurred.
when: a material grows steadily and keeps a trace
why: Growth carries the trace away from its origin over time

text: An abridged version can remain the standard reference long after a full text is available, so the distortion keeps shaping belief.
why: Familiar summaries are reused more than full originals.

text: When one side refuses to meet and reconcile accounts, the signed contemporaneous record becomes the only fixed reference point for the disputed events.
when: Parties refuse a meeting to resolve a dispute
why: Without agreement, the earlier written record stands alone

text: A journal entry can cross-reference a clipping from an earlier location, linking two independent sources for the player to find.
A consistent record shows the story is consistent, not that it is true; the item may have passed through hands unnoticed.
A fully executed document is hard to undo, so errors in its wording are costly once it has been signed.
when: drafting a binding agreement

text: A person asked to sign a partly hidden document cannot know what she attests, so she cannot judge the commitment she makes.
when: A contract or pledge is shown only in part

text: An exhibit linked to a suspect may prove presence or contact only, not the act itself; test what it actually shows.
A code known to only one person loses its security when that person is captured.
A shared record proves a common connection but not necessarily a significant one, so weigh it before drawing conclusions.
A dated record reflects only what was recorded at that instant, so a claim must be checked against entries both before and after the event.
An excerpt that reads smoothly is not thereby complete; smooth prose can hide cuts that only a comparison with the full text reveals.
Absence of a recorded inquiry is not proof that no inquiry took place.
A record kept by a distracted or inexperienced clerk can be corrupted by mixed-up goods, change and entries, making the total uncertain and misleading.
when: Planting ledgers or tallies as in-game evidence.
why: Confused record-keeping can mislead as much as having no record at all.

text: Identity evidence depends on accurate records; a match is only possible if the original distinctive features were recorded.
when: Using records to match physical traces.
why: Without a recorded baseline, the match cannot be made.

text: Personal writings reflect the writer's self-image and mood as much as events, so their damaging lines may be read as moods rather than plans.
when: A diary or journal is offered as evidence.
why: Writers often exaggerate or express feelings in low spirits.

text: A reference record with a wrong name or date produces false matches or mismatches, so the provenance of every record must be verified.
when: When relying on an archive of identifiers for identification.
why: Errors in labels propagate into every comparison made against them.

text: A humble record such as a plain headstone can carry more intimate evidence than a grand monument, so humble records should not be dismissed.
when: Weighing the evidential value of different kinds of records.
why: Plain records often reflect personal, individual detail rather than public display.

text: 1) State the suspect's false claim. 2) Refute it with authenticated records. 3) Present a parallel case showing how such an impostor could be built. 4) Link the suspect to the impostor identity.
when: when a suspect has built a false identity

text: 1) Record each exhibit at handover. 2) Note who handed it over and who received it. 3) Link the exhibit to its role in the case.

1) List every known fact as a short numbered entry. 2) Group entries by event. 3) Record who was or could have been present at each event. 4) Read all entries together to find connections between them.
when: many facts seem to conflict and no unifying idea has emerged

text: 1) Check the document for formal defects such as a missing witness. 2) Trace any appeal to the highest authority that rules on it. 3) Compare the disputed document with later documents. 4) Decide the outcome from the formal result, not from intent alone.
when: A claim depends on a disputed will or similar instrument.
why: Formal requirements decide validity, and later documents can override earlier ones.

text: 1) Collect constable returns and warrants with dates. 2) Order them chronologically. 3) Read the sequence of pursuit and arrest to place each person's movements at each date.
when: reconstructing a series of arrests or pursuits
