Showing the source of a threat too early removes the dread, while blurring every detail leaves the audience unable to judge what was actually perceived.
why: suspense depends on partial information that is still clear enough to follow

text: 1) Introduce a plausible suspect backed by evidence. 2) Add a second suspect with a stronger, timed claim. 3) Expose a disguise that breaks that claim. 4) Doubt the witness. 5) Reveal who held the key. 6) Overturn the belief with a document. 7) Expose the motive.
when: designing a multi-stage mystery reveal

text: 1) Explain the solution to the relevant characters. 2) Back the explanation with a proof arranged in advance, such as a demonstration, a comparison, a physical search or a letter. 3) Show the consequences briefly.
when: When resolving a mystery before the affected characters.
why: A prepared proof makes the solution verifiable rather than merely asserted.

text: 1) Interrupt the scene with a sudden event. 2) Have a trusted figure authorise the reveal. 3) Present evidence in order, dismissing rumours first. 4) Place the decisive fact last. 5) Close with a question that tests the listeners' judgement.
when: Structuring a reveal scene where the solution must land with impact.
why: Escalating beats and sanctioned disclosure build tension and make the conclusion feel earned.

text: 1) Gather the suspects in one room. 2) Explain the false solution. 3) Expose its flaw with a physical proof: a trap, a recovered object, a confession or an on-the-spot experiment. 4) Resolve the culprit's fate.
when: Staging the final reveal of a mystery.
why: With suspects present, each reaction is visible and the proof is public.

text: Do not stage a reveal before its key evidence is set out and the audience is ready; without evidence, the naming feels arbitrary and fails to persuade.
when: Planning when to deliver a major or climactic reveal.
why: The reveal depends on its evidence; a naming before the evidence lacks grounds.

text: A reveal resting on surprise alone, a detail or culprit first shown at revelation, feels cheap or unfair; plant it earlier so the audience can reconsider prior scenes.
when: writing identity reversals or any late reveal
why: The audience cannot reconsider earlier scenes without the clue.

text: Make reveals fair by planting visible partial clues earlier, even if a mask or role hid the person; show how any framed suspect's trail was built.
why: Audiences can reconsider earlier scenes once the clue is visible, and an unbuilt frame feels unfair.

text: A culprit careful in one respect may be careless in another, so each category of trace should be judged separately.
when: evidence shows mixed care across different traces
why: Care is rarely uniform across all actions

text: Doubt about unverifiable testimony spread slowly and unevenly: some kept a general belief yet refused specific accusations, while others stayed firm.
A two-stage twist first makes the player accept a supernatural explanation, then reveals a mundane living cause beneath it, so each resolved belief opens a second, plainer one.
Source a second reveal from a witness whose silence was deliberate, withholding the secret until a late account such as a deathbed confession.
when: a story needs a late reveal after earlier answers
why: a motivated silence keeps the secret hidden without breaking credibility

text: Narrow the distance between two suspects in stages, with each clue moving suspicion closer to the real link, without naming the link until the late reveal.
when: Structuring a mystery where the answer is one hidden person
why: Gradual narrowing keeps the audience engaged while the final connection feels earned rather than abrupt.

text: Hold an out-of-scheme motive back for a late reveal, so players who reason only from familiar categories are surprised.
when: Designing the final twist of a mystery
why: Players who trust the categories have no box for the true motive

text: Make a large reveal checkable through concrete, verifiable links such as dates or events, so a surprising claim feels fair.
when: When delivering a major revelation.
why: Verifiable details lend credibility to claims that would otherwise seem arbitrary.

text: Force proof at the reveal through a lure, a staged appearance, or an open admission.
Uneven heating reveals some marks before others, so partial clues appear first and invite the investigator to repeat the action.
Revealing background facts gradually through interviews changes which suspect looks plausible, so each conversation can shift the leading suspect.
A reversal that re-reads an object the audience has already seen collapses the first solution and makes the final answer feel earned.
when: designing a mystery reveal
why: The audience already holds the evidence, so the new reading feels fair rather than invented.

text: Layer reveals so each depends on the previous one: once the alibi trick is known, a second cover-up becomes explicable.
why: Chained dependence makes the later reveal follow from the first.

text: A layered misattribution twist runs through a trusted party's setup, a false culprit, a contradiction, an empty reward, a reinterpretation, and a final reversal of the culprit.
when: Designing a mystery with several reveals
why: Each stage explains the previous one, so the player's beliefs about guilt and reward shift together.

text: Revealing the aim, evidence or culprit early alerts the subject, who can prepare a consistent false account or lose the chance of an unguarded slip; hold details and hints until confrontation.
when: planning when to show evidence or hints to a suspect or the audience
why: A suspect who knows the evidence can prepare a consistent false account, and early hints weaken the reveal.

text: A search that appears unfair can turn the group against the investigator and provoke protest.
when: Conducting a search of a group.
why: People resist searches they see as unequal or unjust.

text: A reveal that jumps to a conclusion without intermediate reasoning feels unfair to the audience or player.
A private fact that looks minor alone can favour one theory over another, so members tend to underrate what they hold.
why: a fact's bearing often depends on other facts that only show up when combined

text: 1) Give the audience the same clues the solver has, showing each before the reveal. 2) Confront the suspect with the clues in order. 3) State the decisive reversal last, once it follows from them.
when: building a late or final-act reveal that must feel fair in hindsight
why: Clues shown in order let the audience recognise the reversal once named and check the solution against facts it already holds.

text: 1) Establish the accuser's version convincingly. 2) Plant a checkable clue earlier, such as a recalled voice or phrase. 3) Have the investigator name the true culprit with it, exposing the accuser and reframing earlier scenes. 4) Let the physical outcome follow the investigator's word.
when: designing a late twist where a character takes credit for or falsely accuses others
why: A reversal set up by earlier clues feels earned, while an unsupported one feels arbitrary.

text: 1) Overturn the expected identity through a sworn statement or testimony. 2) Follow with a confession that explains the disguise, substitutions and method in order.
1) Build each reveal layer on its own proof. 2) Make the first proof a documentary record. 3) Make the second a physical clue, such as a portrait. 4) Make the last a confession.
Let the player's action drive the climax: stage the confrontation with suspects present so the player produces the proof, and trigger the arrest by the player's signal, not a cutscene.
when: designing the final confrontation or sequence of a mystery
why: Player-produced proof and player-triggered arrest make the resolution feel earned.

text: Resolve several earlier unexplained clues in one explanatory scene, such as how the killer entered, why an object was taken and why an innocent suspect looked guilty.
when: writing the climax of a mystery with many planted clues or open threads
why: One explanation tying clues together is more satisfying than piecemeal explanations.

text: Avoid questions that assume the answer or ask about what the witness cannot know, since they may be blocked or struck.
Give players two plausible suspects supported by different clues, so the witness they choose to question decides which theory survives.
when: designing a choice between leads
why: the player's choice tests the rival theories

text: Use a mid-game reveal in which NPCs who accepted an early claim are shown the gap in it.
when: an early claim was accepted without verification
why: Exposing the gap rewards players who questioned the claim and changes NPC standing.

text: Make a mystery's reveal a physical breach or exposure of the mechanism, so the answer is shown directly rather than only described.
when: Staging the reveal of a hidden mechanism.
why: Seeing the mechanism makes the answer concrete and self-verifying.

text: Pair a closing theory with concrete events the player witnessed, and end the reveal with a concrete explanation of the main threat.
when: Ending a level's reveal
why: Concrete grounding makes the explanation satisfying

text: Overturn a confidently wrong conclusion with a new fact instead of erasing it, so earlier evidence gains a second meaning and the twist feels earned.
why: Earlier clues stay meaningful and connect to the twist, which the player already partly knows.

text: In the solution, replay collected clues and reinterpret evidence already shown, showing each item's place in the solution; the final speech only ties facts together.
when: when writing a solution
why: Audiences accept reveals grounded in earlier evidence.

text: A reveal can invert who is victim and who is manipulator, provided the earlier facts support both readings and the apparent target is shown to be the trap's designer.
A final reveal supplies the missing link, recasting earlier facts so events that seemed puzzling or misleading fall into place and fit the solution.
when: a central fact is disclosed
why: A new frame changes how earlier details connect, and earlier facts gain meaning from the solution.

text: A reveal can reframe an earlier ambiguous image: a scene first read as threatening can be recast once the explanation supplies its true cause.
when: When an early image was left open to more than one reading.
why: The explanation gives the image a new meaning without changing what was shown.

text: A game that tracks the player's working theory can reveal facts that do not fit once the theory is pursued too far, turning a wrong conclusion into a discovery.
when: Designing mystery systems where players form and pursue theories
why: Contradictions that surface after commitment make the player reassess, which deepens the twist.

text: A control device such as an oath, shown early as romantic flavour, reads as harmless until revealed as the mechanism of the crime, reframing earlier scenes.
A route assumption that looks like the killer's path can be reversed late by a timing clue, forcing players to reread earlier evidence with the corrected timeline.
when: An entry or exit path seems to explain the event
why: A timing clue that contradicts the path changes how all earlier evidence is interpreted.

text: Let a reveal reclassify a map element, such as a patrol that proves to be a shelter, while another unexplained element keeps tension alive.
when: designing reveals in a level
why: Partial resolution maintains tension.

text: Hint a hidden motive early and let the reveal reframe earlier suspicion, so the twist does not feel arbitrary.
In the reveal, explain point by point why the misleading emphasis was wrong, so the player sees exactly where attention went astray.
A chance confirmation verifies a suspicion by accident rather than by deduction, so the player confirms a belief instead of solving a mystery.
Keep the aftermath brief and often ironic, ending soon after the culprit is exposed or handed to an authority; the final word usually goes to the editorial or narrating voice.
Deliver a climax before its full explanation when the scene works without context, and fill in the context afterwards.
when: The climax is effective without full context.
why: Later explanation adds meaning after the fact.

text: After the main reveal, close a minor side thread, such as a valuable revealed as worthless, to tie off loose ends.
when: A subplot remains open after the climax.
why: Settling small threads quickly lets the main reveal carry the story's weight.

text: End on a short, clean line the reader will quote, since a memorable final phrase carries the reveal in memory.
Hiding a purpose so completely that the later reveal feels arbitrary makes the reveal unsatisfying.
when: Planning when and how a hidden purpose is revealed.
why: Players cannot connect a reveal to earlier clues they never saw.

text: A human agent introduced only at the reveal, with no earlier signs, feels arbitrary, and an inconsistent supernatural frame makes the solution look like a cheat.
when: Revealing a human cause behind a supernatural frame

text: Make the final explanation use only clues already seen, and account for every flagged gap, such as a stray item or an empty container.
when: when writing the solution of a mystery
why: New facts at the reveal feel unfair and leave flagged gaps unexplained.

text: Close a mystery with an external report, such as a newspaper, so the player learns the outcome without further investigation.
Reverse the victim's role late: reveal the victim's own action, like paying for an arrangement, aided the plot, or a seeming loss is a gain for protagonist or hidden party.
when: Choosing the strongest late twist for a victim-centred plot or a late-stage twist in a heist story.
why: Revealing the victim as complicit or as gaining reverses the audience's assumption about who is harmed and recasts the whole scheme.

text: An audience expecting danger from outside is changed when a character in the room confesses, reversing their view of who is trustworthy and who is the threat.
when: A confession reveals the culprit is among those trusted.
why: The reversal overturns expectations the audience built from earlier cues.

text: Revise a first impression of an NPC, whether composed or quick to agree, with a later second encounter or scripted check that corrects the player's initial reaction.
when: Designing NPCs whose early demeanor or responses should be doubted later.
why: A delayed check or second encounter corrects a false first impression that later evidence would overturn.

text: Stage a reversal by returning to the scene while the threat is still alive and visible, rather than explaining it in retrospect.
when: Revealing that the apparent threat was a human mechanism
why: A live reveal keeps tension and lets the player witness the exposure directly.

text: When a target looks unbreakable, seek the single assumption that fails rather than attacking every safeguard at once.
when: Facing a system that appears airtight
why: A plan must defeat every check together, so one failing assumption can open the whole route

text: Undo a theory with a source the player did not weigh earlier, such as a witness's motive to please or a financial record.
when: revealing that a planted solution was wrong
why: A new kind of source reverses the conclusion without introducing a new suspect

text: When a vanished person reappears in the same sealed room, the puzzle is reframed, and the audience needs a cause for the return as well as the disappearance.
when: A missing person returns to the room they vanished from.
why: The return adds a second question that the story must answer.

text: A later event such as a light change can reverse an earlier reading of a scene, forcing the player to reinterpret what they saw.
when: Designing a scene whose meaning changes with conditions.
why: New information recasts earlier observations and rewards attention.

text: Place the late counter-proof cluster at roughly 80-86% of the way through, and the final reconciliation at roughly 92-97%.
when: pacing a multi-solution mystery

text: A reversal-driven plot has seven stages: premise, false solution, investigation pressure, escape and misdirection, crisis, complication and reversal, and reveal with aftermath.
A reversal-driven mystery runs: hook, opening misdirections, suspicion on the household, false solution, reconstruction crisis, second false solution, climax, aftermath.
when: outlining a mystery built on reversals
why: Each segment tests and overturns a belief about the culprit

text: An informant can be right about the outcome and wrong about the cause, so hearsay is unreliable for mechanisms or amounts.
when: A rumor reports a result and an explanation for it.
why: Partial reporting can get the result right while the explanation is wrong.

text: 1) Disprove the identification of the suspect. 2) Show that the witness never existed. 3) Expose the purpose of the lure. Each stage removes one layer of the false belief while keeping the player engaged.
when: breaking a false belief in a mystery
why: Breaking the belief in stages keeps the player from losing the whole case at once

text: At the final proof, show a physical object that contradicts a common belief, such as a corpse that looks lifelike, to overturn the audience's assumption.
when: Climax proof of a supernatural identity.
why: A reversal makes the proof memorable and undermines the expected sign.

text: Resolve the legal or material consequence of a reversal, such as acquittal and inheritance, to show who benefits from the new truth.
when: Closing a mystery whose solution changes ownership or guilt.
why: Showing the consequence makes the reversal concrete rather than only a changed suspicion.

text: Show the physical result of a trick before its cause, so the audience registers the effect first and the explanation later confirms it.
A reveal that re-reads evidence already present, e.g. attacks recast as harm prevention or theft as planned fraud, makes every clue fit one consistent logic and feels always there.
when: Evidence is already on the table and read one way, or a final explanation reinterprets a prior clue.
why: Reinterpretation changes the meaning of evidence the player has already seen.

text: Reversing apparent culprit and victim, with the investigator as culprit, recasts earlier clues against a new suspect; a blackmailer-victim swap turns expected motive into its opposite.
Reverse a wrongful accusation at the end with a specific new clue proving innocence, using it to open a second suspect thread and close the innocent party's arc.
when: Ending a story that clears a falsely accused character.
why: An evidenced clearing is credible and keeps the story moving.

text: A suspect who turns questions back on the questioner may be deflecting rather than admitting anything.
After an apparent unmasking, continued threats show that the first explanation was incomplete and re-read earlier events.
when: A threat seems resolved but signals continue
why: The first explanation covered only part of the cause

text: Treat a reversed order as a hypothesis to test: damage may follow its event, a method may follow an owned item; let it reorder which records to check first.
when: Physical damage is read as evidence of how an entry happened, or an assumed sequence of decisions is taken for granted.
why: Damage can be produced either before or after the action, so the apparent order can be reversed.

text: When one reading is plausible, check whether the reverse reading fits equally well; if a fragment's reverse holds only unrelated content, rule that side out.
when: When one reading of an identity is plausible, or a fragment is printed on both sides.
why: Quickly rules out a candidate reading or source.

text: After a reversal exposes a false accusation following an irreversible act, show its cost via petitions, compensation or public confession; the act cannot be undone.
when: A reversal is revealed after the verdict is carried out.
why: Consequences make a reversal emotionally weighty rather than only informative; irreversibility increases the stakes of the lie.

text: A sympathetic first impression can be reversed by a later, independent source, provided earlier cues such as fear and secrecy fit the new explanation.
when: a character was presented as a victim
why: Consistent early cues make a reversal feel earned rather than unfair

text: If access is unclear, check whether the victim was watched more closely than they watched others, which can reveal hidden access.
when: when a locked or closed space has no obvious means of entry

text: A line near the reveal that hints at the reversal signals it to the audience without spelling it out in full.
A reversal lands only if the audience still remembers the earlier facts, so plant them early enough to be recalled.
when: designing a late reversal
why: recontextualising needs the original fact to be remembered

text: Instead of asking who wanted a clue read a certain way, ask what the victim could have intended by the object's state.
when: a staged clue points at a convenient time or suspect
why: the victim may have left the sign themselves

text: Place a reversal at the end of a chapter to give it strong emphasis.
Let a decisive reveal arrive after the audience believes the situation is lost, since a reversal at that point carries the most momentum.
why: Apparent defeat raises stakes, so a sudden turn feels stronger.

text: A theory that looks impossible can still be the one to pursue if it explains the facts better than the ordinary explanation.
When evidence fits two candidate targets, test the assumed intended victim, because a plan that seemed to misfire may have succeeded against someone else.
when: A reconstruction where every inquiry points one way but the planned outcome is unverified.
why: A flawed premise about the target can make every new fact fit a wrong reading.

text: A character who seemed unable to act can later perform the key act, and this reversal increases the impact of the admission.
when: A passive character is positioned to make the final statement
why: The contrast with earlier passivity makes the act more striking.

text: A trusted character can be the culprit as a reversal, provided the proof is delivered in order.
A reversal at a moment of apparent defeat works when the protagonist's plan was signalled earlier, so the audience accepts the twist in hindsight.
when: The protagonist seems trapped and the audience expects rescue or disaster.
why: Planted signs make the twist feel earned rather than convenient.

text: Reuse one twist shape, such as impersonation, across a collection so players learn to expect it and the next reversal feels both fair and surprising.
when: writing a multi-case mystery collection

text: A reversal that shows an apparently voluntary event was forced can reframe the apparent schemer as a manipulator who offered a misleading account.
A late reveal that the apparent evidence was manufactured or the suspect was a scapegoat reverses earlier clues, recasting the accused as innocent and the scheme as deliberate.
when: Fair-play structure has planted the clues the reversal depends on; apparent evidence is later shown manufactured.
why: Reinterpreting planted clues recasts the accused as innocent and the scheme as deliberate.

text: A firm inference or witness's certain account can be overturned by an objective record or expert physical examination, forcing a fresh reading of earlier events.
when: A witness account seemed certain, or an apparent cause is accepted.
why: An objective record or examination can outweigh a recollection.

text: When a reveal clears the wrongly accused and exposes the real culprit, earlier suspicions are recast as errors and the investigator's trust in appearances breaks.
when: at the close of a mystery
why: Reversing the target of suspicion gives the ending lasting weight.

text: A sudden reversal, such as a surprise visit or news item, can turn a stalled situation into a plan and shift the mood at once.
when: when a quiet investigation has stalled
why: Unexpected information breaks the waiting and gives characters a direction

text: A safeguard a character trusts can be reversed later, so the same condition that protected him removes his means of calling for help.
when: a reversal turns an earlier reassurance into the cause of harm
why: the condition that reassured also isolates the character

text: A second discovery that contradicts the working theory forces a reassessment and raises suspense.
Reversing apparent roles, so those who seemed criminal prove to be agents, reframes the whole situation for the audience.
A minor background character dismissed early can be revealed as a wanted culprit later, provided the early dismissal is shown as a judgment the player can revise.
when: Planting a key suspect in a mystery.
why: A fair reveal depends on the earlier judgment being visible and open to revision.

text: A case that first points toward the occult, then reverses that belief through a late cluster of physical evidence, keeps the player's assumptions active until the turn.
One overlooked qualifying word in a settled document can reverse a claim the reader already accepted, once the document is checked against its exact wording.
when: A property, ownership or rights claim has been treated as settled.
why: Readers trust a settled claim and rarely recheck its exact terms.

text: A reveal can overturn a prevailing belief with dated documents; it lands best when the contradicting texts are already in the reader's hands, needing only comparison.
when: Designing a mystery where the truth is found in records rather than announced.
why: Documents let the reader reassess a settled belief without confrontation; self-discovery by comparison makes the reversal feel earned.

text: A reversal mystery leads the audience to a false solution, then exposes the true one through a physical fact that the false solution cannot satisfy. Pages to avoid this: the true culprit is hidden in plain sight as the apparent victim.
A polemical argument can work like a mystery: each rebuttal turns on documents whose dates, omissions and attributions reshape what the reader believes.
Treating a reversal as a resolution is a mistake; a reversal reframes the case, and closure needs further steps.
A physical reveal that can be undone or reversed leaves the evidence unrecorded or incomplete.
A verdict reversed by a higher court can conceal a flawed first stage, so the whole case path should be reviewed, not only the result.
A reversal that depends on a convenient rescue, or contradicts the protagonist's established capability, weakens the character and makes the audience feel cheated.
when: Resolving a tense scene with a turn of events.
why: Rescues the protagonist did not cause undercut their established competence.

text: 1) State the events in their true chronological order. 2) Link them with dated records. 3) List unresolved possibilities and note whether they change the outcome. 4) Stage the final proof as a visible demonstration.
when: Presenting a solved case whose events were discovered backward.
why: Discovery order differs from true order; the explicit timeline lets the audience follow the logic.

text: 1) State the assumed order of events. 2) Trace each object's custody chain. 3) Test whether reversing the order fits the custody facts. 4) Adopt the order that the custody evidence supports.
when: A timeline built on assumed sequence conflicts with object custody.
why: Custody facts can overturn an intuitive order of events.

text: 1) Re-read every object under the reversed purpose. 2) Rebuild the events as an ordered timeline. 3) Check that each clue planted earlier explains its place in the timeline.
1) Start from the outcome. 2) Read the earlier events backward. 3) Ask how each event led to the next. 4) Treat an event as part of the plan only if it links to the chain.
when: after a crime, to test whether it was prepared
why: reading backward shows how ordinary events connect to the result

text: A late reversal is fair and credible only when its overturning clue appears earlier and explains, rather than replaces, clues already shown; unplanted reversals feel arbitrary and break trust.
when: Planning a late twist or a turn to break a stalled investigation.
why: Readers accept only reversals they could have checked against earlier evidence.

text: Plant setup before an empty reveal, such as misleading weight, a lost key or a forced lid, so the audience reads the emptiness as meaningful.
when: Building a reversal
why: Without setup the reversal has no weight

text: Plant the clue that supports a late reversal in the earlier narrative, and make the related character's absence visible, so the audience can recognise its significance.
why: a reversal relying on information the audience never had feels like a cheat

text: Recognizable enemy groups can be used for misdirection if their reveal is later reversed.
when: When planning a late twist on a known enemy type
why: Players trust familiar groups, so reversing them creates surprise

text: Reveal a wrongdoer's error late, since revealing it early removes the suspense the later reversal depends on.
Reverse the perceived victim and culprit within one visual scene, so the audience's belief changes in a single moment.
when: Staging a late twist that overturns the assumed threat
why: One scene carrying both the body and the empty room forces an immediate re-reading of the whole situation.

text: Stack two twists so the player resolves one belief and then discovers a second, more mundane belief underneath it.
Build the reveal so it reverses the premise object, such as showing it never moved, so the search must look inward rather than outward.
Let the player revisit a refused topic after gaining another clue, so the refusal pays off later.
when: when designing dialogue branches
why: Later context changes what the refusal means.

text: Return to an earlier hesitation the witness did not volunteer, since pressing it can expose an uncertainty they had concealed.
A witness who was advised to omit something may reveal it later, once the reason for silence no longer binds them, so re-question them after their protection changes.
when: A witness withheld facts on someone else's advice or to protect themselves.
why: The motive for silence weakens when the witness's risk or obligation changes.

text: 1) Let a questioner leave after a first answer. 2) Return after a short delay. 3) Compare the new answer with the first to test consistency.
when: When an answer may not be final.
why: A returning questioner tests whether the story holds.

text: Revisit a dismissed open item when new reasoning reframes its absence as evidence.
when: When an item was earlier judged unrecoverable.
why: A reframed absence can carry more information than the item itself.

text: Reward players who exhaust a cooperative contact's knowledge before that contact becomes unavailable.
Let players notice a mismatch between an NPC's energy and the subject at hand, and reward that attention with a new lead.
Let an NPC offer a small aside that opens a new line of questioning, so attentive players are rewarded.
when: Designing dialogue that should reward careful listening.
why: A passing remark that opens a lead makes attentiveness pay off in the game's progression.

text: Offering a reward to anyone who brings help quickly enlists passers-by as a summoned guard.
when: a protected person needs help during the night
why: the reward makes passers-by an extra layer of protection

text: A reward or wanted notice can rise in value as the player learns more, reversing the sense of a small task into a serious one.
when: A minor task is linked to a larger plot thread
why: New information changes the stakes of an apparently small task

text: Anyone who responds to a payment offer may be after the reward, so verify each claim independently.
Design NPCs who reveal a detail or change a confession under mild pressure, and reward patient questioning and noticing the shift.
when: When designing NPC dialogue

text: Reward the dialogue choice that brings a rambling NPC back on topic, since patience and a good pretext unlock the key facts.
when: when a conversation has many digressions

text: Reward the player for finding the lone dissenting witness, whose testimony costs them something to give.
when: Designing a mystery or investigation where dissent is risky.
why: Testimony given at personal cost carries more weight and rewards careful searching.

text: A riddle with no reachable key gives players nothing to act on, so the key must exist somewhere in the game.
when: Designing riddles
why: Unsolvable clues stall play

text: 1) Map each riddle phrase to an instrument, direction or landmark. 2) Find the single vantage point from which the clue becomes visible. 3) Take bearings on the spot.
when: a riddle encodes a physical location

text: 1) Record the unexplained phrase verbatim. 2) Turn it into a list of constraints such as count, time and landmark. 3) Test each candidate against every constraint. 4) Keep the candidate that meets all of them.
when: Solving a clue whose meaning is initially hidden.
why: Checking constraints one at a time narrows the answer to a single fit.

text: Rivalry over the same person or prize is itself a motive; rivals readily suspect each other, and quarrels and insults in the record reveal it.
when: two characters compete for the same prize, person or resource

text: A rival who wants to protect their own share may reveal what others were hiding.
when: conflict exists among people involved in a plot

text: People tend to overstate a rival's motive when the rival is already disliked.
when: a rival is already disliked by the observer
why: prior dislike biases how ambiguous evidence is read

text: Rivals tend to correct or contradict each other when pressed, which reveals facts that either would conceal alone.
Rival authorities may resent outsiders and hold back facts, and their cooperation depends on who receives credit.
when: A rival agency shares a case.
why: Credit and status shape what rivals are willing to reveal.

text: Weigh a rival's claims, denials or accusations for envy and self-interest; they do not settle which theory is right.
when: a rival disparages another investigator or theory; rivalry shapes what officials and witnesses say
why: rivalry can distort warnings and statements

text: A rival NPC who attacks witnesses by inventing their views should reward a player who asks them to name the claim they are answering.
Old social rivalries, such as competition over a marriage, can supply a motive for a present crime and should be recorded.
when: Reconstructing a family's social history during an investigation.

text: Test a rival suspect separately, even at some cost, to remove doubt about a psychological reading.
A boastful rival leaks information: what they brag about reaches the source, who repeats details and reveals how the rival learns things.
when: When a rival is in a competitive relationship with a source.
why: Competitive boasting and flattered sources spread details between parties.

text: Pitting two rivals against each other lets one death remove a threat while the surviving rival absorbs the blame.
when: Scheming to eliminate someone and frame another.
why: The survivor has motive and is visibly connected to the fight.

text: A rival pursuing the same goal may watch the same endpoint, complicating the operation; a second character's inquiry about the same target can reveal such a rival tracker.
Include a rival character who challenges the player's neat theory aloud or holds a confident solution that may be wrong, so the player must test it.
when: designing investigator characters or when a theory is presented as the answer
why: it rewards checking rather than trusting boldness; spoken objections expose gaps a player may otherwise accept

text: Rivals working the same case can agree explicit rules: one may not publish what it learned only from an official source, and each may keep back a vital discovery.
when: Two agents hold different sources and agendas
why: Agreed limits let them cooperate without giving up all advantage

text: A rival faction can plant decoy evidence whose lie becomes visible to players who cross-check it.
Let rival factions respond to earlier reveals by moving or hiding evidence, so the player's timing changes what the rival can do.
when: designing a game with rival factions and clue reveals
why: Timing changes how opponents respond and builds tension

text: A rival's sworn claim is an accusation to be tested, not an established fact.
Before accepting a supernatural or occult reading, test ordinary human explanations such as motive, secret or circumstance; keep the supernatural open only while they fail.
when: A mysterious cause is claimed or an occult hint has a possible human cause.
why: Ordinary causes often explain outcomes attributed to unusual ones; testing them keeps the story fair.

text: When an ambiguous message is read aloud, a character who tests several readings before the facts arrive keeps the audience weighing competing explanations.
when: an ambiguous hint is received before evidence

text: Rival theories can read the same object in opposite ways, so each reading must be tested against the full set of evidence, not a single item.
Rivals informally test ideas with each other, and both gain, because a theory challenged by a rival is improved or dropped sooner.
When many similar traces in a scene differ in condition, players compare them to infer timing or order of events, turning scattered clues into a hypothesis.
when: A scene holds many similar objects with varied damage or position.
why: Comparison reveals which differences track when or how each object was involved.

text: Two appeals to a person's character, one from pattern and one from personal knowledge, can compete without either settling the question.
Test simpler explanations first, such as a spare item, and prefer the simpler human one when it fits; set aside elaborate mechanisms the evidence does not need.
when: Choosing between explanations for an apparently impossible or elaborate action.
why: Testing simpler causes first avoids unjustified complex conclusions.

text: Offer rival motives for an unexplained act, such as bribery, a promised payment, romantic interest, attention-seeking or embarrassment, and test each against the other evidence.
when: A person's cooperation or conduct has several plausible motives.
why: The same act can have different causes, so each motive must be checked.

text: A rival who suspects another character can serve as a red herring, so players should check opportunity before accepting motive as the answer.
when: A rival's suspicion points toward an innocent character

text: Make a rival NPC who gains from a false accusation a natural red herring, and give the player a way to check that rival's motive.
when: designing mystery suspects in a game
why: A checkable motive makes the red herring fair.

text: Alternate viewpoints so each step toward the answer is paired with another character's fear.
Compare the chosen location with nearby alternatives to see which one satisfies the actor's needs.
when: explaining why an act took place at a specific spot

text: Deductive reasoning is only as reliable as its list of alternatives, so an omitted explanation can make the correct one look impossible.
Build a detailed alternative explanation that fits the same facts, and keep it open until a fact contradicts it.
when: The official case rests on items that each have innocent explanations
why: Tested rivals expose weak links that a single account hides

text: Judge any explanation by whether it accounts for all the evidence, not only the part it was built to cover.
A competing explanation, such as food slowing absorption, must be weighed against how large the gap actually is before it is accepted.
Avoid claiming much knowledge; a boast invites checks, while modest claims keep the other side guessing.
Keep a rival explanation open, such as a real criminal framing an innocent person, until evidence rules it out.
When a physical object matches a claim, weigh rival explanations of how it came to be that way before accepting the claim.
when: when a found object seems to confirm a testimony
why: the same object may fit a different account of events

text: Use the situation's goals, such as speed and secrecy, to narrow candidates by distance and destination.
when: when candidates differ in distance or destination
why: the goals of the situation favour some candidates over others

text: Ask whether the proposed theory is consistent with the charge being made; a mismatch exposes a gap in the reasoning.
when: A theory is offered to explain a specific accusation
why: Inconsistency between theory and charge reveals unsupported links

text: Identify the evidence each hypothesis depends on, since the same evidence, such as regular large payments, can fit opposite stories.
when: A single piece of evidence supports more than one explanation.
why: Shared evidence cannot decide between explanations on its own.

text: Test each innocent explanation a suspect offers for a trace rather than accepting it, since each trace can be given a harmless source.
Test every leading theory, simple or convenient, against the evidence before accepting or rejecting it.
why: A theory that fits the investigator's hopes can warp how facts are read.

text: Include a checkable rival explanation, such as an accident, so the player's first theory can prove wrong.
when: Designing a mystery with a tempting first solution.
why: A live alternative keeps the investigation from closing too early.

text: Reasoning that starts from one favoured explanation may overlook the others, so keep several explanations open until facts separate them.
when: when an investigator has a favourite explanation early
why: a favoured explanation can filter out evidence for alternatives

text: Offer a competing mechanism late in the mystery so players can test their reconstruction against it before the true method is revealed.
A plausible alternative explanation for a fact creates reasonable doubt, even when no direct evidence contradicts the prosecution's account.
Parallel cases competing for the same authority's attention slow an investigation, since limited attention is split.
when: several cases share one decision-maker
why: Divided attention reduces progress on each

text: Each theory generates predictions; checking them by measurement or search tests whether the theory holds.
Mixing rival theories, or a single story explaining every fact, yields a conclusion that fits everything, explains nothing, cannot be tested, and hides alternatives fitting the same evidence.
when: Combining explanations of the same evidence, or accepting a single story that explains every fact.

text: Two incompatible explanations can fit the same residues, so residues alone rarely settle who acted or how.
An appealing alternative theory can replace the evidence if the investigator stops checking it against facts.
Do not treat the most detailed version of an account as the most accurate.
A theory that fits one suspect while leaving the others unexamined is incomplete; test every candidate against it.
Fixating on one clue blinds the investigator to the rest of the evidence, so the whole picture is lost.
when: Many clues conflict and attention narrows to one
why: Overweighting a single item hides how the others fit together

text: An explanation that fits the narrator's own framework can make every outcome seem to confirm the theory, while remaining untestable against the scene.
A supernatural explanation can be a cover story, so check whether it explains the traces better than a human agent does.
when: A supernatural explanation is offered for physical traces.
why: A human agent may be hiding behind the appearance of the supernatural.

text: A narrator with partial information can form a confident wrong theory, and acting on it can lead to an unjust accusation.
when: When an observer sees only part of events
why: Missing facts can look like complete ones

text: Treating an outsider theory and an insider theory as mutually exclusive can hide a lead, since both can be tested.
Confirming a rival narrative, such as blaming an outside group, while the simpler explanation goes untested, leads the investigation to the wrong conclusion.
when: Several stories compete to explain an event.
why: A dramatic rival explanation attracts attention and can displace testing of ordinary causes.

text: 1) List each reading the evidence allows. 2) Name a test that confirms or rules out each. 3) Keep rivals open and test each against every new fact. 4) Run tests before settling; discard any the facts break, since a single fitting fact rarely separates rivals.
when: Evidence fits several explanations and facts are incomplete.
why: Keeping rivals open prevents premature conclusions; a fixed first answer can fit part of the evidence while being wrong.

text: 1) State each alternative as a separate theory. 2) List the physical traces or records it predicts. 3) Check them against the scene, records and expert knowledge. 4) Keep theories whose traces match; drop any a test removes. Plausibility or mood alone establishes nothing.
when: Several explanations fit early clues or a plausible explanation is not yet verified.
why: Explanations that fit mood but not traces should not survive testing.

text: 1) Recreate the suspected cause, such as a trap or animal, under the original conditions. 2) Compare its damage pattern or effect with the observed one. 3) Reject the hypothesis if the effects differ.

1) Accept a new hypothesis for argument. 2) Derive what it implies about other parts of the case, such as an act that must have been done in parts. 3) Check whether the earlier theory survives, and reject any hypothesis whose implications do not fit.
when: Two or more explanations fit the same facts.
why: Consequences expose contradictions that a theory alone hides.

text: 1) Name the innocent or familiar explanation. 2) List what it cannot explain, such as why a target was chosen when more valuable items were left. 3) Check each physical detail against what it would produce. 4) Adopt it as a working presumption only if it fails.
when: An obvious convenient theory rests on a common category and has not been checked against physical details.
why: A plausible explanation can leave real evidence unexplained; unexplained details can reveal a different motive.

text: 1) Name each rival explanation, such as accident, suicide or murder. 2) Test each against specific clues. 3) Count the coincidences each requires as costs. 4) Drop any hypothesis a single clear clue contradicts. Keep separate questions apart so one does not block the others.
when: A case or trace has more than one plausible explanation.
why: Systematic exclusion is more reliable than favouring one explanation early.

text: 1) List the supernatural explanation alongside every plausible human one, such as a prank, a concealment or a precedent. 2) Test each against the physical traces. 3) Keep open any the facts do not yet rule out.
when: An odd or apparently impossible event invites a supernatural reading but evidence is limited.
why: Physical checks separate plausible explanations from unfounded ones.

text: 1) Name the explanation offered for a sound or trace. 2) Ask whether the suspect would have produced that sound or trace. 3) If not, weaken or drop the explanation.
when: a sound or trace is explained away as harmless

text: 1) List candidate explanations for an act. 2) Ask a witness who saw the actor about alertness, gaze and gait. 3) Discard explanations those answers contradict.
when: one witness observed the actor's condition closely
why: Testimony about physical and mental state can rule out explanations

text: 1) When one testimony or trace fits two sources, assign each reading to a different tester. 2) Have each test every new fact against their reading. 3) Compare which reading accumulates contradictions.
when: When evidence supports two explanations equally well.
why: Parallel testing against the same facts exposes which reading fails.

text: 1) Test the new theory against all the facts the old theory used. 2) Check whether any expected reaction, such as a silence, fails to appear under the new theory. 3) Revise until every trace is explained.
when: Re-examining a case after a reversal.
why: A reversal that leaves facts unexplained will not hold.

text: 1) State each motive hypothesis. 2) Note the kind of victim and planner each implies. 3) Find one check whose result separates the hypotheses.
when: Several motives fit a case
why: A distinguishing test lets the investigator choose between hypotheses instead of holding them all.

text: 1) Ask which facts the rival theory leaves untouched 2) Note each concrete contradiction 3) Seek evidence that resolves each contradiction.
when: a neat explanation fits the main fact but must be checked
why: A theory can fit its central fact yet fail on details.

text: 1) Keep the accurate observation. 2) Set aside the supernatural or improbable explanation. 3) Ask which ordinary act would produce the same appearance, then test it against all other details.
when: A striking observation has an improbable cause and an ordinary cause could produce the same appearance.
why: Keeping the observation avoids discarding real evidence with the false explanation.

text: 1) Collect each account of the same behaviour. 2) Read the rival account aloud so each speaker can answer it. 3) Test both against known facts and choose the account that fits best.
when: Two people explain the same observed act differently.
why: Setting accounts against each other and facts exposes which claims hold up.

text: 1) Identify the single strong fact. 2) Ask who else could have produced it and when. 3) Build a rival explanation that accounts for the same fact. 4) Test it against known facts. 5) Look for corroboration.
when: one fact points one way and no rival explanation exists

text: 1) Compare the proposed explanation with the victim's character and routine. 2) Check the physical setting for fit. 3) Check the suspect's account against the other people's positions.
when: A death is presented as self-inflicted or accidental.
why: Each check can expose a staged explanation.

text: 1) List every account the evidence allows of how a death occurred. 2) Add hypotheses such as a third party being shielded. 3) For each account, state the conduct it would predict. 4) Test each against observed behaviour before settling.
when: When the cause of a death is contested.
why: Different accounts predict different behaviour, so testing separates them.

text: 1) List each explanation that fits the body. 2) For each, state which trace it predicts. 3) Note which traces contradict each explanation. 4) Keep both open until the traces decide between them.
when: when a death could be self-inflicted or caused by another person
why: each trace narrows the field only if its prediction is explicit

text: 1) List every explanation that fits the locked state. 2) Identify the physical change each explanation requires. 3) Test each change against the scene. 4) Discard explanations the evidence contradicts.
when: when a locked state has been broken or disturbed

text: 1) List each competing reading of an event. 2) For each, state the traces a true version would leave. 3) Check the scene for those traces. 4) Treat an expected trace that is missing as evidence against that reading.
when: when an account could be a real act or a staged one

text: 1) State each candidate explanation for the anomaly. 2) Test each against the timeline. 3) Reject any explanation that fits one fact but fails the timing.
when: When several explanations fit the observed mismatch
why: An explanation must fit all facts, not just one

text: 1) List each competing explanation for an event. 2) Work out what behaviour each would predict afterwards. 3) Compare each prediction with what was observed and drop explanations that conflict.
when: Two or more explanations compete
why: Each explanation implies different behaviour afterwards.

text: Give NPCs competing goals and plan culprit actions under time limits, then check whether the traces left are consistent with that plan.
when: When generating or designing a murder mystery
why: Time-constrained plans leave checkable traces, letting players choose among plausible reconstructions.

text: 1) List each candidate explanation. 2) Mark each part that lacks a supporting trace or witness. 3) Test each part against physical evidence and the timeline. 4) Drop any explanation that the evidence contradicts.
when: Several explanations compete for the same evidence.
why: Testing each part separately exposes weak links that a tidy whole story hides.

text: 1) Note where the object was found. 2) Note what it was used for. 3) Test the suspect's innocent explanation against both before accepting it.
when: A common object appears at a scene where harm was attempted
why: Context can reveal an innocent story to be incomplete

text: 1) Identify the object or act the official account requires. 2) Perform or imagine that act. 3) Check whether the object would have been needed and whether it was present.
when: an accepted explanation rests on a single object or inference
why: a required object that is absent counts against the account

text: 1) Reconstruct the observation conditions: distance, light, weather and wind direction. 2) Propose a known mechanism. 3) Check whether it reproduces each reported detail, including timing and how the sight faded.

1) Fix a timeline from known dates. 2) Use it to limit when each suspect could have acted. 3) For each rival, request an independent record. 4) Keep the rival until confirmed or ruled out. 5) Combine timeline and records to narrow the search.
when: multiple explanations fit the known facts and each can be checked against records

text: 1) State the hypothesis as an untested supposition. 2) Build its strongest case: motive, means to conceal, a substitute, and a disposal site. 3) Ask how each fact bears on it. 4) Invite a challenger to question each step.
when: an investigator needs to test a damaging theory before believing it
why: explicit testing exposes weak links that a confident argument hides

text: 1) Infer who used a place from small objects and worn paths. 2) Write the theory as numbered points. 3) List the facts it leaves unexplained. 4) Weigh each anomaly by how much it damages the theory. 5) Judge the theory by how many anomalies it covers.
when: a theory explains most facts and needs a checklist of its gaps
why: listing anomalies shows what the theory must still account for

text: 1) Test each explanation against all the circumstances. 2) Group small, individually weak facts that point the same way. 3) Judge each explanation by how well it covers them. 4) Compare with alternatives that may be just as strange.
when: Choosing among several candidate explanations
why: Weak facts gain force when they converge, and alternatives must be judged on equal terms

text: 1) Offer an alternative source for a damaging trace. 2) Compare the trace's properties, such as colour, length and condition, with that source. 3) Reject the alternative if any property does not fit.
when: A physical trace is assigned to a suspect by rival explanations.
why: Property mismatch disproves an alternative owner.

text: 1) Give each suspect a visible motive. 2) Supply a second, equally plausible explanation for the event. 3) Test each explanation separately against the evidence.
when: Investigating an event with several suspects or possible causes.
why: Testing alternatives separately prevents a single visible motive from settling the case.

text: 1) List ordinary explanations: conspiracy, disordered mind, illness, shadow, misremembered sight, coincidence. 2) Test each against all the evidence. 3) Consider a supernatural cause only after ordinary ones fail.
when: unexplained events occur
why: ordinary causes are checked first so a strange cause is not accepted by default

text: 1) Name each candidate explanation for a strange event. 2) For each, list the facts it explains and the facts it leaves unexplained, testing against the whole pattern. 3) Keep the best-fitting explanation as the working answer until it fails.
when: when a strange event could have a supernatural or human cause and several candidate explanations are available
why: No single candidate accounts for every occurrence, so only testing against the full pattern shows which explanation survives and where the residue lies.

text: 1) List all plausible explanations for the event, making sure none is omitted. 2) Test each against known motives, opportunities and behaviour. 3) Eliminate an option only when the evidence is decisive. 4) Accept the remaining option only after confirming the list of alternatives is complete.
when: A player or investigator must choose among rival explanations, or elimination has left a single explanation standing.
why: An incomplete list makes the remaining option look inevitable when it may not be, and a missing alternative makes an elimination-based conclusion unsound.

text: 1) When a new story fits the known facts, list each link of the existing chain. 2) Test each link against the rival story. 3) Keep links the rival does not explain. 4) Re-judge the verdict from the surviving links.
when: A credible rival explanation appears against a circumstantial case
why: Rejecting the whole chain discards links that may still hold

text: 1) List the human explanations for each strand: fabrication, coincidence, error, malice. 2) Test each against the evidence. 3) Note which strands resist every human explanation.
when: When a mystery has both a rational path and an apparently supernatural cause.
why: Systematically failing human explanations lets the player see when the uncanny is the only fit.

text: 1) Separate what is known from what is merely asserted. 2) Weigh the source's knowledge and motives. 3) Check the timeline the explanation depends on. 4) Test each layer of the account separately.
when: A second party offers an explanation for a hidden event
why: Confident explainers can be wrong or self-interested

text: Hold several explanations open at once, each accounting for all known facts, and keep each provisional until evidence separates them; dropping or committing to one early hides the right answer.
when: Early in an inquiry while facts are thin, or when several explanations fit the same events.

text: Keep a merely possible rival provisional and test it before accepting it; present any conclusion as probable, not settled, until tests support it, since possibility alone does not establish truth.
when: A rival explanation is proposed or a conclusion is being formed.

text: Offer two or three plausible explanations for one puzzling clue, such as a folk reading and a mundane one, each backed by different clues, so only one survives all tests.
when: Designing a mystery or puzzling physical clue with a single true cause.
why: Players must test explanations to find the one consistent with all evidence.

text: Let a community or rumour system keep rival explanations of one event alive, each with some support (personal killing, a fight, deliberate disappearance), so players must weigh them.
For an unexplained disappearance, keep rival explanations open and test each, such as death, imprisonment, extracting information, wagering on outcomes or demanding ransom.
when: An unexplained disappearance occurs.

text: Before committing to a theory, list every competing explanation it must beat, keep a record of each alternative, and weigh each against the evidence.
Before reading silence as evidence, check whether an innocent cause such as fear or distance fits the timing; a fear that did not yet exist cannot explain it.
why: silence has many causes, and only a cause present at the right time can account for it

text: Include a rival NPC who reaches a confident early conclusion, so the player sees the cost of acting on partial proof.
Test a hostile witness's account against a neutral witness when the two share a household and may have rivalries.
Keep rival explanations open when judging odd behaviour, and do not settle unresolved questions by assumption.
when: Interpreting a suspect's or witness's unexplained actions.
why: Assumed answers hide alternatives that may be true.

text: Test a comforting explanation against facts before accepting it; do not present an argued theory as tested when it has not been checked.
when: a theory offers relief from a painful outcome
why: comfort is not evidence

text: Test each plausible explanation against a specific observed detail, and reject it when that detail contradicts it, not merely because it seems unlikely.
when: A plausible theory is offered and an observation can test it.

text: A plausible but unproven alternative does not disprove a case; test each link of the main case independently.
Give rival NPC investigators preconceived theories that the player must expose by finding contradicting evidence.
when: Designing competing investigators in a mystery.
why: Players then engage in reasoning by testing rather than accepting the first answer.

text: Test every theory, including elegant and complete ones, against physical constraints such as strength, reach, and distance before accepting it.
when: several explanations are on the table
why: An elegant, complete theory can still be wrong, and physical constraints are what rule out impossible acts.

text: A theory that clears a suspect of the worst charge must be tested against the evidence like any other theory.
Give rival readings of a document to different NPCs so the player must judge which interpretation is trustworthy.
when: Designing competing interpretations in a mystery.
why: Conflicting authorities make the player weigh credibility.

text: Before building a theory on an odd detail, test each rival explanation for it, such as the person fled versus was never there.
when: when a single unusual detail is central to a theory

text: Put rival hypotheses to an expert so they must commit to one or back away, exposing the limits of their opinion.
Let two NPCs describe the same evening with matching outlines but different details, so the player must compare them.
List each clue with its plausible innocent alternatives so the reader or player can weigh them instead of accepting the intended reading.
when: Designing evidence in an investigation story or game.
why: Unmentioned alternatives make weak evidence look conclusive.

text: Let a suspect finish personal explanations before judging him, since background such as motive often explains erratic behaviour.
Test a companion's ready explanation of odd behaviour before accepting it, because accepting it lets the explainer control the story.
when: someone offers an explanation before examining the behaviour
why: an unexamined explanation can close inquiry prematurely

text: Keep a second solution path open so a player who discards a red herring can still reach the answer.
Stage scenes with props suggesting a struggle or gang attack so players form a false theory that they must test.
when: Designing crime scenes for investigation

text: Test a theory's logic with a hypothetical method; a joke about method is not evidence but can expose a flaw in the theory.
when: Evaluating an elaborate suspect theory
why: Pushing a theory to an absurd case reveals whether its logic holds

text: Give every explanation a credible rival so the player keeps a theory but never a certainty.
when: Misdirected investigation stage.
why: Competing readings sustain doubt.

text: Factions may choose committee members precisely so the opposing party's influence cannot sway decisions.
when: a committee is contested between factions
why: Control of decisions is the goal of the selection.

text: A refused favour or trade between neighbours can later be recorded as part of a grievance and used in a serious charge against the refuser.
when: when a community has small quarrels before a serious accusation
why: Earlier friction gives later suspicion a ready motive

text: Illness or harm striking several neighbors at once can be blamed on one invisible agent.
when: Several people in a community fall ill or suffer harm together

text: Accusers are often neighbors with a stake in the accused's land, livestock, debts or reputation, so accusations cluster around existing local disputes.
when: In small communities where resources are shared or contested.
why: Shared boundaries, animals and insults create quarrels that witnesses then act on.

text: Common fame is general reputation used as grounds for an accusation, alongside sworn testimony.
Committee and seating assignments can reveal rivals linked by family, marriage and land.
Rivalry often runs along several axes at once, such as romance and status, so separate the axes to learn which one drove an action.
Households beside a dispute's origin are often where an affair begins, so check neighbour proximity when tracing a charge.
when: when tracing where an accusation started
why: nearby households share the dispute and its witnesses

text: Common everyday goods, such as a widely sold brand, do not identify anyone, so they should not be used to name a person.
Do not confront a watcher in public, because a public scene gives the opposing side a legal or social pretext.
when: Discovering a tail

text: Someone playing a role often betrays it through actions that depart from a real resident's routine, such as entering a familiar place without the expected ease.
when: When observing someone claiming a familiar place or identity
why: Real routines are habitual, while a role must be consciously performed.

text: A role index pairs each person with the pages where they appear and a role label, such as arrest, examination, trial, execution, or excommunication.
A role label records what happened to a person but not why it happened.
Keep speech and conduct consistent with the assumed role, since outward plausibility often does more than detailed questioning.
when: Maintaining a cover during an investigation
why: Plausible conduct keeps the cover intact without constant probing

text: Give a character only the knowledge that serves their role, because irrelevant facts blur their profile and crowd out useful ones.
why: A focused knowledge set makes the character's purpose legible

text: Read trace features such as print size, stride and boldness of movement together to infer who assisted and who acted.
when: Several people left traces at one scene.
why: Combined movement features indicate roles.

text: Count the roles a plot requires separately from the people visible in it; a threat that seems to need several parties may need only one.
when: a threat appears to need several outside parties
why: one person can fill more than one role

text: A person's seat or role determines which stage he could have witnessed, so check who sat where before judging whether he was present.
when: inferring whether an official saw a particular stage

text: Judge an official or witness by their practical role in proceedings, not only by public reputation, which can hide real influence.
when: assessing how much an official shaped a proceeding

text: Treating a partial participant as the main offender, or the reverse, leads to wrong expectations about who will respond and what they know.
why: a character's role determines their likely behavior and knowledge

text: Eliminating a suspect because their role seems to rule them out, without checking the timing, can wrongly clear the guilty.
Group characters by role topics such as afflicted or confessors, and use those groupings to decide which characters the player is told to watch.
Compare a character's claimed role with observed behavior; if the role implies one conduct and the observed conduct differs, treat the mismatch as a contradiction to pursue.
why: Conduct inconsistent with a stated role exposes a false claim or hidden motive.

text: Physical traces reported after each visit to a booked room, such as disturbed bedding, can show what occurred there.
Read a private room's furnishings, decoration and collected objects as evidence of the occupant's profession, wealth, spending, taste and associates.
when: a character's personal life must be inferred from the environment, or players need a profile before speaking to the character
why: private spaces reflect habits without the occupant speaking

text: Room condition, such as dust or ash, gives a time window: a spotless room with no dust suggests that a document was written and torn recently.
Read a room's books and unfinished work as a record of what its occupant studied, feared or was preoccupied with.
Disorder confined to one spot marks a localized event; rooms beyond that look orderly suggest the struggle did not spread.
when: When assessing the extent of a disturbance at a scene
why: The spread of disorder shows where an event occurred.

text: Treat an interpretation of a room's objects as a hypothesis, not as proof of a person's motive.
1) Ask where the witness sat and where light sources and the sun fell. 2) Rebuild the scene from their own vantage point. 3) Ask about peripheral objects such as wall pictures.
when: a witness has been in a location and gives an account of it
why: Peripheral details show whether the room was really observed

text: Ask where a meeting happened as well as who attended, since the room shows who else was nearby.
Round numbers are only suspicious in context; treating every round figure as a clue produces false motives.
when: When reviewing ordinary records such as receipts or ledgers.
why: Round sums are often ordinary, so context must decide their meaning.

text: A timeline is only as precise as its times, so a rough interval leaves the gap it covers uncertain.
why: Precision cannot exceed the precision of the recorded times.

text: 1) Count the rounds in the weapon. 2) Account for each empty chamber and each wound. 3) Check that the remaining count matches the expected total.
when: A shooting must be reconciled with the weapon's ammunition.
why: Each shot is then either accounted for or shown to be missing.

text: Traces such as remains, ruts and debris accumulate over time. Read in sequence, they reveal a route and what happened along it, even without a witness.
A multi-stop route limits where an item could first have been sent, so the posting port narrows where to search.
when: tracing an item through a multi-stop route

text: A fugitive who avoids busy lit streets, cuts through gaps and goes around obstacles likely knows the area.
why: Route choices reveal familiarity with the local layout

text: Reconstruct a substitution method by asking what each participant had to do at each step of the route.
when: Investigating a staged route or alibi
why: Stepwise reconstruction exposes the required actions and the people who performed them

text: Check the stops along a suspect's route for places where an object could be left, collected or handed over.
when: A suspect's movements are tracked and an object may have moved with them.
why: A stop on a route can serve as a hidden drop point for moving an object.

text: Infer a movement route from the street layout and from the only direction a site can be reached.
when: reconstructing how a prisoner or cart travelled
why: terrain and street plans constrain possible paths

text: Judge each entry route by how easy it is, how noisy it would be, and who could have observed it, rather than accepting the first plausible one.

1) Find objects away from the body. 2) Confirm each object's owner, for example through servants or records. 3) Order the finds along a plausible route. 4) Check the route against the layout, such as tunnels, gates and roads.
when: a trace is found away from the body

text: 1) Mark a trail by blazing trees or cutting bark. 2) Clear brush so horses can pass; where roots or stones block the way, the track is a bridle-path. 3) Widen it for ox-carts, making it a road. 4) Add gates or bars where it crosses fenced land. 5) Fence both sides to make a public highway.
when: describing how a route matured over time

text: 1) Collect dated, checkable events: asset sales, cash withdrawals, transport changes, and last sightings. 2) Order them by time. 3) Mark the point where the record stops as the place to begin the search.
when: A person has vanished and the record ends at a known point.
why: A chain of dated events shows where the trail goes cold and where to look next.

text: 1) Start from the final resting place. 2) Follow the water route upstream toward the likely starting point. 3) Confirm the route against the layout of the surroundings.
when: A body or object was moved by water
why: Backward reasoning from the endpoint narrows the starting location

text: Test a witness's described route against physical evidence, such as the state of a door or wall, before accepting the route.
when: A witness describes how someone entered or left
why: A route that conflicts with the scene signals an inaccurate or false account.

text: Provide a physical route that fits the thief's size, so the solution can be checked against the environment.
when: designing the entry solution of a locked-room mystery
why: A checkable physical route makes the solution verifiable in play.

text: A stopped, altered, or suddenly reworded routine is often the first sign of a changed situation, even before the cause is known.
why: Routines are stable, so their interruption or alteration marks a change in circumstances.

text: Treat routines as a baseline: a deviation or intrusion becomes evidence only when it breaks an established pattern, and then stands out at once and often carries meaning.
when: When a scene or conduct should follow a known pattern.
why: Regularity makes a missing or changed element noticeable at once.

text: Use a regular habit or witnesses' reports of habitual acts, such as routine orders or nightly pacing, as a dependable time reference for when events or arrivals occurred.
when: When estimating when a person arrived or acted, or when witnesses report habitual actions.
why: Routine gives regular observers a dependable reference and anchors when events happened without explanation.

text: A single unusual absence from a settled schedule can look more significant than it is; many interruptions are routine and carry no hidden purpose.
when: When interpreting one unusual absence or change in a settled schedule.
why: A well-established pattern exaggerates the anomaly.

text: 1) Establish the normal routine of a place, household, device or person. 2) Note each break and record when it occurred. 3) Ask what each break signals and compare it to the routine. 4) Confirm the timeline with another source such as access logs or witness entries.
when: When a setting follows a known rhythm with no direct evidence, or an event happens at a time that breaks a known pattern.
why: Deviations are meaningful only against an established baseline, and a second source checks the timeline.

text: A sudden emotional collapse during a public event breaks the scene and lets a quieter bystander speak privately to the investigator.
when: a performance or gathering is disrupted by one person's distress
why: The disruption lifts the social pressure that kept the bystander silent

text: A person who normally avoids a certain look may break that habit when news matters to them, so a changed glance can signal concern.
when: A character's usual habit of gaze or manner changes during a conversation.
why: Breaking an established habit signals that the subject has become important to the speaker.

text: A broken arrangement, such as a missed meeting replaced by a message, can signal a shift in intent before the message is read.
Observers judge conduct against shared time norms, so being out past a conventional hour is noticed and read as a breach.
when: A social setting with customary hours for rest or departure.
why: Shared expectations give observers a baseline against which deviations stand out.

text: Players who meet an innocent, mundane scene doubt their working theory, and a well-built red herring rewards those who keep investigating.
when: when a scene seems to contradict a theory
why: ordinary surroundings make a conspiracy look unlikely

text: People ignore familiar routine noise, but unusual or prolonged noise can wake sleepers and draw attention.
when: when a noise is used to cover movement
why: Habituation hides expected sounds, while novel sounds break through.

text: Watchers kept still in a dark, silent room with no activity perceive time as passing slowly, and the wait feels longer than it is.
when: Long, quiet waiting periods in a dark space
why: Little stimulation makes elapsed time feel stretched

text: Planners neglect small details they never allowed themselves to consider, so a trivial circumstance can upset the whole plan.
A prejudiced listener can miss a contradiction, treating a detail only one person can perceive as confirmation rather than as a reason for doubt.
when: a detail conflicts with the expected conclusion
why: belief blinds the listener to the conflict

text: A fall in a person's visit frequency can signal that the household has changed.
when: when a regular visitor notices fewer admissions or contacts
why: Routine contact breaks down when the household's situation shifts.

text: A break in routine, such as a skipped meal, late return, or unusual outing by people who never went together, prompts investigation and a timeline check.
when: When a regular pattern is interrupted or a character's action departs from their routine.
why: Routine is the baseline against which deviations are noticed, and unusual actions often mark where a hidden event lies.

text: When a person known for steady habits breaks one, the break itself is a strong signal that something has changed.
A departure from a usual schedule, such as an earlier return than normal, is the first signal of a suspicious event and needs explaining.
when: comparing a person's movements to their routine

text: Routine observations, such as a change in how much someone eats, can serve as a second line of evidence beside physical traces.
Establish routines, such as a standing meal or a standing guard, as scripted states that the audience can check against later scenes.
why: a routine sets an expectation that a later scene can confirm or break

text: A scene arranged for an activity at a time when none is expected signals that someone has been there and merits investigation.
when: a routine or expected timing is broken in a scene
why: an out-of-routine arrangement betrays recent or unexpected presence

text: Establish the normal arrangement of keys before judging a deviation, since household routine defines what counts as unusual.
when: A locked room is part of the evidence.
why: A deviation is meaningful only against a known baseline.

text: A minor detail that breaks an ordinary habit can reveal more than a major fact; ask what a normal person would have done and treat departures as questions.
when: when reconstructing a sequence of actions

text: A break from a known routine at the time of a crime signals unease, but it does not prove guilt on its own.
