when: someone who knows the person's habits notices an odd act
why: nervousness shows in out-of-character behavior

text: Treat unexplained cancellations, especially two that match in time or place, as possible signs of a concealed link between people.
when: A minor schedule change seems to connect two people
why: Matching gaps can hide a relationship

text: Retained routines such as sleep and appetite can indicate that affliction was less severe than reported.
when: Judging the severity of a reported condition.
why: Severe conditions usually disrupt basic routines.

text: A person who consistently avoids the main entrance and uses a side or private door suggests a separate relationship with the place.
when: when a suspect's movements diverge from the public routine
why: Habitual use of an unusual entry indicates privileged or hidden access.

text: Routine duties reveal who handled an object: its maintained condition shows who managed it, and service routines show who may enter a room or handle it.
when: When an object is normally maintained by a particular person.
why: Routines establish a baseline and reveal what must be done with an object.

text: A routine task performed by staff, such as laying a table, can arrive at the wrong moment and end a private encounter.
Discovering a broken assumption triggers a chain of consequences, such as realising another person could have entered, which forces a reassessment of the whole scene.
Scheduled NPC routines, such as a stop at a friend's before arriving at a location, force the player to reconstruct their movements.
when: When designing NPC schedules that feed investigation.
why: Hidden intermediate steps make the timeline something the player must assemble.

text: Routine checks can hide a clue, so the investigator must know what a routine check would have revealed before trusting it.
Overlooking a small observable sign is the usual reason a player or reader fails to solve a case.
Assuming a disguise hides everything can make an observer miss the habit that identifies the person.
why: Observers focus on the visible disguise and overlook unconscious behaviour.

text: A single odd choice may have an innocent cause, such as an obstacle on the shorter path, so verify the alternative route before treating the anomaly as evidence.
when: When an unusual route choice is treated as suspicious
why: Unseen physical obstacles can explain choices that look like deliberate concealment.

text: Trapped occupants who ignore small anomalies, such as an unresponsive switch, can miss the hidden mechanism.
When an audience already knows a performer's habits, a staged joke reads as deliberate.
when: the audience has seen the performer's habits before
why: familiar patterns reveal the act

text: 1) State the suspect's routine claims. 2) Check each against physical features of the scene, such as plants, structures and times. 3) Record contradictions.
when: A suspect explains their presence with a routine.

text: Note every procedure breach, such as taking an unauthorised visitor into a restricted area or leaving a door unlocked.
Log a broken meeting as a game state change, then place a follow-up note from the same person so the player must read it to learn what changed.
Let a scheduled NPC movement, such as an arrival at the same hour each night, be watched from a fixed vantage point.
when: designing recurring NPC behavior for player observation
why: a fixed time and place makes the event predictable and watchable

text: A forced entry risks injuring bystanders or the victim, while waiting risks a life; choose by how immediate the threat is.
Routine canvass and background checks find witnesses and rule out leads cheaply, but tend to miss inside knowledge when a crime is deliberately designed.
Witnesses, even if interviewed apart, that agree may share one source, rumour or leading questions; count origins, not voices, since one error can appear as several confirmations.
when: A set of accounts seems to corroborate each other
why: Repeated accounts may trace back to a single origin

text: Do not rely on a sighting or rumour that cannot be traced to a source; check single-source rumours against records before treating them as fact.
when: When a sighting or rumour is used as evidence
why: A single source can mislead.

text: A matching document shows a shared source for two pieces of evidence but does not identify who wrote or handled it.
When several separate accounts repeat the same odd detail, suspect one earlier source, such as coaching or rumor, rather than independent observation.
when: reports seem independent but share an unusual specific detail
why: An unusual detail recurring independently is improbable, so a common channel is the likelier explanation.

text: Rumours or in-world articles can be fallible sources that players learn to cross-check against physical clues.
when: Designing information the player receives from in-world media.
why: Cross-checking teaches players to weigh sources by evidence.

text: Separate claims based on sight from claims based on rumor, and do not accept fearful claims at face value.
why: Accepting them unchecked spreads error.

text: Repeated claims sharing one origin look like independent corroboration, though none has been checked and each repeat merely echoes the first.
when: when a claim appears in many accounts, such as neighbourhood gossip, that share a single origin
why: Repetition along a chain is mistaken for corroboration; agreement reflects spread rather than verification.

text: Make NPC rumours and post-quest gossip partly true and partly false, rewarding players who verify before acting on them.
when: when writing NPC gossip, tips or post-quest gossip
why: Mixed accuracy rewards checking and prevents players from trusting every tip blindly.

text: Gossip can supply a motive and make a suspect seem guilty before any act or evidence appears, redirecting the inquiry and pressuring the player to clear or convict.
when: early in an investigation, when a community forms opinion about a suspect or suspicion forms before any specific act is documented
why: A motive narrative directs attention; social expectation of a motive makes the accusation seem plausible in advance.

text: Public agreement, crowd size or social standing is not proof that a claim is true; it must be tested against the evidence.
when: when a claim is judged by how many people believe it or several people repeat the same belief
why: Numbers and status measure belief and influence, not accuracy; a shared error can look like consensus.

text: Family gossip about a quarrel is background context, not proof of motive; a real grudge can exist without being the cause of the accusation.
Vivid, sensational or often-repeated rumour is not necessarily the likeliest truth; repetition makes unverified theories seem established before they are checked.
when: when a dramatic event is covered by media or gossip
why: Striking explanations are more memorable and widely shared than cautious ones.

text: Relayers color speech with their own opinion, praise, disapproval and irrelevant speculation, so relayed speech is not neutral.
when: when information passes through a helper or relayer who has opinions about the subject
why: Relayers color reports with their own attitudes, which do not bear on the facts that matter.

text: Community opinion, public condemnation or neighbourhood consensus naming a suspect is not evidence of their actions; hostility can make an innocent person look guilty.
when: when a community names, condemns or judges a suspect by reputation or local opinion
why: Opinion reflects reputation, hostility and prejudice, not conduct; a prejudiced audience can make a later verdict look predetermined.

text: Partial information spreads faster than it is verified, so a group may learn a threat exists before learning its identity, breeding suspicion.
when: A group receives an incomplete message
why: Rumor outpaces checking

text: Unverified rumour can outrun fact and trigger panic within minutes, and its origin may remain unclear.
when: when a whispered or unchecked story reaches a crowd
why: Rumour travels faster than verification, so people react before facts are known.

text: An unverified claim gains force as it passes from person to person, and in a charged moment few stop to test it before acting.
when: during tense or emotional events
why: momentum carries the story into action

text: A crowd tends to echo the first confident version of an event, so a group's agreement can make a claim seem settled.
when: Several bystanders describe the same incident together
why: Social agreement lends a claim false credibility

text: A single definitive statement about a closed house shapes a crowd's suspicion toward the people inside, even before it is tested.
when: When a group hears a categorical claim about who could have acted.
why: Definitive statements anchor group judgment.

text: Speakers often deliver claims with more confidence than they have earned, which makes rumour sound like fact.
Curious onlookers often give empty or contradictory accounts, while a few witnesses give precise details.
when: many people gather after a public event
why: Curiosity draws in people who have little to report.

text: Rumour offers rival motives for an act, and audiences may accept the loudest one without evidence.
A witness who has heard public talk may reshape an account from rumour rather than memory, so later statements can reflect talk.
when: rumour about the case is circulating

text: Whom a community chooses, invites or consults as arbiter can reveal what it believed about a person's allegiances, even without direct testimony.
when: Direct statements are missing and group belief must be inferred from actions.
why: Selection choices reflect collective judgment about trust and sympathy.

text: A listener eager for adventure accepts an unusual story quickly, especially when it offers danger and excitement.
when: the listener is primed for adventure
why: appetite for the unusual lowers scrutiny of claims

text: Onlookers' reactions, such as screams or a stampede, are witness material and should be recorded as data about who saw what.
Once a verdict is voiced publicly, a crowd hardens it quickly, and reversing it costs the speaker face, so people keep defending it.
when: a noisy group reacts to an accusation
why: public commitment raises the social cost of changing one's mind

text: A suspect who learns a witness was present reconstructs what the investigator now knows from what could have been overheard.
when: When a hidden witness is revealed after an interview.
why: Hearing the exchange lets the suspect infer what was asked and admitted.

text: When opposing a prevailing belief is dangerous, doubters may stay silent, so the record looks more unanimous than the community actually was.
when: Dissent is punished, whether as heresy or as a crime.
why: Silencing doubters removes visible disagreement and makes the consensus appear complete.

text: A bewildered group that wants a verdict can overlook contradictions, letting a caught liar escape exposure.
when: group is confused and seeks a resolution

text: Publicized claims draw curious visitors, and the expectation that a respected figure will attend can draw larger crowds.
when: When news of an unusual event spreads locally.
why: Curiosity and anticipation of authority bring people to witness it.

text: Neighbourhood whispers can influence a formal proceeding even before any charge is laid, because the court may weigh the community's talk.
when: Rumour circulates about a person before a trial begins.

text: Gossip driven by rivalry tends to exaggerate or contradict, as speakers compete to score points.
when: when speakers are rivals
why: competition rewards contradiction

text: A suspect with a position of trust can spread a counter-accusation through a trusting listener, who may repeat it without testing it.
when: when the investigator is isolated or acting alone
why: Trust makes the listener an effective channel, so a claim can reach others before the investigator responds.

text: A group awaiting a stranger grows more excited as news and a shared letter are passed along and re-read.
when: characters or players are waiting for an announced newcomer
why: Each retelling adds attention and speculation, so expectation builds before the newcomer is seen.

text: A person may know that a secret exists and who it touches while knowing none of its particulars.
Grudges within a community often trace to disputes over money, housing and voting rights, which are the concrete stakes people contest.
A dated newspaper notice can carry news across a distance, so anyone who reads it can learn of events they did not witness.
when: Information must travel between distant places in a story.
why: Printed notices reach readers far from the event.

text: Rumour changes with each relay, sounding certain while contradicting itself on details; verify information passed through several people before acting.
when: when information passes through multiple people
why: Each retelling adds, alters or loses details, and every retelling can add distortion or lose the original detail.

text: Give rumour-spreading NPCs a visible bias so players learn to discount their claims; let gossip repeat a suspect's reputation so players test it against facts.
when: when designing gossip characters or a suspect's public image in a mystery
why: A known bias lets players correct for the source and separate reputation from evidence.

text: Give some sources a bias or motive and make a source that refuses to explain itself a suspicious clue.
when: Designing lore sources for a mystery
why: Biased sources add ambiguity and reward critical reading.

text: Do not discard a biased source outright, since its bias may itself be the clue.
Overheard hearsay in a crowd, such as bystanders describing a body, can supply the first decisive lead.
A social acquaintance can supply a quick profile of a target, such as their standing and habits, without revealing why the questioner wants it.
Seed a runaway NPC with a debt, a routine and an unfinished deal so the player can rule out explanations by checking the same records.
when: when designing a missing-person or runaway quest
why: elimination gives the player a reasoning path

text: Use rumours to add atmosphere and alternative suspicion; do not use them for clues a player must reliably deduce from.
When facts are withheld, audiences fill the gap with invented news; rumour gathers around the unknown into a fanciful account that explains everything without hard evidence.
when: when key information is delayed or withheld and people fill the gap with rumour
why: Invention resolves uncertainty, and a dramatic story feels complete without evidence.

text: Bad weather, low traffic or non-market days delay rumours and news, so people in some areas lack information others already have.
when: when rain, wind or a non-market day reduces travel along a route, or rumour spread is tied to travel or weather
why: Fewer travellers means fewer carriers of news; delayed travel delays the information carried with it.

text: Withholding facts from one person does not stop news; it travels through staff, servants and tradespeople, who pass on partial information to the wrong people.
A rumour that is partly right and partly unverifiable can be confirmed or contradicted later by inspection.
Hearings held before a packed crowd let the crowd's outrage feed back into officials' conduct.
when: when officials hold public hearings amid strong feeling
why: officials respond to the pressure in the room

text: Overheard rumours and crowd reactions keep observers uncertain, sustaining tension while the decision is pending.
when: A waiting audience hears partial information.
why: Partial, unconfirmed news prevents the tension from resolving.

text: A suspense timer built on an unconfirmed rumour lets the player wait, check and decide while the threat stays uncertain.
In a crowded, noisy gathering, important remarks are lost among overlapping conversations.
Gossip in a shared space such as a tavern spreads information, letting the player test who heard what and when.
when: When designing social spaces where NPCs exchange news.
why: Shared channels spread details between NPCs.

text: Gossip that spreads findings can warn culprit NPCs, so a discretion rule can gate how far a discovery propagates.
Third-party gossip can reveal motive by naming who gains and who loses from a death, such as inheritance or will terms, while sounding like idle talk.
when: a character speaks about a third party's wealth
why: concrete beneficiary facts connect a person to a motive

text: An investigation can grow from a few visible disturbances into a community-wide hunt, with public demand deciding which names get offered.
when: when a mystery depends on public suspicion

text: Early accusations can trigger guards, arrests and public notices, and each step makes the next accusation more credible to other characters.
when: When a local rumour gains official force.
why: Each official action serves as apparent confirmation for later claims.

text: Mass accusation can fill prisons, halt business and drive people to flee, as fear replaces normal economic and social life.
when: when accusations spread widely through a community
why: Fear disrupts trade, work and households at once

text: Passion in one person can set off the same feeling across a crowd, and the force of the spread grows with the zeal of those affected.
A rumor spread by an NPC after a confrontation can damage the player's credibility, making later quests or requests harder for others to accept.
when: after the player confronts an NPC with accusations
why: Reputation damage carries forward, so later interactions start from a lower trust level.

text: Trust relationships between NPCs can carry a rumor to a respected figure first, so the player must repair that standing to restore trust.
when: when NPCs have tracked trust ties
why: Rumors travel along trust links, so the most trusted listener shapes how the player is perceived.

text: Theories built from partial observation diverge widely, so each NPC's rumor reflects only what they personally saw.
when: NPCs who witnessed fragments of an event
why: Incomplete information produces competing guesses.

text: Public theories spread faster than evidence and can settle on a suspect from sympathy alone, ignoring an alibi the evidence supports.
when: A popular theory forms about a suspect before the facts are established
why: Sympathy and narrative appeal move through a public faster than verification

text: Public gossip and opinion can steer an investigation toward the wrong suspect; most loose suspicions are red herrings that connect to a claim without establishing it.
when: when a name is raised in gossip or a disputed document circulates among the public
why: Crowd belief can substitute for evidence and pull attention before facts support it.

text: Witnesses often repeat rumour as confirmed fact and blur dates and causes; separate what they saw from what they heard, and ask what the speaker actually witnessed.
when: when a witness states a claim confidently or testimony is gathered from locals or secondhand sources
why: Confidence and repetition make hearsay sound firsthand, and repetition mixes observation with hearsay.

text: Ignoring who supplied information is a mistake: a source may have a motive to mislead, favour one side or exaggerate, so check biased claims independently.
when: when gossip comes from a staff member, a rival or another biased source
why: A supplier's motive can distort the picture, so biased claims need independent checking.

text: A discovery witnessed by many can still be misremembered, shaped by who arrived first and who was afraid.
A shared fear can make a crowd settle on one story that no member individually witnessed.
when: Many observers saw a frightening event
why: Fear and group agreement override individual perception.

text: A witness who gossips tends to overstate what they heard, so treat their account of others' words with caution.
when: The witness is known to repeat rumour
why: Habitual repetition inflates partial hearing into confident quotation

text: A reputable informant can still repeat a claim they did not witness, and a good reputation alone does not confirm the claim.
Asking a witness to pick from a crowd can mislead when the description is vague, because several people may fit.
When accusers ask strangers in a crowd for their names, identical or similar names can lead to the wrong person being recorded and detained.
when: Shared or similar names exist in one community.
why: Identification by name alone is unreliable in a crowd.

text: A community verdict built on one incident and gossip is not independent corroboration.
why: its sources reduce to the same single event

text: Trusting a story because several people repeat it consistently. Identical details from an interested circle may reflect coordination rather than fact.
when: When several witnesses from one interested group give matching accounts
why: Agreement among parties who share a stake is not independent corroboration.

text: Gossip volunteers much irrelevant material; without a clear question, the investigator must sit through unrelated detail to find what matters.
when: Interviewing gossipy informants.

text: A thief who heads straight for the expected hiding place may have heard household gossip, so the choice reveals a source rather than a real hiding place.
Relayed news is partial: an absent character only learns what the sender wrote down, so unreported actions stay hidden.
when: Information passes through a messenger or report
why: The receiver knows only what was transmitted

text: Judging how often crimes are solved from reported cases alone overstates success, because unreported and never-found cases are never observed.
when: forming beliefs from reported or discovered incidents
why: The observed sample is filtered by what gets noticed

text: Secondhand routines from insiders can be stale, exaggerated or wrong, so they should be verified before a plan commits to them.
when: Relying on rumour or household gossip about a target's habits.
why: Hearsay is not observed evidence of actual movement.

text: In crowds, a person not seen is not proof of absence, because movement through dense crowds hides people.
when: Assessing whether someone was present in a crowded space such as during an interval.
why: Crowds obscure people from observers.

text: Acting on unverified hearsay can make the investigator look as unreliable as the people they distrust.
One person changing their belief does not automatically change the beliefs of others who share the same framework.
A leaked report can be exaggerated, and it may create panic rather than useful information.
when: Outside rumor or press reaches the investigation.
why: Partial and inflated accounts spread faster than accurate ones.

text: A jest or teasing remark is not proof; it only opens a line of inquiry that later evidence must confirm.
when: When a remark seems to implicate someone.
why: Words said in banter can be exaggerated or meaningless.

text: Shared talk about a decoy can make witnesses assume a link to the real crime that does not exist.
when: A decoy is widely discussed in a community
why: Common talk creates expectations of connection

text: 1) Plant a false rumour on an in-world notice board. 2) Track which characters change behaviour. 3) Unlock a confession dialogue once the player supplies a checkable fact.
when: Designing a suspect who reacts to rumour
why: Behaviour changes reveal who is concealing and gate a confession behind player evidence

text: Treat gossip as a lead to check, not as proof, and note the speaker's motive; keep a sourceless rumour unconfirmed until its source is traced.
when: when the rumour is repeated without a source

text: Let unproven rumours change NPC prices or trust before the truth is shown, so false stories carry in-game cost, such as spoiled goods cutting trade.
Tie rumor and news-style reports to facts the game currently knows, so they stay consistent with player progress.
when: a game system generates in-world news or rumor
why: Reports that match known facts build trust

text: Generate journals and NPC gossip as partial secondhand accounts with omitted details, so players must cross-check other sources.
when: Designing quest text and rumors in games.
why: Makes players verify information rather than accept it at face value.

text: Give rumoured names and histories small conflicts, so the player must verify them before trusting any single account.
when: when writing NPC rumours about people or places
why: Small inconsistencies make checking necessary and prevent accepting rumour at face value.

text: Gossip-driven motives can be plausible red herrings, but they must stay unproven, or they stop distracting and start resolving the case.
when: a rumor is used as a motive
why: plausible but unverified gossip misleads without closing the case

text: Community memory fills gaps that records leave, but it is biased and adds little once complete documents exist.
when: when choosing between local testimony and written records

text: Neighbourhood gossip about a person's strength or habits is hearsay, not proof; require physical evidence to corroborate it first.
when: Evidence rests on reputation or talk rather than direct observation
why: Secondhand talk cannot confirm what the speaker did not see.

text: Do not treat gossip or an unverified report as evidence or verdict; treat it as a lead to test, since any link in the passing-on chain may be wrong.
when: Early information is hearsay
why: relayed claims lose accuracy as they pass between people

text: Treat gossip about relationships as a lead, not fact, until its source is verified; use it to choose what to check next, not as the basis for an arrest.
when: Using acquaintance testimony about a suspect.
why: Gossip can be inaccurate or biased.

text: A vain source may first mock or withhold information to enjoy the other's discomfort, then release it as a favour.
when: Dealing with a status-conscious source who holds information.
why: Vanity makes the source enjoy displaying power over the questioner.

text: Hearsay gains the appearance of fact when it is repeated and when the speaker personally checks it, even if the original source is anonymous.
when: Rumors circulate in a shared workplace or community
why: Repetition and apparent verification lend credibility to unverified claims

text: Let a paid informant sell partial or mixed true and false details; the player must verify a few before acting on the rest.
when: Designing an NPC who sells information.
why: Partial verification lets the player estimate the reliability of unverified claims.

text: Neighbours' gossip about lovers and bad character may be prejudiced or malicious, and can be used to cover other facts, so it must be checked.
when: When rumour is the main source about a victim's conduct.
why: Gossip reflects social bias and can distract from real connections.

text: Check whether a witness verified the source their claim relies on, such as a postmark or record, before accepting the claim.
when: when a claim rests on a document or mark
why: Witnesses often pass on claims they never checked.

text: Use a family member's knowledge, such as the institutions they have used, as a starting point for narrowing where to check.
when: when searching for a concealed person
why: Close relations know habits and places.

text: Treat a relayed witness report as a lead to verify rather than a fixed fact, especially when the teller admits uncertainty.
Give an NPC a personal history the player learns in fragments, and let its resentments bias how the NPC treats suspects, so the player checks his account against the scene.
when: When generating a dialogue-driven NPC who gives the player information.
why: A biased source forces the player to verify claims instead of accepting them.

text: When told a person is somewhere, go and check the place yourself rather than accepting the claim.
when: A claim about someone's location comes from an interested party
why: Secondhand statements can be false

text: Test a claim against people who would have known the fact, rather than accepting it because someone reports it.
A hearsay report with an unreliable tone can still contain a useful lead, such as an agitated visitor's enquiries.
when: Evaluating gossip whose tone is biased.
why: Concrete actions and details can be accurate even when framing is not.

text: A witness whose key claim rests on rumor is weakened once they must concede the rumor was only rumor.
when: Cross-examining a witness whose key claim came from hearsay
why: Admitting the source was rumor removes the claim's basis

text: Weigh vague gossip by the credibility of its speaker; a suggestive hint from an unreliable source should direct further questions, not establish a motive.
when: when a rumour suggests a hidden relationship or motive
why: Vague hints are easily misread and mislead if treated as established fact.

text: Test a supernatural rumour first by asking whether the story matches how real people behave, before accepting any uncanny explanation.
when: when a place or person is surrounded by lurid rumour
why: rumours that no one who has been inside can confirm are often unfounded

text: A faction or NPC that disbelieves the player can be shown wrong through evidence the player gathers, proving the player's minority conclusion later.
when: Designing NPCs who doubt the player's findings
why: Gathered evidence turns a disputed conclusion into a verified one

text: NPC social routines such as gossip exchanges or community meetings can serve as channels through which the player earns introductions to target characters.
when: Designing an insular community with social networks.
why: Routine social interactions naturally provide reasons and openings to meet targets.

text: Gossip can be wrong, garbled or incomplete, with similar names or places easily confused; its accuracy may only be confirmed after events.
Gossip can spread faster than verified information, so a reputation built in one public setting may not reflect the facts.
Gossip errs both ways: a true document can be rejected for bad reasons, and a false one can pass on the word of a sworn witness.
Gossip about a suspect's temper can colour how others see him and bias the investigation.
when: Witnesses repeat reputations rather than observed facts

text: Vague or amused witnesses add colour that may be unreliable, so useful details must be separated from embellishment.
A vague excuse for knowing a restricted fact is not proof of guilt, since it may be innocent gossip.
Gossip repeated as fact by one speaker can mislead, and a contested denial shows the rumor is disputed rather than proven.
Attributing knowledge to a vague source such as the town names no channel and does not explain how the fact spread.
A date taken from a single second-hand source can be wrong, so check it against another source before building a timeline on it.
1) Contact the place through a separate channel. 2) Confirm whether the named person is absent and who is in charge. 3) Record what remains unverified before acting.
when: a tip names a place and a person
why: an independent channel reduces the chance the sender controls the check

text: 1) State the suspicion. 2) Find an independent reference that can confirm or deny it. 3) Build on the suspicion only if the reference confirms it.
when: A suspicion comes from memory or intuition
why: An unverified hunch can be wrong

text: Do not accept a source's claim on its word; have an independent observer check it in person or find an independent link to confirm or contradict it.
when: a secondhand report affects a decision

text: Let NPC gossip or an insisting NPC present a wrong theory, and give players evidence to weigh so their findings decide which explanation holds.
Give witness NPCs reliability values that drop with intoxication, fear, distance, poor lighting or date mismatch, so players must cross-check their statements.
Give each NPC witness a reliability tag or level, such as sobriety or honesty, that raises or lowers how much testimony counts; players learn over time which to trust.
Let NPC rumours spread through chains of NPCs, adding a slight distortion at each hop, so players must trace a claim back to its origin before relying on it.
when: when generating an NPC gossip system
why: distortion makes unverified claims unreliable

text: Record informal talk with its source, verify it independently against a record before relying on it, and weigh disclosure consequences; servants may repeat or exaggerate rumour.
when: Information comes from informal talk.
why: Unverified gossip can be inaccurate or self-serving.

text: Separate reported gossip from confirmed fact, and require corroboration before counting a rumored affair or debt as motive.
when: A witness offers rumor about relationships or money.
why: Rumor can be false or exaggerated.

text: Verify claims repeated in press reports, such as a stated family relationship, against independent sources.
Confirming that a story's names, dates and sources are sound does not establish that the story itself is true.
why: Accurate details can sit inside a false or unproven account.

text: Let NPCs protect or obstruct the player, so testimony must be weighed by the speaker's interest.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that carries clues
why: Interested testimony teaches players to weigh sources critically

text: NPC rumors can carry accurate facts, so give players world-state checks such as a stopped clock or a cold stove.
when: when designing NPC testimony

text: Keep an NPC's reported interpretation separate from its raw observations, so players can reach a different conclusion from the same evidence.
A trustworthy NPC gives specific details the player can check; an evasive NPC contradicts an earlier line.
Model witness credibility through bystander NPC reactions that laugh at or dismiss a speaker, signalling how much to trust them.
Track quarrels between NPCs in a reputation system, and flag a new accusation that falls near an old feud as suspicious to the player.
when: when a game world contains NPC conflicts
why: a link to an old feud gives the player a lead

text: Give each rumor a way for the player to test it, and store competing rumors in a log so the player can compare claims against physical evidence.
when: Designing rumors that circulate in a town or household
why: Testing lets the player separate rumor from fact.

text: Before treating a rumour as a finding, 1) ask who first observed or made the claim. 2) Note each person who relayed it, including you, and check each link. 3) Note any link whose source cannot be named. 4) Rate by how close the first teller was to the event.
when: a claim arrived through other people
why: Each relay can add, drop or shift details, or add embellishment or bias, distorting the original facts.

text: Let players trace a rumor back along the NPCs who passed it on to its first witness, to judge whether later reports are independent.
Facts restated, questioned and challenged between speakers arrive in a form the listener can check.
Check whether the person spreading a rumour was also a source of it, and whether their own impairment shaped what they said.
Let a rumor spread through several NPCs while keeping one originating source discoverable, so players learn to trace apparent agreement back to a single origin.
when: designing a rumor that appears to be confirmed

text: Once a secret leaks to an enemy, it becomes a time-limited danger, since the enemy must act before the advantage is gone.
when: Information about a plan reaches the opposing side.
why: The enemy's knowledge creates urgency that forces an earlier response.

text: 1) List everyone who knew of a planned event and which facts each was given. 2) Identify what the culprit wanted. 3) Compare what each person could have passed on. 4) Check the list rather than trusting it.
when: a secret plan has leaked or an NPC reveals an undisclosed fact

text: 1) List every route by which a detained person could have learned outside information, such as insiders or visitors. 2) For each route, identify the record it leaves, such as a permit or logbook. 3) Check each record against an independent source.
when: A detained person seems to know things they should not
why: Each route leaves a checkable trail, and independent checks reduce reliance on any single account

text: 1) Note each claim about movements or timing. 2) Compare it with an external record such as a schedule or programme. 3) Ask an unrelated question to shift the topic and test attention.
when: an informal witness gives timing or motive claims
why: external records expose contradictions and an abrupt topic change tests attention

text: Track the source of each lead, because a cover story may later conflict with testimony and expose itself.
Check each informal detail against a dated source before accepting it.
Let a rumor-spreading NPC repeat an authority's framing, and plant a clue that reveals the influence behind it.
when: An NPC's gossip echoes an official explanation
why: Players can detect where a story was shaped

text: Let false in-world claims spread through a rumour system, and require the player to trace who started a story and check it against evidence.
when: when a game world carries false reports
why: Tracing sources teaches the player to weigh claims rather than accept them.

text: Track who asserted what about whom, so that a second rumour can be flagged as hearsay rather than treated as fact.
Give each rumor an NPC source with a recorded grudge, so players can weigh the speaker's motive against the accusation.
when: Designing rumors players must evaluate.

text: Design rumors to be checkable: a player who gathers an alibi or witness should be able to lower a rumor's credibility.
Use a rumour that contains a true lead even when its tone is unreliable.
when: Designing rumours that guide player action.
why: A mix of accurate lead and biased framing rewards careful evaluation.

text: After an incident, rumour splits into rival camps, such as political insult, prank or supernatural explanation, each favouring the reading that suits it.
when: Gossip circulates about a disputed event.
why: Each group has its own reason to prefer its explanation.

text: A published item about an investigation is a sign that someone outside is watching, not evidence of the underlying crime.
when: Interpreting a public mention of an ongoing inquiry.
why: The item reveals observation, not what was found.

text: Let a town rumor or newspaper announce the player's actions so an NPC demands answers before the player is ready.
when: Designing pressure from a game world on the player's investigation.
why: Public exposure forces the player to act on the timeline the world sets.

text: A witness's account can change after they consult another source, so a second source can correct an earlier report.
when: When a witness's story changes between statements.
why: The witness's view follows the influence of whoever they last spoke to.

text: Rumour grows as it travels, and each new teller can add embellishments.
when: A story passes through many people
why: Each retelling adds invented detail

text: 1) Ask a direct question first. 2) Ask how the witness knows the answer. 3) If the witness changes subject or becomes distressed, return to the question with a firm demand for a direct answer. 4) Ask whether that is all they know.
when: Interviewing a witness whose claims may rest on hearsay.
why: Asking for the source shows whether the claim is observed or repeated.

text: 1) Ask the person directly implicated in the rumor. 2) Note whether the answer confirms or denies the claim. 3) Treat silence or admission as evidence only the involved person can supply.
why: Only the person concerned can resolve the gap in a secondhand report.

text: Design rumour chains passed among NPCs, each adding, dropping or slanting detail, so players can trace them to a primary source and weigh each link's reliability.
when: Designing rumours or legends spread through characters.
why: Distortion turns information gathering into verification, and layered retelling makes the source a discovery task.

text: Make the messenger's motive visible, and trust a hostile or gossiping source less than a neutral witness.
when: Designing rumor delivery in a narrative or NPC system.
why: The motive shapes how reliable the report is.

text: Treat a report delivered in secret, rather than confronted openly, as less reliable.
when: Judging a damaging claim whose source avoided direct confrontation
why: Whispered accusations avoid the scrutiny that an open claim would face, which weakens their credibility.

text: A prosperous NPC can become the target of a whispered accusation; let the rumor change as it passes between NPCs.
when: designing social pressure on a character
why: Mutating rumor makes the source harder to trace.

text: A hidden party acting on a false belief about one person can form a second false belief about another. Both errors can then be exploited.
when: A culprit suspects a witness knows more than they do
why: An error in one belief carries into later judgments about other people

text: A false alarm draws attention to a harmless cue before the real threat arrives, misdirecting the audience's focus.
A false public solution, such as an announced arrest, can make the audience doubt the investigator too early, so it must be resolved in the reveal.
why: Competing accounts create doubt that the true reveal must answer

text: Overusing false alarms or rumours teaches the audience to disregard later cues and flattens suspense; each false lead should have a real consequence.
A false report can alarm people who did nothing, and they may act on it.
when: A planted story reaches innocent people
why: Believed falsehoods cause real action by those who had no part in events

text: Let some rumour clues be false in the level data, and reward players who trace the chain back to its origin.
A court created quickly, by reversing an earlier decision under claimed emergency, can move from trial to execution within about a week, leaving outside bodies no time to intervene.
why: Compressed timelines remove the window for review.

text: Rushing a frightened witness, or pressing them about their own wrongdoing, can make them shut down and stop volunteering information.
when: When a witness fears blame for what they overheard or did.
why: Fear of punishment makes witnesses guarded.

text: A rushed entry can injure bystanders or the victim, so speed must be balanced against the risk inside.
Rushing an arrest because a witness may slip away risks acting on incomplete evidence.
Gaps caused by a rushed event, such as a hurried levy or a fire, can explain why a town's archive is incomplete, giving the world a believable reason for missing records.
when: When designing why a town's archive lacks certain documents.
why: A cause for the gap makes missing records feel plausible rather than arbitrary.

text: A person may falsely confess to a killing to protect another, and the confession can be exposed by checking the objects the confessor claims to have used.
when: A confession seems to close a case too easily.
why: The confessor's claimed actions may not match the physical evidence.

text: Design a lure so that a wrong guess about the target only leads them to think the notice rested on a misleading detail, without exposing the investigation.
when: the investigator is unsure of the target's knowledge
why: a failed lure should cost the investigator nothing

text: Check which party a proposed safeguard disadvantages; a restraint that removes the subject's means of escape serves the proposer, not the safety it claims.
when: A test or condition is proposed as a precaution
why: Precautions can hide an attack on the person they supposedly protect

text: A vague but plausible official statement can reassure the public while committing the source to very little.
when: when an authority must say something before facts are settled
why: Limited commitment keeps the source flexible as the facts develop.

text: When confession promises safety, accused people may confess to many crimes to secure it.
when: confession is offered as a way out
why: the promised safety outweighs the cost of false admissions

text: Sarcasm can invite a witness to explain in full, leaving the questioner embarrassed.
1) Control the suspect's hands and pin the arms before any search. 2) Withdraw the arm from a pocket slowly. 3) Check the outside of the pocket before reaching in.
when: Searching a suspect who may be armed or may struggle.
why: A restrained suspect cannot strike quickly, and checking the exterior first reduces the risk of a hidden weapon.

text: When a suspect is about to harm themselves, switch from questioning to protecting life.
Design suspect tests so they cannot harm innocent people.
Grant a reprieve where a judge doubts a verdict, and grant bail to anyone accused only through unverifiable testimony.
Hide a clue among objects of the same kind rather than in a secret place, where no one expects to look.
when: when concealing evidence in a scene

text: The same act, such as a suicide attempt, can be read as a danger to manage or as a clue, depending on who observes it.
when: When interpreting a suspect's self-harm
why: Observers with different roles weigh the same act differently

text: Confusing 'same victim' with 'same culprit' is a central error, since a shared victim does not identify a shared culprit.
when: Two cases involve the same person.
why: Shared circumstances are treated as proof of identity without support.

text: Assuming all traces at a scene come from the same moment blocks the two-phase explanation and hides the real sequence of events.
A letter may refer to an event that happened the day before it was written, so do not assume the event and the document share a date.
Scatter a culprit's neutral-looking actions across separate scenes so players must reassemble them to see the pattern.
A container that breaks and releases several small items gives the player a set of objects to sort and connect into a sequence.
Place the parts of a mechanism in ordinary containers early so they read as trivia, and combine them only at a final puzzle.
when: Setting up a multi-part solution to be assembled late.
why: Separated, innocuous parts do not signal the solution, and combining them at the end makes the climax a deduction.

text: Accounts recorded after events, including memories formed after reading press coverage, are not independent evidence and make matches with reported facts look stronger than they are.
when: A witness reports a recollection after reading a public account of the event, or any account is recorded after the event.
why: The later account may be shaped by what was read.

text: Neither disorder nor tidiness proves innocence or guilt; disorder may result from one event rather than a struggle, so establish its cause before inferring a fight.
when: Investigating a disturbed room.
why: Assuming a struggle can point the investigation at the wrong people.

text: Occupants who want no identifying trace may wear gloves and rubber soles, leaving only indirect marks behind.
A character's posture or line delivery that changes after an emotional scene gives players a readable cue about that character's state.
why: Visible shifts in demeanour signal how the scene affected the character

text: After an outcome, characters summarise events through their own bias, such as romantic, legal, social or club concerns, so their conclusions differ.
when: When characters discuss a resolved case.
why: Each speaker's personal interest shapes what they take from the same facts.

text: A sudden event tends to generate rumours with specific physical details, and these can outlast the facts behind them.
Reconstructing events from a scene's leftovers, marks and arrangements lets an investigator infer who was present and what happened, without any witness.
when: a scene has no witnesses

text: An object found at a scene does not show who left it or when; physical traces such as a fresh stain may be the only timing clue.
A reenactment shows only that a mechanism could have been used, not that it was used; the demonstration does not prove the act happened.
when: interpreting a reconstruction of an impossible exit
why: Possibility and actual occurrence are different claims.

text: End a case with a reconstruction screen replaying the player's deductions in order, labeling each theory and the clue that revised it, so the player sees how clues connect.
when: Concluding an investigation sequence, such as a dungeon's solution summary.
why: A summary links clues to the outcome.

text: When the culprit is unknown and has no record, work from the crime and the traces it leaves, studied closely.
when: no records or informers apply
why: The scene itself is then the only material available.

text: Present a reconstruction of events one claim at a time and watch the suspect's reaction to each claim.
Reconstruct the crime as a plausible, step-by-step story, including how the act was carried out, so the suspect can see how the evidence fits together.
when: the evidence supports each step

text: Let players assemble a reconstruction of events from physical traces, such as blood, weight or displacement, found among scene objects.
A game can reconstruct a past event for the player from a map, timestamps and damage to an in-world object.
when: when the player must learn what happened before the scene
why: the player can infer the sequence from consistent traces

text: Scene traces can reveal how many people were involved: one person's methods, such as a single drag trail or an improvised carrying device, differ from what a group would need.
when: Deciding whether a crime at a scene was committed by one person or several.
why: A group could lift and carry directly, while a lone actor needs aids and may return for items.

text: Check the trim and cut edges of a sheet, since cutting can remove the marks that would link it to its source.
when: A sheet's origin matters and its edges have been altered.
why: Trimming erases the evidence that connects a sheet to a stack or bundle.

text: In dialogue, let the player present collected events and let the NPC confirm, deny or correct each one, with each reply opening a new branch.
when: designing a dialogue tree for investigation

text: Delivering a reversal in conversation after the event reveals facts without interrupting the scene itself.
Use sequence reconstruction when a witness account and the physical record disagree.
when: Testimony and physical evidence conflict
why: Reconstruction can reconcile the two sources

text: A matched trace, such as a hair, places a person at a location but does not by itself show who else was present.
why: Traces establish presence at a place, not the full set of people there.

text: Test whether a scene supports a theory by checking whether its traces fit the proposed action.
when: A theory about an event is being evaluated against the scene.
why: Traces inconsistent with the proposed action count against the theory.

text: Rehearse the actual steps of a plan instead of trusting reasoning alone, since untested steps hide failure points.
when: Before committing to a multi-step plan

text: An entry added to the original after a copy was made appears only in the original, so its absence from the copy marks when it was added.
An explanation after a reveal can recast a feared group as amateurs who chose dramatic trappings yet faced real danger.
Royalty and copyright value can rise sharply after a death through renewed sales, so the financial stake can grow after the event.
when: Estimating the value of a legacy after a death.
why: Renewed attention increases sales of the deceased's work.

text: A projectile in an unexpected spot that conflicts with the intended story prompts the player to search more deeply.
when: Designing a mystery that should reward closer inspection
why: Contradictions with the expected story create curiosity and a reason to continue searching

text: Trampling by many people blurs or erases overlapping prints, so the order of events becomes unreadable; keep observers still and away from the scene.
when: Several people cross a surface holding footprints or evidence before it is examined.
why: Foot traffic overwrites the impressions being studied.

text: Small unrecorded details, such as misplaced props or loose litter, can break a faithful reconstruction of an earlier scene.
when: A scene is rebuilt from memory or an incomplete record.
why: Minor changes alter the conditions in ways the test does not account for.

text: Reproduction tests are weak when the scene has already been disturbed, because they then recreate a changed situation rather than the original event.
Revealing the answer before the audience has the clues to reach it, or covering a gap in the chain with assertion instead of evidence, breaks the sense of fair play.
when: Writing a mystery or puzzle reveal
why: The audience cannot verify or reproduce a conclusion whose supporting clues were withheld

text: A body may be moved and its limbs arranged before the investigator arrives, so the original position of the body is lost.

1) Gather every surviving source: court papers, diaries, letters, minutes, itineraries, later official reports, and site visits. 2) Date each one. 3) Check each claim against an independent dated source. 4) Do not rely on one partisan account when others exist.
when: Later reconstruction of a disputed event documented only in fragments, with some records lost or withheld.
why: Independent dated sources can check a partisan narrative and confirm or refute individual claims.

text: 1) Sort surviving documents, family memory and local tradition by date and provenance, and check the sites and remains they mention. 2) Match each source against the others. 3) Distinguish details the sources support from details invented to fit. 4) Note how well each part is supported.
when: Rebuilding an old incident or incomplete record from partial sources of differing reliability.
why: Combining sources of different kinds exposes gaps and can corroborate or contradict a written account, keeping the account honest.

text: 1) Identify the original conditions: room state, objects, people, routine (walk and meal timing) and subject's mental state. 2) Restore each condition, refurnishing the room exactly as before. 3) Repeat the act and record the outcome. 4) Count a mismatch against the theory; a repeated result supports it.
when: A theory of how an act happened depends on conditions that can be restored, such as room state or the subject's routine.
why: Reproduction can confirm or weaken the theory; matching the original setting and the subject's condition keeps other variables from distorting the comparison.

text: 1) Form the timing hypothesis and identify every step the act requires. 2) Perform each step in order at realistic pace, timing the whole run. 3) Compare total time with the available window or the witness's account. 4) If it fits, the claim is possible; if not, it is ruled out.
when: A suspect's alibi, access or disputed timing depends on a short absence or fixed time window.
why: Measured durations tested against the real steps of an act reveal feasibility better than guesses.

text: 1) Separate traces by who left them. 2) Identify the traces that belong to the event. 3) Read each mark for the action that made it. 4) Order the actions into a sequence. 5) Combine several traces before concluding.
when: a scene can be read from traces of movement

text: 1) List each physical trace and the person's condition. 2) For each, ask who could have produced it and in what state. 3) Combine them into one story. 4) Test that story against what nearby people do next.
when: a scene holds several small traces that together imply a sequence

text: 1) Build one ordered chain of who, when, what and why from partial accounts. 2) Check that every observed detail fits the chain. 3) Disclose the chain step by step so each conclusion follows from evidence already shown.
when: Concluding an investigation where the solver must justify the answer to the audience
why: A reveal feels credible when each step follows from evidence and no link is covered by assertion

text: 1) Build a motive-based account of the crime. 2) Test it against facts the audience has already seen. 3) Confirm it explains every earlier oddity. 4) Deliver it as a reconstruction.
when: when the reveal should be earned through facts shown earlier
why: a reconstruction built only on shown facts feels fair and satisfying

text: 1) Recount the case from the point the investigator entered it. 2) Label each early impression. 3) Name the clue that revised each impression. 4) End with the complete chain and final reversal.
when: Closing a mystery with a fair-play reveal.
why: The reader can check each step against facts already shown.

text: 1) Replay events in order from first act to last. 2) Explain how each act was set up. 3) Reinterpret earlier oddities as clues now that the solution is known.
when: all clues have been collected and the reveal should reward re-examination
why: Hindsight shows how earlier details fit the solution

text: 1) Collect the old sources: letters, court records and witness memory. 2) Test the present claim against each source. 3) Note which accounts agree and which conflict.
when: A present accusation depends on events from long ago.
why: Independent sources can confirm or break a claim that no single source can settle.

text: 1) Reconstruct the scene under the original conditions, including the same door, bolt and observers. 2) Use only improvised tools that were plausibly available. 3) Perform the mechanism step by step with witnesses present. 4) Let skeptics test the result directly before accepting it.
when: testing whether a locked-room claim depends on a physical mechanism others doubt
why: A reenactment turns an abstract theory into something observers can check for themselves.

text: 1) Start from the final remark or conclusion. 2) Work backward through the chain of associations. 3) Check each link against an observed act. 4) Treat any link lacking an observed act as a guess.
when: inferring what someone thought but did not say
why: backward tracing exposes a chain that looks incoherent forward

text: 1) Estimate the offender's intelligence and assume the simplest effective method. 2) Identify the physical constraints of the task. 3) Infer the number of people and their positions. 4) Look for marks the proposed sequence should leave. 5) Check the scene's disorder against the sequence.
when: A hidden event must be rebuilt from physical traces
why: A capable offender tends to choose the simplest workable route, and the method leaves checkable marks.

text: 1) Note where the body lies relative to the access routes to infer how it arrived. 2) Record absent traces, such as missing blood or items. 3) Match trace positions against the setting's physical mechanics. 4) Test each fact against one unified hypothesis, and check it against the known schedule.
when: Cause and place of a death are in doubt and the physical layout can be checked
why: Physical position and absences constrain how the event could have happened

text: 1) Describe the scene step by step from each participant's viewpoint, including non-human ones. 2) Check each step for plausibility. 3) Build one account covering every observed fact.
when: A closed scene with an unusual mechanism needs a full explanation.
why: Viewpoint steps expose actions that cannot physically happen as described.

text: 1) Document the scene and body positions before anything is moved. 2) Check each exit separately. 3) Search every plausible hiding place for the weapon. 4) Note untouched valuables. 5) Exclude each explanation that needs an exit, step by step.
when: a death occurs in an apparently sealed space

text: 1) Inspect the arrangement of objects, openings and the culprit's own records. 2) Infer the sequence of actions these arrangements imply. 3) Check whether that sequence explains every trace.
when: when a scene offers no witness or confession
why: Arrangements and records hold traces that show how an act was done

text: 1) Collect each trace found at the scene. 2) Record which person each trace fits. 3) Give no decisive weight to a trace until its owner is established.
when: a scene holds several traces whose owners are unknown

text: 1) Walk the approach and note side entrances. 2) Trace paths hidden behind cover to the body's position. 3) Search the ground closely over a wide area. 4) Ask what could be seen from outside. 5) Sketch the room and inventory its contents.
when: Surveying a crime scene
why: Each step reveals a different kind of information about access, concealment and disturbance

text: 1) Reproduce the scene with the same people, positions and props. 2) Speak the lines as originally spoken. 3) Test whether sound or line of sight from the disputed spot matches the witness's account.
when: a witness describes an action that can be physically replayed
why: a replay tests the account against physical conditions

text: 1) Describe the pose and fall direction a claimed wound would normally produce. 2) Compare the body's pose and the positions of its belongings with that description. 3) Note each mismatch for follow-up.
when: The stated cause of death and the body's posture or belongings seem inconsistent.
why: A wound produces a predictable fall, so departures from it reveal a different sequence of events.

text: 1) Record where the witness was and what that position allowed them to hear. 2) Identify speakers by voice traits. 3) Order the heard events into a sequence. 4) Check each step against physical evidence. 5) Mark which steps are inference.
when: witness heard but did not see the event
why: a sequence built from sound must be tested against the room to be trusted

text: 1) Note damage to objects, such as a torn fence or broken railing. 2) Infer the victim's position from it. 3) Use scorch patterns to estimate range. 4) Check the ground for tracks to infer routes.

1) Collect dated grants and later deeds for the site. 2) Note the natural features each cites as boundary points. 3) Compare neighboring records that cite the same features. 4) Track renamed landmarks across periods. 5) Check which authority issued each record. 6) Converge on the most consistent line.
when: a site's boundaries survive only in documents that use changing names and perishable markers
why: no original survey of the markers survives

text: 1) Note what the official record omits and test any claimed event against it. 2) Date each document against the events it supposedly relates to. 3) Track participant attendance to find when a view changed. 4) Match that change with the arrival of a key document to infer cause.
when: A narrative's sequence conflicts with dated records and attendance data exists.
why: Dates and attendance reveal decisions that no record states outright.

text: 1) Identify each source and whether its writer witnessed the events. 2) Mark direct testimony apart from summaries. 3) State where the record ends and what is missing. 4) Say whether chosen examples illustrate a pattern or count all cases.
when: building an account from records you did not witness
why: readers can judge reliability and avoid overreading selected cases

text: 1) Read prints and ash against each other. 2) Note the order of marks. 3) Infer what was carried and where the boots went from missing steps.
when: Reconstructing a sequence of actions from physical traces
why: Comparing marks and their order reveals carried objects and removed footwear

text: 1) Log timestamped player actions during play. 2) Reconstruct the sequence afterward. 3) Use it to test an alibi or to check which event happened first.
when: Designing mysteries where players must verify alibis or event order.
why: A reconstructable log lets designers and the game check consistency.

text: 1) Mark the seated victim's position, the firing spot and the wall impact point. 2) Join them with a straight line. 3) Use the line to determine which side of the victim the shot came from.
when: A shot's origin and direction must be tested against who could have stood where
why: A straight line from impact back to source fixes the shooter's side and approximate position

text: 1) Record each damaged item's force direction and posture of the victim. 2) Test whether the damage matches the victim's own movements or an attacker's. 3) Test whether each item was damaged before or after the event. 4) Accept the explanation that fits all force directions.
when: injuries and damage seem to conflict with the stated sequence
why: Force direction and object position reveal the order of events.

text: 1) Establish the door state. 2) Build the timeline from sound and light. 3) Mark objects that moved. 4) Note physical traces. 5) Check the order in which people entered.
when: a closed room holds a body or disturbance
why: each witness sees only part of the event, so the sequence must be rebuilt from each vantage point

text: A trial run must use the real steps, strength, timing and attention of a realistic performer; timing only the fastest version of an act misstates feasibility.
when: Setting up a timed re-enactment of a suspect's action.
why: An ordinary person acting under stress differs from a trained or unhurried performer, so unrealistic conditions produce a misleading result.

text: A reenactment must match the original conditions in angle, height, and sequence; small differences can make the test prove nothing.
when: running a physical reconstruction to test a claim
why: The result is only valid if the test reproduces the conditions it claims to verify.

text: To understand an actor's conduct, reconstruct what people of the time accepted as true and as evidence, rather than judging by later knowledge.
Give a generated map shifting place names and dated land records, so players must reconcile old and new labels to locate a site.
when: designing a world with renamed locations

text: When a scene has been altered, reconstruct its original positions from witnesses rather than the current layout, unless the changes were recorded.
when: furniture or objects were moved before examination
why: the current layout no longer reflects the event

text: Assembling a full reconstruction is useful after facts are gathered, but early on gathering facts matters more than building a theory.
Named places can anchor timing when confirmed as the event site; a place named in a dying message is not automatically the crime scene or the killer's home.
when: When documents name a place whose timing is uncertain.
why: Named places give fixed points witnesses cannot easily alter, but a name alone does not prove where the event occurred.

text: A postmark from a post office near a venue, within a stated time window, links the sender to that place and time.
when: a parcel was posted near the scene

text: A preserved location, such as a common field kept unbuilt, can carry memory of past events into the present.
Positional details such as an open door or a displaced rug can establish when and how a room was used.
when: reconstructing a sequence of events in a room
why: Physical positions record past actions and can fix a timeline.

text: Read the body and surroundings for traces of the victim's movements and the attacker's position, since wounds, clothing and objects each record part of the sequence.
when: At the scene, before it is moved or cleared
why: Physical traces are lost or altered once the scene changes

text: The choice of observation position is itself evidence: a watcher who picks a spot facing outward was probably looking for someone.
when: An unusual position is chosen.
why: The position reveals the watcher's purpose.

text: Test a physical direction given by an examiner, such as which side a wound came from, against the positions of people in the scene.
when: A finding implies who could have been where
why: Positional facts can confirm or exclude a suspect's account

text: Powder development works best on smooth, non-porous surfaces. On rough surfaces the powder cannot hold fine detail, and smeared prints are hard to recover.
when: when choosing whether to dust an object

text: A nearly empty place at a set hour limits witnesses, so it defines the opportunity for an act to go unseen.
Check a place named in records against a map, tying boundaries to landmarks such as bridges or compass lines.
when: a record describes a location's bounds
why: maps can confirm or reveal inconsistencies

text: A location can hold the memory of an event for someone who witnessed it, and that witness may describe or avoid the place accordingly.
when: When a character's account is tied to a place where a death or event occurred.
why: Vivid recollection attaches to the setting where the scene was experienced.

text: A location with a known history is a strong clue, but the route taken to reach it can tie a suspect to the place.
when: Evidence is found at a site connected to past events
why: The path to the site creates a link between person and place

text: Test a reconstruction across layout, stains and witness account; no single detail should carry it alone, and all must agree.
when: testing a reconstruction against a witness account

text: A location where a person's routines and objects were concentrated is a useful place to search for evidence.
when: Choosing where investigators should look.
why: Concentrated personal objects and habits make relevant traces more likely to be found there.

text: A place with a known entry point but no recorded exit can serve as the probable site for further investigation, where a missing person may still be.
when: A person entered a location and was never seen leaving it.
why: The unrecorded exit makes the location itself the most likely place to search.

text: In an open, empty area with no cover or witnesses, an attack leaves few traces, so the investigation depends on the scene's silence and brief sightings.
when: When an attack occurs in a location with no cover, witnesses or footprints.
why: Without cover or witnesses, there is little physical or testimonial evidence to collect.

text: A witness's memory of a place can be reliable in feeling but unreliable in detail, so it is not proof of what happened there.
when: When using a recalled scene as evidence.
why: Emotional intensity preserves impressions better than accurate specifics.

text: 1) List physical traces: lock state, window access, broken foliage and ground firmness. 2) Test each possible route against them. 3) Reject routes the traces contradict and keep those they allow.
when: a scene shows evidence of how a person could have entered or left

text: 1) List known positions by hour. 2) Mark each as confirmed by a reliable witness or only claimed. 3) Check each leg of movement against a timetable.
when: an alibi covers a span of time with some verifiable points
why: Feasibility depends on both fixed points and the travel between them.

text: 1) State what the scene claims happened. 2) Work out the disturbance that event would cause. 3) Apply it to the arranged objects. 4) Check whether they react as claimed or whether the arrangement came later.
when: a scene includes an arranged object the victim's last acts would not plausibly produce

text: 1) Inspect the whole structure, attic to ground floor, not one damaged spot. 2) Check each hole or mark for a matching mark on the opposite side. 3) Note expected traces that are absent. 4) Read how objects are displaced or left intact.
when: a dramatic event must be explained from its physical scene
why: one spot or one testimony can mislead

text: Assuming a place is deserted from a quick look at the ground floor can miss evidence of a hurried departure or recent presence.
when: When a location appears empty after a brief survey
why: Partial surveys miss traces of recent occupation

text: 1) Note checkable signs such as bearing, dress, footwear, and carried items. 2) Tie each inference to one specific sign. 3) Chain the signs into a working hypothesis. 4) Test the hypothesis against later evidence.
when: when a person is seen only briefly
why: Each inference stays checkable and can be revised.

text: 1) Derive lot dimensions and a building's position from land descriptions. 2) Compare the present structure with that footprint. 3) Note which parts are original and which were altered.
when: testing where a building stood at an earlier time
why: later appearance may not match the original

text: Compare records with fixed entry positions, so a missing entry appears as a blank gap too narrow for the next group of entries.
when: Entries sit in set positions on the page
why: Position-based layout turns absence into a visible space

text: Check floors and furniture edges, since small items can lie out of sight and be missed on a casual first pass.
Start an investigation at a fixed scene fact, such as a body or sealed room, and have the player work back to the method, then test whether a suspect's motive fits.
when: Designing deduction puzzles
why: A fixed fact anchors reasoning and gives a checkable endpoint.

text: A gap in a fitting, such as shutters that barely meet, can permit a view into a room from outside.
why: Small gaps can admit sight even when they block passage

text: A food or drink item can carry quality or origin data that signals a second character was present.
Make a missing object the focal clue, since locating it can lead to the culprit.
1) Hold a position with line of sight to the target. 2) When the target moves, go at once to the exit they are likely to use. 3) Intercept there.
when: a target may escape through a crowded space
why: a route to the exit is faster when planned in advance

text: 1) Fit the found fragment against its supposed source, such as the torn edges of a garment. 2) Compare the material and weave. 3) Record whether the fit confirms the claimed origin.
when: a clue's source is known and must be matched
why: a successful fit confirms the claimed origin

text: 1) List each room's visitors. 2) Note the times each room is cleaned or prepared. 3) Find rooms left unvisited at night. 4) Ask where you would hide an object from the offender's side.
when: Locating where a concealed object could survive
why: Routine leaves some rooms unobserved for long periods

text: 1) Note the changed conduct of the creature that hid the item. 2) Infer its motive, such as protecting a precious object. 3) Search the sites that motive would choose, not the usual storage place.
when: a hidden item was placed by a creature or agent with predictable habits
why: A creature's motive predicts a hiding place that differs from its normal one.

text: Let an NPC fetch an item as a quest step, since the retrieved item can reveal the next clue.
Ask what an object held when it left its origin, to fix its contents before any later change can be claimed.
when: an object's contents are disputed
why: the origin record sets the baseline against which later changes are judged

text: Objects found at a scene can be tested against witness claims about a product, place or time.
when: When a witness makes a checkable claim.
why: Objects are physical facts that can contradict testimony.

text: A crime scene is a set of competing claims: who has authority, who touched what, and who says what happened.
Do not treat saw nothing as nothing happened until you have checked the observer's coverage of the route.

1) Inspect the scene before interviewing household members. 2) Keep witnesses apart from the scene and each other while they wait. 3) Interview each witness in a chosen order. 4) Compare each account with those already taken.
when: when several witnesses may influence one another
why: keeping witnesses apart stops their accounts from contaminating each other

text: 1) State what the crime would have required at the location. 2) List the physical signs that act would leave. 3) Compare the observed signs with those expected. 4) Treat a mismatch as evidence the body or crime was moved.
when: When a body or object's placement does not fit the act.
why: A set of agreeing traces is needed; a single odd detail is weak.

text: Separate who committed an act from how the scene was staged; identifying the perpetrator matters more than correcting a misdirected scene.
Keep what a scene shows separate from what the people in it claim until both have been compared.
A distinctive scent or brand choice on an object can link it to the person who handled it, while a strong masking odour can indicate an attempt to hide a trace.
A smell can be planted deliberately to mislead, or tested to show which object carried it, so scent works both as a decoy and as a link between objects.
Scorching on fabric indicates that a shot was fired at close range.
Confused or scuffed prints suggest deliberate concealment, but the observer must judge whether the disturbance is careless or intended.
when: Tracks are disordered or partly erased.
why: Disturbance can come from haste or from a deliberate attempt to hide movement.

text: A planner who scouts a location in advance creates evidence of intent, so reconnaissance can expose the planner as well as inform the act.
A suspicious employer's penetrating gaze can unsettle an impostor and lower their confidence, breaking a prepared cover.
when: An impostor faces direct questioning or inspection.
why: Nerves reduce the composure needed to keep a rehearsed story consistent.

text: 1) Send one observer forward to look through a window. 2) Keep the rest of the group waiting. 3) Have the observer report back to the group.
when: when the group needs a close look without exposing everyone

text: A scripted distress display has a fixed sequence: collapse, rigidity, shrieking, then being carried toward the accused, and it can be repeated on cue.
Give a suspect's scripted excuse, account, or bluff about a character's nature a conflict with facts found later, so players who test it against other evidence are rewarded.
when: Designing NPC testimony in a mystery.
why: Rewards players who compare claims with the rest of the evidence.

text: Give an NPC a dialogue branch that tests the player's accusation, so a correct accusation produces a telling reaction and an incorrect one produces none.
when: Designing NPC dialogue for accusations.
why: Telling reactions reward correct reasoning and give feedback to the player.

text: Script a suspect to make a revealing move, such as a visit or moved item, only after apparent inaction, and provide a fallback path for a suspect who does nothing.
when: Designing investigation triggers for a suspect NPC.
why: A delayed trigger rewards patience while the fallback prevents a stalled case.

text: Script an NPC to behave differently when alone or unobserved, giving players a reason to spy on them and watch for tells.
when: Designing characters with hidden motives
why: Players who watch unobserved moments gain evidence the NPC hides in public

text: A scripted NPC rebuttal can be answered only by presenting a specific item, so dialogue branches depend on whether the player holds the decisive proof.
