A non-player character running a fake ritual can use scripted effects such as lights out or prepared answers, which the player must uncover by spotting props.
when: When designing a deceptive NPC ritual or performance.
why: Scripted effects rely on props and rehearsed responses that a player can detect.

text: A character who instructs others what to say fixes their account in advance, so later questioning meets a prepared story rather than spontaneous memory.
when: A suspect can influence the people who will be questioned.
why: A pre-set story answers questions before they are asked.

text: 1) Hold the character in isolation for a period. 2) Stage an emotional meeting with a relative. 3) Branch later dialogue on the player's earlier choices.
when: when scripting an interrogation scene

text: 1) Script in-world news or NPC hints that push players toward a suspect. 2) Plan a later reveal that corrects the record.
Script NPC reactions to probing questions and news as readable tells, such as a changed tone, sudden request, or guilt or relief, so players can test which reading is correct.
Script NPC replies to show sharp reactions or topic changes on sensitive subjects, giving the player a clue to follow up.
when: A question touches a sensitive subject
why: Reactions reveal what the NPC is hiding

text: Script NPC reactions as data, so a changed expression at a specific character's arrival flags a hidden relationship for the player.
when: Designing NPCs who hide a relationship with another character.
why: Recorded reactions give the player a readable signal to investigate.

text: Set a scripted reveal for a later event in a specific location, after the player has collected the needed clues.
when: designing a scene that resolves a mystery
why: the reveal then rewards the player's earlier investigation

text: Trigger an overhearing NPC with a scripted line the player can watch for a reaction to, and make hidden enemies react to the volume and position of player dialogue.
when: When designing stealth or eavesdropping encounters
why: Tying reactions to speech volume and position makes the listener's behaviour legible to the player.

text: Script a series of NPC warnings or rumours to set up a later event, and log who spread each one so the player can trace the motive back.
when: When designing a game event that should appear foreshadowed.
why: A traceable chain makes the event feel prepared and lets players reason about motive.

text: Script a suspicious NPC to name a rival when questioned, creating a trust puzzle the player must resolve.
when: when the player questions the NPC about a crime
why: deflection gives players a conflicting source to weigh

text: Script the order in which information reaches the player, since whichever contact the player meets first can shape how later events are interpreted.
when: designing a sequence of NPC encounters

text: Script a town event in advance and trigger it from earlier clues, so the player arrives into an already charged crowd.
when: designing town or community events

text: Hide a key item with a minor NPC, such as a servant, so the player is surprised when authorities produce it.
when: scripting a reveal that depends on a secondary character
why: a minor NPC holding the clue creates a fair but unexpected turn

text: 1) Seal the found item in protective material, handing it over unopened if its authenticity may matter later. 2) Mark it with a personal identifier. 3) File it with related documents under a clear label.
when: An investigator finds physical evidence and wants to keep it usable.
why: Securing and labelling evidence keeps it usable for later reasoning.

text: Hard surfaces such as gravel leave no prints, so the route across them must be inferred from indirect traces.
when: a route passes over unmarkable ground
why: only soft ground records impressions

text: Prefer bare physical features such as scars, ear shape or facial features over beards, glasses or clothing, since disguises rarely alter them.
when: when judging an identification by sight in good light
why: disguises rarely reproduce or alter the underlying features

text: Re-test a sealed flap after a delay; a seal that opens at once, without sticking or tearing, suggests the letter was handled.
when: a document's contents matter and others can reach it
why: properly sealed gum should hold firm when pressed later

text: A seal impression's shape can point to a specific object, since few common objects share an unusual outline.
why: Distinctive outlines narrow identification

text: Track who holds each key and each handover, since custody determines who could have entered a sealed room.
when: An event happens in a room sealed from outside or access depends on one key.
why: Custody history shows who could have entered and when.

text: A room can look sealed from outside while one latch or window is left so the culprit has a route out.
Handling a soft object can restore its original shape, so creases and indentations that carried the record disappear.
why: soft materials spring back and fill the marks left by a record

text: Absence of tracks is weak evidence no one passed: hard surfaces and short grass hold few marks, so an empty search may have mundane causes.
when: checking whether a person took a route or came to a place
why: hard surfaces hold few marks

text: A sealed-looking scene can hide a path that the witness account does not reveal.
A trace reads as a clock only if undisturbed; if it was handled or replaced, the reading reflects the handling, not the time.
Handling an item before it is photographed and recorded contaminates it and can make its traces unusable as evidence.
Using force on delicate evidence can destroy clues; handle fragile items gently.

1) Write a letter naming the suspect, the knowledge source and what the recipient should do. 2) Seal it with a fixed release time unless you return first to cancel. 3) Deliver it and obtain written acknowledgment. 4) Keep the acknowledgment and put your papers in order.
when: before confronting a dangerous person alone
why: Evidence still reaches others if the investigator is harmed

text: 1) Record each clue where and how it was found. 2) Keep related finds together. 3) Check the area for further clues before moving any item on.
why: keeps the context of each find intact

text: 1) Issue a written instruction for access. 2) Bring the required tradesman. 3) Enter together with witnesses. 4) Record the state of the room before removal. 5) Seal and transport removed objects.
when: when evidence integrity may be challenged later
why: Witnessed, documented access prevents any one person from being accused of private alteration.

text: Restrict a sealed key item to one named recipient or NPC, so opening it requires finding that person; withhold critical facts until a chosen story point.
when: designing a restricted sealed item or a critical fact withheld in a story
why: restricted access controls when information reaches the audience; a single gatekeeper creates a clear, meaningful goal

text: Seal sensitive evidence and entrust it to a trusted custodian with a fixed opening time, so opponents cannot learn its contents early.
when: disclosure could endanger people or alert a suspect
why: early disclosure would let enemies act first

text: Track which NPCs handled each item, since a cleared handling record hints at deliberate cleanup, which is a clue in itself.
when: designing object histories for NPCs
why: Missing handling data is itself evidence of concealment.

text: State the release condition for a sealed document plainly so the eventual reveal feels earned rather than arbitrary.
when: when a sealed or withheld document gates a reveal
why: An unstated or unclear condition makes the reveal feel arbitrary.

text: Store sealed, blind-labelled evidence so the player can compare results later without bias.
when: Designing evidence checks in a case

text: Secure empty containers before routine handling or shipping removes them, since they may hold key evidence.
Sealed evidence prevents leaks but cannot be checked before its deadline, so it risks dismissal or acceptance on faith alone.
Holding evidence private until the decisive person has read it lets that person choose, but delays public action.
when: Evidence affects a person who must decide how it is used
why: Early exposure can preempt the decision of the rightful party

text: Record a provisional conclusion in sealed form, to be opened only once the truth is established, as a check on one's own earlier error.
A sealed or delayed disclosure keeps the audience waiting for its contents, so the reaction to it carries suspense.
when: When a key fact should arrive at a later moment
why: Waiting for contents sustains attention

text: A subject writes a private event before a reading and seals it, so the reader later names it and the subject confirms, creating the appearance of insight from hidden knowledge.
when: Staging a reading or interrogation where the subject should feel the reader knows something private.
why: The subject cannot check the reveal before it lands, and the sealed slip hides the source of the insight.

text: 1) Write the expected identity and seal it before the reveal. 2) Record the solution in sealed form and set an opening condition, such as a deadline or trial event. 3) Perform the reveal. 4) Have a third party open the sealed note only when that condition is met and compare it with what was revealed.
when: An investigator or game must show that a reveal was fixed in advance and not improvised.
why: A prediction or sealed record fixed before evidence is seen cannot be shaped by later observation or altered after the fact.

text: 1) Privately write one suspect's name. 2) Have the hidden answer checked against it. 3) Confirm or deny the name, showing whether the reasoning matches the evidence without revealing the rest of the deduction.
when: The game has a hidden identity or fact the player must deduce, and a theory must be checked without giving the answer away to the group.
why: A fixed answer written in advance gives an unambiguous way to judge the player's reasoning.

text: Record a signed, sealed verdict in writing so that any later change can be detected by comparing it with the original.
when: when a judge's ruling could be altered
why: Written records outlast spoken rulings and leave a fixed trace.

text: Log each NPC claim with its in-game timestamp and seal it before the player learns the outcome, then compare it with the event time.
A sealed, unread reply prevents the sender from editing it, but the checker still depends on the questions asked; a neutral source tied to the claimant offers no real check.
when: Deciding whether a third-party reply can be trusted
why: Sealing protects the answer, while independence protects the source

text: Test every door, servant entrance and connecting passage of a sealed room, not only the occupant's route, since an overlooked exit may remain.
when: when a sealed-room claim must be checked or a room is fastened from the inside
why: A sealed door shows only that one route is blocked; looking only at obvious exits leads to a wrong conclusion.

text: Treating a sealed room as a complete alibi is an error, because anyone inside could have left before the seal began.
Apparent proof that a room is impossible to enter or leave can be false, since an overlooked exit may remain, and abandoning the method for a convenient conclusion closes the case wrongly.
when: Investigating a seemingly sealed scene.
why: Looking only at obvious exits leads to a wrong conclusion.

text: 1) Confirm room sealed and object missing. 2) Rule out occupants as takers, testing them and what they consumed. 3) Check windows, locks, ceiling, floor, sills and outside ground for traces. 4) Sound walls and cellars for hidden passages. 5) If insiders are cleared and routes fail, conclude a third party used another route and reason from the culprit's known style.
when: a room is sealed and an object is missing, or a theft seems impossible given the locks and seals
why: Eliminating insiders and ruling out routes shifts attention to an unexpected entry path that traces can confirm.

text: 1) Estimate time of death from bodily signs. 2) Compare that estimate with the last confirmed contact. 3) Log every entry, with items left and the lock state on leaving. 4) Test each entrant's claim against what they could actually have seen.
when: a sealed room or impossible-access case

text: 1) Establish the seal: confirm entries and windows were closed and nothing was disturbed. 2) Take the last-seen timeline from the final person to leave. 3) Record the scene as found. 4) Note what witnesses could not perceive. 5) Only then seek an explanation.
when: when a scene looks closed and an account of the last hours exists
why: Ordering the evidence before theorising keeps the explanation tied to facts.

text: 1) Check traces at the edges of a closed door, such as odor through a crack. 2) Read ambient smells as clues to the hazard inside. 3) Force the entry from a position out of the line of any rush. 4) Vent the room before treating anyone inside.
when: A closed space may hide a hazard that outweighs the cost of forcing it.
why: A closed door can hide lingering fumes that become deadly in small spaces.

text: 1) List every opening on each floor, including basement doors, kitchen windows, dining-room windows and living-room windows. 2) Record each opening's state: bolted, boarded, barred or sash-locked. 3) Note what each opening leads to, since some open only onto an inner court. 4) Eliminate secured openings. 5) Test the remaining route against the premise that the victim may have admitted the visitor.
when: A scene looks sealed and the choice is between an outside intruder and a visitor admitted from inside.
why: A complete survey shows which routes were open, but an admitted visitor leaves barriers intact.

text: 1) List every entrance to the room. 2) Note when each was last checked or used. 3) Record any inconsistency, such as a lock on one side and an open window. 4) Use each recorded action as a timestamp to bracket possible entry.
when: when a room appears sealed
why: Each constraint narrows when an intruder could have acted.

text: A puzzle room sealed by several locks should track which key is missing and where it was last seen, so the player can rebuild the route.
when: Designing a locked-room puzzle.
why: The player needs traceable state to deduce the route.

text: Show the physical facts of a sealed room early, but leave the method and timing for the confession to explain.
when: sealed-room mystery design
why: players hold early facts and reinterpret them at the reveal

text: Give the culprit a delivery or service role, which justifies movement across the setting while drawing no scrutiny from others.
when: the culprit must move through a restricted setting
why: An ordinary messenger is seen everywhere and so is rarely questioned.

text: A social barrier, such as an assertion that no one goes somewhere, restricts access less than a physical barrier, and open access can still allow tampering.
when: A space is guarded by a stated rule rather than a lock.
why: People respect verbal restrictions unevenly, and unlocked spaces remain open to anyone who chooses to enter.

text: A simple barrier such as a weight or spring can be passed by anyone who knows it is there.
when: A space is guarded only by a lightweight mechanism.
why: Knowledge of the mechanism is enough to defeat it.

text: A room used by several groups can mislead an observer who assumes it serves a single purpose; objects may reflect multiple overlapping routines.
when: Inferring a room's use from its objects.
why: A single room can host the habits of several distinct groups, each leaving different traces.

text: 1) Call the missing person's name and search hiding places. 2) Test each exit in turn and confirm whether it is still locked. 3) Rule out ordinary routes before considering unusual ones. 4) Widen the search across the house and grounds.
when: A person vanishes from a sealed room.
why: Checking exits in order closes ordinary routes and keeps the impossibility open.

text: 1) List every possible way into or out of the room. 2) Test each route against the physical facts. 3) Test each against the people present and their sightlines. 4) Eliminate failed routes; the remainder is the answer.
when: When a room seems closed or unreachable.
why: Elimination against facts and witnesses narrows the routes to the plausible one.

text: 1) Map every route out of the room. 2) Map what each witness could see from where they stood. 3) Time the blind intervals between sightlines. 4) Test the story against physical evidence such as noise from a latch. 5) Accept the sealed-room claim only after all routes are checked.
when: A person appears to have vanished from a sealed space.
why: Apparently impossible disappearances usually depend on what observers could not see.

text: An empty search can still confirm the hypothesis being tested when that hypothesis predicted the location would be empty.
Court files covering wills, contracts, boundaries and slander show ordinary relations between neighbors, not only crimes.
when: when reconstructing a community from records
why: daily disputes were recorded alongside serious offenses

text: Record dates precisely so that intervals between events can be calculated.
why: interval arithmetic depends on exact dates

text: Track which open questions lack supporting evidence, so players know to search new areas rather than rereading old notes.
Before treating a physical search as proof, ask who searched, when, and what they expected to find.
when: A physical search is offered as proof of guilt or identity
why: Expectations and timing shape what searchers report

text: A search-driven reveal has four parts: a question, a misleading visible marker, a convincing inference, and a closing record that restores trust in the conclusion.
An empty search does not prove a fact never existed or that someone is innocent, since records or evidence may have been destroyed or removed beforehand.
when: when records may have been disturbed or a suspect's premises are searched and find nothing
why: Destroyed or removed evidence leaves nothing to find, so negative results are weak evidence.

text: Searching an exposed scene later may find nothing, which wrongly suggests nothing happened there.
why: Erasure removes the physical trace, not the event that caused it.

text: Skimming an object misses hidden evidence, which is found only by checking every leaf or surface.
when: An investigator searches a book or similar object.
why: Evidence hidden inside an object is only reached by a complete search.

text: A search should cover everyone equally, including the most senior people, and should not begin unless it can be completed for all.
when: An inquiry requires checking the belongings or rooms of many people.
why: A partial search is perceived as unfair and invites suspicion.

text: A failed match or identification does not prove innocence or guilt, since the person may be absent from the collection or unseen by witnesses.
when: Interpreting a lineup, witness check, or database comparison where no match is found.
why: Witnesses may not have seen the person or the timing may be wrong; absence from a database is not non-involvement.

text: When a thorough search of a closed area finds nothing, but contrary evidence remains, the missing intruder becomes a puzzle in its own right.
when: A locked-room style search returns no results despite signs of a presence
why: A failed search contradicts the evidence, so the premise itself is questioned.

text: Record null results, such as searches or background checks that find nothing, as information rather than ignoring them.
why: A null result is still information and can be reconsidered later.

text: When no candidate's marks match, widen the search, since a negative result only excludes those already checked.
when: A comparison yields no match against the current suspect pool
why: Exclusion does not identify the culprit

text: Searching right after an ambush, or after any long delay, lets the attacker flee or let suspects move or remove hidden traces, weakening what the search finds.
when: When an attacker has fled before the search starts, or a long time passes before searching.
why: Each extra hour gives a suspect time to alter or remove evidence, and delay gives the attacker time to escape and remove traces.

text: A room ransacked in a targeted way, with containers forced and bedding emptied while valuables remain, suggests the culprit sought documents rather than goods.
when: When reading a crime scene for the intruder's real goal.
why: Searchers look for what they want and ignore what has no use to them.

text: Searchers check the nearest plausible hiding spots to a crime scene or findspot first, before examining places farther away.
when: when a hidden item is linked to a known location
why: spots nearest the object are the most likely hiding places

text: A search inventory is a numbered record of found objects, each with its location and condition, so that traces can be read together rather than alone.
The person directing a search chooses which places are checked, so the findings reflect what that guide chose to show.
Hand marks on a fence or rail show someone searching by touch, while a direct path to a target suggests the person already knew the way.
when: Judging whether someone was searching or knew the location.
why: Searching requires groping; prior knowledge allows a direct route.

text: Searching only the prominent objects misses traces, which often sit in gaps, containers, and corners.
Assuming a hidden item is kept where things are normally stored leads to a failed search.
why: Agents hiding something valuable often avoid their usual place.

text: 1) State the object a claim predicts must exist. 2) Search behind and under furniture with a light source. 3) Leave any find undisturbed until it is recorded.
when: A claim predicts a particular small object is present in a room
why: A clear target and careful handling prevent overlooking or destroying evidence

text: Allow an NPC to destroy evidence before the player searches their quarters, so a failed search is a meaningful outcome.
when: when designing searchable NPC spaces

text: Keep local incident history as a searchable log that the player can check against recent events.
Give different NPCs different search results depending on what each one expects to find.
when: Designing a search mechanic with multiple searchers
why: Expectation-driven results create believable, varied clues

text: Treat objects arranged too neatly as a sign of staging by a non-thief, and give players reason to suspect it as a second deduction layer.
when: items look placed rather than dropped, or a scene's evidence is suspiciously complete
why: Orderly placement signals a different cause from the obvious one, and noticing the staging is a deduction in its own right

text: A grammatical slip, such as a plural written in singular form, can reveal that a second person wrote the note.
Have a second independent witness inspect the same mark, because a witness may confirm a mark simply because they expect to.
A second questioner can ask about a topic nobody covered, such as clothing, and surface details the first pass missed.
when: A first round of questioning has finished without a full description.
why: Different questions open different lines of recall.

text: A second person who holds a damaging secret becomes as dangerous to the culprit as the first holder, so the culprit may act against them too.
when: Someone else besides the culprit knows the hidden past
why: Exposure threatens the culprit whoever reveals it

text: A second character entering a stalemate can produce a confession the first refused to give, especially when they claim responsibility to shield the other.
when: when two characters are protecting each other

text: A perpetrator who joins a crowd in a public place after an act can be seen there, creating a second alibi for the same night.
A second round of questioning can make a witness look guilty through tone and position rather than through evidence.
A satisfying explanation for one anomaly can hide a second, more serious one that the first does not account for.
when: Resolving an apparent puzzle with a plausible answer
why: Closure on the first anomaly reduces scrutiny of the rest

text: Keep questioning while a second observer watches the subject, since the questioner alone can miss tells that the observer catches.
Bystanders and staff may recognise a visitor and report the encounter to the suspect, which can expose a covert visit.
when: When an investigator visits a suspect's household or workplace unannounced.
why: Staff who notice a visitor tend to pass on what they saw to the people they serve.

text: A minor cut on the hand opposite the main wound can indicate that the blade's path continued beyond the main injury.
when: when an injury has additional small marks
why: Secondary marks show the motion behind the main wound

text: Run a secondary character's hidden history beside the main plot, so the audience knows more than the protagonist does.
when: when the protagonist is unaware of an important backstory
why: the audience's extra knowledge sustains tension in scenes with that character

text: An injury that does not match the claimed fall, such as one on the back of the head, may have a separate cause and should not be assumed to come from the fall.
when: A medical report lists an injury inconsistent with the stated event.
why: A single event rarely explains injuries in several places on the body.

text: Treat a later reference's claims, such as a named relative or description, as unverified until an independent source confirms them.
A second, unrelated story can absorb attention and offer a rival explanation, pulling the audience toward a wrong motive.
when: A false trail is needed to hold interest until a turn.

text: A secondary source's judgment of a person can shape later readers' view of the event, so their character assessment must be checked against the documents.
Collect secondary descriptors such as height, build, complexion, facial hair, and clothing, and separate clear observations from uncertain ones.
when: interviewing a witness about a person
why: secondary details test whether the primary identification holds

text: A character may withhold evidence when delivering it would cancel an advantage they hope to gain, treating silence as a tradable good.
when: Evidence would undo a benefit the holder is pursuing
why: Holders weigh disclosure against the value they expect from keeping it hidden

text: Ask what a suspect knew about a key fact, and treat a silence on that point as a meaningful clue.
when: A suspect avoids a topic central to the case.
why: Omission on a relevant point can indicate knowledge or concealment.

text: Make the protagonist's self-deception the obstacle, and let the reveal rest on contradictory physical evidence the protagonist must confront.
When a character reads part of a secret decision, such as a document, they may draw a plausible but wrong conclusion about its motive, creating suspense for an audience who knows more.
when: A hidden decision is partly visible to a character.
why: Partial information yields a guess shaped by the character's own interests.

text: A group that agrees on a shared fiction can hide real beliefs from one another, with both sides knowing the fiction without either stating it.
when: Members of a group maintain a comforting pretence about a loss or uncertain event.
why: Unspoken agreement lets a fiction persist while private beliefs diverge from it.

text: Telling a witness too much about the investigation can cause a leak, so keep the real plan from anyone who might blurt it out.
when: When a witness is connected to the suspect or the crime
why: Careless talk alerts the culprit and destroys the element of surprise.

text: A routine can also hide things, because an actor who blends into the pattern is harder to notice.
when: when a character's behaviour fits the expected pattern
why: Expected activity draws less scrutiny than unusual activity.

text: An official who refuses to disclose a source should be treated as information in itself.
when: When an official withholds the origin of a fact.
why: The refusal narrows what can be known and signals that a source exists.

text: 1) Give the hidden stash or secret room a backstory. 2) Link an NPC's personal loss to the device guarding it. 3) Let the player discover the backstory through the old lore and a newer private use.
when: Designing a secret room or stash in a level
why: Lore-based discovery makes the guarded object meaningful and the mechanism believable

text: Resolve every withheld matter eventually, since unanswered gaps frustrate rather than engage the audience.
End sections on a turning point: a changed state such as a found object, new name, new body, physical clue, message, or hidden visitor, that raises a question.
End a section on anticipation, deferring the answer so the audience waits for the result.
Each section should advance the story through a new discovery, setback, or deadline, keeping the audience's attention active.
Set up a consequential action as a small, concrete step, then close the segment on its consequence.
when: Ending a chapter or scene on a decisive choice

text: End a section on a reversal of the expected outcome, such as apparent safety followed by a sudden loss, to shift pacing and sharpen suspense.
when: the audience or player expects safety or resolution

text: 1) Scan the text for places where characters are unusually close together. 2) Use those spots as division points. 3) Read the resulting phrases. 4) Test the phrases against meaning before trusting them.
when: Recovering a message whose words are run together.
why: Unusual crowding marks likely phrase boundaries, but any split is only a hypothesis until checked.

text: End each scene or chapter on an open question that reopens the case rather than resolving it, making the next objective urgent because unresolved curiosity pulls the audience forward.
when: Structuring a sequence of scenes or chapters in a mystery or investigation narrative.
why: Unresolved curiosity carries momentum into the next section.

text: End a section on a concrete visible action whose purpose is not yet stated, rather than on a summary of mood.
when: closing a chapter or scene that hands off to the next
why: an unexplained action pulls the audience forward

text: Close a section on a new shock to push the audience into the next part.
when: ending a section mid-tension
why: An unresolved shock creates pull toward what follows

text: End a section on the accusation so the next section opens with its consequence.
when: Structuring chapters or scenes around a reveal
why: A closing accusation creates a hook that carries into the next scene

text: End each case with a short aftermath that closes the loop, such as arrests, rescues, a confession, or an escape that cannot be traced.
when: When concluding a mystery case.
why: Closing consequences give the player a sense of resolution.

text: Examine a scene before anyone handles it, and leave it unchanged until its traces are recorded or a full search is made, so the search starts from the original state.
when: A scene has just been discovered or is being investigated and may hold evidence not yet examined.
why: Handling erases or alters traces; disturbed objects destroy clues, mislead later searchers, and prevent later accounts from being checked against the original state.

text: Secure physical evidence or hard-to-replace identifying sources as soon as their value is recognised, before they are altered, consumed or lost, and protect them.
when: Evidence may be destroyed or used before collection, or a source provides hard-to-replace identification.
why: Acting late can allow a second harm; an unprotected source may be lost or damaged.

text: Seizures took livestock, crops, household goods and tools from estates, reaching several households at once.
When a suspect owns only one book, that volume is likely the key and can be requested for inspection.
when: Numeric correspondence exists and the candidate key book can be identified and seized.

text: Store sealed evidence in a secure vault rather than close at hand, so an adversary cannot track where it is.
Seizing one person's property can extend to spouse and relatives, who may be jailed or stripped of provisions.
A preserved scene can still hide evidence, so preservation does not replace a thorough search.
when: Investigating a locked-down scene.
why: Freezing the room protects evidence from disturbance but does not reveal what is hidden in it.

text: 1) Close the door and keep others away from the scene. 2) Send for the qualified examiner. 3) Clear the room of everyone not required to stay. 4) Leave the scene unaltered until the examiner views the body and surroundings. 5) Search only after that viewing.
when: At the discovery of a body or crime scene, before evidence is moved, examined or cleaned.
why: Early visitors and disturbance can alter the scene, and a search from a disturbed state finds less.

text: 1) Count and record the prisoner's money and personal effects against him in the register. 2) Measure height and note removed items such as boots. 3) Keep scene clothing as evidence and issue standard garments.
when: A prisoner is booked into custody.
why: Written inventory fixes what can later be disputed or altered.

text: 1) Photograph the item. 2) Request any fingerprints on it. 3) Alert the institution holding the funds to stop payment to the suspect.
Keep a sample from any test item and keep an item consumed by only one person intact for analysis, since an unpreserved item cannot clear anyone.
when: For test items, or when only one person consumed the item.
why: Analysis confirms the reaction reading; no other eater can vouch for a solitary item, so only its own evidence can clear it.

text: Collect small residues, such as dust, that routine cleaning would otherwise erase, so the trace survives for later analysis.
Secure a distressed witness's help by acknowledging their courage and framing the request as painful but necessary.
when: asking a witness to face a distressing task
why: Recognition and framing make cooperation more likely.

text: When a key item is still missing, keep the suspect or area under watch so the item cannot be disposed of.
when: When a suspect may destroy or hide a key item
why: Watching the suspect keeps the missing link recoverable

text: Keep the original form when the exact wording is itself evidence.
when: Presenting old records as evidence
why: Modernizing can erase the detail that matters.

text: Reward the player for preserving a trace before it is disturbed by player or NPC actions.
when: a scene's evidence can be contaminated
why: preservation rewards careful play

text: Avoid searching methods that destroy the only evidence of a secret; restore the scene where possible so it can be checked again.
when: a fragile or single clue must be inspected
why: destroyed evidence cannot be used later

text: A selected, non-random set of documents or examples shows a pattern but not its frequency; conclusions drawn from it need caution and may misstate how common an event was.
Investigators tend to draw the deduction that matches their own method, so contradictory conclusions can look equally convincing.
when: when several investigators reach different conclusions from the same evidence

text: Do not treat every object as a clue. Check whether each one would actually be needed for something before reading it as evidence.
When a claimed harm would hit everyone who meets its source equally, not only a chosen target, treat the claimed mechanism with suspicion.
when: when evaluating a claimed curse or gaze-based power

text: Reading witness details in one direction distorts a case, since emphasising only incriminating points produces a biased conclusion.
when: Presenting evidence against a suspect
why: Omitted exculpatory details leave the conclusion unbalanced

text: A framing built on chosen conditions is an argument rather than a neutral survey, so the selection of conditions should not be taken as the full picture.
when: Reading an account that presents context to support a conclusion.
why: The author's choice of pressures shapes which causes appear important.

text: 1) Release one fact to a witness. 2) Observe the reaction, such as surprise or relief. 3) Use that reaction to judge what the witness already knew or feared.
when: A reaction is more useful than the fact itself.

text: Record only the dates that bear on the case, and pass quickly over idle intervals.
when: Building a chronological record of a case or quest.
why: Irrelevant entries dilute the sequence that matters.

text: A character who knows the full story may omit damaging or decisive parts when retelling it, so the listener hears a partial version that seems whole.
when: A detailed account seems full but hides a critical fact.

text: Choosing which true facts or readings to present can steer conclusions wrong, making a weak case or ambiguous clue look conclusive by hiding the omitted facts or reverse reading.
when: Summarizing for a decision-maker, or presenting or evaluating a case or clue in a persuasive context.
why: Omission shapes the decision as much as falsehood; omission can make a weak link look strong, and ignoring the reverse reading hides the ambiguity.

text: A weak witness may respond to only one particular questioner, which limits who can effectively extract testimony.
when: Several people try to question a distressed or confused witness.

text: A witness may notice one striking detail while missing a plainly visible object nearby, so an omission is weak evidence.
A side dispute with no bearing on the main problem can absorb attention so fully that the investigator loses interest in the central question.
when: a vivid side quarrel runs alongside the main inquiry
why: the immediate side issue pulls focus away

text: A character who feels safe may later volunteer what they concealed, without being pressed.
when: when trust has been built through patience
why: low pressure lowers the cost of honesty

text: A witness who answers a casual question readily may still omit a detail that emerges only under gentle follow-up.
Attention is selective. A fact in full view often goes unnoticed until the frame of inquiry changes and the observer looks at it differently.
when: Repeatedly reviewing evidence without finding a solution
why: A fixed frame filters out facts that do not fit it

text: A suspect may offer identity details to seem open while refusing to explain their conduct; openness about facts is not openness about motive.
A culprit who keeps some records but removes others leaves a selective trail that reveals their habits.
when: An offender manages receipts or documents
why: Choosing which records to keep is itself a habit

text: Press reports that credit the wrong party for an action can mislead readers about who acted, while the true actor keeps the substance of the gain.
when: a public account of a resolved event is printed
why: Readers trust the printed version, so the misattribution persists and shapes their view of the outcome.

text: When one party selects all members of a council, those members owe their seats to the selector, so loyalty shapes their votes.
when: a body's members were appointed rather than independently chosen

text: Ordinary theft takes everything of value, so a selective pattern of removal points to a specific, rule-bound motive.
when: when loss follows a consistent pattern

text: A reputation or trust meter can drop when the player withholds findings from a quest-giver.
when: When a quest-giver expects shared findings
why: Withholding information damages the relationship with the one who expects it

text: Assume each character holds something in reserve; no one tells everything, so evasions and gaps are worth reading.
A guarded witness often opens up after the investigator shares something real first, so a partial disclosure invites the other person to reciprocate.
when: A witness holds information back and has a reason to guard it
why: Reciprocity builds trust and makes the witness feel the exchange is fair

text: A quest journal or rumour system presenting accurate but selective information rewards players who compare sources.
Quoting only part of a source, such as a single line or its cautionary qualifier, can reverse what readers believe the source says.
when: Summarizing a source or citing a single line from it.
why: Dropping the qualifiers reverses the impression.

text: Selectively reading symptoms or matching precedent features tends to validate the hypothesis favored before evidence accumulated, so readers of one precedent can reach different suspects.
when: Interpreting symptoms or matching evidence to a precedent.
why: Each reader emphasises the matches that suit their preferred answer.

text: Reveal one finding at a time to a suspect, watch whose reaction it unsettles, and use that reaction to choose the next question.
Compare an accuser's quotation of a witness with that witness's full dialogue to find any distortion.
when: A witness is quoted in an accusation

text: Let NPC announcements state only true facts while hiding the key ones, so players must work out what was left out.
when: when designing NPC public statements

text: Do not infer bad faith from a selective excerpt alone; test each claim against specific evidence first.
An investigator's own carelessness, such as leaving belongings in plain view, can become evidence that others read.
Check a postmark against the sender's whereabouts, since a sender who posts an item personally takes a risk and may gain an alibi from the timing.
when: the sender posted the item personally
why: posting in person is a risk taken in exchange for an alibi

text: An item that degrades or burns when exposed makes its own loss a clue, pointing toward whoever had access to it at the critical moment.
when: a document must be known to exist yet be unavailable when it matters
why: its destruction is traceable to the people present

text: A copy you make yourself carries little formal weight; a certified copy from the official keeper may be needed to prove a record's contents.
when: The finding must hold up in a formal proceeding
why: Self-made copies can be disputed

text: A suspect's explanations introduce new claims others can check, so each explanation adds a new point where the account can be contradicted.
when: a suspect explains away evidence
why: every stated detail becomes testable

text: Document each of your own actions, since they may later have to be described as testimony.
A participant's written account often justifies their motives, casting accusers as the real slanderers, and mixes admissions of fear and confusion with claims of entitlement.
when: A participant writes or tells a statement about their own role, especially when a campaign faces later scrutiny.
why: Self-protection against reprisal shapes the framing; they have a stake in how they are judged and how the record reads.

text: Lower the weight of a statement from someone who gains from the outcome, such as a paid or rewarded witness, since personal gain biases what they choose to say.
when: A witness was paid or otherwise rewarded.
why: People who profit from a conviction tend to speak first, and their interest may selectively shape the account.

text: A statement against the speaker's own interest carries more weight than one serving it; do not accept a self-protective denial at face value, especially when safety is at stake.
when: When judging whether a denial or admission is credible.
why: A speaker gains little by inventing a claim that hurts them; self-interest shapes what a speaker admits.

text: Claims about another's wealth or one's own ruin, from a party who stands to gain or lose, are self-serving; discount them and verify against records outside the party's account.
when: A character makes financial claims, or a source has a financial or reputational stake.
why: Claimants benefit from how their money story is told.

text: Treating a self-serving statement or self-defense as neutral history or established fact gives the writer's agenda unexamined authority; test its claims against other sources.
Relatives, acquaintances or grieving parties who defend their interests or speak for each other give partial testimony on a victim's relationships, motive or state; weigh it as biased.
when: Gathering accounts from family members or others about a victim.
why: Shared interest colours what is reported.

text: Advice or an offer to drop the matter from someone close to the case may protect the giver's interest in keeping the truth out of reach rather than the truth.
when: Receiving a warning or offer from someone close to the case.
why: Protective motives and self-interest can overlap in the same message.

text: A witness with a stake, or who wants to avoid blame, frames events in their own favour; accepting that self-serving framing at face value yields a skewed picture.
when: A witness tells their own part in events, or testimony about a disputed event is weighed.
why: Self-interest biases the account.

text: Records made by someone with a stake in the dispute may be biased or wrong on particular points; check them before trusting and invite correction.
when: A record's author gains from its contents.
why: Stakes can bias what is written.

text: Corroboration from stakeholders, whether a self-interested endorsement or interested parties signing each other's accounts, only repeats their own position and is not independent.
when: A writer or party with a stake vouches for their own record, or interested parties sign each other's accounts.
why: A stakeholder's praise confirms their claims, not the facts.

text: Testimony from a witness who wants an outcome or protects a reputation carries less weight alone; check details favouring the teller, like insisting on a key action, against independent accounts.
when: A witness has a stake in the outcome or protects a reputation.
why: Self-interest shapes what is reported and how firmly it is held.

text: Witnesses who fear consequences or gain from an account shape it to protect themselves: pushing blame onto others, stressing helpful facts, or relying on people who cannot be checked.
when: A witness is involved in or near an incident with possible consequences, or has reason to move suspicion away from themselves.
why: Self-interest bends recollection and biases which facts are volunteered.

text: When a large reward and a pardon are offered to members of a group, one member tends to betray the others early.
when: a group of accomplices faces pressure or an offer of clemency
why: the incentive to talk outweighs loyalty for the individual

text: A narrator personally affected by events filters what he reports toward his own comfort and irritation, dismissing others' concerns and misjudging people he dislikes.
when: A participant with a personal stake narrates events the player must interpret.
why: Personal stakes shape attention and judgment, so details that matter to him dominate while others are waved away.

text: A person's offered help often carries expectations of gratitude or obedience, and their motive shows in how they picture their own standing.
when: a character gives help, money or a proposal
why: people value what makes them feel equal or superior to others

text: A person who deceives others can come to half-believe their own claim and act on it, so a human scheme can produce results nobody planned.
when: A character runs a deception that depends on a shared belief.
why: Self-deception makes the schemer's actions sincere but still produce unintended outcomes.

text: A witness who benefits from the story may let personal satisfaction color their account.
when: When a witness reports an outcome that reflects well on them.
why: Self-interest shapes what is remembered and emphasized.

text: A witness counts as interested if they have a stake in the outcome, including an investigator who found the key object.
A suspect's own recorded words about the sequence of events can serve as proof of their role in that sequence.
Know who holds an interest before trusting testimony or verdicts; interest shapes who testifies and how an ambiguous sign is read as evidence, through the lens of those who benefit.
when: Weighing testimony or a verdict from a party with a stake, or an ambiguous sign used to support a verdict.

text: Let an NPC informant tell a full story with a hidden motive, flagging self-serving parts in dialogue or with an interest tag so players can separate them from confirmable facts.
when: Designing informant dialogue or witness records.

text: Weigh an informant's or witness's account against what they gain, lose or fear, since a stake may shape the story, especially when they are the only source for key events.
when: The informant or witness has something to gain or lose, such as a career, reputation or grievance at stake.

text: When a person's acts work against their own interest, look for a hidden controller who gains from them, and compare acts and statements for the pattern.
when: A suspect's behavior makes no sense for their own benefit
why: Actions that hurt the actor often serve someone else's stake

text: A character with a stake who declares that no proof exists is making a one-sided claim, which the audience can test against the people involved.
when: A character claims evidence has been fully destroyed
why: Self-interested reassurance is incomplete while witnesses still exist

text: Evidence handed over by people who benefit from the outcome arrives already sorted, so check what was kept, returned or removed before trusting it.
why: the handler can shape what the audience sees

text: A speaker who asks to be judged fairly in advance is presenting their own case, so that framing should be noted.
when: a speaker pleads for a fair hearing before giving an account
why: The request shapes how the listener is expected to receive the claims

text: A mark repeated across incidents may signal a group rather than one person, which changes the pool of likely suspects.
when: the same initials or token recurs across several events
why: a shared sign can belong to an organisation, not a single individual

text: Several witnesses giving the same account usually outweigh a single voice, and a clear timeline backed by them can outweigh a weak identification.
Expect that many self-described witnesses will stretch facts to be helpful, and weigh each account by the witness's position and motive.
Treat information offered in exchange for a favour as possibly self-interested, since the informant expects something back.
An alibi from someone who fears scandal or has their own name at stake should be weighed as shaped by that interest.
when: the witness is protecting a partner or their own reputation
why: the witness has a motive to make the account favour the protected person

text: An account that turns toward self-pity and requests for sympathy suggests the speaker is shaping the story for their own benefit.
when: when a witness asks for sympathy
why: sympathy-seeking reveals a motive for shaping the account

text: A writer who claims to have doubted events should be checked against their other writings from the same period.
why: Self-defense can contradict earlier public statements.

text: Accept an account from someone with a stake in the outcome provisionally, then test it for what it leaves out.
when: The witness has motive to shape the story and the official version rests on it
why: Plausibility is not truth, and interested witnesses smooth over disputes or motives

text: A witness who undercuts her own accusation in the same passage invites the audience to weigh the claim as weak.
Evidence that reads as proof to an in-world authority can read as malice to the player, because the player sees the motive behind the testimony.
when: Testimony is presented to a court, jury, or other in-world judge.
why: The player has access to context that the authority lacks, so the same statement carries a different meaning.

text: A self-authored account is shaped by a writer who protects their own position and chooses what to reveal and how to present themselves; check its claims against other records.
A self-serving narrator who tells events from their own viewpoint, flattering themselves or minimising or overstating guilt, is a biased source; check the timeline against other sources.
A motive offered by an interested party, such as a threat-maker, may be leverage or sympathy; check it against their own gain, and treat appeals to honesty as persuasion.
when: Evaluating a confession, explanation or motive from a party pursuing their own aim.
why: The teller may shape the account to gain sympathy; the source may use the claim for leverage rather than to reveal the truth.

text: Questioning witnesses in front of others or signalling suspicion to a whole group contaminates answers; they may close ranks or invent accounts to escape scrutiny.
when: Questioning a group of witnesses together.
why: Collective fear encourages coordination or fabrication to avoid blame.

text: A single witness whose account serves their interests produces a misleading picture, and a lone corroborating witness is insufficient if they could share the suspect's interest.
A witness with a personal stake may frame events to protect his standing; separate his feelings from the verifiable facts.
when: interviewing a client who has a stake in the outcome

text: A timeline built from a suspect's own account is easy to bend, so it must be cross-checked against objects and other witnesses.
A dying suspect's account can be self-serving, so verify it against other evidence before relying on it.
Pressing a suspect for more details can produce self-serving versions of events that favour the suspect.
Theories offered by people with a stake in the outcome steer the investigation toward their preferred answer.
when: a character advances a theory that favours a particular suspect
why: Interested parties shape what others look for, so their theories need independent verification.

text: A cover built on an interest backfires if the target knows more about that interest than the persona does.
An interested witness may supply a motive that strengthens a case while also biasing the account they give.
why: personal stake shapes what is reported

text: Vague, self-serving accounts often reveal the witness's bias more than the truth.
Accepting one faction's account of its own fairness is unreliable, because the faction benefits from that account.
when: a faction describes its own proceedings

text: A witness who says they always opposed a practice may have supported it, so their claim of objection needs checking against the record.
why: Self-justifying accounts shape how the witness describes their own past conduct

text: Officials who profit from an accusation process have an incentive to keep it going.
when: when officials gain fees, property or status from convictions
why: Personal gain from the process rewards its continuation

text: A long monologue can slow the reveal, and the teller's partial, self-serving account should be tested against other evidence.
when: A character gives an extended explanation
why: Length and self-interest both reduce reliability

text: A victim's or employer's own timeline can be wrong or self-serving, and confidence in a person's honesty does not establish the facts.
when: When an account comes from someone with a stake in the outcome or a trusted reputation.
why: Trust and personal interest bias recollection and reporting.

text: A motive reported by an interested party may be coloured by jealousy or grievance.

1) Gather suspects, witnesses and officials in the scene room and treat them alike. 2) Have people re-establish object and personal positions on site. 3) Let them discuss freely. 4) Record each claim that conflicts with the physical layout.
when: Individual interviews have stalled and the scene can be reconstructed; suspects and witnesses replay it together.
why: Physical positions force people to commit to specifics that separate interviews may let them avoid, so contradictions surface.

text: 1) Ask the group to mentally return to the moment of the event. 2) Invite each to report any impression, however trivial. 3) Narrow volunteers' accounts with follow-up questions on time, appearance and clothing. 4) Question each person separately, out of earshot of others. 5) Schedule a second interview, since forgotten details can return later.
when: group shared one viewpoint and memories are still fresh
why: Group settings suppress shy witnesses, and private questioning prevents copying or revision of answers.

text: 1) Announce a general claim that everyone present is hiding something. 2) Watch who looks away or over-explains. 3) Approach each person in turn and note who reacts most.
when: Several suspects share a secret and none has volunteered it privately.

text: 1) Question the group in a fixed order 2) Record each member's answer on a key event 3) Compare the answers for agreement and conflict.
when: a household or group shares one event
why: a fixed order keeps answers comparable

text: Check the account of a witness who is implicated, controls the scene, or gains or loses from the outcome against physical traces and other statements before trusting it.
when: A witness is implicated in the events, under suspicion, or has a stake in the outcome.
why: A personal stake gives reason to shape the account; people shade accounts to protect themselves.

text: Interest is a reason to check an account, not to reject it; test a self-interested claim or corroborated alibi against facts rather than dismissing it.
when: Evaluating testimony from a motivated witness, or an alibi backed by a close witness.
why: Self-interest explains why someone may lie, but truth depends on evidence.

text: Treat a suspect's account of motives, past or sequence of events as a lead revealing motive and method, accepting only parts confirmed by other witnesses and records.
when: A suspect volunteers an account or confession.
why: A self-written account is not final proof; the speaker benefits from how it is received.

text: Give an NPC a self-serving retelling with visible motive, and let the player check its claims against documents or other NPCs.
when: Writing a character who withholds or distorts information.
why: Visible motives teach players to question claims rather than accept them.

text: A witness who admits wrongdoing loses some trust but may have reason to avoid trouble, so weigh both the lost credibility and the motive.
when: the only witness has a self-interested record
why: an admission lowers trust while revealing a motive to speak

text: Treat each witness as having a stake, and check their claims against physical evidence before accepting them.
when: A witness also controls the scene or answers for an event
why: Self-interest can shape what a witness reports about the scene.

text: Test a suspect's self-description against facts, such as what support was actually provided, before accepting a claimed grievance.
when: when a suspect claims neglect or suffering
why: a claimed grievance may not match the record

text: A perceived detail contradicting an easy explanation keeps the question open, but an unverified sound under fear is not evidence even when reasoning says it is unlikely.
when: an offered explanation conflicts with what was perceived: keep the question open if the perception is verified; discount it if unverified under stress
why: Direct perception is harder to dismiss than a general theory, but unverified perception under stress is unreliable because fear shapes what is heard

text: A witness who learns she was overheard may change her tone, so impressions formed before and after that point cannot be compared directly.
when: A witness discovers that her words were heard by someone who is investigating.
why: Awareness of being observed changes how she presents herself.

text: A single distinctive sensory cue, such as a scent or a fragment of a voice, can anchor a witness's memory of a person they never saw clearly.
when: a witness recalls someone seen only briefly or poorly
why: A vivid partial cue gives memory a fixed point, so the recognition feels firm despite weak sight.

text: Witnesses usually hear more than they see, so a sound from a room confirms presence there but not the identity of whoever made it.
A witness can attest only what their senses reported; a sighting may be false through a deluded sense, a deceiving appearance, or a real figure mistaken for its likeness.
when: when a claim rests on a sighting
why: perception can be deceived in several distinct ways

text: Odd smells and similar easily dismissed sensory cues can identify a cause that visual evidence misses.
when: Investigating an event with limited visibility

text: Present a vivid sensory image before explaining what it means, so the audience experiences it first and interprets it second.
Ask precise, seemingly trivial sensory questions, since a fabricated account rarely anticipates concrete detail.
Binding and blindfolding remove visual cues, so the candidate must rely on the group's spoken signals.
when: group initiation trials
why: Removing one channel forces reliance on another

text: A familiar scent or object can trigger partial recall of associated past events, giving access to memory without direct questioning.
when: A character has lost or partly lost access to a memory.
why: Sensory input links to memories through association, so a cue can reactivate them.

text: Smell or sound rarely marks when an event began or ended, and a witness may mistake a sound for another event, so verify a sound-based time before fixing the timeline.
when: a witness relies on smell or sound to place someone or anchor a timeline
why: Sensory impressions persist without marking when they began or ended

text: A missing trace proves little when the observer was too far away or lacked the sensing range needed to detect it.
1) Ask targeted questions about sound, smell, light and handwriting. 2) Ask about physical state, such as dust or disturbed objects. 3) Check each answer against what the scene should show.
when: reconstructing an account after a frightening or confused event
why: Targeted questions recover details the witness did not consciously record

text: Log timed in-game events and have NPC witnesses report them with sensory cues, such as a clock striking or a hinge creaking.
Judge sound testimony by the listener's position, distance from the source and any barriers between them.
when: a witness reports hearing something rather than seeing it
why: Hearing depends on position and obstruction

text: Do not treat a smell or other sensory impression as identifying contents; confirm the contents with a test.
when: a sensory clue points to a substance
why: smell alone does not establish what something is

text: Pair each twist with a proof the player can check through an in-world sense such as touch, smell or taste, not sight alone.
why: The player can verify the answer by the same means the investigator uses

text: Ask an eager witness to separate what they actually observed from what they assume, since a helpful witness may add assumed detail.
Separate incidents before combining them, since one explanation for two different attacks may be wrong.
when: Several attacks or incidents are being explained together
why: Different incidents may have different causes

text: A crime stays hidden while its related events remain separate, because unconnected incidents form no visible pattern.
when: Several incidents occur without a visible link
why: Only a shared element can join events into a pattern

text: Give a hidden household its own entrance so it never passes through a shared business below.
Keep the fabricated lead clearly separated from genuine evidence so the decoy does not contaminate later findings.
when: A false lead has been planted to provoke a reaction.
why: Mixing fabricated and real traces makes later conclusions unreliable.

text: Model identification and cause-of-death examination as separate steps from discovery, each with its own person and time.
Track a remorse value separately from guilt so that the player's choice of confession or defiance changes how other characters treat them.
when: implementing reputation or social systems
why: guilt and remorse are different signals that others read differently

text: Servants or others who share a secret tend to look away and give short answers, and their silence is itself a signal to investigate.
when: When a group of witnesses is questioned about a shared secret.
why: Shared secrets create coordinated reticence.

text: Gossip from servants or doormen can reveal a hidden routine, such as a secret exit used at night.
when: checking a suspect's movements
why: staff observe habits the investigator cannot see

text: Remarks from people who serve the occupant, such as a landlady on payment and meals, add a second layer of testimony on their habits.
Question the servants of a likely recipient, since a servant who sees an object can recognise it or react, confirming the link.
A household servant's memory of who called and when gives an independent check on residents' accounts of their visitors.
when: A household has its own record of visitors

text: Routine tidying by household staff carries a dropped item through the household toward its intended reader.
Have household NPCs remark on a suspect's changed behaviour or routine, giving timed clues and early unease before the cause is known.
when: designing household NPC dialogue or seeding early unease in a setting

text: Question household members separately, since slightly different accounts of an absence can expose a false alibi.
when: checking an alibi through servants

text: Treat staff who served throughout as witnesses and assess how reliable each one is.
when: Staff handled or served the food.
why: Their accounts are evidence, but only as trustworthy as their observation.

text: Place low-status NPCs as witnesses who saw more than the powerful suspected, rewarding players who talk to them.
When newspapers and outside contact are scarce, a regular gathering becomes the main place to hear and retell news.
when: few other news sources exist
why: Scarcity makes the gathering the only dependable channel.

text: Assuming that a beautiful rural landscape means safety. A pleasant appearance can conceal a hidden history of cruelty.
why: Appearance says nothing about what has happened inside a place.

text: A striking outside theory that fits public fears of danger attracts wide attention and can push quieter, more mundane facts into the background.
when: A dramatic rival explanation is publicised
why: Vivid stories compete more strongly for attention than intimate detail

text: Public sermons that picture accused people as servants of the devil can intensify popular fear.
when: Religious or political speech during accusations.

text: A location's layout, sounds and decay can reveal its history, hint at what happened there, and suggest who may be present.
when: a place should function as a clue
why: the present state of a place records its past

text: Use a series of minor cases to set expectations of harmlessness, then place a serious item within one of them.
when: Structuring a sequence of investigations for a reveal
why: Established expectations make the later reversal land with surprise

text: A crime can be fitted to the season and landscape where it occurs, so the setting shapes what the audience sees first.
when: designing a crime scenario tied to a specific place and time
why: Setting determines the visible surface of an event and the expectations the audience brings to it.

text: Test whether a decoy motive fits its setting; a financial dispute rarely escalates to violence, so a more serious motive may explain the same facts better.
Barriers, nearby listeners and watching staff reduce what a witness will say, so statements recorded in such places are incomplete.
when: Interviews held in shared, noisy or monitored spaces
why: People guard their speech when they expect to be overheard

text: Memory of a stranger is likely in quiet places and unlikely in busy hubs, so failed checks in crowded places do not prove a lie.
when: Judging whether a witness should remember a person.
why: Quiet settings make a visitor stand out and be recalled.

text: A sensational setting does not make a case remarkable, and ordinary conduct can be misread as strange, so surface oddness is weak evidence.

Settlement closes disputes fast but leaves truth and culprit unestablished; investigation costs time but finds liars. Quiet settlement after confession suits cases where public trial would harm innocents.
when: when a dispute can be bought off, or when a culprit confesses and public trial would harm innocents
why: A public trial can harm innocent parties, so mercy can be the stronger choice

text: Frame a timing question as a yes-or-no matter first, since it settles quickly, and defer longer questions until timing is fixed.
when: several questions compete during an investigation

text: A dated record of an agreed settlement can show that a later arrest for the same debt breached it.
End a mystery by hushing the matter up through a settlement or offer rather than justice, leaving the social situation closed.
when: When the culprit has a strong motive to conceal the truth.

text: When rival readings clash, settle the dispute by returning to a fixed written record rather than continuing to argue.
Settle who is present before questioning, because a witness may refuse to dismiss others and an investigator without authority cannot force it.
A single reliable, independent positive identification can settle an open clue question, after which the result can be acted on.
when: a specific check can confirm a clue
why: One trustworthy confirmation may be enough to proceed.

text: A suspect's startled reaction to a pointed question or recognition, such as turning away or urging a companion back, is worth recording; it can reveal what a cover story hides.
when: when questioning a suspect with a cover story, or when a suspect is recognised
why: a sudden reaction can betray what the suspect is trying to conceal

text: A witness's visible shock or evasive parrying at news of a death can signal guilt, innocent distress or performance; test it against other facts.
when: when a witness reacts strongly to news in an interview
why: strong emotion can signal guilt or innocent distress

text: A sudden accusation or shocking revelation can provoke a physical reaction, such as grabbing at the accuser, standing abruptly or gripping furniture, that shows the stakes.
when: when a witness is confronted with an unexpected fact or accusation
why: strong emotion produces involuntary bodily tension

text: Removing the pressure behind a character's choices, through financial relief or learning a feared document is unrelated, can sharply change mood, willingness and attention.
when: a debt is eased, a sum is received, or a suspect learns an expected document is unrelated to the crime
why: the pressure that drove their choices has lifted; fear of a crime link is suddenly removed

text: A witness who changes subject, hesitates, asks to be excused or resists details is often holding back a sensitive fact; it shows concealment rather than guilt.
when: when a witness avoids a topic or changes the subject abruptly
why: reluctance signals that testimony touches something sensitive; slips and redirections carry the hidden concern

text: A witness who hesitates to swear an oath may have a stake in the answer that they are reluctant to admit.
A person who recognizes someone in an unexpected meeting may cover the reaction with an excuse, and the excuse can reveal the fear beneath it.
when: A character unexpectedly meets someone who knows their secret
why: People reach for a pretext to hide an involuntary fear response

text: A witness who fears a hidden person often shows relief when a named candidate is not that person, revealing which names are safe.
when: when a witness is shielding an identity
why: Relief signals elimination, not the target.

text: A strong, emotionally loaded first impression, such as a recognized costume, can make observers accept an identity before checking details.
when: when a body or event is identified under shock
why: emotional shock slows checking of details

text: A character asked to spy on others may feel uneasy about the role, which can shape how willingly they carry out the watch.
when: A character must observe someone they would rather not spy on.
why: Covert watching conflicts with personal ethics and trust.

text: A startling moment can fix overheard words in memory, so a witness may repeat them exactly while misreading what they meant.
when: a witness overheard remarks that shocked them
why: strong emotional arousal strengthens memory of the words

text: A frightened or sleeping witness often holds real sensory detail that they cannot recall unprompted, while fear can also add imagined details.
when: after a frightening event the witness experienced at close range
why: shock weakens recall and mixes perception with fear

text: A character who reacts sharply to a seemingly harmless remark may have a personal stake in the subject, and the reaction is worth following up.
when: a remark touches a character's private concern
why: strong emotion shows investment beyond the words spoken

text: A sudden change in a person's face and eyes at a known figure's arrival reveals fear or guilt before any explanation; most onlookers miss it.
when: a known person appears near a suspect
why: onlookers attend to the arrival, not to the suspect's reaction

text: Accusers' distress eased only once the suspect was bound, and the authority recorded this as meaningful.
when: when accusers' relief follows the suspect's restraint
why: the timing was taken as confirmation of the charge

text: A target may accept a short delay as a source of hope, which a manipulator can then exploit.
when: when a requester offers a brief wait

text: People who process shocks alone rather than seeking company are better left unprompted for a while, and pressing them with questions can backfire.
when: A witness has just received shocking news and has a known habit of withdrawing
why: Their stress response is internal, so interruption disrupts processing

text: A shocked witness gives approximate intervals and may lose a minute or two, so their sequence of events is blurred.
when: a witness recounts an event under horror or fear
why: shock distorts the sense of time

text: Hints that earlier choices mattered produce dread in the audience without revealing answers.
when: a retrospective frame signals that events were serious
why: suggested stakes outrun the facts the audience actually has

text: Under shock, people reveal what they know through unguarded reactions such as turning away, pale faces, mutual glances and recoiling from the scene.
when: when people are confronted with a body or key clue
why: shock lowers control over expression

text: Observers often attribute unease to external causes such as weather or age rather than to a specific threat.
when: A character or player feels unexplained apprehension.
why: People look for a plausible, non-threatening explanation for vague fear.

text: When nearly everyone believes in an unseen threat, most people accept accusers' claims and only a few distrust them.
why: Shared fear lowers scrutiny of claims.

text: A casual, offhand remark can revive an unsupported theory, and the listener supplies its meaning, reading hidden intent into tone or look.
when: A character holds a wishful theory and hears an ambiguous comment.
why: Listeners project their hopes onto ambiguous signals.

text: A shaken witness can lose the ability to reason and obey without question.
A witness can be sane and honest yet have no recall of events before a certain point, a known pattern that can follow severe shock.
when: A witness's account depends on a period that may have been disturbed by trauma.
why: Severe shock can block recall of earlier events without impairing honesty.

text: Relief at elimination is ambiguous, not proof: a witness may mislead on purpose, so weigh each relief reaction against other evidence before concluding guilt or concealment.
when: interpreting a witness's sudden relief
why: relief may come from being cleared of suspicion, not from hiding something

text: A reluctant or hesitant answer is a signal to verify, not proof of guilt or falsehood; hesitation can come from loyalty rather than deception.
A sudden unexpected disclosure can probe a suspect's reaction when the suspect's composure is known to slip under surprise.
when: When the shock will not endanger anyone

text: When several observers share the same unease, do not dismiss it just because the lead investigator has not seen it.
Have other characters notice and comment on a sudden reaction, so it becomes a shared fact in the scene that players can recall later.
when: planting a clue through reaction
why: a witnessed reaction is harder to dismiss

text: Shocks temporarily renew a character's energy, and once the stimulus is removed, strength fails quickly.
A startled reaction can come from fear, surprise, embarrassment, drink or private shame, so innocent causes must be ruled out before reading it as guilt.
when: interpreting a reaction to an exposed object
why: many emotions produce the same response; a visible reaction does not identify its cause

text: Relief that is too long or too complete drains tension, so the next threat reads as repetition instead of escalation.
Emotional shock can cut a survey short and leave the scene incompletely recorded.
when: the investigator or a partner is distressed

text: Victims in shock may not describe what they saw clearly, so their accounts need checking against the scene.
Relying on shocks without clues that make them meaningful weakens tension, because the audience cannot connect the shock to a question to pursue.
when: Designing scares or sudden reveals
why: Unexplained shocks produce startle without investigative engagement.

text: Relief at clearing one suspect can lead a group to drop others too quickly, so earlier assumptions still need rechecking.
A witness who readily accepts an offered explanation may be relieved rather than truthful, since the offer itself shapes the answer.
Being accused of fabrication can make investigators doubt their own valid work, even when the evidence is sound.
Missing powder marks on clothing suggest a shot was fired from a distance.
when: examining a gunshot victim's clothing
why: Powder residue travels only a short distance from the muzzle.

text: Natural shooting posture bounds estimated shooter height, producing a range rather than a single figure.

1) Fix the victim's posture and facing from observed facts. 2) Work out the single spot from which the attack could have been made. 3) Mark that spot on the scene. 4) Test each route and exit against the facts. 5) Note items that are missing.
