when: a body's posture or furniture constrains where an attacker could stand

text: 1) Count the empty chambers or missing cartridges in a dropped weapon. 2) Treat the count as the number of shots fired. 3) Do not treat the count as proof that any shot hit.
when: A weapon is recovered at a scene with some cartridges missing.
why: Missing cartridges show the weapon was discharged, but not whether the discharges struck anything.

text: A voice heard through a door or from afar is taken as proof of presence, but a brief reply does not confirm location or that the person was alive then.
when: A witness hears a familiar voice through a door, from afar or in the dark, or a reply is the only evidence of presence.
why: They cannot compare it with the real voice, and a voice does not confirm location or time.

text: A hard-of-hearing witness hears only part of what happens and may build their own explanation, which can diverge from the facts.
why: Missing information gets filled by the witness's own interpretation.

text: Distance or absence from a room can prove a listener could not have heard the important content, which narrows suspicion.
A distant or chance witness can confirm a suspect's identity or a location, but only for what he personally saw.
when: An identification or location must be confirmed from far away or by accident.
why: A witness's knowledge stops at the edge of his own observation.

text: Treat a heard sound as a timed event, and record the listener's delay before acting, since that delay narrows the window for when the event occurred.
when: Reconstructing when a shot or similar sound happened.

text: A distant visible sign can convey information that cannot be heard or reached, and a change in its pattern can reveal activity out of sight.
when: when a character must learn of a hidden event from afar

text: Each additional locked room between a trapped person and others adds distance and blocks sound, cutting off help.
A distant sighting can misidentify the person; discount detailed identification claimed beyond the range the witness could plausibly see, since recognition weakens with range.
when: when a witness saw someone from far away

text: Partially heard or recalled speech gets filled with assumptions and associations; mark each detail heard or inferred, and never treat a remembered phrase as exact.
when: A witness reports an overheard or recalled exchange.
why: Partial hearing leaves gaps filled by assumption; unmarked inference is later taken as a full transcript.

text: Once an accusation drops distance as a limit on the suspect's reach, any location-based alibi can be dismissed.
Witnesses estimate distance from perceived speed and duration, and these estimates can be badly off, so a confident distance claim still needs checking.
A distant observer busy with other work cannot reliably say who was seen or fix the time, so such a sighting is weak.
why: Distance and divided attention limit identity and timing.

text: A trail that sends the investigation abroad can leave the case unresolved for days, slowing progress.
A witness who hears poorly may miss part of a question, so a plain yes or no can be misread as a confession or a slip.

1) Establish the witness's exact position. 2) Test what could be seen from it, ideally by re-enacting with a companion. 3) Identify what was unseen and propose a route that explains it. 4) Verify the route.
when: A witness's account depends on what they could see from one position.

text: Treat sounds heard at a distance as support for a timeline, not as identification of a person.
why: distant sound lacks identifying detail

text: Check a witness who heard nothing for sleep depth and sensitivity; a known light sleeper makes silence informative.
A hearing can deliver facts that are new to both protagonist and reader while keeping their true meaning hidden until later.
when: Structuring an information reveal in a scene.

text: Follow a suspect at a distance to learn who they meet, where they go, and how long each visit lasts.
when: When the suspect's whereabouts are disputed or a meeting may be hidden.

text: Let a hard-of-hearing or distracted suspect mishear a question, creating a branch where the player must clarify.
Let players test a witness's claim about what was seen from a window with a line-of-sight check.
A vanished suspect or missing item invites a conclusion of flight or supernatural cause, so test several innocent or misleading explanations before accepting either.
when: a suspect, NPC or item vanishes or goes missing
why: Disappearance is ambiguous and can mislead; absence should not automatically point to a supernatural cause.

text: Repeated sightings, especially by several witnesses who build on earlier reports, reinforce a legend and make mundane explanations less likely until the whole community shares the alarm.
when: a rumour is repeatedly confirmed by witnesses, especially several people
why: Accumulated, mutually reinforcing reports shift belief toward the supernatural.

text: Identifications from a single or brief view, such as a momentary voice, glimpsed figure or partial silhouette, are unreliable; witnesses may say only that a person resembles them.
when: a witness saw the person once or identifies someone from fleeting cues
why: Brief exposure limits recall, and witnesses fill gaps by inference, so a confident identification is unreliable.

text: Viewing from afar or in weak light gives shadowy figures little detail, and witnesses fill gaps with expectation; assuming a fleeting distant shape matches someone known misidentifies them.
when: a sighting is made from far away or under weak light
why: Limited line of sight and light force the mind to supply missing features from prior belief.

text: 1) Ask how the witness perceived the event, including distance, cover and light. 2) Ask what else the observed person carried and whether they saw the witness. 3) Test whether each person involved can be identified. 4) Check whether minor errors undermine the core claim. 5) Judge whether the report rests on perception or imagination.
when: A witness's account depends on sight, hearing, distance or memory, especially at night, briefly or in fright
why: Perceptual limits can undermine identification even when core words are recalled; each question separates observed detail from imagined detail.

text: Do not accept a sighting or let a single unverifiable report carry a verdict until a second independent witness confirms it, since one report cannot separate truth from error.
when: Evidence rests on a single unverifiable report
why: One mistaken witness cannot decide the case; a report cannot separate truth from error.

text: Recognition, such as hearing a familiar name or seeing a known person, can trigger an involuntary reaction like pallor or a sudden movement.
when: Confronting a suspect with a familiar name or person, or a disguised person is in the presence of someone who knows them
why: Physical reactions are harder to control than spoken words; recognition triggers an unconscious physical response.

text: A person who sees someone often over a long period may still fail to recognize them later.
when: a witness has had frequent contact with a person over time
why: recognition depends on attention, not exposure alone

text: People who pass a familiar place daily often see it without observing it, so they cannot count or describe its specific details.
when: Someone has passed a place many times without attention.
why: Passive seeing does not record countable facts.

text: People are seen far less often in empty settings, such as quiet Sunday mornings when most people are indoors, so sightings depend on the hour.
when: when judging whether a witness could have seen someone
why: few people are out to observe

text: A suspect's habitual action, such as a repeated song at a set time, can be a signal to outsiders.
when: A routine action recurs at a fixed time.
why: Habits can carry hidden communication.

text: People trying to match a changed face to a remembered one may fail on overall appearance yet accept one stable feature as enough to settle identity.
when: Someone must identify a person altered by time, disguise or illness
why: A constant feature can anchor recognition even when most other traits have changed

text: A person who seats themselves with light behind them makes their face hard to read, which may be deliberate.
when: A person chooses a seat facing a window.
why: Shadow hides expression from the observer.

text: People who benefit from a visible pattern may hear the warning, accept the facts, and still refuse to draw the conclusion.
when: A recognised pattern threatens a group's interests
why: Those who gain from the status quo resist its implications.

text: Observers unaware of a concealed mirror can misread its reflection as a separate, possibly distorted figure, especially in silhouette.
when: when a reflective surface lies outside the observer's view
why: the observer cannot see the mirror

text: A suspicious sighting explained at once with a simple, plausible reason closes the lead for the audience.
when: a suspicious sighting is given an easy explanation
why: a plausible explanation ends the need for further thought

text: A familiar, old exchange device, such as a returned dropped item, can act as a signal that an observant person recognises as a hidden link.
when: Two parties exchange an ordinary-looking object.
why: Observers who know the convention read the exchange, while others see only the object.

text: A repeated chance encounter turns a coincidence into unease, and people read repeats either as design or as fate.
when: The same person is met by chance more than once.
why: Repetition suggests a pattern, which invites an explanation beyond chance.

text: When a witness recognises the key figure at a reveal, the mood shifts from searching to shock.
when: At the climax of a staged reveal
why: Recognition makes the discovery personal

text: Asking a witness whether they are entirely certain of a speaker's identity can make them reconsider and reverse an earlier assumption, reordering other facts.
when: when a witness has identified someone from a voice or call
why: a suggested alternative reopens doubt

text: A silhouette or backlit outline confirms presence and shape but not identity or activity, because interior detail is lost.
when: a suspect's location matters with only partial evidence, or a figure is backlit or seen from a distance in a dark space
why: Light behind a subject removes the surface detail needed for recognition.

text: Bystander sightings give a direction of travel but not an exact position, so they should not be relied on alone for tracking.
when: Tracking a fugitive through a crowd or street.
why: Direction from several witnesses narrows the search area without fixing where the person is.

text: A report attributed to an eyewitness cannot be verified from the text alone; the reader needs independent corroboration.
Common objects with angular outlines, such as a hat with corners, can distort a silhouette so that it looks inhuman.
An empty room after a sighting does not disprove the sighting, since the observed figure may already have moved away.
when: When a search finds nothing after a reported sighting.
why: A search that occurs later may miss a person who has left.

text: Treat a sighting that is the only link between a person and a place or time as tentative until it is checked.
when: A single witness sighting is the main evidence

text: Treat a brief flicker of recognition as data, recording its strength and how quickly it fades.
when: Observing a subject during cued recall
why: Partial and fading recall shows the shape of a memory

text: A witness with repeated direct contact with a subject, such as a driver who often carries the same person, is a reliable source of routine facts.
why: Repeated first-hand contact gives direct knowledge.

text: Learning a target's new lodging quickly suggests the target has been followed since arrival.
when: when a target reaches a new location soon after being seen

text: Record how often an observer watched, since the number of sightings depends on how much time they spent watching.
when: when weighing a count of repeated sightings
why: A count means little without the watch frequency behind it

text: A visitor who enters and leaves by the same route repeatedly without hindrance suggests familiarity with that route.
Log NPC sightings with game time so players can rebuild an event by cross-referencing them.
Investigators weigh whether a revealed fact can support the case, and withhold testimony that would hurt an innocent party without helping the case.
when: When deciding how to use a witness's disclosure.

text: An unwitnessed claim can gain support by preserving any document it refers to, which serves as corroboration.
when: when a claim has no witness

text: Two different callers asking about the same valuable item on the same day is a warning sign, especially if one caller's name matches a known alias.
why: Coordinated or repeated interest in one item suggests a threat.

text: A repeated object detail may be explained by an origin the story has not yet mentioned, so check for unseen history before reading the detail as a clue.
A small, harmless errand, such as returning a dropped item, gives a reason to revisit the same spot repeatedly.
when: when watching a location over time without drawing attention

text: A subtle tell, such as an NPC repeatedly looking at one object, can point to a hidden link without any dialogue.
A witness who cannot follow the question gives answers that carry no information and should not be weighed as evidence.
A flawed or unreliable witness can still reveal part of the truth, so do not dismiss them entirely.
when: When a source's reliability is in doubt.

text: Two documents sharing an impossible date suggest a systematic pattern rather than a single clerical error.
when: when a record's dates fail a check

text: Make an object's testimony repeatable, so a second copy or second examination yields the same contradiction, which strengthens its reliability.
when: When an artifact is meant to serve as evidence.
why: Consistent results across attempts reduce the chance of a fluke.

text: A sighting is weak when the witness's times are approximate or the lighting was poor.
Repeated pressure on one surface leaves a mark at a consistent position. That position can reveal the person's occupation or habit.
why: the same motion recurs in the same place

text: Each link in a sighting chain gives the next investigator a place and time to check, so the chain advances forward in time.
A recognition flicker in the eyes lasts only a fraction of a second, making it hard to fake and easy to miss.
Shopkeeper identification made near closing time, under pressure, should be weighted against time of day and customer volume.
when: When a shopkeeper identifies a buyer during a busy or closing period.
why: Pressure and crowding reduce the accuracy of recognition.

text: Fluent, smooth or detailed speech is weak evidence: it can pass checks while hiding gaps, rehearsal, guesswork or motive; gaps surface only under direct demand.
when: a witness's story sounds complete, consistent, fluent or detailed
why: Smooth or detailed talk feels trustworthy and can mask lapses the speaker is unaware of or wants to conceal.

text: Once a theory forms, the investigator may fit vague reports to it, and witnesses who share information may look independent when they are not.
when: When a suspect theory is already formed and witness reports arrive.
why: Confirmation bias and shared gossip make weak evidence look strong.

text: A witness description that matches a record may still be false; compare the witness account with the official record, not with the first person named.
when: When identifying a person from a witness description and a record
why: Matching to the first name on a record ignores that the record may name the wrong person

text: A disturbance can hide an act from observers but not necessarily their report, so a witness may still log the sighting even if no one can act on it.
when: An escape is partly masked by noise or confusion.
why: Observers may still record what they saw, even when the noise prevents an immediate alarm.

text: A sighting with no conversation confirms that a person was present, but not their state of mind or intent.
Witnesses may misplace a sighting in the wrong room or compartment, so its location must be checked against other evidence.
A narrator close to the detective may flatter him, so audiences should weigh praise separately from evidence.
when: Presenting an investigator through a loyal narrator.
why: Admiration can colour the reported reasoning.

text: A person who handled an object once may have handled it again in an unmapped window, so each access period must be tracked.
when: when reconstructing who touched an object
why: single known access is not the full access history

text: A dramatic reveal loses force when repeated, so later reveals must add new information.
A sighting that dissolves when approached cannot be verified and makes poor evidence; record who saw it and from where.
A fabricated sighting can hold up if its travel and timing seem plausible, so each detail needs independent checking.
when: When accepting a claimed later sighting.
why: Surface plausibility does not establish that the sighting occurred.

text: 1) Note the time and place of the reported sighting. 2) Establish the suspect's verified location at that time. 3) If verifiably elsewhere, treat the sighting as false. 4) Otherwise check whether the person could physically have reached that place then.
when: a witness places a suspect at a scene
why: A person cannot be in two places at once, and physical reach limits where they could have been.

text: 1) Check overhead openings such as skylights first. 2) Check roofs and the eaves for ladders or external objects. 3) Check any overlooked routes before accepting a sealed-room explanation.
when: When a sealed room's occupant has vanished
why: Vertical and overlooked routes are often missed when attention is fixed on doors and walls.

text: 1) Identify the last verified trace, such as a messenger, luggage or ticket. 2) Test each link in turn. 3) Follow unanswered letters or wires as further traces.
when: A suspect disappears.
why: Each verified link narrows where the person went.

text: 1) Steer repeatedly to named people and specific points. 2) Note the few concrete details. 3) Set aside opinion and digression. 4) Return to any point met with hesitation.
when: A verbose witness knows a social circle and facts are buried in digressions.

text: 1) Reassure the witness 2) Present the contradicting fact 3) Ask about one small detail and note whether the account holds.
when: a witness's account depends on a fleeting view
why: gentle steps reveal whether the detail survives challenge

text: 1) List every plausible approach to a spot. 2) For each, ask whether a watcher with a clear view would have seen it and was facing that way. 3) Remove failing routes; the remainder points to a hidden route.
when: When several watchers report a sudden appearance or disappearance
why: Visibility and attention together determine which routes could have gone unnoticed.

text: When a night has no witnesses, offer other ways to resolve it, such as footprints, receipts or a stranger's description, rather than making the gap decisive.
when: designing an unwitnessed period
why: A single gap should not settle the question alone.

text: Do not use a fevered or half-conscious witness's vivid impressions as evidence.
when: the witness is in a fevered or half-waking state

text: Repeat an observation before trusting it, because a single look can be misread.
when: verifying a suspicious act
why: a second look checks perception

text: Recount any bundle whose count surprises you before drawing conclusions, since a first miscount can look like a discovery.
why: Counting errors are common, and a wrong count can mislead an investigation.

text: A sighting from a different night bears only on that night and cannot settle the time of a separate event.
Test a claimed observation against conditions such as darkness and weather; a face seen through glass in rain and dark would require contact with the pane.
why: Physical conditions limit what can be seen

text: Design an apparent victim with a hidden plan to vanish, revealed through a ledger or letters the player finds.
When a character seems to vanish, ask who holds a key or knows a route, and do not assume a secret passage without evidence of a key or door.
when: investigating an apparent disappearance
why: keys and known doors are the usual explanation

text: Treat each sighting as a boundary on time, not as a precise point in time.
when: Converting witness sightings into a time estimate
why: A sighting shows only that something was true before or after a moment

text: Use an unresolved suspicious figure as a plausible false lead, but do not use it where a clue must be clean and unambiguous.
when: Designing misdirection in a mystery
why: A lead the player cannot resolve keeps suspicion alive without confirming guilt

text: If a witness saw an object at one point, account for the time it was out of sight before assuming it is still there.
when: when an object's location is reported at an earlier time
why: the object could have been moved during the unobserved interval

text: Treat an unwitnessed claimed activity, such as walking the streets, as an unverified gap rather than as an alibi.
why: Without a witness or record, the claim cannot confirm where the person was.

text: Design clues where the pattern of a repeated action, not any single action, reveals the culprit's purpose.
Recognition may rely mainly on the first-seen setting, so a changed setting can hide a known person; yet habits or expressions can reveal a disguised person in a new setting.
when: A pursuer has seen the suspect only in another setting; a known person reappears in a new setting
why: Setting cues can dominate recognition, while habits and expressions survive a change of appearance.

text: An observer who arrives just after destruction and says nothing directly can still send a signal that the destroyer feels read.
when: A witness discovers someone has just destroyed something.
why: Silence and timing convey knowledge without confrontation, which the destroyer interprets.

text: Check a witness's vantage point: light, distance, obstruction, windows, glass partitions and floor surfaces determine what they could see or hear from where they stood.
when: Evaluating an eyewitness account or whether a witness could have observed an event from their position.
why: Each factor can enable or block sight and sound; a witness cannot report what their position hides from view.

text: Use a separate observer who sees the figure from another angle to expose a disguise, since that witness may mistake the stand-in for the person.
when: Testing a disguise or false alibi
why: A separate sighting can reveal the substitution that the household accepted

text: A second reading taken from a different position narrows where a hidden source can be, because the two bearings intersect at a single point.
when: a source's direction is known from one spot
why: intersecting bearings fix a point that one bearing cannot

text: Use a sighting of the supposed dead as the hinge of the twist, with the deduction following from it rather than replacing it.
when: Constructing the moment a presumed death is overturned.
why: A concrete sighting gives the player a fixed point to test the deduction against.

text: A single sighting can be explained in many ways, so it cannot identify anyone on its own.
when: Drawing conclusions from one partial observation.
why: One data point leaves too many explanations open.

text: Treating one directional reading as proof of a source is a mistake; the nearest structure on the bearing is not necessarily the source and must be checked.
1) Map windows, glass partitions, lamps and surfaces on a plan. 2) Mark the witness's position. 3) Check whether light, distance and obstruction allowed the claimed observation.
when: Testing a witness claim of seeing or hearing something.
why: A plan lets each claimed observation be checked against physical constraints.

text: Before accepting that no one passed unseen, list the doorways, check whether an open door or a standing person blocks view of both entrances.
when: When a room has several openings and people may have moved through them.
why: Sightlines decide whether an action could have gone unnoticed.

text: Treat a deliberate signature as a mindset clue, not confession or proof of literacy or guilt; compare it with a known sample, since it can mislead.
when: interpreting a deliberate act left at a crime scene
why: deliberate acts reflect intent but can be used to mislead

text: Players read a sign repeated at a second scene as a deliberate signature, which strengthens a false pattern built from it.
when: a clue reappears at a later crime scene
why: repetition suggests a pattern

text: A signature is a distinctive mark or token repeated at each incident or communication, identifying one author across separate events that look unrelated when judged alone.
A deliberate mark left at a scene is a signature: a message that says who acted and why, meant to be read by others.
when: A culprit wants to send a message, claim a grievance or identify a group
why: Marks carry intent beyond the act itself

text: Signature analysis treats a deliberate act as an expression of the doer's temperament, so a familiar analyst can infer the actor from the act's style.
when: When a crime shows a distinctive, planned style and candidates are known
why: Planned acts reflect personal habits and character

text: Copying a signature is easier than copying a full handwritten text, so a long hand-written passage is harder to forge convincingly.
when: Assessing whether a handwritten document is authentic.
why: A signature is short and can be practised, while a whole text reveals many habitual letter forms.

text: A message signed with a name shows only that someone sent it under that name, not who the real sender is.
Multiple signers can confirm what was seen, but they do not confirm what caused it.
A recurring private phrase that an NPC repeats can signal its weakening mental state when it shifts toward self-accusation.
when: Designing NPCs whose psychological state changes over time.
why: Changes in a repeated phrase make inner tension readable.

text: A figure who appears at several points in the same events can be a witness, a rival, or a coincidence. Keep that reading open rather than fixing on one early.
when: A figure appears at two or more points where each appearance could be innocent or purposeful
why: Early fixation on one reading can mislead, and several appearances are not yet evidence of a single purpose

text: Repeat a location name or warning across scenes and pay it off with a concrete event later, since repetition without consequence loses force.
when: Using motifs to build foreboding
why: Each recurrence gains weight only when it connects to a new event.

text: A known thief's signature technique can recur across a game world, and a found clue such as an old journal or newspaper can tie it to a present crime.
when: designing a mystery world with repeat offenders

text: Familiar misdirection tricks recur in different cases, so a known pattern can be recognized from its outline.
why: Methods are reused because they have worked before

text: Track a phrase that repeats across a document even when its meaning is unclear, because repetition marks it as significant and later evidence must explain it.
when: a recurring fragment could be a code, location or timing cue
why: repeated wording signals intent even before its sense is known

text: Before calling a witness's statement contradictory, check whether the wording refers to a recurring service or routine rather than the specific day in question.
when: a statement conflicts with a fixed fact and its wording admits two referents
why: routine references renew daily, so they can point to a different occurrence

text: Use a crime's signature when material evidence is ambiguous or has an innocent explanation, and test the suspect's guilt against the psychology the crime shows.
when: material evidence is ambiguous

text: A reused signature can predict the next act, so an investigator can anticipate where the author will strike.
when: A signature recurs across more than one act

text: A timekeeper that sounds at a fixed interval and halts activity each time builds tension toward the final stroke, because the same pause keeps recurring.
when: A recurring sound marks time during an event.
why: A steady rhythm makes the expected moment feel closer with each repetition.

text: A recurring in-game cue such as a song or gesture can be a signal; players who trigger it themselves can trace the contact on the other end.
when: Designing hidden communication in games.
why: Mirroring the cue exposes the receiving party.

text: A recurring event at a similar time each night lets observers learn its pattern and predict when a threat will return.
when: an event repeats on a regular schedule
why: Repetition gives observers a pattern they can anticipate and track.

text: A signature list shows who was willing to sign, not who agreed with the content, so counting names alone can overstate consensus.
Give a recurring thief a signature method, such as a calling card or entry style, that the player learns to recognize across several crimes.
when: Designing a recurring antagonist
why: Recognizable habits let players predict the culprit

text: Give each location a signature debris set, such as sawdust in a workshop or pile fibres in a carpeted room, so the player can match residue to rooms.
Physical clues can be manufactured, so a behavioral signature can test them; but the signature is itself interpretive and can be as subjective as intuition.
when: when physical evidence is in dispute

text: A person may call out a community signal to someone they expect, even before seeing them, so the call reveals whom they were expecting.
when: a victim uses a signal before seeing the person they expect
why: the call was intended for a known recipient

text: A character's unexplained sense of doom, even when rationally rejected, leaves a lasting impression of threat on the audience.
when: when building suspense before a reveal
why: the feeling stays on record and primes the audience to expect danger

text: Witnesses without knowledge of optics or electricity read unusual sights, such as reflections or lightning, through belief rather than natural cause.
when: observing a rare phenomenon with no known explanation
why: the science to explain it was not yet available

text: A recognisable idle behaviour that appears at a key moment, especially when repeated across scenes, is noticed as evidence of what the actor was waiting for.
when: A character performs a distinctive posture or pause matched to a critical event.
why: A repeated gesture linked to the timing of an event invites the observer to connect it to the actor's intent.

text: Signs of deliberate human arrangement include stones placed along edges, debris-free paths, few straight lines and a repeated curve seen from only one or two viewpoints.
Smearing oil or grease on the outside of a lamp's glass cuts its glare, especially on a dusty road, so a dim lamp can be a sign of tampering.
when: when a light is unexpectedly dim

text: An anomaly resisting every obvious explanation should stay open as an unresolved clue, not forced into a convenient theory or discarded; meaning may appear when linked to other evidence.
when: A trace has no obvious explanation.
why: Its significance may only appear when combined with other evidence.

text: Do not abandon a theory at the first detail that cannot be explained at once; test it further with time, patience and research.
when: A suspect's account is smooth and one detail resists explanation.
why: An unexplained detail may hide a flaw that more work can find.

text: Ruling out a line of inquiry does not resolve an unexplained detail, which may return later and deserve a second look.
when: when a discarded line of inquiry leaves a detail unexplained

text: Open with small unexplained events, such as a figure at a window or failing lights, so later events read as a continuation.
when: setting up a mystery before the main crime or threat
why: small anomalies build unease and prepare the audience for escalation

text: Treat a common decorative symbol with no tie to the event as non-evidence; a symbol is clue-worthy only when it connects to the event.
Unexplained odd impressions or hints of darker meaning keep the audience curious and speculating without proof, setting up a later payoff.
Giving each conspirator a partial map marked with a shared sign lets any one of them recover the cache without the others knowing.
Failing to explain why evidence was kept, rather than destroyed, leaves a gap in the theory.
Mistaking a sign for a firm conclusion: a mended object shows attachment to it, not a trait of character.
when: When reading personality from an object's condition
why: One sign supports a narrow inference, not a broad judgment

text: A conflict between an early stated fact and a later event, left unexplained, reads as a mistake rather than as a clue.
why: without an explanation, the audience cannot tell error from intended misdirection

text: A signal works only if the partner enters the room and notices it, and nothing guarantees either.
Assuming a deliberate sign was made by the culprit, when the victim could equally have made it.
Treating strange knowledge, a remark later confirmed by events, or unusual skill as proof of guilt lets suspicion attach to almost any detail.
A sign with no natural explanation cannot be checked, so it should carry only presumptive weight, never serve as proof.
An evidence loss that is never explained reads as a cheat; make sure the lost object or person can be found again.
1) Stage the suspect's routine at a set time. 2) Reproduce the cue yourself. 3) Watch for a response from outside, such as a thrown object.
when: A suspected signal needs confirmation.
why: Mirroring the cue draws out the external response.

text: 1) Identify the reference the speaker relies on. 2) Infer what expectation that reference implies about the speaker. 3) Check whether that expectation explains the speaker's conduct and words.
when: A suspect's words seem out of place for their setting.

text: 1) Log small unexplained incidents as they occur. 2) Revisit the log as new facts arrive. 3) Fit related incidents into a pattern.
when: Minor events seem unrelated at first
why: Small incidents may connect to a larger pattern only once more facts are known

text: 1) Guess the language from its letters and grammar. 2) Test whether the message makes sense in that language. 3) If it does not, try another language, since the message may fit a different one.
when: a signal is in an unknown language

text: 1) Send a controlled signal to the suspects. 2) Record who responds and how. 3) Compare each response with what that person should already know.
when: several suspects could be involved in an event
why: the pattern of responses shows who is informed

text: 1) Keep a record of facts that fit no current theory. 2) Ask the person most likely to explain each fact directly. 3) Compare accounts with third-party remarks. 4) Accept an innocent explanation only after it fits all other facts.
when: when a working theory leaves facts unexplained

text: Make a symbol or signal readable through in-game sources: a codex, a translating character, or an earlier scene teaching it, such as a swung lantern, before it matters.
when: When a symbol or signal must carry meaning for the player later in the game.
why: Meaning must be reachable through in-game sources; learned codes let players interpret the signal when it matters.

text: Withhold a fact from the reader only with some hint; concealment that is never signalled feels like cheating.
Build a code on a category the reader can learn; once the scheme is known, every message in that category becomes readable.
when: a code must be used by people who need to read it
why: a learnable scheme lets its readers decode each message

text: A watcher should respond only to a signal pattern both sides already understand, and may require the signal to be repeated before answering.
when: when a signal could be an accident or a trick

text: Tie each physical sign to a specific plausible cause before using it in a conclusion.
Avoid signals that a watcher could also recognise, since the same cue that reaches a contact can alert the enemy.
when: Choosing a covert signal in a monitored setting.
why: Any signal visible to a contact is also visible to a watcher.

text: Make a signal simple enough to read but unlikely to occur by chance.
Check that a physical sign was read by people with the relevant skill, and that any request for re-examination by skilled examiners was answered.
when: when a bodily sign or physical evidence decides a case
why: untrained or biased readings can mislead

text: Place a signature block or endorsement at the end of a late document that reassigns credit the title or body implied, so a careful reader sees who acted.
Silence or a sudden demeanour shift may signal concealed knowledge that raises stakes, or loyalty, fear or private reasons rather than complicity; weigh which before treating it as proof.
when: when a witness or suspect withholds information or goes quiet about their own movements
why: silence depends on feelings, protecting a shameful secret can outweigh telling the truth, and silence has many possible causes, while a shift in behaviour is read as concealed knowledge

text: Experienced offenders often stay silent, since a defense takes time to build and a careless remark at arrest can hurt them in court.
when: at or after arrest
why: Early statements carry legal risk.

text: Silence signals that nothing is happening, yet it also prevents intervention, so each choice made during silence carries risk.
when: A scene is held quiet while a character waits or observes.
why: Players and audiences read stillness as both safety and danger, which raises stakes.

text: Prolonged exhaustion can make a person sign a false confession, then deny it once the pressure ends.
when: after extended sleep deprivation and forced movement
why: exhaustion overrides the ability to resist a demanded statement

text: A request for silence about specific names or dates signals that the stakes are high.
A character's earlier silence that looked like evasion can gain a clear motive when a late explanation reveals its reason.
when: Writing a reveal that reinterprets a character's behavior.
why: Reinterpreting known behavior makes the reveal feel earned.

text: Weigh whether a secret was volunteered or extracted when assigning blame, since an extracted disclosure implicates the person differently.
when: assessing a revealed motive
why: How a secret was obtained affects how much it counts against the person.

text: When a targeted appeal for a witness finds nothing, treat the failure as a signal to refine the target rather than as proof the witness is absent.
when: a narrow appeal for a witness brings no result
why: the failure narrows what the witness is likely to be

text: Staying silent when a visitor hesitates gives the observer more time to read them.
Extended silence pressures a suspect or opponent to fill the gap, an interrogation or verbal tactic; nervous suspects often reveal more than direct questions draw out.
when: when a suspect is being questioned or both parties are trying to learn what the other knows
why: people tend to fill silence with explanation to end an uncomfortable pause

text: Deliberate silence lets a frightened witness recover composure and gives the interviewer time to organise questions.
when: A witness is frightened or overwhelmed during questioning.
why: Pauses reduce the witness's fright and let the interviewer think, so the next question lands better.

text: A witness's silence can harm the person they are trying to protect, so withholding is not automatically safe.
Too many secrets can make readers feel manipulated, so limit how many facts are kept back.
Record contradictions in signs, sources and behaviour faithfully rather than explaining or smoothing them over early, so careful players can catch them later.
when: when comparing accounts or tracking a person's behaviour
why: early closure can hide evidence that later proves important

text: Record a witness's silence in response to a question as a fact, without treating it as proof of anything.
when: when a witness does not answer a pointed question
why: silence is observable but ambiguous

text: Make a target's attendant or associate the vulnerability the player exploits, rather than the target itself.
when: designing indirect routes to a protected NPC

text: Present facts to an investigator committed to a theory, expecting them to be misread in predictable ways, and use that misreading as a lever.
when: a detective NPC has committed to an early verdict
why: the verdict filters what the investigator accepts

text: Plant a deliberate silence, such as an item no NPC mentions, as a lead rather than a dead end.
when: Designing case files or quest logs with gaps.
why: A gap that players can notice and act on gives them a reason to keep investigating.

text: A silent occupant of a locked room may be asleep, drunk, ignoring noise or incapacitated, so silence alone shows neither unawareness nor refusal.
when: an occupant does not reply after being warned at a locked room, or a lack of reaction to a sound inside a locked room
why: Silence has multiple causes, and an investigator should not assume refusal; several states produce the same lack of response.

text: A refusal marks its subject as sensitive, such as a weapon or wound, and the shape and conditions of the refusal reveal where hidden material lies.
when: a witness declines to answer about a sensitive detail, or a character withholds answers during questioning
why: Refusal often signals the detail is secret or important; refusals and conditional offers signal concealment, so listeners draw conclusions from them.

text: Silence about an event a person would certainly learn of or a witness would normally report is evidence, such as unmentioned widely reported news or a requested visit.
when: only where the event would be widely reported, or a witness fails to mention something memorable such as a requested visit
why: A living person would normally respond to such news; a witness would normally report it, so omission suggests reluctance or refusal.

text: Do not treat a suspect's silence or reaction as an admission unless no other explanation exists and fact-based confirmation supports it.
when: A suspect remains silent under accusation; a witness gives no spoken answer but reacts visibly to a question.
why: Silence and reactions are ambiguous; a fair question must be answerable in fact before evasion carries evidential weight.

text: A silent accused, often read as weak, or a witness refusing to explain, looks as though hiding something; an unanswered charge before an audience weighs heavily.
when: a charge is made in front of an audience
why: Silence is taken as a sign the charge cannot be refuted.

text: A questioner's pause or minimal prompt after an answer or contradiction pressures people to fill the silence with more detail, confidences or concessions.
when: interviewing a motivated source, in a one-sided quiet conversation, after an answer, or after a specific contradiction is put to a witness hiding something
why: People feel pressure to fill silence and elaborate, so a quiet listener often gathers more than an active questioner, and a partial liar may volunteer more.

text: After a disclosure, silence signals the other party's turn; pausing before disclosing a fact invites the listener to fill the silence, revealing what they know.
when: a conversation pauses after one party reveals something; the listener may hold relevant knowledge
why: People read silence as an open turn and feel pressure to fill it, and tend to fill silence with talk.

text: A refusal to answer may mean guilt or protection of someone who holds the secret; a suspect under direct pressure may accept loss of position rather than name them.
when: a witness or suspect is pressed on a sensitive point or refuses a direct question
why: Loyalty to a confederate can outweigh the suspect's own interests, so refusal has more than one meaning.

text: Refusal and stalling end or delay the exchange, but they still reveal what is being withheld, so the questioner can infer from what is left unsaid.
Holding back after stating a goal, and watching the listener's reaction, can make a witness fill the silence and volunteer information they meant to hide.
when: When a witness seems to know more than they are saying.
why: People feel pressure to fill silence, and unguarded remarks can slip out before they are asked about the topic.

text: A witness who refuses to name the cause of tension may be protecting someone, and the refusal itself is information to record.
when: A witness declines to explain a strained relationship.
why: Protecting others can produce refusal without guilt.

text: A silent suspect cannot be cleared, and an audience may read the silence as guilt.
when: a suspect refuses to explain a key time window
why: without an account, an open gap looks like concealment

text: When a person reveals nothing of her past, neighbours know little about her history, and that absence can itself be information, though it may also be deliberate concealment.
when: When witnesses cannot describe a victim's background.
why: Those with secrets may hide their past on purpose, so silence does not mean no connections.

text: Absence of expected follow-up can be read as proof of a convenient explanation rather than as evidence.
when: Expected contact stops after an anomaly

text: Silence or turning away from a question can itself be a tell, since the absence of speech carries the signal.
when: a person is pressed on a topic

text: An offerer may recast a refusal as a wrong done to them, shifting blame and claiming the moral high ground.
A reluctant answer from a witness may be the most important one, and the witness controls what they choose to reveal.
when: A witness withholds details out of delicacy or self-interest
why: Withholding signals content worth checking

text: A suspect who refuses to speak appears guilty, but silence can also protect innocent people from making errors, so it leaves investigators with no information either way.
when: A suspect declines to answer questions during an investigation.
why: Silence is ambiguous and yields no new evidence.

text: Silence in news or reports can be read as a sign of further events, even when nothing is confirmed.
when: A story is missing expected coverage
why: Absence of information invites speculation

text: Silence on one topic may come from loyalty or shame rather than guilt.
A refusal to explain how an item came to be somewhere, or to name its true owner, is a clue to weigh for hidden motive.
A missing reaction counts as evidence only against a clear expectation. A guard animal that stays quiet for a visitor suggests the visitor was known to it.
when: A known reaction should occur for an arrival and does not.
why: Silence means something only when the reaction is normal and reliable for that animal or person.

text: When an expected consequence of a crime fails to appear, such as a sale or report, its absence is evidence about what happened.
when: an expected timeline of reactions is reliable
why: without a reliable expected timeline, silence means nothing

text: When a suspect stays silent, look for a motive and outside support, such as who would be paid to keep quiet.
when: a suspect's silence is unexplained
why: Silence that persists needs a reason.

text: Treat a group's silence as a statement, since saying nothing about an event shapes how others' accounts are received.
when: Witnesses saw an event but say nothing about it.

text: Treat a refusal or a short reply such as 'I do not know' as information: it means the captive is either ignorant or resisting.
Test a witness's claim to have heard nothing against what would normally have been audible; an accepted explanation for silence can hide a contradiction.
when: witness says they heard nothing

text: When a person refuses entry to a place, consider whether they are avoiding being seen there.
when: a household member blocks access to a room

text: A silence in the record, such as no one seeing a person leave a place, is a gap worth treating as the next question.
when: Reviewing an assembled timeline
why: Unexplained gaps point to unexamined movements

text: A pause after an emotional admission can act as an assurance, since both sides expect the next words to be truthful.
when: A witness has just confessed a feeling or strong statement.
why: A quiet pause signals that the next answer will be sincere.

text: A party who stays silent while others speak in a dispute is a clue, since their absence in a timeline can signal reluctance.
when: When a timeline shows some parties acknowledging an issue and others not.
why: Absence within a dated sequence can mark avoidance.

text: Repeated polite non-answers suggest the matter concerns private feeling rather than public fact.
when: A witness evades many questions with courteous but empty replies.
why: Courtesy paired with silence signals a personal reason for withholding information.

text: People who meet danger tend to cry out, so an absent cry where a sound could carry suggests the person met someone they did not fear.
when: When a person vanished in a place where a cry would have been heard.
why: Fear usually produces an audible reaction, so its absence points to a calm encounter.

text: Refusing a proposed condition makes the refuser look suspicious, so a stated safeguard can become a trap the target cannot safely decline.
when: A condition is framed as a reasonable safeguard in front of an audience
why: Declining signals guilt to observers

text: A refusal that comes with a stated threat spells out the stakes within the exchange itself, so both sides understand what is at risk.
when: A proposal is rejected by a party with leverage.
why: Explicit consequences make the refusal a message that can be acted on.

text: An official who stops acting on accusations can become a target, and refusal can draw accusation onto their own family.
Silence can be designed so its meaning depends on the institution interpreting it.
Silence has many causes, such as distance, fear, a sleeping household or illness, so an absence of sound supports a conclusion only after other causes are considered.
when: when reasoning from a lack of noise
why: Several unrelated conditions can produce the same quiet.

text: A witness's failure to hear does not prove an event such as a struggle did not occur; inferring no struggle assumes what the witness could hear.
when: when a witness reports not hearing something
why: Hearing depends on distance, sleep and attention, so absence of report is weak evidence.

text: Do not conclude an event did not occur because a record is silent; records are often incomplete or lost, so compare against surviving series first.
when: concluding that nothing happened because no record exists
why: Records are often incomplete or lost.

text: Reading an accused's refusal to plead or confess as further guilt, especially after the institution has decided, makes denials impossible to disprove.
when: an institution has already decided, or an accused is pressed to confess or affirm a claim
why: Silence is misread when the institution has already decided.

text: Silence that is advised or a deliberate legal tactic, such as a suspect's or witness's, is no testimony and not evidence of guilt.
Taking a silent or uninformed witness as proof that nothing happened is a mistake.
Reading silence as sleep or refusal without testing the assumption leads to wrong conclusions about a person's state.
Reading a refusal through an existing belief lets it confirm a theory already formed, so the test becomes circular.
when: the tester already holds a theory
why: Interpretation is shaped by prior belief

text: A witness's silence is not an alibi, and readers or investigators can misread it.
A silent wait that adds no new information drags and loses the audience's attention.
when: A scene is held in silence for a long stretch.
why: Tension needs new input to keep growing; without it, waiting becomes boredom.

text: A refusal to speak ill of the dead may be sincere, so it alone is not evidence of guilt.
when: A witness declines to criticize the victim.
why: Respect for the dead is a common reason to refuse.

text: A writer's silence about a rival does not prove that the writer worked independently; check the citations themselves.
Refusing to continue an accusatory process can itself be read as guilt, turning accusers against anyone who hesitates.
Treating a suspect's refusal to account for their whereabouts as proof of guilt is a mistake, since the silence may hide something unrelated.
when: when a suspect will not give an alibi
why: concealment can have many causes

text: A witness's first answers can be vague or evasive, and a point may be admitted only after pressing.
Treating a refusal as a denial is a mistake; the listener often reads it as confirmation that something is being hidden.
when: A character declines to answer a question
why: A refusal carries implied information that a flat denial would not

text: Treat a refusal as information: record it, then re-ask a narrower question with the refusal in view.
Do not treat a refusal as proof of guilt; record it as a clue needing explanation, weigh it with other evidence, and move on if nothing else supports it.
when: a witness or suspect refuses a reasonable request or to answer questions
why: Silence has many causes, including hidden personal matters unrelated to the crime, and one reaction rarely settles a question.

text: Record refusals and withheld answers alongside what was said, as facts that shape later suspicion, since what a subject avoids is evidence.
Set a dialogue flag on a refusal, not only a plain 'no', so it unlocks or blocks later branches and an objective, and repeated questioning opens further branches.
when: designing NPC dialogue trees or systems; a silent or defiant NPC, or a tense scene staged around a sensitive subject
why: Refusal then has consequences instead of dead-ending, and refusals can reveal that a hidden matter exists.

text: Do not infer an outcome from silence in a record. An unrecorded verdict or fate is unknown, not implied.
when: When a case ends without a documented result.
why: Records can be incomplete for many reasons unrelated to the outcome.

text: Let a witness refuse or shorten answers when a pressing question seems to expose a secret, and treat the refusal as a clue.
when: A question touches a concealed matter.
why: A refusal signals that the question hit something real, which the player can use.

text: A claimant who refuses to explain their past should fail a verification check, unless the examiner accepts a partial answer.
Do not treat an empty search as clearance for someone who refused to be searched.
when: A person refused a search and the search found nothing.
why: Refusal leaves the person unverified, so an empty result proves nothing about them.

text: Refusing to answer can be read as complicity and draw formal threats, while answering gives up information; the questioner must weigh both costs.
when: when a suspect is pressed to talk

text: Silence in a legal record, such as an unanswered petition, shows that the request was not weighed by the court.
when: when reviewing how a court handled requests
why: omissions in the record reveal gaps in the process

text: A routine register that is brief and never mentions an event can itself be evidence, when compared with its coverage of other events.
Silence in an official record does not prove that nothing happened.
Silently log harmless-seeming dialogue questions so a later clue can be checked against what the NPC said.
In a tense silent exchange where both characters privately think of the same thing, the one who looks away first is read as conceding the point.
when: Two characters share a secret and hold a steady look.
why: Breaking eye contact signals that the holder has lost nerve, so the moment is decided by it.

text: A suspect who shows no visible reaction to an incriminating object may still recognise it, so an absence of emotion is worth noting but is not proof.
when: a suspect is shown an object linked to a crime

text: A suspect who refuses to account for their whereabouts leaves the investigator to supply the answer.
when: when the suspect stays silent under direct questioning

text: A suspect who refuses to defend himself or who admits damaging facts to shield another can look guilty even when innocent.
when: A suspect withholds a fact that protects someone else.
why: Authorities read silence and self-damaging answers as guilt, unless the hidden reason is discovered.

text: Questioners can halt a colleague with a slight gesture, such as a head shake, without any spoken order.
If the accused and the only witness who can confirm the timing both stay silent, neither is fully cleared and the case reduces to one person's word against the other's.
Judge a silent or absent party by their own written words, which can show whether they knew the secret being kept.
when: A witness has said nothing directly about a secret

text: A dog that does not react to a visitor suggests the visitor was someone the dog knew.
when: when an intrusion occurs and a guard animal is present
why: Animals usually bark at strangers.

text: A witness who heard nothing carries little weight if their room lay far from the event, since distance limits what can be heard.
when: the witness claims to have heard nothing
why: distance limits what can be heard

text: A door that opens without noise suggests its hinges were oiled beforehand, so silence can indicate preparation rather than normal use.
Model a silent suspect as a game state that only other evidence can break.
Strongly shared beliefs can treat disagreement as heresy, silencing sceptics; unvoiced doubt lets rumours grow unchallenged, so early voiced doubt can stop an escalating accusation.
when: when a community strongly holds a belief or an accusation starts to spread
why: social pressure discourages doubters, and silent doubt leaves rumours unchecked

text: Assuming a silent room holds an empty or sleeping occupant, without a timed check, can mislead the investigation.
A silent cross-examination does not concede that the evidence is sound.
At official premises, observe and collect information without commenting, since comments can reveal your hypotheses.
Silent listening draws more from a witness with a motive to talk, but direct questioning is faster when a fact is needed now from a hostile witness.
A silent witness builds suspense but delays the clue, while a witness who speaks plainly delivers information quickly but offers less mystery.
when: When deciding how fast a story must deliver a clue.

text: Treat a silhouette, shadow, or single sighting as evidence of presence, not identity; name the person only after a clearer view or a second check.
when: when a figure is seen only as a shadow or outline, or briefly in poor light
why: A shape alone cannot distinguish one person from another; a resembling silhouette can belong to someone else.

text: Observers viewing a shadow or silhouette at distance see only outline and profile, so a similar figure can be mistaken for another person.
when: The observer sees shape through a screen, blind, or at distance.
why: Silhouettes convey shape and profile but not facial features.

text: Make NPCs identifiable by silhouette at range, such as a distinctive cloak or gait, while close-up verification of the face remains needed.
Partial clues, such as build, clothing, or a witness's silhouette-only sighting, narrow suspects without naming one; the player must combine them to identify a person.
when: Designing witness clues with limited detail.
why: Partial clues reward combining them with other evidence.

text: A single sighting is a weak basis for a long watch, and a watch that one message can break is fragile.
Let an item or NPC leave a recognizable scent, and add masking scents as deliberate cover-ups the player must see through.
when: Designing scent-based clues in a generated dungeon.

text: Give each scent profile to only a few NPCs, so each scent test is a real narrowing step rather than a dead end.
when: Designing scent-based deduction in a dungeon.

text: A stealth or deduction game can use scent as a clue type, where the player sniffs NPCs or objects and the game matches the profile against a list.
when: Designing a deduction mechanic.

text: Make a figure seen only as a silhouette identifiable by matching its outline to a known character, so the player must recognise the shape.
when: When designing identification challenges in level content
why: Outline recognition turns observation into a puzzle

text: Speakers often give a brief account of an event that closes the topic, leaving out motive and detail.
when: a speaker wants to avoid further questions
why: A short version discourages follow-up.

text: Observers tend to accept a simple remaining explanation once every alternative has been closed off.
when: all other routes of an apparent impossibility have been ruled out

text: One theory holds that simple, concrete details catch a cunning person more often than complex traps do, because the person prepares for complexity.
When an unexplained figure appears at a place, the simplest candidate consistent with the records usually beats the most dramatic identity.
Ruling out the simplest explanation first, such as an agency allocation, makes the remaining anomaly stronger evidence of deliberate action.
Treating the simplest explanation as proven is an error; simplicity is a guide to likelihood, not certainty.
1) Start from the most probable explanation. 2) Question everyone who knows the event most closely. 3) Compare their accounts. 4) Consider supernatural causes only after human causes are tested.
when: An event could be human or supernatural
why: The probable explanation is tested before rarer ones.

text: Prefer the simpler explanation when it fits evidence, not rejecting it merely for being neat; yet a crime looking simple and above-board deserves suspicion, since culprits betray themselves covering tracks.
when: Prefer simple when a complex explanation is being built around scene details; suspect simple-looking crimes when they appear above-board
why: Clever reasoning invents elaborate accounts when a plain one is available; culprits usually betray themselves while covering their tracks.

text: Sincerity does not guarantee accuracy: an honest witness can omit, misremember or misperceive details, so check their account against other facts.
why: Honesty and accuracy must be assessed separately; sincere witnesses can omit or misremember details.

text: A quoted fragment without its surroundings can mislead readers into a meaning the speaker never intended, so check dates and surrounding text before accepting it.
why: Missing context invites wrong interpretation; isolated quotations can imply a sequence the surrounding text contradicts.

text: A witness's sincere belief, including a claimed persecution, does not confirm the reported event occurred; sincerity reflects belief, not evidence.
why: Sincerity reflects belief, not evidence.

text: Vividness, detail, confidence or sincerity does not establish accuracy; a witness's interpretation must not replace observable facts. Check accounts against independent evidence.
when: weighing any account, memory or testimony
why: Vividness and certainty do not establish accuracy.

text: A guarded party who hears a partly wrong accusation often corrects the wrong half, which reveals what they already knew.
when: Confronting someone with a partial and partly wrong claim
why: They assume the interviewer already knows the other half

text: A person may lie to avoid being linked to a crime they fear being blamed for, even when the lie hides an innocent act.
when: A suspect had been near a crime scene.
why: Fear of being blamed makes an innocent act look suspicious, so people conceal it.

text: Finding an ordinary source for a claim does not prove the witness is lying; it only shows the knowledge did not require a supernatural explanation.
Distinguish original editions from later reprints, and note which originals have become rare, when judging a source's reliability.
A witness can be accurate on key facts while padding the account with irrelevant detail, so separate the core facts from the embellishment.
when: when a testimony is long and digressive
why: Accurate core facts can make irrelevant or wrong padding seem credible

text: Judge a participant's sincerity separately from whether their conduct was mistaken, since both can be true at once.
When a character's grievance sits beside professed devotion, the audience must judge where sincere feeling ends and a hidden motive begins.
when: A character claims affection while resenting obligations
why: Mixed signals keep the question open

text: A victim's correspondence or relationship log can carry motive hints that players piece together over time.
Separate characters who sincerely act on false information from those who hold the facts, since their demeanour may differ.
When a witness adds a step to explain an earlier point, the new step may clash with another part of the account.
when: A witness corrects or extends an earlier statement under questioning.
why: Each added detail creates new claims that can conflict.

text: Treat a witness's honesty and the certainty of what was decided as separate questions; an honest witness can still be wrong about the decision.
when: a witness is trusted but reports only what was said
why: Sincerity concerns the speaker, while certainty concerns the decision.

text: When a questioner remarks on a disguise detail, fold the remark into a plausible explanation that the persona could give.
when: when a questioner comments on a prop or detail

text: Once a corrected sequence shows two events were nearly simultaneous, a person's belief about their own chances of success can change.
when: A reconstructed timeline contradicts what the person assumed.
why: The revealed order changes which actions were possible, altering their sense of control.

text: An agent who feeds false information while believing it serves a cause can drift into a confused, double position between truth and deception.
when: when judging a character who seems to act a part

text: Confidence and visible distress are not verification; sincerity does not establish what a witness perceived, and a private sworn observation stays uncorroborated.
A suspect's frankness, tears or sincere-sounding confession can be a performance shaped by self-interest; judge the explanation by its content, not apparent sincerity.
when: when weighing a suspect's account or confession
why: Sincerity of tone does not guarantee an accurate account of motive.

text: Sincerity measures conviction, not correctness: a sincere person may hold false beliefs, flawed reasoning or be a poor judge of what they report, yet act with integrity.
when: when judging a character or witness who believes something false
why: Honest belief can coexist with flawed reasoning.

text: A party can take a witness's remark out of context and use it to back a claim the witness never made.
when: Hearing a witness quoted in a dispute

text: A public apology may be sincere or self-serving, and the two are hard to tell apart.
Emotional hints from a witness may be sincere or self-protective, so they need checking before they shape an investigator's theory.
why: the motives behind a hint are often mixed

text: Believing a witness from intuition is not evidence; a sense that someone is sincere must be tested against proof.
A witness who talks freely is not necessarily accurate; the account may be vague, repetitive or distorted.
Dismissing a route because it was absent at an earlier check. The scene may have changed since, so recheck.
when: When a route was checked at an earlier time
why: Someone may have altered the scene after the first check.

text: Information about a room's layout from one person's memory may be outdated, especially if it is more than a year old, so verify before relying on it.
Treating a sincere witness as accurate ignores physical limits such as distance or walls that restrict what they could have perceived.
when: A witness is sincere but positioned poorly
why: Honest testimony still fails when the witness lacked access to the event.

text: Older textbook rules for cooling and rigidity can mislead an expert, so estimates should not lean on them uncritically.
why: rules of thumb may not fit the case

text: Confidence about an object's origin from general knowledge is not a confirmed link to a particular person.
An old photograph may not show a subject's current appearance, so it can mislead identification.
Guessing a person's appearance from cosmetic shades is weak inference and should be treated as opinion.
Clues that depend on one habit or one witness are not independent, so counting them separately creates false confidence.
Assuming an accusation is sincere ignores the accuser's motive when a land or family dispute gives them one.
An old title can outlast the office that gave it, so a title can mislead about current authority or real wealth.
A clause removed from a later revision can still be quoted as if it remained in the newer version.
when: The source exists in several editions or revisions.
why: Earlier wording looks current when revision history is ignored.

text: Confidence drawn from one's own inspection is not a test; an untested conclusion can be wrong.
when: Assessing whether a concealment succeeded.
why: Self-assessment lacks an independent check.

text: Reading too much into omissions, or confusing a writer's habits with their intent, is a common error, especially when the reader is hostile to the writer.
when: when interpreting a writer's omissions or habits
why: The reader's feelings shape what they notice and how they interpret it

text: A sincere believer may notice contrary facts less, not more, because the belief already explains them away.
when: a person's conviction is strong and shared
why: A fixed premise filters out evidence it cannot explain.

text: 1) Record the original's details precisely. 2) Compare the item presented as found against that record. 3) Note any difference in detail.
when: provenance of an item is disputed and an exact original exists
why: precise originals expose swaps

text: 1) Accept a partial payment first. 2) Raise the offered amount. 3) Watch how the client responds to judge seriousness.
Judge a witness's sincerity separately from their account's truth; tone and sincerity are not tests of truth, since sincere-sounding accounts can be wrong or false.
when: when weighing testimony
why: Sincerity and accuracy are independent.

text: A single confession, even freely given, is not proof; without independent checks it remains one party's version, since sincerity does not establish accuracy.
when: A confession is the only source offered for a motive, or a witness volunteers history unprompted.
why: A self-serving speaker shapes the record, and honest delivery can rest on wrong memory or motive.

text: Ask what was actually done or said by the original source rather than relying on a summary given by someone in between.
Unrefuted does not mean true in every detail; separate an account's core claim from its exact wording before trusting either.
A red herring must be correctable by evidence the player can later find, because an uncorrected false lead leaves players feeling cheated.
when: Designing a misleading clue or suspect in a mystery.
why: Players accept misdirection only when it is later explained and resolved.

text: Correct imprecise wording in testimony, separating what was seen from what was identified, because loose phrasing can mislead later.
Use transcription errors or damaged records as in-world clues, such as a misnumbered page that conceals a timeline.
Witnesses may be sincere yet mistaken, so their honesty should not be taken as proof that their account is accurate.
when: when assessing a witness whose belief drives their account
why: sincere belief can distort perception as much as deliberate lying distorts testimony

text: Do not rely on a single found object or shared detail; treat the link as provisional until other evidence confirms it.
when: A lone object or shared detail appears to implicate or link a person.
why: One matching detail can coincide without a real connection.

text: A single physical clue, such as powder, can fit several explanations or event sequences; do not read too much into it alone.
No single clue should carry the case: it can mislead, and another trace may exonerate its suspect, so test each clue and treat it as one of several.
when: Building the evidence chain for a mystery.
why: If one clue fails to land, the solution collapses.

text: Fixating on one vivid clue blocks other lines of thought.
Making one sealed document the only clue makes the story depend on a single object, so losing or missing it stalls the whole mystery.
when: when designing a withheld-information reveal
why: All progress rests on one item.

text: Treating one reaction as proof of a hidden trait leads to a wrong conclusion; independent confirmation is still needed.
when: When interpreting a suspect's response to a test
why: A single reaction can have several causes, so it is only a lead until corroborated.

text: Let a clue depend on one assumption the player must test, rather than stating the conclusion outright.
when: designing a clue that points toward a suspect
why: A testable assumption lets the player reach the conclusion through their own reasoning.

text: A theory built on one person's movements stays unverified until independent evidence supports it.
A single shared habit is weak evidence easily dismissed as coincidence; treat it as a lead to test, since many people share the same habit.
when: Only one habit links a suspect to a witness's description

text: Do not assume motive from one relationship without checking the others, since a single tie may mislead.
when: A motive appears to rest on one relationship
why: Other ties may explain the act better or rule the suspect out

text: If one perpetrator is assumed for linked events, a suspect with a sound alibi for one event may be eliminated from the others as well.
when: Several crimes are assumed to share a culprit.
why: Presence elsewhere during one event excludes the same person from the other.

text: If re-entry needed a key and only one person could open the door, a missing key suggests a single actor did the act.
A single-killer mystery pins the death first on an outside rival, then on a trusted suspect, and surfaces the real killer only in the final stretch.
Attributing the whole plot or event sequence to one suspect hides other participants' roles and distorts the account; check each participant's part separately.
Relying on a single watcher, or on the guardian's own presence alone, creates one point of failure.
A theory that explains every fact through one motive can fit many people, so it may point confidently at the wrong one.
Assuming one beneficiary behind every accusation misses the wider pattern in which many officials and tradespeople each profited.
Treating greed as the only motive misses feuds and gossip. Accusations often have mixed motives that must be weighed together.
Do not treat one suspicious act as proof of intent or guilt; require a sequence of acts pointing the same way, since one act can misdirect an investigation.
when: When deciding whether a suspect's behavior justifies action.

text: Settling on one untested explanation stops the search for alternatives, makes rivals harder to raise and can hide contradictory evidence; keep rivals open, since without them no test separates causes.
when: An examiner has chosen a cause before running any tests.
why: Without rival hypotheses, no test can tell the competing causes apart.

text: One reproduction or replacement with one person proves little, especially when reactions vary between individuals; repeat tests across several people before confirming a theory about behaviour.
when: A re-enactment is used to confirm a theory about a person's behaviour.
why: Individual variation means one run cannot guarantee the same outcome.

text: A single stop or departure from routine reveals little; read several small actions together and test it against other evidence before concluding about plans.
why: One act can have innocent causes.

text: A single search or empty storage place proves little; absence conclusions need a thorough search, and each new arrival or visitor can change what should be checked.
when: When concluding an item is missing from a place.
why: One unchecked location may still hold it.

text: A torn or missing page alone is not conclusive, since it may be an ordinary lapse; read it alongside other evidence before concluding.
when: when a physical gap is the only clue
why: gaps can have innocent causes

text: Separate the one checkable fact a rambling witness gives from the remarks around it, and trust that fact more than the rest.
Eliminating one mechanism does not prove that the whole class of similar explanations is wrong.
If one observer covers the only route in or out, every movement must pass that point, so the observer's blind spots decide whether an alibi holds.
when: When a building or area has one controlled route
why: A single checkpoint constrains all movement through it

text: Keep a supernatural explanation available but partial, so it excuses events without settling them.
when: A curse or supernatural cause is offered within a mystery.
why: Leaving the explanation unsettled keeps the player weighing mundane and supernatural readings.

text: A chain of plausible inferences can fail at one link, and a plausible alternative can neutralize a clue; test each link against independent evidence before trusting the whole sequence.
when: A reconstruction relies on several connected inferences, or a suspect offers a plausible alternative.
why: One wrong step can invalidate later conclusions that depend on it.

text: Declaring a case solved on one damning or matching link, such as past record, fingerprint match or sudden departure, skips how the trace came to be where it was found.
why: A single link can make a chain of reasoning feel complete when it is not.

text: Acting on a single broken edge without further checks risks a wrong conclusion about how the damage occurred.
when: a damage site is used to decide what happened
why: one feature may be misleading

text: Noticing one error, such as a spelling mistake, can cause the more telling features of a document to be overlooked.
when: Reading a document for clues about its origin
