why: A single salient error draws attention away from the full pattern

text: A single wrong detail may be chance; the argument for knowledge rests on several errors pointing in the same direction.
A route that seems to exclude one candidate may still permit another, so test every candidate rather than only the first.
A trapped room with only one exit invites physical struggle when the target is cornered, so the confrontation can turn violent.
why: With no other route, a cornered target has little to lose by fighting.

text: A single inspection of each route can miss a route built to look sealed. Recheck routes that appear closed.
when: When eliminating entry routes in a sealed room
why: Deliberately disguised openings can pass a quick check.

text: Assuming the cover story is the only version in circulation is risky, since other versions may exist.
when: when an event has been described to several people
why: other accounts may contradict the cover story

text: One answer to a control question is a single sample, not proof of candour or guilt.
when: interpreting a control question
why: one response can be coincidence

text: Treating a short gap as the only possible gap can miss other opportunities, such as an act done on an earlier day.
when: when a timeline seems to allow only one window
why: Acts can occur over many days, not only in one short interval.

text: Concentrating on one line of enquiry, such as the victim's private life, can produce repeated dead ends while other possibilities stay unexplored.
Supernatural and human causes can be stacked in one explanation, so each layer must be tested separately.
when: An explanation mixes a supernatural cause with a human one

text: Do not rest a timeline on a single estimate when other evidence is available.
when: Building a timeline
why: One estimate can be off, and corroboration reduces error.

text: Do not treat one estimate, such as rigor timing, as settling the time of death.
when: Fixing a time from a single physical sign
why: Rigor timing varies, so the estimate is a range

text: Avoid resting the entire plot on one misleading clue; attentive readers who spot the gap will judge the story unfair.
Agree on one story and tell it plainly to every audience, adding no embellishment.
when: when facing repeated questioning
why: a consistent, plain account is hard to attack

text: Do not treat a single disagreement as proof of forgery. Confirm it against the original first.
when: when a record conflicts with one account
why: A single conflict can have other explanations.

text: A single incident can lead an observer to revise their reading of a person's feelings, so one event can reshape the whole picture of their character.
One past incident can become decisive character evidence, and a reputation built on it spreads through gossip and hints rather than fresh observation.
when: a community forms a verdict on a person
why: rumour repeats the incident without new observation

text: Do not treat one involuntary reaction (flinch, startle, probe response) as proof of guilt or future conduct; fear, grief, embarrassment, or innocence can cause it. Seek corroboration.
when: the reaction or behaviour is the only evidence available
why: the reaction does not identify its own cause

text: Do not confirm one striking clue or test result, such as an animal's response, until other facts corroborate it; a lone observation may be incomplete or mistaken.
when: one dramatic clue points to a named culprit, or an identity test yields one striking result
why: one observation can mislead, so corroboration is needed

text: Give the player one pointed question with clear options to an NPC that confirms a hidden state, such as a key holder or changed routine, not a long dialogue tree.
when: designing dialogue where the player must pursue a line of inquiry
why: clear options keep the questioning moving

text: A single recalled phrase is weak evidence, so use it as a lead that directs inquiry rather than as proof of motive.
Depending on a single person to carry a reveal is fragile, because a delay or absence can make the reveal fail.
when: Planning how a reveal will reach its audience.
why: One point of failure can stop the reveal from happening.

text: A quiet reaction has many causes, so infer hiding only from a surrounding pattern of behavior, not from one silence.
Do not treat one emotional moment as proof of inner life; it is a hint to be weighed with other evidence.
Singed hair or scorching around a wound indicates firing from close range, which bounds how far away the shooter could have been.
when: when a wound shows signs of burning or singeing
why: residue and heat effects fall off with distance

text: A partial seal impression may carry no trace of origin, so physical evidence on an anonymous note can lead nowhere.
when: When an anonymous note has a seal or stamp that is incomplete.
why: Partial marks often lack the features needed to identify a source.

text: Treat a route inferred from one object as a hypothesis until other traces confirm it.
A single trace fragment is not proof; it only suggests a place that must be checked.
Do not treat one unguarded look as proof of a hidden motive; it is only a clue to weigh with others.
A single mark can support a reconstructed sequence of events, using its size, thickness and border to infer how it was made.
when: no witness saw the events

text: Put the decisive proof in a single controllable artifact, such as a negative, a measured photograph or a footprint, so the evidence is clear and checkable.
Identifying a person or origin from one feature, such as foot size, costume, planted item, dialect or haircut, misleads; confirm only with several independent matching features.
when: when identifying a person or confirming a suspect
why: Matching needs multiple independent features.

text: One out-of-character item is not proof on its own; it needs independent confirmation before it is treated as evidence.
A single trace can support several stories, so test each candidate story against the other traces.
A single memorable feature can dominate a witness description and mislead searchers who look only for it.
when: Using a description to find a suspect
why: Striking details draw attention away from others

text: Treating one key position as proof ignores exceptions, such as a private room sometimes locked from inside by ordinary choice.
why: Household arrangements vary, and mixed arrangements weaken any general rule.

text: An innocent cause can explain mud or a wet boot, so a physical trace needs a second source.
Building a full profile from one trace overreaches; a single worn surface supports only a probable diagnosis.
when: Drawing conclusions from a single physical feature.
why: One feature rarely determines a condition, symptoms, and behavior together.

text: A behavioural habit proves nothing on its own; it needs a matching moment in time and a second independent observation to count as evidence.
why: Habits are common, so one match can be coincidence.

text: A single trace, such as a hair, smell, mud or wet boot, has several possible sources; confirm it with reference data or a second independent trace before concluding.
Do not build a conclusion or signature from one suggestive detail or sign that several explanations could fit; check each link on its own before relying on it.
when: when a small sign could support more than one explanation
why: Ambiguous signs need corroboration before they support a conclusion.

text: A confident conclusion from one trace can be wrong; when its conditions are disputed and no further evidence is in hand, hedge and promise further proof rather than overclaim.
why: Overclaiming a contested trace invites easy rebuttal.

text: Do not treat a single mark as conclusive without checking it against records.
Do not treat a single unusual trace as proof of guilt; a trace with an innocent cause needs corroboration before anyone is accused.
A single missing item from a set is a meaningful gap only if it is known that a full set existed.
Do not treat a single trace as proof of an absent person's identity or traits.
when: concluding about a missing person from a scene
why: one misread object can mislead the whole profile

text: Do not infer that a scene was staged from one oddity alone; require other evidence before drawing that conclusion.
when: A single detail seems arranged.
why: One unusual detail can have an innocent explanation.

text: Do not treat a single trace as proof; build a case from several pieces of evidence.
when: When one object seems to point decisively to a person or event.
why: A single trace may have an ordinary explanation.

text: A matching trace can confirm a reconstruction when its position fits the proposed action; an admitted physical trace may reveal a sealed room, while other traces need a second trace.
A key fact or alibi resting on one witness stays provisional and unbacked until independent proof arrives, especially if that witness is missing or unreliable.
when: When one witness is the only link to an alibi or key identifying fact.
why: Single sources can be wrong, lying, or absent.

text: A single deposition or vivid witness account is not proof or corroboration; the witness's mood and interests can shape what they report.
Do not read one brief or distant observation as proof of motive or purpose; aim and intent are inferred, not confirmed.
when: A lone sighting is interpreted.
why: Brief distant views are easily misread; one observation cannot establish intent.

text: A timed account from one witness can hold suspicion on one suspect and leave other candidates unexamined.
A dying or unwell witness may be the only source of a critical fact, so their testimony can be lost before it is checked.
A single witness backing a dramatic claim should be treated as unconfirmed until other evidence supports it.
when: One testimony supports an extraordinary claim
why: A lone account, however vivid, lacks independent support

text: A case built on inference can be overturned by one credible first-hand account.
Before accepting a strange claim from a single witness, check whether an ordinary cause such as intoxication, injury, fear or known capability explains it.
when: A supernatural or unusual claim rests on one witness
why: Witness state and ordinary causes often account for the report

text: A single sight-line from a vantage point supports a claim about what was seen but cannot establish a location on its own.
A timeline resting on one witness for a whole day or time block is unverified and fragile; a second, independently checkable source makes it much harder to break.
why: No second source exists to check the account.

text: Treating one matching cue or identification as decisive closes inquiry early; a skilled challenge can undo it unless other evidence supports it.
when: An identity question carries significant consequences.
why: Stopping at one matching feature skips checks that could reveal a mismatch.

text: Relying on one witness with a stake, such as a grudge or self-protection, distorts the picture even when they supply a useful fact.
when: A single witness with a stake supplies the only key detail or key source for understanding events.
why: Self-interest, grudge and self-defense shape what a witness reports and omits.

text: When the only witness is the one reporting a private perception, the claim cannot be tested, so its reliability cannot be judged.
A single visual detail, such as facial hair, is weak identification because it can be false or worn as disguise. Seek more durable marks.
when: when identifying a watcher

text: A witness's recall of a single evening may be wrong, however clear it feels to them.
Taking a judgement of someone's character from a single old memory as settled is a mistake; test it against other evidence.
When the only witness who could confirm a document disappears, officials may treat the matter as closed, though the claim remains unverified.
A single watcher in a crowded or complex space can easily lose the subject.
A detail noticed by one character can have an innocent explanation, so check the object's history before drawing a conclusion.
A reveal that skips the early impressions leaves the audience unable to see why the earlier theory was wrong.
Each impression needs a plausible explanation; a deep mark alone does not prove a posture, so check it against other traces.
A single observation with no baseline proves little on its own.
why: Without an earlier state there is nothing to compare against.

text: A plant seen by only one witness depends entirely on that witness's reliability and view, so decide in advance how well they could see it.
why: One observer is a single point of failure for the clue's validity.

text: A watch drawn from prominent people can name its own rivals and neighbors as suspects, a bias that the system itself does not correct.
when: Watchers are chosen by standing rather than neutrality.

text: A last-seen time from one witness is a single data point and may be wrong; confirm it before building on it.
A clue seen by only one character, and not by the person it concerns, is easy to lose.
when: A clue is witnessed by someone other than its subject

text: 1) Record the observer's distance, eyesight, lighting and when they began attention. 2) Identify core facts repeated consistently. 3) Discount details shaped by fear or self-interest. 4) Check core facts against a second independent source.
when: When a clue rests on one witness.
why: Viewing conditions limit what a sincere witness can perceive.

text: Before accepting a key clue from one witness, weigh their state, fears and expectations; do not treat an agitated witness's unverified sighting as settled.
when: When a key clue rests on one witness.

text: Do not establish an unseen act or guilt on one witness's account or on accusers' testimony alone; require a plurality of witnesses and further evidence before conviction.
why: Accusers' accounts can be mistaken or can feed on each other.

text: Do not rely on one partial observer for what was said or who started an exchange; check the sequence against other sources and show what they missed.
when: Evaluating an eyewitness report from a distance, behind a barrier, or with partial access.
why: Distance, angle and missed sound limit what one observer can know; partial knowledge misleads.

text: Flag a clue only one character can perceive as unconfirmed and pair it with a player-checkable trace, such as a second witness, physical trace, or unfakeable test.
when: When designing a clue that depends on a single witness, trigger or perception such as a vision.
why: No one else can test the detail.

text: Do not treat one witness as decisive or rely on their description when it conflicts with physical evidence; check each account against traces left at the scene.
Avoid relying on one costume when the target has reason to suspect outside agents.
Never let one sighting be the whole case; a crime must be established on independent grounds in addition to identification.
when: when deciding whether an identification is sufficient
why: A single report, however sincere, can be wrong and needs corroboration.

text: Treat a single anecdote about a physical trait as unconfirmed; verify it through the object itself or a second independent source.
when: Using a secondhand report to support an identity claim.
why: One account can be mistaken or incomplete, so corroboration is needed before relying on it.

text: Maps show layout but not ground traces, may be outdated or incomplete, and modern ones may misrepresent period routes. A map cannot replace a site inspection.
when: when relying on a map, especially to infer a historical route

text: A memorial is placed for visibility or convenience, so it can stand near an event without marking its exact location.
when: A marker is offered as the site of a death or burial
why: Placement follows practical factors, not necessarily the precise spot

text: 1) Check the whole space, including books, cupboards, boxes and clothing pockets. 2) Note which places were disturbed. 3) Use the pattern to map how far the search went.
Meet where observers' sightlines do not reach, such as a third party's rooms reached by a separate route.
when: a covert meeting must avoid being observed
why: A watcher can only report what falls within their line of sight

text: A skill that few people can perform narrows the set of likely owners of a trace to a small group.
A person's abilities, such as speaking a language, can reveal where they have lived or traveled.
when: Deciding who came from where in a story
why: Acquired skills reflect past experience.

text: A list of skills, even deep ones, rarely reveals a single unifying role. The designer must supply the purpose that ties the skills together.
when: when a character's skills seem to have no common calling
why: Skills alone do not imply one role

text: Let a skilled culprit leave a few traces for the investigator to find, since a flawless act removes the tension of the investigation.
when: when writing a clever antagonist's crime
why: Players need something to test in order to feel the challenge

text: Friendliness or goodwill can conceal hidden opinions or intent to harm, so don't take a friendly witness's account at face value or treat goodwill as proof of innocence.
when: Assessing testimony from a sympathetic witness
why: Friendliness can conceal a shared opinion that colours the account; flattery can conceal intent to harm.

text: A forced laugh after a calm answer can betray fear of discovery that the spoken answer hides.
when: the investigator is caught observing the witness's surroundings

text: Track forms of address in dialogue as a clue-bearing record of relationships; a formal title in place of a given name usually signals emotional distance.
when: Reading personal correspondence or dialogue.
why: Forms of address encode the speaker's relationship to the person named.

text: Use an unexpected foreign word spoken by a character as a flag that something in the scene is not what it seems.
A rule forbidding the accused to look at accusers makes any glance an offence, so ordinary behavior becomes apparent proof of guilt.
Give a friendly NPC a brief tell, such as a hard glance after a warm greeting, and let the player decide whether to trust it.
Let a friendly NPC's gaze repeatedly settle on one object or door, a small tell hinting at a second motive that a later check can reveal.
when: Writing a helpful character who has an undisclosed agenda.
why: Players who noticed the tell gain an advantage when the motive surfaces.

text: Offices that conferred standing included minister, deacons, parish clerk, constable, magistrates and military officers.
A shared office's push to gain its house and land may be read as a bid for influence as a landholder, not simple greed.
When a document names an office instead of a person, find the holder from dates and circumstances rather than from the title alone.
In a small community, hostility often has several sources, so one visible grudge does not settle a case.
An organisation that depends on one hidden leader may collapse if that leader is removed.
when: Analyzing a group structured around a central figure.
why: Centralized control means the group has few functioning substitutes for its leader.

text: Personal or social details may or may not bear on the crime, so check their relevance before acting on them.
An NPC's social network can reveal relationships, debts or grudges that the player can use as motives.
when: Designing NPC relationship systems that feed investigation.
why: Relationship data becomes actionable motive information.

text: A spreading accusation cascade halts trade, drives people to flee, and can reach respected members of the community, since no one feels safe.
Investigators may hesitate before powerful suspects, letting high-status culprits escape while smaller suspects are caught.
when: when a suspect's rank is high
why: Social pressure can weaken the willingness to act on the same evidence.

text: Trusting a witness because of social standing rather than checking the times they give.
Social standing can push investigators toward hasty conclusions.
Make an honest skeptic's doubts partly correct; a skeptic written as plainly foolish makes the misdirection unfair.
when: Writing an expert who doubts a suspect
why: Players need a fair chance to side with the skeptic.

text: Model a solution as required links, such as each party's location, whether they met, and whether there was time to act, which the player must supply before the case closes.
when: When designing or analyzing a mystery's answer or win condition.
why: Breaking the answer into facts makes its gaps visible; explicit links give the player a checklist and make the final step feel earned.

text: Reveals not backed by clues the player has already met read as tricks, so make every solution path rest on seen clues and replay key evidence in a final sequence.
Solutions are usually explained after the fact, often by a detective to a witness, using available proof: a document, a physical trap, a reconstruction, or a confession.
why: A clear explanation tied to available proof resolves the case for the player.

text: Resolve mysteries by inference from physical objects rather than by confession; a confession may follow, but the proof should not depend on it.
Layers that rest on one contested fact all fall when that fact fails, so the whole case collapses with a single weak link.
when: a case is built from stacked inferences
why: the layers share one foundation

text: Treating one small detail as proof of a conclusion overreaches, since trifles support other conclusions rather than standing alone.
when: Drawing conclusions from minor physical details
why: A single small detail can have innocent explanations and needs corroboration

text: Presenting a solution as a list of conclusions, without the steps that led to it, leaves the audience unable to check it.
when: when writing a reveal
why: unverifiable conclusions cannot be trusted or tested

text: 1) Walk the listener through the reasoning in order. 2) Tie each step to a fact the listener has already seen. 3) Let the listener check each step. 4) Hand over results to those who must act.
when: an official team must act on the reasoning

text: 1) Gather the group at a set place and time. 2) State the frame of the problem. 3) Present reasoning in a clear sequence. 4) Test each item with a pause before its result. 5) Stop before the final step to show the outcome, then name the culprit.
when: The verdict depends on checks the audience can follow
why: Visible steps and pauses make the accusation feel earned

text: 1) State the stumbling block that rules out the obvious suspect. 2) Name the anomaly in the evidence. 3) Infer the hidden actor from the anomaly. 4) Explain the motive and means.
when: when delivering a final reveal
why: ordered steps let the audience follow and verify each inference

text: Outline the solution's skeleton before placing decoys, so the hidden answer stays consistent as red herrings are added.
Check the inner edge of a sole separately from the rest of the shoe, since that area carries different wear and residue.
Give each case an official solution complete enough that a single hidden detail reframes the existing evidence.
when: authoring a mystery whose twist must recontextualize clues
why: A reversal only lands if the first reading was coherent and the new detail explains what it had left unresolved.

text: A bluff finale closes the case quickly by provoking a confession but leaves no legal proof; a proof-based finale is slower but gives players a verifiable solution.
when: Choosing how a mystery resolves when evidence is incomplete
why: Forcing a reaction ends the case quickly, but players may feel the solution is unverified.

text: A hidden person can produce rapping or knocking sounds with a body part, such as a foot, from behind a concealing screen.
Sound-based inference is unreliable when sounds are masked or many people arrive at once.
Build dread with repeated sensory cues such as heat, smell, pale light, and silence, so the player senses a threat before it is shown.
when: Preparing a player for a danger that has not yet appeared.
why: Recurring sensations accumulate into an expectation of threat.

text: Symptoms that ease when a subject is away and return on exposure point to a source inside the environment they left.
when: Locating a recurring cause in a known environment

text: Relying on one sense can miss cues from another; combine what is heard, smelled and seen where possible.
A volatile poison can leave no trace in the body and carry a smell that is easy to miss, so a death can appear natural.
when: Routine examination finds no cause of death
why: Standard examination does not test for volatile substances, so the method stays hidden.

text: Mark elapsed time with everyday sounds such as shutters opening, footsteps and clock strikes, so the countdown feels present.
when: when a countdown must feel present

text: Undamaged clothing on a victim suggests they were taken by surprise rather than in a struggle.
when: Reading a body's physical condition at a crime scene

text: A witness's account of when an item was left and collected fixes the window in which it was unattended.
Soft ground that holds only expected marks suggests nobody else used that route.
when: when the ground is intact

text: Traces such as dampness, overgrowth, or a dropped item show that time has passed and a place has been unused, but not who passed through.
when: When estimating how long a location has been empty.
why: Wear accumulates with time, independent of who visited.

text: Calls for help, a sudden scream of an animal, and an abrupt silence each raise tension in a scene where sight is limited.
A fresh coat laid over still-wet oil dries unevenly, leaving dull and glossy patches that expose a recent overpainting.
when: a new coat is applied over paint that has not fully dried
why: parts of the surface set at different rates depending on the wetness beneath

text: A sound with no visible source leads an observer to assume an identity, and the assumption is overturned when the true source is revealed.
when: A reveal should reframe a familiar setting.
why: The observer fills the missing source with the most familiar explanation.

text: In a silent, dark setting, ordinary small sounds become distinct and ominous, which heightens tension as a central fact approaches.
when: At the moment before a major reveal
why: Isolated sounds stand out when surrounding noise is absent, so each one feels loaded with meaning.

text: Actions can differ sharply in noise: seating an object may be almost silent while removing it clangs, so a heard sound can point to the opposite action.
when: A witness identifies an action only by sound
why: Sound depends on the specific movement, not just the object

text: Physical marks recorded without a stated medical or physical check leave their cause open, so their meaning stays ambiguous.
A forged substitute keeps its content and goes unnoticed only if the target never inspects it closely or lacks the means to check.
when: Replacing a document in front of its owner
why: Inspection is the only point where the change can be seen

text: Drug behaviour can be uncertain and experts may disagree about dose and effect, so conclusions should allow for that uncertainty.
when: Relying on expert pharmacology.
why: Pharmacology has real uncertainty.

text: Keep an uncertain or uninformative physical clue as a possible lead, not proof, and send it for further checking rather than concluding on the spot.
when: when a found object might connect to the case
why: further testing can resolve ambiguity

text: End a section on an unexplained sound, such as a sob in the night, to close on a question and pull the player forward.
when: at a section or session end

text: Do not treat an uncertain sound as proof that someone entered a place.
Plant a fair clue to a hidden source, such as the skill or rhythm of the sound, so a reveal reads as surprise rather than a trick.
when: Designing a reveal where the source is hidden at first.
why: A hidden source that is never hinted at feels like cheating.

text: Reliability of a source depends on its purpose and its access to events, not on how exact or official its facts seem.
when: Comparing conflicting accounts
why: Precise-sounding statements can still serve a motive

text: Asking who initiated a message or meeting can reverse the apparent motive behind an event.
when: an arranged meeting or message is central to a case

text: Record the source of each piece of quest information; a rumour from a third NPC should carry less certainty than a fact the player witnessed.
when: when designing quest information in a game
why: Players weigh information by how it reached them

text: 1) Stage an early favor by arranging a threat the target can be rescued from, which builds trust. 2) Accept the grateful target's invitation. 3) Use the new access, including restricted rooms, to observe the target's household.
why: Trust and access to restricted rooms come from the staged rescue.

text: 1) Restate the claim as a question about its source. 2) Wait for the witness to commit to a name, place or circumstance. 3) Check that detail against a second source before building a theory on it.
Discard a dubious clue source without discarding the questions it raised, which may still be meaningful.
Read each source or relayed account for what its author or relayer had reason to say, given their stake in the outcome; loyalty and social wishes shape what is told.
why: Authors and relayers emphasize what serves their own interests

text: Weigh each informant's interest before trusting them: a lender who profits from ruin may exaggerate, and a paid informant may shape what they report.
when: receiving an account from a financially or commercially involved person
why: incentives distort reports

text: A reported harm whose outcome benefits the alleged victim, or a victim who refuses to prosecute, warrants a check for staging.
when: A claimed victim gains financially or socially from the event.
why: Gain from the event gives the claimed victim a reason to arrange it.

text: Warnings about a witness from people with their own stakes do not prove the witness is unreliable; a speaker's character does not disprove what they said.
when: Hearing negative opinions about a witness from interested parties
why: Interested warners may be motivated by loyalty or dislike

text: Criminal records of fingerprints, measurements and photographs, plus underworld informers, together identify offenders who have a past.
when: the culprit is a known offender
why: Records and contacts supply a background to match against.

text: If a suspect asks who told the investigator a fact, the investigator needs a believable answer, or the bluff collapses.
when: when a challenge reveals knowledge the suspect did not expect
why: the suspect will test the source of the claim

text: Make threats specific and plausible; concrete consequences create more tension than vague general warnings.
when: A character or antagonist warns of consequences

text: Reveal a witness's financial stake through dialogue so that players can judge how far to trust them.
when: Writing witness characters

text: Tag each NPC or witness claim with source and access level, such as witnessed, heard, believed, eyewitness, rumour or second-hand, so players weigh claims by how directly they were known.
when: NPC testimony or a case rests on several accounts, such as frightened, drunk, or secondhand witnesses.
why: Explicit source tags let claims be weighed by how directly the source knew the event.

text: Tag each record with its source type so documents, witness testimony and inference can be told apart.
Let an NPC's wording reveal its source, so players can infer who told them and where to look next.

1) Arrange facts in dated order. 2) Log each timed fact with its source, separating testimony from independently confirmed facts; a plausible story is not a source. 3) Set entries against the crime's time window. 4) Mark gaps: undated periods and claims resting on one source.
when: establishing whether a person could have been present, or whether a movement claim can be checked
why: Mixing unverified claims with confirmed facts hides which parts of the timeline are reliable

text: A case file in a game can record each clue with its source, so the player can weigh who observed it.
when: Clues come from multiple characters or observations.
why: Recorded sources let the player judge reliability.

text: Send a messenger immediately and press on before the opponent can react; speed is the counter to a timed obstruction.
when: when an obstruction is timed to an opportunity
why: Delay gives the opponent free rein.

text: Split a quest log into separate threads, and let a player test a theory against evidence before committing, so a red herring can fit one thread but not the others.
when: designing a mystery with multiple parallel leads
why: separate threads reveal inconsistencies that a single thread hides

text: Ask how a witness knows a time: direct observation, a personal watch, or a chime heard while distracted. Each carries different reliability.
when: when a witness gives a time

text: Mark a source's claim as the source's claim, not an established fact, when footnotes or testimony describe an unverified trait.
when: A document asserts a trait that cannot be checked.
why: Separating asserted claims from established facts prevents false certainty.

text: Do not rely on memory for a recurring pattern when a written schedule can confirm it, and leave unconfirmed points open until a source settles them.
when: A witness claims a pattern but cannot confirm details about other events.
why: Confident recollection of a pattern can be wrong without a source.

text: A speaker who asks not to learn the investigator's findings keeps his own involvement vague and gains a reason to say nothing more.
when: the speaker has a stake in the matter
why: Staying ignorant limits what he must reveal

text: A speaker's eagerness to pass on a story can colour what they repeat, so their enthusiasm is part of what the listener must weigh.
A long, documented stretch of unchanged state makes a single later change stand out clearly.
why: Contrast with a stable baseline reveals the deviation

text: Limit each speaker's authority to what they personally observed, so a long-serving NPC is reliable about one matter and only guessing about another.
when: when writing testimony from several characters
why: A witness's claim covers only their direct experience.

text: Have a speaker pull back at the last moment and change course, which keeps tension alive without resolving it.
A speaker's agitation and sudden exclamations can be as telling as the answers they give.
Use hallucination or guilt effects sparingly so the player is never sure whether a figure is real.
Attempts to interrupt or steer a conversation may suggest the speaker wants something kept back.
when: A witness tries to stop another person from answering.
why: Interruption can be an effort to control what is revealed.

text: Match a witness's detail to the exact placement of an item, such as the finger a ring is worn on, rather than to the item alone.
when: A witness recalls a specific, unusual detail about someone's appearance
why: Exact placement is more distinctive than the item

text: A fast response shows speed, not identity. A timeline narrows the field of possible leakers but cannot by itself name the one responsible.
Counting two spellings of one name as two witnesses or two accused people inflates the cast and corrupts the timeline.
Assuming an attacker's identity from a whispered phrase alone is unsafe; the phrase must be tied to other evidence.
when: When a single overheard phrase links to a suspect.
why: Words can be reused, coincidental, or misheard.

text: 1) Have a watcher confirm that no one entered or left, fixing the sequence of arrivals. 2) Give each watcher a position and a signal. 3) Tell the witness to speak only if certain. 4) Reveal the face suddenly under light. 5) Accept a one-word confirmation.
when: when a suspect was seen briefly in poor light and must be identified
why: fixed sequence and separate roles prevent leading the witness

text: Give overheard speakers distinct pitch, tone, phrasing or a repeated rhyme, so listeners can tell them apart and match a recited phrase to a known event without seeing them.
when: speakers are heard through a wall or door
why: voice traits remain distinct without visual contact

text: Let a character appear to be in conversation while being silent or dead, so the player notices the gap between what they see and hear.
when: Designing a scene with multiple characters.
why: Mismatches between visual and audio cues prompt the player to re-examine the scene.

text: Specialist knowledge is the lore that lets a distinctive trace be matched to a small set of possible sources, such as a tobacco ash type, a footprint or a trade-shaped hand.
when: when a trace is distinctive
why: lore converts a trace into a narrow set of candidates

text: A physical sign reads as clue only with the specialist knowledge behind it; without that lore, residues such as ash read as noise, so the lore must be learned first.
when: a sign depends on specialist knowledge
why: a sign has meaning only within the knowledge that interprets it; meaning depends on recognising the material

text: An animal's species indicates its habitat, so a creature found in a place can show where it has been living.
Test a claimed expert by asking specific questions about names, dates and context in their field, and judge the answers rather than their confidence.
when: Identity or expertise matters and a real expert's knowledge is available as reference
why: A real practitioner answers specific questions easily while a pretender cannot

text: Extend appeals to specialist trade journals, where a sale record of a distinctive garment may be traced.
Specialist analysis of physical traces can narrow a search, for example by showing that original documents exist rather than copies.
when: When a search is unfocused and a specialist can examine traces.
why: Analysis tells the searcher what kind of object to look for and where it may be.

text: A specialist NPC giving a skill-based verdict, such as amateur or professional, can narrow the suspect list for the player.
Do not claim a species identity without a matching reference; leave the name open until the evidence fits.
An unusual technique may narrow culprits to skilled people, but if applying the method needs little know-how, don't assume a specialist background.
when: A rare technique suggests specialist skill; when the know-how required is small, the method implies nothing about background.
why: Specialist skill is rarer than general ability, yet the know-how needed to apply a substance may be small.

text: Make claims specific by naming the act, victim, place, slope, or time, since specific details can be checked against other evidence while vague claims cannot be tested.
when: when writing or evaluating witness accounts, appearance details, or quest accusations
why: Specific details can be verified unlike general impressions; precise claims are falsifiable and let players act on evidence.

text: Specific details feel like proof and raise credibility but are not corroboration; detailed names, dates and measurements are often chosen to persuade, not to make an account true.
when: A vision names objects that match people or events in the world.
why: Specificity raises perceived credibility, though it is not independent corroboration.

text: Judge witness claims by small specific details, such as build, age, accent, overheard speech fragments, or observations tied to a known routine, rather than by general impressions.
A detail a witness insists on can be more stable than the identity they claim, so test each detail separately.
A capability claim gains weight when several witnesses describe specific acts, such as lifting heavy objects.
when: when assessing whether someone could have moved something

text: Press a witness with narrow questions about details that a true account would have to get right, so each answer can be checked.
when: When a witness's account touches a physical or medical point.
why: Specific claims expose inaccuracies that vague claims hide.

text: When interviewing a reluctant witness, keep questioning on specific facts such as threats and motive rather than general impressions, since witnesses often don't know which details matter.
when: when interviewing a reluctant witness
why: Witnesses often don't know which details matter, so ask the specific question instead of waiting for them to volunteer it.

text: Pair dream, vision, trance or spirit clues with a checkable anchor, such as an object, time or location the player can physically confirm or rule out.
when: Designing supernatural or mystical clues.
why: Independent physical evidence separates true clues from misleading ones.

text: A supernatural effect in a staged setting may be performance, since skilled performers such as jugglers or ventriloquists can imitate spirit contact.
when: A supernatural effect appears in a staged or performed setting, or is claimed by performers.
why: Recognizing the performance mechanism prevents accepting the claim at face value; performance skill can produce the reported effects.

text: Spectral evidence is testimony that an accused person's apparition harmed or appeared to the afflicted, an unseen or supernatural figure no outside observer can independently check.
Spectral sight is a claimed ability to perceive a person's spirit rather than their body, used as evidence against them.
Spectral sightings are weak evidence because an unseen agent may take the shape of an innocent person, so a face seen in a vision may not match the real one.
Give eerie horror events, like phantom footsteps, spectral sounds or sleeping guards, human causes testable through tracks, dropped keys, disturbed dust, a spent torch or a gas jet.
when: Designing supernatural-seeming events in horror content.
why: Players feel the supernatural reading is earned yet false when it can be tested physically; visible traces let players reason to an ordinary cause.

text: When a supernatural explanation points at a person, keep the human actor open and check it against motive and knowledge, since the label can conceal an ordinary cause.
when: A supernatural claim or diagnosis points at a person or their behaviour.
why: Premature acceptance of the supernatural answer leaves the human cause unexamined.

text: Before accepting a supernatural event, check whether a person gained from the fear it caused.
when: an event favours one person in a place with a reputation
why: a staged event serves its beneficiary

text: A dream or vision can echo real events, so separate its supernatural framing from the human elements it reflects and check those elements against evidence.
when: A character experiences a dream or vision that seems prophetic.
why: Gothic framing can make ordinary events seem supernatural.

text: Check a frightening account against plain physical facts before accepting any supernatural explanation.
when: A scene seems uncanny but has no clear source
why: Most eerie impressions have an ordinary cause once inspected

text: When a mystery calls for dread, let the investigation confirm a human explanation and leave a supernatural remainder unexplained.
when: when a horror story must keep an element of mystery after investigation
why: A remainder keeps the player's model open and sustains tension.

text: A supernatural-seeming effect that others can reproduce on demand is exposed as mechanical, turning the claim into a demonstrable trick.
when: a reported effect appears only when a particular person is present
why: Reproduction gives an independent, checkable explanation.

text: A supernatural-seeming haunting can be resolved by a mechanical illusion, where an apparition is produced by reflections and an operator with access to the staging.
when: designing a haunting mystery with a mundane explanation
why: Players accept the supernatural frame until a mechanism explains each escalating event.

text: A supernatural explanation can seem to fit a time window; check the window against physical access before accepting it.
when: Evaluating an explanation for an event within a time window.
why: Physical access constraints can rule out a seemingly fitting explanation.

text: 1) Identify which parts of a scene have ordinary causes. 2) Check the supernatural explanation against a physical or behavioural event. 3) Give it the same corroboration as any other claim.
when: when an event seems supernatural but may have ordinary causes
why: Separating ordinary causes from the supernatural core shows what the explanation actually supports.

text: Mark spectral clues the player cannot verify as unverifiable, and give an independent check or second source before any puzzle or case depends on them.
when: A clue cannot be checked by the player.
why: Unverifiable clues cannot settle a case alone.

text: Give a supernatural-seeming event a concrete human cause players can uncover through the same records, testimony and traces as other clues.
when: Designing an in-world event that looks uncanny, prophesied or magical.
why: Keeps the mystery solvable through fair evidence; players feel satisfied when apparent magic resolves into traceable human action.

text: Unverifiable testimony may justify an inquiry and strengthen other presumptions, but should not convict without further evidence.
Being seen as a spectre by the afflicted is not enough to commit or convict someone.
Give each supernatural or hidden claim a checkable consequence, such as a time, place, or object that must move, so it can be shown false.
when: Designing a supernatural mystery
why: Claims without consequences make a weak mystery.

text: Design a mystery where the supernatural solution implicates an NPC's inner state, and let the player test whether a human-scale motive fits the clue.
when: when designing a supernatural mystery involving NPCs
why: A testable motive makes the supernatural answer engage with human behaviour.

text: People who believe no one is listening speak unguarded and may reveal knowledge or motive, with hints whose meaning is unclear at first.
when: a person is alone and emotionally shaken, or a character speaks while assuming no listener
why: the belief of being alone or unheard lowers their guard, and speakers do not guard their words

text: A witness may reveal hidden knowledge through an answer given before any question on that subject is asked, such as denying a cause nobody has raised.
when: When a shocking announcement is delivered and the witness responds unprompted.
why: Guilty knowledge can surface in reflexive reactions before the witness can guard it.

text: An unguarded reaction to a mentioned fact, such as a pause, setback or sudden change of topic, can reveal knowledge the speaker would deny if asked directly.
when: A key fact is mentioned in conversation with a suspect.
why: Surprise or concern escapes self-control before the speaker can conceal it.

text: A spoken explanation gives listeners a reason to accept an odd situation, lowering their scrutiny.
when: an odd situation is seen only in part
why: a stated reason satisfies the question before it is asked

text: A listener can sense concealment from a manner that seems unnatural, even after the listener has agreed to a plan.
People tend to speak frankly in front of someone they believe is unconscious, so a feigned victim can overhear their plans.
when: a character feigns unconsciousness near others who are talking
why: They assume the person cannot hear, so they reveal what they would otherwise hide.

text: Investigators may read an unguarded remark as a self-revelation rather than a guess about the external cause.
when: when a suspect's words are overheard in a tense situation
why: Attention shifts from the outside problem to the speaker's own state.

text: Harsh words spoken about a person can later support a slander claim and damages, so spoken accusations carry legal weight.
Speech cues can suggest a suspect's origin or identity, but treat them as partial; corroborate a single slip, such as a foreign phrase, before trusting it.
when: identifying a suspect from witness testimony, or identity is uncertain and only casual speech is available
why: speech cues are informative but incomplete, and one slip can have an innocent explanation

text: A victim who shows no reaction to an approaching person suggests the approach was expected or came from someone known to them.
when: when a victim seems undisturbed by an approach
why: people usually react to unexpected strangers

text: People who cannot be woken and respond unnaturally suggest a drug rather than ordinary sleep.
when: Witnesses in a crime scene are unresponsive
why: Ordinary sleep does not produce that response

text: Give non-player characters a consistent speech habit, then let a single out-of-character statement serve as a detectable tell.
why: a break in an established pattern is easy for players to notice

text: When observed behaviour fits none of the competing explanations neatly, suspect that one of the shared assumptions is wrong.
Specific, checkable statements count for more than emphatic but vague denials.
Recurring nursery or idiom references in NPC speech can echo a later signature or code, linking dialogue to a puzzle.
when: Writing NPC speech that connects to a puzzle or clue.
why: A familiar register makes a later match feel earned.

text: A remark revealing knowledge the speaker could only gain by being present is a trace that exposes their presence.
when: when a suspect describes a detail they should not know

text: An explicit warning not to repeat words confirms that the words touched a real secret.
when: When a character responds to an overheard remark.
why: Urgency to suppress information signals its importance.

text: Hesitation appears first at ordinary-sounding words, and trigger words then cause a sharp reaction and loss of composure.
when: A subject conceals a secret under questioning.
why: Pressure builds gradually until charged content breaks composure.

text: A reveal that depends only on a character's word feels weak; a visible physical detail gives the audience something to verify.
A countersign spoken aloud can be learned by anyone within earshot, so the check is compromised once overheard.
when: A password is exchanged in public or within earshot of others
why: Audible passwords spread to listeners

text: Do not treat silence as evidence until the expected reaction is confirmed as normal. A sound sleeper or an unreliable guard can fail to react for unrelated reasons.
why: Without a baseline, a missing reaction can be explained by the observer or the animal rather than the event.

text: A confrontation that becomes a speech no one interrupts loses tension and stops feeling like a contest.
Guarding the obvious communication channels does not mean all channels are closed; a protected plan can still have a gap.
when: Securing a plan against leaks.
why: Overlooked routes, such as public news, bypass the controls placed on known routes.

text: A hiding place mentioned in conversation reveals the owner's habits to anyone listening.
Making every character evasive drains their hints of force.
Evidence that the victim spoke to someone proves they were alive at that moment, not afterward.
when: Using a late conversation to set a time of death.
why: Being alive at one time says nothing about later times.

text: Assuming an exit is open because it is unguarded is an error; check its timing before accepting the route.
Spelling and handwriting cannot establish a writer's intelligence or literacy.
Overlooking how a crowd, a leader or a physical contact shapes what a witness later says leads to misreading their testimony.
Check several independent facts: one failure can be explained away, but several converging facts raise the overall case and are hard to dismiss.
when: A verdict rests on accumulated circumstantial facts
why: Converging independent-looking facts raise the overall probability of guilt

text: Stacking weak indicators or coincidences before verifying each builds conclusions on untested links; check each for an innocent explanation before weighing the total.
when: the player must weigh minor indicators rather than one decisive proof
why: A large pile of items can feel conclusive even when each item is ambiguous

text: Stacking several pressures in quick succession, each adding to the last, keeps tension rising through a sequence.
when: building a run of setbacks or threats

text: Following one misdirection with a second unrelated disturbance pulls attention further from the main case.
Stacked pressures such as raids, debt, lost leaders and a feared enemy make hostility and suspicion feel earned to those living through them.
when: A region is under several strains at once.
why: Accumulated hardship and fear normalize extreme responses.

text: Player confidence in a hidden truth rises as several weak, partly contradictory clues accumulate, even when no single clue proves it.
when: a reveal built from a sighting, a lie, a courtesy and an unexplained habit
why: Each clue is ambiguous alone, but together they point one way.

text: Repeated evasions read as filler and stall an investigation unless each one narrows the question or points somewhere new.
when: Several witnesses refuse or deflect without adding new evidence.
why: Refusals that yield no new direction leave the player with no progress.

text: Each inference built on the last compounds uncertainty, such as moving from 'she went out' to 'someone locked up after her'; test each link separately.
why: Chained conclusions can seem solid while each step rests on assumption.

text: Stacking inferences until they form a full person can build a convincing but false character, since each guess may be wrong.
when: multiple weak traces are combined into one profile
why: each added guess compounds the error

text: Several independent motives strengthen a case more than one alone, but unchecked stacked motives can make a weak case look strong; check each separately.
Stacking evidence toward one reading sets a firm conclusion that later review can overturn, but too much leaves no alternative reading for the audience.
when: presenting a case whose evidence seems to point one way

text: Household staff reveal routines and private habits when sympathetic people comment on events, but deflect pointed questions; unlock their gossip through friendly conversation, not direct questioning.
when: Investigating through servants or other staff.
why: Direct questioning signals a motive and gets refused, while sympathy invites talk.

text: Service staff who distrust police give guarded answers, so cooperation from them is limited.
when: questioning hotel or service staff as an official
why: Distrust of authority makes witnesses withhold information

text: Staff who change employers can carry knowledge of a household to outside places, opening new routes for information.
A staff member's recollection can supply a vehicle type and a departure time that written records do not contain.
A long-serving household member can supply reliable knowledge of routine and local history that cannot be observed directly.
when: Gathering background information from a servant or local resident.
why: Long familiarity gives access to patterns and history that a visitor would not know.

text: Shop staff can act as witnesses who confirm buyers and say whether they recognize a suspect.
when: when a trade record must be verified against people who handled it
why: Staff can confirm records that documents alone cannot establish.

text: Track staff changes before a death, since a replacement may be the person present at the critical moment.
when: When staff were replaced shortly before a death.

text: Ask household staff who recently left and whether the victim had recent guests, since answers can point to a specific person.
when: Investigating a household crime

text: A high number of special formal meetings within a short period signals that a dispute has been pushed into formal procedure.
when: tracking a conflict through community records
why: Frequency of formal meetings reveals how far a conflict has been formalized.

text: Culprits plant clues such as a card, moved object, forced entry or false footprints to imply an outsider or false motive; test each apparent clue separately.
when: A scene's items suggest a stranger acted, its evidence fits too neatly with one suspect or contradicts the entry point, or a clue conveniently implicates an outsider or a single date.
why: Investigators who accept a clue at face value follow the path the planner intended while the real plan proceeds elsewhere; staging makes evidence seem to support a conclusion the act does not.

text: Dents on the nose from spectacles indicate regular wear, and they can suggest a visual condition.
Planted evidence can serve as a red herring that the player must test against independent facts.
when: designing misleading evidence
why: Tested red herrings reward careful players

text: Evidence that is too neat, complete or pointed at one person may be arranged; real evidence is vague. Judge planted items by whether their placement is natural for the owner.
when: A case looks too clean against one suspect, or an item is found where its owner would not normally keep it.
why: A frame-up is built to point one way, unlike messy real traces; staged placements show unnatural order or convenience.

text: A staged loss fools only those who do not look closely; an outcome that is too tidy is the usual giveaway.
An item that looks stolen but still holds valuables may be a decoy, so test whether the robbery was staged.
when: when a scene suggests a robbery

text: Test signs of a multi-person attack for staging before accepting them, and do not accept a suspect as framed merely because a relative or gang is named.
why: Naming a plausible culprit does not prove the plant

text: Test a claim that a suspect could not have reached a remote scene by asking whether they would have been seen in a busy area nearby.
why: a known person's presence in a busy place can be checked

text: Test an apparent conclusion against every detail; one anomaly is enough to reopen a case that otherwise looks settled.
when: a scene's reading seems complete
why: Each detail must agree with the conclusion for it to hold.

text: Treat a detail that overdoes its own style as possibly a staged imitation, since a genuine author rarely performs the style so exaggeratedly.
when: when a detail is too neat or theatrical
why: Imitators tend to exaggerate the expected signs

text: Stage an alarm to find a hidden object only if the owner's priorities are predictable; avoid it if the target lacks attachment or would spot the staging.
when: the object's location is unknown but its owner's priorities are predictable

text: When opponents watch, make a visible move that looks genuine while the real move happens elsewhere, unnoticed.
when: When the opposition is known to observe and follow
why: Watchers act on what they see, so the staged move draws them away.

text: A show of searching for a document, or a readily handed-over suspect copy, can signal a decoy meant to make the document seem to have existed earlier.
when: a person's theatrics around a document seem out of proportion to its importance
why: Staging can manufacture an impression of an earlier record

text: A claimed locked state can be tested directly; a lock that opens at a touch contradicts the claim and the account behind it.
when: a suspect describes a secured object or fastening

text: Assume anything visible was seen by the culprit too; a clue in an unusual place, given the victim's normal habits, may have been arranged to mislead.
when: A clue seems too neat or placed oddly
why: A clever offender can anticipate what the investigator will notice

text: A sudden staged outburst shows whether a person is rattled, since a rattled person reacts visibly.
Fabricated traces and invented similar incidents can shift suspicion away from the person who made the marks.
when: A disturbed scene needs an innocent explanation

text: Compare recovered remains with witness descriptions of age, height and missing teeth to test a claim.
when: a grave or body is found and the records describe the person
why: physical evidence can confirm or contradict testimony

text: A staged crime or attack, a blind, fake vehicles or fake officers give investigators a plausible false trail, so the real method, motive or route looks normal.
when: A real cause, motive or route must stay hidden.
why: A plausible explanation ends the search for alternatives; a false trail misdirects the search.

text: A staged false rumour can provoke a reaction that exposes the true antagonist, because the antagonist acts on information they believe is real.
when: the true antagonist is hidden from the player

text: A staged clue that copies a known pattern can mislead people who have not seen the precedent, but an investigator who checks the precedent sees through it.
when: A scene looks arranged, too tidy or copied from elsewhere
why: The copied pattern reveals its artificiality to anyone who knows the original

text: A killing staged as an open, formal contest looks fairer than a hidden attack, so the death draws less suspicion and attention shifts to the spectacle.
when: A planner wants a murder to pass as a legitimate fight.
why: Observers judge public, rule-bound conflict as acceptable.

text: A staged sound or movement triggered by the player can mislead other characters into a false conclusion.
when: Designing a trick that other characters observe.
why: Observers reason from the effect they perceive and may reach a wrong conclusion.

text: Observers' reactions can be staged on cue, so apparent symptoms seem to confirm the examiners' claims.
when: an examination relies on displays by accusers
why: Performed symptoms look like independent proof.

text: A test that seems to confirm guilt can be staged or flawed (blindfolds, cued reactions, pins readied in advance); its flaws may be discoverable, so it is not independent proof.
A dramatic or sensational detail can absorb attention and hide the rational plan behind a case.
A made-up badge shown to a child can spread the story further than intended, exposing the cover to people who talk.
when: Using a false credential to win an insider's trust.
why: Children and casual listeners repeat what they see and hear.

text: A staged scene can produce a reaction that is not a confession; the real admission may come later, after the moment, not during it.
A displayed object can be staged for the occasion, so confirm it was actually in use when the outcome occurred before treating it as an explanation.
when: when a suspect presents tools or items as proof of innocence
why: items displayed later may not reflect the earlier reality

text: 1) Know how the material actually fails. 2) Check whether the reported result fits that failure pattern. 3) Check whether the required forces and edge conditions can really occur.
when: when a physical damage claim is central to a case

text: 1) Predict how an honest person of the claimed class would react. 2) Apply a controlled stimulus. 3) Compare the actual reaction with the prediction. 4) Treat a mismatch as a clue.
when: A suspect's class or background is in doubt and the stimulus can be controlled.

text: 1) Present a plausible cover story to the suspect. 2) Arrange a moment where they must react to it. 3) Observe their unscripted reaction, which reveals more than their words.
when: a true motive must stay hidden, or a suspect's reaction is needed to test them

text: 1) Ask whose item the trace belongs to. 2) Ask how its owner accounts for being present. 3) Establish the time window in which the mark could have occurred. 4) Test the inference against other facts.
when: a physical trace seems conclusive

text: 1) Ask whether the claimed act would have been audible. 2) Check any mechanism involved, such as a lock. 3) Attempt the act or an equivalent. 4) List each required step and judge its credibility. 5) Ask the witness to explain each detail.
when: a claim depends on sound, strength or how an object or lock works
why: Physical checks expose claims that cannot happen as described.

text: 1) State each inference from a specific sign. 2) List the alternative causes that would produce the same sign. 3) Eliminate alternatives the sign contradicts. 4) Hold remaining inferences loosely.
when: When an object's signs have several plausible causes
why: A sign may fit more than one cause and must be checked before it is trusted

text: 1) Let the opposing side believe the investigator has left. 2) Route that news through a channel the investigator controls. 3) Return and act when the suspects have dropped their guard.
when: the suspect watches the investigator and would be alerted by knowledge of the investigation
why: A false belief of absence removes suspicion, letting the investigator act unseen.

text: 1) List each clue that points to an outside agent. 2) Test each against physical evidence, such as whether a trace matches a suspect's object. 3) Note any mismatch between clues. 4) Accept the outside explanation only if the tests hold.
when: A scene's clues point neatly to an outsider, especially early and conveniently.
why: Staged traces can mislead; testing against physical evidence separates real clues from planted ones.

text: 1) Ask which body part was affected. 2) Ask whether another part could have done the task. 3) Ask whether the claimant could perform the task at all.
when: when a witness claims a physical reason for being unable to act
why: Specific, checkable questions expose excuses that cannot hold

text: 1) Measure or describe the suspicious item precisely. 2) Compare it with the suspect's known possessions or marks. 3) Note whether the match is exact or only similar. 4) Discount items that contradict measured facts.
when: an item seems to point at one person
why: Measured comparison separates real matches from convenient resemblance.

text: 1) List the possible answers to a question the object could settle. 2) Note that every answer is itself a usable fact. 3) Run the test and use whatever result it gives.
when: When an object seems unimportant but a test could resolve an open question about it.
why: Each outcome gives information, so the test is worth running whatever it shows.

text: 1) Check whether the object's type is widely owned. 2) Check whether a matching object belonged to someone else. 3) Note whether it lies in an obvious place. 4) Match it to physical evidence. 5) Test rival explanations against the timeline.
when: when a striking object seems to point to one person
why: a single-owner inference needs the object to be rare and placed by its owner

text: 1) Ask who benefits from the suspicion. 2) Check whether the suspect was already an easy target. 3) Test each neat fact for a contradiction, such as an alibi that breaks it.
when: when evidence points too directly at one person
why: A frame-up needs a convenient scapegoat and tangible proof, so it can be checked on both.

text: 1) Treat a blank page as possibly hiding text. 2) Consider and reject simpler explanations, such as a decoy or nothing being there. 3) Test the page with a suspected reagent or heat source.
when: A recovered document appears blank.
why: Invisible writing is revealed only by a specific action, so blank pages must be tested before being discarded.

text: 1) Identify the route the apparent effect uses. 2) Secure that route, such as locking a door. 3) Observe whether the effect still occurs; if it does, that route was not its cause.
when: a door or object appears to move on its own
why: a physical effect depends on access that the test removes

text: 1) Check whose object it really is, using markings or initials. 2) Test whether the attached explanation is plausible. 3) Check whether any witness account changed after talking to someone else.
when: when an object or statement fits the expected story too neatly

text: 1) Note the marked or unusual object. 2) Ask whether it could be a deliberate message or pure chance. 3) Check its meaning against a second, independent source. 4) Discard it if no source confirms it.
when: when an object seems to carry a message

text: 1) Place the key object where the subject will see it 2) Keep its significance unannounced 3) Arrange a predictable reason for the subject to enter 4) Observe from concealment 5) Define beforehand which reactions count.
when: testing whether a subject knows about an object
why: a prepared setup makes reactions interpretable

text: 1) Note where the clue sits and what is normal for that object or person. 2) Propose an innocent explanation for its placement. 3) Propose a staged explanation. 4) Choose the explanation that a habit or placement rule can test.
when: Judging whether a clue is genuine or planted
why: An innocent and a staged explanation must be tested against a fact the player can check

text: 1) Establish a person's habits through people who know them well. 2) Compare each planted item with those habits. 3) Note how each item breaks a habit, such as how it is stored or used. 4) Count how many items break the same habit.
when: A scene looks arranged to implicate someone.

text: 1) Describe what the site would have looked like and how hard it was to reach. 2) State what the claimed procedure would demand. 3) Compare that picture with the claim and with surviving traces.
when: A site or procedure is part of the evidence for a claim.
why: Physical constraints can confirm or contradict a claim about how an event happened.

text: 1) Offer the tester a substitute object or method chosen by the other side. 2) Watch whether they accept it. 3) Treat refusal to use a neutral substitute as evidence that the test is rigged.
when: when a test's result depends on an object or method controlled by the tester
why: A fair test should give the same result with any neutral substitute.

text: 1) Show the physical clue early with no explained meaning. 2) Let suspicion attach to a wrong suspect. 3) Demonstrate the clue's mechanism. 4) Link the mechanism to a social leak that reveals who acted.
when: Revealing how a locked or hidden mechanism worked in an investigation.
why: Separating the object, the demonstration and the social chain keeps the mystery moving while the method is confirmed.

text: Test a proposed explanation against conditions it cannot easily explain, such as undressing in deep cold beside an open window.
When an NPC stages evidence, ask who benefits from what remains, since the staging usually serves a particular person's interest.
when: When an NPC could be framing another character.
why: Staged evidence is built to favour one conclusion over others.

text: Ask who could have placed an item, why, and whether its owner genuinely used it, rather than accepting a name or mark as proof.
when: Evaluating a clue that points to a particular person
why: Names and marks can be copied or stamped, so they are weak proof of ownership or use.

text: Make scent clues testable by letting the player compare items that were in contact, so the player can see which one carried the odour.
When placing a staged item to implicate a non-player character, give it a true owner that the player can discover, so the decoy can be exposed.
when: Designing a red herring built on a planted object.
why: A discoverable owner lets players test the clue instead of accepting it at face value.

text: Each new device invented to save a theory from a contradiction must come with its own test that could prove it wrong.
Turn a witness's claim into a testable one by tying it to a physical fact, such as a bell or door that would have sounded.
when: When a witness says they heard or saw nothing.

text: Tie accuser reactions to the suspect's movements so the player can test whether a reaction is real or staged.
A thief may rely on the owner not needing a taken item for a short while, so the absence goes unnoticed for a time.
when: When an item is taken from a place where the owner is unlikely to check soon.
why: Delayed need for an item delays discovery of its theft.

text: Give the first suspect a plausible prop, such as a weapon or piece of jewelry, that later reads as staged, so the framing becomes visible in hindsight.
when: designing a red-herring suspect
why: A prop that seems incriminating early can later show the scene was arranged.

text: Test an outsider-thief theory against insiders' gains, since a theft can be staged by beneficiaries using a fake loss.
when: A theft appears to be committed by an outsider.
why: Staged crimes benefit someone inside the circle, which outsider theories ignore.

text: A culprit can arrange a scene, with a false identity, disguised body and fake records, so inspection finds nothing damning or points at someone else.
when: A scene must be read as a false story.
why: Each prepared element is built to survive examination.

text: A cause of death or harm that matches a recognised natural pattern can pass examination, because examiners compare signs against known natural causes.
when: The apparent cause is strong and the physical signs match a natural event
why: Examiners read the body against familiar patterns, so a plausible match can hide a planned act

text: A staged-crime mystery moves through disappearance, a charge against a suspect, misdirection, a confession that splits suspect from threat, and a reversal.
1) Announce the newcomer through a letter or rumour. 2) Delay the arrival with weather or a timed event. 3) Let the wait build tension. 4) Reveal the character at the arrival.
when: a new character should be surrounded by expectation before being seen
why: Alternating waiting and arrival makes tension rise before the meeting.

text: 1) Keep the suspect engaged in conversation to hold their attention. 2) Have a second person search their belongings. 3) Accept that a failed search costs the investigator standing.
when: Circumstantial evidence points to hidden papers and the suspect can be kept occupied.
why: Divided attention prevents the suspect from interfering while the search proceeds.

text: 1) List every strange occurrence from the outcome. 2) For each, ask who could have produced it. 3) Check the means, opportunity and access for that person. 4) Keep items that resist every explanation separate and state them plainly.
when: When an event looks supernatural and a concealed human action is suspected.
why: Testing each anomaly item by item shows which ones have ordinary mechanisms.

text: Display stolen items in an odd arrangement and have a note mark the arrangement as meaningful so the player must decode it.
when: when designing staged-scene puzzles

text: A staged corpse is a substitute body placed so the apparent victim escapes, hiding who actually died; close associates may be complicit.
when: A mystery where a death is reported and the identity of the dead is in doubt.
why: Readers assume a body is the person named, so the substitution hides the true actor.

text: A self-staged crime is one where the apparent victim arranges their own abduction to pressure another person, so it reads as a third-party crime.
An apparent disappearance can be explained by the missing person's own choices, such as relocating without notice, rather than by an external cause.
when: Resolving why a character seemed lost

text: A staged element traced back to its original owner shows that its removal served a purpose other than the one it appeared to serve.
Let the player reconstruct a faked crime from clues such as a dropped object or a thrown item, proving the scene was staged by someone the player trusted.
when: Revealing that a crime scene was fabricated.
why: Physical evidence that the player can verify makes the staging believable.

text: A staged death, sham funeral, or natural-seeming illness can hide a deliberate, targeted plot, so an ordinary cause may turn out to be malice.
when: An apparent misfortune is staged or convenient for someone.
why: Audiences accept an ordinary cause until a concrete event contradicts it.

text: A second body found mid-story reverses suspicion when it contradicts the first theory, forcing the player to rebuild the whole reading.
when: midpoint of a mystery
why: A new fact that undoes the current explanation resets the player's suspicions.

text: When a danger is revealed as a performance, earlier sounds and details that matched the act become evidence the player can reread.
why: The performance leaves traces that fit the staged frame.

text: Evidence that a death was staged, such as a wound inflicted after death, overturns earlier theories about who killed the victim and why.
when: a reconstruction shows a scene was arranged
why: Killer theories depend on the assumed sequence of events

text: 1) Release findings first where they touch the other side's theory. 2) Hold the most damaging facts back until later. 3) Hear the other side's account before revealing inferences.
when: Presenting evidence to a party who holds information you need.
why: Ordering disclosure for effect tests the other side's theory and protects your advantage.

text: 1) Appear in public in one guise at a known place. 2) Change identity out of sight. 3) Appear again in the second guise, so staff sightings cover the gap.
when: Designing or analysing a staged alibi.
why: Public sightings in each guise make the switch invisible to witnesses.

text: 1) Hold back a central fact until the listener is ready to receive it. 2) Watch the listener's hesitation and reaction. 3) Reveal the hidden matter in small steps, each adding one piece. 4) Let the listener supply facts where possible.
when: when a hidden fact would harm a third party if revealed too early or the listener must be prepared
why: Gradual disclosure prevents shock and keeps the listener engaged in reasoning.

text: 1) Circulate a false report that implicates one suspect. 2) Summon each suspect separately. 3) Watch each reaction for the one that exposes the guilty party.
when: when logic alone cannot separate suspects
why: The guilty party may react to the bait where innocent suspects do not.

text: 1) Let a character be identified as dead early. 2) Present a sighting of that character alive later. 3) Have the solver reconstruct the disguise from details already reported.
when: Building a twist where a presumed victim turns out to be the killer.
why: Reusing reported details makes the reversal feel deduced rather than invented.

text: Surprise has several causes: at an unexpected figure it can signal missing information and a lead; at a stated deduction, being found out or embarrassment.
when: observing a character's reaction to a figure or to a deduction put to them
why: The same visible reaction can have different causes, so an observer must not read it in isolation.

text: Learning who now benefits from a discovery can lead an investigator to keep it secret when speaking would help no one.
when: deciding whether to disclose a discovery
why: The value of disclosure depends on who would gain from it.
