when: an accusation follows an earlier dispute
why: a matching history makes the motive plausible

text: Check a public act of kindness against who benefits from it, though a kind act may still be genuinely kind.
when: Judging a character's motive from a generous gesture

text: A sharp change in a witness's manner around one topic or person, such as blushing, blinking, or blocking a passage, can signal a hidden motive.
when: A witness's manner shifts sharply around one subject or person.
why: Emotional reactions can leak concealed reasons, but they are signs to test, not conclusions.

text: When a character's stated reason can be measured, compare its cost or scale with the act it explains. A reason too small to justify the act points to a hidden motive.
when: A character gives a reason for an action that can be checked against a sum, count or other fact
why: A mismatch between claimed purpose and measurable scale signals the real want

text: A victim's earlier threat of self-harm makes a suicide reading plausible, but it explains the scene only if the physical evidence agrees with it.
when: A victim has voiced suicidal intent before dying

text: Events close together in date can link a motive to an action, which is a hypothesis to test rather than proof of guilt.
A gap between a person's claim of not desiring an office and their recorded actions is evidence of motive.
when: a candidate disclaims interest in a contested post

text: Judge culpability by both inward intent and outward act, since a minimal physical act can carry grave intent.
when: Assessing a character's responsibility for a past death.

text: Decide the next investigative step before a trail goes cold, such as checking a witness's account of the time.
when: During a surveillance or tracking sequence.
why: A ready next step keeps momentum when the target's trail is lost.

text: Stating the penalty an attacker would face can make a reluctant witness weigh the cost of silence against the cost of speaking.
when: witness refuses to name a suspect
why: a stated cost changes the balance between speaking and staying silent

text: Plans that rely on routine sequences fail where the planner assumed something would stay fixed; a single cancelled event can break the whole chain of dependent steps.
when: A plan depends on a sequence of routine events the planner cannot fully control.
why: Each assumed fixed event is a link; if one changes, every later step that relied on it breaks.

text: Assuming the claimant's gain is obvious while the holder has no reason to act misses other suspects.
A pretext that insults a suspect can damage the investigator's standing with allies who witness it.
when: Using a provocative test on a suspect in front of others.
why: Observers may side with the suspect when the test seems unfair.

text: Matching an object's kind is not matching its source. A widely sold item fits many possible owners, so the match only supports a line of inquiry.
Accepting a clean physical match while the motive stays unexplained leaves the case open, since the act may not serve the suspect's apparent goal.
when: A violent act does not fit the suspect's apparent purpose
why: A mismatch between act and goal suggests the motive is incomplete.

text: A clean motive picture can hide a deliberate reset, where the person later reappears under a new name with a new family.
when: when an absence seems to have no motive

text: Accepting the first stated motive, such as a bad temper, without checking records like wills and estates can miss documents that contradict it.
why: Records often show circumstances that contradict the common story.

text: Reading an owner's intention into an object from its storage place alone, without other evidence, is unsupported.
Compare a suspect's stated plan or reason with actual conduct; the gap often holds the real motive, so ask which explanation the conduct fits better.
when: a stated plan or explanation conflicts with actions, or an absence needs explaining
why: conduct that contradicts a plan reveals the real intent; behaviour reveals what words conceal

text: Give each non-player character a hidden financial stake, such as inheritance or debt, that surfaces only through certain dialogue choices or questions on adjacent topics.
when: writing suspect dialogue
why: hidden pressure rewards questioning and keeps early suspicion open

text: Separate intent from action: documents that show a plan do not prove it was carried out.
Compare an object's stated purpose with how well it actually serves that purpose; if another use fits better, the stated purpose may be false.
When a document is destroyed, give a stated motive, because destruction without a reason reads as a plot convenience.
Design an NPC whose hidden motive turns the player's first reading of a threat into a second reading of protection once the motive is unlocked.
when: designing NPC secrets
why: Reinterpretation rewards exploration.

text: Check a witness's stated reason for being present against the calendar before accepting it.
when: when a witness explains their presence at a place tied to the case
why: A plausible reason can be false when the date does not fit

text: Measure a beneficiary's gain against the prior state, not against a disputed document; the wrong baseline can reverse who appears to gain.
when: inheritance or ownership is contested
why: a disputed document may itself be false

text: Give a victim character a hidden financial motive that the player can uncover through documents or records.
when: Designing a character whose motives are not obvious.
why: Discoverable motives reward investigation and make the character's conduct intelligible.

text: Check any testimony given after a payment or reward for influence, because an inducement can shape what the witness says.
Separate what a character intended from what their actions caused. Someone may produce an outcome without knowing it, so do not infer conspiracy from consequences alone.
Place a closing question that reaches a suspect's hidden motive to open a confrontation or a new objective.
Model a quest giver who offers a large reward for an item and refuses to name its owner as a hidden-motive NPC.
Do not rely on intent-reading when a document is formally valid and clearly worded.
when: A document meets formal requirements and its terms are plain.
why: Clear wording makes inference about intent unnecessary.

text: Heated insults such as calling a witness a liar carry no evidential weight unless specific statements are shown to be false.
Track a suspect's purchases and errands, so that items bought together can reveal a plan the player must assemble.
Compare a person's stated reason for going somewhere with the first questions they ask there; a mismatch exposes a false explanation.
when: when a character gives a reason for an action that others can observe
why: Actions that do not serve the stated purpose reveal the real intent.

text: Ask by stating what you already know, rather than a yes-or-no question, so the suspect must answer or reveal a lie, even if the claim cannot be checked.
when: When a suspect is likely to deny being present or involved, and the investigator can afford to be wrong about the stated knowledge.
why: A direct yes-or-no question invites an easy denial, while a stated claim presses the suspect to respond.

text: Weigh a suspect's spoken accounts of their inner state against their observed behavior, since self-reports are often unreliable.
when: when a character describes their own feelings or condition
why: Spoken claims about one's state can be false, while behavior is observed directly.

text: State a plausible wrong theory openly, so attentive players can later compare it with the true account and find where it failed.
why: a visible wrong theory rewards careful reasoning rather than surprising the player

text: Have characters state the limits of what they know, such as having a strong idea but no proof. This keeps their reasoning credible.
when: A character offers a theory without full evidence.
why: Acknowledged uncertainty makes a character more believable.

text: Check quoted wording and copies against the original; copies hide omissions, misfiled items, copying slips, and a single transcription error in an address.
when: Relying on a copy of a record or quoted wording
why: Treating a copy as the original document can mislead investigators.

text: A single word or overheard phrase can carry several meanings; keep each reading open, since a first reading may be wrong until a fact or fuller conversation selects one.
when: a key remark has no clear referent, or a partial overheard line is interpreted
why: Meaning depends on the surrounding exchange.

text: An ambiguous line from a character can carry a harmless reading and a revealing one, and which reading wins depends on what the listener already suspects.
A witness may deny having used a word that the questioner clearly remembers them saying, so disputes over wording are settled only by a written record.
when: A witness disputes the exact words used
why: Memories of specific wording are unreliable on both sides

text: Record transcription corrections separately from original wording and spelling, so originals stay recoverable and readers know what was altered before trusting a word.
why: Altered words can change how a name or claim reads.

text: Make overheard, through-wall or phone-call NPC speech ambiguous about who is speaking, so players must question witnesses to resolve the speaker.
when: designing speech heard through doors or walls

text: Read a note for what it implies as well as states, since insinuation can alarm more than claims; treat it as a motive source, not settled proof of cause.
when: Analyzing a written message whose meaning goes beyond its literal content.
why: Implication carried by phrasing can affect a recipient more than explicit claims do.

text: A dying NPC's cryptic line can point at several people; the player's record of who was present and what they knew should decide the reading.
when: designing ambiguous last words
why: knowledge state resolves ambiguity

text: Keep clue wording short and ambiguous enough that players must test it rather than take it at face value.
Test each ambiguous word in a statement against the speaker's situation and knowledge to decide whether it was meant literally or figuratively.
Do not rely on a public witness appeal as the main line of inquiry, since the subject may have travelled in a private vehicle unseen.
When a witness's story is told both impaired and sober, weigh the sober telling more heavily.
Record who reported each statement and to whom, since the source of a clue is part of the clue itself.
when: writing a case where information travels through several people
why: the chain of reporters determines how much the player trusts it

text: Reading a suspect's own recorded words back to him can expose a contradiction he cannot easily deny.
when: Recorded remarks conflict with his later account.

text: An ambiguous remark or overheard phrase, even an offer of help heard as a threat, can carry many meanings; reading guilt into it before weighing context is speculation.
when: a remark can be read two ways
why: Meaning depends on context and what the listener knows.

text: Quoted speech is only as reliable as a witness's memory and honesty; a single misheard or misremembered word can invert a retold report's meaning.
when: a witness repeats another person's words
why: partial observation distorts recalled dialogue

text: Translated or unrecorded wording can lose nuance, so readings based on it need caution.
A translation can carry the commissioner's assumptions, and later readers who trust it inherit those assumptions.
A suspect's own words, quoted out of context, can be used to build a case out of genuine feeling.
Ambiguous words spoken in anger can mean different things. Read the final words against tone and manner, not the wording alone.
when: when a last remark might signal intent
why: delivery can reverse the apparent meaning of words

text: One incorrect detail in a witness account, such as a wrong station name, can shift the whole sequence. Check each detail against a reference source before building on it.
why: Errors propagate through every later inference.

text: Stressing one word in a witness's wording can read as doubt, though it may be only a feeling.
A refusal to answer can come from shame or from protecting someone else, so it cannot be read as a confession.
An interviewer who responds only to tearful appeals can be drawn away from the questions that matter.
when: when a suspect shifts to pleading
why: emotion can crowd out the factual line of questioning

text: A statement read back to a witness and sworn to is not the same as an account first taken independently from them.
why: Reading back can shape or harden the first version.

text: A pleading voice from behind a barrier can be read in more than one way, so listeners may disagree about what it means.
1) Read each statement back and fix it on record. 2) Sort it as lead, background or proof. 3) Treat detailed length as no evidence of proof. 4) Note absences without treating them as proof.
when: A large set of statements must be assessed for a case
why: Statements serve different purposes and must be sorted before weighing

text: 1) Put each accuser's claim to the suspect. 2) Record the suspect's answer to each claim. 3) Keep the answers on record so they can be checked against the full examination later.
when: when examining a suspect against several accusations
why: a summary can misreport what was said

text: 1) Record each statement in order. 2) Note new names or details that appear. 3) Check whether they arrived after outside information was introduced, which suggests they were supplied, not recalled.
when: comparing a suspect's successive statements

text: 1) Standardize spelling to one modern form. 2) Leave words and sentence structure unchanged. 3) Adjust punctuation to carry the original sense. 4) Keep archaic forms where the old wording affects meaning.
when: Publishing a modernized edition of old records
why: Consistent edits keep meaning intact while improving readability.

text: 1) Ask who said what, in what words, and to whom. 2) Ask whether the original speaker used those words. 3) Obtain the original document where possible before reacting.
when: A witness repeats another person's disputed words.
why: Summaries and relays can shift meaning, so the source must be tested.

text: Write NPC dialogue so one line reads two ways and signals different things by player knowledge, leading to a different suspect or location.
when: designing a clue delivered as dialogue
why: a second reading rewards returning with new knowledge

text: Write down small errors that favour the accused, even when none is damaging, and check them.
when: a witness's account has minor inaccuracies
why: Minor errors can hide patterns that matter.

text: Give a suspect two dialogue states: a public face in company and a private one when the player finds them alone.
Answer an alternative explanation with new evidence rather than by restating the original conclusion.
when: When a suspect or rival disputes an inference.
why: Repetition does not distinguish between the two explanations.

text: Make NPC references such as the usual service or the night watch ambiguous, and let the player ask follow-up questions to resolve contradictions.
Track each version of a captured enemy's or NPC's account in dialogue, and let contradictions unlock the next investigation step.
Let players confront the source to check exact wording, since a mismatch can unlock a new line of questioning.
when: Designing rumour verification mechanics.
why: Verification gameplay rewards players who compare relayed and original words.

text: A witness who repeats one stock explanation yields little, while a talkative witness can offer useful facts when followed up.
when: questioning a witness
why: A stock answer closes the topic, whereas open talk exposes details

text: A stereotype-based inference can be built as a trap that rewards players who test the assumption.

Accounts forced into stock phrases or matching a familiar stock figure are shaped by expectations, stripping atmosphere and motive; treat them as interpretation, not raw observation, and distrust them.
why: Witness expectations shape such accounts, and stock phrasing strips atmosphere and motive, so retold accounts are interpreted rather than raw observation.

text: Judging who could be harmed or who is the culprit by assumed traits (reputation, cheerfulness, gender or other stereotypes) is weak; test such assumptions against evidence before narrowing suspects.
when: judging who could be a target or culprit, or building a profile from assumed traits
why: Reputation and temperament do not determine who is harmed or who did it; stereotypes can exclude or include suspects for the wrong reasons.

text: Inferring a person's appearance from national stereotype treats an assumption as evidence and can send the investigation the wrong way.
why: Stereotypes are not observations of the individual.

text: Give a stock explanation for a missing ally that contains a contradiction the player can find.
A thief may take a single unit and keep it in reserve, so a one-item shortage can be deliberate rather than accidental.
when: A small, single item is missing from a controlled store.
why: One unit may be enough for a purpose that the thief plans to use later.

text: Information that raises the value of an object makes theft a more plausible motive for targeting it.
Known valuables carried by a person weigh against suicide and in favour of homicide, suggesting a motive.
when: When a death involves a person known to carry valuable property.
why: Valuables give a plausible reason for an attack.

text: When a theft ignores obvious valuables and takes one item, treat that item as the target rather than general loot.
when: a theft skips valuables

text: Small, portable losses narrow the likely type of thief.
when: a series of thefts takes only easily carried items
why: The kind of goods taken points toward a kind of thief.

text: A stolen item that needs the owner's personal authorisation is useless to thieves, so taking it reveals that they misjudged their target.
when: When evaluating a theft

text: A stolen-object chase follows an item through successive owners, and the thief is often a trusted insider rather than the most suspected person.
when: Designing a theft mystery
why: The item's chain of custody gives the player a path, and the insider's position hides the thief.

text: An unsold stolen item does not prove the theft was pointless; the thief may be waiting for a safe moment to sell.
when: When stolen goods have not yet surfaced
why: Delayed resale is a normal pattern

text: 1) Offer a promise of no prosecution in exchange for information. 2) Name a price for the stolen items. 3) Use the agreement to learn where the goods are held.
when: Stolen property is held by a third party such as a receiver.
why: A deal gives a holder of stolen goods reason to disclose their location.

text: 1) List everyone told the object existed. 2) Add household members deliberately kept ignorant, since they are still inside the house. 3) Add anyone who could have received the knowledge through an informant.
1) Establish what was valuable and where it was kept. 2) Identify who knew of the hiding place. 3) Check the financial picture. 4) Note the victim's routines and who watched them.
when: A theft is assumed to be the motive but has not been tested

text: Stolen goods carry provenance, so a found item matching a known loot list can link to a specific theft and to its hideout.
when: Designing items taken from a crime and placed in the world

text: Give stolen items an engraved name or crest that points the player to the owner or to an NPC linked to that owner.
when: Designing a stolen item clue
why: A readable mark links an item to a person

text: Plant a tempting motive, such as a valuable item whose value or purpose does not match the crime, so players must look for the larger plan.
when: In mystery design

text: A direct seizure from a dangerous, guarded target risks the taker's life, while a covert swap avoids confrontation but depends on a controlled diversion.
Record when a found watch or mechanical timer stopped and compare that moment with the event timeline, since a stopped mechanism freezes a datable time.
when: a watch or mechanical timer is found halted
why: A stopped mechanism freezes a moment that can be dated against the schedule.

text: A stopped timer fixes an event time only if it was running then and stopped because of that event, not from an unrelated cause such as running down.
when: a stopped clock is used as a timestamp
why: A clock not running at the event cannot record its time, and coincidental stops mislead.

text: Shock or unconsciousness leaves a witness's sense of time imprecise, so their timing becomes approximate.
when: a witness has fainted or been in distress
why: Unconsciousness and distress disrupt how the witness judges elapsed time.

text: A stopped clock shows only the moment it stopped, so any later time must be inferred from other references.
A steamship arrives almost as fast as its letter, while a sailing ship is slow. A long gap between letter and event suggests sailing travel.
why: steam removes most of the delay

text: Mechanical timers often stop when physically shocked, so a stopped timer may mark the moment of an impact.
when: a timer was on a body during a violent event
why: shock can disrupt the mechanism

text: A lamp still burning in daylight shows someone was active in the room recently.
when: A light source is found running at an unexpected time
why: Fuel burns only while someone keeps it lit or leaves it on

text: Compare a suspect's stated plan with the reconstructed timing; a mismatch in the stated hour can expose an alibi.
A stated wish, such as a request to be woken early, fixes when others expected a person to be active.
An object that should be running but has stopped may carry a false time or a deliberate sign, so its reading must be examined before it is accepted.
when: an object's state contradicts its expected state
why: a stopped object can mislead about when an event happened

text: Fixed clocks, watches and calculated doses fix a timeline and can expose what someone knew or intended.
when: A timeline must be proven or a suspect's account of time must be checked.
why: Objective time records are harder to dispute than recollection.

text: Do not accept a stopped or moved clock as event-time proof unless checking whether it stopped by accident or was set by hand; mechanisms fail or are manipulated.
when: a stopped or moved clock is used to fix when an event happened
why: Clocks can be set or stopped by hand or fail mechanically, so they can suggest a false hour.

text: Record each change to a fixture with its time and origin, then test any official explanation for it against what witnesses saw.
Pair each fixture state change with a plausible in-world excuse, and let players find that the excuse conflicts with the recorded facts.
This structure map divides a mystery story into setup, clues, suspicion, misdirect, pressure, oddities, reveal and resolution, with percentages marking their positions in the text.
A mystery story can use a convenient suspect and a false theory, with the decisive clues placed in environmental details rather than human motives.
Clue flow has three phases: front-loaded opening clues, a steady trickle during the main action, and a late cluster that turns the reader toward the resolution.
when: Planning clue placement across a story
why: Each phase serves a different job

text: A trial-then-investigation mystery opens with the prosecution's case, then an amateur inquiry reverses it through a chain of false solutions, each supported by a real clue.
1) Hook and premise, 0-3% of length. 2) False frame, 3-8%. 3) Complication, 8-25%. 4) False solution, 25-42%. 5) Reveal, 48-59%. 6) Crisis, 65-82%. 7) Aftermath, 88-98%.
when: pacing a mystery across its full length
why: Fixed phases keep the reveal in the middle third and the peak of danger late.

text: A stranger cannot be released on his own word; without a known local guarantor, detention lasts longer.
when: when a protagonist lacks local standing
why: Release depends on someone vouching for the detainee.

text: Claims from a stranger, including a reveal resting on his word alone, may be wrong or guessed and are treated as suspicious until checked before believing or acting.
1) Ask for a general physical description first. 2) Ask about height relative to the witness, build, face, skin and marked features. 3) Follow with a direct recognition question.
when: A witness's memory of a brief encounter with a stranger is the main lead.
why: Staged questioning moves from general to specific features, which improves recall.

text: Emotional strain can distort an investigator's judgement and push them to abandon investigation altogether.
Stress and confusion reduce recall, so a witness's silence on details may reflect the circumstances rather than concealment.
when: a witness is questioned about a frightening period
why: Stressful events impair memory of the details

text: A person under strain may brood, lash out at work and neglect routine duties, all of which are visible to colleagues.
Sudden physical changes such as draining color, averted gaze, dry lips, or repeated mouth wiping often appear when a witness hears a sensitive name or fact.
when: When a questioner raises a topic the witness wants to avoid.
why: Stress produces involuntary bodily reactions that betray concealed knowledge.

text: An NPC's stress threshold can trigger a volatile outburst that mixes true clues with false accusations.
when: an NPC is under sustained questioning
why: pressure lowers control over what is said

text: A declaration signed in haste under emotional strain may read as hysteria rather than remorse, so it is unreliable as an account of facts.
when: When a statement is written under pressure

text: A tester who holds the wrong reading explains away contrary facts with increasingly strained inferences rather than abandoning the reading.
when: When a favored hypothesis faces growing contradictions.
why: Commitment to a reading makes each contradiction seem explainable.

text: Financial strain can look like motive even when the accused is not personally responsible for the loss that caused it.
Give a character a composure or stress meter so players notice holding back through behavior rather than through statements.
Hairstyle and dress reveal an item's period, so stylistic features can date a photograph to an earlier time.
why: fashions change in recognizable ways

text: When a writer's style is more formal than their education supports, the statement's aim becomes too visible to hide.
A stray original document can be decisive, but it can also be wrong, so it must be tested like any other source.
why: Originals carry authority but can contain errors or be superseded.

text: Doubt based on style or precision is evidence about the text, not proof of falsehood; the core claim may still be true and should be weighed separately.
why: Stylistic oddity and factual error are different things.

text: Store document contents as structured text so the game can show exactly what was promised and to whom.
when: Building letters, contracts or notes that carry promises
why: Structured records let the game check and display exact terms

text: A weaker final act may point to a different perpetrator, but style alone can mislead since one person may behave differently at a case's end.
when: Comparing a case's final act with its earlier acts to judge whether the same perpetrator committed them
why: A perpetrator's style can differ from earlier acts, yet one person may also behave differently at the end of a case.

text: Ordinary human behavior, such as imaginative play, can explain strange conduct and make it less alarming, but this does not make the person's account trustworthy.
when: a witness's odd conduct has a harmless-looking explanation

text: Early small signs, such as a repeated wish to visit a location, can point to the real human cause before the reveal.
when: Planting a hidden human cause behind a supernatural event
why: Prevents the reveal feeling arbitrary

text: Offer a supernatural or official explanation early to absorb the first theory of an impossible event, so the audience sets it aside once evidence appears.
when: at the opening of an impossible-event mystery
why: an easy answer satisfies the first question until evidence contradicts it

text: Give a stated cause for a missing marker, such as forced sale or seizure, so its absence feels explained rather than arbitrary.
A dream sequence that leaves a physical state change on waking, such as an injury or status effect, makes the illusion checkable, so the deception is fair.
when: when a story or game stages apparent events, such as dreams or hallucinations, that are later undercut
why: The physical sign gives the audience a checkable clue, converting an apparent event into evidence they can verify.

text: Dreams often borrow imagery from recent experience, with places and people reappearing in altered form, so strange content can have a rational origin.
when: An uncanny image appears that may trace back to the character's recent experience.
why: Dream content recombines what the mind recently encountered, so the source is often ordinary.

text: Revealing that a feared threat was a dream or delusion recasts earlier encounters as possibly imagined, reframing the story after the fact.
A reasonable false explanation keeps the audience calm; when the true cause appears, it reads as a correction rather than a cheat.
when: a reveal overturns an explanation the audience accepted
why: The audience had a plausible account they can now see was wrong.

text: Cases can be sorted into three classes: subjective, external, or mixed, which helps judge how far each explanation can be trusted.
A clue shown to the reader and later explained away must still match the physical facts, or the reader will notice the gap.
when: Writing a clue that is dismissed by an in-story explanation
why: Mismatch between explanation and physical facts breaks reader trust

text: Explaining away an odd detail, such as an unusual voice or mask, without asking what it rules out lets a flawed theory survive.
when: when an anomaly fits a convenient explanation
why: Dismissing anomalies removes the evidence that would expose the error.

text: 1) Split each strange event into its component sensations. 2) Assign each sensation a candidate ordinary cause. 3) Test each cause against the physical scene. 4) Keep the explanation provisional until physical evidence supports it.
when: A sequence of odd events seems supernatural but each piece might share a common cause
why: Separating components exposes which parts a rational cause fails to cover

text: Use a dream or vision as a foreshadowing cue whose details map to real NPCs and places, so the player can check them.
when: Designing a foreshadowing sequence.
why: Checkable details turn foreshadowing into a clue the player can verify.

text: If the story should remain supernatural, rule out the human explanation explicitly.
when: Writing a genuinely supernatural mystery.
why: Without explicit elimination, readers assume a grounded cause and the supernatural claim loses force.

text: In a place with almost no animal life, a fresh animal sign is conspicuous and carries more weight than it would in a crowded setting.
when: when an isolated setting has few animals
why: The rarity of animal activity makes any sign stand out.

text: Many apparent hauntings are solved by thorough search and an open mind, and human devices such as wire, hidden bells or ceiling gaps often explain them.
when: Unexplained events occur and a human agent is plausible
why: Ordinary mechanisms are more common than supernatural ones.

text: A previous in-world incident can reveal the hidden mechanic that explains a present contradiction.
when: Designing lore that supports a present-day puzzle
why: Players connect the past record to the current puzzle and infer the mechanic

text: A local legend regarded as a tale becomes credible when physical evidence in place ties it to a specific site and a written account confirms it.
A local legend can serve as a false frame that a human plot exploits, so the belief in the fable becomes part of the crime's power.
when: Building a locale with folklore that hides a real antagonist
why: The antagonist gains influence from the community's acceptance of the myth.

text: Build an apparent supernatural event around a hidden or disguised human actor; give the human cause the same visible traces, so investigators check arrangement, not label, weighing both explanations.
when: A story offers a supernatural explanation for a frightening event

text: If every character dismisses a legend, players have no reason to take it seriously; give at least one character a reason to believe it.
Plant a lore fact early, then pay it off with a physical injury or mark on a character, turning an abstract myth into verifiable proof.
when: Designing a reveal the player can check.
why: A matching physical sign ties a myth to a specific character.

text: Scatter a torn lore document across rooms with straight edges and overlapping words as solvable constraints, and let later pieces resolve ambiguous text.
when: Designing a document-assembly puzzle for a player
why: Physical fit and later context give the player a checkable way to reconstruct the text

text: Use an in-world reference such as a note or book to point to deeper lore, so an unresolved detail becomes an optional follow-up.
when: Leaving a minor detail unexplained in a level
why: A referenced source turns an open question into an invitation rather than a defect

text: Let the player suspect a legend exists before revealing its link to a place, so the discovery answers a question they already hold.
Item-by-item human explanations suit cases where most events have ordinary mechanisms. Forcing a human frame onto thin evidence overreaches.
when: When deciding whether to explain an anomaly through a concealed human action.

text: Renaming an impossible feat with a different label, such as telepathy or levitation, does not change what the act physically requires; the label is not an explanation.
when: A rational or mystic label is offered for a strange event.
why: Labels describe an effect without showing its mechanism.

text: 1) Trace each link in the chain of testimony back to whoever witnessed the event. 2) Check whether each witness was present. 3) Accept the supernatural claim only if every link holds.
when: when a supernatural explanation is offered for an event
why: Testing each link exposes the mundane explanation hidden in the chain.

text: Resolve a supernatural threat through a relationship or social act rather than a kill, so the climax carries emotional resolution.
when: When the threat stems from a hidden personal desire or conflict
why: Ending the threat through a human change gives the climax emotional weight instead of only combat payoff.

text: When a game offers a curse or ghost explanation, check whether each event has a human motive, planning and a beneficiary; if so, make the human explanation discoverable.
when: Designing a supernatural mystery with a hidden human cause
why: Players reward a mystery whose rational answer is findable.

text: Check the source of a supernatural claim before accepting or dismissing it; approach the sound and identify its origin.
when: Evaluating a local legend or eerie report in a mystery setting.
why: Rumours can mask ordinary causes that direct observation exposes.

text: A fake supernatural effect exposed by a single captured frame lets the reveal rest on one controllable piece of evidence that the eye missed.
when: Designing a hidden mechanism meant to look occult
why: A photograph can record a detail that observation during the event did not register, so one artifact can overturn the supernatural reading.

text: Not every superstition or false belief signals guilt; treating a characterisation device as evidence against someone is a mistake.

1) Separate the claimed cause, such as madness, curse or inherited taint, from observable conduct. 2) Ask whether a physical agent with a motive could have acted. 3) Trace who could reach the object or location, and check planning and beneficiary. 4) Prefer the human explanation with clear motive and execution that fits these physical and motive constraints.
when: An unusual or uncanny event is explained as irrational or supernatural
why: Most apparent supernatural acts reduce to a physical mover with a reason to act; physical and motive constraints separate plausible explanations from implausible ones.

text: 1) Identify the mundane mechanism a legend could hide, such as a concealed key or passage. 2) Search the fabric of the place, including ground and fixtures, for it. 3) Accept the explanation only after the physical search confirms it; skipping this hides human action.
when: A legend or seemingly impossible event explains a disappearance or anomaly and the place may hide a mechanism.
why: Acting on the hypothesis verifies it rather than relying on testimony; physical records often explain apparent impossibilities.

text: 1) Name each non-human explanation offered, such as a curse or accident. 2) Check each against where every object lies. 3) Compare when an injury occurred with when the damage happened. 4) Set aside explanations that cannot be tested.
when: In a game with supernatural elements, when a curse or accident story is offered

text: 1) For each claimed effect, list the physical conditions it requires, such as sound, movement, or a hidden body. 2) Identify who could produce those conditions. 3) Test the candidate mechanisms until one separates from the others.
when: An unverified effect is offered as proof of an unseen cause
why: Specifying requirements turns a claim into checkable conditions

text: Surplus stock sold at auction often carries markings, such as on collars or waistbands, that identify it as condemned stock.
Bulk stored raw materials found without their finished form indicate what was being made or prepared.
when: A scene holds large quantities of unfinished material.
why: Stock reveals the activity that consumes it.

text: Regular movement of food or supplies toward a location implies someone is being fed there, even if no one is seen.
Total a person's transactions over a period, since repeated sales or payments can add up to a large, deliberate sum that single entries hide.
A store lead can yield several candidates; a label narrows the field without naming the person.
Count a remaining supply against its recorded amount to rule out or confirm an extra dose or missing item.
when: When a substance or item may explain a death or event.

text: Show planted clues, such as hidden messages, weapons or objects, openly before the reveal, so the later explanation feels fair in hindsight.
when: Planting a hidden message, weapon or object that will matter later.
why: Visible but unremarked evidence makes the reveal feel fair and rewards attentive players when its role is revealed.

text: Surfaces in prolonged contact with a person, such as a bed, are likely places for residue, so sample them most carefully.
why: Long contact transfers more material to the surface.

text: Plant a decisive marker, such as a name marked on an item, in plain sight, where it reads as meaningless until the interpretation changes.
when: Designing clues for a substitution reveal
why: The clue is visible from the start, so its meaning comes from a later change in framework.

text: A prolonged waiting period strains watchers, and small noises can mislead them.
when: a trap requires a long wait
why: fatigue and noise degrade observation

text: Keep findings quiet, especially from associates of a suspect, so no one is warned.
when: When an investigation is still active.
why: Warning a suspect or their friends lets evidence be hidden or altered.

text: A surveillance log is a day-by-day timeline of a suspect's visits, meetings, meals, calls and money movements, with times, places, companions and contacts, read as a sequence.
Surveillance means posting a watcher at a fixed point, such as a house opposite, to record a suspect's movements and contacts over time.
Documented facts such as sworn statements, a medical certificate, a funeral and recognition by family outweigh interpretations of a witness's mental state.
when: a claim is judged on the record
why: checkable records resist psychological explanation

text: Partial physical records can survive destruction, and a fragment such as an unburned edge can still carry a date or detail that anchors a reconstruction.
Surveillance shows behavior but rarely proves contact; use it to test what a suspect does next, not to confirm a link.
Organise case notes into one record per person plus one for loose facts, so contradictions between accounts become visible.
when: from the first day of an investigation, when facts arrive unsorted
why: Separate records make conflicting statements easy to compare

text: A photographer's studio records can identify a portrait's sitter and supply the sitter's address.
when: an unknown person appears in a photograph
why: studios keep sitter details

text: Store each claimed detail, such as place, time and companion, so the player can later compare an NPC's statements against other evidence.
when: designing NPC dialogue and quest state

text: Cases that left a documentary trail may not represent the rest; surviving records can give a distorted picture of how common an event was.
A watch that begins after an event will miss an entry that happened before it started.
when: Relying on surveillance to bound a time window.
why: Coverage gaps before the watch leave the earlier window unobserved.

text: Trace the chain of succession by asking who inherits if the present heir dies, since title and land may pass along a fixed line.
when: an heir stands to gain from a death
why: A successor beyond the heir can also be a motive holder.

text: 1) Watch the target over a long period from a hidden vantage. 2) Wait for a single window of opportunity. 3) Act in that window and remove traces afterward.
1) Identify each beneficiary's share. 2) When one beneficiary dies, check whether their share passes equally to the others. 3) Recalculate what each survivor would receive if only one remains.
when: when a series of deaths might be linked to inheritance
why: survivorship clauses shift shares as beneficiaries die

text: In closed-case mysteries the culprit is usually someone already present in the scene, so the question is which person in the room could have acted.
Rank suspects by access and relationship to the victim, not equally; ranking narrows the field but establishes neither motive nor a deed.
when: a timeline is partly fixed, or when designing a suspect list the player can investigate

text: When several characters have motives, test each one's claims against facts before accepting any accusation.
when: more than one suspect has a plausible motive
why: shared motives do not identify the actor

text: Let a rational authority supply a human suspect, then let that suspect fade, so the player must decide who the real threat is.
when: when the mystery should move from a mundane explanation to an open question
why: A discarded suspect shifts the player's suspicion and keeps the threat ambiguous.

text: At the start of a theft mystery, map the inheritance chain and rank suspects by who gains, not by who is loudest.
when: Beginning a theft investigation with family or estate ties
why: Gain from the object is a stronger signal than noise

text: Make each named suspect a separate branch the player checks in turn, so the investigation has a clear order of tests.
when: Designing a mystery with several named suspects.
why: Separate branches give the player a manageable sequence rather than one tangled question.

text: Make an innocent suspect a plausible false solution by tying them to one incriminating fact, and let the player see the gap.
Let the investigator catch the suspect before the motive is known, so the final act concerns meaning rather than who did it.
when: a mystery whose motive lies in a hidden past
why: a solved whodunit leaves the late story to explain why

text: A mystery can be built as a chain of hunts, where a dismissed explanation gives way to a secret investigator who follows successive suspects, each overturned by the next.
when: structuring a detective investigation
why: A chain of overturned theories keeps the player moving forward while the true explanation stays hidden.

text: If no human suspect is raised before a supernatural reveal, the eventual ghost explanation has no alternative to test against and feels arbitrary.
when: Building a mystery that ends in an occult explanation
why: A human alternative that the player can consider and reject makes the final explanation feel earned.

text: 1) Weigh each suspect's motive, means and access separately. 2) Check whether the suspect could have known the terms that make the motive work. 3) Ask who was present when each physical clue was recovered. 4) Treat background pressures as context only.
when: narrowing a list of suspects with overlapping access where the evidence must be weighed fairly
why: Motive, access and evidence reliability are distinct, and mixing them produces unfair accusations; a suspect may fit one factor strongly and fail the others.

text: 1) Ask who could physically reach the victims. 2) Ask who knew and trusted them. 3) Ask who had a reason to harm them, using background history to answer.
when: Physical traces are thin and suspects must be narrowed

text: 1) List everyone who could have placed the cause. 2) List who could obtain the means. 3) List who gained from the result. 4) Tie each list to a record that can be checked independently.
when: several people had access and the case turns on who could both obtain and benefit from the means

text: Give each suspect its own evidence trail: one clue that makes them seem the answer, then a new fact that clears or rebalances them, so the player revises the theory.
when: writing a rotation of suspects in a mystery
why: Each specific new fact keeps shifts in suspicion grounded and believable, and testing each suspect keeps the search alive.

text: Test an unfashionable line of inquiry before deciding it is wrong; dropping it merely for being unpopular is an error.
Give suspects access and daily routines that conflict with a supernatural story, so the player must check the human explanation.
when: When designing suspects in a mystery
why: Conflicting routines make the human explanation testable

text: Give each secondary suspect a full cycle of spotlight so no single false solution lasts too long.
when: Balancing a cast of suspects
why: Rotating focus keeps the mystery moving and prevents fatigue.

text: A witness may hide a visit by someone who had little good feeling toward the victim, because its discovery would make the household seem implicated.
when: a visitor had a grudge against the victim
why: the visit would implicate the household

text: A warning given in ordinary conversation can conceal its purpose, which the listener may only understand afterwards.
when: A character warns a suspect casually
why: Ordinary framing lowers the listener's guard

text: A visible irregularity can belong to a separate, innocent secret rather than to the main event.
A detective-style case can hinge on a victim who is secretly the agent, so the reveal reverses who is blamed for the disturbance.
An obvious early motive or visibly angry suspect can pull attention from the real trail; track it for later contradiction instead of chasing it.
when: Designing or reading a mystery with an early apparent motive
why: Players tend to accept a visible motive as the answer before checking other evidence

text: A hidden mastermind is often an unnoticed servant or clerk who stays out of view while others hold the visible roles.
Leave visible an item whose removal would look odd, such as one the owner was known to possess.
when: when a search would notice an absence
why: removing a known item draws suspicion

text: A visible threat can make one party carry a message to another without alerting them to a concealed plan.
A villain's written lore or journal can reveal the vanity or fixation that players can exploit, and NPC traits can be tied to predictable mistakes such as returning to a scene.
when: Designing antagonists whose weaknesses should be discoverable
why: Self-revealing writing gives players a way to anticipate the character's errors.

text: Make the hidden agent someone close to the protagonist, such as a household member or party member.
when: Designing the source of a mystery's threat.
why: Proximity raises stakes and makes suspicion shift inward.

text: A key figure hidden among many similar background characters is hard to identify, so investigators can move unnoticed.
A villain who acts on misinformation creates an opening, because a player who learns the false belief can use it against them.
A hidden director may set accusation order through visible actors; players should check who sets the sequence, which may be older or hidden figures, and be able to expose the director.
An ideal offender must be meticulous, unseen, without friends or dependents, and quick in mind and body.
when: When designing or judging a perfect criminal.
why: These requirements define an ideal that real offenders fail to meet.

text: A mystery can run as a ladder of decoy suspects: each is raised to presumptive guilt, then cleared, while the true culprit stays in view from the opening scene.
why: Repeated reversals keep the player's attention moving away from the culprit.

text: A planned crime is idealised and leaves out incidental difficulties; real execution introduces errors the plan does not contain.
A vivid reaction hides the performer's control over it, so observers who do not test it let staging pass as genuine.
Overplaying a suspect's confidence makes the reveal seem arranged rather than earned.
when: Writing a suspect who is certain they will not be caught.
why: Excessive certainty reads as authorial convenience, weakening the reveal.

text: Give every suspect a genuine non-criminal secret or small domestic oddity, set up early, so a wrong suspect is reasonable and suspicion shifts naturally once the mechanism is visible.
why: A plausible wrong suspect keeps the solution fair.

text: Show an NPC's behaviour before revealing the threat behind it, so players must later reconcile the behaviour with the hidden cause.
Make a villain's signature, such as a particular lure, drink or device, appear in two earlier incidents so players infer the pattern and expect it again.
when: Designing a recurring antagonist.

text: Give each suspect a visible gain from an event, such as a vacancy or a rival's removal, so players can reason about motive.
when: Designing suspects in narrative or dungeon generation.

text: Give a suspect NPC a warm dialogue style that conceals motive, and provide a documented record that contradicts the spoken story.
Hide opportunistic accusers among genuine witnesses, so the player must separate private gain from honest report.
Make an intermediary NPC who quietly suppresses reports to curry favor a hidden mechanic that the player can uncover.
when: designing hidden plot mechanics

text: Make the most convincing suspect a trusted insider, so the reveal reverses a belief the player already holds.
when: When choosing the apparent culprit for a mystery.
why: Reversing a strong belief creates a more satisfying reveal.

text: Give a culprit NPC a realistic capability level so the solution is reachable without requiring a flawless plan.
when: Designing an antagonist's competence for a mystery puzzle.
why: Realistic capability keeps the puzzle solvable and the culprit credible.

text: Give antagonists a concrete, checkable motive, such as a debt or a rival's gain, that players can discover through documents or NPCs.
when: when designing an antagonist's backstory
why: Discoverable motives reward investigation and make villains credible.

text: Cast doubt on a second trusted figure before the final reveal, so the last unmasking carries higher stakes.
when: the hidden antagonist is a late-revealed ally
why: A prior doubt makes the final suspect feel like a real risk

text: Spread suspicion across several characters who each have a motive and an alibi, so attention does not settle on one suspect or location.
when: Multiple incidents occur in different places.
why: Diffused evidence weakens the pull toward any one suspect.

text: Use the skill a task requires to filter suspects: work that can be done from memory needs no physical copy, while copying requires the physical materials and training.
when: When the object's theft depended on a specialized skill.
why: Only some suspects could have produced the result with their abilities.

text: A single fast answer is only a lead until corroborated, so it should be noted and checked rather than pressed immediately.
when: Receiving a quick answer from a witness
why: Fast answers can be managed and are unverified

text: Keep separate leads apart, such as a record, a deal and a named person, until evidence connects them.
when: A case has several unrelated threads

text: Most cases are explained by the simplest account; the real difficulty is proving it rather than finding it.
Let the wrong suspect be a sincere actor who believes what they see, which makes the false solution convincing.
when: designing a false solution
why: A sincere mistake reads as credible, unlike a clear liar.

text: A single alternative explanation can be as unsupported as the claim it challenges, so it must be tested like any other.
Treating every incident as the work of one person can hide a second actor, so test whether the events truly share a single perpetrator.
when: When a series of events is attributed to one suspect
why: Assuming a single source overlooks a second party with separate goals.

text: A detective's first argument can be wrong and reversed by a later confession, so mysteries should allow the leading theory to be overturned.
when: structuring suspicion across a scenario
why: Players who commit to one theory feel cheated if the reversal is unsupported.

text: 1) Identify the uncanny event. 2) List plausible human or mundane sources. 3) Check each against available evidence. 4) Mark the event open if no source is confirmed.
when: An unexplained event could have an ordinary cause that has not yet been tested.
why: Assuming the supernatural before testing ordinary causes leads to unfounded conclusions, while assuming ordinary causes without evidence hides real unknowns.

text: Question suspects apart from one another so their accounts cannot be aligned or reconciled with each other.
when: When more than one suspect is linked to the same act.
why: Separate accounts reveal contradictions that shared accounts conceal.

text: Make each new piece of evidence reframe the suspect list rather than only add to it, so the player feels the culprit has changed.
Elimination reaches a sound conclusion only when all of its premises are true; one false premise undermines the whole deduction.
when: Concluding the culprit by eliminating other suspects.
why: The conclusion inherits any weakness in its premises.

text: When a crime is suspected, check whether the body could practically be disposed of; if disposal would be implausible, doubt the crime explanation.
when: Testing a murder theory against physical evidence.
why: Murder requires removing the body, so the logistics constrain which explanations are credible.

text: A fact the investigator already holds can rule out a hypothesis that a clue seems to support.
Give the public a false culprit with physical evidence, so the player must test that evidence rather than accept it.
when: the public has already named a suspect
why: Testing the evidence forces the player to reason about it instead of following the crowd.

text: Treat only facts that agree across several independent accounts of the same event as firm; conflicting versions are not reliable.
when: when sources disagree about an event

text: A system that looks airtight may depend on a human habit, such as forms relaxing over time, that becomes the real weak point.
when: Assessing the security of a procedure-bound system
why: Human routines can bypass formal safeguards

text: Do not accept a door as an exit merely because it is near a trail's end; its direction and distance must match the prints.
Keep the question of how someone entered separate from why they entered, since a thief who left an item behind poses a different problem.
Make the character who controls entry to a sealed space the culprit or hazard, with that control shown on the page from the start.
why: players trust that character, so the lock is the trust placed in them

text: A source who turns pale, refuses to discuss a matter, or gives only a limited assurance signals concealment, even though the reaction reveals no fact directly.
when: the source is questioned about a sensitive matter
why: distress and evasion show that the source is hiding something

text: A guilty suspect confronted with a precise question about the victims can panic and act in ways that expose their guilt.
when: an interrogation scene near the climax
why: Direct questions about a hidden act can overwhelm a guilty person's composure.

text: A guilty character's fear of discovery can make innocent events look like threats, because the fear is built on their own guilt.
when: when a concealing character hears a summons, noise or questions
why: Guilt primes the character to read ordinary events as danger.

text: A character can be guilty of a lesser wrong, such as sending a note, while innocent of the central crime, such as the killing.
why: Involvement in a plot and guilt for the act are separate questions

text: Flag a protagonist's reticence early, so that a later disclosure of guilt feels earned rather than sudden.
A supernatural excuse offered for failure can signal that a method is being concealed rather than that the effect is genuine.
when: An interested party explains a failed effect with an unseen cause
why: Excuses often protect the mechanism behind an effect

text: Separate two questions in a mystery: whether events form a deliberate pattern, and whether that pattern can be proved and punished.
when: designing or analysing a case where the culprit may be known without proof
why: knowing the answer and being able to prove it are distinct states

text: Reading fear as proof of guilt in the main crime is a mistake when it may only reflect the false news; check it against what the bait said.
A visible personal motive such as rivalry or jealousy draws suspicion onto anyone it connects to, even when the real scheme lies elsewhere.
when: when several characters have openly stated conflicts with a victim or each other
why: Conspicuous motives attract attention and are assumed to be decisive.

text: When unlikely failures cluster, ask whether they were arranged and who benefited, rather than only what bad luck occurred.
when: Several unrelated failures occur together.
why: Coincidences can be produced by someone who knows the weak points.

text: A weak identification can still drive an arrest when motive and missing alibi are strong.
when: An arrest rests on an identification plus other circumstantial evidence.
why: Strong motive and alibi gaps can make a weak identification seem sufficient.

text: Let self-interested NPC admissions unlock dialogue branches, but let players verify them. Unverified remarks from interested sources are not independent evidence and lead to false motive conclusions.
when: when an NPC volunteers a motive, or a motive rests only on a single informant's remarks
why: Verification keeps performed candor from being taken as proof; interested sources are not independent evidence.

text: Give a wanted description several specific traits, such as eye colour, hair and a distinctive habit, and unlock identification only when a combination of them matches.
when: a player must identify an NPC from a description
why: a single common trait would otherwise trigger a false match

text: Show players the letters needed to verify a name clue, since a clue they cannot check feels unfair.
when: A character hides behind a new name.
why: Verifiable evidence lets the player earn the connection.

text: Give each suspect a plausible motive and a clue that is weak alone, so the group must weigh the evidence rather than accept it.
when: designing a set of suspects
why: Weak individual clues require comparison, which keeps the group deliberating

text: Treating offenders as types, such as a stock criminal profile, is quick but skips the individual motive; reasoning from inside the culprit's motive reveals who would act.
when: Choosing how to reason about a suspect
why: Types describe categories, while motive explains one person's choice.

text: Check whether the accused had direct contact with the people in the accusation, since a missing contact leaves a gap in the story.
when: an accusation depends on a relationship between two people
why: Without contact, the claimed motive or plan has no route to act on

text: Require a claimant to describe the item's wear or contents before receiving it, which filters out impostors.
when: When designing a lost-item quest
why: Details known only to the true owner are hard for impostors to fake.

text: A contact close to a victim, such as a teacher or companion, can reveal attention, gifts or routines that suggest a relationship.
when: Investigating a person's private relationships.

text: Test a claim of regular access against the normal pattern of contact; if that contact would be unusual, the claim of constant presence is weak.
when: Someone says they were always in touch with a person or place
why: Routine patterns show whether frequent access is plausible

text: Building cases against several suspects without verifying the connections between them lets red herrings accumulate unchallenged.
when: Multiple suspects each appear guilty
why: Unverified links make innocent suspects look connected

text: 1) Identify a person with sole access to something that could be altered. 2) Check it at uneven intervals over several days. 3) Enter without warning. 4) Inspect the item, the person's contacts, and their handling of the subject.
when: The subject is medicine, food, a locked object or similar
why: Surprise checks catch what scheduled visits miss

text: 1) Obtain the earlier case's records, such as press reports. 2) Identify the earlier offender's accomplices. 3) Check whether those accomplices connect to the present crime.
when: a present method has been matched to an earlier case
why: the earlier network may reveal the present culprit

text: Before naming a suspect, check a matching description against measurable features such as height, and never rely on a single report.
Under questioning, a suspect's voice, posture, gaze or pallor can reveal knowledge, but observers can misread these signs, so they are leads rather than proof.
when: When questioning a suspect or a person about a sensitive matter.
why: Pressure weakens control over the body and voice, but reactions are informative yet ambiguous and should not be treated as proof.

text: A suspect confronted with a specific claim may show pallor, sweating or an outburst, signalling a reaction to the claim.
when: When a specific hidden fact is put to the suspect.
why: The claim touches something concealed, and the body betrays the strain.

text: A suspect who recognises a displayed object may start and try to seize it, which confirms a connection the investigator could not yet prove.
when: A physical clue is shown during a confrontation
why: Guilty knowledge produces an involuntary reaction when the object is recognised

text: Noting an accused person's reaction to evidence gives suspicion a human basis that a later reveal can redirect to another character.
when: Early suspicion falls on one character and must later shift to another.
why: A visible reaction makes the initial suspicion feel earned, so the redirect feels like a correction.

text: Give each suspect a real but explainable lie; suspicion stays high even though the suspect is innocent.
why: An evasive but explicable lie keeps the audience suspicious without proving guilt.

text: A suspect who believes the investigator knows where hidden evidence lies may act on that belief, such as fetching the item, and expose themselves.
when: When the hidden item is outside the suspect's knowledge.
why: If the suspect knew the item's location, they could deny everything instead of acting.

text: 1) Ask a follow-up that invites a checkable detail. 2) Identify who or what could confirm it. 3) Verify or contradict the claim before committing to a theory.
when: A suspect gives a vague excuse for their movements
why: A vague answer can hide an invented story that a specific question exposes.

text: 1) Compare the stated purpose of an action with independent records, such as travel times. 2) Note any mismatch between purpose and conduct. 3) Record changes in the suspect's manner as timeline details.
when: A suspect's explanation is plausible but unverified
why: Independent records can confirm or refute a plausible account.

text: 1) Start from the witness's own account of the problem. 2) Ask targeted follow-up questions about why key actions did not happen. 3) Ask about mechanics: when, where and how payments or meetings occurred. 4) Ask what was feared.
when: when a witness is hiding a motive
why: Moving from the stated problem to its mechanics reveals concealed motives.

text: 1) Ask the key question without lead-in, just after a disorienting moment. 2) Record the immediate answer as a lead. 3) Watch the speaker's follow-up hedges and whom they glance at. 4) Check the answer against other witnesses and the timeline before relying on it.
when: A suspect is among others who may coordinate their stories and is off guard
why: A fast answer shows less managed content, and a glance can reveal coordination

text: Make a suspect's recognition tell subtle so careful observers catch it while those who only read dialogue miss it.
when: designing a suspect's reaction to a trigger
why: subtle tells reward attentive play without giving the answer away

text: Give each suspect a plausible guilt pattern, then clear them with a new fact rather than a twist, testing and dropping each false solution before raising the next.
when: building a mystery with multiple suspects
why: Repeated testing keeps the audience engaged and uncertain

text: Repeated glances toward a hidden spot and watching through a gap in a door show a suspect is monitoring the investigator.
when: A suspect's attention keeps returning to the investigator's activity.
why: Monitoring reveals concern about what the investigator might find.

text: Keep a shortlist of suspects with plausible motives open until direct physical evidence narrows the field.
when: several suspects have plausible motives
why: Early conclusions drawn from one reading can send the investigation down a false path.

text: Seed two or three suspects per level, each with a plausible alibi that a single physical test breaks, such as a mold, a reflection or a trapped demonstration.
when: When populating a level with suspects.
why: Each alibi that one test can break gives the player a discrete, fair check.

text: Each identity reveal re-sorts the suspect list, so suspicion passes from one character to the next in sequence.
when: A mystery with several identity reveals.
why: A new identity changes who had motive, access and opportunity.

text: Move a suspect out of earshot before discussing the threat, so the group can speak freely while the suspect is watched without being alerted.
when: A suspect is present while the group plans
why: Speaking openly in front of a suspect may alert them and disrupt observation.

text: When laying out suspects, write motive, opportunity and counter-evidence side by side.
when: Comparing several suspects in a mystery.
why: Side-by-side layout exposes which suspect has the strongest combined case.

text: A suspect's private monologue can state motive directly, giving the player dramatic irony that the other characters do not share.
when: A suspect is alone and reacting to a threat.
why: Private thought shows what the suspect hides from others.

text: When a suspect attacks a witness's reliability, the attack can expose a personal motive that the player can use later.
when: A suspect responds to an accusation with personal insults
why: Emotional attacks often reveal the attached stake behind the suspect's fear

text: A stated motive that seems too slight to explain the outcome suggests a deeper cause, such as an older grievance.
Stack several suspects who each carry a real motive so that each accusation carries weight and the player keeps reconsidering.
when: designing a mystery's suspect set
why: Suspects with credible motives sustain doubt, while a single weak suspect is dismissed quickly.

text: Give the reader a suspect's reasons and emotional state early, so a later reversal of the suspicion feels earned rather than arbitrary.
why: Established motive makes the reader's earlier judgment visible, so reversing it reads as a correction.

text: A suggested outside culprit can shield whoever proposes it, drawing attention from the true cause; treat such an excuse, including a recanting witness's outside power, as unproven.
when: when someone proposes an intruder
why: A false external threat shifts blame away from those present.

text: Widen suspects to everyone who knew an item existed, including staff, dealers, visitors and advisers, then to whom those people might have told.
when: After an item goes missing, or when the obvious names are checked and the case is still open
why: Knowledge of an object enables a theft, and the suspect list is often incomplete.

text: Households and police tend to pursue a plausible outside suspect first, which can delay attention to causes inside the household.
when: one obvious outside suspect exists
why: an external culprit explains the event conveniently

text: A scapegoat is a decoy figure placed to absorb suspicion, shielding a hidden organiser who is the real planner.
Widen the inquiry to surrounding circumstances, including the sources that spread a theory, since seemingly minor details can carry much of the truth.
An outside danger, such as a hostile fugitive, can serve as a rival threat and alternate suspect that diverts attention from the main mystery.
when: when a case needs a second source of menace

text: After a first theory, check whether the figure central to the case could also be involved, instead of stopping at the first suspect.
why: The first theory can be wrong, and a central figure may have both access and interest.

text: When a disappearance seems impossible, ask where the missing person would least likely be sought.
when: a missing person cannot be found in expected places

text: A stolen or planted object can connect to a larger hidden group, so one clue may point beyond the single suspect it seems to name.
when: A clue is linked to a theft or a crime with several possible actors.
why: Objects move through networks, so their origin can reveal more than their immediate owner.

text: When an interested party urges dropping an inquiry, weigh their interest in avoiding scandal against the advice.
when: a relative or stakeholder discourages investigation
why: Interest in avoiding exposure can bias advice toward stopping.

text: Do not assume every name on an accusation list is guilty, since such lists grow through fear and kinship as well as evidence.
when: when evaluating a list of accused people
why: Accusations spread along family and neighbourhood ties, not only through proof

text: Use a conclusive clue to settle one question, then open a second question about who could reach it, and plant a plausible second suspect near the scene.
when: Structuring a mystery's clue sequence
why: A settled answer shifts the mystery to access, and a second suspect tests the first theory

text: A method that requires specialized knowledge narrows the suspect pool to people with access to that knowledge, either as practitioners or as those who instructed them.
when: An identified method demands an uncommon skill or knowledge
why: The skill requirement limits who could plausibly have executed the method

text: Keep one name recurring through the investigation so it keeps drawing attention even after it is shown to be wrong.
when: a suspect has been cleared but may still matter
why: A persistent name keeps the player's attention on a thread that could still lead to the truth.

text: Accusations spread outward from a suspect or central source to officials, neighbours, the wealthy and neighbouring places; tracking locations reveals their direction and reach.
when: when a process reaches people of every social rank
why: Suspicion extends along existing relationships, institutions and geography.

text: A scapegoat is chosen who has visible access and debts, and the frame needs only their name attached, since the disgrace lands whoever acted.
when: The investigators will look no further than the visible suspect
why: Visible motive and access make the scapegoat plausible without proof

text: Whether an authority accepts a planted scapegoat depends on its incentives, such as preferring a clean record to a doubtful case.
when: when a frame is used to close a case
why: officials act on what they are rewarded for

text: Widening a candidate list overwhelms players unless a second constraint filters it down.
Judging a character by profession or outward piety can mislead, since respectability does not rule out violent capacity.
A framed scapegoat can unravel the plan by generating fresh leads or by confessing.
when: when a frame is used to close a case
why: a questioned fall-guy may point back to the real object

text: 1) Search beyond the scene along the route the actor likely took. 2) Repeat searches at places not yet covered. 3) Read identifying marks on each recovered item to fix its owner.
when: Initial searches of the scene fail to turn up key items.
why: Items may be discarded along a route rather than left at the scene.

text: A profile fitting many people leaves the pool wide; narrow it with physical evidence such as footprint sizes or footwear, not alibis alone.
when: A mystery where alibis are unreliable or easily faked.
why: Physical filters remain checkable when testimony is contested.

text: Point a rumour or dying word at an outside faction while the real mechanism lies inside the locked setting, so the false trail fails under inspection.
A scapegoat setup should leave a trail that can be rechecked later.
A scapegoat must be an almost certain candidate for the blame, so choosing the patsy is part of designing the frame.
when: when planning a frame
why: a weak candidate lets the frame fail

text: When a topic is raised indirectly, the subject may step into the frame and place themselves at its centre before anyone names them.
A culprit who believes the investigator lacks key knowledge tends to fortify a position and commit to it, giving the investigator time to find a clue.
when: The investigator waits quietly rather than confronting the culprit.
why: Committed positions are harder to abandon, and the commitment exposes more evidence over time.

text: Repeatedly using a diminished or altered name for a person can shape how readers perceive them.
when: A writer refers to an accused person in demeaning terms.
why: Repeated naming frames the reader's view.

text: A testator who revises a will often makes a sudden new beneficiary, even an outsider, less surprising to those who handled the estate.
A suspect's admission of intent, such as an offer of money or a readiness to do anything, states a motive that investigators can test.
A departure from known routine is evidence: a change in a familiar pattern or a new object in an empty place is often the first sign something happened.
when: Judging an actor's likely action or identity, or when an observer knows a place or household's normal state well.
why: Routine gives a baseline against which anomalies stand out, making deviations both noticeable and credible.

text: A public image of cheerfulness or respectability may conceal private pressure, so question the surface of a case when a respected figure is involved.
when: a public figure's image may hide private strain
why: Public presentation and private circumstances often diverge, and the gap can supply motive.

text: Public causes or respectable activities may be a front for a private link that actually explains the gathering.
A pin or badge paired with a habit can indicate membership of a fraternal group.
when: a person wears a group emblem and shows matching habits
why: paired signs make membership more likely than a single sign

text: Keep investigative actions separate from raw facts so the chain of reasoning stays transparent.
when: A case is being documented or reviewed
why: Mixing actions with facts hides which conclusions rest on which evidence

text: An agent's choice of action reveals what they believed; ask what they would have known to explain it.
A former admirer or rival of the victim should be treated as a suspect to be cleared or confirmed.
when: Asking about a victim's other admirers or romantic history
why: Past rivalries can supply motive that current relations hide

text: A recent change in a person's plans, such as a withdrawn commitment, can reveal a motive worth probing even when the stated reason seems weak.
when: motive is unclear and the victim's personal life offers a lead

text: A sequence of actions shows what was done but not why; the same actions can fit several motives, which must be assessed as a separate question.
when: when a reconstruction establishes what happened
why: Actions are observable, while motives must be inferred from other evidence.

text: Judge a suspect's apparent folly against the likely intelligence of the culprit. A clever culprit would not act so openly, so the folly may show the plan was not the suspect's.
when: when a suspect behaves in a way that seems out of character
why: Someone else may have arranged the damaging actions.

text: Flag implausible details in a witness's description, such as a disguise that seems false, and note them for checking later.
Track a suspect's motive, access and behaviour as separate entries, so the player must combine them before making an accusation.
when: designing a suspect board for players
why: separate entries force the player to link evidence rather than match a single clue

text: An actor's need to avoid suspicion explains why some traces were wiped and others left behind.
when: Accounting for uneven traces in a scene.
why: Concealment is selective, so the wiped and missed traces reflect what the actor feared being caught doing.

text: Character profiles can narrow a suspect field but cannot identify one culprit alone, since many people may fit the same profile.
