when: ranking suspects when alibi evidence is incomplete
why: Personality fit is weaker evidence than physical or alibi facts.

text: Ask what subject was discussed at a past meeting, since a shared subject can link that meeting to evidence found later.
Reasoning about what an actor would prefer, such as avoiding a patrolled room, is the weakest location evidence and should carry the least weight.
when: Location is argued from the killer's habits rather than physical traces.
why: Preferences are guesses; physical and timing facts can be checked.

text: Judge individuals rather than groups; a person's role alone does not reveal their intentions.
Show who was positioned to influence each decision, so readers can see how one stage made the next possible.
when: explaining a chain of decisions

text: A portrait may look unfriendly because its subject dislikes being seen, so the witness may be distorted by the subject's own behavior.
when: When judging a likeness that seems to contradict a reputation.
why: The subject's reluctance can alter the recorded appearance.

text: Keep a contract's cost unknown until revealed, and give players an informed NPC or a search to read the full terms.
when: Designing a sign-or-refuse choice
why: Players can then decide with information they earned

text: The strongest item often completes a case that other items have already built.
Begin an investigation by treating every suspect as possible, then narrow the list as facts arrive, to avoid committing early.
when: when several people could plausibly be responsible
why: early commitment can lock in a wrong suspect

text: Attaching small traits to NPC bodies or rooms, such as stains, ash or nail marks, lets a suspect's profile narrow as the player gathers clues.
when: Designing environmental evidence that identifies a suspect
why: Each trait removes candidates, so the profile converges as evidence accumulates

text: Inheritance can set the suspect list, since each heir has a motive tied to the estate.
when: A death or crime concerns property that passes between relatives.

text: A sighting that contradicts a locked door, held privately by observers, keeps a puzzle open until an ordinary, checkable explanation appears.
when: when planting an apparently impossible entry or exit
why: Unresolved contradictions drive players to keep reasoning

text: Confrontation can require the player to show a physical item, such as a bottle or stub, before a suspect's claim changes.
A compartmented plan can use four roles: a naval liaison, a construction supervisor, a local labour and pilot organiser, and a promoter who supplies information and guides the expedition.
when: when organising a multi-part covert operation
why: each role covers a separate function

text: An elimination conclusion is only as good as its candidate list; a missing agent, route or location carries its gap into the verdict, so a certain-seeming answer may be provisional.
when: Using elimination to explain an effect.
why: Unlisted causes cannot be excluded, and the remaining answer depends on the list being complete.

text: Warning or alarming a suspect before others are questioned lets them coordinate answers or coach witnesses, weakening later checks.
Choosing suspects for surface traits such as name, habit, timing, poverty, past failure or social standing, rather than evidence, shows only thin evidence and does not establish guilt.
when: A suspect is picked for superficial reasons, or a theory rests on reputation.
why: Surface traits and social judgment substitute for proof.

text: Investigators may fix on one suspect because evidence against that person is easiest to gather, narrowing attention before alternatives are weighed.
when: several people have motives and opportunities
why: convenient evidence draws attention away from stronger but harder leads

text: Offering too many alternative explanations stalls the investigation and makes the audience lose interest.
Treating visible agitation as proof of guilt misreads grief, since grief and anger can look identical.
when: Judging a suspect by how upset or agitated they appear

text: A stated reason may be an afterthought, so it should be weighed as a claim rather than accepted as the true motive.
A theory whose named suspect would have no reason to perform the action it describes explains its clue only loosely.
Assuming a companion was present, based on a single object, can mislead the investigation.
when: inferring who was with a person from one clue
why: one object rarely proves who was present

text: A conclusion that the real document differs from the displayed one is a working hypothesis, not proof, until the real document is found.
why: Behaviour around a document is suggestive but not conclusive

text: A subject who quietly fills an interviewer's slip with a near match can make a false account look consistent.
Stacking too many grudges makes none of them stand out, so each suspect's motive loses weight.
Legal title and physical occupancy can point to different people, so the visible defender of a plot may not be its legal owner.
why: Each party's stake depends on the kind of claim it holds

text: Choosing a more favorable court can be procedural pressure that hides weak evidence behind a convenient verdict.
Counting only helps when the production record is complete, so the investigator must verify records directly with the maker.
why: missing records make the count unreliable

text: Investigators often record a statement and forget the behaviour that contradicts it.

1) Start from a response that seems wrong for the stated reason. 2) Replay the scene: who was present, what could be said openly, and what each person did next. 3) Ask which motive makes each act natural, and test rival motives against the same acts.
when: A person's conduct contradicts the reason they give for it.
why: Acts reveal relationships that spoken accounts conceal.

text: Build a full roster covering household members, neighbours, tradespeople, professionals and acquaintances who could affect the case.
when: when the cast is still unknown
why: A missed suspect is costly early on.

text: 1) Compare two observations of the same person. 2) Find the recorded event between them. 3) Test whether a witness could perceive that event from their position. 4) Link the event to a motive.
when: two accounts of one person's behavior differ with no stated reason

text: 1) For each suspect, list what they want, what they fear, and whom they fear most. 2) Use these to explain why they hide, refuse or invent. 3) Test the motive against their behavior and the physical evidence.
when: the investigation depends on predicting a suspect's next move

text: For each suspect, build one sequence: who wanted money, who learned of the will, and who had access to the means.
when: Assessing motive and opportunity across suspects.
why: A single chain shows whether each suspect could have acted.

text: 1) Check ordinary outgoings against receipts to find discrepancies. 2) Isolate regular unexplained payments. 3) Chart income by period. 4) Match income timing against spending changes.
when: Reconstructing a person's finances from records.
why: Separating explained from unexplained flows exposes the hidden transactions.

text: 1) Map each person's sums owed and interest rates. 2) Note whether debts were rolled into principal. 3) Record stated figures to check later contradictions. 4) Verify figures with a second source.
when: A death or disappearance changes someone's financial position
why: Debts and stakes show motive, but figures are often hidden or overstated

text: Give each suspect a distinct personality and motive profile, such as debt, reputation or need for an item, checked against their character and the value of any stolen object.
when: Designing suspects for a theft or a deduction puzzle.
why: Distinct profiles let players match behaviour and motive to evidence.

text: Gate the final accusation until all statements and clues are gathered and earlier reveals logged, each unlocked from collected clues; optional timers or guard actions add pressure.
when: The game has a final accusation step.
why: Gating holds the reveal until the evidence is complete.

text: Change appearance fully when re-entering a scene where a suspect has already seen you, so that person does not recognize you.
when: Returning to a scene with a previously observed suspect
why: A full change is what made the disguised figure unrecognizable to a prior observer

text: Name a suspect only after checking who could plausibly have made the change, given their recent capability.
Learn which hand an item suits by trying it on a person, rather than asking anyone directly about their hand use.
when: a suspect might deny or hide a physical trait
why: A fitting test reveals the trait without the question being asked.

text: Let a character's changed employment open new questions, such as when and why they left their previous post.
Attach strength or mobility values to each suspect and check them against the physical demands of the scene, such as moving a heavy object.
when: Building suspects whose capability matters to the crime
why: Lets the player test whether a suspect could have acted

text: When an answer does not come out whole, suspect your own working before blaming the evidence.
when: a theory leaves loose ends

text: Let the public story stand while investigators keep their real suspicions hidden, so the culprit does not realise they are suspected.
when: Investigators are setting a trap for a culprit.

text: Let a hung jury delay a case rather than resolve it, so the case remains open for later stages.
Research the background of everyone connected to a case for past scandal that could reveal a motive.
when: Building a suspect list

text: 1) Choose a gesture or phrase the disguised character cannot easily drop. 2) Use it at each appearance. 3) Let players connect it to the earlier profile, even when faces differ.
why: A recurring tell lets players recognize a disguised suspect.

text: A pause and fixed stare when a witness requests secrecy show that this one demand matters more to them than the rest of what they said.
when: a witness reacts strongly to one request
why: a strong reaction exposes which concern is central

text: A suspect's flicker, pause, sudden return to a subject, or overly quick denial can reveal knowledge they would not state directly.
when: An interviewer probes a subject the suspect knows about
why: Concealing knowledge produces involuntary tells in reaction to a probe.

text: Show a character's reaction before explaining its cause, and explain the cause only afterward.
why: Delaying the reason keeps the reader curious and invites them to read the trace.

text: A speaker can reduce disbelief by admitting they once held the listener's view and changed their mind under evidence.
when: The claim is extraordinary.
why: Shared past skepticism shows the speaker reasoned their way to the claim.

text: Attach predicted reactions to a suspect's dialogue, such as a denial or a shock, and let the player test the prediction by choosing what to say.
when: Designing a dialogue-driven accusation or interrogation system.
why: Letting the player check a prediction makes interrogation an active test rather than passive reading.

text: Use a visible character reaction, such as a flustered remark, to signal that a recalled fact now matters.
when: Revealing that a previously mentioned detail is significant.
why: A visible reaction draws attention to the detail without stating its importance outright.

text: Reread excessive praise as possible mockery or a hidden motive once the group's real purpose becomes clear.
when: Praise is later revealed to serve another goal

text: Answer a blanket accusation with specific, checkable items rather than a general denial, since each defeated item weakens the sweeping claim.
Tagging dialogue lines with the emotional reaction they cause lets a game check whether a rivalry was actually touched.
when: In dialogue systems that track NPC relationships.
why: Reaction tags turn a line into a checkable state change rather than mere flavor.

text: A suspect who expected the visit, after seeing the investigator with a known associate, will have prepared responses, so early contact can reveal that the investigator's approach is already known.
when: A suspect has seen the investigator's movements before the formal visit.
why: Prior observation lets the suspect prepare for the inquiry.

text: A tell or flinch may reflect nervousness or distress rather than guilt or a specific mark, so test it against other evidence before concluding.
when: Interpreting a suspect's glances, manner changes, or physical reaction as evidence of guilt or identity.
why: Agitation and distress have many causes unrelated to the crime or the identity being tested.

text: Treating a stranger's unusual attention as hostile without checking the pattern of movements, or missing that perfect indifference is itself the clue.
when: Interpreting a group's unnatural calm toward an outsider

text: Use a planned denial as a clue: have a later witness who saw the connection contradict the denial, revealing the hidden relationship.
when: Designing an NPC who must deny knowing a contact.
why: The contradiction lets the player discover the concealed link.

text: Post-crime conduct is evidence: leaving openly before witnesses is hard to reconcile with a hidden body, yet such behavior has many explanations and proves neither guilt nor innocence.
when: Weighing a suspect's flight, abandonment of an accomplice, or conduct after an alleged act.
why: Post-crime conduct has many explanations and does not establish guilt or innocence.

text: A suspect who keeps refusing stays plausible but risks a dead end; players need some clear answers soon to stay engaged.
when: a suspect must hide a motive
why: repeated refusals with no progress frustrate

text: Keep the proof incomplete until a late clue arrives, so the first theory has to be argued rather than simply confirmed.
when: A mystery's first theory is pivotal.
why: Argument keeps the theory contested and the player engaged.

text: The most helpful character is often the one who casually dismisses clues, so treat such dismissal as a warning sign.
when: evaluating an NPC who guides the investigation
why: Dismissing evidence can hide its authorship.

text: A leaked detail such as a map or description can trace back to one NPC, creating an optional investigation into who leaked it.
when: Designing optional side content around information leaks
why: Tracing a leak gives the player a self-contained goal with a specific culprit

text: A linked mystery collection repeats a shape: a bold claim or impossible event, small physical clues logged without explanation, a plausible wrong solution, a crisis, then a reconstruction that reruns the clues.
when: designing a series of mystery cases with a shared solver
why: The shared shape lets players learn to distrust the first explanation while the mechanisms vary.

text: Ignorance by request can look like a plot convenience. Make it costly by showing a visible consequence, such as an unresolved crime.
when: when a character asks not to be told the truth
why: Without a cost, the choice reads as a shortcut rather than a meaningful decision.

text: Letting the audience assume an investigator knows more than the narrator without signalling the gap.
when: Writing a mystery from a limited viewpoint
why: Unsignalled differences in knowledge mislead the audience about who knows what

text: 1) Note the remark and who was present. 2) Note the target's reaction. 3) Infer a personal sensitivity from the reaction. 4) Ask who could most easily exploit that sensitivity. 5) Seek that person and confirm with later evidence.
when: When a social remark might point toward a person connected to an event.
why: Each step is a small inference, and later evidence is needed before the lead is trusted.

text: A suspect's tidy story can be designed to convince, so the player must test it for a flaw rather than accept or reject it on first sight.
Witnesses named by the suspect may have been arranged to be absent or unable to confirm, so their corroboration carries limited weight.
when: the suspect supplies the witnesses
why: the suspect controls who can be checked

text: Delaying the moment of looking, by hiding the face and fixing attention elsewhere first, builds suspense before a reveal.
Suspense grows as repeated setbacks, partial results and small disturbances delay a payoff, including a pursuer's repeated failures and a long gap between a wrong and its revenge.
when: A reveal must carry weight and the audience needs to feel the wait.
why: Each false alarm or partial find keeps the expected payoff pending while anticipation builds.

text: Suspense grows when a stretch of uncertain waiting is followed by a sudden escalation, so the next event lands harder.
when: pacing a sequence of events
why: The wait raises expectation, and the escalation then feels sharper against it.

text: Each stretch of waiting must include new signals, such as a sound or movement, so the build does not stall.
when: a sequence built on patience
why: a wait without change stalls the build

text: Each delay in a withheld reveal or waiting period should add a new detail, such as a gesture or sound; repeating the same cue or stalling without new information dulls tension.
when: the reveal is held back across several beats, or a waiting period reuses one sound, light or sign
why: stalling without new information only frustrates, and a cue that brings no new progress stops signalling approach

text: Observers notice pauses before a subject's answer and read them as meaningful.
when: During a staged questioning

text: Tension rises during a long wait even without new information, because anticipation itself keeps the stakes high for the audience.
when: a long idle wait with no new events
why: anticipation sustains stakes without new facts

text: Small sounds, such as a rustling bush, raise tension so that even careful people hesitate or make mistakes.
when: A team is waiting or moving in silence near a target.
why: Heightened alertness makes ordinary noises feel threatening.

text: Restraint rather than action can drive tension, as a silent observer's held breath and imagined threats build suspense.
when: a scene with a hidden observer
why: an unspoken threat builds suspense

text: A sudden change in tone when answering a sensitive question can betray concealment more clearly than the content of the answer.
when: a person answers a sensitive question
why: tone is harder to control than wording

text: A crime story can reveal the culprit at the start, shifting suspense from who did it to whether concealment will hold under mounting pressure.
when: when the murder occurs early and the audience knows the killer
why: Suspense then comes from concealment and pressure rather than from a mystery.

text: Pause before a reveal and narrate listener reactions during long explanations, letting the audience form theories and anticipate the twist so tension rises when it lands.
when: a reveal is about to happen, or an NPC or narrator delivers a long explanation before a reveal
why: anticipation primes the audience and lets them form their own theories

text: When outside authorities are approaching, model the time limit in event sequences and demand a rapid account, since the suspect has less time to build a prepared story.
when: when outside authorities are close to arriving
why: little time limits how much a story can be prepared, and time constrains what could have happened

text: Make relief between threats real but partial: the character feels better, yet a lasting problem or required preparation keeps the next threat pressing.
Use time pressure to raise suspense by showing the cost of delay before the outcome is known.
when: when pacing a story or quest with a deadline
why: Known costs make the player feel the urgency.

text: Restate the stakes at each stage of a sequence, such as what the outcome means for a life, so the audience keeps the consequences in view.
why: Repeated reminders keep tension high between events.

text: Alternate moments of hope and despair in narration, such as hesitation followed by a decisive sound, to sustain tension.
when: Pacing a tense sequence
why: Shifts between hope and despair keep the audience engaged and anticipating the next outcome

text: Compare restraints with their claimed purpose: a captor who fears escape binds tightly, so loose restraints suggest the bound person could free himself.
when: A reported abduction or confinement involves physical restraints.
why: Restraint tightness reflects what the restrainer actually feared.

text: Ask the question plainly and then wait; giving the witness time lets them recover details they would otherwise skip.
when: A witness hesitates over a detail
why: Recall takes time

text: Add a timed quest with a fixed reply deadline, where a missing answer changes the story state.
when: Designing quests that wait on replies
why: A fixed deadline creates pressure and a state change on failure.

text: Use a dated, timed detail, such as the hour and date of a death, as the hinge that makes a match undeniable.
when: Confirming a claim made by an unverifiable source.
why: A precise time is hard to explain away as coincidence.

text: A departure or deadline opens a short window, and the outcome of a scene turns on what happens inside that interval.
when: A scene where the result depends on a short window of time

text: Time gaps between events, such as days of fruitless search, increase tension and sharpen a sense of deadline.
A brief line can cover a long, dull stretch, letting tension be saved for the decisive scene that follows.
when: A stretch of waiting, sneaking or other low-event time must be passed
why: Keeps attention on the moments that matter instead of idle time.

text: Interrupting a scene at its peak raises the stakes, and the next scene can open in a different place.
A remedy that brings brief relief is often taken as proof of a natural cause, so short-term improvement can mislead observers about what caused a condition.
when: When a treatment appears to work at first and then fails or changes.
why: Observers attribute the change to the remedy or the cause they already expect.

text: A partial, poorly lit view makes an observer react before the nature of the object is shown, so suspense grows from the gap in what is seen.
when: A scene must build tension before showing its cause.
why: The observer's reaction signals a discovery while the cause stays hidden.

text: When a character lets others feel informed until they discover they were outsiders, the reveal creates suspense and reframes earlier conversations.
when: Designing a reveal in a mystery narrative
why: Characters who believe they know more than they do keep the audience engaged until the gap is exposed

text: Repeating an event with increasing intensity, closer approach or new detail builds suspense and forces the investigator to act.
when: A recurring threat is used to build pressure across scenes
why: Each stronger repetition raises the stakes and narrows the choices

text: A restrained suspect can still nearly overpower the investigator, so restraint must be complete.
Resolving every cliffhanger in the next scene removes the suspense that the interruption built.
A scene built only on sound becomes exhausting if no release or later explanation follows.
1) Alternate slow, rich sensory description with sudden shocks. 2) Let each shock land after a calm passage so it reads as a break.
when: Building suspense in a scene
why: Contrast between calm and abrupt events heightens tension

text: End a tense wait with a clear event that resolves the tension and gives the player or audience its next objective.
when: a suspense sequence reaches its climax
why: A resolved climax releases tension and tells the audience what to do next.

text: Use a late confession to open a timed window in which the player can act before the outcome is fixed.
Structure escalating events in tiers, moving from a mild form to obstruction to direct harm, and place a second NPC who witnesses the event as a check on the player's account.
when: Designing escalating events with witnesses
why: Escalation builds stakes, and a second observer corroborates the sequence

text: An unread document can be given any meaning readers want, so its unknown contents fuel speculation.
when: A sealed document's contents are withheld from everyone.
why: Without the actual content, imagination fills the gap.

text: Audiences guess at causes when the true reason is hidden; offering two or three plausible wrong explanations before the true one sustains speculation.
when: a key cause is withheld
why: each wrong guess is tested and keeps the true answer open

text: Suspense can come from clocks, departures and late arrivals, each of which sets a window in which a scene's outcome is decided.
Treat motive inferred from relationships and circumstances as speculative until it is tested against known facts.
Treat a theory that needs a special exception, such as a surname used as a first name, with suspicion.
Warn the audience that the outcome may differ from expectation, so the eventual reveal is read as deduction rather than trickery.
Public speculation can outrun proof: a seemingly settled case may rest on one unverified lead, and early conclusions spread by public reports harden before evidence is checked.
when: When public opinion has formed around a suspect.
why: Repetition and sensational framing create confidence that outpaces the evidence.

text: Presenting a theory as idle speculation when it is a direct accusation leaves the audience unsure what it means.
Speculation that a death was an accident or a plan is often wishful or spiteful; treat it as a lead to test, not a fact.
when: when a third party raises a suspicion about a death

text: Speculating about side details without evidence, such as rumoured honours or status, adds noise and weakens the main inference.
when: building a motive from gossip or hearsay
why: unsupported details can crowd out the evidence that matters

text: A hopeful surface line set against a grim remark makes the audience doubt the hopeful line.
when: Dialogue where a cheerful statement is followed by a dark comment.
why: The contrast invites the audience to question the surface.

text: Pretending to agree with a delirious person hides the listeners' own knowledge but does not stop the leaks.
when: listeners humour a delirious speaker
why: the speaker still voices what they know

text: An unseen opponent who repeatedly thwarts the player's plans makes the player feel watched, and tension rises as the player suspects someone knows their intentions.
when: the opponent is never seen but keeps anticipating the player's moves
why: the player infers that an unseen agent is tracking them

text: Dramatic tension can make an observer lose track of the procedure, so the test's steps must be kept explicit.
when: Running a high-stakes reproduction or test
why: Emotional pressure distracts from following the method

text: Audiences can learn that a threat is moving before the characters do, which builds tension through the gap in knowledge.
when: A pursuit or threat is shown from the hunter's side.
why: Knowing more than the characters makes their unawareness tense.

text: A traveller who forms doubts en route may later change the account of what they intended.
when: during a journey

text: A group that believes it fights a world-scale enemy reads ordinary events as parts of that struggle, so its motive becomes collective.
Dread can arise from a sensory cue, such as a gust of air, before any visible evidence appears, and wrongness may show only on closer approach.
Unresolved possibilities unsettle more than confirmed ones, and withholding a threat's content sustains suspense better than showing it, because doubt keeps the audience imagining.
when: Building tension before a major reveal
why: Uncertainty keeps the mind actively imagining; anticipation of an unknown threat keeps the audience engaged more than a fully visible one.

text: Use a pointed hint when a suspect has a plausible cover; avoid it when the hint might alert the suspect or expose the questioner's knowledge.
Uncertainty about whether a target has noticed the observer creates suspense, but it must be resolved eventually.
when: building tension in a stealth scene
why: suspense without resolution frustrates players

text: Keep shocking details separate from proof of the crime, so that horror does not stand in for evidence.
A response that follows an event after a very short gap implies the responder had a direct channel to the source, not a long chain of intermediaries.
when: Timestamps are reliable and the order of events is known
why: Information needs time to pass through each intermediary, so a very short gap suggests a direct link

text: Carry tension through reactions and small turns, such as a contradicting witness or a seized document, rather than through delay alone.
Short, sharp commands and a sudden stop drive the pace of a tense sequence.
when: writing dialogue or events during an escape

text: Use slow, peril-heavy pacing before a turning point, or when a character must gather information under difficult conditions.
Note a detail that does not fit the expected result, such as a wound lacking expected mess, and withhold judgment until an expert report confirms it.
when: when physical evidence contradicts the expected outcome

text: Light humour during a strained interview can ease the moment and make disclosure easier.
when: The interview has become tense.
why: A lighter tone lowers the emotional cost of speaking.

text: Grim humour in a precise, planned crime can signal a planned release of tension by a person who thinks carefully.
when: A crime is carefully planned yet includes playful or grim touches

text: Use a labelled, staged reveal only when the solution depends on many objects; a single clear piece of evidence needs no staging.
Split an arrival into short, dense scenes, each ending on a question.
Use a deadline when the character's choice is the point of the scene, not when the player simply needs an answer quickly.
List each possible reading of a motionless figure, such as thought, sleep or death, with the signs supporting it, and keep several open until evidence decides.
Give players a dated event log to reason from, and schedule recurring hazards at set intervals to drive pacing.
when: structuring a long, time-based sequence
why: a visible timeline and rhythm guide expectation

text: Offer two or three plausible stories, each backed by a visible clue and contradicted by a hidden clue the player must find to progress.
when: Designing a case with several possible explanations

text: Surface signs such as colour change, breaking surf over shallows, and exposed humps of sand reveal hidden hazards beneath, so design these cues to warn observant players.
when: when a hazard lies below the water surface
why: the surface shows where the seabed rises

text: Attach a character's dread to a real situation, such as a delayed letter or long absence, so the fear stays concrete.
when: Writing a character's fear about a future event.
why: A concrete source keeps dread believable and prevents it from becoming abstract.

text: Long runs of failed leads erode focus, and repeating a failed search method yields no new information and drifts toward unstructured searching; each failure should yield some information.
when: An investigation or search stops producing answers at a lead.
why: Repeated failure without feedback erodes motivation and the clarity needed for structured reasoning.

text: Suspense rises from the mismatch between a known deadline and an unknown agent, so the threat's identity can stay hidden.
when: Designing an anonymous threat
why: An unknown source sustains dread

text: Rumours of progress raise hope and refusals to delay dash it, so each rise and fall keeps suspense alive.
An unseen presence, signaled by a touch in the dark or a breath nearby, escalates a confinement scene by adding a second threat.
when: A trapped character is already under physical danger.

text: Showing a character's dread before stating its cause builds suspense, as the audience anticipates the worst before learning the actual matter.
when: When a reveal will turn out to be less severe than feared
why: Anticipation of the worst raises tension

text: An unexplained demonstration of knowledge creates curiosity, because the gap between what is shown and what is understood gives the audience a reason to keep engaging.
when: Introducing a character whose competence should be felt before it is explained
why: The unresolved gap motivates the player to seek the answer

text: News of a death paired with a frightening or supernatural framing pushes a group toward a supernatural reading, so the atmosphere governs their reactions more than the facts do.
when: a death is announced in an uncanny or frightening setting
why: Dread shifts a group's frame of interpretation, so mundane evidence is overlooked until the fear fades.

text: A hazard that shifts with tide or season changes a location's danger over time, so the same place is safe or deadly at different phases.
A timed threat runs regardless of player actions, so a counter-plan must land inside the window the threat allows.
Doubt is punished: after an authority's verdict it looks like disloyalty, and amid accusers hesitation can mark one as a target, so doubters fall silent.
when: when an authority has issued a verdict, or when accusers strike at anyone who questions them
why: Accusers may treat hesitation as a sign of complicity.

text: Do not rely on coincidences or on circumstances that seem to favour your wishes; expecting them is a gamble, and plans built on them can fail.
why: Coincidence cannot be relied on.

text: A participant with doubts can break a conspiracy, so the weakest member is best removed from the scene before the trap springs.
when: A group plan depends on every member acting together.
why: A hesitant member is the likeliest point of failure.

text: Words shouted in distress can be misheard, so an ambiguous word should be compared with candidate meanings by sound and form.
An informant who distrusts the listener may leave out the most important point.
when: the informant does not trust the questioner
why: distrust makes the witness withhold the critical detail

text: A defence built only on doubt can clear a suspect without establishing who actually did it.
Holding back a suspicion can slide into complacency when the observer still knows the other person only shallowly.
when: when the relationship is new
why: waiting without understanding yields no clear picture

text: 1) Keep a suspect detained while the explanation is unconfirmed. 2) Check the innocent explanation physically against the scene. 3) Release only after it is confirmed.
when: A suspect's innocent explanation has not yet been verified.
why: Confirming the explanation prevents clearing a suspect on an untested story.

text: 1) Summarize quiet stretches of time in one entry. 2) Expand the detail when events become active.
when: Presenting a long stretch of game time to the player.
why: Compressing idle periods keeps focus on the events that matter.

text: Use a hunch to decide whom to question or examine next, but do not treat it as a conclusion until evidence another observer can verify supports it.
Hold a timed threat back with a conversation or puzzle that releases new information at each stage.
End a section on a hook when the next scene must be entered with a question in mind.
Do not dismiss an official verdict on suspicion alone; doubt must be backed by evidence before the finding is overturned.
Keep the trigger for a reaction short and ordinary, so the clue is easy to overlook on a first reading.
Make timed hazards gate access, so the player must visit at the right phase to find or hide an item.
when: When designing timed hazards

text: Pace the wait with ambient tension, then release it on the arrival event.
Hold the most perilous encounter back until players hold enough evidence to identify the danger.
Keep a confession or summary scene apart from physical evidence, so players can test the story against late evidence before the level ends.
Fear by itself is not enough to hold an audience; combine dread with other qualities such as warmth or wit.
when: building sustained tension
why: combined qualities hold attention better than dread alone

text: Suspense arises from urgency, reversals, time gaps, unexplained anomalies, and watcher presences; staged reveals plant clues for later payoff.
A recurring image that returns with small new details gathers force each time, so the threat becomes clearer and more alarming.
when: when a dream, vision or motif recurs
why: Each return adds information and reinforces the association.

text: Suspense before a revelation can be built with five devices: a vague stranger's warning, a disguised figure, a reassuring authority, fear displaced onto a legend, and a held-back threat.
when: a story or level needs tension before the real danger is revealed

text: Suspense needs the audience to glimpse that a secret exists; a secret never hinted at creates no tension.
A character rehearsing a deception in front of the audience tells the reader the secret while the other characters remain ignorant, creating dramatic irony.
when: a secret plan is carried out by a character the audience can observe
why: The audience holds information the cast lacks, so tension builds from waiting for it to be discovered.

text: The gap between what a character sees and what they understand drives suspense, and hindsight makes missed patterns clear.
when: Structuring a mystery's reveal
why: Readers track the difference

text: Removing sight forces characters to rely on sound, touch and guesses about direction, which raises tension.
when: a dangerous scene where visibility is cut off
why: Uncertainty about the environment and each other's position sustains dread.

text: Blocking sight of a threat at the critical moment withholds its appearance, so tension builds and the eventual reveal lands with more force.
when: at the climax of an investigation or encounter
why: Delayed sight keeps the audience anticipating the answer

text: A mysterious witness who confronts without revealing information builds suspense before any clue is delivered.
Delaying a reveal while a listener risks discovery raises tension, because the listener's fear is felt by the audience.
when: When a hidden listener is present
why: Discovery risk increases anticipation

text: Showing an ominous action without its purpose builds suspense, because the audience senses danger without knowing the full picture.
when: Story needs tension before the reveal.

text: Withholding information a character holds sustains suspense when the audience already has the clues needed for the reveal or the hidden purpose is disclosed in time.
when: A character withholds a known solution or knows more than the audience while building toward a reveal.
why: Visible groundwork lets the audience anticipate the reveal; withheld knowledge sustains tension while the eventual disclosure rewards attention.

text: Withholding a threatening figure's face keeps the audience's curiosity alive until the reveal.
when: when a threat is shown before its identity is known
why: The unresolved feature invites the audience to speculate.

text: Withholding the nature of a crime while showing its effects on people builds suspense, because the audience knows something terrible happened and waits for the reveal.
when: The reveal would be spoiled by early disclosure but the consequences are already visible.
why: Unresolved consequences create pressure that drives attention toward the hidden act.

text: A decision the character cannot make, such as whether to leave, raises tension, and changes in habits such as sneaking or hesitating signal rising fear.
when: building suspense through a constrained choice
why: an unresolved choice keeps pressure rising without a visible threat

text: Waiting carries no risk when the witness is already in custody, so an appointment-based suspense device loses most of its force.
when: Witness is in custody

text: Suspense is built from three combined sources: prolonged waiting, small physical signs of agitation, and an abrupt sound that breaks the silence.
Suspense grows when repeated episodes escalate in intensity, moving from small signs to physical blows to violent confrontation.
when: Structuring a multi-stage threat
why: Rising intensity keeps tension building across episodes

text: Suspense can be built from three sources: anticipated horror that still lands hard, reversals at section endings, and a sense of an unseen observer who anticipates the player's moves.
Suspense rests on three parts: escalating threats, brief relief between them, and early setups that are paid off later.
A mystery can delay its answer by stacking false solutions, then shift the central question from who the culprit is to what the culprit is to the protagonist.
when: Designing a mystery with a late reveal of a hidden relationship
why: Changing the question late gives the audience a fresh frame, so the reveal adds meaning rather than only a name.

text: A threat left undefined in a character's mind often feels worse than a known one.
when: A character receives vague warning of danger
why: Without a definite shape, the imagination fills the gap with greater fears.

text: Delay the full explanation and give partial hints. Suspense comes from anticipation and open questions more than from the answer itself.
when: The audience must gather evidence before the reveal.
why: Unresolved questions keep the audience moving toward the next event.

text: Visible anticipation, such as every eye turning to a door or a stir at a small gesture, builds tension before a key reveal.
when: A scripted reveal is about to happen and the audience must wait.
why: Repeated expectant cues keep attention fixed on the coming event.

text: A summons demanding immediate action and secrecy makes the recipient fear more than the stated facts, so unnamed dread grows.
when: A message calls a character to act quickly and keep it quiet
why: The request for secrecy and haste suggests a hidden threat larger than the message states.

text: Building expectation around an unseen arrival, then delaying it, raises tension and turns the eventual appearance into a reveal.
when: introducing a new character who should be anticipated
why: A withheld payoff keeps curiosity active until the character appears.

text: Repeating a test at a fixed time while withholding its result builds suspense, since the audience expects the next occurrence.
when: evidence is incomplete and the answer depends on a later observation
why: a fixed schedule creates anticipation while the outcome stays hidden

text: 1) Start with a distant sound. 2) Move to a closer sound. 3) Insert a pause in which the threat seems near. 4) Release the tension with a sharp event.
when: Building suspense as a threat approaches slowly
why: Escalation in steps keeps tension rising until release.

text: Lay out the full case against a character before showing the defence, and hold back the decisive answer. This keeps the audience waiting.
when: when the audience needs suspense before a counter-argument

text: Interrupting an account at a moment of tension creates immediate suspense that holds attention until the next revelation.
why: Unfinished tension keeps the audience engaged

text: Repeated interruptions frustrate the audience without adding tension, so limit them and keep each one moving toward the answer.
when: Delaying a reveal
why: Delays that repeat the same hint feel like padding.

text: Let a staged crisis escalate in steps so each event looks more supernatural, while each step still has a mundane mechanism.
when: authoring a sequence of staged events in a haunting
why: Escalation sustains the illusion of the supernatural, while each mechanism remains recoverable.

text: Limiting the character's perception, through darkness, silence and brief light, creates dread because the character's limited awareness is itself the source of tension.
when: stealth or tense scenes
why: Restricted sensing forces the audience to imagine threats the character cannot yet see.

text: Stretch perceived time through repetition, such as a character pacing the same path or a clock hand that does not move.
when: When building suspense during a wait
why: Repeated actions make waiting feel longer to the reader

text: Distracted or absorbed companions can heighten a character's solitude during a wait.
when: When a character must wait alone in a tense scene
why: Inattentive others leave the character alone with their fear

text: Pace the waiting between repeated tests with other events, which separates the tests and raises pressure.
when: structuring time between repeated observations
why: interleaved events make waiting feel longer and more tense

text: Delaying a known, unavoidable event extends the wait and danger, sustaining tension as each delay heightens stakes and the audience stays alert.
when: When a known outcome is awaited and cannot be avoided; when pacing an approaching threat.
why: Each delay heightens stakes while the character imagines worse outcomes; extended anticipation keeps the audience alert.

text: Suspense grows when the audience waits with uncertain timing while small sensory cues each bring the expected event closer without yet delivering it.
when: an event's timing is uncertain and must be waited for
why: Each cue shows time passing and the threat approaching, which raises anticipation.

text: A timed wait with no contact builds suspense, so a later message that changes the plan lands with more force.
when: when a story needs a turn after a quiet period
why: the absence of contact raises expectation before the message arrives

text: Repeated waiting without new information or change erodes patience, letting impatience replace tension, so delays should be used sparingly.
when: Designing an anticipation scene such as a delayed arrival.
why: Players tolerate delay when it is rewarded, but repeated empty waiting erodes patience.

text: A reassurance that the threat is over buys time before the next pressure point, but it risks deflating tension if held too long.
when: Pacing a mystery's middle section
why: The promise lowers alertness briefly, so the next pressure point hits harder, at the cost of lost momentum if the pause runs long.

text: Withholding a key fact or name until late, while slowing the scene with close physical detail, keeps the audience waiting and builds suspense.
when: A reveal can be delayed for effect and the audience needs to anticipate it
why: Expectation and suspicion grow while the answer is held back

text: Keep repeated observations ambiguous so no firm answer comes, sustaining tension until more evidence arrives.
when: designing repeated sightings or tests
why: unresolved ambiguity holds attention without resolving the mystery

text: Suspense grows when characters who know more refuse to explain, so the gap between audience knowledge and character knowledge becomes the source of tension.
when: some characters know the truth and the audience does not
why: an open question keeps attention fixed on the hidden fact

text: Suspense builds when a sealed document's contents are withheld and the decision to open it is delayed to a later moment.
when: A reveal must be postponed or handed to a character's choice
why: The unknown outcome keeps the audience uncertain and attentive

text: A deferred reveal frustrates the audience if the eventual choice carries no new information.
when: Withholding a reveal behind a decision
why: A delay without payoff reads as stalling

text: Use a locked gate or refusing NPC whose reason is held back to create suspense, and resolve the reason later.
when: designing an obstacle that should keep the player curious
why: An unexplained barrier keeps the question open until the reason is revealed.

text: Withholding a reveal builds suspense, but holding it too long reads as evasion and frustrates the audience. Balance the delay against the payoff of the reveal.
when: when deciding how long to hold back an explanation
why: Delay that is too long reads as unfair withholding.

text: Stillness or a long delay reads as padding and drains tension unless a reveal follows or a clear threat is approaching.
when: Using quiet or ambient tension scenes, or delaying without a clear sense of approach
why: Tension with no resolution or direction loses its effect.

text: Repeating a false alarm without a payoff weakens later suspense.
when: Building tension with recurring warnings
why: The audience learns that warnings do not lead to real danger.

text: Withholding that the player can see through quickly loses tension.
when: When a character conceals information with obvious tells.
why: Predictable concealment removes the suspense of the reveal.

text: Ambiguous repeated tests frustrate an audience if no other route to the answer is offered.
when: designing repeated ambiguous tests
why: players need an alternative path to resolve repeated uncertainty

text: If the reveal disappoints after a long build, the accumulated tension is wasted, so the payoff must match the anticipation.
Suspicion travels along property lines, family ties, quarrels and self-appointed groups, so accusations often follow existing social connections.
when: when a community begins naming suspects
why: existing ties and shared interests decide whom people believe and blame

text: In a small, isolated community, residents judge newcomers and people of unfamiliar appearance as suspects, so prejudice can point at the wrong people.
when: A closed group with shared routines has a crime to explain.
why: Limited contact and visible differences make outsiders stand out and invite suspicion regardless of evidence.

text: A new face in a household can raise a careful suspect's suspicion, so a stand-in should be used with care.
when: when substituting household staff to create cover
why: Unfamiliar people are noticed and questioned by those who know the routine.

text: When witnesses die one after another, each death may look natural, but their accumulation makes players suspect a link.
when: When several people who hold knowledge die in a short span.
why: A cluster of deaths tied to shared knowledge suggests deliberate silencing even if each death alone is explained.

text: Stage a crowd moment such as a scream or alarm to force an identity into the open, rather than resolving it through private dialogue.
when: The reveal needs to land at a set moment with several witnesses present
why: A shared reaction makes the revelation public and hard to dismiss.

text: A crowd's prior expectation determines whether a genuine call for help is believed, so a real plea can be dismissed as a prank.
when: A character signals real danger to a group that expects them to joke.
why: Expectations filter incoming evidence, so the group discounts what it has already categorized.

text: Witness agreement supports an explanation but does not prove it; a group sharing one viewpoint can agree on a wrong account, adding little independent evidence.
when: Presenting testimony as evidence, or several witnesses report the same event together.
why: Consensus can be shared error; shared conviction feels like verified fact.

text: Concentrate plan-revealing details in a single cluster, with a late burst of specifics, so the audience can assemble the mechanism at once.
when: a hidden method must be revealed
why: a clustered set of clues makes the method legible

text: Treat a suspicion about a rival's supposed discovery as a hypothesis to test, not as established fact.
Plant suspects and grievances through ordinary business such as land, debts and lawsuits long before the crisis, so later accusations read as continuations of known feuds.
when: Opening the first fifth of a mystery or conflict-driven story.
why: Familiar disputes make a sudden crisis feel like an escalation the player already understood.

text: Do not dismiss a suspect because his apparent interest runs against the crime; check whether the benefit depends on conditions or sequence.
when: A suspect seems to have reason to keep the victim alive.
why: A reward that depends on conditions or order can reverse an apparent interest.

text: 1) Ask what a stated suspicion rests on. 2) Check that basis against observed facts. 3) Weigh the suspicion according to how well its basis holds.
when: someone states a suspicion about another person
why: Suspicions often rest on impressions rather than evidence

text: Suspicion of a person can already exist among some people well before any formal charge or arrest is made.
when: When tracing when an accusation first began.
why: Informal talk precedes official action.

text: A panel with a prior suspicion or fixation on one suspect reads the same ambiguous sign differently from a neutral examiner and accepts or rejects evidence too quickly.
when: when an examination panel has a prior suspicion
why: prior belief shapes how ambiguous evidence is interpreted

text: An authority figure who pushes a confident theory and dismisses motive is trusted, so the audience does not suspect them until a reversal.
Judging guilt from appearance, such as disliking a face, or from strong emotional reaction is prejudice, not a finding; it favours some suspects and closes off others.
when: when an investigator forms early judgments
why: Premature judgment on looks removes alternatives from consideration.

text: Attach each suspicion to a checkable observation, so players eliminate theories by consulting witnesses rather than guessing.
when: designing a suspicion system
why: Checkable observations make elimination fair

text: Let the player test whether an NPC's hint served the NPC, by comparing it with later evidence.
when: designing dialogue hints that may be red herrings
why: comparison separates a true clue from a self-serving one

text: Suspicion directed at the investigator can cut off access to the information needed to clear them.
when: when authorities suspect the investigator
why: Blocked sources prevent exoneration.

text: Audiences first suspect a conveniently marked outsider, such as a servant, lover, rival or foreigner, then shift toward an overlooked cause.
when: during the middle of a mystery
why: Suspicion follows family, class and reputation lines, so social markers steer blame.

text: Audience suspicion moves from victim to liar to new suspect when each claim is tested against a physical fact such as a route, a receipt or a search result.
when: a story where claims can be verified against objects or places
why: each check confirms or breaks a claim, reassigning belief

text: Accusation spreads from long-troubled, outspoken figures to newcomers and then to respected members, before turning back on the accusers.
when: A crisis where accusations multiply through a community.
why: Each accusation widens the circle until it reaches people with standing, which exposes the process.

text: Rotate suspicion among plausible suspects with real motives or grounded facts, such as watched, half-explained figures around a missing person, keeping the culprit in plain sight.
when: Choosing suspects for a whodunit or keeping a mystery open while the culprit is unknown.
why: Credible motives keep every suspect plausible until the reveal; shifting suspicion keeps players engaged without inventing unsupported guilt.

text: A cluster of closely timed coincidences draws suspicion, and concealment of those coincidences adds weight to it.
when: Several related events occur within a short span, especially if hidden from parties.
why: Matching timing and concealment are unlikely under innocent explanations.

text: Suspicion rotates among spouses, friends, servants, rivals and outsiders, moving when a physical, routine or official fact contradicts or points elsewhere.
when: A mystery with multiple groups of suspects, when a new fact or pressure event appears.
why: A contradicting fact removes the current suspect's credibility; each new candidate gives the audience a different target to test.

text: Clear, expose or reclassify each disguised stand-in as the next impostor appears, so suspicion keeps moving instead of settling on one face.
when: Structuring who the player suspects across a mystery.
why: A suspect who is cleared quickly leaves the player searching for the next one.

text: Suspicion moves to a suspect only after testimony reframes all earlier clues, so the same explained events are reread as evidence against that suspect.
when: Late testimony names a hidden identity.
why: A named motive turns previously dismissed oddities into evidence.

text: Suspicion shifts from an outsider to a trusted companion after a concrete event such as a corpse, a disappearance, or a physician's letter.
when: The story has reached a turning point with a visible event.
why: A concrete event makes the trusted person's involvement harder to dismiss.

text: Suspicion cascades through successive suspects, as each reveal implicates a new party until even the victim appears complicit.
when: A mystery with several reveals in sequence.
why: Each new revelation resets trust and pushes suspicion onto whoever is next exposed.

text: Suspicion moves in waves as gains and clues surface, and the final suspect gathers clues slowly until a late cluster makes the accusation certain.
when: when a story has several suspects over time
why: clues accumulate and shift belief in stages rather than all at once

text: Suspicion cycles: a convenient suspect falls first, then an innocent party is cleared by a specific alibi or test, and the true author emerges from a dismissed clue.
why: Each cleared suspect narrows belief toward the real culprit

text: Suspicion moves from the most visible outsider to the least obvious insider once a physical trace is read; official suspicion follows easy-to-present evidence, while the investigator follows evidence hard to fake or easy to overlook.
why: Easy-to-present evidence like bloodhounds or prints gets acted on, while subtle traces like dust, hairs or pipe bore expose the real culprit.

text: Suspicion can widen gradually through successive suspects, each dropped when a new dated document or record removes it, so the investigation grows in scope.
Suspicion moves to a new suspect whenever the player's current belief breaks, so each reveal inverts the suspect list.
when: a chain of false solutions
why: The player's last belief is what holds the current suspect in place

text: A suspicion-reversal mystery moves suspicion across several suspects, each shift backed by a clue, so the final answer must survive every earlier false suspect.
why: Each reversal keeps the player's attention on a new candidate until the true culprit is exposed.

text: Suspicion voiced by one witness can shape how others interpret later events.
when: A witness publicly suspects a person.
why: Shared suspicion biases interpretation of subsequent evidence.

text: Sympathy for an accused person can shape which suspects are considered, and the investigator may conceal that influence from others.
when: An investigator is emotionally invested in a suspect's innocence.
why: Emotional bias steers the search without being openly acknowledged.

text: Suspicion based on appearance, such as a foreign look or unusual facial hair, is bias, and audiences notice when a story leans on it.
when: Building a suspect's characterisation or a suspicion.
why: Appearance is not evidence, and readers reject suspicion that rests on it.

text: A suspect's suspicious movement may have been caused by a call or summons from someone else, which the supposed caller later denies.
when: a suspect's timing looks incriminating
why: A misattributed summons can explain the movement and mislead the group

text: 1) Open with a misleading observation that suggests an accident or innocent visitor. 2) Reveal murder through a clue. 3) Arrest a suspect justified by real evidence. 4) Introduce a clue that partly contradicts that suspect. 5) Shift to a rival theory. 6) Repeat with a second false solution. 7) End with a partial confession.
when: Structuring the reveal sequence of a whodunit or investigation scenario.
why: Each step is justified by evidence yet leaves the next link open, so no suspect is cleanly cleared.

text: Suspicion in a community tends to follow family ties, shared land and old quarrels more than any act the accused was shown to have done.
when: a community decides who to blame or distrust
why: Existing ties supply ready explanations for blame

text: When a person has open quarrels and threats and unrelated misfortune follows, observers tend to read the misfortune as malice caused by that person.
when: a community linking a person to local losses
why: recent hostility is taken as the cause of later harm

text: When the threat is inside a trusted household, suspicion usually moves from outsiders to family members after a physical test exposes the insider.
when: Designing the progression of suspicion in a closed-circle mystery.
why: Outsiders are the default suspects, so the insider is revealed only after a test shows them to be the actual threat.

text: Suspicion by association assigns guilt because of a relative's guilt, but kinship alone is weak evidence of accomplice intent: relatives share household access, not necessarily intent.
Observers guess at hidden wrongdoing using the fears fashionable in their era, so their suspicions reflect general anxieties more than anything they have seen.
when: An observer knows little about the person being suspected.
why: Familiar fears supply ready explanations when direct observation is absent.

text: Do not settle on a suspect's guilt from rumour or ambiguous gestures alone; wait for corroborated evidence before committing.
when: a suspect's behaviour could be read two ways
why: ambiguous signs can mislead when read without corroboration

text: Every suspicion rests on some base, even when appearances mislead. Find that base and test it before acting on the suspicion.
when: when a character or player forms a conclusion from observation
why: a conclusion can feel certain while its foundation is an unchecked assumption

text: Let suspicion of a protagonist's guilt rise gradually across the story rather than all at once.
Estrangement or old feuds are reasons to look closer, not proof of guilt.
when: When a suspect has a motive-related history
why: A grievance explains a motive but does not establish action

text: Let each false suspect explain one clue and leave one contradiction unexplained, so that suspicion shifts while the final answer stays open.
when: Designing a chain of suspects before the true culprit is revealed
why: Partial explanations make each suspect plausible, and the leftover contradiction points toward the real answer.

text: Hold every suspect open until each person's whereabouts are known, rather than fixing suspicion on a favourite.
when: When assessing suspects during an investigation
why: Premature fixation on one suspect causes the investigator to overlook evidence against others.

text: Keep the frame on an innocent suspect active until the final act so the player continues guessing.
when: Pacing the suspect arc of a mystery
why: An unresolved suspicion sustains tension and delays the reader's conclusion.

text: A suspicion value can rise with each clue or rumour and fall when the player supplies an innocent reading of an item.
when: building a system that tracks how suspicious a suspect appears
why: Letting players reduce suspicion through explanation keeps evidence open to interpretation

text: An NPC suspicion meter rises when the player reveals knowledge the NPC believes was private, so exposing hidden information makes the NPC defensive.
Give each suspect a gain tied to a fixed event, such as an inheritance or a deadline, so suspicion shifts along each gain line as the story unfolds.
when: when several characters could plausibly be guilty
why: a clear motive makes a character a plausible suspect at each stage

text: Too many false alarms make the audience stop reacting to real threats.
Gossip can drive a suspicion value that changes townsfolk reactions independent of what a character actually did.
when: when designing NPC reputation systems

text: An investigator may doubt a case because its evidence looks too neat, even before the reason for that doubt is shown.
An observer who already suspects a target reads odd behaviour, such as feigned drunkenness or lingering, as purposeful rather than accidental.
when: When an observer already suspects the target
why: Suspicion gives ordinary acts a hidden purpose

text: Treat a suspect's self-description of impulsiveness as a claim to check against their conduct, not as a verdict on intent.
when: When judging whether a suspect's account of intent is credible or reconstructing whether an act was spontaneous or prepared.
why: A self-description can hide a planned act, and it carries the same uncertainty as any other claim.

text: Suspecting a particular person can lead a witness to report seeing that person, so check any such sighting against other evidence.
When an outsider or supernatural suspect is introduced early, a visible insider detail gets dismissed and household members holding the inside plot go unchecked.
when: an outsider or supernatural suspect is presented early or set up as the obvious culprit
why: The outsider explanation absorbs attention, leaving the detail unweighed.

text: Once evidence exposes a substitution, cover-up or frame (a proof, or a witness's described physical act even without the object shown), suspicion shifts to whoever arranged it.
when: A substitution or cover-up is exposed
why: The party who arranged the concealment becomes the logical source of the deception.

text: Under public accusation, suspicion is shifted onto a third party through rumour, and the accuser's own honesty may be attacked.
when: When characters face a public accusation
why: Pointing at someone else deflects attention from the accused

text: Make an innocent suspect's flight a turning point in the middle of the case, not the ending.
when: a suspect runs or disappears before being cleared
why: A midpoint flight keeps suspicion high while the investigation continues.

text: Let a trusted helper who guards, searches or assists the player be a suspect in plain sight, with clues that look procedural rather than suspicious.
when: Placing a culprit among the investigators
why: Routine actions look like normal duty, so their suspicious meaning is missed until late.

text: Suspicion that moves outward to an external group and then back inward to staff can hide an insider until tool evidence lines up.
when: Shifting suspicion across factions during a mystery
why: An external suspect absorbs early attention, so the return to insiders feels like a fresh discovery.

text: Make the external threat believable before revealing the internal one; a credible outside culprit gives an insider cover to act unseen.
when: Designing a mystery where the culprit is a trusted insider
why: Players accept the outside suspect first, so the insider's real motive stays hidden.

text: Suspicion falls on whoever a timeline places nearby or last interacted with the scene, the most available culprit by default.
when: a group feels threatened by an investigation, or a threatening character is found dead
why: Blaming the nearest person deflects attention from the group's own exposure, and the nearest actor is blamed by default, so the protagonist can be framed by their own actions.

text: Suspicion shifts when a document, disguise, or witness contradiction breaks the current theory, even before proof, and moves to whoever that evidence points at, even a trusted narrator.
when: When designing suspicion shifts, or when evidence contradicts a narrator's or a figure's account.
why: Concrete breaking evidence gives the player a reason to revise the theory; a contradicted narrator can become the suspect.

text: Each new fact that clears or incriminates a suspect shifts suspicion to someone else, not only through elimination; no candidate settles while unexplained clues stay open until late confessions.
when: when the audience tracks suspects across a story
why: Repeated invalidation keeps several candidates alive instead of settling on one early.

text: Suspicion lands first on the most visible suspect, then moves to a less likely or unseen party with a motive, driven by new physical or testimonial detail, not confession.
when: Pacing suspect changes across a mystery.
why: Visible suspects draw early attention, and new evidence redirects it.

text: Clearing a suspect, including with a search, redirects attention to the remaining candidates, so the final one becomes the focus of the explanation.
when: several suspects are eliminated in turn
why: clearing one suspect redirects attention to the remaining candidates

text: When every member of one group seems innocent, investigators tend to shift suspicion to a different group.
when: candidates are cleared one by one without a strong suspect
why: Lacking a clear culprit, attention moves to whoever remains unexamined.

text: When one suspect is discharged, suspicion often moves to another person named by the same rumor, so the matter returns in another form.
when: a first accusation fails or is dismissed
why: The rumor behind the first accusation outlives its target.

text: Suspicion settles on the character with the most visible secret, while the true actor is hidden in plain view as a helper, judge, second or servant.
when: a scene with several people who have something to hide
why: Visible secrets draw attention away from quieter, trusted figures.

text: Suspicion in a case often moves from the most obvious party to an outsider, then to the investigator's own theory.
when: a case with several plausible culprits

text: Players distrust the first culprit once a midpoint crisis collapses it, so suspicion moves from an outsider to a visibly guilty insider and then to a quieter insider with a hidden motive.
when: a mystery shifts suspicion across the cast over its run
why: Each reversal of a visibly guilty suspect exposes the previous reading as incomplete, pushing attention toward hidden motives.

text: After a misdirect has settled, concentrate decisive clues in the middle of the mystery so suspicion moves from the first suspect to the true target.
when: when a mystery builds a reputation for one suspect before revealing another
why: the first half establishes the spectacle, then the middle clues redirect attention

text: Move suspicion between supernatural and living enemies, so the reader is always assigned a human suspect before the story turns again.
Ask who benefits from each false lead; a suspicion or rumour that serves one party's cover story is likely planted.
when: Evaluating suspicions, rumours or accusations
why: Planted leads serve the planner's interests, so their beneficiary points toward the planner

text: Suspicion should be a tool that shifts from one suspect to another as each new fact arrives, rather than being the subject of the mystery itself.
when: Structuring a multi-suspect investigation.
why: Moving suspicion keeps the method and the suspect chain separate, so the method can be revealed while suspicion still moves.

text: Suspicion stays diffuse until the deduction names a place, then moves at once to the people tied to that place.
when: Designing how a mystery narrows its suspects.
why: Without a location there is no basis for singling out individuals, so the focus shifts only when one is named.

text: Once a mechanism is exposed, shift suspicion to those who relied on it rather than to the accused.
when: a reveal undermines a group's accusation
why: The exposed mechanism now implicates its users.

text: Suspicion that moves between human and supernatural causes, with each human suspect failing a test, leads the player to accept a larger explanation.
when: When structuring the escalation of a mystery's explanation.
why: Each failed human explanation removes alternatives until only the larger cause remains.

text: Suspicion can move from the first accused to a new group when later clues connect a past conflict to a second suspect.
When suspicion moves from an outside accomplice to the household and then to the disguised agent, each shift reframes earlier evidence.
when: structuring suspicion across a mystery
why: Reframing earlier clues makes the final reveal recontextualize the whole episode.

text: When suspicion shifts from a living accomplice to the dead principal, the reader's model of who planned the crime reverses, so the late reveal lands as a reversal.
why: Moving blame to someone the reader thought was out of play overturns the earlier model rather than confirming it.

text: Suspicion moves from one suspect to another once a clue establishes who owned a key object, because guilt reassigns to the person that owner was connected with.
when: a clue resolves ownership of an object at the scene
why: Identifying the owner changes which relationships the player treats as suspicious.

text: Suspicion moves when the next discovery tests a suspect's motive, so each new clue shifts blame to a different character.
why: A motive is only as strong as the evidence that survives testing

text: Suspicion moves onto a culprit when their motive is tied to a document and their own statements conflict with each other.
when: in the middle act of a mystery
why: A motive plus contradictions gives the player a concrete reason to suspect that person.

text: Suspicion shifts in waves, each triggered by a new contradiction or link to the victim, so each suspect receives a full cycle before the next takes over.
when: Pacing suspects across a mystery
why: Short cycles keep any single false solution from lasting too long.

text: Suspicion moves in a sequence from one character to another, each shift triggered by the newest witness having a motive the player has just been shown.
when: A mystery where the suspect list changes over the course of the story.
why: Each new motive redirects suspicion, keeping the player uncertain about who is responsible.

text: Keep the accused's guilt as the default from the start, and let the reversal come from the witness with the most to lose.
Make each new clue shift blame to a different household member, so the audience must keep re-evaluating the whole group rather than one suspect.
Let each apparent solution be undone by a verified fact that removes one suspect cleanly.
when: when a suspect is cleared
why: A clean refutation prevents the player from keeping doubt about a cleared suspect.

text: Shifting suspicion by reinterpreting existing clues can work without new discovery; otherwise each shift needs a new fact, motive, or contradiction, since unsupported shifts feel arbitrary.
when: when rotating suspects across a mystery's cast
why: Fact-driven shifts feel earned and keep trust; reinterpreting known evidence can overturn a suspect without any new discovery.

text: Suspicion driven by grudges, property claims, rank, class or kinship rather than factual evidence misleads investigations; accusations need a factual basis.
when: Investigating a death with several possible culprits, or when a suspect is chosen because of rank, class or kinship.
why: Social motives can outweigh the available evidence, and status-based suspicion has no factual grounding.

text: Suspicion can radiate out from a few households to neighbours, relatives and distant people, until neighbours turn on one another.
Suspicion can pass along a chain of suspects and return to an earlier one when new evidence appears, so the culprit is not fixed early.
when: in a mystery with several plausible suspects
why: New evidence re-weights earlier suspects, keeping the question open.

text: After a main suspect is cleared, the player's suspicion does not move cleanly to one new person but splits across several candidates before narrowing.
when: A main suspect's alibi collapses mid-story
why: Suspicion is anchored to the old theory, so it scatters before a new target forms.

text: Suspicion can spread so widely that the group collapses before the investigator can exploit it.
Keep suspicions tentative until a test or corroboration confirms them, on case boards or clue journals, so the suspicion-to-proof gap becomes a playable mechanic and theories aren't treated as facts.
when: designing a clue journal or tracking multiple suspicions during an investigation
why: Unconfirmed theories should not be treated as established facts.

text: Use suspicion to decide where to look and whom to watch, not as the sole basis for an accusation or arrest.
why: Suspicion guides investigation, but accusation requires proof.

text: Pair a sympathetic detail with a suspicious one in the same scene so that neither settles the question and the player stays torn.
when: designing an ambiguous accused character
why: the two details pull the player's judgment in opposite directions

text: Treating a complainant's suspicion as proof of the culprit's identity confuses accusation with evidence.
when: A complainant names or suspects a person without direct evidence.
why: Suspicion is a belief and does not establish identity.

text: A character can hold suspicions without confirmed knowledge, and the two should be kept distinct when tracking what each person knows.
when: Tracking characters' beliefs about a hidden event.
why: Suspicion is not proof, so treating it as fact misstates what the character can act on.

text: A witness who agrees too quickly may be performing rather than telling the truth, so the agreement should be re-examined.
when: A witness immediately accepts a claim that favours them.
why: Immediate, convenient agreement can hide a motive.

text: A clue that seems to implicate someone too neatly may instead be the strongest evidence of their innocence, so check the mechanism's constraints first.
when: Evaluating a clue whose timing or content looks incriminating.
why: Convenient fit can be a sign of staging or of a flawed inference rather than guilt.

text: Distinguish suspicion from proof; do not charge or accuse on suspicion, opportunity, or motive alone.
when: When a convergence of clues points to a suspect but no decisive fact exists.
why: Accusing too early risks losing the case if the suspicion is wrong.

text: Suspicion that shifts without an anchoring clue reads as indecision rather than misdirection.
when: suspects change with no new clue
why: the audience sees no reason for the change

text: Close attention to a speaker's belongings may be read as suspicion.
A brief change in a claimant's expression while a document is identified can reveal more than their testimony.
when: A person is questioned about a document they stand to benefit from.
why: Involuntary reactions can betray knowledge the testimony hides.

text: Hiding or fleeing from authorities fits guilt, but also fits an innocent person afraid of being wrongly charged. Such conduct is weak evidence alone.
when: Evaluating a suspect's evasive behavior
why: Fear of false accusation produces the same visible actions as guilt
