text: A person who takes precautions more elaborate than the situation needs draws attention, even though each precaution alone looks ordinary.
when: a suspect's conduct is examined
why: The pattern across the steps, not any one step, reveals design.

text: A member who suspects a leader may sell that leader out to the authorities to protect themselves.
A quick, ready explanation for a suspicious noise should be checked rather than accepted, since cover stories can be offered at once.
when: someone explains away a noise connected to an event
why: An immediate explanation may be prepared in advance, so it is not evidence that the noise was harmless.

text: An invented errand used to clear the room can later be noticed as suspicious.
Overly curious questions alert the person being investigated, so a scout's questions must look ordinary to avoid suspicion.
when: a visitor gathers information from an occupant
why: unusual questions signal intent

text: When a character reacts to an object without a shown cause, the audience tends to blame the person rather than examine the object.
when: a reaction is shown without explanation
why: the reaction has no visible cause to attach it to

text: When an act looks inexplicable and the actor cannot or will not give reasons, audiences generate rival motives to fill the gap.
when: an act has no stated reason
why: An unexplained act leaves a gap that people fill with guesses.

text: A suspect who tries to undo a warning by acting on it often produces the very act that exposes them.
when: A suspect reacts to a warning with an outgoing message or move
why: The reaction itself becomes visible evidence

text: Neighbours who cannot explain a rival's sudden large gain tend to suspect envy or wrongdoing, even without evidence of either.
when: someone with little visible means acquires a large holding
why: Unexplained advantage invites suspicion and resentment

text: Involuntary tells include a facial spasm, a suspicious glance at passing strangers, and a voice that cannot be steadied.
Money that moves in ways the neighbours cannot explain, such as loans, cash payments and large spending, shows a hidden source of funds.
when: When a victim's finances do not match her known means.
why: Unexplained income often points to the motive behind a killing.

text: An official's anxious interest in a suspect that exceeds the stated reason is a strong clue to a hidden relationship.
when: An official shows concern beyond their stated role.
why: Real motive shows in excess concern that the stated reason does not justify.

text: Let an unexplained reaction unlock an interview with a third NPC, making it a valid lead the player can follow.
when: A reaction points to a relationship the player cannot yet explain.
why: A third character can supply the missing context and move the investigation forward.

text: An unexplained change in an NPC's plans, paired with a stated reason that does not fit, can serve as a clue hook for the player to pursue.
when: Designing story hooks.
why: A mismatch between action and reason invites investigation.

text: A firm ultimatum, such as threatening to inform the authorities, can move a reluctant person to speak.
when: a person refuses to cooperate voluntarily

text: Introduce a specific name with no context and watch for abrupt shifts in posture, colour or tone; a quick guard going up is a tell, not proof.
when: testing whether a witness's denial holds
why: a guarded reaction can have many causes beyond knowledge of the subject

text: When a reaction is much stronger than expected, treat the gap between expectation and result as information to study.
why: an unexplained gap may point to knowledge the investigator lacks

text: A large offer with no explanation, especially one promising no questions, warrants scrutiny of the real motive.
when: when the reward is out of proportion to the item

text: Withheld information, such as secrecy or a motive, reads as a cheat or misdirection unless the audience later learns why it was held back.
A sudden change of manner that is not explained can read as an authorial trick rather than as character.
when: A character abruptly changes demeanour
why: Without motivation the change feels contrived to the audience.

text: A stranger's unusual interest in an investigation may be either a clue or a red herring, so treat it as ambiguous until tested.
A pretext that leaves the host uneasy can deepen the very secrecy it was meant to uncover.
when: when the host is suspicious after the entry
why: Unease makes the host more guarded.

text: A question whose purpose is unexplained can seem odd, so others may dismiss it before its answer matters.
Announcing a new arrest without detail can confuse the audience about who is guilty.
when: A reversal introduces a new suspect
why: Vague announcements leave the guilty party unclear

text: A denial with no explanation leaves a suspect exposed, even when the suspect is innocent.
Underestimating a cool-headed suspect's reaction can lead to injuries to officers.
A reveal that leaves one action unexplained frustrates the audience, even when the rest of the solution holds.
Reasoning from constraints assumes behavior that no record confirms, so the conclusion is only as strong as that assumption.
when: The act being inferred is undocumented
why: An unverified behavior may not have happened as assumed

text: A reaction that an innocent person also triggers identifies no one, and explanations offered afterward for that result are not controls.

1) Prepare a question plan in advance. 2) Open calmly and let the suspect commit to a defence. 3) Gauge composure, then pause to reconsider rather than push harder. 4) Ask a pointed question about a specific time, place and detail. 5) Follow with narrow, checkable details.
when: when the suspect has given a smooth, prepared account
why: a specific, unanticipated question tests whether the account holds

text: An unexplained fact, such as a large purchase, shows only motive. Rule out ordinary explanations like overheard gossip or third-party relay before concluding guilt; physical evidence is needed.
when: when a suspect has an unexplained large purchase or resource, or knows something with no recorded route

text: A tip that arrives at a convenient moment may be bait, so ask whether the suspect could have written it and would gain from the timing.
when: a tip arrives just when the suspect benefits
why: a convenient tip may serve the suspect's own plan

text: An unusually clean or pristine surface or impression suggests deliberate preparation; check how the mark was produced instead of accepting it as ordinary.
when: when evidence looks too perfect
why: a surface can be polished before a mark is placed on it

text: When a clue seems fabricated, look for the extra step the staging required, since that step is where the fabrication shows.
when: When an investigator suspects a clue was placed to mislead.
why: Staging needs actions beyond the crime itself, and those actions leave traces.

text: A planted clue that looks too convenient is suspect; test how well it fits the scene before trusting it.
when: a clue arrives exactly when it resolves a question
why: convenient finds are often planted

text: Damaging finds that each look incriminating, and together look overwhelming, may have been selected rather than found; question how the set came together.
when: several damaging items point the same way at once

text: Measurements that agree too closely across several tracks are more likely staged than coincidental, so judge how tight the agreement is.
when: when judging whether tracks are genuine
why: real walkers rarely match exactly

text: An account that is too complete and convenient deserves scrutiny; its ease can hide weak points.
A culprit whose rationalization is too neat reads as a plot device, so the contradictions in their reasoning must stay visible.
when: Writing a culprit's motive.
why: Overly tidy justification removes the human texture that makes motive believable.

text: A clue that survives when it could easily have been destroyed may have been left on purpose, and such deliberate clues can backfire on their authors.
when: A key item survives in a place where destruction was easy.
why: Culprits who leave clues to mislead take the risk that the clue exposes them.

text: A trace that is too neat, or that leads exactly where investigators will look, may have been placed deliberately and should be tested.
when: a clue seems conveniently placed
why: Staged evidence often points directly at the investigation

text: Keeping a feigned condition convincing over many days is hard and carries real risk to the person faking it.
when: A staged incapacity must last a long time
why: Each day of performance adds a chance of exposure and personal danger

text: If a secret has held among several people who had reason to talk, the secret is probably real.
when: several people share a secret and each had incentive to reveal it
why: pressure to betray would usually have broken the silence

text: Sweeping a whole group can cause panic and rumour that bury the facts the investigator needs.
1) Assume every witness statement is false. 2) List which physical facts fit that assumption. 3) Note which physical facts contradict it.
When one line of questioning fails, change angle, such as asking about access to a room, rather than repeating the same question.
With an evasive witness, switch to another source instead of pressing the same person again.
A single controllable switch makes its operator a suspect once the lights return and the scene is reviewed.
Track motive for both sides of a conflict, so the player can shift suspicion when a new record changes the picture.
1) Appoint named examiners and swear them. 2) Have them search for the sought sign. 3) Write their findings, sign them and attest them before an official. 4) File the report as a formal record.
when: When physical evidence needs an expert eye and a formal record.
why: The oath and attestation give the report weight, which is why its content must still be checked.

text: Treating an account as firm evidence simply because it is sworn and detailed.
Do not treat an oath as proof: sworn form records what was said, not that it was true.
why: an oath fixes the statement but not its accuracy

text: 1) Identify the sworn account's source, date and signatories. 2) Check its account against the written record line by line. 3) Locate the points of disagreement. 4) Judge whether each difference changes substance.
when: Verifying a witness account against documents.
why: Structured comparison separates real contradictions from minor wording variation.

text: A sworn or formal statement can raise a witness's weight in the eyes of listeners even when their general standing is low.
why: Formal commitment signals accountability

text: Sworn testimony written down before a hearing creates a durable evidence trail that fixes a witness's version for later comparison.
when: when a claim must be checked after the event
why: a written commitment resists drift in memory

text: Weigh a sworn witness's account against other evidence, since a sworn witness can be mistaken and dismissing their word needs justification.
Where the accused requests it, testimony should be sworn rather than given in writing before the account is accepted.
when: when a party asks for sworn evidence instead of a written attestation
why: an oath binds the witness more firmly to the account than a written attestation

text: A motive built from a symbol alone is speculation; a symbolic grievance needs independent corroboration before it implies intent.
A symbol with a known meaning, found on victims, can reveal which group carried out an act.
A drawn sign can look meaningless until a specialist recognizes its source, and its meaning depends on the tradition it comes from and who reads it.
when: a symbol appears at a scene and its origin is unknown

text: Symbols can carry unrelated readings from different traditions; treating one meaning as certain when the evidence allows others produces false attributions, so an identification must be weighed first.
Compare a specialist's identification of a symbol with other sources before acting on it, and record which reading the evidence supports.
when: a symbol has been identified by a single source

text: A sympathetic NPC can give the player a biased tip; rewarding cross-checking of that tip against the scene encourages evidence-based reasoning over trust.
why: Affection for an NPC can shape how much the player believes that NPC's information.

text: Make the most sympathetic claimant the actual danger, so a player who trusts the wronged party is led into the reveal.
when: designing a mystery with a claimant or heir
why: Sympathy lowers the player's guard against the true threat.

text: Give a suspect a sympathetic motive and a lawful errand whose timing contradicts the stated purpose, so the player can catch the mismatch.
A sympathetic witness chosen to observe an act is likely to support the story rather than question it.
why: Sympathy makes the witness less inclined to scrutinise the framing

text: Let a sympathetic witness hold the final key, so the reveal is pulled from them rather than discovered alone.
A sympathetic profile should not excuse a harm; weigh the harm itself separately from the character's good qualities.
when: Assessing a character who did both good and serious wrong.
why: Sympathy can hide the cost to victims.

text: A sympathetic backstory can lead the audience to trust a character's conclusions too quickly, even when his grudges may bias them.
when: When a character is both sympathetic and the source of key interpretations.
why: Sympathy is read as reliability, so biased claims go unchecked.

text: Let the player explain a device to frightened characters during a confrontation so that they earn the characters' trust.
when: Designing an arrest or boss-confrontation sequence

text: Trusting a sympathetic witness or dismissing one who confesses dislike skips the corroboration step.
Clues that cut against a sympathetic reading can feel unfair to the audience until the confession that explains them arrives.
Sympathy for a distressed witness lowers an investigator's scrutiny, leading them to accept the witness's framing and trust sincerity over the facts.
when: when the witness is distressed or vulnerable and the investigator is moved or grows attached to them
why: Empathy and emotional engagement reduce distance from the evidence and lower scrutiny of the witness's account.

text: A confident, sympathetic witness can seem more reliable than a better-evidenced one, and readiness to name a culprit can outpace what they actually saw.
when: when comparing witnesses of differing status or warmth
why: social appeal can substitute for evidence

text: Balance a witness's emotional account against what the witness actually saw, because sympathy can distort reporting.
when: Evaluating testimony from a biased or attached witness

text: Audience sympathy and appealing stories can settle a verdict over complex evidence, because audiences fill gaps with the most natural story.
when: A case is presented with emotional framing or an emotionally appealing explanation.
why: Emotionally satisfying stories are accepted over complex evidence.

text: Sympathy from listeners, including for a grieving witness, can make a witness's account seem more credible than the evidence supports.
when: Evaluating testimony that reveals a hidden personal matter.
why: Emotional reaction can make a witness seem more credible than the evidence supports.

text: 1) Have a colleague watch for loss of focus in the sympathetic investigator. 2) Warn when personal engagement starts to affect judgment. 3) Keep the team's distance from the witness.
when: A witness is vulnerable and the team risks losing objectivity
why: An outside observer can notice bias that the involved person cannot see.

text: Sympathy factions that defend or shield a suspect can act as allies or obstacles to the player, independent of the clues.
Gentleness can make an interviewer drop a point they needed, so sympathy trades completeness for the witness's comfort.
Sympathy for a victim can turn into prejudice against a suspect, shaping public belief and possibly how a jury reacts.
when: A victim is widely pitied and a suspect is publicly known.
why: Feelings about one person spread to judgments about another.

text: Physical symptoms a confessor reports after speaking can be read as proof of sincerity, though they say nothing about the claim itself.
Check whether observed symptoms fit the claimed cause; symptoms that the claimed cause would not produce make that cause doubtful.
A shaking hand, irritability and poor sleep are physical signs that can point to a cause, though one sign alone does not establish a diagnosis.
when: Observing a person's physical signs as possible evidence of a condition.
why: Several causes can produce the same set of signs.

text: Symptoms gain evidential value once they fit a recognized pattern, so compare observations with a reference description of each candidate cause.
Give several ambiguous physical signs of death in one scene so they form a conclusion only when read together.
when: Revealing a death through indirect evidence.
why: Individually weak signs are easy to dismiss, but together they point clearly to one conclusion.

text: A chain of branching questions moving from a symptom toward its cause lets players follow a logical path to the hidden explanation.
1) Read a physical trace as a condition. 2) Infer the likely diagnosis from it. 3) Infer symptoms, then the way of moving. 4) Present each step as probable, not certain.
when: Building a profile from skeletal or bodily evidence.
why: Each layer depends on expert knowledge and is less certain than the one before.

text: 1) Examine the hair. 2) Examine the jaw. 3) Examine the arms. 4) Examine the hands, using magnification for small signs. Record what each part reveals about occupation.
when: at the start of an interview when the person's background is unknown
why: a fixed order ensures no part is missed and small signs are caught

text: Adhesive that is still tacky indicates a very recent application, so it can date a replacement to the most recent period.
Record admissions made while an NPC is incapacitated as evidence but tag them less reliable, so trust can vary.
Tag each NPC claim as true or false in the game data, so that a later retraction can resurface the earlier line as a clue.
when: when NPCs make statements the player may later revisit
why: Stored truth values let the game connect retractions to earlier dialogue.

text: Have gossip NPCs spread rumours about each other, tagging each with the speaker's status, grudge, source and bias, so players judge how far to trust partly accurate claims.
when: Designing gossip systems or gossip NPCs whose information is partly true.
why: Source bias makes players weigh claims, and explicit bias lets players calibrate trust in partly accurate rumours.

text: Tag NPC testimony and relayed rumours with their source, confidence or self-interest, and hop count, so players can weigh reliability and cross-check claims against map or item data.
when: when a game records what characters say about events or passes information along through dialogue
why: tags let players judge reliability; visible hop counts show how far a claim is from its source

text: 1) Record each claim's source and basis as seen, heard, or assumed. 2) Mark hearsay as unconfirmed. 3) Upgrade a claim to confirmed only after a direct witness or independent record supports it.
when: players collect multiple statements or a journal or rumor system presents hidden events
why: knowing how a claim was obtained changes how much weight it deserves, and players need to know which information is provisional

text: Tag each NPC clue fragment with the observer's distance or conditions so players can judge how reliable it is.
Record each NPC hint or testable claim with a confidence level so a later check against evidence can flag weak claims or red herrings.
when: NPCs or a dialogue system deliver hints or statements the player must evaluate later
why: Logged claims allow later comparison against evidence

text: Tag each NPC claim with its stated premises so players can find the hidden assumption that fails.
Write NPC rumours as partly true clues with a known source and bias, so the player must weigh them.
when: When designing tavern tales or rumours in a game world
why: Known bias gives the player a way to judge reliability

text: Tag each non-player statement as seen, heard or assumed, and let players weigh each tag differently.
when: when writing NPC dialogue that reports events
why: Players can cross-check claims only when they can classify them

text: Log an NPC's reaction as a flag the player can later weigh against other statements.
when: tracking NPC responses to evidence
why: stored reactions allow later comparison with other testimony

text: 1) Record every stop the target makes. 2) Note each small deliberate act. 3) Read the acts together to infer the target's plans.
when: shadowing a suspect's routine
why: habits and plans show in small acts

text: Use a tail when a target's movements are the only way to find a contact or hiding place.
A captive NPC released under tail can reveal a hidden faction through where he goes, letting the player learn the group's location.
when: Designing quests around captive NPCs.
why: The NPC's movements expose associates.

text: 1) Post a tail to follow the target. 2) Learn where the target is at a set time. 3) Plan the confrontation for that time, expecting the target to be present.
when: the target must be found again after a gap

text: Tailor-made clothing normally carries sewn strips naming the maker and client, and often the date, so missing strips are unusual.
A talkative NPC can hold useful clues among filler dialogue, so the game should give players a way to filter for them.
when: Designing an NPC with a lot of chatter.
why: Players need a way to separate the usable clues from the noise.

text: Let a talkative witness run on rather than cutting them off, then sift the talk for the few usable facts it contains.
when: A witness gives long, rambling answers.
why: Useful clues can sit among filler dialogue, so interrupting may lose them.

text: Let a talkative or elderly witness speak at their own pace, and steer back to the subject in small steps rather than with sharp, direct questions.
when: when the witness digresses and the needed facts are scattered through background talk
why: sharp questions make digressive witnesses lose the thread

text: 1) Check innocent causes first, such as too little moisture or defective gum. 2) Rule each one out. 3) Only then consider deliberate tampering.
when: a seal fails
why: simpler causes are more probable

text: Use a dim light or odd object as a tampering clue that careful players notice and impatient players miss.
A signal that fails to ring when touched suggests its mechanism was disturbed, which can indicate tampering by someone with access.
when: A tripwire or bell cord does not respond as expected
why: Failure of a signal is itself evidence that someone interfered.

text: Give players targeted questions for NPCs, and let each answer unlock the next deduction.
Order a lab test for a specific hypothesis rather than a general scan, since a question-driven analysis is easier to interpret.
when: Choosing an analysis for an unexplained death.
why: Results from a vague test are hard to interpret.

text: Choose a stimulus that bears directly on the hypothesis being tested, since an unrelated trigger produces a result that proves nothing.
when: When provoking a suspect to reveal a hidden trait
why: Only a stimulus linked to the hypothesis produces evidence that bears on it.

text: When accusers choose targets from rumor, the targets often cluster in one community or congregation that accusers already hear spoken of with hostility.
why: Shared hostility in one group makes its members easy to name.

text: The choice of victim can suggest a targeted attack when the victim's vulnerability matches the mechanism's effect.
when: A harmful act appears to affect a particular person
why: Matching vulnerability to the method implies deliberate selection

text: A pattern of teasing without new information exhausts the audience, and interruptions that feel arbitrary weaken the scene.
Complicated technical terms can make an uncertain cause seem settled when it is not.
Check a technical term's professional sense and the sources it cites before relying on it, rather than accepting the everyday reading.
A technically true but incomplete answer can conceal a key fact and serve as the planted clue to that concealment; the listener must judge what was omitted and why.
when: When a character has a motive to hide part of a truth.
why: Accurate but selective statements can mislead without a lie.

text: Include true but selective statements in NPC dialogue so the player can catch the omission later.
when: When writing dialogue that conceals part of a truth.
why: A later-caught omission rewards attention to what was left unsaid.

text: A person who appears impassive on blunt questions may brighten sharply on a topic where they feel at ease, revealing their comfort zone.
when: A reserved person is asked about varied subjects.
why: Comfort and discomfort show in changes of expression and energy.

text: Establish each character's normal manner before reading a tell, since a tell gains weight only when it contrasts with that baseline.
when: Interpreting a reaction as evidence of knowledge or guilt.
why: Without a baseline, ordinary behaviour is easily mistaken for a meaningful signal.

text: Overly casual indifference that follows a reaction can be a cover for the first response and is worth noting.
when: A suspect's calm seems forced right after a visible reaction.
why: Overacting calm is an attempt to conceal the earlier reaction.

text: Cross-check guarded speech against involuntary signs, since a mismatch between calm words and a flushed or fidgeting body is a usable clue.
when: A suspect's words and physical cues disagree
why: The contradiction points to agitation the words conceal

text: A single bodily tell is weak evidence, since fear, shame or privacy can cause it; confirm it with a second source, such as a mirror or another witness, before acting.
when: When a witness's nervousness or a suspicious tell is interpreted as guilt
why: Fear, shame or privacy can produce the same signs as concealment

text: Record each answer and each reaction in a journal so the player can use the accumulated pattern to narrow a secret.
when: Designing a dialogue puzzle that uses yes or no questioning
why: A written record lets the player follow the pattern of answers and tells

text: Use a behavioral tell, such as a physical reaction, only to choose the next line of questioning, never as sole ground for an accusation or proof of guilt or knowledge.
when: When a tell appears during questioning.
why: Tells signal where to look but prove nothing alone; fear and discomfort have many sources.

text: Ask the suspect a question whose answer would be telling if they were guilty, such as asking about symptoms that would appear after poisoning.
when: Testing a suspect's guilt without decisive evidence.
why: A guilty suspect's answer or reaction can betray knowledge they should not have.

text: Treat observed tells as questions to test against evidence, never as conclusions; demeanour alone cannot support a case.
Present the culprit's method as a proposal the player can test, not as a settled fact, so the solution stays open to checking.
when: when the culprit has not confessed
why: A testable claim lets the player verify the method.

text: Tells such as flushing, paling, nail-biting, sudden silence, averted eyes or folded hands can signal concealed distress, yet also stem from illness, anger or embarrassment.
when: when a suspect's inner state shows only through visible behaviour, particularly when an investigator probes a hidden secret
why: Involuntary reactions reveal distress the subject would not state, but the same signs are ambiguous across causes.

text: Plant a behavioural tell on an antagonist early, so that its later recognition feels earned rather than sudden.
when: Building a reveal in which a character is identified by appearance or gesture.
why: A tell seen earlier lets the player recognise the antagonist before the protagonist states it, which makes the payoff satisfying.

text: Let tells point to hidden items, so the player connects an NPC's reaction to a location.
Give in-game documents telltale features, such as inconsistent detail, odd phrasing or broken sentences, so close readers can judge whether a note is finished or a rough draft.
when: Writing notes, journals or ledgers for players to read.
why: Careful readers use textual signs to judge authenticity.

text: A small object left on a surface can transfer to a visitor's clothing and later reveal that they were present.
when: a hidden visitor must be exposed later
why: objects pick up material from whatever touches them

text: A sharp reply to a warning is evidence of how a person may react under pressure, so record it.
A passionate motive is unlikely for a suspect whose calm, profit-seeking conduct contradicts anger; temperament can rule a motive out.
when: a passion-based motive is proposed for a suspect
why: Motives show in how a person acts under pressure.

text: Infer a culprit's temperament from their method: a crime copied from earlier patterns suggests an imitative rather than inventive mind.
when: The method of a crime seems to point to a type of mind
why: Method reflects habits of mind

text: Treating a character's rudeness or temper as evidence of crime confuses temperament with motive; a motive built from temperament alone fits many people and needs physical or situational support.
Judging a person's character by temperament is open to bias, and assumptions about how people behave can mislead an investigation.
when: An investigator concludes that a suspect would or would not act a certain way.
why: Character assumptions are subjective and can exclude a real culprit.

text: Let a villain's stated reason for an action be a claim the player can test against other evidence in the level.
when: A game antagonist explains his actions
why: Testable motives turn the player into an investigator

text: Give each enemy or NPC a temperament that governs how it carries out a deed, so a scene that breaks the temperament signals a different actor.
when: Designing cast behaviour for a mystery
why: Consistent temperament lets players spot staged or mismatched scenes

text: People who hold land only as tenants, without legal title, are unlikely to bury someone permanently on that land.
when: Judging where a person without title might have acted
why: Lack of title removes both the right and the security needed for such an act

text: A tenant's legal standing to claim land depends on the owner's title, so possession and title can belong to different people.
when: A tenant and an owner both have some connection to the same land
why: The tenant's right to act for the land derives from the owner's legal claim

text: Without a valid will, an estate typically passes to blood relatives.
when: under typical inheritance rules

text: Compare where each party leaves marks. One person's traces together with another's absence of traces can show who moved and how.
A calm baseline sharpens tension through contrast: a composed character or calm social scene makes an unresolved problem or threat feel more pressing.
when: a character works through confusing evidence while others remain calm; calm social scenes are mixed with threatening ones
why: Contrast with the calm makes the difficulty or threat stand out more strongly.

text: State the limits of an expert's tentative opinion explicitly, such as being unable to tell which wound came first.
why: Unstated limits leave room for false certainty

text: Giving a precise date from a rough biological clue overstates what the evidence supports; state a range instead.
when: Reporting exposure time from biological traces.
why: Such traces only bound the time approximately, and local conditions vary.

text: Treat a witness's hedged recognition as no identification, including when an identification weakens once the witness is asked whether they are certain.
when: A witness hedges a recognition claim.
why: Hedged recognition gives no basis for singling out a person.

text: Hold a theory tentatively and accept that partial correctness is possible; competing views may each capture part of the truth.
when: Two explanations for the evidence conflict
why: Each view may account for different clues, so both can be partly right

text: Label a reconstruction of events as a tentative hypothesis until evidence confirms it.
when: Proposing how a crime was committed before proof exists.
why: Presenting a guess as a finding can mislead the investigation.

text: Define abstract terms early in a dialogue and hold them fixed, since loosely used words drift in meaning over time.
when: A conversation relies on abstract concepts that the answers depend on.
why: Drift in meaning makes replies from different points in the exchange hard to compare.

text: A repeated numeral written larger each time suggests a code, but treat that reading as a hypothesis to test against other evidence.
when: A repeated symbol appears in a final message
why: Repetition invites a code reading that may be coincidence.

text: 1) Draw each boundary the grant describes, such as rivers, lines and widths. 2) Compare the drawn lines with each claim. 3) Locate where the claims overlap or conflict.
when: a boundary dispute depends on grant wording
why: Plotting the description shows where a conflict actually arises.

text: 1) Identify a phrase with more than one plausible sense. 2) Check each sense against verifiable facts such as membership and dated events. 3) Accept only the sense the facts support.
when: An ambiguous claim about relationships or affiliations matters to the case.
why: Reading an ambiguous phrase only in the favoured sense leads to false conclusions.

text: Let a character state the terms of a bargain themselves, so the motive shows through the offer rather than through narration.
Keep a testimony log that the player can check against inventory items, so statements can be verified against physical objects.
when: Designing a game where witness statements matter
why: Cross-referencing statements with items turns testimony into evidence to be weighed.

text: Weigh each testimony by the witness's stake and by whether it fits the physical facts, not by how confident it sounds.
when: Several accounts conflict

text: Test a human-error verdict against the physical record, such as a signal's displayed state, since the record may show the operator acted correctly.
when: investigating an accident blamed on a person
why: The mechanical record can overturn testimony that seems self-serving

text: Weigh testimony by who gives it and what that person could plausibly know, since access to information makes some claims more or less credible.
when: Assessing witnesses
why: A claim outside a witness's access is less reliable than one within it.

text: Test a witness's account for the sounds or traces it should have produced; a missing shot or a missing stain exposes a false story.
NPC notes written in terse, guarded language when they hide something let the player learn to read hesitation as a signal.
when: Designing a note or journal system for NPCs.
why: Consistent guarded phrasing teaches the player to treat brevity as a clue.

text: A confident or sworn statement may only vouch for a person's character rather than describe events, so it is not proof of what happened.
when: When evaluating a deposition.
why: Character testimony and event testimony answer different questions.

text: 1) Track which witnesses are present, sober or absent during each event. 2) Let the player discover what each witness saw. 3) Make conflicting testimony discoverable, so a bribed account can be checked against an honest one.
when: Designing events with several witnesses
why: Presence and state decide who can contradict a story

text: 1) Have the witness indicate the location of a sensation before anyone examines the body. 2) Examine only the area needed. 3) Show the physical sign to observers at the same moment. 4) Match the sign to the witness's earlier description.
when: A testimony describes a bodily experience that can be checked directly.
why: Recording the pointed location first fixes the baseline, and a visible sign that matches the account moves the case from words to evidence.

text: 1) State what the witness would ordinarily do in this situation. 2) Compare the stated excuse with that routine. 3) Check the excuse against verifiable facts such as weather. 4) Note what the witness leaves out. 5) Flag any mismatch as a possible planned departure.
when: When a witness's report is the main source of information and can be tested against routine or physical facts
why: Conflicts with habit, facts or omissions reveal lies that sincere-seeming testimony can hide.

text: 1) Ask for a plain account of recent events. 2) Collect names, origins and arrival details. 3) Walk through events in order, step by step. 4) Record each concrete detail as a checkable claim. 5) Test every claim against independent sources.
when: When a witness is emotional, confused or doubted but holds specific, checkable details
why: Ordered, concrete recall yields verifiable facts even when the witness's interpretation is unreliable.

text: 1) Compare each witness's description of clothing or features with the physical evidence. 2) Note any conflict as a clue. 3) Question the witness further before accepting or rejecting the account.
when: A witness's claims conflict with physical evidence
why: Detailed but wrong descriptions can mislead, and conflicts point to a next question.

text: 1) Ask the witness to give the full account first. 2) Have them repeat it, and note corrections. 3) Ask pointed follow-up questions on each detail. 4) Let each answer shape the next question.
when: Building a sequence of events from one witness
why: Repetition brings out corrections and new facts, and chained questions test each detail.

text: 1) Take each second-hand or trance-derived account. 2) Compare it with independent records. 3) Trust only the details that the records confirm.
when: A key claim rests on a sensitive's or witness's report
why: Second-hand testimony is unreliable until checked against independent sources.

text: 1) Ask for raw symptoms and observed facts first. 2) Keep answers brief and specific. 3) Ask for impressions afterwards and tag them as less certain. 4) Withhold conclusions until the account is complete.
when: Interviewing an emotional or vague witness.
why: Raw observation before theory keeps the investigator's ideas from shaping what the witness reports.

text: 1) Extract the time, place, companions and the witness's reactions from the account. 2) Separate what was perceived from what was felt. 3) Check each part against the environment.
when: A player must judge how much to trust a witness report.
why: Breaking the account into checkable parts lets each claim be tested independently.

text: Sort each testimony into firsthand observation, secondhand report or rumour, or account shaped by feelings or interests; firsthand carries most weight, and secondhand reports can be excluded.
when: Several accounts of one event conflict, come through intermediaries, or a case rests mainly on rumour.
why: Each category deserves a different level of trust.

text: Do not treat folk testimony as verified fact; present it as a story whose truth is uncertain.
when: Writing or using oral accounts and legends in a setting.
why: The teller's claims cannot be checked and may be partly wrong.

text: Track whether the player opened a topic or was prompted on it, so later dialogue can reflect what the player volunteered.
when: Designing branching NPC conversations.
why: Recording who initiated a topic lets later responses reflect the player's own choices.

text: Treat witness statements as evidence, not proof; weigh them by the speaker's position, firsthand access, motive, and whether the physical scene supports them.
when: Weighing a witness statement or several accounts of the same events.
why: Each witness has different access and motives; the physical scene can confirm or undercut an account.

text: Testimony lacking legal weight can still direct a search or confirm a line of inquiry, so judge it for investigative use as well as proof.
when: A statement is too weak to convict but points somewhere useful.
why: Leads and confirmations drive investigation even when evidence is not decisive.

text: A later witness can supply the mechanism linking a financial oddity to a motive, turning an unexplained anomaly into a usable explanation.
when: When an anomaly has no explanation yet.
why: Testimony about actual payments or dealings gives the anomaly a cause.

text: Compare testimony from people who knew the land during the original owner's lifetime to settle how a boundary was drawn.
when: a boundary is disputed decades after it was set
why: Those who knew the land at the time have direct knowledge of its layout.

text: Witness testimony has three layers: first-hand observation, reported speech, and inference. Each layer must be separated before a single claim is trusted.
when: when a witness is the only source for a key fact
why: the layers differ in reliability

text: Store each witness testimony as separate claims for identity, time and place, so the player can press on the weakest claim.
when: a witness-NPC system is designed

text: Treat testimony from any witness, official or doctor as a claim to test before accepting it as fact, even when the speaker is sincere.
Test a symbol's proposed meaning against testimony about the events it claims to explain, since a witness's account can rule out a reading.
when: a symbol has a rival reading tied to an event
why: Factual testimony can eliminate an interpretation that the physical evidence allows.

text: Judge testimony by the cost the speaker accepts, and weigh it against available proof before accepting the account.
Separate what a statement proves from what it cannot prove. Estimate both before deciding how much weight the statement carries in a case.
when: Evaluating any witness statement.
why: A statement may prove one fact while leaving the link to the main charge unproven.

text: Record your own state while observing, since your account is also testimony that others may test.
when: Reporting what you saw during a tense event
why: Your condition affects your reliability as a witness

text: Treat a claim that cannot be checked against any other source, with only witnesses' reports as the record, as unverified rather than established.
A listener who believes they are unseen reacts more honestly than one who knows they are being watched.
when: A hidden listener is within earshot of a staged conversation.
why: A person who thinks they are unobserved drops their guard.

text: A witness may feel strongly threatened yet be unable to name the threat or any act behind it, so the fear alone is not evidence.
when: a witness reports dread with no specifics
why: Fear can be felt before its cause is understood

text: Unverifiable testimony is a claim about something only the reporter says they perceived, such as a vision or unseen presence, that no one else can confirm.
Feelings such as anger or guilt are hard to check directly, so weigh how well each account fits the other facts.
when: A testimony rests on a speaker's inner state.
why: Inner states leave few observable traces, so fit with other facts becomes the best test.

text: A narrator with no stake in the outcome, whose account is confirmed by other evidence, needs less testing.
When an official says a message was received but cannot name where a reply should go, flag the gap and treat the claim as unverified.
Do not plan evidence around a witness's memory returning, since recovery can come suddenly at an unpredictable time.
when: A key witness has lost recall.
why: Recovery cannot be timed.

text: A sincere but emotionally primed account is weak evidence; treat it as grounds for suspicion rather than as proof.
A claimant NPC can be introduced as an unverified lead with a registry object the player checks to confirm or rule out the claim.
when: Designing NPC identity claims the player must verify.
why: A checkable record turns a rumour into a testable question.

text: Witnesses or evidence holders who cannot testify openly or be questioned again, such as through failing health or dying, cannot be tested; the result rests on agreement or narrator's judgment.
why: Untested evidence cannot be verified, so its effect depends on the agreement around it.

text: An unverified claim can shape the questioner's theory even after it has been shown to be false.
why: early assumptions persist after correction

text: A story about a third party who cannot be found is impossible to verify and must be tested before it supports a conclusion.
Pressing a witness without independent evidence gains little, because repeated denial costs the witness almost nothing.
when: the questioner has no independent evidence
why: denial is cheap for the witness

text: Accepting an account whose supporting records are lost or unverifiable means the account rests on the teller alone.
Accepting a claim that someone would have noticed an intruder, without asking about line of sight or the noise a person would make, can hide an opportunity.
when: when a witness claims they would have noticed
why: Lack of sight or quiet movement can allow access without detection.

text: Acting on an unverified report can alert the suspect or waste time.
A person claiming to know someone's hours may be bluffing, so the claim should be checked against other sources.
A statement that is filed but never re-examined shows what was said, not whether it was true.
why: recording a claim does not test it

text: 1) Treat an unverifiable claim only as a lead. 2) Open an inquiry into the accused's life. 3) Require independent corroboration before any verdict.
when: An accusation rests on a private perception

text: Treat unverifiable testimony, such as visions seen only by the afflicted, as grounds for suspicion, not proof, especially when the accuser's reactions are read as evidence.
when: the vision cannot be physically checked
why: private perception cannot be confirmed by others

text: Let an NPC report a sound or sighting the player cannot verify, and provide a timer or event log so the player can judge its reliability.
when: designing NPC testimony in a game
why: A checkable record lets players weigh the report instead of accepting or rejecting it outright.

text: Keep a witness claim open rather than accepting it when the claimed evidence cannot be found on search, however sincere the witness.
Do not treat a denial as established until other statements or physical traces have been compared with it.
when: a denial is the main claim on a point
why: A denial alone is only a claim

text: Keep a speaker's claims about their own name or home marked as statements until independent evidence confirms them.
Do not let a list of points against a suspect harden into a verdict before each entry has been tested.
when: an investigator compiles a list of accusations
why: listed claims are only unverified until checked

text: A claimed blackout is hard to disprove, so treat it as an unverifiable gap rather than as a lie.
when: a witness claims to have lost memory of an evening

text: Give NPCs confident but unverified opinions so the player must decide what to trust.
when: designing dialogue for investigation

text: Treat information from a source that cannot be re-questioned, or that remembers nothing of giving it, as an unverified clue until outside evidence supports it.
when: The source is a trance, oracle or other subject with no recall.
why: The source cannot confirm or correct its own account.

text: Admitting unverifiable testimony lets a case proceed, but leaves anyone open to accusation without checks.
when: a rule-holder decides whether to accept unverifiable testimony

text: Test any offered explanation against the timeline; do not fill an unknown interval with an unverified event to fit a preferred suspect.
when: when a discovery contradicts an earlier account, or a timeline has a gap
why: timing reveals gaps an explanation may hide, and assumed events hide the true alternatives

text: An untestable mood-based explanation, which assumes anything may mean something, lets any fact fit and makes every outcome look like support.
when: when a theory rests on mood rather than specific evidence
why: a theory that explains everything cannot be checked against facts

text: Supernatural claims about invisible agents cannot be sworn or checked and absorb attention without producing evidence; weigh them skeptically.
when: when central evidence is a claim no one can check or a theory cannot be tested practically
why: an untestable explanation lures investigators away from the facts

text: An elegant or internally consistent theory can seem proven to its proposer yet be wrong; test it against physical facts before committing.
when: when a theory explains everything heard so far or feels elegant
why: consistency with testimony does not confirm the theory

text: 1) List each premise a conclusion or explanation requires. 2) Test each premise against evidence. 3) Judge by whether the premises hold, not how neat it sounds; check whether it survives if any link fails.
when: when a conclusion depends on several assumed links, or a suspect offers a neat explanation for an odd act
why: a chain fails if any one premise is false; an explanation is only as strong as its premises

text: 1) Hold the current theory as provisional and use it to direct inquiry. 2) Identify the most unexplained fact. 3) Test whether the theory accounts for it. 4) Revise the theory if it does not.
when: pursuing a working theory, especially when a neat theory leaves a key behaviour unexplained
why: facts it cannot explain show it covers only part of the evidence and can expose a red herring

text: Make a mystery's explanation testable, and make each competing explanation predict something checkable so the player can rule options out.
when: when designing a mystery's explanation or competing explanations
why: untestable answers give no route to the truth

text: Untestable clues invite folk remedies, and a remedy that brings brief relief before relapse can seem to work and give false confidence.
why: temporary improvement looks like a cure

text: Test a neat, emotionally complete explanation at its weakest checkable point until it fails or survives, rather than judging it by coherence.
when: when an early account explains everything through one motive, before its facts are checked
why: a satisfying story can stop checking

text: A theory that explains a motive but not how the act was done, or how access or location was gained, is incomplete; revise or reject it.
when: evaluating competing explanations
why: a theory must account for the method as well as the motive

text: A single reading or physical trial can be wrong or prove little; test each early conclusion against a second observation or repeated trial.
why: a first reading of evidence can be wrong

text: Confirm a route or trace only when several traces agree; one comparison, odd detail, or single match can be coincidence.
when: verifying a route or a scene's objects as the main record of events
why: multiple independent traces are harder to explain away; a trace matching only one hypothesis is not proof

text: Lay out the chain of reasoning aloud and let a skeptical listener, including the person it concerns, challenge each link before trusting a hunch.
when: when a provisional conclusion about a person rests on inference and emotion
why: challenge reveals gaps, and a chain that cannot be explained to others may rest on fixation

text: Treat an explanation that cannot be checked, such as an unknown intermediary, as a weak point to press rather than a settled answer.
Some phrases in a prearranged code cannot be deduced, so test a pattern before assuming arbitrary wording is meaningful.
Test a proposed explanation by reproducing its mechanism under the same conditions; a matching result gives the explanation real support.
when: checking a solution to a puzzle or mystery
why: reproduction turns a plausible story into a tested one

text: Before accepting a deduction, check whether it tests a claim against new evidence or only restates the claim in other words.
when: evaluating an argument or in-world inference
why: A restated claim looks like proof but adds no support.

text: Present a stated theory to a reluctant witness as a test, since the response to it reveals more than a direct question.
when: When a witness will not answer a direct question.
why: Accepting, rejecting, or challenging a theory shows what the witness knows and fears.

text: Small differences between cases compound through repeated steps, much as a small early error grows larger with each later step.
when: reasoning from a close match through a long chain of inference
why: each step carries the early difference forward and enlarges it

text: If a case rests on one category of unverifiable testimony, a single ruling excluding that category can leave the proceeding with no working basis.
when: a case's evidence depends on one testimony type

text: Untestable explanations such as blood in the ears or agitation can dismiss a detail without checking the scene or other witnesses; prefer testable answers.
when: when a witness reports a sound or event, or a detail is explained away
why: such explanations are easy to offer and hard to check

text: A solution that works in outline but lacks checkable data, or rests on evidence the audience never sees, cannot be tested and fails under scrutiny.
why: the audience cannot test a claim whose supporting data is missing or hidden

text: A vivid, far-fetched idea matching one clue, or a single matching word, can seem convincing while other evidence contradicts it; check every clue.
when: when evaluating a compelling hypothesis that has not been checked
why: vivid ideas and striking details draw attention before they are tested

text: Observers' expectations, including a reader's belief in guilt, shape how results are read, so a single success or repeated test is not established without separating results from expectations.
A smooth story built from correct facts can hide unsupported links and be false; test the whole story and mark each link with its evidence.
why: fluent narration makes gaps harder to notice

text: An accused claim can be shielded by an excuse that resists checking, which ends the test without settling the claim.
why: An untestable excuse leaves the examiner no way to confirm or refute the claim.

text: Endless untestable theories cloud judgement and produce nothing that can be checked.
Building an entry or exit theory on one missing trace is risky; check the surrounding evidence first.
Without weather records and witness statements, a physical trace proves little because it cannot be dated.
when: Relying on a physical mark as evidence
why: Undated traces cannot place events in time

text: Treating a frightened tipster's account as the full story is risky. A single explanation, such as guilty conscience, may be incomplete.
A correct prediction can still fail if the response is too slow to act on it before the moment passes.
when: acting on a timed prediction
why: Scheduled events do not wait for investigators.

text: Overconfidence in a character's plan makes a reversal sharper, but it feels contrived when no earlier setup supports that confidence.
A theory that fits one hiding place may collapse when another candidate is tested, so every candidate must be checked in turn.
when: Building a deduction around a concealment
why: Fit with one location does not establish fit with others

text: A gut conviction without a specific flaw can persuade characters but not readers or players.
A single-object explanation fails if the physics cannot explain how the tainted item stayed separate from the rest of the contents.
why: Physical properties like settling can contradict a theory.

text: Speculating that a professional burglar was involved, based only on gloves or a forcing tool and without supporting evidence, misleads the investigation.
Assuming a single cause for a missing item can hide an accomplice who took it.
when: An item's absence seems explained by one actor
why: Other people may have been involved

text: Letting an untestable source decide something that affects a person's life causes real harm.
A test can alert the person being watched, and an unknown timing makes the test impossible to schedule, so check both before acting.
when: when setting up a timed observation

text: 1) State the theory as a story accounting for the facts. 2) List each fact it must explain and check it against the evidence. 3) Mark facts it cannot explain as weak spots. 4) Drop or revise it when a contradiction holds.
when: when a plausible explanation is proposed and must be checked before anyone acts on it
why: listing facts exposes where an explanation breaks; a theory fitting some facts can still be wrong

text: 1) State the key premise plainly. 2) Present each inference to a sceptical colleague, who challenges each link. 3) Answer each objection with a new fact or reason. 4) Drop, revise or rebuild any link that fails.
when: testing a deduction or a complicated theory before relying on it
why: objections expose weak links that stay hidden while the theory is held only in the mind

text: 1) State a provisional theory covering all current facts. 2) Name what else must be true, or predictions that would confirm or break it. 3) Check those consequences against new facts. 4) Drop or revise it if one fails.
when: deciding whether a suspect theory deserves pursuit, or evidence is incomplete and action is needed before certainty
why: accepting a theory without testing its consequences lets weak explanations survive; predictions make a hypothesis testable

text: 1) Build a reconstruction from the object's features and location, labelled provisional. 2) Choose two checks, such as revisiting the scene for a predicted physical trace, that would confirm or refute it. 3) Run them with knowledgeable people before acting on it.
when: an object found at a scene is used to explain an event
why: stating observable predictions lets a reconstruction be refuted, so it is tested rather than assumed

text: 1) State the theory. 2) List the strongest objections, including motive and contrary evidence. 3) Answer each objection with a specific explanation. 4) Check whether all answers rest on one assumption.
when: Before acting on a theory.
why: Forcing rebuttals exposes weak links that a neat story can hide.

text: 1) Consider an unwelcome theory seriously. 2) Examine it from every side. 3) Act on it only after that full review.
1) List each physical trace and each witness observation. 2) For each, ask whether the hypothesis predicts it. 3) Keep the theory open for any trace it cannot explain.
when: A working theory depends on where an object was found or on a partial witness account.
why: A theory that fits the main facts can still fail on small details it does not explain.

text: 1) Summarise the plot from the clues already found. 2) Compare the summary with the late witness's account. 3) Deduce what remains, then confirm it against facts.
when: When a late witness account is available to check a theory
why: A reconstruction is only trustworthy once it matches independent testimony.

text: 1) Build a full story from known facts. 2) Test each element against facts. 3) Keep the parts that survive and discard those contradicted.
when: Roles or relationships in a story are unclear
why: Plausible theories can contain errors that only testing reveals.

text: 1) List every act a theory requires of the culprit. 2) For each, ask whether a sensible offender with goals such as silence and escape would perform it. 3) Rank theories by how plausible their acts are.
when: Several explanations fit the physical facts
why: Checking each act against a rational actor ranks theories by how plausibly the culprit would have acted.

text: 1) Choose a cheap test whose outcome depends on whether the theory is true. 2) Perform it. 3) Read the reaction to decide whether the theory holds.
when: A trace suggests a theory and a cheap test is available
why: A test whose result depends on the theory discriminates it from alternatives better than assertion

text: 1) State the hypothesis as depending on one checkable fact. 2) Ask a precise question whose answer confirms or defeats it. 3) Seek a second independent source for that fact.
when: A working theory must be tested against the record.
why: A single precise fact gives a clear test, and a second source reduces error.

text: 1) State the conclusion as a hypothesis with a stated likelihood. 2) List the other explanations that could produce each matching fact. 3) Narrow the location in stages, from wide to specific. 4) Check the narrowed location physically.
when: When a few indirect clues point to a small set of places and a cheap check can confirm or refute the claim.
why: Staged narrowing keeps checks cheap and makes the hypothesis testable.

text: 1) List every oddity in the scene. 2) Propose a hypothesis. 3) Check it against each item. 4) Reject any hypothesis that leaves an item unexplained.
when: a set of oddities resists a single account

text: 1) Identify the central claim the solution depends on. 2) Ask for checkable specifics only the presenter could know, such as names, descriptions and dates. 3) Press the central claim before any minor points.
when: the solution rests on identifications or documents not yet shown to the group
why: a claim that cannot be checked, or that resists pressure, is the likely weak point

text: 1) Note the missing detail. 2) Check whether the account is false on that point. 3) Look for a simple cause, such as the person never having looked.
when: A gap in a suspect's account seems suspicious

text: 1) Form a hypothesis from observed differences. 2) Predict the outcome of the next case before it occurs. 3) Compare the prediction to the result. 4) Revise the hypothesis when predictions fail.
when: Checking whether a pattern in game evidence or design holds.
why: Predictions made in advance test a hypothesis; recalling outcomes afterward does not.

text: 1) Identify the points where the theory needs knowledge or actions it cannot explain. 2) For each gap, test whether a proposed explanation closes it against independent facts. 3) Check who knew what and when in each explanation. 4) Reject the theory if gaps remain unanswered.
when: When a theory has been built and needs vetting before it is acted on
why: A theory can look sound while resting on untested assumptions or ad hoc patches

text: 1) Match the scene to documented precedent cases with the same method. 2) Verify background facts in primary records. 3) Let each new fact confirm or reject the working theory.
when: when the crime follows a known pattern and reliable records exist
why: Two independent checks, method and history, confirm or reject the theory.

text: 1) Form a theory, accepting it may be guesswork. 2) List facts that must hold if it is right. 3) Assign each check to a separate party, splitting queries so no one learns the purpose. 4) Treat the theory as proven only if all predictions are independently confirmed.
when: Verifying a theory the investigator cannot check alone.
why: Independent checks test the theory without revealing it to checkers.

text: 1) Ask whether anything was taken. 2) Check whether the witness still has valuables. 3) Look for physical disturbances such as a missing key or displaced furniture. 4) Test whether the cause fits a human search.
when: A witness reports a strange event.
why: Physical facts can discriminate between human and supernatural causes.

text: 1) State the theory. 2) Ask what it predicts that an alternative would not. 3) Check each contradicting detail against it. 4) Drop the theory if a detail it cannot explain is physically or testimonially confirmed.
when: when a tidy explanation is being accepted for an event
why: A theory must survive checks against details, not merely fit the overall story.

text: 1) Note a character's sudden reaction to a stimulus, such as a flinch or flight, and keep it as a clue. 2) Later, use that same stimulus deliberately while testing a hypothesis about the character. 3) Read the reaction as evidence only after its meaning is understood.
when: When a hidden trait would appear only under pressure
why: A deliberate stimulus chosen for a reason exposes a trait, and the earlier reaction gives the result its meaning.

text: 1) Form several candidate explanations for a person from their surroundings. 2) Treat each as an open option to test. 3) Keep the one that survives further evidence.
when: Forming a first judgment about a person from their environment.
why: First impressions from surroundings alone are often wrong, so they should be held open.

text: 1) Identify an improbable pattern and treat it as a suspicion, not proof. 2) Test it with controlled trials while a helper records observations independently. 3) Use an instrument that reacts to the hidden cause. 4) Reveal the physical evidence first, then explain the mechanism.
when: A pattern could be chance or deliberate control and you can test which.
why: Layered revelation with independent corroboration makes the conclusion checkable.

text: 1) Test the explanation against the facts it must explain. 2) Test it against other cases it should also fit. 3) Check whether the speaker could actually have observed what they claim.
when: A confident explanation is about to close a case

text: 1) Check the location for signs of the suspected act. 2) Test the theory rather than assuming it. 3) If the suspect is caught doing something suspicious, check what they actually did before accepting the theory.
when: When a motive-rich suspect appears to explain an event
why: Confirming a suspect's presence does not confirm they caused the whole event

text: 1) List reasons a suspect might want the victim gone. 2) Separate wish from resolve. 3) For each element, name the fact that would confirm or drop it. 4) Check that fact and update.
when: Building a suspect case before physical proof exists.
why: Each element becomes testable instead of a general suspicion.

text: Treat a conjecture or a cause reached by elimination as a theory: test it against all known facts, and do not treat it as certain while its grounds allow challenge.
when: forming a conclusion from partial evidence
why: a conjecture that fits some facts may fail others, and unverified grounds leave the conclusion open

text: Test each candidate theory against every known clue and physical fact, listing unexplained clues, and drop any explanation that requires what the evidence rules out.
when: choosing between competing explanations of a mystery
why: a theory must fit all clues, not only the one that makes it seem convincing; one explaining only some is incomplete

text: Do not treat a complete-looking chain as proof until its premise and each link are tested; solid-looking facts can build a convincing case against an innocent.
when: evaluating a prosecution-style case or a player's accusation

text: Withhold unverified theories, whether assumed motives or gossip, from the wider group until checked, since they can steer an investigation without evidence.
Do not build a theory or reversal on a single name, silence or fact, since disproving that one premise collapses the whole reconstruction.
when: evaluating a theory or a bold reinterpretation of a case
why: a theory built on one premise is fragile

text: Before using an expert's or witness's theory as evidence, test it against exact physical evidence, samples and testimony, however authoritative its source; drop it when a detail contradicts it.
To test a witness's vague judgment about someone, ask for specific words, actions and dates that support it.
when: when a witness says someone never seemed worried or was always something
why: specifics can be checked, while generalities cannot

text: Test the first hypothesis against other possible motives before accepting it, especially when it looks too neat.
A theory that fits the known facts may still be wrong, so test it before accepting it, and keep it separate from the true solution.
when: Several theories fit the facts

text: Let the player present a deduction to an NPC who raises objections, and win the NPC over only with answers backed by evidence.
when: Designing a theory-presentation mechanic
why: Requiring evidence rewards linking clues rather than guessing

text: Reject a colleague's theory only on evidence, not on a hunch about a suspect's nature; find evidence that supports or refutes it.
when: when weighing competing explanations

text: Plan safety for anyone placed at risk in a test, and arrange a fallback such as moving them to a safe place afterwards.
when: A test exposes a person to danger.
why: Testing a theory carries a moral and practical cost.

text: When a subject's reaction could come from knowing about a test, rerun the test with the trigger hidden from the subject.
when: A test result depends on what the subject could see or guess
why: Hidden triggers separate real reactions from reactions to knowledge

text: Adopt an unfamiliar test only after checking established reference guidance, and avoid any test whose lawfulness or validity is disputed among practitioners.
Following one essential clue is faster, while following all clues in full is slower but catches leads that would otherwise be missed.
when: Choosing how to investigate with several open leads.
why: Speed and completeness pull in opposite directions.

text: A test that reproduces the effect supports a natural explanation, while a test that fails narrows the field without proving an unexplained cause.
when: Interpreting the outcome of a source test.
why: Failure to reproduce a sound rules out one cause but does not establish another.

text: Test a mundane explanation against time, place, circumstances and physical facts before accepting a supernatural or insane one.
when: A clue has a mundane explanation, or an eerie or confusing report comes from a possibly unreliable witness.
why: Ordinary causes often leave traces that a frightened witness cannot see.

text: 1) Identify a claim about a past physical condition or a central case claim, such as wasted muscle. 2) State what traces it predicts: marks on a body, object or place, or follow-up actions such as searches. 3) Check those directly. 4) Record whether they match.
when: A witness or suspect makes a claim about a past physical condition or names a physical detail, or a claim is central to a case.
why: A claim that predicts a trace can be confirmed or refuted by a match or absence.

text: Make a witness's theory or an NPC's accusation, including a suspect's motive, disprovable by facts the player can reach.
when: Designing NPC accusations or witness theories.
why: Testable accusations let the player reward careful investigation.

text: Test each claim against the scene, physical record and world facts such as item size or route length, not the witness's status or sympathy.
when: Accounts conflict, a witness's motive to lie is plausible, or designing NPC testimony that may contain errors.
why: Physical contradictions give players a checkable way to find lies or mistakes.

text: Test a witness's excuse against the layout and other people's movements before accepting it, especially when it is too convenient.
when: A witness explains away their presence somewhere.
why: Excuses that fit perfectly can be constructed to cover a gap.

text: Test an alarming label against all observed evidence before acting on it, since a dramatic word can feel decisive while adding no support.
when: Judging a suspect's apparent guilt or a witness's odd behaviour.

text: Treat an accepted official story as a possible misdirection and test each of its links before relying on it.
when: When a prosecution, faction or NPC authority presents a settled account.
why: An accepted narrative may be built to hide the key fact.

text: Avoid a lead that is disproved without new information, since that resets the search rather than narrowing it.
Test a claimed identity by asking staff about routine details a stand-in would need to know, since answers reveal the impersonation.
when: a person may have been replaced
why: A stand-in must know the routine to pass as the real person

text: Store proven facts as case flags, and keep true but unprovable theories out of the official record, or note them separately.
when: when designing a mystery's case file

text: Test a witness's claim against physical conditions, such as whether a hat could have stayed on in the wind that day.
when: a claim depends on weather, distance, or lighting
why: physical conditions can make a claim impossible

text: Specific, itemized objections to a record can be tested and answered; a blanket charge that the whole record is false carries little weight.
when: A disputed record is challenged
why: Only itemized claims can be checked against evidence

text: Test a stated reason for an act against the actor's own doubts about it, since those doubts show whether the reason holds up.
when: Judging why a character undertook a trip, errand or visit.
why: Stated reasons often fail under the actor's own scrutiny.

text: Test a newly offered motive against the objection it was built to answer and against the known facts, not by how neat it sounds.
when: A new motive is offered to explain an act.
why: A tidy motive can still fail under scrutiny of the evidence.

text: Test whether a method could have been copied by comparing it with a published similar case.
when: an outside source describes a method used in the case

text: Test a confession's grand or heroic justification against its practical consequences; self-justifying framing often fails when measured against the facts.
when: when a culprit explains an act in idealistic terms
why: Self-serving framing hides costs and contradictions that the facts reveal.

text: A false confession that physical evidence can easily disprove works only as a short distraction.
when: physical evidence can contradict the confession

text: A theory absorbing every fact, dismissing contrary details as tricks, or unchangeable by any fact is unfalsifiable and halts the search. Reject a detail only with a specific check.
when: when evaluating a confident case against a suspect, or when a theory absorbs contrary evidence
why: the theory explains everything, removing pressure to test it; an unfalsifiable case cannot be corrected by evidence

text: Reading all evidence that favours a suspect as proof of skill lets a theory absorb contrary evidence and stop being testable.
A claimed partnership with a scapegoat is a lie that the victim can test, and someone who knows the scapegoat may reject it immediately.
when: A culprit invents a partner to implicate an innocent person
why: Personal knowledge of the accused exposes the invented link

text: A reconstruction can be plausible yet unprovable once the physical evidence that would confirm it has been destroyed.
Presenting a theory without linking each claim to a checkable source lets the audience dismiss it.

1) Find the unstated premise the claim needs to hold. 2) Rebuild the physical or causal reasons behind the rule. 3) Check whether the claim ignores a distinction it itself draws. 4) Look for statements that contradict each other.
when: judging a report, witness or rule that presents a timing or physical claim as settled

text: 1) Search the rooms the person would use. 2) Ask others who might have seen them. 3) Record which places were examined. 4) Treat the claim as unverified until confirmed.
when: when a character's absence is central and a claim of departure must be tested

text: 1) Take the speaker's full account first. 2) Ask targeted questions about each person involved. 3) Pursue passing details with short confirming questions. 4) End with a next step, not a verdict.
when: a story centres on one person who may be disguised or hiding a motive

text: 1) Send a short query asking whether a person is at his post. 2) If he is absent, send a message that must be delivered to his own hand and answered.
when: Checking whether a person is present at a location.
why: A direct query confirms presence, and a required reply confirms absence.

text: 1) Record each conflicting claim exactly. 2) Ask what the speaker gains by making it. 3) Compare any revision under re-questioning with the first version. 4) Check which version the physical facts support.
when: two statements about one event conflict
why: Motive and physical evidence together show which claim is more reliable.

text: 1) Ask who saw the event. 2) Ask how close they were. 3) Ask whether they gained anything. 4) Check whether their statements agree over time.
when: Judging a witness's claim.

text: 1) Describe the claimed method. 2) Compare it with every known natural method. 3) If none fits, flag the claim as unresolved instead of accepting it.
when: Assessing a claim that something impossible occurred.
why: Systematic comparison separates claims that fail from those that remain open.

text: 1) Establish the suspect's character as the source of their opinions. 2) Compare each assertion with established facts. 3) Check whether the claim can be tested or rejects every alternative in advance.
when: Evaluating a suspect's denials or explanations.
why: Character explains a stance, but only fact-checking shows whether it holds.

text: 1) Speak a neutral trigger word near the person. 2) Watch the eyelids and breathing for any sign of awareness. 3) Treat a single brief twitch with caution before concluding unconsciousness.
when: When deciding whether an apparently sleeping person can hear
why: A neutral trigger reveals awareness without tipping off the person.

text: 1) Repeat the claimed act exactly. 2) Listen or watch from the witness's position and distance. 3) Compare what could be seen or heard with the witness's account.
when: A witness's account depends on what could be sensed
why: Re-enactment shows what the witness could and could not have perceived

text: 1) Reproduce the suspicious effect independently 2) compare the same witness's statements over time 3) gather retractions and depositions 4) test whether the original evidence still holds.
when: judging a contested trial
why: Documentary and comparative checks reveal what a single record hides.

text: Let a companion voice a wrong assumption that the player can disprove with evidence found in the game world.
when: when writing companion dialogue about a mystery
why: the player can test the assumption and overturn it

text: Plant a believable false lead that a player can disprove by checking it against an anomaly the lead cannot explain.
