Test an accused person's claim that someone supplied false information against the physical facts before accepting it.
A test produces a reaction the observer can read and reproduce, while an emotional appeal moves the observer without a checkable result.
when: Choosing how to challenge or clear a suspect.
why: Only reproducible results can serve as evidence.

text: A suspect who reacts with sudden violence to a harmless-looking test item shows the item was meant to harm the tester.
when: when a test item is offered to a suspect

text: A water ordeal is a trial where the accused is cast into a river and the result is read as the verdict: drowning means guilt, surviving means innocence.
A merchant NPC can offer a side wager that grants access to his records, rewarding players who check the odds.
A quest can require the player to secure a vow from an NPC, tracked in state so the vow can be broken later with consequences.
why: tracked promises create consequences that can trigger later

text: A community decision later declared void can still drive later conflict, because the record shows what the parties were fighting over.
A visibly staged test can alert the guilty party, who may then become careful or start investigating the test itself.
when: when the test is noticed by the people being investigated
why: the suspect gains time to react before the result is read

text: A test with a visible result can look honest while its operator controls the outcome, so a convincing demonstration is not proof of accuracy.
when: when the operator of a test also benefits from its result
why: The person administering the test can shape what appears to happen.

text: 1) Offer a small wager on a checkable fact. 2) Let the informant consult his own records to prove his point. 3) Check the records he reads aloud against other sources.
when: an informant holds records but refuses direct questions

text: 1) Form a theory. 2) Send a warning based on it. 3) Observe the recipient's reaction. 4) Compare the reaction and later news with the reasoning.
when: when a theory predicts how someone will respond
why: the response confirms or refutes the reasoning

text: 1) Place a candidate object into the dent and check for an exact fit. 2) Set it on a smooth surface and look for a second impression. 3) If both match, conclude it lay there earlier.
Make a warning line produce a branch so that non-response leads to a forced entry with its own consequences.
when: Scripting an NPC warning before a forced entry.
why: Branching gives silence a meaningful consequence rather than a dead end.

text: A reasoner with a firm conclusion tends to examine new contrary evidence closely before reversing their view.
when: a new document contradicts a strong prior belief
why: certainty raises the bar for revision

text: Stating that one fact may overturn a theory keeps suspects and readers guessing, since the theory is presented as provisional.
when: an investigator holds a theory openly
why: a provisional theory keeps others uncertain

text: A witness who begins a question, stops and corrects it may reveal knowledge they have not admitted, and the gap can be completed to expose it.
A witness first confronted with a physical object often revises an earlier account.
when: a witness is shown an object that ties to their story
why: Denial becomes harder when the object contradicts the first version.

text: Conflicting public theories of a theft each act as a lead, and only the one that fits the physical record survives checking.
when: Several competing explanations circulate about one event
why: False leads are cheap to produce, but physical evidence constrains which story can be true

text: Correcting a widely circulated text after the fact is slow and incomplete, so earlier errors persist, even after their author changes view.
A verdict reached on present evidence is provisional and may be revised when further evidence appears.
A theory that fits neatly, or appears to prove itself, still needs each assumption and piece of evidence checked; a sense of fit is not confirmation.
Revise an official's conclusion when a later physical report arrives, since new evidence can overturn an early, comfortable reading.
New evidence, such as spare plain clothing, should revise a working theory rather than simply confirm it.
When a found object contradicts the working explanation, revise the explanation rather than forcing the evidence to fit it.
when: a scene object does not match the expected story
why: a contradicting object often reveals a second story

text: Ask questions that let the witness name their own wishes or choices, rather than leading them to a predetermined answer.
when: Eliciting an opinion or intention from a witness.
why: Self-stated answers are more reliable than answers the questioner suggested.

text: Entertain a suspect's rival explanation provisionally, without endorsing it, to lower their guard.
An act that works against the culprit's own aims, such as a noisy weapon for a silent escape, lowers a theory's standing without disproving it.
why: Real offenders sometimes act oddly, so implausibility weakens a theory without ruling it out.

text: Let a late reversal reduce certainty without fully closing doubt, so the ending stays open to checking.
when: the reversal overturns the answer but cannot yet be confirmed

text: Hold a provisional hypothesis to give the inquiry direction, and replace it as soon as later facts require.
when: early in an investigation

text: Keep a private inference provisional until a comparison can show it to others; a hunch is not confirmation.
why: Premature conclusions can be wrong

text: Do not convict or clear a suspect on bodily timing alone; weigh it against routine and other evidence.
why: bodily signs give only rough estimates

text: Revise a first explanation of an odd action once a stated reason is known, since the reason can change how the whole act is read.
Test a self-inflicted explanation by asking what purpose it would serve once the attacker's goal has already been achieved.
when: when a victim's condition could be self-inflicted or imposed

text: Give an NPC's odd behavior more than one possible explanation, and tie each explanation to a check the player can run.
A solution that explains a crime's mechanics but conflicts with the characters or their behaviour is not yet trustworthy, even if it closes every gap.
when: when judging a complete explanation of a mystery
why: Mechanism alone does not account for how people actually act

text: Check whether an injury could have been made by the victim's own hand; if it could not, self-infliction is ruled out.
when: Deciding whether injuries were self-inflicted.
why: Physical reach limits what a person can do to themselves.

text: Hold suspicion as a score that is revised as each new fact arrives, rather than locking it when a suspect is accused.
when: Tracking suspicion during an investigation.

text: Plant a later correction on a page that predates it, so a player who checks dates can detect that the record was altered.
when: designing a document that hides a later edit
why: Date mismatches reward careful readers.

text: Dialogue that contradicts itself within one exchange can serve as a fair-play clue that rewards close reading.
when: Designing clues in character dialogue
why: Players who read carefully can catch the inconsistency and gain information

text: Use the self-growing hearing pattern when a public proceeding should expand by itself; not every accusation spreads this way.
An object or statement that fits the expected story too neatly deserves scrutiny before it is accepted.
A fixed belief must give way when a new witness detail contradicts it.
Treat an inference about hidden feelings as provisional until a second independent fact confirms it.
Each new conviction or arrest adds names to the list of suspects, so an accusation process can feed on itself and widen steadily.
when: when accused people are asked to name accomplices
why: Each verdict supplies new names that prompt further charges

text: When a character's own careless act triggers the worst threat, stakes rise because the danger traces back to a choice the character made.
when: a character's imprudent action drives a crisis

text: A correction written later than the date of the page it sits on shows that the record was revised after the events it describes.
when: checking whether a compiled record is contemporaneous
why: Later insertions can carry earlier page dates.

text: Model a confession as a revisable statement, so a later retraction changes game state instead of deleting the earlier line.
when: Implementing confessions that can be withdrawn
why: Keeping both versions preserves the history of the case

text: An unverifiable accusation can sustain itself with no new facts, since each reaction and each reported harm reinforces the next accusation and appears to confirm it.
Neatness alone does not prove staging; test a suspected arrangement against the physics of the claimed event before concluding anything.
why: orderly scenes can occur naturally

text: A frame that is too neat can make the investigator suspect the planted object itself.
A neat collection of evidence can persuade observers to stop looking for whoever arranged it.
A rival theory checked only by the investigator's own reasoning can survive by default, so independent sources are needed to confirm or break it.
Trusting a neat tip over the physical evidence that accompanies it can mislead an investigator.
An account can be internally consistent yet contradict external records, so consistency alone does not establish truth.
when: evaluating a polished witness story
why: a story can be coherent while still being wrong

text: A reconstruction that fits neatly can still be a story built around a preferred suspect rather than the facts.
A reply that is too neat makes a clue look like the answer rather than an open question for the player to weigh.
A theory can undermine itself: if a supposed ally inflicts the harm, the alliance it claims becomes contradictory.
Once a suspect is named, every harm can be attributed to the suspect, so alternative natural causes are overlooked.
when: when an accusation has been made against a specific person
why: the accusation becomes the lens through which later events are read

text: Confessors may name innocent people to shield themselves, so accomplice names from a confession are not reliable without verification.
when: A confessor names others
why: Naming others can reduce a confessor's own blame

text: A theory with a missing link fails even when every other fact supports it.
when: Assessing a theory built from many supporting facts
why: Knowledge of a possibility is not proof of the specific intent the theory requires

text: An explanation that fits a favored theory elegantly can still be wrong; test it against independent sources.
A plausible picture of a suspect's mind remains a guess until physical evidence agrees with it.
when: when a suspect fits a motive profile
why: character fit alone can mislead without corroboration

text: 1) State the current hypothesis or reconstruction from the facts available. 2) Compare each new fact, recollection or witness detail with it. 3) Revise it whenever a new detail contradicts or adds to it, rather than keeping the earlier view.
1) Name the feeling toward the suspect. 2) Reflect on whether it persists when calm. 3) If it persists, treat it as a conflict and recuse; if it fades, continue with explicit checks.
when: an investigator notices strong anger or affection toward a case figure
why: passing emotions can be separated from lasting bias

text: 1) Replay the whole observation afterward. 2) Test each inference against what was seen and said. 3) Discard or flag any inference that fails.
when: after an interview or tail
why: errors often survive until checked again

text: 1) Ask about a third party's ability in a way that requires a direct answer. 2) Listen for phrasing that reveals the respondent's own knowledge. 3) Treat a refusal to answer as informative.
when: when the suspect is likely to answer with habitual or instinctive language
why: A reply about someone else can expose the respondent's own skill or access.

text: 1) Collect small objects and habits that fit together, such as a key matching a hidden door. 2) Link them into one theory. 3) Test the theory before having proof, using knowledge of the person's character.
when: Circumstantial evidence accumulates without a clear proof.
why: Small connecting items can form a coherent theory that a test can confirm or refute.

text: Revise or drop a working explanation once a new clue or account contradicts it, rather than defending it against later evidence.
when: when a new clue or account does not fit the current explanation
why: Facts outrank the theory built before them; a theory built on early clues can fail the next one, and clinging to it misleads the investigator.

text: Treat a timeline as a provisional hypothesis: it may fit while resting on unverified steps, so revise it when new evidence arrives or awkward timings remain unexplained.
when: when reconstructing events from records
why: New evidence can overturn an order that looked settled.

text: Mark motive-based conclusions provisional until questioning or evidence confirms them, since a motive is not proof; a delegated brief is not established fact.
why: A motive is not proof.

text: Let expert NPC opinions be revised after the player challenges them with new evidence.
when: when an expert NPC states a firm conclusion
why: Revisable opinions reward players for pressing with evidence.

text: Offer the player a way to revise a conclusion, such as a second witness or an object to inspect, so that an early judgment can be corrected.
when: Designing a case the player can reopen.
why: Allowing correction keeps the investigation open and rewards further checking.

text: Keep a hypothesis open to revision, since a new fact such as a stain or a message can overturn a theory built on older facts.
Treat each theory as provisional until it has been tested against evidence.
when: Forming an investigative conclusion
why: Untested theories can be wrong.

text: Treat an inference from a clue as a lead that may point somewhere, not as proof, and confirm it with a separate test before acting on it.
when: A deduction rests on a single clue or a single witness.
why: A plausible inference can be wrong, and a second check guards against acting on it.

text: Keep working assumptions about identity or motive provisional, and do not treat them as settled before confirmation, since that prejudices the inquiry.
Do not treat an exclusion as final until the access evidence behind it has been checked.
Do not treat a neat alibi as proof of innocence until its travel and timing facts have been checked against independent sources.
When new evidence contradicts a character's hypothesized role, reassign the role, such as puppet, accomplice or mastermind, rather than keeping the original assignment.
when: Tracking suspects' roles in a mystery.
why: Roles are hypotheses, and contradicting evidence shows the earlier role does not fit.

text: Carry out the critical checks yourself rather than delegating them, since the conclusion is only as strong as the checks behind it.
When a contradiction persists, revise the theory or add an outside agent that explains it, rather than discarding the observed fact.
when: A reconstruction cannot explain a fact without extra factors.
why: Keeping the fact and changing the story preserves the evidence.

text: Make an NPC's arrest or suspicion provisional, so a player-supplied alibi can clear them and release them.
why: A wrongly held suspect should be releasable once the alibi appears.

text: Hold a witness's own theory as provisional, since it may serve that witness's interests.
Let a motive label be revised as understanding grows, updating the player's view without contradicting earlier clues.
Do not adopt a neat theory until evidence supports each link; keep several explanations open until evidence narrows them.
when: Several suspects or explanations remain possible

text: When a lead seems to answer the main question but carries signs of a separate motive, test whether it explains the facts or belongs to a different crime.
when: When an official-looking or politically charged clue appears
why: A dramatic lead can be a side effect of an unrelated crime, not the activity under investigation.

text: Test a proposed cause by comparing it with when the person was last observed well; a theory that fails the timing is weakened.
Offer a false solution the player can test and fail; the closed trail teaches the player which evidence to doubt.
Each suspect theory feels strongest just before a test breaks it, so the player's confidence peaks and then reverses sharply.
when: pacing suspicion toward a reversal
why: Confidence peaking before a test makes the disproof a sharp turn.

text: A theory defended from pride or attachment can outlast its evidence, causing investigators to ignore disconfirming facts.
when: An investigator has committed to an early theory.
why: Personal investment in a first theory resists revision.

text: 1) List every fact the suspect or explanation must account for. 2) Check whether it explains each one. 3) Reject it if a central contradiction remains, since a convenient explanation may be a decoy.
when: A single suspect or explanation appears to explain everything, or fits only part of the evidence.
why: A theory that fails on some details is likely incomplete, wrong, or a decoy.

text: 1) Accept a surprising claim or supernatural frame as unverified. 2) List other explanations that fit the same facts, testing ordinary ones first. 3) Test each directly, including the original claim, before acting on any of them.
when: A single surprising fact seems to settle a question, or a supernatural frame is proposed.

text: 1) Record the witness's explanation for a physical mark. 2) Judge the mark's apparent age against the stated date. 3) Examine its pattern against the explanation. 4) Have a second observer confirm the reading.
when: A witness explains a bruise, wound or other physical trace
why: Mismatches in age, pattern or cause expose a story that does not fit the evidence.

text: 1) Assume the most ordinary cause, such as an echo. 2) Reproduce the conditions by stamping or walking briskly. 3) Check whether the sound returns each time. 4) Search the area for a source. 5) Repeat the test rather than accepting one result.
when: An unexplained sound or sign has a possible mundane source that can be tested on the spot.
why: Repeatable tests separate natural causes from the unexplained without relying on a single observation.

text: 1) Take hold of the first loose clue. 2) Follow it step by step in every direction it leads. 3) Continue until the whole connected clue is gathered.
when: A single clue opens onto several connected leads.
why: Following each thread in turn builds a complete picture from a small start.

text: 1) Identify the favoured suspect. 2) Check the suspect's location at the relevant time against the alibi. 3) Check whether a motive exists. 4) Drop or revise the theory if the alibi holds and motive is absent.
when: Before building an accusation on a suspect theory.
why: A plausible theory that lacks motive and has a confirmed alibi fails regardless of its appeal.

text: 1) Build motive from relationships among characters. 2) Record the facts that contradict the theory. 3) List questions the theory cannot answer. 4) Test the alibi against its supporting witnesses. 5) Keep open questions alive until resolved.
when: Laying out suspects and a working theory.
why: A theory is useful only if it explains known facts and the facts that cut against it.

text: 1) Propose the apparent purpose behind how remains were handled. 2) Check the purpose against the physical traces. 3) If it does not fit, propose another purpose and check again.
when: Judging whether a proposed explanation for remains matches the evidence.
why: Traces constrain purpose; a mismatch signals the explanation is wrong.

text: Make at least one death testable, such as through records or an autopsy, so the player can confirm foul play rather than merely suspect it.
when: When a conspiracy depends on suspicious deaths.
why: A checkable death lets the player move from suspicion to proof.

text: Investigators committed to a theory, accusation or obsession dismiss, ignore, twist or miss contrary facts and testimony; test each contrary fact instead of discarding it.
when: an investigator or decision-maker has settled on a theory or accusation
why: Expectation and commitment filter out evidence that does not fit.

text: Once committed to a view, people find it hard to back away from a contradicting fact, so a confident wrong theory persists and must be actively revised.
when: after a view is committed and a contradicting fact arrives
why: Commitment to a theory resists correction.

text: Committing to a test meant to prove a theory can make empty results look like confirmation of that theory.
when: observer has publicly committed to a plan
why: investment in the plan biases interpretation of the outcome

text: A pause and a night's rest can let a solver revisit the evidence with fresh eyes and notice the ordinary explanation.

when: when the reference event is controlled or shaped by the investigators
why: The anchor can distort reports of when things happened.

text: Bind events to a regular cycle such as tides, so gaps and overlaps between events become visible and checkable.
when: Reconstructing a sequence or checking an alibi for events bounded by a repeating cycle.

text: Anchor the timeline to a household routine, such as when a house was last locked up, to fix times that witnesses can be checked against.
when: sightings are loosely timed
why: fixed routines give reference points

text: Place an object where its target will encounter it during habitual routines, such as near a bedside or a favoured item, so it is likely to be noticed.
Repeat one constant image that stays steady while everything else moves, giving the audience a fixed point to hold on to.
Check whether each witness's routine actually places them where they claim to be at the time.
when: when verifying a witness's presence during a window
why: Routines reveal whether a claimed location is plausible.

text: Record a person's usual visit schedule to establish when and by whom a resource can be reached.
Ask witnesses about routine tasks near the event, since routine actions anchor the timeline.
An action observed in the house, such as a door being locked, can serve as a timestamp that bounds when an intruder could have entered.
when: when reconstructing a timeline around a locked room
why: Known actions give fixed points against which other events can be placed.

text: A daily routine limits when a trace could have been made: writing on a surface that is changed every day dates from the last change.
when: a timeline depends on a written or observed routine
why: routine resets erase earlier traces

text: Varying clothing, names and hair across an NPC's appearances while keeping one small mark constant lets players recognise the NPC by the mark rather than the costume.
when: Designing a disguised NPC the player must recognise.
why: Players then learn to look for constant features, which rewards careful observation.

text: Two fixed points, such as a clock strike and an estimated later moment, define an interval that can be tested against other evidence.
when: Only approximate times are available between anchors.
why: The interval bounds the event, turning a rough estimate into a checkable window.

text: Fixing a time around one striking object, such as a missing item, can hide a more reliable source and lead the whole investigation wrong.
why: a vivid anchor feels decisive, so it is rarely re-checked

text: Making every interrogation a chain of helpful suggestions from one person makes players notice the steering and distrust the scene.
when: Writing interrogation scenes with a recurring helper.
why: Players detect a character who always steers, which breaks the sense of a natural exchange.

text: A routine event such as a weekend return is ordinary, so a timeline entry for it proves little on its own. Corroborate it with other evidence.
A timeline fixed by a single later sighting, such as a man reporting a death an hour earlier, can be checked against the suspect's movements.
when: Building a timeline for an alibi or suspect movements
why: A fixed time anchor lets each claimed movement be tested

text: 1) Start from fixed transport times such as departures and arrivals. 2) Add the visible acts performed in between. 3) Fill the gaps with what the suspect must have done next.
when: When reconstructing a suspect's movements from timed sources.
why: Anchored times make each step checkable against records.

text: 1) Collect each dated document. 2) Order them by their dates. 3) Link each document to the one it answers or causes. 4) Recover event order even when the narrator reports events late.
when: The plot depends on who knew what and when, or on the sequence of a decision.
why: Each document anchors its event by when it was written and what it triggered, so order survives late reporting.

text: 1) Find a certified or written date as a fixed anchor. 2) Place the certified events first. 3) Fit undated testimony around them using its order of events and references to other people's movements.
when: Witnesses disagree or give no dates.
why: A fixed point lets event order be recovered even when calendar dates are lost.

text: 1) Identify the one event whose date matters. 2) Find a fixed anchor it depends on. 3) Gather several independent sources, each giving a point or range. 4) Calculate from the anchors. 5) If a source fails, move to the next instead of accepting the gap.
when: A timeline must be built from patchy records and at least one fixed anchor exists.
why: Several sources narrowing a range are more robust than any single source.

text: 1) Fix the anchor time from a timed object. 2) Chain inferred events forward and backward from it. 3) Mark each link with how strongly it depends on unstated assumptions.
when: Reconstructing when events happened from a single recovered clue.
why: Anchored chains show which links are solid and which are guesswork.

text: 1) Fix anchor points such as the last transport, the arrival time, the moon's position, first light and any gap of unconsciousness. 2) Place each claim between anchors. 3) Check each claim against the anchors and flag conflicts.
when: A witness is the main source of time or place.
why: Fixed events constrain estimates the witness cannot make directly.

text: 1) Fix the timeline on a few dated events, such as a disappearance, the last recorded message and the night of a death. 2) Order all other observations against those anchors.
when: when reconstructing the order of events from several sources
why: Everything else is placed relative to the anchors, so their accuracy matters most

text: 1) Identify each step of a subject's route. 2) Note what ordinary people would normally see or do at each step. 3) Compare the result with witness accounts.
when: When rebuilding events from routine behaviour.

text: 1) Fix anchor times first: meals, messages, arrivals at a site and departures. 2) Note the gap between each pair of anchors, such as time spent at a place. 3) Attach each claim to its nearest anchors.
why: Anchors give a fixed frame for testing every other claim.

text: 1) Fix a few reliable times as anchors. 2) List every possible exit or route. 3) Check each route's timing against every anchor. 4) Eliminate routes that fall outside the window.
when: A locked space must be explained by a route in or out
why: Hard times rule out routes that seem convenient

text: 1) Fix shared, checkable anchors such as a departing vehicle and a station clock. 2) Note each timepiece's known error and correct readings against it. 3) Place each character's claimed movements against those anchors.
Do not rely on one witness's sequence when it is in doubt; anchor the timeline to surviving records, since timing claims need matching records to be trusted.
when: A timeline depends on memory alone with no surviving record.

text: Attach each recorded event to a fixed date so the order and spacing of events can be checked.
why: Fixed dates make sequence and gaps testable.

text: Confirm place and dates early in questioning, because later timelines and conclusions depend on them.
when: Reconstructing a sequence of events.
why: Errors in early anchors propagate into everything built on them.

text: Give NPCs fixed routines, such as a guard on a set patrol, so that a change in routine signals an event elsewhere in the world.
when: Designing NPC schedules that players should read as clues.
why: A visible baseline lets players notice when something is wrong.

text: Attach dated events to NPC locations so players can test a claimed presence against a timeline.
when: building a timeline-based investigation

text: Physical capacity and criminal skill answer different questions, so a suspect unable to do the physical work may still be involved through an accomplice.
Infer event order from traces: if an organism can only settle after soft tissue is gone, the exposure must have preceded its settling.
when: Reconstructing the order of events from physical traces.
why: Each trace requires a prior condition, so its presence implies that condition came earlier.

text: 1) List each witness's timed claims in order, such as hearing a sound, coming downstairs, calling, and help arriving. 2) Place them on one shared clock. 3) Use events shared by two or more accounts as anchors. 4) Flag times resting only on one person's memory. 5) Mark remaining gaps no account explains.
when: several witnesses give overlapping accounts or had windows of opportunity
why: fixing times across accounts bounds where each person could have been, and shared anchors keep the timeline reliable

text: 1) Record each stated time, such as a planned meeting, a death or an arrival. 2) Add durations and travel distances. 3) Check each account against the resulting sequence.
1) Start recounting events from a fixed date. 2) Anchor each event to a date taken from a written record. 3) Cross-check time-stamped entries against each other to expose contradictions.
1) State the account a suspicion would require to be true. 2) List every fact that must hold for it. 3) Choose a test for each fact. 4) Begin with the most accessible fact.
when: When a suspicion is broad and needs a plan of attack.
why: Separate checkable facts make progress measurable.

text: 1) Start from the simplest fact whose purpose is clear. 2) State each next inference. 3) Attach each inference to its source clue. 4) Check that every link holds before revealing.
when: explaining a solution at the end of a mystery
why: tracing each link to a clue keeps the reveal verifiable

text: 1) Create a false paper trail, such as a fabricated report supporting a plausible story. 2) Place an object belonging to another person where it points to that person.
when: a culprit needs suspicion moved to someone else
why: Documents and objects make the false story feel supported

text: 1) List the known facts. 2) Join them into a step-by-step sequence of who was where, what was done and what was hidden. 3) Check each step against the evidence. 4) Mark the sequence as provisional.
when: When forming a theory from evidence.

text: 1) List every dated event, such as meetings, purchases and illness episodes. 2) Order them chronologically. 3) Scan for near-matches that cluster together.
when: a chain of events may connect a person to a result
why: ordering makes near-coincidences visible

text: 1) Fix times that independent observers can confirm, such as routine arrivals. 2) Fill gaps between fixed points with stated durations. 3) Record the tolerance of each interval. 4) Separate the onset of an event from the moment help is summoned.
when: Reconstructing the order of events from testimony and routines.
why: Anchored times and explicit tolerances prevent estimates from distorting the sequence, and separating onset from discovery avoids misplacing events.

text: Sounds of arrivals by different routes, such as a lift and a stairway, reveal the order in which people came.
when: Visual evidence is unavailable.

text: Record bearings and distances between locations, since a scene's position and layout determine what can be reached from where.
Accepting a conventional start date for a disappearance without checking the last certain sighting can mislead the whole inquiry.
when: An investigation adopts a start date from common assumption.
why: The question asked then concerns the wrong period.

text: 1) List every time stamp with its source. 2) Mark each as measured (clock, bell) or estimated (guess, duration). 3) Chain the intervals between anchors and note gaps with no witness. 4) Check estimates against the chain; where they disagree, the gap is where the account can be bent.
when: Investigators rebuild who was where and when from many time readings.
why: Chaining measured anchors exposes estimates and unwitnessed gaps that hide movement.

text: When a witness cannot give a precise time, record the account as a range or estimate rather than an exact time.
when: A witness is unsure of the exact time of an event.
why: Treating an approximate time as exact creates false precision in the sequence.

text: Require each timeline clue's date to be confirmed by two unrelated in-world events, such as a festival, delivery, or death, before the player can rely on it.
when: When designing a timeline system for player-discovered clues.
why: A single anchor can be wrong, so independent confirmation makes the timeline trustworthy.

text: Log NPC positions, transit times and arrivals with minute-level timestamps so players can test alibis, check travel at walking speed, and find schedule gaps.
when: When designing NPC schedules, alibi checks, or puzzles that depend on where a character was at a given time.
why: Ordered, precise timestamps make movement claims checkable against one another and reveal where an NPC could have acted.

text: An unreliable sense of time, such as an NPC's distorted perception, can be used deliberately to create confusion that the player must work through.
when: a story needs the player to doubt a character's timing
why: Players must cross-check conflicting times, which adds challenge and mystery.

text: 1) Record each dated event, such as visits, refusals and deliveries. 2) Order them by date. 3) Look for the point where the pattern changes.
when: when several dated events must be ordered to locate a change
why: A sorted sequence exposes when a shift began.

text: A witness's last sighting of a person alive sets the earliest possible time of death and the latest moment known alive, anchoring the timeline and bounding what happened afterward.
when: Reconstructing a timeline
why: The victim cannot have died before being seen alive; a last-known time anchors the sequence.

text: Laudanum acts in three phases: a stimulating phase, then a sedative phase, then deep sleep.
The largest unknown interval in a timeline is the most important gap to investigate, because it hides the most about when the event occurred.
A later independent sighting of someone who left an event bounds when that event could have ended, which helps order events.
A journey broken at an intermediate stop, such as a port, gives the traveller opportunity to make calls or send messages.
A witness pressed in one meeting may give less than on a later, unpressured visit, so revisit witnesses once pressure is removed.
when: When a witness was cautious or evasive in an earlier meeting.

text: A known countdown raises tension because each passing moment is a loss, and tension grows as the count approaches zero.
when: when a timed reveal or discovery threat is set
why: each passing moment reduces the remaining time

text: A new incident can connect earlier unlinked incidents when it shares a location, person or record with them.
when: A later event shares an element with earlier separate events
why: The shared element makes the earlier events visible together

text: Equating the last witnessed moment with time of death or event time is a mistake; death or the event may have occurred later, and later changes can hide it.
when: Timing an event from witness sightings
why: The last sighting only bounds the event from one side; the scene may have been changed afterwards.

text: Do not treat a late return as guilt without checking the gap it leaves, weighing weather, route and stated reasons first.
1) Identify who last saw the person. 2) Record exactly what each witness saw. 3) Note what the person carried or did just before being seen.
when: when a person has vanished
why: the last moments narrow where to look next

text: 1) List each successive moment after the event. 2) Count who was present to observe at each. 3) Rank moments by fewest observers. 4) Treat the lowest-count moment as the most likely escape window, after stating assumptions.
when: a crowded timeline in which witnesses change position
why: An escape is most explainable when the fewest people could have seen it.

text: 1) List each recorded departure and arrival time. 2) Compute the gaps between connections. 3) Sum the gaps to estimate how far ahead the adversary is.
when: Working out who could have acted before whom.
why: Summing known travel and waiting intervals gives a lead estimate from records.

text: 1) Date the event the witness describes. 2) Ask who in the witness's life could have told them. 3) Check whether that source existed and was in contact with the witness in time.
when: A witness claims knowledge they could not have witnessed.
why: The check shows whether the knowledge could have been obtained through ordinary means.

text: Record each person's last certain sighting and anything heard afterwards, since these set the boundary of what is known.
Do not use photographs taken long after an event to answer questions about its timing.
when: Using recorded images as evidence
why: Later images may show a changed scene

text: Tie each sighting to a clock reference such as a departure, a sound, or the moment of sleep, so its timing can be checked even when identity is uncertain.
when: when recording testimony about a sequence of events
why: Timing anchors make a witness's account usable as evidence even when identity is weak.

text: An independent timestamped record, such as a receipt or cloakroom ticket, can contradict a suspect's stated times without relying on anyone's memory.
Confirm a claimed time against an independent clock or record, such as a call log or relayed signal, not the witness's or suspect's own account or watch alone.
when: when a witness or suspect states a time that matters
why: An outside record does not depend on any one account.

text: Anchor a sequence with independent times such as an arrival or a meal hour, which together set the window for each event.
when: when witnesses give conflicting or incomplete times

text: Time each step of an alibi with a different witness, so one faulty clock cannot break the whole chain.
why: A failure is contained to one link when sources are independent.

text: An independent physical estimate, such as time of death, gives a second window against which a witness's timeline can be tested.
An independent source fixes a time or place only if it does not depend on the suspect. Uncertain recognition or incomplete records may fail to do so.
An event that happens at the most inconvenient moment may be more likely staged than accidental.
When no direct time is recorded, infer one from a related event, such as arrival at a scene, and work from the resulting window.
when: an event lacks a recorded time
why: A bounded window still constrains who could have acted.

text: Give each NPC a narrow, sometimes wrong time window so players must merge them into a schedule to find contradictions.
when: designing NPC testimony for players to reconcile
why: Merging partial accounts rewards players who compare them.

text: Combine several record types with surviving physical sites, since each source type checks the others.
when: documents conflict or are incomplete and sites can still be inspected
why: Independent sources expose errors that any single source would hide.

text: A moving shadow or light patch can act as a slow clock that places an observer in time.
Use a fixed external schedule, such as a timed power cutoff, as a constraint that explains why an act had to occur at a particular time.
when: Building a timeline or motive argument

text: A time-stamped dialogue record can serve as a timeline that later puzzles check, so events reported in conversation become verifiable facts.
why: Stored timestamps let later game logic test a player's claims against what was recorded.

text: Market prices can react to an event before any report appears, so a price series can fix when the event happened.
when: Direct witnesses or reports are unavailable.
why: Sharp drops and later recovery mark the event's date.

text: A gap under about 45 minutes can be too short for a multi-step preparation, making an act in that window implausible.
when: judging opportunity inside a narrow window
why: multi-step tasks need time to complete

text: A shared window open only about 2.5 hours in each 12-hour cycle leaves every coordinated part needing to finish inside it.
when: when a plan depends on a tidal or periodic window
why: short windows leave little slack for error

text: A timeline built from partial observations can mislead. Gaps in the record can make an innocent explanation look impossible or a guilty one look certain.
when: Reconstructing events from scattered observations

text: A very short time window invites improbable escape routes to be proposed, so check each proposed route against the timing.
why: Tight windows tempt people to accept routes that would not fit the clock.

text: Assuming dates from a vague or uncertain witness are exact leads to false conclusions.
why: Uncertain recall carries error that must be weighed before comparing.

text: Taking the last known sighting as the moment something happened misplaces the event, which may have occurred earlier.
when: when placing an event in a timeline
why: The last observation is only a bound, not the cause.

text: 1) Identify a process with a known duration. 2) Get witness-reported start and end times. 3) Compute the earliest completion time. 4) Treat events before that time as possibly having altered the trace.
when: A trace such as a stain or mark depends on when a timed process finished.
why: A known duration converts a vague account into a checkable time limit.

text: 1) Collect the time ranges each witness gives. 2) Intersect them to find the interval all accounts allow. 3) Test that interval against physical evidence.
when: several witnesses give overlapping times

text: 1) Put each witness's timestamped events in sequence. 2) Check overlaps and gaps between witnesses. 3) Test each claim against physical access limits, such as whether a window could admit a person. 4) Confirm key details directly, not by secondhand report. 5) Mark unknown gaps rather than guessing.
when: several people describe one night's events

text: 1) Fix the crime's time to a clock reading. 2) Work backward from that time to test each witness's estimate. 3) Record each sound with its time. 4) Turn gaps and overlaps into follow-up questions.
when: several witnesses heard or saw events during one night

text: Use separate independent references, such as a stopped device, a celestial position and a tidal state, each to anchor a different part of one sequence.
Each new reliable sighting shortens the possible interval and shifts the odds, so an argument that ignores known sightings is weakened.
Testimony gains value when the person it implicates can no longer deny it, so a planted link is set to matter only after that person is dead or silenced.
when: a witness's account will decide an accusation
why: an accusation cannot be contested by someone who is gone

text: Small mismatches between witnesses, such as times or appearance details, often mark the weak point of a case and should be tested rather than dismissed as sloppiness.
when: When two sworn accounts disagree on time or description.
why: Discrepancies can expose a false alibi or a misidentification.

text: Test a stated routine, such as where valuables are kept each night, against the physical evidence before accepting it, since the scene may contradict it.
Cases become more testable when events are fixed in order and each crucial moment has several independent observers.
Be cautious when testimony seems to fix a time that physical evidence does not firmly support, since the apparent fixed point may be an assumption.
when: Physical or medical evidence gives only a loose time range
why: Witness timing can be assumed rather than observed

text: Record when and before whom each statement was given, so its timing relative to the event can be placed and weighed.
Build fair-play deductions from timestamps, schedules and time-zone differences that the reader can check, so the timeline itself carries the solution.
why: A checkable timeline lets the reader test the detective's reasoning against stated facts.

text: 1) Record the date of each incident from written entries. 2) Compute the intervals between them. 3) Form a provisional schedule theory. 4) Predict the next incident date. 5) Check the prediction against new records.

1) Obtain the exact sequence of events after the first sound or event. 2) Check whether each step is physically possible in the time allowed. 3) Reenact the sequence while timing it. 4) Reject any account that cannot be performed in the time.
when: when a witness's account depends on how long actions took
why: a story that cannot be performed in the available time is false, however plausible it sounds

text: 1) Mark checkpoints such as first contact, key handover, observation period and discovery. 2) Place each suspect's movements against those checkpoints. 3) Mark which movements conflict.
1) Fix times using observable landmarks such as the moon's position or a lit window. 2) Use each landmark as a checkpoint in the timeline. 3) Check which accounts each landmark corroborates.
when: when reconstructing a night timeline
why: Environmental markers give checkable reference points independent of memory.

text: Check stiffening against the stated time of death, adjusting for temperature, and corroborate before relying on it.
when: Comparing a body's state with an account of death time
why: Temperature shifts rigor timing

text: A time window is only as firm as its endpoints, so verify each endpoint before relying on it, especially when it comes from memory rather than records.
when: when a window is built from several witness times or its endpoints come from memory
why: One unchecked or misremembered endpoint can wrongly open or close the span and change who fits.

text: A window of possible times is not the act itself; the exact moment stays open until other evidence fixes it.
when: when a time window has been established but not narrowed further
why: Confusing a possibility range with a fixed time leads to premature conclusions.

text: Ask why someone with a fixed schedule changed it, because the change may reveal the reason behind the unusual act.
when: a regular routine is broken

text: Known departure and return times of household members bracket the period in which an intruder could have acted.
when: when several people's movements are known
why: Absence periods define the window when the house was unwatched.

text: 1) Use an early document to fix a time or place 2) search the physical scene at that target 3) confirm the finding with traces.
when: when the answer must be proven by something checkable

text: 1) Find an upper bound: a known event that would have removed or altered the deposit. 2) Find a lower bound from its physical state. 3) Check whether the bounded window fits a known disappearance date.
when: judging when an object or body was deposited
why: Two bounds from independent evidence narrow the timing

text: Do not build a timeline from a window too wide to mean anything, or from events whose times were never recorded.
why: Without a meaningful window or recorded times, any overlap is arbitrary.

text: Do not use process-time arithmetic when the duration is unknown or witnesses disagree about when the process started.
why: Without agreed start and duration values, the computed window is unreliable.

text: Timeline reconstruction from spending means recalling small payments, summing them, and checking the total against cash still held to rebuild a sequence of events.
Unexplained gaps often hide the critical act and matter more than fixed anchors; investigate them first, as closely as anchors, since a gap may hide guilt or an innocent reason.
when: a timeline has a period with no accounted events
why: Investigators overlook missing time, and key actions are concealed where no one is watching.

text: An unaccounted gap matters as much as recorded times but proves neither guilt nor innocence; keep it open and corroborate with a second source before treating it as wrongdoing.
when: A person's time cannot be accounted for.
why: Gaps often have ordinary causes, and a gap shows where the investigation should look next.

text: An unaccounted interval near the event carries the most weight in an alibi check: anyone unaccounted for within it stays a possible participant and cannot be cleared.
when: when laying a witness timeline against an event
why: Gaps near the event are where a story can hide an opportunity; an unheard return can keep suspects uncleared and outweigh other links.

text: Note periods a person cannot be found or accounted for, such as alone in a room; they are an alibi's weakest point and must be flagged and accounted for.
why: Unwitnessed spans allow actions no witness can confirm; minutes nobody can confirm are where an act could occur.

text: Store NPC whereabouts with timestamps and explicit gap markers, so the player must rebuild the timeline from partial recollections; a gap gives a concrete question to pursue.
when: Designing quest logs, NPC memory, or investigation content with NPC alibis
why: Overlapping absences that coincide with an event create gaps the player must reason about.

text: A complete-looking sequence or silent witness can hide unobserved action between events; silence is not evidence of inactivity, so check those intervals; a gap is itself information.
when: Reconstructing a witness's timeline or reviewing a record
why: Overlooked gaps let hidden action pass unexamined and can conceal movement or events.

text: 1) List each unobserved interval the suspect cannot account for. 2) Mark corroborated parts. 3) For each uncorroborated gap, ask what could be done in it and whether the suspected act fits. 4) Treat uncorroborated gaps as the core of the case.
when: When a suspect's movements are only partly observed.

text: Routine absences, such as a scheduled staff break or a task that draws attention away, leave rooms unobserved, letting an actor move unseen.
when: A scheduled break leaves an area without attendants.
why: Routine absences remove the people who would notice an intruder.

text: A timeline records where each person was over time, and a brief window when no one can vouch for someone is an opportunity for an act.
when: Analysing who could have committed a crime
why: Gaps in witnessed movement show which suspects had access

text: Gap estimates such as about half an hour carry error, so a timeline should record its tolerance rather than treat them as exact.
when: Filling intervals between anchored events.
why: Estimated durations are imprecise, and unrecorded tolerance can make a sequence appear more certain than it is.

text: An unexplained interval between known times marks a place to look for an encounter, such as a meeting or a stop along the way.
when: a timeline has an unexplained interval

text: Treat a pause before access to a building as a lead to investigate, not a conclusion, since it may indicate time needed for someone else to act.
when: An access delay or unavailability appears in a timeline
why: Delays can conceal preparation by another party

text: Keep one timeline variable genuinely indeterminate, so an alibi-style timing argument fails without needing a new witness.
Once a witness admits the timing was never recorded, a confident identification loses its support, even if the identity is never directly disputed.
Witness sightings that cover only some time slots, with the uncovered slots shown as unknown, let the player see which intervals remain unresolved.
when: When designing witness-based clues in a game.
why: Explicit unknown intervals direct the player's further investigation.

text: Recorded or stated times are only as reliable as their clock or memory; guesses, stopped clocks, missing stamps and estimated travel times mislead, so verify against an independent source.
when: when building a timeline from recorded or witness-stated times
why: Individual timekeeping and travel speeds vary, and unchecked times can silently fix the whole timeline on a wrong point.

text: Without a recorded time for an event, later reconstructions of the sequence become unreliable, since exact times can only be recovered from readings taken at the moment.
A gap that no witness or record can fill makes the sequence impossible to fix, and hidden parties can exploit that blur.
A timetable cannot be fully trusted, since a delay such as fog can break a schedule-based conclusion, so plans built on schedules need margin.
when: when a plan relies on published times
why: real travel is disrupted by weather and other delays

text: An unobserved gap is not proof of tampering. The real question is whether the gap was long enough for the change to occur.
An unknown anchor time breaks a backward-calculated timeline, because the chain of estimates has nothing fixed to start from.
Vague timing leaves gaps that a suspect can exploit; the last confirmed sighting must be pinned down.
why: Unpinned timing lets an alibi hide inside an unmeasured span.

text: 1) Record each person's movements with times. 2) Compare the windows of absence. 3) Find gaps where the act could have happened. 4) Test each candidate gap against independent checks.
when: When several people have short, overlapping absences
why: Gaps not covered by any alibi identify the candidates who had the chance to act.

text: 1) Log each detail with its source and whether it is first-hand or relayed. 2) Record the witness's awareness window. 3) Flag unexplained details as unresolved, not explained. 4) Check flagged details against primary sources.
1) Find the last confirmed sighting of the object in place. 2) Find when it was first noticed missing. 3) Treat the interval between them as the custody window.
when: Establishing who could have handled an object.

text: Mark timeline gaps explicitly as unknown, not blank or guessed, so no one reads absence of record as absence of events.
when: a timeline has a stretch with no reliable information, or witnesses cannot place events in time
why: A blank can be read as nothing having happened.

text: Record each unobserved interval, and any gap a suspect will not explain, as an open unresolved item rather than a settled fact, even if last seen entering a place.
when: A witness's account stops at a doorway, staircase or room, or a suspect will not explain a gap.
why: Seeing someone enter does not show they left, so the exit remains unverified.

text: Do not date an event using a process whose rate is unknown.
why: without a rate, the condition shows no elapsed time

text: For every unobserved interval, ask who can speak for the person during that time; an interval with no witness is a gap.
when: Testing an alibi that has unobserved periods.
why: Gaps are where an alibi can hide an opportunity.

text: Treat unexplained intervals in a timeline as the places where further questions belong.
when: when no account covers a period between known events

text: Do not assume guilt from unaccounted time. A person need not account for every minute, though an unwitnessed gap leaves no alibi.
Leave a timeline gap that the player can close by visiting a second location.
Treat an account of hours you did not witness as testimony to be checked, not as established fact, even when it is told confidently.
when: Reconstructing events from a later account.
why: Confident telling does not make unobserved events reliable.

text: Time overlap shows opportunity, not action, and can be arranged; treat timing and reaction inferences as hypotheses to check.
why: Such inferences are probable, not proven, and reading too much into them misleads.

text: Boundary disputes and releases between neighboring towns appear as entries in an ownership chain, marking where claims overlapped.
Where traces cross or overlap, the mark laid over or partly erasing another was made later, so overlap order fixes the sequence of passage.
when: Several traces cross or overlap on one surface.
why: Later passes disturb earlier impressions; reading overlap backwards reverses apparent direction of travel.

text: Express an event's time as a window built from several approximate estimates; overlapping independent estimates narrow it, and other evidence can test the band.
when: Evidence is approximate or witness times are estimates.
why: Overlapping estimates give a band that other evidence can test.

text: Ask witnesses for a bounded time window, such as the last few minutes, because a window narrows the search for a passer-by.
A claim or denial covers only the period it names; events outside that window remain unexamined, so check the timing of each claim.
when: A witness denies involvement or makes a claim.
why: The denial is bounded in time.

text: Long gaps between dated events, such as a weekend, can hide movements that a timeline cannot show.
when: a timeline has large unrecorded intervals
why: Unrecorded time can conceal what happened

text: A timeline with many unverifiable steps makes readers lose track of who can confirm what, weakening the whole deduction.
when: Constructing a long sequence of movements.
why: Each unverifiable step adds doubt that spreads to the steps that could be verified.

text: 1) Fix the earliest and latest moments the act could have occurred, using reliable witness times. 2) Exclude any time outside the window. 3) Weigh times inside the window by the actor's incentive.
when: when an act must be placed in time from several clock-based accounts
why: A bounded window narrows the search, and incentive points toward likely timing.

text: 1) State the inference, such as a recent arrival. 2) Ask a direct question that would confirm or deny it. 3) Accept or revise the inference by the answer.
when: A timing-based inference needs a quick check before it guides further reasoning.
why: A direct question turns a plausible story into a testable claim.

text: 1) Fix the last moment the item was known to be present. 2) Fix the first moment someone needed it. 3) State the window between them explicitly. 4) Test each witness against that window.
when: A small or personal object disappears and the question is who had opportunity.
why: A bounded window limits which people and times remain possible.

text: Test whether an act could fit the entire interval at any hour, not only the hour a favored theory prefers.
when: when a theory depends on when something happened

text: Record witness claims with explicit time windows, so players can check whether each claim covers the events they care about.
when: authoring witness statements in a game
why: Undated claims cannot be tested against the timeline

text: Check whether the official time window is established or only assumed before judging any alibi against it.
Turn a short time window into a puzzle where the player must confirm each suspect's location during that interval.
Do not present a time-of-death window as an exact time; it records only what can be shown.
when: Reporting a reconstructed time of death
why: Bounds from sightings are limits, not precise measurements

text: Frequent time checks sustain tension but slow the pace, so they must be balanced with action.
when: Writing a timed sequence

text: Let players log timed sightings or note timestamps and sort them into a timeline to reconstruct routes, alibis or suspects, making the timeline itself a puzzle.
when: designing deduction puzzles from in-world records
why: Sorting timed entries reveals sequences players must reason about, showing who could have seen what.

text: Fix each recurring event's timestamp on a timeline so gaps, returns and sequences show whether events are connected or a natural cause explains them.
when: when events recur irregularly, or any clue is built from repeated small events
why: Dates expose patterns that memory blurs; timing and recurrence separate a pattern from chance.

text: 1) Record each suspect's arrivals, departures and returns with times. 2) Compare these with the offence time and any sightings. 3) Flag each claimed alibi or location that conflicts with the record.
when: testing alibis or whereabouts
why: A shared frame exposes alibis that do not fit the timing; contradictions with the record are the basis for challenging an alibi.

text: 1) Gather dated entries from depositions, warrants, letters and later memoirs. 2) Date each source and note each author's motive. 3) Reconcile conflicting figures. 4) Sort all entries and build the full timeline before concluding intent or plans.
when: several documents disagree or mention events
why: Dating and motive-weighing show which conflicts matter and which can be resolved.

text: 1) List each person's stated movements with times and locations. 2) Compare them with what independent witnesses observed. 3) Map distances and check each leg against the time it takes. 4) Chain events in order. 5) Mark gaps and implausible speeds as weak points.
when: several accounts must fit together within time windows, or whether a sequence was physically possible is being tested.
why: Stories fail where stated times conflict with observations or physical limits; timed legs and distances expose impossible sequences.

text: 1) Collect arrival and departure times and stated times from every account. 2) Lay all events on one timeline. 3) Check whether overlapping accounts can both be true. 4) Mark which claims are independent and which rest on one witness; cross-check disputed vehicles or times before accepting them.
when: when several accounts give times for the same event or witnesses report movements around one event
why: Overlapping events on one timeline expose contradictions that single accounts hide; the timeline shows which statements corroborate each other.

text: 1) Collect every account. 2) Sort all events by time into one sequence per person, covering every party. 3) Look for long empty stretches. 4) Test the sequence against physical limits such as travel distance and speed; test each alibi against it, not on its face.
when: when several accounts conflict, one date decides whether a person could have been at a scene, or several suspects claim locations around a crime
why: A single ordered schedule covering all parties exposes gaps and impossible movements.

text: Give suspects and NPCs timestamped movement and transport records so players can check alibis against a schedule.
when: when designing alibi or movement puzzles
why: A timestamped schedule gives a concrete, checkable basis for accepting or rejecting an alibi.

text: Use timetables, drifting or misset clocks, ticket records, transport logs, servant testimony and NPC schedules that players must order and reconcile to notice disagreements.
when: when designing a timeline or movement-based mystery
why: Requiring players to order and reconcile records makes the puzzle depend on reasoning rather than a single clue.

text: An unexplained absence or undisclosed visitor leaves a gap that observers fill with guesses, keeping the question alive.
when: the source of a gap is hidden
why: people prefer a guess to an open question

text: A person who does not know they are watched shows conduct they would otherwise hide, so a hidden observer can capture it.
when: an observer stays out of the target's view
why: concealing the watch keeps behaviour natural

text: A long wait builds tension but can dull watchers' attention, as companions grow restless and fidget.
People often underweight a soft deadline and keep searching past the point where they should leave.
when: a deadline is flexible rather than fixed
why: A deadline that seems negotiable loses its urgency

text: Felt time in a tense wait can far exceed real time; a few minutes of watching a risky object can seem like an hour.
when: A watcher waits with attention fixed on a risky object or sound.
why: Attention to each small change stretches perceived duration.

text: At peak suspense a character can forget their next plan, leaving them stuck between options.
Establishing when an event could have happened means testing the time window, verifying alibi documents, and asking whether a person could realistically have been seen.
Trace inference runs backward from a mark or residue on a surface or object to the body or item that produced it.
Timeline reconstruction builds an ordered sequence of events from a witness's approximate durations, order of actions and the gaps between them.
when: a witness saw events only in pieces
why: an ordered account is needed for the investigation

text: A reconstructed timeline is a sequence of dated events and fixed checkpoints, with undated actions placed between them.
A locked-room puzzle can be solved by asking when a closure was made, not only how an opening was sealed or forced.
when: A room seems closed and rules out an outside intruder.

text: A time-of-death estimate is a range, not a precise moment, so it should be treated as a window and not as an exact time.
when: using an examiner's or any time-of-death estimate
why: Post-mortem timing depends on conditions, so it has limits.

text: A timeline removes hiding places but alone forces no confession and settles no guilt, since the same timeline can support opposite prosecution and defence conclusions.
when: relying on a timeline to extract a confession or prove guilt
why: Pressure from facts does not compel admission of guilt.

text: A reliable timeline combines the sequence of events, sounds, movements and physical remains.
A case story can open with the commission before the crime's facts, so the audience meets the frame before the details.
Where an object is found and where it is later delivered are fixed points that constrain the timeline and must both be checked.
Timeline reasoning about messages weakens when messages can travel by unrecorded means.
when: Messages may be sent by unrecorded means.

text: Time of death is hard to fix when a body is found after prolonged exposure, such as cold, and the medical estimate may span many hours.
when: When a body is found long after death or in harsh conditions
why: Environmental effects alter decay, so the estimated window can be wide.

text: A reconstructed timeline shows what was possible, not what happened, so physical evidence is still needed to confirm it.
Treat witness time estimates as approximate and provisional; cross-check them against other sources or a public clock before relying on them.
when: a timeline depends on witness statements or estimated absence durations
why: Human time estimates drift and are often imprecise; an independent clock gives the firmer fix.

text: Events with a known clock time, such as a striking clock or gunshot, serve as fixed anchors; anchor each witness's report to them so accounts can be sequenced.
when: several witnesses describe the same short event
why: A shared time reference lets accounts be compared and sequenced.

text: Before rejecting a theory over conflicting witness times, identify each clock's reference; a fixed offset is corrected by subtraction, so fifteen minutes fast turns twenty past into five past.
when: witness times from different locations or sources appear inconsistent
why: A hidden fixed offset between clocks can make a contradiction vanish.

text: Check whether each event could occur before the events that depend on it; an effect appearing before its cause signals a broken order.
Objects left in their final state, such as a half-played board or lights still burning, can serve as time markers.
Use a timing cue such as weather or a dried puddle to date an event for the player without any NPC stating it.
Combine time sources that are vague or disagree into the narrowest window that all of them allow.
when: Several time sources disagree or are vague.
why: The overlap of independent estimates is tighter than any one of them.

text: Place events relative to a fixed, timed object with a known installation time; this is more robust than an unanchored estimate.
when: when the question is when something happened

text: A wind-up mechanism that runs about fourteen to fifteen hours shows, when stopped, the time it was last wound or touched, if its start time is known.
when: A scene contains a timed object whose running state can be read.
why: Its running time is predictable, so its stopped position fixes when someone interacted with it.

text: A timeline gives an interrogator a structure for questions, since each timed step is a point where the suspect's account must fit.
when: When questioning a suspect about their whereabouts.
why: Each checkpoint forces a specific, testable answer.

text: Combine separate approaches by the same person into one timeline, which can show that preparation came before the key event.
Leave a margin for error when planning a route so that one party arrives before a set hour and another is in position before a later one.
when: Planning a timed sequence of movements
why: Uncertain travel time makes a zero-margin plan fragile

text: Work backwards from the critical window to test whether a suspect could have been in two places at once.
An event during a pending transaction, such as the death of the party who must honour it, makes failure likely.
why: The transaction cannot settle once the required party is gone.

text: If an occupant's first outing comes right after moving in, the person who arrived may not be the person who later returns.
when: comparing an occupant's arrival and departures
why: a sudden change in routine can mark a substitution

text: A witness may know that someone was present without knowing when they arrived or left, so test witness times against each other.
when: Reconstructing a timeline from witness accounts.
why: Partial knowledge yields gaps in the timeline.

text: Set a specific time for a reveal, which makes the wait concrete and public and turns impatience into anticipation.
when: A reveal is deliberately delayed.
why: A named moment gives the audience a fixed endpoint to wait toward.

text: Before counting a disordered detail as a sign of haste, check whether ordinary sequence explains it, such as outer clothing being put on last.
when: when a detail seems out of place
why: routine order of actions often explains apparent disorder

text: Check event order: if an early stimulus would have produced a reaction, any later feigned response must begin after that stimulus.
Compare a witness's account against an outside fixed point, such as a dated message, to check whether the sequence of events holds together.
An alibi that shifts under questioning and has no fixed anchors is weak. Test it against fixed points such as transport records or timed events.
when: When the account changes on repeated questioning.

text: Choose which witnesses to visit first by the specific hour each one can cover.
Shadow a suspect toward the likely hiding place rather than confronting him early.
when: a suspect may hold the object somewhere not yet known
why: early confrontation alerts the suspect and can end the trail

text: Judge what an absence implies by trip length: someone leaving a base takes different things than someone away for a weekend.
when: interpreting missing belongings
why: the items needed depend on how long the person expects to be away

text: When one link in a chain is missing, work from the known parts and ask what must have been true for the rest to fit.
A known period when a character is away from their post fixes the window in which another party's visit or action can occur.
Demonstrate a suspected position with your own body so others can test and accept a reconstruction.
An independent witness's sighting, including confirmation that no one passed, can fix a scene at a particular time.
Break an accusation into ordered steps, each tied to a named person, so every step can be checked on its own.
when: when reconstructing a disputed incident
why: a single unified claim hides which step can be verified

text: A step that appears out of sequence, or a required step that is missing, can expose a disputed or irregular action worth investigating.
Check whether key evidence arrived after decision-makers had formed their view, since the weight of late evidence depends on that timing.
Let the player disprove a frame by finding a timing or motive gap in the accusation.
when: Designing a murder mystery with a framed suspect
why: Discoverable gaps give players a route to clear the innocent and find the culprit

text: Use travel time between locations as a pacing tool, with brief waits that let players review their clues.
why: Pauses restore attention before the next step.

text: Make a timeline puzzle require the player to track when each character could reach a location.
when: Designing a time-based deduction challenge
why: Reachability over time turns alibis into a checkable puzzle

text: Reward players who work out which production method produced a forged item, not only those who notice that it looks wrong.
when: When a forgery puzzle has more than one solution path.
why: Reasoning about method tests deeper understanding than surface inspection.

text: Backward timeline planning should be used only when timings are known; with guessed timings it produces false precision.
when: when the durations are estimates
why: exact-looking results rest on unverified numbers

text: A scene-reconstruction system can require the player to check a claimed action against the traces the true event would leave, such as disturbed objects or reacting NPCs.
Require players to test a reconstructed story against dated events before a final accusation unlocks.
Reconstruct a timeline only when several actions depend on timed conditions; without fixed points, there is nothing to anchor it.
when: deciding whether timeline analysis applies
why: fixed points supply the anchors that windows are measured from

text: Narrow the window of tampering by timing, placing it after the event and before the scene is formally examined.
when: Evidence of tampering must be dated.
why: Timing bounds which people could have had access.

text: Leave a watch post before staying becomes conspicuous to staff and customers, since familiar faces may begin to notice or question you.
when: Maintaining a long stakeout in a public place.
why: Repeated presence draws attention and undermines cover.

text: A trace that places a suspect at a different time can eliminate that suspect from the event being investigated.
when: Comparing a suspect's confirmed movements against the time of the event
why: A person cannot be present at two places at once, so a timing mismatch rules them out

text: A person's movements can be rebuilt from hotel registers, telephone logs, mail and staff recollections, and no single source needs to be complete.
when: The person has left a trail of institutional records

text: Store a disputed mechanism, such as a dragged body, as a reenactment puzzle that resolves only when the correct movement is replicated.
why: Requiring the right action makes the mechanism a skill-based challenge.

text: A stopped in-game clock can hint that a power cut or tampering happened.
when: when designing environmental clues

text: A timeline that rests on witnesses who may misjudge the hour or place is weak and should not be trusted alone.
when: Witness accounts are the only source for event timing

text: Ask witnesses for an orderly, lucid account, since the order of their statements exposes gaps.
A timed observation fixes that a person was present at one moment only, so it narrows the window but does not prove presence later.
when: when a witness reports someone at a specific time
why: A single sighting is a snapshot, not continuous proof.

text: A stand-in's timing can give the trick away, for example by leaving late when the house is quiet.
when: Testing whether a visible presence was the person it appeared to be
why: Unusual timing contradicts the expected behavior of the person being impersonated

text: Deliver a new piece of information when the protagonist's resolve is weakest, so tension restarts.
when: A protagonist is wavering or close to giving up.
why: Fresh information at a low point reignites conflict.

text: Give a timing clue an early, dismissible explanation, then bring it back with a stronger witness so the player is taught to discount it before it matters.
when: A clock or timer clue is central to an alibi or timeline.
why: A clue dismissed early and reraised later with better testimony pays off without feeling sudden.

text: Timelines are weak when all times are estimates with no fixed events to anchor them.
when: Reconstructing events from witness estimates only.
why: Without anchors, errors in each estimate accumulate unchecked.

text: Start a disappearance timeline at the last moment the missing person was reliably seen, not at a later rumour or sighting.
when: A disappearance is being investigated and its start is disputed.
why: A convenient later start date can hide the true window of opportunity.

text: A discovery that coincides with a party beginning a legal or financial action is suspicious timing that can point toward whoever controlled the discovery.
Place dated records of orders, deliveries and events side by side, so timing can be checked against each suspect's access.
when: a case depends on when means were obtained relative to when effects began
why: Matching dates across separate records can confirm or break a suspect's link to the cause.

text: Resolve an impossible state by reordering events already shown, not by adding new ones; the reveal feels fair because the timing was set out early.
when: when a sealed or impossible scene needs an explanation
why: the audience already holds every piece, so the solution feels earned

text: Use a timed event, such as a stop that reopens an alibi, as the hinge of the case, forcing the reader to decide which witness to believe about it.
when: Constructing an alibi that seems closed but may be reopened.
why: A time window converts a settled alibi into a live question without new characters.

text: Scheduled events such as appointments, patrols, train arrivals or NPC routines can serve as fixed points from which a player reconstructs a timeline.
when: designing timeline-based puzzles
why: Fixed events give the player reference points to order other events.
