text: A timeline view logging timed departures, arrivals, shots and each character's claim lets players cross-check accounts against each other and scene evidence; short blocking intervals can create or break an alibi.
when: players must verify NPC whereabouts or accounts
why: Checking claims against a shared timeline turns testimony into a puzzle.

text: Store each game event with its game time, location and presence list, including room entries, trap triggers and sightings, so designer and player can rebuild an intrusion and see who is excluded.
why: Players can check which characters are excluded from each event.

text: Travel times between locations set timing constraints: an arrival message or lead calculation shows how soon a character can reach a place, defining the window in which to act.
when: designing timed NPC movement or player action windows
why: Travel time bounds what is possible.

text: A timed weather event gives a time boundary: marks made after a snowfall began date to the interval since then, and tracks lying on fresh snow were made after it stopped.
when: using a timed weather event as evidence of when movement happened
why: A known start point lets traces be dated relative to it.

text: Travel times between areas can be tuned so that a player who stops to listen or carry a burden runs out of time before a scheduled event.
when: When designing timed sequences in a game.
why: Movement costs and pauses change how much time remains, creating tension.

text: A plot built on a precise schedule fails when one fixed date falls out of order, because later steps cannot undo an event already fixed earlier in the sequence.
when: A scheme depends on a strict chain of dated steps, such as substitutions or false identities.
why: Each step assumes the prior date held, so a single conflicting date can collapse the whole arrangement.

text: A fixed deadline makes each lost day shrink the characters' options; a flexible deadline loses tension.
when: the deadline is firm and cannot be delayed

text: Fixed mechanical records, such as a timed device that logs an event, can pin down the moment something happened.
when: When a crime or event must be dated.
why: Automatic recorders give times independent of witness memory.

text: When each backstory event triggers the next, the timeline carries a motive's logic and reveals it in order.
A timeline puzzle that gives timestamps, travel durations and messages lets the player work backward to when an event occurred.
when: Designing a time-based deduction puzzle
why: Known durations constrain the possible time of the event

text: A second timer can trigger a routine at regular intervals, such as renewing air roughly every forty minutes, so recurring actions happen without a person present.
when: an action must recur while the character is unobserved
why: the second timer schedules the routine

text: An object shown to have moved after an event the audience thought was earlier overturns prior assumptions and changes which characters are suspected.
when: when the reveal depends on the order of events
why: reversing the sequence reinterprets every earlier clue at once

text: Fix a narrow event window from two bounds: a physical estimate of when the event happened, and the last confirmed sighting of the person alive.
when: early in an investigation
why: Two bounds turn vague timing into a testable interval.

text: A timeline built from clock times, dates and events shows the order in which people were where, which is the basis for checking claims.
when: reconstructing who was present at what moment
why: Ordering events exposes contradictions that isolated accounts hide

text: A scene reveals how a body or visitor arrived through five trace types: disturbed ground, broken growth, wheel marks, left objects, and food provenance.
why: Each trace type records a different part of the arrival or departure sequence.

text: A timeline built on one party's account, whether suspect's or accuser's, distorts events or can be wrong; each step needs corroboration from witnesses who can confirm it.
why: Other accounts can contradict or confirm that party's version.

text: A timeline resting on one disputed or unconfirmed hour or date fails, since every event placed relative to it inherits the error; ask how a claimed hour was established.
why: All other placements inherit the error; unverified numbers can lock an argument onto a false time.

text: A timeline is only as good as its dates: check every date against its source, and treat a mismatch as an argument, not proof, until confirmed.
when: using a date mismatch to challenge a story
why: Calendar dates are often misremembered, and unverified dates can be disputed.

text: A witness can be accurate about events yet wrong about intervals and finish times, so confirm start and end points with observers before using a time reckoning.
when: a timeline relies on witness recollection of durations
why: Recalled events are often correct while recalled gaps and finish times are not.

text: Confusing the order of events can make chance overlap look like cause.
why: a cause must precede its effect, so a wrong order creates false links

text: A timeline built on one household's account inherits every gap in that household's knowledge, so it needs outside corroboration.
when: Building a timeline from one group's testimony
why: One source carries its own blind spots

text: A witness's sense of time can be shifted by clocks, a late bell or a suggested remark, so timed alibis based on memory are weak.
A witness who knows that times matter to investigators may shape their time reports rather than give them neutrally.
Calculating backwards from remembered intervals fails when those intervals were never logged, and one missed entry can break an otherwise sound chain.
when: Reconstructing dates from memory or sparse logs.
why: Unrecorded intervals have no reliable value to calculate from.

text: Fragments taken out of order can support several readings, so a partial exchange can be misinterpreted.
when: a listener assembles partial dialogue
why: sequence is needed to fix meaning

text: A witness's time estimate loses weight when conditions such as fog are admitted to have allowed faster travel than claimed.
Adding approximate durations together accumulates error, so the total can drift far from the true span.
when: summing several estimated intervals
why: each approximation carries its own error

text: Reading intent backward from the outcome can make coincidences look like a deliberate plan.
Assuming that an arrest or other event caused a recovery, without testing other causes, can attribute healing to the wrong factor.
when: when suffering stops around the time of a notable event
why: Recoveries often coincide with events for reasons unrelated to them.

text: Timeline puzzles where the player aligns ages, intervals and places from several testimonies should be solvable, with one contradiction that the player can find.
when: When designing investigative puzzles from multiple testimonies.
why: A puzzle with no findable contradiction, or with several, gives the player no clear path to a solution.

text: A single transit record shows only a route someone travelled, and can push a search toward the wrong place.
when: when a record is used to locate someone

text: Events following each other show only time order, not cause; a threat followed by harm needs checks of what else happened in that period.
A character's stated timing can be wrong, and a mismatch against a clock or log becomes a checkable clue rather than a plot error.
when: when an alibi or timing claim is given
why: Stated times can be checked against recorded events

text: A person woken from sleep has an unreliable sense of timing, and sounds seem louder or closer than they were.
when: when a witness was asleep before the event
why: Sleep disrupts time perception and sound localization.

text: Time estimates made under stress are unreliable, even when counted with a steady rhythm.
when: when a person is frightened or under strain
why: stress distorts perceived elapsed time

text: A reconstruction can only approximate original conditions, so its results carry some uncertainty.
when: when a scene cannot be fully recreated
why: small differences in conditions can change timing results

text: A timeline is only as reliable as its inputs; if clocks cannot be read in the dark, the plan's timings become unusable.
when: Time readings depend on poor light

text: Uncertainty about the hour of death can itself be exploited by a defence to challenge the timeline.
when: When the time of death is only approximately known
why: A wide window gives an opponent room to dispute the prosecution's timeline.

text: A timeline built on one record can break if that record is incomplete or partly preserved.
when: The central date rests on one document or one witness's word.
why: A single source has no check if it is damaged or misremembered.

text: A timeline built from one account can look exact while resting on guesses.
why: Precise times in one telling hide the approximation underneath.

text: A walk or car journey can take far longer than expected, so claimed travel times must be checked against realistic durations.
when: A suspect's account relies on a quick journey.
why: Travel delays are easy to underestimate.

text: 1) Fix the last moment the victim is known alive. 2) Anchor the timeline on objective clocks or markers. 3) Convert each witness claim into a window. 4) Compare windows for gaps and overlaps. 5) Test every suspect's movements against that moment.
when: Several witnesses give differing times, or a timeline for a death is being built.
why: Events cannot be placed without a known starting point; fixed references and windows reveal who could have acted when.

text: 1) Collect each witness's timed statements, such as a departure, a sighting or a late check. 2) Attach a source to each point and anchor it to events others heard or saw. 3) Lay the points in one sequence. 4) Examine the gaps between points, where the open questions lie.
when: Several partial accounts or witness times must be joined into one ordered sequence.

text: 1) Date each event from documents or witnesses, such as letters, a rupture, a visit or the crime. 2) Order all events by date. 3) Test each claim against the sequence and mark the gaps between consecutive events.
when: reconstructing a sequence of events
why: Gaps show where time is unaccounted for.

text: 1) Verify each date against a reliable record. 2) Lay out the events in order. 3) Test whether the sequence explains the motive and the awkward timings.
when: events are spread over years and their order is the key clue
why: Verified dates make the chain trustworthy; testing against awkward timings exposes gaps.

text: 1) Have the witness recount their day step by step in fixed order, from first contact through each later event. 2) Check each small decision against independent sources. 3) Repeat the account and compare each repetition with notes.
when: A witness's day must be fixed in time, such as at the start of an interview.
why: Ordered recording with repetition exposes shifts and contradictions.

text: 1) Write a clear history of the event and state each claimed time or event. 2) For each claim, ask how it is known and name an independent witness who could confirm it. 3) Accept a time as strong only when an independent source confirms it. 4) Test whether stated durations are plausible.
when: reconstructing a timeline from witness accounts or testimony
why: Speakers may not be telling the truth, so each claim needs an independent check.

text: 1) Record each person's movements in time order, such as departures, appointments, returns and visits, with location and time. 2) Attach a witness to each leg. 3) Compare records, marking gaps where no one is accounted for and overlaps where two conflict.
when: several people's movements must be reconciled or who was where during a time window must be reconstructed
why: Gaps and overlaps reveal windows of opportunity and false alibis; ordered, witnessed legs expose gaps that scattered statements hide.

text: 1) Collect movement reports of the same person over the same hours from several staff or witnesses. 2) Anchor each report to appointments or schedules and place events in order. 3) Test each entry against the others, records, physical facts and stated plans, noting gaps.
when: several people report the same person's movements, or alibis must be tested
why: Several independent reports anchored to schedules are harder to distort than one account.

text: 1) Fix the time and place of each event in order, listing each person's movements with times. 2) Anchor the list to the estimated event time, even when times are approximate. 3) For each moment, mark who could have been at that place and compare each position with the timing of the threat.
when: several events must be placed in order and the question is who could reach a place at a given time
why: A shared time anchor brackets the event and shows who had access to it.

text: 1) Have an unremarked observer follow the suspect, close enough not to lose them but far enough to avoid notice. 2) Log each stop and meeting in order. 3) Check each stop against known facts. 4) Read gestures when words cannot be heard; leave blank stretches empty.
when: a suspect's movements over hours must be tracked, or the subject may move or meet others

text: 1) Store each witness time estimate as a range. 2) Collect the last confirmed events, such as a door fastened at a known hour, and add the medical window. 3) Add each range as a boundary. 4) Narrow the overlap to the smallest shared window.
when: several sources give overlapping or differing times
why: Overlapping ranges bound the true interval better than any single estimate.

text: 1) Anchor timed sightings, such as arrival, an overheard exchange, movement, entry and any later call, to clock times. 2) Order unclocked events using sounds such as locks, shots or calls for help. 3) Write each step in clock order and check each movement against the time it requires.
when: multiple witnesses describe the sequence of an event
why: Clocks and sounds give fixed points, and travel checks expose accounts that move faster than possible.

text: 1) Start from the present result or surviving physical evidence. 2) Ask which earlier event or act would produce it. 3) Link each earlier stage to the next by evidence such as a sale, visit, letter or death. 4) Repeat until the chain reaches the root cause, checking each step against independent facts.
when: Tracing a present crime or situation back through its background, or the cause is hidden by later damage or change.
why: Working backward keeps each step tied to what it explains; surviving traces constrain what could have happened and expose gaps.

text: 1) Anchor the timeline to one reliable time reference or known event. 2) Work outward, estimating when other events happened from witnesses' sense of time, treating each event as its own link. 3) Mark each person's position at each moment and note gaps.
when: Several accounts overlap in time and must be ordered, or when events happened is being reconstructed.
why: A fixed anchor lets uncertain times be placed relative to each other.

text: 1) Record each person's evening and morning as timed events, collecting each witness's times for the night. 2) Anchor them to fixed times and order arrivals and departures on one timeline. 3) Test overlaps: who saw whom in the same room at the same time. 4) Find gaps where a suspect is unaccounted for and check each time against an independent source.
when: several people claim to have been somewhere at a particular hour or give times for the same night

text: Have a witness narrate their actions in sequence, anchoring each step to the event, to place them in time.

1) List each timed event a witness reports. 2) Record each time from an independent source, such as separate watches. 3) Compare the sources and mark disagreements. 4) Accept only events whose times agree.
when: when a witness's timeline depends on clock readings
why: independent sources expose errors that one clock hides

text: 1) Fix a known starting event and its time. 2) Add each leg's duration in order: departure, travel, waiting, walking. 3) Sum to predict the arrival time. 4) Compare it with the recorded time.
when: Checking whether a suspect's claimed movements fit a tight timeline

text: 1) Record the time each event starts and ends. 2) Find scheduled fixed points such as transport arrivals. 3) Subtract the time needed for movement and actions to find the window available. 4) Check whether the plan fits within that window.
when: When checking whether a person could have been at a place and acted within known times.
why: Fixed times define the window in which the events must have occurred.

text: 1) Fix anchor times, such as the last sighting and the discovery. 2) Compute the gap between them. 3) Compare the gap with how long a natural process takes.
when: when a case hinges on whether a timeline is physically possible

text: 1) List each dated interval, such as time held before burial or time since a space was last disturbed. 2) Treat each interval as a checkable claim. 3) Compare each claim against remains and reports.
when: rebuilding when events happened

text: 1) Assign a named watcher to the suspect. 2) Instruct the watcher to stay unseen and say nothing. 3) Also watch any companion who may carry the object or plan. 4) If the subject travels, place a hidden observer in the same transport.
1) Fix a bounded interval from one witness's time. 2) Narrow it with a second witness's upper or lower limit. 3) Check each window against the witness's routine and what they could perceive.
when: when accounts must be fitted together and the order of events is uncertain
why: Overlapping bounded windows fix the sequence of events more reliably than any single account.

text: 1) Reconstruct a suspect's movements step by step using transport and sightings. 2) Turn each gap in the timeline into a question. 3) Answer each question with evidence.
when: A suspect's movements must be verified.
why: Gaps in the timeline are the weak points that an investigator must close.

text: 1) Rebuild each suspect's known movements as a timeline. 2) Mark the gaps. 3) Look for a gap in which an unseen round trip could fit.
when: When several suspects' movements are uncertain
why: Unexplained gaps are where a hidden trip would have to occur

text: 1) Fix the time with a reliable instrument reading. 2) Fix the position with a second reading. 3) Inventory equipment and supplies. 4) Separate what is intact from what is missing. 5) Record each result when it is found.
when: reconstructing what happened after a disruption
why: a recorded sequence of readings keeps later reconstruction reliable

text: 1) Record when each absence begins. 2) Record when it ends. 3) Treat the two dates as the window in which the relevant event must fall.
when: a person is away from the scene
why: Absence dates fix when that person could not have acted.

text: 1) Take a fragment of the victim's words. 2) Infer the secret it implies. 3) Infer who had reason to hide it. 4) Turn each guess into a testable hypothesis.
when: when the victim's last words are among the few clues

text: 1) Have the witness narrate one stage at a time: each place, action, meal or drink. 2) Record estimated durations and place events on a clock. 3) Mark blank periods explicitly. 4) Anchor each gap with outside points.
when: a witness was impaired and the order of events determines who was where
why: Fragmentary memory can still yield an ordered account if gaps are marked and anchored

text: 1) List dated events in order. 2) List every treatment or action given, with its time. 3) Compare each witness account against both lists. 4) Flag each mismatch for investigation.
when: the answer depends on order and timing
why: Timing claims can only be checked against records

text: 1) Establish whether the marked item exists. 2) Identify whose item it is. 3) Ask its owner to account for their whereabouts during the time window.
when: A physical trace links an item to a suspect and the time of an event.
why: Each answer narrows the next question, so the inquiry stays on course.

text: 1) List each event with the time it occurred. 2) Order the events relative to one another. 3) Mark events that fall within the same short window.
when: Several actors acted within a short period and their actions might be related.
why: Ordering events exposes overlaps and sequences that scattered accounts hide.

text: 1) Start from the earliest event that gave the plotters a chance to act. 2) Step forward, noting what information each step needed. 3) Check each step against what they could obtain.
when: Explaining a plot or a criminal's sequence of actions.
why: Ordering the plan reveals which information each step depended on.

text: 1) Establish what the culprit wanted. 2) Read the setting for materials and ignition sources. 3) Order the events from the traces. 4) Weigh each alternative by probability and by the culprit's expectations. 5) Label the result as a theory.
when: physical traces and a known motive together suggest a sequence of events

text: 1) List every fixed date in the timeline. 2) Compare each against records from separate sources. 3) Find the entry that conflicts. 4) Treat that single conflict as the key clue.
when: The mystery depends on who was where and when.
why: A single conflicting date often exposes the whole plan, while one isolated error may be only clerical.

text: 1) Anchor the sequence on checkable facts such as delays, arrival hours or missed connections. 2) Record durations as well as clock times. 3) Note who was awake or present to witness each event. 4) Fix a later known time to anchor the next sequence.
when: A witness's account of timing must be checked against independent facts.
why: Checkable facts and durations create a sequence that can be tested against other accounts.

text: 1) Fix each event to a time source that others can confirm. 2) Lay out each person's day in order, including idle periods. 3) Check the stretch between each pair of anchors for gaps. 4) Compare each alibi with an independent account.
when: the central question is who was where and when
why: gaps and contradictions only show once every stretch is timed

text: 1) Anchor the timeline to a known event. 2) Ask whether an interval exceeded a set duration. 3) Repeat with a larger duration to shrink the window. 4) Test each bracket against the next question.
when: a suspect's presence during a crime window must be established
why: each answer either survives or fails under the next question

text: 1) Confirm the person's real identity through a search. 2) Match a date to a transport or passenger record. 3) Check photographs with people who dealt with them. 4) Assess background traits to judge motive.
when: the case depends on identity or a past connection held only in records
why: each record narrows identity, timing or motive

text: 1) Identify the known start point of a transaction. 2) Count the procedural waiting days. 3) Estimate its status on a given day. 4) Compare it with other events during the waiting period.
when: A suspect's financial or administrative action leaves a trail with known waiting times.
why: Counting from a known start yields a checkable timeline.

text: 1) Start from the last firm account, such as a departure time or stated plan. 2) Infer the likely next event. 3) Check it against independent witnesses. 4) Repeat until the sequence is complete.
when: A suspect's movements are disputed and independent witnesses exist
why: Turns intuition into a checkable sequence of times, places and people

text: 1) Establish the timeline of the event. 2) Check whether the suspect had time to take the clue. 3) If not, look for another person present who could have taken it.
when: When a clue seems to point at one suspect.

text: 1) Establish the timeline of the hours before the event. 2) Identify the window that matters most. 3) Test each candidate theory against that window. 4) Keep the theories that survive.
when: When a hostile or emotional exchange was heard but not fully understood
why: Timeline checks remove theories that conflict with known movements

text: 1) Establish the routine that sets the window of opportunity. 2) Estimate time from physical signs. 3) Compare with known patterns. 4) Check each witness account against the routine.
when: A case depends on who could be present at a specific hour
why: Routines and physical signs constrain when events could have happened.

text: 1) Date each event from records or timestamps. 2) Infer elapsed time from physical signs of change. 3) Order events in sequence. 4) Check each interval against witnesses.
when: when events, witnesses and physical signs must be placed in sequence
why: Combining dated events with physical change gives a sequence no single source provides.

text: 1) List each account's stated times. 2) Overlay the accounts on one timeline. 3) Check whether each witness was placed to hear or see the event. 4) Mark which accounts conflict.
when: several accounts must fit one clock

text: 1) Collect each witness's remembered sounds and their approximate times. 2) Test what could be heard from each location with doors open or shut. 3) Move the event time to the sound that matches what was audible. 4) Check the witness's hearing before relying on her account.
when: Witnesses give approximate times and a remembered sound might be the crime.
why: Audibility tests can show that a recalled sound was the event, not a later one.

text: 1) Record each event with its time and source. 2) Attach a margin to each approximate time. 3) Compare gaps and conflicts between events. 4) Check unusual timings against known routines. 5) Keep the timeline provisional and revise it as facts arrive.
when: Several witnesses give times and events must be put in order.
why: Anchoring events and testing conflicts narrows the window for the act.

text: 1) Start from an undeniable physical fact. 2) Reason backward to the causes that could produce it. 3) Reason forward from motive. 4) Treat the point where both chains meet as the likely truth.
when: The outcome is fixed but its cause is uncertain
why: Agreement between a physical chain and a motive chain narrows the answer.

text: 1) Check each source's own record 2) Confirm that each person did what the cover story claims 3) Seek formal authority only after the checks are complete.
when: an investigator must clear several sources before acting

text: 1) Timestamp every event: letter posting, message relayed, instructions given, warning delivered. 2) Compare the gaps between events. 3) Use the speed of each hop to narrow who could have relayed information.
when: A leak is suspected and events have clock times or dates
why: Gaps between events reveal how information traveled and who had a direct channel

text: 1) Establish the ordinary routine as a baseline. 2) Anchor events to shared time markers that others can check. 3) Record each attempt or event with its time. 4) Cross-check times against a second source.
when: a suspect's account depends on times or relative positions
why: deviations only mean something against a baseline and checked times

text: 1) Collect times from everyone who handled the subject. 2) Mark each time as a last or first sighting. 3) Test the sequence for gaps and contradictions.
when: Establishing when a person was last seen and where they went next.
why: Separate witnesses fix times more firmly than a single source.

text: Recount the whole account in order, fact by fact, to expose weak points in the reasoning.
when: before presenting a solution

text: 1) Fix the witness's last known contact to build a timeline. 2) Check each answer against earlier ones. 3) Ask what the witness expected when they claim ignorance. 4) Press on hesitations before moving on.
when: interviewing a witness who may conceal information
why: A structured timeline exposes gaps and contradictions.

text: 1) List each event with its time or duration. 2) Mark uncertain times as approximate. 3) Note what the witness could not see. 4) Order the events to rule sequences in or out. 5) Add the elapsed time since the event.
when: building a timeline from witness accounts
why: each step keeps the account accurate and bounded

text: 1) Derive the shot's direction from the wound path. 2) Match that angle to a position in the layout that gives the needed height. 3) Test the resulting position against witness timing.
1) Ask each witness who saw whom. 2) Ask what was said. 3) Ask how long it lasted. 4) Ask what happened next. 5) Test each answer against facts already known.
1) Record the state of each observable object at every visit. 2) Compare consecutive states to find what changed. 3) Order the changes, anchoring them to any timed event heard.
when: a witness returns to the same place at intervals
why: changes between visits reveal when events happened

text: 1) Start at the beginning of the case. 2) Present each clue in the order it was found. 3) Label conjectures as conjectures. 4) Confirm or drop each one with later facts. 5) Explain hidden details once their supporting facts are shown.
when: The player has seen the clues and needs them connected

text: 1) Record each trace's position and flow direction. 2) Use gravity to infer the orientation when each formed. 3) Order traces by which overlays which. 4) Check the sequence obeys physical rules.
when: reconstructing what happened to a body
why: traces give a timeline only once ordered and checked

text: 1) Place each known event, including estimated times, on a timeline. 2) Check whether events line up in sequence. 3) Group facts under a plausible motive. 4) Record each reasoning step so it can be tested against each fact.
when: When there are several dated facts and a suspected motive.
why: A timeline and motive organise facts into a testable explanation.

text: 1) List each observed trace. 2) Compare it with the person's usual routine. 3) Record contradictions without forcing a single story. 4) Delay conclusions until enough of the scene is examined.
when: when several traces must be sorted against a known baseline
why: a baseline shows which changes are meaningful

text: 1) Ask the witness for exact times, the sequence of events and who said what. 2) Place each item on a timeline. 3) Anchor each item to a clock time and to independent physical facts. 4) Mark gaps and fill them from other sources.

1) Lay the chart out as a shared reference and trace the claimed route on it. 2) Order dated records into a timeline. 3) Inventory physical traces left behind. 4) Check each trace and environmental variables such as tide against the sequence.
when: when rebuilding a complex, spatial, time-dependent event
why: combining map, dates and damage tests a claimed sequence from several sides

text: 1) Write each step of a witness account in order with its time. 2) Check every step against the others for consistency. 3) Flag steps that rest on only one source.
when: Reconstructing what happened from one or more accounts.
why: Each step can be tested against the rest, exposing gaps or contradictions.

text: 1) List ordinary records such as logbooks, consumed supplies and deliveries. 2) Date each record. 3) Cross-check each against the others and the witness accounts. 4) Note what the timeline does not prove.
when: a case depends on where people were and when
why: independent routine records corroborate or contradict witness accounts

text: 1) Find an object or mark that does not fit the expected scene. 2) Match it to a likely source. 3) Rebuild the sequence step by step, checking that each action explains the next trace.
when: Reconstructing events from small remnants
why: Each step must be consistent with the physical record

text: 1) Establish when writing or tearing happened. 2) Establish when cleaning happened. 3) Establish when scraps were disposed of. 4) Confirm the order with a witness account.
when: Reconstructing what was discarded from a tidied scene.

text: 1) List each dated event with its source. 2) Anchor the sequence on fixed checkpoints such as a stopped watch, a departure time or a medical window. 3) Place each undated event in the only interval consistent with all constraints. 4) Test the derived sequence for contradictions.
when: several events carry times from different sources that must be reconciled
why: checkpoints give a fixed frame, and a derived time is credible only if it fits everything else

text: 1) Reconstruct the victim, household, evening, doctor's visit, morning discovery and inquest, in that order. 2) Note the gaps where the order breaks down.
when: building a case from witness accounts

text: 1) List every fixed point the timeline assumes. 2) Ask which one could be wrong. 3) Propose an alternative window that fits both accounts. 4) Check that window against witnesses before discarding the original timeline.
when: Two testimonies seem to conflict about when an event happened

text: 1) Identify the last firm sighting of each person. 2) Check each clock and routine against it. 3) Place medical and physical findings within the resulting window.
when: the order of events matters and clocks disagree
why: A fixed reference point anchors the rest.

text: 1) Fix an exact time for the key meeting. 2) Place each person's route around that time. 3) Check that each stage can be confirmed by someone.
when: several people claim to be in different places
why: A fixed time and a documented route make claims testable.

text: 1) Collect time-stamped statements from independent witnesses. 2) Convert medical estimates into time windows. 3) Check which events fit inside the windows. 4) Flag any event that fits none as unexplained and explain it separately.
why: Events that fit no window must not be forced into the timeline.

text: 1) Pin down the key time points: when a sound was heard, when the body was found, when death was estimated. 2) Mark the gaps between them. 3) Test each account against those gaps.
when: Several accounts of who was where conflict
why: Ordering events exposes which alibis clash and which can be set aside

text: 1) Collect dated objects and records. 2) Set each event's possible window. 3) Compare expert estimates with the dates. 4) List rival explanations side by side against the timeline.
when: several events must be placed in order
why: the combined timeline tests which explanations fit

text: 1) Let each witness give their account in their own words first. 2) Compare accounts covering the same movements. 3) Anchor memories to datable events. 4) Narrow a time window using several estimates. 5) Mark agreements, conflicts and silences.
when: When a single witness's time is vague or several sources must form one sequence
why: Unprompted accounts avoid shaping, and comparison exposes what is reliable

text: 1) List every handoff of the item in order. 2) Time how long each holder had it alone. 3) Identify each person who could see each handoff. 4) Check each observer's sightline against the room layout.
when: Investigating who could have tampered with an item or dose.
why: Summaries of access can hide short or wider windows, so each handoff must be timed and each observer identified.

text: 1) Anchor the timeline to the most regular daily events, such as meals and departures. 2) Have the witness recount the day in order without skipping stretches. 3) Mark the last confirmed sighting. 4) Mark the first unexplained gap. 5) Record each time as a range, not a single point.
when: Reconstructing when a person left, where they went, and when they were due back.
why: Routine events give reliable timestamps, and ranges absorb recall drift.

text: 1) Track each NPC's location and actions over time. 2) Let the player compare claimed movements against that record. 3) Use mismatches to expose opportunity.
when: Designing an investigation where a character's opportunity is tested.
why: Players can only check alibis if the world records where characters were.

text: 1) Identify each time's source and known error. 2) Correct each reading by its offset. 3) Anchor the sequence to a fixed reference time. 4) Check adjusted times against independent sightings. 5) Record every correction.
when: several sources give disagreeing times, or cause and effect order matters
why: Corrected, cross-checked times let someone else verify the chain

text: 1) Attach a witness's vague date to a fixed public event. 2) Ask whether they accept that anchor as close enough. 3) Use the anchored date to order other events.
when: The witness needs to place an event in time and the event is recent enough for a public anchor to exist.
why: Fixed events give vague memories a reference point that can be checked.

text: 1) Record each known event with its time. 2) Note which periods each observer covered. 3) Narrow the window to uncovered intervals. 4) Mark hours without cover for evidence from elsewhere.
when: several people had chances to act at different times
why: Coverage rules out action during watched periods, leaving a smaller window.

text: 1) Collect a record of each movement, such as tickets, luggage labels, routine patterns, and transport bookings. 2) Order the movements by time. 3) Check each time reading against the clock or source that produced it. 4) Build the sequence only from readings that pass the check.
when: When a case depends on the order and timing of movements
why: A sequence built on a single unverified time reading can point to a false conclusion

text: 1) Build a timeline of events and object states. 2) Record each state change. 3) Design each false testimony detail as a visible inconsistency against the timeline.
when: Authoring a mystery with testimony that players can check.
why: A timeline gives players a fixed reference to catch false details.

text: 1) List every timed event from testimony in order. 2) Overlay the events to narrow the window of the crime. 3) Use fixed departure or arrival times as boundaries. 4) Eliminate routes that conflict with the timeline.
when: A time of death or crime is disputed and testimony gives times

text: 1) Map each witness's position. 2) Check what that position could hear, given distance, stairs and closed doors. 3) Place each sound in sequence against the others. 4) Explain any unexpected silence.
when: the sequence of events depends on what people heard
why: Positions limit what each witness could have perceived

text: 1) Mark known gaps and environmental conditions as fixed boundaries. 2) Place each act inside the window those boundaries allow. 3) Test each act against all windows in sequence, not from a preferred conclusion.
when: several acts depend on timed conditions
why: placing acts without testing them can hide conflicts between windows

text: Build the timeline from fixed household routines, such as a set breakfast hour, a daily wake-up call, or a habitual walk, to serve as reference points.
when: People follow predictable daily habits
why: Routines give checkable times against which claims can be measured

text: 1) Record and order by time every timed event, including handovers, notes, arrivals and independent arrival and departure records. 2) Mark each person's movements on the timeline. 3) Find unwatched windows, such as a visitor no one can place in a crowd. 4) For each window, list who could have been present and who has no confirmed location.
when: when several people have overlapping, unverified movements, or when reconstructing who was where during an incident
why: Unwatched windows are where an alibi or act can hide, so mapping them focuses the investigation; independent records anchor the timeline so gaps stand out.

text: 1) Fix the deadline or anchor time, such as a departure. 2) Estimate each leg's minimum duration, including any required wait, and set a maximum for each travel duration. 3) Subtract the legs from the deadline to find the latest start. 4) Subtract every delay from the remaining margin.
when: when an event is tied to a fixed time and place, or several events must line up around a fixed time such as a train or rendezvous
why: Counting backward reveals whether the plan is feasible and how much margin remains for delays.

text: 1) Recreate the original conditions: exact positions and props, temperature, locks, latches, who is present or asleep, and what could be heard. 2) Act out the disputed steps. 3) Time each step.
when: when a claim about access, timing or audibility is disputed
why: Reenactment is valid only when conditions match; small changes in positions or props can alter what is heard or seen.

text: 1) Anchor each witness account to an approximate time or nearby identifiable event, such as a noise, departure or arrival. 2) Place the accounts in order. 3) Check each against the others to test alibis and sightings.
when: when a witness cannot state the exact time, or witness times are approximate and must be compared
why: Relative order can be fixed from anchored events, and ordered anchors reveal which accounts agree and which conflict.

text: 1) Take the witness's account of activities. 2) Tie each activity to a set hour. 3) Test each timed point against an independent source.
when: A witness gives a sequence of activities.
why: Anchoring each activity to a time makes gaps and contradictions visible.

text: 1) Fix the stages of an event in order. 2) Place each witness's claimed actions within those stages. 3) Compare the placements for gaps or mismatches.
when: when several witnesses describe one evening or event
why: Order exposes an account that does not fit.

text: 1) Establish the order of events, such as the crime first and the cleanup after. 2) Note which cleanup method was chosen at each step. 3) Use each step to narrow the set of possible culprits.
1) List each person involved. 2) Fix each person's time and place using calls, memos, or guard logs as time-stamped witnesses. 3) Cross-check each claim against a first-hand source.
when: A case depends on who was where between two known times
why: Time-stamped records make alibis checkable

text: 1) Log each event with its time. 2) Require the player to place events in order. 3) Accept an alibi as confirmed only after the order holds.
when: Designing a timeline-based puzzle
why: Ordering checks make alibis testable

text: 1) Note the time of waking. 2) Estimate time lost to sleep. 3) Cross-check against routine events, such as a recurring noise at a fixed hour, to bound the sequence.
when: reconstructing when events occurred during the night
why: routine markers give independent anchors for uncertain time

text: 1) Separate what the witness saw from what they heard reported. 2) Cross-check the fragments against other witnesses and dated records. 3) Order the events using outside references.
when: Rebuilding a sequence of events from a partial witness account.
why: Independent references keep a timeline from relying on one unreliable memory.

text: 1) Record the time of each event from a clock or in-game timestamp. 2) Place each claimed urgency on that timeline. 3) Note any gap between claimed urgency and elapsed time.
when: Testing a witness's sequence of events or claim of urgency.
why: A gap between a claimed emergency and the clock is a signal worth noting.

text: 1) Fix a clock time for each event. 2) Measure the intervals between events. 3) Compare each person's claimed whereabouts against the timeline. 4) Re-check the account wherever an interval is tight.
when: Several statements about the same period must be checked against one another
why: Short intervals often decide whether an alibi holds

text: 1) Mark statements that lack dates. 2) Order them using other dated records. 3) Compare each witness's earlier and later accounts to find when and how they changed.
when: undated testimony

text: 1) Fix each dated entry as a point on the timeline. 2) Pair parallel records from different offices to see both sides of a dispute. 3) Check names against original documents for clerk errors. 4) Mark outcomes missing from the record. 5) Use a later account only after checking its author's position.
when: a key outcome is missing from official records
why: Dated fragments from several sources can be ordered into a sequence even when one outcome is unknown.

text: 1) List every accusation with its date. 2) Record its target and order. 3) Compare the sequence against who gained from each step. 4) Judge whether the pattern suggests planning.
when: Testing whether accusers acted in concert
why: Ordered timelines reveal planning that single events hide.

text: 1) Date the earlier connection. 2) Link it to the later outcome. 3) Note each figure's official position. 4) Note new authorities' arrival and first impressions. 5) Date the setup and start of any institution. 6) Record its proceedings and any later suppression. 7) Compare key figures' later views with earlier conduct.
when: an outcome may have roots in earlier events
why: ordering the stages shows how one stage enabled the next

text: 1) Record a witness's claim with its time before any confirmation arrives. 2) Wait for independent news of the event. 3) Compare the claimed time with the confirmed event time.
when: testing a witness's account of a distant or hidden event
why: Early written records prevent a match being fitted after the fact.

text: 1) Record each threat, later harm and recovery with its date. 2) Order the events. 3) Check whether each recovery lines up with an event or with a natural cause.
when: when reconstructing a sequence from testimony with uncertain dates
why: Ordering events makes it possible to test which cause fits the timing.

text: 1) Measure how much flows in a set time. 2) Adjust the flow restriction until the target duration matches. 3) Repeat calibration before relying on the device.
when: a timer depends on a fixed flow rate
why: the flow must match the intended duration

text: 1) Identify the source of the materials. 2) Infer the tools from the cut and residue marks. 3) Note any gaps where the maker resorted to a fallback. 4) Read placement and disguise to infer state of mind. 5) Record null results. 6) Weigh competing readings by likelihood.
when: A physical artifact is the main clue and its making can be reconstructed
why: Working backward from the object to its production yields evidence about the maker, their tools and their conditions

text: 1) List the chain of events that had to follow the event in question. 2) Note each delay between them. 3) Subtract the delays backward from the moment of the later event. 4) Use the result to fix when the event occurred.
when: Establishing the time of an event from later records
why: Each required step bounds how early the event could have happened

text: 1) Anchor each event to a shared public clock reference, such as a striking clock. 2) Place events relative to the last recognised strike. 3) Order arrivals and departures from those fixed points.
when: when witness times are vague and a shared public clock is available
why: Shared references let separate accounts be combined into one sequence.

text: 1) Identify the record the claim implies, such as a payment date tied to a scheduled event. 2) Check the date against that record. 3) Confirm with a source separate from the claimant.
when: when a suspect or witness gives a timed account
why: Records the claimant does not control give an independent test of the claim.

text: 1) Record when each character was known to be in each place. 2) Check whether each event was possible given those positions. 3) Note which knowledge each character had at each time.
when: Testing who could have been present at an event
why: Timelines built on incomplete knowledge of movements can mislead

text: 1) List each outflow with its recipient and amount. 2) Sum the list. 3) Compare the total with cash still held. 4) Use any difference to check or infer missing payments.
when: A timeline depends on many small transactions that are easy to forget one by one.
why: Summing recalled payments against remaining cash gives a rough cross-check on memory.

text: 1) List departure and arrival times for each leg of the journey. 2) Note every stop and its time. 3) Estimate the arrival at the final location. 4) Confirm the hour with an independent source.
when: when reconstructing a person's movements or an alibi
why: Chained times expose impossibilities, and an independent source confirms the reconstruction.

text: 1) Fix the central date from an external record. 2) Link any false statement to that date to test whether it was prepared in advance. 3) Use a stated hour and place to narrow the window. 4) Treat absence of later sightings as evidence. 5) Label the working conclusion as belief until proven.
when: Several dated facts can be checked against each other.
why: Records outside any one memory make a timeline testable and resistant to a single witness's errors.

text: 1) Anchor each event to a routine such as meals, shift changes or timetables. 2) Check any clock that may be unreliable before use. 3) Mark spans with no sighting as windows to explain. 4) Check each source against the others before accepting it.
when: A claim about the time of an event is needed to test an alibi or movement.
why: Routines give more trustworthy anchors than estimated hours, and unreliable clocks can mislead the whole reconstruction.

text: 1) Log each dated, specific sighting. 2) Look for a repeated pattern. 3) Form a candidate explanation that fits the pattern.
when: Investigators must reconstruct an unexplained behaviour.
why: Dated repetition turns scattered observations into evidence.

text: 1) List the stated schedule. 2) Gather independent facts such as letters, sightings and hiding places. 3) Order them to reveal the hidden sequence. 4) Check each step against a witness or trace.
when: Reconstructing a suspect's true whereabouts
why: Independent facts reveal gaps that a stated schedule conceals

text: 1) Fix anchor times from each account. 2) Record observation conditions such as light and distance. 3) Compare routes and streets. 4) Check whether the parties saw each other. 5) Test each admission for new timeline gaps.

1) Anchor events to marked times. 2) Fix each person's state, awake or asleep, and location. 3) Compare witnesses' accounts for conflicts. 4) Discount sensory reports made in fear, fatigue or poor visibility.
when: when several people were present at different points in a night
why: Timed anchors and fixed positions make alibis checkable

text: 1) Fix when each person arrived, was last seen, and was heard. 2) Identify the last confirmed presence of the victim. 3) Check each account against independent facts. 4) Note gaps where attention was distracted.
when: Multi-witness cases with a time-bounded window.
why: A timeline anchored to fixed points lets each account be tested.

text: 1) Anchor the timeline with fixed events such as telegrams, departures, deaths, and clock times. 2) Measure distances and travel times between places. 3) Compare arrival and departure times across the whole route.
when: Several people give times for overlapping events.
why: Fixed events and measured travel make claimed presence testable.

text: 1) Note timed events such as clock strikes and recurring sounds. 2) Check physical markers, such as seals, each morning. 3) Compare markers across rooms to see whether a disturbance stayed in one place. 4) Check the timeline against the markers before trusting any account, including your own.
when: Deciding whether an intruder was human
why: Physical markers that persist provide an objective check on recollection.

text: 1) Start with the earliest documented event. 2) Add each dated item in order, recording its author, date and claim. 3) Note the gaps between items, since short and long intervals show urgency and hesitation. 4) Test later claims against the line. 5) Mark missing dates rather than filling them with assumptions.
when: when a case depends on who knew what and when
why: A single ordered line exposes contradictions and gaps that scattered records hide.

text: 1) Record each person's movements as times and places. 2) Overlay them on the moment of the event. 3) Mark the windows when each person could have reached the object or room.
when: Several people claim different whereabouts and the event depends on who could reach a place
why: A time-ordered record exposes who could have acted and when an object could have been moved

text: 1) Normalize all event dates to one calendar, adjusting for time-zone or date-line offsets. 2) Place events from separate sources on one timeline. 3) Look for several independent matches within a window.
when: When clues from several locations must be compared by date.
why: A date recorded on different sides of a date line can be a day off, so unnormalized dates create or hide coincidences.

text: 1) Fix a few checkable clock times for key events, such as arrival, departure, a celestial cue and a deadline. 2) Leave other times vague. 3) Use the anchors to verify the sequence of events.
when: Timed ordeal or investigation where an alibi window or deadline matters
why: Few firm times keep the sequence verifiable without dulling the scene

text: Treat a reenactment as evidence of what is possible, not proof of what happened; urgency and vivid performance can make a plan feel more convincing than the evidence supports.
when: A theory has been tested by reenactment under time pressure, or a reconstructed sequence is offered as an explanation of events.
why: A plausible route does not establish that the suspect took it; vivid performance feels like confirmation even when it only shows what is possible.

text: Every step and witness time must agree with the rest, since one conflicting window or time can shift or break the whole timeline.
when: Several witnesses give times for the same events.
why: Inconsistent times can shift the whole timeline.

text: Record each time's source and reliability: discount times recalled from memory and trust times tied to something the witness saw or heard; ask how they know a time.
when: when a witness gives a time
why: Approximate or memory-based times can shift an apparent sequence; the basis of a time shows its reliability.

text: Do not rest a timeline on one interested or single witness; require independent corroboration from clocks, objects or other people, since one mistaken or biased witness can distort the sequence.
when: when a key sequence depends on a single account
why: Without a second source, one mistaken or biased witness can distort the whole sequence.

text: Let players fill a timeline board from partial clue cards, checking placements against in-game schedules and checkpoints drawn from watches or schedules.
Let players rebuild events from scattered or timestamped receipts, travel records and witness sightings; a late-discovered record can re-date the plot, forcing revised theories.
when: when designing deduction puzzles
why: Re-dating makes earlier conclusions revisable and rewards careful reconstruction.

text: Merge NPC accounts into one timeline and show gaps between confirmed events, highlighting where an NPC could have acted unseen.
when: when building a mystery with multiple NPC witnesses or player-facing investigation tools
why: Gaps in shared knowledge create investigation targets.

text: Give NPCs timestamped schedules and logged sightings; players build a clock from statements and cross-check each against another NPC's schedule to find the one who could not have been present.
when: when designing a mystery with multiple suspects
why: Consistent, time-stamped data lets players test contradictions and verify a reasoning path.

text: Model travel distances and fixed travel times between map locations, with dated messages from distant NPCs, so players can test whether a claimed route or alibi is physically possible.
when: when designing movement or NPC alibis between locations
why: Impossible travel exposes false alibis; known travel times make a claimed movement checkable.

text: Do not treat the order of any stretch a witness cannot recall as certain; record the witness's inability to fix a time as information.
when: when a witness reports an unrecalled gap

text: Attach to each timeline step its named time source and supporting proof, such as documents or notes, so every interval can be checked on its own.
when: when reconstructing a sequence of past events
why: An interval with no stated reference cannot be checked by anyone; attached proof lets each link be checked rather than trusted as a whole story.

text: Store each timeline event with its source tag and reliability, so first-hand reports, relayed reports and physical traces are weighed separately rather than treated as equally trustworthy.
when: when witnesses are scarce or their accounts overlap only partly
why: Sources differ in how directly they observed events, so their reliability differs.

text: Store event time ranges and flag conflicting times, such as two NPC witnesses' accounts, as a visible puzzle the player must resolve with another source.
when: when two NPCs give conflicting times
why: An unresolved conflict drives the player to seek more evidence.

text: Ask for exact times: when an event ended, how long a person was away, and whether they had returned before the next event began.
when: When an alibi depends on intervals
why: Precise intervals are needed to measure whether a trip fits

text: Keep the seal and the crime separate in time; a seal applied afterwards can be an afterthought that does not reflect the event.
In a timed travel system, record each leg and place an NPC witness at each stop who can confirm that leg.
When a predicted time and a recorded time disagree, look for a source of error before trusting either figure.
Provide a field-notes journal that logs observations as facts and a timeline of movements, so the player can check who was where and when.
when: Designing a game where the player gathers and interprets observations
why: Separating logged facts from interpretation lets the player build their own conclusions

text: State a concrete deadline early and repeat it, so every later delay carries a cost.
when: an action or investigation must feel urgent
why: Repetition keeps the clock visible throughout the story

text: Record your own path before examining tracks, so your disturbances are not mistaken for evidence.
when: Investigating a scene with soft ground
why: Own movement can overwrite or add prints

text: After a clock correction removes a contradiction, re-test the corrected timeline against the other facts rather than treating it as proof of the favoured explanation.
why: a resolved conflict does not confirm the investigator's preferred story

text: Delay sensitive reveals, such as an accusation, until the required evidence is in the player's log.
when: when a reveal would be unfair if made early
why: Evidence should precede the accusation so the player can verify it.

text: Author the event timeline so that every trace is explicable by some sequence of actions.
when: Designing a crime with physical evidence
why: Unexplained traces make the solution feel unfair

text: Test a disputed movement by reenacting it with a person of similar height and weight over the same ground.
when: The physical feasibility of a movement is contested.
why: A reenactment shows whether the movement is actually possible.

text: Do not treat the authority that orders an action, such as issuing a warrant, as the same authority that decides on it, such as judging the case.
why: Different roles in one process carry different responsibility for a failure.

text: Generate timing coincidences as background noise, so players learn that a single timing match does not prove intent.
why: noise teaches players to weigh coincidence correctly

text: Make the date of a watched event visible to the player so they can plan around it.
For a puzzle that asks players to reconstruct events, let them replay a suspect's path and have the game check whether the timing fits.
when: when designing a deduction puzzle with a timed sequence
why: timed replay turns the player's theory into a testable check

text: Let a clock, timer or valve in a level show a state the player must explain, such as stopped while still holding stored run.
when: designing an environmental clue

text: Encode a timeline in physical state: soot, a burnt-down candle, a bullet hole, a casing and footprints each reveal a different time or position.
why: Each prop then gives the player a separate clue to the sequence.

text: Let NPC witnesses supply timing details, so players verify a document's date by questioning them rather than being told by a narrator.
Use stopped clocks, NPC routines and staged scenes to create a timeline the player must reconstruct from clues.
when: designing timed investigation content
why: Players then build the sequence of events themselves.

text: Store each stage of a faction's history as a timeline event so players can rebuild the causal order from in-game records.
when: generating or authoring faction histories

text: Ask players to order a set of events and identify the single event that changes the plan.
when: Designing a puzzle or challenge built on a sequence of events.
why: Ordering requires players to reason about cause, sequence and consequence.

text: Design a reclassification step in which secondary traces, such as residue or lock marks, reverse the first reading of a scene.
when: a scene looks like one kind of event
why: contradicting traces should overturn a surface reading

text: Give time-of-death estimates as ranges rather than exact times, so the timeline remains a problem the player must solve.
when: when a game reports a death time to the player
why: Exact times would remove the deduction work

text: Make an unexplained interval in a level's timeline a lead that players can investigate in the world.
when: designing movement or timeline puzzles
why: Players can pursue gaps through locations and encounters

text: Design timestamp puzzles in which door logs, patrol routes or burn times must be reconciled, and each claimed action must fit the available minutes.
when: Designing a time-based deduction puzzle.
why: Players can then catch impossible accounts through arithmetic.

text: If in-world clocks drift, give players a calibration method such as a watch or sundial before timestamps on notes or witness statements can be trusted.
when: Designing time-based clues in a world with unreliable clocks.
why: Players need a reference to correct timestamps.

text: Give the world a clock and log each NPC's position against it, and make physical states such as a warm corpse or a dry puddle readable clocks the player can inspect.
when: designing evidence the player uses to infer time
why: readable physical state lets the player bound events without witnesses

text: Build a fair timeline puzzle from a table of timestamped events that the player compares against witnesses' differing clocks.
Show two characters at different times, and reward a player who notices they were never present together.
when: designing a character who may be one person in disguise

text: Official or public records, such as a published timetable, can fix the timeline accounts must match, yet official times can be hasty, so check them against physical signs.
when: accounts disagree about timing, or when reviewing an official report
why: Public records are independent of witnesses, but official conclusions may not match physical evidence.

text: If the item was already owned, tracing it to its owner is less likely; if the method came first, the item must be sought and the search leaves traces.
Anchor the timeline to fixed, objective times where available, such as a stated departure or arrival, and check witness accounts and other evidence against them, since memory shifts more easily.
when: When a person's timeline is central to the case.
why: Fixed times are harder to shift than memory, so a precise anchor makes contradictions in other evidence visible.

text: Tie a witness's own movements to checkable details such as clocks, bells or purchases, so staff can confirm them and the reveal is fair.
Chain timed events in order, so each confirmed time anchors the next claim.

1) Fix the date of the last confirmed sighting. 2) Place later events such as deliveries, sales and visits against it. 3) Check each claimed later sighting for travel time and physical feasibility. 4) Note who benefits if the date is moved.
when: When a disappearance or death depends on a date.
why: Exposes sightings that are impossible or staged to shift suspicion.

text: 1) List each witness's claimed times for one event. 2) Place all claims on one shared clock. 3) Mark the gaps and conflicts between them; these are the first leads to pursue.
when: Several accounts of one event must be reconciled

text: Store an event timeline the player can check against NPC statements, so a shifting date becomes a detectable contradiction.
Use dates and relationships as checkable facts, so the player can test a confession against the timeline.
when: A story reveal depends on a past connection between characters.
why: Testable facts let players verify a confession and feel the reveal is earned.

text: Give a late return a route and reason that players can check, so the return can clear a suspect as well as condemn them.
A time written in a message gives a fixed point for ordering the events around it.
A sudden physical sign with a timestamp, such as an animal's paralysis, can narrow a timeline and confirm an earlier suspicion.
when: A health change in a person or animal is observed
why: A dated onset places an event within a known window

text: Tying a mismatch to a timestamp lets players date the clean-up against other events.
Give each timestamp a source, such as a watch or chime, so the reader can test it.
when: Presenting times as evidence in a mystery.
why: A time with no stated source cannot be checked, so it cannot support a deduction.

text: Pair a clue with a timeline stamp, such as an arrival date, so players combine two weak facts into a reliable inference.
Give notes and letters in the game world timestamps and copy counts so players can build a timeline from paperwork.
when: Designing in-world documents for a mystery
why: Paperwork then becomes a checkable timeline source

text: A timestamped check-in or arrival record brackets where a person must have been after a given event.
Store NPC and witness claims as timestamped statements so players can line up accounts, assemble a timeline, and spot agreements, contradictions, or unverifiable claims.
when: Designing testimony or witness data for a game or timeline puzzle
why: Timestamps let statements be compared automatically or by the player, and make contradictions findable.

text: Anchor an account with precise clock times and durations between events, so readers can rebuild the order and pace of what happened.
when: when readers must trust the sequence of events

text: Store NPC alibis as timestamped events that the player checks against a shared time window.
when: designing suspect alibis

text: Provide a timestamped log or journal so the player can catch a false claim about when something happened.
when: Designing clues that test a player's reasoning about timing.
why: Recorded times give the player a fixed reference to contradict claims.

text: Approximate witness times and stated durations are soft and may be wrong or deliberately low; walking or travel estimates often underestimate, so carry a margin of uncertainty unless measured.
when: A timeline depends on approximate witness times or stated durations.
why: Poor measurement conditions and approximate recollections vary widely and can hide gaps that matter to an alibi.

text: Precise timing turns vague claims into checkable facts, because a measured duration can be tested against a known limit.
when: A claim depends on how long something lasted

text: Times resting on one witness's watch or memory are weak; check them against a second independent device or record that could corroborate or contradict them.
when: A timeline rests on one witness's account.
why: A second independent source can confirm or break the claim.

text: A fair-play timing twist misreads trusted witnesses and a visible object until a late reinterpretation reverses the apparent timeline.
A small error in one witness's time spreads through every timeline built on it, shifting the whole sequence enough to clear or implicate someone.
If no event follows the deadline, the countdown goes slack and tension collapses.
Presenting a time of death as a single point rather than a range overstates the precision of the estimate.
One small detail, such as who knocked at a door or who set down an object, can carry the timing of a whole episode.
when: Reconstructing a sequence of events
why: Minor actions often serve as the hinges of a timeline

text: Mark vague times as soft and precise times from reliable sources as firm, and keep the two categories separate in the record.
Check how long a sound lasted and how far it could carry before accepting a timing claim.
when: a witness gives an exact time for a sound
why: Duration and range limit when a sound could be placed

text: Measure an interval from a clearly defined start event to a clearly defined end event.
when: Timing an action for a rule check

text: Compare a measured duration with the rule's limit; any interval beyond the limit is a breach of that rule.
when: Checking a time-limited rule

text: Timing of actions close to a key or scheduled event can suggest a motive linked to that event, such as acts on the eve of a planned departure.
when: when a sequence of actions follows a key occurrence or a behaviour coincides with a scheduled event
why: Timing links the actions to the event or expectation that prompted them

text: Keep the timeline separate from the question of motive. An opportunity window alone does not identify who acted.
when: when a suspect has access but no clear reason to act
why: Access and motive must both be established to point at one person.

text: Check the timing of a lawful act: a legitimate duty performed at the wrong moment can displace a more important one and hide a harmful purpose.
when: judging a suspect's alibi or errand

text: When a death falls on a date the victim had feared or announced, check the coincidence against the rest of the evidence rather than treating it as confirmation.
when: When a death matches a previously stated fear or prediction.
why: A matching date is striking but does not establish cause.

text: Coincidences occur by chance, so a single timing match does not prove deception or intent; treat it as suggestive until tested, keeping a deadline-created motive separate from proof.
why: Chance produces many matches, so one match is expected by chance

text: Timing alone does not prove intent; a replacement or change can be innocent even when it coincides with a suspicious event.
Timing evidence alone rarely proves an alibi or route: it sets limits other facts must fit, so corroborate any timed result before trusting it.
when: A timing result is used as evidence.
why: Time windows constrain without establishing presence or absence, and one measurement can mislead without corroborating evidence.

text: Time each arrest after enough evidence and suspicion have built, so the group's distrust matures before it is used.
A dated, repeating pattern gives the audience a clock, so they can predict the next event and feel the timing of the threat.
when: a recurring threat appears on a schedule
why: Predictable intervals make the audience anticipate the next event and feel tension.

text: A timing link or match alone is weak evidence: it suggests a connection without proving one, and witness uncertainty and reporting-chain time reckoning limit its value.
Timing logic can point suspicion at a witness; a sworn denial must be checked against evidence rather than dismissed or accepted by default.
why: A plausible sequence can be wrong even when it singles out someone.

text: A timing estimate is only as reliable as its assumed burn rates and the weather conditions it assumes.
why: wrong rates or conditions shift the estimated duration

text: 1) Fix the event time from objects still in place, such as cards on a table or unmoved chairs. 2) Use a suspect's departure as the boundary after which he could not have acted. 3) Narrow the window to the interval between these markers.
when: An event must be timed from a scene
why: Unchanged objects record the moment the scene was last left alone.

text: An accusation, warrant, arrest and examination can all occur within a single night, so a false accusation can escalate very quickly.
Establish the order in which people were woken and where they went first, since that sequence reveals who was alerted.
when: reconstructing a night's events

text: When a witness cannot supply key timing facts, question the people who handled transport or logistics, since they may give more direct evidence.
when: Timing facts are needed and the peripheral witnesses are unhelpful.
why: People directly involved in logistics tend to know schedules and timings more precisely.

text: Payment for a shady arrangement is typically made in advance, before the outcome, when the payer can no longer back out.
when: Assessing when a covert payment is likely to occur
why: Paying early locks in the agreement and reduces the payer's option to withdraw

text: Being woken abruptly can be a timing clue suggesting that another party acted at a specific moment.
when: when a character's sleep is interrupted during an event
why: The interruption fixes when outside action occurred

text: Estimate how long a cause needs to act, using a comparable test, and count that delay when placing events; an apparently late event may have begun earlier.
when: an event's timing depends on how long a cause takes to take effect
why: a cause may act slowly, so the observed time is not the start time

text: A locked door explained too quickly loses its tension, so an unexplained cause should stay open for a while.
why: Premature explanation removes the uncertainty that drives the scene.

text: Acting early against a small agent lets the larger figure escape.
Reading a room too quickly causes obvious traces in plain sight to be missed.
Delivering news in a way that signals its significance can alert the suspect before the planned moment.
Let an informant's stated fatigue limit how many questions can be asked in one session.
when: When designing an informant scene

text: A surprise arrest while the suspect is off-guard leaves no time for a prepared defence, but acting on presumption alone risks a wrongful arrest that cannot be undone.
when: when deciding whether to arrest before evidence is complete
why: Speed favours the investigator only when the evidence is already sound.

text: Acting at once keeps momentum but risks rushed conclusions; a reflective pause yields clearer reasoning but can invite wild guesses while it lasts.
when: choosing between immediate action and reconsidering an open case

text: Witness tone, confidence, stammer or attitude is not evidence: a stiff or evasive manner is not proof of guilt, and sincere protest can sway listeners even after gaps are exposed.
why: Attitude changes reflect feeling, not facts; a reader's judgment of tone can stand in for evidence, so conclusions about people can outrun what was observed.

text: A disguised speaker's ironic or mocking remark can betray their identity to someone who knows their manner of speech.
when: a disguised character speaks
why: Habitual tone and wit persist beneath a disguise.

text: Alternate light and grim scenes; abrupt contrast, such as a calm domestic scene followed by violent news or banter followed by grim news, heightens tension and keeps the audience unsettled.
when: When pacing a sequence of scenes or moving a scene from relaxed to ominous.
why: Contrast with the prior mood sharpens the impact of the next discovery or news, and abrupt tonal change keeps the audience uneasy.

text: Letters or journal entries can change wording with an NPC's mood, so players learn to read tone and omission as clues.
when: Designing written NPC communication.

text: Use a change in dialogue tone as a tell the player tracks over time, not as a fixed verdict.
when: Designing NPC reactions as clues
why: A tell suggests a question without settling it.

text: Following a grave scene with a light one sets expectations for tone and hints at character stakes such as financial strain.
Firmness draws out evasive answers but can close a witness down; a friendlier tone and questions about the past draw out a holding-back suspect's background. Use firmness only for evasion.
when: A witness refuses to answer or talks around a matter; a suspect is holding back on a topic.
why: Firmness signals that evasion will be noticed, but it can also end cooperation.

text: 1) Record the regular pattern of the impression. 2) Infer the tool shape that could leave it. 3) Collect each candidate object, such as a boot or horseshoe. 4) Compare each directly against the impression. 5) Confirm or exclude each, linking a match to a specific item and owner.
when: When an impression or indentation may identify a tool, object or person.
why: Matching a pattern to a source converts an unexplained mark into evidence.

text: Do not read a physical mark as a sign of a specific cause until ordinary explanations are ruled out, since innocent events and many people can leave the same mark.
when: When a physical mark is found on an object or surface and used to attribute a cause.
why: Many common marks have ordinary explanations that look identical to the sought sign.

text: Silence can be read as honour or as evasion, and which reading prevails often depends on who speaks for it.
A physical mark's color, size and shape may be redescribed as time passes, so later descriptions are less reliable than first observations.
when: When a mark is recorded days or weeks after it was first seen.
why: Memory and suggestion reshape descriptions as the mark changes or is discussed.

text: An expert can identify a tool by a peculiar nick in its blade and its dimensions, linking it to earlier crimes with the same tool.
when: A tool mark at a scene is compared with marks from other scenes.
why: Distinctive wear on a tool leaves a repeatable signature in the marks it makes.

text: A strong physical trace links a body, object or location to a place that the accepted account rules out.
A specialist can infer the instrument that made a mark, and the skill behind it, from the shape and placement of the damage.
A soft surface such as snow keeps a record of movement, including who passed, in what order, how fast and where people hesitated.
when: The ground holds fresh soft impressions.
why: Soft materials deform under weight, preserving traces of passage.

text: A mark pressed into a surface can identify the object that made it, such as a cap's peak impressed in brushed snow.
Dry, hard ground often fails to hold tyre impressions, so tracks cannot be read there.
when: Reading vehicle tracks across a surface.

text: Marks left on an object can show it was opened with an improvised tool rather than the one a witness would expect.
when: when a witness describes how an object was opened
why: Tool marks carry evidence of method that witnesses may not have observed.
