text: Magnification reveals structure only when the observer knows which features separate one candidate cause from another.
A crossed-out entry can be the only trace of a fact, and the struck line can reveal what an official tried to correct or hide.
Walls, gates, wells, trees and roads keep traces of old boundaries, which can be compared with deed descriptions.
when: Deed bounds must be checked against the ground
why: Physical features can preserve the location of boundaries recorded in old documents

text: Physical marks on a surface, such as a blade scrape on a door panel, are concrete evidence, while stories about the place are legend.
Odours and residues persist in rooms and on clothing, so they mark where a person has been.
Objects keep impressions, stains and fresh marks that can show posture, recent handling and what happened in a room.
Reversed impressions left on absorbent blotting paper can be read in a mirror, revealing writing from a sheet that was pressed against it.
Count a gap as meaningful only if the record was meant to hold that entry.
when: A record is incomplete and the missing part might matter.
why: Ordinary gaps are otherwise mistaken for deliberate concealment.

text: Look for struggle signs such as trampled earth, broken bushes and torn fabric, and for dragging signs such as displaced fences, to reconstruct how a body moved.
Treat a bruise from a grip as a record of force, not only as a sign of pain.
when: when assessing physical marks as evidence
why: Marks show how an action was done, which can matter for judgement.

text: A rough, uneven cut on an object's end suggests a blunt tool rather than teeth or a sharp blade.
when: An object's end shows a cut.
why: Tool edges leave characteristic marks.

text: Physical traces such as mud or marks can anchor a sequence of events to a specific place and moment.
when: ordering events at a location

text: Any tool or method that touches a scene leaves residue, such as fibers, scorch marks or scratches, that can be traced back to the tool.
when: when designing or reading a scene where something had to be handled
why: physical contact transfers material between objects

text: A personal trace such as a hair can connect a person to a room, so collect and keep it for comparison with suspects.
Examine small fragments under magnification for material and curvature; a fragment of different glass with a different curve may come from another object.
If a person bears a mark but no wound, look for an injury on the other party, such as cut knuckles, that could have caused it.
when: a mark has no obvious source
why: an injury on the attacker can leave a mark on the victim

text: Traces that survive a heavily disturbed scene are worth checking, since they may still carry usable time signatures.
when: A scene has been trampled or handled by many people
why: Disturbance removes many traces but not all

text: Partly erased shoe prints can still reveal who moved a body.
Hiders often mark a hidden spot with an object chosen for private amusement, so an odd, personally meaningful object can point investigators toward the concealment.
when: when investigating a hiding place
why: Hiders tend to express their own humour or habits in how they mark things.

text: Persistent personal marks, such as carved initials, can identify a character across time and remain as traces after they leave.
when: Designing environmental clues tied to a character's past.
why: Physical marks survive the character's presence and link them to places.

text: Scrapes on a chest or disturbed floor tiles can encode what action happened and how hurried it was.
when: designing environmental clues

text: Persistent ground marks such as footprints or flattened grass give players a route-checking puzzle they can solve by reading the scene.
A physical trace, such as a fragment caught in a bolt, can reveal a passage route that a sealed door appears to rule out.
A torn or partial document can leave one detail for the player to find while the rest of its content is revealed.
when: Designing a reveal that should hold back a single fact
why: The missing detail becomes a final objective

text: When a clue's location and presence change over time and are saved, players can deduce hidden NPC activity from the record of removals and returns.
when: Designing items that change state during play
why: Recorded state lets players reconstruct an unseen actor's behavior

text: Scatter several traces, like footprints, a glove and a torn map piece, each linked to one NPC, so players must work out which belongs to whom.
A supernatural-looking event can be explained or excluded by the absence of expected traces, so a no-trace check lets players rule out a cause.
A lock that has been taken apart and reassembled shows that someone had access to the door.
when: When investigating whether a locked space was entered.
why: Disassembly and reassembly leave a physical record of access.

text: Not every absence is meaningful: items can simply be lost and indifference explains much neglect, so corroborate a gap or silence before reading it as a clue.
when: An item is missing without a pattern, or a character fails to mention something.
why: Ordinary loss and simple indifference produce the same gap or silence as concealment.

text: A partial match on one letter form is not proof of authorship and should be treated only as a lead.
when: Attributing handwriting to a suspect.
why: Letter forms can be similar across writers, and one match is weak evidence.

text: Reading a mark as proof of identity alone misleads, because it shows what the culprit wanted others to believe; check it against physical facts.
when: Interpreting a message left at a scene
why: Signatures can be staged

text: A trace surviving a fire may be partial or misleading, so record both what survives and what is missing.
when: Physical evidence has been damaged.
why: Missing parts can change the reading of the rest.

text: Removing one trace does not remove others, such as a message's content or the sender's habits, which can still reveal origin.
when: A culprit hides a trail by erasing marks
why: Other traces remain behind

text: Two accounts of one meeting can agree on words but differ in meaning, so compare interpretation as well as wording.
when: Comparing witness accounts of the same exchange.
why: Identical words can carry different intent depending on the listener.

text: Scratches on a tool or catch have many causes, and others may own similar tools; a tool-to-mark match is an inference, not a certainty.
why: Similar marks and objects can come from different sources.

text: Marks left by a previous reader, such as pencilled lines and queries, can link an object to a case but do not reveal what a message means.
Traces cut both ways: a player may only notice their own traces later, so check your own trail as well.

1) Examine the mark under magnification rather than judging its general look. 2) Look for variation in intensity within it. 3) Propose concrete candidate instruments. 4) Test each against the observed pattern. 5) Keep the interpretation open.
when: the mark is the main physical trace and its cause is disputed

text: 1) Create a pretext for the suspect to show their hands or body. 2) Watch the reaction as they comply. 3) Note any hidden mark, wound or stain revealed.
when: The crime may have left marks on the attacker.
why: A pretext that asks for the body lets the investigator observe the result and the reaction together.

text: 1) Prepare an object that records handling. 2) Show it to each suspect separately. 3) Compare their answers for consistency. 4) Examine what they discarded afterwards.
when: when the question is whether a suspect has seen or handled a specific object
why: separate questioning keeps witnesses from coordinating answers

text: 1) Note the mark, such as a scratch or notch. 2) Ask what action could have produced it. 3) Reproduce the mark with the suspected tool. 4) Check that the tool is strong enough for the job.
when: A trace could have been made by more than one action.
why: A reproduced mark tests the link between tool and trace rather than assuming it.

text: 1) Subdue the suspect with a minimal, controlled hold. 2) Let one officer focus on handcuffing while another keeps watch.
when: A suspect has been subdued after an outburst.

text: 1) Attach a speaker to each line of a rumour. 2) Keep the line order. 3) Let the player compare adjacent lines to find which link added a new detail.
when: when a rumour is shown to the player as a chain of statements
why: Speaker attribution lets players locate where the change entered

text: Mark uncertain items and object-based inferences as guesses, such as with a question mark, and list those needing outside confirmation before treating them as fact.
when: When recording notes or drawing conclusions from room evidence.

text: Store footprints, mud, dust and traces left by vehicles and NPCs as persistent world state so players can reconstruct who passed through, when, and their route.
when: Designing environmental storytelling in a game world.
why: Persistent traces let players infer past events.

text: Before accepting a tool, check it could survive the force needed on the material; one that would break or bend is ruled out, since fitting a mark is not proof.
when: A proposed tool fits or fails to match the damage.

text: Treat a distinctive mark seen in passing as a lead needing corroboration, since another person may share the same feature.
when: linking a person to an earlier sighting by one visible feature
why: Common features can match several people, so uniqueness must be checked.

text: Mark an unknown interval as unknown rather than filling it with assumption.
Flag secondhand, exaggerated, or paraphrased material as such, and state where the account is still vouched for, so readers can calibrate trust per claim.
when: when a text mixes sources of different reliability
why: readers need per-claim trust signals

text: Mark withheld information as withheld so the player knows there is more to learn.
when: Designing a reveal that is intentionally postponed.
why: Explicit withholding keeps curiosity active rather than causing confusion.

text: A partial wall inscription placed low on the floor can point the player toward the culprit or a hidden item.
when: Designing a victim-message clue.

text: Read a mark's position together with timing evidence before drawing conclusions, rather than dismissing a mark because others were nearby.
when: When a mark's location seems to conflict with the timeline.
why: Position and timing must be read together.

text: Reuse the same phrasing or images for key facts, so the audience recognises each fact when it returns later.
when: a fact will matter again in a later reveal
why: repeated wording makes the fact easy to recall

text: Mark each informant's interest in the outcome so players know how far to discount what that informant says.
Let a relic taken from a hidden event persist as physical evidence after the event ends, so the player can revisit and examine it.
Mark each gap where a chain of ownership breaks, and label any link that depends on guesswork.
when: Records of ownership are incomplete
why: Unmarked guesses can be mistaken for documented transfers

text: Mark which observations are unreliable and why, so the player can check them rather than having a real clue silently discarded.
when: Writing reports or sightings that a player must weigh.

text: Mark a character's wishful theories as hope rather than fact, so readers do not mistake them for established knowledge.
when: Writing a character who holds an unverified belief.
why: Readers accept stated beliefs as truth unless the text signals otherwise.

text: A moved movable object should leave a misaligned footprint; a player who checks alignment can detect tampering.
when: A level has rugs, shelves or similar movable objects.

text: Use a worn or partly hidden maker's mark as a lead to a second location, rewarding close inspection.
when: When designing hidden clues on items.
why: Inspection-rewarding clues make careful players feel rewarded.

text: Confirm a mark is recent by checking the scene against its earlier recorded state.
Let environment states, such as an unfastened latch or a burned document, record past events so players can rebuild the sequence from them.
when: In mystery or puzzle spaces meant to be reasoned out

text: Plant mud-over-print layering on an object so that careful inspection of the object rewards the player with a sequence of events.
when: Designing an environmental clue on an object
why: Layer order turns an object into a readable event record

text: A hidden physical tell can be found by touch or close contact after a visible disguise has passed, since gloves and coats can conceal it.
Prints on an object show that a particular person handled it, which can point to a second person when the expected handlers are excluded.
when: When physical traces on an object conflict with the stated account.
why: Traces record contact, so unexpected prints reveal additional involvement.

text: Ask about each surface a person could have touched, testing every route by which the evidence could have been handled or entered.
when: tracing who handled an object or entered a space
why: Covering every route prevents a missed contact from being overlooked.

text: Mud, dust and wet ground preserve physical marks such as ruts and footprints, which can later be read as evidence.
when: A scene holds marks that witnesses cannot supply
why: Soft surfaces retain marks for later inference

text: Physical traces include fingerprints, footprints, cigarette ash, mud and handwriting, each supplying facts rather than final answers.
why: raw traces need interpretation before they explain an event

text: Collect each small physical trace separately, marking its origin, even before its meaning is known, since it may connect to another source later.
when: Gathering physical evidence at a scene.
why: Mixed or unlabeled samples cannot be linked back to their source, and an unexplained trace can gain meaning once another clue is found.

text: Let a merchant NPC sell a suspect's discarded item, so the player can test a physical clue before making an accusation.
when: Designing clue-testing in a game.

text: 1) Cut a small sample from inside a seam. 2) Seal it. 3) Label it with owner, item and date before sending it to a specialist.
when: a stain or residue must be tested by a lab
why: keeps the sample's identity and custody clear

text: 1) Record each trace in a numbered list. 2) Test each one by smell, taste or fresh examination. 3) Keep samples sealed so they can be re-examined.
when: Investigating a scene disturbed by many people
why: Systematic records keep traces comparable and reliable

text: Record and document each mark in place before interpreting what it means.
when: Examining a scene

text: A trace proves identity only with independent confirmation, such as weather, a garment's cut or a disinterested witness; trace inference alone is not proof.
A trace's description can shift as an observer looks closer, moving from a vague label to a specific and more serious one.
why: Close inspection changes what the observer sees and names.

text: Dust, mould and mud record shapes; a mark that looks like a shapeless smudge can hold a clear pattern when examined closely under magnification.
when: when a trace first looks uninformative
why: fine detail survives in soft deposits and is missed at a glance

text: Material facts such as times, distances and records differ from inferences drawn from a suspect's character or behaviour.
Trace evidence is faint physical residue, such as a shallow floor depression or spilled particles, that shows where an object once stood or what was moved.
A physical trace shows that movement, entry or an object's presence occurred, not who caused it or handled it; treating it as proof of who moved something is a mistake.
when: When a trace is used as evidence
why: The trace records the disturbance, not the identity of the one who caused it

text: Fingerprints, mud, hair, fibres, dust, debris and small clothing damage record where a person has been and what they did.
when: When a person's whereabouts are in question or a scene is examined for presence
why: Each object carries physical traces of contact.

text: When material facts seem to exclude a suspect favored by character tests, the conflict stays unresolved until a method is found.
Under magnification, the shape of hairs and fibres identifies their material or source, so a small trace can point to a particular animal or material.
Matching initials or markings can link two people to one object, and testing true ownership can reverse a conclusion.
A matching object shows two items are alike, not who owned them or why they were there.
Hair torn out with tissue still on its roots indicates that the pulling force was great.
when: reading force from a physical trace
why: tissue tearing with the hair shows strong pulling

text: A message built from cut-out printed words carries evidence in its paper, typeface and fragments, which can reveal where it came from.
A smear or stain can place an object at a location, and a name written on it can tie the object to its owner.
Certain materials, such as tarred twine, are associated with particular trades, so the material can suggest a sender's occupation or environment.
when: When identifying the origin of a packaged object
why: Materials tend to be tied to specific workplaces and crafts

text: A trace that connects two separated places can show that an event happened even when no witness saw it.
A trace proves contact, not guilt; treat a trace link as a lead, not a verdict, since innocent contact and trades can produce the same trace.
when: Interpreting a trace as evidence against a person or linking a trace substance to a suspect's item
why: Contact is common and does not establish intent.

text: Match small traces such as soil or grit to the places where that material occurs, comparing them with comparable samples, to narrow where a person recently went.
when: when a person's movements are unknown
why: A distinctive material links the trace to a location.

text: Read wear, stains and odd or repetitive marks as records of a person's habits, methods and activities; untrained observers see only appearance.
when: examining people or objects for evidence; a trace is odd or repetitive and its purpose is unclear
why: Traces record repeated behaviour.

text: A match on an unusual detail, such as a paper watermark, rare tobacco blend or unusual match type, ties a common object to one owner; a common detail is weak.
when: asking who made, owned or used a common object

text: Residue that looks uniform to the naked eye can break into recognisable fragments under magnification, so examine samples under a microscope.
when: when analysing dust or residue
why: fragments identify the substances and sources

text: A physical trace can have several possible makers, so do not identify a person from it until you have considered who else could produce it.
when: A trace could have been made by more than one person.
why: Shoes, sizes and borrowed items let different people leave the same mark.

text: A trace is strong evidence when its location matches where the event should have occurred.
when: Checking a stain or mark against a hypothesised event

text: Note precisely where a trace sits: a deposit in one narrow spot is stronger evidence than a diffuse smear.
Compare scene fragments side by side with items from a suspect's rooms, matching by material, colour and damage.
when: when two locations may share a trace

text: Physical traces that match an account test its consistency, not its truth, because a planned alibi can also fit the physical evidence.
when: when a detailed account matches the scene
why: A carefully prepared story can account for every visible trace.

text: Materials and craftsmanship reveal an owner's care and class, and can rule out a careless owner.
Compare a fragment's material, not only its shape, since a matching outline can come from a different cloth.
when: matching a found piece to its claimed source
why: shape alone can match by chance

text: Choose a trace that splits the suspects, so a trait carried by few candidates narrows the field at once.
when: Selecting a clue for an elimination test.

text: Do not force a closed door when the traces show no danger; the traces should decide whether to act.
when: Deciding whether to open a closed space.

text: Treat a reading of a trace as a hypothesis to test; it may show staging without explaining how the event itself happened.
when: interpreting a suspicious physical detail
why: a staged detail is evidence about behaviour, not the mechanism of the act

text: Read a physical trace against each competing hypothesis, because one mark can support two opposite accounts of the same death.
when: Cause of death is disputed between accident, suicide and murder
why: Scratches and marks have several possible causes, so the same trace can fit different stories

text: Check each physical trace against other known facts before trusting it, and build conclusions only from several small facts that can be checked separately.
Matching prints across several objects link one person to all of them, but the timing of each print must still be established.
Compare dirt or soot on a floor with material from outside the location. Similar residue suggests the same route was taken.
when: when a trace is found inside and the route is unknown
why: Matching materials links an interior trace to an exterior path.

text: Match bruise patterns to the places where fabric is torn to infer how a person was gripped.
when: Grip-like marks and torn fabric are both present.
why: Marks at matching locations point to a shared cause.

text: Game maps can carry trace evidence such as disturbed soil, cut vegetation or boat marks, letting players reconstruct events by asking what the terrain would have allowed.
why: Physical traces make past events discoverable without direct testimony.

text: Particles found across an entire item suggest the air of where it habitually hangs, while particles on one side suggest traces picked up along the way.
when: when comparing particle distribution across an item

text: A combination of particle types found in only one district can narrow the locality when checked against a directory of local trades.
when: when particle types indicate local industries
why: unusual combinations tie to few places

text: Missing dirt can be as informative as present dirt: if a claimed route should have left sand, gravel or earth on shoes, its absence contradicts the claim.
when: a claimed route crosses a surface that leaves traces
why: the route would have deposited that material on footwear

text: Estimate a document's age by comparing it side by side with a newer sample, since visible wear such as yellowing and thickness differences reveal age.
when: A clue depends on when a material was produced.
why: Side-by-side comparison exposes differences that are hard to judge from one sample alone.

text: Collect and label small trace objects such as cigarette ends before any testing; an unlabeled or mixed trace cannot be reliably linked to its source.
when: A small object might connect a person to a scene
why: Preserving the link between trace and source is what makes the trace usable as evidence

text: Physical traces that look incriminating, shown before the innocent explanation is available, lead the audience to settle on a wrong suspicion.
Overlapping marks on one object can form a puzzle in which the player separates two sets of traces and attributes each to a person.
Offenders remove traces by wearing gloves, brushing or drying mud and clothing, disposing of tools or keys, and altering a victim's hair or face.
when: An offender tries to hide their presence
why: Each method targets a different kind of trace

text: A physical trace identifies a person only by matching a stored record, such as a fingerprint file; without that record the trace proves little.
when: a trace may link to a known record
why: identification depends on a database entry to compare against

text: A cigarette lit with matches typically uses about three matches, so a count of spent matches estimates how many cigarettes were lit.
when: matches are the only available measure of smoking
why: each light consumes a roughly fixed number of matches

text: Over-reading a trace common to many occupations or a widely owned object convicts the wrong person; it does not prove who owned or used a particular item.
when: Linking a common trace substance or widely owned object to a suspect
why: A widely shared substance or item cannot single out one person.

text: Assuming a trace belongs to the culprit can wrongly implicate an innocent visitor or a household member.
Physical traces can be misread, and a timing inference drawn from one, such as a liquid level, is a guess that may not match the true time.
Reading a surface detail as old without checking its freshness can lead to a wrong conclusion, so judge freshness before drawing inferences.
when: when interpreting labels or marks
why: A new label can look like an old one.

text: Weather, light and handling degrade traces, and a suspect can exploit these conditions to cast doubt on physical evidence.
when: When a trace is collected under poor or changing conditions
why: Degraded conditions give a suspect grounds to dispute the trace

text: A small print can be misread as belonging to a child or a small person; only comparison with a reference reveals its true type.
when: when interpreting a print's size or owner
why: a single trace gives an unreliable first impression

text: A physical trace that contradicts a witness may expose either the witness or a second party, so check the trace before trusting either.
when: Physical evidence disagrees with a testimony
why: Either account may be wrong, and the trace may reveal a hidden actor

text: Assuming a sequence from one trace, or overlooking small ones such as a towel or knuckle marks, produces a wrong reconstruction.
A dull, patchy surface is easily taken for simple shabbiness, and its meaning is missed unless someone reads the pattern.
A mark that looks intentional may come from natural forces, and a mark that looks natural may be deliberate, so each mark's physical logic must be tested.
Linking two cases through a shared trace is often an assumption rather than a finding, especially when the investigators already know each other.
why: Acquaintance does not establish that one actor left both traces

text: An investigator's own lapse, such as an unlocked door, can become the decisive gap, so record exact times of each opening and closing.
why: undocumented times make one's own mistake indistinguishable from a culprit's

text: Faint or smeared marks can make layering ambiguous, so a confident reading of their order may be wrong.
when: Marks are faint, smeared or partly covered
why: Unclear edges make the overlap order uncertain

text: A trace placed where a casual visitor will meet it may be disturbed, but one placed where a visitor avoids it will record nothing.
when: When positioning a trace or trap
why: Placement determines whether the expected visitor interacts with it

text: 1) Find the physical trace. 2) Find candidate objects that could have made it. 3) Accept a match only when the object fits exactly. 4) Only then link the mark to that person.
when: when a trace could belong to several people
why: an unmatched print proves nothing about who made it

text: 1) List every physical trace in the scene. 2) For each trace, list people who could have made it and test their capacity for that act. 3) Keep only suspects consistent with all traces.
why: Isolated traces mislead; matching each one to possible makers turns it into evidence.

text: 1) Treat each trace as a question, since it usually supports several explanations. 2) Record it and state its probable meaning. 3) State at least one alternative reading. 4) Withhold judgement until both readings are tested.
when: Interpreting physical evidence at a scene, early before further tests return
why: Logging before judging keeps an early theory from dismissing traces that fit another reading.

text: 1) Count the links between you and the account. 2) Trace each link back to its speaker to find the first witness. 3) Check which relays were actually verified. 4) Treat repeated phrasing as a possible sign of a single origin.
when: Several people or agencies seem to confirm the same account.
why: Repetition can hide a single original report.

text: 1) Examine soles and garments with a lens and naked eye, and inspect seams under magnification. 2) Lift fibres or particles with tweezers, not fingers. 3) Seal each sample at once in a labelled envelope, noting its source. 4) Wrap the item in clean paper and keep it for later analysis.
when: Trace material is small enough to be lost
why: Fingers and loose handling contaminate or lose fine traces.

text: 1) Record each sample's exact location on the object and when it was collected; undocumented samples weaken evidence. 2) Seal each in its own labelled container so materials do not mix. 3) Keep records for later comparison.
when: When collecting small, easily overlooked or easily destroyed trace samples for analysis.
why: Exact location and time allow later comparison; separate containers prevent cross-contamination.

text: 1) Record the unknown trace's shape and features. 2) Create or obtain a known reference of a candidate source. 3) Place the reference beside the unknown trace. 4) Note which features match and which differ.
when: when an unknown mark must be attributed to a source
why: a side-by-side comparison exposes differences a lone trace hides

text: 1) Compare the object's outline with the trace on the body 2) Check whether a fixed part, such as a buckle prong, fits the most-worn position.
when: a body trace may belong to a seized object

text: Collect trace evidence with care, such as fibres under a victim's nails or cloth cut from where a weapon was wiped, before the scene is disturbed.
when: processing a crime scene
why: traces are small and easily lost

text: 1) Collect loose material from the suspect, such as dust from their feet. 2) Collect a matching sample from the place in question. 3) Compare the two samples side by side. 4) Seal and preserve each item until trial.
when: A suspect denies presence at a place and a trace from that place is available
why: A match between suspect and scene material tests the denial, and sealing preserves the chain of custody

text: 1) Compare the paper colour of the two sheets side by side. 2) Hold both to light and compare their appearance. 3) Align the edges and check whether ruling lines match. 4) Note distinctive defects that recur across consecutive sheets.
when: A document's paper can be compared with a known stock.
why: Shared physical features across sheets point to a common source.

text: 1) Obtain a known sample from the item's original source. 2) Compare its traits, such as colour and thickness, with the found item. 3) If they match, conclude the found item came from that source and that someone else had access to it.
when: an item is found in a place where it should not be
why: a verified match turns an odd find into evidence

text: 1) Examine the sample under low magnification. 2) Sort visible particles by type, such as fibres, dust, skin and residue. 3) Identify the residue substance. 4) Link the substance to a trade or activity.
when: An object carries residue or debris that may tie it to a person or trade
why: Sorting particles by type and identifying the substance gives a traceable lead

text: 1) Cut a small sample from the stained area. 2) Mount it in a fluid reagent on a slide. 3) Examine individual cell or fibre shapes under magnification. 4) Compare them with a labelled reference collection to identify the source.
when: When a stain or small object could link a suspect to a place, animal or setting.
why: Microscopic structure distinguishes sources that look alike to the naked eye.

text: 1) Judge the trace's freshness to tie it to a time. 2) Check where the item is sold. 3) Rule out household members who use it. 4) Compare the trace with the suspect's own possessions.
1) Record a physical trace immediately, with its time. 2) Compare it against the suspect's known profile. 3) Store the match result in the case file.
when: investigating a physical trace such as a bite or mark
why: Immediate recording prevents loss of the trace and keeps the comparison checkable.

text: 1) Collect traces from the body and its footwear. 2) Identify each trace's material under magnification. 3) Compare the materials with candidate locations. 4) Exclude traces the investigators carried in themselves.

1) Collect trace material onto a clean surface in the suspect's presence. 2) Divide it, giving the suspect's custodian a portion to seal. 3) Seal the portion in front of the suspect. 4) Record the custody chain.
when: A trace must later be matched to a location and the suspect might dispute it.
why: Sealing in the suspect's presence prevents a later claim that the sample was switched.

text: 1) Discard trampled central paths. 2) Inspect the edges and surroundings of the path where impressions remain distinct. 3) Note marks that differ in walking pattern. 4) Read overlapping prints so the later step cuts into the earlier one. 5) Follow each trail to its endpoints and look for turns, doubling back or struggle.
when: Interpreting footprint evidence in a scene
why: Contaminated paths mislead and overlaps and endpoints show order and cause

text: 1) Fire test projectiles through the same cloth and layers as the suspect garment. 2) Compare their marks with the recovered projectile under matching conditions. 3) Treat a partial impression judged by eye alone as weak evidence.
when: A recovered projectile must be linked to a garment

text: Before treating a trace as proof, check it fits the injury's location, direction and finality; a trace that does not fit the wound proves little and can support rival readings.
when: When traces seem to support a theory or evidence is weighed against an injury.
why: Odd traces are easy to over-read, and mismatched traces can support rival readings.

text: A trace becomes evidence only when matched to a second object or record that could have made it and to a record of who held it.
when: when a physical trace is used as a clue
why: A trace without a comparison cannot link to a source.

text: Match footwear found at the scene to the prints by fitting pattern and wear, and treat an identifying mark such as a worn heel as a unique identifier.
when: when a suspected shoe is recovered
why: Specific wear patterns can tie a print to one item.

text: Compare suspect fingerprints with case prints only when a clean, reliable record exists; without one, a match cannot be confirmed.
when: When using fingerprints to link or exclude a suspect.
why: Poor or incomplete records prevent a reliable identification.

text: A matching trace shows a link, not a sole explanation; weigh each object against the rest of the evidence.
when: when a trace matches a suspect

text: Avoid placing traces whose meaning is never tied to any character or event, since players cannot use them.
Examine a document's material properties, such as paper stock, printed marks and envelope, as well as its words.
when: A document lacks a name or signature
why: Physical traits can reveal origin and handling

text: When a clue depends on a matched pair and the expected partner is missing from its usual place or found elsewhere, the theory built on that clue must change.
when: a clue relies on an item having a matching partner
why: the pair no longer fits the theory

text: Do not settle a cause of death from physical traces alone; read them together with motive and timing.
when: Choosing between accident, suicide and murder
why: Traces are ambiguous and gain weight only when combined with other evidence

text: Every physical trace and dated record must fit the proposed sequence of events; a sequence that fails any one trace is rejected.
when: when evaluating a reconstructed sequence
why: each trace is independent evidence of how the event happened

text: Keep a master key in the calculation unless its guarding is strict enough to rule out its use.
when: A master key exists and is guarded.

text: Use wear and material on a gate or post as a dating clue for a room's history.
when: Designing a space with a layered history
why: Physical wear reveals approximate age and changes over time

text: Turn small material disputes into motive records so players can identify which rival holds the strongest grievance.
Cover remaining fragile traces with boxes or boards so they survive until they can be recorded.
when: Traces cannot be captured immediately.
why: Physical covers slow the damage from thaw or weather.

text: Distinguish a faint trace from an identifiable impression, and do not treat an ambiguous mark as a print until other evidence supports it.
when: Interpreting a faint mark at a scene
why: Hopeful investigators can read ambiguous marks as definite prints

text: Make the final proof multi-part and physical, combining items such as document fragments, a lab extract and a found object.
when: Assembling the evidence for a mystery's climax.
why: Several physical pieces together are harder to dismiss than a single claim and give the reveal weight.

text: Fine, stretchable threads give more reliable traces than adhesive glue, because they are nearly invisible and do not give a false disturbance.
when: When choosing a material for a trap or trace that must not be noticed
why: A material that is hard to see and sensitive to contact records movement more reliably

text: 1) List each small trace and witness report. 2) Assign each one checkable cause. 3) Chain the causes into a candidate sequence of events. 4) Test each link against independent evidence, including the subject's own account. 5) Keep untested links labelled as hypotheses.
when: a stranger arrives with several small traces, or events must be reconstructed from physical traces and witness reports
why: each cause can be checked, and the subject's account tests the whole chain

text: Changes after an event mark where things happened but do not show what happened; a place can look trivial once ordinary life has moved in.
when: revisiting a disturbed scene

text: A trace consistent with poisoning can coexist with death from natural causes, so the trace alone may settle nothing about the cause.
when: When a trace suggests a harmful substance.
why: Presence of a substance does not establish it caused the death.

text: Ordinary crimes leave traces in rough edges and small inconsistencies; a botched act leaves them everywhere.
Dropped objects, witness sightings and the physical state of a body can each serve as a link in a chain of traces that reconstructs events.
A physical trace becomes evidence only after it is checked against weather, measurements, and timing; an unchecked trace is only a suggestion.
when: when interpreting prints, marks, or other residue at a scene
why: environmental conditions determine whether a trace could have formed when claimed

text: An unknown culprit can be identified from small objects and habits, with each trace weighed for what it implies about the person who left it.
when: The culprit is unknown and several small objects at the scene may share one source.
why: Converging minor traces can narrow a large suspect pool to one person.

text: A pronoun slip or a missing stop may have an innocent cause, so each should be treated as a lead to test, not as proof.
Treating a trace only as a record of position misses what it implies about sequence and events.
when: Interpreting physical evidence.
why: A single mark can carry more than one fact.

text: 1) Ask the same question of each record. 2) Collect the answers into one list. 3) Look for a common beneficiary across entries. 4) Treat the result as direction, not proof of who ordered each action.
when: Evidence is many small records
why: Consistent questions make entries comparable, and the list reveals where value flows.

text: 1) Ask the household where an accident victim was taken. 2) Ask about the time, the vehicle and any visitors.
when: A person is involved in a roadside accident.

text: 1) List each odd sensation a witness reports. 2) Assign each a mundane cause, such as a hidden person or a moved object. 3) Treat anything resisting mundane explanation as a possible real anomaly, not as dismissed.
when: a witness's account contains an apparent anomaly

text: Let a clue carry a traceable source, such as a page number or printed text, that players can match to a specific book in the world.
Give a missing NPC or closed door at least two plausible causes so players must choose which to test.
Judge a trace against its setting: a smear that fits the wrong context is itself a clue.
when: a residue or mark appears in an unexpected place
why: context mismatch signals a different source

text: Observers often signal one another, so a timed escape should be planned as if it is being watched.
when: Watchers are posted near an escape route
why: Coordinated signals reveal the watch to the escaper

text: When a trail ends, search for a new trace such as faint vehicle wheel marks, which can explain the stop.
when: a trail stops at a point in slush or mud

text: The point where a track stops suggests where the walker entered cover, so search there.
Footprints that lead to an edge and stop indicate the direction of travel, so the search should move to that edge.
when: Tracks that end abruptly at water, a wall or a drop.
why: A trail that ends points to where the person likely went next.

text: A servant's exclamation can act as a warning signal that alerts a hidden person inside to an approaching visitor.
when: servants interact near a concealed person
why: Audible greetings carry information to anyone who hears them.

text: A physical signal line between a trapped person and someone outside can reveal an action without any noise.
A single signal is unreliable: it cannot be repeated once given, and a passing obstruction can hide it, so use more than one cue.
why: the signal is the only channel between observers

text: Thaw, slush and passing traffic erase prints, and weather can remove a trail entirely.
A trail that returns on itself misleads an investigator who follows only the first leg.
A tail can be noticed, so the follower must keep distance and avoid losing the subject.
when: During active following of a suspect.

text: An object's trail can be lost after its first sale; tracing later buyers may depend on someone who knows them.

1) Follow a track as far as it runs. 2) Search where it ends, looking for where someone stood or waited and examining that spot closely. 3) At a crossing, choose the next route by the following physical clue, not by guess.
why: A pause point often holds more evidence than a passing track.

text: 1) Identify who is most likely to carry news of an escape to the hidden party. 2) Follow that intermediary discreetly rather than the fugitive. 3) Let the fugitive go once the trail is known.
when: A suspect escapes and the accomplice is unknown.
why: The intermediary is more likely than the fugitive to reach the real target.

text: 1) Follow the clearest prints first, since distinct prints are easy to track. 2) When the trail is lost, mark the last known print. 3) Search the ground around it in widening passes.
when: a moving target leaves prints on soft or mixed ground

text: 1) Post a second watcher near the exit. 2) When the first follower is seen, the second takes over the watch. 3) The first withdraws without being noticed.
when: the target is alert, has several exits, or may flee
why: a handoff keeps the trail after one follower is spotted

text: 1) Work out the method the culprit must have used. 2) List the residue it would leave and where it would sit. 3) Check which surfaces would keep it. 4) Search in a fixed order, including vehicles. 5) Inspect closely under good light. 6) Stop when light fails and resume next day.
when: when planning a search for the traces of an act
why: searching from the method gives the expected traces

text: 1) The signaller watches the route and gives the agreed signal when the target appears. 2) The signaller does not act. 3) The second observer approaches and sees the target's face first.
when: a watch depends on one observer identifying a target that another observer reports
why: identification happens before any confrontation

text: Agree on a physical signal in advance, such as a visible change in light, where its appearance means discovery and its absence means the watch continues.
when: observers must communicate across a distance
why: a physical cue can be read from afar without alerting the target

text: Coordinate guard movement with a shared signal, such as a called word or a fired shot, so the group acts together.
when: multiple agents must move at the same moment
why: a common trigger keeps timing consistent across guards

text: Make the player's signal a deliberate in-world action, and let the AI respond by its own route, so the player must plan around the blind spot.
when: designing player-triggered guard responses
why: the AI's independent route creates a planning challenge for the player

text: Reward players who read a pattern of several signs, not one clue, with a safe way to disarm the threat.
A single revealed trait can recast earlier events for the player, changing how they read facts already known.
A trade shapes the hand, so hand form can reveal a person's occupation, including slaters, sailors, compositors and diamond-polishers, and can help identify unclaimed bodies.
when: when examining a hand or body for occupation
why: repetitive trade work leaves lasting physical marks

text: A body, its belongings and its surroundings carry evidence about habits, wealth and recent history that an expert can read as clues.
A trait matching a clue can be a decoy; corroborate it with independent evidence, such as other candidates' possessions or recalled habits, like which hand they use for cards.
when: a trait points to one suspect and needs support
why: Independent observations test whether the trait is distinctive.

text: A trait introduced as a light joke or teasing point can later become a key identifying clue, if it is recalled when it matters.
Compare a suspect's visible trait, such as an injury or gait, with records kept by those who treated them. A surprising trait may be staged.
when: When a visible trait is central to a suspect's identity.
why: Records made by people with no stake in the case are harder to fake.

text: A small personal trait can change how a motive reads and can explain an action that physical evidence leaves unclear.
Treating a physical trait as proof of identity, without checking when the trait first appears in the record, is an error.
Add a character trait that rules out an action, so players can clear a suspect by reasoning from who that person is.
when: a suspect is wrongly implicated
why: trait-based reasoning gives players a legitimate way to eliminate suspects

text: A trap that protects a decoy can fail to protect the true target, so the audience's belief about where danger lies can be turned against them.
when: a protective trap is set around a decoy
why: the trap assumes the threat comes from outside, which the twist overturns

text: A staged trigger raises a relevant subject unexpectedly while a person is off guard, to prompt a slip or a confession.
Make a trap a welcoming space, with warm hosts and a locked exit appearing only after the player has relaxed, so the reversal hits harder.
when: Designing a sanctuary that turns hostile.
why: Contrast between comfort and threat intensifies the reversal.

text: A sudden visible change of mood can make a careful target suspicious, so the shift should be gradual or plausible.
when: Using a quarrel to steer a target who is alert.
why: Abrupt emotional change reads as staged to a watchful person.

text: Naming an unseen agent can satisfy an audience while leaving unanswered how the agent acts; the mechanism must still be explained.
A bluff can drive a frightened person to self-harm, so a sting should not be used on fragile suspects and medical care must be planned in advance.
when: Planning a confrontation that relies on fear of exposure.
why: Acute fear can push a vulnerable person to a dangerous act.

text: Taking a tidy-looking room for innocence is a mistake, because a closed drawer may hide a search.
A late threat with no earlier planted cause feels like a cheat, and over-neat resolution removes the suspense built by escalation.
when: Resolving a multi-stage threat
why: Unearned threats and tidy endings both undercut tension

text: 1) Make a false clue or forged message. 2) Deliver it to the suspect. 3) Watch the suspect's reaction to reveal their guilt.

1) Adopt a false identity that unsettles the suspect's expectations. 2) Invent a plausible consequence, such as a prosecution by a named authority. 3) Place the suspect in a room with a route to act. 4) Station a backup outside, ready to enter when the suspect acts.
when: A suspect is guilty of a lesser crime and can be made to fear exposure.
why: Control of setting and timing lets the investigator intervene at the moment of action.

text: 1) Learn the suspect's hiding place. 2) Inform the authorities of the location. 3) Schedule their arrival to control the timing of capture.
when: A pursuit has a clear location and a timed final moment.
why: Controlling arrival timing turns an apparent escape into a controlled capture.

text: 1) Let the suspect proceed so the act incriminates him fully. 2) Fix a time window from his stated conditions. 3) Place watchers out of sight and conceal the potential victim. 4) Signal the suspect to the decisive point. 5) Close the trap as he enters.
when: the suspect's plan is known in outline and timing can be controlled
why: intervening at commitment yields evidence from the suspect's own act

text: Use a staged trap, such as a feigned illness or bait advertisement, so the culprit acts on his own assumption and exposes himself before the investigator.
Tie the protagonist's want, such as escape or romance, to the lever the trap uses against them.
Before treating a discovery's timing as evidence, identify who controlled its trigger, such as who ordered the works that exposed it.
why: Coincidence stays a suspicion until control of the event is shown

text: Watching a suspect rather than confronting them lets them reveal more over time, at the cost of delaying resolution and sustaining tension.
when: An investigator can gather more by observation than by direct questioning.
why: Patient observation can surface clues that a confrontation would end early.

text: Within a gap between two confirmed events, measure walking time between the locations; travel time limits what a person could do and can rule a route in or out.
when: Judging whether a person could act or travel during a gap between two fixed times at different places.
why: Travel time limits what movement is physically possible within the gap.

text: Prisoner transport is guarded by mounted escorts, warders in the van's passage and on the driver's box, and a holding cell at the courthouse.
A person's movements across places, recorded in travel or passenger lists, can serve as timeline clues in an investigation.
A stop during a timed trip leaves a window in which someone could slip in or out unseen, even if the driver noticed nothing.
A traffic-based check can show a hiding claim is implausible, but it cannot prove when an object was placed.
A trace found by tracking can explain an otherwise unaccounted movement, such as a return made by an indirect route.
Compare a suspect trace with a record of the scene from before the event. A mark absent from the earlier record must have been added afterward.
when: When a trace is suspiciously convenient or a pre-event scene state is available.
why: A mark absent before the event cannot have been made by the event itself.

text: Station a watcher at a transit point to log arrivals and departures, and place the watcher where travellers actually pass.
when: tracking who comes and goes

text: Delay explaining a twist until players hold the same clues as the protagonist, keeping the reveal fair.
The gap between a call and an arrival bounds how long a witness could have spent elsewhere.
when: checking an alibi against response times
why: the time gap limits the window in which the witness could have acted

text: Compare a player's stated route or time against logged events, so an NPC's question can hinge on a fact only that player could know.
Include routes the investigators themselves used earlier; these are easy to overlook yet can be the real access path.
when: a death or disappearance has no obvious access point
why: familiarity makes a used route seem already ruled out

text: Wheel marks and trampled ground around a spot show that a vehicle was backed up to it.
Travel times, such as a walk plus a scheduled train, fix when a person could have departed or arrived.
when: A movement must be placed within a time window.
why: Scheduled transport gives a hard constraint on movement.

text: Tracking whether a player keeps a promised meeting arranged through a public channel lets the game respond to that choice.
when: A promised meeting is set through a public channel.

text: An arrival made too early or too late can alter the target's behaviour, and the target may leave before the party arrives, defeating the plan.
why: The plan assumes the target stays put until the chosen moment.

text: A fixed departure time forces a scene to end early, so a fixed schedule acts as a ticking clock that shapes how characters behave.
Environmental states like weather gate when an action is possible, and can hide or expose objects.
A stated arrival is possible only if verified distance divided by realistic walking or running pace, lowered by fatigue, fits the time available.
when: Testing whether someone could reach a place in time.
why: Independent travel records set a hard bound on movement.

text: A claimed meeting is impossible if the travel time exceeds the window; a fifteen to twenty minute trip cannot fit a ten-minute window.
when: Checking a timed alibi.
why: Physical travel time bounds what a witness could have done.

text: Estimate travel time between two known points to infer where a person could have spent an unexplained interval.
when: A person is missing for a stretch and the window of possible locations is needed.
why: Known travel times bound the places reachable within the gap.

text: An arrival has five ordered parts: vehicle stops, passenger steps down, luggage left, knock, vehicle leaves. A witness can rebuild them as a timeline.
Travel-time timeline tests depend on assumed mode and speed; establish how the person moved first, or present results as probabilities, not proof.
why: Travel time estimates depend entirely on the mode and speed of movement, and the method does not establish vessel type.

text: Dismissing a route as impassable or merely unlikely, without checking the map, can eliminate the true answer or leave the real access path unexamined.
when: Constraints are assumed rather than checked against the map.
why: Players and designers who skip verification lose valid candidates.

text: Each stage of a concealment plan carries its own exposure, and moving a body is often the riskiest stage.
when: When planning a multi-step cover-up.
why: Physical movement risks discovery by people who would otherwise not notice anything.

text: Trusting the first recorded destination of an object can hide its real movement.
An old name such as a simple track label can understate how developed a route became, and a newer name can hide an older track.
A route dismissed without checking its timing makes the final solution look like cheating to the player.
Travel estimates vary, so allow a few minutes more or less before calling a timeline gap suspicious.
when: When judging whether a travel-time gap is suspicious
why: Small variations in travel time are normal and would falsely flag innocent accounts.

text: 1) Fix the times the suspect was known to be elsewhere and note the claimed departure place and time. 2) Estimate walk or travel time for each leg to the next claimed place. 3) Add the legs and any meeting length. 4) Compare the total with the time elapsed or gap available, checking whether the claimed arrival is physically possible.
when: Testing whether a suspect's claimed route or timed alibi fits the available window.

text: 1) Stage a transfer with an insecurely locked van door, or offer a timed opening in a transport section. 2) Track the prisoner's response and choices as clues to intent. 3) Accept the risk of a real escape chance.
when: A prisoner's response to an opening is informative and the transfer or section can be staged safely.
why: Timed openings let player and NPC choices reveal intent; a suspect who takes the chance may reveal a plan.

text: 1) Measure the total gap between two known times. 2) Subtract fixed intervals such as intermissions. 3) The remainder is the time available for the trip and any act.
when: When checking whether a suspect could leave and return during an event
why: Fixed intervals reduce the free time a movement must fit into

text: 1) Transfer the captive to another prison before release. 2) This cuts off warnings from outside friends.
when: Preparing a controlled release.
why: Distance from allies prevents warnings during surveillance.

text: 1) Collect each character's sightings and sounds. 2) Order them in time. 3) Check whether any character could have been in two places at once.
when: testing alibis

text: 1) Name the trace that seems to prove something. 2) Ask whether it was left before, during or after the event. 3) Write what each timing predicts for other traces. 4) Keep the timing that other traces support.

1) List each specific physical detail a witness gives about a route. 2) Walk the route yourself. 3) At each named point, search for the predicted objects or marks. 4) Note the order in which they appear.
when: a witness describes a location and an event that can leave traces
why: checking predicted marks tests the account against the ground

text: 1) Time the real trip between the two locations. 2) Compare the measured time with the claimed window. 3) Conclude only that the movement was feasible, not that it happened.
when: A suspect's movements depend on travel time
why: A timed route shows possibility, not use

text: 1) List every role a person holds across the case. 2) Order those roles by stage. 3) Check for a shift from witness to accused and trace the path to the outcome.
1) Identify the procedure that filled the post. 2) List each candidate and how each was declined or passed over. 3) Note who was excluded at each stage.
when: analysing a contested appointment

text: Check the route length between the suspect's location and the scene, since a short side exit can make a trip feasible within a small window.
when: When a trip must fit a short window
why: Shorter routes make brief absences plausible

text: Plan a witness's arrival from published schedules rather than guessing, so the meeting time is known in advance.
when: A witness is travelling to meet an investigator.
why: Calculated arrivals allow the investigator to prepare the meeting without waiting.

text: Log every quest-relevant transaction with a timestamp so players can rebuild what was owed or promised on any given day.
Let a note arrive through a messenger the player never clearly sees, so attribution rests on the note's content.
when: Designing anonymous delivery

text: Gate puzzle solutions by in-world travel time, so an NPC cannot be in two places within the game clock and players can test accusations against it.
A taxi leaves a traceable record while a bus or underground leaves less, so a careful suspect prefers the less traceable option.
when: when a suspect chooses how to travel during a crime

text: People who travel alone, rarely stay in one place, and rarely follow the news are hard to trace, so an alibi resting on them is less likely to be challenged.
when: Assessing whether a cover story will be tested
why: Few independent checks reach such people

text: Once a visitor leaves, a lone occupant's movements can go unobserved, so their alibi rests on their own word.
when: A character is alone after another has departed
why: No one else is present to confirm what they did

text: Record each sighting of a clue or suspect in the player's map or journal, so later payoffs and movements can be traced back to earlier appearances.
when: when a clue recurs across an area
why: a traceable record makes a payoff feel connected to earlier play

text: An unused ticket or travel item shows intent to make a journey, not that the trip was completed.
Let quest-givers or hideouts be known only by partial names, so the player must work to link a name to a place or person.
when: a mystery requires the player to discover identity
why: partial names turn identification into a task

text: A suspect who adds an unverifiable stop to fill a gap widens the window, so check whether the total time leaves room for that stop.
when: A suspect offers a new stop to explain a gap.
why: Extra stops consume slack that the account already lacks.

text: A lettered diagram of where each sample sits on an item gives players a map to reason from.
when: when presenting sampled evidence to players

text: A traveller whose destination no one knows is hard to trace afterward.
Travel times are estimates, and a wrong figure can clear a guilty party or convict an innocent one, so verify it before relying on the result.
Assuming where a crime happened without evidence makes every timeline built on that assumption unreliable.
Building a timeline on checkpoints that cannot be verified gives a false sense of precision.
when: sources are unreliable

text: Accepting a witness's story that stops exactly where its claims can no longer be verified leaves the key claim untested.

1) Record the vehicle's fuel level when it was left. 2) Record the level of spare supplies. 3) Compare consumption with mileage. 4) Fix the travel window by matching the vehicle's location at a known time.
when: witness times are unreliable or absent

text: Provide a sketch-map tool where players record room layouts, doors, windows and furniture; spatial notes persist as the level is explored and can be compared with later evidence.
Do not treat a witness's guess about direction or place as fact until another source corroborates it.
when: a witness is unsure where they were
why: guesses are not observations

text: Provide a search action that sweeps in lanes and reveals items hidden under cover, rewarding methodical play.
Sort matched prints by hand and by room, so the game can show where each character has been.
when: when displaying forensic results to players
why: Location-sorted matches reveal movement patterns.

text: Make each location visit return a clear yes-or-no answer, and show the visited-location list so the player sees progress and what remains.
when: the player is canvassing locations
why: a visible record shows progress and prevents repeat visits

text: Show confidence levels on a map, such as certain, remembered, traces only, or guessed, so players can judge which locations are reliable.
Track whether ordered official actions were carried out, since a later petition can reveal that a committee was never convened.

1) Indict, naming the accused, charge and alleged harm. 2) Take the plea. 3) Swear a jury to decide on the evidence. 4) Adjourn if no agreement, keeping the accused in custody. 5) Seek written legal opinions on contested questions. 6) Reach a verdict. 7) Let a later court refuse to enforce it. 8) Allow appeal to a higher authority.
1) Read the formal charge and take the accused's plea. 2) Hear the accusers' evidence. 3) Introduce related prior acts. 4) Hear the defence. 5) Deliver the verdict.
when: when building a courtroom or case-file sequence

text: 1) Identify who had authority to order each action. 2) Identify who only relayed or filtered complaints. 3) Check whether the record supports the favoritism charge. 4) Assign blame to the actor who actually shielded the suspect.
when: a suspect seems exempt from scrutiny while others are pursued on the same grounds
why: Blame lands on the wrong actor when intermediaries, not the senior figure, did the shielding.

text: Offering a suspect a trial with a not-guilty plea or a full confession with mercy trades a contested outcome for a surer, lighter one.
Build a character's sympathy in plain sight, such as sincere principles stated in a calm scene, then invert it as hidden facts surface so the exposure lands with force.
why: The reader accepts the virtue at face value, so the reversal contradicts a belief the reader actually held.

text: Trusting a sales pitch, staff assurance or credible source's attributed claim stops checking; omitted parts or wrong attribution carry forward unless tested.
why: Trust in the source stops the reader from testing the claim.

text: Witnesses are more likely to share sensitive information after the questioner states a clear purpose and offers a verifiable identity.
when: When a witness is initially reluctant to disclose a location or private fact.
why: Trust depends on the questioner appearing legitimate and transparent.

text: Nonverbal reactions from an expert, such as a dismissive gesture, signal doubt and let the audience gauge how far each expert is trusted.
when: Experts disagree and their reactions are shown.
why: Reactions reveal trust levels without explicit statements.

text: A victim who trusts the person delivering a claim and cannot easily verify it is likely to accept the staged story.
when: The victim cannot check the document or destination directly.
why: Trust removes the motive to question the claim.

text: Let the hired protector become part of the trap, so the character the reader trusts is the means of the theft.
when: writing a mystery where the victim hires help
why: Betraying trust reverses the reader's expectation of safety.

text: Looking only at total gain and ignoring the order of events misses how a sequence can shift a claim.
when: Analyzing a motive tied to multiple events.
why: Gain depends on sequence as well as amount.

text: Accepting the appearance of a natural cause without checking the mechanism behind it allows a planned act to pass as fate.
when: Judging whether an event was accidental
why: Appearances can be arranged to match a natural cause, so only the mechanism reveals the truth

text: Asking a helpful witness for favours spends their trust; abusing it can end their cooperation and damage later investigation.
when: when relying on a sympathetic character to deliver a favour
why: Cooperation depends on trust, which is finite and easily lost.

text: Judging a witness's reliability by appearance or social status, rather than by checkable position, leads to accepting false testimony.
when: Assessing whether a witness can be trusted.
why: Appearance and status do not establish where a witness actually was or what they saw.

text: An unusually good offer can be a lure: its oddities may hide a fabricated identity or a trap, so such offers should be treated as clues rather than luck.
when: A character offers an unusually favourable deal.
why: The offer conceals a motive, and its oddities expose it.

text: A trusted NPC's result can be correct only if the player verifies the process, so reliance on the NPC's reputation trades speed for risk of error.
when: When designing a puzzle where an NPC provides a test result.
why: Trust can hide a gap in the procedure, and verification costs time.

text: Sympathy can open information to the player while lowering their guard, a tradeoff that a trust or composure meter on an NPC can model.
A single short note can be written in alternating words by two people, and their differing stroke strength and letterforms reveal who wrote which words.
Check both sides of a document, since one object can carry several kinds of information that a single glance would miss.
when: The object has writing or information on more than one face.

text: A scroll that quotes a second character's report gives the player two sources, each with its own bias, to weigh against each other.
when: when writing in-world documents
why: Competing sources make players judge reliability.

text: Divide the explanation between an outside witness account and an insider confession, so the second part adds new information instead of repeating the first.
when: Delivering a late reveal that needs both an external view and internal motive
why: Two sources cover different ground, so the audience gets both how and why.

text: Evidence falls into two tiers: grounds that justify examination, and proofs that can sustain a verdict, namely a voluntary confession or two credible witnesses to a specific act.
when: when grading evidence before an accusation
why: separating leads from conclusive proof prevents weak indicators from becoming a conviction

text: 1) Plant the link as two separate facts in the first scene. 2) Keep a plausible separate-person explanation in place. 3) Have an outside witness show the transformation. 4) Follow with a confession that gives motive and mechanism.
when: Revealing that a surprising figure is a transformed or hidden version of another character
why: A witnessed demonstration makes the reveal believable, and the confession adds history the witness could not provide.

text: Give clues two plausible readings, one harmless and one damning, and let context, a second item, or later confirmation settle which holds, so the player weighs and chooses.
when: Designing evidence documents or visual clues for players.
why: A clue with one obvious reading gives no reason to deliberate, and players who read context reach different conclusions.

text: A typeface identifies a machine model, but many machines share that model, so a typeface match alone is weak evidence about who used the machine.
why: the model is widely used across offices

text: Each typewriter has individual defects such as a chipped letter, misaligned character or uneven shape; compare typed letters for matching defects, which point to one machine.
why: Wear and damage are unique to each machine

text: Assuming who physically produced a document can hide the person who supplied the knowledge or tools used to make it.
1) Classify each NPC answer as denial, partial admission or reframed admission. 2) Weight the type by the NPC's experience. 3) Use the weighting as one signal, not as proof.
when: Designing NPC interrogation responses.

text: Before accepting an uncanny explanation, list ordinary causes, including a non-human creature used by a person, and check which fit every physical trace.
when: When an event seems supernatural or impossible.
why: Most apparent uncanny events have ordinary causes visible in the physical traces.

text: A supernatural claim that gives concrete, checkable details and is later confirmed by independent news makes the audience carry the claim forward on trust until the match arrives.
when: A story presents an unverifiable supernatural source whose details can be tested later.
why: Withholding verification keeps the claim in play, and a dated, timed match then resolves the doubt.

text: Let supernatural language describe a character's mind while actions are explained by ordinary means.
when: writing horror-tinged narration or dialogue
why: it keeps the atmosphere while grounding events in plausible causes

text: Keep an unexplained event open rather than assuming it is ordinary; but when resolving a supernatural mystery, leaving the uncanny unexplained or explaining it without trace support frustrates players.
when: A sound or event has no confirmed source; or when resolving a supernatural mystery.
why: Presenting an open question as settled removes its tension and misinforms the reader; players need answers the evidence can support.

text: A ready explanation, such as having a reason, can end inquiry too early, so the investigator should ask what that reason actually is.
when: A person offers a justification for an unusual request.
why: Accepting a stated reason without probing leaves the real purpose hidden.

text: 1) List each symptom. 2) Assign it to the proposed cause if that cause explains it. 3) Collect the symptoms left over as the unexplained residue.
when: when a witness offers a natural explanation for a strange condition
why: Separating explained effects from the remainder shows whether the cause is complete.

text: 1) Identify the claim the whole inquiry depends on. 2) Ask whether anyone verified it. 3) Propose a rival explanation, such as impersonation, that would explain the facts. 4) Work out who the alternative actor is and why they would act that way.
when: An investigation or deduction rests on a claim that no one has checked.
why: Testing a foundational assumption can reopen the full set of explanations, even though it proves nothing by itself.

text: Treat a document's emotional tone as a sign of possible bias, not as proof of its claims.
Suppress theorizing while observing, because speculation shapes the imagination and distorts what is seen.
when: Recording events as they happen
why: Speculation fills gaps in perception with imagined content.

text: Treat an inferred belief drawn from another person's reading of behaviour as a lead to pursue, not a settled fact.
when: A belief is inferred second-hand from observed behaviour.
why: The inference is itself an interpretation and may be wrong.

text: When evidence supports several explanations, state the uncertainty openly rather than forcing one answer.
when: evidence is genuinely ambiguous on a side matter
why: openly stated ambiguity reads as realism rather than carelessness

text: Do not accept an interval, motive or route as settled until independent records confirm it; a record certifying itself does not count as confirmation.
why: Trusting a record because its own source certifies it, without independent checking, can hide errors.

text: NPCs who accept a faction leader's stated lineage without checking let players later discover the claim was never verified.
when: a faction leader makes an unverified claim of rank or descent
why: Acceptance without checking leaves a gap the story can later expose.

text: An explanation that depends on actions no witness saw is weak; mark which links are unconfirmed so the player can judge them.
A claimed link between a suspect's act and a witness's bodily mark can be accepted without any test of that link.
Inferred links reflect what the reconstructor expects to find, and without an outside check they can distort the result.
A single observer's expectation can be wrong, such as assuming a household is sleeping in, yet fit the reasoning without being checked.
A vague presentiment that is never tested can be left unexamined and forgotten.
Rejecting an inference only because it is uncomfortable is as biased as accepting it for that reason, so the inference must be tested.
when: When an inference points toward a person the investigator would rather not suspect.
why: Emotional preference distorts judgment in both directions.

text: Once a deduction is explained it looks simple, which leads people to underrate the method that produced it.
Accepting a proposed solution before checking it against physical traces, such as an open window, risks a wrong conclusion.
Without an explicit comparison to the stated source, a mismatch may go unnoticed.
Odds quoted as evidence are only as sound as the comparison behind them, so they should be checked before being relied on.
A clever theory can survive simply because nobody checks its assumptions about how the people involved would behave.
Assuming a required preparation step is impossible for a suspect, without checking how the object is normally used, can wrongly clear that suspect.
when: when a suspect is ruled out by a claimed constraint
why: A constraint may be less strict than assumed, so it needs testing.

text: A premise accepted without checking can carry an error through every later step of the deduction.
Accepting a coincidence without checking it can hide a real pattern, and a speculative theory of fate is not evidence.
A conclusion preserved without its method looks more authoritative than it is, because the reasoning that produced it cannot be checked.
Relying on the most recent or most detailed explanation without testing it lets a persuasive but wrong account stand.
Holding a theory privately lets new facts test it fairly, but it can go unchecked for too long if no new facts arrive.
when: when an investigator keeps a theory without publicly committing to it
why: early public commitment creates pressure to defend the theory rather than test it

text: Treat claims citing unnamed authority, or undated letters bearing only a bare name, as unverified; a name alone does not show who made the claim or request.
when: when assessing reported claims
why: Nothing ties the text to a checkable author or moment.

text: Record an odd observation, such as a missing object or strange visitor, in a journal with no explanation so it can be linked later.
when: a game has a log or journal system
why: unexplained entries become clues when later facts arrive

text: An unexplained name in a guest or access record flags a possible uninvited person; trace the record's source before dismissing it.
Use an object that is known to exist but unavailable at the critical moment; avoid this device if the audience must examine the object itself.
when: the plot needs evidence that cannot be inspected at the key point
why: examination requires the object to remain intact

text: A withheld letter or a message with no return address can serve as a quest flag that the player must chase down.
when: When designing quests around communication.

text: Undocumented transfers of an item between holders open room for tampering or doubt, making the evidence unreliable.
when: when evidence changes hands informally
why: Without a record, no one can confirm the item's condition.

text: Without dates, an order inferred from message content may be wrong.
when: Reconstructing a sequence of messages that lack timestamps
why: Content-based order depends on assumptions about what each message presupposes

text: A notice or sign can be placed or removed by someone with an interest, and the official record may not show who did it.
Evidence obtained without authority may be inadmissible, so how a document was obtained matters as much as what it shows.
Treating an undated, uncited journal line as authoritative only because it is old.
when: A document is used as the only authority for an event
why: Age does not establish accuracy or a date

text: Undated documents or facts give no anchor for when events occurred; do not place them in a timeline, since that invents precision the evidence does not support.
Treat a paper lacking the usual attestation and oath as unfinished and unofficial, and never present it as evidence that was offered.
when: reviewing loose records
why: missing formal attestation shows it was never presented
