text: A witness who hides one fact often hides others, so verify each statement separately rather than trusting the whole account.
Check a worker's claimed skill with a practical test, since a written credential can be false.
when: A character's stated expertise matters to the plot or to a decision.

text: Let an NPC with a grudge give accurate sightings mixed with self-serving claims, so the player must cross-check them with another NPC.
when: designing NPC testimony
why: Mixed reliability rewards verification.

text: Treat a witness's claim to have thought they heard someone as something to verify, not as a fact.
when: A witness reports hearing or seeing with uncertainty.
why: Hedged perception is weak evidence until checked.

text: Write witness dialogue so players can verify its details, since an NPC may be right about an event and wrong about its cause.
when: an NPC reports a sighting

text: Keep an accusation checkable through physical evidence, so a rumour about the accuser's reliability cannot fully replace testing the original claim.
when: Designing a discredited witness or rival rumour
why: Verifiable evidence lets the player separate the claim from the attack on the accuser

text: Human remains keep permanent identifiable structures over long periods, and identification has been possible from remains recovered from furnace ashes.
when: Assessing whether remains can later be identified after attempted destruction.
why: Bone and structure persist through many destructive processes.

text: Burned remains can still identify what was destroyed; compare how the residue burns and look for less-charred fragments that reveal the original item.
when: An object was partly or fully burned.
why: Burn patterns and surviving fragments preserve enough of the original to be recognized.

text: When a face is too damaged to recognize, identify a person through lasting features: build, carriage, hair colour and small distinctive marks.
when: identity must be fixed from disfigured remains or partial evidence
why: Such features persist when the face is unusable.

text: Let a victim refuse to name an attacker early, as a visible anomaly that hints the scene was staged.
when: staged-crime design
why: a supposed victim's silence signals that the scene was arranged

text: 1) Find a specific, idiosyncratic physical mark on the remains. 2) Compare it with the known record of the candidate. 3) Accept identity only if the mark matches.
when: Confirming identity from remains.
why: A specific mark is harder to fake than a general resemblance.

text: 1) Publish a reward notice describing the body, clothing and jewellery in detail. 2) Place it where the victim's circle or trade will read it. 3) Follow each lead that comes back.
when: the victim is unknown and ordinary inquiry has failed

text: 1) Recover the object and link it to the body part or fragment. 2) Document the discovery process and location. 3) Check whether the identifying item is unique before accepting an identity.
when: Establishing identity from items found separately from remains.
why: An object is only as strong as its uniqueness and the chain of discovery that connects it to the person.

text: Establish the victim's identity first, since every later deduction depends on it.
Give an NPC's corpse a distinguishing mark, such as a scar or a missing item, that players can compare with the NPC's known description.
when: Designing an identifiable body in a mystery.

text: A victim's described symptoms, such as numbness, tingling, drowsiness, and warmth, can help identify the drug involved.
when: A poisoning is suspected and the victim can describe symptoms.
why: Symptom patterns are specific enough to narrow the possible drugs.

text: A person who arranges an alibi is probably engaged in something criminal, so the arrangement is a clue to hidden intent.
when: the victim's own preparations reveal intent investigators did not see
why: Precautions reveal behaviour that ordinary explanations would not produce

text: To reason about a victim's message, imagine their confinement, remaining time and options, then infer what they would most likely choose to do.
when: A victim may have left a record in a confined space.

text: Profile a victim's habits, wealth display, impressionability and superstitions to identify who could exploit them.
Rebuild a victim's history from prior investigations, old partnerships and rumours; a background gathered over years yields the strongest list of possible motives.
when: When many past associations could explain a motive.
why: Each past association can be checked against records.

text: A theory requiring a victim to act against their known habits or the scene's layout is weak and should be tested first.
when: when evaluating a crime theory
why: Known behavior constrains what the victim could have done.

text: 1) Ask who the victim was and where she came from. 2) Ask what she did, how she lived, her habits and morals. 3) Ask her company, her enemies and whether she was thought rich.
when: When a victim's past is unknown and a motive must be found.
why: These questions cover the places where motives and secrets usually sit.

text: Use the victims' appearance and condition as a clue to what they experienced.
A victim of high social standing may refuse to prosecute and resolve matters privately, so the investigator's findings may never reach the courts.
when: when the victim has social influence
why: Social standing gives the victim leverage to avoid public process.

text: Let the injured party be a possible culprit, so the investigation tests the player's trust in the victim.
when: A crime is staged or the victim has a hidden stake.
why: A victim who may have caused the crime turns the investigation into a question of trust.

text: Let the victim's own belongings become the evidence that moves suspicion, so an ordinary object shifts the theory.
when: Introducing a physical clue in a mystery.
why: A personal item ties the crime to the victim and redirects suspicion.

text: Keep the victim's identity uncertain, with conflicting accounts, until the reveal, since confusion over who died can be a deliberate design tool.
when: the reveal depends on who the victim was
why: Uncertainty holds attention and makes the eventual identification a payoff.

text: Subverting the expected victim: make the apparent target the one drawn toward the threat, so the reveal reverses the audience's assumption about who is in danger.
when: When designing a stray-animal or monster mystery with a companion NPC
why: Players who expect the victim to be passive are surprised when the victim is the agent, which strengthens the reveal.

text: When a victim's own information, such as a schedule, is used by an opponent, that information becomes the means to predict and intercept the opponent later.
when: a character's ordinary information is visible to a threat
why: Turning the victim's knowledge against the thief lets the pursuer anticipate a waypoint.

text: A document the victim left behind can reverse an accusation, showing the death was self-inflicted and clearing the suspect.
when: a suspect is blamed for a death that the victim may have caused
why: the victim's own record reframes the motive and removes the apparent killer

text: Do not treat a victim's movements as proof of identity until other traces confirm the path.
when: Tracing a victim's route
why: An unconfirmed route can lead to the wrong suspect.

text: Make the victim's identity the hidden variable, and keep a checkable description such as hair color or a physical feature that players can compare against the body.
when: authoring a murder mystery with an identity twist, or designing a body discovery scene
why: A checkable description lets the player detect the mismatch, so the reversal is fair; a recognition or hesitation turns a passive body into an active lead.

text: A threatened target's reactions, such as contacting authorities, hiring protection or seeking help, can each move them closer to a planned trap.
when: a threat has been issued to a target
why: Each protective action is a step the threat-maker can anticipate and exploit.

text: A victim who does not report an attack and waits a long time before disclosing it limits what can be checked and may conceal the attack's cause.
when: When an attack victim stays silent or delays disclosure.
why: Delay erodes physical evidence and gives the victim time to control the story.

text: When a charge names specific victims, its proof rests on the victims' accounts of their injuries.
When the manner of death is unclear, examine the victim's recent activities and relationships for motive, enemies, or offences.
when: the cause of death is ambiguous

text: Examine the dead person's finances, debts and obligations, since they can reveal a motive that points to a different culprit.
A victim's diary naming incidents and wrongs gives a list of people with cause for revenge, widening the field of suspects.
when: reviewing a victim's records

text: A victim who trusts a public name and a published notice can be steered to seek a specific figure, without verifying that figure's identity.
when: The victim has a reason to seek help and a trusted information channel that can be influenced.
why: Trust in a public source replaces independent verification of the person it advertises.

text: A motive can reverse the apparent victim: the dead man was planning harm against the killer, making the death the outcome of a plot rather than a random attack.
Victims may downplay harm out of loyalty or fear, so the record can understate events; a victim's minimizing account is not the full measure of harm.

1) Identify the victim's preparations. 2) Infer the criminal enterprise they imply. 3) Identify who that enterprise targets. 4) Treat that target as a likely suspect. 5) Test the theory against the facts.
when: a victim's arrangements suggest a hidden plan
why: A victim's plan can point to the person it was aimed against

text: Victim's fits or reaction to a look or touch is no infallible proof of guilt; it may be a red herring for an innocent character, so test against other evidence.
when: designing mystery clues

text: Key witnesses move, travel or settle abroad, so an investigator can arrive a day too late and find the witness gone.
when: witnesses are not fixed in one place during an inquiry

text: A trapped victim who expects a search may write a message where the attacker is unlikely to look, since paper is easy to find or destroy.
when: A victim is trapped and wants to name an attacker.
why: Paper can be found or destroyed.

text: A target hurrying to answer a lure leaves traces such as transport use and timetable inquiries, which investigators can follow to the destination.
when: The target acts quickly on a forged request.
why: Haste forces unplanned actions that reveal the route taken.

text: A victim's remarks about a past marriage or hidden means, along with unusual visitors, hint at a concealed history that may explain the crime.
when: When reconstructing a victim's secrets from scene evidence.
why: Offhand statements and callers reveal connections the victim did not disclose.

text: A missing key witness who holds the proof gives the story a clock, keeping the case open and driving the search.
when: the story depends on the witness's return

text: Check a suspect's movements over a long period, and weigh a record of unexplained absences as evidence.
when: assessing a suspect's opportunity
why: Patterns of absence reveal opportunity over time.

text: Ask a suspect to describe a claimed experience in detail, such as a game move by move, to test whether they actually know it.
when: A suspect claims familiarity with an activity.

text: Work backward from a victim's schedule to plant questions about unexpectedly early actions that players must solve from the evidence.
Trace the victim's last movements as well as the suspects' movements; the route can reveal who followed the victim and why.
when: The suspect list is wide and the victim's route is unexplained
why: A victim's path often points to an unlisted pursuer.

text: Lights or traces showing where a victim was fix the victim's position and so the likely place of attack.
when: Establishing where a crime occurred
why: A victim's position is evidence of the attack location.

text: Mud that is dried or freshly made after rain tells marks left on entry apart from marks left on exit, so the order can be fixed by the mud's state.
when: after rain falls between two visits
why: rain changes how marks look over time

text: Overlooking that the victim could keep moving after dosing changes the timeline and can make a suspect look impossible when they are not.

1) Lay out each person's movements against a clock, sequencing departures, arrivals and destinations. 2) Mark intervals when no one saw them. 3) Test whether those intervals let each person reach the scene. 4) Shared destinations or meetings then stand out.
when: several parties' movements fall within a short window, or when locating opportunity in a case
why: Ordering movements in time exposes shared destinations and meetings; unobserved intervals are where opportunity hides

text: 1) Start from the victim's known behaviour and dates, not the suspects. 2) Check each stated time against independent physical facts such as distance and travel time. 3) Test the date of any message against when it was used.
when: a suspect's account of when something was known conflicts with independent timing

text: Log the player's movements after a discovery so witness NPCs report flight and calm differently, letting one action read as guilt or innocence.
Make a suspect's death close one thread while opening another, so the case moves forward rather than stalling.
when: Killing a suspect in the middle of a mystery
why: A death removes a false lead and creates a new question about who was responsible.

text: People who do not know a colleague's hidden past judge them only by present conduct, while a few confidants know the history.
when: a person's past is known to only a few
why: secrets are shared selectively, so few people can explain later reactions

text: Internal bleeding can hide a serious wound from bystanders, so an apparently unhurt person may be badly injured.
A gentle or friendly appearance is no guide to guilt; a suspect's history and background give better evidence.
Check a suspect's past dealings with the victim, such as an earlier charge, as a possible hidden tie that explains the link.
when: Reviewing motive and connections.
why: Prior contact can reveal motive or a concealed relationship.

text: Agreement among several writers can hide a single origin when all of them draw on the same source, so they should count as one witness.
when: multiple accounts appear to confirm one another
why: shared sourcing is easy to miss

text: 1) Keep a central figure's past out of the main action. 2) Have an outside witness reveal one fragment of it in passing. 3) Give the witness a reason to be reluctant or a personal stake. 4) Add a contrasting view from another character.
when: A victim's past must matter later but cannot be stated outright without spoiling the reveal.
why: A witness with a stake makes the fact feel earned and lets readers weigh sources.

text: Place a key fact with a side character who may disclaim its relevance. Its significance should become clear only when it fills a gap in the player's notes.
when: when designing clues delivered through dialogue
why: Delayed meaning rewards players who keep and compare information.

text: A villain who explains the plan while the captive is still active can leak information the captive uses to reverse the trap.
why: Explanation scenes give the trapped party facts they can act on

text: Assuming a lone actor without checking for others can misdirect the whole timeline and the suspect list.
A villain who makes lethal attacks should have a motive the player can discover in proportion to the threat.
Allow a character the player likes to be a suspect, and provide clues that test that affection against the evidence.
when: Designing a suspect the player is fond of
why: Affection otherwise replaces evidence in the player's judgment

text: Let the villain die by the same means used on the victims; the matching end gives strong closure without a separate trial.
when: Resolving a story whose antagonist used a hazard or tool against others.
why: A poetic mirror satisfies the player's sense of justice more directly than an off-screen resolution.

text: Make the obvious suspects plausible, then reveal the culprit as a trusted insider.
A visitor who leaves visibly shaken signals that the news they carried was grave.
when: a visitor leaves visibly upset after a conversation

text: When an expected visitor enters, a trigger can change an NPC's behavior, with preset detention or dialogue outcomes.
why: a scripted state change responds to the arrival of a specific character

text: Visits to an isolated person can serve as channels that carry names and claims out to outsiders.
when: when a confined or isolated person receives regular visitors
why: Visitors pass on what they hear to others

text: A person who visits a crime scene is not necessarily the culprit; a later intruder may be a different party.
when: Interpreting a stakeout's results.
why: Assuming a single identity for everyone who returns leads to wrong conclusions.

text: A shared description such as approximate age or poor clothing is a weak link on its own and should not be treated as proof of identity.
when: Matching an unidentified body or person to a known individual.
why: Many people share such general traits.

text: 1) Compare the name a visitor gives with what the employer and other witnesses reported. 2) Check whether the visit matches the normal official process. 3) Count independent sources supporting the claim.
when: A visitor gives a name, acts eccentric and refuses to wait, or an authority figure asks for something valuable that cannot be checked directly.
why: A mismatch in name, process or sources can expose impersonation.

text: 1) Collect visit accounts from several witnesses. 2) Build a combined visit history with dates and entry points. 3) Check each entry against at least one other source. 4) Look for a repeated pattern.
when: a timeline depends on entries that a single checkpoint does not record
why: cross-checked sources reveal patterns that one record would miss

text: Do not treat a glimpse made under stress or at night as proof of identity.
Ask what an unauthorized visitor came to obtain, since the purpose points to something overlooked in the scene.
when: Someone entered a place without authorization
why: Purpose reveals targets the scene may still hide

text: A voice heard through a closed door is weak identification. The listener may be unable to name the speaker and may only believe it matches a voice heard earlier.
when: identifying a speaker by sound through a barrier
why: muffled, indistinct sound carries little identifying detail

text: A sound few other sources could make, such as a known door creak, can pin a witness's timing to one event or show who moved when.
when: the sound is distinctive and witnesses know it well
why: A sound only one source can produce pins the listener's timing to one event.

text: A shift in narrative voice can suggest the writer's identification or bias; treat it as a lead to test, not as proof.
A strong, distinctive voice suits imitation: listeners remember its traits, and the copy need not be perfect.
Use a voice imitation as cover only when witnesses hear it at a distance, not when a witness can see the face clearly or handle the body.
Voice recognition is untested until the witness hears the voice again; ask whether they would know it, and then test it.
when: A witness claims to recognise a voice from an earlier event.
why: A recognition claim made from memory alone may not hold up when the voice is heard again.

text: A disguised voice can sound unnatural to someone who knows the speaker, so familiarity can expose a disguise.
when: A witness heard a voice through a door or at a distance.
why: Known speakers have characteristic pitch and cadence that a disguise alters.

text: Accepting a voice on the telephone without a second check lets an impersonator pass as a trusted contact.
Assume a voice heard through a barrier may belong to someone other than the expected person until sight or a second clue confirms it.
when: When identifying a speaker by voice alone
why: Voices are easy to mistake behind a door

text: 1) Choose a line the victim said earlier. 2) Practise it aloud until delivery feels natural. 3) Build the cover story around that line.
A voice heard without sight is hearsay about who was present; it establishes presence, not identity, so ask how the witness excludes another speaker.
when: when a witness names someone from a voice heard without seeing them, or reports a second person they did not see
why: A voice may belong to more than one person; hearing a voice does not confirm who spoke.

text: Every concealment plan has a weak point, often a post-event step that invites suspicion; without direct evidence, look there for the culprit's gap.
why: plans have logical gaps

text: Test a reconstruction against its weakest point, meaning the single detail it explains worst. If that point fails, the account is incomplete.
when: A reconstruction fits most facts but leaves one contradiction.
why: One unexplained detail can overturn an otherwise tidy story.

text: Focus on the moment a victim becomes vulnerable, such as during exhaustion, rather than on the device used, because that moment reveals the real opening.
when: analyzing how a defended target was reached
why: focusing on the device hides the opening

text: A case checklist is only as strong as its weakest entry, so a missing element such as an unrecovered weapon leaves a visible gap.
when: When assessing an accusation against a checklist
why: One unfilled element can invalidate the whole case

text: Label a hypothesis that rests only on one interested party's suspicion as weak, even while still pursuing it.
why: Honest labelling prevents a thin lead from being treated as established.

text: A defence can discredit a whole inference chain by finding its one thin or unexplained point and casting doubt on everything built on it.
when: a case relies on a chain of reasoning
why: sceptics judge the chain by its weakest link

text: A reconstructed chain is only as strong as its weakest link, so check each link; a step without an observed cue is a guess that breaks the inference.
why: a plausible whole can hide one unanchored step

text: A chain that reads as complete can hide a weak link, so each step needs independent checking rather than repeated reading of one document.
when: when a single written source supports several steps
why: Re-reading one source confirms its claims, not their independent truth.

text: Weak links accumulated together do not automatically form a strong chain.
when: When many small pieces of evidence point to one suspect
why: Quantity of weak evidence does not raise its quality

text: Give a faked death a visible weak point, such as a body mismatch or a witness, so a careful player can expose it.
when: designing a staged death in a story or world
why: a fair weak point rewards careful players without making the fake obvious

text: Make false leads resolvable: reveal missing support, such as an accuser without proof, or the motive behind a false tip, so players can dismiss it.
when: Designing red herrings or misleading NPC information.
why: Players gain confidence in their reasoning when a false lead can be ruled out by evidence or an understood motive.

text: People who spread large payments across many institutions often want to hide their total wealth from others.
when: Transactions are split across several banks
why: Spreading funds keeps anyone from seeing the full amount.

text: Physical wear such as dirt, tears or crumpling makes an object read as worthless, so players dismiss it even when it matters.
when: An important item is shown in a damaged state.
why: Players judge value from appearance and condition.

text: Visible valuables draw the eye and hold attention even when a viewer tries to look away from them.
when: A valuable object is displayed in a shared scene
why: Conspicuous objects capture visual attention

text: A wealthy person who holds no office and is not old is seated with ordinary members, so money alone does not earn deference.
when: community ranks by age and office
why: age and office set rank, and property does not

text: An estate can be split so one party holds life use while another inherits the remainder after that party's death.
when: dividing property between a surviving spouse and heirs
why: Splitting interests in time lets each party's claim be honoured.

text: Spending beyond known income is a lead, not proof of hidden funds: trace where the surplus came from and verify it, since a second money source may exist.
when: when a visible lifestyle or expensive possession exceeds a suspect's known income or declared means
why: Spending beyond declared means points to a second source of money that must be verified.

text: A merchant or quest-giver who displays wealth can be marked as a suspect, and an item left in view can be made inspectable as a clue.
when: Designing NPCs and scene objects for a mystery

text: Worn footwear combined with carefully kept nails suggests a person whose appearance does not match their apparent occupation.
when: Judging a disguised or misrepresented social station.
why: Physical upkeep reflects daily habits that disguise rarely covers completely.

text: An item worn in one specific way points to habitual, repeated use by one person, which can identify an owner.
when: reading personal items for routine
why: repeated handling leaves a consistent pattern

text: A comfortable display of wealth can hide private ruin, so surroundings do not reliably show a person's finances.
when: when judging a character's financial state from appearances
why: Comfort and exhausted funds can coexist.

text: Spending alone does not prove theft, because the suspect may have legitimate sources such as a pension, salary, loan or sold assets.
when: When treating lavish spending as evidence of a crime.
why: Lifestyle shows spending, not the source of the money or who acted.

text: Showing only a suspect's wealth hides the motive; the debt and its urgency are what give a reason to act.

1) List the suspect's visible possessions, clothing and receipts. 2) Compare them against a baseline, such as a comparable household. 3) Check each stated income source before concluding that spending exceeds means.
when: When testing whether a suspect's lifestyle is supported by known income.
why: A baseline makes the contrast visible, and checking sources prevents conclusions from unverified assumptions.

text: Give a merchant or lord NPC a visible debt record, and use a shop or bank event that reveals financial trouble to trigger a quest offer.
when: designing NPC bargains in a town or dungeon
why: the player can see why the character accepts or refuses a deal

text: Make a debt discoverable through social systems, and give a second NPC an unexplained gap that complicates the motive.
A weapon's owner, loaded count and physical condition are checkable facts, so each can confirm or dispute a claim about the weapon.
when: A weapon's history is part of the investigation

text: Where a projectile lodges in an object constrains the shooter's position relative to the victim's body.
Treat an item-fit clue as weak when the item could have been worn on either hand or its owner is unknown.
when: an item-fit clue is used to narrow suspects
why: Without a fixed hand or known owner, the fit says little about the wearer.

text: A weapon that belonged to a known household links the crime to that household, so tracing an object's owner gives a lead.
Check whether a weapon was actually fired; undischarged chambers can weaken an explanation that assumes it was.
Linking a weapon to a specific item of the victim's clothing, such as a hat with a matching hole, ties the object to the victim.
when: Establishing ownership of a weapon through a matching item.
why: A physical correspondence between two items connects them.

text: A soft bullet fired through woven cloth usually picks up an impression of the weave, so a recovered bullet can link to the garment it passed through.
Reading a cut or tear as a weapon mark without checking the garment's style or whether the weapon was drawn is a common error.
Striking bone can flatten one side of a bullet, erasing its fabric marks there; the unflattened side may keep them, so match only if some surface stays intact.
when: A bullet is recovered for comparison

text: Track who has handled a weapon or item, since each handling can change what it can prove and an unknown chain makes it unreliable.
when: an item is moved, grabbed or struggled over
why: handling can add or remove traces

text: Do not identify a person from the visible hilt of a weapon alone.
when: A weapon is found at a scene
why: A weapon's visible part is shared and does not establish who held it

text: Weather changes falling between two traces bound when an intrusion or event could have occurred, so its timing can be read without a witness.
Wheel ruts and hoof marks in wet ground can show that a vehicle was present during a period of rain, dating the marks when the rain's timing is known.
when: Dating a mark against weather
why: Rain timing bounds when the mark could have formed

text: Wet or muddy clothing can contradict a claimed alibi, especially when the weather or location says the person should have stayed dry.
when: a witness claims to have stayed indoors

text: Deliberate dusting or wiping of surfaces suggests the actor knew their own traces were already on those objects.
Weathering dates an object only when its starting age is known; with an uncertain origin, decay evidence misleads.
Wet ground and busy footpaths can multiply or erase tracks, so sorting them can defeat the whole approach.
when: Tracks are collected from a site with heavy use or wet conditions
why: Overlapping and washed-out prints are hard to attribute

text: A clean surface suggests deliberate wiping by a careful culprit, but when a surface shows no traces, first check whether it could hold one, since the material may explain the absence.
when: A surface shows no prints or traces
why: Absence can come from the surface rather than from deliberate action.

text: Let weather echo a character's emotional state, so storms and debris outside mirror disorder inside.
Bad weather moves a crowd into fewer indoor venues, concentrating listeners and changing who hears what.
Weather cues such as still air or unexplained movement in leaves warn that a storm or turning point is coming before it arrives.
when: Building suspense before a reveal or turning point.
why: Audiences read environmental signs as predictions and feel tension while waiting.

text: A windowless room with one thick door cuts off outside help and muffles violence, so it suits a final confrontation.
when: Staging a climactic confrontation.
why: Isolation removes rescue and hides noise, raising the stakes of the scene.

text: Vivid, certain impressions and feelings of insight from someone impaired, distressed, or under a perception-altering drug are not evidence of accuracy; verify them independently.
when: Receiving testimony or observations from someone impaired, distressed, or under a perception-altering effect.
why: Impairment can produce confident, detailed recollections, and elation or sensory intensity can feel like insight while being inaccurate.

text: When a suspect pleads a mental defence, the central question moves from who committed the act to whether the suspect's mind can be judged responsible, which a specialist must assess.
when: A suspect's confession is paired with a claim of madness.
why: A plea of insanity changes what must be proven and who is competent to prove it.

text: A witness's senses can be confused by fear, fatigue, or outside influence, so a striking perception must be checked against a second observer.
when: when a witness reports a frightening sight
why: Strong emotion and tiredness distort perception, and a second observer can confirm or refute it.

text: A testator can redirect property by changing a will, so both the current heir's plans and the existing will determine who gains.
when: assessing who will inherit
why: A will can override the default succession.

text: A will's detailed provisions reveal relationships and who was expected to provide what within a household.
A will's pious wording can conceal the testator's real aims. Compare its stated intentions with the arrangements it actually makes.
when: when reading a will as evidence
why: Stated intentions may hide self-serving aims.

text: Do not use a will as direct evidence of guilt or of what happened after death; it shows the testator's intent, circumstances and allies, not what a person did.
Model a will or entail as a quest rule that the player learns through documents or conversation, revealing the heir and succession chain.
when: designing inheritance mysteries
why: Gradual discovery sustains the investigation.

text: Witch is the only term among overlapping labels for suspected magical practitioners that carries a compact with the Devil; the other terms do not convey that idea.
when: Interpreting the label applied to a suspect in a record.
why: The label determines which alleged allegiance and offence is presumed.

text: Early statutes made witchcraft a capital offence only when the practice had caused a death, so the harmful result was the test of guilt.
A 17th-century charging formula defined witchcraft as keeping familiarity with Satan and doing works beyond the course of nature.
Hold back an investigator's reason or a fact the player lacks, so the later reveal reframes earlier scenes and makes the action look suspicious first, then sensible.
when: When an action would look odd before the reveal, or when planning reveals in a mystery.
why: Delayed explanation keeps the player's reading open and rewards them when the reason is shown; withheld knowledge makes earlier events look different once disclosed.

text: Precautions shown without a stated purpose invite the audience to keep a question open until it is answered.
when: characters take protective steps without explanation
why: unexplained action creates curiosity

text: A story can hold back the protagonist's past guilt until late, so the threat's logic becomes readable only in hindsight.
when: when the threat is tied to the protagonist's history
why: A late disclosure reframes earlier clues and sustains suspense without an early explanation.

text: Open the story with a threat whose purpose is withheld, so the audience senses danger before it knows the reason behind it.
when: Opening a mystery with a sinister event.
why: An unexplained purpose keeps the audience reading later events for meaning.

text: Avoid pursuing a sensitive area when each question could start a chain of disclosure that the questioner cannot control.
Leave one method of the solution unexplained at the end to keep an element of mystery and room for a merciful resolution.
when: closing a mystery in which the guilty party has repented
why: A partial answer keeps the ending open while still resolving the main question.

text: A detective who privately holds a conclusion while sharing only part of it creates tension rather than a plot hole.
when: The investigator has identified the truth but not yet revealed it.
why: Withheld knowledge keeps the audience anticipating the reveal.

text: Stating a stark fact while withholding its outcome keeps tension high, because the audience waits for the next update.
when: Between revelations in a story.
why: Unresolved outcomes keep attention on what comes next.

text: An investigator who claims to hold decisive proof but refuses to reveal it keeps fear alive after a trap has failed.
when: when a trap or interrogation has not produced a confession
why: Unnamed proof leaves the suspect uncertain how much is known.

text: Withheld information can be read as evasion or concealment, eroding trust, so the reason for the delay must be clear to the audience and to allies.
when: Withholding information from allies or witnesses, or when a character or reveal delays information
why: Withheld information can be read as concealment, eroding trust.

text: Withheld knowledge needs a concrete, satisfying payoff; unpaid secrets make the audience feel cheated, and vague threats left unresolved read as filler.
when: Designing secrets, hidden knowledge, or delayed reveals.
why: Audiences need a resolution to feel the withholding was purposeful; suspense without resolution loses trust and interest.

text: Withheld or forgotten testimony still matters, and the investigator should note the gap rather than ignore it.
when: A witness cannot or will not give an account

text: Clues shown early but left uninterpreted keep tension, yet a clue that is never explained leaves the player with nothing to act on.
when: when designing a mystery reveal
why: Withholding meaning sustains suspense only until the reveal makes the clue's purpose legible.

text: Let NPCs withhold a key fact until the player presents evidence, then release it in stages that depend on the player's choices.
when: Designing NPC disclosure in a game.
why: Staged release rewards evidence-building and keeps information meaningful.

text: Do not hold back facts that the other person needs in order to act.
when: when deciding what to withhold from a listener

text: Withholding outcomes holds tension, but it blocks a reader who needs a clear answer before taking the next step.
when: The audience must understand the situation to follow what comes next.
why: Withholding trades clarity for suspense.

text: Keeping a trap's method secret preserves its effect, but frustrates helpers who cannot follow the reasoning.
when: Investigators hold a plan that would be weakened if revealed.
why: Disclosure would warn the target, while silence costs the team understanding and cooperation.

text: Explicitly promise that a withheld answer will come later; the promise keeps the question open while an unpromised delay reads as evasion.
when: the audience is asked to wait for an answer
why: The promise gives the audience a reason to keep attention; an unpromised delay frustrates.

text: Leaving a detail or mechanism unexplained keeps the reveal open, but frustrates or reads as evasion unless the unknown is clearly marked as deliberate or its reasons are given.
when: the effect or detail is central to the story
why: Players tolerate a gap they know is deliberate; explaining makes the solution feel fair.

text: Keeping a plan private prevents leaks to opponents, but leaves allies uninformed and feeling excluded, and exposed to unforeseen danger.
when: Deciding whether to share suspicions or a plan during an investigation.
why: Secrecy protects the plan while costing trust and shared reasoning.

text: A witness with a theory but no proof may keep it private, since voicing an unsupported opinion can be dismissed and expose the speaker's own secrets.
when: A witness suspects wrongdoing but lacks evidence.
why: Officials dismiss claims that come without support.

text: A person of rank may give no explanation unless asked, so their silence about a matter is itself a fact to record.
when: Someone is questioned about why they were somewhere.
why: People of standing do not volunteer explanations they are not asked for.

text: When an investigator shares facts but withholds conclusions, the audience reasons toward the answer alongside them, which builds suspense.
when: when the audience should reach the conclusion themselves
why: Hidden reasoning invites the audience to test their own guesses.

text: Keep suspicions private while questioning, revealing at most that you have an idea; early disclosure lets the source adjust or harden answers to fit your view.
when: when questioning a witness or suspect who may adjust to your view
why: A stated opinion biases the source's responses; early disclosure warns the suspect.

text: Withholding the working conclusion until evidence is complete keeps the question open, so anticipation and tension hold the audience's attention.
why: Unrevealed conclusions create expectation; the unresolved gap holds attention.

text: A detective NPC can hint that something is off and reveal the full logic only after the player visits the right location, so the reasoning rests on facts the player has already seen.
when: Designing staged reveals of an NPC's deduction.
why: Delayed reveal keeps the reasoning reproducible from what the player has gathered.

text: Scattering clues while holding back their connection gives the audience the tools but not the link, sustaining suspense until the reveal.
when: the story must delay a reveal

text: Withholding reasoning too long, or never delivering it, reads as cheating or an unfair reveal even when every fact was given; keep the chain fair, checkable and revealed after testable evidence.
when: Structuring a mystery reveal
why: Audiences need checkable clues to engage with the solution.

text: Withholding reasoning too long, or without stated reason, erodes trust, mystifies companions or loses the audience, looks arrogant, and cheats readers who missed early clues.
when: when an investigator holds back an inference
why: Unexplained teasing reads as condescension, not skill.

text: A withheld plan feels like cheating when the audience needs it to make a choice before the reveal.

1) Form the conclusion and write the suspect's name down before any arrest. 2) Delay the arrest until the suspect can be reached. 3) Confirm through an independent report and a verbatim, carefully recorded confession.
when: the solver wants certainty before acting on a case
why: a privately held answer needs confirmation before it is pressed

text: Let NPC dialogue withhold a theory or a relevant visit until the player asks the precise question or presents the right evidence, rewarding careful questioning.
Keep theories unstated and limit who hears them until evidence tests them; early disclosure lets others interfere or tip off suspects, and untested theories may mislead.
when: while an investigation is open and a theory could alert suspects or allies, or affect others if spread early
why: Untested theories may mislead; unstated theories can be revised without public loss of face.

text: Withhold the culprit's name and the detective's suspicion until the final reveal, so the audience can test the clues before the answer is given.
when: the audience has all the clues and the reveal is the payoff
why: Naming the culprit or revealing suspicion early removes the chance to test clues and turns the reveal into confirmation.

text: Let a magical effect's mechanism stay partly hidden while a plausible natural reading remains; hold back a discriminating clue so the player tests both readings.
when: when designing a mystery with competing explanations
why: Delayed evidence lets the player hold both readings and choose on proof.

text: Keep your strategy and discoveries from the opponent when an early disclosure would let them prepare a counter.
when: when the opposing side can adapt

text: Do not reach a firm conclusion when witnesses disagree or the evidence is only partial.
A character may withhold their true purpose, but the withheld information must be present in the story so the reason can be reconstructed later.
when: Writing a guide or investigator whose aims are concealed.
why: Concealment is fair only when the player can later reconstruct the hidden reason.

text: Keep a real plan from a helper when telling them would make them interfere, and deflect their questions with a plausible unrelated topic.
when: telling the truth would make another person interfere or change behaviour

text: Declare a clue conclusive without explaining why, so the player must reconstruct the logic behind it.
Withholding a conclusion until verified guards against premature blame, error and tipping-off, but delays action while an innocent person may suffer or danger continues.
when: when a suspicion involves a possibly innocent person or danger may continue
why: Fairness to hypotheses competes with the cost of delay to the person affected.

text: Withholding reasoning or purpose keeps suspense and dread high, but costs trust as characters and audience feel excluded; fair-play puzzles frustrate without a clear fact to reason with.
when: a detective holds back a deduction
why: Suspense rises while the audience feels shut out.

text: An NPC who withholds a conclusion gives the player a choice of when to act, but risks frustrating players who prefer to move immediately.
Hold the decisive revelation, witness line or central name that flips the hypothesis back until pressure has built, approaching it indirectly first; early disclosure drains suspense.
when: A scene's reversal, culprit identity or quest hypothesis depends on one revelation.
why: Delay concentrates the audience's attention on the reveal.

text: Concealing a discovery or hypothesis too long makes it look like deception once revealed, making innocent later statements seem suspect and damaging trust.
when: When an investigator keeps a theory or discovery from partners for an extended period.
why: Delayed disclosure reads as hidden intent once the reasoning emerges.

text: Withholding evidence, a sealed document or an answer too long frustrates and feels cheated; once revealed it must pay off quickly, or it reads as a dead end.
when: A mystery holds back key evidence, a sealed document or an explanation.
why: Players tolerate suspense only while they expect the answer to arrive.

text: Withhold the decisive fact or solution while investigators keep asking questions and stay active, so tension and anticipation persist until the next clue.
when: A story needs sustained tension before the next clue.
why: Repeated questions signal that an answer exists, creating anticipation.

text: Do not withhold information the audience needs to reason toward the answer; give the decisive clue before the tests begin, not at the final moment.
when: Building suspense through concealment or designing a mystery reveal.
why: Unfair concealment prevents reasoning toward the answer; players need the means to deduce it.

text: Give each withholding character a believable motive; if they could simply speak, unexplained silence reads as arbitrary, contrived or lazy plotting, breaking trust and suspense.
when: Deciding whether a character should delay disclosure.
why: Audiences tolerate delay when the silence seems motivated.

text: Withholding a central fact builds suspense, but holding it too long loses the audience. A character may keep a theory private without lying, limiting talk to public facts.
when: When staging the disclosure of a central fact, or when a character holds a private theory while others seek answers.
why: Suspense depends on the listener having context to judge what is withheld; delay past a point costs clarity.

text: Withholding a suspect's name guards people and serves legal caution and drama, but leaves a listener with authority unable to verify or act on the claim.
when: When the listener has authority or a personal stake and could alert the suspects.
why: Partial disclosure guards people at the cost of the listener's ability to check the account.

text: Witnesses may withhold evidence or suspicions for honest reasons such as personal reticence, avoiding endorsement of a superstition, or protecting property value, not guilt.
when: A witness has something relevant but does not mention it, or gives a partial account.
why: Silence can come from temperament or social or reputational motives rather than guilt.

text: A witness with direct access may hold back the decisive fact out of fear of blame, loyalty, shame or embarrassment or a promise, while truthfully telling everything else.
when: A witness has relevant knowledge or a legitimate reason to stay silent.
why: Self-protection and loyalty suppress disclosure.

text: Witnesses withhold what they judge unimportant or unrecognized, or out of delicacy, pride or feeling, and may recall it only when asked a precise question or after reflection.
when: A witness is questioned about a sensitive event or the night of a crime.
why: Witnesses judge relevance from their own view, assuming authorities would ask if it mattered; feelings and reputation shape disclosure.

text: A short, unusually light message that gives no cause but a new address leaves the reader to supply the danger.
when: Delivering a warning that must be delayed or hidden
why: A missing cause invites the audience to imagine the threat

text: A character may offer a plausible alternative route while holding stronger suspicions in private, leaving others unsure what the character actually believes.
when: a character proposes a theory that differs from their own

text: When an ally shares a plan but refuses to discuss the personal reason, listeners expect a confidence that never comes, and their expectations shift.
when: an ally discloses a goal and withholds the personal side
why: withheld information changes what the listener expects

text: Characters often keep unconfirmed discoveries private, and the audience sees the reservation only later.
Withholding the source of a document can prompt the suspect to accept questioning, since the questioner appears to know more than they reveal.
when: Questioning a suspect about a document whose origin is undisclosed.
why: Unknown knowledge on the questioner's side creates implied pressure, encouraging cooperation.

text: A questioner who demands information while hiding their own knowledge can make the other party refuse to continue.
why: the other party sees the exchange as unfair

text: A stoic character may hold back information for a stated reason that the player learns only after earning trust.
when: A reserved NPC conceals knowledge
why: Trust unlocks the true motive behind the silence

text: A character may deliberately refuse to learn facts in order to avoid a duty or to protect someone, and this refusal shapes what the story can reveal.
when: when a powerful witness would be harmed by knowing a crime
why: Choosing not to know spares the character a painful burden or a dangerous obligation.

text: Withhold the cause of a disturbance or visual evidence so characters speculate; speculation sustains tension, but concrete facts released early end it.
when: The audience must feel pressure but does not yet need facts to act on.
why: Withheld visual evidence leaves partial descriptions that keep speculation open.

text: Keep part of your knowledge in reserve when questioning a witness who may hide facts, revealing it only to get confirmation; early full disclosure makes hostile witnesses close down.
when: Questioning a witness who may hide facts.
why: Hostile witnesses close down under direct probing.

text: A witness may confirm a decision yet withhold its reason, and the gap between the two is where the hidden motive usually sits.
when: A witness acknowledges an action but refuses to explain it.
why: The unexplained reason often concerns something the witness wants kept private.

text: Keep a key NPC out of reach until late, so their account reframes the clues the player has already gathered.
when: When designing a narrative twist
why: Late testimony gains weight when earlier clues have built up unresolved questions.

text: An official's refusal to show a document can itself be a clue, since the refusal may protect the official's own position.
Holding back part of a payment and naming a smaller figure can draw a witness's interest without revealing the full value of the offer.
when: Negotiating a bribe or payment for information.
why: Partial withholding keeps the witness engaged while preserving leverage.

text: Withhold a procedural hint only when a second clue exists that corrects the first failed attempt.
when: Designing a puzzle that requires a specific procedure.
why: Without a correcting clue, players cannot recover from a wrong attempt.

text: Do not hold back evidence that helps the accused if the opponent can recover it quickly on its own.
why: Concealment is exposed when the other side finds the item anyway

text: Let NPCs give partial answers and reward players who ask the correct follow-up question.
when: Designing dialogue that hides part of its information.
why: Partial answers keep the player engaged and reward precise questioning.

text: Withholding strong contrary evidence while a belief hardens makes the eventual reversal more striking, since the prior conviction is stronger.
when: a character holds a firm conclusion that new evidence will overturn

text: Withholding an early suspicion from those who could act loses evidence that would otherwise have been available at the time.
when: A witness notices something but does not report it.
why: Delay lets evidence degrade or disappear.

text: When feuding families withhold their payments, the official who depends on them goes unsupported, which deepens community turmoil.
Withholding is staged disclosure: the holder controls what is seen and when, and reveal timing drives suspense.
when: When a character controls access to information.
why: Paced reveals keep the investigator uncertain and engaged.

text: Prolonged stasis drains tension: a long wait without a turn, peril without change, or a hesitating speaker. Recovering attention needs a sudden shift in action.
A participant who keeps part of their knowledge back leaves the shared picture incomplete, misdirecting helpers or theories built on it.
when: Pooling information across several parties, or a helper acts on partial information.

text: Evidence a witness withholds to protect someone can mislead the investigator later, even when the motive is kind.
when: a witness keeps back an item to spare an ally
why: The omission hides facts the investigator needs.

text: Withholding information can conceal truths that matter to other people who are entitled to them.
when: Keeping an investigation private

text: Withholding findings from a client can cost goodwill and trust, even when the withholding is strategically sound.
when: When an investigator keeps key findings from the party who hired them
why: Clients expect information and may judge the investigator negatively for silence

text: Holding evidence back from authorities lets an investigator steer the case, often in directions nobody planned.
Keeping a finding from a companion can leave them confused and suspicious, weakening the working relationship.
when: When an investigator withholds a discovery from a partner.
why: Partial information breeds distrust.

text: A bluff can appear to fail for a long time, so observers may grow frustrated before its payoff arrives.
when: a misdirection is running
why: The payoff is delayed by design, and impatience can undermine it.

text: Refusing to name the source of a trace breaks its chain of custody, so the trace stays unlinked to anyone.
Withholding can frustrate the audience if they have no reason to keep following the investigator.
A recipient who hesitates to share an anonymous letter may hide its real impact, which can delay the investigation.
when: When a recipient is reluctant to show a threatening message.
why: Embarrassment or fear can make the recipient withhold the most important detail.

text: Holding back a theory can let a wrong verdict stand and leave a dangerous person free.
A cut-off line of inquiry can leave the audience believing a hidden answer exists, which raises suspicion of the authorities who blocked it.
when: when a question is blocked without explanation
why: people infer concealment from unanswered questions

text: 1) Hold one specific clue back from a suspect or companion. 2) Watch whether they repeat or reference it later. 3) Treat any repetition as evidence of their knowledge.
when: when testing a theory without alerting others

text: When a narrator or reveal omits steps or knowledge, state the omission openly and keep the basis of reasoning visible; unstated gaps look like missing evidence.
when: A reveal depends on reasoning the reader cannot see, or a narrator chooses not to reveal everything.
why: Unstated omissions look like gaps in evidence rather than deliberate choices.

text: Do not withhold a fact the audience needs to follow the next scene or keep the goal in view; a missing fact breaks comprehension rather than building suspense.
when: The next scene depends on that fact.

text: Withhold your knowledge, a document's source, a find's origin or a check's method when disclosure would let a suspect tailor their account, warn them, or ruin a trap.
when: During questioning or when sharing case details.
why: Revealing the source or method lets the suspect adjust their account or conceal evidence, and preserves leverage.

text: Let an NPC withhold information until a condition such as player goodwill is met, giving a timed, specific account players can check against map locations and other NPC accounts.
when: Designing an NPC who controls access to information.
why: Tying disclosure to goodwill makes social actions affect information flow.

text: Keep a finding from the public when publishing it could alert suspects.
when: publicity would warn culprits

text: Let the game hide some evidence from the player while keeping the deduction chain checkable from clues the player has already seen.
When a character who holds information leaves or is removed, make that information available from another source so the player is not blocked.
when: when an information-holding NPC can exit the game state

text: Hold back a key object and tease its owner before linking the two, so the player connects them only at the reveal.
Withhold the conclusion until the evidence has been shown; signal only the next questions so the player assembles the pieces.
when: when designing a reveal that depends on player deduction
why: Players who build the answer themselves value the reveal more.

text: Withhold key clues during the first part of a mystery and release them in clusters before each reveal, so the player's reading of the case is only overturned at the right time.
when: Pacing clue release in a short mystery.
why: Early disclosure of reasoning removes suspense, while clustered release lets the reveal recontextualise several clues together.

text: Let a helper character withhold a key timeline fact, with a clear tell, so the cost of withholding drives the mystery's core.
Withholding a find or suspicion protects leverage, but colleagues or allies lose information and may act on an incomplete picture; weigh the cost of silence.
Withholding a theory or key fact from a partner keeps control and misdirects them, but leaves their theory incomplete and risks strain, humiliation on discovery, or failure if circumstances change.
Keeping partners uninformed protects the lead from interference but costs trust, and can turn cooperation into rivalry or leave sent-away partners angry and suspicious.
Withholding decisive evidence or the answer builds dread and engagement, but withholding too much makes the reveal feel withheld rather than earned, frustrating a reader who cannot reach it.
when: Deciding how much of the answer or a delayed reveal to hold back, including through secondhand sources.
why: Withholding creates engagement but risks frustration if clues do not reach a reachable conclusion.

text: Keeping a state ambiguous builds suspense, but if it stays unresolved when players need clarity, it becomes frustrating.
when: when a character's condition must stay uncertain

text: Withholding the answer from an accused person keeps the reveal intact but costs them the chance to respond, while telling them gives hope but risks spoiling the reveal.
when: Deciding how much an accused person should know before a set reveal.
why: Information given early can help the accused but weakens the surprise.

text: Keeping back a discovery protects a rival advantage but weakens shared evidence and slows progress for both sides.
Withholding facts keeps leverage and lets a questioner reveal them at the right moment, but too much secrecy can make the questioner seem arbitrary and stall progress.
when: A character knows facts the player or party does not and should reveal them selectively.
why: Revealing too early warns the other party; revealing nothing leaves them stuck.

text: Withholding a true clue can prevent authorities from reading it as support for a mistaken explanation, but it can also distort the case and leave a private reading unchecked.
when: When a true clue would reinforce a false impression if disclosed
why: Selective disclosure protects against misreading but risks the investigator's own judgement being wrong

text: Withholding a solution gives a stronger proof but can prolong suspense for others, which may be regretted later.
when: Deciding how long to keep a conclusion private.
why: Delay protects the case while imposing emotional costs on people kept in the dark.

text: Under a suggested theory, a witness can move from certainty about one account to tentative agreement and then to belief in the suggested account within a short exchange.
when: a theory is put to a witness repeatedly
why: Social suggestion can reshape recall.

text: A witness who first claims to have heard nothing may recall a specific detail after hearing another account repeated.
when: after exposure to other testimony or a repeated prompt
why: new information reshapes memory

text: A witness's account is shaped both by how questions are asked and by what the witness wants to hide.
when: interviewing a person who has a reason to be guarded
why: both the question framing and concealment change what is reported

text: A witness who later realises a threat stood close by may overturn their own earlier account, so earlier statements need re-checking.
A source's account of events can shift over time as its author's stake in how those events look changes, so one person may tell different stories at different dates.
when: the source has a personal stake in the outcome
why: later reputational or political pressure changes what the author wants to emphasize

text: Witnesses who compare notes or discuss the event blend what they heard with what they were told and may recall incidents that never happened; warn them not to discuss it.
when: when witnesses have compared notes, discuss the matter with friends, or want to seem important
why: Gossip, conversation and emotion reshape what people report and recall.

text: Changes in minor details across retellings can be ordinary memory drift, not deliberate lies. Treating every change as deception misjudges the witness.
when: Comparing successive accounts from one witness
why: Memory reconstructs events each time it is recalled

text: 1) Record the order of each witness's statement. 2) Check whether that witness heard earlier accounts. 3) Compare statements to see whether they echo one another.
when: several witnesses give accounts of the same event
why: echoed accounts can look like independent corroboration

text: A witness may retract or change an account under questioning; compare each revision with the first account, since changes can signal honest correction or a shift toward concealment.
when: A witness retracts or revises a statement during an interview

text: A witness who blurts a name and then quickly tries to take it back may be shielding a person the group is concealing.
when: a witness shows fear or over-protectiveness
why: Fear of exposing someone can make a witness hurry to retract a name.

text: One witness report can be valued differently by one audience as a lead and by another as material for publicity, shaping how it is presented.
when: A witness report is passed to officials or the press.
why: Audiences with different goals select which parts of an account to use.

text: Under emergency pressure, first impressions may be wrong, and details recalled later can reverse an earlier judgment.
when: a witness or responder made a quick judgment during a crisis
why: hurried observation misses cues that reflection later surfaces

text: Testimony can be shaped by fear, strong emotion, other people's input and written preparation, so it is not a pure record of what a witness experienced.
One testimony can support two opposite inferences, so note what each detail rules out before using it as proof.
when: a single witness statement is used to argue both guilt and innocence
why: Details that seem to help one side often cut against it when read closely

text: A witness who revises a story under pressure undergoes a state change that the player can detect and use to test other statements.
when: a character is questioned repeatedly
why: Revision is a visible signal that the earlier account is open to challenge.

text: A witness may omit a fact another witness reports, and their silence about it becomes evidence when they are asked directly.
when: Two witness accounts cover the same event and one leaves out a detail
why: Omission may reflect forgetfulness, embarrassment, or concealment, so it is a lead rather than proof.

text: Let a witness revise her account when she recognises a companion, so the player must cross-check testimony against physical evidence.
Recalling a suspect after a break can produce a more guarded second account, which observers notice and which can alter the picture.
when: Re-interviewing a central suspect after an adjournment or new evidence.
why: A suspect who knows more evidence exists becomes more careful.

text: When the accuser who makes a charge also confirms it, testimony stands in for evidence and nothing independent is checked.
1) Ask the witness a question in plain terms. 2) Compare the answer against any earlier written statement. 3) Press loose phrasing with repeated, plainer questions until the precise fact emerges.
when: A witness's phrasing may hide a fact.
why: Loose wording often conceals a specific detail that surfaces under repeated plain questioning.

text: 1) Check the account's claims against contemporary documents. 2) Check its physical claims against the landscape, such as sight-lines. 3) Judge whether the independent evidence converges on the claim.
when: evaluating a legend or memoir written long after events
why: convergence strengthens a claim without proving it

text: Log each revision of a witness's story as a discrepancy instead of overwriting the earlier version.
when: when a witness changes their account under questioning
why: The sequence of revisions is itself evidence of inconsistency.

text: Make witness NPCs repeat their statements under pressure, and keep those statements stable unless new evidence changes them.
when: designing dialogue for witness characters
why: stable statements let players test them against other evidence

text: Model witness statements as partial records with gaps, and let players compare accounts to find where they agree and conflict.
when: designing testimony in a game

text: Test witness accounts against physical traces, layout, dates and timeline before accepting or building on them, especially when the witness may mislead; memory is often partial.
when: taking witness accounts; a story must be checked for consistency; a reader or player must judge whether a story holds up; a witness gives an account that will shape the next step
why: memory can be partial or wrong; stories can conflict with geography or schedules; partial truths and fabricated details can send an investigation after a wrong target; dated claims and physical checks expose contradictions a bare story hides

text: A witness who first denies that anything happened may later give a detail they did not intend to reveal.
when: When a witness's account shifts during questioning.
why: Narrowing questions pulls out specifics the witness had not planned to share.

text: Witnesses can disagree on a physical detail such as an object being carried. Such conflicts become points of doubt that prompt further checking.
when: Witnesses give conflicting accounts of a physical object
why: Memory of small physical details is often unreliable and contested

text: Test a timeline and explanations against a neutral record, such as a timetable or staff memory, before accepting them, since smooth answers can be prepared.
when: an independent timetable or log exists; a suspect explains suspicious actions, especially involving travel times or movements
why: smooth, complete answers can be prepared; only checks against independent records expose contradictions

text: Keep the number of people who could contradict a staged timeline low, such as by refusing outside visitors.
when: A false timeline must survive official review
why: Each witness is a chance for the false account to be exposed

text: Ask a witness whether they would swear to a claim when much is at stake, and request concrete specifics, since vague recall is weaker evidence.
when: A witness gives a dramatic or important account.
why: Specific, committed detail is harder to invent or drift from than general recall.

text: Witness NPCs can have shifting memory, stated grudges and partial knowledge, so the player must cross-check their account with a second source.
when: when designing witness NPCs for an investigation
why: Unreliable single accounts force players to compare sources, making the investigation more active.

text: Assuming a witness who saw a man speaking with a victim also saw the man who committed the crime.

1) Split the account into separate checkable claims (dates, places, names, possessions). 2) Test each against physical traces, public records and other accounts. 3) Accept claims the traces support; set aside and note contradicted claims. 4) Treat a missing object as a clue in its own right.
when: a witness reports a physical event that leaves traces; a witness makes factual claims
why: checkable facts can expose false accounts

text: 1) Separate what the witness saw from their conclusions and hedged inference. 2) Check checkable details, such as route, timing and conditions, against reference data and independent accounts. 3) Weigh the witness's motive. 4) Offer innocent alternative readings and test each against precise details and other evidence. 5) Accept only the parts that survive; hold judgement until more evidence arrives.
when: a witness's account is emotional or hurried; a single person's memory is the only source for an event; a case depends on what someone saw or heard
why: the same visible facts can support several stories; a witness with a stake may present events in a favourable light; fluent narration and sincere confidence can hide guesswork or error

text: 1) Ask exactly what the witness saw and where they stood. 2) Establish distance, vantage and light, and check whether they allow the reported detail. 3) Test each detail against other facts and normal practice. 4) Check reported injury against surrounding objects and the account. 5) Treat odd details as possible deliberate action.
when: when a witness is the only source for a key fact
why: physical limits and ordinary practice reveal whether a claim is plausible

text: 1) Compare the current account with the earlier statement or sworn record. 2) Press one specific point where they conflict; read the earlier statement aloud and ask them to reconcile. 3) Pause in silence. 4) Test recognition with unrelated names. 5) Reassure them their statement is safe. 6) If they refuse to reconcile, treat them as hostile and weigh answers accordingly.
when: questioning a witness whose statement can be checked against other sources; a witness's account conflicts with a prior statement
why: narrow contradictions and silence push a witness to correct or extend a false account; confronting them with their own record forces reconciliation or exposes evasion

text: 1) Collect a specific account. 2) Pick its checkable claims. 3) Confront the implicated person with those claims and compare their response.
1) Record the predicted event and its time. 2) Wait until that time. 3) Observe whether the event happens. 4) Raise the source's reliability if it does, and lower it if not.
when: a witness or NPC predicts a future event
why: A correct prediction is evidence about the source's reliability

text: 1) Compare the account with physical objects, fixed times and other statements. 2) Record how it is delivered. 3) Note any revisions made under pressure or confrontation.
when: testing a witness's account

text: 1) Separate firsthand observation from secondhand talk and rumor. 2) Compare versions of the same event. 3) Test details the speaker volunteers. 4) Check names and wording across records. 5) Ask whether the claimed feat was needed. 6) Mark withdrawn or never-sworn testimony as unsworn.
when: A case depends on testimony, reputation, rumor or stories about a person
why: Each step reveals whether an account is reliable, consistent and checkable

text: 1) Record the witness's first, unprompted account. 2) Log each later confirmation separately. 3) Note which terms the investigator supplied before the witness used them.
when: Interviewing a witness over several sessions
why: Separating first accounts from confirmations shows what was observed and what was suggested.

text: Test each witness statement against independent sources and other known facts, such as other statements and timings, before accepting it; update earlier statements when later evidence contradicts them.
when: when multiple testimonies or new evidence accumulate
why: descriptions are strongest when checked against physical facts rather than memory alone

text: Check whether a witness's statements stay consistent after their emotion settles; content that holds when the performance fades is more reliable.
when: judging how much of a witness's account to trust

text: Separate what a witness reports from how the witness wants to be seen, since self-protective framing can shape an otherwise frank account.
when: A witness gives a key fact while defending their own reputation
why: Self-interest colors testimony even when the witness seems trustworthy

text: Check whether a witness could distinguish direction before trusting a precise location they report.
when: when a witness places a sound or figure at a specific spot
why: A witness who cannot separate one side from the other gives a location that is not reliable.

text: Test a witness's condition, such as intoxication, before accepting their account.
when: A witness may be impaired by drink, drugs or distress
why: Impairment changes how reliable the report is

text: A witness who has forgotten or is unavailable can still offer clues that the player must confirm through other means.
when: A key witness cannot give a full account

text: A witness-reliability system can check an NPC's statement against world state such as weather, time or location before accepting it.
when: When designing dialogue whose claims can be contradicted by the game world.
why: Checking claims against state makes testimony a puzzle rather than a fixed fact.

text: Assuming a witness could see from a spot without checking light, distance and obstruction produces false conclusions.
when: Accepting a claimed observation at face value.
why: Visibility depends on physical conditions that are easy to overlook.

text: 1) Read exactly what the report states. 2) Compare its specific items with the case facts. 3) Go to the source holding the specifics before treating the link as confirmed.
when: when a news item, report or rumor seems connected to an investigation
why: A dramatic report can seem conclusive while its specifics do not match; the best source for specifics gives reliable confirmation.

text: 1) Ask what each witness could actually see from their position, given distance, speed of movement and posture. 2) Ask about physical details noticed and how sure they are of each. 3) Ask whether the observed figure matches the suspect and weigh the match against those observer conditions.
when: when testing a witness's identification or describing a person they only partly saw
why: Partial sightings often produce confident but limited descriptions; perception conditions determine how much the match can bear.

text: 1) Identify concrete, checkable details such as time, place and object. 2) Check each against independent facts or sources; independent confirmation adds weight. 3) Accept general impressions only as hypotheses.
when: when weighing a witness account or assessing testimony in an investigation
why: Precise details can be verified, while vivid impressions can mislead; a specific detail confirmed by another source is harder to dismiss.

text: 1) Record the witness's account in detail. 2) Identify a physical check the account implies. 3) Perform that check on the relevant people or objects. 4) Compare the result with the account.
when: When a witness account makes a claim that can be physically verified.
why: Physical checks tie testimony to evidence that can confirm or contradict it.

text: 1) Ask narrow questions about how the witness came to act. 2) Compare the answer against the facts of the situation. 3) Ask for a yes or no to remove qualification and expose evasion.
when: When a witness's account depends on a claim that can be tested.
why: Narrow questions reveal what a broad account hides.

text: 1) Have the witness act out their positions and movements in sequence. 2) Check what could have been seen from the suspect's spot through doorways and angles. 3) Anchor each step to physical objects the witness confirms.
when: testimony is reluctant or the sequence of events is unclear
why: physical reconstruction shows what was possible from each position

text: Treat an alibi from a single second-hand source as a claim to verify, not as settled fact.
Ask a reluctant witness directly for their own suspicions, and explicitly allow them to answer honestly without fear of blame.
when: questioning a reluctant witness

text: Do not rank a witness's reliability by status alone; weigh sobriety, fear and whether the account is first-hand.
when: Ranking witnesses in an investigation
why: Status does not guarantee accurate observation

text: Keep witnesses in the area until a scripted later event and require attendance at further questioning unless prevented; highest-stakes claims also need physical presence.
when: when a statement must be tested in person, or a scripted investigation has a later hearing
why: a filed statement alone cannot answer new questions; witnesses who leave the scene cannot be used in later stages

text: In settings where most people are indoors or unwell, fewer people move about, so a suspect is less likely to be seen.
when: crowded or sparse settings such as a rough crossing
why: Fewer people are present to notice the suspect.

text: Order witness lists by urgency so the most perishable leads come first.
when: designing a timed investigation

text: When a witness did not report something she would probably have seen, such as paper in a person's hand, that absence can count against a theory.
when: A witness was positioned to observe a detail that the theory requires.
why: A predicted observation that never appears weakens the theory.
