text: Witnesses who cover different segments of the same night can jointly support an alibi that no single witness could, since each fills gaps the others leave open.
when: when several household members or associates account for one period
why: combined coverage closes gaps left by any one account

text: When a witness's account is the only account, ask who was prevented from speaking with that witness.
when: Assessing a single-source account.
why: Restricted access signals that the account has not been checked.

text: A large number of witnesses is not proof when they may share a single source, so count independent sources rather than people.
Test a witness's account against known facts only if the witness had access to the events in question.
why: a witness without access cannot confirm or refute the record

text: Separate the witness pool so an NPC linked to the accuser's faction cannot vouch for the accused.
when: designing NPC testimony systems

text: Check each witness's motive, such as reward, loyalty, family tie or self-interest, before weighing their account, since it can bias what is reported in either direction.
when: several witnesses have different relationships to the suspects

text: A grudge lowers trust in a witness's judgement and conclusions but does not prove falsehood; test the account and separate accurate observations from biased interpretation.
when: testimony comes from someone with a stake in the outcome; a single informant is the main source
why: grievance shapes interpretation, so a true observation can come with a biased conclusion

text: When designing NPC witnesses, give them a reason to lie (self-protection, status, fear), tag motives and biased statements, and show bias in dialogue or reactions so players can judge reliability.
when: Designing NPC witnesses for a mystery, or witnesses give conflicting accounts of an event
why: Reactions expose the witness's stake and perspective

text: A witness's prior belief about a suspect or household can skew observation, recall and identification, so record their stated opinion alongside testimony.
when: witnesses share a household with the suspect or hold prior opinions about them
why: prior belief can bias observation and reporting

text: Judge a partisan source's claims on factual merit against the record, not by its aim; a partisan's repetition adds tone but no proof.
when: a character defends a claim through a biased or interested source
why: Conviction and self-interest colour how a chain of testimony is presented.

text: Check a witness's motives and prior stance before weighing their objections; a grudge or prior conflict can let accurate evidence be dismissed as invented.
when: a witness has a grudge or prior conflict with the authorities
why: Objections to a source can reflect the objector's convictions, and bias can discredit accurate observations.

text: Witnesses with financial, reputational, family, inheritance or neighbourly/workplace ties can carry a party's interests into their account.
when: when witnesses share ties with the parties
why: stakes and close ties create partisan interests

text: Witnesses with personal ties, group membership or their own alibi can bend timing claims, since a suspect witness may set discovery time to fit their alibi.
when: witness testimony is used to fix a time
why: The witness controls the discovery and has a stake in the result

text: Loyal friends defend a suspect regardless of evidence, citing familiarity as character proof, reluctant to see them as killers; loyalty establishes no fact.
when: a witness is attached to or backs the person being questioned
why: attachment and loyalty outweigh logic and shape how the witness argues

text: Personal liking or dislike selects what a witness reports, so favoured people look better and disliked worse, making guilty seem innocent or innocent guilty.
when: the witness is partial toward or against someone
why: Feeling selects which details get told

text: A witness's admission that they hoped blame would fall on another person can shift suspicion toward someone new.
when: a witness reveals their own motive
why: Motive statements reframe who appears to benefit

text: A witness's view of one person can swing from disparagement to praise to outright hatred within a few entries, shaped by mood and circumstance.
when: first-person testimony from a teller close to events and emotionally invested in them
why: Mood, outside pressure and prior feelings shape what the teller reports about a person.

text: A witness's stance toward an accused can flip after personal contact, such as a touch or a heartfelt conversation, turning earlier hostility into defense.
when: a witness has direct social contact with the accused or a confrontation
why: personal bonds and contact can outweigh earlier impressions

text: Players and characters tend to read a distressed witness as mad, which can cause a true report to be dismissed.
when: A character gives an agitated or unusual account of events.
why: Agitation signals unreliability, so accurate content is discounted with the delivery.

text: Even brief, unreliable or weak-theory accounts usually hold some correct facts; separate reliable details from vague ones rather than dismissing the whole account.
why: partial views usually contain some accurate material

text: Weigh a witness's dislike, hostility or grief before trusting their praise, blame or description of a person; weigh their opinion apart from facts and check with neutral sources.
why: bias shapes what is noticed and reported

text: A record written by one party, like a losing candidate's diary, is framed: it chose what to include and how to describe opponents, so verify its claims independently.
when: relying on a record written by a party to a dispute, especially near a conflict's end
why: A party controls what it records.

text: A person with a stake in a document may be ineligible as a witness. The choice of witnesses can therefore reveal who benefited from the signing.
when: judging a disputed document
why: Eligibility rules exclude interested parties

text: Tag witnesses with motives and prior disclosures so players can judge reliability, and spot a rehearsed story through its inconsistencies.
Doubt a witness's testimony when the witness has a clear reason to lie, rather than treating the testimony as reliable.
when: the witness has a motive to deceive

text: An informant NPC who lied once can still give a true tip, so track trust per claim rather than per character.
when: Designing NPCs who have been caught lying.
why: Trust tracked per claim lets a liar remain useful.

text: A partisan narrator can leak the truth he meant to hide, because his frankness and blindness to how his words will be read reveal facts against his own side.
Weigh a witness's grudge against a party as a source of bias, since resentment can color what they choose to say.
when: when a witness has a personal grievance against someone involved
why: Grievances shape memory and emphasis even when the witness is sincere.

text: Witnesses or rebuttals produced by the accused's allies are partisan, not neutral checks, so the defense must show their knowledge is firsthand.
when: when witnesses or rebuttals are chosen or produced by one side's supporters
why: Allies share the same interest in the outcome.

text: Eagerness, tangential motive or agitation can make an honest witness seem unreliable, while dramatic delivery can make a weak or unreliable account sound convincing; judge content, not performance.
why: tone, motive and performance distort how testimony is judged

text: A persuaded witness can appear reliable while only repeating what was suggested to them.
when: when a witness repeats a story after being told what to say
why: consistency can reflect suggestion rather than observation

text: Do not treat a neutral-seeming witness as impartial. Check his links to other parties, such as shared arrival times or initials.
why: Hidden connections can turn an apparently disinterested witness into an accomplice.

text: Personal interest, such as attraction to the victim, can colour testimony and should be asked about directly.
when: a witness has a personal link to the people involved
why: undisclosed feelings can shape what a witness reports

text: Reading a source only up to the matching line can hide the context that shows whether the link matters.
A witness's opinion of others' competence, such as police seeming sleepy, may reflect the witness's own bias rather than real performance.
Letting a witness's contempt for a rival shape the whole picture of that rival produces a distorted understanding of the case.
when: When a single hostile witness is the main source about a person.
why: Hostility biases description and selection of facts.

text: A witness close to the suspect may soften the account unconsciously, so test the facts rather than the witness's character.
A witness who wants to please an authority may name the person they think the questioner expects.
when: A witness is questioned by someone whose approval they want
why: The desire for approval can override accurate observation.

text: Trusting a frightened witness's own story can produce a false account, and a confident denial can still be wrong.
when: Reconstructing an event from one emotional witness
why: Strong conviction does not guarantee accuracy

text: Set a reviewer's personal assertions, such as claims about what someone saw or read, apart from documented fact when weighing an argument.
A witness eager to help grows less forthcoming over time, and may hold back facts they shared freely at first.
when: the cooperative witness is interviewed later rather than immediately
why: Their zeal cools, so later interviews yield less than the first meeting.

text: A witness can steer conversation toward general reflections to keep it away from the case itself.
A courteous verdict can still be a strong condemnation in substance, so judge the content rather than the tone.
Blunt demands make reluctant witnesses and suspects evasive; courteous, apologetic questioning in their own language lowers guard, so they share more detail even while pressing for facts.
when: Witness or suspect is hostile, evasive, or defensive.
why: Disarmed people are less guarded and cooperate more; manner and rapport affect how readily a witness speaks.

text: Open an interview with a courteous, non-threatening tone, since a comfortable witness talks more; a severe manner can soften into a kind one once rapport forms.
when: a witness is cooperative but reserved
why: comfort makes the witness talkative and willing to volunteer detail

text: A courteous request for a handover signature may still be taken as an accusation, but the procedure should be followed anyway.
when: requesting custody marks from people who handled an item

text: Frame a question as shared interest in stopping a wrongdoer, since suggesting the suspect's name is being misused can win cooperation.
when: A witness is initially hostile or defensive.
why: Appealing to a shared interest lowers the witness's resistance.

text: Remarks let fall in casual conversation can support belief without proof, which pushes the audience to look for a physical or documentary link.
when: the solution rests on offhand remarks
why: hints create belief but not demonstration

text: Several messages that all point to the same suspect group suggest coordinated misdirection rather than independent reports.

1) Ask the holder of records for permission to examine them rather than demanding access. 2) Frame the request around a third party's transactions, not a named suspect. 3) Let the holder reach the suspicion himself. 4) Share only the case detail the auditor needs.
when: A records holder is willing but reluctant to speak about a suspect
why: Framing protects the holder from appearing to inform and keeps the request neutral

text: 1) Ask a trusted intermediary who understands the witness to explain the real aim. 2) Wait a day. 3) Let the witness speak freely without interruption. 4) Do not laugh at trifling details.
when: Interviewing a witness who is ashamed, distrustful, or unable to recall on direct questions
why: A trusted intermediary lowers the witness's guard, and the witness will share small details only if they are not mocked

text: Do not count two accounts as corroboration if the witnesses might have coordinated their stories.
Give a reluctant witness a graceful exit, such as a pause or withdrawal to another room, so they can regroup and return on their own terms.
when: A witness is distressed mid-interview.
why: Space lets the witness recover and makes their return more candid.

text: A witness is reliable only for what they directly perceived; a narrator who never heard a sound cannot describe it, and a signed record verifies nothing beyond observation.
why: Testimony covers observation, not identity or unobserved links

text: A witness's account depends on their opportunity to observe, condition at observation, interest in the outcome, and whether others or independent records confirm it.
when: weighing any witness account
why: Opportunity, condition and corroboration determine how far a report can be trusted.

text: Weigh a witness's admitted doubt about their perception, and doubt reports from drowsy or just-woken witnesses, since fatigue or haste can distort what was seen or heard.
when: A witness raises uncertainty about their own observation, or is drowsy or has just woken.
why: Impaired or hurried perception can distort what was seen.

text: Verify dramatic or self-centred accounts, and check whether fear or dream produced an impossible, emotionally charged detail, since strong emotion or embellishment can add false detail.
when: A witness delivers an account with strong embellishment or a personal stake; evaluating a report with a prior motive.
why: Dramatic framing can add or inflate details, so checking is needed; vivid false detail can come from emotion.

text: Judge a writer by what they state, not by spelling, grammar or craft quality, which say little about intelligence, honesty or motive.
when: assessing a writer's competence or reliability
why: Poor technique may reflect lack of training rather than a sign of guilt.

text: Weigh testimony by who speaks, how they speak, what they omit or gain or lose, and whether neutral observers can confirm it.
when: testimony rests on a single source or a source with a stake, or conflicting accounts
why: stake and corroboration shape how far an account can be trusted

text: A witness can be accurate on one point and self-serving or wrong on another; judge each claim separately rather than the teller as a whole.
when: the witness has a stake in the outcome, or reliability is mixed
why: Motive biases some claims but not all; the teller of a claim is not the claim itself.

text: A story or view repeated without retraction, even word-for-word as if memorized, shows persistence, not accuracy; repeated questioning validates flimsy accounts as readily as honest ones.
why: stability under pressure is not the same as accuracy

text: 1) Check the basis of the witness's knowledge. 2) Corroborate with independent sources; a single account is easily wrong or biased. 3) Compare with other accounts. 4) Look for bias and motive. 5) Track changes under repeated questioning. 6) Test claims against physical facts.
when: a single testimony would decide a verdict or a claim is important
why: Single accounts are easily wrong or biased.

text: Give in-game witnesses an explicit stake, such as a cause to defend, so players must weigh and check their testimony against a conflicting source.
Do not dismiss a witness merely for motive, ridicule or name change; discrediting the teller does not impeach testimony, so test the claims on their own grounds.
when: a witness's motive or background is in question
why: An accusation of motive is an attack, not proof that testimony is false.

text: Label each reported fact as seen directly, heard secondhand, inferred or rumor, and weigh each category differently.
when: presenting witness accounts or designing in-game testimony
why: Mixing sight with rumour and guesswork hides how much each claim is worth; source type determines evidential weight.

text: A witness with a stake in the outcome filters what they report through their interests, feelings and self-image, so the same event can be told in a self-serving way.
when: the witness has a personal stake or strong moral views about the matter
why: Interests and self-image determine which details are emphasised and how they are framed

text: A verdict reached early by intuition, especially one tied to the judge's self-image, resists revision and treats contradiction as a personal attack.
when: the witness has a prior personal investment in the opinion
why: defending the opinion protects the judge's sense of self

text: A questioner may avoid pressing details, so vague questioning is safe for the witness.
when: when the questioner has not yet formed a suspicion
why: close probing could reveal the questioner's own suspicion

text: A shift from firm knowledge to hesitation, such as 'let me think', signals weakening certainty and is worth recording.
when: witness is questioned about a specific detail
why: hesitation can mark the edge of what the witness actually knows

text: Witnesses often avoid a concrete event with a vague word such as things, and a gentle follow-up on that word can open the matter.
when: A question touches a specific event.
why: Vague words let witnesses avoid committing to details.

text: An unsure witness tends to adopt the first plausible option the questioner offers, then describes it with growing confidence.
when: Witness is uncertain and eager to help, and options are offered
why: Agreeing pleases the questioner and relieves uncertainty

text: A witness whose testimony proves useful may be released, which suggests usefulness rather than innocence drove the release.
when: a witness is freed after giving key testimony
why: release can serve the accuser's aims

text: Speaking up for someone at personal risk, such as during dangerous times, signals sincerity and gives the testimony added credibility.
when: Speaking for an accused person is dangerous.
why: Costly action is hard to fake, so observers read it as sincere.

text: A party criticized in a published account may annotate its copy, which signals that the account was being read and taken seriously.
when: a published account attacks a named person

text: Telling a resisting suspect that another witness has already spoken tends to make them stop resisting and speak.
when: a suspect is withholding information
why: Corroboration removes the point of continued resistance.

text: Only a newcomer lacking background has no preset reading of a scene, so their first interpretation is free of expectation.
when: a witness joins without prior accusation
why: background knowledge sets expectations

text: An accused person whose argument is undercut by a trusted witness may be left speechless, since the blow is emotional as well as logical.
when: the witness was trusted and did not expect to speak against the accused
why: the reversal hits both reasoning and feeling

text: A witness who is pressed may give a self-protective account and stop at the point where it becomes dangerous, cutting the story short at a convenient spot.
when: A witness's account is shaped by self-interest and is being questioned.
why: Self-protection makes the witness avoid the most incriminating part of the story.

text: A suspect cannot tell whether a stranger who accuses them saw the crime or is only trying to frighten them.
when: When a stranger silently follows a suspect and accuses them.
why: The stranger's knowledge, motive and reliability are all unknown.

text: A vivid or emotionally certain account tends to be accepted, even though certainty does not make it accurate.
when: when a witness speaks with conviction
why: emotional force is mistaken for evidence

text: Witness testimony does not substitute for documents or physical evidence that can be examined directly.
A witness's value depends on how precisely events are recorded, how checkable the account is, and whether the sighting is physically possible.
A witness's confidence in what they heard does not establish that the account is accurate.
A signer may not know witnesses are watching, yet the formality is still met. Witnesses can later swear the signing was properly done.
Rank testimony by directness: seen directly outweighs heard directly, which outweighs heard secondhand; a claim passed through two or three people ranks lowest.
when: deciding how far to trust a witness report
why: direct access reduces distortion

text: Weigh each witness by state (grief, drink, emotion), closeness to events, motives and reticence, and whether independent checks confirm; a sober eyewitness outweighs a grieving or drunk one.
when: Several witnesses with different access to events, or interviews with several witnesses.
why: Emotion, drink, grief and access to events each distort what is reported; accounts vary in reliability and motive.

text: Check a witness's stake (financial, legal, social, or a theory protecting them) before accepting their claim; never treat their word as settled, and lower weight for prior history.
when: A witness benefits or risks from the result, or has a prior history or personal stake.
why: A stake gives a reason to shape testimony; bias from history or investment distorts reports.

text: A witness's weight depends on what they could have known and on what might have constrained them from speaking plainly.
when: Weighing a witness's testimony
why: Access to events and social restraint both affect how reliable and how candid an account is

text: Testimony is strongest when many independent people agree on the same action, and weaker when a witness was present but did not notice the detail in question.
when: Weighing several witnesses to one event.
why: Independent agreement is hard to fake, while inattentive presence gives no real evidence on the disputed detail.

text: Before trusting a witness, check who saw, from what distance and position, and how the account reached you.
when: weighing testimony from hidden or distant observers

text: A witness's account is credible only if they were positioned to perceive what they claim, so test the basis of an alibi, not just the claim itself.
when: when a witness offers an alibi or clearing testimony
why: a claim can be sincere yet rest on a vantage point that could not have supplied it

text: Judge a witness's report by how well they had access to the event and whether they have a motive to shape what they say.
when: evaluating any testimony in a story
why: Access limits what was observed, and motive biases what gets reported

text: Weigh testimony by the witness's motive, senses and standing, not only by what they say.
when: When a case rests on what someone heard, saw or said about a person.
why: Content alone can hide bias, perceptual limits or social pressure.

text: A witness's account can be bent by emotion, self-interest and selective sharing, so weigh it against documents and other statements.
why: Testimony filtered through feeling or motive can drift from what actually happened.

text: Weigh each witness by what they gain or lose: grief, grudge, loyalty or rivalry can shape what someone says and what they leave out.
when: witnesses give conflicting accounts of a person's motives or behaviour
why: Personal interest distorts reporting

text: Weigh each witness's account by their position, attention, motives and habits, rather than accepting or dismissing it wholesale.
when: when several witnesses give partial or unhelpful accounts

text: Test a new accusation against what you already know of the accuser's behavior, asking why they waited or never asked earlier.
when: A claim comes from someone whose past conduct is known
why: Gaps in behavior make a claim look improbable

text: Consistency checks lose force when a claim rests on a physical object or document the target cannot dismiss.
Judge testimony by its source, its consistency with other accounts, and whether it covers the period that matters.
when: weighing any witness claim
why: Each factor exposes a different way an account can mislead

text: A witness who states the basis of a belief and admits faults on their own side is usually more credible, but the concession must be genuine.
when: Challenged about bias or motive.

text: A witness NPC with a stated stake, such as a payment or debt, can be probed by asking for the basis of their testimony.
A person asked to report a traveller's progress to someone else becomes a witness to that journey.
Avoid writing witnesses as simply truthful or simply false; give each a limit or motive so judgment is required.
when: when writing witness characters
why: flat reliability removes the need for careful evaluation

text: A witness whose presence at the time has a plausible, independent explanation is more credible.
Judge testimony by the witness's position, bias and evasions as well as by the words used, since each shapes what the words are worth.
Test an offhand comment against concrete facts; it matters only when it conflicts with something physical.
Openly clearing one suspect can make the rest of an investigator's case more credible, if the method behind the clearing is shown to be sound.
Weigh a witness's account against their stake in the outcome; someone who owns the weapon used has a motive to protect themselves.
when: a witness has a personal interest in the event
why: Self-interest can shape how an account is told, including what is stressed or left out.

text: Weigh testimony against motives such as resentment or trust, since a personal accusation or a vouching may not reflect the facts.
when: ranking witness statements
why: Motives color testimony, and vouching is not proof.

text: A witness's assurance of having no personal stake cannot be taken as certain, since witnesses are not always impartial about their own feelings.
why: People are poor judges of their own bias, especially when emotionally involved

text: Avoid treating a suspect's appearance or reputation as proof of guilt or innocence.
when: weighing a suspect against the evidence
why: Appearance and reputation are not evidence of the act itself.

text: Explain away each anomaly in a witness's account on its own terms, but do not dismiss core observations that resist explanation.
when: a witness reports alarming or unusual events
why: dramatic accounts may be exaggerated yet still contain real observations

text: Errors that all fall on the same specific true points suggest the writer knew those facts well, whereas random falsehoods scatter across unrelated details.
when: assessing whether a document's inaccuracies are chance
why: a person lying by chance gets some facts right and misses others at random

text: Vagueness about amounts or dates is a reason to check the account, not to accept it, and gaps should not be filled by the investigator's own assumptions.
when: When a witness is vague on key facts.

text: When probing a suspect, make only truthful but vague statements, so nothing checkable is given away while the other side fills the gaps.
Treat an oddly vague phrase as a clue, since a speaker who meant a specific person would usually have named them plainly.
Judge a witness's account by their position, attention and certainty. A witness can be sure of one fact and only guess at another.
when: Weighing any witness testimony
why: Each part of an account depends on what the witness could actually perceive

text: A motive becomes credible when the prize is stated in concrete terms, such as commercial value or the interest of rival powers.
Weigh a witness's account by how much the witness gains from one version of events, and whether an impartial observer saw the same thing.
when: Several accounts conflict and one speaker controlled evidence or benefited from its outcome.
why: A witness who gains from an outcome may shape the account toward it.

text: Opponents may attack both a witness's perception and their motives or sobriety; assess each attack separately.
when: when a witness's rival disputes their account
why: character and perception are separate questions

text: Weigh a witness's statement only as far as the witness is reliable, disinterested, and believed by the audience; do not treat a denial as proof when the witness has a personal stake.
when: Deciding how much a witness's statement can support a conclusion.
why: Personal stakes, grudges, loyalty or kindness can bias testimony as much as malice.

text: Judge witness accounts by the speaker's name, age, role and the specific acts they can attest to.
when: when a witness account is central to a case
why: concrete identity and acts make claims checkable against the speaker's position

text: A checkable detail makes a weak test when it is common or easily guessed, because a lucky guess can match it by chance.
when: Choosing which detail a witness must get right.
why: Common details give correct answers by coincidence, so passing them proves little.

text: When a motivated source's story stays consistent across its core details, treat that core as credible even while doubting its emphasis or framing.
when: a source with a stake gives an account

text: When a group assures that a practice rarely endangers the innocent, test that assurance against actual cases rather than treating it as settling objections.
when: a group defends a practice by claiming it rarely harms innocents

text: A witness's own standing and a large petition from long-known neighbors add weight to character evidence.
Vague answers such as 'I do not know' or 'about' give nothing to test; press with precise questions on distance, direction, time, names or places, or seek a second source.
when: a witness gives non-specific replies
why: Vague answers cannot be tested against other sources.

text: Test what each state of a witness knows, rather than dismissing the witness as unreliable altogether.
Weigh testimony from a source with a record of dishonesty as weak evidence, and test its claims against physical facts.
when: A witness has a criminal or dishonest record
why: Such testimony is often self-serving and unreliable

text: Count a secondhand report as credible only when a named, reliable witness vouches for it, and mark the rest as uncertain.
Rumor and folk legend carry little weight until traced to firm sources, though they can point investigators toward a suspect.
Weigh a witness by motive, character, corroboration, and whether they admit their own wrongdoing; an admission of wrongdoing strengthens testimony because it is costly to make.
when: When testimonies conflict or the only witness is compromised.
why: Each factor shows whether the witness gains from lying and whether the account is likely to be true.

text: Let players check a witness's report against conditions like distance, distraction or fatigue.
when: When designing testimony the player must weigh.
why: Checkable conditions let players judge reliability themselves.

text: Judge a witness's reliability by reputation, by others' opinions, and by how the record was made, and check secondhand warnings against the testimony itself.
when: Deciding whether a source is trustworthy or whether a record may have been altered
why: Reputation and transcripts each give partial, sometimes misleading evidence

text: Do not treat a witness's confidence about a brief look in poor light as proof of identity.
when: A witness claims to recognize someone from a short or dim observation
why: Confidence does not guarantee accuracy under poor viewing conditions.

text: Give NPC witnesses a reliability rating based on distance, training, grudges or fear, since frightened witnesses give vaguer descriptions, so players weigh their accounts differently.
when: designing NPC witnesses
why: visible reliability shapes how players use testimony

text: A testimony's reliability should rise only when an independent second clue supports it, so a single NPC's account cannot solve a case.
when: when designing NPC testimony in a game

text: A witness's account is limited by what they could perceive, whether they had reason to shade the truth, and how well it fits other testimony.
when: Weighing overlapping testimonies
why: Sincerity does not guarantee accuracy when perception or motive is limited.

text: A witness's standing can be a stored value that changes how other characters weight that witness's testimony, independent of what was observed.
A rule that counts several accusers as one person reduces corroboration, so their joint account carries less weight.
When one witness discredits another, the competing accounts must both be weighed, changing how each is trusted.
when: A witness is warned against another witness
why: Pressure on one account reshapes trust in the other

text: A later judgment can discredit a witness's supernatural testimony after the verdict, citing possible fraud or outside influence, which weakens the verdict it supported.
when: a conviction that rests on a witness whose status is reassessed
why: the verdict depended on that witness's credibility

text: A witness's reliability depends on position to observe, attention or hearing, memory, and honesty or motive; a weakness in any one can make the account unreliable.
when: when weighing a witness account

text: Judge a witness by four things: why they were present, their habits, their tools such as clocks, and whether other accounts contradict them.
Testimony is weighed on three factors: corroboration by other observers, the witness's reliability, and counter-claims made against the accuser.
when: judging a disputed accusation

text: Vagueness, especially about dates, is mistaken for evasion or lying though it often reflects honest memory gaps; dismissing such a witness discards accurate testimony.
why: Imprecision is read as motive rather than memory limits

text: Treating one sworn, vague or partisan statement as settled proof is a mistake, whichever way it points; the public often assumes the defence will never answer it.
Accepting a witness's credibility from social standing alone lets an arranged alibi pass unexamined.
Vague witnesses can be wrongly taken as hiding something, so each claim needs its own source before it is trusted.
Treating a vague recollection as confirmation of a claim leads to false certainty.
why: A vague memory cannot confirm specifics

text: Accepting an emotionally invested account without checking it against neutral sources hides the observer's slant.
why: Bias goes unnoticed without independent comparison

text: A witness's grievances and self-interest colour part of the account, so their statements need checking.
A consistent story can still be partial, so consistency alone does not establish the whole truth.
An account can be internally consistent yet still mislead, and a theory that fits its own facts can fail against the physical scene.
A rough sketch may read as a gag, leading viewers to write off a real clue as sloppy art.
A listener's promise to keep a secret does not limit what they do with the information next.
Assuming a witness cannot speak to a topic narrows an inquiry and can send questions to the wrong people.
when: Planning which questions to ask whom.

text: A vague question such as did she look strange invites agreement; narrow questions give the witness less room to shape answers.
why: open wording lets the witness mirror the questioner

text: A witness who made an earlier mistake, or whose time depends on an unchecked clock, is a weaker source even when delivering a firm figure.
when: Assessing a time or figure from a witness
why: Prior errors and unverified instruments undermine precision

text: If the antagonist's shock at the reveal is not credible, the reversal feels staged and loses its impact.
Knowledge learned for one occasion covers only what was studied and tends to break under unexpected questions.
when: Testing whether someone's expertise is genuine
why: Surface knowledge lacks the depth to answer unplanned questions

text: A witness's embarrassment can lead them to undervalue accurate details they did notice.
A weak-sounding excuse is not proof of guilt, and a dismissive judgment about it must still be tested against records.
Once a clue is destroyed, the case rests on testimony about it and on who had access, so those witnesses must be credible.
why: weak witnesses cannot carry the case once the physical evidence is gone

text: Reading a vague phrase as a list of suspects can mislead the investigation.
Assuming a witness would notice a substitution is an error when their contact with the real person was only momentary and their impression is weak.
If a witness's reason for staying silent is weak, the omission reads as contrivance rather than character.
Attacking a witness's character can make the witness shut down and stop sharing information.
Confidence does not reflect precision; test a witness's certainty against what they could observe, and record exactly what each saw and for how long.
why: Confidence does not reflect precision.

text: Loyalty or kindness can make a witness knowingly lie, such as repeating a false time for a partner; lower their credibility, including corrected accounts, when allegiance is disclosed.
when: a witness knows a fact that would harm someone they care about, or allegiance is disclosed
why: Loyalty can outweigh accuracy; protective motives produce knowing false testimony even when no rule excludes the witness.

text: Attacking a witness's character does not prove the accused innocent or answer the evidence; it removes one support, so other evidence must still be examined.
Witnesses can be wrong about the hour, the person involved or what they checked; ask each whether an identity or date error is possible, and test the account against other records and witnesses.
when: a case depends on who was where and when
why: Observation and memory are fallible and can conflict.

text: Sympathy, distress or charm lowers scrutiny; accepting a sympathetic or pleasant speaker's account unchecked leads to false conclusions and missed withheld facts.
why: Emotional appeal lowers scrutiny.

text: Fully believed or fully dismissed witnesses remove the need for deduction, and heavy unreliability signals make audiences distrust everything; balance credibility and keep verifiable anchor facts.
when: writing NPC reports the player must evaluate
why: Balanced credibility keeps the player reasoning about evidence.

text: Witnesses under pressure or eager to please may confirm a suggested identity; ask them to confirm only when fully sure, since the answer may mirror the questioner's expectation.
when: a witness is asked to confirm identity
why: Pressure and suggestion can override uncertain memory; willingness to please makes identification reflect expectation rather than what was seen.

text: A stated reason that sounds weak may still be the true one, so an inferred hidden motive needs confirmation before it is treated as fact.
Interviewers who move quickly, pass over weak or unexpected answers, and repeat the question to another witness steer the collective result.
Judgments of whether a witness is credible or an act is beyond human strength depend on what the judge already believes is possible.
when: Weighing extraordinary testimony.
why: Prior beliefs decide what counts as impossible, so the same account can be accepted or rejected.

text: Reading too much into a witness's words can invent meaning; confirm the intended sense with the witness where possible.
when: Interpreting a witness's phrasing or tone.
why: Wording and memory can differ from what the investigator infers.

text: Eliminating a route on the word of a single witness is fragile, since that witness may be mistaken or the account may itself be disputed.
when: When ruling out an access route based on one person's observation
why: Unverified testimony can wrongly close a route that was actually open.

text: Relying on a single witness for a destroyed document leaves the only record as that witness's account, which may be unreliable.
when: When a key document was destroyed and only one person saw it.
why: Without a second source the account cannot be verified.

text: Affection or sympathy for a witness can bias how their behaviour is read, so an investigator should check for it.
when: when a witness is personally liked or close
why: sympathy shapes interpretation of ambiguous signs

text: A witness who clings to a theory despite contrary facts is not automatically guilty; loyalty or fear can drive the stubbornness.
Guards who testify about each other's sleep are not independent witnesses, so their accounts need an outside check such as a third party who was awake.
when: when guards vouch for each other's whereabouts
why: Mutual testimony shares the same bias and gap

text: A witness's reliability can be challenged on grounds such as fatigue, so testimony needs corroboration.
when: When a witness contradicts a suspect
why: Fatigue or other conditions can make a witness's account unreliable

text: Discounting a witness because they are fearful of the supernatural or hysterical does not establish that they are wrong, and such a witness may have seen something real.
when: When a witness's temperament is used to dismiss their account.
why: Emotional state affects delivery, not necessarily the accuracy of the observation.

text: 1) Tag each claim as directly seen, heard, inferred or admitted. 2) Note the witness's known bias for each claim. 3) Check each claim against other evidence before relying on it.
when: a witness is credible on some points and suspect on others
why: Sorting claims by source shows which parts can carry weight

text: 1) Check whether the source's manner, such as unusual precision, fits how real witnesses speak. 2) Check whether the claimant's actions match the claim. 3) Check the text's form for signs of a private draft.
when: A claim's authority depends on who published it, or a document seems unintended for publication.
why: Credibility can be judged from the text before its facts are weighed.

text: 1) Ask the same short question at intervals. 2) Wait through silences instead of filling them. 3) Record each answer exactly, including contradictions. 4) Follow up with consistency probes.
when: Questioning a weak or confused witness whose replies come slowly.
why: Short repetition reduces confusion, and exact records preserve evidence of contradiction.

text: Test a suspect's story for consistency with physical details, such as a claimed residence abroad or the condition of their hands, and ask them to explain any mismatch.
when: A suspect tells a detailed personal story
why: Physical details can contradict claimed experiences

text: 1) Trace the claim to its source. 2) Ask whether a true knower would have given specifics, since silence about details suggests partial knowledge. 3) Note whether the witness's condition could make the claim less reliable. 4) Check the claim against independent facts.

1) Ask the witness for the exact words used. 2) Record them verbatim, including every claimed link and claim about others. 3) Mark which names and places remain unknown. 4) Search independent records for mention of them.
when: A witness's account is the main evidence and must be tested.
why: Exact wording lets the listener judge what was actually said and gives a fixed basis for checking.

text: 1) Note the witness's state, such as fear, intoxication or distance from the event. 2) Note whether the witness knows the source direction of a sound or event. 3) Separate what the witness saw from what they believed or were told.
when: Assessing a witness's account
why: Emotional state, perception and inference each affect accuracy

text: 1) Check the witness's condition, such as drink or fatigue. 2) Check distance and light. 3) Check the date of the sighting against the event. 4) Use the account only if all pass.
when: a witness's account is the only source for a time or identity
why: each factor distorts perception

text: 1) Ask about the witness's stake and feelings toward those involved. 2) Separate observed facts from interpretation. 3) Compare answers over time and flag changes. 4) Check key claims against physical traces. 5) Record half-remembered details as uncertain.
1) Check what the witness could actually have observed. 2) Rate how sure they are. 3) Look for embellishment or self-interest. 4) Weigh the account accordingly.
when: Assessing a witness's account.
why: Access, confidence and embellishment each affect reliability.

text: 1) Check the witness's name and qualifications. 2) Confirm membership in a relevant professional body. 3) Vet the witness before trusting them, since enemies can send a false witness.
when: a witness supplies key evidence
why: enemies may plant false witnesses

text: 1) Check the conditions of perception and the witness's state. 2) Seek corroboration from others or from evidence. 3) Check named details against known places and timing.
when: a claim rests only on what one witness perceived

text: 1) Check how precise the witness's times and details are. 2) Verify what they could physically see or hear from their position. 3) Fix timing with device logs. 4) Probe for personal bias. 5) Cross-check with other witnesses.
when: a case depends on who passed a single choke point
why: each check tests a different way a confident witness can still be wrong

text: 1) Tell the witness and any attending party the time limit, and keep within it. 2) Open with a short, reassuring statement of who is asking and why. 3) Ask one question at a time. 4) Use gentle, repeated prompts to recover a fact the witness has lost track of.
when: The witness is the only source for a fact and cannot be interviewed at length.

text: 1) Trace who told whom along the chain. 2) Separate first-hand reports from second-hand ones. 3) Look for agreement among independent accounts. 4) Reconcile differences with a plausible scenario. 5) State what remains unknown.
when: when no document names a place but people's accounts of it survive
why: Oral accounts gain weight only when their transmission and independence are established

text: 1) Ask a precise question whose answer can be checked against the physical scene. 2) Compare the answer with the evidence. 3) If it conflicts, re-run the same procedure with one controlled change. 4) Keep instructions identical across trials so differences come from the change.
when: A witness's directions or memory must be turned into a physical action that can be verified.
why: Identical repetition isolates the variable responsible for any difference in outcome.

text: 1) Let a long-talking witness speak without interruption. 2) Filter out digression. 3) Record material facts about routine, deviations and people. 4) Note the witness's conclusions separately as opinion.
when: When interviewing a witness who speaks at length and knows a routine
why: Material facts are often buried under filler, and conclusions can be wrong even when observations are accurate.

text: 1) Ask about a specific person at a specific time. 2) Let the witness volunteer contrasts with other people. 3) Use volunteered contrasts to identify the person sought.
when: When a witness is unlikely to recall a person from general questioning
why: Specific questions and volunteered contrasts reach memories that broad questions miss.

text: Weigh each witness by sleep, fear, drink, drowsiness, sobriety, distance, light, duration and attention; brief, distant or poorly lit sightings carry little weight.
when: evaluating any eyewitness testimony
why: Impaired perception and poor viewing conditions distort what a witness reports, so the same account can carry very different weight.

text: Keep a witness's stated doubt attached to the statements it qualifies, naming which claims are shaky, so the audience can weigh the weakest parts.
when: the witness admits being unsure what they perceived
why: Unnamed doubt cannot be checked; marking it shows the least reliable parts.

text: Track each witness's reliability and motive as a visible stat, since a dramatic witness may add a sighting the player must verify.
when: designing multi-source testimony or witnesses whose statements the player evaluates
why: Visible reliability tells the player which accounts need checking rather than accepting them as fact.

text: When a witness is a participant or beneficiary, accept only the parts corroborated by other evidence, and weigh each claim separately.
when: the witness gains money, status or protection from their account
why: A stake can colour the whole account

text: Check an alibi witness's reliability before accepting it, including any record or habit that could discredit their testimony.
when: Relying on an alibi from a witness.
why: An alibi is only as strong as its witness.

text: Tie a trace to a specific craft or class so players can narrow suspects without receiving a direct answer.
Give the player a clue that contradicts the crowd's account of a suspect, so the community verdict can be tested.
when: villagers push a convenient suspect
why: a contradiction lets the player question the consensus

text: Tag each testimony with a confidence level and a verification status that the player can update as new evidence arrives.
when: designing player-facing clue systems

text: Tell a witness that the whole truth is wanted, so they feel free to include details they might otherwise skip.
when: opening an interview

text: Use a drug- or state-driven amnesia to explain an out-of-character act only when a plausible trigger and a known state are present.
when: Explaining an act by someone who cannot remember it.
why: Without a trigger and known state, the explanation is an unfalsifiable excuse.

text: Mark an unreliable guide with visible cues, such as drunkenness or self-absorption, so players know to weigh their hints.
when: a guide gives useful but suspect hints
why: the player can judge how far to trust them

text: Threaten only with consequences you can actually carry out, since a failed bluff ends cooperation.
Test a witness's assumptions, such as believing an illness is a known recurrence, before treating their account as fact.
when: a family member explains a medical or personal event
why: A belief can replace the investigation that would confirm it

text: Do not accept a story merely because it is consistent with known facts; consistency can be engineered.
when: when an account fits the physical evidence
why: A coordinated story can be built to match known facts.

text: Record testimony the game cannot confirm and leave the player to judge which governing rule applies.
Make an in-world pamphlet credible by naming its author, letting copies circulate, and allowing rival NPCs to contradict its claims.
when: designing a document players should be able to trust or doubt

text: Give NPC witnesses slightly different versions of one event, so the player must find the consistent core that all versions share.
when: Designing an event that players reconstruct from witness accounts
why: Variation forces players to compare accounts and identify what is reliable

text: Do not rely on a single witness's description of a person's class or height.
when: A single witness estimates a person's social class or stature.
why: Such estimates are easily wrong and need corroboration.

text: Judge a witness's coverage of the time window rather than attacking their character, since a truthful witness can still have a narrow view.
when: a witness seems respectable and honest
why: A credible witness gives an accurate but partial window that must be measured.

text: Do not assume a witness is unreliable merely because their story sounds odd.
when: when weighing an unusual testimony

text: Past similar deceptions make a new false story more believable, but when reputation is contested, judge by consistency, candour and conduct, not standing or past accusations.
when: A suspect has a history of deception, or a witness's reputation is disputed without direct evidence.

text: A witness may give an earlier date for a recent transaction to move it away from the crime, reasoning that older matters draw less suspicion.
when: A dated transaction is linked to a crime
why: Older-seeming events are assumed to attract less suspicion

text: Times reconstructed from memory are vague, and witnesses often cannot say exactly when someone left.
when: A witness is asked to date an event.
why: Human sense of elapsed time is approximate.

text: Timeline reasoning is weak where no time records exist and every account depends on memory.
when: no logs or stamped records are available
why: memory-based accounts drift and cannot be compared precisely

text: Old records can give dates in ambiguous forms, such as split years, and these must be resolved before events are put in order.
when: when placing events from historical documents in sequence
why: Calendar conventions differed, so one date can have two readings

text: Dates recalled from memory are weaker than dates tied to a public signal; mark them approximate so a vague recollection is not treated as a precise timeline point.
when: a witness gives a date without a public anchor
why: Memory of when something happened is less reliable than an external marker, so the timeline should carry its own margin of error.

text: A timestamped in-world journal lets the player build a timeline, but a self-serving or incomplete journal can mislead, so its entries should be checked against other sources.
An approximate witness time, such as 'about three', is useful only after it has been tested against other anchors.
when: a witness gives a rounded or estimated time
why: Estimated times can be off, so they gain value only when confirmed.

text: Present in-world newspapers or ledgers with timestamps so players can build a timeline of NPC movements and find where a claimed alibi breaks.
When witness times are approximate, state a reconstructed sequence as a range rather than a single exact point.
why: Imprecise anchors cannot support a precise conclusion.

text: Check an in-world letter's date against its supposed author's recorded location; a letter dated while that author is off-map is a clue that the document is false.
when: Lore documents carry dates and an NPC has a travel log
why: Authors cannot write from places they were not

text: A timeline built from memory is approximate, and a time given from memory can be wrong; verify critical times against dated records, such as a timetable.
when: a witness reconstructs durations or dates
why: Memory of time is imprecise.

text: Dates recalled from memory can be wrong and distort the apparent pattern, so take dates from written, dated records.
Treating approximate witness times as exact creates false certainty and can hide the window that decides an alibi, since small rounding errors erase it.
when: a witness gives a rounded or vague time
why: Small rounding errors can erase the window that matters.

text: Approximate times such as 'nearly six' or 'about twenty-five minutes after ten' are estimates; small errors shift the whole sequence, so don't trust them as exact or trust an unknown clock.
when: Building a timeline from witness-reported times.
why: Approximate or differently sourced times shift the apparent sequence, and small estimate errors can move every dependent conclusion.

text: Treat stated clock times and watch checkpoints as approximate ranges, not exact proof, until a second source confirms them.
when: Building a timeline from clocks, rounds, or a witness's recollection of times.
why: Clocks and patrol checks are imprecise, and recalled times are often wrong by a margin, so precise conclusions need corroboration.

text: Narrator times and distances are often rough estimates, and second-hand details drift from the original, so they should not be treated as exact.
Witness dates shift between tellings, so elapsed-time answers should be treated as ranges rather than exact dates.
when: a witness gives an approximate time since an event
why: recollected durations are imprecise and can change

text: An earlier event, weeks or months before, can be essential to a witness's chain, so timing must be checked across the whole span.
Times estimated from memory can be off by minutes, which can decide whether a suspect could have arrived in time.
when: A timeline relies on recalled estimates rather than fixed records.

text: Treating an approximate body sign as an exact clock can build an alibi or accusation that collapses under cross-examination.
A clock wound in haste or misset by an hour gives a systematically wrong time, so any event timed by it is off by that amount.
when: When a time reading comes from a personal or hastily set clock
why: A small setting error can make a timeline appear to contradict or support a theory

text: Recollections of when an activity ended are often wrong, so remembered times need verifying.
A timeline built from one person's memory may contain wrong dates and invented causes, so it must be checked against other sources.
Approximate times drift, so accepting one timeline too quickly can hide a gap between claims.
Later retellings can misdate an order; check dates against records kept at the time.
when: reconstructing when a ruling took effect

text: 1) Collect each witness's account separately. 2) Record only what each person saw and in what order. 3) Merge them into one timeline. 4) Mark the intervals no one witnessed.
when: when several witnesses describe the same events
why: the merged timeline shows where events lack any witness

text: Record uncertain witness times as approximate values or ranges, such as around eleven or about midnight, so the timeline keeps its margin of error rather than false precision.
when: When witnesses estimate times from memory, from other events, or give an approximate time.
why: Estimated times carry real margins of error, and false precision misleads later reasoning.

text: Keep an in-world event log with dates and speakers, and let players build timelines from dated letters, rumours and proclamations by checking entries against each other.
when: When designing investigation content spread across documents.
why: Players reconstruct the sequence themselves.

text: Date in-world documents with write dates, hedged phrasing, and ink fade or page wear so players can catch backdated entries or later rewrites.
Anchor a claimed whereabouts to in-world clocks or events so the claim can be checked.
when: Designing timelines for suspect or NPC alibis.
why: Anchored claims can be verified against the world state.

text: Stamp story events with in-game times so the player can assemble a timeline from journal entries or overheard conversations.
when: a story unfolds over several in-game days or hours
why: Timestamps let players order events they discover in different places.

text: Matching accounts aren't independent proof: they may reflect a true alibi or coordination, weighed against character and motives; shared untestable experience also makes them dependent.
when: Two or more accounts match
why: Matching can result from shared story as well as truth.

text: Loyalty biases even a sincere NPC's account, including their view of others; weigh statements by the speaker's relationship to the subject and cross-check claims against other sources.
when: Assessing a witness close to a suspect
why: Affection influences what is noticed and reported.

text: A loyal witness may lie to shield the person they feel loyal to, offering a convincing but false explanation; the motive is personal tie, not self-interest.
when: the witness has a personal connection to the suspect
why: a well-built story can still be untrue

text: A loyal witness may refuse to say more, or withhold a name or soften a statement; the account is fair in form, shielded in content, and refusal can signal hidden knowledge.
when: when a witness has reason to protect a suspect
why: loyalty withholds information; loyalty can override full disclosure

text: Loyalty can delay suspicion: a witness who withholds another person's history postpones an inquiry line.
when: a witness protects someone
why: protective silence hides relevant background

text: Strong loyalty or emotion can make testimony less reliable rather than more, since it pushes the witness toward defense over fact.
when: A witness defends a suspect with strong feeling and no proof
why: Advocacy displaces observation

text: A denial to a question about disloyalty confirms loyalty, while hesitation reveals a secret, so loyalty questions can expose hidden contacts.
when: when a questioner asks whether a contact spoke against the group
why: the timing and tone of the answer are read as signals

text: A witness with a grudge or lost position may speak frankly and volunteer key objects after receiving only a partial answer from the questioner.
when: A witness has a motive to talk and the questioner gives a guarded reply
why: Resentment and a wish to share information lower the witness's guard

text: A witness who lies about their whereabouts can serve as a plot lever rather than the culprit, which supports branching investigations.
A suspect can be held as a material witness to keep them available for questioning without a full arrest.
Keep the persona by feigning innocence and refusing to explain, so the accusation cannot be pinned on the speaker.
when: when the accuser is confronted after a veiled accusation

text: When a witness's confusion appears, test repeatedly to decide whether it is a passing disturbance or a deliberate act, rather than judging early.
when: A witness's confusion could be real or feigned
why: Early judgement can be wrong, so repeated testing separates the two

text: A witness who seems to confirm the theory can be exposed by one test question that only the genuine person could answer.
when: a witness or ally is presented as proof
why: A single decisive check cheaply separates a fraud from a real ally.

text: When a criminal group keeps losing members to arrest, survivors ask how the authorities knew, and that question turns into an accusation of a hidden informer.
when: a network has suffered repeated losses
why: Shared loss history makes members doubt one another.

text: NPC dialogue branches can depend on affection or loyalty, so a protective lie becomes available only through that relationship.
Marriage ties across households shape who is protected, because in-law connections can shelter a member from consequences.
Staying loyal to a theory after its key link has failed wastes time and stalls the investigation.
when: a reliable source has contradicted the theory
why: sunk effort tempts the investigator to keep defending it

text: Hide the truth behind a loyal character's denial, making the lie checkable: give a visible tell and a motive players can uncover; reward players who spot the mismatch.
when: Designing a character who conceals the truth to protect someone.
why: Players can only challenge a cover story if the story contains something checkable.

text: Witness may show pauses, pallor, fidgeting, changed wording or shifts in voice, pace or composure, even when body stays still; these signal concealment or anxiety.
when: Pressed on a denied or secret matter.
why: Concern about exposure shows in speech before the body; anxiety alters delivery even when speech stays calm.

text: Witnesses in a district run by a violent group stay silent out of fear of retaliation, not from lack of knowledge.
when: A group threatens anyone who would testify against it
why: Testifying risks a victim's life, so fear rather than ignorance keeps people quiet.

text: A witness's sudden strong reaction to a found item signals that the discovery matters to them, but it does not reveal what they are reacting to.
when: An NPC shows fright or shock at a discovery.
why: Emotional response indicates significance while leaving its cause open.

text: A character whose words contradict their facial expression or posture gives the audience a readable cue that something is wrong.
when: A character speaks reassuringly while showing a contrary expression.
why: Audiences read nonverbal signals and notice mismatches with speech.

text: A worried frown after a question about others involved signals that the question has reached a sore point.
Witnesses close to an affair may hold back or bend their statements, and their manner under questioning is itself evidence to weigh.
when: when witnesses have a personal stake in the outcome
why: Loyalty or self-interest pushes people toward favourable or evasive answers.

text: A sudden change in a witness's demeanour, becoming unusually animated or unusually still, marks a subject of interest worth examining.
when: Questioning a witness and noticing shifts in their manner.
why: Abrupt change in behaviour signals that a topic touches something sensitive.

text: A witness who balances professional secrecy against self-protection often resists publicity and gives minimal answers.
when: a witness has a professional or personal reason to avoid exposure
why: exposure carries a cost to the witness

text: A prior assessment of a witness's condition may not describe their state at the time of testimony, especially when their health is declining.
when: Relying on an older medical or mental evaluation of a witness
why: Health and composure change over time

text: Testimony loses weight when a witness's motive or state of mind is unclear; strong feeling colours both content and delivery, so separate facts from manner.
when: Witness is emotionally charged or visibly shaken.
why: Audience cannot separate report from feeling; fear colours both content and manner.

text: Lower a witness's testimony weight when afraid, intoxicated, sleep-deprived, fatigued, feverish or injured; check their perceptions against other sources.
when: Witness's condition was impaired at the time, or when weighing their account.
why: Fear, drink and fever can distort sensory memory.

text: Read a witness's temperament and frame choices so they have no easy way out, avoiding wording the witness will not tolerate.
when: when interviewing a volatile witness

text: Asking what people talked about and how they seemed adds context that a bare timeline lacks.
Before relying on a witness or confronting them, check whether their mental state and health can bear the strain of testimony.
when: A witness's reliability depends on mental state or physical health, or a confrontation is planned
why: A strained witness may break and reveal more than intended

text: An account from a witness who is drinking heavily or nearly drunk is weakened and needs heavier checking against other evidence.
when: the witness was intoxicated when observing or when speaking later
why: Intoxication impairs attention and memory, so the account may be incomplete or inaccurate.

text: Witnesses may describe a fixture's state from a different day or time, so their account of its condition needs a date check.
A witness who has learned to be impassive gives little to read, so the investigator should watch for the one topic that breaks the pattern.
when: Questioning a witness who maintains a controlled manner.
why: A practiced composure hides most signals, so the exception is the informative point.

text: Record each witness's stake, fear and state at the moment of speaking, and show these as dialogue tags players can weigh.
Treat a witness's manner as a reason for follow-up questions rather than as proof of guilt.
when: A witness's demeanor seems to conflict with their stated feelings.
why: Grief, shame, or fear can produce the same signs as concealment.

text: Confident or vivid delivery of a vague description is mistaken for accuracy, though broad categories or a strong impression without specifics cannot single out one person.
when: A witness describes a person only in broad categories or gives a strong impression without specifics.
why: Confidence and vividness are mistaken for accuracy; a clear mental picture may still lack the detail that identifies its subject.

text: Use a verbal description only as a lead, never as firm evidence; recognition from a description alone does not confirm identity, and vague sightings mislead if treated as proof.
when: When a suspect is known only through description.
why: Descriptions are indirect and cannot establish that the person met is the one described.

text: Some witnesses who never saw faces say they would not recognize the people involved, because such people do not stand out in memory.
when: Asking witnesses whether they would recognize a disguised culprit.
why: Unremarkable appearance leaves weak memory traces.

text: Loose descriptions of age, clothing, vehicles or manner narrow the field slightly, fit many people, and cannot separate the person seen from similar people; a partial fit is not proof.
Do not identify a suspect from a vague witness description alone; require a second clue such as a distinctive item or scar. Give NPC witnesses vague sightings by default.
when: Identifying a suspect from a witness, or designing identification in a mystery.
why: Generic traits match too many candidates; vague descriptions should not resolve a case alone.

text: Vague or inconsistent descriptions of an object weaken any timing inference drawn from it, so compare accounts across sources first.
Vague or generic features make a reveal feel arbitrary rather than earned.
A description too vague to single out a person identifies no one, so a disguise that defeats recognition also defeats the evidence.
A frightened witness may describe a human being as a monstrous or unnatural thing, so the description should be checked before it is believed.
when: A witness reports a terrifying sight
why: Fear distorts perception and description

text: 1) Record the witness's account exactly as given. 2) Ask specific questions about clothing, features or details to narrow a vague description. 3) Ask follow-ups that eliminate candidates one at a time.
when: When a witness recalls a person only vaguely or describes a group of possible suspects.
why: Specific questions turn a vague memory into a usable description and separate candidates.

text: Name the exact target item so searchers can flag near-matches, such as a similar but wrong object, for closer checking.
A witness with fixed expectations may dismiss real evidence as useless before examining it, such as marks the authorities have already disturbed.
when: when a witness has preconceptions about a scene
why: expectations filter what the witness considers worth attention

text: A witness who hears a clue-bearing remark often does not recognise its importance and treats the words as trivial.
when: the remark is heard before its context is known
why: the witness lacks the later fact that links the words to the event

text: A witness who has already heard others' stories can repeat them convincingly.
A witness who merely echoes another's claims is likely coached, and comparing their statements exposes the echo.
when: two witnesses give similar accounts
why: Coaching produces repetition rather than independent recall.

text: Treat a retold account as partial when the intermediary admits omitting or altering details; infer what was left out from the marked gaps.
when: evidence reaches the investigator through an intermediary
why: Marked omissions show where the record is incomplete

text: Repeat a single word a witness has used, which can prompt them to name a person or place they had kept back.
A pattern that explains one clue but not the rest is a candidate, not an answer; test it against every other detail first.
when: a scene's details echo a known story or name

text: A witness who repeats the investigator's exact wording may be echoing an earlier answer or the investigator, so the claim needs testing.
Accepting an account because a second agrees confuses agreement with independent proof; accusers who drew on the same suggestions count as one source, not many.
A witness's account can be shaped by what they have already heard, including the investigator's own words, so later agreement is weak evidence.
when: Questioning a witness after the investigator has named a theory
why: A witness who adopts a term offered to them may not have observed the thing described.

text: Treat an embedded narrator's account as testimony to check against outside facts, since the narrator's claim of truth confirms nothing.
when: when a narrator swears the account is true
why: A narrator who has a stake in the outcome can shape what is remembered.

text: Confidence does not measure accuracy: do not rank a more confident witness as more reliable, and test strong claims, including whether the reported event happened.
when: A witness is sure of an identification, especially by conspicuous features when identity matters, or claims they could not be mistaken about someone they know.
why: Sincere, detailed accounts can still be unreliable perception, and confidence reflects assumptions as much as observation; check motive and memory.

text: A witness tied to a suspect or faction by friendship, rivalry, kinship, debt or loyalty has a stake and may point toward a rival, so their account is not neutral.
when: The witness has a personal, financial, kinship or factional tie to the suspect, or protects an allied group.
why: Loyalty, interest or a stake in the outcome colours what the witness reports; record the reasons for their stance.

text: Do not discard a biased witness; test each reported fact separately against independent evidence, such as possessions or payments, since observed facts may hold even when interpretation does not.
when: The witness was present but has bias, a grievance, hostility to the questioner, or reasons to shade their account.
why: Bias can distort what a witness reports even when sincere; weigh each claim by the speaker's prejudice and state of mind.

text: A first-person narrator with romance, self-interest or hindsight may give a clean record that omits their own contact with the victim; weigh it against other sources.
when: The narrator benefits from how events are recorded.
why: Self-interest shapes which events the record includes.

text: Affection, hostility or past history can make a witness minimise, idealise or omit facts; weigh their account against that history and their attachment and defensiveness.
when: A companion, relative or another character describes a person they are close to, hostile to, or have history with.
why: Past relations and emotional closeness colour present judgments and what is reported or omitted.

text: Watchers blended among ordinary people make a hiding place seem safe to its occupants.
Minor witnesses may give information grudgingly, so extract it bit by bit and check each piece.
Even a confident, disciplined witness can be sure of an outcome they never saw; separate what they observed from what they inferred, since reliability does not extend beyond their view.
Confidence in a face or seal does not confirm dates, timing, settings or names; check those details separately.
when: When weighing a witness's confident recognition or seal identification.
why: Confidence reflects the witness's feeling about memory, not the accuracy of its details; they may be certain about the wrong moment.

text: Confident tone does not prove direct knowledge or accuracy; emotion, drink, rumour or admitted personal lapses can sound convincing, so separate testimony from actual knowledge.
when: Assessing a convinced witness whose knowledge is central to the case.
why: Confidence is a delivery quality, not access to the event; a person can believe they know more than they do.

text: Companions who are also suspects or friends may give biased accounts of a suspect's whereabouts.
Witness descriptions of an object's cost or use may be exaggerated or coloured by the witness's motives and should be checked against other evidence.
when: Relying on witness testimony about objects.
why: Witnesses may have reasons to distort what they saw.

text: A half-seen listener, such as a glimpse of a coat or a moving door, is not proof of identity and is easily misidentified.
when: a listener was only partly seen or heard

text: A forceful lay observer can be right for the wrong reasons, so a reveal should rest on evidence rather than on how confidently someone speaks.
when: Weighing competing explanations

text: A confident witness may still misremember a physical detail, so the answer must be asked directly and recorded exactly.
A detailed, confident statement can still be wrong, because fear can inflate what a witness imagines seeing.
when: When a witness under fear gives a vivid, complete account.
why: Fear and imagination can produce confident but mistaken detail.

text: Do not treat a confident group account as proof when light was poor or observers were frightened.
when: Many observers agree on a crime's details
why: Agreement among uncertain observers is not independent confirmation.

text: Design an NPC who protects one faction as a source of bias, so their statements can mislead the player toward a rival.
when: Writing NPC dialogue and clues
why: Biased sources add verification work for the player

text: Do not assume a witness is lying because they are wrong on a detail, since error and deceit are different and must be assessed separately.
when: A witness is shown to be wrong on a specific point.
why: A mistaken detail does not by itself prove intent to mislead.

text: Plant a witness's honest mistake, such as hearing one place but being told another, so it reads as innocent first and as a clue later.
why: A clue hidden in an innocent error is recognised only once its meaning is known.

text: A biased witness adds emotional texture and misdirection, but a clean, unbiased witness is needed when the player must learn the event accurately.
when: choosing a witness to an event

text: Hedged or technically true wording, declining to speculate, or stated motives for silence can hide how a speaker knew something or intended, signalling a self-serving or incomplete account.
when: A statement is smooth but its source or purpose is unclear, or a witness narrates events with qualifiers or a reason to conceal.
why: Careful phrasing avoids admitting hearsay, self-interest or a hidden plan; committing to claims exposes the witness to contradiction; speakers soften claims they are unsure of.

text: Evasion, refusal or curt reply signals concealment, not proof of guilt, innocence or a specific fact; record and test it against other evidence, since fear or caution may cause it.
when: A witness refuses, postpones or curtly answers a direct question, even with other details offered, avoids eye contact, over-protests, turns hostile, or is asked about a claim they may have reason to hide.
why: Refusal can reflect fear, principle, irrelevance or caution rather than concealment of fact; a lost trail alone should not confirm wrongdoing; a witness may deny doubt while still evasive.

text: Failing to defend oneself or reacting with anger toward accusers is an interpretation and weak evidence, not proof of guilt or innocence.
when: An accused person fails to defend themselves or confronts or drives off accusers.
why: Anger under accusation can arise from injustice as easily as from guilt.

text: Make an NPC's account incomplete or omit one important fact, so a later clue or second source exposes what was left out.
when: Designing NPC statements that change over the game.
