why: Delayed exposure rewards players who keep and compare clues.

text: Witnesses often give vague phrases and admit key facts only when pressed, so a brief answer signals reticence; the admission can reframe earlier events they reported.
when: Questioning a witness who may have something to hide, or whose account seems incomplete.
why: Fear of consequences keeps witnesses silent.

text: Under direct questioning, evasion shows as sharp refusals, claimed forgetting, sudden subject changes, flat replies, comfort or lies, and reluctance to discuss a hobby.
when: A suspect is questioned directly about a sensitive matter.
why: Fear, pride, indifference or self-protection can each produce evasion that hides the truth.

text: A subject who changes the topic or answers a key point with irrelevant questions is stalling; note the redirection and return to it later, as evasion marks a sensitive area.
when: A subject steers away from a topic, or is questioned about a key point.
why: Avoidance points to a matter worth revisiting; the redirection itself draws suspicion.

text: Evasive witnesses show hesitation, delayed replies, folded arms, hands working together, shrugging, nervousness, blame-redirection or a watchful manner replacing a warm greeting.
when: During questioning, especially when hesitation or body language conflicts with a flat denial.
why: Such signs are leads to follow up, not proof of guilt; discomfort or shock can produce them innocently, so weigh unprompted disclosures above answers given only when asked.

text: Hospitality, small talk and flattery build rapport and make a guarded witness talk more freely, especially one short of money.
when: A witness is unhelpful at first or in financial need.

text: Calm, gentle questioning, or warm talk about a topic a person enjoys, makes a guarded witness share more fluently than direct questions do.
when: A witness answers in short or guarded replies to direct questions.
why: A relaxed interviewer or conversation lowers the witness's guard.

text: Framing questioning as help, and stating openly that full candor serves the witness, can make a reluctant witness accept and tell everything.
when: A witness holds back information but needs help.

text: Careful characters avoid writing anything that could later be used against them, and word notes so only the intended reader grasps their purpose.
when: a message could incriminate its sender
why: written words become evidence that outsiders can use

text: A witness with failing memory may hide the lapse and recall a point only when a specific cue, such as a named event, prompts it.
when: questioning someone whose memory is impaired
why: People conceal lapses to protect their standing, so recall may appear only when a precise cue is offered.

text: A witness who refuses to become complicit and asks how silence can be secured reveals their own stake, which is itself evidence.
when: a witness is asked to keep quiet
why: Reasons for silence show what the witness fears

text: An evasive witness answers a direct question with mockery, compliments and topic changes rather than a direct reply.
when: A witness is pressed on a point she wants to avoid.
why: Deflection keeps control of the exchange and avoids the substance of the question.

text: A witness with a grudge against a target tends to color statements about that target, even when the details they give sound precise.
when: the witness holds open hostility toward the subject
why: a motive to harm shapes what they emphasize or invent

text: A person who knows the attackers but will not name them, or who overstates a vague danger, is likely hiding a personal secret.
when: An attacked person is evasive about who attacked them.
why: Refusal to answer and overstated fear signal where the real stakes lie.

text: A witness bound by silence may speak once a serious charge threatens someone who cannot speak for themselves.
when: a secret is held and an absent person is accused
why: the reason for speaking limits how far the account can be trusted

text: A witness who initially hides what they know may have been pressed for silence by the subject, so the reluctance is itself evidence.
when: A witness had direct contact with an unknown subject.
why: Pressure to stay quiet shows in the witness's hesitation.

text: Answers under questioning can be evasive; vague replies, such as excuses about poor visibility, should be recorded and tested rather than accepted.
when: a witness gives vague answers about conditions
why: vagueness can hide the true vantage or motive

text: A character may bind others to secrecy and still refuse to explain why, so the reason stays hidden even after the secret is shared.
A guarded suspect often probes with questions about the topic at hand, so the pattern of those questions reveals what they care about.
when: a suspect is questioning the investigator

text: Several suspects who each hide a private engagement look alike, which can disperse suspicion across the group.
when: Multiple suspects conceal similar private activities.
why: Shared secrecy makes innocent and guilty concealments hard to tell apart.

text: A witness who speaks around a subject, or fixates on an unrelated detail, may be passing on a suggestion without stating it outright.
when: speech is circumlocutory, reluctant or oddly fixated
why: the witness avoids stating the fact directly

text: A witness who keeps avoiding a specific object, or sounds strained when it is mentioned, may know more about it than they say.
when: Behavior contradicts their words in a narrow, specific way
why: Awareness of the object can cause avoidance

text: Hostility toward a group can grow without any open act, from resentment of its rise or of its separate standing in the community.
when: a family or group stands apart from the wider community
why: resentment and suspicion can spread without a specific offense

text: In a divided community, ordinary acts are read as hostile, and evidence is gathered to fit each camp's position.
when: a community split into rival parties
why: Existing hostility shapes how each side interprets events.

text: A creature guarding something valuable shows it through altered posture, head movement and repeated inspection of one spot.
when: a creature has hidden or protects an item
why: Guarding changes the creature's ordinary conduct.

text: When neither side makes careless errors, the winner is the player who anticipates the opponent's likely mistakes and exploits them.
when: a reduced endgame where both players play carefully
why: small, predictable mistakes decide the result

text: When two parties sense a trap, they test each other with indirect questions and answer carefully, each reading the other as calculating.
when: mutual suspicion in a conversation
why: each side fears the other is steering the exchange

text: A pretender who answers probing questions with indignant refusal rather than answers tends to be read as evasive and suspicious.
when: A claimed expert is pressed with specialist questions
why: Anger in place of answers gives the test away and invites suspicion

text: A witness who answers indirectly can be pressed with a sequence of narrow, direct questions, and bystanders often judge the resulting account to be untrue when it is evasive.
when: A witness refuses or deflects direct questions about money, relationships or motive.
why: Narrow questions remove room for vague answers, and evasion under pressure reads as deception to observers.

text: A guarded professional's refusal or rebuff to questions signals that they know something relevant, and their suspicion of the questioner's motives often reveals this.
when: An NPC refuses to answer or reacts with suspicion
why: Withholding information is a sign of knowledge or concern

text: A guarded character may defend a claim with a plausible explanation, then retreat when asked a specific follow-up about its practical details.
when: A character's explanation is pressed with a concrete follow-up question.
why: A prepared surface story often lacks the details needed to answer follow-ups.

text: Characters often withhold information by default, so trust between them is partial on all sides.
A witness who is evasive or strained, or repeats a last-seen account word for word and denies too quickly, may be guarded; this warrants more questions, not proof of guilt.
when: When a witness shows discomfort or reluctance during questioning
why: Strain and quick denials can come from concealment, or from ignorance, fear or innocence.

text: A pressed witness often answers with a rejoinder that deflects suspicion without adding information.
when: When a witness is questioned on a point they would prefer to avoid.
why: Deflection protects the witness while appearing responsive.

text: A witness who repeats an answer rather than adding detail, or refuses to commit when asked who had access to a suspected substance, may be protecting someone.
A secret can be priced in money, and the person holding it may raise their demands over time.
when: when a secret is used as leverage

text: In a small community where watchers exchange tales, secrets are hard to keep because observations spread from person to person.
Everyone inside a guarded, sealed room is a witness for everyone else during the seal, but only for the period the seal lasted.
Insider knowledge spreads widely, so a narrow circle of knowers is a hypothesis to test; knowledge many share, like a weapon's location, narrows suspects only slightly.
when: Narrowing suspects by what they knew.
why: Routines, schedules and leaks can give outsiders the same facts.

text: When a witness says 'I don't know' to a point they plainly can answer, name that directly and re-ask from a different angle or in plainer words.
when: A witness repeatedly declines or says 'I don't know' to a specific question.
why: They may be guarded rather than ignorant; reframing can reach information withheld without the witness knowing it.

text: A witness who lies about several unrelated details, or takes the blame, may be shielding another person, so look for a motive to protect someone else.
Mention a guessed name or relationship as already known, then read the witness's reaction, which confirms the link more reliably than a verbal answer and exposes anxiety.
when: A witness may confirm a suspect's identity, or an interviewer wants a guarded witness to reveal anxiety.
why: Witnesses react to perceived knowledge held by the questioner.

text: Make threats a player option with consequences, such as a witness who turns hostile and refuses further talk.
When two people share the same hesitation and avoid the same subject, infer that a secret is being kept from the investigator and others.
when: Witnesses withhold the same topic

text: Read a hostile or biased source against its grain; its false claims can reveal what its writer wants to hide.
when: A source is malicious or self-interested

text: Give NPC dialogue a false justification that the player must test against a clue, such as a note or letter.
A suspect's weak point can be found in a secret that gives leverage, and the conspirator with a separate personal motive is the one to pressure when another will stay silent.
when: One conspirator is unlikely to talk
why: A second, personal motive offers a lever the silent party lacks.

text: Establish a person's usual behaviour first, so that a departure from it stands out as meaningful.
when: when watching a suspect's reactions
why: Change is only visible against a known pattern.

text: A refusal to give a name or identity is not evidence in itself, but it signals that the claim needs independent checking.
An NPC who holds a damaging secret can serve as an early warning, because the culprit may target that NPC.
when: Designing an NPC whose secret drives a later threat

text: Answer a direct question evasively to keep it open and build suspense.
when: a character is asked a question they are not ready to answer
why: an unresolved question keeps the audience pressing for the answer

text: Keep an unidentified figure as a default suspect, which prevents the search from closing on the first plausible culprit.
when: a mystery has several viable suspects
why: an open unknown keeps the search from closing early

text: Ambiguous, guarded parting lines leave a character unsettled and keep tension open between scenes.
Treat each hostile act, such as a bribe, threat or staged fight, as evidence of the opponent's plan.
Holding back indications that are not yet confirmed keeps an inquiry open and prevents premature conclusions.
A minimised claim about one's own timing, such as being a few minutes late, should be checked against external records because it can conflict with what actually happened.
when: a witness reports their own arrival or movements
why: self-reports tend to soften timing

text: A stranger who offers a drink at once while watching the target's reaction is giving a second warning sign of an ambush.
Do not assume every reported remark is strategic, since ordinary candour can explain advice as well.
when: When judging the motive behind a piece of counsel.
why: Sincere advice is also common.

text: Record what a source withholds as well as what it gives, since omissions can be informative.
when: interviewing a guarded witness
why: refusals can point to hidden facts

text: A contact that someone omits from their account is a fact to check, because the silence can be an inconsistency.
when: Comparing a character's account against records
why: Omissions can conceal relevant connections.

text: Hold a key alibi witness back behind fear or confrontation, so the witness gives their account only after the player resolves a related threat.
when: designing a critical witness who will not speak freely
why: Earned testimony carries more weight and ties the witness to the story's stakes.

text: A witness withholding out of care for someone may reveal the fact only after repeated contact, trust or the right evidence; a single appeal to confidentiality does not compel disclosure.
when: A witness protects someone they care about, or an NPC withholds a fact for an understandable reason.
why: Motive to conceal outweighs a single request, so repeated contact or evidence is needed to change the position.

text: A witness NPC's choice to reveal or withhold a fact can change how other characters judge the suspect.
when: a witness holds a fact that bears on a suspect
why: Other characters weigh the suspect according to what they are told

text: Tie a secret to a trust or reputation value, so revealing it changes how other characters respond to the player or NPC.
Revealing a secret that the other person finds shameful can turn an outwardly steady relationship into hostility.
Prolonged questioning through standing, sleep loss, and repeated urging by several questioners in turn wears prisoners down until they agree to nearly anything.
when: An interrogation is long and rotates through multiple questioners.
why: Exhaustion and repetition erode resistance and blur memory.

text: Harsh pressing, mockery or provocation can make a witness refuse cooperation, give contradictory or false information, hide the key detail, and turn into an enemy.
when: Pressing a witness who is already defensive or frightened.
why: Pressure triggers defensiveness, lowering account quality and making later checking harder.

text: Stalling an answer without new clues frustrates characters and players, reads as evasion rather than suspense, and worsens the longer it lasts.
when: The investigator must wait for information, or a central answer is delayed over many scenes.
why: Anticipation needs visible progress to stay engaging; players may stop caring about the answer.

text: Withholding a fact without a visible motive shifts audience sympathy away from the holder and frustrates players, so the holder needs a clear reason.
when: Writing secrecy into a character's actions.
why: Unexplained concealment seems unfair to the audience.

text: Withheld information is not proof of guilt: witnesses may conceal from fear of suspicion, to shield another, or to keep a private matter or innocent errand hidden.
when: A suspect or witness keeps a secret.
why: A suspect who keeps a secret can look guilty though innocent.

text: Asking a witness to keep a secret can compromise their neutrality later.
A staged confrontation fails once suspects compare notes, because the separation that makes the test work is lost.
when: Running a separated-suspect reaction test.
why: The test relies on suspects not knowing about each other's summons.

text: Assuming a secret is a loan or financial transaction by default causes investigators to miss the real nature of the hidden item.
when: A hidden object or payment is found without its contents being checked
why: A familiar explanation is accepted before the evidence is examined

text: Withholding an outcome without sensory clues leaves the scene unclear and the audience unable to follow it.
Guarding against one risk can create another, such as an escape route that implicates a third party.
A guarded answer is not always a lie; a witness may speak only about what she was permitted to see.
A witness who feels confided in may overshare or say what the listener wants to hear, so a single conversation can distort testimony.
when: when a witness has been drawn into a sympathetic exchange
why: Sympathy and flattery bias what a witness reports.

text: A host who steers the talk toward personal matters may be shaping the interview, so keep returning to the investigative question.
A guard's account of who passed is only as reliable as his attention during the watch.
when: a guard is the only source of who used an exit

text: A leading hypothetical read as a trap hardens the suspect's defences, so the probe gains little.
when: The suspect suspects the frame is a trap.
why: Once the frame is seen, the suspect refuses to engage.

text: Confessions that repeat the accusers' described acts may reflect shared sources rather than independent fact.
Accepting the first tidy answer without asking what it fails to explain is a common investigative error.
Sharing a theory with a single official can expose the trap to rivals or the press.
Refusing to hear a witness can lose evidence, since a witness who insists on telling their story may hold what the investigator needs.
when: When an investigator wants to avoid a witness's account.
why: Declining to listen discards testimony the witness is willing to give.

text: A witness who refuses to confront a supposed source may be hiding a human cause, so the refusal itself deserves scrutiny.
when: A witness avoids investigating a claimed threat.
why: Avoidance can protect a concealed mundane explanation.

text: A forgetfulness explanation can cover a timeline mismatch, so it should be treated as a claim to test rather than a fact.
when: When an anomaly is explained by a person's lapse of memory
why: Memory-based explanations are easy to accept without verification

text: 1) Match the hostile witness's tone so she does not dismiss you. 2) Reveal your purpose only after she accepts you and presses for it. 3) Press one precise point repeatedly without pause. 4) Record unguarded remarks and watch behaviour after the exchange.
when: Interrogating a guarded witness with a hidden tie to a suspect.
why: Rapport lowers defences, precise triggers provoke reactions that broad questions do not, and rapid repetition leaves no time to compose a reply.

text: 1) Identify the topic the NPC avoids. 2) Assign the NPC a motive to shield another, such as loyalty or fear. 3) Unlock the motive when the player asks the correct follow-up.
when: Authoring a guarded NPC whose secret involves another character.
why: A stated motive gives the player a concrete path to the hidden truth.

text: 1) Appraise the witness before pressing. 2) Adopt a relaxed, sympathetic manner. 3) Accept a stated point, even a doubted one, to keep the witness talking. 4) Verify accepted points later.
when: A witness is guarded and a direct question would simply be denied.
why: Lowering the guard keeps the witness talking, but accepted points may be unreliable.

text: Make an evasive or off-topic answer a cue that prompts the player to follow up.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that hides knowledge

text: Have NPCs withhold information by default so players must cross-check claims rather than trust a single source.
Let a friendly NPC whose kind conduct conflicts with other clues hide a hostile objective that the player uncovers later.
Keep an investigator's answers neutral and unconcerned when a suspect is listening, so the suspect gains nothing to read.
when: when a suspect may be probing what the investigators know
why: revealed reactions let the suspect adjust

text: A performer's rules can protect the deception by treating refusal to answer as acceptable while forbidding admission of ignorance, so silence becomes a non-answer.
when: When a performer is questioned about something it cannot answer.
why: Refusal preserves the illusion, while admitting ignorance would expose it.

text: Let a hostile reply end the conversation or open a different route, rather than simply failing the player.
Do not treat a pleasant or hospitable manner as proof of innocence; judge by behaviour rather than courtesy.
Give a secret-holding NPC a trust flag that the player's promise sets, controlling which other characters may learn the information.
when: Designing NPCs who share information conditionally
why: Conditional disclosure makes the player's promises matter

text: Give dialogue trees evasion flags, with I don't remember options that unlock or lock later questions.
Remove a witness from the scene with a plausible errand for a set time so the rest of the scene can be searched unobserved.
when: when a search must happen without a witness watching
why: The witness is absent while the errand lasts.

text: Sharing enough evidence wins cooperation, but revealing the core theory can warn the suspect; share evidence and hold the theory back.
when: When questioning a cooperative suspect

text: Guarding answers strongly to a curious stranger protects secrets but can cost goodwill with a contact who may later prove useful.
Keeping plans to oneself limits leaks, but it leaves allies guessing and unable to act on accurate information.
Locking a secret clue to one character until a later choice creates a real dilemma between sharing it and keeping it private.
when: When designing information gating in a mystery.
why: Withholding carries risk, so the player must weigh the cost.

text: Revealing a backup witness early proves a point at once, while holding them back keeps evidence in reserve for use only if the main evidence is challenged.
when: Deciding when to disclose a second witness.
why: Early disclosure gives up the option to use the witness as a fallback.

text: A sudden hostile exchange releases built-up tension but closes off the lines of inquiry that were open.
A heated quarrel witnessed by bystanders establishes both a motive and a checkable record, since others can corroborate or contradict the account.
when: when a public disagreement may bear on a death
why: witnesses give independent confirmation of what was said

text: A witness at a fixed vantage point gives specific sightings, and an item missing from one person later found elsewhere can corroborate a link.
1) Ask the witness to fetch the physical evidence. 2) Accompany the witness to where it is kept. 3) Observe the item in its original place.
when: a physical record is needed to test a claim

text: 1) Ask the witness to sketch the scene roughly. 2) Mark where key objects stood. 3) Check those positions against the real layout.
why: a sketch turns vague memory into testable positions

text: Give witness NPCs a source field of saw, heard or inferred, and let players ask how each claim is known, since a claim's reliability depends on its source.
when: when writing NPC testimony or when a witness's account is central and its basis is unclear
why: Explicit sources let players test claims

text: Let NPC-signed in-world records serve as fixed reference points for disputed events, so players have a trustworthy anchor to weigh conflicting testimony against.
when: Multiple NPCs have sworn to an event
why: Witnessed records anchor contested accounts

text: A fixed gaze at an object can silently prompt a speaker to mention that object, even without a question being asked.
when: during conversation about a relevant object

text: A witness who repeatedly glances at a scene element and looks away quickly shows awareness of it.
A gesture toward something the observer cannot see is clear in intent but unexplained, so it can read as madness or as a hint.
when: A character points at a hidden object.
why: Missing context leaves the gesture open to interpretation.

text: A witness who only glimpsed an event and cannot describe it or agree with others provides little more than a witness who saw nothing.
when: Several witnesses report the same event
why: Unidentifiable or conflicting sightings cannot be matched to a suspect

text: Watching a hidden person take a delivered object can briefly reveal their condition through their face.
when: a hidden person is observed at a handover

text: Reading a witness's hesitation or glance toward a person as confirmation of identity is a mistake.
when: A witness hesitates or looks at someone during an identification.
why: A glance is ambiguous and can be shaped by the room's expectations rather than by recognition.

text: 1) Record the accused's movements. 2) Check whether an accuser shows a reaction or marks at that moment. 3) Repeat the movement deliberately. 4) Record whether the reaction matches each time, and include a control.
when: Physical traces are claimed to follow a suspect's movements
why: Repetition with a control separates a real link from a chosen pattern

text: A single glimpse rarely identifies a person; pair it with a physical item such as a uniform or emblem.
why: the item links the partial description to a known source

text: Witnesses often notice details by chance without knowing they matter, so their sightings can be incidental.
when: a witness observes an event before its significance is known
why: attention goes to what seems ordinary at the time

text: A witness can be confused in one task yet lucid in other matters on the same day, so reliability should be judged task by task.
A person impaired by drug use can misjudge elapsed days and insist on the wrong day, so their timing should be checked against other sources.
when: a witness is intoxicated or otherwise impaired
why: Intoxication distorts a person's sense of time.

text: As a witness's physical strength weakens, their recall of old events may become fragmented and out of order, while memory may remain the least damaged faculty.
when: Questioning a witness whose health is declining
why: Memory can persist even as other abilities fail

text: Record passing vehicles and bystanders even when they are mentioned only in passing, since a brief detail can later serve as a witness.
when: a scene is being documented
why: incidental details can become decisive later

text: A witness who faints or cannot tell sleep from unconsciousness is weak on timing and perception, even where a physical detail they report proves true.
A witness under drugs or stress can misreport or fade, so observers' descriptions must be read in light of that condition.
Giving an NPC witness a reliability value that drops when impaired produces vague or contradictory dialogue.
when: designing witness dialogue

text: Perception-altering drugs can dilate pupils, shift heart rate, produce elation and a sense of superiority, and intensify colors and shadows, changing what the user observes.
when: An observer has taken a perception-altering substance

text: Intoxication or poor sight, such as dim light, makes a witness's identifications and accounts untestable, so they need outside support before being relied on.
when: A witness had drink or lacked a clear view
why: Impaired perception makes claims unverifiable or unreliable

text: Judging what a witness saw without considering intoxication, a fall or fear mistakes a distorted perception for an accurate record.
Vague time estimates, such as roughly an hour, can shift a timeline's window; verify them before drawing conclusions.
why: Imprecise recollection can place an event on the wrong side of another.

text: A witness's inability to describe someone may be real or a dodge, so test it against other evidence.
An impaired witness may recall vaguely or refuse to describe what they saw.
An informant who is impaired or self-absorbed may still give useful hints, but their reliability is lower.
A drowsy or inattentive witness weakens a transfer record, and their later claim to have attended is itself uncertain.
when: When the witness is tired or distracted during the exchange.
why: A record only counts if the witness actually observed the exchange.

text: Assuming a silent witness has nothing useful to add.
Relying on a witness with impaired hearing without checking what she could actually perceive can lead to a wrong timeline.
when: A witness with hearing loss gives testimony about sounds.
why: Her account of silence may reflect her limits rather than what happened.

text: Assuming a pre-existing illness rules out a human cause. The illness may only make the victim vulnerable while a deliberate trigger still acted.
Altered time perception can make an honest witness seem to have been in two places at once, so a fixed clock is needed before claiming an intruder.
1) Set a sworn statement beside a statement by the same person made earlier or later. 2) Ask whether the witness could have been reliable when the first statement was made.
when: a witness has conflicting statements

text: 1) List each witness's claims. 2) Check official records for past perjury or punishment for deception. 3) Argue the evidence itself is false, not only the witness's character.
when: challenging testimony in a hearing

text: A sincere but impaired witness, such as one drugged, is unreliable because impairment corrupts perception; weigh their statements against other evidence and give them less weight.
when: a witness was drugged or otherwise impaired
why: impairment corrupts perception even when the witness is honest

text: Challenge a witness when their motive or earlier statements conflict with what they now claim.
Use an in-world witness, such as a ticket seller or guard, as an independent record that confirms or breaks a claim.
Deliver an absent NPC's account as a note or recollection, and let the player judge how reliable it is.
when: the witness is absent from play

text: Rest an impeachment on documents and several sources, since a retraction can itself be discounted as unreliable.
Test the most obvious motive against the evidence before accepting it; valuables left untouched argue against robbery as the real purpose.
when: When a crime scene suggests theft but the evidence does not fit it.
why: A wrong motive sends each later inference in the wrong direction.

text: Test an alibi against timed evidence before trusting a theory, because a plausible theory can collapse once the timed evidence is laid out.
when: a tidy theory is forming
why: timelines expose impossibilities that theories hide

text: Delay sensitive findings from people who are not yet ready to hear them, especially when the news may hurt them.
when: a finding may distress those affected

text: Start with an easy-to-check fact that narrows the field, rather than the hardest fact, which can waste time before progress is made.
when: When several facts remain to be tested.
why: Early narrowing reduces the cost of later checks.

text: Test a single anomaly against the other facts before acting on it; resolve to check it first rather than concluding at once.
when: a lone fact contradicts an otherwise strong case

text: Test each compartment of a container separately, since scent can concentrate in one small space while the rest is clean.
When a setting seems too ordinary for the threat described, test the surface with further inquiry rather than accepting the impression.
when: the setting contradicts what the investigator was told to expect
why: a mismatch between expectation and appearance is a warning sign

text: A light teasing remark that touches a sensitive point tends to fail and can damage rapport.
when: when a companion has a hidden weakness
why: the remark exposes what the other person is protecting

text: Ask follow-up questions in an order where each answer points to the next place or person to check.
why: each answer narrows the possibilities

text: A test can reveal a different substance from the one suspected, and that single result can redirect the whole investigation.

1) Fix the time and surroundings of the witness. 2) Walk through events in order, one fact per question. 3) Check what the witness could physically see. 4) Test indirect observation such as reflections. 5) Confirm the end state of objects and doors. 6) Ask whether the witness may have dozed during any gap.
when: A witness describes a sequence of actions and her vantage must be judged
why: A fixed order exposes gaps and tests whether the account fits the physical setup

text: 1) Interview witnesses one at a time in a set order, such as by rank. 2) Compare each short report with the others. 3) Check each informal claim against known facts.
when: When several witnesses share a household
why: Patterns and contradictions appear only when reports are compared

text: 1) State the known sequence of events one step at a time. 2) Ask the witness to confirm or correct each step. 3) Record confirmed steps as facts and corrections as what the witness knew.
when: interviewing a witness who has partial knowledge
why: Confirmations lock in facts, and corrections reveal the witness's actual knowledge.

text: 1) Ask a general question about a witness's whereabouts. 2) Narrow it to a time window. 3) Narrow it again to specific places. Each answer sharpens the next question.
when: Interviewing a witness about a timed event.
why: Narrowing in steps prevents the witness from answering with vague generalities.

text: 1) Fix a starting moment, such as when people woke. 2) Walk forward through the day in order. 3) Press vague intervals for a concrete time or last occurrence. 4) Record each person's movements. 5) Mark where accounts disagree for later checking.
when: When several people moved through the same space over a day.
why: A sequenced account exposes inconsistencies that a bare timeline hides.

text: 1) Demand the full account at the outset. 2) Ask about one step at a time: who acted, what was done, in what order, and why. 3) Test each link against facts already held. 4) Get partial admissions on record. 5) Use each admission to check later denials.
when: when a suspect's account depends on a chain of decisions
why: each link can be checked, so weak links surface

text: 1) Begin with low-stakes witnesses who give partial testimony. 2) Question the household member whose answers matter most. 3) Question the central suspect. 4) Hold a decisive witness for last. 5) End on an unresolved question.
when: Structuring an inquiry where several witnesses each shift the picture.
why: Ordering witnesses by rising stakes builds pressure and makes each answer more consequential.

text: Require a sequence of approaches, such as flattery then payment, before an NPC reveals a simple fact.
when: designing NPC dialogue gates

text: Hold back a sensitive question until the suspect has revealed the relationship that makes it relevant.
When one witness's meeting is emotionally heavy, schedule it so that witness is not left upset and then sent away immediately afterwards.
when: Multiple witnesses are seen in a fixed order
why: Order can protect a distressed witness from a harsh exit

text: Test a witness's sight line before relying on a reconstruction built from it.
Pass sensitive material through a trusted person in a sealed note rather than an ordinary messenger.
when: when information must stay secret across a team

text: Run fingerprint checks only after trace analysis, so that handling for prints cannot disturb the trace.
when: Trace evidence and prints are both needed
why: Print handling can disturb or contaminate the trace

text: A questioner who is emotionally attached to a distressed witness often drops a pressing question and turns to comfort, so the witness's distress can end the questioning.
when: The questioner cares about the witness and the answer matters to the case
why: Affection pulls the questioner's attention from the question to the witness's well-being

text: A suspect who turns suddenly polite and guarded is often sensing pressure, so a sharp change in courtesy signals that scrutiny is building.
when: A suspect becomes aware of an investigation
why: Guarded courtesy often masks awareness of pressure.

text: Distressed, grieving or dazed witnesses often have trouble with time and sequence, so a single account from them may be unreliable.
when: A witness is emotionally shaken or confused
why: Strong emotion disrupts memory of order and timing.

text: A witness can give many words and promises yet reveal very little, so an investigator should judge what is actually disclosed, not how much is said.
Appearing inattentive lets an observer take in more than those around them.
when: Visual evidence is blocked or the observer wants to stay unnoticed.

text: Emotional display, such as distress or appeals to feeling, can hide the truth or serve to avoid answering, so emotion must be separated from content.
when: A witness becomes emotional during questioning.
why: Emotional display can obscure what is actually said.

text: 1) Ask permission before raising a delicate matter. 2) Start with a neutral past fact the suspect can confirm. 3) Get a clear answer before linking it to the present event. 4) Corroborate the fact with a third-party source. 5) Present the theory in steps, checking each with a short question. 6) Watch the suspect's expression throughout. 7) Rule out frightening alternatives to calm the suspect.
when: Questioning a vulnerable or sympathetic suspect when information matters more than confrontation.
why: Gentle, step-by-step questioning gathers information without alarming the suspect.

text: 1) Start with indirect or harmless questions. 2) Raise a specific claim as a test. 3) Note whether the witness accepts, rejects, or challenges it. 4) Escalate to pointed questions only as the witness reveals defensive moves.
when: When questioning a reluctant witness who will not volunteer facts.
why: Staged pressure reveals defensive reactions, which yield partial admissions rather than full confessions.

text: 1) Let the witness finish without interrupting. 2) Tell them their account is what is needed. 3) Once they calm, ask practical questions about location and expenses. 4) Only then ask harder questions, promising they will be believed.
when: when a witness is angry, grieving or frightened but key facts are needed
why: Letting emotion pass keeps the account coherent and encourages a fuller telling.

text: Gentle questioning gathers information with less alarm but may yield only partial agreement, while confrontation risks defensiveness.
when: Choosing an approach for a suspect.
why: Each approach has costs in what it reveals and how the suspect reacts.

text: Reasoning about an ambiguous clue tends to swing between readings until a fact decisive enough to separate them is found.
when: no decisive fact is yet available
why: each reading stays plausible until it is tested

text: A witness's failure to see a person clearly, due to poor lighting at meetings, is itself a fact to record.
when: when a witness could not identify someone they met
why: The limit on observation shapes what the testimony can establish.

text: An observer's intoxication, excitement or emotional state can distort their sensory reports and their reading of others' tells, so check it before accepting the account.
when: When a witness reports a sensory impression under poor conditions, or when reading another person's tells.
why: Impaired or agitated observers give weaker accounts, and their impressions may be imagined.

text: Several independent identifications of an object, especially one located near a body, strengthen a case; a second witness repeating a shared source adds no confirmation.
when: When linking a weapon or item to an event, or when two witnesses agree.
why: Independent identifications reduce the chance one mistaken witness drives the conclusion; repeated information looks like corroboration but adds no independent evidence.

text: Let an observant character register what others miss, and give a dismissive remark that acts as a hint for a careful player.
when: Writing dialogue where a character dismisses a clue
why: Careful players can separate the dismissal from the truth.

text: An observer who admits limits on their own judgment makes a physical description read as objective observation rather than flattery.
An NPC witness can give accurate information whose reliability depends on conditions the player can verify, such as light, distance and line of sight.
when: when designing NPC testimony in a game
why: Making reliability depend on checkable conditions lets players weigh what they are told.

text: Reveal a disguise through a witness directly observing the change rather than through a confession.
when: Staging the exposure of a disguised character
why: Seeing the transformation is more convincing than a spoken explanation.

text: Overhearing part of a private exchange reveals a forming decision and can shift a listener's view; in design, holding back the remainder creates curiosity and a later payoff.
when: When a character waits where a conversation about her can be heard, or when designing restricted-access eavesdropping scenes.
why: The overheard decision is raw information about how she will be judged; partial information creates curiosity and gives the full meaning a later payoff.

text: Overlooking sound is a mistake, since a creak can reveal a hidden watcher as surely as a glimpse.
when: Assessing whether a hidden observer could have been detected.
why: Sound can betray presence even when sight is blocked.

text: An observer's excitement can pass to witnesses and spoil their independent behaviour, so the observer should stay calm and passive during a test.
when: Running a test in which witnesses react to the scene
why: Witnesses pick up the observer's cues, which contaminates their reactions.

text: Separate what a witness saw from what they assumed, since confident witnesses often present assumptions as observations.
Have different characters report different phenomena at the same event, so the mismatch becomes a deduction puzzle for the player.
when: Designing conflicting NPC testimony
why: Mismatched reports invite the player to reason about who saw what

text: Let an NPC witness a suspicious act and report it, but have others dismiss the report because of that NPC's reputation, so the player must recover it from rumour.
when: when designing NPC testimony and rumour systems

text: Separate a witness's observations (saw, heard) from inferences and feelings, and check each against what they could actually know; feelings are not evidence.
when: when a witness reports an event, states a conclusion, or is emotional
why: Each kind of perception has different reliability; conclusions and emotions can outrun what was perceived.

text: Real witnesses blend what they saw with what they concluded, so testimony mixes observation and inference rather than giving exact, formal descriptions.
when: taking testimony from a witness

text: Witnesses can report the same observed symptoms yet reach different interpretations, and a confident wrong explanation can shape what they do next.
when: Several characters describe one shared observation.
why: People attach their own assumptions to observations, so identical facts yield divergent conclusions.

text: Witnesses of an impossible event may stay unsure whether to believe their own senses when no mechanism is given to settle the doubt.
when: after witnessing an impossible event
why: no explanation is available to resolve what was seen

text: A witness may report speech or actions they could not see directly, such as through thin walls or a shared space, so their knowledge is limited by vantage point.
when: Assessing what a witness could have perceived
why: Sound and sightline limits restrict what a witness can know firsthand.

text: A witness's report of nothing unusual, or a vivid detailed account, reflects only their view and attention; ask what lay outside their frame.
when: When a witness's report is taken as proof nothing happened, or a detailed account is taken as the whole story.
why: Observation is limited to the witness's position and attention; a detailed account can still omit the decisive moment.

text: Letting the player stand where a witness stood and view what was visible from there teaches sightline reasoning and tests the witness's account.
A brief obstruction that pauses a moving person can give a watcher time to see an object dropped and picked up by someone else.

1) Identify what the witness directly observed. 2) Verify that observation against physical facts. 3) Evaluate the witness's explanation separately, since interpretation can change on later reflection; apply extra scrutiny if the witness has a grievance.
when: Weighing testimony that mixes observed facts with explanations or identifications.
why: An observation can be accurate while the interpretation built on it is wrong; sensory facts are firmer than the cause assigned to them.

text: 1) Present the plain observed facts first. 2) Present the writer's analysis separately. 3) Let the reader check one against the other.
when: when a found text mixes events and interpretation
why: Separating the two lets the reader test the interpretation against what was actually seen.

text: Separate a witness's assumptions and general impressions from firm observations; treat recall under brief, faint, or poor views cautiously, recording them as tentative impressions, not identifications.
when: Taking testimony about events or appearances; when a sighting rests on a brief or poor view.
why: Assumptions often enter memory and get reported as observations; confident testimony can exceed what was perceived.

text: Ask witnesses for their impressions as well as their facts, since interpretation is part of testimony.
Give each witness a stated vantage point so the reader can judge what they could and could not have observed.
when: Presenting witness testimony in a mystery
why: Knowing the vantage point lets the reader weigh silence and conflicts correctly

text: Rapid, sustained questions on specific checkable details can break a witness's composure faster than attacks on the witness's character.
when: a witness is questioned in quick succession on narrow points
why: specific gaps are harder to defend than general credibility

text: Emotional distress can cause an evasive witness to end questioning, leaving a contradiction unresolved.
when: A witness is pressed on a weak point.
why: Distress shifts the witness's response from answering to withdrawing.

text: A legal hold on a witness can be challenged within about forty-eight hours, so investigators cannot keep a witness held indefinitely.
when: the legal system allows a rapid challenge to a material-witness hold

text: A witness who suddenly goes quiet or looks frightened after a conversation may be under pressure rather than simply reticent.
when: interviewing a witness who has just spoken with another party
why: A sudden change in manner often follows an intimidating exchange

text: A witness glimpsed just before a reveal adds pressure without new information, reminding the audience that someone is watching.
when: A reveal is about to happen with an observer nearby
why: Visible observation raises stakes without adding facts.

text: Even a witness of good character may be pressured into silence or changed testimony by fear.
when: When a witness has reason to fear consequences.
why: Fear overrides character in shaping what is reported.

text: Pressing a volatile witness at close range raises the interviewer's fear sharply and can turn the interview hostile.
when: A witness reacts strongly and is physically close.
why: Close proximity to an agitated person escalates threat and fear.

text: 1) Use a direct light or controlled setting to unsettle the witness. 2) Ask a sudden, pointed question. 3) Watch the mouth and hands rather than the eyes for reactions.
when: Questioning an evasive witness.
why: Mouth and hand movements are harder to control than gaze.

text: Make intimidating a witness in a pending case a serious offense, with the most severe penalty when the case involves a life.
when: when designing a court or witness system
why: Threats against witnesses corrupt testimony before a verdict.

text: Pressing an evasive witness can open up partial knowledge, but pressing one with nothing to give tends to harden them.
when: when deciding how hard to press a witness
why: pressure only helps when the witness is holding something back

text: People who fear future interference with their papers or affairs often take protective legal steps in advance.
when: a person worries that others will tamper with their records
why: advance protection guards against later meddling

text: A witness's protective actions, like moving valuables or defending a source, reveal what they stand to lose; note when defending someone tells you something.
when: A witness takes protective action after an event.
why: Protective actions show what the person stands to lose.

text: A witness who protects another may be shielding them or exposing their own involvement; test this, and treat any revealed exposure as a new line of questioning.
when: A witness's conduct seems evasive, or a witness defends another character.
why: Protective conduct can hide another person's involvement. The risk they accept makes their own involvement a new lead.

text: Set up protection before a threat acts, since an enemy who senses danger may move quickly.
Protect a child witness by placing them somewhere safe and limiting visitors to those with written authorization.
when: A child witness may be exposed to a sensitive investigation.
why: Controlled access reduces exposure and pressure on the child.

text: A sole-check witness who can confirm or break an alibi becomes dangerous to its beneficiary and may be removed; protect them before relying on their testimony.
when: A witness is the sole independent check on a suspect's whereabouts.
why: Their testimony threatens the person whose alibi is at stake. Loss of the witness removes the only check.

text: Delay and interrogation intensify a witness's fear, and that fear lowers the reliability of their later statements.
when: A witness is kept waiting or questioned at length.
why: Fear compounds with each delay, degrading the accuracy of what the witness reports.

text: Guards can be defeated, so protection lowers risk but does not guarantee a witness's safety.
A promise of protection can make a witness's cooperation depend on what they want kept hidden.
when: A witness is promised anonymity in exchange for information

text: 1) Move a threatened witness out of reach immediately. 2) Expect the opposition to target them next, since they are the remaining witness.
when: A witness is endangered by an opponent.

text: When a document may have been tampered with, copy its contents and destroy the original to limit what a watcher can later use.
when: a document is exposed to others
why: the original is the most useful evidence

text: Check that a suspected protector had access or power to act, since emotional motive alone does not establish opportunity.
When a witness's safety is threatened because of what they know, assign watchers to follow and guard them.
Gate a protected informant or leave-alone order behind more than one clue, so its reveal rests on accumulated evidence.
when: designing quest branches involving a protected character
why: Multiple clues make the branch depend on evidence rather than a single lucky find.

text: Do not reveal which witness supplied a clue during questioning, so the source stays protected.
Do not dismiss a witness's fear entirely when it inflates an ordinary sign, since the reaction may still reflect something real about the listener.
when: a witness's fear may be inflating an ordinary sign

text: A witness who sees the listener as an ally, or who feels flattered and at ease, may reveal hidden motives or say more than intended.
when: when the witness sees the listener as an ally or the interview is relaxed or flattering
why: Comfort or perceived shared sides lower the guard that normally limits disclosure

text: A witness who feels their account is taken seriously volunteers background and gossip freely, even without prompting.
when: when the interviewer shows mild familiarity with the subject
why: the witness does not feel their story is being dismissed

text: Asking several witnesses or searching old papers can help recover details, though it may still leave questions open.
when: a key memory is vague
why: Second sources add partial recovery without guaranteeing answers

text: When a witness closes up, switch to a narrower question that secures the one fact still needed, rather than pressing on the broader topic.
Build rapport with a witness before raising a point that threatens their account, so they relax and are less guarded when the point is made.
when: Before confronting a witness with a timing or consistency problem

text: When a character is re-read after the player learns more, the meaning of that character's earlier lines can shift.
Track rapport as a state value: blunt questions lower it, and a well-judged approach raises it and unlocks deeper answers.
when: Designing dialogue systems for guarded NPCs
why: Rapport gates which information an NPC will reveal

text: Rapport can make a witness protect the suspect, so the questioner hears mainly what is comforting.
why: Sympathy for the suspect filters what the witness chooses to say

text: A remark that someone is improving is not a statement that travel or activity is safe; reading it as one is a common reasoning error.
when: Interpreting a witness's comment on a person's condition

text: 1) Calm a witness who breaks down. 2) Return to the question asked. 3) Recover the sequence of events in order.
when: when a witness becomes too distressed to answer
why: Distress blocks recall until the witness is steadied

text: 1) Build rapport with hospitality and compliments. 2) Ask for a physical description. 3) Ask for independent identifiers such as handwriting or a photograph.
when: a witness is needed to identify a person

text: 1) Identify the group most likely to have seen the subject. 2) Frame each request as a specific question with a time window and location. 3) Use separate requests for separate sightings. 4) Name one contact point. 5) Run the notice for a fixed period unless cancelled.
when: when the witness is unknown and the event was public enough that someone may have noticed

text: Let a lost memory return by placing the character back in the same state or location where it was formed.
when: Designing a memory-recovery moment in a story.
why: Returning to the original context can trigger recall.

text: Offer small, concrete rewards to a child or servant, then negotiate upward if needed, since a loosened tongue can open talk among the adults around them.
when: A household is guarded
why: Small rewards build rapport cheaply

text: Design dialogue for rambling NPCs so off-topic answers still hold hints that players can recover by asking the right follow-up.
when: when writing long conversations with talkative characters

text: Indirect rapport-building yields more disclosure but needs time; a deadline forces a direct question that usually gets less.
when: Choosing how to question a guarded witness under time pressure.
why: Trust-building takes time that a deadline may not allow.

text: Witnesses keep the gist of a conversation but not exact words or every promise, and recollections of brief exchanges are vague, so accounts diverge on details.
when: several witnesses recall the same conversation or someone recounts a brief earlier exchange
why: Memory keeps the gist more reliably than wording; brief exchanges are weakly encoded

text: Figures seen in passing are often forgotten, since attention goes to the errand or to tracking a fast mover, so little detail is encoded until later facts link them.
when: a witness is busy with another task or a fast-moving figure passes through view
why: Attention is spent on the errand or tracking, not on memory encoding

text: Overheard words gain meaning once a witness learns of an event; a warning reported after the harm may be recalled afterwards, so it is not proof of prediction.
when: a witness recalls overheard words or a warning after learning of an event
why: Later knowledge reshapes memory and can add significance that was not there

text: Recollections formed later are shaped by suspicion or a prior favourable view of one side, so they may differ from what was said and are weak evidence.
when: When testimony rests on an old recollection the witness admits is uncertain, or a witness holds a view of one side.
why: Later suspicion or prior opinion can reshape what was remembered.

text: Approximate ages and appearance estimates vary with the witness and year, so they should narrow the suspect pool and be checked against a register, not identify one person precisely.

1) Note visible cues in sequence, such as shifts in mood, gesture, gaze or expression, rather than waiting for words. 2) Tie each cue to the thought or need it implies. 3) Adjust your behavior to what they seem to need. 4) Test each reading against other sources or the subject's own account.
when: When a witness's account is partial or impaired, or when inferring a subject's train of thought from observed cues.
why: Silent or impaired people signal through behavior, and single readings can mislead; linking each cue to a thought makes the reading testable.

text: Tag NPC testimony with any interest or stake the speaker has, such as a rival or beneficiary, and lower its confidence so players weigh the claim against motive.
when: when generating NPC testimony or an NPC gives information about another character
why: the speaker's stake affects reliability

text: Record each witness's exposure time, distance, lighting, angle and vantage range with a confidence value, so distant or secondhand identifications rank below close-range ones.
when: when NPCs report what they saw, from afar, in poor conditions, or heard secondhand
why: Players need to weigh reports of different reliability; these conditions determine how much a statement can support

text: Tag each witness with conditions such as intoxication, illness, fatigue, deafness, distraction, injury or strong emotion that lower accuracy and completeness, so players can discount their sightings.
when: a witness has a known condition affecting observation or when designing testimony systems
why: Such conditions reduce the accuracy and completeness of recorded details; a visible condition gives players a basis to judge reliability

text: Reminders, leading questions or offered answers can alter recall; details unlocked this way are less reliable than spontaneous recall, and uncertain witnesses tend to adopt suggestions.
when: a witness is prompted, reminded or offered a possible answer
why: Recall is rebuilt on each retrieval, and uncertain witnesses adopt suggestions rather than admit they do not know

text: Perception fills gaps in fast, brief, partial or dim views with expectation, so a detail can feel vivid yet be wrong; a spinning light can read as a continuous ring.
when: motion is too fast or partial to resolve, or a witness sees someone briefly or in dim light
why: Expectation supplies the missing frames and gaps get filled by what the witness expects

text: Shock, panic or waking can leave a person confused and unable to recall events, so they must rebuild them from others' accounts.
when: a statement is given just after waking, or in shock or panic
why: Memory of recent events is disrupted in that state.

text: A later repeated name, place or phrase can link a half-remembered earlier fact, but the player must notice the match before the link forms.
when: a new clue repeats a name, place or phrase from an earlier one
why: Recall is cued by matching words

text: Failure to recall is often failure to retrieve: cues succeed where open questions fail, bringing back forgotten remarks suddenly or gradually, and partial impressions of long-unseen people.
when: a witness cannot recall unprompted or is asked to identify someone not seen for a long time
why: Cues trigger memories that open questions miss; memory is searched by association

text: Witnesses recall costume or disguise traits, such as hair and eyewear, rather than fixed features, so a vivid distinctive description can misidentify the real appearance.
when: using testimony about a suspect described as vividly distinctive or disguised
why: Costume details are more salient than underlying traits and get attributed to the wearer

text: A witness showing alarm, avoiding eye contact or refusing when a pointed question touches a hidden relationship or their movements has revealed a point to check, not proof of guilt.
when: questioning a witness about a sensitive topic or their own movements
why: Fear of exposure causes visible distress and refusal signals a sensitive point

text: A decisive detail or throwaway line in a passing text is often overlooked and recognised only once later context reveals its meaning; without it the fact seems unimportant.
when: a clue is placed in a passing text or a decisive fact was received early
why: The meaning becomes clear only with later context

text: Impaired memory comes back as scattered, vivid fragments with gaps, and images may recur dreamlike, blurring perceived with imagined.
when: a witness was drunk or impaired, or reports vivid memories from a sleep-disrupted period
why: Impairment disrupts the sequencing and continuity of memory and entangles perception with imagination

text: Witnesses often revise timing recollections once a reconstruction of events is offered. Check revised accounts against the known schedule.
when: When a reconstruction is shown to a witness.
why: Witnesses may adopt the proposed sequence without a real memory of it.

text: A partial view, such as a reflected image, is incomplete, and what it appears to show depends on what the observer already believes.
when: observation is indirect or obstructed

text: Witnesses confident about small mechanical details often grow vague under questioning, and once damage is repaired their memory becomes the only record.
when: a physical state has been altered after the event
why: repair removes the physical evidence that could check their account

text: A forgotten object in a place the culprit should have left suggests the culprit returned there for a reason.
Readers who receive a fragile note often memorise it nearly word for word, turning a physical clue into stable mental evidence.
when: a physical clue is easy to lose or damage
why: memory keeps the clue even if the object is lost

text: Repeatedly trying to recall details can make a person certain of something that never happened, since memory is easily reshaped.
when: a witness is pressed for details
why: recall itself reshapes memory

text: Witnesses reliably recall the main event but often lose side details such as a minor bet, so a detail missing from some accounts is weak evidence.
why: minor details fade faster than the central event

text: Memories can resurface during reflection, so a late recollection can be sincere yet conflict with earlier statements.
when: A witness recalls a detail well after the event.
why: Reflection and a personal stake can bring back or reshape recall.

text: A witness often ties a visual detail to the moment they first became suspicious, which makes recall specific yet more open to challenge.
when: when a witness explains why they noticed something
why: the anchoring moment gives a detailed memory that can be attacked

text: Ordinary witnesses rarely recite a routine day smoothly; they reconstruct it from habit rather than replaying events.
when: when asked about a routine period days earlier
why: routine guides reconstruction, not a stored sequence

text: Witnesses pressed on false testimony may minimize it as trivial, describing it as sport or play.
when: a witness admits a sworn statement was false

text: Memory of an event weakens over time, and the witness may come to doubt their own senses about it.
The key content of a destroyed document can survive in memory and keep shaping a character's choices.
Players keep a memorable, odd-looking figure in mind as a suspect, even when that figure has no role in events.
when: A figure has a distinctive manner or prized possessions.
why: Distinctiveness makes the figure stick in memory.

text: A half-remembered clue often surfaces suddenly after the person has stepped away from the problem and reflected on it.
when: A player is stuck on a puzzle or unexplained observation.
why: Reflection away from the problem can release associations that focused search missed.

text: Witnesses often cannot recall their own recent hours yet give precise dates for events years old, so recent recall needs more checking.
when: when a witness is asked to place their own recent activity

text: People forget ordinary-looking individuals easily and cannot identify them reliably later, especially when their clothing, movement and speech match many others.
when: A witness must recall or recognise a person who looks like many others.
why: Without distinctive features to anchor memory, a common appearance blends into the crowd.

text: Stressed witnesses may report impossible physical sensations, which should be weighed as unreliable testimony rather than accepted as proof.
when: Witnesses describe a suspect's presence in ways that defy physical evidence.
why: Acute stress distorts perception and memory.

text: A vivid colour can be remembered sharply while the outline of the person stays uncertain.
when: a witness recalls a striking feature from a partial view
why: strong colour is easier to retain than shape in a glimpse

text: A practical concern that was pushed aside by a frightening event returns to mind only after the emotional spell is broken by a reminder of the mundane issue.
when: a group has been gripped by an uncanny or frightening moment
why: Fear suppresses ordinary priorities, which resurface once the emotional state eases.

text: Witnesses can recall a single word differently from the original, and the difference can change the timeline.
when: a replay reveals a differing word
why: a small wording change can shift a stated time

text: A witness's impression of a voice or tone can change on reflection, as a quick first judgement is revised.
A nearby word or item can prime a reader toward a different reading of a clue, even when the reader is careful.
when: clues read in context
why: mental association steers interpretation

text: A witness recalls a memorable event clearly, and that memory also reveals what their attention was focused on.
when: When judging how reliable a witness's detailed recall is
why: Vivid events anchor memory and show where attention went

text: Witnesses often do not register an absence until asked a specific question about it.
when: questioning a witness about a missing item
why: An unmarked absence is not stored in memory as a notable event, so it surfaces only when a cue prompts it.

text: Bystanders remember sudden physical reactions such as a start, pallor or tremor and keep them in the record even before anyone knows what they mean.
when: A tense moment with a sudden bodily reaction
why: Vivid bodily signs are noticed and stored as memory even without an explanation.

text: A hurried answer can make a person forget a fact they would otherwise remember, such as a date or a presence.
when: A person must answer quickly under pressure.
why: Haste reduces recall of details.

text: An incident that once drew notice tends to resurface as a reason for suspicion long after it has lost relevance.
when: A past event has been publicly noticed
why: Attention keeps the event available as an explanation

text: Players quickly notice when every clue result points the same way, and then stop trusting the investigation.
when: A puzzle's outcomes all lead to one answer
why: Uniform results reveal a predetermined answer

text: Obscurity in local records can result from circumstances such as hurried recruitment or a fire, rather than from a lack of importance.
when: When a person or event is poorly documented.
why: Rushed departures and disasters leave records unfinished or lost.

text: Enemies or fleeing NPCs that check for witnesses and take cover before acting give players a readable stealth cue.
when: when designing NPC behavior around observers
why: Visible caution signals that observation matters.

text: An NPC that has only seen clumsy thieves may conclude thieves are always caught, because its beliefs are built from the sample it observed.
when: an NPC forms beliefs from its own observations
why: Its observed sample contains only failures

text: A witness who treats assumptions as facts can be steered to react as a manipulator predicts, which makes such witnesses exploitable.
when: when a character is prone to accepting suggestions
why: Assumptions acted on as facts make responses predictable

text: Lapses of attention can erase both the thought being pursued and the intended destination, leaving gaps in a person's account of their own route.
when: A person falls into prolonged brooding while moving.
why: Attention drifting away means the thought and goal are not held in memory.

text: Sudden or stressful events distort witnesses' sense of order, so recalled sequence may be wrong; reconstructing the moment can recover forgotten details.
when: when a witness describes a stressful or sudden event from memory
why: sequence memory is weak and re-living a moment cues it

text: Quoted text recalled from memory rests entirely on the reciter's memory, even when delivered word by word.
when: A witness reproduces a document from recollection.
why: Memory can alter wording, so precise quotation does not guarantee accuracy.

text: An embarrassed or distrustful witness may give confused or unhelpful answers to direct questions and only open up later.
when: A witness is ashamed, wary, or unable to recall under direct questioning
why: Direct questioning can make the witness shut down

text: Witnesses often remember behavior, a voice, a gesture, or a clothing fragment, but not faces, especially after a brief glimpse.
when: A witness observed people briefly or in poor light
why: Attention goes to actions and details more than to faces seen for a moment.

text: A witness reports only what angle, distance, light, attention and memory let them perceive; a brief glance in poor light yields a sparse, shaky picture of features.
when: a witness had a brief or poor view
why: Limited light, time, angle and attention restrict what is actually perceived

text: Identification from memory is weaker than a receipt or record and must be checked against it, since partial impressions are fallible.
when: a witness's recollection conflicts with a documented sale or record
why: Memory is fallible in ways written records are not

text: A detailed witness description can still be partial: height, age or dress may be recalled while other traits, like eye colour, are not.
A witness's memory of writing seen in unusual conditions, such as floating in air, may be unreliable for judging gender or style.
when: Relying on a witness to identify a writer.
why: Unusual viewing conditions limit what can be reliably observed.

text: Witnesses often cannot confirm whether a specific bolt was engaged, even when they know a related door was usually locked.
when: when questioning witnesses about door states at night
why: routine knowledge of one door does not transfer to others

text: Witnesses to a document signing often see the manner of the process rather than the contents, so their reports describe behaviour, not text.
A witness's remembered details, such as a distinctive physical feature, are only as reliable as the memory behind them.
when: A witness supplies specific remembered details, especially under duress.
why: Memory can be incomplete or mistaken even for vivid details.

text: A clue's physical size does not determine its value; a large object can be overlooked while investigators search for small traces.
when: Judging the importance of physical evidence.
why: Size is a poor proxy for evidential relevance.

text: Identifying someone by voice through a wall is only as strong as the voice's distinctiveness and the listener's attention, and distinctive voices are often easy to imitate.
when: when a single auditory witness is the only evidence someone was present
why: The trait that makes a voice memorable also makes it easy to mimic.

text: An honest witness can still be wrong, and a memory lapse, possibly from illness or exhaustion, is a limit of observation, not proof of lying.
when: a witness fails to recall a detail or shows confusion after sleep or sickness
why: Fever and fatigue genuinely impair recall, and a gap in memory is not proof of deception

text: Anchor witness times to fixed or scheduled events, such as lamps being lit, a shop closing or a timed climax, so approximate recollections can be checked against the clock.
when: witnesses recall times loosely or place an event relative to a scheduled cue
why: A shared or independent reference point gives memory something to be checked against

text: Reveal witness memory in fragments that players must assemble, rather than a complete memory at once, keeping them reasoning toward the full picture.
when: designing memory reveals or traumatic, confused witness scenes
why: Fragments keep the player actively reasoning toward the full picture

text: Limit NPC witnesses' perception, such as by a wall, deafness or partial vision, so testimony covers only part of the scene and players must work out what each could know.
when: designing witness NPCs for an investigation
why: Limits make testimony a puzzle rather than a fixed fact source

text: Treat a witness's lost stretch of memory as possible evidence that someone deliberately arranged it.
when: a witness cannot recall a period of time

text: A witness who cannot recall events is evidence about the witness's condition, not proof that nothing happened, and should prompt a check of what the witness consumed.
when: Witnesses have gaps in memory after a shared drink or meal.
why: A common substance can explain memory loss and point to a tampering route.

text: Recalling a planted detail at the point it becomes important reminds the reader of it.
when: a clue's meaning is about to be revealed
why: The reminder links the early detail to the moment of payoff.

text: A witness's recollections can show that documents said more than a narrow reading allowed, so memory should be checked against the record.
Use short prompts that extend the witness's own recollection, such as asking whether they knew someone before a certain date.
when: A witness is recalling past events.
why: Small prompts let the witness lead and carry the memory forward.

text: An alibi or sightline is only as strong as the witness's position, attention and record; check where each witness stood and what they were doing.
Recall-probing questions check what a witness observed, not what they intended, so they cannot establish motive.
A habit of attention, such as methodical detail-by-detail scrutiny, can hint at a person's training or background.
when: when forming early hypotheses about a person with few hard facts
why: how someone attends to the world reflects their past

text: Witnesses often forget names and minor details, so accepting a gap can be better than pressing for it.
when: when a witness cannot recall specifics

text: Verifying a witness's claim about where someone is staying can reveal that another person has been asking about the same target.
when: A witness's account of a location cannot be confirmed.

text: Read a witness's evasions, mood and stake in the outcome alongside their words, since each affects how far the account can be trusted.
when: assessing any witness
why: The shape of an answer carries information the content does not.

text: A partial view can confirm a general impression, such as a person's presence, but not a specific identity.
Recall a witness after other evidence has come in when their account conflicts with what was later revealed.
when: a witness's account conflicts with later evidence

text: A small detail recalled late, such as part of a number, can be checked quickly and may yield either a confirmation or a new lead.
Whether the watched person saw the witness reveals the witness's own risk, which raises the urgency of protecting them.
Distance and poor conditions limit what a witness can reliably report, so a lead should stop where the observation actually ends.
When a witness's account has a gap, test it against another person's record of the same events before trusting or dismissing it.
when: the missing detail matters to the case
why: a lapse can be genuine or convenient, and only corroboration tells them apart

text: Weigh a witness's new recall by specificity, consistency and checkability. Details that grow vaguer or harder to verify deserve less weight.
when: A witness's memory changes over time

text: Let an NPC witness's memory improve with dialogue progress, but tier each new detail and make it checkable against world state.
when: Designing NPC memory that unlocks through conversation

text: A guard who saw someone leave but dismissed it can hide a clue, giving the player reason to question the testimony.
when: designing unreliable witnesses
why: expectations hide what the witness saw

text: Offer players the choice between accepting a suspect's reaction at face value and testing it against other evidence.
when: designing accusation scenes
why: choice makes evidence checking a deliberate act

text: A harmless-looking NPC can carry hidden knowledge; an offhand remark by another NPC hinting the cover is false lets players catch it.
when: When designing a low-status NPC who holds important information
why: Hints make the mismatch discoverable

text: Place an incidental remark that reads innocently at first and gains meaning once the player's assumption is overturned.
when: Scripting dialogue meant to pay off after a reveal.
why: A remark that is reinterpreted later rewards attentive players without signposting the answer.

text: Counting containers and their marks can show how many people were present, and a discrepancy in the count can overturn a theory.
when: Reconstructing who took part in a gathering.
why: Each person leaves traces such as wet rings or used glasses, so a mismatch shows an absent or extra person.

text: Recalling a suspect while their emotions are still raw may prompt a confession sought as relief, though a calm suspect may still refuse.
