when: right after an emotionally charged scene
why: the suspect may want to relieve distress

text: Treat witness approximations, such as 'about' times or 'four or five days', as ranges, not exact values, and distrust a sudden precise clock time from someone vague elsewhere.
when: Reconstructing events from witness accounts.
why: Approximate estimates are common and witnesses often cannot recall exact numbers or times; a sudden precise figure may be unreliable.

text: A witness's impression of a person's mood can count against a reading that implies deliberate harm, so compare it with the physical evidence.
when: When a witness describes a victim's state of mind before an event.
why: An unsuspecting mood argues against a deliberate act.

text: Readings of involuntary cues depend on background knowledge of the subject, so an observer without that history should treat a confident reading as unreliable.
when: When interpreting a subject's cues without knowing their history
why: Each link in a cue chain relies on known background

text: Trust a sensory report according to what that sense can reliably tell, so a firm sound from a known direction outweighs a cry of uncertain source.
when: when judging a witness who heard something without seeing it
why: Senses differ in localization and identification accuracy.

text: Preserve or restate a clue in persistent written form so players can work it out at their own pace.
when: When a puzzle needs sustained thought rather than a quick reaction
why: Players solving over time need the clue available again without relying on memory.

text: Collect independent reports from several observers before revealing your own conclusion, then compare them to expose disagreements.
Choose a reconstruction timing window when observers are distracted, since people absorbed elsewhere notice little.
when: Testing whether an act could go unseen
why: Distraction determines whether a sequence could have passed unobserved

text: Compare who wrote each account, what access the writer had, and what the writer stood to gain before relying on it.
when: When the primary record is lost or the writer had a stake in the outcome.
why: Access shows what a writer could know, and interest shows what they might distort.

text: Assume a trained agent memorised a document after a brief look, rather than assuming it was carried away.
when: when judging what a trained agent has learned from papers
why: trained agents memorise closely

text: Give each NPC's knowledge a confidence value, and have the player cross-check two or three NPCs before acting on a clue.
when: Designing NPCs with partial or uncertain knowledge.
why: Confidence values and cross-checks keep unreliable clues from being trusted alone.

text: Treat details outside a witness's attention focus as unrecorded: the most vivid memory marks where attention was fixed, and divided attention may leave a detail never recorded.
when: when weighing a witness's memory of a brief, fast or chaotic event

text: A witness's account is more reliable when backed by notes written at the time, with dates and hours.
why: Notes made close to the event resist later distortion.

text: A witness who knows the household's routines and the person's appearance well carries more weight as an identifier.
when: when weighing a close associate's identification
why: Intimate knowledge makes recognition more reliable.

text: Plant a precise number in an offhand witness memory, so the audience can re-read it later as evidence.
when: a witness gives a casual account
why: A detail recorded as trivial becomes decisive once its exact value is checked.

text: An NPC whose memory state persists can drift, contradict itself, or revise its story when pressed, so each contradiction becomes a usable investigation tool for the player.
when: In interactive questioning systems.

text: Players who reach a related puzzle later can recall earlier dialogue, so the payoff rewards attention rather than luck.
when: A puzzle depends on information given earlier
why: Recall turns noticed details into solutions

text: A witness's presence changes both what speakers say and how the witness later remembers the exchange, even when the witness is told to keep out of the way.
when: when a third party listens to a private talk
why: speakers adjust their words, and an overhearer still records the whole exchange

text: Perceived brightness of a room depends on the observer's position and the light source, so the same room can seem bright or dark.
Two partial views of the same scene can conflict because the physical state changed between observations.
when: An observer sees the scene only through a gap or limited angle.

text: Recall can be tied to conditions the witness experienced, such as distance, weather, or lighting, so vague memories follow from the environment.
when: designing witness memory in a game world
why: environmental conditions make the vagueness a designed result rather than arbitrary

text: A hidden NPC behind a locked door can reveal later that the player's earlier actions were overheard.
A fresh sighting can reframe an earlier memory, turning something first read as carelessness into deliberate concealment.
when: A new observation contradicts an old impression
why: New evidence changes how past events are interpreted

text: An NPC's claim of a distant event can be checked against line-of-sight and distance rules, so a player can catch an impossible claim.
when: When designing NPC testimony in a game with spatial rules.
why: Spatial constraints give the player a way to test testimony.

text: An interrogation system can track hesitation and conflicting times as witness states, which the player resolves by cross-checking records against each other.
when: When simulating witness behavior in an investigation game
why: Persistent witness states give the player contradictions to resolve through records.

text: A detail planted too far before its payoff may be forgotten entirely, so the payoff must come within reach of the player's memory.
Leading questions and emphasis can plant false memories, so agreement with a supplied detail proves little; the witness may agree with the questioner instead of recalling.
when: When a questioner supplies or stresses a detail the witness should confirm.
why: Suggestion can replace recall.

text: Witnesses fill gaps in later recall with assumptions or expectations held at the time, so observed facts must be recorded apart from inferences.
Identifications from partial views or incomplete recall can be wrong despite confidence, as similar coats or builds produce the same recognition; corroborate uncertain matches with a second source.
Frightened or motivated witnesses' firm answers, and confident recalled dates or exact times, can be wrong; keep time windows open until independently confirmed before timelines count as proof.
when: Relying on a witness's confident directions, recalled dates or timelines.
why: Confidence in delivery or recall does not guarantee accuracy.

text: Recalled speech and letters are reconstructions, so exact wording is approximate; check quoted letters against originals, and write down statements when heard, since no other listener can verify private talk.
when: When a witness recalls or reads aloud speech, a private conversation, or a letter.
why: Recall of wording degrades, and exact-wording memory depends on listener memory and attention.

text: Recaps repeat old errors or add new ones and spread hearsay; each retold item should add a correction or new link, since repetition delays the answer without adding information.
Single observers see only part of a scene and tend to overstate partial glimpses, so ask what they did not see and check their account against other accounts and traces.
when: When a single observer describes a scene or a partial glimpse.
why: A glimpse such as a few lines read from a distance is easy to overstate.

text: Old memories of events decades past are reconstructed and blurred, so sworn testimony about them, including childhood memories, can sound more certain than it is.
when: When a witness recounts events long past, such as early life or decades-old events.
why: The oath does not fix the facts; reconstruction can feel more certain than it is.

text: Observers who break agreed protocol or report different kinds of result make the group's record incomparable and unreliable; a record is comparable only when everyone follows the same protocol.
when: When several observers or investigators report one event or progress.

text: Sensory impressions such as drafts, smells or sounds are easily misremembered, and a recalled sound may not be the one that matters, so they should not carry a claim alone.
why: Witnesses may also misremember times or sounds.

text: A witness who suddenly recalls more, or recalls a sound after the fact, may assign it to a convenient person without evidence, shifting blame.
when: When a witness suddenly names a person or recalls a sound, especially after a threat or deadline.

text: Absorbed observers drift from their posts, and eager ones who move or peer around cover give themselves away to the subject, so undisciplined watchers cannot be trusted.
Routine records such as laundry days are easy to misremember under stress, so they need checking against other sources.
when: Relying on a witness's recall of household routines
why: Stress degrades memory of ordinary events

text: A single witness's recollection can miss the decisive fact, and gossip channels often carry it, so ignoring servants and tradespeople is a mistake.
when: Investigating how information spread.
why: Lower-status channels move news between households and often hold the key detail.

text: A deadline mentioned once and then dropped loses its pressure, so later scenes no longer feel like a race.
Approximate times and descriptions can be wrong without any intent to deceive, so error and lying must be told apart.
A link that exists only in memory may be coincidence or a recall error; re-check the original wording before relying on it.
Relying on a witness's memory that items were unchanged is only as strong as that witness's reliability.
when: When the argument depends on a witness recalling the state of a place or object
why: Unchanged-item testimony can be wrong or misremembered

text: A deliberate habit such as keeping a clock fast can be forgotten when a witness reconstructs an event later, shifting their reported times.
when: Reconstructing times from memory.
why: The bias may not be in the witness's mind when they recall the event.

text: A witness's inventory count can be wrong or self-serving, so the inference from a mismatch depends on the count being accurate.
when: When relying on a witness's account of possessions.
why: Witnesses may misremember or misreport, which can create a false mismatch.

text: Staff recollections are approximate and may conflict, so they should be cross-checked against records.
Dismissing a report because the accused cannot remember the event is a mistake, since memory failure does not disprove the report.
when: Evaluating a report against a suspect's claimed lack of memory.
why: Forgetting is not evidence that the event did not occur.

text: An examiner who misreports another witness's words to the accused can mislead them into admissions.
A key fact can be missed when it is buried under filler, and a deviation can be mistaken for noise because the witness shrugs it off.
when: When a witness delivers a long account with several details
why: The witness's casual tone can hide the significance of a detail the investigator needs.

text: Revealing a fact in a way that lets the suspect trace it can expose the source to retaliation, so the source must be protected.
when: The disclosed fact came from a named or identifiable source
why: A suspect who turns blame onto the informant can damage a useful contact.

text: A distressed client may withhold the real reason for a request and give less precise answers, while sympathy can lead the investigator to accept the account too quickly.
when: Interviewing an emotionally distressed client
why: Distress reduces precision and sympathy lowers scrutiny.

text: Treating a later summary as an eyewitness record overstates its reliability.
when: When a secondary account is cited as if it came from a witness.
why: Summaries pass through another writer's selection and memory.

text: A verbal credential that is never verified lets a false claim pass as true at a checkpoint.
Small details recalled from memory, such as an accessory or whether something was left in place, are often wrong unless closely noticed; check the object itself.
when: when witnesses are asked about personal accessories or small details
why: unnoticed details are rarely remembered accurately, and the object itself is more reliable than recall

text: A witness's confident time estimate may be inaccurate, and a rambling answer can hide that the witness did not notice the time.
when: Relying on a witness's stated duration
why: Certainty and detail feel reliable but do not measure elapsed time

text: Witnesses record details that seem unimportant to them, such as whether a house was dark, and forget details the inquiry needs.
when: Collecting witness testimony for an investigation
why: Witnesses judge relevance by their own experience, not by the inquiry's needs.

text: A witness who recalls a detail only after reflection may have that memory shaped by later thinking, so early and late accounts should be compared.
when: when a witness remembers a detail after a delay
why: Reflection can reconstruct or alter what was originally perceived.

text: Timelines built from memory are unreliable and should be anchored to records where possible.
when: When reconstructing an event sequence from witness recall
why: Memory drifts, so records give firmer anchors

text: 1) List each event with its source. 2) Mark which times are firm, from logs, and which are recollections or estimates, so players know which entries to doubt. 3) Leave gaps unfilled rather than assuming what happened in them.
when: Several witnesses give partial times for the same events.

text: 1) Open with a free-recall prompt and let the subject narrate as far back as they can; the sequence should come from them, not your questions. 2) Note gaps, hedges and self-protective remarks. 3) Branch to narrower questions based on what they said. 4) Re-ask key points later.
when: At a first interview or NPC dialogue before anything is checked.
why: Unprompted narration reveals what the subject chooses to include and omit.

text: 1) Identify the dated claim in a recollection. 2) Anchor it to an independent dated record, such as a journal, note or receipt. 3) Accept only the dates that match.
when: A witness cannot recall when something happened or needs a memory of dates or times.
why: Recollection drifts, but independent dated records fix it.

text: 1) Record vague descriptors such as height, age and dress. 2) Compare them against physical evidence. 3) Narrow the suspect pool, then confirm with a physical or documentary source.
when: A witness describes a person who is not known to the investigator.
why: Witness descriptions are imprecise, so they only narrow the field until corroborated.

text: 1) Assign one person to record events in real time. 2) Take notes of everything observed. 3) Build the account from those notes, either condensed or verbatim.
when: Testimony will need to be checked or retold later.

text: 1) Have the witness write what was worn or carried. 2) Compare that list with what is actually missing. 3) Name a specific omitted detail and ask again, waiting for recall.
when: A witness can recall events but not every item

text: 1) Ask about the most recent entry the witness is sure of. 2) Ask what came before it. 3) Use the layout of the record to fix position. 4) Bring in other people as anchors. 5) Confirm each inference, moving from general points to particular ones.
when: When a witness cannot give a free account of a past day but can recall specific fixed points.
why: Each confirmed fixed point cues the next, rebuilding the sequence step by step.

text: 1) Ask when the witness first remembered a fact. 2) If memory appeared only after prompting, weigh the recollection as weaker.
when: A witness suddenly recalls a fact useful to the case.
why: Recall triggered by a prompt may reflect suggestion rather than observation.

text: 1) Establish where the witness was posted. 2) Establish what they were busy with. 3) Ask what they could not see. 4) Identify every entry and exit they were meant to watch.
when: When an alibi rests on a single observation point
why: Blind spots define where unseen movement could happen

text: Name a specific occasion, such as a particular day, to anchor a witness's memory, then ask who else was present.
1) Ask the same question again later. 2) Ask what happened just before the event. 3) Compare the answers with independent records.
when: a witness claims not to remember
why: repeated and sideways questions reveal whether a blank is real or convenient

text: 1) Identify the clue's symbol system. 2) Link its imagery to a known lore reference. 3) Form a reading. 4) Test the reading against later events or actions.
when: A clue is written in a language, code, or symbol system the player or investigator does not know.
why: A reading validated by consequences is more reliable than one based on a single matching symbol.

text: 1) Choose cues with a known link to the matter. 2) Present them one at a time. 3) Watch for recognition or unthinking reactions. 4) Record partial recall and how quickly it fades.
when: A subject's memory is in question
why: Deliberate cues can bring up memory the subject cannot report on demand

text: 1) Invite the witness to a discussion. 2) Present several facts at once. 3) Ask about specific familiar objects in a comfortable setting, which may trigger recall.
when: when a witness's knowledge is essential but not surfacing

text: 1) Confirm the witness's identity and route. 2) Ask for specifics such as names, places and mood. 3) Test the stated timing against an independent source such as a phone call. 4) Compare with physical traces.
when: A single witness's account needs corroboration
why: Specific, independently checked details separate reliable accounts from vague ones.

text: 1) Identify the vantage point, such as a hill, where the event could be seen. 2) Estimate how many people could fit within clear view. 3) Use that number to judge the scale of the event.
when: When estimating how many witnesses an event could have had.
why: Visibility limits the audience, which constrains the event's likely size.

text: 1) Separate the advice a document gives from the outcome it endorses. 2) Check clauses that grant grounds for action against those that restrain it. 3) Compare the document with the later record of what was actually done.
when: Evaluating a formal or hedged source whose conclusion matters.
why: Advice, permissions and actual outcomes can diverge.

text: 1) Ask the witness for a description of the person or event. 2) Note how vivid and specific the answer is. 3) Treat a vague answer as a weak link.
when: When a witness claims to remember a person or event.
why: A description reveals how much the witness actually observed, and vague memory limits what can be built on.

text: Read partisan documents, such as a minister's account or a critic's tract, with care, and weigh each against the rest of the evidence rather than relying on one for motives or moral state.
when: When a source has a clear side in the dispute.
why: Partisan writers shape events toward their position.

text: Separate what a witness saw directly from what they heard in part or inferred; inferences from calls or sounds are weaker than observed facts, so note overheard gaps.
when: When a witness saw only part of an exchange.

text: Gate NPC memories behind triggers such as a matching question, a revisit, a set in-game time, or a second NPC or document, so players must investigate rather than listen passively.
when: When designing NPC dialogue that reveals event details or witness recall.
why: Gated detail rewards investigation; NPCs can hold partial memories.

text: Establish the light, distance, noise and duration of each observation before weighing a witness's account; at distance identity may be impossible, and unseen or inaudible events cannot be reported reliably.
when: When a witness description, identification or testimony comes from a noisy, chaotic or distant scene.
why: Observation conditions determine how much detail can be trusted.

text: Treat memory-based clues as leads: memory can fail, be reshaped by later events or drift, so verify even a second agreeing memory with documentary support before it drives a conclusion.
when: When a witness recalls something only vaguely or a clue comes from memory.
why: Memory alone is incomplete and can drift.

text: Record hearsay apart from confirmed facts and let each retelling embellish it, so players can trace a claim to its first source and test it against what another character saw.
when: When NPCs pass on information they did not witness, in rumour systems.
why: Tracing the source is the only way to test a claim.

text: Let NPCs log what the player has said, so a later question that contradicts an earlier answer or cover story can prompt a confession or revision.
when: Designing dialogue-driven interrogation or social deduction.
why: Recorded answers give the player a basis for contradiction, which makes the confrontation meaningful.

text: Test a witness's alertness, such as whether they dozed or sleep lightly, before weighing their account.
Give a memorised NPC story gaps about unanticipated specifics, so that the player's precise question about a time or place can break it.
when: when designing an interrogation puzzle
why: stories rarely cover exact details

text: Tie a witness's memory to a physical object that can be shown again, so the claim can be checked rather than merely believed.
when: when a witness recalls an item or document
why: presentable objects allow verification

text: Treat a written memory aid, such as a list of positions, as a clue to how a combination is meant to be operated.
when: A note lists symbols or positions
why: It records the operating sequence

text: Do not press a witness in shock for a full account; schedule fuller questioning for when she is stronger.
when: witness is still in shock

text: Stop witnesses who volunteer theories or conclusions and keep them to what they observed.
when: A witness moves from observation to speculation.
why: Theories from witnesses can replace evidence and mislead the record.

text: Let a recall bring a suspect back once new evidence is found, and let a closing summary list the verdict options.
when: designing investigation mechanics

text: Give each witness one memorable event so that their recall feels specific and plausible.
when: When writing witness dialogue for a deduction scene
why: A single vivid anchor makes testimony feel credible

text: Recheck a witness's claim by searching the area they described, such as a stairway they said was guarded.
Let an NPC's forgotten detail return through a journal, another witness or a physical item, so the player reconstructs it instead of hearing it repeated.
when: designing an NPC who loses a quest detail
why: reconstruction turns a lost memory into a discovery

text: Let a drunk or concussed NPC recall the night as shuffled fragments that the player must sort into order.
when: Designing an NPC whose memory of an event is impaired.
why: Sorting fragments turns recall into a puzzle the player solves.

text: Track each witness's position, line of sight and distance; limit reports to what they could perceive, e.g. a figure seen from behind gives height and clothing, not a face.
when: designing NPC perception and witness reports, or an NPC has partial information about an event
why: keeps testimony consistent with what the NPC could perceive

text: Log which NPCs were in each location at each time so that detailed knowledge can be traced to a witness.
when: building an NPC location and knowledge system

text: Tag NPC recollections made long after an event with a decay marker, prompting players to verify them against a second source.
Make the path to a hidden name run through an informant with a tie to the record-keeper, so the player must earn it through trade or favours.
when: A key identity is locked behind a non-player intermediary
why: Earned access gives the player a reason to invest in relationships

text: Add an informant NPC with a grudge who reveals a hidden detail, rewarding players who talk to disgruntled characters.
why: Grudges make NPCs willing to disclose secrets

text: Let information travel only through defined channels such as letters, staff and rumours, so the player can trace any leak back to its source.
Give an in-world expert's claim a visible basis, so the player can judge whether that expert's authority applies to the clue at hand.
when: when generating expert NPCs who vouch for clues
why: players need grounds to weigh authority against evidence

text: Test whether a witness was awake and positioned to perceive an event, and do not assume that a sound heard by one person was heard by all nearby.
when: Comparing accounts of who heard or saw something.
why: Perception depends on location, sleep and attention.

text: Place each observer at a fixed vantage point hidden from the subject, with a retreat position nearby in case the subject looks back.
when: the subject might turn and notice an observer
why: a noticed observer changes what the subject does

text: Position light sources so their glare does not hit the subject's eyes, and move or extinguish a light at the key moment to keep observers concealed.
when: observing during a staged or timed moment
why: light can expose observers or dazzle the subject

text: Enforce observer silence with agreed hand signals and quiet footwear, so observers can follow the subject without being heard.
Check a chance remark that links to an existing lead before weighing it, since coincidences are common.
why: An unchecked remark can look meaningful while being pure coincidence.

text: Let a stealth NPC believe the player has been fooled while the player prepares an ambush.
A voice disguise mechanic should let guards who have heard the NPC up close recognise the difference.
Track which claims the player volunteered, so later NPCs react to what was already admitted.
when: when multiple NPCs question the player
why: NPCs should not ignore disclosures made earlier

text: Two crimes with the same design and execution suggest the same mind is behind both.
when: a new case resembles an older one
why: a repeated signature is harder to attribute to coincidence

text: Store each NPC's reactions to named people as relationship data that dialogue and behaviour can draw on.
Let a player place a fuzzy NPC memory on a known game event, such as a bell ringing or a guard shift change.
why: Shared anchors make vague testimony usable.

text: Verbatim repetition shows retention of wording, but reconstruction under pressure can keep the memory while the wording drifts, so the test is less reliable then.
when: A witness is asked to reconstruct a statement under pressure.
why: Stress can change phrasing even when the underlying memory is intact.

text: A witness's memory is weak evidence on its own; it becomes strong when an independent record fixes the same facts.
A witness with a criminal record may give a vivid account, but the record makes the account suspect until confirmed independently.
Record each witness answer with its source, who saw what and when, and a firsthand flag, so players can cross-check contradictions, overlaps and single-source gaps.
when: Witness testimony matters to the solution or players must investigate it.
why: A player can only check contradictions if observations are recorded; structured metadata makes corroboration and single-source gaps visible.

text: Track each witness's lighting, distance and fear level, and let these determine how many details they report, so the player can probe for gaps.
when: Designing witness NPCs
why: A perception record makes testimony consistent and gives the player something to test.

text: Store each claim a player hears from a witness and check it against world state, such as a hole present or an object absent.

1) Note whether the witness perceived the event directly. 2) Check whether the witness might have been noticed. 3) Estimate how strong the witness's emotion was. 4) Record the witness's stated uncertainty with the report.
when: A witness's report is primary evidence for an event
why: Direct perception, exposure and emotional state each shape how far the report can be trusted

text: Order the case file so the player reads one witness's record before another's, mirroring a court's sequence.
when: Presenting multiple witness records in a case file
why: A deliberate sequence helps players assemble the account as a court would.

text: A witness's own report is not enough to establish an impossible event when no physical trace supports it.
when: Evaluating an account of an impossible appearance or disappearance.
why: Without physical evidence, the claim rests only on the witness's perception or memory.

text: Bystander NPCs who witnessed a public confrontation can confirm or contradict an accuser's account; players must compare their counter-statements against it.
when: when designing a scene where a public argument matters later
why: multiple witnesses let the player check testimony

text: Witnesses who did not notice are not automatically lying, and a deceptive witness is not merely busy; test any failure to notice against the environment.
Bystanders' reactions to a question, including who looks to the investigator for cues, reveal who has a stake in the answer.
when: several people are present during questioning

text: A listener's frown or unease when a gap appears is evidence in its own right and should be recorded alongside the speaker's account.
when: someone reacts to a witness's lapse
why: the other person's reaction can reveal knowledge the speaker is hiding

text: A witness who saw a stranger only briefly often gives a generic description, such as height and common clothing, that fits many people.
when: The witness had a short or distant view.
why: Brief observation captures only broad features.

text: Brief visits followed by a quick return are easily overlooked in memory and records.
when: a visit was short

text: A bystander describing others may shape the account to distance himself from them, so his portrait needs independent checking.
when: A peripheral acquaintance describes the people around them.
why: A wish to avoid being linked to those people biases the account.

text: Workers and passers-by who notice an odd visitor asking strange questions tend to report the visit, making them witnesses.
A bystander who seems neutral may be watching for their own reasons, so every observer in a scene can be a possible interested party.
Brief, poor-light, or unrepeated sightings and identifications are less reliable than prolonged contact; a confident account from a glimpse needs close questioning and confirmation.
why: Fleeting, unconfirmed perceptions are often misreads

text: A witness with a limited view and believable gaps is more credible than one who recalls every detail; check her claims against independent sources.
when: A servant or attendant reports events from a narrow position
why: A limited view should produce a limited account

text: A witness's vantage bounds what they could have known, so sightings of some people alongside disclaimers about others can both be consistent.
A bounded estimate, such as a range of days, is more useful than a false precise guess from a witness.
when: A witness is unsure of an exact date

text: Bystanders remember exact words, so a slip made in a group becomes testimony that can be used later.
when: When a slip occurs in front of other listeners.

text: In a crowded setting with many people, no one can reliably confirm another person's movements, so testimony about them becomes unreliable.
when: Many people share a location and witnesses are asked about a specific individual.
why: Attention is spread across too many people for any one person's movements to be remembered.

text: A brief observer lacking context about someone's history or reasons may judge their sanity or honesty from manner alone and misread intent.
when: When forming a lasting impression from a short encounter without context.
why: Odd manner is noticed quickly, while reasoning and context take longer to appear; missing context leads to reading intent or character incorrectly.

text: Assuming bystanders saw what happened, when they saw only a normal action, leads to wrong conclusions about the event.
A brief glance can mislead a watcher who assumes a figure seen in a place is the person who should be there.
when: A watcher checks a room or cell briefly.
why: A constructed presence, such as a figure on a bed, looks like the real occupant.

text: A timed trick that relies on an unwitting bystander to mask its noise fails if that bystander leaves early.
Overt bullying can silence a witness and undo progress already made. Pressure works better paired with reassurance.
when: Questioning a frightened or threatened witness.
why: Intimidation makes a witness withdraw, while reassurance lets them finish the account.

text: A brief explanation offered under challenge should be tested against the full record, not accepted because it sounds plausible.
Have each narrator record only events they personally saw or did, and state where their knowledge ends, so gaps stay visible.
when: multiple narrators tell parts of one story
why: clear limits let readers separate seen from heard

text: Treat a bystander's theory about motive, such as a quarrel, as a suggestion to test rather than as proof.
Record the identity of an uninvolved driver used in an evasion and pay them afterwards, so the innocent party is not harmed.
Model a busy NPC whose attention is limited by workload, so the player learns that a missing memory is itself information.
A bounded-room reveal works only while suspects cannot flee, so a prepared cordon must be in place before the accusation.
when: a suspect can escape once accused
why: exposure gives the suspect a reason to run

text: A detailed message can make its recipient less cautious, because specifics feel like proof of genuineness.
when: the message's details fit what the recipient already knows

text: Vagueness about what differs between a suspect and the witnessed person is evidence about witness reliability, not proof of innocence.
when: A witness cannot explain a difference in a lineup or identification.
why: Vague answers signal weak recall, which neither confirms nor clears the suspect.

text: A smooth, detailed account is not proof of reliability; test its details against the scene and independent evidence before treating it as settled.
when: A witness or suspect gives a vivid, complete, or detailed story.
why: Detail can mask bias, error or invention.

text: Check each candidate explanation against every detail; one specific detail that does not fit can rule an explanation out.
when: choosing between explanations
why: the obvious reading may fail on a single detail

text: A witness can be designed to be wrong, such as reporting a struggle that was really a startled gesture.
A detail that does not fit the official account easily, such as mixed voices heard at one time, is worth treating as significant.
Minor details gain weight when they explain a mismatch between testimony and the physical record.
when: A witness account conflicts with the physical evidence
why: Small details can resolve the conflict

text: A mismatch between a reported detail and known facts may mean the story changed in retelling or that two items were confused.
A detail that looks wrong, such as a poorly fitting wig, can be a discoverable clue in dialogue or inspection.
A repeated detail is strong evidence of common origin only if it is unusual in itself; common details can arise independently.
when: judging whether repeated testimony is copied
why: Only rare details carry enough information to act as a fingerprint.

text: A witness distracted during the event recalls little, and a witness with a stake in the outcome may minimize their own role when pressed.
when: When weighing how much to trust a witness's account.
why: Distraction weakens memory, and self-interest shapes what a witness admits.

text: Accumulating contradictory details can deepen the sense of mystery, since each new conflict makes the overall case feel less coherent.
when: Many clues appear to conflict
why: Unorganized contradictions raise uncertainty without suggesting an answer

text: A detailed itinerary or suspect's story can look credible because of its detail, and detail can cover a false account; detail alone does not verify a claim.
A large volume of trivial detail can bury the important point in a witness timeline.
when: when many small observations are collected

text: Assuming a witness sure of one detail is equally reliable about other details.
when: Weighing a witness's full account.
why: Confidence varies across facts, such as a person's condition versus their face.

text: A detached observer who believes they can read people completely is often wrong about them.
Added detail in a retold story does not raise its accuracy, so trace the chain of reporters before trusting extra specifics.
Trusting the most confident or most detailed witness as the most accurate one is a mistake; detail and certainty do not guarantee accuracy.
when: Weighing conflicting testimony.
why: Confidence and detail can be produced by sincere but wrong memory.

text: A witness may give a time with apparent precision while only estimating it; check whether the witness could actually see a clock.
when: Witness times are used to fix a sequence of events.
why: Precision in speech does not guarantee the observation behind it was exact.

text: 1) Assess the witness's access to what they observed and the quality of their source. 2) Assess memory of dates and details, including impairment such as drinking. 3) Assess stake, motive and feelings. 4) Weigh facts accordingly before accepting them.
when: When several witnesses give accounts of the same events.
why: Each factor limits how far a witness's account can be trusted; interested or impaired witnesses may distort what they report.

text: Do not drop a distinctive detail after introducing it; record it and pay it off when the scene is reconstructed.
when: Introducing clues to the player.
why: An unpaid detail leaves the mystery unresolved.

text: Let a field report carry exact details, dates and first impressions, so an absent character can judge progress without visiting the scene.
when: A character must follow events they cannot witness
why: Specific reports let the absent character assess progress

text: Let a quest-giver NPC answer a fixed set of questions, and have the player's notebook build a suspect profile from the answers.
when: When designing investigation quests in a game.
why: A fixed question set makes the profile consistent and easy to match.

text: Attach a reliability marker to a character's account given while poisoned, drunk or frightened, prompting players to corroborate it before acting on it.
when: A character's testimony is delivered under impairment or stress.
why: A visible marker tells players the account needs checking.

text: Examining one detail intensely reveals a few points clearly but loses the whole picture; organized breadth of hypotheses keeps the full situation in view.
Strict detachment from people improves clarity of reasoning but can make the investigator seem cold or inhuman to colleagues.
Repetition across many people, or stacking many testimonies, makes a story feel more reliable even though repetition adds no evidence and weak accounts stay weak.
when: When a case relies on many witness accounts of varying strength or a story is retold through many people.
why: Familiarity from retelling and sheer volume of accounts are mistaken for confirmation.

text: When a claim is restated in a form that exposes its weakness, listeners often draw the damaging conclusion themselves rather than accepting it from the speaker.
when: When trying to undermine a theory without direct argument.
why: Self-drawn conclusions feel more credible than conclusions handed over.

text: Events inside a sealed space may have only one witness, the person who was inside, so no eyewitness can check their account.
Secondhand reports carry the uncertainty of their origin; treat them as leads pointing toward a danger, not proof, and verify before acting.
when: When information comes through a relayed or second-hand source.
why: Relayed accounts can be incomplete, altered, or retracted by the original speaker; reconstruction is only as reliable as its sources.

text: When a central inference rests on one witness whose evidence is doubtful, treat the case as only as strong as its weakest link.
when: When assessing a case built on few witnesses.
why: Partial support from other witnesses does not replace full corroboration.

text: Specific personal detail anchored to a witness's own movements or family events gives a statement more weight than general impressions.
when: When comparing the detail of several witness accounts.
why: Specific, checkable detail is harder to invent than vague impression.

text: Short, identical, unembellished answers can signal a rehearsed or guarded witness.
when: Assessing a witness's reliability from the form of their replies
why: Rehearsal and guardedness reduce spontaneous detail

text: When two sources disagree about one person, weigh each source's familiarity with that person and interest in how they are seen before accepting either account.
when: Two witnesses give conflicting accounts of the same individual.
why: Familiarity and self-interest shape what a witness says.

text: Trace a story that has passed through several people back to its original source before accepting its time, place, and witness.
Repeat an identification test with the sample order changed, and require consistent correct matches, since one correct answer may be luck.
when: When a single correct identification could be a lucky guess.
why: Changing the order prevents a repeated pattern from reproducing a correct answer by chance.

text: Store a witness's observations separately from their beliefs so the player must decide which parts to trust.
when: When designing an NPC who gives both facts and interpretations
why: Separation makes the player evaluate evidence rather than accept or reject the whole account.

text: Ask what conditions produced both reports rather than who is lying when two credible witnesses contradict each other.
when: Two credible accounts flatly conflict and no direct evidence exists
why: Shifting the question to conditions can reveal that both witnesses were sincere

text: Use a second witness's testimony to confirm an identity that the first witness could not see clearly, so the reveal rests on two accounts.
when: Confirming a disguised identity late in a mystery.
why: Two independent accounts make the identity credible.

text: A sharp shift in a writer's tone between two statements, from mild concern to accusation, signals that something happened in between that the writer may not describe.
A character who repeatedly admits earlier statements were false teaches the audience to distrust the next version, so each new account needs checking against evidence.
when: a deceptive character gives several accounts in sequence
why: each retraction shows that stories can be false, which lowers trust in later claims

text: Sincere and tactical emotion or helpfulness look alike, so trusting apparent sincerity can end questioning too early; judge by checkable inconsistencies with routine or facts.
when: Judging whether a suspect's or NPC's distress, surprise, or helpfulness is genuine, including when an NPC may conceal involvement.
why: Strong emotion can be real or used to close off questioning, and visible sincerity is easy to mistake for innocence.

text: A timeline built on one witness's times may be entirely that witness's invention.
when: Relying on a single source for times
why: Without independent confirmation, the sequence rests on one account.

text: Trusting an account from a source who has a stake in how the subject is seen can distort the picture of that subject.
when: A witness benefits from a particular portrayal of someone.
why: Interest pushes testimony toward the witness's purposes.

text: A teller losing control may repeat real facts in the wrong order, so comparing sequence as well as content can expose them.
when: A suspect's retelling becomes disorganized or rushed.
why: Real memories keep their original order even when the teller loses control of the narrative.

text: When a witness repeats another person's words, their own opinion can filter what is passed on.
when: when a witness relays what someone else said
why: Repeated speech carries the reporter's interpretation, which can distort it.

text: Accepting a secondhand report as if the object were directly inspected invites error and should be verified.
when: Judging an identity claim based on a published account.
why: Reports can misstate details that an examiner would catch on inspection.

text: Two witnesses who seem independent may have heard the same false source, so their agreement becomes the trap rather than proof.

1) Record testimony without interrupting, letting the witness describe impressions freely. 2) Ask for concrete detail. 3) Separate reported incidents from sensations or feelings. 4) Interpret only after the record is complete, and verify only the perceived parts.
when: Taking a witness statement that mixes events, sensation, and interpretation.
why: Interrupting or interpreting early blurs fact with feeling, and feelings such as enchantment or being watched cannot be checked directly.

text: 1) Separate what the witness saw and heard from what the witness concludes. 2) Offer a natural explanation for each perception. 3) Test the supernatural claim against the ordinary explanation. 4) Ask for checkable details before accepting the conclusion.
when: A distressed witness claims a supernatural cause without checkable evidence.
why: Separating perception from inference shows which parts of the account can be tested.

text: A non-suspect who has seen a hidden act may use that knowledge as leverage, offering mutual silence in exchange for silence.
when: A minor character witnessed the protagonist's secret.
why: Knowing a secret gives the witness a bargaining position.

text: A person who turns away from the observer while reading or speaking hides the face the observer would otherwise read for tells.
when: someone reads or answers with their back turned

text: A witness loyal to a suspect is more likely to speak when told honest answers are safe and the matter can be handled discreetly.
when: witness is fond of or loyal to the suspect
why: fear of exposure or public scandal keeps witnesses silent

text: Let a witness be both source and suspect, so the person who reports a sighting is later investigated in turn.
Give a torn witness a constructive step, such as speaking to the suspect themselves, so they feel involved rather than accused.
when: witness is split between loyalty and suspicion
why: feeling accused makes witnesses defensive

text: Use a witness report, such as a description of an unusual person, to locate the real figure behind an apparent attack.
when: Designing how a detective finds the true culprit.
why: A witness's description narrows the search and leads to a confession or proof.

text: A witness who switches sides may be deliberately staging the turn; treating it as mere delusion misses the deception.
when: a witness changes allegiance mid-case
why: The turn itself can be the tactic.

text: Plant the sleight in plain view with a detail that seems minor to the characters but is noticed by one witness.
Witnesses giving sympathetic but vague accounts work as red herrings, while witnesses giving precise, verifiable details work as reliable clue sources.
when: Designing NPC testimony for a mystery.
why: Vague testimony misleads without contradiction, while precise testimony can be cross-checked by the player.

text: Cut off detained suspects from outside contact so they cannot coordinate a story; isolation also removes witnesses who could corroborate them.
when: after arrest
why: Limits coordination with accomplices or witnesses and removes sources of corroboration

text: Question witnesses away from anyone who intimidates them, and note who briefed them first, since a present threat or prior briefing can undo or steer testimony.
why: A prior briefing can filter or steer testimony without the investigator knowing.

text: Separate mutually suspicious accomplices so they cannot coordinate, since their distrust makes them easier to isolate and their coordination is the main threat.
when: When several participants are mutually suspicious and their coordination is the threat.
why: Accomplices who distrust each other gain little from contact and are easier to pick apart.

text: Few nearby residents limit the number of possible witnesses, which narrows the set of people who could have seen events.
when: when assessing a remote scene

text: When two witnesses might coordinate their accounts, check whether they can meet, since shared time allows alignment of stories.
when: Two witnesses may be sharing a location
why: Coordination is possible when they can communicate before speaking to the investigator.

text: Isolation, such as a long drive from help and servants who keep leaving, removes easy assistance and raises the stakes.
when: a setting is placed far from outside help
why: distance and loss of staff make the situation harder to escape

text: Advice can be framed so that following it cuts the listener off from their allies, binding them more closely to the speaker.
when: When a powerful speaker offers counsel that seems neutral.
why: Acting on the advice removes the listener's other sources of support.

text: A pattern can go unnoticed when each event is recalled separately; comparing event dates side by side reveals it.
Separating witnesses stops them coordinating, but a suggestion all of them received can still shape their matching accounts.

1) Summon each suspect separately under a pretext so neither knows the other is coming. 2) Place each in a position where their reaction to the accusation can be observed. 3) Voice the accusation and watch for reactions an innocent person would not show.
when: Two or more suspects could have committed a crime and a reaction to an accusation may separate them.
why: Separation and concealed observation prevent coordinated responses and expose unusual reactions.

text: 1) Interview each person in a chain of action separately. 2) Ask the same routine questions. 3) Note each time marker. 4) Line the markers up against one another. 5) Separate first-hand sight from assumption. 6) Map the exact sequence of handovers.
when: When several people were involved in a chain of actions
why: Separate, comparable accounts reveal disagreements about who was where and when

text: Keep a frightened witness's account private and away from household talk, so the testimony stays uncontaminated.
Keep witnesses or NPCs describing the same event separated so agreement or contradiction stays testable; compare details like menu and preparation, since contradictions point to a liar.
when: several witnesses or NPCs describe the same event
why: Coordinated stories hide contradictions

text: Define each NPC's knowledge and guilt separately, so an NPC can be innocent of the main crime yet still hold a clue.
why: separate axes prevent innocence from erasing useful knowledge

text: Track living and dead NPCs separately in game state, so a corpse can still be counted by an observer who does not know its status.
when: NPCs can die while remaining in view
why: A count based on presence alone will include the dead and mislead the player.

text: Separate characters so that one faces the danger alone while the others can only hear it or help from a distance.
when: building a peril scene
why: Isolation heightens fear and makes the rescue depend on indirect information.

text: Record when and by whom each trace or object was seen; an object recognised by several independent observers links to a person more strongly than any single recognition.
when: When physical traces or objects are used as evidence.
why: Dated, multiply seen traces can be rechecked; agreement across separate observers reduces the chance of a single mistake.

text: Follow-up questions, especially about date or hour, pin a witness to narrower details than a vague first account and can change the meaning of what was seen.
when: when a witness gives a vague first account
why: Precise prompts force the witness to commit to details they might otherwise leave out.

text: A brief partial view, limited by distance, obstruction, light or reflection, raises a question without settling it; reflections distort and occlusions hide detail, so assuming clarity misleads.
when: An observer sees something out of place, or relies on a reflection or obstructed view for key information.
why: Missing detail leaves the identity open.

text: Recalled details can be mistaken, so confirm them against the physical scene before acting on them, since a recalled answer is only as reliable as the memory behind it.
when: when a player relies on a recalled detail to draw a conclusion
why: Recall reconstructs the scene and can introduce errors.

text: A witness's first account may be incomplete rather than false, and later answers can change under pressure to include omitted activity.
when: A witness claims to have stayed at a post or location.
why: People often leave out uncomfortable details until pressed.

text: Under repeated questioning, a witness's account may change in stages, with each admission arriving later and vaguer than the one before.
when: A witness is pressed over several sessions
why: Fear of consequences and pressure from questioning

text: An observer with a personal stake reads events through that stake, so feelings can impair judgement about the people involved.
when: the observer has a relationship with those involved
why: Emotional investment colours perception of others' behaviour

text: Actions taken in one drug state may be recalled when the same state returns.
when: A character has lost memory of an act done under a drug.
why: Memory can be linked to the state in which it was formed.

text: Observers trained to read signs draw more precise inferences from the same brief glimpse than untrained observers do.
when: when judging a stranger from a brief observation
why: Reading signs is a learned skill that sharpens with practice.

text: A witness close to events but bound by family ties may speak indirectly, so the wording of their account becomes evidence.
when: A witness has close access to events but a loyalty that limits what they can say
why: Ties of loyalty restrain direct statement, so the witness signals meaning through phrasing

text: A witness who flinches under a direct question has shown they understood it before denying knowledge, which is evidence worth noting.
when: A direct question touches a sensitive fact.
why: A reaction can reveal knowledge that a denial conceals.

text: Witnesses often volunteer useful details as the questioner leaves, such as an unprompted remark about an injury.
when: When an interview is ending and the witness has relaxed.
why: Relief and the lessening of pressure loosen the witness's control over what they reveal.

text: Witnesses who saw only hands, a sleeve or a back give little identifying help, and such partial sightings narrow the suspect pool only slightly.
when: Evaluating witness reports of a disguised person.
why: Fragmentary details are shared by many people.

text: A witness who saw only part of a person, such as a chin under a large hat, may still feel sure they would recognise the item again.
when: when a witness recalls a distinctive but partly seen item
why: Confidence about recognition can exceed what the partial view actually recorded.

text: Accounts of overheard speech often break off just before the words that matter, leaving the critical content missing.
when: when a witness reports overheard speech

text: A document that promises a fuller account later signals that it is withholding facts.
Independent witnesses who give the same description or answer at different points strengthen each other's reliability, since separate confirmation reduces the chance one observer is mistaken.
when: When weighing the reliability of a sighting or answer.
why: Independent confirmation reduces the chance that one observer is mistaken.

text: NPC dialogue can be a tree where information unlocks only through precise questions, or the right keyword or topic, rather than a verbose release.
when: Designing NPC dialogue or conversation systems for an investigation.

text: Independent observers who track a party's movements can expose an assembled or staged accusation.
when: group testimony appears to support one account
why: group testimony can be built to back a single story

text: Two witnesses who recall the same sound corroborate each other even if neither knows its source.
Treat an unexpected NPC reaction as a clue with several possible readings rather than as a failure state.
Each new independent witness adds detail that narrows the suspect pool.
Adjust manner to each witness: deferential with long-serving staff, careful and guarded with one who resists.
Check a character's account of their own movements against an independent sensory cue, such as a sound or footstep.
when: a character's whereabouts are disputed
why: Sensory cues are harder to shape than a spoken account.

text: Do not accept a confident recollection as accurate when the witness admits large gaps in memory.
when: Assessing a witness's account of an event.
why: Confidence does not repair missing memory.

text: Two credible witnesses who are present and give sworn accounts of the same physical act carry strong weight, while a single account carries little.
when: A claim involves an act that ordinary means cannot explain.
why: Independent corroboration reduces the chance that one person's error or invention alone decides the outcome.

text: Test a claim that nobody passed by asking whose role was excluded from the count, since a person seen but not recorded may still have passed.
when: A witness statement rules out all movement
why: People are counted by their expected roles, so an unexpected role can pass unrecorded.

text: A detail that feels familiar but cannot be placed should be held open, since recall of its source may come later and make it significant.
when: A detail is noticed but its source is unknown.
why: A stray observation can gain meaning once a related fact surfaces.

text: A hidden witness the culprit does not know about can defeat an apparently safe barrier, so a locked hiding place should not be treated as guaranteed to conceal the act.
when: designing a scene where a character might observe a crime from concealment
why: Physical barriers can hide the act from the culprit's view while leaving an observer inside.

text: An interrogation mini-game can log each answer and flag variations, so the player sees a contradiction build over repeated questions.
when: designing a questioning mechanic
why: Visible logs make inconsistency a playable clue.

text: Let an NPC's testimony carry withheld details that unlock after trust or corroboration, and mark omissions in logs so players know the record is partial.
when: designing NPC dialogue and journals
why: Players learn what is missing and earn the rest

text: The person at the centre of a case can fill gaps that intermediaries could not see, making their own account the strongest confirmation.
when: Resolving disputed events in a case

text: Accept hesitant, partial answers and let the witness reach the conclusion themselves rather than stating it for them.
A single reinterpretation of one timestamp can recolour all earlier testimony that relied on it, so earlier scenes change meaning without being altered.
When a culprit stages a non-player witness to observe an event, the account that witness later gives the player carries that staging and can be checked against other accounts.
when: a non-player character reports an event the culprit arranged
why: staged observations leave traces that differ from honest ones

text: Record whether a witness was pressured during an interview, so later dialogue reflects the change in their attitude.
Placing a witness to see an object or person creates a memory link, and later questioning can steer that recollection toward a chosen target.
when: suspicion may later fall on the intended target
why: recollection of a link is open to suggestion once the witness is asked about it

text: A guard's logged observation with time and description gives players a time window and object to match against suspects' records, narrowing suspects without a full identity.
when: Designing clue logs for an investigation puzzle.
why: Partial, timed observations let players eliminate suspects without a full identity.

text: A watch whose effectiveness drops the longer it runs can model player boredom and fatigue during long stakeouts.
When a character doubts their own perception, such as whether a sound was real, the audience is pulled to question what they know.
when: when a narrator's senses are unreliable under stress
why: Making perception itself uncertain raises doubt about what is true.

text: A witness or subject knows only what they saw and may give an incomplete account, so every statement must be checked against other evidence rather than accepted for its detail.
Damaging hearsay often comes from someone with a stake in the outcome, and that stake should lower its weight.
Judging a witness only by whether the statement contains false facts misses accounts that are accurate yet hide the decisive event.
why: A fully accurate account can still omit the most important fact.

text: Vague recollections of an earlier meeting leave gaps that must be filled from records or other sources rather than trusted alone.
when: Relying on a witness's memory of a past meeting
why: Memory of an event years old is unreliable

text: Trusting direct observation is not enough, since even what one sees can mislead when read without checking.
A story that depends on the audience's indifference fails once they become curious.
A character's stated temperament is useful evidence, but it can be misread and should be weighed with other facts.
when: Judging whether a victim would have acted in a certain way.

text: A routine described by staff may not match what happened on the critical occasion, since memory tends to reflect general practice.
when: when testing an access claim against a stated routine
why: people describe usual practice rather than a specific event

text: A witness questioned informally may give a first version later discounted as a lie, which damages the record.
Trusting a witness's conclusion over their observations is a mistake, since the conclusion may be an interpretation that outruns the evidence.
A witness list built at the scene can be incomplete, since people in a crowd may go unnoticed until later.
Treating a true detail supplied by a spirit as proof that the accused is guilty confuses an accurate fact with a guilty identity.
An eavesdropper who hears only part of a conversation may misjudge the whole, because she hears one side of a judgment without its reasons.
when: A character acts on fragments of an overheard talk.
why: Missing reasoning makes a partial hearing misleading.

text: 1) Speak loudly to one person so a nearby listener hears. 2) Act as if unaware of that listener. 3) Aim the words at a known emotional weak spot. 4) Read the listener's reactions as evidence. 5) Repeat the point if interrupted.

1) Start from the person's last known record. 2) Send inquiries to registries in other places. 3) Publish rewards and appeals. 4) Watch the likely return point. 5) Filter incoming leads before acting.
1) Identify the original source of a claim. 2) Check whether that source can be reached directly. 3) Note each intermediary and what they might gain from relaying it.
when: Assessing information that arrived secondhand.

text: 1) Confirm the detail is unusual. 2) Show it circulated before the later accounts. 3) Identify a plausible carrier. 4) State any remaining gap in the chain.
when: testing whether separate accounts are independent or copied

text: 1) List each public note's details. 2) Order the act, the time gap and the note's appearance. 3) Infer which observers could have seen the act and passed it on.
when: Working out who witnessed a private act from unsigned public messages.
why: Timing and content narrow the set of possible watchers.

text: 1) Avoid asking the hidden question directly. 2) Raise a related side topic. 3) Wait for the target to volunteer the desired name or detail.
when: When a hostile or guarded character shuts down direct questions.
why: Direct pressure can harden resistance, while a side approach lets the answer surface on its own.

text: 1) Ask the witness to describe the person they saw. 2) Record the description. 3) Match it later against suspects.
when: when a witness saw an unidentified person
why: A recorded description allows a later match.

text: 1) Take each household member's account separately. 2) Record their routines and sleep times. 3) Check reported sounds and their timing against claimed movements. 4) Check missing items against each report. 5) Search every space large enough to hold the object in question.
when: The household was active during the relevant time and staff can describe it.
why: Separate accounts with timings expose gaps that a single neat story hides.

text: 1) Open with reassurance and a reward, making clear the witness is not the main target. 2) Bluff about what you already know. 3) Watch for flinches under direct questions. 4) Apply a visible time limit. 5) State the stakes, including legal consequences. 6) Move to a private room once the witness starts talking. 7) Remove other interviewers so the witness does not feel watched.
when: The witness has a clear fear that the interviewer can address.
why: Each step lowers the witness's fear or raises the cost of silence.

text: 1) Run standard screens for all common agents first. 2) If nothing matches, suspect an unfamiliar substance. 3) Identify it by weighing its properties together, not one at a time.
when: Cause of death is clear, the agent is unknown, and standard tests return nothing useful.
why: Common agents must be excluded before rarer ones are considered.

text: Voice can identify a hidden face, but never treat sincere certainty as proof; verify with a second sense or source, since mimicry and honest error look alike.
when: when the face is hidden or a witness identifies a character only by sound
why: An honest mistake looks the same as a deliberate lie, and a stranger or accomplice can imitate the voice.

text: Vary the expected responses so that a refusal is informative but not automatically damning.
when: scripting NPC reactions to requests
why: Players should not treat every refusal as proof of guilt

text: Unlock interrogation options only after the player presents a specific document or object that justifies them.
when: designing NPC questioning in a game

text: State how information was obtained, since testimony from a hidden or unverified source can be dismissed later.
why: The source determines how much weight the reader gives the testimony.

text: Keep witnesses apart so their accounts stay independent and cannot be shaped by one another.
when: Several witnesses must be questioned about the same event.
why: Overheard answers let a witness adjust their story to match others.

text: Weigh a statement that earns release with the same suspicion applied to other coerced statements, since the reward gives the speaker a motive to say what is wanted.
when: A statement is offered in exchange for release or leniency.
why: An inducement creates an incentive to tell the questioner what they want to hear.

text: Weigh independent testimony from fellow prisoners or witnesses against a witness's later statements rather than letting the later statement override it.
when: A witness recants earlier claims
why: Earlier independent accounts can contradict a later turn.

text: A signaler must watch the observer's reaction and change the act immediately if the observer seems to notice it.
when: when a covert signal is in progress
why: An irritated remark shows the signal was registered as noise.

text: Notice when a question's framing points toward one reading of the evidence, since it steers how the evidence is weighed.
when: Posing a question about ambiguous evidence to a judge or player.
why: Framing shapes which interpretation seems natural.

text: Track a witness NPC's knowledge as game state, so their removal changes which alibis remain checkable. Log guard patrols, door openings and cart movements so players can test whether a suspect's route was possible.
when: designing NPC knowledge and environmental logs
why: State and logs let consequences of removing witnesses be felt and tested

text: Give little weight to testimony hedged with phrases like 'I think' or 'it might have been' when it concerns dates.
when: when judging a witness's answer about a date
why: Hedged answers do not fix a specific date.

text: Use an NPC guard or doorman as an alibi witness, letting the player ask about times and routes.
when: When designing a location with a stationed NPC
why: A stationed witness gives the player a source to question

text: Add a witness-log record, such as a taxi entry or guard roster, that confirms or contradicts claimed alibis.
when: Designing alibi checks in a game.
why: A neutral log gives the player a source independent of the suspect.

text: Model interrogation pressure as escalation steps such as repetition, rephrasing and language switch, each raising the chance that a scripted answer cracks.
when: Building an interrogation minigame.
why: Graduated steps give the player meaningful choices about how hard to press.

text: Track interviewed NPCs, and when every lead loops back to the same people, prompt the player to reassess their line of inquiry.
when: Designing investigation progression.
why: Looping leads signal a stalled line.

text: Make testimony count only when a second witness is present, so players must find a second witness before the gate opens.
when: a puzzle or quest needs corroboration

text: Let witness-only claims raise suspicion without granting conviction, and require the player to find physical traces before a verdict is possible.
when: when designing accusation mechanics around unseen or private perceptions
why: Private claims can be false, so they should guide inquiry, not settle the outcome.

text: Give NPC witnesses partial, emotionally coloured testimony, and let the player cross-check positions and times to resolve it.
when: Designing NPC witness accounts

text: Do not discard a distorted witness entirely; they may still hold one true detail worth cross-checking.
when: A witness is unreliable but may have seen something real.

text: Make NPC knowledge partial so players must choose which questions to ask and which answers to trust.
when: An NPC holds information relevant to a mystery.
why: Incomplete knowledge makes the player's choices matter.

text: Plant character clues in dialogue, such as who refuses a test or arrives for a specific reason, so the player can recall them later.
when: Writing dialogue for witnesses or suspects.
why: Small, memorable details in conversation become useful evidence when the player connects them later.

text: Physical traces show what moved, was hidden or was altered, but testimony is needed to explain how the trace came to be there.
when: the case depends on a moved, hidden or altered object

text: Witnesses close to a suspect or victim give partial accounts covering different windows, and may disagree about a key event.
when: statements come from family or close associates
why: Personal feeling shapes what they recall and what they emphasise.

text: Persistent, sincere requests lead residents to give cooperation and information about the building and its residents.
when: when a canvasser keeps returning with a sincere manner
why: Persistence and sincerity build willingness to help.

text: A suspect asked to recount events in their own words cannot prepare answers for questions they have not yet been asked.
when: Before direct questions are put to the suspect
why: Direct questions allow prepared answers, whereas open narratives expose the suspect's unprepared account

text: A formal questioner usually opens gently with fact-gathering questions, then escalates to firm, direct questions on the point that matters most.
when: Formal questioning of a witness

text: Each witness observes a different slice of events, so no single account gives the complete sequence.
Witnesses can agree on a general impression while none can name the specific feature responsible.
when: when several witnesses describe the same person
why: General impressions can align without identifying specifics.

text: Give NPC witnesses partial, uncertain details, such as a random subset of traits, height, clothing, an accessory or direction, so players must combine several witnesses to identify a suspect.
when: designing NPC witnesses for identification puzzles
why: Partial information keeps players inferring, and combining partial views rewards careful comparison.

text: An NPC's stated theory may contain deliberate errors or explain only some clues, such as not the placement of key items, so players should check each claim against objects and testimony.
when: a case is delivered through an NPC's account
why: Unchecked claims can mislead the player in a designed way.

text: Give a reticent NPC a trust value: pressing too early lowers trust, while a non-committal answer unlocks a narrower follow-up question.
when: Designing dialogue for NPCs who withhold information.
why: Trust gates what the player can learn and keeps interrogation meaningful.

text: Program an NPC who refuses to discuss a topic to reveal information only after the player meets a condition or presses for a set number of answers.
when: Designing NPC dialogue gated by conditions.
why: Gated disclosure makes persistence a meaningful player choice.

text: Recover items under formal authority with a documented search, so the trace is recorded rather than merely noticed.
Let an NPC witness's retraction depend on whether the threatening faction member is present, so separating them preserves testimony.
when: designing NPC witnesses linked to a faction

text: NPC witnesses should report only what they observed, while the player decides which inferences to voice.
when: Designing inquiry scenes with NPC testimony.
why: Separating observation from inference leaves the reasoning to the player.

text: Open a confrontation with a frank statement of what is known, including the witness's withheld link to the event.
when: the interviewer has established facts about the witness
why: Plain disclosure signals that the investigator knows enough to continue.

text: An NPC can recall a detail the player has not yet linked, letting the player make the connection through a new conversation.
Give NPC witnesses partial, slightly wrong knowledge, such as an almost-right name, so the player must cross-check them against other evidence.
why: a witness who is nearly right forces verification instead of acceptance

text: Re-questioning only helps with a new angle; repeating the same questions mostly yields the same answers.
when: questioning a witness a second time
why: without new framing, the session produces repetition rather than new facts

text: Partial witness detail is weaker than a full description. A witness who recalls nothing specific about a person supports nothing about that person's identity.
when: Assessing a witness who saw someone but cannot describe them.
why: Identity needs distinguishing features, which partial recall lacks.

text: Non-player characters can answer vaguely unless the player asks precise, neutral questions, and their answers can be marked as suggestible when the player offered a suggestion.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that tracks question framing
why: Tracking suggestion lowers the reliability of replies and rewards careful questioning.

text: Put a family lead, such as a relative's trade or service, into an NPC's chatter, and place visitors and money trails that point to a hidden past, so the player reconstructs the motive.
when: When generating NPC dialogue and environmental clues for a mystery.
why: Scattered small leads let the player assemble a motive without a direct explanation.

text: An NPC interview tree can ask background and routine questions first, unlocking pointed questions only after baseline facts are gathered.
when: designing NPC dialogue trees
why: baseline facts make pointed questions meaningful

text: Release a late witness only after players hold enough evidence to judge whether that testimony fits.
An NPC can answer some questions and refuse others, signalling which topics are protected.
when: Designing NPC dialogue for an investigation.
why: Selective refusal tells the player where the secret lies.

text: An NPC can report a true observation while omitting context, so players should cross-check it against other NPCs' accounts.
when: Designing NPC testimony in a mystery or dungeon.
why: A single account can be accurate yet incomplete.

text: Give witnesses conflicting accounts of the same presence. Their disagreement becomes a clue that points to one staged source the player must reconcile.
when: When a supernatural presence is the central mystery.

text: Give each NPC claim a source, and make recall reliability depend on conditions such as lighting, distance, time of day or setting; quiet places retain memories, busy hubs do not.
when: designing witness NPCs whose accounts vary by conditions
why: Conditional reliability forces players to judge sources.

text: An NPC can describe a figure or object accurately while wrongly assuming its identity, so players must separate the reliable detail from the unreliable claim.
When an NPC's testimony conflicts with the timeline, the player must reconcile the two.
Incomplete recall of a door or object can be built into an NPC, so players must work around it with other evidence.
A witness who speaks only to protect one side can be attacked as partial, which weakens the whole record.
why: Visible bias lets opponents discredit the testimony as a whole

text: A respected witness can be accurate for one time window and silent about another, so trustworthiness does not extend their account to every period.
when: a witness covers only part of the night or day
why: observation is limited to where the witness was

text: Facts relayed quickly under time pressure, such as by telephone, are incomplete and should not be treated as the full picture.
