Assuming a sworn, signed, written report is objective because it is formal ignores the examiner's beliefs and the guide they used.
Treating a formal apology as closing a dispute, without watching for later misconduct, leads to wrongly judging the matter resolved.
A witness may deny that a trait is conclusive while admitting it matches; record the denial and the admission separately.
when: When taking testimony on a physical comparison
why: Merging the two loses the witness's real assessment.

text: 1) Give the witness a formal warning that the statement may be used against them. 2) Record the statement in writing afterward so it becomes an official record.
when: when the witness could become a suspect
why: A formal warning changes the legal weight of the statement and creates a record that later accounts can be checked against.

text: Tag each NPC testimony with its basis (saw, heard, inferred or assumed) and the speaker's bias; verify biased rumours against physical items before relying on them.
when: designing NPC dialogue or knowledge systems that report events
why: Players weigh testimony differently once its source is visible, and tags show which claims can be verified physically.

text: Give each NPC statement separate, checkable claims, such as a timestamp, ledger, guest book or shift roster entry, matching logged world records, a clock or other NPCs' accounts.
when: when designing NPC testimony or interrogation dialogue
why: Separate claims let players verify one at a time and reward comparing accounts.

text: Log NPC timed statements, leaving approximate times and unconfirmed intervals, such as an unexplained long wait, so players build the timeline from several sources and question the gaps.
when: when designing NPC alibis or timelines
why: Unconfirmed intervals create investigable gaps.

text: Ask a witness for the whole account, word for word, even when it seems to harm the accused, since an answer's bearing cannot be judged in advance.
why: A clear standard for testimony keeps the full record available.

text: Give several NPCs partial, inconsistent accounts of one sound, creature or item, so their shared trait or mismatch becomes a puzzle clue the player resolves.
Treat poor-visibility witness detail, such as a sound or brief glimpse, as true but partial, probabilistic clues the player must interpret rather than firm identification.
when: witnesses saw a person briefly, at a distance, in disguise or in poor light

text: Present an NPC's stated theory as a hypothesis the player can disprove, not as a fact the game asserts.
when: when an NPC explains an event
why: keeps player reasoning active and avoids handing out settled answers

text: Deliver a charge in a formal set phrase to mark the move from suspicion to action and show that the scene has escalated.
Let an NPC who warns and then retracts leave a verifiable hint, so a player who returns to the question is rewarded.
when: designing NPC warnings
why: A retraction that leaves evidence keeps the warning useful.

text: Treat a frightened witness's partial, emotional first account as a statement to be checked against facts, not as a complete record.
Treat a witness report that gives a time and an object but no person as a usable lead, and test it against other accounts before relying on it.
when: A witness gives a time and object but cannot identify a person.
why: A partial sighting can narrow a timeline, but untested it remains unreliable.

text: Treat an NPC's remark about the player's state as a witness statement that the player can later challenge or explain.
Trigger NPC reports when a player or suspect revisits a changed location and asks the wrong questions.
A formal defect, such as a missing witness, can invalidate a document regardless of what its author intended.
when: A document is disputed on grounds of form.
why: Legal validity depends on meeting formal requirements, not on the author's wishes.

text: Design odd NPC behaviour so two motives fit the early acts, and only the true motive explains the later ones.
when: Designing an NPC whose behaviour the player must interpret.
why: Staged evidence lets the player discriminate between motives over time.

text: Make an NPC's costly choice a visible tell, and give players a record that lets them check the motive they infer from it.
Let NPCs make specific, checkable claims that players can verify in the world, and reward players who record them with a later payoff.
when: Designing NPC dialogue or notes that feed later encounters
why: Verifiable claims let players feel their notes matter

text: Give a witness NPC only a general direction, so the player must follow up at a later location to narrow it down.
when: Generating NPC information in a dungeon or level
why: Partial hints create a reason to explore and link locations.

text: Let careful inspection reveal a reversal through several features, such as a scar or tattoo, so players who examine the full body find the truth.
when: when designing a mistaken-identity twist

text: Build NPC dialogue where the player presents a claim and the NPC checks it against facts the player gathered earlier.
Give an NPC a prepared cover story using one true detail, so the player exposes the contradiction only by bringing a second source.
Record each NPC's claimed location at each time, and let players find witnesses who confirm or break those claims.
Let a character with a stake in a theory push that explanation, giving players a biased source to weigh.
Let an NPC give information only when the player claims a role; record the claim and let the NPC retract the information if the claim proves false.
Provide an authority NPC, such as a lawyer or constable, who can confirm or refute a rumour, rewarding a visit to the right place.
Let non-player witnesses identify a face from a photograph, and give them a hidden incentive that explains their cooperation.
Give a comic or minor NPC a real motive or action that is later explained, and let the player test that NPC before discarding them.
when: building a suspect NPC for a mystery
why: A testable suspect makes the dismissal a player choice rather than an arbitrary cut.

text: Flag an NPC's claim that conflicts with an event the player witnessed, so careful play is rewarded.
Let an NPC withhold a fact it dislikes sharing, and let the player recover it by cross-checking with a second NPC.
Let an interrogated NPC keep consistent rebuttals under pressure, so the player can test contradictions against its earlier answers.
when: when designing an interrogation mechanic

text: Log minor disputes as timestamped world events, so a later accusation can recast an ordinary quarrel as motive.
Let NPCs' later choices, such as refusing a marriage or leaving a village, serve as clues to what they know.
Let child NPCs give partial or false clues, with adults having reasons to dismiss them; a child's warning can be a valid hint for the player to check.
when: when designing NPC hints

text: Witnesses should report all relevant facts, since each fact's value depends on the others; a shortened account can suit a puzzle when the full version is available from other sources.
Informal talk over tea can yield more detail than formal questioning, but it mixes fact with rumour and spreads quickly.
when: When gathering accounts from a household

text: A confession explaining everything can read like a lecture, while ending it abruptly leaves a gap the audience must accept rather than resolve.
when: Deciding how completely to explain a solution
why: Full explanation risks tedium, and a break risks an unresolved detail

text: A character who cuts off an account at the key moment signals that they already understand it, and the delay itself adds tension.
when: A witness's story reaches its central point
why: The interruption shows the listener's knowledge and withholds the answer.

text: Sudden arrivals, messages or ambient sounds can reset tension in a scene, resolve a confrontation without answers, and give the witness time to recover.
when: A scene risks losing momentum or the investigator needs a pause.
why: Breaks change the emotional pace and can help the witness and the player reconsider.

text: A second witness or record that describes the same event independently serves as a check on the first account.
when: Testing a key claim from one witness.
why: Independent sources reduce the chance that a single account is wrong or invented.

text: Choose witnesses that respond in different ways, so that one witness's state is not simply copied by another.
when: Using several animal or NPC witnesses to detect a hidden factor
why: Witnesses that react identically give one signal, not independent evidence.

text: Seek an independent witness outside the suspect's household for any claimed whereabouts, rather than accepting the suspect's word.
when: when a suspect's alibi relies only on their own account
why: Independent confirmation is required to test the claim.

text: Plant an insider motive, such as a dismissal or grudge, that the player can connect only after the outsider theory fails.
when: a crime first blamed on an outsider
why: A late-connected motive makes the insider reveal feel earned rather than arbitrary.

text: The length of time between dated exchanges reveals how urgent a matter was and how long parties hesitated.
when: when reading a sequence of dated letters or replies

text: When suspicion moves from a client's relatives, it usually lands on insiders such as an employer, family member, or servant who has access to the object.
when: Investigation moves beyond the obvious suspects
why: Insiders have the access the crime requires.

text: Split a decisive fact across partial accounts, each adding a piece, to delay the reveal and build suspense, only when the audience need not know the core fact early.
when: the answer must feel earned; the audience does not need the core fact early in order to follow the events
why: each account adds a piece while holding back the decisive fact

text: A suspicious detail with an innocent origin can still shape events, because it is out of character and invites speculation before its cause is known.
when: A character performs an uncharacteristic act that others misread.
why: Out-of-character behavior stands out and suggests a hidden plan even when the cause is mundane.

text: Incomplete or self-correcting NPC dialogue after a scare makes the player assemble a likely truth from fragments, rather than receive a complete explanation.
when: Writing NPC dialogue after a frightening event.
why: Fragments invite the player to reason and feel more involved.

text: When the key to a mystery lies in a memory the character cannot access, the player cannot verify it until a staged test makes it observable.
when: The reveal depends on a forgotten or drugged action
why: Neither the character nor the player has the information, so the test is the only route to proof.

text: A witness with no records can be accurate about facts, but that accuracy is harder to prove.
when: Evaluating a witness who lacks written support.
why: Without records, accuracy cannot be independently checked.

text: A witness who heard but did not see can support only limited claims, and corroboration from a witness who saw an object but not the act does not link a person to the act.
when: When weighing witness testimony by sensory channel.
why: Sensory detail limits what a witness can establish about who did what.

text: Use the ages and timing of remembered events that players can rebuild from dialogue into a timeline.
when: Past events must be reconstructed from character accounts.
why: A consistent timeline lets players test claims against each other.

text: Set up a trusted but limited NPC's limits early, so a later reveal recontextualizes them.
Give the final reveal an independent source whose credibility the player can verify through a separate artifact, such as a dated record that matches the reveal's details.
when: When the reveal is a claim the player must accept over the investigator's skepticism.
why: A checkable external artifact makes an account credible without requiring the player to trust a single voice.

text: Give an innocent suspect a visible mark of guilt, so the accusation is earned and the later clearing evidence is credible.
when: building a list of suspects
why: Visible marks make the suspicion reasonable, so clearing the suspect feels like a real turn.

text: A witness at a narrow view, such as a keyhole, sees only a fragment and may give a precise-sounding account covering only part of what happened.
when: A witness observes through a small or partial opening or gap.
why: The limited vantage restricts what can be seen, so the account covers only a part.

text: Neutral facts such as a denial or an unrelated record can fit either rival explanation, so they settle nothing between them.
when: comparing two competing explanations
why: Consistency with both sides is not discrimination

text: Two nearby places let each identity gather many witnesses while no one sees both identities at the same time.
In disputes with factions, the accused party may choose a council of witnesses, and outside pressure can force additional members onto it.
why: Each side's selection of witnesses shapes who judges the case.

text: Phrase questions neutrally and openly, without presuming an answer or revealing how much you know; presumed premises steer witnesses, and visible interest makes them shape or withhold answers.
when: When questioning a witness about identity or events.
why: Witnesses tend to accept the premise a question carries, and showing too much interest in one point makes them shape or withhold the answer.

text: Give more weight to a neutral witness who had no reason to shape the account, such as someone who only overheard talk.
why: Without a stake, a witness is less likely to bend the account toward a purpose.

text: Trust a neutral witness for plain facts such as who was present in a place, even when that witness cannot say what it meant.
why: Neutral testimony can fix a simple fact without requiring an interpretation.

text: Introduce a detail in neutral, ordinary description early, so that its later return reads as a payoff the audience could have anticipated.
when: when the final reveal depends on a physical detail
why: the audience accepts the detail without suspicion

text: Even narrow sensory testimony, such as a felt touch of cloth, can support a usable inference about an unseen person's clothing or position.
Open an interview with neutral everyday topics such as books, hobbies or a meal to lower a guarded witness's defences before the painful subject.
when: A distressed or defensive witness is questioned and there is time to build trust.
why: Relaxed talk makes a witness more willing to disclose.

text: A witness who has only just taken up a post may not have seen the arrivals they are asked about, so check their tenure before weighing their memory.
Have more than one observer watch a subject's reaction, so a signal is confirmed by others before it is relied upon.
When two accounts agree in nearly every detail, their exceptions mark exactly where the later event differed, so examine those points first.
when: Two accounts of similar events are compared
why: Differences are where the accounts' independent content lies

text: Observation at night yields less because sight fails; sound may still reveal what sight cannot.
when: Covert observation extends into darkness.
why: Vision degrades in low light while hearing does not.

text: Overlooking a nearby busy road as a source of witnesses. Even an isolated house may be watched from a highway in view.
when: When assuming a location is isolated
why: A public route in sight of a building can supply observers.

text: Giving NPCs biased opinions about one another while the player arrives neutral lets the player assess the scene independently of the group's prejudices.
when: When designing a mystery where characters hold opinions about each other
why: Neutral observation lets the player detect gaps in the group's consensus.

text: Treating a suspect's helpful fact as neutral can hide the motive it reveals.
when: A suspect offers evidence that seems to help them.
why: Helpful facts often carry an interest that goes unexamined.

text: 1) Ask an open question without proposing an answer. 2) Only if no answer comes, probe for the existence of a memory. 3) Record suggested answers and any hedged acceptance separately from firm recall.
when: Judging how much a witness's account can bear
why: Neutral questions reveal whether a real memory exists before it is shaped.

text: 1) Collect accounts from everyone present after the event. 2) Compare them for any report of the disputed event. 3) Weigh the absence of reports as evidence of limited confidence, not proof.
when: When a disputed event occurred in a crowded setting.
why: Comparing accounts reveals whether anyone else perceived the event.

text: 1) State your own stake openly, accepting the risk of exposure. 2) Read the witness's reactions as well as their answers. 3) Press on the specific word that produces a strong reaction. 4) Hold ground under threat.
when: A witness has a clear reason to conceal and reacts strongly to one subject.
why: Honest stakes and reaction cues reveal where the witness's knowledge lies.

text: 1) Identify the specific claim a witness makes. 2) Ask a question that tests that claim, not one that repeats the report. 3) Ask about related conditions the report did not cover, such as weather.
when: When interviewing a witness whose account fixes a time or place.
why: Repeating the report yields no new information; testing questions expose gaps.

text: 1) Accept the account as reasonable to keep the witness talking. 2) Raise a plausible alternative that a challenger could argue. 3) Watch whether the witness or others react with new details or defensiveness.
when: Questioning a witness whose account may be shaped by motive
why: Pressure on a plausible story can expose undisclosed disputes or knowledge

text: Keep your reactions neutral when questioning, since visible shock signals the question matters and may silence the witness.
when: interviewing an emotionally involved witness
why: Reactions reveal what is important and change what the witness says.

text: A neutral question with no stated purpose can measure whether a witness answers candidly.
when: a truthfulness check is needed without revealing which fact matters
why: the question hides the purpose of the test

text: Give watchers narrow orders, such as recording all entries but stopping only exits, so they gather more information.
Use neutral wording in public notices, such as saying a person died rather than was murdered, so the culprit is not alerted.
why: loaded wording can warn the person who committed the crime

text: Flag ambiguous expressions as neutral facts and reveal their meaning only once corroborating evidence is found.
A witness's admission explaining one sighting opens a new timeline to test; a careless admission can open a hidden area rather than a direct search.
A witness who accuses another character may have a personal motive, so listeners weigh the accusation against the witness's character and affections rather than accepting it at face value.
when: A character reports suspicious behavior or madness in another character who is tied to them by family, marriage or inheritance.
why: Personal stakes can bias a witness, and doubting the witness can imply something about the witness's own judgment.

text: A person who searches the listener's face and asks them to confirm what they know is checking how much the listener already knows.
A witness may regain composure and gain new ideas during an interruption, so breaks in questioning can help both the witness and the investigator.
when: Questioning is intense and the witness appears distressed.
why: Time away from pressure can restore composure and prompt fresh thinking.

text: Character and evidential value are independent: poor reputation lowers weight without cancelling it, and respectable witnesses may give weak evidence depending on how obtained; check against internal and external evidence.
when: When judging a witness's testimony, especially one with a damaged reputation.
why: A flawed person can still report true facts.

text: A witness who confesses a costly lapse or admits doubts tends to be more convincing on other matters and more candid about the admitted points.
when: When a witness confesses a personal lapse or admits doubts.
why: Admitting costly faults or doubts signals willingness to report unflattering facts.

text: A biased witness may still be substantially true; keep the factual part of their account and test it rather than dismissing it outright.
when: When a witness has a motive against the accused.
why: Dismissal discards true information along with the bias.

text: When one witness might fail, secure backup testimony in advance so the case does not depend on a single source.
when: A case relies on a witness who may change sides or be unreliable.
why: Backup sources keep the case intact if the main witness fails.

text: A witness's isolated, sedentary life and craving for excitement can inflate self-regard and colour what they report.
Check testimony heard through a barrier against what the witness could actually perceive from their position.
when: When a key line reaches the investigator secondhand or through a door
why: Partial perception limits reliability

text: Let objects that undercut the official explanation pile up before anyone states the conclusion, so the player reaches the inference first.
A final explanation built from many converging pieces of testimony and objects, rather than one trap, makes the solution feel proven and complete.
when: the case is resolved at the end of a mystery
why: Convergence of independent sources lets the reveal carry weight without a single dramatic test.

text: Bargained or bribed testimony, such as for immunity, is shaped by the witness's incentive and may hedge or please the payer; payment or protection is not proof of truth.
when: When a witness speaks after a promise of protection or after being paid.
why: The incentive shapes the content and certainty of what they say; payment creates an incentive to please the payer.

text: Strong emotion, drinking, fear and second-hand hearing each bias a witness's interpretation, even when the witness reports events honestly.
when: Assessing witness reports, especially when a witness has a strong emotional stake.
why: Emotion and impairment colour interpretation even when the witness is honest.

text: Corroboration from a source sharing the same bias is weaker than it appears.
when: Two sources agree but may share a viewpoint or interest.
why: Agreement from a biased source adds little independent support.

text: An explanation offered by someone with their own purpose should be weighed alongside that purpose, since the explainer may want a particular outcome.
when: Receiving a supernatural debunking from an interested party.
why: The source's motive can shape which explanation they offer and what they want the listener to do.

text: 1) Make a child NPC give rumours and partial truths rather than authoritative hints. 2) Require the player to verify them. 3) Let leaving a child out of an investigation or protecting them change lead availability or NPC trust.
when: Designing child NPCs in an investigation game.
why: Unreliable child information keeps verification as the player's task, while choices about the child have consequences.

text: Verify a private exchange reported second-hand against another source, and check the exact wording before building conclusions on it.
when: A key fact about a private conversation reaches you through a go-between
why: Second-hand reports can alter wording, and unconfirmed accounts can mislead

text: Let an NPC's testimony be checkable against another NPC's recorded position, rather than accepted as given.
when: Designing NPC statements about events.
why: Cross-checking against another character's position turns testimony into a verifiable clue.

text: Treat a witness's account of their route or events as partial, and probe a brief account of significant events with follow-up questions.
when: Reconstructing where a person was from their own account, or a witness gives a short account of events they should know well
why: Lapses of attention leave holes the witness cannot fill; brevity can hide omissions that a fuller account would reveal

text: A single uncorroborated account is weak support; treat it as a lead and require a second independent clue, such as a physical trace or another witness, before resolving a case.
when: A case rests mainly on one person's account of another's conduct
why: A lone account can be mistaken, motivated or shaped by suggestion

text: Read a limited statement at its scope: a witness who could not observe a stretch cannot confirm or deny it, so a servant's 'heard nothing' says little about entry.
when: A witness reports no sighting of a key event or route segment
why: Silence from a witness who could not see the stretch is weak evidence on its own

text: Record what each witness can and cannot confirm: a hedge marks a memory limit, and a sincere 'I don't know' is not a denial but stops rumour filling the gap.
when: Recording witness testimony, or a witness is unsure about a key point
why: Admitted uncertainty prevents unsupported claims from filling the gap

text: Crowds, engine noise, screams and cross-talk drown out quiet speakers and key details, so listeners lose track of who said what and clues go unnoticed.
when: Dialogue or a scene occurs over ambient, crowd or chaotic sound
why: Attention is drawn to louder sources, so competing sensory input hides quiet speakers and the important detail

text: A witness can report a detail without understanding its significance, so the detail may carry more information than the witness recognises.
when: Interpreting a casual remark from a witness
why: Observers record what they see without knowing what it means.

text: A witness whose states never share memories can truthfully forget what they knew in the other state, so their accounts conflict.
when: a witness's knowledge depends on time or condition
why: Separate states do not carry recollections across.

text: Players often see the link between scattered details only after an outside prompt, such as a name appearing in a document.
when: after gathering clues but before connecting them
why: Placing details side by side is what makes a hidden pattern visible

text: An unconscious action in response to a cue, such as an instruction spoken without thought, can reveal memory that a conscious answer would conceal.
when: A stated memory loss is doubtful
why: Unthinking acts are harder to control than deliberate answers

text: Observers overlook people carrying ordinary objects such as trays or wearing uniforms, treating them as background rather than as possible actors or movers.
when: Service or staff figures appear in a scene
why: Routine objects make a person's role seem unremarkable, so their movements are not recorded.

text: Under stress, witnesses may forget a detail that returns after hours, days or weeks.
when: witness under stress
why: Memory recall can be delayed, so revisiting a witness pays off.

text: A creaking floor or other sound reveals a presence before anything is seen, so sound can warn a character or player of danger.
when: Sound is audible while vision is limited.
why: Hearing gives early cues when sight cannot.

text: Under sudden alarm, people make reflexive corrections, like shutting then reopening a door, and these visible actions can later reveal them.
when: Under sudden alarm
why: Panic drives repeated actions before reasoning catches up

text: Attacks reported from sleep or half-waking are often nightmares shaped by bodily discomfort, heavy meals, unfamiliar lodging and fear.
when: the witness was asleep or half-awake when it began
why: perception is unreliable in that state

text: Observers attend to a person's pleasant manner and miss a mismatch between it and where that person's attention actually goes.
when: A friendly character's gaze keeps returning to one place.
why: Admiration for pleasantness hides the discrepancy.

text: A limited witness narrator observes and reports a scene but sees less than the investigator and may misjudge the method, so the account reflects the witness's blind spots.
A witness with limited hearing may report only that something was noticed, so accounts of sounds carry limited weight.
Check how well each witness actually knows the person in question, and whether an identification rests on direct contact or only gossip or reputation.
when: Weighing testimony about a person's character or identity
why: Recent or biased acquaintance can distort a witness's account, and inferred identities may come from gossip

text: Too many missing or changed items in one scene drown out the important one, so include only the absences that bear on the question.
when: designing a scene with several missing or changed items
why: crowded clues make the key one hard to notice

text: A suspect who speaks at length gives the examiner more material to check, though a fluent or sincere account can still hide the central fact.
when: When a suspect volunteers a long account
why: Extended speech creates testable details, and sincerity does not confirm truth

text: A witness who guards their own words often still volunteers history about their relatives, lodgers and associates.
A witness who admits they cannot swear to an identity is more credible than one who insists on it.
A witness with limited memory can still reliably report an absence, such as that a certain request was never made, which narrows the search.
when: A witness cannot recall a specific person but is sure of what did not happen.
why: An absence of action can be remembered even when individuals are not.

text: Check what a witness's claim rests on, such as observed behaviour, rather than what the people involved said.
when: A witness states a conclusion about a relationship.
why: Conclusions drawn from observation may not match the parties' own accounts.

text: Deliver sudden news of a death and watch for an immediate, unguarded outcry; a natural shriek and protest suggests genuine ignorance rather than an act.
when: testing whether a witness already knows the truth
why: unguarded reactions are too natural to be easily staged

text: The information a public source can report depends on which witnesses are still available; if key witnesses vanish, the account is missing crucial details.
Revealing later that a damaging testimony came from a witness with limited access rewards players who compare accounts.
Observers can register details without conscious attention, and replaying a scene later can surface them, but only details that were registered at the time can be recovered.
when: when a player or character passed through a scene without focusing on certain objects
why: Recall depends on whether the detail was encoded at the time, so an unnoticed detail cannot simply be summoned on request.

text: Investigator cues, including naming a topic, can plant ideas or steer a witness toward a choice; record which details came from the witness and which from the investigator.
when: An investigator names a topic or guides a witness toward a particular person
why: A witness may look where directed and confirm the cued choice, so the result may reflect the prompt as much as memory

text: A casual glance misses small anomalies, such as cut or pasted labels, that only close, magnified, methodical inspection reveals; casual viewers take surface appearance at face value.
when: Inspecting an object that looks ordinary at a glance but may carry a trace
why: Key anomalies are small and visible only under close checking

text: A witness can be sincere yet have limited access, such as seeing someone only at work; sincerity does not extend their knowledge beyond that access.
why: honesty does not supply missing observation

text: Witnesses use related words loosely, so a general term may stand for a more specific physical state than they actually saw.
why: Everyday words blur distinct conditions

text: A witness proves an item existed at a time, not where it is now, and does not prevent concealment over a long period.
why: Time allows an item to be moved or hidden.

text: A witness kept uninformed about a task's purpose may later repeat what they saw, which weakens secrecy.
when: when witnesses are used to hide an operation
why: Those kept in the dark may talk to others.

text: An apparently empty window may still be watched by someone who did not notice, so roles and attention matter as much as presence.
when: Judging whether a window was unobserved.
why: People present but inattentive do not register events.

text: A corroborating light or witness covers only one household or area, so it does not confirm wakefulness across the whole group.
when: when one witness's observation is used to vouch for many people
why: Corroboration applies only to what that observer could see.

text: 1) Separate what the witness saw from what they heard or inferred, keeping observed facts apart from inferences. 2) Identify which sense supports each identification. 3) Ask negative questions to find the limits of their knowledge. 4) Cross-check details against independent facts.
when: Assessing a witness's identification of a person, or reporting something they could not fully observe
why: A claim is only as reliable as the sense and circumstances behind it; reasoning from inferences as if observed leads to errors

text: Trust a witness's judgment only within what they could know, and ask what they do not know; certainty beyond that is not evidence.
when: A witness offers views on a relationship or situation beyond their direct knowledge
why: Limited contact limits what a witness can reliably report; someone who never met a partner can say little about the relationship

text: Reveal only the evidence a witness must answer and keep the key detail from everyone, since full disclosure or spreading word lets the witness shape the account.
why: Word spreads and shapes later answers; showing the whole case lets the witness shape the account

text: Limit a captive's means of reply, such as a gag, bound hands or only a note, nod or single word, so answers are short and precise.
when: An interrogator must extract a single fact
why: Players must ask precise questions to get useful answers, and answers stay pointed rather than free-ranging

text: Ask whether a witness read the whole record or only a summary, since a doubt carries weight only if the witness knows the full evidence.
when: when the evidence is documentary

text: Record each witness's knowledge and bias in design data so players can judge how reliable each account is.
Limit further arrests to cases of necessity, and restrict printed or public discourse that can feed quarrels.
when: When an accusation spreads and detentions multiply.
why: Unchecked arrests and public debate escalate suspicion.

text: Script a witness's sighting of a suspicious figure to stay ambiguous until a later check, such as an autopsy, overturns or confirms it.
when: Writing an NPC testimony that the player must weigh.
why: A deferred check keeps the testimony open without making it false by default.

text: Witnesses who hear the outcome may sincerely reinterpret earlier sensory details as linked to it, so compare later accounts with the original record.
when: witness hears news after the event
why: new information reshapes memory of earlier sensory details

text: A routine settles within days so can anchor inferences, but visitors and disturbances can change it; witnesses may describe ideal practice, so verify actual routine first.
when: When deciding whether a character's usual schedule or routine can anchor an inference.
why: Schedules become stable quickly, yet unexpected events can break them, and ideal routines often differ from actual practice.

text: Character can be checked through public records, but good standing does not prove testimony; relatives' or associates' character testimony may be partial and needs independent knowledge.
when: Witness reliability is attacked
why: Character and content are separate matters.

text: Testimony from intoxicated, frightened or retelling witnesses is weak; separate what was seen from details added later, and check the most confident details, which may exceed the facts.
when: Weighing gossip, a drunk's recollection or a story retold through several people.

text: Give two sources conflicting accounts, such as a messenger versus a sender or a protective lie, and let physical evidence or a record decide which holds.
when: Designing a conflict between witnesses or an intermediary NPC.
why: Conflict forces the player to weigh evidence; physical evidence or a record gives a neutral way to settle the clash.

text: Each retelling reshapes an account: tellers pick what to repeat, links drop details or qualifiers like 'I think', listeners embellish; trace accounts to their source.
when: information passes through several people before reaching the investigator
why: Every link filters and reshapes the account, and each depends on the one before, so later versions can outgrow the original.

text: Extraordinary claims from respectable, conventional, calm, sincere or distressed witnesses get trusted over their content; check every unverifiable claim against facts, not manner, deference or standing.
when: weighing a witness whose status or demeanour looks reassuring
why: appearance and standing trigger trust before content is checked

text: Agreement is not corroboration when witnesses share a vantage, expectation, fear, grievance or source; they may echo one assumption, motive or told story, even the same wrong time.
when: when several witnesses give the same time estimate or account
why: social pressure, shared assumptions and common motives align their errors; repeated testimony may trace to one story

text: Do not equate a motivated witness with a liar, or discard their account for bias alone; corroborate it against independent evidence before weighing it.
when: a witness is prejudiced or has a stake in the outcome
why: A biased source can still report true facts, and dismissing them loses evidence.

text: Tag NPC testimony with a visible stake or grudge, so players must weigh it against inspectable traces and other clues before accepting it.
when: designing an in-game witness whose account may be self-serving
why: Visible bias lets players judge a claim instead of accepting it as fact.

text: Do not accuse a person on an overheard keyword or lone testimony; require confirmation from a second source, such as a records terminal, first.
when: narrowing down speakers of an overheard clue before accusing anyone
why: A single hearing cannot establish who spoke

text: Keep reported speech, such as what another person said, separate from the speaker's own words, and note when the speaker confirms a statement.
when: A witness quotes someone else, or statements are recorded in a case file or dialogue log.
why: Mixing the two blurs who said what; confirmed speech is stronger evidence than secondhand report.

text: Witnesses with a stake, grudge, hostility toward one party, a wish to promote another, or a strong moral or religious framework bias reports, fusing checkable facts with judgments.
when: a witness has a personal stake, grudge, or strong moral or religious framework
why: Bias colours perception and reporting, so factual claims and verdicts arrive fused together.

text: Wary informants clam up when their information seems important or no assurance has been given; pressing early yields silence, while those feeling heard under protest may give more.
when: questioning a wary or reluctant informant before any assurance has been given
why: Perceived importance and fear of exposure make witnesses guard what they know.

text: An excited or elated witness mixes their own feelings into the facts, so the listener must separate what is felt from what is known.
when: A witness is biased, emotional or distracted
why: Strong emotion colours how the witness reports events

text: Excited observers inflate what they saw, reporting impressions of closeness or detail as if they were measurements.
when: A striking event is observed by an excited group
why: Emotion turns impressions into confident claims

text: A sincere young witness may report accurate concrete details while drawing sweeping, emotional conclusions from them.
when: a child reports events they witnessed
why: Feelings and loyalties shape interpretation.

text: A child's vivid testimony can seem supernatural because of the child's age, which makes it harder to dismiss.
Rising agitation in a witness signals that the testimony is coloured by emotion and should be checked against other evidence.
when: A witness's account becomes more anxious or emotional as it proceeds.
why: Anxiety distorts perception and recall, making the account less reliable.

text: A partner whose trust wavers may be steadied by receiving full written detail of each step, which also creates a shared record.
when: Trust between conspirators is shaken
why: Complete disclosure reduces suspicion and ties both parties to one account

text: A witness's temper and the questioner's manner both shape how the witness's answers are heard and interpreted.
when: a witness is questioned under pressure

text: A witness pressed to explain herself by an accusatory questioner answers briefly and turns away to signal objection.
when: An interrogator shifts from enquiry to accusation.
why: Insistent demands turn the exchange into an accusation, so the witness protects herself through minimal replies.

text: A correct detail from an unreliable witness can be coincidence, so it needs independent checking before it is trusted.
when: When a drunk, hostile or self-interested witness gives one checkable detail.
why: Partial accuracy from an unreliable source does not establish the rest of its account.

text: People assume a familiar routine held to the end, so a person's unusual final hours often go unchecked by others.
when: when someone describes a routine they follow daily
why: others assume the usual pattern without checking it

text: A brief glimpse under shock can feel certain yet be wrong, and memory of the period after a shock is often unreliable.
when: When a witness reports a vivid memory formed under stress.
why: Shock impairs perception and memory, producing confident but inaccurate recall.

text: An agitated witness may volunteer useful detail but may also drift off topic.
when: a witness is emotionally charged during questioning
why: emotion loosens recall and focus at the same time

text: Accounts taken soon after an event, from a household or crowd that is agitated and gossiping, tend to be muddied as recollections blend together.
when: when early accounts are collected from an unsettled group
why: Shared talk and emotion blend individual memories.

text: A witness's story can shift step by step under precise questioning, such as moving from one location to another, and each shift is a signal to check against other evidence.
when: When a witness is questioned closely about a timeline or location.

text: Witnesses recall routine events poorly, and their memory of which day it happened fades further as questioning is delayed.
when: asked about a repeated daily event
why: a routine occurrence blends into others, so single days are hard to separate

text: A confessor may swear an oath without understanding what it means, so a sworn statement is not automatically informed.
when: judging a sworn confession
why: the oath may have been taken without understanding its weight

text: An instinctive physical withdrawal can signal unease the person cannot justify, and the other party may read it as a slight.
Distracted observers often fail to notice a small deliberate action performed in front of them and treat it as incidental.
when: attention is pulled elsewhere during the action
why: unattended actions are not registered

text: Bystanders filter testimony through their assumptions, dismissing a speaker as mad and missing content that may matter.
when: a witness speaks in an emotional state
why: prior assumptions shape what is heard

text: A distant observer who cannot hear an exchange must infer its meaning from gestures, which can be staged or misread.
when: Judging a conclusion drawn from a watcher far from the event.
why: Gestures are visible but ambiguous, and they cannot reveal the words spoken.

text: People who are not careful distinguish observed traces from suppositions tend to accept every detail as certain once a theory is presented to them.
when: Presenting a theory to a sceptic or a listener.
why: Without marking which links are supported, all links feel equally proven.

text: A fixed date gives memory a starting point, so witnesses supply more detail than they do from vague recollection.
when: recalling events without a fixed reference point
why: fixed anchors cue memory

text: A minor witness may confirm a basic event but give no name or direction; when follow-up answers stay empty, the investigator should accept the limit and move on.
when: Minor witness is the only source for a basic event
why: Such witnesses often lack identifying detail, so pressing further yields nothing.

text: Players and observers notice hidden things through reflections or partly blocked views, so information visible only indirectly still registers as a clue.
when: The relevant object or person is out of direct line of sight.
why: Indirect views reveal what direct views hide, and players can be trained to look for them.

text: Memory of minor details, such as the position of a fixture, degrades after repairs or distress, so such details deserve less trust.
when: when a witness recalls small physical details after a change or upsetting event
why: Changes and distress disrupt memory of incidental features

text: Witnesses who see the same shadowy shape describe it differently, filling gaps with their own expectations and fear.
when: When several witnesses report on one brief or poorly lit sighting
why: Observers complete ambiguous shapes with what they expect or fear

text: Light, teasing exchanges can calm a witness and loosen their account, so they begin to speak more freely.
when: when a guarded witness has stopped offering detail
why: relaxed rapport lowers defensiveness and encourages disclosure

text: A witness may leave a stop out of a summary and admit it only when asked directly, so an account that seems complete can still be incomplete.
when: a witness narrates a journey in brisk summary
why: Summaries compress the route and omit legs the speaker does not volunteer

text: A figure that boards unseen and leaves at the last moment is identified only when two observers recognise it together.
when: when a single observer might miss a fleeting figure
why: independent confirmation raises confidence in a brief sighting

text: A plausible wrong answer is attractive because it fits what the audience already expects.
when: The audience holds a prior expectation about the solution
why: Fit with expectations hides the error

text: A witness questioned repeatedly may adopt a feature they were led to notice, and retract it only when pressed again.
when: a witness faces leading questions
why: a suggested detail can come to feel like something seen

text: A witness who knows about a reconstruction may act differently, so the test can be compromised.
when: a witness learns the purpose of a replay
why: awareness changes behavior

text: Witness descriptions of a person in a role shrink to generic traits such as rough height, clean-shaven face and ordinary clothes.
when: A witness recalls someone seen briefly in a familiar role.

text: An eager informant who is keen on their own theory can push an inquiry forward without checking the source, leading to costly action.
when: A witness proposes a suggestion and presses to act on it quickly.
why: Enthusiasm and pride can override verification.

text: Discovering a discrepancy in presented evidence can reverse a witness's trust in the investigator who presented it.
why: the witness reads the difference as a trap

text: A witness who was asleep, drowsy or distracted may have registered a sound or sight without noticing it at the time.
why: attention is reduced, so perception is weak but not absent

text: A witness who answers only exactly what is asked volunteers little, leaving the investigator with little to work with.
when: when interviewing a reserved or literal witness

text: Distinctive costume items are easier to recall than faces, so they work well as search keys for finding an unknown person.
when: searching for someone seen only in passing
why: unusual visual elements stand out in memory

text: A concealed listener who gathers information may keep returning and improve their position for further listening, showing that eavesdropping is itself rewarding to them.
when: Designing a concealed observer character.
why: Listening yields both knowledge and enjoyment, which encourages repeat visits.

text: An emotional witness may confirm an identity too readily, so the examiner must press for firm, definite answers.
when: A grieving or distressed witness is confirming identity
why: Emotional state can push a witness toward quick agreement.

text: When others present deny a witness's perceived event, the witness's account is often not withdrawn.
A witness with a motive may describe a subject in vivid terms that reveal the witness's own feelings more than the subject's character.
when: when testimony comes from someone with a stake
why: motive shapes what the witness notices

text: A highly impressionable observer at close range may feel a crowd as a pull, while observers behind cover see only the disturbance, not its cause.
when: A concealed observer watches a crowd up close.
why: Limited vantage shows effects without their sources.

text: A witness approached unexpectedly may be badly startled and fail to recognize a familiar person until reminded of an earlier contact.
when: when an investigator approaches a witness from behind
why: Surprise impairs immediate recognition

text: Stunned witnesses in a shocking event give fragmentary, weak accounts, and repeating a single phrase is not a reliable identification.
when: Witnesses describe an event in high-emotion, chaotic conditions
why: Shock narrows what a witness can recall and say clearly

text: Hope for an outcome or admiration for the person seen can colour recollection, shifting reports toward the wish or favourable detail rather than what the witness knew.
when: when a witness has an emotional stake in the result or admires the person described
why: Emotional response shapes memory and reporting.

text: Dramatic or erratic conduct alone does not show falsehood, since performance and clear thinking coexist; yet a convincing performance is not proof of sincerity either.
when: A witness shows extreme or theatrical behavior, or delivers a performance.
why: Performance and clear thinking can occur together in one person, and emotional convincingness distorts evidence as much as dismissal does.

text: A frightened or angry witness may be sincere yet wrong; suspicions colored by fear are persuasive but unverified and must be tested before they shape the case.
when: A witness is driven by fear, distrust or grief.
why: Strong emotion shapes what is perceived and reported, so fear-colored suspicions are not established facts.

text: A witness who seems certain may hedge or retract when frightened, so record the hedge as a sign of weak evidence.
when: A witness is pressed under pressure
why: Fear can weaken a stated certainty

text: When many observers praise the same person in identical terms, the praise may reflect what observers want to see rather than what the person did.
when: A character's reputation rests on many similar accounts
why: Shared expectations shape how observers describe someone.

text: Local oral tradition can explain a present event through a causal account, but its claims are hard to verify, so the investigator must often rely on the teller's word alone.
when: A setting has a long oral history but the physical proof has decayed.
why: Inherited memory supplies explanations and past procedures, yet no independent check is available.

text: A teller may move his own situation to another place or period, telling his account at a safe distance.
when: A suspect tells a story whose setting differs from his real situation.
why: Distance from the real events lowers the teller's perceived risk of exposure.

text: Laughter, a darkening face, stillness or sudden distrust signal where a witness's concealed knowledge lies.
when: Questioning a reluctant witness on a sensitive subject.
why: Involuntary reactions betray emotional stakes that answers may hide.

text: A witness's interpretation of events, such as a belief in a conspiracy, can be wrong while the observed facts remain accurate.
when: When a witness reports strange or frightening conclusions
why: Emotional or confused witnesses often mix accurate observation with unreliable explanation.

text: Witnesses often confuse what they heard reported at an inquest with what they personally saw.
when: Taking testimony from a witness after a public proceeding.
why: Repeated information blends into memory and feels like firsthand experience.

text: A precise, sequential account with checkable facts feels more credible to listeners, who use it to test against what they already know.
when: when a witness gives a detailed, ordered account
why: Specific details give the listener something to verify.

text: Witnesses often believe they watched continuously when they were in fact away from the key sightline during a blind interval.
when: A witness reports an unbroken view of a door or route.
why: Attention and movement take witnesses out of the critical sightline without their noticing.

text: A witness may state a negative fact with firm certainty while having never checked it, reasoning that they would have noticed if it were present.
when: A witness's denial is the main support for a conclusion.
why: Certainty can rest on an assumed observation rather than an actual one.

text: Players accept an eyewitness account as proof of guilt until a new explanation reframes what the witness saw.
when: A witness reports a suspect's act with confidence
why: A direct report feels like firm evidence, so it stays settled until another reading challenges it.

text: A hidden witness is someone present in a scene who knows what was said but goes unnoticed by the people being observed.
A witness can confirm one part of a story and not another, such as a man's presence without being able to describe a masked companion.
Signs such as stiffening vary widely between individuals, so they give limited precision on when death occurred.
Even a genuine report may be compromised, since observers and detectives can be bribed.
When a person dies without a written will, survivors' accounts of his spoken wishes become the main evidence of what he intended.
when: a death occurs with no written will
why: No document remains to record his decisions.

text: Routine signed entries, such as payment receipts, create many known samples of a person's hand that can be compared later.
when: a record book is kept over a long period

text: A witness who gave harmful testimony can carry lasting personal cost, shown in later decline.
A witness with no knowledge of the matter can still be questioned, and their ignorance is itself evidence about how reliable their confident claims are.
when: A witness gives a confident answer on a subject they could not have observed

text: A witness's assurance about someone's character reflects the witness's belief, not proof of what that person did.
when: When weighing a character judgment about a suspect.
why: Belief about character is not evidence of specific conduct.

text: An account that reports another person's words passes that person's version on only secondhand, through the narrator's own framing.
A witness who avoids news and conversation may lack key facts, such as a victim's identity or an innocent party's arrest.
when: A witness's knowledge is compared with what happened in the wider world
why: Isolation limits what a person knows about the events they describe.

text: Let witness NPCs describe a room correctly in one respect and wrongly in another, so players test every statement; a witness wrong about everything undermines all clues.
Compare a witness's first account with later ones; changes after pressure or new facts reveal errors or concealment and are warning signs.
when: a witness's account changes over repeated questioning or after new evidence emerges
why: pressure and new facts expose inconsistencies that first accounts conceal

text: Witnesses who deny knowing each other, or omit a prior link they consider irrelevant, may still be acquainted; ask directly and check hidden connections.
when: witnesses give matching denials or are interviewed about people involved in an incident
why: Denials are easy to make and hard to verify, and participants omit links they judge irrelevant until asked directly.

text: A late witness can overturn or reframe the theory; keep theories open until late evidence is checked, since a witness held back can supply the missing motive and sequence.
when: late in the inquiry when key facts are still unknown
why: Late firsthand accounts fill gaps that physical clues alone cannot explain.

text: Never treat a later account as equal to contemporary records; check its author's position before use, since long-after writing may inflate tradition and temperament; its praise and claims need caution.
Disagreement about what an image or perception shows hints at hidden content; an NPC who perceives something others don't can signal a hidden event without revealing it.
when: characters disagree about what an image depicts, or an NPC's perception conflicts with others'
why: The disagreement signals that something hidden is happening without revealing it.

text: When accounts conflict, a trait they all share may be a more telling pattern than any single description, and it may form the reliable core; disputed traits mark uncertainty.
when: accounts conflict and none settles the matter

text: Read an honest gap in recall as possibly a trauma effect, not deceit, and test where recall ends; admitting inability to identify people keeps the account credible.
when: a witness cannot account for a period or describe a person
why: Trauma can erase recall without intent to mislead, and an honest gap is more believable than a full description.

text: Volunteered detail growing under pressure may be invented, and precise detail about a briefly seen stranger may be unreliable; vagueness can be honest.
when: a witness's account grows more detailed under pressure, or describes a briefly seen stranger

text: Judge reliability per claim: a witness can be accurate on one point and wrong on another, or hide a lie or relationship among many accurate details to protect someone.
when: a witness's account is checked and is mostly accurate
why: Errors and accuracy occur independently across details; accurate details make a false one look reliable.

text: A witness who is frightened or stunned gives a less reliable account, so weigh their testimony accordingly unless another check exists.
why: fear distorts observation and memory

text: A late witness can reshape a timeline, and holding the strongest testimony for last can sway a judge who is already wavering.
Narrow questions about a person's routine habits can expose unusual nervousness or inconsistency with their normal behaviour.
Let witness NPCs be accurate on some fields and vague on others, such as an emblem seen clearly while the face stays hidden.
Differing serial numbers across items in one outfit suggest it was assembled from different sources.
Gather pieces of the story from several people who each saw only part of it, rather than relying on one witness who knows the whole picture.
when: Reconstructing a past event from accounts.
why: Each partial witness contributes a fragment, and their independent accounts can be compared for consistency.

text: Make some rumours true and some false, and let players verify them against records, so gossip is useful but not trusted blindly.
Grade a witness by listing what they can fix, such as events, sights and sounds, and what they cannot, such as exact dates or intervals.
when: Assessing how far to trust a witness's account

text: Learning a suspect's routine, such as where they work, can answer a question about a missing item without asking them directly.
when: An item is missing and the suspect would not answer directly

text: A close associate of a victim often supplies more useful names, habits and rivalries than a casual witness does.
Give NPC testimony as raw observations, letting the player supply interpretations and test them against other clues.
Use a witness's detail as a lead when it can be checked against the physical setting, such as a window's height or the presence of a ladder.
An alibi holds best when strangers with no stake in the outcome remember the suspect being present, not just when the suspect claims it.
Do not read evasion into a statement reported second-hand until you have checked that the wording was not paraphrased.
when: A statement reaches the investigator through other people.
why: Paraphrase can change the meaning of a narrow answer.

text: Check whether a disappearance has a known routine explanation, such as habitual short-notice departures, before reading the absence as guilt.
when: A person vanishes without warning.
why: A familiar pattern can explain the absence without any crime.

text: Check each suspect's statements against outside records. A claim that records contradict, such as a denied sum later found elsewhere, is evidence to pursue.
when: a suspect's account can be compared with financial or other records

text: Give suspect characters varied reactions to pressure, so the player must read behaviour rather than assume guilt from demeanour.
why: uniform reactions let players shortcut to a verdict

text: A routine, neutral observer carries more weight than the investigator who arranged the observation.
why: Independence from the investigation makes the testimony more credible.

text: A local observer with no stake in the matter can supply a dated sequence of arrivals, departures and occupancy at an empty site.
when: A site is found empty and its occupancy history is needed
why: A disinterested witness reports without bias

text: When a location is closed, nearby passersby may be the only source of information, so ask them for leads.
A reported sighting in a distant place or at a given hour may be mistaken or used to escape notice; check it against independent sources or records.
A sighting at a distance, through a window, in poor light or as a brief glimpse is weak evidence of identity; state the conclusion as tentative.
when: when judging an identification made from far away, in low light or from a brief glimpse
why: Reduced detail makes recognition unreliable.

text: An admitted lie neither proves nor disproves later claims; admitted trivia can buy credibility, so weigh each claim on its own evidence and track unresolved key gaps.
when: when a witness has admitted a lie or confesses small falsehoods
why: Candour about trivia can distract from unresolved key facts.

text: Give disguises or suspects a visible tell, such as a mask seam, mismatched detail, bandage, stain or glove, that a careful player can check with an examine action.
when: Designing clues on a suspect character or disguise.
why: A visible tell gives the player a concrete test without needing dialogue.

text: Keep routine steps brief and vary sources during long waits: repeated steps and time stamps drag and dull a final disclosure, while new sources keep attention on the stakes.
when: when a wait extends over a long period or routine testimony runs long
why: New sources keep attention on the stakes, and brief routine keeps the final disclosure impactful.

text: A well-known person meets only a small share of a city, so someone walking many routes can pass unrecognized; overestimating recognition leads to false claims that a movement was seen.
Before accepting a claim, trace it to its origin and ask whether the accuser saw it directly; second-hand claims from friends or motivated sources, unchecked against records, are weak.
when: when a claim rests on a single relayed source
why: Relayed claims lose verification and motivated sources bias what is passed on.

text: Honest failure to notice under heavy workload differs from a wish to conceal; the investigator must distinguish the two before judging a witness.
when: when a busy staff member cannot recall a visitor

text: Unqualified confidence in a witness's account is a warning sign, while honest hedges should be recorded as meaningful.
A respondent who offers no proof of identity deserves suspicion, since an impostor sent by the suspect would normally arrive carrying proof.
An NPC who saw the player can be asked open questions first, then shown a sketch, with answers graded by specificity and hedging.
when: designing an identification by an NPC witness
why: graded answers reward careful questioning

text: Rank witnesses by how certain they are, how closely they saw the subject, and whether other witnesses agree before accepting a claim.
when: several witnesses give overlapping accounts
why: each factor independently affects how much a claim can be trusted

text: Evidence gained by watching or listening unseen can confirm a suspicion that a direct question would alert the target to.
when: a target would react to being asked
why: Concealment keeps the target's behavior natural.

text: Do not dismiss a late account as false merely because it came late.
why: Delay alone does not show deception.

text: Treat a statement cut off before its key point as an open question to return to, not as a closed fact.
The person who knows the suspect best may be first to see through a display of feeling, so track their reactions.
Let an unreliable witness contradict themselves later, so attentive players can detect the problem by comparing statements.
when: Designing a witness whose reliability should be discoverable

text: Keep a witness's report in reserve as intelligence to use later when it becomes relevant.
when: A report is incomplete or does not yet bear on the case.
why: Early reports can gain value as other facts emerge.

text: A damaged document can make one answer unreadable, leaving the player to infer it from context and other testimony.
when: designing partially legible evidence
why: Inference rewards cross-referencing sources.

text: Use distance from neighbours and public roads as a parameter for how likely a crime in the world is to be noticed.
when: When generating locations where crimes or hidden events may occur
why: Proximity to witnesses and authority controls detection likelihood.

text: A witness NPC present during dialogue can act as a verifier whose confirmation unlocks a claim the player cannot confirm alone.
Tie a witness's reluctance to a specific stake, such as a job or debt, that a later player choice can remove.
Let an NPC react visibly to an unseen threat before players learn its source, so the threat is felt before it is shown.
when: When a threat will be revealed later in the level
why: Visible reactions create dread without explanation

text: Give characters a sore-spot trait that determines which accusation provokes anger, so the same claim lands differently on each NPC.
Tie any lie-detection cue to checkable world state rather than NPC animation or voice tone, which players can learn to exploit.
when: Designing a lie-detection mechanic
why: Demeanour cues are easy to exploit

text: Before assigning an order to a suspect, check who could have heard it, since a witness's expected reaction can rule them out.
why: Someone who heard an order would have reacted to it.

text: Seek a second witness who reports the same fact from a different angle, and note what that witness did not say.
when: Verifying a witness statement.
why: Independent angles and omissions reveal more than repetition.

text: A complete account that stays the same across retellings is treated as a sign of truthfulness, even when the teller's motive is doubted.
when: Judging a witness or suspect's account
why: Consistency is hard to fake across repeated tellings.

text: Keep an event log with timestamps from different NPCs so players can spot where two accounts of the same events disagree.
when: Designing NPC accounts of shared events

text: Two characters who repeat each other can be built as a trap when they share a motive, so the player must check whether their accounts are linked.
when: Designing paired NPC witnesses.
why: Apparent corroboration hides a common interest that the player must uncover.

text: Ask a concealing witness what they fear and address any fear of retaliation before asking for cooperation, since fear often explains refusal.
when: A witness's cooperation becomes selective.
why: Fear makes witnesses hesitant to testify and often explains the refusal.

text: Attach a reliability value to each NPC's information and let players check it against a second source before acting on it.
Give each NPC statement a reliability level; intoxicated or frightened NPCs give vague or contradictory directions while sober ones are precise, so let statements conflict for cross-checking.
when: Designing NPC dialogue for investigation or directions.
why: Witness state changes the precision and consistency of what they report; cross-checking against physical clues tests conflicting statements.

text: Separate a witness's firsthand observations from impressions and feelings about a person; trust concrete, testable facts such as clothing or arrival time over sympathetic opinions.
when: When a witness is emotional, gives opinions, or is invested in the person described.
why: Sincere emotion can distort details; emotional investment makes descriptions more favorable than the evidence supports.

text: Weigh a sighting by the witness's prior familiarity with the person; a witness who never knew them gives weak identification and should not anchor a timeline.
when: A key identification or last-seen timeline depends on a witness who may not have known the person.
why: Without prior knowledge, the witness cannot distinguish the person from look-alikes, so an unfamiliar witness may misidentify them.

text: A hostile dismissal of a frightened witness can make her seem more sincere to the audience, since her fear is visibly real.
when: Writing a suspect who shuts down a witness
why: Audiences read hostility toward a weak accuser as a sign that the accuser may be right

text: Let NPCs give conflicting accounts of one figure, each shaped by their own interests or vantage point.
when: Designing a mystery around a disputed figure
why: Conflicting accounts push the player to weigh sources.

text: A witness can be friendly and detailed yet still know nothing past a certain date, so check each account's coverage window before relying on it.
when: Interviewing a witness who knew the subject only for part of their history
why: Detail and friendliness do not extend knowledge beyond the time the witness actually had contact

text: Treat an exaggerating witness's claims as unverified until corroborated, even if the room accepts them as entertainment.
when: A witness boasts or exaggerates in front of others.
why: Exaggeration makes testimony unreliable though it may hide real clues.

text: Test a source's claim of insider knowledge by weighing what only insiders could know, such as a private confidence or a spouse's jealousy.
when: when a masked or anonymous speaker claims special knowledge
why: Private details are hard to fake and reveal whether the claim is credible.

text: Show each rival expert's reasoning so a dispute reads as a genuine disagreement rather than simple ridicule.
when: Two experts disagree on a cause.
why: Visible reasoning lets the audience judge each expert's trustworthiness.

text: Make an informant useful but self-interested, so that their testimony is shaped by a secret they are protecting and must be checked against documents.
when: Designing witnesses who hold partial truths.
why: A biased source gives real information while keeping the player doubting its completeness.

text: Vivid observations are hard to fake but still subjective, so they support a claim without proving it.
A witness can be accurate about some details and wrong about others, so judge each claim separately rather than discarding or accepting the whole account.
when: Evaluating a witness whose testimony mixes reliable and unreliable claims
why: Reliability varies across different parts of an account

text: A witness's own slip, such as glancing toward a family, can draw suspicion onto that family, so the slip should be noticed and its effect weighed.
when: When a witness's unguarded movement is seen by an audience
why: Observers attach significance to small involuntary actions.

text: Place a watcher with a non-committal expression in the crowd to hint that they know more than they show.
when: Staging a reveal where an informed character should be signalled without being exposed.
why: A subtle cue invites the player to suspect the watcher without confirming it.

text: Do not treat a witness's claim as proof until a physical record confirms it, such as a sketch or journal that shows only scribbles.
when: A character's account rests on a record that proves less than claimed.
why: Subjective impressions can exceed what the physical record supports.

text: Reliability rests on consistency of central facts and on the witness's manner, not on polish. Peripheral details may shift across retellings while the core stays stable.
when: Weighing a witness whose retellings vary
why: Stable central memory is a better reliability sign than uniform wording

text: Let a disguised character act as a witness, and reveal the impersonation later as a second-phase confrontation with the culprit.
when: a key witness is missing or unreliable
why: A later reveal recasts earlier testimony and raises the stakes of the final confrontation.

text: Test a witness's professed neutrality against what they gain from each outcome, since a neutral stance can hide a lean toward one side.
when: A witness claims impartiality while an undisclosed gain depends on the outcome
why: Financial or other interest can shape influence even when the stated stance sounds reasonable

text: Read a witness's physical signs, such as tiredness, colouring or steady eyes, as clues to their state, but treat them as support for judgement, not as facts about events.
when: when assessing an upset or exhausted witness
why: Body signals reflect condition but do not confirm what happened.

text: Stage a reproduction in front of sceptical witnesses so its outcome cannot be dismissed as luck or staging.
when: A test is meant to prove a hidden mechanism
why: A sceptic's presence makes success harder to explain away.

text: Let a dying witness speak the largest secret, so a single scene delivers a major reveal.
Let a witness's mistaken sighting count as a clue that is dismissed at first and later proves to be a key fact.
when: A witness reports something the characters initially reject.
why: Dismissed testimony stays in the reader's memory and gains weight when the reveal returns to it.

text: Explain a fabricated name or detail with a real object in the world, such as a printed title or label, so the discovery feels earned.
why: The reveal then feels grounded rather than arbitrary

text: Discredit the witness before the reveal, so the audience is unsure whose account to trust when the testimony arrives.
Let a character's vision or testimony be accurate but leave its source unexplained, so the player must weigh its reliability.
when: A character reports something the player cannot verify.
why: Unverified but accurate testimony keeps the player uncertain about the character's sanity or insight.

text: NPC answers can depend on whether a cover story is believed, so each persona needs a backstory that holds under light townsfolk questioning.
when: Designing disguises, infiltrator NPCs, or a false persona or pretext.
why: Light questioning is how players are most likely to probe a cover.

text: A witness's reputation changes how much weight a listener gives their word, so a discredited witness may be dismissed whatever the truth of the account.
A hypnotised subject can only reflect what the operator already believes, so apparent insight traces back to the operator.
Evidence relayed through several people is filtered at each step, so its reliability depends on who speaks, who translates and who has a stake.
when: An account reaches the player through intermediaries
why: Each relay can lose core facts or add bias

text: NPC dialogue can let enemies discredit witnesses in advance, so the player must find evidence that cannot be explained away.
When one impression lies over another, the mark on top was made later, so overlapping marks reveal the order of events.
when: When soft ground records impressions that overlap.
why: Physical layering preserves temporal order.

text: Pressure on an emotional NPC can make its dialogue volatile and reveal hidden knowledge, while calmer tone options keep the conversation on track.
Multiple NPCs giving slightly different versions of an event let the player cross-check and rank their accounts.
when: designing an event witnessed by several NPCs
why: variation gives the player material to test and compare

text: If NPC decision-makers weigh different factors, such as manner, physical proof or grudges, identical evidence can produce different verdicts.
when: Designing a tribunal or jury system in a game.

text: NPC witnesses can carry confidence levels, so 'I think it was him' sounds different from 'I saw his face.'
when: designing NPC testimony
why: graded confidence tells the player how much weight to give a claim

text: A timed answer system that causes details to be forgotten under pressure models hurried recall and rewards slower, careful questioning.
A witness hidden behind a locked door who overhears an interview reframes earlier pressure as a setup when revealed at the end.
A single rumour can gain a new name with each retelling, until a whole faction turns against one character.
Reporting a remark to rivals can change factional trust and set a conflict in motion between the speaker and the reporter's opponents.
when: When a character passes a private remark to an opposing group.
why: Rivals react to the content, altering alliances.

text: When a claim says an unseen agent acted regardless of location, no alibi, distance or good character can rebut it.
when: A witness reports harm by an agent only the accuser perceives.
why: The claim is defined so that no ordinary evidence can contradict it.

text: A vendor can recognise an NPC face shown from a portrait or poster, so a canvassing mechanic can link a purchased object to a character.
when: When designing a canvass or shop-inquiry mechanic.
why: Vendors remember customers' faces, letting players connect objects to people.
