text: Each false statement adds a new fact that must be defended, so a lie made to explain one anomaly increases the chances of exposure.
when: A person maintains a deception to cover an anomaly.
why: Every added claim creates another point at which the story can be contradicted.

text: A witness afraid of trouble may change their story, so their account must be weighed against their motive to protect themselves.
when: When a witness faces possible consequences.
why: Self-protection motivates altered testimony.

text: Players who cross-check NPC accounts against each other and against their own observations can reach conclusions the game never states directly.
when: When a game presents several conflicting NPC accounts.
why: Comparison across sources yields inferences that no single source provides.

text: An echo copies the listener's own rhythm, so footsteps that pause or change tempo independently argue against a simple echo.
when: Judging whether a sound is an echo.
why: An echo can only reproduce what was made, so independent timing reveals another source.

text: A claim resting only on a dead person's word cannot be checked, so it stays weak evidence even when stated with certainty.
when: Evaluating a testimony whose only source is unavailable.
why: Without a living or recorded source, the claim has nothing to be tested against.

text: When testimony is too vague to link a suspect to the event, the investigation can end without a finding of responsibility.
when: when the available accounts cannot connect a person to the act
why: Without a link between person and act, the case cannot reach a conclusion.

text: A dying character's ambiguous late remark can reopen an answer the player believed settled, adding doubt without new proof.
when: when a settled answer needs a late jolt
why: ambiguity invites reinterpretation of earlier evidence

text: Witnesses' confident accounts can supply a false culprit; a mystery can use their testimony as the misdirect and reread the scene to expose it.
when: A crime where several observers describe an intruder
why: Confident group testimony is accepted as evidence, so the false culprit persists until the setting is reinterpreted.

text: Cooperative subjects may guess what the questioner wants and confirm it; eager agreement or cued reactions can reflect politeness rather than real memory, and they may accept suggested identifications.
when: interpreting reactions to cues, or a witness seems eager to help or agrees after being shown material
why: People respond to perceived expectations and want to please questioners, not only to memory.

text: Accepting a witness's moral judgments as facts, or ignoring an inconvenient account because its source is biased, both corrupt the evidence base.
why: Verdicts are opinion, and discarding inconvenient testimony hides real evidence.

text: Sustained pressure or a tense questioner pushes witnesses toward answers that end questioning or please the questioner, making their statements unreliable.
when: under sustained pressure or when pressing a witness for specific answers
why: distress favours quick answers, and pressure pushes witnesses toward what the questioner wants to hear

text: Sincerity does not establish accuracy: honest witnesses can be wrong or partial, and an honest-looking account can still hide a puzzle.
when: evaluating any testimony
why: Sincerity and accuracy are separate properties.

text: Confident judgement from a witness outside their competence, such as physical ability or a non-expert's opinion, is a guess to check, not evidence.
why: Confidence does not turn a guess into evidence.

text: Speech recalled from a stressful moment or an overheard confession is only as reliable as the witness's exact memory; a key phrase may be misremembered.
when: Relying on an overheard admission as evidence
why: Memory of spoken words is imperfect and can be disputed.

text: Confirmations extracted after a fact is stated, or accounts shaped for a witness, may be repeated unchecked; treat them as leads to check against independent evidence.
why: Witnesses may agree to end pressure, and shaped accounts replace observation.

text: A mismatch does not prove fakery: an honest witness whose account conflicts with a suspect's can be suspected, and honest interests can look like camouflage.
when: when accounts are compared
why: Suspicion spreads to whoever does not fit, and a mismatch alone does not prove one fact is fake.

text: Rewards or pardons offered for testimony can shape accounts toward the incentive and encourage invented detail; tag such testimony as motivated.
when: a witness gains from testifying
why: incentives distort recall and reporting

text: A witness who is overwhelmed or unwilling can leave the room, creating gaps in the record that later testimony cannot fill.
A witness who carried out instructions faithfully can be honest and still wrong about what those instructions actually did.
A witness drawn in by a wager can be overconfident, so every fact he states should be checked against the records.
A witness recovering from stupor or shock may give no usable timeline at first, so their sense of time should not be trusted early.
Routine checks can confirm the wrong story when each source is asked only about its own record.
A witness with a motive to hurt the accused is easy to dismiss, which can hide real facts within their account.
An identification made under pressure or suggestion can be wrong, so a later denial should not be dismissed merely because it came later.
when: Assessing a witness who has identified or refused to identify a suspect.
why: Suggestion and pressure distort memory, so either the identification or its denial may be unreliable.

text: Cross-examination can shift a witness's timeline, such as a medical estimate of time of death, creating doubt without any new fact.
when: when questioning focuses on exact times or details
why: pressure on details can produce apparent inconsistency

text: Counting everyone who saw a routine as a suspect, without evidence that they acted on it, inflates the suspect list.
Relying on a routine examination to rule out a hidden cause, or treating a natural death as settled before checking small signs, misses concealed causes.
Witnesses who testify in a hurry tend to tangle their accounts further, adding conflicts rather than clarity.
when: A witness is rushed or pressed to answer quickly

text: A concealed witness may be the culprit, so readers may suspect the helper too late for a reversal to land.
Stating a claim with more precision than the evidence supports can reveal the investigator's mistake to the suspect.
why: A suspect may recognize an overly specific claim as wrong.

text: Interrogating an innocent but uninformed witness for information can mislead, since they can only offer inference.
when: when a witness lacks direct knowledge
why: their answers reflect guesswork

text: Dramatic retellings tend to grow in the telling, so compare them against what the teller could actually have seen.
why: Each retelling adds detail the original source never had

text: Witnesses can differ in how much of a condition they really observed, so confirm each person's view separately.
when: Several witnesses describe the same object
why: Confident accounts may rest on partial observation

text: A plausible identification, such as matching a figure to a known person, can take an investigator far from the truth if unchecked.
when: An identification rests on a partial view or resemblance.
why: Investigators tend to stop testing a conclusion once it seems to fit.

text: Trusting a first-person account written after the fact is risky, because its author controls which events appear.
why: Selection by the author can remove key events without any false statement.

text: A guarded witness may withhold the core fact at first, so early accounts are partial and should not be treated as complete.
when: Initial questioning of a guarded witness.
why: Core facts are often hidden until trust develops.

text: A confirmed return time does not prove the earlier part of the account, which needs its own checks.
Impressions formed after the fact are unreliable, so observer agreement should be checked before it carries weight.
An account repeated to others before it is tested hardens into apparent fact, making later verification harder.
when: A witness shares an unverified claim with people who will repeat it.
why: Repetition gives an untested claim the look of corroboration.

text: Pressing too hard can close a witness down, leaving answers at blanket denials until questions reach a painful subject.
when: An investigator keeps pushing a defensive witness on the same line.
why: Sustained pressure raises defensiveness, so the witness stops offering anything new.

text: Overstating a trivial remark before corroboration can mislead the reader or investigator into a false conclusion.
Vague times and generic descriptions from one witness, such as shortish or a mustache, cannot identify anyone alone and need a second source.
Attacking minor points can look like quibbling and distract from the central claim, which is the one that needs testing.
Do not assume a witness's account is spontaneous or truthful when the witness was chosen and briefed by someone with an interest in the outcome.
why: A chosen witness can serve the briefing party's timeline rather than the truth.

text: Do not treat a confession as settled when the speaker is feverish, exhausted, or defending a theory of their own.
A witness who is both pitiable and unreliable can make the audience trust emotion over verifiable facts; keep the two apart.
An adult's casual dismissal of a witness's report can close a question prematurely, so the report should be weighed on its own terms.
A secondhand report written years later may describe a different place or time than the event it claims to describe.
Testimony given under fear or relief may be incomplete, skewed and dramatised, so it should be checked against other evidence.
why: Strong emotion distorts memory and attention and shapes how the witness tells the account.

text: Quantity of detail is not proof of accuracy; rehearsed or fluent accounts can be highly detailed without firsthand knowledge or checking.
when: A witness gives a long, elaborate, confident account.
why: Detail reflects rehearsal as well as genuine observation, and volume and fluency feel like reliability.

text: Testimony from a witness loyal to a suspect, such as a close associate or trusted manager, is hard to assess and may be coloured by that loyalty.
when: When a witness has a clear interest in protecting a suspect.
why: Loyalty and interest distort judgment and can lead an investigator to discount conflicting evidence.

text: Drunk or agitated witnesses often misremember distances and durations, and alcohol distorts both speech and recall, so timing claims need checking.
when: When a witness is drunk, agitated or talking over drink.
why: Intoxication lowers the reliability of both speech and memory.

text: Children's testimony against a family member, given under pressure, is unreliable evidence and should be weighed with great caution.
when: When children are questioned in a charged case against a parent.
why: Pressure can shape what children say.

text: Motive claims often arrive with reliability attacks in the same breath, so test each claim separately rather than letting one carry the other.
A sincere alibi can still be wrong, and trust in the source is not evidence of the fact.
when: When evaluating an alibi from a trusted or sincere witness
why: Belief reflects the witness's confidence, not the event itself.

text: Pious or formal phrasing can make a troubling conclusion sound acceptable, so look past the wording to the claim it carries.
why: Tone can disguise an idea that would be questioned if stated plainly

text: Treating an angry or distressed remark as a confession without knowing the question that prompted it.
when: A remark is made during questioning or after a dispute
why: The prompt often determines what the words mean

text: Remarks recalled after an event can be reshaped to fit it, so they are weak evidence of prior intent.
A writer who admits bias can still steer an account through what they choose to stress.
Agreement among accusers who describe the same vision can come from shared fear or shared expectation, so it must be checked rather than read as independence.
Elimination reasoning fails if the starting state is misremembered, because the excluded agents depend on an accurate baseline.
when: Reasoning from a remembered earlier state.
why: A wrong baseline breaks the chain of exclusions.

text: A witness's sincere belief that no one could have guessed a secret does not rule out a leak.
A test seems valid when it sometimes gives the expected result, but occasional agreement does not establish that it is reliable.
when: when evaluating a test or puzzle mechanic

text: Crowded scenes with weeping, knocked-over furniture and fleeing people distort observation and make accurate recording harder.
A character's known habits often come from other people's accounts rather than measurement, so a baseline built on testimony is only as reliable as those accounts.
why: habit claims are themselves unverified

text: Confident recognition can be wrong, especially when suspicion colours the memory.
when: A person believes they recognise someone and suspects them.
why: Suspicion biases memory toward confirming the suspicion.

text: Discarding a whole account after one falsehood can throw away its true parts. Check each part separately before deciding what to keep.
when: A single claim in an account is shown to be false.
why: One false claim does not make every claim false.

text: A witness's guess about nationality or language, drawn from accent, should not be treated as fact.
when: A witness infers a person's origin from speech.
why: Accent-based inference is unreliable and easily wrong.

text: A witness who swears that an event was impossible is making an inference, not reporting an observation, and the inference needs checking.
A witness who says they just got an impression may be right, or may be recalling what they expected to hear.
An NPC witness can report an event at the wrong hour or from the wrong door, so the player must reconcile its report with other sources.
when: an NPC reports events it observed
why: NPC perception and recall can be incomplete or wrong

text: Treating a delirious accusation as fact, or dismissing a witness as simply mad, misreads what the words show; judge the content over the label.
when: Weighing testimony from a feverish or disturbed character.
why: Such speech shows inner fear, so it is neither proof of events nor noise; dismissing it can hide real information.

text: A witness who glimpsed someone in passing may be wrong about the person or the day.
when: The identification rests on a brief or incidental sighting.
why: Brief observation gives little opportunity to confirm identity or date.

text: Dismissing a witness's account too quickly can hide the real physical evidence.
when: Investigators weigh a witness's testimony against other explanations.
why: Premature dismissal stops the search for corroborating traces.

text: A witness may be sure a route was clear only because nothing happened in front of them; test such claims against timing.
Telling a witness they are wrong can talk them out of a correct observation.
when: A witness has just made a valid identification
why: Discouragement can override a sound memory.

text: An unclear sighting in fog can be dismissed as imagination without a record, so the observation is lost.
when: Encountering an ambiguous visual event
why: Without a written note, the unclear observation cannot be compared with later evidence.

text: Accepting a witness's claim of prior ignorance without checking can mislead, since people may not recognize their own exposure to a subject.
A confident witness can be certain of a wrong detail, so confidence is not evidence of accuracy.
when: when assessing a witness's firmly stated claim
why: Certainty reflects the witness's manner, not whether the observation was correct.

text: Verified details lend credibility to unverified claims only by association, and the investigator must note this.
when: Some of a witness's claims are confirmed and others are not.
why: Confirmed facts can make unconfirmed claims seem reliable without justification.

text: A witness left uncross-examined is not thereby believed; silence may reflect a tactical choice rather than acceptance.
when: When evaluating testimony that went unquestioned.
why: Lack of challenge may be strategic and does not confirm the account.

text: A confident explainer who claims to know the victim's inner thoughts may be trusted too easily, even when nothing is corroborated.
when: Someone offers an explanation with unusual certainty about another person's mind
why: Apparent insight into a person's thoughts is mistaken for reliability

text: A frank, practised performance can read as honest at first and then as deceptive once contradictions appear, so players may swing their trust sharply.
when: a suspect's story is delivered with confidence
why: Confident delivery is ambiguous, and each contradiction flips the reading of earlier statements.

text: A claim that cannot be checked is treated as unreliable by default, so the audience may dismiss it unless concrete details are given.
when: A story depends on an unverifiable source to move the plot.
why: Without testable details the audience has no basis to trust the source.

text: 1) Pick a concrete, checkable detail in the account, such as a garment or a number. 2) Find an independent object from the same period. 3) Compare the detail with the object.
when: a witness gives a specific detail and an object survives

text: 1) Open with yes-or-no prompts to settle the witness. 2) Ask open questions about the event. 3) Have key terms defined in the witness's own words. 4) Repeat any surprising question to check the answer. 5) Record pauses, tone and phrasing changes.
when: Interviewing a witness whose recall is impaired by a trance, fever or similar state.
why: Staged prompts reduce confusion and make replies comparable across attempts.

text: 1) Record each witness's account as points: what they saw, when, what they did, and what they could not swear to. 2) Keep the firm claims and the uncertain claims in separate lists.

1) Choose a hiding spot with sightlines over the likely return point, ideally covering two approaches. 2) Stay hidden and wait until the subject arrives. 3) Approach the subject by a route they can see.
when: when a person is likely to return to a place to finish an action

text: 1) Repeat the witness's own phrases back to them. 2) Pose a hypothetical about their intent instead of naming a crime. 3) Reverse a sentence's form to test for automatic agreement. 4) Add one unexpected provocation to test the reaction. 5) Stay quiet and still so they keep talking.
when: Witness is intoxicated, drowsy, evasive or hard to reach, and the questioner can stay with them over time.

text: 1) Predict a suspect's behaviour from observed habits. 2) Ask an independent witness. 3) Compare the answer with the suspect's claim.
1) Restore the witness's composure before questioning. 2) Ask for the account as an ordered sequence, without interruption. 3) Ask targeted questions only after the narrative is complete.
when: when the witness is agitated and an ordered account is needed
why: A calmer witness gives a clearer timeline, and the investigator keeps details that interruption would lose.

text: 1) Identify the specific loss the witness fears. 2) Find who can waive it. 3) Obtain a signed guarantee against that loss. 4) Present it and state your belief in the witness's innocence.
when: a witness's silence rests on fear of a specific loss
why: a guarantee that removes the fear can make the witness speak

text: 1) Split the witness statement into separate claims such as names, appearance, times and actions. 2) Check each claim against independent evidence. 3) Accept or reject each claim on its own result.
when: a witness gives several details of different kinds
why: claims of different kinds can have different reliability

text: 1) Hold back specific facts. 2) Ask broad questions first. 3) Narrow them to times, places and objects. 4) Have the suspect commit to exact claims. 5) Check each claim against evidence.
when: when a suspect's account can be tested
why: committed specific claims can be proven false later

text: 1) Identify a distinguishing physical feature the witness noticed. 2) Ask the witness to specify it exactly. 3) Have the witness commit to that specific answer.
when: When a witness's identification must be precise.
why: Forcing a precise answer exposes vague or invented claims.

text: 1) List the physical traces the claimed event should leave. 2) Work out where each would land from the actor's position. 3) Inspect those spots. 4) Schedule any check that needs time.
when: A witness describes physical events that leave traces
why: Physical traces can confirm or contradict a witness's account.

text: 1) Restate a vague answer as a specific figure, such as a distance or time. 2) Ask the witness to confirm or correct it. 3) Note any claim that cannot be checked.
when: questioning a witness who answers loosely
why: Specific figures expose inconsistencies that vague answers hide.

text: 1) Collect time-stamped reports from each observer. 2) Lay them on one timeline, interval by interval. 3) Mark who was out of sight at the critical moment.
when: The crime window is narrow and observers cover overlapping views
why: Overlaying reports shows who could not have seen the event

text: 1) Establish a witness's regular pattern, such as meetings or visits, as a baseline. 2) Ask independent witnesses to confirm each element of it. 3) Compare the accounts for agreement.
when: when a witness describes a regular routine
why: independent confirmation tests a single account

text: 1) Ask direct questions about the witness's relationship to the victim and about the critical time. 2) Accept the first account only as a hypothesis. 3) Check specific details independently. 4) Record which claims are verified.
when: A witness gives a timeline covering the critical window
why: Initial belief must be tested before it is relied on

text: 1) Check the witness's claims against other evidence and records. 2) Note the witness's stake, bias and reasons to justify themselves. 3) Test the wording for a contradiction hidden inside a passage.
when: A witness's account is self-justifying, the witness had something to gain, or a private account conflicts with public records
why: Self-interest and loose wording can make an account look reliable when it is not

text: 1) Collect each earlier written or recorded statement by the suspect. 2) Compare them with later statements. 3) Reuse them only as recorded, and flag any contradictions.
when: when a suspect's account changes across sessions
why: earlier statements can be reused in later sessions, so their accuracy matters

text: 1) Reconstruct the time a witness claims. 2) Reproduce the event under the same conditions. 3) Check whether the witness could have heard or seen it from where they were.
when: a witness's account of time conflicts with the physical setting
why: the setting limits what can be perceived from a given place

text: 1) Identify the alibi's sole link, usually one witness's statement. 2) Re-question that witness, possibly with a different investigator. 3) Apply pressure or a counter-threat. 4) Check whether the testimony changes.
when: When a suspect's alibi rests on one witness who may have a reason to lie
why: Pressure on a weak link can produce a changed account that exposes a false alibi.

text: 1) Record every account and what each witness saw or did not see. 2) Compare accounts and note contradictions and their reasons. 3) Note what a witness chose not to report and why. 4) Test each account against physical traces. 5) Ask neutral follow-up questions checking accounts against evidence.
when: Several people share one event and their accounts must be reconciled.
why: Comparison separates reliable details from errors, distortion or influence; physical evidence and probing questions separate accurate reports from mistaken ones.

text: 1) Remove unnecessary people from the room. 2) Limit listeners to those whose presence serves the goal. 3) Speak with the informant alone when they will reveal more without others present.
when: When an investigator needs a candid account from a witness.
why: Controlling the room controls who the witness will speak to freely.

text: 1) Stage an ordinary-looking role, such as a disguise, that asks the suspect for a short written reply. 2) Collect the reply. 3) Compare it with the original document's distinctive features. 4) Accept the link only if several features agree.
when: A suspect's written link to a document must be verified without alerting them
why: A controlled test produces comparable evidence while staying inconspicuous

text: 1) Collect each firsthand account. 2) Collect secondhand accounts of the same person. 3) Compare each against the firsthand record and against each other.
when: Several witnesses describe the same person or event.
why: Secondhand reports can carry the observer's guesses rather than the subject's facts.

text: 1) Ask about details that are hard to fake and rarely noticed. 2) Compare the witness's answers with what was actually observed. 3) Note the gap between confident claims and detailed recall.
when: Testing whether a confident identification rests on real observation.
why: Unnoticed details expose assumptions that the witness did not actually check.

text: 1) Treat each statement as a claim. 2) Check it against documents, physical traces, and other witnesses. 3) Accept it only if it survives the cross-check; reconcile any contradictions before relying on it.
when: Weighing statements that may conflict or come from people with a motive.
why: Statements that have not been tested against independent sources can be wrong or self-serving.

text: Give each witness one precise, checkable detail, such as a ring or a clock chime, that can be matched against other clues.
why: A distinctive detail becomes a usable identifier or timing anchor.

text: Give witness NPCs an age, a role and a list of acts they can attest to, so players can weigh each account.
when: when creating NPC witnesses
why: shared attributes make accounts comparable

text: Have NPC reports state their basis (saw, heard, or deduced) so players can weigh each claim.
when: designing NPC testimony
why: Stated sources let players judge reliability

text: Give NPC witnesses a bias value that shifts with their relationship to the player and their emotional state, so their statements vary.
when: designing NPC testimony

text: Check whether anything observed about a person contradicts their claimed routine or availability.
Do not rely on a shaken or frightened witness's account; distress, fear, shielding someone or betraying a confidence can distort what they say even when sincere.
Track NPC reputation separately from claim accuracy, so the player can see when trust is doing the work instead of evidence.
Do not treat answers from an impaired or altered-state witness as verified fact; hold them until independent checks confirm them and note the limit in the record.
when: A witness's recall or judgment is impaired by altered state or a possible physical cause.
why: Such answers reflect the witness's view, can be shaped by questioning, and cannot confirm or rule out events.

text: Do not rely on a witness's account or its specific details until they are checked against independent accounts or physical evidence.
when: Testimony is the main basis for a conclusion, or one witness supplies a specific fact that will drive the investigation.
why: Testimony can be incomplete, biased or misremembered and needs corroboration.

text: Treat facts that a suspect or NPC volunteers, or supplies as the only source, as unverified until an outside source confirms them, and weigh why the source offered them.
when: A suspect or NPC volunteers unrequested information, or is the only source for a fact.
why: Accepting offered facts at face value can send the investigator down the wrong path.

text: Show a narrator's blind spots openly, and include later corrections that reveal what an earlier account shielded, so readers can weigh the witness against the investigator's reading.
when: A narrator reports a scene the investigator reads differently, or a narrator's statement is partial.
why: Otherwise readers may doubt the investigator rather than the witness, and later corrections let them verify claims.

text: Question even helpful witnesses about unobserved gaps, checking the timing of sightings as well as the count, since a few seconds is enough to slip away and rejoin.
when: Testing who could have moved unseen between two points.
why: Cooperation does not remove unobserved gaps, and counts alone miss short windows.

text: Give NPC witnesses varying reliability through conditions or bias, such as drowsy, drunk, frightened, prejudiced or a confident noble, so players must cross-check their statements.
when: Designing NPC testimony.
why: A conditioned or biased witness is less reliable and should not be taken at face value.

text: Make some NPC witnesses unreliable or only partly accurate, giving partial or conflicting details that players must cross-check or confirm before acting.
when: Authoring NPC testimony for a mystery.
why: Partial reliability makes verification a required step.

text: Limit each NPC's account to its own vantage point, giving partial or conflicting information, so players must assemble the truth from several partial logs.
when: Designing several NPCs who saw the same event.
why: Vantage-based variation makes cross-checking necessary.

text: For an event that will be publicly doubted, choose witnesses with standing and wait for them to be present before acting.
when: An event's account will face public disbelief.
why: Credible witnesses give the account weight.

text: Question a child carefully, since leading questions can draw out details but can also shape the answer.
when: interviewing a minor

text: Do not accept an unnamed or unlocated witness as proof; rate their account with low credibility.
when: a sighting cannot be traced to a named person
why: An untraceable source cannot be checked.

text: Take a cooperative witness's full account at the first meeting, while they are willing, rather than planning to return for the rest.
when: the witness is cooperative and holds partial knowledge
why: Willingness can end, and a return visit may yield much less.

text: Vary a gatekeeper NPC's refusal wording so it reflects the reason behind the refusal, rather than repeating identical lines.
when: A gatekeeper NPC refuses the player more than once.
why: Varied wording gives the player a signal about the underlying motive.

text: Store each NPC's exact words and what it actually saw, so later contradictions can be checked against the record.
when: Designing NPC testimony in a game

text: Do not rely on a witness who only repeats one explanation; move on to someone who engages with details.
why: Repeated explanations add no new information

text: Keep atmospheric description purposeful; each detail should carry information or tension, since long passages slow the scene.
when: When writing scene descriptions.

text: Offer a feigned-disinterest dialogue option that unlocks more detail from talkative NPCs.
Compare accounts from several witnesses; when they describe the same strange effect in similar terms, a common cause is likely.
when: Several accounts cover the same event
why: Shared descriptions point to one source

text: Let NPC witnesses state a confidence level with a reason, and let the player's follow-up question change what they say.
when: designing NPC testimony in dialogue
why: confidence and reasons make testimony feel earned and revisable

text: Check each witness answer against the question actually asked, since witnesses sometimes answer a different question.
when: Interviews about access or timing
why: An answer to an unasked question can seem relevant while leaving the real question open

text: Place a witness in hiding beside the action, so the audience learns events through a limited, close view.
when: When a scene needs tension and must be seen through one character's limited view.
why: A close, restricted view keeps the audience uncertain.

text: Give an NPC who offers a theory a motive for steering the player, so players learn to question sources.
when: Writing NPCs who suggest explanations
why: Players must weigh a suggestion by its origin

text: Let an NPC's stated opinion be wrong, and reward the player for checking it against other evidence.
when: When an NPC gives a verdict or interpretation of events
why: Checking opinion against observation teaches the player to separate conclusions from facts.

text: Ask every witness the same yes-or-no question and compare answers, giving no visible reaction to any reply.
Observe a group from a concealed recess with a view of its entrance and stairs, learning its structure without entering the room.
when: You need to learn who meets and how members are admitted without contact.
why: Watching arrivals reveals structure without risking exposure through entry.

text: Give guard or townsfolk NPCs a memory of a player or suspect, tied to a world event the player also witnessed.
Vary NPC witness descriptions by lighting, distance and observation time so the player must weigh each account.
when: designing witness dialogue
why: Differing conditions make accounts differ in detail and trust.

text: Start questioning from what the witness actually perceived, separating features they saw, such as clothing and build, from features they never saw, such as the face.
when: the witness had a partial view
why: Claims should match the observation actually made.

text: Let a pressured or bargaining NPC give the player's next clue, and show the reason for their cooperation in the dialogue.
when: designing NPCs who reveal information under pressure
why: A visible motive makes the disclosure believable.

text: Unlock an NPC's recall of a fact only after a prompt, to model delayed memory.
when: Designing NPC memory in a mystery game.
why: Gated recall mirrors how real memory surfaces under prompting.

text: Give each witness request a different category of witness, so the player must decide which channels are worth their time.
Do not rely on an exact-detail comparison when the original is remembered only in general terms.
why: vague memory cannot reveal small differences

text: Give NPCs memories that cover only regulars, so a stranger is noticed only when the player asks in the right way.
when: When designing NPC knowledge of the people in their environment
why: Selective memory makes investigation depend on precise questioning rather than general queries.

text: Generate a mix of true alibis, false but checkable alibis, and alibis resting on one witness with a motive to lie.
when: When designing a set of NPC alibis for a mystery
why: Mixed reliability keeps the player verifying claims rather than trusting them all equally.

text: Assign each witness NPC a reliability score and a set of statements, and flag any statement that conflicts with physical state for the player.
when: designing an NPC witness system
why: explicit reliability lets players weigh testimony against the world

text: Admit uncertainty openly and do not present a provisional premise as proven.
when: When presenting a deduction.
why: Keeps the reasoning honest and checkable.

text: Keep the identifying photograph hidden from other observers during a witness check so that official presence does not influence the witnesses' answers.
when: Running an identification with witnesses in the presence of other people.
why: Visible photos or observers' reactions can steer what witnesses report.

text: Let an NPC's account be checked against its earlier retellings, and let consistency across retellings raise the player's trust.
when: An NPC repeats information to the player over time
why: Stable retellings signal reliability and can be compared against the record.

text: Do not end questioning when a witness becomes difficult, since that removes the chance to test their story.
when: A witness's account changes or they become uncooperative.

text: Give NPC witnesses a reputation score, so honest, consistent witnesses are trusted even when they testify against the player.
Give NPC witnesses varying reliability, so their statements about a door or object may be wrong or self-serving.
Give NPC witnesses sight and hearing limits so players must cross-check what each one could actually perceive.
Let NPC dialogue sound threatening or mocking when it is routine, and reveal its real meaning later through another NPC or an object.
Check claims made during fits or claims to see hidden things before relying on them.
Assign reports a confidence value that drops for sightings made at range or relayed through rumour, and let it govern how much the report counts.
when: When the game models NPC or player witness reports.

text: Show players the last-seen times of NPCs so they can compare them against a process clock.
when: Designing investigation clues that depend on timing.
why: Players need the last-seen data to apply the process clock.

text: An NPC's response to a planted item can vary with its motive and knowledge, so quests should account for different responses.
when: Designing a quest where an NPC reacts to a planted item
why: Motive and knowledge drive different reactions

text: Let players catch NPCs in contradictions by comparing dialogue choices against items and other NPCs' statements, with lower reliability for impaired speakers.
when: designing NPC dialogue and clues
why: cross-checking statements rewards careful players

text: Let lights, silhouettes and routines act as sightings that players interpret, with explicit rules stating when a sighting counts as identification.
when: when designing observation-based clues
why: Players can reason from sightings only when identification rules are clear

text: Design an NPC's claimed shared past so a document or another NPC can confirm or contradict it.
when: an NPC claims a personal history with another character
why: Outside checks let players test the claim

text: Let a character pause while memory catches up instead of forcing an early identification.
when: recognition is partial and the character is still searching
why: A premature answer can lock in a wrong identity.

text: Give an impaired or tired NPC witness vague timings and uncorroborated sightings, and provide a physical trace the player can use to check them.
Give NPC witnesses a reliability score and known biases, and mark each of their claims as first-hand or rumour.
Place a silent NPC at a hidden exit so it records the player's return and can use that knowledge later.
Count two witnesses as corroboration only if they saw the same thing from the same place without collusion; crowd agreement that is only shared belief is not independent evidence.
when: When assessing whether two witnesses or a crowd support each other.
why: Shared motive, coordination or belief makes agreement worthless as corroboration.

text: Do not treat a witness's agreement as independent confirmation when they are simply accepting what they are told.
when: Evaluating a witness who responds with 'if you say so' or similar deference
why: Deferential agreement reflects the questioner's prompt, not the witness's memory

text: Make two in-world reports agree on mundane facts but differ on uncanny ones, so the designer controls how far the player can trust each.
when: Designing competing in-world reports.
why: Agreement on ordinary facts grounds trust, and disagreement on the uncanny tests it.

text: Let one NPC discredit another so the player must weigh competing accounts.
when: Designing conflicting testimony in a mystery
why: Conflict forces the player to evaluate sources rather than accept the first one

text: Trust the facts of strained testimony while discounting its tone, since distress changes how a witness speaks without changing what they saw.
Do not rely on one witness's sense of gender or identity when physical evidence contradicts it; weigh it against other evidence.
when: Witnesses disagree about a suspect's identity characteristics.
why: Perception of identity under stress is unreliable.

text: Do not accept a single informant's explanation of a hidden event until its claims about dates, people and places are checked against independent records.
when: A single informant is the only source of an account

text: When the protagonist's own memory is unreliable, source the decisive proof from an external record or witness rather than from their recollection.
when: The solver's memory conflicts with the truth
why: A mistaken memory cannot prove what happened, but an independent record can.

text: Show NPC reliability as a visible rating with factors like distance, light, motive or intoxication, or only via state like fright; ratings ease checking, state requires inference.
when: Designing NPC witness reliability.
why: Visible factors let the player judge trust; hidden state requires inference.

text: Hiding a body's face prevents identification but invites suspicion about why it was hidden, so concealment can backfire.
why: Deliberate concealment reads as a sign of intent

text: Witnesses present during a fit can attest only to the words and convulsions they saw, not to the unseen apparition the speaker described.
Give each NPC witness a different partial slice, such as a gesture, cloak color, or carried item, so players combine fragments and weigh them against physical traces.
when: Designing NPC testimony in a game.
why: Combining fragments makes the player reason toward identity rather than receive it; partial, conflicting knowledge makes players investigate instead of accepting one account.

text: A witness's independence depends on their actual views and conditions for taking part, not on the role they nominally hold.
why: Position alone does not show whether a witness holds a separate opinion

text: A witness may report who gave an instruction without knowing the identity of the instruction's author, so do not assume the witness saw the culprit.
when: relying on a witness account to identify a culprit
why: Witnesses often hear instructions without seeing the person behind them.

text: A witness is usually more reliable about her own actions and thoughts than about other people's motives or characters.
when: Weighing a witness's account

text: Record a witness's own limits, such as absences, scruples and reliance on others, when weighing how much of their account to trust.
Give witnesses two kinds of testimony: precise, cross-checkable facts and vague impressions that fit several suspects.
when: when designing NPC testimony for deduction
why: Precise facts allow verification, while vague impressions create ambiguity.

text: Witnesses at stations and on trains notice more than they intend, and their partial accounts combine into a picture of a pursuer's movements.
when: a pursuer moves through public places
why: incidental observers record details without knowing they matter

text: A sincere, accurate witness can still mislead, because a sighting records what happened in one moment and not why it happened.
when: A single confident witness anchors the case.
why: A sighting captures the event but not the motive or context behind it.

text: 1) Ask each witness what they remember exactly. 2) Ask whether they remember the gist or the exact words. 3) Record which parts they can vouch for and which they cannot.
when: when taking testimony about a conversation
why: a witness may vouch for only part of an account, and the gaps must be recorded

text: 1) Plant early a detail about the key object that reads as routine. 2) Present witness accounts that contradict each other on where a character went. 3) Make each account checkable against physical evidence. 4) Reveal the culprit when the contradictions are stacked.
when: Building a late-stage reveal in a mystery.
why: Checkable contradictions let the player reconstruct the truth themselves, and routine early details become meaningful in hindsight.

text: 1) Ask the witness to state their own position at the time of the event. 2) Ask who else was nearby and where objects were left. 3) Reconstruct the scene from the answers and check it against the evidence.
when: Building a reconstruction of an event from a witness's account.
why: A witness's own position and surroundings constrain what they could have seen or done.

text: Count a witness's observations as evidence only after separating them from inferences, labeling theories as opinion, and checking them against other accounts and tests.
when: Recording or weighing a witness statement.
why: Sincere witnesses can be wrong about cause, and keeping observation apart from opinion keeps testimony credible.

text: Keep a witness to what they actually witnessed, and do not let them draw others into the account or do the work of proof for the listener.
Treat a witness-only account as a lead to investigate, not as proof of guilt.
when: when the only evidence is a claim perceived by one person

text: Weigh a witness by what they directly saw, their perception conditions (distance, lighting, hearing, time precision), stake, prior feelings and past record before accepting.
when: when deciding how much to trust any eyewitness, witness or NPC report
why: Perception quality and motive shape what a witness reports, so raw testimony can mislead.

text: Weigh secondhand reports by what the speaker can know and why they would say it; rank sources by access and motive; intermediaries may sound pessimistic or confident from incomplete information.
when: when information comes through an intermediary or several witnesses describe the same person or event
why: Limited access, incomplete information and motive shape how secondhand claims are framed.

text: A witness's past run-in with the law can colour their caution, so weigh their reluctance with that history in mind.
List the possible sources of a witness's bias, such as outside pressure, prior prejudice and unclear evidence, so the audience can weigh the testimony.
when: when a witness's opinions shift sharply
why: Named sources let the audience discount the testimony accordingly.

text: Weigh a single witness against physical traces and other accounts, and discount a witness's identification when they seem stunned.
when: Several accounts or physical evidence conflict
why: Emotional state reduces the reliability of a single account

text: Weigh testimony by how well the witness recalls facts that matter and whether they flag what they do not know; admitted gaps can make a witness more trustworthy.
why: Honest acknowledgement of gaps signals careful reporting

text: Weigh a witness's account by their known temperament and reliability, then check it against independent facts before accepting it.
when: When accounts conflict or a claim needs support.
why: Reliability of the witness shapes how plausible a claim is, but independent verification is needed to confirm it.

text: Weigh an unconfirmed account by timing and consistency with other facts rather than by the witness's confidence alone.
when: a key witness account cannot be corroborated by another witness
why: Confidence does not measure accuracy, while timing can be checked against records.

text: Weigh a sworn account by the time elapsed since the event, the witness's age then, and the witness's stake in the outcome.
when: evaluating a deposition taken long after events
why: Time, age and interest all shape what a witness can reliably recall and report.

text: Do not discard a whole account because its teller is unreliable, and do not accept it whole either; separate usable facts from noise by corroboration rather than the witness's manner.
when: When evaluating an intoxicated, hostile or hearsay witness.
why: Corroboration is a more dependable test than how the witness behaves.

text: When two accounts conflict, a witness with a poor reputation for honesty or sobriety can be discounted in favour of the more credible account.
when: when testimonies contradict each other
why: reputation signals how far a witness's perception can be trusted

text: Dismissing a witness as mad can hide a real crime, so their account should be tested before being discounted.
when: A witness's account seems implausible.
why: A real event may be mistaken for delusion.

text: Accepting a witness's conclusion instead of the observed facts beneath it skips the evidence that actually supports or undermines it.
when: when a witness states a verdict such as 'it was murder'
why: The conclusion carries the witness's bias and may not follow from the observations.

text: 1) Note who gave the account and any stake. 2) Check whether they observed it directly and under what conditions. 3) Compare with other witnesses' accounts of the same moment. 4) Check any motive to shade the story. 5) Test each version against physical facts.
when: evaluating witness accounts of an event, especially when they disagree or an account is the only route to a crime
why: Testimony is weighed by source, observation, corroboration and physical support.

text: 1) Ask how each witness recognized the person or object. 2) Note how certain they claim to be. 3) Separate what they saw from what they heard. 4) Combine partial accounts into one timeline.
when: several witnesses give partial accounts that must be combined
why: recognition, certainty and sense channel determine reliability

text: 1) Note each speaker's position and length of service. 2) Note their interests and grudges. 3) Discount remarks those interests would shape. 4) Keep hearsay as evidence of motive, not of fact.
when: collecting staff or bystander gossip
why: each speaker's status and grudges bias what they say

text: 1) Record the remembered remark exactly as spoken. 2) Note what context is missing. 3) Consider the witness's position and stake. 4) Note when the remark was first disclosed. 5) Check secondhand reports against the original source.
when: using a witness's memory of someone's words

text: 1) Decide whether the statement proves the claim or was introduced for effect. 2) Read the circumstances that produced it. 3) Offer innocent explanations for each reported fact. 4) Assess the speaker's stake and bias. 5) Cross-check against independent sources.
when: A sworn statement is central to a dispute or accusation.
why: Separating proof from effect and testing each fact prevents a biased account from deciding the outcome.

text: A timeline from testimony orders the times witnesses give, anchors them to events all sides can confirm, and marks gaps, showing who was where and when.
when: when the case depends on who could have been where at a given hour

text: A suspect's day is usually reconstructed from witnesses who each saw only part of it, not from one complete account.
A witness's timing depends on when they woke, which is itself uncertain, so their account is weakened.
when: when a witness's testimony depends on waking or sleeping times
why: The reference point they use for timing is unreliable.

text: 1) Extract every duration, date and time of day each witness mentions. 2) Order the times into one sequence, linking separate movements into one route. 3) Mark conflicts and gaps. 4) Note each witness's limits before trusting the times.
when: reconstructing event order or alibis from several witnesses
why: combining accounts exposes the full sequence of movements

text: 1) Anchor the timeline on independent, verifiable points such as departures and arrivals, before relying on memory. 2) Place each witnessed event at its stated time, in sequence. 3) Check each claim against what that witness could physically perceive. 4) Mark agreements, conflicts and gaps; leave gaps unfilled by guesswork.
when: several witnesses give times for overlapping events, accounts disagree, or a person's possible movements must be located
why: Independent records are less error-prone than recollection, shared fixed points let contradictions surface, and an unexplained gap is evidence in itself.

text: 1) Collect each witness's time window. 2) Overlay the windows on one timeline. 3) Mark overlaps, conflicts and gaps. 4) Ask precise questions about exact wording to expose weak points.
when: reconstructing an event sequence from several accounts

text: 1) List each witness's location at each time. 2) Compare these with the times of key events. 3) Mark accounts that place a witness where they could not have been.
when: testimony conflicts or relies on a witness's own position
why: timing shows which accounts can be true

text: 1) List each reported step in the order given, with any time marker the speaker supplies. 2) Separate firm anchors from soft ones. 3) Test the sequence against fixed points such as appointments or deadlines. 4) Check claimed rest periods against other witnesses.
when: When several accounts must be fitted together.

text: 1) Assemble a timeline from transport records and places. 2) State it as established fact. 3) Let the suspect confirm, deny or stay silent. Each fixed point removes a place to hide.
when: When confronting a suspect with precise movement records.
why: Specific, proven details leave the suspect fewer ways to evade.

text: 1) Convert each stop in the account into a timestamp. 2) Lay the timestamps against known event times. 3) Mark which intervals are unaccounted for. 4) Ask for times and places, setting aside remarks about character. 5) Note where the relayer hedges.
when: when checking a relayed alibi against physical facts
why: Testable detail can be checked, unlike character remarks.

text: 1) Build the timeline from the witness's own stated times. 2) Compare subjective durations against an objective clock. 3) Mark gaps and sudden changes to show when an effect began.
when: when a witness's account of time conflicts with records or a room seems sealed
why: A fixed reference settles disputes that memory cannot

text: Deliver testimony as dated facts that the player assembles into a timeline.
Oral tradition mixes fact with rumour and fable, and dates or causes shift on each retelling; sifting them is slow and may not begin until after the account is written.
Local tradition tends to lose details such as who owned a place while keeping the story of the place itself, which survives longer within a family.
when: when an account has been passed down for more than a century
why: Stories tied to emotional or family memory are retained better than administrative facts

text: A feud that was never written down survives only in oral tradition, so its motive rests on retelling rather than documents.
Give one partial clue, such as a disturbed chair or a fragment with partial details, and leave its cause or the remaining details for the player to infer or find elsewhere.
when: when designing unsettling rooms, or message and note clues
why: the player completes the picture; exploration completes the clue

text: Place rare lore needed to use a trap, lock, or potion in one book or with one NPC, so the method becomes a clue to who set it.
when: Designing a dungeon element whose use requires specialised knowledge.
why: Limiting the lore's source makes the method's user traceable.

text: Leave some cache contents unknown so the player must decide whether the cache matters to the plot.
when: Designing caches tied to plot decisions.
why: Uncertainty about contents creates a choice about the cache's importance.

text: Keep tradition and rumor shaped by local pride or jealousy separate from records written at the time.
when: Local stories are used as evidence
why: Interest can color oral accounts

text: Explain an odd custom in human terms, such as burial rites or inheritance rules, so that an uncanny location feels grounded.
when: when writing lore for an unusual place or custom
why: a human basis makes a strange custom credible and understandable

text: Establish the world's governing explanation before the case clues, so later evidence feels pre-explained.
when: scripting a mystery or trial
why: Players then interpret each clue within the frame the designer chose.

text: Long-lived oral tradition can be persistent yet unverifiable; record it as tradition rather than established fact.
why: persistence across generations does not confirm an event

text: Oral tradition about a celebration is less reliable than recorded acts, so do not build conclusions on it alone.
1) List each uncanny claim. 2) Test whether a human motive, such as grief, withdrawal or devotion, explains it. 3) Keep only the claims no human motive covers.
when: when a rumour mixes ordinary and supernatural claims
why: most claims often have a mundane cause, leaving few that need the uncanny

text: Treat oral tradition as useful but uncertain; never use it as sole proof, and corroborate it with other clues or later documents.
when: when designing local lore or NPC testimony in a game, or when tradition is the main basis for a claim about a place or event
why: players weigh unverified sources instead of accepting them outright; retold accounts drift and need corroboration

text: Seed generated lore with legends of old feuds that are partly false, and let the player find the true origin through records.
when: when generating background lore

text: Plant a previous unsolved incident in a world's history that shares a trap signature with a current one, so players who research it can infer a copycat or red herring.
when: Building backstory for a mystery in a generated world.
why: Historical parallels give players a line of inference.

text: Log death and event dates in world state so players can rule out candidate NPCs by timeline.
When a character argues that a harmful act is justified, ask whether the speaker would perform it personally; a retreat to 'just arguing' exposes a hollow justification.
when: a character defends a deed in dialogue
why: unwillingness to act suggests the argument lacks conviction

text: A changed plan, such as a canceled departure, can be a visible world-state flag whose timing is itself informative.
when: When designing world-state changes that follow a revealing event.
why: A reversal right after a slip shows the event's effect on the character.

text: Avoid plot links that the world's own rules cannot support, since players will reject contrived connections.
when: Designing story links and reveals.
why: Connections that violate established rules break trust in the deduction.

text: Flag recurring locations or names across quests in a world-state log to prompt players to connect a chain of events.
Check a witness's statement against world facts only a present character could know, and flag statements that contradict the current state of the scene.
Separate what the game world records as true, such as quest state or faction status, from what is physically true, so NPCs can act on recorded facts the player knows are false.
when: Designing world state in narrative games.
why: Creates believable NPC behavior and dramatic irony.

text: A wound's entry point and angle constrain both the victim's posture at the time of the shot and the shooter's position relative to them.
when: when interpreting a gunshot or stab wound
why: geometry links the wound to body position and direction of force

text: A wound's depth and outline can indicate the kind of object that made it.
A wound below the heart bleeds before the victim falls, while a later wound leaks as the victim lies across a surface, so bleeding order helps reconstruct positions.
when: reconstructing a victim's position from wounds
why: Bleeding depends on the body's posture at the time each wound was made.

text: A projectile entering high and leaving lower, or an oblique downward path, suggests the shooter stood above the victim, such as on a staircase, especially at close range.
when: reconstructing a shot from wound geometry
why: The trajectory angle reflects the shooter's height.

text: A wound's side, angle and extent indicate roughly the hand used; a blow from behind favours the attacker's likely handedness. Record direction and extent when describing an injury.
when: reading an injury to infer how it was inflicted, or a wound is inflicted from behind
why: Stance and reach favour one hand; angle and extent constrain who could have made the wound.

text: Judge wound state (fresh, clotted or dried) to set order against a fatal injury; a bloodless wound may be post-mortem, added to suggest a cause that did not kill.
when: a surface injury could come from a fatal event or earlier violence, or a murder method seems excessive or senseless
why: Bleeding and drying change over time; a heart that has stopped produces no bleeding.

text: A fatal wound matching no weapon found on the scene suggests the victim struck a broad surface, such as a wall, during a struggle.
A wound and its dressing can serve as independent proof that contradicts a verbal account.
when: A person's story about an injury is questioned.
why: Physical injuries are hard to fabricate convincingly.

text: Check whether a wound's position fits the claimed act; a wound in an unexpected place may indicate a staged scene.
when: a scene suggests a particular cause
why: Physical injury must match the method claimed

text: A shot placed in a victim's back suggests the attacker stood close behind them.
why: a rear wound implies close following

text: Two wounds with suspiciously similar angles suggest the victim was not in the position the shooter's account requires.
when: Reconstructing shooter position from wounds

text: A wound-order argument fails if its assumed direction of impact is wrong, so verify the assumed source of the injury first.
why: The conclusion depends on the relative position of the injury and the cause

text: Estimates of height or distance from a wound angle are rough, and a small error in distance can distort them considerably.
when: inferring a shooter's position from an entry angle
why: Angle-based estimates are sensitive to small measurement errors.

text: 1) Sort wounds by type, such as blunt or sharp. 2) Separate injuries by depth and location. 3) Identify which wound could have caused a fatal injury.
when: Examining a body after a violent death.
why: Wound types point to different weapons and causes.

text: A distinctive mark tied to one region points to a homeland, and the inference strengthens when a second item from that region agrees.
when: a person carries a regional mark or item
why: specialist knowledge links the mark to a place and a second item corroborates it

text: A call or signal used within one community reveals a person's background, so a single cry can indicate where the speaker has lived.
when: an everyday call is heard
why: the call belongs to a particular community

text: Compare a document's spelling, vocabulary and products against its claimed origin, since regional wording can reveal a false source.
when: A document claims an origin that may be false
why: Language habits are hard to disguise consistently

text: Use a formal register when a message must signal authority, distance or the seriousness of an accusation; avoid it when warmth or plain clarity is needed.
when: when choosing the tone of a written message
why: Register sets the reader's sense of the author's stance.

text: Regularised spelling hides the original form of a name, which may be needed to identify the person.
when: when a modernised edition is the only source used
why: Original spellings can carry clues that normalisation removes

text: 1) Inspect the register entry for the claimed alibi. 2) Compare its handwriting with other entries known to be written by the same person.
when: a suspect's account names a guest or visitor register

text: The same document can support opposite readings, such as a warning sign or a sign of trust, so decide between them using independent evidence.
when: A will or record drawn shortly before a death.
why: Its meaning depends on the reading chosen, not on the text alone.

text: An ambiguous item, such as a blank stub or emotionally loaded note, fits several explanations and gains meaning only when combined with other facts.
A witness may answer from a prepared document rather than memory without noticing, and may repeat another person's claims as their own.
when: when the witness was coached or shown papers
why: Written scripts blend memory with other people's assertions.

text: Ambiguous legal wording, such as an unclear term, can be read in opposing ways, making a motive look stronger or weaker than it is.
A route described as mostly shut may be open at set times; ask what the phrase actually means before dismissing it.
Before acting on ambiguous wording, shorthand, or an unexplained name such as a place or person, confirm its meaning with the issuer.
when: A written term has two plausible senses, is shorthand, or names an unexplained place or person
why: Readers can misread a word in good faith

text: Make a payment or ledger support more than one NPC's story, so dialogue lets players argue for either reading.
when: Designing ambiguous documents in dialogue-driven investigations.
why: Ambiguity makes players weigh evidence instead of accepting the first reading.

text: Give ambiguous in-world signatures a disambiguating context the player can gather, such as rank, location and who was present, rather than leaving the identity unresolvable.
when: An NPC signs with a name shared by several characters
why: Players must be able to solve the ambiguity from clues

text: Writing fixes exact terms and settles oral disputes, but later instruments may not match the original oral promise. Trust writing when accounts conflict; doubt it when only later records exist.
why: Writing preserves exact wording, but a later record is a new statement, not a copy of the original understanding.

text: A letter's tone can colour how readers take its factual claims.
when: reading a personal letter as evidence
why: Mood and manner shape the reader's trust in the content.

text: A written note requesting a small private gathering limits the number of witnesses, so events can happen with few people able to confirm them.
A 1666 order required testimony in writing, kept on file by the court clerk, which made later reconstruction possible.
Written procedural cautions do not guarantee restraint; authorities can later move quickly to prosecution if the cautions go unenforced.
Self-written accounts give times, places and event order as their writer chose; judge them by author, date, and whether complete or selective, asking what they omit.
when: when a suspect's or witness's written account is a main source, such as a letter, diary or deposition
why: Writers can admit some facts while keeping others out of view, so reliability depends on what was included.

text: Treat letters written by a person as primary documents that can answer charges about their character, and date them to place them in sequence.
A letter whose point of view shifts can hint at the writer's bias, giving the player a clue to the writer's identity.
Check a letter's date and place before deciding whether it is a plea, a fraud or an honest warning.
when: A written message is used as evidence
why: Date and place reveal whether the letter fits the claimed circumstances.

text: A suspect's writings reveal where admiration and contempt lie; read them as character evidence.
Check address books, handwriting samples, and written notes to trace who was told a secret.
when: a secret may have spread in writing
why: written communication leaves a checkable record

text: Treat a written instruction as evidence in its own right, not only as a means of communication.
when: a letter directs a hidden action

text: When every witness to an old understanding is dead, the written instrument becomes the only fixed record of it.
when: settling a claim based on an old, undocumented understanding
why: No living person can confirm the original terms.

text: Correspondence between communities can carry suspicion from one place to another, spreading an accusation beyond its origin.
when: Leaders in separate communities exchange letters on a shared belief.
why: Letters transmit endorsement and encouragement across distance, making local fears appear more widespread.

text: A written approach can be used later, so every phrase must be exact.
1) Write the speaker's account down as they say it. 2) Have the speaker sign it. 3) Have a second person witness the signature, which gives the record standing.
when: Recording a confession or testimony that may later be relied on.
why: A signed, witnessed record is a fixed account rather than a memory that can be disputed.

text: 1) Choose a private, quiet setting. 2) Show the suspect how silence will harm an innocent person. 3) Have the suspect write the account in own words and read it through. 4) Have a respected third party witness the signatures. 5) Pass the document to the proper authority.
when: When a suspect's account can clear an innocent person and the core facts are largely known
why: A witnessed, self-written statement carries weight and cannot easily be disowned

text: Weigh the risk of discovery before opening another person's correspondence, since interception can expose the investigator.
A written document placing a suspect elsewhere at the relevant time can serve as an alibi, but it must still be checked against the timeline.
when: when a document claims a suspect's location

text: An adult may dismiss a child's detailed report at first, then reconsider when pressed to check the scene herself.
when: When an adult hears an unusual report from a child.
why: Adults may resist disturbing claims until they test them directly.

text: A young or frightened witness's identification can be challenged easily, so it should be corroborated by other evidence before it carries weight.
when: The sole identifying witness is a child or highly distressed.
why: Fear and limited understanding make recall vulnerable to challenge.

text: Companions' waiting or worry does not independently confirm where a person was, since it reflects expectation rather than observation.
Assuming a claim is supernatural because the witness was too young to remember the event hides the likelier channel, such as someone who passed it on.
Let one NPC vouch for another suspect's alibi, so the player must reopen a room they had considered settled.
when: Placing NPCs whose statements alter what is known about a location.
why: A vouching witness gives the player a reason to revisit settled areas.

text: When a second character's testimony clears a suspect, open a new suspect's room instead of ending the quest.
when: a level gates progress behind suspect verification
why: Clearing a suspect changes which location the player must investigate next.

text: Make a suspect's alibi a set of rooms to check, where one entrance record contradicts another only when two linked rooms are compared.
when: when generating a level with suspect alibis
why: The contradiction exists only across linked spaces, so the player must visit both.

text: Use a dispute between NPCs to draw the player to a location, and reveal the dispute's real purpose later.
when: Designing a quest that begins with a conflict.
why: A visible conflict motivates the player to act while hiding the manipulation behind it.

text: Let a reckless player action attract witnesses or guards, so impulsive play carries a visible cost.
when: Designing responses to reckless player behaviour.
why: Consequences tie impulsive choices to outcomes the player can learn from.

text: Resolve a suspect with a lure-and-trap encounter in place of a dialogue confession, so the player controls the confrontation.
Place a false solution gate near the midpoint, where the apparent boss dies or flees, so the party believes the threat is contained.
when: pacing a dungeon's middle section
why: Apparent containment releases tension before the real threat

text: Trigger a late ambush by a sound or silhouette while the player is away, so the threat appears during an apparent safe moment.
when: designing a late-game surprise
why: Absence and a cue create dread before the attack

text: Create a trap room where the player waits for an NPC to break in, with a threatening weapon visibly loaded but in fact harmless.
when: Generating an ambush encounter.
why: A visible threat drives tension, and hidden harmlessness lets the designer control the outcome.

text: Use a timed checkpoint, such as a station stop, as a lock: the world state before and after it determines which NPC could have acted.
when: Gating a suspect's alibi behind a location and time.
why: A time-based lock turns a closed alibi into a question the player must resolve.

text: Schedule a scripted ambush around mid-level, after the player has formed a wrong theory, to force re-evaluation.
In a bluff encounter the player confronts a boss with fake evidence, and the boss's reaction reveals whether the accusation is true.
why: The boss's response to a false accusation exposes guilt without a direct admission

text: 1) Place an NPC companion with an ordinary action that hides a planned move. 2) Let the player learn the schedule. 3) Use it to intercept the thief at a waypoint. 4) Reveal the captive's crime to raise stakes.
when: building a travel or chase encounter in generated content
why: A planted, ordinary clue lets the player predict and intercept the threat, and the late reveal changes the reward.

text: 1) Schedule several simultaneous events such as a theft, a shooting and a flight in one night. 2) Let the player sequence them to recover the truth.
when: Designing a climactic time-limited section.
why: Simultaneous events force the player to order and prioritise information.

text: Build a timed escort whose final destination is reached only after the player rejects the first trail.
when: generated escort or rescue missions

text: Make investigative actions such as warrants or canvasses limited resources the player spends, each use bounded.
when: Designing investigation mechanics in a game

text: Chain areas so each apparent answer is overturned by an item found in the next area, such as a name on a garment undoing a substitution.
when: Designing a sequence of mystery areas
why: Each new item gives the player a reason to revise the previous conclusion.

text: Create a puzzle space where the player reproduces a test to prove a claim.
when: Designing a late-level proof moment.
why: Reproducing the test lets the player verify the solution themselves.

text: In a room-based investigation, front-load a few clue rooms and gate the deeper ones behind checks that clear suspects.
when: designing a multi-room investigation
why: Early clues build a theory while gates test it

text: 1) Put one true clue and one misleading decoy in each area or suspect's room. 2) Make inspecting the decoy unlock the real trail. 3) Order rooms so the first false solution is the one intended. 4) Chain rooms by a traceable item.
when: Generating a multi-room or multi-area investigation level or dungeon.
why: A decoy gives the player a false conclusion, and inspecting it reveals the real path.

text: 1) Give the player a service role inside a target location under a planted cover identity. 2) Drop an item that prompts a guilty NPC reaction. 3) Let the NPC's reaction reveal guilt.
when: Generating an infiltration mission inside a manor or similar closed location.
why: Cover roles grant access and a planted item creates a reaction the player can read.

text: Furnish each location with objects that reveal its routine, so players can infer who uses the room and what happens there.
when: Designing rooms or locations whose occupants should be inferable by the player.
why: Players read objects as evidence of habits, turning furnishing into an observable clue.

text: A breachable steel door gives players a choice between fast entry with damage and slow entry without it.
when: Designing a locked room or raid location.
why: The breach option trades time against the cost of damage.

text: Give a haunted room a concrete hidden mechanism, such as a concealed key, panel and passage, that the player can discover to explain the legend.
when: Designing a ghost story for a location.
why: A discoverable cause lets the player resolve the legend through play.

text: A finale room can chain several tests in sequence, each with a pause, ending in a choice for the player.
when: Designing a generated or authored finale
why: A chained structure builds tension toward a meaningful decision

text: Place a test room that recreates the original conditions, with NPC witnesses observing the player's reproduction.
when: Generating a reconstruction challenge
why: Observed reproduction makes the result credible within the game.

text: Chain confirmation stages so each partial proof unlocks the next area, with the final confession held by the antagonist.
when: Designing progression through a mystery
why: Gating by proof ties progress to understanding rather than combat.

text: Design a death event where a hazard or monster turns out to be a memory or visitor from the player's past rather than a combatant.
when: Generating a quest where the threat is non-combat.
why: A non-combat resolution surprises players who expect a fight and reframes the threat.

text: Build a staged-death puzzle so the cause of injury is checked after the player's first assumption, changing the level's threat once it is re-examined.
when: Generating an encounter around a corpse or apparent death.
why: The first assumption drives the player's actions, so a later check can change the threat.

text: Gate the final confrontation behind a physical experiment, such as applying heat or a chemical reagent, that exposes hidden text or mechanism.
when: Designing the climactic encounter of an investigative level.
why: A deliberate experiment gives the player an action that unlocks the confrontation.

text: Re-skin one boss enemy as a different impostor on each floor, with each disguise revealing the next floor's layout or key.
when: Generating a dungeon with a recurring antagonist across floors.
why: The same enemy in new disguises gives variety while carrying story forward.

text: A layered boss has three stages: a dead underboss, a fake leader, then the true leader, each revealed in a separate room or cutscene.
when: building a multi-stage antagonist
why: Separate reveals keep each layer distinct for the player

text: 1) Put a corpse bearing a unique mark in the opening room. 2) Put an object proving the body is someone else in a second room; the official death record is a false document the player must challenge. 3) Later, bring the living person back as a character who verifies the swap and hands over a token as proof.
when: building a dungeon investigation or generating narrative twists
why: Contradicting an official record creates a reveal the player works to earn.

text: 1) Show the ghostly event first as an ambiguous sound in a neutral location. 2) Later show it as a concealed cabinet-based source. 3) Reward players who revisit the scene with a new tool.
when: when an NPC-driven supernatural event is part of a dungeon or level
