why: Revisiting with new information turns the same event into a second, mundane explanation.

text: 1) Make the first enemy a disguised figure the player identifies through items it leaves behind. 2) After it is defeated, reveal a second, hidden enemy.
Make a supposed corpse an NPC that can be found alive, with its own movement path and visible traces such as a missing coat or a cleaned room.
when: generating a level with a found body

text: Create a two-stage threat in one room: stop the copying threat first, then retrieve the original, giving the player two objectives.
Hide a trained creature or item carrier as an NPC's pet, with a testable behavior cue, such as biting an object, that the player can observe.
Have an NPC watch from a location the player assumed was empty, revealed by a late trigger.
Plant an early environmental clue or foreshadowing line that pays off later, so the reveal reads as recall and early text gains meaning on return.
when: generating clues that a later reveal depends on
why: Recognition of an earlier clue makes a late reveal feel fair.

text: A clue ledger logs unexplained clues such as predictions, hints and sightings, each matched to a later explaining event; early plants pay off many rooms later as decisive proof.
when: when generating or scripting a mystery with linked clues across a dungeon or town
why: Delayed payoffs make the player reassess earlier discoveries, and matching logged clues to later events makes the payoff feel set up.

text: 1) Split a clue into two fragments, such as a staging record and its confession. 2) Place one at a scene and its twin in a suspect's room. 3) Let the player connect them.
when: when designing paired or multi-part clues
why: Connecting separated clues is a satisfying discovery.

text: Show decisive items as routine objects, such as a half-read note, cold cup or stored item, in the opening room, so meaning surfaces only at payoff.
when: when placing key items in a level
why: Familiar objects regain meaning once the situation changes, and early visibility keeps the payoff fair rather than arbitrary.

text: Place discardable clues, such as a torn note, receipt or partial item in trash containers, that players retrieve from a filing place and reassemble, each fragment unlocking a lead.
when: Designing puzzles where a trace must be recovered later, or collectible clues hidden in waste.
why: Retrievable discards reward attentive inventory management, and reassembly rewards exploration and advances the investigation.

text: Use a physical trait, mark, object, hat or tool matching a character already met or seen in an earlier room, so the clue links to a known person.
when: Designing a clue that points to an NPC, or generating a level with a shop or workplace.
why: Linking a trait to a known character lets the player connect the clue without extra explanation.

text: Include a few unexplained environmental details, such as a rumour or marked book, as optional clues rewarding only players who explore.
Place the only full version of a secret in one locked or guarded source, so the player must reach it to learn the whole account.
when: Designing a mystery where partial clues are spread across NPCs.
why: A single authoritative source gives the player a clear goal for resolving the mystery.

text: Plant a false-suspect item, such as a weapon near an innocent NPC, and let the player clear that NPC with a second test.
when: generating placed evidence near an innocent character
why: A second test lets the player correct the first conclusion.

text: Place a fact that contradicts the apparent cause early in the scene, such as a weapon in an unexpected hand or a body in an unexpected place, so careful players can reconstruct the sequence.
when: Designing a scene where a 'dead' or defeated character is a trap or twist.
why: Early, checkable contradictions let players solve the scene by reasoning rather than by luck.

text: End an investigation arc on a transportable object as a lead to an off-screen suspect, with confirmation arriving later through an NPC.
Place an odd substance early in the level that later reveals how a trick was done.
when: Seeding clues that pay off in a later reveal.
why: A strange early detail gives the player a fair chance to connect it to the solution.

text: Show a locked room or unexplained item early and let the player use it later.
when: Seeding a space that pays off in a later act.
why: An early unexplained object becomes a payoff that feels planned.

text: Plant an unexplained lore fragment, such as an unexplained name or slip, that players can pursue after the main reveal.
when: Building a world with post-reveal content
why: A lead that outlasts the main twist extends engagement into follow-up play.

text: Build a late evidence board where items gathered from earlier rooms combine to reveal the answer.
when: Designing the endgame of a deduction-based generated level.
why: A shared board rewards the player for remembering and linking items across the whole level.

text: Use a single traceable item as the spine of a puzzle chain: each holder unlocks a new location, and the item's wear can serve as an evidence check.
Make partial, ambiguous reports, such as NPC remarks about hands, sleeves or clothing or a delayed passive record, each narrow the field slightly so the player must combine them.
when: Building identification puzzles from witness reports or designing sensor or camera clues.
why: Each partial report narrows the field only a little, and a partial record is more believable and requires corroboration.

text: 1) Scatter one repeated visual or item across several rooms. 2) Reveal new information at each stage. 3) Let its meaning shift until the final reveal.
when: Building a narrative item that spans multiple areas of a level.
why: Revisiting one item with new context reinforces the mystery without adding new objects.

text: 1) Decide the intended discovery path. 2) Add false leads, such as a red-herring item that fits poorly, a hastily hidden item or a conflicting rumour. 3) Ensure each can be disproven by evidence elsewhere, letting the player reject it through reasoning.
when: Building a mystery or investigation scenario
why: The player must be able to reconstruct the truth from available evidence.

text: 1) Generate a pool of rumours. 2) Mix true clues with false ones. 3) Vary the sources so players practise sorting reliable from unreliable claims.
1) Create several small facts, each innocent alone. 2) Make them converge on one hidden cause, such as matching timestamps across rooms. 3) Let the player assemble the pattern.
when: Designing a puzzle where the answer emerges from many weak clues.
why: Individually innocent clues that align reveal a cause only when combined.

text: 1) Place a witness NPC at a window or tower with a limited field of view. 2) Pair each claim the witness makes with a recoverable object, such as a bullet or torn cloth. 3) Let the player verify the claim by finding that object.
why: The player can cross-check testimony against a physical trace in the world.

text: 1) Split a multi-part item across several zones as collectible pieces. 2) Leave one piece missing. 3) Point the missing piece to a hidden container that holds the answer.
when: when designing a collection that leads to a hidden reveal
why: the missing piece gives the player a clear next step

text: 1) Place a testable rumour in the first room. 2) Add a sealed room where the rumour's effects can be observed and recorded. 3) Hide one physical artifact that exposes the mechanism. 4) Let hidden human actors use the same mechanisms the player sees.
when: Generating a level whose apparent threat is a hidden human mechanism
why: Testable setup, a recording opportunity and a single decisive artifact reward careful observation and reframe the threat as human.

text: 1) Hide a found object such as an inscription or plaque in the final room. 2) Make it resolve the identity of the threat. 3) Optionally tie it to a character's ancestry to suggest a follow-up threat.
when: Designing the final room of a level where the threat's identity is the reveal
why: A late artifact that names the threat delivers the reveal and can open a sequel hook.

text: 1) Show the player the outcome first. 2) Plant a checkable clue earlier in the level. 3) Let the player discover the mechanism by connecting the clue to what they saw.
when: Designing a puzzle whose mechanism must be discovered
why: The player gets a fair path to the answer and a satisfying payoff.

text: 1) Give a murdered non-player character a last route through the level. 2) Place the pursuer's trace on that route. 3) Let the player find the antagonist by retracing it.
when: Designing a murder mystery
why: Retracing the victim's path gives the player a concrete way to find the antagonist.

text: 1) Place a small set of props in each room. 2) Give each prop a stated but unexplained purpose. 3) Reuse the props in the solution path.
when: generating rooms that will host a mystery's clues
why: Props with stated purpose gain meaning when the solution reuses them, linking setup and payoff.

text: 1) Present a set of candidate sites. 2) Let the player eliminate them one at a time. 3) Reveal the last remaining site through a document. 4) Gate the reveal behind late signals that only appear in combination.
when: Designing a map whose true location is found by elimination.
why: Eliminating candidates in turn turns exploration into deduction, and combined signals make the final answer appear only when several are met.

text: 1) Place a countable object whose absence is a clue. 2) Let the player notice the count is off. 3) Make the missing item point to a hidden actor.
when: Designing a generated room or scenario with a hidden faction.
why: Players question anomalies they can count, which drives them toward the hidden actor.

text: 1) Place a missing item clue. 2) Place an out-of-place tool clue. 3) Place a dated note clue. 4) Require the player to combine all three to decide who a figure really is.
when: Designing an identity deduction puzzle.
why: Combining independent clues forces active reasoning rather than single-clue answers.

text: 1) Hide a confession object in a location the player will not check until late. 2) Let it resolve the puzzle only after the player has committed to a theory.
when: Designing a late-resolving puzzle proof.
why: Committed theories make the confession land as a correction rather than an answer.

text: Make in-world entries carry clues that only make sense together, so a player who connects two related entries can link a feud to a present conflict.
Make the reference needed to decode an NPC's remark learnable inside the game world, such as through a map name, local saying or historical fact, not only outside knowledge.
when: Designing a dying or cornered NPC who leaves a clue.
why: Players who lack outside knowledge cannot decode a clue that depends on it.

text: Let players compare a body against a checklist of marks, so one mismatched tattoo or item reveals a substitution.
Leave one genuinely unstaged detail in a staged scene, such as a tool that cannot have caused the claimed damage, so a careful observer can detect the artifice.
when: building a staged scene that a player should be able to unmask
why: A single inconsistent detail gives an attentive player a verifiable lead.

text: Place a clue in an item the player has already passed, then reveal its meaning late to reverse the leading theory.
when: When designing a late-game reversal.
why: Revisiting an earlier item rewards attention.

text: Design clues with several readings, such as a torn map pointing to several places, and let other clues settle which reading is correct.
Place a distinctive object in an early room whose detail matches a document found later, so players can connect them when they meet it.
when: Generating a hidden-identity puzzle

text: Let NPC hopes or rumours steer players toward a red herring, and place clues to the real threat in less obvious locations.
when: Designing misleading information in generated content.
why: Players follow the strongest social lead first, so real clues must sit off that path.

text: Give an occult clue two possible explanations, one human and one magical, and include a test that separates them.
when: Designing an eerie clue or ward in a game.
why: A testable separation lets the player resolve the ambiguity through play.

text: Use a transport or service NPC as a witness whose description narrows a suspect in the final act.
A hidden residence and account can serve as a clue trail, letting the player find a second address through documents.
when: when planting clues to a secret location
why: Document trails reward investigation and reveal the hidden arrangement gradually.

text: Tag each clue with the suspect it implicates, then show which links survive when a new witness statement is added.
when: Building a deduction system in a game
why: Tagged clues let the system re-evaluate a case as new testimony arrives

text: A dropped glove or cloak sized for a small body can narrow the suspect list by a height or build attribute.
when: Generating a clue based on clothing size.
why: Clothing fit reveals a body attribute the player can use to filter suspects.

text: Design a dialogue puzzle in which a secondary NPC reacts to an object or word the player brings into the room, revealing a hidden fact.
Give a hidden entrance a sound cue that alerts a specific room, so the player can test testimony about who could have entered.
Disguise a container as a standard decorative object, such as a sarcophagus or display case, and make its contents discoverable only by a scanning tool acquired later.
when: when a level hides a key item in a decorative container
why: the disguise hides the contents until the player gains the right tool

text: Spread several copies of a clue-bearing lore document across locations so the player is less likely to miss it entirely.
when: when a lore document carries an essential clue
why: Multiple placements raise the chance that the player encounters it.

text: Spread mismatched physical evidence across several rooms so the player reconstructs the contradiction unaided, with no cutscene.
Have two separate sources, such as a journal and an NPC's memory or a second independent NPC, confirm a location, name or detail before the player acts on it.
when: When a lead is important enough to need confidence, or testimony gates player action.
why: Independent confirmation raises trust in the lead and lets players corroborate testimony before committing.

text: Give a forged letter, ledger or message a checkable property (paper from the wrong room, ink the victim would not use, typewriter, seal) that matches or contradicts a record elsewhere.
why: The player can verify the forgery only by visiting the other location; a cross-reference gives a concrete way to test authenticity.

text: Let players test a legend or partial NPC explanation against physical traces or a later record (ledger, dated inscription) before trusting it, since it may be partly false.
when: Designing legends or NPC lore for a mystery.
why: Legends and partial explanations can be partly false, so physical traces or later records verify them.

text: Tag each log entry and NPC statement with its source type (first-hand or relayed), confidence and hearsay depth so players can weigh how far to trust each and what to cross-check.
Mark an NPC's answer as unverified until the player checks it in the world, with a risk that a quick confession alerts enemies.
when: Generating information from captured NPCs.
why: Verification keeps players from trusting coerced answers without evidence.

text: Design each trace to fit a route the player can test, such as a gate, a wall or a path visible from a window.
when: Building routes that a suspect must have used.
why: Testable routes let players confirm or rule out access.

text: Scale verification to stakes: a minor clue may accept a written note, while a critical claim requires the witness present in the scene.
when: when deciding how a player can verify a claim
why: higher stakes justify costlier confirmation

text: Give a witness NPC a confident answer the player can test against a map, log or actual location, even when the NPC has no direct knowledge.
when: Generating witness NPCs whose statements should be checkable
why: Testable answers reward investigation and expose unreliable witnesses

text: A clue found by a trusted character carries more weight in a scene than one found by a stranger.
when: assigning which character reveals a document
why: Who discovers a clue shapes how much the player believes it.

text: Let a companion NPC mark planted clues as suspicious after testing them against layout and access records.
when: designing companion dialogue about evidence
why: a companion's check models careful reasoning for the player

text: A document surviving only as a copy can lead players to hunt for the original, letting them judge whether that copy deserves trust.
Let the player gather traces from characters and match them against evidence, eliminating candidates one by one.
when: When building an investigation mechanic around physical traces.
why: Gathered traces give the player a concrete method for narrowing suspects.

text: A portrait or sketch can be matched to a historical record to identify a hidden antagonist, with the matching done by the player.
when: Designing identification puzzles for a hidden antagonist
why: Player-driven matching turns identification into an active deduction.

text: Plant a decoy trail, such as a note or dated item, that points to an NPC with a clean alibi, and let the player test that alibi.
when: generating a misleading lead for the player
why: Testing an alibi turns a false lead into a verifiable step that rules out the NPC.

text: A disabled alarm can be a clue that someone with access tampered with it.
when: Designing a security system with a hidden actor
why: Disabled systems point toward a specific suspect.

text: Hide a clue in content that fits its genre, such as an essay or poem, so it reads as ordinary material to casual readers.
when: when a clue should blend in and be decoded only by a knowing reader
why: Readers skim genre content without suspicion, so the clue survives casual reading.

text: Use an artifact from an outside source, such as a clipping or log, as the verifying key for an in-world manuscript, so the player can cross-check the account.
when: When generating a document-based reveal that must feel credible.
why: A separate, checkable artifact lets the player confirm a claim instead of accepting it on trust.

text: Use a recurring clue as a generated seed so that the same name or object reappears in later roots or documents.
when: generating connected clues across a level
why: Repetition of a seed object links rooms and keeps earlier clues relevant.

text: Give the player a document or object that must be tested with a specific tool before it can be trusted.
when: Building an evidence-based puzzle in a generated level.
why: Testing the object, not accepting it, turns a passive find into an active deduction.

text: A found object such as a purse or key can lead the player to a wrong NPC, and a second search reveals who placed it.
when: when designing a planted-evidence puzzle
why: A visible found item drives an accusation that a deeper search later overturns.

text: Plant evidence that the player can check later, such as footwear sized to match tracks, so that a late trap pays off a mid-game clue.
when: Generating clues for a multi-stage mystery.
why: Evidence placed early and verified later creates a payoff the player can follow.

text: Confirming a lead by checking its source, such as a rack or locker, can be an optional sub-puzzle that either narrows or closes a path.
why: Each check either adds a suspect location or removes one from consideration.

text: A clue with a misleading surface reading, corrected by a second source such as a note or log, keeps first-look interpretations from deciding the outcome when rewards wait for confirmation.
when: When designing clues in a generated level.
why: Requiring corroboration before reward prevents players from acting on the first, wrong reading.

text: NPC testimony that includes a checkable detail, such as a garment, arrival time or false name, lets the player confirm the claim against an item or location.
when: Generating clues for an investigation dungeon.
why: Verification against game objects turns testimony into a playable deduction.

text: Identifying marks visible only under a scanner or x-ray view can be placed in a level, and matching them to a records dossier lets each match confirm identity independently.
when: Designing body-search or identification puzzles
why: Hidden information rewards the right tool and reading, and independent matches build conviction

text: A detection device can give an accurate reading while the player's interpretation of its meaning is wrong, producing a false solution even though the instrument itself is trustworthy.
when: Designing a puzzle or mystery built on a sensor, detector or lantern signal
why: The error lies in the assumption attached to the reading, not in the reading, so the false conclusion feels earned.

text: In an interrogation system, unverifiable explanations raise suspicion, while verifiable explanations lower it.
when: A player questions a suspect who offers an account of their actions.
why: Verifiable claims can be checked and cleared, while unverifiable ones leave suspicion in place.

text: A frame journal puzzle is a player-found manuscript whose margins or erasures contradict its own claims, and the contradiction is the solvable clue.
when: when designing a document-based clue in a dungeon
why: Contradictions in the record let the player solve the puzzle from the document itself.

text: 1) Give an item or symptom that contradicts the obvious poison. 2) Provide a diagnostic test that reveals the masking agent. 3) Use the mismatch between result and expectation as a second test or pointer to the hidden substance.
when: When building a poison or pill puzzle, or a poisoning puzzle with a diagnostic tool.
why: A symptom that disagrees with the obvious cause points the player to a hidden substance.

text: 1) Tag each scene object as fitting or contradicting the main theory. 2) Rank leads by the number and strength of contradicting tags. 3) Present the contradicting items as the primary investigation targets.
when: building a clue system that lets players rank their leads
why: Ranking by contradiction directs the player toward the most informative anomalies.

text: 1) Create in-world logs, ledgers or diaries. 2) Have each confirm or contradict an NPC claim. 3) Let players compare the record with the claim.
when: Designing NPC testimony that players can verify.
why: Written records give players an independent check on NPC statements.

text: 1) Place a contradictory detail, such as an unexplained item on a shabby NPC, in dialogue or an inventory. 2) Log it for the player. 3) Give the NPC a plausible reason to skip follow-up. 4) Keep the flag available for a later check.
when: Designing NPC dialogue or inventories that hold mysteries
why: The clue stays discoverable and revisitable without forcing an immediate answer

text: 1) Have an NPC tell a fable embedding real vault details, such as trap order or key location. 2) Let the player match the fable against the map to deduce the route.
when: Designing puzzle-driven vaults where NPCs hold partial knowledge.
why: Players can reconstruct real layout from a disguised account they can verify.

text: 1) Make each NPC statement checkable through a physical action the player can take. 2) Let the player combine several partial statements to rebuild events. 3) Track each suspect's position through a shared timeline.
when: When designing NPC testimony in a mystery game.
why: Checkable and combinable statements let players reconstruct events from partial, sensory-limited accounts.

text: 1) Have the player gather a testimony from one NPC. 2) Require verifying it against archive documents. 3) Only then allow naming the culprit.
when: Designing a culprit reveal in a mystery quest
why: Cross-checking testimony before naming the culprit makes the reveal earned and fair.

text: 1) Collect sample items from each suspect's location. 2) Run a comparison test at a lab node against the evidence. 3) Use the match to reduce the suspect list to one person.
when: when a scenario has several suspects and physical evidence
why: Comparing against every suspect's samples narrows a large set to one.

text: 1) Take a control sample from a neutral site. 2) Take a target sample from the suspected site. 3) Compare the two so the difference is easy to read.
when: when a scenario uses environmental sampling to find a hidden agent
why: A paired control makes the signature in the target sample clear.

text: 1) Let the body's identity be inferred from items at the scene. 2) Place a late item, such as a letter or receipt, that reverses the identification.
when: Designing a dead-NPC investigation puzzle.
why: A late reversing item rewards players who tracked the scene's details.

text: 1) Place a test object in a trap room. 2) Observe the reaction it provokes. 3) Use that reaction to narrow the suspect list.
when: Designing a trap or test that identifies a suspect in a level.
why: A reaction to a neutral test object is a diagnostic clue that narrows possibilities.

text: Split in-game documents and NPC testimony into observed facts and interpretation, feeling or gaps, so players can cross-check which parts to trust.
when: Designing found journals, letters or NPC testimony in a generated world.
why: Cross-checking against logs, objects or other NPCs lets players judge reliability instead of accepting text or testimony whole.

text: Mark some NPC testimony as drawn from an unverifiable source, so players must cross-check it against physical clues.
when: when designing mystery testimony
why: unverifiable claims need independent support

text: Link a financial clue to a later witness so the player must cross-check two sources before accepting a motive.
when: When placing motive evidence in a quest.
why: Requiring corroboration makes the motive feel earned.

text: Before placing a planted fact such as sight range or light level as a clue, verify it against the world's own rules.
Tag false objectives or traps as staged, and build clue trails from timing and placement so careful players can detect them.
Track means, motive and opportunity as separate verified flags, so the player sees which part of an accusation is still unsupported.
Give an NPC portrait or wall painting a subtle flaw as a hint, and tune its art style so the hint is easy to misread.
when: Generating environmental visual clues

text: Show overlaps between two sources only after the player has collected both.
why: Premature overlap removes the discovery of the link.

text: Keep names hidden from the player until a second, independent source confirms them.
when: A dialogue system reveals identities tied to a secret
why: Early disclosure removes the deduction and a single source may be unreliable

text: Let players uncover the truth by spotting a mismatch, such as a weight too light, an initial belonging to someone else, or a room too clean.
when: Designing a discoverable deception.
why: Noticing an inconsistency rewards careful observation.

text: Let a journal or ledger list several named witnesses, each giving a separate detail, so players can cross-check the story.
when: Designing in-world records of events.
why: Multiple sources let players verify the account.

text: A puzzle can present a note that must be matched to a character using two visible features, such as slant and letter shapes, that differ on the surface.
when: when designing a document-matching puzzle
why: Two features give the player a concrete comparison to make.

text: Log where each document arrived, such as a door, post or messenger, so the player can test its provenance.
when: when designing documents that carry route clues
why: Recorded delivery lets players judge a document's origin.

text: Make wanted-poster or sketch mechanics use partial, contradictory descriptions so the player must visit the suspect to confirm identity.
when: when designing description-based identification puzzles
why: Contradictory sketches push the player toward direct confirmation.

text: An NPC can give a true report that other NPCs dismiss. Let the player verify it through a physical object, which then restores the NPC's credibility.
when: Designing NPC reports that peers reject
why: Physical verification gives the player grounds to trust the report over social consensus

text: Plant a hidden weak point in a concealment, such as an item moved too late, as a thread the player can pull to expose it.
Let an eavesdropping mechanic deliver partial NPC lines, and require a second source before the player can confirm them.
A document puzzle can let the player compare an item's physical property against each suspect's stored samples, and false names on documents should be made misleading.
when: Designing document or item clues in a game
why: Property comparison gives players a fair, checkable path to attribution

text: Give each in-world claim, such as a journal entry or gossip, a physical record or second non-player source the player can use to check it.
when: Generating clues or lore for a mystery
why: Unchecked claims leave the player's reasoning resting on the designer's word alone.

text: Let a recorded clue tell the player which question to ask, then close the mystery with a scene that confirms the answer through recovered items.
when: when designing a mystery's ending
why: the player connects evidence to the answer through the items gathered

text: Generate a glyph with a plausible but misleading reading, and place a translation NPC in the same room to correct it.
Use item-based clues, such as ammo counts or footprints, that the player can ignore at first and reinterpret after later information.
Give a dying NPC a last line that the player must decode against the scene to reach the answer.
Place a misleading item the player must recognise as deliberately placed before the final solution is accepted.
when: generating a dungeon structured as a mystery

text: Make the final physical check, such as an object fitting a body part or a wear mark, a discoverable puzzle so the player confirms the accusation themselves.
Let the player accept or challenge a confession, and record whether it was extracted, so its reliability can be checked later.
when: confessions are used as evidence in a generated world
why: The game can later reveal whether trust in that evidence was warranted.

text: Show players when a testimony lacks corroboration, but still require them to act on it to progress.
when: a quest relies on unverified claims
why: Players can recognise the risk while the choice still matters.

text: Have one NPC echo another's testimony and let the player catch the echo by comparing the two statements.
when: generating NPC testimony
why: Comparison turns coaching into a discoverable clue.

text: Hide an omitted passage in a copied document, so a player who compares the copy with the original discovers what was removed.
Create a confession quest in which an NPC explains a haunting's source; the explanation becomes the key that unlocks the next area.
Place a false confession encounter mid-late, with the real evidence hidden in a later area.
when: pacing a deduction dungeon
why: A believed confession sends the player back to test it

text: An interrogation room is an NPC investigator who sets trap questions and withholds the decisive fact, forcing the player to answer or stall.
when: when designing a dungeon encounter with a questioning NPC
why: The withheld fact keeps the player under pressure without a fight.

text: 1) Pick one fixed location for the final confrontation. 2) Gather the documents and clues from earlier zones there. 3) Present them to the antagonist to resolve the case.
when: Designing the climactic area of an investigation level.
why: A single location lets earlier clues converge into one payoff scene.

text: 1) Let an NPC give a detailed confession. 2) Expose its weak points through environment cues such as blood, sounds or footprints. 3) Reveal the true events when the cues contradict the confession.
when: generating a false-confession encounter
why: Environmental cues let the player test the confession rather than accept it.

text: In an accusation scene, pause the action, dim the room, and highlight the key clue before the player names a suspect.
when: Designing the accusation moment in a game.
why: Visual and temporal emphasis focuses the player on the decisive evidence.

text: Script an accusation that prompts a designated NPC to act, exposing him to the player.
Stage a trap-and-confession room in which the villain must speak before a poison or trap triggers on death.
when: designing a boss finale
why: Forced speech delivers the reveal before the boss dies

text: A witnessed confession can resolve the case without a public accusation, while an accusation built on procedural faults, with escalating pressure, can also end in confession without hard proof.
when: staging the climax of a mystery encounter
why: Both avoid requiring physical proof; the two positions differ on whether the climax includes a public accusation.

text: Give a damning-looking scene or damaged room a second, non-obvious cause, such as third-party pressure, so players must reason back rather than accept the obvious reading.
when: designing a scene players will read one way and later revise; designing environmental storytelling
why: A single obvious cause removes the reasoning the player could otherwise do.

text: Plant staged or damaged evidence early, such as a moved body, hidden object or damaged item implying another event, then reveal it later as a clue.
when: generating a room or level with a staged or ambiguous event
why: A late reveal recontextualises a clue the player already saw.

text: Let the player reconstruct a trap or proof with movable objects or NPCs, such as a weight-and-string setup, so the mechanism is revealed and confirmed by their own physical actions.
when: designing a trap set-piece or proof puzzle in a generated level or dungeon
why: A physical reveal can be seen and tested in the world, and performing the test lets the player confirm the mechanism.

text: Cleaning removes earlier marks from a surface, so evidence may be absent wherever a floor has been washed.
when: Evidence depends on marks on a surface that may have been cleaned
why: Washing eliminates the impressions that would otherwise persist

text: Place a body or object away from the true origin; fragments, fibres or ash matched to a room layout, or timing and lock clues, reveal where the event really happened.
when: building a puzzle where the crime scene and origin differ; designing a dungeon where a false location draws the player first
why: Fragments and residue in the first room point the player to the real location, and a convincing false room is exposed by timing or lock details.

text: Stage a plausible external attack hiding a swapped body, object or added evidence; a forensic or identifying-mark check of the body reveals the staging.
when: generating a staged crime scene
why: Identifying marks and forensic checks give the player a test the staged scene cannot easily fake.

text: Identifying a device's maker links the object to a specific source and a known person.
Reason from how a trap device works to a likely method for an earlier crime with a similar mechanism.
Make a crime scene's disorder match the claimed event, and give players a contradiction between neat display and violent backstory to detect through inspection.
when: designing a staged or disputed scene
why: mismatch lets players detect staging

text: Place flammable props beside a light source in procedural scenes, so players can infer an accident from burn patterns.
A crime-scene system can store drag marks, prints, hair samples and posture so players must reconstruct events from them.
Present a room's event as layers of sound, light and object position, each witnessed from a different spot, so players must combine them to reconstruct what happened.
when: designing an investigation puzzle room

text: Encode past events in room geometry, such as a stain pattern on bare stone or a rug edge that marks where something fell, so players can read what happened.
Attach a plausible institutional verdict, such as a diagnosis or coroner's ruling, to an unresolved encounter so players can accept or contest it.
Use a corpse with false identifiers, plus a missing-companion clue, as an identity puzzle that unlocks the truth when the companion is found.
when: generating a body discovery puzzle
why: A mismatched companion exposes that the identifiers were planted or wrong.

text: Place a victim's message, such as a scrawl on a wall, in a room the player must decode.
when: adding a late clue to a generated room
why: Decoding the message makes the player an active participant in the reveal.

text: Build a locked-room puzzle whose apparent victim or intruder is inverted by a late artifact that contradicts the first scene.
when: Designing a locked-room scenario.
why: A late contradiction forces the player to revise the whole picture of the crime.

text: Seed a locked room with objects that support two readings, such as an open window that fits an intruder or an insider, and reveal the true reading after a second event.
when: Generating a mansion or interior level with a mystery.
why: A second event forces the player to re-read the same scene, which keeps the mystery alive.

text: Leave a cause of death as an open puzzle with partial evidence, allowing more than one valid resolution.
when: Designing an investigation whose outcome should depend on player inference.
why: Partial evidence supports several conclusions, so the player's reasoning determines the outcome.

text: A cleanup action that removes each trace with some chance of missing one leaves a surviving trace that becomes the clue.
when: When designing evidence removal in a level.
why: Imperfect removal produces residual evidence the player can find.

text: A trail of blood on plants and disturbed ground can lead a player to a body, using the same trace system as vehicle tracks.
A cleaning NPC who erases traces adds a time limit to an evidence-gathering stage, since clues vanish unless collected first.
when: Designing an evidence stage where traces can be removed
why: Removal of traces creates urgency to collect them before they disappear

text: Model corpse examination as a sequence of actions, each recording a state change that police NPCs can detect, so careless handling leaves a trace.
when: When designing investigation interactions with a game corpse or scene.
why: Recorded state changes let the game judge whether the player preserved the scene.

text: A generated crime scene with a dismissed official explanation and hidden traces forces the player to re-read the room.
when: generating a scene meant for investigation
why: Traces the official explanation ignores reward the player who looks again.

text: A loose floor tile or turned rug can conceal a stash, and an NPC's admission can unlock access to it.
Traces such as leftover food or ash can be checked against a second occupant, letting players prove a hidden person was present.
Reproducing a suspected event with an identical prop and a matching disposal device can produce damage that matches the original scene, proving how the scene was made.
when: An early physical mark was dismissed and the player needs to prove its origin.
why: A test with the same object and method leaves the same mark, which confirms the mechanism that produced it.

text: Shot range can be estimated from the force that carries the bullet to a wall and from the absence of powder marks on the target; a shot with no powder marks suggests more than a few feet of distance.
when: Estimating how far a shooter stood from a target
why: Powder residue burns onto close targets and is absent at longer range

text: The army Colt bullet weighs 230 grains and the ordinary Colt bullet 200 grains, so bullet weight can distinguish pistol types.
when: Identifying which pistol fired a recovered bullet
why: Different pistol types use bullets of different standard weights

text: Light, a sudden flare, or a noise can disrupt a concealed effect, and a device that slips or shows under movement can reveal the trick.
when: Relying on a concealed mechanism during a performance.
why: Environmental change and movement expose the hidden mechanism.

text: 1) Take in the scene as a whole. 2) Record its facts in order. 3) Then hunt for traces. The scene itself becomes evidence, so the order of inspection matters.
when: investigating a scene
why: order of inspection preserves evidence

text: 1) Sort incidents by victim. 2) Check whether incidents fall in the same period. 3) List everyone with access. 4) Ask who knows the target best. 5) Write the answers down.
when: A set of incidents has several victims and several people with access
why: Mapping victims, timing and access shows which accounts are consistent

text: 1) Hold the object by a handle that avoids contact. 2) Dust it with fine powder that sticks to oily residue. 3) Tap to spread the powder. 4) Blow off the surplus. 5) Photograph the revealed ridges.
when: when prints are invisible on a smooth, non-porous surface
why: powder adheres to the oily residue a touch leaves behind

text: 1) Replay the scene in its real layout, with the same rooms, connections and stops. 2) Play each participant in turn, so every person's view of the others is tested. 3) Note any timing or access flaw the replay exposes. 4) Check door and access states directly rather than trusting reports.
when: Use when a theory depends on movement, timing or who could reach which space.
why: Physical replay exposes timing and access problems that reading a written account misses.

text: 1) Close the exits and post guards at every door. 2) Cover the outside routes. 3) Keep the audience seated and rope off standing spectators. 4) Check each person individually. 5) Isolate the body and performers.
when: A crime occurs in a closed public venue and witnesses must stay available.
why: Sealing exits and tracking each person prevents suspects leaving and keeps the scene intact.

text: 1) Narrate the culprit's preparations in order. 2) Continue through the act itself. 3) End with the escape, so each step's role is visible.
when: when revealing a complex plan at a mystery's climax

text: 1) Label each past crime in a game's history as impulsive or premeditated. 2) Mark impulsive crimes with disorderly traces. 3) Mark premeditated crimes with preparation and tools placed in advance. 4) Let the player infer intent from the scene.
when: When generating a game world with a history of crimes the player investigates.
why: Scene evidence lets the player reason about intent from physical setup rather than from stated motives.

text: 1) Examine fragment fibres under magnification. 2) Build a reference set of samples from many paper types to show how rare the fibre type is. 3) Collect samples from every candidate source. 4) Compare fragment to each sample.
when: A document is destroyed but material fragments remain.
why: Matching needs a complete comparison set so rarity is meaningful.

text: 1) Examine both sides of a fragment before identifying it. 2) Compare its surface features with known methods. 3) Identify the technique from residue, not the person.
when: Fragments are found where prints are absent.
why: A smooth backing can resemble a glove, so one side alone may mislead.

text: 1) Build a sealed room with a death whose mechanism is not visible. 2) Place the objects needed to reconstruct it inside the room. 3) Let the player assemble the mechanism from those objects.
when: when creating a locked-room or impossible-death scenario
why: The player solves the impossibility through reconstruction rather than guesswork.

text: 1) Let a suspect die or be removed before the full explanation. 2) Place remaining props and contrivances in the level. 3) Require the player to rebuild the mechanism from those props.
when: Designing a late reveal in a level with a removed suspect
why: Reconstruction from remaining props turns the reveal into a deduction the player performs.

text: 1) Place a corpse with personal effects. 2) Place a living figure carrying matching effects elsewhere. 3) Require the player to match the effects to identify who is dead.
when: generating an identification puzzle around a body
why: Personal effects that can be carried by someone else turn identification into an inference the player must make.

text: 1) Place a personal object on a body that identifies the victim. 2) Make it visible but unread by the player. 3) Have the reveal read it as the identity key.
when: generating a corpse whose identity must be reconciled
why: A visible but unread object lets the player overlook the identity key until the reveal.

text: 1) Place objects where a struggle would leave them. 2) Let the player infer the sequence of events from their positions. 3) Arrange positions so only one reconstruction fits them.
when: generating the aftermath of a past fight
why: Player inference from positions supports deduction of the sequence of events.

text: 1) Model the scene as seats, objects and timestamps the player can cross-check. 2) Place one deliberately mismatched item that resolves later. 3) Stage a forged lure that draws the antagonist into a controlled room.
when: Generating an investigation scene with a hidden culprit
why: Cross-checkable details let the player reason toward a solution, and a late lure forces the antagonist to act.

text: 1) Provide a physical-match check, such as a bite or footprint. 2) Let the match give the player one solid anchor. 3) Let the player build the case from that anchor.
when: Designing an investigation that needs one reliable piece of evidence.
why: A single firm anchor gives the player a stable basis for the case.

text: Do not assume a recording occurred without evidence that the device existed.
when: a recording is suggested but not shown
why: an unsupported device claim is a guess

text: Ask players to match two independent traces, such as a fuel gauge and a receipt, so each successful cross-check feels earned.
when: designing a clue that the player must confirm
why: independent confirmation rewards reasoning

text: Record key custody as a visible log so that alibi claims, such as a claimed illness, can be checked against recorded movements.
when: designing a vault or locked container
why: Players can test claims against the log.

text: Let players challenge a coroner's time estimate with a documented modifier, so the stated time can be contested.
Before treating an out-of-place object as meaningful, check whether it could have been moved by ordinary means, such as knocked over during a struggle.
when: an object lies in an unexpected position in a disturbed scene
why: Some anomalies have natural causes, so significance must be checked against the physical layout.

text: Tag memories recalled after a cross-reference as possibly contaminated, so the player can weigh them.
A crime scene puzzle room can start with a guard holding the room and offer a short list of named witnesses to question in turn, logging each statement as a fixed record.
when: When designing an investigation room.
why: Fixed records let the player detect later contradictions.

text: Build clues that eliminate a cause, such as a search finding nothing, as sequential checks the player performs in order.
when: Designing a puzzle where the player rules out explanations one by one.
why: Ordered elimination gives the player a clear path to the remaining explanation.

text: Attach a checkable physical residue, such as warmth, footprints or a mark, to a supernatural-seeming event so players can test the human explanation first.
when: Designing an eerie or unexplained event.
why: A testable residue lets players reason toward an answer.

text: Lock a crime scene until its designated official arrives, and snapshot its state at the first witness's arrival so later changes can be compared.
when: Building investigation scenes in a game.
why: Locking reflects real procedure, and a snapshot lets the player detect what was touched.

text: A body-identification puzzle can let the player match a corpse to a roster, while planting one item that contradicts the body.
when: Designing a corpse identification puzzle.
why: A contradicting item tests whether the player checks the evidence against the body.

text: A staged crime scene should mislead guards away from the real target and leave a trail that can be checked later.
Build sealed-room puzzles from authored anomalies such as a bolt operable from outside, a key on the wrong side, or a gap in a timeline.
when: Generating or authoring a locked-room puzzle.
why: Each anomaly can be explained by a hidden action, giving the puzzle a solvable answer.

text: Build a false trail with decoy clue objects (decoy item, misleading key, misplaced body) pointing to a different suspect, so players must test each clue and revise their reading.
when: Designing investigation puzzles with red herrings or generating clue sets for a mystery
why: Players must verify clues rather than accept them at face value; forced revision makes clues do more than simple collection.

text: Place a decoy and an original in the same room so the player must compare and physically test which is wrong; a common prop can hide the key item that testing reveals.
when: Designing hidden-item puzzles or generated rooms that contain a target item
why: Players must compare and physically test objects rather than just search containers or trust a resembling object.

text: Design harassment or traps that look random but all guard one item or chamber, so a player who spots the shared target solves the puzzle.
when: When designing enemy encounters that should feel like a pattern
why: A hidden common target turns scattered hazards into a discoverable clue.

text: Hide a key item inside a decoy object, such as an ornament, that the player can inspect only after an identity puzzle is solved.
when: Placing items that depend on earlier puzzles.
why: Gating inspection ties the item's discovery to the puzzle's progress.

text: Place a burned or damaged decoy in a secondary location so the player wrongly concludes that the main item is gone.
when: Designing a search route around a key item.
why: A visible loss ends further search, so the decoy redirects the player's effort.

text: A generated level can present a convincing culprit and a sealed room that seems to confirm them, then reverse the belief through a later clue.
when: generating a mystery-driven level
why: The later clue reframes the earlier evidence, producing the same belief shift as a written plot.

text: 1) Build a misleading clue against a second NPC. 2) Make it plausible. 3) Provide a timeline or witness that can check it. This lets players separate true leads from red herrings.
when: Designing clues that point at a second NPC in a mystery
why: Checkable clues let players distinguish truth from deflection

text: Plant a convenient suspect or object early, then build a reveal in which it explains only part of the evidence.
when: when designing a mystery's misdirection
why: A partial explanation misleads the player while leaving a fair path to the real answer.

text: Schedule an innocent NPC inside a suspect's window so the player must resolve the overlap as a red herring.
Place a decoy clue set in a distant area and make the true site reachable only after the player reconsiders the first clue.
when: generated investigation maps

text: Make a lookalike or disguise puzzle hinge on a lasting trait, such as a scar or ring, not outfit or name, matched across rooms to unlock the true identity.
when: When designing identity-based puzzles or NPC mix-ups where rooms have NPCs under different names.
why: Lasting traces remain reliable while outfits and names can be swapped or copied.

text: Make a rescuer NPC who helps the party and is the boss in disguise, giving him one visible combat act and one tangible tell, such as an object he handled.
when: generating a hidden-boss encounter
why: Helpful behaviour lowers suspicion while the tell allows later detection

text: Use a twin or lookalike NPC for a two-stage identity reveal: a disguise item first, then a written record that confirms the link.
when: Generating a dungeon with a mystery NPC.
why: A lookalike explains an apparent contradiction, and a record makes the link verifiable.

text: Give a disguised NPC a checkable record, such as a gate log or register, so a player who questions the identity can break the false alibi.
when: Designing an NPC disguise a player can investigate.
why: A time-stamped record turns a suspicion into a verifiable test.

text: A physical marker, such as a name or brooch, or a mismatched item, reveals that one character was substituted for another, contradicting the player's assumed identity without a cutscene.
when: Generating identity-based puzzles or hidden-character encounters.
why: The marker contradicts the assumption; the changed physical clue lets players deduce the substitution through inspection.

text: A generated character's identity can be drawn from a set of traits, letting the player's evidence determine which trait is true.
when: generating a suspect whose identity is revealed through play
why: Evidence-driven resolution lets the same generated character support multiple readings.

text: Each new item the player finds for the same name unlocks a deeper identity, so one name becomes a ladder of reveals.
A recognition signal that is easy to copy can be used by someone else, so the identifier needs to be hard to replicate.
when: Designing a meeting token or password.
why: Anyone who sees the signal can reproduce it and pass as the intended contact.

text: 1) Present a corpse with disputed identity, or spawn several NPCs who each claim it. 2) Give the player identity marks such as scars, teeth or hair. 3) Let the player match or test each claim against the marks; the matched result decides identity.
when: Generating a corpse-identification encounter or body-swap puzzle.
why: Testing competing claims against checkable marks turns identification into a solvable player task.

text: 1) Give two people matching halves of a symbol, such as complementary marks on paired objects. 2) Have each carry one half. 3) Let them identify each other by matching the halves in a crowd.
when: Two characters must find each other among many people without speaking openly.
why: A matched pair of marks lets strangers verify identity quickly and discreetly.

text: 1) Place an NPC performing an ordinary task near the victim's room. 2) Make the NPC wear the victim's costume. 3) Let the player discover the costume only after the victim's time of death has been estimated.
when: Generating a scene where a disguised NPC delays discovery of a body.
why: Delaying the costume reveal keeps the time-of-death estimate misleading until the player checks it.

text: 1) Let an NPC aid the player. 2) Tie the NPC's hidden identity to an object the player already holds. 3) Reveal the identity when the player checks that object against the scene.
when: Designing an ally whose true role is hidden in plain view.
why: The player uncovers the truth through an item they already control, not through exposition.

text: Give NPC disguises consistent fixed features, such as a nose, teeth or gait, that a perceptive player can notice.
when: when generating or designing disguised characters
why: Consistent features reward attentive players with a way to recognise a disguised character.

text: A naming generator should reject names that exactly rearrange existing character or faction names, unless the anagram is intended as a clue.
when: Generating names for NPCs, bosses or factions.
why: Accidental anagrams create false or confusing links.

text: Give each disguised NPC a hidden faction or floor and a recurring tell, so the player can identify its group across the level set.
Store a feud or old debt in a generated archive so that a late room unlocks the reason behind a character's behaviour.
when: generating backstory the player discovers late
why: Archived history gives a late room a payoff without relying on dialogue alone.

text: Use forged messages to split the party, with a detectable detail such as an NPC's handwriting for the player to spot the fake.
when: creating a split-party mid-game event
why: A detectable detail rewards attentive play

text: Hide a second text layer on a container that is revealed only when the player applies heat or light to it.
when: Placing readable documents or containers in a level.
why: A hidden layer rewards experimentation and turns an inspection action into a discovery.

text: Messages sent by telegraph or courier can take time to arrive, so a request and its answer are separated by a short wait.
when: Designing communication between distant characters.
why: Transit time creates a pacing gap between asking and receiving.

text: Chain forged or edited papers across rooms, each traceable to its room and retiring a prior theory, or stack correcting documents in one secure container.
when: Placing story documents in a level.
why: Each correction changes the player's belief in turn, which sets the pace of the reversal.

text: Place the same sigil on several persistent objects across the map, such as carts, tabards or banners, so players can link an unseen figure to a known faction.
when: Designing masked NPCs that should be traceable.
why: Repeated, persistent marks let players build a match over time.

text: Write lore entries as unreliable oral accounts and tell the player the tale may be partly true.
when: Designing lore for a generated or authored world.
why: Uncertain lore invites investigation without giving away facts.

text: Put the rules of an enemy or artefact into in-game lore, inscriptions or manuscripts before the player must rely on them.
when: Designing puzzles that depend on a hidden rule
why: Players can reason with rules they have already read.

text: Give a merchant or craftsman non-player character records of who commissioned each item, so the player can trace a dropped object to its owner.
when: Designing item provenance in a game
why: Commission records give the player a route from an object to a person

text: Date in-world notes by the game clock so they can corroborate or contradict later non-player recollections.
when: Designing records a player can find
why: A dated record made at the time carries more weight than a later recollection.

text: Let an improvised item replace a missing key, so its presence shows the key was lost before that point in the scene.
In a missing-item puzzle, place a duplicate elsewhere so the player must compare the two to see which one is out of place.
when: designing missing-item puzzles
why: comparison reveals the misplaced item

text: A dropped item or exchanged token can work as a signal between two NPCs, which a player who notices can interpret.
when: Designing NPC interactions that imply a hidden link.
why: Players who notice the exchange gain a clue without explicit exposition.

text: 1) Place a treasure in a fireplace or chimney base. 2) Place an earlier search that missed it. 3) Let the player find it only after reasoning about why the earlier search failed.
when: generating a hidden reward that requires reasoning
why: Explaining a failed search shifts the puzzle from looking to reasoning.

text: Make treasure or quest items convincing copies, detectable via a performable material test (scraping, cutting or weighing) or a clue revealing the wrong copy.
when: designing item-based puzzles or placing valuable objects in a dungeon
why: Forgeries make close inspection matter, and a detectable test rewards careful inspection.

text: Flag a set of items that match too closely, since a detection system can use the same logic that exposes repeated copies.
when: Checking generated content for suspicious repetition
why: Near-identical items indicate a shared template and can be caught by similarity checks.

text: Give the house an inventory baseline so players can rule out items that belong there.
Make an empty tomb or vault seem explained by a documented transfer, then place a journal item revealing the real treasure elsewhere.
when: Designing a hidden reward behind a plausible false explanation.
why: The cover story misleads the player until the record exposes it.

text: A dungeon's fake exchange works best with a sealed package whose contents only reveal themselves when opened.
Hide the motive, such as a buried treasure, under the scene's own architecture so the player must search the structure to find proof.
when: placing evidence for a treasure motive in a generated space
why: Architecture-hidden motives reward search and tie the reveal to the space itself.

text: Give a ghost-like or supernatural-seeming creature a concrete hidden mechanical or chemical cause, leaving examinable residue or scuffing so players can verify it before committing.
when: Designing supernatural-seeming encounters or monsters with a hidden mechanical cause.
why: Verifiable mechanisms let players test a hypothesis, which makes discovery fair and satisfying.

text: Place early warnings, half-sentences or inscriptions about a hazard, like a weak floor or dangerous room, and pay them off when a matching area appears and the line is reread.
when: Level design with environmental hazards or trap hints.
why: A fair setup lets the player connect the early hint to the danger, and the hint stays hidden until the matching area appears.

text: Signal a trap, ambush or staged lure with a small suspicious detail or recognisable warning cue, such as a sugared drink or dark house, that the player can notice before it triggers.
when: Placing traps or ambushes in a level.
why: Visible warnings give fair notice and reward attentive play.

text: Disused objects or neglected grandeur, like old fittings, worn thresholds or unused lamp hooks, suggest a past the player must reconstruct, including a missing occupant.
when: Designing an environment that should imply a backstory or missing person.
why: Traces of former use or contrast with present emptiness invite inference and make absence feel felt.

text: A slow-filling vessel or drip can serve as a countdown that triggers a door, flood or guard change, and players can measure its rate to learn it.
when: designing timed hazards or events
why: a measurable rate makes the countdown readable

text: Give a sealed chamber a rising hazard such as stale air or heat, so the player can read it as a visible timer.
when: Generating a room meant to trap the player.

text: Set a trap's trigger in advance inside an innocent-looking object, and make the cover action a minor visible event the player can notice in hindsight.
when: generating traps that must look incidental
why: hindsight lets the player connect cover and trigger

text: Use a sound cue with no response, such as a key turn met by silence, to build dread and make the cue matter later.
when: Designing tension in a locked or closed room.
why: An ambiguous silence invites the player to remember and interpret the sound later.

text: Let a hidden enemy or NPC be heard before it is seen, with its sound's character planted as a fair clue to its identity.
when: Designing encounters with concealed enemies.
why: Hearing a source first builds expectation and gives players a clue to what it is.

text: Place a visible background helper whose presence hints at the real source of a hidden sound.
when: Designing a scene where a sound's source is concealed.
why: A background figure can point toward the hidden source without giving it away.

text: Narrow a hidden location by elimination: a room flanked by occupied neighbours is less likely to hold a captive, since occupants would hear a struggle.
when: Locating a hidden captive among a row of rooms.
why: Occupied neighbours make noise and raise the risk of discovery, so the middle empty room is the likely choice.

text: Let room lighting create a shadow or reflection suggesting a presence, then let the player verify it with a light source they control.
when: Designing ambiguous lighting in a level.
why: Player-controlled verification separates real threats from light effects.

text: Give most spooky events in a game a traceable mechanical source, and mark a few as deliberately unexplained to keep ambiguity without making the system feel arbitrary.
when: Designing supernatural or ambiguous encounters
why: Traceable causes reward deduction, while a few unexplained events preserve mystery.

text: Place trip wires, fragile threads or pressure tiles in rooms and let the player check them on return, so a broken marker signals passage.
when: Generating rooms that an enemy may cross while the player is away.
why: Persistent broken markers let returning players reconstruct what passed through.

text: Use the boss's own tool or trap as the final hazard, so the encounter echoes earlier threats the player already witnessed.
when: Generating a boss arena tied to a prior storyline.
why: Reusing a known tool connects the climax to earlier events and makes the threat legible.

text: In a flooded location, leave debris and marine growth on a victim's wounds and nearby objects so the player can judge whether a death was accidental.
when: a victim is lost in water
why: Traces showing how and when a body was struck let the player reason about cause.

text: Generated encounters can offer several false solutions, each disproven through a different sense channel such as sound, blood, or a physical trace, before the true one.
Plant growth or item decay can act as an in-world clock, so the player estimates how long an item has been missing by reading its condition.
when: designing a missing-item or reset puzzle
why: a known rate turns condition into elapsed time

text: A hazard that causes the injury can be placed where the player must inspect a specific spot to find it, so the injury becomes proof of an environmental cause rather than a human attack.
when: A dying NPC or suspect shows an injury that reads as guilt, and the true cause is an unseen environmental hazard.
why: The player must examine the right location to discover the hazard, and the same injury then clears the suspect.

text: Reflective surfaces or mirrored panels can turn an apparent intruder into the observers' own reflections when the reveal is made.
when: A room where an apparent enemy is seen
why: A mirror makes the viewer's own image look like a separate figure, which the reveal then explains.

text: A hidden passage can be gated by a disturbed-object clue, such as displaced threads or marks, so players infer the route from physical traces rather than a map.
when: Designing a secret route in a level with environmental storytelling.
why: Physical traces give players a discoverable inference path that rewards observation.

text: 1) Place an NPC who seems alive or threatening in a sealed room. 2) Have the NPC already dead when the player enters. 3) Add small tells such as a stopped clock, unwound object, hidden face or stain. 4) Observant players read the tells as proof of death.
when: Building a discovery scene or encounter that reverses the expected danger.
why: Multiple tells let observant players reach the true state without it being stated outright.

text: 1) Let the player remove blood or clothing from their character during stealth. 2) Leave other traces that a later search can detect. 3) Reward inspection that finds the remaining traces.
when: When designing stealth systems where concealment is possible.
why: Partial concealment keeps evasion meaningful while rewarding thorough investigation.

text: 1) Tie a guardian threat to the removal of a key item. 2) Place the item's holder as an in-world NPC. 3) Use scorched or smoke-trail clues that lead to the hidden excavation.
when: When generating a tomb or ruin with a guardian
why: A trigger linked to an item and an NPC gives players a logical path from clue to source.

text: 1) Make each zone look safe on entry. 2) Place the real threat in the next zone past an apparent refuge. 3) Seed NPC tells in earlier rooms. 4) Pay off the tells in a later confrontation. 5) Add a collapsing-stair escape after the solved puzzle.
when: Generating a dungeon whose layout carries a narrative of false safety.
why: Layering apparent safety over real threat keeps players uncertain and makes later reveals earned.

text: Give a mysterious effect a mundane, testable cause, such as a human or trap, as the first hypothesis; reveal any magical cause only afterward or leave it unconfirmed.
when: Designing a curse, haunting or unexplained effect in a level.
why: A testable mundane cause rewards investigation and gives a fair first step, while the magical reading keeps atmosphere.

text: Script a haunted, cursed or ghostly event with a rational human or object cause, such as a hidden or sleeping NPC or moved object, that clues let the player discover.
when: Designing a spooky, cursed or supernatural-seeming event or encounter.
why: A discoverable ordinary cause preserves atmosphere and rewards investigation.

text: Place a small object or tell, such as a misplaced key or open drawer, that contradicts the obvious explanation or surface story, positioned where the player walks past it.
when: Staging scenes or generating rooms that carry a mystery element.
why: A visible contradiction rewards careful players without needing a hidden trigger.

text: Companion animals' distinct reactions, such as one cowering and another staring, signal hidden threats; watching a companion over a short stay can reveal which of two similar hazards is active.
when: Designing a haunted or stealth scene with companion creatures, or two hazards with similar visible effects.
why: Distinct reactions give separate cues about a threat without requiring the player to risk harm.

text: Use a light that appears or moves in a sealed or unreachable area to warn the player that an encounter is underway elsewhere.
when: when generating environmental storytelling in a level

text: Use a hollow-sounding wall as a hint to a hidden room, and let breaking the surface reveal the reward.
when: designing hidden areas

text: Clear gas or fume hazards through venting, giving the player a concrete reason to open windows or vents.
when: Designing gas hazards in a generated dungeon.

text: Mark key rooms with recurring uncanny sightings so the final location feels already occupied before the event.
when: when a generated level must carry a supernatural sense
why: Repeated marking primes the player to read the final room as threatening.

text: Place a small wrong detail at a level entrance, such as a misaligned inscription, that the player can ignore but that later matches a hidden room.
when: Designing hidden areas that reward attentive players.
why: Subtle mismatches let players reconstruct the hidden layout without explicit hints.

text: Use limited light radius, fog and smoke as deliberate design tools that make some details ambiguous, creating real uncertainty for the player.
when: Designing visibility in a horror or stealth area
why: Deliberate ambiguity creates tension without hiding essential information.

text: Build a hidden compartment that the player can test through interaction, such as knocking, to reveal a concealed object or creature.
when: generating a concealed area in a dungeon

text: Stage a dummy or mannequin over a blood or evidence trace, so the player must look beneath the object to find the real scene.
when: placing evidence in a staged scene
why: Requiring the player to inspect beneath objects rewards thorough search.

text: Place an inscription or portrait early in a room and let its text change once the player finds a second source.
when: Placing a clue in a generated level.
why: A later source gives the player a reason to reread the earlier clue.

text: Point to a captive's building with physical traces such as mud, footprints or a covered window, so the player can locate the captive before identifying the culprit.
when: When a hidden captive must be found before the antagonist is confronted
why: Location traces let players progress by deduction without needing to resolve who is responsible first.

text: Build a puzzle chain where a visible landmark gives a measured bearing to a dig site, with one offset that changes the result.
Keep one location or item unresolved after the test, seeding a follow-up quest.
when: Generating a reveal sequence
why: A leftover gap gives the player a reason to continue.

text: Hide a critical map piece behind a fog or tide mechanic, revealed only when the player reads an environmental cue such as soundings.
when: Placing an essential item or room in a generated level.
why: Environmental cues let a careful player find the piece by deduction rather than by search.

text: Use a shared container, such as a cup or flask, as the clue, with a short list of NPCs who could have touched it.
when: placing a clue that identifies the culprit
why: A short suspect list keeps the deduction fair and solvable

text: Hidden items can be recoverable from unexpected locations such as laundries, drains or vehicles, and a retained piece like a stamped label can identify the source.
when: Designing where concealed items can be found in a game world.
why: Unexpected storage points give players alternative paths to evidence.

text: 1) Place the hidden item inside a sealed container. 2) Give the container an exterior outline or weight that reflects the item. 3) Add a decorative layer that conceals the item but not the outline. 4) Allow the player to test the container's inventory label against the object.
when: When generating a sealed container that hides a key item the player must deduce.
why: The outline and weight give the player a clue, and the label is a claim the player can verify.

text: Give found items a traceable condition, such as an unremovable ring, broken trinket, unlabelled bag or initials-only bag, readable in inventory descriptions, each implying a different inference about the owner.
Hide a key or trace object in a decor container or behind furniture, revealing it only when the player searches a specific spot or performs a specific interaction.
when: Designing hidden clues in a game room
why: A targeted search rewards deliberate player action rather than random discovery

text: In stealth levels, let extra precautions generate records: excess cleanup leaves traces, and added locks leave access logs.
Give the player a concealed observation item, such as a mirror or camera, paired with a routine action that hides its use.
when: when designing stealth or investigation options

text: Place a concealed hiding spot near a bed or chest so players can overhear NPC confessions triggered by their actions.
when: generating NPC-driven dialogue scenes
why: Overheard confessions reveal hidden motives without a scripted cutscene.

text: Hide the final evidence in a container that needs a tool the player has already seen, tying a physical clue to the final accusation.
when: generating a late-game reveal
why: Reusing a seen tool links the clue to the solution.

text: Record which NPCs hold keys to each door and whether each door is locked at each time; let players find key copies through receipts or records.
when: Designing key-based access and suspicion in a game
why: Tracked key ownership and door state let players deduce who could reach a room and trace a path to the culprit

text: Let a small key open a container found elsewhere in the level, linking two locations through one item and using its tag as a clue to its origin.
Let players test a seemingly bolted door, since an untried route may still reach the bolt.
Scattering identical key items across rooms and characters forces the player to determine whose item each one is and what the pattern implies.
when: Designing puzzle or quest items that must be matched to owners.
why: Ownership and pattern become the puzzle, so duplicates add inference rather than redundancy.

text: An NPC guard or clerk can run a routine check that a player triggers with a plausible reason, unlocking a record or door without a key or fight.
when: designing a locked record or door
why: procedural trust in routine requests bypasses hard locks

text: Let a visible cipher or heat-revealed document be solved in stages, each stage unlocking the next map location.
Include ordinary furnished containers in the candidate pool for key items, not only procedurally hidden spots, so generated rooms do not teach players to search only nooks.
when: when generating rooms that hold a key item
why: a varied candidate pool keeps search behaviour from becoming predictable

text: In a locked room, place a decoy mechanism that looks like the way in or out; hide the real route behind it and let the player reveal it by testing.
when: Generating a sealed room with a hidden exit or entry.
why: Testing a decoy rewards the player with the real route and makes discovery feel earned.

text: Put a document and a locked container in the same room so the player finds the proof together.
when: placing a key clue and its supporting evidence
why: Finding both pieces together makes the proof credible and removes search friction.

text: Plant a lock's combination digits in an NPC's notebook or dialogue early, then require the player to use them late.
why: The early plant makes the later solve feel fair

text: A key or tool broken into two halves and found in different rooms requires the player to find and combine both parts.
when: Designing a puzzle that spans multiple rooms.
why: Dividing an item across locations forces exploration before the item can be used.

text: A locked vault can require two separate items: a physical key and a knowledge item such as a secret word, so neither alone opens it.
when: Designing a locked container or vault in a level or investigation scenario.
why: Splitting the lock into a physical and a social half forces the player to gather items from separate sources.

text: 1) Place a visible state change on the lock early, such as a fresh scratch. 2) Let an NPC or document later explain it. 3) Use the explanation to unlock a new route.
when: Designing environmental clues for a locked room.
why: A visible change noticed early and interpreted later rewards attention and feels earned rather than arbitrary.

text: 1) Require three keys to open a safe. 2) Hold only some keys with known characters. 3) Place a duplicate of one key elsewhere. 4) Let the duplicate's location drive the next investigation step.
when: generating a safe-room investigation
why: Tracing who holds a key and where a copy exists turns possession into a suspect filter.

text: 1) Place a locked room with a sealed main entry. 2) Add a secondary opening passable only by a small character. 3) Place a climbable object as a bridge to that opening.
when: generating a locked-room puzzle with size-dependent entry
why: The bridge and opening together make the small-intruder route discoverable.
