why: The cry contradicts the accident and gives players a reason to look for a human cause.

text: A single piece of evidence can support several competing conclusions, so a clue that seems to prove one story often fits an equally plausible alternative.
when: Evidence appears to support one conclusion but has another plausible reading.
why: Evidence is consistent with multiple explanations until further clues discriminate between them.

text: Ambiguous actions such as carrying a weapon or hiding a letter read as guilt of one kind, so they can conceal a true identity until a trap closes.
why: Players read ambiguous behaviour through the most available suspicion.

text: Emotional reactions such as blushing, evasiveness, fainting, terror, embarrassment or shock are suggestive but have innocent causes, so weigh them against other evidence before taking them as proof.
when: Judging a person's nervous or emotional reaction, including to a revealed fact.
why: Such reactions have multiple plausible causes and can be performed by a practised person.

text: The same gesture, joke, deflection or sudden silence can signal opposite emotions such as anger, grief or guilt, so weigh both readings before taking it as evidence.
why: One signal rarely settles its meaning.

text: An observer's sympathy or prejudice shapes which signals seem significant, so the reading may reflect the observer more than the subject.
A detour may be a deliberate stall to gain time or simply aimless walking, so players can misread it unless the game gives a clue.
when: a character takes an indirect route under time pressure
why: the same movement fits both intentions

text: A victim's silence about an attacker can mean many things, including shielding someone unrelated to the crime.
when: when interpreting a victim who refuses to name an attacker
why: Silence has many motives and does not identify the culprit

text: Someone already looking for a culprit may read a suspect's sternness, silence or dark smile as evidence of guilt.
why: Ambiguous expressions become suspicious when the accuser wants a culprit.

text: Trust in an observer's inference is weakest when the observer is annoyed or afraid.
A tell can be a coincidence such as heat, drink or lighting, so confirm it before treating it as evidence.
when: when reading a reaction as a sign of guilt
why: Ordinary causes can produce the same visible sign.

text: A lack of reaction does not prove ignorance, since both innocence and deliberate performance can produce the same silence.
when: Interpreting a stranger's failure to react to a name.
why: Silence is ambiguous and can conceal either truth or a performance.

text: A visible reaction from a target can be read as confirmation of a guess, but it may mean something else, so treat it as a signal rather than proof.
when: When interpreting a suspect's reaction to a hypothesis.
why: Reactions have many causes, and the same reaction can follow a wrong guess.

text: A strong reaction can point at the wrong person, so the first reading of a reaction may not be the full story.
when: interpreting a dramatic response in a confrontation
why: emotion can be directed at someone other than the presumed culprit

text: Observers who hold strong expectations tend to perceive and report what they expected, so a seen reaction may reflect expectation rather than conduct, and confident testimony can override checking.
when: a witness must identify someone or judge a claim; observers already believe a suspect is guilty; witnesses in a haunted or eerie setting
why: expectation guides perception, so the expected result is seen; expectation shapes what observers see and report

text: An investigator with a strong prior theory reads new or ordinary signs as confirming it, lowering the standard for conclusive evidence and making the account neater than the evidence supports.
when: after forming an initial theory, including a supernatural cause; interpreting witness behaviour or traces
why: expectation shapes perception, so ready-made conclusions absorb contrary signs; expectation decides which details count as proof

text: Examiners with a prior belief read unfamiliar or ordinary features as the sought mark, judging them against expectation, and treat a lack of reaction as confirmation.
when: an examiner holds a prior belief about the sign; a physical examination is guided by a prior belief
why: prior belief sets the baseline against which features are called unusual; expectation shapes perception and interpretation

text: Observers stop checking people whose presence or role fits their expectation, so impostors pass, ordinary workers draw little attention, and departures go unnoticed.
when: a person's presence fits the observer's expectation; a person is encountered in a familiar role such as a delivery worker or attendant; a witness expects a person to be elsewhere
why: expected people receive little scrutiny; expectations filter what is perceived; expectation overrides perception

text: Observers absorbed in a conversation, task, form or distraction, such as admiring a disguise, miss outside events, fail to challenge newcomers and overlook items in plain view.
when: engaged in conversation during a critical interval; busy with tasks or distracted; an inspection involves paperwork; a surveillance team watches a moving subject
why: attention is limited, so absorbing activity crowds out other events; recognition depends on attention, and attention spent elsewhere is unavailable for tracking

text: A sudden disturbance or striking figure draws observers' attention to the most salient event, so nearby actions or the person who matters go unnoticed.
when: a sudden event occurs in a room with other people present; several figures pass a watch point
why: attention is limited and drawn to what stands out

text: Expectation fills perception gaps: observers feel sure of wrong sequences, listeners infer unheard speakers, and witnesses believe they saw what they assumed, so separate sight from inference.
when: an overheard fragment is unclear; questioning witnesses about another person's movements
why: expectation shapes what a listener hears; memory fills gaps with expected events

text: Strong emotion or prior preparation makes ambiguous behaviour or objects read as confirming the expected outcome: innocent items look like evidence, calm as menace, inaction as help.
when: a witness has prepared for a feared scenario; the observer is under strong emotion
why: expectation shapes how ambiguous sensory input is interpreted

text: An observer who is alone, uneasy and expecting something may let imagination run ahead of what is actually seen.
when: a character observes a tense, eerie or lonely scene
why: expectation fills gaps in perception and reads ambiguous cues as confirmation

text: When a group moves in staggered order, with one person ahead, another following and a passer-by unaware, observers fail to see the members as connected.
when: Members of a group travel separately through a public space.
why: Spacing in time and position hides the shared purpose from casual observers.

text: Respondents under questioning adopt the vocabulary and details their questioners expect, so the story matches the expected one.
A player can know a change is coming yet still be surprised when it arrives at an unexpected moment, since surprise depends on timing.
when: a predicted change occurs at an unexpected point
why: knowing a fact in advance differs from having it in mind when it takes effect

text: People dismiss a sound that is routine for their household, even when it matters, because expectation filters what is heard.
when: a normal noise occurs during a crime window
why: expectation filters perception

text: A publicly announced event sets observers' expectations so that a real action looks like a continuation of a known pattern.
when: the audience already holds a settled expectation
why: observers read the new event through the old one

text: Observers focused on faces and doors overlook traces at ground level, so clues placed low in the environment are easily missed.
when: Players scan a scene for people rather than for ground-level detail
why: Attention is drawn to human figures and entry points.

text: Players notice an object in a state that breaks expectation, such as an open door expected shut, and remember it even before understanding it.
why: A violated expectation draws attention and stays in memory until it can be explained.

text: Seated players stand, walk and leave the table during long calculations, so brief absences are normal and easy to overlook.
when: A player is deep in a long decision or calculation.
why: Long thinking creates a natural break in presence that no one expects to record.

text: A detail shown during danger is registered without being weighed, because attention is focused on escape.
when: a character is fleeing or in danger when the detail appears
why: Attention is on survival, so the detail is noticed but its significance is missed.

text: People who expect an action to have an effect can show that effect even when someone else performs the action, because imagination drives the reaction.
when: when a claimed power is tested on people who know who is acting
why: belief and expectation can produce an apparent effect without the claimed cause

text: A lone character is more likely to be noticed by whoever is nearby, so isolation raises exposure rather than providing safety.
when: a character is alone in a space that others can reach or see
why: a figure standing apart draws attention from anyone nearby

text: Those with close daily access to a person, such as an attendant, can notice hidden strain through physical reactions and signs of concealed appearance.
when: When a character is observed by someone who sees them in private, unguarded moments.
why: Close access reveals what a public face hides.

text: A long, silent stare at a clue with no guiding question produces no conclusion at all.
when: A player studies a visual clue without a prompt
why: The observer's state limits the reading.

text: A witness in a crowded or distracting scene often gives vague testimony because attention was divided.
when: When a witness saw an event amid many distractions.
why: Divided attention leaves weak impressions even of events the witness observed.

text: Reassurance and light topic changes can ease anxiety and draw attention away from an open question without resolving the doubt beneath it.
when: When an ally offers comfort or changes the subject during an unresolved investigation.
why: Mood relief lowers tension but leaves the underlying uncertainty intact.

text: A long silence before speaking makes a room go still and attentive, so the audience waits for what comes next.
when: A speaker pauses at the climax of a reveal.
why: Silence raises expectancy and focuses the audience.

text: A hidden figure rising from a space already shown empty makes players feel their earlier observations were right, rewarding attention.
when: When a reveal follows an earlier, explicit showing that the hiding space was empty.
why: The surprise validates the player's prior check of the evidence.

text: Observation means recording specific, countable facts that can be checked later, which is different from merely having seen something.
when: Clues must be gathered and used in an investigation.
why: Only recorded details can support inference.

text: A beneficiary's death can leave each survivor's expected share unchanged in arithmetic while narrowing the remaining pool of heirs.
when: when comparing the effect of a death on each survivor
why: the share arithmetic and the pool size change differently

text: Investigation grounded in systematic observation, not conjecture, is the method credited with opening the study of nature; it is not a rejection of all reasoning.
why: Observation supplies the evidence that deduction alone cannot.

text: Observing a phenomenon directly on first contact is hard, because suspicion must not be aroused in the occupants.
when: Investigating an event inside someone's home or private space.
why: Early observation risks alerting the source and ending the lead.

text: Use a decoy sting only when the method is rare and identifiable and the investigator controls the lure.
when: deciding whether to set a trap; avoid when the target would recognize the ruse or bystanders could be harmed
why: stings fail when the target sees through them and endanger others when uncontrolled; they are likelier to succeed when the target cannot practically test the set-up

text: Choose lodging that has sightlines onto the target's traffic and a separate private route for one's own movements.
when: An observer must watch a target without being seen moving in and out.
why: Sightlines reveal the target's comings and goings, while a private stair keeps the observer's movements hidden.

text: A character whose appearance contradicts expectations can serve as a disguise that lowers the observer's guard.
when: Designing a character who should seem harmless or unlike a stereotype.
why: Players rely on appearance to predict behaviour, so a mismatch conceals intent.

text: Watch a location unseen to learn who arrives, departs and connects, without any conversation.
when: direct questioning is dangerous or unavailable

text: Watchers who expect an arrival and keep checking for it cover open approaches, so attention matters as much as line of sight.
when: When judging whether an approach could have gone unseen
why: A watcher's direction of focus determines what they can detect, not just what is visible.

text: A stakeout suits a target expected to leave a known location at an uncertain time; it is less useful if the target can be arrested safely at its hideout.
when: when choosing between surveillance and direct action
why: Waiting for an uncertain move wastes effort when a safe direct arrest is available

text: An enemy can feign leaving, then return quietly to watch a suspected activity before intervening, so the player is caught in the act.
why: Watching first confirms the activity and gives the enemy a clear reason to act

text: In busy, lit rooms, NPC recognition should depend on their expectations of role rather than on sightlines.
when: Designing NPC awareness in crowded spaces
why: Expectation shapes what NPCs notice more than line of sight does.

text: After a search finds nothing, set a watch on the location, since a guilty character may return to it on their own.
when: A suspect has been searched at a scene without direct evidence being found.
why: A culprit may be drawn back to the place where the deed happened.

text: Once a reliable observer covers a place from a given time, movement or action there after that time is ruled out, so the possible window narrows.
when: an observer is posted at a fixed time
why: Coverage proves nothing happened during the watched period, leaving only the uncovered interval.

text: When a fortune-teller's checkable prediction fails under player testing, the town's regard for the legend should drop.
when: Designing a prophecy NPC
why: Predictions only shape belief if outcomes can contradict them.

text: A constant companion becomes background to an observer, so its loss goes unnoticed until the loss is very close.
when: when an observer is occupied with other matters
why: habituated elements stop drawing attention

text: A shared belief in an explanation primes people to read ordinary events as confirming it, so the belief helps produce the reported phenomena.
when: when a community strongly expects a certain kind of cause
why: observers interpret events through the expected explanation, so each event seems to confirm it

text: Enemies who watch a meeting learn who the witness is, so a witness's visible contact with investigators can make them a target.
A stakeout meant to catch a habitual secret act should run at least two weeks, across more than one night.
Excitement over a discovery can make investigators accept a theory quickly, skipping detail-gathering, or treat an ordinary sign as a decisive clue the environment could produce unaided.
when: a striking revelation arrives
why: speed of conclusion can replace careful collection of detail; enthusiasm can override baseline checks

text: Relying on expectation lets investigators overlook facts and accept leads matching the expected suspect type without testing.
Excessive self-distrust can make an observer misread clear evidence too.
Treating a failed physical test as proof of lying is a mistake, since a removed object can make a true account impossible to confirm.
Judging a person's state from a few moments of watching can mislead, even when the reading later proves accurate.
when: Deciding whether to proceed based on a quick read of a suspect.
why: Short observation gives limited data, so the judgement carries more risk than it seems.

text: A watcher who holds a steady gaze can reveal their own suspicion, because the watched party can read the watcher's intent in return.
when: A character tries to read another's face through prolonged eye contact.
why: Gaze and expression are readable in both directions.

text: Watching by a suspect can look like an accident and go unnoticed until the investigator checks for it.
when: A suspect is watching from a partly hidden position.
why: Surveillance blends into ordinary behavior.

text: 1) Choose a hiding place with natural cover and a clear view of the target. 2) Keep the target unaware of being observed, placing watchers so they see without being seen.
when: watching a target at a distance; a target will leave a known location at an uncertain time
why: concealed watchers keep the target unaware and let the team react to its movement

text: 1) Map the exits and sight-lines of the location. 2) Confirm there is no unwatched exit. 3) Take a concealed position with a view of the observable door. 4) Watch everyone who enters and leaves.
when: before watching a suspect

text: 1) Use a trusted contact to gain access to a crowded venue. 2) Observe the target from within the crowd. 3) Check whether the target shows recognition.
when: watching a target without being approached
why: a crowd allows observation at low risk

text: 1) State the reaction a person would ordinarily show in these conditions. 2) Observe whether it occurs. 3) If it is missing, the explanation must account for the absence.
when: a witness or suspect claims an event had no effect on someone
why: Ordinary human response is a baseline for judging claims.

text: 1) Write a complete list of expected people or items. 2) Match each recovered item to one entry. 3) Mark each match off. 4) Treat unmarked entries as leads.
when: when the expected set is known in advance
why: Unmatched entries point to the next line of inquiry.

text: 1) Hide behind a screen with a small opening. 2) Log each arrival and departure against clock times. 3) Build a timeline of visitors and movements across the watch.
1) Prepare the watch at the known location. 2) Wait for the timed arrival signal. 3) Detain the arrival before questioning. 4) Let the detained person speak first, before interrogation begins.
when: The trap relies on a timed arrival at a known place
why: Detaining first keeps control, and letting the person speak reveals their real reaction

text: 1) Survey candidate spots. 2) Reject spots that catch the target only by chance or from the wrong direction. 3) Choose the choke point the target must pass, not the target's likely destination.
when: Picking a fixed post to watch a subject.
why: A post on a required route yields reliable sightings.

text: Use a hidden vantage only with the authority to do so, and keep it concealed from the suspect.
when: Planning covert observation of a suspect.
why: Unauthorised or detected surveillance undermines the case.

text: Make failed leads return information, such as a locked door revealing a guard's post, and log open and closed threads in a quest log.
when: Designing investigation content where leads can fail
why: Information from failure keeps the player's effort useful and shows remaining leads

text: Show an NPC's expectations through dialogue so the player can judge which bait will work.
Place several observers so that whoever acts is identified by more than one witness.
why: a single observation can be disputed

text: Do not stage a decoy without an observer ready to see and follow the result, since an unseen reaction gains nothing.
Do not let personal feelings pull attention away from the observed person, since this causes the questioner to miss reactions.
when: While observing or questioning someone
why: Distraction makes the observer miss the brief reactions that carry information.

text: Keep a steady manner and avoid appearing to examine minutely, so that others do not change their behavior or remarks.
when: Inspecting evidence while others are present
why: Visible scrutiny provokes guarded or altered remarks

text: Audience reactions such as cheering, acceptance, laughter, or oaths and mockery signal a speaker's social standing, and listeners weigh them as evidence when judging credibility.
when: when a case is judged in front of a crowd or a speaker addresses a crowd
why: people treat others' acceptance as evidence; group reactions indicate social standing

text: A strong reaction in a shared space draws bystanders and can unbalance the witness, so the probe has social consequences.
when: the probe is made in a public or shared place

text: Other people nearby may notice an exchange and draw their own conclusions from it, so an observed reaction can spread.
Bystanders often ask their own questions about why someone is asking, and may hold back where the asker comes from.
when: A stranger is questioned about another person.
why: Curious bystanders weigh the asker's motives.

text: When an audience splits behind rival explanations, each camp rejects the other's theory and may refuse proof that goes against its own.
when: A public investigation offers several competing explanations.
why: Committed supporters defend their chosen theory against contrary evidence.

text: Onlookers accept a brief absence as ordinary but grow suspicious as the wait lengthens, turning confusion into rumor and scandal stories.
when: a character leaves a public gathering without explanation
why: A short gap has innocent explanations, while a long unexplained gap does not.

text: A group that falls silent and turns away on the player's approach signals hidden activity or a nearby concealed area.
when: A group of NPCs is encountered in a space.
why: Sudden silence and avoided eye contact read as concealment, prompting the player to search.

text: A person whose dramatic act goes unnoticed may doubt their own perception and adopt the explanation that restores their composure, even against the evidence.
when: A loud or significant action draws no visible response from the group.
why: People prefer explanations that protect their sense of self and calm.

text: Shared emotion between two witnesses can make a coincidence feel like proof of a connection.
why: Emotional resonance feels like confirmation even when it is not evidence.

text: The mood of spectators can run ahead of the evidence, so their awe or hostility shapes how testimony is heard and read.
when: testimony is delivered in front of a charged audience
why: Emotional pressure leads listeners to read implication as accusation before facts support it.

text: To test a claimed event, check whether the people present reacted to it. Missing expected reactions weigh against the claim but do not prove it false, since attention is directional and most of a crowd may have been facing elsewhere.
when: One witness reports a dramatic event that others seem not to notice.
why: Real events usually leave traces in other people's behaviour.

text: A suspect reveals plans in steps when kept away from others or believing no one can hear, so overheard speech can disclose details directly.
when: when a suspect is separated from companions or emotionally pressed and thinks they are alone with a rival
why: Lowered guard and emotion loosen disclosure.

text: Under threat or force, people confess to escape danger, so confessions track fear and questioner methods more than facts, and can be false, especially when reasoning from a theory.
when: A confession is obtained through threat, force or deprivation.
why: Confession offers a way out of present harm; pressure produces statements regardless of the facts.

text: Coerced statements may be shaped by pressure rather than events, or be wrong, so verify them against outside facts; a statement that stops at a boundary is incomplete.
when: A witness or detained subject yields under threat or pressure.
why: Pressure rewards speed over accuracy and can produce inaccurate, convenient or partial claims; stopping points signal missing information.

text: Pressure from a doubtful document or a credible threat of formal charges can move a reluctant witness to disclose, though the document may be unreliable.
when: A witness refuses to cooperate or stays silent while holding information.
why: Pressure from a document or credible consequences raises the cost of silence.

text: Coercive questioning often repeats in a cycle: the questioner demands every detail, the victim says all has been told, and the questioner insists there is more.
when: when a suspect questions a captive or weaker party
why: The questioner rejects each answer as incomplete, so the pressure continues.

text: A coerced NPC may report only partial truths, which prompts the player to examine the evidence personally.
when: when designing an NPC under pressure
why: Partial testimony makes the player look for corroboration.

text: A speaker who reads a listener's distress can stop, change the subject and hold back information, releasing the confession in partial, chosen parts.
when: A confession made to a family member or sympathetic listener
why: The speaker adjusts how much to reveal based on the listener's reaction.

text: Witnesses under pressure may recant or deny a confession when pressed, and coercion can be used to force a retraction as well as a confession.
when: A witness is questioned by authorities with a stake in the outcome
why: Pressure can push testimony in either direction

text: A culprit who has concealed all physical evidence may still confess under mounting internal pressure, when a private thought becomes a self-accusation spoken aloud.
when: Physical evidence has been removed and the culprit is under psychological strain.
why: Guilt and fear can overpower the wish to stay silent.

text: A statement made in delirium at the moment of death feels like a confession because listeners lower their guard.
when: a dying person makes an accusation
why: solemnity reduces scepticism

text: A host uneasy about a stranger often yields only after pressure from an introducer she trusts, not from the stranger alone.
when: when a host hesitates to admit a visitor
why: Trust transfers from the introducer to the visitor.

text: A witness who believes the investigator already holds the facts may concede details to protect their own position.
when: a witness is holding back information

text: A person asked to delay an action, with a reason given, visibly weighs the request before agreeing.
when: A witness is asked to postpone something for an investigative reason.

text: An odd question from a character early is easily dismissed as a joke, and players may recall it when a related clue appears.
when: a character asks an unusual question early in the story
why: the question stays in memory until a later clue gives it meaning

text: A person hiding a damaging fact often denies it first and admits it only when pressed on a related point.
when: questioning someone whose interests are at stake
why: Direct admission carries more risk than a partial or delayed concession.

text: Direct questions to a guarded person often get short refusals, while a playful, flattering tone can lower that guard.
when: questioning a hostile or reluctant person

text: A confession made later, unforced and consistent with the facts, is weighted as more credible than an earlier confession.
when: a false confession came first
why: it comes without pressure and fits the known facts

text: A controlling person can use isolation to shape how any accusation would be judged, arguing that it would be hard to prove.
A nervous suspect with thin evidence may confess when offered a lighter outcome for confessing, framed as a momentary lapse.
when: Evidence is thin and the suspect is impulsive.
why: Reduced stakes make disclosure feel less costly.

text: A free but watched suspect tends to circle the questioner, and a nervous one may eventually confess or act rashly through his own temperament.
when: a suspect is free to move, feels watched and is high-strung
why: the pull of the investigation exploits the suspect's own nervousness

text: Earlier minor acts can bind a person to later, graver acts they did not plan.
when: A character makes small early choices that seem harmless.
why: Each step commits the actor to the next.

text: A witness who breaks down under continued pressure may then give an account they first withheld.
when: Pressure is kept up after an initial show of distress

text: A suspect who has tried to appear in control may visibly react when confronted with a detail only the culprit could know, and then give up the account.
when: A guilty party's hidden knowledge is exposed by a precise detail
why: Recognising that the investigator has matched their plan removes the basis for maintaining composure

text: A detained subject may tell a long account and then stop at specific points, and questioning on those points rarely recovers the withheld information.
when: When a suspect withholds key information during questioning.
why: Some subjects hold firm boundaries that pressure does not move.

text: Players accept a confession as completing the case, so a later clue that reopens it lands as a surprise.
when: when a confession appears to explain all the evidence
why: The confession seems to close the question

text: A retracted confession primes players to distrust later confessions, so a second reversal lands more easily.
Build up an NPC's inner tension before a confession, so the confession feels like a consequence rather than an arbitrary ending.
when: Designing confession or self-betrayal endings.
why: Unprepared confessions read as convenient rather than earned.

text: Stage a formal questioning with observers present and the suspect in the central seat to raise pressure on a lying witness.
when: a witness's lie must be confronted directly
why: visible scrutiny makes evasion costlier

text: Pair a confession with an interruption that forces an immediate departure.
A person is more likely to confess when the truth is already known or likely to be found out, though this is a starting point, not a guarantee.
when: Judging whether a confession reflects real discovery pressure.
why: Discovery pressure drives many admissions, but not all.

text: Bringing a suspect face to face with someone close to them can produce a slip or confession through emotional pressure.
when: when a suspect's relationships are known and a loved one is available
why: affecting scenes unsettle the accused

text: Holding a suspect alone for days wears down resistance, so a confession gained this way may be hurried rather than true and needs checking.
when: before an emotional interview
why: isolation erodes resistance

text: Confessions multiply accusations: a statement given for release names accomplices, and each confession raises belief in the plot, drawing in more accusers.
when: A suspect is pressed for a statement that promises release.
why: Questioners' expectations shape content and each named person adds further accusations.

text: A statement given over repeated sessions can grow more extravagant each time, so comparing transcripts across sessions reveals coaching.
when: A confession is taken in several sessions on different days.
why: Each session builds on the prompts of the last, adding detail that the earlier version lacked.

text: Confessions obtained after the charges were read aloud may reflect pressure rather than independent truth, and should not count as independent proof.
when: when a confession follows the reading of specific accusations to the accused
why: the accused hears the charge and may give way under pressure, so the admission reflects the accusation as much as the facts

text: A deadline attached to a distress threat makes refusal feel like complicity in harm, pushing a reluctant target toward compliance.
when: when a request is backed by a threat
why: refusal is reframed as causing the harm

text: Under a severe personal threat and a short deadline, a group under pressure may confess in unison to the same claim, and the pressure, not the facts, produces the answer.
when: When a group is pressed to name a culprit under a timed, severe threat.
why: Fear of a worse outcome drives the confession more than knowledge of the actual event.

text: A confession extracted under fear is weak evidence, yet a court may treat the recorded admission as proof, and the accused often withdraw it before trial.
Confessions drawn out by affecting scenes can be unreliable, because emotional staging can produce a performance rather than the truth.
Frustration with slow progress can push an investigator toward harsh coercive methods, which is a sign of distress rather than sound practice.
when: When an investigation stalls under pressure
why: Stress shifts judgment toward coercion

text: Pressure on a suspect can end in serious harm, including tragedy, so a forced confession should not be treated as a neat resolution.
when: Writing a confession scene in a story or game
why: Coercion carries real human costs that a resolution can obscure

text: Public confession under repeated hearings can look like coercion, and a record shows only what the recorder chose to write.
Withholding a mystery's answer frustrates other characters and players and can damage trust, especially if the delay later fails.
when: when a reveal is held back for a long time
why: Players and companions expect progress and clarity

text: 1) Let the speaker hesitate and ask for privacy. 2) Release documents selectively in date order. 3) Hold the decisive reversal until late. 4) Produce proofs when the listener demands them.
when: when a key fact should change how earlier scenes are understood
why: Delay and partial disclosure build suspense while a timeline forms for the listener.

text: 1) Secure most of the facts. 2) Ask the room an open question aimed at the guilty person. 3) Let the accused speak. 4) Answer with facts they cannot dispute.
when: in a confrontation once evidence is largely secured and a confession is likely
why: giving a chance to speak pressures the guilty party without premature naming

text: 1) Choose a private place out of earshot of others. 2) Open with an indirect appeal to duty and to the risk silence creates for others. 3) Withhold full evidence and reveal a fragment to test the response. 4) Once confession begins, lower pressure, offer protection, and ask for the full account.
when: interviewing a reluctant witness who is likely to lie
why: Staged pressure and reassurance let the witness move from denial to disclosure.

text: 1) Have the subject fix an exact day and hour for their account, then ask who could confirm it. 2) Establish their ties to named people and places before showing related records. 3) Reveal findings one at a time, most damaging last. 4) Record answers verbatim for later checks.
when: When the subject will talk and each answer can be checked against records
why: Fixed, checkable answers let later evidence test them

text: 1) Open with a firm demand for the truth and state the consequences of refusing. 2) Ask narrow, checkable questions about a past event. 3) Link dates to test answers. 4) On visible panic, switch to gentle, specific suspicion and reassure the witness.
when: A witness is evasive about a past connection and answers can be tested against dates.
why: Each phase builds pressure, then narrows the facts, then lowers the witness's fear enough to confess.

text: 1) Open with the speaker's hesitation at the threshold. 2) Ask the listener to guess the answer. 3) Show the listener's reaction. 4) Only then state the explicit fact.
when: A reveal should be earned in steps rather than simply told
why: Each stage builds tension and lets the listener reach the answer first.

text: 1) Read your notes aloud to the witness. 2) Include a deliberately wrong detail. 3) Invite correction, which draws out agreement on the true facts.
when: Dates or details must be confirmed with a reluctant witness.
why: People correct errors more readily than they volunteer facts.

text: Record threats and promises made to a suspect, and tag any confession obtained by force or under them as coerced and unreliable; reward checks against independent clues.
when: Recording confessions in an interrogation system.
why: The tag signals that the statement needs corroboration.

text: Record who ordered a confession or apology and tag it coerced when an authority NPC orders it; sincerity shows only in that party's later behaviour over several in-game days.
when: A statement is produced under a superior's direction or social pressure, including designed NPC apologies or confessions.
why: Compliance and sincere guilt can look identical in the words spoken; ordered apologies reveal intent only through later actions.

text: When a final push draws no response, end the session rather than keep pressing.
Give the player repeated windows to press a secret NPC, and raise a tension value with each missed window.
when: an NPC guards a secret

text: Let a final suspect's confession reveal one or two mechanics the player missed, such as a hidden access route or consumable, while confirming the rest of the reconstruction.
when: when writing the endgame reveal in a game investigation
why: it rewards the player's reconstruction with new information

text: End a scene or chapter on an unresolved moment that the next scene must answer.
when: when closing a section of a narrative
why: an open question pulls the player forward

text: Let an NPC's final words encode a foreign place name, and supply a glossary or in-world map so the player can decode it.
Build interrogation dialogue in stages, such as appeal, reveal, bluff, pressure and confession, each showing tells like a fear meter or body language.
when: designing interrogation scenes

text: Make a confession option available only after the player presents the matching evidence.
Stage a village hearing with NPC witnesses so players watch escalation across repeated sessions.
Do not treat a silence or submission obtained through force as evidence, since it is not a documented admission and establishes no fact a third party can check.
Trust a confessed person's admission of their own act more than their accusations of others, and treat named accusers as leads needing independent verification.
when: assessing testimony in an investigation or trial
why: Naming others is less reliable than admitting one's own guilt.

text: Add a beat of silence after a reveal in dialogue, with an option to wait, so the player can watch an NPC's reaction before responding.
when: Designing a dialogue scene with a shocking reveal
why: Silence gives the player time to read the NPC's reaction

text: A full confession confirms the investigator's conclusions but removes the deduction, so use it only when the audience already holds enough clues to suspect the answer.
when: when deciding whether to include a confession
why: A confession that states the answer leaves nothing for the audience to solve.

text: A pressed suspect may accuse someone else to draw suspicion away, often with an early defensive remark before any accusation; timing and reaction to questioning reveal it.
when: when pressed by questioning, or when a defensive remark is raised before any accusation is made
why: diverting attention is an instinctive response to suspicion; fear of being named prompts early redirection

text: Confronted accused often counter-accuse, shifting focus onto the questioner; such rebuttals read as malice, and an accuser lacking complete proof can find the dispute turned against them.
when: when confronted before evidence is complete, or when a rebuttal names others
why: rebuttals naming others read as evidence of malice; the accused can reframe the dispute by attacking the accuser's conduct

text: Accused NPCs answer a player's accusation with a counter-claim opening a new dialogue branch; the accusation succeeds only with proof, otherwise dialogue turns against the player.
when: Designing confrontation dialogue.

text: Deflecting a direct question signals concealment, but it is not proof of guilt alone, since fear, pride or indifference can also cause evasion; weigh it with other evidence.
when: when a character changes the subject when asked directly
why: evasion signals concealment to the listener, but evasion has many causes and proves nothing alone

text: A guarded suspect may answer with counter-questions, humor or remarks on the questioner's restlessness, leaving the question unanswered; the questioner must keep returning to the point.
when: when a guarded character is asked about intentions or a sensitive question is deflected
why: redirecting keeps control of the exchange and avoids disclosure; humor and counter-questions dodge exposed points

text: Confronted with contradicting evidence, a suspect may attack its source: claiming a plot, blaming the informant, or saying investigators manufactured the evidence, rather than addressing the claim.
when: when physical evidence is presented to an articulate suspect, or a stated account is contradicted and its source is identifiable
why: shifting doubt onto the source weakens the evidence's force and redirects attention from the suspect's own story

text: A character hiding a fact can offer lesser scandals in its place, so the questioner collects many stories but no verified fact.
when: a character must hide a fact without appearing evasive
why: a lesser scandal absorbs attention

text: Listeners who correct a speaker's phrasing tend to scrutinise the wording and examine the substance of the report less.
when: a relayed claim is challenged on grammar or form
why: Attention moves to the form of speech.

text: A courteous, specific explanation can lower an audience's guard toward an unexplained entry, even when the only support is the stranger's own word.
when: An unexpected visitor arrives without a clear reason.
why: Politeness and detail make the account feel trustworthy.

text: Digressions from the main question often reveal tensions a direct question would not elicit, because the speaker is not guarding those topics.
when: talkative witness
why: unguarded talk lowers the speaker's defences

text: Grooming or checking a mirror during questioning can be deflection, signaling the subject treats the topic as of secondary interest.
A character who confidently dismisses ghost talk with a natural cause may be nervous, so the rational argument can serve as a defense.
when: When a character rejects a supernatural explanation with visible unease
why: Rational explanations can mask fear

text: A person under questioning may avoid a direct answer through silence, or by making a counter-demand that turns the exchange toward the relationship between them.
when: An interviewee has a reason to postpone the truth.
why: Silence and counter-demands shift the exchange and buy time without outright refusal.

text: A witness who does not want to answer may fill the conversation with flattery, physical courtesies, changes of subject and appeals to an earlier promise.
when: A person is avoiding a question they would rather not answer.
why: Charm and digression move the talk away from the subject, so the question loses its grip.

text: A suspect who offers a rival suspect often invents a motive for that rival to answer an objection, and invented motives tend to show strain such as hesitation and repetition.
when: A suspect points at an innocent party with a thin case against them.
why: A motive built to fill a gap is assembled under pressure rather than remembered.

text: A subject who keeps changing the topic may be steering away from the real matter on purpose, so the questioner should keep the goal in view.
when: A subject diverts a line of questioning.
why: Diversion can be deliberate evasion rather than a random whim.

text: A suspect who believes no trace was left may become overconfident, mocking, and careless, and may unknowingly leave evidence behind.
when: A suspect's confidence rests on a belief that evidence cannot be found.
why: Certainty that no trace exists reduces vigilance against leaving one.

text: A counter-narrative is an official or flattering account that fills the gap left by the truth, and the audience can compare it against earlier evidence.
A counter-witness is not automatically decisive; many defense depositions can still fail to overturn a prosecution.
Give the obvious suspect a counterweight of comparable weight, such as another suspect with a hidden motive, so the answer is not handed over too easily.
when: the obvious suspect has a clear motive
why: an equal rival keeps the reader or player from settling early

text: A counsel-like NPC can challenge the weakest link in the player's case, forcing the player to reinforce that link before accusing.
when: the player makes an accusation in a trial-like scene
why: the challenge exposes gaps the player must fill

text: A target who anticipates the investigator can reverse the situation by staging a false scene that draws the pursuer away.
A counter-narrative that contradicts clues the audience has accepted, without showing why, weakens the mystery.
A plausible alternative explanation, such as suicide or delirium, offered by a suspect can divert players from the decisive clue.
when: when a suspect offers a convenient explanation
why: a ready explanation feels like a resolution

text: 1) Collect the alibi witnesses' accounts of time and place. 2) Check the claimed travel against the schedule. 3) Weigh a precise, multi-witness alibi above a single witness's claim of an earlier meeting.
when: An accused person has an alibi that conflicts with a prosecution witness.
why: A precise alibi supported by several witnesses and a fixed schedule is harder to dispute than one uncorroborated claim.

text: 1) Find one half of an action. 2) Search thoroughly for its missing counterpart. 3) Record whether the counterpart was found before drawing conclusions.
when: a small trace implies a second part of an action

text: Use a quick-deflection dialogue option to flag a topic the NPC wants to avoid, inviting the player to investigate it.
Offer a character-reference NPC as a counterweight, so the player chooses which witness to trust.
Casual teasing among acquaintances often reveals personal sensitivities, because speakers do not guard what they say in social settings.
when: When listening to conversation in social settings.
why: Relaxed speakers reveal rivalries and tensions they would hide under direct questioning.

text: Unguarded moments, such as speech during sleep, can reveal what a subject fears more directly than deliberate answers.
when: A subject is not in control of their speech.
why: Without deliberate control, fears surface in speech.

text: Witnesses who glance toward a group, or mention a name, draw crowd glances and shrugs, and the crowd begins to read them as guilty.
when: When a suspect's conduct is observed by many people at once
why: Public observation shifts attention to the person named or glanced at, even before facts are weighed.

text: Witnesses may withhold information from social pressure, and silence can itself function as testimony.
when: Witnesses are with people whose opinion matters to them, such as at an inquest.
why: Social obligation can keep people quiet even when they know something.

text: A deliberate pause after a key point lets the audience fill the silence with its own reaction, raising tension without further input.
when: When pacing a revelation in front of a group
why: Silence invites the audience to supply the emotional response themselves.

text: Viewing a familiar image inverted can change its emotional character; a pleasant face may look sinister when seen upside down.
when: A known image or object is shown in an unusual orientation.
why: An unusual orientation disrupts recognition and changes the affective reading of the image.

text: Calm composure or warm, helpful conduct lowers observers' guard, so they search less carefully and stop checking the person's real motives.
when: A suspect is composed, or offers generous, friendly help to others in a group.
why: Surface calm or kindness reads as trustworthy.

text: Do not read a composed or lucid moment as innocence, or a cunning act or strong self-control as guilt, without surrounding context; the same signal can have opposite causes.
when: A witness shows strong self-control, or a lucid or cunning act is observed.
why: Composure under strain can be read as guilt or as grief, so the investigator should weigh context before choosing.

text: A calm, correct, formal demeanour is often misread as concealment, yet it may reflect discipline or reserve or hide guilt; record it as a lead, not a finding.
when: A suspect or witness is calm, precise and correct under questioning about a crime.
why: Observers read composure as hiding something, but calm and reserved people are not necessarily hiding anything, and impressions of faces are unreliable.

text: Judging character, sincerity or hypocrisy from composure or displayed emotion is unverified: restraint can hide grief, and open display can hide calculation.
when: Forming a first impression, or judging sincerity from demeanour alone.
why: Apparent feeling can be an act, as when someone performs grief or fear while acting coldly for gain; honest conduct is hard to tell from performance, so verify before it guides inquiry.

text: Do not read calm as innocence or fear as guilt: rehearsed composure and genuine shock appear in guilty and innocent people alike, and innocent reactions get misread as tells.
when: When judging a suspect or witness by demeanour, composure or fear.
why: Demeanour is weakly tied to inner state, an impassive face is a poor guide to feelings, and appearance, nerves and calm are weak evidence in either direction; observers read the same calm differently.

text: Make a witness's reaction a repeatable, animated trace the player can verify, such as words conflicting with posture or tone, not a claim the witness vouches for.
when: Designing witness reactions or dialogue that hints at hidden intent in a game.
why: A visible mismatch gives players a way to infer concealed attitudes.

text: When a precise question touches a withheld or sensitive fact, a witness may pause, flush, freeze or turn evasive, and the break signals the hidden point.
when: A precise question touches a withheld fact, or a specific event or the dead person's character is raised.
why: Embarrassment, guilt or a wish to keep something hidden disrupts composure before the witness speaks.

text: Observers' expectations shape how they read outward signals: silence may be read as shock, and a sudden noise as part of the show when it fits the expected pattern.
when: A witness describes someone else's inner state, or a sudden noise occurs during a staged or expected event.
why: Expectations and feelings shape how observers interpret outward manner and new stimuli.

text: Repeating instructions and asking for small signs of listening keeps a witness compliant during a conversation controlled by someone else.
when: an intimidating party needs a witness to stay silent
why: Small confirmations commit the witness step by step to the silence demanded

text: A small object left conspicuously unused, such as new footwear kept unworn, signals a person's standing to observers who know the norm.
when: observers share social expectations about the object
why: a deviation from expected use is noticed and read

text: A character may keep returning to the site of a death out of compulsion, even while wishing to shut it away.
when: a character is tied to the site of a traumatic death
why: A compulsion to confront the scene keeps it in use.

text: When an interviewer shows how much they already know, the witness may become suspicious and defensive, and may stop cooperating.
when: when an interviewer overplays their knowledge
why: the witness realises they have been observed or tested

text: A provoked suspect's involuntary reflex, such as a cry of pain when a marked limb is struck, reveals a hidden mark more persuasively than a verbal denial.
when: a suspect is safely provoked by a test on the marked body part
why: Reflexes are not controlled by deliberate speech, so they expose what the suspect tried to hide.

text: A witness's confusion, anger or sudden sulkiness when questioned about an observation can be as revealing as the answer itself.
when: When directly questioning a witness about a claimed observation.
why: Emotional reactions can expose doubt or concealment.

text: A brief shift such as a fading mouth line or relaxing fingers can reveal a reaction the witness cannot fully control.
when: A pointed question touches something the witness had not considered.
why: Involuntary physical responses betray internal reaction.

text: A suspect is more likely to concede once their own conduct needs explaining than when only the victim is under discussion.
when: Pressure is applied to a guarded suspect
why: Personal exposure outweighs the cost of speaking

text: Concern directed at someone other than the victim can reveal whose welfare a person prioritizes.
when: news of a harm reaches several people
why: reactions expose priorities that direct answers hide

text: Observers read others by their conduct, and a gaze, posture or passing glance is read as meaningful even when it may be incidental.
when: A character watches someone in a crowd or a social scene.
why: People interpret visible behavior as a sign of inner states such as interest or longing.

text: A character who repeatedly checks doors, windows and bolts, and keeps doing so after others answer, shows compulsion rather than a single precaution.
when: a character repeatedly checks entry points
why: the ritual persists regardless of reassurance

text: A person hiding something often loses composure first under a steady, penetrating gaze, so their reaction reveals the concealment before any admission.
when: When a questioner holds steady eye contact with a suspect.
why: Sustained scrutiny strains concealment, and the hider's composure gives way first.

text: A sudden shift from anger to controlled calm can show a person hiding emotion behind deliberate composure.
People reveal what they know through eye contact, voice, household mood, and the subjects they choose or avoid.
when: when physical evidence is ambiguous and the question is what someone knows

text: Shifting tone from easy to cold and back to light can make a suspect lose composure at the right moment.
when: when an interrogation has stalled
why: unpredictable pressure disrupts the suspect's control of the exchange

text: Decision-makers may count a suspect's demeanour as evidence, even when no link in the evidence chain is broken.
when: A verdict is reached by lay people rather than experts.

text: A detached, clinical manner toward others can be read as snobbery, which lowers how much people trust the observer's judgment.
Players judge an NPC's sincerity from detailed emotional display, such as flushing, stamping or unhidden tears.
why: Visible physical emotion reads as genuine feeling.

text: A changed glance or stern whisper from a character can signal a shift in loyalty, and the people close to that character may not notice.
when: A character's manner changes subtly during a scene.
why: Subtle shifts are often missed by those who are emotionally close.

text: Respondents from different groups answer with different strength and specificity, and those differences reveal who is sensitive, motivated, or suggestible.
when: Comparing answers across distinct audiences in a collection of statements.
why: Groups differ in sensitivity, motivation and suggestibility, so their answer patterns carry information about the source.

text: Players enjoy deductions drawn from a character's appearance because they display the investigator's skill in plain sight.
Judge a character's traits by repeated concrete habits, such as reactions to threat, handling of animals and manner toward others, not by claimed or performed traits.
why: Repeated behaviour is harder to fake than stated or performed character.

text: Judge feelings from several signals, not one manner or small act; a cool manner may reflect setting or strong emotion, and sleeping, grooming or murmured words can mean several things.
when: Watching a suspect through a narrow window, or judging after one exchange.
why: Small signs are ambiguous clues, not proof, and tone after one exchange can mislead.

text: Record a witness's emotional outbursts, requests and sudden shifts in manner between sessions as data, not noise, since they can reveal fear, motive or a rehearsed reply.
when: Interviewing witnesses, including across repeated interviews.
why: Behaviour under stress can point to hidden knowledge or interests; a bright change after grief may signal a rehearsed reply.

text: Pause to let a distressed witness recover composure before the next question, since a steadier voice signals readiness to continue.
when: A witness is in acute distress.
why: Pressing on during distress yields unreliable answers.

text: Read a speaker's fear and distress alongside the words to infer motives the words do not state.
Weigh a witness's calm demeanor against what was overheard, since a composed performance can replace an earlier emotional display and hide a shift in position.
when: A witness's composure appears after an emotional moment that was observed or overheard.

text: Compare a denial with the manner in which it is given; a calm answer that conflicts with a reaction to a name suggests concealment.
when: a witness denies knowing a person or event
why: manner and tone can betray what the words hide

text: A neutral, composed manner keeps listeners from guessing the answer early.
when: Withholding a conclusion from an audience

text: A witness's reluctance can signal that something important lies beyond the next question, and should be used to build anticipation.
when: Writing a witness who avoids a topic
why: Reluctance suggests a hidden fact the audience wants revealed

text: Posture, eye contact and avoided tasks are weak evidence of guilt; use them to decide where to look next, not who is responsible.
when: judging a suspect's behaviour during an inquiry
why: Nervousness and discomfort have many causes unrelated to wrongdoing

text: Rising breath, pallor, or glances toward another person during recall can mark where an answer is being withheld.
when: when a witness is being questioned in front of others or on a sensitive point
why: physical signs reveal stress that the spoken answer hides

text: Read a set of facts as one composition organized around a unifying idea, rather than as a record that includes everything without selection.
why: selection and organization reveal connections that a complete list hides

text: Weigh a source's reliability by how a claim was delivered, such as a withheld name or shifting reason, not only by what it says.
Choose a distraction that fits the actor's known traits, so observers accept it as genuine rather than out of character.
why: observers judge a distraction against what they know of the person

text: Track posture, sleep and appetite as indicators of a person's mood and state.
when: monitoring a subject's emotional condition
why: physical signs often reflect mood changes before words do

text: A concealing gesture, such as a hand placed over a gap, can hide a staged loss from observers.
Judging a stranger's honesty, conduct or social class by appearance, manner or company is an untested assumption, not evidence, and can mislabel them and lead investigators to the wrong suspect.
when: When an outsider or messenger is present at an incident, or a status is inferred from looks.
why: A first impression can be proven wrong by the outcome, and appearance and associates say little about actions; test against other evidence.

text: Reading too much into an adversary's courtesy or sudden change of mind can lead to a wrong conclusion.
A drink or visible nerves is not proof of guilt on its own; the reaction should be checked against other evidence before it is trusted.
when: When a witness shows strain after a probe.
why: Strain can come from fear, shock or stress unrelated to the crime.

text: A visitor's posture hints at the category of their problem, not at its solution, so treat it only as a starting guess.
A speaker who knows the people well still offers speculation, not evidence, when describing their motives.
A composed suspect can ignore a staged outburst, so the test yields no information.
A witness's calm composure is taken as evidence that the event was real, but composure does not establish that an event happened.
A companion's impression that a suspect was always with them should not override the timing evidence when deciding whether the suspect could have acted.
when: When a companion's testimony conflicts with recorded times.
why: Timing records are more reliable than memory of being together.

text: 1) Note changes in the speaker's voice and manner. 2) Notice any silence, colour change or grip after the news. 3) Hold back questions while the witness processes. 4) Speak once their reaction has settled.
when: Interviewing a witness after delivering difficult information
why: Reactions reveal what the witness knows and feels before they speak

text: 1) Ask what the sender could have seen or realised at that exact moment. 2) Test that explanation against what is found on site.
when: when a signal breaks off at a dated moment
why: The cause of the break is inferred from the sender's knowledge and must be confirmed by evidence.

text: 1) Note speech rhythm and whether it sounds rehearsed. 2) Note posture and grip. 3) Note eye direction. 4) Check whether the words match the physical reactions. 5) Judge only from several signs together, never from one.
when: when the words alone seem scripted
why: single signs can mislead

text: Treat a witness's flush, flinch, pallor, forced composure, defiant tone or posture as a prompt for further questions or checks, never as proof of guilt or honesty.
when: A witness's posture or pauses seem to contradict a denial, or a flush, forced composure or defiant tone appears, or reactions are used as evidence.
why: A single sign has many causes and can be innocent stress; a nervous tell such as an altered voice or averted gaze is not a confirmed lie. Reading it as proof of deception is an unreliable personal theory. Ask what the speaker gains by speaking and check against evidence before clearing or convicting.

text: Do not believe a speaker because you like their face, manner or bearing; check the account against records and corroboration, since likeable delivery is mistaken for reliable content.
when: A witness is persuasive or liked.
why: Liking a speaker is a common but weak basis for belief; demeanour does not establish accuracy.

text: Read emotional reactions such as relief, anger, fear or shock as responses to new information, not proof of guilt or prior planning, since grief, amusement and shock can look alike.
when: Judging a suspect's reactions.
why: Emotions are ambiguous evidence, and each reaction has many causes.

text: Confirm any hesitation, reaction or slip with a second probe before acting on it; a single pause or ambiguous reply has innocent causes and can read two ways.
why: A presenter's careful answers can signal a weak point, but one pause alone is not proof of guilt or error.

text: Let an NPC notice a witness's emotional tell and recall it later, linked to a concrete motive, so the player can verify it against a later scene.
when: Scripting NPC observations or explaining a suspect's reaction after the fact.
why: A remembered reaction becomes a verifiable clue that ties an observation to a concrete motive.

text: Judge an emotional display by what it is aimed at, not by how sincere it looks.
when: when an emotional appeal accompanies a question
why: a sincere-looking appeal can still mask a real motive

text: When a witness's reaction does not fit the obvious reading, test each assumption about what the witness knew and whom they believed they were seeing.
when: a witness reacts oddly to an event
why: a wrong assumption about knowledge or identity can make a reaction look inexplicable

text: Learn a character's established traits and beliefs before judging which behaviour is probable for them.
why: probability judgments depend on knowing the person

text: Do not assume a flat, unemotional witness is hiding something, or that an emotional witness is telling the truth.
Do not make NPCs judge demeanour unless the player can see the cues, since hidden cues make the judgment feel unfair.
Demeanour can be counted as testimony because listeners read composure as reliability, but nervousness does not prove guilt and calm does not prove innocence; check it against evidence.
when: Judging a witness during an interrogation.
why: Listeners treat a steady voice as a sign of reliability, but demeanour is weakly tied to inner state and cannot settle a question alone.

text: A puzzle solver may act oddly on purpose, such as swinging or dropping an object, to hide their method from companions.
In a crowded room, a swap of similar objects can pass unseen because attention is spread across many people.
Ill-fitting clothing, a high collar hiding the head, or sleeves without visible hands suggest borrowed garments and a changed appearance.
when: When a person's clothing does not match their build or role
why: Borrowed clothing rarely fits the wearer's body

text: Small physical tells, such as wax on a false feature that spots in damp weather or an unnaturally crooked shape, betray a disguise.
when: When an artificial feature is worn to conceal identity
why: Materials and fit behave differently from natural features under real conditions

text: A face seen once in passing is stored and recognised later when a new cue links it to a name, sometimes suddenly.
when: A person is seen briefly before their identity is known.
why: Memory keeps the visual trace, and a later cue retrieves it with the name attached.

text: A decoy can mislead the audience even when the investigator within the story has already dismissed it.
when: A story where the investigator sees through a suspect the audience does not
why: The audience has less information than the investigator and relies on surface cues

text: A character who appears to be the investigator's ally can secretly control the situation, and the reversal lands only when earlier signals and motives were shown beforehand.
when: Designing a twist where an ally is revealed as the antagonist.
why: Earlier trust in the ally's signals is what gave them control.

text: Attentive observers can spot concealed wiring or devices that look innocent, so concealment is a chance of avoiding detection, not a guarantee.
when: Players search a scene for hidden elements
why: Careful attention picks up small details that look slightly out of place.

text: A performer who believes in the role performs more naturally than one merely acting, so conviction sustains a disguise.
when: when a disguised character must hold up under questioning
why: performance from conviction avoids the stiffness of acting

text: A visitor who controls her appearance before a meeting can shape the first impression that a gatekeeper will report.
when: A character prepares to be judged on looks before an audience.
why: A reported impression depends on what the reporter sees, so presentation changes the outcome.

text: A widely publicized failed attempt makes a later real attempt look routine, so the real route passes unnoticed.
Absorption in playing a disguise can make an investigator lose sight of the meeting's purpose.
when: Maintaining a long disguised conversation
why: Attention shifts from the goal to the act

text: When targets realize they were tricked, they may react aggressively or destroy remaining evidence.
when: A deception is exposed while evidence is still at risk
why: Exposure gives the target a motive to protect themselves

text: Overacting in a disguise can alert the suspect before the trap is set.
when: A disguised character performs a role for an observing target.
why: Exaggerated behavior reads as suspicious and gives the target time to prepare.

text: 1) Change apparent age, hair, complexion, dress and social manner. 2) Apply the same change to any partner, including gait and mannerisms. 3) Test the cover by passing people who know the usual appearance and checking for recognition.
when: Preparing a disguised surveillance team, or a watcher following a subject through public spaces where known faces could be spotted.
why: A full cover is confirmed only when people who know the wearer fail to recognise them; partial changes leave cues such as gait or manner that familiar observers still notice.

text: 1) Note the suspect's habits and fixed marks. 2) Compare them with a witness who knows the real person's features closely. 3) Confirm identity only when the close witness agrees.
when: A look-alike may pass a casual observation
why: A twin or double can pass a casual look, while intimate knowledge reveals mismatches.

text: 1) Choose a cover role that fits the target setting. 2) Make its details ordinary and unremarkable. 3) Use the community's routine social channels to gain introductions. 4) Send findings through a private channel.
when: Investigating an insular community where gossip and introductions provide access.
why: A plausible, unremarkable cover opens doors that a conspicuous outsider cannot reach.

text: Observers fixated on costume may miss a constant feature, yet close or repeated observation later reveals hard-to-change traits such as the eyes.
when: Recognising a disguised or changed-appearance person: brief observation may fail, while close or repeated observation succeeds.
why: Costume draws the eye while constant bodily features go unremarked, but a costume masks surface features, not all of them.

text: A disguise covering one clue can leave others; writers and characters must cover every identifying trace, since one missed mark can expose the person.
when: A writer disguises one clue, or a character hides behind costume or a false injury.
why: A single missed trace can identify the person; partial concealment leaves traces observers can use.

text: Relying on one memorable or striking trait to identify someone fails, since traits can be hidden, copied or performed deliberately, and recognition may be delayed.
when: Identifying a disguised person by one feature.
why: The trait may be a deliberate performance, and a witness may need time to connect a detail to a person.

text: Judging identity by face or outfit is unreliable, since disguises defeat appearance checks and removable markers can be swapped; use a lasting feature or a different test.
when: Characters or NPCs must be told apart and the marker used is clothing or another removable item.
why: Removable markers can be exchanged, and appearance-based recognition is defeated by disguise.

text: Build, gait and fixed marks persist across disguises, unlike colour or size. Voice, accent and speech habits are contested: easily changed (avoid) or often surviving costume changes (use).
when: Identifying a disguised suspect or NPC from a description or observation.
why: Conspicuous traits can be erased by simple changes, while stable features and hard-to-change traits survive costume changes.

text: A calm, ruminative manner can hide an active search, so others misjudge how much the investigator already suspects.
when: When an investigator appears passive while gathering evidence.
why: Apparent inaction conceals ongoing reasoning.

text: When a face is hidden, observers identify people through durable marks such as clothing, luggage, servants, voice and manner rather than the face.
when: A suspect's face is obscured by veil, muffler, wig or circumstance.
why: Non-facial marks remain visible when the face cannot be seen.

text: A crowded masked event hides identities and lets people observe others without being recognised.
when: when a suspect hides in a crowd or costumed event
why: Masks and numbers reduce individual recognition.

text: People recognise a close acquaintance by face and expression even when clothing and setting change.
when: A witness knows the subject well and sees them only briefly.
why: Identity rests on familiar features more than on costume.

text: A witness who identifies a person may later retract under pressure, so recognition should be re-checked rather than treated as settled.
when: An identification is made and later challenged
why: Recognition from memory is fragile when pressure is applied

text: Let NPCs react to a disguise, an accent or an inconsistent story, and trigger a suspicion dialogue check when a lie goes too far.
Make disguise details like clothing condition, stated occupation or tagged items inspectable, so NPCs accept or reject the cover and a false trace, such as a footprint, can be exposed.
when: Designing a stealth or infiltration system with disguises.
why: Concrete, inspectable details make the disguise's credibility depend on player choices.

text: Give NPCs recognition chances based on attention, elapsed time and familiarity, so a disguised player is sometimes passed and sometimes exposed.
Identifying a disguised figure from a brief glimpse is error-prone, since the observer's expectations fill in details the viewing did not supply.
when: A face seen once in disguise is matched against someone expected
why: Expectation supplies detail that the glimpse lacked

text: A cover that depends on someone else's introduction fails if that person is questioned.
when: The cover rests on a referral from a third party.
why: The cover is only as strong as the weakest link in the chain of introductions.

text: A disguised investigator who meets the suspect face to face risks recognition, so the scenario must explain why the suspect fails to identify them.
when: The disguised character interacts directly with the suspect.
why: Without a stated reason for non-recognition, the disguise breaks and the trap fails.

text: A disguised NPC's wound or gait must match a medical or service record stored in the world. A mismatch can trigger suspicion.
Let an NPC recognise a player's name or item, and let that recognition unlock further detail in place of a face or description.
Prioritise identifying a target over capturing them, and treat capture as optional.
when: a watch aims to confirm who appears on a route
why: a confirmed identity gives the group more value than a rushed capture

text: Mask the scent of any metal in a concealed trap, since scent can reveal it even when the surface looks undisturbed.
when: Concealing a metal trap from a creature.

text: Clothing and silhouette are recalled better than faces in poor light, yet a quick costume change often goes unnoticed; clothing can identify but also mislead.
when: A witness glimpses someone briefly, in dim light, or with the face partly covered.
why: Clothing is more visible than facial features under those conditions, yet poor light makes a disguise easy to sustain.

text: Shock, fear, distraction or illness lower a witness's reliability, so statements made in that state need careful checking before being relied on.
when: A witness is frightened, distressed, unsteady, distracted or ill.
why: An impaired state reduces observation, recall and clear reporting.

text: Pressing a distressed witness on painful details can make them shut down and degrade the account, so keep them calm and move on when needed.
when: Questioning a distressed or grieving witness about traumatic events.
why: Repeated distressing recall harms the witness and degrades the account.

text: Tears, hoarseness, evasion or agitation may signal concealment, yet distress alone does not prove deception or guilt, since fear, shock or grief also cause it; record both readings.
when: When a witness or suspect is questioned about a sensitive matter or reacts to a revealed fact.
why: Distress has many causes, so the same cue can signal concealment or an innocent reaction.

text: Frightened, excited or fainting witnesses perceive and report unreliably, so their reports may conflict with calmer observers and need weighing for fear as well as accuracy.
when: A witness is under strong emotion during an observation or reports a sighting while frightened.
why: Fear and panic shape what is perceived and reported.

text: Observers treat an unverifiable claim as proven when the witness shows visible distress before them; distress lends credibility without making the claim true, so weigh them separately.
when: Witnesses suffer visibly before a group.
why: Distress reads as sincerity, which seems to confirm the claim.

text: A person in distress may not notice sounds or events, so a witness who heard nothing may still be telling the truth.
when: a witness reports no sound during a stressful moment
why: strong emotion narrows attention

text: In darkness, distances estimated by counted steps accumulate error, and one lapse in the count can reverse the whole spatial conclusion.
when: a space is crossed without sight
why: Counting errors compound over a walk

text: Sudden distress when a question is put bluntly can be read as dread rather than proof of guilt, and should be weighed as such.
when: when a witness reacts strongly to a direct question
why: fear and guilt produce similar outward signs

text: A guarded witness may show distress through color changes, eyelid movement or forceful repeated denials, which can expose what calm answers hide.
when: witness is emotionally guarded
why: strong emotion leaks through when composure slips

text: A person who hears a case built against them may visibly collapse, such as losing colour from the face and fainting.
when: When a suspect is confronted with circumstantial evidence against them.
why: Strong stress can overwhelm the body and cause a sudden physical reaction.

text: A grieving or exhausted character may notice a contradiction yet ask no follow-up questions, so the clue is logged but left unexamined.
when: A character is emotionally overwhelmed during a scene that holds a clue
why: Grief and exhaustion reduce the drive to pursue details

text: A frightened observer may explain away a sighting with a convenient cause, such as a shadow, and avoid closer inspection.
when: When an observer is afraid and then sees nothing on a second look.
why: Fear pushes the observer toward a reassuring explanation rather than a test of it.

text: When questioning nears the truth, a suspect may shift abruptly into distress, apology or pleading, which ends the line of inquiry.
when: A suspect has been caught in an inconsistency under questioning.
