why: A sudden emotional pivot shifts the focus from facts to the relationship, so the questioner often yields.

text: Terse, guarded wording that omits explanation can signal a controlled mind under pressure rather than a calm one, and readers sense the strain without it being stated.
when: Reading a written message from someone who is hiding distress.
why: Restraint in what is said and what is left out reveals tension that direct statement would hide.

text: After a shock, witness accounts tend to be fragmentary, self-correcting, and garbled, with frequent admissions of uncertainty.
when: Interviewing people soon after a frightening event.
why: Fear disrupts memory and coherent speech.

text: A reluctant witness who becomes curt and defensive signals that the question touched something they would rather not discuss.
when: Questioning someone who has a plausible story with one weak point.
why: Defensive reactions reveal sensitivity around the point being probed.

text: A witness who is pressed with specific gaps often shows visible agitation before the first admission, which signals that the gap was real.
when: A witness is confronted with a list of unexplained facts.
why: Specific, checkable gaps create discomfort that a general question does not.

text: A collapse or genuine distress proves the emotion, not that the witness reported facts accurately; judge emotional state and factual reliability separately.
why: Emotional state and factual content vary independently.

text: A confession mixing accusation, self-reference, an imagined second self, contradictions or a delusional tone, or made during crisis, may be false; check it against facts.
when: When reading a spoken or written confession, or a suspect confesses during a mental or physical crisis.
why: Strain and delusion distort the account.

text: Strong fear produces physical symptoms such as trembling, nausea and sweaty grip, which degrade perception and recall of events.
when: A witness or player experiences a frightening or stressful event.
why: Stress impairs motor control and the accuracy of what is perceived and remembered.

text: Distraction, confusion, fear or fatigue can cause witness error without intent to deceive, so a confused witness should not be assumed to be lying.
why: Attention moves elsewhere, and sleep, fear or fatigue distort time sense; such errors differ from deliberate falsehood.

text: Distress can make a witness's report sound more certain than their perception allowed, so the stated confidence should be discounted.
when: The witness was frightened or disgusted while watching
why: Strong feeling raises the sound of certainty beyond what was perceived

text: Once a world-level cause is established, each new misfortune is read as its work and suspicion forms before evidence is weighed, so later cases need no separate justification.
when: a world's governing explanation or single cause for all bad events is given before the mystery's cases
why: The existing frame supplies the interpretation later evidence is read through, absorbing every new event as confirmation.

text: When a discrepancy is presented as an open question before its answer, players engage with it as a puzzle and try to solve it alongside the investigator.
when: a clue is shown without an explanation at first
why: An unresolved anomaly invites active inference, which makes the eventual answer more satisfying.

text: A suspect's strong anger or indignation at being questioned is not evidence of guilt or of innocence.
when: When a suspect reacts emotionally to questioning.
why: Emotional reactions are common among innocent and guilty people alike, so they reveal little.

text: When a physical event seems impossible, people may doubt their own senses, asking whether they were awake or mistaken.
when: When an observed event contradicts expectations about the physical world.
why: Unexplained observations threaten trust in one's own perception, so people question themselves first.

text: Players discount trivia presented as color, such as a pet's routine, until a reveal reframes it as the method.
Players who receive only part of a conclusion from an ally feel frustrated and distrust the ally.
when: a guide character withholds conclusions
why: they feel kept in the dark and lose a sense of control over the investigation

text: Players learn to cross-check NPC dialogue against the world state when some NPCs are known to hold grudges that could color their statements.
when: An NPC with a stated grievance describes events or other characters.
why: Visible grudges signal that the NPC's interpretation may be unreliable, prompting verification.

text: Dismissing every strange detail as coincidence makes players feel cheated when a pattern later becomes undeniable.
when: When an investigation explains away unusual clues too often.
why: Repeated dismissal removes the player's trust that the unusual details matter.

text: An oddly high reward for pointless work signals a hidden purpose, so players feel the anomaly before they understand it.
A reversal lands hardest when the audience has already accepted a resolution, such as a pardon or escape, as settled.
when: when a resolution has been shown as final
why: Accepted closure makes the overturn feel like a shock

text: Players are drawn into each reading of shared evidence and reconsider only when the next reading overturns it.
when: a mystery offers several readings of the same clues
why: Each reading uses real evidence, so it feels convincing on its own terms

text: Without independent proof, players may act on a belief the accused denies, treating the reveal as a conviction rather than a settled fact.
when: the accused denies the secret and no one else can verify it
why: The discoverers hold the only evidence, so their belief drives action.

text: Offer the player two rival readings of the same pattern, each with a visible cost, so that choosing between them is a real decision.
when: Designing an ambiguous pattern the player must interpret.
why: A choice carries weight only when both options have real costs.

text: When a suspect group shares a belief system, the belief itself becomes a clue to their origins and aims.
when: When a group's members hold a common set of beliefs.
why: Shared belief reveals structure and connections that individual statements may not.

text: Accepting an apparent accident, suicide, or plausible explanation like mislaid papers ends checking early, leaving the real route undiscovered unless a clue shows an item left the building.
when: When an initial reading of a scene or a completed search seems conclusive.
why: A settled explanation discourages further checking, and a completed search makes the room feel exhausted.

text: Accepting an official or authority theory without testing its facts can close off the true trail.
when: When an authority's explanation is available for an event.
why: Authority conveys confidence, which discourages independent checking.

text: Making too many deaths look like accidents-with-suspicion causes players to assume a conspiracy behind every death and tires them.
when: When many witness deaths are presented in a game.
why: Constant suspicion exhausts players and removes the impact of the deaths that matter.

text: 1) Open with broad recall questions. 2) Move to narrow factual questions. 3) Check narrow answers against facts already given by other sources.
when: When a character holds scattered facts that must be cross-checked.
why: Moving from general to specific keeps the exchange flowing and lets later answers test earlier ones.

text: A believable invented opportunity or public lure gives a hidden suspect a plausible reason to come forward, letting the player force a confrontation on their own terms.
when: When a suspect is hidden and a public lure or believable opportunity is available
why: A lure lets the player force a confrontation on their own terms.

text: Once doubt is planted about a trusted person, the recipient tends to read later events as confirmation of it.
Outside possibilities, such as unseen watchers or contacts elsewhere, can pull attention away from the core line of inquiry.
when: Several leads are open at once
why: Plausible distractions compete for attention

text: An anonymous message with no named sender can steer suspicion toward a person the reader has had a prior encounter with.
when: the sender is unknown
why: A known acquaintance fills the gap left by the unknown author.

text: Confident, knowledgeable speakers attract trust, so a frame they offer, such as a lecture on a criminal world, can steer an investigator toward a false lead.
when: An expert NPC confidently describes a domain relevant to the investigation.
why: Authority and vivid detail make claims feel reliable without verification.

text: Players accept a false cause when each oddity gets a plausible natural explanation from a trusted character, so the real threat stays hidden.
when: Several odd events occur before the threat is named.
why: Each explanation closes the question before the player connects the events.

text: A delay can be justified by a future event that is hard to refuse, which buys time and keeps the truth out of reach.
when: A character postpones disclosure by pointing to an upcoming event.
why: A weighty future event makes the questioner accept waiting rather than press.

text: A character with a plausible emotional motive, such as jealousy, can draw attention away from the real question and act as a red herring.
when: A character reacts strongly to a situation unrelated to the mystery.
why: Strong emotion looks significant, so players may chase it instead of the actual clue.

text: People under fear often hear ordinary sounds as supernatural. Reattributing such sounds at the end reads as a misdirect rather than a second twist.
when: When a character is nervous or alone in a tense scene.
why: Fear magnifies ordinary noises, such as a shifting tripod leg or nerves.

text: Two individually weak lures that support each other can draw in a cautious target more effectively than either lure alone.
when: when the target is careful and would reject a single lure
why: Each story lends apparent credibility to the other, and their combination feels independently confirmed.

text: A false solution is more persuasive when it rests on real, sympathetic clues, such as a suspect's agitation or refusal to cooperate, rather than arbitrary evidence.
when: Designing a wrong suspect that the player is meant to believe for a time.
why: Grounded clues make the false theory feel reasonable, so its later refutation is more satisfying.

text: A red herring works because it is plausible and invites action, not because it is weak.
when: When designing misleading leads
why: Players act on leads that look reasonable, so implausible leads fail to misdirect

text: A plausible story can be built for almost any set of facts, so each step of a reconstruction needs evidence rather than being accepted because it reads well.
when: When an investigator has settled on a convincing account
why: Narrative coherence is easy to produce and does not establish that events happened.

text: Overplaying a performance gives the test away, so keep the speaker's behaviour consistent with normal talk.
when: When staging speech to draw out a listener
why: Unnatural behaviour alerts the listener that a test is underway.

text: Other people asked about a pretext may later reveal the approach, so the story must survive being checked.
Trusting prints that could be planted by someone who knew they would be read leads to false conclusions about movement.
why: A deliberate planter can fake a trail.

text: An official report presented as a finished solution can end the player's search early, so it should be checkable for contradictions.
when: when an authority presents an explanation as complete
why: a trusted source makes the question seem settled

text: 1) Identify what the delay gains the person requesting it. 2) Decide whether pressing now or waiting serves the investigation. 3) Test the delay by checking whether the stated reason holds.
when: An interviewee asks for time before answering.
why: A delay can be honest or deceptive, and asking what it gains reveals which.

text: Use a pretext to get an answer when disclosing the real purpose would make the witness refuse.
A pretext that exploits a known weakness, such as vanity about expertise, can draw a target into a location; it works only if the target's weakness is known to the lure's author.
when: Designing a lure or deception.
why: The bait must match a real desire to be believed.

text: A private conversation with no witnesses feels like candid talk rather than arrest, which lowers a suspect's guard.
when: An investigator questions a suspect alone.
why: The lack of witnesses makes the exchange feel safe and informal.

text: Publicly disciplining someone who investigates deters others from investigating, even without any physical barrier.
when: A community punishes an individual who seeks outside information.
why: Social cost works as a lock, so people avoid inquiry to protect themselves.

text: Enforce questioning procedure when public curiosity pressures it, so that testimony remains usable.
when: Public or crowd pressure disrupts an interview
why: Procedural breaches can make testimony unusable

text: Wait out silence rather than prompting: calm, unhurried pauses make a reluctant witness fill them with extra detail, and a subject may recover a lost thread.
when: A subject goes quiet or loses track mid-answer, or a witness has denied something and holds back a detail.
why: Prompting too early interrupts recall; silence creates discomfort the witness relieves by speaking.

text: Pressing a witness with anger, force or repetition can make them withdraw or invent a story or detail to please or escape, corrupting evidence; check any changed account.
when: A witness's account changes or they are pressed hard.
why: A coerced witness may invent a different story to escape pressure.

text: A talkative source who is flattered and deferred to becomes eager to speak and volunteers opinions about themselves and their institution.
when: Source enjoys talking and responds to attention.
why: Attention and deference feed the source's self-image, so they disclose more.

text: Pressure from authority figures in a formal hearing makes witnesses more anxious, which can change what they say.
when: Questioning a witness in a formal or hostile setting
why: Anxiety affects memory and disclosure

text: Pressure in questioning raises the chance of contradictions, including from innocent people.
when: A witness or suspect is questioned under strain.
why: Stress makes accounts harder to keep consistent.

text: A threat aimed at a third party can silence a witness, who stops speaking to protect that person and leaves her knowledge unavailable.
when: a witness fears harm to someone else if she talks
why: Concern for others outweighs the witness's wish to report what she knows

text: A composed suspect who has already settled how to resist can hold firm against emotional pressure.
when: when the suspect has prepared a stance

text: A witness facing a rushed, agitated speaker may keep a valid objection to themselves rather than argue.
when: a forceful, intimidating speaker questions a witness
why: Intimidation suppresses challenge even when the witness is right.

text: Vague hints that a resolution is imminent create pressure, which a skeptical observer may read without accepting.
when: Authorities or NPCs signal progress without evidence.

text: A suspect confronted with a detailed account may fall silent, then offer a partial version whose corrections expose the parts they most want to protect.
why: specific, checkable detail is hard to deny outright

text: A person who believes he has won tends to relax, which leaves him open to a counter-attack from behind.
when: An attacker assumes the confrontation is over.
why: Relaxed attention cannot respond quickly to a sudden reversal.

text: A witness's direct questions can reveal their own concern or which explanation they already trust.
A hostile party tests an offer by pointing out one-sided terms and expects an answer it can verify.
when: a bargain is offered to a hostile party
why: Distrust makes unverifiable promises look like traps

text: Pressing someone for hidden knowledge tends to provoke resentment, so an investigator's standing as an independent observer affects what they can learn.
Waiting feels longer than it is, so a person on a stakeout may believe hours have passed when only a short time has gone by.
when: when a character or player waits with nothing happening
why: Attention on an empty interval stretches perceived time.

text: Hinting that you know more than you do can make a suspect's reply reveal what they fear, showing their worry and what they are protecting.
when: When confronting a suspect who holds information back.
why: The suspect reacts to the implied threat before deciding what to say.

text: An observing partner who holds back interruptions and saves a question for later lets the questioner finish a line of inquiry without losing the observation.
when: A second character is present while another conducts questioning.
why: Interrupting a line of questioning disrupts it and can cost the observation its moment.

text: A reluctant witness may open up when the matter is framed as serious and they are among peers rather than authorities.
when: when a witness is unwilling to gossip or disclose

text: A silent, fixed stare from one character shapes how others interpret a scene, acting as a message without words.
when: A tense scene where one character says nothing
why: Others read the silence as meaningful and adjust their interpretation.

text: Blame-assigning phrases and conditional threats are pressure devices that try to control another person's choice.
when: a written message urges a decision

text: After a costly accusation episode, communities resisted renewed accusations of the same kind, because they remembered what it cost.
when: after a costly episode of unverifiable accusations
why: the cost of the episode was remembered

text: Demanding phrasing such as 'must' can provoke indignation and harden a witness's resistance, though limited facts may still come out.
when: A witness is pressed with a direct demand
why: The demand is felt as pressure.

text: A speaker who reads evasion as fraud or cowardice pushes the listener to reveal more than intended.
when: when a listener refuses to answer directly
why: Accusation of cowardice creates pressure to disclose.

text: A suspect who fears exposure to someone powerful can be pressed harder by a questioner than one who fears only the questioner.
when: the questioner holds leverage over the suspect's secret
why: The threat of the feared person's anger does much of the work.

text: An interrogator's manner, including sarcasm and direct questions, shows which claims will be pressed and which are accepted.
when: observing how a questioner treats a witness's statements
why: pressure is applied selectively to claims the questioner doubts

text: Praise or matching a talkative witness's manner can loosen a guarded witness, though they may overreach, be cut off, or volunteer unplanned remarks that help or mislead.
when: Questioning a guarded or talkative witness who responds to praise.
why: Witnesses who feel esteemed talk more freely.

text: Open with a warm, relaxed, light tone and let the witness talk; this lowers resistance more effectively than blunt cross-examination.
when: Interviewing a witness who resists pressure or is unwilling to help.
why: Lower tension makes the witness more willing to explain.

text: Use flattery only with status-motivated sources; a principled source with no reason to be flattered will see through it.
A persecution that is mostly show signals that the threatened exposure may never happen.
when: Judging whether an intimidation or exposure threat is real
why: A threat meant to pressure rarely needs to be carried out

text: A threat's menacing or flattering wording can signal its author's fear, since threats are often used to frighten others; verify this reading against other evidence.
when: Interpreting an anonymous or hidden party's threat.
why: Intimidation is often a sign of insecurity.

text: Judge a person's danger by whether they can reach help when they choose. Someone who can reach town at will is not personally threatened, even in a dangerous place.
when: When assessing whether a victim in a remote place is at risk
why: Ability to escape or summon help limits the threat, even if the setting itself is hazardous.

text: Introduce a threat through a physical token, such as a card or note, that names the threat, its nature and a time.
why: A concrete object makes an abstract danger tangible and specific

text: A threat carries little weight when the accuser holds nothing that could convict, so judge the threat by the accuser's actual evidence.
when: A suspect is said to have feared an accuser.
why: Fear requires a credible capacity to harm, not only a stated accusation.

text: Before acting on an overheard threat, check whether it concerns an immediate act or a future intention.
why: A threat about the future does not call for immediate action.

text: A direct, personal question about a person's conscience can break defiance more effectively than a legal demand.
when: a witness is defiant but reachable through loyalty or conscience

text: Use open questions before leading ones, since leading questions reduce what a witness can later be shown to have volunteered.
when: Questioning any witness whose account matters.
why: Leading questions push the witness toward an answer, weakening the value of what they say unprompted.

text: Watching how a shocked witness behaves often yields more than pressing them with direct questions.
Ask a suspect what made them think you were wrong; their answer can reveal which witness or fact they fear.
when: A suspect has rejected a confrontation and you want to learn their concern
why: The reason offered for doubt often points at a specific person or fact they are worried about.

text: Open a questioning exchange by getting the subject to talk about their own affairs before approaching sensitive matters.
when: Questioning a guarded or evasive subject.
why: Talking about familiar matters starts the conversation without triggering defensiveness.

text: Press a subject when their composure or clarity starts to fade, since that is when they can least deflect.
when: A subject's alertness is declining during questioning.
why: Reduced clarity lowers the subject's ability to resist or evade.

text: Keep questions short and quick so the informant cannot build a coherent story between them.
when: When gathering facts from a witness who might prepare or shape an account.
why: Brief questions limit the time available to construct a consistent but false narrative.

text: Use the origin of a revealed object as the next pressure point, since learning where it was found can deepen a witness's distress.
when: a witness reacts to a revealed object and asks where it came from
why: the object's location links it to the witness's world, intensifying the reaction

text: Repeating the same questions with more force hardens a reserved or committed person; change the approach instead of pressing the same point.
when: A character confronts someone who is reserved or has already committed to a position.
why: Opposition hardens a determined person's commitment rather than changing their mind.

text: A threat pressures only a target who fears the next step; fear, not physical restraint, drives obedience.
when: A character is threatened with harm.
why: Fear, not restraints alone, determines obedience.

text: Keeping a purpose or threat alive during quiet periods leaves the audience feeling pressure even when little seems to happen.
when: a story or level has a slow stretch
why: The unresolved threat keeps tension active between events

text: Showing a threat's effect through a brief sensory test builds more dread than an immediate explanation, because the audience feels danger before understanding it.
when: a threat must feel serious before its nature is known
why: Partial exposure to horror sustains anticipation better than full disclosure.

text: Threatening a reluctant witness with punishment tends to produce anger and defiance rather than useful information.
when: interrogating a reluctant witness
why: Coercion raises hostility, which blocks cooperation.

text: Information from a source eager to look clever may be shaped by that wish, so it needs independent checking.
Flattery reveals the flatterer's aims as well as the subject's views, and the subject's self-image can colour what they report.
Questioning under armed pressure can produce a confident denial rather than the truth.
Flattery and drink can make a witness exaggerate or invent details.
Threats without evidence can produce only more evasion; the shift to narrow questions is what moves the witness.
when: An investigator relies on a stern warning alone.
why: A threat without support gives the witness nothing to respond to except denial.

text: Flattery in a private letter may accompany a practical request, so check what was being asked.
why: Praise can be a means to a concrete end.

text: Asking the same question twice in front of others may prompt a witness to refine the answer rather than reveal the truth.
when: Re-asking a question in a group setting
why: Repetition gives the witness time and cues to adjust the account

text: Threatened witnesses give partial truths; check each claim against other evidence.
A witness's evasion may come from grief or embarrassment rather than guilt, so reluctance alone is not proof of wrongdoing.
when: A witness is reluctant to answer personal questions.
why: Emotional states such as grief or shame produce evasive behaviour in innocent people as well as guilty ones.

text: Waiting too long lets the suspect escape or the danger return, so patience must be bounded by the threat's urgency.
when: The investigator chooses to hold back while the threat continues
why: Delay gives the perpetrator time to act again or disappear.

text: Passive waiting without a clear plan frustrates partners and can lose momentum.
A single firm holdout can freeze a group's outcome, so small impressions may outweigh technical arguments.
A rival investigator's pace can tempt the protagonist into acting too early.
when: a competitor is progressing faster
why: Competition pressures the protagonist to commit before the evidence is ready.

text: A questioner's own agitation can colour how they read a witness, and the witness can turn the same reading back on the questioner.
Pressing hard on a painful subject makes the subject's distress close the conversation, so the questioner learns less.
when: Raising a topic tied to grief or loss.
why: Distress makes the subject withdraw and refuse further answers.

text: Emotional appeals can push an investigator toward promises of confidentiality that later limit what they can do.
when: when a distressed witness asks for secrecy
why: Promises made under pressure may be impossible to keep.

text: 1) Admit your own error or weakness. 2) Praise the other person's experience so they feel invited to share. 3) Keep your real goal and the specific fact you want hidden. 4) Let the source volunteer what they know.
when: Extracting information from a rival or authority figure who guards it.
why: Lowering the other's guard makes them more willing to talk.

text: 1) Remove the suspect's companions. 2) Read the suspect's temperament and choose the pressure that suits them. 3) Make the threat credible with a plausible consequence. 4) Offer a single exit under a time limit.
when: A witness is hostile and holds key information, with little time to spare.
why: A credible, time-limited threat leaves the suspect only one choice.

text: 1) Press the subject with intimidation. 2) If they brace against it, switch to warmth that appeals to honour, love and family ties, and recalls a happier past. 3) Invoke an absent person whose fate depends on the answer, offering easier conditions for speaking.
when: when a subject's resistance is emotional and physical evidence is incomplete
why: a braced subject responds to emotional appeals more than to threats

text: 1) Ask a direct, unexpected question about a sensitive personal matter. 2) Watch the reaction as closely as the answer. 3) Claim more knowledge than you have. 4) Let the witness leave.
when: a witness holds back on a sensitive matter and has a stake in the outcome

text: Ask who planned, who benefits and who was close to whom in sequence, so each answer narrows the set of possible actors.
when: Narrowing suspects in an investigation.
why: Ordered questions reduce candidates step by step.

text: 1) Keep tone calm and firm. 2) Repeat the same direct question without changing wording. 3) State an unverified fact as a probe. 4) Watch for denials and physical tells. 5) Offer a plausible face-saving reason for concealment.
when: Questioning a witness who is holding back a specific detail.
why: Repetition, a bluff and an excuse each push a guarded witness toward partial disclosure.

text: 1) Ask a narrow question. 2) When the witness changes the subject, return to the original topic using their own words. 3) Repeat until the witness states the answer plainly.
when: An interviewer must get a direct answer from a charming or digressive witness.
why: Repeated, narrow return to the topic keeps control of the conversation.

text: Keep threatening letters as evidence for later use, since they can help identify the sender.
when: Receiving a threat from a hidden party.

text: Limit surveillance and destruction beats, since repeated threats lose their force.
Trigger a threat event, such as a dangerous character entering, to interrupt an interview and raise tension.
Let an NPC become more forthcoming when dialogue choices flatter them, unlocking gated lore.
Interrupt a digression that pulls the conversation away from the goal rather than letting it run on.
when: A subject steers talk away from the matter at hand.
why: Unchecked digressions let the subject control the topic.

text: When a source resists, reassure them that the questions only gather facts and imply no accusation, and make the reassurance sincere.
when: When a witness or informant is protective of someone or unwilling to answer.
why: Protective sources withhold information when they feel accused; sincere reassurance lowers that resistance.

text: Threats can force quick speech, but it may be untrue and the suspect may shut down entirely; use threats only when the next step is clear and verify the answer.
when: Threats would be the only source of leverage.
why: Coerced speech shows willingness to talk, not accuracy.

text: Authority and firm manner can compel an answer; payment, especially to a witness with financial need, can secure cooperation or silence, but may bias answers toward what the questioner wants.
when: A witness is evasive or has a financial need.

text: Players denied an answer may read the delay as evasiveness or as being mocked, especially when they already suspect the investigator.
when: an investigator withholds conclusions
why: withholding looks like hiding the result

text: A brief pause or change in a person's routine action when a key word is spoken can signal that the topic matters to them.
when: Questioning someone who has hidden knowledge.
why: Involuntary reactions reveal interest even when the person says nothing.

text: Concessions such as 'I can't say' give little information but still signal that the witness is holding something back.
when: A witness deflects a direct question.
why: Evasion is itself a reaction that reveals constraint or concealment.

text: A calm reaction to a known name can mean guilt, practiced composure, or innocence, so a single reaction is ambiguous.
when: A suspect shows no visible reaction to a name the investigator tested.
why: Several causes produce the same calm surface.

text: In an interview both sides may hold information back to test the other, so disclosure often proceeds in alternating turns.
when: Two parties each hold information the other wants.
why: Each side fears giving away an advantage before learning the other's position.

text: Witness emotional shifts, such as fear turning to cunning, may signal concealed knowledge or reflect fear or grief; use them to choose where to press, not as proof of guilt.
when: Observing a witness during questioning.
why: Emotional signals are ambiguous and can have innocent causes; they indicate where to look, not evidence in themselves.

text: Weigh a remark by the target's observed reaction rather than by the words alone; a jest that visibly lands marks a real personal sensitivity.
when: When interpreting teasing or jokes between people.
why: The same words carry different weight depending on how they affect the listener.

text: Severity or a sudden harsh tone halts a frightened witness's answers, so the interviewer should avoid it.
when: Questioning a witness who is already afraid.
why: Fear reduces willingness and ability to speak.

text: Silence or a partial reaction can look like a confession when it actually reflects fear or loyalty, so it must be weighed against other evidence.
when: When interpreting a witness who avoids the central point under pressure.
why: Emotional states such as fear or loyalty produce the same outward signs as guilt.

text: Bluffed disdain or feigned ignorance can be read by the other party as puzzlement, so bluffing does not reliably hide knowledge.
when: A party uses feigned ignorance to conceal knowledge.
why: Odd manner signals uncertainty rather than control to the listener.

text: Record repeated 'I don't remember' answers as information rather than as empty results, and stop pressing once further questions yield nothing.
when: When a source repeatedly claims no memory of an event.
why: Persistent non-recall can signal a sensitive area, and continued pressure produces diminishing returns and distress.

text: Wait out a pause instead of rushing to the next question, since silence often prompts the witness to speak.
when: A witness has stopped answering.
why: Silence creates pressure that can draw out information.

text: Attention absorbed by a loud, dramatic or comic scene makes people miss a new sound or a quieter, sensitive exchange nearby.
when: During a noisy, dramatic event, or when a character needs cover for a sensitive exchange.
why: Listeners filter for expected noise and follow the spectacle, so they miss new sources or the real subject.

text: Players overlook mundane carriers such as carts or delivery routes that they do not classify as threats, so an ordinary route can hide an event.
when: when an ordinary object or traveler moves through a scene
why: Players screen objects by threat category, not by their role in the event

text: An unseen intruder may call out to test whether anyone is present, so staying silent hides the observer.
when: an intruder is near and the observer is unseen
why: A call with no answer tells the intruder the area may be empty

text: Loud noise can drown out a search's sounds, but it also hides sounds from anyone on the other side of the wall, so the searcher may miss a listener.
when: Searching in a space where others may be nearby
why: Masking works in both directions

text: Attackers who plan a breach often observe a target over an extended period before acting, gathering routines and identities first.
when: A protected place has staff or regular visitors whose routines can be watched
why: Long observation supplies the information that makes a later direct entry succeed without force

text: An intruder can leave a physical object, such as clothing, that may identify him later even when he is not seen.
Treat intuition as a hypothesis to verify: do not dismiss it, but a hunch with no stated basis must not replace evidence or pass as fact.
when: When a reasoner reaches a conclusion by feel.
why: Intuition can be wrong without verification.

text: Infer an intruder's build and method from several combined traces, such as footprints, reach and time taken, rather than from any single mark.
when: When a scene is disturbed and the intruder cannot be seen.
why: Combining independent traces narrows the range of possible explanations.

text: In a locked-room problem, ask what the suspect needed others to believe, not only how the room was entered.
when: When a room appears sealed and a single exit seems to explain the event
why: Staged traces are built to create a false belief, so the intended belief reveals the plan.

text: A person who leaves a room and locks it behind them gains time, because pursuers must spend effort forcing a strong door.
when: A pursuit begins after an escape from a sealed room.
why: Forcing a door takes time and tools that pursuers may not have at hand.

text: A route missed from the enumeration can make an elimination look airtight when it is not. Confirm the list is complete before concluding.
when: When solving a locked-room problem by elimination
why: An omitted route can carry the real answer while the rest appear closed.

text: A self-caused disturbance can be mistaken for hostile action, and the reverse also happens, so the cause stays unclear.
when: Interpreting an unexplained change to a barrier
why: Clumsiness and external influence can produce the same visible result

text: 1) List every door, partition, window, wall, gate, stair, balcony and access path into or out of the space. 2) Check each route against physical signs and known state at the time. 3) Weigh against timeline; eliminate routes strong evidence rules out. 4) Examine the remaining route, which often points to an insider.
when: When a closed room or crime seems to admit no entry or exit.
why: Systematic elimination of all recorded routes reduces an apparently impossible entry to a tractable question and prevents overlooking the real one.

text: Give NPC intuition a mechanically distinct status from confirmed evidence, such as a hint, so players can tell the two apart.
Faintness or strong emotion, including terror, can come from heat, fatigue, illness, grief or a different wrongdoing, and bodily arousal cannot tell fear from guilt.
when: Interpreting physical or emotional reactions during questioning.
why: Many causes and emotions produce the same response, so reactions show feeling, not guilt.

text: A hesitation before answering a precise detail or fetching something may reflect a rehearsed account or nerves; record it as a weak lead, not proof.
when: a witness is asked a precise detail about a claimed event, or pauses when asked to fetch or check something
why: Nerves and many innocent causes also produce hesitation, so it must be checked against other evidence.

text: Changed voice, shifting gaze or sudden starts under questioning can reflect stress as much as concealment, so they signal stress, not proof of a lie.
when: a witness is questioned directly on a sensitive point or a suspect is under pressure
why: Guilt and stress look alike from outside.

text: Visible discomfort, like lowered eyes, blushing, a changed manner, shifting posture or tone, or a repeated denial, often marks concealed feeling or a sensitive point worth pressing.
when: a question touches a sensitive fact or subject and the witness's manner changes
why: Concealed knowledge or feeling produces visible discomfort, which often marks evasion.

text: Under incriminating evidence or unwelcome news, the body may show pallor, sweat, trembling, fidgeting, flushing, a tight grip, collapse or fainting while speech stays controlled, signalling a near break.
when: a suspect is shown incriminating evidence they fear, or a listener hears unwelcome news
why: Physical reactions are harder to control than speech.

text: A name raised in questioning can trigger a visible flush, caught breath, stiffening or scream before composure returns, exposing a link a denial hides.
when: a person is named in questioning, especially if the witness denies or avoids them
why: Emotion leaks through the body when a person is surprised by a name, despite verbal control.

text: A suspect who fears being blamed may show pallor, hesitation or panic and look guilty even when the facts point elsewhere, since fear mimics concealment.
when: a suspect is at risk of being blamed or shows visible panic
why: Fear of suspicion produces the same physical strain as concealed knowledge, and anxiety is easy to read as guilt.

text: Haste leaves visible traces, such as half-finished clothing or tasks, snatched remains, emptied drawers, forced locks or overturned furniture, revealing urgency or a targeted search.
when: a character is interrupted by an urgent call, invents a reason for being present, or a ransacked room is examined
why: Attention shifts to the urgent event before routine finishing; an excuse made in a hurry is performed roughly; urgent searching is disorderly and targets a goal.

text: Haste under alarm makes careful actors forget precautions, leaving a single slip, such as a light left burning, that undoes the plan; check hiding steps before leaving.
when: an actor must leave quickly after an unexpected interruption or while departing under pressure
why: Haste reduces attention to small details, and urgency crowds out planned precautions.

text: An unplanned first reaction to a shown object, such as a stammer or pause before denying, reveals a connection to probe, more than a prepared answer.
when: an object is shown unexpectedly and the suspect is questioned about it
why: Immediate reactions come before a denial is constructed; hesitation signals knowledge the character would rather not share.

text: A loaded phrase or planted lure touching a hidden fact provokes a visible involuntary reaction in someone holding a related secret, while an uninformed listener stays unmoved.
when: a suspect hears a phrase tied to a hidden fact, or a guarded suspect is exposed to a provocative item
why: Knowledge of the secret gives the phrase weight, and fear that the hidden fact will come out drives the reaction.

text: A calm or blank face is ambiguous and may signal innocence or concealment; unexpected calm under a humiliating stimulus may hide feeling, so the reaction can count as evidence.
A character hiding a secret leaks it through brief reactions, such as a glance, held breath, paleness, stopped gesture or hand moving toward pocket, even when words stay calm.
when: the character is asked about or reminded of the concealed matter, or cannot be asked directly
why: Involuntary movements can leak what speech withholds or conceals.

text: Observers trust involuntary bodily signs, such as flushing, fidgeting or averted gaze, over a person's composed words when judging temper or guilt.
when: A character's spoken words are guarded or calm while physical signs show agitation
why: Uncontrolled signals are harder to fake than speech

text: A sudden change in a person's colour or manner at a new arrival can reveal a prior connection the observer does not yet understand.
when: A particular figure arrives within the person's sight or hearing.
why: Emotion shows before the person chooses what to say, exposing a hidden relationship.

text: A character corrected mid-meeting can show alarm and reveal knowledge they meant to hide, once their expectation proves false.
when: a wrong identity assumption is corrected in front of them
why: being corrected exposes what they already knew

text: A pause, pallor and a sudden specific answer after an aborted sentence can signal the person already knows the detail and is deciding whether to reveal it.
when: a question touches a detail the witness is hiding
why: the hesitation shows an internal choice to disclose

text: A suspect may slip by using a name only an insider would know, then ask how it was known; such slips reveal knowledge the suspect denies having.
when: questioning a suspect who denies knowing a person or object

text: A witness who hesitates before confirming a known fact may have heard or seen more than they admit.
when: when a known fact is put to a witness
why: Hesitation can signal a withheld detail.

text: A speaker who revises a hypothetical toward a concern may be signalling a worry they do not voice.
when: a speaker reshapes their wording mid-sentence
why: Word changes can reveal what the speaker is holding back.

text: Pressed about a known link, people often admit only the true minimum and reveal nothing further, protecting what they hold back.
when: someone is asked about a connection to a person tied to a hidden event
why: a short, partly true reply closes the topic

text: A body placed in a doorway communicates refusal more clearly than spoken words do.
when: A gatekeeper blocks a visitor from a room.

text: Restless listening and shifting tone signal that a character is hiding expectation, and observers read these tells before any cause is explained.
when: when a character conceals a motive
why: people read behavioral signs as evidence of inner state

text: An emotionally involved witness may volunteer detailed alibi information unprompted while complaining or boasting.
when: a witness is close to the suspect and speaks freely
why: Emotion lowers the guard over what is revealed.

text: A suspect's first reaction, such as stunned disbelief or a low admission, reveals his state of mind and can serve as evidence.
when: immediately after an arrest or accusation
why: unguarded reactions expose inner state

text: Warm appeals work on emotionally exposed subjects but fail against self-controlled ones, who keep their composure under them.
when: when a subject is interrogated for information
why: emotional openings differ between subjects

text: Involuntary reactions such as recoil, hiding, sudden departure or colour change can carry meaning, and each has both an innocent reading and a significant one.
Experienced observers read tells by pattern recognition built from many past cases, noticing early signs that a person is deteriorating.
when: the observer has long experience with similar people
why: past cases provide a basis for comparison

text: A gesture that comes before a quick verbal reply can signal concealment, even when the face and words show no change.
Hesitation before a specific answer that changes when a particular name or topic arises can signal a stake, though grief or fear of blame can also cause it.
when: Reading a witness's pauses during questioning
why: Hesitation is ambiguous; it tracks emotional stakes as much as guilt

text: Suspects under pressure may shiver, glance back, or turn suddenly angry when followed, and observers may read these signs as guilt.
when: when being followed or questioned
why: stress produces physical signs

text: Frequent pauses between words can signal that a witness is holding something back.
when: when interviewing a witness whose answers seem guarded
why: hesitation suggests the speaker is choosing what to reveal

text: A suspect's involuntary reaction to a name can be caught by a second observer who is watching them.
when: A name is raised during questioning.

text: What a person grabs under alarm depends on their life situation, so a lure should match the target's circumstances.
why: different attachments, such as family or valuables, drive different reactions

text: Excited or agitated suspects reveal more than calm ones, so emotional state is a cue for when to press.
when: A suspect is emotionally engaged in the conversation.
why: Heightened emotion lowers guard.

text: A sharply personal question can produce a visible reaction such as sobbing, turning away or hiding the face. Such a tell is a reaction, not proof of guilt.
when: when a pointed question touches a named relationship
why: emotional reactions arise from the question's personal weight

text: Pallor, a strained voice or a sudden flash of anger can indicate that a challenge has landed, and the suspect may then leave.
when: when reading a suspect during an interrogation
why: involuntary physical responses betray stress under a successful challenge

text: A listener can notice when a speaker's energy shifts sharply toward a harmless subject as a sensitive one comes near.
when: when a sensitive topic is close

text: A person's unguarded reaction to a place or inscription can expose interests they deny aloud, so a strong reaction that contradicts stated indifference is a clue.
when: when someone reacts strongly to an object or place while claiming not to care
why: involuntary responses are harder to control than spoken words

text: A calm, idle-seeming investigator leads observers to assume no lead exists, though the investigator may be tracking the real one.
when: an investigator appears uninterested
why: low visible urgency is read as low threat

text: People accept odd behaviour from an injured or shocked person as a result of the injury, so a substitute's oddities go unquestioned.
when: A substitute acts strangely after an apparent attack
why: Injury provides a ready explanation that suppresses suspicion

text: A suspect who receives a fact that matters to them may show a brief flicker of discomposure before changing the subject.
when: A relevant fact is delivered to a suspect.
why: The fact touches something the suspect cares about hiding.

text: A witness who turns cold and gives routine answers when pressed on a sensitive person may be unpracticed at deception and say no more.
when: A witness is asked about a sensitive past connection.
why: Deception is uncomfortable for people who do not practise it.

text: Small reactions after a tense exchange, such as a flush or a private smile, reveal the emotional cost to the people involved.
when: A tense exchange has just ended.
why: Brief involuntary responses leak feelings that were suppressed during the exchange.

text: A suspect may know more than they are willing to admit, and concealing knowledge does not by itself make them the culprit.
Brief involuntary signs, such as a slight drooping of the eyelids, can reveal a flicker of disturbance when the rest of the face shows nothing.
A listener's visible interest in an offhand remark sets it apart from other remarks, so an attentive audience notices it.
when: a casual remark is later needed as evidence
why: visible interest signals importance

text: Paleness combined with visibly weighing options reads as calculation rather than plain denial.
when: A accused person who pauses to weigh a way out
why: Observers take visible deliberation as a sign of strategic thinking.

text: A nervous target reads ambiguous gestures as threats, so indirect probing can unsettle innocent people as much as guilty ones.
A brief pause or sharp reaction to a recognised name or place, cut off before control, signals a hidden connection, since recognition is hard to suppress.
when: A name or place is spoken aloud, or a suspect hears a trigger they recognise.
why: Sudden reactions read as concealment, and recognition causes a split-second change that is hard to suppress.

text: Under pressure, involuntary reactions such as a sudden start, fixed stare, eye or colour change, posture shift or dropped object can leak knowledge words hide.
when: A suspect or witness is confronted with a difficult question, or a subject they have a stake in and try to conceal.
why: Involuntary reactions bypass deliberate control, so they leak what speech would suppress.

text: Pressing on a subject a guarded witness cares about can shift their expression between emotions; the flicker marks where pressure lies and prompts questions, not proof.
when: A guarded witness is questioned face to face about a sensitive topic after a calm opening.
why: Pressure on a personal concern exposes emotions kept controlled, and a single flicker has many possible causes.

text: Words spoken in a delirious or disturbed state repeat a dominant preoccupation, so they reveal what a character fears more than what actually happened.
when: A character speaks while feverish, drugged or otherwise impaired and the listener wonders whether the words are true.
why: Altered mental states bring the dominant preoccupation to the surface, so the content reflects inner fear rather than events.

text: Retelling can re-enact the experience, with voice and manner shifting. These changes are evidence of the witness's emotional state, separate from the events.
when: A witness retells a distressing or embarrassing event
why: Recalling an experience re-activates the emotions attached to it

text: Involuntary signs, such as restless eyes, a brief flicker of recognition or guilt, or shifting gaze, brow or mouth, betray inner state more reliably than a composed face or words.
when: words are guarded or composed
why: Speech and looks are easier to control than involuntary reflexes.

text: A protective secret can be exposed by a single careless disclosure from an intoxicated insider, so one slip can grant access that layered rules were meant to prevent.
when: A secret protects a secured asset
why: People under the influence reveal what they should keep quiet

text: A gradual change in orientation may leave no internal sign, so players need an external cue to notice it.
Saying 'I did not see it' is a narrow claim, while 'I know nothing of it' is broad and easier to disprove.
when: Evaluating a witness's carefully limited answers
why: Broad denials make more claims that can be checked against other sources

text: A witness can speak only literal truths yet still create a false impression through what they leave out.
when: When evaluating testimony or NPC dialogue that is accurate but incomplete.
why: Omission can mislead as effectively as falsehood.

text: A pause, delayed or strained answer, or bitten-back half-finished reply often marks a sensitive point worth a focused follow-up, though not proof of guilt.
when: a witness pauses, answers late, or starts and stops on a direct or easy question
why: Hesitation marks where the account is weakest and can reveal what the witness meant to hide, but it has innocent causes too.

text: A character who breaks off mid-name or nearly says a secret tells the listener more than a flat denial, so a cut-off can point toward hidden knowledge.
when: A character has reason to hide knowledge but must still speak to others.
why: The listener completes the unfinished thought, so the implied secret feels more concrete than a denial.

text: A hesitant or over-precise denial can be written as a dialogue signal that an NPC is hiding a link, without proving that the link exists.
when: Writing NPC responses to a shown item.
why: Signalling concealment gives the player a lead while keeping the truth open.

text: Dialogue can carry two meanings at once, the stated words and a hidden intent; judge a line by its tone and by what it leaves unsaid.
when: reading a line that may hide a purpose

text: Shifts in routine across days, such as cancelled orders, unusual smoking, or burnt letters, mark a change in a person's state.
when: when reading a timeline of a suspect

text: Use changed behaviour, such as drinking, restlessness or avoided eye contact, to build suspicion without a direct accusation.
when: when an audience must suspect a character without being told outright

text: When a person acts against expectation, treat the reversal as a clue and make explaining it the focus of the investigation.
when: a character breaks an established pattern
why: the break often reveals hidden intent

text: A fair clue is usually one small slip within an otherwise careful plan, not a large or conspicuous mistake.
Use mild teasing to test whether a witness shows irritation, since a sharp reaction can expose what they are protecting.
when: a witness seems guarded but not openly hostile
why: a small provocation can reveal a stronger reaction than direct questioning

text: A suspect's glances toward exits or windows, followed by a decision, can expose a plan of action.
when: a suspect is under pressure or about to act
why: Attention to escape routes often precedes movement, revealing intent before action.

text: Show a character hesitating before a hard question, weighing reluctance against the need for truth, so the cost of asking is visible.
why: visible cost makes the question weigh on the audience

text: Treat a sudden departure as a lead, since haste suggests fear and fear suggests the matter is significant.
A body arranged neatly rather than sprawled is unlike someone stabbed while standing or struggling, and may suggest the body was placed after death.
A sudden recognition can redirect the whole line of questioning mid-conversation, so stay open to changing focus partway through.
when: during an extended interview

text: A suspect who insists on a formal inquiry when offered a safe settlement is anomalous and must be explained, since guilt would normally favour the settlement.
when: when a suspect's choice seems to work against their own interest
why: Unexplained choices can reveal the true motive

text: Treat hesitant identifications as leads to pursue, not as proof of identity.
when: a witness hesitates on identification
why: hesitation means the match is uncertain

text: Deliver a final reveal as a monologue the player triggers, limiting the suspect's options to confess or refuse.
when: designing a dialogue-based confrontation
why: a limited option set focuses the scene on the reveal

text: Check whether a suspect's behaviour fits the crime window, since conspicuously open or noisy conduct right after the act argues against guilt.
when: judging a suspect's behaviour near a crime time
why: a recent killer would likely avoid drawing attention

text: A character's suspicion or cruelty makes sense once the reader knows what that character feared.
when: Judging a character whose hostility seems extreme.
why: Fear of a specific threat shapes behavior that would otherwise be unexplained.

text: In hidden-information games, opponents' handling of played cards, hesitation and facial expression reveal what they hold.
when: reading opponents' concealed holdings
why: habits of handling leak information

text: A desk or other barrier shields an examiner and lets him hide surprise by bending over papers, though giving up the barrier can read as weakness to a dangerous person.
when: Choosing whether to stay behind a barrier during questioning.
why: Protection visibly used can signal either caution or vulnerability.

text: Do not expect a disguised person to look awkward; an effective disguise works by avoiding awkward behaviour.
when: when assessing whether someone is disguised
why: awkwardness is the wrong signal for a well-built disguise

text: Infer from the reaction a person would normally give; a missing response can be as informative as an observed one.
when: A silent scene is interpreted.

text: A suspect can stage a result, so watch what the suspect does rather than what the suspect says.
when: When a suspect's account conflicts with observed evidence
why: Statements are easier to fabricate than sustained actions.

text: A listener who avoids a subject or does not ask who benefits may be concealing knowledge of it.
when: Questioning a suspect about a scenario.

text: Physical traces such as warmth, arrangement or disorder can contradict a witness's account of recent activity.
when: A witness describes an action that leaves a checkable physical state
why: Recent activity leaves traces that cannot be reconciled with a claim of inactivity.

text: A dialogue system can store every NPC line verbatim; when a later statement contradicts it or shows hesitation, it can offer a contradiction action unlocking new questions.
when: designing NPC dialogue the player can interrogate
why: Stored statements let the game detect conflicts and reward the player for catching them.

text: A dialogue system can track tells such as hesitation, blushing, word choice, repeated phrases or topic changes as flags, letting NPCs react or unlock targeted follow-up questions.
when: NPC dialogue is generated from player-driven conversation

text: A corpse showing agitation suggests the victim foresaw death, while a sudden natural death usually leaves no such expression.
when: Reading a body to infer how death occurred
why: Expression reflects the victim's state at death, which differs by cause

text: An NPC's response changes with how much of the player's reconstruction is correct, so its dialogue can disclose its motive as the player's deductions improve.
when: in a confrontation scene with a boss or NPC
why: The NPC reacts to accurate points and revealing lines, giving the player feedback on their reasoning.

text: Authored body-language cues such as hesitation or a tightened grip can point the player toward a line of questioning.
when: Designing NPC reactions to sensitive questions.
why: Nonverbal signs of unease guide the player to the topics that matter.

text: Mystery works by drawing thought away from a simple fact, not by hiding the fact itself.
A long, consistent lie is hard to sustain, because each invented detail adds a new point where it can be contradicted.
when: A witness or character gives a detailed story across several statements.
why: Every extra specific claim creates another checkable surface.

text: Hesitation or nervous answers are cues for follow-up, not proof of guilt; fear, shame, confusion or stress, and innocent people's contradictions, produce them too.
Nervous gestures or a blush may reflect distress, embarrassment or other feelings, so neither is proof of guilt on its own.
A slip of the tongue or unintended admission may be harmless; treat it as a lead needing corroboration, not proof of wrongdoing.
Accurate tells invite plausible but wrong explanations: observers take concealment for surprise, dismiss threats, or explain clues away, so they go unused.
when: a clue is easy to interpret incorrectly
why: Observers tend to accept a plausible explanation for a reaction.

text: Hesitating too long before acting can expose innocent people to harm, so reluctance carries its own cost.
Reading mood or motive from behaviour, such as cheerfulness, new habits, smiles, a startle or a locked door, is a guess until checked, though witnesses present it as fact.
when: A witness or investigator interprets mood, motive or an odd action without direct proof.
why: Behaviour is ambiguous and invites confident reading.

text: Judging a speaker's honesty by appearance, manner or charm is unreliable and reflects the judge's generalizations, since a pleasant manner says nothing about truth.
Reading silence or omissions as concealment relies on projected motives or assumed normal conduct, which may be wrong, and observers cannot tell deliberate from unconscious silence.
when: Interpreting an ambiguous silence or omission from a suspect.
why: Projection supplies a sinister explanation for silence that may have no hidden purpose.

text: Hesitation, glancing or eye movement can come from fear, loyalty or nervousness, so record it as a reason for further checking, not as proof of guilt or identification.
when: When a witness pauses or glances during questioning.
why: Nervousness has many innocent causes, so such signs only justify further checking.

text: Hesitating at the first touch can delay the check that matters most, so the most decisive test should not wait on reluctance.
when: When an observer is reluctant to touch a person.
why: Reluctance postpones the decisive evidence.

text: Excessive or insincere praise is easy to detect and undermines the approach.
A witness caught in a minor lie may still conceal the central fact, so one exposed contradiction does not resolve the case.
A lie that rests on one claim can be undone by a single document or source from outside the conversation.
when: A speaker relies on an unverified falsehood
why: An external record can contradict the one claim the lie depends on

text: A charitable excuse offered for a visible sign can conceal the truth rather than explain it, and the excuse itself may signal protection.
Dismissing exits too quickly makes an impossibility feel like a cheat; listing each check carefully keeps it credible.
Dramatic phrases are often assumed metaphorical, but literal statements can also be taken as figures of speech, so check each.
Pressure to dispose of a body quickly can destroy evidence before the cause of death is settled.
A hasty or confident first verdict, even from a local examiner, can be wrong; require careful examination before naming a cause.
A first reading of silent gestures can be wrong when the missing sound would have explained the behavior.
when: interpreting a scene without audio
why: missing context leads to a wrong reading

text: A stranger's gaze can cause a guilty-looking action that has an innocent cause.
Reading meaning into a single gesture can confirm a suspicion the observer already held.
Readers and officials often hear a qualified denial as a full denial, or as a confession.
when: A narrow statement is summarized or reported later.
why: People tend to simplify statements into the stronger version they expect.

text: Strong anger can make a concealed real name slip out during a denial, exposing the identity.
An invented excuse that is too neat or eager makes the target wary.
Different stated reasons for skipping the same event can signal a concealed motive rather than a neutral choice.

1) Ask about a specific detail of a threat or act. 2) Watch for colour changes, twitches, stiffness, growing hesitation or shifting details. 3) Press with follow-up questions until the answer changes or firms up.
when: A witness hesitates or changes answers under specific questioning.
why: Repeated specific questions expose shifting details and signal the need for a full account.

text: 1) Record what each NPC has told the player. 2) Compare new statements against that record. 3) Surface contradictions as clues.
when: Running a mystery with many NPC conversations
why: Logged statements let later contradictions become discoverable evidence

text: 1) List the traits the crime required. 2) Test a suspect's behavior in a controlled situation against those traits. 3) Record how far the behavior matches.
when: when physical facts seem to clear the suspect

text: 1) Identify a rare, recognizable method the suspect has used. 2) Build a lure that imitates a credible threat. 3) Fix the time and place yourself. 4) Station a watcher with orders to intervene at once when the suspect acts.
when: The investigator wants proof from the suspect's own act
why: The suspect's action supplies proof that reasoning alone cannot

text: 1) Give the NPC two motives that conflict with an item the player found. 2) Let the player detect the lie by comparing answers. 3) Ask a follow-up that forces one reason. 4) Record which reason the NPC avoids.

1) List each sudden change in a person's behaviour or attitude with its date and place. 2) Attribute known changes to known causes. 3) Mark unexplained changes as the target. 4) Work backward from who could have triggered them.
when: Motive is unclear and behaviour changes are recorded with dates.
why: Anchoring on dated changes gives deduction a fixed target.

text: Design brief reactions that read two ways and need pairing with another clue; a single reaction can mix anger, fear and uncertainty.
when: Writing NPC reactions as clues or interpreting a single visible reaction.
why: A tell with one reading gives an answer instead of a deduction.

text: Give NPC dialogue readable tells, such as changed stance, new option, pause or changed wording, that players learn to notice on key subjects or in false or evasive answers.
when: Designing NPC dialogue that may conceal information.
why: A noticeable tell rewards attention and makes deception discoverable.

text: Flag dialogue remarks that reveal knowledge the speaker should lack as designed tells, so players can notice the slip as a sign of concealment.
when: Designing NPC dialogue with hidden knowledge.
why: Unexpected knowledge is a detectable signal of concealment.

text: Flag hesitation before confirming a fact, or a hesitant or wrong identification, as a visible cue that an NPC is unsure or hiding something, prompting follow-up.
when: Designing NPC responses to questions or witness scenes.
why: Hesitation gives players a visible cue to follow up.

text: Let minor tells, such as fidgeting near an object, raise suspicion without settling it; combine them with physical facts, not nerves or a pale face.
why: Innocent people also become unsettled.

text: Let an NPC who believes they are speaking to someone else give away information in dialogue that the player can use.
when: an NPC is mistaken about who they are talking to

text: Plant a casual dialogue line that becomes a key only when combined with another clue.
when: Designing dialogue that feeds later deduction.
why: Delayed significance rewards players who remember and connect details.

text: Give dialogue a hidden reaction state, shown through text or animation, that the player must notice when a specific fact or item is mentioned.
why: lets players test an NPC's knowledge through dialogue options

text: Make hesitant non-player characters share only a fragment unless pressed, so persistence in questioning is rewarded.
when: Designing reluctant NPCs.
why: Gating fuller answers behind pressing rewards inquiry.

text: Separate evasive behavior and strong motive from proof of presence and action before judging guilt.
when: deciding whether a suspect is guilty
why: Suspicion and motive do not establish that someone was at the scene or acted.

text: Audiences and players adopt a convincing early theory from first clues and keep it until a later clue directly contradicts it, testing new evidence against that fixed frame.
when: a mystery's first act supplies several clues, or a plausible wrong explanation is introduced early
why: Early facts that fit a theory make it feel credible, so it becomes a fixed frame for later evidence.

text: Do not settle a character from one account or one action; await repeated observation, since single impressions are shaped by the speaker's aims and rarely capture whole character.
when: a character is described in strong terms by one witness, or a judgment about a person rests on one observed action
why: One action rarely captures a full character, and the inference may be wrong.

text: Do not conclude guilt from revulsion, reluctance to believe someone guilty, or a strong reaction alone; fear, shame or unrelated grief can produce the same response.
why: Emotional responses reflect the reasoner's feelings, not the suspect's actions.

text: Observers judge a distressed or unsteady person by appearance, labelling them drunk or mad, and may end the encounter without checking facts.
when: someone looks intoxicated or in distress
why: Visible condition shapes the observer's assumptions.

text: People judge a mild or pleasant-looking person as innocent, so appearance can mislead judgments of guilt.
when: assessing a witness or suspect
why: appearance shapes trust

text: Observers anchor on a striking, memorable feature and treat any figure that shows it as one stable identity.
when: when a suspect appears in several scenes
why: distinctive features serve as shorthand for identity

text: A busy reader skims a document quickly and labels it by first impression, which shapes how its content will be judged.
when: A professional reader receives a document in a routine setting.
why: Quick scanning relies on surface style and sets expectations before the substance is read.

text: A person who is partly undressed or without usual appearance elements will only admit someone they do not mind seeing them that way.
when: Inferring who a victim would have let in.
why: People accept visitors selectively when they are not presented normally.

text: A comforting natural explanation closes the question, so players stop investigating further once they accept it.
when: A character offers a reassuring cause for a troubling event.
why: Closure relieves the need for further inquiry.

text: A character's belief in the supernatural can make them careless or nervous, so superstition can act as a motive or misdirection.
when: A character acts on an occult belief during an investigation.
why: Fear or belief alters decisions, producing observable mistakes.

text: Investigators can be pushed by a wish for a suspect's innocence or by superiors' firm conviction. Both pressures must be discounted when weighing evidence.
when: An investigation is shaped by personal sympathy or institutional certainty
why: Hopes and authority distort how evidence is weighed

text: People who believe a streak predicts the next outcome keep chasing a repeated result, and grow angry when it repeats.
when: a person is losing and sees a number or outcome repeat
why: They assume past random results shape future ones, so they seek a pattern to win back losses.

text: Players tend to act on confident expert verdicts, so incomplete ones must be checked before acting on them.
when: An NPC gives an authoritative conclusion.
why: Authority makes a claim feel settled even when its evidence is partial.

text: Stiffening after death gives a rough clock, since rigor follows a known order of onset and passing off.
when: Estimating time of death from a body
why: The predictable sequence allows an estimate

text: Rigor begins in the face and jaw, spreads through the body, usually lasts about a day, and passes off in the same order.
Reject a proposed motive or claim when a well-established character trait or habit does not fit the act, even if the motive is neat.
when: Judging a suicide or other self-directed theory against character evidence, or a claim conflicting with a well-attested trait when no physical evidence settles it.
why: Behaviour inconsistent with a person's habits signals a weaker explanation; judgments about what a person would do rest on established character.

text: Discrepancies about who knows what can point toward concealment, but firm judgement should wait until more evidence arrives.
Valuables left on a victim argue against robbery as the motive.
when: A killing where the victim's possessions are still present
why: Money left behind contradicts a theft motive

text: Judge an unlikely coincidence by weighing its likelihood against the alternative, rather than dismissing it by instinct.
when: when a strained coincidence explains a key event
why: Instinct can wrongly accept or reject coincidences.

text: Rigid objects that handling cannot alter need less protection than soft, deformable objects, which change easily when touched.
Keep an unexplained clue on record and postpone assigning its meaning until later events can test it.
when: when a clue's owner or significance is uncertain

text: Identify a ring-shaped floor impression as the rim of a heavy container by measuring its diameter and comparing it with candidate objects.
when: when a circular mark is found on the floor
why: the rim diameter should match the base of the object

text: A witness's poor judgement in the past can weaken confidence in their current assessment of a situation.
Do not dismiss every anomaly; a candidate mechanism must account for the specific details reported, not merely exist in general.
when: Evaluating an unexplained event
why: Generic explanations fit any report and test nothing

text: Check how a claim was known, not only what it says; the same words can hide hearsay or first-hand knowledge.
when: evaluating a claim from a witness or official

text: A disguise supports a cover when the questioner's only reference, such as a photograph, shows a different appearance.
when: when the questioner knows the real person from an image
why: the reference no longer matches the disguised person

text: When a claim cannot yet be checked, judge the teller by demeanour, personal cost and steadiness, since a fabricator tends to offer a milder, more believable story.
when: an extraordinary claim must be acted on now
why: a fabricator makes the story plausible rather than risky

text: Judge an account by whether its content rings true and coheres internally, not only by who delivered it, especially after a previous source has misled.
when: a teller has been unreliable before
why: internal consistency is an independent sign of truth

text: Store a wrongful sentence as a world-state flag that a later scene can revoke, changing NPC dialogue and standing.
A verdict system with guilty, innocent and not proven outcomes, each with different consequences, lets an unresolved case carry its own distinct result.
when: Designing a court or accusation mechanic in a game.
why: A third outcome lets the game represent insufficient proof.

text: Deference to an authority or famous investigator, or a junior hiding a sound view, can suppress questioning of a reconstruction and delay a useful correction.
when: A subordinate disagrees with a superior's theory, or others are considering whether to question a reconstruction.
why: Deference suppresses the correction the case needs.

text: Odds stated in a rhetorical argument are not measured probabilities and should not be treated as data.
Judging an offer by its amount misleads, since money may be an instrument of a scheme rather than its end.
Beliefs about what a type of person would do can be wrong, so a mismatch resting on such a judgment needs independent support before it overturns a case.
Judging a case by its apparent stakes can end the inquiry before the key clue appears, and small objects can carry large consequences.
when: Deciding whether a small problem deserves full investigation
why: Low apparent stakes can hide serious consequences tied to a minor item

text: Investigators often notice an absence early but fail to analyze it until later, when other urgent tasks have crowded it out.
when: Many tasks compete for attention during an investigation
why: Urgent work pushes unexplained gaps aside

text: Assuming a broad category such as a region from one feature, without checking the trace's details, leads to a wrong identification.
when: Matching a trace to a population or region
why: A single shared feature rarely distinguishes a broad group from its neighbours

text: A firm belief in a person's character can bias judgement about their actions, so it should be checked against the evidence.
when: A witness or investigator judges a person's likely behaviour.
why: Prior belief about character filters how evidence is read.

text: Judging a suspect by stereotyped appearance or background can lead the investigator away from the real culprit.
Character-based judgments depend on how reliable the source describing the person is, and the assessor's own psychology can shape the trait model.
when: Using a trait model to doubt an account.
why: The trait model is built from testimony and interpretation, not hard fact.

text: A read on temperament can mislead, because the same psychological signs can be interpreted in more than one way.
Fear about personal stakes can push a person to accept the nearest or most alarming explanation of an observation without checking alternatives.
when: The observer has a strong personal stake in the outcome
why: Emotional investment favors answers that confirm the fear

text: Compassion lowers an investigator's guard and can let a suspect take control of the exchange, sometimes escalating into physical overstep.
