Vividness and certainty are not evidence of accuracy. A memory can feel more real than ordinary life and still be wrong.
when: Evaluating a witness's emotionally charged testimony.
why: Emotional intensity strengthens conviction regardless of truth.

text: 1) Take the account as given. 2) Ask whether its claims make one outcome clearly more probable than its opposite, given the speaker's own situation. 3) Test any claim against independent evidence where that is possible.
when: A suspect offers an explanation that cannot yet be checked.
why: An explanation can be judged on its content, but it is not proof until checked.

text: 1) Take each rival theory in turn. 2) Credit the specific facts it handled correctly. 3) Separate correct observations from wrong inferences. 4) Note any point the theory left unanswered before giving the final answer.
when: several characters have offered competing theories; skip when only one theory exists
why: a tally shows which facts each theory handled

text: Judge people by evidence, not by charm, repellence, appearance or manner; these do not indicate guilt or innocence, and many traits have ordinary explanations.
when: when assessing a person whose manner might sway judgment
why: emotional response clouds clear reasoning; appearance and manner are weak evidence, and conclusions from them alone often fail when checked

text: Feelings such as compassion, vanity or jealousy can skew credibility judgments; when a subject touches personal feelings or rivalries, guard against your own bias and check judgment before acting.
when: An interview touches on personal feelings or rivalries.
why: Emotion colors how credible an account seems, and personal feelings can distort judgment without the investigator noticing.

text: Each link in an inference chain must be defended, since knowing who is guilty differs from proving it; the chain holds only while every step, including the final one, is justified.
why: A case needs every link, and a coherent chain can hide untested steps.

text: Do not form a theory before the facts are in, since a held theory makes the mind bend facts to fit it.
when: during evidence gathering
why: early theories bias interpretation of later facts

text: Set an account aside until the facts are gathered, then compare it with the speaker's manner.
Ask a sceptic to probe the weakest steps of a theory and to say which step is only a guess.
when: Before treating a theory as established.
why: Coherent accounts can hide untested links.

text: List each claim made about a scene and mark whether the physical evidence supports it, keeping supported and unsupported claims separate.
Separate a suspect's actions from what they knew at the time, and ask what they knew before judging the act.
when: when a suspect's acts look damning but their knowledge is unclear
why: Acts done in ignorance carry different blame.

text: Score each NPC claim for internal consistency and for fit with what is already known, and let the player decide whether the account holds.
when: Building a suspect-dialogue system.

text: Use a contradiction between a witness's knowledge and the public record as a puzzle hook.
when: designing NPC knowledge in mysteries

text: Judge an NPC's claim by whether records or witnesses can support it, not by how plausible it sounds.
Withhold an action's outcome when it matters more than its display, and reveal it once the immediate threat has passed.
when: A scene's tension depends on what is not yet known

text: Do not let a high reliability score replace checking, since scores assist judgment but do not establish facts.
when: acting on a highly rated source
why: ratings are estimates, not verification

text: When a trace falls outside one's expertise, such as the detail of a lens prescription, refer it to a specialist who can read it precisely.
Do not treat a found scrap as conclusive until you know who wrote it and when.
when: Interpreting an unattributed note.
why: Undated, unattributed notes can mislead.

text: Defer an emotional witness who presses for attention until the wider household has been heard.
when: when one witness demands immediate contact

text: Judge a past event's actors by the law and the knowledge in force at the time, not by what later readers know.
why: conduct depends on what contemporaries could know and were bound by

text: Let a later rule invalidate a category of perceived-only testimony, so verdicts that rested on it are questioned.
Defending one detail does not defend the whole account; judge each challenge against the specific claims it targets.
Treat argumentative skill as separate from evidence; a persuasive speaker should be checked against facts, not trusted for winning an exchange.
Listeners read hidden significance into ambiguous phrases or rumor; a prior belief makes a short phrase confirm it, such as romance rather than money.
when: A witness or listener hears a short ambiguous phrase or vague rumor.
why: Preconceptions and a search for hidden significance shape how fragmentary words are read.

text: Listeners adopt a ready explanation of odd conduct, such as a cover story or superstition, as default and suspect a trick only once a detail contradicts it.
when: A listener already holds a theory, or someone's theory frames the odd conduct.
why: The ready explanation seems to confirm itself until a contradiction appears.

text: A listener's feelings about a speaker, such as disgust toward a repellent one, bias how the account is weighed.
when: a speaker is repellent
why: emotional reaction biases evaluation of content

text: Lay audiences read the same facts in opposite ways (a quarrel as real or staged) through everyday assumptions and irrelevant prejudice; their verdicts are not expert analysis.
when: A case must be argued to or judged by non-experts.
why: Non-experts weigh ambiguous facts through everyday assumptions and feelings entering untrained judgments.

text: A witness who has rehearsed a story can shift its emotional tone to suit each listener while its facts stay the same.
when: a witness has given statements to several people
why: Rehearsal separates delivery from content.

text: When a spoken name ties two people together, a listener's sudden start, flush or abrupt change of topic reveals more than the words do.
when: a name links two characters in conversation
why: unplanned reactions betray recognition

text: Stories with multiple versions can absorb new signs flexibly, and pride and credulity shape which versions survive.
when: a legend has several versions across a community
why: Flexible variants fit whatever evidence appears, and social motives select which survive.

text: A listener who hesitates or answers with a pointed question often reveals uncertainty about how much the speaker actually knows.
when: A speaker makes an unverified claim in a tense exchange.
why: People betray doubt through pauses and probing replies while they weigh the claim.

text: Publicly printed news of a new rule makes that rule known to anyone who reads it, so a motive based on knowing the rule must consider who had access to the news.
when: A motive depends on whether a suspect knew a rule.
why: Public announcements spread knowledge widely, including to people who were not directly involved.

text: Inherited reputation can make a person the first suspect even with no direct part in the event.
when: A suspect's ancestor had a notorious past.
why: Gossip carries the ancestor's guilt onto the descendant.

text: A listener who hopes for conflict reads a calm exchange as hostile, so expectations bend how overheard tone is interpreted.
when: Listening to ambiguous or muffled exchanges.
why: Expectation shapes perception of tone.

text: A listener who doubts a speaker's state of mind judges their account harshly, even when the doubt is never voiced.
when: A surprising claim comes from an emotional or distressed speaker.
why: Perceived judgment shapes trust before evidence is weighed.

text: A suspect's grief, tears, keepsakes or emotional appeal can move an investigator and make them less guarded.
when: A suspect displays strong emotion during questioning.
why: Emotional display invites sympathy, which lowers defenses.

text: A listener with an emotional stake in hearsay reacts to its emotional weight more than its accuracy, believing or doubting it on mood.
when: A rumor concerns something the listener hopes for or fears.
why: Hope and fear weigh more than evidence.

text: A flattered guest may notice that praise is excessive yet dismiss the mismatch as harmless.
when: A character receives exaggerated praise for a simple action
why: Flattery is pleasant, so its excess is easily overlooked

text: Audiences share a protagonist's belief in a windfall until a twist shows it is worthless, because they experience events through the protagonist.
when: when the protagonist believes they have gained a reward
why: audiences take the protagonist's view of events until shown otherwise

text: Expectation primed by a known signal, such as a legend, or by tension makes listeners anticipate the effect and find mundane sounds significant, so fear arrives on cue.
when: A known signal is set up in advance, or listeners are tense or primed to expect a threat.
why: Heightened expectation raises the perceived meaning of mundane sounds.

text: A sincere witness can be disbelieved, and group dismissal does not make a report false; following the crowd's view misleads, because a visible motive is not evidence.
when: A witness's report is mocked or dismissed by a group, or a player follows the crowd's view.
why: Social dynamics and prior expectations override perceived sincerity.

text: A listener's motives can shape how they hear and report a remark, so the reported wording may differ from what was said.
when: A remark is passed on by a witness or informant
why: Listeners may be motivated to hear it a certain way

text: A dramatic reaction invites an audience to decide the outcome before the evidence has been weighed.
when: presenting a strong emotional reaction as evidence
why: vivid moments create conclusions faster than evidence supports

text: A single reaction, such as to a staged reveal, can mean surprise, fear, recognition, shock or guilt, so judge it only against other facts and later accounts.
when: A single reaction is used as evidence about a person's knowledge or guilt.
why: The same visible reaction has several possible causes.

text: An investigator often accepts a smooth explanation that resolves an anomaly and moves on without rechecking the contradiction it covers.
when: A plausible explanation is offered for a contradiction.
why: Resolving the anomaly reduces the urge to check further.

text: Investigators should test human explanations, such as access, motive and timing, before accepting an uncanny cause, because a mundane cause is usually ruled out only through checking.
when: A supernatural explanation is tempting but a human one has not been fully ruled out.
why: Premature acceptance of an uncanny cause skips checkable evidence of access and timing.

text: Players and investigators can infer a hidden opening from the sound of breaking glass or from a character's habits, even when no opening is visible.
when: A room's apparent seal conflicts with an audible or habitual clue.
why: Sound and habit are indirect evidence that reveal a route the layout hides.

text: Players are persuaded more by the pattern of several matching dates than by any single date.
when: When several independent records are presented on one timeline.
why: Accumulated matches form a convincing whole that single matches cannot.

text: Players who accept a sealed room as impossible stop questioning who controlled access, so the assumed seal becomes the real lock on the solution.
when: a sealed room is presented as proof of an impossible death
why: trust in the seal suppresses checks on the person who opens it

text: When an intruder vanishes from a sealed space, audiences first assume a hidden passage, keeping belief in a physical explanation rather than the impossible.
when: a figure disappears from a space with all exits closed
why: a hidden route feels less impossible than no route at all

text: Players who decode a partial code by pattern can deduce a missing entry and feel progress, then commit to a theory before its contradictions appear.
when: A puzzle gives a partial code or cipher with a discoverable pattern
why: Pattern completion gives a sense of progress, which makes players trust the theory built on it.

text: Separate what can be known from a silhouette, its outline, from what cannot, its interior details, and state the distinction explicitly.
when: When reporting or judging an identification from a backlit view
why: Blending outline with assumed detail produces unwarranted confident identifications

text: An alternative explanation of evidence still needs its own corroboration before it can be accepted.
when: offering a counter-reading of an item
why: a counter-theory can overreach by relying on unverified claims about who touched what

text: A reconstruction shows that a method is possible, not that it was actually used. Drama can make a plausible method feel proven, so check it against physical evidence.
when: When evaluating a staged reconstruction or presenting one as an explanation of an event.
why: Feasibility and drama do not establish actual cause.

text: Calling a chain of reasoning elementary does not make it correct, and overconfidence makes a sound method seem trivial even when it solves serious cases.
when: Presenting or judging a deduction
why: Simplicity of statement is mistaken for weakness of reasoning.

text: Once a legal principle is declared settled, participants may be told that questioning it is not their role.
An investigator who tests a prediction may read a confirming result as proof while overlooking evidence that the prediction failed.
when: Interpreting the outcome of a reaction test.
why: Investigators tend to favour results that match their own view.

text: Lack of reaction can mean inattention or masking, not absence of the event. Treating silence as proof that a claim is false is a mistake.
when: Others present did not respond to a reported action.
why: Noise, distraction, or preoccupation can hide an event from observers.

text: Consistency between two baits can be mistaken for proof that both are true.
when: when a target evaluates linked stories
why: Agreement between separate sources feels like corroboration even when both are planted.

text: 1) List each apparent proof against a suspect. 2) Test each separately. 3) Mark each as confirmed, weak or contradicted. 4) Judge the suspect only on the points that survive testing.
when: A case rests on several apparently strong points
why: Chains of plausible points can hide weak links

text: 1) Compare what was found with what the situation leads you to expect. 2) Check the absence against the normal routine. 3) Note the anomaly. 4) Confirm that every fact needed for the inference is already available to the player.
when: Solving a case from a gap such as a missing item, entry or step.
why: A deduction is only fair when the facts that support it are already on the page or in the scene.

text: 1) List each damning item in a case. 2) For each, propose an alternative explanation that does not require the accused's guilt. 3) Ask who else could have produced the item.
when: testing a case built on several incriminating items
why: alternative explanations expose whether each item actually supports the theory

text: Audiences and players accept the first plausible motive, such as money or a convenient legal or romantic explanation, as complete and stop searching for the real cause.
when: a visible financial motive or a convenient legal or romantic explanation is put forward
why: A plausible surface explanation resolves the need for an answer quickly.

text: Reading a motive into a gap before ruling out an ordinary lapse in record keeping, or filling a silent record with an unsupported motive, produces false conclusions.
when: when a record has a gap or is silent about why someone acted
why: people often assume intent behind an unexplained gap; plausible motives feel like answers but evidence does not establish them

text: Personal grudges can bend an investigator's judgment: they turn neutral evidence into apparent proof and disguise private scores as public duty, so conclusions need checking for this influence.
when: investigator has a personal stake or past dispute with the suspect
why: Revenge mixed with duty distorts assessment of evidence; old quarrels can make accusations serve a grudge rather than the truth

text: A listener may explain away an accusation as the product of an old family feud, where love turned to hatred, and stop checking the claim.
when: the accuser is tied to the target by family history
why: a plausible motive offers an easy reason to dismiss the charge

text: A hidden motive tends to surface through behaviour, such as leaving early or avoiding witnesses, well before any confession.
when: a character conceals a plan
why: concealment shows in actions

text: A player who wants a target to be guilty, or wants to damage them, will pursue an accusation eagerly and tend to over-read ambiguous evidence in its favor.
when: A lead comes from an accusation against a person the player dislikes or wants to harm.
why: The wish for a particular answer shapes how the evidence is weighed.

text: A suspicious act can read as a threat until its hidden motive is known, after which the same act may read as protection.
when: an act has an unexplained reason
why: Motive determines how the act is interpreted.

text: An open, visible container signals that its contents are at risk, letting observers judge how confident the owner is.
A hidden personal attachment can explain why someone stays silent and can turn that silence into a possible motive.
A witness's account can be bent by affection, jealousy, prejudice, or self-protection, so statements should be weighed against the speaker's stake in the outcome.
when: a witness has a personal stake in the case
why: Motive colours what a person reports before it reaches the listener.

text: Intent formed when an opportunity appears may be impulsive, and the moment the decision was made is often impossible to know.
Community expectations supply motives quickly, and audiences accept a motive that fits local expectations, such as a widow expected to remarry.
when: a motive is assigned from social norms
why: familiar roles make motives feel plausible without proof

text: A person facing imminent financial ruin may see a death or loss as the only way out, making financial danger a strong candidate motive.
when: A suspect is under severe debt or threat of losing their standing.
why: Under extreme pressure, people may consider drastic acts they would otherwise reject.

text: A witness who profits from others' secrets, such as through blackmail, has reason to hide what they know.
why: Personal gain from concealment motivates denial.

text: Players readily link a later misfortune to an earlier grudge or threat, treating the sequence of events as proof of cause.
when: a threat is recorded shortly before harm occurs
why: Temporal order feels like causation, especially when a motive is already on record.

text: Strong feelings after a sudden loss, such as a fire, make people eager to find a culprit and quick to name a rival who had a recent dispute.
when: right after a sudden loss

text: Wrongdoers often see their own harmful acts as impulsive, while imagining planned crimes as requiring cold, deliberate calculation they feel they lack.
when: When a character or player judges their own culpability or intent against an imagined model of premeditation.
why: Self-image is measured against an idealized picture of the premeditated criminal, which can make gradual wrongdoing seem less culpable.

text: Motive is often inferred from a person's words and conduct, but the inference depends on the reader's assumptions about what those signs mean.
when: Reading a suspect's letters or behavior to infer motive.
why: Signs are open to interpretation, so the same conduct can support different motives.

text: A witness who stresses one particular word or claim often signals a motive the questioner has not yet asked about.
when: a witness answers with unusual emphasis on a specific point
why: Emphasis exposes what the witness cares about, which can point to an unexplored motive.

text: Suspicion moves to whichever suspect's secret or motive the player is most inclined to believe.
when: when several suspects each have a motive
why: Believability decides which suspect holds attention.

text: Players suspect the character with the strongest emotional motive first, especially when that character also flees the scene.
when: a mystery with a visible motive and an apparent flight
why: Motive and flight are read as guilt before evidence is examined.

text: A settled future event, such as an engagement, creates a motive pressure that the audience can track through the story.
when: Building a plot around an approaching commitment
why: A fixed date gives motives a deadline

text: Motive and opportunity establish only motive and opportunity, not proof of an act.
when: Judging whether a case has been proven.
why: Those two factors leave the act itself unshown.

text: A crime without ordinary motive removes the easiest explanation, so investigators must look for other causes.
when: Analyzing a crime with no obvious motive.
why: Absence of motive shifts attention to psychology and opportunity.

text: Avarice is a common passion behind the destruction of a wealthy person, so financial motive can drive killing alongside other passions.
when: Assessing motive in a case involving a rich victim
why: Money is a frequent driver of deliberate harm

text: When the apparent actor seems unable to have acted, or an act looks purposeless, ask who profits; a beneficiary who controls money is a strong suspect.
when: the visible perpetrator seems unable to have acted, or many people could have taken an object whose purpose is unknown
why: Financial interest reveals who has reason to arrange the act.

text: Accused people are often already in quarrels or factional disputes, so existing rivalries are a good predictor of who gets named.
Check the date of a change in a document against the date of the crime, since a change made long before an event was not a reaction to it.
when: A document change seems linked to a later event
why: Timing determines whether a change could have motivated the act

text: Have NPCs push one theory with messages pointing the same way, so players must weigh who gains from the accusation.
A recorded feud can explain conduct that otherwise looks unexplainable, so compare historical records against observed behavior.
Ask why a particular room or target was chosen; the choice often reveals whether the actor knew the building's layout and routines.
Ask why someone did a small act at the time, such as putting out a light. The reply can reveal a choice made under pressure.
Ask who needs the death to be believed, not only who gains from it.
Read a rival's earlier acts together, in hindsight, as steps toward one goal, and weigh rival explanations against that pattern before accepting a motive.
when: a wrongdoer's act has been witnessed only in part
why: Intent is inferred from the sequence rather than from a single act

text: Asking who last saw the victim alive is a sound starting point, but a gossip claim naming someone is itself a claim to test.
Ask what an unusual, risky act gained the actor and what would have happened without it, then reason backward to the actor's need.
when: A suspect's behavior looks needlessly complicated.
why: A costly act must serve a goal that outweighs its risk.

text: Start a murder investigation by asking who gains from the death, and build the case around the strongest motive.
when: when many clues are weak but a financial relationship can be documented

text: A suspect's real secret dealings with the victim can be a red herring that does not explain the death.
when: a hidden relationship is discovered
why: Real but unrelated facts can mislead.

text: Each group that gains from an outcome also has a stake in the story told, so ask who benefits from a claim and who defends it.
when: When assessing a claim pushed by a group with power or interest.
why: Stakes give groups reason to shape and protect the narrative.

text: Show the investigator's motive so the player can tell a case built on evidence from one built on a grudge.
when: when a player must judge an NPC investigator's conclusion

text: Judge a suspect's likely action by what they stood to lose, not only by whether the reasoning about them is neat.
when: Weighing whether a suspect would act in a given way.
why: Human choices are driven by stakes such as shame, which can outweigh self-interest.

text: With audio only and no faces, intent must be inferred from words and from the character's later behavior.
when: observation relies on sound alone
why: faces and gestures are absent

text: Test a proposed motive against observed action rather than assumed sentiment, and check each candidate cause against whether it fits the change.
when: Evaluating a motive or eliminating a suspect.
why: Sentimental stories can feel convincing but fail against the actual behaviour.

text: When a character's stated reason for an action seems thin, look for a hidden fear beneath it, such as exposure, debt or lost reputation.
when: a suspect's behavior does not match the reason given
why: fear often explains actions better than the stated reason

text: When an ordinary explanation seems to undercut a theory, ask why the cover exists and test that reason before abandoning or accepting the theory.
when: when a plausible explanation threatens a working theory
why: a cover story can be innocent or an active disguise

text: A purchase or preparation for an event can signal planned intent.
when: assessing whether a subject plans an appearance or event
why: preparations reveal intentions that have not been stated

text: An impersonal or fanatic motive makes a crime open, while a personal motive tied to the victim confines suspects to people who dealt with the victim.
when: Choosing how wide the suspect pool is.
why: Motive determines who had reason to act.

text: A lapse of will and judgment is theorised to build before an act, peak during it and fade afterwards, causing the traces detection depends on.
Who-benefits reasoning misleads: the obvious beneficiary may not be the actor, first apparent gains must be measured, and some crimes are pathological with no rational gain.
Inferring intent from manner alone is unreliable; a long courtesy walk may be ordinary courtesy, so treat motive read from manner as a hypothesis to test against other evidence.
when: forming an early read on a suspect's motive
why: Manner is weak evidence of intent and can mislead.

text: Fitting facts to a convenient motive, or rebuilding a motive to fit any set of facts, misses the real plan; a reconstructed motive still needs independent evidence and testing.
A motive that fits one time window may fail for another, so motives must be checked against when events happened.
A motive theory built from several cases can mislead when a suspect has a different need, so test it against each individual.
when: applying a general pattern of motive

text: Turning one motive inference into a general claim about human nature overstates what a single case can show.
when: an investigator reasons from one character to people in general
why: one case cannot support a general rule

text: Accepting the first reading of a motive is risky: a withheld letter can make an innocent act look guilty and a guilty one look harmless.
when: a motive is first suggested
why: concealment can flip the apparent meaning

text: A motive that seems very large can make investigators overlook smaller, personal motives that explain the act better.
A flashy spender may be innocent, so the sudden-spending shortcut can point at the wrong person.
Reading motive into hedged wording overreaches when the hedging has an ordinary explanation such as politeness or caution.
when: Interpreting hedged or indirect statements
why: Not every indirect phrase hides a secret opinion

text: Adding a suspect to the opportunity column only for being present is weak evidence, and crossing someone off on motive alone can also mislead.
when: Building a suspect grid
why: Presence and low apparent motive are weak grounds for inclusion or exclusion

text: Behavior-based reasoning assumes a rational culprit, so a panicked or unusual culprit can break the expected pattern.
when: When a culprit's emotional state is unknown.
why: Panic produces actions that rational models do not predict.

text: Judging motive by the amount of money alone, without considering the people and feelings involved, misreads why someone might act.
when: Assessing a financial motive
why: Feelings such as burden or resentment can outweigh the sum

text: A failed check on a story does not prove criminal guilt, since a lie may be protective rather than culpable.
when: Interpreting a contradiction in a witness's or suspect's account.
why: People lie for many reasons, including to shield someone.

text: Settling on the first motive that fits, or reading guilt into nervous behaviour, leads to false conclusions when several causes are possible.
when: when interpreting motive or guilt from behaviour
why: Nervousness and evasion have many causes besides the one suspected

text: Letting a gossip-based motive decide the target before physical evidence confirms it leads the inquiry down a misleading path.
when: choosing a suspect or line of inquiry
why: motive is easier to find than proof

text: Revealing a key motive too soon removes the audience's chance to form its own view.
when: when pacing a mystery reveal

text: Infer motive by ruling out alternatives. 1) List what was left untouched or unstolen. 2) Remove motives the physical evidence contradicts, such as robbery when valuables remain. 3) Examine motives tied to people close to the victim. 4) Test each remaining motive against evidence.
when: when narrowing possible motives for a crime or determining why an act occurred
why: Contradicted motives are removed and remaining ones are tested rather than assumed

text: 1) Check the attacker's background, income and risks. 2) Test whether their stated motive makes sense given what the act would cost them. 3) Ask who gains from the act. 4) Confirm the suspected beneficiary by questioning.
when: an attack or crime seems unmotivated for the person carrying it out

text: 1) Write the subjective reading, based on the actor's intent. 2) Write the objective reading, based on what was actually done. 3) Weigh each against the evidence before choosing one.
when: an act could mean opposing things

text: 1) Identify the earlier event that gave the absent party a motive, such as a document, fear or secret. 2) Build the sequence forward from that motive. 3) Ask why the party did not act directly earlier. 4) Test each link against physical facts.
when: when a crime depends on a hidden past
why: motive chains explain both timing and method

text: 1) Identify who had a motive. 2) Identify who could physically have acted. 3) Match witness descriptions of height, build, and appearance to each candidate. 4) Keep only people who fit both.
when: Several suspects had access to the scene.
why: Motive alone or opportunity alone does not identify a culprit; both together narrow the field.

text: 1) Work out what the accuser would gain if the act succeeded. 2) Note who it would help and who it would hurt. 3) Match each gain to earlier conflicts. 4) Present the result as interpretation, not proof.
when: a hidden motive lies behind a visible act
why: gains often reveal motives that surface actions hide

text: 1) Infer planning level from the method. 2) Infer the likely emotional driver. 3) Identify a likely source of that emotion. 4) Add conditions on who knew, what they felt and when. 5) Test the motive against the timing of events.
when: Reasoning about the motive for a violent act.
why: Conditions and timing reveal motives that fit only some circumstances.

text: 1) Let the player infer a likely motive from the victim's dependencies. 2) Let that motive point to probable evidence. 3) Confirm the inference with a physical find.
when: Structuring a clue chain in a mystery game.
why: Reasoning first and confirming second makes the player's deduction feel earned and checkable.

text: 1) Give significant NPCs a motive profile of several weighted traits, such as ambition, vanity, fear and sincere belief. 2) Let player evidence decide which trait becomes visible.
when: Designing important NPCs in a dungeon or story.
why: Visible motives that shift with evidence reward investigation.

text: 1) List what a suspect acquired. 2) For each item, ask what it is for and whether its cost or type fits the stated purpose. 3) Test candidate purposes against the known facts.
when: A suspect's purchases or possessions do not match their stated reason for them.
why: Mismatches between stated and actual use reveal intent.

text: 1) Ask who inherits or benefits from a death. 2) Check whether the witness knows the contents. 3) Ask who loses, to see whether the answer shifts from gain to grief.
when: Establishing motive early in questioning while relationships are still open
why: Probing gain and loss reveals a witness's knowledge and framing

text: 1) Set out what the records already establish. 2) Assign a helper to check the unknown parts of the background. 3) Combine both into the suspect profile, weighing each source.
when: A suspect's background is partly unknown.
why: Delegating checks spreads the work and keeps each source's weight visible.

text: Prioritize suspects by who knew the valuables were present, ordered by how directly they knew; knowledge of the goods is a stronger lead than general access.
when: stolen valuables were known to a household or a theft requires an insider
why: Leaks often come from people informed about the goods; knowledge of the target is a strong filter.

text: Give suspect characters motives with explicit gain and risk values so the player can judge whether an accusation fits.
when: Designing motives for suspects in a mystery.
why: Measurable stakes let players test accusations rather than accepting labels.

text: Track debts, policies and beneficiaries in a motive ledger so players can see who gains when an NPC dies.
when: designing npc motives

text: Have an NPC flag a hidden motive early in dialogue, then pay it off in a later quest step.
Check motive against what each suspect knew, since a benefit a person did not know about gives that person no motive.
when: Assessing a suspect's motive
why: Motive requires awareness of the benefit

text: Treat money trouble as evidence of motive and strain only, not as proof that a person committed an act.
when: Evaluating a suspect with financial pressure
why: Motive is necessary context but does not establish action

text: Do not use motive as the only filter when many NPCs share the same motive.
when: When designing suspect filtering
why: Shared motives leave too many candidates

text: Let players either accept an NPC's stated motive or contest it with evidence from a logged interaction record.
when: an NPC confronts the player with a pattern of past actions

text: Dependents or sources with a stake in the outcome may shape accounts to keep favor, shifting after promises and offering rumour, or steering questioners toward or away from people.
when: Assessing testimony from servants or dependents tied to someone in authority; when a source controls access to information or to people needed for questioning
why: Continued favor gives the witness a stake in the outcome; a source's own stake shapes what they reveal and withhold while still appearing helpful.

text: A person under heavy debt may pursue a costly claim because it may be the only realistic way to repay what is owed.
when: debts are pressing
why: Limited alternatives raise the value of the claim.

text: Once one suspect fits an expected pattern, investigators tend to dismiss other motives for the same reason, leaving those leads unexamined.
when: A suspect looks obviously guilty early
why: Confirmation of the favoured suspect lowers interest in alternatives.

text: A concealed family relation can explain a witness's interest in the victim, since fear of exposure creates a motive to stay close to the case.
when: When a witness hides a relationship with a party in the case
why: Concealment reveals the stakes the witness is protecting

text: Denials about a missing object can reveal more than admissions, and a contradiction can give others a motive to name a rival.
when: when witnesses are questioned about an item
why: Being caught in a contradiction shifts suspicion onto others.

text: A person who pushes past others to reach a scene shows a strong need to control it, which is worth noting.
People often read a change of fortune that favors them as a reward for their own merit, which colors their guess about the motive behind it.
when: A character learns of a decision that benefits them.
why: Self-interest biases the interpretation of another's reasoning.

text: A person who hides to protect someone will break cover when they fear that protected person is in danger.
when: A hidden person's concealment is driven by loyalty to someone else.
why: Protective motives can outweigh the wish to stay hidden.

text: Relatives with a financial stake in an estate tend to keep guarded distance from each other and show mutual suspicion.
when: an inheritance is at stake

text: Strong attachment can produce contradictory behavior: contempt for a partner can coexist with refusing to leave, so both signals point to the same underlying bond.
when: when interpreting a character's conflicting feelings and actions
why: Attachment alone can keep people in relationships they openly resent.

text: Players suspect whoever stands to lose most from the truth, so motive-linked suspicion guides their reading of ambiguous evidence.
when: when a mystery hinges on who benefits from concealment
why: players assume that a loss creates a motive to lie

text: Sincere piety and a sense of justice, good in themselves, can push passions toward harsher action when combined with personal motives.
A disturbance is noticed only by someone who knows the usual arrangement, so the observer's familiarity decides which changes are recognised.
when: Looking for signs that something was moved or removed
why: A person who knows a normal order notices when it breaks.

text: Observers notice a missing element before they understand it, reasoning from a prior pattern that the element should be present.
when: when a familiar pattern is broken
why: expectation makes absence noticeable

text: Household members who notice a watch feel their privacy violated, which spreads suspicion through the group.
Someone can notice a hidden object and choose not to act on it, so noticing and reporting are separate acts.
when: when a witness sees something that could expose another person
why: Discretion or loyalty can outweigh the urge to disclose.

text: A hunch from memory can feel like a real connection while being imagined; checking it against a document separates the two.
Observers form first impressions from looks and manners, then test them against later conduct; a mismatch becomes the first suspicious clue.
when: when a suspect's public charm conflicts with private signals

text: Skilled players watch other players' habits, not only the rules, and the difference between players lies in knowing what to observe.
when: competitive play with hidden information or other players
why: observing opponents shapes decisions more than rule knowledge does

text: Posture, gaze and small physical tics of a listener reveal more about their state than their spoken answers.
when: Reading a character's hidden knowledge or emotional state.
why: Involuntary behavior is harder to control than speech.

text: In low light, people rely on faint sounds, touch and an unseen presence, and often misjudge what these cues mean.
when: scenes where sight is limited
why: sound alone rarely settles where a source is

text: Witnesses often miss a brief involuntary gesture, and notice it mainly when they saw the same gesture in an earlier encounter.
when: a gesture is brief or glimpsed
why: recognition requires a stored memory of the gesture to match against

text: A silent observer may notice when a companion's reasons are hidden and begin to wonder what they are holding back.
A target absorbed in its own thoughts often fails to notice a follower until it reaches its destination.
when: the target is distracted or emotionally engaged
why: attention on inner concerns reduces awareness of surroundings

text: A target who recognises a watcher will close the door and end the surveillance, so the watcher loses the advantage.
Loud, comic, or emotional public events pull player attention away from quieter clues, because the more visible event dominates focus.
when: A noisy or dramatic scene occurs near a subtle clue.
why: Salient stimuli capture attention before quieter evidence is registered.

text: Companions who cannot read the signs depend on the leader and may fall behind or lose confidence in the chase.
when: when a party includes members without the tracker's skill
why: Tracking knowledge is not shared automatically

text: Observers who describe a person as ordinary or unremarkable tend to record little detail, so their overall impression hides what a trained eye would notice.
when: A witness gives a summary impression rather than an itemized account.
why: A category label like unremarkable reduces the attention paid to specifics.

text: Early physical details about a character, such as worn marks or footwear, read as background until a later deduction turns them into evidence.
Set a 'noticed' flag when an NPC reacts to a displayed item, so the clue surfaces implicitly rather than as stated text.
Picture what might have happened, act on the picture, and check it against the ground.
A fabricated supernatural creature can be built from real, mundane effects, such as a luminous substance that makes an animal look infernal.
when: designing a fake monster or supernatural sighting
why: Real effects make the illusion physically plausible.

text: Do not explain every perception error; let the audience infer it from the setting.
An NPC dialogue system that records which events each NPC mentions can flag the events it omits, letting the player press the NPC about them.
An NPC witness system can record which details an NPC noticed with a confidence level, and let the player test those details against other sources.
when: Designing NPC witnesses whose knowledge the player must verify.
why: Recorded confidence lets the player weigh each detail.

text: Being noticed while following a suspect can let their employer hear of you, turning the tail into a warning.
why: the target and employer learn of the observer

text: Identifying a watcher from clothing or appearance alone is a guess that may be wrong.
A witness who could not see a figure should not be trusted to identify it, even when a voice seems familiar.
why: darkness makes recognition unreliable

text: An impression of magical vanishing is not an explanation; the answer must be found in the door, the key or the route.
when: a disappearance seems dramatic
why: drama hides mundane mechanics

text: A rehearsed impression is still only an impression, not proof that the person was actually present.
Trusting a witness who recalls only a vague impression can place an event at the wrong time.
why: impressions lack precise detail

text: Assuming a witness saw someone just because that person was present in the room leads to wrong conclusions about who was there.
An observer whose attention is elsewhere, such as under a drug or stress, may miss signals from others in the room.
when: Interrogating while the observer is impaired or distracted
why: Limited attention filters out secondary cues

text: 1) Ask the witness for the exact words used. 2) Ask for the order of events. 3) Ask exactly when the conversation broke off. Note hesitation and interruption as well as content.
when: when an account depends on a voice, feeling or half-heard exchange
why: precision separates memory from expectation

text: 1) Gather suspects under a neutral pretext. 2) Seat the observer where hands and reactions are visible. 3) Raise stakes quickly so each suspect's risk appetite shows in choices. 4) Record each suspect's attitude and any refusal with its reasons.
when: physical evidence cannot separate a few suspects and character must help decide
why: Behaviour under stakes is treated as evidence of character to be matched against the crime's demands.

text: 1) Stay silent. 2) Move slowly. 3) Keep to dark paths away from the light. 4) Head for a safe boundary or help.
when: passing an unseen threat in darkness
why: avoids alerting a hidden person and reaches safety

text: Record a witness's impressions of mood, emotion or temperament separately from established facts, treating them as less reliable than physical features.
when: A witness reports a feeling or temperament about a person or scene
why: Impressions add atmosphere but do not establish facts; they depend on the witness's perception and fear, not observable traits.

text: Do not build a case on an impression alone; impressions can be wrong and are not measurements, so confirm the detail with another source.
when: the key detail is a described impression
why: impressions can be wrong

text: Keep a time-stamped log of NPC sightings, sounds and actions so players can order events and find the one account that conflicts.
when: when NPCs describe overlapping events
why: Lets players assemble the timeline from fragments.

text: Limit NPC dialogue to observations and let theories come from the player's deduction.
when: Writing NPC dialogue for a deduction-based game.
why: Keeping interpretation with the player preserves the deduction challenge.

text: Add a notice board or newspaper that posts time-windowed witness requests, so the player's reply options determine which witness NPC appears.
Log how long and how closely each NPC has observed the player, and weight their statements by that familiarity.
when: designing NPC reputation systems

text: A tiny swap of one object for a look-alike can strongly signal to observers that someone acted deliberately in that space.
when: when an observer notices a changed object in a familiar setting
why: small unexpected changes stand out against a known baseline

text: A visible object can reveal that its wearer expected a specific threat, such as a blow, so its state carries information about preparation.
when: an object's protective features suggest anticipated danger
why: Equipment chosen for a particular threat signals what its wearer foresaw.

text: Listeners trust a story that seems plausible to them, even when their own expectations shaped how it was rebuilt.
when: A rumour or report fits what the listener already expects
why: Expectations fill gaps in what was actually observed.

text: People repeat what was printed in the press as if it were settled, so press reports strongly shape a group's views.
Whether an object is noticed depends on its setting: the same item goes unseen in a crowded, shabby place but is remembered in a quiet one.
when: The item's surroundings contain many similar items or people.
why: Ordinary detail blends into its context, while an item that departs from its surroundings draws attention.

text: When rumours contest an in-world document, players must judge its truth themselves, so credibility stays an open question until the end.
when: The document's claims are publicly disputed
why: Competing rumours force players to weigh evidence

text: Read an object's wear, damage and condition as a record of its owner's habits and body, then test that record against everyone who could have handled the object.
when: Investigating who recently used a place or object when personal items are present
why: Wear accumulates from repeated personal use, so it carries identifying information about the user.

text: The one item that differs from the rest of a set, such as an unmarked or differently handled object, is often the most informative clue.
when: Comparing a group of similar personal objects
why: A deviation from the shared pattern stands out and points to a distinct user.

text: Investigators read people from outward traces such as clothing fit, hair movement, silhouette, lantern-lit faces and small signs; a discrepancy from expected appearance is often the key clue.
when: When identifying a person or detecting a disguise
why: Mismatches between appearance and expectation reveal concealment

text: An object placed well back from a table edge suggests a careful person who guards against being knocked off.
when: reading a person's habits from small placements
why: careful people position things to avoid accidents

text: People who need an item quickly tend to keep it close at hand and keep related secret items together, which narrows where it is likely hidden.
when: Predicting where an owner has stored an item.
why: Convenience and secrecy drive storage habits.

text: A single item of evidence can support opposing theories, and one fact about its source or circumstances can overturn the reading.
when: an investigation rests on one interpretation of several items
why: each item may have an innocent explanation that competes with the guilty one

text: Faint, indistinct or sparse traces, such as a lone mark on moss or lichen, invite over-reading and invented patterns; support only tentative conclusions until corroborated.
when: Judging ambiguous, scarce or faint traces, such as marks on moss or lichen ground
why: A single ambiguous mark fits several possible makers, and indefinite details invite over-reading and false conclusions.

text: A trace that matches the investigator's theory can be over-read, because confidence in the match comes from the investigator rather than from the evidence.
when: Matching common materials such as soil or dust to a location.
why: Common materials can match many places, and a favoured theory makes the match seem stronger than it is.

text: Staged evidence can look too convenient; comparing treated traces with untreated ones reveals what was deliberately spared.
when: When a clue seems to fit the conclusion too neatly.
why: Staging leaves differences in how traces were handled.

text: Trusting a single observed tell too much ignores whether the observer's reaction depended on earlier, stored observation.
Treating a single letter or document as absolute proof overstates what it establishes, since it may still fit several explanations.
when: Weighing one document as decisive.
why: A document often proves less than it appears to.

text: Footprint patterns from overshoes can match many people, so a pattern alone rarely identifies a single individual.
why: Common footwear produces shared patterns.

text: A visible trace such as blood often carries an obvious default reading that first impressions get wrong until an expert examines it.
A verdict built on status, popularity or wealth can sound decisive while answering a different question than the one asked.
when: No plain statement of the facts is available.
why: Proxies correlate with reputation, not with the truth of a dispute.

text: An observer can misread an object or gesture, interpreting a puzzling item in the wrong light at first.
when: an observer encounters an unexplained object
why: without context, first impressions of an item can mislead

text: 1) Identify objects unique within a household. 2) Trace who handled them and when, including washing, ironing and carrying. 3) Compare those dates with the suspect's account.
when: An object's ownership is clear and its movements can be traced through routine tasks
why: Custody records can contradict a claimed presence or alibi

text: 1) Measure a set of prints. 2) Compare the size with objects found in the house. 3) If a size matches, link the prints to that object. 4) Then question the object's history.
when: prints match a size of an object in the house
why: A confirmed size link ties the trace to a specific object and raises questions about it.

text: Do not assume an object was used in a crime just because it was found near the scene; check its custody chain first.
when: An object is found near a crime scene
why: Proximity alone does not show use or ownership in the act

text: Compare physical traces such as footprints, footwear, fingerprints and weapons against each candidate, clearing or keeping each one, and record where the search could not reach.
when: a suspect list is long and physical traces exist to sort it
why: Systematic matching narrows candidates, and recording gaps prevents false clearances.

text: Treat physical evidence as meaningful only once a witness links it to a specific person.
when: an object such as a cloth, weapon or document is found
why: An unattributed object does not identify who was involved.

text: Reading guilt into ordinary events, such as a nosebleed or dry shoes, misleads when their cause is unknown; small details may mean much or nothing; many reactions have harmless causes.
An observer drawn to someone by pity, anger, admiration or affection colours perception and report, may read a deliberate test as cruelty, so the account is partial.
when: An observer is emotionally involved with, or drawn to, the person under questioning.
why: Emotional involvement shapes perception and report.

text: Outside pressure, from an outsider urging an investigator or from passion, fear and gossip in a stressed community, speeds decisions and accusations before evidence is weighed.
when: an outsider presses an investigator to act, or fear or gossip circulates in a community under stress.
why: Pressure from others changes the pace of decisions; emotion and talk can outrun judgement.

text: A nickname or recent attention can lead observers to attach a familiar name to a stranger or shape what a witness expects to see, distorting identification.
when: recent context fills the observer's attention, or a nickname is given to someone.
why: Priming makes familiar names and faces surface before observation, shaping perception.

text: Witnesses primed with a cause or legend before an event tend to report sightings matching it, so prior belief shapes what they perceive.
when: people are primed with a preconceived explanation or told a story before an event.
why: Expectation shapes perception.

text: An investigator who states a suspicion as certainty reads each later detail as confirmation, ignoring details pointing elsewhere and keeping that suspect until a physical trace contradicts.
when: a player or investigator commits to a suspect before proof arrives, or the obvious story points at one suspect.
why: A favoured theory filters new evidence toward the held conclusion.

text: An investigator's assumption, or a sign pointing toward a suspect, is a presumption that justifies closer examination but not guilt; a deduction is a conclusion drawn from evidence.
An observer's own feelings or prejudices, such as hostility, jealousy or bias, colour how they read another's tone, manner or tells, turning anger or grief into apparent guilt.
when: Interpreting another character's or witness's tone, manner or tells.

text: Pinning suspicion or a repeated word onto whoever is nearest or most hostile is often a reflex, not evidence; words gain meaning from speaker and listener.
when: linking an overheard keyword or suspicion to a person physically nearby.
why: Ordinary words gain meaning from speaker and listener, not from proximity.

text: Do not convict on presumption or suspicion alone; without physical traces or sufficient proof, a sceptical reviewer rejects the accusation and a presumption slides into conviction.
when: when deciding whether to convict, or the accusation rests on suspicion without physical evidence
why: presumption can be wrong, and conviction needs proof; reviewers reject unsupported belief

text: Separate a recorded presentiment, feeling or speculation from the events it describes; a diary or log entry of inference is not established fact.
when: reviewing a written record or diary.
why: The boundary between inference and observation is easily blurred.

text: An emotionally attached observer reads a suspect's behaviour in the most favourable light, so innocent acts look guilty or guilty acts innocent, favouring readings that match existing conclusions.
when: The observer has affection or dislike for the suspect, or is emotionally invested.
why: Emotional attachment and confirmation bias shape which signs are noticed and how they are weighed.

text: Prejudice against a witness or claimant, or an advance warning, offers a ready explanation, so sound claims are dismissed as known delusion before being examined.
when: A listener is warned about a claimant in advance or holds strong assumptions about them.
why: The warning or prejudice replaces scrutiny of the claim with a ready explanation.

text: An eerie mood or haunting setting, such as moaning wind, ghostly cues or a ghostly presence, primes players and investigators toward a supernatural explanation before evidence is weighed.
when: a mystery or investigation uses eerie atmosphere.
why: Mood and atmosphere shape expectations and interpretation of ambiguous events.

text: Nerves (a startle, dropped item, shaking hand) and ordinary acts (yawning, unrelated lesson before an inquest) are read by observers as guilt or indifference, feeding suspicion without showing guilt.
when: a character is addressed or questioned, or behaves ordinarily around an inquest.
why: Observers read involuntary tension or indifference as guilt.

text: A witness's prejudices and deference to rank shape how they describe people, so their descriptions reveal their attitudes.
why: Social attitudes colour observation

text: A sudden bright light can blind an observer at the critical moment, leaving them unable to say what was happening.
when: An event happens during a sudden disruption.
why: Vision and attention can fail exactly when they are most needed.

text: People find a theory that fits a prejudice easier to hold than one that fits the facts.
when: Two explanations compete and one matches existing feelings.
why: Prejudice gives an easier, more familiar explanation.

text: A guilty party may attend the investigation, stay silent, listen closely and watch the investigators, so their quiet interest and nervousness are cues an investigator can record.
when: When a person present at an investigation reacts unusually to what is said.
why: A guilty person has reason to monitor what investigators know.

text: An observer busy with their own goal may notice a clue, accept a casual explanation and file it away without following up.
when: the observer has a competing errand
why: a plausible, open-sounding reply discourages further questions

text: Listeners who already hold an accusation read an ambiguous word as aimed at the person they suspect.
when: an ambiguous statement follows a known accusation
why: preset belief selects the interpretation

text: Mentioning a suspect's close family can trigger visible emotion, which an interrogator can read as a sign of the suspect's weak point.
when: Probing a suspect's emotional attachments

text: Suspects who assume others share their own bad motives read every silence and evasion as hidden purpose, so innocent reticence can be mistaken for scheming.
when: When a character interprets another's silence or evasion through their own intentions.
why: People project their own motives onto others, so ambiguous silence gets a sinister reading.

text: An observer's prejudice against a person can persist even against the plainest proof.
why: Prior feelings filter how new evidence is read.

text: A mind occupied by one mystery can make an ordinary place feel charged or haunted, so first impressions formed then are unreliable.
when: a searcher visits a location while preoccupied or in poor light
why: attention is fixed on the problem and misreads neutral features

text: Omens such as circling scavengers lead players to read later clues as signs of death.
when: A setting must prepare players to interpret what follows.
why: Early cues shape expectations and set how later evidence is read.

text: Prior meetings with a person, room, or object color what an observer later perceives, so repeat observations differ from a first impression.
when: when an observer has encountered the subject before
why: memory of earlier encounters shapes new perception

text: Experts can be biased by prior knowledge, such as already knowing an outcome, so their estimates may be shaped before the evidence is examined.
when: when an expert estimates from evidence after learning a result
why: Known outcomes shape how evidence is interpreted

text: Outsiders' first questions reveal their assumptions, such as whether a family member is among the victims.
An official present during an interview can change how a witness speaks.
when: when interviews happen in front of an observer

text: People accept a stillness or behaviour as normal when it fits the context they expect, so a wrong timing can go unnoticed by everyone present.
when: a character's behaviour is normal in its setting but wrong in timing
why: Expectation of context hides the anomaly, since others treat the behaviour as part of the scene.

text: A listener's preconception can distort their picture of a person, so a stated fact such as age can correct a mistaken impression.
when: When forming an impression of a witness described by others.

text: Investigators who know household members personally often reject them as capable of a crime, narrowing the suspect list before the evidence is checked.
when: when suspects are close to the investigator
why: Personal affection and moral assumptions override what the traces show.

text: A personal connection to a case brings motivation and intimate detail about the people involved, while detached outside inquiry may miss what ties would reveal.
when: Gathering information from people in a case.
why: Personal ties open access and motivation.

text: Players judge a newly arrived character by appearance, clothing and manner before any dialogue, reading his role and self-image from them.
when: a character enters a scene and has not yet spoken
why: visual and behavioral cues are read before words

text: When some accused people are shielded while others are pursued, players read the unequal treatment as proof of a hidden hand and assume corruption.
when: Outcomes depend on who the actor is rather than on the stated rule.
why: Visible inconsistency is taken as evidence of secret influence.

text: People who treat trivial incidents as omens of good or bad fortune will read ordinary misfortune as malice.
when: when a community interprets minor events as signs
why: a belief in omens converts chance misfortune into evidence of intent

text: A claimed mesmeric or hypnotic effect can be strongest in the person who believes in it, so belief can make the effect seem real.
when: A character or player reports an influence they expect to feel.
why: Expectation shapes perception, so the believer experiences the effect most intensely.

text: A strong emotion can lead an investigator to read an ambiguous clue as confirming a fear, forming a hostile interpretation before testing it.
when: When the player holds a strong emotional stake in the outcome of the investigation.
why: Emotion shapes perception, so a feared conclusion seems confirmed by evidence that does not actually establish it.

text: A person hiding a secret who visibly changes habits, such as greeting, posture, or avoidance, is noticed by observers, who may look back or comment.
when: When a character deviates from a known routine while concealing something.
why: Deviations from a baseline are conspicuous to others, who register them as unusual.

text: A primed observer's recall is shaped by mood and expectation, so they find resemblances and patterns that may not exist.
when: when a witness is emotionally primed
why: mood and expectation reshape perception

text: Officials first accept self-inflicted death when the victim seems unlikely to resist the method.
when: A death is presented as self-inflicted.
why: Assumed behaviour of the victim shapes the first verdict.

text: A witness who appears exactly where the investigator arrives is read as coincidence, and the absence of that person would also have looked like coincidence.
when: A witness's presence at a key moment needs explaining.
why: Both presence and absence can be framed as suspicious, so coincidence alone rarely settles the matter.

text: Observers attribute uncanny insight to investigators whose method is hidden from them, though a careful, systematic process usually explains it.
when: when an investigator seems to know things by intuition
why: Unseen reasoning looks like supernatural ability to outsiders.

text: When clues about one suspect are front-loaded and dense, players lock onto that suspect early and hold the belief even as other clues arrive.
when: A mystery front-loads evidence against one character.
why: Dense early evidence forms a settled theory before later clues can challenge it.

text: Players read ambiguous new evidence through the theory they currently hold, so a forgery is first assigned to the group they already suspect.
when: when a group is framed as conspirators
why: Current suspicion sets how new clues are interpreted.

text: Players keep suspecting whoever the official account favours until a new physical contradiction or a second body moves their suspicion.
when: a multi-suspect mystery
why: An accepted explanation anchors belief until new evidence challenges it.

text: Players and characters overlook familiar service figures in plain view, so an insider in an everyday role stays unsuspected even when present in every scene.
when: a service or staff character appears throughout the story
why: Repeated, expected presence makes the character part of the background to attention.

text: Different observers of the same person see different sides, so their accounts may conflict until they are compared.
Some argue the presumption of innocence becomes largely formal once an accused is arrested and treated like a criminal.
Reputation, a report from a fellow practitioner, harm following cursing, harm following enmity, and close association with a convicted person all count only as presumptions.
A known extreme prejudice against a group can recast a relationship as a possible motive, though it is not enough alone to establish that someone acted.
when: Evaluating an attitude as motive
why: Attitudes shape choices but need corroboration to show action

text: Ask a question assuming a detail, such as which person was involved; a witness who hesitates or refuses to name someone confirms the premise rather than volunteering it.
when: a partly cooperative witness holds back information.
why: Hesitation after a presumptive question reveals acceptance of the premise.

text: Record an observer's silence, unusual interest or sudden withdrawal and weigh it against other facts, not as proof; silence has several meanings, so test a reading before acting.
when: an observer's reactions seem significant during an inquiry, or a silence could have an innocent cause.
why: Behavior is ambiguous alone but meaningful when combined with other evidence.

text: Several independent observers reaching the same result, such as agreeing an item looks different, corroborate a finding; a single check is weak evidence.
Ask what a viewer would perceive first, such as body orientation; a wrong first detail shows the writer never pictured the scene.
Use a concealed observer to tell the player something a character does not know, so tension builds through that gap.
Knowing a witness's regular schedule lets investigators infer what they could not see directly, such as whether a light was on or someone was absent on a given night.
when: when a witness passes a location at predictable times
why: Habitual observations reveal changes in state indirectly

text: An observer with relevant expertise can notice hidden states behind a calm front that untrained watchers miss.
Look for a feud, boundary dispute or hard words exchanged before an accusation, since these give people reasons to resent the accused.
when: When an accusation involves neighbors, land lines or earlier quarrels.
why: Existing grievances supply motive and an audience for suspicion.

text: Prior experience of violence, such as wartime service, is often taken to lower the barrier to killing.
An observer's romantic interest can colour what they notice and how they interpret it, so impressions should be checked against physical facts.
when: A narrator or observer is emotionally invested in the subject.
why: Attraction shapes attention and trust, distorting perception.

text: A mind primed for the strange sees ordinary details as strange and looks less for mundane causes, so an exotic explanation diverts attention from mundane suspects.
when: A dramatic or exotic story is presented before facts are checked, or an observer strongly expects a supernatural event.
why: Expectation filters what is noticed and how it is interpreted.

text: Suspicion from class, background, looks or reputation, not evidence, repeated through prejudiced framing passes for proof; it makes the investigator look foolish and must be handled carefully.
when: a group forms a verdict about a suspect.
why: Prejudice carried by framing and noise is mistaken for proof.

text: Model gaps in a witness's observation explicitly, so the player must work out what the witness missed.
when: A witness was absent from part of an event.
why: Unobserved moments leave the player to reconstruct the missing information.

text: Prejudice from a person's job, class, wealth, style or group colours how demeanour is read as sincere or calculating; such readings reveal the observer and are only evidence to weigh.
when: An observer forms a view of someone from background, appearance or group.
why: Prejudice shapes perception, so the reading reveals the observer as much as the subject.

text: Observers' timing errors distort the chronology built from their reports, so their time stamps need checking.
Stale air, heat and a confused head degrade an observer's counts and timings, including the investigator's own.
Earlier cases can colour an investigator's view of new people, turning a recognised pattern into prejudice.
Ruling out a motive from general beliefs about people, without checking it against the evidence, can wrongly close a line of inquiry.
why: Assumptions about human behaviour may not hold in a specific case

text: Following one motive too early hides the others. Keep all leads open and defer choosing a motive until evidence arrives.
when: several motives remain plausible

text: Accepting a stated motive, such as valuables, before checking the financial details can lead investigators to the wrong explanation.
An observer can misread a witness's motive, judging curiosity as ghoulish when it has another cause.
An observer who lacks perceptiveness can take a suspect's display of feeling at face value and miss what it conceals.
Questions that presume guilt make the answers seem to confirm it, so the transcript records the questioner's assumption more than the witness's knowledge.
when: designing or reviewing interrogation dialogue
why: Framing supplies the conclusion that the answer is then read as proving

text: An observer who was himself out of his usual routine that night weakens any claim about what others were doing at that time.
In public observation, the watchers can become the ones who decide what counts as a sign of guilt.
An observer may excuse a reaction by a trait they share, such as irritability, which biases the reading.
Observers may over-read an averted gaze and invent meaning where none exists.
when: Interpreting a character's eye movements as clues.
why: Ambiguous signals invite projection of the observer's own suspicions.

text: Acting on personal dislike of a suspect rather than on evidence distorts which suspects are pursued.
A witness who believes no one followed them may be wrong, since a skilled watcher can escape notice.
when: Assessing a claim that surroundings were clear
why: Absence of observed pursuit does not prove absence of pursuit

text: A place's reputation can make people see or report what they expect, and atmosphere such as gloom or decay can lead an investigator to read ordinary facts as signs.
when: when a location carries a frightening legend
why: Expectation and mood bias observation and interpretation.

text: Jealousy toward a rival can make an investigator see that rival as guilty, or wrongly treat a suspect as innocent.
why: Rivalry biases the investigator's view of both people.

text: Investigators attached to a finished theory react defensively when a single fact undermines it, often prioritizing reputation over the evidence.
when: a confident theory is challenged by one fact
why: self-satisfaction and reputation concerns resist revising a conclusion

text: A vivid impression formed from holding a written message does not prove the writer's situation, because the reader's expectations shape what is reported.
when: Forming a view of a writer through a physical object or intuition.
why: Expectation colours perception, so impressions need comparison with the writer's later account.

text: Fear can persuade a person that a supernatural cause is more likely than an ordinary one.
Before accepting a witness's report, establish where they stood, distance, obstructions, attention, and any impairment such as drinking or irregular watching.
when: a witness claims to have seen, heard or noticed something, especially at night or at a distance.
why: A report is only as reliable as the view and assumptions behind it.

text: Give characters watching from the dark a reason to be there, or the scene reads as contrived.
when: Placing hidden observers in a scene

text: Keep observers in darkness and out of sight, since a visible light or noise can warn the target and spoil the test.
Check any presumed time of death against later sightings; a living person seen after that time removes the murder window.
Let a character's prejudice color their hints, so the player learns to test each NPC's claims.
when: writing NPC dialogue in a mystery
why: Testing claims teaches players to distrust unverified opinion.

text: Give each NPC a quarrel, land claim or rivalry that exists before the crime, so suspicion has an existing path to follow.
when: When designing NPC relationships for a mystery.
why: Pre-existing conflict makes accusations believable to other NPCs.

text: Let the accused receive a presumption of innocence until fuller evidence exists, and do not add burden to people already suffering.
when: A community is deciding whether to judge a suspect.

text: Observers vary and one impression can mislead; a lone observer unswayed by others may keep a truer record when accounts conflict or consensus forms fast, though background assumptions still mislead.
when: relying on a single account of a scene; or when many accounts conflict or consensus forms quickly.
why: Attention varies between people; lacking social bias keeps a record nearer raw evidence, yet background knowledge can mislead.

text: Audiences may overestimate an investigator's confidence and assume a puzzle is equally puzzling to the investigator, which misleads them.
when: a narrator reports a puzzle they cannot solve
why: the narrator's uncertainty is projected onto the investigator

text: A frightened person often acts on instinct, so their actions may not follow a neat plan and may contradict a rational explanation.
when: Judging an act made immediately after a violent event
why: Instinct rather than reasoning drives action under fright.

text: Offenders often give themselves away by spending or celebrating freely soon after a crime.
when: shortly after a crime
why: the sudden change in behaviour draws notice

text: Pride in a method can lead an offender to disclose it, for example by writing to show how clever he was.
when: An offender who considers his method clever or has grown conceited
why: Vanity drives the wish to be recognised, which exposes the offender.

text: A person accused of a wrong may defend it by weighing one questionable act against many blameless ones, a common self-justification.
when: when defending a single misdeed
why: tallying good acts feels like a fair balance

text: A person is more likely to reveal guilt when a relevant subject comes up unexpectedly while they are off guard.
why: Surprise lowers the composure that normally hides guilt.

text: Offenders may betray themselves through vanity, a need to confess, flight without covering tracks, reckless confidence, or a return to the scene.
Under threat and exposure, a suspect's words and movements can reveal knowledge they meant to hide. Watch for sudden lunges, insistence, or statements that go beyond what the evidence allows.
when: A suspect is cornered and the situation is under the investigator's control
why: Stress lowers control over what a person says and does

text: Owners of a puzzle often assume it was missed for lack of skill, but clues kept in separate sources are rarely joined.
when: A puzzle's parts sit in different documents
why: No one holds all the parts together

text: Under group questioning, people interrupt or steer talk toward their own concern, so interruptions reveal who wants to control the topic.
when: A group discussion turns to sensitive matters.
why: People with something to protect try to direct the conversation.

text: Impressions made from one fixed template repeat each other exactly, while genuine ones vary, so uniformity across a set can expose forgery.
when: Several impressions are available side by side
why: A flat template produces identical results, whereas a natural source varies with each contact.

text: A person who hears only part of a tense private exchange misreads it, filling gaps with their own fears or jealousy.
when: overhearing fragments
why: missing context is filled by emotion

text: Each person reads the same events from partial information, so accounts diverge depending on what each was told.
when: people share an event but not its hidden details
why: withheld facts change interpretation

text: A witness who watches the wrong side of a scene can miss a remarkable event entirely, so partial sight can hide what actually happened.
when: A witness's position covers only part of the action.
why: A witness is only as reliable as the angle they look from.

text: A suspect who has lied earlier may later admit part of the lie with a sincere-sounding reason while still denying the central accusation.
when: Witnesses already contradict the suspect's first account.
why: Partial admission reduces the cost of the lie and keeps the core denial intact.

text: A confirmed but tangential secret offers a ready explanation for odd behaviour, so people treat the case as explained and stop testing the rest.
