when: A partly true personal secret is revealed alongside a suspicious act
why: Partial truth makes the remainder easier to accept

text: A speaker who starts to reveal something and then stops leaves the group guessing and holds their attention.
Partial credit for correct observations gives players a sense of progress even when their final accusation fails.
why: credit for valid reasoning is felt as achievement

text: In shouting, drunken or confused crowds, a listener may catch only one firm fact while everything else stays lost in noise.
when: when an argument is conducted loudly
why: overlapping voices prevent a full account

text: People recognise an item from a partly visible label by its word shape, not a full reading, and this recognition can be wrong.
when: text is only partly visible
why: recognition relies on familiar word shapes

text: A witness who leaves out what they cannot say shows it through hesitation and changed manner, and attentive listeners can sense the omission.
when: A witness gives a partial account of a painful or difficult event.
why: Emotional resistance shows in behaviour even when the words are incomplete.

text: Players accept a false suspect when clues arrive as isolated fragments, because no frame connects them until the final reconstruction.
when: Clues are scattered and held back until the end of a case.
why: Without a frame, each fragment looks like a separate oddity rather than part of one plan.

text: A source's knowledge is bounded by their role and when they joined, so a denial may reflect limited access. Ask what they could have seen before judging them unhelpful.
when: when choosing which NPC to question, or when a source denies knowing something
why: Role and timing determine access to information, and a denial may reflect limited access rather than absence of information.

text: Emotional displays such as hostility, devotion, fear, candour, surprise, or calm can be feigned, and a composed denial may reflect innocence or practised control, so no single reaction proves guilt, innocence, or a claim.
why: Reactions and demeanour are performed and cannot be read reliably in isolation.

text: Feigned boredom or distraction, while the questioner keeps listening closely and hides their real aim, can make a guarded subject talk more freely.
when: A guarded witness must be drawn out without revealing the real line of inquiry.
why: Lowered perceived pressure reduces the witness's guard; a relaxed questioner seems less of a threat.

text: A smooth, polished, prepared defense may signal a careful suspect, so look for hesitation before it, since real answers often contain visible hesitation.
when: A suspect denies ownership or wrongdoing with polished logic.
why: Prepared reasoning sounds clean, while a real answer often contains visible hesitation.

text: Feigned disbelief can loosen a talkative source, who grows more forthcoming when contradicted.
when: the source is talkative

text: Feigned memory loss gives a plausible reason to avoid answering questions, so questioners meet confusion instead of information.
A guilty party who volunteers unprompted reassurance or overstates innocence draws attention to the very thing being hidden.
when: Observing a suspect's speech during an investigation.
why: Excess defense signals concealment and invites scrutiny.

text: A witness who carefully prepares appearance and expressions may be read as artful and concealing, because observers link polish with deception.
when: A witness presents a carefully staged appearance.
why: Observers associate deliberate presentation with hidden intent.

text: A person who performs devotion in company can keep a harsher private side hidden, and observers do not look for the rest when the public side is managed carefully.
when: A suspect's public behavior appears neat and complete
why: A flawless surface reduces the search for a hidden side.

text: A narrator who admits a story is hard to believe and begs to be taken seriously shows strain, not evidence that the story is true.
when: a reporter asks for trust without supporting facts
why: an appeal for belief reflects the reporter's emotional state

text: A person who yields verbally to a challenge may still show defiance in face or posture, so the spoken answer does not reveal the full reaction.
when: a challenged character responds
why: People mask feelings while conceding

text: Actions that fit a performer's expected role, such as tumbling or leaping, look harmless even when they hide suspicious movement.
when: A character moves within an expected role during a show or event.
why: Observers judge movement by what the role predicts.

text: A character may keep a light or mocking surface while silently calculating, so visible calm does not reveal their actual thinking.
when: A character is under pressure but must appear unconcerned.
why: Performing composure protects the character while the real reasoning happens out of view.

text: A witness given a plausible, face-saving reason for concealing something tends to accept it and then give more detail.
when: A witness is hiding a fact out of fear of blame.
why: The excuse lowers the social cost of admitting the truth.

text: A character who claims to have held back questions out of courtesy plants the impression that they know more than they say.
when: a character must seem unconcerned while hinting at knowledge
why: the restraint reverses the direction of suspicion

text: Generous offers can win a neutral bystander's sympathy even when the giver has a hidden purpose.
People act differently when they believe no one is watching, so an unguarded expression can contradict their public manner.
when: A character is seen alone
why: Without an audience, the character drops the public mask

text: A claimed injury can explain months of absence from public duties without any direct proof of where the person went.
when: a person is unavailable for a long period with a medical reason

text: A feigned weakness in a language is easy to keep up when the listener suspects nothing, so mispronunciation makes a weak tell.
Prepare a plausible excuse before being challenged; giving one just before a brief transaction draws observers' attention away from the face and lowers scrutiny.
when: A person is somewhere that needs explaining, or an impostor meets a clerk or guard briefly.
why: An excuse draws the observer's attention away from the face.

text: When a suspect claims not to recall a name, press gently to tell genuine memory gaps from invented ignorance.
when: A suspect professes not to remember a name or detail.
why: Gentle pressure separates forgetting from deliberate concealment.

text: Use a false claim, such as a stated conclusion, to see whether the suspect reacts as a guilty person would, but only when the investigator knows the claim is false.
when: Probing a suspect's reaction without revealing evidence.
why: The reaction to a false claim can expose guilt while keeping the investigator's position safe.

text: A casual offer to check a companion's story can prompt a suspect to name someone they had not mentioned.
A victim's appearance can be a performance that casts the bound person as the wronged party and steers attention away from them.
when: When a bound or injured person seems to be the victim
why: Staged victimhood directs suspicion toward someone else

text: Conduct done openly in front of others, such as asking directions, is a weak signal of innocence, since a person planning a crime tends to avoid attention.
why: People who want to avoid notice usually act less conspicuously.

text: Feigned courtesy looks like evasion when the investigator is already pressing a specific line of questioning.
when: an investigator is committed to a line of questioning

text: Admitting uncertainty and keeping a stated promise makes an offered deal feel fair to the suspect.
A feigned collapse draws others to tend the apparent victim, which frees the feigner to act or watch unnoticed.
when: a character pretends to be unconscious, injured, or dead
why: Attention shifts to the apparent victim, leaving the feigner free.

text: Feigned disinterest or over-acting that seems too obvious or too well timed reads as dismissal or suspicion, silencing or driving off sources; it must sound natural.
when: Using apparent disinterest to draw out talk.
why: Transparent tactics breed distrust.

text: A feigned state can be exposed by an expert who knows how to test the pretence.
when: when the captor is a specialist

text: A dying witness may be deliberately misleading, so a convincing death scene can be a staged trap rather than genuine testimony.
Feigned familiarity can lead a witness to claim more knowledge than they really have, so verify what they say.
A witness who feigns sleep gives unreliable timing for when they stopped being awake.
Misdirection holds only briefly; once a single observer stops watching the show and checks the real scene, the cover fails.
Flattery and light banter can hide a lack of real progress from the questioner, who then mistakes rapport for results.
A distraction that breaks the actor's established character makes observers suspicious and can provoke indignation.

1) Keep questioning centred on an apparent suspect. 2) Admit openly that proof is weak. 3) Watch the culprit's reactions closely. 4) Keep one's own team partly uninformed so their reactions look genuine. 5) Explain the stratagem afterward.
when: physical or legal proof is thin and the culprit is likely to act
why: A believed false focus can prompt the culprit to reveal themselves.

text: 1) Answer the witness's pitch with an off-topic remark while still listening. 2) Introduce a seemingly trivial name without comment. 3) Let the witness talk freely. 4) Return to the real line of inquiry later.
when: Concealing real interest from a guarded witness.
why: Digression lowers guard and hides which detail matters.

text: Do not use a feigned plan when allies would be exposed to an armed opponent without warning.
when: The suspect is known to carry weapons.

text: Make an opponent believe you are more hurt or less watched than you are, so their caution drops.
when: Caution by the opposition is the main obstacle.

text: Do not trust an apparent disability at face value; test it by observing the witness when they believe no one is watching.
Script an impostor NPC to show genuine fear when an unexpected event occurs, so that players can catch the mismatch with the NPC's act.
An investigator who holds a correct minority view can be worn down by ridicule, isolation and long hours, weakening the conviction needed to continue.
when: When a correct conclusion is disputed by most colleagues and remains unproven
why: Social pressure and anxiety erode confidence even when the investigator is right

text: Erratic emotions invite a single neat explanation that can settle observers' minds, though rejecting it leaves the behavior unexplained.
when: a character's mixed emotions have no clear cause
why: a plausible story closes the question quickly

text: An observer's liking for a person can overturn a firm prior belief within days, and the observer may be puzzled by the change.
when: when a person's appearance or manner contradicts the observer's stated principles
why: Warm feeling shifts judgment faster than explicit principles are revised.

text: Public commentators can turn a crime into a moral lesson, absorbing it into existing prejudices rather than the evidence.
Listeners may accept a witness's account because it fits what they hope to hear, rather than because the evidence supports it.
when: When a witness's story matches a listener's wishes.
why: Expectation and hope bias evaluation of testimony.

text: A speaker who wants to avoid a sensitive subject may fill the talk with an absorbing side topic, pulling attention away from it.
when: when one party is steering away from a real subject

text: Showing knowledge of one specific detail makes a suspect assume the rest of the questioner's account is already known.
when: The questioner reveals a detail the suspect did not expect them to have.
why: The suspect treats the known detail as evidence of wider knowledge.

text: A personal clash with a group leader can harden a participant's position, so group decisions partly depend on interpersonal dynamics.
Audiences watching a high-stakes display treat it as a physical test rather than a claim, which makes it persuasive.
when: a public display with high stakes
why: it feels like an experiment with a visible result

text: Lavish gifts and favors can be experienced as pressure by the recipient rather than as kindness.
when: when a generous offer comes from someone with an agenda
why: The recipient may sense the obligation hidden inside the generosity.

text: People in desperate straits cling to the most improbable hopes, and the less solid ground they have, the flimsier those hopes become.
when: A character faces prolonged financial or social pressure.
why: Unsupported hope substitutes for the missing support.

text: When a forbidden act is framed as necessary, people search for reasons it is lawful rather than questioning whether it should be done at all.
when: an act is presented as required
why: A feigned need makes the act seem required, and the mind then looks for justifying reasons.

text: A small reward offered to a source can reveal that the reward was noticed, and the source's reaction shows that the offer changed the exchange.
when: when offering a tip to open a conversation
why: Small payments prompt a visible reaction that signals interest.

text: An investigator who is nervous or feels imprudent can become the one being studied, and their unease reveals how easily control is lost in questioning.
when: The questioner is under pressure during an interview.
why: Nervousness is visible to the subject and shifts the balance of the exchange.

text: A person's guard lowers when the conversation turns to a subject they enjoy, and they may mention physical traits such as scars or missing teeth without prompting.
when: Talking with a suspect about a topic they care about
why: Enthusiasm shifts attention away from the investigator's purpose

text: A witness under pressure may reverse a stance, moving from doubt to a claim of connection.
when: a witness is confronted with a matching object or fact
why: emotional pressure can override an earlier position

text: Fear of exposure can motivate a person to pay a demand and stay silent rather than report it.
when: when a witness has complied with threats without reporting them
why: Fear of consequences outweighs the wish to seek justice.

text: Players accept a false frame when the characters in the scene accept it, and keep trusting it until a detail contradicts it.
when: a story where characters share a wrong explanation
why: Players take their cues about what is true from the characters' reactions.

text: Candid disclosure comes more readily within established trust, via a direct question rather than an accusation, and in a friendly informal tone, especially when flattered.
when: Questioning a frightened client or witness who holds key information, or trying to draw out a complaint or resentment.
why: Trust and informal warmth lower defensiveness.

text: An impatient client is restrained only by a clear, timed plan that shows when action will happen.
Crowd agreement can result from social pressure, since people hesitate to contradict a powerful figure.
when: When a group appears to agree with an authority figure.
why: Deference to status can suppress dissenting observations.

text: Charm can make an interviewer feel answered when the question has not been answered, so the interviewer should ask the witness to state the answer plainly.
when: A pleasant conversation leaves the key question unresolved.
why: Pleasant tone creates a sense of resolution that the content does not support.

text: Missing expected traces, such as fingerprints on a surface where contact is expected, can signal deliberate care or technique, such as gloves, rather than innocence.
when: Expected marks such as fingerprints are missing from a crime scene, object, or surface.
why: Removing or avoiding traces requires planning, so the absence is informative; a skilled actor's method may itself leave a distinct residue.

text: A witness who checks a locked door at one time and assumes it stays locked will report a state that may have changed later. The time of each check matters.
when: When a witness reports a door's state
why: People infer a door's state from an earlier check, so the reported state may be outdated.

text: A person who leaves a bloodied outgoing trail may later return to the same place, leaving a fresh trace over the earlier one.
when: A fresh incoming trace overlies a bloodied outgoing one.
why: The later entry shows an unplanned return to the scene.

text: A smeared, whitened, slightly greasy mark reveals that someone attempted to remove a stain, and the method used exposes the cleaner's tools and skill.
when: A stain shows signs of an incomplete or improvised removal attempt.
why: Visible residue and method betray the attempt's quality and available resources.

text: A culprit may remove the vessels or tools used for incapacitation quickly, eliminating the physical evidence that could reveal what was used.
when: A hidden means of incapacitation must be concealed.
why: Removing the physical object destroys proof of the method.

text: A thorough inspection of a wall's top with no climbing traces suggests a sealed vault or a different entry route.
when: checking a wall for signs of climbing
why: Absence of traces after a thorough search narrows the possible entries.

text: A spotless or clean spot among dusty items or surfaces suggests recent handling; check handles, knobs and object tops, and a bright, fresh item suggests recent insertion or replacement.
when: Objects in shared dusty storage are compared, or surfaces in a dusty room are inspected.
why: Hands wipe away dust where they touch, leaving a clean mark; sealed items keep their finish longer than exposed ones.

text: A single ambiguous trace can support two readings, such as carelessness or agitation; the chosen reading is a probability, not a certainty.
when: Interpreting one physical trait of a clue
why: The same visible feature can result from different causes

text: Ask whether a weapon was chosen or merely available nearby, since the choice reveals planning while availability suggests opportunity.
when: Found objects are used in a scene.
why: Choosing an object implies intent and preparation, while grabbing one implies impulse.

text: Prefer explanations grounded in ordinary, checkable detail over elaborate dramatic theories, and test each theory against every detail it must explain.
when: A theory is attractive but untested against physical and financial facts.
why: Dramatic detail can pull reasoning away from the mundane facts that decide the case.

text: Prints that never overlap, or that hug the far edge of a narrow path, suggest a walker avoiding their own tracks, since a normal walker would usually double back over some.
when: a narrow path shows prints that avoid overlapping
why: Deliberate avoidance of one's own prints is unusual for ordinary movement.

text: Tickets bought in bulk may have been destroyed once no longer needed, so gaps in the count are not always evidence of an absent person.
when: A purchase record shows bulk buying with no matching stubs.
why: Buyers who want privacy may discard unused tickets.

text: When an explanation for disposing of objects is given, check whether a simpler, less risky option was available to the actor.
when: an actor's chosen method of hiding or disposing of something is questioned
why: an unnecessarily complex or exposed choice undermines the stated motive

text: 1) Find an accidental feature present in both the source and the suspect copy. 2) Check whether the source itself could have produced the feature. 3) Compare the feature's dimensions and position on both. 4) Judge the match against the chance that two independent events would coincide.
when: A source item and a suspect copy both exist
why: A forger does not intend to reproduce accidental features, so a shared one points to direct copying.

text: Public opinion forms quickly and can treat an accused person as guilty before trial, because repeated belief substitutes for proof and people assume authorities charge only with cause.
when: A group consensus forms about a suspect, or an accusation is discussed informally before formal proceedings.
why: Repeated belief substitutes for proof; people assume authorities charge only with cause.

text: A suspect with a negative reputation is blamed before evidence links them to a crime, and shunning and collective attention spread suspicion through the group.
when: A person has a negative reputation in a family or community, or a community already distrusts them.
why: Prior resentment lowers the bar for suspicion; social cues amplify it.

text: A reluctant figure forced to choose between two options in front of others tends to commit publicly, because evasion becomes costly.
when: the figure wants to avoid the matter and an audience is present
why: public witnessing raises the cost of staying vague

text: A socially prominent suspect makes an ordinary crime seem important, and the story spreads through every social class.
The public can hold condemnation and sympathy for the same suspect at once, so opinion is firm yet contradictory.
A famous or prominent name on a found item draws disproportionate attention, even when the person named had no involvement.
when: A found item names a respected figure
why: Prominence makes a name feel significant

text: An audience can largely accept a well-ordered motive reconstruction even without proof, because clear, sequential reasoning makes a motive feel established.
when: a character presents a chain of reasoning to others
why: logical order persuades people more than missing evidence deters them

text: A critique can gain public favor despite strong institutional opposition, so public reception does not track the strength of the argument.
when: when a reasoned critique meets an established authority
why: popularity and argument quality can diverge

text: Adults' repeated rumors spread to children, who catch panic more readily than adults and absorb unverified claims.
A death often reveals a person's character more clearly than their life did, so the community re-judges them and their reputation may rise or fall.
when: After a person dies.
why: Death prompts a retrospective reckoning.

text: Social decorum keeps gossip in private circles, so it spreads without being voiced openly in public.
A public appeal may go unanswered even when repeated, because witnesses may not realize their information is valuable.
when: An investigator publishes a missing-person appeal
why: Most readers do not respond.

text: Audiences favour a rumor that is dismal and sounds plausible over one with evidence, so unsupported theories spread through groups.
when: Partial information circulates among a group of observers
why: Vivid or dismal explanations feel credible even without support.

text: A motive offered as gossip without evidence can take root in an investigator's mind before anyone checks it.
when: A speaker supplies a motive for a suspect without proof.
why: Unchecked claims are easily accepted and remembered.

text: Doubt spread through friendly remarks and gossip, rather than direct accusation, lets the speaker avoid suspicion while still reaching an audience.
when: When someone wants to discredit a claim without being identified as the source.
why: Indirect remarks carry socially without drawing scrutiny to the speaker.

text: A recurring image appearing across many sources gains weight with the perceiver, so an imagined threat can come to feel real.
when: when the same image keeps recurring
why: repetition makes an idea haunt the mind

text: Public rumor and press consensus form quickly and persist, so overturning them requires contesting each claim in turn.
when: When a case is widely reported before its evidence is examined.
why: Repetition lends a claim authority that a single objection does not remove.

text: Audiences hold competing readings of an unseen threat, such as a real leader or an invented rumour, until evidence settles which one is true.
when: the threat is discussed only through vague talk
why: Vague accounts leave two plausible explanations open

text: Present a theory to an official in a way that does not wound their pride, since a blunt challenge can close off cooperation.
when: Sharing a conclusion that contradicts an official view
why: Wounded pride makes the official less willing to act on the theory

text: Public talk and press reports can draw investigators onto one suspect, expanding the inquiry around that suspect and discouraging later checks.
when: when public attention builds around one suspect
why: Early attention locks investigators onto a narrative before evidence is tested

text: A prior report about a known culprit primes people to read later events as that culprit's work, so they form suspicions before evidence arrives.
when: A rumour or news item precedes an incident.
why: Expectation set by a story shapes how new events are interpreted.

text: Accepting public talk as analysis is unreliable when the talk itself admits it has no explanation.
when: Weighing community opinion about a case
why: Rumor has no verified basis

text: In a group, each listener repeats an accepted claim as settled, so one unchecked error multiplies across the group.
Once a theory forms, suspicion between groups can spread faster than the facts supporting it, so accusations outrun evidence.
when: After an initial theory of culpability takes hold among participants.
why: Established theories make people read ambiguous evidence as confirmation.

text: A prepared or repeated cover story can become a sincere belief for its teller, even though it is false, especially when it rests on an untestable, half-remembered precedent.
when: A character justifies a wrong to themselves over time.
why: Repeated rehearsal and an untestable justification make the rationalization feel true.

text: Precise recollection or a neat phrase repeated word for word may reflect rehearsal or someone else's wording, so precision alone does not prove accuracy.
when: A witness gives unusually detailed testimony or repeats a precise time or phrase word for word.
why: Preparation or supplied wording sounds exact without being recalled from experience.

text: Under pressure a rehearsed account is brittle: it may shift from implying one thing to conceding another, and nonverbal signs like a shifting gaze or faltering line can contradict it.
when: A witness is pressed for detail or repeats a prepared account under questioning.
why: Rehearsed lines do not adapt to new questions, and body language leaks discomfort.

text: Retellings are shaped by the speaker's stake, the questions asked, and the crowd's reaction, so hints and sneers can pass as facts.
when: Gossip, secondhand accounts, or reports about a person.
why: A personal stake colours what is repeated, and the shape of questions and reactions shapes what is reported.

text: A person who opens a conversation with a rehearsed angle may not be listening to what is actually said.
A suspect with a memorised account may stammer or repeat phrases when asked about an unanticipated specific time, buying time to reorganise.
when: when a pointed question targets an exact moment
why: rehearsal rarely covers precise specifics

text: Shifting accounts that move suspicion between suspects force players to keep re-weighing each one.
A full retelling only exposes contradictions if the story has not been rehearsed; a practised account can be repeated without inconsistency.
when: When asking a witness to repeat their account
why: Rehearsed stories hold together on repetition, so the test only works on unrehearsed accounts.

text: Confessors who later withdraw their statements often say they were labeled and worn down until they agreed to anything, so a retraction can expose the methods used.
when: A confession is retracted after the pressure ends.
why: The retraction is the accused's attempt to correct a record made under duress.

text: A person who fears discovery may script a denial for an accomplice, and the planned denial itself reveals that a connection exists.
when: A suspect asks an accomplice to disclaim knowing someone.
why: A deliberate denial signals a hidden connection the speaker wants concealed.

text: People who share a story often glance at an ally after answering a question, which can reveal that the answer was coordinated.
when: Questioning several connected people together
why: Witnesses look to allies for cues when they are unsure of the answer

text: Test a rehearsed answer with an unexpected neutral question; contradictions from general questions fail against rehearsed stories, so they must target what the witness did not anticipate.
when: A witness's answer sounds too smooth or practiced, or the witness has prepared an account.
why: Rehearsed answers already cover expected questions and break down when the question leaves the expected path.

text: Rehearse a staged performance so its timing and delivery are controlled before it is used on the target.
when: when a deceptive scene depends on precise delivery

text: Check whether a witness's account matches a rehearsed script or follows a partial confession the accused made in advance.
when: A witness's account sounds prepared or matches a prior disclosure

text: A speech repeated in the same words and tone suggests rehearsal; treat it as a warning sign to test further, not proof of a lie.
when: when a character gives the same account more than once
why: Scripted repetition can mask an unverified story.

text: A retraction repairs the record but may not restore trust; a group committed to an explanation may read it as deception and absorb the counter-evidence.
when: A community committed to an explanation doubts the retraction.
why: The explanation already accounts for reversals, so counter-evidence is absorbed rather than accepted.

text: A quick, rehearsed-sounding excuse is not proof of guilt; note it as evidence but withhold judgment until more is known.
when: A character leaves a room with a hurried, practiced excuse or an unexplained presence.
why: Quick explanations are normal under surprise, and a judgment made too early can mislead.

text: Ignoring a shared template is a mistake: a set of identical items from one source should raise suspicion.
when: Reviewing a collection of similar items
why: Copies from one source repeat each other, so their identical appearance signals a common origin.

text: A witness whose story matches yours too neatly looks coached, and agreement between a bribed witness and a self-interested party is weak evidence.
Treat written notes a witness uses to rehearse answers as a sign of coaching or possible tampering with the witness.
Rehearse a concealed effect in front of a mirror to reduce the visible movement needed to trigger it.
when: Performing an effect that relies on a hidden mechanism.
why: Reduced visible movement makes the mechanism harder to detect.

text: Re-examining the same unchanged clue, even while angry, adds no information; repetition rarely reveals a hidden link without new evidence or a different frame or test.
when: Stuck on a puzzle with no new angle, or a player keeps revisiting one clue without new evidence or changed state.
why: The clue's content is fixed and the unchanged frame keeps directing attention to the same details, so only new evidence or a different test changes the conclusion.

text: Audiences trust a helpful or credentialed investigator's conclusions and rarely check them, so one revealed as the culprit hides in plain sight and makes a sharper twist.
when: the investigator or expert is also the culprit and their authority or helpful role goes unchallenged
why: Trust in the helper's visible role or authority lends the account credibility the audience rarely checks, which hides the culprit.

text: An investigator may prefer a harder solution because it earns more credit, so judgment is partly shaped by reputation rather than facts alone.
when: When a person has professional incentives tied to the outcome of an investigation
why: Expected recognition for a difficult answer can pull conclusions away from the evidence.

text: When the protagonist cannot tell whether information is real, the audience comes to share that doubt.
when: a character faces unverified information
why: Keeping the character's uncertainty visible links the audience to the character's state.

text: A bad reputation makes ordinary losses and accidents read as accusations, so suspicion attaches to a person's name rather than to any specific act.
when: when a community already distrusts someone
why: people blame a known figure for unexplained misfortune

text: A true observation can be dismissed when the witness has a poor reputation or when a plausible cover story was offered at the time, and survives only as gossip.
when: when a witness report conflicts with a stable reputation or fits a familiar explanation
why: Reputation and a ready explanation make the report seem like eccentricity rather than evidence.

text: A sympathetic reading of a relationship can outweigh technical proof with some decision-makers.
A witness who readily admits not knowing, and reacts openly to a question, tends to be more reliable.
A reputation for helpfulness can raise a player's trust in a charming NPC, so the player's trust becomes part of the trap.
when: NPC reputation system influences dialogue trust
why: Trust based on reputation makes the hidden threat harder to see.

text: Reputation can mislead, and the most suspicious-seeming candidate may turn out to be innocent.
Familiar objects and faces are seen through habit, so a daily-handled object can be swapped for a near copy unnoticed; changing viewpoint exposes hidden details.
when: an object is handled or a scene or person is observed routinely or many times without close examination
why: Habitual viewing lowers attention to small changes; expectation filters out unexpected detail.

text: Sudden breaks in routine, such as hurried staff, ignored calls, an unexpected official visit, or a routinely documented person's records stopping, signal a change before it is announced.
when: a setting with a familiar pattern is suddenly disrupted, or a routinely documented person's records stop
why: Deviations from expected routine signal a cause; a break in a regular trail is noticed because the routine set an expectation.

text: Ordinary routine acts, like tidying after an incident or shared practices, should not alone be read as concealment or hidden alignment; they can look suspicious only in hindsight.
why: ordinary actions can look suspicious in hindsight

text: Busy routines consume attention, hiding real absences and the true hour while a victim's condition changes; test each habitual explanation, like a night outing, against the timeline.
when: an absence goes unnoticed for a period or seems ordinary, during a busy routine task or habitual activity
why: Attention is consumed by the task, and ordinary-seeming absences are accepted without checking.

text: People ignore routine-looking figures such as postmen, servants, or regular travellers, so someone in an ordinary role goes unremembered by witnesses.
when: a character's role is familiar and unremarkable; asking a witness whether they saw a specific person at a specific time
why: Familiar roles are screened out of attention; constant presence makes individuals indistinct, so witnesses do not register them.

text: A person who does not regularly check a supply may fail to notice its loss for a while, and may not remember whether they used it themselves.
when: When a resource is drawn from containers the owner rarely inspects.
why: Routine habits reduce attention to small changes, so depletion goes unnoticed.

text: Observers stop noticing routine sights, such as a regular delivery, so a routine event can hide a deliberate act.
when: a familiar recurring event happens near a crime
why: Repeated exposure makes people stop registering the event

text: When characters show no surprise at a concealed guest, the concealment reads as normal and observers stop questioning it.
when: when a household routinely hides identities
why: absent reaction signals that the concealment is expected

text: People judge an unusual event against their usual routine, so a time outside the routine can lead them to misread what caused a sound.
when: When a witness hears something at an atypical hour
why: Expectations built from habitual patterns shape interpretation of new events

text: Players learn recurring hazards, such as a gate that closes on a set day or a trap on a cycle, and can exploit or be caught by them once the pattern is recognized.
when: A hazard follows a repeating schedule or cycle.
why: Predictable repetition allows players to form and act on expectations.

text: People overlook what is familiar and close, and do not examine it, so an ordinary nearby object or person is easily missed.
when: A scene contains a dramatic explanation alongside everyday items or people.
why: Attention is pulled to the unusual, and the familiar is not checked.

text: Identify one habitual act that is typical of a person rather than gathering many weak signs, then use it to infer how they will respond in new situations.
when: A quick judgment of a person's likely conduct is needed before fuller evidence exists
why: A characteristic action can reveal a consistent pattern across situations

text: A culprit can avoid suspicion by moving openly in a role that observers expect, because observers stop noticing a familiar role.
when: A suspect must be seen repeatedly yet go unrecognised
why: Shared costume and habit suppress scrutiny more than concealment does.

text: Witnesses fill gaps with expected routine, so a missed deviation can feel as though the usual pattern held.
when: A habitual person behaves differently on one day
why: Expectation overrides attention to change

text: A reverted habit is a clue only to someone who knows the person's baseline; a stranger cannot recognize it.
when: An observer tries to detect a disguised person by their habits.
why: Recognition requires knowledge of the earlier behaviour.

text: 1) Record a subject's routine over several days. 2) Note deviations from that routine. Deviations carry more meaning than any single act.
when: watching a subject to infer intent
why: a stable baseline makes changes stand out as signals

text: Players who observe NPCs in a room can match behaviour to the room's objects, confirming or rejecting an inference about its use.
when: NPCs act within a furnished space that carries routine-revealing objects.
why: Matching behaviour to objects lets players test their inferences against evidence.

text: An investigator's own movement can disturb a barrier or clue, so the investigator becomes a possible source of the disturbance.
when: The investigator moves near a protective barrier or evidence
why: Physical movement can knock or shift objects without intent

text: Ask whether the occupant usually locked the room. If the normal habit is locking, an unlocked door at the later check is an unusual change worth investigating.
when: When a door's state at a time of discovery conflicts with expectations
why: A departure from routine marks a change in the scene that may be significant.

text: A vehicle can be identified by tire marks and damaged plates, and a report of a found vehicle may match it.
when: Physical traces of a vehicle exist at a scene.
why: Distinctive marks narrow the set of possible vehicles.

text: Note where objects are kept, hidden or repeatedly handled, since a concealed or often-touched item can reveal intent.
when: observing a subject's relationship to objects
why: concealment and repeated handling suggest significance

text: Changing the light on a scene, such as moving a candle to throw light through a gap, can reveal details previously hidden and raise the observer's certainty.
when: When an observer reports a detail that was hard to see under the original lighting.
why: Lighting determines what is visible, so a new angle can confirm or refute an earlier observation.

text: A room left unsearched is a blind spot, and a missing item may still be there, so the gap must be recorded rather than ignored.
when: a house-wide search excludes a room
why: Unsearched space can still hold the item being sought.

text: When an unexpected visitor abruptly disturbs a household member, observers infer that the news is important and not routine, even before any explanation is given.
when: An unannounced arrival visibly startles someone in the group
why: Timing and the host's reaction carry meaning that people read as a sign of significant news

text: When treatment fails and no natural cause is apparent, practitioners who accept an unseen malicious agent tend to attribute the failure to that agent.
when: belief system accepts unseen malicious agents

text: Players trust a set of clean negative test results and stop questioning, missing the item the tests could not check.
when: a lab or test clears a suspect
why: clean results feel conclusive

text: A large number of containers can make a search feel hopeless before it starts, discouraging the player from trying.
when: A room holds many shelves or containers to check.
why: Sheer volume makes the task seem endless.

text: Searchers who assume an item is hidden skip ordinary visible objects and repeatedly check secret-looking spots.
when: when hunting a missing item in a furnished space
why: they model the target's location as secret rather than ordinary

text: A sudden switch to a language the suspect may know tests comprehension, so the suspect keeps a blank face to avoid revealing it.
when: when a questioner switches language without warning
why: a flicker of recognition would expose understanding

text: Asking who would benefit from ending a target's activity narrows the field to a short list of likely suspects with a motive.
when: A threat or harm is suspected but the perpetrator is unknown
why: Motive filters the many possible actors down to those with a stake in the outcome.

text: Irritation and fatigue can make a searcher close a container unexamined and move on, missing the item it held.
1) Identify a measurable trace such as footprint size, height or gait. 2) Measure the trace against each suspect. 3) Drop any suspect who fails the test, whatever other evidence points to them.
when: Before committing to an interview or arrest.
why: A failed measurable test is decisive, while hopes and convenient theories are not evidence.

text: 1) Identify a claim that rests on one person's word. 2) Find a neutral third party who can answer. 3) Ask a few closed questions the claimant cannot shape. 4) Compare the sealed or unedited reply directly with the claim.
when: A claim depends on one person's word and an independent source exists
why: Closed, independently framed questions limit what the claimant can steer and make the answer checkable

text: 1) Identify the sign expected for the suspected appearance. 2) Check whether it is present. 3) Treat its absence as evidence when the subject should show it.
when: When testing whether a person matches a claimed identity, such as wind-blown hair
why: Missing an expected sign can be as informative as spotting one

text: 1) Confirm the change is shared by several observers. 2) Vary the lighting, the viewing angle, or the surroundings. 3) Check whether the change persists under each variation. 4) Only then report or act on it.
when: When an observed detail seems to change and must be checked before it is reported or acted on
why: A change that survives varied conditions is more likely real; one that disappears was likely an artifact of conditions

text: Narrow a suspect list by testing motive, opportunity and physical access; when ordinary explanations fail, consider the remaining possibility even if it seems improbable.
when: suspect pool is small and access can be tracked
why: Systematic elimination converges on the answer when intuitive explanations are exhausted

text: Treat a failed verification as information for revising the reading of the scene, not as grounds to abandon the search.
when: A witness's directions produce a wrong result when acted on.
why: A failure reveals which assumption about the scene is wrong.

text: Treat a resident's assumption about who owns an object as a claim to be verified, not accepted as fact.
when: A local person states ownership of personal objects
why: People who live with objects can be wrong about who used them.

text: Let a witness's character inform how much you trust them, but never let trust replace checking their information.
Test a witness's perception against the physical traces the event left behind, such as dust, scorch marks, or decay, before accepting the account.
when: A witness's detailed account cannot be squared with the scene.
why: Physical evidence is less affected by emotion than memory is.

text: Stress or fatigue can reduce a player's noticing of details and bias how they read text or objects, producing predictable slips.
when: When a player is under stress or fatigue during an investigation.
why: Emotional state can bias interpretation of the same material.

text: Limit an NPC's witness reports to events its position let it perceive, and let the player check them against physical evidence.
when: When writing dialogue for NPCs who witness events.
why: A witness's knowledge is bounded by where she stood.

text: Qualify each NPC sighting with its conditions (distance, lighting) and a confidence value like 'startled' or 'may have been seen', so players weigh it against what the witness could see.
when: An NPC reports seeing a player or event in a game.
why: Qualified reports reward cross-checking rather than blind trust.

text: In dim light or fog, faint points or moving patches get misread as other objects, and their apparent shape shifts as visibility or the observer's viewpoint changes.
when: Sighting made in poor or dim lighting, or when visibility is low.
why: Reduced visual information and changing viewpoint alter what is perceived.

text: A faint signal can be easier to notice from the edge of the gaze than when stared at directly, since fixed direct attention can make it fade.
when: searching for a faint visual clue
why: peripheral vision is more sensitive to faint light than central focus

text: A person intently focused on one target often fails to notice others nearby, even in the same room, and strong emotion makes this blindness worse.
when: a scene where one person dominates attention
why: attention narrows under focus and emotion

text: An observer who sees only part of a figure fills in the rest with their own assumptions.
when: Observing through a partial view.

text: A sound such as a footstep announces a figure before it is seen, and the listener infers identity from cues like gait, so the face stays hidden until close.
when: When an approaching figure should be revealed gradually
why: Hearing precedes sight, so inference from sound builds anticipation

text: Two people hearing the same ambiguous sound may interpret it differently, so shared perception of an unclear sound is weaker evidence than it seems.
when: Multiple witnesses report an ambiguous sound.
why: Agreement on a sensation does not fix its cause, since each person supplies an interpretation.

text: A person who appears unconscious can still hear conversation and react, sometimes with a visible shift in expression.
when: When a seemingly unconscious character is near a conversation
why: Apparent sleep does not guarantee that hearing has stopped.

text: An observer who sees a figure vanish is likely to read it as impossible unless the layout and elapsed time are measured against the available exits.
when: A figure disappears or appears suddenly in a space.
why: Brief sightings lack detail, so the sense of impossibility comes from unchecked assumptions about routes.

text: A dazed or unsettled observer misjudges distances and scale, seeing familiar places as smaller or larger than they really are.
when: when the observer is unsettled
why: altered perception distorts spatial judgement

text: Reflections in windows or shifting lamp shadows can make players perceive watching figures or changing room sizes, which are effects of light rather than real presences.
when: Dim or moving light sources in a room.
why: Light patterns change with movement and are easily read as agents or shape changes.

text: An impaired observer may report clear reasoning and speech while their perceptions are distorted, so calm articulation does not guarantee reliable sensory reports.
when: A witness has been drugged, exhausted, frightened, or otherwise impaired
why: Impairment can distort perception while leaving the ability to speak and reason intact

text: One observer may perceive a detail others miss, and that detail can remain unexplained even to the observer.
when: Observers report unequal details at one event
why: Individual attention and state select different features

text: Fear and sudden glare distort an observer's timing and perception, making a room feel more hostile than it is.
when: during a frightening or dazzling event

text: Players dismiss anomalies when the protagonist doubts their own senses, so a rival can stay hidden behind the protagonist's self-doubt.
when: when the viewpoint character is unreliable
why: the protagonist's doubt becomes the reader's reason to disbelieve

text: Failing light shortens the time available for observation, so sightings made near dusk are less complete and less reliable.
when: when observing near dusk
why: low light limits what can be seen

text: Headlights or bright light blind observers to what lies outside their lit circle, limiting what they can see of the dark around them.
when: when a witness is looking into darkness from a lit position
why: Bright light reduces visibility of unlit areas.

text: Sounds only establish that someone was present, not who, so rate voice- or sound-only identifications weaker than seen events, requiring seeing the person or other evidence.
when: A witness reports sounds from another room or at a distance, or identifies someone only by voice or sound.
why: Sounds from a household routine can be produced by anyone nearby; sound alone is ambiguous and can come from many people.

text: Give stationed NPCs at doors, counters and gates timestamped sightings, so the player assembles a sequence by visiting each and checks reports against other evidence.
when: Designing a mystery that depends on a timeline.
why: Distributed sightings make the player rebuild the sequence through exploration.

text: A faint change in light or a sound from overhead shows the outside world has responded, even when no actor is seen.
Small disturbances in fabric, such as ruffled threads on a trouser leg, may show a snag on a nail or fence.
An NPC can recognise the player by naming a past event, and the player can check the claim against what they remember.
when: Designing recognition and trust between NPCs and the player
why: Shared memory makes recognition feel earned and verifiable

text: In thick fog, sound is hard to locate, so shouts and shots give no reliable direction.
when: Dense fog or similar weather covers the area where a sound occurs.
why: Fog scatters and dampens sound, so the listener cannot judge where it came from.

text: An intent flag in dialogue or quest systems can distinguish a deceived accomplice from a knowing one.
when: when quest outcomes depend on what an NPC knew
why: A stored intent state lets outcomes differ for the same act.

text: A real object just below the horizon can have its reflection projected onto clouds, so it appears in the sky before its outline is directly visible, then vanishes as light changes.
when: An observer is near a hidden object and lighting and weather are right
why: Optics can carry an image of an unseen object into view

text: A drugged character can be unable to move or speak while keeping full awareness, so they witness events but cannot act on them.
when: A character is incapacitated by a shared drink or substance at a critical moment.
why: Incapacitation can disable action while leaving perception and thought intact.

text: A small interruption during a task can cause a detail to be dropped from the result.
when: When a witness or agent is interrupted mid-task.
why: Attention shifted mid-task loses the item being processed.

text: A first impression of an unidentified loud sound can be wrong, so it should be revised once its source is located.

Give each NPC a schedule and log timestamped positions, conversation states, movements, last-seen and left-at times, so players build alibi grids and spot contradictions, absences, and impostors in two places.
when: When designing alibi-based deduction in a game's event system.
why: Timed records make absence detectable and let players reconstruct events from evidence.

text: Store each character's habits, such as smoking, drinking or eating, and possessions as data, so the game can flag scene traces or planted clues that do not fit them.
when: Implementing scene-consistency checks and clue validation for suspects.
why: Stored data lets the game detect contradictions and test clues against the accused character automatically.

text: Give a witness who saw events in darkness or dim light only partial clues, such as touch, scent or footsteps, that the player must interpret and test with follow-up questions.
when: When designing a witness who saw events in darkness or dim light.
why: Partial sensory evidence keeps the solution open to deduction.

text: Let the player find a physical check, such as a latch bolted from one side, to confirm or contradict a witness.
Do not enter a room that may hold danger until its layout has been confirmed from outside.
when: Approaching a building with unknown interior layout.
why: Outside observation reduces the chance of walking into an ambush.

text: Log NPCs the player has seen only once in their notes, so the entries resurface when a new name or clue appears.
when: Designing a system where players recall earlier sightings.
why: Stored sightings let a later clue pay off earlier encounters.

text: Make each NPC's room match its character profile, so a room that contradicts the profile signals a visitor or a planted clue.
when: furnishing NPC living spaces
why: Mismatches become deliberate signals the player can read.

text: Give NPCs different levels of perceptiveness, so a sharp one catches a tell that a dull one misses and players learn whom to trust.
Let a witness NPC report visions or dreams, but flag them as unverifiable and let other NPCs dispute them.
why: the player must then weigh the claims

text: Give NPCs sensing powers only under a rule that each claimed sensing event can be tested against physical location.
Show an NPC through fresh traces like footprints, pruned growth or residual heat before the player sees them.
Have several non-player witnesses each give a time range, and require the player to reconcile the overlapping windows.
A witness can report accurately but partially, so a game can let the NPC be right while the player must confirm it.
when: when designing NPC testimony

text: Let players find a second witness who can confirm or contradict an NPC's logged, timestamped statement.
when: when a claim is central to a mystery
why: independent corroboration tests a single account

text: Log which surfaces and containers a search has checked, so later targeted actions can reach hidden items that a general sweep missed.
Store NPC state as raw observations, such as last location and dialogue lines, separately from the impressions shown to the player, so both can be weighed.
Store the investigation question, such as what is missing and how it left, as the first state the game tracks.
when: Implementing a mystery or investigation system.
why: A defined question gives later clue evaluation a fixed target.

text: Record hidden actions in game state so they can be revealed later, and place an observer who can notice them.
when: When a hidden action should pay off in a later scene.
why: Unrecorded actions cannot be revealed, and unnoticed ones stay hidden.

text: Log overheard speech but mark what could not be heard, since muttered or unclear words are not evidence.
when: recording observations of overheard speech
why: unclear words can be misremembered and inflate the record

text: Fear may heighten a witness's perception so they notice phenomena sooner, yet a pounding pulse from fear can dull hearing and make sounds doubtful.
when: When observers are under strong fear or high stress.
why: Heightened arousal changes what the mind registers, while stress reduces auditory clarity.

text: A witness with incomplete memory often recalls forgotten details only when given a specific prompt, not general questions.
A single damning fact can revive suspicion of a figure already thought settled, so suspicion can rise and fall as evidence arrives.
when: when a suspect appears cleared
why: one fact can reopen a question closed by earlier reasoning

text: A vivid, specific detail makes an admission feel credible and hard to disprove, though the detail may also be invented to persuade.
when: A suspect explains a past action.
why: Specificity signals honesty to listeners, whether or not the detail is true.

text: Players and characters quickly judge a trap by its results, so a failed sting is often read as proof the bait was never real.
when: A trap yields no capture.
why: Absence of outcome is interpreted as a flaw in the scheme, damaging the investigator's standing.

text: Reward players who test the weakest link in a claimed schedule instead of the whole story at once.
when: When designing alibi or timeline puzzles.
why: Focused testing is how players progress through a chain of claims.

text: Building a theory or actor profile on one detail, such as a back wound or odd clothing, misleads: the detail may have an innocent cause or other evidence may disagree.
when: When an odd detail or single feature is the main basis for a conclusion or profile.
why: Many details have ordinary explanations that only wider evidence can separate; a single detail can mislead when the rest of the scene points elsewhere.

text: Searching only at one scale, such as tiny fragments, causes an investigator to miss evidence in plain view.
when: Surveying a scene for evidence.
why: Attention fixed on small items overlooks large, conspicuous objects.

text: Revealing a clue too early wastes the chance to observe how the target reacts to it.
when: Deciding when to show evidence to a suspect.
why: Once the target knows the clue, the reaction it would have produced is lost.

text: 1) Hold one independent fact that you know to be true or false. 2) Ask the witness to restate the whole account. 3) Press on the single checkable point rather than the whole story.
when: When you have one independent fact that can test a witness's account
why: Full restatements expose inconsistencies, and a single checkable point gives a clear test without needing outside corroboration of everything.

text: 1) Pick one fact only an informed person would react to. 2) Reveal it and observe the reaction. 3) Repeat the same claim and see whether the reaction changes. 4) Choose the next question from the response. 5) Hold back other details for later.
when: You need to know whether a suspect is informed about a named object or person
why: A consistent or changing reaction to repeated cues indicates knowledge; held-back details preserve leverage.

text: 1) Have a witness commit to a description first. 2) Reveal the matching object suddenly, without explanation. 3) Watch for a start or change in composure, and in voice and body.
when: a witness has already described an object or person
why: prior commitment to a description makes a match to a sudden object meaningful

text: 1) Speak a trigger word or place where the suspect can hear it, without addressing them. 2) Watch for a small stop in movement. 3) Record the reaction as a probability, paired with other evidence.
when: a suspect denies knowledge of a place, name or event
why: an unaddressed trigger reveals recognition without alerting the suspect

text: Treat demeanour, manner or belongings as hypotheses, not proof; test them against stronger evidence such as records or dental or physical checks.
when: When inferring a suspect's background from behaviour or choosing how to confirm an identity.
why: Manner is easily performed and can mislead; stronger tests are less easily faked than personal items.

text: Ask a targeted question that could confirm or refute a new lead, such as asking staff whether they have seen a person with a specific feature.
when: When a new lead needs checking.
why: A specific question produces a result that clearly supports or contradicts the lead.

text: Offering several sympathetic openings instead of confronting a guarded or ashamed witness lowers their defenses, so they disclose hidden details more readily than under direct pressure.
when: A witness is holding back, or is ashamed or embarrassed and the detail is essential.
why: A reduced sense of threat and open invitations let them choose to disclose, whereas pressure can make people withdraw.

text: Searching or excluding only some people, without a stated reason, reads as unfair or dismissive; the excluded become resentful, guarded or outburst-prone and withhold cooperation.
when: An investigation checks one group but not others, or a character is removed from a scene without a stated reason.
why: Selective treatment reads as unfair or as dismissal, so people resist and withhold help.

text: A witness's sympathy for a person shapes what they notice and how they describe it.
when: witnesses have personal feelings about a suspect
why: Feeling directs attention and colours interpretation

text: When judging a general case, people with a personal stake often show it through colour changes, long pauses and half-finished sentences.
when: the case touches the subject's own situation

text: Sympathy for a possibly innocent suspect creates reluctance to act, and this pressure should be noticed rather than left to shape decisions unseen.
when: a costly step such as an arrest is pending
why: sympathy and doubt push toward hesitation

text: A suspect who believes he was observed and faces a threat may bargain for his safety, changing his behavior toward the investigator.
when: When a suspect's actions are exposed in detail in private
why: Perceived surveillance and risk make compliance more attractive than resistance

text: A suspect who believes the listener is helpless and cannot act tends to speak freely and boast about what was done.
when: The suspect thinks no one can use what he says
why: Lowered guard removes the caution he would otherwise show

text: A witness with a stake in the outcome who needs the investigator's help tends to return after walking out.
A subordinate who does not know who employs them has less loyalty to lose, so is more willing to betray that person.
People of high status tend to avoid engaging with a servant as either an inferior or an equal, so they fail to question him.
when: witnesses of different social rank are in the same scene
why: Social conventions discourage questioning across class lines, so relevant information goes unasked.

text: A target who discusses events in conversation can unknowingly supply information that a planner uses to adjust the plan.
when: when a character is watched by someone with a hidden plan
why: the target's casual talk reveals habits and reactions

text: A witness may recall a relevant sighting, then dismiss it by doubting their memory or fearing that speaking will cause harm.
when: a witness realizes a detail may matter to the investigation
why: Doubt and fear of consequences push them toward silence.

text: People know little about one another beyond a few narrow shared facts, so most knowledge of others is inference.
when: people who share only a limited context
why: shared context covers only a narrow range

text: Repeated failure blamed on one object can turn that object into a symbol, and resentment toward it can grow into a wish for revenge.
when: a persistent failure is linked to a specific object or person
why: Discouragement attaches a cause to a single symbol.

text: A person busy with a task often fails to notice someone leaving, so their inattention can serve as evidence that a movement went unseen.
when: an NPC is occupied when a movement occurs
why: attention is focused elsewhere during the event

text: Reluctance to intervene, such as not wanting to knock, can delay the discovery that a routine has broken.
when: when acting would intrude on someone
why: politeness postpones checking

text: A listener with a large stake in an answer accepts the claim more readily and lowers their guard against error.
when: The reward for a particular answer is large.
why: Motivation makes a wanted answer feel true.

text: Forcing a suspect to publicly acknowledge or deny a relationship in front of witnesses can distort how they behave and how others judge them.
when: A relationship is put to the test in a group setting.
why: Public exposure makes a quick response decisive for the observers' view of the person.

text: A source who refuses to repeat or expand on a sensitive claim, or later denies it, signals that the topic is delicate, so the refusal is worth noting as information.
when: when questioned about a dangerous or private matter
why: People often withdraw from statements that expose them or others.

text: A listener may be outside a window rather than in the room, so speak as if they are present and make the lure cover all likely positions.
when: When staging talk to expose an unseen eavesdropper
why: Eavesdroppers can be positioned outside the room where the speaker cannot see them.

text: Long service gives a source full knowledge but does not guarantee cooperation; such a source may speak only when given a reason.
when: when a veteran NPC holds the most complete knowledge
why: Knowledge and willingness to share are independent.

text: When witnesses feel embarrassed or uneasy, their discomfort slows their response and draws attention away from physical traces.
when: a sudden social moment disrupts a group
why: Emotional reactions compete with factual observation, so witnesses respond to the mood rather than the evidence.

text: A suggestion from one observer can shape what others perceive, so group agreement may reflect shared expectation rather than an actual change.
when: When several observers agree on an anomaly after one of them proposed an explanation
why: Shared expectation can produce agreement that looks like independent confirmation

text: An investigator who enjoys a friendly conversation can forget the real purpose of the visit.
when: Building rapport over social activities such as meals.
why: Pleasant company diverts attention from the goal.

text: With a reluctant or guarded person, wait for a natural break before raising the subject, and stop when they halt; forcing it before rapport ends cooperation.
when: Interviewing a subject who is reluctant, afraid, or guarded.
why: Pushing too hard shuts reluctant speakers down, while a relaxed target reveals more; timing decides how much they say.

text: A loud, absorbing spectacle, including ceremony, silence or dance around a trick, draws attention away from the quiet act or hidden channel producing the effect.
when: A festival, performance or crowd event is underway, or a performance includes a spectacle around its trick.
why: Attention is consumed by the expected display and moves away from the mechanism.

text: Treating a witness's theatrical distress, such as a faint, as proof of innocence or guilt is a mistake, since staging or questioners may arrange such reactions.
when: An interview or confrontation scene where a reaction is treated as decisive evidence.
why: Staging and the setting of the scene can cause distress or fits that observers misread as confirmation.

text: A deceptive statement is designed to sound small and reasonable, and a deceiver's apparent sympathy adds to its credibility.
People tell small lies to serve a larger purpose, such as hiding a deficiency or steering a visitor's choices.
when: A character gives an account that seems to protect something or direct the listener
why: A minor falsehood can conceal a bigger concern

text: A suspect who drops the performance during a crisis reveals how much of the earlier manner was staged.
when: when a suspect faces sudden pressure
why: Under stress the performance gives way to natural composure.

text: Under accusation, suspects often answer with questions and counter-demands instead of volunteering information.
when: when accused or pressed with claims
why: deflection avoids giving away useful facts

text: A target's reaction to a veiled accusation escalates in stages: calm, then agitation, then an attempt to rise, then near-faintness.
when: when a suspect hears a hinted accusation

text: A suspect who shows no alarm at a staged spectacle may already know it is staged, so the lack of reaction is itself informative.
when: when a staged event is shown to a suspect
why: a person who knows the staging does not react as a believer would

text: Witnesses often reveal information in stages, first denying or minimising, then admitting more under pressure or after a direct question.
when: A witness has a reason to withhold a detail
why: Witnesses protect themselves or others and yield only as far as pressed

text: A suspect who believes a message comes from a trusted source will act on it and attend the meeting, even when the message is a trap.
when: When a message appears to come from someone the target trusts.
why: Trust in a familiar source overrides caution about the message's origin.

text: Only a rare observer with specific trick-spotting knowledge notices an inconsistency in a skilled performance, while most of the crowd notices nothing.
when: A performance is watched by a mixed audience.
why: Detecting a trick requires knowing how the trick is done.

text: Manipulative lures are fitted to a target's current condition, so a character's present need reveals which temptation they are most likely to fall for.
when: a character may be manipulated
why: Manipulators exploit the specific circumstances of their target.

text: In a staged meeting, the witness may be shaken while the suspect remains calm, so their reactions can diverge.
when: a witness and a suspect meet unexpectedly
why: people differ in how well they control involuntary responses

text: A strange, apparently pointless act can draw attention to its absurdity while the real purpose is achieved in the background.
when: when an odd act seems irrational and its effects might serve someone
why: Observers label the act as madness or quirk and stop looking for a purpose.

text: A target who expects a valuable exchange will act on a fake prize when the deal's cues, such as a code and a price, seem credible.
when: a staged exchange trap
why: Expected gain can outweigh suspicion of the package.

text: Skilled performers can control facial expression, voice, breathing and colour, and produce fits or rigidity on cue, deceiving trained, skeptical observers such as judges, clergy and jurors.
when: A witness performs a condition that cannot be checked directly.
why: Performers with fine control over their bodily signals can imitate symptoms convincingly.

text: Study fabricated accounts to see how false reports persuade readers, but do not treat their claims as evidence of truth.
A plausible account is only as strong as the checks it passes, and it cannot replace physical evidence.
Design NPC dialogue in stages: a direct challenge, then a pause, then a reassurance option that unlocks a hidden clue.
when: An NPC is meant to reveal a clue only after pressure.
why: Staged pressure with a face-saving option makes a reluctant NPC more likely to disclose.

text: Plant a suspect before any crime by establishing a standing grudge, a visible watcher and rumors that supply a motive.
when: the audience must hold a suspect with motive and opportunity before the incident
why: the reader gets a reason to suspect early

text: Treat a visible quarrel between allies as possibly staged when their accusations follow a coordinated sequence.
when: Allies appear to fall out
why: Staged disputes can hide joint action.

text: Before accepting that a source knows a private fact, check who else could have heard it, including intermediaries and prior arrangements.
when: A source repeats a private statement exactly.
why: A leak or prior arrangement can explain apparent knowledge without any supernatural source.

text: A missing reaction in a staged test is also information and may mean the setup failed.
when: a planned reaction test produces no visible response
why: absence of response can reflect a failed setup rather than innocence

text: A staged setback that convinces opponents the investigation has failed can lure them into relaxing or revealing their hand.
Skilled offenders are rarely caught and their failures are seldom seen, so the visible cases are mostly clumsy ones.
why: Detection shows the offenders who failed, not those who succeeded

text: A performer can seem to know private facts through a hidden intermediary who relays information from the questioner to the performer, so apparent insight may be a human channel.
when: A supposed supernatural or omniscient source reveals private information.
why: A hidden relay can pass overheard words to the performer, producing apparent knowledge.

text: A deception can be built so that each likely challenge has a prepared answer, steering audience attention toward effects rather than facts.
when: When a character's apparent power depends on hiding how an effect is produced.
why: Prepared responses deflect scrutiny before it reaches the mechanism.

text: A sudden, convenient injury invites doubt, since a genuinely suffering person is watched and their health is asked about openly.
when: an injury appears just when someone is needed elsewhere

text: A staged illness draws attention to the person faking it, who may then be watched more closely.
why: Sudden illness is noticed, and the one who feigns it becomes the focus.

text: A questioner who stops at the general principle may miss decisive facts such as names or hiding places; probing further reveals what the abstract answer hides.
A staged rebuke can mislead the very person it protects, since that person has no warning and may react as if the public scene were real.
why: the cover story is not shared with its own beneficiary

text: A suspect who recognises a manipulation tactic may call it out, which can end cooperation.
Reading a deliberately ordered sequence of effects as random chance, or as proof of the supernatural, leads to wrong conclusions.
1) Present the suspect as helpful and reasonable. 2) Frame requests as sympathy or duty. 3) Let the skeptic appear obstinate. 4) Keep the suspect's real motive separate from apparent motive.
when: Designing a suspect who should be revealed only later
why: Apparent helpfulness hides motive, and a discredited expert reinforces the misdirection.

text: 1) Rebuild the sequence of actions behind a convenient clue. 2) Check each action against the time available. 3) Check each action against the risk of being observed.
when: When a convenient escape route or clue appears too easily
why: Timing and observation constraints reveal whether a staged trace is physically possible.

text: 1) Arrange an unannounced meeting between a witness and a person she may fear or love. 2) Place a distant observer to record the first emotional reaction. 3) Use a signal and separate rooms or vehicles to avoid a public scene.
when: identity is the open question and a reaction can narrow it
why: an unwarned meeting exposes involuntary reactions that the parties cannot prepare for

text: Escalate a scare in stages, from an ambiguous noise to a cry to a visible figure, so tension builds before the visible event.
when: when a sighting is the turning point of a scene

text: Supplying proof to authorities who want it before acting secures their cooperation, but gives up control over when the evidence is revealed.
when: when authorities demand proof before acting

text: Social standing shapes who is believed and who is suspected: higher standing carries credibility, while poor, marginal or disliked people draw suspicion away from the investigator.
when: when a land quarrel between unequal households is revisited, or during suspect rotation
why: higher standing carries more credibility in the community

text: Listeners overwhelmed by a self-claimed title or praised talent accept it without probing; confident delivery and high-status labels substitute for verification.
when: a speaker announces or describes their own high rank, prestige or talent
why: Status, a confident manner and welcome praise substitute for verification in the moment.

text: Suspicion moves from a visible enemy to a trusted ally, because players trust the character closest to the protagonist's desires.
when: Late stages of a mystery with a hidden betrayer.
why: Trust in a close helper lowers guard.

text: Judging rank from manners, servants and an elegant carriage produces false confidence in a stranger's identity.
when: An observer infers social status from outward signs.
why: Appearance signals can be staged or misleading, so they are not proof of identity.

text: Figures whose standing rises by fighting a threat may have reason to keep people afraid of it.
when: a role's status depends on opposing an enemy
why: their standing rises as fighters against that enemy

text: A plan that depends on a short window of opportunity is fragile, so each step needs a fallback route.
when: when a lure depends on a brief moment of absence
why: Delays or early returns can break a plan that has no alternative.

text: Let players discover the difference between real and assumed locks, so their access assumptions can be tested.
when: Designing doors whose lock status differs from what players assume.
why: Discovering that an assumed lock is not real rewards testing and revises the player's model of access.

text: Judge a person's routines, such as meals and daily habits, to choose a visit time when they are reachable and not disturbed.
when: Planning to approach a character for information.
why: Routines determine when people are available and receptive.

text: Security that relies on keys, passwords or records held by individuals can be defeated by someone who obtains copies of those items while using the system legitimately.
when: A system's access control depends on items held by people rather than on the system itself
why: Legitimate use exposes procedures, credentials and duplicable items that an attacker can gather and reuse

text: A searcher risks being caught, and the consequences of discovery add tension to a slow, careful search.
when: When a player searches someone else's belongings.
why: Fear of exposure raises the stakes of each action.
