text: Acting alone to test a theory carries real risk and fear, which should be planned for in the design of a solo investigation.
why: Solitary risk raises stakes that the player must manage

text: A test subject who bears real discomfort should be compensated, for example with rest, and the test should not cause lasting harm.
when: Using a companion or character as a test subject
why: Ethical limits protect the subject and keep the test valid

text: Under exertion, fear, disorientation, or disrupted events, people misjudge elapsed time and distance, so a timing gap or conflict with records is not necessarily a lie; check against a dated record.
when: when a player or witness is under strain or disorientation, when reconstructing how long ago events occurred, or when a witness's timing conflicts with records
why: strain and disorientation distort the sense of time and distance

text: Sedatives or altered states can stretch or shorten perceived time, so a short action may feel far longer or shorter than its measured duration.
when: when a witness was under drugs or extreme stress
why: Altered states distort the sense of duration

text: A witness overwhelmed by a strong emotional moment may miss what happens next, so their account of the aftermath can be incomplete.
when: When a witness is present during an intense scene
why: Emotion narrows attention

text: A traveller can lose track of elapsed time while absorbed in a task, so a casual remark about the hour can signal lost attention.
when: A character is absorbed or distracted during a timed scene
why: Attention on a task removes awareness of passing time

text: An observer's sense of responsibility can add strain that distorts what she later reports.
when: an observer is under pressure to produce a correct identification
why: stress and responsibility bias recollection and reporting

text: A protector facing exposure of someone they shield may act in fear, so a killing can be sudden and unplanned rather than premeditated.
when: a protector faces exposure of a loved one
why: Fear of consequences can drive an impulsive act.

text: Grief draws a room together and quiets sceptics, so the emotional mood is not evidence of guilt.
when: at a death or funeral
why: shared solemnity feels like consensus

text: Players can hold a firm conviction about a suspect's guilt that formal standards of proof would reject, which creates doubt and delays accusation.
when: a suspect seems guilty but no direct proof exists

text: Public attention to a case rises and falls, so a community may return to an event now and then and then forget it again.
A suspect who fits the audience's expected profile draws suspicion away from the real culprit once named.
when: the audience already holds a stock picture of the culprit
why: the match makes the accusation feel obvious

text: Declining an offer of help from locals raises suspicion, so refusing a request is itself a risk to the cover.
An investigator who finds progress too easy suspects the opponent is letting them advance, reading the open path as a lure.
when: An adversary seems to permit or ignore the investigator's moves.
why: Easy progress conflicts with expected resistance, prompting a search for the hidden purpose.

text: When told that everyone present is hiding something, people look away, over-explain, or let their attention drift toward a private worry.
when: Several people share a secret and none has volunteered it in private questioning.
why: Group pressure makes it harder to hold a story alone, so concealment shows in reactions.

text: Investigators may pursue a lead they doubt is directly connected to the crime when it is conspicuous enough, such as through an area-wide search.
Listeners are often persuaded by a witness's vehemence and conviction even when the physical detail remains disputed.
when: when a clue depends on testimony without physical proof
why: passion is easily taken for accuracy

text: People who doubt a cascade stay silent, because voicing doubt risks being named next, so doubt builds unseen.
when: Accusations are spreading and naming is dangerous.
why: Fear of being the next target suppresses open dissent.

text: Many members of an accusing crowd show no personal grievance and simply follow suggestions from others who hold grudges.
A single-perceiver claim gains strength from how the group reacts to it, not from any independent check of the event.
when: only one witness perceived the event

text: A pattern of messages that escalates from teasing to hostility changes how the target reads the author's intent.
when: A target receives repeated anonymous notes.
why: Escalation makes harmless teasing look deliberate.

text: A wrongly accused suspect cleared by a second investigator's independent deduction is more convincing than one cleared by the first investigator's correction.
when: Designing a case where an innocent suspect is released and later vindicated.
why: Independent reasoning from a fresh viewpoint reads as proof, while a correction from the original investigator reads as a retraction.

text: Once a charge is public, authorities and press treat the accused as guilty, and later evidence is read to fit that guilt.
when: an early accusation becomes the working frame
why: the initial charge becomes the default frame

text: Criminal careers mostly start between ages sixteen and twenty-one, and most criminals show no mental abnormality.
Do not accuse a suspect while evidence is thin; an accusation warns them and reveals that you suspect them.
when: Suspicion is strong but proof is weak and action would alert the suspect
why: A premature move lets the suspect hide, adapt, or escape before the case is solid.

text: Sufferers and suspected people form opposing factions, each pressing its cause to extremes, so every accusation reinforces the others.
Showing the material and social cost of a wrongful accusation, such as anonymous payments or lost standing, makes the injustice visible and raises player investment.
when: a false suspect bears consequences in the story
why: Concrete harm to an innocent party increases the emotional stakes of the mystery.

text: Stereotyping a person by sex, class, group or past record misreads their account and decides which signals seem meaningful, so such bias needs checking.
A suspicion that arises during distraction or desperation can feel more convincing than the evidence supports.
when: An investigator is under pressure and grasping for an explanation.
why: Stress lowers the threshold for accepting a convenient explanation.

text: Settling on the person with the easiest access without checking whether they had time to act leads to the wrong suspect.
when: Assessing suspects in a small group
why: Access shows opportunity but not the timing needed to act

text: As clues arrive, suspicion moves from the obvious suspect to new ones and swings when a clue changes a suspect's apparent role; the first suspect stays in doubt until a confrontation.
when: Several suspects are introduced, or NPCs carry state tied to evidence.
why: Each new clue redirects attention, and an unresolved accusation keeps earlier suspicion alive.

text: A suspect frightened by a credible warning grows uneasy, seeks confirmation, and may leave hastily to move the item.
when: A suspect receives a tip that threatens their safety or freedom
why: Fear of exposure pushes the suspect to act before they are caught

text: Players keep a suspect under suspicion until an alibi clears them, then reopen suspicion when a new witness contradicts that alibi.
when: a suspect has a witnessed alibi
why: A fresh, specific witness account reopens the case.

text: Suspicion can move from accident to unknown visitor to a named suspect within one section when a single physical clue reframes the case.
A suspect who refuses to look at evidence can be read by an audience as suspicious, and the crowd reacts with murmurs.
when: When a suspect declines to engage with an exhibited clue in public
why: Observers interpret apparent indifference as a sign of concealment.

text: A suspect with both opportunity and a stake in the outcome draws attention whether or not they are responsible.
when: Opportunity and motive are visible.
why: People read proximity and motive as guilt before proof appears.

text: In obsession mysteries, suspicion centers on the protagonist's sanity rather than on a criminal until a trick is revealed.
why: The protagonist's conduct is the most salient anomaly on the page.

text: Suspicion moves from the most vivid suspect to the least expected one, often the person closest to the victim or the one who seems most innocent.
when: a mystery with several suspects
why: Players weigh vivid suspects first and rarely suspect the quiet insider.

text: Players fix on the most visible suspect when a quarrel and a weapon by the body point to that person, and keep the reading until contrary evidence appears.
when: early in an investigation with an obvious motive and weapon
why: an accusation backed by motive and a weapon at the scene looks settled

text: A detained suspect presented as the planner makes the case look closed, so the player may accept a false solution.
when: after the arrest of a plausible suspect
why: a detention signals that the case is resolved

text: Suspicion attaches to the accused from the start while the accuser's motive goes unexamined until a confession.
when: the accuser is presented as credible
why: Players accept the first testimony and do not check the source's motive.

text: When several explanations compete, each new clue reshuffles which one the audience suspects most.
when: a mystery with multiple possible explanations
why: Each clue reweights the candidate explanations.

text: Player suspicion moves to whichever newer, confident voice displaces the last one, so each fresh accuser briefly redirects blame.
when: several characters offer competing accounts of a wrongdoing

text: Visibly valuable objects in disorder suggest a theft motive, so a player may accept a robbery reading unless the scene is checked against it.
when: When a scene holds valuable objects that look disturbed
why: Value and disorder together make theft a plausible motive.

text: Reading a witness's distress or hesitation as guilt can be a mistake, since fear or grief can produce the same signs.
when: Interpreting a witness's nervous behavior.
why: Innocent emotional states look like concealment.

text: 1) Count and separate the detained group, identifying those hurt or dead. 2) Question each individually. 3) Record each claim with what can and cannot be checked.
when: When handling a group of detained suspects.
why: Separation prevents coordinated stories and sorts verifiable claims from unverifiable ones.

text: Players move suspicion to the next candidate only after the prior one is cleared, and hold each new suspect until a test or physical detail contradicts it.
when: a mystery with several plausible suspects or competing explanations
why: Each dismissal or collapse opens a new lead and earns trust in the next layer; each accusation feels resolved until contradicted.

text: Players feel progress when a candidate list shrinks through checks they perform themselves, even when the remaining uncertainty is still high.
when: A suspect search narrows through in-world checks
why: Each elimination gives visible evidence that the search is advancing.

text: A speaker who asks what they revealed while feverish shows they are weighing the risk of exposure.
when: someone who was feverish or raving
why: they cannot tell how much was kept back

text: Accusations tend to fall on neighbours with unusual habits, unpopular standing or irregular lives rather than on strangers.
when: A community is building a case against someone

text: Public sympathy for one suspect can steer which person is pursued, even when other suspects have comparable opportunity.
when: A sympathetic suspect is set against unsympathetic ones
why: Sympathy shapes whom people are willing to investigate

text: Investigators hold suspicion on one suspect until a link to a wider group forces a fresh look, which can revive a previously cleared suspect.
A verified alibi clears a suspect, but a later question about it can flip belief back to suspicion and then to release.
when: when a suspect's alibi is checked and then challenged
why: each new test of the claim moves belief again

text: A late evidence cluster can point at the least-suspected character, because the player has spent suspicion on others.
when: after several suspects have been cleared
why: Earlier suspicion was exhausted on other characters.

text: Shared common traits, such as a recurring habit, age, height or build, narrow suspects but do not prove identity, since many people share them.
when: Matching a disguised person or description to a known profile.
why: Shared traits apply to large numbers of people, so they are weak evidence on their own.

text: Identify the evidence that actually supports a suspicion, then press it with questions to see whether it survives.
when: Evaluating a theory built on a suspicious detail
why: Suspicions often lack the evidence that would support them once examined

text: A single unusual physical trait can narrow identity sharply, but only after it is checked against the original missing-person record, since the record may omit it.
when: Using a distinctive trait to match a found body or item to a candidate.
why: A rare trait is strong evidence only if it was actually recorded earlier; an unrecorded trait cannot confirm or exclude anyone.

text: Treating an access rule, such as a required presence, as absolute can hide gaps that a timed test reveals.
when: An investigation relies on a rule about who may enter a room
why: Rules of presence often have timing or procedural gaps

text: Checking only the suspects you already favour causes missed culprits.
when: When an investigator has a preferred suspect
why: Narrow focus skips other people who had the same access and opportunity.

text: 1) Start with the last people who housed or employed the subject. 2) Record what each saw directly versus heard secondhand. 3) Collect any letters or papers they can provide. 4) Fix dates using dated sources. 5) Note where each trail ends and pick the next lead from that gap.
when: A person has moved away and their past survives only in others' memories and papers
why: Each witness covers only a partial window of contact, so the full history is assembled from overlapping partial accounts

text: 1) Identify a checkable claim and locate a physical trace, such as a room, schedule or empty space. 2) Compare the claim with the trace; if it contradicts, discount the claim and treat the witness as mistaken or untruthful. 3) Eliminate candidates whose known features differ from the trace. 4) Test alibis against independent records.
when: A character or witness gives an account that can be checked directly against physical traces.
why: Physical traces are more reliable than unverifiable testimony, and contradictions between accounts and evidence are the basis for new leads.

text: A suspect's tidy excuse, such as a sudden claim to have discarded a ticket, should be treated as a claim to test against physical details, not accepted as fact.
when: suspect offers an excuse checkable against physical details

text: A suspect who sees the investigator already knows the details is more likely to give a full, honest account.
when: during a confrontation with verified evidence
why: lying gains nothing when gaps will be exposed

text: A suspect under pressure often shifts to charm or frankness and presents their actions as provoked, placing blame on the victim.
when: A cornered suspect is questioned about their motive.
why: Self-justification protects the suspect's standing and shapes their account.

text: A listener who cannot check a stated fact at the moment tends to accept it as true.
when: when verification is unavailable during the exchange
why: unchecked claims feel settled

text: Culprits often assume that small concealment steps are safe, but a discarded item or replacement object can point to a particular person or habit that the culprit did not anticipate.
when: a suspect tries to erase or replace evidence
why: The culprit judges risk from their own view and misses knowledge other people hold about common objects.

text: A teller filters what an audience learns by deciding which details count as unnecessary.
A suspect may accept only part of a theory, so the remaining gaps must be followed up rather than assumed resolved.
when: Questioning yields partial agreement.
why: People often accept the parts that fit their experience and resist the rest.

text: Silence about one's movements protects against self-incrimination but tends to make a case look worse to observers.
when: A suspect declines to explain their movements
why: Observers read unexplained silence as concealment

text: A person who never complained of pain leaves vague or inconsistent testimony about it, and that absence of complaint is weak evidence.
when: Witnesses describe the health of someone who did not report symptoms
why: Witnesses who did not watch the person's health closely cannot give complete accounts

text: Players read an innocent suspect's self-incriminating remark as guilt until a later clue gives it another meaning.
when: a wrongly accused character says something that fits the accusation
why: the remark matches the accusation on first reading

text: A sudden change in a speaker's voice, manner or routine can make an explanation sound less natural and signal a shifting account worth closer checking.
when: A speaker's demeanor, voice or routine changes while explaining, or a witness's behaviour changes.
why: Altered conduct often precedes or accompanies a change in what someone will say.

text: When a suspect volunteers a statement that seems unnecessary, ask why they mentioned it, since the motive can reveal what they want to conceal.
when: A suspect offers an unprompted or unexplained remark
why: Unrequested statements often serve to steer or hide something

text: Compare a suspect's strong reaction with the excuse they give afterward, since a gap between them points to a concealed matter.
when: A suspect's reaction is out of line with their stated reason
why: A thin excuse covering a strong reaction suggests something hidden

text: Test a claimed precaution against the actual actions, since an item that contradicts the stated care reveals the claim as unreliable.
when: a witness claims someone took care to avoid notice
why: actions that undercut the stated precaution expose the explanation as false

text: Vague, open-ended answers fit many questions, so they can seem to match a question more than they actually do.
when: A source gives short, interpretable replies.
why: Broad answers let the listener supply the match themselves.

text: A suspect's rationalisation of an earlier failure can sound convincing in the moment, so its internal contradictions must be checked before it is accepted.
when: When an exposed suspect offers an explanation for past conduct
why: Plausibility in the moment is not evidence of truth

text: An unseen accomplice blamed by a suspect should not be accepted without a way to test the claim.
when: When a suspect attributes wrongdoing to unidentified others.
why: Untestable claims can shift blame without producing evidence.

text: 1) Separate what the witness saw from what they heard, and mark verdicts and theories as opinion. 2) Keep the few concrete, checkable facts and discard verdicts. 3) Verify each fact against independent evidence. 4) Record conflicts and who could know what.
when: A witness is talkative, emotional, or has a stake in how others are judged, or multiple witnesses give conflicting or emotionally charged accounts.
why: Fluent detail can hide that most of an account is opinion or second-hand report. Judgments cannot be tested, but facts can be corroborated, so separating them keeps the usable evidence.

text: 1) Separate minor claims from the main claim. 2) Identify each item's single source. 3) Check the source's stake in the outcome, since a party profiting from an accusation has reason to press it. 4) Compare claims against records or independent witnesses. 5) Check claims against observable facts such as stated income versus spending.
when: When judging an accusation or evaluating testimony or papers in a case.
why: Separating and tracing claims shows which parts are supported and which depend on one biased source, since stated interest can bias what a witness reports.

text: 1) Ask whether the information was actually read or heard. 2) Ask its general drift. 3) Ask the source's identity. 4) Ask who it concerns. Each answer narrows the inference.
when: Learning a secondhand or accidental disclosure
why: Stepwise narrowing tests reliability before inference

text: 1) List what the person knew at each step. 2) Ask what they would plausibly do if they held each candidate belief. 3) Compare the resulting route with their stated account.
when: When checking whether a suspect's movements fit their story
why: Reconstructing actions from beliefs exposes mismatches that the account hides.

text: 1) Start from a known event. 2) Ask what the suspect must do next given their danger and options. 3) Give each step a plausible reason. 4) Check each step against the time available and the evidence.
when: When facts are incomplete and the suspect's options can be listed
why: Anchoring each step to a motive and a deadline turns a story into a testable sequence.

text: 1) Break the account into individual details. 2) Test each detail against physical traces in the scene. 3) Compare it with the teller's earlier statements. 4) Note which details fail. 5) Keep each verified part separately.
when: A detailed account can be compared with objects, traces or other testimony.
why: A detail that fails one check can expose the rest of the account, while true parts may still survive.

text: 1) Have the suspect state their account fully first. 2) Hold back a fact that contradicts it. 3) Once committed, state the fact flatly without argument. 4) Observe whether the suspect retracts or escalates.
when: You hold one reliable fact contradicting a stated alibi
why: Commitment before disclosure forces the suspect to choose between retraction and a harder denial, revealing more than an argument would.

text: 1) State a relevant fact to the suspect in a controlled setting. 2) Compare the suspect's verbal claims with their manner or word choice. 3) Note any slip that conflicts with a claim of ignorance. 4) Check the slip against other evidence before concluding.
when: Testing whether a character is concealing knowledge.
why: A reaction that contradicts stated words can expose concealed knowledge, but needs corroboration.

text: A suspect's own testimony is weak when they are implicated; whether they are watched matters more than whether they are detained.
when: When a suspect gives an account of their movements.
why: An implicated person has a motive to shape their account.

text: Test each element of a gossip-driven theory against physical facts, and do not dismiss a stock type that has direct support.
when: When a story seems to account for everything
why: Stock roles are false only when used in place of evidence

text: Treat a fact reported by one interested party as unproven until someone who did not hear it from that party confirms it.
when: A key fact rests on one person's word.
why: Shared origin makes apparent corroboration unreliable.

text: Treat a generous or insistent alibi as a reason to probe further, not as a settled answer.
when: When an alibi is offered with unusual force or detail.
why: Insistence can signal a stake in the outcome rather than accuracy.

text: A subject who feels unwatched, or is questioned gently and attentively, lowers their guard and discloses details they would otherwise withhold.
when: A subject is unaware of being watched or is questioned in calm, open terms.
why: Feeling safe or gentle questioning lowers defensiveness, so unguarded phrases reveal what the subject knows.

text: Arousal or a brief startle is not proof of guilt: fear, recognition, surprise, coincidence or hearing one's name can cause it, and guilty subjects may stay calm.
when: Interpreting a physical arousal, startle or pause response.
why: Several causes produce the same signal, so it is not specific to guilt.

text: Treating a tell as proof of guilt misleads, since anger, grief, fear and nervousness produce the same visible cues; tells only raise suspicion.
when: Reading a suspect's physical signs or nervous gesture during questioning.
why: Anger, grief, fear and nervousness have many innocent causes.

text: Under pointed questioning about a name, event or sensitive act, a guarded witness shows involuntary bodily tells or verbal slips that betray what they fear or know.
when: A witness is pressed with a direct question or confronted with a specific name or event.
why: Pressure produces involuntary signs and slips that reveal concealment.

text: An out-of-proportion reaction to a revealed fact, or a too-quick answer or relief at a term, suggests the character already knew the subject.
when: A character reacts strongly to a revealed fact or is questioned about a specific subject.
why: Reaction out of proportion to the news, or speed of reply, implies prior knowledge.

text: A suspect's reaction to an unexpected fact, such as startling, gesturing wildly or covering the mouth, is recorded evidence, though not proof on its own.
when: Observing how a suspect responds to news of the event or an unexpected fact.
why: Observed reactions are data that can raise or lower suspicion.

text: A suspect whose presence is ambiguous at key moments can become a red herring for the investigator.
when: when a suspect's whereabouts at crucial times are unclear
why: Uncertainty invites focus on the wrong person.

text: A visible change in face, posture or tone at the wrong moment, such as going pale or sitting up, is read by others as a sign that a remark struck home.
when: A speaker hears a remark that touches a hidden matter.
why: Involuntary reactions are harder to control than words, so they leak the emotional impact of the remark.

text: An anxious suspect paces, works their hands, and starts then breaks off questions when weighing how much they are exposed.
when: A suspect feels threatened by an investigator's knowledge
why: Their attention is split between defence and fear of exposure

text: A witness who first denies or is unsure may later admit specific detail when asked about a particular place or action.
when: when questioning about a specific location or action

text: People reveal hidden intent through small unplanned cues such as glances, hesitation, slips, stumbles, lip movement, posture change, stray words, and how they handle objects.
when: a character withholds a thought but is observed
why: unplanned acts leak what speech conceals

text: Showing a suspect that the investigator already knows everything can make surrender seem the only option.
when: when confronting a suspect during questioning
why: A visible command of the facts removes the suspect's hope of a successful defence.

text: A witness under emotional strain may hide feelings by looking away and speaking in controlled sentences.
when: the witness is protecting a family member
why: self-control conceals distress

text: A person discussing someone they care about may slip a pet name or nearly say that name in an altered form.
A strong emotional reaction to an accusation can signal guilt or simple offence, so it needs corroboration before being treated as a confession.
when: When a suspect reacts angrily to a bluff or accusation.
why: Guilt and offence produce similar outward responses.

text: A sudden reaction to one loaded word can reveal a concern the speaker is trying to hide.
when: when a keyword touches something the speaker fears or regrets
why: involuntary startle exposes what a person wants concealed

text: Waiting and watching often makes a suspect act again, committing them to a course that leaves a definite clue.
when: The threat is not immediate and the investigator can observe quietly
why: A suspect who believes the threat has passed may repeat the act and expose themselves.

text: A suspect who reacts to a detail they should not know, after a small wording slip, reveals that they already know about the event.
when: when an investigator uses a deliberate wording trap
why: a reaction to an unknown-but-supposedly-private detail signals prior knowledge

text: Listeners experience a speaker's hesitation and interruptions as dramatic tension, so pacing can come from the telling itself, not only the structure.
A calm or unexpected reaction from a suspect can mislead observers about that suspect's motive.
when: A suspect reacts unexpectedly to news
why: Observers read emotion as a sign of guilt or innocence

text: A threatened suspect may reveal a hiding place once resistance seems hopeless.
when: the suspect faces a stronger party
why: the suspect judges resistance futile

text: A witness's sharp, angry denial of a theory can signal a private suspicion they will not admit.
when: Someone rejects a suspicion more strongly than the situation calls for.
why: Strong denial can conceal a belief the speaker already holds.

text: People readily hurry to put a displaced object back in place, so an object moved out of position draws the hand.
when: When an object in a familiar space is visibly out of position
why: The eye catches the disorder and the urge to tidy overrides caution.

text: A suspect who learns the investigator's real role may react with a sharp, visible startle, and agitation can grow as a hypothetical case unfolds.
when: an investigator reveals a role during a visit
why: Guilty knowledge can trigger alarm when the topic comes close

text: A small disagreement with an expert about a fact can reveal a certainty the speaker should not have.
when: when a person is questioned about a detail they claim to know
why: certainty about a detail can betray inside knowledge

text: Each speaker frames facts to suit their own stake, so accounts from people with different interests can conflict while all sounding sure.
when: when people discuss an event they have views on
why: each teller has an interest in how the event is framed

text: Short flat answers paired with closed posture, such as folded hands and a tight mouth, often signal deliberate withholding rather than simple shyness.
when: A witness is questioned about events they may be hiding.
why: Closed posture and clipped speech reflect a conscious effort to give nothing away.

text: Questions about a witness's personal past can produce visible reactions such as a changed expression or flashing eyes, marking a nerve worth pursuing.
when: Questions touch on family, past connections, or personal history.
why: A sore subject makes the witness react involuntarily, which exposes concealed information.

text: A sudden, plausible outburst draws every observer's gaze, so attention leaves the critical spot and a hidden action goes unnoticed.
when: when a hidden action must happen in plain sight
why: people turn toward an unexpected remark and away from what they were watching

text: A character shaken by a sudden event may stall even when the chance to act is still open.
when: an event removes a character's momentum
why: resolve drops after the shock

text: A suspect's reaction that conflicts with a literal answer, such as a nervous laugh or repeated touching of an object, suggests that more is being withheld.
when: A character gives a technically true or narrow answer during questioning.
why: Physical tells expose discomfort that the verbal answer conceals.

text: A suspect's quick glances toward an accomplice, or sudden stalling such as claiming to fetch a key, can signal guilt or nervousness.
when: Questioning a suspect who refuses access or avoids a point.
why: Stalling and glances reveal discomfort, though they have many causes.

text: A listener hiding a strong reaction will often use a physical shield or change the subject to keep composure while a sensitive detail is revealed.
when: A key detail is revealed in a socially tense scene.
why: Composure must be maintained without showing emotion to others present.

text: Words spoken to oneself, overheard by another, are often more revealing than statements made to the listener.
when: When a character's self-directed speech can be overheard.
why: Unguarded speech shows private concern not shaped for the listener.

text: Visible tells such as paling, hesitation, or shifting eyes can serve as evidence alongside spoken words when judging whether someone is lying.
when: A character is being questioned and their demeanor is observable.
why: Physical and tonal cues carry information that the words alone may not.

text: A suspect who is nervous shows visible cues such as color change or hesitation, which intensify when a trap is announced.
when: A suspect is present while an investigation is announced.
why: Fear of exposure appears in the body before it appears in words.

text: A suspect's sudden agitation, such as a bodily tell, an odd sound or a sudden offer of money, can be read as evidence of knowledge.
when: A suspect reacts strongly to a presented object or claim.
why: Involuntary or excessive reactions often accompany concealed knowledge.

text: A suspect who insists on personally handling key evidence, claiming it will be ruined otherwise, may be trying to control or alter it.
when: A suspect resists others touching or examining a set of records or objects
why: Control over evidence can hide its contents or condition

text: A witness who sidesteps a direct question often knows more than they admit, so the evasion itself is useful information.
when: A witness avoids answering a question about a specific matter.
why: Deflection can indicate knowledge or concern that the witness does not want to share.

text: Two opposed theories describe guilty answers: flat denial of everything, or admitting unavoidable facts and reframing them. Each theory can be used to argue either innocence or guilt.
when: Judging how a suspect's interview answers reflect guilt.

text: Make a dependant's behaviour readable enough that players can check it against what the adults say.
when: Designing household characters in a story
why: Checkable behaviour lets players test claims rather than accept them

text: Ambiguous relations, such as owning an object versus it fitting someone, can hide a reinterpretation the audience has already seen.
when: designing a clue that can be read two ways
why: the distinction is easy to overlook until it is pointed out

text: Give a staged intruder a logical target, such as a search for a specific person, so the break-in looks purposeful rather than random.
A witness's habitual tells can give them away when they lie, so watch whether their manner changes during a specific claim.
when: A witness is making a statement that may be false.

text: Unnecessary effort in a clue, such as closing a door no one could see into, is a signature of a deliberate plan.
when: When a detail seems to require odd or wasteful actions
why: Staging demands steps that serve the deception rather than the stated purpose, which leaves an awkward trace.

text: Do not treat a confident speaker's certainty as proof of the underlying event.
Nervous looks, winks or shyness during an exchange are weak signs of deception; treat them as less reliable than a physical check.
when: Judging whether a speaker is telling the truth
why: Demeanor is easily misread, while physical evidence can be inspected directly

text: A visible pause before answering marks a point for follow-up questioning, especially before a witness names another person.
when: a witness hesitates before answering
why: Hesitation often signals reluctance or information being weighed, which warrants closer questioning.

text: Alternating warmth and seriousness, such as offering water after shouting or whispering after a shout, keeps a suspect off balance and hard to settle.
why: unpredictable mood changes disrupt the suspect's composure

text: An anxious suspect may answer slowly for innocent reasons, so delay alone does not prove guilt.
why: Being tested causes stress unrelated to the crime.

text: Anxiety about one question is easily mistaken for guilt about the whole matter; keep the two apart.
A character's strong reaction can be triggered by an unrelated concern such as gossip or a marriage, not the question at hand.
An early theory fixed on one suspect shapes how later reactions are read, so ambiguous behavior gets forced to fit it.
Treating a single answer pattern as proof misleads, because innocent people also deny or admit facts in similar ways.
A witness who is not rattled by a bluff will not return, so the approach fails with anyone who has nothing to gain.
Assuming that variation always indicates a genuine source is a mistake, because the forger can control variation in both sets.
when: Judging authenticity from variation alone
why: Variation can be manufactured, so it is evidence only when the process producing it is understood.

text: Dismissing a suspect because one strong point is weak is also a mistake, since the other points must be tested as well.
when: One piece of evidence against a suspect fails
why: A failed point does not clear the remaining points

text: Illness, nervousness and an observer's own agitation produce similar signs, and an emotionally invested observer may read guilt into innocent behavior.
Treat a tell as a lead to verify, never as proof; pair it with an independent fact or other signs, since one gesture cannot convict.
why: The same reaction can come from innocence, fear or performance.

text: Give evasive NPCs readable tells such as pauses, repeated denials, changed tone or animation, so players can tell the character is concealing something.
when: Designing NPC dialogue or animation for evasive characters.

text: Give a companion who cannot speak plainly readable signals such as pacing, turning away, or brightening at a song, and let players test interpretations against other evidence.
when: designing non-verbal companion NPCs

text: Leaving two plausible wrong theories open at once keeps the audience uncertain about who is responsible and what happened.
when: Midpoint of a mystery with competing explanations
why: Neither explanation yet fits all the clues.

text: Accusers who joke about their own fits or treat them as sport reveal that the display was deliberate rather than involuntary.
when: witnesses display levity about the accusations
why: A casual attitude indicates performance.

text: Visible progress toward a reveal, such as a widening gap or a countdown, builds suspense because players anticipate the outcome.
when: Staging a slow reveal of a hidden object or a timed reveal in play.
why: Visible progress raises anticipation as players track the approaching moment.

text: An in-game warning before a major reveal raises the stakes and gives the player a chance to stop, which can work as a difficulty choice.
when: Designing a dramatic discovery the player may not want to face.
why: Advance warning lets the player decide whether to continue, which increases investment in the choice.

text: 1) Stage the event with a stand-in at the original position. 2) Have a witness help set it up. 3) Trigger the mechanism as it originally occurred. 4) Reveal the hidden part through a visible lever or catch. 5) Reset and repeat the trigger to show it works.
when: When a verbal explanation would be hard to believe or physical proof is available
why: Showing the mechanism persuades witnesses more than describing it, and a witness-run reset proves function

text: People instinctively attribute a series of deaths to the supernatural, which lets an ordinary killer strike unnoticed among them.
when: when a run of deaths is believed to have a supernatural cause
why: the instinct to blame curses draws attention away from human action

text: A body stiffens after death, holding its posture until limbs are moved, so the pose at discovery must be recorded first.
when: A corpse is found in a seated or posed position.
why: Rigor holds the position until someone straightens the limbs.

text: A person's temperament governs how they carry out a deed; an impulsive, bold person acts openly and leaves different traces than a planned, careful one.
when: Judging whether a method fits a suspect
why: Temperament shapes the style, care and visibility of an action

text: A character acting on strong emotion makes poor tactical choices, such as a reckless chase, which draws attention and undermines their goal.
when: A character is pursuing a target while emotionally aroused.
why: Emotional intensity overrides careful planning, causing collisions and exposure.

text: A disguised or changed person tends to drift back toward old habits and speech, while deeper character structure remains stable.
when: A person returns to ordinary life after a major change or disguise.
why: Surface change such as opinion or manner fades, while stable traits persist.

text: A person's temperament predicts the kind of crime they would commit: someone whose values are already satisfied by fantasy is unlikely to commit an act that conflicts with them.
when: when judging whether a suspect fits a crime
why: people act on the motives their temperament makes salient

text: Let interrogation dialogue use temperament tags, with silence and private scenes available as tools the player can choose.
when: Designing a suspect interrogation system.

text: Physical strength does not guarantee the temperament to harm someone directly, so ability alone should not settle a theory.
Assigning suspects to stock character types lets every trait be read as evidence for the type, and the type then absorbs contradictory facts.
when: When a theory is built from stereotypes rather than observed facts
why: Once a type is assumed, nearly any detail can be fitted into it

text: Impressions of temperament are easily mistaken for facts about a person, so they should not be recorded as identifying traits.
why: Impressions reflect the observer's reading as much as the person.

text: Concealment through distraction ends when attention returns, making the hidden danger visible to everyone at once.
when: When a cover depends on directed attention.
why: Cover based on distraction is temporary by design.

text: Long waiting in darkness or silence, with something seeming imminent, raises tension and sharpens the senses before any event occurs.
when: players wait in the dark or during a stakeout or watch before an encounter or delayed action
why: Anticipation builds tension more than immediate action in uncertain conditions

text: Fear from an uncanny sight or eerie setting can persist after its mundane explanation is known, so feeling and cause can be separated.
when: after an uncanny image or eerie setting has been explained or has a mundane source
why: Emotional reaction follows feeling, not only explanation; physical fear responses do not determine what actually causes the sensation

text: A hinted or unstated threat unsettles more than a stated one, because listeners fill the gap with their own worst-case conclusion.
when: a threat is suggested or hinted at rather than shown or stated
why: the mind supplies its own worst-case picture and suspicion

text: People who believe they are unobserved may take watchers for routine activity, such as passing boats, and fail to notice the observation.
when: when people keep a secret near observers
why: they read familiar sights as harmless

text: When two observers independently reach the same unease about one event, the shared reaction reads as stronger evidence that something has happened.
when: Two characters react to the same disturbance without coordinating
why: Independent agreement reads as corroboration

text: A lone watcher in a dark, still building tends to imagine footsteps and grows more fearful as the wait goes on.
when: Watching alone in a dark, silent place
why: Isolation and silence amplify the perception of small sounds

text: A visible looming threat keeps players expecting a payoff during a stalled investigation.
when: the investigation pauses without resolution
why: Anticipation sustains attention while progress is slow.

text: Deaths and livestock losses are attributed to people who earlier made threats or curses, linking misfortune to grudge.
Players waiting for a promised event tend to imagine threats worse than any real danger, which produces dread.
when: An anticipated moment is delayed while nothing visible happens.
why: Uncertainty leaves a gap that the imagination fills with worst cases.

text: A person who senses that others are watching or suspicious tends to feel hunted, and that fear can grow and push them to overreact.
when: When a suspect perceives observers' attention.
why: Perceived scrutiny raises anxiety, which can change behavior and reveal more.

text: A target can become terrified by a completely invented threat, such as a watcher who does not exist, so the fear comes from the story alone.
A sudden quiet after repeated noise is treated as more threatening than the noise itself, because silence can hide a threat.
when: A threat has been signalled repeatedly and then stops
why: Players infer that a quiet period may conceal danger

text: A victim who reasons from a belief that the threat is contained will dismiss a credible warning, letting the threat proceed.
when: a warning arrives that conflicts with the victim's belief about the threat
why: People trust a prior conclusion over contrary evidence when that conclusion is comforting.

text: Physical reactions described in a scene, such as a sick feeling or prickling skin, heighten the sense of threat.
when: Building tension in a frightening moment

text: A fear state can make it unclear whether an action was chosen or forced, which creates doubt about one's own agency.
when: A character is under fear or stress
why: Impaired judgment blurs the line between intent and impulse

text: Uncanny sensations or disturbing images, such as dread or unease, are not evidence of a cause and must not be taken as proof of one.
when: a character or player relies on feelings or a disturbing image to identify a source
why: Sensations are shaped by expectation and cannot be traced to a specific origin; odd sights can stand in for evidence

text: A setting's mood can make an observer read more danger, or a supernatural cause, into an ordinary event than the evidence supports.
when: interpreting a dark, tense, or threatening location, or an unexplained event within an atmospheric setting
why: Atmosphere heightens perceived threat and primes people to read ambiguous sensations as unnatural, independent of actual evidence

text: Silencing a witness through threats hides the trail from the investigator and removes evidence.
Fear can decide how an ambiguous clue is read before the evidence settles it, producing a confident but unsupported interpretation.
when: A character or player is frightened while interpreting a scene.
why: Emotional state biases interpretation toward the most threatening reading.

text: Sincere witnesses' recalled times and durations are approximate; they can misjudge by hours without noticing, especially when tired or asleep.
when: A witness reports a duration or time of an event from memory.
why: Subjective time perception is unreliable and the error is not felt by the witness.

text: A cluster of similar events can look random until the intervals between them are calculated and compared.
when: When players review a log of repeated events.
why: Interval patterns are only visible when the entries are listed together and measured.

text: Players keep suspecting a person whose clues are real but whose timing is misread, until an alibi breaks that reading.
when: when physical clues fit a suspect but times conflict
why: Real clues carry weight even when their timing is wrong.

text: Players spend their attention on suspects' motives rather than on timing evidence, so a clock-based mechanism can stay hidden.
when: mysteries where suspects are chosen on motive
why: Motive draws focus to people, away from the clock.

text: Check a witness's time references against each other and against the event sequence; descriptions that point to different periods signal a conflict to resolve.
when: A witness's timing matters to a theory about who was present.
why: Timing contradictions can rule out accounts that cannot fit the sequence.

text: A covert act timed to a climax, when attention peaks, is more likely to pass unnoticed than one done during a quiet moment.
when: Planning or designing a covert action during a scripted event.
why: Peak attention is directed at the main moment.

text: A witness who cannot recall a date may recall an event when it is linked to a separate, vivid detail such as a harvest, a garment, or a season.
when: Trying to recover a memory that cannot be reached by direct date questions
why: Concrete associated cues give memory retrieval a route that dates alone do not provide

text: A traveller who sleeps or cannot see the route misjudges how much time passed, so their estimate of duration can conflict with people who were present.
when: A witness was asleep or enclosed and cannot see the route or clock
why: Sensory cues are limited, so duration is inferred from sound and feel

text: Treating an approximate medical estimate as an exact time, or missing that a fast-acting method implies the perpetrator was close to the victim.
when: When reasoning from a medical timing estimate
why: Overprecision and missed implications lead to wrong suspect lists.

text: A delay that seems arbitrary to the audience can lose their goodwill, especially when the request to wait irritates them before its purpose is clear.
when: a reveal is postponed without a visible reason
why: unexplained waiting reads as stalling

text: A witness who slept between checks cannot vouch for the hours in between, so those intervals must stay unverified.
1) Order events chronologically. 2) Attach each event to its source. 3) Draw conclusions only after the ordered sequence is complete.
when: Reconstructing a case from multiple sources.
why: Ordered, sourced events make each conclusion traceable to evidence.

text: 1) Ask the witness for the longest time they were away. 2) Record each answer as an upper bound, keeping the tightest ceiling. 3) Ignore digressions that do not answer the question. 4) Compare the bound against a fixed event. 5) Conclude whether the time was sufficient for the purpose.
when: A witness's timing matters but their memory is unreliable or their attention was elsewhere
why: A maximum bound is more robust than a precise guess, and fixed events anchor the estimate

text: Do not dismiss a clue as fake merely because it is convenient; test its timing first.
when: When a clue seems too neat to be genuine
why: Convenience alone does not prove staging, and a suspicious detail may be innocent.

text: A depicted face can suggest a character's hidden traits, but exaggerated color and hard detail shape the impression the viewer forms.
when: A viewer reads a portrait as a character clue
why: Stylistic choices bias the reading.

text: People tend to accept newcomers who look polished and admirable without checking their claims, so appearance can persuade more than verification.
when: When a newcomer presents a credible look and a letter or claim, and no check is made.
why: Polish and appearance create trust that bypasses scrutiny.

text: Quick, over-eager agreement with a point can be a sign that the speaker is concealing something.
when: A witness agrees too readily with an interviewer's statement.
why: Unusually fast endorsement can signal an attempt to steer the conversation.

text: Identity clues tend to arrive in a fast cluster after a long buildup, so understanding accelerates near the climax.
Players dismiss a place's folklore or ghost reputation as a hoax, treating a hidden room as rumor until physical evidence shows it is real and reachable.
when: When a location has a supernatural reputation and no physical evidence yet.
why: Players discount unverified stories about haunted places, so physical proof is what changes their belief.

text: Audiences move suspicion away from whoever seems most helpful, so a helpful figure can hide the true antagonist.
when: a helper is also a potential suspect
why: Helpfulness reads as loyalty and lowers scrutiny

text: Players read a sudden death under a relative's care as a family quarrel over money until evidence contradicts that reading.
when: early in a case involving a will or an inheritance

text: A protagonist's own misconduct weakens the credibility of their accusations, so players discount what that character claims afterward.
when: the protagonist has been caught in wrongdoing earlier

text: Give a starting persona a visible idle trait, so later careful play feels like growth rather than a sudden skill jump.
why: A visible baseline makes improved play feel earned to the player.

text: A published description of a person that is unusually detailed can reveal how much the authorities already suspect.
when: Reading a public description issued in a missing-person case
why: Detail beyond what a search needs signals private suspicion

text: Keeping the accuser powerless for too long drains player interest.
A surprising claim made by a credentialed expert can seem settled before the other evidence has been weighed.
when: When an authoritative figure presents an unexpected conclusion
why: Perceived expertise lends weight that the evidence has not yet earned.

text: A witness who turns reluctant or detached when questioned, or shows guilty unease or a composed face over visible misery, is often withholding information.
when: when questioned about a sensitive matter or while hiding information
why: Discomfort, loyalty or embarrassment makes people withhold details; visible discomfort signals concealment without a direct statement.

text: Secrets leak through unguarded talk: relieved beneficiaries reveal past scheming or money strain, and unaware speakers' offhand remarks reveal adjacent facts listeners connect.
when: a character receives a large gain in company, or a few people know a secret while others talk freely about related matters
why: Relief lowers guard; speakers see no significance in offhand remarks.

text: A witness's withholding may be harmless, such as timing disclosure or loyalty, or may signal guilt; ask why a detail was held back before weighing it.
when: a witness stays silent about a recognized object or delays revealing a relevant detail
why: Silence is easily read as guilt, and the reason shapes how the detail is weighed.

text: Witnesses may withhold facts that seem meaningless, protect a third person, or stem from fear, often without intent; each side in a relationship may conceal from the other.
when: when a cooperative witness's partial knowledge matters or a witness's silence affects the case
why: The witness may not know the fact's importance.

text: Vague answers about future plans can make a listener suspect a rival, especially when the listener is already jealous.
when: a partner withholds intent
why: uncertainty invites the worst interpretation

text: A character who gives an urgent warning and then calls it a whim has taken it back, but the retraction does not erase what was said.
when: a character reverses a warning
why: The original words still carry information the listener can use.

text: When a witness answers everything else but withholds one answer, the withheld point marks a clue worth pursuing.
Witnesses may leave out a detail when someone suggests omitting it, then add it in a later, less pressured telling.
when: When a witness's first account was given under pressure or influence.
why: Pressure or suggestion shapes what gets reported.

text: A person who explains a suspicious detail before being asked tends to set the frame of the conversation and steer how the listener reads it.
when: A suspicious detail is present and the speaker volunteers a reason.
why: An offered reason becomes the default interpretation.

text: A person under strain keeps close observers at a distance and shields themselves by locking doors, especially on the day they feel most exposed.
when: When a character is trying to hide a vulnerable state from those near them.
why: Distance and locked doors reduce the chance of being seen before composing themselves.

text: A character who believes a key person is dead has no reason to search for them, so they keep relevant evidence hidden without lying outright.
when: A character holds a false belief about a central figure's fate
why: Mistaken beliefs remove the motive to disclose, producing misdirection

text: Restrictions on information can break down under pressure when another character argues that the situation cannot get worse.
when: When a character has withheld information and others push back.
why: A perceived lack of further harm reduces the value of secrecy.

text: A person who refuses to discuss their own experiences, saying they lack the right yet, signals restraint and possible secrecy.
when: A character declines to speak about their experiences.
why: Declining to speak reads as hesitation or a reason to keep silent.

text: A witness who states an unpublicized fact, or mentions a detail before anyone told them, has revealed earlier access; trace such knowledge to a channel.
when: a fact is known only to a few who handled or witnessed the scene, or the witness's knowledge seems to outrun public information
why: An unprompted mention or unpublicized fact shows earlier access, and knowledge should trace back to a channel.

text: Withholding evidence, facts or terms too long leaves the player no route to them, loses the audience's thread and trust, and weakens the payoff before the confrontation.
when: when delaying evidence, facts or a confrontation
why: Unresolved withholding erodes trust and leaves the audience guessing.

text: Withholding reasoning, or a fact that never appeared in the story, makes a fair-play reveal feel arbitrary or like cheating; keep clues available for the audience to check.
when: when the reveal is delayed or depends on hidden reasoning
why: Without checkable clues or visible logic, the eventual answer feels arbitrary rather than earned.

text: A reveal resting on an account the audience never witnesses feels like a summary rather than an investigation.
when: when the solution is delivered only as reported narration
why: the audience did not see the deduction happen

text: Keep the meaning of a trigger phrase hidden from observers so that the reaction is not shaped by explanation.
when: Testing whether a suspect's reaction reveals private knowledge.
why: Explaining the phrase beforehand would let the reaction reflect the explanation rather than the suspect's own knowledge.

text: Keeping companions or a trusted partner in the dark breeds frustration, suspicion and less cooperation, as they react before understanding; partial information also looks like hiding.
when: deciding how much to share with a partner or group
why: Partial information frustrates collaborators and can invite their suspicion.

text: A distressed witness may be unable to track times, and answers can shift when a tangible reward is offered.
when: Questioning a witness whose fear distracts from the facts.
why: Distress consumes attention, and rewards change how willing the witness is to answer.

text: A minor hesitation in a witness's answers can shape how the rest of their testimony is read.
when: Evaluating a witness's account of events.
why: Small signs of uncertainty color the perceived credibility of everything else they say.

text: Testimony from people who observed a suspect closely can contradict the suspect's own account, revealing the real motive.
when: when a suspect's self-description conflicts with observers' accounts
why: observers see the suspect's conduct, which a self-description can hide

text: Emotional display in a confession, such as tears, tells observers little about truth, since it can accompany false confessions.
when: a confession is delivered with visible emotion
why: Emotion is not diagnostic of honesty, yet observers tend to read it as sincerity.

text: Weigh an informant by checking specific, verifiable details against other evidence; precise, checkable particulars count for more than general or sympathetic accounts.
when: Several sources describe the same person and each can be checked on at least one point.
why: Specific claims can be confirmed or refuted, while vague or emotionally colored claims cannot.

text: When several sources describe the same events differently, record every conflicting version rather than choosing one early, then sort the contradictions to see which claims can hold together.
when: Two or more accounts of the same events clash and no single source is clearly reliable.
why: Early selection hides contradictions that may reveal the true sequence.

text: When witnesses report hearing nothing, ask what physical arrangement would explain the silence rather than discarding the answer.
when: a witness says nothing unusual was heard or seen
why: A lack of sound or sight is informative when it points to a constraint such as distance or separation.

text: Testimony arrives in layers: physical facts first, then household staff, then an intimate confidante whose account narrows the field of suspects.
when: a case is built from several witnesses of differing closeness to the victim
why: Each layer adds knowledge and closer witnesses reveal more about motive and who knew what.

text: 1) Meet the witness in a neutral place away from others. 2) Offer payment to secure cooperation. 3) Reassure them they will not be punished. 4) Ask open questions first, then narrower ones. 5) Build a timeline of when events occurred. 6) Follow up contradictions until the account settles. 7) Do not reveal what you already know.
when: Questioning a frightened, lower-status witness who saw something relevant.
why: Neutral setting, reassurance and payment lower fear and encourage honest, sequenced answers.

text: 1) Discover a contradiction in a witness's account. 2) Hold it back rather than confronting immediately. 3) Use it at a later confrontation.
when: Questioning a witness whose account conflicts with known facts.
why: Withholding a contradiction preserves leverage for a stronger later challenge.

text: Witnesses fill gaps in unusual or unintelligible events with plausible inferences from their expectations, mixing interpretation with observation and closing questions too early.
when: An unusual act is observed without a clear reason, or a tense exchange is overheard in a language or context the witness cannot follow.
why: Expectations and guesses replace missing detail, which the witness then reports as if observed.

text: Witness confidence does not establish accuracy, especially for partly perceived details such as timing and loudness; reliability depends on condition, vantage and motives, and questioning separates seen from assumed.
when: Evaluating a brief sighting, poor light, or a witness giving firm statements about events only partly perceived.
why: Confidence can exceed what was actually perceived, and certainty and accuracy vary independently under stress.

text: Do not dismiss a biased or eccentric witness outright; weigh the bias, since concrete details can be correct even when interpretation is wrong, and check them against other evidence.
when: A witness openly admits feelings toward someone involved, or is discounted because their account seems unlikely.
why: Bias affects how a witness reports but does not automatically make the facts wrong.

text: A witness with a personal stake, such as payment, unpaid wages, loss or grudge, may exaggerate or shade the account, so weigh the stake when assessing reliability.
when: When assessing testimony from a witness who has a stake in the outcome.
why: Material interest or grudge distorts what the witness reports, such as haste, urgency or sequence.

text: Testimony is only as reliable as the witness's vantage, attention, conditions and precision in locating what was perceived; gaps are filled unconsciously; distant or stressed sightings are partial evidence.
when: When a witness's information is used to establish facts, such as a single witness to a vanishing or appearance.
why: Distance, light, direction and attention limit what was known, so unchecked accounts can mislead.

text: Shock, fear, exhaustion or poor visibility degrade a witness's memory of dates and sensory detail more than calm observation in good conditions; verify timing before trusting it.
when: When a witness has been emotionally shaken, frightened, exhausted, or reports events in poor visibility.
why: Traumatic experience, fear, fatigue and low visibility disrupt memory of when things happened and perception.

text: Witnesses of the same event perceive different things because position, hearing, lighting and attention differ, so each account reveals only a slice.
when: Several observers report on the same event from different places.
why: Distance, hearing ability, lighting and attention limit what each person registered.

text: A report of a sound or voice from an empty place cannot be checked directly, so its weight depends on the witness's state and the timing of events.
when: a witness reports something no one else can confirm
why: Perception under stress is unreliable, and timing offers the only available check.

text: Witnesses differ in how precise their knowledge is; a vague answer often reflects limited knowledge rather than deliberate concealment.
when: When a witness gives a vague or partial account.

text: A warning works only when the target has a reason to fear the threat; otherwise the target may read it as bluff and test it.
when: A warning is delivered to a target
why: Without a reason to fear, a warning looks like empty pressure.

text: A witness with a stake in the outcome may show over-courtesy, stock phrases, sudden topic shifts, or pressure to end the conversation.
when: A witness has a motive to shape their account.
why: Such manner can signal avoidance or self-protection, though it is not proof.

text: Children who are taught to be quiet often report unusual things without interpretation, which can make their accounts more direct and candid.
when: When a child witnesses an unusual event.
why: Children tend to describe what they see without filtering it through expectations.

text: Stories passing through several hands gain or lose details at each step, so secondhand accounts of impossible events are weak evidence.
when: when an event reaches the listener through intermediaries
why: Each retelling can add, drop or alter details.

text: Answers given as a story with their own shape are hard to check on the spot, and a relaxed or flattering setting makes them seem more reliable than they are.
when: A subject recounts their past in a comfortable conversation.
why: Narrative form and a warm setting lower the listener's inclination to verify details.

text: Other people often notice what a subject hides, such as unusual movements or sounds, and their observations can corroborate or contradict the subject's account.
when: A subject's account conflicts with what others observe.
why: Witnesses see patterns the subject does not disclose.

text: Under fear or shock, a witness can give a vivid, confident account that the physical scene later contradicts, and rarely checks their own account.
when: A witness experiences an overwhelming sensory event.
why: Overwhelmed senses prevent the witness from noticing their own errors.

text: A witness's account reflects what they believe happened, colored by feelings, embarrassment and memory gaps. Confident detail can sit beside real gaps, so it is evidence to weigh, not proof.
when: The only source for events is one emotionally involved witness
why: Emotional involvement and memory gaps distort recall even when the witness is sincere

text: Observers who saw a person only briefly often misplace times by hours.
when: A witness glimpsed a person briefly and is asked to place the time of the sighting.
why: Brief observation gives weak temporal memory, so timing errors are common.

text: Players accept an authority figure's misdirect more readily, so an expert's confident reading must be challenged before the player doubts it.
when: when an expert NPC presents a wrong conclusion
why: Trust in authority lowers the chance that players test the expert's claim.

text: Fear sharpens perception of small noises and makes them seem vivid and real, so a frightened witness's certainty is not reliable evidence.
when: A witness is frightened or tense during an uncanny event
why: Heightened fear amplifies ordinary sounds and distorts judgement.

text: A witness can describe a real fear while also suspecting a prank, and holding both views is common.
when: An NPC reports a frightening event with some doubt about its nature.
why: Fear and skepticism coexist, so an account can be sincere and still uncertain.

text: A witness's prior belief can shape how they report a sighting, so their account is framed by expectation even when the physical details are accurate.
when: When a witness holds a strong belief related to the event they describe.
why: Expectation guides attention and interpretation of what was seen.

text: A witness who recognises a voice but never saw a face can identify a person only by voice and half-remembered words, so such identification is fallible.
when: a witness reports recognition without having seen the face
why: recognition is limited to what was actually perceived

text: Written statements can hide lies that a face-to-face account would reveal, so written testimony is not safer than spoken testimony.
when: when evaluating letters or written references
why: Writing removes the visible cues that help judge honesty

text: A child's statements about who they love or trust show attachment, not reliable recognition of a stranger.
when: A child is questioned about identifying an unfamiliar person.
why: Children's expressed bonds reflect emotional attachment rather than accurate identification.

text: A sighting establishes what was seen, not its meaning; after a traumatic event, weigh concrete sensory details more heavily than interpretive statements about their cause.
when: Evaluating a witness who reports an event and explains it, especially a frightened witness after trauma.
why: Observation and interpretation can be wrong independently; basic sensations are less distorted than conclusions drawn under fear.

text: Weigh a witness's account by her position, what she could actually see, and whether a detail surfaced unprompted or only after a question. Keep vague impressions as weak leads.
when: When evaluating what a witness reports
why: Position limits perception, and prompted recall or unverified feelings can be unreliable.

text: Do not treat a witness's conclusion about a cause, such as suicide or proper burial, as evidence; record it as opinion separate from observation.
when: When a witness offers a verdict on what happened
why: Opinions can be wrong even when the observations behind them are accurate.

text: Match each witness to the question they can actually answer; a witness weak on one point may be reliable on another.
when: When several sources offer information on different aspects of the same case.
why: Witnesses differ in what they observed and remember, so their reliability varies by question.

text: Test an account delivered with strong emotion against evidence before accepting it.
when: A suspect's account is delivered with intense feeling.
why: Emotion can make a weak account feel convincing.

text: Judge a witness's reliability by the conditions of observation, such as position, distance and fatigue, rather than by the witness's category.
when: When evaluating testimony.
why: Perception depends on where and how the witness observed, not on who they are.

text: A witness whose account contradicts itself should be judged claim by claim, not accepted or rejected wholesale.
when: A key witness has lied about one point but the rest of their account is still needed.
why: One falsehood does not invalidate everything else the witness says.

text: Weigh a witness's stake in the outcome and their physical vantage point before accepting their account. Interested witnesses, whether hostile or loyal, can distort what they report.
when: When several people give accounts of where someone was during a fixed time window.
why: A witness's motive and limited view shape what they report, so their testimony is evidence to test, not a conclusion.

text: Testimony that works against the witness's own interest, such as a rival confirming another's whereabouts, is harder to fabricate and deserves more weight.
when: When assessing whether a witness is likely to be lying.
why: Statements costly to the speaker are less likely to be invented.

text: Two independent sightings of the same physical detail corroborate each other, even if neither witness understood what they saw.
when: When two witnesses who did not share information report matching details.
why: Independent agreement is unlikely to arise from coincidence or shared error.

text: Fatigue, such as dozing during watch, limits what a witness can observe, so later sightings rest only on moments they were awake.
when: When a witness keeps watch over time.
why: Sleep removes observation for the dozed interval.

text: Vivid or emotionally intense recollection, including confident accounts of what others said, does not prove accuracy; emotion fixes details in memory regardless of correctness.
when: Relying on a witness's strongly felt or confident memories or accounts of what others said.
why: Strong emotion fixes memories in mind regardless of accuracy, so vividness can mislead.

text: Witnesses sharing a rumour, household or expectation are not independent and may reinforce one mistaken identification; agreement in number does not establish accuracy.
when: When counting corroborating witnesses, or several sources agree but drew on one common expectation or source.
why: Shared sources produce matching accounts without independent confirmation.

text: A distracted witness may sincerely claim certainty they cannot support, so check where each witness was actually looking.
when: When relying on eyewitness reports of a sudden appearance
why: Sincere confidence does not guarantee that the witness was attending to the relevant area.

text: A vivid, prejudiced account is easy to remember and repeat, so its colour should be discounted and only checkable claims kept.
when: A teller is hostile to the person they describe.
why: Emotional detail feels convincing and spreads easily while carrying no evidential weight.

text: Relying on a single witness's sighting in poor light, without a physical test or corroboration, makes the identification weak evidence.
A long gap between an event and the interview can blur a witness's memory of it.
Hostility can make a true alibi sound false, and loyalty can make a false alibi sound true. Mere presence in a place does not prove what happened there.
when: When judging testimony from witnesses with strong feelings toward the parties involved.
why: Emotional stake distorts how credible an account seems, and location alone says nothing about actions.

text: 1) Record each account a witness gives. 2) When a new account conflicts with an earlier one, mark the earlier void and ask for it to be restated. 3) Test every explanation alone, then side by side with the other explanations and physical facts. A retraction may be sincere or a second lie; do not assume either.
when: A witness gives two or more accounts touching the same facts, offers several explanations touching shared facts, or revises an earlier statement.
why: Plausible explanations can fail only when placed beside another claim, and a retraction may be honest or deceptive, so each version must be tested rather than trusted.

text: 1) Begin with harmless background questions about a shared subject. 2) Hold sensitive questions until rapport is set. 3) Record answers for brevity, repetition, and lack of embellishment. 4) Read non-verbal signs such as pauses and color changes.
when: A witness's reliability matters and direct questions would produce defensive answers
why: Neutral openings reduce defensiveness, and consistency and guardedness signal how much the witness is holding back

text: Treat testimony that proves little alone as corroboration that can strengthen a case built from other facts, not as proof.
when: Evaluating a witness account that is unreliable or indirect
why: A single detail cannot convict but can support a case built on other evidence

text: Keep witnesses with fixed beliefs or a strong stake apart from others during an inquiry, so their conviction does not shape what other witnesses notice.
when: A witness holds a fixed belief or has a stake in the outcome.
why: Strong preconceptions blur subtle clues and bias what other observers report.

text: Do not read a contradiction between testimony and the scene as proof of lying. A sincere witness may have had compromised perception.
when: A witness's account conflicts with physical evidence.
why: Mistakes under shock are more common than deliberate deception.

text: Give witnesses condition modifiers such as fear or intoxication that change how reliable their statements are.
when: Designing NPC testimony that the player must evaluate
why: Varying reliability forces the player to judge sources

text: Contradiction testing is most useful when a witness's claims lack independent records; it is less useful when records independently support the explanations.
when: deciding whether to use contradiction testing
why: independent records can confirm or refute claims without relying on the witness's consistency

text: Accepting the most dramatic account because it appears in print, and overlooking that a mundane cause must also fit every fact, leads to wrong conclusions.

1) Identify the person most useful to the inquiry who is least willing to accept help. 2) Offer help informally, without pressure or an obligation to pay. 3) Assign each investigator to the person they can best approach.
when: The most useful witness refuses direct assistance.
why: Pressure breaks the trust later needed, and matched roles make the approach feel natural.

text: 1) Collect each item and place it in a numbered container. 2) Record the owner against the number in a separate key. 3) Keep the key away from the person doing the testing.
when: Testing samples whose source must stay hidden from the examiner.
why: A blind label prevents the examiner's expectations from influencing results.

text: Do not dismiss an expert outright; verify the specific source and test the conclusion before accepting or rejecting it.
when: An expert's claim conflicts with another conclusion.
why: Experts can be refuted by a more careful reading of details, not by dismissal.

text: Adding a solvent to a sample can reveal a chemical identity through whether a precipitate forms.
when: Confirming a chemical identity in a sample.
why: Precipitate formation is a checkable reaction signature.
