text: 1) Set a deadline and plan backward from the gathering time. 2) Assemble all suspects and expert witnesses in one room, with an observing official. 3) Present evidence in sequence, narrowing the group at each step. 4) Test each suspect physically. 5) Switch to full light at the decisive moment to reveal the result.
when: A climax where all suspects can be assembled and the evidence is ready
why: Scheduled, sequenced staging builds suspense and a clear reveal

text: Keep a control subject beside a test subject, with only one receiving the treatment, to establish a baseline.
when: Running a controlled experiment on test subjects.
why: Without a control, an observed effect cannot be separated from ordinary variation.

text: 1) Test each source on the same subject. 2) Compare the resulting effects. 3) Link sources that produce the same effect. Shared effect on one test subject can connect two samples.
when: Physical samples must be tied to a common origin.
why: Identical responses on the same test subject give a traceable link between samples.

text: 1) State a hypothesis and predict the result. 2) Change one factor while holding all others fixed. 3) Compare the outcome with the earlier baseline. 4) Restore the variable and retest to confirm.
when: Testing a suspected cause in a system with several interacting parts.
why: Isolating one variable shows whether it is the true cause.

text: Covert collection avoids alerting suspects but carries ethical and personal cost, and is justified only when suspicion has a real basis.
when: Deciding whether to gather evidence secretly.
why: Secrecy protects the investigation but can harm trust if no cause for suspicion exists.

text: 1) Open with neutral prompts to set a quick, automatic rhythm. 2) Switch suddenly to charged prompts while the subject is off guard. 3) Keep the pace fast so there is no time to compose an answer. 4) Time each response and log it alongside a physiological reading.
when: A subject hides one specific piece of knowledge and likely trigger words can be guessed.
why: Hesitation and physiological spikes on charged words can reveal the concealed knowledge.

text: 1) Compare a body's observed features with a written description. 2) Count the matched features and separate common traits from distinctive ones. 3) Confirm only with distinctive traits that can actually be checked.
when: Deciding whether a found body matches a missing-person description.
why: General agreement across common traits fits many people, so only a verifiable distinctive trait can confirm identity.

text: An investigator's emotional commitment can lead them to assume an error before checking the record, distorting the review.
when: Reopening a case the reviewer feels strongly about
why: Conviction can precede evidence

text: A small discrepancy in an estimated measurement, such as height, is better explained by the uncertainty of the estimate than treated as a contradiction.
when: Comparing an estimated measurement to a recorded value.
why: Estimates carry error, so small gaps do not by themselves rule out a match.

text: 1) Check whether the absence matches a reported missing person with that condition. 2) Establish whether removal happened before or after death. 3) Ask why the part was removed. 4) Test each candidate reason against personal detail.
when: a body part is absent from remains
why: Checking records, timing, motive and personal facts in order separates accidental, natural and deliberate causes.

text: Tool force shows what the tool required, not who used it; a single matching trial proves little, so repeated comparison is needed.
why: Similar marks can arise from different people and forces.

text: Do not run a test that risks lethal harm without protective measures and a witness.
when: Designing a test that could cause serious injury.
why: Hazardous tests need protection and oversight to limit danger.

text: 1) Image the body with X-ray or scanner to reveal hidden structures. 2) Note each mark: dental work, surgical metal, old fractures, tattoos. 3) Match each mark against its own independent record. 4) Treat identity as conclusive only when several markers each match their own record.
when: Body is unrecognizable or hidden and reliable records of teeth, surgery or injuries exist
why: Each independent record confirms identity separately, and several confirmations together are far stronger than one

text: 1) Obtain a full written description of the missing person, including illnesses, injuries and names of treating doctors and dentists. 2) Prioritise dental records. 3) Compare each known injury with the matching part of the remains.
when: Remains are found and a known person is the candidate
why: Dental records can identify a skull found later, and injuries must be checked against the correct body side

text: Omit a key fact from in-world records as a hole that players fill from other documents or witnesses, such as an alibi revealed later.
when: Designing investigation content or a case file with missing entries.
why: Discovery through comparison rewards attention.

text: Absence of a record entry does not prove an event did not occur; logs may be incomplete and record survival depends on chance. Check what a log records first.
when: Checking a log, ledger, or expected record, or when an archive search finds nothing.
why: Records capture only some treated or logged events, so silence in the record does not disprove them.

text: Do not fill missing evidence with assumed explanations or guessed text, such as assuming someone has left; state missing or damaged records and mark unknown durations as unknown.
when: Records are missing, damaged, or incomplete, or a duration is unknown.
why: Assumed answers make an incomplete case feel complete, and guessed text can pass as evidence and distort the reconstruction.

text: Gap suggests deliberate removal if the record should have existed and someone had access; otherwise it may reflect no action or non-recording.
when: A record appears incomplete.
why: Gaps can reveal tampering, but a missing entry only means something if it was expected to be there.

text: Official files may be closed to private inquirers without a legal order, so an investigator may need another route to the facts.
Records reveal transactions without anyone speaking, so they can confirm or contradict witness testimony.
when: Testimony and documents may disagree
why: Documents are a physical trace independent of what people say

text: Older specialist reference works still hold useful knowledge and should not be neglected in favour of recent sources.
Surviving records of past events are often imperfect and scattered, so accounts must be assembled from fragments and stated as such.
when: When reconstructing events from historical documents.
why: Few complete records survive, so reconstructions rest on partial evidence.

text: Important facts can survive only in documents made for another purpose, such as an estate dispute, so such records can settle questions that official rolls leave open.
when: When a primary record of a relationship or identity is lost.
why: Disputes force people to write down facts that would otherwise go unrecorded.

text: Reread records and cross-check all known facts against each new clue, since a decisive detail missed or left unused can resolve an unexplained clue.
when: A case rests on written testimony or records, or a clue seems unexplained despite earlier information.
why: Recall drops details and facts already in hand go unused unless cross-checked; fresh reading reconnects them.

text: Record deliberate gaps in a document as well as its contents, since an author's omissions can point to knowledge they expected to recall.
when: reading a written account with unexplained absences
why: gaps can signal knowledge the author did not write down

text: A record can exclude a suspect even when it cannot confirm one, so use records to rule candidates out as well as in.
when: When checking candidates against records
why: Negative results narrow the field even when no positive match is found

text: An incomplete cosmetic detail, such as paint covering only part of the mouth, is an observation the investigator must explain.
Records of one dispute may be filed in different offices, each holding part of the terms, so search every office where related deeds or bonds may be filed.
when: a land or ownership dispute involves several agreements
why: The full terms can appear only when the scattered parts are compared.

text: When records have a gap, check whether a known personal event, such as a lawsuit, falls in that period before linking the two.
When repeating an earlier condition, check whether the original record likely underreported the amount, and adjust to match the real conditions.
when: A reproduction must match an earlier dose, quantity, or input recorded in a log.
why: Records often miss part of what was actually applied, so the recorded value may be too low.

text: A design log that records every room-layout change lets a playtest result be traced to the exact configuration that produced it.
when: Layouts are changed between playtests.
why: Tracing results to configurations makes it clear which change caused which effect.

text: Back a disputed document's authenticity with expert comparison and independent witness checks; a single recognition or signature match is not sufficient alone.
when: A will, letter or receipt is contested.
why: Forgeries can pass one check but fail when corroborating witnesses are asked.

text: Incidental records such as expense lists can reveal conditions and practices that no narrative states directly.
when: When formal narratives are silent about conditions or circumstances.
why: Records made for accounting or other purposes often contain details the writer did not intend to preserve.

text: Treat two independent gaps, such as missed payments and unclaimed belongings, together as stronger evidence than either alone.
when: two separate routine trails stop around the same time
why: Two unrelated lapses converging on one date make a shared cause more likely.

text: Movements unseen by others leave holes in the shared record, and events inside those holes stay hidden until reconstructed.
when: when a person's whereabouts were unknown to the household

text: A records check that finds no person matching a claimed identity removes the main support for that claim.
Elimination is valid only if the candidate list is complete; an omitted possibility, inherited from an incomplete source, makes a wrong answer look certain and yields a dead-end search.
when: Excluding candidates one by one, such as hiding places, or key facts are still missing.
why: An unlisted place is never checked, so the search can end without finding the object.

text: Condensed, recopied, or summarized notes can drop details or blend opinion with fact, distorting the sequence and making later checking harder.
Records may stop at the last known point, so later stages depend on people's memories, which are less reliable.
why: Documents rarely cover the full trail

text: A quick explanation that ignores a pagination gap can miss the real story, so examine the object before accepting an explanation.
A late confession can be staged to hide a worse fact, so a later admission is not automatically the complete account.
when: A witness finally admits a detail after earlier denials
why: Partial admissions can conceal the most damaging facts

text: A record written by an interested party is not neutral, and an official summary can smooth over or distort what happened.
when: When a minister, official or participant produced the main surviving record.
why: Participants shape the record to their own position.

text: A later marginal note can reflect hindsight rather than the moment of the event, so it should not be read as contemporary.
when: When a note was added after the original entry.
why: Later writers know the outcome and may reinterpret the event.

text: One misnumbered or unnumbered item in a transcription can shift all later references, misleading anyone who cross-checks them.
Do not conclude a death from a missing record alone, since lapses, absence abroad and clerical failure can produce the same gap.
when: a person's records stop without positive evidence of death
why: A gap has several possible causes, and only positive evidence settles the fact.

text: Trusting a key's history without checking whether it was returned, lent or copied lets a duplicate remain in circulation unnoticed.
when: Access items pass between owners, services or returns
why: A returned key may be a copy, so the chain of custody is broken silently

text: Keeping a record book of names, codes and signatures where many people can photograph it lets an attacker assemble the information needed to pass checks.
when: Verification relies on written records of credentials
why: Photographed records together supply identities, codes and signatures that defeat verification

text: 1) Report observed facts without interpretation, marking any guess as a guess. 2) Name priority subjects such as relationships and new details. 3) Record which prior checks were negative. 4) Build a timeline of who was together and when they separated.
when: One person observes in the field and another reasons about the observations
why: Separating facts from theory keeps the reasoner unbiased and makes the timeline checkable

text: 1) Gather older reference sources covering every way the event could have occurred. 2) Extract and classify their notes by method. 3) Review the classified notes before the investigative visit.
when: a case has many possible causes
why: Prepared knowledge covers every contingency, and preparation is rarely wasted even when the case proves simple

text: 1) After a split result, record each decision-maker's stated reasons. 2) Identify which argument moved which person. 3) Adjust the next presentation to address those specific reasons.
when: A case failed to reach agreement and will be presented again.

text: 1) Classify each marginal figure as a money amount or a time using context. 2) Check each time against a fixed event to confirm what it refers to. 3) Read earlier times as arrivals or glances at a watch, and later times as planned meetings.
when: A victim left written numbers and their meaning is uncertain.
why: Context and fixed events disambiguate figures written without labels.

text: Keep an observation log that records the order in which facts were learned, so later reasoning can be traced to its source.
when: Tracking evidence during an investigation
why: Knowing the sequence of learning reveals which conclusions were influenced by earlier information.

text: 1) Watch the event without theorizing. 2) Write down the observations once the moment has passed. 3) Mark which details are uncertain.
when: Recording a stressful or fast event
why: Notes made soon after the event are more reliable than recollection later.

text: Record every fact, including those that seem irrelevant or were withheld, because significance and meaning may only emerge later.
why: Significance may appear later, and withheld evidence's meaning depends on who later learns its source.

text: Verify a claimed identity against a reliable register, such as a directory of titled people, rather than trusting appearance, a card, or a title.
when: A person claims a rank or identity that affects trust or access.
why: A reliable register exposes false claims that appearance cannot.

text: Judge an explanation by whether it fits the independent record, not by how reasonable it sounds.
Let a game's records system filter an archive by fixed fields, leaving a short candidate list that the player must visit to confirm.
when: When designing archive or record mechanics in a game.
why: Fixed fields keep the search manageable and meaningful.

text: Write in-world archives as footnoted documents with cited sources, some wrong or contradictory, so players must cross-check them.
Document a minority conclusion carefully, so it can be defended when supporting evidence arrives.
when: When a conclusion is held against the views of colleagues
why: Careful records let a conclusion be defended later

text: Require every attendee to show a ticket, and log lost tickets and any whose printed seat differs from the seat they occupy.
Record errors found in a published work and promise their correction in any reissue.
Assuming a witness's description is complete when the witness did not closely observe the person's health.
when: Relying on witness descriptions for identification
why: Gaps in observation produce gaps in the description

text: 1) Work from a fixed written checklist. 2) Count each bone or part against it. 3) Take your own measurements. 4) Compare with the official findings. 5) Record evidence at once and sketch positions on site. 6) Ask few questions, listen closely, and follow up leads the observations suggest.
when: An investigator must confirm or challenge another party's findings on a limited visit
why: Independent measurement and a fixed checklist expose gaps and errors in the official account

text: A recorded mark can identify a person even when its cause is not recorded, so identification does not require knowing how the mark arose.
when: Matching a recorded scar or mark to remains
why: Identity depends on the mark's presence and description, not its origin

text: A body that matches a poison's appearance is not proof of poisoning, because a natural illness can produce similar signs.
when: an investigation rests on physical appearance
why: Similar symptoms can have different causes.

text: When testing a suspected toxin, increase the dose in measured steps, log the effect at each step, and set a ceiling for safety.
when: Testing a toxic substance.
why: Stepwise dosing with a limit reveals the response curve while bounding harm.

text: Quoting a rule without reading the case it cites can produce a false exception that seems to overturn the rule.
why: The omitted detail in the source case is what resolves the anomaly.

text: The more general a proposition, the more certain it tends to be, and the less it tells about any single case.
when: Reasoning from a broad rule to a specific individual or event.
why: Broad statements average over many cases, so they lose predictive force for one.

text: An accepted explanation can be used to dismiss evidence, and it may persist for generations without testing.
when: Evaluating an explanation that closes a case.
why: A plausible story that fits one striking fact can stop further examination.

text: Before treating a motive as proof, check whether other parties had the same motive; a shared motive can point to a rival as readily as the accused.
when: a real motive is found for one suspect
why: A motive that applies to several parties does not single out one of them.

text: When a wider party with power and reason to act emerges, reopen the question of who benefited from the victim's death.
when: new testimony names an enemy with power and motive
why: A new candidate with means and motive can overturn an investigation built on a single suspect.

text: Reason from physical properties: if a material's bulk moisture would have to be overcome first, a theory that depends on intense heat is unlikely.
when: Evaluating a theory that requires extreme heat to produce an effect.
why: Water content acts as a barrier that absorbs energy before the object can burn.

text: When one observation could have several causes, list every plausible source, compare each against the other known facts, and keep the conclusion open until one candidate clearly fits best.
when: A single sighting or clue has multiple possible explanations
why: Accepting the first explanation risks error, especially when fear or emotion favors the nearest answer

text: Claiming to know the answer before reading the evidence can blind an investigator to contrary facts.
when: Starting an investigation with a strong prior belief.
why: Confidence without evidence filters out information that does not fit the belief.

text: A document can seem to confirm what the reader already believes, so strengthened conviction should prompt a check of the reasoning.
when: Reading a document that matches a prior theory.
why: Readers accept evidence that fits their belief more readily than contrary evidence.

text: Arresting suspects who do not match the trace profile wastes time and misleads the investigation.
when: Suspects are detained based on general suspicion rather than the evidence.
why: Unmatched arrests are released, and the actual culprit stays free.

text: Do not assume an odd absence means foul play before ordinary explanations are checked.
when: a physical absence appears suspicious
why: Accidental, natural or routine causes are more common and must be ruled out first.

text: Do not accept a common motive without checking whether it fits all the traces of the act.
when: a familiar motive explains only part of the evidence
why: A motive that leaves some traces unexplained is probably incomplete.

text: Eliminating alternatives only works when the list covers every possibility; an incomplete list can lead to a confident but wrong conclusion.
when: Building the set of alternatives to test.
why: A missing option can survive elimination unnoticed, so the remaining answer may be false.

text: Ruling out an alternative using assumptions about a person's character or habits, instead of evidence, weakens the elimination.
when: Testing an option during elimination.
why: Unverified assumptions about character can dismiss a possibility that the facts do not actually exclude.

text: Rejecting a hypothesis because it is unpleasant rather than improbable biases the analysis.
when: Weighing candidate explanations.
why: Emotional aversion removes viable candidates without evidence.

text: Alerting a person whose interests are affected while checks are still running can destroy evidence or let them prepare an account.
when: Investigating a case where an interested party is involved.
why: Early disclosure gives the interested party time to influence what the checks find.

text: A certain but uninformative statement, such as a trivially true disjunction, does not advance an investigation.
when: Evaluating a conclusion that is certainly true.
why: Certainty alone carries no information about which explanation holds.

text: When the one feature that would confirm a match cannot be examined, the case stays ambiguous and cannot be closed.
when: The key distinguishing evidence is missing or unexaminable.
why: Without the decisive feature, general agreement cannot resolve identity either way.

text: Guessing the cause of an unrecorded mark and presenting the guess as fact.
when: Writing up identifying marks from a report
why: An unrecorded cause is speculation, not a recorded fact

text: A single outcome or a long run of results is not proof of deliberate control on its own.
why: Unlikely events still occur by chance.

text: 1) Settle the foundational fact of the case, such as the identity of remains. 2) Only then examine who acted and why, avoiding motive speculation while basic facts remain uncertain.
when: An investigation has a basic fact question and a later question about motive or culpability that depends on it
why: Motive built on an unsettled fact tends to fit evidence to a preferred story, and culpability cannot be assessed reliably until the fact is established.

text: 1) List every rival explanation early, including human, medical and psychological ones. 2) Find a test that separates them. 3) Check whether the phenomenon depends on place, routine or particular people. 4) Test each rival against the same facts.
when: A phenomenon is reported and could have a supernatural or human cause
why: Each rival predicts different results, so a decisive test can discriminate between them

text: 1) List every possible outcome that covers the case. 2) Test each against the facts. 3) Discard options that conflict with evidence. 4) Check whether the remaining option is the only one left standing.
when: A case has a small set of alternatives that can be exhaustively enumerated.
why: Eliminating alternatives against facts reaches a definite answer, but only if the list truly covers all possibilities.

text: 1) State every candidate explanation up front and number it. 2) For each, list what it would require to be true. 3) Dismiss candidates on evidence, keeping physically possible but remote ones labelled as remote. 4) Stop once one explanation is confirmed by direct proof.
when: Several explanations fit the facts and a wrong choice is costly.
why: Listing all candidates prevents premature dismissal and ensures each rejection rests on evidence.

text: 1) Restate the conclusion. 2) List the premises it is drawn from. 3) Ask whether it follows from them or depends on an unstated link. 4) Ask for the specific circumstances behind the link.
when: Testing whether a claimed anomaly or conclusion is logically sound.
why: A conclusion may seem valid while resting on a premise nobody stated, which specific questions expose.

text: 1) List every explanation the facts allow. 2) Sort them into outside and inside groups by whether they involve the named parties. 3) Dismiss outside explanations with a conclusive item. 4) Test each remaining suspect in turn. 5) Set motive aside until the list is formed.
when: Starting an inquiry where facts are known but motives are not.
why: Setting motive aside first keeps the probabilities balanced rather than fitting facts to a favoured suspect.

text: 1) Use idle time to build explanations from partial reports. 2) Keep each theory private until new facts arrive. 3) Test the theory against those facts before committing to it.
when: when an investigator has partial reports and must weigh facts
why: withholding a theory avoids bending later facts to fit an earlier public claim

text: 1) Separate established facts from asserted claims. 2) List each competing explanation. 3) Test each against measurable traces, using controlled experiments where needed. 4) Conclude only after tests are complete and the evidence chain holds.
when: Several explanations fit the same facts and each has a credible expert behind it.
why: Expert opinions can conflict, and only measured traces can separate them.

text: 1) Check the physical facts first, such as fire damage, soot pattern and undamaged surfaces. 2) Test each candidate cause, exotic or mundane, against those facts. 3) Accept only the cause that fits every fact.
when: Evaluating competing causes of an unusual death or event.
why: Physical facts constrain every candidate, so a cause must match all of them.

text: 1) Test the theory alone or with a second visit before informing others. 2) Confirm the mechanism is present before acting on it.
when: An investigator has a theory that could lead to a false accusation
why: A verifying return prevents error and protects against acting on a single frame

text: Investigate improbable possibilities and long-shot leads before excluding them; dismissing them on assumption leaves an unclosed branch that can later undermine the conclusion.
when: A conclusion depends on a fact that is probably false but unproved, or when deciding whether to continue a long-shot lead
why: An unlikely claim can still be true, and only inquiry shows whether it is; a hopeless-seeming lead may still need closing to make the conclusion defensible.

text: Hold every competing explanation to the same test: it must account for all facts and physical marks, not only the dramatic ones.
when: Choosing between or evaluating rival explanations
why: A theory explaining only striking details can mislead, and applying one standard prevents any theory from escaping scrutiny.

text: Start from the assumption that an error may exist and look for it in the record, rather than accepting a verdict as final.
when: Reviewing a case that was closed by a verdict
why: Even expert work can contain mistakes

text: Prevent parties from exchanging open accusations early, since public accusation can escalate a private dispute into a scandal or criminal matter.
when: Investigating a dispute between people who may distrust each other.
why: Once accusations are public, witnesses become guarded and the investigators lose control of the situation.

text: 1) Compare symptom onset with the time since the suspected dose. 2) Check whether the dose and timing fit a poisoning pattern. 3) Test tissues for traces, since a long, small dose should leave them. 4) Weigh the result before deciding.
when: physical signs look like poisoning but may have a natural cause
why: Timing, dose and tissue evidence separate poisoning from illness that merely looks similar.

text: A negative finding, such as normal bones, still narrows the field of possibilities even though it names no one.
when: An inspection finds nothing abnormal
why: Eliminating options is progress toward identification

text: Confusing a long run of negative results with real progress, or volunteering conclusions beyond one's qualifications, such as an exact identity.
when: Reporting on a limited inspection
why: Negatives narrow options only slowly, and non-experts overreach when they state definite identities

text: Weight each objection by its actual strength: overstating a weak one wastes effort, and ignoring a strong one misleads.
why: objections carry unequal weight

text: A theory survives objections about detail, but objections to its overall structure require rebuilding the chain of reasoning.
when: Evaluating which objections to a theory matter
why: Detail errors can be patched while structural errors undermine the whole argument

text: A repeated or odd request, or a cover that a third party can check, can draw suspicion and cause the pretext to collapse.
when: a pretext is repeated or can be verified
why: repetition and checkable details give observers grounds to doubt the cover

text: 1) Note the ambiguous pattern without acting. 2) Set a clear trigger for escalation, such as a suspect trying to leave the area. 3) Act only when the trigger fires.
when: When a suspect's behavior is suspicious but not conclusive.

text: Warn your superior before acting alone on a doubted conclusion, so that later success is credited to your earlier judgment rather than to ambition.
when: A lead has closed a case and a subordinate disagrees with it.
why: Early warning protects standing and makes independent work look principled.

text: Answer a strong opposing view with a specific reason tied to the case, not a general appeal to how things usually go.
when: Defending a conclusion against a counterargument.
why: General appeals to base rates do not address why this particular case differs.

text: Watch the test result directly and use a written instruction, rather than relying on a verbal report.
when: Running a test that requires precise execution.
why: Direct observation and written instructions reduce error and misreporting.

text: Old healed fractures, long scars and distinctive tattoos are lasting features that can identify a person when the body is later found.
when: A body may never be found and identity must rest on unchanging features
why: These features do not change over time, unlike appearance

text: Signs of careful planning, such as a cut pane with bolts slipped and a key turned, indicate deliberate entry; assuming forced entry was the only route makes investigators miss them.
when: Assessing how a break-in or secured-space entry was carried out.
why: Planned entry leaves precise, quiet traces unlike forced entry, and quiet methods are easy to overlook.

text: Physical traces such as trampled ground or disturbed objects can connect a crime to a specific location and help reconstruct the route.
when: Investigating a crime scene with outdoor or disturbed areas.
why: Traces link actions to places and times.

text: A trace check must include overhead and elevated access points, such as roofs and gutters, when considering how someone could have entered.
when: Investigating a possible entry route
why: Entry can be made from above, not only from doors

text: A location chosen by a suspect can reveal a connection to the scene, since a familiar setting makes presence look normal.
when: Assessing why a suspect chose a particular meeting place.
why: Familiar settings let a person's presence pass without notice.

text: A defence that relies on one barrier, such as a lock, is weak if the secondary barrier requires little force to defeat.
when: Evaluating a secured space's protection.
why: An attacker only needs to pass the weakest layer.

text: Use a legitimate-looking cover, such as viewing a property that is for let, to justify physical access to a space.
when: entry to a restricted space needs a plausible reason
why: a plausible reason is less likely to be questioned

text: A lock opened with its own key implies the thief had access to that key, which points toward someone inside the household or with close access.
when: Investigating a break-in where no force was used.
why: Only key holders can open a lock without damaging it.

text: Uncertain key counts and unknown key holders weaken any claim that access was impossible.
when: When reasoning about whether a locked space could have been entered.
why: An impossibility claim depends on knowing every key and who held it.

text: Being near the scene is not the same as having access to the victim.
when: When judging whether a suspect could have acted.
why: Proximity without contact or means does not establish opportunity.

text: 1) List every possible entry and exit point. 2) Check each one's state, such as locks, grilles and sightlines. 3) Test its strength physically. 4) Record each route checked. 5) Narrow suspects to those already inside.
when: Deciding who could have entered or left a sealed room, before the scene is disturbed.
why: A claim that nothing could pass depends on testing every opening, not only the obvious one.

text: 1) Test every door and record whether it is open, locked or barred. 2) Record where each key is and how it is turned. 3) Search each room and remove it from the candidate list. 4) Treat a missing key as a clue that points to the likeliest route. 5) Continue until only the unsearched room remains.
when: Investigating a closed house or set of connected rooms to find who could have moved between spaces.
why: Systematic elimination narrows the possible routes until the remaining one is the probable explanation.

text: Check the physical route an impostor could take, such as the bolts on a garden gate, as well as appearance when testing an alibi.
when: An alibi relies on movement between locations.
why: Physical access constraints can rule out or support an alibi.

text: Do not conclude a thief is an insider from a lock alone; check whether a key could have been copied or taken.
when: A lock-based clue points to a specific key holder.
why: Keys can be obtained by outsiders, so access does not prove insider status.

text: An object changed in a partial way that fits no obvious motive signals an unfinished plan or a second actor, so it deserves investigation.
when: an object is altered only in some places
why: A change that does not serve its apparent purpose suggests the plan was interrupted or someone else acted.

text: Whoever holds the lease or ownership of a space governs who controls it and can order its occupants to leave.
A destroyed document can be linked to its source by matching the material it was written on, such as paper fibres, even when the writing is illegible.
when: Text is lost but fragments remain and candidate material samples can be gathered.
why: Material properties persist after ink and content are gone.

text: Read physical remains such as overgrown roads, broken walls, cellar remains and surviving houses as evidence of former settlement and of links between living families and documented events.
when: When written records are sparse and the site still exists.
why: Landscape and structures can preserve traces of past occupation that documents omit.

text: Use physical sites such as grave markers and burial places as evidence of a person's fate and location, read alongside dated documents.
when: When a person's end or location is uncertain from written records alone.
why: Physical remains provide an independent trace that can confirm or narrow a documented fate.

text: A host who sets out special items, such as a clean cloth and a dedicated glass, for a guest signals the guest's higher social standing.
when: A scene shows a prepared meal or hospitality arrangement.
why: Hosts prepare distinct items for people they wish to honour.

text: A spotless room suggests recent cleaning, so a disturbance before that cleaning is likely hidden rather than gone.
when: A scene has been tidied after an event.

text: A mark's position can show a forced action, such as a thumb-mark above a heel suggesting someone pulled off a boot by force.
when: A mark sits in an unusual position on an object
why: Placement reveals how the object was handled

text: Note what is missing from a set of remains as carefully as what is present, since an absence can carry as much information as a found part.
when: a set of remains is incomplete
why: The missing part may point to a cause that the found parts alone would not reveal.

text: Record an odd physical detail even when it seems trivial, so it can be explained once more context emerges.
when: an object has an unexplained feature
why: A dismissed anomaly is lost, while a logged one can connect to the solution later.

text: Spatter patterns from a victim's position show which surfaces were struck and can suggest where the attacker stood.
A tight ring on a swollen or thickened finger may be cut free by removing the finger, and the left hand is usually slightly smaller, so a tight ring would more often sit there.
when: an unexplained finger is missing and a ring was worn
why: Physical fit of a ring can drive a deliberate removal of a digit.

text: Any disturbance can have an innocent cause, so a trace must be checked against the expected routine before it is taken as evidence.
when: When interpreting a disturbed trace
why: Ordinary activity can disturb a trace and be mistaken for intrusion

text: A physical record that is collected but never compared is inert and yields no evidence.
when: Records are gathered without a planned comparison step.
why: The value of a record comes from the comparison the investigator makes.

text: A skill inference is only as reliable as the evidence for each step, so each trace must be checked separately before inferring skill.
when: Drawing a conclusion about a perpetrator's skill from several traces.
why: Weak evidence for one step can distort the overall profile.

text: Tool marks show that a tool was used, not who used it or why, so they should not be taken as proof of a particular culprit.
when: Physical marks are used to identify a perpetrator.
why: Marks confirm a method but not an actor or motive.

text: A material match proves only the material, not the person; linking it to a person requires a representative sample set covering every candidate.
why: A rare fibre in an incomplete comparison set is not persuasive.

text: A test reaction can mislead when a harmless natural substance produces the same signal as the suspected agent.
when: Interpreting a chemical or reagent result.
why: Without checking benign sources, a reaction can be wrongly taken as proof.

text: Trusting a developed image without checking the conditions under which it was made can lead to wrong conclusions.
why: Capture conditions affect what a photograph shows

text: 1) Have the subject pick up natural skin oil by drawing fingers through hair. 2) Press each fingertip onto smooth glass to leave a ridge pattern. 3) Write the name and date on the strip at the moment the sample is taken, not later.
when: A reference sample is needed to later match a physical trace to a person, or when building a reference archive of physical identifiers.
why: A labeled, dated reference allows a later comparison to be checked against a record, and contemporaneous labels preserve the link between sample and person because after-the-fact labels are unreliable.

text: 1) List every object and trace in the scene. 2) Check each against the known habits of the people said to have used it. 3) Flag traces that contradict the claimed sequence.
when: A scene seems deliberately arranged to suggest a particular sequence.
why: Staged scenes often contain small traces that a careful observer can match against habits.

text: 1) Record exactly what was observed, including colour, size and position. 2) List every plausible source, including distant ones. 3) Compare each candidate with other known facts such as distance, direction and concurrent events. 4) Hold the conclusion open until one candidate fits clearly better.
when: Interpreting an ambiguous observation

text: 1) Record each subject's traces with name, hand and date on a labelled strip. 2) Repeat the recording at set intervals. 3) Compare the takings to reveal change over time.
when: Identity or a change in identity must be checked against an earlier baseline.
why: A series of consistent, labelled records shows change, but only when compared.

text: 1) Examine objects for signs of origin, such as packaging quality or workmanship. 2) Test what can be tested. 3) Separate conclusions from unidentified remainders. 4) Mark what stays unknown.
when: Sorting a set of found objects to decide what matters
why: Separating definite findings from unknowns prevents partial readings from being treated as conclusions.

text: After a broad test flags a substance, run a specific follow-up reaction, such as adding a solvent and watching for precipitate, to narrow the field to one substance.
when: A first test indicates a class of substances rather than a single one.
why: A specific follow-up separates candidates that the broad test cannot.

text: Removing evidence from a scene, even temporarily, can compromise it and make later findings harder to trust.
when: When an investigator handles objects outside official procedure.
why: Disturbed evidence loses reliability.

text: A broken seal proves a door was opened but not who opened it or how; an intact seal can still be bypassed by a mechanism.
when: When interpreting a seal check after a closed-space test
why: Seals record entry without identifying the actor or method

text: Sensational press coverage can force action before the facts are settled.
The value of a word-association probe depends on the timing of the switch to charged prompts, not on the neutral opening.
when: Designing a word-association probe.
why: The neutral opening sets up the rhythm, and the switch produces the signal.

text: Ask what else could cause a reported symptom before treating it as evidence of one body part or condition.
when: Interpreting a witness's account of a symptom such as a limp or pain
why: A single symptom often has more than one cause, so it does not point clearly to one site

text: Shield the parts that are not under test so that the only changed variable is the one being examined.
when: Running a controlled test on a machine or system.
why: Stray changes in other parts can confound the result.

text: Read back notes only with a clear record of when they were taken, because undated notes are open to challenge.
when: Presenting written or recorded statements as evidence
why: Missing timestamps let opposing parties dispute reliability

text: Record the position and orientation of finds with sketches on site, since placement may matter for later analysis.
when: Recovering physical evidence at a site.
why: Positional context can be lost once objects are moved.

text: A physical marker is only as strong as the document that matches it; without a trustworthy record, the marker cannot establish identity.
when: Using hidden marks to identify a body
why: The match depends on the reliability of the comparison record

text: 1) Identify the referee named in the application. 2) Verify the referee through an independent source such as a directory. 3) Request a written reply. 4) Judge the reference against the claims made.
when: Verifying a person's background through the people who vouched for them
why: A reference is only as reliable as its writer, and independent checks reduce the risk of error.

text: Changing several variables at once, such as travel, company, routine and treatment, makes it impossible to tell which change caused the difference in outcome.
when: Re-running a test after a failure.
why: Attribution of cause requires isolating one variable.

text: Test a physical assumption directly, such as whether a sound carries, instead of assuming it, then check whether anyone reacts.
when: when a theory depends on sound or sight reaching a person
why: perception depends on physical conditions that are easy to misjudge

text: Do not treat one successful test as proof, because a single unnoticed breach in the setup can undo the result.
when: Interpreting results of an isolation or control test
why: Controlled setups depend on the enclosure being complete

text: Record control samples under the same conditions as the event, including the investigator's own movement, since any nearby movement contaminates the record.
when: Collecting reference data for a sensitive measurement.
why: Uncontrolled activity can disturb the instrument more than the signal being measured.

text: Comparing samples side by side under identical conditions can rule out a cause quickly.
when: Two samples may differ in origin and conditions are easy to match.
why: Identical conditions remove lighting or setup as explanations for the difference.

text: A surprising result that contradicts the expected outcome can force a revision of theory, but an incidental action can destroy the subject before the result is confirmed.
when: A controlled test is interrupted before it is repeated or verified.
why: A single unconfirmed surprising result remains weak evidence, and losing its source removes any chance to check it.

text: A controlled experiment reproduces one suspected cause in isolation, showing whether that cause alone can produce the effect.
when: Several causes could explain one outcome.
why: Isolating a single variable reveals whether it is sufficient on its own.

text: The operator's manner and expectations shape the subject's response but are often unrecorded, so results cannot be fully checked afterward.
when: running an interrogation or measurement test
why: the operator is part of the measurement

text: A wager or prior claim by the tester can bias how a test is set up and read, so keep the expected result out of the setup.
Outside people with their own plans can disturb a test, so their interference should be treated as a threat to the setup.
when: Others outside the test team can affect the subject or setting.
why: Unplanned contact changes the conditions the test depends on.

text: A reproduction that misses a key condition makes a failed result meaningless, so it cannot refute the theory.
A reproduction by a different person can give a different result, because strength and angle change where the object lands.
when: Repeating an action with someone other than the original actor
why: The physical result depends on the actor's force and angle

text: Do not treat a material explanation as proven just because it could happen in principle.
when: a natural cause is proposed for an observed change
why: Possibility is not confirmation, and the explanation needs a test.

text: Repeating an experiment until it yields the result a theory needs corrupts the test.
A replica that differs from the original in position or detail can change the result, and without a standard fixed action comparing trials is meaningless.
1) Run the test with the subject aware of the trigger. 2) Repeat it with the trigger hidden. 3) Compare results; a reaction that disappears when hidden came from knowledge.
1) Hide the claimed source from the subject. 2) Have a substitute perform the same action. 3) Compare the reactions; equal reactions mean the source is not causing the effect.
when: when testing whether a claimed effect is real
why: separates the real effect from the subject's expectations

text: 1) State the claimed action, such as a throw or a drop. 2) Repeat that action under matching conditions. 3) Compare the resulting mark or position with the evidence found on site.
when: Checking whether an object could have moved as a theory claims
why: A reproduction shows whether the claim is physically possible

text: 1) Recreate the suspect's likely actions in the real location. 2) Time the operation. 3) Predict the physical marks it would leave. 4) Search for those marks. 5) Judge whether the sequence was possible.
when: A sequence of actions is claimed impossible or implausible and the location can still be recreated
why: A physical trial shows feasibility and tells investigators where to look for traces

text: 1) Separate whether a person believes an act happened from whether the effect could have occurred at the claimed time. 2) Check the substance's timing against the claimed hour. 3) Test by analysis when possible.
when: A dosing or death time is disputed
why: Physical facts settle claims that testimony cannot

text: 1) Name the claimed cause and the action that should end the effect. 2) Perform that action once as a controlled trial. 3) Watch whether the state changes. 4) Collect other reports of the same action and check for a pattern.
when: A state is claimed to respond to a specific action that can be repeated.
why: A deliberate intervention helps separate a real cause from coincidence.

text: 1) Once a theory explains the evidence, arrange conditions where the subject performs the act under observation. 2) Remove interfering observers. 3) Watch each stage and match it to the original incidents.
when: A theory explains the evidence but no direct witness can confirm it.
why: A reproduced act confirms the theory more strongly than argument alone.

text: Run a calm, fixed pre-event routine so the game can log a baseline that later deviations are measured against.
when: Setting up a scene where a change must be detected
why: A stable baseline makes later changes measurable.

text: 1) State the candidate environmental cause, such as softening, heat or moisture. 2) Check known cases where the material behaved that way. 3) Treat the result as plausible until it is confirmed.
when: an alteration might come from a material change rather than a human act
why: Testing a natural mechanism against known cases separates it from a human explanation.

text: 1) Identify the mechanism the explanation relies on. 2) Recreate that mechanism under controlled conditions. 3) Observe whether the expected result occurs. 4) Reject the explanation if it fails.
when: Testing a theory about how an event happened.
why: Demonstrating the mechanism directly checks whether it could produce the observed result.

text: 1) Measure force with a pressure gauge while applying a tool to a test surface. 2) Reduce force in repeated trials until marks match the original. 3) Use the lowest force that reproduces the marks as the estimate.
when: Tool marks are present and the tool can be reproduced in trials.
why: The force needed to make the marks reveals how strong an intruder must have been, and which defence was weak.

text: 1) Rebuild the suspected setting, matching layout, materials and key positions. 2) Run each candidate action in the same fixed sequence. 3) Compare outcomes trial by trial. 4) Restore the scene so the test leaves no trace.
when: An event was heard but not seen, and its source depends on location.
why: A faithful replica with fixed actions makes trials comparable and the location variable testable.

text: 1) List each anomaly as its own question, including small ones. 2) Propose an ordinary mechanical or sensory cause for each. 3) Check that the proposed mechanism physically works by rebuilding and testing it. 4) Label any event that stays unresolved.
when: Before accepting a supernatural explanation for uncanny events
why: Each strange event may have a traceable cause, and testing separates real causes from guesses.

text: 1) Identify the physical mechanism that produces the evidence. 2) Reproduce that mechanism with the tools a forger would use. 3) Compare the result with the disputed evidence to test whether it was genuine.
when: when a piece of evidence may be forged
why: Reproducing the method lets the player demonstrate forgery rather than assert it.

text: Prepare and test equipment, such as a lock, and check the wiring and placement of any tripwire or alarm before relying on it during an investigation.
when: Before entering a space with equipment, or when using a tripwire or alarm to fix timing.
why: Untested equipment can fail at the critical moment, and an unverified signal can fail silently and mislead the timeline.

text: Playtest route durations against the timings given to players, by walking the routes yourself, before relying on them in a mystery.
when: during level and schedule validation
why: Self-testing catches impossible timings.

text: Check the identity and purity of test reagents and samples yourself rather than trusting their labels, and confirm that samples cannot be swapped.
when: When a test result depends on materials and one operator.
why: Labels and operator trust can hide errors or tampering in the procedure.

text: Rereading a record without the person who knows its context can miss background that only that person can provide.
when: Reviewing documents without consulting people involved
why: Some context exists only in people's memory

text: 1) Reread the original record line by line. 2) Ask where the earlier process could have failed. 3) Check for missing evidence, uninvestigated circumstances, unwatched suspects, and oversights by the defense.
when: A closed case still has an unresolved question and the original documents are available
why: Systematic rereading can expose errors that the verdict hid

text: Cross-contaminating samples or using unlabelled containers makes results untraceable to their source.
when: Handling and storing multiple samples.
why: Mixed or unlabelled items cannot be reliably linked to an owner or origin.

text: Do not move a body, tidy objects or touch a scene before its traces are recorded, since handling destroys position evidence and other traces.
when: a scene is being examined, especially one with small displaced objects
why: Early handling destroys evidence, and moving objects erases the position evidence they carry.

text: A subordinate who continues a closed case alone must manage three things: authority over the case, rivalry with peers, and access to the scene.
The more grotesque or unusual an incident, the more closely it should be examined, since such incidents often yield the key trace.
when: when investigating a bizarre or gruesome scene

text: Examine a scene early, since marks found long after an event may be altered or weathered.
why: Time and handling degrade or change traces.

text: Early precautions, such as preserving samples and withholding closure, largely determine whether a death is questioned at all.
when: A death is first assessed
why: Choices made at the start limit what can be checked later

text: Giving the player physical scene facts before dialogue lets them test each account against evidence.
Anyone handling a body or scene before it is recorded, including patrol officers, staff, officials or investigators, can alter or contaminate evidence; control and document early access.
why: Early disturbance destroys the original state; record who had access before trusting a trace.

text: Foot traffic from early searchers, police or household members can erase faint marks like footprints; before concluding from tracks, note who disturbed the scene and which traces are lost.
when: first entry to a scene, or many people move through it before investigation
why: Foot traffic erases or obscures faint marks.

text: Contamination from the investigator's own hands, clothing or previous samples can confuse scent matching.
when: Sampling several suspects in sequence.

text: Stopping a search after the first useful find hides further evidence in the places not yet checked.
Evidence recovered by a private party can break the chain of custody and be dismissed, so the handling of each trace must be documented.
when: When a clue is recovered outside official procedure.
why: An unrecorded chain of handling lets opposing parties challenge the evidence's integrity.

text: 1) Take control of the location and forbid anyone touching or tidying anything. 2) Keep everyone present within reach. 3) Remove nothing; leave loose debris and fragile traces such as warm residue untouched. 4) Record every object handled before investigators arrive.
when: First arrival at a scene, before anything is moved or cleaned, when first responders reach it
why: Early handling changes the evidence and who is known to have been present; clearing or handling a scene can destroy the most important trace.

text: 1) Seal each entrance so any opening breaks the seal, and place a sensitive indicator before it. 2) Remove objects that could confound the test and search the enclosed space beforehand. 3) After each interval, check every seal and marker, recording broken and intact states. 4) Interpret conflicts between markers before concluding.
when: Checking whether a closed space was entered between visits, or markers are used during repeated absences
why: Broken seals and indicator states record entry without relying on memory; markers yield evidence only when inspected after each interval.

text: 1) At first viewing, record the body or object position before anything is moved. 2) Note what looks natural and what looks wrong. 3) Spend time on details that seem odd.
when: Examining a scene before it is disturbed.
why: Moving the body or objects destroys evidence of their original position.

text: 1) Record first impressions of the scene as soon as possible. 2) Revisit after the scene has been disturbed. 3) Note which marks survive. 4) Compare surviving marks with your recorded memory of the event.
when: a scene has been disturbed or cleaned
why: Memory is checked against what remains

text: 1) Remove other people from the room first. 2) Examine the body and its props. 3) Note each item's exact position. 4) Restore every item to its original state. 5) Keep observations private until the official inquiry begins.
when: When access to a scene is limited and the official examination still needs the scene intact.
why: Restoring items prevents the examination from being detected or from corrupting later evidence.

text: 1) Choose a helper with access to the target and a motive to cooperate. 2) Supply sealed, clean containers. 3) Tell the helper to open them only at collection. 4) Specify exactly what to collect and how to seal and deliver it. 5) Limit the number of people involved and enforce secrecy.
when: a target would refuse a request for ordinary physical samples
why: clean sealed containers prevent contamination and limit exposure

text: 1) Read every surface and note all fragments. 2) Loosen the top layer gradually, by moistening and waiting, rather than forcing it. 3) Peel only when edges separate. 4) Secure the revealed lower layer immediately. 5) Keep the discovery private from observers.
when: An object has been relabelled, repainted or overwritten
why: Forcing the top layer risks tearing the record beneath

text: 1) Search in a fixed order, starting at the scene of the event and moving outward. 2) Record each item where it was found. 3) Seal and carry items to a secure holder so no one can alter them unseen.
when: Collecting physical evidence that must survive formal challenge
why: Recorded location and sealed custody make later tampering visible

text: 1) Search the site thoroughly at the start. 2) Trace each event to a concrete mechanism. 3) Ask whether the perception could be false. 4) Seal or mark the scene so any real change can be proven. 5) Accept partial explanations honestly.
when: Investigating unexplained events where a human agent is plausible
why: Thorough search and controlled conditions separate human causes from illusion.

text: Lock or guard a scene when leaving it, since an accomplice could return and move or hide items; clues then survive until investigators return.
when: Leaving a crime scene for any period, or before finishing analysis
why: Clues can be lost or disturbed if the scene is left open.

text: Photograph the body, wounds and marks before anything is moved, so the original scene survives for later analysis.
A scene check narrows possible routes but does not identify a person, so combine it with other evidence before naming anyone.
Relock each door after inspecting it so the room stays intact for later checks.
Record scene evidence such as the number of shots fired from a weapon, since it can contradict a quick verdict.
Remove an unwitting bystander who could interfere by giving them a harmless false reason to withdraw, such as a story that sends them to bed.
Name each object aloud so a partner can confirm it, keeping both observers working from the same picture of the room.
when: two investigators examine a scene together
why: A shared description prevents missed or misremembered details.

text: Record apparently unimportant facts immediately, since trivial-seeming details can gain meaning later; noting only significant ones leaves nothing to reconsider when the picture changes.
when: Many small facts must be compared later, or evidence is gathered before its significance is known.
why: Memory of minor details fades before they become relevant, and facts that seem trivial can gain meaning as the question clarifies.

text: Searching only for planned, obvious or theory-predicted evidence misses plain-view details and the real mechanism; investigators find what they expected.
when: Reviewing evidence against a theory or searching a crime scene for clues.
why: A fixed hypothesis or expected evidence filters out ordinary but telling details.

text: Relying on others' descriptions without direct inspection can carry a false account forward, so an object known only through reports should be treated as unverified.
when: The only evidence for a scene or object is what others said or described.

text: Repeating an earlier pass's obvious places wastes effort, yet a quick first survey misses small objects in gaps, so re-search where events cluster.
when: Re-searching a room or area after a first pass.
why: Obvious spots are already cleared, while gaps escape quick passes.

text: Expectation focuses search on likely locations, so searchers sweep open ground and overlook containers holding decisive evidence; hunting hidden compartments makes plain containers missed.
when: Searchers know which objects or hiding places to expect.
why: Prior expectation directs effort toward likely spots and away from ordinary containers.

text: Long fruitless searches erode motivation and method: searchers tire, lose ordered inference, and rely on chance effort.
when: A long pursuit or bounded search yields repeated failed leads or empty zones.
why: Repeated negative results weaken both hope and systematic reasoning.

text: Players often overlook a key they saw early, because it looks like an ordinary item rather than a puzzle tool.
when: A hidden object is opened by an item seen earlier in the game
why: Familiar, mundane-looking items fail to draw attention as solutions

text: A player or investigator overlooks an object already in view when an earlier assumption makes it seem irrelevant to the case.
when: a working theory conflicts with the object's meaning
why: Wrong assumptions suppress recognition of evidence.

text: Items hidden but never used reveal the hider's state of mind and intent, not only a theft.
After repeated searches come up empty, searchers lower their suspicion of that place.
when: the hiding place looks ordinary
why: A negative result reduces perceived risk

text: A room that appears sealed from within leads players to assume no one could have left, which makes it an effective locked-room effect.
when: A room is bolted or locked from the inside
why: The apparent impossibility suppresses the search for alternative exits

text: People hesitate to open sacred or ancestral resting places, so a hiding place protected by a social or ritual barrier is rarely searched.
when: A hiding place is protected by a strong social or ritual taboo.
why: The taboo deters searching, which lets concealment succeed.

text: Players tend to overlook back routes that read as scenery, so routes shown as background may be missed.
when: a route is visually plain or dull
why: it resembles set dressing

text: In a crowded scene, unexpected empty places stand out to observers and get filed as facts that need explaining.
when: A crowd is present but certain positions are unexpectedly empty.
why: Conspicuous gaps stand out against a dense background.

text: Players treat an item revealed in a public search as self-proving, even when the holder never knew it was there.
when: An object falls from a target's pocket during a search watched by a crowd.
why: Discovery in front of others makes the finding feel conclusive.

text: A safe opened without being picked implies the opener had its key, which shifts the question from how someone entered to who could reach the key.
when: When a locked container opens without signs of forcing
why: Absence of forced entry points to legitimate access, narrowing suspects to key holders.

text: Treat small anomalies seriously and follow them up rather than dismissing them; the first explanation may be only half right, and dismissing an odd light can nearly close a lead.
when: A minor odd observation seems explainable away.
why: Dismissed anomalies can hide the real lead.

text: An object left in an unusually disordered state for its owner suggests someone may have deliberately altered it.
A dry item left where it was set down shows an action was prepared for but never completed.
A party who takes a document to an unfamiliar firm, with an unexplained reason, is a detail to scrutinize rather than accept.
when: A claimant changes the usual professional channel for a document.
why: Unusual routing can signal an attempt to avoid scrutiny.

text: Untidy details, such as unturned cuffs, loosely tied laces or an item in the wrong pocket, signal that a change of clothes was rushed.
Examine correspondence closely for signs of tampering, paying most attention to official or franked envelopes.
when: private correspondence could have been read by others

text: Too much scrutiny of one object narrows attention so that faint clues vanish; stepping back to survey the whole scene helps.
when: a player fixes on one object and finds nothing
why: intense focus excludes the surrounding details where clues sit

text: Ask why a perpetrator would choose a harder method when an easier one was available; an elaborate method can hint that the scene was staged.
when: A break-in looks unusually elaborate.
why: Staged scenes often use methods that a real intruder would not pick.

text: A partial or first search does not prove absence: missing traces may sit in unexamined parts or small items, so check the rest before concluding.
when: Inspection covers only part of a site, or an early search comes up empty.
why: Unseen parts or small items can hold the fact that decides the question.

text: A failed search may reflect the method used rather than the object's absence, since searchers without knowledge of habits look in the wrong places.
Do not assume the better tool was actually in the actor's hands; a timing inference built on the fallback depends on that assumption.
Collecting several traces without tying each to a location makes the set hard to interpret.
when: When gathering multiple physical traces from a scene
why: Without location links, traces cannot be interpreted together

text: Do not accept an explanation for disorder without checking when the space was last serviced, since an untidy room can act as a dated record.
Missing documents can be read as concealment, but a gap alone does not prove intent.
when: When a destroyed or absent record is noticed.
why: Gaps have innocent explanations as well as sinister ones.

text: Anxious searchers look where they fear the target is rather than where it could plausibly be.
Sending a field agent without a clear list produces unusable material, and missing a time limit lets the subject return or the scene change.
when: Directing field work during an investigation.
why: Unfocused collection wastes effort, and delay lets conditions change.

text: Rejecting one route after a single inspection can miss a second route, and a hypothesis rejected at once may still be correct under different conditions.
when: Testing exits or hypotheses in a sealed-room investigation.
why: Each assumption must be checked explicitly rather than assumed excluded.

text: A search radius that is too narrow can miss the place, and one that is too wide wastes time.
when: Setting the scope of a location search
why: Scope errors either exclude the target or bloat the search

text: A routine sweep of leads may produce no direction for several days; routine work alone does not guarantee a result.
when: An inquiry relies only on standard searches and questioning
why: Routine tasks cover known ground but do not themselves generate a new lead

text: Assigning a searcher unsuited to a space or person, such as a male searcher for a restroom, is an improper plan that needs correcting.
Linking a found object to a suspect from memory and suspicion, without testing the object, produces a fragile inference.
Clues recalled from a scene are unreliable unless the observer noticed the objects when first seen.
when: Reconstructing a scene from memory after the fact
why: Objects not attended to at the time are not accurately recorded

text: 1) State the suspicion as a physical claim about distance, access or structure. 2) Inspect the site directly. 3) Confirm or reject the claim before acting on it.
when: when a theory depends on physical facts
why: a suspicion becomes testable only once it names a checkable property

text: 1) List every object on the floor, including damaged ones. 2) Count containers and their marks. 3) Test residues. 4) Look for mismatches with the working theory. 5) Check for signs the scene was altered after people left. 6) Search corners. 7) Measure and draw a plan.
when: Several people were present and objects have been moved, broken or left.
why: A systematic survey exposes details that a first impression misses.

text: 1) List each incriminating fact as a numbered item. 2) Beside each, write its most plausible innocent or alternative explanation. 3) Note which items no explanation covers and mark them as unresolved.
when: Mixed evidence has accumulated and a clear overall view is needed
why: Pairing each fact with a counter-explanation exposes which suspicions remain after ordinary explanations are spent

text: 1) Inspect the exterior first for soiling, smells, re-sealing, altered dates and cover handwriting. 2) Examine the sides and backing. 3) Check fastenings. 4) Open and examine the contents. 5) Record each finding in writing as you go.
when: Examining a sealed or wrapped object that may have been handled by others
why: Staged inspection exposes tampering in order, and written notes prevent loss of detail before inference.

text: 1) Inspect how each restraint was made. 2) Determine whether the bound person could have tied it themselves. 3) Test whether the restraint can be loosened.
when: When a bound person's restraints look like evidence of violence
why: Restraint craft can reveal self-binding or a staged arrangement

text: 1) Inspect ordinary furnishings as well as obvious evidence. 2) Note objects that do not fit the owner's public image. 3) Check the state of room controls such as shades and lights. 4) Ask what normal use the room shows and what has been disturbed.
when: Investigating a room early, before it is disturbed.
why: Routine objects and odd details reveal habits, visitors and recent events that main evidence can miss.

text: 1) Check each shelf row by row, from the highest down. 2) Note books pulled out and returned out of alignment. 3) Compare each disturbed book's dust against its neighbours.
when: inspecting a shelf for recent handling
why: Recently handled items are clean and misaligned, distinguishing them from long-undisturbed ones.

text: 1) Begin the inquiry immediately after being summoned. 2) Examine the scene while traces are fresh. 3) Question everyone present, including guests and servants, early. 4) Record evidence before it decays.
when: when running an investigation of a crime scene
why: Delay and exposure destroy evidence and fade witness memory

text: 1) Confirm that damage sits where the claimed method would place it. 2) Count the marks and check they match that method. 3) Check whether a dropped object shows signs of its fall. 4) Check any denial against the physical evidence.
when: A scene looks like a break-in but the damage or placement seems arranged.
why: Mismatched damage, marks or placement reveal that the scene was arranged.

text: 1) Set the frame and who is present. 2) Collect every raw impression, including passing fancies. 3) Only then interpret the observations.
when: Gathering reports about an event where interpretation could contaminate recall.
why: Impressions recorded before a theory fills the gap stay uncontaminated and can be checked later.

text: 1) Look for a physical signature, such as discharges or interference that starts and stops with an event. 2) Check which variable changes the effect. 3) Propose a physical and human explanation. 4) Confirm by tying the phenomenon to a person.
when: An effect seems beyond explanation but leaves measurable traces.
why: A signature and a controllable variable point to a physical source, and a person confirms the cause.

text: 1) Record the same place under two different conditions. 2) Compare the records with measuring tools rather than general impression. 3) Note exactly what changed between records. 4) Trace the change to its cause.
when: A scene seems to change between observations or a detail seems inconsistent
why: A measurable difference between conditions exposes hidden structure that a casual look misses

text: 1) Check whether your own movement could have caused the disturbance. 2) Rule out self-caused causes before concluding an outside agent acted. 3) Re-check each sudden impulse for its origin.
when: A barrier or clue is found altered or a sudden disturbance occurs
why: The first explanation may be wrong, and self-caused breaches are easy to mistake for hostile action

text: 1) Start by assuming an ordinary cause. 2) Test each ordinary explanation. 3) Accept an unusual cause only after the ordinary ones fail several tests.
when: Investigating an anomaly in a setting where both natural and unusual causes are possible
why: Earned supernatural conclusions feel more credible than assumed ones

text: 1) Survey walls, floor and ceiling with basic tools. 2) If the first pass finds nothing, repeat the search where events cluster. 3) Probe gaps and under fixtures with a tool. 4) Use a sound cue on contact to locate the object. 5) Retrieve the object and test a hypothesis about it.
when: When a first survey fails and an event repeatedly centres on one spot
why: Small objects in gaps are missed by a quick survey, and sound cues reveal contact out of sight

text: When an alibi depends on a companion who cannot be found, test it through records that do exist, such as hotel registers and travel timetables.
why: An untraceable companion leaves the alibi unverified.

text: Weigh several anomalies together rather than concluding staging from one oddity, since a single unusual choice can have ordinary causes.
when: A scene shows one or more unusual features.
why: An isolated oddity may have an innocent explanation.

text: A search that looks only in expected places, or feels thorough, can miss items, so a negative result does not prove absence; check methodically.
when: When searching a scene or area for evidence or a hidden object, especially after finding nothing.
why: Searchers can miss hiding places they did not consider; confidence in a search does not guarantee every item was found.

text: A confined person can infer hidden observation from others' behaviour, such as a helper avoiding eye contact or dimming a light, before the watching is confirmed.
when: A person is held in a room that may be overlooked.
why: Unusual conduct by companions signals that they are being watched.

text: Concealed observation places silent witnesses where they see a subject unseen, so their reports stay reliable and the subject's natural behaviour is undisturbed.
An investigator can establish that a person is present, and roughly who, from recent orderly traces, before ever seeing that person.
Long surveillance on foot can be tedious and may last weeks, so it demands sustained patience from the watcher.
when: Planning a long surveillance task.
why: Covert following on foot is slow and repetitive.

text: Broad coverage of peripheral locations or searches of all household members often yields nothing, so aim effort at the likely source.
when: When investigators consider broad surveillance of peripheral locations or searching all household members.
why: Wide coverage not aimed at the likely source is unproductive; staff rarely keep stolen property on the premises, and broad searches produce protest that costs goodwill.

text: A reflective surface can reveal that a character is watching someone, allowing observation without confrontation.
Test indirect observation, such as a reflection, by asking how it showed each movement, since indirect views can miss details.
when: A witness saw an event only through a mirror, glass or similar reflection
why: Reflected views are partial and can distort what is visible

text: Once a target is lost in a crowd, infer where they went from what is already known about their goals.
why: known intent narrows likely destinations

text: A hidden item's likely location can be inferred from its owner's character, such as a tidy person keeping papers in a particular cubby.
when: The owner's habits are known and the target is likely hidden by routine.

text: Avoid a costly search built on a weak premise, because a long empty search damages credibility.
when: When deciding whether to commit resources to a physical search.
why: Failed searches cost time and erode trust in the investigator.

text: Examine concealment spaces such as linings and closets by hand when an object may hide something.
when: A suspect's belongings may conceal a small item.
why: Hidden compartments are common places to conceal items.

text: Concluding a missing item such as tickets left the building is unreliable if its search, or a paired object's search, was not exhaustive.
when: A search for missing items was not exhaustive.
why: Small items can be concealed on a person and missed by a limited search.

text: An indirect search from outside the room, such as probing with a tool through a window, can miss small traces that close examination would reveal.
when: When an investigator cannot enter the scene.
why: Indirect tools reach only surfaces they touch, not fine details.
