text: A search run without clear procedure can waste time and find nothing, even when the target is nearby.
when: When a search area is covered without a defined order or method
why: Unstructured searching misses ground and time runs out

text: Relying on one channel, such as newspapers, misses people who could identify the target by description.
why: Each channel reaches a different audience.

text: Searching a large collection of records is slow, and effort can be wasted on the wrong samples.
when: When comparing a trace against many records by hand.
why: Manual comparison scales poorly with collection size.

text: A recording may confirm that an event happened without identifying its cause, such as a door half open in a photo.
1) Build rapport with a helpful side character. 2) Ask about habits and routine during ordinary conversation. 3) Record routine facts without it looking like an interrogation.

1) Return to the scene and record any changes. 2) Compare repeated marks with earlier copies. 3) Ask others discreetly about unfamiliar people. 4) Combine these clues to infer what the witness will not say.
when: a witness will not disclose the decisive fact

text: 1) Post someone to guard the body or scene. 2) Request fingerprints and physical evidence. 3) Question staff only in a general way. 4) Send investigators to search the rest of the premises, such as basement and yard.
when: at the start of an investigation

text: 1) List every exit and what lies beyond it. 2) Check whether a route out exists. 3) Post watchers at the points a person's route must pass.
when: Verifying whether a person could leave a building unseen.
why: Known exits and watched chokepoints determine which routes are possible.

text: 1) Compare a specific written plan or map against the actual layout. 2) Pace out the measured distances and mark the indicated spot. 3) Clear any growth or cover from the candidate surface. 4) Tap and scrape the surface, marking hollow or changed sound or texture to dig. 5) Bring in a helper with tools once the search narrows.
when: A concealed feature is documented but its exact position is lost.
why: Combining documented measurements with direct physical testing narrows the search to a precise spot.

text: 1) Place a marker where a hidden intruder would have to disturb it. 2) Test the marker by opening the door yourself to confirm it responds. 3) Check the marker's state after each event to learn what happened unseen.
when: A space must be watched when no witness can stay there
why: Tested indicators provide a trustworthy physical record of passage

text: 1) Sound out the floor, ceiling and walls of the space. 2) Check each surface for marks. 3) Record findings before sealing or leaving the space.
when: Searching a room for a hidden mechanism or object
why: Covering every surface avoids missing marks left by a device

text: 1) Photograph the scene by day from a fixed position. 2) Return at night from the same position and take a second picture. 3) Compare the two images for changes.
when: Checking whether a scene changed overnight
why: A fixed viewpoint makes differences attributable to events, not framing.

text: 1) Rig a camera and light to the point of interest. 2) Record any opening or movement. 3) Use the recording to separate a hoax from the event.
when: Testing whether a reported event is real
why: A recording captures what witnesses cannot reliably report.

text: Keep each NPC's current room or position in the game state, and update records whenever someone moves, so answers to player questions stay accurate.
when: A room or sleeping arrangement changes during play.
why: Unreported changes send investigators and players to the wrong place.

text: Search a small area around a paced mark rather than a single point, because paced distances are approximate.
when: Locating a site from measured distances.
why: Pacing introduces error, so the true spot may lie nearby.

text: Testing a suspected poison on oneself can be dangerous and nearly fatal, so it should not be imitated.
when: Considering testing a toxic substance on a person.
why: Human exposure to toxins can cause severe or lethal harm.

text: Treat a dramatic or exotic explanation as a hypothesis to test like any other, rather than dismissing or accepting it on its presentation.
when: A death is framed as strange or unexplained by the public.
why: Presentation can make an unlikely cause seem more credible than the evidence supports.

text: A conclusion resting on a single study or experiment is weak evidence. Treat it as provisional until other trials confirm it.
why: One result can reflect chance or unusual conditions, so acting on it as settled can mislead.

text: Change only one variable at a time and record each change, since changing two at once hides which one mattered.
when: Running a test to identify a cause.
why: Simultaneous changes make the result impossible to attribute.

text: A relaxed social setting, such as a meal, can make a reluctant person more open to help than a formal meeting.
when: Choosing where to approach a proud or guarded person.
why: Informal settings lower defensiveness, though they must not be used to press a point.

text: Applying a statistical generality to predict one individual, such as a single suspect or victim, confuses group tendency with individual outcome.
when: Drawing a conclusion about one person from a population-level rule.
why: Group statistics describe a population well but say little about any one member.

text: A structured inquiry establishes the victim's identity first, then addresses how, when and by what means death occurred, reporting only what is actually established.
when: When investigating a death or similar case with several open questions.
why: Identity anchors every later inference; skipping it leaves conclusions without a foundation.

text: A small assigned task can split a group, so one member leaves while the others wait, creating a window in which the remaining people are unobserved.
when: Staging a scene that needs separated suspects
why: Members absent from the group cannot witness or be witnessed

text: Each extra person on a covert mission multiplies the chances of being spotted, so splitting a team into a mover and a guard reduces exposure.
Two companion roles can share an investigation: one character questions while the other watches, records and notices details, so more facts are tracked at once.
when: A case has many facts to track and questioning and observing must happen simultaneously.
why: One role cannot pursue a line of questioning and keep scanning the scene at the same time.

text: Keeping the plan secret from one's own team makes members anxious and less able to act well, and can damage trust once the plan is revealed.
when: when a team member needs to act on the plan, or members are kept partly uninformed
why: Those kept in the dark may feel deceived.

text: Fixing on one suspect, through focus or early arrest, makes investigators overlook traits or evidence pointing elsewhere or favouring the accused.
when: A case has a dominant suspect, or a suspect is arrested before the inquiry is finished.
why: Early commitment blocks alternative filters, so contrary facts are discounted to fit the chosen account.

text: An investigator who keeps findings from superiors risks never having them heard, and superiors can cut off a presentation before it ends.
Rivalry between colleagues invites petty treachery, such as undermining a rival's claim to credit for a finding.
Disagreement among team members about escape risk can break an ambush; agree procedure in advance.
Checks made openly can reveal the direction of your suspicion, so verification may need to be done quietly.
when: When investigating a suspect who could react to being checked.
why: Early disclosure lets the suspect adjust the story.

text: Teammates may read aimless-seeming questioning as wasted time, so keep the purpose clear to yourself even when the team cannot see it.
Admitting a case is stuck is useful only if it leads to a new plan of action.
when: An investigation has stalled.
why: Acknowledging failure without acting on it wastes time.

text: Sympathy for a person can override method when judging evidence, so investigators should apply procedure consistently regardless of feeling.
when: When an investigator feels strong sympathy toward one side of a case.
why: Emotional attachment can bias which evidence is accepted and how it is weighed.

text: 1) Assign each evidence type to a specialist with its own method. 2) Have each specialist report results. 3) Tie each result to a shared timeline.
when: a case involves several kinds of physical evidence
why: Dividing work by specialty gives each trace expert analysis while keeping results comparable.

text: In a co-op scenario, split the knowledge so each player holds one compartment, and reveal the full plan only by combining their reports.
when: when designing a multiplayer secret plan
why: players must cooperate to assemble the whole

text: Do not drop a disagreement merely because one side has named its frame; weigh both views against the evidence.
when: when more evidence can still arrive
why: Naming a frame does not settle the facts.

text: Share a concealment plan with the people who need to know before acting, so they can raise objections.
Withholding your conclusion tests collaborators' observations and keeps control, but frustrates them and can reduce their willingness to contribute.
when: Only when collaborators' reasoning is what is being tested

text: Keeping facts private preserves each theory's independence from others' influence, while pooling facts shares evidence sooner but reduces the independence of each member's reasoning.
when: a group of investigators shares one case
why: independent reasoning and shared evidence pull in opposite directions

text: 1) List each independent line of inquiry. 2) Assign each line to a suited, different investigator. 3) Set a fallback for each line. 4) Require progress reports at fixed times. 5) Close each line with evidence before concluding.
when: several independent leads or checks, such as records, movements and contacts, can each be worked alone
why: Dividing leads among people keeps several threads moving without losing track of the whole, lets each be closed separately, and reduces the chance one is skipped.

text: Let an intermediary tabulate mass replies, so the investigator works from a summary rather than every response.
when: many replies arrive from an appeal
why: summaries save time and surface the strongest responses

text: A formal vote on accepting a solution forces each listener to commit, and a dissenter can openly declare the solution wrong and promise proof.
when: a group must accept or reject a proposed answer
why: a recorded commitment makes dissent visible and testable

text: A lead gathers short reports from several agents, each pursuing one narrow line of inquiry, then decides what each fragment adds and sets the next task.
when: Several parallel threads must be coordinated and cross-checked.
why: Separate lines yield partial results that only gain meaning when one coordinator combines them.

text: A bystander told only part of the plan may help or hinder the outcome in ways the organiser did not expect.
An investigator may have found a clue before the player or another character, so who discovered an item can be uncertain.
when: Recording or reconstructing who found a clue.
why: Searches overlap, and the first find is not always clearly recorded.

text: 1) Split the work into separate lines of inquiry. 2) Each line pursues its own theory. 3) Reconvene to compare findings.
when: Two plausible theories are both worth pursuing.
why: Independent lines test theories in parallel and can be combined later.

text: 1) Re-search the scene and the victim's papers after the first sweep. 2) Canvass the victim's associates and usual haunts. 3) Trace unidentified objects to their owners. 4) Run a city-wide search for any vehicle, using public advertising. 5) Check background of minor witnesses. 6) Assign each task to a distinct team so work does not overlap.
when: At the start of an inquiry with no single clear lead and many threads to cover
why: Covering many threads in parallel finds leads that a single line of questioning would miss

text: 1) Define the witness window by time and place. 2) Trace physical records, such as where documents were sent from. 3) Send typed or written evidence for expert analysis. 4) Build background reports on the victim's habits and associates. 5) Station watchers near the scene.
when: A case has many possible witnesses and records.
why: Dividing work into tasks with clear scope makes parallel progress trackable.

text: 1) Ask each expert only questions within their field. 2) Record what they confirm. 3) Record explicitly what they decline to answer and who they refer it to.
when: Gathering answers from specialists during an investigation.
why: Experts give firm answers within their competence and decline speculation outside it; mixing the two inflates weak conclusions.

text: Have investigators work privately for a set period from the same facts, without discussing the case, so each forms an independent solution to compare later.
when: a group solves one mystery together or runs a group investigation exercise
why: Shared discussion would contaminate independent reasoning, while independent solutions expose different readings of the same evidence.

text: Name each parallel line of inquiry and track it separately, so facts from one thread are not used as support for another.
when: several threads of investigation run at the same time
why: mixing threads makes unrelated facts appear to confirm a theory

text: Quick casts from ready materials give acceptable but softer edges than careful casts, and the loss of sharpness can be challenged.
when: Capturing a fragile trace under time pressure.
why: Haste trades fine detail for quantity, and detail is what a sceptic will question.

text: Parallel investigation tasks can duplicate or interfere with each other unless responsibilities are clearly divided between teams.
when: Several teams or agencies work the same case at once
why: Without a clear split, teams step on each other's work

text: 1) Attempt a physical probe that would be blocked if the object were solid. 2) Note whether it passes through with no resistance. 3) Try a rational or natural explanation before accepting the anomaly.
when: A witness must check an ambiguous or impossible object
why: A physical test separates real objects from illusions, and a rational check should be attempted before concluding the sighting is supernatural

text: Explaining a case aloud to a listener exposes weak points in the reasoning, because the speaker must state each link.
when: A chain of reasoning feels finished but has not been checked
why: Stating each step forces the speaker to justify it

text: Do not air a half-formed theory before superiors, who may dismiss an unfinished idea as the work of an unsound mind.
A listener who rejects a reasoning chain may be wrong too, so a failed explanation tests communication as well as the truth of the chain.
when: When someone fails to accept an investigator's reasoning.
why: Rejection can reflect poor explanation or the listener's own bias.

text: Letting the most dramatic explanation set the terms of an inquiry leads to dismissing ordinary people who were present and could have acted.
when: An investigation or puzzle has a showy outside explanation.
why: The method checks who was present, not who seems exotic or dramatic.

text: 1) State each candidate explanation as an explicit question at the start. 2) Write a concrete physical reason for and against each. 3) Mark which reasons depend on assumptions. 4) Revise the list when a major fact arrives.
when: Early in a case with several plausible causes and physical evidence.
why: Explicit candidates and recorded premises make it clear which conclusions must be reconsidered when a fact changes.

text: Treat a plausible explanation as conjecture until physical evidence confirms it, because a confident first explanation can hide the real cause.
when: When an explanation rests on reasoning about what a suspect would want to hide, or on an initial belief about an object's location.
why: Unconfirmed reconstructions can mislead the investigation if accepted too early, and confidence in a first explanation can prevent discovery of the real cause.

text: Present a working theory as your own opinion rather than forcing it on others.
Test a clock's error against a second source before using it; when a witness's time conflicts with other sources, trust whichever independent clock is more reliable.
when: A timeline depends on a clock or watch, or a witness's time conflicts with other sources
why: Unknown error can shift a whole window; independent fixed references anchor a timeline better than one person's memory

text: The window to claim a dropped object can be very narrow, with a rival arriving only about thirty seconds after the first.
when: Designing timing for a race to an object.
why: A short gap creates tension and makes speed decisive.

text: Act on physical traces as soon as possible, because some clues degrade or disappear within hours if left unattended or handled.
when: Arriving at a scene where traces may decay or be cleaned
why: Delay lets fragile traces evaporate or be lost.

text: Physical evidence such as mismatched torn stub halves can show that two people entered at different moments.
when: Paired physical tokens are used to date entry.
why: Tokens torn at different times fail to line up.

text: A killer who expects a later discovery plans a wider window than the actual one, so the real window is often narrower than intended.
when: Reasoning about when a culprit planned an act to be discovered.
why: Earlier discovery shrinks the safe window the culprit assumed.

text: Estimate the start of a long-running dispute by subtracting each witness's stated age from the event's date, then compare the results across witnesses.
when: When a witness gives an age and the dispute's duration is unknown.
why: Ages stated at a known event fix an approximate date for earlier events.

text: Reconstruct events from a range of source types, including testimony, petitions, diaries, expense records and earlier histories, and weigh each against the others.
when: When key events are known only from scattered papers.
why: Different source types reveal different facts, and cross-checking reduces the risk of relying on one biased account.

text: Confirm an individual's stated dates and recurring intervals against other observers, since a precise count from one witness may still be wrong.
when: A recurring event must be checked against a timeline
why: Precision signals care but does not guarantee accuracy

text: When witness times are approximate, such as 'five minutes to eleven, or thereabouts', treat any overlap conclusion as only as precise as the estimate.
when: When matching approximate times across witnesses.
why: Estimated times carry an error band that can decide whether windows overlap.

text: A neatly ordered timeline with gaps filled by assumption looks more complete than the evidence supports; mark unobserved intervals as unknown instead.
when: When presenting or accepting a reconstructed timeline, or when a witness was asleep, absent or not observing
why: Unrecorded periods look resolved though nothing is known about them; visual order suggests coverage

text: Starting a trace from the present can bias the search toward a story already formed in the investigator's mind.
why: The starting frame shapes which records seem relevant.

text: An alibi that fits a timetable can still be false, so the timetable itself should be confirmed before relying on it.
when: An alibi is judged against a schedule.
why: Schedules may be wrong, changed or misread.

text: 1) Group marks by likely source and label each group. 2) Check which mark lies on top of which; the mark on top was made later. 3) Read where each mark sits. 4) Chain the layers into a sequence. 5) Present the result as checkable inferences.
when: Several traces touch the same object and their order is uncertain
why: Layering reveals which events came first, since physical marks record the order in which they were made

text: 1) Gather every report about the event. 2) Arrange all reports by date and time. 3) Compare adjacent entries to find gaps where the sequence is unexplained.
when: several accounts each cover part of an event
why: ordering exposes missing intervals

text: 1) Start with the earliest dated record. 2) Add each later record in order, such as grants, purchases, petitions and debt discharges. 3) Note when each debt was cleared. 4) Cross-check against neighbours' records. 5) Anchor entries to public events.
when: reconstructing a family's or party's history from scattered paperwork
why: Ordered dated entries reveal turning points and gaps that others sources can check.

text: 1) Anchor the timeline to an independent forecast of when the event will occur. 2) Log each change with a clock time or interval. 3) Log unchanged intervals too. 4) Have a second person keep notes.
when: a sequence of states must be reconstructed and its timing will be disputed
why: Independent anchors and two records make the timeline checkable

text: 1) Establish the household's normal routine as a baseline. 2) Record each witness claim with its time. 3) Flag claims that contradict each other. 4) Note which events were seen and which only heard.
when: Building a timeline from staff who were awake but did not watch events
why: A baseline makes deviations visible and contradictions and weak sources easier to mark

text: 1) Order the events by time. 2) Follow one actor's sequence at a time. 3) Anchor each stage in physical traces or witness reports. 4) Mark which steps are supported and which are inferred.
when: Reconstructing a death or incident from overlapping events.
why: Separating sequences by actor and anchoring them in evidence prevents overlap from misleading.

text: 1) Date the warrants or orders. 2) Note the place of each examination. 3) Record the names of officers involved. 4) Use these anchors to order the events.
when: When ordering events from scattered official documents.
why: Dates, places and names are fixed points that can be matched across records.

text: 1) Find each undated record's date by linking it to an independent event that is unrelated to the others. 2) Confirm each date with a second unrelated anchor. 3) List dated entries side by side to reveal recurring intervals.
when: When a witness's memory of a date is doubtful or a sequence must be rebuilt from several records.
why: A single date with no independent check can be wrong, and recalled dates drift, while patterns only show when entries are compared.

text: 1) Start with the earliest event. 2) Record each fact in its own brief numbered line. 3) Re-read the log, mark doubtful entries, and correct errors by erasure or annotation. 4) File it apart from routine records.
when: events happened across several places and their order is uncertain
why: numbered, ordered entries turn scattered recollections into a reviewable timeline

text: 1) Fix a dated starting point and a dated earlier point. 2) Define the window between them. 3) Request every record within the window. 4) Mark each stage as known or unknown, never filling gaps by guess. 5) Use each stage to name the next source to ask.
when: Reconstructing a person's history against a fixed period
why: A complete, bounded window prevents gaps from being missed and keeps assumptions out of the record.

text: 1) Collect the witness's own checkpoints with time, observed state, and whether they got a response. 2) Order them. 3) Mark the intervals the witness is unsure of and any stretches they were asleep. 4) Record impressions separately from observed facts. 5) Find the window between last confirmed normal state and discovery.
when: An event happened out of sight and a regular attendant made routine checks
why: Fuzzy times and unverified gaps must be separated from solid observations to narrow when the event could have happened

text: 1) Order events by time. 2) Trace each person's route between them. 3) Fix anchor points such as calls or arrivals. 4) Record what each person could know at each point.
when: When an alibi or a suspect's whereabouts must be confirmed, or an arrival must be explained.
why: Sequence and knowledge together show whether someone could have acted.

text: 1) Collect time estimates from several witnesses for the same window. 2) Mark each person's unaccounted intervals. 3) Find where a suspect's absence overlaps the moment of harm.
when: When several witnesses give times for a narrow window.
why: Opportunity appears only where unaccounted time coincides with the event.

text: 1) Anchor the sequence on a fixed clock time. 2) Log each witness's perceptions at each checkpoint. 3) Record self-observed events with a timestamp. 4) Compare overlapping testimony across witnesses.
when: When several witnesses observed parts of the same night or event.
why: Common clock anchors let separate perceptions be aligned and compared.

text: 1) Gather dated records from independent sources such as newspapers and schedules. 2) Record witness times. 3) Build a timeline. 4) Identify gaps and impossibilities against each suspect's alibi.
when: An alibi or the movement of goods is in question and dated records exist.
why: Independent sources can contradict claims that rely on memory.

text: 1) For each suspect, check whether their motive is strong enough to commit the act. 2) Check whether the motive could be denied as proof. 3) Consider whether a weak motive could still drive a fearful, lesser act.
when: Several suspects have partial or weak motives for a crime.
why: Motive strength and denial separate the plausible culprit from the one who merely fears blame.

text: Do not treat a trusted expert's word or reputation as proof that the process was clean; test the process itself.
when: When a result depends on one operator's work.
why: An argument that someone would not do something is not a check that they did not.

text: Interpreting a scan or image without knowing its context can lead to a wrong conclusion, such as taking old remains for recent ones.
when: Reading imaging or physical evidence
why: An image has no meaning until the context that produced it is known

text: 1) State the claimed fact. 2) Find a primary record such as a list, booking or log. 3) Check whether the record supports or contradicts the claim.
when: When a witness or suspect asserts a fact that a record could confirm.
why: Primary records give checkable evidence independent of memory.

text: Check an authority's cited rule against the specific case it describes, since the source may contain an omitted fact that explains the apparent exception.
when: A conclusion relies on a textbook rule, published case, or expert opinion.
why: A rule may appear overturned only because the cited case omits a relevant condition.

text: Weight or gait narrows a suspect pool but does not single out one person; other evidence is required.
why: Many people share similar body weights and gaits.

text: Relayed or remote reports stay unverified until checked on the ground or against independent records, since each relay can alter times, wording or order.
when: Findings come from a distant source or a timeline relies on accounts relayed by other people.

text: 1) Keep other people out of earshot during one-on-one questioning. 2) Have a neutral second observer record statements so accounts can be compared afterward.
when: Interviewing a witness, especially in sensitive one-on-one questioning.
why: Isolation reduces outside influence, and a second observer guards against misrecording.

text: 1) State who you are and why you are asking. 2) Ask the witness's opinion first and record it. 3) Ask what was actually seen or said. 4) Name any witness bias and weigh the account accordingly. 5) Trace third-hand information to its source. 6) Compare opinion with physical clues; revisit only if new evidence contradicts it.
when: Interviewing a witness with a personal stake or close connection, or when early fixation on one suspect risks closing the investigation.
why: Stating your purpose lowers defences, and separating opinion from observation shows what the witness actually knows. Recording an unprompted judgment stops early fixation from shaping later answers.

text: A witness may turn pale or fall silent when another person points out a gap in their account, which may suggest the point is sensitive.
when: an inference about their timing is put to them
why: an inference touching their account can cause visible discomfort

text: Evasive people often disclose more when questioned one-on-one than in front of others, since others' presence raises their guard.
when: questioning someone who has reason to conceal information
why: Being watched increases self-protection

text: A witness given a real choice, such as deciding whether the questioner stays, becomes more willing to talk.
when: A guarded witness is being questioned.
why: Feeling in control lowers defensiveness.

text: A witness who admits one lie may still be shielding other parts of the story. An admission of one lie does not verify the revised account.
when: After a witness corrects an earlier statement

text: A tentative witness can be overridden by a more confident one in group settings, so corrections must be checked for real observation.
when: group interview
why: Confidence is not the same as accuracy.

text: When the subject says little, a witness's fear and excitement can supply the characterization, so the account reflects the witness.
when: when the subject gives few words
why: the listener fills the gap with feeling

text: Give the witness the role of corrector rather than accuser, which lowers resistance and makes candid answers more likely.
when: interviewing a witness who is ashamed, frightened or hostile
why: A corrector role feels less threatening than being accused.

text: Keep a second person close enough to restrain a suspect during a confrontation.
when: Questioning a suspect who may become violent.
why: Physical proximity allows a fast response if the suspect turns dangerous.

text: Choose sceptical witnesses for a test, since a result that convinces them cannot easily be disputed.
when: A result must withstand challenge from others.
why: Doubt from a critical observer forces the evidence to be strong.

text: Control a subject's unstable state, such as sleeplessness or nervous sensitivity, before relying on a reproduction.
when: The subject's condition varies unpredictably between tests.
why: An uncontrolled variable makes the result of a reproduction unreliable.

text: Expect a rambling interview to yield few usable facts, and plan to sift for them rather than judge the interview as pointless.
Corroborate a timeline with a witness who saw the victim alive at a stated time.
when: Establishing when a person was last alive.
why: An independent sighting supports a stated time.

text: Ask whether anyone entered or left the area during a witness's stay; a clear answer can close off a route.
when: Checking whether an unseen person could have passed through a location.
why: A witness who was present for the whole stay can rule out entry or exit.

text: Keep a faithful, timed record of a witness's exact words, since it is the only reliable basis for settling later disputes about what was said.
when: A statement may be contested later
why: Memory of wording is unreliable and disputes are settled by the record

text: An identification resting on one witness is weak, so seek independent confirmation and check the witness for a motive that could shape it.
when: Identifying a body from a single source.
why: A lone or interested witness may be mistaken or biased.

text: Check a party's stated belief against its conduct, since actions that contradict the claim reveal the true position.
when: Assessing a witness or interested party's testimony.
why: Conduct inconsistent with a stated belief is stronger evidence of their real view than the words.

text: A sympathetic listener may accept a weak theory too quickly, so their agreement is not proof that the reasoning holds.
when: when a friendly reviewer hears a theory
why: Goodwill can override scrutiny.

text: Answering an objection by repeating the original claim rather than giving a new reason fails to address the objection.
when: Defending a theory against a challenge
why: Restatement adds no evidence to the argument

text: Vague witness answers leave gaps that can be misread as confirmation.
when: Accepting a witness's non-specific answers
why: Silence or vagueness is not corroboration.

text: An interviewer's private theory forming before the account is complete can steer which answers get recorded and which are overlooked.
when: Interviewing while the account is still incomplete.
why: A premature conclusion biases what is noticed and recorded.

text: A witness who has already been alarmed may give a different account on a second telling, so repeated accounts should be compared for shifts.
when: Re-interviewing a witness after an initial alarming questioning.
why: Alarm can alter recall, so differences between tellings are signals to examine.

text: A date misremembered by a witness can break a chain of reasoning, so the date should be checked against a record rather than memory.
when: A timeline relies on a witness's recollection.
why: Memory is unreliable for specific dates and times.

text: Accepting a plausible, on-topic reason for a witness's presence at face value can hide a real motive.
when: Evaluating a witness's stated reason for being present.
why: Innocent-looking reasons are easy to give and hard to verify without checking.

text: A physiological spike can reflect nervousness rather than guilt, especially when the questioner already suspects the secret.
when: Interpreting a stress reading during questioning.
why: Anxiety from suspicion produces the same response as guilt.

text: 1) Ask whether the witness knows anything beyond what others told them. 2) Separate personal knowledge from secondhand report. 3) Ask a direct follow-up when a rumor is denied to see whether the denial holds.
when: A witness has a personal stake or knowledge of others' actions and answers seem carefully limited
why: Narrow answers can hide a key fact known through another person

text: 1) Fix the last sighting in the witness's own words. 2) Raise a quarrel neutrally and let the witness volunteer the reason. 3) Probe unvolunteered points, such as whether a parting was friendly on both sides. 4) Test the account against independent records.
when: When interviewing a witness about a sequence of times, claims and contacts
why: Establishing fixed facts first and letting motives surface unprompted reduces the risk of answers shaped by the question.

text: 1) Ask one concrete question at a time: who, which way, whether they spoke. 2) Record the answer. 3) If answers stay empty, accept the limit and move on.
when: Interviewing a minor witness
why: Single focused questions extract usable detail without overwhelming the witness.

text: 1) Separate each claim into what was perceived and what was assumed later. 2) Note who was present and when. 3) Check each claim against physical evidence and other witnesses.
when: when several people were awake or present at an event
why: Mixing perception with later assumption hides the claims that need verification.

text: 1) Reread the account as if no one had told it. 2) List every unusual feature of the scene. 3) Check the state of physical objects against what the witness described.
when: when a testimony is complete and consistent but the scene may disagree with it
why: A coherent story can still be false, and objects often reveal small contradictions.

text: 1) Write notes promptly after the conversation, within about five minutes. 2) Review the notes together, separating reported facts from interpretation. 3) Record uncertain characterisations as tentative.
when: after any informal interview whose account may be needed later
why: Recollection drifts within minutes, so delayed notes lose accuracy.

text: 1) Record each version of a witness account as it is given. 2) Compare versions against each other. 3) Set contradictions against one another to find what changed and why.
when: A witness's account changes across interviews
why: Tracking versions exposes shifts that a final account hides

text: 1) Collect each party's account. 2) Test contradictions against physical facts such as wounds, weapons and sounds. 3) Identify which accounts cancel out. 4) Check whether any witness will formally testify.
when: Several accounts of one event conflict
why: Physical facts break ties that testimony alone cannot resolve.

text: 1) Record distance, light, obstruction and the witness's emotional state. 2) Check the account against other witnesses. 3) Accept an identification only after these conditions are weighed. 4) Do not treat a description matching a suspect as proof of identity.
when: Testimony is the only evidence that a figure was present or who it was
why: Observation conditions and witness state determine how reliable a sighting is

text: 1) Write down the exact observed detail at the moment of sighting. 2) Keep competing readings open. 3) Check the detail against an independent record. 4) Treat a match as a verified link, not proof of motive.
when: When a precise sighting may connect a person to a place or fact.
why: A recorded, independently checked detail separates a real link from chance overlap.

text: 1) Record the witness's words as they are given. 2) Have the witness retell the events in order, including details already mentioned. 3) After each stage, summarise it and get confirmation before continuing. 4) Pair statements with the witness's reactions. 5) Hold conclusions until the full sequence is confirmed.
when: A witness has given an informal account that needs to be fixed before testing against other evidence.
why: Recording and confirming step by step prevents the account from shifting and exposes gaps.

text: 1) Read the complete case record before acting. 2) Form a working theory of who committed the act, kept separate from the official charge. 3) List every witness who can speak for the accused. 4) Visit each witness, state who you are and what you want, and ask direct questions. 5) Let each answer choose the next step rather than following a fixed script.
when: An investigation must reach beyond formal channels and needs a stepwise method.
why: Evidence-first reasoning and adaptive questioning reach information formal routes cannot.

text: 1) Take notes in shorthand during the exchange. 2) Transcribe them into full text. 3) Make fair copies and check them against the original.
when: Recording a witness's statement for later use
why: Shorthand is useless until transcribed and verified

text: 1) Ask a pointed question the witness has no easy reason to answer. 2) Note the stated reason for presence. 3) Note any deflection or redirected question. 4) Note whether the response shows any expressive reaction.
when: Watching a witness for evasion during questioning.
why: Evasion and deflection reveal more than a plausible answer, and a lack of reaction is a weak signal either way.

text: 1) Choose a routine request that looks ordinary. 2) Let the other party's own procedure produce the record. 3) Accept the answer without stating the true purpose.
when: the true purpose would be refused if stated openly
why: routine requests draw less scrutiny than direct questions

text: Have each observer sign a plain written account of what they saw, so their testimony is fixed before later discussion alters it.
why: written accounts fix testimony

text: Flag NPC lines repeated in identical wording and tone so the designer can see scripted rehearsal and vary the lines.
when: when reviewing dialogue
why: Repetition makes scripted behavior obvious to players.

text: Track the source of each clue so the game can tell whether a conclusion rests on independent evidence or one shared inference.
when: When a game system evaluates whether an accusation is supported.
why: Shared origins can make a conclusion appear better supported than it is.

text: Record a last-seen state for each NPC, and let a staged sighting in another location create or remove suspicion.
when: Implementing NPC tracking and suspicion systems.
why: Lets the game respond to false or misleading information in a consistent way.

text: Track the player's current theory as game state, and when a new clue contradicts it, prompt re-evaluation instead of silently keeping the old theory.
when: When a game lets players hold explicit suspicions about events.
why: Explicit tracking makes contradictions visible so the player can revise their beliefs.

text: Track each object's location and change history, including moves by NPCs or the player, so visible shade or wear differences and disturbed evidence can be traced to recorded moves.
when: Objects can be moved during play or change off-screen, or when implementing interactions that can affect clues
why: A recorded history explains visible state changes; recorded changes let players detect what happened before they arrived; a change log shows whether a scene has been altered

text: Track which character holds which document as game state, since access to a copy can open or close a route.
when: Designing quests where documents gate progress.

text: Give vehicles, lamps or torches a fuel or charge count that falls with use, so players can work out how long each was active.
Store item wear, condition and location values so an object's use and handling can be read from its record.
when: When designing inventory or loot data
why: Recorded history lets the player infer how an object was used.

text: A sealed item's state flag, or an object's position, can record that it was opened, letting the player test whether it was tampered with.
why: flags record handling as game state

text: Record which items should exist in a scene and which were removed, so a missing item is detectable and checkable as a clue.
when: A puzzle depends on items removed from a scene or designing item tracking for a scene
why: Comparing expected and actual state exposes the gap; tracked removals make the missing item checkable

text: Track wet or muddy clothing as a state flag on each NPC, so it can disprove a claimed alibi when the check is made.
Store item wear with a timestamp so the game can distinguish fresh damage from old damage.
why: Clues that depend on recency need the game to know when the damage happened.

text: Store a bleed state and a time-of-wound flag on a corpse, so a blow applied after death reads as a staged injury.
when: Building a corpse-inspection system
why: Recorded timing lets the game distinguish pre-death and post-death injuries

text: Give bodies and objects state tags such as fragmentation pattern, residue, decay level and submersion position so players can deduce origin and handling.
when: Designing physical remains or objects that players should interpret.
why: Structured state tags make physical evidence readable and consistent.

text: A snag usually splits fabric into two rents at right angles that meet where the object entered.
when: when modelling how fabric tears from a point impact

text: A piece with two free edges can be torn off by one force, while a piece with one edge or a hemmed edge is much harder to remove.
Light containers may float rather than sink, so water is a poor disposal method for small boxes.
when: Choosing a disposal method for an object.
why: Buoyancy can bring an object back into view.

text: Treat a rough physical test as a filter that rules some explanations out, not as proof that a specific explanation is true.
when: a cheap experiment is used on a complex event
why: a simple model cannot capture every factor

text: Buoyancy depends on weight versus displaced water; added weight sinks a submerged object, removing it lets it float; decay gas, body fat, bone size and water temperature alter surfacing.
Include real ground shape in a physical test: slopes or banks can roll or deflect a falling object so it ends far from its first contact point.
when: testing a claimed fall from height, or an object falls across a curved slope or embankment
why: intermediate motion and the slope change the direction of travel

text: Impact type shapes the fragment pattern: a drop yields a few large pieces, while crushing grinds material into many small grains.
why: the energy and contact type determine how material separates

text: A trajectory system that records where a thrown item lands lets players reconstruct an event from what remains in the scene.
Physics-driven props respond to forces, so a staged display can collapse or shift on contact, revealing whether it was disturbed.
A recording instrument with a damper that stops motion after each shock can register the next shock cleanly, whereas undamped instruments keep vibrating and blur the record.
when: Detecting small vibrations from movement.
why: Residual oscillation from one shock masks the next.

text: A flash-lit camera capture can reveal a fine wire or trigger that dim ordinary light hides from view.
when: A decisive moment involves a mechanism too fine to see in normal lighting
why: Flash exposure freezes an instant with light the eye does not get

text: A freshly washed surface fixes a timeline: footprints on it show whether anyone walked there since the washing.
when: A surface was cleaned or wetted at a known time
why: Any print made after the wetting records a later passage

text: Tides and currents can carry objects and bodies from one place and strand them in eddies at another.
when: A body or object lies far from its origin
why: Moving water transports material and drops it where flow slows

text: 1) Replace the moving object with a simple stand-in 2) Launch it at a set force 3) Note where its path ends relative to the scene 4) Repeat several trials.
when: a physical event must be tested against a scene
why: a stand-in gives cheap evidence about plausibility

text: Derive damage and wear from material properties, so a damaged item shows which force caused it.
Rule out deflection before trusting a straight trajectory: a steep impact angle and high velocity keep a projectile on a straight path.
Trace a ray from a recorded hit point back along the shot's path to narrow a sniper's probable location.
A game can split evidence processing into roles, where a lab tool gives a range or a match rather than a single answer.
when: designing forensic tools in a game
why: Probabilistic results keep players reasoning rather than receiving a final answer.

text: Let a formal verdict fire on sworn-style testimony and revise it only when new evidence is introduced.
when: Implementing legal or verdict systems in games.
why: Matches the logic of record-based decisions and keeps state changes intentional.

text: A deduction board lists competing theories side by side, each with clues it explains, contradicts or leaves unexplained, flags the best-supported theory, and records motive and opportunity.
when: Players must choose among competing theories
why: Explicit support and gaps make the choice reasoned; parallel theories let the player compare and track open questions.

text: A theory board can require each rival explanation to survive every clue before the player accepts it.
when: Designing a deduction interface for a mystery.
why: Requiring full consistency prevents premature acceptance of a partial explanation.

text: Let players cross-reference lists, rumours and staff statements in a case-file screen to eliminate suspects.
when: Designing an investigation interface

text: Keep suspect boards cheap to revise so players do not lock onto the first accusation.
when: Designing a suspect-tracking interface

text: A final-act screen can let players assemble evidence into a case, choose presentation order, and see each link checked.
when: Designing a mystery resolution interface

text: 1) Record each collected fact in the case notes. 2) Mark whether it bears on the central case. 3) Let the player separate the marked facts to learn relevance.
when: when designing a case-notes or evidence-tracking interface
why: sorting facts by relevance trains the player to discriminate evidence

text: A case board marks each entry as observed or deduced, and each theory step as backed by evidence or an assumption, so players see which conclusions rest on evidence.
when: When designing a player notebook or theory tool.
why: Separating evidence from guesses supports better reasoning.

text: Let a deduction board chain clues, such as physical trait, skill and location, into a provisional hypothesis confirmed only by a third clue or witness.
when: Players combine clues to form theories

text: Show the player's earned deductions as a checklist in confrontation dialogue, so they can see which conclusions their evidence supports.
why: Makes progress in reasoning visible and rewards correct chains of inference.

text: On a theory board, give each competing explanation a single checkable contradiction the player can test.
Provide a deduction board where players compare evidence such as handwriting and labels, gating the solution on the evidence the player has collected.
when: players must confirm an identity from documents

text: When an NPC gives an alibi or explanation, show the claims it depends on and let the player mark each as confirmed, contradicted or unverifiable.
Give the player a notebook recording each suspect's supporting facts, so the final reconciliation is a puzzle rather than a guess.
why: Recorded facts let the player check claims instead of relying on memory

text: Let the player magnify or enlarge a clue so the comparison is visible and fair.
when: When a clue depends on fine detail to be matched.
why: Visible detail lets the player make the comparison themselves.

text: Let players compare items side by side so matching and merely similar features can be told apart.
when: When designing a comparison interface for clues
why: Direct comparison separates true matches from superficial resemblance.

text: Poor lighting or viewing one clue at a time narrows how much a viewer can read from an image.
Presenting evidence to a group of NPCs with the match shown on screen lets the player see the fit that the NPCs judge.
when: Designing an evidence-presentation scene.
why: Shared visual confirmation makes the match legible to both player and NPCs.

text: Keep a witness log that separates first-hand clues from rumors, and accept only first-hand clues as proof.
Design environmental hints as ambiguous shapes whose meaning becomes clear only after the player obtains the matching key item.
when: Designing environmental puzzles or hints.
why: Gating the reading behind an item ties the clue to progression.

text: Record a player's knowledge of an alibi gap as an open question, giving a clear next objective.
when: A player has identified an unexplained time window
why: An explicit open question tells the player what to investigate next

text: Use confirmation prompts to lock in clue facts before a new dialogue branch opens, so the player's confirmed knowledge is fixed before progressing.
when: Designing branching investigation dialogue.
why: Checkpoints ensure the player has accepted key facts before the story moves on.

text: Score a player's description of a suspect against specific generated attributes rather than a vague impression, so recall is rewarded for accuracy.
when: Building a describe-the-suspect mechanic.
why: Specific scoring rewards precise observation over general summary.

text: Observers can misjudge a scene where an impossible result appears, reacting in ways that mislead about what happened.
when: An unexpected or impossible result is observed at a scene
why: Surprise can distort interpretation and response

text: Flag biased, distressed, or impressionistic claims in item descriptions or dialogue so players know which details to verify before acting on them.
when: Writing NPC dialogue or item descriptions that carry uncertain, emotional, or biased claims.
why: Explicit marking tells the player which claims require checking.

text: On a magnification scale, 1x shows original size, a multiplier above 1 enlarges, and a fraction below 1 reduces.
when: Showing a zoomed view of a small object

text: A supply cache found in an unlit cell signals that an unseen actor is active nearby.
Count the sheets in each bundle; the bundle one sheet short of its expected total is the likely source of a removed sheet.
when: The source stack is complete enough to be counted.
why: A missing sheet from a known bundle links the forged or removed sheet to that bundle.

text: An item people do not normally carry, found with a suspect, is strong evidence of intent.
Leave a faction's relic or tool at a scene as a calling card so players connect the scene to that group.
when: Designing scenes that point to a group
why: A recognisable token links evidence to identity

text: Test where a route ends by checking its carriers for signs of their environment, such as whether they are wet or dry.
A bulky device that needs a container narrows the list of people who could have carried it away.
when: a missing object is large or awkward to carry
why: carrying it requires a container and access to it

text: Question a carrier's staff and records, since they hold handover times and signatures.
A document's intended recipient can be deduced from its container, forming a puzzle chain.
Explain an abstract standard with everyday comparisons so non-specialists can apply it to the facts.
when: Presenting a technical or legal standard to a lay audience.
why: Familiar comparisons make abstract thresholds usable.

text: Keep evidence items persistent so players can reference them during confrontation.
when: Designing a mystery game's evidence system

text: A rival who finds a hidden cache first can take its contents and replant the marker, so the original message is used against its finder.
when: when a cache can be discovered by others

text: A container puzzle with identical containers can let the player reason from stated odds, with hints that progressively narrow the candidate set.
when: Designing a container-finding puzzle
why: Stated odds and hints give the player a rational search order

text: Containers in a game can show locked, forced, or empty states as clues, so the player infers which NPC had access to a key or a reason to remove items.
why: Container states encode who had access and what was taken, letting the player deduce actors.

text: A concealed mechanism such as a light wire can move only light objects, so it fails with heavy furniture.
when: Designing a hidden mechanism that moves objects.
why: Load beyond the mechanism's strength defeats it.

text: A traceable item may have been taken innocently and in bulk, so its source can implicate a whole group rather than one person.
Borrowed items can point to their owner rather than their user, so tracing a borrowed object may implicate the wrong person.
when: An item used at a scene belongs to someone else.
why: The item's source and its user are different people.

text: Treating a brand as an identity is an error, because many people can share the same product.
when: a product is used to name a person
why: Common products do not single out one owner.

text: Owners who held land only briefly do not show long-term ties, so their presence in a later list is weak evidence of connection.
1) List every carried item. 2) Record identifying details such as maker, serial number and any addresses. 3) Note each item's location on the character.
when: when a character's possessions may reveal identity or movement
why: Identifying details link items to people and places

text: 1) Examine the trace in both transmitted and reflected light. 2) Calibrate the magnified view against a reference scale. 3) Hold the view perfectly still during capture. 4) Take a backup capture in case the first fails.
when: A fixed image must be compared at high magnification
why: Light, scale and stillness each affect whether the comparison is reliable

text: Show expected and actual inventory contents side by side, or keep inventory visible and consistent, so players can detect swaps and work out what was taken.
when: When players are expected to deduce item changes.
why: Deduction from mismatch requires that the player can see both the expected and actual state.

text: Show a zoomed clue view with a visible magnification scale and a reference, so players can compare fine details accurately.
when: Puzzles depend on reading small marks such as runes or prints
why: Without a scale, players cannot judge size or match a detail to a reference

text: Carry a trace found in an open area into later scenes so other characters can see it and react to it as evidence.
An item an NPC carries stays with them, so a message they took can be found on their body or at their destination.
Store a building's or plot's history as a chain of owners, so players can trace who held it at any given time.
Make a parcel or item moved between rooms a traceable clue, and check its location against the carrying NPC's routine.
when: designing item-based clues
why: a routine-based location lets players reconstruct the path

text: Hide clues in mundane containers that fit a character's habits, so the player finds them by searching.
Place depletable resources such as fuel or rations in containers a player must inspect, so that a missing amount can serve as a clue.
when: When designing a resource clue for a level.
why: A depleted container must be checked by the player to reveal the discrepancy.

text: Keep a fragment inventory for breakable objects with a known total; a surplus or gap signals the object was broken elsewhere and moved.
Place a cache at a specific world location named by an NPC's confession, and let the player verify it by finding the items.
when: Designing a hidden item cache tied to an NPC's story.
why: A concrete, checkable location turns dialogue into a followable lead.

text: Let the player clear suspicion by presenting physical items at the scene, such as tools, ledgers or receipts, that explain the outcome.
when: when designing accusation resolution in a mystery
why: physical items let the player prove an innocent explanation

text: After a trap or event, show the player a checklist of changed inventory, with one unexplained missing item as the clue.
when: a game event changes the player's inventory
why: a visible list of changes gives the player a concrete clue to pursue

text: Let the player's journal record expected inventory so that a discrepancy becomes a prompt for investigation.
when: the player tracks items in a space
why: A logged expectation turns a missing item into a visible question.

text: Let players compare a found item against an NPC's inventory screen as a deduction step.
when: a found item may belong to an NPC
why: A direct comparison turns discovery into a reasoning step.

text: Show the original quote beside the recorded summary when a record has altered a statement, so players can compare what was said with what was written.
An item-examination interaction can use a powder tool to reveal latent marks that then appear on the item, and a comparison screen can let the player match them to candidates.
when: Designing evidence examination in a game
why: Visible reveal and comparison make forensic clues accessible to players

text: Tag each record or claim with its creator, source and reliability, and let rumours change as they pass between NPCs, so players can spot misleading sources.
when: Designing a player-facing record of clues

text: After a puzzle is solved, replay events in discovery order, showing how each clue supports the solution and marking decoys and missed clues.
when: after a puzzle or mystery is solved
why: Replay shows how the solution followed from visible clues

text: Give players a recap that lists collected facts and asks them to mark the ones that matter, so the reveal rests on evidence they already saw.
when: the solution depends on several earlier facts

text: A journal or recap screen that lists relevant observations rewards player attention and helps them connect clues.
when: Players gather many observations over a mystery
why: A recap makes relevant clues visible without relying on memory

text: Note what is missing as well as what is present, because an absence can be a clue in an investigation.
when: when the space will be used for investigation

text: A record book in a level can hold dates that must match a key item's engraved date, so a mismatch becomes a puzzle clue.
when: when designing puzzles around documents
why: Players can check the mismatch themselves.

text: Record each trace's position relative to the path edge so its placement can be reasoned about later.
Place verifiable records, such as registers or case files, in a distant location so that a trip to verify them is rewarded.
when: when designing investigation content with travel
why: Physical travel to obtain records gives the player a meaningful verification step.

text: Summarising confirmed links at the end gives the group a shared model of the situation.
Record failed operations and their causes so the lessons remain available to the wider team.
when: A planned operation does not achieve its goal.
why: Unrecorded failures leave no reference for avoiding the same mistake later.

text: Count a recurring category, such as ministers, across two periods to make a structural comparison that a single anecdote cannot provide.
when: When comparing turnover or patterns between periods of a community's history.
why: Counts across periods reveal patterns that individual cases obscure.

text: A case notebook that indexes every name and alias the player meets lets a name in one source connect to a name in dialogue.
A reading action can list each visible cue beside the conclusion it supports, so players see the chain of reasoning.
A recap screen can order the clues the player has collected into a timeline, showing how the pieces connect before the final accusation.
when: A mystery needs the player to review evidence before a final decision
why: A visible ordering helps the player verify the chain before committing

text: A player journal can tag each entry with a confidence level, marking entries made in darkness or under stress as uncertain.
when: Designing a player-facing evidence log
why: Confidence tags let the player weigh observations by how they were gathered.

text: A journal that records each clue lets players reconstruct a solution on their own, so it should hold the details that reasoning needs.
when: Designing investigation journals
why: Players reason from recorded evidence

text: Logging each attempt in a journal lets the player compare outcomes across tries.
when: Designing a puzzle that requires comparing repeated attempts.
why: A record of prior results makes patterns across trials visible.

text: A journal or rumour mechanic can spread public blame that later proves false.
when: Designing in-world information systems

text: A deduction journal can reopen a dismissed candidate automatically when a new discovery removes one of its opposing reasons.
when: Designing a player-facing case log that tracks candidate explanations.
why: Removing an opposing reason restores a candidate's plausibility, so it should return to view.

text: A case review can turn into a tally where the most-cited points win regardless of quality; weigh each point by its strength.
when: when summarising evidence for several suspects

text: Proofreading can miss a writer's own name errors, so mistakes in identifying people can survive into print.

1) Define the injury or service the missing person would need. 2) List the institutions likely to have provided it within a set radius. 3) Visit or check each. 4) Match each record against the timeline. 5) Treat each negative as information.
when: A missing person must have sought care or a service at a known location
why: Systematic elimination narrows the search to the place that fits

text: 1) Have each investigator report. 2) State the central working theory. 3) List outstanding tasks. 4) Review each suspect separately, listing evidence against and in favour. 5) List conditions still unproven.
when: when several suspects remain and the evidence points in different directions
why: a fixed format stops one clue from growing into a theory

text: 1) Locate the order to hold the trial. 2) Locate the indictment. 3) Locate the plea. 4) Locate the finding. 5) Locate any later reversal by a higher body. 6) Order the entries by date.
when: When reconstructing a trial that appears across several records.
why: Each stage leaves its own record, and their order shows how the case moved.

text: 1) Let the player record theories in a journal. 2) Let new clues prompt revisiting each recorded theory. 3) Let the player mark theories as confirmed or ruled out.
when: when designing a journal for deduction gameplay
why: the record supports repeated cycles of speculation and testing

text: After a puzzle is solved, offer a journal recap listing each deduction beside its supporting clue so players can audit each step.
when: a puzzle or mystery is resolved
why: players can check their conclusions against the evidence they saw

text: Let players log examined details and dialogue facts in a time-stamped notebook or journal so earlier observations can be compared later.
when: Designing a clue-gathering interface
why: Recorded observations are easily lost, and comparison across findings drives deduction.

text: Let a journal log every odd or unexplained detail, so players can test whether the accumulated oddities form a pattern and connect them to later findings.
why: players can connect earlier oddities to later findings

text: Record traces and each object's original position and condition before the scene is disturbed or handled, since rain, visitors or handling erase the first state.
why: Once moved, the original evidence cannot be recovered

text: Show a numbered case journal of facts with the player's links and contradictions, revised as new evidence arrives, so the reasoning chain stays visible.
when: Players must combine clues

text: Track which clues the player has found and use the final recap to show how those clues connect, so the reveal rewards the player's work.
when: Designing an end-of-case cutscene or NPC monologue.
why: A recap grounded in found clues confirms the player's deductions.

text: Record silent periods as results. A window with no passage is data, not a failed watch.
why: An empty window can rule out a movement.

text: Open a puzzle with a sparse log describing a seemingly impossible state, such as a sealed room holding a body, and place the clue needed for the answer within it.
when: when designing a puzzle that begins with a mystery

text: Record a surprising test result in a durable form before any step that could interrupt or destroy the test subject.
when: A test has a single unexpected outcome that may be lost.
why: Without a record, the result cannot be checked or reasoned from after the subject is lost.

text: Keep a written record of every instruction, change, and concession, so the test can be audited afterwards.
when: A test or reproduction is being run.
why: Written records let others check whether the conditions were met.

text: Record searches carefully, since a search done while the occupant was absent can be challenged.
A journal can hold several NPC diaries, with prompts that send the player to compare the same night across them.
Give the player a journal of suspicions that other characters cannot read, so the player tracks evidence the NPCs do not share.
when: the player is solving a mystery alongside NPCs
why: private tracking supports deduction

text: A journal should highlight repeated names, places and phrases when a new entry arrives, prompting the player to connect related clues.
Show an explicit empty slot in the player's case notes for a known-missing link, so the player knows the gap exists and can search for it.
when: when a case requires a fact the player has not found
why: A visible gap directs search and prevents players from assuming the case is complete.

text: Provide a case-review screen at the end of a generated mystery that scores each player theory against the true chain of events, listing matched and missed facts.
why: the player sees which parts of their reasoning held

text: Let players mark log entries for review and return to flagged events later, like pencil marks on a working record.
when: a case log is in use
why: suspicious entries stay available for reconsideration

text: Provide a journal that logs each NPC tale so players can compare stories against facts they have already found.
when: Players receive multiple narrated accounts that may contradict or confirm discovered facts.
why: A record lets players cross-check claims, turning storytelling into deduction.

text: Keep a visible list of known occupants in a journal so anomalies stand out against the expected set.
when: Players must notice unexpected presences.
why: An anomaly is only recognizable against a clear baseline of what is normal.

text: NPCs that recognize a returning player can change their dialogue or alert state, so repeated presence has consequences.
when: A player repeatedly visits the same area or NPC.
why: Memory of the player's earlier presence changes how NPCs react.

text: When a scene has no audio, display facial and gesture cues so players can infer the characters' intent.
when: a scene is observed without sound

text: Give each NPC a visible trait that survives disguise, such as a scar, limp or ring, so the player can spot them in a costumed crowd.
when: when designing NPCs in masked or costumed events
why: Persistent traits let the player identify characters despite costumes.

text: Offer the player a choice of questions where conspicuous-feature answers seem sufficient, while detail questions expose the witness's error.
when: Designing a witness-testing interaction.
why: Players who stop at obvious features miss the errors that detailed questions would reveal.

text: Show NPC reaction tells, such as pauses and tone changes, as readable signals so players learn to interpret them; an unperceivable tell cannot be used to judge a bluff.
Add visible tells, such as a glance toward an accomplice or a sly sidelong reaction hinting at a secret unstated aloud; let players confirm them before accusing.
when: Designing NPC behavior that hints at a secret or NPC reactions during dialogue.
why: Confirmation lets the player act on evidence rather than guesswork; non-verbal hints reward observant players.

text: Show NPC reactions on a visible meter so the player can track escalation from calm through agitation to collapse.
when: when NPCs react to player provocation
why: makes reaction stages readable

text: Give NPCs visible cues, such as flushing or fidgeting, that change with suspicion so players can read them as clues.
when: Designing NPC presentation for a deduction or social game
why: Visible state changes give players readable evidence

text: Use a brief visual cue or dialogue line to show the player that a character has been recognised.
Signal a death or loss through an NPC's reaction rather than a text box, before the details appear.
when: the player should sense loss before learning specifics
why: A reaction draws the player in more than a caption.

text: Show NPC credibility as a meter that changes with emotional state, so players can weigh the NPC's claims.
when: An NPC makes claims the player must evaluate.
why: A visible credibility state makes trust a readable choice.

text: Show a witness's visible reluctance or apology as a readable cue, so the player can judge how far to trust the account.
when: Presenting a reluctant or self-effacing NPC
why: Visible demeanor helps players calibrate trust without a meta-label

text: Give visible feedback when a protective barrier is breached so the player can tell self-caused breaches from enemy action.
when: Designing a barrier the player can breach accidentally
why: Clear feedback lets players attribute causes correctly

text: A covert signal, such as a blank card or a set gesture, can let the player send a result to an NPC without naming them.
when: Designing a secret communication mechanic.
why: Signals convey results without exposing the player or the target.

text: A reflective surface can reveal a hidden watcher behind the player, showing the player was observed without the watcher being seen directly.
when: when designing a reveal of an unseen observer
why: The reflection gives the player a visual clue to a presence they could not otherwise perceive.

text: Give different feedback for solid and hollow surfaces when the player probes them, so probing becomes a readable skill.
when: Players search walls or floors for hidden features.
why: Distinct responses let the player infer what lies beneath.

text: Under a perception-altering status effect, show a clear warning and mark observations unreliable, since visual cues may mislead while the logged state stays accurate and checkable.
when: The player's character has an active status effect that alters display
why: Altered perception can mislead the player, so the authoritative state should be available to verify.

text: Tag symptom logs by cause so players can see which effects are resolved and which remain.
when: when presenting a list of effects in a game
why: Grouping by cause makes remaining mysteries visible.

text: Give players a timeline board filled from testimonies that logs NPC movements and flags entries conflicting with alibis, checked against locked doors, timestamps and items left behind.
when: When players track multiple witness statements or must test several accounts of the same hours
why: Visual placement makes contradictions and gaps easy to spot

text: A game case log can store each event as a numbered entry so the player can rebuild the timeline and spot gaps.
when: the player must reconstruct the order of events across locations
why: an ordered record makes missing steps visible

text: Store the timeline in the quest log so the player can check when an NPC was present and when events happened.
when: A mystery depends on the order of events
why: Lets the player verify claims

text: Provide a replay or timeline view so players can compare each character's movements with the events they witnessed.
when: When players must check character accounts against recorded actions
why: Side-by-side comparison makes mismatches between stated and actual movement visible.

text: A case board should store time-stamped events and let the player sort witnesses and vehicles by time window.
Show a timeline that records when each event became known, so players can see where information lagged behind events.
when: information arrives at different times
why: the gap between event and knowledge changes what players infer

text: Present a case file or journal in chronological order, separating dates, confirmed facts and open questions clearly.
when: A game presents accumulated investigation facts to the player.
why: Clear separation shows what is known and what remains open.

text: Give players a timeline board listing each visit and its duration, with the window where an object could change hands highlighted.
when: When designing investigation interfaces for a game.
why: A visual board lets players see overlaps and gaps without tracking them in their heads.

text: Listing deadlines in a quest log, together with their consequences, helps players plan.
when: Presenting timed objectives to the player.
why: Visible deadlines and penalties let players prioritize.

text: A game timer shown as an in-world date or hour that players can check repeatedly keeps the clock visible rather than hidden.
why: Repeated checking keeps the deadline present in the player's mind

text: A timing condition that is not stated clearly makes players fail for reasons unrelated to the puzzle itself.
Provide game-clock or instrument timestamps and log timed events in order, so players can arrange them on a timeline and spot gaps.
when: the player must reconstruct the order of past events
why: timestamps let players order clues without guessing; ordering exposes missing intervals

text: Make deadlines visible: give a timer or sound cue at each countdown stage, and show a fixed deadline's remaining window on the player's map.
when: a timed sequence or mission depending on a timed event is active
why: visible stages and remaining windows keep the deadline readable and let players plan around it

text: Log witness statements with timestamps so the player can notice when accounts conflict.
when: the player collects several statements
why: Timestamps make inconsistencies visible.

text: Display clocks as fair timers, and let a disguise swap be possible only during a window the player can see closing.
when: A timed disguise mechanic is used
why: The player can judge the remaining time and act on it

text: Mark gaps in in-game logs with visible placeholders so attentive players can spot where information was withheld.
